units.la: Venerando Seni, PETRO MOLINÆO, S. Litterarum in Ecclesiâ, & Academiâ Sedanensi Doctori celeberrimo.
units.tr: To the venerable elder, Peter Molinaeus, Doctor of Sacred Letters in the Church and in the Academy of Sedan, most renowned.

units.la: Venerande Senex, neque enim aliud quod est, quo gratius compellari possis, quodque in summâ doctrinâ tuâ, paribusque de Ecclesiâ meritis excellentius, quàm te esse ordinis nostri Theologum maximè veteranum. Hoc virtutis, eruditionis, honoris, ætatis denique tenes nunc fastigium: quod quo rarius, eo majorem omnibus admirationem, tibi gloriam conciliat. Ista est corona pretiosissima, quam in viis justitiæ reperiri, senectutem bonam, Sapiens affirmat.
units.tr: Venerable sir, there is no other title by which you could be addressed more pleasingly, or one more excellent given your great learning and your equal merits to the Church, than that you are the most senior theologian of our order. You now hold the summit of virtue, learning, honour and, finally, age. The rarer this is, the greater the admiration and glory it wins you from everyone. This is the most precious crown, which the Wise Man affirms is found in the ways of justice: a good old age.

units.la: Vera θεολογία: unde Græcorum dicti calogeri: & cujus argumenti ultimum atque emortuale Affinis tui scriptum est, quo & nos, pro suâ benevolentiâ, dodonavit, de Senectute bona. Quid enim optatius homini hac in vita contingere queat, quàm viram sic agere & sic producere, ut in ipsâ quoque canitie fructus, eosque optimos doctrinæ & librorum, quod tu eâ quâ nunc es ætate nunquam definis, proferat? Alia cum ætate marcescunt atque intercidunt, tu verò vegetam adeo florentemque agis, ut nunc maximè vivere videaris, quo magis in propinquo ex communi humanæ vitæ cursu mors reputatur. Esque eâ jam ætate, nisi & superaveris, quâ Cato Major, quando apud Ciceronem, de senectute disputabat; & quod ille de se, tibi quoque dici patieris, plane nec enervasse eum, neque affixisse senectutem: atque quartum agebat annum supra octogesimum.
units.tr: True theology [θεολογία], whence the Greeks called the monks kalogeroi, "good old men." The last and deathbed work on this subject was written by your kinsman, who, out of his goodwill, dedicated it to us: On a Good Old Age. For what could be more desirable for a man in this life than to conduct and prolong his life so that, even in grey hair, it bears fruit, and the best fruits of learning and books, which you never cease to produce at the age you now are? Other men wither and fail with age, but you remain so vigorous and flourishing that you seem to be living most fully now, the nearer death is reckoned in the common course of human life. And you are now at that age, unless you have already passed it, at which Cato the Elder was when he discussed old age with Cicero. What Cato said of himself you will allow to be said of you too: that he had neither enfeebled nor burdened his old age. He was then in his eighty-fourth year.

units.la: Rara hominum ætas, illorum præsertim qui à juventute acri semper occupatione studiorum suos pridem spiritus detriverunt. Quomodo Tu, qui ab anno ætatis vigesimo quarto publicæ in Academiâ professioni admotus fuisti. Utque mirabili Dei providentiâ, quando puer ad necem quæreba-
units.tr: Such a long life is rare among men, especially among those who from youth have worn out their spirits in the keen and constant pursuit of study. How you were called to a public professorship in the Academy in your twenty-fourth year, and how, by the wonderful providence of God, when you were a boy you were being sought for slaughter...

units.la: rebaris, in horrenda clade Bartholomæa, servatus ancillæ maximè industriâ fuisti; ita diutius vivere, propter illos, qui ipsam tibi vitam, nedum longam invidebant, debuisti, ut hoc quasi foenore illis invisæ vitæ studium remunerares, scirentque, nullo alio te tum omine servatum fuisse, quàm ut illis diutissimè superesses. Atque hinc tibi primam constantemque hæsisse curam oppugnandi & confundendi Papatus, à tenéris adeo impressam commendatamque, colligimus. Quo in opere quantâ cum assiduitate, dexteritate, fructu & felicitate versatus hactenus sis, nescio an Nos, an Adversarii magis sentiant. Certè totus orbis scripta tua loquitur & veneratur, gaudebuntque posteri Molinæum, & tamdiu, tamque bene aliorum quam suis commodis vixisse. Venerabilis Beza annorum erat septem supra octoginta, quando quiescebat: magnus Rivetus, affinis ille tuus, meique, dum viveret, amantissimus, & qui in postremis suis ad me, de Te prolixe loquutus, annos attigit lxx ix.
units.tr: ...you were being sought, and in the dreadful Bartholomew massacre you were saved chiefly through the diligence of a maidservant. You ought therefore to live on, and to live long, for the sake of those who grudged you even life, let alone a long one, so that you might repay their hatred of your life by your zeal, and they might know that you had been spared at that time for no other purpose than to outlive them by many years. Hence we gather that from your tender years there clung to you a first and constant care to attack and overthrow the Papacy, a concern impressed and commended to you from the start. How greatly, with what assiduity, skill, fruit and success you have been occupied in this work so far, I do not know whether we or our opponents feel more. Certainly the whole world speaks of your writings and reveres them, and posterity will rejoice that Molinaeus lived so long and so well, as much for the benefit of others as for his own. Venerable Beza was eighty-seven years old when he rested. Great Rivetus, that kinsman of yours and of mine, who loved me most dearly while he lived, and who in his last letter to me spoke at length about you, reached seventy-nine years.

units.la: Illâ ætate legimus Athanasium; provectiori etiam Hieronymum fuisse. Adeo notata à Veteribus quoque ætas, quando in eminentibus in Ecclesiâ Viris eam singularem, & solito grandiorem observarunt. Neque ullis magis vovenda, aut gratulanda ubi adest, quam iis, qui viam justitiæ ingrediendo, eamque alios docendo, hoc ejus præmium referunt, ut longævi sint. Est bonum signum, dicunt Hebræi, senex in domo: atque ita quoque in Ecclesiâ, cujus regimen non aliis quàm senioribus committitur: ut ne quidem quæstioni locus hic sit, quam Plutarchus egregiè tractat; an seni gerenda sit respublica? quum talis ad docendam regendamque Ecclesiam ita præ aliis idoneus habeatur, ut nisi senili instructum bene prudentiâ sapientiâq; ad illam admittere liceat neminem. Ex quo vel solo, quę muneris nostri sit ratio, quidque requiratur in homine, qui illud digne obiturus sit, perspicuum. Senes, בעלי tales, זקנים. [illegible, ~6 letters] venerandi, non qui solis annis & canitie tales, vel senectutem ignavam, molestam, aut turpem, sed qui gravem, & omni virtutum genere decoram, semperque in publicum utilem ducunt, hi seu numina quaedam, coelestem abitum quasi in nostri gratiam comperendinantia, suspicendi. Sic vivis tu jam, & totus aliis vivis, ut tibi vivere, & tibi mori peraeque fere negligere videaris. Deo interim gratias, quod eo adhuc es vigore & robore, ut munus in Ecclesiâ, & Academiâ,& in scribendis etiamnum libris alacriter & constanter peragere valeas: quodque juvenes senem audiant, quem juvenem senes audiverunt; ut, quod de se Augustus olim, hic usurpem. Si causam roges, (quamvis non rogabis) quid Te compellem? vel librum hunc, Controversias dictarum in orbe religionum, aut illarum capita exponentem, (ut alii, ut studiosi illa in promtu habeant, magnâ absque hoc difficultate colligenda: additis de statu religionum hodierno Dissertationibus) tuo nomini inscriptum eam? cau-
units.tr: We read that Athanasius was of that age, and Jerome was older still. The ancients too noted this age, observing it as singular and greater than usual in eminent men of the Church. There are none to whom a vow or congratulation is more due, where they are present, than to those who walk the way of righteousness and teach others, and who receive this reward for it, that they live long. "It is a good sign," the Hebrews say, "an old man in the house." So also in the Church, whose government is committed to none but elders, so that there is not even room for the question which Plutarch treats excellently, whether government should be entrusted to an old man. For such a man is regarded as so much more fit than others to teach and govern the Church that no one may be admitted to it unless he is furnished with senile prudence and wisdom. From this alone it is clear what the nature of our office is, and what is required in a man who is to discharge it worthily. Old men, [בעלי] such as these, elders [זקנים], are venerable: not those who are such merely by years and grey hair, or by an idle, troublesome or shameful old age, but those who lead a grave life, adorned with every kind of virtue, and always useful to the public. These we regard as certain divinities, who, as it were for our sake, put off their heavenly departure, and we ought to revere them. So you now live, and wholly live for others, and you seem almost equally to neglect living for yourself and dying for yourself. Meanwhile I thank God that you still have such vigour and strength that you can discharge with eagerness and constancy your office in the Church and the Academy, and still write books; and that young men hear an old man whom old men once heard when he was young. So, what Augustus once said of himself, I may use here. If you ask the reason (though you will not ask), why do I address you, or why do I inscribe to your name this book, setting out the controversies of the religions in the world, or their chief heads (so that students may have them ready to hand, which otherwise would be gathered with great difficulty, with dissertations on the present state of religions added)? cau-

units.la: causam me nunc justam satis expósuisse confido: atque hanc exspectavi occasionem, ut Tuis ad me litteris, quamvis tardius, publicè responderem: Hoc denique precatus, in quo finio, ut Deus Te diutissime Ecclesiæ, nobisque sospitem conservet: atque tandem æternùm beet.
units.tr: I trust that I have now sufficiently explained my reason, and I have waited for this opportunity to reply publicly, though rather late, to your letter to me. Finally, I pray this, with which I end: that God may keep you safe for the Church and for us for a very long time, and at last make you eternally blessed.

units.la: Aeternus obductis quaeritur Lux Alma tenebris Tartareâ se fulse meri, strepitusque nefandos.
units.tr: The eternal kindly Light is sought through shrouded darkness; it shone forth from Tartarean depths, amid unspeakable din.

units.la: Ætherea ne damnare minus, prob numina gentem. Sic se Erebi ostens aut acies, sauceque dolique Et quicquid nex dira parit. Vesana libido Heu! demissis grassatur agris, nec meta furori est. Quis mihi Cajanos, Alogos, Bassosque; Secundosque Angelicos, Blastosque canat (sed nomina priscis Nota) Dietrepbi, Garthaeis, ac fata Menandri? Quis mihi vel fando memoret Barbasq;, Naetosque, Ammonios, Baddasque, & cetera nomina gentis Barbarie celebrata gravi. Renovare dolores Impatiens mens horret adhuc. Si Tartara plaudant Ut vis est vesana illis, si vincere cordi est Et Domini calcare acies longo ordine, gyris Inflexis, nec scire modum; Tu surgis in hostes Impavidus, vir magne, truces, & vindice coelo Dissicis unanimem magno discrimine gentem, Sicque alios, Te ipse beas. Nihil arma Pelagi Mentibus officiunt cautis, nihil arma Socini
units.tr: Lest the heavenly powers condemn the nation less, they are shown to be gods. So the ranks of Erebus show themselves, and the wounds and cunning deceits, and whatever cruel death brings forth. Alas! Frenzied lust rages through the abandoned fields, and there is no limit to its rage. Who will sing to me of the Cainites, the Alogi, and the Bassi; of the Secundians, the Angelicals, and Blastus (names known to the ancients), of Diotrephes, of the Garthaeans, and the fate of Menander? Who will tell me, even by speech alone, of the Barbasians, the Naetians, the Ammonians, the Baddaeans, and the other names of a barbarous race made famous by its grievous deeds? My mind, unable to bear it, still shudders at renewing its sorrows. If the Tartarean powers rejoice, as their frenzy wills, if it is dear to them to conquer and to tread down the ranks of the Lord in long lines, with bent circles, and without knowing any measure; you rise against the fierce enemies, great man, fearless, and with heaven as avenger you scatter the nation united in great danger, and so you bless others, yourself. The arms of Pelagius do not harm minds that are wary; the arms of Socinus, made subject to your rule, do nothing.

units.la: Imperio subjecta tuo. Deus esse trinus Creditur invitis tenebris, quas mentibus almis Objicit, & propriis cadit incurabilis armis.
units.tr: God is believed to be triune, in spite of the darkness, which he opposes to nourishing minds; and the incurable one falls by his own weapons.

units.la: Non Christi vis ulla perit, dum Filius astra Deserit, & patrias sedes, aeternaque regna In terris prognatus homo. Non illa potestas Quâ mortem devicit, & omnia mortis amara Fregit, & inferno vitam produxit ab alveo, Queis mortis stat certa fides & gloria Fati. Sic age, sic Domini bellum gere servę fidelis, Sic Domino sic victor eris vincente fideli, Et Magnus majora dabit, sic gloria immatum [?] Te vehet excelsum numen, sic gloria coeli Impotet audaces animas queis gloria vilis Et meritum coeleste jacet, sonderque prophanum. Matte animo, Vir magne, Tuos, Christique triumphos Asserere, & invictas Te defensore tiaras.
units.tr: No power of Christ perishes, while the Son, born a man on earth, leaves the stars and his paternal seat and eternal kingdom. Not that power by which he overcame death and broke all the bitterness of death, and led life up out of the depths of hell; in which lies sure faith in death and the glory of fate. So act, so wage the war of the Lord as a faithful servant; so you will be a victor for the faithful Lord who conquers, and the Great One will give greater things; so the glory of the Divine Power will lift you high, so the glory of heaven will strike bold souls, for whom base glory and heavenly merit lie low, and the profane... Be of good courage, great man, to assert your triumphs and those of Christ, and with you as defender the unconquered tiaras.

units.la: Siquid ego vel Praeco quoeam, facilisque [illegible, ~3 letters] In laudes id verto tuas, nomenque per orbem Diffundi me vate velim. Mysteria Nomen Si quae habeat, Vir celse, Tuum, mysteria redde (Sepe vel externa latentia Oracula voce) Summaque diffuso fundatur Copia Cornu.
units.tr: If I, as herald, can achieve anything, and thus turn it to your praise, I would wish your name to be spread abroad through the world by my song. Lofty man, if your name holds any mysteries, give back the mysteries (often hidden even under outward oracular voice), and the sum is founded in an overflowing horn of plenty.

units.la: EPIGRAMMA IN EANDEM SUMMAM, Et lusus ad Nomen HOORNBEEK.
units.tr: EPIGRAM ON THE SAME SUMMA, and a play on the name HOORNBEEK.

units.la: Vloqueris, voxque illa Dei est, Tua bella, triumphus. Et quae vix cupias, perficis arte gravi: Sic urges, sic ora domas, sic hostibus instas, Et potuit qui vult vincere, velle mori. Quid mirum est, Vox illa Dei, tua Copia Cornu est, Et Tu qui Cornu Copia, Summa Dei es.
units.tr: You cry out, and that voice is the voice of God: your wars, your triumph. You accomplish, by weighty skill, what you could scarcely wish for. Thus you press on, thus you tame mouths, thus you assail the enemies, and he who wished to conquer was able to be willing to die. What wonder is it? That voice of God is your horn of plenty, and you, who are the horn of plenty, are the Summa of God.

units.tr: You are called (and that voice is God's voice): your wars, your triumph. What you scarcely wish for, you accomplish by weighty skill. Thus you press on, thus you subdue mouths, thus you pursue your enemies, and he who wills it can conquer; he could even die willingly. What wonder is it, that voice of God? Your plenty is a horn, and you, who are a horn of plenty, are the sum of God.

units.la: Exprimis hâc Summâ. Licet hæc permulta requirantMagnum opus, at tamen id pagina parva refert.Et, quod miramur, varia arma dolosa retundis, Atque hostes proprio sic jugulas gladio. Cætera quæ promunt breviter solideque refellis,Quin simul incautos hos superare doces. Controversarum fidei compendia rerum, Sic igitur tuto, te Duce, scire licet. Nunc Summas Scotista tenax, Thomistaque essset, Ut bene digestas commemorare suas. Sunt miseræ, elumbes, vana, sunt denique falsa,Quæis tua non unis conferenda modis.Hâc gravior, brevior, succinctior, aptior haud est, Solaque, quam scribis, Summa probanda venit. Judicio Summistaprobo si perlegas illam, Ut Symmystatibi, sic mihi testis, erit.
units.tr: You set forth in this Summa what would otherwise need a great work, and yet a small page contains it. And, what we marvel at, you blunt the many deceitful weapons and so cut down the enemies with their own sword. The rest you refute briefly and solidly, and you also teach that these incautious men are overcome at the same time. Here are compendia of the controversies of the faith, so that with you as leader we may know them safely. Now the stubborn Scotist and the Thomist would have their summas recalled as well digested. They are wretched, feeble, vain; in short, they are false, and yours is not to be compared with them in any one respect. No work is weightier, briefer, more concise or more apt, and only the Summa you have written deserves to be approved. If a judge who approves of the Summists reads it through, it will be a witness for you, and so it will be for me.

units.la: DISSERTATIO, DE CONTROVERSIIS, ET Disputationibus Theologicis.
units.tr: DISSERTATION ON CONTROVERSIES AND THEOLOGICAL DISPUTATIONS.

units.la: C ontroversiarum alię, sunt illæ, vel problematicæ, vel fidei. Hæ aut cum infidelibus, aut Hæreticis, aut Schismaticis. Infideles, illi, sunt Gentiles, cum Judæi, denique Mahommedani. Hæretici sunt, Papistæ, Anabaptistæ, Enthusiastæ & Libertini, Socinani, Schismatici, sunt Luterani, Remonstrantes, additâ distinctione, Brownistæ, atque in Oriente multùm Græci. De controversiis Theologicis, Disputatione, & studio controversiarum in Scholis. Controversiæ primæ exordium, & præcipua capita ostendantur in disputatione Diaboli cum Adamo. Genes. iii. Primùm est religio, cum circa eam error; ex errore, controversia; hinc disputatio. Religio quid naturalis, Mosaica, vel Vet. Testamenti; Christiana. Adversus illam est Gentilismus, adversus illam Judaismus; contra hanc, cum plena apostasia, Mahommedismus. Quid Schisma, quid Hæresis: & qui, sive Hæretici, sive Schismatici. Supremus erroris, atque apostasiæ gradus est, peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum: hoc quid sit. Controversiam alius est qui movet, & qui eam sustinet ac repellit alius. Videndum quis moveat, & quare, & quomodo. Quidam ex sola concertandi libidine, de rebus facilibus, de verbis disputant, & multiplicant quæstiones, non minus illorum contentio vehementia. Attendenda probè non res solum, sed quoque animus opponentis. Quæstio est vel primaria, vel secundaria. Differentia inter controversiam, & momentum ejus. Hæc neque elevandam nimis, neque aggravandam. Effica- cia. turque, ad fundamentum fidei, praxim, communionem Ecclesiæ, & ad status hominum. In responsione ad controversiam, videndum insuper quis, & quando respondeat, tum quomodo. Disputatio alia ore fit, alia scripto: privatim, aut publicè. Usus, & modus disputationum. Quæ non etiam cuivis concedendæ. In Censura librorum non solum libri examinandi, sed primum Auctor, cui concedi scriptio debeat; & libri, antequam scribatur, argumentum, atque delineatio. Disputatio alia habetur cum Orthodoxis, alia cum Hereticis. Finis illius est duplex, vel convincere, vel componere. De studio controversiarum. Alia in studioso requiruntur, alia in studiis. Ibi ante omnia ut sit probus, & diligens, & modestus. Hic prærequiritur studium linguarum, Hebraicæ præsertim, Græcaeque; etiam Philosophiæ. Studium controversiarum inchoanti necessaria semper precatio, & jugis lectio Scripturæ. Notitia controversiarum prima habetur rudis, tum distincta, ex scriptis utriusque partis electiis. Adversaria. Lectio librorum. In disputatione bene ponendus controversiæ status: non festinanter prosiliendum ad argumenta: tenendum filum veritatis: non multis argumentis standum, sed validis. Disputandi dexteritas.
units.tr: Some controversies concern problems, others concern the faith. The latter are conducted either with unbelievers, with heretics, or with schismatics. The unbelievers are the Gentiles, the Jews, and finally the Mahometans. The heretics are the Papists, the Anabaptists, the Enthusiasts and Libertines, and the Socinians. The schismatics are the Lutherans and the Remonstrants, to which is added, by a further distinction, the Brownists, and in the East chiefly the Greeks. On theological controversies, on disputation, and on the study of controversies in the schools. The beginning of controversy and the chief heads of it are shown in the disputation of the Devil with Adam, Genesis 3. First there is religion, and where there is religion there is error about it; from error comes controversy, and from controversy, disputation. Religion is either natural, Mosaic (or of the Old Testament), or Christian. Against the first stands Gentilism, against the second Judaism, and against the third, which is complete apostasy, Mahometanism. What a schism is, what a heresy is, and who are heretics or schismatics. The highest degree of error and apostasy is the sin against the Holy Spirit; what this is. One person raises a controversy, and another sustains it or repels it. We must see who raises it, why, and how. Some dispute about words and easy matters from a mere lust for contention, and multiply questions, with no less vehemence in their quarrelling. One must carefully weigh not only the matter but also the mind of the opponent. A question is either primary or secondary. The difference between a controversy and its importance. The latter is neither to be raised too high nor weighed down too far, and its force reaches to the foundation of faith, to practice, to the fellowship of the Church, and to the state of men. In answering a controversy, one must further see who answers, when, and how. Disputation is carried on partly by word of mouth and partly in writing, privately or publicly. The use and method of disputations; these are not to be granted to everyone. In the censure of books one must examine not only the book but first the author, to whom writing ought to be permitted, and also the subject and outline of the book before it is written. Disputation is held either with the orthodox or with heretics, and its end is twofold: either to convince or to reconcile. On the study of controversies: some things are required in the student, others in the studies themselves. In the student, above all, he must be upright, diligent, and modest. For the studies, a knowledge of languages is required beforehand, especially Hebrew and Greek, and also of philosophy. For one beginning the study of controversies, constant prayer and continual reading of Scripture are always necessary. The first knowledge of controversies is rough, then distinct, drawn from the writings of both parties, chosen with care; notes and the reading of books. In disputation the state of the controversy must be well laid out; one must not rush hastily to arguments; the thread of truth must be held; one should rely not on many arguments but on strong ones. The skill of disputing.

units.la: Postquam eo tandem religionis res devenerunt, ut disputationibus præcipue agi videantur, peculiare & non minimum Theologici studii argumentum fuit hoc quod in tractandis ejus occupatur controversiis. Siquidem non instituere solum & tradere dogmatica Theologiæ, vel solam praxim (prout nunc res sunt) urgere sufficit, nisi & in singulis etiam Theologiæ capitibus Adversarios denotemus, & movere controversiam, ac discutere, disputationem instituere, & vel corroborare argumentis veritatem, vel falsitatem & errores redarguere etiam, atque diluere queamus. Unde in nullo doctrinæ genere tot vel libri deprehenduntur, vel quod libros tantopere extendit & excrescere facit est aliud, quam quod habetur elenchicum.
units.tr: After things of religion had come to such a point that they seem to be chiefly carried on by disputations, the particular and by no means minor subject of theological study has been the handling of its controversies. For it is not enough merely to set out and teach dogmatic theology, or to press practice alone (as things now stand), unless in each head of theology we also mark the adversaries, stir up controversy, examine it, institute disputation, and are able either to strengthen the truth with arguments or to refute and also refute falsehoods and errors. Hence in no kind of doctrine are so many books found, and what makes books swell and grow so greatly is nothing other than what is called the elenctic method.

units.la: Duum autem generum controversiæ nostræ sunt. Aliæ problematicæ, inter Orthodoxos ipsos, vel de rebus fundamentum fidei non proxime concernentibus: problema etiam Tertullianus vocat, lib. de fuga in per-fecut. quod pertinet frater ad tuum problema, habet sententia nostra exhortationem & exhortationem. Alia sunt controversiae fidei, quae Ecclesiae sunt cum extraneis, cum Infidelibus, cum Haereticis, adde & cum Schismaticis. Illae graviores, proindeque cum majori animorum contentione, & divortio agitatae; in quibus etiam cognoscendis & decidendis majus momentum haeret, atque necessitas. Ea scire omnium interest, qui ad se aliqua ratione pertinere putant, discrepantes in Christianismo sectas, aut extra cum generales illas, quibus maxima mundi pars subjacet, superstitiones, & infidelitatem nosse. Non quod ad rationem fidei requiratur, etiam alia ab ipsa, & repugnantes ubique errores scire: satis est tenere simpliciter religionis capita, neque necesse errores, vel quascunque in religionis negotio cognoscere quaestiones; hoc enim tu interrogaberis, quod ipse, non quid alii crediderint. Verumtamen ad declinandas varias in vita nostra fideique cursu cautes & scopulos, dum ubique & sub singulis fere capitibus errorum aut haeresium latibula tenet Diabolus, valde expedit comperta habere errorum aut omnium, aut praecipuorum saltem, nobisque viciniorum, argumenta. In Theologo certe id summe necessarium: quippe cujus hoc est negotium, quoscunque a fide aberrantes erudire, & convincere; dum non potest, vel saltem, & scire tum a quibus extricandi homines sint malis, tum in quem perducendi veritatis portum; ac asylum. Quare de eo dubitare nolumus, nos aliquam gratiam a Theologiae Studiosis nostris, quorum formandis in omnem Ecclesiae operam studiis a Domino praepositi sumus, inituros esse, si hac etiam in re juvare illorum labores conemur, ostenso illis omnium per Theologiam controversiarum indice, juxta singulas sectas falsosque ditas religiones; facto ordine à Gentilibus, ad Iudæos, tum Mahommedanos, quos omnes merito pro Infidelibus habemus; inde pergendo ad Hæreticos, Papistas, Anabaptistas, Enthusiastas & Libertinos, Socinianos; denique ad Schismaticos, Lutheranos, Remonstrantes, Brownistas, seu Separatistas; postremo & in Oriente Græcos. De illis omnibus agere strictim instituì, & præformare disputationem. Nam & controversias ordine enumerabo, & quis tum singularum pseudo-religionum genius sit, tum quo modo disputandum ubique; quique celebres hic ibi disputatores, quid ultra agendum, meo quidem judicio, videatur, ad singula exponam. Quibus proinde singulares inscribo libros, nequidquam exiguâ eorum mole deterritus: ubi cum me aliorum tueri possim exemplo, tum præsens res, materiæque momentum, & diserepantia adeo argumenta, &, quod præsertim hic respexi, studiorum Theologicorum forma ac manuductio, quibus diversi libri, Auctores, adversaria, & cursus ουσιας conveniunt, divisionem illam nostram effagitare visa fuerunt.
units.tr: Now there are two kinds of our controversies. Some are problematic, arising among the orthodox themselves, or concerning matters not closely touching the foundation of faith; Tertullian also calls these problems, in his book On Flight in Persecution, where he says that a brother's ... pertains to your problem, and our opinion contains exhortation and exhortation. Others are controversies of faith, which the Church has with outsiders: with unbelievers, with heretics, and add also with schismatics. These are weightier, and are therefore carried on with greater contention of minds and with division; in knowing and deciding them lies greater importance and necessity. Everyone who thinks that he is in some way concerned has an interest in knowing these things: the sects that differ within Christianity, or those outside it, and the general superstitions and unbelief to which the greatest part of the world is subject. It is not required for the reason of faith to know other errors, both those different from it and those that contradict it everywhere; it is enough simply to hold the heads of religion, and it is not necessary to know the errors or whatever questions arise in matters of religion, for you will be asked about what you yourself believe, not what others have believed. Nevertheless, in order to avoid the various snares and rocks in our life and course of faith, since the Devil holds his hiding places of errors or heresies everywhere and under almost every head, it is very expedient to have learned the arguments of all the errors, or at least of the chief ones, and those nearest to us. This is certainly most necessary for a theologian, since his business is to instruct and convince all who wander from the faith, and he cannot do this unless he knows both from what evils men may be extricated and into what harbour of truth and refuge they may be led. Therefore we do not doubt that our students of theology, whose studies for the service of the Church the Lord has placed in our charge, will receive some favour from us, if we also try to help their labours in this matter, by setting before them an index of all the controversies throughout theology, according to each sect and each false religion; the order being made from the Gentiles to the Jews, then the Mahometans, whom we all rightly regard as unbelievers; from there proceeding to the heretics, Papists, Anabaptists, Enthusiasts and Libertines, and Socinians; finally to the schismatics, Lutherans, Remonstrants, Brownists or Separatists; and lastly, in the East, the Greeks. I have resolved to treat all these things briefly and to sketch out a disputation. For I shall both enumerate the controversies in order, and explain for each the character of each false religion, how one should dispute in each case, and which celebrated disputants are here and there, and what further, in my judgment, ought to be done. For this reason I have inscribed separate books to them, not deterred by their small bulk; since while I can be defended by the example of others, the present matter, the weight of the subject, and the arguments so diverse, and, what I have especially considered here, the form and guidance of theological studies, with which the various books, authors, notes, and the course of the substance [οὐσίας] agree, seemed to demand this division of ours.

units.la: De tribus impræsentiarum dicendum arbitror, de controversiis Theologicis; de disputatione, super illis; denique de Studio controversiarum, in Scholis bene instituendo & prosequendo. Initium omnis controversiæ & disputationis Theologicæ est à contentione primâ Diaboli, cum Protoplastis, Genes. iii. Ubi adversus hominem, quin Deum quoque, (ita omnis disputatio contra fidem, utramque impetit) de gravissimis & fundamentalibus religionis articulis suscepta disputatio fuit, de Deo; de ejus obedientiâ & cultu; denique de hominis salute, an in Deo, an extra eum collocandâ: quæ deinceps tria summa capita manserunt, in quibus oppugnandis & evertendis omnem posuit Diabolus industriam. Genes. iii. etiamne dixit] Deus, non comedetis de quolibet ligni arbore? vers. 5. Verùm novit Deus, quo die comedetis ex eâ, oculos vestros aperiendos, & sicut Deus vel futuros, cognoscentes bonum ac malum: Quo attentius sæpiusque hæc verba considero, eo certius in iis præcipua, adeoque fundamentalia disputationis de religione capita deprehendo. Etenim hinc origo omnis Theologicæ disputationis petenda, & summa articulorum controversorum, qui potissimum semper agitati à Diabolo contra hominem, ejusque religionem, & salutem fuere. Primò omnium dubitationem homini injicit, quæ ut fidei soliditatem ac constantiam vellicat, ita primam infidelitati, atque apostasiæ januam pandit, ac viam: adeone dixisset Deus? Primus aberrandi gradus est, de veritate dubitare; & Diabolus, qui non ausit statim objicere homini apertam à Deo defectionem, eam sub incautæ dubitationis formâ proponit, & urget. Dubitationem movit Dæmon de Dei veritate: an Deus id dixisset? videlicet hoc prostrato, ut non amplius Deum credamus verum aut veracem esse, nihil religionis ultra superest. Insuper quasi malus esset Deus, ita eum homini depingit, invidum nempe felicitatis humanæ: unde sponte jam sequebatur, non esse quod tali Deo, ejusque mandatis amplius obtemperaret. Atque hoc est homini suadere, Deum tentare, probam videlicet ejus capiat, experiaturque, annon, contra ac minatus erat, per fructum arboris illius vetitæ gustatum, ad divinam perventurus fuisset sapientiam, adeoque felicitatem. Quippe & hoc distinctum controversiæ caput erat, disputatione hâc mire involutum implicatumque, in quo consisteret hominis felicitas: an in præcisâ absolutâque Dei & mandati ejus obedientiâ? quod unicè impugnatum ivit suâ tentatione Diabolus. Et sanè evictis illis omnibus, facillimum est Satanæ seipsum Dei loco ingerere, apud illos quibus ista persuaserit. Et hoc ejus in jugi, quâ homines vexat, disputatione molimen, hic scopus est, dejectâ Dei reverentiâ & cultu, ejus thronum locumque invadere, & se Deum facere. Manifestum id quoque in
units.tr: I think three things should be spoken of at present: on theological controversies; on disputation concerning them; and finally, on the study of controversies, to be well organised and pursued in the schools. The beginning of every theological controversy and disputation is from the first contest of the Devil with our first parents, Genesis 3. There a disputation was undertaken against man, and indeed against God as well (for every disputation against faith assails both), concerning the most weighty and fundamental articles of religion: concerning God; concerning obedience and worship of him; and finally concerning the salvation of man, whether it is to be placed in God or outside him. These three have remained the chief heads, and in attacking and overthrowing them the Devil has spent all his effort. Genesis 3: Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden? verse 5: For God doth know that in the day ye eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened, and ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil. The more attentively and often I consider these words, the more surely I find in them the chief and therefore fundamental heads of the disputation about religion. For from here must be drawn the origin of all theological disputation, and the sum of the controverted articles, which have always been chiefly stirred up by the Devil against man, and against his religion and salvation. First of all he casts doubt into man, which, while it shakes the firmness and constancy of faith, opens the first door and way to unbelief and apostasy: Has God indeed said so? The first step of straying is to doubt the truth, and the Devil, who did not dare at once to object to man a plain defection from God, proposes it and presses it in the form of a careless doubt. The Demon raised doubt about the truth of God: did God really say this? Clearly, once this is overthrown, so that we no longer believe God to be true or truthful, nothing of religion remains beyond it. Further, as if God were evil, he depicts him to man as envious of human happiness; whence it followed at once of its own accord that there was no reason to obey such a God and his commands any longer. And this is to persuade man to tempt God, that is, to take his trial and to see whether, contrary to what he had threatened, by tasting the fruit of that forbidden tree he would attain to divine wisdom, and so to happiness. Indeed this too was a distinct head of controversy, wonderfully involved and entangled in this disputation: in what man's happiness consists, whether in the bare and absolute obedience of God and his command? This was the one thing the Devil went about attacking by his temptation. And certainly, once all these were overcome, it is very easy for Satan to thrust himself into God's place among those whom he has persuaded of these things. And this is the aim of his effort in the continual disputation with which he harasses men: to cast down the reverence and worship of God, to invade his throne and place, and to make himself God. This is also manifest in

units.la: gcgemina tentatione, qua Christum initio adortus est, Matth. iv. Ita sc. oportuit, utrumque Adamum non multum dissimili tentatione aggredi, eventu licet longe dispari. Uti illic, ita & hic, Christum a Deo avocatum avulsumque voluit & subjectum sibi, tum, ne se Dei filium crederet, quin praeberet clientem Diaboli, cum adoraret & coleret. Convenicbat praeterquam in re, etiam in modo, tentatio ac disputatio utraque, initio, vel hypothesi facta a dubitatione: ibi, num Deus dixisset? hic, num verum, quod itidem dixisset Deus, Christus sciebat, se esse Dei filium? Observemus ergo, praecipua, quae in contentionem Diabolus trahit, capita super religionis negotio, haec semper i. est de Deo dubitatio, sive de natura ejus, sive de verbo. ii. an Deus per omnia verax? adeoque an fides ei semper habenda sit? Noverimus, Diaboli esse has objectiones, quarum nunc instituimus analysin. iii. an omnino bonus Deus? iv. an ubique & semper ei obediendum? v. quid, annon tentare cum aliquando conveniat? vi. in quo hominis sita sit beatitudo? an in individuo cum Deo nexu & conjunctione? vii. si non forte praestet Diabolum pro Deo accipere & colere? Haec illa sunt capita, quae ut in prima Diaboli tentatione omnia ceu totidem spicula conjuncta & contortiplicata (ut Plauti verbo utar) fuerunt, ita postquam his cessit homo miserre victus, perpetuum fuerunt disputationum adversus hominem, & quam Deus praescripsit homini religionem, Diabolo argumentum. Credo quid in omni errore & peccato Diabolus agit, vel committit peccator homo: quam ut de Deo dubitet, & Deum tentet, neque ei obediat? nec etiam eatenus in solo Deo, ejusque cultu, & communione summum bonum collocet. Et hoc quanto studio quaesitum a Gentilibus fuit, in quo situm esset? idque omne ex prima illa Disputatione, secutaque ad eam infelici hominum deviatione & lapsu. Omnis disputatio aliquo nititur crroerrore, ut eum vel inducat, vel amoliatur: atque ubi errori nullus, non quoque disputationi seriae locus est. Utrumque hic spectatur, quatenus cadit in negotium religionis, seu error, aut controversia, vel disputatio: illaque se ita mutuo subsequuntur, ut super religione primum nascatur error, inde controversia, demum de controversia disputatio.
units.tr: The twofold temptation with which he first attacked Christ (Matt. 4) was like this: the two Adams were assailed by temptations not very unlike each other, though the outcomes were far different. Here as there, the aim was to draw Christ away from God and make Him his own, so that He would not believe Himself to be God's Son but would instead become a client of the Devil, worshipping and serving him. Both the temptation and the dispute had the same form, not only in substance but in manner: they began from doubt, or a hypothesis. There the question was, "Has God really said?" Here it was, "Does Christ know that what God has likewise said is true, that he is God's Son?" Let us observe, then, the chief heads on which the Devil brings contention in matters of religion. They are always these: (i) there is doubt about God, whether about His nature or about His word; (ii) is God true in all things, and so is He always to be believed? Let us note that these are the Devil's objections, whose analysis we now undertake. (iii) Is God wholly good? (iv) Must we obey Him always and everywhere? (v) Is it sometimes fitting to test Him? (vi) In what does man's blessedness consist: in an individual bond and union with God? (vii) Is it perhaps better to take the Devil as God and worship him? These are the heads which, in the first temptation of the Devil, were all joined together like so many darts, twisted and intertwined (to use Plautus's word). Since man yielded to these and was miserably overcome, they became the constant subject of disputes against man, and the Devil's argument against the religion which God prescribed to man. I believe that this is what the Devil does in every error and sin, or what the sinful man commits: to doubt God, to test Him, and not to obey Him; and in this way not to place the highest good in God alone, in His worship and communion. And how eagerly the Gentiles sought to know in what this good consisted! All of this came from that first dispute and the unhappy straying and fall of men that followed it. Every dispute rests on some error, either to bring it on or to remove it; and where there is no error, there is no room for serious dispute either. Both are considered here, insofar as they fall under the matter of religion: error, controversy, or dispute. These follow one another in such a way that error first arises about religion, then controversy from error, and at last dispute about the controversy.

units.la: Religio, vel strictè sumitur, pro cultu Dei specifico, qui primâ legis tabulâ injungitur, & solum Deum habet pro objecto immediato, ac proprio, quae aliter pietas εὐσέβεια dicitur; vel latè, pro omni virtutis probitatisque officio, sive Deum proximè, sive homines concernat, à Deo nobis in lege, seu utrisque Decalogi tabulis, imperato. Vti elogium justi in Sacris, quando homini tribuitur, vel quomodo in Scholis dicitur justitia universalis; pari latitudine accipitur etiam religio. Certè in epistolâ Jacobi, cap. 1. verf. ult. & penult. religionis dicitur esse linguam suam bene cohibere, viduas & orphanos invisere, quae praecepta aliàs referuntur ad secundam tabulam. Eodemque tendit distinctio Scholasticorum de religionis actibus, in proprios & immediatos seu elicitos, per quos homo ordinatur ad solum Deum; quod convenit cum religione, priori & strictâ acceptione: & in actus ejus imperatos, quos producit mediantibus aliis virtutibus: omnes tamen ultimò in cultum ac reverentiam Dei ordinantur, qui elicitive sunt suarum virtutum. v. g. visitare orphanos viduasque, actus elicitus à misericordiâ; & immaculatum se custodire à mundo, actus temperantiae: sed imperantur à religione, à quâ habent, ut omnia haec religiosè fiant; quod convenit cum religionis acceptione nostrâ secundâ, latiori. Vide Thomam II. II. qu. lxxxı. art. 1. Quâ ratione Religio commodè definiri vel describi potest, ex Clementis Alexandrini Paedagogiâ, Paedag. lib. I. cap. VII. παιδαγωγία ἡ θεοσέβεια, quae est doctrina divini cultus, & eruditio ad adsequendam veritatis agnitionem, & recta institutio, vitaeque agenda ratio, quae in coelum deducit. Religionem Graeci θρησκείαν, Hebraei דת dicunt, quod servitutem sonat: atque religionem omnem falsam, & nominatim idololatriam, iidem appellant הדרה עבודה, contracte עבד, de quo extat integer codex in Talmude. Graeci θρησκεία & θρῆσκος, quod utrumque occurrit Jac. 1. versibus indicatis, a θρᾶξ, θρῇξ Thrax, (unde & θρησκείας ventus), quia apud Thraces scilicet Orpheus primus Deorum cultum introduxerit, derivant: in Sacris N. Testamenti in genere pro religione venit, sive de vera Jac. 1.26. 27. sive de falsa sermo sit, uti Pharisaismum suum Apostolus, Act. xxvi. 5. vocat τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἵρεσιν τῆς ἡμετέρας θρησκείας. & Coloss. ii. 18. θρησκείᾳ τῶν ἀγγέλων. Religionis vocem alii a relegendo derivant, uti Cicero; & ex eo Isidorus, qui omnia, quae ad cultum Deorum pertinerent, diligenter pertractarent, & quasi relegerent, sunt dicti religiosi a relegendo. Alii a religendo, ut dicat, nos Deum religere atque redamare: qui potius in verbo lusus videtur, quam ejus derivatio. Cum Lactantio malimus a religando vocem trahere, lib. iv. de vera sap. cap. xxviii. ubi & Ciceronis illam sententiam rejicit: diximus nomen religionis a vinculo pietatis esse deductum, quod hominem sibi Deus religaverit, & pietate constrinxerit: quia servire nos ei, ut domino, & obsequi, ut patri, necesse est, melius ergo id nomen Lucretius interpretatus est, qui ait, religionum se nodos exolvere. Quo & Augustinus respexit, dicens: religet nos religio uni omnipotenti Deo, lib. de vera relig. cap. iv. atque paulo ante: ad unum Deum tendentes, & ei uni religantes animas nostras, unde religio dicta creditur. Omnis vera religio, & quae a Deo, triplex unquam fuit, Naturalis, ex principiis & jure naturali: Mosaica, in Veteri Testamento; Christiana, in Novo: illa omnium hominum fuit, & prima; ista Judaeorum; haec nunc est Christianorum: nisi quod ante Mosaicam Dei popupopulus praeter naturalem etiam institutum habuerit, cum Mosaicâ postmodum subsecutâ convenientem, quaeque utrobique & legem, & Euangelium variè docuit; atque ita alia post aliam successit religio, vel diversus Deum colendi modus, priore plenior, ad salutem una semper eademque, usque ad postremam hanc nostram Christianam consummatissimam: non quod legi, aut doctrinæ morum sub antiquo etiam Testamento quidpiam defuerit, sed quod τὴν τρόπου religionis, alia perfectior atque abundantior œconomia fuerit surrogata, superducto Euangelio expunctore totius veteris vetustatis, inquit Tertullianus, lib. de Oratione.
units.tr: Religion is taken either strictly, for the specific worship of God which is enjoined in the first table of the law, and which has God alone as its immediate and proper object (and this is otherwise called piety, εὐσέβεια); or broadly, for every office of virtue and uprightness, whether it concerns God directly or men, as commanded to us by God in the law, that is, in both tables of the Decalogue. Just as the praise of the righteous in Scripture is given to a man in this wider sense, or as in the Schools it is called universal justice, so religion too is taken with equal breadth. Indeed, in the epistle of James, chapter 1, the last two verses, religion is said to be to bridle one's tongue and to visit widows and orphans, precepts which are elsewhere referred to the second table. The scholastic distinction of the acts of religion points the same way: into proper and immediate acts, or elicited ones, by which a man is directed to God alone (this agrees with religion in the first and strict sense); and into its commanded acts, which it produces by means of other virtues. All of these, however, are finally directed to the worship and reverence of God, and they are elicited by their own virtues. For example, visiting orphans and widows is an act elicited by mercy, and keeping oneself unstained by the world is an act of temperance; but they are commanded by religion, from which they receive that all these things are done religiously. This agrees with our second, wider sense of religion. See Thomas, II. II. qu. lxxxi. art. 1. For this reason religion may conveniently be defined or described from Clement of Alexandria's Paedagogus, Book 1, chapter 7: παιδαγωγία ἡ θεοσέβεια (piety is the training), which is the teaching of divine worship, and instruction for attaining knowledge of the truth, and right education and the conduct of life, which leads to heaven. The Greeks call religion θρησκείαν, and the Hebrews דת (dat), which means servitude. The same people call every false religion, and idolatry in particular, הדרה עבודה (avodah zarah), in contracted form עבד, about which a whole treatise exists in the Talmud. The Greeks derive θρησκεία and θρῆσκος, both of which occur in James 1 in the verses cited, from θρᾶξ or θρῇξ (Thrax), whence also the north wind θρησκίας, because Orpheus, as they say, first introduced the worship of the gods among the Thracians. In the Sacred Books of the New Testament the word in general means religion, whether the discourse is about true religion (James 1:26, 27) or false. So the Apostle calls his Pharisaism τὴν ἀκριβεστάτην αἵρεσιν τῆς ἡμετέρας θρησκείας (the strictest sect of our religion), Acts 26:5, and in Colossians 2:18 we read θρησκείᾳ τῶν ἀγγέλων (worship of angels). Others derive the word religion from relegere (to read again), as Cicero does; and from him Isidore, who says that those who carefully went over and as it were re-read all that pertained to the worship of the gods were called religious, from relegere. Others derive it from religere, as if to say that we bind God to us again and love Him in return; but this seems rather a play on words than a true derivation. With Lactantius we prefer to draw the word from religare (to bind), Book 4, de vera sapientia, chapter 28, where he also rejects that opinion of Cicero: "We have said that the name religion is derived from the bond of piety, because God has bound man to Himself and constrained him by piety; for we must serve Him as Lord and obey Him as Father. Lucretius has interpreted the name better when he says that he loosens the knots of religion." Augustine also had this in view when he says: "Religion binds us to the one almighty God," de vera religione, chapter 4; and a little before: "Tending to the one God and binding our souls to Him alone, from which religion is believed to be named." Every true religion, and every religion from God, has always been threefold: Natural, from the principles and natural law; Mosaic, in the Old Testament; and Christian, in the New. The first was for all men and was the first; the second belonged to the Jews; the third is now that of Christians. Except that before the Mosaic law the people of God had, besides the natural religion, an institution agreeing with the Mosaic one which followed afterwards, and which in both respects taught the law and the gospel in various ways. So one religion succeeded another, or one different manner of worshipping God, each fuller than the last, yet always one and the same for salvation, up to this last Christian religion, the most complete. This was not because anything was lacking to the law or the doctrine of morals even under the Old Testament, but because another, more perfect and abundant dispensation was substituted for the manner of religion, the gospel having been brought in as the expunger of all the old antiquity, as Tertullian says in his book de Oratione.

units.la: Jam errores quod spectat (circa vocem non hærebo, quæ deviationem quamvis denotat, ἁμάρτημα, inde quodcunque peccatum error habetur, reveraque est: & nos hic, à veritate quando peccatur, errorem appellamus) sunt ii super religionis nunc dictæ negotio, vel adversus Naturalem, aut Mosaicam, aut Christianam. Adversus illam errando peccant Gentiles; istam, Iudei; contra hanc totam videlicet, ex universali & plena apostasiâ, Mahommedani: nam adversus Christianam religionem ex parte erratur, sub nomine etiam Christiano, tab hæreticis, aliisque. Ex Naturali Theologiâ aut religione convincendi sunt Gentiles; ex Mosaicâ, Iudæi; ex quâcunque, & Naturali, & Mosaicâ, & Christianâ, Muhammedani, quia illam omnem aliquâ ratione admittunt, & in quamcunque etiam peccant.
units.tr: As for errors (I shall not dwell on the word, which denotes a deviation, ἁμάρτημα; hence any sin is regarded and really is an error, and here we call error whatever sin departs from the truth), they concern the matter of religion just described, either against the natural, or the Mosaic, or the Christian religion. The Gentiles err against the first; the Jews against the second; the Mohammedans against the whole of the third, through a complete and universal apostasy. For against the Christian religion men err in part, even under the Christian name, as do heretics and others. The Gentiles must be refuted from natural theology or religion, the Jews from the Mosaic, and the Mohammedans from every religion, both natural, Mosaic and Christian, because they admit all of these in some way, and yet err in each of them.

units.la: Succedunt Hæretici, qui sub professione Christianismi, religionem tamen Christianam vehementer lædunt, ejusque veritatem in multis oppugnant: atque uti isti religionis hostes sunt, quamvis sub unâ ejusdem prosessione; ita Schismatici sub unâ haberi volentes aut visi Ecclesiâ, tamen in nonnullis huius, & quoque sincerae religionis adversarii existunt. Religionis ergo trium generum homines inimici sunt, vel qui extra omnem religionem & Ecclesiam Christianam sunt, Infideles; vel qui sub eadem religione Christiana se quasi obtegunt, Haeretici; vel qui etiam sub eadem fere Ecclesia, Schismatici. Quum enim a nostra parte se tenent & religio, & Ecclesia, apud quam religio est, adversarii tum religionis, tum Ecclesiae, vel extra utramque degunt, & nihil sibi cum utraque commune volunt, quales sunt primae classis infideles; vel religionem eandem impugnant, nihil cum eadem commune habentes Ecclesiâ, Haeretici; vel quasi fere ejusdem Ecclesiae, & huic tamen, illique in nonnullis adversi, Schismatici. Omnium illorum errores, & vel Infidelitas, vel Haeresis, vel Schisma, alterum altero majus est, aut minus. Infidelitatem apostasia facit, eâ minor est Haeresis, hâc Schisma, omnium una mater Error, ex errore contentio, inde tum reliqua. Unde Apostolus signanter utrumque conjungit, schismata & contentiones, 1. Cor. 1. 10. ne sint in vobis schismata: v. 11. indicatum mihi de vobis, quod lites inter vos sunt. Sic à Scholasticis, apud Thomam, 11. 11. qu. xxxvi 1 r. de contentione: altera sequente quaestione agitur de Schismate.
units.tr: Next come the heretics, who, under a profession of Christianity, nonetheless grievously harm the Christian religion and attack its truth in many points. Just as these are enemies of religion though they share one and the same profession, so schismatics, who wish to be held, or to seem, members of one and the same Church, are nonetheless opponents of that Church and of sincere religion in some respects. There are therefore three kinds of men who are enemies of religion: those who lie wholly outside the Christian religion and Church, the Infidels; those who cover themselves, as it were, under the same Christian religion, the heretics; and those who, while under almost the same Church, are schismatics. For since both religion and the Church in which religion is found hold to our side, the adversaries of religion and of the Church either live outside both and want nothing in common with either, like the infidels of the first class; or they attack the same religion while having nothing in common with the same Church, the heretics; or they are, as it were, of the same Church, yet opposed to it and to that religion in some points, the schismatics. Of all these errors, whether unbelief, heresy or schism, one is greater or less than another. Apostasy makes unbelief; heresy is less than this, and schism less than heresy. Error is the one mother of all; from error comes contention, and from contention the rest. Hence the Apostle deliberately joins the two: "schisms and contentions" (1 Cor. 1. 10), "that there be no schisms among you"; and at v. 11, "it has been reported to me concerning you that there are quarrels among you." So the Scholastics, in Thomas, II-II, qu. 36, art. 1, treat of contention, and the following question treats of schism.

units.la: Schisma, uti & Haeresis, vel late sumitur (quin vox haeresis aliquando in bonam etiam partem, & quaelibet sententiarum animorumque scissura schisma quasi aliquod est: scinditur incertum studia in contraria vulgus), vel stricte. Nam sensu Ecclesiastico illa fere opponi solent, ut minus haeresi schisma sit. Hoc, propter aliquam (sed hic, vel ibi majorem) causam doctrinae est, aut disciplinae, quae uti proponitur, per se & primo non videtur tollere fundamentalem religionis articulum, haeresis immo. Quo sensu doctrinam Lutheri, ex quâ Lutherani judicandi; tum Brownistarum Anglorum; etiam Arminii, unde Arminiani (distinguendo illos semper à Socíniano-Remonstrantibus), denique & Graecorum in Oriente Ecclesiarum, inter Schismata numeramus. Quae unitatem Ecclesiae, cujus communionem non videri voluerunt omnino abjicere, ledunt alia aliis graviora. Oportebat quidem nihil non fovere, ne Ecclesiam Dei scinderent, scribit apud Eusebium lib. vi. cap. xlv. Dionysius Alexandrinus Novato. Hæreses, nec propter doctrinarum divortia, nec animorum, possunt aut volunt Ecclesiæ ejusdem unitatem colere; sed quæ fundamentales fidei articulos aperte convellunt, religionis, & Ecclesiæ æque inimici sunt. Horum censentur nobis Papistæ, Socinian, Enthusiastæ ac Libertini, si aliqua ipsorum religio dicenda sit: Anabaptistæ, quia varium hominum genus est, & ignorans passim, vixque aliquando præter anabaptismum, aut juramenti, & officii Christiano-politici negatum sibi usum, & ignoratam carnis Christi originem præ se ferens, alias vero ultra procedunt ad Pelagianismum, & Socinianismum, pro re natâ ferendum de illis judicium erit. Hæresis Schisma (de quâ diximus etiam in Apparatu ad Confutationem Socinianismi); illam apostasia superat, peccati & malitiæ gravitate. Apostasia est præterquam in doctrinâ, alia in vitâ. Et Schisma, & hæresis, & apostasia est vel nascens, vel consummata: quâ de distinctione conferlis Iohannis Raynoldi, eruditissimi Theologi, prælect. 1. de libris Apocryphis. Summus erandi gradus est apostasia; apostasiæ autem gradus summus peccatum, quod dicitur, in Spiritum Sanctum, ubi non solum deficit aliquis à veritate, verum & eidem, & convictioni de eâ apud conscientiam suam claræ opponit se quantum potest maliciose, & persequitur eandem, ac blasphemat, unde non peccatum solum, sed blasphemia dicitur: quod quid sit, ob rei difficultatem, lubet penitius investigare.
units.tr: Schism, like heresy, is taken either broadly or strictly. (Indeed the word heresy is sometimes used in a good sense, and any splitting of opinions and minds is, as it were, a kind of schism, since the crowd is divided into opposing pursuits.) In ecclesiastical usage, however, these terms are usually set against each other, so that schism is less than heresy. Schism arises from some cause of doctrine or discipline, greater or lesser as the case may be, which, as it is put forward, does not of itself and primarily seem to overthrow a fundamental article of religion, as heresy does. In this sense we count among the schisms the doctrine of Luther, from which Lutherans take their name; the doctrine of the English Brownists; that of Arminius, whence the Arminians (always distinguished from the Socinian Remonstrants); and finally the schism of the Greek churches in the East. These churches did not wish to cast off the unity of the Church altogether, nor to appear to abandon its communion, but they harm it in different ways, some more gravely than others. "Indeed one ought to leave nothing untried, lest they divide the Church of God," writes Dionysius of Alexandria to Novatus, in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 6, chapter 45. Heresies, whether through divergence of doctrines or of minds, can neither wish nor manage to preserve the unity of the same Church; those which openly overthrow the fundamental articles of faith are equally enemies of religion and of the Church. Of these we reckon the Papists, Socinians, Enthusiasts and Libertines, if any of them is to be called a religion at all. The Anabaptists are a various and ignorant sort of men, who in many places scarcely go beyond anabaptism, or the denial of the oath and of Christian civil office, and who hold an ignorant view of the origin of Christ's flesh; in other cases they proceed further to Pelagianism and Socinianism, and our judgment of them must be formed as the occasion requires. Heresy surpasses schism (which we also discussed in the Preface to the Confutation of Socinianism), and it surpasses apostasy in the gravity of sin and malice. Apostasy is either in doctrine or otherwise in life. Schism, heresy and apostasy are each either beginning or completed. On this distinction compare John Reynolds, the most learned theologian, Prelection 1 on the Apocryphal Books. The highest degree of erring is apostasy, and the highest degree of apostasy is the sin said to be "against the Holy Spirit." Here someone not only falls away from the truth but also maliciously sets himself, as far as he can, against that truth and against the conviction of it clear in his own conscience; he persecutes it and blasphemes it. Hence it is called not merely a sin but blasphemy. What this is, because of the difficulty of the matter, we are pleased to examine more thoroughly.

units.la: Blasphemiam esse βλασφημίαν τὴν φήμην, famam alicujus nocere, Græci tradiderunt. Hebræi dicunt פגר opprobrium, contumelia. נאצה: & חלל, & קלל maledictio. ברך utrumque & benedixit significat, & maledixit. Ira secundum inter septem universalia Noachi præpræcepta, tantopere à Iudæis deprædicata, est, ברכה de maledictione Dei. Ac Iobi primo, & secundo capite hæc vox ברך ipso sequiori sensu occurrit, atque etiam alibi: an per antiphrasin, ut multis placet, pro minime benedicere? quemadmodum bellum, quasi minime bellum, apud latinos: an benedicere, pro maledicere, atque hoc demum pro renuntiare, seu numen abnegare? uti apud Seldenum, de Iure naturali Ebr. Lib. II. cap. 11. Martinus de Roa, annon potius, quod & Seldeno placet, pro singulari linguæ sanctæ idiotismo, in utramque partem æque pro circumstantiâ loci accipiendum? ut apud Latinos, sacrare, & imprecari: etenim in ברך nihil proprie, quo, juxta Hebræos, benedicere aut maledicere significetur.
units.tr: The Greeks have taught that blasphemy is "harm to someone's reputation" [βλασφημίαν τὴν φήμην]. The Hebrews use פגר (reproach, insult), נאצה and חלל, and קלל (curse). The word ברך means both bless and curse. The second of the seven universal precepts of Noah, so greatly extolled by the Jews, concerns the cursing of God [ברכה]. In the first and second chapters of Job this word ברך occurs in the latter sense itself, and elsewhere too. Is it used by antiphrasis, as many think, to mean not at all to bless? So in Latin bellum is said, as if it meant "not at all pretty." Or does to bless stand for to curse, and this in turn for to renounce, or deny the divine majesty? So Selden, On the Law of Nature among the Hebrews, book II, chapter 11. Or rather, as Martín de Roa holds, and as Selden also agrees, is it to be taken in either sense equally, according to the circumstances, as a peculiar idiom of the holy tongue? So in Latin sacrare and imprecari serve both senses. For in ברך there is nothing that properly signifies, according to the Hebrews, either to bless or to curse.

units.la: Blasphemia in genere dicit contumeliam alicui impactam, ad ejus honorem vel excellentiam deprimendam. Committitur vel in Deum, vel in Creaturas; præcipuè quidem sanctos, & Angelos; vel homines. Tit. III. 1. neminem blasphemare. ubi proximè respicit magistratus & potestates, quibus vers. 1. subjectionem deferri & obedientiam, imperat. Eph. IV. 31. omnis blasphemia tollatur à vobis. 1. Reg. XXI. 10. contrà Nabothum, ברך maledixisti Deo, atque Regi. Iudas, epist. vers. 8. κυριότητα ἀθετοῦσι. δόξας δὲ βλασφημοῦσιν. Sed & hæc in Reges, qui Dei sunt ἀγγέλους, blasphemia, in Deum ipsum indirectè vergit.
units.tr: In general, blasphemy is an insult directed at someone to diminish his honour or excellence. It is committed either against God or against creatures, chiefly against the saints and angels, or against men. Titus 3. 1: "to speak evil of no one," where he is chiefly thinking of the magistrates and powers, to whom he commands in the same verse submission and obedience. Eph. 4. 31: "let all blasphemy be put away from you." 1 Kings 21. 10, against Naboth: "you have cursed God and the king" [ברך]. Jude, v. 8: "they despise dominion, and they blaspheme the glorious ones" [κυριότητα ἀθετοῦσι. δόξας δὲ βλασφημοῦσιν]. But blasphemy against kings, who are God's agents [ἄγγελοι], also tends indirectly towards God himself.

units.la: Multipliciter & haud uno modo committitur in Deum blasphemia. Quatuor ejus habes species 1. quando contumeliosè, atque per summum contemptum quis in genere de Deo malè loquitur: uti Pharao, quid est Dominus? &c. Exod. V. 2. 11. Quando quis detrahit Deo ea, quæ ipsi debentur & propria sunt: ut si quis neget Deum justum, sapientem &c., vel Deo filium &c. III. Quando attribuuntur Deo, quæ ei neutiquam conveniunt, & cum divinâ ejus naturâ aperte pugnant. Ut quando Pharisæi Christum dicebant hominem edacem, ac bibonem. Matth. xi. 19. vel quod per Beelzebub daemonia ejiceret, Luc. xi. 15. similiaque plura. iv. Denique quando creatoris adscribitur, quod soli Deo proprium est: ut quando homini adscribunt potestatem remittendi peccata. Blasphemia alia magis directe, alia fit magis indirecte: atque apertior alia est, alia magis palliata. Apertae, atque directae exemplum habrendum dedit P. Julius II. ad disputo de Deo, blasphemia Italis usitatiori: de qua, an blasphemia sit, & ut ab hoc crimine usum suum loquendi purgent, quaerant Iurisconsulti, Baldus de Vbaldis, Vol. 3. Consil. 3. 6. & Thomas Grammaticus, decis. Neapolit. 50. nobis res illa extra quaestionem ponitur, ac dubium.
units.tr: Blasphemy against God is committed in many ways and not in one way only. You have four species of it. (1) When someone speaks evil of God in general, with insulting words and the greatest contempt, as Pharaoh did: "Who is the Lord?" etc. (Exod. 5. 2). (2) When someone detracts from God what is due to him and proper to him, as if he denied that God is just or wise, or that he is the Son of God. (3) When things are attributed to God that by no means belong to him and openly clash with his divine nature, as when the Pharisees said that Christ was a glutton and a drunkard (Matt. 11. 19), or that he cast out demons by Beelzebub (Luke 11. 15), and many similar things. (4) Finally, when what belongs to the Creator alone is ascribed to a creature, as when men ascribe to a man the power of forgiving sins. Blasphemy is committed in one way more directly, in another more indirectly; and one kind is more open, another more disguised. As an example of open and direct blasphemy, Pope Julius II gave the more usual Italian form of blasphemy, I dispute about God. Whether this is blasphemy, and whether men may purge their manner of speaking of this charge, lawyers may inquire: Baldus de Ubaldis, Vol. 3, Consil. 3, no. 6, and Thomas Grammaticus, Decisions of Naples, no. 50. For us that question lies outside our present inquiry and is doubtful.

units.la: Quid blasphemia in Spiritum Sanctum, explicari debet ex Matth. xii. 31. 32. quodnam hoc peccatum sit? quare dicatur irremissibile? denique quomodo dignoscatur?
units.tr: What blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is must be explained from Matthew 12. 31-32: what this sin is; why it is called irremissible; and finally how it is recognised.

units.la: 1. Quis Spiritus S. adversus quem hoc peccatum proprie dicitur committi? quid peccatum, vel verbum, vel blasphemia? quibus vocibus & notionibus peccatum hoc in Scriptura designatur. Per Spiritum Sanctum, sunt qui intellexerunt, ipsam Dei essentiam; nomine Spiritus S. essentialiter sumto. Sunt qui tertiam in S. Trinitate, Spiritus S. personam: vel Spiritus Sancti dona, effecta, & operationes in homine. Hoc bene: ita tamen, ut peccatum adversus opus Spiritus S. in veritate hominis ostendendae, etiam adversus Spiritum S. Deumque (nam blasphemia proprie personam respicit) commissum habeatur. Syrus, & Arabs habent, in Spiritum S.: in Graeco est τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον. Non omne peccatum in vel adversus Spiritum Sanctum est blasphemia. Contra Spiritus S. personam, etiam opera, gratiam & dona peccatur, non semper tamen ex malitia, vel cum blasphemia. Hoc peccatum quod dicitur blasphemia, atque in Spiritum S. a multis varie explicatur. Toletus in Lucam cap. xii. 1. octodecim ejus affert expositiones: quas Corn. à Lapide in Matth. Matth. xii. ad septem contrahit. Nos nec has, neque illas sectamur, quae videri suis locis possunt, atque examinari. Attamen quia aliorum sententias in hujusmodi quaestionibus audire quam maxime convenit, primo sunt qui intelligunt hoc peccatum, de peccato ex malitia, aut peccatum ex ignorantia, peccatum contra Patrem; ex infirmitate, contra Filium; sic ex malitia quod peccatur, esse hoc peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum: quae sententia placuisse videtur Magistro Sententiarum, II. dist. xliii. & Thomae, 22. qu. xiv. sed rejicitur, & refutatur a Bellarmino, lib. II. de poenitentia, cap. xvi. vide & Sixtum Senens. bibl. lib. VI. annot. lvi. Ejusce peccati constituunt tum sex species, sc. desperationem, praesumtionem; impoenitentiam, obstinationem, impugnationem veritatis agnitae, & invidentiam fraternae gratiae. De quibus Thomas, ut. II. Et ante eum, Alex. Alensis, part. II. qu. clxvii. num. III. Secunda sententia est, exponentium hoc peccatum, de finali impoenitentia; quae fuit Augustini: redarguitur autem ab Erasmo, in Notatis contra Bedam, pag. 17. 18. Bellarmino, Gomaro, in Matth. xii. Tertia sententia exponit, de peccato post baptismum; quae fuit Origenis olim: sed ab Athanasio, aliisque merito rejecta. IV. intelligitur ab aliis, de negatione fidei in persecutione. V. de odio, convitio ac contumelia in Deum VI. de peccato simonia. VII. de Pneumatomachis, negantibus Spiritus S. Deitatem. Verum hisce omnibus omissis, quae judicamus rem non explicare; refutare autem non est hujus loci: dicimus; blasphemiam in Spiritum Sanctum, esse peccatum, quo, qui de veritate religionis Christianae satis certo & evidenter est convictus, idque Spiritus S. gratia & operatione, tamen tandem illam, de qua adeo persuasus est, veritatem scienter, volenter, malitiose, ac totis viribus abnegat, oppugnat, blasphemat. Materia peccati est, veritas doctrinae Sacrae, omnis quidem ejus, legis gis & Euangelii, potissimum tamen Euangelii, Christique: non enim videtur aliud singulare & specificum peccatum esse irremissibile, & irreconciliabile peccatori apud Deum, quam quod mediatorem Christum impetit, eamque & ejus notitiam ac fidem destruit. Requiritur in homine sic peccante, ut sit illuminatus, persuasus & convictus de sacra veritate, sufficienter, ne accipiat aliqua se quidem veræ doctrinæ scire, non autem præcipua, nedum omnia capita. & certò: quisquE enim dubitat de veritate, qualis tempore Christi multi inter Iudæos erant, non est convictio, neque ex malitia abnegatio, vel oppositio. denique etiam evidenter: ne obscuritatem, vel tenebras ignoratæ veritatis prætendat.
units.tr: 1. Which Holy Spirit is it against whom this sin is properly said to be committed? What is sin, or word, or blasphemy? By what words and notions is this sin designated in Scripture? Some have understood by the Holy Spirit the very essence of God, taking the name Spirit essentially. Others understand the third person of the Holy Trinity, the Holy Spirit, or the gifts, effects and operations of the Holy Spirit in man. This is good, provided that sin against the work of the Holy Spirit in showing forth the truth is also held to be committed against the Holy Spirit and God, since blasphemy properly regards a person. The Syriac and Arabic versions read "against the Holy Spirit"; in Greek it is "the Holy Spirit" [τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον]. Not every sin in or against the Holy Spirit is blasphemy. Sin is committed against the person of the Holy Spirit, and also against his works, grace and gifts, though not always from malice or with blasphemy. This sin, called blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, is explained in many different ways. Toletus, on Luke 12:1, gives eighteen explanations of it, which Cornelius a Lapide reduces to seven on Matthew 12. We follow neither these nor those, which can be seen and examined in their own places. Yet since in such questions it is very useful to hear the opinions of others, first there are those who understand this sin as a sin of malice, as opposed to a sin of ignorance; a sin against the Father, as opposed to a sin of weakness against the Son. In this view, it is the sin of malice that makes it the sin against the Holy Spirit. This opinion seems to have pleased the Master of the Sentences, Book II, dist. 43, and Thomas, 2-2, q. 14; but it is rejected and refuted by Bellarmine, Book II on Penance, ch. 16. See also Sixtus of Siena, Bibliotheca, Book VI, annotation 56. This sin is held to comprise six species: despair, presumption, impenitence, obstinacy, attacking the truth once recognised, and envy of a brother's grace. On these Thomas writes, as above. Before him, Alexander of Hales, part II, q. 167, n. 3. The second opinion, of those who explain this sin as final impenitence, was Augustine's; but it is refuted by Erasmus in his Notes against Bede, pp. 17–18, by Bellarmine, and by Gomarus on Matthew 12. The third opinion explains it as sin after baptism; this was once Origen's, but it was rightly rejected by Athanasius and others. Some understand it, fourthly, of the denial of faith under persecution; fifthly, of hatred, reproach and insult against God; sixthly, of the sin of simony; seventhly, of the Pneumatomachi, who deny the Deity of the Holy Spirit. But setting aside all these, which we judge do not explain the matter, and whose refutation does not belong here, we say that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is a sin by which a person who has been sufficiently, certainly and evidently convinced of the truth of the Christian religion, and this by the grace and operation of the Holy Spirit, nevertheless at last knowingly, willingly, maliciously and with all his strength denies, attacks and blasphemes that truth of which he has been so persuaded. The matter of this sin is the truth of sacred doctrine, all of it indeed, of law and gospel, but above all of the gospel and of Christ. For no other single and specific sin seems to be unforgivable and irreconcilable to the sinner before God than that which assails the Mediator Christ and destroys the knowledge of him and faith in him. In a man who sins in this way it is required that he be enlightened, persuaded and convinced of the sacred truth sufficiently: not merely that he knows some parts of true doctrine, but not the principal ones, much less all the heads of it. And it must be certain: for whoever doubts the truth, as many among the Jews did in Christ's time, is not convinced, and his denial or opposition does not come from malice. Finally it must also be evident, so that he cannot plead the obscurity or darkness of a truth that is unknown to him.

units.la: At, dices, quomodo id fieri potest; ut quis sic contra mentem suam, illuminatam & instructam probè, peccet? quomodo id possibile, per naturam? præsertim si statuamus, voluntatem semper intellectum sequi, ab eoque determinari, neque posse ab ejus dictamine vel regulâ abire, ne in incognitum, aut malum feratur, quâ malum? Hæc quidem objectio gravissima est, contra illam sententiam de determinatione voluntatis à judicio intellectus, atque maximè ab aliis urgetur in contrarium: solvi tamen potest perquam commodè, unâ vel alterâ adhibitâ distinctione.
units.tr: But you will say: how can it happen that someone sins in this way, against his own mind, which is well enlightened and instructed? How is this possible by nature, especially if we hold that the will always follows the intellect, is determined by it, and cannot depart from its judgment or rule, lest it be carried toward the unknown or toward evil as evil? This objection is indeed very serious against that opinion which holds that the will is determined by the judgment of the intellect, and it is pressed most strongly by others on the opposite side. Yet it can be answered very conveniently by introducing one or two distinctions.

units.la: Quare notandum primò, aliud esse judicium intellectus theoreticum, aliud practicum. Theoreticum peccantibus in Spiritum S. benè constat, eoque satis superque norunt veritatem sibi patefactam, persuasamque; sed practico, quo judicatur, quid agendum, vel sequendum sibi sit, aberrant: hoc enim speciem boni malo imponit, quando determinat sequendum, quod in se theoreticè videt quidem malum, at, vel ut malitiam suam offendat homo & experiatur, ob φαινόμενον, sequendum tamen arbitratur. Deinde etiam distinguendum in judicio intellectus practico, absolutum vel comparatum. Absoluto quidem videt homo, caveri à ri à se oportere peccatum istud; at judicio comparato, circumstantiis omnibus expensis, & sui suæque malitiæ habitâ potissimum ratione, videns quamtumvis meliora, probandsque, deteriora tamen mavult sequi. Vti fur, qui in se absolute, & theoretice novit satis furtum malum esse, & sibi quoque cavendum, at lucrum respectans, hoc præfert summque commodum, & furatur. Vel judicium practicum distingue, in primum, & ultimum. Primo judicas facile aliquid non agendum, quod mutato consilio, & ex ultimâ προαιρέσει secus statuis amplectendum. Videre itaque licet, quomodo, quantumlibet in peccato adversus Spiritum S. mens peccatoris bene sit illuminata, etiam contra eam peccare nihilominus fœde homo queat. Alterum requisitum est ad hoc peccatum, præter convictionem & persuasionem de S. veritate, ut quis à Spiritu S. sit illuminatus, & convictus, forte & sentiat in se hoc effectum Spiritus S. esse, illuminantis, quamvis non sanctificantis. Designandum enim in doctrinâ hujus peccati venit, quare non contra veritatem adeo dicatur peccatum, ac quidem contra Spiritum Sanctum: quod hinc petendum. Formam peccati constituit veritatis istius, atque per Spiritum S. illuminationis abnegatio. Deinde oppugnatio, in se, & in alios. Oppugnat veritatem & ejus auctorem Spiritum Sanctum, βλασφημ, vel συκοφαντ, atque ejusdem professores fideles. Quia veritatem illam oppugnat in se, ideo & in aliis quoque: pari odio armatur in eandem veritatem quomodocunque, & contra ejus promotionem, Auctoremque ipsum. Denique accedit veritatis, & Auctoris blasphemia: non enim peccatum est simpliciter, vel peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum, sed blasphemia, unde veritas, ejusque auctor Spiritus Sanctus dirissime calumniantur, & quæ quis sentit esse divinissima, damnat tamen, clamatque esse Diabolica. Atque hæc adjuncta peccati sunt, ut homo faciat scienς contra conscientiam, tum volens, atque ex odio & malitia, & omni adeo conatu, totisque viribus. Vide sententiam, & explicationem synodi Lingonensis, de peccato in Spiritum Sanctum, anno 1404 apud Bochellum, Decret. Ecclesiae Gallicanae, lib. I. tit. IX.
units.tr: First, then, it must be noted that the judgment of the intellect is one thing when theoretical and another when practical. Those who sin against the Holy Spirit are well aware of the truth revealed to them and convinced of it, and they know it fully and more than enough in theory; but they go astray in the practical judgment, by which one decides what must be done or followed. For this judgment puts the appearance of good upon evil, when it determines that something is to be followed which one in theory sees to be evil, yet one judges it must be followed because of the apparent good [φαινόμενον], although the man feels and experiences his own malice.
