Next, the practical judgment of the intellect must also be distinguished as absolute or comparative. In an absolute judgment a man sees that he must beware of this sin; but in a comparative judgment, when all the circumstances have been weighed and above all his own malice has been taken into account, he prefers to follow the worse things, though he sees better and more approvable things. So it is with a thief, who knows absolutely and in theory that theft is evil and that he must beware of it, but who, looking to gain, prefers that and seizes the greater advantage, and steals. Or the practical judgment may be distinguished into first and last. By a first judgment you judge that something is not to be done easily; but when your purpose has changed, and by your final choice [προαιρέσει] you decide otherwise and embrace it. It is thus evident how, however well the mind of the sinner is enlightened, a man may nonetheless sin shamefully against it, even against the sin against the Holy Spirit. The second requirement for this sin, besides the conviction and persuasion of the holy truth, is that a person be enlightened and convinced by the Holy Spirit, and perhaps also feel in himself the effect of the Holy Spirit as enlightener, though not as sanctifier. For it must be shown in the doctrine of this sin why it is said to be a sin not so much against the truth as against the Holy Spirit; and this must be sought from here. The form of the sin consists in the denial of that truth and of the illumination given by the Holy Spirit. Next comes the attack, both on oneself and on others. He attacks the truth and its author, the Holy Spirit, by blaspheming [βλασφημεῖ] or slandering [συκοφαντεῖ], and likewise its faithful professors. Because he attacks that truth in himself, he does so also in others; he is armed with the same hatred against that truth in whatever way, and against its promotion and its very author. Finally there is added the blasphemy of the truth and of its author: it is not simply a sin, or a sin against the Holy Spirit, but blasphemy, by which the truth and its author, the Holy Spirit, are most bitterly slandered, and what a man feels to be most divine he nonetheless condemns and declares to be diabolical. These are the accompanying features of the sin, that a man acts knowingly against his conscience, both willingly and from hatred and malice, and with every effort and with all his strength. See the sentence and explanation of the Synod of Langres, of the year 1404, on the sin against the Holy Spirit, in Bochellus, Decret. Ecclesiae Gallicanae, lib. I, tit. IX.

units.la: Quaeritur, an ad hoc peccatum necesse sit, omnem ac totam veritatis doctrinam atque capita oppugnare, an vero satis sit, nonnulla, sed ea praecipua & maxime fundamentalia, impetere? Resp. non requiritur necessario ad hujus peccati constituendam essentiam, ut omnis veritas, & quaecunque religionis capita blasphementur; sufficit si unum, sed illud praecipuum, v. g. Christus. Ut siquidem Pharisaei peccarint, vel eorum aliqui hoc in Spiritum S. peccato, non necesse neque etiam verisimile, illos, ut Christum, sic quoque Mosem, & omnem religionis Mosaicae vel Judaicae veritatem oppugnasse: quamvis facile ad illud peccatum hoc sequatur, ut ab uno articulo ad reliquos blasphemandos pergat hominis impietas. Vide de hoc Justum Fewrbornium, Theologum Lutheranum, in singulari hujus argumenti Commentario, lib. de peccato in Spiritum S. cap. XI. Quaecunque ad hoc peccatum diximus pertinere, conjungenda, neque divelli quidpiam debet. Alioqui facile evenit, ut quis etiam optime de veritate persuasus, atque a Spiritu Sancto, eam tamen neget, qui non ideo in Spiritum Sanctum dicetur peccare: quales qui in persequutione labuntur, qualis etiam Petrus Apostolus; at defuerunt hic posteriora ad peccarum illud pertinentia: quippe quamvis negavit ille Christum, contra animum egit, neque Christum oppugnavit, vel blasphemavit, non ex malitia, pronoque vel toto animo. Contra, Paulus ἐμαινόμην ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου, ex odio quidem Christum, ejusque veritatem blasphemavit, sed defuerunt priora: non enim negavit sciens, volens, aut de veritate instructus, vel convictus.
units.tr: Question: whether for this sin it is necessary to attack the whole of the doctrine and all the heads of the truth, or whether it is enough to assail some, but those principal and most fundamental ones. Answer: it is not necessarily required, for the essence of this sin to be constituted, that every truth and all the heads of religion be blasphemed; it is enough if one is, provided it is the principal one, for example Christ. For if the Pharisees sinned, or some of them, in this sin against the Holy Spirit, it is neither necessary nor even probable that they attacked Moses, and every truth of the Mosaic or Jewish religion, just as they attacked Christ; although it easily follows from that sin that the wickedness of a man proceeds from one article to blaspheming the rest. On this see Justus Feuerborn, the Lutheran theologian, in his singular commentary on this subject, Book de peccato in Spiritum S. cap. XI. Whatever we have said belongs to this sin must be taken together, and nothing ought to be separated from it. Otherwise it easily happens that someone, though very well persuaded of the truth and enlightened by the Holy Spirit, nevertheless denies it, and yet will not for that reason be said to sin against the Holy Spirit. Such are those who fall in persecution, as also the Apostle Peter. But the later elements that belong to that sin were lacking here; for although Peter denied Christ, he acted against his own mind, and he did not attack or blaspheme Christ, nor did he do so from malice, nor with a settled or whole mind. On the other hand, Paul, breathing threats and slaughter [ἐμαινόμην ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου], out of hatred did blaspheme Christ and his truth; but the earlier elements were lacking. For he did not deny knowingly, willingly, or while instructed in or convinced of the truth.

units.la: 1. Tim. 1. 13. Antea qui fui blasphemus & persecutor & contumeliosus. lamniator; sed misericordiam consecutus sum. [?] quia ignorans feci in infidelitate. [?], non est particula ἀλλὰ[?] sed διαχρίνων[?], peccatum Pauli describens, & discernens ab aliis peccatis, etiamque ab hac in Spiritum S. blasphemia.
units.tr: "Before, I was a blasphemer, a persecutor and an insolent man; but I obtained mercy, because I acted in ignorance and unbelief" (1 Tim. 1. 13). The particle here is not ἀλλά [alla] but διακρίνων [diakrinōn], describing Paul's sin and distinguishing it from other sins, and also from this blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Quid jam quod hoc peccatum dicitur irremissibile? namdicitur non remittendum, ὡς ἀφιέμενον[?], tum ὡς ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι[?] τῷ μέλλοντι[?]. Irremissibile volunt aliqui non absolute & simpliciter intelligendum esse, sed vel quod ut plurimum & ordinarie non remittatur; vel difficulter: quod fere eodem redit; quod enim difficulter, id ut plurimum vix fieri solet: illud Bellarminus, aliique. Deinde alii putant irremissibile dici, videlicet nisi peccator istius nominatim peccati seriam egerit pœnitentiam; sic Socinus explicat in Ioann. v. sed sic fere omnia peccata dicenda erunt irremissibilia esse, non hoc peccatum solum. Existimamus autem hoc peccatum dici irremissibile, quod revera, & simpliciter nunquam à Deo remittatur alicui hoc peccati genus. Non quod impossibile Deo sit per absolutam potentiam, quod Dei vel Christi impotentia hic aliqua sit in remittendo aut expiando: nec sufficit, meo judicio, dicere peccatum hoc irremissibile esse non propter se, sed propter aliud, sc. ob finalem impoenitentiam; nam ita omnia peccata irremissibilia: sed per justitiam Dei impossibile esse hoc genus peccati alicui remitti, quia nempe de isto peccato ita constituit Deus, ne remittatur alicui, & hoc juste quidem, propter summam istius delicti atrocitatem, quod contra unicum salutis medium, & gratiam Spiritus Sancti, qui solus conversionem, fidem & salutem efficere potest, tam indigne committitur, dum is, ejusque gratia in Christo nobis revelando, procaciter contemnitur, oppugnatur, atque ex mero, & contra conscientiam, odio blasphematur. Hoc est, quod Apostolus dicit, iterum crucifigentes sibi Filium Dei & profitnentes. Heb. vi. 6. quod vero ἐξυγίως causa Christus addit, non remissum iri peccatum istud in hoc, neque in futuro seculo, neutiquam Purgatorio extruendo facere, ut quidem Papistae vulgò velint, hinc satis manifestum. 1. quia nullo modo sequitur, peccata in altero seculo remittuntur, vel non remittuntur; ergo datur, vel necesse est hic intelligere Purgatorium. 2. imò punitio huius peccati etiam secundum Papistas non potest intelligi in Purgatorio fieri, nedum remissio, quia peccatum hoc in supremo gradu mortale, non in Purgatorio, etiam secundum ipsos, sed in inferno puniendum. III. In Papistico Purgatorio dicuntur puniri, qui purgantur, & poenis debitè perpessis superiores tandem evadunt: at peccatum in Spiritum S. dicitur nunquam non puniendum; ergo non in Purgatorio.
units.tr: What of the fact that this sin is called unforgivable? For it is said not to be forgiven, that it is not remitted (ὡς ἀφιέμενον [hōs aphiemenon]), and that it is not forgiven in the age to come (ὡς ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τῷ μέλλοντι [hōs en tō aiōni tō mellonti]). Some want "unforgivable" to be understood not absolutely and simply, but to mean either that it is for the most part and ordinarily not forgiven, or that it is forgiven with difficulty, which comes to much the same thing, since what is difficult is usually for the most part hardly ever done. Bellarmine and others hold this view. Others again think it is called unforgivable, namely unless the sinner has performed a serious repentance for this particular sin by name; Socinus explains it this way on John 5. But on that reading almost all sins would have to be called unforgivable, not this one alone. In my judgment, this sin is called unforgivable because in truth and simply it is never remitted by God to anyone who commits this kind of sin. This does not mean that it is impossible for God by his absolute power, as if there were some weakness in God or Christ in forgiving or atoning; nor, in my judgment, is it enough to say that this sin is unforgivable not in itself but on account of something else, namely final impenitence, for on that reasoning every sin would be unforgivable. Rather, by the justice of God it is impossible for this kind of sin to be forgiven to anyone, because God has so decreed concerning this sin that it shall not be forgiven to anyone; and this decree is indeed just, on account of the great atrocity of this offence. It is committed so wickedly against the one means of salvation and the grace of the Holy Spirit, who alone can effect conversion, faith and salvation, while Christ's grace revealed to us is insolently despised and attacked, and, out of sheer and conscious hatred, is blasphemed. This is what the Apostle means: "crucifying again to themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt" (Heb. 6. 6). That Christ adds that this sin will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come (ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τῷ μέλλοντι [en tō aiōni tō mellonti]) is clearly not to be taken as building a Purgatory, as the Papists commonly wish, and this is sufficiently plain from the following. First, it in no way follows that sins are remitted, or not remitted, in the other age; therefore there is a Purgatory, or it must be understood here as Purgatory. Second, the punishment of this sin cannot even on the Papists' own view be understood to take place in Purgatory, much less its remission, since this sin is mortal in the highest degree and, even by their own account, is to be punished not in Purgatory but in hell. Third, in the Papist Purgatory those are said to be punished who are purged and, having duly suffered their punishments, at last rise to higher things; but the sin against the Holy Spirit is said never not to be punished; therefore it is not in Purgatory.

units.la: IV. Neque in hoc, neque in futuro seculo, non distinguit remissionem, alia ut hic, alia ut tum fiat; sed durationem non-remissionis, sive punitionem perpetuam significat: unde Vulgata, Marc. iii. 29. appellat, aeternum delictum. V. Remissio peccatorum aliqua fiat in futuro seculo; at non ideo in purgatorio: sed in judicio post resurrectionem supremo & universali. Futurum istud seculum non incipit à morte: sed à resurrectione. Luc. xx. 34, 35. filii huius seculi uxores ducunt, & nuptum dantur. hoc est, ut benè Gomarus, hoc super negotio, in Matth. xii. qui ante finem & consummationem huius seculi erunt, illi nubent; & ut Luc. xvii. 26, 27. qui verò digni habiti fuerint, ut consequantur illud seculum & resurrectionem ex mortuis, neque ducunt uxores, neque nuptum dantur. Sic Marc. x. 36. Eph. i. 21. hoc seculum, & futurum opponuntur. Hebraei dicunt עולם הבא & העולם הזה. VI. sensus phrasis simplicissimus est, nec respiciendum proprie ad saecula; quod remittetur nunquam his neque in futuro. Marc. iii. 29. Quid quod inter Papistas ipsos non defuerunt, qui hunc locum pro Purgatorio confirmando frustrà adduci viderunt: qualis fuit Petrus à Soto.
units.tr: Fourth, the phrase "neither in this age nor in the age to come" does not distinguish one remission here and another remission then; it signifies the perpetual duration of non-remission, or perpetual punishment. Hence the Vulgate, at Mark 3. 29, calls it "an eternal sin." Fifth, some remission of sins takes place in the age to come, but not therefore in purgatory; it takes place at the final and universal judgment after the resurrection. That coming age does not begin at death but at the resurrection. Luke 20. 34, 35: "The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage," that is, as Gomarus rightly says on Matthew 12, those who are before the end and consummation of this age will marry; and, as in Luke 17. 26, 27, "those who are counted worthy to obtain that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage." So too Mark 10. 30 and Eph. 1. 21 set this age and the age to come against each other. The Hebrews say olam ha-ba [עולם הבא] and ha-olam ha-zeh [העולם הזה]. Sixth, the simplest sense of the phrase is that it is not to be referred strictly to ages: the sin will never be remitted, either in this age or in the next (Mark 3. 29). Moreover, even among the Papists themselves there have been some who saw that this passage was vainly brought forward to confirm Purgatory; Peter à Soto was one of them.

units.la: Difficillima est peccati illius dignotio, quo pacto vel argumento cognoscatur. Habetur autem, vel per divinam manifestationem extraordinariò, cui fini in primâ Ecclesiâ, inter dona & charismata Spiritus S. extraordinaria, fecisse διὰ χρίστις πνευμάτων [?] multi existimant, vel etiam προφητείαν [?], 1. Cor. xii. 10. quamvis hanc proprie in alium & magis communem usum serviisse credibile. Cognitio ejus per Spiritus ordinarium & humanum judicium, habetur ex effectis, peccatis sceleribusque illud demonstrantibus: atque vel peccatori ipsi se ostendit, vel etiam aliis: illud certius est: Spiritus enim hominis, qui in ipso, novit quae hominis sunt. 1 Cor. 11. 11. At de altero judicare, num peccet in Spiritum S. id sane per quam difficile, ni impossibile: tum quia difficulter statui de animo alicujus potest, an de veritate doctrinae S. probè sit convictus; tum etiam an ex merâ malitiâ, & contra conscientiam se opponat: quod negat veritatem, atque oppugnat eam, etiam blasphemat, facilè sciri & videri atque audiri potest; sed quo animo id faciat, in quo tamen ratio hujus blasphemiae & peccati specifica quaeri debet, id quis facilè de altero dixerit? Quare omninò caute de peccatore hoc judicandum, vel potius suspendendum judicium, atque Deo istud pie resignandum. Tum etiam ideo, quia videmus judicia de hujusmodi peccatoribus nonnullis, qui pro talibus vulgo habiti, incerta valde esse. Pharisaeos, quibus Christus loquitur, vulgo hujus peccati reos faciunt: at Christi sermonem & textum potius admonitorium esse adversus hoc peccatum, quò quidem tendere illos Christus videbat, quam indicatorium peccati hujus jam reorum, si intelligamus cum Georgio Vechnero, conc. in hunc locum, Germanicè, incertum faciet illud de Pharisaeis commune judicium. Sane si contextum verborum Christi respiciamus, illud necdum voluisse Christum eos peccati istius reos esse probabile sit, praeterquam ex verbis non signanter hoc pec-
units.tr: The recognition of that sin is very difficult, and it is hard to say how or by what sign it may be known. It may be known either by extraordinary divine revelation, a gift which many think served that end in the primitive Church among the extraordinary gifts and charismata of the Holy Spirit, "the discerning of spirits" (διὰ χρίσεις πνευμάτων [dia kriseis pneumatōn]), or even by prophecy (1 Cor. 12. 10), although it is credible that prophecy served a different and more common purpose. Knowledge of it through the ordinary and human judgment comes from its effects, from sins and crimes that demonstrate it; and it shows itself either to the sinner himself or also to others. The first is more certain, for "the spirit of a man, which is in him, knows the things of a man" (1 Cor. 2. 11). But to judge of another, whether he sins against the Holy Spirit, is certainly extremely difficult if not impossible. First, because it can hardly be determined about a person's mind whether he has been properly convinced of the truth of the Holy Spirit's doctrine. Second, whether he opposes it out of pure malice and against his conscience, which is what is at stake, since the nature of this blasphemy and sin must be sought in the specific motive: that he denies the truth, attacks it, and blasphemes it can easily be known and seen and heard; but with what intention he does it, and it is this that determines the specific character of his blasphemy and sin, who could easily say that of another? Therefore one must judge about such a sinner with the greatest caution, or rather suspend judgment and devoutly leave it to God. Third, because we see that the judgments made about some such sinners, who are commonly regarded as such, are very uncertain. Many people make the Pharisees, to whom Christ speaks, guilty of this sin. But if we understand with George Wechner, in his sermon on this passage (in German), that Christ's word and text are rather a warning against this sin, toward which Christ saw that they were tending, than a declaration that they were already guilty of it, then that common judgment about the Pharisees becomes doubtful. Indeed, if we look at the context of Christ's words, it is probable that Christ did not wish them to be already guilty of this sin, apart from the mere words which do not expressly name this sin

units.la: { } peccatum Pharisæis exprobrantibus, etiam ex occasione accepta, ideo dico vobis: videlicet pro fideli admonitione, quicunque verbum dixerit contra &c. quasi dixerit hactenus gravissimè peccastis in Dei Filium, quod si pergatis, contra tam apertam veritatem, & Spiritus S. omnimodam convictionem per tam manifesta mea opera & verba, vos opponere, & addere blasphemiam; videte, ne peccetis & blasphemetis in Spiritum S., peccato adeo atroci horrendoque, ut nullo unquam tempore sit expiandum. Et, si voluisset Christus significare illos peccati istius jam reos esse, vel ibi, vel postea, ubi sæpe acriter in eos invehitur, hypocritas, cæcos, viperas appellando, incitatior credo & hic fuisset Christi adversus eos oratio. Ex adverso quamvis cum edacem, bibacem, Samaritanum, Diabolicum passim calumniati fuerint, pro illis tamen precari haud destitit, etiam in cruce, addità hac ratione, diversitatis peccati indice, Pater remitte iis, quoniam nesciunt, quid faciant: Luc. xxiii. 34. Non quod ausim affirmare, Pharisæorum nullos tum temporis in Spiritum S. peccasse, quod me utique latet, neque ego eos absolvo; sed indico duntaxat quam difficile sit illud judicare, & ex Christi sermone probari id satis certo non posse. Idem fere de Iuliano Imp., famoso isto in historiâ Ecclesiasticâ apostatâ, dixero: in Spiritum S. illum peccasse, fere omnes statuunt; sed quia (non absolvo hominem, neque ei patrocinium volo) haud facile ostendi potest, an probe convictus & persuasus de veritate religionis Christianæ fuerit, annon potius simulavit illam professionem, in gratiam Constantii Imp. cui successor destinabatur, usque dum liceret animum & religionem prodere, studiis & Scriptis Libanii Sophistæ, & præceptoris sui Maximi Philosophi semper nimium addictus, haud immerito de illius peccato, aut peccati genere judicium quis cohibeat suum. Fuit peccator gravissimus, & apostata, & blasphemus, sed non omnis blasphemia est haec quae dicitur in Spiritum Sanctum. Certè quando pater ejus Constantius sedulò caverat, ne Iulianus gentilem audiret praeceptorem, & nominatim illum non Libanium, Constantinopoli ejectum, vetabatur autem Iulianus eum accedere, Nicomediae agentem, eo quod religione gentilis esset ; nihilo tamen minus libris ejus delectabatur, illisque clanculum comportatis utebatur. Et alter ille Maximus Philosophus, quem postea Valentianus praestigiatorem necari jussit, Nicomediam, in gratiam Iuliani, convolavit, cumque apud hunc Iulianus philosophica gustasset, confestim etiam Praeceptoris religionem imitari coepit, qui eiquoque imperandi ambitionem indidit. Cujus rei fama ad Imperatorem delata, quo offensam ejus devitaret & periculum amittendi imperii Iulianus, tonsus monasticam vitam simulat, sed & clanculum philosophica exercet, manifestè vero Sacra Christianorum scripta legit, & Nicomediane ecclesiae lector constituitur. Additque, qui haec refert Socrates, histor.Eccles.lib.III.cap.1. & haec quidem propter metum facit, spem autem imperandi interea non abjicit. Quibus rite expensis, quis certò de Iuliani animo sibi persuadeat, cum de veritate religionis Christianae sufficienter ac manifestò convictum fuisse; atque postea, quum Ethnicismum palam fovere ac promovere decrevit, contra conscientiam egisse, & ex mero odio Christianismum oppugnasse, non potius illum semper à Praeceptoribus Gentilismum retinuisse, & religionem Christianam contra conscientiam & simulatè fuisse professum? Adeo dubia haec sunt, quae alterius animum, nostrumque de eo judicium concernunt. Interim valde blasphemum fuisse hominem, eumque peccandi modum prope ad blasphemiam in Spiritum S. accedere, nemo negarit: praecipue qui illa consideret, quae refert Theodoretus hist.lib.III.cap.xxv. illum in mortis articulo, sagitta mirabiliter transfossum, dixisse; sed ex relatione aliorum habet: Iulianum quidem vulvulnere accepto, implesse manum suam sanguine, & sparso illo in aera dixisse, vicisti Galilæe, simulque & vi-ctoriam confessum & maledictum animam esse, ita eras astonitus.
units.tr: { } (the sin being thrown in the Pharisees' faces), and which he said as a consequence: "Therefore I say to you," namely as a faithful warning: "whoever speaks a word against" etc., as if to say: "Hitherto you have sinned most gravely against the Son of God; but if you go on, setting yourselves against such plain truth and the Holy Spirit's complete conviction through my works and words so manifest, and adding blasphemy, take heed lest you sin and blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, a sin so atrocious and horrible that it can never at any time be expiated." And if Christ had meant to say that they were already guilty of this sin, either there or afterwards, where he often inveighs fiercely against them, calling them hypocrites, blind, and vipers, then, I believe, his speech against them here would have been more vehement. On the other hand, although they slandered him as a glutton, a drunkard, a Samaritan, and a devil everywhere, he did not cease to pray for them, even on the cross, adding this reason, which marks the difference of their sin: "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23. 34). I do not dare to affirm that none of the Pharisees at that time sinned against the Holy Spirit, which indeed is hidden from me, nor do I absolve them; but I only point out how difficult it is to judge this, and that it cannot be proved with sufficient certainty from Christ's words. I would say much the same of Julian the Emperor, that notorious apostate in ecclesiastical history: almost everyone holds that he sinned against the Holy Spirit. But since it cannot easily be shown (I do not absolve the man, nor do I wish to defend him) whether he was duly convicted and persuaded of the truth of the Christian religion, or whether he rather feigned that profession in order to win the favour of the Emperor Constantius, for whose successor he was destined, until he could betray his mind and religion, being always far too devoted to the studies and writings of the sophist Libanius and of his tutor, the philosopher Maximus, no one can justly restrain his judgment about the nature of his sin or the kind of sin it was. He was a most grievous sinner, an apostate and a blasphemer, but not every blasphemy is that which is called blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Certainly, when his father Constantius had carefully taken care that Julian should not hear a pagan tutor, and had expressly forbidden him to approach Libanius, who had been expelled from Constantinople, "Julian, while living at Nicomedia, was forbidden to approach him, because he was a pagan in religion; nevertheless he delighted in his books and used them, having got them secretly." And that other philosopher, Maximus, whom Valens later ordered to be put to death as a charlatan, flew to Nicomedia for Julian's sake; and "when Julian had there tasted philosophy under him, he at once began to imitate the religion of his teacher, who also instilled in him the ambition to rule." When news of this reached the Emperor, Julian, to avoid his displeasure and the danger of losing the empire, "pretended a monastic life with a tonsure," but secretly practised philosophy, and openly read the sacred writings of the Christians, and was appointed reader in the church at Nicomedia. Socrates, who reports this (Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 1), adds that he did this out of fear, but meanwhile did not abandon hope of ruling. Having duly weighed these things, who can be certain of Julian's mind, since he was sufficiently and manifestly convicted of the truth of the Christian religion, and afterwards, when he decided to openly foster and promote paganism, acted against his conscience and attacked Christianity out of pure hatred? Is it not rather more likely that he had always retained paganism from his pagan teachers, and had professed the Christian religion against his conscience and pretending? So doubtful are these matters, which concern the mind of another and our judgment of him. Meanwhile, no one will deny that the man was very blasphemous, and that his manner of sinning came close to blasphemy against the Holy Spirit; especially if one considers what Theodoret reports in his history (book 3, chapter 25): that when he was at the point of death, miraculously pierced through by an arrow, he said (but Theodoret has it from the report of others) that "Julian, having received the wound in his liver, filled his hand with blood and, scattering it into the air, said: 'You have conquered, Galilean,'" and that at the same time he confessed defeat and that his cursed soul was astonished at this.

units.la: Denique est & alius, cujus recentior historia, Franciscus Spira, à quo peccatum in Spiritum S. commissum, in veritatis Evangelicæ, coram nefando isthoc Johanne Casâ, Papæ Venetiis legato, annis abhinc centum, abnegatione, vulgò existimant: sed temerè meo quidem judicio, qui hunc, ex iis quæ de eo constant ex historiis & relationibus Basileæ editis Anno 1550. in epistolis Caelii S. Curionis, Grybaldi, Calvini, Henr. Scoti, Geloji, Borrhai, Vergerii Apologiâ, Sleydano, lib. xxi. atque aliis, ad hoc crimine vindicandum censeo. Negavit veritatem, non tamen illam oppugnavit, nedum quod blasphemarit; & quodcunque egit, contra conscientiam quidem, non autem ex malitiâ odioque, sed ex infirmitate, metu honoris, opumque amittendarum sibi & familiæ, commisit: sed de eo etiam alio loco diximus, imo neque enim in censu reproborum collocavero, ob profundos illos dolores, pœnitentiam & suspiria, atque ad gratiam anhelantes emicantesque, inter horrendas angustias & tentationes, ejectiones. Quomodo etiam de eo, & benignius judicant, Musculus, in loc. Comm. de desperatione; Voetius, de desert. Spiritual. & alii. Gomarus item à peccato in Spiritum S. commisso eum absolvit; non item à desperatione.
units.tr: Finally there is another case, the more recent history of Francis Spira. People commonly suppose that he committed the sin against the Holy Spirit when, in Venice, a century ago, he renounced the truth of the Gospel before that wicked man Giovanni della Casa, the Pope's legate. In my judgment, however, that is a rash view. I think he should be cleared of this crime, judging from what is established about him in the histories and accounts published at Basel in 1550, in the letters of Caelius Secundus Curio, Grynaeus, Calvin, Henry Scott, Gelous, Borrhaus, in Vergerius's Apology, in Sleidan's twenty-first book, and in other sources. He denied the truth but did not attack it, much less blaspheme; and whatever he did, he did against his conscience, yet not from malice or hatred but from weakness, fear of dishonour, and fear of losing his wealth and family. I have said more about him elsewhere. I would not even count him among the reprobate, on account of those deep sorrows, repentance and sighs, and his longing and striving for grace amid the dreadful anguish and temptations he suffered. Musculus, in his Commonplace on despair, and Voetius, in his work on spiritual desertion, and others also judge him more kindly. Gomarus likewise absolved him of the sin committed against the Holy Spirit, though not of despair.

units.la: De peccato Angelorum quaeritur, an fuerit peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum? Formaliter secundum omnia membra idem hoc peccatum fuisse, & quidem contra Christum, qui illis se revelatus, ut futurus mediator, cui unico accepta ferenda esset omnis Angelorum hominumque beatitudo &c. & cui se noluerint Angeli submittere, ut nonnulli sentiunt, neutiquam dicendum: verum peccatum Angelorum huic in Sp.S. criminì analogum, & in multis similis fuisse, quod spe-ctat état apostasiam, & blasphemiam, contra manifestam veritatem, atque ex odio seu malitia, mtius asseras. Unde & nomen retinuerunt, ut διάβολοι dicantur, & prima Diaboli tentatio, quâ tum homines aggressus, tum Christum, ad blasphemiam fuit, in Deum: adeoque illorum peccatum, supra hominum, fuit irremissibile. Hæc de illo peccato obiter diximus, cujus cognoscendi difficultate Deus nos exercere voluit, cum in omnibus Scripturis Sanctis forte nulla major, nulla dissicilior invenietur, haud sine causâ loquitur Augustinus serm. xi. de Verbis Domini. Quare etiam, in sermonibus ad populum, quæstionis hujus difficultatem & molestiam se vitare solitum, ibidem testatur. Erasmus inter loca in Euangelio inexplicabilia, suâ quidem sententiâ, & illum habuit de peccato in Spiritum Sanctum. Quod censuram Natalis Bedæ non effugit. Socinus, in Notis ad Dialogum, de Iustificatione, ubi hujus Auctor dixerat, Quia præsens salutis tempus non solum contemnunt, sed & agnitæ veritati contradicunt, quod est peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum, apponit, præstat hæc verba non addere. Nam enim adhuc controversum est quid sit peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum. Unde quæ ejus tum temporis super hoc sententia fuerit, colligas.
units.tr: It is asked whether the sin of the angels was a sin against the Holy Spirit. It must by no means be said that it was formally the same sin in all its parts, and indeed against Christ, who was revealed to them as the future mediator, to whom alone all the blessedness of angels and men was to be attributed, and to whom, as some think, the angels refused to submit. Rather, the sin of the angels was analogous to this sin against the Spirit and in many respects similar: it concerned apostasy and blasphemy against the plain truth, and arose from hatred or malice, as I shall maintain. Hence they keep the name, being called devils (διάβολοι), and their first temptation, by which they attacked both men and Christ, was blasphemy against God. Therefore their sin, beyond that of men, was unforgivable. I have touched on this sin only in passing. God wished us to be exercised by the difficulty of understanding it, since perhaps no sin is greater or more difficult to be found in all the Holy Scriptures. Augustine, in his eleventh sermon on the Words of the Lord, rightly says so. For this reason he testifies, in the same place, that in sermons to the people he was accustomed to avoid the difficulty and troublesomeness of this question. Erasmus, among the passages of the Gospel he thought inexplicable, certainly included this one, the sin against the Holy Spirit, in his own opinion. This did not escape the censure of Natalis Beda. Socinus, in his Notes on the Dialogue on Justification, where its author had said, "Because they not only despise the present time of salvation but also contradict the truth once recognised, which is the sin against the Holy Spirit," adds: "It is better not to add these words, for it is still disputed what the sin against the Holy Spirit is." From this you may gather what his opinion on the matter was at that time.

units.la: Atque hæc de erroribus, & errorum variis modis, ac gradibus; de Schismate, Hæresi, Apostasiâ, deque supremo erroris crimine, Peccato in Spiritum S. Pugnant hi omnes adversus unicam veritatem, quæque ipsam tenet, religionem, denique & quæ hanc, Ecclesiam. Nos ex adverso illis fortiter obsistere, & repugnare debemus, armis videlicet Theologicis, hoc est, disputando, & convincendo. Atque uti in bello spectatur fortitudo, & alacritas, ita in hoc conflictu, ubi sunt militiæ Domini, sanctus pro Dei causâ ardor, & in contendendo dexteritas, ac vis. Hæc à studiis est, quibus primùm controversias discimus, & tum quid Adversarii sentiunt, aut pro se adferunt, tum quibus im-pupugnandi & deiiciendi sint armis, sive argumentis. Quem in finem ea Theologiae pars facit, quam elenchticam nominamus, seu Controversiarum.
units.tr: So much for errors, and the various kinds and degrees of error: on schism, heresy, apostasy, and the supreme crime of error, the sin against the Holy Spirit. All these fight against the one truth, against the religion that holds to it, and finally against the Church that is its home. On our side we must resist them vigorously and oppose them, with theological weapons, that is, by disputing and convincing. As in war courage and eagerness are looked for, so in this conflict, where the soldiers of the Lord are engaged, we need holy zeal for God's cause, skill in contending, and force. This belongs to the study by which we first learn the controversies, then what our adversaries think or bring forward for themselves, and then with what arms, that is, with what arguments, they are to be attacked and overthrown. To this end serves that part of theology which we call elenctic, or controversial.

units.la: Controversia dupliciter sumitur, vel pro re & materia quaestionis; vel pro ipsa, quae super illa movetur, disputatione: hinc dicimus, statum controversiae; & controversiam movere: quorum illud materiam spectat controversam; hoc, disputationis actionem. Vti apud Graecos ζήτημα, & ζήτησις, vel συζήτησις (συζητεῖν, in Novo Testamento aliquoties) ἀμφισβήτημα, & ἀμφισβήτησις. Apud Quintilianum, Institut. Orator. lib. III. cap. x. videbis discrimen inter ζήτημα, ἀπορον χρινόμενον.
units.tr: The word controversy is used in two ways: either for the thing and matter of the question, or for the disputation itself which is stirred up over it. Hence we speak of the state of the controversy and of raising a controversy. The former concerns the disputed matter; the latter, the act of disputing. So among the Greeks there are ζήτημα [zētēma] and ζήτησις [zētēsis], or συζήτησις [syzētēsis] (the verb συζητεῖν [syzētein] occurs several times in the New Testament), and ἀμφισβήτημα [amphisbētēma] and ἀμφισβήτησις [amphisbētēsis]. In Quintilian's Institutes of Oratory, Book III, chapter x, you will see the difference between ζήτημα [zētēma] and what is called ἄπορον κρινόμενον [aporon krinomenon].

units.la: Controversiam alius est qui movet; alius, qui motam sustinet, & repellit. Illud primo attendere omni curâ oportet, quis, & quare, & quomodo controversiam moveat. Nam talis potest esse Auctor, qui contemni potius, quam ut serio ei quis se opponat, merebitur. Et vel nulla, vel levis forte, quae eum impellit, causa: quod si gravis aliqua, justa hinc oritur disputatio. Sed quis, qualisve sit, & quo animo in campum prodeat, modus quo utitur, tum in re, quam agit, tum erga personas, quibus se objicit, faciet manifestum. Sunt, quos sola eaque pervicax contendendi libido in arenam protrahit, quorum inquies animus primum & jugiter ipsos vexat, inde alios: quod hic quidem eo perniciosius, quo conscientias hominum, & religionem turbare, res est pessimi facinoris & exempli. Atque hinc immensa quaestionum undiquaque seges, non obleta, sed indagata, & multa ab ipsis vi protracta. Ne nihil sc. agerent homines, in res inquisitivae runt valde futiles, non in Scholis Litteratorum tantum, uti, quem numerum remigum Ulisses habuerit; prior scriptane sit Ilias, an Odyssea; tum, an ejusdem Auctoris; uti haec Senecâ false ridet: vel qualibus Grammaticos suos passim vexasse Tiberium Imp. scribit Suetonius. us, quae mater Hecubae; quod Achilli nomen inter Virgines fuerit, quid Sirenes cantare solitae? sed & in Scholis quoque Theologorum hujusmodi: ubi quanta curiositate Scholastici, qui vulgò appellantur, se immiserint in quaestiones multùm inutiles, audaces, ἀντιζηλωτικὰς, omnibus notum. Inde illae, quas Apostolus nominat βεβήλους κενοφωνίας, 1. Tim. VI. 20. & ejusdem capitis versu 4. qui languent περὶ ζητήσεις & λογομαχίας; quae Scholasticae Theologiae haud immeritò adaptat Nicolaus Clemanges. Scripsit eximium de Quaestionibus opusculum, Iulius Rugerius, Pronotarius, uti appellant, Apostolicus, & Abbas Lamularum, ubi, an, & quales quaestiones movere Theologo liceat, & quae stultae, quae utiles censendae, exponit.
units.tr: One person is the one who raises a controversy; another is the one who takes up the matter once raised and beats it back. First of all we must attend with every care to who raises the controversy, why, and in what manner. For there may be an author who deserves to be despised rather than seriously opposed. Perhaps the cause that impels him is nothing, or slight. If it is some serious cause, a just disputation arises from it. But what sort of man he is, and with what purpose he comes into the field, will be made clear by the method he uses, both in the matter he treats and towards the persons he attacks. There are some whom a sole and stubborn love of contention drags into the arena. Their restless spirit troubles first themselves and constantly, and then others. This is all the more pernicious, since to disturb men's consciences and religion is a matter of the worst crime and example. From this comes an immense crop of questions on every side, not reaped but dug up, and many of them forced out by violence. So that men might not be idle, they inquired into matters that were very trivial, not only in the schools of the learned, such as how many oarsmen Ulysses had, whether the Iliad or the Odyssey was written first, and whether both had the same author, which Seneca mocks as false; or what kind of grammarians the Emperor Tiberius was said by Suetonius to have harassed on all sides; or who was the mother of Hecuba; what name Achilles bore among the maidens; what the Sirens were accustomed to sing. Such questions were also raised in the schools of the theologians, where everyone knows how eagerly the so-called Schoolmen plunged into very useless, bold, and contentious questions (ἀντιζηλωτικάς [antizēlōtikas]). From this come those profane babblings (βεβήλους κενοφωνίας [bebēlous kenophōnias]) which the Apostle names in 1 Timothy 6:20, and those who, in verse 4 of the same chapter, dote about questions and strifes of words (περὶ ζητήσεις καὶ λογομαχίας [peri zētēseis kai logomachias]). Nicolas Clemangis fittingly applies these words to Scholastic theology. Julius Rugerius, protonotary, as they call him, of the Apostolic See, and Abbot of Lamulae, wrote an excellent little work on questions, in which he sets out whether and what questions a theologian may raise, and which are to be judged foolish and which useful.

units.la: Etiam in Scholis Theologorum nimis frequens concertatio de verbis, λογομαχία, quasi nil rerum, de quo quaeratur, amplius superfit. Quos Critolaus Phaselites, apud Clementem, Stromat. lib. II. non inepte vocavit ὀνομαχοτρίβας, id est, qui pugnant de nominibus. Hujusmodi innumera ubique, & magnâ animorum contentione agitantur, quippe contendendi studioso peraeque est, de re, an de umbrâ, modò disputetur. Atque hi quaestionem semper, ubi aliqua forte videtur, in plurimas extendunt, & multiplicant. Quod nuspiam sit majori praejudicio, adeo in controversiis fidei, inter diversarum (ut sic dicam) religionum sectas. Vbi alii ex ἀπειρίας & defectu judicii, alii ex malitiâ, illas multiplicant, quo ostendant scilicet, haud sine causâ bellum concitari, vel ut divortium, quod non invenitur, ipsi faciant, aut promoveant, extendantque. Pessimi prosectò, quos cum sua professio ad quaestiones minuendas vel tollendas movere oportebat, animo potius & rixandi cupiditati indulgentes, sepem quam communire debebant, discindunt, ac perrumpunt; & hiatum non obstruunt, sed dilatant. Quales sunt, qui dum aliis doctrinam attribuunt ab ipsorum opinione remotam, tam, unde & controversiam faciunt, & ex consequentiis, suo arbitrio formatis, quaestiones iterum alias. Id quod nonnullis Lutheranorum, adversum Nostros disputantibus, nimis quam familiare. Unde tam & tanta vehementia rixosi homines disputant, clamant, tumultuantur, nihil attendentes, nec se, nec alios, neque quod agunt argumentum, omnia potius commovent & commiscent, perfringuntque, quam ut vel desistant, vel defervescant; unde illorum χολη nil videtur aliud, quam quod de Euclidis, Diogenes, χολη; eorumque ἀπαθεία, quod idem de Platonis, κατάληψις. Quare magni refert in disputatione, praeterquam ad rem, attendere etiam ad disputantis animum, quo animo sua agat, quid respiciat, quo collimet: Atque hinc saepe apparebit, unam thesin ab illo teneri, non adeo propter se, ac propter aliam.
units.tr: In the schools of the theologians too there is too frequent a contest about words (λογομαχία [logomachia]), as if nothing of the matter in question remained. Critolaus of Phaselis, in Clement's Stromata Book II, not unfittingly called such men onomachotribas (ὀνομαχοτρίβας), that is, those who fight about names. Such contests occur everywhere in countless numbers and with great heat of spirit, since to the man who loves contention it makes no difference whether the dispute is about a thing or about a shadow, so long as there is a dispute. And these men always extend and multiply a question wherever one seems to appear. This is nowhere done with greater prejudice than in the controversies of faith between the sects of the different religions, so to speak. There, some multiply the questions out of inexperience and lack of judgment, others out of malice, so as to show that the war is not fought without cause, or to create or promote and enlarge a divide that does not exist. Surely the worst are those who, whose profession should have moved them to diminish or remove questions, indulge instead their own spirit and desire for quarrelling. They tear and break through the hedge they ought to have fortified, and they widen the gap instead of closing it. Such are those who, while attributing to others a doctrine far from their own opinion, thereby both create the controversy and, from consequences formed at their own pleasure, raise yet other questions. This is all too familiar to some of the Lutherans who dispute against us. Hence contentious men dispute with such vehemence and such noise, shout and riot, paying no attention to themselves, to others, or to the argument they are handling. They stir up and mix everything, and break through everything, rather than either stopping or cooling down. So their bile seems to be nothing other than what Diogenes said of Euclid's bile (χολή [chole]), and their lack of feeling is what the same man said of Plato's apatheia (ἀπάθεια [apatheia])... Therefore in disputation it matters greatly, beyond attending to the point at issue, to attend also to the disputant's mind: with what intention he acts, what he has in view, what he aims at. From this it will often become clear that someone holds one thesis not so much for its own sake as for the sake of another.

units.la: Unde discrimen controversiarum sequitur; in primarias, & secundarias, vel principales, & consequentes, quae ex praecedentibus oriuntur. Verbi gratia, in controversiis Arminianis, prima fuit de negotio praedestinationis: de apostasia Sanctorum dubitanter primo, dein assertive docuerunt, nempe ubi senserunt, ex prioribus de praedestinatione thesibus, prout eam explicabant, sequi tum alteram opinionem circa vires liberi arbitrii, tum illam de apostasia, Arminio primum non ita pervisa. Sic quoque apud Papistas, praecipua contentio est de authoritate Ecclesiae, vid. Romanae, suae, neque enim alio velint facere quodcunque de Ecclesia tantopere disputant; & deinde de authoritate & potestate Romani Pontificis: hinc, si examines, constabit omnia fere Theologiae ipsorum capita derivari. Quae multum refert in ipsa disputatione nosse, apud Adversarios quid ex quo sequatur, & qua facturā isthic omnia nascantur.
units.tr: Hence follows the distinction between controversies: some are primary, or principal, and others secondary, or consequent, arising from the earlier ones. For example, in the Arminian controversies the first question concerned the matter of predestination. They taught concerning the apostasy of the saints at first with hesitation and only afterwards assertively, namely when they judged that from their earlier theses on predestination, as they explained it, there followed both the other opinion about the powers of free will and that about apostasy, which Arminius had not at first fully foreseen. So too among the Papists the chief contention concerns the authority of the Church, that is, of their own Roman Church (for they do not wish to make anything else of the Church, though they dispute so much about it), and then concerning the authority and power of the Roman Pontiff. If you examine this, it will be clear that nearly all the heads of their theology derive from these. In the disputation itself it is very important to know what follows from what among the opponents, and from what source all their claims spring.

units.la: Deinde ex illis sequitur aliud hic etiam discrimen observandum, inter controversiam, & ejus momentum: illic qualitas, sic controversiæ quantitas attenditur. Nam prout grave aut leve est momentum, ita controversia æstimatur, & vel incitanda est, vel remittenda. Multi solam spectant controversiam, sæpeque (quod dicitur) factus movent in simpulo, dum vix tanti res erat, ut in contentionem veniret, fortassis non in tantam. Pro veritate ut respondeatur, ipsa exigit; sed quantum respondéri debeat, ex ejus dijudicandum momento; præsertim quando veritati vindicandæ jam factum satis videri queat, & observari ultra debet, ne à charitate latius, quam à veritate, discedatur. Momentum controversiæ alii elevant nimis, alii plus justo aggravant. Magna requiritur prudentia, nec hic temere, vel, aliter quam oportet, judicemus. Optimum de controversiæ momento examen instituitur ad fundamentum fidei, quatenus ei accedit, vel derogat; ad vim & praxim pietatis, prout eam vel promovet, vel evertit; ad communionem Ecclesiæ, quid hæc patiatur; denique ad statum & conditionem hominum, quatenus ea diversa est, aliique quos Apostolus infantes & carnales appellat; spirituales, adulti, perfecti alii. 1. Cor. 111. 1. Ephes. IV. 13. Heb. V. 13.14, ista omnia respicere oportet cum, qui de momento ventilandæ controversiæ statuat.
units.tr: From these distinctions there follows another point to be observed here, between a controversy and its importance: the one is judged by its quality, the other by its quantity. For according as the importance is great or small, so the controversy is valued, and it must either be pressed or let go. Many look only at the controversy itself, and often (as the saying goes) they make a storm in a teacup, when the matter was scarcely worth coming to contention, and perhaps not to such a degree. The truth itself demands that it be answered; but how fully it ought to be answered must be judged from its importance, especially when it can seem that enough has already been done to vindicate the truth, and care must be taken not to depart further from charity than from truth. Some raise the importance of a controversy too high, others weigh it down more than is just. Great prudence is required, and we must not judge rashly or otherwise than we ought. The best examination of a controversy's importance is made with reference to the foundation of faith, insofar as it adds to or detracts from it; to the force and practice of piety, insofar as it promotes or overturns it; to the communion of the Church, and what this suffers; and finally to the state and condition of men, insofar as it differs, and to those whom the Apostle calls infants and carnal, and others who are spiritual, adult, or perfect (1 Cor. 3:1; Eph. 4:13; Heb. 5:13, 14). All these things must be kept in view by anyone who decides on the importance of a controversy to be debated.

units.la: Præterea & alia etiam respondturo ad motam controversiam tenenda, ut, quis respondeat; neque enim hoc quorumcunque, vel sibi assumere, vel ut ipsis concedatur: tum & quando respondeatur. Est in disputationibus, ut in rebus aliis, permultum situm in bene captanda temporis opportunitate, quam qui omittit, ut non tum respondeat quando res agitatur, & hominum expectatio responsionem efflagitat, &c. in eximii usus negotio, insuper ubi ad respondendum lacessitur & provocatur, æque rei negligens habendus est ac sui, si post transactam tempestatem & fervorem contentionis idem iterum recoquat argumentum, & post bellum aciem restaurat, & nec rei quid adeo necessariæ, neque que id suo tempore, proferat. Aliud est, ubi nova provocatio, & rei momentum, prælium perennant. Sed ferè quemadmodum in ludis puerilibus videmus, per totum annum habere singulos suas periodos, extra quas nemo illos multum æstimat vel sectatur, ita & controversiarum nonnullarum in Scholis sua sunt tempora, quibus maxime florent.
units.tr: Moreover, the one who is about to reply to a controversy that has been raised must also consider other matters, such as who should reply; for this is not something anyone may claim for himself or have conceded to him, and also when a reply should be made. In disputations, as in other affairs, much depends on seizing the right moment, and the one who misses it, by replying not when the matter is being discussed and people's expectation calls for an answer, etc., in a business of the greatest use, and moreover when he is challenged and provoked to reply, is to be regarded as no less careless of the matter than of himself, if after the storm and heat of the contention is past he stirs up the same argument again and restores his battle line after the war is over, and brings forward something not so necessary, nor at its proper time. It is another matter when a new challenge and the importance of the question keep the fight alive. But, just as we see in children's games that each has its own seasons during the year, outside of which nobody values or pursues them much, so too some controversies in the schools have their own times, when they flourish most.

units.la: Denique & diligenter observandum, quomodo in disputatione respondeas, quo animo, animique moderatione, aut servore, & quam diu: tum ut discrimines rem, & personam, & quo pacto utrumque excipias. ἀμφισβητεῖν μὲν, ὑμεῖς δ' ἐμοί, inquit Plato, in Protagorâ: quamvis difficulter se contineat animus inter disputandum, quin in contentionem & rixas facile erumpat. Sed viri sapientis est se temperare, suique nunquam non esse compotem, tum ut mens judicio semper polleat, promptaque sit in eruendâ veritate; tum ut huic sua constet apud omnes reverentia & dignitas, quæ inter jurgia vehementer concutitur, & tantum non amittitur. Præterquam quod aliis etiam per strepitum pulvis offunditur, ut à studio & indagine veritatis abstrahantur, ad tumultum potius audiendum, quam veritatis necessariæ disquisitionem.
units.tr: Finally, one must also observe carefully how you reply in a disputation: with what spirit, with what restraint or heat of mind, and for how long; and also that you distinguish the matter from the person and know how to receive each. "You dispute, but I [...]," says Plato in the Protagoras [ἀμφισβητεῖν μὲν, ὑμεῖς δ' ἐμοί]. Although the mind can hardly restrain itself during disputation, and easily breaks out into strife and quarrels, it is the mark of a wise man to control himself and never to lose possession of himself, so that his mind always excels in judgment and is ready for bringing out the truth, and so that his reverence and dignity, which among wranglings are violently shaken and almost lost, remain constant before everyone. Besides, dust is thrown into the eyes of others by the noise, so that they are drawn away from the zeal and search for truth, to listen to a tumult rather than to the necessary inquiry into the truth.

units.la: Scripsit Erasmus, in epistolarum initio, ad Petrum Barbirium, anno MDXXI. Mihi sane adeo est invisa discordia, ut veritas etiam displiceat seditiosa. Zuinglius, in Comment. de verâ & falsâ relig. Tam mihi infensæ sunt contentiones illæ, quæ citra fratrum offensionem vulgari sequuntur, præsertim de iis rebus, quæ rem Christianam non produnt, ut nullum videam nocentius venenum subdi posse adolescenti Christo, quam contentionem. Oecolampadius, in præfatione libelli sui anno MDXXV, de genuina verborum Domini, Hoc est corpus meum, expositione, ad Doctores Suevicos: error condonari potest, inquit, modo fides adsit in Christum. Discordiam, neque si sanguinem fundamus, expiabimus.
units.tr: Erasmus wrote at the beginning of his letters, to Petrus Barbirius, in the year 1521: Discord is so hateful to me that even a seditious truth displeases me. Zwingli, in his commentary on the true and false religion: Those contentions which commonly follow without offence to the brethren, especially about those things which do not betray the Christian cause, are so hateful to me that I see no more harmful poison that can be given to a young Christian than contention. Oecolampadius, in the preface of his little book of 1525, on the genuine exposition of the Lord's words, "This is my body," addressed to the Swabian teachers: An error, he says, can be pardoned, provided faith in Christ is present. Discord, not even if we shed our blood, will we expiate.

units.la: Disputatio omnis fit vel voce, vel scriptò: vel privatim, vel publicè. Publica quae coram inter partes instituitur, plurimùm potest in exordio controversiae, quando primum nascitur; vel ubi singularis aliqua se offert occasio, & spes fructus per illam consequendi non vulgaris: caeteroquin ex solâ animi quâdam generositate illam inire, vel contendendi (ut ferè fit) studio, id quanto plus rararum, eo minùs usus habet ac commodi. Cujusmodi Colloquiis verissimè adscribas luculentum judicium, quod olim dedit Petrus Mosellanus de disputatione Lipsicâ, a.cIↄ Iↄ x i x. habitâ inter Eccium & Carolostadium, in epistolâ ad Bilibaldum Pirckamerum, quam ex bibliothecâ Pirckameri exhibet in Annalibus Reformationis, ad annum jam nominatum, Abrahamus Scultetus: Mihi (inquit) hoc disputandi genus theatricum numquam visum est mansuetissimâ Christi doctrinâ dignum. Nec adduci possum, ut credam: Spiritum Sanctum, pacis authorem, ad ejusmodi pugnas unquam se demittere. Christiane Theologiae veritas citius impetratur orando, quàm invenitur disceptando. Atque inde existimo, in talibus Colloquiis, post Deum, & nominis divini invocationem, (cui primae semper partes ante actionem omnem tribuendae: quod egregiè à Nostris, cum magno Adversariorum pudore observatum fuit in Colloquio Poissiaceno) prius quam ad rem, ipsos Actores descendere debere in se ipsos, & bene se examinare, illudque polliceri, quod depositò omni contendendi vincendique studio, nil propriis daturi sint affectibus, sed ita se intentos fore veritati, ut à quâ parte illa deprehensa fuerit, etiam si ab adversâ, tam lubentes manus daturi & sequuturi eam sint, quam si essent victuri, atque omninò componendae, quantum fieri potest, controversiae, animisque, operam se daturos; ad solam Dei gloriam, & Ecclesiae aedificationem. Unde Zuinglius, in epist. ad Matthaeum Alberam Rutlingensem ministrum, (est operum ejus Tom. II.) sententiam de Coena Domini expositurus, sic praefari non veretur: Deum ergo Opt. Max. precor, ut vias nostras dirigat, ac siquibi similis Bileamo in morem veritati pertinaciter obluctaturi, Angelum suum opponat, qui machaera sue minus hunc asinum (insciitiam & audaciam dico nostram, si saltem ex audacia gloriaeque cupiditate quicquam nobis hic agitur) sic ad maceriam affligat, ut fractum pedem, hoc est impurum illotumque carnis sensum auferamus, ne ultra blasphememus nomen Domini Dei nostri. Modeste & pie, ut qui ostendit se memorem suae imbecillitatis, & Deum verens; tum disputaturum debere omnino a se amovere omnem arrogantiam & φιλαυτίαν. Secus, quid attinet disputare, & concitare molestiam, si quis in principio moneat, quemadmodum Ioachimus Westphalus in Colloquio cum Martino Micronio anno clɔ lc lɪv. d. III. Martii: Non quidem nostri, sed vestri duntaxat causa disputabimus: Summa enim de nostra (in quiebat) doctrina certa. Ex quali colloquio, vel hominum genere frustra tibi aliquem fructum pollicearis; quo imo in deterius omnia abeunt, & ruptúram faciunt longè quam prius erat immaniorem.
units.tr: Every disputation takes place either by word of mouth or in writing, either privately or publicly. A public disputation held face to face between the parties is most effective at the beginning of a controversy, when it first arises, or where some special occasion presents itself and there is hope of a fruit from it that is not ordinary. Otherwise, if one enters upon it from mere generosity of spirit, or from the eagerness to contend (as usually happens), the rarer this is, the less use and advantage it has. To such colloquies you may most truly ascribe the excellent judgment which Petrus Mosellanus gave of the Leipzig disputation held in 1519 between Eck and Carlstadt, in a letter to Bilibald Pirckheimer, which Abraham Scultetus sets out in his Annals of the Reformation for the year just named, from Pirckheimer's library: To me, he says, this theatrical kind of disputing has never seemed worthy of the most gentle doctrine of Christ. Nor can I be persuaded to believe that the Holy Spirit, the author of peace, ever lowers himself to such battles. The truth of Christian theology is obtained more quickly by praying than it is found by disputing. And from this I think that in such colloquies, after God and the invocation of the divine name (to which the first place must always be given before any action, as our people observed well, to the great shame of their opponents, at the Colloquy of Poissy), before they come to the matter itself, the very participants ought to descend into themselves and examine themselves well, and promise this: that, having laid aside all zeal for contending and conquering, they will concede nothing to their own passions, but will be so intent on the truth that, from whichever side it is discovered, even if it is the opposing side, they will as willingly give their hands to it and follow it as if they were going to win, and that they will labour, as far as possible, to settle the controversy altogether and to calm their minds, solely for the glory of God and the edification of the Church. Hence Zwingli, in his letter to Matthaeus Alber, minister at Reutlingen (it is in Volume II of his works), when about to set out his opinion on the Lord's Supper, does not hesitate to preface it thus: I therefore pray to God, most good and most great, that he may direct our ways, and if anywhere, like Balaam, someone stubbornly struggles against the truth, that he may set his angel against him, who with his sword may so beat down this ass (I mean our ignorance and boldness, if indeed anything is being done here from boldness and a desire for glory) against the wall, that we may take away the broken foot, that is, the impure and unwashed sense of the flesh, lest we blaspheme any more the name of the Lord our God. He speaks modestly and piously, as one who shows that he remembers his own weakness and fears God; and he says that anyone who is about to dispute must altogether put away from himself all arrogance and [φιλαυτίαν] self-love. Otherwise, what is the point of disputing and stirring up trouble, if someone at the outset declares, as Joachim Westphal did in his colloquy with Martin Micron on 3 March 1554: We will dispute not for our own sake but only for yours; for the sum of our doctrine is certain. From such a colloquy, or from such a kind of men, you may promise yourself no fruit at all; rather everything goes from bad to worse and produces a breach much more savage than it was before.

units.la: Sed ante omnia cave, ne imparatus unquam & non bene instructus munitusque disputationem incipias, ne vitus magnum scandalum existas alteri, & confirmati erroris causa. Quod Augustino ante conversionem saepe obtigisse, ipse serio postmodum doluit. lib. de duobus animabus, contra Manichaeos, cap. IX. quedam nocia victoria penè mihi semper in disputationibus proveniebat differenti cum Christianis imperitis.
units.tr: But above all take care never to begin a disputation unprepared and not well instructed and equipped, lest you become a great stumbling-block to another and a cause of confirming error. Augustine himself later grieved seriously that this had often happened to him before his conversion. (On the Two Souls, against the Manichaeans, ch. 9): a certain harmful victory almost always fell to me in disputations when I argued with unlearned Christians.

units.la: Iam Scriptis quae institutur disputatio, haud minus observat quae polumus, quin eo magis, quo quae chartis inscribuntur ad plures perveniunt, atque perdurant. Ubi primum & nimis vulgare vitium hoc in Scriptoribus est, quod adeo promiscuò quilibet, & valde leviter scribunt. Quod uti inter causas, cur disciplinae meliores intereant, retulit Maturinus Simonius, in eximio mio de literis perennibus libello; ita non minus inter dispendia rei ecclesiasticæ poni debet, quando in Theologiâ negligitur. Certè ut non omnibus committenda est præsens disputatio, quæ ore fit, quam nec quivis arripiet; ita neque scribere omnium est. Haud tolerandum, ut quicunque vult, scribat; sed ut qui potest scribere, velit, hoc urgendum. Benè ac sapienter habetur librorum censura: sed uti libri examinantur, ita velim ut primùm ipse Scriptor dignus æstimetur, sive per Censores, aut Verbi Ministros, aut Theologiæ Professores, (sic Synodus Emdana anno 1571. art. 51.) ex ratione professionis suæ, aut experientiâ & usu, qui ad scriptionem cum fructu se applicabit. Nam ut pro arbitrio quisque calamum sumat, & Theologiæ controversiis se immiscéat, plurimorum malorum exstitit causa. Scribunt aliqui ea quæ ipsi nesciunt, qui nec seipsos attendunt: alii quoque sciunt, & fere ideo solum quia sciunt; sed ii parum respiciunt an ista alii ignorent: hi quidem non adeo male, sed uti sui causa illud agunt, non aliorum; ita is demum dignus Scriptor est, qui omissis quæ obvia & passim haberi possunt, in illis pedem figit, eaque pro sequitur ulterius, quæ restant, aut indaganda, aut in usum referenda meliorem. Scite Bernardus, serm.xxxvi. in Cantica: Sunt namque qui scire volunt eo tantum sine ut sciant, & turpis curiositas est. Et sunt qui scire volunt ut sciantur ipsi, & turpis vanitas est. Qui profectò non evadunt subsannantem Satyricum, & ei qui ejusmodi est decantantem, scire nihil est, nisi ie scire hoc sciat alter. Et sunt item qui scire volunt, ut scientiam suam vendant, verbi causa pro pecuniâ, pro honoribus, & turpis quæstus est. Sed sunt quoque qui scire volunt ut ædificent, & charitas est. Et item qui scire volunt, ut ædificentur, & prudentia est. Horum omnium soli ultimi duo non inveniuntur in abusione scientiæ, quippe qui ad hoc volunt intelligere, ut benefaciant. Scripsit Franciscus Sanchez libellum facetum magis quam utilem, de malmultum nobilis & primâ universali scientiâ, quod nihil scitur: ubi, o quantum est hominum, qui etiam quae nescivunt, sciunt, inquit. Duo autem ut agamus ista fere supersunt, tum supra cognita, alia adinvenire & producere; tum quaecunque habentur, suo maximo usui adaptare, & elocare. Adeo hodie qui scripturus, oportet sit nonnullae lectionis, quo sciat antequam ad scribendum se accingit, ea quae vulgo sciuntur, ut, non nota & dicta aliis, & longe saepe ac ipse facturus sit melius, sed alia, & aliquam partem aut meliora, aut utiliora, aut quo vis pacto necessaria, proferat. Sic Jacobus Acontius, in epistolâ ad Johannem Wolfium, de ratione edendorum librorum, non indignâ lectu: tum autem videndum, quid extet, quid desiderari posse videatur. Ne ad idem argumentum proferam magni judicii virum, Franciscum Verulamium, quem nominasse sufficerit. Non satis est ut quis bona scribat, nisi quoque se aliquâ commendent necessitate. Hieronymus, ad Rusticum Monachum, ne ad scribendum cito prosilias, & levi ducaris insaniâ. Multo tempore disce, quod doceas. Virgo Vestalis (auctor est Plutarchus, in vitâ Numae) primis decem annis discebat ea quae officii sui erant; altero decennio ea exercebat; tertio, eadem alias docebat. Quod autem non major ratio habetur eorum quibus scribere liceat, facit quod tot habemus, & incondita, & superflua Scriptorum volumina, quaeque rebus nostris, quibus tamen explicandis aut defendendis data videri volunt, haud parum intercedunt, & nocent. Nec in Censurâ librorum sufficere videtur, ut Auctorum habeatur solum ratio, sed omnino antequam liber scribatur, & de argumento, & scripti dispositione velim haberi consilium, an e re forte futurum sit operam hic impendere, annon potius in alterius argumenti negotio? tum quia aegre adducitur quis ut omittat, aut deleat quod aliquo labore jam perfecit opus, & in profluentem abjiciat, quod agebant olim Gentiles, qui in Scriptorum tertámine ad aram Lugdunensem in Galliis Poetæ aliive Scriptores succubuissent: tum quod difficulter (quamvis habeamus ante nos exemplum Augustini, & post eum Thomæ Aquinatis, atque Æneæ Silvii) sua quis retractet. Iam olim in Ecclesiâ ratio & censura librorum habita fuit; nec quivis promiscue tolerati scriptores: quin canon Apostolorum (uti dicitur) lx, deponendum dicit, qui scripta divulgat δημοσίευει ἐπιλοίμῃ τῆς λεῳ τῆς κλήρῳ. Ergo non quivis scribat; sed nec quodvis.
units.tr: Now in writing a controversy, one must be no less careful about what we publish, all the more so because what is committed to paper reaches more people and lasts longer. Here the first and most common fault among writers is that anyone at all writes, and does so very carelessly. Mathurin Simonius, in his excellent little book on enduring literature, lists this among the causes of the decline of good disciplines; and in the same way it must be counted among the losses of the Church's affairs when it is neglected in theology. Just as a live disputation should not be entrusted to everyone, since not everyone will take it up, so writing is not for everyone. It cannot be tolerated that whoever wishes should write; the point to press is that whoever is able to write should also be willing. The censorship of books is rightly practised, but I would like the author himself to be judged worthy first, whether by censors, ministers of the Word or professors of theology (so the Synod of Emden in 1571, art. 51), judging from his profession, or from his experience and practice, whether he will apply himself to writing with profit. For when each person takes up the pen as he pleases and mixes himself into theological controversies, this has been the cause of very many evils. Some write what they themselves do not know, and do not examine themselves. Others do know, and mostly only because they know; but they pay little attention to whether others are ignorant of these things. These do not act so badly, but they do it for their own sake, not for others'. So the only writer worthy of the name is one who, leaving aside what is obvious and commonly available, fixes his foot on matters that are not, and then pursues what remains, either to be investigated or to be turned to better use. Bernard well says in sermon 36 on the Song of Songs: There are those who want to know only for the sake of knowing, and that is shameful curiosity. And there are those who want to know so that they themselves may be known, and that is shameful vanity. These certainly do not escape the mocking satirist, who sings that to know nothing is to know this, unless another knows that one knows it. There are also those who want to know so that they may sell their knowledge, for money or for honours, and that is shameful gain. But there are also those who want to know so that they may build up, and that is love. And likewise those who want to know so that they may be built up, and that is prudence. Of all these, only the last two are not found in the abuse of knowledge, since they wish to understand for the sake of doing good. Francis Sanchez wrote a little book, more witty than useful, on the nothing-knowing of the most noble and first universal science, that nothing is known; in it he says: O how many people there are who even know what they do not know! There remain, to be sure, two tasks in such work: to discover and bring to light things beyond what is already known, and to adapt whatever is available to its greatest use and to set it forth. So today whoever is going to write must have read widely enough, before he sets himself to write, to know what is commonly known, so that he may produce not things already known and said by others, and often said far better than he himself would do, but other things, or some part that is better, more useful, or in some way necessary. So Jacob Acontius, in his letter to Johann Wolf on the method of publishing books, which is worth reading: one must then see what exists and what seems to be wanting. I need not bring forward for the same point the man of great judgement, Francis Verulam, whom it is enough to have named. It is not enough that someone writes good things, unless they also recommend themselves by some necessity. Jerome to the monk Rusticus: do not leap quickly into writing, and do not be led by a light madness. Learn for a long time what you are to teach. The Vestal Virgin (Plutarch is the authority, in the life of Numa) spent her first ten years learning what belonged to her office, the second decade practising it, and in the third taught others. But because the same care is not taken over those who are allowed to write, we have so many disorderly and superfluous volumes of writers, which, though they claim to explain or defend our affairs, do no small harm. Nor does it seem sufficient in the censorship of books to consider only the authors; rather, before a book is written, I would wish counsel to be taken about both the subject and the arrangement of the work, whether it will in fact be worth the labour to spend effort here, or rather on some other matter. This is because it is hard to persuade someone to omit or delete what has already been completed with some labour, and to throw it into the stream, as the ancient Gentiles did, when poets or other writers were defeated in the contest of writers at the altar at Lyons in Gaul. Likewise it is difficult for anyone to retract his own work, although we have before us the examples of Augustine, and after him Thomas Aquinas and Aeneas Silvius. Already in the ancient Church the judgement and censure of books was practised, and writers were not tolerated indiscriminately; indeed, the canon of the Apostles (as it is called), number 60, orders the deposition of one who publishes [δημοσιεύει] writings for the laity. Therefore not everyone should write; but neither should anything at all be written.

units.la: In criticis eo diligentius secernenda res est quæ agitur, à persona, & adversario, quo majus hic periculum, si utrumque imprudenter aut malitiose commisceas, & à realibus transeas ad personalia, seu quod tum fere fit, ad convitia, quibus plus noceas, quam causæ cæteroquin bonæ, aliàs prosis. Refert de amplissimo Thuano Casaubonus, & hæc illius verba, in epistolis, ep. cxc. Memini divinum virum Thuanum, quum illi sæpe quorundam è nostris scripta commendarem: solitum respondere, non posse ferre se illos, qui genere scribendi plus destruerent, quam doctrinâ ædificarent. Is, quocum disputatur, vel est heterodoxus; vel orthodoxus, in quæstione nempe problematicâ. Vbique in disputando requiritur eruditio, sed hic insuper magna prudentia, ut eo religiosius personam caveamus, quo ejusdem nobiscum est & fidei & societatis: adeoque vel nomen ejus à nobis sileatur prorsus, vel debite ubique veneremur, observemusque semper ut alteri faciamus, prout nobiscum fieri cupimus.
units.tr: In controversial writing the matter at hand must be separated with greater care from the person and the opponent, since the danger is greater here if you mix the two carelessly or maliciously, and pass from things to persons, that is, as usually happens, to abuse, by which you do more harm than good to an otherwise good cause. Casaubon reports this of the most distinguished de Thou, in his letters, letter 190: I remember that when I often commended to that divine man de Thou the writings of some of our own people, he used to reply that he could not bear those who by their manner of writing destroyed more than they built up by their learning. The person with whom one disputes is either a heterodox person, or an orthodox one, in a question that is open to debate. In every disputation learning is required, but here great prudence is required besides, so that we guard the person all the more scrupulously the more he shares our faith and fellowship. Therefore either his name should be passed over in silence entirely, or he should everywhere be duly honoured, and we should always observe what we wish others to do to us.

units.la: Duplex disputaturo propositus sit finis oportet, ut convincat, vel ut componat, id est, ut vel alium in suam perducat sententiam, & ab errore dimoveat; vel (ubi id quidem datur: non enim ubique hoc licet) sententias & controversiam componat. Zuinglius, in exegesi Eucharistici negotii, ad Lutherum: fecialem tibi mitto librum, non qui res repetitum, sed compositum veniat. Atque illud valde attendere unumquemque oportet, qui non unius adversarii majorem habere cupiat rationem, quam totius Ecclesiæ, ejusque tranquillitatis. Verum in tuto collocatâ ante omnia veritate, de pace cogitandum, & communione mutuâ. Quod est ἀληθεύειν ἐν ἀγάπῃ, Ephes. iv. 15. Quomodo Cyrillus, in Concilio Ephesino, scripsit ad Nestorii quendam amicum: tantum fides integra & salva sit, & carus amicus omnibus ero. Neque alli concedam ut religiosissimum Episcopum Nestorium ardentius amem, quam ego. In Actis Conc. Ephesini. part. 1.
units.tr: The one who is to dispute ought to have a proposed aim, either to convince or to reconcile; that is, either to bring the other person to his own opinion and turn him from error, or (where this is granted, for it is not always permitted) to settle opinions and the controversy. Zwingli, in his exegesis of the Eucharistic business, to Luther: I send you a fecial book, which comes not to repeat matters but to settle them. Each person who does not want to have greater regard for one opponent than for the whole Church and its tranquillity ought to attend very carefully to this. But truth must first be placed in safety, and then we must think of peace and mutual fellowship. This is to speak the truth in love [ἀληθεύειν ἐν ἀγάπῃ], Ephesians 4:15. So Cyril, at the Council of Ephesus, wrote to a certain friend of Nestorius: only let the faith remain whole and safe, and I will be a dear friend to all. Nor will I allow anyone to love the most religious bishop Nestorius more ardently than I do. In the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, part 1.

units.la: Sed ultimo nunc loco de Studio Controversiarum bene dirigendo sermo nobis instituendus. Ubi primum in studioso, tum in studiis nonnulla requirimus. Illic quidem ut tribus illis sit præditus virtutibus, ad quas studiosum quemque examino, ut de eo capiam præsagium, si sit probus, & diligens, & modestus, quæ singula vitam ejus, & studia, & mores effingunt, commendantque. Nihil istorum in vero studioso deesse patior. Nisi etenim coram Deo probus, & apud se diligens, erga alios modestus sit, si in aliquo deficiat, ubique hæret. Quippe ista illorum omnium est inter se affinitas, & cum studioso sociabilis necessariaque cognatio, ut nisi adsint, vel dici studiosus nequeat. Non ferro vitæ improbæ aut non satis castigatæ juvenem, præsertim qui nostri ordinis esse cupiat, cujus alioqui exiftit merum dedecus & propudium. 1 Paral. xxix, 5. At dixit eis Rex Iehiskia, auscultate mihi O Levitæ: jam sanctificate vos, & sanctificate domum Iehovæ Dei majorum vestrorum. Nehem. xii. 30. Quumque mundassent se Sacerdotes & Levitæ, mundaverunt populum. Primum illi sancti, hinc populus; quem non sanctificabunt, nisi prius sanctificati ipsi. Hebræi: ornate ipsum, & postea ornate alios. Certe multum potest vita Theologi, ad ædificationem si bona sit, sin mala, ad destructionem: & grave ejus judicium futurum est, qui moribus doctrinæ suæ adversis vita plus obobest, quam doctrina prosit. Dixit Nilus, in Ascetici: neminem manent certiora supplicia, quam illum, qui multos vitiorum suorum facit discipulos. Quamvis in istis imitandus magister non sit, tamen qui se magistrum scit, peccans, eo gravius delinquit. Et temere aliorum curam suscipiunt, qui suas nondum curaverint cupiditates: uti Idem ibidem loquitur. Qui historiam hodiernorum Bachmannum in India, nuper scripsit Abrahamus Rogerius, refert, illorum religiosos, quos Sanjasios appellant, ut ad rerum divinarum meditationem se dignos praestent, primum operam dare in debellandis sex quos appellant hostibus, cupiditate, ira, avaritia, superbia, amore mundano, & vindicta: quibus superatis sic demum aptos se putant qui rerum Sacrarum contemplationibus vacent. Atque ii Gentiles. Commendo nostris hominibus, huic fini ut legant elegantissimos Chrysostomi libros, quos scripsit de Sacerdotio. Summum viri Theologi est elogium, quod Polychronio Apamenorum Ecclesiae Antistiti fert Nicephorus, lib. xiv. cap. xxx. & optime vixit, & optime docuit, vita scilicet ex aequo doctrinae respondente. Etenim erubescit quam vis praeclara doctrina, quam propria reprehendit conscientia, uti bene Hieronymus, in Epitaphio Marcellae. vel uti Abbas Antonius, in Melissis: nihil doctore frigidius, verbis tantum philosophante: hoc enim non doctoris, sed histrionis est.
