units.tr: But now, last of all, we must discuss how the study of controversies should be rightly directed. Here we must require some things first in the student and then in his studies. In the student, he should indeed be endowed with those three virtues by which I examine every student, to form a forecast of him: whether he is upright, diligent, and modest. Each of these shapes and commends his life, his studies, and his character. I do not allow that any of them be lacking in a true student. Unless he is upright before God, diligent in himself, and modest towards others, if he falls short in any one of them he will stumble everywhere. These qualities are so closely related to one another and so bound up with the student that, without them, he cannot even be called a student. I do not want a young man, especially one who wishes to belong to our order, to be unchastened in his life or morals, for such a man is a mere disgrace and reproach to it. 1 Chron. 29:5. But King Hezekiah said to them: Listen to me, O Levites; now sanctify yourselves, and sanctify the house of the LORD God of your fathers. Neh. 12:30. And when the priests and the Levites had purified themselves, they purified the people. First those holy men, and then the people; those whom they do not sanctify, unless they are first sanctified themselves. The Hebrews say: adorn yourself first, and afterwards adorn others. Certainly the life of a theologian can do much, for building up if it is good, and for tearing down if it is bad; and his judgement will be grave, since he whose life does more harm than his teaching does good, by conduct at odds with his doctrine. Nilus said in his Ascetic writings: No one has more certain punishment awaiting him than the man who makes many disciples of his vices. Although such a man is not to be imitated as a teacher, yet he who knows himself to be a teacher and sins sins all the more gravely. And those who have not yet cared for their own desires rashly undertake the care of others, as the same author says in the same place. Abraham Rogerius, who recently wrote about the present-day Brahmans in India, reports that their religious men, whom they call Sanjasi, first labour to subdue six enemies, which they name: lust, anger, avarice, pride, love of the world, and revenge. Only when these are overcome do they think themselves fit to devote themselves to contemplation of sacred things. And these are Gentiles. I commend to our people, for this purpose, that they read the most elegant books of Chrysostom which he wrote On the Priesthood. Nicephorus, book 14, chapter 30, gives the highest praise a theologian can receive to Polychronius, bishop of the church of the Apamenes: he both lived excellently and taught excellently, his life, that is, corresponding evenly to his teaching. For however splendid a doctrine may be, it blushes when one's own conscience reproves it, as Jerome well says in his Epitaph on Marcella. Or as Abbot Antony says in the Melissae: nothing is more lifeless than a teacher who only philosophizes in words; for that is the mark not of a teacher but of an actor.

units.la: Tum diligentiam in studiis adhibeat oportet, qui proficere annititur, & acquirere multi magnique operis titulum, καλὸς ἐπισκοπῆς. 1. Tim. iii. 1. ad exemplum maximi virorum Calvini, qui uti semper, vel indignantibus amicis, sollicite agebat, ne ipsum Dominus veniens otiosum deprehenderet; ita nihil frequentius in ore habebat, quam nullam sibi acerbam vitam esse, praeter otiosam. Scribit Ludovicus Vives Budeo, est in Centuria epistolarum Goldasti: equidem ἀβίωτον ipse dicit, & plane ζωὴ ὁμοίως existimo esse eam vitam, quae absque ingenii cultu traducitur. Juxta illud Senecae: otium sine litteris
units.tr: Then he who strives to make progress and to win the title of a great and good work, a good work of oversight [καλὸς ἐπισκοπῆς], 1 Tim. 3:1, must apply diligence to his studies, after the example of the greatest of men, Calvin. Just as he always acted with anxious care, even when his friends were annoyed, lest the Lord should find him idle on his coming, so he had nothing more often on his lips than that no life was bitter to him except an idle one. Ludovicus Vives writes to Budé, in the Centuria of letters of Goldast: he himself calls it [ἀβίωτον] unlivable, and I plainly think that life is likewise [ζωὴ ὁμοίως] no life at all, which is passed without cultivation of the mind. In accordance with that saying of Seneca: leisure without letters [is a grave to the living].

units.la: terris teris mors est, & vivi hominis sepultura. Bene iterum Hieronymus, ad Rusticum Monachum: facite aliquid operis, ut te semper Diabolus inveniat occupatum. Cavere nobis atque ingenio nostro debemus quam maxime, ne unquam simus plane otiosi, quia alioqui hoc ipsum otium negotium facessit, & non tantum ardorem mentis extinguit, verum etiam multo infelici lolio animum conferit. Semper in opere & labore sit, si non manus, saltem mens nostra. Perpetuum hoc mobile quiescit nunquam, atque idcirco occupari quam optimis debet continuo, & utilissimis. Quomodo Alexander ajebat, quod mundi dominus brevi adeo factus esset, ὠνδὲ ἀναβαλλόμενον. Musaeo Zachariae Ursini scis quid inscriptum fuerit? Amice, quisquis huc venis: Aut agito pauca, aut abi: aut me laborantem adjuva. Simile fere, pro foribus Oporini, celebris Typographi: Quisquis es, rogat te Oporinus, etiam atque etiam, ut, si quid est, quod à se velis, perpaucis agas: deinde abstinebis ... nisi, tanquam Hercules, defesso Atlante veneris suppositurus humeros: semper enim erit, quod tu agas, & quotquot huc attulerint pedes.
units.tr: It is a death, and the burial of a living man. Jerome again well says to the monk Rusticus: Do some work, so that the Devil always finds you occupied. We must guard ourselves and our minds as much as possible, that we are never wholly idle, for otherwise that very idleness creates business, and not only quenches the ardour of the mind but also sows it with a most unhappy darnel. Let there always be work and labour in us, if not in the hands, at least in the mind. This perpetual motion never rests, and so it ought always to be occupied with the best and most useful things. Alexander used to say that, although he had become lord of the world, he had become so in a short time not postponing anything [οὐδὲ ἀναβαλλόμενον]. Do you know what was inscribed on the door of Musaeus, Zacharias Ursinus's house? Friend, whoever you are who come here: either do a few things, or go away; or help me while I labour. Much the same is written almost at the door of Oporinus, the famous printer: Whoever you are, Oporinus asks you again and again that, if you have anything you wish to have done by him, you should do it in a few words; then you will refrain ... unless you come, like Hercules, to put your shoulders under Atlas when he is tired; for there will always be something for you to do, and as many more as the feet bring here.

units.la: Denique modestia praecipuum juventutis ornamentum, adeo studiosum & Theologum decet, ut hac sola deficiente, studia quaevis operi sint, non honori. Modestia videlicet, qua quis humillime semper de se sentit, aliis omnibus se postponit, & neminem facile offendit vel experitur inimicum. Hinc non tantum apud Gentiles, qui sapientes censebantur, se submissionis causa amatores sapientiae, philosophos, non sapientes appellari volebant; sed quoque apud Judaeos, Doctores & Rabbini veniunt eodem nomine, quo discipuli, & dicuntur non modo חכמים sapientes, sed תלמידי חכמים discipuli, aut studiosi sapientiae, vel sapientum. Non admodum multi inter studiosos, qui eruditione excellunt, pauciores modestia: adeo, quae aetatis istius est lubricitas, difficile, modestiam profiteri: quae tamen virtus, quam corpori gratiam pulchritudo, istum moribus decorem conciliat, & pluris facienda, majorique studio passim ambienda quam vulgo fit. Eruditus, sed immodestus juvenis pari pretio est, atque apud Salomonem mulier forma praestans, & simul impudica. Quod in viris, prudentia id modestia est in juvenibus, utque ibi nullus usus eruditionis est, nisi illam adjunctam habeat, ita neque hic suum ei pretium, nisi sociata modestiâ. Modestos Iudaei vocant Abrahami discipulos; alios, Bileami. Quinam discipuli Abrahami? quibus est oculus bonus, spiritus contritus, & anima humilis. Huc spectat Iulii Rugerii opusculum, de Auditore Theologiae, ubi qualem eum esse oporteat, moribus, & externis disciplinis, imprimis vero Philosophiâ, imbutum, copiose & eleganter edisserit.
units.tr: Finally, modesty, the chief ornament of youth, so befits the student and the theologian that, if this alone is lacking, all his studies serve dishonour rather than honour. Modesty, namely, by which a man always thinks of himself most humbly, puts all others before himself, and easily offends no one nor finds an enemy. Hence not only among the Gentiles, who were thought wise, did men who out of humility wished to be called lovers of wisdom call themselves philosophers rather than wise men; but also among the Jews, teachers and rabbis are called by the same name as disciples, and are called not only wise men [חכמים] but disciples of the wise [תלמידי חכמים], or students of wisdom or of the wise. Among students, not very many who excel in learning are modest; so difficult is it, given the slipperiness of that age, to profess modesty. Yet this virtue, which gives grace to the body as beauty does, lends a grace of character to the other, and is to be valued more highly and sought with greater eagerness than is commonly the case. A learned but immodest young man is of the same worth as the woman who is beautiful in Solomon's eyes and at the same time unchaste. As prudence is in men, so modesty is in young men; and just as learning is of no use there unless it is joined to prudence, so here too it has no worth unless modesty is joined with it. The Jews call the disciples of Abraham modest, and others the disciples of Balaam. Who are the disciples of Abraham? Those who have a good eye, a contrite spirit, and a humble soul. To this purpose belongs the little work of Julius Rugerius, On the Hearer of Theology, in which he discusses fully and elegantly what sort of man he ought to be, imbued with morals and external disciplines, and above all with philosophy.

units.la: Nam Studia ut bene instituat, eaque quae porro cognoscendis agitandisque controversiis (de quo impraefens) occupantur, praerequiritur ante omnia cognitio linguarum, & usus philosophiae: absque quibus nemo unquam feliciter disputavit. Linguarum puta, Hebrea, & Graeca, quas nonnemo, eximius scilicet magister, fontes omnium haeresium esse, coram Rege Galliarum Francisco, adstante litteratissimo Budaeo, vocabat. Si Platinae fides, P. Paulus II, promiscue haereticos appellabat omnes in Academiis studiosos: adeo humanitatis studia, & nomen Academiarum oderat atque detestabatur. Quibuscum confero, quod in Talmude Ierosolymitano, tractatu Peah, sol. 15. col. 3, lego, Rabbi Iehosuam interrogatum, quando quis doceret filios linguam Graecam יון, respondisse: tempore, quo neque dies sit, neque nox. Quoniam sc. scriptum: & meditaberis in lege [die, ac nocte. Quam eandem ob causam, juxta eum, prohibitum quoque fuerit docere artes liberales. Acute! Auctor Iuchasin, maledictum pronunciat אררי, qui filium suum docuerit disciplinam Gentilium. Attamen Graecam linguam facilius concedunt Iudæi ut quis addiscat, vel eâ utatur, atque illâ etiam scribat sacra. Verùm omnino necesse est Theologo linguas illas scire, ut ipsum Scripturæ textum (de quo inter Theologos omnis vertitur disputatio) in originibus intelligat; & non per interpretem agere, sed propriis frui oculis & judicio, in discernendis verbis verborumque sensu, queat. Inde Clementina est, lib. v. tit. de Magistris, (quæ confirmata in concilio Basileensi, sess. xix. & hoc sæculo anno cIↄ Iↄ cx. à Paulo v.) de constituendis omnibus in Scholis, Romanâ, Parisiensi, Oxoniensi, Bononiensi, Salamantinâ, aliisque Professores linguarum Hebraicæ, Arabicæ, & Chaldeæ. Illo consilio Zwinglius Epistolas Paulinas omnes Græce sua manu descripsit, memoriæ mandavit, adeò ut Græcè postea facilius illas sciret, quam Latinè: qui illius codex asservatur in Bibliotheca Tigurinâ. Atque de eo ipse, in Exegesi Eucharistiæ ad Lutherum: de me ipso coram Deo testor, Evangelii vim atque summam, cum Ioannis, Augustinique tractatuum lectione didici, tum diligenti Græcanicarum epistolarum, quas hisce manibus ante undecim annos exscripsi; quum tu annos jam octo regnasti. Beza in senili adeo ætate, debilitatâ fere omnium memoriâ, tamen ex juvenili studio, usque perpetuo hoc retinuit, ut totos Psalmos Hebraicè, & quodcunque caput ex epistolis Pauli Græcè recitaret. Solida jaciunt fundamenta, qui inde à Scholis se assuefaciunt primigenio Sacrorum librorum sermoni, quem postmodum quibusvis linguis adaptando, nequaquam id molestiæ sentiunt, quod non immani per omnia studia fructu se compenset. Victorinus Strigelius, dum adhuc in Papismo hæreret, quatuor causas recensebat, ob quas Lutheranorum Scholas præferret Papisticis; quod illic vigeret studium linguarum, eloquentiæ, Historiarum, & denique propter docendi Methodum magis expeditam & facilem, quam ullibi.
units.tr: For to pursue his studies well, and those which are occupied with the investigation and discussion of controversies (on which I am now engaged), the knowledge of languages and the practice of philosophy must be required beforehand above all: no one has ever disputed successfully without them. By languages, I mean Hebrew and Greek, which a certain outstanding teacher, in the presence of the King of France, Francis, with the most learned Budé standing by, called the sources of all heresies. If we trust Platina, Pope Paul II indiscriminately called all who studied in the universities heretics; so much did he hate and detest the study of the humanities and the name of universities. With this I compare what I read in the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Peah, fol. 15, col. 3: when Rabbi Joshua was asked when one should teach sons the Greek language, Javan, he replied: at a time that is neither day nor night, since it is written: and you shall meditate on the law [day and night]. For this same reason, according to him, it was also forbidden to teach the liberal arts. Shrewd! The author of Juchasin pronounces a curse, Cursed be [אררי], on the man who has taught his son the learning of the Gentiles. Yet the Jews more readily allow a man to learn the Greek language, or to use it, and even to write sacred things in it. But it is absolutely necessary for a theologian to know those languages, so that he may understand the text of Scripture itself in its original (on which the whole dispute among theologians turns), and so that he may not act through an interpreter but may enjoy his own eyes and judgement in discerning the words and the sense of the words. Hence the Clementine constitution, book 5, title On Teachers (confirmed at the Council of Basel, session 19, and in this century in the year 1610 by Paul V), ordains that professors of the Hebrew, Arabic and Chaldee languages be established in all schools: at Rome, Paris, Oxford, Bologna, Salamanca and elsewhere. With this purpose Zwingli copied out all the Pauline epistles in Greek with his own hand and committed them to memory, so that afterwards he knew them in Greek more easily than in Latin; that copy is preserved in the Zurich library. He himself says of it, in his Exegesis of the Eucharist, to Luther: I testify before God concerning myself that I learned the force and sum of the Gospel, partly from reading the tractates of John and Augustine, partly from careful study of the Greek epistles, which I copied out with these hands eleven years ago, when you had already reigned eight years. Beza, even in his very advanced old age, when his memory was almost entirely weakened, nevertheless retained from his youthful study this habit throughout his life: that he could recite the whole Psalms in Hebrew and any chapter of the epistles of Paul in Greek. They lay solid foundations who from their schooldays accustom themselves to the original language of the sacred books, which, afterwards adapted to any other languages, they find no trouble at all, since it repays them with a rich fruit in all their studies. Victorinus Strigelius, while he was still stuck in Popery, enumerated four reasons why he preferred the Lutheran schools to the Papist ones: because there flourished there the study of languages, of eloquence, and of history, and finally because of a method of teaching that was more expeditious and easier than anywhere else.

units.la: Sanè necessariæ προσωδίαι sunt ad Theologica, litteratura, & philosophia. Quò facit Abrahami Sculteri Oratio, de conjungenda Philologia, cum Theologia, in Curriculo vitæ, pag. 103. Nam magna dicendi facultate sacerdoti est opus, quin etiam Dialectices valde peritum esse oportet, dixit Abbas Antonius, Melissarum lib. II. Dialectica, non qualis olim in Scholis, ex Tartaretis, Bricot, Perversore, Eckiis, Copulatis Bursæ Montis, Exercitiis Taurinis & Caninis docebatur, quibus se conqueritur Melanchton (orat. de Studiis corrigendis) totos fere sex annos detentum fuisse & excarnificatum, sed quæ, cum cætera philosophia eò dirigatur, ut mentem hominis in veritatis investigatione fortiter juvet, atque studiis omnibus quam maximè conducat. Hujus proba cognitio mentem dirigit tum in percipiendâ recte veritate, tum in deprehendendo facilius errore, eoque destruendo. Ostendit hoc exiguo, sed egregio, tractatu Lambertus Danæus, quem scripsit de Elenchis Hæreticorum: ubi per omnes Sophismatum species cundo declarat, quomodo ex iis ad propositas objectiones promptè respondéri possit. Ne Faustum Socinum dicam, qui quoque de Elenchis Sophisticis inter opera, tractatum reliquit, exemplis Theologicis quidem, sed iis ad subversionem fidei factis, illustratum. De usu Logices in Theologicis vide etiam lectionem XIV. Iohannis Prideaux, habitam in Vesperiis. Illa ergo sive Dialectica, sive philosophica scire Theologum oportet, nec scire perfunctorie, sed usum illorum habere familiarem promtumque, quid ni & facultatem, ubi opus aliquando, quod persæpe fit, docendi? Uti in Argentoratensi Scholâ Martyri evenit, & Zanchio, Professoribus Theologis, quorum illi vacante Philosophicâ professione, impositum Aristotelis Ethicam exponere; huic, Physicam, alternis septimanis. Novimus quidem philosophiæ abusus, atque uti Tertullianus loquitur, etiam de philosophorum ingenijs omnem hæresim animari; sapientia sæcularis temeraria interpres divinæ naturæ & dispositionis, uti in libro Præscriptionum Idem. Eodem libro: quid ergo Athenis & Hierosolymis? quid Academiæ & Ecclesiæ? quid hereticis & Christianis? nostra institutio de porticu Salomonis est, qui & ipse tradiderat Dominum in simplicitate cordis esse quærendum. Viderint qui Stoicum, & Platonicum, & Dialecticum Christianismum protulerunt. Platonem, omnium haereticorum condimentarium appellat, lib. de anima. Et de Aristotele, inquit, nescio an sua paratior implere, quam aliena inanire. In Apologia: Quid adeo simile Philosophus & Christianus? Graeciae discipulus & coeli? fame negotiator & vitae? verborum & factorum operator? rerum aedificator & destructor? amicus & inimicus erroris? veritatis interpolator & expressor, furator ejus & custos ejus antiquior omnibus ni fallor? similia ejus discipulus Cyprianus, lib. de bono patientiae. Sed vitium illa sunt, non philosophiae, verum philosophorum, ista abstentium. Quomodo repudiamus saecularia studia, sine quibus divina non possunt? inquit alibi, lib. de Idololatria.
units.tr: Certainly the necessary aids of accent and pronunciation [προσωδίαι] are needed for theology, literature and philosophy. Abraham Scultetus's oration on joining philology with theology, in his Curriculum vitae, p. 103, makes this point. For, as Abbas Antonius said in the second book of the Melissae, a priest must have great skill in speaking, and indeed must be very well versed in dialectic. I do not mean the dialectic once taught in the schools from Tartaretus, Bricot, Perversor and Eck, from the Copulata of the Bursa Montis, and from the Taurine and Canine exercises, by which Melanchthon (in his oration on correcting the studies) complains that men were held for almost six whole years and tortured. I mean the dialectic which, since the rest of philosophy is directed to it, strongly helps the human mind in the search for truth and is most useful for all studies. Sound knowledge of it guides the mind both in grasping the truth correctly and in detecting error more easily, and so in destroying it. Lambert Daneau shows this in his small but excellent treatise on the refutation of heretics, where he goes through every kind of sophism and explains how replies to the objections put forward can be given readily from them. I say nothing of Faustus Socinus, who also left a treatise on sophistical refutations among his works, illustrated with theological examples, but examples made for the overthrow of the faith. On the use of logic in theology, see also the fourteenth lecture of John Prideaux, delivered at the Vespers. The theologian must therefore know these subjects, both dialectic and philosophy, not superficially but with a familiar and ready use of them. Why should he not also have the ability to teach them, when occasion sometimes requires it, as it very often does? This happened at the school of Strasbourg with the theology professors Martyr and Zanchius: when the chair of philosophy was vacant, the first was charged with expounding Aristotle's Ethics, the second with the Physics, on alternate weeks. We know well the abuses of philosophy, and, as Tertullian says, every heresy is kindled by the wits of philosophers: worldly wisdom is a rash interpreter of the divine nature and arrangement, as he says in the book On Prescription of the same author. In the same book: What then has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What has the Academy to do with the Church? What have heretics to do with Christians? Our instruction comes from the portico of Solomon, who himself taught that the Lord is to be sought in simplicity of heart. Let those look to it who have produced a Stoic, Platonic and dialectical Christianity. He calls Plato the seasoner of all heretics, in the book on the soul. And of Aristotle he says: I do not know whether he was more ready to fill his own mind or to empty the minds of others. In the Apology: What is so alike between the philosopher and the Christian? The disciple of Greece and of heaven? The merchant of fame and of life? The worker of words and of deeds? The builder and destroyer of things? The friend and enemy of error? The corrupter and expounder of truth? Its thief and its guardian, older than all, if I am not mistaken? His disciple Cyprian says similar things in the book On the Good of Patience. But those faults belong to philosophers, not to philosophy, and it is those who abstain who are at fault. How do we reject secular studies, without which divine things cannot be understood? he says elsewhere, in the book On Idolatry.

units.la: Clemens Alexandrinus, Stromatum lib. I. Alii autem philosophiam etiam cum maximo malo & ad hominum perniciem venisse in vitam existimant, ut quae profecta sit a maligno aliquo inventore: ipse vero probat esse divinae originis, Ἡμεῖς ἐργον σοφίας τῆς Φιλοσοφίας. Ostenderunt quidem passim veteres, varios in philosophia gentili errores, Christianae veritati inimicas, Iustinus Martyr, libr. Ἀνατροπή, sive Eversio quorundam dogmatum Aristotelicorum; Tatianus, in Oratione contra Graecos, statim in initio; Epiphanius, Panarii lib. I. Tom. I. Augustinus, de Civit. Dei, lib. VIII. sed neque negarunt, boni permultum fructusque in philosophia esse, eamque continere talia, quae non modo cum sacris bene queant conciliari, sed & ex iis defluxerint. Unde in Apol. Tertullianus, quis Poetarum, quis Sophistarum, quis non omnino de Prophetarum fonte potaverit? inde igitur Philosophi suum ingenii sic rigaverunt, ut qua de nostris habent, ea nos comparent illis. Atque doctissimus Seldenus, nus, lib. 1. de jure Natur. Hebr. cap. 11. ex Iudaeis, Patribus Christianis, & Paganis ostendit, veteres philosophos Pythagoram, Platonem, Aristotelem, aliosque multa cum Iudaeis communione, hinc varia in philosophiam suam transtulisse. Quare ab ea se non continuerunt Patres, sed reddiderunt sibi admodum familiarem. De Origene nemo nescit. Videantur compendio ejus Philocalia, cap. xiv. & Homil. xiv. in Genesim. Augustinum adde, de Doctrina Christiana lib. 11. c. xl. Et contra Cresconium Grammat. lib. 1. cap. xii. xiii. xvii. De Clemente. Hieronymus, epist. ad Magnum. Clemens Alexandrinus, presbyter Ecclesiae, meo judicio omnium eruditissimus. Quid in illius libris indoctum? imo quid non e media philosophia? Apud Iudaeum Maimonidem, More Nevochim part. 1. caput. v. est, non esse ad contemplationem rerum divinarum accedendum sine praesente cognitione & intelligentia aliarum scientiarum, & sine emendatione vitae. Vide hoc caput, & etiam cap. xxxiii. Non esse cursum studiorum ab ipsa Theologia incipiendum, sed exercendam prius animum in aliis artibus & disciplinis, adde cap. xxxiv. & lv.
units.tr: Clement of Alexandria, in the first book of the Stromata: Others think that philosophy came into life even with great evil and to the ruin of men, as if it had proceeded from some malign inventor; but he himself proves that it is of divine origin: philosophy is a work of wisdom [Ἡμεῖς ἔργον σοφίας τῆς φιλοσοφίας]. The ancients indeed showed in many places the various errors in pagan philosophy that are hostile to Christian truth: Justin Martyr in his Refutation, or Overthrow of certain Aristotelian doctrines; Tatian at the very beginning of his Oration against the Greeks; Epiphanius in the first book, first volume, of the Panarion; Augustine in the eighth book of The City of God. Yet they did not deny that there is much good and fruit in philosophy, and that it contains things which not only can be reconciled well with the sacred writings but have even flowed from them. Hence Tertullian in the Apology: What poet, what sophist, what one at all has not drunk from the fountain of the prophets? From there, then, the philosophers watered their minds in such a way that what they have from our writings they provide to us in return. And the most learned Selden, in the first book of On the Law of Nature among the Hebrews, chapter 11, shows from Jews, Christian Fathers and pagans that the ancient philosophers Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle and others, having much in common with the Jews, borrowed many things from them for their own philosophy. Therefore the Fathers did not keep themselves from philosophy, but made it quite familiar to themselves. Nobody is ignorant of what Origen did. See his Philocalia in summary, chapter 14, and Homily 14 on Genesis. Add Augustine, On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 40; and against Cresconius the grammarian, book 1, chapters 12, 13 and 17. About Clement, Jerome, in his letter to Magnus: Clement of Alexandria, presbyter of the Church, in my judgment the most learned of all. What is unlearned in his books? Or rather, what is not drawn from the midst of philosophy? Among the Jew Maimonides, in the Guide of the Perplexed, part 1, chapter 5, it is said: one should not approach the contemplation of divine things without first having knowledge and understanding of the other sciences, and without the amendment of life. See this chapter, and also chapter 33: the course of studies should not begin from theology itself, but the mind should first be exercised in other arts and disciplines; add chapters 34 and 55.

units.la: Neque ipsam prorsus Scholasticam excludo, cujus mentionem facio; quia ad philosophiam potius, quam Theologiam referenda videtur: ut hos multi potius (de Scholasticis loquitur) philosophos appellandos censeant, quam Theologos, inquit Beatus Rhenanus, in praefat. ad Tertullianum. Sed hi consulendi, quemadmodum Chamierus in epistolis Iesuiticis, ad Cottonum, scribit se fecisse, non aliter, quam si quis aliquando palatium visitans, post aularum, cubiculorum, coenaculorum magnificentiam, etiam latrinas non dedignetur aspicere, sed parce, ob foetorem. Non soli nostri Scholasticam variis ob causas reprobarunt. ipsi Doctores Papistici saepe, multisque illorum studium reprehendunt, acutum quidem, sed audax, protervum, litigiosum, & inane, multam videlicet partem. Neque nos simpliciter illos rejirejicimus, sed cum distinctione, & cum judicio aliquando fructum etiam aliquem ex iis colligere annitimur: quemadmodum, similis enim fere ratio, studio Rabbinico, non propter deliria ipsorum & nugas, sed propter aurum, quod etiam ex stercore colligitur, & ut adversarios eådem armaturâ retundamus, sic Scholastica, sive Theologiâ, sive Philosophiâ utimur, eamque commendamus. Twissus, Vindiciar. de Electione, lib. 1. part. 11. pag; 281. Neque hoc ideo obtinere volo, quia sic visum est Scholasticis; sed quoniam optimâ mihi videatur ratione niti. Verum nollem etiam à nostris ista rejici, propterea quod sic visum sit Scholasticis. Neque enim fingunt omnia Cretes. Et quamquam in multis plus justo curiosi deprehenduntur, & vani; attamen quamplurima, præsertim de Deo & attributis divinis, solidâ ratione fundata apud ipsos comperiuntur. Et quis unquam è Scholasticis, tot tantaque opinionum portenta procreavit, quot quantaque & parturivit & peperit Conradus Vorstius, & consimiles Socsimani, dum nihil magis crepant, quam non audiendos esse Scholasticos, cum suis inanibus, & vanis ratiocinationibus? Qui eâdem Digressione, se in laudes eximii Theologi, Iohannis Piscatoris multum diffundit, propter accuratam ejus Theologica non vulgariter, sed scholastice tractandi rationem, quam assecutus fuerit solâ sacrarum litterarum professione, communibus tantum disciplinis in subsidium vocatis, Grammaticâ, Rhetoricâ, & Logicâ, ut in eo exemplum extare Deum voluisse censeat, quo demum accuratæ & scholasticæ in rebus ad salutem conducentibus eruditionis, vel ex solâ sacrarum scripturarum lectione, assiduâ meditatione, in eàsque commentatione provchi possimus, missis Summistis, Sententiariis, & Scholasticis ad unum omnibus. Ut nil necesse habuerit adversum nos disputationem instituere Gabriel Vasquez, Scholasticus operosus, in 1. Tom. 1. qu. 1. disp. in de utilitate Theol. Scholastica. non enim Nos omnem Scholasticam contemnimus mus, quod vel sola exempla Danaei, Junii, Trelcatii Iun. Twissi, Ferrii, Spanhemii, Rhetorfortis, aliorumque evincunt, sed quidem meram scholasticam: uti Lutherus ajebat, Thomisticam purum, esse asinum verum, sive sit Italus, sive Germanus, in Resp. ad Catharinum. Eaque ratione non soli haeretici, quos appellant, sed nonnulli etiam catholici in Scholasticam Theologiam ita invehuntur, ut Vasquez haereticos facit adversus eam objicientes. Vide Cornelium Agrippam lib. de vanitate scientiarum, cap. xcvi i. & Melchiorem Canum, loc. Theol. lib. ix. cap. vii. ubi ad inanes illorum subtilitates inquit: puderet me dicere, non intelligere, si ipsi intelligerent, qui haec tradiderunt. Ex Nostris & Protestantibus, quid de Theologia illa Scholast. haberi debeat, vide, ex ipsis adeo Papismi Doctoribus confirmantem, Iohannem Gerhardi, Confess. Cathol. lib. i. part. i i. cap. xv. Robertum Parkerum, obiter, Polit. Eccles. lib. i i. cap. xxxiv. Et venerandum nostrum Voetium, in peculiari de eâ Disputatione. Atrox vero in Scholasticos, & Nostros, veritatem autem maxime, est calumnia Socini, quasi a Scholasticis demum doctrinam de satisfactione Christi accepissemus, part. i v. de Christo servat. cap. i i i. Non mala sunt, quaecunque Scholastici tenent, neque ab ipsis primum nata quae tuentur omnia. Sed cum propter res a Theologica veritate & modestia alienas, tum tractandi eas modum, non satis castum & religiosum, posthabentur. Vbi in aliis probatae fidei articulis saepe egregios se praebent. & acutos disputatores. Iohannes Staupicius, Lutheri & praeceptor, & promotor, Conradum Summerhard, Theologum Tubingensem saepe haec verba usurpare solitum, retulit; Quis me miserum tandem liberabit ab ista rixosa Theologia! Scholasticos invenus. Vere rixosa Theologia: quando, uti bene observavit virorum judiciosissimus Verulamius, in Novo Organo, Scholastici, praeterquam quod Theologiam satis pro potestate in ordinem redegerint, & in artis cefinxefixerint formam. hoc insuper effecerunt, ut pugnax & spinosa Aristotelis philosophia corpori religionis, plusquam par est, immisceretur. V Vetselus Gansfortius, lux mundi suo tempore dictus, trium Facultatum Doctor, inter duces Reformationis merito numeratus, quando in disputationibus sibi authoritas Scholasticorum, hinc Thomæ, inde Seraphici Doctoris objiceretur, haud insciter sic respondere erat solitus: Thomas fuit Doctor, quid tum postea? & ego Doctor sum. Thomas vix latine intellexit, & unilinguis fuit: ego trium principalium linguarum mediocrem peritiam assecutus sum. Thomas vix umbram Aristotelicam vidit: ego Aristotelem Græcum in ipsâ Græciâ didici. Nam in Græciam peregrinatus, Græca addidicerat, & à Græcis sibi nomen retinuerat Basilii.
units.tr: Nor do I altogether exclude the Scholastic theology which I have mentioned, since it seems to belong more to philosophy than to theology: so that many would rather call these men (he speaks of the Scholastics) philosophers than theologians, says Beatus Rhenanus in his preface to Tertullian. But these men should be consulted, as Chamier writes in his letters to Cotton against the Jesuits that he did, and not otherwise than if someone visiting a palace, after the magnificence of the halls, bedchambers and dining rooms, did not disdain to look at the latrines too, but did so sparingly, because of the stench. Not only our people have rejected Scholasticism for various reasons; the Papist teachers themselves often do so, and many of them criticise its study as keen indeed, but bold, pert, quarrelsome and empty, at least for the most part. Nor do we simply reject them; with discrimination and judgment we sometimes strive to gather some fruit even from them, just as with the Rabbinic learning, which we use not for their follies and trifles but for the gold which is also gathered from dung, and in order to repel adversaries with the same weapons. So we use Scholastic theology, or philosophy, and commend it. Twisse, in Vindiciae de electione, book 1, part 2, p. 281: I do not wish to hold this merely because it has seemed right to the Scholastics, but because it seems to me to rest on the best reasoning. Yet I would not want these things to be rejected by our people merely because they have seemed right to the Scholastics. For the Cretans do not always lie. And although in many matters they are found to be more curious than is right, and vain, nevertheless very many things, especially about God and the divine attributes, are found among them founded on solid reason. And which of the Scholastics ever produced so many and such great monsters of opinion as Conrad Vorstius and his like the Socinians gave birth to and brought forth, while they cry out nothing more than that the Scholastics, with their empty and vain reasonings, are not to be heard? In the same digression he spreads himself widely in praise of the eminent theologian John Piscator, for his accurate handling of theology not in a vulgar but in a scholastic manner, which he attained from the profession of sacred letters alone, with only the common disciplines called in to help, grammar, rhetoric and logic. Twisse thinks God wanted an example of this in him, so that we might at last advance to accurate and scholastic learning in matters conducive to salvation, even from the reading of the sacred Scriptures alone and from constant meditation and commentary upon them, dismissing all the Summists, Sentence-men and Scholastics without exception. Gabriel Vasquez, the laborious Scholastic, had no need to set up a dispute against us, in the first volume, question 1, disputation on the usefulness of Scholastic theology. For we do not despise all Scholasticism, as the examples of Danaeus, Junius, Trelcatius the younger, Twisse, Ferry, Spanheim, Rivetus and others prove; but we despise pure Scholasticism, what Luther called Thomism, which is a real donkey whether it is Italian or German, in his reply to Catharinus. For this reason not only so-called heretics but also some Catholics rail against Scholastic theology in such a way that Vasquez makes heretics object against it. See Cornelius Agrippa, the book On the Vanity of the Sciences, chapter 96, and Melchior Cano, Theological Places, book 9, chapter 7, where he says of their empty subtleties: I would be ashamed to say they do not understand, if those who handed these things down understood them themselves. On what our own people and the Protestants should think of that Scholastic theology, see John Gerhard, Confessio catholica, book 1, part 2, chapter 15, confirming it from the very doctors of Papism; Robert Parker, in passing, in Ecclesiastical Polity, book 2, chapter 34; and our venerable Voetius, in his special disputation on it. But the calumny of Socinus, as if we had received the doctrine of Christ's satisfaction from the Scholastics, is atrocious against the Scholastics and against us, and very false, in part 4, On the Preservation of Christ, chapter 3. Not all that the Scholastics hold is bad, nor were all the things they defend first originated by them. But they are set aside, partly because of matters foreign to theological truth and modesty, and partly because of a manner of handling them that is not sufficiently chaste and religious. Yet in other articles of well-attested faith they often show themselves to be excellent and acute disputants. John Staupitz, the teacher and promoter of Luther, reported that Conrad Summerhart, the Tübingen theologian, was often accustomed to use these words: Who will at last free me, wretched man, from this quarrelsome theology! We find the Scholastics so. Truly a quarrelsome theology, since, as the most judicious Verulam wisely observed in the Novum Organum, the Scholastics, besides having reduced theology to order as far as they could and fixed it in the form of an art, have also brought this about, that the combative and thorny philosophy of Aristotle is mingled with the body of religion more than is fitting. Wessel Gansfort, called the light of the world in his time, doctor of the three faculties, rightly numbered among the leaders of the Reformation, when in disputations the authority of the Scholastics was thrown at him, on the one hand Thomas and on the other the Seraphic Doctor, used to answer not unskilfully: Thomas was a doctor; what then? I too am a doctor. Thomas scarcely understood Latin and knew only one language; I have acquired a moderate skill in the three principal languages. Thomas scarcely saw the shadow of Aristotle; I learned the Greek Aristotle in Greece itself. For having travelled to Greece, he had learned Greek there, and from the Greeks he had kept the name Basil.

units.la: Ad controversias quandocunque acceditur, sive inquirendas, cognoscendas, aut tractandas, precibus ad Deum semper communire animum oportet, & implorato anté divino Spiritu, sic demum se committere isti pelago. Quemadmodum quibus periculum est ab infecto aëre, aliquo adversus venenum antidoto se corroborant; ita ubi inter hæreses & errores multi farios versandum nobis est, opus habemus singulari Dei gratiâ, quâ conservemur. Lutherus Georgio Spalatino studiorum methodum præscribens, hoc inter alia monuit, ut à sacrâ ad Deum oratione semper inchoaret: nullus enim, bene ait, est divinorum verborum Magister, præter ipsummet verbi sui auctorem. Tom. I. Operum Lutheri Lat. Bene orasse, inquiebat Idem, est bene studuisse. Iac. 1. 5. Si quis eget sapientiâ, petat à Deo. Bernardus, Serm. ad fratres de monte Dei: quo Spiritu Scripturæ factæ sunt, eo Spiritu legi desiderant, ipso etiam intelligende sunt. Psalm. cxix. 18. Unde in legibus Academiæ Vittembergensis, à Melanthone conscriptis, fuit: sic pie mentes studia inchoent, ut ardentibus votis hanc precationem assiduè repetant; fac cum servo tuo seeundum misericordiam tuam, & justificationes tuas doce me. Retege oculos meos ut intuear mirabilia legis tuae. Augustinus, Serm. 112. de tempore: qui vult cum Deo semper esse, frequenter debet orare, & legere. De Didymo Alexandrino Veteres referunt, quod miscuit precibus studia, & laborem, Ruffinus, histor. lib. 11. cap. vii. Quod ipsum Senex ille suasit Iustino, qui veram sapientiam, quam frustra in Scholis Philosophorum, apud Pythagoricos, Platonicos, & Peripateticos quaesiisset, nullibi repertum iri monebat, quam apud Christianos in S. Scripturis: Tu, inquiebat, votis & precibus tibi ante omnia lucis portas aperiri opta: neque enim ab aliquibus perspicientur aut intelligentur, praeterquam si Deus & Christus eis concesserint intelligentiam.
units.tr: Whenever one approaches controversies, whether to investigate, examine or handle them, one must always fortify the mind with prayers to God, and, having first implored the divine Spirit, only then commit oneself to that sea. Just as those who are in danger from tainted air strengthen themselves with some antidote against poison, so when we must move among many heresies and errors, we need the singular grace of God to keep us safe. Luther, prescribing a method of study to George Spalatin, advised among other things that he always begin with sacred prayer to God: "for no one," he rightly says, "is a master of divine words except the very author of his word." Tom. I. Operum Lutheri Lat. Luther also used to say that to pray well is to have studied well. James 1:5: "If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God." Bernard, Sermon to the brothers on the mountain of God: "by the Spirit by whom the Scriptures were made, by that same Spirit they desire to be read, and by that same Spirit they are to be understood." Ps. 119:18. Hence in the statutes of the University of Wittenberg, written by Melanchthon, it stood: "let pious minds begin their studies in such a way that they constantly repeat this prayer with burning desires: deal with your servant according to your mercy, and teach me your statutes. Uncover my eyes that I may see the wonders of your law." Augustine, Sermon 112 on the time: "whoever wishes always to be with God ought to pray and read frequently." The ancients report of Didymus of Alexandria that he "mingled prayers with his studies and labour," Rufinus, History, book 11, ch. 7. That same old man advised Justin, who had sought true wisdom in vain in the schools of the philosophers, among the Pythagoreans, Platonists and Peripatetics, warning him that it would be found nowhere but among the Christians in the Holy Scriptures: "You," he said, "above all desire that the gates of light be opened to you by vows and prayers; for they cannot be perceived or understood by anyone unless God and Christ grant them understanding."

units.la: Deinde qui velit Controversias Theologicas bene discernere & tractare, se addicere debet S. Scriptura, & continuae ejus lectioni: hinc enim omnis veritas, & de dogmate quovis Theologico habetur judicium. Quilibet Israelita, dicunt Iudæi, tenetur aliquam partem dici & noctis consecrare studio legis, propterea quod scriptum: & meditaberis in ea die ac nocte, Menasse ben Israel, in libro Hispanico, Thesoro dos Dinim, part. 11. cap. 1. Quanto magis Theologus id agat, & Theologiae consecraneus? Biblia Sacra, Institutiones Calvini, Confessio Bezae, & Grammatica Hebraea Cevallerii, Bibliothecam Francisci Junii, quando primum studio Theologico Genevae incumbebat, constituerunt, quibus solis libris diu, sed diligentissime, usus fuit. Et in agrum Limburgicum Idem quando postea excurrit, Evangelii annunciandi causa, solis quae secum sumeret, Bibliis contentus fuit. Apud V Valdenses, qui Sacris destinabantur, nihil ferme ultra studebant, quam ut integros S. Scripturae libros ediscerent: unde apud illos plurimi extitere, etiam ex vulgo, qui universas Pauli epistolas, alii qui Proverbia Salomonis, librum Iobi, aut Psalmos Davidicos memomoriâ tenerent. Idemq; usus obtinuit olim in Collegio Monachorum Augustinianorum Fesulano, quod Florentiâ distat unum lapidem, quo tempore ei se aggregavit Petrus Martyr; ut qui memoria valerent integros ex S. Litteris libros memoriae mandarent, recitarentque. Quod si nostri quoque Studiosi imitarentur, magnum hinc fructum ad studia, quæ Verbo Divino ceu coelestibus aquis jugiter irriganda, redundaturum, certum est. Hoc est Testamenti Christi studiosum esse, quemadmodum Gallicana Ecclesia Irenaeum denominat, in epistolâ commendatoriâ ad Eleutherum, episcopum Romanum, apud Eusebium, lib. v. cap. 1 v. Siquidem non male dixit, quisquis ille fuerit Dionysius, lib. de divinis nominibus, Scripturam esse substantiam nostri Sacerdotii. Et quare non S. Scripturae recitatio, aut repetitio æque haberi vel introduci posset, atque concionum? Erasmus, de Ratione verae Theologiae: nec, meâ sententiâ, fuerit inconsultum divinos libros ad verbum edisce-re, vel non intellectos, autore Augustino.
units.tr: Next, whoever wishes to discern and treat theological controversies well must devote himself to Holy Scripture and its continual reading, for from there comes all truth, and judgment on any theological doctrine. The Jews say that every Israelite is bound to dedicate some part of day and night to the study of the Law, because it is written: "and you shall meditate on it day and night" (Josh. 1:8). Menasseh ben Israel, in his Spanish book Thesoro dos Dinim, part 2, ch. 1. How much more ought a theologian to do this, and be dedicated to theology? The Holy Bible, Calvin's Institutes, Beza's Confession, and Cevallerius's Hebrew Grammar made up the library of Francis Junius when he first applied himself to theological study at Geneva, and he used these books alone, for a long time but most diligently. And when he later went out into the Limburg region to proclaim the Gospel, he was content with the Bible alone, the only thing he took with him. Among the Waldenses, those destined for the sacred ministry studied almost nothing beyond learning whole books of Holy Scripture by heart; hence among them there arose many, even from the common people, who held in memory all of Paul's epistles, others the Proverbs of Solomon, the book of Job, or the Psalms of David. The same practice once prevailed in the Augustinian monastic college at Fiesole, a mile from Florence, when Peter Martyr joined it: those who had good memories committed whole books of Holy Letters to memory and recited them. If our students too imitated this, it is certain that great fruit would flow from it for their studies, which must be watered continually by the Divine Word as by heavenly waters. This is "to be a student of Christ's Testament," as the Gallic Church calls Irenaeus in his letter of commendation to Eleutherus, bishop of Rome, in Eusebius, book 5, ch. 4. Indeed, whoever Dionysius was, he rightly said in the book on the divine names that Scripture is the substance of our priesthood. And why could not the recitation or repetition of Holy Scripture be held and introduced just as well as sermons? Erasmus, on the method of true theology: "nor, in my view, would it be unwise to learn the divine books by heart word for word, even without understanding them, as Augustine advises."

units.la: Atque illis subsidiis ad ipsas dignoscendas controversias feliciter jam se accinget, & tum privatim apud se, tum publice, & cum aliis, & sub aliis studia sua provehet. Primùm leviter & rudi magis cognitione capita controversiarum, ex libris obviis addiscet: deinde distinctius, ex primis & praecipuis utriusque partis antagonistis Scriptoribus, cognoscet ipsam disputationem. Nam, quemadmodum in trivialibus classes sunt, & per gradus adscenditur, ita in toto studiorum cursu ordo observatur, ut ad altiora non praeruptè, sed ordine quodam perveniatur. In litterario ludo, verba sunt Origenis, quibus ille rationem Scholarum suo tempore observatam nobis significat, ubi pueri prima elementa suscipiunt, abecedarii dicuntur quidam, alii syllabarii, alii nominarii, alii jam calculatores appellantur. Sic in Academiâ quoque gradatim itur, & qui ordo est in naturâ, idem etiam in Scholâ, ut à rudioribus bus initiis progressus fiat ad perfectiora. Ita in Controversiis Studiosus confusam primo earum habet notitiam, tum distinctam; & quae non agit in curriculo Academico, ea persequitur postquam illum superavit. Nam qui multorum mos, ut post emensa non infoeliciter studia Academica, & adeptum gradum aliquem, aut nactam promotionem, studiis fere nuntium mittant, saltem iis non insistant, neque ea promovere ulterius, & pergere indies indefesso pede laborent, pessimus est, & causa quod tam pauci gradum suum tueri possint, vel doctrina aliquando excellant.
units.tr: With these aids he will now set about these controversies themselves with good fortune, and advance his studies both privately with himself, publicly, with others, and under others. First he will learn, lightly and with a rather rough knowledge, the heads of the controversies from the books that come to hand; then, more distinctly, he will come to know the disputation itself from the first and chief writers of each side who oppose one another. For just as in the elementary schools there are classes and one advances by steps, so in the whole course of studies an order is observed, so that one reaches higher things not abruptly but by a certain sequence. "In the school of letters," are the words of Origen, by which he tells us of the arrangement of the schools observed in his time, "where boys take up the first elements, some are called abecedarians, others syllabarians, others nominarians, and others now calculators." Thus in the academy too one proceeds gradually, and the order that is in nature is also in the school, so that progress is made from rudimentary beginnings to more perfect things. So in controversies the student first has a confused notion of them, then a distinct one; and what he does not pursue in the academic course, he pursues after he has got through it. For the custom of many, who, after they have finished academic studies not unsuccessfully and obtained some degree or promotion, send their studies almost a farewell, do not keep at them or advance them further, and do not labour day by day with untiring foot, is the worst, and the reason why so few can maintain their degree or ever excel in learning.

units.la: Apud Chinenses, gentem usquequaque sollertem, lex obtinet, ut quam in opificiis vel artificiis urgent ubique apud suos diligentiam & laborem improbum, similem studiis praescribant, eumque non ab illis tantum, qui operam dant ut gradum aliquem assequantur, sed a promotis jam quotannis etiam efflagitant. Quippe tenetur hic eidem se examini singulis annis sistere, uti quando primum promoveretur, nempe ut videatur, an & quos progressus fecerit, & num ad altiora evehendus, vel gradu privandus sit, aliisque multandus poenis. Unde fit, ut omnes quotquot se studiis unquam dedere, diligentiam adhibere summam debeant, aut ad assequendum gradum, aut ad retinendum. Et se vidisse hominem senem, qui quamvis quadragesimum ageret ab accepto gradu annum, tamen continuo se affligebat exercendo poliendoque stylo, & memoriae mandandis facultatis suae libris, quomodo apud nos adolescentes in trivialibus solent, scribit in epistola, de statu rei Chinensis, anno cIↄ Iↄ xcviii. ad Claudium Aquavivam, Iesuitarum Generalem, Nicolaus Longobardus.
units.tr: Among the Chinese, a people everywhere skilled, there is a law that they prescribe for studies the same diligence and tireless labour that they everywhere press upon their people in crafts and trades, and they demand it not only from those who strive to attain some degree but also every year from those already promoted. For such a man is bound to present himself to the same examination each year, just as when he was first promoted, namely so that it may be seen whether and what progress he has made, and whether he is to be raised to higher things or deprived of his degree and punished with other penalties. Hence it follows that all who have ever devoted themselves to studies ought to apply the greatest diligence either to attain their degree or to keep it. And Nicolas Longobardi, in his letter de statu rei Chinensis, written in 1598 to Claudius Aquaviva, General of the Jesuits, writes that he had seen an old man who, though he was forty years past his degree, nevertheless constantly exercised and polished his style and committed to memory the books of his learning, as our young men in the elementary schools are accustomed to do.

units.la: Denique & facit jam Noster sibi Adversaria, seu Locos, quod ajunt, communes Controversiarum, in quae observata hinc inde colligit & conservat, quod si ita videatur, singulis sectis aut religionibus distinctos libros; quem in finem nos quoque in hac Summa totidem libros fecimus. Sunt illa Adversaria ad instar cisternarum, quae aquam undiquaque collectam servant. Quare is fere eruditorum mos est, ut memoriae imperfectioni, imparis ad omnia quae continuo ei obveniunt retinenda, tali adjumento occurrant, praesertim in initio. Isaacus Casaubonus, in Exercitationibus ad Baronium, loquens de libro Nicolai Cabasilae; legi eum librum, inquit, magna cum voluptate, & more meo excerpta confeci nonnulla. Ita quoque veteres. Inter libros Aristotelis meminit Diogenes Laërtius, Τὰ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ Πλάτωνος. Τὰ ἐν τῇ πολιτείᾳ. Τὰ ἐν τῇ Τιμαίῳ. Atque ita jam quaevis legit Studiosus, & ex omnibus observat, quae in suos singula usus seponat. στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀγγελίας commendat Apostolus Timotheo. 1. Tim. v. 13. Legendum autem, quomodo Ambrosium legere solitum Augustinus scribit, Confess. lib. vi, cap. iii. cum legebat, oculi discurrebant per paginas, & cor intellectum rimabatur, vox autem & lingua quiescebant.
units.tr: Finally, our author now makes for himself Adversaria, or, as they say, common places of controversies, in which he gathers and keeps what he observes here and there; and, if it seems good, separate books for each sect or religion, to which end we too have made as many books in this Summa. Those Adversaria are like cisterns that keep water collected from every quarter. Hence it is almost the custom of learned men to meet the weakness of memory, which is unequal to retaining everything that continually comes its way, with such an aid, especially at the beginning. Isaac Casaubon, in his Exercitations against Baronius, speaking of the book of Nicolaus Cabasilas, says: "I read that book with great pleasure, and in my manner I made some excerpts." So too the ancients. Among the books of Aristotle, Diogenes Laertius mentions "the things in Plato's Laws" [Τὰ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ Πλάτωνος], "the things in the Republic" [Τὰ ἐν τῇ πολιτείᾳ], "the things in the Timaeus" [Τὰ ἐν τῇ Τιμαίῳ]. And so the student now reads whatever he reads, and from all of it notes what he sets aside for his own use, each thing separately. The Apostle commends "the elements of the message" [στοιχεῖα τῆς ἀγγελίας] to Timothy, 1 Tim. 5:13. We should read as Augustine writes that Ambrose used to read, Confessions, book 6, ch. 3: "when he read, his eyes ran over the pages and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were at rest."

units.la: Lectioni succedit meditatio, absque qua illa sarcinam menti facit, non fructum. Multa lege quidem, sed plura meditare: illud est cibum in os ingerere, hoc ac si illum stomacho tuo digereres, & sic demum in succum sanguinemque ille revera convertitur. Multa legere, & in lectione subsistere, est onus in se accipere, sub quo fatiscas; meditatio autem explicat illa, & superat, & fructum inde capit utilem jucundumque. Atque non solum docendi in Scholis sunt homines, legere varia: verum etiam meditari posse, & ruminare, disponere, uti denique posse lectis. Hoc pacto mens acuitur, quae alias nimium legendo facile obtunditur. Quae si observes, tum animum tuto dispergere per quosvis libros: nam hinc jam vera erga libros oritur cupiditas & ardor. Non libros, aut librorum titulos, vel pretium, aut raritatem nosse; sive magna librorum strue & bibliotheca te offerre, quasi hoc virum doctum arguat: sed libros, quia boni, quia utiles, atque necessarii, licet pauciores, habere convenit. Non refert quam multos, sed quam bonos habeas, Seneca, epist. xlv. Non tam multos quam optimos libros colligere, inquit Bessarion Cardinalis, in epistola, quâ Venetis suam donat bibliothecam, quæ extat in Centuriâ Epistolarum Philologicarum Goldasti; & prima est inter epistolas Principum, collectas ab Hieronymo Ruscelli, ex Italico Gallice factas, per E. Belleforest. In istius epistolæ initio (scripsit eam anno MCCCCLXVIII.) sic loquitur, & studium erga libros quale suum sit, exponit: Equidem semper à tenerâ fere puerilique ætate omnem meum laborem, omnemque operam, studium, curamque adhibui, ut quoscunque possem libros, in omni disciplinarum genere, compararem. Propterquod non modo plerosque, & puer, & adolescens manu mea conscripsi, sed quicquid pecuniolæ sepponere interim parca frugalitas potuit, in his comparandis absumpsi. Nullam enim magis dignam atque præclaraм suppellectilem, nullum utiliorem præstantioremque thesaurum parare mihi posse existimabam. In quem finem est quoque Richardi Buri Episcopi Dunelmensis scriptum Philobiblion, ubi cap. III. Auctor, nullam caristiam (parcitatem intelligit) hominem debere impedire ab emtione librorum, cum sibi suppetat quod pro iisdem petitur; nisi, inquit, in duobus casibus: vel quando videtur cedendum esse malitiæ venditoris; vel tempus emendi exspectandum opportunius. Capite secundo autem non male dicit, quod contemplatio veritatis nunquam est persectior quam per libros. Apostolus quoque quam suorum librorum curam habuerit, indicat illis ad Timotheum verbis, in posteriori ad eum epistolâ, circa finem: τὸν φαιλόνην, quem Troadæ reliqui apud Carpum, adfer cum venies, & libros, maxime membranas. Τὸν φαιλόνην penulam. Syrus vertit ܦܠܝܛܐ ܡܣܦܪܐ: domum scriptorum habet Tremellius, arcam quâ scripta conservantur: vide de penulâ hâc, præter alios, Baronium Tom. I. ad annum animum lviii. exactissime autem istud argumentum tractantem Bartolum Bartholinum, Casp. F. in singulari de Pœnis Commentario, ubi vestimenti genus fuisse, & quale, multis atque eruditè ostendit, & membrana, Syrus יהודה ... ספירה ... explicat.
units.tr: Reading is followed by meditation, without which reading burdens the mind rather than feeding it. Read much, but meditate on more. Reading is putting food in the mouth; meditation is digesting it in the stomach, and only then is it truly turned into juice and blood. To read much and stop at reading is to take on a load under which you will collapse. Meditation, however, unfolds what you have read, masters it, and draws from it useful and pleasant fruit. Men should be taught in schools not only to read widely but also to meditate, to ruminate, to arrange, and finally to make use of what they have read. In this way the mind is sharpened, whereas by too much reading alone it is easily dulled. If you observe these things, you may safely range over any books at all, for from this a true desire and zeal for books arises. One should not know books only by their titles, their price, or their rarity, nor present oneself with a great pile of volumes and a library, as if that proved a learned man. Rather, it is fitting to have books that are good, useful and necessary, even if they are fewer. It does not matter how many you have, but how good they are, Seneca, Letter 45. Not to collect so many books as the best ones, says Cardinal Bessarion in the letter with which he gave his library to the Venetians, which is found in the Centuria Epistolarum Philologicarum of Goldast, and is the first among the letters of princes collected by Hieronymus Ruscelli, translated from Italian into French by E. Belleforest. At the beginning of that letter (he wrote it in 1468) he speaks thus, and sets out what his zeal for books has been: From almost my tender and childish age I have applied all my labour, all my effort, zeal and care to acquiring whatever books I could in every kind of learning. Therefore not only did I, while still a boy and then a youth, copy out with my own hand a great many, but whatever small sums my thrifty frugality could set aside I spent on acquiring them. For I judged that I could provide no more worthy or splendid furnishing, no more useful or excellent treasure, for myself. To the same purpose is the work Philobiblion of Richard de Bury, Bishop of Durham, where in chapter 3 the author says that no scarcity (he means lack of money) ought to keep a man from buying books, provided he has what is asked for them, unless, he says, in two cases: either when it seems necessary to yield to the greed of the seller, or when a more opportune time to buy is to be awaited. In the second chapter he says not badly that the contemplation of truth is never more perfect than through books. The Apostle also shows how careful he was of his books, in those words at the end of his later letter to Timothy: The cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, bring when you come, and the books, especially the parchments. The cloak is a penula. The Syriac renders it as a case for scrolls, and Tremellius has "a house of writings", that is, a chest in which writings are kept. On this penula, besides others, see Baronius, Vol. I, at the year 58, and for one who treats this subject most exactly, Bartolus Bartholinus, son of Caspar, in his singular Commentary on the Punic (Pœnis) matters, where he shows, learnedly and at length, what kind of garment it was and what it was like; and he explains the parchment (membrana), which the Syriac renders as yehuda ... sefira.

units.la: In libris autem controversiarum evolvendis, & præcipuè in scriptis hæreticorum multo cum judicio versari oportet, ac prudentiâ: quomodo Dionysius Alexandrinus, apud Eusebium, lib. vii. cap. vii. scribit se fecisse, quum jam sciret omnia bene expendere & judicare, ideoque illorum sermonibus non modò non commoveretur, sed usum quoque inde apud se hunc faceret, ut illa diluceret, & magis postea abominaretur. Cribrum se præstare æquum est, quod excussò furfure similam retinet; non saccum, qui facem, post expressum vinum, servat. Quomodo Judæi dicunt, quadruplicem discentium sortem esse: alios spongiarum instar, omnia promiscuè attrahere; alios clepsydræ in modum, quod unâ aure accipiunt, altera mox amittere; tertios, quasi saccos facientes, optimos, cribris similes esse. Duo hæc præcertim, quæ circa illa multum peccari animadverto, observanda in studio controversiarum morosum imprimis attendantur ad sanum controversiæ bene constituendum; in quo nimis ofcitanter multi versantur, & quasi nsummum ab aliis acceptum, quem vix semel vertunt, inhærent, citra diligentius examen, formæ quæstionis, prout ab aliis sæpe facta est, levitor jacta est: quum tamen hinc, ut justissimè ponatur controversiæ terminus, non modò multum lucis accedat toti disputationi, sed & ipsa levior reddatur, & fructum, quem oportet, felicius sic assequamur. Hoc est, quod Tertullianus dicit, summam quæstionis certis lineis determinare, ad lineam disputare: ad unam lineam congressionem dirigere. Alioquin id multoties evenire cernimus, ut nec de eadem re disputent sæpe, qui non leves tamen turbas cient; nec se mutuo (fermè quasi id unum studiose inintenderent) intelligant. Plures quaestiones facilius in initio, circa positionem controversiae, finiuntur, quam post inchoatam, vel habitam disputationem. Ego semper sic ago, & agendum alios doceo, ut in statu quaestionis genuine formando signandoque potissimum operae impendatur: quo ita quaestio melius intelligitur, & alieni nihil Adversario tribuimus, faciliusque argumenta ex re bene posita, quodam naturali ductu quasi profluentia, capiuntur. Plus equidem hic semper sum sollicitus, quam de argumentis: haec etenim, res bene intellecta de se sponte satis promit, suggeritque. Bene Plato, in Cratylo, sub finem: [illegible, ~20 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] Debet quisque circa rei cujusque principium stabilendum multa disserere, diligentissimeque considerare, utrum recte descrip-sit necne, quod quidem sufficienter examinato, caetera jam principium sequi debent.
units.tr: In reading controversial books, and especially the writings of heretics, one must proceed with much judgement and prudence. So Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, Book 7, chapter 7, writes that he did this when he already knew how to weigh and judge everything well; and therefore he was not only not disturbed by their arguments, but made use of them in this way, to clarify them to himself and afterwards to abhor them the more. It is right to act like a sieve, which after the bran is shaken out keeps the fine flour, not like a sack, which keeps the dregs after the wine has been pressed out. The Jews say that there are four sorts of learners: some are like sponges, soaking up everything indiscriminately; some are like a water-clock, which let in through one ear what they receive and let it out at once through the other; some, like sacks, retain the worst; and the best are like sieves. These two points especially, which I observe are where people commonly go most wrong, must be attended to in the diligent study of controversies, for the sound establishment of a controversy. In this many are too careless, and, as if they had received the matter from others as something finished, they cling to it, hardly ever turning it over again, without a more careful examination; the form of the question, as often laid down by others, is lightly stated. Yet from this, if the boundary of the controversy is rightly set, not only does much light come to the whole disputation, but the disputation itself is made easier, and we reach the fruit we ought to reach more happily. This is what Tertullian means when he says that one should define the sum of the question with fixed lines, dispute along a line, and direct the engagement to a single line. Otherwise we often see that those who are not trivial in stirring up disturbances often do not even dispute about the same matter, nor understand one another (as if they were earnestly aiming at nothing else). Many questions are settled more easily at the start, in the statement of the controversy, than after the disputation has begun or been carried on. I always proceed in this way, and teach others to proceed, so that the chief effort goes into forming and marking out the true state of the question. In this way the question is better understood, we attribute nothing alien to our opponent, and arguments are more easily taken from a well-stated matter, flowing, as it were, by a natural course. I am always more anxious about this than about the arguments, for a matter that is well understood brings forth and supplies arguments of its own accord. Plato rightly says in the Cratylus, near the end: [the Greek is illegible in the scan]. Everyone ought, in establishing the starting point of any matter, to discuss much and consider most diligently whether it has been rightly described or not; and once this has been sufficiently examined, the rest should follow from the starting point.

units.la: Alterum quod etiam monendum duxi, est de argumentis, vel disputatione ipsa, ubi non uno peccatur modo. Primum quod nimis festinanter multi ad argumentandum prosiliunt, antequam bene facto quaestionis cardine, inter partes convenerit, quid illud proprie sit de quo controvertitur, vel priusquam tentatum sit, an non forte alio quo modo transigi res possit, quam contentione. Perinde ac si in bello, vel alia quavis discordia mox ad arma quis properet, ubi species modo dissensionis apparet. Deinde non satis accurate attendunt ad filum veritatis, ut sic illud appellem, quo hoc ante omnia indagentur, teneant, & per certa eaque proxima vestigia premant ac sequantur. Est quippe, uti in fodinis, ita in veritatis indagine vena, cujus aliquod caput ubi habes [illegible, ~12 letters], per continuum ductum, nullo facto saltu, religiose id sequaris oportet, fermè uti in disciplinis Mathematicis solemus, pens : quamquè agendi rationem multum secutus Bradwardinus, in disputatione de causâ Dei, contra Pelagianos : nisi quod hic servandum semper fidei principium solum Dei verbum, ex quo regula eorum quæ tenenda sunt, construenda, & quæ neutiquam cum naturâ vel ratione commiscenda vel confundenda est: ut hoc pacto per certa vestigia veritatem ex Dei verbo acquiramus, & simul caput controversum quod spectat, Adversarius se potenti quasi & continuo fluxu delatum in veritatis portum, mirabili & certâ viâ, sentiat. Veritas ubique sibi est similis, omnesque ejus articuli ita sunt inter se conjugati, ut levi, dummodo prudenti & non desultoriâ, declinatione unum ex alio ad oculum fere sequatur. Quare mihi semper probata fuit ratio disputandi Socratica, quâ per continuas pressasque interrogationes & responsiones, veritas in fine ita certo colligitur, concluditurque, ut assensum sui ab omnibus facile impetret: quam cum alibi, tum præcipuè observat Plato in Hippiâ, ubi de pulchro disputatur; eamque se à Parmenide accepisse, ait in Sophistâ: adde ejusdem quoque Theætetum, vel, de scientiâ; & alium, Politicum. Quo quidem modo impossibile fere est in errorem incidere, nisi vel non bene primò arripueris filum illud, quod dixi; vel, non fueris recte sequutus, aut aliquid prætermiseris, & non bene collegeris vestigia. Vel in limine erraris & non apprehenderis veritatis portam illam necesse est, vel saltus feceris, quibus à recto tramite facile tum aberratur. Quorum illi occurres, si meditatò pedem fixeris in thesi manifestâ, & ab utraque parte agnitâ, quantumvis à τοῦ προσκόπου remotiore: huic, si quod in malè subducto calculo fit, per proxima repedes, quantum fieri potest, vestigia, & sensim pedem promoveas in apertiora. Quod errorem quis committit hinc est, quandoquidem ex abrupto in rem mens involat, & non mature, & gradationis secura, temerarios insultus facit, progressus nullos.
units.tr: Another point I thought should also be noted concerns the arguments, or the disputation itself, where errors are made in more than one way. The first is that many rush too hastily into argument before, the pivot of the question having been well fixed, the parties have agreed what precisely that is about which they dispute, or before it has been tried whether the matter might not be settled in some other way than by contention. It is like someone who rushes to arms in war or any other discord as soon as the mere appearance of disagreement shows itself. Next, they do not attend closely enough to the thread of truth, as I may call it, by which all things must first be sought out, held, and followed along certain and nearby tracks. For in the search for truth, as in mines, there is a vein; when you have found its head, you must follow it religiously along a continuous course, without any leap, somewhat as we are accustomed to do in mathematical disciplines. I have followed this method largely, as did Bradwardine in his disputation On the cause of God against the Pelagians; except that here the principle of faith must always be kept, namely God's word alone, from which the rule of what is to be held is to be constructed, and which must by no means be mixed or confused with nature or reason. In this way we acquire the truth from God's word by sure tracks, and at the same time the opponent, carried along as by a strong and continuous current on the head of the controversy that concerns him, perceives that he has been brought into the harbour of truth by a wonderful and certain way. Truth is everywhere like itself, and all its articles are so joined to one another that, by a light, prudent and not wandering turn, one can follow almost by sight from one to another. Therefore the Socratic method of disputing has always pleased me, in which, through continual and close questions and answers, the truth is at the end so surely gathered and concluded that it easily wins assent from all. Plato observes this everywhere, but especially in the Hippias, where the beautiful is discussed; and he says in the Sophist that he received it from Parmenides. Add also his Theaetetus, or On Knowledge, and another, the Politicus. Indeed, by this method it is almost impossible to fall into error, unless you did not first rightly seize that thread which I have mentioned, or did not follow it properly, or omitted something and did not gather the tracks well. Either you must err at the threshold and not grasp the gate of truth, or you will make leaps, by which one is easily led astray from the straight path. You will meet the first if you have firmly planted your foot on a manifest thesis, acknowledged by both parties, however far it may be from the look-out [τοῦ προσκόπου]. Against the second, if something has gone wrong in a badly reckoned sum, go back along the nearest tracks as far as you can, and gradually advance your foot into more open ground. The error that a person commits comes from this: the mind flies at the matter all at once, and not maturely, and without the security of gradual steps, makes rash assaults and no progress.

units.la: Vltimum quod moneam est, ne arbitremur numero & copia argumentorum in disputationibus rem agi. Sunt qui putant solâ fere multitudine victoriam obtineri, quos sua ratio vehementer fallit. Non numero, sed pondere argumenta æstimanda, & pauca mala, quam plura. Argumentum mihi est, non quælibet ratio, quæ in disputatione forte adferri, sed quæ consistum sustinere potest integrum, & sibi sufficit, ut adversus omnes exceptiones perstet. Talia vero haud adeo multa sunt, quæ rebus ipsis quasi enata & ordinem suum, & vim omnibus commonstrant, simulque Disputatoris probant tum judicium, tum eruditionem. Ad quæ demum ultimo loco accedit, eorum bene utendorum dexteritas: scilicet ne de nobis dici possit, quod de Carolostadio Zuinglius, idem ei accidisse, quod Tyroni, cui arma quidem ad pugnandum non deessent, sed armorum peritia.
units.tr: The last point I would advise is that we should not think a dispute is decided by the number and quantity of arguments. Some believe victory is won almost by numbers alone, and their reasoning greatly misleads them. Arguments are to be weighed, not counted, and a few good ones are better than many bad ones. By an argument I mean not any reason that might happen to be brought forward in a dispute, but one that can hold its ground entire, that is sufficient in itself, and that stands firm against every objection. Such arguments are not very many. They arise, as it were, from the matters themselves, and they show their own order and force to everyone, while at the same time they prove the disputant's judgment and learning. Last of all comes dexterity in using them well, so that it cannot be said of us what Zwingli said of Carlstadt: that he had the same experience as a recruit who has weapons for fighting but no skill in handling them.

units.la: Atque hæc nos impræsentiarum de Controversiis, & Disputationibus Theologicis. Confersis quæ habet eximius Theologus, Georgius Sohnius, Tom. I. de verbo Dei, lib. II. de tractatione Scriptura Sacra elenchica, id est de disputatione, seu disputandi ratione. Chemnitius, in Prolegom. ad locos Theologicos. Nam libellum Matthiæ Hõe, de Disputationibus Theologicis, ne commendem, ipse satis facit futilis: nisi convitiari & calumniari malis, quam quod est vere & Theologice disputare. Ego vero potius suadeo, ut hoc in loco legantur Augustini libri quatuor, de doctrina Christiana, (quibus, quando Scriptorem hunc commendo, jungere soleo ejusdem Confessionum libros.) Scriptorum ejus facile optimos, inque primâ editione Basileensi Amorbachianâ, ante alteram Erasmi, eâdem parte, quartâ videlicet, conjunctos) addito ejus quoque Enchiridio, tum ob doctrinæ utilis materiam, tum ob gustum aliquem capiendum Scriptorum antiquorum, quibus quantum debeamus, soli ignorant, qui ea non legerunt. Atque, ex Augustino quidem, & libro quem diximus, Confessionum x i. cap. 1 1. [?] hanc, ante studia dicendam precationem, nobisque saepe usurpatam, hic exhibere, tandem ut finiam, haud inconsultum duxi:
units.tr: So much for now concerning controversies and theological disputations. Compare what the distinguished theologian Georg Sohn has written in volume I, on the Word of God, book II, on the handling of Holy Scripture in refutation, that is, on disputation, or the method of disputing. Chemnitz, in the Prolegomena to the Theological Commonplaces. As for the little book by Matthias Höe, On Theological Disputations, I will not recommend it, since it is rather trifling in itself, unless you would rather revile and slander than dispute truly and theologically. I would advise instead that at this point one read the four books of Augustine on Christian doctrine (which, whenever I commend this writer, I am accustomed to join with the books of his Confessions), as well as his best writings, which in the first Basel edition of Amerbach, before Erasmus's, were gathered together in the same part, namely the fourth, with his Enchiridion added, both for the useful matter of its teaching and so that one may get a taste of the ancient writers, to whom we owe so much that only those who have not read them do not know it. And from Augustine, indeed from the book I have mentioned, the Confessions book XI, chapter 1 [?], I have thought it not unwise, to conclude, to set out here the prayer to be said before study, which I have often used myself:

units.la: Deus meus, intende orationi meae, & misericordia tua exaudiat desiderium meum; quoniam non mihi soli est natum, sed usui vult esse fraternae charitatis; & vides in corde meo, quia sic est, ut sacrificem tibi famulatum cogitationis, & linguae meae, & da, quod offeram tibi. Inops enim & pauper sum, tu dives in omnes invocantes te, qui securus curam nostri geris. Circumcide ab omni temeritate, ab omnique mendacio interiora, & exteriora labia mea. Sint casta delitiae meae scripturae tuae, nec fallar in eis, nec fallam ex eis. Largire inde spatium meditationibus nostris in abdita legis tuae, neque adversus pulsantes claudas eam. Neque enim frustra scripsisti voluisti tot paginarum opaca secreta, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, qui sedet ad dexteram tuam, & te interpellat pro nobis, in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae & scientiae absconditi. Amen.
units.tr: My God, give ear to my prayer, and let your mercy hear my longing, since it is born not for myself alone but is meant to serve brotherly love; and you see in my heart that it is so, that I offer you the service of my thought and tongue, and give me what I may offer you. For I am needy and poor, but you are rich toward all who call upon you, you who care for us without anxiety. Circumcise from my inner and outer lips all rashness and all lying. Let your Scriptures be my chaste delight; let me not be deceived in them, nor deceive others from them. Grant room to my meditations on the hidden things of your law, and do not shut it against those who knock. For you did not write those dark secrets of so many pages in vain, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Amen.

units.la: Summae Controversiarum RELIGIONIS. Liber Primus, DE GENTILISMO.
units.tr: Summa of Controversies of Religion. Book One, On Gentilism.

units.la: Multa huc spectantia rejiciuntur in Tractatum alium. Interim necessitas harum disputationum commendatur, & argumenti praesentis Scriptores, antiqui & posteriores, recensentur. Schema & series controversiarum cum Gentilibus.
