units.tr: Many matters that bear on this subject are reserved for another treatise. Meanwhile the need for these disputations is commended, and the writers on this subject, ancient and modern, are listed. The scheme and sequence of the controversies with the Gentiles.

units.la: VUm constitutum nobis sit, singulari tractatu agere de Conversione Ethnicorum, ubi data opera in statum Gentilismi, praecipuè hodierni, sumus inquisituri; tum disputationem, ac denique de eorum conversione dissertationem instituturi, illa quae eò spectant, jam omittere, & in ipsum locum servare visum, annotatis hic duntaxat controversiarum hujus argumenti capitibus, quantum studioso scire ad disputandum, & tum ad studia, tum collegia elenctica instituenda necesse videbitur. Neque omnino abs re in hoc negotio, quod sulcus multis videri posset peregrinum nimis, si non supervacuum, ubi tanta scilicet aliarum & inter Christianos agitatarum quæstionum, quæ nos exercent, copia, occupantur: quinimo propter idipsum laudabile videri debet propositum nostrum, quod, quum ultra modum ferè Christiani inter se litigent, provido consilio, neque neglectis quæ alibi sunt justis controversiis, Veteres Romanos, & Germanos imitati, qui quos domi habebant bellicosos spiritus, ad externa & remotiora destinabant, ita nos juvenum animos ad disputandum pronos, in illa subinde revocamus quæ Ecclesiæ cum extraneis supersunt, ne hæc ignorent, vel ne curent minus, neutiquam sanè levioris momenti, quam reliqua. Quomodo Germani, Romanique, ita & Alexander, apud Græcos, pro inferendo Persis bello, olim disseruit: Domestica quieti ea ratione prospectum iri, amotis occupatisque longinquâ militiâ, qui ociosi discordiis & audaciâ res turbare consueverint.
units.tr: Since I have resolved to treat the conversion of the Gentiles in a separate treatise, in which I shall deliberately inquire into the state of Gentilism, especially as it stands today, and then set out the disputation and finally the discourse on their conversion, I have decided to leave out for now the points that belong there and to keep them for that place. Here I shall only note the heads of the controversies on this subject, as far as a student will need to know them for disputing, and for setting up both the studies and the elenctic colleges. Nor is this undertaking entirely out of place, though it may seem to some too remote a furrow, if it is not superfluous, since so many other questions are debated among Christians and occupy us. Indeed our purpose ought to seem praiseworthy for this very reason. Christians quarrel among themselves beyond measure, and so, with a wise plan, without neglecting the just controversies that exist elsewhere, we imitate the ancient Romans and Germans, who directed the warlike spirits they had at home toward foreign and more distant enemies. Likewise we turn the minds of young men, which are prone to disputation, back again to those matters that remain between the Church and outsiders, so that they do not ignore these or care less for them, though they are by no means of lesser importance than the rest. As the Germans and Romans did, so Alexander, among the Greeks, once argued for making war on the Persians: domestic quiet would be secured in this way, when those who are used to stirring up trouble through idleness, discord and boldness are removed and kept busy with a distant campaign.

units.la: Multos quidem magnique nominis Theologos pro nobis habemus, qui Theologiæ hoc cum Gentilibus tractarunt argumentum, præcipue inter Veteres, quando ex Gentilismo Ecclesia quotidie colligebatur, & augescebat; etiam inter Posteriores, qui quamdiu Gentilium tanta ubique copia est, & officium nostrum perpetuum pro illorum invigilare conversione, non omnino hic omittendum bene censuerunt, quos tum sequimur, & hoc in loco recensemus, ut studio huic se tradituri cognoscant, quos Auctores vel volumina consulere liceat. Inter Veteres sunt, Iustinus Martyr, Athenagoras, Theophilus Alexandrinus, Tatianus Assyrius, Clemens Alexandrinus, Origenes, Eusebius, Athanasius, Nazianzenus, Chrysostomus, ex Græcis. Inter Latinos, primus Tertullianus, Minucius Felix, Cyprianus, Arnobius, Lactantius, Augustinus. Hi antiqui. Ex Posterioribus, Thomas Aquinas, Marsilius Ficinus, Raimundus Sebon, Ludovicus Vives, Joh. Fridericus Lumnius, Ludovicus Granatensis tensis, Petrus Charron, Philippus Mornaeus, Antonius Possevinus, Thomas à Jesu, Martinus Fotherby, Iohannes Yates, Alexander Ross. Hugo Grotius, Mirelius, Amyraldus. De quibus omnibus & singulis judicium alibi interponimus.
units.tr: We indeed count among our allies many theologians of great name who have treated this subject of theology with the Gentiles, especially among the ancients, when the Church was daily gathering and growing out of Gentilism. Among the later writers too, since there is such a great multitude of Gentiles everywhere, and since our continual duty is to keep watch for their conversion, they have thought it not right to omit this subject here. We follow them and list them in this place, so that those who are about to devote themselves to this study may know which authors or volumes it is permitted to consult. Among the ancients are Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Theophilus of Alexandria, Tatian the Assyrian, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Eusebius, Athanasius, Gregory Nazianzen, and Chrysostom, from the Greeks. Among the Latins, first Tertullian, Minucius Felix, Cyprian, Arnobius, Lactantius, and Augustine. These are the ancients. Of the later writers: Thomas Aquinas, Marsilio Ficino, Raymond Sebond, Ludovicus Vives, Johann Friedrich Lumnius, Luis de Granada, Pierre Charron, Philippe Mornay, Antonio Possevino, Thomas à Jesu, Martin Fotherby, John Yates, Alexander Ross. Hugo Grotius, Mirelius, Amyraut. On all of these, both individually and together, we give our judgment elsewhere.

units.la: Omnis autem cum Gentilibus disputatio est, vel de illis quae ex natura ostendi, docerique possunt, vel de aliis, quae supra naturam, aliunde ex supernaturali revelatione aut Theologia, quae in Dei verbo est, petuntur. Quippe cum duplex omnino sit Theologia, naturalis prima, sed imperfecta; altera supernaturalis, & consummata: quarum illa Gentiles abutuntur, hanc ignorant, utraque illos docenda venit, illiusque defectus hinc supplendi, ut ad fidem, atque salutem perducantur. Super illius, Theologiae naturalis puta, capitibus disputamus ex communi principio naturae, & rationis, quamdiu aliud non habent. Inde ad persuadendum hoc supernaturale divinae veritatis principium, per remotionem omnium adversus id, quae habere possint, praejudiciorum & objectionum, progredimur.
units.tr: Every disputation with the Gentiles concerns either those things that can be shown and taught from nature, or those things that lie above nature and are sought from supernatural revelation, or from the theology that is in the Word of God. For theology is altogether twofold: the natural, which is first but imperfect, and the supernatural, which is complete. The Gentiles misuse the former and are ignorant of the latter. Both must be taught to them, and the defects of the first must be supplied from the second, so that they may be brought to faith and salvation. On the heads of that natural theology we dispute from the common principle of nature and reason, as long as they have nothing else. From there we proceed to persuade them of this supernatural principle of divine truth, by removing all the prejudices and objections they may have against it.

units.la: Etenim praeter defectum Theologiae naturalis, ostendimus hic nihil rationis adversus Dei verbum adferri posse, quo minus divina ejus veritas, tot testata insignitiis notis, aliisque argumentis, agnoscatur; ubi nec improbabile, tale aliquod Dei verbum dari, quum & ipsi Gentiles hic sua jactent, sive oracula, sive Sacros codices; uti Brachmanni suum Vedam, alii alia, manente quaestione, utra lex, illorum, an nostra, & quam habemus, Scriptura S. praeferenda sit? Ad Theologiam naturalem, juxta capita Decalogi, quaestiones dispartiri possunt in illas quae Deum, & quae hominem concernunt. Ibi quaeritur, de Dei primum natura, seu essentia, an, & quid, & quis sit? Deinde, de ejus operibus, nempe de creatione, tum providentia. Tertio de cultu Dei, in genere primum, tum in specie: nam diversi generis Gentiles sunt: alii barbaricam professi, ex adververbo speciem saltem quasi religionis, alii: utrique peccant, illi quia nullam, hi quia malam habent, & sequuntur religionem. Ergo & colendum Deum esse, & non per idololatriam, aut multiplicem superstitionem, sed & abjurata omni (cui plurimi inter illos sunt addictissimi) magiâ, docendum. Secundo, post Deum loco, agendum de homine, deque eo considerato primum in se, tum erga alios. Ibi de animae humanae immortalitate, hominis antipathia; de animarum metempsychosi: quae postrema apud multos Gentilium in usu, & creduntur.
units.tr: For apart from the defect of natural theology, we show here that no reason can be brought against the Word of God that would prevent its divine truth from being acknowledged, a truth attested by so many remarkable marks and other arguments. Nor is it improbable that some such word of God has been given, since the Gentiles themselves boast of theirs here, whether oracles or sacred books: thus the Brahmans have their Veda, and others have others. The question then remains: which law is to be preferred, theirs or ours, that is, the holy Scripture we possess? According to the heads of the Decalogue, the questions of natural theology can be divided into those that concern God and those that concern man. Here the first question is about the nature or essence of God: whether he is, and what and who he is. Next, about his works, namely creation and then providence. Third, about the worship of God, first in general and then in particular. For the Gentiles are of different kinds: some profess a barbarous religion, others a kind of religion only in appearance; both err, the former because they have no religion, the latter because they have a bad one and follow it. Therefore it must be taught both that God is to be worshipped, and not through idolatry or manifold superstition, but also with all magic renounced, to which very many among them are most devoted. Second, after God, man must be treated, considered first in himself and then in relation to others. Here we speak of the immortality of the human soul, of man's antipathy, and of the transmigration of souls, which last is in use among many Gentiles and is believed.

units.la: Homine considerato in societate humanâ, ut cum aliis, & inter eos vivit, controversiam facit primum audita corporis, palam in hominum conviictu usitata inter Gentilium multos, qui absque vestimentis incedunt; ipsorum feritas, quâ se mutuo caedunt & dilaniant; tum vulgata inter ipsos fornicatio, incestus etiam, & polygamia. Haec hactenus capita ex lege & Theologiâ naturali decidi queunt: praeter quae, ut vides, multa adhuc ad veram religionem & salutem cognitu sunt necessaria; sed quae ex illo naturali principio non habentur. Quare altius figere pedem jam necesse est, & sublimiorem rerum sphaeram adscendere, videlicet ad veritates Theologiae supernaturalis, quae ex sola Dei revelatione habentur, & verbo.
units.tr: When man is considered in human society, as he lives with others and among them, the first controversy concerns the nakedness of the body, which is openly practised in the company of men by many Gentiles who go about without clothes. It concerns their savagery, by which they slaughter and tear one another apart. It concerns the fornication commonly practised among them, incest too, and polygamy. These heads can be settled so far from the law and from natural theology. Apart from these, as you see, many things are still necessary to know for the true religion and salvation, but these are not available from that natural principle. Therefore we must now plant our foot more deeply and ascend to a higher sphere of things, namely to the truths of supernatural theology, which are had from God's revelation alone, and from the Word.

units.la: Sed in antecessum duo praelibanda mihi videntur, quorum primum ad superiora pertinet, & claudit ea, nimirum de vanitate philosophiae & philosophorum, in ordine ad salutem, tum, quod ad sequentia spectat aliud, de praestantia religionis Christianae, in genere, quae ipsa praesertim in eo consistit, quod librum istum, quo superiam veritatem consignavit Deus, possidet. Hic ergo de verbo Dei agendum prius, ejusque divinitas quibuscunque adstruenda argumentis. Tum ex isto Dei verbo plenius jam ostendenda illa capita, quae supra ex naturali cognitione aliquantum, sed imperfecte exexpösita fuerunt : circa Deum, de Personarum in Deo Trinitate, de hominis creatione, & lapsu: de Christo, de justi-ficatione, sanctificatione, denique de hominis extremis, de resurrectione, judicio, cælo, & inferno. Inter quæ sunt, quorum nulla apud Gentiles, vel in illorum Theologiâ strictura apparet, ut de S. Trinitate, Christo, vel nostra ex mortuis resurrectione, alia nonnullam partem nota illis fuerunt, quamvis obscure & imperfecte: hæc jam ex Dei verbo confirmantur, & docentur plenius. Verùm sciendum, quod illa, quæ ex Dei verbo dicimus ultimo docenda esse, non per disputationem, sed solâ ex Dei verbo ostensione & expositione debeant peragi, admissâ semel Verbi divinitate, post quam fide accipere oportet quæ à Deo nobis revelantur, non ea rationibus disceptari, nisi quod scrupuli interim, & si quas habent aut movent, difficultates excindendæ ac solvendæ semper sint. Atque illa quæstionum capita, ex quibus formandæ controversiæ, super quibus cum Gentilibus instituitur disputatio.
units.tr: But before that, two things seem to me to need to be set out in advance. The first pertains to what has gone before and closes it: namely, the vanity of philosophy and of the philosophers with respect to salvation. The second, which concerns what follows, is the excellence of the Christian religion in general, which consists especially in its possession of that book in which God has deposited the higher truth. Here, then, we must first treat of the Word of God, and establish its divinity by whatever arguments. Then, from that Word of God, we must now show more fully those heads which were set out above, to some extent but imperfectly, from natural knowledge: concerning God; concerning the Persons in the Trinity of God; concerning the creation and fall of man; concerning Christ; concerning justification and sanctification; and finally concerning the last things of man: the resurrection, judgment, heaven and hell. Among these there are some of which no trace appears among the Gentiles or in the strictures of their theology, such as the Holy Trinity, Christ, or our resurrection from the dead. Other points were known to them in some part, though obscurely and imperfectly; these are now confirmed from the Word of God and taught more fully. But it must be understood that those things which we say must be taught last from the Word of God should be carried out not by disputation, but solely by showing and expounding the Word of God. Once the divinity of the Word is admitted, we must accept by faith what is revealed to us by God, and such things should not be contested by reasons, except that any scruples and difficulties they have or raise should always be cut away and resolved. These are the heads of questions from which the controversies are to be formed, on which the disputation with the Gentiles is set up.

units.la: Controversiæ autem hæ sunt, vel super hisce capitibus: nam pro re natâ illas vel sub interrogatione, vel assertivè proponere visum fuit.
units.tr: These controversies are either on the following heads: for, as occasion requires, it has seemed right to put them sometimes as questions and sometimes as assertions.

units.la: I. Deum esse, certis ex naturâ rationibus probari potest, & debet.
units.tr: I. That God exists can and must be proved from certain reasons drawn from nature.

units.la: II. Deus est ens perfectissimum.
units.tr: II. God is the most perfect being.

units.la: III. An Deus sit unus? an plures Dii. Resp. prius.
units.tr: III. Whether God is one, or whether there are many gods? Answer: the former.

units.la: IV. Deus est incorporeus, & incorruptibilis.
units.tr: IV. God is incorporeal and incorruptible.

units.la: V. Quis sit Deus? Resp. Creator cæli, terræque.
units.tr: V. What is God? Answer: the Creator of heaven and earth.

units.la: VI. An mundus à Deo sit creatus? Aff.
units.tr: VI. Was the world created by God? Affirmative.

units.la: VII. An quoque Deus mundum à se creatum providentiâ suâ sustentet, ac gubernet? Aff.
units.tr: VII. Does God also sustain and govern the world he created by his providence? Affirmative.

units.la: VIII. Deus ille omni religione à nobis colendus est.
units.tr: VIII. That God is to be worshipped by us with all religion.

units.la: IX. Nulli, præter istum unum Deum, Dii alii habendi, aut venerandi.
units.tr: IX. No other gods besides this one God are to be held or venerated.

units.la: X. Nullæ Dei faciendæ sunt imagines, aut si-musimulachra ulla religiose habenda.
units.tr: X. No images of God are to be made, nor is any idol to be held in religious reverence.

units.la: XI. Vana est omnis superstitio, ut & divinatio.
units.tr: XI. All superstition is vain, and so is divination.

units.la: XII. Nefas est Magiam exercere.
units.tr: XII. It is wrong to practise magic.

units.la: XIII. An anima hominis sit immortalis? Aff.
units.tr: XIII. Is the soul of man immortal? Affirmative.

units.la: XIV. Hominem seipsum interimere, est contra naturam, & rationem.
units.tr: XIV. For a man to take his own life is contrary to nature and reason.

units.la: XV. Num à morte hominis, ejus anima commigret in alienâ corpora, sive hominum, sive bestiarum? Neg.
units.tr: XV. Does the soul of a man, after his death, pass into other bodies, whether of men or of beasts? Negative.

units.la: XVI. Hominem nudo corpore incedere, & versari inter homines, indecorum.
units.tr: XVI. For a man to go about with a naked body and mix among men is unseemly.

units.la: XVII. Alium cædere, nedum interficere, aut devocare, haud humanum est.
units.tr: XVII. To strike another, let alone to kill him or call him to account, is not human.

units.la: XVIII. Fornicari, vel incestum committere, aut polygamiam exercere, illicita.
units.tr: XVIII. Fornication, or committing incest, or practising polygamy, is unlawful.

units.la: XIX. Gentilium Philosophia nequit hominem perducere ad verum & summum bonum, vel salutem.
units.tr: XIX. Gentile philosophy cannot bring a man to the true and highest good, or to salvation.

units.la: XX. Sola salutem praestat religio Christiana.
units.tr: XX. Only the Christian religion gives salvation.

units.la: XXI. S. Scriptura complectitur verum Dei verbum estque divinae authoritatis.
units.tr: XXI. Holy Scripture contains the true Word of God and is of divine authority.

units.la: XXII. Ex Dei verbo certò docetur:
units.tr: XXII. From the Word of God it is taught with certainty:

units.la: In Deo Personarum Trinitas.
units.tr: That in God there is a Trinity of Persons.

units.la: Hominem fuisse creatum sanctum, ad Dei imaginem.
units.tr: That man was created holy, in the image of God.

units.la: Per peccatum primorum Parentum prolapsum fuisse hominem in omnem miseriam, peccati, & poenae.
units.tr: That through the sin of our first parents man fell into all misery of sin and punishment.

units.la: Christum Θεὸν [?]ἄνθρωπον esse nostrum redemptorem.
units.tr: That Christ is God-man [?] and our Redeemer.

units.la: Homines coram Deo justificari per justitiam Christi.
units.tr: That men are justified before God through the righteousness of Christ.

units.la: Nos à Deo per ejus Spiritum sanctificari.
units.tr: That we are sanctified by God through his Spirit.

units.la: Post mortem iterum hoc in corpore nos resurrectu-ros.
units.tr: That after death we shall rise again in this body.

units.la: Ad generale omnium judicium.
units.tr: To the general judgement of all.

units.la: A quo beatos manet in coelo aeterna felicitas.
units.tr: From which eternal happiness remains for the blessed in heaven.

units.la: Improbos gehenna.
units.tr: The wicked to hell (gehenna).

units.la: Liber Secundus. DE JUDAISMO.
units.tr: Book Two. ON JUDAISM.

units.la: Necessitas studii Controversiarum Judaicarum. Scandalum aut non, aut male hic disputantium. Notitia & usus linguae Hebraeae. Controversiae.
units.tr: The necessity of the study of Jewish controversies. Whether scandal arises, or not, from those who dispute here badly. Knowledge and use of the Hebrew language. Controversies.

units.la: QVod in legibus Atheniensium erat, ἀσεβείας ἐδίκ ταλαιπωρίας, cumque Dei legem multis modis conveniens, ut aberrantibus viam ostendamus, id sicubi locum habet apud Iudaeos certe, miseram hodie, quantum olim felix, gentem omnibus verè Christianis magnâ operâ observandum venit: dispersi, palabundi, & cali & sedi sui exsortes vagantur per orbem sine homine sine Deo rege, quibus nec advenarum jure terram patriam saltem vestigio salutare concedituy, inquit de illis Tertullianus, in Apolog. & post eum, de iisdem similiter ejus discipulus, Cyprianus. Quinam ubicunque homines miserandum magis in modum errant, quam Iudaei, qui ante Deo proximi, soli gaudebant verae religionis notitiâ, & salutis aeternae spe, quâ utrâque nunc juxta carent. Scripturam retinent adhuc, & non quotidie minus, quam Sabbathis legunt, vectigali libertate, uti Tertullianus amat loqui: Sed & Iudei palam lectitant, vectigalis libertas vulgò editur, sabbathis omnibus. Verùm eo infeliciores, quo non intelligunt illa, quae sola iis pridem indulta, quaeque, quo minus ab ipsis capiuntur, capiunt eos, & per ipsorum vitia tenent magis sectari tos. Interim pristini temporis memoria, & futurae, forte etiam instantis, liberationis spes ut magis animum erga eos nostrum commovet, & ad commiserationem provocat, ita alacriores facit ad studium & negotium. gotium omne nostrum ipsorum conversioni quanto ocyus impendendum. In quo nolo ut meorum ullus desit, & opus detrectet, ob omissam hac in parte, si qua à me fieri possit, institutionem; aut non excitatum animum, zelumque, meâ quà doctrinâ, quà exemplo. Quippe dignius nullum novi argumentum, in quo occupemur, & ubi majori spe opera nostra collocetur, quam hic. Alii aliter sentiant, ac malint vires ingenii animique sui convertere in proximiores ipsis Christianos, ego à primo studiorum, quin adolescentiæ tempore, singulari me impetu erga Iudæos, & eorum disputationes, conversionemque actum scio: unde, ante quemcumque. Theologum [?]elencticum, legisse memini, quia alium hujus argumenti copiosiorem ignorabam, Galatinum. Ex quo hæsit animo, ut in Academiâ vel præcipuè Iudaica commendem, & tum publicis, tum privatis Lectionibus, & Disputationibus hoc in argumento me, aliosque, crebrius exerceam, si forte placeat Deo, ut periodus, quam populi istius conversioni præscripsit, sit præ foribus, ibique nostrâ, vel nostrorum eâ in re operâ uti.
units.tr: What existed in the laws of the Athenians as a charge of impiety [ἀσεβείας ἐδίκ], and what suits the law of God in many ways, so that we may show the way to those who have gone astray, is certainly to be pursued with great effort by all who are truly Christians, wherever it applies among the Jews, a people now as wretched as once they were happy. Scattered and wandering, without heaven and without their own soil, they roam the earth without a man and without a God as king, and not even by the right of strangers is the land of their fathers granted them to set foot upon, says Tertullian of them in his Apology, and after him his disciple Cyprian says the same of them. Nowhere are men more wretchedly in error than the Jews, who once stood nearest to God and alone rejoiced in the knowledge of true religion and in the hope of eternal salvation, and now lack both alike. They still keep Scripture, and read it every day no less than on the Sabbaths, by the freedom of tribute, as Tertullian likes to put it: But the Jews also read it openly; the freedom of tribute is given out to all the Sabbaths. But they are the more unhappy because they do not understand those things which were once granted to them alone, and which, the less they are grasped by them, the more they grasp them, and hold them to be pursued through their own vices. Meanwhile, the memory of former times and the hope of a future, perhaps even impending, deliverance move our minds toward them, and as it stirs our compassion, so it makes us more eager for study and labour. All our effort should be devoted as quickly as possible to their conversion. In this I wish that none of my people be lacking, or shrink from the work, on account of the neglect, in this respect, of instruction (if any can be made by me), or an animus and zeal not stirred up by my teaching and example. Indeed I know of no more worthy subject to occupy ourselves with, nor one in which our labour may be placed with greater hope, than this. Others may think otherwise and prefer to turn the powers of their mind and spirit upon Christians nearer to themselves. I know that from the first of my studies, indeed from my youth, I was driven by a singular impulse toward the Jews, their disputations and their conversion. Hence, before any other theologian of controversy, I remember reading Galatinus, since I did not know of another more copious on this subject. From this it has stuck in my mind to commend this subject above all in an academy especially Jewish, and to exercise myself and others more often in it, by public and private lectures and disputations, if it pleases God by chance that the period which he has prescribed for the conversion of that people is at the doors, and that we may use there our labour, or that of our people, in this matter.

units.la: De Conrado Pellicano scimus; cum à primâ juventute vehementi ardore flagrasse erga Hebraica; hâc occasione, quod puer audisset aliquando disputantem cum Iudæis Christiânum, adeo infœliciter, ut non à Iudæo solum, sed etiam Iudæâ muliere Doctor Theologus turpiter confunderetur: id quod animum Pellicani tantopere cruciabat, ut hinc insatiabili studio ad Hebraica & Iudaica pernoscenda indesinenter agitatus fuerit, inque iis adeo profecerit; quamvis summâ difficultate, maximâ quę istius temporis erat, librorum Hebraicorum & Magistrorum penuriâ, ut in Rabbinicis, Chaldaicis, Talmudicis etiam, quod fere miraculi loco habebatur, multo cum fructu versaretur. Equidem valde vereor, ne quod Pellicano videre obtigit, multis nostrum quoque evenire, si quando cum Iudæis committerentur: quod quam turpe & infandum est, tam ne contingat, omni modo singulis providendum, tum sibi, tum aliis; de his præsertim hoc dixero, qui formandi in Scholis veniunt Theologiæ Candidati. Iulianus Pomerius Toletanus, in præfat. libri de sexta mundi ætate, contra Iudæos disputaturus, inquit: ubi de Deo, vel contra Deum aliquid agitur, periculosum est pastori, si taceat; infame, si fugiat: mortiferum, si succumbat. Verissime, & in negotio quidem Iudæorum, ante omnia probrosum. Nota est Augustini historia, quodque de se testatur, ut in Manichaismo detentus fuerit per infœlices quas videbat Manichæorum à Christianis, in frequentibus disputationibus, reportatas victorias.
units.tr: We know of Conrad Pellicanus that from his earliest youth he burned with a fierce ardour for Hebrew. The occasion was that, as a boy, he once heard a Christian disputing with Jews so unhappily that a doctor of theology was shamefully confounded, not only by a Jew but even by a Jewish woman. This so tormented Pellicanus's mind that, driven by an insatiable zeal, he ceaselessly applied himself to learning Hebrew and Jewish matters, and made such progress in them, although with the greatest difficulty, which was the chief obstacle of that age, the scarcity of Hebrew books and teachers, that he engaged with great profit in the rabbinic, Chaldee and even Talmudic writings, which was then almost regarded as a miracle. Indeed I greatly fear that what befell Pellicanus may happen to many of us too, if at any time we should be pitted against the Jews. How shameful and unspeakable that is; so that it may not happen, every means must be taken by each of us, both for ourselves and for others, and I say this especially of those Candidates of Theology who come to be formed in the schools. Julian Pomerius of Toledo, in the preface to his book On the Sixth Age of the World, about to dispute against the Jews, says: When something is discussed concerning God, or against God, it is dangerous for the minister to be silent; disgraceful to flee; deadly to give way. Most truly, and in the matter of the Jews, above all, shameful. The story of Augustine is well known, and what he himself testifies: that he was held in Manichaeism through the unhappy victories which he saw the Manichaeans win over Christians in frequent disputations.

units.la: Vulgare impedimentum in re Iudaica ex lingua ignorantia est, quod ante omnia depellendum, nunc præcipuè, ubi Deus tam copiosa suppeditat linguarum Orientalium omnium discendarum media, præ illis temposuit, quando vix codices istarum erat reperire, quum, quod Lavaterus scribit, se à sene Pellicano haud semel audivisse, per totam Germaniam nullum Græcum Testamentum, quamvis multo emendum, prostaret: primum quippe ejus exemplar ex Italia allatum fuit. Ioh. Reuchlinus (Hermolaus Barbarus ei Germanicum Reuchlin, commutavit in nomen Græcum Capnionis) quando primus Grammaticam Hebraeam composuit, præceptori Judæo, à quo linguam discebat, pro singulis horis totidem tribuebat aureos, & maximum rarissimumque munus merito æstimabat Biblia Hebræa M. S. quæ ei Imperator, ad quem legatus à Duce V Vittembergico missus fuerat, donabat, trecentis aureis æstimata. Per Dei, & magnam certe eam, gratiam hodie commodior & vulgatior illarum linguarum habetur institutio, & librorum copia. Hieronymus, Tom. II. epist. ad Sun. & Fretelam: Quis hoc crederet, ut Barbara Getarum lingua Hebraicam quaereret vetiveritatem: & dormitantibus, imo contendentibus Graecis, ipsa Germania, Spiritus Sancti eloquia scrutaretur? Ut, quemadmodum, post primam Apostolorum praedicationem, in Reformatione Ecclesiae, linguas renituisse observatum, hoc omnis instar nunc quoque haberi queat, instantis circa Iudaeos & eorum conversionem, periodi. Dicunt Iudaei, in Pirke abbot, cap. IV. ּפְּרוֹפִּיתָה, prepara te ipsum in vestibulo, ut intres in triclinium. Quod si ullibi, omnino cavendum hac in re, ne quis imparatus, ne viribus impar in disputationem cum Iudaeis prodeat, ne vel victus, vel dubia alea discedens, causam prodidisse judicetur. Accipe consilium Victoris à Carben, ex Iudaeo converși Christiani, (qui postea Coloniae docuit in templo Vrsulano, unde ibi in foribus templi ferro inscriptum, & jam vetustate fere exesum: Victor olim Iudaeus) lib. 1. adverf. Iud. cap. ult. Commonendus hic es, si tibi congrediendum est cum Iudaeo aliquo in certamen disputationis, cogites prius necessarium fore uti sagittis telisque pharetram resertam habeas, quibus te ab incursione illius tueri possis. Quibus vero si careas, consilium meum plane est, nequaquam tibi cum illo conferendas manus esse, quin abstineas potius. Nam ut & alias te saepe commonefeci, illorum mos est à pueritia ferme, & ab incunabulis ad disputandum adversus Christianos institutos esse, atque indies instituti à suis majoribus. Enim id ita cautum apud eos, imprimis de doctrina sua legis, sibi prospiciant semper ut sciant in promptu respondere unicuique vel haeretico suae sectae, vel alias utcunque infideli, ut ipsi arbitrantur, si quid scisciitatus ille ab eis fuerit. Praecipuum quidem hujus rei adjumentum situm in linguae Iudaicae cognitione, citra quam nihil agitur. Unde Clementina, in concilio Viennensi edita, de Professoribus linguarum Orientalium, in Academias introducendis, ut instructi & edocti sufficienter in linguis hujusmodi, fructum speratum possint (Deo auctore) producere, fidem propagaturi salubriter in ipsos populos infideles.
units.tr: A common hindrance in dealing with Jewish matters is ignorance of the language, which must be removed above all, and now especially, when God supplies such abundant means for learning all the Oriental languages, which were scarcely available in earlier times, when there were hardly any books of those tongues to be found. As Lavater writes, he had heard from the old Pellicanus more than once that throughout the whole of Germany no Greek Testament was on sale, though it could have been bought for a great price; its first copy had been brought in from Italy. Johann Reuchlin (Hermolaus Barbarus changed his German name Reuchlin into the Greek Capnion) when he first composed a Hebrew grammar, paid his Jewish teacher, from whom he learned the language, as many gold coins for each hour, and rightly valued at a high price, and as a very great and rare gift, a Hebrew manuscript Bible, which the Emperor gave him, to whom the envoy had been sent by the Duke of Württemberg, valued at three hundred gold coins. By God's grace, and certainly a great grace, the teaching of those languages and the supply of books are today more convenient and more widespread. Jerome, in volume II, in the letter to Sunnia and Fretela: Who would believe it, that the Barbarian tongue of the Getae should seek the Hebrew truth, and that while the Greeks slept, or rather quarrelled, Germany itself should search the oracles of the Holy Spirit? So that, as after the first preaching of the Apostles the languages were observed to flourish in the Reformation of the Church, this too may now be taken as a sign of the period at hand regarding the Jews and their conversion. The Jews say in Pirke Abot, chapter IV: [פְּרוֹפִּיתָה] Prepare yourself in the vestibule, that you may enter into the dining room. If anywhere, certainly in this matter one must take care that no one comes forward unprepared and unequal in strength to dispute with the Jews, lest he be judged to have betrayed the cause, either defeated or withdrawing from a doubtful contest. Take the counsel of Victor of Carben, a Jew converted to Christianity (who afterwards taught in the church of St Ursula at Cologne, whence there is an inscription cut with iron on the church door, now nearly eaten away by age: Victor, once a Jew), in the first book against the Jews, last chapter: You are to be warned here: if you must engage some Jew in a contest of disputation, think first that it will be necessary for you to have a quiver full of arrows and darts, with which you may protect yourself from his attack. But if you lack these, my advice is plainly that you should by no means join hands with him, but rather abstain. For, as I have often warned you elsewhere, their custom is to be trained almost from boyhood, from the cradle, to dispute against Christians, and they are trained daily by their elders. For it is so provided among them, especially concerning the doctrine of their law, that they always take care to know how to answer at once, whether a heretic of their own sect or any other unbeliever, as they think, should question them about anything. The chief aid in this matter lies in knowledge of the Jewish language, without which nothing is accomplished. Hence the Clementine decree, issued at the Council of Vienne, concerning the introduction of teachers of Oriental languages into the academies: so that, instructed and sufficiently taught in such languages, they may (God being the author) produce the hoped-for fruit, and propagate the faith usefully among the unbelieving peoples themselves.

units.la: E Quod Hieronymi fuit, de suo in linguam Hebræam studio, (quod sub variis Rabbinis multo labore excoluerat, jam sub præceptore Tiberiense, tum sub alio Barrabano, qui timebat (inquit) Iudeos, & mihi alterum exhibebat Nicodemum,) encomium & testimonium, idem omnium nostrum esse debet, quod perhibet in Epitaphio Paulæ, his verbis: Hebræam linguam ego ab adolescentia multo labore ac sudore ex parte didici, & indefatigabili meditatione non desero, ne ipse ab ea desciscar.
units.tr: The praise and testimony that Jerome gave to his own study of Hebrew (which he had cultivated with great labour under various rabbis, first under a teacher from Tiberias, then under another named Barrabas, who feared (he says) the Jews, and who showed me another Nicodemus) should be the same for all of us. He writes in the Epitaph of Paula: I learned Hebrew from my youth, in part by great labour and sweat, and by untiring meditation I do not give it up, lest I myself fall away from it.

units.la: Unde nemo opinor mirabitur, non dicam visлo vertet, quod Studiosos cum in aliis, tum in hisce, idque vel imprimis, manuducimus controversiis, quæ res concernunt Iudaicas. Neglectum quamvis à nonnullis studium, non minus tamen utile semper est, & valde necessarium: atque cogitare hic debemus illud Athenienfium solemne juramentum, pugnabo pro Sacris solus, & cum aliis. Vel Hebræorum vulgatum admodum verbum, במקום in loco ubi nemo vir, tu te virum præsta. Satis bene & diligenter illa apud nos traduntur, tractanturque, quæ spectant controversias Christianorum, quæ sunt v. g. cum Pontificiis, Anabaptistis &c. sed hoc uti bene agitur, ita neque illud, quod de Iudæis diximus, omittendum fuerat. Vulgus, neque omnino absque ratione, reprehendit in Politicis nostris, quod arma Christiani Principes in se vertunt mutuo, quæ adversus Turcas potius, pro redemtione oppressorum Christianorum, contorquenda essent: idem annon multam partem Theologis quoque juste exprobari possit, viderint, quorum interest, Christianos quidem acriter inter se decertare, sed raro cum Infidelibus, cum Iudæis, aliisque istius generis: vehementer illos inter se pugnare, sæpiuscule de apice aliquo, & subtili magis quam necessario articulo, viderique potius ingenii certamen esse quam fidei, interim paucos istorum disputationem sustinere posse cum Iudæo, vel cum eo in arcarenam descendere. Ita nobis contingit, quod Isidorus Peluliota scribit, lib. 11. epist. cxxx ix. τί γὰρ τὸ ἐκῶν τῶν μόνον σκοπεῖν, τὸν κοινὸν ἐχθρὸν ἀφιέντες, καὶ τὰ ἀλλήλων ἐπιζητοῦμεν. Proprias domesticas respicientes, communem hostem negligimus, armamur adversus nos invicem. Frivolum est, quod Papa Romanus observat inter solemnitates suae coronationis, ut processuro sibi ad Ecclesiam Lateranensem, sub montem Iordanum Iudaei obviam veniant, legem offerentes, eamque commendantes, quibus ille tum nihil aliud scilicet respondeat, quam ex formula: Sanctam legem cari Hebraei laudamus et veneramur, utpote quae ab omnipotente Deo per manus Moysi patribus vestris tradita est: observantiam vero vestram, et vanam interpretationem damnamus, atque improbamus: quia Salvatorem, quem adhuc frustra expectatis, Apostolica fides jam pridem advenisse docet, et praedicat, Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum: Qui cum Patre, et Spiritu S. vivit, et regnat Deus, per omnia saecula saeculorum. Uti haec legantur in Pontificali Romano, sol. 47.
units.tr: Hence, I think, no one will be surprised that we guide students, not to say turn them, in other controversies as well, and above all in these, which concern Jewish matters. Although some have neglected this study, it is always no less useful and very necessary. We should keep in mind the solemn oath of the Athenians: I will fight for the sacred things alone, and with others. Or the well-known Hebrew saying: במקום [in the place] where there is no man, be a man yourself. The controversies of Christians among themselves, such as those with the Papists, the Anabaptists and so on, are handled among us well and diligently enough; but just as this is done well, so the matter we have raised about the Jews should not have been left out. The common people, and not entirely without reason, criticise our statesmen for turning the arms of Christian princes against one another, when they ought rather to be aimed against the Turks, for the rescue of oppressed Christians. Whether the same charge could not justly be brought against most theologians, let those judge whom it concerns: they contend fiercely with one another, Christians against Christians, but seldom with unbelievers, with Jews and others of that kind; they fight bitterly among themselves, quite often over some peak or subtle point that is less necessary than it is subtle, and it seems more a contest of wit than of faith; yet few of them can hold a disputation with a Jew, or go down into the arena with him. So it happens to us, as Isidore of Pelusium writes, book 2, letter 139: τί γὰρ τὸ ἐκῶν τῶν μόνον σκοπεῖν, τὸν κοινὸν ἐχθρὸν ἀφιέντες, καὶ τὰ ἀλλήλων ἐπιζητοῦμεν. Looking at our own domestic affairs, we neglect the common enemy; we arm ourselves against one another. It is a trifling thing that the Roman Pope observes among the solemnities of his coronation: as he proceeds to the Lateran Church, Jews come to meet him below Mount Jordan, offering the Law and commending it, to whom he then replies, of course, only with the set formula: We praise and revere the holy law of the Hebrews, dear to us, as it was given by almighty God through Moses to your fathers; but we condemn and reject your observance and your vain interpretation, because the Apostolic faith teaches and proclaims that the Saviour, whom you still wait for in vain, has already come: our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, for ever and ever. These words are read in the Roman Pontifical, p. 47.

units.la: Controversiae Iudaicae variae sunt, interque eas, uti notum, praecipua, et tritissima de adventu Messiae, Tertullianus, nec alia magis inter nos et illos compulsatio est, quam quod jam venisse non credunt. Profecto non de ascii umbra, uti Celsus, apud Origenem, lib. 111. improbe calumniatur; sed de summa et centro religionis ac salutis est concertatio. Quamvis an, quod vulgo quidem fit, inde semper incipienda disputatio sit, ego dubitem; magis forte consultum aliquando, quod prudentiae disputantium relinquo, non hinc exordiri, ubi ad singula fere promtas habent responsiones exceptionesque, sed vel a veritate aut praestantia religionis Christianae, a Christo, vel articulo de hominis coram Deo justificatione, aliisve, pro re nata. Sed de hoc, et de aliis huc spectantibus quia in singulari huius argumenti opere ex professo ago, ila jam omitto, solum-
units.tr: There are various Jewish controversies, and among them the chief and most worn is the one about the coming of the Messiah. Tertullian: Nor is there any other quarrel between us and them, than that they do not believe he has already come. Truly this dispute is not about the shadow of the ass, as Celsus wickedly slanders, in Origen, book 3; it concerns the sum and centre of religion and salvation. Whether the debate should always begin here, as is commonly done, I doubt. It may sometimes be wiser (I leave this to the judgement of the disputants) not to start here, where the Jews have ready answers and objections to almost every point, but from the truth or excellence of the Christian religion, from Christ, or from the article on man's justification before God, or from whatever else the occasion requires. But since I deal with this and other matters that bear on it ex professo in a separate work on this subject, I now pass them over, and will set out only a brief synopsis of the controversies, which is the purpose of the present undertaking.

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] (printer's mark at bottom right, not text) modo syllabum controversiarum, quod praesentis instituti est, exhibiturus. Quod vero ad controversiarum dispositionem & seriem, alio eas ordine collocavi alibi, quam hic, neque in eo quidpiam situm, quo loco, modo bene, tractes, & liberum cuique variare haec, prout visum. Quaeritur ergo,
units.tr: I have arranged the dispositions and sequence of the controversies in a different order elsewhere than here; nor does it matter in what place or manner one treats them, and each person is free to vary these things as he sees fit. The questions, then, are these:

units.la: I. Num Moses, in monte Sinai quum esset, praeter legem scriptam, acceperit quoque oralem שבעל פה traditiones, viva tantum voce docendas? Neg.
units.tr: I. Did Moses, while on Mount Sinai, receive, besides the written law, also an oral law, שבעל פה [shebe'al peh], traditions to be taught by living voice alone? No.

units.la: II. Num Talmud, quo contineri (ajunt) legem oralem, ad ejus usque conscriptionem non nisi ore traditam, tradendamque, tandem autem propter temporum injuriam colligendam & consignandam, sit divinae certitudinis, atque authoritatis, & juxta, si non supra Scripturam, amplectendum? Neg.
units.tr: II. Is the Talmud, which (they say) contains the oral law, which was passed on only by mouth until its writing down, and was at last gathered and committed to writing because of the injuries of the times, of divine certainty and authority, and to be embraced equally with, if not above, Scripture? No.

units.la: III. Num Kabalistica Judaeorum doctrina, quae consistit potissimum in litterarum permutatione, per Temurah, uti appellant; vel in earundem supputationem arithmetica, per Gematriam; & vocum diversarum ex singulis formatione, per Notaricon; praeter reliquos modos vel regulas, quas in universum tredecim faciunt Judaei, praeter jam dictas, Zura, Rasetebotve sophe tebot, Chafer Vmela, Setumot Vpetuhot, Kare vela Quetib, Quetib vela Kare, Ketasnot Vgedolot, Hiluf, Nekudot, Taamim, num illa doctrina divinae sit originis, & authoritatis? Neg.
units.tr: III. Is the Kabbalistic doctrine of the Jews, which consists chiefly in the permutation of letters, called Temurah; in the arithmetical calculation of the same letters, called Gematria; and in the formation of various words from the individual letters, called Notaricon; together with the other methods or rules, which the Jews make thirteen in all, besides those already named (Zura, Rasetebotve sophe tebot, Chafer Vmela, Setumot Vpetuhot, Kare vela Quetib, Quetib vela Kare, Ketasnot Vgedolot, Hiluf, Nekudot, Taamim), of divine origin and authority? No.

units.la: IV. Num divisio librorum S. Scripturae, ut apud Judaeos fit, in Pentateuchum utrumque, Prophetas, & Hagiographa, sit optima? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Is the division of the books of Holy Scripture, as the Jews make it, into the two Pentateuchs, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa, the best? No.

units.la: V. An in Deo uno sint tres Personae, Pater, & filius & Spiritus Sanctus? Aff.
units.tr: V. Are there three Persons in the one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit? Yes.

units.la: VI. Num aliqui Angeli sint corporei, compositi ex aere & igne, & alati, quique cibis vescantur, generent, atque etiam moriantur? Neg.
units.tr: VI. Are some angels corporeal, composed of air and fire, winged, and do they eat food, beget children, and even die? No.

units.la: VII. Num Daemones sive Diaboli secundo creationis die, cum inferno, creati sint; vel, ex Angelorum cum mulieribus congressu aliqui nati, aut ex coitu Adami cum Lilith, aliisve Dæmonum matribus? Neg.
units.tr: VII. Were demons or devils created on the second day of creation, along with hell; or were some born from the intercourse of angels with women, or from the union of Adam with Lilith or other mothers of demons? No.

units.la: VIII. Num omnium hominum animæ sint creatæ simul primo die, & pares seu conjuges? Neg.
units.tr: VIII. Were the souls of all men created together on the first day, and paired or married? No.

units.la: IX. Num cœlum sit animatum, & quidem animâ rationali? Neg.
units.tr: IX. Is heaven animated, and indeed with a rational soul? No.

units.la: X. Peccatum Adami primum fuit commune totius naturæ humanæ, unde omnes homines nascuntur cum peccato originali.
units.tr: X. Adam's sin was the first sin of the whole of human nature, whence all men are born with original sin.

units.la: XI. An Messias, in Scripturâ S. promissus, & expectatus olim, omnino venerit, eoque, quo prædictum à Prophetis fuit, tempore? Aff.
units.tr: XI. Did the Messiah promised and long awaited in Holy Scripture indeed come, and at the time foretold by the Prophets? Yes.

units.la: XII. Num Messiæ regnum debeat hâc in terrâ esse mundanum? Neg.
units.tr: XII. Ought the kingdom of the Messiah to be worldly on this earth? No.

units.la: XIII. An Iesus Christus, in quem Christiani credimus, sit verus ille Messias? Aff.
units.tr: XIII. Is Jesus Christ, in whom we Christians believe, the true Messiah? Yes.

units.la: XIV. An Euangelium Iesu Christi sit veritatis, & authoritatis divinæ? Aff.
units.tr: XIV. Is the Gospel of Jesus Christ of truth and divine authority? Yes.

units.la: XV. An Iesus Messias sit verus Deus & homo? Aff.
units.tr: XV. Is Jesus the Messiah true God and man? Yes.

units.la: XVI. An, & Messiæ erat, & Christus pro peccatis nostris passus fuerit, atque satisfecerit? Aff.
units.tr: XVI. Was it, and was it necessary for the Messiah, that Christ suffered for our sins and made satisfaction? Yes.

units.la: XVII. An per illam Iesu Messiæ, nostri loco præstitam satisfactionem & justitiam, coram Deo justificemur? Aff.
units.tr: XVII. Are we justified before God through that satisfaction and righteousness of Jesus the Messiah, offered in our place? Yes.

units.la: An vero per nostra ipsorum opera? Neg.
units.tr: Or rather through our own works? No.

units.la: XVIII. Num homo ex se, & suis naturæ viribus valeat præstare bona religionis opera? Neg.
units.tr: XVIII. Can man of himself, by his own natural powers, perform the good works of religion? No.

units.la: An vero per singularem Dei gratiam, & virtutem Sp. S. ut convertatur necesse habet, & hinc sanctificetur, ut cultum Deo præstare potens sit & idoneus? Aff.
units.tr: Or rather does he need to be converted through the singular grace of God and the power of the Holy Spirit, and thereby be sanctified, so as to be able and fit to render worship to God? Yes.

units.la: XIX. Annon omnia contra Dei legem peccata sint mortalia? Aff.
units.tr: XIX. Are not all sins against God's law mortal? Yes.

units.la: XX. Num Iudæi ex Dei præcepto teneantur facere Tephillim, vel ligamenta coriacea, quibus inscriptæ sint quatuor ex lege sectiones, ubi habetur addiatum, ut sit tibi in signum ad manum tuam, & in memoriale inter oculos tuos. videl. Exod. xiii. à versu 2. ad 10. Ibidem à verf. 11. ad 16. Deut. vi. à verf. 4. ad 9. Et cap. ejusdem libri xi. à verf. 13. ad 21. quæ inter precandum gestant alligata fronti, & sinistro brachio? Neg.
units.tr: XX. Are the Jews, by God's command, bound to make the Tephillim, or leather straps bearing the four sections of the Law where it is written: and it shall be for a sign upon your hand, and for a memorial between your eyes, namely Exod. 13, verses 2 to 10; there also verses 11 to 16; Deut. 6, verses 4 to 9; and chapter 11 of the same book, verses 13 to 21, which they wear bound to the forehead and left arm while praying? No.

units.la: xxi. Non licet jurare vel per hominem, vel per creaturas alias.
units.tr: xxi. It is not lawful to swear either by man or by any other creature.

units.la: xxii. Sabbathi Iudaica observatio est superstitiosa, & carnalis.
units.tr: xxii. The Jewish observance of the Sabbath is superstitious and carnal.

units.la: xxiii. Polygamia, & repudium sunt illicita.
units.tr: xxiii. Polygamy and divorce are unlawful.

units.la: xxiv. Improba est Iudæorum, in Christianos quam exercent, usura.
units.tr: xxiv. The usury which the Jews practise against Christians is wicked.

units.la: xxv. Num mendacium aliquando sit licitum? Neg.
units.tr: xxv. Is a lie ever lawful? No.

units.la: xxvi. Num homo legem Dei in hac vita perfecte implere possit? Neg.
units.tr: xxvi. Can a man perfectly fulfil the law of God in this life? No.

units.la: xxvii. Homo fidelis & pius potest ac debet divinæ erga se gratiæ, & salutis suæ esse certus.
units.tr: xxvii. A faithful and pious man can, and ought to, be certain of divine grace towards himself and of his own salvation.

units.la: xxviii. Lex Mosis cæremonialis & politica nos non ultrius obligant.
units.tr: xxviii. The ceremonial and political law of Moses no longer binds us.

units.la: xxix. Populus Iudaicus, inde à contemto ab ipsis vero nostro Messia, à fœdere Dei rejectus fuit.
units.tr: xxix. The Jewish people, from the time they despised our true Messiah, were rejected by God from the covenant.

units.la: xxx. Tandem etiam populi Iudaici futura est ad Deum & Christum conversio.
units.tr: xxx. Finally, a conversion of the Jewish people to God and Christ is also yet to come.

units.la: xxxi. Non transeunt animæ, post hominum mortem, in alienà corpora.
units.tr: xxxi. Souls do not pass, after a man's death, into other bodies.

units.la: xxxii. Omnium & singulorum hominum futura est ultimo die resurrectio.
units.tr: xxxii. The resurrection of all and each of mankind is to take place on the last day.

units.la: Liber Tertius. DE MUHAMMEDISMO.
units.tr: Book Three. ON MUHAMMEDISM.

units.la: De Muhammede, ejus ortu, vita, & tradito ab eo Alkorano. Hujus versiones; & Scriptores adversus Christiani. Nomen Sarracenorum, Turcarum
units.tr: On Muhammed, his birth, life, and the Alcoran handed down by him. Its translations, and the writers against it. The name of the Saracens, Turks

units.la: carum unde. Origo sectae Muhammedicae. Schisma Turcarum, & Persarum; ejus causae, & capita. Musulmannus. Janizari. Controversiarum Muhammedicarum ordo. De illorum curanda conversione.
units.tr: whence the name. The origin of the Muhammedan sect. The schism of the Turks and Persians, its causes and heads. Musulman. Janizaries. The order of the Muhammedan controversies. On how their conversion is to be pursued.

units.la: NAtus dicitur Muhammed Abulcasimus, celebris & execrandus impostor, anno supra sexcentesimum vigesimo: alii, non hoc tempore natum, sed celebrem fuisse, asserunt; natum autem anno D xcv i i. imperante Mauritio, quum illud sub Heraclio, qui Arabibus Herchil, fuerit. Baronius obitum ejus refert in annum cxxx. Marquardus Frcherus, in sua, ad jus GraecoRomanum Leunclavii, Chronologia, anno Dlx. natum, & obiisse anno Dcxxx i i. ait; quo etiam quidem anno obiisse eum, at natum anno Dxc i i i. scribit in Lexico, Scindlerus. Erpenius, circa anno Dlxxx. Elmacinus, in historia Sarracenica, quem multi sequuntur, ponit annum, juxta nostrum computum, Dlxx i. Alii paulo aliter. In eo omnes consentiunt, post initium anni sexcentesimi, circa vigesimum istius seculi, aut trigesimum annum, natum, vel notum maxime fuisse, quippe ad istud tempus omnes istius mentionem faciunt. מחמד est a חמד dagessato, quod significat valde celebravit: unde participium passivum מחמד valde celebratus, celebris; convenitque cum Chaldaeo חמד desideravit, optavit. חמוד desideratus. Daniel cap. ix. 23. & x. 11. איש חמודות vir desideriorum; desideratissimus. Latine, Desiderius. Parentes Muhammed habuit Abdalla (quod servum Dei עבדאללה significat) & Eminam, vel Amenam, VVahebi filiam, non, uti vulgo persuasum, ignobili & abjecta, sed ex illustri familia, quamvis tum temporis forte inopi & paupere, fuit, & prosapiae inter omnes Arabes praecipuae, de tribu Koreischitarum, qui Mecca rerum potiebantur, anque Muhammedis primi & summi adversarii, tribulum ac civem suum, quam primum res novas moliretur, urbe expulerunt: cumque iis dein bello decertavit Muhammed, à Medinensibus acceptus & adjutus, illosque iterato prælio superavit. Avum ejus Abdalmutalibum Schickardus, in præfat. ad Tarich, inter Arabiæ reges refert. Mecca prognatus Muhammed, non Medinâ, uti multi scribunt: sed Meccâ à Proceribus Koreischitis (quos in Alkorano sæpius diris devovet, ut præcipuos suos hostes) pulsus, ob novas quas disseminare incipiebat opiniones & leges, anno ætatis suæ LIII. vel LIV. quod fuit anno decimo quarto novæ suæ religionis, diciturque incidisse in annum Christi I𝔇CXIV. secundum alios XXII. Medinam, antea dictam Iathrib (distat Meccâ itinere decem dierum) aufugit, à quâ ejus fugâ Muhammedani æram suam inchoant, quam Hegeram appellant, quod significat fugam; uti Iudæi, à mundi initio; Græci, à primâ Olympiade; Romani, ab urbe conditâ; pos Christiani, à nato Christo annos supputamus; & urbs illa Iatrib, per antonomasiam, Medina & Medinath-alnabi, hoc est civitas Prophetæ dicta. Mecca urbs est Arabiæ, non Felicis, uti ostendit Gabriel Sionita, de nonnullis Orientalium urbibus cap. VII. sed Desertę: magnitudine accedere ad Amstelodamum, dicit Erpenius: ubi natus Muhammed, educatus, & plurima Alkorani capita sibi revelata, alia autem Medinæ, in Alkorano scripsit. Hic & templum illud religiosissimum, de quo mira fabulantur, & quod laboriosissimis invisunt Muhammedani peregrinationibus: de quo nos in sequentibus. Genealogiam Muhammedis usque ad Adamum explicant ejus asseclæ, & per omnes generationes, ajunt, jubar aliquod in fronte istorum refulsisse, ex quorum linea esset aliquando oriundus Muhammed, quod in hoc se totum denique effudit baesitque. Admiranda fingunt cum nato Muhammede, præterquam in ipso, etiam alibi contigisse. Per universum orbem thronos omnes & judiciociorum sedes concidisse, illi videlicet factúras locum; & terrae rerumque omnium, adeoque & hominum magnam sterilitatem eo nato solutam; idola omnia se tum inclinasse; Lucifervm, prae aliis timentem sibi, ausugiisse; adfuisse Muhammedi in nativitate ex improviso obstetrices mirum quam speciosas & elegantes; aves advolasse rostris hyacinthinis, ab Oriente in Occidentem usque fulgentibus, & nescio quae non, ementita omnia, nec ipsis eo tempore Arabibus, nec in mundo aliis unquam comperta. Scribit Leunclavius, Hist. Musulmanae Turcorum lib. 1. circa illud tempus sacrum Persarum ignem, Orimasda appellant, quemque, antiquissimo cultu, Solis loco venerabantur, extinctum fuisse. Muhammedani hoc in gloriam Muhammedis trahunt, quasi igne sponte extincto: at certius edocent nos Historiae, factum illud ab Heraclio Augusto, in expeditione contra Persarum Regem Cosroem, quodque tum Christiani milites idolum hoc suftulerint. Ridiculum valde est, quod Muhammedi quatuor annorum puero contigisse ajunt, ab Angelis (quorum custodiae videlicet datus fuerit, patris sui posthumus), qui tres puerum acceperint, & in montem seorsim abductum diffecuerint circa ventrem, citra ullum tamen dolorem, intestinaque adeo pulchre laverint, ut nive fuerint facta candidiora; cor etiam diffecarint, atque ex eo nigrum granum, vel atram guttam (quam singulis inesse, ceu semen aliquod Diaboli, quo homines vexantur, credunt) abstulerint. Denique redditis ei sic intestinis, & corde, bene lotis purgatisque, nitidus puer ad suos reversus dicitur. Vecors certe sit, hisce qui fidem adhibeat: quae tamen sic narrant Muhammedani, uti videre est apud Johannem Andream, Consus. Secte Muhammed. cap. 1. 8: in Alkorano Germanico, cap. 1 v. Sed ad vitam Muhammedis quod facit, mercatoriis rebus operam primo dedit, serviitque Domino suo in conducendis & agendis camelis, reliquoque immento, familiari Arabum commercio, usque dum illo mortuo, viduam ejus prædivitem in matrimonium accepit Chadigam, qui primus ei emergendi gradus extitit. Sed quum morbo laboraret epileptico, & hinc Chadiga animo ab eo fieret alienior, ut quam pœnitere inciperet, viro tam abjecto & imbecilli nupsisse, ille jam majora animo versare, falsidita mercatura, occœpit, & ad comminiscendas ecstases & divinas Angelicasque apparitiones, insomnia ac enthusiasmos animum transtulit: ad quod frequens iste morbus prætextum & occasionem suppeditare videbatur, dicendi esse paroxysmos cœlestium revelationum, quas tum pateretur scilicet, quando epilepsia corripiebatur; unde in Alkorano vocatur vir pannis laneis opertus, Surat. VII. quibus illum ejus morbum significari haud frustra creditur. Atque sub Diabolico illo fascino capita vel fustula Alkorani sui è cœlo accipere se fingebat. Non enim integrum Alkorani codicem vel simul edidit, aut accepisse se commentus est, sed per partes & membranulas jam hoc, tum illud caput, vel versum, pro re natâ, prout videbat hoc vel istud de se credi consultum esse, & ad adversarios suos (Meccensis præcipue) coarguendos, iisque os quasi cœlestibus oraculis obstruendum, protulit: unde ille materiarum toto Alkorano est nusquam cohærens ordo, ac mera confusio, unum alteri raro conveniens. Anno ætatis suæ quadragesimo cœpit jactare revelationes & prophetias, quas acceptas vel confictas primum manifestare solitus erat uxori Chadigæ, inde aliis, neque reliquit nisi acervum schedarum prophetias suas continentium, quas non ipse redegit in istum, quem habemus, codicem, sed successores ejus collectas in unum, ita prout nunc sunt, compegerunt. Jam dicunt, per particulas ei singula à Gabriele Angelo (quocum fuerit valde familiaris) adducta & revelata fuisse: jam à Deo ipso in cœlis, quò admirandâ equitatione pervenerit, accepisse. Sic ipse aliquando suis narravit Muhammed, se quâdam nocte, dum cu-baret inter undecim (tot enim habebat) uxores, excitatum ab Angelo Gabriele fuisse, jussumque mulum conscendere Alborach, pervicaciter primò recalcitrantem, quousque promissum accepisset, quod una cum Muhammede Paradysum esset ingressurus, quo vectus illâ nocte pervenerit Jerusalemum, ibi juxta scalam de terrâ in cœlum erectam ascenderit cum Gabriele, qui eum manibus prehendebat, vel (juxta alios) gestabat humeris, ad primum cœlum usque. Hic Adamum, primum hominem conspexit, unaque terrenarum rerum omnium formas, ideas opinor, hominum, animalium, atque ita porro; inter cætera, gallum ejus magnitudinis, ut pedibus consisteret in cœlo infimo, & caput secundo insereret, cujus cantillantis vocem reliqui qui aderant gallorum figuram habentes Angeli excipiebant, à quorum clamore expergefacti terrestres galli clamorem edant infra. Salutato Adamo, in cœlum perrexit secundum, ubi offendit Noachum, quo etiam inter mutuos complexus & commendationes valedicto, atque observato inter alia ibidem procerae staturae Angelo, qui caput tertio hinc cœlo inferret, abiit. Ad tertium ubi appulit, Abrahamum vidit, Angelum etiam cui bini, suo oculi distabant à se itinere mille & septuaginta dierum: erat hic (ne nesciatis) Angelus mortis, valde occupatus assiduè in annotandis, sive qui nascuntur, sive qui moriuntur, hominibus. In quarto cœlo (quod totum erat smaragdinum) Iosephum Iacobi patriarchæ filium conspexit, plurimos item Angelos, interque eos aliquem continuo plorantem, nempe hominum peccata, & conditionem damnandorum. In quinto cœlo Moses commorabatur, cum longe adhuc pluribus Angelis. Sextum tenebat Iohannes Baptista, cum Angelis aliis. Septimum incolebat Christus, qui se scilicet Muhammedi ulterius ad Deum tendenti commendabat: hic AnAngelos vidit omnium maximos, vel millies toto etiam mundo majores, quibus singulis erant septuaginta mille capita, totidem linguae, quaeque totidem emittebant, quotiescunque, nempe sonabant, voces, quibus tantus dabatur sonus, ut nisi alii aures obturassent suas, ocyus obsurduissent. Hic Gabriel socio Muhammedi valedixit, quem comitari ulterius non licuit: Muhammed vero, voce Dei ut propius accederet, invitatus, per excelsa montium nivesque aquasque ad Dei solium perrexit, usque ad duos fere sagittae jactus, Deinque faciem vidit, nempe septuaginta mille velis luminis caelestis obductam. Haec si quaeras, num vera? ab eo pete, qui Drusillam euntem in caelum vidit, Idem Claudium vidisse se dicet iter facientem, non passibus aequis. Descripta autem reperies, apud Ioh. Andream, cap. VIII. In Alkorano Germanico, lib. I. cap. V. apud Richardum, Confut. legis Saracen. cap. XIV. Ioh. Cantacutzenum, orat. VI. in Muhammedem. Philippum Guadagnolum, Apolog. pro Christ. relig. contra Achmedem Persam, cap. II. sect. II. Thomam a Iesu, de Converf. Gent. lib. X. pag. 674. Ipseque Muhammed illa ita de se credi voluit, Surat. LXIII. Sed uti satis indicat, a suis haec minime tum accepta fuisse, ita praemisso vano juramento rem confirmare annisus est: per Stellam vespertinam (sequor latinam versionem Retinensis) nullatenus erraus, nil ex proprio velle, nisi tantum divinitus sibi mandatum loquitur: qui sublevatus ad orizontis celsitudinem ad Deum ipsum instruentem illum atque docentem efficaciter accessit, tanti tamen spatii intervallo, quantum sagitta arcu missa bis transcurreret. Qui tunc praecepta Deum sibi dicentem audiens, animum minime dubitantem inde tulit, ubi nec vas eum de divina visione calumniemini. Miror quod illa apud aliquem sanae mentis hominem assensum reperire possunt, conficta unice ab Auctore ad fidem sibi comparandam, & stolidis nugis, ridiculis falsitatibus, mendaciis, calumniisque in Sanctos Prophetas, Christumque que, refertissima. Sed bene est, quod fabulam hanc inter ipsos Muhammedanos sunt qui dedignentur, negantes unquam Muhammedem in coelo cum Deo locutum fuisse. Alii ab Gabriele acceptam legem, dicunt: contra alii, ab hominibus compositam, viris sapientibus ac disertissimis. Surat. xxi. sequenti xxii. dicitur, a Deo compositam, atque ab eo ad homines missam per Angelum Gabrielem, primo ad Muhammedem, Surat. xlix. & l. & li. Uti azoara liii, & liv. quod noctu a Deo fuerit tradita Muhammedi. Azoar. lv. quod ipsius Dei scripta fuerit manu. Azoar. lvi, & lxvi. jurat a Deo compositam, per lucem octasue Stellarum, quod magnum scientibus est sacramentum, hic Alkoran optimus a Rege mundi compositus est atque positus. Az. lxxxi. mihi divinitus missus est. Una & tempus significat, quando ei de coelo missus sit, azo.cv. i. in nocte alchidera, nocte sc. omnium foelicissima. Tandem ex febri obiit, aetatis anno lxiii. quorum xl. transegit, ante inchoatum sc. Propheticum suum munus. xiii. annos Meccae; decem reliquos, post fugam, vel Hegiram, Medinae.
units.tr: Natus was Muhammed Abulcasimus, the famous and accursed impostor, in the year 620 after Christ. Others assert that he was not born at this time but was already famous, and that he was born in 571, under the emperor Maurice, when that Heraclius who was called Herchil by the Arabs was reigning. Baronius places his death in the year 630. Marquard Freher, in his Chronology, which accompanies Leunclavius's edition of the Greco-Roman law, says that he was born in 510 and died in 632. Schindler in his Lexicon also gives the year of his death as 632 but says he was born in 593. Erpenius puts his birth around 580. Elmacinus, in his Saracen history, which many follow, gives 571 by our reckoning. Others differ slightly. All agree that he was born, or at least became very well known, a little after the beginning of the seventh century, around the twentieth or thirtieth year of that century, since all writers who mention him refer to that time. Muhammed [מחמד] is from [חמד] with a dagesh, which means "he greatly celebrated," so the passive participle [מחמד] means "greatly celebrated, famous." It agrees with the Chaldee [חמד], "he desired, he wished," and [חמוד], "desired." In Daniel 9:23 and 10:11 we have [איש חמודות], "a man of desires," that is, most desired; in Latin, Desiderius. Muhammed's parents were Abdalla (which means "servant of God," [עבדאללה]) and Emina, or Amena, daughter of Wahab. He was not, as is commonly believed, of low and humble birth, but came from a distinguished family, though at that time perhaps poor and needy, and of a lineage the most eminent among all the Arabs, namely the tribe of the Koreishites, who held power in Mecca. These same Koreishites, Muhammed's first and greatest enemies, drove out of the city their own tribesman and citizen as soon as he began to introduce new things. Afterwards Muhammed fought a war against them, received help and support from the people of Medina, and defeated them again in battle. Schickard, in the preface to the Tarich, lists his grandfather Abdalmuttalib among the kings of Arabia. Muhammed was born in Mecca, not in Medina, as many write. Driven out of Mecca by the Koreishite nobles (whom in the Koran he often curses as his chief enemies), because of the new opinions and laws he had begun to spread, he fled in the fifty-third or fifty-fourth year of his life, which was the fourteenth year of his new religion. This is said to have fallen in the year of Christ 614, or according to others 622, from Mecca to Medina, formerly called Yathrib, a ten days' journey away. From this flight the Muhammedans date their era, which they call the Hegira, a word meaning flight, just as the Jews reckon from the beginning of the world, the Greeks from the first Olympiad, the Romans from the founding of the city, and we Christians from the birth of Christ. That city of Yathrib was also called, by way of distinction, Medina and Medinath-alnabi, that is, the city of the Prophet. Mecca is a city of Arabia, not the Happy one, as Gabriel Sionita shows in his work On Some Cities of the East, chapter 7, but of the Desert. Erpenius says it is about the size of Amsterdam. Here Muhammed was born and brought up, and here he was given most of the chapters of the Koran by revelation; others he wrote in the Koran at Medina. Here too is that most sacred temple, about which they tell wonderful stories, and which the Muhammedans visit on their most laborious pilgrimages; of this we will speak below. His followers trace Muhammed's genealogy back to Adam, and they say that through every generation a certain radiance shone on the forehead of those from whose line Muhammed was at some time to come, and that in him it at last poured itself out and rested entirely. They invent wonders that they say happened elsewhere, not only in him, at his birth: that all thrones and seats of judgment throughout the world were overturned, as if to make room for him; that a great barrenness of the earth, of all things, and even of men, was ended by his birth; that all the idols then bowed down; that Lucifer, fearing for himself above others, fled; that midwives, wonderfully beautiful and elegant, were suddenly present at Muhammed's birth; that birds flew in with hyacinth-coloured beaks, shining from East to West, and I know not what else. All these things are invented, and were unknown not only to the Arabs of that time but to anyone else in the world. Leunclavius, in the Muhammedan History of the Turks, book 1, writes that about that time the sacred fire of the Persians, which they call Orimasda, and which they had venerated in place of the sun with the most ancient worship, was extinguished. The Muhammedans claim this for Muhammed's glory, as if the fire had gone out of its own accord. But the histories teach us more reliably that this was done by the emperor Heraclius on his expedition against the Persian king Chosroes, and that Christian soldiers then destroyed this idol. It is very ridiculous that they say there happened to Muhammed, when he was four years old (since he had been born after his father's death and was therefore committed to the care of angels), that three angels took the boy and cut him open around the belly, away on a mountain by himself, without any pain, and washed his intestines so beautifully that they became whiter than snow; they also opened his heart and removed from it a black grain or dark drop, which they believe is in everyone, like some seed of the Devil by which men are troubled. Finally, when his intestines and heart had been put back, well washed and cleansed, the boy is said to have returned to his people shining. Surely whoever gives credit to these things must be mad; yet the Muhammedans tell them in this way, as can be seen in John Andreas, Consus. Secte Muhammed., chapter 1, section 8, and in the German Koran, chapter 1 v. But as for what concerns Muhammed's life: first he devoted himself to trade, and served his master in leading and managing camels and the rest of the business, the common commerce of the Arabs, until, after his master's death, he married his wealthy widow Khadija, which was the first step of his rise. But since he suffered from epilepsy, and for this reason Khadija became more and more averse to him, so that she began to regret having married such a base and feeble man, he now turned to greater things. He gave up honest trade and turned his mind to inventing ecstasies and divine and angelic appearances, dreams and enthusiasms. This frequent illness seemed to offer him a pretext and an occasion: he said that the fits he suffered whenever he was seized by epilepsy were the paroxysms of heavenly revelations. Hence in the Koran he is called "a man wrapped in woollen cloths," Sura 7, by which it is believed, not without reason, that his illness is meant. Under this diabolical enchantment he pretended to receive from heaven the chapters or small pieces of his Koran. He did not publish or claim to have received the whole Koran at once, but in parts and small pages, now this chapter, now that one or verse, as the occasion required, as he judged it best that this or that should be believed about him, and he brought them out to confute his adversaries (especially those of Mecca) and to stop their mouths, as it were, with heavenly oracles. Hence the material of the whole Koran has no coherent order anywhere, but is pure confusion, one part seldom agreeing with another. In the fortieth year of his life he began to put forward revelations and prophecies, which at first, whether received or invented, he used to disclose to his wife Khadija, and then to others. He left nothing but a heap of loose sheets containing his prophecies, which he did not himself arrange into the codex we now have; his successors gathered them together into one and put them together as they now stand. They say that each part was brought and revealed to him by the angel Gabriel, with whom he was very intimate; at other times they say he received them from God himself in heaven, to which he came by a wonderful ride. So Muhammed himself once told his followers that one night, while he was sleeping among his eleven (for that many wives he had), he was roused by the angel Gabriel and ordered to mount the mule Alborak, which at first stubbornly kicked back until he received the promise that he would enter Paradise together with Muhammed. Carried on it that night, he came to Jerusalem; there, beside a ladder set up from earth to heaven, he ascended with Gabriel, who held him by the hands or (according to others) carried him on his shoulders, as far as the first heaven. Here he saw Adam, the first man, and at the same time the forms, I suppose the ideas, of all earthly things, of men, animals, and so on. Among other things there was a cock of such size that it stood with its feet in the lowest heaven and put its head into the second; the other angels present, who had the figure of cocks, received the voice of its crowing, and at their cry the earthly cocks, awakened, crow below. After greeting Adam, he went on to the second heaven, where he met Noah; after mutual embraces and commendations, and after leaving him, and noticing among other things an angel of great stature there who was to bring the head into the third heaven, he departed. When he reached the third, he saw Abraham, and also an angel to whom each of his eyes was distant a journey of 1,070 days. This, lest you do not know, was the angel of death, very busy constantly in recording men, whether those who are born or those who die. In the fourth heaven (which was entirely emerald) he saw Joseph, son of the patriarch Jacob, and many angels too, and among them one who was continually weeping, namely for the sins of men and the condition of the damned. In the fifth heaven Moses dwelt, with still more angels. John the Baptist held the sixth, with other angels. Christ inhabited the seventh, who commended Muhammed as he pressed on further towards God. Here he saw the largest of angels, a thousand times greater even than the whole world, each of whom had seventy thousand heads, and as many tongues, and each of these tongues sent forth as many voices as it spoke, so that such a great sound was given that, unless others stopped their ears, they would soon become deaf. Here Gabriel took leave of Muhammed, his companion, whom he was not permitted to accompany any further. But Muhammed, invited by the voice of God to draw nearer, went on through the high mountains, snows and waters to the throne of God, almost two bowshots away; and then he saw the face of God, veiled, namely, by seventy thousand veils of heavenly light. If you ask whether these things are true, put the question to him who saw Drusilla going up to heaven; the same man will say that he saw Claudius walking, not with even steps. You will find these things described in John Andreas, chapter 8; in the German Koran, book 1, chapter 5; in Richard, Refutation of the Saracen Law, chapter 14; in John Cantacuzenus, Oration 6 against Muhammed; in Philip Guadagnoli, Apology for the Christian Religion against Ahmed the Persian, chapter 2, section 2; and in Thomas a Jesu, On the Conversion of the Gentiles, book 10, page 674. Muhammed himself wished these things to be believed about him, Sura 63. But as he sufficiently indicates, these things were by no means accepted at that time by his own people, so he strove to confirm the matter by first making an empty oath: "By the evening star" (I follow the Latin version of Retines), "we do not err at all; he speaks nothing of his own will, except what has been divinely commanded to him; he, raised to the height of the horizon, drew near to God himself, who instructed and taught him effectively, yet at a distance that a bowshot would cover twice." He who then heard God speaking to him carried away a mind in no way doubting, so that there was no fault to be found in him concerning the divine vision. I wonder that such things can find assent from any man of sound mind, since they were invented solely by the author to win belief for himself, and are full of foolish trifles, ridiculous falsehoods, lies, and slanders against the holy prophets and Christ. But it is well that among the Muhammedans themselves there are some who disdain this fable, denying that Muhammed ever spoke with God in heaven. Some say that the law was received from Gabriel; others, on the contrary, that it was composed by wise and most eloquent men. In Sura 21, and the following 22, it is said that it was composed by God and sent by him to men through the angel Gabriel, first to Muhammed; Suras 49, 50 and 51, and likewise 53 and 54, that it was delivered to Muhammed by God at night; Sura 55, that it was written by the very hand of God; Suras 56 and 66, that God composed it, swearing "by the light of the eight stars, which is a great oath to those who know, that this best Koran was composed and set down by the King of the world." Sura 81: "It was sent to me by God." It also indicates the time when it was sent to him from heaven, Sura 105: "in the night of Alkadr," that is, the most blessed night of all. At last he died of fever in the sixty-third year of his life, forty of which he had spent before he began his prophetic office; thirteen years at Mecca, and the remaining ten, after the flight or Hegira, at Medina.

units.la: Alkoran dicitur אלקוראן, al articulus est & vel קוראן koran vel Alkoran est lectio; aliis videtur, quod sit praeceptorum collectio: aliis a קרא confessus fuit, confessio, aliis, quasi correctio Veteris sc. & Novi Testamenti. A Muhammedanis, & in Alkorano appellatur Alphorhan a פרק divisit: vel, ut sit quasi distinctionum volumen, i.e. distinctis regulis & capitibus traditum: vel, discretivum boni & mali; sic versio Roberti Retinensis Angli. Sed quemadmodum Koran, vel Alkoran, a legendo dicitur, quomodo מקרא vel מקרא apud Iudaeos Scriptura Sacra; ita & Phorcan, sive Alphorhan, Capitum liber & sectionum, quod apud Hebraeos est פרק, sive פירקא. Quomodo & Graeci Scripturam S. appellarunt Biblos, inde & nos vulgo, Biblia. In Korano, Surata, xxi. vel secundum translationem Retinensis xxxi.
