Etiam quondam dedimus Mosi & Aaroni Alphurcan, lex Mosis intelligitur, eo quod & hæc distinguit bonum à malo, licitum ab illicito. Cardinalis Cusanus librum suum Cribrat Alcorani, sic incipit: Est liber legis Arabum Alchoran, ob præceptorum collectionem, atque Alphurcan ob discretam capitum separationem nominatus. Potior tamen est illa altera Alphurcani denotatio. Quod Arabice sunt Alkorani capitula surata, souraton, vel cum articulo assourata, Latinus interpres dixit Azoara: Postellus, lib. 11. de orbis Concordia, ubi Alkoranum refutat, usar: rem attendens Euthymius Zigabenus, μυθικὰ fabulas appellavit. Quando latinam versionem indicamus, azoara vulgo dicimus, vel surata, & cum pronomine suo, assurata: מורה Arabicè, idem est quod apud Rabbinos מר, vel הלכה, regula, lex, canon. מר Arab. ivit ambulavit. συγχεῖν τὰ κανόνι Apostolo dictum, Gal. v 1. 16.
units.tr: The Alkoran is called אלקוראן [al-qur'an]. Al is the article, and קוראן [koran] or Alkoran means reading. Some think it means a collection of precepts. Others derive it from קרא, to confess, and take it to mean confession. Others take it as a kind of correction of the Old and New Testaments. The Muhammedans also call it, in the Alkoran, Alphorhan, from פרק, he divided. Or it may be understood as a volume of distinctions, that is, handed down with distinct rules and chapters. Or it means the discriminator of good and evil*; so the version of Robert of Ketton, the Englishman. But just as Koran or Alkoran comes from reading, as מקרא among the Jews means Holy Scripture, so also Phorcan, or Alphorhan, is the book of chapters and sections, which among the Hebrews is פרק or פירקא. Just as the Greeks called Holy Scripture Biblos, from which we commonly say Biblia. In the Koran, sura 21, or according to Retinensis' translation 31: We also gave to Moses and Aaron the Alphurcan. The law of Moses is meant, because it too distinguishes good from evil, lawful from unlawful. Cardinal Cusanus begins his book Cribratio Alcorani thus: It is the book of the law of the Arabs, called Alchoran from the collection of precepts, and Alphurcan from the distinct separation of chapters. Yet that other explanation of Alphurcan is the stronger one. The chapters of the Alkoran are called in Arabic surata, souraton, or with the article assourata, which the Latin translator rendered Azoara. Postellus, in book 11 of De orbis concordia, where he refutes the Alkoran, calls them usar. Euthymius Zigabenus, considering the matter, called them μυθικὰ, fables. When we cite the Latin version we commonly say azoara, or surata, and with its pronoun, assurata. מורה in Arabic is the same as מר or הלכה among the rabbis: rule, law, canon. מר in Arabic means he went, he walked. The Apostle speaks of walking by this canon [στοιχεῖν τῷ κανόνι], Gal. v 1. 16.

units.la: Capita continet liber Alkorani cx iv. Secundum latinam versionem cxx iv. quorum alia inscribuntur Meccensis, alia Medinensis, quod partim Mecca, partim Medinæ dixerit Auctor sibi ea tradita fuisse: tantæque vulgò sanctitatis habetur apud Muhammedanos liber, ut nisi à toto mundoque attrectari nefas ducant: quare ejus corio extrinsecus litteris majusculis inscribere solent: ne tangat eum nisi mundus. אלמטהר אלא ימסה את In varias sæpe linguas Alkoran conversum est. In Latinam, anno clɔ cxl iii. translulit, jussu Petri Abbatis Cluniacensis, Robertus Retinensis, Anglus, cum Hermanno Dalmata; quam versionem anno clɔ lɔ l. cum multis aliis eò spectantibus, præcipue Refutationibus Alkorani, edidit Theodorus Bibliander, doctus Tigurinorum Professor, istorumque unus, qui Biblia Tigurina procuravit, obiitque anno clɔ lɔ lxvi. succedente ei in Scholâ, Ioh. Guilielmo Stuckio: quæque illius viri in studiis Arabicis fuerit diligentia, ex epistolis ejus ostendit Hottingerus, in Præfat. Histor. Orient. atque ejusdem Bibliandri Apologiam pro editione Alkorani recudi curavit, ediditque una cum Testamento Muhammedis, de quo post, Ioh. Fabritius. De Latina Alkorani versione Roberti Retinensis sciendum, non ex Alkorano, sed ejus paraphrasibus concinnatam fuisse; unde tanta istius versionis cum aliis, ipsoque Alkorano, diversitas: quod docet David Chytraeus, in Orat. de statu Ecclesiarum in Graecia, pag. 29. ubi in haec verba: ex publicis historiis, & Alcorano ipso, ac refutationibus Basileae conjunctim editis, studiosi cognoscent. Quos, si dissimilitudine editionum Alkorani offendentur, illud moneo, quod ex Jacobo Palaeologo Graeco, Pragae didici, libros unde illae translatae sint, non ipsum Alkorani contextum, rhythmis Arabicis constantem, sed paraphrases Alkorani, majori verborum copia, diversis ab interpretibus institutas, continuisse.
units.tr: The book of the Alkoran contains 114 chapters, or according to the Latin version 124. Some are headed Meccan and others Medinan, because the author said that he had received them partly at Mecca and partly at Medina. Among the Muhammedans the book is held in such reverence that they think it wrong to touch it unless they are clean from the whole world. So they usually inscribe on its outside cover, in large letters: Let none touch it but the clean [al-mutahharu illa yamassuhu]. The Alkoran has often been turned into many languages. In 1143 Robert of Ketton, an Englishman, translated it into Latin with Hermann the Dalmatian, at the command of Peter, Abbot of Cluny. This version, in 1550, was published by Theodor Bibliander, the learned Professor at Zürich, together with many other works bearing on it, above all refutations of the Alkoran. Bibliander, one of those who procured the Zürich Bible, died in 1566, and was succeeded in the school by Johann Wilhelm Stuckius. How diligent that man was in Arabic studies, Hottinger shows from his letters in the preface to his Historia Orientalis. Johann Fabritius also had Bibliander's Apologia pro editione Alkorani reprinted, and published it together with the Testament of Muhammed, of which more later. On Robert of Ketton's Latin version it should be known that it was compiled not from the Alkoran itself but from its paraphrases. Hence the great difference between that version and others, and the Alkoran itself. David Chytraeus teaches this in his oration de statu Ecclesiarum in Graecia, p. 29, where he says in these words: Studious readers will learn this from public histories, from the Alkoran itself, and from the refutations published together at Basel. If those who are offended by the dissimilarity of the editions of the Alkoran want to know why, I advise them of what I learned at Prague from Jacob Palaeologus the Greek: the books from which those translations were made did not contain the text of the Alkoran itself, which consists of Arabic rhythms, but paraphrases of the Alkoran, made by various interpreters with a greater abundance of words.

units.la: Transferendi quoque Alkorani in Latinum, animum habuit Nicolaus Clenardus, celebris iste apud nos Grammaticus, qui Lovanii docuit, & Salmanticae frequentissimo Auditorio; inde studiis Principis Henrici Regis fratris praepositus, raro, pro conversione Muhammedanorum promovenda, exemplo flagrans, relicta Lusitania, & in Africam suscepta peregrinatione, in Arabum Academia celeberrima Fesana diligentem operam dedit non linguae magis ipsorum, quam religioni perscrutandae, circa annum MDXXXV. cupidus tum Alkoranum vertere in linguam nostram, tum confutare, & instruere melius Muhammedanos: incitante ad haec cum valde Francisco Victoria, magni nominis inter Dominicanos Theologo. De illo suo studio, inter alia, ad praeceptorem Latomum sic scripsit: nisi mihi librorum defuerit copia, stat sententia fideliter Latinis dare, quidquid in ea superstitione positum est. Sed tum librorum, tum temporis penuria non perfecit quod propositum erat. Fesae agens, parcissime libros Arabicos nancisci potuit, invidente illos non modo solito Muhammedanorum in Christianos odio; verum etiam Christiani cujusdam perfidiâ, qui ut semper nostrae res infidelibus per pseudoChristianorum quorundam scelera proditae fuerunt, tantum effecerat apud Regem Fesae (quem Arabice salutare & alloqui Clenardus jam valebat) ut ne quispiam Clenardum doceret, neve libros quis ei traderet: inde & praeceptorem quem habebat, amisit, & tantum non discrimen capitis incurrit, sed &, nort diu post obiit, circa annum clɔ Iɔ xlii. Illiberi, hodie dicta Granata: reliquitque Grammaticam Arabicam, quae M. S. asservatur in Hispaniâ, apud Perusium Valentinum, virum doctissimum. Caeteroquin in unâ Bibliothecâ Fesanâ triginta duo millia voluminum Arabicorum fuisse, Er penius, ex testibus oculatis & fide dignissimis, retulit, in Orat. i. de ling. Arab. Uti in secundâ Orat. apud Arabes multa repeperiri, quae nos desideramus, Scriptorum monumenta, Titi Livii libros omnes, Pappi Alexandrini Mathematici, Hippocratis, Galeni multa, atque aliorum. Sed & Nicolaum Clenardum ibidem haud semel memorat, ejusque fidem, ut horum scientissimi, obtestatur. Clenardum certe adeo Arabicorum amantem fuisse legimus, ut saepe auditus fuerit dixisse: malle se fructum panis edere apud librum Arabicum, quam in magno hominum strepitu multum versari. Verum ad Alkoranum revertendo, ejusque tum versiones, tum confutationes: in Arragonicam se transtulisse, cum glossis, & librum Zunae, scribit Iohannes Andreas, Maurus, ad fidem Christi conversus. In Italicam curavit transferri Andreas Arrivabene, edidítque anno clɔ Iɔ xlvii. Hanc nos saepe consulimus & sequimur, ubi Latina obscurior est atque difficilior. In Germanicam vertit Salomon Swiggerus, Concionator Norimbergensis: eaque transiit in nostrum sermonem Belgicum. Haud ita pridem in Gallicum, ex Arabico transtulit Du Ryer, addit is subinde Variorum glossis, Gelaldin, Bedaoi, Teffitans Ioabir, Commentatore Alkorani Turcico, aliisque.
units.tr: Nicolaus Clenardus also intended to translate the Alkoran into Latin. He was a famous grammarian among us, who taught at Louvain and at Salamanca, to a very crowded audience. Then he was appointed tutor in the studies of Prince Henry, the king's brother. He was a rare man, burning with zeal for promoting the conversion of Muhammedans. Leaving Portugal and undertaking a journey to Africa, he devoted diligent effort at the celebrated Arab academy at Fez, around 1535, to examining their religion more than their language. He was then eager both to translate the Alkoran into our language and to refute it, and to instruct the Muhammedans better, and Francisco Victoria, a theologian of great name among the Dominicans, strongly urged him to this. About this project he wrote, among other things, to his teacher Latomus: Unless I run short of books, I intend to give faithfully in Latin whatever is set down in that superstition. But the shortage of books and of time did not allow him to accomplish what he had proposed. While at Fez he could get Arabic books only very sparingly, since the Muhammedans' hatred of Christians made them envious, and a certain Christian's treachery too. As always, our affairs were betrayed to unbelievers by the crimes of some false Christians. He had so much influence with the King of Fez (whom Clenardus by then knew how to greet and address in Arabic) that no one was to teach Clenardus, and no one was to hand him books. So he lost even the teacher he had, and ran almost into danger of his life. Not long afterward he died, around 1542, at Illiberi, today called Granada. He left an Arabic grammar, preserved in manuscript in Spain with Perusium Valentinus, a most learned man. Otherwise, Erpenius reports in his first oration on the Arabic language, from eyewitnesses and most trustworthy sources, that there were thirty-two thousand Arabic volumes in one library at Fez. In his second oration he says that among the Arabs many monuments of writers are to be found that we miss: all the books of Titus Livy, Pappus of Alexandria the mathematician, many of Hippocrates and Galen, and others. He also mentions Nicolaus Clenardus there more than once, and vouches for his reliability, as one of the most learned of these men. We read that Clenardus was so fond of Arabic books that he was often heard to say he would rather eat the crust of bread beside an Arabic book than be much involved in the great noise of men. But to return to the Alkoran, and to its translations and refutations: John Andreas, the Moor converted to the faith of Christ, writes that Clenardus had translated it into Aragonese, with glosses, and also the book of Zuna. Andreas Arrivabene had it translated into Italian, and published it in 1547. We often consult and follow this version where the Latin is more obscure and difficult. Salomon Swigger, preacher at Nuremberg, translated it into German, and from that it passed into our Dutch language. Not long ago Du Ryer translated it into French from the Arabic, adding now and then the glosses of various commentators: Jelaleddin, Beidawi, Tefsir Ioabir, the Turkish commentator on the Alkoran, and others.

units.la: Adversus Muhammedanos, & Alkoranum scripserunt Varii, de quibus videri potest venerandi D.Voeti Bibliotheca Theol. lib. 11. Ant. Possevinus, Biblioth. de Iudeis. cap. VIII. Scriptores aliquos contra Alkoranum edidit, unà cum versione istius latinà, Bibliander. Tales sunt, ut potissimos nominem, Ludovicus Vives, Hieronymus Savanarola. Disputatio Christiani cum Saraceno, ex Vincentii Lirinensis Speculo historiali, lib. xxiv. Nicolaus de Cusa. Cardinalis scripsit Cribrationem Alkorani, libris tribus. Richardus Praedicatorii Ordinis Monachus, Confutationem legis Mahometicæ. Iohannes Cantacutzenus, Constantinopolitanus primùm Imperator, postea Monachus, Apologias, & Orationes contra Muhammedem. Septem Castrensis, Auctor anonymus, de Moribus Turcorum, cum praefatione Lutheri. Æneas Sylvius, epist. cccx. ad Machometem principem. Euthymius Zigabenus, Panopl. part. ii. quod primum est, inter Saracenica Sylburgii, Graece & Latine, Theodorus Abucara: extat in Bibliothecâ Patrum. Euodius, Monachus. Nicetas Choniates, editus cum Gregorii Nysseni Catechetico majori. Ioh. Andreas, Maurus. Philippus Guadagnolus Apologiam edidit, pro Christianà Religione, adversus Ahmed, filium Zin Albedin, Persam Asphahensem, Latinè primum Romae a. MDXXXI. & postea Arabice, cujus exemplar habeo, a. MDXXXVII. Atque Ahmedis Persae illum librum, cui tit. Deterfor Speculi, scriptum fuisse adversus Iesuitae alicujus lib. Speculum veritatem monstrans, uti ex Guadagnolo discere potuimus, ita ejus authorem, proindeque harum disputationum & scriptionum primum fuisse Hieronymum Xavier, eundem qui turpiter Historiam Christi, Persice conscriptam, mendaciis & fabulis conspurcavit, docuit nos Ludovicus de Dieu, in praefat. ad Historiam Christi Persicam Xavierii, à se versam in Latinum, atque Animadversionibus in eam suis digne castigat stigatam. Guiljelmus Postellus, lib. 11. de orbis concor-dia. Auctor Epitomes Bellorum Sacrorum, apud Canisium, Antiq. Leƒt. tom. vi. Nominare hic an debeam Thomam Campanellam, lib. Atheismus triumphatus, cap. xi. ambigo, Addentur melius, Thomas à Iesu, de Convers.Gent.lib.x. Iohannes Forbesius, Instruct. Theolog.lib. iv. Ficinus, de Relig.Christian.cap.xi.&c. Grotius, lib. ult. de Relig. Alexander Ross, Anglus, lib. Anglico, A Caveat for reading the Alcoran. Avidissime exspectamus viri in rebus Hebraeorum, & Muhammedanorum juxta doctissimi, Ioh. Henrici Hottingeri, celebris apud Tigurinos Professoris, & linguarum Orientalium hodie Promotoris maximi, Commentarios de Religione Muhammedica; item Theatrum Muhammedicum: quorum spem egregiam tum promiss, tum specimine exhibito dedit in Thesauro Philologico, iterum in Historia Orientali; in cujus praefatione etiam Bullingeri scriptum de religione Turcica memorat: praeterquam quod in libris Historiae Ecclesiastica, quolibet seculo, inde à septimo, peculiari sectione secundâ, quod singulare ei est, prosequatur semper historiam Muhammedismi. VVilhelmus Schickardus, in Proœmio Turich pag. 76. mentionem facit libri à se scripti, de Orbo Dei Saracenorum, in quo errorem Alkorani confutet, Mariam matrem Christi confundentis cum Mirjam Sorore Aaronis: sed liber an editus sit, nescio.
units.tr: Various writers have written against the Muhammedans and the Alkoran, and one may consult the venerable D. Voetius, Bibliotheca Theologica, book 11. Antonio Possevino, Bibliotheca, on the Jews, chapter 8. Bibliander published some writers against the Alkoran together with its Latin version. To name the chief ones: Ludovicus Vives, Hieronymus Savonarola, the Disputatio Christiani cum Saraceno from Vincent of Lérins' Speculum historiale, book 24, and Nicolaus de Cusa, the cardinal, who wrote Cribratio Alcorani in three books. Richard, a monk of the Order of Preachers, wrote Confutatio legis Mahometicae. John Cantacuzenus, first Emperor of Constantinople and later a monk, wrote Apologias and Orations against Muhammed. Septem Castrensis, an anonymous author, wrote On the Customs of the Turks, with a preface by Luther. Aeneas Sylvius wrote Epistle 310, to Mahomet, prince. Euthymius Zigabenus, Panoplia, part 2; this is the first of the Saracen works in Sylburg's collection, in Greek and Latin. Theodorus Abucara is in the Bibliotheca Patrum. Euodius, a monk. Nicetas Choniates, published with Gregory of Nyssa's Greater Catechetical Oration. John Andreas the Moor. Philippus Guadagnolus published an Apologia for the Christian religion against Ahmed, son of Zin Albedin, a Persian of Isfahan. It was first published in Latin at Rome in 1531, and afterwards in Arabic; I have a copy of the Arabic edition of 1537. From Guadagnolus we learned that the Persian Ahmed's book, entitled Deterfor Speculi, was written against a Jesuit's book, Speculum veritatem monstrans. Ludovicus de Dieu taught us, in the preface to his Latin version of Xavier's Persian History of Christ, and in his own Animadversions on it, that the author of this, and so of these disputations and writings, was first Hieronymus Xavier, the same man who shamefully defiled the History of Christ, written in Persian, with lies and fables, and whom de Dieu rightly castigates. Guilielmus Postellus, book 11 of De orbis concordia. The author of the Epitome of the Holy Wars, in Canisius, Antiquae Lectiones, vol. 6. I am uncertain whether I should name Thomas Campanella, Atheismus triumphatus, chapter 11. It is better to add Thomas à Jesu, de Conversione Gentium, book 10; John Forbes, Instructiones Theologicae, book 4; Ficino, de Religione Christiana, chapter 11, and so on; Grotius, the last book de Religione; Alexander Ross, an Englishman, in his English book A Caveat for Reading the Alcoran. We eagerly await the commentaries of the most learned man in Hebrew and Muhammedan matters, Johann Heinrich Hottinger, the celebrated Professor among the Tigurini and the greatest promoter of Oriental languages today, on the Muhammedan religion; likewise his Theatrum Muhammedicum. He gave excellent hope of these, both in his promises and in a specimen shown in his Thesaurus Philologicus and again in his Historia Orientalis. In the preface to the latter he also mentions Bullinger's writing on the Turkish religion. Besides this, in his books of Ecclesiastical History, from the seventh century onwards, in each century, in a special second section, which is peculiar to him, he always pursues the history of Muhammedism. Wilhelm Schickard, in the preface to his Tarich, p. 76, mentions a book written by him, on the Saracens' Orbo Dei, in which he refutes the Alkoran's error in confusing Mary, mother of Christ, with Miriam, sister of Aaron. But I do not know whether the book was published.

units.la: Scriptores vero pro Muhammedisimo apud Arabes sunt plurimi, atque in Alkoranum quidem scripsere oppido multi: centum & quinquaginta enumerat Sidi Ali, in suo de Dogmatibus Moslemannorum libro, Descript. Arab. cap. xii. Circumfertur Testamentum Muhammedi, quod ab ipso in favorem Christianorum compositum fuisse dicitur, ut hi pari conditione cum suis ubique haberentur, vitâ, commercio, atque omni denique auxilio, vicissimque ut apud Christianos Muslimici omni fruerentur favore & privilegiis. Testa-men mentum hoc primus in Gallia protulit, ex sua versione Gabriel Sionita; iterum anno clɔ Iɔ cxxxvɪɪɪ. Iohannes Fabritius, Dantiscanus; Grotius, in epist. ad Salmasium, anno xxx. suppositum à Christianis existimat, ut sub obtentu tanti nominis Muselmannis æquioribus uterentur. Cui etiam accedo, & tum in mercatorum, tum Monachorum gratiam conditum arbitror. In fine ejus minatur, quod, qui conditionibus in eo contentis non satisfecerit, non fruiturus sit privilegio in favorem Praesulum Monachorum Christianorum indulto. Non videtur mihi exordium, quod nec est solitum illud in nomine misericordis Dei, neque eo spiritu inflatum, qui Muhammedi, proprius, ut nec finis satis pro authoritate, quam sibi arrogabat, testibus pluribus testamentum hoc confirmantibus, convenire cum genio Muhammedis & stylo.
units.tr: The writers on Muhammedism among the Arabs are very numerous, and many have written on the Koran. Sidi Ali, in his book on the doctrines of the Muslims (Descript. Arab. ch. 12), lists one hundred and fifty. There circulates a Testament of Muhammad, said to have been composed by him in favour of the Christians, so that they would be treated on equal terms with his own people everywhere, in living, trade and every other kind of help, and in return that the Muslims would enjoy the same favour and privileges among the Christians. This Testament was first published in France by Gabriel Sionita, in his own translation, and again in 1638 by Johannes Fabritius of Danzig. Grotius, in his letter to Salmasius, thinks it was forged by Christians so that under the cover of so great a name the Muslims would be treated more fairly, and I too agree and think it was drawn up for the benefit of merchants and monks. At its end it threatens that whoever does not satisfy the conditions contained in it will not enjoy the privilege granted in favour of the prelates and monks of the Christians. Its opening does not seem to me Muhammad's own: it is not the usual formula "In the name of the merciful God", nor is it inflated with that spirit which belonged to Muhammad, and the ending too does not fit the authority he claimed for himself. Several witnesses also confirm that this testament does not agree with Muhammad's character and style.

units.la: Arabes (an ita dicti ab occasu, עֶרֶב Vesperam significat, quasi ἑσπέριοι, populi occidentales, ad occidentem vel occasum siti; quod Scaliger, in Castigat. ad Festum, voce Erebum, sensit; Vossio lib. 1. de Idolol. c. xxvi. minus verosimile, qui à עֲרָבָה planities, desertum mavult derivare, primoque id nomen tributum Arabiae deserta incolis autumat; vel an à עֵרֶב mixtus, quia gens est ex variis mixta, colluvies hominum: nisi forte utrumque hoc facile conjungas, gentem ut significet mixtam; quae deserta loca habitat, quod Scindlerus, in lexico) etiam Hagarenos, & Sarracenos appellari, omnes sciunt; sed non ita, unde istud nominis. Illud obvium, ab Hagare, Abrahami ancillâ, Ismaelis matre dici. Sed quod erubescant, vel indignentur ex serva se nominari, & quasi malint à Sara Saraceni dici, multis visum, at temere; inter Christianos non modo, praecipue Veteres, ut Hieronymo, in Ezech. lib. 8. Sozomeno, hist. lib. vi. cap. xxxviii. Ut autem notam illegitimae originis & Agar matris ignobilitatem expungerent (fuit enim illa serva) Saracenos se vocarunt, quasi à Sara uxore Abrahae dcdescenderint. Sed & inter Iudæos R. David Ganz, in Chronologiâ pag. 313. Atque ex Mauris, Iohannes Andreas, Consus. secte Mahom. cap. 1. ejusdem sunt sententiæ, satis vulgaris, quam qui Muhammedica scribunt ex aliorum relationibus potius, quam fide & inspectione rerum Arabicarum, omnes communiter sequuntur. Et Michael Baudier, Histoire de la Religion des Turcs liv. 1. Sed frustra, quum à Sarâ nequeat derivari Saraceni, nedum Sarracenì: etenim in radicali hic ponitur ק, quæ in voce Sara non est: neque datam rationem obliterandæ Hagaris Muhammedani agnoscunt, à cujus filio stemma suum aperte deducunt, & honori hoc reputant, non vero habent ignominiosum. Couvarruvias, Variar. Resol. lib. 11. cap. 1x. Si à Sarâ derivaretur, non Sarraceni, sed Saraceni dicerentur. Inter Veteres Damascenus, à Sara quidem etiam, sed ex aliâ ratione derivat, lib. de Hæresibus Σαρακηνοὶ δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς κολῶν εἰς ἐπὶ Σαρρᾶς κεκλημένους, διὰ τὸ ἐρημίαν ἐσθαι ὑπὸ τῆς Ἀγαρηνοί, Ἀγαρηνοί, Σαρρᾶς κεκλῆσθαι. Saracenos vero eos appellant, ut ex Sara vacuos, eo quod Agar Angelo dixerit, Sara dimisitme vacuam. quomodo originem suam haberet quasi ex Σαῤῥᾶς κενή. quod in Codicibus Palatinis quoque, post Zigabeni fragmentum, καὶ Σαρακηνῶν legisse se testatur Sylburgius, in Notis. Nugæ. Et quod Erasmus, in vitâ Hieronymi, dixit: abdidit sese in solitudinem, quæ inter Syros & Agarenos, nunc corrupto vocabulo Saraeas dictos, nescio quid sibi velit. Neque nomen hoc venit à Saraca, urbe vel regione Arabiæ, sic dictâ, quod Stephano de urbibus placuit; Couvarruviæ; Guevaræ, in epistolis; Pinto, in Dan. vi 1. Sed ab Arabico פשט predari, latrocinari; nomine hoc à Vicinis impositio propter vitæ genus ληστεύειν, quod illi exercebant: Ita Scaliger, Scindlerus, Fullerus, Miscellan. lib. 11. cap. xii. Brerewodus Anglus, lib. de Inquisit. lingua cap. xiii. Ioh. V Veemsus, Scotus, in Decal. praec. vii. Exercit. iii. Buxtorfius, in Lexico. Bochartus, Geograph. S. lib. IV. cap. 11. Hottingerus, Histor. Orient. lib. I. cap. 1. Id quod Genes. xxxv 11. 25. Hebraice est, caterva Ismaelitarum, Targum habet דרקי מכבר ... caterva Saracenorum. Epiphanius, in principio Panarii: Ismaelita, qui nunc Saraceni vocantur. Chaldaeis inanem significat, quod Hebraeis בר ... viri inanes, Iudic. IX. 4. 11. Sam. VI. 20. Alii Saracenos à Sarra, Arabice desertum, derivant, & Sakan, habitavit, quia habitant in deserto: unde Graecis ἐρημίται dicuntur. Vide Cl. Georg. Hornium, ad Sulpit. Sever. lib. I. pag. 33. Certe Libyam interiorem hodie etiam Sarra appellari, ideo quod deserta sit, notum. Sed praeferenda illa, quam dixi, vocis origo ab Arabico Sarak, quod est praedari. Nisi cum Pocockio, in Notis ad Specimen Historiae Arabum, placeat derivare à Sharhion, & in plurali Sharhiun & Sharhiin, quod Orientales significat, ut idem sit Saracenus, & Orientalis, seu Orientis incola.
units.tr: Why the Arabs are so called is uncertain. Is it from the Hebrew word for evening [עֶרֶב], as if they were ἑσπέριοι, western peoples, situated toward the west or sunset? Scaliger in his Castigationes on Festus, under the word Erebum, took this view. Vossius (De Idololatria, bk 1, ch. 26) thinks this less probable, and prefers to derive it from [עֲרָבָה], a plain or desert, and holds that the name was first given to the desert of Arabia and then to its inhabitants. Or is it from [עֵרֶב], mixed, because the nation is mixed from various peoples, a mixed crowd of men? Unless perhaps you combine both, so that the word means a mixed people which inhabits deserted places (as Schindler says in his lexicon). Everyone knows that they are also called Hagarenes and Saracens, but not everyone knows where this name comes from. The obvious view is that they are named after Hagar, Abraham's maidservant and Ishmael's mother. Many have thought, but rashly, that they blush or are offended to be named after a female slave, and would rather be called Saracens after Sarah. Among the Christians, not only the older writers, such as Jerome (on Ezekiel, bk 8) and Sozomen (History, bk 6, ch. 38), say: "In order to wipe out the mark of illegitimate origin and the lowliness of Agar their mother (for she was a slave), they called themselves Saracens, as if they were descended from Sarah, the wife of Abraham." Among the Jews too, R. David Ganz holds this in his Chronology (p. 313), and among the Moors John Andreas (Consus. sectae Mahom., ch. 1) shares the same view. This opinion is fairly common, and nearly all who write on Muhammad follow it, relying on the reports of others rather than on faith in and examination of Arabic sources. So too Michael Baudier (Histoire de la Religion des Turcs, bk 1). But it is in vain, since Saracen cannot be derived from Sarah, let alone Sarracen. For the root here contains the letter [ק], which is not in the word Sarah. Nor do the Muhammadans acknowledge the explanation given, which would erase Hagar; they openly trace their lineage from her son, and count it an honour, not a disgrace. Covarruvias (Variae Resolutiones, bk 2, ch. 9): "If it were derived from Sarah, they would be called not Sarraceni but Saraceni." Among the ancients, Damascene also derives it from Sarah, but on a different ground, in his book On Heresies: "They are called Saracens, as if empty of Sarah [Σαρρᾶς κενή], because Hagar said to the angel, 'Sarah sent me away empty.'" Sylburg testifies in his notes that he read the same reading in the Palatine manuscripts, after the fragment of Zigabenus: "and of the Saracens". Trifling things! And what Erasmus said in the life of Jerome: "He hid himself in the desert which lies between the Syrians and the Agarenes, the people now called, by a corrupted word, Saraceni; I know not what he means by this." Nor does the name come from Saraca, a city or region of Arabia so called, as Stephen in his book On Cities thought, and Covarruvias, Guevara in his letters, and Pinto on Daniel 6:1. It comes rather from the Arabic [פשט], to plunder, to rob, and was given by their neighbours because of their way of life, which was to live by raiding; so Scaliger, Schindler, Fuller (Miscellanies, bk 2, ch. 12), the Englishman Brerewood (On Languages, ch. 13), John Vermeyden (Scotus, on the seventh commandment, exercise 3), Buxtorf (in his lexicon), Bochart (Sacred Geography, bk 4, ch. 11), and Hottinger (Oriental History, bk 1, ch. 1). This agrees with Genesis 37:25, which in Hebrew reads "a band of Ishmaelites", and the Targum has "a band of Saracens". Epiphanius, at the beginning of the Panarion: "The Ishmaelites, who are now called Saracens." In Chaldee [the word] means "empty", as the Hebrew [בר] means "empty men" (Judges 9:4; 11; 1 Samuel 26:20). Others derive Saracens from [Sarra], Arabic for "desert", and [Sakan], "he dwelt", because they dwell in the desert, and so the Greeks call them ἐρημῖται, hermits. See Georg Horn on Sulpicius Severus, bk 1, p. 33. It is certainly known that even today inner Libya is called Sarra, because it is a desert. But the origin of the word I mentioned, from the Arabic [Sarak], to plunder, is preferable. Unless one is pleased, with Pococke (in his notes to the Specimen Historiae Arabum), to derive it from Sharhion, and in the plural Sharhiun and Sharhiin, which means Orientals, so that a Saracen and an Oriental, or inhabitant of the East, are the same.

units.la: Turcarum (alii contendunt dicendum esse Turcorum) & nomen, & origo aeque incerta. Videsis Schickardum, in Proemio Tarich, pag. 40. & Hottingerum, Histor. Eccles. Part. I. Cap. VIII. pag. 517. Primus apud quem nominis huius mentio, est Pomponius Mela; inde apud Plinium, lib. VI. cap. VII. Ille in fine lib. I. Geograph. juxta Maeotim & Riphaeos montes, Turcas ponit: juxta Thyrsagetae Turcaeque vastas silvas occupant, alunturque venando. Unde ex Scythis oriundos se & ipsi, & alii communiter statuunt. Multorum hac super re sententias vide diligenter collectas à Ioh. Cuspiniano, de Turcorum origine, unde, à quibus, & quando primum in Persiam ac minorem Asiam prodierint, ignobili manu, & tenuissimis primordiis, palantes, praedantesque, pastoralis turba, quousque opibus & vi aucti cum Saracenis, quorum acceperant religionem, aliquoties confligere, & illustres erigere familias ac regimen inceperunt, tandem in primo ipsorum Rege Osman, qui Othomannus primus Turcorum Rex appellatur, anno cIↄ ccc. longe latèque Christianis & Sarracenis ademtâ multâ regione, fundarunt vastum hoc amplumque, quod hodie est, Turcarum, vel Othmanidarum imperium. Qui inter Christianos res Muhammedis scripsere, eum adjutum dicunt in confingendâ suâ lege partim à Iudæis, partim à pseudo-Christianis, in quos, dum iter hinc inde faceret, sæpius incidebat. Interque istos præcipue memoratur monachus quis hæreticus Monothelita, juxta alios Arianus, Sergius Constantinopolitanus, mansionis Callistrati, quem Græci Scriptores ψευδάββαν appellant, urbe propter hæresim expulsus, atque inde in Arabiam profugus, ubi ei cum Muhammede fuerit commercium. Leunclavius, Histor. Muselm. Turc. lib. 1.
units.tr: The name and origin of the Turks (others insist it should be Turcos) are equally uncertain. See Schickard in his Proemium to Tarich, p. 40, and Hottinger, Church History, part 1, ch. 8, p. 517. The first author in whom this name is mentioned is Pomponius Mela, and then Pliny (bk 6, ch. 7). At the end of the first book of his Geography, Mela places the Turcae near the Maeotian and Riphaean mountains: "Near the Thyrsagetae and the Turcae, they occupy vast forests and live by hunting." Hence many, like others in general, hold that they themselves are of Scythian descent. For a careful collection of the opinions of many on this matter, see John Cuspinian, On the Origin of the Turks: from whom and where, and when they first came into Persia and Asia Minor, a pastoral horde, wandering and plundering, of humble hand and very slender beginnings; until, grown in resources and power, and having adopted the religion of the Saracens, with whom they had fought on several occasions, they began to raise illustrious families and to govern. At last, under their first king Osman, who is called Othman, the first king of the Turks, in the year 1300, they took much territory from both Christians and Saracens, far and wide, and founded this vast and extensive empire of the Turks, or Othmanids, which exists today. Those among the Christians who have written about Muhammad say that he was helped in fashioning his law partly by Jews and partly by pseudo-Christians, whom he often met on his travels here and there. Among these a certain heretical monk is especially mentioned, a Monothelite, or according to others an Arian, Sergius of Constantinople, a resident of the Callistratus house, whom the Greek writers call Pseudobbas [ψευδάββας], expelled from the city on account of heresy, and who then fled to Arabia, where he had dealings with Muhammad. Leunclavius, Muslim and Turkish History, bk 1.

units.la: Alii vero non Christianum illum fuisse, sed Christiani cujusdam Meccensis gladiarii servum, cum quo colluserit Muhammed, existimant. Guadagnolus, cap. x. sect. 1. pag. 331. Illumque uxorem Muhammedis Chadigam, quando maritus morbo suo corripiebatur, monuisse, ajunt, ne consternaretur animo propter illos paroxysmos, quia sicuti Muhammed affereba, ita eo tempore, istoque sub symbolo Angelus ei apparebat Gabriel, qui cum eo de rebus cœlestibus & divinis confabulabatur, cujus conspectum non ferens istum in modum concuteretur. A judæis etiam in componendâ suâ lege adjutum scribunt, eosque Iudæi dicunt fuisse Phineam, & Abdiam ben Salon. Quippe ex Christianismo & Iudaismo hinc inde aliqua mutuatum cum, jamque his, tum illis acclamate, constat. Glycas, Annal. part. iv. Idem Mahometus in Palestinam profectus, quum in Iudæos, Arianos, & Nestorianos incidisset, quasi collectam quandam ab omnibus congesit, peculiaremque religionem suis tradidit. Prima fuit quæ religioni ejus fidem habuit, Chadiga uxor, tum servus Zeidin, Ali, Abubeker, Orman, aliique, qui Muhammedi postea successerunt Chaliphæ, quod vicarium notat, quasi Muhammedis locum in terra tenentes. חליפה à חלף permutatus fuit, successit. Rabbini dicunt חליף Halife Lulahe vicarius Dei, ποτογκράτος θεῦ. Mortuus fuit Muhammed (רסול apostolum appellant, tum נבי prophetam, rasul allah רסול אללה apostolum Dei) aetatis suae anno lxiii. anno fugae vel Hegirae, xi. die Lunae: ejusque tam accuratam tenent iconem, ut Nic. Clenardus scribat, in epist. ad Latomum, suum praeceptorem; se libellum legisse Arabicum, in quo ipsorum Propheta tam distincte ad unguem ab illis descriptus & expressus erat, ut ne quidem canos capillos omitterent, sed numerarent illum canos habuisse quatuordecim. Obiit in urbe sua Medina, ibique sepultus est. Quod de pendulo ejus Meccae sepulchro, vi magnetica in aerem attracto, vulgo narrant, fabula est. Gabr. Sionita, Descript. Arab. cap. viii. Primus post Muhammedem Chalipha fuit, socer ejus Abubeker, cujus filiam Ische secundam uxorem habuit Muhammed. Secundus Omar, itidem Muhammedis socer. Tertius Othman: & hic Muhammedis socer, qui pluribus uxoribus multos soceros adscivit. Quartus Hali, Muhammedis gener, ducta in uxorem Fatima, Muhammedis filia, quae die quadragesimo, vel septuagesimo post mortem patris, obiit. Quatuor isti primi sunt Chalipha, & qui Prophetae suo in vita astitere: sed post mortem gravis oborta dissensio, & Scisma inter assectas Hali, quem Persae; & Omar, quem Turcae sequuntur. Abubeker imperavit post Muhammedem, biennium. Omar, annis decem. Hic Alkoranum in volumen redegit, instituitque jejunium Ramadam, quod a Muhammedanis quam religiosissime servatur. Tertius Otman, duodecim, quibus regnavit annis, subegit Cyprum, Mauritaniam &c. tandemque domi suae occisus est. Quartus Hali, quem valde venerantur, & praeceptorem, & Regem fidelium appellitant, a Persis tantum non supra Muhammedem collocatur, suisseque ei dicunt, quod olim Mosi Aharon. Quin ajunt, Gabriēlem Angelum quando Alkoranum de cœlo adferret, in mandatis habuisse tradere istud Hali, sed quod per imprudentiam id dederit Muhammedi: quem tamen errorem Deus leviter tulit, quum sciret Muhammedem etiam virum probum esse ac fidelem. Verùm mortuo Muhammede, quum Hali, per ejus testamentum, successor designatus esset, & tamen Abubeker, postque eum insuper duo illi Omar, & Otman, variis artibus imperium ad se raperent, exclusò Ali, hic tyrannidem fugiens in speluncam se abdidit, usque dum illis è medio sublatis, tandem Chalifatus ad ipsum delatus fuit. Unde Persæ adeo execrantur priores illos tres Chalifas, ut dicere vulgò solent: Maledictus Abubeker, Omar, & Otman, atque clementia Deus utatur erga Hali, inque eo sibi complaceat. Neque illos pro Chalifis agnoscunt, eorumque acta & scripta si quando reperiunt, igne comburunt.
units.tr: Others, however, think that he was not a Christian but a slave of a certain Christian swordsmith of Mecca, with whom Muhammed used to associate. Guadagnolus, cap. x. sect. 1. pag. 331. They say that when her husband was seized by his illness, his wife Chadiga advised him not to be dismayed by those fits, because, as Muhammed claimed, the angel Gabriel was appearing to him at that time under this guise, and talking with him about heavenly and divine matters; and that he was so shaken by the sight of him that he could not bear it. They also write that he was helped in composing his law by Jews, whom they say were Phineas and Abdias ben Salon. Indeed, it is clear that he borrowed some things from Christianity and some from Judaism, and that he cried out for both. Glycas, Annals, part iv. The same Mahometus, when he had gone into Palestine and fallen in with Jews, Arians and Nestorians, gathered together, as it were, a certain religion out of all of them, and handed down a peculiar religion to his own followers. The first to believe in his religion was his wife Chadiga; then his servant Zeidin, Ali, Abubeker, Orman, and others, who afterwards succeeded Muhammed as caliphs, a word that means vicar, as if holding Muhammed's place on earth. [חליפה] is derived from [חלף], to exchange, to succeed. The rabbis call the [חליף] Halife Lulahe, vicar of God, [παντοκράτωρ θεοῦ] (Pantocrator of God). Muhammed died (they call him rasul, apostle, and nabi, prophet; rasul allah, apostle of God) in the sixty-third year of his age, in the eleventh year after the flight, or Hegira, on a Monday. They hold his likeness so exactly that Nicolaus Clenardus writes, in a letter to Latomus, his teacher, that he had read an Arabic book in which their Prophet was described and portrayed by them so precisely, down to the fingernail, that they did not even omit his grey hairs, but counted them and said he had fourteen grey hairs. He died in his own city of Medina and was buried there. The popular story about his tomb at Mecca, where a pendulum is drawn into the air by magnetic force, is a fable. Gabriel Sionita, Description of Arabia, cap. viii. The first caliph after Muhammed was his father-in-law Abubeker, whose daughter Ische was Muhammed's second wife. The second was Omar, likewise Muhammed's father-in-law. The third was Othman, and he too was Muhammed's father-in-law, who by his many wives gained many fathers-in-law. The fourth was Ali, Muhammed's son-in-law, who had married Fatima, Muhammed's daughter, and she died on the fortieth or seventieth day after her father's death. These four were the first caliphs, and they stood by their prophet during his life. But after his death a serious dispute and schism arose between the followers of Ali, whom the Persians follow, and those of Omar, whom the Turks follow. Abubeker ruled for two years after Muhammed, Omar for ten. He reduced the Koran to a single volume and instituted the fast of Ramadan, which the Muhammedans keep most scrupulously. The third, Othman, reigned twelve years, during which he subdued Cyprus, Mauritania, and so on, and at last was killed in his own house. The fourth, Ali, whom they greatly venerate and call both teacher and king of the faithful, is placed by the Persians almost above Muhammed, and they say he stood to him as Aaron stood to Moses. Indeed, they say that when the angel Gabriel was bringing the Koran down from heaven, he had been commanded to hand it over to Ali, but through carelessness gave it to Muhammed; yet God lightly bore this mistake, since he knew Muhammed was also an upright and faithful man. But after Muhammed's death, although Ali had been designated successor by Muhammed's will, Abubeker, and after him those two Omars and Othman, seized the government for themselves by various devices, and Ali was shut out. Fleeing this tyranny, he hid himself in a cave, until those men were removed and the caliphate at last came to him. Hence the Persians so curse those first three caliphs that they commonly say: Cursed be Abubeker, Omar and Othman, and may God show mercy to Ali and be pleased with him. Nor do they acknowledge them as caliphs, and if they ever find their deeds or writings, they burn them in fire.

units.la: Quatuor annis regnasse Hali, scribunt, ejusque acinacem vaginā eductum solitum fuisse se diffindere in duplicem, quo tum infideles, tùm Christianos instar segetis demessuerit. A suis nihilominus occisus fuit, & quoque in Sanctorum numerum relatus. Iuramentum si quando Persæ faciunt, id per nomen Muhammedis concipiunt, & Hali. Tantum Turcarum erga Persas odium est, ut Turcam ad Persas declinantem non secus execrentur ac si ad Christianos abiisset, mortisque afficiunt supplicio; immo Deo plus placere ajunt, si quis unum Persam, quam si septuaginta interficiat Christianos. Nata ea dissensio, vel tota præsertim fuit ex diversā interpretatione Alkorani, de quā non sine causā dixit auctor Septem-Castrensis, lib. de moribus, & religione Turcorum, cap. xx. De lege autem eorum & Alkoranu vel Mahometa tanta est inter eos disrepantia dicendorum, & narrationis diversitas, ut si centum de eis de hujusmodi interrogati fuerint, nullus eorum respondebit ad propositum alterius. Narrant, rant, post excessum Muhammedis, tantam copiam diversarum narrationum, legum, librorumque de gestis dictisque Muhammedis sparsim fuisse (quae de tanta hic confusione dicunt, eo minus mirum, quo non integrum Alkorani codicem Muhammed vel confecit, vel compegit ipse, sed farraginem capitulorum nequidquam concordantium tantummodo reliquit) ut Rex ipsorum jusserit Doctores comportare omnia sua exemplaria Damascum, exploratum quae servari vel aboleri oporteret. Vbi primum ex ducentis Doctoribus sex electi, qui librum Zuna composuerunt de dictis & factis Muhammedis, cui omnes in posterum acquiescerent: quod & factum, nam hi confecerunt ejus sex libros, singuli unum: caetera exemplaria omnia quae advexerant, tot numero ut ducentos camelos onerarent, in profluentem demersa. Neque sic extinctae illorum dissensiones fuerunt, quin manserunt sectae praecipuae quatuor; quarum Ductores, Melich, Assafihi, Alambile, Abuhamife, quorum inter se disputationes potissimum sunt de rebus matrimonii, repudii, de orationibus, jejuniis, balneis &c. in quibus istud genus hominum, ut religionem ponunt suam, ita vehementissime altercantur. Vide Ioh. Andream, Consus. secta Muhammed. cap. III. Iohannes Cotovicus Vltrajectinus, in Itinerario Hierosolymitano, cap 1. de illis sic loquitur:
units.tr: They write that Ali reigned four years, and that he was accustomed to draw his scimitar from its sheath and split it into two, with which he cut down unbelievers and Christians alike like a crop of grain. Nevertheless he was killed by his own people, and was also counted among the saints. When the Persians swear an oath, they frame it in the name of Muhammed and Ali. The hatred of the Turks toward the Persians is so great that they curse a Turk who turns to the Persians just as if he had gone over to the Christians, and they put him to death; indeed they say that God is better pleased if someone kills one Persian than if he kills seventy Christians. This dispute arose, or chiefly arose entirely, from the different interpretation of the Koran, about which the author of Septem-Castrensis, in his book on the customs and religion of the Turks, chapter xx, rightly said: Concerning their law and the Koran or Mahomet there is such disagreement in what is to be said, and such diversity in the telling, that if a hundred of them were asked about these things, none of them would answer to the purpose of another. They relate that after the death of Muhammed there was scattered such an abundance of varying traditions, laws and books about the deeds and sayings of Muhammed (and it is less surprising that there is such confusion here, since Muhammed himself neither composed nor compiled the whole codex of the Koran, but left only a heap of chapters that by no means agree) that their king ordered the teachers to bring all their copies together at Damascus, so that it might be determined which should be kept and which abolished. Then six were chosen out of two hundred teachers, who composed the book called Zuna about the sayings and deeds of Muhammed, to which all would afterwards assent. This was done, for these men produced six books, one each; all the other copies they had brought, enough in number to load two hundred camels, were sunk in a flowing river. Yet their disputes were not thereby put out, and four principal sects remained. Their leaders were Melich, Assafihi, Alambile and Abuhamife, whose disputes among themselves concern especially matters of marriage, divorce, prayers, fasts, baths and so on; in these matters this kind of people argues most vehemently, just as they make these things their religion. See Johannes Andreas, Consus. secta Muhammed. cap. III. Johannes Cotovicus of Utrecht, in his Jerusalem Itinerary, chapter 1, speaks of them thus:

units.la: Proximi in regno successores fuere Ebubeccir, Omer, Osman, denique Alim: qui tanquam sacrorum reges supremi legis Mahometicae Caliphae, plurima Mahometis scripta addiderunt. Hos, itemque Ebubanisfen, Malichim, Schaaffin, & Achmetem Sembelim, velut eximios Mahometicae legis doctores, seu Imamos, aut Santones, Turcae, Arabes, Tartari, Indi, Africanique Mahometani omnes venerantur. Contra Persae hos omnes, Alisicu Hali excepto, velut hereticos detestantur: scripta & libros eorum, ubicunque reperiant, flammis exurunt; crudeliter etiam in eorum observatores animadvertunt; Scheihadarus vero atque Harusiu doEtrinam veluti legitimam, ac caeteris sinceriorem, & saniorem amplectuntur; quos tamen reliqui Mahometae secta cultores execrantur. Hinc cruentum & vehemens inter Persas & Turcas jamdudum ortum est bellum, atque ingens odium, ut in se mutuo, tanquam hostes acerrimos, & haereticos pestiferos, crudeliter saeviant. Is autem Schiechadar a multis non habetur pro alio ab Erdebil, patre Ismaelis Sophi, Persarum regis, quod faciunt Cotovicus, & Leunclavius, qui antistitem fuisse dicunt, qui novae vitae & rigidioris instituto nomen famamque sibi acquisivit: idem est Haider vel Schich Haider, Scheich caput, Doctorem, regem, proprie senem significat. Erdebil non fuit ejus nomen, sed oppidi, cujus erat dominus. Sultani istius Haider filius fuit Ismael, istius nominis inter Persiae Reges primus, & familiae, quae etiam hodie Persis imperat: Sophi appellatur, propter vitam religiosam, quam sectabatur. secundum alios religiosum; alios, laneum significat, id est, virum laneo tegumento opertum: nam hoc discriminis loco Persae inter alia habent a Turcis, quod hi lineo & subtilissimi operis tulipanto caput involvant, Persae laneo utantur tegumento. Nisi alia sit vocis Sophi derivatio, ab antiquo Aegyptiorum nomine, quod sapientiam significat, & Graecis est σοφία. Vide Hottingerum Histor. Orient. p. 372. Ismael Sophi maxime sectam Hali, quam sequebatur, in Persia observari fecit, atque armis propagavit. Vide Descript. Persiae, ex Petro della Valle, pag. 188. Et pag. 175. originem Sophinorum, ex Leunclavio. Tantaeque apud suos Ismael Sophi est venerationis, ut & per ejus caput jurent religiosissime, & comprecaturi alicui, voveant, ut ille desiderium ipsorum expleat. Nummis suis ab una parte inscribi jubebat solitum illud: la illahe illallahu. Muhammedun resul allahe, id est; non est Deus praeter unum Deum: Muhammed Dei nuncius. Ex altera: Ismail halife lullahe. Ismael vicarius Dei. Leunclavius, Histor. Musulm. lib.
units.tr: The next successors in the kingdom were Ebubeccir, Omer, Osman, and finally Alim: who, as supreme caliphs and kings of the sacred law of Mahomet, added very many writings of Mahomet. These, and likewise Ebubanisfen, Malichim, Schaaffin, and Achmetem Sembelim, as outstanding doctors of the Mahometan law, or imams and santons, are venerated by all the Turks, Arabs, Tartars, Indians and African Mahometans. The Persians, on the other hand, detest all these, except Alisicu Hali, as heretics; wherever they find their writings and books, they burn them in flames; they also punish their followers cruelly. But they embrace the doctrine of Scheihadarus and Harusiu as legitimate, and purer and saner than the rest; yet the other followers of the Mahometan sect curse them. Hence a bloody and violent war between Persians and Turks has long been waged, and an immense hatred, so that they rage cruelly against one another as most bitter enemies and pernicious heretics. Now many do not regard this Schiechadar as different from Erdebil, the father of Ismael Sophi, king of the Persians, as Cotovicus and Leunclavius do, who say that he was a bishop who gained a name and fame for a new life and a stricter rule. Haider or Schich Haider is the same; Scheich properly means head, teacher, king, and an old man. Erdebil was not his name but the name of the town of which he was lord. The son of this Sultan Haider was Ismael, the first of that name among the kings of Persia, and of the dynasty that still rules Persia today. He is called Sophi on account of the religious life he followed. Others say it means woolen, that is, a man covered with a woolen garment; for in this matter of distinction the Persians differ from the Turks in other ways too, since the Turks wrap their heads in linen and most finely worked turbans, while the Persians use a woolen covering. Unless the word Sophi comes from another derivation, from the ancient name of the Egyptians, which means wisdom, and is sophia in Greek. See Hottinger, Historia Orientalis, p. 372. Ismael Sophi caused the sect of Ali, which he followed, to be observed most of all in Persia, and spread it by arms. See the Description of Persia, from Pietro della Valle, p. 188, and p. 175, on the origin of the Sophis, from Leunclavius. Ismael Sophi was held in such veneration by his people that they swear most solemnly by his head, and when they wish to pray for someone, they vow that he may fulfil their desire. He ordered that on one side of his coins be inscribed the well-known formula: la illahe illallahu. Muhammedun resul allahe, that is, there is no God but the one God: Muhammed is the messenger of God. On the other side: Ismail halife lullahe. Ismael vicar of God. Leunclavius, Histor. Musulm. lib.

units.la: xvi. Primum dissensionis inter Turcas Persasque caput est, super autoritate Chalifae Hali, nam hunc sequendum solum Persae dictitant, priores tres Abubekerum, Omarem, Otmanem execrandos. Tum, quod jam diximus, in operimento capitis istam diversitatem observant, ut Turca in capite gerat Tulipantum, lineum capitis involucrum, φακιόλιον[?] Graeci dicunt; Persarum vero secta praecipit, ne caput ex fastu quodam lineis ejusmodi spiris ornent, sed tegumento duntaxat è lanâ, & vili pretio, confecto. Quod quia plicas habet duodecim, Enafler, sive duodecim, ab Arabicâ voce, & Enafferlarii vocantur: denique quia tegmen hoc rubri coloris est quod gestant, etiam kisselbassilarii, id est, capita rubra, dicti. Hoc ergo pacto se à reliquis Muhammedanis Osmannicis illi distinguunt. Apud Musulmannos qui coloris viridis gestant in capite involucrum, eo significare prae caeteris volunt splendorem prosapiae, atque à Muhammede se oriundos, quemadmodum ea de causa Tartari in universum omnes ejus coloris habent tegumenta, quod de Muhammedis familiâ prognatos se jactant; & Rex ipsorum magnus Cham, Chitaunus dicitur, à capitum tegumentis istiusmodi è filtro factis: & familia Haly similiter eum in finem viridi colore utitur: quin in Tarich idcirco, uti observat Schickardus, series & posteritas Haly, quasi religione quadam & privilegio singulari, litteris viridibus descripta. Nempe isto colore, terrae gratissimo quasi indumento, Muhammed ipsorum Propheta jam senescens peculiariter gavisus fuisse dicitur. Ater color Muhammedanis (verba sunt V Vilhelmi Schickardi in proœmio ad Tarich) profaedo habetur & infausto, ut pullus incedat nemo Turcarum, nisi calamitatem aliquam insignem passus. Unde & Christianorum legatis olim vitio versum est Constantinopoli, quod nigrâ veste, coloris inauspicati, Bassas accederent, quo se habitu si non spernî, contaminari tamen hilaritatem quaerebantur. Multo ei praeferunt Rubrum, magis vero belli quàm pacis tempore, quod sanguinem refertur. Huic tantùm excellere putatur Coerulaeus, quantum & ipsum coelum inferiora superat; unde Alkorani vestibulum, tanquam coeli portam, eo plerumque pingunt, ut non semel observavi. Rursus hunc excedit Flavus, auriin terrâ, & in coelo Solis aemulus, cum tamen ipsum antecedit Candidus, velut immaculatus, & innocentiae signator, Luna proprius, quam circa Kalendas cum Iudeis venerantur, & in edium culminibus ac vexillis, ubique representant. Super omnes hos eminere creditur Viridis. In Babylone, scribit Petrus Martyr Mediolanensis, legat. Babylon. lib. III. Muhammedanos velamine capitis uti albo, Christianos glauco, Iudaeos croceo: Mahometha populus velamen fert, multis gyris lineis, quemadmodum & Iudaeus & Christicola, insimulatum. Sed Christicola glauco, Iudaeus croceo, Mahometha albido, coloribus discernuntur.
units.tr: xvi. The first point of disagreement between the Turks and the Persians concerns the authority of the caliph Ali. The Persians insist that he alone must be followed, and they curse the first three, Abu Bakr, Omar and Othman. Then, as we have already said, they also differ in the covering of the head. The Turk wears on his head a tulipant, a linen head-wrap, which the Greeks call [φακιόλιον?]. The Persian sect, however, forbids men to adorn their heads with such linen coils out of pride. They must use only a covering of wool, made at little cost. Because this covering has twelve folds, it is called the enafler, or "twelve," from an Arabic word, and its wearers are called enaffarii. Finally, because the cap they wear is red, they are also called kisselbassilarii, that is, "red heads." In this way the Persians distinguish themselves from the other Ottoman Muhammadans. Among the Muhammadans, those who wear a green head-covering want by it to signal above all others the splendour of their lineage and their descent from Muhammad. For the same reason the Tartars in general all wear head-coverings of this colour, since they boast that they are descended from the family of Muhammad. Their great king, the Khan, is called Chitaunus, from head-coverings of this kind made of felt. The family of Ali likewise uses green for this purpose. Indeed, in the Tarich, as Schickardus observes, the line and posterity of Ali are described in green letters, as if by a certain religious privilege. Muhammad, their prophet, is said to have especially rejoiced in this colour, which is most pleasing to the earth, as a kind of garment, when he was growing old. Black is regarded by the Muhammadans as ill-omened and unlucky (these are the words of Wilhelm Schickardus in the preface to the Tarich). No Turk walks in black, unless he has suffered some notable calamity. For this reason the Christian envoys at Constantinople were once blamed for approaching the pashas in black clothing, a colour of ill omen, since by such dress they sought, if not to be scorned, at least not to spoil the cheerfulness of the court. Much preferred is red, and red is thought to be especially suited to a time of war rather than of peace, because it signifies blood. Blue is thought to excel this colour as far as the heavens exceed the lower things. For this reason they usually paint the entrance of the Koran, as the gate of heaven, in that colour, as I have observed more than once. Again, yellow surpasses this, being gold on earth and a rival of the sun in heaven, though white comes before it, as spotless and a sign of innocence, belonging to the moon, which they venerate about the calends together with the Jews, and which they display everywhere on the roofs of houses and on banners. Green is believed to stand out above all these. Peter Martyr of Milan writes in his Embassy to Babylon, Book III, that in Babylon the Muhammadans wear a white head-covering, the Christians a blue-green one, and the Jews a saffron one: The Mahometan people wear a head-covering, wound with many coils of linen, just as the Jew and the Christian do, though they are distinguished by colours. The Christian is marked with blue-green, the Jew with saffron, the Mahometan with whitish.

units.la: Tertium in quo discrepant à Turcis Persae, circa ipsorum religionem, est in precibus: quippe precationes, quas Namasi vocant Muhammedani, Schach Ismaël alias, & novas, atque à formula Muhammedis diversas instituit. A Schach, quod Persis dacem, regem significat, (nam quod apud Arabes est Sultan, Tartaros (vel potius Tataros) Chan, Persis est Schach) nomen ludi vulgaris Schaccorum, vel latrunculorum dici, atque Persicae originis ludum, nomenque ejus esse, jam pridem à Doctis annotatum. Alias inter Muhammedanos in Africâ sectas vide memoratas Leoni Africano, lib. III. in descriptione exactissimâ Fessae, seu Regni Fessani.
units.tr: The third point on which the Persians differ from the Turks concerning their religion is in prayers. The Muhammadans call their prayer-forms namasi, and Shah Ismail, among others, instituted new ones, different from the formula of Muhammad. The word shah, which in Persian means "leader" or "king" (for what the Arabs call sultan, and the Tartars, or rather Tatars, call khan, is in Persian shah), is said to be the name of a common game of chess, or of draughts, and scholars have long noted that this game and its name are of Persian origin. For other sects among the Muhammadans in Africa, see those recorded by Leo Africanus, Book III, in his most exact description of Fez, or the Kingdom of Fez.

units.la: Turcae Persas Gauros appellant, id est, hereticos aut infideles, quo convitio vulgo etiam Christianos designant. Matthias à Michou Cracoviensis Medicus, qui scripsit Sarmatiam Asianam atque Europaeam, quorum illa Russos complectitur & Lithuanos, qui antiquis Getae; haec Tataros, lib. I. cap. VI. de Tataris inquit, quod à quo tempore Muhammedismum susceperunt, quod factum anno cIↄ ccxlvı. sub P. Innocentio iv. Christianos Ϛινtεις, id est, paganos, & γαυρ, id est, infideles & sine religione, appellarunt.
units.tr: The Turks call the Persians gaurs, that is, heretics or infidels, and by this term of abuse they commonly designate Christians too. Matthias of Miechów, a physician of Kraków, who wrote about Asian and European Sarmatia, of which the former includes the Russians and Lithuanians (the ancient Getae), and the latter the Tartars, says in Book I, chapter VI, concerning the Tartars: since the time when they adopted Muhammadanism, which happened in the year 1246 under Pope Innocent IV, they called the Christians kafirs, that is, pagans, and giaurs, that is, infidels and without religion.

units.la: Musulmannos ﭘﻮﺴﻠﻤﺎﻥ nominant Muhammedani asseclas, & perfidiæ suæ assentientes omnes. Quod quidem alii explicant salvatos: Vide Scindlerum, in Lexico; alii autem melius, credentes, fideles, obtemperantes. Gabriel Sionita, Arab.cap.xiv. Ita Leunclavius in Onomastico: Musulman orthodoxus, recte credens.
units.tr: The Muhammadans call their followers and all who assent to their perfidy Musulmans, in Persian. Some explain this as saved; see Schindler in his Lexicon. Others, better, explain it as believers, faithful, obedient. Gabriel Sionita, Arabic, chapter xiv. So Leunclavius in his Onomasticon: Musulman, orthodox, rightly believing.

units.la: Inter Genitzaros, quomodo prætorianum peditem Turcæ appellant, quorumque origo refertur ad Sultanum Muratem. 1. anno cIↄ ccc lxiii. plures sunt Christianæ originis, ex quintâ mancipiorum parte, quæ Sultano tribui solet, corroganda aut ex Turcis, aut Christianis, qui primò agricolis Turcicis ad operam præstandam, discendamque cum linguâ ipsorum etiam religionem traduntur, & hinc ad portam Imperatoriam mittuntur, in comitatu Sultani futuri, adscituriique Genitzarorum nomen, qui numero sunt, referente in epistolis Busbequio, duodecim mille, atque uti splendori & robori sunt Principi, ita ab illis ei maxime metuendum esse, viri magni merito observant. Vide Historiam Musulm. Turc. Leunclavii, lib. 1. & Philippi Camerarii Meditat. Histor. Vol. 11. lib. 11, cap. 1v.
units.tr: Among the Janissaries, as the Turks call their praetorian infantry, whose origin is traced to the Sultan Murad I in the year 1363, many are of Christian origin. They are drawn from the fifth part of the captives which is usually assigned to the Sultan, or from Turks or Christians who are first handed over to Turkish farmers to do their work and to learn their language and religion, and from there are sent to the Imperial Gate to accompany the Sultan and to be admitted to the name of Janissaries. According to Busbecq's letters, there are twelve thousand of them. As they are the glory and strength of the prince, so, as men of great distinction rightly observe, he has most reason to fear them. See the Turkish Muhammadan History of Leunclavius, Book I, and Philipp Cluverius's (Camerarius's) Historical Meditations, Vol. II, Book II, chapter IV.

units.la: Quod spectat Mubammedanorum dogmata, & pessimæ religionis articulos, sunt ii varij. Elmacinus, in initio Historiæ Saracenicæ, circa duodecim recenset capita, quæ Muhammed in exordio prædicationis suæ potissimum spectarit: nempe quod credere homines jussit in solum Deum ;eum colere & adorare; quod destruxit cultum idolorum;præcepit circumcisionem; instituit Jejunium mensis Ramadan; quinque orationes: peregrinationem ad templum Meccanum; prohibuit esum sanguinis, morticinii, & carnis porcinæ; sed & credi quoque voluit Prophetis & Apostolis: Christum filium Mariæ & prophetam esse, sed vero majorem illo; tum legem & Euangelium à Deo esse tradita. Hottingerus, Histor. Orient. lib. 11. cap. 111. ex Muhammede ben Abibecer refert, Muhammedis Pseudo-Prophetæ ipsorum quadraginta capita fidei & religionis fundamentalia, quæ si quis servet, salutem certo sit adepturus. Habet Mogbabed à Salman, qui à Prophetâ audivisse se refert, quòd dixerit: Qui è populo meo quadraginta servaverit dicta aut consilia, Hortum (Paradisi) ingredietur, eumque excitabit Deus excelsus, cum Sapientibus & Prophetis, ultimo die. Diximus: O Apostole Dei, quæ sunt quadraginta illa dicta? Respondit Muhammed. Si credis in Deum, & diem ultimum. Esse item librum Prophetas. Resuscitationem post mortem, Providentiam circa bona & mala. Si testaris, non esse Deum, nisi τὸν Θεὸν, neque Apostolum ejus. Si statis temporibus tuas preces peregeris, premissa ablutione seu purificatione larga, suo quoque tempore convenienti (solent enim Muhammedani superstitiosâ membrorum, manuum cum primis, ablutione ad singulas precandi vices se præparare)& consummatione incurvationum, & inclinationum, precibus singulis destinatarum. Si decimas dederis. Si mense Ramadam jejunaveris. Si Meccanum iter, ubi potes, feceris. Si singulis diebus & noctibus duodecim Recaas ordinarias oraveris; tres autem ex superabundanti pietatis studio. Si à fenore abstinueris. Nec vinum biberis. Nec per Deum in vanum juraveris. Nec contra quemquam Deum testem appellaveris, sive propinquum, sive remotum. Nec præcipitanter judicaveris. Nec fraudaveris fratrem tuum, vel à facie, vel à tergo. Neque mulierem castam abegeris aut repudiaveris. Neque suum cuique exprobraveris nævum. Neque vi quenquam coegeris, aut ludibrio habueris. Neque afflictionis seu cruciatus causa Dei timorem omnem abjeceris. Neque quæ inter homines sparguntur calumniose effutiveris; vel, si non fueris obtrectator. Si Deo gratias egeris pro quolibet accepto beneficio. Si patientiam probaveris in calamitatibus & afflictionibus. Si de misericordia Dei non desperaveris. Si cognoveris, quod omne id, quod evenit tibi, a te non aberraverit, (id est, non fortuito tibi evenerit, quasi alii jam fuisset destinatum) si enim a te aberrasset, tibi non obtigisset. Neque Dei iram in te propter gratiam creaturarum concitaveris. Neque hunc mundum, pro futura vita, elegeris. Si aliquid abs te frater tuus fidelis (Moslemannus) petierit, avare non denegaveris. Si in negotiis religionis observaveris eum, qui supra te est: in rebus vero mundanis (elegantissimam Arabismus habet paronomasiam) eum qui infra te est. Neque juraveris. Neque cum Sathana amicitiam contraxeris. Si vanitati valedixeris. Facultates orphani non rapueris. Clamorem auditum non suppresseris. Familiam tuam & liberos tuos si instituteris, in iis quae usui ipsis esse possunt apud Deum, eosque Deo ter Opt. Max. adduxeris. Si vicinis tuis benefeceris, neque ab iis, si misericordia tua egent, eam cohibueris. Nulli creaturae maledixeris. Laudes Dei, jubilationes, celebrationes, & magnificationes (detur venia novo vocabulo ad Emphasin Arabismi exprimendam nobis extorto) si multiplicaveris. Si in Alkorano in omni statu semper legeris, nisi cum fueris immundus. Si non deserueris septa cætus. Si tandem feceris alis quicquid gratum esset si tibi fieret. Hi sunt articuli religionis Muhammedicae fundamentales, ejusque summa, ad salutem Muhammedicam scilicet obtinendam. Adde & quae ad idem argumentum plura eodem capite adfert, ex aliis quoque Muhammedicis Doctoribus, celebris vir Io. Henricus Hottingerus. Pocockius, in Notis ad Specimen Arab. Abul Faraji, pag. 52. ex Pharestanio, quod roganti Gabrieli, speciem & habitum Arabis induto, quid esset Islamismus, respondit: ut confitearis non esse Deum praeter Deum illum, & me esse Apostolum Dei, & ut tempora precum statuta diligenter observes, & Eleemosynam praestes, & mense Ramadani jejunes, & ut ad Caabam, si commode possis, peregrinationem religionis ergo instituas. Et pag. 301. dictum refert a MuMuhammede, Islamismum fundatum esse in quinque rebus, Confessione hac, non est Deus praeter Deum illum, & Muhammed Dei Apostolus; Orationibus constanter celebrandis, largiendis Eleemosynis, Peregrinatione religionis ergo, & jejunio Ramadani. De quibus singulis egit, ex Muhammedanorum sententia, in sequentibus. Bernhardus Varenius Medicus, post Descriptionem Japoniae, commentariolum addidit de Diversis Gentium religionibus, ubi pag. 259. etiam Muhammedanorum, secundum praecipuos articulos, religionem breviter exponit.
units.tr: As for the doctrines of the Muhammadans and the articles of this most wicked religion, these are various. Elmacinus, at the beginning of his Saracen History, lists about twelve points which Muhammad chiefly aimed at at the start of his preaching: namely, that he ordered men to believe in God alone, to worship and adore him; that he destroyed the worship of idols; that he prescribed circumcision; that he instituted the fast of the month of Ramadan; five prayers; a pilgrimage to the temple at Mecca; that he forbade the eating of blood, carrion and pork; but he also wished it to be believed that the prophets and apostles were from God, and that Christ was the son of Mary and a prophet, but greater than him; and that the law and the Gospel were handed down by God. Hottinger, Oriental History, Book II, chapter III, reports from Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr that the forty fundamental articles of faith and religion of their pseudo-prophet Muhammad are such that whoever keeps them will certainly obtain salvation. Mogbabed has, from Salman, who reports that he heard it from the Prophet, that he said: whoever among my people keeps forty sayings or counsels shall enter the garden (of Paradise), and God Most High will raise him on the last day with the wise and the prophets. We asked: O Apostle of God, what are those forty sayings? Muhammad answered: If you believe in God and the last day; in the book of the prophets; in the resurrection after death; in providence concerning good and evil. If you bear witness that there is no God but God, nor any apostle but his. If you perform your prayers at the appointed times, having first made a full ablution or purification (for the Muhammadans are wont, in superstitious fashion, to prepare themselves for each act of prayer by washing their limbs, above all their hands), and completing the bowings and inclinations appointed for each prayer. If you give tithes. If you fast in the month of Ramadan. If you make the pilgrimage to Mecca, where you can. If you say the twelve ordinary prayers each day and night, and three more out of extra zeal for piety. If you abstain from usury. Nor drink wine. Nor swear by God in vain. Nor call any God to witness against anyone, whether near or far. Nor judge rashly. Nor defraud your brother, whether to his face or behind his back. Nor send away or repudiate a chaste wife. Nor reproach anyone for his blemish. Nor force anyone by violence, or make him a laughing-stock. Nor cast off all fear of God for the sake of affliction or torment. Nor spread slanders that circulate among men, or, if you are not a detractor. If you give thanks to God for every benefit received. If you prove your patience in calamities and afflictions. If you do not despair of the mercy of God. If you know that whatever happens to you has not passed you by (that is, it has not happened to you by chance, as if it had already been destined for another), for if it had passed you by, it would not have come to you. Nor provoke God's wrath against you on account of the favour of creatures. Nor choose this world in preference to the future life. If your faithful brother (a Moslem) asks anything of you, do not refuse it grudgingly. If in matters of religion you observe him who is above you, but in worldly things (the Arabic has a most elegant paronomasia) him who is below you. Nor swear. Nor make friendship with Satan. If you bid farewell to vanity. Do not seize the property of an orphan. Do not suppress a cry you have heard. If you instruct your household and your children in those things which can be useful to them before God, and bring them to God, the Best and Greatest. If you do good to your neighbours, and do not withhold mercy from them if they need it. Curse no creature. If you multiply the praises, rejoicings, celebrations and magnifications of God (let a new word be allowed, wrung from us to express the emphasis of the Arabic). If you always read the Koran in every state, except when you are unclean. If you do not desert the enclosures of the assembly. If finally you do to others whatever you would wish done to you. These are the fundamental articles of the Muhammadan religion, and its sum, namely for obtaining Muhammadan salvation. Add also the many other points which the famous John Henry Hottinger brings forward on the same subject in the same chapter, drawn from other Muhammadan teachers. Pococke, in his Notes to the Specimen of Abu'l Faraj the Arab, p. 52, from Pharestanius, reports that when Gabriel, appearing in the form and dress of an Arab, was asked what Islam was, he replied: that you confess there is no God but that God, and that I am the Apostle of God; that you diligently observe the appointed times of prayer, give alms, fast in the month of Ramadan, and, if you conveniently can, make a pilgrimage to the Kaaba for the sake of religion. And on p. 301 he reports a saying of Muhammad: that Islam is founded on five things: the confession that there is no God but that God and Muhammad is the Apostle of God; the constant performance of prayers; giving alms; pilgrimage for the sake of religion; and the fast of Ramadan. Each of these, according to the opinion of the Muhammadans, is treated in what follows. Bernhard Varenius, a physician, after his description of Japan, added a short treatise On the Various Religions of the Nations, where on p. 259 he also briefly sets out the religion of the Muhammadans according to its principal articles.

units.la: Praecipua nobis contentio iiscum est de Muhammede, an Propheta sit; & de recipiendo, vel repudiando Alkorano. Plura quidem omnino, sed in illis definiendis situm est fundamentum Muhammedismi. De Deo etiam sive S. Trinitate; de Christo, Dei filio, & Deo; de rebus creatis varia, mundo, coelo, Angelis &c. Sed ante haec omnia, ordinem tractationis Theologicae, secundum methodum capitum, si spectemus, quaestio est d; S. Scriptura, ejusque integritate, vel corruptione. Videlic. I. de Scriptura. II. de Muhammede. III. de Alkorano. IV. de Personarum in Deo Trinitate. V. de Christi Deitate. VI. de rebus creatis variis. denique VII. de extremis mundi: judicio; & paradyso, atque inferno. Haec Theologiae capita. Alia sunt capita religionis Muhammedicae, quae in praxi eorum observantur & constituunt: nam distribuimus, ordinis causa, capita, in Theologiae, & religionis ipsorum: nempe I. circumcisio Muhammedanorum. II. lotiones. III. preces. IV. Juramenta. V. jejunia. VI. peregrinationes. VII. polygamia, & repudium. VIII. prohibitio vini. denique IX. considerandi etiam veniunt ipsorum religiosi, & Monachi. Atque haec sunt capita, super quibus agitatur disputatio cum Muhammedanis.
units.tr: The main dispute we have with them concerns Muhammad: whether he is a prophet, and whether we should accept or reject the Qur'an. There are, of course, many other points, but the foundation of Muhammadanism rests on settling these. There is also the question of God or the Holy Trinity; of Christ, the Son of God and God; and of various created things, the world, heaven, the angels, and so on. But before all of these, if we look to the order of a theological treatise arranged by topics, the question is about Holy Scripture and whether it is whole or corrupted. Namely: I. on Scripture; II. on Muhammad; III. on the Qur'an; IV. on the persons within the Trinity of God; V. on the divinity of Christ; VI. on various created things; and finally VII. on the last things of the world: the judgment, paradise, and hell. These are the heads of theology. There are other heads of the religion of Muhammadanism, which are observed and make up their practice. For the sake of order we divide the heads into those of their theology and of their religion, namely: I. the circumcision of the Muhammadans; II. washings; III. prayers; IV. oaths; V. fasts; VI. pilgrimages; VII. polygamy and divorce; VIII. the prohibition of wine; and finally IX. their religious men and monks also come to be considered. These are the heads on which the disputation with the Muhammadans turns.

units.la: Praemitti illud debet, quod diximus de Scriptura Sacra; ut quod est principium, aliquatenus saltem utrimque qúe agnitum, à nobis integrum, sed quod Muhammedani ajunt corruptum esse, & mutilatum. Norunt illi Vetus, atque N. Testamentum, sed non omnes eius libros: præ reliquis tenent, legem Mosi datam, Psalterium Davidi, & Christo Euangelium. In Surata de mulieribus dicitur: Equidem nos inspiravimus tibi, sicut inspiravimus Noe, & Prophetis post eum, & apparuimus Abrahamo, & Ismaeli, & Isaaco, & Iacobo, & Tribubus, & Iesu, & Iob, & Ionæ, & Aaroni, & Salomoni, & dedimus Davidi Psalmos. Et quosdam Apostolos jam olim recensuimus tibi, quosdam vero non. Et colloquutus est Deus Moysi facie ad faciem. Truncata & confusa vides adduci Sacra: adduci autem, non in borum gratiam adeo, ac pro stabiliendâ Muhammedis auctoritate, quasi cum illis similiter modo à Deo inspirati. Quis ille ordo, Aaronem post Ionam, & Iesu; Salomonem ante Davidem, & post illos Mosem constituere? Alibi, cap. de Mariâ, Esdram etiam memorat: mentionem fac in libro de Esdrâ, quoniam ipse fuit justus, Propheta, & extulimus eum in locum excelsum. His sunt quibus beneplacitum est Deo ex Prophetis. Nisi non Esdras ibi intelligatur, ut quidem accipit Guadagnolus, Apolog. pag. 7. Sed Enoch, quem Arabes appellant Edris: quod confirmari videtur ex eo, quod additur, de Edris seu Enochi misericordi, & extulimus eum in locum excelsum. Sed de nullis crebrior in Alkorano mentio quam de Mose, ejusque torâ, lege; & Christo, atque ejus Euangelio. Surata xiI. Christo Mariæ filio commisimus Euangelium, quod est lumen & confirmatio testamenti, ad complendam legem. Ideoque omnis Euangelii servus judicium præceptorum ejus sequatur, quia alias pœnâ dignus erit. Faciunt Scripturæ S. libros centum & quatuor. Quorum decem ajunt missos ad Adamum; quinquaginta, ad Seth; triginta, ad Enoch; decem, ad Abrahamum; legem, ad Mosem; ad Davidem, Psalmos; ad Isa, seu Iesum nostrum. Euangelium; denique Alkoranum, ad Muhammedem.
units.tr: What we said about Holy Scripture must be put first, since it is the starting point, and is at least in some measure recognized on both sides: we hold it to be whole, but the Muhammadans say it is corrupted and mutilated. They know the Old and New Testaments, but not all their books. Above the rest they hold the law given to Moses, the Psalter of David, and the Gospel of Christ. In the sura On Women it is said: Indeed we have inspired you, as we inspired Noah and the prophets after him, and we appeared to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron and Solomon, and we gave David the Psalms. And some of the apostles we have already related to you, and some we have not. And God spoke with Moses face to face. You see that the Sacred books are brought in mangled and confused, and brought in not so much for their sake as to establish the authority of Muhammad, as though these men were likewise inspired by God in the same way. What order is this, placing Aaron after Jonah and Jesus, Solomon before David, and Moses after them? Elsewhere, in the chapter on Mary, he also mentions Ezra: Make mention in the book of Ezra, for he was just, a prophet, and we raised him to a high place. These are those among the prophets with whom God is well pleased. Unless Ezra is not meant there, as Guadagnolus understands it, Apology, p. 7.
