Rather it is Enoch, whom the Arabs call Idris; this seems confirmed by what is added about Idris, or Enoch: merciful, and we raised him to a high place. But of no one is there more frequent mention in the Qur'an than of Moses and his Torah, or law, and of Christ and his Gospel. Sura 12: To Christ, the son of Mary, we gave the Gospel, which is a light and a confirmation of the covenant, to complete the law. Therefore let every servant of the Gospel follow the judgment of its precepts, for otherwise he will be worthy of punishment. The Holy Scriptures make up one hundred and four books. Of these they say ten were sent to Adam; fifty to Seth; thirty to Enoch; ten to Abraham; the law to Moses; the Psalms to David; the Gospel to Isa, or our Jesus; and finally the Qur'an to Muhammad.

units.la: Hinc varias historias Sacras in Alkoranum relatas legere est, ut de vacca rufa, ex Numer. xix. quod caput Alkorani inscriptum ideo de Vacca; & noster D. Ravius Latinè dedit. De Saule, Goliathe, Eliâ, Elisæo, et libris V. T. historicis: de Zachariâ, Iohanne &c. ex Scriptis N. Testamenti: quæ ita lacera & corrupta in Alkorano adferuntur, ut vix dignosci queant. Nec tamen integros scripturas libros admittunt, conscii quam multa iisdem continentur quæ falsitatis arguerent ipsorum factas inde relationes, & instituto suo maximè adversantur. In Scripturâ Novi Testamenti imprimis quæruntur, nullam Muhammedis extare mentionem, quum Christum aliquando dixisse volunt: annuncio vobis nuncium bonum, quod pone me venturus est apostolus & propheta, nomen ei Muhammed. quod à Christianis erasum calumniantur. Atque ita pro arbitrio Scripturam admittunt, vel rejiciunt, fingunt refingunntque, & corruptam eam depravatamque in genere, sed frustra, clamitant. Quippe in Auctores istius objectæ corruptionis si primùm inquiramus, quinam erunt ii? Christiani, an Iudæi, an utrique? Non illi, quos præterquam religio à tali designando flagitio cohibet, nec historiæ memorant tale quid unquam aggressos, nec si tentare eorum aliqui id voluissent, ab aliis præteriti fuissent diversarum Sectarum (in quas Christianismus perpetuo scissus fuit) hominibus, non meliorem illos arguendi & damnandi occasionem habituris, quam si scelestas isti operi manus unquam adhibuisse convinci potuissent. Neque à Iudæis corruptæ Scripturæ, gente ad superstitionem usque pro servandis illis sollicitâ. Nedum ab utrisque, adeo inter se religionis diversitate & studiis discrepantibus. Tum si vel à quopiam ejusmodi facinus tentatum, aut à multis etiam fuisset, non ideo ab omnibus, imo fieri non potuisset, ita ut pariter vel Iudæi, vel Christiani, aut simul omnes conspirassent in idem scelus, ut non alii magis sani piique restitissent, & superstites mansissent saltem Scripturæ aliæ, ex quibus illa depravatio coarguì, & præcipuè deletum ex iis nomen Muhammedis, (ob quod unum hæc adeo vexant & disputant Muslimi) ostendi posset. Unde alterum adversus Muhammedanos hinc surgit argumentum, quod si vel aliqua corruptio Scripturarum facta fuisset, à quocumque demum Auctore (hoc ut largiamur, quamvis salsissimum), possent deberentque proferri alia Scripturæ exemplaria pura, vel saltem non in universum corrupta, antiquiora ipso Muhammede, ex quibus tum ostendi forte vitium, tum corrigi posset. Vel si nec hoc, saltem in aliis Auctoribus, ubi Scripturæ passim allegantur, istius deprehendi aliquod deberet documentum.
units.tr: From this one may read the various sacred histories related in the Qur'an, such as the red cow from Numbers 19, the chapter of which is therefore titled On the Cow; our Ravius has translated it into Latin. Likewise concerning Saul, Goliath, Elijah, Elisha, and the historical books of the Old Testament; concerning Zachariah, John, etc., from the writings of the New Testament. These are cited in the Qur'an so mangled and corrupted that they can scarcely be recognized. Yet they do not admit the books of Scripture whole, being aware how many things they contain which would prove the accounts they have made from them to be false, and which are especially opposed to their purpose. They complain above all about the New Testament, that there is no mention of Muhammad anywhere in it, though they claim that Christ once said: I announce to you a good messenger, who will come after me, an apostle and a prophet, whose name is Muhammad. They accuse the Christians of having erased this. Thus they admit or reject Scripture at their pleasure, feign and refeign it, and cry out, but in vain, that it is in general corrupted and depraved. Indeed, if we first ask who the authors of this alleged corruption would be, who would they be? Christians, or Jews, or both? Not the Christians, whom religion itself restrains from committing such a crime, and whom history records as never having attempted anything of the kind; nor, if some of them had wished to try it, would they have escaped notice by the men of the various sects into which Christianity has been perpetually divided, who would have had no better occasion to accuse and condemn them than if they could have been convicted of having ever laid hands on such a wicked work. Nor the Jews, a nation anxiously superstitious in preserving those books. Still less both together, so much at odds with one another in religious diversity and in their zeal. Moreover, even if such a deed had been attempted by some one of them, or even by many, it would not have been done by all, indeed it could not have been done, so that either the Jews or the Christians alone, or all of them together, conspired in the same crime, without others who were more sound and pious resisting, and without other Scriptures surviving at least, from which that depravation could be exposed, and especially the name of Muhammad, removed from them (on account of which alone the Muslims vex and dispute these matters so much), could be shown. Hence another argument arises against the Muhammadans: if any corruption of the Scriptures had been made, by whatever author (let us grant this, though it is most absurd), other pure copies of Scripture, or at least not wholly corrupted, older than Muhammad himself, could and ought to be produced, by which the flaw might either be shown or corrected. And if not this, at least in other authors, where the Scriptures are cited here and there, some evidence of such corruption ought to be detected.

units.la: Tertiò, si adulterare Scripturam adversus Muslimorum religionem & nomen, Christianis fuisset unquam animus, & facultas, quis credat non alia majora & graviora adversus istos eâdem opera in Scripturis apposituros illos fuisse, ubi jam nihil adeo sigillatim istos concernens reperitur. Quod si prophetiam Christi de venturo Muhammede demere potuerunt, annon similiter prædictionem aliquam inserere speciatim adversus Muhammedem, vel Muslimos, atque nominare venturum pseudoprophetam, & detestrimum impostorem Muhammedem?
units.tr: Thirdly, if the Christians had ever had the intention and the ability to falsify Scripture against the religion and name of the Muslims, who would believe that they would not, by the same work, have inserted other, greater and more serious things against these men in the Scriptures, where nothing at all now is found concerning them in particular? But if they could remove Christ's prophecy about the coming Muhammad, would they not likewise be able to insert some prediction specifically against Muhammad or the Muslims, naming Muhammad as the coming false prophet and most execrable impostor?

units.la: IV. Si semel dicas, depravata esse Sacra volumina, quî certus eris vel ipse, vel alios certos facies, de non corruptis ibi quoque, ubi tu censeas vera, vel admittenda pro veris esse, & quæ in Alkorano quoque ex Scripturâ adducuntur? siquidem in illis etiam corruptionem æque evenisse dicet alius, ac tu eam alibi ponis, semel traditâ Scripturæ S. integritate & puritate. Idem hic dixero, quod Augustinus, eâdem fere in causa, Manichæis, lib. xvii. cap. iii. contra Faustum: undique tergiversatio vestra confunditur, aperte dicite vos non credere Christi Euangelio: nam qui in Euangelio quod vultis creditis, quod vultis non creditis, vobis potius, quam Euangelio creditis. V. Vel quomodo, siquidem talia sint nostra Biblia, adeo corrupta & depravata, Muhammed in Alkorano eadem probat commendatque, ut & jubeat in dubiis Christianos consulere, qui illa jugiter volvunt? Cap. Iona: si suspicio tibi obvenit de his quae in hoc Alkorano misimus ad te, consule eos, qui legunt Scripturas pristinas ante te. Atque huc, pro Scriptura integre recipiendâ adducere licet, quod dicit Sur. Vacca: nunc creditis aliquibus Scripturis, & aliquibus non creditis? at non erit merces ei qui facit talia ex vobis, nisi confusio in praesenti vitâ, & quod in die resurrectionis tradetur acerbissimis tormentis, & non negligit Deus quod operamini. Ne hoc denique afferam, quod illam semper curam gerit Deus verbi sui, ut juxta vaticinium Matth. v. 18. nunquam futurum sit, vel coelo ac terrâ intereuntibus, ut apex aut jota ex eo intercidat; aliaque, quae hic pro astruendâ divini verbi perpetuâ puritate in medium adduci possent.
units.tr: IV. If once you say that the sacred volumes are depraved, how will you yourself be certain, or make others certain, that they are not corrupted even where you judge them true, or to be admitted as true, and also where the passages are drawn from Scripture in the Qur'an? For another will say that corruption has equally happened in those passages as you assert it elsewhere, once the integrity and purity of Holy Scripture has been surrendered. I would say here what Augustine said, in nearly the same cause, to the Manichaeans, book 17, chapter 3, against Faustus: On every side your evasion is confounded; say plainly that you do not believe the Gospel of Christ: for you believe in the Gospel what you wish, and what you do not wish you do not believe; you believe yourselves rather than the Gospel. V. Or how, if our Bibles are so corrupted and depraved, does Muhammad in the Qur'an approve and commend the same books so much that he even bids Christians, who constantly turn them over, to consult them in doubtful matters? Sura of Jonah: If any suspicion comes to you about those things which we have sent down to you in this Qur'an, consult those who read the Scriptures that were before you. And here, to urge that Scripture be received whole, one may bring forward what the sura of the Cow says: Do you now believe some Scriptures and not others? But there will be no reward for one of you who does such things, except confusion in the present life, and in the day of resurrection they will be delivered to the most bitter torments; and God is not unmindful of what you do. Finally, not to mention that God always takes such care of his Word that, according to the prophecy of Matthew 5:18, it will never happen, even with heaven and earth passing away, that one stroke or one jot will perish from it; and other arguments which could be brought forward here to establish the perpetual purity of the divine Word.

units.la: Objiciunt, quantum observare potui, pro sententiâ suâ Muhammedani haec duo. 1. Deletum è libris Sacris nomen Muhammedis. Hoc exprobrant Christianis, deinde etiam Iudaeis. Illis, quod Christi tale aliquod verbum eraserint ex Euangelio: annuncio vobis nuncium bonum, quod post me venturus est Apostolus & Propheta, nomen ei Muhammed. His tale quid objiciunt: Iudaei accesserunt ad Caabum filium Aschraphi, immutarunt legem, & scripserunt librum, in quo mutarunt totam Apostoli Dei Muhammedis. Resp. 1. Probare factum & crimen hoc debent vel Christianorum, vel Iudaeorum, in corrumpendis Sacris libris commissum, testibus & documentis aliquibus, certisque, ni, quam falsi dicam intentant aliis, incurrant ipsi: quod revera fit, dum nullo argumento, id quod hic confingunt, probare Muhammedani possunt aut confirmare. 11. quaero, quo in libro, capite vel loco Scripturae, legis aut Euangelii lectum aliquando nomen Muhammedis fuit? ut in Codicibus, aut Commentariis, vel loci antecedentibus & consequentibus, contextu denique, aliquod ejus vestigium aut monumentum ostendi possit. III. quin omnes sacri libri, antiquissimi probatissimique, & ipso Muhammede vetustiores constanter eadem ubique legunt, cumque illis nostri hodie Codices conveniunt. Quomodo si tam exserte notatum alicubi sive in lege, sive Euangelio nomen Muhammedis fuit, ita nullibi hoc servatum, sed ex omnium Codicum, scriptorum, impressorumque, Commentariorum, hominum denique omnium fide & memoriâ exciderit? IV. Sed hoc plane commentum arguit, quod ipse Muhammed, & in Alkorano, de hoc conqueri visus fuit: atqui quâ ratione vel ante ortum notumque Muhammedem, vel quo tempore in vivis adhuc fuit, Christiani, & omnes ubique falsationem illam Biblicam in nomine Muhammedis instituissent? quid obsecro minus verosimile dici à quoquam potest? V. Quod si sufficiat dicere, nomen Muhammedis olim lectum in Bibliis, vel inter dicta & conciones Christi fuisse, atque inde ablatum; idem possunt facile dicere vel Persæ de nomine sui Hali, vel Turcæ de Homar, in gravibus, quas inter se mutuo exercent, contentionibus, quibus tamen simile dicentibus ideo fidem non adhibebunt: quare nec nos pari commento, de nomine Muhammedis. Denique & quilibet impostor, mendax, seductor de se suoque nomine idem afferere poterit, hoc si sufficiat. Vel quid ni & de Alkorano, hoc nomen quoque in Bibliis expressum antea fuisse? vel in Alkorano olim fuisse forte hujus aut illius nomen &c? quae quis omnia tam facile, quàm vanè confingat. Confer & Ficinum, de Relig. Christian. cap. xxxv i. Iohannis Cantacuzeni Apol. contra Mahomet. IV. Et Richardi Prædicatoris Confut. legis Surrac. cap. III. Etiam Guadagnolum, cap. IV.
units.tr: As far as I could make out, the Muslims bring two arguments for their view. (1) They charge that the name of Muhammed was erased from the Holy Books. They reproach the Christians with this and then also the Jews. Against the Christians they say that they removed from the Gospel a saying of Christ such as: "I announce to you good news: after me there will come an Apostle and Prophet whose name is Muhammed." Against the Jews they allege something like this: "The Jews went to Kaab, son of Ashraf, altered the law, and wrote a book in which they changed everything about the Apostle of God, Muhammed." Reply: (I) They ought to prove this deed and this crime, committed in corrupting the Sacred Books by Christians or Jews, with certain witnesses and documents, or else they will themselves fall into the very fault they charge on others, which in fact happens, since the Muslims can prove or confirm by no argument what they here invent. (2) I ask: in which book, chapter, or passage of Scripture, of the law or of the Gospel, was the name of Muhammed ever read? Can any trace or record of it be shown in the codices or commentaries, or in the preceding and following verses, or in the context itself? (3) Indeed all the sacred books, the most ancient and most approved, and older even than Muhammed himself, read the same everywhere, and our present codices agree with them. How then, if the name of Muhammed had been plainly noted somewhere in the law or the Gospel, has it nowhere been preserved, but has vanished from the faith and memory of all codices, writers, printed editions, commentaries, and indeed of all men? (4) But this fiction plainly betrays itself, since Muhammed himself seemed to complain of it in the Alkoran. Yet by what reasoning could Christians, and everyone everywhere, have carried out that Biblical falsification in the name of Muhammed, either before Muhammed arose and became known, or at a time when he was still alive? What, I ask, can anyone say that is less probable? (5) If it is enough to say that the name of Muhammed was once read in the Bibles, or among the sayings and sermons of Christ, and was taken away from there, then the Persians may just as easily say the same about the name of their Ali, or the Turks about Omar, in the bitter disputes they wage among themselves; yet no one will give credence to those who say similar things, and so we likewise will not give credence to a like invention about the name of Muhammed. Finally, any impostor, liar, or seducer could make the same claim about himself and his own name, if this were sufficient. Or why not also say that this name too had been expressed in the Bibles before, or that the name of this or that person once stood in the Alkoran, and so on? Anyone may invent all such things as easily as he does idly. Compare also Ficinus, On the Christian Religion, chapter 36; John Cantacuzenus, Apology against Mahomet, book 4; Richard Prædicator, Confutation of the Law of the Saracens, chapter 3; and also Guadagnolus, chapter 4.

units.la: Secundo objiciunt Muhammedani illa Scripturæ loca, quæ inter se, vel cum veritate pugnare videntur, ex quibus corruptionem Scripturæ demonstrare satagunt. Vti, dissonantiam genealogiæ Christi, apud Matthæum, & Lucam, Euangelistas: quod legitur de Cainan, apud Lucam: diversam narrationem vocationis Petri, & Andreæ, apud Iohannem cap 1. & Matthæum cap. IV. 18. Quod dicitur Matth. XI. 13. omnes Prophetas usque ad Iohannem prophetare, cum alibi dicatur, Christum adhuc Prophetas mittere, & Scribas, & Doctores. Quod Ioan. 1. & apud Marcum legitur, Iohannem manducasse locustas & mel sylvestre; at apud Matthæum XI. 18. neque manducasse, neque bibisse. Quod alibi Petrus dicitur beatus; alibi diabolus. Christum esse Deum; & tamen visum fuisse: quum apud Iohannem dicatur cap. I. 18. Deum nemo vidit unquam. Quod Ioan. v. 31. Christus jam negat se testimonium de seipso perhibere; jam affirmat. Quod Christus Ioan. x. 18. sibi potestatem dicit esse animam suam ponendi, & assumendi; quum impossibile videatur, ut quis seipsum resuscitet. Matth. XXV. signa dicuntur edenda per pseudoprophetas; quum nemo possit miracula facere, præter Deum. Objiciunt dissensum apud Euangelistas, in diversa narratione de negatione Petri; de blasphemante in cruce Latrone, an Latronibus. Quod Matth. XII. 40. Christus tribus diebus & noctibus futurus dicitur in corde terræ; nec tamen tamdiu inter mortuos fuit. Marc. XVI. 16. dicitur condemnandus qui non crediderit; quum tamen non videamus puniri omnes, qui increduli sunt. Suscitatio filiæ Archisynagogi non eodem modo facta narratur apud Euangelistas. Tum quod Christus Matth. v. videtur legem Mosis abrogasse, quoque adferunt. Item, quod dicitur Marc. ult. Ite, prædicate Euangelium, quasi alium hic Christus librum tradiderit Apostolis, ab eo, quem nunc habemus. Ista adversus integritatem & ἀφθαρσίαν S. Scripturæ, omnia, uti videmus, ex historia N. Testamenti, nil ex Vetere, objiciunt Muhammedani, interque eos Ahmed Alabedin Persa lib. Politor Speculi: cui respondit Apologia pro religione Christiana, Philippus Guadagnolus. Haec autem objecta dissolvit, Apologiae suae cap. IV. potissimum cap. VII. ut operam in exponendis illis, & confutandis siculneis objectionibus, & contradictionibus tam leviter confictis ponere nihil necessum arbitremur, praesertim quum & illa obvia sint apud quoscunque Scriptores Christianos, & in Commentariis abunde solvantur. Recensere tamen haud inconsultum judicavi, ut sciretur quaenam illa sint, quae hac in re pro se adducunt Muhammedani, & simul ut imprudentiam illorum inter Christianos notaremus, qui in illis & similibus Scripturae locis nimis tralatitie errorem sive Scriptorum, sive Scripturae concedentes, manus infidelium hac in parte haud oscitantes firmant, quum absque illo aliter & melius ad singula responderi, & αὐτοφωνίας commode tolli possint. Haec prima est cum Muslimis disputatio, super Scriptura Sacra, ejusque invictiata puritate: hic cardo disputationis, ut non immerito scripserit Nicolaus Clenardus, ad praeceptorem suum Latomum, quando de Muhammedis doctrina inquit: negat Christum a Iudeis crucifixum, negat eum redemtorem humani generis. Atque haec cum asseverent, ajunt se credere Evangelio & V. Testamento: verum & nos, & Iudaeos non habere libros incorruptos. Hic est disputationis cardo.
units.tr: Secondly, the Muslims object to those passages of Scripture which seem to conflict with each other or with the truth, and from which they strive to demonstrate the corruption of Scripture. Such are: the discrepancy between the genealogies of Christ in the Evangelists Matthew and Luke; what is read of Cainan in Luke; the differing accounts of the calling of Peter and Andrew in John chapter 1 and Matthew chapter 4:18; what is said in Matthew 11:13, that all the Prophets prophesied until John, when elsewhere it is said that Christ still sends Prophets, and scribes, and teachers. Also that John, according to John 1 and Mark, ate locusts and wild honey, but according to Matthew 11:18 neither ate nor drank. That Peter is elsewhere called blessed and elsewhere the devil; that Christ is God and yet was seen, whereas John 1:18 says that no one has ever seen God. That in John 5:31 Christ now denies that he bears witness of himself, and now affirms it. That Christ in John 10:18 says he has the power to lay down his soul and take it up again, whereas it seems impossible for anyone to raise himself. That Matthew 25 says signs will be shown by false prophets, although no one can work miracles except God. They object to disagreement among the Evangelists in their differing accounts of Peter's denial, and of the thief blaspheming on the cross, whether it was one thief or two. That Matthew 12:40 says Christ would be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, yet he was not among the dead so long. Mark 16:16 says that whoever does not believe will be condemned, yet we do not see all unbelievers punished. The raising of the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is not narrated in the same way by the Evangelists. They also adduce that Christ in Matthew 5 seems to have abrogated the law of Moses; likewise that Mark's last chapter says, "Go, preach the Gospel," as if Christ here handed the Apostles a different book from the one we now have. All these objections against the integrity and incorruptibility [ἀφθαρσίαν] of holy Scripture, as we see, are drawn from the history of the New Testament, and nothing from the Old; the Muslims, and among them Ahmed Alabedin the Persian in his book Politor Speculi, raise them. To him replied Philip Guadagnolus in his Apology for the Christian Religion. Guadagnolus resolves these objections chiefly in chapters 4 and 7 of his Apology. I therefore judge that it is unnecessary for me to spend effort in expounding and refuting these objections and contradictions, so lightly contrived, especially since they are obvious in all Christian writers and are amply answered in the commentaries. Yet I thought it not unwise to list them, so that it might be known what these are that the Muslims adduce in this matter, and at the same time so that we might note the thoughtlessness of those Christians who, too readily conceding error in these and similar passages of Scripture, either to the writers or to Scripture itself, confirm the hands of the infidels, which are not idle on this point, whereas without that concession each point can be answered otherwise and better, and self-contradiction [αὐτοφωνίας] can be conveniently removed. This is the first disputation with the Muslims, about Holy Scripture and its unshaken purity; this is the hinge of the dispute, as Nicolaus Clenardus rightly wrote to his teacher Latomus, when speaking of the doctrine of Muhammed: "He denies that Christ was crucified by the Jews, he denies that he is the redeemer of the human race. And while they assert these things, they say they believe the Gospel and the Old Testament; but we and the Jews, they say, do not have uncorrupted books. This is the hinge of the dispute."

units.la: Illud de principio religionis, S. Scriptura: unde disputationem melius quis ordiatur in tractatione controversiarum, quam in praesenti cum Adversariis actione: quippe hic potius a Muhammede, vel Alkorano, seu utriusque authoritate exordium instituetur. De Muhammede primum, utpote Alkorani Auctore, quem non Prophetam solum habent, sed & majorem Christo. Tres vulgo celebrant Prophetas. Mosem, Iesum, Muhammedem; sed hunc tantum Christo praecellere ajunt, ac is Mosi. Mosi lex, Christo Euangelium, Alkoran Muhammedi traditum. Vnde ultimus Prophetarum dicitur, quem scilicet Deus miserit. Surata xliii. xlv. xlviii. l. & lvii. Benefacientes, & veritati in Muhammedo positæ credentes, ipsius Dei viam & veritatem sequuntur. Vnde ista ejus vox erat: qui obedit mihi, ipsi Deo obedit; qui adversatur mihi, ipsi Deo adversatur: qui Principi meo paret, mihi paret; & qui Principi repugnat, mihi repugnat. Hic de quo vulgo in ore habent, quod & portis cœli inscriptum fabulantur: לא אלה non est Deus, nisi Deus ille; & Muhammed, Dei nuncius. In Alkorano, Surat. ix. qui sequitur Legatum, imitatur Deum. Quare ergo malevoli non credunt Alkorano? Atque passim conjungitur Muhammed, cum Alkorano suo, ut utrique par videlicet exhibeatur reverentia, & cultus. Surata x. Viri boni credite Deo, & legato ejus, & libro divinitus misso de cœlo. Refert Clenardus, in epistolis, quod quum Fesæ degeret, Arabicæ linguæ addiscendæ ergo, Doctor aliquis Muslimus in periculum fere capitis venerit, ideo quod in Scholâ docuisset: Muhammedem non quidem peccasse unquam, potuisse tamen leviter peccare, in surripiendo forte à puero per jocum pomo, aut simile quid. Tanti habetur apud illos, tamque ἀναμίρτητον, & omni ex parte ἀμαμον Muhammed.
units.tr: Let us start with the principle of religion, Holy Scripture. A disputation in treating controversies is better begun from this point than in the present action with our adversaries; for here the starting point will rather be made from Muhammed, or the Alkoran, or the authority of both. We shall take Muhammed first, as the author of the Alkoran, whom they regard not only as a Prophet but as greater than Christ. They commonly celebrate three Prophets: Moses, Jesus, and Muhammed; but they say that Muhammed alone excels Christ, and Christ excels Moses. To Moses was given the law, to Christ the Gospel, to Muhammed the Alkoran. Hence he is called the last of the Prophets, that is, whom God sent. Suras 43, 45, 48, 50, and 57: "Those who do good and believe in the truth set forth in Muhammed follow the very way and truth of God." Hence this was his saying: "Whoever obeys me obeys God himself; whoever opposes me opposes God himself; whoever obeys my Prince obeys me; and whoever resists the Prince resists me." This is the man whom they commonly have on their lips, and whom they fable is also inscribed on the gates of heaven: [לא אלה] "There is no God but God, and Muhammed is the messenger of God." In the Alkoran, Sura 9: "He who follows the Messenger imitates God. Why then do the malicious not believe the Alkoran?" And Muhammed is constantly joined with his Alkoran, so that equal reverence and worship are shown to each. Sura 10: "Good men, believe in God, and in his messenger, and in the book sent down from heaven." Clenardus relates in his letters that, while he was staying at Fez to learn the Arabic language, a certain Muslim teacher came close to losing his life for having taught in a school that Muhammed indeed never sinned, but could nevertheless have sinned slightly, by perhaps stealing an apple from a boy in jest, or something of the sort. Such is the esteem in which they hold Muhammed, so sinless [ἀναμάρτητον] and in every respect faultless [ἄμωμον].

units.la: Sed primò, quodnam ipse ullibi quæso argumentum dedit Prophetæ, vel imo justi hominis? adeo nil nisi bella ejus, prælia, & depopulationes ipsi Muslimorum narrant historici. Christus, aliique Prophetæ se probarunt vulgo dupliciter, dictis, tum factis. De Iesu hoc manifestissimum. Luc. xxiv. 19. qui fuit propheta, potens in opere & verbo; coram Deo & omni populo. Act. i. 1. quæ capit Iesus facere & docere. Præter alia ei ab aliis, atque præsertim à Deo Patre suo data testimonia. Ioann. v. 3. 32. 36. 37. 39. alius est qui de me testatur, & novi quod verum sit testimonium, quod testatur. statum de me. Vos misistis ad Iohannem & testimonium perhibuit veritati. Ego autem habeo testimonium majus Iohanne, nam opera quae dedit mihi Pater ut illa perficerem, illa ipsa opera quae ego facio, testantur de me quod Pater me miserit. Et qui misit me Pater, ipse testatus est de me. Ubi vero Muhammedis tale aliquod testimonium, nedum majus, dum se Christo cupit praeferri? Ubi Deus de eo testatus, vel alius Propheta, exceptione major, qualis pro Christo fuit Baptista Iohannes? vel, quae sive docuit divina, sive patravit miracula, quae fidem tam extraordinario Prophetae concilient? Vbi ex adverso interrogatus aliquoties de miraculis, frigida responsione eludere homines consuevit: quod ex ipso patet Alkorano. Surata XVI. petentibus ut eis virtutes miraculaque Dei faciat, dic, Deum omnipotentem illa facere. Iterum Surat. XVII. quum dixerint tibi, quare non facis miracula? respondé illis, non missum ad aliud quid, quam ut exponeres mandata Dei. Quali responsione omnino vocationem suam non suspectam solum reddidit, sed damnavit, ac ostendit falsam; quum Deus Prophetas suos extraordinarios, ad novum statum Ecclesiae inducendum, missos, nedum quale negotium visum fuit Muhammedis, dono & potestate miraculorum instruere solitus sit: quod de Christo, & Apostolis fatentur Muhammedani. Prodigiosa quae de Propheta suo narrant, tum res ipsa arguit conficta esse, tum nullius etiam testimonio fide digno confirmantur, & non in propatulo, sed clam, in angulo, vel privatim & noctu, procul ab arbitris testibusque, contra ac in tali negotio fieri solet, accidisse perhibent, id est, propriae narrationis indicio ipsi omnia confutant. Quale, ne hoc etiam praetermittam, quod Abdalla Muhammedem, ubi Medinam venisset, ex facie dignoscens (scilicet ita Prophetae explorari vel deprehendi solent) propositis ei tribus quaestionibus, quas hactenus Prophetarum nemo solvisset, ex argutâ responsione Prophetam tam collegit. Audire gestias sublimes istas interrogationes. Prima erat, quidnam primum in die judicii eventurum esset? respondit Abulcasimus, ignis primum homines congregabit ab Oriente in Occidentem. Altera: quo primum cibo in Paradyso vescerentur beati? respondit: jecore piscis. Tertia: unde fiat quod puer aliquando in Patrem magis, aliquando in Matrem feratur? respondit Candidatus: hoc accidere ab emisso in coitu femine, sive patris primum, sive matris. Dignum videlicet tanto Prophetâ examen, & judicium! nam ita vel ex facici lineamentis, vel per propositas quaestiones, easque futiles & nugaces, Prophetae explorari probarique solent, scilicet. Deinde, nec probavit se Prophetam Muhammed, neque tantus Propheta esse potuit: quandoquidem post Iohannem Baptistam, de quo dictum: Lex & Prophetae usque ad Iohannem: inde regnum Dei evangelizatur. Luc. xvi. 16. & Prophetam illum magnum Christum, cujus ille erat phosphorus, nulli de novo alii, ultimo hoc tempore, exspectari Prophetae debuerunt, minus major qui omnibus praecedentibus esset, & ipso adeo Christo excellentior. Neque id argumentum, quia ex Novo sumtum Testamento, ideo eludere possunt Muslimi: quia nec Novum Testamentum integre rejiciunt, neque Iohannis Baptistae historiam, quae cum patris sui Zachariae, distinctum in Alkorano facit caput. Tum iii. quamvis istud non obstaret, redargueret Prophetam hunc satis, quae eum commendare deberent, sua ipsius tum doctrina, tum vita. Et haec quidem quam impia, quam turpis fuit? quid Prophetam? vix hominem retulit. Nam quum vita ejus vitiis & sceleribus fuerit cooperta, tum in duobus insigniter probrosa semper extitit, libidine videlicet, & in alios crudelitate. Homo impurissimus legem tulit de pluribus simul capiendis uxoribus, quatuor nempe aut quinque, quod spurcae mentis dilucidum fuit argumentum: & quo ostenderet se
units.tr: But first, I ask, what proof did he ever give of being a prophet, or even of being a just man? The Muslim historians themselves tell of nothing but his wars, battles and plunderings. Christ and the other prophets, as the common view holds, proved themselves in two ways, by their words and by their deeds. In the case of Jesus this is very plain. Luke 24:19: who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people. Acts 1:1: all that Jesus began both to do and to teach. Besides these, he had other testimonies from others, and above all from God his Father. John 5:31-32, 36-37, 39: There is another who bears witness of me, and I know that the witness which he bears of me is true. You sent to John, and he bore witness to the truth. But I have a greater witness than John, for the works which the Father gave me to finish, the very works which I do, bear witness of me, that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness of me. But where is any such testimony for Muhammad, let alone a greater one, since he wishes to be preferred to Christ? Where did God bear witness to him, or another prophet, with an exception as great as that which John the Baptist made for Christ? Or what divine teaching or miracles did he perform that would win faith for so extraordinary a prophet? Whenever he was questioned about miracles, he was accustomed to put people off with a feeble answer, as the Alcoran itself shows. Sura 16: To those who ask that he should show them the powers and miracles of God, say: God almighty does those things. Again, Sura 17: When they have said to you, why do you not work miracles? answer them: I was sent for no other purpose than to expound the commands of God. By such an answer he did not merely make his calling suspect, but condemned it and showed it to be false, since God was accustomed to equip the prophets he sent to introduce a new state of the Church with the gift and power of miracles, and this was not what Muhammad's mission seemed to need. The Muslims themselves confess this of Christ and the apostles. The prodigies they tell of their prophet are shown to be made up by the very nature of the thing, and they are not confirmed by the testimony of any reliable witness. They say they happened not in public but in secret, in a corner, privately and by night, far from onlookers and witnesses, contrary to what usually happens in such matters. In other words, by the evidence of their own narrative they refute all these things themselves. I will not pass over this also: when Abdallah came to Medina, he tested Muhammad by his looks (for prophets are usually tested or recognised in this way), and after putting three questions, which none of the prophets had answered up to that time, he concluded from his clever reply that he was a prophet. Listen to these sublime questions. The first was, what will happen first on the day of judgment? Abu al-Qasim answered: fire will first gather men from East to West. The second: with what food will the blessed first feed in Paradise? He answered: with the liver of a fish. The third: how does it come about that a child sometimes takes after the father and sometimes after the mother? The candidate answered: this happens from the seed emitted in coition, whether the father's or the mother's comes first. A test and judgment indeed worthy of so great a prophet! For in this way, by the features of his face or by questions put to him, and those trifling and silly, prophets are usually tested and proved. Furthermore, Muhammad neither proved himself a prophet, nor could he have been so great a prophet, since after John the Baptist, of whom it was said: The law and the prophets were until John; from then the kingdom of God is preached (Luke 16:16), and since that great prophet Christ, of whom John was the forerunner, no new prophet ought to be expected in this last time, least of all one greater than all who went before and even more excellent than Christ himself. Nor can the Muslims evade this argument on the ground that it is taken from the New Testament, since they neither wholly reject the New Testament nor the history of John the Baptist, which, together with that of his father Zechariah, forms a separate chapter in the Alcoran. Moreover, even if this were no obstacle, his own teaching and his own life would sufficiently refute this prophet, and they ought to have commended him. And what was his teaching, how impious and how base was it? As for his life, it hardly showed him to be a man, let alone a prophet. For though his life was covered with vices and crimes, it was always notoriously disgraceful in two respects, namely in lust and in cruelty towards others. That most impure man passed a law allowing several wives to be taken at once, four or five, which was a plain proof of a foul mind. And to show that he surpassed all men in lechery, he had eleven wives; others credit him with seventeen, besides concubines. And he often boasted of this, not only that he had known each of them in a single night, but that this had happened to him alone, a remarkable proof of a prophet, namely that he could …

units.la: omnes superare luxuria, unus undecim uxores habuit; alii ei tribuunt septemdecim, praeter concubinas: inque eo subinde gloriatus fuit, non modo quod singulas una nocte cognosceret, sed quod singulare hoc ei contigisset, eximium scilicet Prophetae argumentum, ut quadraginta viros fortissimos coëundi facultate aequaret. Monstrum hominis, & libidinis plus quam humanae mancipium. Aliis severe ipse interdicit, cap. de mulieribus, ne quascunque & consanguineas ducant: ne commiscemini cum mulieribus, quae cognitae fuerunt a Patribus vestris, quoniam turpe est & malum, & iniquum: prohibitae sunt vobis matres vestrae, & filiae vestrae, & amitae vestrae, & patrueles vestrae, & filiae fratris vestri, & filiae sororis vestrae &c. Sibi vero licentiam tribuit, quasi ex oraculo divino, quâlibet potiundi. Cap. de haeresibus, vel sectis: O Propheta, nos certe concedimus tibi, inquit ei Deus, potestatem in uxores tuas omnes quibus dederis mercedes suas, & quascunque acceperis manus tua, & filias patris tui & filias amitae tuae & filias fratris matris tuae, & filias matertera tuae, quae peregrinatae sunt tecum, & quamcunque mulierem credentem, quae se tibi Prophetae prostituere voluerit, idque tibi speciatim, & singulariter concedimus; non vero aliis quibuscunque. Dignum certe Prophetâ privilegium. Et post: copulare cum quacunque ex illis tibi libuerit, & tecum fac inhabitare quamcunque volueris; & non erit tibi criminii, vel ad hanc accedere, vel ab illâ recedere. Hoc autem parum est: verum etiam gratum habeant ipsae quidquid tibi libuerit, & non contristentur, & complacéant sibi de quacunque re quam illis dederis. Propudium hominis! sibi primas in promiscuâ & turpissimâ libidine explendâ concedens partes. Haec nimirum istius prophetae est singularis sanctitas & castitas, qui ea sibi indulget, quae in ipsam naturam incurrunt, & naturalem modestiam: sed quae astuto turpique consilio sic edicebat, quo palliaret suum cum servi Zaidis uxore adulterium, & raptum; istam enim confuprpatam mox quasi ex divino iterum oraculo sibi desponsavit in uxorem, quamvis novem aliis stipatus. Quare ut, tum aliis hoc indignantibus factum, tum servo Zaidi satisfaceret, introducit in Alkorano, capite citato, Deum se reprehendentem, quod cogitasset uxorem Zaido reddere, ob offensam, quam hinc nempe homines capiebant: & cum diceres illi, cui Deus beneficia contulit; & tu quoque contulisti: accipe tibi uxorem tuam, & time Deum; & abscondebas in corde tuo quod Deus operabatur, & timebas homines, & Deus dignior est ut timeas eum. Cum ergo Zaidus illam cognoverit seu defloraverit eam, nos copulavimus eam tibi, ne sit fidelibus peccatum in uxoribus desideriorum eorum, cum cognoverint eas, & imperium Dei completum est: non est imputandum ad culpam Prophetae illud, quod Deus illi speciatim permisit. Ita Deus, ejusque nomen sceleri huic induendum fuit, ut improbus Nebulo impurissimae suae libidini quod opponeret, haberet patrocinium: neque sufficiebat homini, etiam sub mendacito Prophetiae titulo & pallio, sic delinquere, nisi & Deum socium atque Auctorem peccati una faceret. Ibidem egregium scilicet epiphonema hoc additur: Non licebit tibi posthac O Mahomet, ut auferas uxores a viris suis, etiamsi earum pulchritudine captus fueris. Postquam videlicet facinus illud cum Zaidis uxore Propheticum patrasset, atque libidinem explesset suam. Ubi & id quoque notandum, leges istas in suorum facinorum patrocinium, excogitatas ab ipsomet semper fuisse, post commissa illa, non ante: ut ita manifestissime liqueat, ista in criminum suorum excusationem vel defensionem ab eo commenta dolo pessimo fuisse. Atque ista persuaderi rudibus istis hominibus, an brutis, potuerunt! atque illum adhuc atra guttā, vel peccati fomite a prima aetate per Angelum liberatum fuisse dicent? proh hominum fidem! Talem istud quod de Muhammede narrant, cum cum puellā formosā, sed infra aetatem, Marinā in adulterio de-pre prehensum à conjugibus suis Aasa & Chadiga juramento adactum promisisse, modo tacerent, ab isthac puella posthac se abstenturum; quod tamen non servavit: unde illae cum deseruerunt, & ad patrias reversae fuerunt aedes. Quem tumultum ut sedaret iterum, more solito, divinum commentus hoc responsum fuit, quod est cap. de prohibitione, quo datur viris cum ancillis suis congrediendi potestas (ancilla quippe Muhammedis erat illa Marina), quando & quousque liberet, nequidquam reclamantibus & aemulantibus uxoribus. Sed jam ante hanc confectam legem id facinus commiserat, & fidem de non committendo interposuerat, perjurus, adulter & stuprator. Vide de hisce plenius Iohannem Andreatam, confut. Mahum. cap. VII. Et Philippum Guadagnolum, contra Ahmedum Persam, cap. V. sect. III. & cap. X. sect. II. & III. ubi quoque respondet Auctor ad Muhammedanorum, pro suo Prophetā, exceptiones, & excusationes. Est & apud Vincentium Lirinensem Specul. histor. lib. XXIV. disputatio Christiani, cum Muhammedano, super illis Prophetae turpitudinibus ac flagitiis; etiam ejus saevitiā ac crudelitate. Quid enim aliud per totam vitam egit, quam praedari, praeliari, & stupris rapinisque se facere celebrem & metuendum? Apud Elmacinum, cap. I. historiam ejus si quaeras, nil praeter bella & praelia leges, praedā mulierum, puerorum, rerumque aliarum inter socios distributā. In Alkorano saepe ad bella homines conclamat & ad caedes, praesertim ad interficiendos, qui sibi obtemperare nollent. Surata XIX. converti nolentes, ubicunque repertos, mensibus Haram peractis, sumite atque interficite, omnibus viis insidiantes illis. Et Surat. LXXI. O boni homines: exite ergo in bellum in nomine Dei cum pecuniā vestrā, & cum animabus vestris. Hac via bona est, atque ob hoc Deus vobis dimittet peccata, dabitque optimam habitationem in Paradyso. Scilicet Paradyso, ubi rapaces, praedones, homicidae, homines improbi injusti-quae que præmiandi erunt. In quibus egregie præivit illis vitâ & exemplo suo Muhammed. Quæ ut vitam ostendunt prorsus improbam: ita talem designant ejus auctorem, qui à Spiritu prophetico maxime sit alienus. IV. Quin & contraria Prophetis & Apostolis plurima docuit, ut legenti Alkoranum, & cum verbo Dei conferenti cuilibet est manifestum. Ex quo eò magis redarguì, ut potest facile, ita & debet doctrina ejus, quo in Alkorano Surata de lampadibus, salsissimè inquit: non aliud tibi dicitur, nisi quod dictum est ante te Apostolis. V. Quid dico adversa Prophetis & Apostolis? contraria imo sibi ipsi docuit ac dixit plurima. Vt, ne alia proferam, de ipso religionis Muslimicæ principio Alkorano, jam dicit illud à Deo in cœlo sibi traditum; jam missum per Angelum Gabrielem: nunc à Deo, tum ab hominibus compositum esse. VI. Nihil unquam suturorum prædixit, quod tamen proprium Prophetarum, ut se hinc etiam Prophetam declarasset. Quæ eo magis in ipso requirimus, quò Christo reliquisque Prophetis longe præstantiorem se dicens, etiam omnia quæ in Prophetis locum habent, ei copiosius adfuisse oportéat. Vel imo prædixerat ex stolidâ Christi æmulatione, tertio se ab obitu die in cœlum assumendum, in quo falsus fuit, & alios ἀναλήψει mortui frustra exspectantes turpiter fefellit, qui putrescens & fœtidum cadaver tandem nudum in terram projecerunt, uti Humbrem retulit; vel ut alii, lotum, vestibusque tribus superindutum mandaverunt terræ. Æque verax scio suturus in prædictione, quâ brutis etiam animalibus promisit partem fore in Paradyso. VII. Quid vero necesse ut comparationem instituamus inter Christum & Muhammedem, ut ostendamus quam hoc falsum & blasphemum, quod Muhammedani tamen credi volunt, ideoque probare etiam ipsis incumbit, Christo Muhammedem supercellere? Indicare hoc argumentum sufficit, quod confirmare nemo opus dicet. Conferan-turtur utriusque & vita, & doctrina, & miracula, & propagandæ religionis ratio, proh quam immane inter utrumque discrimen, neque nisi apud infideles, ubi res exegerit, ostendendum! Videlis Richardum, Confutat. legis Saracenæ cap. xv. & Guadagnolum, Apolog. cap. x. sect. xi. Denique adversus Muhammedem illud quoque adferri omnino debet, quod dum viveret vulgo pro homine stulto, fanatico, & dæmoniaco habitus non sine causa fuit: tantum abest ut pro Propheta. Quare de illo etiam ipse sæpius conquestus graviter fuit. Surata xxxi. sibi vulgo objici significat: Iste nil aliud quam homo, sicut & nos, cum arte sua magica nobis accedit, cujus volumen allatum vel somnium est, ejusque figmentum. Sur. xxxv. Illi etiam credentibus intimant, ne sequamini virum illum, dæmoniacum & amentem per incantationes, comedit ut ceteri, atque per fora vagatur. Idem Sur. xxxvii. lxxi. xliv. dicunt, hic homo non est nisi magus & mendax, universum commentum est quod ab ipso affertur. Surata xlviii. lvi. & lxii. & lxxviii. nuncupat dæmoniacum. Surat. lxxxiv. & xci. jurat pro more suo: per stellas combustas & retrogradas atque rectas, & noctem obscuratam & auroram, hoc verbum est boni Prophetæ, ipsumque absque augmento diminutioneque ferentis, qui coram Deo potens est, ei devote serviens, & præceptum ejus nunquam transgrediens, nullatenus autem est dæmoniaci, seu Diaboli. Surat. lxxix. Iterum: Per res visibiles & invisibiles, nuntii verbum bonum est à Deo mundi conditore compositum, non autem vel ab incantatore vel Mathematico. Ex quibus apparet, pro quo vulgò habitus à suis Muhammed fuerit, homine stulto, fanatico, vagabundo, præstigiatore, mago, dæmoniaco: neque hoc ex temerario aliquo vulgi judicio, sed suo merito & culpâ. Nihil enim Prophetam quod saperet, edebat unquam, sed ea præ se ferebat committebatque quæ hominis amentiam simul argüerent, & improbitatem, à diabolis valde vexatum fuisse, est certissimum: nam ut hoc emolliret apud homines, qui illo haud parum videbantur offendi, commentus versiculum fuit, quasi à Deo iterum prolatum: nos nunquam Prophetam misimus, qui non esset tentatus. Nam hic mos ei assiduus erat, omnibus suis scandalis occurrere remedio versiculorum, à Deo sibi, in patrocinium vitiorum sc., traditorum. Et versum illum produxit, quum aliquando lecturus capitulum Stella, ubi idolorum fit mentio, ea execrare volens, contrà commendaret, diceretque, Deos excelsos esse: & saepius animadversum, eum, ubi Dei nomen esset prolaturus, Diabolum commiscuisse. Quae ex perverso illo vitae instituto haud parum corroborata, quando totos saepe dies in speluncam sese abdens, vacuus, & inedia macceratus, visiones & colloquia Angelorum comminiscebatur, ab ipsa uxore Chadigâ aliquoties propterea increpatus, monitusque Diabolicas illusiones esse, & delira, atrae bilis, haud parum adhuc residuae, figmenta. Unde ex animi aegritudine se de summo praecipitem aliquando dedisset, nisi (ajunt) ab Angelo Gabriele diligenter fuisset servatus. Quae similiter observare est in ipsorum religiosis, nam vexationi Diabolicae & incantationibus tribuenda sunt, quae adeo prodigiosa de illis referunt, de illorum ἀναισθησίᾳ, quod vix aliquem quantacunque frigoris aut caloris sensum habeant, & sive corpus illorum incidas aut amburas, vix moveantur; de illorum ecstasibus, quas adeo vehementes patiuntur, ut in signum earum catenas in collo gestent brachiisque, & quo tempore illis corripiuntur, daemonis acti afflatu, carmina multa canant & edant; tantamque homines hi sanctimoniae prae se ferunt speciem, ut nec nati a parentibus, ceu alii communi more, existimentur. Sed extra coitum, absque virili semine procreati, quos Nefesoglì appellant. Auctor Septem Castrensis, commendatus praefatione Lutheri, lib. de moribus & relig. Turc. cap. XIV. XV.
units.tr: Though all others surpassed him in lust, he himself had eleven wives; others credit him with seventeen, besides concubines. He often boasted of this, not only that he lay with each of them in a single night, but that this singular gift had been given to him, a remarkable proof of his prophethood, namely that he matched forty of the strongest men in the capacity for intercourse. A monster of a man, a slave of lust more than human. He strictly forbids others, in the chapter Of Women, to marry any close kin: Do not marry women whom your fathers have known, for it is shameful, wicked and unjust. Your mothers, your daughters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters and your sisters' daughters are forbidden to you, etc. For himself, however, he grants a licence, as if by divine oracle, to take whomever he pleases. In the chapter Of Heresies or Sects: O Prophet, we grant you, says God, the right to take as wives all those to whom you have given their dowries, and whoever your right hand has taken, and the daughters of your father and your paternal aunts' daughters and your maternal aunt's daughters, and the daughters of your mother's brother, and the daughters of your mother's sister, who have migrated with you, and any believing woman who wishes to give herself to the Prophet, and we grant this to you alone and specially, and not to any others. Certainly a privilege worthy of a prophet! And afterwards: You may lie with any of them you please, and take into your house whichever one you will; nor will it be a sin for you to approach or to leave any of them. And this is not all: let them even be glad of whatever you please, and not be grieved, and let them be content with whatever you give them. Shameless man! He grants himself the first place in satisfying a promiscuous and most shameful lust. This, no doubt, is the singular holiness and chastity of that prophet, who indulges himself in things that run against nature itself and natural modesty. He issued these rules with a crafty and base design, so as to cover his adultery and seizure of Zaid's servant's wife. For after he had defiled her, he soon took her as his wife, as if by another divine oracle, though he already had nine others. So that he might satisfy both those who were indignant at what was done and Zaid his servant, he introduces into the Koran, in the chapter cited, God rebuking him for having thought of returning the wife to Zaid, on account of the offence which men would take at this: And when you said to him to whom God had shown favour, and to whom you also had shown favour: take your wife to yourself, and fear God; and you hid in your heart what God was about to bring to pass, and you feared men, when it is more fitting that you fear God. Then, when Zaid had known her, or deflowered her, we joined her to you, so that there might be no sin for the believers in respect of the wives of their adopted sons, when they have had their desire of them; and the command of God was fulfilled. That which God specially permitted to the Prophet shall not be imputed to him as a fault. Thus God and his name had to be put on this crime, so that the wicked rascal might have a protector for his most impure lust. Nor was it enough for the man, under the false title and cloak of prophecy, to sin in this way, unless he also made God the partner and author of his sin. In the same place this remarkable epiphonema is added: It shall not be lawful for you hereafter, O Muhammad, to take wives away from their husbands, even if you are captivated by their beauty. That is, after he had committed that prophetic deed with Zaid's wife and satisfied his lust. Here it should also be noted that these laws, devised to excuse or defend his own misdeeds, were always invented by him after the deeds had been committed, not before. Thus it is most plainly clear that these were inventions of his, made with the worst cunning, to excuse or defend his crimes. And could such things be persuaded to those rude men, or to beasts? And will they still say that he was freed from the spark of sin, or from the tinder of sin, from his earliest age by an angel? Good heavens, what credulity! Such is what they tell about Muhammad: that he was caught in adultery with a beautiful girl, though under age, named Maria, by his wives Aisha and Khadija, and was compelled under oath to promise that, provided they kept silent, he would henceforth abstain from that girl; yet he did not keep this promise, and so they left him and returned to their father's houses. To quell this uproar again, in his usual way he devised a divine answer, which is in the chapter Of Prohibition, by which men are given the power to lie with their female slaves (for Maria was indeed Muhammad's slave), whenever and as long as they please, though his wives protested and were jealous in vain. But he had already committed that deed before this law was devised, and had given his pledge not to do it again, being a perjurer, an adulterer and a ravisher. On these matters see more fully John Andreas, Confutation of Muhammad, ch. 7, and Philip Guadagnoli, against Ahmed the Persian, ch. 5, sect. 3, and ch. 10, sects. 2 and 3, where the author also answers the Muslims' objections and excuses on behalf of their prophet. There is also, in Vincent of Lérins, Speculum historiale, book 24, a disputation between a Christian and a Muslim over those baseness and crimes of the prophet, and also over his cruelty and savagery. For what else did he do throughout his whole life but plunder, fight, and make himself famous and feared through debauchery and robbery? In Elmacin, ch. 1, if you seek his history, you will read nothing but wars and battles, and the plunder of women, boys and other goods shared among his followers. In the Koran he often calls men to war and to slaughter, especially to the killing of those who would not obey him. Sura 19: those who refuse to convert, wherever you find them, once the sacred months are past, seize and kill them, lying in wait for them in every way. And Sura 71: O good men, go forth therefore to war in the name of God with your money and with your souls. This way is good, and for this reason God will forgive you your sins, and will give you the best dwelling in Paradise. In Paradise, namely, where robbers, plunderers, murderers and wicked, unjust men are to be rewarded. In these things Muhammad went before them with his life and example. Just as these show his life to be utterly wicked, so they mark him as an author far removed from the prophetic Spirit. IV. Indeed he also taught many things contrary to the Prophets and Apostles, as is plain to anyone who reads the Koran and compares it with the Word of God. For this reason his teaching is refuted all the more easily, and it ought to be, by the same means. In the Koran, in the Sura of the Lamps, he says very foolishly: nothing is said to you except what was said before you to the Apostles. V. Why do I speak of things opposed to the Prophets and Apostles? He has taught and said many things even contrary to himself. To mention no others: concerning the very foundation of the Muslim religion, the Koran, he now says that it was delivered to him by God in heaven, now that it was sent through the angel Gabriel, and now that it was composed by God and by men. VI. He never foretold anything of the future, which is nevertheless the proper mark of the prophets, by which he might have declared himself a prophet. We require this of him all the more because, calling himself far greater than Christ and the other prophets, he ought to have had all that belongs to the prophets in fuller measure. Indeed, out of foolish rivalry with Christ, he had foretold that on the third day after his death he would be taken up into heaven; in this he was false, and he shamefully deceived others, who waited in vain for his ascension [ἀναλήψει]. They, when the rotting and stinking corpse was at last cast out naked on the ground, as Humbert reports, or, as others say, washed, clothed in three garments, committed it to the earth. I know that he will be just as truthful in the prophecy by which he promised that even brute animals would have a share in Paradise. VII. But why is it necessary for us to draw a comparison between Christ and Muhammad, to show how false and blasphemous it is, though the Muslims want it believed, that Muhammad surpasses Christ? It is enough to point out this argument, which no one will say needs confirming. Let the life, the teaching, the miracles and the manner of propagating the religion of each be compared; how immense the difference between them, which need only be shown among unbelievers, where the matter requires it! See Richard, Refutation of the Saracen Law, ch. 15, and Guadagnoli, Apology, ch. 10, sect. 11. Finally, this also must by all means be brought against Muhammad: that while he lived he was regarded by the common people as a foolish, fanatical and demon-possessed man, and not without cause; so far was he from being regarded as a prophet. Therefore he himself often complained bitterly about this. In Sura 31 he indicates that the common people objected to him: This man is nothing but a man, like us, who comes to us with his magic art; his book which he brings is but a dream and his invention. Sura 35: They also warn the believers, do not follow that man, possessed by a demon and mad through his enchantments; he eats as others do and wanders through the markets. The same in Sura 37, 71 and 44: they say, this man is only a magician and a liar; the whole fiction that he brings is his own. In Suras 48, 56, 62 and 78 he calls him one possessed by a demon. In Suras 84 and 91 he swears, as is his custom: by the stars that burn and go backward and forward, and by the darkened night and the dawn: this word is that of a good Prophet, who carries it without addition or diminution, who is powerful before God, serving him devoutly and never transgressing his command, and is in no way possessed by a demon or by the Devil. In Sura 79 again: By visible and invisible things, the messenger's word is a good word composed by God, the creator of the world, and not by an enchanter or an astrologer. From these it appears what Muhammad was commonly held to be by his own people: a foolish, fanatical, wandering, deceitful, magical, demon-possessed man. Nor was this from some rash judgment of the common people, but from his own merit and fault. For he never produced anything that was wise, but displayed and did things which at the same time proved his madness and wickedness. That he was greatly troubled by the Devil is most certain. To soften this in men's eyes, who seemed to be not a little offended by it, he invented a little verse, as if again uttered by God: We never sent a prophet who was not tempted. For this was his constant practice, to meet all his scandals with the remedy of verses, given to him by God, namely as a protection for his vices. He produced that verse once when he was about to read the chapter The Star, where mention is made of idols, wishing to curse them, but instead he praised them and said that the high gods were exalted. And it was often observed that when he was about to utter the name of God he mixed in the Devil. These things are much confirmed by that perverse manner of life of his, for often, shutting himself up in a cave for whole days, empty and wasted by hunger, he invented visions and conversations with angels; his wife Khadija often rebuked him for this and warned him that these were diabolical illusions and ravings, the fictions of black bile, which still remained in him in no small amount. Hence, in his mental distress, he once threw himself headlong from a height, had he not (they say) been carefully saved by the angel Gabriel. Similar things can be observed among their religious men, for the strange things they relate about them, their insensibility [ἀναισθησίᾳ], that they scarcely feel any degree of cold or heat, and that whether one cuts or burns their body they hardly move; their ecstasies, which they suffer so violently that as a sign of them they wear chains on their necks and arms, and at the times when they are seized, driven by the breath of a demon, they sing and utter many songs; and these men show such an appearance of sanctity that they are thought not to be born of parents in the common way, as others are, but to have been produced outside intercourse, without male seed, and they are called Nefesoglì. The author of the Seven Castrensis, recommended by Luther's preface, book on the customs and religion of the Turks, ch. 14 and 15.

units.la: Redeundo ad Muhammedem, quod magus perfectissimus simus fuerit, astruitur in disputatione Christiani, cum Muhammedano, apud Vincentium Lirinensem, & exemplo ejus aliquo commonstratur. Platina in vita P. Honorii 1. de Muhammede verba faciens magum dicit: magicis artibus Asianos & Africanos deludens. Ne dicam, quod apud Persas, præcipuè nobiles, Magiæ studium valde est familiare. Sed de Muhammede hæc quidem dicta obiter sunt, ad coarguendam ejus insaniam, utque ostendatur, nihil minus quam pro Propheta habendum illum fuisse.
units.tr: Returning to Muhammed: that he was a most perfect magician is argued in the disputation of a Christian with a Muslim, reported by Vincent of Lérins, and is illustrated by an example from his life. Platina, speaking of Muhammed in the life of Pope Honorius I, calls him a magician: deluding the Asians and Africans with magic arts. Not to mention that among the Persians, especially the nobles, the study of magic is very common. But these remarks about Muhammed have been made only in passing, to expose his madness and to show that he was by no means to be regarded as a prophet.

units.la: Scire tamen cupias forte, nunquid argumentorum, quæ speciem habeant, pro illo adferant Muslimici? dicam. Imo pro eo argumentari volunt, ex Veteri, & ex Novo Testamento; aliisque, Prophetam commendantibus argumentis. Gregorius Abul Farajii Malatiensis, in historiâ, de Origine & moribus Arabum, edita à Pocokio, pag. 14. Porro asserunt Islamitarum docti, factam fuisse mentionem Mohammedis, in libris à Deo demissis, sc. in lege, isto textu, Venit Deus à Sina, & ortus est à seir, & manifestatus est à monte Paranus. Deut. XXXIII. 2. quibus verbis indicari dicunt, descensum legis ad Mosem, Evangelii ad Iesum, & Alcorani ad Muhammedem. Porro in Psalmorum isto textu, Manifestavit Deus è Sione Aclifan Muhmudan: coronam laudatam. Psalm. 1. 2. per coronam indigetari ajunt regnum, per Muhmud, i.e. laudatam, Muhammedem. In Evangelio denuum, isto textu, Si ego non abeam, Paracletus ad vos non veniet. Joann. XVI. Confer & notas Pocockii. pag. 183. &c. Ad quæ perfacilis est responsio. Sed & adferunt ex Deut. XVIII. 15. Prophetam è medio tui è fratribus tuis, sicut me, suscitabit tibi Iehova Deus tuus; auscultate ei. Quod exponunt de Muhammede. Inepte, & calumniosè, quum de Christo Jesu intelligi debere, præterquam textus argumentum, convincit etiam historia Novi Testamenti. Act. III. 22. & VII. 37. Ioann. I. 45. Muhammedi verò sequentia apud Propheta potius applicentur. verf. 20. 21. 22. Veruntamen Propheta ille, qui sibi arrogarit loqui aliquid in nomine meo, quod non praecepero ei eloqui, aut qui loquetur in nomine Deorum alienorum; omnino morietur propheta ille. Quod si dicas cum animo tuo; quomodo cognoscemus verbum illud, quod non loquutus fuerit Iehova? Quod fuerit loquutus ille Propheta in nomine Iehova, si non erit illud verbum, neque evenerit, hoc illud est verbum quod non loquutus est Iehova; superbè eloquutus illud est propheta ille, ne timeto ab eo.
units.tr: Perhaps you wish to know whether the Muslims offer any arguments for him that have some appearance of weight. I will tell you. Indeed, they want to argue for him from both the Old and the New Testament, and from other arguments that commend the prophet. Gregory Abul Faraj of Malatya, in his history of the origin and customs of the Arabs, published by Pococke, p. 14: Moreover, the learned among the Muslims assert that mention of Muhammed was made in the books sent down by God, namely in the law, in this text: "God came from Sinai, and arose from Seir, and was manifested from Mount Paran." Deut. 33:2. By these words, they say, is indicated the descent of the law to Moses, of the Gospel to Jesus, and of the Koran to Muhammed. Moreover, in this text of the Psalms: "God has manifested from Zion Aclifan Muhmudan, the praised crown." Ps. 1:2. They say that by "crown" the kingdom is meant, and by "Muhmud," that is, "praised," Muhammed. Again, in the Gospel, in this text: "If I go not away, the Paraclete will not come to you." John 16. See also the notes of Pococke, p. 183 etc. An answer to these is very easy. But they also cite Deut. 18:15: "The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet from the midst of you, from your brethren, like me; hear him." This they explain of Muhammed. Foolishly and calumniously, since that it must be understood of Christ Jesus is proved not only by the argument of the text but also by the history of the New Testament: Acts 3:22; 7:37; John 1:45. The following words of the passage are rather to be applied to Muhammed: vv. 20–22: "But the prophet who shall presume to speak anything in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who shall speak in the name of other gods, that prophet shall surely die. And if you say in your heart: How shall we know the word which the LORD has not spoken? When the prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, and the thing does not come to pass nor happen, that is a word which the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously; do not be afraid of him."

units.la: Interim figmentum est, quod in Novo Testamento; pro Muhammede, confingunt dictum à Christo Iesu fuisse: nuncium vobis adfero, de nuncio post me venturo, cujus nomen Muhammed. Surata lxx. Post Mosem venit Christus, filius Mariae, dicens: O filii Israëlis ego ad vos missus Dei nuncius, affirmo per Testamentum meum, quod in manibus habeo (quasi Euangelium jam tum Christus in manibus tenuisset, antequam scriptum fuit, atque per istud jurasset) quod post me venturus sit nuncius aliquis, cui nomen Muhammed; quem dicent magum esse. Ex versione Cl. Golii, cap. lx i. Aciei est: & quando dixit Iesus, filius Mariae: O filii Israël, equidem ego missus ad vos legatus Dei, verum asserens, qui coram me, librum Mosis, & laeta annoncians de legato venturo post me, cujus nomen Ahmed. Et postquam ad eos venisset cum evidentibus signis, dixerunt: hoc fascinum est manifestum. Bene est quod conscius Magiae suae illum confessus ipse sit Auctor, cui remedium pro more attulit ex confecto oraculo. Quodque dicitur in Euangelio lectum fuisse de Muhammede, quam falsum sit, supra ostendimus, & hinc insuper confirmatur, quod si tam illustre testimonium venturo Muhammedi perhibuisset unquam Christus, non hoc semel & uno in loco, sed a pluribus sacris Scriptoribus variis in locis memoratum, repetitum, confirmatumque sine dubio fuisset, ut non unius loci depravatione obliterari tanti argumenti negotium nomenque potuisset. Quemadmodum de Christo Meslia quod promissum antea fuit in V. Testamento, id non semel vel uno in loco, sed innumeris continebatur; ita quod Muhammedem concernat, praesertim si hic Christo sit tanto illustrior, non semel dictum scriptumque fuisset, sed pluribus in locis, quam ut ita deleri, nullo sui relicto alicubi vestigio, potuisset. Vel in Commentariis aliorum in Scripturam, qui adeo multi semper fuerunt, aut narrationibus historiisque Ecclesiasticis, extitisset illud uspiam. Accedit, quod quum de ista corruptione (ita ad hominem loquor) Muhammed conquereatur in Alkorano, facta illa fuerit jam ante sua tempora; quod quam insulsum sit quis est qui non videat? eccur enim praecedentes istud nomen erasissent, antequam ipsis cognitum, quid hominis futurus esset Muhammed? vel quomodo non, si vel ab aliquibus designatum hoc facinus, in aliorum Commentariis relatum fuisset? Deinde praedictiones futurorum, vel quia minus explicatae, vel minus metuendae, religiose servari prae aliis solent, praesertim de nuntio aliquo bono & fausto, quale hoc Muhammedis, si Auctoribus fides, fuerit. Quis ex Apocalypsi unquam suffulit, vel delere conatus fuit nomen, aut praedictionem alicujus aut hominis aut rei ibi factam, quamvis gravis, quamvis admirandae, nedum desideratissimae? Denique Ioann. xvi. nomen ejus qui a Christo promittitur, dicitur, παράκλητος: in Alkorano, Ahmed, vel Muhammed, quod non παράκλητος significat, sed περίκλυτος inclytum, laudatum. Quod observavit Cl. Golius: nempe η & υ eodem modo efferebant Graeci, & quidem ut ι, prout etiam in Syriaco, & in Canticis Ecclesiae exprimitur: Verum sacer Codex habet παρακλητος: quae vox consolatorem significat; non Ahmedem. Sed putidiora haec sunt, quam ut iis immoremur.
units.tr: Meanwhile it is a fiction that they invent, that in the New Testament Christ Jesus said something about Muhammed: I bring you tidings of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Muhammed. Sura 70. After Moses came Christ, the son of Mary, saying: O children of Israel, I am sent to you as a messenger of God; I affirm by my Testament which I have in my hands (as if Christ had already held the Gospel in his hands before it was written, and had sworn by it) that after me there will come a messenger, whose name is Muhammed; and they will say that he is a magician. From the version of the illustrious Golius, ch. 61. The sense is: And when Jesus, the son of Mary, said: O children of Israel, truly I am sent to you as an envoy of God, confirming the book of Moses before me, and announcing good news of an envoy who will come after me, whose name is Ahmed. And when he had come to them with evident signs, they said: this is manifest sorcery. It is well that the author himself confesses that he was conscious of his own magic, for he brought a remedy, as is his custom, drawn from a fabricated oracle. And that it is said to have been read in the Gospel concerning Muhammed, how false this is we have shown above; and this is further confirmed by the fact that if Christ had ever borne so illustrious a testimony to the coming Muhammed, it would not have been mentioned once and in one place only, but would without doubt have been recalled, repeated and confirmed by many sacred writers in various places, so that the matter and name of so great an argument could not have been obliterated by the corruption of one passage. Just as what was promised beforehand concerning the Messiah Christ in the Old Testament was contained not once or in one place but in countless places, so what concerns Muhammed, especially if he is so much more illustrious than Christ, would have been said and written not once but in many places, far too many to be deleted without leaving any trace of it anywhere. Either it would have existed somewhere in the commentaries of others on Scripture, which have always been very numerous, or in ecclesiastical narratives and histories. Add to this that, since Muhammed complains in the Alcoran (to speak to the man in his own terms) that this corruption had already taken place before his time, who does not see how foolish that is? For why would earlier writers have erased that name before anyone knew what sort of man Muhammed was to be? Or how is it that, if this crime had been committed by anyone, it was not recorded in the commentaries of others? Furthermore, predictions of future events are usually preserved more scrupulously than others, either because they are less explicit or less alarming, especially concerning some good and happy messenger, such as Muhammed, if we believe his supporters, was. Who has ever removed from the Apocalypse, or tried to erase, the name or the prediction of any person or thing there foretold, however grave or however admirable, let alone one most eagerly desired? Finally, in John 16 the name of him whom Christ promises is Paraclete [παράκλητος]; in the Alcoran it is Ahmed or Muhammed, which does not mean Paraclete but periclytus [περίκλυτος], illustrious, praised. Golius, that illustrious man, observed this: the Greeks pronounced η and υ in the same way, indeed as ι, as is also expressed in the Syriac and in the Canticles of the Church. But the sacred codex has paraklētos [παρακλητος], a word that means comforter, not Ahmed. But these things are too silly for us to dwell on them.

units.la: 111. Pro Muhammede etiam afferunt visionem ejus, aut raptum in coelum, quando jumento Alborach illud conscendit, & cum Angelis, cum Deo ibi collocutus dicitur. Fabulæ, quemadmodum Arabes dicere consuerunt, de Tasmo. iv. Miracula ejus etiam aliqua. Sed quæ, qualia quæso? an, quod cum animalibus & avibus sermonem contulisse dicitur? profecto hominis insani argumentum. an quod arbores ei gratulatæ dicuntur, accepto Alkorano? vel etiam quod vocatæ ab ipso, sibi alvum in campo exoneranti umbram dederint? aut quod impingens aliquando ad arboris truncum, illa jussu ejus diffisa iter transeunti aperuerit? nugæ, nugæ. Vel an dicent, atram cordis guttam ab eo per Angelos tempestive avulsam, ut à peccato & Diabolo liber esset? homo, si quis alius, utrique per totam vitam miserè & fœdè mancipatus.
units.tr: 111. For Muhammed they also cite his vision, or his rapture into heaven, when he mounted the beast Alborach and is said to have conversed there with the angels and with God. These are fables, as the Arabs are accustomed to say, from the Tasm. 4. Some of his miracles too. But what sort of miracles, I ask? That he is said to have conversed with animals and birds? Surely the argument of a madman. That trees are said to have congratulated him on receiving the Alcoran? Or that, when he was relieving himself in the field, trees called by him gave him shade? Or that when he once struck against the trunk of a tree, at his command it split open and let the passing traveller through? Trifles, trifles. Or will they say that a black drop was plucked from his heart by angels at the right moment, so that he might be free from sin and the Devil? A man, if ever there was one, who was wretchedly and foully enslaved to both for his whole life.

units.la: Cæterum decem plerumque narrant Muhammedis miracula: primum, quod sine dolore prodierit ex utero matris, circumcisus & hilaris. Secundum, quod in ejus natali omnia idola per totum orbem corruerint. Tertium, quod Lucifer arreptus ab Angelis, tunc immersus sit in profundum mare. Quartum, quod venti, aves & nubes de ejus educatione decertarint. Quintum, quod asina, voce humanâ, eum vocarit sigillum Prophetarum. Sextum, quod nubes atra semper, etiam cœlo sereno, ejus capiti incubuerit. Septimum, quod Lunam bipertito divisam conjunxerit & compegerit. Octavum, quod Angelus ei sit locutus. Nonum, quod ficus ab eo evocata, humiliter se inclinarit, Decimum, quod bos & agnus ei, quasi maximo Dei nuncio, locuti sint. Vide & Cornel. à Lapide, comment. in Apocalyps. xiii. 11. Gregorius Abul Farajii, de Origine & moribus Arabum, sect. i. Narrantur etiam de eo Muhammede, miracula quædam, qualia, Lunæ fissura, arborum ei obviam euntium processus, quod à lapidibus salutaretur, & quod aqua inter ipsius digitos scaturiret, quod turbam multam exiguo cibo saturaret, quod ipsi adgemiscerent trabs, quod apud eum quereretur Camelus, quod ei testimonium perhibuerit ovis assa, cujus armus ipsi dixerit, cave ne comedas, veneno siquidem infectum. Quam egregia scilicet illa miracula ? solius Muhammedis, vel assentatoris alicujus fide innixa, & sic temeraria, ut suā se futilitate coarguant. Miracula etenim quae aliquando à Prophetis, vel Christo facta fuerunt, in confirmationem doctrinae & veritatis, in gratiam aliorum, quò crederent, & praesentibus aliis, & coram hominum multitudine facta leguntur; non in angulo, vel campo aut antro locove solitario, sed inspectantibus, qui ad fidem perducerentur, aliis; tum etiam non solent miracula à Prophetis exhiberi in rebus vilibus ac nihili, qualia quae Muhammedis circumferuntur trunci scissi, iterumque consolidati, arboris eradicatae &c., sed in rebus seriis & gravioribus miracula sua Deus ponere solet, quae aliquid eximii praestent, atque miraculo digna sint. Denique & quando fiunt, alicujus & non exigui usus gratia fiunt, ut fructum quem adferant aliis; verbi, causa; ut aegri sanentur, ut mortui resurgant, tempestas sedetur &c., uti videmus in miraculis Christi & Prophetarum, quae palam, multis praesentibus; & in rebus non momenti solum alicujus, sed & usus fructusque eximii, exhibita: contra quia se habent omnia, quae finguntur, Muhammedis miracula, ut nec 1. praesentibus aliis; nec 2. in rebus momentosis, aut 3. cum usu & fructu ullo in alios, facta perhibeantur, seipsa satis produnt; atque condemnant. Quare Gregorius Abul Pharajii inquit; Doctiores inter Islamitas, diffidentes illis miraculis, ad Alkoranum recurrere, & in hoc potius uno miraculum constituere, quod quum eloquentissimi laborarint par aliquid Alkorano procudere, ne capitulum quidem unum ei conferendum producere potuerint. Dignum videlicet patella operculum.
units.tr: Moreover, they commonly relate ten miracles of Muhammed. First, that he came forth from his mother's womb without pain, already circumcised and cheerful. Second, that at his birth all the idols throughout the whole world fell down. Third, that Lucifer, seized by the angels, was then plunged into the deep sea. Fourth, that the winds, birds and clouds contended over his upbringing. Fifth, that a she-ass, with a human voice, called him the seal of the prophets. Sixth, that a dark cloud always hung over his head, even when the sky was clear. Seventh, that he split the moon in two and joined and fitted it together again. Eighth, that an angel spoke to him. Ninth, that a fig tree, summoned by him, bowed down humbly. Tenth, that an ox and a lamb spoke to him as to the greatest messenger of God. See also Cornelius à Lapide, commentary on Revelation 13:11. Gregory Abul Faraj, on the origin and customs of the Arabs, sect. 1: Certain miracles are also related of Muhammed, such as the splitting of the moon, the advancing of trees to meet him, that he was greeted by stones, that water gushed out between his fingers, that he satisfied a great crowd with a little food, that beams groaned for him, that a camel complained to him, and that a roasted sheep bore witness to him, saying to him: beware of eating my shoulder, for it is poisoned. How remarkable, indeed, are those miracles! They rest solely on the faith of Muhammed or of some flatterer, and are so rash that by their own triviality they convict themselves. For the miracles that were sometimes performed by the prophets or by Christ were performed for the confirmation of doctrine and truth, for the benefit of others, that they might believe; they are read of as done in the presence of others and before a multitude of people, to be seen by those who were being brought to faith, not in a corner, or in a field, or in a cave or some solitary place. Nor do miracles by the prophets usually concern worthless and trifling things, like the split and re-joined trunks or uprooted trees attributed to Muhammed, but God is accustomed to work his miracles in serious and weightier matters, which accomplish something remarkable and are worthy of a miracle.
