Finally, when they happen, they happen for some purpose of real and considerable use, so as to bring some fruit to others: for example, that the sick may be healed, the dead raised, a storm calmed, and so on, as we see in the miracles of Christ and the prophets, which were performed openly, in the presence of many, and in matters not of trivial importance only but of remarkable use and benefit. On the contrary, since all the miracles of Muhammed that are invented have the opposite character, so that they are not reported as done 1. in the presence of others, nor 2. in matters of weight, nor 3. with any use or fruit for others, they betray and condemn themselves. Hence Gregory Abul Faraj says: the more learned among the Muslims, distrusting those miracles, have recourse to the Alcoran and place the one miracle in this alone, that although the most eloquent men have laboured to produce something like the Alcoran, they have not been able to produce even one chapter to compare with it. Surely a lid worthy of a dish.

units.la: v. Denique ex sectae Islamicae successu, qui brevi tempore satis magnus & prosper undiquaque fuit, pro veritate Prophetae sui, argumentantur. Sed quod argumentantur. mentum ipse Alkoran, quotiescunque, quod saepe facit, nos vetat respicere ad improborum felicitatem, infringit: praeterquam quod & Scriptura, & experientia satis docent, ex nudo eventu de rerum & consiliorum bonitate haud esse statuendum. Tum non vi solâ doctrinæ suæ, quod in religione Christiana, populos gentesque subegit, quibus potitur, Islamismus, sed armis & bellorum metu, & immani imperandi saevitiâ: quibus Nimrod aliquis aestimatur, non verus Doctor & Propheta: nam & felicissimi saepe successus sequuntur facta omnium improbissima. Hinc adeo extollit in lege suâ, pugnantes pro eâ. Caput Assaffi, vel Surata Aciei, §. 4. ex paraphrasi Persicâ: Virtque Deus diligit eos qui pugnant in semita ipsius, scilicet pro causa Dei, ad exaltandum in terra Dei verbum, & propugnandam propagandamque ejus legem atque religionem; prelia ineuntes contra hostes, acie instructâ, obfirmatis etiam, junctisque simul animis, talem in modum, ac si ipsi existant structura solide juncta, vel murus ferrominatus. Eaque causa est quod tam acriter agunt in bellis Turcæ, instigante eos ad hoc lege sua, & promittente occumbentibus in prælio immediatum in Paradysum ingressum. Aliaque sunt, quæ ut causas celeris progressus rei Muhammedicæ, adfert Alexander Ross, in libello Anglico A view of all Religions, sect. 6. i. Continuæ & frivolæ multæ Christianorum, inter se, de religione disputationes. ii. Vita Christianorum, tum laicorum, tum Christianorum, improba. iii. Victoriæ Muhammedicæ, quæ ipsorum promoverunt doctrinam. iv. Et hæc carni magis grata, quam Christiana. v. Turcarum in Christianos tyrannis, & præmia iis propósita, qui Islamismum amplectuntur. vi. Licita apud illos polygamia. vii. Prohibitæ de Alkorano disputationes, ejus translatio ac venditio interdicta. viii. Prohibitio Philosophiæ. ix. Dogma ipsorum, quod quivis, modo bene vivant in religione suâ salvari possunt. x. Quod damnati mnatı ex inferno, post perpessas poenas, liberantur xi. In honestate externa superant Christianos. xii. Concedunt vindictam privatam, amq; putant licitam. xiii. Superstructa communi religio est Arianismo, qui Orientales iam corruperat Ecclesias. xiv. Non sinunt quem piam blasphemare Christum, aut Moysen. xv. Semper diligentes admodum fuerunt in lucrandis, citra vim tamen & coactionem, proselytis. Neque sunt illæ causæ omnes de nihilo, ut per eas tantos subitosque progressus fecerit Muhammedismus. Quas mature expendere oportet cum, qui curandis illis operam daturus sit.
units.tr: v. Finally, they argue for the truth of their Prophet from the success of the Islamic sect, which in a short time became very large and prosperous everywhere. But the Alkoran itself refutes this argument, since it forbids us, as it often does, to look to the prosperity of the wicked. Scripture and experience also teach well enough that the goodness of a teaching or a plan cannot be judged from the bare outcome. Moreover, Islam did not subdue the peoples and nations it holds, in the Christian religion, by the power of its doctrine alone, but by arms, by fear of war, and by monstrous cruelty in ruling. For these reasons he is esteemed a Nimrod rather than a true teacher and prophet, since the most wicked deeds are often followed by the most fortunate successes. From this he extols in his law those who fight for it. In the chapter Assaffi, or the Sura of the Battle Array, §4, in the Persian paraphrase: And God loves those who fight in his way, namely for the cause of God, to exalt the word of God on earth and to defend and spread his law and religion, joining battle against the enemy in ordered ranks, with their minds also made firm and joined together, in such a way as if they were a structure solidly joined, or a wall bound with iron. This is why the Turks fight so fiercely in their wars, since their law urges them to this and promises an immediate entry into Paradise to those who fall in battle. Alexander Ross, in his English booklet A View of All Religions, sect. 6, gives other causes of the rapid progress of the Muhammedan cause: (i) the many continual and trivial disputes among Christians over religion; (ii) the wicked life of Christians, both laymen and clergy; (iii) the Muhammedan victories, which advanced their doctrine; (iv) and this doctrine is more pleasing to the flesh than the Christian one; (v) the tyranny of the Turks over Christians, and the rewards offered to those who embrace Islam; (vi) polygamy, which is permitted among them; (vii) disputations about the Alkoran are forbidden, and its translation and sale are prohibited; (viii) the prohibition of philosophy; (ix) their dogma that anyone may be saved in his own religion provided he lives well; (x) that the damned are released from hell after suffering their punishments; (xi) in external decency they surpass Christians; (xii) they allow private vengeance and think it lawful; (xiii) their common religion is built upon Arianism, which had already corrupted the Eastern churches; (xiv) they do not allow anyone to blaspheme Christ or Moses; (xv) they have always been very diligent in winning proselytes, yet without force or compulsion. Nor are all these causes without foundation, so that Muhammedanism made such great and sudden progress through them. Whoever means to set about dealing with these matters must weigh them carefully beforehand.

units.la: Pro Muhammede praeterea adfert Ahmed Persa, contra quem disputat Guadagnolus, varia Scripturæ loca, Iesa xxi. 7. juxta Vulgatam versionem: & vidi currum duorum equitum, adscensorem asini & adscensorem cameli. Per adscensorem asini, Christum; & per adscensorem cameli, Muhammedem intelligunt. At nec ita ibi vere legitur, minus autem id quod volunt intelligitur, ubi sermo de excidio Babyloniæ per Persas & Medos, quos accelerantes Prophetæ annunciat; dicitque speculatorem vidisse, currum equitum, currum asinorum & currum camelorum, certum pro indefinito.
units.tr: Besides this, Ahmed the Persian, against whom Guadagnolus disputes, cites various passages of Scripture in favour of Muhammed, such as Isaiah 21:7 according to the Vulgate: "And I saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on an ass and a rider on a camel." They understand by the rider on an ass Christ, and by the rider on a camel Muhammed. But the passage is not read that way at all, and the meaning they want is even less apparent, since the passage speaks of the destruction of Babylon by the Persians and Medes, whom the Prophet foretells as hastening on. He says that the watchman saw "a chariot of horsemen, a chariot of asses and a chariot of camels," where the camels are an indefinite number.

units.la: Objiciunt etiam Dan. xiv. vers. 34. quod de lapide, absque ulla ope manuum excisio, qui percussit imaginem ad pedes ejus ferreos & luteos, ut eos conterebat &c. Quo absit ut Muhammedes intelligatur, quod is scilicet omnes religiones in unum coegit, & commisceret. Christus ille lapis est, vers. 44.
units.tr: They also object to Daniel 2:34, about the stone cut out without any help of hands, which struck the image on its feet of iron and clay, so that it crushed them, etc. Far be it that Muhammed should be understood here, since he is supposed to have gathered and mingled all religions into one. That stone is Christ, as verse 44 shows.

units.la: Etiam ad Muhammedem trahunt, quod dixit Christus de mittendo Paracleto, Ioann. xv. & xvi. 7. 8: nisi enim abiero, Paracletus non veniet ad vos: si vero profectus fuero, mittam eum ad vos. Et veniens ille &c. Intelligitur Spiritus S. Apostolis ut promissus, ita in eos postea copiose collatus. Neque puto Muhammedanis placere, ut dicamus, Muhammedem à Christo missum, quem Christo longè præferunt, quod tamen hic expresse dicitur de mittendo à Christo Spiritu Sancto;
units.tr: They also apply to Muhammed what Christ said about sending the Paraclete, John 15 and 16:7–8: "For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I depart, I will send him to you. And when he comes, etc." It is understood that the Holy Spirit, as promised to the apostles, was afterwards poured out upon them abundantly. Nor do I think the Muhammedans would be pleased for us to say that Muhammed was sent by Christ, whom they put far above Christ, although this passage expressly speaks of the Holy Spirit being sent by Christ.

units.la: Adferunt insuper quasi de Muhammede dictum, Genes. XVIII. 20. de Ismaële etiam exaudivi te: quod de ipso illo Ismaële intelligendum, neque quidquam ad Muhammedem.
units.tr: They further bring forward, as if it were something said about Muhammed, Genesis 18:20: "I have also heard you concerning Ishmael." This must be understood of that very Ishmael, and has nothing to do with Muhammed.

units.la: Deut. XXXIII. 2. Dominus de Sinai venit, & de Seir ortus est nobis, apparuit de monte Pharan. Quasi de Meccâ & Muhammede; quum sermo sit de Moyse, cui Deus πολυμερῶς, & istisque montibus singulariter apparuit.
units.tr: Deuteronomy 33:2: "The Lord came from Sinai, and rose up for us from Seir; he appeared from Mount Paran." They take this as referring to Mecca and Muhammed; but the passage is about Moses, to whom God appeared in many ways (polymerōs), and on these mountains in a singular manner.

units.la: Psalm. 71. iuxta Latinam, at LXXII. 10. Reges Sabæi & Sebâ dona offerent. Denique incurvabuntur ei omnes reges, omnes gentes servient ei. Non per Sabā Meccam; sed de Christo Psalmum intelligendum esse, cuivis ex textu constare potest. Hæc de Muhammede.
units.tr: Psalm 71 according to the Latin, or 72:10: "The kings of Sheba and Seba will offer gifts. Finally all kings will bow down to him, all nations will serve him." Sheba does not mean Mecca; and anyone can see from the text that the psalm must be understood of Christ. So much for Muhammed.

units.la: Iisdem quoque Alkoran, quibus ejus Auctor, confunditur argumentis: nam ut ibi spectamus, quis, quidque egit, ita hic quod paria docuit, in libro, cujus alioquin divinitatem nobis persuasum omnino cupiunt. Innumera sunt & magna elogia, quibus seipsum hic liber ad nauseam usque commendat. Quod certe non pro dignitate gravis Scriptoris, nedum divini est, propriis tu rgere laudibus, neque alio se probare argumento, quam ridiculâ & inani sui ipsius commendatione. In ipso statim initio: Hic liber est sine falsitate, & sine errore a liquo veridicus, iis qui in se habent amorem Dei, qui timent atque colunt eum, & qui se oblectant in orationibus, atque eleemosynâ, & legem tibi cunctisque tuis. Prædecessoribus à Deo cœlitus datam observant, & spes futuri seculi comprobavit sectam hanc esse veracem, quam qui sequitur, ab ea trahitur summo bono, ut contra incredulis minatur perpetuum malum; & quæ ibidem, plura enim sunt, sequuntur. Sur. v. sic incipit: Deus pius & misericors,
units.tr: The Alkoran is also refuted by the same arguments by which its author is refuted. For as we look at who did what and what he did, so here we look at what the book taught on the same matters, a book whose divinity they otherwise wish us most firmly to believe. Its countless and great praises, by which this book commends itself to the point of nausea, are innumerable. Indeed, it is certainly not in keeping with the dignity of a serious writer, let alone a divine one, to praise himself, nor to prove himself by any other argument than a ridiculous and empty self-commendation. At the very beginning: This book is without falsehood, and without error from anyone truthful, for those who have in themselves the love of God, who fear and worship him, and who delight in prayers and alms, and who keep the law given to you and to all your people by God from heaven before you, and the hope of the future age has confirmed that this sect is true; whoever follows it is drawn by it to the highest good, while for unbelievers it threatens perpetual evil; and what follows there, for there are many more things. The fifth Sura begins thus: God, merciful and compassionate,

units.la: virtus vivus & altissimus, supra quem non est alter Deus, & qui primo hominibus in viam rectam dedit Testamentum, & postea Euangelium, ultimo veracissimum librum, videlicet Alfurcam vestra legis, confirmatorem superiorum. Surat. ix. Liber hic vobis caelitus missus. Surat. x. Librum veracissimum tibi de caelo mandavi. Surat. xxi. Verba huius voluminis composita sunt per sapientissimos & eloquentissimos. Quomodo ergo Muhammedi in coelo, vel per Gabrielem in caverna tradita? ut in initio Sur. xxii. dicitur: In libro hoc Alkorano Arabico a Deo composito, nostra declaratur conversio &c. Surat. xxiii. & xxiv. & xxv. in initio ubique & xxvii. Deus quidem glorificandus est, gratiaque ei habenda, quod suis hominibus dederit librum purum & sanum sine aliqua falsitatis mixtura. Sur. xxxiv. In hoc capitulo a Deo composito, scripta sunt multa quae manifesta hominibus & memorabilia sunt. Sur. xxx. in initio. Surat. xxxvii. xli. xlv. xlvi. xlviii. xlix. li. Hic liber a Deo pio sapienteque compositus, nec mendacium aliquod praesens nec futurum indicat, nec a Prophetis praeteritis contraria nuncuat. & Surat. lx. &c. Hinc adeo fides Alkorani in ipso imperatur. Surat. lxxiv. In Deum itaque operum vestrorum cognitorem, atque Prophetam, & hunc vobis divinitus missum credite. Surat. lxxv. lxxxv. Alkoran nobis missum, quare non credidistis? & pluribus locis similia per universum Alkoranum occurrunt. At vero neutiquam librum Alkorani, uti volunt, divinum esse, divinaeque authoritatis, facile quoque ostendi in transcursu poterit. 1. sive respiciamus Auctorem Muhammedem, hominem bipedum omnium nequissimum, fanaticum, & diabolicum: qualis ab eo vel doctrina, vel liber provenire potuit, praesertim ad Magistri ideam si, uti hic factum, efformatus, ad comprobanda & justificanda quaeque ejus, etiam maxime enormia, flagitia? 11. Contradicit sibi, circa originem suam turpiter. Iam enim dicitur Alkoran a Deo factus, jam ab hominibus: iterum Muhammedi tradituss traditus in coelo; tum in terrâ, ab Angelo. III. Vera quæ aliqua videtur adducere ex historiâ Vet. Test. mutilat & pervertit, neque illa sana habet amplius; nedum alia & propria. Uti fit Surata II. in historia Saul Regis: tum Gedeonis. In Surat XXII. Josephi, cujus innocentia dijudicata fuerit ex interulâ cuptâ post, non ante. Surat. XXXVIII. de Salomone, quod intellexerit garritum avium; quodque coacto ex hominibus, bestiis, & Diabolis magno exercitu, contenderit in regionem formicarum. &c. Surat. XLVI. de immolatione Isaaci Surat. XLVIII. de Salomone iterum, & ejus equis. Surat. I. de familiâ Imram, quod Maria mater Christi sit Mirjam, soror Aaronis, filia Amrami. Qualis quoque inepta Patrum series recensetur Surat. XV. Abraham, Isaac, Iacob, Noah, David, Salomon, Ioseph, Mose, Aaron, Zacharias, Iohannes, Iesus, Helias, Samuel, Hiskia, Loth. Et hoc IV. assignari potest adversus dignitatem Alkorani, ejus ἀμωθοσία: quod nullus omnino ordo seriesve rerum habita vel observata sit, vitio hic supra quam in vulgaribus scriptis manifesto, atque fastidiendo: vere rudis indigestaque moles. V. Atque ipsi Muhammedani fatentur, multa in Alkorano esse, quæ emendata & castigata sunt, centum & quinquaginta versus dicuntur fuisse per alios correcti & retractati, revocatorii, Arab. nacehamas fog. Iohn. Andreas Conf. sect. Muham. cap. II. Retractavit Muhammed, quod prius dixerat de precando versus Ierusalemum, edixitque ut ad Meccam se orantes converterent. Ieiunium item, more Iudæorum observatum antea, rejecit in mensem Ramadam: multaque de ancillis, & concubitu cum illis licito, de testamentis, aliisque rebus mutavit. Vide Guadagnolum cap. VII. sect. III. Sed & VI. mutilum magna parte Alkoranum sit oportet, quod compilatum ex scriniis à muribus arrosis, & humiditate, atque ærugine multum absumtis, & hinc inde ex schedis variè disjectis, divulsis, ruptisque in farra-
units.tr: the living and most high God, beside whom there is no other God, who first gave to men the Testament on the right path, and afterwards the Gospel, and last the most true book, namely the Alfurcan of your law, confirming what went before. Sura 9: This book has been sent to you from heaven. Sura 10: I have commanded the most true book to you from heaven. Sura 21: The words of this volume have been composed by the wisest and most eloquent. How, then, was it handed down to Muhammed in heaven, or through Gabriel in a cave? As it says at the beginning of Sura 22: In this book, the Arabic Alkoran composed by God, our conversion is declared, etc. Suras 23, 24 and 25, at the beginning throughout, and 27: God indeed is to be glorified, and thanks are to be given to him, because he has given his people a book pure and sound, without any mixture of falsehood. Sura 34: In this chapter composed by God many things are written which are manifest and memorable to men. Sura 30 at the beginning. Suras 37, 41, 45, 46, 48, 49, 51: This book, composed by a pious and wise God, indicates no lie either present or future, and announces nothing contrary to the earlier prophets. And Sura 60, etc. Hence faith in the Alkoran is commanded within it. Sura 74: Believe, therefore, in God, the knower of your deeds, and in the Prophet, and in this one sent to you from God. Sura 75 and 85: The Alkoran has been sent to us; why then did you not believe? Similar things occur in many places throughout the whole Alkoran. But that the book of the Alkoran is divine, and of divine authority, as they wish, can easily be shown in passing. (1) Whether we look at its author, Muhammed, the most wicked, fanatical and diabolical of two-footed men, what teaching or book could come from him, especially if, as here, it was shaped according to the idea of a master, to confirm and justify all his crimes, even the most monstrous? (2) It contradicts itself shamefully about its own origin: for now the Alkoran is said to have been made by God, now by men; again, it was handed down to Muhammed in heaven, and then on earth through an angel. (3) It mangles and perverts the true things it seems to bring from the history of the Old Testament, and does not keep them sound, let alone other things that are its own. This happens in Sura 2 with the history of King Saul, and then of Gideon. In Sura 22, Joseph, whose innocence was judged from a torn shirt, afterwards and not before. Sura 38, about Solomon, that he understood the chattering of birds, and that, having gathered a great army of men, beasts and devils, he marched into the region of the ants, etc. Sura 46, about the sacrifice of Isaac. Sura 48, about Solomon again, and his horses. Sura 1, about the family of Imran, that Mary the mother of Christ is Miriam, the sister of Aaron, the daughter of Amram. Such an absurd succession of the patriarchs is also recounted in Sura 15: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Noah, David, Solomon, Joseph, Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John, Jesus, Elijah, Samuel, Hezekiah, Lot. (4) This can also be charged against the dignity of the Alkoran, its disorder (anomothosia): no order or sequence of matters is observed or kept anywhere, a fault more manifest, and more tedious, than in ordinary writings: a truly rude and undigested mass. (5) And the Muhammedans themselves admit that many things in the Alkoran have been emended and corrected: they say that a hundred and fifty verses were corrected and retracted by others, the revocatory verses, in Arabic nacehamas fog. John Andreas, Confutation of the Sect of Muhammed, chap. 2. Muhammed retracted what he had said earlier about praying toward Jerusalem, and ordered those who prayed to turn toward Mecca. Likewise he rejected the fast, previously observed in the manner of the Jews, to the month of Ramadan; and he changed much about female slaves, lawful intercourse with them, wills and other matters. See Guadagnolus, chap. 7, sect. 3. But the Alkoran must also be largely mutilated, since it was compiled from chests gnawed by mice, much consumed by damp and rust, and from pages scattered and torn this way and that, and forced into the chaotic heap of chapters that we now have, where the chapter on conjunctions, which once equalled the chapter on the cow in length, is now seen to be half as long. (6) It also contains many things that contradict one another, as about the use of wine, which it now forbids and now seems to allow. Sura on the Bee:

units.la: facraginem capitum, quae nunc habemus, coactum, ubi caput de conjunctionibus, quod olim magnitudine aequavit caput de vacca, hodie dimidio minus conspicitur. VII. Multaque habet sibi invicem contraria. Ut de vini usu, quem jam prohibet, jam concedere videtur. Sur. de Ape: Et ex fructibus palmarum & uvarum inebriabimini, & futurabimini, seu potum & victum sumatis. Nunc mandat castimoniam; iterum libidinem promiscuam & Venerem, suo vel exemplo, comprobat, atque indulget. Aliquando Christianis videtur salutem adjudicare, & quod salvari in sua quidem religione possint; alibi negare idem, & tollere. Iam neminem cogi vult ad fidem: tum vim & arma intentare in adversum sentientes praecipit. Et quae istius commatis a Spiritu contradictionis profecta ibidem plurima. VIII. Mendacia insuper, fabulae, figmenta innumera: ut de Angelo mortis, cui oculi a se mutuo distent itinere dierum mille & septuaginta: de Angelis in coelo sexto, quorum unus habeat capita septuaginta mille, & totidem linguas, quaeque edant totidem voces. De bove sub terra, cui sint quadraginta cornua, atque ab eorum uno ad alterum iter mille annorum. De Angelis, Dei thronum in coelo portantibus, quibus tanta sint capita, ut avis nec per mille annos continuos volando perveniat ab aure una ad alteram. Karonem quendam Mosis subditum ajunt fuisse tam opulentum, ut solae thesauri ejus claves Camelum, qui eos portabat, oppresserint. Surata XXVIII. habet fabulam de septem dormientibus, pro vera historia, & mysterio non exiguo: nam & disputari ajunt, quot numero illi dormientes fuerint, an tres, an quatuor, an quinque, an vero sex, cum cane; at nonnullos, dicit, existimare, septem illos fuisse, octavum canem. Digna videlicet operoso examine, & quorum Alkoran meminerit. Ne quod de Alexandro nugantur memorem illum ad occasum Solis pervenisse, ipsumque locum vi-deri derit, ubi Sol se in calidum abdit fontem. Quorum nonnulla vide etiam adducta, & exagitata apud Richardum, Confut. leg. Sarac. cap. ix. Ioh. Andream, Confut. Sectae Mahom. cap. iv. verf. x. Ioannem Cantacuzenum, orat. ii. in Mahometem. Ioh. Forbesium, Instruct. Historico-Theolog. lib. iv. cap. xiii. Thomam à Iesu, de Convers. Gent. lib. x. pag. 666. &c. ix. Nec sola mendacia & fabulas continet Alkoran; sed insuper spurca, foeda, improba permulta; qualia quae de mulieribus, polygamia, repudio passim occurrunt. Confer Ioh. Andream, cap. vi. Thomam à Iesu, pag. 677. Guadagnolum, cap. vii. sect. i. Tale & quod cap. i. in Alkorano legitur: uxores vestrae sunt aratura vobis, idite ergo araturam vestram ad libitum. quod glossa explicat, adite eas, sive secundum, sive contra naturam, scelus! Tum quales hic instruat homines inde quoque patet, quod Paradysum suum adinstar lupanaris formet, inque eo sitam coelestem felicitatem credi velit, quod copia futura sit formosissimarum virginum ad coitum. x. Simul ad saevitiam & crudelitatem, bella, & caedes instigat doctrina sua homines, quae cum humana haud conveniunt disciplina, nedum divina. Illis paradysum pollicetur, qui maxime fuerint belficosi. Surata vi. ix. xviii. xix. xxxi. xli. lvi. lviii. Dix. lxxi. Atque ad vindictam mutuo hortatur homines, alitcrac pro charitate, & sacra doctrina convenit. Surat. ii. vinu etiam vestram facite similem, ut liberum pro libero, servum pro servo, mulierem pro muliere. Surat. iii. vindicans se post injuriam illatam, nequaquam dem exstitit. Huc & illud spectat, quod aliis religionem istam persuadere, atque vi cogere ad fidem homines docuit, locis Alkorani illis jam citatis. xi. Etiam hoc contra fidem Alkorani adferri potest, quod nullo unquam miraculo, ut quidem tale Scriptum, quod se tanto opere jactat, decerret, comprobata sit. Secus doctrina Mosis, & doctrina Christi, quibus se multis tamen paparasangis illud temere praefert. xij. Et quia singulariter se supra Christi Euangelium extollit, uti expresse Ahmed Alabedin, perfectionem suae legis ultra Euangelium deprædicat, apud Guadagnolum pag. 352. instituatur in disputatione collatio utriusque, secundum omnia quae in Scripto attendi debent, Auctoris, materiae, formae, styli, finis, antiquitatis, & reliquorum capita, patebit, tantum distare ab Euangelio Alkoranum, ut hoc ipsum infra dignitatem Euangelii maxime videri debeat, cum Alkorano conferri. Haec adversus Alkoranum obiter attulimus, quamquam in disputatores contra istud graves diras evomat. Surat. xi. ut ita qualemcunque rerum harum notitiam nostri habeant. Pro illo nihil omnino video quod adferre possint, ita nec insita, nec adscita ulla habet argumenta, quibus se apud bene sanos commendet. Illa quae forte objiciant, de doctrinae suae felici successu, & per multas orbis regiones diffusione, imperio, duratione, & imperii Muhammedici prosperitate, infra, ubi praejudicia illorum, in negotio conversionis, discutiemus, pressius examinabuntur. Haec interim de praecipuis fidei Muslimicae capitibus breviter disseruimus, de Alkorano, Muhammede, & ante omnia de Scripturae Sacrae integritate & fide. Superstunt ea quae religionem Christianam propius concernunt, vel peculiares religionis Muhammedicae articulos, ut ibi articuli de Trinitate, Christo, creaturis; hic, de Muslimorum circumcisione, lotione, precibus &c. de quibus, quia hunc campum nunc sumus ingressi, quid ni etiam paucula eodem stylo annotemus?
units.tr: the hodgepodge of chapters that we now have, put together in a heap, where the chapter on the conjunctions, which once matched the chapter on the cow in length, is now seen to be half as long. VII. It also contains many things that contradict one another. For example, about the use of wine, it now forbids it and now seems to allow it. Sur. on the Bee: And from the fruits of the palms and grapes you will get drunk, and you will take your drink and food. Now it commands chastity; again it approves and indulges promiscuous lust and sexual intercourse, even by its founder's own example. At one time it seems to grant Christians salvation, and to say that they can be saved in their own religion; elsewhere it denies the same and takes it away. Now it wants no one forced to the faith; then it orders force and arms to be turned against those who think otherwise. Many other such contradictions, arising from the spirit of contradiction, are found in the same place. VIII. Besides, there are lies, fables and countless fictions: for example, about the Angel of Death, whose eyes are a journey of a thousand and seventy days apart; about the angels in the sixth heaven, one of whom has seventy thousand heads, and as many tongues, each uttering as many voices. About an ox under the earth, which has forty horns, and from one of whose horns to another is a journey of a thousand years. About the angels who carry God's throne in heaven, who have so many heads that a bird flying continuously for a thousand years could not get from one ear to the other. They say that a certain Karon, a subject of Moses, was so rich that the keys of his treasures alone weighed down the camel that carried them. Sura XXVIII. contains the story of the seven sleepers, presented as a true history and a not small mystery: for they say there is debate about how many of those sleepers there were, whether three, four, five, or six, with a dog; but some, it says, think there were seven of them, with an eighth, the dog. Clearly these are matters worthy of laborious examination, and the Koran mentions them. Not to mention what they tell about Alexander, that he reached the setting of the sun and that the place itself seemed to be where the sun sinks into a warm spring. Some of these things may also be seen cited and dealt with at length by Richard, Confut. leg. Sarac. cap. ix.; John Andreas, Confut. Sectae Mahom. cap. iv. vers. x.; John Cantacuzenus, orat. ii. in Mahometem.; John Forbes, Instruct. Historico-Theolog. lib. iv. cap. xiii.; Thomas à Jesu, de Convers. Gent. lib. x. p. 666, &c. IX. The Koran contains not only lies and fables, but also very many filthy, foul and wicked things, such as those about women, polygamy and divorce, which occur everywhere. Compare John Andreas, ch. vi.; Thomas à Jesu, p. 677; Guadagnoli, ch. vii. sect. i. Such also is what is read in chapter i. of the Koran: your wives are your field to you; go, then, into your field at will, which the gloss explains: approach them, whether according to nature or against nature, a crime! Moreover, what kind of people it forms is also clear from this, that it shapes its paradise like a brothel, and wants the heavenly happiness there to consist in the abundance of the most beautiful virgins available for intercourse. X. At the same time, its teaching urges men to cruelty and savagery, to wars and slaughter, a doctrine that agrees neither with human discipline, let alone divine. It promises paradise to those who have been most warlike. Suras vi. ix. xviii. xix. xxxi. xli. lvi. lviii. Dix. lxxi. And it urges men to mutual revenge, which agrees neither with charity nor with sacred doctrine. Sura ii.: and do ye also make retaliation like to it, a free man for a free man, a slave for a slave, a woman for a woman. Sura iii.: one who takes vengeance after the injury inflicted on him is by no means... To this also belongs that it taught men to persuade others to this religion and to compel them to the faith by force, in the passages of the Koran already cited. XI. Also, this can be brought against the faith of the Koran: that it has never been confirmed by any miracle, as such a Scripture, which it boasts of so greatly, ought to have been. It is otherwise with the teaching of Moses and the teaching of Christ, which it rashly sets itself above by many parasangs. XII. And because it lifts itself up singularly above the Gospel of Christ, as Ahmed Alabedin expressly proclaims, preaching the perfection of its law beyond the Gospel (see Guadagnoli, p. 352), let a comparison of the two be made in the disputation, according to all the things that must be considered in a writing: its author, matter, form, style, purpose, antiquity, and the rest of the heads. It will then be plain that the Koran is so far from the Gospel that it should especially seem beneath the dignity of the Gospel even to be compared with the Koran. We have brought these points against the Koran in passing, although it vomits grave curses against those who dispute against it (Sura xi.), so that our people may have some knowledge of these matters, of whatever kind. For that religion I see absolutely nothing they could bring forward; it has no arguments, either innate or acquired, by which it could commend itself to sensible people. As for what they may perhaps object, concerning its happy success and its spread through many regions of the world, its empire, its duration, and the prosperity of the Muhammadan empire, these will be examined more closely below, where we shall discuss their prejudices in the matter of conversion. Meanwhile we have briefly discussed the chief heads of the Muslim faith: the Koran, Muhammad, and above all the integrity and trustworthiness of Holy Scripture. What remains are those matters that concern the Christian religion more closely, or the peculiar articles of the Muhammadan religion, such as, there, the articles on the Trinity, Christ and creatures; here, on the circumcision, washing, prayers, etc. of the Muslims. Since we have now entered this field, why should we not also note a few of these in the same style?

units.la: Ad Controversiam de Personarum in Deo Trinitate
units.tr: On the Controversy concerning the Persons in the Trinity of God

units.la: duo haec nobis cum Muhammedanis agenda sunt: primo ut ἀποφάσεως & διαστολικῶς tollamus Infidelium omnes adversus veritatem exceptiones, objectiones, & praejudicia; tum ut ex Scriptura, quam non omnino ab Adversariis repudiari supra diximus, veritatem tem doctrinæ fidéque nostræ ostendamus. Hoc (in tractatione doctrinali ordo sæpe jubet præmittere, quæ in præsenti disputatione forte secundum obtinerent locum) ex illis fit Scripturæ S. locis, quæ sive ex Veteri, sive N. Testamento pro asserendâ illa veritate adferri solent, & omnibus nota obviaque sunt: ex illis libris, locisque Sacris, quos neque Adversarii forte repudiabunt. Deinde in Alkorano etiam aliqua notanda, quæ in præjudicium Muslimorum circa hanc veritatem adferri possunt: non solum quod passim Deus introducitur loqui plurali numero, nos misimus Mosem &c. Sed & quod verbi divini, ac Spiritus etiam mentio fit, ubi de Deo est sermo. Sur. de mulieribus: Iesus Christus apostolus Dei & verbum Dei quod misit ad Mariam, & Spiritus ex Deo. Surata primâ, sive de vaccâ, Deus de Christo dicit: Sanctificavimus eum Spiritu Sancto. Surata de fœderibus: memento ô Iesu, fili Mariæ, beneficii mei erga te ac matrem tuam, tum te corroboravi Spiritu Sanctitatis: alloqueris enim homines in cunabulis, & adultos, & creabis de luto volatilia, insufflabis enim in luteam formam, & creabis volucres permissu meo &c. leprosos mundabis, cæcos illuminabis, ac denique mortuos resuscitabis. In quibus mentionem audimus fieri tum Verbi, tum Spiritus; quæ pro doctrinæ Christianæ haberi possunt vestigiis & reliquiis: nisi quod per Spiritum illos intelligere Angelum Gabriëlem, Ahmed Persa dicat. tum præter eximia illa in Christum elogia, argumentum inde construi pro Christi deitate potest, quod ei tribuitur facultas miraculorum, quam Deo propriam esse adeo tenent Muhammedani, ut (quemadmodum supra annotatum) ex eo arguant locum Matth. xx i v. falsum, quia Pseudoprophetis videtur adscribere vim miraculorum, soli Deo competentem. Sed de Christi Deitate mox. Ad præsentem disputationem conferri possunt, Richardus, Prædicatorii ordinis Monachus, Confutat. legis Sarac. cap. xv. Iohannis Gantacutzeni Apologia r contra Muhammedem & eratio. III. Philippus Guadagnolus, Apolog. pro Christianis, tractatu III. de Trinitate. Ioh. Forbesius, Instruct. historico Theol. lib. IV. cap. V. Descriptio Arabiae cap. XVII.
units.tr: There are two things we must accomplish with the Muhammadans. First, by negation [ἀποφάσεως] and by distinction [διαστολικῶς] we must remove all the exceptions, objections and prejudices the unbelievers raise against the truth. Second, we must show the truth of our doctrine and faith from Scripture, which, as we said above, the adversaries do not wholly reject. Here (in doctrinal treatment, order often requires that what in the present dispute might perhaps hold a second place be put first) we draw on those passages of Holy Scripture, from the Old or the New Testament, that are customarily cited to prove this truth and are known and familiar to all, from those books and sacred passages which the adversaries perhaps will not reject either. Next, some points in the Qur'an also deserve notice, which can be brought forward to the prejudice of the Muslims concerning this truth: not only that God is everywhere introduced as speaking in the plural, we have sent Moses, and so on, but also that mention is made of the Word of God and of the Spirit where the discourse is about God. In the Sura Of Women: Jesus Christ is the apostle of God and the word of God which he sent to Mary, and a spirit from God. In the first Sura, or The Cow, God says of Christ: We sanctified him with the Holy Spirit. In the Sura Of Covenants: Remember, O Jesus, son of Mary, my benefit towards you and your mother, when I strengthened you with the Spirit of holiness; for you spoke to men in the cradle and as adults, and you will create birds from clay, for you will breathe into the clay form, and by my permission you will create birds, etc. You will cleanse lepers, you will give sight to the blind, and finally you will raise the dead. In these passages we hear mention made both of the Word and of the Spirit, which may be regarded as traces and remnants of Christian doctrine; except that Ahmed the Persian says that by the Spirit they understand the angel Gabriel. Moreover, besides those outstanding praises of Christ, an argument for the deity of Christ can be built from the fact that to him is ascribed the power of miracles, which the Muhammadans hold so strictly to be proper to God that (as noted above) they argue from this against the passage Matthew 24, as false, because it seems to attribute to false prophets a power of miracles belonging to God alone. But more on Christ's deity shortly. For the present dispute the following may be consulted: Richard, a monk of the Dominican order, Confutation of the Saracen Law, ch. 15; John Gantacuzenus, Apology against Muhammad, and his refutation, book III; Philip Guadagnolo, Apology for the Christians, treatise III, on the Trinity; John Forbes, Instructio historico-theologica, book IV, ch. V; Description of Arabia, ch. XVII.

units.la: Objectionum adversus fidem nostram habent duplex genus Muhammedani: aliud adversus rem ipsam; aliud contra rei vel fidei expositiones Scholasticas, plerunque (fateor) inanes, & scandalosas. Vt quod Scholastici, de processionibus in Deo personalibus, dicunt, Filium per actum intellectus divini procedere: Spiritum Sanctum per voluntatem, quod ita Infideles offendit, ut hinc istae nascantur Ahmedi Persae objectiones; scientia, & amor in Deo, illud actus quasi intellectus, hoc voluntatis, essentialia sunt, non ergo relationis personalis fundamentum. Iterum, si per actum intellectus producitur in divinis Filius, ergo vel per intellectum & scientiam in Deo omnem, vel non: si illud, ergo & per intellectum Filii ipsius quoque, seu Verbi: si per aliquam demum, ergo per scientiam aliam etiam alius Filius produci posset, & sic in infinitum. Ego vero neutiquam probo illam expositionem Scholasticorum, quare nec vindico: sed scire hinc licet, Doctores Muhammedanos etiam subtiliter disputare; longe aliter, ac Muhammed in Alkorano, qui ineptus & vanus est, prae Alkorani interpretibus, & Doctoribus Islamismi haud parum saepe acutis. Aliter adversus ipsum Trinitatis articulum disputant, & argumentantur. I. Quia unus Deus. Hinc crebra illa unitatis divinae in Alkorano professio, non adeo est in gratiam hujus veritatis, ac in oppositionem ad Christianam fidem de Trinitate. II. quia Deus simplicissimus. III. Quia Deo non est uxor, ergo neque Filius. IV. Quia videtur illis sequuturum, ex aliis Dei attributis plures Personas iidem nasci. V. Vel Filium, & Spiritum Sanctum esse alterius a Patre naturae, seu essentiae, videlicet minoris. VI. Dissidium forte oriturum aliquando inter diverversas Personas. quod attingit Surat. xxx i ii. Ad illa multis respondere nihil necesse; quia & levia sunt, nulli non facillimè solvenda, & nobis magis propositum enarrare Muslimorum res, quam refutare, vel multum super iis disputare. Præterquam de S. Trinitate, in pluribus circa Deitatem errant opinionibus, sed quia earum nulla eminentior est illâ negatæ Trinitatis, hanc ante omnia censuimus explicandam. Cui connexa est altera circa Christi deitatem: quam quoque tollunt.
units.tr: The Muhammadans have two kinds of objections against our faith: one against the thing itself, and another against the Scholastic explanations of the thing or of the faith, which are for the most part (I admit) empty and scandalous. For example, what the Schoolmen say about the personal processions in God: that the Son proceeds through an act of the divine intellect and the Holy Spirit through the will. This offends the unbelievers so much that from it arise the objections of Ahmed the Persian: knowledge and love in God are essential, the one being as it were an act of the intellect, the other of the will, and so they are not the basis of a personal relation. Again, if the Son is produced in the divine nature by an act of the intellect, then either he is produced through the intellect and knowledge that is in God as a whole, or not. If the former, then the Son is also produced through the intellect of the Son himself, or of the Word; if through some other, then through another knowledge some other Son could also be produced, and so on to infinity. I, however, by no means approve that explanation of the Scholastics, and so I do not defend it. Yet from this one may learn that the Muhammadan doctors also dispute subtly, far unlike Muhammad in the Qur'an, who is inept and empty, compared with the interpreters of the Qur'an and the doctors of Islam, who are often not a little sharp. They dispute and argue against the article of the Trinity itself in other ways. (1) Because God is one. Hence that frequent profession of the divine unity in the Qur'an is not so much for the sake of this truth as in opposition to the Christian faith concerning the Trinity. (2) Because God is most simple. (3) Because God has no wife, and therefore no Son. (4) Because they seem to think it would follow that several Persons would be born from the other attributes of God. (5) Or that the Son and the Holy Spirit are of a different nature or essence from the Father, namely of a lesser kind. (6) That perhaps a dissension will at some time arise among the different Persons, which Sura 32 touches on. It is not necessary to answer these many things, since they are light, and easily resolved by anyone; and our purpose is rather to set out the affairs of the Muslims than to refute them or to dispute much about them. Apart from the Holy Trinity, they err in many opinions concerning the Deity; but since none of these is more prominent than the denial of the Trinity, we have judged that this should be explained above all. Connected with it is the other question concerning the deity of Christ, which they also deny.

units.la: De Christo nonnulla tenent Muhammedani vera, at falsa quam plurima. Natum credunt, ex Mariâ virgine; sed in Mariâ designandâ stupendum committunt errorem, quod illam filiam Amrami dicunt, & confundunt cum Mirjam, sorore Mosis. Quatuor fuisse mulieres perfectas memorant, inter quas & hæc. Asia, filia Merahæ; Maria filia Amrami, quam & matrem Christi nugantur; Chadiga, filia Hubald, Muhammedis uxor; & Fatima, Muhammedis filia, quæ nupta Hali. De Mariæ cibatione in templo miraculosâ, cœlitus ei cujusvis generis subministratis cibis, æstivis etiam quum hiems esset, & hibernis in ipsâ adeo æstate, fabulantur multa, uti quoque de Mariæ conceptione, & partu. Salutationis Angelicæ meminit Alkoran, Surata v. Concepisse, quum esset annorum tredecim; atque peperisse octavo à conceptione mense, qui partus nunquam vitalis præterquam in Iesu. Peperisse adjunt, ad truncum palmæ, quæ per multos annos infrugifera, nato Christo, eoque matrem suadente ut illam frugis accipiendæ causa concuteret, mox floruit ac dedit dactylum recentem, cujus esu Maria à partu refocillata fuerit. Varia in Alkorano de Christo extant elogia, quod Propheta fuit, & quod ei datum Euangelium, quodque miracula fecit, leprosos mundavit, mortuos in vitam resuscitavit, inter quos etiam collocant Sethum, Noæ filium, aliaque plura, quæ ex scri scriptis Muhammedanorum huc facientia collegerunt Gabriel Sionita, Descript. Arab. cap. XVII. Schickardus, in Proœmio Tarich, à pag. 97. & deinceps. Seldenus, ad Eutychii Origines Ecclef. Alexandrinæ, pag. 89. Levinus VVarnerus, in Compendio Muhammedano de Christo, & Christiana relig. Hottingerus, Histor. Orient. lib. I. cap. III. Vulgo Christum loquentes Muhammedani, dicunt: propheta Isai, super quem salue. Ipsum Christum mortuum non volunt, sed assumi ex Apostolis, vel sociis Christi, ejus loco, ipso in cœlum sublato, quem tamen se crucifigere Judæi crediderint. Surata xi. Dicunt illi, nos occidimus Christum Iesum filium Mariæ, Dei Apostolum, cum non occiderint, nec crucifixerint eum, sed occidere visi sibi sint. Qui autem diversum hic sentiunt, & ipsi dubitant de eo, nec certi quidquam scientes, opinionem tantum sequuntur: revera eum non interfecerunt; sed sustulit eum ad se Deus, qui potens est & sapiens. Illum ex sociis Christi aliquem, qui se Christi loco dederit ἀντίψυχον, ajunt à Christo selectum fuisse, monito, ut hoc pacto Judæorum malitiam eluderet: quodque proinde interrogarit suos: cui vestrum placet, ut induatur imagine meâ, & occidatur, ac crucifigatur, & sic ingrediatur paradysum? Tum vir quidam ex illis, ego, inquit. Confestim ei Deus effigiem Christi imposuit, atque is occisus & in crucem actus fuit. Unde postea contentio inter homines orta fuerit, an Christum ipsum sustulissent, annon? si Christum, ubi ille socius esset? si hunc, ubi ergo Christus? Conveniunt hæc cum Basilidis in primâ Ecclesiâ hæresi, & forte inde sumta, qui docebat, non ipsum Christum, sed illius loco Simonem Cyrenensem crucifixum: & quod Christus præsens omnia aspectans illorum errori illuserit.
units.tr: The Muhammadans hold some things about Christ that are true, but very many that are false. They believe he was born of the Virgin Mary; but in identifying Mary they make a stupendous error, for they call her the daughter of Imran, and confuse her with Miriam, the sister of Moses. They relate that there were four perfect women, among whom is this one: Asia, daughter of Muzahim; Mary, daughter of Imran, whom they also absurdly call the mother of Christ; Khadija, daughter of Khuwaylid, the wife of Muhammad; and Fatima, daughter of Muhammad, who was married to Ali. They tell many fables about Mary's miraculous feeding in the temple, with food of every kind supplied to her from heaven, summer fruits even when it was winter, and winter fruits in the very summer. They tell similar tales about Mary's conception and delivery. The Qur'an mentions the angelic salutation, in the Sura v. She conceived when she was thirteen years old, and bore the child in the eighth month after conception, a birth that was never viable except in the case of Jesus. They add that she gave birth at the trunk of a palm tree, which had been barren for many years; that, when Christ was born, at her mother's urging she shook it to get fruit, and it at once flourished and gave a fresh date, by eating which Mary was restored after childbirth. The Qur'an contains various praises of Christ: that he was a prophet, that the Gospel was given to him, and that he worked miracles, cleansing lepers and raising the dead to life; among those raised they also place Seth, the son of Noah, and many other things. Gabriel Sionita, Description of Arabia, ch. XVII, has collected these and other matters bearing on this from the writings of the Muhammadans; so too Schickard, in the Preface to the Tarikh, from p. 97 onward; Selden, on Eutychius' Origines Ecclesiae Alexandrinae, p. 89; Levinus Warner, in A Muhammadan Compendium on Christ and the Christian Religion; Hottinger, Historia Orientalis, book I, ch. III. Commonly the Muhammadans, speaking of Christ, say: the prophet Jesus, on whom be peace. They do not hold that Christ himself died, but that someone was taken in his place from among the Apostles or companions of Christ, Christ himself having been taken up into heaven; yet the Jews believed they had crucified him. Sura xi.: They say, we have killed Christ Jesus, son of Mary, the apostle of God, though they did not kill him nor crucify him, but it seemed to them that they did. Those who hold a different view on this are themselves in doubt about him, and knowing nothing certain, follow only opinion. In truth they did not kill him; but God took him up to himself, who is powerful and wise. They say that one of Christ's companions, who offered himself in Christ's place as a substitute [ἀντίψυχον], was chosen by Christ, who had warned him that in this way he would thwart the malice of the Jews; and that therefore he asked his followers: which of you is willing to be clothed in my likeness, and be killed and crucified, and so enter paradise? Then a certain man among them said: I am. At once God put the likeness of Christ upon him, and he was killed and fastened to the cross. Hence later a dispute arose among men whether they had taken Christ himself or not: if Christ, where then was that companion? If that companion, where then was Christ? These things agree with the heresy of Basilides in the early Church, and are perhaps taken from it, for he taught that not Christ himself but Simon of Cyrene was crucified in his place, and that Christ, standing by and seeing everything, mocked their error.

units.la: Ad naturam Christi divinam æque offenduntur Muhammedici, quam in eo negant, & impugnant. Unde Christianos per contumeliam appellant Associatores, quod Deo socium sc. & filium adjungant; & plures hinc in Alkorano ajunt, Deo non esse socium: quod quotiescunque occurrit, adversus Christianos dictum existima. Surata Locmanni, xxx i. à Clariss. Golio versa, §. 10. 12. 14. aliisque capitibus, & locis fere innumeris. Ac proinde qui ab illis ad Christianismum accedunt, in anathematizatione pristinae perfidiae distincte docentur rejicere, inter alias Muhammedicas constitutiones, & hoc, quod Muhammed τὰς χεσιανὰς ἐνδίζων [?] ἀφεντὰς ἐνομάζει [?] τῇ κοινωνητὰς [?] τῇ ἐπιπερίας [?], convitians Christianos nominat Negatores, & communicatores; & sodalitiarios. apud Sylburgium, in Saracenicis. Azoara, vel Surata xi. ex versione Retinensis: summopere quidem cavendum, ne lege vestra quid indignum & injustum proferatis, nec de Deo quidquam nisi verum dicatis. Iesus Mariae filius, Dei nuntius, sauque Spiritus, & verbum Mariae caelitus missum exstitit. In Deum itaque, illiusque suo legato credentes, ne dicatis Deos tres esse, cum non sit nisi Deus unus, qui filio caret; eique omnipotenti universa caeli terraeque subjecta sunt. Christus quidem ipse negare minime poterit, sicut neque Angeli Deo propinqui, quin Dei subsit imperio. Tum adversus S. Trinitatem, tum adversus Christi deitatem haec dicta. Illam multis in locis impetunt. Surat. xvii. xxv. xxvii. xxix. xxxv. cxxii. In Colloquio Muhammedis cum Abdia Iudaeo: Deus non habet socium, aut filium. Fideles appellant eos, qui istud credunt. Surat. xii. Et xiii. Sur. iiii. Christus non fuit nisi vir tantum, cui multam bonitatem contulimus, Doctoremque filius Israel proposuimus. Narrant, Christo in caelos assumto, interrogatum eum a Deo fuisse, numquid dum Christiani dicunt, docentque eum Deum, & Dei filium esse, ipse unquam se pro Deo gesserit, aut haberi voluerit? Surata, de mensa: Iesu fili Mariae, tune dixisti hominibus, assumite me & matrem meam pro Dis, praeter Deum. Respondit, absit: non mejum est, ut dicam, quod revera mihi non competit. Si dixissem istud, utique jam illud scires, qui noris quid in mea sit anima. animâ, ego vero nescio quid sit in tuâ, cum secreta tua cogitata habeas. Nihil quidquam iis dixi, nisi quod à te jussus sum: celite Deum Dominum meum, & Dominum vestrum. Hoc testatus sum illis, quamdiu ime egi apud illos. Nugae, quin calumnię, & blasphemiae. Non Christiani eres Deos faciunt, aut Mariam numen, neque Christus se Deum fecit, sed ostendit, & qua verbis, qua factis probavit, testimonium divinitatis, & quod filius Dei esset, ei multifariam perhibente etiam de coelis Deo. Omnia ex Scripturis & comportare testimonia, & argumenta ad Christi probandam deitatem supersedeo, quum sit res & Christianis nota satis, & probatu facilis, tum ab instituto nos longius, hoc si pro dignitate persequeremur, abduceret, vel extra necessitatem hunc nostram digressionem extenderet. Interim volo ut omnes Christiani hoc bene observent, pro fidei nostrae haud levi confirmatione, quod Muhammedani aperte fatentur, in Novi Testamenti Epistolis Paulinis clare & exserte Christi Deitatem legi, unde adversus nos hac super re disputantes. Paulinarum epistolarum illam ob causam authoritatem declinant, & ajunt, illas à Christianis adulteratas esse. Ubi hoc saltem veritati à suis hostibus testimonium, quod eam, juxta ipsos, Pauli epistolae confirmant: & quicunque in istis illud vel non vident, vel tergiversantur, & contrà disputare audent ex Christianis, liquet minus candidos & perspicaces esse Muhammedanis: qui ut ut in eo latius divagantur, quod ipsarum Epistolarum authoritatem tollunt; hoc tamen æquiores sunt, quod illis praedicari id, quod in quæstione versatur, Christi deitatem, libere agnoscunt & fatentur, quod Christianus etiam qui audire vult sæpe negat audacter, eique oblatrat. Guadagnolus, in disputatione adversus Ahmed Persam: verum frustra (inquit) ex epistolis Pauli plura tibi afferuntur testimonia, qui in tuo libro fateris, Apostolum Paulum, Christum Deum & hominem praedicare. Sufficit hic tantum probasse, EEpistolarum Pauli authoritatem esse divinam, sicut & caeterarum Scripturarum. Quod si fateris, Paulum clarissimè Christum Deum & hominem asserere, debes etiam Christum Deum & hominem, prout asseruit Paulus, confiteri. Ergo, ut qui authoritatem istarum Epistolarum admittit, attamen negat Christum illis dicteri Deum, Muhammedanis ipsis hac in parte magis infidelis videri jure potest, [illegible, ~3 letters] ἐν ὀλίγῳ χρόνῳ ... 1. Tim. v. 8. Numirum ita evenit, ut quem Judaei contumaciter fateri abnuunt, Centurio praedicet: revera Dei filius hic fuit. Matth. xxvii. 54. Hoc ad argumenta nostra, vel Sacram & Paulinam Topicam, ex quâ vel maximè hic solemus disputare. Ad rem spectat, quod verba illa de Christo filio Dei dicta Psalm. 11. 7. Muhammedani etiam non differentur de eo accipienda esse: nam in libro Camus, magnae apud illos authoritatis sic legi, Guadagnolus pag. 478. auctor est: & ex eo dictum Dei omnipotentis & excelsi, ad Iesum, cui orationes Dei & pax: tu es filius meus, & ego hodie genui te. Quae aperte Dei filium agnoscunt Iesum Christum; quare & Deum. Hic quam vellem extaret, vel nobis notior esset liber V Vilhelmi Schickhardi, cit: Deus orbus Saracenorum! cujus mentionem fecit in procemio ad Tarich Persarum: sed an prodierit, ignoro.
units.tr: The Muhammedans are as offended by Christ's divine nature as they are opposed to it, and they deny it and attack it. Hence they insultingly call Christians Associators, because they join a companion to God, namely a son. Many passages in the Qur'an say that God has no companion, and whenever this occurs you may take it as said against the Christians. See the Sura of Luqman, 31, translated by the most illustrious Golius, §§ 10, 12, 14, and in many other chapters and almost countless places. Accordingly, those who come over to Christianity from them are expressly taught, in renouncing their former unbelief, to reject, among other Muhammedan doctrines, this one: that Muhammed, reviling the Christians, calls them [τὰς χεσιανὰς ἐνδίζων ἀφεντὰς ἐνομάζει τῇ κοινωνητὰς τῇ ἐπιπερίας] deniers, associators and sodalists. See Sylburg, in the Saracen matters. Azoara, or Sura 11, in the version of Retinensis: You must take the greatest care not to say anything unworthy and unjust in your law, nor to say anything about God but the truth. Jesus, son of Mary, was the messenger of God, and the Spirit and Word of God sent from heaven to Mary. Therefore believe in God and in his messenger, and do not say that there are three gods, since there is only one God, who has no son; and to him, the Almighty, all things in heaven and earth are subject. Christ himself can by no means deny this, any more than the angels who are near God can deny that they are under God's rule. These words are aimed both against the Holy Trinity and against the deity of Christ. They attack the former in many places: Sura 17, 25, 27, 29, 35, 122. In the Colloquy of Muhammed with the Jew Abdias: God has no companion or son. They call those who believe this infidels: Sura 12 and 13, Sura 4: Christ was no more than a man, to whom we gave much goodness, and whom we set forth as a teacher for the children of Israel. They relate that when Christ had been taken up into heaven, God asked him whether, since the Christians say and teach that he is God and the Son of God, he had ever claimed to be God or wished to be regarded as such. In the Sura of the Table: Jesus, son of Mary, did you tell men: take me and my mother as gods besides God? He answered: God forbid. It is not mine to say what is not truly mine. If I had said it, you would surely already know it, for you know what is in my soul, though I do not know what is in yours, since you know your secret thoughts. I said nothing to them except what you commanded me: worship God, my Lord and your Lord. I bore witness to this among them as long as I was with them. These are trifles, or rather calumnies and blasphemies. Christians do not make God out of Christ, nor Mary a divinity, nor did Christ make himself God; rather, he showed and proved by his words and deeds the testimony of his divinity, and that he was the Son of God, God himself bearing witness to him in many ways, even from heaven. I refrain from gathering all the testimonies and arguments from Scripture to prove Christ's deity, since the matter is well known to Christians and easy to prove, and because pursuing it as it deserves would lead us too far from our purpose, or extend this digression beyond what is necessary. Meanwhile I want all Christians to note well, for no small confirmation of our faith, what the Muhammedans openly confess: that Christ's deity is clearly and plainly read in the Epistles of Paul, which is why they, disputing with us on this point, decline the authority of the Pauline epistles and say that they were corrupted by Christians. Here at least is a testimony to the truth from its enemies: that, according to them, the Pauline epistles confirm it. And whoever among the Christians fails to see this in them, or evades it, and dares to argue the contrary, clearly shows himself less honest and perceptive than the Muhammedans. Although the Muhammedans go far astray in this, in that they abolish the authority of the Epistles themselves, they are yet fairer in this respect, that they freely acknowledge and confess that what is in question is taught in them, namely Christ's deity, which many a Christian, even one who wishes to listen, boldly denies and barks against. Guadagnolus, in his disputation against Ahmed the Persian: Truly, he says, in vain are many testimonies from Paul's epistles brought to you, since in your book you confess that the Apostle Paul preaches Christ as God and man. It is enough here merely to have proved that the authority of the Epistles of Paul is divine, as also of the other Scriptures. If you confess that Paul asserts most clearly that Christ is God and man, you ought also to confess Christ as God and man, as Paul asserted. Therefore, one who admits the authority of these Epistles yet denies that Christ is called God in them can rightly seem more unbelieving than the Muhammedans themselves in this respect. [illegible] [ἐν ὀλίγῳ χρόνῳ] ... 1 Tim. 5:8. So it happens that the centurion proclaims him whom the Jews stubbornly refuse to confess: Truly this was the Son of God. Matt. 27:54. This bears on our arguments, or on the Sacred and Pauline topic from which we most often dispute here. To the point: the Muhammedans also do not dispute that the words spoken of Christ as the Son of God in Psalm 2:7 must be understood of him. For in the book Camus, of great authority among them, it is so read; Guadagnolus, p. 478, is the authority: And from this the saying of God Almighty and Most High to Jesus, on whom be the prayers and peace of God: You are my son, and I have begotten you today. By these words they plainly acknowledge Jesus Christ as the Son of God, and therefore as God. I wish that the book of V. Wilhelm Schickhard, cited as God, the orphan of the Saracens!, which he mentioned in the preface to the Tarich Persarum, were extant or better known to us; but whether it was published, I do not know.

units.la: Easdem objectiones adversus Christi deitatem habent Muhammedani, quas hac in parte, qui cum iisdem faciunt, afferre solent Pseudo-Christiani, gloriae & deitatis Christi inimici: Ut quod Christus dicitur in Evangelio modo plorasse, modo jejunasse, & passus multa, mortuus tandem, crucifixus &c. quae putant obstare divinae ejus naturae. Illis autem nemo offendetur, qui in Christo, noverit, ex singulari Dei oeconomiâ, utramque naturam esse, praeter divinam, humanam etiam, in quâ illa sustinuit, & cujus ratione illa de Christo narrantur, & sic modo vera sunt. Quo respectu exponendum & quod secundo objiciunt. Matth. xxiv. 36. de Christo dictum, nescire cum horam supremi judicii. Tum quod neminem bonum dixit; Matth. xix. 17. praeter solum Deum. Et Ioann. x: Pater major me est: Sed vers. 22. est, Pater major omnibus: se vero Christus unum ait cum Patre. Et Ioann. xvii. 1. Pater glorifica filium tuum. Et Matth. xxvi. 42. Pater si fieri possit, transeat a me calix iste; verumtamen non voluntas mea sed tua fiat. Ioann. v. 22. neque enim Pater iudicat quempiam, verum omne iudicium dedit filio. Et similia obiiciunt nobis loca, ad quae perfacilis & trita est responsio.
units.tr: The Muhammedans have the same objections against Christ's deity that false Christians, enemies of Christ's glory and deity, are accustomed to bring forward in this matter, siding with them. For instance, that in the Gospel Christ is said at one time to have wept, at another to have fasted, and to have suffered much and finally died, was crucified, and so on, which they think is incompatible with his divine nature. No one will be offended by these things who knows that in Christ, by a singular dispensation of God, there are two natures: besides the divine, also a human one, in which he endured these things, and by reason of which these things are narrated of Christ, and so are true in this sense. In this respect must also be explained what they object secondly: that Matthew 24:36 says of Christ that he did not know the hour of the last judgment; then that he said no one is good (Matt. 19:17) except God alone; and in John 10 the Father is greater than I, but in verse 22 it is, The Father is greater than all; and Christ says that he is one with the Father. Also John 17:1, Father, glorify your Son; and Matthew 26:42, Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not my will but yours be done; John 5:22, For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. And they object other similar passages to us, to which the answer is very easy and commonplace.

units.la: Circa creationem mira & vana sunt, quae fabulantur Muslimi potius, quam docent: principio dicunt creata fuisse, & ipsius Dei manu, pennam, Adamum, thronum Dei, & paradysum. Pennâ Deus conscribit & annotat scilicet omnia quae sunt, quaeque fiunt: est autem ea longitudinis quingentorum annorum itineris; latitudinis, octoginta. In Colloquio cum Abdiâ, Muhammed addit creatam mensam, in quâ nempe omnia cum istâ pennâ scribantur: quae quanta sit, nam pro ratione pennae immensae magnitudinis constitui oportet, non additur. Hominem primum Adamum ex pugillo terrae diversicoloris factum asserunt, & quod hinc varietas ista formae & coloris inter homines sit, ut hic candidus, ater, vel fusci coloris alter exsistat: sed prae omnibus Deum has quatuor nationes fecisse pulchritudine elegantes, Arabes, Persas, Romanos, Indos. III. Thronum Deum sibi ipsi fecisse ajunt; portandum ab Angelis, quorum tanta sint capita, ut avis vix mille annis volando possit ab unâ aurium permeare usque ad alteram. Quarto & Paradysum creavit Deus inter prima, de quo, ex mente Muhammedanorum, etiam aliquid postea dicemus. Mundum & coelum distare inquiunt septem muribus. Stellas scintillare, ideo quod ignem vomant, & ignes quasi faces jaciant in obvios Daemones, qui Paradysum observant, & conantur continuo nuo ingredi, ut quid in cœlo agatur & decernatur scire, & hominibus eadem revelare per oracula sua queant. Cœlum sustentari à monte Kaff, qui eum ambit, & coloris est cærulei, videl. à smaragdis Paradysi, atque hinc esse quod cœlum rubeat. Solem Lunamque æqualis creata magnitudinis, & splendoris; verum Angelum Gabrielem aliquando intempestâ nocte cœlo descendentem, ala sua tam bene Lunam attigisse, ut tantam ei partem abstulerit, ac jam videtur Sole minor esse. Solem occumbentem (dicunt) se in puteum immergere, in fontem aquæ ferventis, ad quem usque pervenerit Alexander, quemque viderit. Terræ centrum collocant in cornu Tauri subterranei, qui quando se movet, terræ motum ciet. Hic stat supra Lapidem candidum, infra quem alius mons: at jam hic quo subsistit? Taurum illum (addunt) facie spectare Orientem, & quadraginta habere cornua, totidem dentes, atque à cornu uno ad alterum esse mille annorum iter. Angelos faciunt alatos, alios duabus, alios tribus, etiam quatuor alis, Surat. xlv. deque illorum uxoribus, an ullas habeant? controversiam movet Surat. I. 1. 1. & lx. 1. 1., & quidem ita sentire nonnullos refert, qui id à Majoribus suis se habere dicunt: sed errare existimat. Diversas Angelis facies formasque addit, alios hominum, equorum, boum, gallorum, volucrium, vel reliquorum animalium effigies habere, quorum nomina apud Deum intercedant: quales in cœlesti suo itinere Muhammedem offendisse supra audivimus. Videatur Roderici Ximenes Toletani Histor. Arabum, cap. v. Cotovici Itinerar. Hierosol. cap. 1 1. Michel Baudier, de la Religion des Turcs li. 1. ch. 1 1. pag. 43. Diabolos docet Alkoran, à Deo creatos, ex igne pestilentiali. Sur. xxv. xv 1. lx 1. quare quum Deus creato homine juberet Angelos coram Adamo assurgere, eumque venerari, resitit Beelzebub negans se facturum, quod ipse igneæ naturæ & originis esset, homo vero infra se terræ. Et quan-do
units.tr: Concerning creation, the Muslims fabricate wonderful and vain things rather than teach them. First, they say that a pen, Adam, the throne of God and paradise were created by the very hand of God. With the pen God writes and records everything that is and everything that happens. Its length is the distance of a five-hundred-year journey, and its breadth eighty. In the Colloquy with Abdias, Muhammed adds that a table was created, on which all things are written with that pen; how large it is, is not stated, since it must be imagined as of immense size in proportion to the pen. They assert that the first man, Adam, was made from a handful of earth of various colours, and that this is why there is such variety of form and colour among men, so that one is white, another black or dark. But above all, God made these four nations beautiful in appearance: the Arabs, Persians, Romans and Indians. Third, they say God made his throne for himself, to be carried by angels, whose heads are so large that a bird could scarcely fly from one ear to the other in a thousand years. Fourth, God created paradise among the first things, of which, according to the mind of the Muhammedans, we shall say something later. They say the world and the heavens are seven myriads of miles apart. The stars twinkle because they vomit fire and hurl flaming torches, as it were, at any demons they meet who guard paradise and try constantly to enter it, so that they may learn what is done and decreed in heaven and be able to reveal the same to men through their oracles. The heavens are held up by Mount Kaf, which surrounds them and is sky-blue in colour, namely from the emeralds of paradise; and this is why the sky is red. They say the sun and moon were created of equal size and brightness; but that the angel Gabriel, descending from heaven at some dark hour, touched the moon with his wing so forcefully that he took away so large a part of it that it now seems smaller than the sun. They say that the setting sun plunges into a well, into a spring of boiling water, to which Alexander came and saw it. They place the centre of the earth on the horn of a subterranean bull, which, when it moves, causes an earthquake. This (they say) stands on a white stone, beneath which is another mountain; but on what does this one stand? That bull, they add, faces east, has forty horns and as many teeth, and the journey from one horn to another is a thousand years. They make the angels winged, some with two wings, some with three, others with four, Sura 45; and whether they have wives, the Qur'an raises a controversy in Sura 1 and Sura 60, and it is reported that some hold this view, who say they have it from their ancestors; but Muhammed judges that they are mistaken. He adds various faces and forms to the angels, saying that some have the likenesses of men, horses, oxen, cocks, birds or other animals, and that their names are mentioned before God; such are the forms in which we have heard above that Muhammed met them on his heavenly journey. See Roderic Ximenes of Toledo, History of the Arabs, ch. 5; Cotovicus, Itinerary to Jerusalem, ch. 11; Michel Baudier, On the Religion of the Turks, bk. 1, ch. 11, p. 43. The Qur'an teaches that the devils were created by God from a pestilential fire (Sura 25, 15, 60), which is why, when God, having created man, ordered the angels to rise before Adam and worship him, Beelzebub refused, saying that he would not do it, since he himself was of fiery nature and origin, while man was below him, made of earth. And when…

units.la: De Muhammedismo.
units.tr: On Muhammedanism.

units.la: do hinc iratus Deus eum de coelo dejecisset, minatus fuit, ei se tamen in terris perpetuo reluctaturum, suasurumque hominibus, ne Deum colant aut veneantur. Quam fabulam in Alkorano saepius repetit ejus Auctor Sur. xvii. xxv. xxvi. & xlviii. De homine dicunt, quod statim ac creatus erat, & consisteret in pedes, sternutarit, & Deo benedixerit, eique simul Angelos fuisset gratulatos. Dormiente homine, animam ei extrahi fingunt, ut moriente, illamque post somnium quibusdam reddi, quibusdam non. Surat. xlix. Arborem ex qua ederit primus homo, dixit Muhammed spicas habuisse septem, quarum unam aufregit ille, quae continuerit grana quinque, quorum duo ipse comedit, duo alia uxor ejus, quintum secum assumsit, quod erat ad mensuram ovi, idque dividit in sexcentas partes, atque inde sc. diversitas colorum nata in seminibus. Quis autem recensendis omnibus istis opinionibus, & fabulis par sit, quibus plenum Alkoran, & referta Muslimorum scripta? specimen illorum hic exhibere ratio instituti postulabat, in quo conquiescimus, examen illorum habentes supervacaneum.
units.tr: Then God, angered by this, cast him down from heaven, and he threatened that he would nevertheless oppose him continually on earth and would persuade men not to worship or revere God. The author of the Alcoran repeats this fable often, at Sura 17, 25, 26 and 48. Of man they say that as soon as he was created and stood up on his feet, he sneezed and gave thanks to God, and the angels at once congratulated him. While a man sleeps, they imagine that his soul is drawn out of him, as at death, and that after the dream it is returned to some men but not to others (Sura 49). Muhammed said that the tree from which the first man ate had seven ears of grain, of which he broke off one that contained five grains. Of these, he himself ate two, his wife ate two, and he kept the fifth, which was the size of an egg; this he divided into six hundred parts, and from this came the diversity of colours in seeds. But who could be equal to listing all these opinions and fables, with which the Alcoran is full and the writings of the Muslims stuffed? The method of our undertaking required that we set out a specimen of them here, and we rest content with it, considering a full examination of them superfluous.

units.la: Pergimus ad religionem Muhammedicam, ut hic specemus illorum superstitionem & ritus, in Circumcisione, lotionibus, precationibus, juramentis, jejunio &c. quo corpus istius religionis habeamus maximam sui parte perspectum. Primo circumcisionem tenent, sed an ex sola aemulatione legis Hebraeorum, ut propterea eam Muhammed instituerit, vel observari praeceperit, an ex antiqua consuetudine, illis gentibus ante Muhammedis tempora etiam usitata, ex instituto & ritu civili, regionis potius quam religionis, ambiguum est. Certe apud istas nationes, & Aegyptios, & Aethiopes, & Colchos [illegible, ~8 letters] inquit Herodotus in Euterpe, circumcisionis usum fuisse, constat. (Diodorus Siculus lib. 11. in initio, & lib. 4.) & apud Idumaeos, atque Ismaelitas, sive antiquos Saracenos. Iosephus, antiquit, lib 1. cap. xxi. de Isaaco, ejusque octavo die circumcisione, postquam dixisset, Iudaeos etiam nunc in circumcidendis suis liberis eundem diem observare: atque Arabes (ait) circumciduntur post annum aetatis tertium & decimum. Nam princeps eorum generis Ismael ea aetate circumcisus est. Sic ante Muhammedem Arabes circumcisi, primaque ejus origo ad familiam Abrahami referenda. Ut quod Ægyptii hic egerunt, aliaeque post eos gentes, ab Israelitis acceperint, non contra, uti Celsus apud Originem calumniatur, lib. 1. contra Celsum. & Herodotus, loco citato, dixit: Phoenices & qui in Palestina sunt, illum morem ab Ægyptiis didicisse. Sed Ægyptii ab Hebraeis; nec ante illud sciverunt.
units.tr: We proceed to the Muhammedan religion, so that here we may survey their superstition and rites: circumcision, washings, prayers, oaths, fasting, and so on, so that we may have a view of most of the body of this religion. First, they keep circumcision; but whether they do so merely from emulation of the law of the Hebrews, so that Muhammed instituted it or ordered it to be observed for that reason, or from an ancient custom that was also in use among those peoples before the time of Muhammed, as a civil institution and rite of the region rather than of religion, is uncertain. It is certain that among those nations, namely the Egyptians, the Ethiopians and the Colchians [illegible], as Herodotus says in Euterpe, the practice of circumcision existed (Diodorus Siculus, book 11 at the beginning, and book 4); and among the Idumaeans and the Ishmaelites, or the ancient Saracens. Josephus, Antiquities book 1 chapter 21, on Isaac and his circumcision on the eighth day, after saying that the Jews even now observe the same day in circumcising their sons, adds: and the Arabs (he says) are circumcised after the thirteenth year of age, for Ishmael, the founder of their race, was circumcised at that age. Thus the Arabs were circumcised before Muhammed, and its first origin must be traced to the family of Abraham. So what the Egyptians did here, and other nations after them, they received from the Israelites, not the reverse, as Celsus slanders in Origen, book 1 against Celsus; and Herodotus, in the place cited, said that the Phoenicians and those in Palestine learned that custom from the Egyptians. But the Egyptians learned it from the Hebrews, and did not know it before that.

units.la: Philo, de Circumcisione: ridetur majorum nostrorum circumcisio, quamvis in non mediocri honore habita, etiam apud gentes alias, praesertim Ægyptiam. Epiphanius, adversus Ebionitas, circumcisionem retinentes, & conjungentes cum Christianismo: quid vero juvat Ebion circumcisionem: quando etiam idololatrae & scelerati Ægyptii circumcisionem habent. Et Samaritae, ac Iudei, & Idumaei, & Homeritae. Plerique vero ex his non propter legem hoc faciunt, sed temeraria quadam consuetudine. Gentiles circumcidebant ex consuetudine, & usu atque observatione politica, quamvis prima apud eos circumcisionis origo ex lege, & praxi Hebraeorum venerit. Nec tantum in Hebraeos, sed etiam in Phoenices, & Arabes haec traditio insolevit, inquit Cyprianus, de Circumcisione.
units.tr: Philo, On Circumcision: the circumcision of our forefathers is mocked, although it was held in no small honour, even among other nations, especially the Egyptians. Epiphanius, against the Ebionites, who retained circumcision and joined it with Christianity: what good does circumcision do Ebion, when even the idolaters and the wicked Egyptians have circumcision? So do the Samaritans, the Jews, the Idumaeans and the Homerites. Most of these, however, do this not because of the law, but from some rash custom. The Gentiles circumcised from custom, and from usage and political observance, although the first origin of circumcision among them came from the law and practice of the Hebrews. This tradition became customary not only among the Hebrews, but also among the Phoenicians and the Arabs, says Cyprian, On Circumcision.

units.la: Clemens Romanus, qui dicitur, Recognit. lib. VIII. Iudaeorum quoque circumcisionem Arabica gentes, aliaeque plurimae ad ministerium suae impietatis imitati sunt. Aliam adhuc observatae apud Muhammedanos circumcisionis causam adfert Septem-Castrensis, lib. de moribus & Religione Turc. cap. xxi. putatque propter crebras & religiosas lotiones, ut ex totum corpus melius perluant, neque arceantur a pellibus praeputii, circumcisionem ab illis adhiberi: mihi videtur (inquit) quod potius [?quantur] circumcisione propter hoc, ut lotio, quâ se æquâ per-fundatur, non sit invalida, remanente aliquâ siccitate sub istâ pelliculâ præputii, sicut superius in 10. & 13. cap. dis-tinctum est. Propterea etiam diligenter incidunt angues & radunt pilos. Inque eandem sententiam propendet Christophorus Ricerius, Comment. de moribus Turcarum, in Descript. Arab. pag. 95.
units.tr: Clement of Rome (so called), Recognitions book 8: The Arab peoples and many others have imitated the circumcision of the Jews as a service to their impiety. Septem-Castrensis, in his book On the Customs and Religion of the Turks, chapter 21, gives yet another reason for the circumcision observed among the Muhammedans, and thinks that they use circumcision because of their frequent and religious washings, so that they may wash the whole body more thoroughly and not be hindered by the foreskin's skin: it seems to me (he says) that circumcision is practised for this reason, so that the washing with which they drench themselves may not be ineffective, with some dryness remaining under this little skin of the foreskin, as I have explained above in chapters 10 and 13. For this reason they also carefully cut away the hair and shave the body. Christopher Richerius, in his Commentary On the Customs of the Turks, in the Description of Arabia, p. 95, leans to the same opinion.

units.la: Tres ergo circumcisionis Muhammedicæ apud Doctos assignantur causæ, ritus antiquus apud istas gentes politicus; æmulatio Moßis & Hebræorum; commodum lotionis: quas vel conjungat aliquis, vel secernat, prout rectius visum fuerit, quamvis postremum istud pro causâ impulsivâ antecedente sumere, nimis mihi quidem dilutum videtur, pro accessoriâ facilius admittendum.
units.tr: Three causes of Muhammedan circumcision are therefore assigned by the learned: the ancient political rite among those peoples; emulation of Moses and the Hebrews; and the advantage of washing.
