One may join these or separate them, as seems best; although to take the last as the chief moving cause seems to me far too weak, and it may more easily be admitted as an incidental one.

units.la: In Colloquio Muhammedis cum Abdiâ, circumcisio ad Adamum usque refertur, qui ab Angelo Gabriele nempe circumcisus fuerit, & detonsum ei capillitium. Circumcidunt Muhammedani, ut Arabes olim Ismaelitæ, non statim à nativitate, octavo, vel alio die, sed post annos aliquot, vel decimum tertium, ad exemplum Ismaelis; vel aliquando septimo, octavo, & sequentibus, ut professionem Islamismi, erecto manus pollice, possint edere, la illah, non est Deus nisi unus, & Muhammed ejus Prophetæ. Neque tum demum illis imponuntur nomina, quando circumciduntur, sed ea accipiunt à nativitate.
units.tr: In the Colloquy of Muhammed with Abdias, circumcision is traced back to Adam, who is said to have been circumcised by the angel Gabriel, and his hair was shaved. Muhammedans, like the Arabs, the Ishmaelites of old, circumcise not immediately after birth, on the eighth day or another day, but after some years, or on the thirteenth year, following the example of Ishmael; or sometimes on the seventh, eighth and following days, so that they may be able to utter the profession of Islam with the thumb raised: la illah, there is no God but one, and Muhammed is his prophet. Nor are names given to them when they are circumcised; they receive them from birth.

units.la: Circumcidi dicuntur apud eos non mares tantum, sed & quandoque fœminæ, at hæ non ex lege, aut necessitate adeo, ac honoris causâ. Sic ex Benlidi, Gabriel Sionita cap. xv. Descript. Arab. At Bartholomæus Georgievitz negat, lib. 1 2. de moribus Turc. fœminæ non patiuntur circumcidi, sed tantummodo jam dicta verba confitentes, Muslimæ efficiuntur.
units.tr: It is said that among them not only males but sometimes also females are circumcised, but this is done not so much by law or necessity as for honour's sake. So Gabriel Sionita, chapter 15 of the Description of Arabia, citing Benlidi. But Bartholomew Georgievitz denies it, in book 2 of On the Customs of the Turks: the women do not allow themselves to be circumcised, but only by confessing the words already mentioned do they become Muslims.

units.la: Circumcidunt in ædibus, opiparo ad hanc solemnitatem instructo epulo, quod per triduum continuant, assato bove integro, cui includitur ovis, huic gallina, & in hac ovum, ad majorem dici & actionis istius significandum splen-do-
units.tr: They circumcise in their houses, with a lavish banquet prepared for this solemnity, which they keep up for three days: a whole roasted ox, in which is enclosed a sheep, in which a hen, and in the hen an egg, to signify the greater splendour and dignity of this day and deed.

units.la: . dorem ac dignitatem. Sed nunquam majori haec cum pompa peraguntur, quam ad circumcisionem proselyti, sive ex Paganis, aut Christianis, qui magnifice primum, comitatus aliquando Proceribus, aliisque viris illustribus, per urbis vicos circumducitur, donariis ornatur, & tertio die circumciditur, itque Musluman, atque à tributo liber. Judæus quando Islamismum accipit, non circumciditur, sed lavatur, & confessus nomen Christi, Dei nuncii ac Prophetæ, tum sacrum carmen istud, La illah &c. inter Muhammedanos venit. Omitto, quod per vim aliquando etiam invitos circumcidunt, nempe si quis contumeliam (secundum ipsos) dixerit Muhammedi, cum non esse Prophetam, vel de Alkorano, non esse eum librum divinum, aut si Turcam conspuerit, ut si cum Muhammedanâ rem habuerit, incendio (juxta ipsorum leges) peribit, vel cogetur circumcidi, & portare Tulipantum.
units.tr: These ceremonies are never performed with greater pomp than when a proselyte, whether from the pagans or the Christians, is circumcised. He is first led magnificently through the streets of the city, sometimes accompanied by nobles and other illustrious men, adorned with gifts, and on the third day he is circumcised, and becomes a Musluman and free from tribute. When a Jew accepts Islam, he is not circumcised but washed, and, confessing the name of Christ as the messenger and prophet of God, he is then admitted among the Muhammedans with that sacred formula, La illah, etc. I pass over the fact that they sometimes circumcise even unwilling men by force, namely if someone has said (in their view) an insult against Muhammed, that he is not a prophet, or against the Alcoran, that it is not a divine book, or if he has spat on a Turk, or if he has had intercourse with a Muhammedan woman; by their laws he will perish by fire, or he will be compelled to be circumcised and to wear the turban.

units.la: Accedo ad lotiones, quas Orientalibus semper valde familiares, Muhammedani crebro, & cum religione utuntur, habentque triplices. Alia enim est domestica, vulgaris, privata, qua post exoneratam vel alvum, vel vesicam utuntur, diligenter caventes, nec ubi lotii vel excrementi aliquid adhaereat, unde inquinentur. Quare nec erecti stantes urinam reddunt viri, sed incurvi cruribus innixi, ut feminæ solent, ne forte conspergantur: & in libro Zuna jubentur, postquam minxerint, siniistræ manus digitis exprimere si quod circa præputium adhæserit urinæ. Non chartâ Bateove anum detergunt, quia illis nomen Dei inscribitur, quod hoc pacto profanari putant, sed aquâ, aut sibi ipsi, aut mancipia hoc Dominis vitis alia, alia & sui sexus fœminis præstant officium, vel aqua si desit, lapillo utuntur, aut panniculo, quo etiam caput virilis membri perstringunt, ne qua urinæ guttula adhæreat, & contaminet vestes. Addit Corovicus in Itinerario, & Clenardus in epistolis, illos etiam quando vel flatum ventris emittunt, lustrationem adhibere. Conferatur Alkorani Surata xii. xxv. Descript. Arabiæ, cap. xv. Tuscia, pag. 82, Richerius, de moribus Turc. pag. 93. Altera lotio est, quam vel ingressuri templum, vel vacaturi precibus peragunt. Unde ante templorum fores ubique fontes habent pulcherrimos, quos conferta multitudine adeunt sub horam precationis, & se diligenter omnes lavant, antequam templa vel Meskitas ingrediantur, quæ ab illoris, & calceis, si quis eos non exuat, contaminari credunt. Lavant denudatis ad cubitum brachiis; primo dextram manum brachiumque, inde partem sinistram, deinceps os, nasum, aures, faciem, & sic totum corpus, præcipue quinque sensus; si nudi sint, pedes, sin calceati, supremitatem calcei madefecisse sufficit, quamvis hoc ipsum de [?] inter causas Schismatis Persarum à Turcis quoque olim fuit, illis quidem calceos tingentibus, his vero id improbantibus. Interim dum se lavant, preces obmurmurant, & tandem linteolo, quod ideo ad zonam appensum ubique gestant, corpus abstergunt. Quod si locus desertus sit, ubi aquæ copia haberi non potest, terra aut pulvere corpus conspergunt. Euthymius Zigabenus, in Panopl. [?] [?] Iubet præterea eos qui se ad preces conferunt, prius purgare: aquâ quidem, si adsit, si minus, humo sossitio: atque tantundem hoc valere, quod alibi lotionem aquæ arbitrantur: nam etiam ad remissionem atque ablutionem peccatorum facere illa, sed leviùm, existimant: adversus gravia delicta adhibent lotionem hanc, quam tertio loco ponimus, magis operosam & religiosam, totius omnino corporis, & singulorum membrorum, in quem finem pilos ubique in corpore radunt, exceptâ in viris barbâ, & in fœminis comâ, & ungues secant tum manuum, tum pedum. Balnea huc in usum ubivis habent magnâ copiâ, quæ dies & noctes papatent viris fœminisque, non promiscue tamen, sed fœ- minis intus se lavantibus, appenso præ foribus linteo, seu signo, monentur advenientes viri ne intrent eo tempore, sed proximum expectent. Balneorum istorum formam usumque latè describit Iohannes Cotovicus Ultrajectinus, in Itinerario cap. iv.
units.tr: I come to the washings, which are always very familiar to the Orientals, and which the Muhammedans use often and with religious care; and they have three kinds. The first is the domestic, common, private washing, which they use after emptying either the bowels or the bladder; they take great care that nothing of urine or excrement clings to them, by which they might be defiled. For this reason men do not pass urine standing upright, but crouching on their legs, as women usually do, lest they be splashed. In the book Zuna they are commanded, after they have urinated, to squeeze out with the fingers of the left hand whatever urine has clung around the foreskin. They do not wipe the anus with paper or a rag, because the name of God is written on it, which they think would be profaned in this way; they do it with water, either themselves or through their slaves, and to other men of their own sex, and women to women, the same office. If water is lacking, they use a small stone or a rag, with which they also wipe the head of the male member, so that no drop of urine may cling and stain their clothes. Corovicus in his Itinerary, and Clenardus in his letters, add that they also perform this cleansing when they let out wind from the bowels. Compare Sura 12 and 25 of the Alcoran, the Description of Arabia, chapter 15, Tuscia, p. 82, and Richerius, On the Customs of the Turks, p. 93. The second washing is the one they perform either before entering a temple or before engaging in prayers. Hence before the doors of the temples they everywhere have very fine fountains, to which the crowded multitude goes at the hour of prayer, and they all wash carefully before entering the temples or mosques, which they believe would be defiled by dust and shoes, if someone did not take them off. They wash with their arms bared to the elbow: first the right hand and arm, then the left part, then the mouth, nose, ears, face, and so the whole body, especially the five senses; if they are barefoot, they wash the feet; if they wear shoes, it is enough to wet the tip of the shoe. This very matter was once among the causes of the schism of the Persians from the Turks: the one party dyed their shoes, the other disapproved of it. Meanwhile, while they wash, they mutter prayers, and finally they dry the body with a little linen cloth, which for this reason they carry everywhere hanging at the belt. If the place is deserted, where a plentiful supply of water cannot be had, they sprinkle the body with earth or dust. Euthymius Zigabenus, in the Panoplia, [illegible] [illegible], also orders those who betake themselves to prayers first to cleanse themselves: with water, if it is at hand, or, if not, with thirsty earth; and they think this has the same force as the washing with water elsewhere, for they believe it also serves for the remission and washing away of sins, though of lighter ones. Against grave offences they use the third washing, which we place last, more laborious and religious, of the whole body and of each of its members; to this end they shave the hair everywhere on the body, except that men keep their beards and women their hair, and they cut the nails of both hands and feet. They have bathhouses everywhere in great numbers for this use, which stand open day and night to men and women; not, however, indiscriminately: while women bathe within, a linen cloth or sign is hung before the doors, and men who arrive are warned not to enter at that time, but to wait nearby. John Cotovicus of Utrecht describes the form and use of these baths at length in his Itinerary, chapter 4.

units.la: Precationes suas fere gestu & varia corporis jactatione æstimant Muhammedani. Nam inclinationes, & prostrationes, quas Erket appellant, & de quibus Suarat lx. gesticulatorias multas adhibent, quando orationes recitant. Quinquies de die solenniter precantur. In Commentario Rerum Turcicarum, pag. 51. dicitur sexies: at Georgievitz, lib. ii. & Gabriel Simonita, cap. xv. & Richerius, Cotovicus, alii dicunt quinquies, ad quas quasi horas canonicas preces suas fundunt. Primo, post ortum Solis, non ante, ne eum videantur adorare. Vide illam precationem, Surat. xxvii. Inde sub meridiem: tum post meridiem, sub Solis occasum: quarto, post Solis occasum, ad primam lucem stellarum: postremò, ad mediam noctem, orationes dicunt varias, & plures paucioresve, utique proclinationes & prostrationes adhibent disparí numero, nunquam plures quam ad medium diei, vel noctis: hæc quindecim inclinationes, & orationes octo: etenim numero ut admonentur Deo preces, ita eo istas definiunt, præterquam quod & hanc rationem dant quare ultima precatio omnium sit longissima, quia oportet (dicunt) accrescere semper devotionem, & finem bonorum operum, nunquam non esse optimum. Primo jusserat illos Muhammed precari conversos ad templum Hierosolymitanum, inde ut se suosque à Iudæis magis distinguerent & removerent, non versus Ierusalem amplius, sed Meccam orare instituit. Surat. i. & xviii. quod factum secundo anno Hegiræ, quo tempore in Meccensi templo antiquum adhuc colebatur idolum lapidis quadrati, Veneris effigiem habentis: de quo Ma-
units.tr: The Muhammedans judge their prayers mostly by gesture and by varied movements of the body. For they use many gestures in reciting their prayers, namely the bowings and prostrations which they call Erket, and of which Sura lx. speaks. They pray solemnly five times a day. A Commentary on Turkish Affairs, p. 51, says six times, but Georgievitz, bk. ii, Gabriel Simonita, ch. xv, Richerius, Cotovicus and others say five, and at these times, as at canonical hours, they pour out their prayers. The first is after sunrise, not before, lest they seem to worship the sun; see that prayer in Sura xxvii. Then comes the midday prayer, then the afternoon prayer after noon, then the fourth after sunset, and finally, at midnight, at the first light of the stars. At each they say various prayers, more or fewer, and they perform bowings and prostrations in varying numbers, never more than at midday or at midnight: fifteen bowings and eight prayers. For they fix the number of prayers as they are reminded to pray to God, and they give this reason why the last prayer is the longest of all: it is necessary (they say) that devotion should always grow, and that the end of good works should never be anything but the best. At first Muhammed had ordered them to pray turned toward the Temple of Jerusalem; then, so that he and his people might be more clearly distinguished from and set apart from the Jews, he decreed that they should no longer pray toward Jerusalem but toward Mecca: Sura i and xviii. This was done in the second year of the Hegira, at which time in the temple at Mecca an ancient square stone idol, having the likeness of Venus, was still worshipped; concerning which Ma-

units.la: ximu zimus Tyrius; sørn. XXXVIII. Clemens Alexandrinus, in Protreptico ad Gentes. Arnobius, contra Gen-tes lib. VI. riderent temporibus prisci Persas fluvios coluisse, memoralia ut indicant scripta, informem Arabes lapi-dem. Euthymius Zigabenus, in Panoplia: dictus lapis caput est Veneris, quam Ismaelite olim adorabant. Si quis accuratius specles, etiam capitis in eo delineamenta non obs-cura erunt. Et in Catechesi Sarracenorum, vel ordine qui observatur cum iis, qui à Sarracenis ad Christianos accedunt, apud Sylburgium, in Sarracenicis, Ἀναθεματίζω τὴν αὐτὴν τὸ οὐς ὁ Μάκε οἶνον τῆς εὐχῆς ἐν φῶς καὶ ἐς μίσην λίθον μέγαν, ἐκ τόπου ἐκ Ἀφροδίτης ἔχοντα ἐμπάθειαν ἐν τοῦτο, ὡς ἐπὶ τοῦ ἐκ Ἀγαρ ἀπο-λύσωντ ἐκ τῆς Ἀβραὰμ ὡς ἀντὶ τὴν κέρμηλον ἀποδικ-ωντ, ὅτι τὸν Ἰσμαὴλ ἐκ μέσου ἄν. Anathematizo etiam ipsam illam precationis domum in Make: in cujus medio jacere ejus lapidem magnum, Veneris effigiem in se habentem: honorari autem ipsum lapidem, quasi Abraham super eo cum Agare coierit; aut camelum ei alligaverit, quem Isaacum erat sacrificaturus. Peregrinantes Meccam, inter alia cultus sui, lapides etiam projicere constat. Johannes Andreas in Confas. sect. Mahom. cap. 1. hoc ab iis fieri dicit, quando superarunt peregrinantes flumen aliquod Batin Muhacil, in quod a colle vicino lapides quosdam de extra jam, Veterum Ethnicorum more projiciunt, in memoriam Abrahae, cui ad immolationem filii proficiscenti Diabolus ibi factus est obviam, et Ismaeli remde sacrificio persecuit; ac refertur in libro Azear, Ismaelem sax is Dominum petiisse. Statuunt quippe Muhammedani, non Isaacum, sed Ismaelem ab Abrahamo immolatum fuisse; quem cum mactare conaretur Parens, & gladius collum dissecare nequiret, intra manus ejus arietem candidum, pinguemque apparuisse, quem Deo pro filio sacrificarit. Clenardus in epist. ad Latomum, refert, hosce peregrinantes ad radices montis Araphat singulos colligere sexaginta tres lapillos, quibuscum recta pergunt Mistam, per quem locum datur Abraham profectus, occisurus filium. Hic tres sunt columnae, certo distantes a se invicem intervallo, & grandi lapidum munita acervo, ad quarum unamquamque singulis diebus peregrini per triduum commorantes, septem ex iis lapillis projiciunt: nempe inde, quod dum Diabolus filium Abrahami ad mactationem sui illac proficiscentem dissuadere opus tentaret, filius illum lapidibus abegerit septem; iterumque vexatus ab eo, alios septem in eum conjecerit, atque sic tertio. Hinc morem illum lapides projiciendi apud illos fluxisse, scribunt. Vide & Pocockium, in Notis ad specim. histor. Arab. pag. 314. etc. Quod vero de ritu Ethnicorum dicitur, ita est, & exponit plenius Auctor iste, cujus disputationem cum Muhammedanis refert Vincentius Bellovacensis, Specul. histor. lib. IV, & ex eo Scaliger, lib. V. de Emendat. temper. aliique; quod nimirum in honorem Mercurii Veteres Indiae populi, soliti fuerint lapides in acervum projicere; atque eo adfert, quod quoque a pluribus, qua Iudaeis, qua Christianis, Prov. xxv. 1. 8. ex editione veteri legitur, sicut qui projicit lapidem in acervum Mercurii. Sic enim Pagani solebant, quia Mercurius viarum dux & lingua quasi credebatur, acervos lapidum in itineribus constituere ejus in honorem, in quem semper lapidem adjiciebat iter faciens, quo ita cumulus augebatur. Illi erant Ἑρμαῖοι λίθοι, Ἑρμαχαί. Hebraei proverbio dicunt, projiciens lapidem in Merkolis. Vide Drusium, in Adagiis. Tisbi in Merkolis quidem nomen idoli esse dicit, Mercuriumque; verum respondisse ei nonnemine haud illum fuisse Mercurii cultum, per ... sed erravit quisquis is fuerit: nam immo isthoc pacto olim Mercurium a Gentilibus cultum, viri horum doctissimi copiose ostendunt. Seldenus, de DIs Syris Syntagm. II. cap. 15. de Mercurii acervo. & Ioh. Gerh. Vossius, de orig. Idolol. lib. II. cap. xxxi. Apud Salouationem, sicut qui mittit lapidem in acervum; non bene versum כצרור אבן במנמה; sed sicut qui ligat lapidem pretiosum, unionem in fundâ, ita est, qui confert stulto honorem. Chaldaeus, הך נקצא רטסא בקלעא ut fragmentum lamine in fundâ. Atque de lapide pretioso explicant Rabbini. Rabbi Levi ben Gersom המרגלית margaritam. Et Hispanica Cypriani de Valera: como quien ligo la piedra en la honda. Italica Deodati, come chi possesse una pietra pretiosa legata, in un mucchio di sassi. Rabbini, inter acervum lapidum. Ralbag, כנל אבני מרגמה שאינו ראי כי שרשים מ הסרגלית inter acervum lapidum, in quo non convenit ponere margaritam. Ritus istius projectionis lapidum apud Paganos usitati, quo & Vetus Vulgata versio, aliique ex eâ respiciunt, mentionem quoque facit in notis marginalibus Deodatus. Ad Latinam: sicut qui mittit lapidem in acervum Mercurii, in margine est: lapidem pretiosum fundâ. Auctor disputationis istius apud Bellovacensem porro indicat, ritum illum projiciendorum lapidum in honorem Mercurii, ab Indis ad Arabes defluxisse: sed qui in honorem Veneris idem egerint: hac ergo consuetudo, inquit, cum ab Indis ad Arabes descendisset, eamque suo tempore apud Mechaм in honore Veneris Machumet celebrari reperisset, sic illam manere praecepit, cum tamen cetera idololatriae praestigia removisset. Unde vero sit, quod in oriente alii Mercurium, Venerem alii hoc honore afficiendam putarint, vide inquirentem Cl. Vossium. Muhammedani vero dicunt, lapidem illum in templo Meccano, esse lapidem Paradysi, qui quando coelo demittebatur, totam collustrarit urbem, sed nunc ob hominum peccata fulgorem suum amisit, ut hoc commento ludant hominum superstitionem, effusâ devotione lapidem illum Veneri olim sacrum, exosculantium & venerantium. In Catechesi Saracenorum quoque: Anathematizo ejus ipsum Meke, & totum ejus ambitum, & qui à Saracenis ibi contra Christianos lacessitur septem lapides. Vcnerem ab Arabibus olim solemniter cultam, certum. In eadem Catechesi, inter anathematismos: Anathematizo eos qui matutinum sidus, sive Luciferum & Venerem adorant: quam Arabum lingua Chabar, id est Magnam, nominant. Glycas, Annal. part. iv. Ismaelitae ad Heraclium usque simulacra colebant. Astarten, quae Luna est, adorantes: quam & chaberam non appellabant, hoc est, magnam. Inde insignia lunularum apud Muhammedanos non nunc solum, vel a tempore Muhammedis, sed a prisicis inde temporibus, & inter ornamenta Ismaelitarum, vel Midianitarum habita, ex Sacris etiam discimus. Iudic. viii. 21. 26. Adeo non a fuga Muhammedis demum origo hujus rei petenda, quia inciderit biduo post Lunae coitum, in initio mensis Muharam, anni Arabici lunaris, corniculante jam Luna, uti Scaliger censuit, lib. ii. & v. de Emendat. temporum: sed multo ante Muhammedem tempore istum Lunularum apud eos usum fuisse, melius ab aliis jam observatum, Seldeno, de Dis Syris, Syntagm. ii. cap. iv. Vossio, lib. ii, de Idolol. cap. xxxi. Atque ab ista consuetudine etiam hodie est usus lunularum in summitate turrium apud Muhammedanos. Eodemque modo dici Veneris solemnitatem retinent, qui eis est, quod apud Iudaeos Sabbathi dies, nobis Dominicus. Diem illum ideo appellitant diem templi, ut & reliquos dies non ex nominibus planetarum (qui loquendi mos mimis quam usitatus est) sed alterum diem post festum, tertium mercatus diem, reliquos ferias nominant. Veneris vero diem prae omnibus eminere dicunt, quemadmodum inter urbes Mecca, & inter menses Ramadan. Eo ajunt, Solem ortum, creatum Adamum, in Paradyso collocatum, atque inde ejectum, eodem futurum diem judicii, atque etiam eodem natum Muhammedem.
units.tr: ximus Tyrius, Sermon XXXVIII. Clement of Alexandria, in the Protrepticus to the Gentiles. Arnobius, Against the Gentiles, bk. VI: The Persians once worshipped rivers in ancient times, as written records show, and the Arabs worshipped a shapeless stone. Euthymius Zigabenus, in the Panoplia: The stone is called the head of Venus, whom the Ishmaelites once adored. If anyone looks more carefully, the outlines of a head will not be unclear in it. And in the Catechism of the Saracens, or the order which is observed with those who come over from the Saracens to the Christians, in Sylburg, among the Saracen texts: [Ἀναθεματίζω τὴν αὐτὴν τὸ οὐς ὁ Μάκε οἶνον τῆς εὐχῆς ἐν φῶς καὶ ἐς μίσην λίθον μέγαν, ἐκ τόπου ἐκ Ἀφροδίτης ἔχοντα ἐμπάθειαν ἐν τοῦτο, ὡς ἐπὶ τοῦ ἐκ Ἀγαρ ἀπο-λύσωντ ἐκ τῆς Ἀβραὰμ ὡς ἀντὶ τὴν κέρμηλον ἀποδικ-ωντ, ὅτι τὸν Ἰσμαὴλ ἐκ μέσου ἄν.] I also curse that very house of prayer at Mecca, in the middle of which lies their great stone, having the likeness of Venus; and the stone is honoured as if Abraham had lain with Hagar upon it, or had tied his camel to it, which he was about to sacrifice as Isaac, because Ishmael was in the midst. It is well known that pilgrims going to Mecca, among other parts of their worship, also throw stones. John Andreas, in Confas. sect. Mahom. cap. 1., says this is done by them when pilgrims have crossed some river, Batin Muhacil, into which they throw certain stones taken from a nearby hill, in the manner of the old heathens, in memory of Abraham, to whom the Devil appeared on the way there when he was going to sacrifice his son, and whom he drove away with a stone; and it is related in the book Azear that Ishmael asked the Lord for stones. For the Muhammedans hold that it was Ishmael, not Isaac, whom Abraham was going to sacrifice; and when the father tried to slay him and the sword could not cut his neck, a white and fat ram appeared in his hands, which he offered to God in place of the son. Clenard, in his letter to Latomus, reports that these pilgrims, at the foot of Mount Arafat, each gather sixty-three little stones, with which they go straight to Mistam, the place to which Abraham is said to have gone, intending to kill his son. There are three pillars there, set at fixed intervals from one another and protected by a great heap of stones; at each of these, on each of the three days the pilgrims stay there, they throw seven of those little stones. The reason, they write, is that when the Devil tried to dissuade Abraham's son from the sacrifice he was going there to make, the son drove him off with seven stones; and when he was harassed by him again, he threw seven more at him, and then a third time. Hence, they write, the custom of throwing stones arose among them. See also Pococke, in the Notes to the Specimen Historiae Arabum, p. 314, etc. As for what is said about the rite of the heathens, it is so, and this author, whose dispute with the Muhammedans Vincent of Beauvais reports in his Speculum historiale, bk. IV, and after him Scaliger, bk. V, On the Emendation of Time, and others, explains it more fully: that the ancient peoples of India were accustomed to throw stones on a heap in honour of Mercury. He brings in support that, in the older edition, which is read by many, both Jews and Christians, Prov. xxv. 1.8: As one who throws a stone onto the heap of Mercury. For the pagans used to set up heaps of stones on the roads in honour of Mercury, who was believed to be the guide of ways and the tongue, and onto which the traveller always added a stone, so that the heap grew. These were the Hermaean stones, the Hermae. The Hebrews say in a proverb, throwing a stone into the Merkolis [מרקוליס]. See Drusius, in the Adagia. Tisbi, on Merkolis, says it is the name of an idol, and Mercury; but someone has replied to him that it was not the worship of Mercury, through ... but he is mistaken, whoever he may be: for indeed in this way Mercury was once worshipped by the Gentiles, as the most learned men show at length: Selden, On the Syrian Gods, Syntagm II, ch. 15, on the heap of Mercury; and John Gerard Vossius, On the Origin of Idolatry, bk. II, ch. xxxi. In the Salvation [Vulgate] translation: as one who casts a stone into a heap; not well rendered as כצרור אבן במנמה [as one who binds a stone in a sling]; but as one who binds a precious stone, a pearl, in a sling, so is he who gives honour to a fool. The Chaldee: הך נקצא רטסא בקלעא [as a fragment of a plate in a sling]. And the rabbis explain it of a precious stone. Rabbi Levi ben Gershom: המרגלית [the pearl]: a pearl. And the Spanish version of Cyprian de Valera: como quien liga la piedra en la honda [as one who ties the stone in the sling]. The Italian of Diodati: as one who might possess a precious stone set in a heap of stones. The rabbis: among a heap of stones. Ralbag: כנל אבני מרגמה שאינו ראי כי שרשים מ הסרגלית [among a heap of stones, in which it is not fitting to place a pearl]. Diodati also mentions this rite of throwing stones used among the pagans, in the marginal notes, as does the old Vulgate version and others who follow it. The Latin: as one who throws a stone onto the heap of Mercury; in the margin: a precious stone in a sling. The author of that dispute, as reported by Vincent of Beauvais, further points out that the rite of throwing stones in honour of Mercury passed from the Indians to the Arabs; but that those who did the same in honour of Venus: This custom, he says, when it had passed from the Indians to the Arabs, and when Muhammed found it being celebrated in his time at Mecca in honour of Venus, he ordered it to remain so, although he had removed the other tricks of idolatry. Whence it is that in the East some thought Mercury, and others Venus, should be honoured in this way, see Vossius, the learned man, who inquires into it. The Muhammedans, however, say that the stone in the temple at Mecca is the stone of Paradise, which, when it was let down from heaven, lit up the whole city, but now has lost its brightness because of men's sins; and so with this fiction they mock the superstition of men, who with poured-out devotion kiss and venerate that stone once sacred to Venus. In the Catechism of the Saracens too: I curse that Mecca itself and its whole circuit, and the seven stones which the Saracens there hurl against the Christians. That Venus was once solemnly worshipped by the Arabs is certain. In the same Catechism, among the anathemas: I curse those who adore the morning star, or Lucifer and Venus, which in the Arabic tongue they call Chabar, that is, Great. Glycas, Annals, part iv: The Ishmaelites worshipped images up to the time of Heraclius, adoring Astarte, which is the Moon, which they also did not call Chabera, that is, great. Hence the crescent emblems among the Muhammedans are not only now, nor only from the time of Muhammed, but have been regarded from earlier times as ornaments of the Ishmaelites or Midianites; we learn this also from the Sacred Scriptures, Judg. viii. 21, 26. So the origin of this thing is not to be sought from Muhammed's flight, merely because it happened two days after the new moon, at the beginning of the month Muharram of the Arabic lunar year, with the moon already a crescent, as Scaliger thought, bk. II and V, On the Emendation of Times; but the use of crescents among them was much older than Muhammed, as others have already observed better: Selden, On the Syrian Gods, Syntagm II, ch. iv; Vossius, bk. II, On Idolatry, ch. xxxi. And from this custom the use of crescents even today on the tops of towers among the Muhammedans is derived. And in the same way they retain the solemnity of Venus, as the day of Friday is to them what the Sabbath is to the Jews and the Lord's Day to us. They call that day the day of the temple, and so, instead of naming the remaining days after the planets (a manner of speaking more unusual in Muslim usage), they name the second day after the feast, the third the market day, and the rest the days of rest. They say that Friday is preferred above all others, just as Mecca is among cities and Ramadan among months. They say that on that day the sun rose, Adam was created, placed in Paradise and expelled from it, that on that same day the day of judgment will come, and that Muhammed was born on the same day.

units.la: Orationes tenentur Muhammedani peragere in templo, in Melkitis suis, (templis rotundis, & aedificii quidem dem fumtuosi, at ornatus intus nulli: nullæ ibi imagines, sola Scriptura hinc inde La illah &c.) nisi quâ sontica causa, aut negotio prohibeantur, tum quovis loco eas absolvunt. Ad templa convocant eos non campanæ, quarum usum hactenus reprobarunt, sive ex strage, ejusque memoria apud eos infausta, quam in initiis regni sui aliquando passi à Christianis fuerint, ad sonum campanæ in illos irruentibus, sive quâ aliâ ex causâ, sed distinguentibus horas clepsammidiis, illasque indicantibus alto clamore & cantiunculâ de turrium fastigiis, (Cl. Golii Lexicon, pag. 59. 60.) religiosis, quos cum in finem habent, & Hoggios appellant: per quos ubi tempus precum est, horribili adeo clamore, ut aures ipsi suas digitis obturare cogantur, ad sacra sua & preces populus confluit. In templo, ubi non promiscuo ordine viri sedent cum mulieribus, sed discreto utrique loco, omnes Hoggium suum respiciunt & contuentur, ut ad ejus nutum se moveant, & vel genua flectant, vel se prosternant, capite in terram inclinato, eam quasi osculaturi, gemitibus, cantiunculis, & prostrationibus rem divinam sc. peragentes.
units.tr: The Muslims are required to perform their prayers in the temple, in their Melkites (round temples, large and costly buildings, but bare inside: no images there, only the Scripture, "La illah," etc., written here and there). They pray at any place only when they are prevented by some criminal charge or business. They are called to the temples not by bells, whose use they have so far rejected, either because of a massacre that they remember with dread, which they once suffered at the hands of Christians at the beginning of their kingdom when the Christians rushed upon them at the sound of a bell, or for some other reason. Instead, the hours are marked by water clocks, and they are announced by loud cries and little songs from the tops of the towers (Cl. Golius, Lexicon, pp. 59-60) by men set apart for this purpose, whom they call Hoggios. When it is time for prayer, the people flock to their rites and prayers at the sound of these criers, shouting so horribly that people are forced to stop their ears with their fingers. In the temple, where men do not sit mixed together with women but each in a separate place, all of them look to and watch their Hoggi, so that they move at his nod, either bending the knees or prostrating themselves, bowing the head to the ground as if to kiss it, performing their worship with groans, chants and prostrations.

units.la: Nullæ ibi audiuntur confabulationes, strepitus, neque quidem sputans aliquis, vel tussiens, (vel siquem natura ad hæc urgeat, tam tacite hæc peragit, ut nemo facile animadvertat) sed inter precandum vel cantandum corpus ita jactant, ut vertiginem sæpe patiantur & animi deliquium: tum continuâ repetitione sui La Illah &c. examinantur quandoque, & spumantes, ultimamque vix syllabam proferentes, in terram concidunt; quod supremum devotionis interpretantur apicem. Communissima illis precationis, quâ utuntur, formula, Elfata appellant, est hæc: In nomine misericordis Dei, Sit laus Deo in æternum, Regi seculorum supremo, propitiatori, & pio Regi judicii. Serviamus igitur illi, quia adjuvabimur. Dirige nos in viam O Deus, & in semitam eorum in quibus tibi complacuisti, & quibus non ira-
units.tr: No conversation, noise, or even spitting or coughing is heard there. (If nature forces anyone to these, he does it so quietly that no one easily notices.) But while praying or chanting they sway their bodies so violently that they often suffer dizziness and fainting. Then, through the continual repetition of "La illah," etc., some of them are sometimes thrown into a trance, and, foaming and barely uttering the last syllable, they collapse to the ground, which they interpret as the highest point of devotion. The most common formula of prayer they use, which they call the Elfata, is this: "In the name of the merciful God. Praise be to God forever, to the supreme King of the ages, the propitious one, and the pious King of judgment. Let us therefore serve him, because we shall be helped. Direct us, O God, into the way and the path of those with whom you have been pleased, and who have not provoked your anger, and who are never ashamed."

units.la: K irraserit, & nequaquam erubescunt. Apud Cotovicum, cap. v.
units.tr: Apud Cotovicum, cap. v.

units.la: In Iuramentis, si uspiam, profani sunt praeunte ipsos Muhammede in Alkorano, quin & ipsius ibidem Deo, qui passim jurat per creaturas non solum, sed & per figmenta, futilia, & vana quaeque. Surata lxi. & sequent: jurat Deus per ventos, per nubes aquosas; naves, Angelos, per montem Sina, librum Alkorani, per domum excelsissimam, per auroram, per noctes decem, per foeminas extrahentes & excavantes profundum, calamum, ficum, olivam, & plura ejusmodi, Surat. lxvi. lxxviii. xcv. xcvi. &c. alibi per Daemonem, Surat. lxxxvi. 1. Per alia jurare, quam per Deum religio est: & Deus, quia neminem se superiorem habet, non nisi per seipsum jurare legitur. Heb. vi. 13. Nullus autem per ea quae infra ipsum sunt jurabit, vel per inanimata, & irrationalia, nedum per ea quae sunt mala.
units.tr: In oaths, if anywhere, they are profane, following Muhammed himself in the Quran, and indeed God himself there, who swears everywhere not only by creatures but also by fictions, trifles and all kinds of vanities. Surat LXI and following: God swears by the winds, by watery clouds, ships, angels, by Mount Sinai, the book of the Quran, by the most high house, by the dawn, by ten nights, by the women who draw out and dig up the deep, by the pen, the fig, the olive, and many such things (Surat LXVI, LXXVIII, XCV, XCVI, etc.), and elsewhere by the devil (Surat LXXXVI, 1). To swear by anything other than God is contrary to religion, and God, since he has no one greater than himself, is read to swear only by himself (Heb. VI. 13). No one, moreover, will swear by things that are beneath him, or by inanimate and irrational things, much less by things that are evil.

units.la: In Ieiuniis, (in quibus, ut rebus externis, & quae devotionem apud homines prae se ferunt, multum vulgo religionis ponere solent, qui vera carent, ἄνευ ἐν λόγῳ μὲν ἔχοντα σοφίας ἀλλ' ἐπιλαθομένα ἐν πανυσφροσύνῃ ἐν ἀφειδίᾳ σώματος) religio Muslimica valde multa est. Integrum, & solemnem mensem habent decimum, quo toto interdiu jejunant; noctu passim helluantur. Appellant jejunium istud Ramadam, a nomine mensis, qui idcirco etiam mensis patientiae seu abstinentiae ipsis appellatur: quo se a cibo, potu, & venere cohibere jubentur, quum apud antiquiores Arabes crapulae & ebrietati dicatus fuerit. Praeter illud jejunium, habent & alia; sed illud est praecipuum, & strictissime observant, adeo quidem ut Iohannes de Laet, in Descript. Persiae referat, a Belga oculato rette se accepisse, quod viderit aliquando duos Muslimos, quod quo tempore jejunandum fuerat, se inebriassent, liquefacto in plumbo fuisse exactos. Quare sub Inspectoribus ribus & Censoribus publicis jejunia celebrantur, ut si quis peccet honestioris notæ, multâ pecuniariâ, alii corpore luant. De nocte, neque prius jejunium solvunt, (quod etiam Iudæi observant) quam stellam in cœlo viderint, vulgare satis ingurgitare se, eamque omni luxuria, comessationibus, tripudiis transigere, vel in ædibus propriis, vel tabernis, quas accensa lumina præmonstrant. Surata de vacca: licet vobis nocte jejunii accedere ad uxores vestras: ipse sunt indumentum vobis, & vos indumentum ipsis; voluit Deus quod vos fraudetis vosmetipsos, & clementer agit vobiscum, & parcit vobis. Igitur commiscemini cum eis, & inquirite quod prascripsit vobis Deus, & comedite & bibite usquedum distinguere possitis filum album à filo nigro ex illucescente aurora. Deinceps complete jejunium usque ad noctem: & ne commisceamini cum eis; sed persistite in templis. Hæc sunt præscripta Dei: non igitur tangatis eas. Quin nec vino, aliás sibi interdicto, tum parci, Auctor Descriptionis Turciæ pag. 53. testatur: aliter tamen Gabriel Sionita Arab. pag. 71. seu cap. xv. (qui & in Descriptione Arabiæ extat, & post Geographum Nubiensem). Forte, utcunque contra legem ipsorum sit, gustare vinum, tamen quando ista nocte se dant omni luxui, contra præceptum, & non ita palam, vino etiam indulgent: quod alias quoque illos avidè imbibere, quando furtim & clam possunt, novimus. Quo pacto sententiæ illæ conciliari possunt. Quale jam post illa sequatur jejunium diurnum, quivis colligat. Pontificii Scriptores quando de eo loquuntur, conferunt cum suâ Quadragesimâ, nempe vivendi more, quum alias illud trigesima tantum sit; unius scilicet mensis, & pro ratione anni lunaris non eodem quotannis recurrente tempore. Dum jejunant, preces recitant multas, & solito prolixiores: eleemosynas præbent copiosas, quas apud Turcas nemo palam poscit, sed egenis extra templum in area sedentibus ultra erogantur: namque, ut scribit Cotovicus, orationem & eleemosynas existimant esse jejunii quasdam quasi alas.
units.tr: In fasts (in which the common people are accustomed to place much of religion, as in external things that display devotion before men, though they lack the truth: "having indeed wisdom in word, but forgetting, in carelessness and neglect of the body" [ἄνευ ἐν λόγῳ μὲν ἔχοντα σοφίας ἀλλ' ἐπιλαθομένα ἐν πανυσφροσύνῃ ἐν ἀφειδίᾳ σώματος]), the Muslim religion is very elaborate. They keep a whole and solemn tenth month, during which they fast all day, and at night they gorge themselves in every place. They call this fast Ramadan, from the name of the month, which for this reason is also called the month of patience or abstinence, in which they are ordered to abstain from food, drink and sex, though among the older Arabs it was devoted to drunkenness and carousing. Apart from this fast they have others, but this is the principal one, and they observe it most strictly. So much so that Johannes de Laet, in his Descript. Persiae, reports that he had received from a sharp-eyed Fleming that he once saw two Muslims who, during the time they were to fast, had become drunk, and were punished by having molten lead poured into them. Therefore the fasts are celebrated under public overseers and censors, so that if anyone of more honourable standing sins, he pays with a fine, and others pay with their bodies. At night, before they break the fast (which the Jews also observe), until they see a star in the sky, they eat their fill, and spend the night in every luxury, feasting and dancing, either in their own homes or in taverns, which lamps lit in front of them point out. Sura of the Cow: "It is lawful for you to go to your wives on the night of the fast. They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. God knew that you were deceiving yourselves, and he has been merciful to you and pardoned you. So now lie with them, and seek what God has prescribed for you, and eat and drink until you can distinguish a white thread from a black thread by the dawning light. Then complete the fast until night; and do not lie with them, but remain in the temples. These are the commandments of God; do not therefore approach them." Nor does the author of the Description of Turkey (p. 53) testify that wine, otherwise forbidden to them, is spared at this time. Gabriel Sionita, however (Arab., p. 71, or chap. xv, which is found in the Description of Arabia and after the Nubian geographer), says otherwise. Perhaps, however much it is against their law to taste wine, when they give themselves over to all luxury on that night, against the command and not so openly, they also indulge in wine. We know that they also drink it greedily at other times when they can do so secretly and privately. How these statements can be reconciled, I leave to others. Anyone can then infer what the daytime fast that follows is like. When the Papist writers speak of it, they compare it with their own Lent, namely in the manner of living, although theirs lasts only thirty days, that is, one month, and does not always fall at the same time each year, according to the lunar year. While they fast, they recite many prayers, longer than usual; they give generous alms, which no one among the Turks begs for openly, but which are distributed more liberally to the needy sitting outside the temple in the courtyard. For, as Cotovicus writes, they consider prayer and alms to be, as it were, the wings of fasting.

units.la: Absoluto solemni jejunio Ramadam, festum quasi Paschale celebrant, per triduum; quod appellant festum magnum, Vlubairam, in memoriam missi scilicet de coelo Alkorani, quando magna copia mactant verveces, atque egregie iterum epulantur, dicunt, in memoriam arietis, qui Abrahamo filium mactaturo ἀντὶ μηχανῆς oblatus; illosque verveces Paradysum etiam ingressuros, & pro dominis suis in die judicii intercessuros, fabulantur. Inde sexagesimo ab hoc festo die, agunt festum minus, quod Religiosorum appellant, peregrinantium ad sepulchrum Meccanum.
units.tr: When the solemn fast of Ramadan is over, they celebrate a feast almost like Easter, for three days, which they call the great feast, Vlubairam, in memory, that is, of the sending of the Quran from heaven. On it they slaughter a great number of sheep and feast again splendidly. They say this is in memory of the ram offered to Abraham, who was about to sacrifice his son, instead of a machine [ἀντὶ μηχανῆς]. They also tell fables that those sheep will enter Paradise and intercede for their masters on the day of judgment. Then, sixty days after this feast, they celebrate a lesser feast, which they call of the Religious, for those who make a pilgrimage to the sepulchre at Mecca.

units.la: Muhammed enim, quo cultum sui augeret apud homines, mandavit peregrinationes ad sepulchrum suum suscipi. In quo primum vanus fuit, quod non alter illas in honorem ejus instituit, sed ipse. Saltem ut semel quivis in vita peregrinationem ejusmodi obeat, & laute celebret, edixit. Surat. II. pecunias vestras propter Deum in peregrinationibus expendite, non desperantes: nec revertamini, nisi primum peractis omnibus, pro facultate vestra, peregrinationi convenientibus, nisi metus a loco prohibeat. Surat. LVII. Et quo magis hominibus Meccanam illam peregrinationem suaderent, commenti sunt, templum Meccanum ab Angelis aedificatum; primum eo peregrinationem instituisse Adamum ipsum; Noachum cum arca septies Meccam circumnavigasse, quae ne tandem ab aquis absorberetur, in sextum coelum fuerit subvecta. Denique ad typum ejus Abrahamo ostensum, atque ab eo primum fundatum templum, Meccam extructam. Surat. II. versus Meccam, temploque medium, quod Abraham primo fundavit. Fanum istud Meccanum hodie est sumtuosissimum, in quod opes Orientis confertim adducuntur, & immensis donariis, auro, argento, serico, & quantivis pretii rebus certatim locupletatur. In templo Meccano est lapis niger, Veneri olim sacer, de quo supra diximus, quem peregrinantes effusissime venerantur. Etiam puteus ibidem, ex quo aquam accipiunt, & secum auferunt quam sacro sanctam opinantur, & sub pedibus Ismaelis enatam ajunt, quando siti pressus ad matrem clamaret, quae visum fontem appellavit Zam Zam, quomodo & hodie eum adhuc nominant, quod est, sta: ste gradum.
units.tr: For Muhammed, in order to increase the worship of himself among men, commanded that pilgrimages be undertaken to his tomb. In this he was vain, because he did not establish them in honour of anyone else, but himself. At least he ordered that everyone should make such a pilgrimage once in his life and celebrate it lavishly. Surat II: "Spend your money for God on pilgrimages, not despairing; and do not return until you have first completed everything fitting for the pilgrimage, according to your means, unless fear of the place prevents you." Surat LVII. And to persuade people all the more to that pilgrimage to Mecca, they invented that the temple at Mecca was built by angels; that Adam himself first instituted the pilgrimage there; that Noah with his ark circled Mecca seven times, and that, lest it should at last be swallowed up by the waters, it was carried up into the sixth heaven; and finally that the temple was shown to Abraham as a type of it, and that Mecca was built around the temple first founded by him. Surat II: "Towards Mecca, and to the middle temple, which Abraham first founded." That shrine at Mecca is today most sumptuous, and the riches of the East are brought into it in a continuous stream, and it is enriched eagerly with immense gifts of gold, silver, silk, and things of every price. In the temple at Mecca there is a black stone, once sacred to Venus, of which we have spoken above, which the pilgrims venerate most profusely. There is also a well there, from which they take water, and carry away with them what they consider sacred. They say it sprang up beneath the feet of Ishmael, when, pressed by thirst, he cried out to his mother, who called the spring that she saw Zam Zam, which is what they still call it today, that is, stop, stand still [sta: ste gradum].

units.la: Jam quod ad res matrimonii, apud Muhammedanos, duo imprimis reprehendimus ista, polygamiam, & repudiandi temeritatem. Indulget suis tot uxores Muhammed, quot alere, & in ordinem redigere possunt: Surat. VIII. Quotcunque placuerit, duas scilicet, aut tres vel quatuor uxores ducite, si timueritis eas pacifi care posse. Tunc enim vel unam, vel pro manus castigare poteris, ducatis. Nempe verberibus compescendas docet. Surat. IX. Quin viros mulieribus praesse Deo visum, ipsi corrigant illas, ipso quibus pecuniam suam expenderint, ipsaque Deum invocent, & maritis pareant, eorumque secreta sibi commissa ut celent, jus aequum postulat. Quae si forte praecepta non observaverint, a vobis corrected & castigata, in domibus lectisve detenta verberentur, usque quo vestris mandatis & praeceptis pareant. Haec constituit, non adeo quod sibi proba viderentur, quam quod, quum ipse hic cum mulieribus suis vixerit, legibus ad eam rem editis tum sua pallidare facinora, tum factorum suorum probatos quasi imitatores habere, hoc pacto allaboravit. Quippe ipse solus undecim fovit uxores, & quod singulis debitum una nocte redderet facillime, etiam gloriabatur impurissimus nebulo. Sultan Amyrath, praeter pelliceis, quarum magnus erat numerus, uxores aluit septuaginta duas: plurimas quippe habent semper Sultani. Licentiam quoque verberandarum uxorum, exproprio suo dedit impostor exemplo: nam quum aliquando durius excepisset mulierum suarum aliquam, & caeteras indignarentur, ipse tum legis patrocinio usus fuit, tum tali
units.tr: As for marriage among the Muhammadans, we chiefly object to two things: polygamy and the reckless ease of divorce. Muhammad allowed his followers as many wives as they could support and keep in order. Surat. VIII. "Take as many wives as you please, two, three or four, if you think you can treat them fairly. But if you cannot, then take only one, or whomever your hand may chastise." Indeed he teaches that wives are to be restrained with blows. Surat. IX. "Since God has judged men to be over women, let men correct them, with what they spend of their own property. Let the women invoke God, obey their husbands, and keep their secrets, as equity demands. If they fail to observe these precepts, let them be corrected and chastised by you, confined in their houses or beds, and beaten, until they obey your commands and precepts." He laid down these rules not so much because they seemed right to him, but because he himself lived here with his women, and by enacting laws for this purpose he tried both to cover up his own crimes and to have approved imitators of his deeds. Indeed he alone kept eleven wives, and that most impure rogue even boasted that he could render the conjugal debt to each of them in a single night. Sultan Amurath, besides concubines, of whom he had a great number, kept seventy-two wives, for sultans always have very many. The impostor also gave a license to beat wives by his own example. When once he had treated one of his women more harshly and the others were indignant, he relied both on the protection of the law and on this distinction: that he had beaten her not as his wife but because she was a detestable old woman. Moreover, so that no woman, or so great a number of them, might be an obstacle to him, if they could not be brought into line even by blows, he established divorce, again starting from his own deed: after he had seized and violated the wife of Zaid, he protected the divorce he had made by another law. Surata lxxv i. "Why, Prophet, do you forbid for yourself the love of your wives? God is pious and bountiful in pardon, Lord of all, wise and incomprehensible; he has granted you to undo your oaths." Sur. iii. "Women divorced by their husbands shall not marry anyone else until four months have first passed; it is good for them to be taken back by their husbands if the husbands wish it. But if not, God hears and sees. Widows shall not marry until they have first been purified for three months. Let them not deny their husbands intercourse (fear God) whenever it pleases them, for it is the head of women. A woman repudiated a second time may marry another; but a woman repudiated a third time may not marry again except to that husband who first put her away. Then, if both are willing, they may be reconciled to their former husbands, or else be honourably dismissed without compulsion. It is wicked and dishonourable to take back anything once given to them. If a woman prepares to flee against her husband's will, let her be recovered by him, but not out of anger or hatred, lest they incur the divine wrath." Surat. lxxv. "Why do you, Prophet, divorce your wives before the appointed and known term is complete? Fearing God, do not cast them out of their houses, nor let them leave unless they have committed some manifest evil." Sur. viii. "When they no longer please you, it is lawful to exchange them."

units.la: {K 3} signature of the gathering at the foot of the page. tali distinctione, quod illam verberasset, non quatenus uxor ejus, sed quod execranda esset vetula. Ac porro ne cui aut mulierum forte aliqua, aut ille tantus numerus obesset, tum si neque verberibus in ordinem cogi possent, repudia constituit: iterum ex suo primum facto, ut rapta & stuprata à se servi Zaidis uxore, divortium quod hic fecerat, lege alia communiret. Surata lxxv i. Cur tu Propheta illicitum statuis tuarum mulierum amorem? Deus pius & venia largitor, omnium Dominus, sapiens, & incomprehensibilis, tibi juramenta delere concessit. Sur. iii. Mulieres à maritis relictae, nemini nisi prius peractis quatuor mensibus nubant, quas maritis volentibus remubere bonum est. Sin autem, Deus audit & videt. Non nubant etiam aliquae relictae, nisi prius emundatae tribus mensibus. Ne negent maritis coitum (timete Deum), ubi illis placuerit, est enim capita mulierum. Secunda vice repudiata potest nubere, ut alia; verum tertia vice repudiata non potest nubere nisi ei marito, qui eam prius rejecit. Tunc autem ipsae volentes, prioribus maritis ante bene reconciliantur, aut vero non coacte honeste dimittantur. Aliquid primo datum illis auferre, nefas & inhonestum est. Mulier ad fugam se praeparans invito marito, recuperetur ab eo, sed non ex ira vel odio, ne iram divinam incurrant. Surat. lxxv. Cur tu Prophetas mulieribus repudium faceris, ante terminum completum & notum, Deum timens, nec a domibus suis illas ejicias, nec ipsae nisi propter res manifeste malas exeant. Sur. viii. Quando illae non amplius tibi placent, commutare eas licet.
units.tr: {K 3} signature of the gathering at the foot of the page. By such a distinction: he had beaten her not as his wife but because she was a detestable old woman. Moreover, lest any of his women, or that great number, should prove a hindrance to him, and if they could not be brought into line by blows, he instituted divorce. He did this first from his own conduct, since after he had seized and violated the wife of his servant Zaid, he sought to protect the divorce that this man had made by another law. Sura lxxv i. Why do you, Prophet, forbid yourself the love of your wives? God is merciful and forgiving, the Lord of all, wise and incomprehensible; he has allowed you to dissolve your oaths. Sura iii. Women divorced by their husbands shall not marry anyone else until four months have passed; if the husbands are willing, it is good for them to take them back. But if not, God hears and sees. Divorced women shall also not marry until they have been cleansed by three months. Let them not refuse their husbands intercourse (fear God) whenever the husbands wish, for women are their field. A woman divorced a second time may marry another; but a woman divorced a third time may not marry anyone except the husband who first put her away. Then, if they themselves are willing, they are fittingly reconciled to their former husbands; otherwise they are honorably dismissed. It is wrong and dishonorable to take back what has been given to them at first. A woman who prepares to flee, against her husband's will, shall be taken back by him, but not out of anger or hatred, lest they incur the wrath of God. Sura lxxv. Why do you, Prophet, divorce women before the appointed and known term is complete? Fear God; do not drive them from their houses, nor let them go out unless they have committed some manifest wrong. Sura viii. When they no longer please you, you may exchange them.

units.la: In cibo & potu, religione abstinent Muhammedani à carne porcina, sanguine, suffocato, denique & vino. Sutata, de mensa, in initio: prohibita sunt vobis morticinium, & sanguis, & caro porcina, & quod idolo sacrificatum est, & suffocatum & combustum, & projectitium, & cornu percussum, & à bestiis occisum. Item Surat. xvi. cap. de animalibus. Dic, non invenio in eo, quod mihi revelatum, esse prohibitum ut comedatur, nisi mor-
units.tr: In food and drink, the Muhammadans abstain from religious motives from pork, blood, what has been strangled, and finally from wine. Sutata, at the table, at the beginning: "Forbidden to you are carrion, and blood, and pork, and what has been sacrificed to an idol, and what has been strangled, and burned, and killed by a fall, and gored by a horn, and killed by beasts." Likewise Surat. xvi., chapter on animals: "Say: I find nothing in what has been revealed to me forbidden to be eaten, except carrion

units.la: tinii. sicinum, aut sanguis effusus, aut caro porci, aut immolatum Idolis. In casu necessitatis connivent, si quis ista comederit, protinusque egerit poenitentiam. Surat. xxvi. Deus quidem nihil fecit illicitum ad victum nostrum, nisi morticinum, & sanguinem, carnemque porcinam, & animal non Dei nomine declamatum. Inde tamen necessitate coactē sumenti, Deus veniam dat: & similiter id facienti nescienter, & postea paenitenti, ac bona facienti opera. In colloquio cum Abdia Iudaeo interrogatus Muhammed, quem cibum comederent coelites in Paradiso, nam in Muhammedico editur ac bibitur pancratice: respondit, quosfibet illis epulandi cibos, quibus delectantur, exceptis istis interdictis, & praecipue porcina. Porcinam vero quam ob causam tam severe detestetur, suasque prohibeat, idem rogatus a Iudaeo, putidissimum dedit responsum: nempe Iesum aliquando rogatum a discipulis, ut ipsis exponeret rationem arcae Noachi, & quomodo in ea vixerint homines cum animalibus, (de qua eadem quaestione sollicitus Iesuita Cornelius illam in exorcismo inter alia a Daemone explicandam proposuerat, quomodo potuerint animalia in arca Noë? sed hoc obiter) accepto homine, eum in sortem aliquam factum proiecisse interram; iussum per nomen Patris resurgere, unde statim surrexit homo ieanus, Iapherus, Noë filius, qui vitae sine cantus, & num tali cantic obrissēt, interrogatus, affirmavit se nequaquam tali vultu mortuum, sed prae metu judicii, ad quod se iam vocari & surgere putabat, adeo incanuisse; qui ergo iussus historiam arcae pandere, sic retulit inter alia. Arcam aliquando pondere & copia fimenti ab aliquo tabulati latere coepisse inclinare, qua re perculsus pater Noach, Deo consulto, elephantem eo loci adhibuit, qui locum tergo sustineret, sicut quamvis humanum suum humano insisteret, ex ea ita commixto natam suam grandem. Annon ergo causae satis, prohibendi bocce ani
units.tr: or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, or what has been offered to idols. In cases of necessity they overlook it if anyone eats these things, provided he then repents at once. Sura XXVI: God has indeed made nothing unlawful for our food except carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and an animal not declared in God's name. Yet God grants pardon to one who eats of these under compulsion of necessity, and likewise to one who does so unknowingly and afterwards repents and does good works. In a conversation with the Jew Abdias, Muhammed was asked what food the inhabitants of heaven eat in Paradise, for in the Muhammedan paradise people eat and drink without restraint. He replied that they may eat whatever foods they enjoy, except those prohibited, and especially pork. When the Jew asked why he so severely detested the pig and forbade it, he gave a most foul answer: Jesus was once asked by his disciples to explain the ark of Noah and how men lived in it with the animals. (On this same question, the Jesuit Cornelius, in his exorcism, had proposed that the demon should explain, among other things, how the animals could fit into Noah's ark; but this is a digression.) Jesus took a man, cast him into the earth as if into a lot, and bade him rise in the name of the Father. At once the man rose, Japhet, son of Noah, who was asked why his hair had turned grey so young. He declared that he had not gone grey from such a cause, but from fear of the judgment, to which he now thought himself summoned and raised. Then, ordered to relate the story of the ark, he told among other things that the ark once began to tilt to one side because of the weight and mass of dung. Noah, alarmed, consulted God, and at God's bidding brought in an elephant to stand at that spot and hold up the side with its back; by this the pig and the elephant mingled, and from them came the great...

units.la: Note: the scanned text is partly illegible; the transcription above is a best reading of the printed Latin. animal ut immundum, Abdia? inquit Muhammed: cui ille, certè satis. Bergit, & iucm jam iterum stercora commovisse, perque universam arcam ista foetide projecisse, refert; unde navis mus sit. Hic vero quia arcam continuò roderet, periculumque hinc non exiguum omnibus crearetur, consulto à Noacho iterum Deo Noach Leoni frontem concutit, qui concitatus, naribus suis felem evomit &c. futiliora enim sunt, quam ut haec diutius prosequamur. Atque ita scilicet in arcâ se continuisse homines, animaliaque narrat, isthoc dialogo Muhammed: & causam prohibitae inter alia porcinae, neque absimilem de prohibito vino, addit. Nempe, fuisse aliquando binos Angelos, Arot & Marot à Deo hunc in mundum missos, ut docerent homines potissimum tria, ne quem occiderent, ne injuste judicarent, ne etiam vinum biberent. Quos, ubi diu se probè habuissent, judicumque munere ritè functos, mulier aliqua formosissima, litem apud illos quandam contestata, quo saventiores experiretur, ad prandium invitat, ibique lautè exceptis hospitibus, etiam vino tandem inebriat, qui inde exardescentes in mulieris formam, congressam optant, quem haec concedit quidem, sed stipulatur, ut prius exponerent sibi alter quo pacto, quibusque verbis semper de coelo descenderet, quibus vero alter adscenderet, quod edocta, atque experiens, confestim ipsa evolavit in coelum. Hoc ubi conspexit Deus, rei insolitae causam indagatus, illam quidem foeminam statim commutavit in Luciferum, ut quae inter mulieres in mundo, eadem inter stellas esset formosissima; sed Angelis iis duobus optionem dedit poenae, quam eligerent, jam vel in altero saeculo quumque nunc puniri praetulissent, pendüli per catenas ferreas demissis capitibus in puteo Babil tenentur usque in diem judicii: Et haec, inquit Muhammed, causa quid ni sufficiens satis probibendi vinum? Quis autem magis anilia, vel puerilia confin-gat. gat, aut proponati Surata. xiii. Vini boni, vinum, & aleas, & fcachos, cum non sint res licitae, sed Diaboli machinas, per quas inter homines inimicitias & abhorritiones (versio Reuinensis) injicere, & eos ab orationibus & invocatione Dei retrahere maximè nititur, praetermittite. Dimittetis igitur, annos? sed Dei mandatum sequentes, Legatoque suo parentes, vobis cavete. Ludum latrunculorum putat, etiam apud nos vulgò in usu. Schach, Arabicè Regem significat, atque tale genus ludi est; ut in capite Regis totâ ejus ratio sita sit, proindeque ejus nomen Arabicum apud nos retentum, monet originis suae, Auctoresque, à quibus illud sumtum. Ludum hunc, cum aleis, vinoque, prohibet Muhammed, ut multarum rixarum, malorumque causas. Surata iii. Scilicet nonnullis demino, schachis, talis, aleis & hujusmodi, dici, peccatum maximum esse hujusmodi potum & ludum: licet autem dulcedinem hominibus, & utilitatem adferant hae peccatorum materies, peccata tamen nacta sunt. E contrario alibi concedit fructum uvarum, cap. de ape, ubi de potu vario, & ex fructibus palmarum, & uvarum inebriamini, & sacramenti, seu potum seu cibum sumatis.
units.tr: Is that not reason enough, Abdias, for regarding this animal as unclean? said Muhammed. To which the Jew replied, "Certainly enough." He goes on to report that the pig again stirred up the dung and scattered this foul filth through the whole ark, and from this the ship's mouse arose. Since the mouse kept gnawing at the ark and no small danger arose from this for everyone, Noah again consulted God, and at God's command the lion shook its forehead, and the cat was roused and vomited from its nostrils... But these tales are too trivial to pursue further. In this same dialogue Muhammed says that men and animals were kept in the ark in this way, and he adds, among other reasons, the cause of the forbidden wine, which is not unlike that of the pig. There were once two angels, Harut and Marut, sent by God into this world to teach men three things especially: not to kill anyone, not to judge unjustly, and not to drink wine. When they had behaved well for a long time and had discharged their duties as judges properly, a very beautiful woman, who was pleading a suit before them, wanting to test which of them was the more gentle, invited them to dinner. There she entertained them lavishly, and at last made them drunk with wine. Inflamed by this, they desired her as she was, and she consented, but on condition that first each should explain to her by what words he always descended from heaven and by what words he ascended. Having learned this, she immediately flew up to heaven. When God saw this unusual thing, he inquired into the cause, and at once changed that woman into Lucifer, so that she who was the most beautiful of women in the world should be the most beautiful of the stars. But he gave the two angels a choice of punishment: either to be punished now or in the next age. They chose to be punished now, and they are hung head downwards by iron chains in the well of Babylon until the day of judgment. "And this," says Muhammed, "is surely a sufficient reason for forbidding wine." Who could invent anything more silly or childish? Compare Sura V: Wine, gambling, dice and chess are not lawful things but devices of the Devil, by which he strives especially to stir up enmity and hatred among men and to draw them away from prayer and the invocation of God. Will you therefore abstain? Obey God and his messenger, and beware. He thinks chess is a game of draughts, which is also commonly played among us. Schach means "king" in Arabic, and it is a game in which the whole strategy depends on the king's head; so the Arabic name, retained among us, shows its origin and the authors from whom it was taken. Muhammed forbids this game, together with dice and wine, as the cause of many quarrels and evils. Sura III: Indeed, to say that wine, gambling, dice and such games are the greatest sin is to say the truth; these matters bring pleasure and some profit to men, but their sin is greater than their use. On the other hand, he elsewhere permits the fruit of the grape, in the chapter on the bee, where he says that you may become drunk on various drinks, from the fruits of palms and grapes, and that you may take them as drink or as food.

units.la: Atqui vinum pollicetur longè optimum in suo Paradyso. Surat. lv. & alibi saepius. Neque vino adeò, quam quidem nullâ abstinent: in vinum, vel quando se liberius ingurgitant, vel eum pro praedâ accipiunt, sumtibusve aliorum, ardentiores. Usitatissimus apud illos ac sapidissimus cibus oryza est, quâ terra illorum abundat, iterumque de eâ fabulantur, quo scilicet ejus saporis originem quoque religiosam faciant, eam natam ex sudore Mahammedis, quem antequam orbi manifestaretur, thronum Dei in Paradyso circumiens, propiusque accedens, & à Deo retrospiciente conspectus, prae timore effuderit: fundebat autem (ut haec recte scias) sex guttas, ex quarum unâ rosa, ex alterâ oryza, ex reliquis quatuor, totidem Muhammedis socii primique Chalifae successores nati fuerint.
units.tr: Indeed, he promises that wine will be by far the best in his Paradise. Sura 55, and elsewhere quite often. They do not abstain from wine altogether, but they drink more heavily when they can do so freely, or they seek it as spoil or at the expense of others. Their most common and most savoury food is rice, of which their land has plenty. They also tell a story about it, to give even its flavour a religious origin: that it sprang from the sweat of Muhammad. Before he was made known to the world, he was walking around the throne of God in Paradise and came closer, and, seen by God as he looked back, he poured it out in fear. He shed six drops (so that you may understand these things correctly), from one of which came the rose, from another the rice, and from the remaining four as many companions of Muhammad and his first successors as caliphs.

units.la: Habet Muslimorum disciplina Religiosos, & Monachos, qui quoque nobis obiter considerandi. Praesit Sacris omnibus, eamque rebus, quam personis, Musti, quem appellant, eique instar Sacerdotis maximi. Hic ipsi Sultano venerationi est, & in summis imperii consiliis adhibetur, absque cujus consilio nihil votum, praesertim in rebus Ecclesiasticis, & religionem quae concernunt, cujus summum est suffragium. Ad quatuor Vezirios, qui intimi & supremi Imperatoris sunt consiliarii, ille accedit quantus, & quid ex doctrina Muhammedica tenendum aut sequendum sit, absque controversia, edisserit.
units.tr: The Muslim system also has religious men and monks, whom we should consider in passing. The Mufti, as they call him, presides over all sacred matters, and over things more than over persons, and he is like their chief priest. He is held in reverence by the Sultan himself and is admitted to the highest councils of the empire, without whose advice nothing is decided, especially in ecclesiastical affairs and matters of religion, in which his judgment is decisive. He goes to the four Vizirs, who are the closest and highest counsellors of the Emperor, and sets out without dispute what is to be believed or followed from Muhammadan doctrine.

units.la: Sub illo proximi sunt, quos appellant Cadileschers, auxilium & consilium suo Musti ferentes, ad instar vel Cardinalium, vel Patriarcharum, quibus singulae attributae provinciae, quarum negotiis Ecclesiasticis occupantur. Unus Romania, vel Europa, Natolia, aut Asia minor alteri; denique (tum tres numero sunt) alius ea, quae in regno Sultanico, Ecclesiastica curat & prospicit. Atque ii sub se habent Cadios, Seriphos, Santones, Hoggios, Talismannos, Dervisios, qui Clerus inferior concionibus, precationibus, & templis intendit, levioraque curat judicia, & lites.
units.tr: Next to him are those whom they call Cadileschers, who give help and counsel to their Mufti, much like cardinals or patriarchs. Each is assigned a province whose ecclesiastical affairs they manage: one for Romania or Europe, another for Natolia or Asia Minor, and finally a third (for there are three) for what concerns and provides for ecclesiastical matters in the Sultan's kingdom. Under them are the Cadis, Seriphs, Santons, Hoggias, Talismans and Dervishes, who make up the lower clergy, attend to sermons, prayers and mosques, and deal with minor judgments and disputes.

units.la: Sed praeter illos varii sunt, qui vota faciunt quasi Monachi. Alii nudi incedunt, obvelatis duntaxat pudendis; alii cibi abstinentiam vovent, egestatem, perpetuum silentium, vitam eremiticam, & solitariam alii. Sunt qui ex peculiari religionis vel superstitionis voto mendicitatem profitentur, qui hospites ac peregrinos suis domibus excipiunt, qui aquam recentem gelidamque in urbem gratis importando & distribuendo se [illegible, ~3 letters]. Praecipui sunt tres ordines, qui nihil proprii possident, & nudi incedunt, quique aliquando devorata herba mistlach in rabiem aguntur, & sibi per totum pectus, item per brachium &c. volitea infigunt. Deinde alii incedunt verpa virilis membri pertusa, cui annulum aeneum [?] librarum ponderis appendunt, quo à coitu secludantur. Tertii rarissimè egrediuntur, sed μονάζοντες in templis, & in eorum angulis, tuguriola sua inhabitant, jejunio atque orationibus continuò vacant, unde divinas (imò diabolicas) revelationes illos accipere creditum: tantæque vulgo sunt æstimationis, ut illos Turcarum Rex moturus bellum primò consulere solcat. Sunt quoque apud illos, quos appellant Nefesogli, tantæ scilicet sanctitatis viri Monachi, ut credant eos sine virili semine natos de quibus vide potissimum Auctorem anonymum Septem-Castrensem, de moribus & religione Turcarum cap. XIV. & XV. qui judicat illud fieri per diabolicum congressum, incubum quem vocant; potest tamen esse, inquit, quod ipsæ matres talium, sint uxores religiosorum, & propter prodigium continentiæ eorum, nascantur eis filii modo non naturali: sed modo alio diabolicæ dispensationis, hominibus occulto. Temere. Unde, addit, propter hoc ipsis Turcis non videtur insolitum, quando Christiani dicunt, imò ipsimet dicunt, & confitentur, Christum ex Maria conceptum & natum sine hominis semine. De Religiosis istis Muslimis vide passim Scriptores rerum Arabicarum, & Turcicarum; atque lib. I. II. III. historiæ Turcicæ Michaelem Baudier, Gallicè. & Hospinianum, lib. I. de Monachis, cap. ult.
units.tr: Besides these there are various people who take vows in the manner of monks. Some go about naked, covering only their private parts; others vow abstinence from food, poverty, perpetual silence, or an eremitic and solitary life. Some profess mendicancy by a special vow of religion or superstition, and they receive guests and strangers into their houses, and bring fresh cold water into the city free of charge and distribute it, and [illegible, ~3 letters]. The chief groups are three orders, who own nothing of their own, go about naked, and sometimes, after eating the herb mistlach, are driven into a frenzy, and pierce their chests, and also their arms, with iron skewers. Others go about with the male member pierced and hang a bronze ring of [?] pounds weight from it, so that they are kept from intercourse. A third group seldom goes out, but lives in cells in the corners of the mosques, constantly given over to fasting and prayers; from these they were believed to receive divine (or rather diabolical) revelations. They are held in such esteem by the common people that the Turkish King, when about to go to war, customarily consults them first. Among them are also those whom they call Nefesogli, monks of such sanctity that they believe them to have been born without male seed. On these see especially the anonymous author from Septem-Castrum, On the Customs and Religion of the Turks, chapters 14 and 15, who judges that this happens through a diabolical intercourse which they call the incubus; yet it may be, he says, that the mothers of such men are the wives of religious men, and because of the marvel of their continence, sons are born to them in a non-natural way, but by another mode of diabolical arrangement hidden from men. Rashly. Hence, he adds, for this reason it does not seem unusual to the Turks themselves when Christians say, indeed they themselves say and confess, that Christ was conceived of Mary and born without man's seed. On these Muslim religious men see throughout the writers on Arabic and Turkish affairs, and Michel Baudier in French, books I, II and III of the Turkish History, and Hospinian, On the Monks, book I, last chapter.

units.la: Ultimo loco cum Muhammedanis agendum de rerum novissimis, judicio, paradyso, inferno. Super quibus tandem etiam illorum sententias audiamus. Primo autem locum aliquem inter medium somniant inter Paradysum & infernum. Surat. XLVI. Inter hos quidem & illos, scilicet Paradysi infernique incolas, in quodam quasi limite sublimi stabunt quidam, discrete scientes horum & illorum faciem, qui nequaquam paradysum ingredientes, sed illud sperando exspectantes in Paradyso visis inquiunt: salvet vos Deus. Vide Alkoranum Gallicè versum de Ryer, pag. 165. In Colloquio Muhammedis cum Abdia Judæo, introducuntur homines in judicii diem eorum primo parente Adamo graviter expostulanlantes, quod eos in miserum istum statum præcipitarit, ideoque ipsum implorant, ut apud Deum intercedat, quo saltem ipsis concedatur locus ille inter Paradysum, atque infernum intermedius. Etiamque preces pro defunctis faciunt Muhammedani: & pro Adamo quidem dicunt filium ejus Seth, una scilicet cum Angelo Gabriele, dixisse preces nonaginta quinque; quum pro demortuo solent modò fundi quinque: at Adamus peculiare quid habuit, puta quinque preces pro eo dictæ sunt, ut hominie, insuper nonaginta, quia reliquorum hominum erat pater. Quodque ridiculum, eo nugacissimæ superstitionis veniunt, ut felibus canibusque stipem elargiantur, assatas & quasque delicatissimas carnes iis præbeant, & aves captas è cavea in libertatem emittant, hac opinione, ut defunctorum animabus hoc pacto scilicet suffragentur & succurrant. Eaque est ratio, quod tam anxiè solliciti sint Muhammedani moriturí, ne discedant hinc nisi solutis omnibus debitis, quod quando vel non possunt, vel nolunt, studient tamen quâ arte vel vi syngraphæ solutionis à Creditoribus nancisci, putantes hoc animam expiari, & culpam quasi obduci, secus graviter post luendam.
units.tr: Last, with the Muhammadans we must deal with the last things, judgement, paradise and hell. On these let us also hear their opinions at last. First, they imagine some place in between Paradise and hell. Sura 46: Between these and those, that is, between the inhabitants of Paradise and hell, there will stand on a kind of high ridge some people who discern the faces of both, who by no means enter Paradise, but waiting for it with hope, say to those in Paradise: God keep you. See the Koran translated into French by de Ryer, p. 165. In the Colloquy of Muhammad with the Jew Abdias, men are introduced on the day of judgement sharply reproaching their first parent Adam, because he plunged them into this wretched state, and so they beg him to intercede with God, so that at least this middle place between Paradise and hell may be granted to them. The Muhammadans also make prayers for the dead; and for Adam they say that his son Seth, together with the angel Gabriel, said ninety-five prayers, whereas for a dead person they usually pour out only five. But Adam had something special: five prayers were said for him as for a man, and ninety more because he was the father of all the rest of mankind. And, what is ridiculous, they go to such lengths of the most trifling superstition that they hand out alms to cats and dogs, offer them roasted and the most delicate meats, and release caged birds into freedom, with the belief that in this way they help and support the souls of the dead. This is also the reason why Muhammadans who are dying are so anxious not to depart hence unless all their debts have been paid; and when they cannot or will not do this, they nevertheless strive by whatever skill or force they can to obtain from their creditors a written release of the debt, thinking that by this the soul is cleansed and the guilt, as it were, wiped away, lest it be grievously punished afterwards.

units.la: Iudicii novissimo die habituri ordinem modumque sic describit Muhammed, ut ante omnia id certissi- mum, & pro articulo fidei præcipuo tenendum incul- cet, futurum judicium.
units.tr: Concerning the order and manner of the last judgment, which Muhammed will hold on the last day, he first of all insists that this is most certain and that the coming judgment must be held as a chief article of faith.

units.la: Quod enim in finem videtur homo vafer egisse, tum ut terrorem hominibus suis, rudibus & Paganis adderet, eoque illos facilius sub imperio contineret suo; tum ut sic etiam affinitatem majorem quasi cum Iudæis & Christianis ostentaret. Omnino judicii istum diem credi ob omnibus suis voluit. Sed & privatum particulare singulorum hominum, ubi mortui sunt, præcedere; quod puerliter valde & ludicrè exponunt. Nempe, defunctum (dicunt) in sepulchro coram duobus Angelis nigris Munkir, & Quære-
