units.tr: For the crafty man seems to have aimed at this: first, to strike terror into his men, who were rude and pagan, and so keep them more easily under his rule; second, to display a greater kinship, as it were, with the Jews and Christians. He wished that this day of judgment be believed by all his followers. But they also set out a private, particular judgment of each man, which comes at the moment of his death, and they explain it in a very childish and ludicrous way. Namely, they say that the dead man in his grave is visited before two black angels, Munkir and Nakir, who question him

units.la: Quaerunt, altero clavam ferream, altero uncum tenente, sisti, animâ corpore ut vestè iterum indutâ, ubi interrogatus de vitâ, suisque in eâ actionibus, & num Muhammedis legem bene servarit, si quidem probe responderit, comites accipit duos Angelos albos, loco illorum nigrorum, quorum qui successerunt Angelorum bonorum alter ei assidet à capite, à pedibus alter, assistuntque sic eidem usque ad diem judicii. Si vero improbus in vitâ, atque de eo convictus coram duobus illis Angelis fuerit, percutitur ei clavâ caput, ita ut septem cubitis subter terram unico ictu statim detrudatur; ab altero Angelorum, ubi ita jam priori vapulavit, ultrà uncino ferreo semper magis magisque attrahitur ad infernâ, usque ad diem judicii. Sepulchra suaserè concava faciunt Muhammedani, quo commodius genua flectere coram Angelis, aliaque officia praestare queant: estque apud illos usitata precatio, quâ orant: Deus noster, libera nos ab Angelo interrogante, à tormento sepulchri, & à viâ malâ. Quemadmodum resurrectionem quidem credunt ad judicium antecedaneam, ita non hominum solùm eam, sed & brutorum animalium statuunt futuram: nempe & illa in judicium, quin quoque in Paradysum suum venient: & ovis isthoc die à percussione & infestatione arietis vindicabitur seu justificabitur, secundum Muhammedem. In Alkorano, cap. de animalibus dicitur: & non est brutum seu jumentum in terrâ, neque avis volans alis suis, nisi gentes similes vobis hominibus. Non apposuimus in libro aliquid superflum, vel injustum. Deinde ad Dominum suum suscitabuntur. Egregiè sic jam bruta nobis similia, & aequiparantur, unius nempe generis gentisque, & resuscitationis simul omnes participes. Resurrectionem quidem hoc pacto futuram fabulantur. Primum scilicet Angelus mortis, quem Adriel vocant, Dei jussu, interimet omnes creaturas viventes, nullâ exceptâ, & Angelos, Diabolos, homines, bestias, aves, pisces, omnia quæ vitam habent: quo facto & ipse ad Deum vocatus, jubebitur pro eo quod omnia occiderit, & se quoque inter Paradysum atque infernum suspendere, qui dicto loco se, in alis suis obvolvens tanto cum clamore, fremituque suffocabit sese, ut hoc solo fragore, nisi jam occubuissent viventia omnia, essent interitura. Surat. lxx ix. dicitur, primo buccinæ sonitu tellus & montes prosternentur, & in pulverem redigentur, horâ veniente cælum fundetur, & debilitabitur, & angeli octo Dei thronum sustentabunt. Hinc mundus quadraginta annis ita consistet vacuus. Postea resuscitabitur in vitam Angelus Seraphiel, cui tradetur tuba sonanda, cujus longitudo sit itinere dierum quingentorum; locus autem, ex quo sonum daturus est, erit Jerusalem. Inde animæ omnium piorum & improborum æque, huc illuc volabunt, atque corpus suum investigabunt singulæ; sonitque illo omnia ossa omnium concurrent. Post quadraginta elapsos annos, Angelus iterum sonabit, & tum ossa carnem & venas recipient: & ubi tertium post alios quadraginta annos sonuerit, remeabunt in corpora sua animæ: quo facto, statim ignis ab occidente Solis accensus, omnes cogeт Ierusalemum versus, quò ubi pervenerint, cessabit. Hic ubi per quadraginta annos in sudore suo navaverint homines, judicium præstolantes, tandem multis defatigati angoribus & molestiis, communem parentem interpellabunt Adamum, Pater Adam, ad quid tu nos genuisti in tantas, tamque acerbas miserias? itane Pater filios tuos pateris in incerto pendere, spem inter metumque? quin potius apud Deum intercede, ut de nobis pronunciet, absolvatque demum quod de paradyso infernoque agere decrevit? at respondebit Adam, se intercessionem pro illis apud Deum non suscipere, quum sciant inobedientem Deo fuisse, tum quando Diabolo suadenti infœliciter obtemperaret: verùm consulet ipsis, ut ad Noachum pergant: quo rogato, pro se ut intercedere dignetur, detrecabit is quoque, ideo quod omnia fecerit ad illos salvandos tempore diluvii, quod jam ultra nihil pro ipsis possit: quare ad Abrahamum illos dimittet, ad quem: Pater omnium fidelium Abraham, nos quaesumus miseros tu respice; respondebit & ille: quid vos a me postulatis, num ignoratis me diu infidelem atque incircumcisum olim fuisse? ego longe impar tanto sum ossicio: quin ad Mosem potius ite: at is quoque dicet, quem appellatis? nonne ego legem vobis dedi, miraculisque abunde confirmavi, & tamen mihi non credidistis? quod si mihi tum credidissetis, jam forte possem quod petitis; sed properate ad Iesum Christum: ad quem conversi dicent, Iesu Christe, Spiritus, verbum, & virtus Dei, moveat te tua pietas & pro nobis intercede: a quo & hoc responsum referent, ego ad vos missus nuncius fui, sed mihi non credidistis: ultimum Prophetam Muhammedem accedite (haec in Colloquio Muhammedis cum Abdia Iudaeo, ubi & Muhammed seipsum designans, ait; illum ipsum Abdia, quocum praesens loqueris), cui denique dicent, o fidelis nuncie, atque amice Dei, quidem peccavimus contra te, attamen nos exaudi &c. Inde pons (dicunt) construitur supra infernum, atque ad pontis caput statera, ad quam appendentur hominum facta, & quorum ea deprehendentur bona, transibunt in Paradisum; alii vero dejicientur in infernum, puniendi. In eodem Dialogo inquit Muhammed, dies judicii duraturos mille annis; atque judicandorum constituendas caterv as viginti & centum, quarum non supra tres sint salvandae, & unaquaeque futura quasi mille annorum itinere longa. In Alkorano Surat. lxvi, turmas judicandorum sistendas dicit a Dei dextera & sinistra; ibi salvandos, hic damnandos: illis traditum iri chartam suarum rationum legendam manu dextera, his sinistra. Sur. lxx ix. & xc iii. liber justorum & salvandorum dicitur asservari in supernis, & liber injustorum in partibus terrarum infimis. Surat. vi‑r. dicitur, facies illorum obfuscandas, & totas fore atras, qui fidem deseruerint, Muhammedanam scilicet, & infideles fuerint; aliorum vero facies candidissimas, Surata lxxxv. cx. xcviii. Alibi de die judicii interroganti respondetur: nemini nisi soli Deo illum esse notum. Surata. lxxvii. lxxxix. Alibi dicit eum exspectandum post spatium annorum quinquaginta mille. Surata. lxxx.
units.tr: They question him, one holding an iron club and the other a hook. His soul is set before them, clothed again in its garment, and he is asked about his life, his deeds in it, and whether he has kept the law of Muhammed well. If he has answered well, he receives two white angels as companions in place of those black ones, and these good angels, who succeed the others, sit one by his head and the other by his feet, and so stand by him until the day of judgment. But if he has been wicked in life and is convicted of it before those two angels, a club strikes his head, so that with a single blow he is driven seven cubits under the earth; and when he has been beaten thus by the first, the second angel drags him ever further down with an iron hook, into hell, until the day of judgment. Muhammedans make their graves rather hollow, so that they may more conveniently bend their knees before the angels and perform their other duties. Their customary prayer is: "Our God, deliver us from the angel who questions, from the torment of the grave, and from the evil way." Just as they believe that the resurrection comes before the judgment, so they hold that not only men but also brute animals will rise: they too will come to judgment, and even into their Paradise. On that day, according to Muhammed, the sheep will be avenged, or justified, against the butting and attack of the ram. In the Alkoran, chapter "On Animals," it is said: "There is no beast on the earth, nor bird flying on its wings, but they are peoples like you men. We have left nothing out or unjust in the Book. Then they will be raised to their Lord." Here brute animals are plainly made like us and put on the same footing, as being of one kind and nation, and all alike share in the resurrection. They invent the resurrection to happen in this way. First the angel of death, whom they call Adriel, by God's command will kill all living creatures without exception: angels, devils, men, beasts, birds, fish, all things that have life. When this is done, he too will be summoned before God and ordered, because he has killed everything, to hang himself between Paradise and hell; wrapping himself in his wings, he will choke himself with such a cry and roar that by this crash alone, if all living things had not already perished, they would have died. In Sura 79 it is said: "At the first blast of the trumpet the earth and mountains will be cast down and reduced to dust; when the hour comes the heavens will be poured out and weakened, and eight angels will bear up the throne of God." Thus the world will remain empty for forty years. Afterwards the angel Seraphiel will be raised to life, and to him will be given the trumpet to sound, whose length is five hundred days' journey; the place from which he is to give the sound will be Jerusalem. Then the souls of all the pious and the wicked alike will fly hither and thither, and each will search out its own body; and at that sound all the bones of all men will come together. After forty years have passed, the angel will sound again, and then the bones will receive flesh and veins; and when he has sounded a third time, after another forty years, the souls will return into their bodies. This done, a fire kindled from the west of the sun will drive all men toward Jerusalem, and when they arrive there it will stop. There, for forty years, men will toil in their sweat, awaiting judgment; at last, worn out by many anxieties and troubles, they will address their common parent Adam: "Father Adam, why did you beget us into such great and bitter miseries? Will you, Father, let your sons hang in uncertainty, between hope and fear? Rather intercede for us with God, that he may pronounce on us and at last absolve us, deciding whether we shall go to Paradise or hell." But Adam will answer that he does not take on intercession for them with God, since they know that he was disobedient to God, when he unhappily obeyed the Devil's persuasion; rather, he will advise them to go to Noah. When they ask Noah to intercede for them, he too will refuse, because he did everything to save them at the time of the flood, and so can do nothing more for them. Therefore he will send them on to Abraham, to whom they will say: "Father of all the faithful, Abraham, we beg you, miserable as we are, look upon us." He too will answer: "What do you ask of me? Do you not know that I was once an unbeliever for a long time and uncircumcised? I am far unequal to such an office. Go rather to Moses." But Moses too will say: "Whom do you call upon? Did I not give you the law and abundantly confirm it with miracles, and yet you did not believe me? If you had believed me then, perhaps I could now do what you ask; but hasten to Jesus Christ." Turning to him, they will say: "Jesus Christ, Spirit, Word, and Power of God, let your piety move you, and intercede for us." And from him they will bring back this answer: "I was sent as a messenger to you, but you did not believe me. Go to the last Prophet, Muhammed." (This is in the Colloquy of Muhammed with the Jew Abdias, where Muhammed, pointing to himself, says: "to that very Abdias with whom you are speaking.") Finally they will say to him: "O faithful messenger and friend of God, we have indeed sinned against you; yet hear us, etc." Then (they say) a bridge is built over hell, and at the head of the bridge a balance, in which men's deeds are weighed; those whose good deeds are found in them will pass over into Paradise, but others will be cast down into hell to be punished. In the same Dialogue Muhammed says that the day of judgment will last a thousand years, and that the companies to be judged will be divided into twenty and a hundred, of which not more than three will be saved, and each will be, as it were, a thousand years' journey long. In the Alkoran, Sura 66, he says that the companies to be judged will be set at the right and left hand of God: the saved on the one side, the damned on the other; the former will be given the paper of their accounts to read in the right hand, the latter in the left. In Suras 79 and 93 it is said that the book of the just and saved is kept on high, and the book of the unjust in the lowest parts of the earth. In Sura 6 it is said that the faces of those who have abandoned the faith, that is, the Muhammedan faith, and have been unbelievers, will be darkened and wholly black; but the faces of others will be most shining white (Suras 85, 110, 98). Elsewhere, when someone asks about the day of judgment, the answer is that it is known to no one but God alone (Suras 77, 89). Elsewhere he says that it must be waited for after a space of fifty thousand years (Sura 80).

units.la: Paradysum autem Muhammedanum, qualem faciant, quantumque, lustremus porro. Constituunt primum coelo suo portas, & claves: portas aureas pensiles, cujus claves asserventur in Dei thesauro: Paradysi vero sedes septem vel locos, ex argento primum, deinde aureum, gemmeum, smaragdinum, adamantinum, sextum e carbunculis ignitum, & septimum ex luce divina compositum. Omnia enim hic aurea argenteaque, mundana, corporalia ac carnalia imaginanda, qualia brutis suis, brutalibusque ingeniis convenire augurabatur vanus Propheta. Pollicetur domicilia hic splendidissima, Surat. xxxv. & liii. talia, quae tota auro obducta sint, conclavia aureis lectis strata, quodque ipsi induentur aureis annulis, coronis, vestibus deauratis, lapidibus pretiosissimis, serico, tapetis, stramentis purpureis, & quod pecuniae habituri sint copiam maximam. Surat. xxvii. xxxi. xli. lxii. lxvi. lxvii. Et ne quid voluptatibus suis, libidinique desit, etiam abundantiam formosissimarum virginum a nullo virorum unquam cognitarum ibi constituit ad animi libitum. Quae certe infernum potius impudicissimorum describere videntur, quam paradysum. Sur. xlvii.
units.tr: Next let us examine what sort of Paradise the Muhammedans imagine, and how great it is. First, they assign to their heaven gates and keys: golden gates hanging aloft, whose keys are kept in God's treasury; and the seats or stages of Paradise are seven: first of silver, then of gold, then of jewels, then of emerald, then of adamant, the sixth of fiery carbuncles, and the seventh made of divine light. For they imagine all things here to be golden and silvery, worldly, bodily and fleshly, such as the vain Prophet supposed would suit his brutish followers and their brutal minds. He promises most splendid dwellings here (Suras 35 and 53), such as are wholly overlaid with gold, rooms spread with golden couches, and that they themselves will be adorned with golden rings, crowns, gilded robes, most precious stones, silk, carpets, and purple coverings; and that they will have the greatest abundance of money (Suras 27, 31, 41, 62, 66, 67). And so that nothing may be lacking to their pleasures and lusts, he also provides there, at their pleasure, an abundance of most beautiful virgins, never known by any man. These seem indeed to describe rather the hell of the most shameless men than a Paradise (Sura 47).

units.la: Habebunt in Paradyso quodcunque illis libuerit, frument-que feminae, quibus oculi clarissimi grandesque ut ova, quos non ad alios quam maritos suos erigent. Item Surat. xlviii & lxii. Timentibus autem, Paradisum possessuris, & ab igne penitus liberandis, dicetur:
units.tr: They shall have in Paradise whatever they desire, and women with very bright and large eyes, like eggs, whom they will raise their eyes to only as their own husbands. Likewise Surat xlviii and lxii. But to those who fear God, who shall possess Paradise and be wholly freed from the fire, it shall be said:

units.la: de fructibus omnimodis vobis datis, optimoque victu comedite atque bibite, ob actiones vestros optimos; & super strumenta formosissima pro modo vestro distumbite, ducturi virgines decentissimas, cum oculis immensis atque pudibundis, nusquam nisi tantum ad maritos suos flectendis. Sur. 1111. Omnes enim qui nostris preceptis crediderint, hodie cum suis mulieribus paradysum possidebunt, gaudium plenum accepturi. Cum cateni's enim & poculis aureis, plenis pro lubitu omnibus deliciis administrabitur illis, istic perpetuo mansuris, omnique voto suo perpetuo potituris, fructusque multiplices consortis. Hasce mulieres statuunt non humanas atq; ex hominibus genitas, sed ab æterno in hunc finem à Deo creatas, & cœlestes esse; suas enim quas hic habuerunt Muhammedani mulieres statuunt exsortes fore Paradysi, atque extra eum foris constituendas, per cancellos eminus virorum gaudia, & cum aliis sc. uxoribus congressus conspecturas. Longe plures ibi credunt fore mulieres, quam viros, singulisque viris plures vel paucióres pro merito addendas, quibus non ad prolem, sed unice ad libitum & satietatem voluptatis usure sint; quin & vires iis submitiistrandas majores cum in finem, ut sæpius coire possint, easque eundem in finem fore mundas & liberas à menstruis. Vah spurcitiem Muhammedici Paradysi! haram pórcorum dicas, vel profitibulum meretricum. Tanta istarum puellarum depraedicatur pulchritudo & gratia, ut si earum modo una aliquando nocu in terra apparerent, totam eam facile effet collustratura: vel si in mare forte despuceret, totam ejus salsedinem extinguecret, inque mel dulcissimum commutaret. Et cibum Paradysi quod attinet, potumque, nam omne genus delitiarum, imo crepundiorum hic narrant, similes habitura labra lactucas. totus Paradysus, inquit Muhammed, est smaragdinus, hyacinthinus, admodum jucundus fertilisque, ubi fontes lactæ, alii melle candido, alii pulcherrimo vino fluentes. Hoc scilicet illis in Paradyso concedit, quo alioqui interdixit in terris: at porcina caro prohibita & ibi quoque erit: exceptâ, omnibus quibus delectantur, affatim potituris. Surata xxv 1 1. Credentes & benefacientes sua non amittent opera. Illi namque Paradysum fontibus amœnum, & annulos, & torques aureos, & ornatus fericeos viridesque & deauratos possidebunt, & in lectis aureatis accumbent. Et hoc est maxima merces & interminabilis. Sur. xxxi 1. Credentibus & benefacientibus Paradysum præbens, illis armillas aureas & margaritas, monilíaque, vestesque sericas adaptabit, viamque rectam, verbumque gratum edocebit. Sur. 1 v. Timentes autem locum hortis & fontibus secundum possidebunt, vestibusque fericeis & purpura vestiendi, puellas ducent cum oculis claris & immensis, quorum albugines candidissimæ, & pupillæ vigerrimæ. Pro libitu suo fructus multimodos absque timore comedent, non gustabunt mortem amplius. Deus eos liberabit à foco, & hoc est grande donum. Surat. 1v 11 1. In Paradyso sunt aquæ dulcissimæ. Suntque rivi saporiferi, lactis, & mellis. Pomaque ibidem omnis generis. & Surat. 11. & xlv 1. & 1 1 1 1. & Surat. 1x 1, acièi, ex versione Cl. Golii, condonabit vobis peccata vestra, & introducet vos in hortos, subter quibus decurrunt fluvii, & mansiones amœnas in hortis Eden. Surata 1xxxv 1. Deus igitur illos ab illius diei malo liberat, dans honorem & ornatum atque mercedem maximam, paradysum videlicet & lectisternia fericea. Ubi nec Solis fervorem, seu frigus sentient: sed arborum umbraculum sibi suos fructus collectos inclinantium, illic habebunt. Et ibidem ex vasis vitreis & argenteis aptissimè compositis, illis potus, velut, Zingiber saporifer, ex fonte Zelzebil administrabitur. Aderunt & juvenes velut margaritæ speciosi, omniumque divitiarum & bonorum copia. Vestes quidem fericeas & deauratas illi juvenes induent, torques argenteos in brachiis ferentes. Vinum quoque benedictum illic Deo dante sufficiet. Surat. 1xxxvi 1 1. de damnatis in inferno ait, nec refrigerium nec vinum ibi habituros, sed ignem. ignem ; at de paradyso, ejusque incolis suo more iterum : sufficienter illic possidebunt hortos palmarum & vitium, puellasque socias & speciosas, papillis brevissimis, vasisque plena, nullum verbum inhonestum, sed mendax auditurí. Surat. xciiii. pulvinaribus & stramentis sericeis in paradyso quiescent, potaturi vinum sapidum & relatu musicas odorisferum: suisque facieb̃ omnibus inerit decor atque pulchritudo. Et bibent vinum commixtum ex fonte Thesiz, &c. idem Sur. xcviii. Ibi nimirum ille fons Alcazar, Muhammedi à Deo speciatim datus, tantae amplitudinis; ut vix septuaginta mille dierum itinere obambulari possit, cujusque aquae nive candidiores, & melle suaviores, & tot vasa cyathique parati ad potandum adsunt, quot coelum stellis scatet. Ibi & arbor maxima Tuba, quae totum implet Paradysum, cujusque folia alterna ex auro & argento sunt, atque inscriptum gerunt nomen Dei & Muhammedis: non est Deus nisi unus, & Muhammed ejus nuncius. Ibique illud paratum Muhammedanis à Muhammede suo convivium, mensaque adamantina, cujus longitudo itinere dierum septingentorum; appositis sellis ex auro argentoque, mappis & linteis ex auro & serico instructa, ad quam mensam festive excipientur omnibus Paradysi epulis, potuque ex fontibus illis pulcherrimis. Tandem convivis singulis ab adolescentibus pulcherrimis epuli administris porrigentur vestes, calceamenta, torques, ornamentaque alia, quibus induentur, ornabunturque; sed inter alia, & mala-citrina singulis exhibebuntur quae ubi odorabuntur, confestim ex iis prosilient virgines formosissimae, singulos Muhammedanos arctius; complexurae, quae per quinquaginta annos iiscum in carnalibus voluptatibus atque deliciis commorabuntur. Post quod tempus, Deus faciem suam Muhammedanis visendam offeret, qui illius fulgorem non sustinentes, inde in terram ilico concident; sed à Deo erecti confirmatique videre cum valebunt: post quam Dei visionem abibunt singuli cum puellis, in sua quaeque palatia, perpetuo cum iis in omni voluptate victuri, & in copia omnium deliciarum, frugum cibi potusque se æternum oblectaturi. Quæ omnia breviter complectitur in colloquio suo cum Abdia Iudæo Muhammed, super statu paradysi ab illo sedulo interrogatus: Paradysi namque solum aureum, inquit, smaragdis & hyacinthis interpositis distinctum; omni fructifera consitum arbore, per amoena decurrentibus fluentis. Quorum alia quidem lac, alia mel album, alia vinum purissimum fundunt. Dies mille annorum ibi erit. Et de vestimentis, eorumque colore sic pronunciat, omnis siquidem colore vestientur, praeter nigro; qui solus concedetur Praeconi Muhammedi, ob singulare ejus meritum. Et de cibis ubi dixerat Muhammed, quod primo ingressis Paradysum, proponeretur vescendus piscis Albebbus, mirabiliter delicatus &c. tempestive rogavit Iudæus, annon quoque cibi isti digererentur, & quæ ratio tum sutura esset excrementorum? respondit lepide, nihil excrementi inde secuturum, ut nihil quoque infans in utero, quamvis vescatur, egerit; si quod tamen superfluui, id per sudorem exituram, odoremque optimum, qualis est musci, fragraturum.
units.tr: Eat and drink the best food and all the fruits given to you, for your excellent deeds; and recline as you wish on the most beautiful couches, to take most comely virgins with immense and modest eyes, who turn their gaze only to their husbands. Sur. 1111. For all who have believed our precepts will today possess Paradise with their wives, about to receive full joy. For they will be served with dishes and golden cups, with every delight they wish, remaining there forever, about to enjoy forever every desire of their hearts, and manifold fruits, and companions. They hold that these women are not human nor born of men, but were created by God from eternity for this purpose, and are heavenly. For they hold that the Muhammadan women they had here will be excluded from Paradise and placed outside it, beyond the lattice, to behold from afar the men's joys and their intercourse with the other wives. They believe there will be far more women than men there, and that more or fewer are to be assigned to each man according to his merit, who will serve not for offspring but solely for the pleasure and satisfaction of lust. Moreover, greater strength is to be given to them, so that they can couple more often, and for the same purpose they will be kept clean and free from menses. Fie, the filth of the Muhammadan paradise! You would call it a brothel of pigs or a stew of prostitutes. So great, they proclaim, is the beauty and charm of these maidens, that if one of them once appeared on earth at night, she could easily light up the whole of it; or if she spat into the sea, she would quench all its saltiness and turn it into the sweetest honey. As for the food and drink of Paradise (for they tell of every kind of delight, indeed of trinkets here), their lips will be like lettuces. Muhammad says the whole of Paradise is emerald and hyacinth, very pleasant and fertile, where there are springs flowing, some with milk, some with white honey, and some with the finest wine. This is clearly granted to them in Paradise, which he forbade on earth; but pork, which is forbidden, will be there too, for them to enjoy in abundance along with everything else they delight in. Surat xxv. Believers who do good will not lose their works. They shall possess a Paradise pleasant with springs, with rings and golden necklaces, and garments of silk, green and gilded, and they shall recline on gilded couches. And this is the greatest and endless reward. Sur. xxxi. To believers who do good, granting Paradise, he will give them golden bracelets and pearls and necklaces, and silken garments, and will teach them the straight way and a pleasing word. Sur. lv. But those who fear the place will possess gardens and springs in due order, and they will take maidens with bright and immense eyes, clothed in silk and purple; their whites most white and their pupils most lively. They will eat fruits of many kinds freely as they please, and will no longer taste death. God will free them from the fire, and this is a great gift. Surat lv 11. In Paradise there are the sweetest waters, and streams of savoury, of milk and of honey. And fruits of every kind there. And Surat ii, and xlv, and Surat ix, acièi, from the version of the illustrious Golius: he will forgive you your sins, and lead you into gardens under which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in the gardens of Eden. Surat lxxxv. God therefore delivers them from the evil of that day, giving honour and adornment and the greatest reward, namely Paradise and silken couches. There they will feel neither the heat of the sun nor the cold; but they will have the shade of trees bending their gathered fruits over them. And there they will be given to drink, from vessels of glass and silver most aptly arranged, a drink like ginger, from the spring Zelzebil. There will also be youths beautiful as pearls, and an abundance of all riches and goods. Those youths will clothe themselves in silk and gold, carrying silver bracelets on their arms. Wine blessed by God will also be enough for them there. Surat lxxxvi. Of the damned in hell he says they will have neither coolness nor wine there, but fire. But of Paradise and its inhabitants he says again in his usual way: there they will sufficiently possess gardens of palms and vines, and companions and beautiful maidens with very small breasts, and cups full, hearing no dishonest word, but only lies. Surat xciiii. In Paradise they will rest on silken cushions and couches, about to drink savoury wine and fragrant wine delivered with music; and all their faces will have grace and beauty. And they will drink wine mixed from the spring Thesiz, etc. The same Surat xcviii. There indeed is that spring Alcazar, given by God to Muhammad in particular, of such size that one could scarcely walk around it in seventy thousand days' journey; its waters are whiter than snow and sweeter than honey, and there are as many vessels and cups ready for drinking as the sky is full of stars. There too is the very great tree Tuba, which fills the whole of Paradise, whose leaves alternately are of gold and silver, and which bear inscribed the name of God and of Muhammad: there is no God but one, and Muhammad is his messenger. And there is a banquet prepared there by Muhammad for the Muhammadans, and a table of adamant, whose length is a journey of seven hundred days; with seats of gold and silver set around it, and tablecloths and linens made of gold and silk, at which table they will be festively received with all the feasts of Paradise and the drink from those most beautiful springs. Finally, to each guest, the most handsome youths who serve the feast will hand garments, footwear, necklaces and other ornaments, with which they will be clothed and adorned; and among other things, to each will be given citrons, which when they smell them, straightway from them will leap forth most beautiful virgins, who will embrace each Muhammadan more tightly, and who will remain with them for fifty years in carnal pleasures and delights. After that time, God will offer his face to the Muhammadans to be seen; they, not able to bear its brightness, will at once fall to the earth; but when they are raised and strengthened by God they will be able to see; after this vision of God each will depart with his girls to his own palace, to live forever with them in all pleasure, and to delight themselves eternally in an abundance of all delights, fruits, food and drink. He briefly sums up all these things in his conversation with Abdias the Jew, when Muhammad was diligently questioned by him about the state of Paradise: For the ground of Paradise, he says, is gold, adorned with interspersed emeralds and hyacinths; planted with every fruitful tree, with streams flowing through pleasant places. Some of these pour out milk, some white honey, some the purest wine. There will be a thousand years' days there. And about garments, and their colour, he pronounces thus: they will be clothed in every colour except black; which alone is granted to the herald of Muhammad, on account of his singular merit. And when Muhammad had said that, on first entering Paradise, a fish called Albebbus, wonderfully delicate, would be set before them to eat, the Jew asked at the right moment whether those foods too would be digested, and what account would then be given of the excrement? He replied wittily that no excrement would follow from them, just as the infant in the womb, though it feeds, passes nothing out; and if anything superfluous there was, it would go out through sweat, and would give off a most excellent odour, such as that of musk.

units.la: Hic scilicet Muhammedis, Muhammedanorumque Paradysus, & cœlum, & omnia; non hominibus, sed brutis, & ultra sensum ac carnem nihil spirantibus, sperantibusque digna. Hæc ille nempe suis persuaserit, mortalium quotquot sunt, stolidissimis, facileque deliciarum tali apparatu inescandis, & spe. Sed qui paulum modo altius assurgunt, ac mente gaudent erectiores, fastidiunt illa in terris, nedum in cœlo; atque tum ex Sacris, tum ratione, levissima opera refutari omnia illa possunt, nisi explodi, ut insulsissima & ab hominis dignitate ac sollicitate alienissima debeant potius, quam serio dilui.
units.tr: Here, then, is the paradise of Muhammed and of the Muhammedans, and their heaven and everything in it: a paradise fit for beasts and for creatures that breathe nothing beyond sense and flesh, and fit only for hopes of that kind. Muhammed no doubt persuaded his followers of this, the most foolish of mortals and easily lured by such a display of pleasures and by hope. But those who rise a little higher and whose minds delight in lifting themselves up despise these things on earth, let alone in heaven. Both from the Sacred Scriptures and from reason, all of this can be refuted with very little effort, or rather dismissed outright, so that it deserves to be mocked as utterly silly and wholly alien to human dignity and concern, rather than to be refuted seriously.

units.la: Uti in cibo potuque delicatissimis gloriam & felicitatem Paradysi sui constituunt Muhammedani, ita infer- ni poenam & cruciatum multam partem in hujusmodi rebus ponunt, quae ingratissimi odoris sunt & saporis, praeter ignem, quem fatentur dirissimum fore, & sempiternum; uti quoque gloria Paradysi illis, aeterna, Surat. lxxxi. Credentes autem & benefacientes tunc veniam adepti, paradysum perenniter inhabitandum, quod est maximum, possidebunt. Increduli vero, vestrisque praeceptis contradicentes, igni mansionique prava perpetuo tradentur. Similiter Surat. xxxii. Ab igne hoc perpetuo ustulantur damnati, & cutis quoties igne absumta, iterum reparatur ad nova semper supplicia. Potus illorum omni felle est amarior, & cibus ex arbore Alzekon, quae in profundo abyssi nascitur, soporis ingratissimi. Muhammed in ementitâ suâ cum Gabriele Angelo per coelum inferosque peregrinatione, dixit se hic vidisse Diabolos diversissimarum figurarum, alios catenis igneis alligatos, verubus transfixos alios; homines mensis instructissimis assidentes, & relictis bonis frugibus, ad appositas malas foetidasque ferri, qui sunt ii scilicet, nam sic Angelus haec interpretabatur, qui in vitâ spretis uxoribus propriis & bonis alias fuerant secutati, id est, qualis ipse quoque Muhammed: alios cernebat haurientes semper plumbum liquefactum, quem effusum resorbebant: hi nimirum erant, qui tutores bona pupillorum defraudarant, eaque fuerant dilapidati. Talia ibi plura, nempe qualia Poetae de suis inferis, Stygé, pomis Tantali, rota Ixionis strenue fabulati olim fuerunt. Infernus, ex sententia Muhammedanorum, septem habet portas. Sur. xxv. adde Sur. lxxix. Et in colloquio quidem cum Abdiâ sic infernum depingit Auctor: Infernî siquidem solum sulphureum, fumosum, multa pice intersertum, ipse totus flamma et tetterrimis est naves. Sunt in eo lacus & putei profundissimi, pleni pice fervente, suppositis flammis sulphureis, quibus quotidie immerguntur damnati. Sunt illic & arboarbores, quarum fructibus vescantur, quo cibo nihil gravius in toto mundo excogitari potest. Quodque ibidem adfert de aliquo post mille annos ex inferni poenis eductando, & in Paradysum constituendo, qui tamdiu maneat in medio inferni, in arcâ vinctus catenis compedibusque, quæ arca in puteo, puteus in gurgite, gurges in vallę, vallis in inferni medio &c. uti reliqua, adeo infalsum & fabulosum est, ut audire ultra pigeat: vereorque etiam, ne fortasse prolixior vel diligentior fuerim in referendis illorum commentis & fabulis, quas scire tamen è re judicavi, ad illorum doctrinam opiniónesque circa sacra noscendam: & quia illa ex variis vel ipsorum vel aliorum scriptis conquirere, non nullius negotii fuit, arduus etiam alicujus, viderint quibus hæc scribo.
units.tr: Just as the Muhammedans place the glory and happiness of their paradise in the most delicate food and drink, so they place most of the punishment and torment of hell in things of the most disagreeable smell and taste. Apart from fire, which they admit will be most dreadful and everlasting, they also hold that the glory of paradise is eternal. Sura 81: Those who believe and do good, having then obtained pardon, shall possess the paradise to be inhabited forever, which is the greatest thing. But the unbelievers, who contradict your precepts, shall be delivered to fire and a wicked dwelling forever. Likewise Sura 32: The damned are burned by this everlasting fire, and as often as the skin is consumed by the fire, it is renewed again for new punishments always. Their drink is more bitter than all gall, and their food, from the tree Alzekon, which grows at the bottom of the abyss, is of the most disagreeable taste. In his fabricated journey through heaven and hell with the angel Gabriel, Muhammed says that he saw here devils of very different shapes: some bound with fiery chains, others pierced through with spits; men sitting at richly furnished tables, and leaving good grains aside, reaching for set bad and stinking iron things. These, namely (for so the angel explained it), were those who in life had scorned their own wives and goods and followed others, that is, like Muhammed himself. He saw others constantly drinking molten lead, which they reabsorbed when poured out; these were, of course, those who had defrauded orphans of their guardians' goods and squandered them. There were many other such things there, just like those which the poets once fabled about their underworld, the Styx, the apples of Tantalus, and the wheel of Ixion. According to the opinion of the Muhammedans, hell has seven gates. See Sura 25; add Sura 79. And in his conversation with Abdias, the author describes hell as follows: The floor of hell is sulphurous and smoky, interlaced with much pitch, and it is entirely made of flame and most horrible things. In it there are lakes and very deep pits, full of seething pitch, with sulphurous flames set beneath, into which the damned are plunged every day. There are also trees there, whose fruits they feed on, a food than which nothing more grievous can be imagined in the whole world. And what he adds there, about someone who after a thousand years is to be led out of the punishments of hell and placed in paradise, who meanwhile remains in the middle of hell, bound in a chest with chains and fetters, which chest is in a pit, the pit in a whirlpool, the whirlpool in a valley, the valley in the middle of hell, and so on as in the rest, is so unreliable and fabulous that it is tiresome even to hear. I fear also that I may have been rather long or thorough in reporting their inventions and fables; yet I judged it worthwhile to know them, for learning their doctrine and opinions about sacred matters. And because it was no small task, and a difficult one, to gather these from various writings, either their own or others', let those for whom I write these things judge.

units.la: Jam postquam Muhammedicæ doctrinæ, tum in iis quæ suæ disciplinæ habent propria, tum quæ adversus fidei & religionis nostræ articulos opponunt, lustravimus διαλογισμοι, superest denique ut in consilium omnia adhibeamus, & videamus, quid ad illorum hominum conversionem forte fieri possit, atque debeat. Certe uti non ego, ita nec meorum aliquem, disputare volo, in tanti præsertim negotii argumento ac hoc est, duntaxat ut disputemus, sed ut disputationis nostræ colligamus fructum usumque, ad hominum conversionem; vel hæc ubi haberi nequit, quod ei proximum, eorum convictionem: Hæc mihi, hæc aliis in disputando semper propono. Quorsum alias contendamus, & multa laterum concussione clamemus alter ad alterum, nisi ut veritate elucescente, ad eam, & salutem suam hoc modo perducantur, qui utriusque fuerint antea exsortes? Et profecto hoc qui non cogitat, ut animas Christo vincat vindicetque, & regnum ejus continuo propaget, sed tantum ut disputet, vel in disputando laudem captet acuminis & victoriæ, ... Ergo & ante disputationem, & in, atque post
units.tr: Now that we have surveyed the Muhammedan doctrine, both in what is peculiar to their system and in what they raise against the articles of our faith and religion (the διαλογισμοι), it remains finally to take everything into counsel and to consider what might perhaps be done, and ought to be done, toward the conversion of those men. Certainly, as I do not wish to dispute for my own sake, nor for that of any of mine, especially in a matter of such great importance, and as this is the case, we should not dispute merely in order to dispute, but in order to gather the fruit and use of our disputation for the conversion of men; or, where that cannot be had, what comes closest to it, their conviction. This is what I always propose to myself and to others in disputing. For what else would we contend for, and shout at one another with much shaking of our sides, unless that, with the truth shining forth, those who were previously without either should be led by it to it and to their salvation? And indeed, whoever does not think about winning souls for Christ and defending them, and about continually spreading his kingdom, but only about disputing, or in disputing seeks the praise of cleverness and victory...

units.la: post pote eam, animum semper oportet in hanc rem intentum habere, & discipere, quibus mediis conversio eorum, cum quibus disputamus, curari optime possit, absque quo & manca, & vana est quaecunque de religione s. scipitur controversia. Hoc ergo cogitanti mihi de Muhammedanis, occurrit primo doctrinae illorum haec consideratio, quod cum ex V. & N. Testamenti Scriptura multa habeat interpolata & adulterata, quae vindicare oportet ab illorum corruptelis & nenis, ita fundamentum hoc praebent, super quo porro disputatio iiscum institui potest, eo futura facilior, quo communie principium religionis aliquatenus saltem agnoscunt, & non operose primum hoc suaderi iis est necesse. Sciunt Christum, norunt Euangelium, & Scripturas multas qua Veteris, qua Novi Testamenti tenent; unde tanto expeditior apud eos opera, quod non ex solo rationis principio, sed ex illo Scripturae etiam agere jam licet. Quod ad opus & certamen cum iis nos invitat, atque feliciorem pollicetur progressum, & victoriam in iis, quae ad illam producta lucem facile conficiuntur. Huc spectat, quod Texeira refert, inter Muhammedanos esse, qui ex reliquiis & segmentis illis quae in Alkorano occurrunt de Christo, Christum etiam haud tralaticie venerantur. Inter illos, prae Turcis Persas scribunt humaniores, dociles magis & tractabiles esse: quos proinde praesertim adoriti & sed ligere, ut ad fidem perducamus, convenit. Sed sola tyrannis est, quae apud eos impedit veritatis agnitionem, dum sub gravi poena inhibentur de lege sua disputare, & commercio cum Christianis, ac precipue libris de religione agentibus interdicuntur. Hoc nisi esset, & non assueta servituti gens, si ingenua magis & liberioris animi, procul dubio facilior praeberet aures, quae jam docta servire & duci ad aliorum plane arbitrium, sublimiorem de Christo & Christiana religione cogitationem omnem respuit & horret. Quo magis & illorum rum libertati, si quo modo, & quorum id fieri potest: studendum à Christianis est, & alliciendi prae aliis ii, qui propius apud nos vivunt.
units.tr: Therefore, both before the disputation, and in it, and after it, the mind must always be fixed on this matter and must consider by what means the conversion of those with whom we dispute can best be brought about; without this, every controversy written about religion is both maimed and empty. So when I think on this about the Muhammedans, this consideration first occurs to me: since their doctrine has much from the Scripture of the Old and New Testaments that is interpolated and corrupted, which we ought to vindicate from their corruptions and inventions, this provides a foundation on which the disputation with them can be further established, and it will be the easier the more they acknowledge at least to some extent a common principle of religion, and the less it is necessary to persuade them of this first point with laborious effort. They know Christ, they know the Gospel, and they hold many Scriptures, both of the Old and of the New Testament; so the work among them is so much quicker, because we may now act not only from the principle of reason but also from that Scripture. This invites us to the work and contest with them, and promises a more fortunate progress and victory, which are easily achieved in those matters that are brought into the light for that purpose. To this belongs what Texeira reports, that among the Muhammedans there are some who, from the remnants and fragments about Christ that occur in the Alkoran, also venerate Christ not in the ordinary way. Among them, the Persians are described as more humane than the Turks, more docile and tractable; therefore it is fitting to make an attack especially on them, and to win them over, so that we may bring them to the faith. But it is tyranny alone that hinders among them the recognition of the truth, since under severe penalty they are forbidden to dispute about their law, and are forbidden commerce with Christians, and especially books treating of religion. If this were not so, and if the nation were not accustomed to slavery but were more ingenuous and of freer spirit, it would undoubtedly offer more willing ears, and would not reject and abhor every higher thought about Christ and the Christian religion, being already trained to serve and to be led entirely at the will of others. Therefore the Christians ought all the more to strive, in whatever way and by whatever means it can be done, for their liberty, and to attract especially those who live closer to us.

units.la: An autem bello resista committi debeat, id est, an ab omni Christianismo junctis armis Turcae oppugnari, & extrudi locis suis, quo ea reddantur Christo & Christianis postliminio ecclesiis & politiis, saepe multumque deliberatum olim, hodieque est. Pontifices Romani semper mirè sagaces solertesque in hac re fuerunt, ut Europaeos omnes Principes in bellum contra Turcas incitarent & extruderent, quo absentibus longe Dominis, Imperatoribus, Regibus, Principibus, tanto melius praedari omnia & auferre terras, bona, & jura ipsorum possent, ac turbare ad arbitrium. Adeo artifices semper tali occasione in rem suam uti, eaque fimbrias suas dilatare à longo tempore didicerunt. Praeterquam quod & hinc praecipuum Bullis suis, Cruciatis, indulgentiis, jubilaeis, non temporali solum & corporali, sed & praesumtae aeque spirituali potestati ac arrogantiae pretium suo modo quaerebant. Adde quod & finis illorum, qui vulgo praetexitur, omnino superstitiosus, quasi pro recuperanda terra sancta scilicet, quae potius maledicta dicenda, pro sepulchro, aliisque soli superstitionem devotis mercibus. Ne jam dicam, quod Lutherum commovit ad obloquendum, cum aliis Papisticae sedis institutis, tum huic bellandi adversus Turcas praetextui, iisque, quas ita nominant, Cruciatis, quod Turcam Christiani nominis hostem considerare nos oportet ceu virgam in manu Dei, per quam affligere res nostras, & per eum ceu lictorem poenas sumere ingratitudinis & improbitatis Christianorum constituit: quod hactenus ferendum bono animo sit, non malo modo atque aequibus eludendum. Eo sensu Lutherus dixit: Preliari adversus Turcas esse repugnare Deo, visitanti iniquitates nostras per illos: quod primo posuit in assertione articulorum, quos dein Bulla P. Leonis x. damnavit, anno cIↄ Iə xx. & hinc perpetuis non oppositionibus & argumentis, sed calumniis impugnarunt Papales, adeo ut haeresis etiam dicam eo nomine Luthero scripserit inter illos Alphonsus de Castro Minorita, lib. III. adversus haeres. tit. bellum, illamque Lutheri haeresim sc. faciat Manichaicā detestabiliorem. Sed Lutherus non negavit simpliciter, contra Turcas praeliandum esse, vel bellum contra eos esse licitum, ut exserte agnovit Bellarminus, lib. III. de Laicis, cap. XVI. ubi hanc quaestionem sigillatim examinat; sed eo modo, quo hactenus, classicum adversus Turcas cani, à Romanis episcopis, suae avaritiae & ambitionis causâ, sub Bullarum Papalium authoritate & veniâ, hoc Lutherus improbavit: de quo in Assertione artic. suorum adversus Bullam P. Leonis dixit, à Turcis exprobrari nobis: nos Bullis & literis veniarum bellare. Altera verò infelicitas, majoris dedecoris & ignominiae, quod tot jam annis passi sumus nos deglubi per impostores & legatos Romanos, toties ad bellum Turcicum, indulgentiis ac facultatibus impudentissimè venditis, pecuniam & substantiam nostram devorantes, quam videmus non solum non venisse, quo mendaces illi & fallaces homines venturam promiserunt, sed etiam in turpissimas eorum libidines & pompas profusam. Verum hoc minor querela. Hoc demum omnium atrocissimum & intolerabile, quod nos indulgentiarum negocio fallacissimo, primum insanissima ceu bruta pecora falsis persuasionibus occupaverunt, & seduxerunt ad universam nostram substantiam compilandam, donec eo ventum sit, ut ne altera quidem sit reliquum, quod non servit Romana avaritiae, semper novis excogitatis imponendi artibus. Sic in vindictam iniquitatis nostrae dedit nobis Deus è Romae truculentiores, crudeliores, insaturabiliores Turcas, quam illi unquam fieri possunt, adhuc pejores hi Turci, nos insensatos praestigiis suis incitant adversus meliores Turcas, tantum, ut interim omnia nostra consumi censeantur, sub titulo belli Turcici. Et in iis omnibus non est aversus furor Domini, necdum intelligi[illegible, ~10 letters] Dei, percutientis nos in corpore & animâ per nos Romanos turcissimos Turcas. Quid ergo dicam ego, quando hic video plus quam quadringentos Prophetas Baal suam Achab circumstare, & ut ascendat in Ramoth Galaad suis Prophetiis animari, & omnia prospera ei nunciare? Forte sicut Micheas & ipse odiosus erat, quia non prophetabat nisi malum, dicam & ipse meo Achab: Ite, praeliamini contra Turcas, ut resistatis virga Dei, & cadatis sicut ille cecidit. Quanto rectius faceremus, si primum ovationibus, imo totius vitae mutata ratione, Deum propitium faceremus? Tum idolo illi Romano Caesar & principes modum ponerent tyrannidis, illusionis, perditionis animarum. Nam ut & ego prophetam semel, licet non audiat, quod scio, nisi Romanus pontifex redigatur in ordinem, actum est de omni re Christiana. Fugiat sicut Christus docuit, in montes qui poterit, aut vitam homicidis Romanis cum fiducia offeras in mortem. Nihil nisi peccatum & perditionem Papatus operari potest. Quid vis amplius? At quis rediget eum in ordinem? Christus illustratione adventus sui, & non alius. Domine, quis credit auditui nostro? Qui habet aures audiendi, audiat, & a bello Turcico abstineat, donec Papa nomen sub caelo valeat. Dixi. Quae rationes fortiores sunt, quam ut a Roffensi Episcopo Confut. Assert. Luther. art. xxiv. facile solvantur. Quippe vult Lutherus, ne sub Papae nomine vel authoritate bellum instruatur, sed illum ipsum prius in ordinem redigendum, siquidem felicem belli exitum cupimus, idque eo magis, quo in multis se adversus Ecclesiam & fideles Turcâ ipso gerat infestiorem: neque ejus vafritie amplius deludendos homines esse, ut ad ejus placitum, & avaritiae satis faciendae causa, in bellum longe abeant, ventosis bulhis inescati, omnia interim sua Papis in praedam relinquentes. Non vel sub Papâ, vel cum eo, aut contra Papanis istis, qui in Papae gratiam soliti sunt conspirare adversus Ecclesiam, prodeundum in bellum Turcicum censuit. Anno MDXXIV. scripsit: In fine Christiastianos omnes adhortor, seu potius obtestor, ut mecum con- iungant preces suas pro tam miseris & fascinatis Principi- bus, quos Deus citra dubium inflammatos ira, tanquam pestes & ad sopes immisit nobis. Ne temere consentiamus ad suscipiendam expeditionem, aut conferendas pecunias ad- versus Tyrannum Turcicum, cum Turca longe solertia, con- silio, integritate, moderatione nostros Principes antecellat. Num sperandum est tam inconsideratis, tam improvidis con- tra Turcam Dativus omnia secundā fore, qui supremum de- o tentare Deum, & blasphemiis afficere non verentur? Est oper. Lat. Tom. II. post exhibita Caesarea, adversus se, suamque doctrinam, Edicta. Istis de causis bellum adversus Turcas dissuasit, quando videlicet Pontificio more geritur, non autem improbavit simpliciter, uti ipse tum dictis locis, tum alibi se declaravit, praecipue singulari hunc in finem conscripto libello anno cIↄ Iↄ xxvii i. de bello Turcico, qui est Tom. iv. Jenens. Erasmus quidem suasit bellum Turcis inferendum, lib. Consultat. de bello Turcico, at non simpliciter; verum, uti Lutherus, quamvis temere visus ab eo dissentire, primum si praecederet apud Christianos digna morum reformatio, neque tam infeliciter ut hactenus bellum istud cederet, quia non Christi negotium egimus, uti bene loquitur, sed adversus Turcas animo Turcico pugnavimus. Praeterquam quod inter causas nostrae infelicitatis, bene & ingenue referat, fractam, autore Papa, a Christianis turpiter fidem, Turcae solemniter datam. Iusiurandum, ejus verba sunt, autore Eugenio violatum, nos in funesta proelia conjecit. Siquidem & hosti servanda fides. Et Bellarminus in hac disputatione ingenue dicit, Lutherum non negare bellum contra Turcas esse licitum, quia putet in genere omne bellum esse illicitum &c. neque quia existimet non habere Christianos justam causam &c. Caeterum si absit nomen Papae, id est, ut nec ejus authoritate, nec Bullis in arma prodeatur; si absit superstitio & opinio terrae sanctae, uti temere di-cicitur; si non id exspectetur demum ut omnes una Principes à Papa quasi ad bellum auctorentur; sed hoc curemus, ut inique oppressis feratur subsidium, ut abrepta per nefas dominia & Ecclesias Christo Christianisque recuperemus, eo casu adversus Turcas Christiani nominis hostes gravissimos bellum juste instaurari, quis ambigat? Certe plures quidem in Turcam Christianorum expeditiones, haud tamen admodum felices multas numerare est. Ab anno cIↄ xcv. usque ad annum cIↄ cclxx. duodecim adversus Turcas & Sarracenos suscepte: atque ultima Ludovici Galliarum Regis, valde infelix extitit. Ita ut nil necesse fuerit, quod Rossensis contra Lutherum, longum facere catalogum Pontificum istorum, qui Reges in istiusmodi bella procitarunt; minus ut Cornelius à Lapide, Prefat. Comment. in Prophetas Minores, inter illos poneret quoque Eugenium iv. cum legato suo Iuliano, quorum nomina, ob perfidiam, & cladem ad Varnam, infestissima merito habentur. Epitomem Bellorum Sacrorum, ut dicunt, legere poteris, Incerti Auctoris, apud Canisium, antiq. Lection. Tom. v i. qui à Ducis Bullionis expeditione, desinit in a.cIↄ.cccccxxi. Addesis Benedicti de Acoltis Aretini, de bello contra Barbaros à Christianis gesto, libros iv. Forbesium, Instruct. Historico-Theol. lib. iv. c. xx. Plurimi consilium inierunt & tradiderunt scripto, quomodo haud difficulter militaris res in Turcam adornari posset, interque eos Philippus Camerarius, Busbequius, ne Callimachi Experientis orationem dicam, de bello Turcis inferendo; ejusque historiam, de Venetis contra Turcas; aliaque istius argumenti voluminibus variis collecta, & edita: neque existimo tantae difficultatis negotium fore, si non inter se Christiani confligerent: at neque tamen etiam abs re monuisse Paulum Fagium censeo, ad Paraphras. Chaldaicam Genes. xvi. 12, ubi de Ismaele dicitur: & ipse erit rebellis inter homines; hoc expendant hodie qui facile esse putant, putant, ut opprimatur Turca, qui ab ipsius origine trahit. Nolo autem meam facere Vberti Folieta, de magnitudine & perpetua in bellis felicitate imperii Turcici, sententiam, vel disputationem, quam ei propterea movit Henricus Stephanus Parisiensis, duabus adversus eum Orationibus, quod Turcarum potentiam supra modum visus fuisset extollere. Sed propter duo expendi haec etiam atque etiam debent, seu bellum instituatur adversus Turcas, seu quocunque modo Christiana res apud istos promoveatur, primo, quia tam late nunc imperitando Saraceni tantam Christianorum Ecclesiarum portionem suo imperio adjungunt, in magnum rerum nostrarum detrimentum; deinde, quod illos, quos suae potestatis faciunt, Christianos dirum in modum vexant, & dis-truciantur miserrima municipia. Nullorum certe, quamdiu vivunt, miserior sors est & conditio, quam Christianorum Turcis captivorum, ab iisque abductorum ad omnem servitutem non solum, sed etiam ad quod illos saepe cogunt, fidei abnegationem, & professionem Muhammedismi, circumcisionem, caeteraque perfidiae istius probra amplexanda. Quem autem non moveat videre alligatos catervatim homines provectae aetatis, juniores, foeminas, uxores, liberos, & promiscue trahi ad gravissimam servitutem, atque ad arbitrium pessimorum hominum prostitui eorum tum corpora, tum vitam? atque id passim apud illos fit, nobis interim altum sternentibus, & gravi socordia negligentibus casum aliorum, quin & nostrum. Aeneam Sylvium ferunt, qui postea factus Papa Pius, ejus nominis secundus, quum aliquoties apud Germaniae Principes in Comitiis, verba faceret de miseriis per Turcarum invasiones in Christianos illatis, Principibus qui aderant saepe lachrymas movisse, proposita dira malorum omnium specie, quae a Turcis Christiani paterentur: & nullus dubito, quin haec ubi hominis, praesertim Christiani animum subeant, quae de inhumana Turcarum erga [?]ergo alios; sed multos aeque ac Christianos, feritate nan- tantur, nedum ut sub oculos veniant, facile commotura mentes sint ad auxilium ferendum captivis Christianis, & prosequendum studium, quod dicimus, de convertendis ad meliorem frugem, vel si qua fieri posset, veram fidem, Muhammedanis...
units.tr: Whether war ought to be waged against the Turks, that is, whether all Christians should join arms to attack the Turks and drive them from their places, so that those lands might be restored to Christ and the Christians, with their churches and commonwealths regained, has been debated often and at length, both in former times and today. The Roman pontiffs have always been remarkably shrewd and skilful in this matter, in urging and pushing all the princes of Europe into war against the Turks, so that while the lords, emperors, kings and princes were far away, they could plunder everything more easily, seize the lands, goods and rights of those men, and throw their affairs into confusion as they pleased. So skilled are these men at using such an occasion to their own advantage, and so long have they learned to extend their borders by it. Besides, from this they also sought in their own way the chief price for their bulls, crusades, indulgences and jubilees, a price not only of temporal and bodily kind but also of that power and arrogance, presumed to be equally spiritual. Add that their stated purpose, which is commonly put forward, is wholly superstitious, namely the recovery of the Holy Land, which should rather be called accursed, for the sake of a sepulchre and other superstitious wares devoted to the soil. I need not add what moved Luther to speak against it, along with other institutions of the Papal see: this pretext of waging war against the Turks, and those things which they call crusades. For we ought to regard the Turk, the enemy of the Christian name, as a rod in the hand of God, through which he afflicts our affairs, and through him, as a lictor, has determined to exact the punishments of the ingratitude and wickedness of Christians; this, so far, is to be borne with a good spirit, and not to be mocked with a bad mind or unfair means. In that sense Luther said: To fight against the Turks is to resist God, who visits our iniquities through them: which he first put forward in his assertion of the articles, which Pope Leo X then condemned in his bull in the year 1520, and from then on the Papalists attacked it not with mere opposition and arguments but with calumnies, so much so that Alphonsus de Castro, a Minorite, even wrote that it was a heresy against Luther in his book Against the Heresies, Book III, title War, and he makes that heresy of Luther more detestable than the Manichaean. But Luther did not simply deny that one must fight against the Turks, or that war against them is lawful, as Bellarmine openly acknowledged in On Laymen, Book III, chapter XVI, where he examines this question point by point. Rather, Luther disapproved of the manner in which, until now, the trumpet against the Turks had been sounded by the Roman bishops, for the sake of their greed and ambition, under the authority and permission of papal bulls. Concerning this, in his Assertion of his articles against the bull of Pope Leo, he said that the Turks reproach us: that we make war with bulls and letters of indulgence. But there is another misfortune, of greater disgrace and shame, that for so many years we have suffered ourselves to be flayed by the Roman impostors and legates, so often for a Turkish war, by the most shamelessly sold indulgences and privileges, devouring our money and substance, which we see has not only not gone to the purpose for which those lying and deceitful men promised it would go, but has been poured out on their most shameful lusts and pomp. But this is a lesser complaint. This is finally the most atrocious and intolerable thing of all: that by the most deceitful business of indulgences they first seized us, the most senseless creatures like brute beasts, with false persuasions, and seduced us to plunder our whole substance, until it has come to the point that not even one part is left which does not serve Roman greed, with ever new devised arts of imposition. Thus in vengeance for our iniquity God has given us, out of Rome, Turks more savage, more cruel and more insatiable than any Turks could ever be; these worse Turks, while we are still senseless, incite us by their deceptions against better Turks, so that meanwhile all our possessions are thought to be consumed under the title of a Turkish war. And in all these things the fury of the Lord has not turned away, and it is not yet understood [illegible, ~10 letters] of God, who strikes us in body and soul through us Romans, most Turkish of Turks. What then shall I say, when I see here more than four hundred prophets of Baal standing around their Ahab, and encouraging him to go up to Ramoth Gilead with their prophecies, and announcing to him all prosperity? Perhaps, as Micaiah too was hated because he prophesied nothing but evil, I too shall say to my Ahab: Go, fight against the Turks, so that you may resist the rod of God, and fall as he fell. How much more rightly would we act if first, by our prayers, or rather by a change of our whole way of life, we made God favourable! Then Caesar and the princes would set a limit to that idol of Rome, to its tyranny, its deception and its destruction of souls. For, as I too have prophesied once, although he does not listen, as far as I know, unless the Roman pontiff is brought back into order, all Christian matters are undone. Let him flee, as Christ taught, to the mountains, whoever can; or else offer yourself with confidence to the Roman murderers to die. Papacy can accomplish nothing but sin and perdition. What more do you want? But who will bring him back into order? Christ, by the illumination of his coming, and no other. Lord, who has believed our report? He who has ears to hear, let him hear, and let him abstain from a Turkish war until the name of the Pope has no power under heaven. I have spoken. What reasons are stronger than these, that they can easily be answered by the Bishop of Rochester in his Confutation of Luther's Articles, article XXIV? For Luther wishes that the war not be undertaken under the name or authority of the Pope, but that he himself must first be brought into order, if we desire a happy outcome of the war, and all the more so because he behaves more hostilely than the Turk himself against the Church and the faithful in many ways; nor should men any longer be deceived by his cunning, so that they go far away to war at his pleasure and for the satisfaction of his greed, enticed by empty bubbles, meanwhile leaving all their possessions as booty for the Papists. He judged that one must not go to war against the Turks under the Pope, or with him, or at the behest of those Papists who are accustomed to conspire against the Church to win the Pope's favour. In the year 1524 he wrote: In conclusion, I exhort, or rather I beseech, all Christians, that they join their prayers with mine for such wretched and bewitched princes, whom God, without doubt, has sent upon us, inflamed with anger, like plagues and pestilences. Let us not rashly consent to undertake the expedition, or to contribute money against the Turkish tyrant, since the Turk surpasses our princes far in skill, counsel, integrity and moderation. Is it to be hoped that God will make all things go well for such inconsiderate and improvident men against the Turk, men who do not hesitate to tempt the Supreme God and assail him with blasphemies? This is in the Latin works, Volume II, after the imperial edicts issued against him and his doctrine. For these reasons he advised against war against the Turks when it is waged in the Papal manner; but he did not condemn it simply, as he himself declared in the places cited and elsewhere, especially in the little book written to this very end in the year 1528, On the Turkish War, which is in Volume IV of the Jena edition. Erasmus indeed urged that war be brought against the Turks, in his Consultation on the Turkish War, but not simply; rather, like Luther, although he seemed rashly to differ from him, he insisted that first there should be a worthy reformation of morals among Christians, and that this war not end so unhappily as until now, because, as he speaks well, we did not carry on Christ's business, but fought against the Turks with a Turkish spirit. Besides, among the causes of our misfortune, he rightly and frankly reports that the faith solemnly given to the Turks was shamefully broken by the Christians at the instigation of the Pope. The oath, he says, violated at the instigation of Eugenius, has driven us into fatal battles. For faith is to be kept even with an enemy. And Bellarmine frankly says in this disputation that Luther does not deny that war against the Turks is lawful, because he thinks all war in general is unlawful, etc., nor because he judges that Christians have no just cause, etc. Moreover, if the name of the Pope is absent, that is, if men take up arms neither by his authority nor by his bulls; if superstition is absent, and the notion of the Holy Land, as is rashly said; if we do not wait finally for all the princes to be enlisted together for war by the Pope as if by a commander; but if we take care that aid be brought to those unjustly oppressed, and that we recover from wicked hands the dominions and churches seized, for Christ and for Christians, in that case who would doubt that a war against the Turks, the most grievous enemies of the Christian name, is justly undertaken? Certainly, more Christian expeditions against the Turks have indeed been made, but it is not easy to count many that were very fortunate. From the year 1095 to the year 1270, twelve expeditions were undertaken against the Turks and Saracens, and the last, that of Louis, King of the French, proved very unfortunate. So there was no need for the Bishop of Rochester, in reply to Luther, to make a long catalogue of those popes who stirred up kings for such wars; still less for Cornelius a Lapide, in the preface to his commentary on the Minor Prophets, to have placed among them also Eugenius IV with his legate Julian, whose names are rightly held in the greatest hatred for their treachery and for the defeat at Varna. You may read an epitome of the so-called Holy Wars, by an unknown author, in Canisius's Ancient Lessons, Volume VI, which ends, from the expedition of Duke Godfrey of Bouillon, in the year 1421. Add the four books of Benedetto Accolti of Arezzo, On the War Waged by Christians against the Barbarians, and Forbes, Historico-Theological Instruction, Book IV, chapter XX. Very many have given counsel and set down in writing how the military enterprise against the Turk could be prepared without much difficulty, among whom are Philip Camerarius, Busbecq, not to mention the oration of Callimachus Experiens, On Bringing War against the Turks; and his history, On the Venetians against the Turks; and other works collected and published on this subject in various volumes. Nor do I think the business will be of so great difficulty, if Christians did not fight among themselves. Yet I think it is not beside the point to have warned, as Paul Fagius does in his Chaldee paraphrase on Genesis 16:12, where it is said of Ismael: and he shall be a wild man among men; let those consider this today who think it easy, to overcome the Turk, who traces his descent from his very origin. But I do not wish to make my own judgment, nor a disquisition, like that of Uberto Foglietta, on the greatness and perpetual success in wars of the Turkish empire, which Henri Estienne of Paris, in his two Orations against him, moved him to make, because he seemed to have exalted the power of the Turks beyond measure. But for two reasons these things ought to be weighed again and again, whether a war is undertaken against the Turks or the Christian cause is advanced among them in any other way: first, because the Saracens, now ruling so widely, add so great a portion of the Christian churches to their empire, to the great detriment of our affairs; second, because they cruelly harass those Christians whom they bring under their power, and most wretched municipalities are destroyed. Certainly no one's lot and condition, while they live, is more miserable than that of Christians taken captive by the Turks and carried off by them, not only to every kind of slavery, but also to that denial of the faith and profession of Muhammadanism, circumcision, and the other disgraces of that perfidy, to which the Turks often compel them. But who would not be moved to see men of advanced age, youths, women, wives and children bound in gangs and dragged indiscriminately into most grievous slavery, and their bodies and lives given over to the will of the worst men? And this happens everywhere among them, while we lie prostrate and neglect with a heavy indolence the fall of others, and indeed our own. They say that Aeneas Sylvius, who was afterwards made pope and named Pius II, when he often spoke before the princes of Germany at the Diets about the miseries inflicted on Christians by the Turkish invasions, often moved the princes present to tears, by setting out the dreadful picture of all the evils which Christians suffered at the hands of the Turks. And I doubt not that when these things come to the mind of a man, especially a Christian, and what is told of the inhuman cruelty of the Turks towards others, but also towards many who are no less Christian, is not only heard but set before the eyes, the minds will easily be stirred to bring help to Christian captives, and to pursue the zeal of which we speak, of converting the Muhammadans to a better course, or, if it could be done, to the true faith...

units.la: Scio, laborare & istos quoque suis hic praejudiciis, sed quae adimi facile possunt ac debent: quo deinceps pergamus, ad persuadendam ipsis Christi fidem ac religionem. Praejudicia alia habent à sua parte; alia petunt à Christianis. Illud commune de Majoribus suis Muhammedismum amplexis, inque eodem liberos instruentibus, prout omnes innata quadam religione lubenter Parentes sequuntur. Quod apud illos quidem eo facili- us solvitur, quo Muhammed suam quum primum hominibus commendaret legem, & facto, & verbis illud obstaculum removit. Unde dicit Surat. 11. hi rogati praecepta divina observare, dicunt, se nullam nisi Patrum suorum sectam secuturos. Patres itaque si stulti ea-que fecerint, eos imitabimini? Item Surata xxx 1. Locmanni, § 20. Et cum dicitur iis, sequamini id quod coelitus demisit Deus, sc. Coranum, atque in eum credite; inquiunt: quia sequimur id, in quo (ut instituisse) invenimus patres nostros. Quid si Satanas instinctu suo, ac veluti traditione quadam, vocaret eos ad tormentum inferni, quo suggestiones ejus & idololatriae ducunt, num sequi eum vellent?
units.tr: I know these people too are held back by their own prejudices, but these can easily and should be removed, so that we may go on to persuade them of Christ's faith and religion. Some of their prejudices come from their own side; others they take from Christians. The common one concerns their ancestors, who embraced Muhammadanism and bring up their children in it, as all parents readily follow a certain innate religious instinct. Among them this objection is the more easily dissolved because Muhammad, as soon as he commended his law to men, removed that obstacle both by his deeds and by his words. Hence he says in Surat. 11: "When they are asked to observe the divine precepts, they say they will follow no sect but that of their fathers. So if the fathers were foolish and did these things, will you imitate them?" Likewise in Surat. 31 (Luqman, §20): "And when they are told, 'Follow what God has sent down from heaven, that is the Qur'an, and believe in it,' they say, 'We follow that in which we found our fathers.' What if Satan, by his own prompting and as if by some tradition, were calling them to the torment of hell, to which his suggestions and idolatry lead? Would they still want to follow him?"

units.la: Majus est, quod sumunt à Muhammedicae sectae felicitate, ejus ingenti à primis initiis progressu, & amplissimo per varias plurimasque mundi regiones dominio. Sed & hoc quoque in Alkorano suo Muhammed sic dissolvit, quod etiam incredulis Deus & impiissimis aliquando multa terrae & mundi hujus bona indulget. Surat. vi. & vii. Tum progressus doctrinae illorum neminem movebit, qui perpenderit, illam non virtute sua, sed armis, & imperio Saracenico, cui incubuit; multaque tyrannide ita dilatatam fuisse, absque quibus ipsa per se nec esset quidquam, nec valeret. Velis doctrinam velis, hoc facile ei augmentum contulit, quia composita ad voluptates omnes est, & libidines. Multam hominum partem pro communi naturæ perversitate quidem occupat, sed illam ob eandem istam rationem, nequaquam optimam.
units.tr: Greater is what they draw from the good fortune of the Muhammadan sect, its enormous progress from its first beginnings, and its vast dominion over many and various regions of the world. But Muhammad also dismisses this in his Qur'an, saying that God sometimes grants even unbelievers and the most impious many of the good things of this earth and world (Surat. 6 and 7). Nor will the spread of their doctrine move anyone who has weighed that it was not spread by its own power but by arms and the Saracen empire on which it leaned, and by much tyranny; without these it would be nothing and could not prevail of itself. Whether it is doctrine or not, this readily added to its growth, because it is framed to indulge all pleasures and lusts. It occupies a large part of mankind, owing to the common perversity of nature, but for that very reason by no means the best part.

units.la: Prejudicia eorum quod concernit, à Christianis sumista; primum capiunt scandalum ex mutuis & discordiis illorum inter se dissidiis, contentionibus, sectis, & bellis. Ad quod primum respondeo, apud Muhammedanos non minus contentionum esse, quam apud Christianos. Quod vel solum satis probat internecinum Persarum, Turcarumque odium, quo hi illos præ Christianis ipsis execrantur & fugiunt, propter causam doctrinæ etiam, quamvis utrique Muhammedicam prosessantur. Præterea dissensiones & varias sectas habent circa religionis suæ radices, ut vocant, id est, de rebus Theologicis; & circa ramos, id est, de rebus juridicis, de quibus agit Gregorius Abul-Farajius, de Origine et moribus Arabum, & Pocokius, in Notis. Tum non hoc Christianismo objiciendum, quod ei per accidens, & per hominum vitia, cum Christi doctrinâ hactenus non convenientium, evenit, quod Christiani inter se multum contendunt; & quod dicit Surata Maria, dissidentes inter se mutuo: minus illum hæc dicere oportet, qui novit, quemadmodum olim in populo Israelitico fuerunt pseudoprophetæ, ita jam quoque futuros inter Christianos falsos doctores prædictum fuisse. Denique in se descendant Muslimi, & culpam in se conjiciant ejus haud levem, dum imprecationibus suis vulgo contra Christianos orant, ut Deus inter illos foveat discordiam & bella: ubi præter seipsos, in malâ ejusmodi compræcatione; & Deum insuper causam istius, quo offendi in nobis videntur, constituunt facinoris.
units.tr: As for their prejudices that come from Christians, first they take offence at the mutual disagreements, quarrels, sects and wars among Christians themselves. To this first point I answer that there is no less contention among Muhammadans than among Christians. This alone sufficiently proves the deadly hatred of Persians and Turks, by which they execrate and shun each other even more than they shun Christians, on account of doctrine, although both profess Muhammadanism. Besides, they have dissensions and various sects concerning the "roots" of their religion, as they call them, that is, theological matters, and concerning the "branches," that is, juridical matters, as Gregory Abu'l-Faraj treats in his work on the origin and customs of the Arabs, and Pococke in his Notes. Moreover, this should not be thrown at Christianity: that it happens to Christians, by accident and through the vices of men who do not agree with Christ's doctrine, that they contend much among themselves. The words of Surata Maria, "differing among themselves," should be said less by one who knows that, just as there were false prophets among the Israelite people, so too false teachers were foretold to arise among Christians. Finally, let the Muslims look into themselves and lay upon themselves no light share of the blame, since in their curses they commonly pray against Christians that God would foster discord and wars among them. In such an evil prayer they make God himself, besides themselves, the author of the very crime by which they seem to be offended in us.

units.la: Præterea graviter adversus Christianos se habere præjudicium publice atque identidem conquerantur, ea culpa cultu tum sanctorum, tum præcipue imaginum, apud nonnullos illorum frequentato. Ubi primò turpiter peccant, qui hoc, quidquid est, Christianismo imputant, quod doctrina Christi ipsa aperte condemnat, &c. non nisi per fœdum aliquorum errorem in Christianismo obtinet. Deinde, nec id ipsum Christianis omnibus tribuendum, quod idola, quod imagines colunt, tantummodo alicui eorum parti, cui ab ipsis melioris notæ mentisque Christianis plurimis continuò reclamatum, qui illa minus ferunt vel probare possunt, quam nulli, quam Turcæ vel Muhammedani.
units.tr: Moreover, they repeatedly and publicly complain that they are gravely prejudiced against Christians by that fault, the worship of saints and, above all, of images, which is frequent among some of them. Here they first sin shamefully who impute to Christianity whatever the doctrine of Christ itself openly condemns, etc., and which holds among Christians only through the foul error of some. Next, this cannot be attributed to all Christians, that they worship idols and images, only to a part of them. Against this, very many Christians of better repute and sounder mind have constantly protested, and they bear such things less, or can approve them less, than anyone else, less even than the Turks or Muhammadans do.

units.la: Præcipuè verò cultus Mariæ ipsos offendit, adeo ut Surat. xiii. introducant Christum à Deo interrogatum, num se & matrem suam pro Diis coli in terris unquam jusserit, docuerit ne? O Iesu, fili Maria; tune hominibus suasisti, ut Deiloco Te, Matremque tuam, duos Deos haberent atque venerarentur? Quod de Christo adducunt, certe non is pro alio vel secundo Deo se coli voluit; sed qui multis argumentis probatus Deus, etiam pro eo, sed uno, & homoufio cum Patre coli debet: neque id adeo abhorrent Muhammedanorum multi, quemadmodum supra audivimus. At de ejus matre Maria juste cantantur, temere eam tali, quo Deus Christusque, honore, id est, divino à nonnullis affici. Vbi & id obiter observari potest, quod, quidquid Mariolatræ distinguunt, cultum Mariæ, à divino, adeo tamen non appareat distinctionis vis, ut nec ab aliis, nec à Muhammedanis, in disputatione adversum Nos, non adeo semper obtusæ mentis, utcumque malæ, capi possit; quin videantur Mariam venerari Papistæ, ut Deum religioso divinoque cultu.
