units.tr: Above all, the worship of Mary offends them, so much so that Surat. 13 introduces Christ being questioned by God: whether he ever ordered or taught that he and his mother be worshipped as gods on earth. "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you persuade men to take you and your mother as two gods besides God and to venerate you?" As for what they cite concerning Christ, certainly he did not wish to be worshipped as another or second God; rather, he who is proved God by many arguments must be worshipped, even as the one God, and as consubstantial with the Father. Nor do many Muhammadans shrink from this, as we heard above. But concerning his mother Mary, they rightly sing that some rashly honour her with such honour as belongs to God and Christ, that is, with divine honour. Here it may also be observed in passing that, whatever distinction the Mariolaters draw between the worship of Mary and divine worship, the force of that distinction does not appear so clearly that it can be grasped by others, or by Muhammadans in disputation against us, who are not always of dull mind, however evil. So the Papists seem to venerate Mary as God, with religious and divine worship.

units.la: Quantopere imaginibus offenduntur, ostendit Surata lxxxi. Neque alio loco habent illas, quam pro rudimento & reliquiis idololatriæ Ethnicæ. Auctor Septem Castrensis, lib de Moribus Turc. cap. xiii. non aliter illos scribit imagines detestari & horrere, religioligiosas videlicet, quam ipsum gehennæ incendium. Adeo ut Christianos ideo idolatras & cultores daemonum vocent, inquit cap. x. Quare idem testatur, quod etiam, in Chio insula quando degeret, & legatis Turcicis forte ostendentibus suorum templa, inque illis imagines, obortaque super illis disputatione, nequiquam satisfacere potuerit, quin identidem regeterent: vos idola colitis. Quod idem sibi quoque evenisse scribit Hugo Linschoten, Itinerar. lib. 1. cap. xliii. quando Maurorum templa ingressus esset cum Lusitanis, qui ex illis interrogabant, ubi forte ipsorum Sancti essent, quos colerent, quum in templis adeo nil imaginis observaretur, solummodo tabula, cui aliquid ex Alkorano Arabicè inscriptum erat: responderbant Mauri, se non, quemadmodum Lusitani, lignum & lapides, sed solum Deum adorare. Turpe profecto, à Mauris, à Muhammedanis, quos nos quidem infidelium loco habemus, ista objici Christianis, & hos se ita gerere, ut aliquâ in re Ethnicis similes arguantur ab illis, quos alias non multum supra Ethnicos ipsi æstimant. Et certe differri non possumus, turpem hac in re; & Ethnicorum idololatriâ haud adeo dissimilem, committi à Papistis, in imaginum veneratione, superstitionem, contra expressum Dei mandatum, cujus violatione pariter Iudæi & Muhammedani, nobiscum offenduntur. Nam & Iudæi primo loco objiciunt, quod imagines Christiani, perinde ac Gentiles idola sua, colunt; & quod hujus rei causa, præceptum in Decalogo secundum, temerario & sacrilego ausu adulterant. Profecto horribilis & detestanda res, in re tam manifeste malâ, quam & Gentilium potiores damnarunt olim, tantum facere religioni præjudicium, & in aliorum conversione sive Muhammedanorum, sive Iudæorum procurandâ, obstaculum! Iohannes Baptista Montalbanus, in Rer. Turcic. Commentario, sententiam Muhammedanorum explicans, ait: non cohibere parietibus Deum. neque in ullam humani oris speciem assimilare, sed magnitudine cælestium arbitrentur. quæ ipsa verba Taciti sunt, describentis mores Veterum Germanorum. Adeo ejusdem sententiæ sunt Muhammedani, cum antiquis Germanis, sub Ethnicismo qui olim fuerunt, atque hac in parte plurimis hodiernis nepotibus, Christianis dictis, parentes multo meliores. Iohannes Cantacuzenus, Apol. III. contra Mahometem: post alia vero crimina, quibus a Musulmanis nos qui Christum profitemur accusamur, etiam in hoc ab iisdem accusamur, quod sanctorum adoremus imagines. Et quid adoramus? profecto nam aliud quam ligna, colores, & lapides. Quinimo justum scandalum inde capiunt rudes illi & increduli homines. Bene hac de re Thomas à Iesu, Carmelitanus Monachus, de conversi Gent. lib. x. pag. 706. Habet hæc secta quedam & probabilia & laudabilia. Deoque grata, ob quæ videntur non sine causa tolerari à Deo. Hæc enim secta maxime odit & detestatur idololatriam, prorsus adeo, ut nullas vel Dei vel Angelorum, vel sanctorum hominum imagines in solum mente colat, sed nullo etiam in loco depingi patiatur, sicut etiam in Veteri testamento, Deus omnium imaginem. Iudaeis veneratio- nem & cultum interdixit. Atque frustrea Idem pag. 644. inter errores doctrinæ Muhammedicæ collocat, quod improperat Christianis adorationem imaginum. Nam non in eo errorem notare debuerat, quod alias urgente conscientia videtur probare & laudare in illis ceu Deo gratum: neque enim aliam ob causam adeo imagines, quam quia idololatriam, refugiunt Muhammedani; & illud ut ethnicum jure habent, in quo Gentilium maxime conspicua semper fuit & execranda idololatria. Philippus Guadagnolus, Apol. cap. VIII. sect. xi. pag. 147. addit, alloquitur adversarium suum Ahmedem Persam, nos in cultu sanctarum imaginum & crucis predicto, idololatriam exercere. Imo vero hoc addit, & quamdiu non omittitis, vos pecca-re fe graviter, & confirmare in infidelitate sua miseros homines objecto isto scandalo, omnes asserimus; eoque gravius, quod illi non id capiunt pro aliquorum inter Christianos vitio, quemadmodum eos hoc interpretari oportebat, sed pro praxi & doctrina omnium Christianorum; quod salsissimum: & Pontificii quando ex Christi doctrina, cultum imaginum comprobare satagunt, maximam sanctissimo nomini impingunt calumniam. Huc etiam spectat, quod in sui temporis historia augustissima refert Iac. Augustus Thuanus lib. xliii, de Mauriscis, quod xx. virgines Christianas ex voto maclassent, quarum capita sparsis capillis pro valvis templi adhuc prostabant, totidemque idolorum cultores, ita Sacerdotes nostros, quod ante imagines procidant, vocant, se sacrificaturos proximo conventu jurassent. Adeo idololatriam interpretatur illa Gens imaginum cultum, & earum cultores idololatras. Refert Matthias a Michou, lib. de Sarmatia Asiatica. cap. v. quod postquam P. Innocentius iv. anno cIↄ ccxlv i. ad magnum Cham misisset Ascelinum, aliosque, pro convertendis ad fidem Christi Tataris; mox etiam, post discessum Christianorum, advenerint legati Sarracenorum, suadentes ut Tatari potius ipsorum, id est, Muhammedicam amplecterentur fidem, additis rationibus, suam esse faciliorem & tolerabiliorem, voluptatibus plenam, utrisque belligeris convenientiorem; Christianorum autem religionem confitendo dicebant esse stultorum, imbecillium, & idololatrarum imagines colentium. Magnum ergo hoc scandalum, pro quo extenuando verbum non facimus, ut quidem Pontificii plurima hic afferre coguntur, ad diluendum istud praejudicium: ubi illis evenit, quod iis qui in coeno volutantur, quo plura ad excusandum malum suum afferunt, eo turpius se dant, quum non nisi omissione & detestatione corrigi hoc quidquid est, possit. Nos interim precamur Deum, ut meliorem mentem indat illis, quicunque culpae istius rei sunt, utque perpendant dant tandem quid sanctum istud, quo inter Christianos veniunt, nomen mereatur, ut amoveant praeter alia, & hoc tantae rei, ac est conversio infidelium, gravissimum impedimentum.
units.tr: The Surah lxxxi shows how greatly they are offended by images. Elsewhere they regard them only as the remnants and relics of Gentile idolatry. The author of the Septem Castrensis, in his book on the customs of the Turks, chapter xiii, writes that they abhor and detest images, meaning religious images, no less than the fire of hell. So much so, he says in chapter x, that they call Christians idolaters and worshippers of demons. For this reason he also reports that when he was staying on the island of Chios, and some Turkish envoys happened to show him their temples and the images in them, a dispute arose, and however hard he tried he could not satisfy them, for they kept retorting: you worship idols. Hugo Linschoten writes that the same thing happened to him in Itinerary, book 1, chapter xliii, when he entered the temples of the Moors with some Portuguese. The Portuguese asked them where their saints were, whom they worshipped, since there was no image at all to be seen in the temples, only a tablet with something from the Alkoran written on it in Arabic. The Moors replied that they did not worship wood and stone as the Portuguese did, but worshipped God alone. It is certainly shameful that Christians should be charged with such things by Moors and Muhammadans, whom we indeed count among the unbelievers, and that these people should behave in such a way that in some matter they are judged by those people to be like the Gentiles, whom in other respects they themselves do not rate much above the Gentiles. And indeed we cannot deny that in this matter the Papists commit a superstition that is shameful and not very different from the idolatry of the Gentiles, in the veneration of images, against the express command of God, by the violation of which both Jews and Muhammadans are offended along with us. For the Jews too first of all object that Christians worship images just as the Gentiles worship their idols, and that for this reason they rashly and sacrilegiously corrupt the second commandment of the Decalogue. Truly a horrible and detestable thing, in a matter so manifestly wrong, to do so great harm to religion, and to create an obstacle to the conversion of others, whether Muhammadans or Jews! John Baptist Montalbanus, in his Commentary on Turkish Affairs, explaining the opinion of the Muhammadans, says: they do not think God is to be confined within walls, nor likened to any form of the human face, but they think of him in terms of the greatness of the heavenly things. These very words are those of Tacitus, describing the customs of the ancient Germans. So entirely of the same mind are the Muhammadans with the ancient Germans, who once lived under Gentilism, and in this respect they are far better parents than many modern descendants who are called Christians. John Cantacuzenus, Apology III against Mahomet: Besides the other crimes for which we who profess Christ are accused by the Musulmans, we are accused by them also in this, that we venerate the images of the saints. And what do we venerate? Surely nothing but wood, colours and stones. Indeed those rude and unbelieving men take just offence from this. Thomas à Iesu, the Carmelite monk, writes well on this matter in On the Conversion of the Gentiles, book x, page 706: This sect has certain things that are both probable and praiseworthy, and pleasing to God, for which they seem not without cause to be tolerated by God. For this sect hates and detests idolatry above all, to such an extent that it worships in the mind no images of God, angels or holy men, and does not allow them to be painted in any place, just as in the Old Testament God forbade the Jews any veneration and worship of an image. And in vain the same author, on page 644, counts among the errors of Muhammadan doctrine that it reproaches the Christians for the adoration of images. For he ought not to have marked this as an error, since in that matter the sect seems, under pressure of conscience, to approve and praise it as pleasing to God. Indeed the Muhammadans have no other reason for shunning images so much than that they shun idolatry; and they rightly regard it as a Gentile practice, in which the most conspicuous and detestable idolatry of the Gentiles has always consisted. Philip Guadagnolo, Apology, chapter VIII, section xi, page 147, addresses his adversary Ahmed the Persian and adds: we, in the aforesaid worship of holy images and of the cross, practise idolatry. Indeed he adds this, and we all assert that as long as you do not give it up, you sin gravely and confirm in their unbelief wretched men, by this stumbling-block; and all the more gravely because they do not take it as the fault of some among the Christians, as they ought to have interpreted it, but as the practice and doctrine of all Christians, which is most false. And when the Papists strive to prove the worship of images from the doctrine of Christ, they heap the greatest calumny upon his most holy name. To this also belongs what Jacques-Auguste de Thou reports in the most august history of his own time, book xliii, concerning the Moriscos, that twenty Christian virgins were sacrificed in fulfilment of a vow, whose heads, with their hair dishevelled, were still exposed as the doors of the temple, and as many worshippers of idols, as they call our priests, had sworn that they would sacrifice at the next assembly, falling down before the images. So that nation interprets the worship of images as idolatry, and those who worship them as idolaters. Matthias a Michou, in his book on Asiatic Sarmatia, chapter v, reports that after Pope Innocent IV in the year 1245 had sent Ascelinus and others to the Great Khan to convert the Tatars to the faith of Christ, soon after the departure of the Christians, envoys of the Saracens arrived, urging the Tatars rather to embrace their own faith, that is, the Muhammadan, adding reasons that it was easier and more tolerable, full of pleasures, and more suited to both warlike peoples. Confessing the religion of the Christians, they said, was the part of fools and weaklings, and of idolaters who worship images. This is therefore a great stumbling-block, and we do not make light of it, as the Papists are indeed forced to bring forward many arguments to remove this prejudice. In this they fare as those who wallow in mud: the more they bring forward to excuse their evil, the more shamefully they behave, since this whatever it is can be corrected only by giving it up and condemning it. Meanwhile we pray God that he may give a better mind to those who are guilty of this fault, and that they may at last weigh what this holy name, under which they come among Christians, deserves, so that they may remove, besides other things, this most serious hindrance to so great a matter as the conversion of unbelievers.

units.la: Sed uti illa sunt praejudicia, ad conversionem Muhammedanorum, quae cavere & corrigere ante omnia oportet, ita ad promovendum opus, duo quidem omnino sunt necessaria. Primum est linguae Arabicae cognitio, qua Alkoran scriptum, tum ejus, qua utuntur Muhammedani, quibuscum nobis forte futura sit res: alterum, missio ad illas oras istorum, qui ei negotio habeantur. apti. | Prae omnibus praedicandum hic exemplum Nicolai Clenardi, Grammaticae illius Graecae Auctoris, quam Vossius postea expolivit & perfecit, & qui in praefatione etiam de Clenardo illud memorat; uti & Possevinus, in Biblioth. lib. ix. cap. ix. de Indeis. Thomas à Iesu, de Converf. Gent. lib. x. pag. 7. 29. Melchior Adamus, in vitis Germanorum Philosophorum, pag. 123. dignum exemplum, quod commendemus, quodque omnibus & Studiosis & Theologis serio proponamus, non ob linguam addiscendam solum, sed ad imitandum etiam viri istius in promovenda Saracenorum conversione studium. Dieštemo, oppido Brabantiae oriundus Clenardus, singulari cupiditate flagrabat linguae Arabicae, quam suâ etiam disciplinâ accendit praeceptor ejus Latomus. Quare non satis habens nosse Graecas Hebraeasque litteras, quas in Academiâ Lovaniensi docebat, linguam Arabicam, cujus gustum ex commentariis Hebraicis jam ceperat, & analogiam cum Hebraeâ viderat, illis adjungere conatus est, usus initio solo Psalterio Nubiensi. Interim in Hispaniam accitus, libros hic Arabicos primum vidit atque evolvit, docuitque Salmanticae Graecas litteras, tanto auditorio, ac usque eo in Hispania visum fuerat nullum, & in Arabicis quidem spatio sex mensium tantum profecit, ut linguam non jam scifeiret solum, sed & alios doceret. Evocatus hinc à Rege in aulam fuit, ad fratris Henrici, Archiepiscopi Braccarensis, institutionem: verùm sedari omnibus illis ardor ejus non potuit, nisi ipsos adiret in Africâ Arabes, & se conferret in celeberrimam Academiam Fesanam, ubi non linguæ adeo (quam jam prompte loquebatur, & quâ ipsum Regem salutare novus hospes poterat), ac quidem religioni ipsorum, & Alkorano pernoscendis haud segniter incubuit. Epistolas ejus habemus Peregrinationum, ac de rebus Muchometicis, scriptas ad Iacobum Latomum præceptorem suum, & Franciscum Howerium, ab anno clo Io xxxv. & deinceps, usque ad annum xli. quum propositisset abesse tantum triennio: de quo in litteris suis ita alicubi conqueritur: putabam me triennio tantum abfuturum, at nonus agitur annus exilii, & nescio quo me jaclet litterarum amor. Litteris istis animum, & rationem studii sui omnem exponit. Eâ, quam Fesâ scripsit, ad Latomum, epistolâ, x. xli. quæque summam ferè comprehendit suarum peregrinationum, inquit: Cum incæpissem Granatæ legere Alcoranum, & miscendis colloquiis cum domestico præceptore, cognovissem quam fædis erroribus dementata esset gens ista Muchometica, sive sic temerè venit in mentem, sive Deus hunc laborem mihi objicere voluit, certè cæpi consilium, ut omissis linguis omnibus, in quibus hactenus studium posuissem, jam in reliquum vitæ spatium me devovarem Arabicis, nec quiescerem, donec sic promovissem; ut & viva voce præsens, & absens tolerabilia calamo, possem cum illis in arenam dogmatum descendere, & simul meo exemplo provocarem, siquis forte hanc Theologiæ partem mecum vellet amplecti. Deinde: Ego vero in Brabantia statui fundamenta jacere, respondique non mea consilia destinari Granatensibus, qui inquisitionis metu simulant Christianismum, sed eos me somniare milites, qui cum Muchometistis ipsis possint confligere: & ibi nobis aliquando pugnandum esse, ubi aperte dogma profitentur Machometicum: nullum esse [illegible, ~3 letters]se certamen, ubi nemo se præbeat hostem. Hunc scopum studiis meis propositi, quòd ita crederem me fructum è capessendis linguis reportaturum, si eas accommodarem pietati. Mundus cœpit Græcari, & Hebraicari, sane ornamentum accessit hominibus studiosis. Verùm si hac via prorogata fuissent Christianæ religionis pomeria, vera gratulandi esset occasio. Quando ergo in Arabismum revoluta est mea peregrinatio, non me movit quod author dicerer professionis Arabicæ, non ut medicis operam præberem restituendo Avicennæ, aut Philosophis, corrigendo Averroës: sed hoc tantum ante oculos fero, ut quemadmodum contra cæteros hæreticos scribunt Latinè, sic adversus Machometistas stylum stringerem Arabicum. Id fieri non potest nisi illorum dogmata penitus habeamus cognita, nec credamus quid in Latinorum libris de illis nationibus jactatum sit. Sed quod suis libris illi ferunt, id arripiamus, & contra id arma capiamus. Præter Alcoranum habent libros Summæ tam ridiculos, ut ipsi sese possint confutare, nisi persuasum esset, Machometum fuisse prophetam veracem. Ex iis deprommenda sunt, contra quæ velis pugnare. Ego igitur putavi hos libros mihi conquirendos, & re communicata cum doctis Theologis, ad me proprie hanc revocandam provinciam, primum ut linguam discerem, deinde rationes doctorum in Arabicam verterem. Neque enim omnes possunt Arabicari, quamvis multi queant Machometum impugnare. Et contra Machometum Latinè scribere, quid pertinet ad tot orbis nationes, quæ solam linguam norunt Arabicam? Non piguit ista ob rei præstantiam describere, & singulis ob oculos ponere, quo videant, quid hac agendum sit. Imo certe veri, & salutaris notitiæ linguarum, cum aliarum, tum Arabicæ fructus est, non ad ostentationem illas circumferre, vel in vertendis aut exponendis scriptis sæcularibus semper hærere, sed homines illarum adminiculo in verâ Christi fide & pietate instruere, infideles convertere, promovendo regno Christi illas consecrare & insumere. Hæc demum sunt Christiani hominis, mis, & in linguis erudit[?] studia. Beatus, qui in istis laborem posuit suum, quemque Dominus adveniens repererit servum multo melius. Matth. xxiv. 46. Post illa Clenardus non diu supervixit, adeo ut exsequi & perficere animi sui instituta minime potuerit, quippe obiisse dicitur anno clɔ Iɔ xlı i. Granatae: verum probatur Deo etiam bonae voluntatis egregium rudimentum, & ad aemulationem volet aliis, quibus Deus mentem, vires, & occasionem ad istiusmodi benignissime elargitur. Iam ante scripserat: Certe non extant apud nos monumenta hujus sectae tam enucleata, ut si cum Machometistis congredi velis, cistra dubium eorum mysteria possis asseverare. Hoc omnino verum puto, non esse nobis eos Arabices, qui cum peritis disceptent, quales habuimus adversus Graecos. Quaeres cum gratia Dei, me nactum videam, ut viam aliquam ad hanc rem muniam, non est negligenda occasio. Nisi mihi librorum defuerit copia, stat sententia fideliter Latinis depromere quicquid in ea superstitione positum est. Ac primum mente tendum est Alcoranus, non ille quidem nudus ejiciendus vulgo, sed adjectis scholiis, & suis, aliorumque Doctorum confessus hic illic jaculis. Quod si tam magno animo Clenardi non defuerint opes (nam Regium somnio somnium) longe majora tentabimus. Quid quaeso? Libri isti Hebraici quos Venetiis imprimit Bomberg, in omnes orbis partes ad Hebraeos navigant, in Africam, in Aethiopiam, in Indiam, Aegyptum, & cetera Judaeorum domicilia. Nos Alcoranos imprimemus, cum versione Latina, & omnibus in locis ubi ab Evangelio defecimus, nostrum habebimus praesidium, tum Latine, tum Arabice. Quam velim ut quis talem nobis aliquando det Alkoranum, juxta cum versione Latina! quod magnum certe in hisce rebus praeberet adjumentum.
units.tr: But just as those are the prejudices that must above all be guarded against and corrected in the conversion of the Muslims, so for advancing the work there are indeed two things absolutely necessary. The first is a knowledge of the Arabic language, both that in which the Alcoran is written and that which the Muslims use, with whom we may happen to have dealings. The second is a mission to those regions where people suited to this task are available. Above all, the example of Nicolaus Clenardus deserves to be commended here, the author of that Greek grammar which Vossius later polished and perfected, and who mentions Clenardus in the preface. So also Possevinus, in the Bibliotheca, book 9, chapter 9, on the Indians; Thomas à Jesu, On the Conversion of the Gentiles, book 10, pages 7 and 29; and Melchior Adam, in the Lives of the German Philosophers, page 123. It is a worthy example, which we commend and which we seriously put before all students and theologians, not only for learning the language but also for imitating the zeal of that man in promoting the conversion of the Saracens. Clenardus, a native of Diest, a town in Brabant, burned with a singular desire for the Arabic language, which his teacher Latomus also kindled by his own instruction. So, not content to know the Greek and Hebrew letters, which he taught at the University of Louvain, he tried to add to them the Arabic language, the taste of which he had already gained from Hebrew commentaries and whose affinity with Hebrew he had seen, beginning with a Nubian Psalter alone. Meanwhile, summoned to Spain, he first saw and read through Arabic books there, and he taught Greek literature at Salamanca to an audience so large that none had ever been seen in Spain up to that time. In Arabic, within a space of only six months, he made such progress that he not only knew the language but could also teach others. Called from there by the King to the court, to instruct the brother of Henry, Archbishop of Braga, he could not, however, have his ardour satisfied by all those things, unless he went himself to the Arabs in Africa and betook himself to the famous Academy at Fez, where he applied himself diligently not so much to the language (which he already spoke fluently, and in which a new arrival could greet the King himself) as to the religion of the Muslims and the knowledge of the Alcoran. We have his letters on his travels and on Muhammadan matters, written to his teacher Jacobus Latomus and to Franciscus Howerius from the year 1535 onwards, until the year 1541, when he had intended to be away only three years. He complains of this somewhere in his letters: I thought I would be away only three years, but it is now the ninth year of my exile, and I do not know to what place the love of letters is driving me. In these letters he sets out his whole purpose and method of study. In the letter he wrote to Latomus from Fez, dated 10 October 1541, which almost sums up the course of his travels, he says: When I had begun to read the Alcoran at Granada, and by mixing discussions with my household teacher, I had learned how that Muhammadan people was infected with foul errors, whether this idea came to me by chance or God wished to place this labour before me, I certainly began the plan, that, leaving aside all the languages in which I had hitherto been engaged, I should devote myself for the rest of my life to Arabic, and not rest until I had advanced so far that I could both in person by the living voice and in absence by the pen, bear myself well with them, and descend into the arena of doctrines, and at the same time by my example challenge anyone who might perhaps wish to embrace this part of theology with me. Then: But I have decided to lay the foundations in Brabant, and I have replied that my plans are not aimed at the Granadans, who pretend Christianity from fear of the Inquisition, but that I am dreaming of soldiers who can contend with the Muhammadans themselves; and that we must one day fight where they openly profess the Muhammadan doctrine: that there is no [illegible] contest where no one presents himself as an enemy. This aim I proposed for my studies, because I believed I would reap fruit from taking up the languages, if I applied them to piety. The world began to become Greek and Hebrew, and surely an ornament came to studious men. But if the boundaries of the Christian religion had been extended by this way, there would have been a true occasion for rejoicing. Therefore, when my journey turned to Arabic, I was not moved by the fact that I might be called an author of the Arabic profession, nor by the thought of serving physicians by restoring Avicenna, or philosophers by correcting Averroes; but I keep this only before my eyes, that just as they write in Latin against other heretics, so I might take up the Arabic pen against the Muhammadans. This cannot be done unless we have thoroughly known their doctrines, and do not believe what is boasted in Latin books about those nations. But let us take up what they themselves put forward in their books, and take up arms against that. Besides the Alcoran they have books of Summae so ridiculous that they could refute themselves, unless it were persuaded that Muhammad was a true prophet. From these must be drawn the things against which you wish to fight. I therefore thought that these books should be sought out by me, and, the matter having been shared with learned theologians, that this task should be undertaken by me in particular: first that I might learn the language, then that I might translate the arguments of the learned into Arabic. For not all can write in Arabic, although many can assail Muhammad. And what is the use of writing in Latin against Muhammad for so many nations of the world, who know only the Arabic language? I have not been reluctant to describe these things because of the importance of the matter, and to set them before everyone's eyes, so that they may see what must be done in this. Indeed, the true and salutary fruit of knowing languages, both others and Arabic, is not to carry them about for show, or always to stick at translating or expounding secular writings, but to instruct people in the true faith and piety of Christ by their help, to convert unbelievers, and to consecrate and expend them in promoting the kingdom of Christ. These, in the end, are the studies of a Christian man, and of those trained in languages. Blessed is he who has put his labour into these things, and whom the Lord, when he comes, will find doing so; a servant who does much better. Matt. 24:46. After these things Clenardus did not live long, so that he could not carry out and complete the purposes of his mind; for he is said to have died at Granada in the year 1542. Yet God also approves the excellent beginning of a good will, and it stirs others to emulation, to whom God most kindly grants the mind, strength and opportunity of this kind. He had already written earlier: Certainly there are not among us any monuments of this sect so clearly set out, that if you wish to engage with the Muhammadans you could assert their mysteries without doubt. I think this is wholly true: that we have no Arabic scholars who can dispute with the skilled, such as we had against the Greeks. You will ask, if by the grace of God I find myself with the means to clear some way for this matter, the opportunity is not to be neglected. Unless the supply of books fails me, I intend faithfully to bring out in Latin whatever is set down in that superstition. And first of all the Alcoran must be attended to, not indeed to be thrown out bare to the common people, but with scholia added, and with confessions from its own and other doctors here and there as darts. But if great-souled Clenardus did not lack resources (for a royal dream is a dream), we shall attempt far greater things. What, I ask? The Hebrew books which Bomberg prints at Venice sail to the Hebrews in all parts of the world, into Africa, Ethiopia, India, Egypt, and other dwelling-places of the Jews. We shall print Alcorans, with a Latin translation, and in all places where we have fallen short of the Gospel we shall have our defence, both in Latin and in Arabic. How I would wish that someone would one day give us such an Alcoran, side by side with a Latin translation! This would certainly afford a great aid in these matters.

units.la: Mirum, quod de Methodo, quâ Mubammedani in Scholis suis docent Arabicam. Clenardus scribit. Est apud eos hic mos: statim à primis annis ad verbum ediIoann. Alcoranum, & insigunt memoriae librum quem non intelligunt. Nec tamen ullis in scholis hic comparet todex: sed ludimagister e memoria depromit pensum, & in tabula lignea describit, id puer reponit in animo, & postridie alterum scribitur pensum, donec annis, aut biennii spatio, totum ediscat Alcoranum. Multo plures reperias qui teneant sic Alcoranum, quam qui ipsum habent domi codicem. Idem de isto docendi discendique in Schölis ordine, ex Leone Africano, refert Descriptio Arabiae, pag. 353. in historia Fesae, cujus urbis Academia est celeberrima: nusquam sic fervet Alkoranus ut hic Fesae. Tunc et florebant & caeterae omnes disciplinae, at Fesae post Grammaticam, totis sunt in Alkorana & Doctoribus Scholasticis, inquit in epistolis suis Glenardus.
units.tr: It is remarkable what method the Muhammedans follow in their schools when they teach Arabic, as Clenardus writes. Their custom is this: from their earliest years they learn the Koran word for word by heart and fix in their memory a book they do not understand. Yet no codex appears in any of their schools. The schoolmaster recites the lesson from memory and writes it on a wooden tablet, the boy takes it into his mind, and the next day another part is written out, until in a year or two, or over two years, he has learned the whole Koran by heart. You will find far more people who keep the Koran in this way than who have a copy of it at home. Leo Africanus gives an account of the same order of teaching and learning in schools, in his Description of Arabia, p. 353, in the history of Fez, whose academy is very famous: nowhere does the Koran flourish as it does at Fez. In his letters Clenardus says that at that time all the other disciplines also flourished there, but at Fez, after grammar, everything is devoted to the Koran and the scholastic doctors.

units.la: Ecquis non jure miretur, quando legerit consilium hoc a Thoma Campanella Monarchę suo suggeri, quod habet lib. de Monarch. Hispan. cap. x. Septimo Scholas linguae Graece & Hebraicae claudat, quia hac imperio exitiosum tulerunt, atque haereses hodie potissimum illis nituntur, contra vero introducat Arabicam, qua Muhametani convincantur, & Transalpini in coarguendis Turcis, non vero Catholici occupati sint? Itane claudet Monarcha Hispanus Scholas omnes linguae Graecae, & Hebraicae? hem barbaram vocem: nempe haereses potissimum illis nituntur. Felices sane haereses; (nihil quam doctrinam nostram intelligit) quae tam excellens habent bonarum litterarum praesidium, & quibus hoc testimonii dat magnus earum adversarius. Contra Maturinus Simonius, in elegānti libello, de literis perennibus, in eos graviter invehitur, qui defectionis causam linguis attribuunt: invitus repeto quosdam turpissime sua defectionis causam linguarum Hebraica, Graeca, & Latina, reflorescentii cognitioni attribuere. Revera autem a Linguis, earumque revirescentia magnum reformationi accessit auxilium & honestamentum. Quod de Arabica dicit Campanella, facile nos, verum una cum Hebraea. brea, Graecaque lingua, & his quidem supra illam, utpote divinioribus, admittimus.
units.tr: Who would not rightly be astonished when he reads the advice which Tommaso Campanella gives to his monarch, in his book on the Spanish monarchy, ch. 10: "Let the king close the schools of Greek and Hebrew, since these have brought ruin to the empire, and heresies today rest chiefly on them; on the contrary, let him introduce Arabic, by which the Muhammedans are refuted, and let the Transalpine peoples be busy refuting the Turks, not the Catholics." Will the Spanish monarch really close all the schools of Greek and Hebrew? Ah, what a barbarous word! Heresies, he says, rest chiefly on them. Happy heresies indeed, which have such an excellent defence of good letters, and to which their great adversary gives this testimony! (He understands nothing but our doctrine.) On the other hand, Maturin Cordier Simon, in his elegant little book On Perennial Letters, attacks severely those who attribute the cause of the defection to languages. I reluctantly repeat that some shamefully ascribe the cause of their defection to the revival of knowledge of the Hebrew, Greek and Latin languages. In truth, the languages and their revival have brought great help and ornament to the Reformation. What Campanella says of Arabic we readily admit, but along with Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and indeed above those, as being more divine.

units.la: Sed de linguâ addiscendâ res minus difficilis, quam de missione ad Mahommedanorum loca & regiones instituendâ: quare quid hic consuli possit, videamus. Vel enim ad hanc rem seminaria in Scholis & Academiis instituenda erunt eorum qui ad hanc provinciam instruantur: quemadmodum ejusmodi seminaria in Ecclesiâ Romanâ ad variorum hominum & partium conversionem habentur Romae, atque alibi. Aut illis totum committendum negotium erit, qui spontaneo motu excitati ad hoc opus eò se lubenter conferunt: aut qui occasione sive mercaturae, quae in illas partes dirigitur, sive Reipublicae nostrae negotiorum, Legati, iisque comites adjuncti Concionatores, homines illos & loca frequentant. Bene autem providere omnes oportet, quid suarum partium sit, quid occulta & efficax in animis Dei vocatio, quid officii ratio, proximorum salus, infidelium conversio, oblataque ad eam occasio, à nobis postulent, siquando Macedonem videmur audire acclamantem: Transiens in Macedoniam, adjuva nos. Act. XVI. 9. Ego existimo, illa in Scholis juventuti, & candidatis Theologiae ac ministerii nonnunquam inculcanda esse, ut sciant omnes, quae quantaque à nobis requirantur, & ut cogitationes ultra parvum aliquorum hominum distractum, intra quem nimis arcte nos incarceramus, & securi aliorum exterorumque fidei vivimus, extendere oporteat, saepiusque exigendam à nobis officii rationem esse, an praeterquam nostris inter quos vivimus, infidelibus quoque & remotioribus, qui salvari nisi vel per nostrum, vel per aliorum ad eos accessum & praedicationem possunt, à nobis satisfiat? quomodo vero credent de quo non audierunt? & quomodo audient absque concionatore? Rom. X. 14. Diligenter expendendum, annon idem quod alii nobis fecerunt, & quas molestias ad nos vel Majores nostros convertendos sumse-runt, vicissim nos quoque aliis impendere decet, & quae plura hanc spectantia ad commovendum animum sibi quis objicere tum potest, tum debet. Ante omnia vero eum, qui operi huic admovendus sit, praeterquam serum suarum bene scientem, & vitae probae atque οικείως esse decet: nullibi enim magis vitae officii improbitas, quam apud eos quos convertere velimus, quique ob imbecillitatem non possunt scandala data fortiori animo ac fide digerere & inoffenso pede praeterire. Eo magis, quo in externa morum disciplina, ipsi saepe infideles Turcae, & Muhammedani cum Christianorum vulgo certare possunt de modestia, aliisque in vita civili moribus: adeo quidem ut Auctor Septem Castrensis hoc argumento se nonnihil aliquando commotum scribat, & tentatum ad illorum sequendas partes. Cap. IX. Quis enim, non dirq-simplex tantum, sed etiam sapiens, quisque, non moveretur primâ fronte, videndo tantam compositionem morum in ipsis insidelibus? omnem enim levitatem in quibuscumque actibus eorum, & gestis, vestitu & apparatu, detestantur sicut ignem, & abominantur sicut pestem. Videntes enim levitatem Christianorum in vestitu & equitatu, & aliis quibuscumque derident, & eas capras & simias vocant. Honestissimum enim modum, imo religiosissimum habens in vestitu tam mares, quam foeminae, tam majores, quam minores, tam curiales etiam quam ipsi rustici & villani. Et ita communem & simplicem, ut omnino nihil indecentiae vel inhonestatis, seu superfluitatis, vel curiositatis vel levitatis in eis possit deprehendi vel notari. De his autem, qui religiosiores & devotiores habentur, quid dicam? tantum enim simplicitatis, & conformitatis & singularis apparentiae & exemplaritatis ostendunt in actibus, gestis & motibus & vestimentis, ut eos aliquem modum regularis observantiae credere profess os. Confer eundem, cap. x. xi. xii. & quae respondet cap. xix. Quando ergo videmus illos haud segniter curare civilem modestiam, nonnunquam Dei iram ... [illegible, ~40 letters] ... convertendos, videlicet à vitâ & viâ malâ ad meliorem. Aute omnia corrigenda & sanctificanda est vita nostra, si quid vel disputatione vel bello contra illos evicturos nos speramus. Fateor equidem, non parvam difficultatem continere hoc, de quo impraesentiarum loquimur, conversionis Muhammedanorum negotium, sed attollendae cogitationes sunt, & tum praestantia, utilitas, atque necessitas operis intuenda, tum respicienda Dei supremi benedictio, & favor, & potentia in opere promovendo, atque sanctificando. Procul dubio qui audierit & observare etiam aliquatenus studuerit illud: ite, docete omnes gentes; experturus quoque est vim annexae promissionis: & ecce, ego vobiscum ero omnibus diebus, usque ad consummationem mundi.
units.tr: But learning the language is a less difficult matter than undertaking a mission to the places and regions of the Muhammedans. Let us see, then, what counsel can be given here. For this work, either seminaries will have to be set up in schools and academies, in which those who are to be trained for this task are instructed, just as such seminaries exist in the Roman Church at Rome and elsewhere for the conversion of various kinds of people and parties. Or the whole business will have to be committed to those who, stirred by a spontaneous impulse, gladly betake themselves to this work; or to those who frequent those lands and places on the occasion either of trade, which is directed to those parts, or of the affairs of our commonwealth, as envoys, with preachers attached as their companions. Everyone must indeed take care to see what is his part, what the hidden and effective calling of God in men's hearts requires, what the reason of duty, the salvation of neighbours, the conversion of unbelievers, and the opportunity offered for it require of us, when we seem to hear the Macedonian crying out: Come over into Macedonia and help us. Acts 16:9. I think these things ought sometimes to be impressed upon young students and candidates of theology and the ministry, so that all may know what and how great things are required of us, and so that they may extend their thoughts beyond the narrow circle of a few people, within which we shut ourselves up too tightly and live securely in the faith of others and of outsiders. And they should often be reminded that we must give account of our duty, whether we have satisfied it not only towards those among whom we live, but also towards unbelievers and more distant peoples, who cannot be saved unless through our approach to them or that of others, and through preaching. But how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? Rom. 10:14. We must carefully consider whether we ought not to do for others what they have done for us, and to undertake, in turn, the troubles they took to convert us and our forefathers; and whatever else bears on this, which one can and should set before himself to move his mind. Above all, the man who is to be put to this work ought, besides being well versed in his own tongue, to be of an upright life and [οικείως] fitting. For nowhere is the disgrace of a bad life greater than among those whom we wish to convert, who, through weakness, cannot bear the scandals given with a stronger spirit and faith, nor pass them by with an unhurt foot. All the more so because in outward discipline of morals the unbelieving Turks and Muhammedans themselves can vie with the common run of Christians in modesty and other civil customs. So much so that the author of the Septem Castrensis writes that he was once somewhat moved by this argument and tempted to follow their party (ch. 9): For who, not only simple but even wise, would not be moved at first sight, seeing such composure of morals in the unbelievers themselves? For they detest every levity in any of their actions, deeds, clothing and equipage as they would fire, and abhor it as they would plague. Seeing the levity of Christians in dress and horsemanship, and in other things, they mock them and call them goats and apes. For men and women alike, greater and lesser, courtiers as well as peasants and rustics, have a most honourable and even most religious manner of dress, so common and simple that in them nothing of indecency, dishonour, superfluity, curiosity or levity can be detected or noted. But what shall I say of those who are held to be more religious and devout? For they show such simplicity, conformity, singular appearance and exemplary conduct in their actions, deeds, movements and garments, that one would believe they profess some form of regular observance. Compare the same author, chs. 10, 11, 12, and his answer in ch. 19. When therefore we see them not idly caring for civil modesty, sometimes [illegible] ... to be converted, namely from an evil life and way to a better one. Above all, our life must be corrected and sanctified, if we hope to prevail against them either in disputation or in war. I admit that this matter of which we are now speaking, the conversion of the Muhammedans, contains no small difficulty; but our thoughts must be raised, and both the excellence, usefulness and necessity of the work must be considered, and also the blessing, favour and power of the supreme God must be looked to in promoting and sanctifying the work. Undoubtedly whoever has heard and has also made some effort to observe that saying, "Go, teach all nations," will also experience the force of the promise attached to it: "And behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the world."

units.la: Ne addam, quod pro rebus terrenis & corporalibus, pro lucro aliquo, honore, alteriusve mundanae rei possessione homines longe graviores suscipiant professiones & labores, quam in hoc sanctissimo maximeque salutari & divino opere ponere necesse esset. Praeterquam quod consolari ac erigere homines hic cum multa alia, tum & hoc praecipue possit, quod ista ratione singularem in modum Apostolos, quin Christum, Deumque imitentur, quando seipsos ita totos offerunt consecrantque promovendae aliorum saluti & conversioni. Praecipue ubi consideraverimus, quantam prob dolor orbis partem Muhammedismus occupet. Vide Edwardi Brerewood Angli, Inquisitionem linguarum & religionum per mundum, cap. xı. Et Iohannis Cotovici, Vltrajectini, Itinerar. Hierosolymit. cap. ı.
units.tr: Not to mention that for earthly and bodily things, for some gain, honour, or possession of some worldly thing, men undertake far more serious professions and labours than would need to be put into this most holy, most salutary and divine work. Besides, among many other things, this above all can console and encourage men here, that in this way they imitate the apostles in a singular manner, nay Christ and God himself, when they so wholly offer and consecrate themselves to promote the salvation and conversion of others. This is especially so when we consider how great a part of the world, to our grief, Muhammedanism occupies. See Edward Brerewood, an Englishman, Inquiry into the Languages and Religions of the World, ch. 11; and John Cotovicus of Utrecht, Itinerary to Jerusalem, ch. 1.

units.la: Magna quidem difficultas operi offertur ex immani Turcarum crudelitate, qua & suis omnibus ex praescripto Muhammedis interdicunt rerum ad religionem pertinentium examine, atque omni super illis disputatione; deinde & saevissime Christianos, excipiunt si quos hoc in opere deprehendant, & videant sollicitare Musulmanorum (uti loquuntur) ad fidem Christianam: sed huic opponi debet tum animus vere Christianus, id est, pro promovendo regno Christi, & conversione infidelium ad mortem & martyrium usque anhelans; tum, illud ipsum esse causae malae & desperatae argumentum, non pati posse quod discutiatur & examinetur. Surat. XIII. de praeceptis huius libri, inquit, quare quis quaestionem querimoniamve movet? post constitutum enim Alcoranum, quidquam inde mutare nefas est. Similiter Surat. XIV. XVII. & XX. Contradicentibus dicito, ut sibi sua sint negotia, tibi tua: ipsique a tuis factis, & tu ab illorum liber. Et Sur. XXV. XXXII. Tecum disputare volentibus dic, Deum solum omnes actus tuos cognoscere, qui die postremo lites omnes & contrarietates discutiet. CXIX. homines incredulos sic alloquere, ego quidem legem vestram atque sectam minime sequar, nec vos meam. Igitur mihi mea manebunt, & vobis vestra. Ex qua eadem causa est, quod typographiam terris suis arcent Muhammedani, & submissos olim a magno Hetruriae Duce typos Arabicos Turca rejecerit, veritus nempe hoc modo in multorum examen legem suam devolutum iri, cui nusquam majus quam in crassa ignorantia praesidium. Prohibuit Muhammed omnem de lege sua disquisitionem, astuto consilio, ut caveret legis suae infirmitati, & suffocaret mentis vel paulum se ad meliora erigentis impetum.
units.tr: Our work faces a great difficulty in the monstrous cruelty of the Turks, who by Muhammad's command forbid all their people to examine matters of religion or to debate them at all. They also treat with the utmost severity any Christians they catch in this undertaking, or whom they see trying to draw the Muslims (as they call them) to the Christian faith. Against this, however, we must set two things: a truly Christian spirit, that is, one longing for the advance of Christ's kingdom and the conversion of unbelievers even to death and martyrdom; and the fact that to refuse to allow a matter to be questioned and examined is a sign of a bad and desperate cause. In Sura XIII, concerning the precepts of this book, it says: "Why does anyone raise a question or complaint? For once the Qur'an is established, it is wrong to change anything in it." Similarly in Suras XIV, XVII and XX: "Say to those who contradict you: let them have their affairs, and you yours; let them be free of your deeds, and you of theirs." And in Sura XXV and XXXII: "Say to those who wish to dispute with you: God alone knows all your actions, and on the last day he will settle all quarrels and contradictions." And Sura CXIX: "Address unbelieving men thus: I will certainly not follow your law and sect, nor will you follow mine. So mine will remain for me, and yours for you." For the same reason the Muslims keep printing presses out of their lands, and the Turk rejected the Arabic type once sent by the great Duke of Tuscany, for he feared that in this way their law would be thrown open to the scrutiny of many, and that nowhere is it more safely defended than in crass ignorance. Muhammad, with cunning policy, forbade all inquiry into his law, so as to guard against its weakness and to smother any impulse of the mind that might rise even a little toward better things.

units.la: Erga Christianos iniquior passim, aliquando & suo modo illis haud perfunctorie videri vult favere. Apud Elmacinum, Histor. Arab. cap. I. dicit Muhammed: benefacite Cophtitis Aegypti, sunt enim vobis genere & affinitate juncti. Item: qui Christianum opprimit, adversarium eum habebit in die judicii. Et: qui Christiano nocet, mihi nocet. Aliquando iis ne quidem salutem aeternam videtur denegare, quin salvari in religione sua possint. Surat. I. sciendum autem generaliter, quod omnis recte vivens, Iudæus seu Christianus, seu lege suâ relictâ in aliam tendens, omnis scilicet Deum adorans, indubitanter divinum amorem assequetur. Ibidem: his qui crediderint, & Iudeis & Christianis & Paganis, ipsis erit merces eorum apud Dominum, & non erit timor contra eos neque contristatio. Contendentibus de lege suâ benignè respondere præcipit: nam contenditis nobiscum de Deo, cum ipse sit Dominus noster, & Dominus vester? & nobis opera nostra, & vobis opera vestra, nosque etiam ipsi Domino nosmet commisimus? Surata Locmanni, xxxi. Dixit quoque Locmannus (est is idem cum Græcorum Æsopo, eædemque fere utriusque fabulæ): o filiole mi, utique si fueris boni piique operis quidquam pondere unius grani sinapis, granorum omnium minutissimi, quod existat in petra, abditâ aliquâ ejus lacunâ, aut in cælis, summo eorum convexo, aut in terra, imo ejus fundo; nempe in parte mundi occulta, suprema vel infima, proferet illud Deus & conspicuum faciet ac coram sistet ut in rationem veniat. ex Persicâ paraphrasi, & versione Cl. Golii. Illud est, quod Iudæi passim docent, Deum nullius opus fraudaturum mercede sua, אין הקנה מקפח שכר כל בריה · Per opera salvatum iri se plerique apud Turcas statuunt; quamvis etiam sint qui non per sua adeo opera, quam per Dei gratiam se salutem suam obtenturos credere videantur.
units.tr: He is generally harsher toward Christians, yet at times he wishes to appear to favour them in his own way, and not in a perfunctory manner. In Elmacin, Historia Arabum, ch. I, Muhammad says: "Do good to the Copts of Egypt, for they are joined to you by kinship and marriage." Likewise: "He who oppresses a Christian will have me as his adversary on the day of judgment." And: "He who harms a Christian harms me." At times he does not even seem to deny them eternal salvation, so that they may be saved in their own religion. Sura I: "It must be understood in general that every righteous living man, whether Jew or Christian, or one who, having left his law, turns to another, that is, everyone who worships God, will without doubt attain divine love." In the same place: "To those who have believed, whether Jews or Christians or Pagans, their reward is with their Lord, and there shall be no fear for them nor any sorrow." To those who dispute with him about their law he commands a gentle answer: "For do you dispute with us about God, since he is our Lord and your Lord? To us our works, and to you your works; and we have committed ourselves to the Lord." Sura XXXI of Luqman: "Luqman also said (he is the same as the Greek Aesop, and the two fables are nearly the same): 'O my little son, if you have in good and pious work even the weight of a grain of mustard seed, the smallest of all grains, which exists in a rock, in some hidden cavity of it, or in the heavens, in their highest vault, or in the earth, in its deepest bottom; that is, in some hidden part of the world, high or low, God will bring it forth and make it visible and set it before him for judgment." This is taken from the Persian paraphrase, in the version of the learned Golius. This is what the Jews commonly teach, that God will not defraud any creature of its reward: "Ein haqqanah mekapeach sekhar kol briyah" [אין הקנה מקפח שכר כל בריה]. Many among the Turks hold that they will be saved by their works, although there are some who seem to believe that they will obtain their salvation not so much by their own works as by the grace of God.

units.la: Salutem dico, à cujus exponenda natura quid ni disputationem aliquando cum Muhammedanis inchoemus? utpote re gravi, & summâ, & cujus maxime quidem nostra refert habere veram cognitionem & fidem. Quippe facile doceri potest, in rebus adeo futilibus & corporalibus sitam haud esse supremam æternamque hominis felicitatem, in quibus illam consistere docent Muhammedani: neque ista tantæ beatitudinis esse si quis possideat, spurca, & bruta, quæ nec cum animæ nostræ, nec beatitudinis præstantia satis conveniunt. Unde Avicenna ipse, quamvis Arabs Muhammedanus, lib. ix. de prima philosophia phia, dixit: lex nostra quam dedit Muhammed dispositionem felicitatis & miseriae, quae sunt secundum corpus; at- tendit. Sed est alia promissio, quae attenditur intellectu. Sapientibus vero Theologis multo major cupiditas fuit ad apprehendendam istam, quam corporum; quae quamvis dare- tur eis, non tamen attenderunt ad eam, nec in pretio habuerunt in comparatione felicitatis, quae est conjuncta cum veritate. Vivant homines lubenter cum Muhammedanis, sed vel hos ipsos malle mori cum Christianis, certum est: adeo anima quando sibi redditur, & magis defæcatur à mundo, quod sub mortem (si quando) fieri maximè solet, uti in rebus mundi tum nullam, ita nec in religione Muhammedica consolationem capere ullam potest, in Christiana vero, si modo cognita, firmam & plenam reperit quietem, salutem, omnia. Bene hoc observavit Richardus ille, ex ordine Prædicatorum Monachus, lib. Confusae legis Saracen. cap. x. quod multi quidem passim à Christiana religione deficiunt ad Muhammedismum, sed in vitâ; in morte nemo. Verum quod jam illi ipsi etiam apostatae velint Christianè mori', aliique Muhammedani in fine vitae liberius Christianismum amplectuntur. Et hujus rei signum in utrisque est, inquit, transmutantur enim quidam Saraceni in Christianos, & Christiani quidam fiunt Saraceni. Christianus quidem nunquam in morte fieret Saracenus, sed in vita: Saracenus autem potius in morte fit Christianus, quam in vita: utrque igitur horum potius eligit Christianus mori, quam Saracenus.
units.tr: I say salvation. Why should we not begin a disputation with the Muslims at some point over explaining its nature? It is a serious and supreme matter, and it is of the greatest importance for us to have true knowledge and faith concerning it. Indeed it can easily be taught that man's supreme and eternal happiness does not lie in such trifling and bodily things, in which the Muslims teach that it consists. Nor, if anyone possesses such things, are they the sign of so great a blessedness; they are filthy and brutish, and agree neither with the excellence of our soul nor with that of blessedness. Hence Avicenna himself, though a Muslim Arab, said in Book IX of the First Philosophy: "Our law, which Muhammad gave, sets out the arrangement of happiness and misery, which are according to the body. But there is another promise, which is grasped by the intellect. Indeed, the wise theologians have had a far greater desire to grasp that than the bodily one; and although it was given to them, they did not heed it, nor did they value it in comparison with the happiness that is joined with truth." It is certain that people willingly live with the Muslims, but that even these themselves would rather die with the Christians: so much does the soul, when it comes back to itself and is more purified from the world (as usually happens, if ever, at death), find neither consolation in worldly things nor in the Muslim religion, whereas in the Christian religion, if only it is known, it finds firm and full rest, salvation, and everything. Richard, that Dominican monk, rightly observed this in Book Confusae legis Saracenorum, ch. x: that many indeed fall away from the Christian religion to Muhammadanism, but in life, not in death. "Indeed," he says, "that even these apostates themselves wish to die as Christians, and that other Muslims at the end of life embrace Christianity more freely, is evident. And of this there is a sign in both cases: for some Saracens are changed into Christians, and some Christians become Saracens. A Christian would never become a Saracen at death, but in life; and a Saracen rather becomes a Christian at death than in life. Both of them, therefore, prefer to die as Christians rather than as Saracens."

units.la: Sed jam tempus est ut finiamus, praeter propositum prolixius in res Muhammedicas hactenus digressi: quae non omnino absque fructu futura sperramus, tum ad cognitionem rerum istarum aliquam impartiendam; tum forte etiam ad accendendos pro, juvandâ illorum conversione, Christianorum animos, qui nimis à nobis pas- sim negligutur. Syllabum quoque, uti de aliis facimus, horum subjiciemus, quae cum Muhammedanis controversiam faciunt.
units.tr: But now it is time to finish, since we have digressed at too great length beyond our purpose into Muhammadan matters. We hope that this will not be entirely without fruit, both in imparting some knowledge of these things and perhaps also in kindling the hearts of Christians, who are too often neglected by us, for the help of their conversion. As with the others, we shall also add a summary of those points which create controversy with the Muslims.

units.la: I. Num Muhammed fuerit verus Propheta, & ipso Christo major? Neg.
units.tr: I. Was Muhammad a true prophet, and greater than Christ himself? No.

units.la: II. Num Alkoran sit liber divinæ & infallibilis veritatis, supra Euangelium? Neg.
units.tr: II. Is the Qur'an a book of divine and infallible truth, above the Gospel? No.

units.la: III. Num S. Scriptura Veteris & Novi Testamenti, quam Christiani habemus, sit corrupta & depravata, multis ex eâ ablatis, aliisque cursus insertis? Neg.
units.tr: III. Is the Holy Scripture of the Old and New Testament, which we Christians have, corrupted and depraved, with many things taken out of it and other things inserted? No.

units.la: IV. An Euangelium comprehendat doctrinam salutis, eaque ex illo solo cognoscenda sit? Aff.
units.tr: IV. Does the Gospel contain the doctrine of salvation, and is that to be known from it alone? Yes.

units.la: V. Deus est infinitus, incorporeus, invisibilis, & invariabilis.
units.tr: V. God is infinite, incorporeal, invisible, and unchangeable.

units.la: VI. In uno Deo sunt tres Personæ divinæ, Pater, & Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus.
units.tr: VI. In the one God there are three divine Persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: VII. Christus Jesus est verus Deus, & ita quoque adorandus.
units.tr: VII. Christ Jesus is true God, and so is to be worshipped as such.

units.la: VIII. Christus ipse vere est crucifixus & mortuus, non alius ejus loco.
units.tr: VIII. Christ himself was truly crucified and died, not someone else in his place.

units.la: IX. Solus Christus est verus & perfectissimus noster mediator, ac salvator.
units.tr: IX. Christ alone is our true and most perfect mediator and saviour.

units.la: X. Justificamur coram Deo non aliâ re, quam sola Christi justitiâ, pro nobis ab ipso præstitâ, atque propter eam obtinemus à Deo remissionem omnium peccatorum, & vitam æternam.
units.tr: X. We are justified before God by nothing other than the sole righteousness of Christ, performed by him on our behalf, and on account of it we obtain from God the forgiveness of all sins and eternal life.

units.la: XI. Num circumcidi oporteat? Neg.
units.tr: XI. Whether one ought to be circumcised? No.

units.la: XII. Num lotiones corporis Muhammedanisufitæ, sint religiosæ, atque expiatoriæ? Neg.
units.tr: XII. Whether the Muhammedan ablutions of the body are religious and expiatory? No.

units.la: XIII. Precari ad certum locum, videlicet Meccam, & per certas corporis proflrationes, est superstitiosum.
units.tr: XIII. To pray towards a certain place, namely Mecca, and with certain prostrations of the body, is superstitious.

units.la: XIV. Num jurare liceat per creaturas, animalia, stellas, Dæmones &c? Neg.
units.tr: XIV. Whether it is lawful to swear by creatures, animals, stars, demons, etc.? No.

units.la: XV. Muhammedanorum jejunia nequaquam sunt recta & sancta.
units.tr: XV. The fasts of the Muhammedans are by no means right and holy.

units.la: XVI. Superstitiosum est, quod Muhammedani in cibo & potu abstinent à carne porcinâ, suffocato, sanguine, & vino.
units.tr: XVI. It is superstitious that the Muhammedans abstain in food and drink from pork, from what is strangled, from blood, and from wine.

units.la: XVII. Contra honestatem & probitatem est Muhammedanorum polygamia; uti & repudium.
units.tr: XVII. The polygamy of the Muhammedans is contrary to honesty and uprightness; and likewise their repudiation (of wives).

units.la: XVIII. Num beatitudo coelestis sita sit in voluptatibus & deliciis carnalibus? Neg.
units.tr: XVIII. Does heavenly blessedness consist in carnal pleasures and delights? No.

units.la: Liber Quartus, DE PAPISMO.
units.tr: Book Four, ON PAPISM.

units.la: Papismus quid. Ortus ejus, ex corruptione disciplinae, & rityum in Ecclesia. Ejus adolescentia, in Bonifacio III. anno. Iocv. Aʼχμη, in Gregorio VII. anno clɔ lxxiv. Hinc oppositiones celeberrimae, Doctorum, Ecclesiarum, Sectarum. Waldenses, anno clɔ clx. Wiclefitae, anno clɔ ccc lx. Hussitae, anno clɔ cccc. Reformatores ἑτέρως dicti, Zuinglius, Lutherus, alii. Inde Papismi casus. Denique ejusdem status desperatus, à Concilio Tridentino, anno clɔ Iɔ xlv. Series controversiarum, & articulorum Papalium, juxta eorundem aetatem de cultu imaginum, Transubstantiatione. Syncretismus: alius in doctrina, cum Doctoribus; alius in praxi, cum simplici & devota plebe, in communibus precibus. Religio nostra ad praxim & salutem tutior. Lectio & studium Scripturae. Disputationes cum Pontificiis. Colloquia ibidem habita, & quomodo habenda: disputatoria alia; alia charitativa, & conciliatoria: ubi expendendae Adversariorum Concessiones, & Consessiones. Quid in scriptione observandum, & praestandum. Argumentorum ratio & classes variae.
units.tr: What Papism is. Its origin, from the corruption of discipline and ritual in the Church. Its youth under Boniface III, in the year Iocv.; its acme [ἀκμή] under Gregory VII, in the year 1074. Hence the famous oppositions of teachers, churches and sects: the Waldenses, in the year 1160; the Wycliffites, in the year 1360; the Hussites, in the year 1400. The reformers, called by a different name [ἑτέρως], Zwingli, Luther and others. Then the downfall of Papism. Finally, its condition was hopeless, by the decision of the Council of Trent, in the year 1545. The series of controversies and Papal articles, according to their age: on the worship of images, on transubstantiation. Syncretism: one kind in doctrine, with the teachers; another in practice, with the simple and devout common people, in the common prayers. Our religion is safer for practice and salvation. Reading and study of Scripture. Disputations with the Papists. Colloquies held there, and how they are to be held: some disputatious, others charitable and conciliatory, where the concessions and confessions of the opponents are to be weighed. What is to be observed and performed in writing. The method of arguments and their various classes.

units.la: PAPISMUS, de quo acturi impraesentiarum sumus, & cujus ante omnia explicandum nomen est, aut strictè sumitur, pro Papalis ordinis in Ecclesiâ Romanâ monarchiâ; quo sensu Cardinalis Perronus, in suis Epistolis, & passim Conclavia mss. distinctionem faciunt Cardinalium Papabilium, à non Papabilibus: aut latè, pro tota Ecclesiæ Romano-Papalis doctrinâ. Neque nomen Papisticum jam ultra indignantur Papales, ut de eo potius gloriosò sc. æquè ac proprio palam gratulentur. Et hoc certè adæquatum ipsis nomen verissimè competit, à quo tempore (referunt autem ad Gregorium VII. in Concilio Romano) nomen Papæ episcopo Romano appropriatum, & non à suis solum, sed & à Græcis, atque à Iudæis in scriptis hoc modo de notari coepit: melius quam per nomen Catholici: quamvis nec hoc usu Ecclesiastico illud dicat, quod multi opinantur, Catholicum, sc. per totum mundum; sed vel per provinciam, aut per dioecesem patriarchalem nominabant Catholicum Veteres episcopum: Salmasius, de Primatu, pag. 210. Aliter tamen de Ecclesiâ dicitur, quod sit Catholica: sed verò hæc simpliciter ita nuncupatur: cæteroquin & particularis aliquando Ecclesia dicitur quoque Catholica. Remigius episcopus, in Testamento suo, apud Flodoardum, lib. 1. Quandoque ego Remigius episcopus de hac luce transfiero, tu mihi heres esto, sancta & venerabilis Ecclesia Catholica urbis Remorum: quod explico, Catholicam fidem professa, vel Catholicæ Ecclesiæ membrum illustre: aut nomen Catholici, vel Catholicæ, quod sibi Roma arrogat, non ideo universalitatem significare putandum sit, quamvis nec quâ parte illud Ecclesiæ veræ est indigetamentum, Romanæ competat. Quippe uti Rainoldus in Thesibus verè posuit, thes. v. Romana Ecclesia nec Catholica est, nec sanctum membrum Catholicæ.
units.tr: PAPISM, which we are now about to treat, and whose name must be explained before anything else, is taken either strictly, for the papal order of monarchy in the Roman Church; in this sense Cardinal Perron, in his Letters, and the manuscript conclaves everywhere make the distinction between the cardinals who are papabiles and those who are non-papabiles. Or it is taken broadly, for the whole doctrine of the Roman-Papal Church. Nor do the Papalists any longer disdain the name Papistic; rather they openly rejoice in it, as if it were a glorious and proper name for them. And this name most truly fits them, since the time (they refer it to Gregory VII in the Roman Council) when the name Pope was appropriated to the Roman bishop, and it began to be used in writing, not only by his own people but also by the Greeks and the Jews, in this way, and to be noted as the name by which he is designated, better than the name Catholic. Although the ecclesiastical usage of that name does not mean what many suppose, namely Catholic throughout the whole world; rather the ancient writers called a bishop Catholic within a province or a patriarchal diocese: Salmasius, On Primacy, p. 210. In another sense the Church is called Catholic, but this is simply how it is named; otherwise a particular church is sometimes also called Catholic. Bishop Remigius, in his Testament, in Flodoard, book 1: When I, Bishop Remigius, pass from this light, you shall be my heir, holy and venerable Catholic Church of the city of Reims. This I explain as meaning either one professing the Catholic faith, or a distinguished member of the Catholic Church. Nor is the name Catholic, or Catholic-ness, which Rome claims for itself, to be thought to signify universality, although it does not fit the Roman Church in that respect in which Catholicity is the mark of the true Church. Indeed, as Rainolds rightly stated in his Theses, thesis 5: The Roman Church is neither Catholic, nor a holy member of the Catholic Church.

units.la: In Ecclesiâ quum tria sint præcipuè consideranda, doctrina, disciplina, & vita, facilior & vulgatior corruptio in vitâ oritur, inde in disciplinâ, quâ per vitiosos & vitiorum proluviem infectâ, tandem illud quod vitæ, quod disciplinæ peccatum erat, & doctrinâ etiam stabiliri incipit, id est, facili compendio ab errore disciplinae pergitur ad corruptionem quoque doctrinae. Ut illud de vita, quod primo loco dixi, omittam, quod etiam, quandiu sana est cum disciplina doctrina, curari per eam optime potest, prima corruptela Ecclesiae fuit in disciplina, in minoribus & levioribus initio, quae parum curata sensim doctrinam etiam occuparunt, unde Papismus suo tempore enatus est. In disciplina levissima videntur quae ritus concernunt, tum quae ordinem; atque eorum depravatio est omnium antiquissima. Primo in ritibus circa res Sacras, & officia, & cultum coepit Ecclesia, ex mala ζηλία, hinc Iudaeos, inde Gentiles imitari, & quasi horreret simplicitas Christi, doctrinam ejus variis ritibus involvere. Haec vetustissima sunt Ecclesiae lemmata: inde progressum ad ordinem Ecclesiasticum mutandum, & alia forma magis ad mundi pompam & monarchiam instituendum, facto discrimine primum inter episcopos, & presbyteros, inde quoque inter episcopos, ut tandem ex illis successerit, qui se postea super omnes ambitiosissime extulit, Papa Romanus. Haec exordia dilapsi status Ecclesiastici a pristina & primaeva puritate; inde circa cultum divinum, Sacramenta, regimen Ecclesiae &c. prava dogmata subsecuta, quae omnia in Romanam Ecclesiam, seu sententiam confluxerunt, inque eadem pertinacissime semper fota fuerunt & retenta. Quae uti olim fidei & doctrinae ratione fuit commendatissima, quando scilicet scribebat illis Apostolus, quod eorum fides in toto mundo praedicaretur Rom. 1. 8. ita (nam corruptio optimi pessima) prae aliis errores, & prava quaeque, ad se magno impetu delata, ut ejus patrocinium, quo de caetero tuta essent, aucuparentur, semper avidius hausit atque defendit.
units.tr: In the Church, since three things are chiefly to be considered, doctrine, discipline and life, the corruption that arises most easily and most commonly begins in life, then passes into discipline, which is infected by wicked men and the filth of vices; and finally that which was a fault of life and of discipline begins to be established also in doctrine. That is, by an easy shortcut the error of discipline proceeds to corruption of doctrine as well. I shall omit that point about life, which I mentioned first, namely that while doctrine is sound together with discipline, it can be very well cured by it. The first corruption of the Church was in discipline, at first in minor and lighter matters, which, being little cared for, gradually seized upon doctrine too, whence Papism arose in its own time. The lightest matters in discipline seem to be those which concern rites, and then those which concern order; and the depravation of these is the most ancient of all. The Church began first with rites concerning sacred things, offices and worship, out of a wicked zeal [ζηλία], first imitating the Jews and then the Gentiles, and as if the simplicity of Christ were distasteful, it wrapped its doctrine in various rites. These are the most ancient beginnings of the Church. From there it advanced to changing the ecclesiastical order, and to setting up another form more suited to worldly pomp and monarchy, a distinction first being made between bishops and presbyters, and then also among the bishops themselves, so that at last from them there arose the one who afterwards raised himself most ambitiously above all others, the Roman Pope. These were the beginnings of the fall of the ecclesiastical state from its earlier and primitive purity. Then, concerning divine worship, the sacraments, the government of the Church, and so on, corrupt doctrines followed, all of which flowed together into the Roman Church, or its opinion, and in it were always most stubbornly cherished and retained. Just as the Church was once most commended for the reason of faith and doctrine, when the Apostle wrote to them that their faith was proclaimed throughout the whole world (Rom. 1:8), so too (for the corruption of the best is the worst), it always eagerly drank in and defended, above others, the errors and every depraved thing that rushed upon it with great force, so that it might gather their patronage, by which they might otherwise be safe.

units.la: Iamque facile adduci potuit Ecclesia illa, & ejus Episcopus, ut se sensim supra alios quosque efferrent, sive fama, fide, authoritate, usurpatione, & quod quidem dem maximum adferebat momentum, urbis & imperii suprematu subnixi. Quod post annum sexcentesimum maxime invaluit, quando Bonifacius III. episcopus Romanus, ab Imperatore Phoca, digno scilicet, per infandum erga Mauritium Imp. ejusque familiam parricidium, Auctore, obtinuit tum ut Ecclesia Romana omnium Ecclesiarum haberetur mater & caput, tum ut Episcopus Romanus diceretur summus & universalis Episcopus, quae facta sunt anno I⋄cv. Inde ad tempora Gregorii VII. haud segniter Pontifices Romani omni opera in id incubuerunt, ut primatum istum suum promoverent, vel suprematum: sic Salmasius dicendum; Paulus Servita Venetus, accommodato novae rei novo & miro vocabulo, totatum dici posse arbitrabatur, quod in epistolis ad Salmasium Sarravius indicat, pag. 220. Post Gregorium ergo hoc egerunt certatim Pontifices, ut potestatem suam, vel omnipotentiam, quę etiam vox ipsis placuit, in Ecclesias omnes, & Episcopos, novis semper augmentis extenderent. Quousque, nec contenti eo, supra omnes politias, regna, & imperia, super omnes nempe homines, hominumque ordinem, & status, pari ambitione se efferrent, quod nimirum ad cumulum imperii & dominationis Antichristianae decerat. Hoc Gregorius VII. dictus Hildebrandus, & Papa factus anno CIↃ LXXIII. ad. x. cal. Maii, curavit gnaviter, & primum ejus documentum dedit in Imp. Henrico IV. quem non satis habens excommunicasse, imperio etiam (quantum in se) privavit, subditosque absolvit juramento fidelitatis & subjectionis, quo erga Imperatorem tenebantur. Hac usus formula, quam Platina in ejus vita prodit. Henricum regem &c. imperatoria administratione regiaque dejicio: & Christianos omnes Imperio subjectos, juramento illo absolvo, quo fidem veris regibus praestare consueverunt. Iterumque in secundo anathematismo: ipsum Henricum ejusque fautores vinculo anathematis colligo: atque iterum regiam ei potestatem adimo, adimo, interdicoque Christianis omnibus illo juramento absolutis, quo fides regibus dari consuevit, ne Henrico ulla in re obtemperent, Rodulphum in regem suscipiant. &c. Cui etiam Rudolpho coronam Imperialem misit, cum famosa ista inscriptione: Petra dedit Petro, Petrus diadema Rudolpho. Adeo nunc omnia a se & sua potestate dependere, & imperium a se accipere Imperatores, suarumque partium esse aliis id dare, vel adimere, similiter regna omnia & dominia in toto Christianismo, quin orbe, quia nimirum vicarius Dei esset & Christi, Petriqueque successor, Papa existimabat. Videlicet is sensus verborum illorum erat, quae in ejus electione observata, atque annotata fuerunt: cum ea potestate Ecclesia Dei praeesse volumus, quâ Petrus Dei mandato quondam praefuit. lib. IV. epist. Gregorii. VII. ep. 111. Ex illis enim intelligitur, scribit ad Germanos, tamquam anathematis vinculo alligatus, & a regia dignitate depositus, & quod omnis populus quondam sibi subjectus a vinculo juramenti eidem promissi sit absolutus. Praecedenti epistola docuerat, Pontifices Regibus longè praestare. Neque adversus Imperatorem Henricum solum illud egit Gregorius, sed quoque Galliae Regi Philippo simile minabatur, lib. I. ep. XXXV. & lib. II. ep. V. Quod si nec hujusmodi districtione voluerit resipiscere, nulli clam aut dubium esse volumus, quin modis omnibus regnum Franciae de ejus occupatione, adjuvante Deo, temptemus eripere. Idemque conclusum adversus Galliae regem, in II. Synodo Romanâ, sub eo habitâ, anno clo lxxv. Libro VIII. ep. ult. singulis per Galliam domibus imponi vult denarium, sedi suae in singulos annos pendendum: dicendum autem est omnibus Gallis, & per veram obedientiam praecipiendo, ut unaquaeque domus saltem unum denarium annuatim solvant B. Petro, si eum recognoscunt patrem, & pastorem suum more antiquo. Astuto [?] mento, ut sic reliquae Ecclesiae agnoscerent imperium Romanae, & in Ecclesias atque in politias parem exerceret ubique tyrannidem dem. Ungariæ regnum Ecclesiæ Romanæ subjectum esse scripsit, illius Duci Geufœ. l. 1 1. epist. lx iii. & epist. xi i, idem ad Salomonem, Vngariæ regem: regnum Vngariæ Sanctæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ proprium est. De regno Hispaniæ similiter, lib. 1. epist. vi 1. & lib. iv. epist. xxvi i 1. de Russia, lib. 11. epist. lxxiv. & quis omnia corroget Papalis fastigii in Ecclesiasticis, in politicis, hoc in homine absoluti, ab eo edita documenta? adeo omnino hic ponenda est Papatus Romani ἀκμή. Lib. ix. epist. 111. mittit ad Abbatem Hirsaugiensem, formulam juramenti, ab Imperatore præstandi, quæ incipit: Ab hac hora & deinceps fidelis ero per rectam fidem B. Petro Apostolo, ejusque vicario P. Gregorio, qui nunc in carne vivit: & quidcunque mihi ipse Papa præceperit, sub his videlicet verbis: per veram obedientiam, fideliter (sicut oportet Christianum) observabo. Et quomodo perfectam Papatus formam fundarit, vide plenius ex his ejus dictatis, quæ leguntur lib. 11. epistolarum, scriptarum anno cIↄ lxxiv. Quod Romana Ecclesia à solo Domino sit fundata. Quod solus Romanus Pontifex jure dicitur universalis. Quod ille solus possit deponere Episcopos, vel reconciliare. Quod legatus ejus omnibus Episcopis præsit in Concilio, etiam inferioris gradus, & adversus eos sententiam depositionis possit dare. Quod absentes Papa possit deponere. Quod cum excommunicatis ab illo, inter cetera, nec in eadem domo debemus manere. Quod illi soli licet pro temporis necessitate novas leges condere, novas plebes congregare; de canonica Abbatiam facere, & è contra divitem Episcopatum dividere, & inopes unire. Quod solus possit uti imperialibus insignis. Quod solius Papæ pedes omnes Principes deosculentur. Quod illius solius nomen in Ecclesiis recitetur. Quod unicum est nomen in mundo. Quod illi liceat Imperatores deponere. Quod illi liceat de sede ad sedem necessitate cogente Episcopos transmutare. Quod de omni Ecclesia quocunque voluerit clericum valeat ordinare. Quod ab illo ordinatus alii Ecclesiæ præesse potest, sed non milit admimo, interdicoque Christianis omnibus illo juramento absolutis, quo fides regibus dari consuevit, ne Henrico ulla in re obtemperent, Rodulphum in regem suscipiant. &c. Videlicet is sensus verborum illorum erat, quae in ejus electione observata, atque annotata fuerunt: cum ea potestate Ecclesia Dei praesse volumus, quâ Petrus Dei mandato quondam praefuit. lib. iv. epist. Gregorii. vii. ep. iii. Ex illis enim intelligitur, scribit ad Germanos, eur sit anathematis vinculo alligatus, & à regia dignitate depositus, & quod omnis populus quondam sibi subjectus à vinculo juramenti eidem promissi sit absolutus. De regno Hispaniæ similiter, lib. i. epist. vii. & lib. iv. epist. xxvi ii. de Russiâ, lib. ii. epist. lxxiv. & quis omnia corroget Papalis fastigii in Ecclesiasticis, in politicis, hoc in homine absoluti, ab eo edita documenta? adeo omnino hic ponenda est Papatus Romani ἀκμή. Petro Apostolo, ejusque vicario P. Gregorio, qui nunc in carne vivit: & quidcunque mihi ipse Papa præceperit, sub his videlicet verbis: per veram obedientiam, fideliter (sicut oportet Christianum) observabo. Et quomodo perfectam Papatus formam fundarit, vide plenius ex his ejus dictatis, quæ leguntur lib. ii. epistolarum, scriptarum anno cIↄ lxxiv. Quòd Romana Ecclesia à solo Domino sit fundata. Quòd solus Romanus Pontifex jure dicatur universalis. Quòd ille solus possit deponere Episcopos, vel reconciliare. Quòd legatus ejus omnibus Episcopis præsit in Concilio, etiam inferioris gradus, & adversus eos sententiam depositionis possit dare. Quòd absentes Papa possit deponere. Quòd cum excommunicatis ab illo, inter cætera, nec in eadem domo debemus manere.
