Quòd illi soli licet pro temporis necessitate novas leges condere, novas plebes congregare; de canonica Abbatiam facere, & è contra divitem Episcopatum dividere, & inopes unire. Quòd solus possit uti imperialibus insignibus. Quòd solius Papæ pedes omnes Principes deosculentur. Quòd illius solius nomen in Ecclesiis recitetur. Quòd unicum est nomen in mundo. Quòd illi liceat Imperatores deponere. Quòd illi liceat de sede ad sedem necessitate cogente Episcopos transmutare. Quòd de omni Ecclesia quocunque voluerit clericum valeat ordinare. Quòd ab illo ordinatus alii Ecclesiæ præesse potest, sed non milt militare, & quòd ab aliquo Episcopo non debet superiorem gradum accipere. Quòd nulla Synodus absque præcepto ejus debet generalis vocari. Quòd nullum capitulum, nullusque liber canonicus habeatur absque illius auctoritate. Quòd sententia illius à nullo debeat retractari, & ipse omnium solus retractare possit. Quòd à nemine ipse judicari debeat. Quòd nullus audeat condemnare Apostolicam sedem appellantem. Quòd majores causa cujuscunque Ecclesiæ ad eam referri debeant. Quòd Romana Ecclesia nunquam erravit, nec in perpetuum scriptura testante errabit. Quòd Romanus Pontisex, si canonicè fuerit ordinatus, meritis B. Petri indubitanter efficitur sanctus, testante sancto Ennodio Papiensi Episcopo, ei multis sanctis Patribus sæventibus, sicut in decretis beati Symmachi Papa continetur. Quòd illius præcepto, & licentia subjectis liceat accusare. Quòd absque Synodali conventu possit Episcopos deponere, & reconciliare. Quòd Catholicus non habeatur qui non concordat Romanæ Ecclesiæ. Quòd à fidelitate iniquorum subjectos potest absolvere. Hæc exhibenda ob oculos fuerunt, ut Papatus genuinam formam & compagem spectaremus, quam hoc tempore à Papâ Gregorio accepit & ut pateret, quàm omnino in hoc istorum Auctore, Papatus vis ponenda sit, qui eum ad suum culmen perduxit. Neque solùm ei debetur auctoritatis Papalis perfectio, quæ quidem præcipue in illis Dictatis respicitur, qualia sunt de Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Pontificis authoritate super omnes; in judicando, in ferendis legibus, supra Imperatores, Principes, Ecclesias, Synodos, de ejus infallibilitate; de necessaria cum Ecclesiæ Romanæ communione &c. ipsissima Ecclesiæ Papalis fundamenta: sed & alia doctrinæ quoque ejus præcipua capita ab hoc Papâ confirmata fuerunt. In Synodo Romanâ I. sub eo habitâ, anno cIↄ lxx i v. primâ hebdomadâ Quadragesimæ, forte eâdem, quâ Dictata illa condita, quippe cujus eodem libro epistolarum meminit, ep. lxi i. in eâ dico Synodo legem tulit de cœlibatu. tu clericorum, aliis quidem inante Synodis saepe etiam vexato, sed jam ab Ecclesia Romana pro articulo seu jugo, quod omnibus Ecclesiis imponeretur, accepto: cui in Germania, ubi hanc suam legem per Legatos promulgabat, omnes Clerici restiterunt, & haereticum, ac vesanum Papam clamarunt, qui non ultra attenderet vocem Domini, dicentis: non omnes capiunt hoc verbum; & Apostoli: qui se non continet, nubat, melius est nubere, quam uri. Ille tamen perrexit, & vi multa obtrusit suum illum canonem, ne presbyteri uxores habeant, habentes aut dimittant aut deponantur. Nec quisquam omnino ad sacerdotium admittatur, qui non in perpetuum continentiam vitamque caelibem profiteatur. In Synodo Romana V, anno clo lxxviii. dixit, ut quicunque se Christianae religionis participem esse desideraret, ab esu carnium, die Sabbathi abstineret. Nec hoc tantum, sed Synodum Romanam VI. anno clo lxxix. habuit contra bonum Berengarium, eumque ad palinodiam coegit, & quamvis contra in Synodo disputante magna parte, maxima autem pars, panem & vinum per sacra orationis verba, & sacerdotis consecrationem, Spiritu sancto invisibiliter operante, converti substantialiter in corpus Dominicum de Virgine natum, quod & in Cruce pependit, & ho sanguinem, qui de ejus latere militis effusus est lancea, asserebat, atque authoritatibus Orthodoxorum sanctarum Patrum tam Graecorum, quam Latinorum modis omnibus defendebat. In quam sententiam itum, & in eam jurare Berengarius adactus fuit. Ergo hoc tempore dogma illud transsubstantiationis vel conversionis substantialis symbolorum Coenae in panem & sanguinem cusum fuit: postquam disputata ab aliquo retro tempore Christi praesentia corporalis in Coena, eaque asserta tandem contra Berengarium fuit, in Synodo primum Romana, ante triginta & novem annos, anno clo l. sub P. Leone IX, tum in Synodo Vercellensi, eodem anno, mense se Septembri. In Turonensi inde, anno cIↄ lv. sub P. Victore ii. præsidente Hildebrando, tunc temporis Ecclesiæ Rom. subdiacono, & Papæ Legato. inde iterum anno cIↄ lix. sub Nicolao ii. ubi ad palinodiam actus Berengarius formulæ isti recantationis, sibi ab Humberto Cardinale, omnium assensu, propositæ subscripsit: Ego Berengarius &c. ubi ex sententia Ecclesiæ Romanæ dixit, panem, & vinum, quæ in altari ponuntur, post consecrationem non solum sacramentum, sed etiam verum corpus, & sanguinem Domini nostri Iesu Christi esse: & sensualiter non solum sacramento, sed in veritate manibus sacerdotum tractari, frangi, & fidelium dentibus atteri. Quæ verba postea ipsis Romanensibus miras difficultates peperere; ut a Capernaitica carnis Christi manducatione excusarent, monente Glossa Juris Canonici, cui formula etiam inserta est, ut verba illa caute acciperentur, secus paritura graviorem haeresim, quam ipsa Berengariana fuerit. Atque ita sub Gregorio vii. in Synodo Romana, quam diximus, anno cIↄ lxxix. ultimum adversus Berengarium sententia Ecclesiæ Romanæ, non modo de præsentia Christi corporali in Cœna, sed etiam de panis & vini substantiali conversione in corpus & sanguinem Christi ratihabita, & in articulum fidei recepta quod ad rem primum fuit. Sententia eadem, at verbum quoque & notio transsubstantiationis primum canonizata in Concilio Lateranensi fuit, quod universale xii. Pontificii ajunt, sub Innocentio iii. a. cIↄ ccxv. cap. i. Una vero est fidelium universalis Ecclesia, extra quam nullus omnino salvatur. In qua idem ipse sacerdos & sacrificium Iesus Christus, cujus corpus & sanguis in sacramento altaris sub speciebus panis & vini veraciter continentur, transsubstantiatis pane in corpus, & vino in sanguinem potestate divina, ut ad perficiendum mysterium unitatis accipiamus ipsi de suo, quod accepit ipse de nostro. Ex quibus palam est, quod uti Papatus adolescentiam in Bonifacio iii. anno Iↄ cv, ita ejus ætatis bene ponamus in Gregorio VII. anno cIↄ lxxiv. & sequentibus, sub ejus videlicet Episcopatu.
units.tr: And that church, with its bishop, could easily be led to raise itself gradually above all the others, by reputation, faith, authority, and usurpation, and, which gave it the greatest weight, by relying on the supremacy of the city and the empire. This grew especially strong after the year 600, when Boniface III, bishop of Rome, obtained from the Emperor Phocas, as fitting reward for the unspeakable murder of the Emperor Maurice and his family, of which Phocas was the author, both that the Roman Church should be regarded as the mother and head of all churches, and that the bishop of Rome should be called the highest and universal bishop. These things were done in the year 606. From then until the time of Gregory VII, the Roman pontiffs strove eagerly by every means to advance this primacy of theirs, or supremacy. Salmasius wished it called suprematus; Paolo Sarpi of Venice, having fitted a new and strange word to a new thing, thought it could be called totatus, as Sarravius notes in his letters to Salmasius, p. 220. After Gregory, therefore, the popes competed to extend their power, or their omnipotence (a word that also pleased them), over all churches and bishops, with ever new increases. Not content with this, they then raised themselves with equal ambition above all states, kingdoms, and empires, that is, above all men, the order of men, and all conditions, which was surely what was lacking to complete the Antichristian empire and dominion. Gregory VII, called Hildebrand, who became pope in 1073 on the 22nd day before the calends of May, zealously carried this out, and gave the first proof of it against the Emperor Henry IV. Not content with excommunicating him, he also deprived him, so far as in him lay, of his empire, and absolved the subjects from the oath of fidelity and obedience by which they were bound to the Emperor. He used this formula, which Platina gives in his life: I depose King Henry, etc., from imperial administration and royal office, and I absolve all Christians subject to the empire from that oath by which they were accustomed to pay fidelity to true kings. And again in the second anathema: I bind Henry himself and his supporters with the chain of anathema; and again I take away his royal power, I take it away, and I forbid all Christians, absolved from that oath by which fidelity is usually given to kings, to obey Henry in any matter, or to receive Rudolf as king. etc. He also sent the imperial crown to this same Rudolf, with the notorious inscription: The Rock gave to Peter, Peter gave the diadem to Rudolf. So far did he think that everything depended on himself and his power, that emperors received their empire from him, and that it was for him to give or take it away from others, and likewise that all kingdoms and dominions throughout Christendom, indeed the whole world, belonged to him, because he was, of course, the vicar of God and of Christ and the successor of Peter. Indeed, this was the meaning of those words which were observed and noted at his election: We wish to preside over the Church of God with that power by which Peter once presided by the command of God. Book IV, letter of Gregory VII, letter 111. For from those things it is understood, he writes to the Germans, that he (the king) is bound by the chain of anathema, and deposed from royal dignity, and that every people once subject to him is absolved from the bond of the oath promised to him. In the preceding letter he had taught that popes far surpass kings. Gregory acted this way not only against the Emperor Henry, but also threatened King Philip of France with the same, Book I, letter XXXV, and Book II, letter V. But if he is unwilling to repent even under this kind of restraint, we want it to be known to no one, clearly and without doubt, that by every means, with God's help, we will try to snatch the kingdom of France from his occupation. The same was decreed against the king of France in the second Roman synod held under him in the year 1075. In Book VIII, last letter, he wishes a penny to be laid on each house throughout France, to be paid yearly to his see: It must be said to all the French, and by true obedience commanded, that each household shall pay at least one penny yearly to St Peter, if they acknowledge him as their father and pastor in the ancient manner. By this crafty device, the other churches were to acknowledge the rule of Rome, and everywhere exercise an equal tyranny over churches and states. He wrote that the kingdom of Hungary was subject to the Roman Church, to Duke Geusa of that land, Book II, letter 63, and letter 12; the same to Solomon, king of Hungary: The kingdom of Hungary is the proper possession of the Holy Roman Church. Likewise concerning the kingdom of Spain, Book I, letter 7, and Book IV, letter 28. Concerning Russia, Book II, letter 74. And who could gather together all the documents issued by him, a man absolute in the matters of the papal summit, both ecclesiastical and political? Indeed, here must truly be placed the zenith [ἀκμή] of the Roman papacy. Book IX, letter 3, he sends to the abbot of Hirsau a formula of oath to be sworn by the emperor, which begins: From this hour onward I will be faithful, in the true faith, to St Peter the Apostle and to his vicar, Pope Gregory, who now lives in the flesh; and whatever the pope himself shall command me, under these words, I will observe faithfully, with true obedience, as a Christian ought. And to see more fully how he established the complete form of the papacy, consult these dictates of his, which are read in Book II of his letters, written in the year 1074: That the Roman Church was founded by the Lord alone. That the Roman pontiff alone is rightly called universal. That he alone may depose or reconcile bishops. That his legate presides over all bishops in a council, even those of lower rank, and may pass sentence of deposition against them. That the pope may depose the absent. That we must not remain in the same house with those excommunicated by him, among other things. That he alone may, as the needs of the time require, enact new laws, gather new peoples, make an abbey out of a canonry, and conversely divide a rich bishopric and unite poor ones. That he alone may use the imperial insignia. That all princes should kiss the feet of the pope alone. That his name alone is recited in churches. That his name is the only name in the world. That he may depose emperors. That he may transfer bishops from see to see as necessity requires. That he may ordain a cleric from any church whatever he wishes. That one ordained by him may preside over another church, but may not hold a lower rank, and ought not to receive a higher rank from any bishop. That no synod may be called a general one without his command. That no chapter and no canonical book is to be regarded without his authority. That his sentence must be retracted by no one, and he alone may retract the sentence of all. That he himself must be judged by no one. That no one may dare to condemn one who appeals to the apostolic see. That the greater cases of any church must be referred to it. That the Roman Church has never erred, nor, as Scripture bears witness, will it ever err. That the Roman pontiff, if he has been canonically ordained, is undoubtedly made holy by the merits of St Peter, as Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, testifies, many holy Fathers agreeing with him, as is contained in the decrees of blessed Pope Symmachus. That by his command and permission it is lawful for subjects to accuse. That he may depose and reconcile bishops without a synodal assembly. That he is not to be counted a Catholic who does not agree with the Roman Church. That he may absolve subjects from the fidelity owed to the wicked. These things were set before our eyes so that we might look upon the genuine form and structure of the papacy, as it was received at this time from Pope Gregory, and so that it might be plain how entirely the power of the papacy must be attributed to this author of it, who brought it to its height. Nor is the perfection of papal authority due to him alone, which is especially seen in those Dictates, such as those concerning the authority of the Roman Church and its pontiff over all in judging, in enacting laws, above emperors, princes, churches, and synods; concerning his infallibility; concerning the necessary communion with the Roman Church, etc., the very foundations of the papal church. But other principal heads of his doctrine were also confirmed by this pope. In the first Roman synod held under him, in the year 1074, in the first week of Lent, perhaps the same in which those Dictates were composed, since he mentions it in the same book of letters, letter 12, in that synod, I say, he enacted a law on the celibacy of the clergy. This had often been troubled even by earlier synods, but now it was accepted by the Roman Church as an article, or yoke, to be imposed on all churches. All the clergy in Germany, where he promulgated this law through his legates, resisted it, and cried out that the pope was a heretic and a madman, who did not heed the voice of the Lord saying: Not all can receive this word; and the Apostle: He who cannot contain, let him marry; it is better to marry than to burn. Yet he persisted, and forced through his canon with great violence, that priests should not have wives, and that those who had them should either put them away or be deposed. And that no one at all should be admitted to the priesthood who did not profess continence and a celibate life forever. In the fifth Roman synod, in the year 1078, he decreed that whoever desired to be a partaker of the Christian religion should abstain from eating meat on the Sabbath day. Nor was this all: in the sixth Roman synod, in the year 1079, he held a council against the good Berengar, and forced him to recant. And although in the synod, most of those disputing against him... the greater part, however, asserted that the bread and wine, through the words of consecration and the consecration of the priest, the Holy Spirit working invisibly, are substantially converted into the Lord's body, born of the Virgin, which also hung on the Cross, and into the blood which flowed from his side by the soldier's spear; and they defended this by every means with the authorities of the orthodox holy Fathers, both Greek and Latin. Berengar was compelled to go over to this opinion and to swear to it. Therefore at this time that dogma of transubstantiation, or substantial conversion of the elements of the Supper into bread and blood, was coined; after the real bodily presence of Christ in the Supper had been disputed for some time, and finally affirmed against Berengar, first in the Roman synod under Pope Leo IX, thirty-nine years earlier, in the year 1050; then in the synod of Vercelli the same year, in the month of September. Then in the synod of Tours, in the year 1055, under Pope Victor II, Hildebrand presiding, who was then subdeacon of the Roman Church and papal legate; and again in the year 1059, under Nicholas II, where Berengar, forced to recant, signed the formula of recantation proposed to him by Cardinal Humbert with the assent of all: I, Berengar, etc. There, according to the judgment of the Roman Church, he said that the bread and wine which are placed on the altar, after consecration, are not only a sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and that they are handled and broken by the hands of the priests, and ground by the teeth of the faithful, not only sacramentally but in truth. These words afterwards caused the Romanists themselves great difficulties; so that they might excuse themselves from the Capernaite eating of Christ's flesh, the Gloss of Canon Law, in which this formula is also inserted, warns that those words should be taken cautiously, lest they bring forth a graver heresy than Berengar's own. And so under Gregory VII, in the Roman synod we have mentioned, in the year 1079, the final sentence of the Roman Church against Berengar was ratified, not only concerning the bodily presence of Christ in the Supper, but also concerning the substantial conversion of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ, and it was received as an article of faith, which was first in this matter. The same sentence, but also the word and notion of transubstantiation, was first canonized in the Lateran Council, which the Papists call the twelfth ecumenical, under Innocent III, in the year 1215, chapter 1: There is indeed one universal Church of the faithful, outside of which no one at all is saved. In it the same Jesus Christ is both priest and sacrifice, whose body and blood are truly contained in the sacrament of the altar under the species of bread and wine, the bread being transubstantiated into the body and the wine into the blood by divine power, so that, to accomplish the mystery of unity, we may receive from him what he received from us. From these things it is plain that, just as we place the youth of the papacy in Boniface III in the year 605, so we may rightly place its maturity in Gregory VII, in the year 1074 and following, that is, under his episcopate.

units.la: Qui nostep calculus adulti hoc tempore Papatus eo certior habendus est, quo ipsi Papatus gnathones summi, & inter eos Baronius Cardinalis, haec tempora ita describit, ut non alio regnasse magis Antichristum etiam hinc certum esse debeat. Quippe is, occasione libri à Petro Damiano Monacho eremita conscripti, de infando scelere, tit. Gomorrheus, quo quadripartita vitia carnis, quibus obrueretur Ecclesia, uti loquitur, perstringit, & de quo libro sibi à P. Alexandro II. postea surrepto conquestus per litteras apud Cardinalem (tum temporis) Hildebrandum fuerat, haec verba protulit, Annal. Tom. XI. ad annum cIↄ xl ix. Caeterum praeter ipsos etiam & frutices illi infelicissimi, vepres infausti, spinae, & urtica agrum Patrisfamilias in immensum oppleverant, qui ex pustore carnis, corruptionis sino turpiter excreverunt. Omnis quippe caro corruperat viam suam: ut non tantum ad eas abluendas sordes videretur satis esse diluvium, sed nefanda scelera ignem e caelo Gomorrheum, quo est exusta Pentapolis, postularent. Iudicet hinc quilibet, an alio, quam hoc tempore Apostasiae Romanae robur & vis summa, ex qua aliquot post saeculis nefandum in modum Papatus imperitavit, ponenda sit.
units.tr: This our reckoning of the Papacy's growth should be held all the more certain because the Papists' own chief flatterers, and among them Cardinal Baronius, describe these times in such a way that it must be certain Antichrist reigned in no other period more. For Baronius, on the occasion of a book written by Peter Damian, a monk and hermit, on the unspeakable sin entitled Gomorrheus, in which he censures the fourfold vices of the flesh by which the Church, as he puts it, was overwhelmed, and about which book he had complained by letter to Pope Alexander II (who later seized it) and to Cardinal Hildebrand (then in office), uttered these words, Annals, vol. XI, at the year 1049: Besides these, those most unhappy shrubs, ill-omened brambles, thorns and nettles had overgrown the field of the father of the household beyond measure, having grown up shamefully from the filth of the flesh and the sink of corruption. For all flesh had corrupted its way, so that the deluge seemed scarcely enough to wash away such filth, and the unspeakable crimes demanded fire from heaven, like the fire of Gomorrah by which Pentapolis was burned. Let anyone judge from this whether the strength and supreme power of Roman apostasy, by which the Papacy after some centuries ruled in an unspeakable manner, ought to be placed at any other time than this.

units.la: Inde Romanae Ecclesiae, ejusque incircumscriptae potestati, usurpationibus, tyrannidi, doctrinae multi se ubique opponere, in Oriente Graeci, in Occidente, praeter plures alios, qui id privatim egerunt, integrae sectae, & Ecclesiae. Namque trium generum constituo opponentes: Doctores, quales innumeri ubique: Ecclesiae, qualis, v. g. Ecclesia Leodiensis, adversus P. Paschalem II. anno cIↄ cvii. denique sectas integras (sectae vocem in bonam partem sumo, uti apud Tertullianum pluries) V Valdensium, in Gallia ad annum cIↄ clx. V Viclefitarum in Anglia, ab anno cIↄ ccc lx. inde Hussitarum, in Bohemia, ab anno cIↄ cccc. SeIam dicit etiam Auctor Chronici Limpurgensis Germanici, citatus in Historia Ecclef. Sclavonica, lib. 1. pag. 5. Moguntiæ Secta quædam innotuit, quæ occultè duraverat per sex secula, aut ultra. Fuere igitur illi homines, ante annum à Christo nato 800. sub Carolo M. Occidentis Imperatore: quo tempore Controversia de Cultu Imaginum maximè viguit: & in Synodo Francofurtensi, sub Carolo M. contra Imagines disputatum est, Anno 794. ita ut factum esset ea anti Synodus Nicena II. Ejus Secta dogmata & articuli erant; Sanctos, nempe defunctos, non esse invocandos: eo quòd pro nemine orent. Deus esse vias hominis post mortem, Cælum vel infernum. Episcopum, vel Papam, nullas dare posse indulgentias, Eleemosynas, Missas, & Jejunia nihil juvare animas à corpore separatas, quarum gratia illa fiant. &c. In hoc etiam nostro Belgio magnam V Valdensium fuisse copiam, post eorum in Gallis oppressionem, & dissipationem, atque ipsius Petri V Valdi accessum; quin & ante hunc, per Tanchelinum, celebrem apud Antverpienses, & vicinas Brabantiæ Flandriæque partes Concionatorem, ad annum clɔ c vı. temere. & per invidiam à Papistis pro hæretico notatum, multosque in hisce regionibus fuisse Papatus & Cleri adversarios, certum. Atque inde adversus optimos V Valdenses primum exercitam hic fuisse Patrum Dominicanorum, ante Hispanicam, sub ortum bellorum nostrorum, Inquisitionem, ignorare neminem sinit Annalium nostrorum fides. Quin & celeberrimo viro Marco Zuerio Boxhornio debemus antiquam V Valdensium Belgarum fidei Confessionem, seu Catechismum per interrogationes & responsiones, publici juris factum, lib. 1. Histor. Belgicæ pag. 36. ad 42. incipitque: wat eischt men van een kerstten. dignum profecto, quod à Belgarum nemine nesciatur. V Valdensium Gallorum Confessionem & Catechismum edidit, in suâ de V Valdensibus Historiâ, Paulus Perrinus V Valdenses sub tempora Reformationis, vel illorum relireliquiæ plurimæ adhuc fuerunt in Galliâ, Bohemiâ & Moraviâ, & alibi: atque dum dispersi hic ibi erant, sæpius suorum aliquos emiserunt per varias orbis partes, quæsitum puriorem Ecclesiam, & melioris doctrinæ homines. Tempore Reformationis Huldr. Zuinglium, Lutherum, Oecolampadium, aliosque accesserunt, quibuscum statum Ecclesiarum suarum communicarunt, & si quæ corrigenda erant, aliterve apud ipsos instituenda, ab illis acceperunt: illud unice satagentes, ut omnes impuritatem Ecclesiæ Romanæ detestarentur, & fugerent, sicut ipsi pridem fecerant. Unde apud eos, inter scripta, sua extitisse à longo tempore antiquum satis librum, de causis secessionis ipsorum à Papatu, La cause del nostre despartiment de la Gleisa Romana, scribit Joh. Paulus Perrin. De Reliquiis V Valdensium in Sabaudia, anno etiam MDLXV. in epistolis suis ad Camerarium Hubertus Languetus, Burgundus, ep. xx. Dux Sabaudiæ expellit ex suâ ditione habitatores convallium Lucernæ & Angroniæ, quibus ante quatuor annos vendidit libertatem in religione, cum ab ipsis victus esset aliquot prœliis. Sunt isti Valdensium reliquiæ, & à ducentis annis semper professi sunt eam religionem, quam jam profitemur; nec impedivit quò minus facerent, Rex Galliæ interea dum est ibi dominatus. Et ad Camerarium filium, ep. xxiv. Fui nuper in Moravia cum Doct. Iordano, qui duxit me Evangelicum, ubi fratres Valdenses habent præcipuam suam Ecclesiam. Loquuti sunt mecum de nostro Efromo, & ostenderunt se valde expetere ejus ad se adventum. & paulo post, Efromum scribit vocatum ab Heidelbergensibus, & Basileensibus, & à Fratribus Valdensibus, animumque ejus magis inclinasse in V Valdenses. Scripsit hæc a. MDLXV. Deque Efromo isto etiam Historia Ecclesiastica Sclavoniæ.
units.tr: Hence many have opposed the Roman Church, its unbounded power, its usurpations and tyranny, and its doctrine, everywhere: in the East the Greeks, and in the West, besides many others who did so privately, whole sects and churches. For I distinguish three kinds of opponents: teachers, of whom there are countless examples everywhere; churches, such as the Church of Liège against Pope Paschal II in the year 1107; and finally whole sects (I take the word "sect" in a good sense, as Tertullian often does): of the Waldenses, in Gaul, up to the year 1160; of the Wycliffites, in England, from the year 1360; then of the Hussites, in Bohemia, from the year 1400. The author of the German Chronicle of Limpurg, cited in the Ecclesiastical History of the Slavs, book 1, page 5, also says: A certain sect became known at Mainz, which had lived in secret for six centuries or more. These people therefore existed before the year 800 after Christ's birth, under Charlemagne, Emperor of the West, at which time the controversy about the veneration of images was most vigorous, and at the Synod of Frankfurt, under Charlemagne, the question of images was debated against them in the year 794, so that the Second Synod of Nicaea was thereby made necessary. The doctrines and articles of this sect were these: that the saints, namely the dead, are not to be invoked, because they pray for no one; that God is the way of man after death, heaven or hell; that a bishop or the Pope cannot grant indulgences; that alms, masses and fasts do nothing to help souls separated from the body, for whose sake they are performed. And so on. In this our Belgium too there was a large number of Waldenses, after their suppression and dispersal in France and the coming of Peter Waldo himself; and even before him, through Tanchelm, a preacher well known at Antwerp and in the neighbouring parts of Brabant and Flanders, around the year 1100 (he was rashly and out of spite branded a heretic by the Papists), and it is certain that there were many opponents of the Papacy and the clergy in these regions. And that the Dominican friars first exercised the Inquisition against the excellent Waldenses here, before the Spanish one, at the outbreak of our wars, no one can be ignorant, as the reliability of our annals shows. Moreover, we owe to the most famous Marcus Zuerius Boxhorn the ancient confession of faith of the Belgian Waldenses, or catechism in questions and answers, published in the first book of his Belgian History, pages 36 to 42, which begins: What does one ask of a Christian? This is certainly worth knowing by every Belgian. Paul Perrin, in his History of the Waldenses, published the confession and catechism of the French Waldenses. At the time of the Reformation there were still very many Waldenses, or remnants of them, in France, Bohemia and Moravia, and elsewhere; and while they were scattered here and there, they often sent some of their own into various parts of the world, seeking a purer Church and men of better doctrine. At the time of the Reformation they came to Huldrych Zwingli, Luther, Oecolampadius and others, with whom they shared the condition of their churches, and from them received whatever needed correcting or otherwise arranging among themselves; their sole concern being that all should detest and flee the impurity of the Roman Church, as they themselves had long before done. Hence, among their writings, there had long existed a rather old book on the reasons for their secession from the Papacy, The cause of our separation from the Roman Church, Joh. Paulus Perrin writes. Concerning the remnants of the Waldenses in Savoy, in the year 1565 Hubert Languet of Burgundy also wrote in his letters to Camerarius, letter 20: The Duke of Savoy has expelled from his lands the inhabitants of the valleys of Luserna and Angrogna, to whom four years ago he had sold liberty in religion, after being defeated by them in several battles. They are the remnants of the Waldenses, and for two hundred years they have always professed the religion which we now profess; nor did the King of France, while he was ruling there in the meantime, prevent them from doing so. And to Camerarius the son, letter 24: I was lately in Moravia with Doctor Jordan, who led me to the Evangelicals, where the brothers the Waldenses have their principal church. They talked with me about our Efromus, and showed that they greatly desired his coming to them. And shortly after, he writes that Efromus had been called by the people of Heidelberg, Basel and the Waldensian brothers, and that his mind had inclined more towards the Waldenses. He wrote these things in 1565. The Ecclesiastical History of the Slavs also speaks of this Efromus.

units.la: Verùm hæc jam tempora sunt Reformationis, quibus pertendit, & perrupit superavitque impedimenta, quibus ante oppressa, cœpitque præcedenti seculo, culo, anno cIↄ Iↄ xvi. per Hudalrichum Zuinglium, in Helvetiâ; & anno cIↄ Iↄ xvii. per Martinum Lutherum, in Saxoniâ. Zuinglium Luthero præpono, quia utut ætate minor, ante Lutherum tamen docere & reformare incœpit, uti testatur, in Explanat. artic. Tom. i. art. xviii. pag. 37. Cepi ego Euangelion prædicare anno salutis decimosexto supra millesimum & quingentesimum, eo scilicet tempore, quum Lutheri nomen in nostris regionibus necdum auditum adhuc erat. Sic autem prædicavi quum Missa adhuc in usu esset Pontificiis, Euangelium quod in Missa legebatur populo propositum explicandum. Explicandum inquam non hominum commentis, sed sola scriptu-rarum Biblicarum collatione. Tametsi tunc temporis vehementer prisci doctoribus, ut qui essent puriores & clariores, addictus essem, quantumvis me & illorum non nihil piget. Testem hujus rei habere possum generosum illum & vere nobilem Theobaldum de Geroldsek administratorem templi Eremitici. In hoc templo, & Glaronæ jam veritatem Zuinglius docuerat, quam à præceptore suo V Vittenbachio olim Basileæ didicerat, de quo in sequentibus: Anno decimonono quum Tigurum concessissem & ibidem prædicare cepissem, indicabam venerabilibus domino præposito cæterisque collegii illius capitularibus, me posthac prædicaturum esse Euangelium Matthæi, idque absque humanis commentationibus ex solis fontibus scripturæ sacræ. Initio ejus anni nemo apud nos de Luthero quidquam audierat, præterquam quod de indulgentiis quiddam prodierat, quod me parum erudire poterat, quum jam antea satis scirem indulgentiarum negotium nihil esse quàm furtum & dolum. Didiceram hoc ex disputatione quadam, quam doctissimus vir Doctor Thomas Wyttenbach Bielensis, patronus & charissimus præceptor meus ante annos aliquot Basileæ in consessu publico in schola ac palæstra theologica licet me absente habuerat. Me tunc in Matthæi prædicatione, Lutheri scriptis parum esse adjutum quis non videt? Obiit Zuinglius, anno MDXXXI. d. xi. Octob. ætatis xliv. vel xlviii. secundum alios. Lutherus autem eo aetate provectior, mortuus est, anno cIↄ Iↄxlvi. d. xviii. Februarii, aetatis anno lxiii. Sic plura pergendi tempus habuit, atque ex eo tempore ante Zuinglium nominatim vulgo solet. Ad horum vero tempus ponendum esse casum Papatus, nemo nescit. Atque ita annotavimus Papatus ortus, adolescentiam, ἀκμήν, casus singula ad Auctores suos, & tempora: quae in hisce Controversiis omnino decet habere praecognita.
units.tr: But these are already the times of the Reformation, in which it extended, broke through and overcame the obstacles by which it had previously been crushed; it began in the previous century, in the year 1516, through Huldrych Zwingli in Helvetia, and in the year 1517 through Martin Luther in Saxony. I put Zwingli before Luther, because although younger in age he nevertheless began to teach and reform before Luther, as he testifies in his Explanation of the Articles, vol. 1, article 18, page 37: I began to preach the Gospel in the year of salvation 1516, at which time the name of Luther was not yet heard in our regions. I preached in such a way, while the Mass was still in use among the Papists, that the Gospel read in the Mass was set before the people to be explained. To be explained, I say, not by the inventions of men, but by the sole comparison of the Biblical Scriptures. Although at that time I was greatly devoted to the early teachers, as being purer and clearer, and somewhat, though I regret it, I still am. I can call as witness of this matter the noble and truly well-born Theobald of Geroldseck, administrator of the Hermit's church. In this church, and at Glarus, Zwingli had already taught the truth, which he had learned long before at Basel from his teacher Wittenbach, of whom more below: In the nineteenth year, when I had gone to Zurich and had begun to preach there, I informed the reverend provost and the other canons of that college that I would from now on preach the Gospel of Matthew, and that without human commentaries, from the sole sources of Holy Scripture. At the beginning of that year no one among us had heard anything of Luther, except that something had come out about indulgences, which could teach me little, since I already knew well enough that the business of indulgences was nothing but theft and deceit. I had learned this from a disputation which the most learned man, Doctor Thomas Wyttenbach of Biel, my patron and dearest teacher, had held some years earlier at Basel, in a public assembly in the theological school and arena, though I was absent. Who does not see that I was at that time helped little in preaching Matthew by the writings of Luther? Zwingli died on 11 October 1531, in the forty-fourth or, according to others, the forty-eighth year of his age. Luther, however, being older, died on 18 February 1546, in the sixty-third year of his age. Thus Zwingli had more time for proceeding, and from that time he is commonly named before Luther. But that the fall of the Papacy must be placed at this time, nobody is ignorant. And so we have noted the rise, the youth, the prime [ἀκμήν] and the fall of the Papacy individually, each with its authors and times, which in these controversies it is altogether fitting to have known beforehand.

units.la: Sed & quintam libet addere Papatus periodum, ejus scilicet desperati, in Concilio Tridentino anno cIↄ Iↄxlv. quando adversus adhibitam diu in eo Reformando frustra operam, se mirum in modum, & contra veritatem obstinavit, ac non tantum priora sua βλασφήμα retinuit pertinacius, sed & ita se adversus omnem admonitionem & doctrinam moliorem obstinavit, ut conclamata exinde Reformationis Ecclesiae istius res fuerit, pronunciato anathemate in puriorem doctrinam, & quoscunque ex ea sentientes. Ab isto tempore desperata facta est ejus salus, quam dum sanare voluimus, curati renuit. Et haec quidem distincta etiam a prioribus habenda est periodus, qua in illam formam se composuit Papatus, qualem antea non habuit, scilicet istam religionis compagem, quam suis omnibus sub aeternae salutis poena tenendam proposuit, denuntiata in deviantes aeterna maledictione. Haec Synodus, uti cum rebus obduratis solet, Papatui corticem & callum adduxit, firmavitque doctrinae tyrannidem: post quam rarius universalis regionum aliquarum, ut quidem antea, contigit reformatio, tam firmiter nempe & pertinaciter se nunc ad sua recipiente Papatu, & sola se tuente contumacia ac tyrannide. Incepit Synodus vel conventus, uti ad eam scripsit Rex Galliae Henricus, sed quam inscriptionem valde indignabantur Patres: Histor. Concil. lib. iv, pag. 356. ipsarum litterarum exemplar exhibet Bochellus, Decret. Eccles. Gallic. lib. v. pag.
units.tr: But I should also add a fifth period of the Papacy, its despairing period, at the Council of Trent in the year 1545. There, after long but fruitless efforts at reforming it, the Papacy obstinately and remarkably set itself against the truth. It not only clung more stubbornly to its earlier blasphemies [βλασφήμα], but resisted every admonition and gentler teaching so obstinately that the reformation of that church was thereafter given up as hopeless, with an anathema pronounced against purer doctrine and against all who thought in accordance with it. From that time its salvation was despaired of: when we wished to heal it, it refused to be cured. This period, too, must be regarded as distinct from the earlier ones, since in it the Papacy took that form it had not had before, namely that structure of religion which it required all its adherents to hold on pain of eternal salvation, with eternal curse declared against all deviants. This Synod, as usually happens with hardened things, drew a crust and callus over the Papacy and confirmed the tyranny of its doctrine. Since then, a general reformation of any region has occurred less often than before, because the Papacy now takes back its own so firmly and stubbornly, defended only by obstinacy and tyranny. The assembly was called a conventus, a meeting, as King Henry of France wrote to it, though the Fathers were greatly offended by that title. Bochellus gives the text of the letter itself, Decret. Eccles. Gallic. lib. v, p. [sic] and Histor. Concil. lib. iv, pag. 356.

units.la: incœpit (dico) Synodus anno cIↄ Iↄ xlv. d. xiii. Decemb. sub Paulo iii. & continuata fuit sub Iulio iii. Marcello ii. Paulo iv. denique absoluta a. cIↄ Iↄ lxiiii.d. 4. Decemb. sub Pio. iv. sessionibus xxv. subscripserunt numero ccl v Patres. Illamque esse fidem suam postquam omnes acclamassent, & doctrinam Ecclesiæ Romanæ perpetuò tenendam, dictum fuit à Cardinale Lotharingio primùm: anathema cuncti is hereticis: inde ab omnibus pariter, clamatum ultimò anathema, anathema: & mox sequenti a. cIↄ Iↄ lxiv.d.xv Ianuarii Concilium confirmavit Papa Pius, atque ab omnibus Christi fidelibus recipi, & inviolabiliter observari mandavit. Hinc jam magno conatu ubique Concilii istius promulgationem & observantiam introducere conati fuerunt Papæ, quamvis cum multorum ingratiis: & non levi Regnorum, & Rerumpublicarum concussione. In Belgio quidem quando anno cIↄ Iↄ lxv. proximo post habitum finitumque anno, obtrudi bonis incolis cœpit, belli facem accendit. Quare Regis litteris, quibus ille anni istius die 11. Octob. Gubernatricem jubebat in suppliciis hæreticorum incunctanter pergere, tum Quæsitores fidei, denique & Concilii Tridentini usum, quâ vi & auctoritate invehere omnem Belgii calamitatem Orangius, aliique acceptam referre confuerunt, inquit Strada, ad istum annum, lib. iv. adde & Thuanum, lib. xl.
units.tr: The Synod began (I say so) on 13 December 1545 under Paul III, was continued under Julius III, Marcellus II and finally Paul IV, and was concluded on 4 December 1563 under Pius IV, in twenty-five sessions. Five hundred and eighty-five Fathers signed it. After everyone had shouted their assent, the declaration that this was their faith and the doctrine of the Roman Church to be held forever was first made by Cardinal of Lorraine: let all cry anathema against these heretics. Then all together shouted at the end anathema, anathema. In the following year, on 15 January 1564, Pope Pius confirmed the Council and ordered that it be received by all the faithful of Christ and inviolably observed. From then on the popes strove with great effort everywhere to introduce the promulgation and observance of this Council, although many were unwilling, and not without considerable upheaval in kingdoms and commonwealths. In the Low Countries, when it began to be forced upon the good inhabitants in the year 1565, right after it had been held and finished the year before, it kindled the torch of war. Hence Orange and others were accustomed to attribute the whole calamity of Belgium to the letters of the King, by which on 11 October of that year he ordered the Governess to proceed without hesitation with the punishments of heretics, then to the inquisitors of the faith, and finally to the use of the Council of Trent, which they introduced by force and authority, as Strada says, book iv; add also Thuanus, book xl.

units.la: Atque in Galliis quos passim tumultus concitarit Concilii introductio, diligentissimus suæ patriæ temporisque historicus, ad quasque illius instantias, annotavit Iac. Augustus Thuanus. Quumque anno cIↄ Iↄ lxiv. primum de observandis Concilii Tridentini per Galliam decretis ageretur, & eorum promulgationem à Rege petitum venissent Legati Pontificis, Regisque Hispaniæ, Carolus Molinæus magni nominis I. C. ac prisca libertatis retinens Consultationem edidit, qua ob multas causas Concilium nullum, vitio indictum, habitum, & termi...catum contra antiqua Patrum decreta & Regni Francici dignitatem ac libertatem contendebat. quam ob rem in carcerem conjectus fuit, & postmodum quidem liberatus, at conditione addita, ne quid in posterum injussu Regis ederet in publicum, Thuanus, lib. xxxvi. Vide de hac re, videlicet introductione Concilii Tridentini, ejusque observantiae in Gallia, eundem historicum, lib. lxviii. lib. xci. anno clo Io lxxxviii. Tandem in ejus acceptionem inclinarunt, sed cum clausula, quatenus neque Regiae dignitati, neque libertatibus Ecclesiae Gallicanae, decreta illius contrariarentur. lib. xcii. De eodem repetita consilia, anno clo Io xcii. Thuan. lib. cv. & lib. cvii. Interque articulos reconciliationis Regis Henrici iv. cum Papa, anno clo Io xcv. xv. Kal. Octob. hic etiam fuit: Efficias ut Concilium Tridentinum publicetur, & observetur in omnibus: exceptis tamen (ad tuam supplicationem & instantissimam petitionem) si quae forte adessent, quae revera sine tranquillitatis perturbatione, executioni demandari non possint. Perron, Ambassades li. 1. pag. 343. Thuanus, lib. cxxii. lib. cxv. in fine, neque nisi sub illa restrictione in Gallia Concilium illud agnoscitur. Adde quod est inter Memoires du Plessis: Advertissement sur la reception du Concile de Trente, en France. Quid vero hac in re actum tandem, & quo astu suis Tridentinam illam Helenam Synodis immiscuerint Praesules Gallicani, nemo melius exponit Laurentio Bochello, in Praefat. ad Decreta Ecclesiae Gallic. anno clo Io xxi. quem audire loquentem expedit. Sic ergo ille: Quantas novissimis temporibus ubique terrarum excitavit turbas Synodus Tridentina, nemo est qui nesciat: cum ob tuptier neglectos Regis Christianissimi Legatos, tum propter nimiam illorum audaciam qui falcem in messem alienam immittentes, plura sibi quam par sit arrogare non sunt veriti: quae de re pleni libri, plenae tabulae publicae. Doctrinam illius probare vel convellere, nihil ad meam Spartam: at scire me non diffiteor, quod nulli
units.tr: And in France, the tumults which the introduction of the Council stirred up everywhere were carefully recorded by Jacques-Auguste de Thou, the most diligent historian of his country and times, at each of its stages. When in 1564 the decrees of the Council of Trent were first under discussion in France, and the legates of the Pontiff and of the King of Spain had come to ask the King for their promulgation, Charles Molinaeus, a jurist of great name who kept the ancient liberty, published a Consultation in which he contended that the Council was null, unlawfully convened, held and concluded, contrary to the ancient decrees of the Fathers and the dignity and liberty of the kingdom of the Franks. For this he was thrown into prison, and afterwards indeed released, but on condition that he should publish nothing in future without the King's command (Thuanus, book xxxvi). On this matter, namely the introduction of the Council of Trent and its observance in France, see the same historian, book lxviii, book xci, in the year 1588. At last they inclined to accept it, but with the clause that its decrees should not be contrary either to the royal dignity or to the liberties of the Gallican Church (book xcii). The same counsels were repeated in the year 1592 (Thuanus, book cv and book cvii). Among the articles of reconciliation between King Henry IV and the Pope, in the year 1595 on 18 September, this also was included: You shall bring it about that the Council of Trent be published and observed in all things, except (at your supplication and most urgent petition) such things, if any there be, as really cannot be put into execution without disturbing the peace. (Perron, Ambassades, book 1, p. 343; Thuanus, book cxxii, book cxv at the end). Nor is that Council acknowledged in France except under this restriction. Add also the treatise among the Mémoires du Plessis: Advertissement sur la réception du Concile de Trente en France. But what was finally done in this affair, and by what cunning the Gallican prelates mixed that Trent Helen into their synods, no one explains better than Laurent Bouchel, in the preface to the Decrees of the Gallican Church, in the year 1621, whom it is worth hearing speaking. Thus he says: How many disturbances the Synod of Trent has stirred up in recent times everywhere in the world, no one is ignorant: partly because the legates of the most Christian King were neglected by some, partly because of the excessive audacity of those who, thrusting their sickle into another's harvest, were not ashamed to claim more for themselves than is right. Of this matter there are full books and full public records. To prove or refute its doctrine is nothing to my Sparta; but I do not deny that I know this, that it is unknown to no one, nor could it be persuaded, even up to now, to our kings or to the supreme courts of the Parliaments, that they should record the most just canons of the Synod in their acts and publish them for observance.

units.la: Note: the scan is in a black-letter-flavoured italic and some words are hard to read; the opening line is a fragment. nulli ignotum est, nec Regibus nostris, nec supremis Parlamentorum Curiis huc usque persuaderi potuisse, ut Synodi iustius Canones in acta sua referrent, & observandos publicarent. Piget etiam refricare, quanto liberius Patres illi conscripti Gallica libertatis assertores & vindices, hanc Synodum procul ab archivis Regiis amandarunt; tanto obstinatius Praesules Gallos illius promulgationem a Principibus nostris efflagitasse, & tandem simul accensas & irritas preces suas, quod regni totius & Ecclesiae Gallicanae iuribus officerent, agnoverunt, conspiratione quadam, venia in quaque Diaecesi cogendi Synodos impetrata, id effecerunt, ut quae in conventu Tridentino decreta fuerant, in omnibus sine delectu Synodos suas infarcirent, & sub anathematis interminatione custodienda Diaecesanis suis proponerent; nedicam ad ipsorum tutelam furias ipsas armarent: ac ne frustra esse id putes, lapides loquuntur, opera interrupta minaeque murorum ingentes aperte testantur. Uniuscuiusque talium, Synodorum bonitas licet omnis, primordium a fidei professione incipit, in qua non solum ad Symbolum Apostolorum, Nicaeni Concilii, & Athanasii auctoritatum satis amplum spondendum, vovendum, ac iurandum est: sed quis feret haec? Caetera item omnia a sacris Canonibus & Oecumenicis Conciliis ac praecipue a sacrosancta Tridentina Synodo tradita, definita, & declarata, indubitanter recipio atque profiteor: simulque contraria omnia ego damno, rejicio, & anathematizo. Hanc veram Catholicam fidem, extra quam nemo salvus esse potest, sponte profiteor, &c. Huc Reges, Principes, huc Nobiles, Patres, huc omnes denique omne genus Ordines animis advertite vestris. Hæc, inquiunt, est vera fides Catholica, extra quam nemo salvus esse potest, indubitanter recipere atque profiteri omnia quae a sacrosancta Tridentina Synodo tradita, definita & declarata sunt, simulque contraria omnia damnare, rejicere & anathematizare. Videte, quaeso, videte quam male vobiscum actum sit, qui animo iam praefracto Synodo Tridentina obsistitis. Iam spei salutis nil est reliquum. Sistite vos judicio Patrum, nostri Tridentini coactorum, sed in ipso Gallia meditullio damnan-dos, & poenis nunquam desituris afficiendos. Neque vero mirari aliquis potest, quod tantopere desudent Papae pro ingerendo ubivis locorum Concilio, qui considerarit hoc esse ipsam Papatus arcem & fastigium, cujus vox, inquit Bellarminus, lib. v. de grat. & lib. arbitrio, cap. xiii. Ecclesia Catholica vox est. Romanam intelligit. Et de quo Jesuitae Professi, in quarto suo voto nuncupando, primo ajunt: Ego N. N. credo & recipio quaecunque sacrum generale Concilium Tridentinum credit & recipit, etiamsi ea in Concilio non fuissent definita. Conveniunt enim illa cum iis quae in Evangelicis & Apostolicis litteris continentur. Deinde de Scripturis dicunt: Praedictis vero Evangelicis & Apostolicis litteris atque aliis, quae praedictum Concilium credi jubet, etiamsi ea in Evangelicis & Apostolicis litteris non inveniantur, credo propter auctoritatem Ecclesiae Catholicae, quae in usu Ecclesiastico praedicta scripta & non scripta recipit. En putidum circulum, Ecclesiae credunt propter Ecclesiam; Concilio Tridentino propter Scripturam quasi, sed huic propter Ecclesiam, Romanam nempe, uti exponunt articulo sequente tertio; hoc est, Ecclesiae Romanae Synodo, propter istam Ecclesiam. Cujusmodi professio desperati status argumentum est, ut quae testatur, illam Ecclesiam nec aliunde salvari ultra posse, neque velle, sed in se & sua pertinacia immori. In hoc ergo Concilio merito nos ultimam Papatus desperabundi periodum assignamus; ipsum autem plenarie epiphaneia manifestatione praesentia suae Christus. II. Thess. II. 8.
units.tr: It also pains me to stir up again how much more freely those Fathers, the assertors and defenders of Gallican liberty, banished this Synod far from the royal archives; and how much more stubbornly the Gallican prelates begged our princes for its promulgation, and at last, acknowledging that their prayers, though heated and vain, were harmful to the rights of the whole kingdom and of the Gallican Church, by a certain conspiracy, having obtained permission to hold synods in each diocese, brought it about that they stuffed their own synods, without distinction, with whatever decrees had been made at the Council of Trent, and set them before their diocesans to be kept under threat of anathema. Not to mention that they armed the very furies for their own protection; and lest you think this is in vain, the stones speak, and unfinished works and the huge threatening walls openly bear witness. Although the goodness of every such synod begins with a profession of faith, in which one must not only pledge, vow and swear to the Apostles' Creed, the Nicene Creed and the Athanasian Creed, but who could bear this? I undoubtedly receive and profess all other things delivered, defined and declared by the sacred canons and the ecumenical councils, and especially by the most holy Synod of Trent; and at the same time I condemn, reject and anathematize all contrary things. This true Catholic faith, outside which no one can be saved, I freely profess, etc. Hither, kings, princes, nobles, Fathers, hither, finally, all orders of every kind, turn your minds. This, they say, is the true Catholic faith, outside which no one can be saved: to receive and profess without doubt all that has been delivered, defined and declared by the most holy Synod of Trent, and at the same time to condemn, reject and anathematize all contrary things. See, I beg you, see how badly it will go with you who, with your minds now stubborn, resist the Synod of Trent. Now there is no hope of salvation left. Submit yourselves to the judgment of the Fathers, our Tridentine assembly, but to be condemned in the very heart of France, and to be afflicted with punishments that will never cease. Nor can anyone wonder that the popes sweat so much to force the Council upon every place, if he considers that this is the very citadel and summit of the Papacy, whose voice, says Bellarmine, book v of De gratia et libero arbitrio, chapter 13, is the voice of the Catholic Church: he means the Roman one. And the professed Jesuits, in the fourth vow they pronounce, say first: I, N. N., believe and receive whatever the holy general Council of Trent believes and receives, even those things which were not defined in the Council, for they agree with those things which are contained in the Evangelical and Apostolic writings. Then concerning the Scriptures they say: Moreover, to the aforesaid Evangelical and Apostolic writings and to the others which the said Council bids us believe, even if those things are not found in the Evangelical and Apostolic writings, I believe on account of the authority of the Catholic Church, which in ecclesiastical use receives the aforesaid written and unwritten things. Behold the foul circle: they believe the Church on account of the Church; they believe the Council of Trent on account of Scripture, as it were, but Scripture on account of the Church, namely the Roman Church, as they explain in the third following article; that is, the Roman Church's Synod, on account of that Church. Such a profession is a sign of a desperate state, since it testifies that that Church can no longer be saved elsewhere, nor wishes to be, but is dying in itself and in its own obstinacy. In this Council, therefore, we rightly assign the last period of the despairing Papacy; and Christ will destroy it by the full manifestation [ἐπιφάνεια] of his presence, II Thess. II. 8.

units.la: Atque ex illo Concilio statim videri possunt dogmata Papalia, & articuli, ob quos illam nos Ecclesiam censemus abominandam esse. Quamvis nec ignoremus, tum ex Historia Concilii Tridentini (cujus auctor est frater Paulus Sarpius, Servita Venetus, qui eam Italice scripsit; & in Gallicum convertit Joh. Deodatus, in Latinum Adamus Neutonus, Scotus); tum ex Iacobo Payva Andradio, Lusitano, (qui Concilio interfuit, ibique scripsit adversus Chemnitium, & ejus de Iesuitarum Theologia librum, Orthodoxas Explicationes de controversiis religionis capitibus, decreta Concilii Tridentini passim explicans) singula magno studio & arte composita esse, & confuta ex mille dolis & amphiboliis. Quod vero Andradius titulum libri fecit, non Explicationem Concilii aut articulorum Concilii, sed ita uti dixi, est quod Concilium hoc expresse vetat, vel Bulla Confirmationis Pii v. ne cuivis liceat Commentarios vel expositiones ejus facere. Ad vitandum praeterea perversionem, & confusionem, quae oriri posset, si unicuique liceret, prout ei liberet, in decreta Concilii commentarios, & interpretationes suas edere; Apostolica auctoritate inhibemus omnibus, tam ecclesiasticis personis, cujuscumque sint ordinis, conditionis, & gradus, quam laicis, quocumque honore, ac potestate praeditis; Prelatis quidem sub interdicti ingressus ecclesiae, aliis vero, quicumque fuerint, sub excommunicationis latae sententiae poenis, ne quis sine auctoritate nostra audeat ullos commentarios, glossas, annotationes, scholia, ullumve omnino interpretationis genus super ipsius Concilii decretis quocumque modo edere, aut quidquam quocumque nomine, etiam sub praetextu majoris decretorum corroborationis, aut executionis, aliove quaesito colore, statuere. Si cui vero in eis aliquid obscurius dictum, & statutum fuisse, eamque ob causam interpretatione, aut decisione aliquâ egere visum fuerit, ascendat ad locum, quem Dominus elegit, ad Sedem videlicet Apostolicam, omnium fidelium magistram, cujus auctoritatem etiam ipsa sancta Synodus tam reverenter agnovit. En fabulam; ex authoritate & instinctu Papae habitum concilium, ab eodem etiam interpretandum: atque uti nihil praeter illius arbitrium decernendum fuit, decretumque, ita nec ab eo aliquid alienum tenere liberum. Vnus Papa illis Concilium, Ecclesia, fides, & omnia. Vnde qui in Concilii Tridentino
units.tr: And from that Council one can at once see the Papal dogmas and articles, on account of which we judge that church to be abominable. We are not unaware that these have been fully treated: in the History of the Council of Trent (whose author is Brother Paolo Sarpi, a Venetian Servite, who wrote it in Italian; John Diodati turned it into French, and Adam Newton, a Scot, into Latin); and by Jacob Payva Andrada, a Portuguese (who attended the Council, and there wrote against Chemnitz and his book On the Theology of the Jesuits, and his Orthodox Explanations of the Chief Points of Religious Controversy, explaining the decrees of the Council of Trent throughout), that each single item was composed with great zeal and skill, and is to be refuted through a thousand tricks and ambiguities. The reason Andrade gave his book a title that is not an explanation of the Council or of its articles, as I have said, is that this Council expressly forbids it, as does the Bull of Confirmation of Pius V, so that no one may make commentaries or explanations of it. "To avoid, moreover, the perversion and confusion that could arise if each person were free to publish commentaries and interpretations of the decrees of the Council as he pleased, we forbid by apostolic authority all persons, ecclesiastical or lay, of whatever order, condition, or rank, and endowed with whatever honour or power (Prelates under penalty of interdict from entering a church, others, whoever they may be, under the penalty of excommunication latae sententiae), that anyone presume without our authority to publish any commentaries, glosses, annotations, scholia, or any kind of interpretation whatever upon the decrees of this Council in any way, or to lay down anything under any name, even under the pretext of a greater corroboration or execution of the decrees, or any other pretended purpose." If anything in them has been said or laid down too obscurely, and for that reason anyone thinks an interpretation or some decision is needed, let him go up to the place the Lord has chosen, namely the Apostolic See, the teacher of all the faithful, whose authority this holy Synod itself acknowledged so reverently. Behold the fable: a council convened by the authority and at the instigation of the Pope, and to be interpreted by him as well; and just as nothing could be decreed except at his pleasure, so nothing contrary to him may be held freely. One Pope is for them the Council, the Church, the faith, and everything. Hence:

units.la: dcndentini Canones scripsit postea Remissiones, Barbosa, continentes Doctorum, qui materias in Canonibus agitatas tractaverunt, diligentes valdeque compendiosas citationes, nonnihil operae posuit in libri sui Prologo, ut se ostenderet nihil egisse contra Pii IV. constitutionem illam & Bullam. Caeterum editae sunt Cardinalium, ad Concilium Tridentinum Declarationes, quae ad ejus explicationem multi usus sunt, post varias in Gallia & Belgio editiones, Antverpiae a. cIↄ Iↄ cxxx ii i.cum aliorum Additionibus, & Rotae Romanae Decisionibus, atque Barbosę illis Remissionibus: quam merito omnibus aliis editionibus & exemplaribus Concilii praeferas.
units.tr: Barbosa, who after the Canons of the Council of Trent wrote the Remissions, containing diligent and very compendious citations of the Doctors who treated the matters discussed in the Canons, took some trouble in the Preface of his book to show that he had done nothing against the constitution and Bull of Pius IV. Moreover, the Declarations of the Cardinals on the Council of Trent have been published, and have been much used for its explanation, after various editions in France and Belgium, at Antwerp in 1630, with the additions of others, the Decisions of the Roman Rota, and the Remissions of Barbosa; these you should rightly prefer to all other editions and copies of the Council.

units.la: Ex Concilii Canonibus quidem, maxime tamen anathematismis, additis Pontificiorum super quovis articulo aut dogmate disputationibus, tum capita dogmatum ipsorum, tum status controversiae erui possunt. Summam religionis Papisticae continet professio fidei, a Pio IV. praescripta: ubi etiam Concilii Tridentini recipitur authoritas, atque haereses illic condemnatae rejiciuntur. Sed nemo compendiosius atque apertius totam Papismi formam & basem simul complexus fuit, quam Silvester Prierias, in Dialogo adversus Conclusiones Lutheri, inscripto Leoni x. (extat operum Lutheri Latin. Tom. i.) fundamentum tertium. Quicunque non inniteter doctrinae Romanae Ecclesiae; ac Romani Pontificis, tanquam Regulae fidei infallibili, a qua etiam Sacra Scriptura robur trahit & authoritatem, haereticus est.
units.tr: From the Canons of the Council, and above all the anathemas, together with the disputations the Papists have added on each article or dogma, both the heads of their dogmas and the state of the controversy can be drawn. The profession of faith prescribed by Pius IV contains the sum of the Papist religion, where the authority of the Council of Trent is also accepted, and the heresies condemned there are rejected. But no one has embraced the whole form and foundation of Papism more briefly and openly than Silvester Prierias, in his Dialogue against Luther's Conclusions, addressed to Leo X (it is in the Latin works of Luther, vol. 1): Third foundation. Whoever does not rest upon the doctrine of the Roman Church and the Roman Pontiff, as the infallible rule of faith, from which even Holy Scripture draws its strength and authority, is a heretic.

units.la: Permultum refert, in Disputationibus Pontificiis inter se conferre doctrinam, theses, & modum disputandi a Papisticis Doctoribus sub initio Reformationis usurpatum; cum hodiernis: tum ut varietatem rerum istarum inter se videamus: tum ut sinceriorem sensus & doctrinae Papisticae habeamus confessionem olim, quam hodie suae religionis incrustatores Iesuitae aliique edere solent. Atque istam ob causam dixi, Controversiarum sensum capiendum praecipue esse ex ipsorum rum disputationibus, non nudis assertionibus, aut propositionibus; & in disputationibus, potissimum quidem ex illorum responsionibus, ad nostra seu argumenta, seu exceptiones: ubi tum præcisius & ad lineam quasi spectatis partium utrimque limitibus, non solum quid controvertant ambæ, sed & quousque ultimò procedant, manifestius apparet. Quantum autem situm sit & in omni disputatione, & in hâc cum Papistis, in statu controversiæ examussim constituendo, quantumque hic ostendatur disputatoris probi judicium, nemo, nisi qui omnem disputandi rationem & momentum, ignorat.
units.tr: It matters greatly to compare with the present ones the doctrine, theses, and manner of disputing that the Papist doctors used at the beginning of the Reformation: both to see how these matters vary among themselves, and to have a more sincere confession of the Papist sense and doctrine from former times, than what their Jesuits and other whitewashers of their religion are wont to publish today. For this reason I have said that the sense of the controversies should be grasped chiefly from their disputations, not from bare assertions or propositions; and in the disputations, especially from their replies to our arguments or objections. There, looking more precisely, and as it were along the line of the boundaries of each party, it appears more clearly not only what both sides dispute, but also how far they finally go. How much depends, in every disputation and in this one with the Papists, on fixing the state of the controversy exactly, and how much the judgment of an honest disputant is shown here, no one can fail to see except one who is ignorant of all the method and weight of disputing.

units.la: Seriem controversiarum Papisticarum multi, verum alii aliter exhibent. Proponunt suo modo illa V Whitakerus, V Willetus, Camero, in Prælect. de verbo Dei pag. 349. alii. Præterea methodus Papistica spectatur, quæ est vel secundum ordinem Concilii Tridentini; vel quem tenuit in suis Disputationum Tomis Bellarminus; aut quis alius ejusdem scholæ & commatis: vel ad ordinem locorum Theologicorum, eorum inter se spectatâ serie & nexu; quod nos sequimur. Denique ad ortum Papismi, & juxta singulorum articulorum quibus quisque temporibus orti, sibique successerunt, velim exhiberi controversiarum nostrarum specimen & tabulam, juxta ea, quæ supra indicavimus, de Papatus ortu, & progressu. Ubi distinguenda tria semper tempora. I. quousque in Ecclesiâ dogma aliquod Pontificium sit ignoratum, id est, ignotus eâ in parte Papismus. II. quando primum intrudi aliquid cœperit, & disputari. III. quando definitum sit, sive à Papis, sive in Concilio à Papis accepto confirmatoque: siquidem decisio articulorum fidei in Ecclesiâ Romana, vel Papalis est, vel Synodica. Vti Gretserus in Colloquio Ratisbonensi III. anno clɔ Iɔ cɪ. Pontifex Romanus, sive solus definiat aliquid, sive definiat cum Concilio Generali. Ista Iudex semper est infallibilis. Verbi gratia, in causa imaginum, tribus prioribus saeculis imagines Ecclesia non habuit, nedum illarum cultum: primùm introduci coeperunt, & disputare super ista quidem materia, à saeculo quarto; sed tantum ut imagines haberentur in templis, memoriae ornatusque causâ: at illarum adoratio saeculo adhuc post demum coepit, id est, quinto, quamvis repressa tum etiam valde, usque quo saeculo octavo confirmata earum adoratio fuit, primùm in Concilio Nicaeno. II. anno cIↄ cc lxxxvII. sub Irene Imperatrice, quod P. Adrianus, legato, & sententiâ suâ comprobavit. Ergo ad annum usque ccc. nullae imagines in Ecclesiâ. Circa hoc tempus introduci coeptae, sed mox ab Eliberinâ Synodo, celebri canone repressae: placuit picturas in Ecclesiis esse non debere, ne quod colitur, aut adoratur, in parietibus pingatur. Circa tempora Augustini, anno cccc. forte adorari coeptae, sed ab imperitâ & errante plebe, reclamantibus Doctoribus. Augustinus, lib. I, de moribus Eccles. Cathol. cap. xxxiv. Nolite mihi colligere professores nominis Christiani, nec professionis suae vim scientes, aut exhibentes. Nolite conseetari turbas imperitorum, qui vel in ipsa vera religione superstitiosi sunt, vel ita libidinibus dediti, ut obliti sint, quidquid promiserunt Deo. Novi multos esse sepulchrorum, & picturarum adoratores; novi multos esse qui luxuriosissime super mortuos bibant &c. Vide quales noret fuisse illos, qui hanc novitatem inchoarent, & cum quibus illos componat. Ipseque P. Gregorius I. sub a. cIↄ c, utcunque imagines tueatur in Ecclesiâ habendas, adorari tamen minimè voluit, ita scribens ad Severum Massilienfem Episcopum, qui, Veterum exemplo & canonibus insistens, imagines omnes frangi & ejici jusserat, lib. VII. epist. CIX. Praeterea indico dudum ad nos pervenisse quod fraternitas vestra quosdam imaginum adoratores aspiciens, easdem Ecclesiae imagines confregit atque projecit. Et quidem zelum vos, ne quid manu factum adorari possit, habuisse laudavimus: sed frangere eandem imagines non debuisse judicamus. Idcirco enim pictura in Ecclesiis adhibetur, ut hi qui litteras nesciunt, saltem in parietibus videndo legant quae legere in codicibus non valent. Tua ergo fraternitas et illas servare, et ab earum adoratu populum prohibere debuit: quatenus et literarum nescii haberent unde scientiam historiae colligerent: et populus in pictura adoratione minime peccaret. Quaestio ergo quum in hoc negotio duplex sit, an habendae in Ecclesiâ imagines? & de usu earundem, an ad cultum adorationemque? primum solum tum adhuc tenuit Romanus Papa, alterum rejecit. In quorum illo uti abiit à sententiâ aliorum sui temporis episcoporum, & à Veterum doctrinâ ac praxi, ita in secundo posteriores Papae similiter ab illo discesserunt, & tam hoc, quam illud, contra omnia jura exemplaque, arripuerunt, nempe in Synodo Nicaena II. quam Graeci sep- timam appellant, anno clo cc lxxxvii. ubi aderant Legati P. Adriani: quamque Tridentina, sess. xxv. in negotio imaginum secuta est, & approbavit. In illâ Nicaenâ, inter alia etiam sanciunt, Act. vii. Qui vero dicunt, sufficere usum imaginum ad memoriam solum, non vero ad salutationem eas habendas, illud quidem recipientes, hoc vero recusantes, semiprobi quadantenus et falsoveri, ut ita dicam, deprehenduntur, altera quidem parte veritatem confitentes, ex altera vero perverse agentes. O insignem quoque horum insaniam. Quae conferantur cum superiori sententia P. Gregorii: atque inde Papismi notetur progressus, & ad deteriora semper prolapsus. Salutationem imaginum intelligunt, cum adoratione, expressius in sequentibus: His ita se habentibus, in confesso et sine ulla dubitatione credimus, acceptam et placitam coram Deo esse venerandarum imaginum depictionem, et earum quae dispensationem domini nostri Iesu Christi exprimunt, et virginis quoque Mariae deipare intemeratae, quinetiam gloriosorum angelorum, et omnium sanctorum, has quoque adorandas et salutandas putamus, qui vero ita non est animatum, sed circa venerandarum imaginum adorationem laborat & dubitat, cum anathematizat sancta & veneranda nostra synodus, quæ efficacia divini spiritus & ecclesiasticis patrum traditionibus munita est & cincta. Anathema autem istud, nihil aliud est quàm separatio à Christo.
units.tr: Many people set out the series of Papist controversies, but not all in the same way. Whitaker and Willet propose them in their own manner, and Camerarius in his Prelections on the Word of God, p. 349, and others. Besides, the Papist method is considered, which is either according to the order of the Council of Trent, or that which Bellarmine followed in his volumes of Disputations, or that of any other of the same school and stamp; or according to the order of the theological places, with their series and connection considered among themselves, which is what we follow. Finally, I would like a specimen and table of our controversies to be drawn up according to the origin of Popery, and according to the times in which each single article arose and succeeded the others, in line with what we have indicated above about the origin and progress of the Papacy. Here three periods must always be distinguished. I. How far some Papal dogma has been unknown in the Church, that is, how far Popery was unknown in that part. II. When something first began to be obtruded and disputed. III. When it was defined, whether by the Popes, or in a Council accepted and confirmed by the Popes; for the decision of the articles of faith in the Roman Church is either Papal or Synodical. As Gretser says in the Colloquy of Regensburg, in the year 1541: The Roman Pontiff, whether he defines something alone or defines it with a General Council, is always an infallible judge. For example, in the case of images, for the first three centuries the Church had no images, much less their worship. They first began to be introduced and disputed about this matter from the fourth century, but only so that images might be in the churches for the sake of memory and decoration. Their adoration, however, began only later, in the fifth century, and even then was greatly restrained, until in the eighth century their adoration was confirmed, first at the Second Council of Nicaea, in 787, under the Empress Irene, which Pope Adrian approved through his legate and his sentence. Therefore up to the year 300 there were no images in the Church. About that time they began to be introduced, but were soon suppressed by the Council of Elvira, by a famous canon: It has pleased us that pictures should not be in the churches, lest what is worshipped or adored be painted on the walls. Around the time of Augustine, in the year 400, they perhaps began to be adored, but by an ignorant and erring crowd, the teachers protesting. Augustine, On the Manners of the Catholic Church, book I, chapter 34: Do not gather for me the professors of the Christian name who know neither the power of their profession nor practise it. Do not chase after the crowds of the unlearned, who are superstitious even in true religion, or so given to lusts that they forget whatever they have promised to God. I know there are many worshippers of tombs and pictures; I know there are many who drink most luxuriously over the dead, etc. See what sort of men those were who began this novelty, and with whom he compares them. Pope Gregory I himself, about the year 600, though he maintained that images should be kept in the Church, nonetheless did not at all wish them to be adored, writing thus to Severus, Bishop of Marseilles, who, following the example and canons of the Ancients, had ordered all images to be broken and cast out (book VII, letter 109): Moreover, we have lately learned that your brotherhood, seeing some worshippers of images, broke and threw out the images in the Church. We have indeed praised your zeal that nothing made by hand should be adored, but we judge that you ought not to have broken the images. For pictures are placed in churches so that those who cannot read may at least read by looking at the walls what they cannot read in books. Your brotherhood therefore ought both to have preserved them and to have forbidden the people to adore them, so that the unlettered might have a means of gathering the knowledge of history, and the people might not sin at all in the adoration of the picture. Since, therefore, the question in this business is twofold, whether images are to be kept in the Church, and about their use, whether for memory or for worship and adoration, the Roman Pope at that time still held the first and rejected the second. As he departed in the first from the opinion of the other bishops of his time, and from the doctrine and practice of the Ancients, so in the second the later Popes similarly departed from him, and seized both this and that against all laws and examples: namely in the Second Synod of Nicaea, which the Greeks call the Seventh, in the year 787, where the legates of Pope Adrian were present, and which the Tridentine Council, session 25, followed and approved in the matter of images. In that Nicene Council they also decree, Act. VII: Those who say that the use of images suffices for memory only, and not for saluting them, while accepting the one and refusing the other, are found to be half-honest and, so to speak, false-true, confessing the truth on the one side, and acting perversely on the other. O the notable madness of these men too. These statements should be compared with the earlier opinion of Pope Gregory; and thence the progress of Papism is noted, and its ever-downward slide into worse things. That by salutation they mean adoration is stated more clearly in what follows: These things being so, we believe without any doubt that the depiction of venerable images is acceptable and pleasing before God, and of those which express the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, and of the glorious angels and all the saints; we also think these are to be adored and saluted. But whoever is not so minded, and labours and doubts about the adoration of venerable images, is anathematized by our holy and venerable synod, which is strengthened and girded by the efficacy of the divine Spirit and the ecclesiastical traditions of the Fathers. This anathema is nothing other than separation from Christ.

units.la: In disputatione de S. Cœnâ, similiter tempus primò poni debet, quo ignoratum transsubstantiationis æque nomen ac dogma, videlicet usque ad sæculum nonum, post tempora Caroli M. id est, post agitatam de imaginibus controversiam. Patres quidem nimiis suis in materiâ Cœnæ Dominicæ rhetoricationibus & hyperbolis imprudenter sæpe locuti fuere, & occasionem errori præbuerunt, sed ipsum tamen dogma, prout Romana tenet Ecclesia, illis tam incognitum fuit, ut omnibus merito nunc horrendum est. Sed quemadmodum voces meriti, sacramenti, altaris adhibuerunt, longe alio sensu, quam eas postmodum arripuerunt Pontificii: ita & mutationis, quam in S. Cœna docebant contingere: mutationis nempe quoad usum, non substantiam: Christum adeo firmiter statuentes in cœlo esse, non in terrâ, ut hinc in celebratione Cœnæ usurparent solemnem ad populum monitionem sursum corda. Sub Carolo Calvo, Caroli M. nepote, circa annum 1 ccc l. controversia super Christi in S. cœnâ præsentiâ moveri cœpit: quâ de re consultus à Rege Bertramus, presbyter, scripsit commendabile opus, uti id appellat Trithemius, in Catalogo, de corpore & sanguine Domini, quod extat inter Orthodoxographa Patrum, & seorsim, commentariolo illustratum à Guilielmo Feuguereo, Leydensi Theologo, a. cI5 I5 lxx ix. ubi quæstionem tum temporis motam Bertramus significat, in prologo, atque libri ipsius initio: Dum enim quidam fidelium corporis sanguinisque Christi, quod in ecclesia quotidie celebratur, dicant, quod nulla sub figura, nulla sub obvelatione fiat, sed ipsius veritatis nuda manifestatione peragatur, quidam vero testentur quod hæc sub mysterii Sterii figura contineantur, & aliud sit quod corporeis sensibus appareat, aliud autem quod fides aspiciat, non parva diversitas inter eos esse dinoscitur: sic in Præfatione. Vbi obserua, inter fideles institutam dici disceptationem: adeo & recens tum erat controversia, & pars utraque in eadem ecclesiâ, neutram adhuc extra suum consortium posuerat, ut in ortu quæstionis solet fieri. Hunc autem quæstionis cardinem fuisse indicat, an in S.
