Cœnâ dicatur corpus Christi esse sub figurâ, id est, sacramentaliter, in signo, an ipsum corpus nude, proprie, verè, substantialiter? utrum ipsum corpus sit quod de Maria natum est & passum, mortuum & sepultum, quodque resurgens & cœlos ascendens, ad dextram patris consideat? uti in libri initio ibidem loquitur: in mysterio fiat, an in veritate? figuram explicat, quod est obumbratio quædam, quibusdam velaminibus quod intendit ostendens, & exemplum dat, uti quando Christus seipsum vitem, discipulos appellat palmites; atque ita in signo vel figura Christi corpus ostendi: quod non sensibus carnis, sed animi fidelis contuitu vel aspicitur, vel accipitur, vel comeditur. deinde: quia panis illic vinumque figurate Christi corpus & sanguis exististi. Eandemque post alios sententiam, sæculo undecimo, anno clo xxx. tenuit Berengarius Turonensis, Andegavensis Ecclesiæ archidiaconus, ipsi, Platinæ celebratus vir sanctimoniâ vitæ & doctrinâ præstans, cujus nihil superest, nisi quod in Synodis adversus eum habitis, & scriptis adversariis, præsertim Lanfranci Cantuatiensis, legitur. Deinde ex eâ, quæ ei præscripta & injuncta fuit palinodiæ formula, apparet, quæ Ecclesiæ Romanæ fuerit, suæ oppolita, sententia, nimirum quod post consecrationem non solum sacramentum sit corporis Christi, sed verum corpus & sanguinem Christi ibi sensualiter manibus sacerdotum tractari, frangi, & dentibus atteri. Horrendum thema, & verè tremendum, uti ipsi solent loqui, mysterium; sed falsum, inane, & verè impium. Atque adeo fe- tum adversus Berengarium oppositum sequior Ec- clesiae factio, quam pro more tuebatur Ecclesia Romana, ut hinc in articulum fidei Romanae transierit opinio de corporali Christi in Coenâ praesentiâ, in variis adversus Berengarium Synodis, ab anno cIↄ l. Romanâ, sub Leone ix. Vercellensi, eodem anno, mense Septembri. Turonensi, anno cIↄ lv. tempore P. Victoris II. cui Concilio legatus ejus interfuit Hildebrandus, postea factus Papa; ubi ad recantationem adactus Berengarius dicitur. Romanâ, anno cIↄ lix. sub Nicolao II, quâ in Synodo illa ei recantationis formula, ab Humberto Cardinale conscripta, propositâ fuit, in quam jurare coactus: Ego Berengarius &c. cujus nunc meminimus. Hic ergo vera sententia condemnata, stabilita erronea, omnibusque, sub poena haeresis, injuncta fuit. De modo, quo Christi corpus & sanguis praesentia essent, supererat adhuc quaestio, nimirum an per mutationem substantialem, panis nimirum in verum Christi corpus, & vini in ejus sanguinem? Sed & hoc non diu post acceptum quoque fuit, ut foecundus error, perfacile alium parit. In Synodo Romana VI. sub S. Gregorio VII. anno cIↄ lxxix. conclusum, converti substantialiter panem in corpus Christi, atque vinum in ejus sanguinem: sed post agitatam diu à diversum sententibus in ipsâ illâ Synodo controversiam: quod indicium est tum demum definitam rem illam fuisse, & pro fidei articulo habitam; secus haud licuisset in alteram partem multum disputare. Ceterum in Concilio Lateranensi, sub Innocentio III. anno cIↄ cc xv. contra Albigenses, & qui fautor eorum habebatur, Almaricum, posita aperte transubstantiatio, Cap. I. transubstantiatis panem in corpus, & vinum in sanguinem. Adeo, quemadmodum super negotio Coenae duplex nobis cum Papistis est disputatio, una de praesentia Christi corporali in Coenâ; de Transubstantiatione altera, Pontificium dogma circa illud agitari caeperit ab anno cIↄ ccc I. definitum vero anno cIↄ I. & cIↄ Ixx ix. hoc autem, nempe Transubstantiatio, a. cIↄ Ixx ix. & cIↄ cc xv. Atque ita in reliquis Papatus articulis ut compendiose ortus & aetas eorundem assignatur, juxta tria quae diximus dogmatis ignorati, disputati, definiti, momenta & periodos, desidero. Quod non tanti nunc operis foret, post omnium fere Papatus articulorum a Multis, ex antiquitate demonstrationem, & sive in Historia Ecclesiastica, sive in Patrum Theologia & scriptis annotationes sedulas & copiosas, Papatus tum emergentis varie, tum etiam repressi. Quod est schema Papatus historicum, doctrinae scilicet istius juxta aetates, & ordinem temporis.
units.tr: In the dispute over the Holy Supper, the first period to be fixed is likewise the one when the term and the doctrine of transubstantiation were both unknown, namely down to the ninth century, after the time of Charlemagne, that is, after the controversy over images had been stirred up. The Fathers, indeed, often spoke imprudently about the Lord's Supper in their excessive rhetorical flourishes and hyperboles, and so gave occasion for error. But the doctrine itself, as the Roman Church holds it, was so unknown to them that it is now rightly horrifying to everyone. But just as they used the words merit, sacrament and altar in a far different sense from that in which the Papists later seized upon them, so also they taught a change that takes place in the Supper, namely a change in use, not in substance. They held so firmly that Christ is in heaven and not on earth that in the celebration of the Supper they used the solemn exhortation to the people, sursum corda ("lift up your hearts"). Under Charles the Bald, grandson of Charlemagne, around the year 850, a controversy over the presence of Christ in the Holy Supper began to arise. On this matter Bertram, a presbyter, was consulted by the king and wrote a work which Trithemius, in his Catalogue, calls a commendable work, On the Body and Blood of the Lord. It is found among the Orthodox writings of the Fathers, and was published separately, with a short commentary, by Guillaume Feugueray, a Leiden theologian, in 1579. In the preface and at the beginning of the book itself, Bertram describes the question that had been raised at that time: "For while some of the faithful say that the body and blood of Christ, which is celebrated daily in the Church, is effected not under any figure or veil, but by a bare manifestation of the truth itself, and others testify that these things are contained under the figure of a mystery, and that what appears to the bodily senses is one thing and what faith perceives is another, a considerable difference is seen to exist between them." So he says in the preface. Note here that the dispute is described as taking place among the faithful, so recent was the controversy at that time, and both sides were still within the same Church, neither having yet been placed outside the fellowship of the other, as usually happens at the origin of a question. The hinge of the question, moreover, was whether the Scripture says that the body of Christ is in the Supper under a figure, that is, sacramentally, in a sign, or whether the body itself is present bare, properly, truly and substantially: "whether it is the very body that was born and suffered of Mary, died and was buried, and that rising and ascending into heaven sits at the right hand of the Father, or whether it is in mystery or in truth." He explains the figure as a certain shadowing, which shows what it intends by means of certain veils, and gives the example of Christ calling himself the vine and his disciples the branches. In this way the body of Christ is shown in a sign or figure, which is seen, received or eaten not by the senses of the flesh, but by the gaze of the faithful mind. Then he adds: "because there the bread and wine are figuratively the body and blood of Christ."* Berengar of Tours, archdeacon of the Church of Angers, a man celebrated by Platina for the holiness of his life and his learning, held this same opinion, after others, in the eleventh century, in the year 1030. Nothing of his survives except what is read in the synods held against him and in the writings of his opponents, above all Lanfranc of Canterbury. Then, from the formula of recantation which was prescribed and imposed on him, it appears what opinion was opposed by the Roman Church: namely, that after consecration there is not only a sacrament of the body of Christ, but that the true body and blood of Christ are there handled sensibly by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth. This is a dreadful thesis, and truly a fearful mystery, as they themselves are accustomed to say; but it is false, empty, and truly impious. And so the offspring of the faction opposed to Berengar, which the Roman Church, as was its custom, defended, passed from there into an article of Roman faith: the opinion concerning the bodily presence of Christ in the Supper. This was established in various synods against Berengar: from the year 1050 at Rome under Leo IX; at Vercelli in the same year, in September; at Tours in 1054, in the time of Pope Victor II, at which council his legate Hildebrand, later made pope, was present, and where Berengar is said to have been forced to recant; at Rome in 1059 under Nicholas II, in which synod that formula of recantation, drawn up by Cardinal Humbert, was put forward, and he was compelled to swear to it: "I, Berengar," etc., which we now recall. Thus the true opinion was condemned and the erroneous one established, and it was imposed on everyone under pain of heresy. Concerning the manner in which the body and blood of Christ were present, there still remained the question whether this happened through a substantial change, namely of bread into the true body of Christ and of wine into his blood. But this too was accepted not long afterwards, since a fruitful error very easily gives birth to another. In the sixth Roman synod, under St. Gregory VII, in 1079, it was concluded that the bread is substantially converted into the body of Christ and the wine into his blood. Yet this came only after a controversy had been stirred for a long time in that same synod by those who held different opinions. This is a sign that the matter was then at last settled and held as an article of faith; otherwise it would not have been permitted to dispute much on the other side. Moreover, at the Lateran Council under Innocent III, in 1215, directed against the Albigenses and against Amalric, who was considered their supporter, transubstantiation was openly laid down in chapter 1: "they transubstantiate the bread into the body, and the wine into the blood." Thus, just as concerning the matter of the Supper we have a twofold dispute with the Papists, one about the bodily presence of Christ in the Supper, and the other about transubstantiation, so the Papist dogma on this point began to be debated from the year 1301, and was defined in the years 1050 and 1079 (for the presence) and in 1215 (for transubstantiation). In this way I point out, in brief, the origin and age of the other articles of the Papacy as well, according to the three moments and periods of the doctrine which I have named: unknown, disputed, defined. It would not now be such a great task, after nearly all the articles of the Papacy have been demonstrated from antiquity by many authors, to make careful and copious observations, both in Church history and in the theology and writings of the Fathers, on how the Papacy emerged at various times and was also suppressed. This is the historical scheme of the Papacy, namely the course of this doctrine according to the ages and the order of time.

units.la: Verum ut se hodie ejus res habent, non aliunde certius, quam ex Concilio Tridentino intelligas, quod, una cum Scriptore aliquo Classico, qualis v. g. Bellarminus (ne quis se pluribus obruat) si quis attente legat & volvat, optime statum & formam Papismi addiscet, quod longe consultius, quam ut minutulis & levioribus libellis se quis addicat, & detineat. In Concilio autem Tridentino ita firmatae res Papisticae sunt, ut illis ne pilum quidem nunc cedere liceat, aut dare locum aliquem veritati, tot diris execrationibus ab ipsis excommunicatae.
units.tr: But as matters stand today, you can learn their true state from nothing more surely than from the Council of Trent. If anyone reads and studies it carefully, together with some classic writer, such as Bellarmine (so that no one is overwhelmed by too many), he will learn the state and form of Papism very well. This is far more advisable than attaching oneself to, and being held up by, small and lightweight pamphlets. In the Council of Trent the Papist affairs have been so firmly settled that now it is not permitted to yield even a hair's breadth to them, or to give any place to truth, which they have excommunicated with so many dreadful curses.

units.la: Ab isto tempore desperata res fuit concordiae, antehac a nonnullis tentatae, frustra tum quidem, sed utnunc etiam aliqui post Concilium syncretismum nostrae religionis & Papisticae moliantur, nae inepte sapere videntur, & nimis lubenter suam isti homines ludere operam. Concilium Tridentinum vel recipis, vel non? Si hoc, jam non te audiet ullus Papista; sin illud, nil tibi cum Reformatis, quos Concilium vel Ethnicis & publicanis habet deteriores. Flectere Synodum ad mentem & sententiam meliorem aut benigniorem, nec potes, nec si posses, paterentur ejus patroni, atque illa vigente, non major sperari potest religionis utrius-que que συμφωνίας vel κοινωνίας, quam lucis cum tenebris Ne de authoritate Papæ dicam, nec inflectendâ, nec vel aliquantulum demittendâ, nedum conciliandâ cum ullâ Reformatione. Quid autem de aliis loquar concordiæ aut emendationis in Papatu innumeris obstaculis? ubi plurimis fortissimisque rationibus tenere id nunc quisque debeat, quod dudum Nicolaus Clemanges docuit, epist. ad Gerardum Marketi, Doctorem Parisiensem: non mentis tantum affectu à Babylone discedendum, sed etiam pedibus corporis. In doctrinâ fundare aut moliri velle syncretismum, res est frustranei laboris & impossibilis omnino, rebus sic, uti nunc à Concilio Tridentino, atque ab authoritate Papæ, stantibus, ac pendentibus: quippe ista duo jam notata, uti in Papatu pro summis habentur tum doctrinæ, tum Ecclesiæ cardinibus, ita occludunt omnem viam Reformationis, vel reconciliationis. In doctrinâ igitur tentari nihil cum Papanis potest, nihil boni ab ipsis sperari, ut in ullâ re aut fateantur erasse se, vel corrigendam doctrinam suam esse, absque quo tamen nulla vel cogitari conciliatio potest. Tantum omnia adversus ipsos nunc in pugnam & destructionem doctrinæ illius conferenda sunt. Atque uti in doctrinâ quidem nihil hic ad concordandas partes superest, nil nisi ab ipsis Papis, & ex Papatu prodeant rei istius consilia, quod frustra exspectes; ita apud Doctores ipsorum parum quoque agendum: quod si aliquid, hoc apud plebem restat, ut missis ipsorum Doctoribus, & ignoratâ, ut vulgò apud eos fit, suorum doctrinâ, veram religionem amplectantur isti vel insciì. Vulgi in Papatu religio consistit fere in externarum aliquarum rerum observantiâ, de cætero valde securi: atque certum est, multorum animos longe aliter affectos esse, ac extus apparent, & sentire eos multum diversa, ab eo quod docentur. De Doctoribus non loquor, quos etiam vis veritatis & conscientiæ tum fateri, tum statuere saltem mente aliter jubet, ac doceri sciunt in suâ Ecclesiâ, forte etiam à seipsis: sed uti hoc est peccatum valde grave, & ad blasphemiam in Spiritum Sanctum inclinans, ita liberiores hâc in parte habemus ex vulgo homines, & magis simplices, quod oportet. In palmario religionis articulo de justificatione, quot sunt in Papatu, neque Cardinales excipio, Bellarminum, Contarenum, praesertim ex simplici plebe, definitiones & distinctiones Doctorum suorum tutò ignorante, qui omnibus difficilis, & meritis justitiâque suâ, in solam recumbunt Dei per Christum misericordiam, neque aliter haec accipiunt quam in nostris Ecclesiis docentur, neque vel sciunt contrarium apud suos praedicari? & hic, atque in pluribus articulis, quos solâ conscientiâ & Spiritu divino duce homines amplectuntur, multa hominum, sub Papatu quamvis viventium, cum nostris est convenientia, atque apud tales, & in talibus concordia quaerenda vel figenda, si qua, est: nulla in doctrinâ, aut Doctoribus. Frustra viri multi in eo laborarunt, ut doctrinam utramque, vel doctores in unum adducerent. Non à superioribus, sed ab imis inchoandum, apud plebem, non Doctores, & non in theoriâ religionis, sed praxi, convenientiae, quae esse possit, collocandum fundamentum. Atque hinc plures sub Papatu simplices, seductos, oppressos, nequaquam ex sensu aut notitiâ Papismi, sed ductu S. Spiritus, & conscientiae religiosae, ut sub multis imperfectionibus, viventes, nobiscum salvandos, & eandem constituere ecclesiam arbitrantur, cum quibus nec communionem denegamus implicitam, & si quoque fieri possit, apertam. Quare isti nobis inquirendi, instruendi, incitandi, atque ad majorem lucem, fidem, & professionem puriorem adducendi diligenter sunt. Ad quod etiam non parum confert, istorum hominum considerare precationes & precationum formulas, quibus utuntur, ab haeresi Papisticâ castigatas, vel castigandas. Quippe, uti relireligionis vis in praxi haeret, ita hujus in vera ad Deum precatione: quo in officio omnes Christiani hominis virtutes junctâ manu concurrunt seque exerunt. Quod proinde singulari cura observandum, ut hinc & de hominibus judicemus, & partem religionis istam eo diligentius curemus, quo ad universam religionem majoris momenti, & hac viâ homines suavius & majori cum fructu duci, instrui, & salvari possunt. Quare haud inconsultum foret, preces scribi, quae comprehendant summam Christianae religionis & salutis, ita ut nullus eis obloqui possit, precationes verè Catholicas & pias, quae non modo neminem offendant, sed ad quarum verum usum dicere liceat: quicunque invocaverit nomen Domini, salvus erit. Rom. x. 13. tanti quippe apud Deum, atque ad salutem momenti est, divini nominis verè invocatio. Neque indignari Papista aliquis potest, quod ab invocatione Dei Sanctos amovemus, quos illi praesertim colunt, quandoquidem satis constat, & Deus novit, ipsique Sancti si adessent scire possent, vel ex Pontificiorum sententiâ ignorare nequeunt, non ex ullo aut religionis contemtu, aut Sanctorum contumeliâ ea à nobis negligi, sed ex solo sensu conscientiae & religionis, quam uni Deo deferendam existimamus. Neque certe ulli culpare possunt (quidquid etiam sit de controversiae circa hanc rem, aut sententiae veritate) quod certiorem insistimus viam, & Sanctorum loco Deum potius adimus, hunc tanto ferventius colimus, quo solum ad omnia cum sufficere nulli, neque etiam Pontificii, Sanctive negare possunt. Ita nostra doctrina (missâ disputatione de ejus veritate) ad conscientiam & praxim relata, omni ratione supra Papisticam tutior est, certiorque ad salutem obtinendam via.
units.tr: From that time the cause of concord was despaired of. Some had attempted it earlier, in vain at that time, and even now some people, after the Council, are trying to build a syncretism of our religion and the Papistical one. They seem foolish indeed, and they are all too willing to waste their effort. Do you accept the Council of Trent or not? If you do, no Papist will listen to you any longer. If you do not, you have nothing to do with the Reformed, whom the Council regards as worse than heathens and tax-collectors. You cannot bend the Synod to a better or kinder mind, and even if you could, its defenders would not allow it. While it stands, no greater agreement [συμφωνίας] or fellowship [κοινωνίας] of the one religion with the other can be hoped for than of light with darkness. I say nothing of the authority of the Pope, which can neither be bent nor even slightly lowered, much less reconciled with any Reformation. But why should I speak of the countless other obstacles to concord or amendment within Papacy? There, for very strong reasons, each person should now hold to what Nicolaus Clemanges long ago taught in his letter to Gerard Machet, a Doctor of Paris: "One must depart from Babylon not only with the affection of the mind but also with the feet of the body." To try to found or build a syncretism in doctrine is a work of fruitless labour and wholly impossible, while things stand and hang as they now do on the Council of Trent and the authority of the Pope. These two, already noted, are held in Papacy to be the highest hinges both of doctrine and of the Church, and so they close off every way of reformation or reconciliation. Therefore nothing can be attempted with the Papists in doctrine, and nothing good can be hoped from them. They will not confess in any matter that they have erred, or that their doctrine must be corrected, and yet no reconciliation can even be imagined without that. Rather, everything must now be directed against them in battle and in the destruction of that doctrine. Just as there is nothing here left in doctrine for reconciling the parties, nothing unless counsels of this business come from the Papists themselves and from the Papacy (which you would wait for in vain), so too little is to be done with their Doctors. If anything remains, it remains with the common people: that, their Doctors being set aside and their teaching (as commonly happens among them) unknown to them, they embrace the true religion, even though they are unaware of it. The religion of the common people in Papacy consists almost entirely in the observance of certain external things, and otherwise they are very secure. It is certain that the minds of many are affected far differently from what appears outwardly, and that they feel quite otherwise than they are taught. I am not speaking of the Doctors, whom the force of truth and conscience also compels either to confess, or at least to judge in their minds otherwise than they know is taught in their Church, perhaps even by themselves. But as this is a very grave sin, leaning toward blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, so among the common people, who are simpler, we have men who are freer in this respect, as is fitting. On the chief article of religion, justification, how many in Papacy (I do not exclude the Cardinals, Bellarmine or Contarini) are there, especially among the simple common folk, who safely ignore the definitions and distinctions of their Doctors? These people rest entirely on the mercy of God through Christ, despairing of themselves and of their merits and righteousness. Nor do they take these matters otherwise than as they are taught in our Churches, and they do not know that the contrary is preached among their own people. Here, and in many articles which men embrace by conscience alone, with the divine Spirit as their guide, there is much agreement between men who live under the Papacy and ours. Among such people, and in such people, concord is to be sought or fixed, if there is any, but not in doctrine or among the Doctors. Many men have laboured in vain to bring the two doctrines, or the two sets of doctors, into one. The beginning must not be made from above but from below: among the people, not the Doctors. The foundation of agreement, such as it can be, must be laid not in the theory of religion but in its practice. Hence several simple people under the Papacy, who are led astray and oppressed, not from any sense or knowledge of Papism but by the guidance of the Holy Spirit and religious conscience, living under many imperfections, we judge to be saved with us and to constitute the same Church. With them we deny neither an implicit communion nor, if it could be done, an open one. Therefore they must be diligently sought out, instructed, stirred up, and brought to greater light, faith, and a purer profession. To this also contributes no little the consideration of these people's prayers and prayer-formulas, which they use, purged or to be purged of Papist heresy. For just as the power of religion lies in practice, so it does in true prayer to God, in which duty all the virtues of the Christian man join hands and show themselves. This therefore must be observed with special care, so that from it we may judge of the people too, and tend this part of religion the more diligently, since it is of greater moment for religion as a whole, and by this way men can be led, instructed and saved more gently and with greater fruit. Therefore it would not be ill-advised to write prayers that embrace the sum of Christian religion and salvation, so that no one can object to them: truly Catholic and pious prayers, which not only offend no one, but of whose true use one may say, "whoever calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved." Rom. x. 13. So great, indeed, before God and for salvation, is the true invocation of the divine name. Nor can any Papist be indignant that we remove the saints from the invocation of God, whom they especially worship. For it is well established, and God knows it, and the saints themselves, if they were present, could know it, or at least even by the Pontifical view they cannot be ignorant, that these things are neglected by us not from any contempt of religion or insult to the saints, but solely from a sense of conscience and religion, which we judge must be paid to God alone. Nor can they blame us (whatever there may be in the controversy on this matter, or in the truth of the opinion) for insisting on the surer way, and for going to God rather than the saints, worshipping Him the more fervently since He alone suffices for all things, which neither any Papist nor the saints can deny. Thus our doctrine, setting aside the dispute about its truth and referred to conscience and practice, is in every respect safer than the Papistical one, and a surer way to obtain salvation.

units.la: Quemadmodum alterum caput si sumamus, quod de justificatione nostri coram Deo, sepositâ disputatione, rogo, utra sententia sit tutior, Papistarum; an nostra sic ita esse, ut Papistae docent, & Deum nos justifica re propter bona opera: attamen annon, quamvis contrarium sentiamus, justificabimur etiam, qui bona interim opera facimus, æque ac alterius sententiæ homines? dum in eo utrique convenimus, necessario bona opera facienda esse, cuicunque salvari volenti: ergo ego, dum bona opera habeam, utcunque errans (loquor per συγχώρησιν) circa opus Dei, & propter quod ille justificaturus hominem sit, salvabor nihilominus, propterea quia habeo id, ob quod ille justificet. At vero si non propter nostra opera Deus justificet, sed ob solam Christi justitiam, vide, si operibus meis nitar & satisfactionibus, non autem Christi, (cujus solius justitiâ standum hic sit, eoque solo per suam justitiam in Salvatorem accepto,) ut jam per illam sententiam, non habens solam illam Christi justitiam, quo justificari contingit, gratiâ misericordiâ excidam. Gal. v. 4.
units.tr: In the same way, if we take the other head, that of our justification before God, setting aside the dispute, I ask which opinion is safer: that of the Papists, or ours? Suppose it is so, as the Papists teach, that God justifies us on account of good works. Yet shall we not, though we think otherwise, also be justified, we who meanwhile do good works, just as much as men of the other opinion? For in this we both agree, that good works must necessarily be done by anyone who wishes to be saved. So I, while I have good works, however mistaken I am (I speak by concession [συγχώρησιν]) about the work of God, and on account of which he is going to justify a man, shall nevertheless be saved, because I have that on account of which he would justify. But if God does not justify on account of our works, but on account of Christ's righteousness alone, consider whether, if I lean on my works and satisfactions, and not on Christ's (on whose righteousness alone one must stand here, and by that alone received into the Saviour), then by that opinion, not having that Christ's righteousness alone by which justification happens, I shall fall from grace and mercy. Gal. v. 4.

units.la: Atque ita in pluribus potest hæc nostræ religionis præ Pontificiâ, ad salutem & praxin ostendi præstantia, qua facilius ad homines, fidei quærentes simplicitatem, illa urgeri, & magno cum fructu ipsis commendari potest, eaque precationibus prudenter ac judiciose conceptis inseri & doceri, citra aliquorum offensionem, utpote ex communibus & confessis Christianæ doctrinæ petita principiis atque fundamentis. Exempli gratiâ, neque enim ad manum habeo quo animi sensum melius exponam, quam si antiquam illam probamque Anselmi formulam Consolatoriam, retineamus, in quibuscunque fere Ecclesiis olim usitatam, vel ejus similes componamus alias: quo pacto arbitror nos optime illam fidelium ubicunque in eadem professionis simplicitate communionem & syncretismum promoturos, melius certe feliciusque quam plurimis aut disputationibus, aut de doctrinæ syncretismo consiliis frustraneis & contentiosis.
units.tr: And so in many respects the excellence of our religion over the Papists can be shown in its bearing on salvation and practice. By this means it can be pressed more easily upon people who seek the simplicity of faith, taught with great profit to them, and inserted into prayers composed prudently and judiciously, and taught without offence to anyone, since it is drawn from the common principles and foundations of Christian doctrine that are agreed on by all. For example (I have no better means at hand of expressing my meaning), let us keep that old and approved Consolatory Formula of Anselm, which was in use in almost all churches long ago, or else compose similar ones. In this way I believe we shall best promote the fellowship and syncretism of the faithful everywhere in the same simplicity of profession, far better and more successfully than by most disputations or by fruitless and contentious proposals about a syncretism of doctrine.

units.la: Formula illa attribuitur passim Anselmo, qui Cantuariensis episcopus factus, anno clo xcIII. d. iv. Decemb. cemb. obiit verò, anno cIↄ cIx. d. xxi. Aprilis: erro- rem in notis putat Bellarminus, lib. de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis, & obiisse existimat a. 1106. quoniam tredecim annos in Episcopatu vixit, quod Edinerus testatur, in illius vitâ, & tamen obiisse hic ipse quoque scribit a. millesimo centesimo nono, qui fuit annus Pontificatus ejus xiii. atqui Pontificem factum ait anno Dominicae incarnationis millesimo xcii. Franciscus Godwinus, in Commentario, de Praesulibus Angliae, dicit eodem tempore illum praesulem factum, vid. anno 1093. & mortuum anno 1109. cum sedisset archiepiscopus annos 19 in quo item error est, quoniam nec ita 19. sed 16. annos sederit. Quidquid sit de annis Pontificatus, in mortis anno conveniunt. Huic quidem Anselmo ab omnibus formula consolatoria tribuitur, sed eam in operibus ejus, sive editionis primae Coloniensis, anno 1560. seu secundae tomo quarto auctioris, anno 1612. non deprehendo: non in ejus Meditationibus, quas indicat Davenantius in Col. ii. 2. nec Epistolis, quem locum alii assignant. Non quidem admodum dissimilia apud eum reperio. In Meditationibus: Quem alium enim dici, jam interfeciorem pro me tibi nescio: nisi hunc qui est peccatis nostris propitiatio; & similia plura: sed non illa, quae sub ejus nomine ubique veniunt. Formula, ejusdem argumenti, alia occurrit longior, brevior alia. Anselmo attribuuntur interrogationes vel septem, vel octo, faciendae moribundo; quibus vel Gerson Parisiensis, vel alii addiderunt alias quatuor. Nam uti Anselmo, ita & Gersoni illa in antiquis libris adscribuntur. Formula alia genuina, quae Anselmi dicitur: adulterata alia, quae Doctorum est sequiorum. Formula utraque occurrit in Tractatu Artis bene moriendi, quod MS. & antiquae editionis aliud est in Bibliotheca Ultrajectina. In Ms. cui tit. Totum bonum, scripto per manus (uti dicitur in fine) fratris Ewedei Boecholt, (ni sallor, Ultrajectini) ordinis Carthusiensis, anno cIↄ cccc
units.tr: That formula is commonly attributed to Anselm, who became archbishop of Canterbury and died on 21 April 1109, having been made archbishop on 4 December 1093. Bellarmine, in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, thinks there is an error in the notes and believes he died in 1106, since he lived thirteen years in the episcopate, as Eadmer testifies in his life of him. Yet this same writer also says he died in the year 1109, which was the thirteenth year of his pontificate, while he says he was made pontiff in the year of the Lord's incarnation 1092. Francis Godwin, in his Commentary on the Bishops of England, says that he was made bishop at the same time, namely in 1093, and died in 1109, after having been archbishop for 19 years. This too is an error, since he held the see not 19 but 16 years. Whatever the truth about the years of his pontificate, they agree on the year of his death. This consolatory formula is indeed attributed to Anselm by everyone, but I do not find it in his works, either in the first Cologne edition of 1560 or in the second, enlarged edition of 1612 in its fourth volume. Nor is it in his Meditations, which Davenant cites on Colossians 2:2, nor in his Epistles, where others locate it. I do find passages there not greatly unlike it. In the Meditations: For whom else can I call, now that I have no other interceder for me with you, but him who is the propitiation for our sins? and many similar things. But not those that everywhere appear under his name. Another formula on the same subject occurs, one longer and another shorter. Seven or eight questions to be put to the dying are ascribed to Anselm, to which either Gerson of Paris or others have added four more. For these questions are found in old books under the names of Gerson as well as of Anselm. One formula is genuine and is said to be Anselm's; another is corrupted and is the work of inferior teachers. Both formulas occur in the treatise The Art of Dying Well, which exists in manuscript and in an old printed edition in the library at Utrecht. In a manuscript titled The Whole Good, written by the hand (as it says at the end) of Brother Ewedeus Boecholt, of the Carthusian order (if I am not mistaken, of Utrecht), in the year 1418 on 6 April, there are full collations on the seven questions of Anselm, introduced in this way: These are the questions and answers made by the Lord and Master Anselm, bishop of the Church of Canterbury, which ought to be put to each of the faithful who is approaching death; and the sick person shall answer in the manner written below. And he to whom these are put shall die securely and shall not see eternal death. The questions are seven, the first of which is this: Brother or sister, do you rejoice that you have been marked with the faith of Christ, and do you glory that you will die in that same faith? The sick person answers attentively and devoutly, and says, yes. Second question. Do you praise the Lord, who has brought you into being in this noble state, that is, the rational state, and has adorned you with the Christian faith? The sick person answers, I praise him. Third question: Do you confess, for your profession of faith and for the grace given you by God, that you have not lived as you ought to have lived, and have not been as pleasing to the Lord as you rightly should have been? The sick person answers, I confess. Do you then accuse yourself? The sick person, I accuse myself. Are you sorry for this? I am sorry. Do you then confess to God and to his saints? The sick person, I confess. And so on. Master Wilhelm Tzewers, canon of Aachen, in the book he entitled The Most Salutary Preparation of the Christian for Death, printed at Cologne by Hermann Boemgart of Ketwich, in Alphabet IX, has the following:

units.la: XVIII. d. VI. Aprilis, continentur prolixe Collationes in septem interrogationes Anselmi, quae hunc in modum praemittuntur: Ille sunt interrogationes & responsiones facta per Dominum & Magistrum Anselmum Cantuariensis Ecclesiae episcopum, quae unicuique fidelium morti appropinquanti fieri debent; & infirmus per modum infra scriptum respondebit. Et cui haec proponuntur, securus morietur, nec mortem videbit aeternam. Interrogationes sunt septem, quarum prima haec est: frater vel soror, laetaris te Christi fide esse insignitum, & gloriaris in eadem fide te moriturum? Respondet infirmus attente & devote, & dicit, etiam. Secunda interrogatio. Laudasne Dominum, quia in hoc nobili esse, scilicet esse rationali te produxit, & fide Christiana te decoravit? Respondet infirmus, Laudo. Tertia interrogatio, fatetisne pro tua fidei professione & gratia tibi a Deo facta, te non ita vixisse, & gratum Domino fuisse, quemadmodum merito debuisses? Respondet infirmus, fateor. Accusas ergo te? Infirmus, accuso. Dolesne de hoc? doleo. Confiteris ergo Deo, & sanctis ejus? Infirmus, confiteor. & sic porro. Magister Vilhelmus Tzewers, Aquisgranensis Canonicus in lib. cui titulum fecit, Praeparamentum salutiferrimum Christiani ad mortem, impresso Coloniae, apud Hermannum Boemgart, de Ketwich, Alphabeto IX. ita habet.
units.tr: These are the questions and answers made by the Lord and Master Anselm, bishop of the Church of Canterbury, which ought to be put to each of the faithful who is approaching death; and the sick person shall answer in the manner written below. And he to whom these are put shall die securely and shall not see eternal death. The questions are seven, the first of which is this: Brother or sister, do you rejoice that you have been marked with the faith of Christ, and do you glory that you will die in that same faith? The sick person answers attentively and devoutly, and says, yes. Second question. Do you praise the Lord, who has brought you into being in this noble state, that is, the rational state, and has adorned you with the Christian faith? The sick person answers, I praise him. Third question: Do you confess, for your profession of faith and for the grace given you by God, that you have not lived as you ought to have lived, and have not been as pleasing to the Lord as you rightly should have been? The sick person answers, I confess. Do you then accuse yourself? The sick person, I accuse myself. Are you sorry for this? I am sorry. Do you then confess to God and to his saints? The sick person, I confess. And so on.

units.la: Ideo qui vult in illa anxietate consolari infirmum, quaedam sibi utilia & brevia proponat, quorum octo ponit Anselmus, sub certis quaestionibus, & Doctores addunt quatuor, cum certis ammonitionibus, & dant consolationem magnam, quomodo infirmus secure moriatur, & poenam evadat aeternam, qui Zelo bono contrito ad ista quaerenda respondet, & regere se vult secundum ammonitiones adjunctas. Et proponentur infirmo cum adhuc sit compos rationis, & bene dispositus circa tempus quando optat venerabilia sacramenta, & in materna lingua &c. Sequuntur interrogationes. Sic primo dulciter ei dicat: Mi frater aut soror, tu tantum vis vivere cum ↄ mecum sancte Matris Ecclesiæ filius aut filia, se gaudeas quod si Dominus præcepit quod in fide Chri-sti standa: non teneris: si dixeris ægrotus: volo viuere, ↄ gaudeas. Tunc dicat Sacerdos aut alter secundo ei proponatur: Gaudes frater aut soror, quod in ista statu, & sub ista regula aut habitu moriendo ex statu aut observantia regularis venebatis, & in hora Domini tuam sæpe graviter offendisti, de quo tamen nunc ex toto corde doles? Respondet, ego sto heu & doleo. ↄ Omnium frater aut soror, super men dolens de tuis negligentiis multis, & quod ita male vixisti, & peccatis tuis Deum multis variis offendisti? Si responderit, etiam Domine, ita tamen sufficienter doleo, &c. ↄ Cum soror, si Domino Deo placuerit tibi diuturnum concedere tempus pœnitentiæ, habere sine benedictionem & propositum, sic velle mutare in vita viuere emendare? Cum dixerit, habeo, si ita libenter volo. ↄ Tu credis frater aut soror, quod Dominus noster Iesus Christus propter te passus est, crucifixus & mor-tuus? Tunc dicit æger, si hoc credo. ↄ Tu ergo tamen gratiæ Deo, quod præter te nec sanctos passus est? Tu credis te non posse salvari nisi per fidem & mortem Domini nostri Iesu Christi? Si dicit, credo, & ita est, dicat astans, carissime frater aut soror, magna nobis Christianis consolatio & siducia est quod omnes homines ab exordio mundi salvati sunt in nostra statu fide & in passione nostri fratris & patris Domini nostri Iesu Christi sunt salvati. Unde etiam veritas est, quod nostris meritis & passionibus tuis temporis nihil nisi temporalem vitam mereri possumus retributionem. Quia ad futuram gloriam omnia illa minus digna æstimatur, sed salvamur æternaliter merito capitis nostri Iesu Christi, qui nos, pro su[?]compassionem [?]dulcissime appetiatur est. Ideo iterum quam mihi animae [?]est in te fiduciam habe in mortem Christi confidens, quod illis salvabeis, non [illegible, ~3 letters] meritis tuis. Et huic morti totum te immitte & commendare. Hanc etiam mortem semper cogita & prae oculis habe, unde de manibus eorum [illegible, ~2 letters] ego crucifixi, sed hunc aspice etiam mentalibus oculis in illum dirigendo, quomodo ipse pro te passus est. Hanc etiam formam crucifixi amplexare, [illegible, ~2 letters] amoris tiinductedinem in representatam refrendo. Sic crucem amplexando cogita, quod spiritualibus amplexibus circumdata dulcissimum [?]rede[?]mptorem & patrem Dominum Iesum Christum, cuius mortis cupis & spera salvari & aeternaliter vivere. Et si iudex velit te damnare, dic humiliter: Domine, [illegible, ~2 letters] mortem Domini nostri Iesu Christi objicio interone & sanctissimum judicium tuum, alter tecum non contendam in hora mortis mea. Et si dixerit iudex, tuis peccatis multa neglexisti, & saepe iram meam incitasti & meruisti, dic ut prius: mortem & vulnera Domini mei Iesu Christi pono inter meas negligentias, peccata & iram tuam, & illi offero pro meritis meis, quae ego debeam habere & non habeo. Et nunc clementissime Deus, veniam & misericordiam supplex deposco, ex contemplatione dilectissimi filii tui Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & sanctissimae genitricis Mariae virginis advocatae nostrae, & omnium electorum tuorum, & signanter illorum qui aliquid in suum singularem recepit devotionem [?]&c. Nam proponitur infirmo, cum ei venerabile sacramentum aliquando ostenditur aut porrigitur, credis Frater mi quod in sacramento altaris post sacerdotis benedictionem verum continetur Christi corpus? &c. Credis etiam quod hic Christus verus Deus & homo, qui sub specie panis continetur, potest habet & aliis mille millibus fecit, quod libenter tibi velit indulgere omnia peccata tua, si in digne pe-nis & desideras: habe etiam voluntatem promtam spontaneam restituendi omnia aliena, quocunque ti-tulo injusto aut illicito ad te venerunt, aut devoluta sunt. &c. XI. Infirmo proponatur, an sibi optet ministrari corpus Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & in eventum si opus fuerit extremam unctionem, &c. XII. Aegro proponatur, an optet ut adsint vel sacerdos cum commendet Domino Deo, beatae Virgini, sanctis Dei, aliis devotis hominibus? &c. Quo prio-res, vel ut Auctor praecedentis libri, Totum bonum, septem interrogationes Anselmianae, uti priores se-quentibus, ita passim isto nomine veniunt, praeque aliis commendandae: atque ex sequiorum Doctorum opi-nionibus superstitiosis, contra priorum mentem ac doctrinam, caetera aspersa; quae tum hic, tum alibi aureae formulae male admixtae legantur, utcunque pro istorum saeculorum Theologiâ, non tamen pro in-tentione Auctor unquam sinquè. Melius & castius idem Hermannus Bumgart, Coloniae, anno 1497 mense Augusto, post Praeceptoritum Nicolai de Lyra, edidit, apposuitque hoc simplici modo ipsam solam Anselmianam formulam, septem interrogationibus. Exemplar apud me asservo: interrogationes faciendae in-firmo morienti. Primo interrogari debet. Si credit omnia quae sunt fidei Christianae. Et respondeat, Credo. Secundo si gaudet se mori in fide Christiana, & respondeat, Gaudeo. Tertio si recognovit se Deum multum offendisse, & respon-deat, Doleo. Quarto si proposuit de caetero ab omni offensa peccati mortalis abstinere, respondeat: Divino auxilio me-diante propono. Sexto si credit se per meritum passionis Christi, & non propriis, ad gloriam pervenire, respondeat tunc. Credo. Septimo debet sibi dicere, si occurreris tibi inimi-cus Diabolus, super eo oppressus merito passionis Christi, Amen. Iam & librum ipsum Caspari Vlenbergii, à Lutheranis ad Pontificios apostatae, Pastoris & Canonici Colonien-sis nactus sum, quem ad hanc formulam comprobandam à multis citari notum: exhibebo autem ejus verba, nescio an ab alio adducta, quidem summam ejus referunt Chemnitius, Persinus, Johannes Gerhardi, alii, sed jam habe ipsa ejus verba, addi-tamque ab eo explanationem. Liber est: Christliche und wichtige Ursachen, warumb die alleinseligmachende Catholische Christen bey dem alten waren Christenthumb bis in ihren tod beständiglich verharren; Coloniae anno 1589. Istius libri c. xiv. cauf. xiv. pag. 416. Wollen allhie nur ein zeugnis führen, wie man zu den zeiten, da die finsternis des Papsthumbs (wie sie reden) am allerdicksten soll gewesen seyn, die leute so gewaltig vñ tröstlich, auff Christum und seinen tod gelesen hat. Ich stinde allhie zu Sanct Cunibert in meiner Pfarrkirchen ein Buch, das man bey den Kranken über hundert jar her gebraucht hat. Ist geschrieben anno 1475. In demselbigen sind etliche sprüche, die der H. Anselmus soll gestellet haben, auff alt, einfeltig Cölnisch teutsch geschrieben: Gehen darauff, wie man bey außspendung der Heiligen Sacramente, einen Kranken auff Christum und seinen Heiligen tod weisen soller und lassen die selbigen also: Gerte Christus Herr, das men alle einen menschen in seyne letzten ende vnd ... ermanen sal. Mensche, erkennestu dich, dat du in dem Christenglouen sterven machs? He antwortde: Ja Ich. Bekennestu, datt du nyet so wael gelevet en haes, als du von rechte solltes haven gedaen? He antwordē: Ja Ich. Beroumet dich dat, ind haes den willen dich zo bessern, off du syt hedes gelovens? He antwordē: Ja Ich. Gelowestu dat vor dich gestorven is Christus Jesus, des waren lebendigen Gottes Son? He antwordē: Ja Ich. Danckes du en des ouch? He antwordē: Ja Ich. Gelo-vestu ouch, datt du nit en machs selich werden, dan overmits synen doet? He antwordē: Ja Ich. Herumb, so lange as du best in dissen leven, so setze al din betrouwen alleyne in diesen doet. Ingeyn and dynsten have betrouwen: Wer alle heyl dat dich in diesen doet, Bedecke dich gans hymede, Mit diesem bode bewant dich alle heyl. Ind wil der Here ordel van dir haven, so antwoir: Den doet myns Heren Jesu Christi setzen ich tuschen dich ind mich, ind dyn ordel. Ind anders en antwordē ich nyet. Syrrhy hey, du haes verdeynt de verdoemenisse. Antwordē: O Here, dair halden ich vor den doet myns Heren Christi Jesu tuschen dich, ind myne quade verdeynste. Wante syne verdeinste offer ich vor dat verdienst, dat ich soulde haven gedaen, ind leyder nyet en haen gedaen. Duch so sage, O Here, yn dyne hande bevele ich myne geyst / Ind dem sieh vielichen / tn so en salto myt den ruygen Doet sien. Bisher aus jenem alten Buch. In margine Auctor: Atque in fine, post allegata illa ex vetusto Rituali, subjungit: Sihe / freundlicher Leser / also hat man sür hundert und etlichen jaren nicht allein allhie zu Cöln / sonder auch in der gantzen Christenheit / auff Christum / und in Christo auff die seligste hett gewiessen; wie wir auch noch thun biß auff den heutigen tag / wen schon diese stagen nicht also von wort zu wort gelesen werden. Solcher zeugnissen weren mehr aus alten büchern beyzubringen, Valde bene, quod ejusmodi testimonia ajat pluria adduci ex veteribus libris posse, de quo nos non dubitamus: sed gratulamur veritati, quod tam illustria sui, in Papatu & olim, & hodie habeat documenta, & quod in eundem sensum, quamvis non iisdem verbis, dicant, se consolationem moribundis impartiri etiam hodie, Papistarum Doctores. Subjungit Vlenbergius, pag. 444. de Bernardo ⁊ S. Bernardi vertrauen auff Christi god in lesten ⁊ eine bestetigung seines glaubens. & pag. 445. Warauff S. Bernardus gestorben ist / darauff stirbt alles was Catholisch ist. Quod si vere & sincere sic sentiant, loquantur, & agant, optimum hoc certe conciliationis, in religionis praxi, fundamentum. Formulam illam olim in Belgio, Germania, Polonia, Sclavonia, Gallia, Parisiis, Italia, Tridenti. Romae quoque, & procul dubio (si illius Anselmus Cantuariensis auctor, uti scribunt Pontificii) in Anglia etiam, id est, quemadmodum Vlenbergius rotunde asserit, in toto Christianismo usitatam fuisse gratulamur: ut nec de Ecclesia nostra, ejusque fide amplius interrogare nos, ubi ante Lutherum fuerit, Papistae debeant; nec aliquis de Majorum nostrorum sub Papatu mortuorum salute esse sollicitus: denique in talium praxi benignius de multis sub Papatu degentibus judicium nostrum fundari, & salutis communio, illa ubi vere agnoscuntur, potest.
units.tr: Therefore, whoever wishes to comfort a sick person in that anxiety should set before him certain useful and brief points. Anselm gives eight of them under set questions, and the Doctors add four more with certain admonitions. They give great comfort in showing how the sick person may die securely and escape eternal punishment, provided he answers these questions zealously and contritely and wishes to govern himself according to the admonitions attached. These are to be put to the sick person while he is still in possession of his reason and well disposed, at the time when he asks for the venerable sacraments, and in his mother tongue, and so on. The questions follow. First, let him say gently to him: "My brother or sister, do you wish only to live with me, a son or daughter of holy Mother Church? Rejoice, for if the Lord has commanded that we stand in the faith of Christ, you are not bound otherwise. If you say, sick one, 'I wish to live,' rejoice." Then the priest or another should put the second question: "Do you rejoice, brother or sister, that you are dying in this state and under this rule or habit, in which you were accustomed to live by the state or observance of the rule, and that in the hour of the Lord you have often grievously offended your Lord, and yet now grieve for it with your whole heart?" He answers, "I do, and I grieve." "Brother or sister, do you grieve over all your many negligences, and that you have lived so badly, and offended God in many ways by your sins?" If he answers, "Yes, Lord, I grieve sufficiently," and so on. "Sister, if it pleases the Lord God to grant you a long time for repentance, do you have the good will and purpose thus to change and amend your life?" When she says, "I have it, and I wish it most willingly." "Do you believe, brother or sister, that our Lord Jesus Christ suffered, was crucified and died for you?" Then the sick man says, "I believe it." "Do you therefore give thanks to God, because he suffered not only for you but for the saints too? Do you believe that you cannot be saved except through faith and the death of our Lord Jesus Christ?" If he says, "I believe it, and it is so," let the bystander say: "Dearest brother or sister, great consolation and confidence is for us Christians that all men from the beginning of the world have been saved in the faith of our state and in the passion of our brother and father, our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence it is also true that by our merits and sufferings we can merit nothing but temporal reward, since all those things are judged of too little worth for future glory; but we are saved eternally by the merit of our Head, Jesus Christ, who, for our sake, most sweetly sought (?) to suffer. Therefore, again, have in yourself that trust which is in my soul, trusting in the death of Christ, that by it you will be saved, not by any merits of yours. And commit and entrust your whole self to this death. Think always of this death and keep it before your eyes, that the hands of those who crucified him ... but look upon him also with the eyes of the mind, directing yourself to him, how he suffered for you. Embrace also the form of the crucifix, ... representing the depth of his love. Thus, embracing the cross, think that, surrounded by spiritual embraces, you hold the sweetest Redeemer and Father, the Lord Jesus Christ, by whose death you desire and hope to be saved and to live eternally. And if the judge should wish to condemn you, say humbly: 'Lord, I set the death of our Lord Jesus Christ before your most holy judgment, and I will not contend with you in the hour of my death.' And if the judge should say, 'You have neglected many things by your sins, and often provoked and deserved my wrath,' say as before: 'I set the death and wounds of my Lord Jesus Christ between my negligences, my sins and your wrath, and I offer them to him for the merits I ought to have and do not have.' And now, most merciful God, I humbly beg pardon and mercy, through contemplation of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the most holy mother Mary, the virgin, our advocate, and of all your elect, and especially of those whom you have received into your singular devotion, etc." For, when the venerable sacrament is sometimes shown or offered to the sick man, it is put to him: "Do you believe, my brother, that in the sacrament of the altar, after the priest's blessing, the true body of Christ is contained?" etc. "Do you also believe that this Christ, true God and man, who is contained under the form of bread, can and has done for thousands of others, and will gladly grant you all your sins, if you repent worthily and desire it? Have also a ready and spontaneous will to restore all that belongs to others, whatever unjust or unlawful title has come to you or devolved upon you." etc. XI. Let it be put to the sick man whether he wishes the body of our Lord Jesus Christ to be administered to him, and, if need be, extreme unction, etc. XII. Let it be put to the sick man whether he wishes the priest to be present, so that he may commend him to the Lord God, the blessed Virgin, the saints of God, and other devout men? etc. Whether, as the author of the preceding book, The Whole Good, calls them, the seven Anselmian questions, just as the former ones follow the later ones, so they are everywhere known by this name and are recommended above others. And from the superstitious opinions of the later Doctors, against the mind and teaching of the earlier ones, other matters have been scattered in, which are read here and elsewhere, badly mixed with that golden formula; though these may be read as the theology of those centuries, the author never intended them. More soundly and chastely, the same Hermann Bumgart at Cologne, in August 1497, after the Praeceptorium of Nicolas of Lyra, published the formula of Anselm alone in this simple form, with seven questions. I keep a copy by me. The questions to be put to a sick man who is dying: First he must be asked whether he believes all that pertains to the Christian faith, and let him answer, "I believe." Second, whether he rejoices to die in the Christian faith, and let him answer, "I rejoice." Third, whether he acknowledges that he has greatly offended God, and let him answer, "I grieve." Fourth, whether he has resolved henceforth to abstain from every offence of mortal sin; let him answer: "With divine help I so resolve." Sixth, whether he believes that he will attain glory through the merit of Christ's passion, and not by his own, let him then answer, "I believe." Seventh, he must say to him: "If the devil, your enemy, should meet you, be overcome by him by the merit of Christ's passion. Amen." I have also obtained the book of Caspar Vlenbergius, a former Lutheran who apostatised to the Papists, a minister and canon of Cologne, which is well known to be cited by many to confirm this formula. I will set out his words, though I do not know whether he took them from another source. Chemnitz, Persinus, Johann Gerhard and others indeed report the substance of it, but here you have his very words and the explanation he added. The book is: Christian and Important Reasons why the Catholic Christians, alone saved, persevere constantly in the old Christianity until their death, Cologne, 1589. In chapter 14 of this book, the 14th cause, page 416, he writes: "We wish to bring forward here only one testimony, to show how, at the time when the darkness of the papacy (as they call it) was said to be at its thickest, people were read to so powerfully and comfortingly concerning Christ and his death. Here in St Cunibert's, my parish church, I have a book which has been used for the sick for more than a hundred years. It was written in the year 1475. In it are some sayings which St Anselm is supposed to have composed, written in old, simple Cologne German. They go with the way one should show a sick person Christ and his holy death when administering the holy sacraments, and they run as follows: [here the German text of the questions follows, in which the sick person is asked whether he will die in the Christian faith, whether he acknowledges that he has not lived as well as he ought, whether it grieves him and he has the will to amend, whether he believes that Christ Jesus, Son of the true living God, died for him, whether he thanks him for it, whether he believes he cannot be saved except through his death; then the sick man is told to set all his trust in this death alone, and when the judge wishes to pass sentence, to answer that the death of his Lord Jesus Christ stands between him and his judgment, and that he answers nothing else; and at the end, to commend his spirit into God's hands.]" Thus far from that old book. In the margin the author adds, and at the end, after citing that old ritual, he subjoins: "Look, friendly reader: in this way, not only here at Cologne but throughout the whole of Christendom, more than a hundred years ago, people were directed to Christ, and in Christ to the most blessed hope, as we also do to this very day, even though these sayings are not now read word for word like that." Such testimonies could be brought forward in greater number from old books. Very well, that he says such testimonies may be adduced in plenty from old books: on this we do not doubt. But we rejoice in the truth, that the Papists, both formerly and today, have such illustrious evidences of this, and that they say, in the same sense though not in the same words, that they impart comfort to the dying even today. Vlenbergius goes on, on page 444, concerning Bernard and St Bernard's trust in Christ's death at the end, and a confirmation of his faith; and on page 445: "Whatever Saint Bernard died upon, upon that dies everything that is Catholic." If they truly and sincerely think, speak and act thus, this will certainly be the best foundation of agreement in the practice of religion. We rejoice that this formula was used of old in Belgium, Germany, Poland, Slavonia, France (at Paris), Italy, Trent, Rome also, and undoubtedly (if its author was Anselm of Canterbury, as the Papists write) in England too; that is, as Vlenbergius confidently asserts, that it was in use throughout the whole of Christendom. Therefore the Papists ought no longer to question us about our Church and its faith, asking where it was before Luther; nor should any of us be anxious about the salvation of our forefathers who died under the papacy. Finally, in the practice of such things, our judgment about many who live under the papacy may be grounded more kindly, and communion in salvation, wherever it is truly acknowledged, may be possible.

units.la: Doctrinale mortis, fratris Iohannis Raulin, Professoris Parisiensis, Parisiis, a. 1518. ita habet Tract. 1. cap.
units.tr: Doctrinale mortis of Brother John Raulin, Professor at Paris, Paris, 1518, thus reads in Tract. 1, chap.

units.la: XXVI. de infirmo exhortando, interrogando, adver- tendo, & observandis circa ipsum.
units.tr: XXVI. On exhorting the sick person, questioning him, advising him, and what is to be observed concerning him.

units.la: Secundo interrogandus est defunctus, de multis & multipliciter. Primo de fide dicendo. Dilecte aut dilecta, vis mori & vivere in soliditate fidei Christianæ, tanquam Dei & domini nostri Iesu Christi verus fidelis & obedicns sanctæ matris Ecclesiæ filius } Et respondere debet, volo: & si opus sit, recitetur vulgari sermone symbolum fidei, & ad omnes articulos respondeat si possit, quod ita credit: & si forte quod absit infirmitatis causa, vel inimici illusione aliter fantasiæ occurrerit, quam fides judicet, illud revocat & pro nullo haberi vult: sed in illa fide vult reddere spiritum. Et potest ei ostendi quomodo in illo lumine fidei & solum per illud transitur ad lumen æternæ gloriæ. juxta illud Sf.[?] in lumine tuo videbimus lumen. Secundo de spe veniæ dicendo, petis à Deo veniam peccatorum tuorum commissorum & omissorum, & quod contra ejus amorem majestatem atque bonitatem egeris, nec eum prout debebas honorasti? & respondeat, peto. Tertio, de proposito suo dicendo; habes tu sincerum propositum, & explicitam voluntatem vitam tuam in melius commutare & corrigere: & de cætero à peccatis abstinere, si vita comes superfuerit? & respondeat, habeo. Et ostendat tunc quomodo poenitentia non est Deo grata, nisi cum tali proposito, & quod pax Deo facienda est, & non treugæ. Deinde super hoc interroget. Rogas etiam Deum, ut tibi gratiam det hoc propositum continuandi, & non recidivandi, veramque contritionem habendi? Quarto de conscientia sua interrogandus est; dicendo. Es tu conscius tibi ipsi alicujus mortalis criminis, de quo non sis confessus? Optasne etiam cor tuum illuminari ad oblitorum criminum si quæ sint habendam notitiam, & si tu libenter ea confitereris, supervenirent ad tui notitiam: & si aliquem scrupulum vel aliquod dubibiuum habeat in conscientia quod illud revelet. Ortato interrogandus est de amore Christi. Indulgeas ex corde omnibus qui notam eius intulerunt, ob reverentiam & amorem Domini nostri Iesu Christi, à quo & veniam speras, & similiter petis indulgeri tibi, & remitti ab his quos verbis aut factis laesisti. Et tunc si qui sunt praesentes quos offendisti, potestis tacite vel publice, ut placeat, veniam postulare & generaliter ab omnibus in generali. Sexto interrogandus est de his quae spectant ad restitutionem, dicendo: Vis ablata per te restitui integraliter quantum ad id teneris juxta suarum facultatum valorem, etiam usque ad omnium bonorum tuorum cessionem & renunciationem, ubi aliàs satisfactio fieri non valeret. Et coram Deo & hominibus veniam in juris petis. Ad quas interrogationes affirmative debet aegrotus respondere, volo. In alio manuscripto Orationum quarundam piarum ac devotarum, super moribundorum dicendarum, ita legi: de interrogationibus. Domine Iesu Christe praeventus tua gratia faciat me ex praecordiis laetari, quia in fide catholica & perfecta charitate moriar. Poenitet namque me quod non melius vixi sicut debui, nec honestius conversatus cum vere fidelibus.
units.tr: Secondly, the dying person is to be questioned about many things in many ways. First, about faith, saying: "Dear brother (or sister), do you wish to die and live in the firmness of the Christian faith, as a true, faithful and obedient son of holy Mother Church, of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ?" He ought to answer, "I do." And if need be, the creed of faith is to be recited in the vernacular, and he should respond to each article, if he can, that he believes it thus. And if, which God forbid, through weakness or the devil's deception, some fancy occurs to him that differs from what faith teaches, he is to retract it and wish it held as nothing; and he is to wish to give up his spirit in that faith. And it can be shown to him how one passes, in that light of faith and through it alone, to the light of eternal glory, according to the words: "In thy light shall we see light" (Sf.[?]). Secondly, about hope of pardon, saying: "Do you ask God for pardon of your sins, committed and omitted, and do you confess that you have acted against his love, majesty and goodness, and have not honoured him as you ought?" And he answers, "I ask." Thirdly, about his purpose, saying: "Do you have a sincere purpose and a definite will to change your life for the better and to amend it, and henceforth to abstain from sins, if life remains with you?" And he answers, "I have." And then it is to be shown how repentance is not pleasing to God unless it has such a purpose, and that peace must be made with God, not a truce. Then question him further on this: "Do you also ask God to give you grace to continue in this purpose, not to relapse, and to have true contrition?" Fourthly, he is to be questioned about his conscience, saying: "Are you aware of any mortal sin of your own, of which you have not confessed? Do you also wish your heart to be illumined, so that if there are any forgotten sins, you may have knowledge of them, and that, if you willingly confessed them, they might come to your notice; and if he has any scruple or doubt in his conscience, that he reveal it." Fifthly, he is to be questioned about the love of Christ. "Do you from your heart forgive all who have injured you, for reverence and love of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom you also hope for pardon; and likewise do you ask that pardon be granted to you, and that you be forgiven by those whom you have wronged by word or deed?" And then, if any are present whom you have offended, you may, silently or publicly, as is fitting, ask pardon, and generally from all in general. Sixthly, he is to be questioned about the matters that concern restitution, saying: "Do you wish what you have taken by force to be restored in full, as far as you are bound according to the value of your means, even to the surrender and renunciation of all your goods, where otherwise satisfaction could not be made? And you ask pardon before God and men in law." To these questions the sick man ought to answer affirmatively, "I wish." In another manuscript of certain pious and devout prayers to be said over the dying, I have read as follows, under the heading "On the questions": "Lord Jesus Christ, anticipated by your grace, may you make me rejoice from the heart, because I shall die in the catholic faith and perfect charity. For I repent that I have not lived as well as I ought, nor conducted myself more honourably with those who are truly faithful."

units.la: Confiteor tibi Deo coeli & omnibus Sanctis, quod te graviter offendi per ingratitudinem: propono ex nunc in antea me juxta fragilitatem meam emendare, si juxta voluntatem tempus & locum concesseris.
units.tr: I confess to you, God of heaven, and to all the saints, that I have grievously offended you through ingratitude. I purpose from now on to amend myself, according to my frailty, if you grant me time and place according to your will.

units.la: Credo firmiter, quod tu piissime Domine Iesu venire pro salute mea turpissima morte mortuus es, reconcilians me inimicum & perditum Patri tuo. Ecce pellem pro pelle, carnem pro carne, vitam pro vita tibi ex penetralibus religno, intende in me & ego irrevocabiliter tibi ut credo, quod aliter quam per effusionem pretiosi sanguinis tui & despectam mortem tuam non possem salvari. Agam gratias ipsi patri tuo te mittenti & tibi meo salvatori pro tam amara
units.tr: I firmly believe, most gracious Lord Jesus, that you died a most shameful death to come for my salvation, reconciling me, an enemy and one lost, to your Father. Behold, skin for skin, flesh for flesh, life for life, I give to you from the innermost depths of my heart; look upon me, and I, as I believe, unalterably cling to you, that I could not be saved otherwise than through the shedding of your precious blood and your despised death. I shall give thanks to the Father himself, who sent you, and to you, my Saviour, for so bitter a life, crucified,

units.la: crucifixa vita quando omittetur anima tua vi poenarum & dolorum separabitur à teneritimo corpore tuo. & in hac sola morte tua meum solamen & fiducia constituo, in nulla alia re fiduciam habeo, quod mors tua mihi sufficiens est ad salutem. Tuae morti me committo. Tua morte me contego. Tuae morti me totum involvo. Si me aliter velis judicare, dico ex nunc prout extunc, & extunc ex nunc, Domine mortem Domini nostri Iesu Christi Salvatoris mei objicio inter te & me & judicium tuum: aliter tecum non contendo. Meritum ipsius dignissimae passionis offero pro merito quod habere debuissem, & hoc non habeo. Mortem tamen Domini mei Iesu Christi pono inter me & iram tuam. In manus tuas Domine commendo spiritum meum.
units.tr: when your soul, by the force of pains and sorrows, shall be separated from your most tender body. And in this death of yours alone I establish my comfort and trust; I place my confidence in nothing else, since your death is sufficient for my salvation. I commit myself to your death. I cover myself with your death. I wrap myself wholly in your death. If you wish to judge me otherwise, I say from now on, as then, and then, as now: Lord, I set the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, my Saviour, between you and me and your judgement; I do not contend with you otherwise. I offer the merit of his most worthy passion in place of the merit which I ought to have had and do not have. Yet I set the death of my Lord Jesus Christ between me and your wrath. Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.

units.la: Credo omnes principales fidei articulos. Detestor omnes haereses & errores atque superstitiones. Recognosco Creatorem meum saepe multipliciter & graviter offendisse. Doleo toto corde de omnibus peccatis meis contra huiusmodi amorem commissis, & de bonis omissis, & gratiis neglectis. Opto ut cor meum illuminetur ad agnitionem oblitorum, ut valeam de eis particulariter. Propono veraciter velle emendare & nunquam amplius peccare mortaliter scilicet si supervixero.
units.tr: I believe all the principal articles of faith. I detest all heresies, errors and superstitions. I acknowledge that I have often and in many ways grievously offended my Creator. I grieve with my whole heart for all my sins committed against such love, and for the good things omitted, and the graces neglected. I desire that my heart be illumined to the knowledge of forgotten sins, so that I may be able to name them one by one. I truly purpose to wish to amend and never again to sin mortally, that is, if I survive.

units.la: Rogo Deum, ut praestet mihi auxilium continuandi & non recidivandi. Indulgeo ex corde omnibus qui quovismodo mihi nocuerunt ob passionem Domini. Peto indulgentiam & remissionem ab omnibus iis quos quovismodo offendi. Volo ut restituantur ablata integraliter usque in restitutionem & renunciationem omnium bonorum meorum. Credo quod per mortem Domini nostri Iesu Christi salvabor. Cui gratias ago quantum valeo. Cui me commendo, cui me committo. Crucifixam vitam ejus quantum infirmitas permiserit ruminabo & meditabor, ut ad resurrectionem cum gloria pervenire merear. Amen. Atque ita ipsa in aliis libris, ac Pastoralibus interrogationum illarum monumenta adhuc conspiciuntur & reliquiae, sed à prioribus multum mutatae. In Pastorali, jussu Mechliniensis Archiepiscopi, edito a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxx ix. His quoque interrogationibus salutì morientium consuli poterit. 1. Nonne vis, frater charissime, & vivere & mori, in soliditate fidei Iesu Christi, tanquam verus Christianus? Resp. volo. 2. Nonne petis à Deo veniam peccatorum, quæ commisisti contra ejus summam majestatem, & quod eum condigne non honorasti? Resp. Peto. Nonne tibi deliberatum est, vitam tuam in melius commutare, si tibi incolumi hoc morbo liberari detur? Resp. Est deliberatum. Atque tales xii. sequuntur ibi interrogationes Formulam, vel Breviarium illud Anselmi, in Belgicis nostris Ecclesiis olim observatum, etiam sub Papatu, ex antiquo, qui penes me est, libello Belgico, cui nec editionis tempus, neque typographi nomen adscriptum, ex stylo apparet satis, esse vetustissimum, didici, quod sic sonat:
units.tr: I ask God to grant me help to continue and not to relapse. I forgive from the heart all who have in any way harmed me, for the Lord's passion. I ask indulgence and remission from all whom I have in any way offended. I wish that what has been taken away be fully restored, even to the restitution and renunciation of all my goods. I believe that through the death of our Lord Jesus Christ I shall be saved, for which I give thanks as much as I can. To him I commend myself, to him I commit myself. I shall ruminate and meditate on his crucified life as far as infirmity permits, that I may deserve to come to the resurrection with glory. Amen. And so monuments and remnants of those questions still appear in other books and in Pastorals, though much changed from the earlier ones. In the Pastoral, published by order of the Archbishop of Mechlin in 1589, consideration may also be given to the salvation of the dying by these questions: (1) Do you not wish, dearest brother, to live and to die in the firmness of the faith of Jesus Christ, as a true Christian? Answer: I wish. (2) Do you not ask God for pardon of the sins you have committed against his supreme majesty, and that you have not honoured him as you ought? Answer: I ask. Is it not decided by you to change your life for the better, if you are granted to be freed from this illness unharmed? Answer: It is decided. There follow there twelve such questions. I learned that the formula, or breviary, of Anselm, once observed in our Belgian churches, even under the Papacy, from an ancient Belgian booklet in my possession, which has no date of publication nor printer's name, and which by its style appears to be very old, runs as follows:

units.la: Hier begint die Commendacie die men leest boer die siecke Mensschen als si leggen op haer uterste. Men vint beschreven in gute anselmus boecken dat men eenen kersten mensche die op sijn verscheiden liet eer hi sterft / ende de wille dat hi hem verweert so salmen hem bragen ende boer leggen aldus. Verbliftu di dat een kersten mensche bist ende int kersten gelove sterven wilt alst die wille Gods is. Ende soo sal dye siecke seggen ja ick. ende soo brachtmen doert Beroumet di dattu alsoo wel niet geleeft en hebste alstu mit rechte gedaen sonde hebben. Jaet. Beroumet u uwe sonden ende hebdi dye wil u leven te beteren of God u spaeren wouden. Jae ick. Geloefstu dat onse heere Jesus Christus die boer dy gestorven is. Ja ick. Dance Danckestu ende loesstu hem daer of. Ia ick. Geloeffse daten niet behouden en moeghste worden ten waer overmits dit voor ons Heren. Ia ick. Soe lobe ende danke Gode alle die wijl daer u leeft ende die sele in dy is ende set alle dijn gelove ende hope ende dijn name in hem ende in anders geen dingen/ende beveelt u selven der passien ende den doot ons Heeren Iesu Christi ende bewint u selven daer in mit gepeynsen ende mit eenen bitteren oberdencken ende bescudet u daer mede. Ende wil u die oberste rechter veroerdelen soo seggot aldus Heere den doot Iesu Christi die sette ick tusschen mi ende dijn oerdeel ende anders en vermete ick mijn geen were ende seyt die heer dan du hebste verdient der verdoemenisse/ soo segt Heere dijn ontfermherticheit ende dinen bitteren doot die voege ick tusschen di ende mi. Ende seggot Heere Iesu Christe levende Goeds Soon ontfermt mijns door uwen bitteren doot. Ende denct een dzoppel dat wten gebenedien lichaem quam ons behouders ons Heeren Iesu Christi genoech hadde geweest om dye werelt mede te verlossen. Ende als die mensch sterft salmen hem voer seggen sijn eyndelijcaers ende dat is aldus. In dinen handen beveel ick minen geest Heere du hebste mi verloest Godt der waerheyt. Verlicht mijn oogen op dat ick nyet en ontslape in mijn doodt ende dat mijn biant nyet en segge ick heb macht gehad regens hem/ Heere Davids Soen ontfermt di mijnre Christe des levende Godts Soen ontferm di mijnre. Soe wie dit leest of boergeseit woz̄dt in sijn uterste of eer hi sterft op dat hi heeft hemelijke ende ronde ... sonden / ende ... goet heeft ... leer gene ... ende ... ende sijn leven wil beteren is dat sake dat hem God wil sparen ende te hebbe ... ende dan soo ... sterven. Subjunguntur postmodum eodem in libello alia ad saeculi superstitionem facta, sed quae ab illa Anselmi commendatione liquido distinguuntur. Omitto, quae alibi ex Hortulo animae, Hosio, Scioppio, Eybbrachto, aliis pro eadem formula attuli, e quibus, ut in omnibus Occidentis Ecclesiis, non Coloniae solum, sed in toto Christianismo, inquit Vlenbergius, Papista Coloniensis, Anglica, Gallica, Italica, Romana ipsa, Tridentina, Germanica, Belgica, Polonica modus ille alloquendi & consolandi moribundos Anselmianus ostenditur notus fuisse atque usitatus. Videre etiam licet, super eodem, Vs-serium, de successione Ecclesiarum, in Occidente, Iohannem Gerhardi, Confess. Catholica, lib. II. part. III. pag. 838. Voetium, Disput. Select. part. II. pag. 738. ubi & alia gemina Anselmianis plura, ex Auctoribus variis, pro immensa sua lectione, atque eruditione, adfert. Addere possem, quod in Missali Trajectensi. Orat. post communionem, ad Deum dicunt: quid tibi digne reddam, pro omnibus, quae retribuisti mihi. Si enim totius mundi merita in unum fuerint congesta, non valerent tuae dignationi aliquatenus comparari. apud Henricum Kyspenning, de medit. mortis, lib. III. in refutandis objectionibus Satanae, ex Bernardi vita adfert, fateor, non sum dignus ego, nec propriis possum meritis regnum obtinere caelorum. Caeterum duplici jure illud obtinens Dominus meus Iesus Christus, haereditate scilicet Patris & merito passionis, altero ipse contentus, alterum mihi donat, ex cujus dono, jure mihi illud vendicans non confundor. ex Augustino: merito mihi spes valida in illo est, quod sanabis omnes languores meos, per eum qui sedet ad dexteram [?] tempus; & te interpellare pro nobis, alioquin desperarem, & similia. Præcipue autem quod hoc in loco annotemus, est Protestatio morituri, quam se confirmat contra tentationes, & ut adsistentes edificet, quam habet Ludovicus Blosius, in Instruct. vitæ Ascetica, lib. II. cap. II. quamquè non alii solum commendant, sed etiam Regem Hispaniæ Philippum II. Hispanice totam moribundâ voce in extremis recitasse, narrat Didacus Vepes, qui Regi erat à confessionibus, hoc modo: Ego peccator indignissimus, redemptus pretiosissimo sanguine Domini nostri Iesu Christi, palam profiteor, me sincero corde ignoscere omnibus, qui quovis modo mihi injuriam vel molestiam aliquam unquam intulerunt: & humiliter rogo tam præsentes quam absentes, omnes, ut mihi vicissim ignoscant & dimittant si in aliquo eos offendi.
units.tr: Here begins the commendation that is read over sick people when they lie at their last. It is written in the good books of Anselm that when a Christian is about to pass away, one should say the following to him before he dies. And if he is willing to be instructed, one shall bring him the following and read it to him in this way. "Do you believe that you are a Christian and wish to die in the Christian faith, if it is God's will?" And then the sick person shall say, "Yes, I do." Then one shall say: "Do you confess that you have not lived as well as you ought to have lived, had you done what was right?" "Yes. I confess my sins and I would wish to amend my life, if God would spare me." "Yes, I do." "Do you believe that our Lord Jesus Christ died for you?" "Yes, I do." "Do you thank him and praise him for it?" "Yes, I do." "Do you believe that you cannot be saved except through our Lord?" "Yes, I do." "Then praise and thank God all the while you live, and while the soul is in you, and set all your faith and hope and your name in him alone and in nothing else. Commend yourself to the passion and death of our Lord Jesus Christ, and comfort yourself in it with thoughts and with bitter remembrance, and protect yourself with it." And if the supreme judge wishes to condemn you, then say thus: "Lord, I set the death of Jesus Christ between me and your judgment, and I put forward no other defence." And if the Lord says that you have deserved damnation, then say: "Lord, I set your mercy and your bitter death between you and me." And say: "Lord Jesus Christ, living Son of God, have mercy on me through your bitter death." And consider that one drop that came from the blessed body of our Saviour Jesus Christ would have been enough to redeem the world.
