And when the person dies, one shall say to him his final words, which are these: "Into your hands I commend my spirit. Lord, you have redeemed me, God of truth. Enlighten my eyes, so that I do not fall asleep in death, and that my enemy does not say, 'I have had power over him.' Lord, son of David, have mercy on me; Christ, Son of the living God, have mercy on me." Whoever reads or says this, when he is at his last, or before he dies, [the text here is corrupt and damaged; it continues about having heavenly and round sins, and about a good life and amendment, and that if God wishes to spare him and to have him, then he will live, and if not, he will die]. Afterwards in the same little book other things are added that pertain to the superstition of the age, but these are clearly distinct from that commendation of Anselm. I pass over what I have elsewhere cited from the Hortulus animae, from Hosius, Scioppius, Eybbrachtus and others for the same formula, from which it is shown that this manner of addressing and comforting the dying, the Anselmian manner, was known and in use, not only at Cologne but in all the Western Churches and throughout Christendom, as Vlenbergius, a Cologne Papist, says: English, French, Italian, Roman itself, Tridentine, German, Belgian, Polish. On the same matter one may also see Usserius, de successione Ecclesiarum in Occidente; Johann Gerhard, Confessio Catholica, book II, part III, p. 838; Voetius, Disputationes selectae, part II, p. 738, where, out of his immense reading and learning, he also brings forward many other things similar to the Anselmian ones from various authors. I could add that in the Utrecht Missal, in the prayer after communion, they say to God: "What shall I render worthy to you for all that you have bestowed on me? For if the merits of the whole world were gathered into one, they would not be able in any way to be compared with your dignity." Henricus Kyspenning, in de meditatione mortis, book III, in refuting the objections of Satan, cites from the life of Bernard: "I confess that I am not worthy, nor can I obtain the kingdom of heaven by my own merits. But my Lord Jesus Christ, who holds it by a double right, namely by inheritance from the Father and by the merit of his passion, is content with the one and gives me the other, and by his gift I, claiming it for myself by right, am not confounded." From Augustine: "Justly is my hope strong in him, that you will heal all my languors through him who sits at the right hand [?] of time, and that you intercede for us; otherwise I would despair," and similar things. But what we should especially note in this place is the protestatio morituri, which a dying person makes to strengthen himself against temptations and to edify those standing by, which Ludovicus Blosius has in Instructio vitae ascetica, book II, chapter II. Nor do others alone commend it; Didacus Vepes, who was confessor to the king, relates that Philip II, King of Spain, recited the whole of it in Spanish with his dying voice at the end, in this manner: "I, the most unworthy sinner, redeemed by the most precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, openly profess that I from my sincere heart forgive all who have at any time done me any injury or any annoyance in any way; and I humbly beg all, both present and absent, that they in turn forgive me and let go, if I have offended them in anything."

units.la: Agnosco me hactenus non vixisse pure nec sancte coram Domino, sicut vivere debueram: agnosco scelera mea multa nimis: agnosco culpas & negligentias meas infinitas. Agnosco quidquid mali, per omnem vitam commisi, & supplici mente à misericordissimo Domino Deo nostro veniam peto: dolens quod unquam eum offenderim, & proponens deinceps vitare peccata.
units.tr: I acknowledge that hitherto I have not lived purely or holily before the Lord, as I ought to have lived. I acknowledge my very many wicked deeds. I acknowledge my countless faults and negligences. I acknowledge whatever evil I have committed through my whole life, and with a suppliant mind I ask pardon from the most merciful Lord our God, grieving that I ever offended him, and purposing henceforth to avoid sins.

units.la: Quamvis autem graviter & multis modis hactenus deliquerim, non tamen diffido de omnipotenti & benignissimâ misericordiâ ipsius Redemptoris mei: sed spero me per meritum passionis & mortis ejus, non autem ita per merita mea, participem futurum æternæ vitæ atque hæreditatis. Ego ipsam passionem ejus sacratissimam, pro refugio munimentoque tutissimo habeo: ego eam inimicis meis invisibilibus semper & ubique, tanquam armaturam inexpugnabilem, objicio; eam sanctæ Trinitati pro meritis, quæ mihi desunt, & pro perfectâ satisfactione de peccatis meis offero.
units.tr: Although I have sinned hitherto grievously and in many ways, yet I do not distrust the omnipotent and most kind mercy of my Redeemer himself; but I hope, through the merit of his passion and death, and not so much through my own merits, to become a partaker of eternal life and inheritance. I hold his most sacred passion itself as my refuge and most sure defence. I always and everywhere set it against my invisible enemies as an unconquerable armour; I offer it to the Holy Trinity for the merits that I lack and for perfect satisfaction for my sins.

units.la: Credo in Deum Patrem omnipotentem, creatorem coeli & terrae: & in Iesum Christum filium eius Dominum nostrum, qui conceptus est de Spiritu Sancto, natus ex Maria virgine, passus sub Pontio Pilato, crucifixus, mortuus, & sepultus. Descendit ad inferos, tertia die resurrexit à mortuis, ascendit in coelum, sedet ad dextram Dei Patris omnipotentis, inde venturus est iudicare vivos & mortuos. Credo in Spiritum Sanctum, Sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam, Sanctorum communionem, remissionem peccatorum, carnis resurrectionem & vitam aeternam. Amen.
units.tr: I believe in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth; and in Jesus Christ, his Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried. He descended into hell, on the third day rose again from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty, whence he will come to judge the living and the dead. I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body and life everlasting. Amen.

units.la: Protestor coram ipso omnipotenti Deo, & coram tota curia coelesti, me cupere & velle in ea fide vitam hanc finire, in qua convenit obedientem sanctae matris Ecclesiae filium mori. Protestor me credere universa, quae ipsa Catholica fides continet, & quae à veris orthodoxisque Christi fidelibus credenda sunt. Quod si vel impugnatione Diaboli, vel violentia morbi pressus, aliquid huic proposito contrarium cogitarem, loqueret, aut facerem, iam illud revoco, & confiteor me nullo modo consentire talibus cogitationibus, verbis aut operibus. Gaudeo, & gratias ago misericordissimo creatori & salvatori meo, cuius mirabili pietate me in sancta fide Christiana moriturum confido. In manus eius sanctissimas animam & corpus meum [illegible, ~3 letters] in hora mortis meae commendo.
units.tr: I protest before almighty God himself, and before the whole heavenly court, that I desire and wish to end this life in that faith in which it befits a dutiful son of holy mother Church to die. I protest that I believe all the things that the Catholic faith itself contains and that are to be believed by the true and orthodox faithful of Christ. If, pressed by the assault of the devil or the violence of disease, I should think, say, or do anything contrary to this purpose, I now revoke it, and I confess that I in no way consent to such thoughts, words or deeds. I rejoice and give thanks to my most merciful creator and saviour, by whose wonderful goodness I trust that I shall die in the holy Christian faith. Into his most holy hands I commend my soul and my body [illegible] in the hour of my death.

units.la: Nihil autem in tota hac [illegible, ~3 letters] integram exhibui, Professionem illam, à Pontificiis quam vt scriptam commendatam, usurpa-tam, [?] sed vt [illegible, ~3 letters] quomodo id commode appellem. Aut saltem quod non utroque pollice comprobaverim, quod non libenter amplector, & nos alios-que consolari, atque Deo in extremis animas nostras committere cupiamus. Adeo illi passim sunt homines, in regulis vitae, & mortis candide prescri-benbendis, usurpandis; & hic quàm uspiam, minus differunt. Quod si ad talia revocare Papistarum suum volunt, & resecare superflua, quae superstitio, & facunda error advexit, saltem nos iis non vexare, certum, quod propius inter nos facilisque convenit. Quid autem de nobis dicere nunc possunt, quid culpare, qui illis stamus, & acquiescimus, quae ex ipsis producimus Papistis, & quibus Nostris ut vivere, & mori cum pace concedant, unice postulamus? Ego nil dubito mihi usurpare consolationem Anselmi, & protestationem Blosii, quâ vel vitus monstrum illud hominis Papalissimi fuit Philippus II. Hispaniarum Rex, Belgarum tyrannus. Quin hoc aegre ferrem, Anselmianam illam formulam, ad liturgiam nostram adjungi, ut sic omnibus constaret doctrinae fidei, & consolationis nostrae consensus cum priscâ & meliori antiquitate, cum illâ consolandi formulâ, quae in medio tristi Papatu, omnibus fere Ecclesiis recepta fuit, & nostrae quoque Belgicae. Iam nihil est quod de maiorum nostrorum salute & fide vel quarant alii, vel diffidant, modo in illâ fide obierint, quae sub extremum ipsius casu traditâ fuit & relicta, cuiusque variis ubique apud Papistas quoscunque monumenta reliqua. Desinant de nobis male loqui Pontificii nos criminati, condemnare qui salutis illa retinemus, ipsis etiam iudicibus fundamenta, quibus suos immoti volunt cum ante, verum etiam post Reformationem. Atque illis ascetices superstruendum iudicium, vel conatus de reducendis Papistis potius quam desendae, mille controversiis involutas.
units.tr: Yet in all this [illegible passage] I have not presented that profession in full, which the Papists commend and use as a written formula, but I cannot say easily how to name it fittingly. At least I do not approve it with both thumbs, nor do I gladly embrace it, though we too wish to console ourselves and others and to commit our souls to God at the end. So widely do men differ in drawing up and using rules for living and dying well, and here they differ no less than anywhere else. But if the Papists want to recall their people to such things and to cut away the superfluities that superstition and eloquent error have introduced, then at least it is certain that we should not trouble them with those things, since what is shared between us agrees more closely and easily. But what can they now say about us, or what can they blame us for, when we stand with them and agree with those things which they themselves put forward, and when we ask only that our people be allowed to live and die in peace? I have no doubt that I may use the consolation of Anselm and the protestation of Blosius, by which even that monster of a most Papal man, Philip II, king of Spain and tyrant of the Netherlanders, was (as they say) comforted at his end. Indeed I would take it ill if that Anselmian formula were not added to our liturgy, so that it might be plain to all that the agreement of our doctrine of faith and of our consolation with the older and better antiquity is shown by that formula of consolation which, in the midst of the sad Papacy, was received by almost all churches, and by our own Belgic church as well. Now there is nothing for others to inquire into or to doubt concerning the salvation and faith of our forebears, provided they died in that faith which was handed down and left to them at the very end of life, of which various memorials survive everywhere among the Papists. Let the Papists cease to speak ill of us, accusing and condemning us for keeping those things that lead to salvation, which are the very foundations by which they themselves, as judges, want their people kept unmoved, not only before the Reformation but also after it. And let judgement be built upon them, rather than attempts at winning back Papists, which are entangled in a thousand controversies, be defended.

units.la: Deinde eundem in finem urgeri debet communis lectio, & studium Scripturae linguâ vernaculâ. Quod dum licere Pontificii nonnunquam nostris respondent (scimus quantum adversus themata pariter sua, & commodo) eo facilius accipi potest, & obtineri. Fuit hoc inter Compactata in Bohemia olim, anno MDXXV. ininter Calixtinos & Pontificios, art. v. hoc tamen, Laicis non prohibetur, ut in aedibus privatis Biblia legantur familiis sine omni additione, seu expositione. Vrgendum, quovis pacto est, ut id vulgo contingat, atque ab omnibus gnaviter frequentetur studium, ad salutem aeque necessarium & utile. Quod, uti argumentum causae nostrae bonae est, dum intrepide non modo concedimus cuivis Sacrae Scripturae lectionem, sed injungimus etiam, & ardentissime expetimus, adeo ut nihil nobis inde metuamus, quemadmodum qui tenebras cupiunt & amplexantur; ita & medium optimum est, quo divina veritas ad animas certius penetret, & ad quoscunque diffundatur. Atque haec res eo diligentius commendari debet, quo in Papatu multi sunt qui quod ipsis prohibetur Scriptura, aegre ferunt, & lectionem ejus usumque urgent. Inter ipsos Hispanos scripsit Fernandus Texeda, conversus Monachus, plures Scriptores extare, qui idem clamant, atque ex illorum adductis testimoniis peculiari libello id ostendit, Londini impresso, anno MDCXXIV. Exhortation of a Spanish converted Monke: collected out of the Spanish Authours them selves, to reade & peruse the holy Scriptures. Qui primus Biblia Belgice edidit a. MCCCCLXXVII. impressa Delphis Hollandorum, apud Jacobum Jacobi, & Mauritium Imants Mediobargensem, in Praefatione, hunc in modum facius suum excusare & defendere necesse habuit: Nochtans wete ick dat het sal werden ter bernt onder die clergie/ hoewel dat sy nochtans weten sullen die ooghaerlijckheyt daer af. Want sommige Clercken tozent, dat datmen de heymelijckheyt der Schriftuere den gemeynen volcke soude ontbinden / ende dat besondere die de minste Clercken sijn / ende en willen niet weten dat Christus Apostelen in alle tongen spraken / ende haer leeringe ende predicatie den volcke Re leerden ende beschreven. Contra & Erasmus in Paraclesi praefixa Athanasio, quae etiam seorsim abeo legitur: Vehementer ab istis dissentio, qui nolunt ab iisdictis legi divinas literas, in vulgi linguam transfusas, sive quasi Christus tam involuta docuerit, ut vix a paucis Theologis possint intelligi, sive quasi religionis Christianae praecipuum in hoc situm sit, ut neglectatur: ob quam causam Idem alibi, lib. xxiv. epist. iv. ad Earol. Vtenhovium, narrat Ludovicum Berquinum, praestantem in aula Regis Francisci I. virum, Lutetiae Parisiorum combustum fuisse, anno clo Ioxxix. eo quod scripsisset, in rem esse pietatis, ut sacri libri in linguam vulgatam translati legerentur a populo. Verum P. Pius IV. in Indice librorum prohibitorum, Regulam iv. posuit de libris sacris non a quovis legendis, tantummodo ex speciali concessione Episcopi, aut Inquisitoris. Videlicet Scripturae Sacrae lectio in censum librorum prohibitorum apud Papas venit. Nos contra in singulorum manus Scripturam tradimus, idque sedulo agimus, ut omnes, & Pontificii vulgo eam habeant, & non aliam, saltem ex ipsorum versione Vulgatam, atque ut eam modo legant.
units.tr: Next, to the same end, the common reading and study of Scripture in the vernacular ought to be pressed. Since the Papists sometimes answer our side that this is permitted (we know how much they say this against their own theses and to their own advantage), it can more easily be accepted and secured. This was once agreed in the Compacts in Bohemia, in the year 1525, between the Calixtines and the Papists, article 5: It is not forbidden to laymen that the Bible be read in private houses by families without any addition or explanation. This must be urged in every way, so that it becomes common among the people and that all diligently take up this study, which is as necessary and useful for salvation. As this is a proof of the goodness of our cause, since we fearlessly grant to everyone the reading of Holy Scripture, and indeed enjoin it and most ardently seek it, so that we fear nothing from it (unlike those who desire and embrace darkness), so it is also the best means by which divine truth penetrates more surely into souls and is spread to whomever it may be. This matter ought to be commended all the more diligently because under the Papacy there are many who are vexed that Scripture is forbidden to them and who press for its reading and use. Among the Spaniards themselves, Fernandus Texeda, a converted monk, wrote that there are several writers who cry out the same thing, and from their testimonies he showed this in a special little book printed at London in 1624: Exhortation of a Spanish converted Monke: collected out of the Spanish Authours them selves, to reade & peruse the holy Scriptures. The first to publish the Bible in Dutch, in 1477, printed at Delft in Holland by Jacob Jacobi and Maurice Imants of Mediobargum, had to excuse and defend his work in this way in the preface: Nevertheless I know it will be a cause of offence among the clergy, although they too will know the danger of it. For some clerics think that the secrecy of Scripture should be withheld from the common people, and especially those who are the least of the clerics, and they will not know that Christ's apostles spoke in all tongues, and taught and preached their doctrine to the people in their own tongue. On the other side, Erasmus, in the Paraclesis prefixed to Athanasius, which is also read separately, says: I strongly disagree with those who do not want the divine letters, translated into the tongue of the common people, to be read, as if Christ had taught things so involved that they could scarcely be understood by a few theologians, or as if the chief point of the Christian religion lay in neglecting them. For this reason the same Erasmus elsewhere, in book 24, letter 4, to Karel Uytenhove, relates that Louis de Berquin, an outstanding man at the court of King Francis I, was burned at Paris in 1529, because he had written that it was for the good of piety that the sacred books translated into the vernacular should be read by the people. But Pope Pius IV, in the Index of Prohibited Books, laid down in Rule 4 that the holy books should not be read by just anyone, but only by special permission of a bishop or inquisitor. Clearly, among the Popes, the reading of Holy Scripture has come under the censure applied to prohibited books. We, on the contrary, hand Scripture over into the hands of individuals, and we take care that all, including the Papists, commonly have it, and not another version, at least their own Vulgate, and that they read it now.

units.la: Interim & disputationem cum Pontificiis non omittendam censeo: quin videndum, ut quovis pacto & quacunque via illos si non convertamus, confundamus & convincamus. Disputatio est duplex, alia ore fit, & dicitur Colloquium, alia scripto, per libros. Colloquiorum inde a Reformatione, cum Pontificiis, a Nostris habitorum, magnus est numerus. Primum fuit Lipsiacum, anno clo Ioxix. d. ix. Iulii, hora septima, & absolutum d. xiv. Iulii, hora octava antemeridiana, eodem anno, inter Carolostadium, una cum Luthero, & Eckium. Disputatio habetur Tom. i. Oper. Lutheri: ac primo quidem de potestate Papae actum fuit, inde de aliis tum temporis non minus controversis articulis, de Bohemis, de purgatorio, indulgentiis, poe-ninitentiâ, &c. Breviter habes quoque eandem descriptam Disputationem, in epistolâ Petri Mosellani, ad Bilibaldum Pirckamerum, quam ex M. S. exhibet, initio Annalium suorum Ecclesiasticorum Reformat. Abrah. Scultetus, ad annum cIↄ Iↄ xix. Sed Teccelius, indulgentiarum primus & praecipuus mango, ubi audiisset consensum in Colloquium Lipsiacum esse, & ibi de rebus suis instituendam disputationem, metuens sibi, indignatusque, dixisse fertur: quin hoc faxis Diabolus, was molt der Teuffel. Interim, sive angore animi, sive aliter, dum disputabatur inter Lutherum, Eckiumque de indulgentiis, ille Lipsiae, in Monasterio Dominicanorum, ad plures abiit.
units.tr: Meanwhile I think that disputation with the Papists must not be neglected either. Indeed we must see to it that, by whatever means and by whatever way, if we cannot convert them, we at least confound and convince them. Disputation is of two kinds: one is oral and is called a colloquy, the other is written, through books. Of colloquies with the Papists held by our side since the Reformation there is a great number. The first was at Leipzig in the year 1519, from 9 July, at seven o'clock, and it was concluded on 14 July at eight in the morning of the same year, between Carlstadt, together with Luther, and Eck. The disputation is found in volume 1 of Luther's works. First the power of the Pope was discussed, and then other articles then no less controversial, on the Bohemians, purgatory, indulgences, repentance, and so on. You also have a brief account of the same disputation in the letter of Peter Mosellanus to Bilibald Pirckheimer, which Abraham Scultetus gives from a manuscript at the beginning of his Ecclesiastical Annals of the Reformation, under the year 1519. But Tetzel, the first and chief champion of indulgences, when he heard that there was agreement for a colloquy at Leipzig and that a disputation about his affairs would be held there, is said to have been alarmed and indignant and to have said: What the devil is this! Meanwhile, whether from anguish of mind or for some other reason, while the disputation was being held between Luther and Eck about indulgences, Tetzel went off to Leipzig, to the Dominican monastery, to several people.

units.la: Alterum abhinc habitum Colloquium Tigutinum, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxii r. d. xxix. Januar. inter Zuinglium, & Iohannem Fabrum, Episcopi Constantiensis Vicarium, in Curiâ Tigurinâ: quò innumeri undique ex agro Tigurino, & vicinis partibus confluxerunt homines, atque singulari Magistratus Diplomate evocati ditionis istius fuerunt Clerici, etiam Constantiensis episcopus, ejusve Legati, qui adfuere, Fridericus ab Anwyli, Ioh. Faber, atque Martinus Tubingensis. Et quamvis disputationem postularet Senatus, ut opponeret quicunque adversus Zuinglium probare se posse consideret doctrinam ejus esse haereticam, identidemque hoc flagitaret Zuinglius ipse, & Collegae, disputationem tamen omnem subterfugiebant Constantienses Legati, nemoque ex Pontificiis alius prodibat. Saepe jam de invocatione Sanctorum, jam de authoritate Scripturae, & Conciliorum, de coelibatu Ecclesiasticorum, disputationem quaerebat Zuinglius, sed partes suas aliis constanter deserentibus, tandem Senatus conclusit: Quoniam vero contra Huldrychum Zuinglium majoris nostrae ecclesiae antistitem et ecclesiasten (quem haeretieum esse multis clam hereticum esse convitiati sunt) post articulorum aut propositionum ipsius promulgationem, nemo proprodire visus est; quibusdam sacra scriptura miraculis convin-cere conaretur, licet non semel eos provocavit, qui illum ano-te haereticum dixere: prudentissimi viri Cas. S. P. Q. Ti-gurinus decreverunt & omnino ratum voluerunt, ut Huldry-chus Zuinglius sacrosanctam Evangelii doctrinam & divi-ni verbi oracula (ut hactenus ab illo facta sunt) annun-tiare & praedicare pergat. Praeterea alienum quemque, quis-quis vel in urbe vel agro verbi ministerio praesunt, est, non quicquam aliud instituere aut docere, quam quod Evangelica doctrina testimonio & sacra scriptura auctoritate per ipsos probari potest. Ab omnibus vero vel haereseos vel alio-rum sectarum criminationibus illos abstinere & in totum sibi temperare volunt. Si qui enim in hoc se immorigeros & rebelles praebuerint, eos de se poenas sumi sinitus, ut se uniquae & iniuste fecisse omnibus testari queant. Actum Tigurii, Januarii XXIX. Anno M. D. XXIII. Non scio aliam disputationem instituturam, habitamque meliori ordine, & majori cum fructu, ac hanc: ad quam, absque tumultu, praeeunte maturo examine, disputatione; omniumque instructione, convictis Adversariis, Ecclesiae Magistratusque unanimi consensu, in urbe & agro secuta fuit felicissima Reformatio. Post actionem, & factum Senatusconsultum Faber, qui antea semper exceperat, se disputare nolle, nisi forte in Academia aliqua Parisiensem nominans, Colonien- sem, aut Lovaniensem. Zuinglio interfuante, quid vero si Erfordia aut Vittemberga huic negotio destinaretur? respondit, minime, quia Lutherus ibi nimis vicinus est: ab aquilone pandit omne malum: scripturum se ajebat adversus Conclusiones, quas Zuinglius eo fine scripserat, ne quis ignoraret, quae de re habenda foret disputatio; tum & ad Concilium propediem habendum, illo, vel proximo (diceas) anno, rem differri volebat: sed finita disputatione, quasi post praelium, loca aliqua Scripturae proferebat, ad quod antea perduci non poterat, nunc pro Ecclesiasticis tradiditionibus &c. decertaas ad quae facillima opera Zuinglius respondit, & leporinum caseum promisit, si quando unam suarum pro possessionum ille subvertisset. Sed quomodo Faber fecerit, vel ex hac ejus ultima responsione colligere; ubi dicebat: nihil omnino certe amice simul & pacifice vivi posset, & si Evangelium nullum esset. Et paulo ante, cum de Scripturis legendis, & per eas confirmandis omnibus fidei articulis Zuinglius monuisset, Pastor Schlierensis subjunxerat: Quid vero illi legendum erit, qui sacerdotii reditus tenuiores sunt, quam ut hos sex mihi libros, Testamentum videlicet, emere queant? Mihi certe sacerdotium est longe tenuissimum. Unde necessitas hoc me dicere cogit. Quomodo vero pro invocatione Sanctorum argumentatus fuerit Faber, scire vis? ecce: Communi, dicebat, & maxime ecclesiae Christianae consensu illud receptum & approbatum est, omnesque denique Christi fideles illud credunt & recipiunt, simulque Litaniae & Canonis Missae auctoritas idem illud confirmat & asseverit, quod nimirum Dei Matrem & sanctos omnes invocare debemus, ut pro nobis intercedere dignentur. Testatur idem ipsa Maria virgo apud Lucam hisce verbis: Ecce hinc me beatam dicent omnes generationes. Et cognata ipsius Elizabet anti-quissime ipsam compellans inquit: Unde mihi hoc, ut veniat mater domini mei ad me? Item, Benedicta tu inter mulieres. Accedit his mulieris Evangelicae testimonium, clamantis: Beatus venter, qui te portavit, & ubera quae suxisti. Quotidiano item ecclesiae ritu celebrant quod canimus, Seniant omnes tuum levamen &c. Porro, si quae nos dicimus vana sunt & pro nugis habentur, mihi prorsus tacendum esse video. Quibus omnibus peractis, atque ubi postremo, pro partibus nostris, V. Volphangus Abbas clara voce dixisset: ubi nunc sunt, qui incendia nobis minati & se lignis allaturos pollicti sunt: Quin nunc in arenam descendunt? Tigurini, non sufficere existimantes, ut Christus & Evangelium, loco inutilium traditionum, annunciaretur, nisi etiam idololatrica omnia & offendicula cultus superstitiosi vbique amo-veri-ent, omnia, hoc quoque non agendum censue-runt, nisi altera indicta Synodo & disputatione, quâ tanti negotii res debite examinaretur, & post habitam, recto ordine caperetur ejus, quod faciendum esset, maturum consilium.
units.tr: Another disputation was held afterwards, the Zurich Colloquy, in the year 1523, on 29 January, between Zwingli and Johann Faber, Vicar of the Bishop of Constance, in the Zurich town hall. Countless people came from all over the Zurich countryside and the neighbouring regions, and by a special decree of the magistrate the clergy of that territory were summoned, as were the Bishop of Constance or his legates who were present: Friedrich von Anwyl, Johann Faber, and Martin of Tübingen. Although the Senate demanded a disputation, so that anyone who thought he could prove Zwingli's doctrine heretical might come forward and oppose him, and although Zwingli himself and his colleagues repeatedly demanded it, the Constance legates kept avoiding any disputation, and no one else from the Papists came forward. Zwingli often sought a debate, now on the invocation of the saints, now on the authority of Scripture and the Councils, now on the celibacy of the clergy, but since the others kept steadfastly abandoning their part, the Senate finally resolved: Since, however, no one has come forward to oppose Huldrych Zwingli, the chief minister and preacher of our greater Church (whom many have secretly and openly slandered as a heretic), after the publication of his articles or propositions, and since he has not been refuted by Holy Scripture, although on more than one occasion he has challenged those who called him a heretic, the most prudent men of the Council of Zurich have decreed and fully resolved that Huldrych Zwingli should continue to proclaim and preach the most holy doctrine of the Gospel and the oracles of the divine Word, as he has done hitherto. Moreover, every other minister, whether in the city or in the countryside, is forbidden to teach or undertake anything except what can be proved by the testimony of the Gospel doctrine and the authority of Holy Scripture. They also wish that all of them abstain from accusations of heresy or of other sects, and altogether refrain from them. For if any prove disobedient and rebellious in this, they shall be punished, so that they may be seen by all to have acted wrongly and unjustly. Done at Zurich, 29 January, in the year 1523. I know of no disputation that was held in a better order, with greater fruit, than this one, in which, without tumult, after a careful examination preceded by the disputation and the instruction of all, the adversaries were refuted, and with the unanimous consent of the Church and the magistrates the most fortunate Reformation followed in the city and the countryside. After the proceedings and the enactment of the Senate's decree, Faber, who had previously always excused himself by saying he was unwilling to dispute, unless perhaps in some university, naming Paris, Cologne, or Louvain, now, with Zwingli present, was asked: what if Erfurt or Wittenberg were appointed for this business? He replied, by no means, because Luther is too near there: "from the north all evil breaks forth." He said he would write against the Conclusions which Zwingli had written for this purpose, so that no one would be ignorant of what the disputation was to concern; and he wished the matter deferred to the Council to be held shortly, in that year or the next (you might say). But once the disputation was over, as if after a battle, he produced certain passages of Scripture, which he had not been able to be brought to before, and now he handed over disputes concerning the ecclesiastical traditions, etc. To these matters Zwingli replied with the greatest ease, and promised a hare's cheese if ever Faber had overturned any one of his positions. How Faber acted may be gathered even from his last reply, where he said: It would certainly be impossible for anyone to live altogether in friendship and peace, even if there were no Gospel. And a little before, when Zwingli had advised that all the articles of faith should be read in Scripture and confirmed by it, the minister of Schlieren had added: But what will those whose priestly incomes are too meagre to let them buy these six books for me, namely the Testament, have to read? For my own priesthood is by far the poorest. Hence the necessity compels me to say this. And how Faber argued for the invocation of the saints, do you want to know? Here it is: By the common and especially the Christian Church's consent, he said, that has been received and approved, and finally all the faithful of Christ believe and receive it; and at the same time the authority of the Litanies and of the Canon of the Mass confirms the same thing, namely that we ought to invoke the Mother of God and all the saints, that they may deign to intercede for us. The Virgin Mary herself bears witness to this in Luke with these words: Behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed. And her kinswoman Elizabeth, addressing her in the most ancient manner, says: Why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? Also, Blessed art thou among women. To these is added the testimony of the Gospel woman, crying out: Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked. Likewise in the daily rite of the Church we celebrate what we sing: May all the saints bring you their help, etc. Furthermore, if what we say is empty and held to be trifles, I see that I must altogether keep silent. When all these things had been done, and finally, when on our side Abbot V. Volphangus had said in a loud voice: Where now are those who threatened us with fire and promised to bring their wood? Why do they not now come down into the arena? the Zurichers, thinking it was not enough that Christ and the Gospel should be proclaimed in place of useless traditions unless all idolatrous things and stumbling blocks of superstitious worship were also removed everywhere, decided that this too should not be undertaken, except after another Synod and disputation was called, in which the matter of so great a business might be duly examined, and after it had been held, a mature counsel might be taken in right order as to what ought to be done.

units.la: Quare denuo disputationem instituunt, in urbe suâ, eodem anno, priore frequentiorem. Cui interfuerunt ex duodecim Helvetiæ pagis undiquaque huc vocati plus minus sexcenti homines, vocatiq; etiam Episcopi Constantiensis, Curiensis, Basiliensis, una cum Basiliensi Vniversitate; sed illi quidem non adfuerunt, neque suos miserunt legatos. De duobus hic, tollendis imaginibus, atque abrogandâ Missâ actum, duravitque disputatio diebus tribus: & tandem postquam Ioachimus Vadianus, qui cum aliis duobus constitutus erat Præses, omnes fuisset obtestatus, ut si quis sibi non satisfactum putaret, sententiam disertis verbis proferret; nemine prodeunte, peroravit breviter Zuinglius, tum Leo Iudæ, post Vadianus, denique Consul Marcus Roistius, atque ita finis impositus huic etiam Disputationi fuit. Et tanto cum ordine, tamque feliciter processit Reformatio Reip. ac Ditionis Tigurinæ.
units.tr: Therefore they arranged a further disputation in their own city, in the same year, more crowded than the first. About six hundred men, more or less, summoned from all twelve regions of Helvetia, attended; the Bishops of Constance, Chur, and Basel were also summoned, together with the University of Basel, but they did not attend and did not send their legates. The disputation concerned the removal of images and the abrogation of the Mass, and it lasted three days. At last, after Joachim Vadian, who had been appointed President along with two others, had entreated all that if anyone thought himself not satisfied he should state his opinion in plain words, and no one came forward, Zwingli briefly gave the closing speech, then Leo Jud, after him Vadian, and finally the consul Marcus Roist, and thus an end was put to this disputation too. And with such order and such success did the Reformation of the commonwealth and territory of Zurich proceed.

units.la: Eodem anno, feriis D. Gregorii, habita Groningæ dis-putatio fuit in ædibus Prædicatorum, inter Dominicanos, atque Sacerdotes Ecclesiæ (uti in Papatu loquuntur) Martini, nempe Magistrum nostrum Laurentium Groningauum, cum fratre Ludolpho, respondente, & Supp-riore Pittinck; atque Hermannum Abringium, juris Doctorem, Ioh. Albertum Timmermannum, Gerardum Pistoris, & Nic. Lesdorpium, Gymnasiarcham. Disputarunt de potestate Papæ monarchicâ, quam isti, contra illos, negabant: Igitur huic Imperialem gladium, quem Patres nostri Romano tribuunt Pontifici, quod Imperator sit, prorsus negamus & Romano, & cuius alii eximii Auctoris. porro: Quod si Romanus Pontifex indicaverit ferias, quas nostra Ecclesia Grouingana Pastor viderit suo populo esse exitio, licebit illi contra Romani Pontificis edicta abrogare ferias, quas videt in perniciem vergere sui gregis. Et quare est pastor, nisi ut prospiciat quae in rem facient commissae multitudini? Romano Pontifici non sunt commissae tuae oves. Praeter illa, & haec Timmermannus dixit: "Ad horarium lectio juris est divini? Quae me novus Apostolus coegit certum psalmorum & precum numerum quotidie emurmurare? Cum Christus doceat, non multis verbis orandum, Ethnicorum more." Denique, quod si jure divino eam monarchiam Romano Pontifici vindicas, nitemur salsissimam assertionem validissimis argumentis eludere. Quid plus Romano Pontifici asseris quam Alexandrino, aut Antiocheno? Si Christi habet monarchicum imperium, qui Christi est vicarius, habent ex aequo omnes, quando ex aequo omnes Christi agunt vices. Neque enim cuiquam peculiariter Christus eam monarchiam tribuit. Quam assertionem si ita accipitis, nitemur eam Evangelicis authoritatibus statuere. Primum igitur negamus Romani Pontificis monarchiam. Ministros suos Christus Apostolos statuit, non monarchas, non satrapas, non Principes, non Rabbinos; hoc est, Magistros potius.
units.tr: In the same year, on the feast of St. Gregory, a disputation was held at Groningen in the house of the Preachers, between the Dominicans and the priests of the Church (as they speak in the Papacy) of St. Martin, namely our Master Laurentius of Groningen, with Brother Ludolph responding, and the Prior Pittinck; and Hermann Abringius, Doctor of Law, Johann Albert Timmermann, Gerard Pistoris, and Nicholas Lesdorp, Rector of the Gymnasium. They disputed on the monarchical power of the Pope, which these men denied against the others: Therefore we absolutely deny that the imperial sword, which our Fathers attribute to the Roman Pontiff on the ground that he is Emperor, belongs to him, and this is the view of another distinguished author. Further: If the Roman Pontiff has proclaimed holidays which our minister of the Church of Groningen sees to be the ruin of his people, it will be lawful for him to abrogate, against the edicts of the Roman Pontiff, the holidays which he sees tending to the destruction of his flock. And why is he a minister, except that he may look after what will serve the multitude entrusted to him? Your sheep have not been entrusted to the Roman Pontiff. Besides these points, Timmermann also said this: "Is the reading of the hours a matter of divine law? Why has the new Apostle forced me to mutter a fixed number of psalms and prayers every day, when Christ teaches that we should not pray with many words, after the manner of the heathen?" Finally, if you claim that monarchy by divine law for the Roman Pontiff, we shall strive to refute this very absurd assertion with the strongest arguments. What more do you claim for the Roman Pontiff than for the Alexandrian or the Antiochene? If he who is Christ's vicar has the monarchical rule of Christ, then all have it equally, since all equally act in Christ's place. For Christ did not give that monarchy peculiarly to anyone. If you understand this assertion in this way, we shall strive to establish it by evangelical authorities. First, therefore, we deny the monarchy of the Roman Pontiff. Christ appointed his ministers as Apostles, not monarchs, not satraps, not princes, not rabbis; that is, rather as teachers.

units.la: Secutae disputationes duae anno MDXXVI: in Rhetia prior, altera in Helvetia: verum hoc utra eo vel ordine, vel successu, quo utraque Tigurina, de quibus modo diximus. Rhetica fuit instituta inter Iohannem Comandrum, Ministrum Evangelicum Curiae Rhetorum, qui octoginta theses ad disputandum conscripserat, & inter Vitaduum Episcopi Curiensis cum Abbate S. Luciae: disputatum de Ecclesia fuit, de purgatorio, & sacramentis, sed in altercationes desinente disputatione, Ordines ut finem imponendum censuerunt.
units.tr: Two further disputations followed in 1526: the first in Rhetia, the second in Helvetia. Neither matched the Zurich disputation, discussed just above, in its order or its outcome. The Rhaetian one was arranged between Johannes Comander, the Evangelical minister of the Court of the Rhaetians, who had drawn up eighty theses for debate, and Vitaduus, the Bishop of Chur, together with the Abbot of St. Luzi. They disputed about the Church, purgatory and the sacraments, but the debate degenerated into quarrelling, and the Estates resolved to bring it to an end.

units.la: Eodem anno, mense Maio, postquam Tigurinae ab aliis Helvetiorum Statibus sollicitati fuissent ad de ferendam reformationem, & Zuinglius din variisque calumniis per Eccium, Ingolstadiensem Professorem, de haeresi fuisset accusatus, variisque inter se scriptis praesertim de Colloquio, & deligendo ei loco, jam per biennium fere egissent, Badenae disputatio, ex arbitrio Cantonum, instituta fuit. Quem locum sibi non satis tutum existimans Zuinglius, abesse coactus, misit tamen Legatis Cantonum Badenae agentibus, ad Eccii tum propositiones, tum Responsiones, quas in Colloquium attulerat, scriptum haud unum: namque disputabant a Pontificiorum quidem partibus Faber, Eccius, Marnerus, praesentesque aderant Constantiensis, Basileensis, Curiensis, Lausonnensis Episcoporum Legati, a nostra vero parte, Oecolampadius, Berth. Hallerus, V. Wissenburgius, aliique nonnulli Basileensium, Scaphusianorum, Mulhusinorum, & Sangallensium concionatores. Sed finis fuit in majorem tumultum, & hominum perturbationem, aliis hanc, illam aliis partem sequentibus: atque a Novem Pagis conclusum, ut Zuinglius excommunicaretur, & Papismus, uti posset, in ditionibus ipsorum retineretur. Videatur Schultetus, part. I. sol. Annalium Ecclesiast. qui germanice, & Latine extat.
units.tr: In the same year, in May, after the Zurich authorities had been pressed by other Swiss states to introduce reform, and after Zwingli had been accused of heresy for a long time and with various slanders by Eck, professor at Ingolstadt, and after they had spent nearly two years in correspondence about the colloquy and the choice of venue, a disputation was arranged at Baden by decision of the cantons. Zwingli, thinking the place not safe enough for him, was forced to stay away, but he sent the cantonal envoys at Baden more than one written paper on the propositions and replies Eck had brought to the colloquy. The debaters for the Papists were Faber, Eck and Marner, and the envoys of the bishops of Constance, Basel, Chur and Lausanne were present. On our side were Oecolampadius, Berthold Haller, Vadian and several other preachers from Basel, Schaffhausen, Mulhausen and St. Gall. But the affair ended in greater tumult and confusion, some following one party and some the other. The Nine Districts resolved that Zwingli should be excommunicated, and that Papism should be kept in their territories so that it could be used. See Schultetus, part I, p. 1 of his Annales Ecclesiastici, which exists in German and Latin.

units.la: Eodem anno Homburgi in Hassia disputationem habeeri jussit Philippus Lantgravius, per Franciscum Lambertum, Avenionensem Gallum, qui Latine, & Adamum Cratonem, Fuldensem, qui Germanice, iis qui Germanice vellent, responderent, de variis per totam Theologiam Thesibus & Paradoxis: ad quam cum venissent tres Pontificii, Nicolaus Herborn Minorita, Guardianus Marpurgensis, & Iohannes Sperberus, post aliquam ventilationem, confusi abierunt: secutaque mox fuit Reformatio Ecclesiarum Hassiacarum, Monachis & Monialibus exactis e Coenobiis, & Monasteriorum redditibus ad Marpurgensem Academiam, & Nosocomia applicata.
units.tr: In the same year Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, ordered a disputation to be held at Homberg in Hesse, conducted by Francis Lambert, a Frenchman from Avignon, who answered in Latin, and by Adam Crato of Fulda, who answered in German for those who wished to hear German. It concerned various theses and paradoxes across the whole of theology. Three Papists came to it: Nicholas Herborn, a Franciscan, guardian of Marburg, and John Sperber. After some discussion they left in confusion. Soon afterwards came the reformation of the Hessian churches, with monks and nuns expelled from their monasteries, and the revenues of the monasteries assigned to the University of Marburg and to hospitals.

units.la: Anno cIↄIↄ xxvi r. d. i. Ianuarii, in Frisia orientali, disputationem publicam sustinuit Norda, Henricus Resius, frequenti omnis ordinis virorum concursu: Resio cuculum induto de surgestu veritatem strenue defendente adversus Gerardum Synellium Nordanum Abbatem, qui ibi convictus a Resio, conticuerat, nullusque post eum certamen restaurare et, victor Resius cuculum coram omnibus posuit, & Monachismum cum universo Papatu abjuravit, unde Ecclesiae Nordanae, quae cum poscebat, Pastor datus, & secuta regimonis illius Reformatio fuit. Vbbo Emmius, Hestor. Frisc. lib. I.
units.tr: On 1 January 1526, in East Friesland, Henry Resius held a public disputation at Norden, before a large gathering of men of every rank. Resius, wearing a cowl and speaking from the pulpit, vigorously defended the truth against Gerard Synellius, Abbot of Norden. Synellius was refuted by Resius there, and fell silent, and after him no one dared to renew the contest. The victorious Resius laid the cowl down before everyone and renounced monasticism together with the whole Papacy. Thereupon a pastor was given to the Church of Norden, which asked for one, and a reformation under that government followed. See Ubbo Emmius, Historia Frisica, book I.

units.la: Eodem anno, in Suecia, Vpsaliae disputarunt M. Olaus, Lutheri discipulus, pro Evangelicis; & Petrus Gallius Professor Vpsalensis Papisticus, vernacula sermone: postquam antea etiam anno cIↄ Iↄ xxiv. disputarant Latine: atque ita triumphum obtinuit veritas, ut Rex Gustavus inde palam, & strenue occaperit reformare, purgare regnum idolis & superstitionibus, atque sacra lingua vernacula: justa parum Evangelii sententiam, peragere jusserit.
units.tr: In the same year, in Sweden, at Uppsala, Master Olaus, a disciple of Luther, disputed on the Evangelical side, and Peter Gallius, the Papist professor at Uppsala, disputed in the vernacular. They had earlier disputed in Latin in 1524. Truth won such a triumph that King Gustavus openly and vigorously began to reform the kingdom, purging it of idols and superstitions, and ordered the sacred service to be performed in the vernacular, in keeping, as far as possible, with the sense of the Gospel.

units.la: Celebris sub hujus anni finem, die videlicet xvii r. Decembris habita est Bernae disputatio: ad quam Senatus finitimos omnes convocavit Episcopos, & Clericos quoscunque, super decem thesibus diu ante impressis, propositisque nostrae partes sudoribus Francisco Colbio, & Bertholdo Hallero, Bernensis Ecclesiae Ministris: ad quae Reformatio superiori anno ibi lata, ita restaurata est, ut abjecto jam integre Papatu, ejus abjurati annum, diemque publice in aere literis columnae inscripserint.
units.tr: Towards the end of this year, namely on 17 December, a famous disputation was held at Bern. To it the Senate summoned all the neighbouring bishops and all the clergy, concerning ten theses that had been printed long before. Francis Kolb and Berthold Haller, ministers of the Bernese Church, had laboured on our side. The reformation introduced there the previous year was then so fully restored that, with the Papacy now completely rejected, the authorities had the year and day of its renunciation publicly inscribed on a bronze column.

units.la: Quarto a. cIↄ Iↄ xxx r. Magistratus Vlmensis, qui jam ab anno cIↄ Iↄ xxii. Evangelium praedicari in urbe sua audierat, pro reformandis plenius Ecclesiis, evocatis Oecolampadium, Bucerum, Blaurerum, Zimbrechtum, & Bartholomaeum Biberacensem; hique capita doctrinæ octodecim fere thematibus comprehendissent, ex urbe & agro convocarunt pastores sacerdotesque numero centum & triginta; quibus illa obtulerunt examinanda: ubi postquam unus & alter ad disputationem prodiit, nemo autem afferret aliquid, nedum dicta themata everteret. Vlmenses, editis Colloquii istius Actis, xvi. Iunii, & sequentibus, volente populo, missam, imagines, festa, & reliquum Papismi apparatum ejecerunt, editis facti sui publico scripto rationibus.
units.tr: In 1530, the magistrates of Ulm, who had heard the Gospel preached in their city since 1522, wished to reform the churches more fully. They summoned Oecolampadius, Bucer, Blaurer, Zimmermann and Bartholomew of Biberach. These men drew up about eighteen heads of doctrine, comprised in nearly as many theses, and summoned from the city and countryside one hundred and thirty ministers and priests, to whom they presented these for examination. When one or two men came forward to dispute, no one brought forward anything, much less overturned the theses. The people of Ulm, having published the Acts of this colloquy on 16 June and the following days, and at the people's wish, cast out the Mass, images, feasts and the rest of the Papist apparatus, and published a written statement of their reasons for what they had done.

units.la: In Reformatione Genevensi, a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxiv. ex Bernensium instigatione, Senatus disputationem curavit haberi inter Farellum, una cum Vireto; & Furbitum Dominicani Ordinis Theologum, hominem dicacem & turbulentum, præsentibus Bernensis Reip. Legatis, in pleno cc. virorum Senatu, de potestate Ecclesiæ in ferendis legibus, de authoritate Pontificis Romani, de traditionibus, & aliis id genus capitibus controversis: ubi Furbitus ad incitas redactus, & damnatus ad palinodiam, eique illudens, à Senatu in carcerem conjectus fuit.
units.tr: In the Genevan Reformation, in 1534, at the instigation of the Bernese, the Senate arranged a disputation between Farel, together with Viret, and Furbity, a Dominican theologian, a witty and turbulent man. The Bernese envoys were present, before the full Senate of two hundred men. The subjects were the power of the Church in enacting laws, the authority of the Roman Pontiff, traditions and other controverted heads of that kind. Furbity was driven to bitter straits and condemned to retract. Mocking him, the Senate cast him into prison.

units.la: Anno sequente à Senatu facultatem disputandi publice impetravit (rem promoventibus Farello, ac Vireto) Iacobus Bernardus, Coenobiarcha Franciscanus, jam conversus, scripsitque themata de justificatione, &c. super quibus disputaretur in diem xxx. Maji, invitatis eò non Genevensibus tantum, sed & Lugdunensibus, & Gratianopolitanis, & quibuscunque veritatis indagatio cura cordique esset. Opposuerunt pro parte Pontificia Carolus Sorbonista, & Chappuisius Dominicanus, protractaque in multas hebdomadas disputatione, tandem fœlix ille diuturnæ dimicationis eventus fuit, qui non alibi, ut non solum antagonistæ illi, raro ingenuitatis exemplo, manus veritati dare, & ab illâ victos se palam testari, atque prædicare eandem, lubentes voluerint; sed per urbem subsecuta commu
units.tr: The following year, Jacques Bernard, a Franciscan abbot who had by then converted, obtained from the Senate permission to dispute publicly, with Farel and Viret promoting the matter. He wrote theses on justification and so on, to be disputed on 30 May. Invited to it were not only the Genevans but also people from Lyon and Grenoble and anyone who cared for and was concerned with the search for truth. On the Papist side Charles, a Sorbonne doctor, and Chappuis, a Dominican, opposed him. The debate was drawn out over many weeks, and at last came the happy outcome of this long struggle. Not elsewhere, but here, those opponents, in a rare example of candour, were willing to give their hands to the truth, to declare openly that they had been beaten by it, and to proclaim the same truth. Then the reformation was carried through the city with the applause and prayers of all.

units.la: — (no further printed text) manii omnium[?] applausu votisque reformatio facta est, cujus ad istum annum monumentum litteris bicubitalibus aere incisum ad valvas curiae perpetuum extare Genevenses curarunt. Legi de hisce potest elegantissima Spanhemii oratio, Genevae editum, atque Benedicti Turretini, Theol. Genevensis epistola, ad Scultetum scripta, quam is suis Annalibus inseruit, Decad. I. pag. 431. ad a. cIↄ Iↄ xxx iv. Eundemque vide, ad annum sequentem, pag. 468.
units.tr: ...with the applause and prayers of all, the reformation was made, and the Genevans had a lasting memorial of it cut in bronze letters two cubits high, placed at the doors of the council chamber, which still stands to this year. One may read about these matters the most elegant oration of Spanheim, Geneva edited, and the letter of Benedict Turrettini, theologian of Geneva, written to Scultetus, which he included in his Annales, Decad. I, p. 431, at the year 1534. See the same author for the following year, p. 468.

units.la: Colloquium V Vormatiense a. cIↄ Iↄxl i. d. xiii Ianuar. habitum inter Philippum Melanchthonem, &c: Ioh. Eccium: ac per quatuor dies disputatum fuit, de peccato originali; quod post abrumpere, & ad Comitia Ratisbonensia rem rejicere, per Imperatoris literas jussi fuerunt. Vide Acta disputationis. Tom. iv. Operum Melanthonis. Colloquium istud nomine Caesaris moderabatur Nicolaus Perrenotus de Granvilla, vir Belgio nostro satis potus, qui concordiam inter dissidentes moliri videbatur, sed minus Nostros inter se committere; prout homo erat ingenio valde astuto, undé de eo Melanthon ad Camerarium scripsit: non videtur hanc legationem suscepturus fuisse, nisi spem haberet, vel de dividendis nostris, vel de controversiis dirimendis. Extat Perrenoti Granvillani Oratio, quam ad pacem & concordiam, si ita placet, conciliandam, in Vormatiensi Colloquio habuit, seorsim impressa, cum Eloquiis Christophori Pannonii, Vique aliquando Genesim ipsam universam Christo Opt. Max. unicam, genuinamque ejus et verae germanum et antiquam[?] restauratam viderunt, & sanctam denique desideraque pacem Christianorum ubi vel dignam, omnibus inimicitiis edita et dissensionibus, quae inter Christianos aptius appellari non possunt, quam intestinae discordiae, in sempiternum delere: cum ante[?] tristia. Sic etiam pessimi & factiosissimi homines loqui possunt & perorare. Melanthon vero, concordiae caeteroquin studiosissimus, & quem Granvillapus dicebat, se scire modestum esse, cum vult, has artes valde detestabatur, & furtive vulgo appellabat moderationes, atque ad Camerarium: non possumus in Conciliationibus illis insidiis sanis vivere. Et sic adeo ex his loquutiis conciliationum non possumus nisi sic contineri, ut non alibi adhaerescant. Eo magis illa displicebant, quod non disputari de Controversiis Granvillanus volebat, sed tantummodo moderari quaestiones, & posse rem subito componi (ajebat) a simulationibus, sicut Judaei stantes agnum sumebant, nam hoc simili utebatur. Ideoque non disceptandum adeo, vel faciendos articulos, sed clam inter Eccium & sui similes fabrefactos proponi, eosque solummodo accipi a Nostris debere, putabat. Super quo agendi modo, uti alias, ita ante habitam disputationem, cum ejus nonnihil subordinatus fuisset, ad Praesides Colloquii dixit Melanthon: Necessarios conciliationes tranquillitatem restituent. Et si de rebus ipsis integre disputari velent, mobi-liem potius agunt, quam cum aliis. Sperumus enim declarationem nostrarum piis mentibus satisfacturam esse. Existimamus autem Invictissimi Imperatoris Caroli Augusti eam esse virtutem, ut veritatem patefieri, et vere modis consulis salutis Ecclesiarum velis. Ideo oramus ut hanc nostram petitionem boni consulatis, utque profecto non ab impudentia, sed a pio quodam studio judicetis. Eckius dicebatur interim in articulo de peccato originis, & justificatione pari cum Nostris sentire.
units.tr: The Colloquy of Worms, held on 13 January 1540, between Philip Melanchthon and John Eck, lasted four days and was disputed on original sin. Afterwards, by the Emperor's letters, they were ordered to break it off and refer the matter to the Diet of Regensburg. See the Acts of the disputation, Tom. iv of the Works of Melanchthon. This colloquy was presided over on behalf of Caesar by Nicholas Perrenot de Granvelle, a man well known in our Belgium, who seemed to be working for concord between the disagreeing parties, but was less inclined to set our men against one another. He was a man of very subtle mind, so Melanchthon wrote to Camerarius of him: he would not have undertaken this embassy unless he had hoped either to divide our side or to settle the disputed points. Granvelle's oration survives, which he delivered at the Colloquy of Worms to achieve peace and concord, if one likes to call it that, printed separately together with the writings of Christoph Pannonius, and at some time they saw the whole of Genesis restored to Christ, the best and greatest, as its sole and genuine true and ancient meaning, and finally wished to wipe out in everlasting oblivion the holy and longed-for peace of Christians, wherever it might be found, together with all the enmities and dissensions that could be more fittingly called civil discord among Christians. Thus even the worst and most factious men can speak and plead. Melanchthon, who was otherwise most eager for concord, and whom Granvelle said he knew to be moderate when he wished, detested these arts greatly and called them, among the common people, secret moderations. He wrote to Camerarius: we cannot live in those conciliatory snares. And so, from these conciliatory phrases, we cannot be held except by not clinging to anything else. The more so, since Granvelle did not want the controversies debated, but only the questions moderated, and said the matter could be settled suddenly by pretences, just as the Jews took the lamb standing; for he used this simile. He therefore thought the articles should not be disputed or drawn up, but proposed secretly, contrived between Eck and men like him, and that only our side should accept them. On this method of acting, as on others, Melanchthon said to the presidents of the colloquy, after he had been somewhat put aside, before the disputation was held: necessary reconciliations will restore tranquillity. If they wish to dispute the matters themselves fully, they are really working to move things rather than with others. For we hope that our declaration will satisfy pious minds. We think, moreover, that it is the virtue of the most invincible Emperor Charles Augustus to let the truth be made clear and to consult the salvation of the Churches by truly appropriate means. So we ask you to take our petition in good part, and to judge that it comes not from impudence but from a certain pious zeal. Meanwhile Eck was said to agree with our side on the article concerning original sin and justification.

units.la: Ad Colloquium ergo Ratisbonense re dilata, quod eodem anno habitum primum, mense Martio & Majo, delectis ab Imperatore Carolo, Pontificiae partis Julio Pflug, Eccio, Gropero; partis Protestantium, Melanthone, Bucero, Nidano gubernatores. Colloquii constituti erant Fridericus Dux Palatinus, & Granvillanus, additis ex Consiliariis Principum variis auditoribus, una cum Comite de Mandersch[?]. Petebant nostri perterri disputationem Vormatiae inchoatam, sed nolebat Caesar, qui tantum viam concordiae & conciliationis tentari jubebat, oblato eum in finem libro, quo articuli religionis omnes continebantur discutiendi, & vel probandi, vel improbandi: nam liberum relinquebat, ut quae non probarentur, exponere liceret, & notare censura. Ibi articulorum nonnulli admissi, de hominis lapsu, libero arbitrio, causa peccati, peccato originis: locus de justificatione ita conceptus fuit, ut neutri parti satisfaceret, quare seposito libro, de re ipsa disputatum, convenitque hanc in formulam: fide propter Christum gratis justificamur, non propter virtutes nostras. Super reliquis rejecta disputatio in aliud tempus.
units.tr: The colloquy at Regensburg was therefore postponed. It was held that same year, in March and May, and was attended by the Papist side's chosen representatives, Julius Pflug, Eck and Gropper, and by the Protestant side's Melanchthon, Bucer and Nidanus, appointed by the Emperor Charles. Friedrich, Count Palatine, and Granvella were present as moderators, along with various counsellors of the princes as listeners and, with them, Count Manderscheid [?]. Our side, alarmed, asked for the disputation begun at Worms to be resumed, but the Emperor, who ordered only that a way toward concord and reconciliation be tried, would not agree. For this purpose he offered a book containing all the articles of religion, to be examined and either approved or rejected. He left it open to them to set out whatever was not approved and to mark it with their criticism. Some articles were accepted there: on the fall of man, free will, the cause of sin, and original sin. The article on justification was framed so that it satisfied neither party. The book was therefore set aside, and the matter itself was debated, and they agreed on this formula: we are justified by faith in Christ, freely, not on account of our own virtues. The disagreement over the remaining articles was put off to another time.

units.la: Hinc tum de libro Caesareo Ratisbonensi, quem legere potes in Actis Colloquii, à Bucero editis, & Tom. IV. Oper. Melanthonis; tum de articulis concordatis varia Principum & Legatorum sequuta, in Actis judicia, inter ipsos quoque Pontificios, quorum alii aliis moderatiis de tota re, & Caesaris propositio judicabant. Nulli rigidius librum repudiarunt, quam Bavari, quibus Episcoporum plerique assentiebantur, huc illos sedulo incitante Eccio, qui etiam Collegas suos Julium & Gropperum eo nomine insimulabat, quod faciliores in concedenda emendatione quondam in Ecclesia abusuum fuissent, sed quos Carolus eo diligentius tuebatur, laudabatque adhibitae majoris moderationis atque prudentiae. Eandem Imperator Cardinalem Tor-tarenum adhibet, quum aliter non videret quo honestiori modo finem Colloquio imponere, multamque à se invidiam depellere posset, qui uno alteroque scripto urgebat totum istud reconciliationis negotium remittendum esse ad judicium Pontificis Romani. Ubi tum nostri aliqui, satis manifestè videbant delusos se hactenus vana spe reconciliationis, longeque aliud quaesitum fuisse quam pacem & concordiam, nihil verò interim de Imperatoris animo, melioris fortè & aperti-ori, quam esset Ecclesiasticorum plerorumque, quos ne-gogotium propius tamen concernebat, judicantes. Ut bene Melanthon hoc de Conventu scripserit: eventus satis ostendit, eos que speraverunt initio adversarios nostros aliquam moderationem, aut emendationem suarum opinionum admissuros, non satis perspexisse eorum voluntates. Tentandos put animos nostros, ut seu inclinatio quaedam seu dissensio fieret, postea suum odium declararent. Atque ab aliquo bene id ibidem observatum refert: Audio, et N. cum viderent frustra tentatas esse has conciliationes, dixisse, Deum fortasse hos conatus impedivisse, qui arcano et mirabili consilio regit Ecclesiam: quod his moderationibus receptis, mala quaedam confirmata fuissent: et eorum stabilita potentia, qui errores praecipue defendunt. Adeoque non mirum, multos fuisse, uti scribit, qui ab hoc toto consilio Conciliationum valde abhorrerent, propter harum periculum: Multa enim sunt, et vetera et recentia exempla, quae admonent, in talibus conciliationibus plerumque decurri ad ambiguos, flexiloquos, fucosos, et fallares articulos, quibus veritas obtuitur, et non sanantur Ecclesiae, sed dissipantur. Quare hinc doceri oportet eos, qui etiamnum Conciliationes somniant, postquam res Pontificiae Ecclesiae in deteriora, et obstinatiora abierunt, quam tum adhuc essent. Qui si haec aliaque exempla sibi proponerent, non tantopere consilia ista, primo quidem valde speciosa, sed perlustrata et applicata praxi, inania, approbarent; ex magna judicii, et historiarum istius rei imperitia. Imperator autem abrupto Ratisbonensi Colloquio, neque obsecundans sanguinolentis aliorum adversum Nostros consiliis, cupiens Ecclesiasticas controversias, non armis, sed aliquando justa Synodo dirimi, pacem certis conditionibus utrique parti mandavit, spem etiam ostendens deliberationum, de emendatione Ecclesiae, habendarum. Neque forte omnino vanum, quod initio Colloquii a multis de Imperatore jactatum, moliri eum novam Ecclesiae reformationem, et doctrinam de justitia fidei propagaturum ad plures alios. Caeterum in isto Ratisbonensi Colloquio, in articulo de justificatione conciliatio ita facta fuit, in hanc formam: Et sic fide in Christum justificamur, seu justi reputamur, id est, accepti per ipsius merita, non propter nostram dignitatem, aut opera, aut propter inhaerentem justitiam, eo justi dicimur, quia quae justa sunt operamur, juxta illud Johannis: Qui facit justitiam, justus est. Et quanquam in renatis semper crescere debent timor Dei, patientia, et humilitas, et aliae virtutes, cum renovatio sit imperfecta, et haereat in eis ingens infirmitas: tamen docendum est, ut qui vere poenitent, semper fide certissima statuant, se propter mediatorem Christum Deo placere. Ut non de justificatione solum, sed et de certitudine salutis, hominisque imperfectione, concordatum jam videretur, et articuli distinguerentur in conciliatos, et non conciliatos. Conciliati placebant valde Imperatori et Principibus: et consentiebant ipsi partis adversae Collocutores, non solum Julius Pflug, et Gropperus, sed et hi in Apologeticis ad Praefationem Colloquii, de Eckio testati fuerunt: Gratia denique Deo, quod et ipsius Eccii manus apud nos est, quae testatum reddere possumus toti orbi, ipsum non in quovis, sed in articulo omnium maximo, qui justificationis est, eam sententiam quam liber Caesari oblatus complectitur, libenter approbasse. Et Melanthon, in epistola, quae est Tom. III epistolarum, Ratisbonae hoc a. MDXLI Kal. Maji scripsit ad Episcopum Vratislaviensem, aliquid spei ostendit duorum praestantium virorum Julii et Gropperi moderatio. Ideo jam de certis articulis formula, ut spero, mediocres propositae sunt.
units.tr: From this came the imperial book of Regensburg, which you may read in the Acts of the Colloquy, published by Bucer, and in Volume IV of Melanchthon's works. From this too came the various judgments of the princes and envoys on the agreed articles, recorded in the Acts, and also those of the Papists themselves, some of whom judged the whole matter and the emperor's proposal more moderately than others. No one rejected the book more harshly than the Bavarians, whom most of the bishops supported, Eck urging them on eagerly. Eck even accused his colleagues Julius and Gropper on this score, because they had once been too ready to concede the correction of abuses in the Church. Charles, however, defended them all the more carefully and praised their greater moderation and prudence. The Emperor likewise employed Cardinal Tortarena, since he saw no other more honourable way to end the colloquy and to turn aside the great odium he had incurred. Tortarena pressed, in one or two writings, that the whole business of reconciliation be referred to the judgment of the Roman Pontiff. Then some of our men saw quite plainly that they had hitherto been deceived by a vain hope of reconciliation, and that something quite different had been sought than peace and concord. Yet they did not judge the Emperor's own mind, which was perhaps better and more open than that of most churchmen, although the matter concerned them more closely. Melanchthon wrote well about this conference: the outcome has shown well enough that those who at the start hoped our opponents would admit some moderation, or some correction of their opinions, had not sufficiently seen their intentions. Our minds ought to be tested, so that if some inclination or dissent arose, they would afterwards declare their hatred. And he reports that someone observed this well at the same place: I hear that N., when they saw these attempts at reconciliation had been made in vain, said that God perhaps hindered these efforts, he who rules the Church by a hidden and wonderful counsel; for if these moderations had been accepted, certain evils would have been confirmed, and the power of those who especially defend errors would have been established. So it is no wonder, as he writes, that many were strongly averse to this whole plan of conciliations because of their danger: For there are many examples, both old and recent, which warn that in such conciliations one commonly runs to ambiguous, equivocating, deceptive and fallacious articles, by which the truth is obscured, and the Churches are not healed but scattered. Hence those who still dream of conciliations must be taught, now that the affairs of the Papist Church have gone into worse and more obstinate states than they were in then. If they set these and other examples before themselves, they would not so greatly approve these plans, which at first sight are very attractive, but, once examined and applied in practice, are empty. The fault lies in their great lack of judgment and of knowledge of the history of this matter. The Emperor, however, broke off the Colloquy of Regensburg. He did not comply with the bloodthirsty plans of others against our people. Wishing the ecclesiastical controversies to be settled not by arms but at some time by a lawful synod, he imposed peace on both parties under fixed conditions, and also held out hope of deliberations to be held on the correction of the Church. Nor was it perhaps altogether empty what many boasted at the beginning of the Colloquy about the Emperor: that he was preparing a new reformation of the Church, and that he would spread the doctrine of the righteousness of faith to many others. Moreover, at this Colloquy of Regensburg, a reconciliation on the article of justification was made in this form: And so we are justified, or reckoned righteous, by faith in Christ, that is, accepted through his merits, not on account of our worthiness, or works, or inherent righteousness. We are called righteous for this reason, that we do what is righteous, according to that saying of John: He who does righteousness is righteous. And although in the regenerate the fear of God, patience, humility and the other virtues must always grow, since renewal is imperfect and great weakness clings to them, nevertheless it must be taught that those who truly repent should always hold, with the most certain faith, that they please God for the sake of Christ the Mediator. Thus it seemed that agreement had now been reached not only on justification but also on the certainty of salvation and on human imperfection, and the articles were divided into reconciled and unreconciled. The reconciled ones pleased the Emperor and the princes greatly, and the opposing participants agreed: not only Julius Pflug and Gropper, but also those men, in their Apologetic writings prefixed to the Preface of the Colloquy, testified about Eck: Thanks be to God, since Eck's own hand is with us, which we can attest to the whole world, that he gladly approved, not in any matter but in the article of greatest importance, which is justification, the opinion which the book offered to the Emperor contains. And Melanchthon, in a letter in Volume III of his letters, written at Regensburg on the first of May 1541 to the Bishop of Breslau, wrote: the moderation of two outstanding men, Julius and Gropper, shows some hope. So now, I hope, moderate formulas have been proposed on certain articles.

units.la: Ubi jam eo utrimque conventum esset, institutum alterum Ratisbonense Colloquium anno MDXLVI, ut post illud dogma conciliatum, pergeretur ad alia, et viderent, num in reliquis etiam via aliqua concordiae iniri posset, cui ad Concilii saltem, sin minus, Comitiorum sequentium tempus utraque pars insisteret, nimirum, ad Ecclesiae, uti dicebant, emendationem et reformationem. mationem, ex eodem Imperatoris, in prorogatione VVormatiensi, superioris anni, decreto. Quia de conciliatione Religionis non potuit hoc tempore tractari, sed dum constitui, & quo hanc necessariam conciliationem adhuc tamen ordine; & quam primum id possibile sit, promovendam obtineamus, & reipsa constituamus, visum esse nobis fore, ad promovendam hanc conciliationem, utile & bonum, versus instituere, & Comitiis indicto praemittere Christianorum colloquium, & collationem aliquot hominum proborum, timentium Deum, aequorum, & commodorum, benefici & patris amantium, & quidem parvo numero. Hic jam quartus erat ab Imp. Carolo conciliationi articulorum religionis destinatus conventus: super qua in variis etiam actum Imperii Comitiis, Ratisbonensi anno XLI. Spirensi, anno XLIV. VVormatiensi, anno XLV. & Augustano, anno XLVIII. A Protestantium parte Collocutores erant Bucerus, Snepfius, Brentius, & Melanthonis loco Georgius Major: pro Pontificiis, Malvenda, Cochlaeus, Billikius, Hofmeisterus: injunctumque ab Imperatore, ut Confessionis Augustanae articuli ordine, missis tribus primis extra controversiam, examinarentur. Sed neque hoc servatum, & conciliatio itā nihil promota ulterius, ut de primā illa articuli de justificatione hic quidem vehementius disceptatum fuerit, quam antea; quaesitumque, an in priori Colloquio conciliatus ille fuisset, an non? & postquam, primum de modo & ordine Colloquii, an per Notarios (quod Nostri urgebant) excipiendi; tum de justificatione iterum, de merito operum, & certitudine fidei aliquantum disputassent, Imperatorio rescripto, & revocatis per suos Principes Collocutorum nonnullis, haec etiam disputatio in fumum abiit. Referit in vitā Buceri Melchior Adamus, ab aliquo tum temporis de Bucero, ejusque cum Hispano Malvendā congressu dictum suisse, ad nomen illius alludendo: er heißt wol Bucer, ich mein er hat ihn aufgebutzt. Praeterea sciendum, ad istud Colloquium, cum Bucero, permissu Senatus Argentinensis, profectum quoque fuisse Iohannem Diazium, qui quia ad Protestantium partes accesserat, à fratre suo Alphonso, altero Caino, postea Neoburgi, in superiori Palatinatu, misere trucidatus fuit.
units.tr: Once agreement had been reached on this point by both sides, a second Colloquy of Regensburg was arranged for the year 1546, so that, after that agreed doctrine, they might proceed to other matters and see whether some way of concord could be entered upon also in the remaining articles. Both parties were to keep to this, at least until the time of a council or, if none were held, of the next Diet, namely for the correction and reformation of the Church, as they called it. This was in accordance with the Emperor's own decree of the previous year, issued at the Diet of Worms: Since the reconciliation of religion could not be dealt with at this time, but while we arrange and effect by deed how this necessary reconciliation may be promoted in good order, and as soon as it is possible, we have thought it useful and good, for promoting this reconciliation, to set up and to send ahead of the Diet a colloquy of Christians, and a conference of some upright men, who fear God, are fair, and are friendly, lovers of peace and of the fatherland, and indeed a small number. This was now the fourth conference which the Emperor Charles had appointed for the reconciliation of the articles of religion. Concerning it, the matter was also discussed at various Diets of the Empire: at Regensburg in 1541, at Speyer in 1544, at Worms in 1545 and at Augsburg in 1548. On the Protestant side the speakers were Bucer, Snepf, Brenz, and, in place of Melanchthon, Georg Major. For the Papists they were Malvenda, Cochlaeus, Billick and Hofmeister. The Emperor ordered that the articles of the Augsburg Confession be examined in order, with the first three set aside as beyond controversy. But this was not kept, and the reconciliation was promoted no further. The first article, on justification, was disputed here more vehemently than before, and the question was asked whether that reconciliation had been achieved at the earlier Colloquy or not. Then, after they had first argued about the manner and order of the Colloquy, namely whether it should be recorded by notaries (as our side urged), and afterwards again disputed a little about justification, the merit of works and the certainty of faith, the imperial rescript and the recall of some of the speakers by their princes brought this discussion too to nothing. Melchior Adam, in his Life of Bucer, reports that at that time someone said of Bucer, and of his encounter with the Spaniard Malvenda, alluding to his name: it is well called Bucer; I think he has cudgelled him. It should also be noted that to this Colloquy with Bucer, with the permission of the Senate of Strasbourg, Johannes Diazius also went. Because he had joined the Protestant side, his brother Alphonsus, another Cain, later had him wretchedly murdered at Neuburg in the Upper Palatinate.

units.la: Sequuta anno clɔ Iɔ xlix. iv. Nonas Maji, disputatio Oxonii, in Angliâ, inter Martyrem, aliosque Pontificios, inter quos cum imprimis adesse debuisset Smythaeus, cujus puer paulo antè Martyrem ad habendam in Academiâ lectionem pergentem schedulâ ad disputationem eâ ipsâ horâ habendam provocârat, quod tempus Martyr non disputationis dicebat sibi esse, sed lectionis, illam in aliud commodius rejiciens tempus, à lectione verò cum Vice-Cancellarius Academiae porrectâ manu apprehensum de cathedrâ vix salvum domum reduxisset, jam tempore, legibusque habendae disputationis scriptis, cum etiam Legati Regii adessent, Smytheus turpiter aufugit, in Scotiam primum, inde in Brabantiam: disputatione nihilominus per quatuor dies productâ inter Martyrem, & tres alios Theologos Pontificios, cujus Acta, testimonio Legatorum Regiorum comprobata, extant.
units.tr: In the following year, 1549, on the fourth day before the Nones of May, a disputation was held at Oxford in England between Martyr and other Papists. Smythaeus should especially have been present there. A little earlier, his boy had handed Martyr, who was on his way to give a lecture in the Academy, a note challenging him to a disputation to be held at that very hour. Martyr replied that this hour was for lecturing, not for disputing, and he put the disputation off to a more convenient time. But when Martyr came down from the lectern, the Vice-Chancellor of the Academy seized him by the outstretched hand and barely led him safely home. Then, when the time had come and the rules for the disputation had been put in writing, and the royal legates were also present, Smythaeus shamefully fled, first to Scotland and then to Brabant. Nevertheless, the disputation went on for four days between Martyr and three other Papist theologians. Its acts, confirmed by the testimony of the royal legates, still survive.

units.la: Sequenti anno clɔ Iɔ I. alia disputatio habita fuit in altera Angliae Academiâ Cantabrigiensi, vi. Idus Augusti, inter Mart. Bucerum, & à parte Pontificiâ, Ioh. Iungum, Sedguicum, & Pernum; de Scripturae libris Canonicis, de fallibilitate Ecclesiae, & operibus non renatorum ante justificationem: quae extat, inter Buceri scripta Anglica, sol. 711.
units.tr: In the following year, 1550, on the sixth day before the Ides of August, another disputation was held at the other English university, at Cambridge, between Martyr Bucer and, on the Papist side, John Young, Sedgwick and Pern. It concerned the canonical books of Scripture, the fallibility of the Church, and the works of the unregenerate before justification. It is found among Bucer's English writings, p. 711.

units.la: Disputationem dicam, an conspirationem sustinuit Oxonii a. clɔ Iɔ liv. d. xvi.
