Aprilis, ex carcere Thomas Cranmerus, additis ei Latimero, & Ridlaeo Episcopis, sed nullum alium in finem, quam ut in arctiora vincula conjectus, tandem etiam, quod biennio post factum, comburendus traderetur rogo.
units.tr: Whether it was a disputation or a conspiracy, I shall leave aside. At Oxford, on 16 April 1555, Thomas Cranmer was brought out of prison, together with the bishops Latimer and Ridley. But this was done for no other purpose than to cast them into tighter bonds, and so that, two years later, he might finally be handed over to be burned at the stake.

units.la: Cui simili fuit alia anno clɔ Iɔ lvi. disputatio, inter ter Convallenses, & Amatum Sanjulianum Præsidem, in speciem magis quam serio: uti loquitur Thuanus, lib. XXVII.
units.tr: A similar affair was another disputation in 1556, between the three Convallenses and Amatus Sanjulianus, the president. It was more for show than in earnest, as Thuanus says in book 27.

units.la: Quod toties tentatum in Germania, ut aliqua religionum maxime dissidentium conciliatio institueretur, iterum aggredi placuit ex decreto Comitiorum Ratisbonensium proxime habitorum, VVormatiæ anno cIↄ Iↄ lv i i. die v. Septemb. præside Iulio Pflug, episcopo Naoburgensi, cuius æquitatem etiam Nostri prædicabant, inter Protestantium Theologos, Melanthonem, Brentium, Iacobum Andream, Pistorium, Eberum, aliosque; & partis Pontificiæ Michaëlem Episcopum Merseburgensem, Canisium, Staphylum, cæteros. Disputatum initio fuit, de norma & judice controversiarum, an Dei verbum esset, an Ecclesiæ consensus: sed postea Pontificii dissensionem inter nostros aucupantes, urgebant condemnationem Zuinglianorum, aliorumque, in quam alii propensiores, dum eam scribi & recitari publicè volebant, & Ienenses Theologi illam Pontificiis publicè exhibebant, scissis inter se Protestantibus, abruptum Colloquium fuit: quod quamvis produci juberet Ferdinandus, Pontificii tamen missum fecerunt, abierunt que.
units.tr: Since this had been attempted many times in Germany, it was decided, by the decree of the Diet lately held at Ratisbon, to take up again the effort to bring about some reconciliation between the most widely divided religious parties. It met at Worms on 5 September 1557, under the presidency of Julius Pflug, bishop of Naumburg, whose fairness our own people also praised. Among the Protestant theologians were Melanchthon, Brenz, Jacob Andreae, Pistorius, Eber and others; on the side of the Papists were Michael, bishop of Merseburg, Canisius, Stapleton and the rest. At first the debate concerned the rule and judge of controversies, whether it was the Word of God or the consensus of the Church. Later, however, the Papists, seizing on the disagreement among our people, pressed for the condemnation of the Zwinglians and others. Some were more inclined to this, and wished it to be written down and read out publicly, and the theologians of Jena publicly handed it over to the Papists. With the Protestants divided among themselves, the colloquy was broken off. Although Ferdinand ordered that it be continued, the Papists dismissed it and left.

units.la: Anno cIↄ Iↄ lix. d. ult. Martii, in Anglia, VVestmonasterii, jussu Reginæ Elizabethæ Disputatio instituta; inter nostræ partis Coxum, Gryndallum, Edwinum Sandes, Iuellum &c. & Pontificias, VVhitum, Baiøum, VVatsonum, Colum, Harpesfeldum, aliosque; ubi de Sacris lingua populari celebrandis, de auctoritate Ecclesiæ, & Missa, paucis sermone vernaculo disceptatum: inde contentione, de modo disputandi, obortâ, revera quia inconsulto Romano Papâ, non auderent, juxta axiomata Ecclesiæ suæ, palam de fide & vulgari linguâ agere, soluta disputatio: secutaque publica Ecclesiæ per Angliam, & Hiberniam, Reformatio, repetitis, quæ Eduardi VI. tempore, circa religionis negotium editae fuerant, pro Papatu eliminando, constitutionibus. Cambdenus, Annal. Elizabetha lib. 1. Prolegomena de vita Iuelli, praemissa ejus Operibus, in sol. p. 48. Richard. Baker, Chron. Angliae, in vita Elizab. Emm. Meteranus, Histor. Belg. lib. 1. Et ex eo Mercurius Gallo-Belgicus, Tom. 1. lib. 1.
units.tr: On the last day of March 1559, in England, at Westminster, a disputation was arranged by order of Queen Elizabeth. On our side were Cox, Grindal, Edwin Sandys, Jewel etc.; on the Papist side were Whitt, Bayne, Watson, Cole, Harpsfield and others. There was a brief discussion in the vernacular about celebrating the sacred rites in the common tongue, about the authority of the Church, and about the Mass. Then a quarrel arose over the manner of disputing, and the debate was dissolved. In truth, since they had not consulted the Roman Pope, they did not dare, according to the axioms of their Church, to treat openly of faith and the vernacular tongue. A public reformation of the Church followed throughout England and Ireland, with the decrees repeated that had been issued in the time of Edward VI concerning religious affairs, to remove the Papacy. Camden, Annals of Elizabeth, book 1; Prolegomena on the life of Jewel, prefixed to his Works, in folio, p. 48. Richard Baker, Chronicle of England, in the life of Elizabeth. Emmanuel Meteranus, History of the Low Countries, book 1. And from him Mercure Gallo-Belge, vol. 1, book 1.

units.la: Post nonnullas illas, in Germania primum, inde Helvetiis, tum in Suecia, & Genevae, in Anglia etiam habitas super religione publicas, inter Nostros & Pontificios, disputationes, in Gallia celebre colloquium institutum fuit, Poissiaci, quod oppidum Sangermano proximum, in aula Monasterii, anno cIↄ Iↄ lxı. d. iv. Septembris. Indictum à Rege Carolo ix. ut disputationibus de religione quotidie increbescentibus, plurimisque Procerum ad Reformatorum partes inclinantibus, videretur tandem, quid agendum esset, & partis utriusque ante omnia constarent sententiae & doctrinae. Quare ad hoc Colloquium, cui ipse Rex interfuit, cum Regina Matre, Fratre Duce Aurelianensi, Margaretha sorore, cum Rege, Reginaque Navarrae, Principe Condaeo, reliquisque Regni Optimatibus, & Consiliariis, magno numero; ex Pontificiis aderant Borbonius, Turnonius, Castellionaeus, Lotharingus, Armeniacus, & Guisius, Cardinales, cum Archiepiscopis, episcopis, circiter quinquaginta, addito magno Sorbonistarum, & Canonicarum numero: ex Nostris eo vocati venerant Beza, Martyr, Marloratus, Viretus, Gallasius, Merlinus, Morellus, Boquinus, Espineus, alii, duodecim numero ministri, additis viginti aliis ab Ecclesiis communiter missis, qui in Sangermano divertebant, & hinc per Regis satellites Poissiacum deducebantur: ubi Rex causam indicti conventus exponens, scire eos dixit, quâ de causâ huc convocati fuerint, nimirum ut turbis, quae passim in suo regno excitantur, salutare remedium ex eorum sententia quaeratur: proinde videant, ut omni offensionis causa praecisa, quae emendatione egeant, corrigantur, & publicæ tranquillitati, quam optime fieri poterit, legitimâ ratione consulatur, curere se, ut non prius discedant, quam omnem operam dederint, ut tandem aliquando compositis dissidiis mutuâ inter majestatis suæ subditos populos concordia ac sincera amicitia sarciatur, quod si fecerint, uti confidat, non commissurum, ut patrocinium, quo à majoribus suis olim protecti sunt, à se suisve magistratibus in posterum possint requirere. Inde Regis Cancellarius, Hospitalius, egregiâ oratione tum Regis animum, tum, sermone ad Antistites converso, horum in rebus istis officium explicuit: verbum Dei sufficere, ad quod tanquam regulam doctrina appendenda & examinanda sit, nec vero erga Protestantes alieno adeo animo nos esse debere; quippe qui fratres sint, & eodem lavacro regenerati eundem Christum nobiscum colant; nec eos praejudicio inauditos condemnandos; sed amplectendos, accipiendos & amice in viam reducendos, sine acerbitate & animi contumacia, nimiâ severitate in eo graviter erraverit. Thuanus, Histor. lib. xxviii. Post quæ, orta quædam adversus Hospitalium, Cardinalis Turnonii, & Lotharingii vitiligatione, Beza dicere jussus, quod neglectum à Cardinalibus fuerat, à precibus exordiitur: inde de singulis religionis capitulis, vernaculo & eleganti sermone differens, cujus quia summâ in Gallicarum Ecclesiarum Confessione, compositâ jam antè, anno cIↄ Iↄ Iv. continebatur, hanc Regi supplex obtulit. Integra illa Bezæ actio & oratio, prout habita, extat in Histoire Ecclesiastique des Eglises Reformees en France, Tom. I. liv. IV. Gallicè; & Latinè, in Commentario Status Religionis, & Reip. sub Carolo IX. part. 1. lib. III. auctoribus (ni fallor) Bezâ, & Gallasio. Nihil autem in totâ illâ Oratione adeo offenderat aures auditorum, & Antistitum, quam quod Beza dixerat in explicandâ transsubstantiationis controversiâ: quod ad locorum distantiam spectat, corpus Christi tantum abest à pane & vino, quanto altius cœlum abest à terrâ. Quamvis id de praesentia corporis, & de ipsius humanitate distincte considerata (ut Thuanus bene) dixerit, prout haec ejus verba fuerant: Si quis interea a nobis quaerat: An Christum a Caena absentem faciamus? respondemus, id minime nos facere. Sin vero spatia locorum (ut necesse est quum de praesentia ipsius corporali agitur, & de ipsius humanitate distincte considerata) respexerimus, Affirmamus ipsius corpus tantum a pane & vino abesse, quantum altius coelum a terra abest, nimirum quandoquidem nos in terra sumus, & Sacramenta item: ipse vero in coelo ita est glorificatus, ut gloria (sic inquit Augustinus) non illi corporis veritatem, sed infirmitatem ademerit. Si quis inde colligat, Nos Christum a Caena absentem facere: male collegerit; hunc enim honorem Deo tribuimus, quod licet corpus Iesu Christi nunc sit in coelo, non alibi: nos vero in terra, & non alibi: nihilominus tamen participes simus corporis & sanguinis ipsius, modo quodam spirituali, & fidei instrumento: aeque vere ac videmus oculis Sacramenta, manibus tangimus, ori nostro admovemus, & in hac vita corporali illorum substantia alimur atque sustentamur. Quibus tamen quia valde offensos videret antistites, qui strepitum parabant, & nisi Regis praesentia fuisset, turbas lubenter concitassent, postridie ad Reginam dictorum suorum explicationem scripsit. Hinc sumta occasione, Cardinalis Turnonius Regem obsecrabat, ne Colloquio ipse interesset, & Ministrorum (sic Nostros appellabant) audiret dissertationes, iisque moveretur. Et postquam diu deliberassent cum Sorbonicis Antistites, quid adversus illam Bezae orationem faciendum ipsis esset, Card. Lotharingus, propter Bezam ingemiscens: utinam aut ille mutus, aut nos surdi fuissemus! inquit. Deinde Colloquium instauratur d. xvi. Septembris, ubi praesentes etiam in hac secunda sessione, eodem loco, erant Rex Navarraeus, aliique Principes. Hic Lotharingus, diu ante meditata oratione egit, quae sibi ne periret, congressum illum adeo contra Turnonii, ac pluQuam Theologorum sententiam exoptaverat (verba sunt Aug. Thuani): in cujus praefatione Regem haud leviter perstrinxit, illum membrum, non caput Ecclesiae dicens, cumque Ecclesiae, & ejus ministris, praecipue Pontifici Rom. subjacere: ac dein pergens explicare duos articulos, de Ecclesia unum, alterum de sacramentis, quos excerpendos, & a Ministrorum vel Bezae oratione vindicandos, ab exitu prioris sessionis Pontificii statuerant, sic concludit, ad Bezae priora illa verba respiciens: tam a vestra opinione absumus, quam altius coelum ab imâ terrâ parte abest. Unde jam Regem, aliosque omnes monere ipse, & Card. Turnonius, ut non aliam, quam istam fidem reciperent, reliquos expellerent, & nisi suae sententiae ac doctrinae ocyus vellent subscribere Ministri, ultra nec audiendos, nec ferendos esse. Quare ut ad Lotharingi orationem responderet ex tempore liceret, frustra petentibus Ministris, & Colloquii continuationem per libellum supplicem a Rege petentibus, vix impetrarunt, ut privato, non publico in loco, porro haberetur. Itaque die xxiv. Septembris tertio conveniunt, non jam Rege Regisque fratre, sed Reginâ Matre, Rege & Reginâ Navarrae, Antistitibus, & duodecim delectis Ministris, paucisque aliis praesentibus: ubi Beza ad praeteritam orationem Lotharingi, de duobus articulis, Ecclesiâ, & Sacramentis copiose disseruit: adversus quae nonnulla, a Lotharingo ad dicendum invitatus, dixit Claudius Espensaeus, Sorbonicus, vir modestus, qui palam profitebatur, se a crudelibus suppliciis, adversus eos, qui religionem nostram amplectebantur, adhibitis semper abhorruisse. Post quem, frustra se ad defensionem parante Beza, Xainctius, eadem repetens, quae jam Espensaeus dixerat, & nonnulla de traditionibus, firmiori quam Scripturae fundamento niti eas, addidit: quem utrumque dein Beza unâ responsione excepit. Tandem Cardinalis Lotharingus, clamorum Xainctii pertaesus,
units.tr: After several such public disputations on religion, first in Germany, then among the Swiss, and afterwards in Sweden, Geneva and England, between our people and the Papists, a famous colloquy was held in France at Poissy, a town near Saint-Germain, in the hall of the monastery, on 4 September 1561, as printed. King Charles IX called it because the disputes over religion were growing daily, and many of the nobles were leaning towards the Reformed side. He wished to learn at last what should be done, and above all to establish the opinions and doctrines of each party. To this colloquy the King himself came, with the Queen Mother, his brother the Duke of Orléans, his sister Margaret, the King and Queen of Navarre, Prince Condé, and a large number of the other nobles and councillors of the kingdom. From the Papists came the cardinals Bourbon, Tournon, Châtillon, Lorraine, Armagnac and Guise, with the archbishops and about fifty bishops, together with a large number of Sorbonne doctors and canons. From our side Beza, Martyr, Marlorat, Viret, Gallasius, Merlin, Morel, Boquin and Espine, and others, twelve ministers in all, had come at the summons, along with twenty others sent in common by the churches. They were lodged at Saint-Germain and were brought from there to Poissy by the King's guards. There the King explained the reason for the summons: they should know that they had been called together so that a healthy remedy for the disturbances breaking out everywhere in his kingdom might be sought by their judgement. Therefore they should see to it that, every cause of offence being removed, whatever needed correcting was corrected, and that public tranquillity was provided for by lawful means as well as possible. He wished them to understand that they should not depart until they had done all in their power so that, the disagreements being settled at last, concord and sincere friendship might be restored among the peoples subject to his majesty. If they did this, he trusted that he would not allow them to demand in future from himself or his magistrates the protection by which they had once been shielded by his ancestors. Then the King's Chancellor, Hospital, with an excellent speech, set out both the King's mind and, turning his words to the bishops, the duty of the bishops in these matters: the Word of God is sufficient, and by it as a rule doctrine must be weighed and examined; nor ought we to be so hostile towards the Protestants, since they are brothers, regenerated in the same font, and worship the same Christ with us; nor should they be condemned unheard on prejudice, but embraced, received and kindly led back to the right way, without bitterness and obstinacy of mind; he who has erred gravely in this by excessive severity... Thuanus, Histor. lib. xxviii. After these things, a certain dispute arose against Hospital, over the censure of Cardinals Tournon and Lorraine. Beza, bidden to speak, began with prayers, which had been neglected by the cardinals. Then, discussing each article of religion in the vernacular and in an elegant style, he offered to the King, as a suppliant, the summary of it, which was contained in the Confession of the French Churches, composed earlier, in 1559. The whole of Beza's action and speech, as it was delivered, is found in Histoire Ecclesiastique des Eglises Reformees en France, Tom. I. liv. IV. Gallicè; & Latinè, in Commentario Status Religionis, & Reip. sub Carolo IX. part. 1. lib. III. by the authors (if I am not mistaken) Beza and Gallasius. Nothing in the whole of that speech, however, had so offended the ears of the hearers and of the bishops as what Beza had said in explaining the controversy over transubstantiation: as far as the distance of places is concerned, the body of Christ is as far from the bread and wine as heaven is higher than the earth. Yet he had said this of the presence of the body, and of his humanity considered distinctly (as Thuanus rightly puts it), in these words of his: If anyone meanwhile asks us, Do we make Christ absent from the Supper? we answer that we by no means do so. But if we look at the spaces of places (as we must when we are treating of his bodily presence, and of his humanity considered distinctly), we affirm that his body is as far from the bread and wine as heaven is higher than the earth; since we are on the earth, and so are the sacraments; but he himself in heaven is so glorified that his glory (as Augustine says) has taken from his body not its truth but its weakness. If anyone infers from this that we make Christ absent from the Supper, he will have inferred wrongly; for we ascribe this honour to God: although the body of Jesus Christ is now in heaven, and nowhere else, and we are on the earth, and nowhere else, nevertheless we are partakers of his body and blood, in a certain spiritual way, and by the instrument of faith; just as truly as we see the sacraments with our eyes, touch them with our hands, bring them to our mouth, and in this bodily life are nourished and sustained by their substance. But since he saw the bishops, who were preparing an uproar, greatly offended by these words, and who would gladly have stirred up disturbances had the King's presence not prevented it, he wrote to the Queen the next day an explanation of what he had said. Taking the occasion from this, Cardinal Tournon begged the King not to attend the colloquy himself, and not to hear the discourses of the ministers (as they called our men), lest he be moved by them. And after the bishops had long deliberated with the Sorbonne men about what should be done against Beza's speech, Cardinal Lorraine, groaning over Beza, said: would that either he had been mute, or we deaf! Then the colloquy was resumed on 16 September, where, in this second session, King Antony of Navarre and other princes were again present in the same place. Here Lorraine, having long prepared a speech, delivered it, which he had wished should not perish, and had greatly desired that meeting against the opinion of Tournon and of more than the theologians (these are the words of Augustus Thuanus). In its preface he lightly touched the King, calling him a member, not the head, of the Church, and saying that he, and the ministers of the Church, and especially the Roman Pontiff, were subject to it. Then, going on to explain two articles, one about the Church and the other about the sacraments, which the Papists had decided after the end of the first session to pick out and defend against the speech of the ministers or of Beza, he concluded, looking back at Beza's earlier words: we are as far from your opinion as heaven is high above the lowest part of the earth. Thereupon both he and Cardinal Tournon warned the King and all the others not to accept any faith other than this one, to expel the rest, and that the ministers, unless they were willing to subscribe quickly to their opinion and doctrine, should be heard no further and tolerated no longer. Therefore, when the ministers petitioned in vain that they might be allowed to reply to Lorraine's speech extemporaneously, and asked the King by a written supplication for the continuation of the colloquy, they scarcely obtained that it should be held thereafter in a private, not a public, place. And so on 24 September they met for a third time, now with the King not present, nor his brother, but with the Queen Mother, the King and Queen of Navarre, the bishops, twelve chosen ministers, and a few others present. There Beza, in reply to Lorraine's earlier speech, discussed at length the two articles, the Church and the sacraments. Against these things, Claude Espence, a Sorbonne doctor, a modest man who openly professed that he had always abhorred cruel punishments against those who embraced our religion, spoke, invited to do so by Lorraine. After him, Beza, preparing his defence, was prevented from speaking, and Xaintes, repeating what Espence had already said and adding some things about traditions, which he said rested on a firmer foundation than Scripture, was answered by Beza in a single reply to both. At last Cardinal Lorraine, weary of Xaintes' clamour,

units.la: vcveritusque, ne sui idcirco à Regina increparentur, quaestioni illi finem voluit imponi, alteramque de Coena, cujus in prima oratione plena mentio à Bezâ facta fuerat, adoriri: rogans, paratine nostri essent Consessioni subscribere Augustanae, eamque recipere? Beza ex adverso quaerebat, an eandem amplecti illis in animo esset? Ietergiversatus Cardinalis scriptum protulit, sibi ex Germania, ut dicebat, missum, sed à Francisco Balduino suppeditatum, cujus opera hac in re utebatur; & quosdam Augustanae Confessionis Theologos evocârat, quos propediem cum Nostris super controversia de Coena committum iri sperabat. Scripto isti ut assentirentur Ministri vehementer ille quidem urgebat, non alio fine, quam ut vel contentionem nostrorum cum Germanis Theologis provocaret; vel, si subscriberent, de illis quasi victor triumpharet. Scriptum continebat formulam, ex Augustanâ Confessione, uti Cardinalis ajebat, desumtam: Fatemur verum corpus & verum sanguinem Iesu Christi vere, realiter & Sacramentaliter esse in Coenâ Domini, & ita exhiberi, & ita recipi ab iis qui communicant. Nihil hic aliud Cardinalis Lotharingus intendit, quam ut commissos retineret Protestantium Theologos invicem, & Ministris eo facilius insultare et, quo Lutheranos nostris aequo infensiores, sibi vero addictiores habebat, quin & nonnullos, quod turpe profecto, stipendiatos. Id quod fide Hier. Zanchii asserto, qui in Responsi ad V. Vilhelm. Holderum, anno 1566 ita scripsit, pag. 20. Certum mihi est, quod jam dicam coram Deo: Audivi ex viro harum rerum perito, & fide digno, se in libro Thesaurarii illius Cardinalis Lotharingi, paucis ante annis vita defuncti, nonnullorum Germanorum Theologiae Doctorum & Pastorum nomina vidisse: quibus pensiones annuae, ex Archiepiscopatu praesertim Metensi assignabantur. In quem vero finem, non fuisse scriptum. Sed si (ut dixi) vera haec sunt, quod ego non ajo, quis fuerit finis, ipse ipsa docet: perpetua bella adversus nos confirmunt
units.tr: Fearing that they would for this reason be rebuked by the Queen, they wanted an end put to that question, and wanted to attack the other matter, the Lord's Supper, on which Beza had dwelt at length in his first speech. They asked whether our men were prepared to subscribe to the Augsburg Confession and accept it. Beza, in turn, asked whether they themselves intended to embrace it. The Cardinal, tergiversating, produced a paper which, as he said, had been sent to him from Germany, but which had been supplied by Francis Balduinus, whose services he was using in this matter. He had also summoned some theologians of the Augsburg Confession, whom he hoped would soon be set against our men in a dispute over the Lord's Supper. He pressed the ministers hard to assent to this paper, and to no other end than either to provoke a contest between our men and the German theologians, or, if they subscribed, to triumph over them as victor. The paper contained a formula which, as the Cardinal said, was taken from the Augsburg Confession: We confess that the true body and the true blood of Jesus Christ are truly, really and sacramentally present in the Lord's Supper, and are so offered and so received by those who communicate. The Cardinal of Lorraine intended nothing else by this than to keep the Protestant theologians at odds with one another, and to make it easier to insult the ministers, since he regarded the Lutherans as more hostile to our men and more favourable to himself; indeed, some of them, a shameful thing, were in his pay. This is asserted on the faith of Hieronymus Zanchius, who in his Response to Wilhelm Holder, in the year 1566, wrote as follows, p. 20: It is certain to me, and I will say it before God: I have heard from a man skilled in these matters, and worthy of trust, that in the account-book of that Cardinal of Lorraine, who died a few years ago, he saw the names of several German doctors of theology and pastors, to whom annual pensions were assigned, especially from the archbishopric of Metz. But for what end the paper was written, he does not say. If these things are true (as I have said), and I do not assert them, the end itself makes it plain: the perpetual wars against us confirm it,

units.la: a Scripto ... eversiones Ecclesiarum nostrarum obsignant: & incrementum Pontificiae tyrannidis palam proclamat atque promulgat. Nulla enim meliori ratione haec obtineri poterant: quam perpetua dissidiorum nostrorum continuatione. Veni Domine Iesu, veni: & dissipa illos, qui bella volunt. Advenerunt autem post finitum Colloquium, Mich. Dillerus, Pet. Boquinus, Heidelbergæ missi, ab Electore Palatino; & V Vittenbergici, Iacobus Andreas, Balthasar Bidembachius, Iacobo Beurlino, eorum Collegæ, Parisiis peste extincto, sed nullo usu cum essent, frustraneo itinere mox domum remearunt. Die xxvi. Septembris reditum ad Colloquium fuit, ubi Beza primum de vocatione Ministrorum, & de S. Coena sermone habito, iterum Cardinalis post aliud quid in oratione Bezae notatum, quaerit: Confessionem Augustanam reciperent, an non? Nostri duo respondebant, primo an illi eandem amplecterentur: sic nempe non incommodam pacis viam inire facile posse: deinde, an quaereret ista Cardinalis suo, an communi nomine? ubi quamvis Collegas acutum intueretur, & vultu quasi singulorum suffragia extorqueret, nemine annuente, Beza subiecit, iniquum proinde esse, quod id adeo a se postularet. Posthæc Sorbonicorum aliquis, ad Bezam, sublato digito: O si te intra Sorbonæ nostræ moenia semel comprehensum teneremus! atqui sic coetus ille, post tumultuantium clamores & confusam turbam, omnia quippe inordinate, & absque Notariis gesta, dimissus, atque Colloquii forma secundum mutata fuit. Cujus tres formas & species statuere liceat, primam Augustissimam, maximeque publice, praesente, duabus sessionibus, ipso Rege: alteram minorem, quasi-privato-publicam, per sessiones iterum binas: tertiam hanc privatam, Reginae tamen iussu, primo inter binos utrimque Theologos, inde Montlucium, & Espenseum, hinc Bezam, & Gallasium, d. xxv i i. Septemb. ubi prima formula, super articulo de S. Coena, postquam alia à Pontificiis solis cusa, & à Regina suppressa fuerat, condita fuit: credimus in usu Cœna &c. Inde xxix. Septemb. inter quinos hinc inde Theologos: Pontificii erant, duo episcopi, Monlucius, & Vallius, tres Sorbonici, Espenseus, Salignacus, Bontelius. Hic relecta prior formula, quæ dicebat verè substantialiter Christi corpus exhiberi: Credimus in usu Cœnæ Dominicæ vere & reipsa ac substantialiter, id est, in ipsa substantia verum corpus & sanguinem Christi spirituali & ineffabili modo esse, exhiberi, sumi, à fidelibus communicantibus.
units.tr: the overthrow of our churches seals it, and it openly proclaims and publishes the growth of Papal tyranny. For these things could be secured by no better means than by the constant continuation of our dissensions. Come, Lord Jesus, come, and scatter those who want war. After the Colloquy had ended, Michael Diller and Peter Boquin arrived, sent from Heidelberg by the Elector Palatine; and five Wittenbergers, Jacob Andreae, Balthasar Bidembach, and Jacob Beurlin, their colleagues, arrived at Paris, after the plague had carried off their colleagues there, but since they were of no use, they soon returned home on a fruitless journey. On 26 September there was a return to the Colloquy, where Beza, after a sermon on the calling of ministers and on the Holy Supper, was asked again by the Cardinal, after some other point noted in Beza's speech: would they receive the Augsburg Confession or not? Our two men replied, first, whether those men would embrace it themselves, for in this way they could easily enter upon a not inconvenient path to peace; second, whether the Cardinal was asking this in his own name or in the common name. Although he looked sharply at his colleagues, and by his expression seemed to extort the votes of each, when no one nodded assent, Beza added that it was therefore unfair that he should demand this of them. After this, one of the Sorbonne men, lifting his finger towards Beza, said: "Oh, if only we had you once caught within the walls of our Sorbonne!" But that assembly, after the shouts of the rioters and the confused din, was dismissed, everything having been done in disorder and without notaries, and the form of the Colloquy was thereafter changed. Its three forms and kinds may be set out: the first most august and most public, in the presence of the King himself, over two sessions; the second less formal, a semi-private and semi-public meeting, again over two sessions; and the third, private yet at the Queen's command, first between two theologians on each side, namely Montluc and Espence on one side and Beza and Gallasius on the other, on 27 September, when the first formula on the article concerning the Holy Supper was drawn up, after another had been struck out by the Papists alone and suppressed by the Queen: We believe in the use of the Supper, etc. Then, on 29 September, among five theologians on each side (the Papists being two bishops, Monluc and Vallius, and three from the Sorbonne, Espence, Salignac and Bontelius), the earlier formula was read again, which said that the body of Christ is offered truly and substantially: We believe that in the use of the Lord's Supper, truly and in fact and substantially, that is, in the substance itself, the true body and blood of Christ are present, are offered, and are taken by the faithful who communicate, in a spiritual and ineffable manner.

units.la: Hæc Petro Martyri minus placebant, qui edito scripto: respondeo, inquit, pro mea parte, corpus Christi non esse vere & substantialiter alibi, quam in cælo: non tamen inficior, Christi corpus verum, & sanguinem illius verum, quæ pro salute humana tradita sunt in cruce, spiritualiter percipi à credentibus, in S. Cœna. Egregie & accurate, cui etiam reliqui quatuor mox assensi sunt. Inde alteram fecerunt formam: Quatenus fides &c. Hæc non probata fuit Espenseo, quia fidei tribueret præsentiam Christi, in sacramento; quam Espenseus tribui volebat Dei potentiæ. Quare die seq. Septemb. tertia formula exarata: Confitemur Iesum Christum in Cœna nobis dare &c. quæ quidem Collocutoribus utrimque approbata, dein Reginæ etiam, & Cardinali Lotharingo, qui palam profitebatur, se nunquam aliter credidisse & multum applausum ubique concitabat, ob partium aliquam, & in primario articulo convenientiam, quam Bezæ profusè gratulata fuit Regina. Verum quantum aliis placuit, tam displicuit Sorbonicis, & Antistitibus reliquis, quando ipsis d. iv. Octobris offerebatur: qui clamabant, formulam esse captiosam, hæreticam, & continere errores plurimos, contra institutionem Sancti Sacramenti altaris. Quos ab illis notatos refert Auctor l' Histoire Ecclesiastique de France ad annum 1561. pag. 609. Quare & Collocutoribus Pontificiis potestas ulterius cum Ministris conferendi negata, ut qui colludere, & se mutuo intelligere, credebantur: aliaque ab illis composita formula fuit, cui nisi Ministri subscriberent, nefas haberetur amplius cum iis agere, quin contra ut haeretici & pertinaces ab Ecclesia judicarentur & poenis ex Regis Edictis afficerentur. Nostri etiam, suae ultimae formulae, ne qua ejus expositione postmodum caperentur, pleniorem addiderunt explicationem: Affirmamus nullam &c. Atque is exitus Colloquii Poissiacensis fuit, d. xix. Octobris, Cardinalium, Episcoporum, aliorumque plurimis discedentibus: quo Colloquio, primum libertas publice de Religione disputandi in Gallia Protestantibus concessa est. Hinc sequenti anno die xvi. Januarii, sequutum primum pro religionis in Gallia libertate, ejusque usu publico in suburbiis, Edictum, quod inde appellatum fuit Januarii. De Colloquio illo legere licet Commentarium Reip. & Relig. sub Carolo ix. part. i. lib. iii. Antonium Fayum, in Vita Bezae; & qui hunc, vel illum, aut utrumque secutus fuit, Thuanum, Histor. lib. xxviii. Et Histoire Ecclesiastique des Eglises Reformées en France, Tom. i. lib. iv Commentarium, de l'Estat de la Religion & Republique, par le President de la Place, lib. vi. & vii. Iosiam Simlerum, in vita Petri Martyris.
units.tr: These words pleased Peter Martyr less, who, when he had published a paper, said: "For my part I reply that the body of Christ is not truly and substantially anywhere other than in heaven; yet I do not deny that the true body of Christ and his true blood, which were given for human salvation on the cross, are spiritually received by believers in the Holy Supper." Excellently and accurately put, and the other four soon assented to it. Then they made a second form: In so far as faith, etc. This was not approved by Espence, because it ascribed the presence of Christ in the sacrament to faith, whereas Espence wished it ascribed to the power of God. Therefore, on the following day, 28 September, a third formula was drawn up: We confess that Jesus Christ gives himself to us in the Supper, etc. This was approved by the speakers on both sides, and then by the Queen also and by Cardinal Lorraine, who openly professed that he had never believed otherwise, and it won much applause everywhere, on account of a certain agreement of the parties on the primary article, for which the Queen warmly congratulated Beza. But as much as it pleased others, so much did it displease the Sorbonne men and the other prelates, when it was presented to them on 4 October. They cried out that the formula was captious and heretical, and contained many errors against the institution of the Holy Sacrament of the altar. The author of the Histoire Ecclésiastique de France, for the year 1561, p. 609, reports these as noted by them. Therefore the Papist speakers were also denied the power to confer further with the ministers, as men who were believed to collude and to understand one another; and another formula was composed by them, to which, unless the ministers subscribed, it would be deemed wrong to deal further with them, but they would instead be judged by the Church as heretics and obstinate persons, and punished under the King's edicts. Our men, too, added a fuller explanation to their final formula, lest they be caught by any later interpretation of it: We affirm that no, etc. And this was the end of the Colloquy of Poissy, on 19 October, with many of the cardinals, bishops and others departing. At this Colloquy, for the first time, liberty to dispute publicly about religion was granted to Protestants in France. Hence, in the following year, on 16 January, there followed the first Edict for liberty of religion in France and its public exercise in the suburbs, which was named after the month, the Edict of January. About that Colloquy one may read the Commentarium Reipublicae et Religionis sub Carolo IX, part 1, book 3; Antoine de La Faye, in the Life of Beza; and whoever followed him, or the other, or both, de Thou, Historia, book 28; and the Histoire Ecclésiastique des Églises Réformées en France, vol. 1, book 4; the Commentarius de l'Estat de la Religion et Republique, by the President de La Place, books 6 and 7; and Josias Simler, in the Life of Peter Martyr.

units.la: Postquam ex Colloquio Poissiacensi reliqui domum essent reversi, Beza autem cum paucis aliis diutius illic haereret, Regina jussit ut anno cIↄ Iↄ lxix. mense Martio conferrent inter se de imaginibus, in Sangermano, à Pontificiis partibus Mallarius, Salignacus, Botilerius, Demochares &c. adhibito viro eruditissimo, Petro Picherello; ex nostris, Beza, Marloratus, Perusellus, Barbastus. Hic Beza primo die, ad duas horas, contra imagines disseruit; sequentibus diebus alii, absque altercatione, aut tumultu. Exitus fuit, quod Monluscius, Espensaeus, Botilerius, Salignacus, Picherelius, imagines Trinitatis, Patris, & Spiritus Sancti simsimpliciter damnarent: reliquas etiam à templis amovendas, exceptâ solâ crucis figurâ, dicerent; sed cultum omnem omnibus absolute denegandum. Atque ista quasi Conventus Poissiacensi post-acta fuerunt.
units.tr: After the others had returned home from the Colloquy of Poissy, while Beza with a few others remained there longer, the Queen ordered that in March 1569 they should confer with one another about images at Saint-Germain. On the Papist side were Mallarius, Salignac, Botilier, Demochares and others, with the very learned Pierre Picherel as adviser; on our side, Beza, Marlorat, Perussel and Barbaste. Here Beza, on the first day, for two hours, argued against images; on the following days the others spoke without quarrel or tumult. The outcome was that Montluc, Espence, Botilier, Salignac and Picherel condemned the images of the Trinity, of the Father and of the Holy Spirit simply; they also said that the rest should be removed from churches, except the figure of the cross alone; but all worship of them was to be absolutely denied to everyone. These things were done, as it were, as a sequel to the Colloquy of Poissy.

units.la: Mihi autem videtur, temere admodum, post multas magnasque super doctrinæ aliquo articulo, & valde oppositas disputationes, laborari de sincerâ in controversiæ puncto convenientia: nisi ubi altera pars in alterius descendit sententiam. Alioqui in ambiguis locutionibus constituta conciliatio, uti nec aliis placet, ita suis Auctoribus, & causæ, propter quam adhibetur, nunquam non magnas parit molestias. Aliter est, si de momento disputiatur controversiæ, an tale sit, ut non salvâ religione, & summâ fidei in ipso controverso articulo, prætiri quæstio, si non omnino, ex eâ saltem parte, quâ acrior videtur, possit; eâque omissâ, veritatis suo semper servato jure integro, talis constitui formula, quæ & summam necessariæ fidei comprehendat, & totum recipiat utriusque partis in se confluxum ac συμφωνίαν. Verbi gratiâ, in articulo & Controversiâ de Cœnâ, velle sententiarum, nostræ & Pontificiæ, sub eandem Confessionem, facere συμφωνίαν, mihi videtur res & impossibilis & infructuosa: at verò si in hoc inquiratur, annon, accipiendo quod utrimque in confesso est, & ad summam religionis facit, ut quis sacramentum cum salutis fructu participet, reliquum controversiæ quod est, in praxi prætériri possit, manente salvâ utrius partis veritate, & super eâ quæstione; res alterius est examinis. Modò pro necessario habeatur, & fidem accipienti sacramentum, & pasturam animi per verum Christum, ejusque & corpus & sanguinem fractum fusumque necessariam omnino esse; omisso interim, an insuper carnaliter ibi Christus & substantialiter præsens sit, & sic edatur quoque. Namque hæc præsentia uti (secundum Pontificios ipsos) non pendet à nostrâ vel fide, vel infidelitate, sed à Dei tum
units.tr: But it seems to me rash to labour over a sincere agreement on the point of a controversy after many large and very opposed disputations about some article of doctrine, unless one side has gone over to the other's opinion. Otherwise a reconciliation framed in ambiguous wording pleases neither side, nor its authors, nor the cause for which it is adopted, and it always causes great trouble. It is different if the question is whether the matter in dispute is of such weight that, without loss to religion and to the sum of faith, the question can be set aside in the article under dispute, if not altogether, at least on the side where it seems sharper; and if that is omitted, while the truth keeps all its rights intact, a formula is drawn up that contains the sum of necessary faith and takes in the whole concurrence and agreement [συμφωνία] of both parties. For example, in the article and controversy about the Supper, to seek an agreement [συμφωνία] between our opinion and the Papist opinion under one and the same Confession seems to me both impossible and unprofitable. But if it is asked whether, granting what is admitted on both sides and belongs to the sum of religion, a person may receive the sacrament with the fruit of salvation, and the rest of the controversy may be set aside in practice, while the truth of each party remains safe and that question is left to another examination, then the matter is different. Provided it is held as necessary that the believing recipient, and the nourishment of the soul, is through the true Christ, and that his body and his blood, broken and poured out, are altogether necessary, and meanwhile it is left open whether Christ is also present there carnally and substantially, and so is eaten as well. For this presence, as the Papists themselves say, depends not on our faith or unbelief but on the truth and power of God; and it will be obtained even by me, however little I believe it (let me speak thus to the Pontiffs), provided I am endowed with true faith in Christ. Therefore, setting aside the Papist dictate and the necessity of their opinion, whose benefit (if there were any such) the faithful too would enjoy even if they did not accept their opinion, someone who spoke of a union of parties rather than of opinions [συνοδίαις], and of a formula of such concord, would be doing something quite different and perhaps more useful. Especially since the Papists themselves can hardly be made to say that knowledge of this point, which is in question here, apart from what is admitted on both sides, can be proved from Scripture to be so necessary for salvation. For one must distinguish the truth itself from the necessity of knowing that truth. But this in passing.

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] veritate, tum potentia, mihi (liceat sic loqui ad Pontifices) quantumvis istam non credenti, dummodo fide vera in Christum sim praeditus, obtinget etiam. Quare omisso sententiae Pontificiae imperio, ac necessitate, cujus bono (si quod tale esset) fruetur fidelis quoque, etsi non admittat eorum sententiam, si jam quis loquatur de partium potius, quam sententiarum συνοδίαις, & de talis concordiae formula, rem longe aliam ageret, & forte magis utilem. Praesertim quum non facile dictuí sint Pontificii ipsi, notitiam istius, quod hic in quaestione, praeter confessa utrimque, ex Scriptura probari posse adeo esse ad salutem necessariam. Nam distinguere oportet, ipsam veritatem, a necessitate cognitionis, quoad illam veritatem. Sed haec obiter.
units.tr: [illegible] truth as well as the power of God, will obtain it even for me, however little I believe it (let me speak thus to the Pontiffs), provided I am endowed with true faith in Christ. Therefore, setting aside the Papist dictate and necessity, whose benefit the faithful too would enjoy (if there were any such), even if they did not admit their opinion, the matter would be quite different, and perhaps more useful, if anyone spoke of a union of parties rather than of opinions [συνοδίαις], and of a formula of such concord. Especially since the Papists themselves can hardly be made to say that knowledge of this point, which is in question here, apart from what is admitted on both sides, can be proved from Scripture to be so necessary for salvation. For one must distinguish the truth itself from the necessity of knowing that truth. But this in passing.

units.la: Pergimus in recensione Colloquiorum, inter Nostros & Papistas habitorum: inter quae quia vix ullum celebrius, certe augustius nullum, praesentibus tot Regiis capitibus habitum, illo Possiacensi, in cujus etiam narratione fuimus prolixiores. Anno clɔIɔ lxvi. Parisiis, in aedibus Nivernianis, ex consilio ducis Mompensierii, instituta disputatio fuit, inter binos utrimque Theologos, Simonem Vigoreum, & Claudium Sanctium, Theologos Pontificios, cum Johanne Spina, & Carolo Barbasto, Protestantibus, cujusque Acta postea Lutetiae publicata sunt, sed isto eventu disputatum, ut post longam et animosam disceptationem, exigua partium nusquam convenientium profectu, et eorum praecipue, quorum causa collatio habita fuerat, utrimque discessum sit. Verba sunt Thuani, Histor. lib. xxxix.
units.tr: We go on to the review of the colloquies held between our people and the Papists. Among them, since none was more celebrated and certainly none more august, held in the presence of so many royal heads, is that at Poissy, in whose account I have also been rather lengthy. In the year 1566, at Paris, in the house of Nevers, on the advice of the Duke of Montpensier, a disputation was arranged between two theologians on each side: Simon Vigor and Claude Sanctius, Papist theologians, and John Spina and Charles Barbaste, Protestants. Its acts were afterwards published at Lutetia, but the disputation ended in such a way that, after a long and heated debate, the parties parted without agreeing anywhere, and with no profit, especially for those for whose sake the conference had been held. These are the words of Thuanus, Histories, book 39.

units.la: Eodem anno Disputatio habita Harlemi, in aedibus Clementis Cornelii, diversorio aurei velleris, inter magni templi Capellanum, atque ab altera parte Johannem Praepositum, Johannem Arnoldi, Reinerium Cant, tertiumque alium, ante meridiem, a nona ad undecimam, & post meridiem à secunda ad quartam, sed quam Consules urbis tumultum civium veriti, abruperunt. Refert Secundo Annalium, Petrus Bor. quod disputatum quidem, non autem quà super sedeo.
units.tr: In the same year a disputation was held at Haarlem, in the house of Clement Cornelius, at the inn of the Golden Fleece, between the chaplain of the great church and, on the other side, John Praepositus, John Arnoldi, Reinerius Cant, and a third person. It was held in the morning from nine to eleven, and in the afternoon from two to four, but the magistrates of the city, fearing a riot of the citizens, broke it off. Peter Bor, in the Second Book of the Annals, reports that it was indeed disputed, but not on the matter in question.

units.la: Anno MDLXXX. in arce Londinensi, ubi tenebatur Iohannes Hartus, quia contra leges Regni, istud subintrarat, Colloquium eorum habuit Iohannes Raynoldus, de Capite Ecclesiae; altera etiam proposita quidem quaestio fuerat de fide, probaturumque se Hartus suscepérat, fidem nostram haud esse veram, & Catholicam; sed eam aggredi noluit, manseritque intacta, dicens ille tandem, longius non progrediar, nisi prius de vita sua securior. Disputarunt scripto, editaque disputatio quidem à Rainoldo fuit, sed quam Hartus approbavit, sic ipse scribens, per literas tum datas ad Rainoldum, tum ab illo acceptas, obtinui ut sermones rationesque mea prout volueram perficerentur. Quare, agnosco veram istic ab illo descriptam esse earum rerum narrationem, de quibus ego & ille inter nos in Colloquio egimus, juxta fundamenta, locaque autorum ipsorum, quos designaram, & quibus me addixeram. Quae valde commendant Rainoldi tum eruditionem, tum aequitatem: quibus ipsi etiam Adversarii alibi dederunt testimonium, in Concertatione Ecclesiae Catholicae in Anglia, part. iii. pag. 222, ubi de Harto suo, ad eum miserunt D. Reynoldum, ministrum Synagogae Anglicanae non vulgarem, qui cum Christii Confessoribus de difficultatibus inter Catholicos & Calvinistas controversis, dissereret; idque sane prae sui diligenter. Libro isti Concertationis, quod obiter dicendum, oppositus fuit alius anno MDLXXXIV. regni Elisabethae xxvi. tit. Iustitia Britannica: scriptus Anglice, & Latine, quo ostenditur, nullos in Anglia, simpliciter & mere ob religionem Papisticam, verum omnes ob perduellionem poenis suis multatos fuisse. Neque candor Harto defuit, quum agnosceret se hoc tanquam coniam conclusionem tenere, eorum opinionem, qui Pontificem temporalem esse Regum Principumque dominum censent, à ratione atque probabilitate prorsus abhorrere. Dignum est Colloquium, quod ab omnibus, super isthoc argumento, & propter plura alia, quae doctissima undique pro eruditione sua Rainoldus adspersit, legatur.
units.tr: In the year 1580, in the Tower of London, where John Hart was held because he had secretly entered the realm against its laws, John Rainolds held a colloquy with him on the headship of the Church. Another question had also been proposed, on faith; Hart had undertaken to prove that our faith was not true and Catholic, but he refused to go into it and left it untouched, saying at last, I will not go further unless first I am more secure about my life. They disputed in writing, and the disputation was published by Rainolds, but Hart approved it, writing thus: Through letters both given to Rainolds and received from him, I obtained that my speeches and arguments should be set out as I had wished. Therefore I acknowledge that the account of those matters, about which he and I argued in the colloquy, is truly recorded there, according to the foundations and places of the authors themselves whom I had marked out and to whom I had bound myself. These things greatly commend Rainolds, both his learning and his fairness, and the Adversaries themselves have given testimony to them elsewhere, in the Concertatio Ecclesiae Catholicae in Anglia, part 3, page 222, where, speaking of their Hart, they say: They sent to him Doctor Reynolds, no ordinary minister of the Anglican synagogue, who discussed with the Confessors of Christ the difficulties controverted between Catholics and Calvinists; and he did this certainly with diligence. To this book, the Concertatio, another was opposed in 1584, in the twenty-sixth year of Elizabeth's reign, entitled Justitia Britannica, written in English and Latin, which shows that no one in England was punished simply and purely for Papist religion, but all for treason. Nor did Hart lack candour, since he acknowledged that he held as a certain conclusion that the opinion of those who think the Pope is lord of kings and princes is utterly abhorrent to reason and probability. The colloquy deserves to be read by everyone on this subject, and for many other things which Rainolds, most learned everywhere, has scattered through his learning.

units.la: Anno cIↄIↄ xcv. d. xii. Octobris Tirani; in Rhetia, disputatio habita, inter Parochos Vulturenos, Stuppanum, Ruscam, Cabassum, Mazzonum, Antonium Consularium, & Antonium Omodeum; atque Ministros Euangelicos Vallis Telinae, Andreossam, Gaffarum, Mey, Calandrinum, ac Cheselium, de mediatorio Christi officio, an secundum utramque, an alteram demum, & humanam naturam, occasione concionis à Simone Cabasso Parocho Tirahensi habitae, in eaque Calvini, & doctrinae ejus diffamationis, contra expressa Trium foederum decreta, quibus cavetur, ne haec pars istam convitiis, contumeliis, vel calumniosis verbis, ac imprimis ne altera alteram haereticam vocet. Eandem prosecuti disputationem fuerunt, in altero congressu anno cIↄ Iↄ xcvi. Kal. Martii: ad quam Praesides pronunciarunt, verba à Cabasso prolata in Joannem Calvinum, eximium Theologum, ac sanctae memoriae virum, ejus bonae famae, & eorum qui cum eo sentiunt, multo modo praejudicare posse, nec debere. Denique in tertio congressu, iterum Tirani, eodem anno, d. 30. Augusti, postquam per Praesides Actis secundi Congressus ad Comitia Curiensia, mense Iunio habita, relatis, eorundemque Comitiorum decreto statutum fuisset: Simonem Cabassum Parochum Tirani palinodiam canere debere eorum, quae in Calvinum dixisset, nec tamen probasset, vel si iterum experiri vellet, num probare illa posset: Disputationem esse continuandam; ea tamen conditione ut utraque pars sufficienter pro expensis caveat; seque intra modestos fines contineat: Nostri obtulerunt scriptum breve, ad quod examinandum cum postero die Adversarii petiissent novem menses, satis manifesto argumento, effugium ab ipsis quaeri, unus iis concessus fuit, dilatumque negotium, ad Cal. Octob. Status Controversiae erat: Utrum Calvinus blasphemasset, eo quod in Institt. lib. II. cap. XIV. scripsit, praedicata illa apud D. Ioannem, praesertim cap. 5. sicut enim Pater excitat mortuos, & vivificat, ita filius hominis, &c. Item, subiectionem illam, de qua D. Paulus 1. Corinth. 15. postquam vero subiecta ei fuerint omnia, tunc & ipse Filius subjicietur ei, qui subjecit sibi omnia. Item, officium Mediatoris, praedicari de Christo secundum utramque naturam simul? Calendis ergo Octobris, die à Praesidibus constituta, quum convenissent Tirani Nostri omnes, Cabassus, neque Parochorum ullus adfuit, nundinas Tiranenses, & proximam vindemiam causati: quae satis futilia omnes videbant: dies etiam disputationis in xv. Novembris dilata, quo tamen nec praestitere Pontificii quod agendum erat: usque dum anni sequentis cIↄ Iↄ xcvii. die xv. Ianuar. Praesides hanc pronunciarunt sententiam:
units.tr: On 12 October 1595, at Tiranum in Rhaetia, a disputation was held between the parish priests of Vulturenum, Stuppanus, Rusca, Cabassus, Mazzonus, Antonius Consularius and Antonius Omodeus, and the Evangelical ministers of the Valley of Telina, Andreossa, Gaffarus, Mey, Calandrinus and Chesel, on the mediatorial office of Christ: whether it belongs to him according to both natures, or only to the human nature. It arose from a sermon preached by Simon Cabassus, parish priest of Tirano, in which he defamed Calvin and his doctrine, contrary to the express decrees of the Three Leagues, by which it is provided that neither side shall use insults, abuse or calumnious words against the other, and above all that one shall not call the other heretical. They continued the same disputation at a second meeting, on 1 March 1596, when the presiding officers pronounced that the words uttered by Cabassus against John Calvin, an outstanding theologian and a man of holy memory, could and should not prejudice his good name or that of those who think with him. Finally, at a third meeting, again at Tirano, in the same year, on 30 August, after the presiding officers had reported the acts of the second meeting to the Diet of Chur held in June, and a decree of that Diet had been issued: Simon Cabassus, parish priest of Tirano, must retract what he had said against Calvin and had not proved; or if he wished to try again, he must show whether he could prove those things. The disputation is to be continued, on the condition that each party gives sufficient security for expenses, and keeps itself within modest limits. Our men offered a short written statement. When the Adversaries, on the following day, asked for nine months to examine it, which was a fairly clear sign that they were seeking a way out, one such period was granted them, and the business was postponed to 1 October. The state of the controversy was this: whether Calvin had blasphemed in writing, in Institutes book 2, chapter 14, that the attributes said of him in John, especially chapter 5, For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them, even so the Son quickeneth whom he will, and so on; likewise that subjection of which Paul speaks, 1 Corinthians 15, And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him; likewise, whether the office of Mediator is predicated of Christ according to both natures at once. So on 1 October, the day fixed by the presiding officers, all our men from Tirano assembled, but Cabassus did not come, nor did any of the parish priests, on the pretext of the Tirano fair and the approaching vintage, which everyone saw to be quite flimsy. The day of the disputation was then postponed to 15 November, but the Papists did not even then do what had to be done, until on 15 January of the following year, 1597, the presiding officers pronounced this sentence:

units.la: Nos excelsorum Trium Foederum Rhaetiae superioris Oratores, & Consiliarii, ex mandato Illustrissimarum nostrarum Communitatum, Curiae, in publicis, & generalibus Comitiis, congregati: Audita expositione coram nobis hodie in publico nostro consessu &c. pronuntiavimus, ordinavimus, ac unanimiter declaravimus, & declaramus &c. In primis praefatum praeceptum ad instantiam praefati Presbyteri Cabassi ut supra emanatum, nullum, casum, & irritum: illudque cum contentis in eo omnino tollimus, & revocamus.
units.tr: We, the ambassadors and councillors of the three Leagues of Upper Rhaetia, assembled at the public and general Diet by mandate of our most illustrious communities and courts, having heard the statement made before us today in our public assembly, etc., have pronounced, ordained and unanimously declared, and do declare, etc. First, we annul, quash and revoke the aforesaid order, issued at the instance of the aforesaid Presbyter Cabassus as stated above, together with everything contained in it.

units.la: Deinde pro bono pacis, & publica tranquillitatis, dictae disceptationi perpetuum indicimus, praecipimusque silentium. Praeterea definimus, praefatum Calvinum eodem citato loco, bene & orthodoxe scripsisse, & sensisse, dictumque Presbyterum Symonem Cabassum (cum nihil unquam sani probare potuerit) iniquè injuria cum affecisse, ac maledictis eum impeimpetiisse; propterea que dictum Presbyterum plectendum, & ad expensas in causa factas persolvendas cogendum fore, statuimus, & ordinamus. Post quae Iohannes Lucius Gugelbergius a Mos Praetor Tiranensis, sententiam Dominorum executus, visis & probatis expensarum hinc inde factarum calculis, Cabassum condemnavit in centum & triginta duos aureos. Quod hic etiam praestitit. Atque is disputationis exitus fuit, festivus certe, & partium nostrarum Theologis admodum honorificus. Neque alio pacto oportet coercere sacrificulorum petulantiam & maledicendi insectandique intolerandam libidinem.
units.tr: Then, for the sake of peace and public tranquillity, we impose perpetual silence on the said dispute and command it to end. Furthermore, we declare that the aforesaid Calvin wrote and thought well and orthodoxly in the passage cited, and that the said Presbyter Simon Cabassus (since he could never prove anything sound) unjustly wronged him and assailed him with insults; we therefore decide and ordain that the said Presbyter shall be punished and compelled to pay the costs incurred in the case. After this, John Lucius Gugelberg, praetor of Tirano from Mos, carrying out the orders of the lords and having examined and approved the calculations of expenses on both sides, condemned Cabassus to one hundred and thirty-two gold coins, which he also paid there. This was the outcome of the dispute, certainly a happy one and very honourable to the theologians on our side. There is no other way to restrain the arrogance of these little priests and their intolerable lust for abuse and attack.

units.la: Anno cIↄ Iↄ xcix. die xiii. Novembris Nannetense Colloquium Catharina, Regis Henr. soror, Religioni Reformatae addictissima, quae nuperat Duci Lotharingiae, sui mariti in gratiam, qui adduxerat Iesuitam Comelet, & Capucinum F. Esprit, probaturos nempe, Catharinae fidem & religionem falsam esse, instituit, cum Iacobo Couet Parisiensi, quem Basileâ, sibi ut à sacris esset, accerserat, (eundem, adversus quem Socinus librum suum scripsit, de Christo Servatore) & D. de Touche. Praesentes fuere, praeter ipsam sororem Regis, ejusque maritum, Dux, & Cardinalis Lotharingiae. Actum de Scripturae authoritate, vel nihil fere: quia quum nostri nullum alium Controversiarum judicem & normam vellent, quam Sacram Scripturam; Adversarii autem non istam, quam in exordio disputationis Iesuita Comelet appellabat litteram mortuam, corticem absque medullâ, librum haereticorum, sed Patres, & quas hi facerent Scripturae expositiones, nostris non refugientibus Patrum audire sententiam, sed infra & post Scripturam, ac quousque cum Scripturâ consentirent, tum ut non istis sed Scripturae servaretur authoritas decidendarum infallibiliter controversiarum, quod nec ulli Patres unquam aliter voluerunt, aut docuerunt; factum, ut nihil ultra iste quidem dem colloquio actum fuerit, Principe Navarræ interim vehementer in fide suâ confirmatâ, & triumphante, quam tantum abest falsam ostendissent vani jactatores, qui ad Scripturæ examen horrebant, atque ut ab eo omninò abstinerent, aliunde etiam sollicitè monebantur. Tandem 15. Decembris Regis Soror, publico Diplomate declaravit omnibus in Galliâ Reformatis Ecclesiis, & fidelibus, quam promptam & egregiam sibi & causæ in Colloquio præstitisset operam Covetus, quodque non nisi ex consilio Ducis discessisset. Quam Declarationem in Historiâ suâ profert etiam Borrius, lib. xxxvi. in fine. Extat & Historia Colloquii seorsim, Gallice edita, à Coveto.
units.tr: In the year 1599, on 13 November, the Colloquy of Nantes was held by Catherine, sister of King Henry, who was most devoted to the Reformed religion and who had married the Duke of Lorraine. She did this to please her husband, who had brought in the Jesuit Comelet and the Capuchin Father Esprit, expecting to prove that Catherine's faith and religion were false. The colloquy was arranged with Jacques Coyet of Paris, whom she had summoned from Basel to serve as her chaplain (the same man against whom Socinus wrote his book de Christo Servatore), and with Mr de Touche. Present, besides the King's sister herself and her husband, were the Duke and the Cardinal of Lorraine. Almost nothing was done concerning the authority of Scripture. Our side wanted no other judge or rule of controversies than Holy Scripture, while the adversaries did not want this. Comelet, at the opening of the disputation, called Scripture "a dead letter, a shell without marrow, a book of heretics," and preferred the Fathers and the interpretations of Scripture that they gave. Our side did not refuse to hear the opinion of the Fathers, but only as subordinate to and after Scripture, and only so far as they agreed with Scripture; the authority to decide controversies infallibly was to be kept for Scripture and not for the Fathers, which no Father ever wished or taught otherwise. As a result, nothing further was accomplished at that colloquy, while the Prince of Navarre was greatly strengthened and triumphant in his faith. The vain boasters, who shrank from the examination of Scripture and were urgently warned from elsewhere to avoid it altogether, were far from showing that this faith was false. Finally, on 15 December, the King's sister issued a public diploma to all the Reformed churches and faithful in France, declaring how prompt and excellent Coyet's service had been to her and to the cause at the colloquy, and that he had left only on the Duke's advice. Borrius also cites this declaration in his history, book 36, at the end. There is also a separate history of the colloquy, published in French by Coyet.

units.la: Anno eIↄ Iↄ c.d. iv. Maji, ab horâ primâ pomeridianâ, ad sextam, habitum fuit Colloquium Fontisbellaquecnse, inter Philippum Mornæum, & Iacobum Perronum, episcopum Ebroicensem, occasione libri à Mornæo Gallicè scripti, de Eucharistiâ, quo adversus Pontificios disputat non ex Scripturâ solum, sed & ex Patribus, atque Scholasticis. Perronus receperat se ostensurum, plus quam quingenta loca ab Auctore depravata, & in sensum alienum adducta fuisse: quare uterque potestatem conferendi à Rege petere, ejusque præsentiam, & Commissarios Regios implorare; qui dati, pro Episcopo quidem, & parte Pontificia Iac. Augustus Thuanus, Franciscus Pithœus, Nic. Faber, cujus locum supplevit Martonus, medicus Regius; pro altera parte, Gofredus Caligno, Philippus Carnajus, Isaacus Casaubonus, qui solus erat religionis Reformatæ. Disputatum, præsente Rege, & primariis Aulæ Principibus, de testimoniis aliquot, Scoti primum, & Durandi, tum Chrysostomi, Hieronymi, demum & aliorum. Dura omnino erat Mornæi ista conditio; ex tempore respondere, non in disputatione de re, quod longe facilius, sed de testimoniis Scriptorum, quæ innumera in libro suo adduxerat, & è quibus quingenta genta se probaturum falsa esse, jactârat Adversarius. Quæ nec ipsa scripto exhibere unquam voluit, ut, quod in tali argumento requiri omnes norunt, non desultorie, sed maturâ collatione, examine, studio, ab objectis vendicaret Auctor. Quodque turpius, quando ad disputationem ventum, non ultra sexaginta Adversarius loca adscripsit, eaque Mornæo horâ demum primâ noctis tradi curavit, leviter notata, Carolus Magnus p. 316. Scotus p. 396. Durandus p. 870, libris, quos conferret, nam alios secum non habebat Plessæus, horâ demum noctis secundâ traditis; quos ad sextam ejus diei, quo habenda à meridie disputatio erat, repetiit alter. Adeo incommodo, brevique tempore virum, ejusque studia urgebant Adversarii, ad Collationem, quam ut Regis, & Principum præsentia faciebat tremendam, ita sustinebat solus Mornæus, uno suæ religionis adjuncto sibi Casaubono; atque cum eo, quem testatur Casaubonus, in Epistolis, octodecim menses & hoc amplius in hanc unicam curam insumsisse, ut si quid in Plessæi libro vel ὄντως vel φαινόμενος μεμψιτὸν inesset, omne rimaretur, & in gloriæ suæ materiem converteret. Atque ut in disputatione de rei probatione, ab humanis auctoritatibus non pendet fidei veritas aut certitudo; ita neque in tali collatione, quæ magis personalis videtur, quam realis, momentum causæ periclitatur, addo nec libri, cujus causa suscepta disputatio illa fuerat. Nam, uti bene monebat Plessæus, quod si ad hanc normam examini subjicerentur omnes libri à Papisticis Doctoribus conscripti, nullus uspiam subsisteret. Et quod ex toto illo libro, totque innumeris Auctorum allegatis testimoniis, primum quingenta, inde sexaginta, tandem novem modo indicata loca, libri & Auctoris fidem summopere comprobavit. Tum loca quod attinet producta à Perrono, ex Scoto, Durando, reliquisque, quam satis bene tueri potuerit Mornæus, apapparet ex Historia Colloquii, mox edita, quae Gallice extat, Anglice, & Belgice: ipsiusque Mornaei secuta & edita Responsione amplissima, ad librum Ebroicensis Episcopi, de Colloquio Fontisbellaqueensi quae conferre oportet, cum iis, quae de isto negotio in variis suis epistolis memorat Casaubonus; & Thuanus, lib. cxxiii.
units.tr: In the year 1600, on 4 May, from one o'clock in the afternoon until six, a colloquy was held at Fontainebleau between Philippe du Plessis-Mornay and Jacques Davy Du Perron, bishop of Évreux, on the occasion of a book written in French by Mornay on the Eucharist, in which he argues against the Papists not only from Scripture but also from the Fathers and the Scholastics. Perron had undertaken to show that more than five hundred passages had been corrupted by the author and drawn into a foreign sense. Therefore each of them asked the King for the power to confer, and called for his presence and royal commissioners. Those appointed were, for the bishop and the Papist side, Jacques-Auguste de Thou, François Pithou, and Nicolas Le Fèvre, whose place was taken by Marton, the royal physician; for the other side, Godefroy de Caligny, Philippe de Carnavalet, and Isaac Casaubon, who alone was of the Reformed religion. The discussion, in the presence of the King and the leading princes of the court, concerned several testimonies: first of Scotus and Durandus, then of Chrysostom and Jerome, and finally of others. Mornay's condition was indeed harsh: to answer off the cuff, not in a discussion of the matter (which would have been far easier), but on testimonies of writers, which he had cited in great numbers in his book, and of which the adversary had boasted that he would prove five hundred to be false. Perron never wished to submit these in writing either, so that the author could not, as everyone knows such a subject requires, defend himself against the objections by careful comparison, examination and study rather than by haphazard replies. And what was more disgraceful, when the time for the disputation came, the adversary cited no more than sixty passages, and had them handed to Mornay at about one in the morning, lightly noted: Carolus Magnus p. 316. Scotus p. 396. Durandus p. 870. The books in which to check them were handed over only at about two in the morning, since Plessis did not have the others with him; the other side demanded them back by six o'clock on that day, when the disputation from noon was to take place. So unreasonable and brief was the time in which the adversaries pressed the man and his studies, for the conference, made terrifying by the presence of the King and princes, was sustained by Mornay alone, with only Casaubon of his own religion joined to him. Casaubon, in his letters, testifies that he had spent eighteen months and more on this single task, to search out everything in Plessis's book that was either ontōs [ὄντως] or phainomenos mempsimoron [φαινόμενος μεμψιτόν] and turn it into a matter for his own glory. But just as the truth or certainty of faith does not depend on human authorities in a disputation about the proof of a matter, so the weight of the cause is not endangered in such a conference, which seems more personal than real; nor, I add, is the weight of the book for whose sake the disputation had been undertaken. For, as Plessis rightly warned, if all books written by Papist teachers were subjected to this standard of examination, none would stand anywhere. And from that whole book, with so many innumerable testimonies of authors cited, the number of supposedly false passages fell first to five hundred, then to sixty, and finally to nine passages only, and this greatly confirmed the faith of the book and its author. As for the passages cited by Perron from Scotus, Durandus and the rest, the account of the colloquy published soon afterwards, which exists in French, English and Dutch, shows how well Mornay could defend them. See also Mornay's very full reply, published afterwards, to the book of the bishop of Évreux on the Colloquy of Fontainebleau. These things should be compared with what Casaubon relates in his letters about this affair, and with Thou, book 123.

units.la: Anno cIↄ Iↄ c 1. d. xxviii. Novemb. habitum Ratisbonae tertium de religione Colloquium fuit, ex authoritate Maximiliani Bavariae Ducis, & Philippi Ludovici Comitis Palatini, inter partis Pontificiae Albertum Hungerum, Velserum, Hannemannum, Gretzerum; Tannerum; & partis Lutheranae varios, à Philippo Ludovico, à Saxoniae Electore Christiano II. alios ab Electore Brandeburgico Friderico, tum à duce VVurtembergico Frederico missos; inter quos praecipui erant Iac. Hailbrunner, Ægidius Hunnius, Runggius, Andreas Osiander, Felix Bidembachius. Disputatum à d. xxviii. Novemb. ad d. viii. Decemb. per xiv. sessiones; de authoritate Scripturae, & judice controversiarum: Gretzero thesin & sententiam suam hunc in modum proponente; Sacra Scriptura non est judex omnium controversiarum fidei, & religionis Christianae. Est quidem norma infallibilis; verum nec sola, nec unica; sed praeter hanc necessario admitti debent traditiones, & Ecclesiae definitiones, Doctorumque Orthodoxorum consensus. Cumque diu satis tergiversati fuissent Pontif. nolu issentque suum controversiarum judicem exponere, authoritate Principum adacti, Gretzerus id fecit: Judex generalis, legitimus, ordinarius omnium controversiarum, quaecunque possunt oriri in negotio religionis, est Pontifex Romanus, sive solus definiat aliquid, sive definiat cum Concilio generali. Iste judex semper est infallibilis, quando ex cathedra definit, ut Pontifex, nulli errori obnoxius; & speramus, hac die, & hac ipsa hora, hoc munere judiciario fungi sanctiss. D. nostrum Clementem VIII. Pontif. Opt. Max. Disputarunt utrimque ex Scriptura primum, argumentis Theologicis, tum ex Patribus: sed nullo, post multos etiam magnosque clamores, effectu. Hic Gretserus impudentissime exsibilans Spiritum Sanctum controversiarum judicem, alta voce clamabat: Iam adest Spiritus Sanctus, iam me condemnat. Iam, iam non potest dicere sententiam condemnatoriam Spiritus Sanctus per hunc librum, ita ut evidenter constet, quae sit ejus sententia. Ergo non potest esse judex. Iam adsum, dicas, erras Jacobe Gretsere. Acta Colloquii a parte una & altera, Ingolstadi, Monachii & VVurtembergae, edita fuerunt: vide & Thuanum, lib. cxxv i.
units.tr: In the year 1601, on 28 November, a third colloquy on religion was held at Regensburg by the authority of Maximilian, Duke of Bavaria, and Philipp Ludwig, Count Palatine. On the Papist side were Albert Hunger, Welser, Hannemann and Gretser, and Tanner; on the Lutheran side were various men sent by Philipp Ludwig, by Christian II, Elector of Saxony, by Frederick, Elector of Brandenburg, and by Frederick, Duke of Württemberg. Among these the most prominent were Jakob Heilbrunner, Ägidius Hunnius, Runge, Andreas Osiander and Felix Bidembach. The disputation was held from 28 November to 8 December, in fourteen sessions, on the authority of Scripture and the judge of controversies. Gretser put forward his thesis and opinion in this form: Holy Scripture is not the judge of all controversies of the Christian faith and religion. It is indeed an infallible rule, but not the only one, nor the sole one; besides it there must necessarily be admitted traditions, definitions of the Church, and the consensus of orthodox teachers. When the Pontifical side had sufficiently evaded the question for a long time and was unwilling to set out its own judge of controversies, Gretser was compelled by the authority of the princes and did so: The general, lawful and ordinary judge of all controversies that can arise in matters of religion is the Roman Pontiff, whether he decides something alone or with a general council. This judge is always infallible when he decides ex cathedra as Pontiff, subject to no error; and we hope that on this very day and at this very hour our most holy lord Clement VIII, Pontiff, Best and Greatest, will perform this judicial office. Both sides disputed first from Scripture with theological arguments, then from the Fathers, but with no result, even after many great outcries. Here Gretser, shamelessly hissing that the Holy Spirit was the judge of controversies, cried out loudly: Now the Holy Spirit is present, now he condemns me. Now, now the Holy Spirit cannot pronounce a sentence of condemnation through this book, so that it is clearly evident what his opinion is. Therefore he cannot be the judge. Here I am, you say; you are wrong, James Gretser. The records of the colloquy, from one side and the other, were published at Ingolstadt, Munich and Württemberg. See also Thou, book 125.

units.la: Anno cIↄ Iↄ c i i. iterum id agente Regis Galliae Henrici iv. sorore unica, Parisiis Colloquium inter Molinaeum, & Cayerum frustra aliquandiu tentatum; tandem, post abitum principis, d. xxv i i i. Maji, inchoatum fuit, & propositia themata de sacrificio missae, adoratione Papae, & Sanctarum imaginum venerazione. Quam adorationis vocem quum aegre ferret Carmelita aliquis in ipso disputationis exordio adhiberi, Cayer, & Doctor Sorbonicus ut bonam tamen retineri voluerunt. Actumque de his & aliis articulis diu fuit, quousque pars adversa Regios ministros induxit, ut, pro imperio, Colloquium dissolverent, ex quo seditio scilicet metueretur.
units.tr: In the year 1602, when Henry IV of France's only sister was again pursuing the matter, a colloquy between Molinaeus and Cayer was attempted in Paris for some time without result. At last, after the prince had left, it was begun on 28 May, and the topics proposed were the sacrifice of the Mass, the adoration of the Pope, and the veneration of holy images. When a certain Carmelite was vexed that the word "adoration" was used at all at the start of the debate, Cayer and a Sorbonne doctor preferred that it be kept nonetheless. The matter of these and other articles was debated for a long time, until the opposing side brought in the royal ministers, who by royal command dissolved the colloquy, since, of course, sedition was feared from it.

units.la: A. cIↄ Iↄ cv i i i. Antverpiae Colloquium habitum inter Franciscum Lansbergium, Concionatorem Rotterodamensem, qui illuc ierat, tempore induciarum, ubi ante occupatam a Parmensi Duce urbem, ministerio fuerat functus, & P. Goudam, praesente Filio Lansbergii Samuele, quoque Pastore Rotterodamensi, & P. Cornelio Cornelii, aliisque octodecim viris honestis, auditoribus: disputatum de transsubstantiatione, & P. Gouda eo absurditatum a Lansbergio adductus fuit, ut palam concesserit, identidemque repetierit, se Christum Deum & hominem in sacramento, non spiritualiter solum, sed & corporaliter, ore corporeo, quemadmodum & mures quoque, ibi consecratam nanciscuntur hostiam, edere, exspuere, addebat & cacare etiam. Quâ audità turpi, sed ingenuâ confessione fidei & doctrinæ Papisticæ, plures ex Auditoribus cum horrore Papatum abjurarunt, & se Ecclesiæ adjunxerunt. Acta disputationis edita sunt,& summam ejus refert in Historiâ suâ Baudartius, Tom. I. lib. III.
units.tr: In 1603 a colloquy was held at Antwerp between Franciscus Lansbergius, preacher of Rotterdam, who had gone there during the truce, having previously served in the ministry in the city before it was occupied by the Duke of Parma, and P. Gouda. Present as listeners were Lansbergius's son Samuel, also a minister of Rotterdam, P. Cornelii, and eighteen other respectable men. The question of transubstantiation was debated, and Lansbergius drove Gouda into such absurdity that he openly conceded, and repeatedly declared, that Christ, God and man, in the sacrament is eaten not only spiritually but also bodily, with the bodily mouth, just as mice too find the consecrated host there and eat it, spit it out, and he added, even defecate it. When this shameful but candid confession of the Papist faith and doctrine was heard, several of the listeners, with horror, renounced Popery and joined the Church. The record of the disputation was published, and Baudartius gives a summary of it in his History, Tom. I. lib. III.

units.la: Anno cIↄ Iↄ cv II I. d. I. Augusti disputavit apud Acidas Swalbacenses Paræus, cum Iesuitis, Becano, Serario, Mulhusino; de Purgatorio, Deo authore peccati &c. quia Becanus ante quadriennium disputationem habuerat Moguntiæ de Deo authore peccati, eâque dixerat, Deum Calvinistarum esse Diabolum: jam in Colloquio Swalbacensi illo, post defensum innocuum Calvini nomen, Paræus eo Adversarios adegit, ut falsi fuerint, ex illâ propositione saltem delendum esse eterum, & quidquid de Calvino sit, male dictum, quod Deus Calvinistarum sit Diabolus. Acta postea Paræus edidit, cum Notis apologeticis.
units.tr: On 1 August 1605 Paraeus disputed at Schwalbach with the Jesuits Becanus, Serarius and Mulhusius, on purgatory, God as the author of sin, and so on. Becanus had four years earlier held a disputation at Mainz on God as the author of sin, and in it had said that the God of the Calvinists is the Devil. Now, in that Schwalbach colloquy, after the innocence of Calvin's name had been defended, Paraeus forced the opponents to admit that they had been wrong; at least the word eterum had to be deleted from that proposition, and whatever might be thought of Calvin, it had been wrongly said that the God of the Calvinists is the Devil. Paraeus later published the proceedings, with apologetic notes.

units.la: A. cIↄ Iↄ cIx. die 19. Septemb.
