Francofurti ad Mænum, inter Clementem Boësium, sive du Boys, Ministrum Hanovien-sem disputatum; & Cosmam Morelles, Professorem apud Prædicatores Coloniæ, qui nundinis Francofurtensibus, Hanoviam profectus, ubi Cappucinum quendam monachum audiverat publice abjurantem religionem Pontificiam, post habitam à Clemente du Boys concionem adeo eximiam, ut ipse Morelles eum Demosthenem Gallicum propterea appellaret, hinc Colloquium cum Nostris expetivit, in quod haud illubentes consenserunt, venerantque Francofurdum prædictus du Boys, Isaacus Genius, quoque minister Ecclesiæ Belgicæ in Hovenbach, cum Timotheo, ejusdem loci Ministro Gallico: ubi disputatum cum Cosmâ Morelles illo, Hispano, de operum meritis; sed cum grossis injuriis & calumniis, uti loquitur Morelles, qui se cholericum nonnihil vivacius & vehementius disputare faebatur, sessione primâ. Colloquium, urgente Nundinarum exitu, finitum, quod & edidit Morelles ex ingenio suo, quantum memoria suggessit, Naturii enim præsentes non interfuere, qui singula quæ & dicebantur & gerebantur annotâssent, sicuti ipse testatur in præfatione, & scripto Coloniæ, super eâdem quæstione, deinceps disputationem prosequutus fuit.
units.tr: On 19 September 1609, at Frankfurt am Main, a disputation was held between Clemens Boësius, or du Boys, minister at Hanau, and Cosmas Morelles, professor among the Preachers at Cologne. Morelles had gone to Hanau during the Frankfurt fair, where he heard a certain Capuchin monk publicly renouncing the Papist religion. After du Boys had preached a sermon so outstanding that Morelles himself called him the French Demosthenes for it, Morelles sought a colloquy with our men, and they agreed to this not unwillingly. The aforesaid du Boys came to Frankfurt, together with Isaac Genius, also minister of the Belgian Church at Hovenbach, and Timotheus, minister of the French congregation in the same place. There the disputation was held with that Spaniard Cosmas Morelles on the merits of works, but, as Morelles puts it, with coarse insults and calumnies, in the first session, in which he claimed to be somewhat more lively and vehement in disputing, being rather choleric. The colloquy was ended, because the end of the fair was pressing. Morelles published it from his own wit, as far as memory suggested, for those present who might have recorded each thing that was both said and done did not attend, as he himself testifies in the preface. He afterwards continued the disputation in a writing at Cologne on the same question.

units.la: Anno cIↄ Iↄ cxvııı. d. xxxı. Iulii Castrieraldi, in Galliâ, institutum Colloquium, ad petitionem locum tenentis regii Pidoux, inter nostræ religionis Iohannem Carre, Paulum Geslinum de la Pittiere, loci ministros, & partis Pontificiæ Iohannem Breard, Doctorem Sorbonicum, Danielem Bandri, Theologiæ ipsorum Baccalaureum: de Purgatorio, invocatione Sanctorum, & Transubstantiatione, sessionibus xıv. quousque authoritate publicâ interdictum ulterius progredi. Quod solitum Adversariorum est artificium, ex illâ figurâ & modo respondere, ad nostram conclusionem. Nam & eodem loci ante, anno cIↄ Iↄ xı. eadem μεθοδῷ disruptum Colloquium, interveniente archiepiscopi Pictavienfis, fuerat, inter Chamierum, & Homblot.
units.tr: On 31 July 1618, at Castres in France, a colloquy was arranged at the request of the royal lieutenant Pidoux, between our religion's John Carré and Paul Geslin de la Pittière, ministers of the place, and from the Papist side John Breard, Sorbonne doctor, and Daniel Bandri, their Bachelor of Theology. It concerned purgatory, the invocation of saints, and transubstantiation, in fourteen sessions, until by public authority it was forbidden to go further. This is the usual trick of the opponents: they answer in that figure and manner to our conclusion. For at the same place earlier, in 1611, a colloquy between Chamier and Homblot had been broken off in the same [μεθόδῳ] manner, through the intervention of the Archbishop of Poitiers.

units.la: Anno cIↄ Iↄ cxxv. d. xıv. Aprilis, indictum authoritate Comitis de Parabere Colloquium fuerat Cognaci, inter Guilielmum Rivetum, & Gilbertum Rousseau, Iesuitam. Quumque Iesuita, ad methodum Veroniamam vellet agere, nec sinere Rivetum argumentari ex Scriptura, per legitime ductas & formatas consequentias, adeoque non convenirent in Colloquii conditionibus, re infecta discessum: Riveto scriptum de vero & recto S. Scriptura usu Gallicum subjungente.
units.tr: On 14 April 1625, a colloquy was called by the authority of the Count de Parabère at Cognac, between William Rivet and Gilbert Rousseau, a Jesuit. Since the Jesuit wished to proceed by the Veronian method and would not allow Rivet to argue from Scripture through legitimately drawn and formed consequences, they did not agree on the conditions of the colloquy, and they parted with the matter undone. Rivet then added a French writing, on the true and right use of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Haud ita pridem anno cIↄ Iↄ cxlv. institutus Conventus Thorunensis fuit, authoritate Regis Poloniæ, Vladislai ıv. d. xviıı. Augusti, fraterna Collatio, seu Colloquium charitatiuum, quomodo appellatur in primâ ejus designatione, anno cIↄIↄ cxlııı. d. xıı. Novembri litteris Synodi Vassaviensis, quibus ut & littera
units.tr: Not long ago, in 1645, the Thorn Convention was arranged by the authority of King Vladislaus IV of Poland, on 18 August, a fraternal conference, or charitable colloquy, as it was called in its first announcement, by the letters of the Synod of Vilnius of 12 November 1643, by which, as also by the letter

units.la: 118 ris Regùs anno cIↄ Iↄ c xlı v. d.xx. Martii Colloquium primò indicebatur in d. x. Octob. anno cIↄ Iↄ c xlıv. quod tempus quia justo angustius, prorogatum fuit. Nostri primum in Synodo Ormoñsi anno cIↄ Iↄ cxlıv. d. xxıv. Augusti, ad Epistolas Regis, & Archiepiscopi, singulas responderunt, & quamvis se multas ob rationes juste vereri dicerent ut is Colloquii foret exitus, quem sperare se Rex significabat, propter ar̄tam illam & absolutam adversæ partis a Papa dependentiam & subjectionem, quo inconsulto nihil quantumvis justum bonumq; (cujus aliqua adferebant exempla) facere illi auderent, propter juramentum quo Papæ essent devincti, & cognita jam essent ipsorum consilia, quod solam cogitarent Nostrorum ad Papatum reductionem, vel nostræ à Papatu secessionis, condemnationem, nullam autem vel Reformationem vel emendationem, sine quâ conciliatio Religionum nulla haberi posset, adeundum tamen Colloquium censebant, quamvis neminę ignorante, alteram partem, cum alia non tantum emendare, sed etiam judicare velit, seipsam ad ullum æquilibrium deducere nolle, uti Nostri respondebant. Scripserat jam episcopus Vilnensis, in suis ad Colloquium evocatoriis, Nostros eò venturos, ad docendum & probandum quomodo illi animas diversarum Nationum & Regnorum, pretiosissimo sanguine Christi redemtas, falsis & perversis suis dogmatibus à veriâ fidei Catholicâ Romanâ Ecclesiâ abducunt, & ad bonorum detrudunt, ad docendum & firmandum in premissô quam se habere pretendunt veritatem. Quæ satis significabant, longe aliud quæri, quam veram conciliationem & concordiam. Initium Colloquii factum anno cIↄ Iↄ c xlv. d. xxvıı. Augusti, inter tres dissidentium Partes, Pontificiorum, Reformatorum, & Lutheranorum, datis singulis partium Præsidibus moderatoribus, Collocutoribus, Notariis, præsente Regis nomine Legato Georgio, Duce Ostrolino. Ex Reformatis præcipui fuerunt, Gorayski, Castellanus Chelmensis. sis ; Theologi, Iohannes Bergius, Reichelius, Georg. Veclincrus, Comenius, Benj. Vrsinus, Ge. Laetus, Samuel Placbta, Ioh. Laetus, Musonius, Reinoldus Adami. Ex Augustanae Confessionis partibus, Hulsemannus, Bothsaccus, Calovius, Cimmermannus, Mochingerus, Iohannes Fabritius, alii. Fateor, leges & normam Colloquii à Rege praescriptam fuisse eximiam, & paucis exceptis, sive scopum, sive modum agendi, & ad scopum perveniendi attendamus, praestantissimam. Articulus primus erat: Imprimis, scopum quem suscepto negotio praefigimus, Concordiam & Unitatem Religionis, ac beatam Ecclesiae Patriaeque Pacem, omnium votis tantopere expetitam, Colloquentes pre oculis habeant, & ut assequantur, totis animi viribus contendant, remotis aliis omnibus intentionibus, quae animos alio, studiaque diverte possunt. Et circa tractationis ordinem, tres faciebant partes, seu periodos: ut prima, utriusque partis sententiae liquido proponerentur: secunda, ad examen veniretur doctrinae: ultima, si quid ad mores dicendum esset, inquireretur.
units.tr: 118 ... the king's letter of 20 March 1645. The colloquy had first been announced for 10 October 1644, but since that time was too short, it was postponed. Our men first answered each of the king's and the archbishop's letters at the Synod of Ormoñsi, on 24 August 1644. Although they said that for many good reasons they greatly feared what the outcome of the colloquy would be, the outcome which the king indicated he hoped for, because of that narrow and absolute dependence and subjection of the opposing party on the Pope, without whose consent they would not dare to do anything, however just and good (they cited some examples of this), because of the oath by which they were bound to the Pope, and because their intentions were already known, namely that they only thought of bringing our people back to Papacy or of condemning our secession from Papacy, and not of any reformation or correction, without which no reconciliation of the religions could be had, nevertheless they judged that the colloquy should be entered upon, although, as our men replied, no one is ignorant that the one side, when it wishes not only to correct but also to judge the other, is unwilling to reduce itself to any equilibrium. The Bishop of Vilnius had already written, in his summonses to the colloquy, that our men would come there to teach and prove how they, by their false and perverse dogmas, lead away from the true Catholic Roman Church the souls of diverse nations and kingdoms redeemed by the most precious blood of Christ, and drive them down to hell; and to teach and confirm in the aforesaid the truth which they claim to have. These words made it plain enough that something quite different was sought than a true reconciliation and concord. The colloquy began on 27 August 1645 between the three divided parties, the Papists, the Reformed and the Lutherans, each party being given its presidents, moderators, speakers and notaries, with the royal legate George, Duke of Ostrog, present. Among the Reformed the leading men were Gorajski, Castellan of Chełm, and the theologians John Bergius, Reichel, George Wejhner, Comenius, Benjamin Ursinus, George Laetus, Samuel Płocki, John Laetus, Musonius and Reinhold Adami. From the side of the Augsburg Confession were Hülsemann, Botsack, Calovius, Zimmermann, Mochinger, John Fabricius and others. I confess that the laws and rules of the colloquy prescribed by the king were excellent, and, with few exceptions, most excellent, whether we look to its aim or its manner of proceeding, and to attaining the aim. The first article was: First of all, let the colloquists keep before their eyes the aim which we set before us in undertaking this business, namely the concord and unity of religion, and the blessed peace of the Church and the homeland, so greatly desired by all, and let them strive with all the strength of their minds to attain it, setting aside all other intentions which can turn minds and efforts elsewhere. And as to the order of the discussion, they made three parts, or periods: first, the opinion of each side was to be clearly set out; second, the doctrine was to be brought to examination; last, if anything had to be said about morals, it was to be inquired into.

units.la: Art. IV. Optamus igitur, ut Collocutores, Tribus generaliter Actionibus, universum negotium complecti velint. Ac in Prima quidem investigent quam accuratissime propriam & genuinam singularum Partium Doctrinam & Sententiam. In altera, de Veritate vel Falsitate Doctrinae conferant. In tertia, si quid circa Fidem & Mores controversum sit, discutiant. Primum appellabant, doctrinae liquidationem & sinceracionem. Art. 5. Primum, id est, perfectam totius Doctrinae liquidationem & Sinceracionem permagnificamus; cum compertum Nobis sit, maximam jam Praesentium malorum causam esse, sinistrae Partium Intelligentiae, & hoc uno fomite, tam luctuosum dissidium in hoc inprimis Regno foveri. Atque id sane bene: nam in omni disputatione permagni momenti est, primum ut constet de statu controversiae, ex partium sincera expositione, missis omnibus adjectionibus, consequentiis, calumniis, vel odiosis explicationibus.
units.tr: Art. IV. We therefore wish that the speakers should be willing to embrace the whole business in three general actions. In the first they should investigate as accurately as possible the proper and genuine doctrine and opinion of each party. In the second they should confer on the truth or falsity of the doctrine. In the third, whatever is in dispute concerning faith and morals should be discussed. The first they called the clarification and purification of doctrine. Art. 5. The first, that is, the complete clarification and purification of the whole doctrine, we greatly commend, since we have learned that the greatest cause of present evils is the perverse understanding of the parties, and that by this one tinder so sad a dissension is fostered, especially in this kingdom. And rightly so: for in every disputation it is of the greatest importance that, first, the state of the controversy be established from the sincere exposition of the parties, with all additions, consequences, calumnies, or hateful explanations set aside.

units.la: Quemadmodum in litteris suis Rex, datis anno clɔ lɔ c xlvı. d. xxv. Martii, post habitum Colloquium: Ergò hæc unica cura sit eorum, qui pacem profligatam revocare cupiunt, ut semotis omnibus officiis, genuina Partium Doctrina in apertum prodeant, illis palam fatentibus quod affirmant, iisdemque nequaquam imputantibus quod negant. Tum verò primum secernatur deerratus error, fiatque periculum an sufficiere tenebræ valeant fulgorem veritatis. Atque, uti paulo ante loquitur: Præcipuus desiderium Nostrorum scopus erat LIQVIDATIO DOCTRINARVM. Iam enim pridem compertum Nobis & persuasissimum est, Arcem præsentis Dissidii esse SINISTRAS INTELLIGENTIAS; caput concordiæ INTEGRATIONEM VERITATIS. Atque ita voluit Rex, priori hac parte agi, non unam hanc vel illam partem veram sentire, sed quid vera sentiat. Deinde alteri parti disputationem assignat, neutiquam vero talem, quæ in contentionem, sed quæ in convenientiam desinat & conciliationem. Art. ix. Quoad alteram Actionem, quâ de Veritate vel Falsitate alterutrius Doctrinæ differendum ducimus, intelligant Omnes, non esse, nec unquam fuisse mentis Nostræ, permittere, ut Partes infestæ hinc inde disputationibus se impetant, à quibus tantopere abhorremus, ut ne quidem disputationis nomen, in tota hac negotio usurpari unquam voluerimus. Didicimus enim, experimento multis seculis, interminatas illas argumentorum conflictationes, in majores fere rixas desinere, & post longos conatus, vix fieri posse, ut Divina Veritas solidioribus & validioribus firmetur argumentis, quam hactenus firmata est. Ego valde hoc postremum noto, & revera observandum est, quod Rex de assiduis per integrum seculum iisdem de rebus disputationibus pronunciat, eo usque eas perductas esse, ut vix videatur ulterioribus rationibus res firmari utrimque posse, quam hactenus firmata est. Adeo ferè idem agitur à variis Scriptoribus, dum ad candem disputationem raro alia adhibentur, quam jam allata à Prioribus fuerunt. Neque minus annoto, ex legibus Colloquii, à Rege prescriptis, undecimam hanc: Quamvis autem certum Nobis sit, quibusvis Religionum dissidiis, sincere difficulter imponi posse, nisi praesit animatus Iudex, qui audiri possit, & cujus sententia necesse sit acquiescere; non diffidimus tamen, pacificam, fraternamque collationem, rite peractam, maximum habitorum momentum, si abrogatis falsis imputationibus, & sepultis, sepultisque veteribus odiis, vel novis diffidentiis, integre & sincere judicare velint. Quibus verbis animatum judicem (qualis Papa) ab hujusmodi actione hactenus removet; neque adeo audiendum censet, cujus loco rem etiam peragere possint alii, quarumcunque partium Theologi, pacificâ, fraternâque collatione. Quae utroque pollice approbanda existimo. Denique id quod articulo XXIV. dicitur, omnibus, praesertim Theologis, atque imprimis Pontificiis commendandum: Priusquam Partes Thoruniò abeant, diligenter Postremis Sessionibus Acta recolligant. Videantque id illud sit, quod maximè obfuit, & deinceps obesse possit optatissimae Pacis & Unitatis: Et quidquid illud sit, tantumne pondus habeat, ut tanto Nos debeat privare bono. Quâ in re felicitè & clementer hortamur, tum Legatum Nostrum, partimque Deputatos, & Moderatores, tum Colloquutores ipsos, ut cordatè introspiciant, quid in re tanti momenti militer consuli statuique possit. Postquam diutius hinc inde de Conditionibus Colloquii disceptatum, tum de titulis ac praesertim de titulo Catholici, in appellatione mutuâ, & scriptione Actorum adhibendo, quem ut sibi proprium Pontificii volebant, ita ut eo nostri pro A Catholicis haberentur, vel quibus non meliori jure nomen Catholici competeret, non ferendum censebant: inde traditis invicem scriptis pro liquidatione doctrinae, Pontificii, de multis sibi temerè attributis opinionibus aut consequentiis circa doctrinam suam de regulâ fidei, de justificatione, de sacramentis, de cultu conquesti fuerunt: Neque refert quòd aliqui per syllogisticas Conse-quenquæstiones istiusmodi propositiones recte se inferre, & juste no-bis imputare existimēt. Videndum enim est cui magis credendum sit, nobis simpliciter, aperte & in terminis terminantibus propositionem negantis, an alteri per Consequentiam (quam ipsam legitimam esse nego) eandem mihi imputanti? Denique quando recusarent Pontificii scripta Nostrorum in Acta referre, quemadmodum alia, & sua, Confessionem & Declarationem doctrinæ Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, quæ postea separatim typis excusa Berolini, anno clɔ Iɔ cxlvi. atque etiam tempus interim Colloquii, à Rege concessum, quod trimestre erat, exspiraret, solutum fuit, mutuâ valedictione & in fraternâ charitate, d. xxi. Novemb. sessionibus xxxvi. Institutum erat, ad sacram Ecclesiasticam unionem atque concordiam, uti expressum in litteris instructionis & missionis, ab Archiepiscopo Gnesnensi ad suarum partium Theologos: unde sess. xvii. Iesuita Schonhoff: dicam brevibus & apertis verbis, Nos pacem & concordiam volumus, per consensum in unam eandemque doctrinam. Deinde cultum. Quâ occasione solerter uti, & qualitercunque oblatam pacis speciem, amputatis omnibus quæstionibus præliminaribus & circumstantialibus, arripere, atque ad rem ipsam protinus accedere, & vel in bonum Ecclesiæ omnia illa veitere, aut animum ipsorum & insidias confestim detegere, oportet. Quod, absque multo prologo, vel verbo haberi potest. Quippe hoc unum duntaxat ipsos interrogo, existimentnè, quo ad illam ecclesiasticam doctrinæ unionem perveniatur, Ecclesiam ipsorum Romanam in doctrinâ corrigi, aut reformari posse, ac debere; an non? affirmandum hic, aut negandum est. Si illud, bene, atque arripimus ut argumentum Ecclesiæ Romanæ fallibilis: sin hoc srustra jam cum illis agimus, qui suam Ecclesiam putant ita non errare, ut neque errare possit. Hieronymus à S. Hyacintho dixit, sess. xx ii.
units.tr: As the King stated in his letter, dated 25 March 1645, after the colloquy had been held: "Therefore let this be the sole concern of those who wish to restore the broken peace, that, with all duties set aside, the genuine doctrine of the parties may come openly forward, each openly confessing what they affirm and in no way imputing to the other what they deny. Then indeed the error that has gone astray will first be separated out, and it will be tested whether darkness can overcome the brightness of truth." And, as he says a little earlier: "The chief aim of our desire was THE CLARIFICATION OF DOCTRINES. For it has long been known and is thoroughly persuaded to Us that the citadel of the present dissension is PERVERSE UNDERSTANDINGS; the head of concord is THE INTEGRATION OF TRUTH." And so the King wished that in this first part the matter should be handled not so that each party may hold this or that as true, but so that it may see what is true. Then he assigns the second part to disputation, yet by no means such a disputation as ends in contention, but one that ends in agreement and reconciliation. Art. 9. "As to the second action, in which we judge that the truth or falsity of each doctrine is to be debated, let all understand that it was never our intention to permit hostile parties to attack one another with disputations on this side and that, from which we so greatly shrink that we have never wished even the name of disputation to be used in this whole business. For we have learned by experience over many centuries that those endless clashes of arguments usually end in greater quarrels, and that after long efforts it is hardly possible that Divine Truth be confirmed by solider and stronger arguments than it has been hitherto." I note this last point strongly, and indeed it must be observed: the King declares that, after constant disputations on the same matters over a whole century, they have been carried so far that the matter scarcely seems capable of being confirmed on either side by further arguments than have already been brought forward. So nearly the same things are being urged by various writers, since for the same disputation scarcely anything is adduced other than what the earlier writers had already offered. Nor do I note less, from the laws of the colloquy prescribed by the King, this eleventh: "Although it is certain to Us that, with any dissension of religions, sincere agreement can hardly be imposed unless there is present an animated judge who can be heard, and whose judgment it is necessary to accept, yet We do not doubt that a peaceful and brotherly conference, duly carried out, will be of the greatest weight, if, with false imputations set aside and old hatreds, or new distrusts, buried and buried again, they wish to judge wholly and sincerely." By these words he hitherto removes an animated judge (such as the Pope) from this kind of action, and does not think it necessary to hear him, since in his place other theologians of whatever parties can carry the matter through by a peaceful and brotherly conference. These things I judge to be approved with both thumbs. Finally, what is said in article 24 is to be commended to all, especially to the theologians, and above all to the Papists: "Before the parties depart from Thorn, let them diligently recollect the acts of the last sessions. Let them see what that thing was which has most hindered, and can hereafter hinder, the most desired peace and unity; and whatever it may be, let them consider whether it has so much weight that it ought to deprive us of so great a good." In this matter we happily and kindly urge both our Legate, and some of the deputies and moderators, and the speakers themselves, to look carefully into what may be wisely decided and settled in a matter of such great moment. After there had been long dispute on both sides about the conditions of the colloquy, and about titles, and especially about the title of Catholic, which the Papists wished to be used as their own in mutual address and in the writing of the acts, so that our people would thereby be considered Catholics, or those to whom the name of Catholic would belong by no better right, they judged this unbearable. Then, when written statements had been exchanged for clarifying doctrine, the Papists complained that many opinions or consequences had been rashly attributed to them concerning their doctrine of the rule of faith, of justification, of the sacraments, and of worship: "It makes no difference that some think that by syllogistic consequences they rightly infer such propositions and justly impute them to us. For it must be considered whom we should rather believe: us, who simply, openly, and in plain terms deny the proposition, or another who imputes the same to me by a consequence (which I deny to be legitimate)?" Finally, when the Papists refused to enter into the acts the writings of our people, as well as others of their own, the Confession and Declaration of the doctrine of the Reformed Churches (which was afterward printed separately at Berlin in 1646), and when the time of the colloquy granted by the King, which was three months, had run out, it was dissolved "with mutual farewell and in brotherly charity" on 21 November, at the thirty-sixth session. It had been instituted "for the sacred ecclesiastical union and concord," as expressed in the letters of instruction and commission from the Archbishop of Gniezno to the theologians of his party. Whence, at the seventeenth session, the Jesuit Schonhoff said: "I shall say in brief and open words: we want peace and concord, through agreement in one and the same doctrine. Then worship." On this occasion one must use skilfully, and seize upon in whatever way offered, the appearance of peace, with all preliminary and incidental questions cut away, and go straight to the matter itself, and either turn all those things to the good of the Church or at once expose their intention and snares. This can be done without much preface, or in a word. For I ask them only this: do they think that, in order to reach that ecclesiastical unity of doctrine, their Roman Church can and must be corrected or reformed in doctrine, or not? Here one must either affirm or deny. If the former, well and good; we take it up as an argument that the Roman Church is fallible. But if the latter, we are wasting our time with those who think their Church does not err in such a way that it cannot even err. Hieronymus à St Hyacinth said at the twenty-second session:

units.la: Nunquam fidem nostram Catholicam antiquissimâ possessione sue certitudinis, tot seculis firmatam, alea presentis Colloquii animus fuit exponere &c. Longe alia est fidei nostrae Catholicae conditio, quam ut disputationibus infallibilis sue veritatis, & certitudinis a nobis subjici unquam debeat, vel patiatur. Hoc si sit, quorsum nobiscum Colloquium petunt, disputationem, unionem? Siquidem nos Reformati ex prima nominis nostri professione, Ecclesiae Romanae doctrinam erroris notamus, eamque corrigendam, in doctrina primo quidem, dicimus: unde quam non in unam eandemque cum iis doctrinam concedere possimus, facile liquet, dum illi quam diximus doctrinae suae infallibilis thesin, constanter tuentur, Nos in illorum doctrinam consentire non possumus, nisi negata nostra, & abdicato nostro nomine, quod tum foret, non Ecclesias consentire invicem, vel duas inter se unire partes, sed transire in alteram. Quemadmodum quando Synagoga ad nos accedit, non fit unio Iudaismi, & Christianismi, vel pax aliqua aut convenientia in eandem doctrinam inter utrosque, vel inter partes; sed simplex illius ad nostras conversio. Atqui hoc si intenderint Pontificii, Nos ad se allicere, utique quid hoc aut novi, aut ut specie Colloquii charitativi, sub σαφνίς unionis Ecclesiasticae, tentaretur? Idque cum tanta disputationis devitatione, ut ab ejus ideo nomine etiam abstinuerit Rex, in Colloquii designatione. Quorsum ista aperte, sincere, nudatis agatur frontibus. Si velint uniri in eandem doctrinam utrasque Ecclesias, Romanam debent sistere emendabilem, secus laterem laveris: si nos tantum velint reducere in suam Ecclesiam, quid ad hoc Colloquio opus; & tali charitativo, quum id universale ipsorum negotium sit? & quomodo id queat aliter peragi quam disputatione, & hac quidem unice? ut quam disputationem videri voluit hoc Colloquium cavere, eam solam quidem ex illa hypothesi sectari debuerit. Quamdiu illa tria tenent Adversarii, Ecclesia suae infallibilitatem, Romani Pontificis authoritatem, & Concilii Tridentini veritatem, seu in rebus religionis canonem, frustra est ut de conciliatione utriusque Ecclesiarum & doctrinarum cogitetur. Atque illa velim protinus iis semper objici, quando specioso conciliationum titulo nos adoriuntur, ut ex responsione tum statim de omni negotio liqueat. Quare dum sess. ix. pro principio ad liquidationem doctrinae suae proponebant Concilium Tridentinum, hoc unum modo petendum, an isti Concilio inhaerent immobiliter ut infallibili principio, an vero patiantur illud ad examen reduci, & emendari? Si illud (neque enim istud dicent), verbum frustra additur, dum quo loco nos Concilium illud habeat, satis notum, certe non pro conciliandis secum in doctrina ullatenus. Ante Concilium Tridentinum, nondum in istam formam vallatis Pontificiorum rebus, per tot tamque dira in Nos anathemata, praecipue ubi non egre admittebatur, Romanam Ecclesiam in nonnullis corrigi debere, & praesertim posse, denique & potestas Romani Pontificis non in istam amplitudinem extendebatur vel agnoscebatur, ac jam major aliquanto apparuit occasio conciliandarum quacunque ratione partium: sed jam post illa omnia validius definita, & amplexa acrius, ut de partium unione serio adhuc agatur, est impossibilia captare, & fere (quod dicunt) luctari cum Coryco. Speciosum quidem, fateor, nomen pacis est, sed sincerae, sed justae, & ubi proponitur non possibilis modo, sed facilis? at ubi omnia secus se habent, & nec proba offertur, neque ex animo, & quam feceris undiquaque inaccessam, est, quod dici solet, thesaurus carbones.
units.tr: "Never has our Catholic faith, confirmed through so many centuries by the most ancient possession of its certainty, been willing to expose itself to the chance of the present colloquy..." &c. The condition of our Catholic faith is far different, so that it ought never to be subjected to disputations about its infallible truth and certainty, nor can it suffer this. If this is so, why do they seek a colloquy with us, a disputation, a union? For we Reformed, from the very first profession of our name, mark the doctrine of the Roman Church as erroneous, and we say that it must first of all be corrected in doctrine. Hence it is easily clear how we can concede no one and the same doctrine with them, as long as they stubbornly maintain the thesis of the infallibility of their doctrine that I have mentioned. We cannot agree with their doctrine unless our own is denied and our name abdicated, and that would mean not that Churches agree with each other or that two parties unite, but that one passes over into the other. Just as, when the Synagogue comes over to us, there is no union of Judaism and Christianity, nor any peace or agreement in one doctrine between the two sides, but simply that one is converted to ours. But if the Papists intend this, namely to win us over to themselves, what is new about this, or what is attempted under the appearance of a charitable colloquy, under the pretext of ecclesiastical union? And this with such great avoidance of disputation that the King, in the designation of the colloquy, for this reason even refrained from its name. Let the matter be carried on openly, sincerely, with faces bared. If both Churches wish to unite in one and the same doctrine, they must present the Roman Church as correctable; otherwise you are washing a brick. If they wish only to bring us back into their Church, what need is there of this colloquy, and of such a charitable one, since it is their universal business? And how can this be done otherwise than by disputation, and indeed by that alone? So the disputation that this colloquy wished to appear to avoid ought, on that hypothesis, to have been the only one pursued. As long as our adversaries hold those three things, the infallibility of the Church, the authority of the Roman Pontiff, and the truth of the Council of Trent, or the canon in matters of religion, it is vain to think of reconciling the two Churches and doctrines. And I would like those points to be always put to them at once whenever they attack us under the specious title of reconciliations, so that from their answer the whole matter may be clear at once. Therefore, when at the ninth session they proposed the Council of Trent as the principle for clarifying their doctrine, the only thing to ask is this: do they cling immovably to that Council as an infallible principle, or do they allow it to be brought under examination and corrected? If the former (for they will not say the latter), the word "in vain" is added, since it is well enough known where that Council places us, and certainly not for reconciliation in doctrine in any way. Before the Council of Trent, when the affairs of the Papists were not yet fortified in that form, through so many and such dire anathemas against us, it was especially not grudgingly admitted that the Roman Church should be corrected in some points, and above all could be; and finally the power of the Roman Pontiff was not extended or acknowledged to that vast degree, and so a somewhat greater occasion appeared of reconciling the parties by whatever means. But now, since all those things have been more strongly defined and more fiercely embraced, to treat seriously of a union of parties still is to seek impossibilities, and, as they say, to wrestle with a Corycian (a sea-urchin?). The name of peace is indeed specious, I admit, but it is of a sincere and just peace, and where it is offered not merely as possible but easy? Yet where all things stand otherwise, and neither a sound offer is made, nor one from the heart, and which, however you approach it, is inaccessible on every side, it is what they commonly call "a treasure of coals."

units.la: A. MDCXLVI. Rex Angliae Carolus disputavit ad Raglani castrum, cum Marchione VVorcestriae Henrico, quae edita disputatio a Thoma Baylie, Theol. Doctore, tit. Certamen religiosum, Anglice. Certe de variis gravissimisque articulis ibi actum, ex tempore primum, imo noctu, dein scripto, & promte accurateque hinc inde responsum, ut non seculares, sed exercitatos Theologos egisse dixeris.
units.tr: In 1646 King Charles of England disputed at Raglan Castle with Henry, Marquess of Worcester. The disputation was published by Thomas Baylie, Doctor of Theology, under the title Certamen religiosum, in English. Many very weighty articles were discussed there, first extemporaneously, indeed by night, and then in writing, and answers were given promptly and carefully on both sides, so that you would say the disputants were not laymen but practised theologians.

units.la: Denique ultima, quam scimus, Disputatio cum Pontificiis per Colloquium habita fuit nuperrime ad finem praecedentis anni clɔ Iɔ clı, d. xvı, Decembris, ad d. xxı ı. ejusdem mensis, scripto; nisi quod d. xx. habita fuerit disputatio ore, dictata ad calamum; omnium in gratiam Ernesti, Hassiæ Landgravii, ad Papatum deficientis; inter Haberkornium, Mentzerum, Happelium, Theologos Aug. Confess. Giessenses; & Valerianum Magnum, Riginaldum Drost, & Paulum Pistorfeld Cappucinos, in arce Rheinfelsā. Cujusmodi Colloquia per χαριν πλιπικὸν magis quaeri tum solent ob praetextum, cui defectionem imputent certò constitutam, quam pro instructione, aut arcendo desectionis periculo. Disputatum hic de primario dissensionis articulo, infallibilitate & primatu Romani Pontificis, ubi istam thesim à se confirmandam proponebat Valerianus: Innocentius Papa x. Episcopus Romanus habet infallibilem jurisdictionem, super universam Ecclesiam Christi. Primum hic observanda, quæ sponte ante conflictum, Act. 11. concesserat Valerianus; nimirum, istam suam thesim non posse probari ex Sacrā S. nullamque in eā mentionem fieri Pontificis Romani, uti nec eandem confirmari posse ex ullā authoritate Ecclesiasticā, vel Ecclesiæ decreto: id est, dico ego, neque ex verbo Dei scripto, neque ex non scripto, quod utrumque ipsorum in rebus fidei est principium. Adeoque fundamentum Ecclesiæ, & articulus religionis ipsorum primarius probari, ipsis palam fatentibus, nullo modo potest.
units.tr: Lastly, the most recent disputation with the Papists that we know of was held by colloquy at the end of the previous year, 1652, from 16 to 21 December, in writing. Only on the 20th was there an oral disputation, dictated to the pen. All of it was held for the sake of Ernest, Landgrave of Hesse, who was falling away from the Papacy. The disputants were, on the Augsburg Confession side, the Giessen theologians Haberkorn, Mentzer and Happel, and, on the other side, the Capuchins Valerian Magni, Reginald Drost and Paul Pistorfeld, in the castle of Rheinfels. Colloquies of this kind are usually sought more for political reasons [χάριν πολιτικόν], to provide a pretext to which they can impute a defection already decided upon, than for instruction or to avert the danger of defection. The dispute here concerned the primary point of difference, the infallibility and primacy of the Roman Pontiff, where Valerian proposed for confirmation this thesis: "Innocent X, Pope and Roman Bishop, has infallible jurisdiction over the whole Church of Christ." First, what Valerian had voluntarily conceded before the conflict, see Act. 11., must be noted: namely, that his thesis cannot be proved from Holy Scripture, that no mention of the Roman Pontiff is made in it, and that it cannot be confirmed by any ecclesiastical authority or decree of the Church. That is, I say, it cannot be proved either from the written Word of God or from the unwritten, which are both the principles of their faith in matters of religion. Hence, as they themselves openly confess, the foundation of the Church and their primary article of religion cannot in any way be proved.

units.la: Audiamus ipsum: Post ætatem D. Petri Pontifices Romani successores ejus habent auctoritatem infallibilem in proponenda, & declaranda universæ Ecclesiæ ex cathedrâ, fidei Christianæ doctrina, & jurisdictionem segregandi à cætu fidelium eos omnes, qui contumaciter eam pernegant. Hanc, inquam, thesin non quæsimus inferre ex solo textu sacro, (siquidem in bibliis nulla sit mentio Pontificis Romani, sed neque ab authoritate Iudicii ecclesiastici possumus praecise sine argumento theologico confirmare illam thesin. Nos enim inter decreta ecclesiastica, fidem concernentia, nullum scimus, quod Pontifici Romano tribuat expresse infallibilitatem authoritatis. Non ex solo textu sacro: ergo neutiquam ex textu sacro. Nam si aliunde, hoc vel ex textu sacro probat, vel ex alio tantum [illegible, ~2 letters], vel utroque: si illud, ergo eo continetur, & ex eo etiam solo hactenus probari potest. Sin illud, ergo neutiquam ex sacris. Et hoc si dicatur, quaero an rei substantia & fundamentum ex sacro textu probari possit, an non? atque pro data responsione, eo vel continebitur, vel non: si non, fundamentum erit ἀγράφον[?]; sin imo, ergo id hactenus ex eo solo etiam probari poterit. Quomodo, Deum esse, & bonum, potentemque potest probari ex Scriptura & ratione; sed quamvis etiam hinc, tamen ex solo textu sacro quoque. Quare quod non ex solo textu sacro probari potest, id hactenus neque ex eo: quoniam ex textu sacro probatio bona instituitur, sive per expressa verba, sive per legitimam consequentiam. Deinde, si in Bibliis nulla sit mentio Pontificis Romani, ergo neque Pontificatus Romani: si enim hoc foret, illud dici non posset. Quare, frustra sunt omnes Pontificii, ipseque adeo Valerianus, qui illum ex Scriptura Matth. xvi. 18. trahere satagit; atque improbum est, vel ejusmodi articulum, nullo Scripturae fundamento subnixum, facere Ecclesiae fundamentum, aut propter eum non agnitum alias Ecclesias, hominesque innumeros condemnare. Temere ergo etiam hactenus alii infallibilitatem authoritatis Papalis ex decretis & authoritate Ecclesiastica conati fuerunt stabilire. Pergit: probamus tamen ab authoritate Iudicii ecclesiastici, has septem propositiones. 1. Pontifex Romanus est successor D. Petri Principis Apostolorum. 2. Pontifex Romanus tenet primatum in universam orbem. 3. Est verus Christi Vicarius. 4. Est caput totius Ecclesiae. 5. Est omnium Christiastianorum Pater. 6. Et Doctor. 7. Cui à Domino nostro Iesu Christo in Beato Petro tradita est plena potestas pascendi, regendi & gubernandi universam Ecclesiam. Patres enim Oecumenicae Florentinae synodi cum Eugenio IV. Pontifice Romano quaestionem de primatu Pontificis Romani definierunt his verbis; Item diffinimus sanctam Apostolicam sedem, & Romanum Pontificem in universum orbem tenere primatum, & ipsum Pontificem Romanum successorem esse Beati Petri Principis Apostolorum, & verum Christi Vicarium, totiusque Ecclesiae caput, & omnium Christianorum Patrem & Doctorem existere, & ipsi in Beato Petro pascendi, regendi, & gubernandi universalem Ecclesiam, à Domino nostro Iesu Christo plenam potestatem traditam esse. Porrò ne quis existimaret eam definitionem esse novam, cautum est his verbis; Quemadmodum etiam in gestis Oecumenicorum Conciliorum, & in sacris canonibus continetur, quae immediatè subsequuntur praefatam definitionem ejusdem Concilii. Nos Pontificem Romanum maiori ratione asserimus nec esse successorem Petri, nec primatum tenere in universum orbem, neque Christi vicarium esse, aut caput totius Ecclesiae, vel omnium Christianorum Patrem, & Doctorem, neque facto, neque jure: & cui talem potestatem dicere traditam in Beato Petro, est delirare verius, quam sapere: utpote qualem quantamque Petrus neque unquam habuit, neque exercuit; & si habuisset, non personalem, sed realem & successivam fuisse, denique ad hos quasi ejus successores Papas Romanos devolutam esse, nemo unquam ullâ vel minimâ specie rationis ostendat. Sed, en Synodum Florentinam. Risum profecto istud debet, ex hac demum Synodo rei illius decisionem petere. Quare non potius ex Synodo Romanâ, sub Gregorio VII. de quâ nos supra diximus? vel an illam ignoravit Valerianus, aut suspectam habuit. Hæc autem Florentina habita anno cIↄ ccccxxviii. Totergo sæculis vel non obtinuit ille primatus Papalis? vel non fuit articulus fidei? neque que in Dei verbo, neque in Ecclesiâ definitus? Et quomodo hic demum definitus? cujus decisioni neque Graeci omnes, qui interfuerunt, interque eos praecipuus Marcus Ephesinus, steterunt, neque reliqui in Oriente, ubi ad eos reversi illi ex Synodo Graeci. Et in Synodo, quando hanc controversiam compositam volebat P. Eugenius, responderunt: Se nullam adhuc respondendi facultatem habere, quare & nolebant consentiente Imperatore, ut de alia quaestione praeter illam de Spiritus Sancti processione, in Unionis litteris ulla mentio fieret. Tandem circumventi & superati à Papâ, haec etiam admiserunt Graeci, & in litteris unionis inserta fuerunt: verum, quod Valerianus inquit, nequis existimaret definitionem esse novam, cautum esse his verbis: Quemadmodum etiam in gestis Oecumenicorum Conciliorum, & in sacris canonibus continetur, quae immediate subsequuntur praefatam definitionem ejusdem Concilii. dolum, vel artem Valeriani ostendunt. Quis enim ista, quae immediate subsequuntur praefatam definitionem ejusdem Concilii, non ita capiat, ut decisioni illi annexa fuerint Conciliorum priscorum decreta? praesertim qui sciat, in illâ Synodo ad agitatam quaestionem de processione Spiritus Sancti multa Veterum testimonia passim adducta fuisse, etiamque ad disputationem illam de primatu Papae, letas esse Graecorum Doctorum de summi Pontificis potestate sententias? & tamen nihil tale in definitione Concilii, ubi haec modo: & gubernandi universalem ecclesiam à Domino nostro Iesu Christo plenam potestatem traditam esse, quemadmodum etiam in gestis oecumenicorum Conciliorum, & in sacris Canonibus continetur. Quare illa Valeriani, quae immediate subsequuntur praefatam definitionem ejusdem Concilii, intelligenda sunt, quae verba; non uti videntur capienda illa verba esse, quae Decreta. Deinde, non dicit ista Florentina, definitionem illam factam fuisse in praecedentibus Oecumenicis Conciliis: nam hoc si fuisset, non dixisset Valerianus, se inter decreta. creta Ecclesiastica, fidem concernentia, nullum scire, quod Pontifici Romano tribuat infallibilitatem auctoritatis; neque missis illis se astrinxisset recenti definitioni Concilii Florentini: sed dicit, qualitercunque tantum Romani Pontificis illam potestatem contineri Concilis. Cui opponimus, quod utcunque Papa Romanus semper quidem studuerit variis modis atque in Conciliis etiam, illam potestatem sibi arrogare, non minus tamen in Conciliis ista ejus arrogantia, à potioribus retusa fuit atque castigata. Quod si canones intelligant Florentini illi Patres, veterum Oecumenicorum Conciliorum, pro illa Papae potestate hic definita, uti in Sacris Canonibus contineri eam expresse ajunt, & sic cum illis Valerianus: aperte dico, illud falsum esse; neque ex ullo oecumenico Concilio (inspectis omnibus quae ipsi adeo Pontificii pro talibus habent, & numerant ante Florentinum hoc, quindecim) canonem illum proferri posse. Quare & Florentinum Concilium falsi arguo, unicum Pontificiae infallibilitatis Ecclesiasticum (juxta ipsos) fundamentum, quod illud asserit; adeo neque Valeriano probatum, ut ante hoc, nullum aliud Ecclesiasticum decretum, vel Concilium pro eadem re scire se palam professus fuerit. Pergit Valerianus in Colloquio, eadem Actione secunda: Et quandoquidem hæc definitio non arctat auctoritatem Romani Pontificis ad Concilium sive Generale sive non Generale: Nos eam pronuntiamus talem, qualem Christus concessit Petro, & Petrus exercuit in actis Apostolorum, qualemcunque Romani Pontifices exercuerunt, & etiamnum exercent, non obstantibus quibuscunque contrarium sentientibus, & demum qualem Patres Oecumenicae Florentinae synodi definiverc. Ergo jam haec tua est argumentatio, non Concilii definitio, quam nos tam facile pronunciamus falsam sictamque, ac tu adfers. Subjungit: Verum, cum Patres illius concilii non tribuant Romano Pontifici verbis expressis infallibilitatem auctoritatis, illam dari theologice argumentamur hoc modo.Hic jam iterum argumentum Ecclesiasticum, quod solum adferre potuit, relinquit, & theologice agendum existimat. Inter Ecclesiasticum vero, & Theologicum ita initio distinxerat: Iudex Ecclesiasticus Iurisdictione directiva proponit, & declarat doctrinam fidei Christianae, quam, qui non crediderit, condemnatur, & coercitiva damnat haeresin, & separat haereticum a coetu fidelium. Theologus vero caret omni potestate coercitiva: directivam autem habet sine ulla iurisdictione, scilicet, non aliam ab illa, quam exercet Orator supra Auditores, vel ad summum Magister supra discipulos. Praeterea, satis expresserunt Florentini Patres, quid Romano Pontifici tribuendum videretur, & tamen non infallibilitatem authoritatis, nec expresse, nec implicite: adeo ut si etiam standum esset Concilio huic Florentino, neque sequeretur tamen ista fundamentalis Ecclesiae Papalis thesis, in tantum neque Ecclesiastice, neque Theologice probabilis.
units.tr: Let us hear the man himself: After the age of St Peter, the Roman Pontiffs, his successors, have an infallible authority in proposing and declaring to the whole Church, from the chair, the doctrine of the Christian faith, and a jurisdiction to cut off from the assembly of the faithful all who obstinately deny it. This thesis, I say, we do not seek to derive from the sacred text alone (since there is no mention of the Roman Pontiff in the Bible), but neither can we confirm that thesis strictly from the authority of ecclesiastical judgment without a theological argument. For among the ecclesiastical decrees concerning faith, we know of none that expressly grants the Roman Pontiff infallibility of authority. Not from the sacred text alone: therefore by no means from the sacred text. For if he proves it from elsewhere, he proves it either from the sacred text, or from something else alone [illegible, about two letters], or from both. If from the former, then it is contained in the text and can be proved from it alone so far. If not, then by no means from the sacred writings. And if he says this, I ask whether the substance and foundation of the matter can be proved from the sacred text or not. Whichever answer is given, it will either be contained there or not. If not, the foundation will be unwritten [ἀγράφον]; but if it is, then it can be proved from that text alone. It is as with the proof that God exists, and is good and powerful: this can be proved from Scripture and reason, but even so, it can also be proved from the sacred text alone. Hence what cannot be proved from the sacred text alone cannot be proved from it at all, since a sound proof is drawn from the sacred text, whether by express words or by a legitimate consequence. Further, if there is no mention of the Roman Pontiff in the Bible, then there is no Roman Pontificate either; for if there were, it could not be said that there is none. So all the Papists are wasting their effort, and Valerian himself too, who labours to derive it from Scripture, Matthew 16:18. It is also wrong to make such an article, resting on no scriptural foundation, the foundation of the Church, or on account of it to condemn the other churches and countless men who do not acknowledge it. So too, hitherto, others have rashly tried to establish the infallibility of papal authority from decrees and ecclesiastical authority. He goes on: Nevertheless we prove these seven propositions from the authority of ecclesiastical judgment. 1. The Roman Pontiff is the successor of St Peter, prince of the Apostles. 2. The Roman Pontiff holds the primacy over the whole world. 3. He is the true Vicar of Christ. 4. He is the head of the whole Church. 5. He is the Father of all Christians. 6. And their Teacher. 7. To him, in blessed Peter, full power of feeding, ruling and governing the universal Church has been handed over by our Lord Jesus Christ. For the Fathers of the Ecumenical Council of Florence, with Pope Eugenius IV, defined the question of the primacy of the Roman Pontiff in these words: "We also define that the holy Apostolic See and the Roman Pontiff hold the primacy over the whole world, and that the Roman Pontiff himself is the successor of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and the true Vicar of Christ, and the head of the whole Church, and the Father and Teacher of all Christians, and that to him in blessed Peter full power of feeding, ruling and governing the universal Church has been handed over by our Lord Jesus Christ." Moreover, lest anyone think this definition is new, it is guarded by these words: "As is also contained in the acts of the Ecumenical Councils and in the sacred canons, which immediately follow the aforesaid definition of the same Council." We assert, with far greater reason, that the Roman Pontiff is neither the successor of Peter, nor holds the primacy over the whole world, nor is the Vicar of Christ, or the head of the whole Church, or the Father and Teacher of all Christians, neither in fact nor in right. And to say that such a power, of such a kind, was handed over to him in blessed Peter is to rave rather than to reason; for Peter neither ever had nor exercised such a power, and even if he had, it would not have been personal but real and successive, and finally, that it has been passed down to these so-called successors, the Roman Popes, no one has ever shown with the slightest appearance of reason. But, behold, the Council of Florence! It is truly laughable to seek the settlement of that matter from this Council alone. Why not rather from the Roman Synod under Gregory VII, of which we spoke above? Or did Valerian not know of it, or did he hold it in suspicion? This Florentine Council was held in the year 1438. So was that papal primacy not in force for all the preceding centuries? Or was it not an article of faith, defined neither in the Word of God nor in the Church? And how was it finally defined here? To this decision neither all the Greeks who were present, nor especially Mark of Ephesus among them, adhered, nor did the rest in the East, where those Greeks returned from the Council. And in the Council, when Pope Eugenius wished this controversy to be settled, they replied that they had as yet no authority to answer, and therefore, with the consent of the Emperor, they did not want any mention to be made in the letters of union of any question other than that of the procession of the Holy Spirit. At last, overcome and worn down by the Pope, the Greeks also admitted these things, and they were inserted into the letters of union. But the words by which Valerian says, lest anyone think the definition new, it is guarded, namely: As is also contained in the acts of the Ecumenical Councils and in the sacred canons, which immediately follow the aforesaid definition of the same Council, show the trickery or the artifice of Valerian. For who would not take those words, which immediately follow the aforesaid definition of the same Council, to mean that the decrees of the earlier Councils were annexed to that decision? Especially someone who knows that in that Council, when the question of the procession of the Holy Spirit was debated, many testimonies of the ancients were cited everywhere, and that even in that dispute about the primacy of the Pope the opinions of the Greek teachers about the power of the supreme Pontiff were brought forward? And yet there is nothing of the kind in the definition of the Council, where it says only: and that to him full power of governing the universal Church has been handed over by our Lord Jesus Christ, as is also contained in the acts of the Ecumenical Councils and in the sacred canons. Therefore Valerian's words, which immediately follow the aforesaid definition of the same Council, must be understood as referring to the things that follow, not, as they seem to be taken, as the decrees. Next, this Florentine Council does not say that the definition was made in the earlier Ecumenical Councils; for if it had, Valerian would not have said that he knows no ecclesiastical decree concerning faith which grants the Roman Pontiff infallibility of authority, nor would he have bound himself, setting those aside, to the recent definition of the Council of Florence. Rather, he says that that power is contained in the Councils in whatever way. To this we reply that, however the Roman Pontiff has always eagerly tried to claim that power for himself in various ways, even in Councils, nevertheless in the Councils that arrogance of his was repulsed and chastised by the more eminent men. But if those Florentine Fathers mean by the canons of the ancient Ecumenical Councils that this power of the Pope is defined here, as they expressly say it is contained in the sacred canons, and Valerian agrees with them: I plainly say that this is false, and that no such canon can be produced from any Ecumenical Council (after examining all those that the Papists themselves count as such, fifteen before this Florentine one). So I also charge the Florentine Council with falsehood, since it is the only ecclesiastical foundation (by their own account) for papal infallibility, and it asserts that; and it is so far from being proved even to Valerian that, apart from this one, he has openly confessed he knows no other ecclesiastical decree or Council for the same matter. Valerian goes on in the Colloquy, in the same second session: And since this definition does not restrict the authority of the Roman Pontiff to a Council, whether General or not, we pronounce it to be such as Christ granted to Peter, and as Peter exercised in the Acts of the Apostles, and such as the Roman Pontiffs have exercised and still exercise, notwithstanding whoever think otherwise, and finally such as the Fathers of the Ecumenical Council of Florence defined. So now this is your argument, not the definition of the Council, which we pronounce as false and fictitious as you bring it forward. He adds: But since the Fathers of that council do not grant the Roman Pontiff infallibility of authority in express words, we argue theologically that it is given, in this way. Here again he leaves the ecclesiastical argument, which was the only one he could bring, and thinks he must proceed theologically. Yet at the start he had distinguished the ecclesiastical from the theological thus: The ecclesiastical judge, by directive jurisdiction, proposes and declares the doctrine of the Christian faith, and whoever does not believe it is condemned, and by coercive jurisdiction he condemns heresy and separates the heretic from the assembly of the faithful. The theologian, however, lacks all coercive power, and has only a directive power without any jurisdiction, namely, no other than that which an orator exercises over his hearers, or at most a teacher over his pupils. Moreover, the Fathers of Florence expressed clearly enough what they thought should be attributed to the Roman Pontiff, and yet they did not express infallibility of authority, neither expressly nor by implication. So even if one were bound to follow this Council of Florence, that fundamental thesis of the Papal Church would still not follow; it is in no way probable, either ecclesiastically or theologically.

units.la: Audiamus tandem Valer. argumentum: Romanus Pontifex est successor D. Petri, Principis Apostolorum. Tenet primatum in universum Orbem. Est verus Christi Vicarius. Est Caput totius Ecclesiae. Est omnium Christianorum Pater. Et Doctor. Cui a Domino nostro Iesu in Beato Petro tradita est plena potestas pascendi, regendi, & gubernandi universam Ecclesiam. Is vero, qui est successor D. Petri, Principis Apostolorum, ac tenet primatum in universum Orbem, estque verus Christi Vicarius, & Caput totius Ecclesiae, omniumque Christianorum Pater, & Doctor, cui a Domino nostro Iesu Christo in Beato Petro tradita est plena potestas pascendi, regendi, & gubernandi universam Ecclesiam, necessario habet auctoritatem infallibilem in proponenda & declaranda universae Ecclesiae, ex cathedra, doctrina fidei Christianae, & jurisdictionem segregandi a coetu fidelium eos omnes, qui contumaciter eam pernegant. Ergo Pontifex Romanus habet auctoritatem infallibilem in proponenda & declaranda universae Ecclesiae, ex Cathedra, doctrina fidei Christianae, & iurisdictionem segregandi à cœtu fidelium eos omnes, qui contumaciter eam pernegant. Ego vero, quamvis sufficeret minorem rejicere, nego etiam majorem, adeoque utramque propositionem: minorem verò principaliter, talem scilicet Papam Romanum Innocentium x. esse, ac hic ex Concilio Florentino per varia ista elogia eum facit esse: neque æternum hoc vel Ecclesiastice, vel Theologice probabit seu Valerianus, seu alius unquam: Sed neque majorem poterit confirmare Adversarius hanc: qui est successor Petri &c. is ideo est infallibilis: nam illorum titulorum conceptum quo facere, & ponere aliquam rationem, etiam extra necessitatem infallibilitatis. Quid enim impedit, Doctorem aliquem dici & Patrem Christianorum, eaque ratione & caput, & Christi vicarium (quamvis male; sed de eo jam non quæritur: attenditur modo, an de se hæc necessario ponant infallibilitatem) & primatum tenere in universum orbem, & successorem Petri esse, ut tamen illa omnia non sit authoritate infallibili? Vide, quam non possit Valerianus ullo modo probare suam tanti ponderis thesim, cui universa Papatus incumbit moles & Ecclesia. Hoc ipse sensit, quare immediate addit: Verum nec definitio illa, neque argumentum nostrum, aut aliud quidpiam ejusmodi, ea sunt, quæ possint captivare in obsequium Christi, & ejus Ecclesiæ, omnem altitudinem intellectus, extollentem se adversus scientiam Dei, nisi Deus statuat intra castra Israel, & castra Ægyptiorum columnam nubis, hinc tenebrosam, illis illuminantem noctem: Nisi, inquam, Deus discernat unicam veram Ecclesiam à cœtibus Hereticorum, signis & portentis, & variis Spiritus Sancti distributionibus. O miseram Ecclesiæ sortem, & statum undequaque desperatum? ut nec hoc quod attulisti hactenus argumentum, qua Ecclesiasticum, qua Theologicum, aut aliud quippiam ejusmodi, te ipso fatente, queat rem evincere, nisi ad aliud medium & locum prolabaris, videlicet miraculorum: de quo nec
units.tr: Let us at last hear Valerianus's argument: The Roman Pontiff is the successor of St Peter, the Prince of the Apostles. He holds the primacy over the whole world. He is the true Vicar of Christ. He is the Head of the whole Church, the Father and Teacher of all Christians, to whom full power to feed, rule and govern the universal Church was handed over in the blessed Peter by our Lord Jesus. Therefore, the one who is the successor of St Peter, the Prince of the Apostles, holds the primacy over the whole world, is the true Vicar of Christ and the Head of the whole Church, the Father and Teacher of all Christians, to whom full power to feed, rule and govern the universal Church was given in the blessed Peter by our Lord Jesus Christ, necessarily has infallible authority to propose and declare to the whole Church, ex cathedra, the doctrine of the Christian faith, and jurisdiction to cut off from the assembly of the faithful all those who stubbornly deny it. Therefore the Roman Pontiff has infallible authority to propose and declare to the whole Church, ex cathedra, the doctrine of the Christian faith, and jurisdiction to cut off from the assembly of the faithful all those who stubbornly deny it. I, for my part, although it would be enough to reject the minor premise, also deny the major, and so both propositions. As for the minor, chiefly, that the Roman Pontiff is such a one as Innocent X, and that by the various praises the Council of Florence gives him he is made such, neither Valerianus nor anyone else will ever prove this, either ecclesiastically or theologically. Nor can my opponent confirm the major: that the one who is the successor of Peter etc. is therefore infallible. For to frame the concept of those titles and to set up some argument from them, even apart from any need for infallibility, is possible. For what prevents someone from being called a teacher and father of Christians, and on that ground both head and Vicar of Christ (though wrongly; but that is not now the question; the only point at issue is whether these titles necessarily imply infallibility in themselves), and from holding the primacy over the whole world and being the successor of Peter, and yet all these things not come from infallible authority? See how little Valerianus can in any way prove his thesis, of such weight, on which the whole mass of the Papacy and the Church rests. He himself felt this, and so he adds straight away: But neither that definition, nor our argument, nor anything else of this kind, are the things that can bring every height of the intellect that exalts itself against the knowledge of God into obedience to Christ and his Church, unless God sets up, within the camp of Israel and the camp of the Egyptians, a pillar of cloud, dark on one side and lighting up the night for the others: unless, I say, God distinguishes the one true Church from the assemblies of heretics by signs and portents and the various distributions of the Holy Spirit. O miserable lot of the Church, and a state despaired of on every side! So that not even the argument you have brought forward so far, whether ecclesiastical or theological, or anything else of this kind, as you yourself confess, can establish the matter, unless you slip into another means and place, namely miracles. Of these, nor

units.la: Concilium Florentinum aliquid, in suâ definitione, neque ullum aliud Concilium, parum abest quin dicam, nec ullus etiam vestrûm Theologus, qui argumentum istud proferat, ad demonstrandam infallibilitatem Pontificis Romani. Adeo in risum abire debet, quem solum miracula Rom. Ecclesiæ jam à multo tempore referunt, fundamentalis ille articulus de Pontificis infallibilitate: vel, sint vera miracula, quis discernet vera, à falsis? certe non quicunque tenetur juxta ipsos, illam credere infallibilitatem: & quale tum istud scilicet ad hoc probandum est medium unicum, vel argumentum, seu nubes illa Israëlitica, hinc illuminans, inde obscurans, tam difficilis cognitu, incerta, rara, nulla? Neque dicimus, quod vera miracula facta ad ostensionem veritatis nihil valeant, ut nos facit dicere Valerianus, pag. 35. sed de miraculis Ecclesiæ Romanæ loquimur: & hæc, negamus aperte, valere ad ostendendam ejus infallibilitatem. Verum cum id quod semel factum est, inquit porro Valerianus, necessariò potuerit fieri: si Pontisex Romanus definiens ex Cathedra erravit aliquando, necessariò potuit errare, seu est fallibilis, nobis verò nulla occurrit ratio, cur non possit errare sæpius, si semel erraverit: quapropter præfatam infallibilitatem non urgebimus, si unus error Romani Pontificis tam certò confirmetur, quam certò v. g. constat Nestorium Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum definivisse ex Cathedra Patriarchali hæresim manifestissimam. Nos enim tametsi existimemus Ecclesiam Catholicam non necessario errare, errante aliquo Pontificum Romanorum, tamen constantissime asserimus infallibilitatem sedis Romanæ, quoad usque evidenti facto nobis, uti supra, probetur, vel unus error in fide Pontificis Romani, definientis ex Cathedra. Huc ergo jam omnis cardo rei devenit, ut errorem Pontificis Romani, ex cathedrâ docentis, ostendamus. Verùm, quamvis illum nequicemus nos indicare, haud tamen inde sequeretur nullum vel esse, vel esse posse, adeoque ipsum esse infallibilem: deinde. à Multis sæpe Paparum errores; quin & hæreses oftensæ fuerunt; & in hoc Colloquio quoque, ad quæ nil respondit Valerianus. Denique, omnino sequitur juxta vos, errante ex Cathedrâ Pontifice, nullam in Ecclesiâ esse infallibilitatem, quia totam hanc uti derivatis ex successione in locum Petri, quam sedi alligatis Romanæ, ita nusquam agnoscitis quam apud Pontificem: quo proinde errante, nullus insuper est infallibilis.
units.tr: The Council of Florence says nothing about them in its definition, nor does any other council; I almost say that none of your theologians who puts forward this argument for proving the infallibility of the Roman Pontiff says anything either. So ridiculous must it be that the fundamental article on the Pontiff's infallibility should for a long time now be supported only by the miracles of the Roman Church. Or, even if the miracles are true, who will distinguish the true from the false? Certainly not everyone who, by their own account, is bound to believe that infallibility. And what sort of means, or argument, is this for proving the matter, that single cloud of Israel, lighting up on one side and darkening on the other, so hard to recognise, uncertain, rare, or nonexistent? Nor do we say that true miracles wrought to show the truth are worth nothing, as Valerianus makes us say on page 35. We are speaking of the miracles of the Roman Church, and these, we openly deny, are worth anything in showing its infallibility. But, since what has once happened, he goes on to say, could necessarily have happened, if the Roman Pontiff, defining ex cathedra, has ever erred, he could necessarily have erred, or is fallible, and yet we see no reason why he should not err more often, if he has erred once; therefore we shall not press the aforesaid infallibility, if a single error of the Roman Pontiff is confirmed as certainly as it is certain that Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, defined a most manifest heresy ex cathedra as Patriarch. For although we think the Catholic Church does not necessarily err when some Roman Pontiff errs, yet we most firmly assert the infallibility of the Roman See, until, as we have said above, it is proved to us by clear fact that even a single error in faith of a Roman Pontiff defining ex cathedra exists. So all the hinge of the matter now comes to this: that we should show an error of the Roman Pontiff teaching ex cathedra. But although we cannot point to it, it does not follow from that that there is none, or can be none, and so that he is not infallible. Besides, the errors of Popes, and even heresies, have often been shown by many; and in this very Colloquy too, to which Valerianus has made no reply. Finally, by your own account it follows altogether that if the Pontiff errs ex cathedra there is no infallibility in the Church at all, since you derive all this from succession to the place of Peter, which you tie to the Roman See, and you acknowledge it nowhere except in the Pontiff; so if he errs, no one further is infallible.

units.la: Hæc ad argumentationem Valeriani in hoc Colloquio, dicenda mihi existimavi, tum quia nuperrime illa contigerunt, tum ut ostenderem in hoc recenti exemplo, quod sæpe dixi, ex quotidianis Pontificiorum scriptis & Actis indicandam semper esse Papismi declinationem, à prisco ipsorum agendi modo, & quo pacto ad nos sensim propius accedant. Certe nonnulla ejusmodi vel ex duobus jam memoratis proximis Colloquiis annotare possum. Ibi, præterquam in toto Actionis scopo, dum nobiscum petunt unionem & concordiam Ecclesiasticam: à quâ multum profecto abfuit, ut eam olim ultro obtulissent: tum etiam, in liquidatione, uti appellant, & sinceratione doctrinæ suæ, ad quam proponendam videtur maximè etiam institutum Colloquium fuisse, ecce de quibus conqueruntur, sibi quasi per calumniam attributis, circa regulam fidei: accusamur, & damnamur, dicunt, quasi ab unica formali & suprema Fidei Regula deficientes, ipsamque sacram Scripturam contemptui habentes, amplectamur humanas traditiones, tanquam fidei nostræ fundamenta & bases, easque DEI verbo, Evangelio Christi, Iustitiæ Fidei, præferamus, concessâ etiam Ecclesiæ & Summo Pontifici potestate, ut nova dogmata, seu Articulos fidei, sine verbo DEI, imò contra verbum DEI, pro arbitrio condat. Scripturas ipsas fastigio Romanæ Hierarchiæ subjicere dicimur, ac si æterna inaiolabilisque DEI veritas, hominum arbitrio niteretur. In potestate Papæ esse scripturas abolere, quas velit, & erigere cultus, ordinare Sacrificia, instituere Sacramenta, mutare Sacramentorum substantialia, figere leges quas velit, dispensare, solvere, quibuscunque legibus velit, &c. Nobis autem quidquid vel Papa, vel Ecclesia contra vel extra DEI verbum statuerit, habendum esse non alio loco, quàm certum DEI oraculum. Quilibet rerum Pontificiarum gnarus, dijudicet, annon, quamvis haud ita omnia, nonnulla tamen istorum verè Pontificiis tribui possint, facileque ostendi, ipsos & talia docuisse, & fundamenta ea in doctrinis & scriptis suis jecisse, quibus illa continentur. Similiter circa justificationem ajunt, Accusamur & damnamur, quasi praetermissâ DEI misericordia, Christoque mediatore, & propitiatore praeterito, ac prorsus sepulto, improbato, deleto, imò spreto Christi merito & gratiâ, Evangelio, de gratuita peccatorum remissione, deque Iustitia fidei penitus abolito, oppressaque doctrinâ Pauli, de gratia Christi, citra fidem policeamur Iustitiam & humanis tantum viribus, quaeramus viam & accessum ad DEVM, & nostris operibus, sine Christo, & extra gratiam facti, obtinere, mereri, emere conemur remissionem peccatorum &c. Quibus similia multa, quin & eadem à Pontificiis doceri, levi operâ, ex collatis aliorum scriptis ac disputationibus, praecipue veterum, ostendi potest, atque ad probandam Papatus declinationem, multo cum fructu, ab iis quibus hic satis otii, diligentiae, & judicii, debebat. Pergunt de sacramentis, & cultu paria recentere: sed in omnibus istam adhibent artem, ut duris & absurdis sophismis, quas circa illos articulos vulgò fovent, hic ibi vocula intermisceant, totam sententiam, ut ipsis verè alioqui solet tribui, facile mutantem.
units.tr: I have thought it right to say these things about Valerianus's argument in this Colloquy, partly because those events are very recent, and partly to show, by this fresh example, what I have often said: that from the daily writings and Acts of the Papists the decline of Papism must always be traced, from their ancient way of acting, and how they gradually come closer to us. Certainly I can note several such things even from the two Colloquies just mentioned. There, besides the whole aim of the proceedings, when they seek union and ecclesiastical concord with us (from which, indeed, they were far removed when they once freely offered it), then also, in the so-called clarification and purification of their doctrine, to which the Colloquy seems chiefly to have been set up, here are the things they complain of, which are attributed to them as though by calumny, concerning the rule of faith: We are accused and condemned, they say, as if we were falling away from the single, formal and supreme rule of faith, and as if we held Holy Scripture itself in contempt, and embraced human traditions as the foundations and bases of our faith, and preferred them to the Word of God, the Gospel of Christ, the righteousness of faith; and as if we granted to the Church and to the Supreme Pontiff the power to frame new dogmas, or articles of faith, without the Word of God, indeed against the Word of God, at their own pleasure. We are said to subject the Scriptures themselves to the summit of the Roman hierarchy, as if the eternal and inviolable truth of God rested on the will of men. As if it were in the power of the Pope to abolish whatever Scriptures he wishes, and to set up forms of worship, to ordain sacrifices, to institute sacraments, to change the substance of the sacraments, to lay down whatever laws he wishes, to dispense and to loosen from whatever laws he wishes, and so on. But for us, whatever either the Pope or the Church has laid down against or beside the Word of God is to be held as nothing other than a certain oracle of God. Anyone acquainted with Papist affairs may judge whether, although not all of these can be fairly ascribed to the Papists, some of them can indeed be attributed to them, and it can easily be shown that they have both taught such things and laid the foundations for them in their doctrines and writings, in which those things are contained. Similarly on justification they say: We are accused and condemned, as if, the mercy of God and Christ our mediator and propitiator having been passed over, and his past work entirely buried, rejected, blotted out, indeed despised, the merit and grace of Christ, the Gospel of the free remission of sins and the righteousness of faith having been wholly abolished, and the teaching of Paul on the grace of Christ having been suppressed, we seek righteousness apart from faith, and seek a way and access to God by human strength alone, and try to obtain, earn and buy remission of sins by our own works, without Christ and outside grace, and so on. Many similar things, indeed the very same, can easily be shown to be taught by the Papists, with a little effort, by comparing the writings and disputations of others, especially the older ones; and this could be done with great profit to demonstrate the decline of Papism, by those who here have enough leisure, diligence and judgement. They go on to recite the same on the sacraments and worship; but in all these they use a particular art: they mix in here and there a little word among the harsh and absurd sophisms they commonly foster on those articles, so that the whole opinion, which otherwise is truly attributed to them, is easily changed.

units.la: Atque in postremo Colloquio Rheinfelsensi, ex Disputatione Valeriani, nota quantam Papatus declinationem: primo, dum auctoritatem Pontificum Romanorum fatetur se non posse ostendere ex solo textu sacro, inde, nullam in Bibliis fieri mentionem Pontificis Romani; tertio, neque ex sola authoritate Ecclesiae posse confirmari illam thesin; praeterea, nullum inter decreta Ecclesiastica se scire, quod Pontifici Romano expresse tribuat infallibilitatem auctoritatis; tantum Patres Synodi Florentinae definivisse primatum Pontificis Romani: neque tamen illos Patres tribuere Romano Pontifici verbis expressis infallibilitatem. Imo, nec illâ definitione, neque argumento Theologico inde facto, neque quopiam alio ejusmodi, posse irrefragabiliter probari illam Papae auctoritatem. Recurrendum ultimò esse ad probam miraculorum. Haec omnia, sex aut septem puncta à Valeriano tradita, in unâ actione Colloquii istius secundâ, ab omnibus notari velim, pro totidem declinationibus rei Pontificiae, in primario quidem Papatus articulo infallibilitatis suae, cui universum ejus incumbit aedificium. Quibus addatur quod, post producta eadem ex Colloquio Thorunensi, Valerianus dixit: Si diabolus ipse afferret contra universam Ecclesiam novum textum sacrum, quem Ecclesia universa violaret, crederem diabolo contra Ecclesiam, secundum Luthero, quantumcunque infami: quapropter cum meis sociis et universa Ecclesia catholica profitemur, protestamurque nullam esse sub Deo auctoritatem contra sacrum textum. At qui è contrario Pontifici S. saepe à suis attribui potestatem dispensandi adversus Apostolum, adversus sacrum textum, quis nescit? Et ubi ignorare scivero Valerianum, lubentissimè ei sum ostensurus, qui hominem ex hoc Colloquio, aliisque ejus scriptis, judicii & candoris non vulgaris, prout decet has ejus virtutes agnoscere, aestimo. Porro quomodo se nunquam extricarit illis angustiis, sed semper magis ac magis irretierit, per totam Colloquii actionem, ex integrâ ejus historiâ cuilibet satis manifestum. In quâ postquam putidam semper commisisset principii petitionem, P. Valerianus, porro sic argumentatus fuit: Innocentius Papa x. successit Petro, supra quem fundata est Ecclesia, contra quam non tom prævalebunt porta inferi. Is, qui talis est habet infallibilem jurisdictionem, scilicet, in decretis fidei, super universam Ecclesiam. Ergò Innocentius Papa x. habet jurisdictionem infallibilem in decretis fidei, super universam Ecclesiam. Breviter, negatur major, & minor. Valerianus: Innocentius Papa succedit Petro in illa jurisdictione, quae conservat Ecclesiam universalem incolumem adversus portas inferi: Atqui: Is, qui sic succedit Petro, necessario succedit in Jurisdictione Monarchica à Christo collata ipsi Petro: Ergò. Innocentius PAPA x. succedit Petro in jurisdictione Monarchica, eidem collata à Christo. Negatur tibi iterum, & major propositio, & minor. Valerianus: sic argumentor ex textu Sacro: CHRISTVS soli Simoni in Novo Testamento mutavit Nomen: Peto ergò à Domino Haberkornio; utrum Christus in hac mutatione nominis voluerit significare insignem aliquam prærogationem Simonis, quæ soli PETRO conveniat. Non quæritur, de insigni aliquâ prærogativâ Simonis; Valeriane; sed de jurisdictione monarchicâ: adde, & infallibili &c. fiat argumentum: negabitur major, & minor, tertium. Et sic semper idem repetiit; vel quod in quæstione turpiter assumsit, probavit autem nihil: præterquam, quod nunc ex textu sacro, & eo quidem solo instituit probare infallibilem Papæ jurisdictionem, quam antea dixerat, ex solo textu sacro inferri non posse. Tandem, post illa sic turpiter tradita, appositit illis geminum de utraque Ecclesiâ argumentum, so. Considero inquit, ab unâ parte Ecclesiam illam, suam nempe, à primo sui exordio usque ad hanc nostram ætatem, fundatam supra petram jurisdictionis præfatâ; ab altera parte, Martinum Lutherum ab anno millesimo quingentesimo decimo septimo stantem adversus universam illam Ecclesiam. misera iterum putidaque petitio ejus quod est in quæstione. Hoc argumentum regulæ suæ est adeo decantatæ, Catholicorum, uti facit, & Biblistarum: quo se & suos Catholicos appellat, sed appellat tantum, utque probet tantum abest, ut ne ullo quidem argumento id conetur. Nos facit Biblistas: bene, accipimus, nos à Sancto Bibliorum studio denominari: sub titulo Bibliistarum comprehendimur illos omnes Haereshiarchas & Haereticos, qui supponentes Ecclesiam erraße in fide, voluerunt corrigere illam ex sacro textu.
