Ineptissime, quasi haeretici Scripturam pro se habeant, vel ex eâ nos agamus adversus Ecclesiam, & non pro eâ, sed adversus Papatum, in fide errantem. Caetera ejus de regula Catholicorum, & Bibliistarum, sunt meri logi, vacui omni ratione, & argumento. Specta quaeso: istam ejusmodi argumentationem: Catholici excommunicarunt à suo coetu, tanquam Haereticos, omnes illos, illosve solos ex Christianis, qui ausi sunt damnare ex sacris litteris doctrinam ejusdem Ecclesiae Catholicae, scilicet omnes Bibliistas. Quid ais? ego vero dico, Catholicos nunquam, nusquam à suo coetu excommunicasse Biblistas, quum ipsi Bibliistae sint. Audi Theodoretum: cum haereticus proferat multa humanae sapientiae argumenta, orthodoxus respondet, ne talia proseras argumenta, ἐγὼ γὰρ μόνῃ τῇ θείᾳ πείθομαι γεγραφῇ. Vel Tertullianum: non recipio quod extra Scripturam de tuo infers. Unde quam inepte, quamque contradictorie faciat Bibliistas damnare doctrinam Ecclesiae Catholicae, liquet.
units.tr: And in the last Colloquy at Rheinfelden, from Valerian's disputation, note how far he declines from Papacy. First, when he admits that he cannot show the authority of the Roman Pontiffs from Holy Scripture alone, he infers that there is no mention of the Roman Pontiff in the Bible. Third, he says that this thesis cannot be confirmed by the authority of the Church alone. Besides, he says he knows of no ecclesiastical decree that expressly grants the Roman Pontiff infallibility of authority; he says only that the Fathers of the Synod of Florence defined the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, and that those Fathers did not in express words attribute infallibility to the Roman Pontiff. Indeed, he says that neither that definition, nor a theological argument drawn from it, nor any other argument of that kind, can irrefutably prove that authority of the Pope, and that one must finally have recourse to the proof of miracles. I would have everyone take note of these six or seven points set down by Valerian in the second session of that Colloquy, as so many concessions of the Papal cause, especially on the primary article of Papacy, that of its infallibility, on which its whole edifice rests. To these may be added that, after citing the same things from the Colloquy of Thorn, Valerian said: If the devil himself were to bring forward against the whole Church a new sacred text, which the whole Church violated, I would believe the devil against the Church, however infamous he might be, according to Luther; therefore, with my colleagues and the whole Catholic Church, I profess and protest that there is no authority under God against Holy Scripture. But on the contrary, who does not know that the Holy Pontiff is often credited by his own followers with the power of dispensing against the Apostle, against Holy Scripture? And if I should find that Valerian is ignorant of this, I would gladly show it to him; for I judge the man, from this Colloquy and his other writings, to have no common judgement and candour, as one ought to acknowledge these virtues in him. Moreover, how he never extricated himself from those difficulties, but was always entangled more and more throughout the whole course of the Colloquy, is plain enough to anyone from its complete history. In it, after he had always committed a foul petitio principii, Father Valerian then argued as follows: Pope Innocent x succeeded Peter, upon whom the Church is founded, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail. He who is such has infallible jurisdiction, namely in decrees of faith, over the whole Church. Therefore Pope Innocent x has infallible jurisdiction in decrees of faith over the whole Church. In short, the major and the minor are denied. Valerian: Pope Innocent succeeds Peter in that jurisdiction which keeps the universal Church safe against the gates of hell. But he who thus succeeds Peter necessarily succeeds in the monarchical jurisdiction conferred by Christ on Peter himself. Therefore Pope Innocent x succeeds Peter in the monarchical jurisdiction conferred on him by Christ. Again it is denied to you, both the major proposition and the minor. Valerian: I argue thus from Holy Scripture: CHRIST alone changed the name of Simon in the New Testament. I ask therefore of Lord Haberkorn whether Christ, in this change of name, meant to signify some outstanding prerogative of Simon, which alone belongs to PETER. No question is raised about some outstanding prerogative of Simon, Valerian; but about monarchical jurisdiction. Add "and infallible," etc., and let the argument be made: the major and the minor, and the third, will be denied. And so he always repeated the same thing, either assuming in the question what he had shamefully taken for granted, while proving nothing; apart from the fact that now he undertakes to prove from Holy Scripture, and from that alone, the infallible jurisdiction of the Pope, which he had said before cannot be inferred from Scripture alone. At last, after having so shamefully set out these points, he added to them a twofold argument concerning each Church, namely: I consider, he says, on the one hand that Church, his own, from its very beginning up to our own age, founded upon the rock of the aforesaid jurisdiction; on the other hand, Martin Luther standing from the year 1517 against that whole Church. Once more a wretched and foul petitio principii of that which is in question. This argument is so much sung of as the rule of Catholics, as he makes it, and of the Biblists: by which he calls himself and his Catholics, but only calls them so, and he does not even attempt to prove it by any argument. He makes us Biblists: well, we accept that we are named from our devotion to the Holy Scriptures. Under the title of Biblists are comprised all those heresiarchs and heretics who, supposing the Church to have erred in faith, wished to correct it from the sacred text. Most absurdly, as if heretics held Scripture on their side, or as if we acted from it against the Church, and not for it, but against the Papacy, which errs in faith. His other remarks about the rule of Catholics and Biblists are mere words, empty of all reason and argument. Consider, I beg you, an argument of this kind: Catholics have excommunicated from their assembly, as heretics, all those, or those alone, of the Christians who dared to condemn from the sacred letters the doctrine of this same Catholic Church, namely all Biblists. What do you say? I for my part say that Catholics never and nowhere excommunicated Biblists from their assembly, since the Biblists themselves are Catholics. Hear Theodoret: When the heretic brings forward many arguments of human wisdom, the orthodox man replies: do not bring forward such arguments; for I am persuaded by the divine Scripture alone [ἐγὼ γὰρ μόνῃ τῇ θείᾳ πείθομαι γεγραφῇ]. Or Tertullian: I do not accept what you infer from your own mind beyond Scripture. Whence it is clear how absurdly and how self-contradictorily he makes the Biblists condemn the doctrine of the Catholic Church.

units.la: Pergit jam de Ecclesiâ Catholicorum, ad alteram suam quasi regulam: Sic igitur probamus Ecclesiam Catholicam esse legitimam, & ejus doctrinam de fide esse veram. Quid vero attinet, probare Ecclesiam Catholicam esse legitimam? quod nemo negat: sed Ecclesiam Romanam esse catholicam illam, hoc probandum erat. Quod autem omnes Coetus Bibliistici, qui extiterunt in orbe Christiano, non sint vera Ecclesiae Christi, neque foveant doctrinam fidei veram, probamus hoc argumento. Coetus Bibliistarum habuerunt in orbe Christiano initium post fundatam Ecclesiam Christi, & desierunt esse. Hoc autem fallum est, Coetus Bibliistarum coepisse post fundatam Christi Ecclesi-am. am, quum sit ipsa Christi Ecclesia, fundata in doctrinâ Biblistarum, seu Prophetarum, & Apostolorum, Ephes. 2. 11. 20. Non vero curamus, quam ipse Bibliistarum faciat descriptionem, quod æque alius posset facere Catholicorum; sed nos rem capimus, prout in se est. Cæterum Theodorus Petreus, Carthusiensis Monachus, in Catalogo hæreticorum pag. 34. Bibliistas ponens, dicit eos docere, solum Scripturarum contextum populo proponendum, legendumque esse, absque ulla interpretatione: quales facit Melanthonem, Carolostadium, qualesque nos fingit esse Reformatos, qui sola Biblia pro fidei & religionis regulâ habemus, non tamen vel alios in rebus aliis, & sacris libros, vel Bibliorum expositionem rejicimus, sed & probamus, & instituimus ipsi. Sic corruit, quidquid de duplici regulâ Valerianus retulit in Colloquio illo, vel scripsit ad Georgium Calixtum, hujus anni MDCXI. d. v. Febr. (quæ epistola impressa Coloniæ) in causa Ernesti Langravii: ubi iterum quam mire disputat! Hisce argumentis exarabimus tuæ eruditioni seriem ratiocinationis, quæ nos cogit ad communionem in fide cum urbis Romæ Episcopo. Hoc præ omnibus scire expeto, quid tantum sit, quod virum magni ingenii animique Ecclesiæ Romanæ astringat. Itaque ex præfata argumentatione nostræ propositiones capitales à nobis demonstrandæ fuerunt tres. 1. Christus contulit D. Petro primatum super universam Ecclesiam. 2. Christus voluit primatum collatum D. Petro transfire ad ejus Successores. 3. Episcopus Urbis Romæ est successor D. Petri. Probamus autem à ratione, Christum debuisse conferre alicui fidelium primatum super universam Ecclesiam: præmittimus tamen differentiam regni Cœlorum, à regnis terrenis. Sed vero, non quid debuerit tuo judicio Christus, id quod temerarium est asserere; sed quid egerit, ostendendum. Tu demonstra, sicut suscepisti, tres illas capitales propositiones. Sic ergo argumentamur. Christus fundavit Ecclesiam suam super doctrina à Deo revelata, que fulgeat ipsi Ecclesiæ certò & infallibiliter usque ad sconsummationem seculi. Is verò, qui fundavit Ecclesiam suam super doctrina à Deo revelata, quæ fulgeat ipsi Ecclesiæ certò & infallibiliter usque ad consummationem seculi, prudentissime constituit in eadem Ecclesia usque ad consummationem seculi unum hominem, aut hominum cætum, pro tempore existentem; qui habeat auctoritatem infallibilem in proponenda universæ Ecclesiæ, ex Cathedra doctrina à Deo revelatas & jurisdictionem segregandi à cætu fidelium eos omnes, qui contumaciter eam pernegant. Ergo Christus prudentissime constituit in eadem Ecclesia usque ad consummationem seculi unum hominem aut hominum Cætum pro tempore existentem, qui habeat auctoritatem infallibilem in proponenda, & declaranda universæ Ecclesiæ ex Cathedra, Doctrina à Deo revelata, & jurisdictionem segregandi à cætu fidelium eos omnes, qui contumaciter eam pernegant. Nos ergo Capuccini postulamus à tua eruditione, & prudentia sententiam tuam de hoc argumento. At quale argumentum? neque enim probat, quod probandum est, neque unam istarum dictarum propositionum infert, quas sibi demonstrandas sumserat, nedum omnes. Concludis: ergo Christus prudentissime constituit unum hominem &c. Imo si constituit, profecto prudentissime constituit: at illud proba, sic eum constituisse. Nos negamus, & sufficere dicimus, quod nobis loco hominis talis alicujus dederit infallibilis auctoritatis suum verbum, quod omnibus opponimus. Tum constituerit talem hominem, negamus illum Papam Romanum esse: tu proba. Præterea negamus nos, omnes illas tuas theses: aut primatum super universam Ecclesiam Petro datum, aut illum, si vel Petro collatus fuisset, transfire ad successores; vel Episcopum Romanum, successorem Petri esse. Ego autem quum Valeriani argumentationem hanc toties usurpatam conside: fere dubito an serio egerit; vel si hoc, an apud animum suum queat certam statuere doctrinam illam, pro quâ tam imbellem videt. aut nullam sibi procedere argumentationem: nescio, que quid tandem Principem Ernestum egerit, ut ad Papismum per illa deficere se credi voluerit, ubi nisi alia schemata intercurrant, ego certus sum, ea apud sanae rationis hominem vim ullam habere neutiquam posse. Methodum suam Valerianus peculiari scripto, anno MDCXLI. tit. Iudicium de Catholicorum & Catholicorum credendi regula, prolixe docuit, & adversus objectiones plurimorum, Ioh. Majoris, Iac. Martini, Ioh. Botsacci, Anonymi, & Conr. Bergii tutari conatus suit. Vbi in praefatione Bibliistas nos, & fratres suos amanter nominat, exponitque scriptionis suae hoc consilium: Eo succurrum Bibliistis fratribus meis &c. Si errantes educere studerem congestis in novi voluminis formam, argumentis ab auctoritate Patrum, Conciliorum, Pontificum, & Bibliorum; actum agerem. Quid vel unum textum perquirat non pridem adductum? Bene agnoscit mecum, hoc pacto, vid. argumentatione ex Scriptura, & auctoritatibus eo usque jam disputatum, ut vix aliquid, quod non pridem adductum sit, proferri ultra queat. Alia ergo ab ipso audiamus. Et certe talem, qui isto animo, ingenioque sit, cum Valeriano, vel ipsum si placet, in religionis & controversiarum nostrarum negotio, exoptem Adversarium, vel disputatorem, qui de disputatis huc usque noverit judicare, & non in eadem semper haerere chorda, sed ad ulteriora nos provocaret, & sua. Mentem, inquit, defixi in duo argumenta. Vno, Bibliistarum credendi regulam everto. Id est: Bibliistae docent, quemlibet & quamlibet posse, ac debere dijudicare ex sacro textu lecto, vel audito, etiam totius Ecclesiae Doctrinam de essentialibus fidei, utrum concordet, aut discordet a sacro textu. Nego, id Bibliistas docere. Non quilibet, vel quaelibet potest, debetque doctrinam totius Ecclesiae examinare, & dijudicare. Quilibet doctrinam probat, 1. Thess. v. 21. id est, examinat, & dijudicat spiritu διακρίνειν, (qui quorumcunque fidelium est 1. Cor. 11. 15. & x. 15) quæ sibi proponitur, num arripienda sit. Hocne absque judicio, seu bruto impetu facit, nescience quid sentiat? Id quod alicui proponitur credendum, varium est, & ab hoc ita, ab illo aliter docetur. Quæro jam an, & quod istorum arripiam, & quomodo? prout quodlibet offertur? at contraria est doctrina altera alteri. Probandum ergo mihi, utrum illorum accipiendum sit. Tu vis ut ad sententiam Ecclesiæ pronunciem, quod credendum sit, quod non, videlicet quod illa jubet, vel improbat. Præter quæstionem de Ecclesiâ, ipse sic cuilibet attribuis judicium de doctrinâ sibi propositâ: solum inter nos discrimen supererit, de regulâ, ad quam judicium faciendum sit, quod S. Scripturam dicimus, tu Ecclesiam, quam frustra nominas, donec ex Scripturâ ostendas, & judicium vel imprimis adhibeamus, ad illam ex aliis dignoscendam. Non ergo docemus, quosvis, & quasvis, doctrinam Ecclesiæ ad examen vocare; sed examinare doctrinam sibi tenendam, an Scripturæ, & sic Ecclesiæ sit, quæ non alio fundamento ædificata est, quam Prophetarum, & Apostolorum. Ephes. 11. 20. Non magis nos doctrinam Ecclesiæ singulis subjicimus, ac Vos ipsi, quando doctrinam propositam (non dices, Ecclesiæ, uti neque nos) singulis dijudicandam dicitis ex authoritate & placito Ecclesiæ; cujus loco nos Scripturam substituimus. Namque illo pacto vos non decideritis quæstionem, vel viam monstratis eximendi feliciter dubii, sed maximam difficultatem injicitis, factâ quæstione, quæ & ubi sit Ecclesia. Denique nihil istorum ex nostrâ sententiâ, ut veretur Valerianus, sequitur, quasi aut in Ecclesiam, aut Sacram Scripturam ullam potestatem, vel judicii authoritatem quibusvis tribueremus: dum non adversus Ecclesiam, sed pro eâ, & pro homine judicio pollente, eoque secundum Scripturam instituto (quod vos potius præjudicio Ecclesiæ occæcatis) loquimur. Certe ista magnum bonae causae sunt argumentum, quod nostram doctrinam quibusvis libere examinandam ex Scripturâ offerimus, neque cujuspiam judicium aut examen reformidamus. Idem in Ecclesiâ Apostolicâ obtinuit, ubi Beroënses supra alios commendantur, quod doctrinam sibi ab Apostolis propositam contulerint cum Scripturis, dijudicantes, an ita haberent, ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφάς. Act. XVII. 11. Hoc ergo argumentum Valeriani primum regulam nostram credendi adeo non evertit, ut stabiliat potius & confirmet.
units.tr: He now moves on to the Church of the Catholics, to what he calls his other rule: Thus we prove that the Catholic Church is lawful, and that its doctrine concerning faith is true. But what is the point of proving that the Catholic Church is lawful? No one denies that. The point that needed proving was that the Roman Church is that Catholic Church. Next, that all the Biblicist assemblies which have existed in the Christian world are not true churches of Christ, and do not hold the true doctrine of faith, we prove by this argument. The Biblicist assemblies began to exist in the Christian world after the Church of Christ was founded, and they have ceased to exist. But this is false: the assemblies of Biblicists did not begin after the Church of Christ was founded, since they are themselves the Church of Christ, founded on the doctrine of the Biblicists, that is, of the Prophets and Apostles (Eph. 2:11, 20). We do not care what description the Biblicists give of themselves, which another could equally well give of the Catholics; we take the matter as it is in itself. Moreover, Theodore Petreus, a Carthusian monk, in his Catalogue of Heretics, p. 34, listing the Biblicists, says that they teach that the bare text of Scripture is to be set before the people and read without any interpretation. He makes Melanchthon and Carlstadt such men, and he imagines that we Reformed are such, since we hold Scripture alone as the rule of faith and religion. Yet we do not reject other books in other matters, or sacred books, or the exposition of Scripture; we both approve them and set them up ourselves. So collapses whatever Valerian put forward about a twofold rule in that colloquy of his, or in his letter to Georg Calixtus of this year 1611, 4th day of February (which letter was printed at Cologne), in the case of Landgrave Ernst. There too, how strangely he argues! By these arguments we shall set out for your learning the chain of reasoning which compels us to communion in faith with the Bishop of the city of Rome. Above all I want to know what it is that binds a man of such great talent and mind to the Roman Church. Therefore, from the aforementioned argument, three chief propositions were to be demonstrated by us. 1. Christ gave Saint Peter primacy over the whole Church. 2. Christ willed that the primacy given to Saint Peter pass to his successors. 3. The Bishop of the city of Rome is the successor of Saint Peter. We prove from reason that Christ ought to have given primacy over the whole Church to some one of the faithful, though we first note the difference between the kingdom of heaven and earthly kingdoms. But what Christ ought to have done, in your judgement, is a rash thing to assert; what he actually did is what must be shown. You, demonstrate those three chief propositions, as you undertook to do. So we argue thus. Christ founded his Church upon the doctrine revealed by God, which shines on the Church itself, certainly and infallibly, until the end of the age. He who founded his Church upon the doctrine revealed by God, which shines on the Church itself, certainly and infallibly, until the end of the age, most wisely established in that same Church, until the end of the age, one man, or a body of men, existing for the time being, who would have infallible authority to set forth from the Chair the doctrine revealed by God to the whole Church, and jurisdiction to separate from the assembly of the faithful all those who obstinately deny it. Therefore Christ most wisely established in that same Church, until the end of the age, one man or a body of men existing for the time being, who would have infallible authority to set forth and declare to the whole Church, from the Chair, the doctrine revealed by God, and jurisdiction to separate from the assembly of the faithful all those who obstinately deny it. So we Capuchins ask your learning and prudence for your judgement on this argument. But what sort of argument is it? It neither proves what needed proving, nor infers any one of those propositions which he had undertaken to demonstrate, let alone all of them. You conclude: therefore Christ most wisely established one man, etc. Indeed, if he established him, he assuredly established him most wisely; but prove that he established him in this way. We deny it, and we say that it is enough that he gave us, in place of any such man of infallible authority, his own Word, which we set against all opposition. Whether he established such a man, we deny that he is the Roman Pope; you prove it. Moreover, we deny all those theses of yours: that primacy over the whole Church was given to Peter; or that, even if it had been given to Peter, it passed to his successors; or that the Bishop of Rome is the successor of Peter. For my part, since I scarcely doubt whether Valerian was in earnest in using this argument so often, or, if he was, whether he can fix in his own mind a settled doctrine for which he sees so feeble a case, or that he makes no argument at all. I do not know what on earth moved the Prince Ernst to want it believed that he had defected to Popery through such arguments. Unless other schemes intervene, I am certain that these can have no force at all for a man of sound reason. Valerian expounded his method at length in a special writing of 1641, titled Judgement on the Catholic and the Catholic rule of belief, and he tried to defend it against the objections of many, namely Johann Major, Jakob Martini, Johann Botsack, an anonymous writer, and Konrad Berg. There, in the preface, he calls us Biblicists and his own brothers in affection, and sets out the purpose of his writing: I come to the aid of my Biblicist brothers, etc. If I were trying to lead the erring out by piling up arguments from the authority of the Fathers, Councils, Popes and the Bible, in the form of a new volume, I would be doing what has already been done. Why look for even one text not already cited? He rightly agrees with me that in this way, by argument from Scripture and from authorities, the matter has already been debated so far that scarcely anything can be brought forward that has not been cited before. Let us then hear other things from him. And indeed, with Valerian, or with himself if he likes, I would gladly have as an opponent in the business of our religion and controversies a man of that temper and talent, one who knows how to judge what has been argued so far and does not stay forever on the same string, but challenges us to further matters, and his own. I have fixed my mind, he says, on two arguments. The first overturns the Biblicist rule of belief. That is: the Biblicists teach that anyone at all may and should judge, from the sacred text read or heard, whether the doctrine of the whole Church on the essentials of faith agrees or disagrees with the sacred text. I deny that the Biblicists teach this. Not everyone may or should examine and judge the doctrine of the whole Church. Each person tests the doctrine (1 Thess. 5:21), that is, examines and judges with the Spirit [διακρίνειν], which belongs to all the faithful (1 Cor. 11:15; 10:15), whether what is set before him is to be accepted. Is he to do this without judgement, or by blind impulse, not knowing what he thinks? What is offered to someone to believe varies, and one teacher teaches it one way, another another way. I ask then whether, and which of these, I am to accept, and how? Am I to take whatever is offered? But one doctrine is contrary to another. So it is for me to prove which of them must be accepted. You want me to pronounce on what is to be believed and what not, according to the judgement of the Church, that is, to accept what it commands or disapproves. Apart from the question about the Church, he himself thus gives to each person the judgement of the doctrine set before him. The only difference between us will be about the rule by which the judgement is to be made: we say Holy Scripture, you say the Church, which you name in vain until you show from Scripture that it is the Church, and that we should first apply judgement to identify it from other things. So we do not teach that anyone at all should bring any doctrine of the Church to examination, but that the doctrine to be held should be examined, whether it belongs to Scripture and so to the Church, which was built on no other foundation than that of the Prophets and Apostles (Eph. 2:20). We no more subject the doctrine of the Church to individuals than you yourselves do, when you say that the doctrine proposed must be judged by each person on the authority and decision of the Church, in whose place we put Scripture. For in that way you do not settle the question, nor show a way of happily escaping doubt; rather you throw in the greatest difficulty by raising the question of what and where the Church is. Finally, as Valerian fears, nothing of this follows from our position, as if we granted authority or power of judgement to the Church or to Holy Scripture over anyone at all; for we speak not against the Church but for it, and for the man endowed with judgement, instructed according to Scripture (which you rather blind by prejudice against the Church). Surely these are a great argument for a good cause: that we offer our doctrine freely for anyone to examine from Scripture, and do not fear anyone's judgement or inquiry. The same held in the Apostolic Church, where the Bereans are commended above others because they compared the doctrine proposed to them by the Apostles with the Scriptures, judging whether it was so, examining the Scriptures [ἀνακρίνοντες τὰς γραφάς] (Acts 17:11). So this first argument of Valerian does not overturn our rule of belief at all; rather it establishes and confirms it.

units.la: Alterum, quo Catholicam fidei regulam confirmare se dicit, non ut simul damnet, quemadmodum loquitur, Biblisticam, hoc est: Communicantes in fide cum Romano Pontifice sunt coetus Christianorum, qui solus claret regeneratis. Simpliciter, & absque ullâ trepidatione, quam in nobis hic multam ridicule imaginatur, illud nego. Quin recolligat, ut ipse hic trepidarit, dum repetens argumentum, ait: quod coetus eorum, qui communicant in fide cum Urbis episcopo sit illustris regeneratis. At omittit illud, in quo unica vis haerebat argumenti, solus: ut solus ille clareat, vel illustris sit regeneratis. Quod in aeternum non probabit Valerianus. Quasi non inter illos etiam qui in fide non communicant cum Romano episcopo, sint regenerati, vel clarentes fide & sanctitate viri. Clarere regeneratis, inquit, est clarere viris conspicuis sanctitate & miraculis. Imperitè, quasi regeneratio sit ad miracula facienda, quemadmodum est ad sanctitatem, vel non clareat ex regeneratione, nisi qui claret miraculis. Sed de his aliquando, ubi Deus otium dederit, lubenter ex professo agemus.
units.tr: The second argument, by which he says he confirms the Catholic rule of faith, does not condemn at the same time, as he puts it, the biblical rule, that is: those who agree in faith with the Roman Pontiff are the assembly of Christians, which alone is illustrious to the regenerate. I deny that simply and without any hesitation, which he imagines to be a great trembling on our part, ridiculously. Indeed he gathers it up, as if he himself trembled here, when he repeats the argument and says: that the assembly of those who agree in faith with the bishop of the City is illustrious to the regenerate. But he omits the word on which the whole force of the argument hung, alone: that only that assembly is illustrious, or distinguished, to the regenerate. Valerian will never prove that. As if there were not regenerate people, or men shining in faith and holiness, among those who do not agree in faith with the Roman bishop. "To be illustrious to the regenerate," he says, "is to be conspicuous to men distinguished by holiness and miracles." That is inexpertly said, as if regeneration were for working miracles in the way it is for holiness, or as if one shone out from regeneration only if he shone out by miracles. But we will gladly treat these things at length some time, when God grants us leisure.

units.la: Hactenus vidimus Colloquiorum inter Nostros & Pontificios, variis in locis, temporibusque, inde à Reformatione habitorum brevem narrationem, eorundem dem materiam, eventum: plerumque ut inde Ecclesia multum lucrata fuerit, sive ad plurimorum instructionem, qui secus alias nihil vel parum de doctrina reformationis inaudierant; sive ad Reformationis plura per loca promotionem & introductionem; sive etiam ad Papalis doctrinae egregiam confutationem, & quod in nuperis Colloquiis observamus, (atque ut in aliis recentibus Papisticorum Doctorum scriptis idem graviter annotetur, sedulo monemus) Papismi declinationem. Haec ergo Colloquia fuerunt, inter Protestantes, & Papistas habita. A. MDXIX. Lipsiacum, inter Lutherum, & Eckium. MDXXIII. Tigurinum, inter Zuinglium, & Fabrum. Eodem anno, Groninganum, inter Dominicanos, atque Sacerdotes Ecclesiae D. Martini. MDXXV. Rheticum, inter Comandrum, & Vicarium Episcopi Curiensis. MDXXVI. Badenum, inter Oecolampadium, & Eckium &c. MDXXVI. Hassiacum Homburgi, inter Franc. Lambertum, & Cratonem; atque ex Pontificiis, Nicolaum Herbornensem &c. MDXXVI. Oldersbemense, in Frisia, inter Laurentium Dominicanum, & Georg. Aportanum. MDXXVII. Nordense, in Frisia, inter Resium, & Synellium. MDXXVIII. Upsalense, in Suecia, inter M. Olaum, & Gallium. MDXXVIII. Bernense, inter Hallerum, & Alexium Grad &c. MDXXXI. Ulmense, inter Oecolampadium, & Georgium Oswaldum. MDXXXIV. Genevense, inter Farellum, & & Furbitum. cIↄ Iↄ xxxv. Genevense, inter Jacobum Bernardum, & Carolum Sorbonistam. cIↄ Iↄ xl ı. VVormatiense, inter Phil. Melanthonem, & Ioh. Eccium. cIↄ Iↄ xl ı. Ratisbonense ı. inter Melanthonem, Bucerum &c. atque Iulium Pflug, Gropperum, Eccium. cIↄ Iↄ xlvı. Ratisbonense ıı.inter Bucerum &c. atque Malvendam &c. cIↄ Iↄ xlıx. Oxoniense, inter Martyrem, & Tresshamum &c. cIↄ Iↄ L. Cantabrigiense, inter Bucerum, & Iungum. cIↄ Iↄ lıv. Oxoniense, inter Crammerum, & VVestonum &c. cIↄ Iↄ lvı. San-Martinense, apud Convallenses, inter VValdenses, & Amatum Sanjulianum. cIↄ Iↄ lvıı. VVormatiense, inter Melanthonem, & Canisium &c. cIↄ Iↄ lıx. Londinense, inter Iuellum &c. atque VVatsonum &c. cIↄ Iↄ lxı. Possiacenum, inter Bezam &c. & Cárdinalem Lotharingum.
units.tr: So far we have seen a brief account of the colloquies between ours and the Papists, held in various places and at various times since the Reformation: their subject matter and outcome. For the most part the Church has profited from them, either for the instruction of many who otherwise had heard little or nothing about the doctrine of the Reformation, or for the wider promotion and introduction of the Reformation in many places, or also for the excellent refutation of Papal doctrine, and (as we observe in the recent colloquies, and as we earnestly warn should be noted in the other recent writings of the Papist teachers) for the decline of Papism. These, then, were the colloquies held between Protestants and Papists: in 1519 at Leipzig, between Luther and Eck; 1523 at Zurich, between Zwingli and Faber; in the same year at Groningen, between the Dominicans and the priests of St Martin's church; 1525 in Rhaetia, between Comander and the vicar of the bishop of Chur; 1526 at Baden, between Oecolampadius and Eck, etc.; 1526 at Homburg in Hesse, between Francis Lambert and Craton, and on the Papist side Nicolaus of Herborn, etc.; 1526 at Oldersbem in Friesland, between Laurentius the Dominican and Georg Aportanus; 1527 at Norden in Friesland, between Resius and Synellius; 1528 at Uppsala in Sweden, between Master Olaus and Gallius; 1528 at Bern, between Haller and Alexius Grad, etc.; 1531 at Ulm, between Oecolampadius and Georg Oswald; 1534 at Geneva, between Farel and Furbity; 1535 at Geneva, between Jacob Bernard and Charles the Sorbonist; 1541 at Worms, between Philip Melanchthon and John Eck; 1541 at Regensburg (first), between Melanchthon, Bucer, etc., and Julius Pflug, Gropper, Eck; 1546 at Regensburg (second), between Bucer, etc., and Malvenda, etc.; 1549 at Oxford, between Martyr and Tresham, etc.; 1550 at Cambridge, between Bucer and Young; 1554 at Oxford, between Cranmer and Weston, etc.; 1556 at San Martino, among the Cévennes, between the Waldensians and Amatus Sanjulianus; 1557 at Worms, between Melanchthon and Canisius, etc.; 1559 at London, between Jewel, etc., and Watson, etc.; 1561 at Poissy, between Beza, etc., and Cardinal of Lorraine.

units.tr: In the same year at Haarlem, between John, priest of the great church, and the provost John Lappius. In 1580, in the Tower of London, between John Rainolds and John Hart. In 1595 at Tiran in Rhaetia, between Stuppanus, Cabassus, etc., and Andreossa, etc. In 1599 at Nancy, between James Covet and the Jesuit Comelet. In 1600 at Fontainebleau, between Philip Mornay and Perron. In 1601 at Regensburg (third), between Gretser, etc., and Egidius Hünnius, etc. In 1602 at Paris, between Molinaeus and Cayer. In 1608 at Antwerp, between Francis Lansbergius and P. Gouda. In 1608 at Schwalbach, between Pareus and Becanus, etc. In 1609 at Frankfurt, between Clement du Bois and Cosmas Morel. In 1618 at Castres in France, between John Carré, Paul Geslin de la Pillière, and John Breard, Daniel Baudri. In 1622 at London, between Doctor Featly and Mushet.

units.tr: In the same year, on 27 June, between Doctor Featly and the Jesuit Fisher. In 1625 at Cogua, between William Rivet and Gilbert Rausseau. In 1645 at Thorn, between the Jesuit Schonhoff, etc., and Berg, Vechner, etc. In 1646 at Uxbridge, between Charles, King of England, and Henry, Earl of Worcester. In 1651 at Rheinfelden, between Haberkorn and Valerian Magnus.

units.la: Quæ ego Colloquia, & si quæ plura, cum eorum Actis, in unum volumen compingi omnia, ne quæ intereant, & ut ab omnibus haberi, atque legi possint, desidesidero. Nam certe ex illis multum, & plus quam ex scripto alio elenctico addisces, ubi quid, & quomodo agendum cum Adversariis, quae validissima argumenta, in quibus plus metuant & deficiant, vel etiam glorientur, evidentissime cognoscitur. Saltem ut nemo in colloquium cum illis descendat & praesentaneam disputationem, nisi istis prius bene lectis, atque examinatis, consulo. Colloquium omne instituitur, aut ex prioribus videre est, vel ad simplicem disputationem, partisque alterutrius confutationem & convictionem; vel ad utriusque amicam conciliationem: qualia in Germania fuerunt VVormatiensia, Ratisbonensia, & nuper Colloquium Thorunense. Pleraque vero disputatoria. Semper attendendum, qua de materia disputandum sit: inter quos Collocutores: quo etiam tempore; quibus praesidibus: praeterea; quibus auditoribus: denique & quo propositio finctu, vel fine. In quibus omnibus quantum situm, ab iisque ut pendeat disputatio bene an secus inchoanda, habendaque, priora satis Colloquia edocent. Ad disputationem evocandi viri docti, ad conciliationem quoque moderati, & prudentes. Et quando cumque offertur, nunquam, ubi commode haberi potest, detrectanda: in offerenda autem videndum; ne ad vanam ingenii ostentationem, ex carnali impetu, vel animositate magis incitatur, quam sancto, pro Dei gloria, & hominum instructione, zelo. Quare nec cum contentiosis, disputacibus, & ambitiosis ingeniis quaerenda, sed declinanda potius: ad exemplum Ambrosii, detrectantis cum Augustino, quamvis mater hoc valde efflagitaret, disputationem: respondit enim me adhuc esse indocilem, eo quod inflatus essem novitate haeresis illius, & nonnullis quaestiunculis iam multos peritos agitassem, sicut illa indicaverat illi, inquit ipse de se Augustinus. Atque de ejusmodi Colloquiis vere pronunciavit Petrus Mosellanus, inter primos Reformatores, epist. ad Bilibaldum Pirckamerum, ubi de Colloquio Lipsiaco, anno
units.tr: I wish that these colloquies, and any others besides, were gathered together with their records into one volume, so that they might not perish and might be had and read by all. For certainly from them you will learn much, and more than from any other polemical writing, where and how one must deal with the adversaries, which arguments are the strongest, which ones they fear and fail at, or even boast of, is most clearly known. At least I advise that no one enter into a colloquy or extempore disputation with them until he has read and examined these carefully. Every colloquy is arranged either, as can be seen from the earlier ones, for a simple disputation, for the refutation and conviction of one side; or for the friendly conciliation of both sides, such as the Worms, Regensburg and the recent Thorn colloquies were in Germany. Most, however, are disputatious. One must always pay attention to the subject to be disputed, between whom the speakers are, also the time, the presiding officers, besides, the hearers, and finally the purpose and end of the proposal. The earlier colloquies teach well enough how much depends on all these matters, and on them whether a disputation is to be begun and conducted well or otherwise. Learned men should be summoned to disputation, and moderate and prudent men to conciliation. And whenever a disputation is offered, it should never be refused where it can conveniently be held. In making the offer, however, one must take care that one is not stirred up by fleshly zeal or animosity, for the display of a vain wit, rather than by holy zeal for God's glory and the instruction of men. Therefore one should not seek disputation with contentious, quarrelsome and ambitious minds, but rather avoid it: following the example of Ambrose, who refused disputation with Augustine, although his mother earnestly urged it: "For he replied that I was still unteachable, because I was puffed up by the novelty of that heresy, and had already harassed many experienced men with some little questions, as that woman had reported to him," Augustine says of himself. And Peter Mosellanus, one of the first Reformers, truly pronounced concerning such colloquies in his letter to Bilibald Pirckheimer, where he speaks of the Leipzig colloquy in the year

units.la: MDCLXIX. Mihi hoc disceptandi genus Theatrum quam nunquam visum est manifestissimâ Christi doctrinâ dignum. Nec adduci possum ut credam, spiritum sanctum pacis authorem, ad ejusmodi pugnas unquam se demittere; Christiana Theologia veritas citius impetratur orando, quam invenia-tur disceptando. Tum, quando disputabitur, videndum ut de articulo gravis momenti, cujusque interest omnium, etiam plebis: qualis v. g. de imaginibus, de communione sub utraque sacramenti parte &c. nam omnino observandum, ut praesente plebe, vel multis auditoribus Pontificiis, disputemus, quò hoc pacto ad eos sensus aliquis verioris doctrinae perveniat, quos alioqui hinc arcere solent Pontificii, & excludere. Non de re minutioni, vel de Patrum duntaxat sententiâ aut testimoniis aliquibus multum contendatur, neque solis praeliminaribus & circumstantialibus, aut personalibus totum tempus transigatur frustra. Semper & Notarii adhibeantur, quod tantopere in Colloquio Ratisbonensi altero urgebant Nostri; quo adversus calumnias, & falsas relationes, quibus mirum, quam se dare solent qui in conflictu succumbunt, semper tuti simus. Idque ex more Veterum, omniumque famigeratorum colloquiorum. Epiphanius, haeres. lxxx. contra Photinianos: Quemadmodum etiam in disputatione adversus Basilium reperimus in his, quae jussi sunt scribere velociter scribendi periti, Anysius diaconus Basilii, & Callicrates excepter Rufini Praesidis provinciae: & Olimpius ac Nicetes memoriter sive à memoria ipsius Basilii: & Entyches ac Theodulus notarii Basilii. In Colloquio Ratisbonensi III. anno MDLXXI, inter conditiones, seu regulas Colloquii, decima erat: Notarii jurati bini ex utraque parte deligantur, qui dicta fideliter excipiant, & singulis sessionibus, finito Colloquio, in praesentia Theologorum & Politicorum, partis utriusque Protocolla conferant, eaque conformata per omnia exemplaribus, reciproce facta subscriptione, & obsignatione permutentur. Sed & par utrius-que tisque partis debet esse ratio, qua in argumentando, quà respondendo, ut non unus semper objiciat, vel respondeat, sed tam hi, quam illi utramque partem, per vices, sustineant. Probæ erant conditiones, quas Theologi Reformati, habituræ disputationis, proponebant in Colloquio Thorunensi, sess. 1. quæ videantur. Uti & quæ Theologi nostri in Admonitione de libro Concordiæ cap. xII. Atque ita æquis conditionibus agendum, argumenta argumentis, ratio rationi opponenda; non calumniis, vociferationibus, minis, tumultu rem agere oportet, non devovendo se, aliosque, quod Pontificiis perquam familiare, qui actum probe, si animam suam vadem stiterint, vel alios præpropere damnarint, opinantur.
units.tr: 1569 (MDLXIX): This kind of disputing seems to me a theatre, never worthy of the most manifest doctrine of Christ. Nor can I be brought to believe that the Holy Spirit, the author of peace, ever lowers himself to such battles; the truth of Christian theology is obtained more quickly by praying than it is found by disputing. Then, when there is to be a disputation, one must see that it concerns an article of grave importance, one in which everyone has a stake, even the common people; such as, for example, images, communion under both kinds of the sacrament, and so on. For it must certainly be observed that we dispute in the presence of the common people, or of many Papist hearers, so that by this means some sense of the truer doctrine may reach those whom the Papists are otherwise accustomed to keep away from it and exclude. The contest should not be carried on at length over some trivial matter, or over the opinion of a Father alone or some testimonies, nor should the whole time be spent in vain on preliminaries and side issues, or on personal matters alone. Notaries should always be employed, as our side urged so strongly at the second Regensburg colloquy, so that we may always be safe against calumnies and false reports, which those who give way in the conflict are wont to produce in wondrous abundance. And this follows the custom of the Ancients and of all the famous colloquies. Epiphanius, heresy 80, against the Photinians: Just as also in the disputation against Basil we find, in those things which he ordered to be written, that Anysius the deacon of Basil, and Callicrates, the one excepted, of the provincial governor Rufinus, quickly wrote down with skill in swift writing; and Olimpius and Nicetes from memory, or from Basil's own memory; and Entyches and Theodulus, notaries of Basil. At the Regensburg colloquy of the year 1571 (MDLXXI), the tenth of the conditions or rules of the colloquy was: Two sworn notaries from each side shall be chosen, who shall faithfully record what is said, and at each session, when the colloquy is finished, in the presence of the theologians and the political officials, they shall compare the protocols of each side, and, once these have been copied word for word, they shall exchange them with reciprocal signature and sealing. But the method of arguing and answering must also be equal on each side, so that not one person always objects or replies, but both sides alike sustain their part in turn. The fair conditions which the Reformed theologians proposed for the disputation to be held at the Thorn colloquy, first session, are worth seeing. So too are those which our theologians gave in the Admonition on the Book of Concord, chapter 12. And so the business must be conducted on equal terms: argument is to be opposed to argument and reason to reason; the matter must not be handled with calumnies, shouting, threats and tumult, nor by devoting oneself and others, which is very familiar to the Papists, who think they have done the thing well if they have pledged their own soul as surety, or have condemned others too hastily.

units.la: Aliud est pro doctrina, ejusque veritate animam suam offerre: aliud pro hominibus, hos ut securos facias, te oppignorare velle & salutem tuam, quod neutiquam licet, cum justus quilibet fide suâ vivat, & omnes coram Christi tribunali apparere oporteat, ut unusquisque referat quod egerit, sive bonum, sive malum. II. Cor. v. 10. Cyprianus, lib. IV. epist. 11. Nobis autem secundum fidem nostram, & divinæ prædicationis datam formam competit ratio veritatis, unumquemque in peccato suo reum teneri, nec posse alterum pro altero reum fieri; cum Deus præmonet & dicat, Justitia justi super eum erit, & scelus scelerati super eum erit. Pro doctrinâ vero se devovere fas est, ut fidem tuam, atque integritatem exponas. Psalm. vii. 5. 6. Lutherus, in epistolâ ad Melanthonem, anno clɔ Iɔ xxx. d. xxx. Iunii, quâ eum valde anxium & consternatum erigit: sol es denn etlos gen seyn / daß Gott seinen Sohn für uns gegeben hat / so sey der Teuffel an meiner stadt. Simili ratione Nostri Sylvæ Ducis anno clɔ Iɔ c xxx. in suo Manifesto, promptos paratosque se dicebant, animas suas pro veritate doctrinæ oppignorare.
units.tr: It is one thing to offer your soul for a doctrine and its truth, and another to offer it for men, so as to make them secure, and to pledge your own salvation for them. That is by no means permitted, since every righteous man lives by his faith, and all of us must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done, whether good or evil. 2 Cor. 5:10. Cyprian, book 4, letter 11: "According to our faith, and the form of divine preaching, the principle of truth requires that each person is held guilty for his own sin, and that one cannot become guilty in place of another; since God forewarns and says, The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him." To devote oneself for the doctrine, however, is right, so that you may set forth your faith and its integrity. Ps. 7:5, 6. Luther, in a letter to Melanchthon, 30 June 1530, which lifts up a man who was very anxious and dismayed: "If it must be that God has given his Son for us, then let the devil have my place." In a similar manner our people of Hertogenbosch, in their Manifesto of 1530, said that they were ready and prepared to pledge their souls for the truth of the doctrine.

units.la: Quod attinet Colloquia charitativa, instituta pro controversiarum inter nos, atque Pontificios conciliatione, quamvis hæc, propter superius dicta, conclamata jam videatur & impossibilis, per prætensam Ecclesiæ Rom. infallibilitatem, Pontificis auctoritatem, & Concilii Tridentini decisiones, Papâ ejusmodi Colloquia, si quæ alia, gnaviter semper dissolvente, & ad se trahente, gaudeatque jam Papatus dici irreformabilis, uti in suis ad P. Innocentium x. litteris ipse loquitur Ernestus Lantgravius, d. vi. Ianuar. clɔ Iɔ clii. attamen quandocunque ab ipsis offertur, & in eum finem petunt Colloquium, amplexandum omnino: quia utcunque ille syncretismus non succedat, nonnulla tamen, ad coarguendam Papismi declinationem, ex illis lucramur, dum in tali negotio videntur nobis velle aliquo modo gratificari, & accedere, ut possunt, propiores. Et juxta illa quæ in Colloquio Thorunensi acta, atque in pace Germaniæ nuperâ conclusa sunt, ut utrique parti sedulo commendetur, de concordiâ quâdam Ecclesiasticâ serio cogitare: hoc, quod agant, adhuc superest. Atque id satius, quam ut ad vim aliam, bella, & persequutiones iterum se convertant. Qui ut in illud potius vires suas omnes intendant, & sine quo id haberi non potest, reformationem admittant, monendi, quemadmodum hæc latius pertractavimus. in Examine bullæ P. Innocentii, adversus pacem Germaniæ, à pag. 169.
units.tr: As for the charitable colloquies, instituted to reconcile the controversies between us and the Papists, although, for the reasons stated above, this seems now to be shouted down and impossible because of the so-called infallibility of the Roman Church, the authority of the Pope, and the decisions of the Council of Trent, and although the Pope, who always vigorously dissolves such colloquies, whatever they may be, and draws them to himself, now glories in being called "irreformable" (as Landgrave Ernest himself says in his letter to Pope Innocent X, 6 January 1652), nevertheless whenever they are offered by the Papists, and they seek a colloquy to that end, we must by all means embrace them. For however that syncretism may turn out, we still gain something from them in exposing the Papists' deviation, since in such a business they seem to wish to gratify us in some way and to come as near to us as they can. And, in line with what was done at the Colloquy of Thorn and concluded in the recent peace of Germany, that a certain ecclesiastical concord should be earnestly considered and commended to both parties: that remains yet to be done, and it is more desirable than that they should again turn to other violence, wars, and persecutions. Those who ought rather to direct all their strength to this, and without which it cannot be had, must be admonished to admit reformation, as we have treated these matters more fully in the Examination of the Bull of Pope Innocent, against the Peace of Germany, from p. 169.

units.la: præterea in illis charitativis, seu Conciliatoriis Colloquiis summopere expendendæ Adversariorum factæ nobis aliquando tum concessiones, tum confessiones. Concessiones appello, factas olim quadantenus conciliationes, ut in Colloquio Ratisbonensi, super primario religionis & controversiarum articulo, de justificatione, & qualia in unum librum collegit Cochlæus, ediditque, valde hic commendanda, quæ propterea hic aliqua describere & exhibere, ad excitandas super iis aliorum cogitationes, haud gravabor. Titulus libri est Quadruplex Concordiæ ratio, & Consideratio, super Confessione Augustanâ, anno cIↄ Iↄ xliv. edita. Vbi, in Explicatione Articulorum Augustæ in Septenorum tractatu, (quo de etiam supra) & Colloquio Haganoæ Regi Rom. &c. tradita d. xvii. Iunii, anno cIↄ Iↄ xl. ad quæstionem sibi à Ferdinando Rege propositam: quid in Augustanæ Confessionis viginti octo articulis esset à Catholicâ Ecclesiâ tolerandum aut acceptandum. Si quo modo in iisce articulis per amicum tractatum cum eis concordari posset? ita ad singulos respondit Auctor. De sancta Trinitate, Art. 1. In hoc articulo nihil mihi displicet ex eorum Confessione. De peccato Originali, Art. 2. Hic concordavimus cum ipsis Augustæ in Delectu. Cui sententiæ adhuc sto & acquiesco. De duabus naturis in Christo, Art. 3. In hoc articulo itidem cum eis per omnia concordes sumus. De justitia fidei, Art. 4. Augustæ in Delectu super hoc quoque articulo concordavimus. Nempe, ut non doceatur, quod sola fides justificet, sed quod omittatur hæc vocula, Sola. Quemadmodum & Cæsarea Majestas una cum aliis Principibus & Statibus in Recessu Imperiali judicarunt atque mandaverunt. De ministerio Verbi, & sacramentis. Art. 5. De hoc quoque articulo concordia in Delectu facta est, quæ permanere & rata haberi poterit. De bonis operibus, Art. 6. De hoc quoque concordatum est, juxta tenorem concordiæ circa Quartum articulum. De Ecclesia, Art. 7. De hoc quoque concordatum est in Delectu. De malis ministris Ecclesiæ, Art. 8. De hoc quoque concordatum ibi fuit. De Baptismo Art. 9. Hic quoque concordatum est cum eis, adversus Anabaptistas. De sacramento Eucharistiæ, Art. 10. De hoc quoque articulo concordatum est cum eis, contra Zwinglianos & Anabaptistas. Nempe, quod reliter est ibi verum corpus & verus sanguis Christi, non solum signum aut figura. De confessione, Art. 11. De hoc articulo non fuit tunc concordatum. Pistea vero protulerunt Potestantes in Delectu sententiam suam in scriptis, sub tribus sane punctis. &c. Quod si hæc tria puncta serio accepta erant erunt ac profiterentur, non foret difficile in his cum eis concordare. De Poenitentia, Art. 12. De hoc quoque articulo concordatum est in Delectu. De usu Sacramentorum, Art. 13. De hoc quoque concordatum fuit in Delectu. De Ordinatione Ministrorum Ecclesiae: Art. 14. Articulus iste in verbis quidem suis reprehendendus non est, in sensu autem adversatur nobis. De Caeremoniis & ritibus Ecclesiae, Art. 15. Hoc in articulo vellemus eis cito consentire, si ex fundamento scripturae demonstrarent, nostras Ceremonias & antiquos Ecclesiae ritus contra Evangelium esse, sicut dicunt. De Potestate saeculari, Art. 16. Hic quoque cum ipsis concordes sumus. De Extremo Iudicio, Art. 17. De hoc quoque articulo concordatum fuit in Delectu. De libero arbitrio, Art. 18. De hoc quoque concordatum est in Delectu. De causa peccati, Art. 19. Et hic per omnia concordatum est. De fide & Bonis operibus, Art. 20. De hoc articulo excitata est scandalosa, supervacanea ac disturna contentio in populo per Lutherum, quae tamen facile tolli posset. De Intercessione & Invocatione sanctorum, Art. 21. De hoc quoque articulo tractatum est in Delectu, sed non plene concordatum. De usu utriusque speciei Eucharistiae, Art. 22. Circa hunc articulum non est plene concordatum in Delectu. De Conjugio sacerdotum, Art. 23. De hoc articulo non est concordatum in Delectu. De Missa, Art. 24. Hoc in articulo bene concordare nobiscum possent Protestantes. De Confessione, Art. 25. De hoc articulo dictum est supra. De Discrimine Ciborum. Art. 26. Quum peterent nostri in Delectu, ut Protestantes velint se universali conformare Ecclesiae, in discrimine ciborum & temporum. In jejuniis & festis diebus, in processionibus & in aliis Ecclesiae Ceremoniis & consuetudinibus: Illi responsum suum in scriptis obtulerunt in hanc sane sententiam &c. Quod si serio ita sentirent circa haec Quinque puncta, bona nimirum forent haec ad unitatem praeparatio, ad invenienda media, quibus se nobiscum & cum universali Ecclesia plene conformarent. De votis Monasticis, Art. 27. De hoc articulo admodum graviter & copiose per multas Scripturas & per exempla sanctorum patrum, in publica Confutatione responsum est. Quod si avaritia & iniquus Mammon eos non obsessos & omnino excaecatos tenet, esset cum ipsis de hoc quoque articulo super tolerabilibus mediis tractandum. De potestate Episcopali Art. 28. Si autem serio ita sentirent, sicut verba supra dicta sonant, sperandum sane foret, ut super hoc quoque articulo possint pax & concordia per licitas media comparari ac erigi.
units.tr: Moreover, in those charitable or conciliatory colloquies, the concessions and confessions of our opponents, which they have at times made to us, must be weighed very carefully. I call concessions the conciliations once made to some extent, such as at the Colloquy of Ratisbon concerning the chief article of religion and of the controversies, justification, and such things as Cochlaeus collected and published in one book. These are very commendable here, and I will not hesitate to describe and set out some of them here, to stir up the thoughts of others on them. The title of the book is Quadruplex Concordiae ratio, et Consideratio, super Confessione Augustana (A Fourfold Plan and Consideration of Concord, concerning the Augsburg Confession), published in 1544, where, in the explanation of the Articles of Augsburg in the treatise of the Seven (of which also above), and in the Colloquy of Hagenau delivered to the King of the Romans, etc., on 17 June 1540, the author responds to each question put to him by King Ferdinand: what, in the twenty-eight articles of the Augsburg Confession, could be tolerated or accepted by the Catholic Church, and whether, if at all, these articles could be reconciled with them through a friendly treatment. On the holy Trinity, Art. 1: "In this article nothing displeases me in their Confession." On original sin, Art. 2: "Here we agreed with them at Augsburg in the Deliberation. To that opinion I still hold and assent." On the two natures in Christ, Art. 3: "In this article too we are in full agreement with them." On the justice of faith, Art. 4: "At Augsburg, in the Deliberation, we also agreed on this article: namely, that it should not be taught that faith alone justifies, but that this little word, alone, be omitted, as His Imperial Majesty, together with the other Princes and Estates, judged and ordered in the Imperial Recess." On the ministry of the Word and the sacraments, Art. 5: "Concord was also reached in the Deliberation on this article, and it can remain and be held valid." On good works, Art. 6: "This too has been agreed, according to the tenor of the agreement on the fourth article." On the Church, Art. 7: "This too was agreed in the Deliberation." On bad ministers of the Church, Art. 8: "This too was agreed there." On Baptism, Art. 9: "Here too we agreed with them, against the Anabaptists." On the sacrament of the Eucharist, Art. 10: "On this article too we agreed with them, against the Zwinglians and Anabaptists; namely, that there is truly the body and true blood of Christ, not only a sign or figure." On confession, Art. 11: "On this article there was no agreement at that time. But the Protestants in the Deliberation presented their opinion in writing, under three points indeed... If these three points were taken seriously and were professed, it would not be difficult to agree with them on these matters." On repentance, Art. 12: "On this article too agreement was reached in the Deliberation." On the use of the sacraments, Art. 13: "On this article too agreement was reached in the Deliberation." On the ordination of ministers of the Church, Art. 14: "This article is not to be censured in its words, but in its sense it opposes us." On the ceremonies and rites of the Church, Art. 15: "On this article we would gladly agree with them quickly, if they could demonstrate from the foundation of Scripture that our ceremonies and the ancient rites of the Church are against the Gospel, as they say." On secular power, Art. 16: "Here too we are in agreement with them." On the Last Judgment, Art. 17: "On this article too agreement was reached in the Deliberation." On free will, Art. 18: "On this article too agreement was reached in the Deliberation." On the cause of sin, Art. 19: "And here agreement has been reached in every respect." On faith and good works, Art. 20: "On this article a scandalous, superfluous, and discordant contention was stirred up among the people by Luther, which yet could easily be removed." On the intercession and invocation of the saints, Art. 21: "On this article too it was treated in the Deliberation, but not fully agreed." On the use of both kinds in the Eucharist, Art. 22: "On this article there was not full agreement in the Deliberation." On the marriage of priests, Art. 23: "On this article there was no agreement in the Deliberation." On the Mass, Art. 24: "On this article the Protestants could well agree with us." On confession, Art. 25: "On this article it has been said above." On the difference of foods, Art. 26: "When our men at the Deliberation asked that the Protestants be willing to conform themselves to the universal Church in the difference of foods and times, in fasts and feast days, in processions and in other ceremonies and customs of the Church, they presented their answer in writing, to this effect, etc. If they were seriously of this mind about these five points, these would certainly be a good preparation for unity, for finding the means by which they might fully conform themselves with us and with the universal Church." On monastic vows, Art. 27: "On this article it was answered very seriously and copiously, through many Scriptures and through the examples of the holy Fathers, in the public Confutation. But if avarice and iniquitous Mammon do not hold them obsessed and utterly blinded, we should treat with them on this article too, on tolerable means." On episcopal power, Art. 28: "But if they were seriously of this mind, as the words stated above sound, it would surely be hoped that peace and concord might be secured and established on this article too, by lawful means."

units.la: Haec Cochlaeus, tum ex sententia Colloquii Augustani, tum sua, de articulis concordandis: quibus, praealiis, insistere licet in judicio de religionum conciliatione formando, vel in quavis etiam iiscum disputatione; ut liqueat quae concessa nobis a Papistis ad reformationem, vel conciliationem dogmata alias fuerint. Qui Cochlaeus deinde in Viis Praeparatoriis ad instaurandam per colloquium concordiam; V Vormatiae, communi Theologorum Pontificiorum nomine anno CIↄ Iↄ xl. via v. posuit, ut articuli Confessionis, Augustae in Septenorum Colloquio concordati, rati utrimque habentur: quippe ubi tantam Collocutores adhibuisse scribit diligentiam, ut sedulo partium disquisitione & amica interpretatione dictorum, ad multorum Confessionis articulorum unanimem sensum & concordiam partium perventum fuerit: repetitque breviter concordatos articulos, post quos pergendum, ad compendifaciendam operam ita existimat: Vt igitur Reverende ac Magnifice D. V. videant, quantum compendii temporisque lucrandi ex priori concordia colloquio utrinque habeamus, si utraque pars ratum habeat, quod tunc placuit, recitabimus hic vobis bona fide bonam partem eorum, quae utriusque partis consensu tunc approbata & concordata fuerunt. Articuli Concordiae Augustensis Colloquii. Etenim in primo articulo, qui est de Trinitate personarum & unitate essentiae divinae, per omnia concordatum est; similiter & in Tertio, qui est de duabus naturis & una persona in Christo, & quidem absque omni dispu-tatioActione aut contradictione. In Secundo autem, qui est de peccato Originali, post nonnullam disceptationem in hac verba concordatum est, quod peccatum Originale sit carentia Originalis justitiae, quae exigit fidem fiduciamque & timorem Dei, quodque Concupiscentia, ex peccato Originali orta, remaneat in homine. Culpa vero Originalis peccati per baptismum tollatur. Id est, quod peccatum Originale tollatur quoad formale, sed maneat quoad materiale. In Quarto deinde, Quintoque, & Sexto articulis ita concordatum est, ut omitti debeat haec vox Sola, quando de fidei justificatione loquimur, ne de catero dicatur, nos sola fide justificari. In Septimo postea, & Octavo articulis iterum concordatum est, per declarationem hujus verbi, Sanctorum, quod utraque pars fateri debeat. In Ecclesia in hac vita esse etiam malos & peccatores. In Nono, qui de Baptismo est, & in Decimo, qui est de Eucharistia, plene concordatum est. Adjecto uno verbo, Realiter, quando dicitur, In Eucharistia corpus & sanguinem Christi vere adesse. Additum est, contra Sacramentariorum fraudulentias, Realiter, Testimonice Wesentlich. Sic & in 13. 14. 16. 17. 18. & 19. pie ac benigne concordatum fuit, ita ut nullus in ejusmodi articulis remaneret inter nos dissensionis scrupulus. In ceteris vero, nisi non per omnia concordare potuerimus, opera tamen precium videtur nobis, Reverendis & Magnificis D. V. commemorare, Quibusdam in punctis ipsis suis propriis scriptis & attestationibus consenserint nobis. &c. Denique idem Auctor, in Discussione Confess. & Apolog. Augustanae, scripta Ratisbonae anno clo Io xli. ad art. iv. v. & vi. de justificatione, iterum sic loquitur: Isti tres articuli, quales habentur in Confessione (non quae nuper variata & excusa est, sed quae Caes. Majestati Augustae exhibita fuit) facile possent concordari, si non obstaret contendendi ac frivole disputandi aviditas & pertinacia. Quemadmodum Augustae concordati fuerunt in septenorum colloquio, in haec sane verba. Justificatio seu remissio peccatorum fit per gratiam gratum facientem & fidem formaliter, per verbis vero & sacramentis instrumentaliter. Conferri possunt Protestantium nonnullorum in eandem rem consilia, scripta ad Guilj. Bellarmum, apud Melch. Goldastum, in Politicis Imperialib. part. xxv i i i. Haec & alia scire eum oportere existimo, qui de rebus Papalibus bene sit judicaturus. Namque nostra plurimum refert, nosse non solum quo pacto disputatio aliqua adornanda adversus illos sit, quibus pugnandum argumentis rationibus, sed etiam quid nostra in re actum jam cum & illis olim vel pridem sit, quod apprime & judicium firmabit, & disputationem. Neque ullam bene sustinebis disputationem, cujus non quoque noris historiam. Id est, quid olim ista super re senserint Adversarii, quid hodie, quomodo tum, vel jam disputent, & ubique scias quae alicubi, ex bono & usu veritatis, concesserint.
units.tr: Thus Cochlaeus, both from the sense of the Colloquy of Augsburg and from his own view, concerning the articles to be agreed. Before these, one may insist on them in forming a judgment about reconciling the religions, or in any disputation whatever, so that it becomes clear which doctrines the Papists have at other times conceded to us for reformation or reconciliation. This Cochlaeus then set out in his Viis Praeparatoriis ad instaurandam per colloquium concordiam at Worms, in the year 1540, on behalf of the Papist theologians as a body, so that the articles of the Confession, agreed at the Colloquy of Augsburg in the year of the Seven, are held as accepted on both sides. For he writes that the conferring parties applied such diligence that, by careful inquiry into each side's position and friendly interpretation of what was said, agreement and a unanimous sense on many articles of the Confession was reached between the parties. He then briefly repeats the articles agreed, after which, to save labour, he thinks one should proceed as follows: So that Your Reverence and Magnificence may see how much time and trouble we may gain from the earlier colloquy of concord, if each side ratifies what was then approved, we shall here recite for you, in good faith, the greater part of those things which, by the consent of both sides, were then approved and agreed. The Articles of the Concord of the Augsburg Colloquy. Indeed, in the first article, which concerns the Trinity of persons and the unity of the divine essence, agreement was reached in all points; likewise in the third, which concerns the two natures and one person in Christ, and that without any dispute or contradiction. In the second, which concerns original sin, after some discussion, it was agreed in these words: that original sin is the lack of original righteousness, which requires faith, trust and the fear of God, and that concupiscence, arising from original sin, remains in man. The guilt of original sin, however, is taken away through baptism. That is, original sin is taken away as to its formal aspect, but remains as to its material aspect. Then, in the fourth, fifth and sixth articles, it was agreed that the word Sola should be omitted when we speak of justification by faith, lest it be said elsewhere that we are justified by faith alone. Afterwards, in the seventh and eighth articles, it was again agreed, by explaining the word saints, that each side must confess that in the Church in this life there are also evil men and sinners. In the ninth, which concerns baptism, and in the tenth, which concerns the Eucharist, full agreement was reached. With one word added, real, when it is said that in the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ are truly present. It was added, against the deceits of the Sacramentarians, real, testimonice, wesentlich. So also in the 13th, 14th, 16th, 17th, 18th and 19th articles agreement was reached piously and kindly, so that no scruple of dissension remained between us on such articles. As for the rest, if we could not agree in every point, it nevertheless seems worth our while to remind Your Reverence and Magnificence that on certain points they have agreed with us by their own writings and attestations, etc. Finally, the same author, in his Discussion of the Confession and Apology of Augsburg, written at Ratisbon in the year 1541, on articles 4, 5 and 6 on justification, again speaks thus: Those three articles, as they stand in the Confession (not the recent altered and printed version, but the one presented to His Imperial Majesty at Augsburg), could easily be reconciled, if the eagerness and obstinacy of contentious and frivolous disputation did not stand in the way. In the same way they were agreed at Augsburg in the colloquy of the Seven, in these words: Justification, or the remission of sins, takes place through grace making one acceptable and through faith formally, but through the words and sacraments instrumentally. The counsels of some Protestants on the same matter, written to Guilielmus Bellarminus, may be compared, in Melchior Goldast's Politicis Imperialibus, part 28. I think a person who is going to judge well of Papal matters should know these and other things. For it matters greatly for us to know not only in what manner a disputation is to be prepared against those whom we must fight with arguments and reasons, but also what has already been done between us and them, once or long ago, which will greatly strengthen both judgment and disputation. Nor will you sustain any disputation well unless you also know its history: that is, what our adversaries once thought on the matter, what they think today, how they have argued then or now, and everywhere you should know what they have, here and there, conceded in the interest of goodness and the practice of truth.

units.la: Deinde Adversariorum Confessiones, in omni disputatione, praesertim Colloquiis, & charitativis, expendi etiam volo: sive Particulares, id est, sententias, quas ex ipsis Pontificiis Doctoribus colligere est, ad singulos doctrinae articulos, & quod multi viri docti ac diligentes egregie praestiterunt, Mortonus, Lamesius, Ioh. Gerhardi, & opus quidem praestantissimum est, quod quotidie magis & magis debet perfici; sive integras accipiamus aliquorum confessiones, quas totas in usus nostros convertamus. Quales Confessio, vel Protestatio, quam Lud. Blosius in Asceticis, & Rex Hispaniae Philippus II. aliique Pontificii tanto in pretio habent, atque in extremis usurpant, ceu tutissimum, cui innitantur, scipionem, quam supra retulimus; vel Consessio P. Pauli Veneti: super quibus si fundare unionem cupiant religiosam Pontificii, age eos audiemus.
units.tr: Next, I also want the confessions of our adversaries to be weighed in every disputation, especially in colloquies and friendly conferences: both the particular ones, that is, the opinions which may be gathered from the Papist doctors themselves on each doctrinal article, which learned and diligent men such as Morton, Ames and Johann Gerhard have done excellently, and it is a most excellent work which ought to be brought to completion more and more every day; and also whole confessions of some men, which we should convert entirely to our own use. Such is the confession or protestation which Ludovicus Blosius in his Ascetics, and King Philip II of Spain and other Papists hold in such high esteem, and use at the last, as the safest shield to lean upon, which we mentioned above; or the confession of Father Paul of Venice. If the Papists desire to found a religious union upon these, let us hear them.

units.la: Caeterum de scriptis, quae in causa Papistica ultro citroque innumera per integrum & quod excurrit saeculum prodierunt, & seu aetatem, seu locum, & materiam consideremus, quam tractarunt, varia sunt, ita statuo: videndum sum in opere quid scribamus, quo post tot egreegregia monumenta, & sæculo huic docto, & quo ipsis Pontificii, nominatim Auctores Colloquii Thorunensis, Valerianus Magnus, & similes ingenuè censent, raro ultra dicta olim & sæpius, alia vel nova afferri, vix scribatur, nisi aut novum aliquod, indictum ante te aliis; vel usum si possis facere dictorum aliquem singularem, ad hanc velad illam occasionem, aut ad adversarium convincendum, vel etiam hoc ipsum tradas fideliter, quæcunque disputatio super quovis articulo inter partes producta sit, queque postrema hinc inde argumenta, exceptiones sint & instantiæ. Super hisce scribas licet, atque superest satis, in quo te exerceas, præcipuè in primo illo, ubi nova afferuntur. Hoc autem est, vel ut Methodum disputandi novam calleas, vel rei quid simile habeas, sive ad convincendos Adversarios, vel etiam debito modo conciliandos. Atque in disputatione novum argumentum est aut artificiale, aut inartificiale, sive ex Patrum qui dicuntur, (ante omnia autem ex Scriptura) monumentis, præsertim ἀνέκδοτα, nondum editis, cui copia est veterum scriptorum, & ad M. S S. patet aditus, in magnis & egregiis Bibliothecis: aut ex hodiernis Papistarum scriptis, ipsos ut reddas magis εὐ παρακολουθητικος. Quo in genere præivit Thomas Iamesius Anglus, libro, A manuduction, or introduction unto divinitie: containing a confutation of Papists by Papists, throughout the important articles of our religion; their testimonies taken either out of the Indices Expurgatorii, or out the Fathers and ancient records; but especially the manuscripts. In his si quid valeas, experire: ut vel nova contra ipsos proferas, vel quæ ipsi nova, evertas. Ego isto consilio recentissimas Paparum Vrbani, & Innocentii Bullas aliquot, religionem imprimis, sed & politiam tangentes, examinavi: in quibus ut ipsi vel recedant in pejus, vel accedere ad nos videantur aliquantulum & reformare, offendi. Non novum dico, quod noviter ineptum: quaquale quod Theodorus Petreus, Carthusiæ Coloniensis Monachus, in Catalogo hereticorum, quem nugacissimum edidit hoc sæculo, a. cIↄ Iↄ c xxv i i r. tamquam diversarum sectarum Auctores & nomina recenset, qui ei appellantur, Bezanitæ, Calvinistæ, Zwinglíani, Bucerìani, Vergeriani, Martyriani, Oecolampadiani, Farellistæ, Boquini, Muscutani &c. Protestantes, Reformati, Hugonotæ, Bisacramentales, tum Anti-Lutherani, Anti-Calvinistæ, Calvino Turcistæ, & nescio quod non hominum genus nominumque: sed quod ineptissimum, pag. 227. ponitur inter hæresiarchas Vincentius à Drielenburch, exortus ad annum 1608. Non possum, inquit Auctor, quin etiam Novatori huic Batavo locum in hoc hereticorum albo assignem. Qui patriâ Ultrajectinus, cum Lugduni Batavorum jurisprudentiæ aliquamdiu operam navasset, juvenili quodam arreptus impetu, anno 1608. diebus circiter quatuordecim ante pascha cum esset Ultrajecti, dixit in oratione matutinâ subitò in se descendisse virtutem Dei, veluti divinam quandam obumbrationem, atque inspirationem, quâ certò intellexerit se esse per Christum justificatum, & à damnatione redemtum &c. Alius porro quidam (sic Batavus Batavum, hereticus hereticum excipit) pressius ipsum designans, cucullum consecit inscriptum hoc symbolo, DrLeLenbVrCh PaVs van alle sotten / id est, omnium stultorum Papa. Quod latine brevius sic dici poterit. DrLeLenbVrCh plane STVLTVS. Ad quæ quis non rideat? quin Scriptorem stolidissimum fustibus excipiendum dicas, qui in haereticis describendis tam stulte insanit? Omnes etenim, qui istum Vincentium, quam apte in Catalogo hereticorum & haeresiarcharum ponatur, novimus.
units.tr: Otherwise, regarding the writings which in the Papist cause have appeared in countless numbers, back and forth, throughout the whole of the past century and beyond, and whether we consider their age, their place, or the matter they treated, they are of various kinds. I lay down this: one must consider what we ought to write in this work, since after so many outstanding monuments, and for this learned age, and as the Papists themselves, namely the authors of the Colloquy of Thorn, Valerianus Magnus and the like, frankly acknowledge, almost nothing is to be set forth beyond what has been said long ago and often, unless something new is brought forward which has not been announced before by others, or unless you can make some singular use of the things said, for this or that occasion, either to convince the adversary, or even to hand down faithfully whatever disputation has been brought forward on any article between the parties, and the last arguments, exceptions and instances on each side. You may write on these matters, and there is enough to occupy you, especially in the first sort, where new things are put forward. This means either that you should acquire a new method of disputing, or obtain something of the kind for the matter, either to convince the adversaries or even to reconcile them in a fitting manner. In a disputation a new argument is either artificial or inartificial, whether drawn from the monuments of the so-called Fathers (but above all from Scripture), especially unpublished [ἀνέκδοτα] writings not yet printed, of which there is an abundance of old writers, and access to manuscripts lies open in the great and excellent libraries; or from the present-day writings of the Papists, so that you make them easy to follow [εὐ παρακολουθητικος]. In this kind Thomas James, the Englishman, has gone before, in his book, A Manuduction, or Introduction unto Divinitie: containing a Confutation of Papists by Papists, throughout the important articles of our Religion; their testimonies taken either out of the Indices Expurgatorii, or out of the Fathers and ancient records; but especially the manuscripts. Make trial of this if you have the ability, so that you either bring forward new things against them, or overturn what they have newly put forward. By this plan I examined some of the most recent bulls of the Popes Urban and Innocent, touching above all religion but also policy, and I found that in them they either go backwards for the worse, or seem to move a little towards us and reform. I do not call new what is newly foolish, such as what Theodorus Petreus, a Carthusian monk of Cologne, sets out in his Catalogue of Heretics, which he published in this century, in the year 1527 (sic), as he lists the authors and names of diverse sects, which are called Bezanites, Calvinists, Zwinglians, Bucerians, Vergerians, Martyrians, Oecolampadians, Farellists, Bocquinists, Muscutians, etc., Protestants, Reformed, Huguenots, Bisacramentarians, then Anti-Lutherans, Anti-Calvinists, Calvin-Turks, and I know not what other kind of men and names. But, most foolish of all, on page 227 he places among the heresiarchs Vincentius à Drielenburch, who arose about the year 1608. I cannot, says the author, refrain from also assigning a place in this white list of heretics to this Dutch innovator. Born at Utrecht, when he had for some time applied himself to law at Leiden, seized by a certain youthful impulse, in the year 1608, about fourteen days before Easter, while he was at Utrecht, he said that in his morning prayer the power of God had suddenly descended into him, like a certain divine overshadowing and inspiration, by which he clearly understood that he was justified through Christ and redeemed from damnation, etc. Moreover, another person (thus one Dutchman receives another Dutchman, one heretic another heretic), pointing at him more closely, made a hood inscribed with this device, DrLeLenbVrCh PaVs van alle sotten, that is, Pope of all fools. In Latin this could be said more briefly: DrLeLenbVrCh plainly STVPID. To which who would not laugh? Indeed, would you not say that the most stupid writer should be cudgelled, who raves so foolishly in describing heretics? For all of us who know him know how aptly Vincentius is placed in the Catalogue of Heretics and Heresiarchs.

units.la: Ad illud de Patrum scriptis, refero etiam Antiquorum Scriptorum à falsificationibus & corruptionibus Papalibus vindicationem: quo in opere gnavum se præbuit eruditumque, ille idem Thomas Iamesius Anglus, Oxoniensis Bibliot. Custos, qui libros impressos Romæ, ex typographia Vaticana, contulit cum antiquis & M. S S. exemplaribus in Oxoniensi, illorumque multiplicem corruptionem notavit & detexit: cujus etiam argumenti scriptum edidit singulare & eximium, lingua Anglica, de Corruptione Scripturæ, Conciliorum, & Patrum.
units.tr: I refer to this also the vindication of the ancient writers from Papal falsifications and corruptions. In this work the same Englishman, Thomas James, Keeper of the Bodleian Library at Oxford, showed himself diligent and learned. He compared the printed books issued at Rome from the Vatican press with the old manuscript copies in the Oxford library, and he noted and exposed their manifold corruption.
