He also published a single, distinguished treatise on this subject in English, On the Corruption of Scripture, of the Councils, and of the Fathers.

units.la: Sed & quorum usum noris pro prudentia ad certos aliquos, ad plures dispergere nova scriptione, excusat eam laudatque, modo ne aliorum ante te dicta optime, ullo modo defraudari tuis cupias. Præterea multi fructus est accuratè ostendere terminos & limites disputationum, ut certo intuitu mox videas quid, & quousque actum rebus nostris sit: quod præterquam aliis, valde conducet tum Controversiarum Studiosis, tum scribere aliquid hac in causa parantibus. Tentavi ego id aliquando in præcipuâ cum Papistis Controversiâ, super Scripturæ Sacræ perfectione, ut, recensitis primo loco iis, qui hac de re ab utraque parte, & quando scripserunt, tum propósito ex scriptis classicis hinc inde Controversiæ statu, ex Concilio Tridentino, & Ecclesiarum nostrarum Confessionibus, addita ejus ex utriusque partis Scriptoribus & disputationibus expositione; tertio nostra ponerem argumenta, & singula à suis exceptionibus vindicarem, argumenta nimirum ex Scripturâ, rationibus, authoritate Patrum, testimoniis Martyrum, confessionibus Adversariorum: denique ultimo loco exhiberem objectiones sententiæ Pontificiæ: omnia ad ultimos usque processus seu instantias, quantum potui: sed si quis majori otio affluens per omnes id præstet controversias, detque quasi Codicem, seu Pandectas Disputationum, annotatis utriusque partis ex optimis Auctoribus Disputationum processibus, ad exemplum eorum, qui in varios Scripturæ libros contexuerunt ex Patribus, qua Græcis, qua Latinis, Catenas; vel ex recentioribus Ecclesiæ Doctoribus Expositiones; sive qui in Auctores optíptimos & Litteratores, Plautum, Suetonium Terentium, Iuvenalem, Florum, Iustinum, Sulpitium, nuper dederunt annotationes ex variis Scriptoribus congestas, qui (dico) ad exemplum istorum, in rebus Theologicis, & Disputationibus idem tentaret, spondere ausum quod is operae pretium fructumque esset relaturus non exiguum. Quippe hoc pacto eximium facturus librorum, sumtuum, & operis in studio collocandi compendium; & tum quae singulis Scriptoribus debeatur laus, tum quid sequentibus agendum super est, breviter ostendens. Ex qua tabula optime perspicietur, quid factum hactenus, quid faciendum restet. Nolim, quod plurimis tamen video in usu esse, propter unum forte vel alterum, quod dicendum habeas, & novum sit, aut videatur, vel adferendum, vel refutandum, de integro iterum ordiri, & rem totam ab ovo (quod ajunt) retractare. Nam quorsum hoc? nisi ut ostendas impotentiam animi judiciique, solum ad fabricandas librorum moles laborantis, & te aeque tuis diffidere, atque invidere alienis? Multo rarior scriptio foret, quam est vulgo, si tam sua & meliora dictis, aut utiliora, usumve singularem habitura Scriptores proferre laborarent, quam aliena, & haec repetere dumtaxat, aut describere, cum maximâ sepe Auctorum injuriâ, & Lectorum onere. Tum & videre oportet etiam atq; etiam, quibus scribas, tuisne, id est, tuae sententiae hominibus, an aliis non dico tibi, quamvis certe sint qui non in commodum aliorum, sed sibi, & pro nominis sui ımani videndoque scriptitent mustaceo. Sed in materia quidem controversiarum Tuis quando scribis, prudenter videndum, num forte te scribere necesse sit: sin aliis, vide quem usum apud illos habere, quae scribis, possint. Nam utcunque utrisque aliquando simul prodesse queant, quae dicis, aliquando tamen non aeque aliis usui erunt illa, quae Tui probant. Iam quae aliis scribis, primum ut ad illorum queant manus perve-
units.tr: But as for those whose use you know, to disperse your work among a few certain people or many with a new writing, he excuses it and praises it, provided that you do not wish to defraud others of what has been said well before you. Moreover, it is very fruitful to show accurately the boundaries and limits of disputations, so that at a single glance you can see what has been done in our cause and how far. This would greatly help not only others but also students of the controversies and those preparing to write something on this question. I once attempted this for the chief controversy with the Papists, on the perfection of Holy Scripture. I first reviewed those who had written on this matter from each side, and when they wrote. Then I set out the state of the controversy from the classic writings, from the Council of Trent and the Confessions of our churches, adding an explanation of it drawn from the writers and disputations of both sides. Third, I would set out our arguments and defend each one against its objections: arguments from Scripture, from reasons, from the authority of the Fathers, from the testimonies of the martyrs, and from the confessions of our adversaries. Finally, in the last place, I would present the objections to the Papal view, carrying everything through to the final stages or instances, as far as I could. But if someone with more leisure were to go through all these controversies and give a kind of Code or Pandects of the disputations, with notes from both sides taken from the best authors on the course of the disputations, after the example of those who have woven catenas on the various books of Scripture from the Fathers, Greek and Latin, or of those who have written expositions from the more recent teachers of the Church; or after the example of those who have recently given notes gathered from various writers on the best authors and grammarians, Plautus, Suetonius, Terence, Juvenal, Florus, Justin, Sulpicius; I say, if someone were to attempt the same thing in theological matters and disputations after that model, I would dare to promise that he would bring back no small profit and reward for his labour. For in this way he would make a remarkable saving of books, expense and effort in study, and would briefly show both what praise is owed to each writer and what remains to be done by those who follow. From such a table it would be seen most clearly what has been done so far and what still needs doing. I would not want, although I see that most people do this, for someone to begin the whole matter again from the start, and to go over the entire thing from the egg (as they say), merely because of one or two points that he has to say, which are new or seem so, or which must be brought forward or refuted. For to what end is this? Unless to show the weakness of mind and judgement of one who labours only to build up heaps of books, and who distrusts his own work as much as he envies the work of others? Writing would be far rarer than it is commonly, if writers laboured to bring forward things that were their own and better, or more useful, or of special value, rather than things that belong to others, which they merely repeat or copy out, often to the great injury of the authors and the burden of the readers. Also, one must look again and again at whom you are writing for: for your own people, that is, men of your own opinion, or for others, I do not say for you, though there certainly are some who write not for the benefit of others but for themselves, for the sake of their own name and to be seen, like those who chase a honey-cake. But in a controversy, when you write for your own people, you must consider prudently whether you really need to write at all. If you write for others, see what use what you write can have for them. For although what you say may sometimes help both sides at once, sometimes those things which please your own side will not be equally useful to others. Now, as for what you write for others, first you must consider that it may reach their hands,

units.la: ni aire, dispiciendum, ne operam luisse, saltem magna ex parte, videamur. Quod ideo dico, quia dum libellis vernaculis nos identidem lacessunt Pontificii, nobis duplex in respondendo incumbit cura, ut Nostros homines adversus illorum vexationes bene muniamus; tum quo pacto ad Pontificiorum manus queant pervenire nostra, ea ut legant, æque ac illorum scripta Nostri. Nisi enim hoc ab illis obtineamus (quod vehementer alioquin impediunt) ut quæ rescribimus vulgari linguâ, ab ipsorum hominibus æque videantur legunturque, ac quæ illi edunt, à Nostris, vide quam impari congrediamur alea. Ergo hoc ante omnia stipulemur ab Adversario, ut nostra legi sinat à suis, perinde ac ejus scripta legantur à Nostris: quod nisi fiat, haud video quid adeo necesse sit, ipsorum scriptis multum respondere, aliterve quam eadem inhibitione librorum adversariorum, quâ ipsi nostros excipere vulgò solent, & arcere. Nunc præsertim, ubi post diuturna graviaque disputationum Theologicarum ultro citroque ultra seculum habita prælia, quid de re sit, quidque pro veritate habendum, sedulo & candido examinatori facile constare queat, etiam citra novam vel ulteriorem scriptionem. Quippe uti bene dixerunt Nostri in Colloquio Thorunensi, sess. I. in Postulatis de ratione Colloquii, art. VIII. Alternationes inter Collocutores, juridico modo congruunt, ultra tamen triplicam non procedatur; cum res ad tot gradus deducta satis patere queat. Imo viris candidis, piis, non partium amore præoccupatis facile patere, post ternam discussionem, veritas controversiæ poterit. Atque illa causa occurrit sollicite aliquando inquirenti, cur jam tam rara sit Papatus reformatio, & conversio Papistarum tam infrequens, contra quam olim, quo tempore urbes & regiones integræ à Papatu reformatæ prius fuerunt, quam jam aliquot homines? nempe, quod veritas in libero examine, maturâ Papatus reformamamatione dilucide statim & facile apparuit, quae nunc formatâ post multas contentiones parte obstinatissimè irreformabili, sed à Papatus tyrannide oppressa & obfuscata, non ita ab hominibus cognoscitur, inde nec accipitur. Primo illo tempore magis ingenua erat multorum de doctrinâ nostrâ professio, quam hodie, &c. in poenam reprobatae veritatis, quam sola intercludit contumacia. Cum nostra confessio, scribit Lutherus, Tom. VII. lib. adversus Papatum Romæ à Satana fundatum, an. 30. coram Imperatore & omnibus imperii statibus Augustæ recitabatur, alterius partis Theologi, num isthæc sacra scriptura refutare possent interrogati, Responderunt, scriptura quidem refutari non posse, sed tantum Patrum & Conciliorum decretis. Ibi nonnulli Principum, risu diffluentes, dicebant: Egregie scilicet nos Theologi nostri defendunt, dicunt enim adversariorum causam Scriptura niti, & nos eâ destitui.
units.tr: so that we do not seem to have wasted our labour, at least for the most part. I say this because, while the Papists keep attacking us again and again with vernacular pamphlets, we have a double concern in replying: first, to fortify our own people well against their harassments; and second, to make sure that our writings can reach the hands of the Papists, so that they read ours just as our people read theirs. For unless we secure this from them (which they otherwise strenuously prevent), namely that what we reply in the vernacular is read and seen by their own people just as what they publish is read by ours, consider how unequal a game we are playing. So above all we must stipulate with the adversary that he allow his people to read ours, just as his writings are read by ours. Unless this happens, I do not see why it is so necessary to answer their writings at length, or to answer them in any other way than with the same prohibition of books by which they usually exclude and keep out ours. This is especially so now, when, after long and serious theological disputations fought back and forth for more than a century, what the truth of the matter is, and what must be held as true, can easily be made plain to a careful and honest examiner, even without any new or further writing. Indeed, as our people rightly said at the Colloquy of Thorn, session I, in the Postulates on the method of the Colloquy, article VIII: the alternations between the speakers accord with legal procedure, but they should not go beyond a triplication, since a matter brought to so many stages can be made plain enough. Indeed, the truth of the controversy can easily become clear to honest, pious men not preoccupied by love of a party, after a third discussion. And this is the explanation that suggests itself to anyone who carefully inquires why the reform of Papacy and the conversion of Papists are now so rare, unlike in former times, when whole cities and regions were reformed from Papacy, when now scarcely a few men are. The reason is that when the truth was free to be examined, it appeared at once clearly and easily in the maturing of the reform of the Papacy. Now, after many contentions, a part has been formed that is most obstinately unreformable, and the truth, though oppressed and obscured by the tyranny of the Papacy, is not so readily recognised by men, and so is not accepted. In that first period the profession of our doctrine was far more open-hearted among many than it is today, for the punishment of the truth that has been rejected, which only obstinacy cuts off. When our Confession was read before the Emperor and all the estates of the empire at Augsburg in the year 30, Luther writes (Vol. VII, in the book Against the Papacy Founded at Rome by Satan), the theologians of the other side were asked whether they could refute this sacred Scripture. They answered that Scripture indeed could not be refuted, but only by the decrees of the Fathers and the Councils. Then some of the princes, dissolving in laughter, said: "Our theologians certainly defend us splendidly! For they say that the cause of our adversaries rests on Scripture, and that we are deprived of it."

units.la: Jam in argumentatione adversus illos disputandum primo quidem loco ex S. Scriptura, inde ratione, tum ex sententia Patrum, quarto ex Confessionibus Adversariorum agendum, uti ultimo testimoniis Martyrum, qui & doctrinam & argumenta nostra suo sanguine confirmarunt. Quam ex Martyrologio topicam, ab Andreâ V Villeto didici, observatam in Synopsi Papismi & post Martyrologium Anglicanum maius, facto catalogo, instruxit Foxus. Quippe quantum verba excedit actio, quâ nulla excelsior martyrio, ita quae martyr dicit, & quidem pro martyrii sui argumento, validissima merito habentur, ad animum movendum & convincendum. Nam in igne manifestabitur, & cujusque opus quale sit ignis probabit. I. Cor. 113. 13. 14. Nemo enim se vel lubens in mortem tradit ob causam frustraneam aut malam, vel suam bonam causam non tum confirmare gestit argumento optimo, gravissimoque.
units.tr: Now in arguing against them, we must first dispute from Holy Scripture; then from reason; then from the opinion of the Fathers; fourth, from the Confessions of our adversaries; and last, from the testimonies of the martyrs, who confirmed both our doctrine and our arguments with their blood. I learned this topical order from the Martyrology of Andreas Quercius (Villetus) and observed it in his Synopsis of Papism; and Foxe arranged his catalogue in the same way after the larger English Martyrology. For just as action goes beyond words, and no action is higher than martyrdom, so what the martyrs say, especially as proof of their martyrdom, is rightly held to be most powerful for moving and convincing the mind. For in the fire it will be made manifest, and the fire will test what sort of work each man's is. 1 Cor. 3. 13, 14. For no one willingly gives himself up to death for a vain or bad cause, nor does anyone who holds his cause good fail to strive to confirm it with the best and most serious argument.

units.la: Cæterum ex ipsorum Adversariorum confessionibus disdisputare docuerunt egregii Scriptores, Mortonus, in Apol. Catholica; Ioh. Gerhardi, in Confess. Catholica, quem librum, vel libros, plures enim sunt, summopere necessarios facio disputaturo cum Pontificiis, quia illis Auctor pro diligentia sua, diffusaque lectione, congessit varia hactenus in Pontificios, praesertim ex ipsis, prolata argumenta, & omnis generis testimonia. Adeo ex ipsis Papistis Papatus confundi potest. In Anglia Iohannes V White, provocavit Adversarium suum, quod de quovis Pontificiae religionis articulo esse toftensurus, repugnare cum S. Scripturae primum, tum Ecclesiae primitivae, denique & aliter cum a Scholasticis, aliisque in Romana Ecclesia doctum fuisse, ac hodie tradunt Iesuitae, & Concilium Tridentinum.
units.tr: Besides, from the confessions of the adversaries themselves, excellent writers have taught us to dispute: Morton, in his Apologia Catholica, and Johann Gerhard, in his Confessio Catholica. I make this book, or these books (for there are several), very necessary for anyone about to dispute with the Papists, because the author, through his careful work and wide reading, has gathered the various arguments and all kinds of testimonies hitherto brought forward against the Papists, especially from the Papists themselves. In this way Papistry can be thoroughly refuted from the Papists' own statements. In England John White challenged his opponent to show, on any article of the Papist religion, that it conflicts first with Holy Scripture, then with the primitive Church, and finally with what the Scholastics and others in the Roman Church taught, as the Jesuits and the Council of Trent now present it.

units.la: Quemadmodum ad Patres provocabat Ioh. Luellus: Si quisquam eruditus adversarius, sive universi simul adversarii nostri ullam laudationem aut ex antiquo & Catholico patre, aut ex vetusto aliquo Concilio, aut a sacrosanctis Dei Scripturis sententiam, ullamve ecclesiae primitivae exemplum in medium proferre possint, unde liquido clareque constet, ullam in toto orbe per sexcentos integros a Christo annos Missam privatam extitisse, ego me manus daturum, atque in contrariam sententiam iurum spondeo. Sic non de Missa solum privata, sed de XXVII, Pontificiae religionis articulis loquebatur. Scriptores autem adversus Papismum praestantiores vide annotatos in Bibliotheca nostri D. Voetii lib. II. Compendio studiosi terant, Amesii Bellarminum enervatum, Riveti Catholicum Orthodoxum, & a parte adversa Concilii Tridentini canones.
units.tr: John Lewis appealed in the same way to the Fathers: "If any learned adversary, or all our adversaries together, can bring forward any praise either from an ancient and Catholic Father, or from some old Council, or from the most holy Scriptures of God, or any example from the primitive Church, from which it may clearly and plainly appear that a private Mass existed anywhere in the whole world for six hundred full years from Christ, I promise that I will give myself up and swear to the opposite opinion." He was speaking not only of the private Mass but of twenty-seven articles of the Papist religion. As for the more outstanding writers against Papism, see those listed in the Bibliotheca of our Voetius, book II. Students should wear them down by working through them: Amesius's Bellarminus enervatus, Rivet's Catholicus orthodoxus, and from the other side the canons of the Council of Trent.

units.la: Tempus est, ut controversiarum Papalium faciamus etiam hic catalogum.
units.tr: It is time that we also give here a catalogue of the Papal controversies.

units.la: I. Annon S. Scriptura ad aedificationem Ecclesiae nunc sit omnino necessaria? Aff. II. Num S. Scriptura omnem suam auctoritatem apud nos obtineat ex auctoritate, & testimonio Ecclesiae Romanae? Neg.
units.tr: I. Is Holy Scripture now wholly necessary for the building up of the Church? Affirmative. II. Does Holy Scripture obtain all its authority among us from the authority and testimony of the Roman Church? Negative.

units.la: III. Num libri, quos Papistæ, juxta Concilium Tridentinum (sess. IV.) præter illos, quos Ecclesiæ Protestantium, & Israëliticæ olim, pro Canonicis S. Scripturæ habuerunt; puta liber Sapientiæ, Judith, tertius & quartus Ezræ, Baruch, Epistola Ieremiæ, libri Maccabæorum, Fragmenta Estheris, & Danielis, ut in Vulgata editione Papistica leguntur, sint sacri Canonici? Neg.
units.tr: III. Are the books which the Papists, according to the Council of Trent (sess. IV), hold as canonical Scripture in addition to those which the Protestant Churches and the Israelites of old regarded as canonical, namely the Book of Wisdom, Judith, the third and fourth books of Ezra, Baruch, the Epistle of Jeremiah, the books of the Maccabees, the fragments of Esther and Daniel, as they are read in the Papist Vulgate edition, truly sacred and canonical? Negative.

units.la: IV. Num universa salutis doctrina, quæ ad Religionem, sive fidem & mores est necessaria, non contineatur in S. Scripturis; sed præterea sit verbum Dei non scriptum, sive Traditiones, de rebus necessariis, divinæ, & Apostolicæ, oretenus ab ipso Christo, aut Apostolis acceptæ, & in Ecclesiâ, continuâ successione, servatæ, quas pari pietatis affectu & reverentiâ, cum Sacris Scripturis, suscipere oporteat, & venerari? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Is the whole doctrine of salvation, which is necessary for religion, that is faith and morals, not contained in Holy Scripture, but in addition there is an unwritten Word of God, or Traditions, concerning necessary matters, both divine and apostolic, received by word of mouth from Christ himself or the Apostles and preserved in the Church by continuous succession, which ought to be received and venerated with equal devotion and reverence as the Holy Scriptures? Negative.

units.la: V. An S. Scripturæ lectio semper omnibus concedenda sit, quin imò in jungenda? Aff.
units.tr: V. Should the reading of Holy Scripture always be granted to all, or rather even be enjoined? Affirmative.

units.la: Ideoque
units.tr: Therefore

units.la: An oporteat, & expediat Sacram Scripturam in linguas vernaculas, usui cunctorum fidelium, transferre? Aff.
units.tr: Ought the Holy Scripture to be translated into the vernacular tongues for the use of all the faithful, and is it expedient? Affirmative.

units.la: Atque,
units.tr: And so,

units.la: An dogmata Religionis necessaria in S. Scripturâ fidelibus perspicuè tradantur? Aff.
units.tr: Are the doctrines of religion necessary to salvation set out clearly for the faithful in Holy Scripture? Affirmative.

units.la: VI. Num Latina Vulgata editio Papistica, sola sit authentica, (non Hebræa Veteris, vel Græca N. Testamenti) & in rebus fidei, Hebrææ Græcaeque præferenda, adeò ut eam nemo quovis prætextu audeat rejicere? Neg.
units.tr: VI. Is the Latin Vulgate edition of the Papists alone authentic (not the Hebrew of the Old Testament, or the Greek of the New), and in matters of faith to be preferred to the Hebrew and Greek, so that no one on any pretext may dare to reject it? Negative.

units.la: VII. Num judicium Controversiarum Theologicarum infallibile alligatum sit, & hæreat solùm apud Papam Romanum, aut Concilium ejus Papisticum, vel Ecclesiam Romano-Papalem; à cujus authoritate omnes debeant petere Sacræ Scripturæ ceetissimam interpretationem, necessariò sequendam in Neg.
units.tr: VII. Is the infallible judgment of theological controversies bound to and resting only with the Roman Pope, or his Papist Council, or the Roman-Papal Church, from whose authority all must seek the most certain interpretation of Holy Scripture, which must necessarily be followed? Negative.

units.la: An verò supremus & infallibilis Controversiarum Theologicarum judex, sit solus Spiritus Sanctus in S. Scriptura? Aff.
units.tr: Or is the supreme and infallible judge of theological controversies the Holy Spirit alone, speaking in Holy Scripture? Affirmative.

units.la: VIII. Num, quia S. Scriptura Religionis omnis est regula perfectissima & sufficientissima, ac sola; ideò in argumentatione Theologicâ ex S. Scripturâ, nullus ratiocinationi, discursui, interpretationi, formandi consequentiis, aut commentationi relinquatur locus? Neg.
units.tr: VIII. Because Holy Scripture is the most perfect and sufficient rule of all religion, and the only one, is there therefore no place left in theological argument from Scripture for reasoning, discourse, interpretation, the drawing of consequences, or commentary? Negative.

units.la: IX. Num Deus praedestinarit homines ad vitam aeternam, propter praevisa ipsorum bona opera, & merita? Neg.
units.tr: IX. Did God predestine men to eternal life on account of their foreseen good works and merits? Negative.

units.la: X. An Deus providentiae suae vi influat in ipsas causas secundas, etiam liberas, eas ad actum movendo, & determinando? Aff.
units.tr: X. Does God, by the power of his providence, act upon secondary causes, even free ones, moving and determining them to action? Affirmative.

units.la: XI. Num justitia originalis in primo homine fuerit supranaturalis, data ad domandam carnis, contra spiritum concupiscentis pugnam naturalem, sive ad naturae humanae defectum, morbum, aut languorem corrigendum? Neg.
units.tr: XI. Was original righteousness in the first man supernatural, given to tame the natural struggle of the flesh against the spirit of concupiscence, or to correct the defect, disease, or weakness of human nature? Negative.

units.la: XII. Num sit aliquod peccatum natura sua non mortale? Neg.
units.tr: XII. Is there any sin which is not mortal by its nature? Negative.

units.la: XIII. Num hominis arbitrium in eam partem peccandi ita sit liberum in utramque partem ut etiam ad bonum religionis indifferens, ac ex se potens sit? Neg.
units.tr: XIII. Is the human will so free to sin in either direction that it is indifferent to the good of religion and able of itself to do it? Negative.

units.la: XIV. Num Maria immunis fuerit ab omni peccato, vel originali, vel actuali? Neg.
units.tr: XIV. Was Mary free from every sin, original or actual? Negative.

units.la: XV. Num Christi anima statim ab ejus ortu perfectè beata, & omni scientiâ repleta fuerit? Neg.
units.tr: XV. Was the soul of Christ perfectly blessed and filled with all knowledge from the moment of his birth? Negative.

units.la: XVI. An Christus sit Mediator, & Mediatoris officium exerceat secundum utramque naturam, divinam & humanam? Aff.
units.tr: XVI. Is Christ the Mediator, and does he exercise the office of Mediator according to both natures, divine and human? Affirmative.

units.la: Num verò solum secundum naturam humanam? Neg.
units.tr: But is it only according to the human nature? Negative.

units.la: xxviii. An Christus in anima etiam immediatè passus sit? Aff.
units.tr: XVII. Did Christ also suffer immediately in his soul? Affirmative.

units.la: xxviii. Num Christus pro omnium & singulorum hominum peccatis indifferenter mortuus sit? Neg.
units.tr: XVIII. Did Christ die indifferently for the sins of all and of each man? Negative.

units.la: xix. Num Christi anima à morte, localiter descenderit ad inferos, ut ibi annunciaret fidelibus V. Testamenti in limbo aliquo hactenus detentis, completam redemptionem, illosque inde secum educeret? Neg.
units.tr: XIX. Did the soul of Christ, after death, descend locally into the lower regions, to proclaim to the faithful of the Old Testament, who had until then been held in some limbo, the completed redemption, and to lead them out from there with him? Negative.

units.la: xx. Num gratia ad salutem sufficiens omnibus & quibusvis hominibus universaliter detur? Neg.
units.tr: XX. Is grace sufficient for salvation given universally to all and every man? Negative.

units.la: xxi. An gratiae convertentis efficacia, veniat ex naturâ & vi gratiae, hominem actu convertentis? Aff.
units.tr: XXI. Does the efficacy of converting grace come from the nature and power of grace itself, which actually converts the man? Affirmative.

units.la: Num verò pendeat ex hominis cooperatione, & voluntate, in cujus arbitrio haereat, illam gratiam vel admittere, vel repellere? Neg.
units.tr: But does it depend on the cooperation and will of the man, in whose power it lies to admit or to reject that grace? Negative.

units.la: xxii. Num virtute, & merito fidei, aliorumque bonorum operum, homo coram Dei judicio justificetur formaliter per propriam suam & inhaerentem justitiam? Neg.
units.tr: XXII. Is a man justified formally before God's judgment by virtue and merit of faith and of other good works, through his own inherent righteousness? Negative.

units.la: An verò solùm propter imputatam sibi justitiam Christi, fide apprehensam? Aff.
units.tr: Or is he justified only on account of the righteousness of Christ imputed to him and apprehended by faith? Affirmative.

units.la: xxiii. Num fides vera, & justificans possit esse sine bonis operibus? Neg.
units.tr: XXIII. Can true and justifying faith exist without good works? Negative.

units.la: xxiv. An omnis fidelis possit, ac debeat certus esse divinae erga se, & in se gratiae, atque suae salutis? Aff.
units.tr: XXIV. Can and should every believer be certain of God's grace towards him and in him, and of his own salvation? Affirmative.

units.la: xxv. An vera & justificans fides semper adjunctam habeat perseverantiam? Aff.
units.tr: XXV. Does true and justifying faith always have perseverance joined to it? Affirmative.

units.la: xxvi. An solus Deus religiosè colendus & adorandus sit? Aff.
units.tr: XXVI. Is God alone to be worshipped and adored with religious worship? Affirmative.

units.la: Num verò etiam Sancti, & Angeli invocandi, votaque iis religiosè nunc cupanda sint? Neg.
units.tr: But are the saints and angels also to be invoked, and are vows to be made to them with religious devotion? Negative.

units.la: xxvii. Salutatio Angelica, Ave Maria &c. seu
units.tr: XXVII. The Angelic Salutation, Ave Maria, etc., or:

units.la: I. Num homo in hac vita legem Dei perfecte & absolute implere possit?
units.tr: I. Can man in this life fulfil the law of God perfectly and absolutely?

units.la: Vel etiam plusquam perfecte, & supra id, quod Deus praecepit, facere? Neg. utrumque.
units.tr: Or even more than perfectly, and do more than God has commanded? Negative, both.

units.la: II. Num opera justorum vere, & proprie sint merito-ria vitae aeternae? Neg.
units.tr: II. Are the works of the righteous truly and properly meritorious of eternal life? Negative.

units.la: III. Num Ecclesia sit coetus hominum eandem fidem profitentium, & Sacramentorum communione viventium, sub Papa Romano? Neg.
units.tr: III. Is the Church a gathering of men professing the same faith and living in communion of the sacraments under the Roman Pope? Negative.

units.la: IIII. Num Ecclesia semper & quibuslibet sit satis visibilis? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Is the Church always and in every case sufficiently visible? Negative.

units.la: IV. Num notae Ecclesiae sint variae illae, quas Papistae suae Ecclesiae faciunt, ut nomen Catholicae, multa antiquitas, duratio, amplitudo, Episcoporum successio, miracula, Prophetiae, felicitas temporalis &c? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Are those marks of the Church which the Papists assign to their Church, such as the name Catholic, great antiquity, duration, extent, the succession of bishops, miracles, prophecies, temporal prosperity, etc., really its marks? Negative.

units.la: An autem veritas doctrinae, certa & perpetua Ecclesiae nota sit? Aff.
units.tr: Is the truth of doctrine, however, a certain and perpetual mark of the Church? Affirmative.

units.la: V. Num Ecclesia Romana non possit errare, ac deficere? Neg.
units.tr: V. Can the Roman Church not err or fail? Negative.

units.la: VI. Num Ecclesiae in terris regimen debeat ab uno aliquo homine, post Christum, esse monarchicum? Neg.
units.tr: VI. Ought the government of the Church on earth, after Christ, to be monarchical under some one man? Negative.

units.la: VII. Num Episcopi jure divino sint supra presbyteros, iisque auctoritate, & potestate majores? Neg.
units.tr: VII. Whether bishops, by divine right, are above presbyters and greater than them in authority and power? No.

units.la: VIII. Num Episcopi urbis Romae, supremam & monarchicam potestatem, jure divino, supra omnes in toto orbe Ecclesias, & Ecclesiasticos habeant? Neg.
units.tr: VIII. Whether the bishops of the city of Rome have, by divine right, supreme and monarchical power over all Churches and churchmen in the whole world? No.

units.la: IX. Num Papa Romanus, in rebus fidei decidendis ac docendis, sit infallibilis, nec possit errare? Neg.
units.tr: IX. Whether the Roman Pope is infallible in deciding and teaching matters of faith, and cannot err? No.

units.la: X. Num Papa, & Episcopi habeant potestatem coactivam, & possint leges condere, in conscientia obligantes? Neg.
units.tr: X. Whether the Pope and bishops have coercive power and can make laws binding on the conscience? No.

units.la: XI. Num Papa Romanus habeat etiam potestatem temporalem summam in omnium Christianorum bona, & res, adeo ut de iis disponere, etiam regna mutare, auferre, aliis conferre, Reges deponere, instituere ere, & leges civiles ferre, vel abrogare, & temporalia quaevis administrare, ac exercere sibi liceat? Neg.
units.tr: XI. Whether the Roman Pope also has supreme temporal power over the goods and property of all Christians, so that he may dispose of them, even depose and set up kings, transfer and bestow kingdoms on others, enact or repeal civil laws, and administer and exercise any temporal affairs whatever? No.

units.la: lxii. An Papa Romanus sit Antichristus? Aff.
units.tr: lxii. Is the Roman Pope the Antichrist? Yes.

units.la: lxiii. Num civilis jurisdictio conveniat personis Ecclesiasticis, ut simul quis sit ecclesiasticus & politicus, pastor & princeps? Neg.
units.tr: lxiii. Does civil jurisdiction belong to ecclesiastical persons, so that one person may be both ecclesiastical and political, both minister and prince? No.

units.la: lxiv. Num debeant esse distincti & sacri Ordines Clericorum, seu Ecclesiasticorum in Ecclesia, Cardinalium, Exorcistarum, Acolythorum, Sub-Diaconorum, Canonicorum? &c. Neg.
units.tr: lxiv. Should there be distinct and sacred orders of clergy or churchmen in the Church: cardinals, exorcists, acolytes, subdeacons, canons, etc.? No.

units.la: lxv. Num electio Pastorum in Ecclesia, nullo modo pertineat ad plebem, neque ejus consensus hic requiratur: verum id totum ad solos spectet Episcopos, atque potissimum ad Papam Romanum, a quo ut capite, omnis Ecclesiasticus ordo, & jurisdictio in caeteros Episcopos, & pastores derivetur? Neg.
units.tr: lxv. Does the choice of ministers in the Church in no way belong to the people, nor is their consent required here, but the whole matter pertains only to the bishops, and especially to the Roman Pope, from whom, as from the head, every ecclesiastical order and jurisdiction over the other bishops and ministers is derived? No.

units.la: lxvi. Num jure & recte personis Ecclesiasticis imperetur perpetuus caelibatus? Neg.
units.tr: lxvi. Is perpetual celibacy rightly and lawfully imposed on ecclesiastical persons? No.

units.la: lxvii. Num Ecclesiastici, eorumque actiones & causae civiles, atque bona temporalia, exempta sint a potestate, ac judicio, & tributis Principum, vel Magistratus saecularis? Neg.
units.tr: lxvii. Are churchmen, and their actions and civil causes, and temporal goods, exempt from the power, judgment and taxes of princes or of the secular magistrate? No.

units.la: lxviii. Num in Conciliis soli Episcopi, non autem presbyteri, habeant suffragium decisivum? Neg.
units.tr: lxviii. In councils, do only bishops, and not presbyters, have a decisive vote? No.

units.la: lxix. Num Romani Pontificis sit, generale concilium convocare, ac praesidere, & auctoritatem suam iis dare, eamque infallibilem? Neg.
units.tr: lxix. Is it for the Roman Pontiff to convene and preside over a general council, and to give it his authority, and that authority infallible? No.

units.la: lxx. Num Concilium Tridentinum ab A.M.D.xlv. & seq. sub Paulo iii. Iulio iii. ac Pio iv. habitum, fuerit legitimum, oecumenicum, sacrosanctum, & infallibile? Neg.
units.tr: lxx. Was the Council of Trent, held from 1545 onwards under Paul III, Julius III and Pius IV, lawful, ecumenical, sacrosanct and infallible? No.

units.la: lxxi. Num praeter, & supra praecepta Dei sint aliqua consilia perfectionis, hominibus commendanda, ut caelibatus perpetui, spontaneae paupertatis, & obedientiae erga Praelatum, quae singularem apud Deum merentur gloriam? Neg.
units.tr: lxxi. Apart from and above the precepts of God, are there some counsels of perfection to be commended to men, such as perpetual celibacy, voluntary poverty and obedience to a superior, which earn a special glory before God? No.

units.la: LXXII. Num vota Monastica, & status, & habitus Monachorum singularis, & varius, peculiaris sanctitatis causâ probari debeant? Neg.
units.tr: LXXII. Should monastic vows, and the particular and varied states and habits of monks, be approved for the sake of a special holiness? No.

units.la: LXXIII. Num ad sacramenti administrandi efficaciam, & perfectionem, necessariò requiratur intentio Ministri, adeo ut sine eâ sit ineffica x? Neg.
units.tr: LXXIII. Is the intention of the minister necessarily required for the efficacy and completeness of administering a sacrament, so that without it the sacrament is ineffective? No.

units.la: LXXIV. Num sacramenta conferant gratiam ex opere operato, sive ex ipsius actionis externae & Sacramentalis vi, ut causâ propriâ, verâ, & immediatè illam efficiente? Neg.
units.tr: LXXIV. Do the sacraments confer grace ex opere operato, that is, by the power of the external and sacramental action itself, as its own true cause, immediately effecting it? No.

units.la: LXXV. An sint duo Sacramenta, S. Baptismus, & S. Coena? Aff.
units.tr: LXXV. Are there two sacraments, holy Baptism and the holy Supper? Yes.

units.la: Num verò septem, & praeter illa duo quoque, confirmatio, poenitentia, extrema unctio, ordo, & matrimonium? Neg.
units.tr: But are there seven, and besides those two also confirmation, penance, extreme unction, orders and marriage? No.

units.la: LXXVI. Num baptismus, ad salutem sit medium absolutè necessarium, adeo ut qui eo, neque suâ culpâ, caret, ideo in aeternum condemnetur? Neg.
units.tr: LXXVI. Is baptism absolutely necessary for salvation, so that whoever lacks it, without his own fault, is therefore condemned to eternity? No.

units.la: LXXVII. Num liceat aliquando quibuslibet etiam baptizare, sive viris, sive foeminis? Neg.
units.tr: LXXVII. Is it ever lawful for anyone at all to baptize, whether men or women? No.

units.la: LXXVIII. Num baptismus administrari debeat sub caeremoniis signandarum crucum in fronte, & in pectore, exorcismo, exsufflatione, gustu salis, tangendis salivâ naribus, atque auribus, ungendo pectore, & scapulis oleo, & chrismate in vertice, & accenso cereo in manus baptizati tradito &c.? Neg.
units.tr: LXXVIII. Should baptism be administered with the ceremonies of signing crosses on the forehead and breast, exorcism, exsufflation, tasting salt, touching the nostrils and ears with spittle, anointing the breast and shoulder-blades with oil, chrism on the crown of the head, and a lighted candle put into the hand of the baptized, etc.? No.

units.la: LXXIX. Num cognatio aliqua spiritualis oriatur ex baptismo, inter Susceptores de baptismo, & baptizatum, ipsiusque Parentes, nec non inter baptizantem, & baptizatum, hujusque Parentes, quae inter eosdem impediat matrimonium? Neg.
units.tr: LXXIX. Does any spiritual kinship arise from baptism, between the sponsors and the one baptized and his parents, and also between the one who baptizes and the one baptized and his parents, which would impede marriage between them? No.

units.la: LXXX. Concupiscentia mali, etiam baptizatis & justificatis, mala, & peccatum est.
units.tr: LXXX. Concupiscence of evil is evil and sin, even in those who are baptized and justified.

units.la: LXXXI. Num baptismus, confirmatio, ordo, imprimant in animâ characterem indelebilem, sive realem & absolutam aliquam qualitatem, quâ quis aptior reddatur ad cultum divinum, configuretur Christo, atque distinguatur ab aliis? Neg.
units.tr: LXXXI. Do baptism, confirmation and orders imprint in the soul an indelible character, or some real and absolute quality, by which a person is made more fit for divine worship, is conformed to Christ, and is distinguished from others? No.

units.la: lxxxii. Num verum Iesu Christi corpus & sanguis corporaliter ac substantialiter praesens adsit in Sacramento Coenae, per totalem substantiae panis & vini in corpus & sanguinem Christi conversionem, sive transsubstantiationem? Neg.
units.tr: LXXXII. Is the true body and blood of Jesus Christ present corporeally and substantially in the sacrament of the Supper, through the total conversion of the substance of the bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ, that is, transubstantiation? No.

units.la: lxxxiii. Num Sacramentum Coenae celebrandum sit in pane azymo, & hostiolis orbiculatis? Neg.
units.tr: LXXXIII. Should the sacrament of the Supper be celebrated with unleavened bread and round wafers? No.

units.la: lxxxiv. Num in Sacramento Coenae fiat Missa, id est, sacrificium verum & expiatorium pro peccatis vivorum ac mortuorum, atque impetratorium omnis generis beneficiorum, Deoque a Sacerdote in altari osseratur corpus & sanguis Christi sub specie panis & vini, jam publice, missa publica, jam privata, ubi solus communicat Sacerdos? Neg.
units.tr: LXXXIV. In the sacrament of the Supper, is a Mass made, that is, a true and expiatory sacrifice for the sins of the living and the dead, and impetratory of every kind of benefit, and is the body and blood of Christ offered to God by the priest at the altar under the appearance of bread and wine, now in a public Mass, now in a private one, where the priest alone communicates? No.

units.la: lxxxv. Num in sacramento Coenae necessarium sit vinum aqua misceri? Neg.
units.tr: LXXXV. In the sacrament of the Supper, is it necessary to mix water with the wine? No.

units.la: lxxxvi. An in sacramento Coenae singulis fidelibus & communicantibus, non panis solum, sed vinum, utraque sacramenti pars tradenda? Aff.
units.tr: LXXXVI. In the sacrament of the Supper, should both parts of the sacrament, not only the bread but also the wine, be given to each of the faithful who communicate? Yes.

units.la: lxxxvii. Num Sacramentum Coenae ad adorationem servari, extra usum, & ostentari debeat? Neg.
units.tr: LXXXVII. Should the sacrament of the Supper be reserved for adoration, outside its use, and displayed? No.

units.la: lxxxviii. Num in inferno sit locus aliquis, seu limbus Patrum, quo fideles V. Testamenti fuerint detenti, usque ad adventum Christi, & limbus infantum, absque baptismo hinc decedentium; & Purgatorium, animis non satis in hac vita purgatis, a peccatis plenarie per poenarum satisfactionem expurgandis? Neg.
units.tr: LXXXVIII. Is there in hell some place, or limbus Patrum, where the faithful of the Old Testament were held until the coming of Christ, and a limbus infantum for infants who die here without baptism, and a Purgatory for souls not sufficiently purged in this life, to be cleansed of their sins fully by the satisfaction of punishments? No.

units.la: lxxxix. Num pro defunctorum animabus instituenda sint, iisque prosint suffragia vivorum, opera quaelibet poenalia & satisfactoria quae appellant, orationes, eleemosynae, jejunia, peregrinationes, missae, &c.? Neg.
units.tr: LXXXIX. Should works of penance and satisfaction, which they call works of satisfaction, such as prayers, alms, fasts, pilgrimages, Masses, etc., be undertaken for the souls of the dead, and do the suffrages of the living profit them? No.

units.la: xc. Num Papa Romanus possit aliquos canonizare, sive que ii ipsi sic in suâ Confessione, editâ Hornæ a. MDXXII. una cum suo Martyrologio; deinde etiam seorsim a. MDXX. diemen Mennisten noemt [?]. Istamque Confessionem ex doctrinâ Mennonis, & Theod. Philippi congestam scribunt in Præfatione. Socinus disputationem contra ipsos inscribit, inter Miscellanea, adversus Mennonitas. Etiam in Lectionibus Sacris, pag. 152. inquit: praeter eos Anabaptistas, qui Mennonitæ vocantur.
units.tr: XC. Whether the Roman Pope can canonize any persons, which they themselves, in their Confession printed at Horn in 1522 together with their Martyrology, and afterwards separately in 1520, call diemen Mennisten noemt [?]. They write in the Preface that this Confession was compiled from the doctrine of Menno and Theodore Philips. Socinus entitles a disputation against them, among his Miscellanea, against the Mennonites. Also in the Sacred Readings, p. 152, he says: besides those Anabaptists who are called Mennonites.

units.la: Originem suam debent superiori sæculo: neque ante id temporis assignabitur in universâ retro antiquitate, non qui in aliquo forte articulo eandem cum Anabaptistis tenuerit sententiam, sed vel una aliqua Ecclesia, vel Doctor, qui doctrinæ systema istud tenuerit, quod ipsi sibi nunc fecere, & sequuntur. Sæculo præcedente in Thomâ Muncero, ejusque cohorte prima sectæ fundamenta posita fuere: nam & illos pro Fratribus suis agnoscit Menno, atque inde in reliquam Germaniam, Belgiumque facta illorum propago. Ad meliorem confusissimæ sectæ historiam oportet tenere ejus distinctas periodos. Quarum prima est Monceri, & Muncerianorum, in bello Rusticano. Inde in Helvetiis: tum Belgio: inde in agro Monasteriensi; ubi bellum eorum Monasteriense. Denique in Frisiâ quas fecerint tum sectas, tum Scismata, spectandum.
units.tr: They owe their origin to the previous century. Nor, looking back through the whole of antiquity up to that time, will one find either a Church or a teacher who held that system of doctrine which they have now made for themselves and follow, not merely someone who perhaps held the same opinion as the Anabaptists on some one article. In the previous century the foundations of the sect were laid in Thomas Müntzer and his band; for Menno also acknowledges them as his brethren, and from them a offshoot spread into the rest of Germany and the Low Countries. For a better understanding of this most confused sect, its distinct periods must be kept in view. The first is that of Müntzer and the Müntzerites, in the Peasants' War. Then came the period in Switzerland, then in the Low Countries, then in the territory of Münster, where their war was the Münster war. Finally, one must observe the sects and schisms they produced in Friesland.

units.la: Anno præcedentis sæculi vigesimo primo, quando foeditatis & tyrannidis Papalis jam diu tæderet homines, primi Nicolaus Storck, Ciconiaï, Thomas Muncerus, aliique, inter quos recensentur quoque Marcus Stubnerus, & Martinus Cellarius, infaustam sectæ anabaptisticæ dederunt originem. Storck Cygneæ natus, ibi cum Muncero coepit res novas moliri: homo indoctus & rudis, jactans colloquia & revelationes Angelicas, quibus multos adeo dementabat, ut in anabaptismum, quem prædicabat etiam, facile adigeret, quasi non aliter salvandos.
units.tr: In the twenty-first year of the previous century, when people had long been weary of Papal foulness and tyranny, the first to give the unhappy origin to the Anabaptist sect were Nicolaus Storck, of Ciconia (Storch), Thomas Müntzer and others, among whom are also counted Marcus Stübner and Martin Cellarius. Storck, born at Zwickau, there began with Müntzer to stir up novelties. He was an unlearned and rude man, boasting of conversations and angelic revelations, by which he drove many so mad that he easily brought them to the Anabaptism which he also preached, as if they could not otherwise be saved.

units.la: Mancerus Stolbergensis erat, & Cygnea tandem exactus, Alsteti, quod Ducum Saxoniae, in Thuringiae finibus oppidum est, concionatorem aliquandiu egit. Cum Luthero aliquoties loquutus, ejus librum de libertate Christiana pessime interpretabatur, in animi licentiam & rerum confusionem, rectiusque monentem Lutherum audire detrectabat, vel sequi. Docebat novum & meliorem mundi instaurare statum, quo excisis impiis, soli pii regnarent: ejus se nunc praeconem, mox vindicem futurum. Impios nominabat omnes a se, & sectā suā alienos. Non sermone tantum, sed etiam scriptis multifariis tam in Papistas, quam in Reformatos, sua gnaviter disseminabat. In Lutherum emisit librum, inscriptum Christo, Principi, uti loquebatur, illustrissimo. Hic exprobrat Luthero, quod enthusiastico spiritu careret, & nil nisi carnalia saperet. Quoque ad Melanthonem epistolam scripsit, cujus haec inter alia, verba exhibet in Chronologia sua Abrahamus Bucholcerus, ad a. cIↄ Iↄ xx iv. Non in solo pane vivit homo: sed in omni verbo, quod procedit de ore Dei. Videte, de ore Dei, & non ex libris profisciuntur. Testimonium quidem verbi veri ex voluminibus est. Nisi enim in corde oriatur, verbum hominis est, damnans scribas versipelles, qui furantur oracula sancta, Ieremie 23. Nunquam eis Dominus locutus est, & ipsi usurpant verba ejus. O carissimi, operam navate ut prophetetis, alioqui theologia vestra non valebit obolum. Considerate Deum vestrum e vicino & non a longo. Missisque quaquaversum per omnem Germaniam epistolis, quas novarum rerum avidi, suique similes homines percupide legebant, hos avertit facile, turbavit omnes. Nec contra Ecclesiasticos tantum se opponere, sed in Magistratum aeque & politicos insurgere, enthusiasmos praedicare instituit, & a Deo sibi ista coelitus revelari, credi omnino voluit. Alsteto ejectus (nam videbat prudens Magistratus in quas ista turbas vergerent) in superiorem Germaniam, Norimrnbergam, atque in Helvetiam concessit: ubi moratus aliquandiu, non destitit omni opera & modo sua dogmata & tumultuum semina spargere, præsertim in comitatu Stulingio; & vicinis locis. Inde reversus in Thuringiam, Mulhusium quod Thuringiæ oppidum est percelebre, sedi suæ elegit: indeq; datis crebris ad varios litteris ita plurimorum animos in mutationem rerum & Ecclesiasticarum & politicarum promiscuè accendit, ut non diu post in bellum quod sequutum, habuerint pronos paratosque. Priusquam tamen Mulhusium venisset, Lutherus per literas Senatum monuit, hominem ut à se arceret, permiciosum, qui quid moliretur, Cygneæ jam, & Alstetii docuisset, & à quo filii turbæ & rerum omnium vastitas esset exspectanda: Scriptæ hæ literæ Vinariæ fuere, anno clɔ Iɔ xxiv. Muncerus autem blanditiis & verborum pompa, ac φαντασμα prophetiarum se ita in animis insinuare noverat, eosque capere, & se verum Prophetam esse à Deo missum dicere, qui contra aliorum tyrannidem & luxum, plebis partes tueretur, mox in libertatem vindicandę, ut Mulhusii efficeret, quo senatu pristino abrogato novus ex voto ejus & Muncerianus constituerentur. Hoc primum dedit animi, spiritusque sui documentum: Iamque tempus putabat, ut missio concionandi officio, galeam & gladium assumeret, quem Gideonis nempe dicebat sibi à Deo traditum, ad tyrannos quoscunque pessundandos, & propugnandam plebis libertatem, erigendumque novum Christo in terris regnum. Interim, erat hoc anno clɔ Iɔ xxv, per Sueviam & Franconiam Rustici, conscripto multo exercitu ad quadraginta, uti referunt, militum millia, in Principes, in Ecclesiasticos, & quoscunque superiores insurgunt, jamque arces, castella, domos, & quaecunque obvia diripiunt, & prosternunt, quibus mox, doctrinâ, scriptis & prædictionibus suis ante incitatis, accessit Muncerus, cum trecentis militibus, qui castra ponebant bant Francusii. Adversus quos Saxoniae Elector Johannes, cujusque patruelis Hassiae Landgravius Philippus, cum Henrico Brunsvicensium Duce, aliam eduxerunt exercitum: & Muncerus quidem suos haud parum consternatos, conspecto Principum militte, & arcu coelesti, qui tum forte apparebat, sed quem in omen victoriae interpretabatur, adversum Principes jubet securos esse, ut tyrannos omnium immanissimos, atque internecioni, quomodo olim Cananaei Principes, destinatos; quorumque pilas tormentis explosas vel ipse solus veste sua effet exceptuus[?]. Collatis signis ubi ad manus ventum, miseri homines qui à temerarii Vatis pollicitationibus potius, quam armis salutem exspectabant, caesi, & in fugam acti conciderunt ad quinque circiter millia, uno prælio: à quo deinde Franculium, quò alii fugerant, capitur, & Thomas Muncerus, quamvis alium se & egrotum mentiretur, deprehensus ex epistola quam in crumena, qui praedam quaerebat miles, ab Alberto Mansfeldio ad Muncerum scriptam, cumque ab incepto dehortantem, reperiebat, ad Saxonem & Landgravium abductus, primum respondit, se omnia ex Dei instinctu & superna revelatione egisse; dein tormentis subjectus, & quum prae dolore exclamaret, increpitus à Landgravio, quod tam multis ille causa extremae cladis fuisset, magno cum risu subjunxit: at hoc voluerunt. Tandem capitis poenam dedit, agnitoque ante mortem errore & delicto, aliqua visus fuit tangi poenitentia. Melanchton scribit in epist. ad Camerarium, quod quum de eo sumeretur in castris supplicium, in corona stans precatus fuerit ut sibi ignosceretur, & flens dixerit, fateri se, quod majora justo suscepisset: quodque cum aliquoties multitudinem arma inducentem voluisset revocare ab incepto, non potuerit; invitusque saepe perrexerit, vulgi voluntati obsecundatus. Accidérunt haec anno MDXXV. Caesorum bello Rusticano, quod aestate unâconfectum, numerus haud pariter ab omnibus refertur: qui minimum, ad quinquaginta millia occisos referunt. Lutherus, tum ne quid commune cum illis hominibus habere videretur, tum ut quam male abuterentur doctrinâ suâ de libertate Christianâ, ostenderet, atque etiam ut homines quoquo modo ad meliorem mentem revocaret, publicis scriptis illorum & res & doctrinam condemnavit, multaque graviis comminatus fuit, ni desisterent: quorum summam in Commentariis suis accurate persequitur Sleidanus. lib. iv. & v. Similiter Melanchton, ad petitionem Principis Palatini, scripsit Responsionem ad articulos Rusticorum. At-que ut omnino detestandum horum hominum fuerit studium, tum rebellionis adversus Superiores, & bellorum, caediumque promiscuarum; tum doctrinae, de novo mundi statu, & excidendis omnibus impiis, & anabaptismo, & quo omnia illa confirmabant, enthusiasmo, ac coelestibus revelationibus, quaeque alia execranda; fatendum certe, intoleranda Superiorum & Politicorum, & Ecclesiasticorum vitia & scandala, atque subditorum oppressiones causam dedisse desperatis illis consiliis: quod neque Lutherus in suis hac de re scriptis dissimulavit. Illa Muncerus suis in acie quando stabant suggerebat, tamquam certaminis causam: Principes Tyrannos esse, qui nec subditis, neque viduis, pupillisque, quod debetur, praestarent praesidium, nec scelera-tos pro meritis plecterent, qui, omnium facultates in se convertentes, rationes solum pro expilanda pecunia excogitarent, qui vitia Ecclesiasticorum non tollerent, sed ferrent ac defenderent, neque reformationem pro eo ac debeant studio promoverent. Et ante Muncerum in Suevia plebeii turbas iisdem fere ex causis moverant, quas edito libello expos uerunt, simul quoque suorum postulata, quae eo tendebant, non ut loco moverent Magistratum a Deo constitutum, sed ut libertatem possiderent Christianis debitam. Primum pepetebant, ut sibi liceret Ecclesiæ ministros eligere, qui verbum Dei purè docerent, nullis admixtis hominum decretis vel constitutionibus. Deinde nolebant posthac ullas pendere decimas, præterquam frumenti, & has ipsas ajebant distribui debere partim in Ecclesiæ ministros, partim egenos, partim in usus publicos. Non oportere ipsos duram adeo servitutem pati, ac hactenus: præter alia nonnulla. Illa non omninò abs re fuere quæ postulabant, abfuissent modo tumultus, & adversus Magistratum à plebeiis, à rusticis exercita pervicacia & rebellio; tum enthusiasmi, aliaque mali Spiritus argumenta. Atque illud fuit, quod viros non malos tum temporis commoverit aliquando in illorum hominum themata & prætextus. Marcum Stubnerum dico, convictorem Melanchtonis, qui vir erat litteratus; Martinum Cellarium; & si forte iis addendus Andreas Carolostadius.
units.tr: Muncer was from Stolberg. After being driven out of Zwickau, he served for a time as preacher at Allstedt, a town of the Dukes of Saxony on the border of Thuringia. He spoke with Luther several times and misread his book On Christian Liberty as a license for the mind and for disorder. He would not listen to Luther's sounder warnings, nor follow them. He taught that a new and better state of the world had to be established, in which, once the wicked were cut off, only the godly would reign. He said that he would soon be its herald and then its avenger. He called all those wicked who were not of his own party and sect. He spread his views energetically, not only by preaching but also in many writings, against both the Papists and the Reformed. He sent out a book against Luther, addressed to "Christ, the most illustrious Prince," as he put it. In it he reproaches Luther for lacking an enthusiastic spirit and for savouring nothing but carnal things. He also wrote a letter to Melanchthon, parts of which Abraham Buchholzer quotes in his Chronology under the year 1524: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God. Note: from the mouth of God, and not from books. The testimony of the true word is indeed in volumes; but unless it arises in the heart, it is the word of man, condemning the crafty scribes who steal the holy oracles (Jeremiah 23). The Lord has never spoken to them, and yet they usurp his words. O dearest friends, labour that you may prophesy, otherwise your theology will not be worth a penny. Consider your God from close at hand and not from afar. He sent letters everywhere throughout Germany, and men eager for novelties, and like himself, read them greedily. He easily drew these men away and threw everyone into confusion. He began to oppose not only the churchmen but also the magistrates and the civil authorities as well, to preach enthusiasms, and he wanted it to be fully believed that these things were revealed to him from heaven. Driven out of Allstedt (for the prudent magistrate saw what disorders these things were tending towards), he withdrew into Upper Germany, to Nuremberg, and into Switzerland. He stayed there for some time, and did not cease by every means and method to spread his doctrines and the seeds of tumult, especially in the county of Stolberg and the neighbouring places. Returning from there into Thuringia, he chose as his seat Mühlhausen, a very famous town of Thuringia. Then, by sending many letters to various people, he so inflamed the minds of very many for a change in both church and civil affairs that, not long afterwards, they were ready and eager for the war that followed. Before he came to Mühlhausen, however, Luther warned the senate by letter to keep this dangerous man away from them. He had already taught at Zwickau and Allstedt what he was now attempting, and from him the sons of tumult and the ruin of all things were to be expected. These letters were written at Weimar in the year 1524. But Muncer knew how to insinuate himself into men's minds by flattery, by a pompous show of words, and by the phantasm [φάντασμα] of prophecies; he knew how to capture them and to declare that he was a true prophet sent by God, who would defend the cause of the common people against the tyranny and luxury of others. Soon he would bring it about at Mühlhausen that they were set free, the former senate being abolished, and a new one, according to his wish and of his party, established. This first gave evidence of his spirit and temper. And he now thought the time had come to lay aside the office of preaching and take up helmet and sword, which he said had been given to him by God, like Gideon's, to overthrow whatever tyrants there were, to defend the liberty of the people, and to raise up a new kingdom of Christ on earth. Meanwhile, in the year 1525, the peasants were rising throughout Swabia and Franconia. They had raised, as they report, an army of about forty thousand men, and they rose against the princes, the churchmen, and all their superiors. They were already plundering and levelling castles, fortresses, houses, and whatever lay in their way. To them, now stirred up beforehand by his teaching, writings, and prophecies, Muncer added himself with three hundred soldiers, who pitched camp at Frankenhausen. Against them the Elector of Saxony, John, and his cousin Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, together with Henry, Duke of Brunswick, brought out another army. Muncer, seeing that his men were fairly dismayed at the sight of the princes' soldiers and at a heavenly rainbow which happened to appear just then, but which he interpreted as an omen of victory, ordered them to be unafraid of the princes, who were the most savage of tyrants and destined for destruction, as the Canaanite princes once were. He claimed that he alone would catch in his own robe the cannonballs fired at them. When the standards were joined and they came to hand-to-hand fighting, the poor men, who were hoping for safety from the rash promises of the prophet rather than from arms, were cut down and put to flight. About five thousand fell in that one battle. Afterwards Thomas Muncer fled to Frankenhausen, where others had fled. He was captured there, although he lied that he was another man and ill. He was recognised from a letter, which a soldier looking for plunder found in his purse, written to Muncer by Albert of Mansfeld and urging him to desist from his undertaking. He was led off to the Saxon and the Landgrave. First he answered that he had done everything by the impulse of God and by heavenly revelation. Then, when he was put to the torture and cried out in pain, the Landgrave rebuked him, saying that he had been the cause of such great disaster for so many. Muncer added, with great laughter: "But this is what they wanted." At last he paid the penalty of death, and before he died, having acknowledged his error and crime, he seemed to be touched by some repentance. Melanchthon writes in a letter to Camerarius that when punishment was taken against him in the camp, he stood in the ring and prayed that he might be forgiven, and, weeping, said that he confessed he had undertaken things greater than was right; and that although he had often wished to call back the multitude that was taking up arms from their undertaking, he could not, and that, unwilling, he often went on, yielding to the will of the common people. These things happened in the year 1525. As for the number slain in the Peasants' War, which was finished in one summer, the figures are not reported equally by all. The lowest estimates put the dead at fifty thousand. Luther, both so that he might not seem to have anything in common with those men and so that he might show how badly they had abused his teaching on Christian liberty, and also so that he might in any way recall them to a better mind, condemned both their deeds and their doctrine in public writings, and threatened them with many grave penalties unless they desisted. Sleidan follows the sum of these in detail in his Commentaries, books 4 and 5. Likewise Melanchthon, at the request of the Count Palatine, wrote An Answer to the Articles of the Peasants. And although the aims of these men were utterly to be detested, both their rebellion against their superiors and their wars and promiscuous slaughters, and their doctrine of a new state of the world, the cutting off of all the wicked, anabaptism, and the enthusiasm and heavenly revelations by which they confirmed all these things, and whatever else is execrable, one must certainly admit that the intolerable vices and scandals of the superiors, the civil authorities, and the churchmen, and the oppression of subjects, gave cause for those desperate plans. Luther did not conceal this in his writings on the matter. Muncer used to put these grievances before his men when they were standing in battle, as the cause of the struggle: the princes were tyrants, who gave neither protection to subjects, nor to widows and orphans, what was owed to them; who did not punish criminals according to their deserts; who, drawing all the resources to themselves, devised only schemes for plundering money; who did not remove the faults of churchmen but tolerated and defended them, and who did not promote reformation with the zeal they ought to show. Before Muncer, in Swabia, the common people had stirred up disturbances for almost the same reasons, which they set out in a published pamphlet, together with their demands, which aimed not at removing the magistrate appointed by God from his place, but at possessing the liberty due to Christians. First they demanded that they be allowed to choose ministers of the Church who would teach the word of God purely, with no admixture of human decrees or constitutions. Then they refused to pay any tithes from now on, except those of grain, and they said that even these ought to be distributed partly to the ministers of the Church, partly to the poor, and partly for public uses. They said that they ought not to suffer such harsh servitude as hitherto, besides some other demands. Those demands were not entirely unreasonable. Only the tumults were lacking, and the obstinacy and rebellion which the common people and peasants practised against the magistrate; and also the enthusiasm and other signs of an evil spirit. And it was this that at that time moved some men who were not bad to take up, at times, the themes and pretexts of those men. I mean Marcus Stübner, a fellow-student of Melanchthon, who was a learned man; Martin Cellarius; and if perhaps Andreas Carlstadt is to be added to them.

units.la: Maximè deplorandum, bonam animam Cellarii istis progressus etiam agitatam fuisse. Vir iste, postquam Vittembergam studiorum causa venisset, ludimagisterium, curante Melanthone, nactus, à Marco Stubnero, in partes factionis illius pertractus fuit, illorumque tenuit sententiam, cum quâ, relictâ Vittembergâ, in Borussiam abiit, ubi jussu Principis in liberam datus custodiam, nonnulla etiam de doctrinâ illâ conscripsit. Quod factum anno xxv. Postea autem animadvertens partes illas labascere indicis, & spem de futuro altero mundi statu frustrare, mutavit in melius sententiam, & sub annum trigesimum sextum venit Basileam, mutato, cum doctrinâ, etiam nomine suo, Latino nempe Cellarii, in Græcum Borrhai: ductâ uxore, quietè hic & honestè vixit, atque sacrorum communionem cum Ecclesiâ habuit. Quia verò vir erat litteratus, qui Tubingæ studiorum tyrocinia posuerat, Heidelbergæ Magister Philosophiæ creatus, Vittembergæ frequentem Scholam privatim habuerat, atque sedulus dulus semper, per istorum temporum de S. Coenae doctrinâ contentiones, victus causa fonestrario opificio se aliquando addixit; demum Basileae inter Professores adscitus, inter Philosophos primum, Rhetoricam explicuit; tum inter Theologos, Vet. Testamenti libros nonnullos eximio commentario illustravit, Pentateuchum Moßis, librum Iudicum, Regum, Iobi, etiam aliquot ex Prophetis; quae praeter alia ejus extant: atque tandem obiit Basileae, anno cIↄ Iↄ Ixiv. Sed ad Muncerum regrediamur. Hic capite plexus fuit post captum à Principibus Francusium.
units.tr: It is most lamentable that the good soul of Cellarius was also troubled by these advances. After coming to Wittenberg to study, this man obtained a teaching post in a school through Melanchthon's care. Markus Stübner drew him into the party of that faction, and he held their opinion. Leaving Wittenberg with it, he went to Prussia, where by the Prince's order he was placed under open custody, and he wrote some things about that doctrine. This happened in 1525. Afterwards, however, seeing that those parties were collapsing under the weight of facts and that their hope of another future state of the world was being frustrated, he changed his opinion for the better. Around 1536 he came to Basel, changing his name along with his doctrine, from the Latin Cellarius to the Greek Borrhaus. He took a wife, lived quietly and honourably there, and had communion in the sacraments with the Church. He was a learned man who had begun his studies at Tübingen, was made Master of Philosophy at Heidelberg, and had held a well-attended private school at Wittenberg. Being diligent always, and during those years of contention over the doctrine of the Lord's Supper, he at one point turned to a manual trade to earn his living. At last he was admitted among the professors at Basel. Among the philosophers he first lectured on Rhetoric; then, among the theologians, he illuminated some books of the Old Testament with an excellent commentary: the Pentateuch of Moses, the books of Judges, Kings and Job, and several of the Prophets. These, besides other works, survive. He died at Basel in 1564. But let us return to Müntzer, who was beheaded after being captured by the princes at Frankenhausen.

units.la: Nicolaus Storck, non Torck, ut aliqui malè, ex proelio profugus, in Bavariam pervenit, ubi in Nosocomio desperabundus obiit. Muncerus ergo fundamenta jecit sectae fanaticae Enthusiastarum atque Anabaptistarum, quamvis fatear inter Muncerum, & sequentes Anabaptistas Monasterienses multum discriminis esse, unde non ut vulgò solet tamquam paria utraque commiscuerò. Anabaptistae Helvetii à Muncero originem trahunt, quem constat, Thuringiá exactum ad Helvetios abiisse, atque ibidem sparso suae doctrinae veneno corrupisse Balthasarem Hubmejerum Pacimontanum, VValshutensium concionatorem celebrem ac dilectum; & Felicem Manzium, Conradum Grebelium, Tigurinos, aliosque, primos apud Helvetios Anabaptistarum parentes, à Muncero quidem ortos, sed Muncerianis aliquantum modestiores. Interim & VValshuti, & Tiguri, & Basileae moverunt turbas: praecipuè super negotio baptismi, tum contra baptismum infantum, tum pro anabaptismo.
units.tr: Nicolaus Storck, not Torck as some wrongly write, fled from the battle, reached Bavaria, and died in despair in a hospital there. Müntzer therefore laid the foundations of the fanatical sect of the Enthusiasts and Anabaptists. I admit, however, that there is considerable difference between Müntzer and the later Anabaptists of Münster, so I do not, as is commonly done, mix the two together as if they were equals. The Swiss Helvetii Anabaptists trace their origin to Müntzer. It is agreed that he was driven out of Thuringia and went to the Swiss, and there he corrupted with the poison of his doctrine Balthasar Hubmaier of Friedberg, the famous and beloved preacher of Waldshut, and Felix Manz, Conrad Grebel of Zurich, and others. These were the first parents of the Anabaptists among the Swiss. They were indeed sprung from Müntzer, but were somewhat more moderate than the Müntzerians. Meanwhile they stirred up disturbances at Waldshut, at Zurich and at Basel, chiefly over the question of baptism: both against infant baptism and in favour of Anabaptism.

units.la: Balthasar Hubmejerus, Fridburgo oriundus, primus VValshutensium à Reformatione concionator, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxv. tum voce, tum scripto multos turbavit: quo factum, ut oppidum facile in partes Austriacas iterum pervenerit, & reductus cum Episcopo Papismus in urbem sit, ei postliminio serviturum. Hoc suis turbis, anabaptismo, & baptismi cum baptisterio proculcatione ille effecit, qui oppido elapsus Tigurum concessit, hic de novo omnia commoturus: verum Senatus suspicatus hominis ingenium turbulentum, quum & clam in urbem irrepsisset, in Praetorio liberâ cum custodiâ servari praecepit, neque vel Imperatori, ad poenam poscenti, tradere voluit. Aliquoties cum Ministris, praecipuè cum Zuinglio (cujus adversus illum habetur Responsio, Tom. 11. Oper. Zuinglii, & Epist. lib. 11.) habità disputatione, postquam Senatui haud semel revocatione erroris institutâ, & de scripto recitatâ turpiter imposuisset, abiit: in eo autem homine, scribit Zuinglius, ad Petrum Gynoraeum, Tom. 11. nihil quam immoderatam rei gloriaeque sitim deprehendisse visus sum ipse mihi. Hinc in Moraviam discessit, & Anabaptistis se associavit, ubi, novos excitans motus, tandem captus, & cum uxore Viennam abductus, igne exustus, & uxor aquis submersa fuit.
units.tr: Balthasar Hubmaier, a native of Friedburg, was the first preacher at Waldshut after the Reformation. In 1525 he troubled many by voice and by writing. As a result the town easily passed back into Austrian hands, and Papism was restored in the town with the bishop, to be subject to him again by right of return. Hubmaier achieved this through his disturbances, his Anabaptism, and his trampling on baptism and the baptistery. He escaped from the town and went to Zurich, where he was about to stir everything up anew. But the Senate, suspecting the turbulent nature of the man, and since he had crept into the city secretly, ordered him kept in open custody in the Praetorium, and would not hand him over even to the Emperor, who demanded him for punishment. He held a disputation several times with the ministers, especially with Zwingli (against whom there is a Response in volume 2 of Zwingli's works, and in his Epistles, book 2). More than once he had instituted a retraction of error before the Senate, and after reading from a written text, he shamefully deceived them, and then he left. Zwingli writes to Petrus Gynoraeus, in volume 2: in eo autem homine, "in that man, however, I myself saw nothing but nihil quam immoderatam rei gloriaeque sitim deprehendisse visus sum ipse mihi," that is, an immoderate thirst for his own cause and glory. Hence he withdrew to Moravia and associated himself with the Anabaptists. There, stirring up new disturbances, he was at last captured and taken to Vienna with his wife. He was burned with fire, and his wife was drowned in the water.

units.la: Tigurî interim Felix Manzius, (de quo, & Balthasare Hubmejero Martyrologium Anabapt. agit ad a. 1526. & in Appendice, tanquam de Sectae suae primis fundatoribus) & Conradus Grebelius, valde pro Anabaptisticâ suâ tumultuabantur, & Zuinglium praesertim adoriebantur: quare Magistratus varias instituit disputationes, inter illos, super articulo baptismi, habendas die xvii. Januarii, d. xx. Martii, iterum vi. Novembris anno cIↄ Iↄ xxv. quando per triduum disputatum, sed omnia frustra: Anabaptistae interim furibunde per urbem clamitabant: vae Tiguro, vae Tiguro, poenitentiam age, quin brevi interibis. Iam edicta in Turbones istos sanciit Magistratus, & gravissima comminatus fuit. Ad illos, Felicem Manzium, & Grebelium a. cIↄ Iↄ xxii. originem suae sectae referunt Anabaptistae Helvetii, qui de eâ epistolam dederunt ad Anabaptistas Belgas in libello aliquo, unde eam descripsit Auctor libri, Successionis Anabaptisticae, seu Babel Anabapt.cap. 11.qui scriptus lingua Belgica à V.P.& Coloniæ impressus a. cIↄ Iↄ c 111. Mentionem illius libri facit etiam Aubertus Miræus, De statu Religionis Christianæ lib. I. cap. xxx, de Belgicarum Provinciarum statu; eumque haudimmerito dignum dicit, qui in Latinum transferatur. Eandem quoque epistolam exhibet Hermannus Modedlib.de initiis Anabap.pag. 146.
units.tr: Meanwhile at Zurich Felix Manz (of whom the Anabaptist Martyrology speaks, under 1526 and in the Appendix, as one of the first founders of their sect) and Conrad Grebel raged violently for their Anabaptism, and attacked Zwingli in particular. Therefore the magistrate arranged several disputations between them on the article of baptism, to be held on 17 January, on 20 March, and again on 6 November 1525, when they disputed for three days, but all in vain. Meanwhile the Anabaptists furiously shouted through the city: "Woe to Zurich, woe to Zurich! Repent, or you will soon perish!" Now the magistrate issued edicts against these disturbers and threatened the gravest punishments. The Swiss Anabaptists refer the origin of their sect to Manz and Grebel in 1522. They gave an epistle about it, in a little book, from which the author of Successionis Anabaptisticae, or Babel Anabapt. chapter 11, copied it. That book, written in the Belgian language by V.P., was printed at Cologne in 1603. Aubertus Miraeus also mentions this book, in De statu Religionis Christianae, book 1, chapter 30, de Belgicarum Provinciarum statu, and he says it is by no means unworthy of being translated into Latin. Hermannus Modes also gives the same epistle, in de initiis Anabap., page 146.

units.la: Additur duobus illis Manzio, & Grebelio tertius Georgius Jacobi, dictus toga cærulea, Blaurock, quem primum Grebelius rebaptizavit, uti postmodum reliquos. Georgius Blaurock, ob repudiatum à se, cum Papatu, sacerdotalem ordinem, aliosque baptismi articulos, publicè concrematus fuit, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxix. de quo in Martyrol. Anabapt. Manzius Tiguri anno cIↄ Iↄ xxv 11. d. v. Ianuar. jussu Magistratus, cujus spretâ authoritate & mandato, nihilo secius in ditione Tigurina, rebaptizandis hominibus pergebat, aquis submersus interiit. Grebelius discipulos plures fecit, quorum unus Laurentius San-Gallum venit, atque auditorium Iohannis Kesleri ingressus, prælegentem ad cap. vi. epist. ad Romanos publice interpellavit, & contra baptismum infantium disputationem exorsus, solidis Kesleri responsionibus retusus abiit. Alterum Sangallensium Professorem Wolfgangum Vlmi-am privatim aggressus avertit, atque in partes suas pertraxit: qui anno cIↄ Iↄ xxv. Scaphusi ipsum Grebelium offendens, ab eo totus nudus in præterfluente Rheno baptizatus, mox revelationes divinas jactavit, sed quas palam edisserere, quamvis rogatus & obsecratus aliquoties, renuit. Tandem hic, cum aliis quinque, V Valsæ anno cIↄ Iↄ xxv 11. à Pontificiis ultimo supplicio affectus fuit, insertusque martyrologio Anabaptistico. Sangallum confluebant passim greges Anabaptistarum, Grebelius ipse, & quaruncunque insaniarum ac enthusiasmorum magistri, inter quos Iohannes Denckius, Bavarus, Norimbergensis dictus, qui docebat, neminem, ne Diabolorum quidem, in æternum perdendum: vir cæteroquin non indoctus, qui VVormatiæ, cum Ludovico Hetzer, concionatorem Euangelicum in istâ urbe alium Jacobum Cautium, dum in vertendis ex Hebraico Prophetis majoribus una occupantur, suis opinionibus infecit, atque ut pro iis publicam sustineret disputationem, adegit. Hetzerus etiam contra Christi Deitatem librum scripsit, à Zuinglio suppressum, ac tandem Constantiæ anno MDXXIX. d. IV. Februarii ultimo supplicio, non absque significatâ prioris vitæ pœnitentiâ, periit, tum propter anabaptismum, tum crebra adulteria. Ab hoc Anabaptistarum antesignano, articulus de Christi Deitate primum impugnari cœpit. Verum Denckii, cujus (opinor) libellos habeo lingua Germanicâ, de Deo, an peccati autor sit; de sublatâ lege &c. non absque acumine scriptos, sed ad enthusiasmos inclinantes, Deus miseritus, operâ Oecolampadii, qui eum in viam reduxit, & ad quem extat Denckii epistola, inter epist. Zuinglii & Oecolampad. l. IV. Basileæ tandem a. MDXXVIII. i. pie mortuus fuit.
units.tr: To these two, Manz and Grebel, a third is added: Georg Jacobi, called Blaurock ("blue coat"), whom Grebel was the first to rebaptize, and afterwards the rest. Georg Blaurock, because he rejected the priestly order along with Papacy and other articles of baptism, was publicly burned in 1529; see the Anabaptist Martyrology. Manz was drowned at Zurich on 5 January 1526, by order of the magistrate, whose authority he scorned and whose command he nonetheless ignored, continuing to rebaptize people throughout the Zurich territory. Grebel made many disciples. One of them, Laurentius, came to St. Gall and entered the lecture of Johannes Kessler. While the professor was lecturing on chapter 6 of Romans, he publicly interrupted him, began a disputation against infant baptism, and was refuted by Kessler's solid answers and left. Another of the St. Gall professors, Wolfgang Ulmer, he approached privately, turned aside and drew into his party. In 1525 Ulmer met Grebel himself at Schaffhausen and was baptized by him, stark naked, in the Rhine flowing past. He soon boasted of divine revelations, but though asked and begged several times, he refused to set them out openly.
