At last he, along with five others, was executed by the Papists at Walsee in 1527, and was entered in the Anabaptist martyrology. Flocks of Anabaptists gathered everywhere at St. Gall, as did Grebel himself and the teachers of every kind of madness and enthusiasm, among them Johannes Denck, a Bavarian called "of Nuremberg," who taught that no one, not even the devils, should be damned for ever. He was otherwise not an unlearned man. At Worms, together with Ludwig Hätzer, an evangelical preacher in that city, he infected Jacob Cautius, another preacher there, with his opinions while they were occupied in translating the greater Prophets from the Hebrew, and he compelled Cautius to undertake a public disputation in their defence. Hätzer also wrote a book against Christ's Deity, which Zwingli suppressed. At last, on 4 February 1529, he perished at Constance by capital punishment, not without a clear repentance of his earlier life, both for Anabaptism and for frequent adulteries. From this standard-bearer of the Anabaptists the article on Christ's Deity was first attacked. But Denck's books, which I think I have in German, on whether God is the author of sin, on the abolition of the law, etc., were written not without acuteness but leaning towards enthusiasms. God took pity on him through the work of Oecolampadius, who brought him back to the right path, and there is a letter of Denck's to him among the letters of Zwingli and Oecolampadius, book 4. At last he died piously at Basel in 1528.

units.la: Antonius Kurfner docebat, quod omnes peccata sua palam confiteri deberent, quæcunque unquam commisissent; abusus loco Iacobi Apostoli, epist. cap. v. 16. Confitemini alii aliis offensas. Alii se, propter dictum Christi: nisi fiatis ut parvuli &c. puerorum instar in vitâ ac moribus gerebant, seque denudabant, & permulta alia indecora committebant. Etiam ex disputationibus eorum apparuit, quas crebras alii voce, alii scripto siscum habuerunt, inter quos præcipuus Ioachimus Vadianus, Reip. Sangallensis medicus, & qui Sangallensibus opitulatum ibat Zuinglius, lib. de baptismo, quod jam non de baptismo solum, sed & de justitiâ operum doctrinam soverent hæreticam. Quæ ut sciamus, & quomodo secta Anabaptistica paulatim ulterius progressa sit, ad alios porro articulos & errores, quod in omni hæresi vel sectâ ante omnia observanVandum, operæ pretium est exponere themata, quæ anno cIↄ Iↄ xxvii. VVormatiæ Iacobus Cautius, de quo dixi, & adversus quem se valide opponebant Collegæ ejus in ministerio Vlricus Preu, & Iohannes Baro, cumque iis Argentinenses Theologi, publicè disputanda proposuit. I. Verbum quod eloquimur, audimus, scribimus, non est vivum & æternum Dei verbum, sed tantum testimonium & signum interni, ut externa etiam satisfiat, II. Nullum externum verbum vel signum vel sacramentum, nulla etiam externa promissio ejus est efficacie, ut internum hominem consolari & confirmare possit. III. Pædobaptismus non est à Deo, sed directè contra Deum & Dei doctrinam per Iesum Christum filium ejus nobis propositam. IV. In Cœna Domini non est essentiale corpus & sanguis Christi. Necdum rectè illa VVormatiæ celebrata est. V. Quicquid in veteri Adamo cecidit & mortuum est, id in secundo Adamo Iesu Christo longè abundantius resurget & revivisçet, idque ordine justo. VI. Iesus Christus Nazarenus nulla alia ratione pro nobis passus est aut satisfecit, nisi insistamus vestigiis ejus, & quam ille triuit, eamus viam, & mandato Patris obediamus, perinde ut filius, quisque suâ mensurâ. Qui aliter de Christo loquitur, sentit aut credit, is ex Christo idolum facit: id quod omnes Doctores Theologi & Pseudo-evangelici cum toto mundo faciunt. VII. Ut externus ejus de pomo vetito neque Adamo neque posteris ejus nocuisset, nisi accessisset interna edendi cupiditas: ita sine interna obedientia & summa cupiditate æterna voluntati obtemperandi corporalis Iesu Christi passio non est vera satisfactio & reconciliatio cum Patre. Vide de illis Abrahamum Scultetum, Annalium Evangelii, seu Historiæ Reformationis, Decade primâ, ad a. cIↄ Iↄ xxv. & Decade II. ad a. cIↄ Iↄ xxvii. Basileæ quoque, & in Suevia passim, Ulmæ, Augustæ, & in Bavaria multo numero Anabaptistæ grassabantur. Illic quidem Oecolampadius resistere, & disputationes habere iisdem publicas, annis cIↄIxxvii. & cIↄIↄ xxix.
units.tr: Antonius Kurfner taught that everyone must openly confess all the sins they had ever committed, abusing for this purpose the words of the Apostle James, ch. 5, v. 16: Confess your faults one to another. Others, appealing to Christ's saying, unless you become like little children etc., behaved like children in their life and manners, stripped themselves naked, and committed a great many other indecent acts. Their disputations, which they held often, some by voice and some in writing, also made this plain. Among these the chief was Joachim Vadian, physician to the government of St Gall, and Zwingli, who went to help the people of St Gall, in his book On Baptism. Their teaching fostered heresy not only about baptism but also about justification by works. So that we may know this, and how the Anabaptist sect gradually advanced to further articles and errors (which, in every heresy or sect, must above all be observed), it is worth setting out the theses which James Cautius, of whom I have spoken, proposed for public disputation at Worms in the year 1527. His fellow ministers Ulrich Preu and John Baro opposed him vigorously, together with the Strasbourg theologians. The theses were: (I) The word we speak, hear and write is not the living and eternal Word of God, but only a testimony and sign of the inward word, so that the outward word may also be satisfied. (II) No outward word, sign or sacrament, and no outward promise of God, has the power to console and strengthen the inward man. (III) Infant baptism is not from God, but directly contrary to God and to the doctrine of God proposed to us through his Son Jesus Christ. (IV) In the Lord's Supper the body and blood of Christ are not essentially present. It has not yet been rightly celebrated at Worms. (V) Whatever fell and died in the old Adam will rise and be revived far more abundantly in the second Adam, Jesus Christ, and that in due order. (VI) Jesus Christ of Nazareth suffered for us and made satisfaction in no other way, unless we follow in his footsteps, walk the path he trod, and obey the Father's command, just as a son does, each in his own measure. Whoever speaks, thinks or believes otherwise about Christ makes an idol of Christ, which all the theologians and pseudo-evangelicals do, along with the whole world. (VII) Just as the outward eating of the forbidden fruit would not have harmed Adam or his posterity unless an inward desire to eat had been added, so without inward obedience and the greatest desire to obey the eternal will, the bodily passion of Jesus Christ is not a true satisfaction and reconciliation with the Father. See on these matters Abraham Scultetus, Annals of the Gospel, or History of the Reformation, Decade 1, for the year 1525, and Decade 2, for the year 1527. Anabaptists also swarmed in Basel, and throughout Swabia, at Ulm and Augsburg, and in great numbers in Bavaria. At Basel, Oecolampadius resisted them and held public disputations with them in the years 1527 and 1529.

units.la: In Bavaria Iacobus Husterus, & cum eo Gabriel Scheerdingus in Moraviam abierunt, primique fuere in iis partibus Anabaptistarum sectae Auctores. In Belgio (domi propemodum nati, inquit Famianus Strada, lib. 11.) quam primum nidulatum hoc hominum genus fuit: sed qui huc Anabaptistica deliria attulit ex Germania superiore primus fuit Melchior Hofmann. Hic anno MDXXVIII. Argentorato Emdam venit, atque strenuè rebaptizavit: quod ubi aliquo tempore fecisset, alterius socii cujusdam & senis prophetiâ ferentis, Argentoratum ut reperteret, ibi per dimidium annI incarcerandus, sed postea multo cum Prophetarum numero, gloria, & successu per omnem mundum, uti alter Elias, additis ei (juxta vaticinium Apocal. xiv. 1.) centum quadraginta quatuor millium ministrorum copiis, praedicaturus Evangelium. Quò cum venisset, & disputationem cum Theologis petiisset, institutâ eâ ad d. xi. Junii anno MDXXXII. confutatus & superatus discessit: pergens autem nihilominus in enthusiasmis & opinionibus proseminandis, turbisque, in carcerem conjicitur: hic mire confisus priori illa Prophetiâ, quam alii quoque ejusdem farinae Prophetae identidem confirmabant, excussis petulanter calceis, projecto pileo, obtestatus Deum, se non nisi aqua & pane vesciturum, quousque digito eum, qui ipsum misisset, monstraret: tandem miser homo in carcere obiit. Hic finis primi Anabaptismi in regionibus nostris institoris, & prophetiarum de eo, fuit.
units.tr: In Bavaria Jacob Huter, and with him Gabriel Scheerdingus, went off into Moravia, and they were the first authors of the Anabaptist sect in those parts. In the Low Countries (almost home-grown, says Famianus Strada, Book 11), this kind of people first nested. But the first to bring Anabaptist delusions from upper Germany here was Melchior Hofmann. In 1528 he came from Strasbourg to Emden and vigorously rebaptized. After he had done this for some time, a certain companion of his, an old man who gave prophecies, told him to go back to Strasbourg, there to be imprisoned for half a year. Afterwards, however, he went out again with a great number of prophets, glory and success throughout the whole world, like another Elijah, and with (according to the prophecy of Revelation 14:1) a hundred and forty-four thousand ministers added to his forces, to preach the Gospel. When he came there and asked for a disputation with the theologians, one was arranged for 11 June 1532; he left refuted and defeated. Nevertheless, going on with his enthusiasms and the spreading of his opinions, and with the disturbances, he was cast into prison. There, trusting wonderfully in that earlier prophecy, which other prophets of the same stamp kept repeating, he shook off his shoes wantonly, threw away his cap, and called God to witness that he would eat nothing but water and bread until God showed him with a finger the one who had sent him. At last the wretched man died in prison. This was the end of the first Anabaptism, and of the prophecies about it, in our regions.

units.la: Reliquerat Emdae Hofmannus, & in locum suum surrogarat Iohannem Trypmaacker, nempe ne vacaret sedes: cui dum cum sociis non bene conveniebat, discessit in Hollandiam, & Amsteldami, Harlemi, Leidae coëgit sectae suae discipulos illos, qui inde tantas, tamque execrandas & omnibus notas dederunt turbas. Ipse quum magnorum Amsteldami, inter plebem, tumultuum auctor existeret, à Magistratu apprehensus, & Hagam missus, flagitiorum poenas dedit.
units.tr: Hofmann had left Emden and, so that the seat should not be empty, had put in his place John Trypmaker. But when he did not get on well with his companions, he withdrew into Holland, and at Amsterdam, Haarlem and Leiden he gathered those disciples of his sect who afterwards caused such great and such execrable disturbances, notorious to all. He himself was the author of great tumults among the common people at Amsterdam; seized by the magistrate and sent to The Hague, he paid the penalty for his crimes.

units.la: Interim Harlemi Iohannes Matthæus, pistor, pertasus uxoris vetulæ, aliam juniorem & magis gratam, filiam Cerevisiarii ad se pellicit, cum quâ Amstelodamum profectus, se Prophetam, & alterum Enochum, à Deo, redimendo ejus populo missum, jactat, strenuèque rebaptizat: quantumvis Melchior Hofmannus Argentorato scripsisset, ut per biennium baptizationes omitterent, ad exemplum Ezræ Haggæique, qui biennio ab ædificando templo fuerant impediti. Elegit quoque duodecim Apostolos, quorum binos, ad exemplum Christi, quaquaversum, Iohannem Beccoldum, Leidensem sartorem, postea Regem Monasteriensem, cum Gerardo Bibliopego, Monasterium: Theodorum Cuyper, cum Bartoldo Bibliopego, in Frisiam: reliquos, Jacobum Campensem, Petrum Vagino-fabrum, Davidem Hornensem, Leonardum Bibliopegum, Cornelium Brielensem, Nicolaum Alcmarianum, Meinardum Delfensem, & Petrum ligni- sectorem, aliorsum misit, omnes divulgatum prophetias, insomnia, anabaptismum & reliquam doctrinam suam, in quâ tradendâ minimè tamen erant concordes. Disputare siquis iiscum aut conferre instituieret, responsi nil aliud referebat à fanaticis, quam ita spiritum dictare, qui non quibusvis contingeret, nec ubique spiraret. Interim librum edunt, Restitutionis titulo inscriptum, in quo hæc congerunt: Christi regnum ante ultimum diem rerum humanarum civile in terra futurum: ubi soli sancti & justi, regibus ferro & vi sublatis, dominarentur. Id autem regnum esse jam captum Anabaptistarum. Magistratum omnem esse delendum: ei omnibus opibus obsistendum. Licet Christi apostolis nullum gladii jus, nullaque regni civilis administratio, nulla item imperii stabiliendi potestas permissa sit, posteris tamen eorum sectatoribus, & iis qui post illos docendi munus in ecclesia suscepturi essent, civile imperium, & jus glagladiis traditum, potestatem faciens, impium Magistratum ferro abSumendi pro libidine. In Anabaptistarum ecclesia nullum impium inveniri: omnes sanctos esse. Neminem servatum iri, qui universas suas facultates in medium non conferret. Lege naturae, cum quae lex divina non pugnet, fas jusque esse, multas habere uxores. Christum corpus ex Dei Virginis carne non induisse. Atque istius commatis plura, quae quantopere & doctrinam Ecclesiae, & pacem Reip. laederent, quivis facile perspiciebat. Amstelodami anno cIↄ Iↄ xxx iv. magna audacia atque impudentia res suas agebant, & nequidquam auditis Imperatoris Caroli v. edictis, & nonnullis alibi capite damnatis, promulgatâque delinquentibus veniâ, perrexerunt: conductis navibus illorum multi abire se responderunt, terram, quam iis Deus ostensurus esset, petituri.
units.tr: Meanwhile at Haarlem John Matthys, a baker, tired of his old wife, enticed to himself a younger and more pleasing one, the daughter of a brewer. With her he set off for Amsterdam, boasting that he was a prophet, another Enoch, sent by God to redeem his people; and he rebaptized vigorously, although Melchior Hofmann had written from Strasbourg that they should suspend baptisms for two years, after the example of Ezra and Haggai, who had been hindered for two years from building the temple. He also chose twelve apostles, and, after the example of Christ, sent them out in pairs in every direction: John Beukels, a tailor of Leiden, later King of Münster, with Gerard the bookbinder, to Münster; Theodore Cuyper, with Bartholomew the bookbinder, to Friesland; and the rest, Jacob of Kampen, Peter the scabbard-maker, David of Horn, Leonard the bookbinder, Cornelius of Brielle, Nicholas of Alkmaar, Meinard of Delft, and Peter the woodcutter, he sent elsewhere. All of them spread their prophecies, dreams, Anabaptism and the rest of their doctrine, in the delivery of which they were by no means agreed. If anyone wanted to dispute with them or confer with them, the only answer the fanatics gave was that the Spirit dictated thus, a Spirit that does not come to everyone and does not breathe everywhere. Meanwhile they published a book entitled Restitution, in which they gathered the following: Christ's kingdom will be a civil kingdom on earth before the last day of human affairs, in which only the holy and the just, with kings removed by the sword and force, shall rule. This kingdom has already been seized by the Anabaptists. Every magistrate must be destroyed, and resisted with all resources. Although no right of the sword, no administration of civil rule, and no power to establish an empire was granted to Christ's apostles, yet to their successors and to those who were to take up the office of teaching in the Church, civil power and the right of the sword has been handed over, empowering them to remove an impious magistrate by the sword at will. In the Anabaptist Church no one is found impious; all are holy. No one will be saved who does not bring all his goods into the common stock. By the law of nature, since the divine law does not oppose it, it is lawful and right to have many wives. Christ did not put on a body from the flesh of the Virgin God. And there were many more articles of this kind, which anyone could easily see would do great harm both to the doctrine of the Church and to the peace of the commonwealth. At Amsterdam in the year 1534 they carried on their business with great boldness and shamelessness. The edicts of the Emperor Charles V were heard in vain, and some were condemned to death elsewhere; and when pardon was proclaimed to the offenders, they went on regardless. They hired ships, and many of them replied that they would leave, seeking the land which God was going to show them.

units.la: Die xxi. Martii quinque viri nudi in publicum strictis gladiis prosiluere, urbem totam pervolantes, & incondito clamore implentes omnia: in nomine Domini. Dei benedictio in veteri urbis parte; maledictio in nova. Hic primus illorum in urbe ista tumultus, qui captis, ut fieri potuit, antesignanis, iisque xxvi. Martii Harlemi, una cum aliis duobus, capitis supplicio affecti, sedavit. Iterum alium excitarunt sequenti anno, mense Februario, quando visi septem, cum quatuor mulieribus, quibus etiam quinta accessit, nudi per urbem mane hora tertia discurrunt, & horrendum clamant: ve ve ve, vindicta vindicta, pater omnipotens; ita ut contremiscere videretur urbs, atque interire. Sed capti illi quoque, & capite multati fuere.
units.tr: On 21 March five men ran naked through the public streets with drawn swords, flying through the whole city and filling every place with a disordered shouting: "In the name of the Lord! The blessing of God on the old part of the city; the curse on the new." This was the first of their disturbances in the city. Their leaders were captured, as far as it could be managed, and on 26 March at Haarlem, together with two others, they were executed, and the disturbance was quelled. They stirred up another the following year, in February, when seven men, with four women and a fifth who joined them, ran naked through the city at about nine in the morning, crying out dreadfully: "Woe, woe, woe, vengeance, vengeance, almighty Father!" The city seemed to tremble and to be ruined. But they too were captured and punished with death.

units.la: Tertium tumultum dederunt ibidem, ejusdem anni mense Majo, quando curiam impetu facto occupabant, & non nisi caesis hinc inde multis, capi, tum puniri pro scelerum merito potuere. Praeterquam Amstelodami, quamvis hic quidem maxime: nam eam civitatem negotiatorum frequentia, & peregrinarum gentium nationes mutuo commercio totam, brevi tempore corrupere. Diversa enim voluntates, diversa judicia, & exterae religiones in urbibus, rebusque sunt perniciosa, inquit Lambertus Hortensius, lib. Tumultuum Anabaptistarum; per totam Hollandiam, Harlemi, Leidae, Hagae - Comitum multum turbarum ab illis hominibus datum fuit.
units.tr: They made a third disturbance in the same city in May of the same year, when they attacked and seized the town hall. Only after many were cut down on every side could they be taken, and then they could be punished as their crimes deserved. Nor was this only in Amsterdam, although it was especially there: for within a short time they corrupted that city, with its crowds of merchants and its mutual trade with the nations of foreign peoples, through and through. "For different wills, different judgments and foreign religions are pernicious in cities and in affairs," says Lambertus Hortensius in his book on the Anabaptist tumults. Throughout all Holland, at Haarlem, Leiden and The Hague, those men caused much trouble to the counts.

units.la: Monasterium missi fuerant Prophetae Iohannis Matthaei Harlemensis Apostoli Iohannes Beckoldus, & Gerardus Bibliopegus. Qui ubi advenerunt anno cIↄ Iↄ XXXIII. ad VII. Kal. Decemb. nocturnos primum coetus agere, multa specie modestiae se in animos hominum insinuare, hypocritas agere exquisitissime, omnium bona communia habere, & nullum divitem admittere, redigere in aequalem sortem omnes. Quo brevi tempore adeo excreverunt, ut anno cIↄ Iↄ XXXIV. in publicam disputationem cum Lutheranis progredi ausi fuerint, quin aliquos in partes suas pertraxerint etiam, inter quos qui illis primum acriter, vere, an simulate ?' restiterat, Bernardus Rotmannus, primus in illa urbe a Reformatione concionator (in quo idem, quod in Thoma Muncero, Dei judicium) Cnipperdollingus, alibi nomen hoc legi Cnoperus Dolling, Hermannus Stapeda Rotmanni Collega, Hem. Rollii, de quo Trajectenses supplicium ob anabaptismum paulo ante sumserant, discipulus, in paedobaptismum semper iniquus atque alii. Hinc ad turbas & tumultus palam itum, & primum per urbem conferto agmine clamitarunt, ut poenitentiam omnes agerent, & rebaptizarentur, alioquin Dei ira confestim excidendi: tum & trucidandos omnes dictis suis minus morigeros, ut ethnicos improbosque, dicebant, & per vim occupata curia, triduum in armis egerunt, & castra civibus magistratuique opposita tenuerunt, quousque compositae utriusque res, ea lege, ut utraque pars ab armis discederet, & quiete viveret, nullis se mutuo convitiis aut injuriis lacesseret, doctrina cuique sua esset esseт integra, & Magistratui sarta tectaque reverentia ac potestas. Interim Anabaptistæ veriti, ne forte de nocte aut improviso obruerentur, ad socios ubique literas dederunt; præcipuè vicinas urbes, Osnabrugam, Vesaliam, Coesveldum, & VVarendorpiam, ut confluerent omnes Monasterium, ceu ad novum à Deo destinatum Ierusalem, & rebus suis concordi animo consulerent. Iohannes Matthæus jam tempus suum adventisse ratus, eò quoque properat, & naves certatim conscendunt homines undique multi, quorum nonnullas jussu & consilio Curiæ Hollandicæ attinuit Magistratus Amsteldamensis, alias duodecim Transisulanian petentes, fraudem suorum edoctæ, mari se dedérunt, & Ditmariam appulere, ubi considentes, nomen Hollandorum ab eo tempore, id est anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxiv. d xxi. Maji, servarunt. Monasteriensis interim videntes quâ hominum turbâ urbs opppleretur, quæque agitarentur, urbe cedebant plurimi. Quod videntes Anabaptistæ, se superiores rati, Magistratum mutarunt, & creárunt consules Cnipperdollingum, & Cippenbrochum, quibus addiderunt viginti & duos Senatores. Iam ad apertum bellum spectabant omnia.
units.tr: John Matthew, the prophet and apostle of Haarlem, had sent out John Beckold and Gerard Bibliopegus to Münster. When they arrived there on 25 November 1533, they first held nocturnal meetings and, under a great show of modesty, insinuated themselves into people's minds; they played the hypocrite most exquisitely, held all goods in common, admitted no rich man, and reduced everyone to an equal lot. In so short a time did they grow that in 1534 they dared to enter a public disputation with the Lutherans, and they drew some into their party as well. Among these was the man who had first and most vigorously (truly, or only pretending?) resisted them, Bernhard Rothmann, the first preacher in that city after the Reformation (in whom the same judgment of God appeared as in Thomas Müntzer). Also Knipperdolling (elsewhere I have read this name as Cnoperus Dolling), Hermann Staepel, colleague of Rothmann, Hendrik Rolle, the disciple of the man whom the people of Utrecht had shortly before executed for Anabaptism, who was always hostile to infant baptism, and others. From this they proceeded openly to riots and tumults, and first they cried out in dense ranks through the city that everyone should repent and be rebaptized, otherwise they would at once be cut off by the wrath of God; then they said that all who were less obedient to their words should be slaughtered, as heathens and wicked men. They seized the town hall by force and spent three days under arms, holding camps opposed to the citizens and the magistrate, until both sides were settled on the condition that each party should lay down arms and live in quiet, neither provoking the other with insults or injuries, that each should keep its own doctrine whole, and that the magistrate should keep its due reverence and authority. Meanwhile the Anabaptists, fearing lest they should be overwhelmed by night or unexpectedly, sent letters everywhere to their companions, especially to the neighbouring cities, Osnabrück, Wesel, Coesfeld and Warendorf, asking that all should gather at Münster as at a new Jerusalem appointed by God, and consult with one accord on their affairs. John Matthew, thinking his time had now come, hurried there too, and many men from everywhere crowded eagerly onto the ships. Some of these, by order and counsel of the Court of Holland, were held back by the magistrate of Amsterdam; the rest, twelve in number, making for Friesland (Transisulania), were warned of their companions' treachery and gave themselves to the sea, and landed at Ditmarsh, where they settled and kept the name of Hollanders from that time, that is, from 21 May 1534. Meanwhile the Münster people, seeing with what crowd of men the city was filled, and what was going on, left the city in great numbers. Seeing this, the Anabaptists, thinking themselves the stronger, changed the magistracy and created as consuls Knipperdolling and Cippenbroick, to whom they added twenty-two senators. Now everything looked toward open war.

units.la: Episcopus Monasteriensis, à Coloniensi Archiepiscopo subsidium, adversus seditiosos petebat, ad liberandam ab eorum tyrannide urbem. Scripto exercitu, eoque urbe occlusâ, Iohannes Matthæus Propheta, totius tragœdiæ auctor & instigator, furioso quam duci similior, postquam aliquos in Episcopi exercitum impetus fecisset, ut videbatur, haud infelices, tandem cæsus, atque corbe à suis in urbem perlatus, frustra exspectata ejus post quartum diem recuscitatione in vitam, humatus fuit. Successit in locum ejus Iohannes Bocoldus, Leidensis sartor, idque ex prophetiâ maxime & revelatione Cnipperdollingi Consulis, quem ut alio beneficio remuneraret Propheta ille, fecit eum suum ac Reip. Lictorem, tradito ad hanc rem solemniter tergladio. Hinc propheta, postquam ex diuturno somnio triduanum præmisisset jejunium, edixit, uni viro licere plures habere simul uxores: unde ipse mox tres sumsit, interque eas viduam quoque prædecessoris sui Iohannis Matthæi. Tantæ vero luxuriæ atque improbitati reclamantes alios, ad quinquaginta, istam solam ob causam, trucidavit. Hinc, ex alterius cujusdam Prophetæ cœlesti iterum revelatione, Rex renunciatur, Rex justitiæ hujus mundi: unde se deincepsregio more per omnia habuit, constituto oratore Regio Bernhardo Rotmanno: quatuor consiliarios elegit, Gerardum Bibliopegum, Bernhardum Crechtingum, Henricum Reckerum, & Gerardum Reningum: aulæ regiæ præfecit consulem Tillebeccum: vasis aureis, argenteisque Gerardum Cippenbrochium: urbis præsecto constituto Cnipperdollingo. Inde ex alia revelatione dixit, a se mitti debere in universum mundum viginti octo ministros, ad prædicandum Euangelium. Interim dum Episcopum tædium caperet diuturnæ obsidionis, fame obsessos enecare, vel ad deditionem adigere instituit. Unde in urbe firmiter undiquaque occlusa omnium rerum inedia, & primum carnis, tum frumenti, herbarum, olerum inopia eos torquebat, & consumtis eduliis, in cibum cedere canes, feles, & mures, imo arborum frondes, coria calcei: quamvis in deliciis & opulentia agente, cum Reginis suis, Rege. Quod quia harum una, nondum penitus exuta omnem humanitatis sensum, reprehendisset, publice ipsius Regis manu, in conspectu reliquarum quindecim uxorum, capite truncata fuit. Capta tandem urbs, captus & Rex fuit, repertaque in tres menses apud eum, pro se & sua Regia, annonæ copia. Is ad vicina primum loca spectaculum missus, ligatus ferreis catenis; tum agnitis errore ac flagitiis, vitæ, ut creditur, servandæ spe, natus duntaxat annos viginti sex, una cum sociis Cnipperdolingo, & Bernardo Crechting, ignitis forcipibus per horam & amplius excarnificatus, tum gladio in cor adacto extinctus est, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxv i. corpora ferreâ cavea inclusa èsummâ primi templi turre suspensa perpetuum posteris monumentum fuere. Scripserunt historiam varii, Henricus Dorpius, civis Monasterienſis, illo ipso anno; Lambertus Hortensius Montfortius, Scholae Nardenae Rector; anno cIↄ Iↄ xlvııı. Sleidanus, anno cIↄ Iↄ lv. Commentar. lib. x. Auctor Successionis Anabaptisticae, belgicè Coloniae impressus liber, anno cIↄ Iↄ c ııı. Ne Scriptores adversus Anabaptistas dicam, Bullingerum, lib. ıı. Hermannum Moded, de Initiis sectae Anabapt. Florimundum Ræmundum, de haeref. lib. ıı. Hondorfium, in Theatro Exemplorum, ad praeceptum Decalogi primum. Excisis Monasterienſibus, causam illorum tuebantur adhuc alii, appellati Batenburgici, à Iohanne Theodorici Batenburg, consule olim Steenvicensi, cujus parens ex nobili Batenburgensium familia, hic filius nothus. Isti reliquos à se dissidentes criminabantur pro perfidis & timidis. Adeo quod semel ex furore, quasi zelo, arripuerunt homines, ægre dimittunt, quin alios μὴ συντρέχειν εἰς τὴν αὐτὴν τῆς ἀσεβείας ἀναχυσιν lubenter etiam blasphemant. 1. Pet. iv. 4.
units.tr: The bishop of Münster sought help against the seditious men from the archbishop of Cologne, to free the city from their tyranny. The army was assembled and the city was shut up. John Matthew the prophet, the author and instigator of the whole tragedy, more like a madman than a leader, after he had made some attacks on the bishop's army, which seemed not unsuccessful, was at last killed; his body was carried into the city in a basket by his followers, and after four days, when his resurrection into life was vainly awaited, he was buried. In his place succeeded John Beckold, a tailor of Leiden, and this chiefly by the prophecy and revelation of Knipperdolling the consul, whom that prophet, to reward him with another favour, made his own and the commonwealth's executioner, handing over a sword to him for this office with due ceremony. Then the prophet, after he had first ordered a three-day fast following a long dream, declared that one man might have several wives at once; whereupon he soon took three himself, among them also the widow of his predecessor John Matthew. Others who protested against such luxury and wickedness, about fifty in number, he slaughtered for this reason alone. Then, by another prophet's heavenly revelation, he was proclaimed king, "King of righteousness of this world"; from then on he lived in every respect in royal style, with Bernhard Rothmann appointed royal orator. He chose four counsellors: Gerard Bibliopegus, Bernhard Krechting, Hendrik Rekker and Gerard Rennink. He placed over the royal household the consul Tilbeck, and over the gold and silver vessels Gerard Cippenbroick, and Knipperdolling was appointed prefect of the city. Then by another revelation he said that twenty-eight ministers must be sent by him into the whole world to preach the Gospel. Meanwhile, as the bishop grew weary of the long siege, he resolved to kill those besieged by famine or force them to surrender. So, with the city firmly shut up on every side and all things cut off, they were tormented first by lack of meat, then of grain, herbs and vegetables; when their food was used up, dogs, cats and mice were turned into food, even tree-leaves and shoe leather, while the king himself lived in luxury and plenty with his queens. When one of these, who had not yet been wholly stripped of all human feeling, rebuked him, she was beheaded by the king's own hand, in the sight of the other fifteen wives. At last the city was taken, and the king too was captured; and there was found with him, for himself and his court, a store of provisions enough for three months. He was first sent to the nearby places as a spectacle, bound with iron chains; then, having acknowledged his errors and crimes, in hope (as is believed) of saving his life, he was tortured for more than an hour with red-hot pincers, he being only twenty-six years old, together with his companions Knipperdolling and Bernhard Krechting; then he was put to death by a sword driven into his heart, in the year 1535. The bodies, enclosed in an iron cage, were hung from the top tower of the main church, a perpetual monument to posterity. Various writers have recorded the history: Henricus Dorpius, a citizen of Münster, in that same year; Lambertus Hortensius of Montfoort, rector of the school at Naarden, in 1548; Sleidan, in 1555, Commentaries, book 10; the author of the Succession of the Anabaptists, a book printed in Dutch at Cologne, in 1603. Not to mention writers against the Anabaptists: Bullinger, book 2; Hermann Moded, on the beginnings of the Anabaptist sect; Florimond de Raemond, On Heresies, book 2; Hondorff, in the Theatre of Examples, under the first commandment of the Decalogue. After the destruction of the Münster men, others defended their cause, called the Batenburgers, after John Theodoric Batenburg, once consul of Steenwijk, whose father came from the noble Batenburg family, while he himself was an illegitimate son. These men accused the others who dissented from them of being treacherous and cowardly. So once men have been seized by a kind of frenzy, passing for zeal, they can hardly be let go, and they gladly blaspheme even those who do not "run with them into the same flood of wickedness" [μὴ συντρέχειν εἰς τὴν αὐτὴν τῆς ἀσεβείας ἀναχυσιν]. 1. Pet. iv. 4.

units.la: In Frisiam Apostolos jam ante miserat Iohannes Matthaeus, Propheta Harlemensis, Bartoldum Bibliopegum, & Theodorum Cuyper anno cIↄ Iↄ xxx ııı, Leovardiam. Hi sibimet persuadentes tam bene Spiritum Sanctum per Iohannis Matthaei χειροθεσίαν se nunc accepisse, ac olim Apostoli in die Pentecostes, primum in coetu quindecim vel sexdecim hominum Prophetae sui deprædicantes coelestem missionem, revelationes, prodigia, miris artibus, ementita authoritate & divino jussu, statim fecere discipulos nonnullos, & in ejus sacramentum rebaptizarunt, inter eos Obbonem Philippi, & Ioh. Scheerder primos. Secutus, cum aliis, Obbonis frater, Theodorus Philippi, qui una cum Men-
units.tr: Earlier, John Matthew, the prophet of Haarlem, had already sent apostles into Friesland, namely Bartold the bookbinder and Theodore Cuyper, to Leeuwarden, in the year 1533. Persuaded that they had now received the Holy Spirit through John Matthew's laying on of hands [χειροθεσία], just as the apostles did on the day of Pentecost, they first gathered a group of fifteen or sixteen people. There they proclaimed their prophets' heavenly mission, revelations and miracles, using clever tricks, a false authority and a claimed divine command. At once they made several disciples and rebaptized them into their sacrament, the first of whom were Obbo Philips and Jan Scheerder. Following them came Obbo's brother, Theodore Philips, who, together with Men-

units.la: ıııı nome Simonis, & David Georgii, ab Obbone facti sedæ suæ episcopi. David Georgii, Delphis Hollandorum; Menno, Groningæ. Neque in Frisiâ, & Groningæ, atque in illis partibus quaquaversum minus tumultuatum ab Anabaptistis, quam alibi, aut in Hollandiâ. Groningæ Henricus Calcearius multam partem denudatus per urbem discurrere & vociferari coepit: occide, occide, occide Monachos, Papas, & universos Magistratus, resipisce, resipisce, prope est tua liberatio. Obbo ille, vir doctus, resipuit postea, & publice fecit palinodiam, quæ legitur in ejus Confessione, editâ Amsterdami, anno MDIX, ex ejus autographo, ubi circa finem dolere se, ait, ex animo, quod aliquem ad istud munus promovisset, in quo tam miserè deceptus ipse sit, & quod non antea destiterit, sed eo adactus esset jam fuerit, ut ad postulatum fratrum, Theodoro Philippi, Davidi Georgio, & Mennoni Simonis idem munus impositurit: quod me valde poenitet, atque coram Deo (inquit) & fratribus meis deplorabo, quoad vixero, istiusque semper reminiscar. Et cum illis valedicerem, Mennonem ac Theodorum monui, missionem meam iniquam, neque in eo circumventum fuisse, ac optare ut nunquam hoc munus accepissent: saltem exonerare coram illis conscientiam visum, culpam & seductionem agnoscendo, de cætero videant quid agant. Ingenuum rarumque apud istud hominum genus, exemplum. Historiam scripto illo contexit primi in his regionibus exordii Anabaptistici, in Melchiore Hofmanno, qui se pro Elia gerebat; tum, illo in carcere Argentorati, miserè, & contra jactatas de se prophetias, extincto, in Johanne Matthæo Harlemensi pistore, qui quaquaversum Apostolos suos miserat, & in Frisiam eos, à quibus in ipsorum ordinem assumtus fuerat, ipse Obbo. Illud solvere apud animum suum hic nequibat; quâ auctoritate vel nomine, aut Melchior Hofmannus, quem evenenventus docuerat falsum, aut Matthæus Harlemensis discipulos facerent & Doctores: quod certe validum adversus totam ipsorum sectam est argumentum, quo probetur, sanctam illam & Christianam esse non posse, quam fundarint homines, ita omnium judicio & sensu maleferiati. A quibus tamen & Menno quoque, & alii istius farinæ omnes ortum suum habent, missionem & baptismum. Hoc urget identidem, & interrogat in suâ Confessione Obbo, quomodo quid boni ex infandis illis Auctoribus prodire potuerit? quisve illis potestatem fecerit docendi agendique illa, quorum se, & fratrem Theodorum, adde & Mennonem, puducerit? Præterea tres illi, à quibus Obbo, uti ab hoc Theodorus, & Menno, aliique missionem suam acceperunt, utcunque prophetarent non amplius persequendos homines, vel fundendum sanguinem, quo se alii pacto adversus vim Magistratus opposuerant, postquam Amsteldami per plateas cursitando & vociferando horrendas dedissent turbas, Harlemum abducti meritas luerunt pœnas, & ultimo supplicio affici conspexit suis oculis Obbo. Ad quam se converterit, postquam illi sectæ valedixit Obbo, non satis constat. Florimundus Ræmundus dicit lib. II. cap. VI. Catholicum factum, sed ex libro ejus illo judico ego potius eum Libertinum factum, uti facilis huc inde progressus est: obiit vero a. MDLXVIII.
units.tr: Menno Simons and David Georgii, were made bishops of their sect by Obbo. David Georgii was from Delft in Holland; Menno from Groningen. Nor was there less uproar in Friesland, Groningen and the surrounding regions, caused by the Anabaptists, than elsewhere or in Holland. At Groningen, Hendrik Calcearius, stripped almost naked, began to run through the city and shout: kill, kill, kill the monks, the popes and all the magistrates; repent, repent, your deliverance is at hand. Obbo, a learned man, later repented and publicly retracted. His retraction is read in his Confession, published at Amsterdam in 1549 from his own manuscript, where near the end he says that he sincerely regrets having promoted anyone to that office, since he himself had been so wretchedly deceived, and that he had not stopped earlier, but had been driven on, so that at the request of the brethren he imposed the same office on Theodore Philips, David Georgii and Menno Simons. "This grieves me greatly," he says, "and I shall lament it before God and my brethren as long as I live, and I shall always remember it. When I took my leave of them, I warned Menno and Theodore that my mission was wrong, and that they had not been deceived in this; I hoped they would never have accepted this office. At least I thought fit to unburden my conscience before them, by acknowledging my fault and their seduction; for the rest, let them see what they will do." A noble and rare example among that kind of people. In that writing he wove together the history of the first beginnings of Anabaptism in these regions: first in Melchior Hofmann, who called himself Elijah, and who died wretchedly in prison at Strasbourg, contrary to the prophecies he had boasted of; then in John Matthew of Haarlem, a baker, who sent his apostles everywhere, and into Friesland, the men by whom Obbo himself had been received into their order. Obbo could not resolve this question in his own mind: by what authority or name Melchior Hofmann, whom the outcome had shown to be a false teacher, or Matthew of Haarlem, made disciples and teachers. This is certainly a strong argument against their whole sect, showing that a church founded by men of such evil character, by the judgment and feeling of everyone, cannot be holy and Christian. Yet Menno too, and all men of that stamp, have their origin, their mission and their baptism from these men. Obbo keeps pressing this point in his Confession, asking again and again how any good could come from such unspeakable authors, and who gave power to those whom he, his brother Theodore, and also Menno, were ashamed of, to teach and act in those things. Moreover, those three men from whom Obbo, and likewise Theodore and Menno and the others received their mission, though they prophesied that men were no longer to be persecuted or blood shed, as others had opposed the violence of the magistrate in other ways, were after running through the streets of Amsterdam and shouting, and causing dreadful disturbances, led away to Haarlem and paid the deserved penalty; Obbo saw with his own eyes that they were put to death. Where Obbo turned after he had bidden farewell to that sect is not sufficiently clear. Florimundus Raemundus says, in book II, chapter VI, that he became a Catholic; but from his book I judge that he rather became a Libertine, as the path from there is easy. He died in 1568.

units.la: David Georgii, Delfensis erat, artem exercens pictoriam, primum ob fortiter repulsum Papatum, inde ob istam suo maxime consilio inter Anabaptistas dissidentes concordiam, in conventu VVestphalico, in oppido Buckholt, celebris, sectam Hofmannicam anno MDXXXIV in inferiore Germaniâ inceptam imprimis firmavit & promovit. Deinde turpia & blasphema plurima docuit, de quibus præter Ubbonem Emmium, ipse Davidis gener Nic. Blesdikius, in Davidis Georgii historiâ, ab eo conscripta, à Cl. viro Iac. Revio vio edita. Obiit Basileæ a. cIↄIↄI, xxv. Augusti, ubi biennio post, iussu Senatus, exhumatus, & cum libris atque effigie sua concrematus fuit.
units.tr: David Georgii was from Delft and worked as a painter. First, because he had strongly rejected the Papacy, and then because of the agreement among the dissenting Anabaptists which he brought about chiefly by his own counsel at the famous Westphalian conference in the town of Bocholt, he greatly strengthened and promoted the Hofmannite sect, which had begun in Lower Germany in 1534. Afterwards he taught many shameful and blasphemous things, about which Ubbo Emmius writes, and David's son-in-law Nicolaas Blesdijk, in the history of David Georgii written by him and published by the distinguished man Jacob Revius. He died at Basel on 25 August 1556, and two years later, by order of the Senate, he was exhumed and burned together with his books and his effigy.

units.la: Menno autem, de cuius missione & doctrina quid sentiendum, ex Obbonis Declaratione colligi potest, natus est anno cIↄ ccccxcv1. in Frisia, prope oppidum Bolswert, in vico VVitmarsum, ubi, postquam in vico Pinnigum, etiam sacerdotem egit. Anno cIↄIↄ xxxv1. deserto Papatu, ab Obbone Philippi rebaptizatus est, & docendi officium, cum solemni manuum impositione, accepit: quod Groningæ, atque aliis postea in locis solerter satis peregit, voce valens, & scripto. Obiit anno cIↄIↄlx1. A Monasteriensibus & Batenburgicis dissentiebant Vbbonitæ seu Mennonitæ, non solum quod tumultus illorum & turbas non probarent, quemadmodum nec Hofmannici, sed ab his & illis discrepabant imprimis in duobus articulis: primo, de futuro instantique alio Christi in terris regno, & admirandâ Ecclesiæ per novam & extraordinariam missionem Spiritus, quemadmodum olim super Apostolos die Pentecostes, restitutione; altero, de uxorum pluralitate, & facili divortio: quorum neutrum Mennonitæ probabant. Quæ pluribus in locis testatus Menno fuit, adversus illos, qui ipsum dicerent cum Monasteriensibus facere, in historia sui discessus ex Papatu, quam scripsit a. cIↄIↄliv. Eundemque in finem est, quod anno huius sæculi vigesimo septimo prodiit scriptum Mennonis, non antea impressum, adversus horrendam & maximam Iohannis Leidensis blasphemiam, qui se pro vero Rege Davide, omnium promisso gaudio, venditat. Attamen, quamvis turbas Monasteriensium Sociorum non quidem probaret Menno, illos tamen etiam pro fratribus agnoscebat: missi quippe erant omnes à Johanne Matthæo Harlemensi, & qui Monasterii primo turbabant, quibus & ipse Iohannes postmodum accessit; & illi, qui in Frisia res novas moliti, liti; Obbonem, & Theodorum Philippi, Mennonem, aliosque suæ sectæ primipilos constituerant. Et passim de Monasteriensibus loquens, fratrum nomine eos indigetat in Confessione, vel Palinodiâ suâ Obbo Philippi. Inter alia: Ende als ick noch om die verleydinge gedencke / die onder den Broederen geschiede tot Amstelredam / int oude kloster tot Hazertsan in den Dam / op het sant / ende boven al tot Munster / soo bedroeft myne sie- le / ende verschrickt daer voor. Ick swoge dan alle die valsche sendingen / prophetien / gesichten / droomen / openbaringen / ende onuytspreeklicke geestelijken hoovaert die terstont van die eerste ure inbrack onder den Broederen. Menno similiter in Fundamenti libro, Monasteriensesë dilectos suos fratres appellat: in Parænesi ad corruptas sectas, (scriptâ, uti apparet, adversus Monasteriensés, & David Joristas): Ick en twyffel daer niet aen ofte onse lieben broeders de en wepnich tegen den Here voorzmaels mishandelt hebben, vermits sy met geweer wolden hoeren gelobe beschermen/ ofte die hebben een genadigen God &c. hoewel sy nochtans in wepnich gedoolt hebben het welcke ons niet behoort om tho volgen, gelijck wy boven geseght hebben, noemplicken als dat sy cenighe wapens gebruyckt hebben anders dan lijdsaemheit unde Godes woordt, het is oock geen wonder dat sy in die tijt gesnoebelt hebben, vermidts sy in die tijt de bepzoebinge der gesten noch niet en hadden. Die opzechte ende droomen heet ick mine susters unde broeders vermits sy onwetende gesnoebelt hebben, men den dobbelhertigen die Godt niet gesocht en hebben met puerder repnder herten hoewel sy su-sters sters unde broeders genoemt waren unde die Princen der verboeringe als bennen Munster unde Amsterdam die laet ick des Heeren handt. sol. 125.126. edit. A. 1616. sed ad correctissimum exemplar Anni 1539. Quae ideo magis ad verbum exscripsimus, quia in aliis exemplaribus non leguntur: tum quoq; ut appareat, nos recte originem Mennonitarum & Anabaptistarum ad Monasterienses illos retulisse. Scripsit Menno pluria, inter quae, uti olim epistola fundamentalis Manichaei, celebris est liber fundamenti: in quo moralia nonnulla, & admonitiones, tum controversiae etiam tractantur, scriptus ab Auctore lingua Frisica, inde translatus in Belgicum, anno 1541. saepiusque impressus. Menno non in solo anabaptismo, & oppugnato paedobaptismo, uti priores, sed nec pro enthusiasmis & revelationibus quemadmodum illi, stetit, sed ulterius progressus, & dogmata alia procudit, novae sectae fundamenta. Iam disputabat de incarnatione Christi ex Maria matre; de officio & vocatione Magistratus Christiani; insuper de disciplina Ecclesiae: nam, uti alii Ecclesiae eripiunt, quae tradunt Magistratui; ita Mennonitae politica, quae Christiano Magistratui auferunt, in Ecclesiam transfundunt, & ejus disciplinam. De qua tamen, ejus forma, modo, rigore & limitibus vehementer inter ipsos disputatur, & hinc scissi in diversa studia animi, ac coetus. Iohannes Calvinus ad Micronium scripsit olim epistolam, in qua contra Mennonem prolixe disputat, super primo articulo assumtae a Christo ex Maria matre carnis & naturae humanae: atque in exordio epistolae observat vir maximus, Mennonis doctrinam e Manichaeorum deliriis haustam esse. Micronius cum Mennone disputationem habuit anno cIↄ Iↄ lii. quae edita Belgice a Micronio, anno cIↄ Iↄ lv. ejusque historiam suae narrationi, de Ecclesia Peregrinorum in Anglia, inseruit Iohannes Utenhovius. Ab anno cIↄ Iↄ
units.tr: Menno, whose mission and teaching can be judged from Obbo's Declaration, was born in 1496 in Friesland, near the town of Bolsward, in the village of Witmarsum, where after serving as a priest in the village of Pingjum he also acted as a priest. In 1536, having abandoned the Papacy, he was rebaptized by Obbo Philips and received the office of teaching with a solemn laying on of hands. He carried out this office diligently at Groningen and later in other places, strong in voice and in writing. He died in 1561. The Obbonites or Mennonites differed from the Monsterites and the Batenburgians not only in that they did not approve of their tumults and disturbances, as the Hofmannites did not either, but they differed from both chiefly in two articles: first, the future and imminent other kingdom of Christ on earth, and the wonderful restoration of the Church through a new and extraordinary mission of the Spirit, as once upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost; second, the plurality of wives and easy divorce, neither of which the Mennonites approved. Menno testified to this in many places against those who said he sided with the Monsterites, in the account of his departure from the Papacy, which he wrote in 1554. To this end too, in the year 1527 of this century, a writing of Menno, not printed earlier, was published against the horrible and enormous blasphemy of John of Leiden, who presented himself as the true King David, promising joy to all. Yet although Menno did not approve of the disturbances of the Monsterite brethren, he still acknowledged them as brothers: they had all been sent by John Matthew of Haarlem, and those who first stirred up trouble at Münster, John himself later joining them; and those who, attempting new things in Friesland, appointed Obbo Philips, Theodore Philips, Menno and others as the leaders of their sect. Speaking of the Monsterites in many places, Obbo Philips in his Confession or Retraction calls them brethren. Among other things he writes, in Dutch: "And when I still think of the seduction that happened among the brethren at Amsterdam, in the old cloister at Hazerswoude, in the Dam, on the Sand, and above all at Münster, my soul is grieved and terrified by it. I therefore reject all the false missions, prophecies, visions, dreams, revelations and inexpressible spiritual pride which broke in among the brethren from the very first hour." Menno writes similarly in the book Foundation, calling the Monsterites his beloved brethren; in the Admonition to the corrupted sects (evidently written against the Monsterites and the followers of David Joris), he writes: "I have no doubt that our beloved brethren have misused the sword against the Lord in former times, since they wanted to defend their faith by force of arms; or that they have a gracious God, etc. Yet they erred with the sword, which we ought not to follow, as we have said above, especially where they used any weapons other than patience and the Word of God. Nor is it any wonder that they stumbled in those days, since they did not yet have the test of the spirits. I call those upright and dreaming ones my sisters and brothers, since they stumbled in ignorance; but the doubters who did not seek God with pure hearts, though they were called sisters and brothers, and the princes of the destruction, as in Münster and Amsterdam, I leave to the hand of the Lord." pp. 125, 126, edition of 1616, but to the most correct copy of the year 1539. We have quoted this more word for word because it is not found in other editions; also so that it appears that we rightly traced the origin of the Mennonites and Anabaptists to those Monsterites. Menno wrote many works, among which the book Foundation is famous, like the fundamental epistle of Manichaeus. In it some moral matters and admonitions are treated, and also controversies. It was written by the author in the Frisian language, translated into Dutch in 1541, and printed many times. Menno did not stand only on Anabaptism and opposition to infant baptism, as the earlier Anabaptists did, nor did he stand on enthusiasms and revelations as they did, but went further and produced other doctrines, the foundations of a new sect. He discussed the incarnation of Christ from Mary his mother; the office and calling of a Christian magistrate; and moreover church discipline. For just as others take from the Church what they hand over to the magistrate, so the Mennonites transfer to the Church the civil matters which they take away from the Christian magistrate, along with its discipline. Yet among themselves they dispute vehemently about its form, manner, strictness and limits, and so they are divided into different opinions and assemblies. John Calvin once wrote a letter to Micronius, in which he disputes at length against Menno on the first article: the assumption of flesh and human nature by Christ from Mary his mother. At the beginning of the letter this great man observes that Menno's teaching was drawn from the ravings of the Manichaeans. Micronius held a disputation with Menno in 1552, which Micronius published in Dutch in 1555; and John Utenhove inserted its history into his narrative about the Church of the Strangers in England. From the year 1543 onwards,

units.la: xliii. Menno, & Theodorus Philippi alios iterum concionatores atque episcopos miserunt: inter quos Adamus Pastor, VVestfalia oriundus, antea dictus Rudolphus Martini, sed qui cum illis non diu fecit, atque cum Mennone aliquoties collocutus, in Arianismum tandem prolapsus est. Franciscus Cuperus, postea resipuit, ac Mennoniticas opiniones, coram Curiae Frisicae praeside Hypolito anno clo lo lxv. publice abjuravit. Adami Pastoris mentionem lego in Anabaptistarum Martyrologio, in historia Iusti Kirt, ad annum clo lo lxi. ubi hic interrogatur, a quo sit rebaptizatus, an dicunt, ab Adamo Pastore, an Davide Georgio?
units.tr: Menno and Theodorus Philippi again sent other preachers and bishops, among them Adam Pastor, a native of Westphalia, formerly called Rudolph Martini, who did not stay with them long. After several conferences with Menno, he finally lapsed into Arianism. Franciscus Cuperus later came to his senses and publicly renounced the Mennonite opinions in 1565 before Hypolitus, president of the Frisian court. I read of Adam Pastor in the Anabaptist Martyrology, in the history of Justus Kirt, under the year 1561, where Kirt is asked by whom he was rebaptized: by Adam Pastor, or by David Georgius?

units.la: Porro concionatorem Menno fecit Leonardum Bouwensen, quem praecipuum in hisce regionibus Magistrum fuisse, lego in libro M. S. Confessionum Anabaptisticarum, quod poenes me est, a Praetore & Magistratu Amstelodamensi anno clo lo lxxi. exceptarum. Ille acerrime res suas egit, & quum inter ipsos oborte fuissent quaestiones ac dissidia super excommunicatione, & de cavendis excommunicatis, an iisdem communis vitae officia obire liceret, edere, mercari, &c.? an vinculum non spirituale & ecclesiasticum solum, sed naturale & politicum excommunicatio frangeret quoque, & tolleret necessitudinem inter parentes ac filios, atque inter coniugatos? an seus, quantumvis poenitens, tamen excommunicandus esset? Leonardus, cum Theodoro Philippi, tracto etiam in consortium Mennonae, rigidiorem excommunicandi disciplinam instituerunt, & sectae ejus auctores exstiterunt, quae inde Rigidorum Excommunicatorum dicta, vel etiam Flandri, atque Mennonita Veteres: cujus doctrinae horrenda passim exempla data sunt, ablegare a marito uxoris, quia ille Reformatae religionis forte esset, vel apud ipsos excommunicatos, haec non, avulsorum a Parentibus filiorum, & similia. Quae ipsorum alii detestantes, alteram Rigidis istis adversam sectam erexerunt, postquam ab iis ob suam in disciplinâ & excommunicatione moderationem excommunicati essent, a. cIↄ Iↄ lvii. nempe Henricus Naeldeman, cum Georgio Heyns, & dicuntur Frisii, vel etiam, quia scilicet ab aliis suorum sectis excommunicatos recipiunt, neque eos rebaptizant, & laxiori vivunt disciplinâ. Barbarita, de Dezchwagen. Inde inter Frisios, atque Flandros gravis extitit semper contentio, ad quam tollendam a. cIↄ Iↄ lxvii. d. xix. Septembris, compromisit bonâ fide pars utraque in duos arbitros, consensu communi electos, Iohannem Willemsoon, & Lubbertum Gerrit-soon, cui Compromisso subscripserunt omnes. Pronunciatâ ab Arbitris sententiâ, non acquieverunt, contra ac polliciti fuerant, Flandri, quantumvis obtestarentur Arbitri, se tam probe hoc in negotio versatos fuisse, ac optarent Deum animis suis propitium. Hinc implacabiliter scissi Flandri, Frisiique, illis Iudices eorumque fidem, his perjurium suis Adversariis & ruptam pacem exprobrantibus: adeo ut quandoque nec una ire, nec ambulare, edere, vel loqui secum, etiam in suprema mortis necessitate, sustineant. Arbitri se Frisiis, judicio suo acquiescentibus, adjunxere, quorum episcopus erat Leonardus Bouwensoon, qui ut Theodorum Philippi, à quo ordinem acceperat, excommunicarat, ita ab aliis quoque excommunicatus fuit, excommunicatione apud illos fere in ludum versâ, quam, ceu pueri pilas, in quosvis promiscue torquent & repercutiunt. Anno cIↄ Iↄ cxxiv. prodiit ab ipsis scriptum, impressum Hornae, quod utriusque partis errores in contentione Flandrorum & Frisiorum ab anno cIↄ Iↄ lxvi. commissos indicat, proque Scismatis praecipuo auctore à parte Flandrorum ponit Ieronymum Timgister, & ex parte Frisiorum Hunc Renicks. Flandris praerant Hans de Weber / Jacobus vander Meulen / Petrus van Ceulen, alii, quibus, uti cum Frisiis, ita nec inter se bene convenit, quin mutuo is exàrderent erga alterum excommunicationibus. Petrus van Ceulen/ cum nonnullis aliis, antea factionis Flandricae, quia cum iis eundem sequi rigorem, & suam solam esse Christi ecclesiam, extraque eam nullam aliam asserere recusabat, excommunicatus, publicam, coram Frisiis, pristini erroris edidit confessionem anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxxix. d. xx. Iulii. Similiter ex Frisiis nonnulli, inter quos primus, Iohannes Henrici Schiedamensis, anno cIↄ Iↄ xc. suos errores in fovendo dissidio publice agnoverunt; quare pacem cum illo Petro Coloniensi acceperunt hi & coluerunt variis in locis; Sic jam alii partes facere & sequi acerrime, alii unire maluerunt: quod postremum certe multum honestius.
units.tr: Menno also made a preacher of Leonard Bouwensen, whom I read was the chief teacher in these regions in the manuscript Book of Anabaptist Confessions, which is in my possession, recorded by the praetor and magistrates of Amsterdam in 1571. He pursued his cause very fiercely. When questions and disputes arose among them about excommunication and about how to deal with the excommunicated: whether it was lawful to perform the common duties of life with them, to eat with them, to trade with them, and so on; whether excommunication broke not only the spiritual and ecclesiastical bond but also the natural and civil bond, and dissolved the kinship between parents and children and between spouses; and whether a sinner, however penitent, must still be excommunicated. Leonard, together with Theodorus Philippi, who had also drawn Menno into partnership, instituted a harsher discipline of excommunication and became the founders of a sect which was called from this the Rigid Excommunicators, or also the Flemings, and the Old Mennonites. Horrible examples of their doctrine were given everywhere: a wife was sent away by her husband because he happened to belong to the Reformed religion; or, among the excommunicated themselves, children were torn from their parents, and the like. Some of their own people, detesting these things, set up a second sect opposed to these Rigid ones, after they had been excommunicated by them for their moderation in discipline and excommunication, in 1557: namely Henry Naeldeman with George Heyns. They are called the Frisians, or also, because they receive those excluded from other sects of their own and do not rebaptize them, and live under a looser discipline, the Barbarita, or de Dezchwagen. From then on there was always a serious contention between the Frisians and the Flemings. To end it, on 19 September 1567 both parties in good faith submitted the matter to two arbiters, chosen by common consent, John Willemsoon and Lubbert Gerritsoon, and all signed the Compromise. When the arbiters pronounced their sentence, the Flemings did not abide by it, contrary to what they had promised, though the arbiters protested that they had dealt so honestly in this matter and prayed that God would be gracious to their minds. Hence the Flemings and Frisians were irreconcilably divided: the one side accused the judges and their good faith, the other charged its adversaries with perjury and with breaking the peace. So much so that at times they will not go together, walk, eat, or speak with one another, even in the extreme necessity of death. The arbiters joined the Frisians, who accepted their judgment, and whose bishop was Leonard Bouwensoon. Just as he had excommunicated Theodorus Philippi, from whom he had received his ordination, so he too was excommunicated by others, the excommunication among them having almost become a game, which they toss and bat about at random, like boys with balls. In 1624 there appeared from their hands a writing, printed at Hoorn, which points out the errors of both sides in the contention of the Flemings and Frisians from 1566 onward. It names Jerome Timgister as the chief author of the schism on the Flemish side and Hunc Renicks on the Frisian side. The Flemings were led by Hans de Weber, Jacob van der Meulen, Peter van Ceulen, and others, who, as with the Frisians, did not get on well with one another either, so that they inflamed each other with mutual excommunications. Peter van Ceulen, together with some others formerly of the Flemish faction, was excommunicated because he refused to follow the same severity with them and to assert that their own party alone was Christ's Church and that there was no other outside it. In 1589, on 20 July, before the Frisians, he published a public confession of his former error. Likewise some of the Frisians, the first of whom was John Henry of Schiedam, publicly acknowledged in 1590 that they had been wrong to foster the dissension. For this reason these men accepted peace with that Peter of Cologne and cultivated it in various places. So some have chosen to take sides and fight most fiercely, others have preferred to unite, and the latter is certainly much more honourable.

units.la: Hi tertii, priorum Schisma detestantur, & in unum aguntur, ex tractu Hollandiae Borcalis, apud nos appellati Waterlanders / vel coetus Johannis de Ries/ & coetus uniti, cepti ad annum cIↄ Iↄ lv. ab Hermanno Timmerman, qui inter Martyres Anabaptisticos ponitur, Antverpiae interemtus, anno cIↄ Iↄ lxix. cujus etiam Hermanni, in ipsorum Martyrologio, brevis legitur Confessio. Huc etiam faciunt, quae apud illos aêtata ab anno cIↄ Iↄ cxxvi. & deinceps, occasione unionis initae inter Harlingenses Anabaptistas, & Frisios, quam Groningenses damnarunt, probarunt autem alii, interque eos Amstelodamenses, quaestione facta, an Frisii Anabaptistae, ab aliis agnosci possent pro populo Dei? unde disputatum de articulis fidei fundamentalibus, de notis filiorum Dei, quo de negotio libellum scripserunt Amstelodamenses Anabaptistae Flandrici, tit. Ramuscula olivae, Oliftacksken/ probatusque à nonnullis ipsorum coetibus, anno cIↄ Iↄ cxxvii. & nuper anno cIↄ Iↄ cxlix. d. xxv. Julii, in ipsorum Synodo Harlemi habita, una cum Confessione Iohannis Sitsen, & Adriani Cornelii, ut quae proxime facerent ad pacem & concordi-amam coetum fovendam. Quis autem dissidia ipsorum, scismata, sectas, casumque causas omnes referat, vel digne prosequatur? Neque uti ipsi loquuntur Opst-tackhen pag. 60. in uno Scismate res stetit, sed post primum varia subsequuta, quae apud multos, longâ consuetudine, & ex animorum abalienatione, humanisque affectibus, diu fuota. Iam scindunt, jam uniunt, jam ob quam causam alios à se, ipsi ab aliis excommunicantur, & omne hoc cum summo acerbissimoque suorum odio & insectatione.
units.tr: These third-group people detest the schism of the former, and are gathered into one. From the district of North Holland they are known among us as the Waterlanders, or the congregation of John de Ries, and the united congregations. It began in 1555 with Hermann Timmerman, who is counted among the Anabaptist martyrs and was put to death at Antwerp in 1569; a brief Confession of this Hermann is also read in their Martyrology. To this also belongs what was debated among them from 1626 onward, on the occasion of the union entered into between the Anabaptists of Harlingen and the Frisians, which the Groningen people condemned, though others approved it, among them the Amsterdam people. The question was raised whether the Frisian Anabaptists could be recognized by others as the people of God. From this arose a discussion of the fundamental articles of faith and of the marks of the sons of God, on which matter the Flemish Anabaptists of Amsterdam wrote a little book entitled The Little Olive Branch, Oliftacksken. It was approved by some of their congregations in 1627, and recently in 1649, on 25 July, at their synod held at Haarlem, together with the Confession of John Sitsen and Adrian Cornelius, as being most conducive to keeping peace and concord among the congregations. But who could recount or properly pursue all their dissensions, schisms, sects, and the causes of each? As they themselves say in Opst-tackhen, p. 60, the matter did not stop at one schism, but after the first came various others, which among many, through long custom, from the alienation of minds and human passions, were long fostered. Now they split, now they unite; now they excommunicate others for one cause, now they are excommunicated by others, and all this with the greatest bitterness and hatred and persecution of one another.

units.la: Ad annum clo Io lxxxvi. Francekerae ob causam emtae domus ab ipsorum episcopo Thoma Beenkens, ubi alii dicebant eum fide non usque bona versatum, alii contra, Scisma Ecclesiarum aliud consequutum: unde hi appellati Huis-hopers Domus emtores; alii Contra Huis-hopers Contra emptores; quibus & tertii accessere Neutrales, qui quidem emtionem illam culpabant, sed propterea Ecclesias scindi nolebant. Scilicet digna causa scismatis in Ecclesia erigendi, sed tali Ecclesiâ, quae ejusmodi ostendit actis se haud esse veram. Et tamen ob illam etiam causam crudelem in modum excommunicarunt, hi illos triginta aliquando & quadraginta homines unâ vice. Ne de alio infami Scismate loquar Mamillariorum, Harlemi nato, ex eo qui puellae mamillas contrectasset, & causam contentionis non solum, sed & scismatis videbatur fecisse, quaestione mota, annon propterea excommunicandus esset: quod hi urgebant, nolebant alii. Qui autem olim dicti fuerint Apostolici, Separati & spirituales, Cathari, Silentes, Bachite sive Precantes, Enthusiastae etiam, Libertini, Hussitae, Augustiniani, vide apud Bullingerum adversus Anabaptistas lib. I. & II.
units.tr: In the year 1586, at Franeker, a dispute arose over a house bought from their bishop, Thomas Beenkens. Some said that he had acted without good faith, others took the opposite view, and a schism in the Church followed from this. Hence those who had bought the house were called the Huis-hopers, the buyers of the house, and their opponents the Contra-Huis-hopers, the buyers' opponents. Third parties also joined them, the Neutrals, who did indeed blame that purchase but did not want the Churches split on account of it. Certainly this was a worthy cause for setting up a schism in the Church, but only in a Church which by such acts shows that it is not the true one. Yet they excommunicated people cruelly even for that reason, sometimes thirty or forty at a time. I say nothing of another notorious schism, that of the Mammillarians, which arose at Haarlem, over a man who had touched a girl's breasts. The question was raised whether he should on that account be excommunicated. This was the cause of the quarrel, and it seemed to have produced a schism as well; one side urged excommunication, the other side refused it. As for those who were formerly called Apostolics, Separatists and Spiritual, Cathari, Silent, Bachites or Praying, also Enthusiasts, Libertines, Hussites and Augustinians, see Bullinger against the Anabaptists, books I and II.

units.la: Dogmata Anabaptistarum sunt qualia ipsi hominum genus, varia, aliaque hae inter eos sectae, diversa istae tenent. Apud nos vulgo noti sunt ex quinque articulis: oppugnati pedobaptismi, erroris primarii, & apud illos
units.tr: The doctrines of the Anabaptists are as varied as the men themselves, and the sects among them hold different views. Among us they are commonly known from five articles: the attack on infant baptism, which is their chief error, and among them the most common of all

units.la: s̈los communissimi ; defensi anabaptismi; negat Chri-sti ex Matris substantia incarnationis; interdicti ipsis omnis generis iurandi ; & officii Magistratus. Sed & alia assumunt, illis nequaquam leviora : liberi arbitrii vires in spiritualibus plus æquo communiter extollunt, negant peccatum originis alii, & justificationem gratuitam absque nostris operibus ; Trinitatem Personarum, in unâ Dei essentia, aliaque, in quibus aut Pelagianorum, aut Socinianorum prava dogmata adoptant, & sequuntur. Enthusiasmi, & anabaptistæ atque oppugnati paedobaptismi primus auctor Thomas Muncerus fuit : de incarnatione Christi ⁊ juramento, Magistratu, & disciplina Ecclesiæ inde disputatum: Christi Deitatem impugnavit inter Anabaptistas primus Ludovicus Hetzerus, & sic alii alia. Verum secundum, ob articulos de baptismo præcipuè, etiam ob non assertam Christi ex matre incarnationem, Martyres ipsorum (utrita iiscum loquamur) passos, non autem ob assertum incarnationis modum, per mutationem verbi in carnem, aut aliter; neque etiam propter alios seu Socinianorum, seu Pelagianorum errores quod ex Martyrologio ipsorum observare promptum est. Nam quum à Papistis vulgo occiderentur, tum ob improbatum nostrum Papatum, unde factum, quod nonnulli & in Nostro, & Mennonitico (ita dicimus ob præmissam ei Mennonitarum fidei confessionem) Martyrologio occurrunt; tum ob addiros de baptismo errores, aliquando etiam de juramento, & Magistratu denique & impastas iis turbas politicas, propterea trucidati fuere. Hinc protestabatur Iacobus d'Auchii anno clɔ Iɔ lv ı ı ı, palam dicitans, nihil sibi cum Monasteriensium, vel Amstelodamensium turbis esse commune. Et quod ad alios religionis articulos, qui anno clɔ lɔ lxxv. in Anglia captivi sub Elizabetha tenebantur, in supplici ad Reginam libello, nil hæretici quod ad dogmata de baptismo, juramento & magistratu admiscere. miscere se, solum, judicium vero de modo vel principio incarnationis Christi, an ex carne matris, suspendere, aeternum & convenire cum Belgicae Ecclesiae ministris ejiebant, in eo etiam quod bona cum conscientia, in re certa & probe nota Deum quidem testem invocarent. Et in Responsione ad Joh. Foxum, Scotum, ita palam loquuntur: sive vivamus, sive moriamur, salutem ponimus non in operibus nostris vel sanctitate, sed solum in Christi morte & resurrectione. Quare quemadmodum doctrinae & religionis alicujus capita discenda sunt tum ex Confessione, tum ex martyrio, unde ob quae quis pati extrema velit, liquet; ita ex Martyrologio Mennonitarum observabis, propter abjuratum Papatum vulgo, additis saepe erroribus catabaptisticis, ratius pro juramenti & Magistratus interdictione, illos mortem subiisse. Ob ista ut a Nostris aliquis occidatur: vel non factum, (aliud est, si turbatio politiae, regnorumque aut etiam dogmata blasphemia accedant) aut ut fiat, non probamus. In Anabaptismi exordio, quando cum seditionibus multis & execrandis opinionibus res ipsorum junctae, tum etiam quia in Sectae exordio semper licet severiori resistere diligentia, si forte opprimi in herba possit, acrius repressi ubivis fuere. Tiguri anno cIↄ Iↄ xxv. tum cIↄ Iↄ xxx. coërciti, quia haec secta ad Magistratuum & honestarum rerum publicarum interitum patissimam spectat: in Edicto suo loquitur Magistratus. Confer ad haec Rud. Gualtheri praefationem in Tom. II. Zuinglii.
units.tr: the most common ones; they defended anabaptism. They deny that Christ's flesh was taken from the substance of his mother in the incarnation. They forbid every kind of oath to their people, and the office of the Magistrate. But they also adopt other positions, by no means lighter than these: they commonly exalt the powers of free will in spiritual matters beyond what is right; some deny original sin; and they hold justification without our works. On the Trinity of Persons in the one essence of God, and on other points, they adopt and follow the perverse doctrines either of the Pelagians or of the Socinians. The Enthusiasts and the Anabaptists, and the first author of the opposition to infant baptism, was Thomas Münzer. Disputes arose from him about the incarnation of Christ, the oath, the magistracy and church discipline. Among the Anabaptists, Ludwig Hetzer was the first to attack the deity of Christ, and so others did other things. But the second group, chiefly because of their views on baptism, and also because they did not affirm the incarnation of Christ from his mother, suffered as martyrs (if we may speak of them in their own terms). They did not suffer for their assertion of the mode of incarnation, through a change of the Word into flesh or otherwise, nor for the other errors of the Socinians or Pelagians, as may readily be seen from their own Martyrology. For when they were commonly killed by the Papists, it was partly because of our rejection of the Papacy (which is why some of them appear in our Martyrology and in the Mennonite one, so called because of the confession of the Mennonite faith prefixed to it), and partly because of their Anabaptist errors about baptism, and sometimes also about the oath and the magistracy, and finally because of the political disturbances they stirred up; for these reasons they were slaughtered. Hence Jacob d'Auchy protested in the year 1555, openly declaring that he had nothing in common with the uprisings of the Münsterites or the Amsterdamers. And as for the other articles of religion, the prisoners held in England under Elizabeth in the year 1575 stated in their petition to the Queen that they mixed in no heresy concerning baptism, the oath or the magistracy; they only suspended judgment on the mode or origin of Christ's incarnation, whether it was from the flesh of the mother, and they declared that they agreed with the ministers of the Belgian Church, also in that they invoked God as witness with a good conscience in a matter certain and well known. And in their Answer to John Foxe, they speak openly in this way: whether we live or die, we place our salvation not in our works or holiness, but solely in the death and resurrection of Christ. Therefore, just as the heads of any doctrine or religion must be learned both from its Confession and from its martyrdom, which shows why anyone is willing to suffer the extreme penalty, so from the Mennonite Martyrology you will observe that, because of their renunciation of the Papacy, they commonly, with frequent additions of Catabaptist errors, and more rarely for the prohibition of the oath and the magistracy, underwent death. We do not approve of anyone among our people being put to death for these things; or else it was not done (it is different if disturbance of the civil order and kingdoms, or blasphemous doctrines, are involved), or, if it was done, we do not approve it. At the beginning of Anabaptism, when their affairs were joined with many seditions and detestable opinions, they were repressed everywhere more sharply, because at the start of a sect one may always resist with greater severity, in case it can perhaps be crushed in the bud. At Zurich they were restrained in the years 1525 and then 1530, because this sect aims most fatally at the ruin of magistrates and honourable commonwealths; the Magistrate speaks to this effect in its Edict. On these matters compare the preface of Rudolf Gwalther to the second volume of Zwingli.

units.la: Regno Angliae illos primum adventantes exegit Elizabetha, singulari edicto anno cIↄ Iↄ lx. Ludovicus Palatinus, anno cIↄ Iↄ xciv. in Churfurstlicher Pfalzer Landesordnung, citv. in Widertäufferischen Irrthumb halb gegebene Instruction / sua ditione exterminat. Omitto crudelia & sanguinaria Imperii Germanici in Anabaptistas edicta: Comitiorum Spirensium anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxix. Iterum, anno cIↄ Iↄ xliv, Augustanorum anno cIↄ Iↄ lr. vel Regis Philippi, in Belgio: de quo ex litteris Regis, ad Gubernatricem, anno cIↄ Iↄ lxv. d. 11. Octob. haec producit Strada, lib. iv. principio in plectendis Anabaptistis, aliisque haereticis, quorum illicunque familiarum sint, nolle quidquam aut remitti, aut differri. Quod à Papatu se segregabant, uti hactenus bene, ira causa fuit odii & persecutionum Papalium adversus illos, aeque ac alios; sed in illos quidem eo gravius, quo praeterea variis heterodoxiis, enthusiasmis & turbis omnia commovebant: quibus & magnumubique creabant Reformationi praejudicium & impedimentum. Unde Zuinglius, qui exordia sectae vidit, & ipso virili oppressit, jam illos schismaticos, jam & haereticos appellat. In epilogo Elenchi contra Catabaptistas, Tom. II. minus non est eos à nobis exivisse. In initio Responsionis, ad libellum Baltazaris Huebmer: Catabaptismum haeresim vel sectam esse neminem obscurum esse poterit, qui primam ipsius originem & institutionem consideraverit. Qui enim apud nos primi hujus authores extiterunt, à nobis flagitare solebant, ut peculiarem & nobis propriam ecclesiam eligeremus. Vbi vero id nullo modo à nobis impetrari posse intellexerunt, in agrum Tigurinum dispersi passim inter simplicem rerumque imperitam plebem inconsulto magistratu, inconsultis ecclesiis, inconsultis denique episcopis vel ecclesiarum ministris, privatim in angulis docere & rebaptizare caeperunt. Idem, Epistola ad Berchtoldum & Franciscum, Ministros Bernenses, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxvii. Tum, in Exegesi Eucharisticî negotii, ad M. Lutherum: Prodierunt enim Catabaptistae, pernitiosum genus haereticorum. Hos merito haereticos appellamus: nam multoties convicti, resipiscere tam abest ut voluerint, ut etiam secessionem fecerint, non ab impiis, Christum aut negantibus aut pontificem asserentibus, sed ab iis fratribus & ecclesiis, quae Christum sanctissime & constanter confitentur, & vitae in melius mutatione colunt: neque alia ratione, quam quod isti perhibent retingi oportere, nostri parte porrò abhorrent à Catabaptismo. Quid enim refert hic ea quoque memorare, in quibus & errant & miscere omnia tentant? Virum Christianum gerere magistratum non posse: iusiurandum non debere Christianum praestare: quo quid aliud quàm magistratus dissolvitur? &c. De iisdem, in expositione fidei Christianae, ad Galliae Regem Franciscum: Qui tametsi à nobis abhorrent quia ex nostris non e-rant; sunt tamen qui nobis omnes illorum errores imputent, vtum acriter contra eos pugnemus quàm quisquam; diversum-que, quam ipsi, in omnibus ante dictis doceamus. Ratione variorum ab illis ex veteribus haeresibus assumtorum dogmatum Melanthon etiam dixit, in suo de illis judicio, ad Fridericum Abbatem Norimbergensem: Nulla est veterum haeresium, quae non videtur his authoribus repul-sulare. Hodie etiam in Socinianismum illorum multi plus aequo propensiores. Polonos fratres appellat Petrus Iohannis Twisck, Hermanus, lib.
