Belgico, de Christi Iutro pag. 51. quamvis videri velit Confessio Mennonitarum illos detestari, et quam art. xiv. de incarnatione, Socini sententiam de Christo vero homine, expressim rejicit: sed quare non idem facit ad seq art. de Christi officio, ubi de Christi satisfactione clarius loquendum, & Socini haeresis aeque rejicienda fuerat? Socinus autem, uti contra illos disputavit aliquando, sita Monasterienses pessimos homines appellat, iisque comparari suam Racoviam aegerrimè fert. Respons. altera ad Volanum pag. 226.
units.tr: England's Elizabeth first expelled these men when they arrived in her kingdom, by a special edict in the year 1560. Ludwig, the Elector Palatine, drove them out of his territory in 1594, in the Electoral Palatine Land Ordinance, and in the instruction given against the Anabaptist errors. I pass over the cruel and bloody edicts of the German Empire against the Anabaptists: the Diet of Speyer in 1529, again in 1544, the Diet of Augsburg in 1555, or those of King Philip in the Netherlands; concerning the last, Strada, in the first book of his work, cites from the King's letter to the Governess of 11 October 1565 the statement that in punishing Anabaptists and other heretics, of whatever families they might be, the King was unwilling that anything be remitted or deferred. That they separated themselves from the Papacy, which indeed is good, was the cause of the hatred and Papal persecutions against them, as against others; but against them it was the more severe, because besides they were throwing everything into confusion with various heterodoxies, enthusiasms and disturbances, by which they created everywhere a great prejudice and hindrance to the Reformation. Hence Zwingli, who saw the beginnings of the sect and suppressed it while it was still young, called them now schismatics and now heretics. In the conclusion of his Elenchus against the Catabaptists, in the second volume: it is no less true that they have departed from us. At the beginning of his Answer to the pamphlet of Balthasar Hübmaier, he says: that Catabaptism is a heresy or sect, no one can fail to see who has considered its first origin and establishment. For those who were the first authors of this among us used to demand of us that we choose a separate church of our own. But when they understood that this could in no way be obtained from us, they scattered throughout the Zurich countryside among the simple and inexperienced common people, without consulting the magistrate, without consulting the churches, and finally without consulting the bishops or the ministers of the churches, and began to teach privately in corners and to rebaptize. The same, in his letter to Berchtold and Franz, ministers of Bern, in 1527. Then, in his Exegesis of the Eucharistic matter, to Master Luther: for the Catabaptists have arisen, a pernicious kind of heretics. We rightly call them heretics; for though they have been convicted many times, they are so far from wishing to repent that they have even seceded, not from the impious who either deny Christ or assert the Pope to be his vicar, but from those brethren and churches which confess Christ most holily and steadfastly and cultivate a change of life for the better; and for no other reason than that these men maintain that things must be rebaptized; our people, on the other hand, shrink still further from Catabaptism. For why should I here recall those points too in which they both err and try to confuse everything? That a Christian man cannot hold the magistracy; that a Christian ought not to render an oath: what else is this but the dissolving of the magistracy? etc. About the same men, in his exposition of the Christian faith to King Francis of France: Although they are abhorrent to us because they were not from among ours, yet there are those who impute all their errors to us, so that we fight against them more fiercely than anyone, and we teach things different from them in all the points said before. Concerning the various doctrines these men took from the ancient heresies, Melanchthon also said, in his judgment on them, to Frederick, Abbot of Nuremberg: There is no ancient heresy which does not seem to reverberate in these authors. Today too many of them are more inclined than is right towards Socinianism. Peter Johannis Twisck, in his Hermannus, in the Dutch book on Christ's Righteousness, p. 51, calls the Poles brethren, although the Mennonite Confession wishes to appear to detest them; in Article 14, on the incarnation, it expressly rejects the opinion of Socinus about Christ as a true man. But why does it not do the same in the following article on Christ's office, where it had to speak more clearly about Christ's satisfaction and reject the Socinian heresy equally? Socinus himself, as he once argued against them, calls the Münsterites the worst of men, and he takes it very badly that his own Racow should be compared with them. Second Answer to Volanus, p. 226.

units.la: Benignius semper iudicarunt Docti, de Adversariorum erroribus, praesertim illis qui circa juramenti usum, & officium Magistratus Omnes fere ex magna bene distinguendi imperitiâ orti videntur. Vt de juramento, & officio Magistratus unde errant? nisi ex neglectâ regulâ de abusu non tollente usum, quodque non distinguant abusum, qui in juramentis solet contingere, & magistratu, à legitimo utriusque officio & usu abutantur juramdi licentia alii, & potestate gerendi Magistratus; an ideo non bonus utriusque usus esse potest? vel vitium personæ quidquamne derogat officio? atque ex abusu gladii apud Monasterienses, & ex infando Iohannis Leidensis exemplo causam sumsisse Mennonem, in gerere disputandi adversus Magistratum Christianum, & usum gladii, legenti Mennonis adversus Iohannem Leidensem librum manifestum, præsertim ex ejus pag. 17. Sed quid hoc adversus legitimum Magistratum, quod, si quid aliud, statum illum probat potius & confirmat, ut justum & necessarium, quando Iohannes Leidensis & Monasterienses suæ non aliter repriminantur, quam legitimorum Principum gladio potuerunt? Similiter quia videre non possunt, quomodo si naturam suam ex carne matris habeat Christus, non etiam aut peccato infectus sit, aut non carnem habeat peccatricem vel minus ἀμαρτωλὸν, & distinguere nolunt naturam ab accedente ejus vitio, à quo immunis debuit esse Servator, ut illius, juxta ac nos, particeps, quod utrumque posse esse Angelus sic docuit: Sanctum quod ex te nascetur; nascetur ex te, neque minus sanctum tamen: inde (dico) quia hic bene distinguere nequiverunt, illorum error de negatâ Christi ex Mariâ incarnatione ortum habet. Atque ita in pædobaptismo hærent, quia utique vident officii nihil ab aliquo præstari extra usum rationis, ita putant absque eo nihil beneficii recipere quemquam posse: quod quantopere ab omni deviet ratione & usu nemo non videt. Hinc tamen est, quod considerantes nonnulli, mitius de illis judicent. Gravissimus autem istorum (loquimur de quinque famosis, supra nominatis) est de incarnatione Christi error: ubi tolerabilius est, si errent non positive, sed privative, id est, veram thesim non capiant, haud vero contrariam teneant, aut mutationem verbi in carnem &c. docent, quæ crassissima hæresis; sed suspendant judicium circa carnis Christi originem, cujus veritatem in dubium nec trahant, nec se trahere videant. Hodie quando illius quid definiunt, corpus Christo in Mariæ utero formatum, quamvis non ex ejus substantiâ, asserunt. Extat Petri Martyris epistola, scripta a. cIↄIↄ lxı.ad Ecclesiam Peregrinorum Londini, in quâ disputat adversus Hadrianum quendam, qui statuebat, opinionem de carne Christi cœlitus allatâ, non sumptâ ex beatâ virgine, Anabaptistis non adimere salutem, quamvis pertinaciter in-eâ hæreant, sed etiam illos in eâ professione cum ad Christum, tum ad ecclesiam pertinere. Contra eundem Hadrianum est epistola Bezæ, nomine Genevensium scripta anno cIↄIↄ lxvı. ad Ecclesiam Gallicam Emdensem, in quâ tum ministerio fungebatur: ubi inter alia ad judicium Capitonis, quod dilerte scripsis-set, quosdam inter Anabaptistas esse bonos, veros servos Dei, Christi martyres, & charissimos fratres nostros; ita respondet Beza: Denique quum innumerabilia pene sint Anabaptistarum dogmata; & quidem inter se dissidentia, quorum alia alii probent, quædam prorsus intolerabilia, quædam stulta & inepta potius quàm perversa, & quidam etiam illarum sint commiseratione digniores quam supplicio, quis Capitonem miretur illos distinxisse? Zuinglium confer, lib. 11. epist. Zuinglii & Oecolampadii, pag. 78. Ad sententiam Hadriani illius facit libellus, vernaculâ linguâ impressus Amsteldami, anno hujus sæculi vigesimo quinto, Breve examen an ad salutem necessarium sit, credere Iesum Christum carnem suam habere à verbo, & non ex Maria? Etiam Erasmus, Anabaptistas commiseratione dignos ajebat, ut qui magnam partem errore potius, quam malitia peccarent. In ipsorum Martyrologio, ex quo judicandos eos, eorumque sectam esse, nullus inficiabitur, neminem occurrere scimus, qui passus fuerit pro errore, hoc in articulo, positivo, sed negativo quidem, dum judicium circa hanc rem suspendit, neque explicat unde carnem Christus suam habeat. Ex libello, quem Nordlingenses Pastores ftores, in initio Reformationis inscripserunt. Reformatio Ecclesiae Nordlingensis, haec ad annum CIↃ Iↄ xxv. in suis Annalibus profert Abrahamus Sculterus: tinginus pueros, tinginus provectioris aetatis, non arcemus ab Ecclesia qui pueros ad tingendum non offerunt, sed manuum impositione et deprecatione Ecclesiae Christo mediatori et servatori nostro commendant. Nullam aetatem praecepit baptismo Christus, sed neque nullam vetuit. Quod judicium neque examino impraesentiarum, neque probo, prudentiae Ecclesiasticae relinquens, quid consultum et ad aedificationem aliorum faciendum sit, vel minus. Vide Philippi Melanthonis Consilium, Tom. II. pag. 166. de baptismo infantium, & an recipiendi sint Anabaptistae; ubi inter alia inquit: Scio plerosque Anabaptistas tollere peccatum originis, & pariter polliceri salutem Judaicis, Turcicis, & baptizatis infantibus, &c. Haec deliria non sunt toleranda. Et de his rebus doctrinam claram tradi oportet in Ecclesia. Et si velis recipere infirmos Anabaptistas, certe adversari huic doctrinae non debebas. Si adversantur, ipsi se sejungunt, cum profecto non satis causae habeant. in fine: Ceteras cavillationes omitte. Non vellem confirmari Anabaptistas. Ideo prudentia opus est, in his vel sanandis, vel reprimendis. Et si fuerit se intelligent, sicut pertinaciores, & plures amplectentur ea deliria. Scribit item Sculterus, ad annum CIↃ Iↄ xxvIII. Fratres unitatis in Bohemia, aliosque tum temporis pios, rebaptizatos fuisse; non quod Anabaptistarum erroribus patrocinarentur, sed quod non viderent, quomodo se aliter a mundo immundo segregarent. Sed & Anabaptistae non tuentur rebaptismum, quasi baptismum secundum, sed quod priorem existimant illegitimum fuisse, ex sua sententia, & nullum. Sic exserte in ipsorum Martyrologio Petrus V Vitses, caementarius, ad annum CIↃ Iↄ IIII. interrogatus, numquid esset rebaptizatus? respondit, se anabaptismum ignorare, ut qui semel tantum esset essel baptizatus, idque, uti rebatur, juxta doctrinam Dei.
units.tr: Learned men have always judged the errors of our opponents more leniently, especially those concerning the use of oaths and the office of the magistrate, and nearly all of these seem to arise from a great lack of skill in drawing distinctions. Where do they go wrong about the oath and the magistrate, if not from neglecting the rule that abuse does not abolish use, and from failing to distinguish abuse, which commonly occurs in oaths, from the lawful use and office of each? Some abuse the licence of swearing, and others abuse the power of exercising the magistracy. Does it follow that there can be no good use of either? Or does the fault of a person detract anything from the office itself? That Menno took his cause, in writing against the Christian magistrate and the use of the sword, from the abuse of the sword among the Münsterites and from the unspeakable example of John of Leiden, is clear from reading Menno's book against John of Leiden, especially at p. 17. But what does this prove against the lawful magistrate? If it proves anything, it rather proves and confirms that office as just and necessary, since John of Leiden and the Münsterites could not be restrained in any other way than by the sword of lawful princes. Similarly, because they cannot see how, if Christ has his nature from his mother's flesh, he would not also be infected by sin, or would not have a sinful [ἀμαρτωλὸν] flesh, and they are unwilling to distinguish the nature from the vice that attaches to it, from which the Saviour ought to have been free, though he shared in the nature as we do, the angel taught both points in these words: The holy thing that shall be born of you; it shall be born of you, and yet no less holy. Hence (I say) because they could not distinguish well here, their error in denying Christ's incarnation from Mary has its origin. And so they cling to infant baptism. They see that nothing of duty is performed by anyone outside the use of reason, and so they think no one can receive any benefit without it. How far this departs from all reason and practice, no one fails to see. Some who consider this judge them more gently. The gravest of these errors (I am speaking of the five notorious men named above) is the error about Christ's incarnation. There it is more tolerable if they err not positively but privatively, that is, if they do not grasp the true thesis, though they do not hold the contrary. But they teach a change of the Word into flesh, and so on, which is a very gross heresy. Rather, they suspend judgment about the origin of Christ's flesh, and they neither call its truth into doubt nor seem to do so. Today, when they do define something about it, they assert that the body was formed in Mary's womb for Christ, although not from her substance. There is a letter of Peter Martyr, written in 1561 to the congregation of foreigners at London, in which he disputes against a certain Hadrian, who held that the opinion that Christ's flesh was brought from heaven and not taken from the blessed Virgin does not take away salvation from the Anabaptists, although they cling to it obstinately, and that they also belong to Christ and to the Church in that profession. Against the same Hadrian there is a letter of Beza, written in 1566 in the name of the Genevans to the French church at Emden, where he then served as minister. In it, among other things, he answers the judgment of Capito, who had expressly written that some among the Anabaptists are good, true servants of God, martyrs of Christ, and our most dear brothers, as follows: Finally, since the dogmas of the Anabaptists are almost innumerable, and indeed mutually discordant, some of them approved by some and others by others, some utterly intolerable, some foolish and silly rather than perverse, and some of them more deserving of pity than of punishment, who would wonder that Capito distinguished them? Compare Zwingli, book 11 of the letters of Zwingli and Oecolampadius, p. 78. A little book printed in the vernacular at Amsterdam in the twenty-fifth year of this century belongs to Hadrian's opinion: A brief examination whether it is necessary to salvation to believe that Jesus Christ has his flesh from the Word, and not from Mary? Erasmus too said the Anabaptists were worthy of pity, as those who sinned in large part through error rather than malice. In their own Martyrology, by which no one will deny that they and their sect are to be judged, we know of no one who suffered for an error on this article that was positive; the error was negative, in that he suspended judgment on this matter and did not explain whence Christ has his flesh. From the little book which the pastors of Nördlingen entitled Reformation of the Church of Nördlingen at the beginning of the Reformation, Abraham Sculteus, in his Annals under the year 1525, brings forward these words: We baptize children, we baptize those of riper age; we do not exclude from the Church those who do not offer their children for baptism, but commend them to Christ our mediator and saviour by the laying on of hands and by the prayer of the Church. Christ prescribed no age for baptism, but neither did he forbid any. I neither examine this judgment at present nor approve it, leaving to ecclesiastical prudence what is advisable and what is to be done, or not done, for the edification of others. See Philip Melanchthon's Consilium, vol. II, p. 166, on the baptism of infants and whether Anabaptists are to be received, where among other things he says: I know that most Anabaptists deny original sin, and likewise promise salvation to Jews, Turks, and baptized infants, etc. These delusions are not to be tolerated. And clear doctrine on these matters ought to be taught in the Church. And if you wish to receive weak Anabaptists, certainly you ought not to oppose this doctrine. If they oppose it, they separate themselves, since they certainly have no sufficient cause. At the end he adds: Omit the other cavils. I would not wish the Anabaptists to be confirmed. Therefore prudence is needed, both in healing them and in restraining them. And if they understand..., the more obstinate and more numerous will embrace those delusions. Sculteus likewise writes, under the year 1528, that the Brethren of the Unity in Bohemia and other pious men of that time were rebaptized. This was not because they defended the errors of the Anabaptists, but because they did not see how otherwise they could separate themselves from the unclean world. But the Anabaptists do not defend rebaptism as a second baptism. They hold that the former baptism was illegitimate, by their opinion, and therefore null. Thus expressly in their own Martyrology: Peter V. Vitses, a mason, when asked in the year 1534 whether he had been rebaptized, replied that he did not know anything of Anabaptism, since he had been baptized only once, and that, as he thought, according to the doctrine of God.

units.la: Anabaptistarum dogmata tripliciter distingui debent. I. in Communia, quae omnes habent, qualia de catabaptismo, contra Christi incarnationem, juramentum &c. II. Singularia, id est, singulis Sectis propria, ob quae inter se dividuntur, & mutuum sibi dicunt anathema. Qualia de excommunicatione inter ipsos, & vitandis excommunicatis, Scismata Flandrorum, & Frisiorum &c. de matrimonio extraneo, sive cum hominibus non suae sectae, deque illis excommunicandis, neque vel si poenitentiam agant recipiendis, nisi adducta persona extranea ad suum quoque coetum, aut demortua. Vel quae olim tenuerunt, sive de bonorum communione Hutteriani, aut Huttiae in Moravia; de non exercendo mercatura, aut cauponaria, alii: de cultu divino non instituendo in templis olim Papisticis, aut idololatricis &c. Eodem pertinet quod illorum nonnulli Agapas observant: de quo Honorius Reggius, id est, vir clariss. Georgius Hornius, de Statu Eccles. in Anglia, pag. 100. quod alii de podonipsia, quasi ad exemplum Salvatoris scilicet Ioh. XIII. cujus praecipuus apud Anabaptistas patronus initio fuit Matthaeus Servatius, unde secta Podoniptarum: dicebantur etiam Apostolici, de quibus Bullingerus, lib. I. adversus Anabapt. cap. IX. Atque illam inter praecepta Christianis observanda, una cum osculo pacis, ponit Consessio Menonitarum, art. XXIII. & quidem non aliter quam si Sacramentum esset, quo erudiamur, ita Christum animas nostras suo sanguine abluisse ab omni peccatorum macula & sordibus. Quare Theodorus Philippi in Enchiridio, inter Notas Ecclesiae illud constituit: & Nicolaus Nicolai, in Confess. ad art. XV. praeceptum & institutionem Christi ait nobis observandam. Dilutum vero est, quod illud absolvit a Sacramento, quum juxta datam ab ipso distinctionem, non hic solum (juxta ipsos) observetur Christi præceptum, sed & spiritualis gratiæ seu nostræ ablutionis per Christi sanguinem significatio intercedat, & quod Apostolus in celebratione Cœnæ præscribit, commemoratio mortis & passionis Christi, quod absque ejus applicatione non fit. Confer Bellarminum, lib. 11. de effectu sacram. cap. xxiv. hâc de re disputantem. Similiter in libello benotico Olijf-tackskken / i. e. Ramus olivæ (conscripto à cœtu Anabaptistarum Flandrorum Amstelodamensium, anno hujus sæculi quadragesimo septimo, approbatoque in Synodo ipsorum Harlemensi sess. 11. anno cIↄ Iↄ c xl ix.) pag. 34. podonipsia ad exemplum, & tanquam ex præcepto Christi commendatur. Adeo omnes, saltem plurimi podoniptæ. Frustra vero hic exemplum Christi, aliaque ex utroque Testamento allegantur, apud quos, utpote locorum & personarum hoc ferente ratione, podonipsia crebro in usu: & non eo exemplum Christi facit, ut istam actionis speciem commendet, nedum in formam alicuius sacramenti, sed in genere officium mutuæ observantiæ docuit, quibusvis actibus usitatis exprimendum. Nisi velimus Cœnam illam in Romanâ Ecclesiâ die Iovis Sancto (uti loquuntur) ante Pascha adhiberi solitam, ubi Prælati, vel etiam Reges & Principes aliorum & pauperum ac subditorum pedes lavant, comprobare. Lege ad hoc argumentum, si placet, Gretserum de Pedilavio. In Pontificali Romano, officium quintæ feriæ in Cœnâ Domini explicatur, ut primo laventur pedes pauperum, hoc modo: Primum itaque circa horam tertiam Pontifex paratus, si velit, amictu, albo, & stola, sine mitra & baculo pastorali egreditur sacristiam cum canonicis & toto clero, & intrat capitulum, ubi parati sunt xiii. pauperes. Quibus sedentibus, ipse flexis genibus lavas pedes & tergit & osculatur. Deinde osculata cuilibet manum, das ei eleemosynam arbitrio suo &c. Adde Scriptores Liturgicos, ad Feriam quintam hebdomadæ majoris. Antiquit. Liturgic. Tom. II. pag. 914.
units.tr: The dogmas of the Anabaptists must be distinguished in three ways. I. Into common ones, which all hold, such as those about rebaptism, against Christ's incarnation, the oath, and so on. II. Particular ones, that is, those peculiar to each sect, on account of which they divide among themselves and pronounce anathema on one another. Such are the dogmas about excommunication among themselves and the shunning of the excommunicated, the schisms of the Flemings and Frisians, and so on; about marriage with outsiders, that is, with persons not of their own sect, and about excommunicating such persons and not receiving them even if they repent, unless the outsider has been brought over to their own assembly too, or has died; or what some once held, such as the communion of goods among the Hutterites, or of the Hutterites in Moravia; about not practising trade or innkeeping, according to others; about not instituting divine worship in temples, which were formerly Papist or idolatrous, and so on. To this belongs what some of them observe, the agapae, concerning which Honorius Reggius, that is, the most distinguished man Georgius Hornius, writes in On the State of the Church in England, p. 100. Others hold to podonipsia, the washing of feet, as if after the example of the Saviour, John 13, whose chief patron among the Anabaptists at first was Matthaeus Servatius, whence the sect of the Podonipti. They were also called Apostolics, of whom Bullinger writes in book I against the Anabaptists, chapter IX. The Confession of the Mennonites, art. XXIII, places this among the precepts Christians are to observe, together with the kiss of peace, and indeed not otherwise than as if it were a sacrament by which we are taught that Christ washed our souls with his blood from every stain and filth of sin. Hence Theodore Philippi in the Enchiridion placed it among the marks of the Church, and Nicholas Nicolai, in the Confession on art. XV, says it is a precept and institution of Christ for us to observe. It is refuted indeed that this frees it from being a sacrament, since according to the distinction given by Christ, not only (according to them) is Christ's precept observed here, but the signification of spiritual grace, or of our cleansing through Christ's blood, also intervenes; and what the Apostle prescribes in the celebration of the Supper, the commemoration of Christ's death and passion, is not done without its application. Compare Bellarmine, book II on the effect of the sacraments, chapter xxiv, disputing on this matter. Similarly, in the notable little book Olijf-tackskken, i.e. Ramus olivae (written by the assembly of Flemish Anabaptists at Amsterdam in the year 1647, and approved in their Synod at Haarlem, session 11, in the year 1649), p. 34, podonipsia is commended as after the example of Christ and as if from his precept. So all, or at least very many, of the podonipti hold it. But the example of Christ and other passages from both Testaments are alleged here in vain, for among them, since place and persons bear it, podonipsia is frequent in use. Nor does the example of Christ go so far as to commend this kind of action, much less as the form of some sacrament; rather, in general, he taught the duty of mutual observance, to be expressed by any ordinary acts. Unless we wish to approve that supper which the Roman Church customarily holds on Maundy Thursday (as they call it), before Easter, where prelates, or even kings and princes, wash the feet of others, namely the poor and their subjects. If you like, read Gretser de Pedilavio on this subject. In the Roman Pontifical the office of Maundy Thursday at the Lord's Supper is explained, namely that first the feet of the poor are washed, in this way: So first, about the third hour, the Pontiff, if he wishes, dressed in amice, alb, and stole, without mitre and pastoral staff, goes out of the sacristy with the canons and the whole clergy and enters the chapter house, where thirteen poor men are ready. When they are seated, he himself, kneeling, washes their feet, dries them, and kisses them. Then, having kissed each one's hand, he gives him alms at his discretion, etc. Add the liturgical writers on the Thursday of Holy Week: Antiquitates Liturgicae, vol. II, p. 914.

units.la: Sed ad Anabaptistas, die Tauffer appellat Ostorodus, in suis institutionibus Socinianis. III. Uti alia sunt dogmata Cœtuum, alia Doctorum, ita à Communibus illorum, & Singularibus Cœtuum dogmatis secernenda sunt propria Doctorum, eaque valde pernitiosa. Qualia, quæ Iacobus Outerman anno cIↄ Iↄ c v. Harlemi docuit, de tribus in Deo essentiis divinis; & essentiæ Patris in cœlo circumscriptione, quod V Veke VValles, in districtu Groningano anno cIↄ Iↄ c xxxv II. de probitate & salute Iudæ proditoris, qui tradendo Christum non peccarit, uti nec sacerdotes & scribæ, juxta suam sententiam; & quod ambo latrones, una cum Christo crucifixi, æque fuerint salvati: quas opiniones tantâ urgebat cum vehementiâ, ut dissentientes, pro satis levi apud ipsos excommunicationis vi & pretio, excommunicaret, tamquam in Spiritum S. blasphemos. In quem proinde Magistratus animad vertere necesse habuit: &, ut ad exemplum Groningensium, rotâ Frisiâ expellerentur alii, instituit Synodus Franekerana a. cIↄ Iↄ c xl iv. Illiusque commatis inter veteres hæreticos nonnulli collocati, qui factum Iudæ aut excusarunt, aut probarunt, propter sequutam nempe (sed non ex facto Iudæ per se) redemtionem: de quibus Philastrius, hær. v I. Epiphanius, hæref. xxxv II. I. Adde Alphonsum de Castro, adv. hæref. lib. VIII. Iudas.
units.tr: But as for the Anabaptists, whom Ostorodt calls the Tauffer in his Socinian Institutions. III. Just as some doctrines belong to congregations and others to individual teachers, so the peculiar doctrines of teachers must be separated from the common doctrines of the congregations and from the particular doctrines of individual congregations. These teachers' doctrines are very pernicious. Such are those which Jacob Outerman taught at Haarlem in 1605 about three divine essences in God, and about the circumscription of the Father's essence in heaven; and those which Veke Walles taught in the district of Groningen in 1637 about the probity and salvation of Judas the traitor, who, by betraying Christ, did not sin, nor did the priests and scribes, according to his view; and that both thieves crucified with Christ were equally saved. He pressed these opinions with such vehemence that he excommunicated those who dissented, using a power of excommunication which they thought rather slight, and he branded them as blasphemers against the Holy Spirit. The magistrate therefore had to take action against him, and, following the example of the Groningers, the Synod of Franeker in 1644 ordered that others be expelled from Friesland. Some of the ancient heretics were placed in this category, namely those who either excused or approved Judas's deed on account of the redemption that followed (though not from the deed of Judas in itself): on these see Philastrius, heresy 61, and Epiphanius, heresy 37.1. Add Alphonsus de Castro, Against the Heresies, book 8, under "Judas".

units.la: Lepidum est, quod inter Doctores Anabaptisticos Franciscus de Knuyt Confessionem & libellos suos hac notâ in fronte præmuniit, Onder verbeteringhe / quod est, salvo meliori judicio, vel sententia: cui Vdemannus responsum oppositit concinno titulo; Noodige verbeteringe / melius judicium. Sed in eo tamen Franciscus egit omnino ex præscripto Remonstrantium, & certe observantius, quam ipsi. Sic enim scribunt in Apologia, pag. 6. Vtiin necessariis & quae super juris sunt, nimis parum est si dicatur, Nos hoc credimus verum esse: Asseverantius loquendum est, Hoc credendum est: Anathema qui id non credit: Ita in iis, quae controversi juris sunt, nimium dicitur, si dicatur, Hoc credendum constanter firmiterque est. Contractius & retinentius loquendum est, Nos expensis omnibus sic credimus, sic statuimus sine cujusquam praejudicio.
units.tr: It is a witty thing that among the Anabaptist teachers Franciscus de Knuyt prefaced his Confession and his booklets with this note on the title page, Onder verbeteringhe, which means "subject to better judgement or opinion". Vdemannus answered him under the neat title Noodige verbeteringe / melius judicium. Yet in this Franciscus acted entirely according to the rule of the Remonstrants, and certainly more carefully than they did themselves. For they write thus in their Apology, page 6: In necessary matters, and those which concern law, it is too little to say, "We believe this to be true". One must speak more assertively: "This must be believed; anathema to whoever does not believe it." So in matters of contested law, it is too much to say, "This must be held firmly and constantly". One must speak more restrainedly: "We, all things considered, so believe and so decide, without prejudice to anyone."

units.la: Postremo disputiciamus, quid facto opus videatur cum Anabaptistis, ad illos vel coercendos, vel convincendos. Pro coercendis aut noviter pullulantibus, aut sua pomaria extendentibus, juxta cum Politicis etiam Ecclesiae est vigilare, praecipue locis illis ubi frequentiores sunt & ab iis plus periculi vel contagii metuitur. Hinc in Frisia edictum adversus illos & eorum Episcopos promulgatum anno cIↄ Iↄ xcvııı. Groningae, anno cIↄ Iↄ c ı.d. vıı. Septemb. proque illo exequendo & renovando institere aliquoties Synodi, praesertim adversus novos Adversariorum coetus, vel loca cultus alia quae extruant, potissimum ubi sua agunt omnia extra consensum Magistratus. Synodus Leovardiensis, anno cIↄ Iↄ xcvııı. art. vı. Bolswardiana, anno cIↄ Iↄ c ı. art. vı. Franekerensis, cIↄ Iↄ c ıı. art. vııı. Doccumana, anno cIↄ Iↄ c ıv. art. xxv. Leovardiensis, anno cIↄ Iↄ c v. art. x. Bolswardiana, anno cIↄ Iↄ c vıı ı. art. ııı. Harlingensis, a. cIↄ Iↄ c x. art. vıı. Snecana, a. cIↄ Iↄ c xıv. art. xıı. Bolswardiana. cIↄ Iↄ c xxıx. Franekerana, a. cIↄ Iↄ c xlıv. aliae. Et quia ex Anabaptistarum Synodo Harlemensi, anno cIↄ Iↄ c xlıx. d. xxv. Iulii, sess. ııı. patuit, quomodo locis istis, in quibus hactenus nulli coetus Anabaptistici fuerunt, aut nulli ipsorum Concionatores, quales recensentur, Daventria, Harderovicum, Arnhemum, Neomagum, Horna, Vesopium, Raropum, Huisdunum, V Vieringae, Delfi, Haga, Schoonhovia, Boscopum, Maeslantsluysa, Haserswouw, Cartovicum maritimum, Vlissingen, Amsterdam, Grootbroek, Rivia, Ruremunda, Rivia, Ruremunda. na, Gorchomum, Buren, Bommel, Maarseveen, & tio Briclana, Ziricæum, jubeant per proximos Coetus & Concionatores provideri: ita & nostrum est obviam ire, qua potest fieri diligentia & prudentia, novis ejusmodi eruptionibus: atque huc pertinet decretum nuperum Illustriss. D. D. Ordinum, in magno Consessu a. cIↄ Iↄ c li. factum, art. i i i. quo statuunt, sectas cohibendas atque in ordinem redigendas, neque permittendum ut in plura loca, quam hodie sint, diffundantur. Quod in causa Anabaptistarum exserte posuit, & ne fieret, censuit Synodus Franekerana, cIↄ Iↄ c i i. Harlingensis, a. cIↄ Iↄ c x. & Franeker. cIↄ Iↄ c xl iv. Edamensis, a. cIↄ Iↄ c xxv, art. xxx i i. Praeterea quo vergat, quod illi incipiunt quoque Synodos cogere, & de anno in annum indicere, ad exemplum nostrarum, ut in ipsorum Harlemensi factum, ubi ex omnibus provinciis & coetibus coierunt ex Hollandia Australi, Selandia, Noorthollandia, Ultrajectina, Flandria, Transisulania varii, & Synodus in sequentem annum Amsterdamum conscripta, omnibus perpendendum. In eo supra modum felices, quod ne quidem rogato Superiorum consensu, suo arbitrio & indicant, & agant Synodos, prout ipsis visum.
units.tr: Finally, let us consider what seems to be needed with the Anabaptists, either to restrain them or to convince them. To restrain those who are newly springing up, or who are extending their orchards, the Church must, together with the civil authorities, keep watch, especially in those places where they are more numerous and where more danger or contagion is feared from them. Hence an edict against them and their bishops was issued in Friesland in 1598, and at Groningen on 7 September 1601, and for carrying out and renewing it, synods have repeatedly insisted, especially against the new congregations of our opponents, or against other places of worship which they build, above all where they do everything outside the consent of the magistrate. The Synod of Leeuwarden in 1598, art. 6; the Synod of Bolsward in 1601, art. 6; the Synod of Franeker in 1602, art. 8; the Synod of Dokkum in 1604, art. 25; the Synod of Leeuwarden in 1605, art. 10; the Synod of Bolsward in 1607, art. 3; the Synod of Harlingen in 1610, art. 7; the Synod of Sneek in 1614, art. 12; the Synod of Bolsward in 1629; the Synod of Franeker in 1644; and others. And since it became clear from the Anabaptist Synod of Haarlem, on 25 July 1649, session 3, how in those places where hitherto there have been no Anabaptist congregations, or none of their preachers, the following are listed: Deventer, Harderwijk, Arnhem, Nijmegen, Horn, Wesep, Raerop, Huizen, Vlieland?, Delft, The Hague, Schoonhoven, Bosch, Maassluis, Hasselt?, Cadzand?, Vlissingen, Amsterdam, Groot-Broek, Rijswijk?, Roermond, Gorinchem, Buren, Bommel, Maarseveen, Brielle, and Zierikzee, they order that provision be made through the nearest congregations and preachers. So it is also our duty to meet such new outbreaks with all the diligence and prudence that can be used. To this belongs the recent decree of the Most Illustrious Lords the States, made in the great Assembly in 1651, art. 3, by which they resolve that sects are to be restrained and brought into order, and that they must not be allowed to spread into more places than they now occupy. This they expressly laid down in the case of the Anabaptists, and the Synods of Franeker in 1602, of Harlingen in 1610, and of Franeker in 1644, and of Edam in 1625, art. 32, decided that it should not happen. Moreover, it points in the same direction that they too have begun to hold synods and to call them year by year, after the pattern of ours, as was done at their Haarlem synod, where various delegates came from all the provinces and congregations: from South Holland, Zeeland, North Holland, Utrecht, Flanders and Overijssel. The synod was appointed to meet the following year in Amsterdam, and this deserves everyone's consideration. They are beyond measure fortunate in this, that they call and hold synods by their own judgement, as seems good to them, not even asking the consent of their superiors.

units.la: Caeterum singularia aliqua haec secta habet: in politiam incurrentia, ob quae adversus eam Politicis diligentius vigilandum: praeter turbas isti connatas, dogmata in pacem & ordinem Reip. peccantia, de excommunicatione & excommunicatorum, quantumvis conjugatorum, mutua fuga, quae domesticam aeque & politicam tranquillitatem infestant. Quare hoc argumentum saepius D. D. Ordinibus exposuerunt Ecclesiae. Synodus Amstelodamensis, a. cIↄ Iↄ xcv. qu. vi i. Hornana, a. cIↄ Iↄ xcv i. art. xv. Emdana, cIↄ Iↄ c i i i. art. xv. Adde Alcmarianam, cIↄ Iↄ c v. art. v i i. Similiter matrimonia illorum clandestina, Synodus Harlemensis, cIↄ Iↄ c. art. xv. Hornana, a. cIↄ Iↄ c xl i. art. xxxv. Enchusana, a. a.MDCXLII. art. XXXV. Edamensis, a.MDCXLIII. art. XXXI, Alcmariana, MDCXLIV. art. XXIX. & XXXIII. Amstelda-mensis, MDCXLVI. art. XXV. Scripsit olim Joh. Schwebelius, Bipontinus Theologus, epist. ad Philippum Melanthonem, a.MDXXX. Meminisse in Conventu Spirensi hortari D. Iacobum Sturmium, ne Anabaptistas in urbem vestram reciperetis, futuros aliquando permolestos hospites: vides in eo genere cum summa infscitia coniunctam incredibilem quandam ἀνοδίαν[?], & opiniones habent nimium aptas civitatibus, de Bonorum communione, & similes fanaticas persuasiones, mihi perinde obsessi videntur, ut olim, qui subito ἐνθουσιασταί[?] quadam rapiebantur ad quaerendas Divorum statuas. Praeterea quia doctrina Anabaptistarum quorundam hodie multam partem inclinat ad Socinianismum, quem Edicta politica dudum regionibus nostris exterminarunt, operae pretium est qua politice, qua Ecclesiastice providere, ne sub illorum nominibus latenter Socinianismus irrepat, quin potius patroni illorum ad hoc tenendi, ut fide jubeant de non intromittenda per se vel directe, vel indirecte exitiosissima haeresi. Certe fere est, uti alias dixi, Anabaptista indoctus Socinianus; Socinianus autem, doctus Anabaptista.
units.tr: Moreover, this sect has some particular features which touch upon the polity, on account of which the civil authorities must watch more carefully against it. Besides the disturbances innate to it, it has doctrines that offend against the peace and order of the commonwealth: concerning excommunication, and the mutual flight of the excommunicated, even when married, which disturb domestic and civil tranquillity alike. For this reason the Churches have often laid this matter before the Most Illustrious Lords: the Synod of Amsterdam in 1595, question 6; the Synod of Horn in 1596, art. 15; the Synod of Emden in 1603, art. 15. Add the Synod of Alkmaar in 1605, art. 7. Likewise, concerning their clandestine marriages: the Synod of Haarlem in 1600, art. 15; the Synod of Horn in 1641, art. 35; the Synod of Enkhuizen in 1642, art. 35; the Synod of Edam in 1643, art. 31; the Synod of Alkmaar in 1644, art. 29 and 33; the Synod of Amsterdam in 1646, art. 25. Johannes Schwebel, a theologian of Zweibrücken, once wrote in a letter to Philip Melanchthon in 1530: I recall that at the Diet of Speyer Jacob Sturm urged that you should not admit the Anabaptists into your city, since they would one day prove very troublesome guests. You see that along with this kind of people there goes an incredible sort of aimlessness [ἀνοδίαν], together with the greatest ignorance; and they hold opinions very suited to the overthrow of cities, such as the common possession of goods, and similar fanatical notions. They seem to me to be as possessed as those who once were suddenly carried away by a kind of frenzy to seek out the statues of the gods, the enthusiasts [ἐνθουσιασταί]. Furthermore, since the doctrine of some Anabaptists today largely inclines towards Socinianism, which the political edicts long ago drove out of our lands, it is worth providing, both by civil and by ecclesiastical means, that Socinianism does not creep in secretly under their names. Rather, their patrons should be made to promise, in good faith, that they will not admit, by themselves or directly or indirectly, a most destructive heresy. Certainly, as I have said elsewhere, an unlearned Anabaptist is nearly always a Socinian, and a learned Socinian is an Anabaptist.

units.la: Quod ad illos convincendos, agendum instandumque disputationibus, & Colloquiis. Quem in finem crebrae iiscum a primis temporibus institutae a Nostris, Zuinglio praesertim, Oecolampadio, Vrb. Regio, Ioach. Vadiano, Mart. Micronio &c. Collationes, & Congressus. Tiguri anno MDXXV. Et quidem isto anno ter, primum d. XVII. Ianuarii; iterum, d. XX. Martii: demum d. VI. Novembris, per triduum integrum, ac postea pluries; ut Zuinglius scripserit, in epist. ad Eslingenses, anno MDXXVI. Doctrina ipsorum septies publicis & liberis colloquiis confutata est. Basileae, ab Oecolampadio, anno MDXXVII. Eodem anno Augustae, ab Vrbano Regio, & aliis. Bernae, anno MDXX
units.tr: As for convincing them, one must press on with disputations and colloquies. To this end, from the earliest times our people, especially Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Urbanus Rhegius, Joachim Vadianus, Martin Micron and others, held frequent conferences and meetings. At Zurich in 1525, and indeed that year three times: first on 17 January, again on 20 March, and finally on 6 November, for three full days, and afterwards many times. As Zwingli wrote in his letter to the people of Esslingen in 1526: Their doctrine has been refuted seven times in public and open colloquies. At Basel, by Oecolampadius, in 1527. In the same year at Augsburg, by Urbanus Rhegius and others. At Berne, in 1528. Again at Basel in 1529, and at Berne in 1531 another disputation was held with them. At Zofingen, in the territory of Berne, in 1532. In the same year at Strasbourg, with Melchior Hofmann. At Geneva, suppressed by Calvin, in 1537.

units.la: xxviii. Iterum Basileae, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxix, Bernae altera cum illis habita disputatio, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxx i. Zofingae, in ditione Bernensi, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxii. Eodem anno Argentinae, cum Melch. Hofmanno. Genevae, à Calvino repressi, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxvii. Georgius Cassander bis cum illis coram disputavit, de quo inter ejus opera fol. 1227. Semel cum Iohanne Kremer a. cIↄ IↄIv iii. captivo in Comitatu Marchiae. Iterum a. cIↄ Iↄ lv i. cum Matthiâ aliquo, Coloniae. Sequuta Protocolla celebria, Francothalense, anno cIↄ Iↄ lxx i. Emdanum, anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxix. Leovardiense, anno cIↄ Iↄ xcviii. quorum posteriorum etiam meminit in Annalibus suis celebris noster historicus, Petrus Borr, lib. xiii. & lib. xxxiii. Et Ecclesiae nostrae semper bonum ac utile censuerunt, Adversarios ad disputationem & Colloquia provocare. Synodus Hornana, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxx & a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxv i. implorata eum in finem Gubernatoris Theod. Sonnoyi auctoritate. Enchusana, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxviii. art. iv. Alcmariana, cIↄ Iↄ xc iii. art. xi. Edamensis, cIↄ Iↄ xcviii. decernit provocandum in disputationem Hans de Ries.
units.tr: 28. Again at Basel in 1529, and a second disputation with them was held at Bern in 1530. At Zofingen, in the territory of Bern, in 1532. In the same year at Strasbourg, with Melchior Hofmann. At Geneva, they were suppressed by Calvin in 1537. Georgius Cassander debated with them twice in person, as recorded among his works, folio 1227. Once with Johannes Kremer, a prisoner, in the county of the Mark, in 1543. Again in 1551 with a certain Matthias, at Cologne. Then followed the famous protocols: at Franeker in 1571, at Emden in 1579, and at Leeuwarden in 1598. Our famous historian Petrus Borr also mentions the last of these in his Annals, book 13 and book 33. Our Church has always judged it good and useful to challenge the opponents to disputation and conferences. The Synod of Hoorn, petitioned for this purpose by the authority of the governor Theodorus Sonnoy, in 1580 and 1575 (sic). The Synod of Enkhuizen in 1578, article 4. The Synod of Alkmaar in 1593, article 11. The Synod of Edam in 1598 decreed that a disputation should be challenged, by Hans de Ries.

units.la: Scripserunt adversus Anabaptistarum errores plurimi, Zuinglius, Lutherus, Melanchton, Oecolampadius, Vrbanus Regius, Iustus Menius, Bullingerus, Ioh. à Lasco, Cassander, Guido de Bres, Ioh. Taffin, Herm. Buschius, Car. Gallus, V Vigandus, Ioh. Tayo, Casp. Heidanus, Ruardus Acronius, Ægid. Hunnius, Luc. Osiander, H. Faukelius, Petrus Pauli, Herm. Modcd. Abr. Cosierus, Gerardus Nicolai, Franc. Lanspergius, Ampsingius, Ioh. Seu, Rob. Puppius, Ainsworth, Adrianus Vossenholius, Vdemannus, Cloppenburgius, Abrah. Dooreslaer, cum Petro Iacobi AustroSylvio, Iac. du Bois, Bontemps, Spanhemius. Iam ab anno cIↄ Iↄ xc ix. Ecclesiae nostrae censuerunt, singulare Volumen Controversiarum Anabaptisticarum, quo praesertim illorum, sententiae, referrentur, & dilulucrentur argumentat, conficiendum: quod operis primum susceperat Arminius, pastor tum Amstelodamensis, & aliquò usque perduxerat, verùm ad professionem Theologicam vocatus in Academiam Leidensem, veritus se, & heterodoxiam suam promere, tum causatus varias operas, & studium positum in consutandis erroribus Papismi, revera in suis evomendis disseminandisque, intermissum fuit & suffocatum. Inque Synodo Alcmarianâ anno cIↄ Iↄ c v, declinati à se illius operis hanc causam dedit, quod inde forte apud aliquos in suspicionem veniret heterodoxiæ alicujus in nonnullis Theologiæ articulis. Inde in Synodo Enchusanâ anno cIↄ Iↄ c xxiv. Ripperto Sixti, & Petro Jacobi Austro-Sylvio injunctum, ut Mennonitarum Confessiones, præsertim recentes omnes diligenter conquirerent, controversias enotarent, discuterentque. Deinde solus in hoc opere relictus Austro-Sylvius, ab anno cIↄ Iↄ c xxvi. cui, postquam id aliquoties petiisset, socius operis adjunctus Abrahamus à Dooreslaar, anno cIↄ Iↄ c xxviii. in Synodo Amstelodamensi, conjunctis operis tandem ediderunt anno cIↄ Iↄ c xxxvii. nostrâ linguâ, Corpus Controversiarum Anabaptisticarum, ubi exactissimè tamquam in tabula variæ Anabaptistarum opiniones, ex propriis ipsorum scriptis (quorum catalogum in operis proœmio exhibent, & exemplaria servantur apud venerandum senem, atque de Ecclesiis nostris hinc adversus Anabaptistas, inde Remonstrantes optimè meritum Abrah. Dooreslaar) tamquam in Digestis enotatæ conspiciuntur. Opus arduum & præstans, quod multam lucem cognoscendis hisce controversiis, & magnum usum præstat ad facile feliciterque disputandum: factum uti ex Synodi Enchusanæ anno cIↄ Iↄ c xxx. Actis, art. xxxiv. video, loco prodromi, ad extruendam hinc plenam Anabaptismi Confutationem, quod levi operâ ad illam controversiarum deductionem & expositionem nem addi nunc posset. In disputatione iiscum observa, ut magis disputes modo Socratico, per pressas interrogationes, quam Aristotelico: sunt enim homines multi versipelles, illiterati, loquaces, qui suis facile constringi & capi possunt thesibus ac verbis, quosq; nimis operosa vel docta responsione non debemus videri majoris pretii facere, aut eruditionis & judicii æstimare, quam revera sint. Sed & videndum quam maxime, ne illis in iis, quæ proba, cedamus ullo pacto, ut in morum simplicitate, non autem fucatâ; in Scripturæ studio & cognitione: quo nomine illos demiratur potius, quam prædicat Florimundus Ræmundus, lib. II. de Origine hæres. cap. III. ubi hæc ejus verba nequidquam dissimulanda: Memini me non nunquam medium inter decem aut duodecim horum mortificatorum (sic enim videri volunt) varia de ipsorum religione cum ipsis disputasse, illosque quamvis nauta essent ac despicabiles homines, ad omnia quaecumque inciderant, Scripturæ aliquem locum in numerato habuisse. Sed hoc Pontificium, in alio quam suæ sectæ homine demirari non novum. Iterum c. seq. de Anabaptistarum moribus: Quum Burdigalam nostram varia nationes e plaga Septentrionali negociandi causa confluere soleant, volupe mihi nonnunquam fuit diversarum religionum homines convenire, ac sermonem cum eis conferre, ac præsertim cum Anabaptistis, ut mysteria ejus religionis perdiscerem. Hic fateor me non semel ingenii perculsum admiratione, quum viderem eos in mediis negociorum turbis eundem vultum atque eundem animi statum semper servare, nec ulla injuria, ira, aut quocumque alio affectu ab eo dimoveri; eundemque vivendi morem atque institutum inter tot nationum colluviem retinere. Quum Anno MDXCVIII. in horum aliquot incidissem, eo tempore quo tota nostra Aquitania extrema fame laborabat, post multa ultro citroque verba, unus ex iis liberrimo vultu & sermone ita infit: An vos Catholici, Christiani dici vultis, qui deliciis immersi, ante fores fatres vestros jacere sinitis? En plateas vestras languentibus & semimortuis plenas, incerea dum mensae vestrae ciborum & vini delicijs redundant. En laceros illos & cutem nudam ostendentes; dum vos byssò & serico vestitis, superbitis. Non hoc apud nos fieri solet. Nemo nostrae religionis panem suum emendicat. Si cui quid defit, id reliquorum fratrum liberalitate ultro suppletur. Nemo apud nos eleemosynam petit; sed nec quisquam otiosam vitam ducit. Omnes laboramus. Quod si quis naufragium aut jacturam faciat, ea communi omnium contributione ex parte resarcitur. Haec scriptor Pontificius, de hominibus, se suisque (fatcor) multum melioribus. Verùm enotemus illorum Controversias, non hujus aut illius Coetus, (scimus enim ab alio saepe improbari, quod hic affirmat) sed quas communiter nobis faciunt.
units.tr: They wrote many against the errors of the Anabaptists: Zwingli, Luther, Melanchthon, Oecolampadius, Urbanus Regius, Justus Menius, Bullinger, Johannes à Lasco, Cassander, Guido de Brès, Johannes Taffin, Hermann Buschius, Karl Gallus, Wigand, Johannes Tayo, Caspar Heydanus, Ruardus Acronius, Egidius Hunnius, Lucas Osiander, H. Faukelius, Petrus Pauli, Hermann Modeus, Abraham Cosierus, Gerardus Nicolai, Franciscus Lansbergius, Ampsingius, Johannes Seu, Robert Puppius, Ainsworth, Adrianus Vossenholius, Udemannus, Cloppenburg, Abraham Dooreslaer, with Petrus Jacobi Austro-Sylvius, Jacob du Bois, Bontemps, and Spanheim. Since the year 1599 our Churches have resolved to compile a single volume on the Anabaptist controversies, in which especially their opinions would be set out and their arguments cleared up. Arminius, then minister at Amsterdam, had undertaken this work first and had carried it some way, but when he was called to a theological professorship at the University of Leiden, fearing that his own heterodoxy might be revealed, he made various other labours his excuse, and with the study he had devoted to refuting the errors of Popery, which in truth he was using to disseminate his own, the work was dropped and suppressed. At the Synod of Alkmaar in 1605 he gave as the reason for his withdrawal from that work that it might perhaps bring him under suspicion of some heterodoxy in certain articles of theology. Then at the Synod of Enkhuizen in 1624, Ripperda Sixti and Petrus Jacobi Austro-Sylvius were charged to diligently seek out all the confessions of the Mennonites, especially the recent ones, to note their controversies, and to discuss them. Afterwards Austro-Sylvius was left alone with this work, from the year 1626. After he had asked for it several times, Abraham à Dooreslaer was joined to him as partner in the work, and in 1628 at the Synod of Amsterdam they at last published together, in 1637, in our language, the Corpus of Anabaptist Controversies, in which the various opinions of the Anabaptists are set out most exactly, as on a tablet, drawn from their own writings (whose catalogue they give in the preface of the work, and copies of which are kept by the venerable old man, Abraham Dooreslaer, who has deserved very well of our Churches against the Anabaptists on one side and the Remonstrants on the other), and they are seen noted down like the Digests. It is a laborious and excellent work, which gives much light for understanding these controversies and is of great use for disputing easily and successfully. I see from the Acts of the Synod of Enkhuizen of 1630, article 34, that it was done as a preliminary to building from it a full refutation of Anabaptism, and that with little effort that setting-out and exposition of the controversies could now be added. In disputation, I observe this: one should argue in the Socratic manner, by close questioning, rather than in the Aristotelian manner. For there are many men who are shifty, unlettered and talkative, who can easily be bound and caught by their own propositions and words; and we ought not to make them seem of greater worth, or judge their learning and judgement greater, by giving them an overly laborious or learned reply, than they really are. But one must also be very careful not to yield to them in any point that is sound, whether in the simplicity of their morals (which is not feigned), or in the study and knowledge of Scripture. On this score Florimond de Raemond admires them rather than praising them, in book 2 of On the Origin of Heresy, chapter 3, where his words must not be passed over in vain: I remember that I have sometimes debated with ten or twelve of these mortifiers (for so they wish to be seen) on various matters of their religion, and that, although they were sailors and contemptible men, they had at their command some passage of Scripture for everything that came up. But for a Papist to admire this in a man other than of his own sect is nothing new. Again, in the following chapter, on the morals of the Anabaptists: Since various nations are accustomed to flock to our Bordeaux from the northern region for the sake of trade, it has often pleased me to meet men of different religions and to talk with them, and especially with the Anabaptists, so that I might learn the mysteries of their religion. Here I confess that more than once I was struck with admiration when I saw them keep the same face and the same state of mind amid the bustle of business, and never be moved from it by any injury, anger, or any other emotion; and that they keep the same manner and rule of life amid such a mixture of nations. When in the year 1598 I met some of them, at a time when all our Aquitaine was suffering from extreme famine, after many words back and forth, one of them, with a most open face and speech, began thus: "Do you Catholics wish to be called Christians, who, immersed in luxuries, allow your brothers to lie before your doors? See how your streets are full of the languishing and half-dead, while your tables overflow with the delights of food and wine. See those ragged ones showing their bare skin, while you pride yourselves in fine linen and silk. This is not the custom among us. No one of our religion begs his bread. If anyone lacks something, it is supplied readily by the generosity of the other brothers. No one among us asks for alms, but neither does anyone lead an idle life. We all labour. And if anyone suffers shipwreck or loss, it is partly made good by the common contribution of all." So writes the Papist author, about men who are, I confess, much better than himself and his people. But we shall note their controversies, not those of this or that congregation (for we know that what one of them affirms is often disapproved by another), but those which they commonly raise against us.

units.la: I. Num sola Novi Testamenti Scriptura, & non etiam Veteris, sit canon fidei? Neg.
units.tr: I. Is Holy Scripture of the New Testament alone, and not also of the Old, the canon of faith? No.

units.la: II. An praeterquam ex Scriptura S. canonicâ, etiam ex libris Apocryphis (qui vocantur) certam articulorum fidei probationem petere liceat? Neg.
units.tr: II. May one seek sure proof of the articles of faith from the so-called Apocryphal books, besides the canonical Holy Scripture? No.

units.la: III. An de Deo Patre, Filio, & Spiritu S. usurpandae voces Personarum, & Trinitatis? Aff.
units.tr: III. Should the terms "Persons" and "Trinity" be used of God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Yes.

units.la: IV. Num in Deo tres sint distinctae essentiae? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Are there three distinct essences in God? No.

units.la: V. An causa praedestinationis divinae, quâ hominum alios in aeternam salutem elegit, alios non, sit solum Dei beneplacitum? Aff.
units.tr: V. Is the cause of divine predestination, by which God chose some men to eternal salvation and not others, solely the good pleasure of God? Yes.

units.la: Num verò ejus causa sit apud homines; ut quos Deus praescivit credituros & obtemperaturos sibi, atque in fide & obedientiâ perseveraturos, ideo eos elegerit; contrà alios, ob praevisam improbitatem, reprobarit? Neg.
units.tr: But is its cause, in men, that God chose those whom he foresaw would believe and obey him and persevere in faith and obedience, and for that reason elected them, while on the contrary he reprobated others on account of foreseen wickedness? No.

units.la: VI. Num voluntas Dei, & praedestinatio sit mutabilis? Neg.
units.tr: VI. Is the will of God and predestination mutable? No.

units.la: VII. An Dei providentia omnia & singula regat, etiam mala, (quâ permittendo, quâ gubernando) juxta aeternum suum de iis consilium? Aff.
units.tr: VII. Does the providence of God govern all things and each thing, even evils, both by permitting and by directing them, according to his eternal counsel concerning them? Yes.

units.la: VIII. An primi homines fuerint creati justi & sancti? Aff.
units.tr: VIII. Were the first men created just and holy? Yes.

units.la: IX. Primus homo, siquidem non peccasset, non suisset moriturus.
units.tr: IX. If the first man had not sinned, he would not have died.

units.la: X. An non omnes nascantur cum peccato originali? Aff.
units.tr: X. Are not all people born with original sin? Yes.

units.la: XI. Num post lapsum etiam permansærint in homine vires liberi arbitrii, ad præstandum bonum spirituale? Neg.
units.tr: XI. After the fall, did powers of free will remain in man for performing spiritual good? No.

units.la: XII. An Christus carnem suam habeat ex substantia matris Mariæ?
units.tr: XII. Does Christ have his flesh from the substance of his mother Mary?

units.la: An vero ex essentia, seu semine Patris (uti loquuntur); aut ex materia, essentia, & mutatione Verbi in hominem; aut alio quo pacto ex cælo attulerit, vel an ignorari debeat, unde sumserit? Aff. prius: Negantur reliqua.
units.tr: Or rather, does he have it from the essence, or seed, of the Father (as they put it), or from the matter, essence and transformation of the Word into man, or in some other way brought it down from heaven? And ought one to be ignorant of where he took it from? Yes to the first; the rest are denied.

units.la: XIII. Num unio naturarum in Christo, divinæ & humanæ ita se habeat, ut divina facta sit visibilis, passibilis, & mortalis? Neg.
units.tr: XIII. Does the union of the natures in Christ, divine and human, so relate that the divine nature was made visible, passible and mortal? No.

units.la: XIV. Num legem Mosis moralem Christus novis præceptis correxerit, atque adauxerit? Neg.
units.tr: XIV. Did Christ correct and enlarge the moral law of Moses by new precepts? No.

units.la: XV. Num Christus morte suâ pro omnium & singulorum hominum peccatis æque satis fecerit? & omnes Adami posteros, a communi, ex Adami peccato, reatu actu redemerit, & reconciliarit Deo? Neg.
units.tr: XV. Did Christ by his death make equal satisfaction for the sins of all and each of mankind, and redeem all the posterity of Adam from the common guilt arising from Adam's sin, and reconcile them to God? No.

units.la: XVI. Num gratia, & spiritus conversionis omnibus hominibus universe offerantur? Neg.
units.tr: XVI. Are grace and the Spirit of conversion offered universally to all men? No.

units.la: XVII. An Deus per solam Spiritus S. operationem, fidem & conversionem in homine efficiat?
units.tr: XVII. Does God produce faith and conversion in man through the operation of the Holy Spirit alone?

units.la: An vero homo per suam cooperationem sibi fidei & conversionis author sit? Aff. prius. Neg. posterius.
units.tr: Or rather, does man himself become the author of his own faith and conversion through his own cooperation? Yes to the first. No to the second.

units.la: XVIII. An nullo unquam casu Christiano homini jurare liceat? Neg.
units.tr: XVIII. Is it lawful for a Christian to swear in no case whatever? No.

units.la: XIX. Num Christiano nefas sit fungi officio Magistratus politici, eoque gladio uti, vel in reos, vel in bello adversus hostes? Neg.
units.tr: XIX. Is it wrong for a Christian to hold the office of civil magistrate and use the sword, either against criminals or in war against enemies? No.

units.la: xx. An Deus ita fideles & filios suos, in Christo conservet, ut non sinat eosdem plane à gratiâ excidere? Aff.
units.tr: XX. Does God so preserve his faithful people and sons in Christ that he does not allow them to fall away completely from grace? Yes.

units.la: xxi. Num eò perfectionis homo in hâc vitâ pervenire queat, ut sit absque omni peccato? Neg.
units.tr: XXI. Can a man attain such perfection in this life that he is without all sin? No.

units.la: xxii. Num inter Ministros Ecclesiæ servari debeat imparitas illa, ut alii sint simpliciter Concionatores, vel Admonitores, alii autem Episcopi, qui præter ministerium verbi, etiam sacramenta soli administrent, & pluribus præsint Ecclesiis, non ita alii? Neg.
units.tr: XXII. Ought that inequality to be kept among the ministers of the Church, so that some are simply preachers or admonishers, while others are bishops who, besides the ministry of the Word, administer the sacraments alone and preside over several congregations, and not the others? No.

units.la: xxiii. An Ministris verbi, ut ministerio suo toti vacent, debeatur certum ab Ecclesiâ laboris sui stipendium? Aff.
units.tr: XXIII. Is a fixed stipend for their labour owed by the Church to the ministers of the Word, so that they may devote themselves wholly to their ministry? Yes.

units.la: xxiv. Num conveniat, ut Minister in publico Ecclesiæ conventu, juxta cum aliis, tacitè precetur?
units.tr: XXIV. Is it fitting for the minister, in the public assembly of the Church, to pray silently along with the others?

units.la: An verò deceat clarâ voce aliis in precando præire? Neg. prius: Aff. post.
units.tr: Or rather, is it proper for him to lead the others in prayer with a clear voice? No to the first: Yes to the second.

units.la: xxv. Num solùm aliqui Davidis Psalmi in Ecclesiâ cantandi? an omnes? Neg. prius. Aff. post.
units.tr: XXV. Are only some Psalms of David to be sung in the Church, or all of them? No to the first. Yes to the second.

units.la: xxvi. An etiam fidelium infantes baptizandi? Aff.
units.tr: XXVI. Ought the infants of believers also to be baptized? Yes.

units.la: xxvii. Num semel baptizatos bene rebaptizent Anabaptistæ? Neg.
units.tr: XXVII. Do the Anabaptists rightly rebaptize those who have already been baptized once? No.

units.la: xxviii. Num Ecclesia peccantem aliquando etiam citra antecedentem admonitionem excommunicare possit, vel debeat? Neg.
units.tr: XXVIII. Can or ought the Church sometimes to excommunicate a sinner even without a previous admonition? No.

units.la: xxix. Num qui peccavit, quantumvis resipiscentiam agat, nihilominus tamen excommunicandus sit? Neg.
units.tr: XXIX. Is a person who has sinned to be excommunicated nonetheless, however much he repents? No.

units.la: xxx. Num excommunicatio Ecclesiastica dirimat vinculum divinum, & humanum, societatis naturalis, domesticæ, & politicæ? Neg.
units.tr: XXX. Does ecclesiastical excommunication dissolve the divine and human bond of natural, domestic and political society? No.

units.la: xxxi. Annon hominum animæ post hanc vitam statim, piorum in cœlis fruantur beatitudine, & impiorum pœnas sentiant infernales? Aff.
units.tr: XXXI. Do not the souls of men, immediately after this life, enjoy blessedness in heaven if they are pious, and feel the infernal punishments if they are wicked? Yes.

units.la: Vel potius omnes ignoto aliquo loco ad diem judicii quiescant, & quasi dormiant? Neg.
units.tr: Or rather, do all rest in some unknown place until the day of judgment, as if asleep? No.

units.la: Liber Sextus DE ENTHUSIASTIS, ET LIBERTINIS, &c.
units.tr: Book Six: On Enthusiasts and Libertines, etc.

units.la: De Enthusiasmo, & Enthusiastis. Primi, Anabaptistae praecedentis seculi. Varium eorum hominum genus. De Theologia Germanica. Controversia cum Enthusiastis, de Davide Georgio: ejus themata, vel quaestiones. De Libertinis: in Belgio, in Gallia. Deistae. Theses Libertinorum. De Henrico Nicolai, & Familia charitatis. De Weigelianis. De Fratribus Roseae crucis. Swenckfeldo. Mathia Vejero. Jesuas Stefelio. Ezechiele Metz. Refutatio libelli, ad legem & ad testimonium.
units.tr: On Enthusiasm and Enthusiasts. First, the Anabaptists of the preceding century. The varied kinds of these people. On the German Theology. The controversy with the Enthusiasts over David Georg: his theses, or questions. On the Libertines: in the Netherlands, in France. Deists. Theses of the Libertines. On Hendrik Niclaes and the Family of Love. On the Weigelians. On the Brethren of the Rosy Cross. On Schwenckfeld. On Matthias Vehr. On Jesaias Stefel. On Ezechiel Metz. A refutation of the little book, by the law and by the testimony.

units.la: Enthusiasmus, sive afflatus in animum aut mentem, alius est bonus, alius malus. Ille, à Deo: sive modo & via ordinaria, communis omnibus fidelibus & sanctis, qui à Dei spiritu aguntur, & reguntur. Ioan. 111. 8. 1. Cor. XII. 3. Sive extraordinaria, qualis Prophetis, & Scriptoribus sacris contigit. 11. Tim. 111. 16. 11. Pet. 1. 21. Malus est, quem à Diabolo homines patiuntur: vel à suis propriis illusionibus: vel quando divinum enthusiasmum fingunt sibi & pingunt, fictum plane, & mentitus. 11. Thess. 11. 2. Hunc impraesentiarum spectamus, in quo nil obstat, quin omnia mali enthusiasmi genera vel species quandoque concurrant, ut idem, qui divinum enthusiasmum temerè fingit, & à suis phantasticis imaginationibus deludatur, & à Satanicis vexetur, in justam mentis fa-cui cri spiritus poenam. Quales Massaliani, vel Euchitæ veteres, de quibus Harmenopulus: vocantur etiam Enthusiastæ, nam agitatione dæmonis occupati, putant eam esse Spiritus sancti. Ementitus enthusiasmus est, quando quis suis opinionibus, doctrinæ, aut factis extraordinarium divini Spiritus prætendit & mentitur afflatum, cœlestesque revelationes. Cujusmodi homines quovis tempore fuerunt varii, qui visiones, & somnia, allocutiones seu Angelicas, seu divinas, & revelationes cœlestes jactarunt. Sub V. T. Pseudo-Prophetæ divinas apparitiones, collocutiones, & mandata commenti. Deut. xiii. 1. 1. Reg. xxii. 11. Et in N. Test. 11. Thess. 11. 2. 1. Ioan. iv. 1. &c. A tempore Apostolorum, in primâ Ecclesiâ, præter Cerinthum fuit Montanus, qui Paracletum in se potius, quam in Apostolos descendisse, dicebat, & assumtis duabus Prophetissis Priscâ, & Maximillâ, ecstatica multa jactabat, atque à Spiritu Paracleto omnia sua provenire dogmata. Hujus id vulgare erat verbum, ab Epiphanio notatum, hæres. xlvii 1. homo velut lyra, & ego velut plectrum. Spirituales se; cæteros autem homines psychicos & animales appellabant. Quę apud Tertullianum non uno in loco occurrunt, ubi in Montanistarum deliria ille tantus vir prolapsus fuerat: quin librum integrum adversus Psychicos conscripsit, de jejunio: cumque de ecstasi libros sex fecisse, author est Hieronymus. Habuerunt olim, quos hoc nomine designarent, Enthusiastas, qui Messaliani, & Euchitæ etiam dicti, in mediam hominum turbam quandoque prosilientes, dein miris gesticulationibus, verbis, strepitu, quasi furore sacro correpti prophetabant, orabant assiduo, & somniis dediti, ἐνθουσιᾶσαι ... κα̈λῶσι, inquit Harmenopulus, lib. de Sectis. Talis etiam Muhammed fuit, impostorum quotquot unquam terram triverunt, maximus, qui sua cum Angelo Gabriele colloquia, & divinas revelationes, raptusque apud agrestem & vesanam gentem crepans, maximam hominum turbam post se & furores suos traxit, perditque. Enthusiasmus non ita in malum vulgò sonat, ac enthusiastæ: unde & titulum libri fecimus, de Enthusiastis, non de Enthusiasmo, uti supra de Anabaptismo, Papismo &c.
units.tr: Enthusiasm, or an inspiration of the soul or mind, is of two kinds, good and bad. The good kind comes from God, either in the ordinary manner and way, common to all the faithful and holy who are moved and guided by the Spirit of God (John 3:8; 1 Cor. 12:3), or in the extraordinary way, such as came to the prophets and sacred writers (2 Tim. 3:16; 2 Pet. 1:21). The bad kind is that which men suffer from the devil, or from their own illusions, or when they feign and paint for themselves a divine enthusiasm, which is wholly fictitious and false (2 Thess. 2:2). It is this kind we are concerned with at present, in which nothing prevents all the kinds or species of bad enthusiasm from sometimes coinciding, so that the same man who rashly feigns a divine enthusiasm is deceived by his own fanciful imaginations and vexed by Satanic ones, as a just punishment of his spirit and mind. Such were the ancient Massalians, or Euchites, of whom Harmenopulus writes: they are also called Enthusiasts, for, occupied by the agitation of a demon, they think it is the Holy Spirit's. A feigned enthusiasm is when someone, by his opinions, teaching or deeds, claims and falsely pretends to an extraordinary inspiration of the divine Spirit and to heavenly revelations. Men of this kind have been various at all times, who have boasted of visions and dreams, angelic or divine addresses, and heavenly revelations. Under the Old Testament the false prophets invented divine appearances, conversations and commands (Deut. 13:1; 1 Kings 22:11), and in the New Testament (2 Thess. 2:2; 1 John 4:1, etc.). From the time of the apostles, in the primitive Church, there was, besides Cerinthus, Montanus, who said that the Paraclete had descended upon himself rather than upon the apostles. Taking to himself two prophetesses, Prisca and Maximilla, he boasted of many ecstatic things and claimed that all his teachings came from the Paraclete Spirit. The common saying of his, noted by Epiphanius (heresy 47), was: a man is like a lyre, and I am like the plectrum. They called themselves spiritual, and other men psychic and animal. These things occur in Tertullian in more than one place, where that great man had fallen into the delusions of the Montanists; indeed he wrote a whole book against the Psychics, on fasting; and Jerome is the authority that he wrote six books on ecstasy. There were once those whom they designated by this name, Enthusiasts, who were also called Messalians and Euchites, leaping out now and then into the middle of the crowd, then, seized as if by a sacred frenzy, prophesied with strange gestures, words and noise, prayed without ceasing, and gave themselves over to dreams; they become enthused ... are called [ἐνθουσιᾶσαι ... καλῶσι], says Harmenopulus, in his book On Sects. Muhammad too was such a man, the greatest of all the impostors who ever trod the earth, who, boasting of his conversations with the angel Gabriel and of his divine revelations and raptures among a rude and frenzied people, drew a huge crowd of men after him, and his frenzies destroyed them. Enthusiasm does not sound so much like evil in common usage as enthusiasts do; for this reason we have made the title of the book On Enthusiasts, not On Enthusiasm, as above On Anabaptism, Papism, etc.

units.la: Nostro sæculo, initia Anabaptistarum ab Enthusiasmis fuerunt, primique sectæ istius authores Enthusiastæ: uti olim quoque Montanistæ enthusiasmum, & anabaptismum una conjunxerunt: de quibus Philastrius Brixiensis auctor est, rebaptizare solitos, quos seduxissent homines. Nostro sæculo, vel ab exordio Anabaptistarum, primi & anabaptismi, & enthusiasmi, (nam & primum Anabaptistarum, quo denotati fuerunt, nomen fuit Enthusiastarum) patroni extitere Nicolaus Storck vel Ciconia; Thomas Muncerus, qui Rusticorum seditiosum quem ducebat exercitum, revelationibus suis pascebat ac gubernabat, ejusque methodum in enthusiasmis servatum breviter memorat Chemnitius, loc. Com. part. 1. de lib. arbitrio cap. VIII. ubi de illo in hunc modum: 1. Ponit ante auditum verbi preparationem seu dispositionem per mortificationem, illam vocat Entgröbung. 2. Studierung/ legere, audire verbum. 3. Verwunderung/ id est, dubitare, an verum sit quod in verbo legis & audis, & petere talem sensibilem revelationem, ne nihil dubitationis vel diffidentiae reliquum sit. Et quidem ita orare potuit suos auditores, exspuentes in cælum: Vater gib mir ins Herz die ausgestrackte Lust zu deiner Gerechtigkeit/ wo nicht/ so will ich dich und alle deine Apostel verleugnen. 4. Die lange Weil/ quando adhuc cum peccato pugnandum est. 5. Besprengung/ id est, in revelatione per vivam vocem Dei erudiantur. Und tempt der Besitzer in das Inwendigst/ und gibt ins Herz ein gewis Urtheil von allen Dingen/ und wird also der mensch den Creaturen entrissen. Anabaptistæ apud Helvetios, Conradus Grebelius, & qui ab ipso in idem præcipitium abductus, Sangallensium antea in Schola la Professor, Wolffangus Vlmian, praeterea Melchior Hofmannus, praesertim Monasterienses illi Turbones, Iohannes Bocoldus Rex, sociique Cnipperdollingus, & Bernardus Crechting; tum Batenburgici qui sic appellabantur, & causam Monasteriensium acriter tuebantur; prae omnibus vero David Georgius, enthusiasmos & ecstases somniabant, urgebantque. Confer Bullingerum, lib. 11. adversus Anabapt. Unde de Enthusiastis sua habet Lindanus, in Dubitantio. Dial. xii. & ex hoc Prateolus, in Elencho Haeresium. lib. v. num. 12.
units.tr: In our century, the beginnings of the Anabaptists arose from enthusiasms, and the first authors of this sect were Enthusiasts; just as the Montanists once also joined enthusiasm and anabaptism together, of whom Philastrius of Brescia reports that they were accustomed to rebaptize those whom they had seduced. In our century, or from the very outset of the Anabaptists (for the first name by which the Anabaptists were marked was that of Enthusiasts), the patrons of both anabaptism and enthusiasm were Nicolaus Storck or Ciconia, and Thomas Muncer, who fed and governed the seditious army of peasants he led with his revelations; Chemnitz briefly records the method he kept in his enthusiasms, Loci communes, part 1, on free will, chapter 8, where he says of him in this manner: (1) He posits, before hearing the Word, a preparation or disposition through mortification; he calls it Entgröbung. (2) Studying/ reading and hearing the Word. (3) Wonder/ that is, to doubt whether what you read and hear in the word of the law is true, and to ask for such a sensible revelation, so that no doubt or diffidence remains. And indeed he could thus pray to his hearers, spitting toward heaven: Father, give me in my heart the outstretched desire for your righteousness; if not, I will deny you and all your apostles. (4) The long while/ when one must still struggle with sin. (5) Sprinkling/ that is, to be taught by the living voice of God in revelation. And the possessor enters into the innermost, and gives into the heart a certain judgment about all things, and thus man is snatched away from the creatures. Among the Swiss, Anabaptists were Conrad Grebel, and those drawn by him into the same precipice, Wolfgang Ulmian, formerly a professor in the school at St. Gall; besides them Melchior Hofmann, and especially those Münster hotheads, John of Leiden the king, and his companions Knipperdolling and Bernard Krechting; then the Batenburgers, as they were called, who vigorously defended the cause of the Münsterites; but above all David Georg, who dreamed of and urged enthusiasms and ecstasies. Compare Bullinger, book 2, against the Anabaptists. Hence Lindanus has his account of the Enthusiasts in his Dubitantius, Dialogue 12, and from him Prateolus, in his Elenchus of Heresies, book 5, number 12.

units.la: Homines Enthusiastici sunt non unius generis, alii haud vulgares faciunt suos enthusiasmos, sed admodum singulares, & revelationes, visiones, somnia, oracula: eaque ad portentosa, extraordinaria, & flagitia insignia peragenda, quales erant Monasterienses, ipsorumque similes. Alii magis communes habent enthusiasmos, etiam aliis a se quin communiter suae sectae hominibus contingentes; qui adversus verbum Dei, & Scripturae S. regulam, suo spiritu duci amant, & ex eo illud interpretari, & fidem, religionem, omniaque instituenda, asserunt. Illos ab hisce haud gravate aliquando damnari continget, quamvis eodem fere utrique genio agitentur, sed ille turbulentus, enormis, truculentus; hic sedatior, & ad religionem, fingendam saltem, magis videtur compositus. Hi omne suum odium in S. Scripturam evomunt, eam simplicem litteram, elementum, alphabetum criminantur, solis pueris, non adultis & spiritualibus, quales ipsi sint scilicet, imperandam aut praescribendam. Spiritum suum ajunt verum Dei verbum, internum, & spirituale normam & judicem Scripturae; hoc audiendum, & sequendum esse, non Scripturae textum aut sensum verbalem: ac prout fastidiunt simplicem & apertum Scripturae stylum, ita obscuris eum, inauditis, & cothurnatis loquendi modis mysticisque exponunt: atque hoc spiritu correptos, ajunt se vulgo deificari. Anabaptistae hodie cautiores, &c & quamvis Spiritum sanctum necessarium quidem faciant ad S. Scripturæ intelligentiam, exserte addunt, hoc non eò facere, quasi Scriptura in se imperfecta sit, sed per Spiritum S. interne aliud extra aut contra Dei verbum doceatur: uti in Confessione sua art. 1. de Scripturâ habet Nicolaus Nicolai, Cl. Cl. quod aperte est contra Enthusiastarum tum axiomata, tum praxim.
units.tr: Enthusiastic people are not of one kind. Some make their enthusiasms not in the common way but in quite singular ways, with revelations, visions, dreams and oracles, and these are carried out for portentous, extraordinary and notorious crimes, such as were the Münsterites and those like them. Others have more common enthusiasms, which also happen to others beside themselves, to people commonly belonging to their own sect; they love to be led by their spirit against the Word of God and the rule of Holy Scripture, and from this they claim to interpret it and to establish faith, religion and all things. The former will not be condemned without severity, although both are driven by almost the same spirit; but the one is turbulent, outrageous and savage, while the other seems calmer and more composed, at least for feigning a religion. These pour out all their hatred upon Holy Scripture, they denounce the plain letter as elementary, as an alphabet, to be imposed or prescribed only on children, not on adults and spiritual people, such as they themselves, to be sure, are. They say that their spirit is the true Word of God, inward and spiritual, the norm and judge of Scripture; this is to be heard and followed, not the text or verbal sense of Scripture. And just as they despise the simple and plain style of Scripture, so they expound it with obscure, unheard-of and high-flown modes of speech and mystical meanings; and those seized by this spirit, they say, are commonly made divine. Today's Anabaptists are more cautious, etc., and although they do indeed make the Holy Spirit necessary for understanding Holy Scripture, they expressly add that they do not do this as if Scripture were imperfect in itself, but because through the Holy Spirit something else is taught inwardly, outside or against the Word of God.
