Nicolaus Niclaes, a most distinguished man, has this in article 1 of his Confession, on Scripture; which is plainly against the axioms and the practice of the Enthusiasts, both alike.

units.la: De Enthusiastis, & adversus illos scripserunt, Philippus Marnixius; & qui adversus Anabaptistas, Bullingerus, Calvinus, Spanhemius, Disputat. AntiAnabapt. XVI. XVII. XVIII. XIX. XX. parumque adeo adversus illos scribendum videtur, qui insanis dogmatis gyrant tum se, tum alios, erudiunt nullos, & quorum tam deploranda est amentia, ut quemadmodum ipsi solent cavere ne cum quopiam agant, nisi jam suæ sectæ se addicente, & simpliciter ad accipienda omnia ipsorum placita tradente: ita ut ab alio, quam vertiginoso & parum sanæ mentis homine illa arripiantur, parum verendum est, plusque constringendi in suis thematis, & ad contradictiones vel absurda adigendi homines, quam ut cum iis serio vel sollicitè multum disputemus. Ipsorum omnia hinc facile coarguenda sunt & confundenda, primò quod apertis frontibus in S. Scripturam incurrunt, eam petulanter repudiant, contemnunt: unde facile quæcunque Enthusiasticus Spiritus dictat, præter & contra Scripturam sunt. Deinde, ad turbas vergunt ipsorum omnia. Denique ille Spiritus sibi mutuo in diversis hominibus, vel aliis alium æque jactantibus Spiritum, passim contrariatur, & variis ac contrariis dictatis ab hoc & illo confunditur facile & coarguitur. Quid ni enim liceat uni exsibilare Spiritum, nullâ certitudine se probantem à Deo esse, quam alteri istum asserere? vel quâ ratione non audietur spiritus aliquis in hoc dictans aliud ab illo spiritu, diversumque, vel forte quid adversum, ac contrarium? Ad duo præcipue attendere semper oportet, ad Scriptu-ram, ram, quam isti homines vilipendunt, & Spiritus proprii enthusiasmos, quos sequuntur & deprædicant. Prout facilis hæc ubique methodus, Deo ejusque authoritate repudiatâ, sibi, quantum quis Deo abstulit, arrogare. Homines hi Dei verbum mancum, mutilum, obscurum dicunt, non omnibus semper, non ipsis videlicet perfectis & adultis simpliciter sequendum, sed Spiritum, ejusque afflatus, & dictata, præter etiam ac contra Scripturam. Quum Scriptura non solum persectissima religionis regula sit, semper & in omnibus sequenda, II. Tim. III. 16. 17. Ephes. II. 20. quæque alias, præter se, regulas respuit, & condemnat. Deut. v. 32. & XII. 31. Apoc. XXII. sed & Spiritus istiusmodi quod attinet, cavere nos jubeat. I. Tim. I. 4. I. Joann. IV. 1. & jactatas frustra confictasque revelationes. Gal. I. 8. II. Thess. II. 2. Iam quod ad hos ipsorum enthusiasmos spectat, spiritumque enthusiasticum, hoc cum imprimis refellit, quod se palam Dei verbo opponit, non authoritati solum ejus, ne eo habeatur loco & honore, quo debet; sed & veritati dictorum, quam non ex ipsis, sed suis φανταςίας cupiunt explicari. Tum, quo se argumento ille spiritus comprobat divinum, audiendumque esse? nullo. Imo exinde, quod dictata ejus sunt improba, blasphema, turbulenta contra Respublicas & Ecclesias, aliter ac Deus qui omnis ordinis & pacis in Sanctorum Ecclesiis, nullius autem ἀκαταστασίας auctor est, I. Cor. XIV v. 33. evertiva S. ministerii, tollentia certitudinem fidei in fidelibus, contraria mutuò, viam pandentia quibusvis spiritibus pessimis & hæresibus, colligitur qualis sit istorum auctor Spiritus. Denique quo festivo adversus illos utitur argumento Marnixius: quum illi nos velint convincere suo spiritu, noster quid ni æque valeat adversus ipsos, certissime testans & clamans omnes illorum enthusiasmos falsos, vanos, atque improbos esse? Quod dicant, suum verum spiritum esse, non ita nostrum, ridiculum est, præsertim ubi genuinum spiritus indicem & probam tollunt, quæ est Scriptura Sancta, & nuda ipsorum asseveratione nos non magis tenemur, quam vel ipsi nostrâ, aut utrique aliorum: & ipsorum quidem spiritus tot ineptis & perversis infandisque effectis satis se ipsum convincit.
units.tr: Those who wrote about the Enthusiasts and against them include Philip Marnix; and those who wrote against the Anabaptists include Bullinger, Calvin, Spanheim, Disputat. Anti-Anabapt. XVI, XVII, XVIII, XIX, XX. Yet it seems hardly worth writing against those who go round in circles with their insane doctrines, both themselves and others, and teach no one. Their folly is so lamentable that, just as they themselves take care not to deal with anyone unless he is already committed to their sect and simply surrenders to accept all their opinions, so it is hardly to be feared that anyone but a dizzy man of unsound mind would be caught by them. We would do better to tie people down to their own theses and force them into contradictions or absurdities than to argue with them seriously or at length. All their claims can easily be refuted and overthrown here. First, they openly run against Holy Scripture, wantonly reject it and despise it. Hence whatever the Enthusiastic spirit dictates is easily shown to be beside and against Scripture. Second, all their doctrines lead to disturbances. Third, that spirit everywhere contradicts itself when different men each claim the Spirit, or one claims the Spirit as firmly as another, and it is easily confounded and refuted by the varied and contrary dictates of this man and that. Why should one not be allowed to hiss at a spirit that proves itself by no certainty to be from God, when another asserts it? Or for what reason will not some spirit, dictating in this man something other than that spirit, and different from it, or perhaps even opposed and contrary to it, be heard? We must always attend to two things: to Scripture, which these men despise, and to the private enthusiasms of the spirit which they follow and proclaim. This is the easy method everywhere: having rejected God and his authority, each man claims for himself as much as he has taken away from God. These men call God's Word incomplete, mutilated and obscure, and say it must not always be followed by everyone, least of all by those who are already perfect and mature, but rather the Spirit, with its inspirations and dictates, beyond and even against Scripture. Yet Scripture is not only the most perfect rule of religion, to be followed always and in all things (2 Tim. 3:16, 17; Eph. 2:20), and it rejects and condemns all other rules besides itself (Deut. 5:32; 12:31; Rev. 22), but it also bids us beware of such spirits (1 Tim. 1:4; 1 John 4:1) and of revelations vainly boasted of and falsely invented (Gal. 1:8; 2 Thess. 2:2). As for these Enthusiasms of theirs, the enthusiastic spirit is refuted above all by the fact that it openly sets itself against God's Word, not only against its authority, so that it is not held in the place and honour it ought to have, but also against the truth of what it says, which they want explained not from Scripture but from their own fancies [φαντασίας]. Then, by what argument does that spirit prove itself divine and to be heeded? By none. Indeed, from the fact that its dictates are wicked, blasphemous and disruptive against commonwealths and churches, unlike God, who is the author of all order and peace in the churches of the saints, and not of any disorder [ἀκαταστασίας] (1 Cor. 14:33), who overturns the holy ministry, removes the certainty of faith in believers, sets them against one another and opens the way to all the worst spirits and heresies, one may infer what sort of spirit its author is. Finally, Marnix uses a witty argument against them: since they want to convince us by their spirit, why should ours not be equally strong against them, certainly bearing witness and crying out that all their enthusiasms are false, empty and wicked? That they say theirs is the true spirit and ours is not is ridiculous, especially when they remove the genuine test of the spirit and proof, which is Holy Scripture. We are no more bound by their bare assertion than they are by ours, or each side by that of the other. Their spirit, in any case, convicts itself by its many foolish, perverse and unspeakable effects.

units.la: Nullius est quod vulgo occinunt, ex 11. Cor. 111. 6. littera enim occidit, spiritus autem vivificat. Neque enim vel per litteram ibi intelligitur verbum Dei, litteris comprehensum, non omne istud, non Euangelium, sed sola lex, quatenus illa, ejusque ministerium opponitur ministerio Euangelii, uti in sequentibus Apostolus illud ministerium mortis, hoc spiritus, illud condemnationis, hoc justitiæ appellat: nequaquam etiam per spiritum intelligit Apostolus Enthusiasticum illum, sed Spiritum Euangelii, vel novi Testamenti, unde dixit: Deus nos fecit ministros novi Testamenti, non litteræ, sed spiritus: littera enim &c. Hinc quasi meri spirituales homines sint nostri Enthusiastæ, quando de re aliqua, vel sacris loquuntur aut scribunt, tam sublimi, cothurnato, & allegorico utuntur sermone, ut nec aliis, nec sibi intelligantur: tantam fundunt in tumore sapientem stultitiam, quod de Valentinianis dixit Irenæus, ut nec spirituales sint, neque litterales. Fuerunt sub Papatu, qui vel inscii, vel imprudentes viam multùm straverunt Enthusiasticis illis, suâ Theologiâ mysticâ, quemadmodum loquuntur, & libellis pietatis: in quibus, terminis & phrasibus duris, mysticis & allegoricis, tum inspirationis, tum deificationis &c. sæpicule usi, qui ab aliis pro enthusiasmis habiti vel accepti postea fuerunt. Quales, Johannes de Schoonhovia, Joh. Taulerus, quem inter Pontificios, Eckius; inter nostros, Marnixius carpunt: defendit autem Lud. Blosius, singulari pro eo apologia: Johannes Ruisbrochius, Belga, qui multa scripsit suo idiomate, & in latinum conversa sunt, atque edita Coloniæ: quem repre-henhendit Iohannes Gerson, at itemum Dionysius Carthusianus, & Blosius defendunt: id enim accidere solet iis, qui scribunt de mystica Theologia, & eorum dicta ab aliis reprehendantur, ab aliis laudentur, quia non eodem modo ab omnibus accipiuntur, inquit Bellarminus, de Scrip- toribus Ecclesiasticis.
units.tr: What they commonly sing, from 2 Cor. 3:6, the letter kills, but the spirit gives life, is worth nothing. For there the letter does not mean God's Word committed to writing, the whole of it, not the Gospel, but only the law, insofar as it and its ministry are set against the ministry of the Gospel. Thus the Apostle calls that ministry the ministry of death, and this the spirit; that the ministry of condemnation, and this of righteousness. Nor does the Apostle by spirit mean that Enthusiastic spirit in any way, but the Spirit of the Gospel or of the New Testament, whence he said: God has made us ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter &c. So our Enthusiasts pretend to be purely spiritual men when they speak or write about some matter, even a sacred one, and use so lofty, buskined and allegorical a style that they are understood neither by others nor by themselves: they pour out in their swelling a foolishness that passes for wisdom, as Irenaeus said of the Valentinians, so that they are neither spiritual nor literal. Under the Papacy there were some who, unwittingly or imprudently, paved the way greatly for those Enthusiasms by their so-called mystical theology, as they call it, and by their books of piety, in which they often used harsh, mystical and allegorical terms and phrases, both of inspiration and of deification, and so on; these were later regarded or accepted by others as Enthusiasms. Among such are John of Schoonhoven, John Tauler, whom Eck among the Papists and Marnix among ours find fault with (but Lodewijk Blosius defends him with a special apology); John Ruusbroec, a Fleming, who wrote much in his own language, and whose works were translated into Latin and published at Cologne, whom John Gerson reproves, and then Denis the Carthusian, while Blosius defends him. For, as Bellarmine says in his book on ecclesiastical writers, this is wont to happen to those who write about mystical theology: their sayings are reproved by some and praised by others, because they are not received in the same way by all.

units.la: In eundem censum refero libellum, Theologia Germanica, pro quo in Belgicum translato legitur commendatio Lutheri, eadem facilitate ac imprudentia, qua Oecolampadius Swencfeldum (non dico Zuinglium, eundem, sed ad alterius argumenti librum: Confutatio Impanationis ac Transsubstantiationis, laudasse) testimonio suo ornārat, pro libello ejus, de cursu verbi divini. Quis auctor libri Theol. Germanica sit, vulgo ignoratur. Videtur sibi Beza, in epistola ad Guljelm. Gratarolum Medicum, quae est epistolarum ejus xlvi. hominem deprehendisse: quaerit modo, an tuto affirmare possit, vel probare testibus & idoneis argumentis, siquidem ille inficietur: vocat, hominem improbissimum: in latinum etiam conversus liber, & impressus Antverpiae, anno cIↄ Iↄ lviii. sub nomine Johannis Theophili. Sacerdos, ex Teutonicorum ordine, aliquibus perbibetur ejus auctor. In scripto quodam fratrum Rosae Crucis, cui tit. Frater crucis Rosae, anno cIↄ Iↄ cxvii, adscribitur Taulero: & hinc commendatur ibidem Pontificiis primum, tum etiam Reformatis, Anabaptistis, Lutheranis, his praesertim, propter commendationem illam Lutheri. Exemplar meum Germanicum anno cIↄ Iↄ lxi. Schwencfeldum authorem praefert. Quidquid sit, fundamenta Enthusiasmi & Libertinismi apud eum occurrere, saltem incauta & prodigiosa sua locutione, ut quando cap. xiv. ait: Vetus homo est Adamus, & inobedientia, ipsceitas, egoitas, & similia, at novus homo Christus & obedientia &c. Antagonistae Libertinismi, & Familismi jam annotarunt Johannes Knewstub, in Dedic. Confutationis H. N.
units.tr: To the same class I refer the little book Theologia Germanica, for which a commendation by Luther is found in the Dutch translation, written with the same ease and imprudence with which Oecolampadius adorned Schwenckfeld (I do not mean Zwingli, that same man, but a book on another subject, the Confutation of Impanation and Transubstantiation) with his testimony, praising his book On the course of the divine Word. Who the author of the Theologia Germanica is, is commonly unknown. Beza seems to have detected the man, in his letter to William Gratarolus the physician, which is letter 46 of his letters; he asks only whether he can affirm this safely, or prove it by witnesses and suitable arguments, since the man would deny it, and he calls him a most wicked fellow. The book was also translated into Latin and printed at Antwerp in 1558 under the name of Johannes Theophilus. Some hold that its author was a priest of the Teutonic Order. In a certain writing of the Brothers of the Rose Cross, entitled Frater crucis Rosae, in 1617, it is ascribed to Tauler, and is commended there first to the Papists, then also to the Reformed, Anabaptists and Lutherans, especially to the latter because of that commendation of Luther. My German copy of 1661 names Schwenckfeld as its author. Whatever the truth, the foundations of Enthusiasm and Libertinism are found in it, at least in its careless and monstrous manner of speaking, as when in chapter 14 it says: Adam is the old man, and disobedience, selfhood, egoity and the like; but Christ is the new man, and obedience, etc. The opponents of Libertinism and Familism have already noted this, John Knewstub in the Dedication of the Confutation, H. N.

units.la: Cum omnibus istius farinæ hominibus neutiquam operosè disputandum est: nam neque id merentur illorum dogmata & opiniones, quæ difficultatem nullam magnam continent, neque illos reddes eo magis dejectos aut convictos; quin uti cum improbitate, audaciæ impudentiæque litare propositum illis, ita inde primus animos sumunt, atque insurgunt arrogantiores, si prolixe refutentur, quasi tanti fiant, & ipsorum sententiæ non levi labore oppugnari possint. Quod in Helvidio notavit Hieronymus, cujus confutationem hoc aggreditur exordio: Nuper rogatus à fratribus, ut adversus libellum cujusdam Helvidii responderem, facere distuli, non quod difficile fuerit hominem rusticanum, & vix primis quoque imbutum literis, super veri assertione convincere: sed ne respondendo dignus fieret qui vinceretur. Ego potius contemnendos existimo, & quantum in illis sanandis plerumque frustra impenditur operæ, tantum aliorum causâ, quos adversus seductionem muniri & moneri oportet, detegenda quidem illorum χρωμα τῆς αἱρέσεως, & τὰ βλάβη, & in quæ principia atque αἰτίας dogmata incurrant, sed absque multo opere & molestiâ, digito quasi ostendenda arbitror: longas multasque adversus illos scriptiones faciendi ego author non sum. Quod tanto impendio abscônditur, etiam solummodo demonstrare, destruere est, inquit Tertullianus: planè uti de Valentinianis. Idem in initio libri, quem adversus illos scripsit: Si bonâ fide quæras, concreto vultu, suspenso supercilio, Altum est, ajunt. Si subtiliter tentes, per ambiguitates bilingues, communem fidem adfirmant. Namque nihil magis curant, quam occultare quod prædicant, si tamen prædicant quæ occultant. Et adversus Enthusiastas quidem hæ controversiæ.
units.tr: We should never argue at length with men of this sort. Their doctrines and opinions do not deserve it, since they contain no great difficulty, and a long refutation does not make them more downcast or more easily convinced. Instead, they treat the attempt as an invitation to shameless and impudent abuse, and they grow bolder and more arrogant if they are refuted at length, as though they were worth so much effort and their views could only be overthrown with great labour. Jerome noted this in the case of Helvidius, and he opens his refutation with these words: Recently, when the brethren asked me to answer a book by a certain Helvidius, I put it off. This was not because it would be hard to convict a rustic fellow, scarcely even trained in the rudiments of letters, of error in his assertion of the truth, but lest by answering I should make him worth conquering. I think rather that such people should be despised. Much effort is usually spent in curing them to no purpose, and I think their colour of heresy [χρωμα τῆς αἱρέσεως] and their harms [τὰ βλάβη], and the principles and causes [αἰτίας] of error into which they fall, should be exposed, but without great labour or trouble, and pointed out almost with a finger. I, for my part, am not the author of long and numerous writings against them. To hide so much at such expense, even merely to demonstrate it, is to destroy it, says Tertullian, quite as he said of the Valentinians. In the beginning of the book he wrote against them, he says the same: If you seek in good faith, they answer with a stern face and a raised eyebrow, "It is deep." If you probe subtly, they affirm the common faith through double-tongued ambiguities. For they care for nothing more than to hide what they teach, if indeed they teach what they hide. These are the controversies against the Enthusiasts.

units.la: 1. Num Scriptura S. non sit verum, & unicum, atque sufficiens Dei verbum, nec perfecta omnibusque semper necessaria fidei regula, explicanda & intelligenda juxta verborum sensum, sed juxta liberum & proprium cujusque spiritum, afflatum, quasi verbum internum, & verum, atque illud terminis & locutionibus novis, sublimibus & miris, supra modum allegorice, mysticéque? Neg.
units.tr: 1. Is Holy Scripture not a true, unique and sufficient Word of God, nor the perfect rule of faith, always necessary to all, to be explained and understood according to the sense of the words, but instead according to each person's free and private spirit, inspiration, as an inner and true word, and that in new, sublime and wondrous terms and expressions, allegorically and mystically beyond measure? No.

units.la: II. Num homini aliquod singulare & proprium sabbathum, vel quies animae suae frequentanda sit, quâ omnium vacuus, in se abire, haerere, ac praestolari debeat coelestem à Deo enthusiasmum, qui tam sit certissimum Dei verbum, & spiritus? Neg.
units.tr: II. Must a person keep some singular and private sabbath, or a rest of his own soul, in which, emptied of all things, he should withdraw into himself, cling there, and wait for a heavenly enthusiasm from God, which is as certain a Word and Spirit of God? No.

units.la: III. Num homines in se, ac spiritu suo omnia habeant, & tantummodo eum sequi, ceu omnium credendorum, & faciendorum normam, debeant? Neg.
units.tr: III. Do men have everything in themselves and in their own spirit, and ought they to follow only that, as the rule of all things to be believed and done? No.

units.la: IV. Num spiritu illo acti, ita in Deum rapiantur, & cum eo uniantur, ut deificari ipsos contingat? Neg.
units.tr: IV. When moved by that spirit, are they carried up into God and united with him, so that it comes about that they are deified? No.

units.la: Enthusiastarum & Libertinorum apud nos coryphaeus fuit David Georgii, Hollandus, Delfis natus, parentibus infimae sortis, ipse litterarum rudis, sed ingenio ad praestigias facto, & fastuoso, qui vitri pictoriam artem primum exercuit, partibusque Anabaptistarum se adjungens, propter concordiam aliquam inter illos, sua potissimum opera, iktam, in oppido V Westphaliae Bockholt, Doctor haberi, & propriam, sed infandam omni ex parte, quâ doctrinae, qua vitae ratione, sectam erigere tentavit, ubi se Davidem secundum spiritum esse, verumque Messiam Christo praestantiorem, suam doctrinam prae Mosaicâ, & Christi esse perfectiorem, polygamiam licitam, & peccati sensum, infernos, Daemones nihil esse, docuit. Coepit ad annum cIↄ Iↄ xxvii. Patria extorris ob edicta & persecutiones contra Anabaptistas, aliosque religioni Papali adversantes, Basileam se contulit, anno cIↄ Iↄ xliv. & multos annos se illic clam, mutato nomine in Iohannem Bruck, vel etiam ab agro & domo, quam emerat, Iohannem Brimingen, magnâque modestiæ specie tenuit, discipulos interim in Belgio varios promissis multis, librisque prodigiosis fovens, solis ejus insciis Basileensibus & Helvetiis, apud quos non tenui fama opum vitæque agebat, usque dum Basileæ mortuus anno cIↄ Iↄ l i i. & honorificè sepultus, detectâ tandem ejus improbitate & imposturis, jussu Senatus per carnificem, triennio fere ex quo obierat, effossus, & publicè una cum libris, quos varios linguâ Belgicâ scripserat, suisque crebro submiserat, & effigie in ejus ædibus repertâ, concrematus fuit anno cIↄ Iↄ l ix. Historiam edidit Academia Basileensis, & exstat conversa in Belgicum, eamque accurate persequutus est Thuanus lib. xxxi. & Nicolaus Blesdikius, Davidis gener, in Historiâ Soceri sui, à quo se circumventum agnovit, & meliora postea sapuit, una cum aliis Davidis, sive Bruckii dicti filiis, & generis, cujus Nicolai Meinardi Blesdikii partem Historiæ Davidicæ aliquam editam debemus Clarissimo viro, & amico nostro D. Iacobo Revio. Denique Vbbo Emmius, Rector Groninganus, libello vernaculo, de Spiritu David-Iuristico scenam hominis nobis pandit atque explicuit. Adeoque quum adhuc in Belgio esset, sub nomine proprio Davidis notus, multis impostuit, ut nobilissimus vir Iohannes à Lasco, sub initium anni cIↄ Iↄ xl iv. ad illum litteras haud semel inscripserit, Dilectissimo fratri Davidi Georgii, verbi divini ministro &c. quarum in suâ historiâ meminit is, quem diximus, Nicolaus Blesdikius. Interim Apologiam scripsit sermone vernaculo, ad Annam Oldenburgicam, anno cIↄ Iↄ xl. quâ omnia fere negat sibi objecta probra, & dogmata. Quod autem revelationibus, & divino alloquio omnia tribuerit, apertissimum est. Fundamentum totius negocii nititur revelationibus, quas sibi accidisse ait in suâ officinâ sedentarià, vel in edium suarum conclavi, idque tertio aut quarto mense post illud Westphalicum collo-quium, inquit Blesdikius, pag. 18. & deinde per omnem vitae ac doctrinae suae cursum ad idem semper recurrit, & revelationes coelestes jactavit incessanter. Quaeritur hic.
units.tr: Among us the leader of the Enthusiasts and Libertines was David Joris, a Hollander, born at Delft to parents of the lowest rank. He was himself unlearned in letters, but of a mind given to trickery and arrogance. He first practised the art of glass painting, and then joined the Anabaptists. Through some agreement among them, brought about chiefly by his own efforts, he was held to be a teacher in the Westphalian town of Bockholt, and he tried to set up a sect of his own, unspeakable in every respect, both in doctrine and in way of life. There he taught that he was David according to the Spirit, and the true Messiah, superior to Christ; that his doctrine was above Moses' and more perfect than Christ's; that polygamy was lawful; and that there was no sense of sin, and that hell and demons were nothing. This began about the year 1527. Exiled from his homeland by edicts and persecutions against the Anabaptists and others opposed to the Papal religion, he betook himself to Basel in the year 1544. For many years he lived there in secret, under the changed name John Bruck, or sometimes John Brimingen after a farm and house he had bought, maintaining a great appearance of modesty. Meanwhile he fostered various disciples in Belgium with many promises and prodigious books, known only to the Baslers and Swiss, among whom he lived in no small reputation for wealth and way of life. He died at Basel in the year 1556 and was honourably buried. At length his wickedness and impostures were discovered, and by order of the Senate, nearly three years after his death, he was dug up by the executioner and burned publicly, together with the books he had written in Dutch and often sent to his followers, and with a likeness found in his house, in the year 1559. The Academy of Basel published a history of him, which exists also in Dutch translation. Thuanus followed the matter closely in book 31, and Nicolaas Blesdijk, David's son-in-law, did so in his history of his father-in-law, by whom he was deceived, and whose wiser opinions he afterwards came to hold, together with other sons and kin of David, also called Bruck. To the most distinguished man and our friend, Mr. Jacob Revius, we owe a published part of the Davidic history by Nicolaas Meinardi Blesdijk. Finally, Ubbo Emmius, rector of Groningen, in a small book in the vernacular, has laid open and explained for us the stage of this man, in his book on the David-Jorist spirit. And so, while he was still in Belgium and known under David's own name, he deceived many; thus the most noble John à Lasco wrote to him more than once, early in the year 1544, addressing him as "To my most beloved brother David Joris, minister of the divine Word, etc." Nicolaas Blesdijk, whom I have named, mentions these letters in his history. Meanwhile David wrote an apology in the vernacular to Anna of Oldenburg in the year 1540, in which he denies almost all the charges and doctrines objected to him. That he attributed everything to revelations and divine speech is quite clear. The foundation of the whole affair rests on revelations, which he said came to him while sitting at his workshop or in a room of his house, and this three or four months after that Westphalian colloquy, Blesdijk says, p. 18. And afterwards, through the whole course of his life and teaching, he always returned to the same point, and he constantly boasted of heavenly revelations. The question here is:

units.la: I. Num Deus ultimo, post Christum, se perfectissima revelatione manifestârit in Davide Georgio, tanquam in altero Christo, eoque prae priori meliori & magis spirituali? Neg.
units.tr: I. Did God, after Christ, reveal himself most perfectly in David Joris, as in another Christ, and one better and more spiritual than the first? No.

units.la: II. Num cum isto Christo Davide Georgio desinere in Ecclesiâ debeat cultus omnis religionis externus, verbi praedicatio, Sacramentorum, & aliarum rerum usus? Neg.
units.tr: II. With this Christ David Joris, should all external worship of religion, the preaching of the Word, and the use of the sacraments and other things cease in the Church? No.

units.la: III. Num Angeli non sint substantiae incorporales, sed tantum animi cogitationes & motus: similiter Daemones, nil nisi carnis adversus mentem rebellio? Neg.
units.tr: III. Are angels not incorporeal substances, but only thoughts and motions of the mind; and likewise demons, nothing but rebellion of the flesh against the mind? No.

units.la: IV. Num vita aeterna, coelum, Christi postremus adventus, judicium, infernus, intra hominem omnia sint, & solum hic, non alibi exspectanda? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Are eternal life, heaven, Christ's last coming, judgement and hell all within man, and to be expected only here and nowhere else? No.

units.la: V. Num peccata omnia singuli palam in Ecclesiâ confiteri debeant? Neg.
units.tr: V. Must each individual openly confess all his sins in the Church? No.

units.la: VI. Num omnis genitalium pudor exuendus sit, & deponendus, atque hoc ad perfectionem faciat? Neg.
units.tr: VI. Must all shame about the genitals be stripped off and laid aside, and does this contribute to perfection? No.

units.la: VII. Num probanda, atque introducenda sit polygamia? Neg.
units.tr: VII. Is polygamy to be approved and introduced? No.

units.la: VIII. Num instituenda bonorum omnium communio? Neg.
units.tr: VIII. Is a community of all goods to be established? No.

units.la: Quae de Spiritu, eadem sunt Libertinorum, qui ita appellantur, & cum Enthusiastis paria faciunt, ita dicti, à praetensâ spiritus sui libertate, quam sectantur. Atque hos non immerito Anabaptistarum prolem constituas. Quare Calvinus eodem opere edidit Instructionem adversus Anabaptistas, atque adversus Libertinos. Libertini nostri ab abusu libertatis, bujusque proprofano praetextu dicuntur, qui nullis verbi divini regulis, nulli disciplinae ecclesiasticae, aut professioni astrictos se opinantur, sed Spiritus sui arbitrio vivendum esse; atque utrinque ex una parte omnem rationem virtutis, peccati, poenarum, ipsiusque etiam inferni flocci faciunt, nullo istorum admisso discrimine; ita ex altera haud quaquam verentur Deum authorem peccatorum, eorum scilicet quae nos pro malis, illi secus, merito habemus, facere. Profana & execranda profecto hominum improbissimorum secta, cujus religio est, nullam religionem aestimare. De quibus vide Bullingerum, adversus Anabapt. lib. I I. cap. X I V. Prateolum, lib. x. num. 4. Pezelium, part. I I. Argument. &c. pag. 2 1 0. de causa peccati, contra Libertinos.
units.tr: What holds of the Spirit holds also of the Libertines, who are so called and who go hand in hand with the Enthusiasts. They are named from the pretended liberty of their spirit, which they pursue. These you may not unreasonably regard as the offspring of the Anabaptists. Hence Calvin, in the same work, published an Instruction against the Anabaptists, and against the Libertines. Our Libertines are so called from an abuse of liberty and its profane pretext. They think themselves bound by no rules of the divine Word, by no church discipline, nor by any profession, but that they must live at the will of their own spirit. On one side they make light of every reason of virtue, sin, punishment, and even of hell itself, without making any distinction among these things. On the other side they do not at all hesitate to make God the author of sins, namely of those things which we rightly count as evils and they do not. Indeed this is a profane and execrable sect of most wicked men, whose religion is to count no religion of any worth. On these see Bullinger, against the Anabaptists, book II, chapter XIV. Pratéolus, book x, num. 4. Pezelius, part II, Arguments, etc., p. 210, on the cause of sin, against the Libertines.

units.la: Calvinus, qui adversus Libertinos masculè & accuratè, quomodo solet, scripsit, illos ait, mitio impudenter & palam solitos fuisse blasphemare Scripturam sacram, & Scriptores ejus divinos. Apud eos Paulus, vas confractum erat; Petrus, abnegator Dei; Iohannes, adolescens stolidulus; Matthaeus, foenerator: sed postea cum viderent se ita loquentes, horrori omnibus esse, vertebant stylum, & obscurius agendum censentes, allegoriis mysticisque locutionibus omnia involvebant, pervertebantque. Auctores recensent primos, Coppinum quendam, Insulanum; & Quintinum, ex partibus Hannoniae oriundum; Bertrandum, cuius illo una ex sartore Doctorem factum, patria sua ob maleficia potius, quam ob verbum Dei, egressos: Claudium Perseualum; denique Antonium Pocquium, sacerdotem. Hi Flandriam primum, & Brabantiam, deinde Galliam suis opinionibus & foeditatibus conturbarunt, atque discipulos reliquerunt ubique plurimos: uti in improbitatem & nequitiam homines facile est reperire & efficere pronos paratosque. Pocquius aliquod tempus Genevae egit, discessurus testimonium & commendationem petiit a Calvino, quo apud alios quosquoscunque aditum sibi & gratiam pararet, sed, quamvis ignoraret adhuc ejus spiritum Calvinus, delirium tamen hominis jam observârat, adeoque nec ad dandum testimonium adduci potuit. Martinum verò Bucerum, addebat Pocquius, concessisse quod ei Calvinus denegavit: adeo decipere bonos viros doctus e-rat, & eorundem abuti nomine ac facilitate. Quod in Reginâ Navarræ evidentius apparuit, quæ quamvis istorum hominum non teneret mysteria, eo usque tamen sermonis fuco & blanditiis fascinata erat, & erga Quintinum ac Pocquium, ceu viros bonos, inclinabat, ut ægerrime ferret illos à Calvino nominatim ad-eò acriterque, in scripto contra Libertinos, castigatos fuisse; arbitrata, quasi se per illorum latus, quod inter domesticos ejus degerent, Calvinus pupugisset. Unde hic necesse habuit scriptâ ad Reginam anno cIↄ Iↄ xlv. epistolâ, crimen istud diluere, & quam imprudenter patrocinium ejusmodi hominibus commodasset, monere. Extat inter epistolas Calvini, pag. 53.
units.tr: Calvin, who wrote against the Libertines manfully and carefully, as is his way, says that they used shamelessly and openly to blaspheme Holy Scripture and its divinely inspired writers. According to them Paul was a broken vessel, Peter a denier of God, John a foolish youth, and Matthew a usurer. But when they saw that such talk horrified everyone, they changed their tune and, judging that they must proceed more obscurely, wrapped and perverted everything in allegories and mystical expressions. Calvin names the first authors as a certain Coppinus from the island, Quintinus born in the region of Hainaut, Bertrand, who had been made a teacher from being a tailor, and who left his homeland because of his crimes rather than for the Word of God, Claudius Perseval, and finally Antonius Pocquius, a priest. These men first troubled Flanders and Brabant, and then France, with their opinions and filthy practices, and everywhere they left very many disciples, since it is easy to find and make men prone and ready for wickedness. Pocquius spent some time at Geneva, and when he was about to leave he asked Calvin for a testimonial and recommendation, by which he might win access and favour with others wherever he went. But although Calvin did not yet know his spirit, he had already observed the man's madness, and so could not be persuaded to give the testimonial. Pocquius added that Martin Bucer had granted what Calvin refused him; so skilled was he at deceiving good men and abusing their name and good nature. This appeared more clearly in the case of the Queen of Navarre, who, although she did not hold these men's mysteries, was nonetheless so bewitched by their varnish of speech and flattery that she inclined towards Quintinus and Pocquius as good men. She took it very badly that they had been rebuked by name, and so sharply, by Calvin in his writing against the Libertines, thinking that Calvin had stabbed her in the side, since these men lived among her household. Hence Calvin had to write to the Queen in the year 1545, to clear himself of this charge and to warn her how imprudently she had lent her protection to such men. It is found among Calvin's letters, p. 53.

units.la: Hoc pacto quidem gnaviter Gallia istâ lue purgata fuit, sed unde ortum, totum fere Belgium eo malo circumseptum, uti Calvinus illâ epistolâ haud falso scripsit: ac nescio quo modo in nostris regionibus adeo hauserit firmiter radicatum, ut hodie quoque pauciores ejus fautores existere optandum esset. Hoc senserunt jam tum de nostrâ Belgarum natione primi Reformatores, nimis leves & petulantes in negotio religionis sibi illos videri. Unde Melanchton, quando cum Bucero Bonnam à Coloniensi Archiepiscopo esset evocatus, ad promovendam in districtu isto reformationem, cum Bucero aliquando ad Rheni ripam obambulans, extensâ dextrâ aliquoties Bucero dixisse scribitur: ne Belgio, ab horrendo sanguinis balneo, & ingeniorum petulantiâ.
units.tr: In this way France was thoroughly purged of this plague, but nearly the whole of Belgium was beset by the same evil from its origin, as Calvin wrote truly in that letter. And I do not know how it has taken such firm root in our regions that it would be a matter for wishing that there were fewer of its supporters even today. The first Reformers already perceived this about the Belgian nation, that these people seemed to them too light-minded and wanton in matters of religion. Hence when Melanchthon, having been summoned to Bonn by the Archbishop of Cologne to promote reform in that district, was walking with Bucer along the bank of the Rhine, he is recorded to have said to Bucer several times, stretching out his right hand: may Belgium be spared from the horrible bath of blood and from wantonness of minds.

units.la: Ad annum cIↄ Iↄ xl. Antverpiæ fuit scandularius aliquis Loy vulgo dictus, unde qui ipsum sequebantur
units.tr: In the year 1540 there was at Antwerp a certain scandal-monger commonly called Loy, and those who followed him

units.la: Loistæ appellati, qui doctrinam Libertinisticam inter cives disseminavit, negata resurrectione, inferno &c. inde per Germaniam, ubi cum Melanchtone disputavit, præsente Luthero, denique reversus Antverpiam, & aliis, & sibi causa extitit ultimi supplicii, combustusque palam est anno {?}MDXLVI. Meteranus, lib. 1. Histor. Belg. Neque hic solum, sed ubique terrarum satis magna Libertinici gregis est copia, illorumque quibus religio ludus est, non dissimiles admodum Cobilâ Tartarorum Rege, de quo Maffæus in epistolis Asiaticis, pag. 332. quod festa & Christianorum, & Iudæorum, & Saracenorum, Idolorumque peræque coluerit. Rogatus causam, respondit: quatuor in orbe magnos Prophetas adorari, à Christianis, Christum; à Iudæis, Mosem; à Saracenis, Muhammedem; ab Idololatris, Sagonombarem Chamum, Deorum primum: quos omnes dum veneror, ajebat, hunc etiam qui in cœlo maximus sit & Deus verior, me honorare existimo. Quæ refer ad librum, non inter Gentiles aut Tartaros, sed Christianos, proh dolor! editum, de Tribus Impostoribus; cujus auctor an Petrus Aretinus, an alius fuerit, jam non inquiro. Quibus succenturiandi, qui hodie in Gallia Deistæ, (alii à Deistis, seu AntiTrinitariis & Arianis Prateoli, de quibus agit lib. 1 v. Elenchi Haeres.) per antiphrasim dicuntur, quasi Deum optimè cognoscant, interim ejus providentiam negantes, aliaque communis Theologiæ capita, carni & rationi suæ minus placita: eaque quia repudiant, quæ Christianorum vulgus simplici fide amplectitur, se appellant fortes, esprits forts, quasi potentes illa devorare, ac nullius facere, ad quæ alii summâ fide & religione contremiscunt; & Degrés dicti, quasi emunctioris naris, & non, uti ceteri, grues. Controversiæ Libertinorum sunt, præter illa, quæ cum Enthusiastis habent communia:
units.tr: were called Loists. He spread Libertine doctrine among the citizens, denying the resurrection, hell, and so on. From there he went through Germany, where he disputed with Melanchthon in the presence of Luther; then he returned to Antwerp and became, through others and through himself, the cause of his own final punishment, and was openly burned in the year 1546. Meteranus, lib. 1 of the History of Belgium. Nor is this kind found only here; there is a fairly large crowd of Libertine flocks everywhere on earth, and of those for whom religion is a game, not unlike Cobila, the King of the Tartars, of whom Maffei speaks in his Asiatic letters, p. 332, who observed alike the festivals of Christians, Jews, Saracens and idolaters. When asked why, he replied that four great prophets were worshipped in the world: Christ by Christians, Moses by Jews, Muhammad by Saracens, and by idolaters Sagonombar Chamus, the first of the gods; and he said that while he venerated all of them, he thought he honoured also him who is greatest in heaven and the truer God. Refer this to the book On the Three Impostors, published not among Gentiles or Tartars but, alas, among Christians; I do not now inquire whether its author was Pietro Aretino or someone else. To these must be added those who today in France are called, by antiphrasis, Deists (others, from Prateolus, who discusses them in book 4 of the Elenchus of Heresies, call them Deists, or Anti-Trinitarians and Arians), as if they knew God very well, while denying his providence and other heads of common theology that are less pleasing to their flesh and reason. And because they reject what the common run of Christians embraces in simple faith, they call themselves strong spirits, esprits forts, as if they were able to devour those things before which others tremble with the greatest faith and religion, and they are called Degrés, as if they had a keener nose and were not, like the rest, cranes. The controversies of the Libertines are, besides those they hold in common with the Enthusiasts, these:

units.la: I. Num unicus tantum omnium viventium sit spiritus, ritus, ubique diffusus, Dei, qui in creaturis sit, & vivat: quare nec animæ nostræ sint proprie substantiæ, vel earum immortalitas sit aliud quid quam Dei ille in nobis spiritus immortalis? Neg.
units.tr: I. Is there only one spirit of all living things, the spirit of God, diffused everywhere, which is in creatures and gives them life? Hence our souls are not properly substances, nor is their immortality anything other than that immortal spirit of God in us? No.

units.la: II. Num omnia quæ homo agit, ipsaque adeo mala & peccata quæ dicuntur, sint opus Dei, & Deus istorum omnium propria & formalis causa? Neg.
units.tr: II. Are all the things that a man does, and indeed those evils and sins so called, the work of God, and is God the proper and formal cause of all of them? No.

units.la: III. Num peccatum revera nihil sit, sed imaginatio modò, seu opinio, quæ facile evanescat & aboleatur, cum istius nulla amplius habetur ratio; quare nec ob illud aliquis sit improbandus, aut judicandus? Neg.
units.tr: III. Is sin really nothing, but merely an imagination or opinion, which easily vanishes and is abolished when no further account is taken of it; so that no one is to be blamed or judged on account of it? No.

units.la: IV. Num infernus nihil, sit, nisi forte mala hominis conscientia? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Is hell nothing, unless perhaps the evil conscience of a man? No.

units.la: V. Num ea demum sit vera & spiritualis libertas, & quam sequi debeamus, omne discrimen boni malique tollere, peccata nihili æstimare; perinde habere omnia, bona sive mala, neque ullâ tangi peccati conscientiâ, aut scrupulo, verùm ut unusquisque sese spiritui suo ducendum committat? Neg.
units.tr: V. Is that true and spiritual liberty, which we ought to follow, the removal of every distinction between good and evil, the reckoning of sins as nothing, the holding of all things, good or bad, alike, and not being touched by any consciousness or scruple of sin, but each committing himself to be led by his own spirit? No.

units.la: Ejusdem cum Enthusiastis & Libertinis est commatis Henricus Nicolai, & quæ ab eo instituta Familia charitatis: quemadmodum Cistercienses Monachi suam regulam appellant charitatis. Sic appellata ab ejus auctore, Abbate Stephano Hardingo, ut est in Chronico Cisterciensi, pag. 33. Natus Henricus Nicolai fuit Monasterii V Westfalorum; sed Amstelodami diu habitavit, & post Davidem Georgium, circa annum MDLVI. nova sua themata & paradoxa cæpit disseminare: homo indoctus, vafer, ad hypocrisin factus, revelationes Angelicas à Gabriele Angelo infusas sibi somniabat, & symbolo utebatur: charitas extorsit; seque primum illuminatum familiæ charitatis seniorem dicebat. Mosi, & Christo palam se præponebat: huic, fidei; illi, spei præconi; se charitatis, utraque majoris, Doctorem præferendum merito esse dictitans; quodque non ut illi, in atrium, vel sanctum, ut Moses & Christus; sed in Sanctum Sanctorum penetraret. Vide de illo Henricum Antonii, Prof. Franekeranum, in Præfat. ad Systema Theol. ubi primordia Ecclesiæ nostræ per Belgium, brevi compendio exponit. Ex Hollandia in Angliam trajecit, ibique permultos ex vulgo operarios, mulierculas, incautam plebem in Sectam suam, quam speciosum charitatis nomen oppido commendabat, allicuit. Nonnulla scripsit, sive epistolas, sive tractatus, titulis semper magnificis: Evangelium Regni; Terra Pacis: Exhortatio, Correctio, quæ ex Belgico etiam in Gallicum translata exstant; & quoque Anglicè: præterquam plures ad diversos Epistolas. In illorum fine semper occurrit illud suum: Charitas extorsit per H. N. Scripturæ loca, qui istorum hominum mos est atque hypocrisis, multâ copiâ, nullo cum judicio, profert, atque illâ ratione simplicibus, qui Scripturas amant, facilius imponit. Epistolæ ejus, quam in Angliâ scripsit ad duas filias V Varwicenses, refutationem oppositit Henricus Ainsworth. Scripsit adversus illum quoque, inter Anglos, Johannes Knewstub, qui confutavit librum ejus, Evangelium Regni, cujus ex primo capite hoc exordium ponit, unde de cæteris quamvis non visis auditisque, facile judicium:
units.tr: Of the same stamp as the Enthusiasts and Libertines is Henry Nicolai, and the Family of Love founded by him, just as the Cistercian monks call their rule the rule of charity. It was so named by its author, Abbot Stephen Harding, as is found in the Cistercian Chronicle, p. 33. Henry Nicolai was born at Münster in Westphalia, but lived for a long time at Amsterdam, and after David Joris, around the year 1556, he began to spread his new themes and paradoxes. A man unlearned, crafty, made for hypocrisy, he dreamed that he had angelic revelations infused into him by the angel Gabriel, and he used the motto: charity extorted it; and he called himself the first enlightened elder of the family of love. He openly set himself above Moses and Christ, proclaiming himself the herald of charity, as Christ was of faith and Moses of hope, and insisting that he deserved to be preferred as teacher of charity, which is greater than both; and that he entered not, as they did, into the court or the holy place, as Moses and Christ did, but into the Holy of Holies. On him see Henry Antonius, professor at Franeker, in the Preface to the System of Theology, where he sets out in a brief summary the beginnings of our Church throughout Belgium. From Holland he crossed into England, and there he drew very many workmen, little women and the uncautious common people into his sect, which he commended under the specious name of charity. He wrote some things, both letters and treatises, always with grand titles: Gospel of the Kingdom; Land of Peace; Exhortation, Correction, which exist also translated from Dutch into French, and in English as well, besides several Letters to various people. At the end of these there always occurs his motto: Charity extorted this through H. N. The manner and hypocrisy of these men is to produce many passages of Scripture without any judgement, and in this way they more easily impose on simple people who love the Scriptures. His letter, which he wrote in England to two daughters of Warwick, was refuted by Henry Ainsworth. Among the English, John Knewstub also wrote against him, and refuted his book Gospel of the Kingdom, from the first chapter of which he gives this opening, from which one may easily judge the rest, though it is not seen or heard:

units.la: H. N. gratiâ & misericordiâ Dei, & per Spiritum sanctum Iesu Christi, excitatus à summo Deo, à morte, secundum Dei providentiam & promissiones: unctus spiritu sancto, in tempore antiquo sacræ cognitionis Iesu Christi: deificatus cum Deo, in spiritu amoris ejus: factus cum Christo heres in cælestibus divitiarum Dei: illuminatus spiritu veritatis cælesti, verâ perfectâ essentiâ luce: electus in Ministrum gratiosi verbi (quod jam ultimis temporibus à Deo excitatum, juxta promissiones ejus) in sanctissimo Christi mysterio sub obedientiâ charitatis ejus: ad manifestandum his ultimis temporibus ex eâdem gratiâ & misericordiâ Dei, & per eundem sanctum spiritum amoris Iesu Christi, bonum nuntium, & quæ sequuntur. Qui tali cothurno incipit, quam orchestram cogitet, satis ostendit. Divinare opus est, quid illis pompaticis verbis sibi velit, & fastuoso, inepto, obscuro loquendi sermone, nisi ut tamquam ex abdito quodam loco proripiens credatur novus μάντις, & deificatus enthusiasta, qui secum alios in deliria agat, & furorem. Adversus Henricum Nicolai primus è Belgis scripsit Theodorus Coornhert, amicus ejus, qui quomodo familiariter eocum plures annos vixerit, & nonnullos ad se, ex ejus familia, aliquando habuerit palam & impudenter asserentes, se Deum esse, edidit libro, qui est Operum ejus Tom. III. vel Dialogo, inscripto Klein monster. Deinde scripserunt adversus illum præsertim Ministri Ecclesiæ Londinensis Belgicæ, ut quos propius hoc malum è Belgio advectum videbantur spectare, Martinus Micronius, & Nicolaus Charinetas. Apud nos ex professo adversus ejus Familiam, vel sectam librum edidit, Belgico idiomate, Caspar Grevinchovius. Nuper eorundem errores, quia cum Antinomis in Anglia repullularunt, agente hoc maximopere Ministro Randallo aliquo, detexit denuo Johannes Etherington: & una perstrinxit, in scripto Anglico adversus Antinomos præcipue adornato, celebris vir Samuel Rutherford. Anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxv. hujus familiæ homines Confessionem ediderc, atque anno cIↄ Iↄ c v. una cum eâ, libellum supplicem obtulere Iacobo Regi: in quo uti se singulariter separant à Brownistis, aliisque, ita Brownistæ quoque in suâ ad Regem Iacobum Apologiâ anno cIↄ Iↄ xcv I. adversus Doctores Oxonienses, se diligenter purgant ab omni cum Familistis communione, quæ impacta ipsis per Oxonienses fuerat. Regina Elizabetha adversus illud hominum genus edictum condidit anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxx. Præcipuum quod hi, ne de enthusiasmis, & deificatione ipsorum dicam, tenent, est quod externam religionis professionem adjunt junt non esse necessariam, neque pro eâ aut loquendum aut certandum, nedum grave aliquod patiendum, aut in altero, quamcunque religionem teneat, aliquid eo nomine reprehendendum esse, sed simulandam pro re nata religionem, ut visum, nec necesse esse ut vitam ad regulam, vel verbum Dei, aut aliquam disciplinam componamus; paedagogicum id atque servile nimis: denique omnia ex charitate, quantumcunque prava sint, interpretanda esse bona. Quae sententia ad placitum carnis & vitae dissolutae, ac licentiosae facta, haud mirum quod fautores reperiat. Quippe nihil hominii, prout naturae jam est summe depravatae, gratius accidere potest, quam ut doceatur simulare, & quemadmodum religionis professionem, ita ejus causâ perpessiones omnes evitare, omnibusque & omni tempori ipsum, sive in malis, sive bonis, accommodare. Praecipue Martyribus infensissimi sunt homines illi, juxta quorum opinionem stultissimi fuerunt qui sive olim, sive hodie Christiani, ob confessionem veritatis pati dura, aut etiam mortem voluerunt.
units.tr: H. N., raised up by the grace and mercy of God and through the Holy Spirit of Jesus Christ, from death by the most high God, according to God's providence and promises; anointed with the Holy Spirit in the ancient time of the sacred knowledge of Jesus Christ; deified with God in the spirit of his love; made heir with Christ in the heavenly riches of God; illumined by the spirit of heavenly truth, with the true and perfect light of essence; chosen as minister of the gracious word (which, now in the last times, has been raised up by God according to his promises) in the most holy mystery of Christ, under the obedience of his love; to make known in these last times, from the same grace and mercy of God and through the same holy Spirit of the love of Jesus Christ, the good news, and so on. Anyone who opens with such buskins shows well enough what stage he has in mind. One must guess what he means by those pompous words and that proud, silly, obscure manner of speaking, except that he is meant to be believed a new prophet [μάντις], springing forth as if from some hidden place, and a deified enthusiast, who drives others with him into raving and frenzy. Against Hendrik Niclaes, the first to write from among the Dutch was Dirck Coornhert, his friend, who, having lived with him familiarly for several years, and having had some from his household who openly and shamelessly claimed that they were God, published an account of this in a book which is in volume III of his Works, or in a dialogue entitled Klein monster. Afterwards, against him, especially the ministers of the Dutch Church in London wrote, since they seemed most concerned with this evil, brought over from the Netherlands: Martin Micron and Nicolaus Charinetas. Among us, Caspar Grevinchoven published a book in the Dutch language directed professedly against his family or sect. Recently, since their errors have sprouted again in England together with the Antinomians, a certain minister Randall pressing this hard, John Etherington uncovered them again; and in an English writing prepared chiefly against the Antinomians, the celebrated Samuel Rutherford censured them along with him. In 1575 men of this family published a Confession, and in 1605, together with it, they presented a supplicatory petition to King James. In it, just as they separate themselves singularly from the Brownists and others, so the Brownists too, in their Apology to King James in 1601 against the Oxford doctors, carefully purge themselves of all communion with the Familists, which had been imputed to them by the Oxonians. Queen Elizabeth issued an edict against that kind of men in 1580. The chief tenets they hold, not to speak of their enthusiasms and self-deification, are these: that an outward profession of religion is not necessary, nor should one speak or contend for it, much less suffer anything grave on its account; that one should not be reproved in another, whatever religion he holds, on that score; but that religion should be feigned as seems fit for the occasion; and that it is not necessary to order our life by a rule, or by the Word of God, or by any discipline, since that is too pedagogical and servile; and finally, that everything is to be interpreted as good out of charity, however perverse it may be. This opinion, shaped to suit the pleasure of the flesh and a dissolute and licentious life, is no wonder in finding supporters. Indeed, nothing can be more welcome to man, as his nature is now most deeply depraved, than to be taught to dissemble, and, just as a profession of religion, so for its sake to avoid all sufferings, and to accommodate himself to everyone and every time, whether in evils or in goods. Those men are most hostile especially to the martyrs, and according to their opinion, those who, whether formerly or today, were Christians and wished to endure hardships, or even death, for the confession of the truth, were the most foolish of men.

units.la: Ex horum numero fuerunt, sub primam Reformationem, Adrianus Vossenhoel, I. C. & Balthasarus, Dominicanorum Antverpiae praefectus. Vsi sunt hoc hominum genus (referente Henrico Antonii, in praesatione modo allegatâ) libris Sebastiani Franci, de quo Lutherus judicavit, quod per omnium hominum oletum perreptassit, & in suo proprio fuisset suffocatus. Ejusdem hactenus sententiae etiam fuit Coornhertus, in lib. Excusatio Romanae idololatriae: quo nec Christianos pro vitandis caeremoniis debere vitae periculum subire, neque exercitium Papalium caeremoniarum, absque animo, idololatriam esse, comprobare nititur. Cui Calvinus, libro illo ex Belgico in Latinum translato à Theologis Belgis, ut eum refutaret, opposuit, quod inter ejus opera est, Confutationem cujusdam Hollandi, ad fratres Belgas: ubi hominem suis coloribus egreegregiè, & stolliditatem ejus depinxit. Iam tempore Origenis cognoscimus ejusdem opinionis nonnullos fuisse, ex ejus Commentario in Matthæum. Homiliâ xxix. explicaturus abominationem desolationis in loco sancto, sic loquitur: Adhuc autem & si quis manifeste quidem videat abominationem desolationis stantem in loco sancto, & si sequatur eam accipiens, sibi excusationem de divinis scripturis, quasi indifferenter liceat Christianitatem negare, dicens denegationem non esse denegationem, & esse immolatorum, quasi nihil nocentes manducanti fuerit arbitratus, proferens de scripturis exempla, & quod indifferenter licet in uno eodemque tempore mulieribus commisceri diversis, quasi & patribus ista facientibus olim &c. Resurrectionem insuper docent illi nullam futuram, aliaque ipsis attribuuntur, quæ vide in libello Belgico, Engelsche Berooerten / pag. 105.
units.tr: Among these, at the beginning of the first Reformation, were Adrian Vossenhoel, licentiate in canon law, and Balthasar, prefect of the Dominicans at Antwerp. They used books of Sebastian Franck with this kind of men (according to Henricus Antonii, in the preface just cited), of whom Luther judged that he had crept through every filth of men and been suffocated in his own. Coornhert was also of this same opinion, so far as, in his book Excusatio Romanae idololatriae, he strives to prove that Christians ought not to undergo danger to life to avoid ceremonies, and that the practice of Papal ceremonies is not idolatry without the intention. Against him Calvin, in the book which the Dutch theologians translated from Dutch into Latin to refute him, set forth Confutation of a certain Hollander, addressed to the Dutch brothers, where he depicted the man excellently in his own colors and portrayed his foolishness. Already in the time of Origen we know that some held this same opinion, as is shown in his Commentary on Matthew. In Homily 29, expounding the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, he speaks thus: Yet even if someone clearly sees the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, and follows it, taking as an excuse from the divine Scriptures that it is permissible to deny Christianity without distinction, saying that a denial is not a denial, and that eating what has been sacrificed harms nothing, and bringing forward examples from the Scriptures, and that it is permitted without distinction to mingle with various women at one and the same time, as if the fathers too did these things of old, etc. Those men also teach that there will be no future resurrection, and other things are attributed to them, which see in the Dutch booklet Engelsche Berooerten, p. 105.

units.la: Henri-Nicolaitarum hæc sunt, quæ quaeruntur:
units.tr: These are the questions concerning the Henry-Nicolaites:

units.la: I. Num charitatis sit, nullam certam habere religionis professionem, sed se omni, quantumcunque etiam falsam religionem docenti, Sectæ adjungere, & simulare, adeoque cum nemine super religionis negotio velle contendere, neque diversa ab aliis errantibus sacra sequi? Neg.
units.tr: I. Is it a matter of charity to have no fixed profession of religion, but to join oneself to any sect, however false the religion it teaches, and to pretend, and so to wish to contend with no one over matters of religion, nor to follow rites different from those of other erring people? No.

units.la: II. Num familia illa charitatis sit hominum planè perfectorum & deificatorum, qui neque peccent amplius, neque à peccato quidquam ultra patiantur, atque ita libere & innocenter inter se vivant, ut scilicet neque se denudare coram sociis pudeat? Neg.
units.tr: II. Is that family of charity made up of men who are completely perfect and deified, who neither sin any more nor suffer anything further from sin, and who therefore live among themselves so freely and innocently that they are not ashamed to strip naked before their companions? No.

units.la: III. Num nulla futura sit corporum post mortem resurrectio; sed omnis resurrectio in hac vita contingat, sitque non alia quam ex peccatis? Neg.
units.tr: III. Will there be no future resurrection of bodies after death, but all resurrection occur in this life, and be nothing other than out of sins? No.

units.la: Valentinus Weigelius, Theologus Augustanæ Consessionis in Misnia, circa annum MDLXXII. doctrinâ suâ novâ multos ita dementavit, ut cjus libri, quos, plures scripsit, linguâ Germanicâ omnes, avidius arrepti, & diversorum manibus versati, nonnullos in
units.tr: Valentine Weigel, theologian of the Augsburg Confession in Meissen, around the year 1572, by his new doctrine drove so many mad that his books, which he wrote in great number, all in German, were eagerly seized and handled by many hands, and led some away

units.la: &c Sectam, quam VVeigelianam appellant, abduxerint, cum Magistro pariter insanientes. Siquidem hic leviter modo doctus, & Scriptis Paracelsicis innutritus, ab hoc praesertim, & Paulo Lautensack, Pictore & Organista Norimbergensi, aliam, quam suam passim vocat, Theologiam cudit, miram, insulsam, quin improbam. Nonnulli adversus illam scripserunt magnis & operosis tractatibus, nos brevem, de Paradoxis & Heterodoxis VVeigelianis anno cIↄ Iↄ c xlvi. dedimus, ad Reverendum virum, & amicum nostrum, Ecclesiastem Amstelodamensem, Iohannem Rulicium: ubi ex scriptis suis hominem, miraque ejus dogmata expressissimus, quem in secunda hac Editione exhibere, haud inconsultum judicamus hic inserere.
units.tr: into the sect which they call Weigelian, going mad along with their master. For he, only slightly learned and nourished on Paracelsian writings, especially from him and from Paul Lautensack, painter and organist of Nuremberg, coined another theology, which he everywhere calls his own: wonderful, insipid, indeed wicked. Some wrote against it in large and laborious treatises; we gave a short one, On the Paradoxes and Heterodoxies of Weigel, in 1646, to the reverend man and our friend, the minister of the Church at Amsterdam, Johannes Rulicius, in which, from his writings, we set out the man and his remarkable dogmas. We judge it not ill-advised to insert that here in this second edition.

units.la: Inter varios hujus nostri saeculi, & Ecclesiae Turbones, censendus venit, idque suo magno merito M. Valentinus VVeigelius, pastor Augustanae Confess. Zscopaunensis in Misnia, qui ex Trismegisto potius, atque Paracelso, quam ex scriptura, de rebus divinis judicium tulit, & circa annum cIↄ Iↄ c xl i. fanaticis libris innotuit, quomodo de eo Ioh. Micraelius, in Syntagmate histor. Fuit homo stolidus, & audax, qui sacris studiis, & philosophiae gustu immaturo abusus, ad paradoxa & putida impotentis cerebri somnia divulganda atque extollenda videtur datus. Nihilque adeo miratus saepe fui, quam hominem ineptum istiusmodi naenias ausum fuisse agitare scriptis, vel etiam animo; maximè verò, tot facile fautores imprudenter reperisse, atque etiamnum alicujus ab ullis fieri. Habet furor hic calamitosissimo hoc saeculo, fautores & laudatores haud paucos, qui magnatum quoque aulas tentant, si quâ ratione capita inficere, & per ea reliqua membra conficere forteam possint, de eodem VVendelinus, in dedic. Theol. sue Christiane, ubi aliqua ejus attingit: & Bohemus in epit. histor. Eccles. pag. 1011. multos in GerGermaniâ, quasi contagione quâdam miserè infecit; etiam in nostris provinciis & urbibus vicinis, multos ex simplicioribus & incautioribus non tantùm, sed & eruditis dementavit. Contra VVeigelium ex professo scripserunt, Nicolaus Hunnius, Theodorus Thummius, lib. cui tit. Impietas VVeigeliana: Iohannes VVeberus, Paulus Vlrici, Andreas Merckius, Frid. Balduinus disp. de communione nostri, Anno cIↄ Iↄ c xvııı. Christianus Becmannus exercitatione Theol. xxı. etiam aliqua in epistagmate ıı. Iosua Stegmannus ad refut. Photinianismi. & spissum tractatum Iohannes Crocius, cui titulum fecit Anti-VVeigelius. Caeterum ut studiosis quoque hujusce Erronis dogmata (non ita fortè cognita, quamvis nomine satis celebri in Germaniâ, libris ejus nisi Germanico idiomate scriptis,) aliquatenus constent, haud abs re fore putavi, ea, quae aliquando studiosè ex libris ejus congessi, occasione datâ exponere, atque si necesse videbitur, refutare: quamvis in istiusmodi παραπολογισμοῖς semper judicem, non adeò de responsione, quam opinionis ipsius indagine, ac genuinâ duntaxat explicatione laborandum esse.
units.tr: Among the various disturbances of this age and of the Church, Master Valentine Weigel rightly deserves to be counted, and to his great discredit, as pastor of the Augsburg Confession at Zschopau in Meissen, who passed judgment on divine matters from Trismegistus and Paracelsus rather than from Scripture, and became known around 1641 through fanatical books, as John Micraelius says of him in his Syntagma historicum. He was a stupid and bold man, who, abusing sacred studies and an immature taste for philosophy, seems to have been given to spreading and extolling paradoxes and the foul dreams of an impotent brain. I have often been amazed that such a fool dared to stir up such trifles in writing, or even in thought; and most of all that so many supporters were imprudently found, and still are found by some. This madness has, in this most calamitous age, not a few supporters and praisers, who try even the courts of magnates, if by some means they can infect the heads and through them destroy the remaining members, says Wendelin of him, in the dedication of his Christian Theology, where he touches on some of his points; and Bohemus, in the Epitome of Church History, p. 1011: he miserably infected many in Germany, as if by a certain contagion; also in our provinces and neighboring cities he drove mad many, not only of the simpler and less cautious, but also of the learned. Against Weigel, professedly, wrote Nicolaus Hunnius; Theodore Thummius, in a book titled Weigelian Impiety; Johannes Weber; Paul Ulrich; Andreas Merck; Friedrich Balduin, in a disputation on communion; in 1618 Christian Becmann, in his Theological Exercise 21, and also something in his Epistagma 2; Josua Stegmann, in his refutation of Photinianism; and Johannes Crocius, who gave the title Anti-Weigel to a thick treatise. Moreover, so that the dogmas of this error may also be somewhat known to students (not perhaps so well known, though celebrated enough by name in Germany, since his books are written only in the German language), I thought it would not be out of place to set out, when occasion offers, those things which I once carefully gathered from his books, and, if need be, to refute them. Yet in such apologetic labors I always judge that the effort should be directed not so much to the reply as to the investigation of the opinion itself and its genuine explanation.

units.la: Ac primum est quod admiremur fastuosam hominis de se, ac suâ Theologiâ jactantiam: suam dico, & ita ipse in praefat. libri, cui titulum fecit Astrologia Theologizata, non semel: hac mea Theologia astrologizata. In Confess. cap. ix: hic omnia ad caelestem, ac terrenam eruditionem necessaria quaerenda sunt, dico propterea, quia talis vera magica Theologia, ac permanebit Theologia VVeigelii, omniumque fidelium, & cap. xviii. accipe Theologiam VVeigelii, atque ad γνῶσιν σαωτῆρι pervenies. Talem & librum scripsit superbo titulo, studii Universalis, quem in libri frontispicio ita nimirum exponit: studium universale, hoc est, quidquid omnino à mundi exordio usque ad ejus finem vixit, quidquid scriptum, aut doctum, vel etiamnum scribi, aut disci possit, quid recte discere. Scire, ac docere sit, quid omnes hoc tempore debeant studere, quam plane facilis, plane difficilis Theologia, omniaque ad discendum sint, quod unice ac solum per preces omnia citra taedium, ac molestiam consequamur ac discamus, etiam de scholis, ac studiis hominum. Quas verborum ampullas, & portentosum, atque ridiculum stylum, non aliter, ac epistolam Manichaei fundamentalem, vel Davidis Georgii, aut Antonii Pocquii, vel Paramira Paracelsica suspicimus. Scripsit etiam librum, tit. Captura aurea, hoc est, ad res omnes absque ullo errore agnoscendas, multis Doctissimis incognita, attamen omnibus scita necessaria. Quid ad haec Scaliger diceret, si videret? qui lib. III. epist. cclxxII. ad Ioannem Caselium: quot Teutonicorum scriptorum portenta nundinae Francofurtenses produxerunt? quis in reliquâ Europâ aut plura vidit, aut petulantiora impotentium animorum argumenta, quam sunt illa lemmata librorum, partim Germanico sermone, partim Latino, sed à Germanis furiis concepta? Quis tam perditus, ut legendis illis bonas horas perdere postulet? &c. Hominis nostri jactantiam accuratius lustremus. In Guothi seauton (& hic ejus libellus, cujus farinae plures) part. III. pag. 36. nullus finis contentionum, &c. usque quo Theologiam Pauli Lautensack & Paracelsi intelligemus. Scilicet ab illis, quos Authores passim deprædicat, orbi dementando natis, pacem suam Ecclesiae tandem emendicare necessum habebunt. Hosque sequitur ut plurimum Authores, quasi laudatissimos & Classicos. Inter Veteres quidem effert Trismegistum, Platonem, Dion. Areopagitam: ex recentioribus, Muncerum, Swencfeldum, Hosiandrum, Taulerum, Paulum Lautensack, qui Pictor & Organista Norimbergensis fuit; maximè autem Paracelsum, hominem sordidum, ebrium, atque impium, si non etiam magum, de quo Oporinus in epist. ad Solenandr. Orare nunquam audivi, neque vidi, neque curabat etiam Ecclesiastica sacra. Ibid. Erat totis diebus & noctibus, dum ego ipsi familiariter per biennium fere convixi, ebrietati & crapulæ deditum, ut vix unam atque alteram horam sobrium eum reperire licuerit. Idem de eo testimonium perhibet Georgius Vetterus, ejus item per biennium individuus comes: nihil magis metui, quoties ebrius erat, erat autem frequenter, quam ut agmina Diabolorum accesseret. Bullingerus idem Tigurì in eo observavit. Ita Paracelsus studiosos Tigurinos in epist. combibones optimos salutat. & Zuingerus Basileæ, vide Beckmann. exercit. Theolog. xx i. Sennertum, de consens. & dissens. Chymicorum, cap. iv. xiii. & in dedicat. Andr. Libavium, in confid. famæ R. C. cap. ix. Melchiorem Adamum in vita Medicorum, de Theophrasto Paracelso. Vicunque de ejus re medicâ varie judicetur, de Theologiâ se continent, vel maximi ejus admiratores.
units.tr: The first thing we should marvel at is the man's arrogant boasting about himself and his own theology. I say "his own," and he himself says so more than once in the preface to the book he titled Astrologia Theologizata: "this my astrologized theology." In the Confession, chapter 9: "here all things necessary for heavenly and earthly learning must be sought; I say this because such a true magical theology is and will remain the theology of Weigel and of all the faithful." And in chapter 18: "Take the theology of Weigel, and you will attain knowledge that saves [γνῶσιν σωτῆρι]." He also wrote a book with the proud title Universal Study, which in the frontispiece he explains as follows: "universal study, that is, whatever has lived from the beginning of the world to its end, whatever has been written or taught, or can still be written or learned, and what it is right to learn." Knowing and teaching what everyone should study at this time is, he says, a theology both perfectly easy and perfectly difficult; and everything needed for learning is obtained and learned without weariness or trouble, solely through prayer, including what is taught in schools and studied by men. We look upon these bombastic phrases and this monstrous and ridiculous style no differently than we would the fundamental epistle of Manes, or the writings of David George, Antoine Pocquet, or the Paracelsian Paramirum. He also wrote a book entitled Golden Capture: for recognising all things without any error, unknown to many learned men, yet known and necessary to all. What would Scaliger say to this if he saw it? In book 3, letter 272, to Johann Caselius, he wrote: "What monsters has the Frankfurt fair brought forth from German writers? Who in the rest of Europe has seen more, or more insolent proofs of unbalanced minds, than those title-pages of books, some in German and some in Latin, but conceived by German madmen? Who is so lost as to wish to waste good hours reading them? etc." Let us examine our man's boasting more closely. In Gnothi Seauton (this little book, and there are many of the same stuff), part 3, page 36: "There will be no end to disputes ... until we understand the theology of Paul Lautensack and Paracelsus." Clearly, those whom he everywhere proclaims as authors born to make the world mad will at last have to beg the Church for their peace. He follows these authors as a rule, as though they were most praiseworthy and classical. Among the ancients he especially extols Trismegistus, Plato, and Dionysius the Areopagite; among more recent writers, Müntzer, Swedenborg, Osiander, Tauler, and Paul Lautensack, who was a painter and organist at Nuremberg; but above all Paracelsus, a filthy, drunken and impious man, if not even a magician. Of him Oporinus writes in his letter to Solenander: "I never heard him pray, nor did I see him do so, nor did he care for even the sacred things of the Church." In the same place: "He was given to drink and gluttony every day and night, while I lived with him familiarly for nearly two years, so that one could scarcely find him sober for an hour or two." Georgius Vetter, who was likewise his inseparable companion for two years, bears the same witness: "Whenever he was drunk, which was often, I feared nothing more than that he would be joined by troops of devils." Bullinger observed the same thing about him at Zurich, where Paracelsus greets the Zurich students in a letter as "excellent boozers"; and Zwingli observed it at Basel (see Beckmann, Exercitationes Theologicae 21). See Sennert, On the Agreement and Disagreement of the Chemists, chapter 4, chapter 13, and the dedication; Andreas Libavius, On the Confidence of the Reputation of the R.C., chapter 9; and Melchior Adam, In the Lives of Physicians, on Theophrastus Paracelsus. However his medical work may be judged, even his greatest admirers keep silent about his theology.

units.la: Quercetanus: Ad Paracelsum vero quod attinet, equidem mihi nequaquam propositi ipsius Theologia patrocinium suscipere: neque ipsi in omnibus adstipulari unquam cogitavi, tanquam in ejus verba jurassem. Et dum ingenium ejus ac scientiam deprædicant, Deo an Diabolo id quodcunque in eo erat, adscribant, ambigunt. Gelius Zemeus, credo, aut quod nera influentia in eo sit naturalis, aut major S. S. gratia in eo, aut immensa dæmonum existentia. Causam, quare hunc Præceptorem adeò observare solent VVeigeliani, Rosencreutziani, qui in Fama fraterna p. 15. illum cum suo fundatore C. R. conjungunt, ut ejusdem instituti hominem, ac similes, reor esse, tum quod amet obscuris, insolitis atque miris loquutionibus sua involvere, nimirum ut saltem hinc à vulgo suspiciantur: tum, quia eodem spiritu sua jactare solcat, & reliquos omnes contemnere. Inde dicere solebat, stultissimum occipitii sui pilum (recalvaster autem erat) plus scire, quam omnes Galeni sectatores & scripta: immo & barbam suam plus experimentorum callere, quam omnes in universum Academias; quod ipse tandem Papam & Lutherum in ordinem esset redacturus, & similia.
units.tr: Quercetanus: "As for Paracelsus, I have never intended to take up the defence of his theology, nor have I ever thought to agree with him in everything, as though I had sworn to his words." And while they extol his talent and learning, they hesitate whether to ascribe whatever was in him to God or to the Devil. Gelius Zemeus: "I believe that either there is some natural influence in him, or a greater grace of the Holy Spirit in him, or a vast existence of demons." The reason why the Weigelians and Rosicrucians so often honour this teacher, who in the Fama Fraterna, page 15, join him with their founder C.R., I think is that he is a man of the same design as they are, and similar to them: partly because he loves to wrap his teachings in obscure, unusual and marvellous expressions, so that at least in this way he may be admired by the common people; and partly because he was accustomed to boast in the same spirit and to despise all others. Hence he used to say that the most foolish hair on his head (he was quite bald) knew more than all the followers and writings of Galen; indeed, that his beard had more experience of experiments than all the academies put together; and that he would at last bring Pope and Luther into line, and similar things.

units.la: Ad V Veigelium. non satis ei sua jactasse, nisi sub poenâ salutis (quasi alter Papa, quem tamen adeò insectatur, simul & aemulatur,) eadem urgeat. In praef. stud. Vniverf. atque hoc meum studium universale tenentur addiscere, si modo aeternum vivere, ac salvari cupiant. In Confess. Cap. IX. Hic omnia ad caelestem ac terrenam eruditionem necessaria, quaerenda sunt. In dialogo de Christianismo cap. IX. introducit Concionatorem ideò damnatum, quod à V Veigelio sc. dissensisset.
units.tr: Weigel did not think he had boasted enough unless he pressed the same claims under pain of salvation (like another Pope, whom nevertheless he so fiercely attacks and at the same time imitates). In the preface to Universal Study: "And they must learn this my universal study, if they wish to live and be saved for ever." In the Confession, chapter 9: "Here all things necessary for heavenly and earthly learning must be sought." In the dialogue On Christianity, chapter 9, he introduces a preacher condemned for the reason that he had disagreed with Weigel.

units.la: Porrò, quò pateat non frustra eum sua vendicare, pansophiam, panepistemon (nihil scilicet Trithemio, aliisque cedens) simul omnia promittit. Titulum studii universalis jam audivimus, denuò illum repeti, nemo, nisi qui molestiam, velit. In praef. inquit: Studium hoc universale, sive encyclopaedia omnium scientiarum, omnes totius mundi homines tangit, atque hoc meum studium universale tenentur addiscere. Ibid. hoc studium universale, non particulare aliquod est, sed omnia continet, quidquid homines in terris addiscere debent, ac possunt. Nemo scientiâ suâ, eruditione, sapientiâ ulterius progredi potest; primum est in mundo, etiam ultimum erit, verissimum studium, quod veritatem omnem absque errore proponit &c. quâ universum mundum, omnesque creaturas cognoscamus &c. eam cognitionem non dabit tibi ars brevis Raymundi Lullii, neque encyclopaedia disciplinarum Scaligeri, neque Trithemius Spanheimensis qui spatio bihorii idiotam latinè docebat. Ideoque accedite huc, quotquot eruditionem mavis &c. Non alio studio fratres Roseae crucis in Confess. cap. IV. extollunt meditationes Patris sui Christiani Rosenkreutzii, (cui originem & fundationem suam affingunt) utopicas, quas super omnibus, quae nunquam à mundi exordio ab hominibus sive per divinam revelationem, sive ministerio Angelorum, acumine ingenii, diuturnâ observatione, exercitio aut experientiâ inventa, excogitata, producta, emendata, aut propagata, hahabuit, egregias adeo ac praestantes, ut si vel omnes perirent libri, & Deo ita disponente, omnium scriptorum, ac totius rei litterariae accideret interitus, tamen posteritas ex hisce solis novum fundamentum ponere, ac novam veritatis confirmationem erigere denuo posset. &c.
units.tr: Furthermore, to show that he does not vainly claim these things for himself, he promises all at once pansophia and panepistemon (yielding nothing, of course, to Trithemius or others).
