We have already heard the title Universal Study; no one would be willing to take the trouble of having it repeated again. In the preface he says: "This universal study, or encyclopaedia of all the sciences, concerns all the men of the whole world, and all must learn this my universal study." In the same place: "This universal study is not some partial thing, but contains everything that men on earth ought and are able to learn. No one can advance further in knowledge, learning or wisdom. It is the first in the world and will also be the last, the most true study, which sets forth all truth without error ... by which we may know the whole world and all creatures ... This knowledge will not be given you by the short art of Raymond Lull, nor by Scaliger's encyclopaedia of the disciplines, nor by Trithemius of Spanheim, who taught an idiot Latin in the space of two hours." Therefore, come here, all you who prefer learning, etc. The Brethren of the Rose Cross in the Confession, chapter 4, praise with no other aim the meditations of their father, Christian Rosenkreutz (to whom they ascribe their origin and foundation), which are utopian, and which, concerning all things that from the beginning of the world have been discovered, thought out, produced, corrected or propagated by men, whether through divine revelation, through the ministry of angels, by sharpness of wit, long observation, practice or experience, he possessed; so excellent and outstanding that even if all books perished, and by God's disposition all the writings and all literary culture were destroyed, posterity could nevertheless lay a new foundation from these alone and raise a new confirmation of truth again. Etc.

units.la: Inscriptionem libri VVeigeliani Captura aurea audivimus; libellus ipse ita incipit: In nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi hunc libellum conscripsi, quo etiam Idiotae eo cognitionis pervenient, ut plures Doctissimos, Doctores, & eruditos superare possint, atque facile ostendere, eruditorum plurimos in singulis tribus facultatibus caecutire. In Gnothi seauton, part. III. pag. 8. adducit litteras Petri Loriotti, Itali (ejusdem, qui commentarium de Contractibus ad axiomata scripsit) ad Sereniss. Saxoniae Elect. Augustum, quibus ille, non sublimium modo & difficillimorum dictorum, verum & universae naturae intellectum promittit per Cabalam numerorum, praecipue ex Apoc. xiii. numeri 666. unde omnia sua expromunt, p. 5. unicus liber Apocalypseos principium, medium, ac finis est universa S. Scriptura, & Theologia. pag. 8. Universa Biblia, & omnes fideles Doctores te ducunt ad numerum bestiae 666. illud noveris, noveris & te ipsum, & omnia: illud agunt Lautensack, & Paracelsus omnibus suis scriptis, pag. 43. &c.
units.tr: We have heard the title of Weigel's book Golden Capture; the little book itself begins thus: "In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ I have written this little book, by which even laymen will attain such knowledge that they can surpass many very learned men, doctors and scholars, and easily show that most learned men in each of the three faculties are blind." In Gnothi Seauton, part 3, page 8, he adduces the letter of Pietro Loriotti of Italy (the same who wrote a commentary on the Contracts in axioms) to the most serene Elector of Saxony, Augustus. In it Loriotti promises an understanding not only of sublime and very difficult sayings but of all of nature, through the Cabala of numbers, especially the number 666 in Revelation 13. From this they bring forth all their teaching. Page 5: "The single book of the Apocalypse is the beginning, middle and end of all Holy Scripture and theology." Page 8: "The whole Bible and all faithful teachers lead you to the number of the beast, 666. Know this, know yourself and all things. This is what Lautensack and Paracelsus do in all their writings," page 43, etc.

units.la: Ut homo vanus reliquos prae se contemnat, Patres, Doctores omnes, cujuscunque religionis quosvis, scientias omnes, artes, scholas, Academias, Ecclesias, quin & condemnet, videamus porro; quo primum hominis genium cognoscamus, & mores, ex quibus tum paria dogmata. Scripsit & peculiarem tractatum, hoc tit: brevis ac dilucida demonstratio, quod hisce temporibus in universa Europa vix ulla in omnibus Ecclesiis, ac scholis cathedra sit, in qua non pseudo-propheta, pseudo-Christus, seductor populi, falsus Scripturae interpres, quique non sub numero caeterum Doctorum comprehendatur, &c. Dicti libri pag. 121. Propono mibi Pontificios, Lutheranos, Calvinianos, quamque sectam seorsim, & confero characteres Antichristi: & ex eorum signaturis facile cognosco quantopere cum pseudo-Prophetis conveniant, atque ulterius dico, universum statum Ecclesiasticum cum omnibus suis scholis in N.Testamento in seculo filii, de maledicta arbore esse, in qua dehinc bonus fructus nec crescit, neque unquam crescere potest. & pag. 123. 125. peccatores in Spiritum Sanctum, illos appellat. De Monasterienfibus Anabaptistis haud absimilia testatur Hortensius, in histor. Anabapt. pag. 39. illud autem palam affirmarunt, à Christi & Apostolorum temporibus verbum Dei pure non fuisse traditum, nec justitiam viguisse. Nicolaus Blesdikius in historiâ soceri sui Davidis Georgii pag. 174. Conscripsit etiam tunc temporis libellum, cui titulum dedit: oratio ad mundi sapientes & Potentes &c. In hoc scripto omnes sua scientia & eloquentia vires explicavit, ut ostenderet, suisque persuaderet, omnes omnium in toto orbe ecclesiarum & sectarum Doctores destitutos esse verâ veritatis luce & efficaciâ: eam autem jam soli sibi caelitus esse revelatam. Quare doctrinam suam, verbum perfectionis appellabat Blesdik. pag. 19.
units.tr: So that a vain man may despise all the rest, the Fathers, all teachers of whatever religion, all sciences, arts, schools, academies and churches, and even condemn them, let us go on and see first what kind of man he is, and his character, from which his doctrines follow. He also wrote a separate treatise with this title: A brief and clear demonstration that in these times there is scarcely any chair in all the churches and schools of the whole of Europe in which there is not a false prophet, a false Christ, a seducer of the people, a false interpreter of Scripture, and one who is not counted among the other teachers, etc. In the same book, page 121, I set before myself the Papists, the Lutherans, the Calvinists and each sect separately, and I compare them with the marks of Antichrist; and from their signs I easily recognise how far they agree with the false prophets. He further says that the whole ecclesiastical state, with all its schools, in the New Testament, in the century of the Son, is a cursed tree, on which good fruit neither grows nor can ever grow. On pages 123 and 125 he calls them sinners against the Holy Spirit. Hortensius, in his history of the Anabaptists, page 39, bears witness to something not unlike this about the Anabaptists of Münster: they openly affirmed that since the times of Christ and the Apostles the word of God had not been transmitted in its purity, nor had justice flourished. Nicolaus Blesdik, in the history of his father-in-law David Georgius, page 174. At that time he also wrote a little book, which he entitled: An address to the wise and powerful of the world, etc. In this writing he set out all the powers of his learning and eloquence, so as to show, and to persuade his followers, that all the teachers of all the churches and sects in the whole world lack the true light and power of truth, and that this truth has now been revealed to him alone from heaven. Therefore Blesdik called his own doctrine the word of perfection (Blesdik, page 19).

units.la: Alios omnes VVeigelius, in Confess. cap. xiv. exortes spiritus sancti appellat. Prioris lib. pag. 128. ideoque statuo, sentio, atque ita apud me concludo, neminem istorum omnium habere donum intelligendi, & interpretandi mysteria sacrarum litterarum. Confess. cap. vi. admodum stomachatur in Lutherum, Philippum, ac Pomeranum, quod Theophrasti commentaria in Matthaeum, & Pauli Lautensack Apocalypsim, non receperint. Regno Dei ideo expelluntur, at sua culpa, quoniam Christum neque audire, neque habere voluerunt. Ejusdem styli exordium supra vidimus libri Capt. aur. Confess. p. 34. Vera Theologia facilis est, neque artes dicendi, Grammaticam, Dialecticam, Rhetoricam, linguas requirit, utpote nullius usus, & Apostoli ac Prophetae absque illis [?]lis nihilominus Theologi fuerunt. Et pag. 31. & 41. Dominica reminiscere: nemo sibi patitur facile persuaderi, Academias omnes exortes esse Christi, & veritatis, quemadmodum ille liber de arbore scientiae boni & mali ostendit. Astrol. Theologiz. cap. xxix. Contemtores huius Astrologiae Theologizatae non solum S. Scripturam rejiciunt; verum & Deum odio habent, qui illos rationales fecerat. Similiter in Patres, Hieronymum, Augustinum, Ambrosium, ex aequo in omnes, & quotquot illorum scripta legunt, vel scientias, linguas, artes addiscunt, impotenter debacchatur. De vita Christi, cap. xliii. In studio Universi passim. Astrol. Theolog. cap. xiv. De sui renuntiat. cap. xliii. Quum tamen ipse homo ineptissimus, ubi modo potest, & ridicule saepe, Graecorum quantulumcumque sapit, etiam citra interpretationem nonnunquam, & Astrologica intermiscet in scriptis, etiam in concionibus ad populum, atque notulis Astronomicis &c. saepius utitur. Cujus quoque commaris est, quod in Postillâ xxi. Domin. post Trinitat. recitat epistolas Abagari Toparchae Esseni ad Christum, & Christi ad illum, apocryphas.
units.tr: Weigel, in his Confession, chapter 14, calls all others strangers to the Holy Spirit (the earlier book, page 128): and so I determine, feel and conclude within myself that none of them all has the gift of understanding and interpreting the mysteries of the sacred letters. In chapter 6 of the same Confession he rages greatly against Luther, Melanchthon and Pomeranus, because they did not accept the commentaries of Theophrastus on Matthew, or Paul Lautensack's Apocalypse. They are therefore cast out of the kingdom of God, and by their own fault, since they were unwilling either to hear Christ or to have him. We saw the opening of the same style earlier in the book Captivus aureus, Confession, page 34: true theology is easy, and it does not require the arts of speaking, grammar, dialectic, rhetoric, or languages, being of no use; and the Apostles and Prophets were theologians without them. And on pages 31 and 41, Dominica reminiscere: no one easily allows himself to be persuaded that all academies are strangers to Christ and to truth, as that book on the tree of the knowledge of good and evil shows. Astrologia Theologizata, chapter 29: the despisers of this Theologized Astrology not only reject Holy Scripture, but also hate God, who made them rational. In the same way he rages without restraint against the Fathers, Jerome, Augustine and Ambrose, and equally against all who read their writings or learn sciences, languages and arts. On the life of Christ, chapter 43; In the study of the universe, passim; Astrologia Theologizata, chapter 14; On self-renunciation, chapter 43. Yet he himself, a most inept man, whenever he can, and often ridiculously, knows a little Greek, sometimes even without translation, and mixes astrological matters into his writings, even into sermons to the people, and uses astronomical notes, etc., quite often. Also a fault of the same kind is that in his Postill, the twenty-first Sunday after Trinity, he recites as genuine the letters of Abgar, ruler of Edessa, to Christ and Christ's to him, which are apocryphal.

units.la: Hactenus hominem vidimus, ejusque indolem; ubi tria observanda, quae totidem principia & causae semper omnium haeresium, schismatum, & turbarum in Ecclesia: Ambitionem puta, audaciam, (uti semper, qui ambitiosi, etiam audaces,) & studium novitatis. De Montano haeretico Eusebius, histor. Eccles. lib. v. cap. xvi. Ficus quidam in Mysia Phrygiae esse fertur, homine Ardabau, in quo primum Montanum quendam, qui nuper ad fidem venerat, sub Grato Proconsule Asiae, immoderata primatus cupiditate captum, aditum ad se adversario praebuisse, lymphaticumque factum, ac subito in mentis obsessione & abalienatione constitutum insanivisse, atque insolita contra traditionem & consuetudinem antiqua successionis sub specie Prophetiae loqui coepisse, ferunt. De Novato idem, lib. vi, cap. xliii. Novatus Romanae Ecclesiae clesiae presbyter, superbia contra lapsos inflatus. Sabbatius itemum, Novatianorum presbyter, in ordine presbyterii sui manere nolens, sed inde ad episcopatum aspelans, inquit Socrates, isdem temporibus ab Ecclesia Novatianorum discessit. lib. VI. cap. V. XIII. De Tatiano, & Severianis, Platina in vit. Pii I. illis quoque temporibus laudabatur & Tatianus Vir doctissimus, quam diu ab opinione Iustini Martyris praeceptoris sui non discessit. Nam postea inflatus opinione sui novam haeresim condidit, quam postea Severus auxit, unde Severiani appellati. Et de Paulo Samosateno, in vita Dionysii I. Is enim inflatus opinione sui ipsius, ac tribunal altius quaerens, negabat Dei Filium e caelo descendisse, sed a Maria cepisse originem, & initium e terra habuisse. Nempe ut Ioannes Climacus, author haud contemnendus, de discretione grad. XXVI, in bibliotheca Patrum, loquitur: hoc autem spiritus immundi in illorum ut plurimum cordibus agere solent, qui inani gloria student, & illorum imprimis, qui externa sapientiae litteris eruditi sunt, ut illos sensum fallentes in haereses, & blasphemias deducant. Vere dixit Salomon Prov. XXVI. 11. 25. Ampluat animo suo miscet contentionem. Vide Deut. XVIII. 20. & Apostolus 1 Tim. VI. 3. ἵνα τετύφωται μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενος &c. vers. 4. addit: τετύφωται μηδὲν nihil sciens, ἀλλὰ νοσῶν περὶ ζητήσεις. Philipp. II. 3. μηδὲ κατὰ κενοδοξίαν [?] duo illa conjungit. De Davide Georgii, Blesdick, pag. 112. quod & apud Vbbonem Emmium est, lib. de Spiritu Dav. Georgii pag. 47. Erat David homo exigue quidem peritiae, sed phrantiae maxime, atque hinc tantum tribuebat suis libris &c. Unde ut in libris ejus perpetuo illud, Nota bene ab Authore ipso suis appositum, & titulum libri admirabilis vah quam fastuosum fecit: Liber Mirabilium, quo quod a mundo conclusum revelatur.
units.tr: So far we have seen the man and his disposition, where three things are to be observed, which are as many principles and always the causes of all heresies, schisms and disturbances in the Church: ambition, I mean, boldness (as always, those who are ambitious are also bold), and a zeal for novelty. Concerning Montanus the heretic, Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 16: They say there is a certain place called Ficus in Mysia in Phrygia, at a village called Ardabau, where a certain Montanus, who had lately come to the faith, was first seized under the Proconsul of Asia, Gratus, by an immoderate desire for primacy, and gave his opponent an opening against himself; becoming frenzied and falling into a sudden obsession and derangement of mind, he began to rave and to speak under the appearance of prophecy, contrary to the tradition and ancient custom of succession. Of Novatus, the same author, book 6, chapter 43: Novatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, puffed up with pride against the fallen. Likewise Sabbatius, a presbyter of the Novatians, unwilling to remain in the order of his presbyterate, but aspiring from there to the episcopate, says Socrates, at the same time left the Church of the Novatians (book 6, chapters 5 and 13). Concerning Tatian and the Severians, Platina, in the life of Pius I: At that time Tatian, a most learned man, was also praised, as long as he did not depart from the opinion of Justin Martyr, his teacher. For afterwards, puffed up with his own opinion, he founded a new heresy, which Severus later increased, whence they were called Severians. And concerning Paul of Samosata, in the life of Dionysius I: For he, puffed up with his own opinion, and seeking a higher tribunal, denied that the Son of God had come down from heaven, but said that he had his origin from Mary and had his beginning from the earth. Indeed, as John Climacus, an author not to be despised, speaks in On the discernment of degrees, XXVI, in the Bibliotheca Patrum: Now the unclean spirit is wont to work this chiefly in the hearts of those who strive after empty glory, and especially of those who are learned in the external letters of wisdom, so that deceiving their senses it may lead them into heresies and blasphemies. Solomon truly said, Prov. 26:11, 25: He who is puffed up in his mind stirs up strife. See Deut. 18:20, and the Apostle, 1 Tim. 6:3: ἵνα τετύφωται μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενος [that he is puffed up, knowing nothing] (v. 4) adds: τετύφωται μηδὲν [he is puffed up, knowing nothing], ἀλλὰ νοσῶν περὶ ζητήσεις [but sick about questions]. Phil. 2:3, μηδὲ κατὰ κενοδοξίαν [nor through vainglory]: he joins those two things. Concerning David Georgius, Blesdik, page 112, which is also found in Ubbo Emmius, On the spirit of David Georgius, page 47: David was a man of little skill, but of the greatest arrogance, and therefore he attributed so much to his books, etc. Hence, as in his books, that phrase constantly appears, noted well by the author himself, and he made the title of his book boastfully grand: The Book of Wonders, in which what has been hidden from the world is revealed.

units.la: Quod ambitio in ejusmodi hominibus concipit, audacia promovet, & pruriens novarum rerum ingenium incunctanter exstimulat. De Apollinari, Ruffinus lib. 11. cap. xx. Vir sane in ceteris instructus, sed dum contentionis vitio nimis agitur, & adversus omne, quod quisque dixerat, ire obvius gestit, jactatione ingenii male fortis, haeresim ex contentione generavit, asserens solum corpus, non etiam animam a Domino in dispensatione suscep-tam. Quo spiritu & Socinus suum illud, disputat contra quivis. de Auctorit. S. Script. cap. 1. pag. 36. & Lection. Sacr. pag. 150. quidquid plerique contra sentiant, proferre solet.
units.tr: What ambition conceives in such men, audacity promotes, and a restless talent for novelties incessantly spurs on. Concerning Apollinaris, Rufinus, book 11, chapter 20: A man indeed well instructed in other matters, but while he is carried away by the fault of contentiousness, and eagerly sets himself against everything that anyone has said, through the boasting of an ill-directed talent he generated a heresy out of strife, asserting that the Lord assumed only a body in the dispensation, and not also a soul. With this same spirit Socinus too is accustomed to put forward his saying, he disputes against whoever (On the Authority of Holy Scripture, chapter 1, page 36; and Lectiones Sacrae, page 150): whatever most people think to the contrary.

units.la: Haud dissimile Valentini V Veigelii ingenium, quod portentosa adeo eructavit dogmata: quae propositurus, lubet iisdem verbis praefari, quibus Irenaeus, ad haereses Valentini, & suorum: Similia quidem nobis loquentes, dissimilia vero sentientes, necessarium duxi, cum legerim commentarios ipsorum, quemadmodum ipsi dicunt, Valentini discipulorum, quibusdam autem ipsorum & congressus, & apprehendens sententiam ipsorum, manifestare tibi dilectissime, portentuosissima, & altissima mysteria eorum, quae non omnes capiunt, quia non omnes cerebrum habent; tu cognoscens ea, omnibus iis, qui sunt secum, manifesta facias, & praecipias eis servare se a profundo insensationis, & ejus, quae est in Deum blasphemationis.
units.tr: Valentinus' disposition is not unlike that of Weigel, which belched forth such monstrous doctrines. As I am about to set them out, I am pleased to preface them with the same words that Irenaeus used against the heresies of Valentinus and his followers: Although speaking similar things to us, yet holding dissimilar opinions, I thought it necessary, since I had read their commentaries, as they themselves call them, of the disciples of Valentinus, and having met some of them and grasped their opinion, to make known to you, most beloved, their monstrous and most lofty mysteries, which not all can grasp, because not all have a brain; you, knowing them, should make them plain to all who are with you, and should instruct them to keep themselves from the depth of unreason and of that blasphemy which is against God.

units.la: Dogmata V Veigelii in duas classes dispono: Communia enim habet cum aliis haereticis; & propria, ac singularia sibi. Vti neutris refutandis diu insistemus, ita minime prioribus, quae ubivis profligata satis & confessa, facileque confutari possunt. Qualia de Scriptura, Deo, Christo, ac nostra salute.
units.tr: I divide the dogmas of V. Veigelius into two classes. Some he holds in common with other heretics, and others are peculiar and singular to himself. I will not dwell long on refuting either class, and least of all on the first, which has been overthrown and conceded almost everywhere and can be easily refuted. Such are his views on Scripture, God, Christ and our salvation.

units.la: De Scriptura, ejusque litterali & spirituali intellectu, nugas Swenckfeldianas, & Enthusiasticas sequitur. Capit autem cap. xx. In praefat. dialogi cap. 11. &c. Micraelius jam dicto loco: Literalem verbi sensum vocat inutilem, quaerit & commendat allegoricum, eumque ex inspiratione Spiritus Sancti discendum credit.
units.tr: From his views on Scripture, and on its literal and spiritual understanding, he derives Swenckfeldian and enthusiastic trifles. He treats this in chapter 20, in the preface of the dialogue, chapter 11, and so on. Micraelius, in the place already cited: He calls the literal sense of the word useless, seeks and commends the allegorical sense, and believes that it must be learned from the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: De Deo, Confess. pag. 44. quod si Deus affectus non hahaberet, nec velle, operari, poenitere, nullam plane Deum habemus, Christum nullum, vel modo Semi-Deum, nobis asui, quemadmodum pseudo-Theologi Trinitatem non recte agnoscunt, teste Augustana confess. & aliis scriptis. Mitto, quae horrenda de Deo, & Christo dicit, ex combinatione Contradictoriorum, de quo mox.
units.tr: On God, Confession p. 44: If God had no affections, neither willing, working nor repenting, we would have no God at all, no Christ, or at most a demi-god for ourselves. In this he, like the pseudo-theologians, does not rightly acknowledge the Trinity, as the Augsburg Confession and other writings attest. I pass over the horrible things he says about God and Christ from the combination of contradictories, which I will come to shortly.

units.la: De vita Christi cap. 1. & . xl iii i. docet, Christi carnem coelitus descendisse, neque ex Maria assumtam: nempe id ut commune haberet cum prisco illo Valentino haeretico, adversus quem Irenaeus, lib. 1. cap. 1. sunt, qui dicunt emisisse eum Christum filium suum, sed animalem, & de hoc per Prophetas locutum esse. Esse autem hanc, qui per Mariam transierit, quemadmodum aqua per tubum transiit. Notate antiquum simile, quo in hoc argumento vel olim haeretici usi fuerunt. Et lib. iii. cap. xi. Iesum per Mariam dicunt pertransisse; quasi aquam per tubum, & cap. xxxii. inscribitur, contra eos, qui dicunt eum nihil de Maria accepisse. Ita etiam Appelles, Marcion, Eutyches: qua de re vide Tertullianum adversus Marcionem; & alio libro de carne Christi. Adversus Appellem, unde materia, si non ex ea qualitate, in qua videbatur? de sideribus inquiunt, & de substantia superioris mundi mutuatus est carnem. Oro vos, si Dei filius non de vulva carnem participaturus descendit in vulvam, cur descendit in vulvam? Per virginem dicitis natum, non ex virgine &c. Vigilius Martyr adversus Eutychem: quae fuit causa Dei verbo per uterum Virginis transitum facere, si nihil inde quaerebat assumere? & lib. iii. in principio. Quorum Eutychiana haeresis in id impietatis prolapsa est errore, ut non solum verbi & carnis unam credat esse naturam, verum etiam hanc eandem carnem non de sacro Maria Virginis corpore adsumtam, sed de coeloditam (juxta infandum Valentini & Marcionis errorem) fuisse deductam, ita pertinaciter verbum carnem adserens factum, ac per virginem ac si aquas per fistulam transisse videatur, non tamen de virgine aliquid, quod nostri sit generis adsumsisse credatur, optimum datur etiam hanc impietatis partem veritatis assertione destruere, & omnem tetri dogmatis nebulosam caliginem penitus dissipare, maximè quod multum ad utriusque naturæ confessionis veritatem proficit, divinis approbare testimoniis, filium Dei humanum corpus de virginis carne assumsisse. Sed de eo ex professo non egimus, ostendimus modò antiquam Valentinianorum hæresim, ab Orthodoxis semper condemnatam, Synodo Carthaginensi iv. confirmatâ sexto concilio in Trullo: carnem ex matris visceribus habere. Addefis i. dist. xxiii c. qui episcopus. Concilium Chalcedonense, sive oecumenicum [uti loquuntur] quartum, contra Eutychem. Videatur & Baltamo in Synod. Chalced. pag. 324. Isidorus, Origin. lib. viii. Ius Canon. cap. xxiv. qu. iii. cap. quidam autem. Decret. de summa Trin. c. i. Conc. Constantinop. vi. cap. lxx ix. &c.
units.tr: On the life of Christ, chapter 1 and chapter 43, he teaches that Christ's flesh came down from heaven and was not taken from Mary. He shares this with the ancient heretic Valentinus, against whom Irenaeus (book 1, chapter 1) writes: there are those who say that he sent forth his Son Christ, but an animal one, and that this was spoken of through the prophets; and that this Christ passed through Mary as water passes through a tube. Note the old comparison, which heretics have used in this argument even in former times. And in book 3, chapter 11, Irenaeus says they claim Jesus passed through Mary as water through a pipe; and chapter 32 is headed against those who say he received nothing from Mary. So too Apelles, Marcion and Eutyches taught. On this see Tertullian against Marcion and in his other book on the flesh of Christ. Against Apelles: whence was the matter, if not from that quality in which he seemed to be? They say he borrowed the flesh from the stars and from the substance of the higher world. I beg you: if the Son of God descended not to take flesh from the womb, why did he descend into the womb? You say he was born through the virgin, not of the virgin, and so on. Vigilius the Martyr, against Eutyches: what was the purpose of the Word passing through the womb of the Virgin, if he took nothing from it? And in book 3 at the beginning: the heresy of Eutyches has fallen into such impiety through error that it not only believes the Word and the flesh to be one nature, but also that this same flesh was not taken from the holy body of the Virgin Mary, but was brought down from heaven (following the unspeakable error of Valentinus and Marcion). It so stubbornly asserts that the Word was made flesh, and seems to have passed through the virgin as water through a pipe, without its being believed that he took anything from the virgin of our kind. It is best to destroy this part of impiety by asserting the truth, and to dispel completely the murky fog of that foul doctrine, especially since it greatly advances the truth of the confession of both natures to approve by divine testimonies that the Son of God took human flesh from the flesh of the virgin. But we have not treated this professedly. We have only shown that the ancient heresy of the Valentinians, always condemned by the Orthodox, holds that the flesh came from the mother's womb, as confirmed by the fourth Synod of Carthage and the sixth council in Trullo. Add Decretum, distinction 23, chapter qui episcopus. The Council of Chalcedon, or the fourth ecumenical [as they say], against Eutyches. See also Baltamus on the Synod of Chalcedon, p. 324; Isidore, Origines, book 8; Corpus Iuris Canonici, causa 24, question 3, chapter quidam autem; Decretum, on the Holy Trinity, chapter 1; Council of Constantinople VI, canon 79, and so on.

units.la: Porrò etiam Mariam à peccato immunem facit V Veigelius, guttbi sean. part. ii. pag. 15. & lib. de situ mundi cap. xv. docet, Christi adscensum non fuisse localem. cap. xviii. inquit: Lucifer è cœlo, & Adam è Paradiso extrusi sunt, citra loci mutationem, manentes eodem loci, quo antea fuerant, sed accidens, Confess. pag. 49. quid eo die responderunt Academiæ, quod Hosiandrum cum essentiali justificatione rejecerunt, & in æternas tenebras ejicientur, cum subjectiva imputativa. Notate hominis candorem, & charitatem. Itidem in Vniversi. cap. vii. es filius Dei, non adoptivè, ut Damnati loquuntur, sed secundum sanguinem, ex Deo ipso, heres Dei. Et in Confess. pag. 52. de Orthodoxis loquitur: Diabolus, Deus & magister est illius Theologiæ. Ita isti homines solent, sua crepare, reliqua & quoscunque secum non sentientes de facili condemnare. In Astrol. Theol. cap. xx. matrimonium, unum è septem Sacramentis facit. Omitto quæ V Vendelinus, vel Micrælius loc. cit. addunt, vel Christianus Beccennus, pag. 358. &c. de simulatione, & hypocrisi; haud absimilia spiritus David-Georgiani, de quo Blesdick. pag. 185. Vbbo Emmius pag. 57. 66. 400. Calvinus contra Libert. cap. VIII. Videlicet, re ita ferente, tutò licet simulare, negare, & contra animi sententiam aliud profiteri, alteri Ecclesiæ se conjungere, atque externâ prosessione aliam mentiri, suam occultare & negare. Ad dogmata VVeigelii, sive paradoxa singularia accedo, quæ non omnia me ponere, immo forte nescire, ingenuè fateor: aliqua exhibebo, & præcipua, eaque, ut in disputationibus, in certa contracta capita, quæ quis alio forte ordine poterit & in varias quæstiones distendere, ac collocare.
units.tr: Furthermore, V. Veigelius also makes Mary free from sin (Guttbi sean, part 2, p. 15). In the book on the situation of the world, chapter 15, he teaches that Christ's ascension was not local. In chapter 18 he says: Lucifer and Adam were cast out of heaven and out of Paradise without any change of place, remaining in the same place where they had been before, but with a different condition. Confession p. 49: what did the Academy answer then, when they rejected Osiander's essential justification and said he would be cast into eternal darkness, while holding subjective imputative justification? Note the candour and charity of the man. Likewise in Universum, chapter 7: he is the Son of God, not adoptively, as the damned speak, but according to blood, from God himself, heir of God. And in Confession p. 52 he speaks of the Orthodox: the Devil is God and master of that theology. Thus these men are accustomed to boast of their own views and to condemn easily the rest, and all who do not agree with them. In Astrologia Theologica, chapter 20, he makes marriage one of the seven sacraments. I omit what Vendelinus or Micraelius add in the places cited, or what Christian Beccennus says on pp. 358 and following, about dissimulation and hypocrisy, which are not unlike the spirit of David Georg (on whom see Blesdick, p. 185), Ubbo Emmius pp. 57, 66, 400, and Calvin against the Libertines, chapter 8. Namely, since the matter so requires, it is safe to pretend, to deny, and to profess something other than one's mind, to join oneself to another church, and by external profession to lie, hiding and denying one's own view. I come to the dogmas of Veigelius, or his singular paradoxes. I frankly confess that I cannot set out all of them, indeed perhaps I do not even know them all. I will present some, and the principal ones, arranged, as in disputations, under certain headings, which another may perhaps order differently and spread out into various questions.

units.la: Paradoxum primum, de principio & origine omnis cognitionis, & scientiæ in homine, ita statuit V. Veige- lius:
units.tr: The first paradox, concerning the principle and origin of all knowledge and science in man, as V. Veigelius sets it out:

units.la: Rerum omnium semina in homine esse, & partem boni, ac mali; idque esse arbores boni & mali in Paradyso. Nullum scibile extrinsecus in nos inferri, sed in nobis latere omnia, indeque excitari. Atque illud est, quod semper inculcat, gnothi seauton. Hominem compositum dicit ex tali limo, in quo universum, & cœli terræque quidquid est, reperitur: idcirco in homine omnia, esse qui constet corpore, animâ & spiritu. Corpus ex limo terræ, scilicet aquâ & terrâ; animam ex igne & aëre, at spiritum ex sideribus & firmamenti esse, unde universum firmamentum, omnia etiam astra in homine, & astronomica quæque ex se discit. Duplicem hominem facit terrenum & cœlestem, atque ex illo omnia mundana & terrena innotescere; scilicet ex illo spiraculo vitæ [limum cœli vocat] quod Deus Adæ insufflavit. Gnothi seaut., part. III. pag. 123.
units.tr: The seeds of all things are in man, and a part of good and of evil; and these are the trees of good and evil in Paradise. No knowledge is brought into us from outside, but everything lies hidden in us and is drawn out from there. This is what he always presses: know yourself [γνῶθι σεαυτόν]. He says that man is composed of such clay that everything in the universe, and whatever there is of heaven and earth, is found in him. Therefore all things are in man, since he consists of body, soul and spirit. The body is of the clay of the earth, that is, of water and earth; the soul is of fire and air; the spirit is of the stars and of the firmament. Hence he learns from himself the whole firmament, all the stars, and every astronomical matter. He makes man twofold, earthly and heavenly, and from the heavenly part all worldly and earthly things become known, namely from that breath of life [which he calls the clay of heaven] which God breathed into Adam. Gnothi seauton, part III, p. 123.

units.la: Ita omnia elementa, firmamentum universum homo in se habet, ac insuper cum mente omnia æterna, æque ac temporalia; inde S. Scriptura studet, Apocalypsi, libro primario, Iesu Christo Deo ac homini, Vet. & N. Testamento. monstro, ex eo enim homo etiam factus, ideoque & universa scriptura in ea, omnis lex, & prophetae. Gnothi seaut. tract. III pag. 23, hic agere ipsi colendus est, nempe ipsemet sibi, ex quo omnia eruat, neque quid aliud studendum homini, quam id, quod ipse est, & unde compositus. pag. 20. & pag. 39. viam hic tibi monstrabo, omnia cognoscendi, tam in caelesti, quam terreno lumine, idque sine errore, sic per quem creavit. Te noris, omnia noris; ex quibus creatus es, id est, quaecunque, omnia enim es, & in te portas omnia, nonminus quam Deus, imo filius Dei es, ipsum ejus regni nostri, habes igitur tantundem, ac Deus. Haec vero cognitio hominem perfectum facit, si cohaeret Christi. Christus autem verus Deus, te noris, nosti & Christum Deum ac hominem, sicut is, ita & nos sumus in hoc mundo. Stud. Universal. cap. VII. Studium universale, si (quantum possibile) à scholis cognosceretur, & amplecteretur, universus mundus illuminaretur, & ad fidem Christianam accederet. Omnes chartacei libri facile comburerentur, unum modo hunc librum emerent. Hic liber pronium librorum liber continet in ludis omnia, extra intus conscriptus, hujusmodi liber non in me solum, sed in omnibus omnino hominibus est. Huc istud Trismegisti citat, p. 40. Video me in omnibus, & omnia in me, ego sum in mari & mare in me, ego sum in coelo, & coelum in me. Ego sum in inferno, & infernus in me. Ego sum in terra, & terra in me. Ego sum in arboribus, & arbores in me. Lib. de bono & malo in homine cap. VII. [illegible, ~20 letters] & in infernum, [illegible, ~20 letters], in hac mente sensus [?] cap. VI: distinguit, quomodo in homine existat cognitio rerum, sc. primo naturaliter, eo quod menti suae se habeat, sive in contemplando, exquirendo, de quo gnothi part. III. pag. 21. quam res aliqua primum ab homine inventa, dicunt, nomen quid est, sit autem jam in homine fuit, modo scripsimus ad id excitaret, agam diligenter excolere coleret. At returm supernaturalium cognitio sit, quando mens quietè & passivè se habet erga Deum, expe-ctans ab objecto infinito, ipso Deo corripi & illumina-ri, frequentando suum Sabbathum, & silentium in a-liquo cordis quasi angulo: attamen neque haec cognitio extrinsecus infertur, capt. aur. cap. xii. Licet quidem à Deo animae tiranti detur; at Deus, Spiritus, verbum in nobis sunt. Anima Sabbatizans expectat passivè operationem Dei, lib. de vitâ Christi c. xxxvi. & gnothi se: part. 1. 1. pag. 8. quicunque Doctor, vel liber te non ducet in se ipsum, te abducit in omnes errores. Atque haec de isto paradoxo, ex mente V. Veigelii sufficient; qualia etiam apud Oswaldum Crollium, in præf. Basil. Chymicæ, legens Sententiam ita explicat Eusch. Bohemus, in epitome histor. Eccles: primò homo ante cognita ac sacris omnia oblivioni tradat. Secundò, infirmatori non contradicat; sed credat. Tertiò, seipsum ex toto deserat.
units.tr: Thus man has in himself all the elements, the whole firmament, and besides, along with his mind, all things eternal as well as temporal. Hence Scripture aims, in the Apocalypse, at the first book, Jesus Christ, God and man, Old and New Testament: I show you, for from it man was also made, and therefore the whole Scripture is in it, all the law and the prophets. Gnothi seauton, tract III, p. 23. Here the only one to be cultivated is yourself, that is, yourself, from whom you draw out all things; nor is there anything else for man to study than what he himself is, and that from which he is composed. p. 20 and p. 39. Here I will show you the way of knowing all things, both by the heavenly and by the earthly light, and that without error, through him by whom he created. Know yourself, you know all things, from which you were created, that is, whatever there is, for you are all things, and you carry all things in you, no less than God; nay, you are the Son of God, you have the very kingdom of our God, and so you have as much as God. This knowledge makes man perfect, if it coheres with Christ. Christ, however, is true God; if you know yourself, you also know Christ, God and man, and as he is, so are we in this world. Studium universale, ch. VII. If the universal study were (as far as possible) known and embraced by the schools, the whole world would be enlightened and would come to the Christian faith. All printed books would easily be burned; they would buy only this one book. This book contains, in the games, all things, written within and without; a book of this kind is not only in me, but in all men without exception. Here he cites that saying of Trismegistus, p. 40: I see myself in all things, and all things in me. I am in the sea, and the sea in me; I am in heaven, and heaven in me. I am in hell, and hell in me. I am in the earth, and the earth in me. I am in the trees, and the trees in me. Book on good and evil in man, ch. VII. [illegible, about 20 letters] and into hell, [illegible, about 20 letters], in this mind the senses [?] ch. VI: he distinguishes how the knowledge of things exists in man, namely first naturally, because it has to do with his own mind, whether in contemplating or in seeking, concerning which gnothi part III, p. 21. When something first discovered by a man, they say, is a name; but it was already in man; I have only written to rouse him to cultivate it diligently. But the knowledge of supernatural things comes when the mind is quiet and passive towards God, waiting to be seized and enlightened by God himself, the infinite object, frequenting his Sabbath and silence in some corner of the heart, as it were. Yet this knowledge too is not brought in from outside. Capt. aur., ch. XII. It is indeed given by God to the thirsting soul; but God, the Spirit, and the Word are in us. The soul keeping Sabbath waits passively for the working of God. Book on the life of Christ, ch. XXXVI; and gnothi seauton, part I, p. 8: Whatever teacher or book does not lead you into yourself, leads you away into all errors. And this shall suffice concerning this paradox, according to the mind of V. Veigelius. Eusebius Bohemus, in his epitome of church history, explains the same teaching, which he reads also in Oswald Croll, in the preface to the Basilica Chymica, thus: First, a man must hand over all things previously known and sacred to oblivion. Secondly, he must not contradict the weak but believe them. Thirdly, he must forsake himself wholly.

units.la: Paradoxum secundum, de Hominis astrologiâ, ejusque renunciatione, ex mente V. Veigelii, ita se habet.
units.tr: The second paradox, concerning man's astrology and its renunciation, according to the mind of V. Veigelius, stands as follows.

units.la: Cuiuslibet hominis nativitatem Planetæ suo subesse, ait, à quo porro dependeat, qualis ipse sit, juxta placita Astrologorum de planetis, eorumque filiis, in Theol. Videlicet Saturnus omnes, qui sub eo nascuntur, colonos, operarios, agricolas, textores, fures, litigatores, iniquos Judices, carbonarios, magos, Tympanistas facit. Jupiter officia Ecclesiasticorum, eruditorum, Politicorum distribuit. Mars arma, ut milites regit, & sic porro. Ita planetae in hominem potiùs agere, quorum influxus ille sequitur: & secundum illorum cursum quomodocunque vivat sex hebdomadas dictos; at septimo, Sabbatho nimirum, etiam sibi nativitatem debet constituere, ac sequi, & priorem planè abnegare, ab ejusmodi operibus & cogitationibus abstinere, quia se nemo talis vel talis, qualis ex planetis est, in regnum coelorum admittitur. Astrol. Theol. cap. xi. sol-licitè licitè id probare satagit, nullum Saturnium, Iovialem, Martialem, Venereum &c. coelos introituum sc. pag. 35. es agricola, nauta, faber? Sub sphaera Saturni sisteris. Iam verò certum, nullum agricolam, fabrum coelos ingressurum; primò, quia in coelo nec aratrum, nec ager, neque securis, neque serra, neque lignum, ideoque omne illud sub Zodiaco manet, & cum eo interit. Secundo, nullus agricola neque faber coelos introibit, quia astrorum filius adhuc, vetus creatura est, quum modo Christianus, nova creatura coelum ingrediatur. Atque ita de omnibus, per totum illum librum progreditur; argumenta capitum nos sequimur modò, quae ad nauseam usque sufficiunt. cap. xii. nullus minerarius, ac avarus coelum introibit, solùs Christianus, utrque enim Saturni filius, qui non ad bona solùm, sed & mala influit, non quod planeta necessitent, sed saltem ducant, & praeludant. Cap. xiv. Nullus Doctor, Magister, Iurisconsultus coelum introibit, magis quam adulter. Cap. xvi. Principes, ac Duces, qui arces, & urbes muniunt, cum omni suâ armaturâ coelum non introibunt. Cap. xviii. Neque Dux, neque Rex coelum introibit, solùm puer & Christianus. Cap. xviii. nullus Aulicus, Consiliarius, Cancellarius. Cap. xix. nullus Pastor Aulicus. Quare? non est ibi aula sc. quae hisce egeat: haec ejus ratio. Bene factum, quod tempestivè hoc monet, ne scilicet aliter quis sibi amens persuadeat. Cap. xx. Conjugatus, vel mulier aeque minus coelum intrabunt, ac fornicator, vel adulter. Cap. xxi. nec parens meus, mater, frater, soror, uxor, liberi, in coelum intrabunt, neque ea cognatione beati sunt, addo neque ipse VVeigelius, solùm qui puer & Christianus. Quae febricitantis animi haec deliria! Cap. xxii. nullus Musicus, vel fidicen poterit coelum ingredi, filius Iovis est, in quinto domicilio laetitiae ac voluptatis Cap. xxiii. Nullus Astronomus, Medicus, Physicus, Philosophus, neque Magister artium, aut linguarum, coelum ingredietur. Nempe Mercurii sunt. Cap. xxiv. Papa, Cardinales, Episcopi, Concionatores, Ludimagistri, Professores caelum non intrabunt. Ratio 1. quia coelum iis non eget. 11. Mercurii sunt, in domicilio religionis, & x. dominatus in Ecclesias, Scholas. Egregie sane. Cap. xxv. Nullus monachus, ordinis religiosi, vel magus caelum intrabunt. Mercuriales sunt, ex ix. & iii. domicilio. Cap. xxvi. Nullus Alchymista: Martis & Mercurii est. Cap. xxvii. Nullus nauta, Tabellarius, Venator. Quare? Non enim in caelo aqua est naviganda, neque urbs, aut terra, quo Tabellarius mittendus, vel cuniculus aut fera captanda. Ohem, quam subtiliter!
units.tr: He says that each man's birth is subject to his own planet, on which in turn depends what he himself is, according to the decrees of the astrologers concerning the planets and their children, in Theol. Namely, Saturn makes all who are born under him into tenant farmers, labourers, farmers, weavers, thieves, litigants, unjust judges, charcoal burners, magicians, and drummers. Jupiter distributes the offices of churchmen, scholars and politicians. Mars rules arms, as soldiers, and so on. Thus the planets act upon man rather, and their influence follows him; and he must live in whatever way according to their course for six days, as they say; but on the seventh, namely the Sabbath, he must also establish and follow his own birth, and utterly renounce the former, abstaining from such works and thoughts, because no one who is such or such, as he is according to the planets, is admitted into the kingdom of heaven. Astrol. Theol., ch. XI. He labours carefully to prove that no Saturnine, Jovial, Martial, Venereal man, and so on, will enter heaven, p. 35. Are you a farmer, sailor, or smith? You stand under the sphere of Saturn. Now it is certain that no farmer or smith will enter heaven: first, because in heaven there is neither plough, nor field, nor axe, nor saw, nor wood, and so all that remains under the zodiac and perishes with it. Second, no farmer or smith will enter heaven, because a son of the stars is still an old creature, whereas only a Christian, a new creature, enters heaven. And he proceeds in the same way through that whole book about all men; we follow only the arguments of the chapters, which suffice even to nausea. Ch. XII: No miner or miser will enter heaven, only the Christian; for both are sons of Saturn, who influences not only good but also evil things, not because the planets compel, but at least they lead and foreshadow. Ch. XIV: No teacher, master, or jurist will enter heaven, any more than an adulterer. Ch. XVI: Princes and dukes who fortify citadels and cities will not enter heaven with all their armour. Ch. XVIII: Neither duke nor king will enter heaven, only the child and the Christian. Ch. XVIII: No courtier, counsellor, or chancellor. Ch. XIX: No court minister. Why? Because there is no court there, which such men need. This is his reason. It is well done that he gives this warning in good time, lest anyone foolishly persuade himself otherwise. Ch. XX: A married man, or a woman, will enter heaven no more than a fornicator or adulterer. Ch. XXI: Neither my parent, mother, brother, sister, wife, nor children will enter heaven, nor are they blessed by that kinship; I add, not even Weigelius himself, only the child and the Christian. What feverish delirium is this! Ch. XXII: No musician or harpist will be able to enter heaven; he is a son of Jupiter, in the fifth house of joy and pleasure. Ch. XXIII: No astronomer, physician, natural philosopher, philosopher, or master of arts or languages will enter heaven. Of course, they belong to Mercury. Ch. XXIV: The Pope, cardinals, bishops, preachers, schoolmasters and professors will not enter heaven. Reason 1: because heaven has no need of them. 2: they belong to Mercury, in the house of religion, and to the tenth house of dominion, in churches and schools. Truly excellent! Ch. XXV: No monk of a religious order, or magician, will enter heaven. They are Mercurial, from the ninth and third houses. Ch. XXVI: No alchemist; he belongs to Mars and Mercury. Ch. XXVII: No sailor, letter-carrier, or hunter. Why? For in heaven there is no water to sail on, nor city or land to which a letter-carrier must be sent, nor rabbit or wild beast to catch. Oh, how subtly!

units.la: Tertium Paradoxum, de cognitionis ratione, & forma docet V. Veigelius, quod cognoscens cum cognitio idem fiat realiter, atque essentialiter. Confess. cap. xiii, pag. 35. cognoscens fit unum cum cognito, sciens cum scito, intelligens cum intelligibili. Verum pseudo-Theologi nolunt ipsi essentialiter a Deo uniri, Christus ac vita ejus in non inest essentialiter; de eo loqui ac concionari quidem possunt, licet extra ipsum sint, hoc illorum negotium, opera, tenebrae, & condemnatio. Pag. 39. Informatorium nostrum hanc fert doctrinam, cognoscens & cognoscibile fiunt unum essentialiter. Mens cognoscendo, intelligendo, tangendo penetrat usque ad unicum essentialem. Et cap. xviii. In Stud. Universf. cap. vii. discens cum discendo essentialiter unitur, immo illud ipsum fit, quod discit, vel in libro legit. Rationem addicit, ex illa humanae naturae cornucopia, qua omnia in se concludit, & est. Ibidem inquit, Aristoteles, aliique philosophi Dialecticam invenerunt, sed lumine naturae ex seipsis, & ego aeque in me eam habui, ac Inventores, & Scriptores. Astrol. Theolog. cap. i. pag. 2. Studium, ac doctrina nostra dat unionem essentialem, ut discens cum discendo unum fiat, de quo schola nihil sciunt, aut scire cupiunt. Ratio in promptu, quia nimirum cum Veigelio non insaniunt. Gnothi seaut. part. iii. pag. 24. realis unio debet esse cognoscentis, & cogniti. Eadem delirria tenuit nuit Esaias Stifelius, unde Stifeliani, contra quem VVeberus scripsit.
units.tr: The third paradox, concerning the nature and form of knowledge, is taught by V. Veigelius: that the knower and the knowing become one thing really and essentially. Confession, ch. 13, p. 35: the knower becomes one with the known, the one who knows with what is known, the one who understands with the intelligible. But the pseudo-theologians refuse to be united essentially with God; Christ and his life do not dwell in them essentially. They can talk and preach about him, though they stand outside him; that is their business, their work, their darkness and their condemnation. P. 39: Our Informatorium bears this teaching: the knower and the knowable become one essentially. The mind, by knowing, understanding and touching, penetrates even to the one essential thing. And ch. 18. In Stud. Universf. ch. 7: the learner is united essentially with the learning; indeed he himself becomes what he learns or reads in a book. He adds a reason, drawn from that cornucopia of human nature in which it encloses and is all things. In the same place he says: Aristotle and other philosophers invented dialectic, but by the light of nature from themselves; and I have it in me just as the inventors and writers did. Astrological Theology, ch. 1, p. 2: Our study and teaching gives an essential union, so that the learner becomes one with the learning, something the schools know nothing of or wish to know nothing of. The reason is ready to hand: of course they are not mad with Veigelius. Gnothi seauton, part 3, p. 24: a real union must exist between the knower and the known. Esaias Stifelius held the same delusion, whence the Stifelians, against whom Weber wrote.

units.la: Quartum Paradoxum, de regula cognitionis, nimirum Combinatione Contradictoriorum. Hoc quidem proprium VVeigeliani spiritus commentum est; & ἰδιον, quod Authori vehementer arridet: toties ac toties idem inculcat, & tantùm non deperit. istud vult, In natura & Scriptura contradictoria esse, & contraria, v. g. in Scriptura, Deum poenitere, Deum non poenitere. In natura, album, non album; sic, caelum, infernus; Deus, Diabolus &c. Illa à mente nostra combinari debere, non per explicationes aliquas, & respectus, ut dicas hoc sensu illud, eâ ratione istud; sed contraria absolutè combinanda esse simpliciter, ac promiscuè. Christus est α & ω; ideoque inquit, in eo principium & principiatum, & contraria omnia absolutè combinanda. Hinc ad absurditates & blasphemias devenit, ut dixerit, & dicere coactus fuerit, coelum & infernus, Deus & Diabolus, Christus & bestia Apocalyptica &c. idem sunt. Haec combinatio neque ex sensu, neque ex ratione à nobis fit; sed mente (aliquando dicit fide) quâ rationi silentium imponitur, & sensui; ratio enim contradictoria absolutè combinari non patitur, sed explicat, distinguit, conciliat &c., & per distinctiones ac respectus absolvit, verum non, per mentem absolutam & promiscua debet, juxta eum, instituì contrariorum combinatio, sive potius bruta confusio: sed non in schola sive lumine sensuali, neque in schola sive lumine rationali, at in schola & lumine mentali, sive fidei, uti loquitur, illud fit. Confess. cap. 1. Duo contraria uniuntur ideo, quia α & ω, principium & finis, aeternitas, & tempus, caelum & terra, Deus & creatura, spiritus & littera, internum & externum conjungenda sunt, alioqui perfecta rerum omnium cognitio non posset obtineri, v. g. Deum poenitet, quia illam nihil poenitet, Deum nihil poenitet, quia eum eum poenitet. Ideoque homo combinare debet æternitatem cum tempore, quia alterum sine altero consistere nequit, v. g. Dei poenitere in tempore nullius usus esset citra non poenitere in æternitate; & ejus poenitere in tempore non posset esse, citra ejus non poenitere. Ideoque unum citra aliud consistere nequit, quia perfectio mundi consistit in contrariis, v. g. die, nocte; calore, frigore, &c. Haec ideo contraria nobis attestatur experientia, ut in hac vita discamus adscendere e tempore ad æternitatem, a creaturis ad authorem, ut omnia combinemus per supernaturalem cognitionem, quae omnia unit: per mentem in caelestibus rerum fit unio. Omnia unum sunt. In terrenis discrimen rerum est, omnia juxta entia, loca, tempora divisa sunt. Idemque per tres sci-holas discendum: est schola sensualis, ubi vel pecus a pecore differt, & ex aliorum relatione, vel libris quis credit, v. g. Deum audire.
units.tr: The fourth paradox concerns the rule of knowing, namely the combination of contradictories. This is indeed a peculiar invention of Weigel's spirit, and his own [ἰδιον] idea, which pleases the author greatly: again and again he presses the same point and hardly ever lets it go. He maintains that in nature and in Scripture there are contradictories and opposites: for example, in Scripture, God repents and God does not repent; in nature, white and not white; so heaven and hell, God and the Devil, and so on. These, he says, must be combined by our mind, not through any explanations or respects, so that you say that this is so in one sense and that in another reason; but opposites must be combined absolutely, simply and indiscriminately. Christ is Alpha [α] and Omega [ω], and therefore, he says, in him are the principle and the principled, and all opposites must be combined absolutely. From this he has fallen into absurdities and blasphemies, so that he has said, and been forced to say, that heaven and hell, God and the Devil, Christ and the beast of the Apocalypse, are the same. This combination is made neither by the sense nor by reason, but by the mind (which he sometimes calls faith), by which reason and sense are silenced. For reason does not allow contradictories to be combined absolutely; it explains, distinguishes, reconciles and resolves them through distinctions and respects. But according to him the combination of opposites must be carried out not through the absolute and indiscriminate mind, but rather it is a brute confusion; and this happens not in the school or light of the senses, nor in the school or light of reason, but in the school and light of the mind, or of faith, as he puts it. Confession, ch. 1: Two opposites are united, because Alpha and Omega, beginning and end, eternity and time, heaven and earth, God and creature, spirit and letter, inward and outward must be joined; otherwise a perfect knowledge of all things could not be obtained. For example: God repents, because nothing repents him; God does not repent, because he repents of nothing. Therefore man must combine eternity with time, because the one cannot exist without the other. For example, God's repenting in time would be of no use without his not repenting in eternity; and his repenting in time could not be, apart from his not repenting. Hence the one cannot exist apart from the other, because the perfection of the world consists in opposites, for example day and night, heat and cold, and so on. Experience attests to us these opposites so that in this life we may learn to ascend from time to eternity, from creatures to the Author, so that we may combine all things through supernatural knowledge, which unites them all: union of things takes place in the mind through heavenly things. All things are one. In earthly things there is distinction; all things are divided according to beings, places and times. And one must learn through three schools: there is the sensual school, where either a beast differs from a beast, and one believes by the report of others or by books, for example, that God hears.

units.la: Cap. II.
units.tr: Chapter II.

units.la: Lumen naturæ, ubi contradictoria juxta se ponuntur, ubi unum absolutè verum est, aliud per respectum. Deus omne audit, non poenitet, contrarium est falsum.
units.tr: The light of nature, where contradictories are placed side by side, where one thing is absolutely true and another true only in a certain respect. God hears everything; he does not repent; the contrary is false.

units.la: III. Lumen gratiæ, ubi meus contradictoria unit. v. g. Deus audit omnia, quia nihil audit, & nihil audit, quia omnia audit.
units.tr: III. The light of grace, where the mind unites contradictories, e.g. God hears all things because he hears nothing, and he hears nothing because he hears all things.

units.la: Cap. II.
units.tr: Chapter II.

units.la: Ideo homo creatus, liberatus, ac spiritu Dei obsignatus est, ut duo contradictoria uniat.
units.tr: Therefore man was created, freed, and sealed with the Spirit of God, so that he might unite two contradictories.

units.la: Cap. III.
units.tr: Chapter III.

units.la: Vera Theologia non est sensualis, neque rationalis, ubi ratio verum a falso discernit, & nunquam duo contraria potest combinare; sed vera Theologia est, ubi principium & finis comprehenduntur, ubi duo contradictoria uniuntur, & vera agnoscuntur. Pag. 10. Qui principium cum fine sumunt, duo contradictoria aliter unire possunt, in Iesu Christum concedunt, rationi valedicunt, quae inimicitia est adversus Deum, & quidem contraria invenire potest, & conferre, at nunquam realiter unire, ut utrumque verum sit simul, & sen. el.
units.tr: True theology is not sensual, nor rational, where reason distinguishes the true from the false and can never combine two contraries; but true theology is where the beginning and the end are comprehended, where two contradictories are united, and both are acknowledged as true. p. 10. Those who take the beginning with the end can unite two contradictories in another way: they concede it in Jesus Christ and bid farewell to reason, which is enmity against God. Reason can indeed find contraries and compare them, but it can never unite them in reality, so that both are true at the same time, and so on.

units.la: Cap. IV.
units.tr: Chapter IV.

units.la: Qui nec deum novit duo contradictoria unire, & pro vero agnoscere, per se in uno principio, nesciit principium cum fine, aeternitatem cum tempore, Deum cum creatura conjungenda esse ad veram & perfectam cognitionem. Immo qui æternitatem cum tempore principatum cum fine non male realiter, nullum Deum habet, extra Christum est, &c. Omnia idipsum sunt, sicut tempus est æternitas, æternitas est tempus; creatura Deus est, Deus est creatura. Omnia in omnibus occultata sunt. Hæc regula referri debet ad combinationem contradictoriorum, seu unionem essentialem illorum. Dei non videre in æternitate, haud potest esse citra ejus videre in tempore, nam si non videt Deus, imo nihilominus videt, & si non videt, videt tamen. Unde perspicere licet, quamvis scriptura & naturalis ratio mundum cum initio pœnam, est tamen ratione mentalis divinæ cognitionis æternus sine principio, sicut Deus æternus sine principio est, idque ideo, quod alterum sine altero esse possit in cognitione divina. Verum ergo manet, Deus est æternus, & non est æternus, tantumdem esse ac Deus principium non habet, quia principium habet: mundus æternus est sine initio, quia Deus æternus est sine initio, mundus initium, & Deus initium habet.
units.tr: He who does not know God cannot unite two contradictories and acknowledge them as true; in one principle he does not know, in himself, that the beginning must be joined with the end, eternity with time, and God with creature, for true and perfect knowledge. Indeed, he who has not rightly joined eternity with time and the beginning with the end in reality has no God and is outside Christ, etc. All things are the same thing, just as time is eternity and eternity is time; the creature is God and God is the creature. All things are hidden in all things. This rule must be referred to the combination of contradictories, or to their essential union. That God does not see in eternity cannot be without his seeing in time; for if God does not see, yet he sees all the same, and if he does not see, nevertheless he sees. Hence it may be understood that, although Scripture and natural reason say that the world had a beginning, the world is nonetheless eternal and without beginning in the mental knowledge of God, just as God is eternal and without beginning, and this is so because in the divine knowledge the one can be without the other. The truth therefore remains: God is eternal and is not eternal, which amounts to saying that God has no beginning, because he has a beginning; the world is eternal and without beginning, because God is eternal and without beginning; the world has a beginning, and God has a beginning.

units.la: C. VIII. Et quia tempus cum æternitate conjungi debet, agnescimus & credimus tres terrenas temporales personas distinctas secundum officia & proprietates, quemadmodum pater est genitor filii, filius verbum est è Patre procedens caro factum, non pater, aut spiritus s. spiritus s. tertia persona, ad utrumque in corda credentium mittitur. Hæc secundum terrenum modum, quomodo se Deus & homo manifestavit; verum secundum cœlestem modum, est Deus Pater, Filius, & Spiritus S. mòdo unus Deus, unitus menti, quamvis divisus rationibus in tempore, & tres unus Deus sunt, omnipotens, æternus, Pater ipse filius est, & Spiritus S., Spiritus S. Pater, & Filius. Filius ipse Pater & Spiritus S. hic nihil prius nec posterius; at in temporali cognitione est majoritas & minoritas personarum, sic & prioritas & posteritas. Et quamvis una persona altera prior sit, & major, nihilominus opposita pars etiam vera est. Etiam licet dicere, spiritus s. creatura, spiritus s. non est creatura. Filius creatus est, filius non est creatus, utrumque verum. Iam adischolas, & concilia nonnulla, ut adversarium suum condemnent, mnent, & anathematizent ipsis archihereticis, quorum multi partem veram agnoscunt, alteram non. In schola verità mentali utraque conjungantur, neque errant: dicunt, Deus non contristatur, Deus contristatur, utrumque verissimum. Nihil hic disputandum, neque contradicendum, nemo hic condemnat, aurea concordia in Iesu Christo, atque ita cum omnibus articulis universæ religionis sese haberet, modo duo contradictoria uniuntur, & agnoscerentur. Cap. XVIII. Numerus bestiæ 666. continet ac comprehendit, immo omnium essentia ac vita est. Numerus 666. eum indicat, qui compendium est totius universi; sc. S. S. Trinitatem, & omnia creata. Neque Trinitas uspiam recte inveniri nisi in numero 666. i.e. Christi humanitate. Multi Theologi putant Verbum caro factum, spiritum s. excludunt, vidissent utique tempus non posse esse sine æternitate, nec vicissim. Tres, unus Deus, caro factus. Deus, id est, Deus Pater, filius, spiritus s. non solum filius, sed & Pater, & Spiritus s. homo, & filius Mariæ factus est. Filius, Christus est bestia illa, numerus ejus 666. Male facis, sic est, quod tantum mysterium hic pono, quod nemo philosophorum invenit, veritas cui manifestum, manifestum, cui occultum, occultum. Recipe Theologiam Veigelii, ac perveniesad gratia mentis. Apage cum isthoc tuo malo mysterio, adeo in eversionem & confusionem omnium veritatum, & Dei, S. Trinitatis, Christi &c. blasphemiam nato! Cap. XIX. Duo contradictoria sunt, quod conjugium sine omni divortio observandum. Christus is est, in quo omnia combinantur, a & q omnia continet. Est cælum beatorum, infernus damnatorum, extra me nihil est. Hactenus audiistis summarium omnis Confessionis, quam totam impendit hoc uno articulo, de combinatione contrariorum, reliquis sparsim intermixtis; ideoque in recitandis ejus verbis prolixior fui, & studiosior, quo mens authoris ex ipsis ejus verbis dextre ab unoquoque percipieretur, atque in aliis etiam ejus sententia facilius constaret; tum propter absurfurdiffima & blasphema, quæ ex ejus mente passim ci-tantur, intelligenda, eorumque fundamentum. Tan-ti habuit hoc suum inventum, ut nullum operosius inculcet, maximo cum tædio. Pauciora sunt, quæ hic illic addit, præter ea, quæ excerpsimus, in hoc Confessi volumine, adeo in repetita crambe se oblectat delira mens. Neque adeo hoc libello id egisse contentus fuit, nisi idem quoque omnibus suis libris ageret, ne forte quis schedulam aliquam introspicieus hoc quoque non statim apprehenderet. Gnothi seaut. part. III. pag. 6. non sariendum partibus, neque ex aliorum relatu credendum, nullus alium condemnet; quis scit utrum verum an falsum sit? nemo: prius numerum bestiæ addisca-mus, id est, veri Theologi efficiamur. pag. 40. Astrol. Theol. cap. x. pag. 30. Mens omnia unit, Deus in ete-ra totus, creatura in Deo tota. Capt. aur. pag. 6. omnia æterna sunt, et simul temporalia. Stud. Univers. c. v. Astrol. Theol. cap. VIII. si addiscas numerum bestiæ in Apoc. comperies Christum illam bestiam esse, et manere, in, cum, et per homines, esseque omnino civitatem illam, illa mulier, meretrix Babylonie, draco, pseudo-prophetæ, iniquitas cum suis sunt. Pag. 23. Quemadmodum firmamentum malum est, in, cum, et per hominem, ita bestia Apoc. 13. est draco, Iesabel, meretrix, Babylon, pseudo-prophetæ. Ita et bonus Deus malus est in eum et per creaturam, citra ejus culpam; absque eo enim creatura se neque movere, neque quidquam cogitare valet, nostra e-rum, qui a et u, qui omnia est in omnibus. Lib. de bono & malo cap. v. apertius se explicat, Deus lux est, neque in eo tenebræ; cælum est, nec infernus; solum bonus, nec malus est, ideoque in eo nequeunt esse tenebræ, solum in creatura, quæ ex malitia horum sibi auctor. Dictum tamen est superius, Deum lucem cum tenebris, cælum cum inferno comprehendere, Angelum et Diabolum, bonum et malum. Ergo in Deo sine tenebra, condemnatio necesse est. Videtur hæc contraria, neque tamen sunt. Deus eeum continens, & concludens & centrum omnium creatu-rarum, bonarum malarumque, neque extra eum quid est, neque diabolus aut improbus sine absque eo vel movere potest; quando ergo Deus tenebras & lumen comprehendit, non haec in ejus essentia insunt, verum in creaturis, quae in tenebras, infernum &c. prolabuntur: quamvis extra Deum esse nequeant, in Deo manere necessum sit. Eadem carent Deo tenebrae non sunt tenebrae, nox ut dies est &c. & sic pag. 23.
units.tr: Ch. VIII. And because time must be joined with eternity, we acknowledge and believe three earthly, temporal persons, distinct according to their offices and properties: as the Father is the begetter of the Son, the Son is the Word proceeding from the Father, made flesh; not the Father, nor the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit, the third person, is sent into the hearts of believers from both. These things are so according to the earthly manner in which God and man revealed themselves; but according to the heavenly manner, God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God in mode, united in the mind, though divided in aspects in time; and the three are one God, omnipotent, eternal; the Father is himself the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Holy Spirit is the Father and the Son; the Son is himself the Father and the Holy Spirit. Here there is nothing before or after; but in temporal knowledge there is greater and lesser among the persons, and likewise priority and posteriority. And although one person is prior to and greater than another, the opposite part is nonetheless also true. It is also lawful to say: the Holy Spirit is a creature; the Holy Spirit is not a creature. The Son is created; the Son is not created; both are true. Now the schools and certain councils, in order to condemn their adversary, condemn and anathematize the archheretics themselves, of whom many acknowledge one part as true and not the other. In the mental school both are joined together, and they do not err: they say, God is not saddened; God is saddened; both are most true. Nothing is to be disputed here, nothing to be contradicted; no one here condemns anyone; there is golden concord in Jesus Christ, and so the whole of religion, with all its articles, would stand, provided that two contradictories are united and acknowledged. Chapter XVIII. The number of the beast, 666, contains and comprehends everything; indeed it is the essence and life of all things. The number 666 indicates him who is the compendium of the whole universe, namely the Holy Trinity and all created things. Nor is the Trinity rightly found anywhere except in the number 666, that is, in the humanity of Christ. Many theologians think that the Word made flesh excludes the Holy Spirit; they would surely have seen that time cannot be without eternity, nor eternity without time. Three, one God, made flesh. God, that is, God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is not only the Son but also the Father and the Holy Spirit; he was made man and the son of Mary. The Son, Christ, is that beast, whose number is 666. You do badly, for it is so: I set forth here so great a mystery which no philosopher has found, a truth manifest to one to whom it is manifest, and hidden to one to whom it is hidden. Receive the theology of Weigel, and you will come to the grace of the mind. Away with your evil mystery, born for the overthrow and confusion of all truths, and for the blasphemy of God, the Holy Trinity, Christ, etc.! Chapter XIX. Two contradictories are such that their marriage must be kept without any divorce. Christ is he in whom all things are combined, and who contains all things. He is the heaven of the blessed, the hell of the damned; outside me there is nothing. Thus far you have heard the summary of his whole Confession, which he devotes entirely to this one article, the combination of contraries, with the other matters scattered and intermixed. I have therefore been more prolix and more careful in reciting his words, so that the mind of the author might be perceived clearly by everyone from his own words, and his opinion in other matters also might be more easily established, and so that the very absurd and blasphemous statements which are cited everywhere from his mind might be understood, together with their foundation. He held his invention in such esteem that he inculcates no other thing more laboriously, with the greatest tedium. Few are the things which he adds here and there, apart from those which we have excerpted from this volume of Confession; so much does the deranged mind delight in repeating the same cabbage. Nor was he content to have done this in this little book, unless he did the same in all his books, lest perhaps someone, glancing at some leaflet, should not immediately grasp this either. Gnothi seauton, part III, p. 6. One must not take sides, nor believe on the report of others; no one should condemn another; who knows whether it is true or false? No one: let us first learn the number of the beast, that is, let us become true theologians. p. 40. Astrol. Theol. ch. x, p. 30. The mind unites all things; God is wholly in eternity, the creature is wholly in God. Capt. aur. p. 6. All things are eternal and at the same time temporal. Stud. Univers. ch. v. Astrol. Theol. ch. VIII. If you learn the number of the beast in the Apocalypse, you will find that Christ is that beast and remains in, with, and through men, and that the city, that woman, the harlot of Babylon, the dragon, the false prophets, and iniquity with them are altogether one. p. 23. Just as the firmament is evil, in, with, and through man, so the beast of Apoc. 13 is the dragon, Jezebel, the harlot, Babylon, the false prophets. So also the good God is evil in and through the creature, without his fault; for without him the creature can neither move nor think anything; our ... who is all things in all. In the book On Good and Evil, ch. v, he explains himself more plainly: God is light, and in him there is no darkness; he is heaven, not hell; he is only good, not evil, and therefore darkness cannot be in him, only in the creature, which by its malice becomes its own author. It has been said above, however, that God comprehends light with darkness, heaven with hell, the angel and the devil, good and evil. Therefore in God, without darkness, there must be condemnation. This seems contrary, and yet they are not. God, containing and enclosing all creatures, good and evil, and being the centre of them all, nothing is outside him, and the devil or the wicked cannot even move without him; when therefore God comprehends darkness and light, these are not in his essence, but in the creatures, which fall into darkness, hell, etc.; although they cannot be outside God, they must necessarily remain in God. The same things lack darkness in God; they are not darkness; night is as day, etc.; and so on, p. 23.

units.la: Paradoxum quintum, de saeculo Spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: The fifth paradox, concerning the age of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: In inscriptione librorum suorum aliquando addit: Vltimo saeculo Spiritus sancti in testimonium, committum prelo. Lib. altero de vit. Christi, quo probat, nullas per Europam scholas aut ecclesias carere pseudo-prophetis &c. pag. 127. ita loquitur: si mihi N. N. credas, magnum tibi aperiam mysterium, nempe hoc, respice Christianae fidei articulos, ut se se invicem sequantur, quae praeteriti, qui adhuc restant, liquebit quid secundum arca Prophetarum jam transierit, & quid adhuc futurum; etiam sub quo articulorum etiamnum vivimus. Illorum articulorum duodecim sunt, sunt itidem duodecim horae mundi, quae in terra omnes adimplendae, antequam in nihilum intereas, hoc praesenti tempore vivimus & summus sub articulo, sedens ad dexteram Dei: ubi hic terminus suum fuerit fortius, cum excipiet alter, unde venturus est judicatum vivos & mortuos; quod non intelligendum de novissimo die, neque de interitu mundi, verum de judicio Filii; Pater enim inimicos suos prima saeculo perdidit diluvio aqueo, Filius altera saeculo Antichristos suos delebit diluvio sanguineo; Ea adimpleta, superest tertium saeculum, nempe Sp. Sancti: qui etiam in terris vigebit, tertius enim articulus de Spiritu S.S. Ecclesia, Communione Sanctorum restat adhuc, ac in terris adimplenda, neque prius interibit mundus, quam omnia impleta sint: hoc tertio saeculo, horrenda ac infernalis generatio in sanctos, qui in terra adhuc, insurgent, cuius simulis non fuerit, verum delebitur ac peribit per diluvium igneum. gnéum, & hoc erit seculum. Δ [ignem putat, quibus nonnulis crebro utitur, etiam in Postillis, nimirum ut gustum astrologicum significaret] Baptismus ignis sc. ignis infernalis. Neque te lateat, aliud esse diem novissimum & judicium extremum seu diem extremum, licet eruditi ita putent: sed hoc arcanum nondum ibi revelat, indicat tantummodo. Oswaldus Crollius in praef. Basilic. Chymic. eadem arcana prodit, & saeculo illo tertio Eliam Medicum, reparatorem omnium expectat pag. 5. Atque haec potissima V Veigeliani spiritus (omnia non dico) paradoxa, de quibus ita porro judicamus.
units.tr: In the title of his books he sometimes adds: Written in the last age of the Holy Spirit, as a testimony, committed to the press. In the second book On the Life of Christ, in which he proves that no schools or churches throughout Europe lack false prophets, etc., p. 127, he speaks thus: If you believe me, N. N., I will open a great mystery to you, namely this: look at the articles of the Christian faith, how they follow one another. From what has passed, and what still remains, it will become clear what has already passed according to the ark of the Prophets, and what is yet to come, and under which of the articles we are still living. There are twelve of those articles, and likewise twelve hours of the world, all of which must be fulfilled on earth before the world perishes into nothing. In this present time we live under the article "and sitteth at the right hand of God." When this period has run its course more strongly, the next will receive it, whence he is to come to judge the living and the dead. This is not to be understood of the last day, nor of the destruction of the world, but of the judgment of the Son. For the Father destroyed his enemies in the first age by the watery flood; the Son will destroy his Antichrists in the second age by a bloody flood. When these are fulfilled, there remains a third age, namely that of the Holy Spirit, which will flourish also on earth. For the third article concerns the Holy Spirit: the Church, the Communion of Saints, still remains, and is to be fulfilled on earth, and the world will not perish before all things are fulfilled. In this third age a horrible and infernal generation will rise up against the saints who are still on earth; there will have been none like it, but it will be destroyed and will perish by a fiery flood. Fiery, and this will be the age. [He thinks of fire, which he uses often, even in his Postils, namely to signify the astrological taste.] Baptism of fire, that is, infernal fire. Nor let it escape you that the last day and the final judgment, or the last day, are different things, although learned men think so: but he does not yet reveal this secret there; he only hints at it. Oswald Croll, in the preface to his Basilica Chymica, sets forth the same secrets, and looks for Elijah the physician, the restorer of all things, in that third age, p. 5. These are the chief paradoxes of Veigel's spirit (I do not say all of them), and concerning them we judge further as follows.

units.la: I. Longe majoris operae ac studii esse, sententiam ejus ac mentem rite indagari, exquirere, & intelligere, quam refutare. II. Ex furnis & fumis HermeticoParacelsicis, & spiritu Chymico adinventa, iisdem tincta, & inflata esse. Ex Philosophia, & artibus si quae unquam didicerunt hujusmodi homines, ea rebus suis Theologicis tam impotenter, fastuose, ac imperite aspergunt & commiscent, ut ignotae plebi mira somniare videantur & venditare stolidi empyrici. Sennertus, de Chymicorum consensu & dissensu in dedicat, Ex Paracelso nimirum, tanquam fonte, dogmata sua hauserunt V Veigelius, Crollius: imo illi ipsi Enthusiastae, qui ante paucos annos in Thuringia religionem Christianam turbare conati sunt, & plures alii ex iis, qui fraternitatis R. C. socii seu clientes videri volunt. III. Vulgaria, & confessa, miris, Chymico-Philosophicis, corruptis verbis ac loquendi modo obscurare solent; ut saltem sermo quid portendat. Calvinus, adversus Libertinos, cap. VII. Peregrina, & insolenti utuntur lingua, quae sic cermicantur, ut nihil plus perspicuitatis insit, quam inane sonus, uti Tertullianus contra Hermogenem inquit: haereticis morem esse, simplicia torquere. IV. Non sermone solum, sed & sensu ac re portentosa, absurda, pessima plurima tenent, atque tradunt. Quae
units.tr: I. Far greater effort and study is needed to investigate rightly, to inquire into, and to understand his opinion and mind, than to refute it. II. His ideas were devised from the furnaces and smoke of the Hermetic-Paracelsian school and the chemical spirit, and are steeped and puffed up with the same. Whatever philosophy and arts such men have ever learned, they so impotently, arrogantly and unskilfully mix and sprinkle into their theological matters that to the ignorant common people they seem to dream wonders, and foolish empirics peddle them.
