Sennert, in the dedication of On the Agreement and Disagreement of the Chemists: Veigel and Croll drew their dogmas from Paracelsus as from a fountain, and so did those very Enthusiasts who a few years ago tried to disturb the Christian religion in Thuringia, and many others of those who wish to appear as companions or clients of the Rosicrucian brotherhood. III. They are accustomed to obscure commonplace and admitted matters with wondrous, chemico-philosophical, corrupted words and manner of speaking, so that at least what the speech portends may be unclear. Calvin, against the Libertines, ch. VII: They use a foreign and unusual language, which is so twisted that it has no more clarity than an empty sound, as Tertullian says against Hermogenes: it is the custom of heretics to twist simple things. IV. They hold and hand down many things that are not only portentous in wording but absurd, very bad, in sense and substance as well. Which things:

units.la: I. Nulla ratione, argumento, vel specie probant; fingunt modò, & quasi pueris, vel amentibus dicta- rent, fanis habent pro arbitrio illa commenti. Agite dum, si omnium istarum, quas tantâ cum patientiâ hactenus audiistis, nugarum allumargumentum, vel probationem obserua veritis? ergo quâ ratione istam sibi potuisse talia persuadere, vel aliis, arbitremini, quibus nulla quidem species rationis fauet, aut obduci vel ab Authore potuit. 1 1. Ideoque tam facile explodantur & respuuntur omnia, quam proferuntur. 1 1 1. Immo æstimenti, operosâ & diligenti, vel doctâ refutatione nequaquam examinanda esse; quæ vel inde sibi nonnullius pretii esse alioqui persuadent. 1 V. Sufficere, ut monstretur, quomodo in communia & certissima principia Theologiæ, ac Philosophiæ impingant, quæ hactenus maximis argumentis eruditis ac sanis constanter probata, non tam leviter nullâ in contrarium ratione, deserenda, & abdicanda sunt. V. In principio iis præcipuè occurrendum, quoquo pacto ecclesiasticè, & politicè, præsertim ad blasphemas & portentosas theses; neque permittendum, ut ad librorum scriptio- nem (scripturire enim impotenter solet istud hominum genus) pergant. V1. Præstiterit quæ cum illis hominibus coram & voce congredi, quam scripto.
units.tr: I. They prove by no reasoning, argument or appearance whatever; they merely invent them and dictate them as if to children or madmen, and they hold these fancies at their own pleasure as sound. Come now: if you have heard all those trifles which you have hitherto listened to with such patience, have you observed any argument or proof? By what reasoning, then, do you suppose that they could have persuaded themselves of such things, or others, when no semblance of reason favours them, nor could the author have been led to them even by himself? 1 1. And therefore all things are as easily rejected and spat out as they are put forward. 1 1 1. Indeed, they are not to be examined by a long, laborious and diligent, or learned refutation at all; for they persuade themselves by this very fact that they are of some worth. 1 V. It is enough to show how they clash with the common and most certain principles of theology and philosophy, which have hitherto been constantly proved by the greatest learned and sound arguments, and which are not to be lightly abandoned and renounced without any reasoning to the contrary. V. At the outset one must meet them, above all, in ecclesiastical and civil ways, especially with regard to their blasphemous and portentous theses; and they must not be permitted to proceed to writing books (for this kind of men is accustomed to scribble impotently). VI. It is better to deal with such men face to face and by voice than in writing.

units.la: 1. Quia ita melius possunt abigi à monstrosis locutionibus ad communes, & usitatas. Primum enim in omni disputatione, ad controversiæ statum, de verborum sensu inquiritur, & sic ad planam sententiæ suæ explicationem dum coguntur, nullo negotio refutantur, juxta illud Tertulliani: hæreticos nosse, debellasse est. 11. Atque ad probationem adigantur, & rationes: quod adeò abhorrent, ut V Veigelius in libel. disput. pag. 3. caveat, & discipulum sedulò moneat, ne contra dictata sua argumentetur, vel se opponat, sed recipiat statim omnia absque ullâ contradictione, nimirum in scholâ mentis vel fidei jam erudiendus: quemadmodum Enthusiastæ solent, argumentis præssi, spiritum suum opponere; ac quia mysteria sua à nemine nisi per illum spiritum percipi posse dictitant, illum primò induci volunt, sine quo de sacris suis handrite quis (ex ipsorum opinione) judicet. III. Scripta vero eorum solent esse prolixa, taediosa & multa: neque facile scriptis vinci se patientur, quin potius centies idem idemque repetent, & promissis saltem, titulo, ac stylo superbis, vanis, falsis, acinusitatis lectorem deludent, atque obtundent. Quod omnibus Enthusiastis, Paracelsicis, V.V eigelianis, Behmistis proprium. Eodemque instituto Johannes VVeits, cujus scripta prodierunt Francofurti Anno 1634. titulos librorum suorum fecit, Revelatio arboris caelestis. Electrum caeleste. Consilium & medicamentum Catholicum &c. Praeter titulorum cothurnos & fumos, nihil. tanquam altius supraque vulgi ingenium spiraturi, si videantur communem sapientiam, ut prophanum vilemque negligere, inquit de Anglis Joh. Barclajus. Neque aliter Manes (a quo Manichaei) quae scribebat, summis titulis proponere solebat, Fundamentum, Mysteria, Thesaurum, suos quoque evomebat libros, appellitans, de quibus Epiphanius haeres. lxvi. Etiam Arius sua Thaliam nuncupabat. Thalia Sotadica dicebatur, cujus exordium ponit Athanasius, Orat. contra Arian. & Baronius, ad Annum cccxxv. num. lxxxi. &c. IV. Fucum facere solent inspersione ac usurpatione thematum aliquorum, quae summam videntur & rigidiorem spirare pietatem, quâ specie incautos fallunt. nulla etiam sonita bibuntur sicut illius Sic V.V eigelius de abnegatione sui ipsius &c. prolixe scripsit, & omnes illius spiritus homines perfectionem creare solent: nempe, id quo longissime absunt, maxime & impudentissime praeferentes. Quid hominum unquam Davide Georgii impurius, ac blasphemius, (ita ob similitudinem ingenii paradoxe portentosi juvat hosce Auctores conferre), qui pudorem genitalium membrorum omnem excutiendam, atque rerum non modò, sed & mulierum promiscuam commixtionem docebat. Nicol. Blesdikii histor. pag. 23. 27 28. 29. 30. 32. 72. 76. 111. 176. & ex eo Vbbo Emmius pag. 14. 244. 257. Se Christum, Davidem secundum spiritum, & peccatum in se quod committeretur, peccatum in Spiritum S. faciebat. Blesdik. pag. 37. 40. 43. 121. 45. 48. 50. 95. Bullinger. advers. Anabapt. lib. II. cap. XIV. Thuanus lib. XXII. Gasparus Grevinchovius. Quare Synodus Enchusana vel conjugium cum istius sectae homine confirmari vetat. Anno cIↄ Iↄ cxvii. & à Baptismi testimonio illos arcet Synodus Edamensis, Anno cIↄ Iↄ cxix. Isti tamen homines haud volunt videri desinere contra peccata declamare; pietatem, & mortificationem hominis magno conatu urgere, & pompose ostentare. Blesdik. pag. 15. 16. 18. 54. 66. 67. 124. Lambertus Hortensius de Anabapt. pag. 44. quod quoque Calvinus in illis hominibus notat, Instruct. contra Libertinos pag. 288. ss. Sed & distinctius ad singula V Veigelii capita aliquid annotemus.
units.tr: 1. Because in this way they can be more easily drawn away from monstrous expressions to common and usual ones. For first, in every disputation, the question is asked, as the state of the controversy, about the meaning of the words, and so, when they are compelled to a plain explanation of their opinion, they are refuted without any trouble, according to that saying of Tertullian: to know the heretics is to have defeated them. II. And they should be driven to proof and reasons. This they so abhor that V. Veigel, in his disputation book, p. 3, warns and earnestly admonishes his disciple not to argue against his dictates or oppose himself, but to accept all things at once without any contradiction, namely as one who is to be trained in the school of mind or faith. Just so the Enthusiasts are accustomed, when pressed by arguments, to oppose their spirit; and because they keep saying that their mysteries can be grasped by no one except through that spirit, they want him first to be brought in, without whom (by their own opinion) no one may judge their sacred matters rightly. III. Their writings, moreover, are usually long, tedious and many; nor do they easily allow themselves to be conquered by writings, but rather repeat the same thing a hundred times, and deceive and wear out the reader with promises at least, with proud titles and style, empty, false and unusual. This is peculiar to all Enthusiasts, Paracelsians, Veigelians and Böhmists. In the same practice Johann Weits, whose writings were published at Frankfurt in 1634, made the titles of his books: The Revelation of the Heavenly Tree. Heavenly Amber. Catholic Counsel and Remedy, etc. Beyond the buskins and smoke of the titles, there is nothing. As if they were going to breathe something higher than the common wit, if they seem to disdain common wisdom as profane and cheap, says John Barclay of the English. Nor did Manes (from whom the Manichaeans take their name) propose his writings under lofty titles otherwise: The Foundation, The Mysteries, The Treasure. He also belched out books of his own, which Epiphanius, heresy 66, mentions. Arius, too, called his own work Thalia. It was called the Sotadic Thalia, whose opening Athanasius quotes in his Orations against the Arians, and Baronius at the year 325, no. 81, etc. IV. They are accustomed to make a show by inserting and using certain themes which seem to breathe the highest and most rigid piety, and by that appearance they deceive the unwary. Nor is anything drunk up with such sound as that. Thus Veigel wrote at length On the Denial of Oneself, and all men of that spirit are accustomed to boast of perfection, namely by most loudly and most shamelessly praising precisely that which they are furthest from. What man was ever more impure and blasphemous than David Joris (it helps to compare these authors with him, since they are alike in their portentous and paradoxical talent), who taught that all shame of the genital members must be shaken off, and a promiscuous mingling not only of things but also of women. See Nicolaas Blesdijk's history, pp. 23, 27, 28, 29, 30, 32, 72, 76, 111, 176, and from him Ubbo Emmius, pp. 14, 244, 257. He made himself Christ, David according to the Spirit, and the sin committed in himself a sin against the Holy Spirit. Blesdijk, pp. 37, 40, 43, 121, 45, 48, 50, 95. Bullinger, against the Anabaptists, book II, ch. XIV. Thuanus, book XXII. Gaspar Grevinchoven. Therefore the Synod of Enkhuizen forbade even a marriage to be confirmed with a man of that sect, in the year 1517 (sic); and the Synod of Emden in the year 1519 excludes them from the testimony of baptism. Yet these men do not wish to appear to cease declaiming against sins; they urge the piety and mortification of man with great effort and display it pompously. Blesdijk, pp. 15, 16, 18, 54, 66, 67, 124. Lambertus Hortensius, on the Anabaptists, p. 44, which Calvin also notes in those men, Instruction against the Libertines, p. 288ff. But let us also comment somewhat more distinctly on the individual chapters of Veigel.

units.la: Quaest. I. An in homine omnium artium, scientiarum, rerum seminal sint, & formae? Resp. I. Homo quidem compendium universi dicitur, omniumque persectionum est ἀνακεφαλαίωσις; sed non ita, ut omnia formaliter in eo sint, & tollatur differentia specierum; sufficit convenientia in genere, ut quod sit quoque, & vivat, & sentiat, atque potissima sui parte sit rationalis, & spiritualis, quo pacto creaturas omnes, tum quae supra & quae infra ipsum sunt, refert, & similitudine sua attingit. Addelis Becmann. loc. cit. pag. 409. Libavium, in examine philos. nova pag. 16. & 101. 11. Quando homo' μικρόκοσμος dicitur, Deus semper excipitur, qui supra eum & omnia, neque ad alicujus constitutionem venit, vel compositionem, ut pars: sic ut dici nequeat, in nobis esse coelum, elementa, Deum ipsum &c. 111. Et jam corruit praecipuum sententiae istius caput, in cujus gratiam illa faciunt, nempe ex homine duci omnium rerum cognitionem, quia omnia sc. in homine sint, neque aliquid extrinsecus inferatur. Quod putide impingit in Theologiam, & Philosophiam.
units.tr: Question I. Are the seeds and forms of all arts, sciences and things in man? Answer I. Man is indeed called a compendium of the universe, and he is the recapitulation of all perfections; but not in such a way that all things are in him formally and the difference of species is abolished. Agreement in genus is enough: he is a body, he lives and he feels, and by his chief part he is rational and spiritual. In this way he relates to all creatures, both those above him and those below him, and touches them by his likeness. Add Becmann, loc. cit. p. 409; Libavius, in Examen philosophiae novae, pp. 16 and 101, 11. When man is called a microcosm, God is always excepted, who is above him and above all things, and who does not enter into the constitution or composition of anything as a part. So it cannot be said that heaven, the elements, God himself, etc., are in us. 111. And now the chief point of that opinion collapses, the point for whose sake they make these claims: namely, that the knowledge of all things is derived from man, because all things are in man and nothing is brought in from outside. This absurdly strikes at both theology and philosophy.

units.la: In Theologiam, tam ratione articulorum fidei supernaturalium, quorum sane notitia non ex nobis, sed duntaxat ex supernaturali, ac coelesti revelatione extra nos haberi potest; quam ratione fidei illius habendae, omniumque virtutum Theologicarum doctrinâ, & praxi ex homine vel ejus naturâ, nullatenus, sed ab extra in hominem, neque alia ratione, quam ex superveniente Dei gratiâ derivandarum. Simile, quod inter articulos Davidis Georgii haereticos, pro xxix. ponitur apud Blesdikium pag. 52. quod docuerit: paradysum, caelum, infernum, Christi postremum adventum, extremum judicium, aeternam vitam &c. non alibi, quam intra hominem observanda & expectanda esse. In philosophiam peccat, per confictam hominis fabricam ex corpore, anima, & suo spiritu, (de quo vide praeter alios, Becmanni exercit. xxv.) Jam quis ex tali rerum omnium, & naturae confusione, & cujuslibet ex quolibet educatione hactenus de natura, adde & praeternaturalibus edoceri potuit, neglectâ natura & gratiâ, solâ hominis & naturae suae contemplatione, ac examine instructus? Ne quidem V. Veigelius dixerit, se sua quae novit, ex se hausisse, & non consueta via addidicisse. Mirum autem ipsum non in se, vel discipulo periculum suae methodi & ἀνυπερίτως aliquod fecisse, quam adeo in contemptum reliquorum studiorum suadet. Committat se quis rotae V. Veigelianae (quin talia etiam inculcat) atque rejectis aliis studiis hac via insistat, profectum & eventum placidè exspectabimus, nisi illum adegerit tandem ista circumgiratio in poenitendam insaniam. Quin & sensus contrarium satis docet. Quid, quando spuritiem aliquam video, vel factorem quis percipit, cuncta ille ex nobis & non ignoti adveniunt? Monuit V Veigelius, ut quilibet agrum suum modo excolat, hinc omnia nos percepturos, & aeque dialecticam atque philosophiam, ac Aristoteles vel philosophus quicunque, percepturos, omnia in omnibus quum sint. an autem videtur quis sibi adeo fecundus, ut nugas VVeigelianas cogitasset unquam, nisi ex scriptis ipsius Auctoris? sane haud facile alicujus agrum ita fertilem credam, ut tales fungos ferat, nisi VVeigelianum. Et hanc habeat sibi laudem propriam. Certum id, quod non ex nobis omnia & solum, sed ab objectis, & aliquando stultissima quaeque etiam inviti percipimus. IV. Quod ergo de sabbato VVeigeliano subnectitur, quo istiusmodi nugas somnient homines, & fabricantis animi similia quaeque phantasmata, ex pretio suo jam aestimare illa licet, & fructu. Quid si somnium vel sabbathum aliquod ingressi, inde doceamur ludibrium suis debere (ne quid gravius dicam) VVeigelium cum omnibus suis somniis & nugis? De hoc vide Maraixium, contra Enthusiastas. Nisi forte nonnulli aliquando rationem meditandi & contemplandi [quam vulgo & omnes scimus, ac probamus] vel ex ignorantia, aut rei praestantia ducti, sive stultā grandiloquentia, sabbathum appellent.
units.tr: In theology, both with regard to the supernatural articles of faith, whose knowledge certainly cannot be had from ourselves but only from supernatural and heavenly revelation coming from outside us; and with regard to the having of that faith, and the doctrine and practice of all the theological virtues, which are derived not at all from man or his nature, but from outside into man, and in no other way than from the grace of God coming upon him. Similar is what is listed among the heretical articles of David Joris (David Georgii), as the twenty-ninth, in Blesdik, p. 52: that he taught that paradise, heaven, hell, Christ's final coming, the last judgment, eternal life, etc., are not to be looked for or expected anywhere except within man. He sins against philosophy through the invented structure of man out of body, soul and his spirit (on which see, besides others, Becmann's Exercitationes xxv). Now who could be instructed about nature, and even about preternatural things, from such a confusion of all things and of nature, and from the education of anything out of anything, neglecting nature and grace and relying only on the contemplation and examination of man and his own nature? Not even V. Veigel would say that he drew what he knows out of himself and did not learn it by the usual way. It is strange that he himself has never made any trial of his method, "ἀνυπερίτως" [anyperitōs], on himself or on a disciple, although he so urges people to despise the other studies. If anyone commits himself to the wheel of V. Veigel (indeed he inculcates such things too) and, rejecting other studies, keeps to this path, we will calmly wait to see the progress and outcome, unless that endless circling at last drives him into a madness he will have to repent of. Indeed, experience teaches the contrary well enough. When I see some spurious thing, or when someone perceives a maker, do all those things come to us from ourselves, and not from things unknown to us? V. Veigel advised that each person should cultivate his own field in this way, and that from it we would perceive all things, and would perceive dialectic and philosophy equally, as Aristotle or any philosopher would, since all things are in all. But does anyone seem so fertile to himself that he would ever have thought up Veigelian trifles, unless from the writings of the Author himself? Surely I would not easily believe that any field is so fertile that it bears such mushrooms, except the Veigelian one. Let it have that praise as its own. It is certain that we perceive not everything from ourselves alone, but from objects, and sometimes even the most foolish things against our will. IV. What is then added about the Veigelian Sabbath, by which men dream up such trifles and similar phantasms of a fabricating mind, one may now judge from their price and their fruit. What if, having entered into some dream or Sabbath, we are taught that we owe mockery (not to say something more serious) to Veigel with all his dreams and trifles? On this see Maraix, against the Enthusiasts. Unless perhaps some people, led sometimes by ignorance, sometimes by the excellence of the thing, or by foolish grandiloquence, call the method of meditating and contemplating (which we all commonly know and approve) a Sabbath.

units.la: At quaerit tamen libell. disp. pag. 11. & capt. cap. 11. & passim; unde ergo, quod non omnes aeque omnia percipiant, si non ex homine haurialtur, quum eadem objecta omnibus aeque proponantur? Siccine? in Talmude nonnumquam quaerit, quare sol in plaga ista oriatur, in altera occidat, & non vice versa? cui respondet Doctor; si ita fieret, ut dicis, idem quaereres. Iustius ego ex V. Veigelio, si ex homine omnia, quare non omnes aeque apprehendunt, atque sapiunt omnia? saltem sequeretur, quod non eam difficultatem experiremur in addiscendis rebus, liquidem omnia in nobis laterent, ut ille credit, quam jam maximam saepe papatimur: quomodo etiam argumentantur, qui contra nonnullos male feriatos disputant, linguam hebraeam non esse homini naturalem, propter addiscendi difficultatem. In rerum perceptione multum quidem situm in diversa hominum indole & ingenio, sed ex ratione objecti, & varia ejus proponendi ratione diversa illa inter homines sapiendi ratio, non totum ex agro nostro interno, vel natura mentis omnium rerum formas & semina complectente. Verulamius, de augmentis scient. lib. 1. caeterum praeclara hoc opinatores, & [si ita loqui licet] intellectualistae, qui tamen pro maximè sublimibus & divinis philosophis haberi solent, recte Heraclitus perstrinxit. Homines inquit quaerunt veritatem in microcosmis suis, non ex mundo majori &c. At illi contra ingenii mentis agitatione urgent & tanquam invocant suos genios, ut reticementur, edunt quae oracula; quibus merito & saepe* decipiuntur.
units.tr: Yet the little book of disputation asks at p. 11, and in the chapter "capt." 11, and passim: whence, then, is it that not everyone perceives everything equally, if things are not drawn from man, since the same objects are set equally before all? Really? In the Talmud he sometimes asks why the sun rises in that region and sets in another, and not the reverse; to which the Doctor replies: if it were done as you say, you would be asking the same question. I ask V. Veigel with better right: if all things come from man, why do not all grasp and know all things equally? At the very least it would follow that we would not experience that difficulty in learning things, since all things would lie hidden in us, as he believes, a difficulty we very often labour under most heavily. Likewise, those who dispute against some badly educated people argue that the Hebrew tongue is not natural to man, because of the difficulty of learning it. In the perception of things much depends on the differing disposition and talent of men, but this difference in the manner of knowing among men arises from the nature of the object and the varied manner of presenting it, not wholly from our inner field or from the nature of a mind that contains the forms and seeds of all things. Verulam, On the Advancement of Learning, book 1: "Moreover, these opinions of those who hold this, and [if one may so speak] the intellectualists, who are nevertheless usually regarded as the most sublime and divine philosophers, Heraclitus rightly censured. Men, he says, seek truth in their own microcosms, not in the greater world, etc. But they, on the contrary, press with the agitation of their minds, and, as if invoking their own genii so that they may be silent, they utter oracles; by which they are rightly, and often, deceived."

units.la: Quaest. II. An homo ex nativitate sua Planetarum proprium habeat, quae ipsum regat, quemque adeo abdicare debeat, ut salvetur? Resp. I. Mirum, qui tam acerbe scientias omnes insectatur, eum paradoxa illa astrologica tam facile adoptare, tot ac tantis rationibus à Phi- losophis & Theologis semper condemnata; nisi forte in hoc studio parum versatior fuerit, quod nullo alio pacto melius ostentari posse sibi visus, quam isto: sicuti antea diximus, istud hominum genus ostentabundum esse & vanissimum. Illa igitur quum assumat, quae salsissima, quaeque nullâ ratione probare allabo- rat, quanti ejus dogmata? II. Pariter aestimari debet, quod huic superstruit ridiculum prorsus & nugat- orium thema, de astri sui renunciatione: quia sc. nemo cum aratro vel armis coelum ingressurus est. Qui studio nugari volet, an aliter facerit, quam hic? Quasi quem hoc anxie torqueat, ne calceatus & ocreatus coelum introeat. Quomodo referunt aliquam scrupu- lum movisse sub obitum, quod verecetur ne uti Antonius
units.tr: Question II. Does a man have from his birth a planet of his own that rules him, so that he must renounce it in order to be saved? Answer I. It is strange that a man who attacks all the sciences so bitterly should adopt so readily these astrological paradoxes, which philosophers and theologians have always condemned on so many and such weighty grounds. Unless perhaps he is more practised in this study than he lets on, and it seemed to him that he could display his learning in no better way than this. As we said before, this kind of men is showy and very vain. Since, then, he takes up those things which are most absurd, and which he labours to prove by no reason at all, how much are his dogmas worth? II. In the same way, we ought to weigh the ridiculous and utterly trifling theme he builds upon this, about renouncing one's star, because, forsooth, no one will enter heaven with a plough or with arms. If someone wants to trifle, does he do anything other than this? As if anyone were anxiously tormented by the worry that he might enter heaven with his shoes and spurs on! They relate that someone, near his death, was troubled by a scruple, fearing that his dogs, which he had loved so dearly in life, would be set over the puppies of Antony [sic]. [The text continues in unit 2.]

units.la: sitis poteris, ipsa catulis praeficeretur, quos tam enixe in vitâ adamarat. ɛɪɪ. Sex diebus quomodo liceat planetam suum sequi, si ut filius planetae damnationem quis incurrat? & quomodo sabbatho omnia abstinenda, quae juxta VVeigelium ex astris provenient, quum etiam multa Ecclesiastica explaneta Iovis derivet, quae sabbatho vel maximè curanda? Neque adeo facile aliquis per totam hebdomadam planetae suo addictus, cum & planetica omnia statim sabbatho, ut poma ex arbore, vel asinus mora (sic loquitur) excutiet? Et quare, ubi de omnibus pronunciavit, illos non posse ita salvari, neque Parentem, filium, uxorem &c. non etiam VVeigelium addidit? neque enim VVeigelius salvabitur, quia VVeigelius, sed si puer & Christianus, prout loquitur. Quam nulla & nugax illa subtilitas! quasi quis unquam tam stolidus, qui opinatus fuerit se salvandum, quia vir aut mulier, faber aut auriga: & non, uti de Iodoco Gallo, Conr. Pellicani avunculo refertur, illum in extremis dixisse; resurrecturum se ad judicium, non ut Sacerdotem & doctorem, sed ut humilem Christianum, (Melch. Adamus in vita Pellicani), ita credamus nos, ut Christianos, salvatum iri, nec aliter.
units.tr: you may be able to... Question III. How may a man follow his planet on the six days without incurring damnation as a son of the planet? And how must everything be abstained from on the Sabbath that, according to Weigel, comes from the stars, since he also derives from the planet Jupiter many ecclesiastical matters which are most of all to be attended to on the Sabbath? Nor can anyone easily, devoted to his planet for the whole week, shake out all planetary things at once on the Sabbath, as apples fall from a tree, or as an ass shakes off its mulberries (so he puts it)? And why, when he pronounced about everyone that they cannot be saved in this way, did he not add Weigel too, and not only parents, son, wife, and so on? For Weigel will not be saved because he is Weigel, but if he is a boy and a Christian, as he says. How empty and trifling that subtlety is! As if anyone were ever so foolish as to suppose he would be saved because he is a man or a woman, a smith or a carter, and not, as is reported of Jodocus Gallus, the uncle of Conrad Pellican, who said at the end that he would rise to judgment not as a priest and teacher, but as a humble Christian (Melchior Adam in the life of Pellican). So we ought to believe that we shall be saved as Christians, and in no other way.

units.la: Quaest. IIII: An cognoscens idem sit cum cognito realiter, & essentialiter? Resp. I. Nisi VVeigelius hoc suo dogmate quid peculiare se docere diceret contra communem, quam etiam damnat, sententiam, judicarem, errorem omnem in terminis consistere, neque in re adeo peccatum esse, quam loquendi modo; sic forte quis terminos illos realiter & essentialiter explicarit: at quia ita se res habet, ut homo crassissime hoc voluerit accipi, aliisque secus sentientibus vel ideo solitum suum anathema dixerit, age, & crasse stoliditati suae vapulet. I. Ex philosophia. An quod quis audit, legit in libro, vel cognoscit, illud sit? & quando Diabolum cognoscit, vel asinum, is statim evadit? immo mimo quando se, vel suum sive asini sui simum cogitat, aut si quid vilius, eam illis idem fit realiter & essentialiter? Obem. Vel, qui VVeigelium cogitat, is VVeigelius realiter fiet? hoc mihi certe nolim; tu tibi forsan, ut totuplex scilicet evadas, & tot VVeigeliana constituas individua. Vel cogitet VVeigelius, sive VVeigelianus adversarium suum, qui omnia ejus themata vehementer rideat, qualis quaeso inde sicut VVeigelianus?
units.tr: Question IV. Is the one who knows really the same as the thing known, both in reality and in essence? Answer I. If Weigel did not say that this dogma of his teaches something peculiar against the common opinion, which he also condemns, I would judge that every error lies in terms, and that the fault lies more in the manner of speaking than in the matter. Thus perhaps someone might explain those terms as meaning "really and essentially." But since the matter stands such that he wanted these words to be understood in the crudest sense, and for that very reason pronounced his customary anathema on others who think otherwise, let him be whipped for his crude stupidity. I. From philosophy. Is whatever someone hears, reads in a book, or knows, that thing? And when he knows the devil, or an ass, does he at once become one? Indeed, when he thinks of himself, or of his own or an ass's dung, or of something even more worthless, does the same thing happen to them, in reality and in essence? Objection: Or, does one who thinks of Weigel become Weigel in reality? That I certainly would not wish; perhaps you would, so that you may of course turn into a thousand-fold being and set up so many individual Weigels. Or let Weigel think of his adversary, or a Weigelian, who vehemently laughs at all his theses: what, I ask you, would he then be, as a Weigelian?

units.la: In Theologiam pessime impingit, & sic videtur ejus causa illud maxime dixisse, nimirum ut hominem deificaret, non se homine contentus, nisi אלהים Genes. III. 5. Deus etiam fieret: quum hoc nec Deo, nec homini conveniat, hominem realiter & essentialiter Deum fieri. In Confess. cap. xv. qui intelligit Deum incomprehensibilem, intangibilem, penetrat ipsum impenetrabilem, & penetratur abilo. Qui penetrat Deum, unitur cum eo essentialiter, hoc fit per ignorantiam, & silentium caeleste, quasi ingimur ei, qui omnem scientiam & intellectum praeterfugit. Atque ita ipse homo per intellectum & cognitionem corporaliter ενθουσιαστης cum Deo unitur, & potest illud fieri, quod cognoscit, nempe Deus aut Dei filius, ita homo illud ipsum fit, quod studet; discit, ac cognoscit, quin seipsum reperit, ac ad se demum redit, esse enim omnia, & in se continet omnia. Fide Christi carnem edimus, & sanguinem bibimus Joh. vi. 1. Ipsa illud ipsum debemus fieri, quod edimus, id est. Christiani sunt per Christum, & cum eo essentialiter unum, non impetative, sed unione essentiali. Quid ergo dicit scriptura respondebunt, quod Hosandrum rejecerunt cum essentialiter satisfactione, quod in Christo essentialiter debemus uniri, sicut palmes in vineâ. Repudiabuntur & in aeternas tenebras exitus rejicientur cum suâ justitiâ imputatione. cap. ix. pag. 25. b. In tractatu de V. ac N. Jerusalem passim pseudo theologos appellat Confess. cap. viii. p. 24. b. citat et Dionysio: In ignorantiâ & suspensis magis unimus Deo, quam animus cum corpore. Confess. cap. IX. pag. 25. pseudo-theologi, qui per imputationem ab extra salvari volunt, nullum Christum habent, extra ipsum sunt, cruces refugiunt, baptismum repudiant, volunt cum-mori, confepelir, repudiant caenam, volunt calicem Domini bibere, sese separant a capite, nihilominus Carnem singulis quatuor temporibus edunt, quod ipsis damnationi est, o quam execrabilis via! Adde Stud. Uni-versi cap. III. Titulus dialogismi de Christianismo promittit explicationem, quomodo homo cum Christo corporaliter, interne ac externe uniatur. Vide ejus cap. I. II. V. Hinc manducationem Christi carnalem etiam urget, in eo a Lutheranis, & Pontificiis, sicut ipse fatetur, diversus, quod non carnem Christi, quasi ex Adamo tradatam, tamen eam ipsam, sicut se in cruce obtulit, corporaliter edi vult, de vita Christi c. XLV I. atque hinc c. XVI. singulis Christianis duplicem adscribit carnem. I. quam ab Adamo habent, cum extremo judicio deponendam; alteram ex Christi carne & sanguine, permanentem in vitam aeternam. Lib. de situ mundi cap. XXII. quid nova & supernaturalis caro aliud, quam spiritificata & deificata caro, quae ex regeneratione, ex carne Christi, & non ex Adamo producta? Homo noster hic neque se, neque alios intellexit. Unimur Deo, Christo, revera, ac spiritualiter, non ut essentia nostra Dei, vel Dei fiat nostra, per aliquam portentosam transmutationem, vel conversionem, quod neque Dei, neque nostri ratio permittit, & vel sensibus refutatur. Justitia Christi, quam nobis loco praestitit, nostra fit per imputationem, & quomodo aliter fieri possit? at & cum Christo etiam animur per spiritum ejus ac fidem: quemadmodum peccatum Adami, quod in actione transeunte consistit, nobis imputatur, qui praeterea etiam eadem natura uniti sumus cum Adamo. Uti in naturali rerum cognitione distinguimus mentem quae cognoscit, & rem, quæ cognoscitur; deinde actum mentis, quo cognoscimus, intellectionem, & rei speciem per quam res recipitur, videtur, atque pernoscitur; ita in spiritualibus nostrâ cum Deo & Christo unione, animam ac Deum, & deinde fidem, quæ actio est animæ supernaturalis, & gratiam Spiritus S. per quam Deus in nos influit, quo per fidem à nobis accipiatur, distinguimus; aliud ut sit Deus & homo, cognoscens & cognitum. Addiscens fabrilia, evadit quidem faber, id est cognitionem eorundem acquirit; at non ipse fit illa fabrilia, ut malleus, securis, ascia, terebra &c. Sic & qui ludos organorum, fistularum, Cytharæ addiscit &c. Haud necesse, diu immorari. Alia est unio essentialis, alia intentionalis, quæ fit per rerum speciem in mente: hujus generis ista est quâ cognitum unitur cum facultate cognoscendi, non illius: in esse cognoscibili & intellectuali, non reali & substantiali.
units.tr: He stumbles very badly into theology, and so it seems that for this reason above all he said it, namely, to deify man, not content with man unless he also became [אלהים, gods] God, Gen. 3:5. Since this suits neither God nor man, that man should become God in reality and in essence. In Confession ch. 15: whoever understands God as incomprehensible and intangible penetrates the impenetrable itself, and is penetrated by it. Whoever penetrates God is united with him essentially; this happens through ignorance and heavenly silence, as if we were drawn to him who escapes all knowledge and understanding. And so man himself, through understanding and knowledge, is united with God bodily and [ἐνθουσιαστής, enthusiastically], and that can happen which he knows, namely that God or the Son of God becomes; thus man becomes that very thing which he strives for, learns, and knows, indeed he finds himself and at last returns to himself, for to be all things is to contain all things in himself. By faith in Christ we eat his flesh and drink his blood, John 6:1. We ourselves ought to become that very thing which we eat, that is, Christians are through Christ, and one with him essentially, not by a command, but by an essential union. What, then, does Scripture say? They will answer that they have rejected Osiander, since he said that we must be united with Christ essentially, as a branch in the vine. They will be cast out and sent into eternal darkness, with the imputation of their righteousness. Ch. 9, p. 25 b. In the treatise on the Vita and the New Jerusalem he everywhere calls the pseudo-theologians, Confession ch. 8, p. 24 b, and quotes Dionysius: we are united with God more by ignorance and suspension of mind than the soul is with the body. Confession ch. 9, p. 25. The pseudo-theologians, who want to be saved by imputation from outside, have no Christ; they are outside him, they shun the cross, they reject baptism, they want to die with him, to be buried with him, they reject the Supper, they want to drink the Lord's cup, they separate themselves from the head, and yet they eat flesh at each of the four seasons, which is damnation to them. O what an accursed way! Add the Studium Universi ch. 3. The title of the dialogue on Christianity promises an explanation of how man is united with Christ bodily, inwardly and outwardly. See his chs. 1, 2, 5. Hence he also insists on a fleshly eating of Christ, in which he differs from the Lutherans and the Papists, as he himself confesses, in that he does not want the flesh of Christ, as if derived from Adam, but that very flesh as he offered it on the cross to be eaten bodily, On the life of Christ, ch. 45, and hence ch. 16. He ascribes to each Christian a twofold flesh: first, the flesh which they have from Adam, to be laid down at the last judgment; second, the flesh of Christ's flesh and blood, remaining unto eternal life. On the situation of the world, ch. 22: what is the new and supernatural flesh, other than spiritualized and deified flesh, produced from regeneration, from the flesh of Christ, and not from Adam? Our man here understood neither himself nor others. We are united to God and Christ really and spiritually, not so that our essence becomes God's, or God's becomes ours, through some monstrous transmutation or conversion, which neither the reason of God nor our own permits, and which is refuted even by the senses. The righteousness of Christ, which he offered in our place, becomes ours by imputation, and how else could it become so? But we are also united with Christ through his Spirit and faith, just as the sin of Adam, which consists in a transient act, is imputed to us, since we are also united with Adam by the same nature. As in the natural knowledge of things we distinguish the mind which knows and the thing which is known, then the act of the mind by which we know, the understanding, and the species of the thing through which the thing is received, seen and thoroughly known, so in our spiritual union with God and Christ we distinguish the soul and God, and then faith, which is a supernatural act of the soul, and the grace of the Holy Spirit by which God flows into us, so that it may be received by us through faith; so that there are God and man, the knower and the known. One who learns smithing indeed becomes a smith, that is, he acquires knowledge of those things; but he does not himself become those tools, such as hammer, axe, adze, auger, and so on. So too one who learns to play the organ, pipes, or lyre, and so on. There is no need to dwell on this at length. One union is essential, another intentional, which happens through the species of things in the mind. Of this kind is that by which the known is united with the faculty of knowing, not the other way round: in a knowable and intellectual being, not a real and substantial one.

units.la: Quæst. IV. An contraria in mente absolutè & promiscuè combinanda sint?
units.tr: Question IV. Whether contraries may be combined absolutely and indiscriminately in the mind?

units.la: Resp. 1. Fons erroris est in prava interpretatione, & abusu & ut Apocalypsi quod de Christo dicitur: hoc enim non docet, contraria omnia combinanda esse: sed modò, Christum principium omnium ex quo, & finem, in quem esse, diverso utrumque respectu, de quo item alibi dicitur, quod non sit in eo etiam & non, sed etiam in ipso. 2 Cor. 1. 19. contra ac V Veigelius audet dicere, utrumque in ipso æque locum habere. Uti si dicam, mare est principium omnium fluminum, & finis, idcirco ibi contraria combinabo? Principium & finis, abstractè & simpliciter quidem sunt contraria; sed nihil impedit, quo minus unum idemque alia & alia ratione dicatur rei principium, & finis. 11. Quodcunque etiam mens de rebus concipiat, nihil rerum naturam mutare potest; verum quæ contraria, manent contraria; & diversa, quæ diversa, omniaque talia ac sunt. Nullo pacto ego mente combinare possum ignem & aquam ut unum, quae combinari contrariâ suâ natura nolunt, multo minus coelum & infernum; Deum cum Diabolo; quidquid enim ego de rebus concipio, invariatae manent; neque si vel stultè eas combinari cogam, ideo desinent esse contrariae. III. Contraria omnia unire, est veritatem omnem tollere, primum enim veritatis principium est, implicationem contradictionis esse fundamentum veritatis, quod est, haud simul quid posse esse, & non esse, atque contradictoriorum alterum tantum esse verum: contrà VVeigelius contradictoria tollendo, omne verum ex rerum natura tollit: ideoque periode ei est, sive dicas Deum esse, an non esse Deum, an Diabolum; quae Scriptura dicit vera esse, an dicas falsa: nam illa utcunque combinabit in suâ mente. Quam haec optima ratio dirimendi controversias? Immò ille aequissimè ferat, quod dico VVeigelium mentiri & nugari, stultum an famam esse. Facilè enim in mente suâ illa combinarit, scilicet. IV. Atque ita etiam falsum semper concipiemus: aliter enim rem concipere, quam se habet, falsum est. V. Quidquid sit, summum scandalum & blasphemia, crudè & intrepidè dicere, coelum esse infernum, Deum Diabolum, Christum bestiam Apocalypticam, &c. quod piae aures non ferunt, & quidem repudiatâ omni explicatione, vel distinctione.
units.tr: Answer 1. The source of the error lies in a wrong interpretation and abuse of Scripture, as with what is said of Christ in the Apocalypse. For that passage does not teach that all contraries are to be combined. It says only that Christ is the principle of all things, from whom they come, and the end, to whom they go, these being taken in two different respects. Something similar is said elsewhere, that in him there is not yes and no, but yes in him (2 Cor. 1:19). Weigel, however, dares to say the opposite, that both hold equally in him. Suppose I said that the sea is the principle and the end of all rivers: would I then combine contraries there? Principle and end are, taken abstractly and simply, contraries; but nothing prevents one and the same thing from being called the principle and the end of a thing in different respects. II. Whatever the mind may conceive of things, it cannot change their nature. Contraries remain contraries, and things that differ remain different, and all such things stay as they are. In no way can I combine fire and water in my mind as one, since by their nature they refuse to be combined, much less heaven and hell, or God and the Devil. For whatever I conceive about things, they remain unchanged; and even if I foolishly force them to be combined, they will not on that account cease to be contrary. III. To unite all contraries is to remove all truth. For the first principle of truth is that the admission of a contradiction is the undoing of truth: that a thing cannot both be and not be at once, and that of two contradictories only one is true. Weigel, by removing contradictories, removes every truth from the nature of things. Hence he is at a loss whether you say that God is, or that God is not, or that it is the Devil, or whether you say that what Scripture declares true is true or false, for he will combine these in his mind in whatever way he likes. What a fine way of settling controversies this is! Nay, let him bear it most fairly if I say that Weigel lies and talks nonsense, and is a fool and a disgrace. For in his own mind he can easily combine these things. IV. And so we shall always conceive what is false as well: for to conceive a thing otherwise than it is, is to conceive what is false. V. Whatever the case, it is the greatest scandal and blasphemy to say crudely and boldly that heaven is hell, God is the Devil, Christ is the Apocalyptic beast, and so on. Pious ears cannot bear this, and it rejects every explanation or distinction.

units.la: Quaest. V. An propediem in terris futurum sit saeculum aliquod spiritus sancti, juxta seriem articulorum symboli?
units.tr: Question V. Whether some age of the Holy Spirit is to come shortly on earth, according to the sequence of the articles of the creed?

units.la: Resp. Illud de saeculo Spiritus S. utcunque videatur ingeniosum, frustra est, neque ullâ ratione solidâ se patitur persuaderi. Quod Filio saeculum datur, est ex ratione dispensatae redemptionis & curatae nostrae salutis, quae antea sub promissione, jam ab exhibitione Christi, nihil ultra exspectandum relinquit quam rerum omnium consummationem, non saeculum hic aliquod distinctum Spiritus Sancti. Dispensatio redemptionis nostrae, quâ solum ratione sæcula distinguuntur, illud non patitur: quum post hanc vitam sæculum vel regnum Trinitatis futurum, non singularis alicujus Personæ, ubi Deus erit omnia in omnibus. Neque in terris talia præstolari nos voluit Deus. Fratres Roseæ Crucis, aliique in Germaniâ plurimi tale sæculum sibi promittunt, quo omnis impietas exulabit, Israelitæ convertendi, quin etiam secundum nonnullos in terram Cánaan reducendi, Turcæ exscindendi, omnium rerum copia, concordia, scientia & sanctitas obtinebit, quomodo primævo ante lapsum mundo, uti declarat Author epistolæ, ante epist. Rogerii Baconis de secret. nat. & art. vide & Becmanni exercit. pag. 361. verum omnia illa frustra. Item tertium sæculum clamabat Philippus Zieglerus, seque istius sanctissimi regni scribebat præconem, in libello Germanico, super isto negotio, adversus Philippum Arnoldum, & Paulum Nagelium. Forte, Germanorum plures eo lubentius in talem futuri felicioris sæculi sententiam eunt, quia homines harum, quibus hactenus graviter pressi, calamitatum pertæsi, facilius sibi persuaderi volunt meliora tempora: atque ut alicubi Ludovicus Vives, in Augustinum loquitur: nulla res est, de quâ liberius homines mentiuntur, quam de futuris, quoniam nihil nos audimus libentius; etiamsi nisi falsum dici sciamus: ita favor in eos noster, qui futura jactant prædicere, licentia eorum irritat, & alit; usque adeo in re mirabili vel voluisse mirandum ducimus. Nisi quod jam olim etiam Muncerus cum suis, & David Georgius perpetuò aliam Remp. aliud sæculum, regnum, & quod à sanctitate se commendaret, creparint. Hortensius, in historiâ Anabapt. pag. 11. inter illorum Paradoxa hoc quidem primum ponit: Paradoxa autem hæc erant. Christi regnum ante ultimum diem rerum humanarum civile in terrâ futurum: hic soli sancti & justi, regibus ferro & vi sublatis, dominarentur. Id autem regnum esse jam coeptum Anabaptistarum. Blesdikius in hist. David. Georg.
units.tr: Answer. However ingenious the idea of an age of the Holy Spirit may appear, it is vain, and it cannot be persuaded by any solid reasoning. The age given to the Son arises from the plan of the redemption accomplished and of our salvation secured. Once the promise was made and Christ was revealed, nothing remains to be expected but the consummation of all things, not some distinct age of the Holy Spirit here. The dispensation of our redemption, by which alone the ages are distinguished, does not allow it. For after this life there will be the age or kingdom of the Trinity, not of any single Person, when God will be all in all. Nor has God wished us to look for such things on earth. The Rosicrucian brothers, and many others in Germany, promise themselves such an age, in which all impiety will be banished, the Israelites converted, and even, according to some, led back to the land of Canaan, the Turks destroyed, and an abundance of all things, harmony, knowledge and holiness will prevail, as in the primeval world before the fall. So the author of the letter declares, before the letter of Roger Bacon, de secret. nat. & art.; see also Becmann, exercit., p. 361. But all these things are in vain. Likewise Philip Ziegler proclaimed a third age and called himself the herald of that most holy kingdom in a German booklet on this matter, against Philip Arnold and Paul Nagel. Perhaps many Germans go more gladly into such an opinion of a happier age to come, because people weary of the grievous calamities by which they have hitherto been oppressed want to be persuaded more easily that better times are coming. And as Ludovicus Vives says somewhere, speaking against Augustine: There is nothing about which men lie more freely than about the future, since we hear nothing more gladly; and yet we know it is only false that is said. So our favour towards those who boast that they can predict the future feeds their licence and encourages it, to such an extent that we think it a marvel to wish for it in a matter so marvellous. Except that long ago Müntzer with his followers, and David Joris, kept crying out for another commonwealth, another age, another kingdom, which would commend itself by its holiness. Hortensius, in his history of the Anabaptists, p. 11, lists among their paradoxes this first one: Now these were the paradoxes: that the kingdom of Christ, a civil kingdom of human affairs, would be on earth before the last day; that there the saints and the just alone would rule, with kings removed by the sword and force. And that this kingdom had already begun among the Anabaptists. Blesdikius, in hist. David. Georg.

units.la: arg.pag. 4. 8. ex Apocalypsi itidem docebant, propediem per novos Apostolicos viros novum Hierosolymam reaedificandam, his templum aperiendum Apoc. 11. 19. & viam ad nuptias Agni aperiendam, Apoc. 19. 7. &c. pag. 37. Iam tertiâ vice, & ultimò Deum se orbi patefacere ajebant, in isto Christo Davidis, qui antea etiam in Mose & Christo, sed in illo umbratice, in hoc corporaliter, jam verò spiritualiter se exhiberet; & doctrinâ suâ postremo saeculo reservatâ, (in quo septima Apoc. tuba resonaret.) torbem ad primaevum mundi, ante lapsum statum retormaret. Atque talem depingunt sibi mundi futuram reformationem fratres Rosae Crucis, universalem in terrenum Paradysum, qualem Adamus ante lapsum possedit, & artium omnium ac sapientiae restitutionem, qualem Adamus, Enoch, Salomon habuerunt, uti contra illos scribit And. Libavius, homo in nostros, etiam illo suo scripto Considerat. infamam & Confess. fraternit. Rosea Crucis, addé etiam Examen philos. nov. pag. 115. 127. virulentior atque inhumanior, nominatim in Cl. D. Lucium, Professorem Basileensem, quem improbè & indignè exagitat; atque etiam ipsi illi fratres contra nostros haud obscurè se declarant, in Fama pag. 30. quam, uti & Confessionem ediderunt hujus saeculi anno XVII. quum demùm nota illa fraternitas coepit esse ad annum XV. Nempe in Fama, quam quinque linguis disparserunt, quasi historiam suae fundationis atque originis continentem, scripserunt, quod Fr. Christianus Rosenkreutzius, nobili inter Germanos familiâ, Monachus, natus An. clɔ ccc lxxxviii. anno suae aetatis decimo sexto peregrinationem ad sepulchrum Christi instituens, ad Magos in Arabiâ, Aegypto, ac Barbariâ divertit, ubi omnia secreta secretorum, Physica, Chymica, Magica hausit, ac didicit, quae in Europam referens, pro universali reformatione humani, ac divini, [ita loquuntur Fam. pag. 29.] instituit collegium, sive fraternitatem; cujus primi socii memorantur pag. 17. atque leges pag. 19., nimirum, I. ut nullam aliam assumerent professionem, praeter ægrorum curationem. II. Nemo fraternitatis causa cogeretur ad certum vestimenti genus; sed morem regionis quilibet sequeretur. III. Fratrum unusquisque quotannis die C. ad S. Spiritus conveniret, vel absentiæ suæ causas transcriberet. IV. Quisque sibi de idoneo successore tempestive prospiceret. V. Signum, vel sacramentum illorum esset R.C. VI. Fraternitas per sæculum taceretur.
units.tr: arg. p. 4, 8. They taught likewise from the Apocalypse that shortly, through new apostolic men, the new Jerusalem was to be rebuilt, the temple to be opened to them (Rev. 11:19), and the way to the marriage of the Lamb to be opened (Rev. 19:7), etc., p. 37. Now, for the third time and finally, they said, God was revealing himself to the world, in that Christ of David who had earlier shown himself in Moses and Christ, but in the latter obscurely, in the former bodily, and now spiritually; and, with his doctrine reserved for the last age, in which the seventh trumpet of the Apocalypse would sound, he would restore the world to its original state, before the fall. The Rosicrucian brothers likewise depict for themselves such a future reformation of the world, a universal earthly paradise, such as Adam possessed before the fall, and a restoration of all arts and wisdom such as Adam, Enoch and Solomon had. So writes Andreas Libavius against them, a man hostile to our side, also in his writing Considerations on the infamy and the Confession of the Rosy Cross Brotherhood. Add also Examen philos. nov., pp. 115, 127, more virulent and inhuman, especially against the distinguished Lucius, professor at Basel, whom he attacks shamelessly and unworthily. Moreover, the brothers themselves declare their position openly against our people, in Fama, p. 30, which they published, as well as the Confessio, in the year 1617, when that famous brotherhood had only just begun to be known, about fifteen years earlier. For in the Fama, which they spread in five languages as if it contained the history of their foundation and origin, they wrote that Brother Christian Rosenkreutz, a monk of a noble German family, was born in 1388. In his sixteenth year, undertaking a pilgrimage to the sepulchre of Christ, he turned aside to the magi in Arabia, Egypt and Barbary, where he drank in and learned all the secrets of secrets, physical, chemical and magical. Bringing these back to Europe, he founded, for the universal reformation of the human and the divine (so they speak, Fama, p. 29), a college or brotherhood. Its first members are named on p. 17, and its laws on p. 19. These were: I. That they should take up no profession other than the healing of the sick. II. No one should be compelled by the brotherhood to wear a particular kind of dress, but each should follow the custom of his region. III. Each of the brothers should meet each year on the hundredth day, at Pentecost, or write out the reasons for his absence. IV. Each should in good time look out for a suitable successor. V. Their sign or sacrament should be R.C. VI. The brotherhood should be kept secret for a century.

units.la: Auctor ille Fr. Christianus Rosenkreutzius mortuus tandem, cum sepulchro suo fratres diutissimè latuisse dicitur, usque dum repertus cum hoc Epitaphio scilicet: Ch. Ros. C. ex nobili atque splendida Germ. R.C. familiâ oriundus, Vir sui seculi divinis revelationibus, subtilissimis imaginationibus, indefessis laboribus, ad cælestia, atque humana mysteria, arcanaque admissus, postquam suam [quam Arabico & Africano itineribus collegisset] plusquam regiam aut imperatoriam gazam suo sæculo nondum conve-nientem, posteritati erundam custodivisset, & jam suarum artium, ut & nominis, fidos ac conjunctissimos heredes instituisset, mundum minutum, omnibus motibus magno illi respondentem fabricasset, hocque tandem, præteritarum, præsentium & futurarum rerum compendio extracto, centenario major, non morbo (quem ipse nunquam corpore expertus erat, nunquam alios infestare sinebat) ullo pellente, sed Spiritu Dei evocante, illuminatam animam (inter fratrum amplexus & ultima osculla) Creatori Deo reddidisset. Pater dilectissimus, Fr. suavissimus, præceptor fidelissimus, amicus integerrimus, à suis ad 120. annos hic absconditus est. Infra scripta Sociorum nonnullorum nomina. Hæc in fama fratern. p. 27. Atque ne longævitatem hujus Patris admodum miremur, A. cIↄ Iↄ c xix. ediderunt Fratres admonitionem ad discipulos suos, quâ illos jubent sibi cavere de falsis fratribus, tit. frater non frater, germanicè, quam communi nomine claudunt & obsignant: Datum 16. Martii ex invisibili nostro nostro domicilio, in Agro Damasceno Anno 1619. Vidit, Hugo Alverda, aetatis suae quingentesimo septuagesimo nono. Edwardus VVoodStrang, Anglus, aetatis suae quadringentesimo tertio. Zacharias Benitz, Francus, aetatis suae ducentesimo octavo. Iacobus Patherius, Pomeranus, aetatis suae ducentesimo quinto. Ad mandatum gloriose fraternitatis proprium subscripsit Irenæus Agnotus C. VV. ejusdem fraternitatis per Germaniam indignus Notarius. Ride, & cogita in Vtopia aliquâ te versari: & tamen hi fratres magno cum strepitu volunt εἶναι π. Quoniam mundus vult decipi, decipiatur. Quaecunque autem fratricelli illi de ordinis sui fundatore & origine promunt, ab illis conficta prorsius, & omni argumento ac ratione, vel historicâ veritate destituuntur; & quantumcunque scribant, tumultuentur, quidve iactitent, credulis duntaxat fumum, & nugas vendunt. Nempe illis verborum ampullis, atque ambagibus, nil nisi lapidem philosophicum occultare voluerunt, & prodere, quomodo illi homines semper solent, dicere & non dicere, promittere & tacere. Indicavit hoc de illis Radtichs Brotoffer in Elucidario majori super Reformationem totius mundi F. R.C. ostenditque, illis illorum scriptis modo contineri ac declarari materiam & praeparationem lapidis aurei. Quippe notum, quomodo illi cum suo lapide solcant omnia polliceri, divina humanaque, atque in ejus gratiam, vulgarem & usitatam philosophandi ac medicandi doctrinam contemnere, & omninò Reformationem velle, scil., reformationem, quae sicuti lapis ille, omnia invertat, renovet, atque deauret quasi in aliud saeculum Poëtarum. Hoc aureum, (ut ad propositum revertamur) Spiritus S. saeculum, & nescio quibus non elogiis appellitant, quod multos hodie dementavit, ac vanâ spe lactavit, inquit Eusch. Bohemus, in epit. histor. pag. 1023. & Micraelius pag. 514. paucis abhinc annis omnium animos suspensos tenuerunt, & nescio quam perfectionem, & summam sapisapientiam justitarunt. In confess. Fr. R. Cr. cap. VIII. in quiunt, quemadmodum homo duo organa auditus, duo visus, ac odoratus totidem habet, voci sonandae modo unum; ita sc. fuerunt saecula, quae audierunt, atque odorata sunt, superesse saeculum elocutionis, cum mundus a sopore suo gravi evigilabit, & obviam ibit novo soli orienti, pedibus nudis, nudo capite, summo cum gaudio.
units.tr: That author, Fr. Christian Rosenkreutz, is said to have died at last, and his brethren to have remained hidden in his tomb for a very long time, until it was found bearing this epitaph: Ch. Ros. C., born of a noble and distinguished German R.C. family, a man admitted by divine revelations, most subtle imaginings and tireless labours to heavenly and human mysteries and secrets. After he had gathered together, through Arabian and African journeys, a treasure greater than any royal or imperial hoard, which his own age was not yet ready to receive, he preserved it for posterity. He also appointed faithful and closest heirs of his arts and of his name, and he built a little world that answers in every motion to that great one. Finally, having drawn out this summary of past, present and future things, and being more than a hundred years old, he gave back his enlightened soul to his Creator God, not because any sickness drove him (he had never suffered from illness himself and never allowed it to trouble others), but because the Spirit of God called him, in the embraces and last kisses of his brethren. Our most beloved father, most sweet brother, most faithful teacher, most upright friend, has been hidden here by his own people for 120 years. Below are written the names of some of the Fellows. In Fama Fraternitatis, p. 27. And lest we wonder greatly at the long life of this Father, in the year 1619 the Brethren issued an admonition to their disciples, in which they bid them beware of false brethren, under the title frater non frater (in German), and they close and seal it with a common name: Given on 16 March from our invisible dwelling in the Damascene field, in the year 1619. Hugo Alverda saw it, in his 579th year. Edward Woodstrang, Englishman, in his 403rd year. Zacharias Benitz, Frenchman, in his 208th year. Jacob Patherius, Pomeranian, in his 205th year. By command of the glorious brotherhood, Irenaeus Agnotus, C. W., unworthy notary of the same brotherhood throughout Germany, subscribed. Laugh, and reflect that you are living in some Utopia; yet these brethren loudly insist to be ... [εἶναι π.]. Since the world wants to be deceived, let it be deceived. Whatever those little brothers say about the founder and origin of their order is entirely invented, and is wholly lacking in any argument, reason or historical truth. However much they write, make a stir, or boast, they sell only smoke and trifles to the credulous. Indeed, with those bombastic and circuitous words they have wished to conceal and reveal nothing but the philosopher's stone, in the way such men always tend to say and not say, promise and keep silent. Radtichs Brotoffer pointed this out in his Greater Elucidarium on the Reformation of the Whole World, F. R.C., and he shows that in their writings the matter and preparation of the golden stone are merely contained and declared. It is well known how they, with their stone, are accustomed to promise all things, divine and human, and for its sake to despise the common and accustomed doctrine of philosophy and medicine, and altogether to want a Reformation, namely a reformation which, like that stone, overturns, renews and gilds all things, as if into another age of the poets. This golden age (to return to our subject) they call the age of the Holy Spirit, with various other titles, and it has driven many mad today and cheated them with vain hope, as Eusebius Bohemus says in his Epitome of History, p. 1023; and Micraelius, p. 514: a few years ago they held the minds of all in suspense, and promised I know not what perfection and supreme wisdom. In the Confession of the Fraternity of R.C., chapter VIII, they say that just as man has two organs of hearing, two of sight, and likewise two of smell, but only one for sounding a voice, so there have been ages which heard and smelled, and there remains an age of utterance, when the world will awake from its heavy sleep and go forth to meet the new rising sun, barefoot, bareheaded, with the greatest joy.

units.la: Cap. VII. Decrevit Deus mundo ante exitium suum eam veritatem, lucem, vitam & gloriam reddere, qualem primus homo, Adam nempe in Paradyso, perdidit, unde postmodum posteri ejus cum eo in miseriam detrusi fuerunt. Illic omnis servitus, fraus, mendacium & tenebrae cessare ac cedere cogentur. Contra illos operose scripsit Libavius, praeter Considerationes in famam & confess. fratern. & Germanice, in examine philos. nov. pag. 262. de philosophia harmonica fratrum R.C. & Analysin Confessionum, &c. Ejusmodi sunt, quae olim & hodie Chiliastae variae opinati: de quibus jam non agemus.
units.tr: Chapter VII. God has decreed that before the destruction of the world he will restore to it that truth, light, life and glory which the first man, Adam, namely in Paradise, lost, and by which his posterity were afterwards thrust with him into misery. There all servitude, deceit, falsehood and darkness will be forced to cease and give way. Against them Libavius has written at length, besides his Considerations on the Fame and Confession of the Fraternity, and in German, in Examen of the New Philosophy, p. 262, on the harmonic philosophy of the brethren of R.C., and an Analysis of the Confessions, etc. Such are the things which Chiliasts, both in the past and today, have variously held; we shall not treat of them now.

units.la: Atque tabula quoque Paracelsum somniasse, & piedixisse referunt; cujus Prognostica qui scire avet, consulat Lectiones Memorabiles V Volfii, Centen. XVI. sol. 484. &c. Quin & Auctor Euangelii aeterni, uti id appellabant Dominicani, (quo S. Euangelium opprimere erat animus, & quod tumultus illos Parisiis inter scholam ac Monachos A. MCCIV. vehementes concitavit,) illud Euangelium dico, tertium mundi statum & Euangelium Spiritus S. promittebat; sive ejus auctor Iohannes Parmensis, & ex scriptis Ioachimi Abbatis congestum fuerit, quod incertum, an alius: nam sedulo Papa librum illum clam comburi, & quaestiones sopiri curavit.
units.tr: Moreover, they report that a tablet shows Paracelsus dreaming and prophesying; anyone who wishes to know his Prognostics may consult the Memorable Lectures of Volfius, Centuria XVI, p. 484, etc. Indeed the author of the so-called Eternal Gospel, as the Dominicans called it (by which they intended to suppress the Holy Gospel, and which stirred up violent tumults at Paris between the school and the monks in the year 1204), that Gospel, I say, promised a third state of the world and a Gospel of the Holy Spirit. Whether its author was John of Parma, and it was compiled from the writings of Joachim the Abbot, is uncertain, or whether it was someone else; for the Pope took careful steps to have that book secretly burned and the questions quieted.

units.la: Verum ista de saeculo Spiritus S. omnia, & qualiacunque, iisdem argumentis refutantur; eo potissimum, quod affirmativam nulla ratione demonstrant, maxime ubi ad particularia aliqua exponenda & promittenda descendunt, quod illis ante omnia faciendum est, siquidem fidem illis adhiberi certam cupiant. Quin repugnant illastatui tum Ecclesiae, tum orbis, quem circa postrema tempora Spiritus Sanctus variis in locis describit futurum haud ita felicem, ac illi homines sibi imaginantur. Matth. xxiv. Luc. xvii. & xxi. 2 Tim. iv. 2 Pet. iii. ut omittam, quod in statum Christi impingunt ea, quae de adventu etiam Christi in terram isto saeculo addunt. Vitae alteri plenissima communicatio Spiritus Sancti ac totius Trinitatis cum omni felicitate, ac perfectione servatur.
units.tr: But all these things about the age of the Holy Spirit, and whatever they are, are refuted by the same arguments; chiefly because they do not demonstrate their affirmation by any reasoning, especially where they descend to explain and promise particular things, which they must do above all if they want their claims to be held with certainty. Indeed, they contradict the condition both of the Church and of the world, which the Holy Spirit describes in various places as going to be not nearly so happy as they imagine: Matt. 24; Luke 17 and 21; 2 Tim. 4; 2 Pet. 3. I pass over that they also assault the state of Christ by adding, concerning this age, the coming of Christ himself upon earth. The other life is kept most full of the communication of the Holy Spirit and of the whole Trinity, with all happiness and perfection.

units.la: A V Veigelio, ad Swencfeldum, eo facilior est transitus, isque necessarius, quod Swencfeldum V Veigelius inter coelestes Prophetas annumerat, dial. de vero Christianismo cap. iv; & quemadmodum V Veigelianismus plures occupavit, ita plerumque illos primum dementavit Swencfeldus, saepiusque nominari hominem audias, quam describi, vel explicari. Graßatur haec Swencfeldiana, inquit Hosius, non modo per Germaniam, verum etiam per Helvetiam, et est ingens eorum numerus qui jactant hunc afflatum, lib. de haeresibus nostri temp. Tom. 1. Atque etiamnum plures istius deliriis tenentur, vixque est, qui paradoxa, & alia a notis sectis sapit, & non apud Swencfeldum somniarit. Historiam ejus breviter tangit Micraelius, Syntagm. histor. lib. iii, pag. 513. Post Anabaptistas fastuosus Casp. Swencfeld de Oßing cum affectis inter Paradoxos merito collocatur. Fuit is nobilis Silesius, et tanquam unus ex Scepticis, neque Papa, neque Luthero, neque Sacramentariis, neque Anabaptistis adstipulatus, sed quaedam ex omnibus approbans, et novam religionis ideam venditans, verbo Dei sepposito, spretoque ecclesiastico ministerio, somnia sua jactitavit, et plurimos, interque eos Valentinum Krautwald et Johannem Sigismund. Werner, illum Canonicum, hunc Pastorem Lignicensem, eloquentia affectata dementavit. Verbum externum ad salutem conferre, carnem Christi non esse nostra similem, legem Dei facile impleri posse docuit, et a Friderico Principe Lignicensi ejectus Silesia, cultissima Germania
units.tr: The transition from Weigel to Schwenckfeld is easy, and indeed necessary, because Weigel counts Schwenckfeld among the heavenly prophets (Dialogue on True Christianity, ch. iv); and just as Weigelianism occupied many, so Schwenckfeld was the first to drive most of them mad. You will hear the man named more often than he is described or explained. This Schwenckfeldian plague, says Hosius, is raging not only through Germany but also through Switzerland, and there is a huge number of those who boast of this inspiration, in his book on the heresies of our time, vol. 1. Even now many are held by his delusions, and there is scarcely anyone who savours of paradoxes or other notions foreign to the known sects and has not dreamed them up with Schwenckfeld. Micraelius briefly touches on his history, Syntagma Historicum, book iii, p. 513: After the Anabaptists, the haughty Caspar Schwenckfeld of Ossig, with his followers, is rightly placed among the paradoxists. He was a noble Silesian, who, as one of the Sceptics, sided with neither the Pope, nor Luther, nor the Sacramentarians, nor the Anabaptists, but approved some things from all of them and peddled a new idea of religion. With the Word of God set aside and the ecclesiastical ministry scorned, he bandied about his dreams, and with affected eloquence he drove many mad, among them Valentine Krautwald and Johann Sigismund Werner, the one a canon, the other a minister at Liegnitz. He taught that the external Word contributes nothing to salvation, that the flesh of Christ is not like ours, and that the law of God can easily be fulfilled. Expelled from Silesia by Prince Frederick of Liegnitz, he wandered through the most cultivated parts of Germany as a false apostle

units.la: nia mie loca tanquam Pseudoapostolus peragravit, & furtivos passim egit conventus, & si verum est, quod de se ipse scribit, intra xxviii. annos plus quam L. libellos idiomate vernaculo typis vulgavit, quos Lutherus ex ipso dixit Diabolum vomere & cacare. Et Eusebus Bohemus in histor. Ecclesiast. epitome. pag. 973. Sparsit autem circa Annum Ch. cIↄ Iↄ xxvi. juxta Osiandrum, & inprimis circa tempus exhibita Augusti Confessionis passim in Silesia puti-dos & factissimos errores, ob quos D. Lutherus, Philippus & alii Theologi eum a factore maleolente Stencfeldium appellaverunt. Ex Silesia autem profligatus, atroque carbone publicè notatus, vagabundus hinc inde per Germaniam oberravit, suique capitis deliramenta passim disseminavit. De quibus omnibus Catal. Hæretic. Schlüsselburgii, libro decimo legas: & Osiandri Hist. Eccles. Cen. 16. lib. 11. cap. 3.
units.tr: ...nia places, wandering like a pseudo-apostle, and he held secret meetings everywhere; and if it is true what he himself writes about himself, within twenty-eight years he published in the vernacular more than fifty little books, which Luther said the Devil himself had vomited and defecated. And Eusebius Bohemus, in the Epitome of Ecclesiastical History, p. 973: "He scattered his errors, according to Osiander, around the year 1526, and especially around the time the Augsburg Confession was presented, in Silesia, foul and most pestilential errors; on account of these Dr. Luther, Philip and other theologians called him the stinking stench-maker Stenkfeld." Driven out of Silesia and publicly branded with a black mark, he wandered hither and thither through Germany, and he spread the ravings of his own mind everywhere. Concerning all these matters you may read the Catalogue of Heretics by Schlüsselburg, book ten; and Osiander's Ecclesiastical History, Century 16, book 11, chapter 3.

units.la: CAP. 3.
units.tr: CHAPTER 3.

units.la: Vir fuit nobilis prosapiæ, ætate provectior, quum litteris & studiis se daret, neque Græca adhuc intelligens, quum de Eucharistiâ docere, & opinionem propriam sequi inciperet; verùm à Cratavaldo, qui in Collegio Canonicorum Lignitii Lectorem egerat, & in Græcis versatior, linguam illam addidicit, postquam eum in sententiam suam pertraxisset. Swencfeld. Tom. 11. epist. 111. & 1v. qui Cratovaldus postmodum Swencfeldianismum valdè promovit. Ipse verò Swencfeldus, postquam in aulâ versatus fuisset, epist. 1., ad Theologica animum applicuit; & dum evitaret nomen & officium Doctoris vel Concionatoris, cum Theologis & Theologicis peramanter versari se, hoc tantùm prositebatur. Tom. 11. epist. ult. confestim tamen ad libros scribendos se applicuit, quasi hoc non cuivis solum, quin & in primis initiis necessarium esset. Contra ac prudentiores semper, & eruditissimi quique judicant, juxta illud Hieronymi: ne ad scribendum cito prosilias, & levi ducaris insania. Multo tempore disce, quod doceas, epist. ad Rusticum Monach. Et ad Nepotianum: disce, quod do[illegible, ~6 letters]eas. Socrates, apud Platonem Alcib. 1. nonne scis opor - tere eos, qui aliquid doctluri sunt, prius quam doceant, intelligere? & egregie Bernardus, Serm. XVIII. in Cantic. Si sapis, concham te exhibebis, & non canalem. Hic siquidem pene simul & recipit, & refundit. Illa vero donec impleatur, expectat, & sic quod superabundat, sine suo damno communicat. Verum canales multos hodie habemus in Ecclesia, conchas vero perpaucas. Tante charitatis sunt, per quas nobis fluenta coelestia emanant, ut ante effundere, quam infundi velint, loqui, quam audire parationes, & promti docere, quod non didicerunt. Gregorius, in praesat. sui pastoral. Sunt plerique mihi imperitia similes, qui dum metiri se nesciunt, quae non didicerunt, docere conceperunt.
units.tr: He was a man of noble birth and rather advanced in years when he devoted himself to letters and study. Not yet understanding Greek, he began to teach about the Eucharist and to follow his own opinion. He learned that language from Cratavaldus, who had been lecturer in the college of canons at Liegnitz and was more skilled in Greek, after he had drawn him into his view. Swencfeld. Tom. 11. epist. 111. & 1v. This Cratovaldus afterwards greatly promoted Swenckfeldianism. Swenckfeld himself, after he had spent time at court, epist. 1. turned his mind to theology. While avoiding the name and office of teacher or preacher, he professed only this: that he was very fond of associating with theologians and with theological matters. Tom. 11. epist. ult. Yet he at once set himself to writing books, as if this were necessary not only for anyone but especially at the very beginning. The wiser men, however, and all the most learned judge otherwise, in line with that saying of Jerome: do not rush headlong into writing, and do not be led on by a light madness. Learn for a long time what you are going to teach, letter to Rusticus the monk. And in the letter to Nepotianus: learn what you teach [illegible]. Socrates, in Plato's Alcibiades I: do you not know that those who are about to teach something must first understand it before they teach? And Bernard, admirably, in sermon 18 on the Song of Songs: If you are wise, you will show yourself a shell and not a channel. For the shell receives and pours out almost at the same moment; but the channel waits until it is filled, and so passes on what overflows without loss to itself. Today, however, we have many channels in the Church, and very few shells. Such is the charity through which heavenly streams flow out to us, that they want to pour out before they are poured into, to speak before they have listened, and are quick to teach what they have not learned. Gregory, in the preface to his Pastoral Rule: Many are very like me in inexperience, who, since they do not know how to measure themselves, have set out to teach what they have not learned.

units.la: Caeterum multis non tam malus initio visus est Swencfeldus, sed ex animi quadam impotentia magis primos errores concepisse, quam improbitate: verum initio dico, ita prudenter distinguenda errorum, turbarum, scismatis vel haeresium principia, ab eorum incrementis & ἀχμῆ. Apud Sculteum, histor. Reform. ad A. M. D. XXV, Bucholcerus inquit: Swencfeldo non tam defuisse probum animum, quam sanum caput. Et Pomeranus, in privatâ cum eo habitâ collatione: credo equidem te non malo animo hac agere; etiam pium te aestimo. Quae inter opera Swencfeldi Tom. II. edit. Anno D. MDLXX. epist. IV. pag. 33. Neque aliter de eo judicat Melchior Adamus, in vita Bullingeri. Peramplum ei testimonium dedit Zwinglius, pro Confutatione Impanationis, ac Transsubstantiationis; atque Oecolampadius, pro ejus tractatu de cursu verbi divini. Tom. II. epist. XXIV. Cui tamen judicio nolim perfacile assentiri tale est: Non hoc agit eruditus & pius Swencfeldus, ut aliquid extremo verbo, ejusque doctrinae, cujus & nullius alterius instrumenti operâ spiritus sanctus utitur, decedat, vel detrahatur; diaboli cum esset, rem adeo salutarem vilipendere. Ipsc videbis, hominem tale quid nihil cogitare. Hoc tantum annititur, quo Deo soli omnis honor, in solidum de-tur. Nolim (dico) hoc simpliciter de illo testari: constabit ex sequentibus, tum ipsius Swenckfeldi testimoniis, tum aliorum judiciis, secius se rem habere: quamvis de eo judicium mihi non arrogem, quo primum animo illa ceperit cogitare & volvere. Lutherus eum acerbissime insectatur Tom. VIII. Ien. oper. anno MDXL. epist. ad Swenckf. Contra Carolostadius perhumaniter eum tractat, epist. ad Swenckf. & Cratovald. inter opera Lutheri Tom. IV. At ipse Swenckfeldus postmodum de Zwinglio nec bene sentiebat, nec loquebatur, me summo odio prosequitur, scripsit libello quo A. MDLIV. Melanthon in praef. ep. ad Rom. Stenckfeldius [ita eum pro Swenckfeldo appellabat] centimanus est: habet milites passim, qui ipsius nomine non solum scribunt, sed etiam seditiones movent; jactitant afflatus, & abducunt homines a publico ministerio, & a lectione & cogitatione doctrinae. Ac nunc quoque adversus me, editis aliquot pagellis nomine Stenckfeldii, repetitur ille xgu xio μι& gratissima cantilena fanaticis hominibus, non cogitatione scripta doctrina Deum communicare se hominum mentibus, sed sine medio. Stanislaus Hosius, lib. de haeref. nostri temp. Tom. I. Oper. pag. 438. quamvis ante Swenckfeldum fuerunt caelestes Prophetae, contra quos justa duo volumina conscripsit Lutherus, quorum dux & antesignanus fuisse creditur Thomas Muncerus, non tamen ii tam aperte a publico verbi ministerio, & a lectione scripturarum homines deterrebant, sicut nunc facit cum suis Swenckfeldius, qui non dubitat etiam ad patrocinium insaniae sua trahere Pauli locum 1 Cor. 13. &c.
units.tr: However, to many people Swenckfeld did not at first seem so wicked. They thought he had fallen into his early errors from a certain weakness of mind rather than from malice. But I say at first, for the beginnings of errors, disturbances, schism or heresy must be carefully distinguished from their growth and acme [ἀκμή]. In Sculteus's history of the Reformation, under the year 1525, Bucholcerus says: Swenckfeld lacked not so much an honest mind as a sound head. And Pomeranus, in a private conference held with him: I believe indeed that you act with no bad intent; I even judge you to be pious. These words are among the works of Swenckfeld, vol. II, edition of 1570, letter IV, p. 33. Melchior Adam judges him no differently, in the life of Bullinger. Zwingli gave him very high praise in his Refutation of Impanation and Transubstantiation, and Oecolampadius did so for his treatise on the course of the divine word, vol. II, letter XXIV. Yet I would not readily assent to that judgment, and this is why: the learned and pious Swenckfeld does not aim to detract from or belittle the ministry of the Word or its doctrine, which the Holy Spirit uses alone and through no other instrument.
