It would be diabolical to despise something so salutary. You will see that the man has no such thing in mind. His only aim is that all honour be given wholly to God alone. I would not (I say) simply vouch for him in this: it will be clear from what follows, both from Swenckfeld's own statements and from the judgments of others, that the matter stands otherwise. Still, I do not claim to judge the frame of mind in which he first began to conceive and turn over these ideas. Luther attacks him most bitterly, in vol. VIII of the Jena works, in the year 1540, in a letter to Swenckfeld. Carlstadt, on the other hand, treats him very courteously, in a letter to Swenckfeld and Cratovaldus, among the works of Luther, vol. IV. But Swenckfeld himself afterwards neither thought nor spoke well of Zwingli, and pursued him with the greatest hatred; in a little book of 1554 he... Melanchthon, in the preface to his Epistle to the Romans, says: Stenckfeld [so he called Swenckfeld] is a hundred-handed monster. He has soldiers everywhere who write not only in his name but also stir up sedition; they boast of inspirations, and draw men away from the public ministry and from reading and reflecting on doctrine. And now, too, against me, with some pamphlets put out in Stenckfeld's name, that old and most pleasing tune is sung to fanatical people: that God communicates himself to human minds through no written doctrine, but without any means. Stanislaus Hosius, in his book on the heretics of our time, vol. I of his works, p. 438: although there were heavenly prophets before Swenckfeld, against whom Luther wrote two substantial volumes, and whose leader and standard-bearer was believed to be Thomas Müntzer, yet they did not turn men away so openly from the public ministry of the Word and from reading the Scriptures as Swenckfeld now does with his followers, who does not hesitate to draw even 1 Cor. 13 etc. into the defence of his madness.

units.la: Vivebat ea tempestate, qua de Ecclesia reformanda & instituenda disputationes agitabantur vehementissimae, omniumque animi huc illuc trahebantur; quare non ille solum, sed & plures circa Ecclesiam haerebant, errabantque. Hinc etiam natae Socino quaestiones, de necessitate inquirendae Ecclesiae, non necessarifarium hoc docens, quo de hominibus maximè laborabant. Sic ejus sententiam explicans Theophilus Nicolaides, tractatu de Ecclesiâ, contra Borkoroski, inquit pag. 9. ego ostendo, Socinum affirmare, quæstionem de Ecclesiâ, non omnem, sed aliquam, nempe quarum & apud quos sit, esse, non simpliciter, & absolute, sed vel pro- pemodum, vel quodammodo inutilem. Ostorodus, Insti- tit, cap. xlii. & Volkelius, de religione lib. v i. cap. xvi. Ideoque & nullius necessitatis esse passim arguunt, de notis Ecclesiæ sollicitum esse, Catechesis Racoviana, cap. de Eccles. Christi, pag. 336. quærit, quia pœnè omnes sibi Ecclesiam arrogant, ex quibus notis Ecclesia dignosci possit? respondet, nullius usus esse, hoc inquirere. Similiter Smalcius, contra Franczium, disp. ii x. de Ecclesia. Atque idem illud est, super quo Andreas Dudithius cum Bezâ, & cum Socino, per epistolas egit. Quin etiam inter Socinianos erant, qui dicebant, Ecclesiam nullam erigendam vel instituendam iterum esse, postquam tam diuturnâ laborarat apostasiâ, prius Apostolicos viros exspectandos & tempora, hoc quæ agerent: atque cum illis Socino multiplex contentio fuit & molestia; quâ super re videri possunt ejus epistolæ ad Matthæum Radecium, & Ostorod. Instit. cap. xlii. & Volckel. lib. vi. cap. ult. Videlicet, istiusmodi quæstiones Swencfeldo, aliisque levioris & procacioris ingenii, quam constantioris, perpetuò dum obversarentur, & Ecclesia certatim quæreretur, quam alii reformabant, formabant alii, quin & qui deformarent (ut tali tempestate fieri solet) non deerant, hinc ille inter omnia hæsit, atque multa quum ubivis carperet, nullis se addixit. Quin, quod omiseram, etiam Batavus ille nostēr, sed indignissimus. David Georgius, decem dialogos conscripsit, inter Theologum nempe, Biblicum, & Sophistam, qui hoc tractant: ubi vera Ecclesia inquirenda sit? Svvencfeldus lib. de triplici hominum vitâ cap.
units.tr: He lived at a time when the most violent disputes about reforming and establishing the Church were under way, and men's minds were being dragged this way and that. So not only he but many others hung about the Church and went astray. From this also arose the questions raised by Socinus about the need to inquire into the Church, he teaching that this inquiry is not necessary, which troubled men especially. Theophilus Nicolaides, explaining Socinus's view in his treatise on the Church against Borkorowski, says on p. 9: I show that Socinus affirms that the question about the Church, not every such question but some, namely which Churches there are and among whom they are, is not simply and absolutely useful, but is in some measure or almost useless. See Ostorodus, Institutes, ch. 42, and Volkelius, On Religion, bk VI, ch. 16. Hence they widely argue that there is no necessity to be anxious about the marks of the Church. The Racovian Catechism, in its chapter on the Church of Christ, p. 336, asks, since almost everyone arrogates the Church to himself, by what marks the Church may be recognized? It answers that there is no use in inquiring this. Similarly Smalcius, against Franck, disp. 10 on the Church. This is the very point on which Andreas Dudith corresponded with Beza and with Socinus. Indeed, among the Socinians there were some who said that no Church should be set up or established again, since it had been in apostasy for so long; they said that apostolic men and times must first be awaited, and then they would act. Socinus had much contention and trouble with these people. On this matter his letters to Matthew Radecki may be consulted, and Ostorodus, Institutes ch. 42, and Volkelius bk VI, last ch. Clearly, such questions always troubled Swenckfeld and others of a lighter and more forward, rather than steadier, temperament, while the Church was being eagerly sought, which some were reforming, others forming, and some even deforming (as usually happens in such a storm). Hence he hung back from everything, and while carping at many things everywhere, he bound himself to none. Moreover, something I had left out: that Dutchman of ours, but most unworthy, David Joris, wrote ten dialogues between a theologian, a biblicist and a sophist, treating the question where the true Church is to be sought. Swenckfeld, in his book On the Threefold Life of Man, ch. 43.

units.la: xliii. Sic loquitur: Non autem talem Ecclesiae reformationem, qualem Chiliastae expectamus: Neque qualem Monasterienses Baptistae, plane perfectam; sed modo speramus, Christum majori cum efficacia ut spiritum in nos effusurum, dispersos Dei filios collecturum, ac copiosius veritatem suam probaturum, adeo ut majori gratia, ac donis quibuscunque Ecclesia sit benedicturus, atque homines magis probi, pii, ac sancti evasuri. Breviter, haec est nostra expectatio. I. Christum ex hisce Ecclesiarum dissensionibus, aliquando etiam syncretismum, ac concordiam inter Papatum & Lutheranismum, ut vocant, daturum: atque plurimos veros pastores, qui solam ejus gloriam, ac hominum salutem sint quaesituri, & sanam Christi doctrinam, ac veritatem absque humanis commentis, sancte docturi, missurum. Etiam Ecclesiae majori numero, ac sanctitate fidelium, qui in spiritu, ac veritate ei sint servituri, benedicturum. Tom. II. ep. xlviii. 653. articulum hunc 36. a Synodo aliqua perpendi, ac examinari vult: Num, ac ubi, hodie omnia Christiane se habeant? Num sub regimine literae, an spiritus simus? Num in caelestem naturam translati, ac in Dei majestatem etiam adoptati? Vel an in media adhuc simus Babylone? Num vera Christi cognitio, in qua vita aeterna consistit, publico patefacta sit? Num rectus sensus, usus, ac dignitas sacramentorum Christi, cum Clavibus restituta sint? vel in quo defectus adhuc haereat: Immo an verum Evangelium, quod non in verbo solum, verum in efficacia, Sp. Sancto, & majori evidentia est, ita ut quidem debet, restitutum etiamnunc sit? Tom. I. ep. VIII. ad Leonem Judae inquit: Apud Pontificios D. sanctum non quaeram. Componat se cum iis, quicunque volet. ibid. Cum Papa, & Luthero in fide convenire nequeo, quoniam me condemnant, & meam fidem, id est, Christum meum in me odio habent. Subjungit iterum: Pro Luthero Deum precari semper, quoniam mihi, aliisque ad cognitionem veritatis multum inservitis. ejusdem Tom. ep. xix. & xx. ad Grynaeum, hisce verbis: Lutherus cum suis adferte fert Christum sine virtute, sine gratia, & divinitate, adeoque sine thesauris suis immensis, & inexhaustis, quem juxta pios ac impios in sacramento distribuit. Annon ab Ecclesia Christi longe absit, qui talem Christum possidet, ut judica. Germanico idiomate jam dixerat: mallem, non semel, sed decies mori, antequam, post agnitam veritatem, ejusmodi βλασφημιῶν[?] erroris, ac idololatriae participem me iterum facerem. Tom. II. epist. xlvi. de doctrina Lutheri: ex Lutheri doctrina solum, nemo coram Deo regenerari, probus & justus fieri potest, & postea: Papam sane apud Deum nullius est pretii (quanquam mundo adhuc pro Lutheranismo melior appareat) etiam Lutheranismus coram Deo necdum valet. Cum Rectores & Doctores Papistae ac Lutheranismi confero, fateri quidem cogor, Lutheranos in principio, praecipue quos Zwinglianos appellant, aliquantum magis pios esse, & plus ingenii, sapientiae ac gravitatis attulisse, etiam Deum plus timentes atque misericordes fuisse. Ubi vero commune vulgus utriusque partis per Dei gratiam intueor, credum, plures adhuc sub Papatu in mediis erroribus pios delitescere, quam sub Lutheranismo. Judicem insuper, iis facilius posse consuli, quam Evangelicis nostris, saltem ex parte, qui vitam suam improbam S. Scriptura, ficta fide, ac satisfactione Christi pallant, neque vix aliquam pietatem alterius curant. Epist. xlviii. ad Friderici Ducem Vratislav. Me quod attinet, libere dico; hodie etiam agnita veritate, si quidem liceret, ad Pontificios, modo conscientia mihi libera concederetur, quam ad Lutheranos, eorumque Missam, & primores transfire mallem. Etiam, quod si res non meliores evaderent, ac quidem hodie se habent (quod speramus tamen) pene praestitisset, sub priori Papatu, ac idolo manere, ubi nobis Deus, sicut parentibus nostris errores non severe adeo imputasset, ac jam verendum, ni doctrina & vita aliter caveamus. Adde ep. xlix. epist. li. epist. liv. & lxxii. & lxxxiv. adeo severe quidem de Lutheranis, benignius autem de Zwinglianis judicat. Valde conquerebatur, neque ininjuste, de mutuis gravibusque Protestantium, & Evangelicorum odiis, contentionibus, ac anathematismis, Tom. I. epist. VIII. & Tom. II. epist. XLV. XLVII. XLVIII. & vel maxime de eo, quod quum non modo vita Evangelicorum saepe non satis sit Euangelica, vel reformationis professioni respondens, essent quoque, qui defenderent, ac docerent, bona opera ad salutem non necessaria, potius noxia esse, Tom. II. epist. LXXX. LXXXIII. & LXXXIV. nempe hoc controversum jam erat inter Amsdorfium, & Georgium Majorem, quorum iste paradoxum illud propugnabat. Ut nihil jam dicam de contentionibus cum Adiaphoristis, Synergistis &c.
units.tr: xliii. He speaks thus: We do not expect such a reformation of the Church as the Chiliasts look for, nor one such as the Münster Baptists imagined, wholly perfect. We only hope that Christ will pour out his Spirit upon us with greater efficacy, gather the scattered sons of God, prove his truth more abundantly, and so bless the Church with greater grace and with all manner of gifts, and that men will become more upright, pious and holy. In short, this is our expectation. I. [He hopes] that Christ, out of these dissensions among the churches, will at some time even bring about a syncretism and a concord between the Papacy and what they call Lutheranism; and that he will send many true ministers, who will seek only his glory and the salvation of men, and who will teach the sound doctrine of Christ and the truth, holily and without human inventions. He will also bless the Church with a greater number and holiness of the faithful, who will serve him in spirit and in truth. Tom. II, ep. xlviii, p. 653. He wants this thirty-sixth article to be weighed and examined by some synod: Whether, and where, everything in Christendom stands well today? Whether we live under the rule of the letter or of the Spirit? Whether we have been transferred into a heavenly nature and adopted even into the majesty of God? Or whether we are still in the midst of Babylon? Whether the true knowledge of Christ, in which eternal life consists, has been publicly disclosed? Whether the right sense, use and dignity of Christ's sacraments have been restored together with the Keys? Or where the defect still lies? Indeed, whether the true Gospel, which is not only in the word but in efficacy, in the Holy Spirit and in greater evidence, as it ought to be, has yet been restored? Tom. I, ep. VIII, to Leo of Jude, he says: I shall not look for holiness among the Papists. Let whoever wishes compare himself with them. Ibid.: I cannot agree in faith with the Pope and with Luther, since they condemn me and hate my faith, that is, my Christ, in me. He adds again: I shall always pray to God for Luther, since you serve me and others greatly in the knowledge of the truth. In the same volume, epp. xix and xx, to Grynaeus, in these words: Luther with his people brings a Christ without power, without grace and without divinity, and so without his immense and inexhaustible treasures, which he distributes in the sacrament to the pious and the impious alike. Is he not far from the Church of Christ who possesses such a Christ, as you judge? He had already said in German: I would rather die ten times, not once, than, after recognising the truth, become again a partner in such blasphemies of error and idolatry. Tom. II, ep. xlvi, on the doctrine of Luther: From the doctrine of Luther alone, no one can be regenerated before God, nor become upright and just; and afterwards: The Pope indeed is of no worth before God (though to the world he still appears better for Lutheranism), and Lutheranism too is not yet of value before God. When I compare the rulers and teachers of the Papists and of the Lutherans, I am indeed forced to admit that the Lutherans, especially those whom they call Zwinglians, were at the beginning somewhat more pious, and brought more talent, wisdom and seriousness, and were also more fearing of God and merciful. But when I look upon the common people of each side, by the grace of God, I believe that more pious people still lie hidden among the errors under the Papacy than under Lutheranism. Moreover, I judge that they can be more easily instructed than our Evangelicals, at least in part, who cover their wicked lives with Holy Scripture, feigned faith and the satisfaction of Christ, and hardly care for any piety of another kind. Ep. xlviii, to the Duke of Friedrich of Breslau: As for me, I say freely: even now, having recognised the truth, if it were permitted, I would rather pass over to the Papists, provided my conscience were left free, than to the Lutherans and their Mass and leaders. Even if matters did not turn out better, as they stand today (though we hope they will), it would almost have been better to remain under the former Papacy and idol, where God would not have imputed errors so severely to us as to our parents, as we must now fear unless we take care in doctrine and life. Add epp. xlix, li, liv, lxxii and lxxxiv, where he judges the Lutherans quite severely, but the Zwinglians more kindly. He complained greatly, and not unjustly, of the mutual and grave hatreds, contentions and anathemas of Protestants and Evangelicals (Tom. I, ep. VIII; Tom. II, epp. XLV, XLVII, XLVIII), and above all of the fact that not only was the life of the Evangelicals often not sufficiently evangelical or in keeping with the profession of the Reformation, but there were also those who defended and taught that good works were not necessary for salvation, and were rather harmful (Tom. II, epp. LXXX, LXXXIII, LXXXIV). This question was already in dispute between Amsdorf and Georg Major, of whom the former defended that paradox. To say nothing more of the contentions with the Adiaphorists, Synergists, and so on.

units.la: Verum enimvero, utut non difficeamur, cum Reformatione etiam scandala nonnunquam data, avidius arrepta fuisse, & neque aliter tum actum, quam ad veritatis percrebescentis periodos fere solet contingere, tamen haud bene factum a Swencfeldo, quod peccata hominum, a veritate doctrinae, & professionem a prositentibus non quiverit, vel noluerit distinguere. Ecclesia ex Papatu, quo hactenus miserè submersa variis in locis jacuerat, eluctata, juvanda erat omni undique auxilio, non deserenda; excipienda, non retundenda. Verum ita fit, homines se magis quaerunt, suumque nomen, quam suis posthabitis solum & unum Ecclesiae communis bonum.
units.tr: Truly, however, although we do not deny that scandals were sometimes given along with the Reformation and were eagerly seized upon, and that things then went no differently than usually happens in the periods when truth is spreading, it was not well done by Swenckfeld that he could not, or would not, distinguish the sins of men from the truth of doctrine, and the profession from those who profess it. The Church, having struggled out of the Papacy, under which it had lain wretchedly sunk in various places until now, ought to be helped by every aid from every side, not abandoned; to be welcomed, not beaten back. But so it happens: men seek themselves and their own name, setting aside their own concerns, and not the one common good of the Church.

units.la: Sed jam ad errores Swencfeldi speciatim designandos, descendamus, quos habuit communes, & proprios. Communes cum Pontificiis, aliisve, de limbo Patrum Vet. Testamenti, Tom. I. epist. IV. & XXXX. & LXIX. de perfectione hominis in hac vita: error nulli non extra Ecclesiam communis: Apostasia sanctorum. Tom. I. epist. XCIV. & lib. de Evangelio. Pedobaptismum oppugnat Tom. I. epist. LXXIV. Tom. II. epist. XX. XXI. XLVI. & in Confess. art. de baptismo.
units.tr: But now let us go down to name the errors of Swenckfeld in particular, which he held, both common and his own. Common with the Papists and others: concerning the limbo of the Fathers of the Old Testament (Tom. I, epp. IV, XXXX and LXIX); concerning the perfection of man in this life, an error common to nearly everyone outside the Church: the apostasy of the saints (Tom. I, ep. XCIV, and the book on the Gospel). He opposes infant baptism (Tom. I, ep. LXXIV; Tom. II, epp. XX, XXI, XLVI; and in the Confession, article on baptism).

units.la: At singulares & propriae ei fuerunt opiniones praesertim de Enthusiasmis, & revelationibus, de verbo Dei, de Christo, & Eucharistiâ. Primùm de Enthusiasmis ejus, à quibus Bellarminus suos Controversiarum libros exorsus est, Tom. II. epist. IV. refertur ejus disputatio habita cum Theologis Vittembergensibus, ubi sententiam suam explicat Swencfeldus, & defendit exemplo Zachariæ, Luc. 1. & Cornelii, Act. x. quibus factas ὀπτασίας dicitur. Atque hinc illud sabbathum Enthusiasticum, quo homines abdicatis & excussis omnibus animo suo cogitationibus, studioso, & pertinaci otio quiescunt, quo supernos & coelestes afflatus excipiant: quod ipsis tum est, animo spiritualiter σιωπᾶν, ut mens intus retracta & vacua, ex sopore isto omnem, atque etiam divinam veritatem eruēt. Adisis Swencfeldi Tom. I. epist. LVIII. pag. 561. Tom. II. epist. IV. pag. 40. Et Apologiam ejus per Theophilum Agricolam, adversus Muhæum. Inter declamationes Melanthonis Tom. II. est oratio Balthasaris Neandri, de doctrinâ Swencfeldianorum, ubi ita describuntur: In nostrâ vicinia Stenckfeldiani Enthusiastæ vociferantur, electis exspectandos esse divinos afflatus, nihil ipsos agere, sed tunc cum se rapi sentiunt invitos, incipiunt invocare Deum: ex hac Manichæa imaginatione incidunt multi in perpetuas dubitationes, multi sunt prophani, indulgent sibi securi, & dicunt se raptos illos exspectare. Sententia, nescio, an quis requirat, ut refutetur, & ejus probetur contrarium: neque enim nobis, sed illis probandi partes incumbunt. Hoc autem probent 1. se debere vacare ejusmodi Enthusiasmis, & divinis revelationibus. II. Ex exemplo Zachariæ, Cornelii, aliorumque, quibus coelestes apparitiones contigerunt, argumentationem procedere, & concludere ad ipsos. III. Revelationes proferant, atque explicent, sibi immediatè factas; non quas per verbum Dei, sed præter illud, ex instinctu divino immediatè habeant. IV. Illas probent aliquo indicio, vel argumento divinas revelationes esse. Sic illis onus probandi incumbit; nobis audiendi: etenim quilibet talia facile de se dixerit, ac somniarit, si absque probatione recipiantur. De sabbatho Enthusiastico, sive phantastico etiam diximus ad VVeigelium. Inter Veteres, primo illud nomen Enthusiastarum haereticis Massalianis datum, de quibus Theodoretus, histor. Eccles. lib. IV. cap. XI. & Hist. Tripart. lib. VII. Eisdem temporibus pullulavit & Massalianorum secta, Precatores vocant, qui Graece nomen illud interpretantur. Habent & aliam appellationem impositam ex ipsa re, Enthusiastarum. Correpti enim numine dicuntur de perceptâ cujusdam daemonis vi, quam Sancti Spiritus praesentiam esse putant: hoc morbo correpti visa somniorum Prophetias nominant. Eadem Baronius, Annalium Ecclesiasticorum Tom. III. ad Annum CCC LX. num. XXXVI. Atque de Cerintho Eusebius, histor. lib. III. cap. XXVIII. Sed & Cerinthus per revelationes, velut a magno Apostolo scriptas, portentosa quaedam nobis, quasi per Angelos sibi ostensa mentitus, attulit.
units.tr: But his opinions were singular and peculiar to him, especially concerning enthusiasms and revelations, concerning the word of God, concerning Christ and the Eucharist. First, concerning his enthusiasms, with which Bellarmine began his books of controversies: in Tom. II, ep. IV, there is reported his disputation held with the Theologians of Wittenberg, where Swenckfeld explains his view and defends it by the examples of Zechariah (Luke 1) and Cornelius (Acts 10), to whom it is said that visions [ὀπτασίας] came. Hence comes that enthusiastic sabbath, in which men, having put aside and shaken off all the thoughts of their minds, rest in a diligent and persistent leisure, so as to receive heavenly and supernatural inspirations; for them it is then to keep spiritual silence [σιωπᾶν] in the mind, drawn inward and emptied, so that out of this drowsiness they may bring forth all truth, even divine truth. See Swenckfeld Tom. I, ep. LVIII, p. 561; Tom. II, ep. IV, p. 40. And his Apology by Theophilus Agricola against Muhaeus. Among the declamations of Melanchthon, Tom. II, there is the oration of Balthasar Neander on the doctrine of the Swenckfeldians, where they are thus described: In our neighbourhood the Swenckfeldian enthusiasts cry out that the divine inspirations are to be awaited by the elect, that they themselves do nothing, but when they feel themselves caught up against their will, they begin to call upon God. From this Manichaean imagination many fall into perpetual doubts, many are profane, they indulge themselves securely, and say that they wait for those raptures. I do not know whether anyone requires that this opinion be refuted and its contrary proved; for the burden of proof lies not with us but with them. Let them prove, however: (1) that they ought to be free for such enthusiasms and divine revelations; (2) that from the example of Zechariah, Cornelius and others, to whom heavenly appearances came, the argument proceeds and concludes to themselves; (3) that they set forth and explain revelations made to them immediately, which they have by divine instinct immediately, not through the word of God but apart from it; (4) that they prove by some sign or argument that these are divine revelations. Thus the burden of proof lies on them, and the hearing on us; for anyone could easily say and dream such things about himself if they were received without proof. We have also spoken of the enthusiastic, or phantastic, sabbath in dealing with Weigel. Among the ancients, the name of Enthusiasts was first given to the Massalian heretics, of whom Theodoret speaks in the Ecclesiastical History, Book IV, chapter XI, and the Tripartite History, Book VII: In the same times there sprang up also the sect of the Massalians, who are called Prayers, which name they interpret in Greek. They also have another name imposed from the thing itself, Enthusiasts. For being seized by the divine power, they are said to be seized by a certain power of a demon, which they think is the presence of the Holy Spirit. Seized by this disease, they call the visions of their dreams prophecies. Baronius says the same, in the Annals of the Church, Tom. III, at the year 360, no. XXXVI. And Eusebius on Cerinthus, Ecclesiastical History, Book III, chapter XXVIII: But Cerinthus too, through revelations, as if written by a great Apostle, falsely brought forth to us certain monstrous things, as if shown to him through angels.

units.la: Altera Swenckfeldi opinio, & error, qui ex priori facile fluit, est circa verbum Dei, ad haud levem verbi, & ministerii divini contemtum, quod proinde litteram vocat, & litteram inefficacem, in praefat. lib. de Evangelio. Ideoque Deum non uti ministerio verbi, ut medio ad hominis conversionem, Tom. I. epist. XCIII. Tom. II. epist. XXXIX. & XLVI. & LVI. & LXXVI, vetus & sophistica est doctrina de causis instrumentalibus gratiae, sine quibus non. Epist. XXXIII. Praedicatio Evangelii non est medium, per quod Deus gratiam suam animis conferat, Deus enim salutem nostram non efficit per externa media. & epist. XXXVI. & XL. Estque inter ejus opera tractatus Simonis Martini, probans, Christum coelestia ac spiritualia dona citra auxilium creaturarum, id explicans, citra externa gratiae media, animis infundere. Tom. II. epist. XLIV. In praefatione libri de cursu verbi Dei, Anno M.D.XXVII. edita pro Swenckfeldo, dicitur: Primum, quod nonnulli hodie libris in Swencfeldum editis, affirment, Verbi Dei cursum, efficaciam, fidem justificantem, cælestem gratiam, & reliqua Spiritus sanctidona, non immediate à Deo, sed per verbum, ut dicitur, vocale, seu medium, in animam & domicilium cordis nostri introduci, hoc est fidem justificantem ex doctrina externa & justificationem per creaturarum media, non à solo Deo, per unicum mediatorem Iesum Christum, citra creaturarum auxilia provenire, quasi Deus omnipotens nullo fidem sine verbo prædicato donare velit, nec absque ministerio ullum hominem justificet, salvumque faciat. Et in ipso libro: prædicatio verbi &c. pro externo homine instituta sunt. Alibi, pro carnis eruditione. Turpiter erravit bonus Vir, ex ignorantia distinctionis, inter verbum vocale, ut sic, quod nulliusin se virtutis est, sed quemadmodum dicitur Ioan. VI.63. Spiritus est, qui vivificat, caro nihil prodest, verba quæ ego vobis loquor, spiritus sunt & vita. Tum inter verbi actionem & suasionem moralem, quæ neque fidem efficere vel conversionem potest. 1 Cor. 11.17. Neque qui plantat est aliquid, neque qui rigat, sed qui incrementum præstat, Deus. Isai. 53.1. quis credidit auditui nostro, & brachium Iehova cui revelatum? atque inter actionem Spiritus, cum verbo operantis, ita ut fides & conversio non sit ex verbo, quasi huic gratia alligata sit; sed ex propria operatione Spiritus, cum & in verbo efficacis. Rom. x.17. Fides ex auditu: auditus autem per verbum Dei. & cap. I.16. Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. Act. 11.37. & xvi.14. Unde patet, quam perverse hæc conceperit Svvencfeldus: Si ex auditu externo esset fides justificans, consequeretur verbum Dei, elementis mundi esse alligatum: imo, quotquot verbum prædicatum audirent, crederent, inquit lib. cit. quod nullatenus sequitur: neque enim fides ex verbo audito; sed ex spiritu una cum verbo fidem præcipiente, atque ad eam adhortante, fidem in animis operatur. Simile est, quod ibid. infert. Ex his siristripata testimoniis, tum ex discrimine ordinis rerum relestium, seu spiritualium, & terrestrium, abunde satis constare putat; cursum Verbi Dei vivi, originemque justificationis fidei immediate à superiis esse, & quantum per visibilia adumbrentur, & externe doceantur, non tamen visibilibus, aut externis adhaerere, quin etiam neque ministerio, neque ministro alligatum esse, sed liberum ordinem obtinere, totumque in invisibilibus quiescere. De Christo plures errores tenuit, de humana natura, & passione ejus, & glorificatione.
units.tr: Swenckfeld's second opinion and error, which follows easily from the first, concerns the Word of God. It leads to no slight contempt for the Word and the divine ministry, and for this reason he calls it the letter, and the letter ineffective, in the preface to his book on the Gospel. Hence God does not use the ministry of the Word as a means of human conversion (Tom. I, epist. 93; Tom. II, epist. 39, 46, 56 and 76): the old and sophistical doctrine of instrumental causes of grace, without which... (epist. 33). The preaching of the Gospel is not a means through which God imparts his grace to souls, for God does not effect our salvation through external means. (epist. 33, 36 and 40). Among his works is a treatise of Simon Martin, arguing that Christ pours heavenly and spiritual gifts into souls without the help of creatures, and explaining that this happens without external means of grace (Tom. II, epist. 44). In the preface to the book On the Course of the Word of God, published in 1527 in defence of Swenckfeld, it is said: First, that some today, in books published against Swenckfeld, affirm that the course and efficacy of the Word of God, justifying faith, heavenly grace and the other gifts of the Holy Spirit are not introduced into the soul and the dwelling of our heart immediately by God, but through the so-called spoken word, or a medium; that is, that justifying faith comes from external teaching, and justification through the media of creatures, not from God alone through the one Mediator Jesus Christ, without the aid of creatures, as if almighty God wished to bestow faith on no one without the preached word, or to justify and save no one without the ministry. And in the same book: The preaching of the word, etc., has been instituted for the external man. Elsewhere: for the instruction of the flesh. The good man shamefully erred, through ignorance of the distinction between the spoken word as such, which has no power in itself, but, as it is said in John 6:63, It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing; the words that I speak to you are spirit and life; and between the action of the Word and moral persuasion, which can neither produce faith nor conversion (1 Cor. 3:7, neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase; Isa. 53:1, Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?); and between the action of the Spirit working together with the Word, so that faith and conversion do not come from the Word, as if grace were tied to it, but from the proper working of the Spirit, which is also effective in the Word (Rom. 10:17, Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God; Rom. 1:16, The Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes; Acts 11:37 and 16:14). From this it is clear how perversely Swenckfeld conceived these matters: If justifying faith came from external hearing, it would follow that the Word of God is bound to the elements of the world; indeed, all who heard the word preached would believe, he says in the book cited, which by no means follows. For faith does not come from the word heard, but the Spirit, together with the word commanding faith and exhorting to it, works faith in souls. He similarly infers in the same place: From these testimonies, and also from the difference between the order of heavenly or spiritual things and earthly ones, he thinks it sufficiently clear that the course of the living Word of God and the origin of justifying faith come immediately from above, and that, although they are shadowed forth by visible things and taught externally, they do not cling to visible or external things; indeed, they are not bound either to the ministry or to the minister, but hold a free order and rest entirely in invisible things. He held several errors about Christ: concerning his human nature, his passion and his glorification.

units.la: Primum de humana Christi natura, quasi ea per summam injuriam diceretur creatura, quâ de causâ Tom. II. epist. lviii. & lviiii. ad Lutherum, adversus Vadianum agit, & peculiari tractatu, adversus Specherum, epist. lxvii. Unde nec Christum filium Adami dici sustinuit, epist. lxxvii. Sed secundum utramque naturam, Dei filium verum ac naturalem fuisse, & sic dicendum, epist. lxx; quin contrariæ sententiæ defensores Antichristos ideo appellare non erubuit, epist. lxxxi. edde & lxvi. Temerè omnia, & imperitè, nisi quoque improbè. Quid evidentius, quam Deum ab homine differre, alium esse Deum, aliud hominem: vel verus homo Christus fuit, & vera ejus natura humana, vel falsus: si illud, id ergo fuit, & non aliud, id solum, cujusque rei quum una tantum sit forma, & per eam res sit, quod est; nequaquam aliquid simul homo & Deus, secundum idem, ad idem: ergo nihil ineptius quam dicere, quod eadem humana natura, simul quoque sit divina: aliud est, quod in unam personam conveniant naturæ, humana ac divina, quæ tum duæ, non una sunt natura; hoc enim fides credit, Deus dicit, sed hominem Christum non esse verè Adami filium, vel secundum utramque naturam Dei Filium esse. & Scripturæ adversatur, quæ ideo genealogiam Christi ad Adamum texit. Luc. III. Matth. I. ut hoc certissimè probet, & passim Christum filium hominis appellat. Matth. VIII. 20. IX. 23. XII. 40. &c. atque seipsum everti t, utramque dicere, & unam naturam. Praeterquam, quod eadem fuit Eutychis haeresis, condemnata in Concilio Chalcedonensi. Duae enim divinitatis & humanitatis naturae post unionem συγχύσεως confusae fuisse, ὡς ἐκ μίας ἀποτελεσθείσης φύσεως, impie docent, inquit de Eutychianis, ad Synodum Chalcedonensem, Balsamon pag. 324. Ubi & hoc quoque de iis addit, ut quod necessario ad illam sententiam consequitur, ὡς ἐκ τῆς Θεότητος ἀποσυμμέζαν τὰ πάθη, Vt quoque affectiones divinitati tribuerent. Similiter Swencfeldus noster, neque in passionibus Christi naturas distingui voluit, quo certius pateat, eandem cum Eutyche haeresim ipsum hic tenuisse, sed ita totum Christum passum voluit, ut ne quidem Deitatem eximeret. Tom. I. epist. IXIII. LXXVIII. & XLVI. non tantum in Christo caro, non tantum humanitas, verum totus Christus, persona, quae & Deus & homo erat, pro nobis miseris peccatoribus, in tormentis, anxietate, passione, ac morte fuit: & postea saepe, ipse Deus passus est. Acriterque in Theologos invehitur, qui distinguunt, Christum secundum humanam, non autem divinam naturam passum esse. Tom. II. epist. III. Si hoc tantummodo voluisset nugator, passionem quoque divinae naturae, sed per tropum, adscribi posse, quomodo Act. XX. 28. pascere Ecclesiam Dei, quam proprio sanguine acquisivit; & I Cor. I. 18. si enim agnovissent, nequaquam Dominum gloriae crucifixissent, nulla hic contentio foret, nec ratio quare dissentientes a se tam severe condemnaret. Vel si hoc voluisset modo, apotelesma passionis, totiusque operis Mediatorii adscribendum esse integrae personae, verum dixisset utique, neque iterum disputatio hic inter nos daretur; sed quod ad mutuam naturarum relationem velit propriam ibi locutionem, ubi quod uni proprium est, alteri quoque in sermone attribuitur, & proprie dicere Deum passum, qui est ἀπαθὴς, contra Scripturam. omnem mnemque rationem est. Iac. 1. 13. Deus non tentatur malis, neque tentat ipse quemquam, verf. 17. apud quem nulla transmutatio, vel mutationis obumbratio. Mal. 111. 6. Ego Iehova non mutor. Quin & supra omnia tam altus Deus, differtque, ut nihil in ipsum agere, passionemque inferre queat. Alioqui etiam Lutherani aliquando defendunt: Christum quoad utramque naturam passum; sed non secundum utramque naturam. Tubingenses in thes. de Christo, Anno 1608. th. 143. Joh. Affelmannus, Prof. Rostochiensis, in Corol. ad disp. de praedestinat. & alibi, in disp. de Christo. Quod ita explicat, quoad, actum notat, ejusque veritatem; secundum, modificationem actus formalem. Verum non modo non modificatio actus, sed nec actus, qui passione designatur, divinae Christi naturae convenit. Neque Svvencfeldus ad ejusmodi subtilitates adscendit, crassiori & rudiori philosophiae adsuetus, vel nulli potius; qualiaque Lutheranis facilè relinquimus, isti praesertim Affelmanno, haud digno qui à nobis nominetur; ita impiissimè peculiari disp. Trias Syllogismorum Anti-Calvinisticorum, hunc primum Syllogismum facit, Deus Calvinistarum est 1. Auctor & causa peccatorum. 2. Verè peccans. 3. Et magis quidem quam homo. 4. Est hypocrita & delusor pessimus. 5. Est iniquissimus & injustissimus. 6. Est Diabolus, immo 7. Diabolo deterior. Contremisco, ac totus horreo, & quis non? quod eo impietatis & blasphemiae animus Lutheranus, isque Theologi abduci potuit; atque illud quidem prolixè instituit probare: quod legere, vel videre diutius non sustinui, nempe ut posset concludere: Ergo non est idem utrorumque, Lutheranorum sc. & Calvinianorum, ut appellat, Deus. Et ejusdem disp. syllogismo tertio: quorum Doctorum tanta est prophanitas, impietas, & abominatio, ut fidem Christianam simpliciter tollant è medio, & quemlibet in suâ religione salvari posse credant, eos certum est causam religionis non agere serio, sed religione ludere, ut tesseris. At Doctorum Calvinianorum tanta est prophanitas, impietas, & abominatio. Ergo. Incipet Deus te Satan, increpet te Deus. Eodem plane spiritu scripsit inter eos aliquis Zachaeus Faber, tractatum satis prolixum idiomate Germanico, Calvinistarum multorum religionem multo deteriorem esse Papistica, ubi in genere de Calvinistis non modo hoc satagit probare, sed & pejores illos esse ipsis, qui Christum crucifixerunt pag. 60. Ethnicis, pag. 89. 118. Turcis pag. 124. quin etiam Diabolo pag. 126. quod pag. 128. multis supra ducenta ac trecenta argumentis se probaturum mentitur, nempe Calvinistarum doctrinam pejorem & damnabiliorem esse ipso Diabolo: quare multis anathematismis execrandam pag. 80. neque in imperio tolerandam, pag. 115. Iudicet Deus, judicent pii: sane aliquando tandem causam suam aget Deus, & ab hisce calumniis, ac Diabolicis insultibus (cujusmodi plures proferre, promptum nobis foret) vindicabit. Sed ad Swencfeldum; interim & ejus memores, quod ante diximus, quomodo ex ipsorum Reformatorum odiis ac dissensionibus, Swencfeldus maxime inceperit, aliter de religione cogitare.
units.tr: First, concerning the human nature of Christ, as if it were said, to his great wrong, to be a creature. For this reason he argues the point in Tom. II, epist. 58 and 59, addressed to Luther, against Vadian, and in a special treatise against Specker (epist. 67). Hence he did not allow that Christ could be called a son of Adam (epist. 77). Rather, he taught that according to both natures he was the true and natural Son of God, and that this must be said (epist. 70). Indeed, he did not blush to call the defenders of the opposite view Antichrists for this reason (epist. 81, and also 66). He handles everything rashly and ignorantly, if not also wickedly. What is more evident than that God differs from man, that God is one thing and man another? Either Christ was a true man and his human nature was true, or it was false. If the former, then it was that and nothing else; since each thing has only one form, and by that form it is what it is, nothing can at the same time be man and God in the same respect and in the same relation. Therefore nothing is more absurd than to say that the same human nature is at the same time divine. It is one thing that the human and divine natures come together in one person, and these are then two natures, not one; for faith believes this, and God says so. But to deny that Christ was truly a son of Adam, or to say that he was the Son of God according to both natures, is contrary to Scripture, which for this very reason traces Christ's genealogy back to Adam (Luke 3; Matt. 1), in order to prove this most certainly, and everywhere calls Christ the Son of Man (Matt. 8:20; 9:23; 12:40, etc.). And so he overthrows himself, when he speaks of both natures and yet of one nature. Besides, this was the heresy of Eutyches, condemned at the Council of Chalcedon. Balsamon, p. 324, writing to the Synod of Chalcedon about the Eutychians, says: They impiously teach that the two natures of divinity and humanity, after the union, were confused (συγχύσεως), as if one nature had been produced from them [ὡς ἐκ μίας ἀποτελεσθείσης φύσεως]. He adds about them something that necessarily follows from that opinion: that they attributed affections to the divinity, as if the passions were separated from the Deity [ὡς ἐκ τῆς Θεότητος ἀποσυμμέζαν τὰ πάθη]. Likewise our Swenckfeld would not allow the natures to be distinguished in the sufferings of Christ, so that it may be clearer that he himself held the same heresy as Eutyches. He wanted the whole Christ to have suffered in such a way that he did not even exempt the Deity. Tom. I, epist. 63, 78 and 46: Not only the flesh of Christ, not only the humanity, but the whole Christ, the person who was both God and man, suffered torments, anguish, passion and death for us wretched sinners; and afterwards often: God himself suffered. He rails bitterly against the theologians who distinguish that Christ suffered according to the human nature and not according to the divine (Tom. II, epist. 3). If this trifler had meant only that the suffering may be ascribed to the divine nature too, but figuratively, as in Acts 20:28, to feed the Church of God, which he purchased with his own blood, and 1 Cor. 2:8, for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory, there would be no dispute here, nor reason why he condemned so severely those who differ from him. Or if he had meant that the effect of the passion and of the whole mediatorial work is to be ascribed to the whole person, he would certainly have spoken the truth, and there would be no further debate between us here. But because he wants, for the mutual relation of the natures, a proper mode of speech there, in which what belongs to one is also attributed in speech to the other, and because he says that God, who is impassible, properly suffered, this is contrary to Scripture and to all reason (James 1:13, God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does he himself tempt anyone; v. 17, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning; Mal. 3:6, I, the LORD, do not change). Moreover, God is so high and so different that nothing can act upon him or bring passion to him. Otherwise, the Lutherans too sometimes defend the view that Christ suffered with respect to both natures, but not according to both natures (Tübingen theses on Christ, 1608, th. 143; Johann Affelmann, professor at Rostock, in his Corollary to the disputation on predestination, and elsewhere, in a disputation on Christ). He explains this, that with respect to marks the act and its truth, and according to the formal modification of the act. But not only is there no modification of the act, nor even an act designated by suffering, which belongs to the divine nature of Christ. Swenckfeld did not rise to such subtleties, being accustomed to a cruder and ruder philosophy, or rather to none at all. We readily leave such things to the Lutherans, especially to that Affelmann, who is not worthy to be named by us. Thus, in a special disputation, Trias Syllogismorum Anti-Calvinisticorum, he impiously makes this first syllogism: The God of the Calvinists is (1) the author and cause of sins; (2) truly sinning; (3) and indeed more than man; (4) a hypocrite and the worst deceiver; (5) most iniquitous and most unjust; (6) the Devil, indeed (7) worse than the Devil. I tremble and shudder all over, and who would not? That a Lutheran mind, and a theologian, could be led into such impiety and blasphemy! He sets out at length to prove this, and I could not bear to read or look at it for long, so that he might conclude: Therefore the God of the Lutherans and the God of the Calvinists, as he calls them, is not the same. And in the third syllogism of the same disputation: Those teachers are so profane, impious and abominable that they simply remove the Christian faith from the midst and believe that anyone can be saved in his own religion; it is certain that they do not pursue the cause of religion seriously, but play with religion as with dice. But the Calvinist teachers are so profane, impious and abominable. Therefore... May God rebuke you, Satan; may God rebuke you. In exactly the same spirit someone, Zachaeus Faber, wrote a rather lengthy treatise in German, The religion of many Calvinists is far worse than the Papistical. There he undertakes in general terms not only to prove this about the Calvinists, but also that they are worse than those who crucified Christ (p. 60), than the heathen (pp. 89, 118), than the Turks (p. 124), and even than the Devil (p. 126). On p. 128 he falsely claims that he will prove, with more than two or three hundred arguments, that the doctrine of the Calvinists is worse and more damnable than the Devil himself. Therefore, he says, it must be cursed with many anathemas (p. 80), and must not be tolerated in the empire (p. 115). Let God judge, and let the godly judge. Surely God will at last plead his own cause and vindicate it against these calumnies and diabolical insults (of which we could readily bring forward many more). But back to Swenckfeld. Meanwhile, let us keep in mind what we said before, how it was chiefly from the hatreds and dissensions of the Reformers themselves that Swenckfeld began to think differently about religion.

units.la: Tertio, eundem errorem circa Christi glorificationem tenuit, quem de naturis inter se, & in passione confusis docuit, dixitque, humanam Christi naturam, per exaltationem, in Deum transformatam, Deificatam; nihilominus, ut vertiginem hominis videatis, manente humana natura, ut simul & verus homo, & in omnem ac aequalem cum Deo gloriam evectus, & deificatus fuerit. In Confess. art. de gloria Christi Tom. II. epist. VI. & XXII. LIII. LVI. LVII. LXVII. Tom. I. epist. XVIII. & XLIII. In libello, cui tit. Coelestis Medicina Christi cap. XXI. Christus ad dextram Dei evectus est, secundum humanam naturam, videlicet ad supremam majestatem, qua non datur superior. cap. XXIII. Christus etiamnum quidem homo est: at in essentia Dei, & divina majestate. Peculiari, & spisso satis tractatu de Christi se-Ergo. (marginal annotation not clearly legible) ralitate in passione, ac gloria, hanc sententiam operosè astruit: Ubi & hæc leguntur, Adversarii tenent, Christum duas diversas naturas distinctis proprietatibus superius in cœlo habere, ubi alteri quid proprium est, quod alteri non competat. Et in margine: Homo in Christo per manifestationem plane deificatus in unam simplicem Dei essentiam adæquatus, & admissus est. Post, Adversarii personam Christi dividunt, cum unam naturam in Deo, in essentiâ divinâ Trinitatis; alteram extra eam, ac infra Deum statuunt; nolunt Christo secundum utramque, æterne unitam naturam, statum ac honorem secundæ in Divinâ Trinitate persona concedere. In epist. mysteriorum de cognit. Christi: Christus secundum utramque naturam unitus in eodem gradu, eadem potentia, gloria, honore, & majestate cum Deo Patre suo, ut secunda persona in divinâ Triade, credendus, & laudandus. Post: nempe omnino divinam, cœlestem, & æternam essentiam, non extincta tamen humana natura, plenissime induit. Atque ita infinitis locis. Eandem chorda pluries oberrat, & ex eodem capite hausta omnia, neglectâ sc. inter naturas differentiâ & distinctione. Homo, & humana natura exaltatur à Deo & beatificatur, non quò Deus fiat, sed à Deo, & sub Deo esse se semper agnoscat: gloriam suam Deus alteri non dat, Iesa xlii 1. & hâc ratione dicitur beatus, solus potens, solus habere immortalitatem &c. 1 Tim. vi. 15. 16. Omnia illa tam naturæ divinæ, quam humanæ, Deo & homini adversantur. Nec Deus hominem in essentiæ vel gloriæ suæ identitatem ac æqualitatem recipit, nec homo eò adscendit, vel adscendere potest. Christus si ita ac eo usque glorificatus esset, nec homo amplius, nec visibilis esset, quum contra vidisse eum Stephanus dicatur, Act. vii. 55. & visibili specie descensurus sit, Act. i. 11. venit ὡς τρόπον ἐθεάσασθε αὐτὸν πορευόμενον εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν. Matth. xxiv. 30. & videbunt filium hominis venientem supra nubes cœli, cum potentia & gloria multa. Adde, & nostra corpora dici ejus cor-
units.tr: Thirdly, he held the same error concerning the glorification of Christ that he taught about the confusion of the natures, both in the passion and otherwise. He said that the human nature of Christ, through exaltation, was transformed into God and deified. Yet, so that you may see his giddiness, he said that the human nature remains and that Christ was raised to the same and equal glory with God, and deified, while still being true man. See his Confession, article on the glory of Christ, Tom. II, epist. VI and XXII, LIII, LVI, LVII, LXVII; Tom. I, epist. XVIII and XLIII. In the little book entitled Heavenly Medicine of Christ, chapter XXI: Christ is raised to the right hand of God according to the human nature, namely to the supreme majesty, above which there is no higher. Chapter XXIII: Christ is indeed still man, but in the essence of God and in divine majesty. In a special and rather dense treatise on the reality of Christ in the passion and in the glory, he laboriously establishes this opinion. There these things are also read: our opponents hold that Christ has, above in heaven, two different natures with distinct properties, so that one has something proper to it that does not belong to the other. And in the margin: Man in Christ, by manifestation, is plainly deified, and is admitted and made equal to the one simple essence of God. Afterwards: our opponents divide the person of Christ, since they place one nature in God, in the divine essence of the Trinity, and the other outside it and below God; they are unwilling to grant to Christ, who is eternally united in both natures, the status and honour of the second person in the divine Trinity. In the epistle on the mysteries of the knowledge of Christ: Christ, united according to both natures, is to be believed and praised in the same rank, with the same power, glory, honour and majesty as God his Father, as the second person in the divine Triad. Afterwards: namely, he has put on wholly the divine, heavenly and eternal essence, the human nature not being extinguished. And so in endless places. He strays on the same string many times, and draws everything from the same source, neglecting the difference and distinction between the natures. Man and human nature are exalted and blessed by God, not so that they become God, but so that they always acknowledge that they are from God and under God. God does not give his glory to another, Isa. xlii 1, and for this reason he is called blessed, the only Potentate, the only one who has immortality, etc., 1 Tim. vi. 15, 16. All those things, both of the divine nature and of the human, are opposed to God and to man. Nor does God receive man into the identity and equality of his essence or glory, nor does man ascend thither or can ascend. If Christ had been glorified in such a way and to such a degree, he would be neither man any longer nor visible, whereas on the contrary Stephen is said to have seen him, Acts vii. 55, and he is to come down in visible form, Acts i. 11, [ὡς τρόπον ἐθεάσασθε αὐτὸν πορευόμενον εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν], in the same way as you saw him going into heaven. Matth. xxiv. 30: they will see the Son of man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power and glory. Add that our bodies are said to be conformed to his glorious body, Phil. iii. 21, yet I do not think we are to be deified, or transmuted into the essence and glory of God.

units.la: ποr pori gloriosò conformanda, Phil. III. 21. neque tamen nos crediderim deificandos, vel in essentiam, ac gloriam Dei transmutandos.
units.tr: We are to be conformed to the body of his glory, Phil. iii. 21; yet I do not believe that we are to be deified or changed into the essence and glory of God.

units.la: Paria somniavit cum Enthusiastis Matthias VVejerus, cujus scripta belgicè primùm An. 1579. & exinde Germanicè An. 1633. Francofurdi prodierunt, at non ipse, verùm post ejus obitum, epistolas ejus, & sermones familiares edidit ejus domesticus Iohannes Spes. Coævus vixit Henrico Nicolai, & Davidi Georgio, quorum insaniam fastidiebat; & hic VVejerus, Serm. lib. III. cap. 11. creaturæ, quibus fruuntur animalia, in animalia nobilitantur, ipsa animalia in hominem. Homo nobilitatur in Deum, atque ista creatura hoc pacto per hominem in Deum redeunt. Et lib. II. cap. I. Novus homo non accrescit, nam novus homo est ipse Deus: quidem homo in novo homine accrescit. Lib. I. cap. XXIV. In tantum homo deificatur, ut nihil præter Deum reperiat, neque seipsum amplius, neque creaturam. Cap. XI. in morte hac anima perit, homo in essentialem Dei vitam ac essentiam abit, ubi sese Christus manifestat, atque ejus commatis plura.
units.tr: Matthias Weyer dreamed the same things as the Enthusiasts. His writings were first published in Dutch in 1579, and afterwards in German at Frankfurt in 1633. He did not publish them himself; after his death his letters and familiar sermons were edited by his household member Johannes Spes. He lived at the same time as Henry Nicolai and David Joris, whose madness he loathed. And this Weyer, in Sermon, book III, chapter 11: The creatures that animals enjoy are ennobled into animals, and the animals themselves into man. Man is ennobled into God, and in this way these creatures return to God through man. And book II, chapter 1: The new man does not grow, for the new man is God himself; indeed, man grows in the new man. Book I, chapter 24: Man is so deified that he finds nothing except God, neither himself any longer nor any creature. Chapter 11: In this death the soul perishes; man passes into the essential life and essence of God, where Christ manifests himself. And there are many more sentences of this kind.

units.la: Ultimò, erravit Swenckfeldus, quamvis non tam graviter, vel hæsit potius, in negotio Eucharistiæ recte explicando: in quâ materiâ plurimi tum titubabant, hinc Pontificiis, illinc Lutheranis, inde Zwinglio, cum suis, articulum illum aliter explicante, incerti quò se verterent. Svvenckfeldus de hac materiâ, in ultimâ suâ confessione acturus, capiti hæc verba præscripsit: major viribus meis articulus; ac verba Christi, de quibus totalis, invertit potius, quam pervertit, & transposuit: hoc est corpus meum; explicans per, corpus meum est hoc, id est, panis est verè spiritualis, ut Joan. VI. 55. caro mea vere cibus est, & sanguis meus vere potus &c. Vide ejus epist. I. II. IV. V. & præcipuè VI. XV. ac peculiarem ejus super eâ re tractatum, epist. Gratovaldi ad Melanthonem Tom. II. pag. 251. Et Zwinglius de iis judicium suum hoc perscripsit, Tom. II. epist. xi. Gratias Deo agimus ubicunque radiantis veritatis, praecipue ubi Vratislaviensium de Eucharistia sententiam hoc in libello vidimus, in quo Luthero contradicunt, Verba S. Caenae hunc in modum explicant, hoc est corpus meum, id est, corpus meum est hoc, videlicet, ita corpus meum animam pascit, nec hoc inconcinnè, quum verba Hebraica zoth, ze, hu, bif, saepe ita accipiantur. Ideoque nostra explicationi non sunt adversi, verum eorum nostra continentur. Atque sic in fundamento rei, ut defenditur contra Pontificios, ac Lutheranos, non erravit, sed verborum Christi tantum aliam secutus est interpretationem. Ubi nos explicamus: hoc est Sacramentum vel signum corporis mei, pro vobis fracti; ille alio ordine verba construens, dixit, corpus meum est sicuti panis, panis animae spiritualis; errore quidem non tanto, tamen eum addere visum, quia de homine, & variis ejus doctrinis commentari erat animus, & institutum.
units.tr: Lastly, Swenckfeld erred, though not so gravely, or rather he stuck fast, in correctly explaining the matter of the Eucharist. Many were wavering on this matter: on the one side the Papists, on the other the Lutherans, and on another side Zwingli and his followers, who explained that article differently, were uncertain which way to turn. When Swenckfeld was about to treat this matter in his last confession, he prefixed to the chapter these words: the article is greater than my strength. He turned the words of Christ, on which the whole question depends, upside down rather than perverting them, and transposed them: this is my body, explaining it as my body is this, that is, the bread is truly spiritual, as in John vi. 55: my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink, etc. See his letters I, II, IV, V, and especially VI and XV, and his special treatise on that matter, the letter of Gratovald to Melanchthon, Tom. II, p. 251. And Zwingli wrote his judgment on them in this way, Tom. II, letter xi: We give thanks to God wherever the truth shines, especially where we have seen in this little book the opinion of the Breslau men concerning the Eucharist, in which they contradict Luther. They explain the words of the Holy Supper in this manner, this is my body, that is, my body is this, namely, so that my body feeds the soul; nor is this inappropriate, since the Hebrew words zoth, ze, hu, and bif are often so understood. Therefore they are not opposed to our explanation; rather, our explanation is contained in theirs. And so, as to the basis of the matter, as it is defended against the Papists and the Lutherans, he did not err, but only followed another interpretation of the words of Christ. Where we explain: this is the sacrament or sign of my body, broken for you, he, constructing the words in another order, said: my body is like bread, bread for the spiritual soul. Indeed, this is not so great an error, yet it seemed to me that he added something, since my intention and purpose was to comment on the man and his various doctrines.

units.la: Atque haec de istis hominibus dixisse, satis sit, satis ad illorum historiam, etiam satis ad istam de illis cognitionem, quâ de iis judicare, quales fuerint, quaeque tenuerint dogmata, requiritur: atque illud hac scriptione spectavimus, non librum facere, vel operosam instituere refutationem, potius narrationem: existimantes, illa nullum lectorem repertura, qui non facile ad ea, ex his quae dicta, sit responsurus, & semper quam brevissimè potest, illa ob oculos ponenda esse solum, neque anxiè examinanda: quia hoc vix merentur, & forte nec illud. August. Retract. lib. II. cap. VI. Quamvis utcunque temperata sit haec ineptia, in eo quod additum est, forte. Cyprianus praef. adv. Judaeos. Sed & legentibus brevitas hujusmodi plurimum prodest, dum non intellectum legentis & seipsum liber longior spargit, sed subtiliore compendio (id quod legitur) tenax memoria custodit.
units.tr: It is enough to have said these things about those men: enough for their history, and enough for the knowledge of them that is required to judge what sort they were and what doctrines they held. In this writing we have aimed not to make a book or to undertake a laborious refutation, but rather a narrative, believing that no reader will find these things without being easily able to answer them from what has been said, and that they should always be set before the eyes as briefly as possible, and only so, not anxiously examined, since they hardly deserve this, and perhaps not even that. Augustine, Retractations, book II, chapter VI: However moderate this foolishness is, in what has been added, perhaps. Cyprian, preface to Against the Jews: Brevity of this kind is also of great benefit to readers, since a longer book does not scatter the understanding of the reader and his own self, but a tenacious memory keeps what is read by a more subtle summary.

units.la: Neque omittendus nobis Jacobus Böhme, alias Teutonicus tonicus Philosophus, cuius scripta Germanice, & jam quoque Belgice nonnulla leguntur, sed revera ἀλλὰς ἀντλλοτις ita verbis ampullatis, contortis, fumosis, sermone non sermone, ad fastum non ad intellectum, scripsit, an deliravit? qui natus Anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxv. prope Gorlitzum, parentibus rusticis, & ipse ruralibus negotiis, pecori, agroque colendo admotus, aetatis anno decimo litteras, ut legere, ac scribere aliquantulum posset, addidicit, atque inde artem calcearium. Anno cIↄ Iↄ c ecstasi spirituali septem diebus se abreptum fuisse ad divina ac coelestia contemplanda, fruendaque dixit, & post iterum, Anno cIↄ Iↄ c x, quum jam in conjugio viveret, & binos filios aleret, cuius rei memoriam libellum conscripsit, cui titulum fecit, Aurora: Libellum, merè nugacem, quem à nemine rectè intelligi, ne ab Auctore quidem, certò mihi persuadeo, non quod tam sublimia doceat, sed quum hoc non agat, tamen tam sublimia loquatur. Astrologica, Philosophica, Theologica, mixturam omnium facit maximè prodigiosam: Et, quaeris, quae à communi Theologiâ tradat aliena? distinctè hoc non magis tibi dixero, quam ipse suarum opinionum, vel sermonum aliquod argumentum, aut probationem. Hoc satis manifestum, illud ab ipso omninò agi, ut Theologia, ejusque tractandi ratio in universum corrumpatur; & amplius perspicuè ac rectè tradi ea vel intelligi non possit: Quare prudenter Magistratus Gorlicensis, illum coram se accusatum, citatumque jussit à scribendo, idiota quum esset, abstinere, libellumque cui Aurorae nomen, supprimere quidem studuit, at haud potuit. Iterum dico, cum istis hominibus nihil prius agendum esse, quam ad distinctam sententiae suae ac dogmatum adigere explicationem, & probationem. Quale illud est! quod apologia primâ adversus Balthasarum Tylchen scribit, à sectione 205. Non ego contorta ad probationem scripta, ex omnibus rebus probare id possum; omnes tres mun-di
units.tr: Nor must we omit Jacob Böhme, otherwise called the German philosopher, whose writings are read in German, and now also in some parts in Dutch. But in truth he wrote in such bombastic, twisted, smoky words, speech that is not speech, aiming at display and not at understanding, that I am left wondering whether he wrote or raved. He was born in 1575 near Görlitz, of rustic parents, and was himself put to rural work, to tending the herd and cultivating the field. In his tenth year of life he learned letters, so far as to be able to read and write a little, and then the trade of shoemaking. In 1600 he said that he was carried away in a spiritual ecstasy for seven days, to contemplate and enjoy divine and heavenly things; and again, in 1610, when he was already married and was supporting two sons, he wrote a little book in memory of that matter, which he entitled Aurora. It is a purely trifling book, which I am firmly persuaded no one rightly understands, not even the author himself: not because it teaches such sublime things, but because, although he does not aim at this, he speaks in such sublime terms. He makes a mixture of astrological, philosophical and theological matter, most monstrous of all. And should you ask what he teaches that is foreign to common theology, I will no more tell you this distinctly than he himself gives any argument or proof of his opinions or words. It is clear enough that his whole aim is to corrupt theology and the manner of treating it in general, so that it cannot be taught or understood more plainly and rightly. Therefore the prudent magistrate of Görlitz, when he was accused and summoned before him, ordered him to abstain from writing, since he was an unlearned man; and he tried to suppress the little book called Aurora, but could not. Again I say, nothing is to be done with such men before they are forced to a distinct explanation and proof of their opinion and doctrines. What a thing it is! In the first apology against Balthasar Tilcke he writes, from section 205: I cannot prove this from writings twisted for proof; from all things I can prove it; all three worlds with all creatures are an argument to me, and nevertheless I am not enlightened: I see, and yet I do not seem to myself to see.

units.la: Non ego contorta ad probationem scripta, ex omnibus rebus probare id possum; omnes tres mundi di cum omnibus creaturis mihi argumento sunt, sunque ne-hilominus non illuminatus: video, nec tamen ipse videor. Domine Pasquil, unde ergo originem Diabolorum vis peti? non concedis, Diabolum magnam Deitatis partem esse, juxta naturam Patris, quum tamen Lucifer ab ipso Christo princeps appelletur: jam vero, quum illud mihi non assentiar, aliam mihi commonstra naturam, ex qua Diabolus creatus sit, praeterquam divinam. 522 fatere quippe debes, Diabolos aliquando Angelos fuisse! jam vero, angeli filii Dei sunt. ex Dei essentia: creaturae sunt, at creatura ex natura ipsa sint aeterni spiritus, atque ex aeterna venerint natura, quae est ipsissima Dei Patris, in initio principii. 524 Improba autem anima ex mundo hoc in tenebrosum vadit, in aeternam naturam, in matrem suam, unde venit, & in qua naturaliter subsistit: quomodo autem alias Deus animam in infernales ignes proiceret, malum, nisi ex eo foret? 522. Anima impiorum una cum Diabolis revertuntur in locum, ex quo in initio creationis sue prodierunt, nempe in centrum naturae, &c. Talia innumera sunt, quae quis intelligat, vel sine taedio devoret? & sensus, & sermo offendit; plurimum. Nec satis habent illi homines errare in sententia, nisi quoque scandalum verbis fecerint. Quomodo cum hiscce monstris aliter agas, quam uti initio dixi, producas solummodo, ad nuda & perspicua themata adigas, atque ad probationem? fugient, sat scio, at vel ita se satis ostendent, liquebitque quod dico, examen & conflictum praesentem illos non sustinere. v.g. quinam illi tres mundi? nude & quomodo coram Atheniensibus solebat, explica. Quid, quod ipse videt, neque videtur? an aliis? forte nec sibi. Horrendum, Diabolum Deitatis partem facere, & quidem magnam, juxta naturam Patris: quid ille Pater? alibi ita loquitur: Deus ab aeterno, solus: essentia ejus dividitur in tres aeternas differentias: una est, mundus ignem: secunda, mundus tenebrosus: tertia, mundus luminosus: est tamen una solum essentia inter se; verum una [illegible, ~10 letters] non est aeterna: Tres illae differentiae sunt similiter aeternae, & infinitae, neque loco neque tempore conclusae: quaelibet differentia se includit in se, in unâ essentiâ; & affectio ejus (quae belgicè) ejus est desiderium, centrum naturae. Quae monstra, quae horrenda! quid vult? quid probat? apage cum diabolico isto & tortuoso apparatu! aliter veritas, & simplicem ac evidentem expositionem amat, non ambages atque labyrinthos; quid illae differentiae, mundi, affectio, naturae centrum &c? atque ut ad superiora, quid, Angelos ex Dei essentiâ esse? creaturam ex naturâ, aeternos Spiritus esse, ex aeternâ naturâ, Dei Patris, in initio principii? quem locum putat animarum separatarum, improbarum, quis ille tenebrosus, aeterna natura, ac materia? quomodo ex eâ venit, in ea subsistit? Quid malum illud, vel affectio, unde anima? ex quo loco initio creationis animae & Angeli prodierunt? quid centrum illud naturae &c? Vides, quot hinc ex sinuoso & prodigioso sermone quaestiones, quot haereses? quis illis digne examinandis tempus frustra terat, vel ab aliquo hoc exigat? quis non illa si nude proponantur, judicare & condemnare noverit, quae seipsa condemnant satis, vel eo, dum non probant. Iam specimen Bohemisticum quoque audivimus, ex quo spiritum licet dignoscere, quo homines illi aguntur: neque puto quempiam plus istorum admodum desiderare; plura tamen, & multis prolixisque libellis scripsit, rescripsitque. Gerre germane, atque edepol lira lira.
units.tr: I cannot prove this from crooked writings; from all things I can prove it. All three worlds of God, together with all creatures, are my argument, and yet I am not enlightened: I see, and yet I do not seem to see myself. Lord Pasquil, then, from where do you want the origin of the devils derived? You do not concede that the devil is a great part of the Deity, according to the nature of the Father, although Lucifer is called the prince of the devils by Christ himself. Now, since I do not agree with that, show me some other nature from which the devil was created, apart from the divine nature. For you must admit that the devils were once angels. Now angels are sons of God, from the essence of God; they are creatures, but a creature from nature itself. Eternal spirits came from the eternal nature, which is the very nature of God the Father, in the beginning of the beginning. 524. But the wicked soul goes out of this world into the dark, into eternal nature, into its mother, from which it came and in which it naturally subsists. Otherwise, how would God cast the soul into the fires of hell, unless it came from there? 522. The souls of the wicked return together with the devils to the place from which they issued at the beginning of creation, namely to the centre of nature, and so on. There are countless such things; who could understand them, or swallow them without weariness? Both the sense and the language offend greatly. Nor are those men content to err in opinion unless they also cause scandal by their words. How should one deal with such monsters otherwise than, as I said at the beginning, by bringing them forward alone, forcing them to bare and plain propositions, and to proof? They will flee, I know well, but even so they will show themselves sufficiently, and what I say will be clear: they cannot endure examination and open conflict. For example, what are those three worlds? Explain them plainly, as he used to do before the Athenians. What about what he himself sees, and yet is not seen? Perhaps by others, but perhaps not even by himself. It is horrible that the devil should make up a part of the Deity, and indeed a great part, according to the nature of the Father. What is that Father? Elsewhere he speaks thus: God from eternity, alone; his essence is divided into three eternal differences. One is the fiery world; the second is the dark world; the third is the luminous world. Yet there is only one essence among them. But one [illegible, about ten letters] is not eternal. Those three differences are likewise eternal and infinite, bounded neither by place nor by time. Each difference includes itself in itself, in one essence; and its affection (which in Dutch is...) is its desire, the centre of nature. What monsters, what horrors! What does he want? What does he prove? Away with this diabolical and tortuous apparatus! Truth loves otherwise, and a simple and evident exposition, not circumlocutions and labyrinths. What are those differences, worlds, affection, the centre of nature, and so on? And to go back to what was said above: what does it mean that angels are from the essence of God, that a creature is from nature, that spirits are eternal, that they come from the eternal nature of God the Father in the beginning of the beginning? What place does he think of for separated and wicked souls? What is that dark, eternal nature and matter? How does the soul come out of it and subsist in it? What is that evil, or affection, from which the soul comes? From what place did the souls and angels proceed at the beginning of creation? What is that centre of nature, and so on? You see how many questions and how many heresies arise from this winding and monstrous discourse. Who would waste time in vain in examining these things worthily, or who would demand this of anyone? Whoever knows how to judge and condemn such things when they are set out plainly will not be at a loss; they condemn themselves well enough, in that they do not prove anything. Now we have also heard a Bohemian specimen, from which one may recognise the spirit by which those men are driven. I do not think anyone could desire much more of them; yet he has written and written back in many and long little books. Gerre germane, atque edepol lira lira.

units.la: Cum V Veigelianis vero istae nobis sunt controversiae:
units.tr: With the Veigelians, these are the controversies we have with them:

units.la: I. Num in homine omnium artium & scientiarum semina sint ac formae, ita ut non ab externo objecto vel principio scientiam haurire oporteat; sed tantummodo ex seipso omnem illam excitare & excutere? Neg.
units.tr: I. Whether there are in man the seeds and forms of all arts and sciences, so that one need not draw knowledge from an external object or principle, but only bring it all forth and draw it out from oneself? No.

units.la: II. Num cognoscens cum cognito, & sic homo cum Deo & Christo, quem cognoscit, fiat realiter & essentialiter unum? Neg.
units.tr: II. Whether the knower and the known become one with each other, and so man with God and Christ, whom he knows, become really and essentially one? No.

units.la: III. Num contradictoriorum absoluta debeat esse siimul & promiscua in mente nostra vel fide combinatio? Neg.
units.tr: III. Whether there ought to be an absolute and indiscriminate combination of contradictories in our mind or faith? No.

units.la: IV. Num quilibet homo à nativitate sua proprium habeat in coelis planetam, qui ipsum regat, & à quo dependeat, at quem, & cujus ductum, si salvari cupit, ante omnia debeat abnegare? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Whether every man from his birth has a planet of his own in the heavens, which rules him and on which he depends, but whose guidance he must, if he wishes to be saved, above all renounce? No.

units.la: V. Num saeculum aliquod Spiritus S. in terris exspectandum, quo mira rerum omnium conversio & felicitas tam corporalis, quam spiritualis speranda sit? Neg.
units.tr: V. Whether some age of the Holy Spirit is to be awaited on earth, in which a wonderful conversion and happiness of all things, both bodily and spiritual, is to be hoped for? No.

units.la: Diximus obiter nonnulla de Fratribus Rosea Crucis, ita appellatis, notisque ab anno hujus saeculi decimo quinto. V Veigelium illi, una cum sui Ordinis fundatore C. R. id est, Christiano Rosenkreutzio conjungunt, in Scripto, cui titulum fecerunt: Fama fraternitatis, quam, una cum Confessione ediderunt a. hujus saeculi XVII. & in altero, cui titulus: Frater Crucis Rosata, Germanicè quoque, ubi praeter V Veigelium, commendant Taulerum, & Theologiam Germanicam, ceu scripta unica, post Scripturam legenda. Libros etiam aliquos scripserunt, praesertim a. XVII. quo illorum nomen, & fama, scriptaque maxime flagrabant: alii rursus adversus illos steterunt praesertim And. Libavius. Mera fabula est & somnium, quod de Ordine suo jactant, & de Christiano Rosenkreutzio, de quo tanquam altero loquuntur Appollonio Thyanaeo quod natus anno clɔ ccc lxxxvIII. Orientem peragratus fuerit, & mira inde retulerit, mortuus denique non ex morbo ullo, quem nec ipse expertus unquam, neque alios infestare siverit, & cujus latuerit sepultura ultra saeculum, tandem prodita cum singulari isto, quod supra vidimus, Epitaphio: Ch. Rof. C. ex nobili atque splendida Germ. R. C. familia oriundus, Vir sui saeculi divinis revelationibus, subtilissimis imaginationibus, indefessis laboribus. bus, ad cœlestia, atque humana mysteria arcanaque admissus &c. Celebrant ex suis socios valde longævos, ut certius sciamus figmenta esse omnia, quingentorum & quadringentorum annorum, alios ducentorum. Nihilque totum illud quod de Fraternitate, sive ad S. Sanctum, ut se appellant etiam, sive Rosæ Crucis, aliud, quam malesanorum capitum de lapide philosophico pompaticæ & vertiginosæ, pro suo more, jactationes. Notum enim, miris & portentosis encomiis titulisque solere illos homines vim artis suæ deprædicare, & arcana ejus ineptissimis loquendi modis obducere, ut non se ipsi, minus alii intelligant. Omnia polliceri, & unâ suâ arte non opes solum, sed vitæ humanæ productionem, & morum sæculique tantam reformationem promittere, nil ut amplius desiderari posse videatur. Et hæc illis mysteriis Fraternitatis occultantur. Quasi homines sint pietatis studiosissimi, ita passim religionem crepant, & vitam Christianam, & morum sanctitatem, quæ suo ordini adscribunt & invento, iterumque eâ verborum vanitate sic obscurant, & verborum ampullis, ut ludere in re seriâ non minus quam in arte suâ, appareat. In scripto Fraternitatis, quod ediderunt tit. Sitentium post clamores, quo respondent ad nonnullorum adversus se objectiones, capitis tertii titulus est: inter arcana Fraternitatis R. C. in Germania comprehendi quoque universalem medicinam, & post Dei cognitionem, Summum bonum. ut dubitare nequeas, quin ex hisce furnis illa Societas enata sit, nihilque aliud quam hominum, quorum in Germania semper magna copia, Alchymiæ & lapidi investigando intentorum conspiratio & secta, qui ut sua magis reddant commendabilia, tanta εισφήσεις uti solent. Societatem appellant, neque tamen illam aliquis aut novit aut format: authorem quod dicunt Christianum Rosenkreutzium, fictum nomen est, & nugatorium drama. Et tamen leges jactant, stant, sive ordinem à Fundatore fraternitatis ipsis constitutum. quæ scilicet in Vtopiâ, aut regno Lunæ obtinent. Velim ego mihi ostendi istorum Fratrum aliquem, si forte aliter sua sacra possit explicare. Et certe si tanti illa secta, ut ab eâ mundi reformatio, & hominis tantum bonum, pro salute etiam animæ, breviter omnia exspectari debeant, non oportet abscondere illam, & ignorari, sed in propatulo omnibus prostare. Quid si etiam quam maxime vellet quis nomen isti suum dare, qui posset? imo si ad annua Comitia die C. ad S. Spiritus convenire, quâ id obsecro liceret facultate aut modo? ita videlicet tandem egregie ludunt homines, & Anticyras ablegant. Parisios Societatis hujus fratres aliqui venerunt anno cIↄ Iↄ c xx iv. & ad angulos platearum affixerunt hujusmodi programmata. Primum: Nos Deputati præstantissimi „Collegii Fratrum Roseæ crucis, gratiâ Altissimi, ad „quem cor justorum se inclinat, in hâc urbe degi„mus visibiliter & invisibiliter. Docemus absque libris, & loquimur quâvis linguâ loci, quo habitamus, „ut homines nobis similes ex erroribus mortis trahamus. Alterum erat: Quicunque ductus curiositate, „nos cupit videre, numquam nobiscum aget, sed si quis „revera vel it albo Fraternitatis nostræ inseri, ei nos „qui cogitationes animi judicamus, promissorum no„strorum veritatem dabimus videndam. Hinc locum „habitationis nostræ non significamus, quandoquidem „ubi cogitationes lectoris cum ejus animo abreptæ su„erint, satis hoc erit ut ipsemet ei, si nobis significet. I, & talibus nugi vendulis te associa, siquidem delitare cupias, & neque sic tamen illos dignosces. Exhibet Nicolaus V Vassenaer, in Historicis suis Relationibus part. v i i i. litteras alicujus ex isto ordine ad se scriptas, quas videat qui volet, sed cui satis firmum adversus vertigines est sinciput, adeo hic omnia χρυσοχυτροληψ. De aliis præterea in Germania (maleficiatorum, & stolidas haereses sectantium valde feraci) turbonibus, & nomen malum inde adeptus, quia nec ipsi tanti, neque illos sequaces habent, dicere supersedeo. Qualis Iesaias [Stiffelius], & qui ab eo Stifeliani dicti, in Thuringia, ab anno cIↄ Iↄ c iv. Ille postquam aliquoties cum Theologis Augustanae Confessionis, in oppido Thuringiae Saltza contulisset, atque ab erroribus praeconceptis discedere nollet, in carcerem conjectus, integrum annum detentus fuit, tandem & liberatus, post praestitam errorum solemnem revocationem, eamque juramento confirmatam.
