Sed postea, praesertim anno cIↄ Iↄ c xxiv. reproduxit errores, numquam bona fide depositos, eosque qua voce, qua scriptis studiose disseminavit. Oppositum se ei potissimum VVeberus. Errores autem erant potissimam partem enthusiastici, de Scriptura littera mortua, &c. forte delusus speculationibus suis, duras & insulsas voces sectarum est magis, quam haereses, de triplici in Deo essentia, Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti; essentiam divinam hominí ingenitam dicebat; peccatum esse malam essentiam, aliaque plura inepta, & pessima. Putant illi homines omnia, quae vera, debere dici essentialia, unde mali essentia apud illos, fideles essentialia Christi membra, essentialiter regenerati &c. quod valde absonum, & magnam conceptuum verborumque συνπλοκῆς notat, presso examine & accurata expositione notionum potius curandam, quam acri vel longa disputatione.
units.tr: We have touched in passing on some matters concerning the so-called Brothers of the Rose Cross, who have been known since the fifteenth year of this century. They join Veigelius, together with the founder of their order, C. R., that is, Christian Rosenkreutz, in a writing entitled Fama fraternitatis, which they published together with the Confessione in the seventeenth year of this century; and in another, entitled Frater Crucis Rosata, also in German, in which, besides Veigelius, they commend Tauler and the German Theology as unique writings to be read after Scripture. They have also written some books, especially in the seventeenth year, when their name, their reputation and their writings were at their height. Others, in turn, have stood against them, especially Andreas Libavius. What they boast of concerning their order, and concerning Christian Rosenkreutz, of whom they speak as though of another Apollonius of Tyana, is a pure fable and a dream: that he was born in 1378, travelled through the East and brought back wonders from there, and finally died of no disease, which he himself never suffered and which he never allowed to trouble others; that his burial place remained hidden for more than a century, until at last it was revealed with that singular epitaph which we have seen above: Ch. Rof. C., of a noble and splendid German Rosy Cross family, a man of his age, admitted by divine revelations, most subtle imaginings, and tireless labours to heavenly and human mysteries and secrets, etc. They celebrate among their companions men of great age, so that we may know more certainly that all these are fictions: some of four or five hundred years, others of two hundred. And that whole story about the Brotherhood, which they also call the Holy Spirit, or of the Rose Cross, is nothing but the pompous and giddy boasting, in their usual manner, of madmen about the philosophers' stone. For it is well known that these men are accustomed to extol the power of their art with wonderful and portentous praises and titles, and to wrap its secrets in the most absurd manner of speaking, so that others understand them no better than they understand themselves. They promise everything: by their art alone not only wealth, but the prolongation of human life, and so great a reform of manners and of the age that nothing more seems left to be desired. And these things are hidden under the mysteries of the Brotherhood. As if they were the most devoted students of piety, they everywhere cry up religion, the Christian life and the holiness of manners, which they ascribe to their order and their invention; and again they obscure these with such emptiness of words and such bombast of expression that it appears they are trifling in a serious matter no less than in their own art. In the writing of the Brotherhood which they published, entitled Silentium post clamores, in which they reply to certain objections against them, the title of the third chapter is: that among the secrets of the Brotherhood of the R. C. in Germany there is also comprised a universal medicine, and after the knowledge of God, the highest good; so that you cannot doubt that this society was hatched from these furnaces, and is nothing but a conspiracy and sect of men, of whom there is always a great number in Germany, devoted to alchemy and the search for the stone, who, to make their own affairs more commendable, are accustomed to use such strained expressions [εἰσφήσεις]. They call it a society, yet no one knows it or forms it; the author, whom they call Christian Rosenkreutz, is a fictitious name and a trifling drama. And yet they boast of laws and statutes, or an order established for the Brotherhood by its founder, which of course hold good in Utopia or in the kingdom of the Moon. I should like someone of those Brothers to be shown to me, if perhaps he could explain their rites in some other way. And certainly, if that sect is so important that through it the reform of the world and the great good of man, even for the salvation of the soul, are to be expected in short, all these things ought not to be hidden and kept unknown, but should be set out openly for all to see. What if anyone wished most earnestly to give his name to them: who could do so? Indeed, if they met at the annual assembly on the day of the Holy Spirit, by what faculty or method, I beg you, would that be permitted? Thus, of course, men finally play their games admirably and send their hearers off to Anticyra. Some brothers of this society came to Paris in the year 1624 and posted notices of this kind at the street corners. The first read: "We, the most distinguished deputies of the College of the Brothers of the Rose Cross, by the grace of the Most High, to whom the heart of the just bows, dwell in this city visibly and invisibly. We teach without books, and we speak whatever language is spoken in the place where we live, so that we may draw men like ourselves out of the errors of death." The second read: "Whoever, led by curiosity, desires to see us, will never have dealings with us; but if anyone truly wishes to be enrolled in the roll of our Brotherhood, we who judge the thoughts of the mind will give him the sight of the truth of our promises. Hence we do not indicate the place of our dwelling, since, once the thoughts of the reader have been carried off with his mind, it will be enough that he himself, if he signals to us, comes." Go, and associate yourself with such trifling trickery, if you wish to lurk in hiding, and even so you will not be recognised by them. Nicolaus Vassenaer, in his Historical Relations, part 8, presents letters written to him by someone of that order, which anyone who wishes may look at; but the one whose head is firm enough against giddiness, is, for all that, a gold-pot-catcher [χρυσοχυτροληψ]. As for others in Germany (a region very fertile in sorcerers and in men following foolish heresies), and the troubles they have caused, and the evil name they have thereby won, because they neither have so many followers nor such, I refrain from speaking. Such was Isaiah Stiffelius, and those called Stiffelians after him, in Thuringia, from the year 1604. After he had several times conferred with the theologians of the Augsburg Confession in the Thuringian town of Salza, and was unwilling to depart from his preconceived errors, he was thrown into prison and held there for a whole year; at last he was released, after making a solemn recantation of his errors and confirming it with an oath. But afterwards, especially in 1624, he revived those errors, which he had never sincerely abandoned, and zealously spread them both by voice and by writing. The one who opposed him above all was Weber. The errors were for the most part enthusiastic: concerning the dead letter of Scripture, and so on. Perhaps deluded by his own speculations, he used harsh and insipid expressions which are more the language of sects than heresies, concerning the threefold essence in God, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; he said that the divine essence is innate in man; that sin is an evil essence; and many other foolish and most pernicious things. Those men think that everything that is true ought to be called essential, whence among them there is an evil essence, faithful believers are essential members of Christ, essentially regenerate, and so on. This is very absurd and marks a great tangle of concepts and words [συμπλοκῆς], to be dealt with by close examination and a careful explanation of the notions rather than by sharp or lengthy disputation.

units.la: In Thuringia, ad idem fere tempus, anno cIↄ Iↄ c xiv. fuit similis spiritus, id est, Enthusiastici, sed minoris roboris & sequelae, Ezechiel Mætz vel Medes, qui Stifelium illum, ceu sponsam Christi praedicabat, cui Iesaiae prophetiae cap. lxv i. applicandae essent: mox, ob scandalosa ac turbulenta dogmata, eorumque tuendorum contumaciam, in carcerem abductus, & Dresdae clam servatus fuit. Rejecit verbum litterale, uti illi amant loqui, seu Scripturam, cum Christi substantia tia seminitum, baptismum nihil esse, uti nec Coenam, & se Michaëlem Principem, dicitur asseruisse. Ducis Saxoniæ edictum adversus Ezechielem illum, & suos complices, præterea duodecim doctrinæ ejus articulos, exhibet in historiâ suâ Baudartius, lib. v i. ad annum cIↄ Iↄ c x i v. quibus continetur totum Michaëlis istius negotium, non dignum quod hic latius persequamur. Vide. & de eodem Epitome Historiæ Ecclesiasticæ Eusebii Bohæmi, pag. 1024. Et Iob. Micraelii Syntagma Historiæ cum, lib. i i i. pag. 506.
units.tr: In Thuringia, at about the same time, in the year 1614, there was a similar spirit, that is, an enthusiastic one, but of less strength and following: Ezechiel Mätz, or Medes, who proclaimed that Stiefel, as the bride of Christ, was the one to whom the prophecy of Isaiah, chapter 66, was to be applied. Soon afterwards, on account of his scandalous and turbulent doctrines and his obstinacy in defending them, he was led off to prison and kept secretly at Dresden. He rejected the literal word, as they like to say, or Scripture, he taught that the seed was from the substance of Christ, that baptism is nothing, and likewise the Supper, and he is reported to have claimed that he was Michael the Prince. The edict of the Duke of Saxony against that Ezechiel and his accomplices, and besides the twelve articles of his doctrine, are set out by Baudartius in his history, book 6, at the year 1614, in which the whole affair of that Michael is contained, not worth pursuing at greater length here. See also, concerning the same man, the Epitome Historiae Ecclesiasticae of Eusebius Bohemus, p. 1024. and John Micraelius's Syntagma Historiae cum, lib. iii. pag. 506.

units.la: Fuit haud ita pridem anno cIↄ Iↄ c xlv. vir non indoctus, præsertim in Hebraicis olim, & vitæ hactenus haud malæ, mihi probè notus, Dominus, amicusque A. B. qui separatum molichatur ab omnibus in Christianismo Ecclesiis coetum, ideo quod putabat, Ecclesiam omnem Christianam ab ævo Apostolico, quamdiu defuerunt Doctores infallibiles, apostaticam esse, quia in eâ docetur & exponitur verbum Dei à ministris non infallibilibus, & tamen nomine Dei: pro quâ suâ sententiâ libellum scripsit, Ad legem & ad testimonium, &c. quem examinavi, eique opposui anno cIↄ Iↄ c xlv i i. ad Reverendum virum, Ecclesiæ Gallo-Belgicæ Amstelodamensis ministrum Henricum Blanchetestæ, Apologiam pro Ecclesiâ Christianâ, non apostaticâ. Responsi nihil hucusque retuli: interim secta evanuit: ut usurpandum mihi hic sit, quod Cicero de Pyrrhoniis dixit, lib. i i. de finib. bon. recte jam pridem contra eos desitum est disputari. Et quantum Noster ex Pyrrhonia habeat, suo loco ostendi. Tantummodo Cl. D. Marcio, qui prior adversus ipsum insurrexerat, insultum opposuit Monitum, unâ brevique schedâ scriptum, quo acerbè & indigne tum Theologum, tum ejus ordinem traduxit, nequidquam pro illâ modestiâ, quam præ se fert, vel pacis ecclesiasticæ cum omnibus iucundæ desiderio ac scopo. Verùm ita videmus vulgo nullos magis homines impotentius ferre dissentientes à se, & suis re-præprehensoribus inclementius dicere, quam qui pacem clamitant cum omnibus sectis inter Christianos incundam, nullasque dissensiones ultra spectandas esse. Atque ita evenit, quod Basilius dixit, epist. lxxi ii. impossibile esse, ut litteris nostris accusantium ora cohibeamus, imo credibilius esse, ut nostros illos apologis irritemus, quo maiora ac pejora contra nos machinentur. Certe si pacis illi filii, oportebat magis pacem suo exemplo praemonstrare, suaque propria in causa vel sententia, quam monitis erga alios acerbis uti, a se maximis de causis dissentientes. Quis tulerit Gracchos de seditione querentes? Mihi deinde, meaeque Apologiae alterum Diploma quasi, aeque ineptum & maledicum, ac prius illud, reposuit. videlicet, Pacis Ecclesiasticae Propensionem: in quo conquisitis dicteriis & contumeliis, quia aliter non poterat, rem suam persequitur, hocque ab omnibus probis & doctis retulit, ut indignum censuerint librum, & institutum, & Auctorem, qui ultra a quopiam audiretur. Futilitatem, & quae non? scripto nostro exprobrat, eo quod sua non articulatim, servato libelli sui ordine, de thesi in thesim examinavimus. Quasi vero tuum sit praescribere Adversario, qua via modoque te aggredi & ferire debeat, dum ad certamen evocatus te opprimit, & hoc ita quidem, ut nihil in tuo illo libro sit, quod non confutatum, & in cujus examen non te provocarit ad Colloquium & disputationem, coram quovis incundam. Ostendenda fuerant, si quae omissa, vel praeterita erant; vel accipienda Colloquii conditio. Accusare Adversarium, & iactare, vel juventutem ei suam exprobrare, crede mihi non est modestorum, non senum, non eorum qui ad disputationem invitant, vel pacem loquuntur. Verum haec facilis, & examino condono (tam extra retaliationem, quam tuum exemplum), ut mihi alias a Deo atque hominibus (te quod offenderim, praeterquam in eo, quod rogatus, tuis conatribus, & convitio de Ecclesia Chriftiana ab ævo Apostolico hucusque apostaticâ occurrerim, nescio) condonari expeto. A quæstione dicis nos aberrasse: sed annon ergo oportuerat quæstionem proposuisse in tuo Monito, & Propemtico, ita ut eam intellexissemus, & vel sententiam tuam accipere, vel refellere licuisset? Ais, nos controversiam non ferire, & eam non formas tute ipse: quod quid aliud est, quam nolle ut disputemus? siquidem ignorata nobis, & involuta negatâque à te quæstionis explicatione, quo quæso pacto disputare possumus? Remittis nos ad tua Erotemata, sed illa adeo intricata & fastidiosa, ut paucis legere lubeat, & nos si insequuti illa pedepressim fuissemus (quod à nobis postulas, quia nosti hoc facile pacto tædium oboriturum) scio quod minus avidos lectores habuissemus, & difficillimè de rei summâ instruendos. Sed quod ego tuam sententiam in propositâ à me quæstione juste & recte expressi, præterquam quod nunc ex Propemtico constat, etiam tum memineram; ex nostrâ de hisce a.cIↄ Iↄ c xl iv. dxv i. Aprilis, sequentibusque, in Selandia, sermocinatione crebra, ex qua sententiam quia satis nova & paradoxa videbatur, aliquot thesibus in mei memoriæ gratiam comprehenderam, cum quibus, statim ac libellum anno sequente editum legi, videbam ut conveniret, & auctorem mihi suum significaret protinus. Præterea Cl. Rivetus p. m. cui scriptum meum miseram, censens, me rem acu tetigisse, eum in finem donavit fasciculo litterarum, ad se ante plures annos tuâ manu scriptarum, hac ipsâ de re simul & Eusebii Meisneri Basileensis, in Typographeo Elzeviriano Leidæ Correctoris ad se litteras a. cIↄ Iↄ c xxxvi. d. vi. Augusti: ex quo tua illa te habere vidi, & Meisnerum ex imaginariis suis visionibus, quibus litteras exorditur, & finit; quique super eodem negotio se dicit a.cIↄ Iↄ c xxx. scripsisse epistolam ad Iohan. Angelium VVerdenhagen, de substantiâ peccati, & de cultu apostolico primitivæ Ecclesiæ. Hunc tuarum opinionum habebas authorem. Quæstionem autem vestram hoc modo proposuit Riveto Meisnerus: Cujus jussu, mandato, & authoritate sabbathum, seu cultum nostrum præcipuum, potissimum sanctificamus nostris concionibus? Censet is, non jussu divino, vel Dei nomine, ac authoritate: quare solas legendas, absque expositionibus, Scripturas: hoc est quod totics dicis, verbum Dei ἀλης insite, indubie, mereque divinum. Pergit Meisherus: Tempore primitivæ Ecclesiæ ἀποστ. τρίτῳ Christus annunciatur, at, eâ defunctâ, in hunc usque diem tantum σωφῶνα perpetuò, non ἀληθές, si vel maxime litterâ τὸς ἀληθὲς. Atque hinc est etiam verum, nullam fuisse, nec esse visibilem ecclesiam veram, post primitivam illam Apostolicam in hunc usque diem: & tamen in omnibus putativis coetibus aliquos vel esse vel esse posse, qui in Christi membra vivificentur. Hoc Tu, Ecclesiam Christianam ab ævo Apostolico & inde esse apostaticam, eo quod prædicat, vel exponit Dei verbum, ejus nomine, & non infallibiliter. Epistolâ tuâ ad Rivetum, sic quæstionem proposuisti: An Reformatarum Ecclesiarum ministri, qui hodierno tempore publicum N. T. cultum mediantibus concionibus, Dei & Christi loco, nomine, & authoritate hominibus exhibent: eundem illum publicum N. T. cultum administrent, qui olim in primitiva N. T. ecclesia, mediantibus concionibus ab ipso Christo, aut ab Apostolis, & Ixx. Discipulis, ordinatisque per eos vocatis ministris, Dei & Christi loco, nomine & authoritate exhibitus fuit? mox explicationis causa addis, (quod tamen in ipso Controversiæ statu poni debuerat, quia eo omnis nititur) te eundem publicum N. T. cultum intelligere, qui ubique habeat divinum N. T. cultus & essentiale ἀγαθόν, infallibilitatem. Hoc verò negamus esse essentiale ἀγαθόν cultus N. T. per omnia ejus tempora, non magis quam per omnes personas. Sufficit initio infallibiles fuisse
units.tr: Not long ago, in the year 1645, there was a man, my friend and lord A. B., who was not unlearned, especially formerly in Hebrew, of a life hitherto not bad, and whom I knew well. He was planning a separate assembly apart from all the churches of Christendom, because he thought that every Christian Church since the Apostolic age was apostate, since infallible teachers had been lacking. In it, he held, the Word of God is set forth and expounded by ministers who are not infallible, yet in God's name. For this opinion he wrote a little book, Ad legem et ad testimonium, etc. I examined it and in 1646 I opposed to it my Apologia pro Ecclesia Christiana, non apostatica, addressed to the Reverend Henricus Blanchetestae, minister of the Dutch Reformed Church of Amsterdam. He has never answered it, and in the meantime the sect has vanished. So what Cicero said of the Pyrrhonists in book 2 of De finibus bonorum may fitly be said here: "It has long been rightly settled that they should no longer be argued with." How much our man has of Pyrrhonism I have shown in its place. He has only set against the distinguished Mr. Marcius, who first rose against him, an insulting little leaflet, the Monitum, written on a single sheet, in which he has abused both the theologian and his order harshly and unworthily, though he professes such moderation and a desire for ecclesiastical peace with everyone. But we commonly see that no men bear dissent from themselves more impatiently, and speak more ruthlessly to their critics, than those who cry out for peace with all the sects among Christians and say that no disagreements should be looked for any further. And so it happens, as Basil said in letter 72, that it is impossible "to silence the mouths of our accusers by our writings; indeed, it is more likely that by our apologies we should provoke them, so that they plot greater and worse things against us." Certainly, if these sons of peace ought to show peace more by their example, and to use their own case and opinion, rather than harsh admonitions toward others, they would be dissenting from themselves on the greatest matters. Who could bear the Gracchi complaining of sedition? Afterwards he answered me and my Apologia with another document, as foolish and abusive as the first, namely Propensio pacis ecclesiasticae. In it, having gathered sneers and insults, since he could not do otherwise, he pursues his cause, and he has brought it about that all good and learned men judged the book, its aim and its author unworthy of being heard any further. He reproaches our writing with triviality, and with other things, because we did not examine his theses one by one, point by point, keeping the order of his little book. As if it were yours to prescribe to your opponent by what road and manner he ought to attack and strike you, when he has been called to the contest and crushes you, and that so completely that there is nothing in your book which has not been refuted, and which he has not invited you to examine in a colloquy and disputation before anyone at all. If there were things omitted or passed over, they should have been pointed out, or the terms of a colloquy accepted. To accuse your opponent and to boast, or to reproach him with his youth, believe me, is not the mark of the modest, nor of elders, nor of those who invite to disputation or speak of peace. But I readily forgive this easy and cheap matter (quite apart from retaliation, and from your example), and I ask that I too be forgiven by God and men for whatever I have offended you (I do not know what, except that, when asked by your companions, I have met your slander that the Christian Church has been apostate from the Apostolic age until now). You say we have strayed from the question. But surely you ought to have proposed the question in your Monitum and Propensio, so that we might have understood it and either accepted your view or refuted it? You say we do not strike the controversy and that you do not frame it yourself: but what else is this than not wanting us to dispute? For since the explanation of the question has been kept from us and withheld by you, how, I ask, can we dispute? You send us back to your Erotemata, but they are so tangled and tedious that one would hardly like to read them through, and if we had followed them step by step (which you demand of us, since you know that weariness will easily arise in this way), I know we would have had fewer eager readers and would have found it very hard to be instructed in the substance of the matter. But that I expressed your opinion correctly and rightly in the question I put forward, I still remembered, apart from its now being clear from the Propensio. From our frequent conversations on these matters in Zeeland, on 16 April 1644 and the days following, I had noted some theses to keep in mind; since the view seemed fairly new and paradoxical, I had them in mind, and as soon as I read the book published the following year, I saw that they agreed, and I at once wished to be told the author. Moreover, the late distinguished Rivetus, to whom I had sent my writing, thinking that I had hit the nail on the head, presented me with a bundle of letters written by you in your own hand several years before, on this very matter, together with a letter of Eusebius Meisner of Basel, then proofreader in the Elzevir printing house at Leiden, dated 6 August 1636. From these I saw that you had those opinions of yours, and Meisner, in the imaginary visions with which his letter begins and ends, and who says that in 1630 he wrote a letter to Johannes Angelius Werdenhagen on the substance of sin and on the apostolic worship of the primitive Church, was the author of your opinions. Meisner put your question to Rivetus in this form: By whose command, order and authority do we sanctify the Sabbath, or our chief worship, chiefly by our sermons? He holds that it is not by divine command or in God's name and authority; therefore only the Scriptures are to be read, without expositions. This is what you keep saying over and over: that the Word of God is truly inborn, indubitable, and purely divine. Meisner goes on: In the time of the primitive Church, in the apostolic age, Christ is proclaimed; but when that age was over, there has been only a [ψευδῶς] counterfeit, perpetually, down to this day, never true, even if in the letter it is the true thing. And hence it is also true that there was not, nor is there, any visible true Church after that primitive Apostolic one until this day; and yet in all the so-called assemblies there are, or can be, some who are quickened as members of Christ. This you hold: that the Christian Church from the Apostolic age and since then is apostate, because it preaches or expounds the Word of God in God's name, and not infallibly. In your letter to Rivetus you put the question thus: Do the ministers of the Reformed Churches, who today offer the public worship of the New Testament to men by means of sermons, in the place, name and authority of God and Christ, administer that same public worship of the New Testament which was once offered in the primitive New Testament Church by means of sermons, in the place, name and authority of God and Christ, by Christ himself or by the Apostles and the seventy disciples, and by the ministers called by them? Soon afterwards, to explain, you add (though this ought to have been placed in the very statement of the controversy, since everything rests on it) that by the same public worship of the New Testament you mean the one which everywhere has the divine essential good of the New Testament, infallibility. But we deny that this is the essential good of the worship of the New Testament throughout all its times, no more than through all persons. It is enough that the Apostles were at first infallible teachers; it is not necessary that those who now teach, always as such, speak in God's name and authority and perform worship.

units.la: Doctores Apostolos, semper ut tales sint, vel nunc, qui Dei nomine & authoritate loquantur, & cultum peragant, necesse non est. Iam vero videant omnes, an ego ex tortuosis erotematis, in quibus nusquam ita clare & thetice agis, ac in epistola, quę certius mentem tuam explicat, quam illa, non bene controversiam sic collegerim & propositerim, quam indagari mihi longe pluris laboris fuit, quam de eâ disputare: Verum Ecclesiæ Christianæ Catholicæ, sive quæ in orbe sunt omnes, fueruntque ab ævo Apostolorum hucusque, à primis earum initiis, sint apostaticæ, eo quod in illis verbum Dei infallibile Veteris ac Novi Testamenti exponatur à Ministris, & concionibus non item infallibilibus, & tamen nomine Dei? Ostende, in quo à mente tuâ, designandâque controversiâ aberraverim. Quod non tua illa verba, θεως insite, mereque divinum &c. servaverim, feci ad majorem intellectum, substituens illis infallibile, quod & melius tuis illis verbum, & significantius rem exprimit, quoque ipse, non tuis illius libelli, sed in epistolâ uteris, quam non vidi nisi post scriptam editamque nostram Apologiam. Sic ergo discas, si placet, non ita perfunctorie & magistraliter rejicere scriptum adversarium, dicendo, controversiam non attractam fuisse, quam tuam ex meo, quam tuo scripto melius intellectam, si non dicant utriusque lectores, tum vero pudorem mihi incussum ingenuè profitebor. Gaudeo interim etiam me intellexisse, cujus araris vitulâ, quoque authore in hæc delíria perductus sis, quorum alios tibi patronos assignavi in meo scripto, præcipue Matthæum Radecium, Franciscum Puccium, ex epistolis Socini; Adolphum Venatorem, celebrem apud Remonstrantes doctorem. Quibus addendus Sebastianus Franck, in epistolâ anno cIↄ Iↄ xl r. scriptâ Argentorato, ad Iohannem Campanum, quâ se credere asserit, Christi externam visibilem ecclesiam, una cum donis & sacramentis suis, per corruptelas ptelas Antichristi, statim ab exitu Apostolorum, abiisse in coelum, & in spiritu ac veritate occultari: & pro certo statuit, à mille & quadringentis hucusque annis nullam Ecclesiæ congregationem, cum Sacramentis suis, extitisse: neque concionatores & ministros ad id vocatos esse quod agunt, vel licere alicui dispersam colligere Ecclesiam, vel sacramenta erogare, nisi extraordinario à Deo vocato missoque, & signis aut miraculis in id confirmato. Ejusdemque cum nostris hominibus opinionis olim fuit Theodorus Coornhert, Amstelodamensis origine, aliquo tempore Harlemensis, ab anno cIↄ Iↄ lxr i. Secretarius, vir ingenii quidem alicujus, sed uti ὀψιμαθὴς (quippe ad annum demum ætatis xxx. linguam Latinam coepit addiscere) ita, quod solent qui immaturis studiis alios docere cupiunt, non ipsi discere, religionis negotio, sola fretus audacia, intemperanter se immiscuit, & ex oppugnata in herbis Reformatione nostrarum Ecclesiarum, præsertim Catechesi, & probata sibi nec nostra Ecclesia, nec aliis, solum intentus carpendis omnibus, & magnis impetendis nominibus, Calvinum dico, Bezam, Daneum, Saravviam, alios, gloriam inanem inter suos aucupatus fuit. Obiit anno cIↄ Iↄ xc. & quod valde observandum, is qui tam impotenter de Prædestinatione multa, sibi nequaquam intellecta, adversus Theologos nostros scripsit, sub mortem, veritatem ejus in se sentire & agnoscere coactus fuit, ad Deum exclamans: se animam suam ab eo „possidere, quam Deo integrum sit pro suo beneplacito „servare, an reprobare, sibi nil esse quod conqueratur. Quod nihil aliud est, quam vim & summam prædestinationis divinæ in nobis aut salvandis, aut abjiciendis, pro Dei summo in omnes arbitrio, proprio sensu confiteri, & in morte sincerius testari, quam multus infrunitis & impetuosis adversus eam scriptis, per vitam. Iste Coornhert passim suis libris, (quos tribus in folio satis crassis voluminibus anno cIↄ Iↄ cxxx. editos nescio quis tanti pretii facere queat, ut emere vel legere velit cum magno temporis, studiorum, nummorumque detrimento) aliquod schema Ecclesiae communis erigendae proponit, in qua, vel solus Scripturae textus legeretur, absque glossis & expositionibus, vel etiam admonitiones ex Scriptura sub aliorum judicio, non autem ex authoritate, aliquando fierent, ad modum alterius & novi Interim, usque dum nova divinaque ad extruendam aliam Ecclesiam, missione accederent ministri, quales Apostoli fuerunt, Ecclesiam ex Christi praescripto novam creaturi, qua jam missione ad erigendam cum Reformatione Ecclesiam omnes, juxta eum, careant. Tomo primo, pag. ult. in delineatione suae Ecclesiae sic loquitur: Raro, aut nunquam utuntur hic humanis glossis, non quod peccatum sit, sed quia incertum, a sole ad stellas, & a fontibus ad cisternas recurrere. Atque ita etiam nemo hic sibi (absque certa & speciali missione) arrogat docendi officium, ut cum authoritate mandet vel prohibeat, bene quidem ut sub meliori sententia admoneat, idque ex Scriptura. Similiter Tomo secundo, lib. Collyrium (Belgice omnia) sub finem. Tomo III[?] in initio, lib. Rudis delineatio Ecclesiae non partialis. Deinde alio; de Ecclesiarum erectione a Baptistis. Denique eodem Tomo, de minuendis Sectis: nam huc praesertim spectare illud suum consilium, de tali Ecclesia Interimistica, Conniventiae opinor alter diceret, ad minuendas, & coeundas in unum Coetum cultumque sectas, arbitrantur. Hoc libello vel dialogo ita sententiam suam exponit: existimem, Magistratui significandum, quod quaecunque scripta humana, glossae, dogmataque aliquid impuri, errores & ambages continent, a quibus omnibus immunis est Scriptura, certam pandens salutis viam. Quare reverenter rogandus esset, ut vellet, ad modum novi alicujus Interim, (& hoc ad tempus usque quo concorditer decretum esset quae doctrina sequenda foret) „omnibus Concionatoribus interdicere, ne è suggestu „populum aliud quid docerent, prælegerent, dicerent“ „ve, præter clarum Scripturæ textum, citra unius syl„labæ aut additionem aut demtionem, quomodo in „Veteri Novoque Testamento solebat fieri. Hoc de„ mum pacto sectas evaniturasPræterea populo sub „multâ injungendum esse, ut omnes suos libros de „Scripturâ tractantes, quæ ipsæ non essent mera Scri„ptura, ad manus Magistratus deferrent, ibique serva„rentur, ut vel redderentur postmodum suis dominis, „vel prout visum foret, de illis disponeretur. Hæc Coornhertus: quæ ut examussim conveniant cum nostri Auctoris conceptibus, nisi inde sua habeat, quis est qui non videt? Speciosum videtur; quod homines hi videntur solliciti esse de uniendis in Christianismo sec-tis, iisque omnibus reducendis ad Scripturam: & certe vellem quam maxime, ut huc saltem perduci sectæ possent; sed quod Ecclesiam inter Sectas illas simpliciter numerant, vel eam nullam uspiam esse dicitant, uno-que ordine omnes habent. & singulorum conditionem æstimant ex opinione adversariorum, ordinariumque in Ecclesiâ ministerium, quod inde à tempore Apostolorum hucusque viguit, jam libere & manifestius, nunc magis occulte, ejusque auctoritatem & vim conculcant & oppugnant, hæc ferri neutiquam aut possunt, aut debent, in illis præsertim, qui pacem tanto boatu clamant, eamque neglectam aliis objiciunt, dum ipsi interim acerbissime à suâ sententiâ alienos exagitant & proscindunt, quâ Doctores singulos, quâ etiam Ecclesias integras. Certe pacis tantæ auctores oportebat præ omnibus benignissime & mitissime agere cum quibuscumque, & dissentientibus, qui hoc tantopere videri volunt damnare in omnibus aliis quod tam egre dissentientes ferunt. Coornhertus palam scribere ausus fuit, inter omnes sectas se nullibi Christi Ecclesiam deprehendere: Romanam nostrâ, quam ne quidem Eccle-siæ siæ nomine dignabatur, meliorem esse, Tom. I. in Dialogis, sol. 484. nec de S. Coena ullibi idcirco participabat, quia veram Ecclesiam, & legitimos ministros desiderabat: unde & communionis necessitatem, quae vulgo docetur, negat quoque, Tom. I. lib. Consistorium, in initio. Tom. III. in Delineatione impartialis Ecclesiae, statim à principio docet, posse quemlibet esse verum Christianum, utcunque non sit membrum alicujus ecclesiae visibilis: rogatusque, quid praestaret, an extra visibilem Ecclesiam vivere, quoad usque ipse Deus per certos ministros Ecclesiam restauraret; an Ecclesiam, infirmorum gratiâ, non valentium vivere absque externa aliquâ formâ, quin ad Sectarum partes prolaberentur, colligere? respondit: prius quidem esse magis certum; at secundum videri sibi necessarium. Collapsam quidem esse Dei Ecclesiam, sed non apparere manifestum mandatum eam restaurandi: attamen ovile aliquod pro infirmis, adversus varios lupos defendendis, sub tali nempe libertate, quâ nemo sibi arrogget, à Deo se ad docendum missum esse, & Sacramentorum baptismi ac Coenae usu relinquatur liber, in infirmorum gratiam habendum; nullum vero istorum urgeri debere praeceptum, aut necessitatem. Unde in carmine aliquo subjecto libello suo adversus Danaeum, cui titulum fecit, Smegma, ad singulas versuum periodos subjicit: quorsum ei vinculum, qui absque eo potest vivere? mat behorst hp hant/ die angebunden leben han / ipsum fundamentum & medulla Libertinismi, in quo gloriatus fuit, quod videlicet nulli se addixerit Ecclesiae, vel communioni. Haec de Coornherto paulo latius, hoc loco, propter magnam illius cum Nostris hominibus, in suis de colligendâ, vel vitandâ Ecclesiâ dogmatibus, affinitatem, utque Nostros docerem, non à se nunc demum ista consilia opinionesque promanare, neque non illa pridem discussa rejectaque fuisse. Quod si hoc unum vellent, ipsum S. Scripturae textum, major irreverentia locoque debere esse apud Christianos, ac vulgo fit, plusque tribuendum ejus lectioni auditionique, etiam nudae citra expositiones, quam homines communiter ei deferunt, utique nos non habere nos repugnantes. Sed cogitent, annon hoc vitium, (vitium quippe est) majus foret, si in omni concione populus nil audiret unquam praeter solam Scripturam, & annon tum hoc, tum alia vitia merito reprehendenda essent ex Dei verbo: quod ubi fieret, quid tum distaret adeo a nostra & communi verbi praedicatione, vel ejus ad particulares casus, quod in concionibus fit, applicatione? atque hoc quidni tum nomine & jussu Dei liceat, ubi tam clarum Dei pro officio sedulo audiendi verbum suum mandatum? quur non cum Paulo dicere hic liceat: ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ ἐν πρεσβείᾳ? unde nomina πρεσβευταὶ πρεσβεύοντες, quasi legatione fungentes: quod sibi ita Origenes applicat, initio lib. VIII. contra Celsum: perinde ac si Deo nos cohortante, ut fervientiore Pauli illo affectu per nos ipsos, & nostram causam peroremus, pro Christo legationem ad homines ineamus. Chrysostomus auditores suos ad crebriorem S. Coenae communionem exhortans, ad Heb. IX. homil. XVII. ita τὰ λεγόμενα. Non enim sunt nostra, sed divini spiritus quae dicuntur: ὁ γὰρ ἡμέτερος λόγος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεύματος τὰ λεγόμενα. Vel hoc misso, tentent illi, cujusvis sectae homines saltem eo adducere, ut ipsum Dei verbum, sit citra quamcumque ejus expositionem, una audire, & colere velint: nos id hactenus non reprehendemus: sed ideo destruere Ecclesias, ordinemque in iis jam a temporibus Apostolorum observatum, in expositione Scripturae; & hoc dicere apostaticum, antichristianum esse, res est ab omni prorsus ratione aliena. Dixerim nostris hic Novatoribus, idem quod Tertullianus olim Marcionitis, lib. de Praescript. Aliquos Marcionitas & Valentinianos liberandae veritatis expectabat: interea perperam evangelizabatur, perperam credebatur, tot millia millium perperam tuae. ela, tot opera fidei perperam administrata, tot virtutes, tot charismata perperam operata, tot ministeria perperam functa, tot denique martyria perperam coronata. Vel, uti adversus Marcionem, lib. 1. O Christe patientissime domine, qui tot annis interversionem praedicationis tuae sustinuisti, donec scil. tibi Marcion subvenirei!
units.tr: Teachers need not be Apostles, either always or now, to speak and act in the name and authority of God. Let everyone see whether I have wrongly gathered and stated the controversy from your tortuous questions, in which you never state the matter so clearly and firmly as in your letter, which explains your mind more certainly than they do. Finding the question was far more work for me than arguing about it. But are all the Christian Catholic Churches, that is, all those in the world and those that have existed from the age of the Apostles until now, from their very beginnings, apostate, because in them the infallible Word of God, of the Old and New Testaments, is expounded by ministers, and in sermons that are not likewise infallible, yet in God's name? Show where I have strayed from your meaning and from the proper statement of the controversy. I did not keep your words, "divine insofar as God is in it, and merely divine" and so on; I made them clearer by substituting "infallible," a word that both suits your meaning better and expresses the thing more precisely. You yourself use this word not in your little book but in your letter, which I did not see until after our Apology was written and published. So, if you please, learn not to dismiss an opponent's writing so casually and dogmatically, by saying that the controversy was not understood, when you have understood my position better than your own writing did. If the readers of both sides do not say so, then I will honestly confess that I have been put to shame. Meanwhile I am glad to have seen by whose calf you were led to plough, and under whose authority you were brought into these delusions. I named other patrons for them in my writing, chiefly Matthew Radecke, Francis Pucci, from the letters of Socinus, and Adolph Venator, a famous teacher among the Remonstrants. To these should be added Sebastian Franck, who in a letter written at Strasbourg in the year 1540 to John Campanus asserts that he believes the external visible Church of Christ, together with its gifts and sacraments, passed into heaven through the corruptions of Antichrist, immediately after the departure of the Apostles, and is hidden in spirit and truth. He firmly holds that for fourteen hundred years no congregation of the Church has existed with its sacraments, and that the preachers and ministers called to do what they do have no right to gather the scattered Church or to administer the sacraments, unless they were sent by God in an extraordinary way and confirmed in it by signs or miracles. Theodore Coornhert, a native of Amsterdam, at one time secretary of Haarlem from the year 1561, held the same opinion as our people. He was a man of some talent, but, like those who are late learners (for he only began to learn Latin at the age of thirty), and as those who wish to teach others while still immature are apt to do, he did not learn himself. Relying on audacity alone, he intemperately threw himself into the business of religion. From the Reformation of our churches, which he attacked while it was still in its infancy, especially the catechism, and from what he himself approved and our Church did not, he was intent only on carping at everything and assailing great names: I mean Calvin, Beza, Danaeus, Saravia and others, and he sought empty glory among his own people. He died in the year 1590. What is especially worth noting is that this man, who so intemperately wrote much against our theologians about predestination, which he had by no means understood, was forced at the end, near death, to feel and acknowledge its truth in himself, crying out to God that he had nothing to complain of, if God chose to possess his soul or to preserve it or to reprobate it, as is right for Him to do according to His pleasure. This is nothing other than to confess with one's own understanding the force and sum of divine predestination, whether for saving or rejecting us, by God's supreme judgment over all, and in death to bear more sincere witness to it than he had borne in life through his many foolish and violent writings against it. This Coornhert, throughout his books (which no one could be found who would value at so high a price, in three fairly thick folio volumes published in the year 1630, as to wish to buy or read them at the cost of much time, study and money), sets forth a plan for building a common Church, in which either the bare text of Scripture alone would be read, without glosses and explanations, or, from time to time, admonitions drawn from Scripture would be given under the judgment of others, not by authority, in the manner of another and new Interim. Meanwhile, until new and divine ministers, such as the Apostles were, come to build another Church, creating a new Church according to Christ's prescription, all now lack, in his view, the mission to build the Church anew with the Reformation. In the last page of the first volume, in his outline of his Church, he speaks thus: "Here they rarely or never use human glosses, not because it is a sin, but because it is uncertain to run from the sun to the stars and from the springs to the cisterns." And so also no one here, without a certain and special mission, claims for himself the office of teaching, so as to command or forbid with authority; they may indeed admonish, in the best sense, and that from Scripture. Similarly in the second volume, in the book Collyrium (all in Dutch), near the end; in the third volume at the beginning, in the book Rudis delineatio Ecclesiae non partialis; then in another, de Ecclesiarum erectione a Baptistis; and finally in the same volume, de minuendis Sectis. For that counsel of his concerning such an interim Church, I suppose someone else would say, looks chiefly to this: to lessen the sects and to bring them together into one assembly and worship. In this little book, or dialogue, he sets out his opinion thus: "I think it should be made known to the magistrate that whatever human writings, glosses and doctrines contain anything impure, errors or obscurities, are things from which Scripture alone is free, since it lays out the sure way of salvation. Therefore he should be respectfully asked to wish, in the manner of some new Interim (and this until it is agreed by common decree what doctrine is to be followed), to forbid all preachers to teach, read aloud or say anything from the pulpit to the people, except the plain text of Scripture, without adding or taking away a single syllable, as was done in the Old and New Testament. In this way the sects will at last disappear. Moreover, the people should be strictly ordered to deliver to the magistrate all their books treating of Scripture which are not themselves pure Scripture, to be kept there, so that they may afterwards be returned to their owners or disposed of as seems fit." So writes Coornhert. That these things agree exactly with the conceptions of our author, unless he has them from there, who does not see? It looks fair that these men seem anxious to unite the sects in Christianity and to bring them all back to Scripture, and certainly I would very much wish that the sects could at least be brought to this. But in that they simply count the Church among those sects, or declare that there is no Church anywhere, and they all share one rank, judging each one's condition by the opinion of its opponents, and now openly and freely, now more secretly, trample on and attack the ordinary ministry in the Church, which has flourished from the time of the Apostles until now, and its authority and force: these things can by no means be borne, nor should they be, especially in those who cry out so loudly for peace and charge others with neglecting it, while they themselves meanwhile most bitterly harass and tear apart those who differ from their opinion, both individual teachers and whole Churches. Surely the authors of so great a peace ought above all to act most kindly and gently towards whomever they deal with, even dissenters, who so wish to appear to condemn in all others what they themselves so hardly bear when dissenters do it. Coornhert openly dared to write that among all the sects he nowhere found the Church of Christ. He judged the Roman Church, which he would not even honour with the name of Church, to be better than ours (Tom. I. in Dialogis, sol. 484), and he did not take the Lord's Supper anywhere, because he longed for a true Church and lawful ministers. Hence he also denies the necessity of communion, which is commonly taught. In the Tom. I. lib. Consistorium, at the beginning, and in Tom. III. in Delineatione impartialis Ecclesiae, he teaches from the very start that anyone can be a true Christian though he is not a member of any visible church. When he was asked what was better, whether to live outside the visible Church until God himself restored the Church through certain ministers, or to gather a Church, for the sake of the weak who cannot live without some external form, lest they fall away to the parties of the sects, he answered: the former is indeed more certain, but the latter seems necessary to him. The Church of God has indeed fallen, but no clear command to restore it appears. Yet some fold should be had for the weak, to defend them against various wolves, under such freedom that no one claims to be sent by God to teach, and the use of the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper is left free, to be held for the sake of the weak; but none of these should be urged as a command or a necessity. Hence, in a poem appended to his little book against Danaeus, which he titled Smegma, he adds after each period of verses: "Why bind yourself to what you can live without?" (Dutch verse, rendered: "Why bind yourselves, who can live unbound?"). This is the very foundation and marrow of Libertinism, in which he boasted that he had devoted himself to no Church or communion at all. I have said this about Coornhert rather more fully here, because of his great affinity with our people in his teachings about gathering or avoiding the Church, and so that I may teach our people that these counsels and opinions do not come from him only now, and that they were long ago examined and rejected. If they wished only this, that the text of Scripture itself be held in greater reverence among Christians than it commonly is, and that more weight be given to its reading and hearing, even bare and without explanations, than men commonly give it, we would certainly not oppose them. But let them consider whether this would not be a greater fault (for it is indeed a fault) if in every sermon the people heard nothing ever except Scripture alone, and whether this and other faults ought not rightly to be rebuked from God's Word. If this were done, how would it differ from our common preaching of the Word, or from its application to particular cases, which is done in sermons? And why should this not be permitted then, in God's name and by his command, since his Word clearly commands us to hear it diligently as our duty? Why may we not here say with Paul: "on behalf of Christ, in an embassy" [ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ ἐν πρεσβείᾳ]? Hence the words "ambassadors" and "acting as ambassadors," as if discharging an embassy: Origen applies this to himself at the beginning of book VIII against Celsus, as if God were exhorting us through ourselves, so that with Paul's more fervent feeling we plead our cause, and enter upon an embassy to men on behalf of Christ. Chrysostom, exhorting his hearers to more frequent communion in the Lord's Supper, in his seventeenth homily on Hebrews, says thus: "For the things spoken are not ours, but of the divine Spirit" [ὁ γὰρ ἡμέτερος λόγος, ἀλλὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεύματος τὰ λεγόμενα]. Or, setting this aside, let those men of any sect at least be brought to the point of wishing to hear and honour God's Word itself, alone and without any exposition of it; we shall not reproach them for that so far. But to destroy the Churches, and the order observed in them from the time of the Apostles, in the exposition of Scripture, and to call this apostasy and antichristian, is a thing wholly alien to all reason. I would say to our innovators here what Tertullian once said to the Marcionites in his book on Prescription: he was waiting for some Marcionites and Valentinians to be freed for the sake of truth; meanwhile the gospel was preached amiss, believed amiss, so many thousands of thousands of faith's works were amiss administered, so many virtues and gifts amiss performed, so many ministries amiss discharged, and at last so many martyrdoms amiss crowned. Or, as he says against Marcion, in book I: "O Christ, most patient Lord, who for so many years endured the overthrow of your preaching, until at last Marcion came to your aid!"

units.la: Iam ut hoc etiam in loco Apologia nostra, pro Ecclesia Christiana, non Apostatica, oppolita libello cui tit. Ad legem & ad Testimonium &c. legatur, non incommodum judicavi. Iustinus Martyr, epist. ad Zenam, & Serenum: Non est igitur molestere resistendum provocantibus & lacessentibus sed constanter placideque respondendum; numquam efficies, ut me dimoveas a proposito. ἀχ ἕτως ἐχ ἕ εχ ἰχύῳ δυνατὸν ἵνα μὴ κρίνησις τὴν ἀφαίρεσιν.
units.tr: Now, that this too may be read in this place, our Apology for the Christian, not Apostatical Church, set against the little book entitled To the Law and to the Testimony, &c., I have thought not out of place. Justin Martyr, in his letter to Zenas and Serenus: It is therefore not necessary to resist those who provoke and assail us, but to answer them steadily and calmly; you will never make me abandon my purpose. [ἀχ ἕτως ἐχ ἕ εχ ἰχύῳ δυνατὸν ἵνα μὴ κρίνησις τὴν ἀφαίρεσιν.]

units.la: Apologias qui scripsere pro Christianis adversus Paganos & Infideles, plurimi quovis seculo fuerunt, eóqs, quo numerosissimi ex Gentilismo ad fidem certatim accederent, celebriores quidem vidit Ecclesia, Iustinum, Athenagoram, Tatianum, Theophilum, Tertullianum, aliosque, nec Clementem Alexandrinum, Origenem, vel etiam Arnobium, Lactantium, Athanasium, Eusebium nunc dicam Caesariensem, sed, qui pro Ecclesiis Christianis apologiam fecerit coram Christianis, nescio an auditum unquam omnibus retro seculis fuerit: quo magis deplorandā venit temporis hujusce nostri, in quod reservati sumus, calamitas, quā qui Christianismum aliàs profiteri se dicunt, in omnem tamen Christianismi & quae olim à primo Apostolorum aevo usque fuit, Ecclesiam insurgere haud quaquam erubescunt, & omnes illas pro Apostaticis habere. Scripsit nuperrime nonnemo, quę est nostri scripturientis ac lascivientis seculi protervia, libellum, cui titulum fecit, Ad legem & ad testimonium; &c. quod ubi primum apud Bibliopolam perlustrassem, contemnebā illicò, indignum responso ratus, quod non nisi interrogare noverat, & responsione nequidquam expectatā temerè concludere, quodque maximè quidem detestabar, in caput omnium totius catholici Christianismi ecclesiarum concludebat, omnes apostasiae impudentissime condemnare. Postmodum significatus Auctor, neque is mihi prius ignotus: etiam responsum ei paratum à Cl. D. Marcio vidi; cui satis habuit insolens Monitum opponere, idemque omnibus notum facere ad instar publicae tabulae, quasi hoc sit respondere posse, quod tacere non posse, uti contra Maximinum Arianum loquitur Augustinus. Grave sane crimen, quod nuperus scriptor omnibus Christianismi Ecclesiis impingit, & forte vix ipsi intellectum quale id sit, quod apostasiam appellat: quomodo enim, si errorem aliquem erroresve in Ecclesiis notes, quale ipsi videtur, quod unice urget, nempe verbum praedicari Dei nomine, & tamen non infallibiliter verum; necdum tamen apostasiam inde concluseris, vel impegeris, vel non ideo, quod verbum Dei, utcunque non infallibiliter, tenetur tamen, docetur quod quam apostasia dicat repudium universale fidei, ac religionis, in eoque ab haeresi differat, quod haec sit, error contrarius aliquibus fidei articulis, illa ab omnibus recedat: quod discrimen adeo notum, ut & apud Theologos, & Iurisconsultos supremo & pessimo loco merito veniat apostasia. Ne nostros dicam, in loco de haeresi, Theologos & Scholasticos sec. sec. qu. xi. de haeresi sequente xi. de apostasia distincte agunt. Atque in jure Canonico, primum de haereticis tum agitur de Apostatis. In jure item Civili, alius & prior titulus in Cod. est, de haereticis & Manichaeis; sequitur de apostatis: & hi quidem deserte Christianae religionis rei sunt. Non certe statim apostasiae crimen intentandum aliquibus, quamvis errantibus, aut etiam graviter peccantibus, non qui errorem admittunt vel diuturnum, ideo omnem fidem repellunt, & ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως ἐναυάγησαν, 1 Tim. 1. 19. Tum & istud omnem superat audaciam, quod Auctor hic nullus addubitet alium coetum, atque ecclesiam erigere, ac facere schisma: parum id quoque considerans, quam gravem incurratis Dei indignationem, Ecclesiam qui temerè turbat ac scindit. Videat, quae scribit Irenaeus, antiquus & gravis Auctor, lib. III. cap. XL. adversus eos qui ex quacunque causa schisma faciunt. Vel etiam lib. IV, cap. XLIII. qui autem scindunt & separant unitatem Ecclesiae, eandem quam Jeroboam poenam perciperunt à Deo, & quae plura ibi graviter contra recedentes à veritate dixit. Aut Cyprianum audiat, de unitate Ecclesiae, & eodem super argumento Augustini sive epistolam, sive librum, contra Petilianum Donatistam: nisi dicere voluerit, & illos pro apostatis scripsisse, adde & Martyres pro eadem obiisse, quod sanè perquam horrendum foret. Hujus Auctoris jam mihi examinare libellum istum, Ad legem & testimonium, animus est, in quod me non adeo sponte mea ingessi, quam invitatus & sollicitatus ad id à variis, quibus denegare hoc quidquid est laboris vix licuit, in supprimenda tempestivè & in herbâ quasi suffocanda, et ἀνυτος instâ sectâ. Neque valde timeo, ubi detecta erunt haec sacra & discussa, multos pellectum eò iri, nisi forte ἀσυμφώνως, & quorum nimis quam fertilis est nostra patria, Libertinos, quibus religio nulla est, dum fere omnem colunt.
units.tr: There have been very many writers of apologies on behalf of Christians against the Pagans and unbelievers in every age, and in the period when very great numbers were eagerly coming over from Gentilism to the faith, the Church saw the more famous ones: Justin, Athenagoras, Tatian, Theophilus, Tertullian, and others. I say nothing of Clement of Alexandria, Origen, or even Arnobius, Lactantius, Athanasius, Eusebius, and now I will mention Caesariensis. But I do not know whether anyone in all past ages has ever been heard who made an apology for the Christian churches before Christians themselves. All the more lamentable is the calamity of this our time, in which we have been reserved: those who say they profess Christianity nonetheless have no shame at all in rising up against the whole Christian religion and the Church which has existed from the first age of the Apostles, and in regarding all of them as apostate. Someone very recently wrote a little book, which he titled To the Law and to the Testimony; etc. Such is the impudence of this scribbling and wanton age. When I first looked it through at the bookseller's, I at once scorned it, judging it unworthy of an answer, since its author knew only how to ask questions and rashly drew conclusions without waiting for any reply. What I detested most of all was that he concluded, most shamelessly, that all the churches of the whole catholic Christian religion stand condemned of apostasy. Afterwards the author was pointed out to me, and he was not previously unknown to me. I also saw a reply already prepared by the learned Mr. Marelius. To this the insolent author thought it enough to oppose a warning (Monitum), and he made it known to everyone in the manner of a public notice, as if this were answering, which is what Augustine says against the Arian Maximinus: that the man who cannot keep silent believes he can answer. It is indeed a grave charge that this recent writer brings against all the churches of Christendom, and perhaps he hardly understands what kind of thing he is calling apostasy. For if you note some error or errors in the churches, such as he alone presses, namely that the Word is preached in God's name and yet is not infallibly true, you have not thereby concluded or charged apostasy. Nor is it apostasy because the Word of God, though not infallibly, is still held and taught. Apostasy means a universal repudiation of faith and religion, and it differs from heresy in this: heresy is an error contrary to some articles of faith, whereas apostasy departs from all of them. This distinction is so well known that apostasy rightly holds the highest and worst place both among theologians and among jurists. I say nothing of our own theologians and Schoolmen, who treat heresy in its place, in question 11 of section 2, and then treat apostasy separately in the following question 11. In canon law, heretics are dealt with first, then apostates. In civil law too, one title in the Code, the earlier and separate one, is on heretics and Manichaeans, and it is followed by on apostates; and these indeed are guilty of deserting the Christian religion. Certainly the charge of apostasy must not be brought at once against some who are erring, or even sinning grievously, who do not reject all faith because they admit an error, even a long-standing one, and "have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith" [ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως ἐναυάγησαν], 1 Tim. 1. 19. Moreover, this author surpasses all boldness in that he does not hesitate to set up another assembly and another church, and to make a schism, giving little thought to the grave wrath of God that he incurs who rashly disturbs and splits the Church. Let him look at what Irenaeus, an ancient and weighty author, writes, book III, chapter 40, against those who make a schism for whatever cause; or also book IV, chapter 43: Those who split and separate the unity of the Church receive from God the same punishment as Jeroboam, and the many other severe things he says there against those who withdraw from the truth. Or let him hear Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church, and on the same subject Augustine, both his letter and his book against Petilian the Donatist; unless he wishes to say that they too wrote on behalf of apostates, and add that martyrs died for the same cause, which would certainly be most dreadful. It is now my intention to examine this author's little book, To the Law and the Testimony. I did not undertake this so much of my own accord as at the invitation and urging of various people, from whom it was scarcely permitted to refuse this labour: namely, to suppress in good time this newly sprung sect, and, as it were, to smother it while it is still in the grass. Nor do I greatly fear that, once these sacred matters have been revealed and discussed, many will be drawn to it, unless perhaps the inconsistent [ἀσυμφώνως] and the Libertines, of whom our country is all too fertile, to whom religion is nothing while they cultivate almost everything.

units.la: Non aliter haereses de quorundam infirmitatibus habent quod valeant, nihil valentes si in bene valentem fidem incurrant, verba sunt Tertulliani, in lib. de praescript. adversus haeret. Vel, ut discipulus ejus loquitur, Cyprianus, epist. III. Graves viros & semel super petram solida stabilitate fundatos, non dico auræ levi, sed nec vento aut turbine commoveris ne animus dubius & incertus variis opinionibus, velut quibusdam ventorum incursantium flatibus frequenter agitetur, & à proposito suo levitatis reprehensione mutetur.
units.tr: "Heresies have no power against the weaknesses of some people, having no strength at all if they meet with a faith that is well established," are the words of Tertullian in his book On the Prescription against Heretics. Or, as his disciple Cyprian says, letter 3: Serious men, founded once and for all upon the rock with solid stability, you must not be moved, I do not say by a light breeze, but not even by wind or whirlwind, lest a doubtful and uncertain mind be constantly driven about by various opinions, as if by the blasts of gusts of wind, and be turned from its purpose by the reproach of fickleness.

units.la: Ita necdum satis haeresium schismatumque in orbe Christiano: non satis divexata à primis incunabilis Ecclesia tot diversis infirmitisque dogmatis ac sectis? ut, ubi nihil fere novi, quod non diu antea commentum, cudi contra veritatem ulterius videri possit, id agi nunc debere credatur, ut variis quasi forte concurrentibus ex pridem notis erroribus, aliud semper ac aliud inde conficiat schisma seductor spiritus λαοσπλάνος πνεῦμα ut dicitur Ignatio, in epistola ad Ephesios. Etenim vix proferri quid ultra potest, quod non ostendatur maxima sui parte, si non omni, ex priscis aliisque defumtum haeresibus sectisque, nisi forte illud, quod scriptor libelli Ad legem, et ad Testimonium, &c. docere handerubuit, omnes ab evo Apostolico Ecclesias Christianas esse apostaticas; caeteroquin in plurimis, ut suo dicetur loco, errores cum aliis communes & hinc inde congestos tenens. Quae causa fuit Apologiam pro Christianismo meditandi, & breviter ostendendi, quam insignis illa Auctoris sit audacia, omnem contemnere & condemnare Ecclesiam, pro sua schismatica, quam Conventicula miro titulo & κατασπάσαντες appellat. Neque sane necessum adeo videbatur libello respondere, ne, ut loquitur adversus Helvidium Hieronymus, respondendo dignus fieret, qui vinceretur, nisi accepissem, etiam sectae Auctorem fieri, libri qui esset; quod illud est, ad quod perpetuo & impotenter contendunt paradoxa & turbida ingenia, familiam ut de suo etiam nomine inter alios ducant, ne quae pars probro vacet: quod, si quis alius, ego vehementer abhorreo, & doleo. Siquidem haud istud leve est, Ecclesiam, pretiosissimum coeli apud nos depositum, scindere, & quod sequi ad haec solet, alia & diversa conventicula erigere ac sequi. Cyprianus, lib. de unitate Ecclesiae: cum haereses & schismata postmodum nata sint, dum conventicula sibi diversa constituunt, veritatis caput atque originem reliquerunt. Παραγονατικός dicunt Graeci. Distinguit Basilius epistola, quae dicitur canonica, ad Amphilochium, αἱρέσεις, χωρισμοί, & ἐκκλησιαστικά. Haereses quidem de iis dicuntur, qui omnino divulsi sunt, & a fide abalienati. Schismata vero, qui ob ecclesiasticas quasdam causas et quaestiones mediabiles inter se disiident. Parasynagogae autem, ms conventus, congregationes, quae a rebellibus suis presbyteris vel episcopis, pis, & ab indocta plebe τῶν ἀπαιδεύτων λαῶν. Ea demque ex Basilio repetit, super eodem consultus τῆς τῶν αἱρέσεων ἐν βασιλεῖ μὲν τῶν Theodorus Studita, epist. iv. ad Naucratium filium. Quò autem referendus sit Auctoris nostri coetus, quem erigit conniventiae; ipse viderit: an verò ad Scepticam? sic certè Diogenes Laërtius, in proœmio ubi de variis Philosophorum sectis disserit, αἱρέσεις δὲ λέγονται ... τὰ φαινόμενα ... ἀγγελίᾳ ... καθ' ὃ ἀλλ' ... Vel an potius ad sequentia, quae de συλλογισμῷ eorum secta, qui ex singulis aliqua sibi quae placerent, seligebant: ἐπὶ δὲ ... Πολέμων ... Ἀλεξανδρίνος, ... αἱρέσεως. Neque miretur quis, si Graeca sine interpretatione subinde posuero: quia nempe sic Auctor noster videtur velle, qui loca Scripturae ex N. Test. integris paginis Graeca descripsit, non sola illa quae asterisco indicavit praecipuè attendenda esse. Nisi Petrum Cotonum Iesuitam imitari ei placuerit, qui cum Danielc Chamiero per litteras disputaturus, Latinae Chamieri primus Graecam integram remittebat, sed duabus iterum Graecis à Chamiero egregiè repulsus, primus etiam in unâ illâ primâ Graecè loqui desiit. Sed ad nostrum: animus est cum eo agere, uti decet, candido atque amico, neque aliter volo, quempiam vel verbulum à me interpretari, quod non ex stylo magis, quàm animo dijudicari exopto; & si quid durius aliquando dictum videri possit, id causae imputandum, cui non possum non saepe graviter indignari; saltem melius à me habebitur, quam quidem ab ipso exceptus fuit Cl. D. Marelius: quod an ipsum decuerit, perstringere modò Adversarium, nec id parum acerbè, aliorum, imò & ipsius esto seriurn judicium. Ego quidem istius reminiscar, quod Chrysostomus monet disputantes contra insanam aliquorum opinionem, qui Deum comprehendi à nobis posse audacter statuebant: quapropter vos fratres charissimi omnes hortor & rogo, curare tentetis pro viribus eorum opinionem, perinde ac insaniam & delirium furentium, cum modestia tamen & clementia. homil. 11. de incomprehens. Dei nat. Cum Apostolo, εἰ αρα πως δώῃ αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς μετάνοιαν εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας. 11 Timoth. 11.25. Spondet quidem noster, meliora se libentissime admissurum, ac semet praebiturum docilem; an vero praestiturus sit, quod de nobis haud gravate pollicemur, exitus ostendet. Decet autem: non enim vincimur quando offeruntur nobis meliora; sed instruimur maxime in his, quae ad Ecclesiae unitatem pertinent & spei ac fidei nostrae veritatem, inquit Cyprianus bene, epist. ad Quintinum, de haereticis baptizandis. Quare, quod etiam vult noster, quo pressius cum eo agam, cominus alloquar, & praesentissime ipsum aggredi placet.
units.tr: So, is there not yet enough of heresies and schisms in the Christian world? Has the Church not been harassed enough from its earliest cradle by so many different weak doctrines and sects? So that, where there is almost nothing new, and nothing that has not been devised long ago, it may still seem possible to forge further against the truth, it is now believed that this must be done: as various errors already well known happen to come together in some chance way, the seducing spirit, "the spirit that deceives the people" [λαοσπλάνος πνεῦμα], as it is called by Ignatius in his letter to the Ephesians, brings forth always one schism after another. For scarcely anything further can be put forward which will not be shown, for the greatest part if not wholly, to be drawn from ancient and other heresies and sects; except perhaps that which the writer of the little book To the Law and to the Testimony, &c. has dared to teach, namely that all Christian churches from the Apostolic age onward are apostate. In other respects, as will be said in its place, he holds many errors common to others and gathered from here and there. This was the reason for resolving to write an Apology for Christianity and to show briefly what remarkable audacity this author has in despising and condemning the whole Church as his own schismatic body, which he calls, with a remarkable title, Conventicles [κατασπάσαντες]. Nor indeed did it seem very necessary to answer the little book, lest, as Jerome says against Helvidius, he should become worthy of an answer who is conquered. Yet I had learned that he was becoming the author of a sect, which is what paradoxical and turbulent minds strive for constantly and without restraint: to lead a following under their own name among others, so that no part of them may be empty of disgrace. If anyone else does this, I greatly abhor it and grieve for it. For it is no light matter to tear apart the Church, which is our most precious deposit from heaven, and, as usually follows from this, to set up and follow other and different conventicles. Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church: Since heresies and schisms have arisen afterwards, while men set up for themselves different conventicles, they have left behind the head and the origin of the truth. The Greeks call such things parasynagogues [παρασυναγωγαί]. Basil, in the letter called canonical, to Amphilochius, distinguishes heresies, separations and ecclesiastical matters: Heresies are said of those who are wholly torn away and alienated from the faith. Schisms are of those who differ among themselves over certain ecclesiastical causes and questions that can be settled. But parasynagogues, that is, assemblies and congregations, are those set up by their rebellious presbyters or bishops, and by the unlearned common people. Theodore the Studite repeats the same from Basil, when consulted on the same matter, in his fourth letter to his son Naucratius. To which class our author's assembly, which he sets up by connivance, should be referred, he himself must see: or is it rather to the Sceptics? Thus indeed Diogenes Laertius, in his preface, where he discusses the various sects of philosophers: "heresies are called ..."; or rather to what follows, concerning the syllogism of that sect which chose for itself from each whatever pleased it: "... Polemon ... of Alexandria, ... of heresy." Nor let anyone wonder if I sometimes set down Greek without translation. Our author, it seems, wishes this: he copied out Greek passages of Scripture from the New Testament, whole pages of them, not only those few he marked with an asterisk as especially to be noted. Unless he has chosen to imitate Peter Coton the Jesuit, who, about to dispute by letter with Daniel Chamier, first sent back Chamier's Latin entirely in Greek; but, being thoroughly rebuffed by Chamier with two Greek letters, he also was the first to stop speaking Greek after that very first letter. But to our matter. I intend to deal with him as is fitting, candidly and in a friendly spirit, and I want nothing else. I wish that no word of mine be judged by its style rather than by its intention. If anything may seem to have been said rather harshly, let it be imputed to the cause, at which I cannot help being often gravely indignant. At least it will be treated better by me than Mr. Marelius was treated by him. Whether it became him to attack the adversary only, and not too bitterly, let the judgment of others and of himself be. I remember what Chrysostom warns those who dispute against the insane opinion of some who boldly maintained that God can be comprehended by us: Therefore, dearest brothers, I exhort and beg you all to try, as far as you can, to cure their opinion as the insanity and delirium of madmen, yet with modesty and gentleness. Homily 11 on the incomprehensibility of God's nature. With the Apostle: "if perhaps God may grant them repentance unto the knowledge of the truth" [εἰ ἄρα πως δώῃ αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς μετάνοιαν εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας], 2 Tim. 2. 25. Our author indeed promises that he will most gladly admit better things and show himself a docile pupil. Whether he will actually do what we without hesitation hope of him, the outcome will show. It is fitting that it should be so: For we are not conquered when better things are offered to us; rather we are most of all instructed in those things which pertain to the unity of the Church and to the truth of our hope and faith, says Cyprian well, in his letter to Quintus, On the baptism of heretics. Therefore, that I may press him more closely, as he too wishes, I will address him face to face, and I am pleased to attack him very directly.

units.la: Ac primo quidem, inquiramus in sententiam tuam, ne in ea constituenda erremus, & tum etiam, quod hinc oriri solet, inter disputandum, ne ut in Monito loqueris, cum larvis nostris luctemur, atque nugemur: in quo tamen venia eo justius nobis debebitur, quod hujusmodi erotematis ab Auctore quaestio non satis aperte proposita, nedum tractata fuit, vel illo ipso articulo xviii. quo tamen luculentissime eam designatam in Monito jactat. Sed patebit illud ipsum manifestius, ubi nos controversiam ad sententiam ejus, accuratius, ut arbitramur, breviús atque significantibus, quam quidem ipse fecerit, formaverimus. Primum, uti dixi, ponamus sententiam tuam; ac deinde super ea ordine disputemus.
units.tr: First, let us examine your opinion, so that we do not go astray in setting it out. Then, as usually happens in disputation, let us avoid what you say in the Monitum, that we wrestle and trifle with our own bogeys. We should be granted all the more indulgence in this, because the Author did not put the question of this kind of erotema clearly enough, let alone treat it, even in that very article xviii, though he boasts in the Monitum that he has marked it out most clearly. It will become plainer still once we have formulated the controversy in relation to his opinion, more accurately, as we judge, and more briefly and pointedly, than he himself has done. First, as I said, let us set out your opinion; then let us dispute about it in order.

units.la: Hoc autem ante omnia & sententiae tuae exponendae, & excutiendae fecerit multum, animum interrogare, quo haec qualiacunque moliaris consilio, quis scopus, quis finis sit, quem intendas? Nimirum, si bene calculum pono, in tribus versaris. 1. ut evertas & destruas communem, usitatam, & Catholicam in Christia. nisi suo Deum publice colendi rationem in S. conciombus, & toto ministerio, quaeque haec praeterea spectant. Non tibi mens impugnandi aliquas denuum Ecclesias, vel aliquos Concionatores; vel alicujus seculi illa; sed quae jam ab aevo Apostolico hucusque invaluit, publicarum concionum forma, atque omnibus & seculis & Ecclesiis communis atque probata fuit, eam oppugnare, atque condemnare. Audax sane facinus, non, si veritatem pro te habens, consuetudinem rejicias: quod perquam laudabile; sed quod ex S. scriptura te putes condemnare posse omnes, quae ab aevo Apostolico hucusque fuerunt, & etiamnum sunt in orbe, Ecclesias. pergo, & hoc ubi obtinebis, in tuis scilicet ideis & circulationibus; nam ut id aliquando revera eveniat, quid tum porro? meliusne orbi futurum arbitraris remoto sole, & abolitis, quae hucusque mundum duxerunt, concionibus? II. Aliam Dei cultum publicum, privatumque substituis, & Ecclesiae formam, quam conniventiam appellas; qua scilicet Deus, jam ob Ecclesiarum omnium diuturnam & pertinacem apostasiam graviter offensus, veram & antiquam Ecclesiae faciem nec dum reducere instituit, sc. Doctorum infallibilium, quales Apostoli erant, & conciones infallibiles, spiritumque ejusdem generis nondum emittit; sed interim hoc rerum statu & pro tempore quasi, Ecclesia sub indulgentia & connivencia divina instituitur, in praecipuis manca, & laborans defectu essentialium ad veram Ecclesiae erigendae constituendaeque formam necessariorum, in solam spem alterius ac melioris forte secuturae suspensa. III. Sic enim promittis tibi, & siquis praeterea amet ire in tuam sententiam, tandem aliquando veram Ecclesiae formam, qua hactenus caremus omnes, caruit fermè semper universus orbis, reductum iri, & conciones infallibiles, quae vere Dei nomine habentur, quales erant Apostolorum aurea tempora! vel seculum spiritus S. adeo apud Enthusiastas omnes dedecantatum! Haec tria tuus spiritus, modo ne in verti-ginem, perpetuò obcrrat. Vin singula probem? quamvis id supervacaneum videri possit; breviter tamen agam, ut primùm de sententiâ tuâ rite constet.
units.tr: Before all else, in setting out and examining your opinion, it will help a great deal to ask yourself what purpose and aim you have in undertaking these things, whatever they are. Surely, if I reckon rightly, you are engaged in three things. 1. To overturn and destroy the common, customary and Catholic manner of publicly worshipping God in Christendom, in the holy assemblies and the whole ministry, and whatever else pertains to these. Your mind is not set on attacking some churches or some preachers, or those of some age; rather, you aim to attack and condemn that form of public preaching which has prevailed from the apostolic age until now, and has been common and approved in all ages and all churches. That is a bold undertaking indeed. It would not be so if, holding truth on your side, you were rejecting custom, which would be most praiseworthy; but you think you can condemn from Holy Scripture all the churches that have existed from the apostolic age until now and still exist in the world. I go on: suppose you achieve this, in your ideas and circles, of course. For suppose it should ever really come about, what then? Do you think the world would be better off with the sun removed and the preachings that have led the world until now abolished? II. You substitute another public and private worship of God, and a form of the Church which you call connivance. By this, God, already gravely offended by the lasting and stubborn apostasy of all churches, has not yet resolved to restore the true and ancient face of the Church, namely infallible teachers such as the apostles were, and infallible sermons; he has not yet sent forth a spirit of that kind. Meanwhile, in this state of things and for the time being, as it were, the Church is set up under divine indulgence and connivance. It is defective in essentials, lacking what is necessary for erecting and constituting the true form of the Church, and suspended only on the hope of some other and better thing perhaps to follow. III. For you promise yourself, and anyone else who loves to go into your opinion, that at last the true form of the Church, which all of us have hitherto lacked (the whole world has nearly always lacked it), will be restored, and infallible sermons which are truly held in the name of God, such as the golden times of the apostles were! Or the age of the Holy Spirit, so discredited among all the Enthusiasts! Your spirit keeps wandering perpetually among these three things, provided it does not get dizzy. Do you want me to prove each one? Though that may seem superfluous, I will nevertheless deal with it briefly, so that first the substance of your opinion is properly established.

units.la: Dixi ergo, te omnia in Ecclesiis mutata, quin pefsumdata velle, praesertim, quae ad rationem concionandi spectant communem, & usitatam. Quare ordinis melioris, ac necessariae methodi causa haec duo quae ad subjectum Controversiae & sententiae tuae spectant; Ecclesias puta, praemitto 1. praesupponi in hac quaestione, Ecclesias quoad doctrinam veras; alioqui de salsis & haereticis, cum omnibus suis concionibus; & ministerio abolendis & devovendis, quis addubitet? intellige ergo conciones in Ecclesiis veras, & doctrinam veram Christi Apostolorumque sonantes: illas si neges alicubi in orbe, vel imo nostras esse, jam tibi non disputatio in nos super forma concionandi, & ministerii, ac cultus divini, illum quod non infallibiles & tamen Dei nomine peragamus, instituenda erit, ut tamen hactenus videris solum id tuo scripto agere, nihil de doctrinae nostrae vel confessionis veritate adhuc dum in dubium trahens; sed capita doctrinae arripienda erunt, superque iis, cum aliis nostris Adversariis lis à te nobis intentanda, ubi tunc quoque te cum reliquis uno ordine habebimus Achivis.
