Therefore, all the faithful, pious and Christian people who have lived anywhere up to now have lived outside the Church, always under a dreadful apostasy and under the most severe anger and indignation of God. How wretchedly deceived were those who thought they were born in the Church and lived in it, and, what they counted no small part of their happiness, died in it. But most wretched of all are those who, deluded by an inexplicable stupidity or madness, eagerly and eagerly competed for death not in the Church but even for her sake. So, by your account, all the martyrs and all the faithful, though they most piously thought they had acted and fallen asleep in the bosom of their mother the Church, were mistaken. You dare to assert that they never saw her, and that they died under apostasy and for apostasy, and not, as they supposed, as a ψυχή and μάρτυς for the Church.

units.la: VIII Argum. Sequitur ex tuâ sententiâ, simul ecclesiam posse esse veram, & apostaticam; quæ est absurdissima implicatio: vera erit, quoniam veritatem ex verbo Dei docet; apostatica, quod eam docet non infallibiliter, & tamen nomine Dei.
units.tr: VIII Argument. It follows from your opinion that the Church can be both true and apostate at the same time, which is a most absurd contradiction. She will be true, since she teaches the truth from the Word of God; apostate, since she teaches it not infallibly, and yet in the name of God.

units.la: IX Argum. Denique non uno modo impingunt illa paradoxa de Ecclesiâ apostaticâ, in veritatem, ac natunaturam Ecclesiae. i. contra ejus necessitatem, dum docetur, tam diu atque adhuc dum nullam veram, omnes esse apostaticas. ii. contra ecclesiae perpetuitatem, quae futura promittitur, ac mansura ἐως τῆς συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος, Matt. xxviii. 20. Quae si quis in dubium trahat, in castra concedit Socinianorum, cui tum opponimus communia nostra adversus istos argumenta. iii. contra unitatem ecclesiae, sive quod spectat convertendos ad Ecclesiam atheos, gentiles, Iudaeos, haereticos, & quoscunque peccatores a Deo ac salute aberrantes; sive conversos, eorumque inter se in & ex Ecclesia quos jugiter petunt salutares fructus. Haec omnia unica tuae sententiae, sed abominanda & nimium quam abominanda spongia deles.
units.tr: IX Argument. Finally, those paradoxes about an apostate Church strike against the truth and the nature of the Church in more than one way. (i) They strike against her necessity, since it is taught that, so long as there is no true church, all are apostate. (ii) They strike against the perpetuity of the Church, which is promised to continue and remain ἐως τῆς συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος [heōs tēs synteleias tou aiōnos], Matthew 28:20. If anyone calls this into doubt, he retreats into the camp of the Socinians, against whom we then set our common arguments. (iii) They strike against the unity of the Church, whether we look at those to be converted to the Church, atheists, Gentiles, Jews, heretics and any sinners who have strayed from God and salvation, or at the converted themselves, and at their mutual fellowship within and from the Church, from which they constantly seek saving fruits. Your one opinion wipes out all these things with a sponge, a sponge that is detestable, and far more than detestable.

units.la: x. Argum. Ultimo, expungis istam doctrinam duos ex fidei Symbolo, quod Apostolicum materialiter dicitur, articulos, illum de communione Sanctorum, & alium de credenda una sancta Ecclesia catholica. Hoc potius manifestissimum est abs te deleri; atque ex eo etiam alterum de communione inter sanctos colenda; nullam quippe ecclesiam verae pastores, regimen, Sacramenta, disciplinam, ac agnoscis; nullam ergo etiam, qualis deberet esse in usu illorum, veram communionem. Vides, quo illa tuorum dogmatum atque erroremum portenta citato cursu ruant? quam omnia sustuleris; quae etiam certissimae probatissimaeque fidei, uno impetu? Jam tibi nihil ecclesia, nihil sancti, nihil martyres, nihil denique totus Christianismus. Quare tempestive videas, atque attentius considere, quid a te agatur, quorsum illa, forte etiam praeter animum ac expectationem, tendant. Sed, arguimur itemur: atque pro veritate Ecclesiae nostrae, non esse tam apostaticam, sic arguimus.
units.tr: x. Argument. Lastly, you erase from the Creed, which is called the Apostles' Creed in its substance, two articles: the one on the communion of saints, and the other on believing in one holy catholic Church. It is most evident that you delete these, and with them also the other article, on the fellowship to be cultivated among the saints. For you acknowledge no church as having true ministers, government, sacraments or discipline; and so you acknowledge no true communion of the kind that ought to exist among them. Do you see where those monsters of your doctrines and errors are rushing with such speed? How much you have taken away, and in one assault, even from the most certain and best-proved faith! Now the Church is nothing to you, the saints are nothing, the martyrs are nothing, and in short all of Christianity is nothing. Therefore see in good time, and consider more carefully, what is being done by you, and where those things, perhaps even beyond your intention and expectation, are tending. But we are again challenged, and for the truth of our Church, that she is not so apostate, we argue thus.

units.la: xi. Argum. i. Quod in illa ministerium, quod adeo exagitas, & abominaris; tantae deprehenditur necessitatis, fructus & efficaciae, adeo ut nemo, credo nec ipse, dissiteri audet, quin sit potentia Dei ad salu-tem. tem, atque valeat ad concutiendas, confringendas, convertendasque hominum ad cultum ac obsequium Dei animas, ad errantium, seductorum, vel ignorantium instructionem clarissimam; commonendos, reprehendendos & convincendos peccatores; etiam ad consolandum, erigendum afflictos, tentatos, &c. id est, [Greek], [Greek], [Greek], [Greek]: adeo ut praesens qui adest, attenditque, cujus [Greek] [Greek] [Greek] [Greek] [Greek], [Greek] [Greek] [Greek] [Greek]. 1 Cor. XIV. 25. quomodo Apostolus ex effectu & fructu ministerii sui, quod non vanum fuisset apud ecclesias, inde argumentari solet ac colligere tum virtutem sui ministerii, tum veritatem ecclesiae apud illos. 1 Thess. 1. 5. Nam evangelium nostrum non fuit apud vos in sermone solum, sed et in virtute, et in Spiritu sancto, et in [Greek] [Greek]. cap. 2. 13. nam accipientes sermonem auditus a nobis Dei, recepistis non sermonem hominum, sed (quomodo revera est) sermonem Dei, qui et operatur in vobis credentibus.
units.tr: xi. Argument. (i) The ministry in her, which you so harass and abhor, is found to be of such great necessity, fruit and efficacy that no one, I believe not even you, dares to deny that it is the power of God unto salvation, and that it is effective for shaking, breaking and converting the souls of men to the worship and obedience of God, for the clearest instruction of the erring, the seduced and the ignorant, for admonishing, rebuking and convicting sinners, and also for comforting and raising up the afflicted, the tempted, and so on. So much so that whoever is present and attends perceives, through the things that are said, that God is among them indeed. 1 Corinthians 14:25. In this way the Apostle was accustomed to argue and conclude, from the effect and fruit of his ministry, which was not in vain among the churches, both the power of his ministry and the truth of the Church among them. 1 Thessalonians 1:5: For our gospel came to you not in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in much assurance. Chapter 2:13: For when you received from us the word of God's hearing, you accepted it not as the word of men, but, as it truly is, the word of God, which also works in you who believe.

units.la: XII. Argum. 1. 2.
units.tr: XII. Argument 1, 2.

units.la: Quae Ecclesia non aliam tenet ac docet veritatem, quamquam in S. literis est, & ex eâ probatur, illa nequit dici apostatica: sed eam veritatem docet nostra Ecclesia. Ergo. Nega majorem, vel minorem. & tum, ut tu soles loqui, de re tota incerta cogitabimus. Sed progredimur ad Ecclesiam conventiculi, quam appellas, atque illam etiam particulatim placet hisce argumentis adoriri.
units.tr: The Church which holds and teaches no other truth than the one found in the Holy Scriptures and proved from them cannot be called apostate. But our Church teaches that truth. Therefore, etc. Deny the major or the minor premise. Then, as you are wont to speak, we shall consider the whole matter as uncertain. But we proceed to the conventicle which you call a Church, and we are pleased to attack it particularly with these arguments.

units.la: XIII. Argum. 1. Proba, ob illa quae in nostris Ecclesiis putas deprehendisse vitia, schisma ab eâ faciendum atque sectandum esse: sit enim, male ibi nonnulla regantur, 1. an illa tanta, ut tolerari salva Ecclesiae unitate non posse videantur, 2. qui ab altera parte anto clamore sectas Christianorum inter se perpetuo axare, solles & perstringere, atque omnes in syncretismum agere? 11. An nos expertus es pertinaces, tuis tom consiliis & monitionibus obstinatè & pervicaciter repugnantes, qui nuidius-tertius demum tua vidimus, & vixdùm audivimus? Ita propere ad erectionem novæ Ecclesiæ, ac coetus, non exspectato responso vel examine ad illa, nedum ecclesiarum aliquo communi & maturo judicio, se accingere? III. An nos tyrannidem tibi opposuimus, vel imò leveriores disciplinæ aliquid à nobis in te tentatum, quam ob causam coactum te dicere possis ad schisma moliendum? perpende quæso, annon hæc præmissa & suppositä atque probata saepius certiusque oporteat, antequam de secessione aut schismate vel cogitetur: & tu, vixdum cognito tuo libello, ac sententiâ, nedum habitis de eo Theologorum judiciis, multo minus iniquâ vel intolerabili oppositione aut condemnatione ullâ Ecclesiasticâ, aliam ecclesiam, alios coetus à nostris erigis, neque vel piis ad nos accedere ultra permittis. Cogita quæso, haec (obsecro te per Deum, ac quidquid Ecclesiæ apud te posit nomen) etiam atque etiam attentius, & apud animum tuum diligentissimè pondera, quid sit, quantique constet homini scandalum aut schisma in Ecclesiâ tentare. Sit, peccetur in concionibus eâ ratione, quâ tu vis, quod scilicet dicantur haberi Dei nomine, quamvis necdum probaveris in eo culpandos nos, nedum damnandos esse: sed demus hoc tibi: ideone schisma, schisma dico moliri? eccur non potius assis sanctissimum tanti Apostoli effatum: quid autem? imo quocunque modo, sive occasione, sive veritate Christus praedicatur; & in eo gaudeo, atque etiam gaudebo. Phil. 1. 18. de illis egerat, qui Christum ex contentione & malo animo annunciarent, verum ex contentione & malo animo annunciarent. Cyprianus, de unit. Eccles. Quisquis ab Ecclesiâ segregatus adulterae jungitur, à promissis Ecclesiae separatur. Nec pervenit ad Christi praemia, qui relinquit Ecclesiam Christi. Alienus est, profanus est, hostis est. Habere jam non potest Deum Patrem, qui Ecclesiam non habet matrem. Si pas- tuis nis evadere quisquam, qui extra arcam Noë fuit, & qui extra Ecclesiam foris fuerit, evadit. Monet Dominus & dicit, qui non est mecum, adversus me est; & qui non me- cum colligit, spargit. Qui pacem Christi & concordiam rumpit, adversus Christum facit. Qui alibi praeter Ecclesiam colligit, Christi Ecclesiam spargit. Si in eo peccetur à nostris, quod se dicunt nomine Dei concionés habere, in formâ concionum peccant, non in materiâ: tu tibi omnia sarta tecta etiam habes, atque accipis: pro illo ipsi respondeant. Augustinus, de unitate Ecclesiae. Ad quaedam quippe illa pertinere possunt, non ad universam orbem Christianum: quem si contagione periisse arbitrantur, dicere, quam multa sancti boni pacis etiam cognita mala in hominum congregatione toleraverint. Certè, ut apud nos istud articulum fidei non facit fundamentalem hactenus sive nomine Dei dicas concionari debere, sive nomine Ecclesiae; ita hanc ob rem solùm vel potissimùm sectam ab ecclesiâ diversam inchoare, argumentum est animi levioris, & valdè schismatutrientis, atque in Ecclesiae bonum & pacem supra modum iniqui, ne dicam improbi. Habeantur catechetica, vel Prophetica exercitia, nomine (uti loqueris) membrorum ecclesiae inter se, salvâ semper doctrinae & ecclesiae illibata veritate ac pace; hoc nequicquam obest concionibus nomine Dei habendis, vel saltem ad schisma neutiquam jubet devenire. Confer tuum erratum clv 111. xiv. Argum. ii. Proba, si omnino instituendum à nostris Ecclesiis schisma, aliam tum ecclesiam, & talem conniventiam, ac describis, erigendam esse. Quo jure hoc agas, quàve authoritate? an Dei? cedò tabulas atque instructionem, uti dicimus: sed ipse nolis Dei nomine hic quicquam agi, quod valde praejudicat tuo conatui, ac sententiae. Ecclesiae nomine? at cujus? quae illa ecclesia, quum nullam in generali totius Christianismi apostasia agnoscas? & tuam illam conniventiae hoc tibi in mandatis dedisse, ut colligeres insanum foret dicere. Deinde, quo jure talem meditaris Ecclesiam conniventiae? cedò regulam ejusce à Deo approbatam & commendatam: Vide enim, omnia agas juxta typum tibi ostensum, Hebr. VIII. 5. secus, quidquid non sit ex fide, illud noveris peccatum esse. Rom. XIV. 23.
units.tr: XIII. Argument. (1) Prove that, on account of those faults which you think you have detected in our Churches, a schism must be made from them and pursued. For suppose some things are badly governed there. (1) Are they so great that they cannot seemingly be tolerated while the unity of the Church is preserved? (2) On the other side, who have constantly torn and attacked the sects of Christians among themselves with such great outcry, and driven everyone into syncretism? (2) Have you found us stubborn, obstinately and pertinaciously resisting your counsels and admonitions, we who only the day before yesterday saw your writings and had barely heard of them? Are you so hasty to set up a new Church and assembly, not waiting for a reply or examination of those matters, let alone a common and mature judgment of the churches? (3) Have we opposed you with tyranny, or has anything more severe than ordinary discipline been attempted against you by us, for which you could say you were compelled to plan a schism? Please weigh this carefully: should these premises not be supposed, proved and established more often and more certainly before anyone even thinks of secession or schism? And you, who have scarcely known your own pamphlet and opinion, let alone obtained the judgments of theologians about it, and who have suffered no unjust or intolerable opposition or any ecclesiastical condemnation, set up another church and other assemblies apart from ours, and you do not even permit the pious to come to us any longer. Consider, I beg you, by God and by whatever name the Church has for you, these things again and again, and weigh carefully in your mind what it is, and how great a scandal or schism it is for a man to attempt in the Church. Suppose that sermons are given in our churches in the way you wish, that is, that they are said to be held in God's name, although you have not yet shown that we are to be blamed for that, let alone condemned. But grant this to you: why then should you plan a schism, I say a schism? Why do you not rather keep before you that most holy saying of so great an apostle: "What then? Whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is preached, and in that I rejoice, and will rejoice" (Philippians 1:18)? He had spoken of those who preached Christ out of strife and with ill will; yet even so, they preached Christ. Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church: Whoever is separated from the Church and joined to an adulteress is cut off from the promises of the Church. Nor does he who forsakes the Church of Christ attain the rewards of Christ. He is an outsider, he is profane, he is an enemy. He cannot have God as Father who does not have the Church as mother. If anyone outside Noah's ark escaped, then whoever is outside the Church escapes too... The Lord warns and says: "He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters." He who breaks Christ's peace and concord acts against Christ. He who gathers elsewhere apart from the Church scatters Christ's Church. If our people are at fault in saying that they hold sermons in the name of God, they are at fault in the form of their sermons, not in their content; you have everything intact and sound for yourself and receive it; let them answer for that themselves. Augustine, On the Unity of the Church: Those things can pertain to certain particular groups, not to the whole Christian world; and if they think that world has perished through contagion, let them say how many evils the saints, good men, have tolerated in the assembly of men, even while knowing them to be evils. Certainly, just as among us that article of faith does not make it fundamental so far, whether you say preaching ought to be done in the name of God or in the name of the Church, so to begin a sect distinct from the Church for this reason alone, or chiefly, is the mark of a light-minded man, one who greatly favours schism and is excessively unfair, not to say wicked, toward the good and peace of the Church. Let catechetical or prophetical exercises be held, in the name (as you put it) of the members of the Church among themselves, with the doctrine and the unbroken truth and peace of the Church always preserved; this in no way hinders sermons from being held in God's name, nor does it at all require a schism. Compare your error at page 111, the fourteenth argument. (ii) Prove, if it is at all to be instituted by our Churches, that a schism, and another church with such connivance as you describe, must be set up. By what right do you do this, and by what authority? By God's? Show me the commission and instruction, as we say; but you yourself do not wish anything here to be done in God's name, which greatly prejudices your attempt and your opinion. In the name of the Church? But of which church? Since you acknowledge no church in a general apostasy of all Christianity, it would be insane to say that your so-called church of connivance gave you this commission to gather. Next, by what right do you devise such a church of connivance? Show me a rule approved and commended by God for it: See that you make all things according to the pattern shown to you (Hebrews 8:5). Otherwise, know that whatever is not of faith is sin (Romans 14:23).

units.la: XV. Argum. III. Et pone tuam Ecclesiam: neque illa adhuc te ipso judice & fatente vera, sed defectuoso statu, quae errores tolerare cogitur, & non sub Dei Abbatia, sed offensione quoque & conniventiâ colligitur.
units.tr: XV. Argument III. Now posit your Church, which by your own judgment and admission is not yet true but is in a defective state, one that is forced to tolerate errors and is gathered not under God's abbacy but also by offence and connivance.

units.la: Quid igitur efficeris, bone vir, quid boni? & tua secundum te corrupta ecclesia, inque eo ipso, in quo apostasiam nobis affingis, scilicet, quod deest nobis verbum orale concionatorium infallibile, sive ὁ λόγος infinitè indubiè merèque verum. quid ergo, & quàm bellè jam nobis provisum per te? scilicet, hoc est quod dici solet, Ἀ'ν ἀγ ἀξ ἀ 'Ηὶ ὁ 'Ιεσούς. vel quod Hebraei, שמעון מזון ידרה ומצי קימה, Rabbi Simeon molit multum, & producit parum. Ex malâ nostrâ, sed tuo solum judicio malâ, dabis nobis tuam longè pejorem ecclesiam: id est, transmuta in omni nostrâ ecclesiâ illam unicam formalitatem, ut sic loquar, ne quid amplius dicatur fieri nomine Dei; quod totum est, si non unicum (nam si ad doctrinam pergas illam item calumniando, oppugnandoque, aliter recurrimus, & tu et jam nobiscum: illa enim, quaecunque hic moveri possunt, in partes jam diu dispositas & in classes adversarias sunt,) quod in Ecclesiis nostris exagitas, mutetur illud, dico, vel aboleatur, an tantum nobis spondere audes, in tuâ Connivencia Ecclesiâ non-plures errores vitiaque fore, quâcunque fortassis etiam ex parte, sive doctrinam, sive disciplinam spectemus? Quam bene igitur collocata erit opera, ac studium, in Ecclesiâ novâ, tuoque ipso arbitratu naevos suos habente, instruendâ? quidquid sit, inique aget, qui Ecclesiam, de quâ nondum, nec per te quidem, convictus esse possit, quod in eâ scandala ferantur cum summo salutis periculo conjuncta, commentari velit cum tuâ, juxta propriam Auctoris sententiam ;. vitiosâ. In superioribus autem vidimus, quo pacto errores admittere in hâc ecclesiâ, neque Sacramentorum, & disciplinæ, &c. sacra adhibere, quæ alioquin ad ecclesiam spectant, consultum eatus fueris.
units.tr: What, then, do you accomplish, good sir, and what good? By your own account your Church is corrupt, and in that very respect in which you charge us with apostasy, namely that we lack an infallible oral preaching of the Word, or the Word [ὁ λόγος], infinitely and undoubtedly true. What then, and how well has this been provided for us by you? Clearly this is what is commonly said, [the saying: "Ἀ'ν ἀγ ἀξ ἀ 'Ηὶ ὁ 'Ιεσούς"], or as the Hebrews say, Rabbi Simeon grinds much and produces little [שמעון מזון ידרה ומצי קימה]. From our evil, which is evil only by your judgment, you will give us a Church far worse than ours: that is, you would alter in our whole Church that single formality, so to speak, so that nothing more is said to be done in the name of God. That is the whole matter, if not the single point. For if you proceed to doctrine and attack it in the same way by calumny and assault, we shall answer differently, and you are already with us; for whatever can be raised here has long since been arranged into opposing parties and classes. You dare promise only this: that in your Church of connivance there will be no more errors or faults, in part or in whole, whether we consider doctrine or discipline, if what is criticised in our Churches is changed or abolished. How well, then, will work and zeal be spent in building a new Church that, by your own judgment, has its own blemishes? In any case, he acts unjustly who wishes to argue that scandals of the greatest danger to salvation are carried on in a Church of which he cannot be convicted, not even by you, while he compares it with yours, which by the author's own opinion is faulty. Yet in what precedes we have seen how you would do well to admit errors into this Church, and to omit the sacraments, discipline, and other sacred things, which otherwise belong to the Church.

units.la: XVI. Argum. XV. Explica, & probia, regimen quale in Ecclesiam tuam velis introductum: regimen enim addere soles, per media item regiminis, mutua mediante sermone edificationis publicæ, inquis: sed quum in nostris Ecclesiis non solum regimen traduxeris; sed reliqua inde sacra exterminaris, in concione preces, cantiones, item catechismos, confessiones, officia Pastorum, Doctorum, Presbyterorum, Diaconorum, ac ceterorum municipium Ecclesiasticorum, Agnostas, Consolatores, conventus, & Assemblea consistorialia, classicalia, synodalia, formulas administrandorum sacramentorum, matrimoniii, &c. Scholas item, studia, ac promotiones & gradus scholares atque Academicos, & quæ istius commaniæ plura, erat. CXLVII. &c. passim: Quæro, ista omnia an etiam velis procul abesse à tuâ Ecclesiâ, & ab ejus statu Continentiæ? quod si ita, mirum quàm indigesta illa moles, vel chaos futurum sit, & tale ut non multum versamur plures à scholis atque ecclesiis nostris hinc abductum iri. Neque tamen, quamvis mentionem feederis regiminis forte aliquius tuo in coetu, ac parasynagoga retinendi, quod tamen æquè cum reliquis in nostris ecclesiis respuetas, ubi ceterorum admittendorum rationem indices vel exponis.
units.tr: XVI. Argument XV. Explain and prove what kind of government you wish introduced into your Church. For you are accustomed to add government, and by means of government, the mutual exchange of public edifying speech, you say. But since in our Churches you not only transfer government but also cast out the other sacred things, namely prayers and songs in sermons, catechisms, confessions, the offices of the ministers, teachers, elders, deacons, and of the other ecclesiastical officials, the admonishers, comforters, meetings, and consistorial, classical, and synodal assemblies, the forms for administering the sacraments and marriage, and so on; also schools, studies, and scholastic and academic promotions and degrees, and the many other things of this kind, which is at CXLVII and elsewhere. I ask whether you also wish all of these to be far removed from your Church and from its state of connivance. If so, it will be strange how shapeless that mass, or chaos, will be, and of such a kind that we, who are much engaged with schools and our churches, will not be drawn away from them. Nor, although you perhaps mention some form of government to be retained in your assembly or parasynagogue, which you equally reject with the rest in our churches, do you indicate or explain the principle by which the others are to be admitted.

units.la: XVII. Argum. V. Si nulla hodie vera Ecclesia, nec nostra, nec imò tua, atque diutissimè sit, quod nunquam aliqua fuerit, ergo nullus conserti vel hæreticus, vel Gentilis, Mahumedanus aut Iudæus potest. Quia quò illum convertes? scio quidem ab hæresi, Muhammedismo, &c. studebis cum abstrahere, sed ad quid? terminum ad quem mihi dicito, ubi illum solveris à pristinâ infidelitate vel errore, quò per te vocandus sit. Instemus paullò pressius in exemplo Iudaei convertendi: scio unde avellendus sit talis homo, videlicet à suo Iudaismo; scio etiam per quod, quo usus medio hoc acturus sis, nempe persuasâ ei veritate SS. Euangelii; sed quaeret miser, quò illum demùm abire iubeas, & ad quam accedere ecclesiam? praesertim, quum illi tanto semper Ecclesiae praejudicio, ac necessitate laborent homines ecclesiis addictissimi. Age, quod studium solebat Adversarius jam noster unicè antea prae se ferre, & ego in ipso non semel depraedicavi, conversionis scilicet Iudaeorum, illud jam ostendat semel atque experiatur; quin sentiet propere, quàm vanus labor & futilis appariturus sit, hasce si sequatur de nullâ certâ ac verâ Ecclesiâ Christianâ hypotheses. Atque hoc etiam solum satis meo quidem judicio fuerit ad explodendam illam sententiam; quod per eam praescinditur omne studium & ratio convertendi Iudaeos, si vel nihil amplius daretur: tantoque illud detestandum magis, quod erat cxlviii, egregiis scilicet suis thesibus adactus, nos jubet supersedere tum à publicâ fidei professione à Christianis deposcenda, tum, à ratione convertendi errantes & ignorantes prescribendâ. Quae mihi jam non absurda videntur, sed abominanda. Quid non cogit homines dicere semel arrepta imprudenter hypothesis, cui omnino constitutum quovis tandem modo ἀγαλλίαν!
units.tr: XVII. Argument V. If today there is no true Church, neither ours nor even yours, and if there has been none for a very long time, because there never was one, then no heretic, Gentile, Muslim, or Jew can be converted. For to what will you convert him? I know you will try to draw a man away from heresy, Muhammadanism, and so on, but to what? Tell me the end to which he is to be brought by you, the point where you will have freed him from his former unbelief or error. Let us press a little harder on the example of converting a Jew. I know from what such a man is to be torn, namely from his Judaism. I know also by what means, and what instrument you will use for this, namely by persuading him of the truth of the holy Gospel. But the wretched man will ask where you bid him go at last, and which Church he is to join? Especially since such men, most attached to the Church, always labour under so great a prejudice and need for a church. Come now: let our adversary, who was accustomed to profess above all else his zeal for the conversion of the Jews, which I too have more than once praised in him, now show it and try it. Indeed, he will soon feel how vain and futile the labour will appear if he follows these hypotheses of no certain and true Christian Church. And this alone, in my judgment, is enough to explode that opinion: it cuts off every effort and method of converting the Jews, even if nothing more were at stake. And it is all the more to be detested because, driven by his outstanding theses, he bids us refrain both from requiring a public profession of faith from Christians and from prescribing a method for converting those who err and are ignorant. These things do not seem absurd to me, but abominable. What does it not drive men to say, once they have imprudently seized a hypothesis, by which they are wholly resolved to reach exultation [ἀγαλλίαν] by whatever means!

units.la: xviii. Argum. vi.
units.tr: xviii. Argument vi.

units.la: Si in tuâ ecclesiâ sufficere existimas solum & merum S. Scripturae textum legi eamque sic prout jacet absque ullis explicationibus pro confessione & Catechismo haberi, quo ita omnes hodie in Christianismo sectae, quae nunc redire sub unum quasi tugurium, & in syncretismum, sequetur inde merus scepticismus, nihil certi habens ex tot incertis Scripturae explicationibus, sed de omnibus tam facile addubitans, quam alicui assentiens, suspiam αλογοφομηδεις: quod fere sola ostendit horum erotematum facies, in quibus semper si, si, & tum de re tota cogitabimus, &c. Vel quod erot. cxxxix. Quid autem ratione qui id dicunt, certi esse poterunt in suo illo ipsorum judicio? quum sexi possit, ut in aliis locis praeteritis, pro opposita parte plura dicantur, &c. merum sapit Pyrrhonismum, qui scis, non contrarium potius verum esse? &c. Vel ut ipsa Pyrrhonis verba erant, quae Gellius refert, lib. xi. cap. v. ὁ μεγάλου ἐντως ἐχει τὸ ὡς, ἡ εἰσὶν ἢ ἀδηλίας. Dicet forte nostèr, se non omnia in dubium trahere, quare inter Scepticos etiam vel Academicos referendus non sit: quare hoc velim ante omnia ostendat, quae certa autumet vel esse, vel esse posse; & annon eo medio, quo caeterorum certitudinem elevat, simul omnium ἀπορίαν introducatur? neq; etiam inter illos Αντιφατικούς olim tantus per omnia consensus fuit, quin alii aliis ulterius perrexerunt, & Arcesilas negabat esse quidquam, quod sciri posset, ne illud quidem ipsum, quod Socrates sibi reliquisset, inquit Cicero Academic. i. quod hoc demum erat, quum nihil posse scire Socrates diceret, hoc ipsum tamen se certò scire asseverabat, quod nihil sciret; vel ut illud discriminis ponit Gellius inter Academicos, & Pyrrhonios, Academici quidem ipsum illud nihil posse comprehendi, quasi comprehendunt; & nihil posse decerni, quasi decernunt: Pyrrhonii ne id quidem ullo pacto videri verum dicunt, quod nihil esse verum videtur. De quibus omnibus recte pronunciat Augustinus, lib. xix. de civit. Dei cap. xviii. Quod autem attinet ad illam differentiam, quam de Academicis novis Varro adhibuit, quibus incerta sunt omnia: omnino civitas Dei talem dubitationem tanquam dementiam detestatur. Cujus etiam libri tres, in quibus disputat contra Academicos, exstant Tom. i.
units.tr: If you think that the bare text of Holy Scripture alone is enough in your Church, and that it should be read just as it lies, without any explanations, and be held as the confession and catechism, then (as things now stand, when all the sects in Christianity are coming back together under one roof, as it were, into a syncretism) there will follow sheer scepticism. People will have nothing certain out of so many uncertain explanations of Scripture, but will doubt everything as easily as they assent to anything, suspending judgment, nothing more [ἀλογοφο μηδεις]. This is almost the only thing that the appearance of your questions shows, in which we always find "if, if," and "then we shall think about the whole matter," and so on. Or, as your question 139 has it: But how will those who say this be able to be certain of their own judgment? Since, as in other places already mentioned, more can be said for the opposite side, etc. This tastes purely of Pyrrhonism. Do you not know that the contrary is rather true? And so on. Or, to use Pyrrho's own words, which Gellius reports (book 11, chapter 5): "it is so, or it is not, or it both is and is not" [ὁ μεγάλου ἐντως ἐχει τὸ ὡς, ἡ εἰσὶν ἢ ἀδηλίας]. Perhaps your man will say that he does not call everything into doubt, and so he should not be counted among the Sceptics or even the Academics. I would like him to show before anything else what he claims is, or can be, certain. Is not the same means by which he undermines the certainty of other things also the means by which the uncertainty of all things is introduced? Nor was there ever such complete agreement among those Academics [Αντιφατικούς], but some went further than others. Arcesilas denied that anything could be known, not even what Socrates had left behind, as Cicero says in Academica book 1. For when Socrates said that nothing could be known, he nevertheless asserted that he himself knew for certain this very thing, that he knew nothing. Or, as Gellius draws the distinction between Academics and Pyrrhonists: the Academics indeed say that it cannot be grasped that anything can be grasped, as if they grasped it; and that nothing can be decided, as if they decided it. The Pyrrhonists say that not even this is in any way true, that nothing is true, which seems to be so. Augustine rightly pronounces on all these matters in book 19 of The City of God, chapter 18: As for that distinction which Varro drew about the New Academics, to whom all things are uncertain, the City of God detests such doubt altogether as madness. There are also three books of his, in which he disputes against the Academics, in Tom. i.

units.la: Et Clemens Alexandrinus, Stromat. lib. vii. atque cum sint quidem tres animae affectiones, ignoratio, opinio, scientia: qui in ignoratione versantur, sunt gentes: qui autem in scientia, vera ecclesia: qui vero in opinione, ii secta-tur haereses. atque in principio libri octavi, sed neque an-tiquissimi philosophi ad contradicendum ferebantur & ad du-bitandum, sedem nos qui amplectimur, etsi quae vere ea philosophiam. Haereticos vero opinatores Theologi veteres αἱρετικούς appellabant: quod apud Eusebium videtur est, lib. v i. cap. x.
units.tr: And Clement of Alexandria, Stromata book 7: since there are indeed three affections of the soul, ignorance, opinion, and knowledge: those who are in ignorance are the Gentiles; those who are in knowledge are the true Church; but those who are in opinion follow heresies. And at the beginning of book 8: but the most ancient philosophers were carried to contradicting and to doubting; we, who embrace the seat of that which is truly philosophy... The ancient theologians called heretics, who are mere opinionists, αἱρετικούς [heretics]; as is seen in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 10.

units.la: Deinde per sententiam tuam introducitur Samaritanismus, omnium errorum, haeresium, & contradictionum foeda commixtio; idem enim sic Sociniano, sic Papistico, sic Remonstrantico, Anabaptistico, vel ab aliis forte orthodoxo modo intelligetur. Unde tum non potest non sequi mira confusio, Babel, discordia, contentiones ac schismata: tantum abest, ut hoc medio lectas & disputationes magis assopitum iri sperandum sit. Pone enim, quod ad lectionem alicujus ex S. scriptura [illegible, ~12 letters] puta de Dei natura, vel S. Trinitate, aut peccato originali, Christi persona [illegible, ~10 letters], satisfactione, vel nostra per Christi meritum & satisfactionem, justificatione, de efficacia gratiae, sanctorum perseverantia, Ecclesia, Sacramentis, officio Magistratus, &c. agentis, eam diversimodè alii ab aliis Auditores intelligant, & ut sit, quilibet suum sensum verum esse, contrarium vero falsum opinetur, contendat; quid hinc aliud exspectari poterit, quàm quod communiter & semper ex hominum disputationibus, maximè vero de religione, oriri videmus? apinmorum, studiorum collegiorum ac coetuum [illegible, ~6 letters], schismata; nisi adeo dementatus tur Ecclesiae formâ, non credas eam ex hominibus constituram, vel meliores eos fore iis, qui sub oculis Apostolorum tamen schismata sectabantur, dicebantque alii se Pauli, alii Petri, alii Apollo esse. 1 Cor. 1. 11, 12. Etenim ἐγὼ μὲν εἰμι Παύλου 1 Cor. 11, 19. Deniquehinc oriatur Libertinismus, quo suisque deque habebunt homines, quid sentiant, doceant, profiteantur, sive Arianum sit, sive Pelagianum. Papisti-cum cum an Anabaptisticum, &c. perinde, modò conticent verborum Scripturæ in superficie teneant.
units.tr: Next, by your opinion there is introduced a Samaritanism, a foul mixture of all errors, heresies and contradictions. For the same text will be understood in one way by a Socinian, in another by a Papist, in another by a Remonstrant, an Anabaptist, or perhaps by someone else in an orthodox way. From this there cannot but follow great confusion, Babel, discord, contentions and schisms. So far is it from being hoped that by this means the readings and disputations will be quieted. Suppose that, when someone reads a passage of Holy Scripture, for instance about the nature of God or the Holy Trinity, or original sin, the person of Christ [illegible], satisfaction, or our justification through Christ's merit and satisfaction, about the efficacy of grace, the perseverance of the saints, the Church, the sacraments, the office of the magistrate, etc., the hearers understand it in different ways, and, as usually happens, each thinks his own sense is true and the contrary is false, and contends for it. What else can be expected from this than what we commonly and always see arising from men's disputations, especially about religion: schisms of opinions, of studies, of colleges and assemblies [illegible]? Unless you were so out of your mind, you would not think that the Church would be constituted from men in this way, or that they would be better than those who, under the eyes of the Apostles, still pursued schisms, and said, some "I am of Paul," others "I of Peter," others "I of Apollos" (1 Cor. 1:11, 12). For indeed "I am of Paul" [ἐγὼ μὲν εἰμι Παύλου] (1 Cor. 3:4). Finally, from this there will arise Libertinism, by which people will make light of, and do what they like with, what they think, teach and profess, whether it is Arian or Pelagian, Papist or Anabaptist, and so on, provided only that they keep silent and hold to the surface of the words of Scripture.

units.la: Nunc ad Ecclesiam tuam quartam assurgamus, quæ erit sicut pristina olim & prima quæ fuit, Apostolica iterum, ubi redibunt tempora, quibus spiritus infallibilis, conciones indubiè veræ divinæque, &c. ac tandem nomine Dei licebit Ecclesiam colligere, & instituere, sacraque administrare, & quæ non? hanc tamen nondum nobis satis explicuisti ex sententia & voto tuo, premis autem & indicas. Ergò adversus eam sic habe.
units.tr: Now let us rise to your fourth Church, which will be like that first and original one which once existed, the Apostolic one, again. In it the times will return when the infallible Spirit will give sermons that are undoubtedly true and divine, and so on. At last, in God's name, it will be permitted to gather and establish the Church, to administer the sacraments, and what not. However, you have not yet explained this sufficiently according to your own opinion and wish, though you press it and point it out. Therefore, be ready to meet it thus.

units.la: XIX. Argum. I. Quod initio argumentorum contra Ecclesiam Apostaticam, & Conniventiæ (nam statum Apostolicum primum mitto) hic iterum contra ultimam tuam ecclesiam primo loco pono ac peto, ut probes, talem Ecclesiæ statum in terris exspectandum: hoc ante omnia nobis proba. Sic enim, atque necessario contra figmenta Chiliastarum, Fratrum Rosææ crucis, V Veigelianorum, ac Seculum spiritus Sancti, quod alii propediem præstolantur, argumentamur: alioqui facillimum foret quodlibet commisci, nisi ejus quod dicimus, præsertim quod pollicemur, peteretur certa probatio, ac spei fideique argumentum. Quod si tibi non jurato vel non argumentanti vis credi, æquè mihi fidem habeto, nam simpliciter rejicienti: sed jam debes fidem, si tibi ex Sacris ostendero, non modo talem statum nusquam prædictum nobis promissumque; sed eum circa ultima mundi tempora dici miserum, deperditum, improbum ac calamitosissimum, ex Matth. XXIV. Luc. XXI. &c. nequaquam ita felicem, ac in primordio & sub Apostolis fuit. XX. Argum. II. Præterea explica, qualis illa Ecclesia Apostolica futura sit, vel quid cum eâ exspectandum nobis? vel sine, si ita vis, abs te hæc quæramus. I. An existimas illam Ecclesiam à Deo approbatam iri, vel instituendam; an vero beneplacitè permittendam solùm? ut soles distinguere. II. An putas, in eâ omnes & singulos Doctores fore infallibiles; an aliquos solùm, instar Apostolorum? III. An omnes locuturos, omniaque sacra tum saltem nomine Dei agenda? IV. An illos docturos hoc idem Dei verbum, quod nos in scriptis habemus; an aliud, & hoc quoque infallibile, & λως insitè indubiè merèque verum? V. Et tale si illorum verbum; an hoc quoque conscribendum: ita ut S. scriptura hinc auctior reditura sit? VI. An quoque populus istius ævi sit futurus indefectibilis & infallibilis, verbum istud λως insitè indubiè verèque accepturus? VII. An semper ad finem mundi usque talis mansura ecclesia, & ejus status? VIII. Annon felicior hic status sit futurus primævo Apostolico? IX. An tum etiam hæreses, sectæ vel schismata? ita in alium orbem mihi pænè videor delatus, vel in sphæram lunæ, aut Utopiam aliquam, quâ ignarus omnium de singulis cogor interrogare: & plura sanè adderem, nisi me jam diu horum, & hujusmodi erotematum cepisset tædium taediosissimum. Φιλως τὸ λεχθὲν γίγνεσθαι ... ut suos jambos contra Philoponum exotdiebatur Georgius Pisides apud Nicephorum, histor. Eccles. lib. XVIII. cap. XLVIII. Baronium, Annal. Tom. VII. ad A. D XXXV.
units.tr: XIX. Argument I. As at the beginning of the arguments against your Apostate Church and the Church of Connivance (for I set aside the first Apostolic state), so here again, against your last Church, I put first and demand that you prove that such a state of the Church is to be expected on earth. Prove this before all else to us. For this is how we argue, and necessarily so, against the fictions of the Chiliasts, the Rosicrucian brethren, the Veigelians, and the Age of the Holy Spirit, which some are eagerly waiting for. Otherwise it would be very easy for anything to be mixed in, unless a certain proof were sought for what we say, and especially for what we promise, as a ground for hope and faith. But if you wish to be believed without swearing or arguing, then believe me too, for I am simply rejecting. But you must now grant belief if I show you from the Scriptures that not only is such a state nowhere foretold or promised to us, but that about the last times of the world it is called wretched, lost, wicked and most calamitous (Matt. 24; Luke 21, etc.), and by no means so happy as it was at the beginning and under the Apostles. XX. Argument II. Furthermore, explain what that Apostolic Church will be like, or what is to be expected from it. Or, if you like, let us ask you these things. (1) Do you think that Church will be approved by God or established, or only tolerated by his good pleasure? As you are accustomed to distinguish. (2) Do you think all and each of the teachers in it will be infallible, or only some, like the Apostles? (3) Will all speak and do all sacred things, at least then, in God's name? (4) Will they teach this same Word of God that we have in writing, or another, and this also infallible, and utterly, undoubtedly and purely true by inner light? (5) If their word is such, is this also to be written down, so that Scripture will thereby be enlarged? (6) Will the people of that age also be unfailing and infallible, and receive that word by inner light, undoubtedly and truly? (7) Will such a Church and its state remain so until the end of the world? (8) Will this state not be happier than the original Apostolic one? (9) Will there then also be heresies, sects or schisms? I seem to myself to have been carried almost into another world, or into the sphere of the moon, or some Utopia, where, ignorant of everything, I am forced to ask about each detail. I would certainly add more, had I not long since been seized with a most wearisome weariness of these and such questions. Let what is said come to pass... as Georgius Pisides used to declaim his iambics against Philoponus, cited from Nicephorus, Historia Ecclesiastica, book 18, chapter 48, and Baronius, Annales, Tom. 7, at A.D. 35.

units.la: XXI. Argum. Hæc de futuro Ecclesiæ statu Apostolico, &c. ac de reliquis sententia, non ita tua est, vel nova, quin multis variisque ex partibus, in pluribus hereodoxis atque fanaticis jam pridem explosa fuerit. Circa futurum Ecclesiæ statum feliciorem quæ tradis, habes communia multàm partem cum deliriis Chiliastarum, Fratrum Rosæ crucis, &c. Paracelsistarum, & VVeigelianorum, de quibus nos in Commentario de VVeigelianis: ne Anabaptistas Monasterienses dicam, & Davidem Georgium, cujus historia ab ejus genero Blesdikio accurate perscripta. Adde istis de Fratribus Roseae Crucis, quae pandit in historica sua narratione Nicolaus VVassenaer Amstelodamensis Medicus, hi-stor. part. VII. à pag. 124. Et part. VIII. à pag. 68. ubi literas profert alicujus ex isto ordine ad se Anno 1624. scriptas, occasione ex illis arreptâ, quae de iis part. VI. & VII. histor. narrat, significârat; explicatque Auctor, quamvis illi invisibiles fratricelli, & humanarum (ut se jactant) cogitationum arbitri, non satis inter se conveniant circa religionem, in eo tamen omnes ἀμεφρονες, & conspirare, quod certò exspectent ac polliceantur sibi generalem mundi, tam quoad politias, quàm Ecclesiam, reformationem; alia tempora, revelationem occultæ Cabalæ, perfectam cognitionem, politiam institutam ad exemplar Reipublicæ Damcareusis in Arabiâ (Vtopiâ sc.) ubi soli sapientes regnant, regnum Spiritus Sancti, pacis generalis, tertium Testamentum, sic loquuntur. Stultiora nescio an unquam legerim illis, quæ isti homines nugantur ac crepant, eaque tanto cum apparatu & φαντασίᾳ de suo ordine, fratribus, & studio, ac exspectatione novi in terris saeculi, quo spiritus S. gratiam & dona quaeque cumulatissima sibi promittunt, certe non ἀνὰ τῶν ἀμφοτερων. Ex eadem schola est, quod Anno 1622. editum Hagæ Comitis ab Andreâ Hobernfeld, Hierosolyma restituta, sive saeculum spiritus Sancti igneum; sub praesentis magna illius tribulationis quaternarii finem magno lumine suum accepturum initium: quo etiam mine interitus Bestiae Romanae & Mahumetismi ad Annum futurum 1624. ex scripturâ sacrâ recensentur & deducuntur. Vbi in praef. ad DD. Ordd. statim probat spiritum suum VVeigelianum Auctor distinctione luminis mentalis, rationalis & sensualis. Κοσμοπολιτ. Etiam de Euangelio aeterno, uti appellabatur, Iohannis Parmensis, tertium mundi statum & tempora spiritus S. somniante, diximus in nostro jam citato commentario: cujus errores vel sententias singulas ordine recensitas legere poteris, apud Bzovium, Annal. Tom. XIII. ad annum 1258. pag. 667. art. XI. Adveniente Evangelio spiritus Sancti, sive claresciente opere Ioachim (quod ab eo dicebatur Evangelium aeternum, sive Spiritus Sancti, &c. Similiter aliud seculum, & statum Ecclesiae in hoc mundo felicissimum docebat seculo sequenti, ex ordine Franciscanorum Iohannes Strinchius Begoardorum sectarius, cujus inter dogmata hoc secundo loco ponitur: Sicut in primo Christi adventu formata est nova Ecclesia veteri Synagoga rejecta; sic & in initio sexti status, vetustas prioris temporis est universaliter repellenda, ut videatur novum seculum, seu nova Ecclesia tunc formari, veteribus jam rejectis, et sicut in sexta aetate, rejecto carnali Iudaismo, & vetustate prioris seculi, renovabitur Christi lex & vita, & crux, &c. Apud Bzovium, Annal. Tom. XIV. ad A. 1254 & Nicolaum Eymerici, in Director. Inquisit. part. II. Ne de Iudaeis dicam, Eliam enixe praestolantibus, אליהו.
units.tr: XXI. Argument. These things about the future apostolic state of the Church, and the rest of your opinion, are not so much yours or new that they have not long ago been put forward, from many and various sides, by a number of heretics and fanatics. On the future happier state of the Church, what you teach has much in common with the fantasies of the Chiliasts, of the Fraternity of the Rosy Cross, and so on, the Paracelsians and the followers of Weigel, about whom I have spoken in my Commentary on the Weigelians. I need not mention the Anabaptists of Münster or David Joris, whose history his son-in-law Blesdijk wrote up carefully. Add to these the Brothers of the Rosy Cross, whom Nicolaas Wassenaer, a physician of Amsterdam, describes in his historical narrative, part 7, from page 124, and part 8, from page 68, where he publishes a letter written in 1624 by a member of that order, prompted by the matters he had related about them in parts 6 and 7. The author explains that although these invisible little brothers, who (as they boast) are judges of human thoughts, do not agree well among themselves about religion, they all agree in this foolishness: they confidently expect and promise themselves a general reformation of the world, both of its politics and of the Church; new times; the revelation of a hidden Cabala; perfect knowledge; a polity founded on the model of the republic of Damcar in Arabia (that is, in Utopia, where only the wise reign); the kingdom of the Holy Spirit; general peace; and a third Testament. Such is their language. I do not know whether I have ever read anything more foolish than what these men babble and boast, and with such show and fantasy [φαντασία], about their order, their brothers, their study, and their expectation of a new age on earth, in which they promise themselves the grace and every abundant gift of the Holy Spirit. Certainly they are not [ἀνὰ τῶν ἀμφοτέρων]. From the same school comes the book published at The Hague in 1622 by Andreas Hobernfeld, Jerusalem Restored, or the Fiery Age of the Holy Spirit, which says that under the present great tribulation, near the end of the quaternary, it will receive its beginning with a great light; there too the destruction of the Roman Beast and of Mahometanism is reckoned and deduced from Holy Scripture for the year 1624 to come. In the preface to the Lords of the Order the author at once proves his Weigelian spirit by a distinction between mental, rational and sensual light. Cosmopolitan. We have also spoken, in our commentary already cited, of the eternal Gospel, as it was called, of John of Parma, who dreamed of a third state of the world and the times of the Holy Spirit. Its errors, or its single opinions arranged in order, you may read in Bzovius, Annals, vol. 13, year 1258, p. 667, art. 11: "When the Gospel of the Holy Spirit comes, or when the work of Joachim becomes clearer (which he called the eternal Gospel, or of the Holy Spirit, etc.). Likewise, John Strinch, a Begard sectary of the Franciscan order, taught in the following century another age and a most happy state of the Church in this world; among his dogmas this is put second: As in the first coming of Christ a new Church was formed when the old Synagogue was rejected, so also at the beginning of the sixth state the oldness of the former time must be utterly driven out, so that a new age, or a new Church, may then seem to be formed, the old things now being rejected; and as in the sixth age, carnal Judaism and the oldness of the former age being rejected, the law and life and cross of Christ will be renewed, etc. See Bzovius, Annals, vol. 14, year 1254, and Nicolaus Eymericus, in Directorium Inquisitorum, part 2. I need not speak of the Jews, who eagerly await Elijah [אליהו].

units.la: Quatenus censes omnes in Christianismo Ecclesias sub apostasia atque defectione esse, & nullam veram, seu quae Dei mandatum pro sua erectione atque approbationem habet, illaque tempora Apostolica exspectanda & novissima, quibus ductu spirituque infallibili vera Ecclesia demum colligatur, convenit sententia tua cum nonnullis inter Samosatenianos haereticos in Polonia, quos signanti ori appellatione Socinianos dicimus, sed cum quibus ipsi Socino hac in parte non parva fuit contentio, qui statuebant, isto rerum atque Ecclesiae statu defectivo, ut & tu iam loqueris, non posse ecclesiam veram Apostolicam erigi, nisi exspectato speciali Dei mandato ac gratia, & spiritu Apostolico: quorum partes ducebat maxime inter illud hominum genus Matthaeus Radecius, ad quem variae extant Fausti Socini literae. Et sane non parum tuam sententiam cum ejus conspirare apparebit ex illis, quae ex Socini literis hanc in rem mox allegabimus. Adeo ut si probabile mihi foret, hujusmodi à te lectos libros unquam fuisse, plurimùm te hinc adjutum dicerem, & ex hac schola edoctum; sed tamen ipse Socinus contra semper disputat, & primâ quidem ad Radecium epistolâ: Cavendum est enim, inquit, omnino ab eorum sententiâ, qui nolunt, hodie ullam vel esse, vel esse posse aspectabilem Christi Ecclesiam, quia videlicet non conspiciantur hoc tempore dona illa coelestia, & Spiritus sancti operationes; quae non solùm Apostolorum aetate, sed etiam post aliquanto fuerunt, ut Iustinus, Irenaeus, & alii scriptores fidem faciunt (unde tamen interim perspicuum est, quod dixi, statim post Apostolos non talem fuisse defectionem, quae omnes aspectabiles Ecclesias suffulerit) neque animadvertunt, conspicua illa charismata ad Christi doctrinam confirmandam ad tempus exhibita esse, nec simpliciter & absolutè Ecclesiae Christi signa, sed pro eo tempore tantum fuisse. Et cum Socinus primâ hac epistolâ ita illorum mentem accepisset, ac si nollent sacros aliquos conventus peragi, & in Christi nomine congregari vel frequentari, meliùs edoctus hoc eos velle, non esse hoc tempore ecclesiam illam Apostolicam & primaevam instaurandam sine speciali aliquo mandato, propterea quia defectio post ipsos Apostolos plena fuerit, adeo ut ipsum quoque fundamentum fuerit sublatum. Sic porrò instat: non video, cur talem ecclesiam instaurare, etiam sine speciali mandato, tentare pii homines non possint; immò cur talis ecclesia & post apostolorum tempora diu fuisse, & hodie esse, diu merito nequeat. Nam quod affirmatis, post ipsos Apostolos plenam defectionem fuisse, sublatumque ex eo tempore ipsum fundamentum esse, hoc mihi nullâ ratione probari potest. Praeterea ejusdem epist. pag. 87. libri epistolarum: Sed urges, ut appareat, plane nullam dari hodie ecclesiam, quae primaevae illi Apostolicae similis sit; vel ob hoc, quod nota ista & tessera apostolicae ecclesiae absit, faciendi miracula, aut certè hac nota & tessera absente, temerarium esse asserere, hodie talem ecclesiam inveniri. Prolixius hâc de re disputat, epist. tet: tertia, refutatis quae pro alia sententia adducta erant, argumentis; atque simul indicat, eandem quoque fuisse Francisci-Puccii sententiam, cujus vitam & facta aliqua istic eādem epistolā describit. Idem ille Puccius, cum quo disputavit Socinus, super statu & immortalitate primi hominis. Epist. pag. 112. nullam neque esse, nec esse posse hodie externam ecclesiam una cum Puccio te sentire ostendis; quae res tandem illi causa fuit ad Papatum revertendi. Vtebatur ipse isdem fere rationibus, quibus interis; & potissimum hoc unum urgebat, post collapsum externa Ecclesiae statum necesse esse ad eundem erigendum, ut aliquis vel aliqui divinitus excitentur; ita ut ex signis &c. Duo praecipue contra Ecclesiae ministerium, ut auctor est Socinus pag. 117. adferebant; primum, eādem aut certè simili ratione instaurandam esse Ecclesiam, quā aedificata fuit; alterum vero, inter tot Christiani orbis dissensiones non posse veritatem dignosci, nisi luce aliquā divinitus, ut Apostolorum tempore, illata. Quae ibidem etiam refutat. Ecce, ut sententia nostri hominis de statu ecclesiae defectivo, & erectione alterius ecclesiae, nimis quam similis sit huic Puccii, Radecii, aliorumque inter Photinianos, sed ab ipsis Socinianis non agnitae, neque ab Auctoribus suis ultra defensae. Hinc apud Socinianos, ubi de Ecclesiā tractant, illam quaestionem semper, ut inter ipsos natam, discussam videre est, à Ioanne Volkelio, lib. & cap. ultimo de Religione Socinianā, Ostorodo, in Institutionib. pag. 405. de quibus nos plenius in Socinianismo Confutato agere proposuimus.
units.tr: Insofar as you think that all Churches in Christendom are under apostasy and defection, and that no true Church exists, or one that has God's command and approval for its erection; and that apostolic and final times must be awaited, in which by an infallible guidance and Spirit the true Church will at last be gathered: your opinion agrees with that of some heretics among the Samosatenians in Poland, whom we call Socinians by a name that stands for a sign, although Socinus himself had no small dispute with them on this point. They held that, with things and the Church in this defective state, as you too now speak, a true apostolic Church could not be set up unless a special command and grace of God, and an apostolic Spirit, were first awaited. Among that class of men Matthias Radecius chiefly led the party, and various letters of Faustus Socinus to him survive. And indeed it will appear, from what we shall shortly quote from Socinus' letters on this matter, that your opinion agrees not a little with his. So much so that if it were probable to me that you had ever read books of this kind, I would say you had been greatly helped by them and taught by this school. Yet Socinus himself always disputes against this view, and in his first letter to Radecius he says: For one must altogether beware of the opinion of those who will have it that today there either is, or can be, any visible Church of Christ, because, forsooth, those heavenly gifts and operations of the Holy Spirit are not seen at this time, which existed not only in the age of the Apostles but also for some time afterwards, as Justin, Irenaeus and other writers bear witness (from which, however, it is meanwhile clear what I said, that immediately after the Apostles there was not such a defection as overthrew all visible Churches). Nor do they notice that those conspicuous charismata were displayed only for a time, to confirm the doctrine of Christ, and were not simply and absolutely signs of the Church of Christ, but existed only for that time. And when Socinus, in this first letter, had understood their mind thus, as though they did not want any sacred assemblies to be held, or people to be gathered or to meet in the name of Christ, he was better informed that they wanted this: that at this time it is not possible to restore that apostolic and primitive Church without some special command, because the defection after the Apostles themselves was so complete that the very foundation was taken away. He presses this further: I do not see why pious men should not be able to attempt to restore such a Church even without a special command; indeed, why such a Church could not rightly have existed for a long time after the times of the Apostles and exist today. For what you affirm, that after the Apostles themselves there was a complete defection and that from that time the very foundation was removed, I cannot be shown to be true by any reason. Moreover, in the same letter, page 87 of the book of letters: But you press the point, so that it appears plainly that there is no Church today like that primitive apostolic one; either because this mark and token of the apostolic Church, the working of miracles, is absent, or else, that mark and token being absent, it is rash to assert that such a Church is found today. He disputes this at greater length in the third letter, having refuted the arguments brought for the other view; and at the same time he indicates that the same was also the opinion of Francis Puccius, whose life and some deeds he describes in the same letter. This same Puccius, with whom Socinus disputed, was concerned with the state and immortality of the first man. Letter, page 112: You show that you think with Puccius that there is today no external Church, nor can there be; a view which in the end was the cause of his return to Papacy. He used almost the same reasons that you use, and mainly urged this one point: after the external state of the Church has fallen, it is necessary for it to be raised up again by some one or some persons being divinely stirred up; so that from signs, etc. Socinus says on page 117 that they brought two main arguments against the ministry of the Church: first, that the Church must be restored by the same or at least a similar method by which it was built; second, that amid so many dissensions of the Christian world the truth cannot be discerned unless some light is divinely given, as at the time of the Apostles. He refutes these in the same place. See how the opinion of our man about the defective state of the Church and the erection of another Church is very much like that of Puccius and Radecius, and of others among the Photinians, though not acknowledged by the Socinians themselves, nor defended further by their own authors. Hence among the Socinians, whenever they treat of the Church, one may see that question always discussed as having arisen among themselves: by John Volkelius, in the last book and chapter of On the Socinian Religion, and by Ostorodt, in Institutions, page 405. We have proposed to deal with these more fully in our Socinianism Confuted.

units.la: Ne de Donatistis dicam, quorum hac in parte errores sic describit Augustinus, de haeresibus, cap. 1x 1x. tamquam Ecclesia Christi propter crimina Caeciliani, seu verè, si in quod magis judicibus apparuit, falsa, de toto terrarum orbe perierit, ubi promissa est, atque in Africā & Donati parte remanserit: in aliis terrarum partibus quasi contagione communionis exiit. Praeterea eadem fere sen-
units.tr: Not to speak of the Donatists, whose errors on this point Augustine describes in De haeresibus, chapter 69: as if the Church of Christ, on account of the crimes of Caecilian (or truly, if it appeared more so to the judges, false), had perished from the whole world, where it was promised, and remained only in Africa and in part of Donatus; in other parts of the earth it had gone out, as if by the contagion of communion. Besides, our author holds almost the same opinion in this matter, which

units.la: [?]entia hac in re Auctori nostro, quæ Turbonibus (Mixtiues diceret Tertullianus) in Anglia, ( quò tam diligenter idcirco undiquaque eodem genio qui ducuntur Socii, contendunt, ut certatim illas Ecclesias quantum in ipsis ultra vexent ac confundant) qui dicuntur Sceptici, sive Quæstionistæ, Querentes, Expectantes. vide Honorium Reggium de statu ecclesiæ Britannicæ hodierno pag. 2. 57. Alii se Expectantes vocant, ullam in orbe terrarum ecclesiam exstare, negantes. Alii Inquisitores sunt, Ecclesiam in deserto latentem quærentes. & inter quatuor ecclesiæ istius jam miserè divexatæ sectas, Antinomios, Anabaptistas, Congregationales, hos pri-mo loco collocat, Querentes, sive Expectantes. pag. 59. Anglicè Seekers & Waiters, Ecclesiam negant alicubi exsistere; sed in futurum expectant miraculosam cætus Christiani per Apostolos restitutionem, & pag. 103. ex concione istorum hominum refert: paulo post, Deum Apostolicos viros excitaturum, qui extraordinarium concionandi donum habituri sint. adde quæ & pag. 105. 110. 114. ejusdem farinæ. Auctor belgici libelli nuper editi, histor. motuum Angliæ pag. 116. de Quærentibus agens ex Honorio Reggio, & Thomæ Eduardi Gangrænâ, primum illorum articulum hunc ponit, quod credant nullam esse Ecclesiam, ministerium, Sacramenta, vel disciplinam ecclesiasticam: atque id ideo, quia jam nullus Apostolus. Inde eos omnia officia reprehendere, ac criminari Ecclesiastica æquè ac politica. Hon. Reggius in Catalogo errorum & hæresium & blasphemiarum in Angliâ exortarum ab Anno 1640. pag. 95. num. cxxx. recenset inter alia: plane illicitum esse concionari tamquam in Ecclesiâ, sed eatenus licet, si concioneris ut expectans discipulus: id est, Christianis non licet concionari positivè, ponendo & asserendo certi quid; sed tantum conferendo, arguendo, disputando: puta ut in coetu Conniventiæ. Et pagina seq. num. cxxxix. Cantiones sacræ & Psalmos Davidis non esse cantandos. Tales omnino inter Philosophos erant Pyrrhonii, vel Sceptici, quos & ἐφεκτικοὺς [?], & ἀπορητικοὺς [?] appellabant. Aulus Gellius lib. xi. Noct. Attic. cap. v. Quos Pyrrhonios philosophos vocamus, inquit, ii Graeco cognomento ἐφεκτικοὶ appellantur. Id ferme significat quasi quaesitores & consideratores. Nihil enim decernunt, nihil constituunt, sed in quaerendo semper considerandoque sunt, &c.
units.tr: the opinion in this matter of our author is almost the same as that of those in England who (as Tertullian would call them, Mixtiues) are carried along with such zeal, all of them, that they strive with one another to vex and confound those churches as much as they can. They are called Sceptics, or Questionists, Seekers, Waiters. See Honorius Reggius, De statu ecclesiae Britannicae hodierno, pp. 2, 57: Others call themselves Waiters, denying that any church exists anywhere in the world. Others are Inquirers, seeking a Church hidden in the wilderness. Among the four sects of that church, now miserably harassed, he places Antinomians, Anabaptists, Congregationalists, and in the first place these Seekers or Waiters, p. 59 (in English, Seekers and Waiters), who deny that a church exists anywhere, but look forward to a future miraculous restoration of the Christian assembly through the Apostles; and on p. 103 he reports from the sermon of these men: soon God will raise up apostolic men, who will have an extraordinary gift of preaching. Add what is said also on pp. 105, 110, 114, of the same kind. The author of the recently published Belgian pamphlet, Historia motuum Angliae, p. 116, treating of the Seekers from Honorius Reggius and Thomas Edward's Gangraena, puts first among their articles this: that they believe there is no church, ministry, sacraments, or church discipline; and this because there is now no Apostle. Hence they condemn and accuse all offices, ecclesiastical as much as civil. Honorius Reggius, in his Catalogue of the errors, heresies and blasphemies arisen in England since 1640, p. 95, no. 130, lists among other things: it is plainly unlawful to preach as in a church, but so far it is allowed if you preach as a learner who is seeking: that is, Christians may not preach positively, affirming and asserting something certain, but only by conferring, arguing, disputing, namely as in a meeting of the Connivents. And on the following page, no. 139: Sacred songs and the Psalms of David are not to be sung. Such among the philosophers were the Pyrrhonists, or Sceptics, whom they called [ἐφεκτικοὺς] suspensive and [ἀπορητικοὺς] aporetic. Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae xi, ch. 5: Those whom we call Pyrrhonian philosophers, he says, are called by the Greek name [ἐφεκτικοὶ] suspensive. That word means roughly seekers and considerers. For they decide nothing, they settle nothing, but are always in seeking and considering, etc.

units.la: Prodiit Anno 1644. Germanicè liber de abusu ministerii in hodierno Christianismo, sub nomine alicujus, qui se vocat Elium Praetorium, Concionatorem Evangelicum, in quo Auctor quidem offensus justè videtur nimiis in Christianismo, Ecclesiis, ipsoque adeò S. Ministerio, vel potiùs ministris, scandalis; ab altera tamen parte inconsideratius ac ferventius invehitur in quorumcunque Ministrorum universum officium, peccans perpetuo (ut dicunt) paralogismo accidentis. Praefatur quidem, sibi id neutiquam in animo esse ipsum S. ministerium impugnare vel vilipendere, pag. 2. atque iterum pag. 98. quaestionem tamen in genere sic proponit, pag. 3. An hodierni cujuscunque religionis, nominatim trium sectarum, ut appellat, quasque satis virulenter prosequitur, pag. 14. non absque gravi calumniâ, quam tamen agendi rationem à se initio penitus ablegasse videri temere voluit (an forte particulariter ab aliquo interea laesus?) an dico hodiernos Ecclesiarum Concionatores in quacunque religione ministerium N. Testamenti probè teneant, eoque funguntur? non absque aliâ priùs ad Deum protestatione, absolutè ac simpliciter negat. Rationes, quas ad confirmationem sententiae suae adfert, omnes facillimo negotio solvi possunt: vel simpliciter negando quod assumit, v. g. in primâ ratione, illorum omnium vocationem non esse divinam, sanctam, & irreprehensibilem: in secundâ, quod omnes cum doctrinâ Christi commiscent glossas philosophicas: in tertiâ, quod omnes essentialia membra S. ministerii tam verbi, quàm sacra-menmentorum adulterent: vel, quod quarto loco adfert, ad illorum ministerium non sequi fructus spiritus S.; quinto, quod in genere dicit de improbitate omnium ministrorum; sexto, non sequi inde carnalis vitae abnegationem & mortificationem; septimo, quod ministri non sunt spiritus ministri, at literae; octavo, quod doctrina & vita sua adversentur doctrinae & cruci Christi; nono, quia illorum ministerium carnale & proprii commodi ac lucri causa habeatur. Quae omnia negamus locum habere in omnibus Novi Testamenti hodie ministris: nam quod in aliquibus, vel etiam multis vitia notari possunt, non idem omnibus attribuendum, nisi & se quoque, qui pro ministro Evangelico se venditat, istorum juxta reum haberi velit. Tum, vitium & scandala ministrorum non sunt conjicienda in ministerium; eique exprobranda, praesertim ubi non docentur per ministerium, quod saltem in Ecclesiis & religione Evangelicorum non fit. Ergo rite distinguendus primum abusus, qui de facto, eoque non universali omnium, sed aliquorum duntaxat, & alicubi, ministris per accidens adhaeret, ab iisque committitur, sed non qua ministris; & ipsius S. ministerii, ut de jure & juxta religionem nostram haberi ac exerceri debet, doceturque omnino sanctissime. Quippe in titulo ipse dixit se actum de abusu ministerii: & pag. 50. satis novit haec distinguere, nisi putet ita deformata hodie esse omnia in Ecclesiis, etiam nostris, ut nil nisi abusus reperiantur: quo tamen manifestissime fallit; 1. quod non omnes ministri, etiam ex eius judicio, aeque improbi, & S. ministerio abutuntur, non qui v. g. similes Iohannis Arnd, cujus libros valde, neque omnino frustra laudat de vero Christianismo: ac Lutheranos perstringit, qui Auctori non exiguam ob ejus scripta attulerunt molestiam, quo de etiam in praefatione istorum librorum agitur. 2. totalis abusus S. ministerii in religione nostra, nisi temere ac calum. humiliosè, asseritur: quia quantumcunque vitiosi ministri alicubi, nullibi tamen secundùm religionem vitia docentur; atque ita doctrina adhuc intemerata manet, ex quâ omnis reformatio instituenda; quæ si in Ecclesiâ asservatur, auditurque, qualem ipse probas, quid est quod omnem nostram religionem temerariè proscribas? Sed ita illi homines solent, facilè ex aliquo deprehenso vel viso sibi errore aut vitio, omnem ecclesiam atque religionem confestim & procaciter infectari. Adeò etiam in reprehendendis peccatis peccatum vix evitamus. Videtur quidem Auctor non omnino malus esse, neque ex improbitate adeò peccare, quam quidem temeritate, quidquid sit de professione Evangelicâ, Papatui saltem nuncium misit; & ex zelo si hæc scripserit, plus scientiæ vellem illi adfuisset, majoremque modestiam optassem Auctori. Loquor de Prætorio. Duo præcipuè videntur ei scandalum circa S. ministerium movisse, 1. vita ministrorum & Concionatorum non satis proba ac castigata, gravis, nec respondens professioni, vel, quam illa exigit, sanctitati. Etiamsi quod ministerium non verentur malis sæpe artibus ambire, & acquirere favore Procerum, ac magistratus, &c. pag. 13. Tum, quod in ministerio plus doctrinæ (si modo hoc etiam) studeant sæpe, quàm vitæ; & disputare assuescant magis docentque, quàm vivere, & quæ istorum hominum (homines quippe sunt ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι) alia solent esse vitia. 11. Et hoc videtur ipsum offendisse, quod in populo ac ecclesiâ non respondeat ministerio suus, qui exspectari possit debeatque, fructus. Quare hinc evidentissimè appareat, perpetuum esse vitium horum hominum, & communem Aristarchorum paralogismum, quod velint & imaginentur sibi ecclesiam absque omni scandalo, & nec in se, nec in hac etiam vitâ ἐγκρατῆ ἀσθενῆ, ... Quum alia sit futura conditio ecclesiæ triumphantis in patriâ, alia ejus & minor hic fit in via: alia quæ præsens & communiter; alia quæ debeat esse. Itaque quando & doctrinâ adhuc sanâ pugnamus etiam ipsi contra vitia ministrorum, pro honore S. ministerii, & quoque nostro; atque vitâ & actionibus in id allaboramus, ut ἀξίως tantâ vocatione & officio vivatur, etiam juxta illa quæ isti homines supercilioși, & noster Auctor perpetuâ per totum scriptum & prolixissimâ paraenesi ac admonitione docet, inculcat, minatur, &c. quid superest, quod in genere & tam rudi atque immodesto modo invehantur contra ipsam religionem, eamque & Ecclesiam acerbissimè, & nullâ adhibitâ justâ distinctione, insolenter proscribant, insectentur, condemnent: verbi gratiâ, quando nos juxta ea, quæ hic Auctor lib. part. iv. pag. 742, &c. nobis facere imperat, nonnullis mutatis, illa saltem quæ præcipua & vitæ sinceram pietatem ac spiritus S. ductum spectant, conamur assequi, quid ultra est, quod ejusmodi libros, & insulsas orationes tam fastuosâ ac dirâ devotione in nos immittant, ceu magnas machinas? Hinc jam perfacilè foret levissimâ castigatione totum librum percurrere & enervare, si operæ pretium videretur: nihil enim in toto illo fastidioso scripto occurrit, in quo non Auctor committat paralogismum in eo observatum, sive ψευδο-συμβιβαστης, sive ψευδο-ἐπιμελητης. Sed in viam ex hoc diverticulo, in quo tamen non extra oleas, & materiam, quam præmanibus habemus, ex lib. ad legem & testimonium, inutiliter fuimus exspatiati.
units.tr: In 1644 a book was published in German, On the abuse of the ministry in present-day Christianity, under the name of a certain man who calls himself Elius Praetorius, Evangelical Preacher. In it the author, indeed, seems rightly offended by the excessive scandals in Christianity, in the churches, and even in the holy ministry itself, or rather in the ministers; but on the other hand he rails too inconsiderately and too fervently against the whole office of any ministers whatever, committing, as they say, a constant paralogism of accident. He does preface that it is by no means his intention to attack or belittle the holy ministry itself, p. 2, and again p. 98; yet he proposes the question in general terms, p. 3: whether the present preachers of the Churches in any religion, namely the three sects, as he calls them, which he pursues quite virulently, p. 14, (not without grave calumny, which however he rashly wished to appear to have wholly set aside at the start of his method; perhaps he was particularly injured by someone in the meantime?) do I say, whether the present preachers of the Churches in any religion hold the ministry of the New Testament rightly and discharge it? He flatly denies it, not without a prior protestation before God. All the reasons he brings forward to confirm his opinion can be solved with the greatest ease, either by simply denying what he assumes: for example, in the first reason, that the calling of all those men is not divine, holy and irreproachable; in the second, that all mix philosophical glosses with the doctrine of Christ; in the third, that all corrupt the essential members of the holy ministry, both of the Word and of the sacraments. Or else: what he brings forward in the fourth place, that the fruits of the Holy Spirit do not follow from their ministry; in the fifth, that he speaks in general of the wickedness of all ministers; in the sixth, that from this there does not follow the denial and mortification of the carnal life; in the seventh, that ministers are not ministers of the Spirit but of the letter; in the eighth, that their doctrine and life oppose the doctrine and the cross of Christ; in the ninth, that their ministry is carnal and is held for the sake of private gain and profit. All of which we deny to apply to all ministers of the New Testament today; for although vices may be noted in some, or even in many, the same cannot be attributed to all, unless he who presents himself as an Evangelical minister wishes to be held, along with them, as guilty. Then, the vices and scandals of ministers are not to be imputed to the ministry, nor reproached to it, especially where they are not taught through the ministry, which at least does not happen in the Churches and religion of the Evangelicals. Therefore one must first rightly distinguish the abuse, which in fact adheres by accident to some ministers only, and somewhere, not to all, and is committed by them, but not as ministers; from the holy ministry itself, as it ought to be held and exercised according to right and according to our religion, and as it is taught most holily in every respect. Indeed, in the title he himself said he was treating of the abuse of the ministry; and on p. 50 he knows well enough how to make these distinctions, unless he thinks everything in the Churches, even ours, has been so deformed today that nothing but abuses are found; yet in this he is most manifestly mistaken: 1. because not all ministers, even by his own judgment, are equally wicked and abuse the holy ministry; not, for example, men like Johann Arndt, whose books he praises very highly, and not without reason, in De vero Christianismo; and he attacks the Lutherans, who caused the author no small annoyance on account of his writings, which is also discussed in the preface of those books. 2. A total abuse of the holy ministry in our religion is asserted only rashly and with calumny, and very humbly; because however vicious the ministers may be somewhere, nowhere are vices taught according to the religion; and so the doctrine remains unimpaired, from which every reformation must be undertaken. If this is preserved in the Church and heard, as you yourself approve, what is the reason for rashly condemning our whole religion? But such men are wont, as soon as they have detected or seen some error or vice in someone, to immediately and insolently inveigh against the whole church and religion. So hardly in rebuking sins do we avoid sinning. The author indeed does not seem altogether bad, nor to sin so much from wickedness as from rashness; whatever he may be professing as an Evangelical, at least he has sent a message to Papacy; and if he wrote these things from zeal, I would have wished more knowledge to be present in him, and I would have wished more modesty for the author. I am speaking of Praetorius. Two things in particular seem to have moved him to scandal concerning the holy ministry: 1. the life of the ministers and preachers, not sufficiently upright and chastened, serious, nor answering to their profession or to the holiness which it demands. Even though they do not shrink from seeking favour of the great and of the magistrates by often bad arts, etc., p. 13. Then, that in the ministry they often study more doctrine (if indeed even this) than life, and are accustomed to dispute more than to teach and live, and the other vices which these men (for they are men, indeed [ἀνθρωπάρεσκοι] men-pleasers) are wont to have. 2. And this seems to have offended him too, that in the people and the church the fruit that could and should be expected does not correspond to his ministry. Hence it appears most evidently that it is a perpetual vice of these men, and the common paralogism of Aristarchs, that they wish and imagine for themselves a church without any scandal, and that neither in themselves nor in this life [ἐγκρατῆ ἀσθενῆ] is there such self-control as they would wish.
