The condition of the triumphant Church in the homeland is one thing, and of the Church on its way here is another, and smaller; the one present and common, the other what ought to be. Therefore, when we fight, with sound doctrine still, even ourselves against the vices of ministers, for the honour of the holy ministry and also of our own, and we labour with life and actions so that one lives worthily of so great a calling and office, even according to those things which these haughty men, and our author throughout the whole writing and in a most lengthy exhortation and admonition, teach, inculcate, threaten, etc., what remains, that they rail in general and in so crude and immodest a manner against religion itself, and proscribe, pursue and condemn both it and the Church most bitterly, and without any just distinction, insolently? For example, when we endeavour to attain, with some changes, those things which this author in book 4, part, p. 742 etc., commands us to do, those which chiefly concern sincere piety of life and the guidance of the Holy Spirit, what more is there that they should launch such books and insipid orations against us, with such proud and dire devotion, as great engines? Hence it would now be very easy, with the slightest correction, to run through the whole book and enervate it, if it seemed worth the effort: for nothing occurs in that whole tedious writing in which the author does not commit the paralogism observed in him, whether [ψευδο-συμβιβαστης] false conciliator or [ψευδο-ἐπιμελητης] false overseer. But let us return to the road from this digression, in which, however, not outside the olive-groves and the matter we have in hand, we have wandered in vain from the book Ad legem et testimonium.

units.la: Cæterum, & hoc denique ad sententiam quam impugnamus, cujusque cum aliorum jam pridem notatis erroribus atque heterodoxiis convenientiam ostendimus, dicendum, eam, quâ ex parte jubet in Ecclesiâ solum S. Scripturæ contextum absque expositionibus legi, haberique pro omni vel catechesi vel confessione, eandem esse doctrinam, quæ olim erat Arminianorum in ipso schismatis initio, quam egregiâ ευφωνία? venditabant primùm urgebantque, usque dum perspiciebant, nihili esse tale consilium, & in idea facilius fingi posse, quam in praxim deduci, ac probari. Isto enim pacto nec hæreses vel sectæ caventur aut imminuuntur, neque sententiæ in Religione diversæ coire aut consopiri ullo pacto possunt, neque etiam Ecclesia erigi, confirmari ac constitui certa; quæ nec agnosci potest, nisi ejus distincta super articulis religionis omnibus, an hoc, an illo sensu ex S. scripturâ deductis, atque intelligendis, (non enim absque tali intelligentia S. scriptura ullo in cœtu legi vel, tractari potest, vel accipi ab aliis, vel communicari) habeatur cognitio, & confessio. Adolphus Venator, inter Remonstrantes primipilus Anno 1617. librum edebat miro & superbo titulo: Theologia vera & mera lactantium & infantium in Christo. Liber fundamentis parvus, dilucidus ac universalis, per meras Scripturas V. & N. Testamenti. Sine præjudicio cujuscunque inter Christianos sectæ, & in usum cunctarum Ecclesiarum. Quæ Christianismus quidem per quatuordecim secula caruit, &c. Ohem! vino venditabili suspensa hedera. Neque tamen Auctor, utcumque hoc promittat & præ se ferat, sine præjudicio cujuscunque sectæ potuit illa meris & nudis Scripturæ verbis, citra allatam in alium sensum Sacræ scripturæ expositionem, absolvere, ac præstare: ecce enim in primis istius libri quæstionibus, quæstione nimirum quarta interrogat, an æternum gaudium futurum sit piis, & infernalis dolor malis? quod initio reclamabit Socinianus, nullam sensibilem pœnam vel dolorem improbis in inferno attribuens, non aliud illorum supplicium agnoscens, quàm æternam annihilationem, quâ non sint. Tum paullo post iterum: Suntne ergo infantes innoxii, eoque in statu constituti, in quo Adamus ante lapsum fuit? &c. responsionem autem affirmativam ponit verbis Dei apud Moisem, Deut. 1. 19. &c.
units.tr: Finally, and this bears on the view we are attacking, whose agreement with the errors and heterodoxies of others we have already pointed out, it must be said that the part of it which bids that in the Church only the text of Holy Scripture be read, without expositions, and be held as the whole of both catechism and confession, is the same doctrine the Arminians once held at the very beginning of the schism. They first flaunted it with a fine-sounding phrase [εὐφωνία] and pressed it, until they saw that such a plan was worthless and could be imagined more easily than put into practice and proved. For in this way heresies and sects are neither guarded against nor lessened, and divergent opinions in religion can never be brought together or lulled to rest. Nor can the Church be raised up, confirmed and established as certain, for it cannot be recognized unless there is a distinct knowledge and confession of its position on all the articles of religion, whether deduced from Holy Scripture in this sense or that and understood in this way (for without such understanding Holy Scripture cannot be read, handled, received from others or communicated in any assembly). Adolphus Venator, the foremost man among the Remonstrants, published in 1617 a book with a splendid and proud title: True and pure theology of babes and infants in Christ. A little book, clear and universal in its foundations, by the bare Scriptures of the Old and New Testament. Without prejudice to any sect among Christians, and for the use of all churches. Which Christianity indeed has lacked for fourteen centuries, etc. Oh! Ivy hung over wine for sale. Nor, however much the author promises this and makes a show of it, could he settle and achieve it "without prejudice to any sect" by the bare and naked words of Scripture, without an exposition of Holy Scripture carried into another sense. See, in the first questions of that book, the fourth question asks: Will there be eternal joy for the pious and infernal pain for the wicked? At the outset a Socinian will object to this, since he assigns no perceptible punishment or pain to the wicked in hell, and recognizes no other punishment for them than eternal annihilation, by which they cease to be. Then a little later again: Are infants therefore innocent, and placed in that state in which Adam was before the fall? etc., and he gives an affirmative answer in the words of God in Moses, Deut. 1. 19, etc.

units.la: An hoc est meris Scripturæ verbis agere, paraphrasim & expositionem eorum falsam palàm inculcare, contra scilicet reatum peccati originalis? Adeo impossibile est illâ methodo quid docere, vel explicare, præcipuè sine præjudicio cujuscunque in Christianismo religionis, vel sectæ, quod isti homines gloriari & promittere solent. Vel, quod idem Auctor, Venator sc. pag. docet, externam pedum ablutionem perpetui usus atque instituti inter Christianos debere esse, ex Ioan. XIII. 1. idque inter prima Christianæ religionis elementa atque fundamentalia; quomodo exmeris (quæso) Scripturis ostendet, vel hoc ille legens ex scriptura & quidem illo sensu intelligens, quomodo sine præjudicio alicujus in Christianismo sectæ audiri possit, velim mihi persuadeatur. Aut quod idem de septem donis Spiritus sancti, vel de novem beatitudinibus, ex divisione apud Papistas usitatâ habet, pag. 5. 31. Aut quod libros V.T. tantùm recenset pro veris & Canonicis illos, qui tales revera sunt, quomodo sine præjudicio Papistarum dixerit? vel sine præiudicio veritatis, hominem ex bonis operibus justificari? pag. 21. taliaque plura, quæ manifestò ostendunt, quam inane omne illud sit, quod tanto mangonio commendare hi solent ad tollenda & componenda schismata meris Scripturæ verbis, ac contextu, missis omnibus expositionibus, vel Inde deductis & formatis confessionibus. Quare etiam Remonstrantes, quamvis ejusmodi consilium illis non displicere initio præ se ferebant, sed & prædicabant; postea tamen vanitatem & falsitatem ejus magis edocti ad Confessiones nomine suorum coetuum edendas, & Apologias, & Catechismos se composuerunt. Indeque in Apologia pag. 5. Confessiones & confessionum formulas, quæ de articulis agunt inter Christianos controversis, distinctè concedunt alias quam meris scripturæ verbis confici posse; oppositè sc. ad ea, quæ præcisè ad salutem necessaria faria credendaque, ideo non aliis, quàm ineris Scriptura verbis proponi volunt: Concludendum certè est, Remonstrantes de formulis istis loqui, quæ versantur circa dogmata non præcisè creditu necessaria, quæque inter Christianos controversæ, ac proinde aliis, quam scripturæ patris verbis, concepta sunt.
units.tr: Is this what it means to work with the bare words of Scripture, to openly press a false paraphrase and exposition of them, namely against the guilt of original sin? So impossible is it to teach or explain anything by that method, especially without prejudice to any religion or sect in Christianity, which these men are wont to boast and promise. Or again, as the same author, Venator, teaches on the same page, the external washing of feet ought to be a perpetual practice and institution among Christians, from John 13:1, and this among the first and fundamental elements of the Christian religion. How, I ask, will he show this from the bare Scriptures? I would like to be persuaded how, when he reads this from Scripture, and understands it in that sense, it can be heard without prejudice to any sect in Christianity. Or what he says of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, or the nine beatitudes, from the division customary among the Papists, pp. 5, 31. Or how, without prejudice to the Papists, can he say that he counts as true and canonical only those books of the Old Testament which really are such? Or how, without prejudice to the truth, can he say that man is justified by good works? p. 21, and many other such things, which clearly show how empty is all that these men are wont to commend with such a show, namely to remove and settle schisms by the bare words and context of Scripture alone, with all expositions and confessions drawn and formed from them set aside. Therefore the Remonstrants too, although at first they showed that such a plan did not displease them, and even preached it, later, being more thoroughly taught its vanity and falsehood, set themselves to publish confessions, apologies and catechisms in the name of their congregations. And so in their Apology, p. 5, they clearly grant that confessions and formulas of confession, which deal with articles disputed among Christians, can be drawn up otherwise than in the bare words of Scripture. They want the things that are strictly necessary for salvation to be set forth in the bare words of Scripture, as opposed to those: It must certainly be concluded that the Remonstrants are speaking of those formulas which concern doctrines not strictly necessary to be believed, and which are disputed among Christians, and therefore were composed in other than the bare words of Scripture.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt contra illam sententiam, quam examinandam nobis propositimus atque discutiendam, argumenta: sequitur, ut etiam videamus Objectiones.
units.tr: These are the arguments against that opinion which we proposed to examine and discuss. It follows that we should also look at the objections.

units.la: Eæ autem, quas vel ipse Auctor, vel alius forte ex ejus libello moverit, huc potissimæ redeunt, ut prima sit de verbo, quod concionamur; altera, de modo quo concionamur, sc. nomine Dei; tertia, de exercitio Prophetico, loco concionum instituendo.
units.tr: Now the objections which the author himself, or perhaps someone else from his little book, has raised come down chiefly to these: the first concerns the thing which we preach; the second, the manner in which we preach, namely in the name of God; the third, the prophetic exercise to be set up in place of sermons.

units.la: I. Prima objectio, de nostris concionibus, vel verbo quod à Præconibus pro concione habetur, eo quod illud non est ὅλως infitè indubiè merèque verum, sive infallibiliter divinum, ideo neque vera, qualem Deus instituit, & probat vel (ut loquitur) Deus inchoari, continuarique voluit concio nostra, vel Ecclesia. Atque huc pleraque ejus tendunt. Resp. In formam redigamus hæc priùs, & sic facilior emerget solutio. Quæ concio non instituitur verbo concionatoris ὅλως infitè, indubiè, merèque vero, illa non est, qualem Deus probat; sed nostra concio talis non est: Ergò. Ad Majorem, illa negatur: probandum tibi, Deum jussisse ac instituisse, ut, post Apostolos fidei præcones infallibiles, semper continuaretur sacra in ecclesiis prædicatio non nisi per concionatores æquè cum Apostolis infallibiles, quorumque verbum semper omni ratione, & materialiter & formaliter, uti illud Apostolorum, esset infallibile; quum ipse Auctor agnoscat particularium Ecclesiarum ministros ab ipsis Apostolis institutos sallibiles fuisse, ac etiam revera aliquando errasse. Distingue ergò & hîc inter Præconcs primos, qui fundamenta & canonem constituerunt; & inter sequentes, quorum non erat Testamentum vel tabulas dictare & scribere, sed consignatum & traditum ipsis, genuinè & secundùm mentem priorum exponere. Quemadmodum id obtinet in politicis, atque ubivis, qui primùm leges condunt, eorum habetur auctoritas certa legum ferendarum, quæ tamen pôstea committuntur explicandæ non authenticis expositoribus, sed qui ad mentem & sententiam legumlatoris adstringuntur rectè exponendam, quamvis & errare possint, ac subinde errent. Vel ut in V. quoque Testamento, infallibili quidem authoritate leges condebat, vel potiùs tradebat, Deo edicente, Moses; sed illis semel constitutis, & in canonem relatis, non addidit Deus, ut solùm ab infallibilibus interpretarentur Doctoribus, sed quibuslibet hoc ex officio committebatur Sacerdotibus, qui fallere poterant & falli; sic quoque jam in Evangelio, ejusque concione sub N. Testamento, qui illud primò docerent, conscriberentque, spiritu infallibili agi necessum fuit, sed ut continuaretur doctrina illa concionum publica. eodem tali spiritus infallibilis ductu in omnibus perpetuò concionatoribus, hoc neque Deum voluisse probari potest, neque necessarium fuit Ecclesiis. 11. ad Minorem, quod in Ecclesiis nostris verbi divini conciones non fiunt verbo λόγος infallibili. distinguimus verbum quod exponitur, quod tractatur; & verbum quo exponitur. Verbum quod, est λόγος infallibile, Scriptura V. & N. T. ut ipse in libri sui titulo agnoscit in nostris Ecclesiis solam Veteris & Novi Testamenti Scripturam pro unico fidei & morum Canone haberi; sed verbum quo illud explicamus, ut jam duplicem habet respectum & relationem, vel ad ipsos concionatores, & personam, quæ loquitur, vel ad verbum Dei, ex quo loquitur: ita priori ratione est fallibile, posteriori verum, neutrâ λόγος infallibile, quale ipsum Dei verbum, quod explicatur: sed illud nequaquam obest sive verbo
units.tr: I. First objection. Concerning our sermons, or the word which is held to be a sermon by the heralds, on the ground that it is not wholly [ὅλως] infallible, indubitable and purely true, that is, infallibly divine, and therefore not the true kind which God established and approves, or (as he puts it) which God willed should be begun and continued as our sermon or Church. To this most of his points tend. Answer. Let us first reduce these to form, and so the solution will emerge more easily. A sermon which is not established by the word of the preacher wholly [ὅλως] infallible, indubitable and purely true, is not the kind which God approves; but our sermon is not such a one: therefore... To the major premise, that is denied. You must prove that God commanded and instituted that, after the Apostles, infallible heralds of the faith, sacred preaching should always be continued in the Churches only through preachers equally infallible with the Apostles, whose word should always in every respect, both materially and formally, be infallible just as the Apostles' word was; since the author himself acknowledges that the ministers of particular churches, appointed by the Apostles themselves, were fallible, and in fact sometimes did err. Therefore distinguish here too between the first heralds, who laid the foundations and constituted the canon, and the following ones, whose task was not to dictate and write the Testament or tables, but to expound faithfully and according to the mind of the first what had been entrusted and handed down to them. This holds in politics, and everywhere, for those who first enact laws: their authority to enact laws is certain, yet afterwards the laws are committed to be explained not to authentic expositors, but to men who are bound to expound rightly the mind and intention of the lawgiver, although they can err and sometimes do. Likewise in the Old Testament, Moses indeed enacted, or rather handed down, laws with infallible authority, God commanding; but once those laws were established and placed in the canon, God did not add that they should be interpreted only by infallible teachers; rather the priests, who could deceive and be deceived, were charged with this as their duty. So too in the Gospel and its preaching under the New Testament, those who first taught and wrote it had to act by an infallible Spirit, but so that this public teaching of the sermons should continue. Yet it cannot be shown that God willed, or that it was necessary for the Churches, that the same infallible guidance of the Spirit should be present in all preachers forever. Answer to the minor premise, that in our churches the sermons of the divine word are not given with an infallible word [λόγος]: we distinguish the word which is expounded or treated from the word by which it is expounded. The word which is expounded is the infallible [λόγος], the Scripture of the Old and New Testament, which the author himself acknowledges in the title of his book is held in our churches as the sole canon of faith and morals. But the word by which we expound it has a twofold respect and relation: either to the preachers themselves and the person who speaks, or to the word of God from which he speaks. In the former respect it is fallible, in the latter true; in neither respect is it an infallible [λόγος] like the word of God itself which is expounded. But this in no way stands in the way of the word being used to expound the word, or of the Church being built up by it, so that a sermon of the divine word is not judged holy, lawful, and necessary for the instruction of the Church.

units.la: 11. ad Minorem: deest. verbo explicando, sive Ecclesiae inde aedificandae, quo minus concio verbi divini talis aestimetur sacra, legitima, atque ad ecclesiae instructionem necessaria. Quamquam neutiquam in hoc argumento verbum Dei, & nostrum concionatorium, qua nostrum, sive potius qua a nobis ex Dei verbo eductum confirmatumque, opponenda sunt sed conjungenda. Verbum ergo concionis undiquaque verum est, videlicet ex sacro Dei verbo petitum, & fundamenti sui ratione, ut medii in argumentatione, infallibile, eoque nulla ratione carpendum vel contemnendum, multo minus pro apostatico deferendum. Deus omnes jussit veritatem tenere ac docere, non infallibiliter indubie, vel infallibilitatem, hoc enim non cadit sub officium; sed merum solius Dei donum est.
units.tr: II. To the minor premise: missing. Whether the Word is being explained, or the Church is being built up by it, the sermon of the divine Word is not thereby made less holy, lawful, or necessary for the instruction of the Church. Yet in this matter the Word of God and our preaching, insofar as it is ours, or rather insofar as it is drawn out and confirmed by us from the Word of God, are not to be set against each other but joined together. The preaching's word is therefore true in every respect, namely drawn from the holy Word of God, and, by the ground of its own authority, as the middle term in an argument, infallible. It is therefore in no way to be found fault with or despised, much less handed over as apostate. God commanded all to hold and teach the truth, not infallibly and beyond doubt, or infallibility itself, for that does not fall under the duty; it is a pure gift of God alone.

units.la: Quamvis verbi divini concio non foret omni ex parte vera, (quam tamen totam veram hic licet praesupponere, ipso Auctore doctrinam Ecclesiarum nostrarum non, quod sciam, saltem necdum oppugnante,) quamvis dico, non foret omnimodè vera, ut hoc facile potest evenire, errorem aliquem etiam & hic admixtu, ubi nihil humani a nobis alienum putamus, non tamen ideo omnis concio proscribenda, vel apostasiae condemnanda, nisi (quod excipio) non simplex error, sed talis sit, qui haeresim vel apostasiam continc: alioquin ex quolibet vel aliquo errore S. concionibus admixto omnem concionum efficaciam atque usum condemnare, error est gravissimus.
units.tr: Although a sermon of the divine Word might not be true in every part (which we may here presuppose as wholly true, since the Author himself, as far as I know, has not yet attacked the doctrine of our Churches), although I say it might not be wholly true, as can easily happen, and some error might also be admitted here, where we think nothing human is foreign to us, nevertheless every sermon is not therefore to be rejected or condemned as apostasy, unless (this I except) the error is not a simple one but such as contains heresy or apostasy. Otherwise, to condemn all the efficacy and use of sermons because of any error at all mixed into holy sermons would be a most serious error.

units.la: IV. Si nostra verbi divini concio minus aestimanda, vel tam gravi crimine apostasiae videlicet condemnanda, ideo quod non fit ὅλως infallibiliter, sed per praecones fallibiles; ergo & S. Scriptura, quā vulgo in versionibus utimur, eadem culpā involvetur, quia & illa per fallibiles interpretes in nostram aliamve linguam data non est ὅλως atque indubie infallibilis vel authentica, erot. cap. 1; sed errorem continere facile potest, saepiusque plures habet. Vide de hoc argumento Cl. D. Marefium de ipsa & honore menta & canonem constituerunt; & inter sequentes, quorum non erat Testamentum vel tabulas dictare & scribere, sed consignatum & traditum ipsis, genuinè & secundum mentem priorum exponere. Quemadmodum id obtinet in politicis, atque ubivis, qui primùm leges condunt, eorum habetur auctoritas certa legum ferendarum, quæ tamen posteà committuntur explicandæ non authenticis expositoribus, sed qui ad mentem & sententiam legumlatoris adstringuntur rectè exponendam, quamvis & errare possint, ac subinde errent. Vel ut in V. quoque Testamento, infallibili quidem authoritate leges condebat, vel potius tradebat, Deo edicente, Moses; sed illis semel constitutis, & in canonem relatis, non addidit Deus, ut solum ab infallibilibus interpretarentur Doctoribus, sed quibuslibet hoc ex officio committebatur Sacerdotibus, qui fallere poterant & falli; sic quoque jam in Evangelio, ejusque concione sub N. Testamento, qui illud primò docerent, conscriberentque, spiritu infallibili agi necessum fuit, sed ut continuaretur doctrina illa concionum publica. eodem tali spiritus infallibilis ductu in omnibus perpetuò concionatoribus, hoc neque Deum voluisse probari potest, neque necessarium fuit Ecclesiis. II. ad Minorem, quod in Ecclesiis nostris verbi divini conciones non fiunt verbo θεος infallibili distinguimus verbum quod exponitur, quod tractatur; & verbum quo exponitur. Verbum quod, est θεος infallibile, Scriptura V. & N. T. ut ipse in libri sui titulo agnoscit in nostris Ecclesiis solam Veteris & Novi Testamenti Scripturam pro unico fidei & morum Canone haberi; sed verbum quo illud explicamus, ut jam duplicem habet respectum & relationem, vel ad ipsos concionatores, & personam, quæ loquitur, vel ad verbum Dei, ex quo loquitur: ita priori ratione est fallibile, posteriori verum, neutra θεος infallibile, quale ipsum Dei verbum, quod explicatur: sed illud nequaquam obest sive verbo explicando, sive Ecclesiae inde aedificandae, quo minus concio verbi divini talis aestimetur sacra, legitima, atque ad ecclesiae instructionem necessaria. Quamquam neutiquam in hoc argumento verbum Dei, & nostrum concionatorium, qua nostrum, sive potius qua a nobis ex Dei verbo eductum confirmatumque, opponenda sunt sed conjungenda. Verbum ergo concionis undiquaque verum est, videlicet ex sacro Dei verbo petitum, & fundamenti sui ratione, ut medii in argumentatione, infallibile, eoque nulla ratione carpendum vel contemnendum, multo minus pro apostatico deferendum. Deus omnes jussit veritatem tenere ac docere, non infallibiliter indubie, vel infallibilitatem, hoc enim non cadit sub officium; sed merum solius Dei donum est.
units.tr: IV. If our sermon of the divine Word is to be valued less, or condemned with so grave a charge as apostasy, because it is not wholly infallible but delivered through fallible heralds, then the holy Scripture, which we commonly use in translations, will be involved in the same fault, since that too, given through fallible interpreters into our or another language, is not wholly and indubitably infallible or authentic, as was said in chapter 1. Yet it can easily contain error, and often contains several. On this matter see the illustrious Mr. Maresius, on the ministry, that is, who established the canon and the Church's tradition...; and among those who followed, who were not the ones to dictate and write the tables of the Testament, but to expound faithfully and according to the mind of the first, what had been handed over and entrusted to them. This holds in politics too, and everywhere: those who first make laws have a certain authority for enacting laws, yet these are afterwards entrusted for explanation not to authentic expositors but to those bound to expound rightly the mind and intention of the lawgiver, although they can err, and sometimes do err. Or as also in the Old Testament, Moses, indeed by infallible authority, enacted, or rather handed on, laws at God's command; yet once these had been established and placed in the canon, God did not add that they were to be interpreted only by infallible teachers, but this duty was committed to any priests whatever, who could deceive and be deceived. So too in the Gospel and its preaching under the New Testament, those who first taught it and wrote it down had to be moved by an infallible Spirit, but so that this public teaching of sermons might be continued. That every preacher should be continually led by the same infallible Spirit, this cannot be shown to be God's will, nor was it necessary for the Churches. [Second] minor premise: in our Churches sermons of the divine Word are not made infallible. We distinguish the word which is explained, which is treated, from the word by which it is explained. The word which is explained, is the infallible divine word, Scripture of the Old and New Testament, as he himself acknowledges in the title of his book; in our Churches only the Scripture of the Old and New Testament is held as the sole canon of faith and morals. But the word by which we explain it, since it has a twofold respect and relation, either to the preachers themselves and the person who speaks, or to the Word of God from which it speaks, is fallible in the former respect and true in the latter, and neither is infallible, as the divine Word itself is, which is explained. Yet this in no way hinders, either the explaining of the word or the building up of the Church from it, that a sermon of the divine Word should be judged holy, lawful, and necessary for the instruction of the Church. Yet in this matter the Word of God and our preaching, insofar as it is ours, or rather insofar as it is drawn out and confirmed by us from the Word of God, are not to be set against each other but joined together. The preaching's word is therefore true in every respect, namely drawn from the holy Word of God, and, by the ground of its own authority, as the middle term in an argument, infallible; it is therefore in no way to be found fault with or despised, much less handed over as apostate. God commanded all to hold and teach the truth, not infallibly and beyond doubt, or infallibility itself, for that does not fall under the duty; it is a pure gift of God alone.

Maresium de usu & honores. ministerii, &c. pag. 14. 22. 23. 28. ubi sentientes, non esse adeo elumbem ac futilem viri istius differtationem contra Auctorem nostrum, ac quidem in Monito suo ridiculè dixit, & duntaxat dicere satis habuit.
units.tr: IV. If our sermon of the divine Word is to be valued less, or condemned with so grave a charge as apostasy, because it is not wholly infallible (ὅλως) but delivered through fallible heralds, then the holy Scripture, which we commonly use in translations, will be involved in the same fault, since that too, given through fallible interpreters into our or another language, is not wholly and indubitably infallible or authentic, as was said in chapter 11; yet it can easily contain error, and often contains several. On this matter see the illustrious Mr. Maresius, on the use and honour of the ministry, etc., pp. 14, 22, 23, 28, where those who think otherwise, that the treatise of that man against our Author is not so feeble and trifling, have said so ridiculously in his Monitum, and were content merely to say so.

units.la: 11. Secunda objectio. At inquies, non hoc adeò ab ipso in Concionibus nostris impugnari, eæ quod habentur à præconibus non infallibilibus; ac quidem, quod tamen nomine Dei, ejusque authoritate habentur, sive Dei loco & tamquam pro Deo legatione fungentes.
units.tr: II. Second objection. But you will say that this is not so much what he attacks in our sermons, namely that they are given by heralds who are not infallible; indeed, that they are given in the name of God, and by his authority, acting in God's place and as an ambassador on behalf of God.

units.la: 2 Cor. 5. 20. Resp. 1. Dei nomine agi ac dici aliquid potest, quamvis non isthâc singulari ratione, Dei loco & persona, atque eâ authoritate: puta, quod Dei mandato & jussu, ejus peculiari ope ac auxilio, & in honorem ac cultum ejus agitur; hoc pacto si conciones habeantur, ut sanè vix negari potest, ecquis tum dubitet dicere, nomine Dei illas haberi? & has esse istius locutionis nomine Dei explicationes ac sensus quoque. supra à nobis ex S. scripturâ ostensum. Quare ergo, non simpliciter negabimus, nomine Dei conciones fieri, illo sensu, quamvis dici æque non possit eas agi loco & authoritate legata à Deo? 11. Jussu & mandato Dei si habentur conciones, habentur etiam authoritate Dei, authoritate nimirum jubentis & mandati; licet illustrior ac major sit authoritas legati, ubi persona insuper jubentis ac legantis sustinetur: prior tamen agendi modu ex mero mandato, non destituitur suâ authoritate; ex Dei autem mandato conciones haberi, prolixè probatum à D. Maresio, quæ diligenter primùm examinanda & confutanda, non inani quo Monito respuenda, si quid hîc refragari Auctori nostro alubescat. 111. Qui Dei loco & authoritate agunt, nullos agere nisi infallibiles ideóque, sint, probandum fuerat: ideo enim negat nos Dei nomine concionari, quia in concionibus errare possumus: proba ergo illum qui Dei nomine, sive loco & authoritate & ex ejus legato gatione agit, hinc non posse falli. Non negamus, aliquos eorum qui Dei nomine agunt esse infallibiles; sed hoc non inde habent, quod Dei nomine agunt, sed quod Dei nomine sic, & infallibiliter ex peculiari gratia & ordine agunt. Scilicet duplex ministrorum, a Deo missorum & legatorum ordo est, primus, supremus, extraordinarius, immediatus Doctorum infallibilium, quales Prophetae ac Apostoli Ephes. II. 20. Secundus inferior, communis & mediatus per Ecclesiae vocationem a Deo ordo est ministrorum & Doctorum non-infallibilium. Ephes. IV. 11, 12. Rom. XII. 6, 7, 8. [illegible, ~30 letters] 1 Cor. XII. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. vide locum. & conf. XI. illi errare nequeunt, non quod Dei nomine, loco & authoritate loquuntur, quod suo modo utrisque commune est, sed quod istius ordinis sunt, atque dono infallibilitatis peculiariter praediti: hi quidem errare possunt, utut ex officio, Dei nomine loquentes, & fallibiliter.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5. 20. Reply 1. Something can be said and done in the name of God, though not in that singular way, in God's place and person, and with that authority: for instance, because it is done by God's command and order, with his special help and aid, and for his honour and worship. If sermons are given in this way, as can hardly be denied, who would then doubt saying that they are given in God's name? And these are also the explanations and senses of that phrase in the name of God which we have shown above from Holy Scripture. Why then should we not simply deny that sermons are given in God's name, in that sense, although it cannot equally be said that they are done in the place and authority of an envoy sent by God? II. If sermons are given by God's command and mandate, they are also given by God's authority, namely the authority of one who commands and of the mandate; although the authority of an envoy is more illustrious and greater, where the person of the one who commands and sends is further sustained. Yet the former mode of acting, from mere mandate, is not deprived of its own authority; that sermons are given by God's mandate has been argued at length by Mr. Maresius, and these arguments should first be carefully examined and refuted, not rejected with an empty Monitum, if anything here should be disputed by our Author. III. Those who act in God's place and authority, it had to be proved that none act except infallible persons: for he denies that we preach in God's name because we can err in sermons; prove therefore that the one who acts in God's name, or in place and authority and by the commission of him, cannot err for this reason. We do not deny that some of those who act in God's name are infallible; but they do not have this from acting in God's name, but because they act in God's name in this way, and infallibly, by special grace and order. For there is a twofold order of ministers sent and commissioned by God: the first, supreme, extraordinary, immediate, of infallible teachers, such as the prophets and apostles (Eph. 2. 20). The second, inferior, common and mediate, is the order of ministers and teachers who are not infallible, through the calling of the Church by God (Eph. 4. 11, 12; Rom. 12. 6, 7, 8; 1 Cor. 12. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; see the passage, and compare chapter 11). The former cannot err, not because they speak in God's name, in place and authority, which is common to both, but because they belong to that order and are peculiarly endowed with the gift of infallibility; the latter indeed can err, although, speaking in God's name from their office, they speak fallibly.

units.la: Neque hoc quod quis simpliciter nomine alterius agit loquiturque, facit ne erret: ut legatus Principis, nomen & personam Domini refert, sed quousque se gerit ex mandato, a quo etiam potest deviare: sic ministri in Ecclesia, Dei nomen personamque repraesentant, dum ex officio docent, quamvis propius, significantius & illustrius illi, qui primi atque immediati ordinis sunt, [illegible, ~12 letters] & Dei locum propius referunt, omnes tamen, etiam communes ordinariique ministri, Dei nomine censentur agere, & authoritate, nimirum quando & quousque juxta commissam sibi instructionem ex tabulis loquuntur, neque evangelizant praeter Evangelium, & id quod ad praedicandum acceperunt, Gal. I. 8, 9. Sic quicunque agit alterius nomine, censetur ex cujus nomine agere, quamdiu sequitur datam fidem, a qua potest & deficere. Duo in mundo status sunt, atque hominum ordines, politicus, & Ecclesiasticus, utrique, & qui Rempublicam regunt Magistratus ὑπερέχοντες, & qui Ecclesiam ministri, Dei nomine agunt, intellige, ex officio; quamvis & in opere ab officio, & praescriptâ sibi à Deo formulâ abire possunt, & authoritate sibi à Deo datâ abuti. Est ubique authoritas, & authoritas regiminis; sed ibi regiminis dominantis ἐξουσία ὑπερέχοντος. hîc ministrantis. Utraque etiam nomine Dei, sed non nomine Dei ex officio, non semper in opere & exercitio: de iure semper, non item de facto: nisi in aliquibus, ordinis primi & infallibiliter actis, qui & ex officio, & in exercitio; de iure & de facto semper Dei nomine egerunt. IV. Υπὲρ Χριστοῦ ἀμβασσευομεν, ὡς τοῦ Θεοῦ παρακαλοῦντος δι' ἡμῶν. Δεόμεθα ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ. Καταλλάγητε τῷ Θεῷ. 11 Cor. v. 20. locus est, ex quo nostrer perpetuò suam de Dei nomine, loco, authoritate, & tanquam legatione pro eo fungendo, interpretationem mutuatur: sed quid ibi est, quò minùs omnes πρεσβευταὶ, qui πρεσβεύουσι & παρακαλοῦσι, & hortantur homines ad salutem ac reconciliationem cum Deo, quales semper in Ecclesiâ esse si probatum velis, adi Marcium, hoc enim ex professo agit, neque mei hic est actum agere, quid est dico, quare illi πρεσβευταὶ, πάντες γὰρ λόγῳ τῆς διακονίας, pro Christo ergo, ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πρεσβεύομεν, &c. Dei nomine non possint loqui, puta ubi eandem certissimam veritatem premunt, docentque, reconciliemini Deo, vel ut Auctor. 11.40. servemini ab hac perversâ generatione? &c. Ipse Auctor erat. x 1. particularium Ecclesiarum ministris, qui etiam ex ejus sententiâ errare possunt, & errant saepè, erat. x11. adscribit huncce locum 11 Cor. v.20. quo idcirco confirmamus nostram responsionem, talem agendi modum vel authoritatem Dei nomine, & pro Deo legatione fungende, non arguere infallibilem debere semper ejus esse qui sic loquitur, doctrinam. v. Sit, peccetur in eo à nobis, quod nomine sive authoritate Dei conciones nostras habemus: an negari potest, si non hoc sensu, Dei nomine habentur, quo ille vult. alio tamen admitti posse? eo nempe, quem ex sacris antea dedimus, ut jussu, auxilio, & in honorem ac cultum Dei habeantur? & an non hoc quoque authoritatem aliquam, talem nempe quam diximus, secum fert? quid ergo est, de quo tantopere exæstuet, & fluctus moveat in simpulo, quod dicunt, eam ob causam, quòd concionesnostræ à nobis fiunt Dei nomine? vel pone etiam, nullâ ratione dici posse, concionesDei nomine à nobis haberi, & in toto illo formali à nobis peccari; hocne omnem concionum materiam & usum ideo tollit, ecclesias dicit apostaticas, & quid non? tu audias illas, & accipias quo nomine placuerit, vel etiam alius eas habeat non tanto authoritatis gradu; & sic omnia emendata ex sensu tuo habueris, & citra schisma: sanè nusquam videbis hujusce rei factum articulum fidei vel fundamentalem; neque etiam tu ex ullo S. scripturæ testimonio ostendes (quod debebas tamen) hanc Dei nomine concionandi rationem esse illegitimam, nosque haud decere. VI. Tantum abest, ut ideo sugiendæ videantur conciones, quod Dei nomine habentur, ut non aliter haberi debeant, vi universalis regulæ, Col. III. 17. Et omne, quodcunque feceritis, sive verbo, sive opere, omnia in nomine Domini Iesu, gratias agentes Deo & Patri per ipsum. omnia vult fieri in nomine Christi. בשם יהוה II Thess. III. 6. Annunciamus vobis, fratres, in nomine Domini nostri Iesu Christi, subducere vos ab omni fratre inordinate ambulante, & non secundum traditionem, quam accepit a nobis. Quotiescunque idem monendum venit aliis similli in casu, quidni liceat ad hoc nomine Christi uti? VII. etiam coetus omnes ecclesiastici & συναγωγαὶ in nomine Dei ac Christi habentur, ac frequentantur, Matth. XVIII. 20. ubi enim duo vel tres sunt congregati εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα, in meum nomen, ibi sum in medio illorum. VIII. Quo, cujus nomine vestra colligitur ecclesia, habenturque mutuæ in coetibus vestris parænesES? non Dei nomine? quo ergo? necesse est, si non Dei nomine, ergo tuo proprio, ita hæc demum sunt opposita. Ioan. v. 43. Ego veni in nomine Patris mei, & non recepistis me: si alius venerit in nomine proprio, illum recipietis. Vides, illud quod non Dei nomine fit, proprio censeri agi? Quod idem est cum illa interrogatione super baptismo Iohannis, an ex cœlo, an ex hominibus? Matth. xxi. 25. quod non ex cœlo & Dei nomine habetur; ex hominibus esse putatur, & nomine fieri proprio. ix. Non sunt opposita, sed subordinata, nomine Dei quid fieri, & nomine Ecclesiæ; adeò non divellenda illa sunt vel opponenda, sed conjungenda, & conciones Dei nomine, & vocatione à Deo per Ecclesiam acceptâ fiunt, alioque respectu ad Ecclesiam: imò quod nomine Ecclesiæ vere & rite fit, non nisi Dei quoque nomine fieri æstimandum est.
units.tr: Nor does the mere fact that someone speaks and acts simply in another's name keep him from error. A prince's envoy bears the name and person of his lord, but only so far as he acts on the commission from which he may also depart. So too the ministers in the Church represent the name and person of God when they teach in their office. Although those of the first and immediate order represent God's place more closely, more clearly and more conspicuously, [illegible, ~12 letters], all ministers, including the common and ordinary ministers, are still considered to act in God's name and with his authority. That is so, of course, when and so far as they speak according to the instruction committed to them from the tables, and do not preach beyond the Gospel or beyond what they have received to preach (Gal. 1:8, 9). So whoever acts in another's name is considered to act in the name of the one whose name he bears, as long as he keeps the pledged faith, from which he is still able to fall away. In the world there are two states and two orders of men, the civil and the ecclesiastical. Both have their own: the magistrates who rule the commonwealth, who are ὑπερέχοντες [hyperechontes, "those in authority"], and the ministers who serve the Church and act in God's name, that is, in their office. Yet both can depart in their work from their office and from the form prescribed to them by God, and abuse the authority given them by God. There is everywhere authority, and an authority of government; but there it is the government of a ruler who lords it over, ἐξουσία ὑπερέχοντος [exousia hyperechontos], and here it is that of one who serves. Both act also in God's name, but not in God's name by office always, nor always in the work and exercise of it. They do so always by right, but not always in fact; except in certain men of the first order, who act infallibly, and who act in God's name both by office and in exercise, both by right and in fact, always. IV. "We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us. We pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God" (2 Cor. 5:20). Υπὲρ Χριστοῦ ἀμβασσευομεν, ὡς τοῦ Θεοῦ παρακαλοῦντος δι' ἡμῶν. Δεόμεθα ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ. Καταλλάγητε τῷ Θεῷ. This is the passage from which our side constantly borrows its own interpretation of acting in God's name, in God's place, with God's authority, and as discharging the function of an ambassador on his behalf. But what is there to prevent all the πρεσβευταὶ [presbeutai, envoys], who act as ambassadors and beseech and exhort men to salvation and reconciliation with God (and if you wish to see that such men are always in the Church, consult Marcius, for he treats this ex professo, and it is not my task here to do the work), what is there, I ask, to prevent them from speaking in God's name? For they are all πρεσβευταὶ, πάντες γὰρ λόγῳ τῆς διακονίας [pantes gar logō tēs diakonias, "all, for the word of the ministry"], and they serve ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ πρεσβεύομεν [hyper Christou presbeuomen, "we are ambassadors for Christ"], etc. Can they not do so, for instance, when they press the most certain truth and teach, be reconciled to God, or as the author says on 11:40, be saved from this perverse generation? The author himself was a minister of particular churches, who, by his own opinion, can err and often do err. He ascribes this passage, 2 Cor. 5:20, to himself as well. We therefore use it to confirm our answer: that such a manner of acting, or such authority, in God's name and in the office of God's ambassador, does not require that the doctrine of the one who so speaks must always be infallible. V. Let it be granted that we sin in this, that we hold our sermons in the name or by the authority of God. Can it be denied that, if they are not held in God's name in the sense he wishes, they can nevertheless be admitted in another sense, namely the one we gave earlier from Scripture, that they are held by command, with help, and to the honour and worship of God? And does this not also carry with it some authority of the kind we have described? What then is the matter about which they make such a fuss and stir up a tempest in a teacup, as they say? Is it because our sermons are made in God's name? Grant even that it cannot be said in any way that sermons are held by us in God's name, and that we sin in all that formal side: does that do away with the whole substance and use of sermons, and call the churches apostate, and whatever else they say? Hear them, and receive them in whatever name you please, or let another hold them with a lesser degree of authority; so you will have everything reformed according to your own sense, and without schism. Certainly you will nowhere see an article of faith, or a fundamental one, made of this matter. Nor will you show from any testimony of Holy Scripture (though you ought to) that this way of preaching in God's name is illegitimate and unbecoming to us. VI. So far is it from being the case that sermons should be avoided because they are held in God's name, that they ought not to be held otherwise, by virtue of the universal rule of Col. 3:17: "And whatsoever ye do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him." He wills that all things be done in the name of Christ. בשם יהוה [bashem YHWH, "in the name of the LORD"]. 2 Thess. 3:6: "We command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us." Whenever the same admonition is needed in a similar case, why should it not be permitted to use the name of Christ for this? VII. Also all ecclesiastical assemblies and συναγωγαὶ [synagōgai] are held and frequented in the name of God and of Christ: "For where two or three are gathered together εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα [eis to emon onoma], in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Matt. 18:20). VIII. In whose name is your church gathered, and in whose assemblies are mutual exhortations held? Not in God's name? In whose then? It must be that if not in God's name, then in your own; so these are finally opposed. John 5:43: "I am come in my Father's name, and ye receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him ye will receive." Do you see that what is not done in God's name is considered to be done in one's own? That is the same as the question about the baptism of John: "Was it from heaven, or of men?" (Matt. 21:25), that is, what is not held from heaven and in God's name is thought to be from men, and done in one's own name. IX. These are not opposed but subordinate: to be done in God's name and to be done in the name of the Church. So those things should not be torn apart or set against each other, but joined: sermons are made both in God's name, and by a calling received from God through the Church, and with respect to the Church in another regard. Indeed, what is truly and duly done in the name of the Church must be judged to be done also in the name of God.

units.la: Neque est quod ad nostra leviter respondeat, ut sæpe isti solent, distinctionibus nos in vanum uti, se nullas agnoscere, plane agendum, &c. Resp. Tum demum plane agi, disputarique, quando accuratè distinguitur, alioqui non philosophia solum, sed Theologia etiam, quin & S. scriptura reprehendenda similiter foret, quæ crebras adhibet distinctiones: atque ipse noster Auctor non semel, ubi verbum tam operose distinguit, ὁ λόγος infinitè indubiè, merèque verum, quid nisi distinctiones tum facit? & erot. cx. ac cxiv. quando addit, quæ tales, annon sollicitè satis distinguit?
units.tr: Nor is there any ground for their light reply to our arguments, as they often do, that we use distinctions in vain, since they acknowledge none, and that we should simply proceed. Answer: the matter is simply proceeded with and disputed only when distinctions are drawn with care. Otherwise, not only philosophy but theology too, and indeed Holy Scripture itself, would have to be censured in the same way, since it uses frequent distinctions. And our author himself, not once, when he distinguishes the word so laboriously, the ὁ λόγος [ho logos, "the Word"], infinite, undoubted and purely true, what else does he do but make distinctions then? And when he adds, in the 150th and 114th questions, "which are such," does he not distinguish carefully enough?

units.la: III. Objectio, ex usu exercitii Prophetici peti potest, quod hactenus urget Adversarius, ut loco concionum nostrarum substitui velit, quo non, ut in nostris Ecclesiis solet, solis Pastoribus loqui concessum, sed omni etiam populo, ex 1 Cor. xiv. vide de hoc erot. cl iv. & clvi ii. Resp. paulo altius hæc res repetenda venit, & ob difficultates nonnullas, quæ in hunc de prophetiæ usu locum 1 Cor. xiv. præterquam à Commentatoribus, moventur etiam à Brownistis, Anabaptistis, & Socinianis, diligentius expendenda. Quæratur ergo primum, quid vox prophetiæ, tie, & prophetare apud Apostolum significet? 11. de facto, quomodo & q. inam ibi prophetarint, vel quo pacto id in illa Ecclesia observatum fuerit? verf. 3. ὁ δὲ προφητεύων, ἀνθρώποις λαλεῖ οἰκοδομὴν καὶ παράκλησιν καὶ παραμυθίαν. 31. Δύνασθε γὰρ καθ' ἕνα πάντες προφητεύειν,
units.tr: III. An objection can be drawn from the use of the prophetic exercise, which the Adversary so far presses, wanting it substituted for our sermons, in which speaking is granted not only to the pastors, as is customary in our churches, but to the whole people as well, from 1 Cor. 14. On this see questions 154 and 282. Answer: this matter must be traced somewhat higher, and, because of certain difficulties which are raised about this passage on the use of prophecy, 1 Cor. 14, not only by the commentators but also by the Brownists, Anabaptists and Socinians, it must be weighed more carefully. Let us ask first, then, what the words prophecy, to prophesy, mean in the Apostle? 11. In fact, how and in what manner they prophesied there, or how that was observed in that Church? Vers. 3: "But he that prophesieth speaketh unto men to edification, and exhortation, and comfort." Vers. 31: "For ye may all prophesy one by one."

units.la: Ad primum. 1. Aliqui, prophetare hic explicant, usu & significatione qua strictè illud sumi solet, propredicere futura: quod facilè refellitur tum ex eo, quod inter Prophetarum horum, quæ sæpius hoc capite repetuntur, munia, semper omittitur futurorum prædictio: non omittenda, siquidem ea intellecta Apostolo fuisset. Tum ex verf. 24. si omnes prophetent, intret vero infidelis aut idiota, &c. adde verf. 29, 31, 32, 34, 35, 36. 11. Alii explicant per interpretari linguas, ut in hoc capite illa opponi perpetuò & conferri solent, linguis loqui, & prophetare; sed arctior illa expositio est quam ut satis sit iis, quæ de prophetiâ hic dicuntur. 111. Alii, de cogitationum cordis occultarum manifestatione, ex verf. 25. nimis etiam arctè. Existimo, per prophetiam significari doctrinam, tractationem, explanationem sacrorum in cœtibus Ecclesiasticis, ad mutuam ædificationem & consolationem instituram, ex S. scriptura, sive alias de articulo aliquo & mysterio religionis. probatur ex verf. 3. 24.31.35. 37. adde 1 Cor. xi. 4. & xii. 8, 10. & xiii. 2, si habuero prophetiam, & novero omnia mysteria, & omnem scientiam. Rom. xii. 6. Ephes. iv. 11. 1 Thess. v. 20.,
units.tr: On the first question. (1) Some explain prophesying here in the sense in which the word is strictly usually taken, namely foretelling future events. This is easily refuted: first, because in the lists of the prophets' functions that are repeated several times in this chapter, the foretelling of the future is always left out, though it would not have been omitted had the Apostle meant it. Second, from verse 24, "if all prophesy, and there come in one that is unbelieving, or unlearned, etc." Add verses 29, 31, 32, 34, 35, 36. (2) Others explain it as interpreting tongues, since in this chapter these are regularly set against each other and compared, "speaking in tongues" and "prophesying." But that explanation is too narrow to suffice for what is said here about prophecy. (3) Others take it as the manifestation of the hidden thoughts of the heart, from verse 25, but this too is far too narrow. I judge that by prophecy is meant the teaching, the treatment and explanation of the sacred things in ecclesiastical assemblies, instituted for mutual edification and consolation, whether from Holy Scripture or otherwise concerning some article or mystery of religion. This is proved from verses 3, 24, 31, 35, 37. Add 1 Cor. 11:4, 12:8, 10, and 13:2: "if I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries, and all knowledge." Also Rom. 12:6, Eph. 4:11, 1 Thess. 5:20.

units.la: 1. Paral. xxv. 2. Ambrosius, vel quicunque Auctor sub ejus nomine commentariorum in epist. Pauli, in hunc locum; quia enim unus atque idem spiritus est, qui tam Prophetis futura dicentibus, quam his qui revelant Scripturas, infundit se pro ratione & qualitate causarum, &c. Sic ergò interpretationem Scripturarum ille hic intelligit: atque ita Hieronymus, qui doctrinam dicit, Primasius, Calvinus, aliique.
units.tr: 1 Par. 25:2. Ambrose, or whoever the author was of the commentaries on the Epistles of Paul published under his name, on this passage: "For since it is one and the same Spirit who pours himself into the prophets who foretell future things, and into those who reveal the Scriptures, he does so according to the measure and nature of the causes, etc." So he understands prophecy here as the interpretation of the Scriptures. Jerome likewise, who speaks of teaching, and Primasius, Calvin, and others.

units.la: Sed majoris difficultatis est, explicare quorum fuerit sic prophetare, & quomodo peragi soleret. I. An hoc ex officio, Ecclesiae istius Pastores, ac ministri ordinati intelligantur egisse? ut multi sentiunt, II. An aliqui ex singulari & extraordinario Spiritus S. charismate? III. An vero fuerit exercitium sacrum commune, in quo ex Ecclesia quilibet, modo ad id idonei, se vicissim [illegible, ~3 letters] exercuerint ad mutuam instructionem & aedificationem? In quo nihil obest, sicut in ordinarium quoque ministerium, ministrosque extraordinaria quae copia spiritus aliquando cecidit, prout illa tempora maximam Spiritus S. in personas quaslibet & officia ubertatem effusionemque ferebant, etiam singulare quod Spiritus S. charisma quandoque intercurrisse, ut tamen exercitium fuerit commune & ordinarium. Papistici interpretes hoc fere solent explicare de illis, qui non nisi ex peculiari afflatu Spiritus & charismate prophetarunt, ac proinde omne extraordinarium fuisse: nimisque insolenter Franciscus Haraeus explicationem, de iis qui obscura Prophetarum & S. scripturae explanarent, communiter Neotericis quibusdam attribuit, atque satis leviter contemnit. Non hoc de mere extraordinario & singulari quo Spiritus S. charismate intelligendum esse, videtur ostendere 1. quod Apostolus hosce Prophetas non reprehendit modo [illegible, ~3 letters], sed eorum doctrinam etiam examini aliorum subjicit, verf. 29. 32. quod non facturus videtur, siquidem illorum doctrina ex mera, immediata, singulari, atque extraordinaria Spiritus S. revelatione, ut id in Prophetis, fluxisset. Praeterquam quod vix videtur, tot Prophetas in una Ecclesia fuisse, quod hic fuisse colligi potest. Neque etiam illiusmodi Prophetis exprobraturus videtur Apostolus fuisse, quot verf. 36. vel as a vobis sermo Dei profectus? Nec denique ab hoc charismate tam sollicite excepisset mulieres, verf. 34. quum alias Prophetissae fuerint Mirjam, Anna, Luc. 11. 36, &c. Quare non de illo prophetandi extraordinario spiritus situs afflatu hanc prophetiam intelligendam esse, hinc patere puto; ut & illud quoque, non videri ista de officio Ministrorum & Pastorum Ecclesiae Vel etiam explicari potest, quod Apostolus cap. xi. quidem loquatur de muliere prophetante, sed quod ideò id non approbet; verùm hactenus satis habeat illum morem pravum in mulieribus castigare, quod ἀκατακαλύπτῳ τῇ κεφαλῇ sacris interessent, de eo enim ex professo agit; sed quod prophetarent insuper, illud servaverit in suum locum, hunc nempe, ubi prophetiis regulam ac modum praescribit, atque ita hic in mulieribus aperte reprehendat, quod antea transierat, nempe quod etiam tentarent loqui publicè, & ἀσφαλῶς [?]. De eadem prophetiâ debet intelligi 1 Thess. v, 20, 21, 22. Spiritum ne extinguite. Prophetias ne vilipendite. Omnia probate, & bonum retinete. 1 Cor. xii. 8. Huic quidem per spiritum datur sermo sapientiae, &c. vers. 10. alteri vero prophetia. Neque forte male hinc explicueris illud 1 Tim. i. 18. ταύτην τὴν παραγγελίαν παρατίθεμαί σοι, τέκνον, κατὰ τὰς προαγούσας ἐπὶ σὲ προφητείας, ἵνα στρατεύῃ ἐν αὐταῖς τὴν καλὴν στρατείαν. Etiam apud Hebraeos in ipsorum sacris usitata fuit prophetia; hinc filii, & collegia Prophetarum, ex quibus Ecclesiarum ministri seligebantur. Quodque propius accedit, in historiâ Euangelicâ & Apostolicâ legimus, Christum Apostolosque Synagogam saepius ingressos, sermonem habuisse, contulisse, disputasse; an putemus Judaeorum Doctores cathedram suam illis concessisse, nec potius tali in exercitio Prophetico haec acta & habita fuisse? ut quod Christum Parentes tandem repererunt in templo sedentem inter Doctores, & audientem ipsos, & interrogantem ipsos, quando omnes admirabantur eius scientiam & responsiones. Luc. ii. 46. Et c. iv. 16. Atque venit in Nazareth, ubi erat educatus: atque intrabat pro more suo, die Sabbati Synagogam; atque surrexit legere. Et dabatur ei liber Esaiae prophetae: librumque aperiens, invenit locum, ubi scriptum, &c. Act. xiii. 14, 15, 16. & intrantes Synagogam die Sabbati, assederunt. Post autem lectionem legis & prophetarum, mitte-bant. bant archisynagogæ ad illos, dicentes: Viri fratres, si quidem est sermo admonitionis apud vos ad populum, loquimini. Assurgens verò Paulus, & movens manu, dixit, &c. De Apollo, Act. xviii. 24, 25, 26. potens in scripturis. Ille erat edoctus κατηχημένος viam Domini: & fervens spiritu, loquebatur & docebat accuratè ea quæ de Domino, noscens tantùm baptismum Iohannis. Hic autem incipiebat παρρησιάζεσθαι in Synagogâ, Atque ex veteri Judæorum in Synagogis more sumta illa de prophetiâ esse, quæ Apostolus ad Corinthios docet, sentiunt interpretes. Hinc commentarius Ambrosii, hæc traditio Synagogæ est, inquit, quam nos vult sectari, quia Christianus quidem scribit, sed ex gentibus factis, non ex Judæis; ut sedentes disputent seniores dignitate in cathedris, sequentes in subselliis, novissimi in pavimento super mattas. Quibus si revelatum fuerit, dandum locum dicendi præcipit, nec despiciendos, quia membra corporis sunt. Ne de Bezâ nostro, ac Petro Martyre dicam, utrisque illam prophetandi morem ex Judæorum Synagogâ petentibus, & explicantibus. Et in Ecclesiâ Christianâ illud viguit saltem in Catechizationibus. Quin ipse Apostolus hoc capite catechismum appellat, vers. 19. sed in ecclesiâ malo quinque verba mente mea λόγῳ & νοΐ μυ loqui, ἵνα καὶ ἄλλους κατηχήσω, ut & alios catechizem, quam mille verba in linguâ: nam toto hoc capite opponi ab Apostolo linguam, & prophetiam, nemo non videt. De Veterum catechizationibus diximus, ubi de Catechizat. & hinc assumti sæpe, quibus concessum publicè concionari. Vide Niceph. Callisth. hist. Eccles. lib. v. cap. xiv. Pro excitio prophetico, quale in Veteri ecclesiâ fuit, ubi commodè haberi potest, non contemnendo, vide Amesium lib. iv. Cas. consc. cap. xxvi. In Harmoniâ Confessionum Belgicarum, (ut sententiam istam etiam authoritate Ecclesiasticâ confirmem,) cap. v. de prophetiâ, ex Synodis Vvestalien si, & Emdanâ, sic constitutum legitur. In omnibus Ecclesiis sive nascentibus, sive vetustis, Prophetiae ordo ex Pauli instituto observetur. II. Ad hoc collegium cooptentur, non modo Ministri, sed etiam Doctores ac ex Senioribus & Diaconis, atque adeo ex ipsa plebe, si qui sint qui donum suum a Domino acceptum in communem Ecclesiae utilitatem conferre velint: ita tamen, ut prius Ministrorum atque aliorum probentur judicio. III. In hoc Collegio ad aedificationem omnium liber aliquis Scripturarum rato ordine explicetur. Ubi autem is, cujus erunt partes, vices suas expleverit, licebit iis qui subselliis eam insequuntur, siquidem visum erit, adjicere quod ad aedificationem pertineat: Ac tum demum, concepta oratione, abeo, cujus erunt partes, actus claudatur. Adde in eandem rem, proque eodem S. exercitio, Synodi Leidensis A. 1629. art. XXXIV. ad explicationem scilicet XXXI artic. Synodi Delphensis. Atque ita in variis Ecclesiis tale exercitium saepe viguit: in Genevensi, tempore Calvini, quando eo Bolsecus itabat, turbasque dabat impudentes. In Londinensi Belgica, Antverpiensi, Dordracena, & sicubi alias. Catechetica quidem (quorum varii gradus & classes) ubivis sedulo retinentur, quorum instar, sed ordinis supremi illa sunt prophetica. Brownistas quod attinet, ii pro exercitio prophetico multi sunt. In Confessione edita A. 1596, atque A. 1598. Anglice, Latinéque, Belgice etiam A. 1612. art. XXXIV. sic loquuntur: Qui ad scripturas interpretandas donis a Deo instructi sunt, ii in coetu Aggelonem seu exercitio Prophetico approbati, studioque sacrarum literarum & doctrinae incumbentes, possunt & debent (ecclesia consentiente & postulantes) pro proportione fidei prophetare, verbumque Dei ad aedificationem, exhortationem & consolationem Ecclesiae explicare: usque dum populo praeparato Deus vires concesserit donis & facultate instructos ad munera ea capessenda, quae Christus publico Ecclesiae ministerio destinavit. Caeterum administratio Sacramentorum nulla sit absque Pastoribus, aut Doctoribus, ad munus suum electis & ordinatis. Eandem habent bent[?] in secundâ petitione, Regi Iacobo oblatâ, quam inseruerunt suæ contra Doctores Oxonienses Apologiæ. Atque Johannes Robinsonus, vir eximius, (de quo alibi diximus, nempe ubi de Brownistis,) in apologiâ, nuperrimè iterum anno 1644. recusâ. cap. VIII. de exercitio Prophetico. Similiter ex eâdem disciplinâ qui scripsit Anglicè, & breviter, A Guide unto Sion. pag. 30. 31. Non omnibus, sed perpaucis tantùm inter suos concedunt prophetare, uni aliquando alterique, pro statu & conditione Ecclesiarum; sed in eo peccant, quod hisce attribuunt, quod Ministris solis licet, Evangelium universim prædicare; uti in Thessalonicensibus contra Oxonienses thes. IV.: probi, fideles, atque idonei viri (quamvis ii necdum in officio ministerii) possunt Evangelium prædicare, & universam veritatem Dei. Quod in illis miror, quum alias vocationem ad ministerium in Ecclesiâ obeundum necessariam etiam docent, Confess. art. XXI. & thesi contra Oxonienses sexta; neque etiam sacramenta administrare illis concedunt, ut supra audivimus. Sed quod singulis prædicare concedunt, & publica coram toto Ecclesiæ coetu divina tractare, in iis maximè castigant ipsorum Antagonistæ, Samuel Rutherfurd in lib. Anglic. pro regimine Eccles. Scotic. contra arg. Robinsoni. Richard. Bernardus, adversus Ainsworthum, pag. 182. quibus addendus Guilj. Apollonius, in Consider. Controv. Anglic. cap. V. qu. III.
units.tr: But it is a matter of greater difficulty to explain who used to prophesy in this way, and how it was carried out. (I) Did those who are understood to have done so act by virtue of their office, namely the ordained pastors and ministers of this Church, as many think? (II) Or were they some who prophesied by a singular and extraordinary gift of the Holy Spirit? (III) Or was it rather a common sacred exercise, in which any members of the Church, provided they were fit for it, took their turns to exercise themselves for mutual instruction and edification? Nothing stands in the way of this last view, just as the ordinary ministry and the ministers were not excluded from the extraordinary abundance of the Spirit which at times fell upon them. Those times brought a very great outpouring and abundance of the Holy Spirit upon persons and offices of every kind, so that a particular gift of the Holy Spirit may sometimes have intervened, while the exercise itself remained common and ordinary. The Papist interpreters usually explain this of those who prophesied only by a peculiar inspiration and gift of the Spirit, and so take it that the whole thing was extraordinary. Francis Harès too rashly assigns the explanation, that it refers to those who expounded the obscure passages of the Prophets and of Holy Scripture, to certain moderns in general, and he scorns it rather lightly. That this must not be understood of a purely extraordinary and singular gift of the Holy Spirit, I think is shown, first, by the fact that the Apostle not only rebukes these prophets, but also submits their teaching to the judgement of others (vers. 29, 32). He would not do this if their teaching had flowed from a pure, immediate, singular and extraordinary revelation of the Holy Spirit, such as belonged to the prophets. Besides, it hardly seems likely that there were so many prophets in one Church, which is what this passage suggests. Nor does the Apostle seem likely to have reproached such prophets with the words of verse 36, Or did the word of God go out from you? Nor finally would he have been so careful to exclude women from this gift (verse 34), since there were other prophetesses, such as Miriam and Anna (Luke 2:36, etc.). Hence I think it is clear that this prophecy is not to be understood of that extraordinary inspiration of prophesying; and also that these things do not seem to belong to the ordinary office of the ministers and pastors of the Church, namely to be done in the congregation, out of honour, or reverence, for the congregation. Or it may also be explained that the Apostle, in chapter 11, indeed speaks of a woman prophesying, but does not for that reason approve it; rather, he is content for the time being to rebuke the bad custom of women who attended the sacred assemblies with uncovered heads (ἀκατακαλύπτῳ τῇ κεφαλῇ). For he treats of that matter expressly there; but as to their prophesying as well, he has kept that for its proper place, namely here, where he prescribes the rule and manner of prophesying. And so here he openly rebukes in the women what he had passed over earlier, namely that they tried to speak publicly and securely (ἀσφαλῶς [?]). The same prophecy must be understood in 1 Thessalonians 5:20–22: Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophesyings. Test all things, and hold fast what is good. And 1 Corinthians 12:8: To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, etc., and verse 10: to another prophecy. Perhaps one may also explain 1 Timothy 1:18 well from this: ταύτην τὴν παραγγελίαν παρατίθεμαί σοι, τέκνον, κατὰ τὰς προαγούσας ἐπὶ σὲ προφητείας, ἵνα στρατεύῃ ἐν αὐταῖς τὴν καλὴν στρατείαν [This charge I commit to you, child, in accordance with the prophecies made earlier about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight]. Prophesying was also customary among the Hebrews in their own sacred assemblies; hence there were sons and companies of prophets, from whom the ministers of the Churches were chosen. And what comes closer still: in the evangelical and apostolic history we read that Christ and the Apostles often entered the synagogue, spoke, conferred and disputed there. Are we to think that the teachers of the Jews gave up their chair to them, and that these things were not rather done and held in such a prophetic exercise? So too Christ's parents at last found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions, when all who heard him were amazed at his understanding and his answers (Luke 2:46). And Luke 4:16: And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up; and he went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, as was his custom, and stood up to read. And there was handed to him the book of the prophet Isaiah; and he opened the book and found the place where it was written, etc. And Acts 13:14–16: And going into the synagogue on the Sabbath day, they sat down. After the reading of the law and the prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them, saying: Brethren, if you have any word of exhortation for the people, speak. Then Paul rose, and motioned with his hand, and said, etc. Of Apollos, Acts 18:24–26: mighty in the Scriptures. He had been instructed (κατηχημένος) in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John. And he began to speak boldly (παρρησιάζεσθαι) in the synagogue. The interpreters agree that the prophesying which the Apostle teaches to the Corinthians was taken from the old custom of the Jews in their synagogues. Hence the commentary of Ambrose: This is the tradition of the synagogue, he says, which we are bidden to follow, because the Christian writes, but as one made from the Gentiles, not from the Jews; so that the elders, eminent in dignity, sit and dispute in the chairs, the following sit on the benches, and the last stand on the floor upon mats. If any revelation is made to these, he commands that place be given to the speaker, and that they not be despised, because they are members of the body. I say nothing of our Beza and Peter Martyr, both of whom derived and explained that manner of prophesying from the synagogue of the Jews. And in the Christian Church it flourished at least in the catechizings. Indeed the Apostle himself calls this chapter a catechism (verse 19): but in the Church I would rather speak five words with my mind (λόγῳ and νοΐ μου), so that I may also instruct others (ἵνα καὶ ἄλλους κατηχήσω), than ten thousand words in a tongue. For no one fails to see that throughout this chapter the Apostle sets tongue against prophecy. I have spoken of the catechizings of the ancients where I treated of catechizing, and from there those often taken up who were allowed to preach publicly. See Nicephorus Callistus, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 14. For the prophetic exercise, such as existed in the ancient Church, which can conveniently be had there, and not to be despised, see Amesius, Cases of Conscience, book 4, chapter 26. In the Harmony of the Belgic Confessions (so that I may confirm this opinion also by ecclesiastical authority), chapter 5, on prophesying, the following is laid down from the synods of Westphalia and Emden: In all Churches, whether newly founded or long established, the order of prophesying shall be observed according to the institution of Paul. II. To this college let there be co-opted not only ministers, but also teachers, and from among the elders and deacons, and indeed from the people itself, if there are any who wish to contribute to the common benefit of the Church the gift they have received from the Lord; yet only so that they are first approved by the judgement of the ministers and others. III. In this college, for the edification of all, some book of the Scriptures is to be expounded in due order. When he whose part it is has fulfilled his turn, those who follow in the benches may, if it seems fit to them, add whatever pertains to edification. And then at last, when a prayer has been offered, the action is closed by him whose part it was. Add, on the same matter and for the same sacred exercise, the Synod of Leiden of 1629, article 34, namely as an explanation of article 31 of the Synod of Delft. And so in various Churches such an exercise often flourished: in Geneva, in Calvin's time, when Bolsec went there and caused disturbances with his shameless behaviour; in the English Dutch Church (Londinensis Belgica), at Antwerp, at Dort, and wherever else. The catechetical exercises (which have various grades and classes) are everywhere diligently retained, and the prophetic ones are, as it were, the model of their highest order. As for the Brownists, there are many among them who favour a prophetic exercise. In the Confession published in 1596 and again in 1598, in English and Latin, and in Dutch also in 1612, article 34, they speak thus: Those who have been equipped by God with gifts for interpreting the Scriptures, if they have been approved in the assembly, as in the prophetic exercise, and devote themselves to the study of sacred letters and doctrine, may and ought (with the consent and at the request of the Church) to prophesy according to the measure of faith, and to expound the word of God for the edification, exhortation and consolation of the Church, until God, the people being prepared, grants strength to those equipped with gifts and ability to take up those offices which Christ has appointed for the public ministry of the Church. Otherwise, the administration of the sacraments shall be carried out by no one without pastors or teachers chosen and ordained for that office. They have the same in the second petition offered to King James, which they inserted into their apology against the Oxford teachers. And John Robinson, an eminent man (of whom we have spoken elsewhere, namely where we treated of the Brownists), in his apology, reprinted most recently again in 1644, chapter 8, on the prophetic exercise. Similarly, the one who wrote briefly in English from the same discipline, A Guide unto Sion, pages 30–31. They allow prophesying not to all, but only to a very few among their own people, to one or another at times, according to the state and condition of the Churches. But they err in this, that they grant to these men what they allow to ministers alone, namely to preach the gospel in general; so in their Thessalonian theses against the Oxford men, thesis 4: upright, faithful and fit men (although they are not yet in the office of the ministry) can preach the gospel and the whole truth of God. This I wonder at in them, since elsewhere they also teach that a call to the ministry is necessary for the office in the Church (Confession, article 21, and in their sixth thesis against the Oxford men). Nor do they grant such men to administer the sacraments, as we heard above. But that they allow each to preach and to handle divine matters in public before the whole assembly of the Church is what their opponents chiefly rebuke: Samuel Rutherford in his English book on the government of the Scottish Church, against Robinson's argument; Richard Bernard, against Ainsworth, page 182; to whom we should add William Apollonius, in Consideratio Controversiae Anglicae, chapter 5, question 3.

units.la: Ergò ut ad nostrum accedam, atque objectioni propositæ respondeam, nego, dato exercitio Prophetico, vel tolli necessitatem vocationis ad ministerium in Ecclesiâ obeundum, quod Socinian i inde cupiunt; vel tolli usum concionum, quod & Anabaptistæ initio urgebant, ut patet ex Apologiâ Anabaptistarum, editâ & refutatâ à Bullingero; tum ex ejus lib. III. cap. adversus Anabapt. In apologiâ quidem ipsi primam causam, quare ad conciones nostras non accedant, dant, quod Reformati non servant Christianum ordinem, quem Evangelium seu verbum Dei docet 1 Cor. 14. nempe ut unus ductor ex officio Christianae charitatis (si quid illi ad aedificationem revelatum fuerit) possit loqui in Ecclesia, et interim alter taceat. quod ipsissimum nostri jam homines sequuntur in coetu suo conniventiae. Quasi vero haec quando observantur, ut in Catecheticis fere solet fieri, tollatur ratio concionandi, qualem observant nostrae Ecclesiae, ac semper etiam usurparunt Christianae. Synodi VI in Trullo habitae cap. lx iv. habet, quod non oportet laicos publicè disputare vel docere, docendi auctoritatem ex se sibi vendicantem, sed ordine a Domino tradito cedere, et autem iis qui docendi gratiam acceperunt, aperire, et divina ab eis doceri, &c. Atque ad conciones quod attinet, earumque usum, non obstante exercitio Prophetico, Chrysostomus in hunc locum 1 Cor. xiv. homilie suae [illegible, ~12 letters], sive applicationem facit ad Auditores ea ipsa de re, ut sedulo sc. conciones sacras frequentent atque attendant. &c. qui propior Apostolorum aevo fuit, Iustinus Martyr, ordinem usumque S. concionum, S. coenae, cantionumque in Ecclesia haberi solitarum, describit in Apologia secunda ad Imp. Antoninum Pium, circa finem, [illegible, ~40 letters], &c. Ne Tertulliani locum, ex cujus Apologia, de sui temporis concionibus, vel Plinii ad Trajanum, lib. x. epist. xcvii. adferam, de quibus in Disp. nostra, de Concionibus Veterum: vel si malis, quem postea nacti super hoc argumento Auctorem sumus, Franciscum Bernardinum vide, de ritu sacrarum Eccles. Catholi. concionum.
units.tr: Therefore, to come to my own point and answer the objection raised, I deny that, even granting a prophetic exercise, the necessity of a calling to the ministry in the Church is abolished, which the Socinians desire to infer from it, or that the use of sermons is abolished, which the Anabaptists also urged at first, as is clear from the Apology of the Anabaptists, published and refuted by Bullinger, and from his book III, chapter on the Anabaptists. In that Apology they give as the first reason why they do not attend our sermons that the Reformed do not keep the Christian order which the Gospel or the Word of God teaches (1 Cor. 14), namely that one leader, out of the duty of Christian love, may speak in the Church if anything has been revealed to him for edification, while another keeps silent. Our own people now follow exactly this practice in their meetings of connivance. As if, when this order is observed, as is usually done in the catechetical lessons, the practice of preaching which our Churches observe and Christians have always used would thereby be abolished. The Sixth Synod, held in Trullo, canon 64, says that laymen ought not to speak or teach in public, claiming the authority of teaching for themselves, but should yield in the order handed down by the Lord, and open the divine things to those who have received the grace of teaching, and be taught by them, etc. As for sermons and their use, notwithstanding the prophetic exercise, Chrysostom, in his homily on this passage, 1 Cor. 14, applies it to the hearers on this very matter, that they should diligently attend and listen to the holy sermons, etc. Justin Martyr, who was nearer the age of the Apostles, describes the order and custom of holy sermons, the holy Supper, and the singing usually held in the Church, in his Second Apology to the Emperor Antoninus Pius, near the end, etc. I shall not cite Tertullian's passage, from his Apology, about the sermons of his own time, or Pliny's letter to Trajan, book X, letter 97, about which we speak in our disputation On the Sermons of the Ancients. Or, if you prefer, see Francesco Bernardino, On the Rite of the Sacred Sermons of the Catholic Church, the author we later found on this subject.

units.la: ANTEPOTHΣEIΣ.
units.tr: Preliminary Remarks [ἀντιπρόθεσις]

units.la: Quod quidam è Philosophis (referente Tullio, IV. Academ.) & ii quidem non mediocres, contra Academicos disputaturi censebant,
units.tr: As some of the philosophers (as Cicero reports in the fourth book of the Academica, and not undistinguished ones) held when they were about to dispute against the Academics,

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] non esse ullam rationem disputare cum iis, qui nihil probarent: id mihi quoque impræsentiarum haud semel perpendendum særiò fuit, in certamen invitato cum Adversario, qui non aliter ac si ex Veteri Academiâ prodiisset, in ipsius religionis sacratissimo negotio non nisi interrogare didicit, ac dubitare: an videlicet, seriò cum eo disputandum mihi esset.
