Erotemata posuit, & quid obsecro, præter erotemata? ut magis ridendum sit, quæ sua illa Thetica putet, præter erotemata, ad quæ in Monito provocat, ejusque (sic loquitur) libelli videlicet sui, vel Thetica refutent, atque ad Erotematica respondeant. Bone vir, primum illa libelli Thetica ab Erotematicis distinctius ostendenda secernendaque à te fuerant, quum totum scriptum nihil aliud videatur esse, quam ut ipse in ejus frontispicio exponis, erotematica propositio, &c. & nulla ferè propositio aliter incipiat, quam à si, si. Verùm quid, quorsum illæ quæstiones, vel potius obErrationes? ita plerumque idem atque idem in iis redit, atque eadem reciprocatur terra. Legeras forte in Talmude, vel Mischnâ, כל המרכה כנריקיח הר quisquis in inquisitionibus multus est, laudem meretur; sed tamen de filio Zacchæi, (forte Rabbi Iohanan is, Hillelis discipulus,) quod additur, qui in ficuum pediculos inquisierit, credo nec ipse es probaturus. Adeò & vitio verti quoque potest, nimium si quæras, vel certa & dubia si labefactare studeas quæstiunculis & hæsitationibus, ac subruere. In Scholis disputari solet, an solùm ille sit hæreticus, qui errorem pertinaciter tenet contra articulum fidei necessarium; an verò non etiam ille, qui dubitat, sive qui in dubium trahit certissima & fundamentalia? vide Melch. Canum loc. Theolog. lib. xi. cap. vi ii. Et Greg. Valent. qu. xi. part. i. dub. ii. Atque qui positivam dubitationem habet, ac pertinaciter fovet contra illos articulos, judicans ambiguos aut incertos esse, de quibus ambigendum neutiquam sit, cum ab hæresi non immunem pronunciat communis sententia. In jure Canonico est: Dubius in fide, infidelis est. Compendio Becanum adi, Theol. scholast. Tom. III. cap. XIV. Sed haec de ἀπιστίᾳ & dubitatione, ἀπαθείᾳ quae affectata, in negotio religionis, atque articulorum fidei etiam discussa à Theologis nostris sunt adversus Remonstrantes, in illorum praefationem, ad Confess. & Apologiam. Verbo dicendo, vel illa, de quibus ambigendum nos haud putamus, vera censes, vel non; ut, exempli causa, quae de Deo, ejus immutabilitate, simplicitate, &c. S. Trinitate, Christo θεανθρώπῳ; vel etiam de Ecclesiâ, ejusque perennitate, S. ministerio, Sacramentis, &c. si vera, ergò dum dubitare de illis ut ambiguis doces, annon veritatem illorum clam sive palam eversum is, saltem elevatum? nam quorsum haec de cunctis dubitandi Pyrrhonica Methodus, eò periculosior; quo sacra tractamus, quae non ὡς ἐπιστήμην & ἀνθρώπων ἀπὸ τῆς μεθόδου ἢ πλάνης, sed cum omni certitudine, πληροφορίας, & ὡς ἐν πίστει βεβαίου recipi volunt, ac doceri. Augustinus, ad Honoratum suum, à Manichaeorum erroribus eum dehortaturus, lib. de utilitate credendi, cap. ult. sic loquitur: Nam istos verbosos & miseros, quid enim aliud, nisi dixerim, penitus desere, qui dum nimis quaerunt unde sit malum, nihil reperiunt, nisi malum; in quâ quaestione saepe Auditores erigunt ad quaerendum. Sed ea docent excitatos, ut vel dormire semper satius sit, quam illo modo evigilare; de lethargicis enim phreneticos faciunt. Sed nos relictâ Auctoritate hac quaerendi, dubitandique ratione ἀπορίᾳ, quae ζητήσεως παρέχει μηδὲν ἀνάγκῃ ἀμφιβολίας ... necesse habuimus nostro, quocum hactenus nobis res, ἀντιπαραopponere, non de fidei quaerentes, nedum ambigentes veritate ullâ, sed in mentem ac sententiam Adversarii inquirentes, ut protrahatur, & quid animi sibi sit in hisce erotematis, sectâ, & quae molitur porrò: ut hinc orbi certius constent, eoque magis caveantur.
units.tr: [illegible] that there is no point in disputing with those who prove nothing. This, too, I have at present had to weigh more than once in earnest, now that I have been invited into a contest with an adversary who, as though he had come forth from the Old Academy, has learned in the most sacred matter of religion to do nothing but question and doubt. I had to consider whether I was really to dispute seriously with him at all. He has set out questions. And what, I ask you, besides questions? So it is more laughable that he thinks his own so-called "Theses" are something apart from questions, to which he appeals in his Monitum: "his little book," as he puts it, "either refutes the Theses or answers the Questions." Good man, you should first have shown clearly and distinguished your Theses from your Questions, since the whole writing seems to be nothing but what you yourself declare on its title page, "a questioning proposition," and hardly any proposition begins otherwise than with "if, if." But what is the point of these questions, or rather of these wanderings? In them the same thing keeps coming back again and again, and the same ground is traversed over and over. Perhaps you have read in the Talmud or the Mishnah: כל המרבה בחקירות זה נמצא נחשב כנריקיח הר "Whoever multiplies inquiries deserves praise," but I believe you will not approve of what is added about the son of Zakkai (perhaps Rabbi Johanan, the disciple of Hillel), that he inquired about the stalks of figs. So too it can be held against a man if he asks too much, or if he strives to shake and undermine what is certain and what is doubtful with little questions and hesitations. In the schools it is commonly disputed whether only he is a heretic who obstinately holds an error against a necessary article of faith, or whether he too is one who doubts, or who calls into doubt the most certain and fundamental things. See Melchior Cano, Theological Places, book XI, chapter 6 and 8; and Gregory of Valencia, question 11, part 1, doubt 2. Moreover, one who holds a positive doubt and obstinately cherishes it against those articles, judging them ambiguous or uncertain, which must by no means be doubted, is pronounced by the common opinion not free from heresy. In canon law it is said: "He who doubts in the faith is an unbeliever." Consult Becanus in compendium, Scholastic Theology, vol. III, chapter 14. But these matters concerning unbelief [ἀπιστία] and doubt, and feigned apathy [ἀπάθεια] in the business of religion and even the articles of faith, have been discussed by our Theologians against the Remonstrants, in their preface to the Confession and the Apology. In short, whether you think true those things which we do not think should be doubted, for example what is said about God, his immutability, simplicity, etc., the Holy Trinity, Christ the God-man [θεάνθρωπος], or also about the Church and its perpetuity, the holy ministry, the sacraments, etc.: if they are true, then while you teach us to doubt them as ambiguous, do you not overthrow or at least undermine their truth, secretly or openly? For what is the purpose of this Pyrrhonian method of doubting everything, the more dangerous the more we handle sacred matters, which they wish to be received and taught not as knowledge [ἐπιστήμη] of men derived from method or error, but with all certainty, full assurance [πληροφορία], and as "firm in faith" [ἐν πίστει βεβαίου]. Augustine, dissuading his friend Honoratus from the errors of the Manichaeans, in the book On the Usefulness of Belief, last chapter, speaks thus: "Those wordy and wretched men, I would say nothing else than: desert them completely, who while they seek too much where evil comes from, find nothing but evil; in which question they often rouse their hearers to seek. But they teach things which, once aroused, it would be better always to sleep than to wake in that way; for they make the lethargic into madmen." But we, leaving aside this manner of inquiring and doubting, which is a perplexity [ἀπορία] that gives rise to inquiry without any necessity of doubt, have thought it necessary to set against our adversary, with whom we have dealt so far, not questions of the faith, still less any doubt about truth, but questions about the mind and opinion of the adversary, so that it may be drawn out, and so that it may be known what he really intends in these questions, his sect, and what he plans further: that thus the world may know more certainly and be the more on its guard.

units.la: Quo teneam vultus mutantem Protea nodo. Neque is ægrè tulerit quæstiones alias sibi referri, easque de suâ ipsius sententiâ, qui omnes Ecclesias suis erotematicis nequicquam erubuit provocare. Quæro jam igitur ipse. I. An sola vera Ecclesia (ex ipsius sensu) fuerit, quæ cum Apostolis, ac Evangelistis, quousque ii infallibiliter nomine Dei, ejus verbum docuerunt, fuit? II. An alii præter Apostolos, & Evangelistas, infallibiliter quoque Dei nomine docuerint? III. An satis ex honore Christi, Ecclesiæque Christianæ sit, si non diutiùs dicatur Ecclesia fuisse vera, quàm cum Apostolis, Doctoribus infallibilibus; vel quando statuitur, ecclesiam Christianam ab ævo Apostolorum usque fuisse formaliter apostaticam? IV. An alicui in culpam adscribi possit, quod nonisit ex ordine & numero Doctorum in Ecclesiâ infallibilium? vel, quod non habeat donum, ac gratiam infallibilitatis? V. Quid si sciviset Ecclesia Christiana à primo istius emententiæ apostasiæ initio, id est, ab ævo Apostolico usque, se apostaticam esse, (quod tamen hactenus toto illo tempore ignoravit,) quid, inquam, factura fuisset, vel etiam facere debuisset, aut imò potuisset, quum tanto illo tempore Deus non concederet Doctores Ecclesiæ, suo nomine infallibiliter docentes, neque Ecclesiæ veram faciem restitueret? VI. Annon vel id solùm satis præjudicet illi sententiæ, quod statuit, tanto temporum intervallo, ac tot seculis in Christianismo ignoratam omnibus Christianis fuisse illam totius Christianismi apostasiam? VII. Quomodo definienda sit apostasia? VIII. An & quomodo salvati Christiani sub istâ pertinaci scilicet apostasiâ? IX. An in Ecclesiâ, vel Christianismo hactenus apostatico, omnes & singuli fuerint apostatæ? X. Quid de Martyribus sentiat, vel ex ejus sententiâ quid dicendum sit de iis, qui vel à Gentilibus, Arianis, Papistis, aliisque, pro Ecclesiâ & veritate martyrium perpessi constantissimè fuerunt? XI. Quis, quæ tempora Antichristi, vel apostasiae Antichristianae? xi. An doctrina & Confessio Ecclesiarum Reformatarum videatur vera? xiii. An Socinianismum ipse abominetur? xiv. An Papismum? xv. Anabaptismum? xvi. Remonstrantismum? xvii. Quinam ei sint & quot articuli religionis & fidei fundamentales? xviii. An quae controversia inter Christianos sunt, vel controverti possunt, ideo incerta sint, nec fundamentalia? xix. An inter omnes in Christianismo sectas instituendus sit syncretismus, & unio Ecclesiastica? xx. An communionem Ecclesiasticam velit colere cum Socinianis, Papistis, Remonstrantibus, Anabaptistis? xxi. An quaelibet & contrariae opiniones, quae videntur probari velle ex S. scripturâ, sine discrimine ad mitti possint, ac defendi? xxii. An recipiat Symbolum, quod Apostolicum dicitur? xxiii. Quid sit haeresis? xxiv. Quid schisma? xxv. An Ecclesia ejus, quam se jactat erigere, Comitientia, vera sit? xxvi. An non, quod alium coetum instituit, eo crimen schismatis incurrat? xxvii. Annon exspectandum fuisset cum erectione alterius Ecclesiae, ex sententia libelli sui, usque dum responsum atque examen libelli serió & quo decet modo ac ordine ursisset, atque accepisset prius? xxviii. Quando illi jam monstrabuntur errores sui ac peccata in suo libro, atque coetu novo instituendo commissa, quo pacto redempturus sit damnum orbi, Ecclesiae, reipublicae, turbatis atque eversis, quae ipsum secutae, animis omnino illatum? xxix. Annon verendum, cum, quamvis monstratis melioribus, pervicaciam oppositurum, & [illegible, ~10 letters] non cessurum? xxx. Quando in coetu suo pro & contra de articulis fidei & ipse quidem disputat, & [illegible, ~12 letters], annon egregium se constituat [illegible, ~8 letters]? auditoresque sic dimissi prorsus conturbentur? xxxi. An necessariam aestimet ad ministerium docendi in Ecclesia vocationem? & qualem? xxxii. Quam ipse ad haec agenda, colligendamque novam Ecclesiam, habeat. & à quo, vocationem? xxxi. Quando in suo coetu, ubi quibusvis licet quâcunque de re & articulo disputare, opponere, vera falsaque, vel nequit satisfieri interroganti ac opponenti, vel inter opponentes non potest convenire, ac pertinaciter nolunt cedere, denique in apertas ac meras contentiones prorumpunt, quid tum consilii in isthoc coetu, vel quis inde fructus? xxxiv. Annon putet ex suo coetu schismata posse enasci? xxxv. An nulla, vel quae in coetu retineat sacramenta? xxxvi. An nullam disciplinam Ecclesiasticam?
units.tr: Lest I hold Proteus changing his face with a knot. Nor will he take it amiss if other questions are referred to him, and questions about his own opinion, he who has in vain been ashamed to challenge all the Churches with his questions. So now I ask. I. Was there, in his own sense, only one true Church, that which existed with the Apostles and Evangelists, as long as they taught infallibly in God's name, God's word? II. Did others, besides the Apostles and Evangelists, also teach infallibly in God's name? III. Is it enough for the honor of Christ and the Christian Church if it is said that the Church was true no longer than while the Apostles and infallible teachers were there; or when it is maintained that the Christian Church from the age of the Apostles onward was formally apostate? IV. Can anyone be blamed for not being of the order and number of teachers who are infallible in the Church? Or for not having the gift and grace of infallibility? V. What if the Christian Church had known from the first beginning of that apostasy, that is from the Apostolic age onward, that it was apostate (which, however, it has so far been ignorant of throughout all that time), what, I ask, would it have done, or even ought to have done, or indeed could have done, since during all that time God did not grant teachers of the Church who taught infallibly in his name, nor restore the true face of the Church? VI. Does it not at least by itself sufficiently prejudice that opinion, which holds that over such a great interval of time, and over so many centuries, that total apostasy of Christianity was unknown to all Christians? VII. How is apostasy to be defined? VIII. Are Christians saved under that obstinate apostasy, and if so how? IX. In a Church or Christianity hitherto apostate, were all and each apostates? X. What does he think of the martyrs, or what, according to his opinion, is to be said of those who suffered martyrdom most steadfastly for the Church and the truth, whether at the hands of the Gentiles, Arians, Papists, or others? XI. Who [are] the times of Antichrist, or of the Antichristian apostasy? XII. Does the doctrine and Confession of the Reformed Churches seem true to him? XIII. Does he himself abhor Socinianism? XIV. Papism? XV. Anabaptism? XVI. Remonstrantism? XVII. Who are, and how many, the fundamental articles of religion and faith? XVIII. Are the matters of controversy among Christians, or those that can be contested, for that reason uncertain and not fundamental? XIX. Should a syncretism and ecclesiastical union be instituted among all sects in Christianity? XX. Does he wish to cultivate ecclesiastical communion with the Socinians, Papists, Remonstrants, and Anabaptists? XXI. Can any and all contrary opinions, which seem to want to be proved from Holy Scripture, be admitted and defended without distinction? XXII. Does he accept the creed called the Apostles'? XXIII. What is heresy? XXIV. What is schism? XXV. Is the Church which he boasts of setting up, the "Comitia" one, true? XXVI. Does he not incur the crime of schism by establishing another assembly? XXVII. Ought he not, according to the view of his own booklet, to have waited with the erection of another Church until a reply and an examination of his book had been seriously made in the proper manner and order, and had first been received? XXVIII. When will his errors and the sins committed in his book and in the new assembly he is setting up be shown to him, and how will he make good to the world, the Church, and the commonwealth the loss inflicted on the minds of those who have followed him, which have been thrown into turmoil and overturned? XXIX. Is it not to be feared that, even when better things have been shown, he will oppose obstinacy and [illegible] will not yield? XXX. When in his assembly he himself disputes for and against the articles of faith, and [illegible], does he not make himself a remarkable [illegible]? And are the hearers so dismissed utterly confused? XXXI. Does he consider a calling to the ministry of teaching in the Church necessary? And of what kind? XXXII. What calling does he have for carrying out these things and gathering the new Church, and from whom does he have it? XXXIII. When in his assembly, where anyone may dispute and oppose any matter or article whatever, true or false, either the questioner and opponent cannot be satisfied, or the opponents cannot agree among themselves and obstinately refuse to yield, and finally they break out into open and mere quarrels, what counsel is then to be taken in that assembly, or what fruit comes from it? XXXIV. Does he not think that schisms can arise from his assembly? XXXV. Is there no sacrament, or any that he retains, in the assembly? XXXVI. Is there no ecclesiastical discipline?

units.la: Sed quaestionum reciprocarum forte satis, nec inficior: & ubi ad hasce respónderit Auctor (respondere sane oportet), ut ejus phrasi iterum utar, tum de re tota accuratè cogitabimus. Denique Monitum, sive subjicio, ut ne putet sibi nobisque factum satis, si ordinem nostrum impudenter proscindat, eosque qui respondent ipsius erotematis, convicietur, atque refutatione indignâ dicat, dum tollere non potest: quod in Monito factum ab illo pessimè. Cordato nulli persuaserit, hoc disputatoris ingenui esse, quaestiones primum infrunitas proponere, omnesque ad respondendum provocare; tum, contemnere leviter, quae contra, & doctè adseruntur, non sine probris in Auctorem, & nullo quidem dato argumento, quo ostendat, nihil prolatum contra se esse alicujus momenti: Vel ita habeat, siquidem sic agere ei constitutum, aliud Monitum, sed gravius nos talibus opposituros esse, ac æquè facile negligere posse sua, quàm ipsum alienâ: judicio interim lectoribus, omnibusque qui ad certamen provocati, relicto. Vel age, insolenti Monito oppono Provocationem, ad præsens sententiæ examen ac disputationem, coram Politicis, & Ecclesiasticis, aliquibus viris doctis & idoneis, qua discutiatur, num rationes habeant aliquas & sufficientes erigendi coetus istiusmodi, quo contra Ecclesiam & doctrinam nostram agat multùm docetque, & sic dogmatum instituatur examen men serium, amicum, pium, ad Ecclesiae, nostrorumque omnium bonum, & salutem, Deique summi majorem gloriam. Hoc faxo, cures. Ita nec in seriis lusisse (agnoscis tua Monita verba), nec conscientiae vim facile putaberis. Sin vero monitionem hanc, provocationemque suscque deque habeas, tibi imputes oritura inde deserti desperatae causae patrocinii, papalisque usurpatae notam arrogantiae, ac quicquid ex hoc neglectu impositorum infectum voles. Si sapis, bene & recte : si autem non sapis, nos vestri curam gessisse non paenitebit: quia etsi cor vestrum ad pacem non convertitur, pax nostra, tamen ad nos revertetur. Sic concludit suam contra literas Petiliani Donatistae disputationem, Aurelius Augustinus.
units.tr: But perhaps there are enough reciprocal questions, and I do not deny it. When the Author answers these (he certainly ought to), then, to use his own phrase again, we will think the whole matter through carefully. Finally, as for his Monitum, or subjicio, let him not think he has done enough for himself and for us if he shamelessly tears apart our order and reviles those who answer his questions, and then, since he cannot remove them, dismisses them with an unworthy refutation. He has done this very badly in the Monitum. No sensible person will be persuaded that it is the mark of a fair disputant first to put forward questions without end and challenge everyone to answer, and then to dismiss lightly, and not without insults against the Author, what is learnedly asserted against him, with no argument at all to show that nothing of any weight has been brought against him. Either let him take this course, if he has resolved to act so: we will oppose to him another Monitum, but a weightier one, and we can as easily disregard his arguments as he ours, leaving the judgment meanwhile to the readers and to all who have been challenged to the contest. Or, come, I set against his insolent Monitum a Provocationem, a challenge to a present examination and disputation of the opinion, before political and ecclesiastical men, some learned and suitable men, in which it may be discussed whether he has any sufficient grounds for setting up a congregation of this kind, which acts and teaches much against the Church and our doctrine. In this way a serious, friendly and devout examination of the doctrines will be instituted, for the good and salvation of the Church and of all of us, and for the greater glory of the supreme God. See that you do this. So you will be seen neither to have played at serious matters (you acknowledge the words of your Monita), nor will you easily be thought to have done violence to conscience. But if you make light of this admonition and challenge, impute to yourself the resulting desertion of a desperate cause and the mark of papal arrogance you have usurped, and whatever you wish to bring on yourself from this neglect of what has been laid upon you. If you are wise, good and well; but if you are not wise, we shall not regret having taken care of you, for though your heart is not turned to peace, our peace will return to us. Thus Aurelius Augustine concludes his disputation against the letters of Petilian the Donatist.

units.la: Liber Septimus
units.tr: Book Seven

units.la: DE SOCINIANISMO.
units.tr: ON SOCINIANISM.

units.la: Haeresis Socinianae malum. Origo. De Lælio, & Fausto, Socinis. Repressus quomodo, & reprimendus Socinianismus. Quo pacto in nostras regiones introductus, & innotuit. Ut ei resistendum. Controversiae.
units.tr: The evil of the Socinian heresy. Its origin. Of Laelius and Faustus Socinus. How Socinianism was repressed, and how it must be repressed. In what way it was introduced into our regions and became known there. How it must be resisted. Controversies.

units.la: Perniciosa cumprimis est haeresis Socsiniana, quâ, inter hodiernas, sub nomine Christiano, nulla aeque detestanda. Non enim hæc articulum aliquem religionis, sed ejus animam & fundamenta concutit, atque fermè evertit. Secundum hanc Christus nihil est, nisi Doctor aliquis, aut Martyr egregius; ejus officium, docere duntaxat, non verè redimere; Euangelium alteram legis justificatio, propter opera contingit; probitas forlummodo ethica aliqua infernus, & animae plurimorum post hanc vitam, nihil, quodque primo loco dicendum fuerat, S. in Deo Trinitas, ludibrium & idolum. Quae omnia, iisque annexa capita & errores quantopere totam Theologiam & religionem infestent ac corrumpant, nemo est qui non sentiat.
units.tr: The Socinian heresy is above all pernicious, and among those of our time there is none under the Christian name to be detested equally. For it does not shake some single article of religion but its very soul and foundations, and well-nigh overturns them. According to it, Christ is nothing but some teacher or an outstanding martyr; his office is merely to teach, not truly to redeem. The gospel is another law, and justification comes through works. Holiness is only a certain kind of ethics, and hell and the souls of most people after this life are nothing. And what should have been said first, the Holy Trinity of God, is a mockery and an idol. Everyone perceives how greatly all these errors, and the chapters annexed to them, infest and corrupt the whole of theology and religion.

units.la: Coepit haeresis abhinc saeculum, à Lælio Socino Senense, qui Serveti blasphemias (ob quas iste Genevae luit anno cIↄ Iↄ lii i.) arripuit, & plura alia contra orthodoxiam dogmata petulanti ingenio sectatus, à Calvino graviter increpatus fuit, epistolâ ad illum scriptâ anno cIↄ Iↄ lii i. quam alibi exhibui: iterum alia anno cIↄ Iↄ lv. quae inter epistolas Calvini legi potest. Hic Lælius Socinus scripsit explicationem in primum caput Iohannis, quam primus refutavit Hier. Zanchius, omisso Auctoris nomine, cujus rationem dat in Praefatione lib. de Tribus Elohim, ubi accuratius hominem sibi bene notum & familiarem (qui ut erat plenissimus diversarum haeresium, ita eas nunquam Zanchio proponebat, nisi interrogans, & disputandi praetextu magis, quam asserendi) describit. Eandem primi capitis Iohannis interpretationem exhibent Auctores maledicentissimi scripti, Ministri consentientes in Sarmatiâ & Transsylvaniâ, Albae Juliae anno 1563. de unitate Dei Patris, Filii, & Spiritus Sancti cognitione vera & falsa, lib. 11. cap. x 1. etiam Franciscus Junius, in Defensione tertiâ Trinitatis. De illâ sic Socinus ipse scribit, epist. 1. ad Dudithium, Nescio an unquam oculis tuis oblatâ sit brevis quaedam explicatio initii primi capitis Iohannis, à Zanchio, & Bezâ, & ex parte à Polonis istis Lælio adscripta: ea vero jam ante annos XVIII. ex officinâ nostrâ prodiit. Lælius etiam dicitur Dialogi, adversus Calvinum scripti, de haereticis jure gladii coercendis, inter Calvinum & Vaticanum, qui passim, & in ipsâ libelli praefatione attribuitur Castellioni. Vti Zanchium, quamdiu cum eo vixit, mirifice fefellit Lælius, similiter bono viro Philippo Melanthoni, quocum triennium exegit familiariter, adeo impositi, ut Philippus pro eo tamquam optimo viro. anno cIↄ Iↄ lvii. intercesserit tum apud Imp. Maximilianum II. tum apud Poloniae Regem Sigismundum, ut horum nomine Legati vicem Venetiis obire, eaque ratione paternam hereditatem, sibi, ob consuetudinem cum Protestantibus in Germania, interclusam, adire tutius liceret. Obiit anno cIↄ Iↄ lx ii. Tiguri, aetatis a. xxxvi i. quo tempore Faustus erat juvenis xxiii. annorum, natus quippe hic fuit Senis, in Italia a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxix,
units.tr: This heresy began about a century ago with Laelius Socinus of Siena. He seized upon the blasphemies of Servetus (for which Servetus paid at Geneva in 1553) and, pursuing with a wanton wit many other doctrines contrary to orthodoxy, he was severely rebuked by Calvin in a letter written to him in 1553, which I have printed elsewhere, and again in another letter of 1555, which can be read among Calvin's letters. This Laelius Socinus wrote an explanation of the first chapter of John, which Hieronymus Zanchius was the first to refute, without naming the author. Zanchius gives his reason in the preface to his book On the Three Elohim, where he describes more precisely the man, well known and familiar to him, who (being full of various heresies) never put those heresies before Zanchius except by way of questioning, and for the sake of disputation rather than assertion. The same interpretation of the first chapter of John is set out by the most slanderous authors of the writing, the ministers who agreed with one another in Sarmatia and Transylvania, at Alba Julia in 1563, on the true and false knowledge of the unity of God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, book 11, chapter 11. Francis Junius too, in his Third Defence of the Trinity. Socinus himself writes of that work as follows, in letter 1 to Dudith: "I do not know whether a brief explanation of the beginning of the first chapter of John, by Zanchius and Beza, and in part ascribed by those Poles to Laelius, has ever come before your eyes. It came forth from our workshop eighteen years ago." Laelius is also said to have written the Dialogue, against Calvin, on the punishment of heretics by the sword, between Calvin and the Vatican, which is attributed everywhere, and even in the preface of the little book, to Castellio. Laelius deceived Zanchius marvellously, as long as Zanchius lived with him, and similarly deceived the good man Philip Melanchthon, with whom he spent three years in close friendship, so thoroughly that Philip, in 1557, interceded for him as for an excellent man, both with the Emperor Maximilian II and with King Sigismund of Poland, that he might be allowed to act as their envoy at Venice and so more safely recover his paternal inheritance, which had been cut off from him because of his association with the Protestants in Germany. He died at Zurich in 1562, at the age of 36. At that time Faustus was a young man of 23, for he had been born at Siena in Italy in 1539.

units.la: Intellecta patrui sui morte Faustus, ocyus Tigurum advolat, crescendae non tam hereditatis, quam Bibliothecae, & scriptorum recondendorum causa, ne in alterius manum venirent, & mysteria illa recluderent quae Lælius praeferat, & Fausto reliquerat suo tempore propalanda. Sic quippe apud amicos nonnumquam de Fausto suo gloriatus perhibetur Lælius, quod is post se omnia felicius mundo esset explanaturus & perfecturus. Cum hac praeda vel thesauro in Italiam abiit Faustus, ubi primum in aula Florentini Ducis, per duodecim annos haesit, inde hac relicta, Basileam venit anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxiv. aetatis xxxv. mansitque triennium: post in Transsylvaniam a celebri medico Blandrata evocatus ad cIↄ Iↄ lxxvi i. tandem in Poloniam, secessit anno cIↄ Iↄ lxx ix. aetatis xl. ubique id unum agens, ut dictata & Theologiam patrui sui plenissime imbiberet & excoleret. Vixit in Polonia Cracoviae, unde circa vitae finem discedens Luclavicias, pagum novem circiter milliaribus Cracovia dissitum, hic post aliquot annos obiit, anno hujus saeculi quarto, aetatis suae lxv.
units.tr: Faustus, on learning of his uncle's death, hastened to Zurich, less for the sake of increasing the inheritance than for the library and the writings, so that they should not come into another's hands and unlock those mysteries which Laelius had kept back and left to Faustus to be disclosed at the proper time. For it is reported that Laelius, boasting to friends now and then of his Faustus, said that Faustus would explain and complete everything after him more fortunately for the world. With this booty, or treasure, Faustus went back to Italy, where at first he stayed for twelve years at the court of the Duke of Florence. Leaving that, he came to Basel in 1574, at the age of 35, and remained there for three years. Afterwards he was summoned to Transylvania by the famous physician Blandrata, in 1576, and at last he withdrew to Poland in 1579, at the age of 40, everywhere doing this one thing, that he might thoroughly imbibe and cultivate the doctrines and theology of his uncle. He lived in Poland at Cracow, and towards the end of his life, leaving it for Luclavice, a village about nine miles from Cracow, he died there some years later, in the fourth year of this century, at the age of 65.

units.la: Libros scribere coepit ab anno cIↄ Iↄ lxx. quos varios ubique locorum, in Italia, Germania, Transsylvania, & Polonia edidit, quorum catalogum, & quae plura ad hujus haeresis historiam spectant, nuper exposui, in Apparatu ad primum Tomum Socinianismi Confesfatati. Interim dum uterque Socinus novum religionis systema & aedificium moliuntur, alii post Servetum Genevae expulsi, easdem haereses profiteminare sategerunt, cum alibi, tum in partibus Transsylvaniae, & Poloniae, quò certatim confugiebant.
units.tr: He began to write books from 1570. He published various ones in many places, in Italy, Germany, Transylvania and Poland. I have recently set out a catalogue of these, and what else pertains to the history of this heresy, in the Introduction to the first volume of Socinianism Confuted. Meanwhile, while the two Socinuses were building up a new system and edifice of religion, others, driven out of Geneva after Servetus, strove to propagate the same heresies, both elsewhere and in parts of Transylvania and Poland, to which they eagerly fled.

units.la: Quales Valentinus Gentilis, Georgius Blandrata, Ioh. Paulus Alciatus, & cum iis alii, qui quando primum innotuere Ecclesiis, & constare coepit eos de Deo & Christo tradere haeretica prorsus, ita dissimularunt ea & palam negarunt, contra animi sententiam, & contrarium ei quod eventus postea de illis docuit, ut majores an haeretici, an tergiversatores initio fuerint, dubium videatur; utrimque nimirum mendaces, & in Deum ejusque veritatem, & in se. Petrus Statorius Tonvillanus, qui istorum unus erat, in Synodum Pinczovienfem citatus, ut responderet de suspicione haeresis adversus se data, propheticam dixit, & Apostolicam doctrinam, quae veram Dei Patris, Filii & Spiritus Sancti cognitionem continet, amplector ac veneror, parique religione, Deum Patrem, Filium, ac S. Spiritum, distinctè secundum sacrarum literarum veritatem colendum, implorandumque precibus, libere profiteor: denique omnem haereticam de Deo Patre, Filio, & Spiritu Sancto blasphemiam, plane detestor, sive Ariana illa, sive Servetiana, Eunomiana, Stancariana fuerit. Factum hoc anno cIↄ Iↄ lix. confessionemque eam propria manu subsignavit. Georgius Blandrata similiter, postquam de eo Ecclesias Polonicas, & Palatinum Vilnensem, Calvinus sollicite monuerat, in Synodo Pinczovienfi anno cIↄ Iↄ lxı. se adversus injurias quasi Calvini defensurus, testatus fuit: Fateor, inquiens, me credere in unum Deum Patrem, in unum Dominum Iesum Christum Filium ejus, & in unum Spiritum sanctum, quocum est essentialiter Deus. Deorum pluralitatem detestor, cum unus nobis sit tantum Deus essentia indivisibilis. Fateor, tres esse distinctas hypostases, & aeternam Christi divinitatem ac generationem & Spiritum Sanctum, verum & æternum Deum; ab utroque procedentem. Et tamen certum est, illos primos ac- cerrimosque hæresis Anti-Trinitariæ in Polonia extitisse patronos & propagatores, cum Francisco Lismani- no, qui in Synodo alia ejusdem anni, se non adeo rem & doctrinam fidei, quam verba Scholastica Trinitatis & similia accusare profitebatur. Attamen magis magisque indies detecti, cum non amplius sub Ecclesiæ nomine & gremio occultari possent, post habitum Colloquium, schismate palam facto in segreges cœtus cibicre, Petricoviæ anno cIↄ Iↄ lxii. Postea anno cIↄ Iↄ lxv, permissu Regis Sigismi. ii. publica instituta disputatio fuit inter Nostros, ac illos: atque ab eo tempore deinceps aperto & diuturno certamine istorum hominum exercita ibi locorum Ecclesia fuit, libriqué pessimi scripti adversus fidem, præsertim S. Trinitatem, ab anno cIↄ Iↄ lxvii. Quibus postea Socinus accessit, uti diximus, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxvii. in Transylvaniam primum, inde in Poloniam. Vide de illis Historiæ Eccle- siar. Slavonicarum lib. i.
units.tr: Such were Valentinus Gentilis, Giorgio Biandrata, Giovanni Paolo Alciati, and others with them. When they first became known to the Churches, and it began to be established that they taught things entirely heretical about God and Christ, they dissembled and openly denied these things, against the feeling of their hearts and contrary to what the outcome later taught about them. So it seems doubtful whether they were greater heretics or greater evaders from the start, liars on both counts: both towards God and his truth, and towards themselves. Peter Statorius of Tongevelen, who was one of them, summoned to the Synod of Pinczow to answer for the suspicion of heresy against him, said: "I embrace and venerate the apostolic doctrine, which contains the true knowledge of God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. I freely profess that God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit are to be worshipped distinctly, according to the truth of the Holy Scriptures, and to be invoked in prayers with equal reverence. Finally, I utterly detest every heretical blasphemy concerning God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, whether it be Arian, Servetian, Eunomian or Stancarian." This took place in 1559, and he signed this confession with his own hand. Giorgio Biandrata likewise, after Calvin had earnestly warned the Polish Churches and the Palatine of Vilna about him, declared at the Synod of Pinczow in 1561, in order to defend himself against the charges of Calvin: "I confess, he said, that I believe in one God the Father, in one Lord Jesus Christ his Son, and in one Holy Spirit, who is essentially God together with them. I detest the plurality of gods, since for us there is only one God, indivisible in essence. I confess that there are three distinct hypostases, and the eternal divinity and generation of Christ, and the Holy Spirit, true and eternal God, proceeding from both." And yet it is certain that these were the first and most bitter champions and propagators of the anti-Trinitarian heresy in Poland, together with Francis Lismanino, who at another synod of the same year professed that he did not so much accuse the matter and doctrine of the faith as the scholastic words of the Trinity and similar expressions. Nevertheless, being detected more and more every day, and no longer able to be hidden under the name and bosom of the Church, after a colloquy had been held they openly made a schism and built separate assemblies at Pinczow in 1562. Afterwards, in 1565, by permission of King Sigismund II, a public disputation was held between our people and them, and from that time on the Church in those places was exercised in an open and long-lasting struggle with these men, and very wicked books against the faith, especially against the Holy Trinity, were published from 1567. Socinus joined them later, as we have said, in 1577, first in Transylvania and then in Poland. See about them the History of the Slavonic Churches, book 1.

units.la: Socinus autem non substitit in uno vel altero adversus Ecclesiam dogmate, non in oppugnanda sola S. Trinitate, & Christo, sed ex suo ingenio totam aliam religionis novamque formam introduxit per singula Theologiæ capita, in quibus proponendis non semper ei æque a suis assensum. Quare omnino ab eo Auctore nova hæc secta, & non per antiquas tantum vel Samosatenianorum vel Arianorum nomenclaturas, supra quos innumera alia adversus fidem ille docuit, appellanda. Eques Polonus, qui vitam Socini scripsit, ut hoc Socinum semper in animo habuisse significat, ut nobilioris fidei doctrinam traderet, ita in eo quidem haud male judicasse mihi videtur, quod circa finem illius historiolæ, de factis & gestis Socini differens, cum comparat Ignatio, Loyolitarum patri; Ignatium quoque, ut alios taceam, majorum nostrorum memoriæ, patriam, a-
units.tr: Socinus, however, did not stop at one or two doctrines held against the Church, nor at attacking the Holy Trinity and Christ alone. From his own genius he introduced an entirely different and new form of religion, through each single head of theology, though in setting these out he did not always win the assent of his own followers. For this reason the new sect must be named after its author, and not only by the old names of the Samosatenians or the Arians, beyond whom he taught countless other doctrines against the faith. The Polish knight who wrote the life of Socinus indicates that Socinus always had in mind to hand down a nobler doctrine of faith, and in this I think he judged well. Near the end of that little history, where he treats the deeds and exploits of Socinus, he compares him with Ignatius, the father of the Loyolites: Ignatius too, to pass over others, had for the memory of our forebears despised his homeland, his a-

units.la: gus. gratias, opes, honores, & alias illecebras contempserat, multos quoque labores, multa discrimina altivò subierat, Zelum gloriae Dei & fidei militiam professus. Non despicio animi magnitudinem, quae in eo aut nonnullis similibus apparuit. Neque enim prorsus molli itinere ad gloriam contenderunt. Sed nondum hic video illud magis arduum, quod quaerimus nobilioris fidei specimen. Non inepta comparatio, utrque novae sectae auctor fuit, aequè execrandae, in cuius gratiam pari studio visi sunt patriam, opes (si quas forte habuerunt), & saecularis vitae nobilitatem deseruisse, eundem gloriae Dei zelum & fidei militiam professi. Sed revera, in Auctor hic ipse prodit, animi magnitudo, & gloriae cupido eos egit in novas erigendas religiones; in Socino quidem eo major, quo alterius etiam fidei typum, vel nobilioris fidei specimen, quemadmodum Auctor loquitur, excogitavit. Videlicet utrique par debebatur ab omnibus & gloria, & merces. Ignatius Socinus aliquantum anterior fuit, utpote natus a. cIↄ cocc xci. [?] mortuus anno cIↄ Iↄ Ivi. [?] Papa Clemens VIII. hoc ne omitterem, anno cIↄ Iↄ cI I ↄ [?] Bullam edidit, vel praeteritam P. Pauli IV. renovavit, adversus negantes Trinitatem: legitur in Bullario Stephani Quarantae, tit. Haeretici.
units.tr: favours, wealth, honours, and other allurements, and had undertaken many labours and many dangers with a lofty spirit, professing zeal for the glory of God and the soldiering of the faith. I do not belittle the greatness of mind which appeared in him or in some similar men. For they did not strive for glory by a wholly easy road. But I do not yet see here that more arduous thing which we are seeking, a specimen of a nobler faith. The comparison is not inept. Each was the author of a new sect, equally to be execrated, and for whose sake they were seen to have abandoned, with equal zeal, their homeland, their wealth (if they happened to have any), and the distinction of secular life, professing the same zeal for the glory of God and the soldiering of the faith. But in truth the author himself betrays it: a greatness of spirit and a desire for glory drove them to set up new religions. In Socinus this was all the greater, in that he devised another faith, or a specimen of a nobler faith, as the author puts it. Clearly both deserved equal glory and reward from everyone. Ignatius was a little older than Socinus, having been born in 1491 and died in 1556. Lest I omit this: Pope Clement VIII, in the year 1599, issued a bull, or renewed the earlier one of Paul IV, against those who deny the Trinity. It is read in the Bullarium of Stefano Quaranta, under the title Haeretici.

units.la: Quo verò magis Sociniani conantur nostris se immiscere & ingerere tum hominibus, tum Ecclesiis, etiam Rebuspublicis, eo diligentius cavendi sunt & coercendi. A primo sectae tempore studuerunt latere sub nominis nostri umbra; vt iam agniti, simul constanter repudiati, condemnatique eorum doctrina fuit, & quantum potuit, omni studio repressa. Ex Polonia, Belgio, Angliâ eliminati. Neque sine causâ, dixit Archiepiscopus Colonienßis Ernestus, intellectis Socinianis quaestionibus & litibus, per Remonstrantes, & Vorstium eiusque discipulos inprimis motis, ad annum huius seculi decimum quartum: iure meritoque omnes tres Religiones, intelligens Papisticam, Lutheranam, & Reformatam, se conjungerent ad hanc sectam communi opera extirpandam.
units.tr: The more the Socinians try to insinuate and thrust themselves among ours, both among men and churches and even commonwealths, the more carefully they must be guarded against and restrained. From the earliest time of the sect they strove to lie hidden under the shadow of our name; but once they were recognised, their doctrine was at the same time constantly rejected and condemned, and as far as possible suppressed with every effort. They were expelled from Poland, Belgium and England. Nor without cause did Ernest, Archbishop of Cologne, say, when the Socinian questions and disputes, stirred up chiefly by the Remonstrants, by Vorstius and his disciples, had been understood, up to the fourteenth year of this century, that all three religions, the Papist, the Lutheran and the Reformed, rightly and deservedly should join together in a common effort to root out this sect.

units.la: Hoc, quo ista scribo, anno, mense Aprili, Catechismus Racoviensis, in Anglia, decreto Parlamenti, igni adjudicatus fuit. In nostris hodie regionibus per contentiones Remonstranticas magnopere innotuit & divulgatus est Socinianismus, postquam a. MDCXXVIII, magno animo & zelo, publico Ordinum decreto, exulare hinc cum Turcica sua doctrina coacti fuerunt auctores ejus Ostorodus, & Vaidovius. Qua eadem diligentia princeps Auriacus VVilhelmus Erasmi Iohannis conatus Antverpiae, ubi Scholae Rector erat, in herba stitit, ne se latius diffunderet, postquam haeresis suae librum aliquem clam emisisset. Vt haec refert Henricus Antonii, Theologus Franekeranus, in Praefat. Systematis Theol. ubi initia Ecclesiae in Belgio aliqua breviter enarrat. Qui Erasmus Iohannis postea in Transsylvaniam aufugit, & Arianismum palam docuit, in coetu Claudiopolitano, cujus minister erat, & cum quo Socinus aliquando disputavit: nam alia Socini erat sententia, dicentis, Christum non extitisse ante Mariam, quem ille ajebat fuisse substantiam spiritualem a Deo ante reliqua creatam, quae postea carnem induisset. Disputationem illam edidit Socinus, interque opera ejus legitur. Ab illo Erasmo Iohannis, haeresis Arianae, quum Socinus Photinianae esset, sectatore factum arbitror, quod ipsis nomina Arianorum & Ebionitarum aliquando & Photinianorum, indita sint. Quod vero pridem exundarit apud nos haeresis Socíniana, cujus antea vix nomen nostris notum erat, factum (uti dico) per infelices Remonstrantium disputationes, primo per Vorstium, Theologum istum, ουσιώδες uti merito appellabat Casaubonus, ei respondurus, postquam ad se scripsisset. epist. ad Thuanum, cclxxxii. & cujus librum de Deo, ita ad Socini mentem compositum, ut nullum æque citent Adversarii, ubi istam materiam tractant, damnatum idcirco à Rege Angliæ, & comburi jussa exemplaria, tum Londini, tum in utraque Academiâ, scribit in Epistolâ ad Perronum Cardinalem, pro Rege suo responsoriâ. Quod ampliss. Magistratus Amstelodamensis secutus nuper fuit, quando in ignem conjici exemplaria librorum Volkelii, ist hic recusorum, laudabili exemplo voluit. Iam quo magis sive clam, sive palam, sive proprio nomine, sive sub alieno se quaquaversum ingerit Socinianismus, eo solertius & validius ei omni modo occurrendum, politicè, & Ecclesiasticè, quodque utriq; inservit, etiam Scholasticè: id est, ut in Academiis diligenter instruantur studiosi de malitiâ & contagio istius hæresis, quibus se artibus vulgò insinuet, quibus nitatur rationibus, tum quo pacto & quibus argumentis confundi & destrui possit. Tempus fuit, quo cum aliis luctandum bestiis nobis fuit: habent quæque disputationes suas quasi periodos. Initio cum Papismo acerrimum bellum fuit, inde cum Anabaptistis, & Enthusiastis, pridem cum Remonstrantibus, nunc cum pessimis omnium Socinianis decertandum venit. Quamvis enim Papistæ graviter errent, tenent tamen adhuc multa religionis fundamenta, sed quæ variarum superstitionum & errorum ἐπισυμβαίνοντα corrumpunt: Socinani vero tollunt omnia. At gravius est carere omnino, quibus carere nequeas, quam habere eadem ut cumque vitiata. Superest hoc: in genere adhuc magni operis argumentum, quod unumquemque exerceat, disputationum adversus illam hæresim. Nos pro modulo nostro inchoavimus, edito Confutati Socinianismi Tomo primo, ad reliqua similiter perficienda accinxi: sed & aliorum in idem opus Domini labores ac studia provocamus, ut unanimi operâ à grege arceamus malum, quo nullum aliud magis inimicum & exitiosum. Quare plura de hoc argumento dicere supersedeo, quæ alibi prolixius tum expósui jam, tum in sequentibus pertractaturus, cum Deo, sum. Interim ad cognoscenda Socinianorum dogmata conducet vel Catechismus Racoviensis, aut Ostorodus, Smalcius contra Frantzium, Volkelius: nam Socini scripta & rarius haberi possunt, & diffusiora sunt, quam ut summam totius doctrinae suae systematicè exhibeant. Tum adversus illa compendio uti possunt Studiosi Strechmanni Photinianismo, aut Andreae Prolæi Manuductio Socinianâ, Cloppenburgii Compendiolo Socinianismi Confutato, vel Nicolai Arnoldi Refutatione Catechesis Racoviana. Extant praeterea nec contemnendi hac in parte tractatus, Theodori Thummii Impietas Photiniana & Calovii Socinismus profligatus. Controversiae autem sunt:
units.tr: In this year in which I write these things, in April, the Racovian Catechism was condemned to the flames in England by decree of Parliament. In our own lands, Socinianism has become notorious and widely spread through the Remonstrant controversies, since in 1628, by public decree of the States and with great zeal, its authors Ostorodus and Vaidovius were compelled to go into exile from here, together with their Turkish doctrine. With the same diligence, William, Prince of Orange, while Erasmus Johannis was Rector of the school at Antwerp, checked his attempts in the bud, so that the heresy would not spread more widely, after he had secretly published some book of that heresy. Henricus Antonii, theologian of Franeker, relates this in the Preface to his Systematic Theology, where he briefly recounts some beginnings of the Church in Belgium. This Erasmus Johannis later fled to Transylvania and openly taught Arianism in the congregation at Klausenburg, of which he was minister, and with which Socinus once disputed. For Socinus held a different view, saying that Christ did not exist before Mary, and that he was a spiritual substance created by God before the rest of creation, which afterwards put on flesh. Socinus published that disputation, and it is read among his works. I think that Erasmus Johannis made himself a follower of the Arian heresy, although Socinus was a Photinian; this is why the names of Arians, Ebionites, and sometimes Photinians have been given to them. That the Socinian heresy, of which hardly anyone among us knew the name before, has now overflowed among us, was brought about (as I say) through the unhappy disputes of the Remonstrants, first through Vorstius, that theologian whom Casaubon rightly called essential [ουσιώδες], intending to answer him after he had written to him (letter to Thuanus, 282), and whose book on God, composed so closely to Socinus's mind that no opponents cite any more often when they treat this subject, was condemned by the King of England, and copies were ordered burned, both in London and in both universities. He writes this in his letter to Cardinal Perron, as a reply on behalf of his king. The very distinguished magistrates of Amsterdam recently followed this, when they wished, with a praiseworthy example, to have copies of the books of Volkelius, a work also reprinted here, cast into the fire. Now, the more Socinianism insinuates itself everywhere, whether secretly or openly, under its own name or another's, the more skilfully and vigorously it must be met in every way, politically and ecclesiastically, and also scholastically, which serves both. That is, students in the universities must be carefully taught about the malice and contagion of this heresy: by what arts it commonly insinuates itself, on what reasons it relies, and also in what manner and by what arguments it can be confuted and destroyed. There was a time when we had to struggle with other beasts. Each has its own cycle of disputations. At the beginning the fiercest war was with Papism, then with the Anabaptists and Enthusiasts, and lately we had to contend with the Remonstrants, and now with the worst of all, the Socinians. For although the Papists err gravely, they still hold many foundations of religion, but these are corrupted by the accidental [ἐπισυμβαίνοντα] errors and superstitions of various kinds. The Socinians, however, remove everything. Yet it is more serious to lack altogether what you cannot do without than to have the same things in whatever corrupted state. One task remains: a great work still in general, to occupy each of us, of disputations against that heresy. We have made a beginning according to our measure, having published the first volume of the Confutation of Socinianism, and I have girded myself to complete the rest in the same way. But I also call on the labours and efforts of others in the Lord's work, so that by united effort we may keep the evil from the flock, since no other evil is more hostile and deadly. Therefore I forbear to say more on this subject, which I have already set out at greater length elsewhere, and which, God willing, I shall treat further in what follows. Meanwhile, for learning the doctrines of the Socinians, the Racovian Catechism will help, or Ostorodus, Smalcius against Frantzius, Volkelius; for the writings of Socinus are both rarer to find and too diffuse to set out the sum of his whole doctrine in a systematic way. Against these, students may use in brief Strecker's Photinianism, or Andreas Prolaeus's Socinian Guide, Cloppenburg's Short Refutation of Socinianism, or Nicolaus Arnoldus's Refutation of the Racovian Catechism. There also exist treatises on this part that are not to be despised: Theodor Thummius's Photinian Impiety and Calovius's Socinianism Overthrown. The controversies are these:

units.la: I. Num in S. Scriptura aliqua revera sit dissensio & repugnantia? Neg.
units.tr: I. Is there in Holy Scripture any real dissension and contradiction? No.

units.la: II. Num S. Scripturae textus authenticus pluribus in locis sit immutatus, atque depravatus? Neg.
units.tr: II. Has the authentic text of Holy Scripture been changed and corrupted in many places? No.

units.la: III. Num aliqui Veteris Testamenti libri sacri perierint? Neg.
units.tr: III. Whether any books of the sacred Old Testament have been lost? No.

units.la: IV. Num sub Novo jam Testamento, Veteris Testamenti lectio non sit necessaria, magnique adeo momenti? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Whether, under the New Testament, the reading of the Old Testament is no longer necessary and of no great importance? No.

units.la: V. Num sine interna, ac singulari illuminatione Spiritus Sancti, S. Scriptura recte & salutariter intelligi, atque servari possit? Neg.
units.tr: V. Whether Scripture can be rightly and savingly understood and preserved without the inward and singular illumination of the Holy Spirit? No.

units.la: VI. Num ratio humana sit judex & norma controversiarum Theologicarum? Neg.
units.tr: VI. Whether human reason is the judge and rule of theological controversies? No.

units.la: VII. Annon aliqua de Deo notitia hominum animis insita sit, & naturalis? Aff.
units.tr: VII. Is there not some knowledge of God implanted in men's minds and natural? Yes.

units.la: An ex rerum creatarum contemplatione, aliqua de Deo notitia acquiri possit? Aff.
units.tr: Can some knowledge of God not be acquired from the contemplation of created things? Yes.

units.la: VIII. Num religio duabus modo contineatur partibus, praeceptis divinis, & promissis? Neg.
units.tr: VIII. Is religion contained in only two parts, the divine precepts and the promises? No.

units.la: Annon etiam notitia credendorum partem faciat? Aff.
units.tr: Does it not also include the knowledge of what is to be believed? Yes.

units.la: IX. Num articuli ad salutem fundamentales sint paucicissimi? iique, quos Socinani pro talibus habent? ut de Deo solùm, quod sit, unus, æternus, perfectè justus, perfectè sapiens, perfectè potens? Neg.
units.tr: IX. Are the articles fundamental to salvation very few, and are those which the Socinians regard as such, namely that God alone exists, is one, eternal, perfectly just, perfectly wise, and perfectly powerful, the only ones? No.

units.la: x. Num Dei æternitas, partes ac successionem temporis habeat, per prius, & posterius? Neg.
units.tr: X. Does God's eternity have parts and a succession of time, before and after? No.

units.la: xi. An Deus essentia suâ sit omnipræsens? Aff.
units.tr: XI. Is God present everywhere by his essence? Yes.

units.la: xii. An Deus habeat omnium scientiam, etiam futurorum contingentium? Aff.
units.tr: XII. Does God have knowledge of all things, including future contingent things? Yes.

units.la: xiii. Num attributa, seu proprietates in Deo sint accidentia, vel qualitates realiter à Deo, atque inter se differentes? Neg.
units.tr: XIII. Are the attributes, or properties, in God accidents, or qualities really distinct from God and from one another? No.

units.la: xiv. An in Deo sint unius essentiæ tres Personæ; Pater, & Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus? Aff.
units.tr: XIV. Are there in God three Persons of one essence: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Yes.

units.la: xv. Num in Deo sint affectus, & variæ voluntatis commotiones? Neg.
units.tr: XV. Are there in God affections and changes of will? No.

units.la: xvi. Num prædestinatio sit Dei decretum æternum, quo voluerit homines in Christum credituros atque in fide perseveraturos, salvare, sed in genere tantum, non in individuo singulari, quos? atque ubi quis actu jam, voluntate suâ bene usus, in Christum credit, diversis alii & alii temporibus, antum demum à Deo, propter ipsorum fidem ac obedientiam, eligantur; & electione modo inchoatâ, & incertâ, atque mutabili, quæ et jam cessare, deficiente in hominibus fide, possit, neque sit completa, & peremtoria, nisi post probatam hominis ad vitæ finem, in fide & bonis operibus perseverantiam? Neg.
units.tr: XVI. Is predestination an eternal decree of God by which he willed to save men, in general only and not any particular individuals, who would believe in Christ and persevere in faith; and, when someone, having actually used his own will well, believes in Christ, at different times and in different people, is chosen by God only on account of their faith and obedience; and this election, begun but uncertain and changeable, which can cease when faith fails in men, is neither complete nor peremptory, unless the man's perseverance in faith and good works has been proved at the end of his life? No.

units.la: xvii. Num Angeli, & materia mundi, ante hujus mundi sex diebus creationem, fuerint creata? Neg.
units.tr: XVII. Were the angels and the matter of the world created before the six days of creation of this world? No.

units.la: xviii. Primus homo annon à Deo fuerit creatus justus ac sanctus? Aff.
units.tr: XVIII. Was the first man not created by God just and holy? Yes.

units.la: xix. Annon omnes homines nascantur cum peccato originali? Aff.
units.tr: XIX. Are not all men born with original sin? Yes.

units.la: xx. Annon mors sit peccati pœna? Aff.
units.tr: XX. Is death not the punishment of sin? Yes.

units.la: xxi. Num homo à natura possit præstare quodvis bonum? Neg.
units.tr: XXI. Can man by nature perform any good whatever? No.

units.la: xxii. An
units.tr: XXII. Whether

units.la: xxi. An Christus sit verus Deus? Aff.
units.tr: XXIII. Is Christ true God? Yes.

units.la: xxii. Num Christus etiam venturus fuisset, quamvis homo non peccasset? Neg.
units.tr: XXIV. Would Christ have come even if man had not sinned? No.

units.la: xxiv. Num Christus, tempore quadragesimalis jejunii, in coelum raptus fuerit, ut ibidem de doctrina hominibus patefacienda instrueretur? Neg.
units.tr: XXV. Was Christ, during the forty days of fasting, caught up into heaven so that he might be instructed there in the doctrine to be revealed to men? No.

units.la: xxv. Num promissio vitae aeternae, & remissionis peccatorum, ac Spiritus Sancti, & salutis in Christo, Patribus etiam facta & oblata sit in Veteri Testamento, ab iisque credita, & proinde ii eadem via salvati fuerint, quâ nos? Aff.
units.tr: XXVI. Was the promise of eternal life, forgiveness of sins, the Holy Spirit, and salvation in Christ also made and offered to the Fathers in the Old Testament, and believed by them, so that they were saved by the same way as we are? Yes.

units.la: xxvi. Num Christus legem moralem perfectiorem, & alias de novo leges dederit?
units.tr: XXVII. Did Christ give a more perfect moral law, and other new laws?

units.la: Videlicet, an ad Primum praeceptum addiderit,
units.tr: Namely, did he add to the First Commandment:

units.la: i. Praeceptum generale, de precibus Deo faciendis?
units.tr: i. A general precept about making prayers to God?

units.la: ii. Formulam Orationis Dominicae?
units.tr: ii. The form of the Lord's Prayer?

units.la: iii. Praeceptum, de invocando & adorando Christo?
units.tr: iii. A precept about invoking and adoring Christ?

units.la: Ad secundum,
units.tr: To the Second:

units.la: i. Praeceptum, de cavendis idolis, eorum habitationis loco, atque idololatriis?
units.tr: i. A precept about avoiding idols, the places where they are kept, and idolatries?

units.la: Ad Tertium,
units.tr: To the Third:

units.la: i. Ne leviter juremus?
units.tr: i. That we should not swear lightly?

units.la: ii. Ut quoque per nomen Christi liceat jurare?
units.tr: ii. That it is also permitted to swear by the name of Christ?

units.la: Quartum praeceptum num sit caeremoniale, & ad Christianos nihil pertinens? Neg.
units.tr: Is the Fourth Commandment ceremonial, and in no way pertaining to Christians? No.

units.la: Num ad praeceptum quintum per Christum additum sit,
units.tr: Was something added by Christ to the Fifth Commandment,

units.la: Quod spectat ad officium Magistratus, & subditorum; maritorum, & uxorum; dominorum, ac servorum?
units.tr: namely concerning the duties of magistrates and subjects, husbands and wives, masters and servants?

units.la: Ad praeceptum sextum,
units.tr: To the Sixth:

units.la: i. Dilectio inimicorum?
units.tr: i. The love of enemies?

units.la: ii. Proximo non irascendum, non convitiandum, neneque vindictam intentandam esse?
units.tr: ii. That one must not be angry with a neighbour, nor revile him, nor threaten revenge?

units.la: Ad septimum,
units.tr: On the Seventh,

units.la: I. Alienae uxoris concupiscentiam, esse adulterium?
units.tr: I. That desire for another's wife is adultery?

units.la: II. Polygamiam, & divortium extra casum adulterii, illicita esse?
units.tr: II. That polygamy, and divorce outside the case of adultery, are unlawful?

units.la: III. Cavendam esse omnem scortationem, impuritatem, turpiloquium, gestus, contrectationes libidinosas?
units.tr: III. That all fornication, impurity, obscene speech, gestures, and lustful touching are to be avoided?

units.la: Ad Octavum,
units.tr: On the Eighth,

units.la: I. Prohibitio avaritiae?
units.tr: I. The prohibition of greed?

units.la: Ad Nonum,
units.tr: On the Ninth,

units.la: I. Omne mendacium & simulationes ac dissimulationes, item detractiones, & condemnationes temerarias peccatum esse?
units.tr: I. That every lie, pretence and dissimulation, likewise detraction and rash condemnation, is sin?

units.la: Qu. Num officiosa mendacia sint licita? Neg.
units.tr: Question: Are dutiful lies lawful? No.

units.la: Ad Decimum,
units.tr: On the Tenth,

units.la: I. Non esse animum oblectandum concupiscentiâ rei alienae, neque ejus fovendam cogitationem?
units.tr: I. That the mind should not be delighted by desire for another's property, nor should the thought of it be nourished?

units.la: Negatur, illa ceu additamenta ad legem à Christo appositá fuisse.
units.tr: Denied, since those were added to the law by Christ as additions.

units.la: XXVII. Num Christus, praeter legem, alia quaedam tulerit praecepta moralia? videlicet
units.tr: XXVII. Did Christ, besides the law, give certain other moral precepts, namely:

units.la: I. De sui abnegatione.
units.tr: I. Concerning self-denial.

units.la: II. Tolerantiâ crucis.
units.tr: II. Concerning bearing the cross.

units.la: III. Denique imitatione Christi? Neg.
units.tr: III. Finally, concerning imitation of Christ? No.

units.la: XXVIII. An Christus passione suâ pro peccatis nostris vere satisfecerit, & salutem meritus nobis sit? Aff.
units.tr: XXVIII. Did Christ truly satisfy for our sins by his passion, and merit salvation for us? Yes.

units.la: XXIX. Num Deus propter opera, vel obedientiam praeceptorum Christi, hominem justificet? Neg.
units.tr: XXIX. Does God justify a man because of works, or because of obedience to the precepts of Christ? No.

units.la: An verò propter imputatam ei, per fidem, justitiam Christi? Aff.
units.tr: But rather because the righteousness of Christ is imputed to him through faith? Yes.

units.la: XXX. An vera probitas sit naturalis, & naturaliter acquisita? Neg.
units.tr: XXX. Is true uprightness natural, and acquired naturally? No.

units.la: An verò à Spiritu Sancto, & singulari ejus efficaciâ hominem actu convertente? Aff. XXXI. Num sint aliqui homines adeo perfecti, ut non peccent? Neg. XXXII. Num aliqua peccata sint per se venialia? Neg. XXXIII. Num renati & fideles plene quidem deficiant à Deo, & ab omni ejus gratiâ? Neg.
units.tr: But rather is it from the Holy Spirit, and from his singular efficacy actually converting the man? Yes. XXXI. Are there any men so perfect that they do not sin? No. XXXII. Are some sins venial in themselves? No. XXXIII. Do the reborn and faithful indeed fall away entirely from God and from all his grace? No.

units.la: XXXIV. Num homini regenito peccanti, & in peccatum crebrius relabenti, quantumvis id doleat & deploret, nullus aditus pateat ad poenitentiam, & ad gratiam Novi foederis, sive misericordiam Dei, & remissionem peccatorum impetrandam? Neg.
units.tr: XXXIV. Is there no access to repentance, and to the grace of the New Covenant, or to the mercy of God and the obtaining of forgiveness of sins, for a reborn man who sins and often relapses into sin, however much he grieves and laments it? No.

units.la: XXXV. Num investigare Ecclesiam, ubi, & apud quos sit, prorsus non sit necessarium, sed propemodum, vel quodammodo inutile? Neg.
units.tr: XXXV. Is it entirely unnecessary, or almost or somewhat useless, to investigate where and among whom the Church is? No.

units.la: XXXVI. Annon professio verae doctrinae nota sit Ecclesiae? Aff.
units.tr: XXXVI. Is the profession of true doctrine not a mark of the Church? Yes.

units.la: XXXVII. Num omnis Ecclesia plane deficere ex mundo possit, ut nulla sit, vel aliquando non fuerit? Neg.
units.tr: XXXVII. Can any Church utterly fail from the world, so that it is no longer, or at some time was not? No.

units.la: XXXVIII. An ad obeundum Sacrum in Ecclesiâ ministerium, necessaria sit vocatio? Aff.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Is a call necessary for undertaking the sacred ministry in the Church? Yes.

units.la: XXXIX. Num baptismus & Coena sacramenta sint, gratiam Dei fidelibus obsignantia & confirmantia? an vero nudae duntaxat fidei professiones, & gratiarum actio? Aff. prius; Neg. posterius.
units.tr: XXXIX. Are baptism and the Lord's Supper sacraments, sealing and confirming God's grace to believers, or are they merely professions of faith and acts of thanksgiving? Yes to the first; no to the second.

units.la: XL. Num Baptismus sit res indifferens, non praecepta? Neg.
units.tr: XL. Is baptism an indifferent thing, and not a precept? No.

units.la: XLI. An etiam fidelium infantes baptizandi? Aff.
units.tr: XLI. Are the infants of believers also to be baptized? Yes.

units.la: XLII. Num prohibitum sit Christiano Magistratui mortis supplicio reum afficere? vel etiam belligerare? Neg.
units.tr: XLII. Is it forbidden to a Christian magistrate to inflict the punishment of death on a criminal, or even to wage war? No.

units.la: XLIII. Num animae post hanc vitam nec subsistant per se, nec vivant, aut sentiant? Neg.
units.tr: XLIII. Do souls after this life neither subsist of themselves, nor live, nor feel? No.

units.la: XLIV. An in resurrectione eadem corpora sint resurrectura? Aff.
units.tr: XLIV. Will the same bodies rise again in the resurrection? Yes.

units.la: xlv. Num improborum poena infernalis nullum cruciatum dicat, solam annihilationem? Neg.
units.tr: XLV. Does the punishment of the wicked in hell involve no torment, only annihilation? No.

units.la: Liber Octavus, DE REMONSTRANTIBUS.
units.tr: Book Eight, ON THE REMONSTRANTS.

units.la: Periodi tres controversiae de Praedestinatione, de Arminio. Vorstio. Simone Episcopio. Remonstrantium nomen. Apologia Socinianismus, de ipsorum tolerantia. Prudenter discernendi ut homines, ita & controversiae ipsorum. Responsio brevis, adversus libellum A. F. P.
units.tr: Three periods of the controversy on predestination, and concerning Arminius, Vorstius, and Simon Episcopius. The name Remonstrants. Their Apology. Socinianism, and the Remonstrants' tolerance. Controversies, like men, must be discerned prudently. A brief response against the little book of A. F. P.

units.la: Ontroversiae de Praedestinatione, quaeque huc spectant, tres in Ecclesia fuerunt magis celebres periodi. Prima, tempore Augustini, adversus Pelagianos, inde & Semi Pelagianos in Gallia, ab anno ccccv. Deinde, saeculo nono, ab anno dccc l. cum Gotschalco, Monacho Orbacensi, Augustini sententiam sequente, & impugnato varie ab Hincmaro, Rabano Mauro, Ioh. Erigena Scoto, aliis, sed & defenso, non minori cum studio, a Remigio, episcopo Lugdunensi, Floro, Prudentio Tricassino &c. tum Synodis etiam pro hac, & illa sententia coactis, agitatisque. Demum hoc saeculo, ab anno cIↄIↄcIII. quo tempore Iacobus Arminius, (nomen vernaculum erat Iacobus Hermanni, quod in Arminium mutarat) Veteraquinas, in Academia Leidensi Professor Theologus damnatam olim ab Ecclesia sententiam renovavit, & contentiones & dissidia illa in Belgicis Ecclesiis mota sunt, ex quibus Schisma Remonstranticum postea enatum fuit. In Arminio quidem mitior animus, & nec ad tot alias opiniones. nes, extra circum Prædestinationis, cujus in doctrinâ rite explicandâ semper hæserat, nimium suis propriis extra Dei verbum, & communem docendi in Ecclesiâ modum speculationibus, neque ad tantas turbas, ac discipuli ejus post ipsum concitandas inclinare visus: interim tamen, ut qui semel compagem aliquam luxant, ad dissolvenda alia prurisse deprehensus fuit, cum aliunde, tum ex Epistola, & articulis perpendendis ad Hippolytum à Collibus. Et Declaratione sententiæ, & Responsione ad xxxi. articulos. Vivere desiit Arminius, a. clɔ Iɔ c ix. In cujus locum designatus quidem erat Conradus Vorstius, sed quum tempestive se prodidisset, præsertim in libro de Deo, non tantum quas partes turbasque foturus esset adversus recte sentientes & docentes in doctrinâ Prædestinationis, sed hæresi Socini imbutum pectus, & varia opinionum monstra à se alii, de quibus & Ecclesiæ nostræ, & Rex Magnæ Britanniæ Iacobus Illustriss. Belg. Ordines monendos existimabant, nunquam hic muneri, ad quod quidem vocatus erat, & cujus occupandi causa Leidam jam cum familiâ suâ venerat, admonitus fuit. Unde factum, quod eam postea Socinianî, ad capessendam apud ipsos Theologiæ professionem, invitarint: quæ in Appendice ad Tom. I. Socinianismi Confut. plenius, ubi ostendendum mihi fuit, quomodo sub nomine Remonstrantium (quo pacto se ipsos lubenter appellant, aut Remonstranto-Reformatos, uti in inscriptione Catechesis suæ: illud nomen ab anno clɔ Iɔ c x. acceperunt ex libello, seu Remonstrantiâ, uti vulgo dicimus, Ordinibus Hollandiæ oblatâ, quam in Collatione Hagiensi, anni seq. clɔ Iɔ c xi. & apud Baudartium in Historiâ, legere est) tum à Vorstio, tum ab aliis, Socinianismus in nostris Ecclesiis innotescere & doceri cœperit.
units.tr: There have been three periods of controversy on predestination and related questions that were especially notable in the Church. The first, in the time of Augustine, was against the Pelagians, and then against the Semi-Pelagians in Gaul, from the year 425. The second came in the ninth century, from the year 850, with Gottschalk, a monk of Orbais, who followed Augustine's opinion. He was attacked in various ways by Hincmar, Rabanus Maurus, John Scotus Erigena, and others, but was also defended with no less zeal by Remigius, bishop of Lyons, Florus, Prudentius of Troyes, and others. Synods were also convened and stirred up for and against this opinion. Finally, in this century, from the year 1603, when Jacobus Arminius (his native name was Jacob Hermanni, which he had changed into Arminius), professor of theology at the Academy of Leiden, renewed an opinion once condemned by the Church, the contentions and dissensions arose in the Belgic churches, and from them the Remonstrant schism later sprang. In Arminius the spirit was indeed milder. He did not seem inclined to so many other opinions outside the circle of predestination, in whose correct explanation he had always stuck, nor to such great disturbances, nor to those his disciples stirred up after him. Yet, as those who have once dislocated some joint are found eager to dissolve others, he was found to do so, both elsewhere and in his Letter, in the Articles to be weighed for Hippolytus a Collibus, in his Declaration of Sentiments, and in his Response to the thirty-one articles. Arminius ceased to live in 1609. Conrad Vorstius had indeed been designated to take his place, but when he revealed himself in good time, especially in his book On God, it became clear not only what parts and disturbances he would stir up against those who rightly thought and taught on predestination, but also that his breast was steeped in the heresy of Socinus and in various monstrous opinions. Our Church and King James of Great Britain, most illustrious, and the States of Belgium thought others should be warned about these. Yet he was never admonished in this office, to which he had indeed been called, and for taking which he had already come to Leiden with his household. Hence it happened that the Socinians afterwards invited him to take up the professorship of theology among them. I have shown this more fully in the Appendix to the first volume of my Confutation of Socinianism, where I had to show how, under the name of the Remonstrants (by which name they gladly call themselves, or Remonstrant-Reformed, as in the title of their Catechism), Socinianism began to become known and taught in our churches, both through Vorstius and through others. They received that name from the year 1610, from the little book, or Remonstrance, as we commonly call it, offered to the States of Holland. It can be read in the Hague Conference of the following year, 1611, and in Baudartius' History.

units.la: In quo haud segnem operam à Simone Episcopio etiam collocatam, nemo inficiabitur. Episcopius ipse, de quo similiter, loco jam à me assignato, dixi, sedulus Arminii discipulus, cuique sua studia potissimum debebat, in locum Francisci Gomari Leidam accitus fuit a. MDCXI. atque postquam à Synodo Dordracenâ a. MDCXIX. una cum aliis Remonstrantium Doctoribus munere exauctoratus fuit, tamen invitâ & Ecclesiâ & Rep. Rotterodamum primùm, inde Amstelodamum, ut Remonstrantium seminario praeesset, & juvenes qui in spem Ecclesiae alauntur in Theologiâ institueret, uti palam de eo loquitur Stephanus Curcellæus, in praefatione Operum Episcopii, repedavit; atque ne Praedestinationis negotium parum Schismati videretur, SocinIana dogmata passim ita suis immiscuit, ut & Remonstrantium fecerit, & Sectæ affricarit, quam ducebat. Hinc, ne Confessionem dicam, quam ita ambiguam & laxam fecit, ut sub eâ, quemadmodum patuit, satis tuto praesidio Socinianismus lateret, Apologiam illius, seu Socinianismi novam Confessionem edidit, Remonstrantium omnium nomine. In quo nescio an gravius peccarit Auctor, an Societas Remonstrantium, quod suo nomine si verint prodire scriptum, quod Socinianismo à fronte & tergo ita totum insignitum, ut manifestissimo fuerit argumento non Arminianismum magis, quam Socinianismum ab ipsis teneri, plusque ab Arminio istos, quam Arminius unquam à Nostris, discessisse. Quid attinebat, ut Episcopius, qui quantopere in scriptis Socinianorum studuerit, & ex illis omnia sua addiderit, in libris nostris contra Socinianos ostendo, in scriptis suis vel alias extra notas controversias adoptaret, & praecipue damnatam Socinianorum haeresim, vel ad hanc nomen Societatis obtenderet, quasi hujus essent, quae adeo non probata sint, ut ne quidem intellecta, & nomen Socinianum ipsorum plurimi adhuc ex animo horreant? Numquid non satis turbarum datum erat per dogmata Arminiana, ut SocinIana insuper in auxilium venire deberent? vel quare non suo solius illa nomine exposuit Epifcopius, suo periculo, immuni ab ista labe servata hactenus Societate, quam certum est nunquam in illa, præter Arminiana, dogmatum capita rogatam unquam, vel consensisse, ut hujus nomine non magis debuerint illa prostare, quam nec suo? Sed hoc spectavit versipellis Auctor, ut venenum suum toti coetui hoc pacto communicaret, & impingeret nomini Remonstrantium, quæ sibi gravius fuisset seorsim ferre. Hinc in Ecclesiam istam, per Doctores suos discipulos Episcopii, plana via hæresis illa subintravit: ut suo exemplo docuerit, non debere unquam coetum ita se tradere τοῖς ἡγεμόσιν, ut pro arbitrio trahant illum in ignota sibi dogmata, suoque ad quamcunque formandam religionem & sectam abutantur nomine. Non ferrent nostri homines, & bene hoc quidem, ut aliquis Reformatam religionem defensurus peregrina intermisceret dogmata, sed & librum talem & auctorem juberent res habere suas, & palam dissensum suum testarentur ocyus atque innocentiam. Nihil etiam necesse est, ut qui Apologiam scribit, ad hoc semper utatur nomine eorum, pro quibus scribit, satis est proprio nomine egisse, ut ad eum solum redeat culpa minus recte à sedatorum, non ad Ecclesiam, vel Societatem. Ut magna Remonstrantium hic fuerit imprudentia, quod siverunt Episcopii Apologiam heterodoxiis variis intertextam prodire suo publico nomine. Quod videre forsan in Apologia Catechesis suæ, per eundem Auctorem scripta, quam post ejus mortem ediderunt, sed non suo, at auctoris Episcopii solius præscripto nomine. Quod æque potuissent facere, imo & longe sanctius fuisset, in scripta Confessionis Apologia, adversus Leidenses Professores, atque in Catechesis suæ alia, adversus Heidanum. Sed turbidi, paradoxi, & mordacis ingenii vir erat Episcopius, ad serendas augendasque contentiones, non ad componendas factus, & cui quale quale caput, certe non adfuit animus Theo-logi logi, id quod in omni tractatione satis evidenter oftendit. Non enim graves & arduas quaestiones de Dei praedestinatione, aliasque Theologicas cum omni reverentia suscipiendas, pro dignitate tractavit, ut homines vel Dei Spiritu, vel argumenti sensu tactum dixisses; sed scurriliter, sed dicacitèr, tamquam res nihili vel levissima ageretur: ut ipse Curcellaeus fateri necesse habeat, forte quaedam leviter dici potuerint, quae ab eo factum fuerit. Neque in Adversarios causa rejici ulla specie potest tam inhonestae tractationis, non dico ipsorum Adversariorum, quod neque etiam decet, sed rei quae agebatur, altissimae & tremendae. Adeo ut, tum per assumta Socinianae haeresis varia dogmata, eaque defensa, tum per acrem & severam Nostros tractandi rationem, seu in scriptis, seu aliter, & ipse & alii ridiculum fecerint suum de tolerantia tantopere jactatâ ὀνομα.
units.tr: No one will deny that Simon Episcopius also devoted no idle effort to this. Episcopius himself, of whom I have already spoken in its proper place, was a diligent disciple of Arminius, to whose studies he was especially bound. He was summoned to Leiden in 1611 in place of Francis Gomarus. After the Synod of Dort in 1619 deposed him from office, together with other teachers of the Remonstrants, he nevertheless, against the wishes of both the Church and the State, went first to Rotterdam and then to Amsterdam, to preside over the Remonstrant seminary and to train the young men who were being reared as the hope of the Church in theology. Stephanus Curcellaeus openly says this in the preface to the Works of Episcopius. And so that the matter of predestination should not seem too slight a cause of schism, he mixed Socinian doctrines everywhere among his own, so thoroughly that he both made them his own and bound the sect he led to them. Here I will not mention his Confession, which he made so ambiguous and lax that, as became clear, Socinianism could lie hidden under it with fairly safe protection. He published his Apology, or new Confession of Socinianism, in the name of all the Remonstrants. In this I do not know whether the author sinned more gravely or the Remonstrant body did, in allowing a writing to come out under their own name which was so stamped from front to back with Socinianism.
