It was a very clear proof that they held not so much Arminianism as Socinianism, and that these men had departed further from Arminius than Arminius had ever departed from our people. What was the point of Episcopius, who studied the writings of the Socinians so zealously and drew all his own additions from them, in our books against the Socinians, but in his own writings to adopt, even outside the well-known controversies, especially the condemned heresy of the Socinians? Or to put forward the name of the Society for it, as if these were its own doctrines, when they are so far from being approved that they are not even understood, and very many still abhor the name Socinian from their hearts? Was there not already enough trouble from Arminian doctrines, that Socinian ones should have to come in to help as well? Or why did Episcopius not set out those teachings under his own name alone, at his own risk, leaving the Society, hitherto kept free of that stain, untouched? It is certain that the Society was never asked, beyond the main heads of Arminian doctrine, and never agreed, that these things should be put forward under its name any more than under his own. But the wily author aimed at this: that he might communicate his poison to the whole body in this way and thrust it upon the name of the Remonstrants, which would have been harder for him to bear alone. Hence that heresy found a smooth path into this Church through Episcopius' disciples who taught doctrine. By his example he showed that a body should never so surrender itself to its leaders [τοῖς ἡγεμόσιν] that they may drag it at will into doctrines unknown to it, and misuse its name for forming whatever religion and sect they please. Our people would not tolerate this, and rightly so: that someone who was to defend the Reformed religion should mix foreign doctrines into it. They would order such a book and its author to be disowned, and would quickly and openly bear witness to their dissent and innocence. Nor is it at all necessary that one who writes an Apology should always use the name of those for whom he writes. It is enough to have acted under his own name, so that the blame for what was done less rightly falls back on him alone, as one of those who stirred things up, and not on the Church or the Society. Great as the Remonstrants' imprudence was here, in allowing Episcopius' Apology, interwoven with various heterodoxies, to come out under their public name, perhaps they saw this too in the Apology for his Catechism, written by the same author, which they published after his death, but under the name of Episcopius alone, as he had prescribed. They could equally well have done the same, and indeed it would have been much more honourable, with the Apology for the Confession, written against the Leiden professors, and the other Catechism, written against Heidanus. But Episcopius was a man of turbulent, paradoxical and biting genius, made for stirring up and increasing contentions rather than for settling them. Whatever his natural endowments, he certainly lacked the spirit of a theologian, as he shows quite clearly in every treatment. For he did not handle the grave and difficult questions of God's predestination and other theological matters, which must be taken up with all reverence, in a manner worthy of their dignity, so that one would have said he was moved either by the Spirit of God or by a sense of the subject. Instead he treated them jestingly and flippantly, as if the matter were of no account or of the slightest importance. So Curcellaeus himself is compelled to confess: "Perhaps some things may have been said lightly, which were done by him." Nor can any excuse be offered for so dishonourable a treatment on the part of the adversaries. I do not mean the adversaries themselves, for that also is not fitting, but the matter that was being dealt with, which is most lofty and awe-inspiring. So that, both by taking up and defending the various doctrines of the Socinian heresy, and by the sharp and severe manner in which they dealt with our men, whether in writing or otherwise, both he and others have made ridiculous their much-boasted name of tolerance [ὄνομα].

units.la: Quid quaeso illud est tolerantiae, quod adeo sibi proprium vendicant Remonstrantes, ut hinc dignosci suam sectam, praeque aliis commendari, velint? Summa huc redit, inquit Curcellaeus, Episcopii successor & praeco, Cum Christiani in praecipuis & fundamentalibus Religionis dogmatibus inter se consentiant, eum qui superest in aliis minoris momenti dissensum impedire non debere, quo minus in unum Ecclesiae corpus coëant, & se ut fratres mutuâ in Christo charitate prosequantur. Si modo qui ista magni aestimant, caeteros diversum sentientes ad ea suscipienda non cogant. Hac enim est tyrannis in Ecclesiâ non ferenda: cujus qui rei sunt, fundamentum evertere & fraternitatis vinculum abrumpere censendi sunt. Quod etiam de idololatris dictum volo. Quae de tyrannide illâ dicit, nullis magis convenire quam suis, apparuit, quando in initio tumultuum non nostros solum Doctores non ferebant, sed tum locis suis extrudebant, tum gravissime persequebantur, multabantque homines (quod & hic factum) etiam extra urbes ad concionem audiendam placidè pièque progredientes. diendam placidè pièque progredientes. Quod de idololatris in unum coetum secum agendis, optime mentem ipsorum explicat, & qualis hinc Ecclesia oritura sit, ostendit: videlicet haræ alicujus instar, vel quale lararium Adriani fuisse dicitur, ubi inter idola etiam Christus aliquis apparuit. Non hoc de idololatris vel ipse Socinus admitteret. Et si institui ejusmodi debet Ecclesia, quid adeo Paulus interdixit communione Christi & Belial, ideo quod nulla συγκατάθεσις templo Dei cum idolis, non magis quam luci cum tenebris, nec justitiæ cum iniquitate? 11. Cor. vi. 14. 15. 16.
units.tr: What, I ask, is this "tolerance" that the Remonstrants claim so much as their own, so that they wish their sect to be known by it and commended above others? Curcellaeus, Episcopius's successor and herald, sums it up: Since Christians agree with one another on the chief and fundamental doctrines of religion, the dissent that remains on matters of lesser importance should not prevent them from coming together into one body of the Church and embracing one another as brothers in the mutual charity of Christ, provided that those who value these things highly do not compel others who think differently to accept them. For this tyranny is not to be tolerated in the Church; those who are guilty of it are to be judged to overthrow the foundation and sever the bond of brotherhood. I wish the same to be said of idolaters. That what he says about this tyranny applies to no one more than to his own side has become clear. At the start of the disturbances they not only would not put up with our teachers, but both drove them from their posts and persecuted them most severely, and they fined people (as happened here too) who had gone out peacefully and piously even beyond the cities to hear a sermon. As for his plan to bring idolaters together into one assembly, it explains his mind very well and shows what kind of Church would arise from it: something like a mixed shrine, or like the household chapel of Hadrian, where, it is said, a certain Christ appeared among the idols. Socinus himself would not admit such a thing about idolaters. And if a Church of this kind is to be set up, why did Paul forbid any fellowship between Christ and Belial, and any agreement [συγκατάθεσις] between the temple of God and idols, just as there is no fellowship between light and darkness, or between righteousness and iniquity? 2 Cor. 6:14, 15, 16.

units.la: Hactenus Reformati idololatris præsertim applicuere verba illa sequentia: ideo exite è medio ipsorum & separamini, inquit Dominus; & immundum ne attingite: atque ego excipiam vos. Iam Reformati qui volent etiam dici, cum idololatris una eundem, & idem incolendum templum, inque idem Ecclesiæ corpus omnibus coeundum esse docebunt? atque alios à se condemnabunt Reformatos, qui hoc nec faciunt ipsi, neque faciendum arbitrantur? Qui hoc quaeso, vel cum professione Reformationis, vel cum puritate cultus divini, & dignitate Ecclesiæ Christi conciliari potest? Dices quidem non te velle reformare Papismum, & illorum aliorumve ideo probare idololatriam, sed siquidem ipsi ferre vos dissentientes in animum inducant, concordiæ locum fore. Ego verò quin facile jam hoc tempore & loco vobis, illâ etiam sub conditione, accessuri sint Pontificii, haud dubito. Agite ergo, & cum illis sub eundem vos abripite pileum, mali bonique æquum tegumentum. Saltem hinc singulos etiam Remonstrantium debere primum nos, nostrasque Ecclesias adire, visuri annon illos admittere in communionem nostram velimus, ne scindere videantur Ecclesiæ unionem, à quâ ipsorum ἀποστασίας abierunt, & ipsos nunc deterrent, cujusque adhuc nomen retinere cupiunt, sequitur. Et non eodem pacto Ecclesias nostras sententie de omniomnibus illorum dogmatibus & hominibus, ipsi non ignorant, ut non putandum sit, quia aliqua per nonnullos ipsorum tradita dogmata extra communionem nostram ponimus,& Doctores illorum, atque pro ratione temporis locique major sollicitudo incumbit,quod erga seductos simpliciter, & in solo praedestinationis negotio rite cognoscendo haerentes,(cui vulgo causam Scismatis tribuere solent) & non factionibus sed pacis studentes, & erga dociles Ecclesia non omni benignitate utatur & prudentia. Quod autem Remonstrantes pro fundamento substernunt suae illius tolerantiae vel potius confusionis promiscuae, omnes hodie Christiano nomine appellatos convenire in fundamentalibus & praecipuis Religionis dogmatibus, quam vanum sit, alibi prolixe, & quam id non ex communi, quod omnes accipiunt, Symbolo sequatur, ostendi. Sententiae illius fundamentum haud aliud est, quam quo nititur Libertinismus, quem tamen videri voluit Episcopius egregie effellisse, lib. IV. Institut. Theol. Sect. 1. cap. XII. XIII. scilicet hoc, quod religiones omnes fere uno sint habendae ordine. Ita disputat in hac Oper. Episcopii praesatione Curcellaeus, ut pares in veritatis vindicatione faciat Calvinistas, (sic pro solita in nos acerbitate loquuntur, quum satis norint nomen hoc nec a Nobis accipi, nec probari: nemo Nostrum se Calvinistam dixit, aut inscripsit, uti illi se Remonstrantes: & qua ratione ipsi se Reformatos adhuc appellant, quam quod aliquando in Ecclesia nostra fuerunt, ex qua temere abierant?) Lutheranos, Pontificios, Mennonitas, Socinianos, eccur non addidit Remonstrantes? vel an judicio decisum est ab horum parte stare veritatem? vel annon alii aeque Remonstrantibus abjudicabunt veritatem, ac hi illis? quod ejus argumentum est, quo hic disputat. Ego autem regero, iniquissimam illam agendi rationem esse, ex aliorum affirmatione aut negatione suspendere rei cujuscunque veritatem, nedum religionis. Alii dicunt se veritatem tenere, & hi, isti, illis verum quid tum? ergo incerta est veritas? Si argumentum tuum pressim sequare, eviceris, nullam esse uspiam veritatem, nam nulłibi tam certa erit, quin insurgent alii, & multi, imo & potissima hominum pars, qui reclamabunt. Quid ergo, quales nos vis homines, scepticos omnes, & quovis vento περιφερόμενοι Ephes. IV. 14.? absit. Sume rem tuam aliquam terrestrem, mundanam, quam certum habeas tuam esse: an ideo cedes, si forte quispiam vel multi etiam controversiam moveant? veritas rei vel certitudo pendet ex opinione adversantis? Dices, hoc certum mihi, illa non. Nempe id revera est, ideo quod incerti estis religionis vestrae, putatis alios verae certos esse non posse. Ad eundem modum quo Papistae, quia ipsi salutis certi esse nec secundum doctrinam suam possunt, neque juxta aliam volunt, opinantur nos salutis certitudinem habere non posse. An ideo nos veritatem doctrinae istius nostrae de certitudine salutis trademus, quod Pontificii eam multis argumentis impugnant; vel ejusne idcirco cedemus certitudinem? & tuum tamen hic etiam obtinebit argumentum, quod Pontificius tam dicet veram esse thesim suam, ac nos nostram. Vides ergo falsam illam esse regulam, quod nequeat constare veritatis certitudo, vel quod haec tum minor sit, ubi alii obloquuntur. Sed inter Christianos opinionibus inter se dissentientes nondum ullo ἀναμφιλέκτῳ judicio est decisum, a quorum parte stet veritas, inquis. Fac conclusionem: ergo nescitur inter Christianos, a quorum parte stet veritas. O abominandam thesim, omnem uno ictu religionem & Ecclesiis, & hominibus profane auferentem. Et quid aliud inferes? nam duo dicis: nondum inter Christianos dissidentes decisum esse a quorum parte stet veritas. Saltem tuam jam causam tradis, & non constare fateris a vestra parte stare veritatem. Tum quae causa & scandalum hinc praebetur Pontificiis inclamandi, quare ergo reformatis, & incertæ opinioni superstitiis certam Reformationem, quam & ipsis persuaderi, serio velim perpendite. Dein dicis, illud haud decisum judicio [illegible, ~8 letters]. Imo in Scripturis omnino: & hoc satis est. Extra eas quid attinet alium judicem exstare, aut quærere? habemus Mosem, habemus Prophetas, insuper & Christum, & Apostolos, quibus illi haud sufficiunt, non veritatem quærunt vel apud quos illa sit, sed tergiversari & vexare. Sed illi non interponunt judicium inter Christianos dissidentes: itane? Reformatus hoc nemo dicat. Pontificiorum themata novimus, quod hic alia sint. An tu negabis, Scripturam decidere, à cujus parte stet veritas, dum alius pro Purgatorio disputat, alius contra, dum unus Sanctos invocandos contendit, alter non, & sic de cæteris? Ego populi istius vices ex animo doleo, qui per tales Doctorum suorum hypotheses in incerta omnia & dubia trahitur, & cui non licet firmâ animi fiducia & [illegible, ~8 letters] amplecti fidei veritatem atque certitudinem. Aliter longè nos docet Dei verbum, aliter ipsius religionis natura & gravitas. Hoc Remonstrantismus, præter alia, mali habet haud vulgaris, quod animos hominum in religionis negotio reddit adeo incertos, lubricos, indifferentes, & de religione ut de re quadam communi, aut fere quasi de secta aliquâ philosophicâ judicantes, ad hominum ingenia, & promiscuam cum omnibus conversationem, & appetitum, non ad naturam illius divinam, cœlestemque. Quando inquit: Si Calvinistæ iniquum esse putant se à Pontificiis aut Lutheranis damnari, quæ id sibi jure in illos aut alios quoscunque usurpant? ipsa certè naturalis æquitas dictat: quod quisque juris in alterum etc. Quasi de re aliquâ propriâ, ubi alterius in alterum jus spectatur, & non de religione, cujus grave & [illegible, ~6 letters] in omnes est imperium, tum ac si in veritatis dissidio par jus sit Pontificiis, atque Reformatis, (quod hos profecto pudendum est asserere) ita loquitur. Damnare si exci-
units.tr: Up to now the Reformed have applied those following words chiefly to idolaters: Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you. Now, will Reformed men who want to be called such teach that everyone must be gathered together with idolaters, and that the same temple and the same body of the Church must be shared with them, and will they condemn other Reformed men who do not do this themselves and do not think it should be done? Who, I ask, can reconcile this either with a profession of the Reformation, or with the purity of divine worship and the dignity of the Church of Christ? You will say that you do not wish to reform Papism, nor thereby to approve the idolatry of them or of others, but that if they allow you to dissent, there will be room for concord. But I have no doubt that the Papists would readily come to you even now, in this time and place, even on that condition. Come then, and let them snatch you under the same cap, the cloak that suits the bad and good alike. At least from this, it follows that each of the Remonstrants must first come to us and to our Churches, to see whether we would admit them to our communion, lest they seem to split the unity of the Church from which they have gone out in their [ἀποστασίας] apostasy, and which they now shun, while still wanting to keep its name. And they are not unaware that our Churches do not judge all of their doctrines and people by the same standard. So we should not think that, because we place some doctrines taught by certain of them outside our communion, we are therefore to use no kindness or prudence towards their teachers, and towards those who are simply led astray and cling only to the proper understanding of the matter of predestination (which people commonly blame for the schism), who seek peace rather than factions, and towards the teachable. The greater concern, given the time and place, is rightly to be felt for these people. As for the Remonstrants' foundation of that tolerance of theirs, or rather their indiscriminate confusion, namely that all who today are called by the Christian name agree on the fundamental and chief doctrines of religion, I have shown elsewhere at length how vain this is, and that it does not follow from the common creed that everyone accepts. The basis of that view is nothing other than what supports Libertinism, which Episcopius nevertheless wished to seem to have skilfully refuted: Lib. IV. Institut. Theol., Sect. 1, cap. XII, XIII, namely that all religions should be regarded as more or less in one rank. Curcellaeus argues this in his preface to Episcopius's works in such a way as to make the Calvinists equal in defending the truth. (They speak this way out of their usual bitterness towards us, although they know well that this name is neither accepted nor approved by us. None of us has called himself or written himself a Calvinist, as those Remonstrants do. And why do they still call themselves Reformed, except that they were once in our Church, from which they rashly departed?) Why did he not add the Remonstrants to the Lutherans, the Papists, the Mennonites and the Socinians? Or has it been decided by judgment that truth stands on their side? Or will not others deny truth to the Remonstrants just as they deny it to those others? That is the argument on which he reasons here. I, however, reply that it is a most unjust way of proceeding to make the truth of any matter whatever, let alone of religion, depend on the affirmation or denial of others. Some say they hold the truth, and these say the opposite of those. So what follows? Is truth therefore uncertain? If you follow your argument closely, you will prove that there is no truth anywhere, for it will never be so certain anywhere that others will not rise up, and many, indeed the greater part of mankind, who will object. What then? Do you want us to be a people all sceptical, and carried about by every wind [περιφερόμενοι] (Eph. 4:14)? Far from it. Take some earthly, worldly matter that you hold to be certainly yours. Will you give it up if perhaps someone, or even many, raise a dispute? Does the truth or certainty of a thing depend on the opinion of an opponent? You will say, "This is certain to me, that is not." Indeed that is so, because you are uncertain of your own religion, and you think others cannot be certain of the true one. In the same way the Papists, because they can be certain of salvation neither by their own doctrine nor by any other they wish to accept, suppose that we cannot have certainty of salvation. Shall we therefore surrender the truth of our doctrine of the certainty of salvation, because the Papists attack it with many arguments? Or shall we give up certainty on that account? And your argument will still hold here too, for the Papist will say that his thesis is as true as ours is ours. So you see that the rule is false, that the certainty of truth cannot be established, or that it is less when others speak against it. But among Christians who differ in their opinions, no decision has yet been reached by any [ἀναμφιλέκτῳ] undisputed judgment as to which side truth stands on, you say. Draw your conclusion: therefore it is not known among Christians on which side truth stands. O abominable thesis, which at a single blow strips religion, Churches and men of all that is sacred! And what else will you infer? For you are saying two things: that it has not yet been decided among Christians who disagree on which side truth stands. At least you are now putting forward your own cause, and you admit that it is not established that truth stands on your side. Then what cause and what scandal is thereby given to the Papists to cry out why the Reformed should seek a certain Reformation, which they themselves are persuaded of, while placing their trust in an uncertain opinion. I would like you to weigh this seriously. Next you say that this has not been decided by any judgment [illegible in the scan]. Indeed, it has been decided by the Scriptures entirely, and that is enough. What is the point of looking for or hoping for another judge outside them? We have Moses, we have the Prophets, and besides these Christ and the Apostles, and these are not enough for those men, who do not seek the truth or ask where it is, but evade it and harass others. But they do not interpose a judgment between Christians who disagree, you say? Does no Reformed man say this? We know the theses of the Papists, which are different here. Will you deny that Scripture decides on which side truth stands, when one man argues for Purgatory and another against it, when one insists that the Saints are to be invoked and another does not, and so on for the rest? I sincerely grieve for the lot of that people, who are dragged by such hypotheses of their teachers into everything uncertain and doubtful, and who are not allowed to embrace the truth and certainty of faith with a firm confidence of mind [illegible in the scan]. God's Word teaches us quite otherwise, and so does the very nature and weight of religion. Remonstrantism, among its other evils, has this uncommon one: it makes men's minds in matters of religion so unsettled, slippery and indifferent, and so judges religion as a common matter, or nearly as a philosophical sect, that they fit it to human temperaments, to promiscuous association with everyone, and to appetite, not to its divine and heavenly nature. When he says: If the Calvinists think it unfair that they should be condemned by the Papists or the Lutherans, by what right do they claim this against those or any others? Surely natural equity itself dictates that whatever right one has against another, etc. He speaks as if of some private matter, where the right of one party against another is in view, and not of religion, whose grave authority [illegible in the scan] extends over all, as if, in a dispute about truth, the Papists had an equal right with the Reformed (which the Reformed would certainly be ashamed to assert). To condemn, if you wish, the distinction is ready at hand, and a very well-known one, between the thing and the person: where the thing is evil, as Popery is in the Church, we condemn it, but we do not condemn the men. And this is not the question now, but the knowledge, certainty and triumph of truth against...

units.la: Oo 4 ... pias, in promtu est destinctio, eaque notissima, rei, & personæ: illam ubi mala est, qualis Papismus in secerto est, damnamus, non tamen homines: & non de hoc jam quæritur, sed de veritatis notitia, certitudine, & triumpho adversus errores ac falsitatem, quæ damnanda omnibus semper est, id est, reprobanda, & cavenda.
units.tr: Oo 4 ... The distinction is ready to hand, and it is very well known: between the thing and the person. Where the thing is evil, as Popery is in its nature, we condemn it, but we do not condemn men. And the question now is not about this, but about the knowledge, certainty and triumph of truth against errors and falsehood, which must always be condemned by all, that is, rejected and avoided.

units.la: Ita nunc Reformatos audimus, iniquum dicere, quod Papismum damnamus? vel æquo jure licere Pontificiis nos damnare, doctrinamque nostram, ac nos illorum? Non hoc Arminius docuit in Disputatione sua, qua assertum ivit: Ecclesias Reformatas a Romana Ecclesia secessionem non fecisse: easque recte facere, quod fidei cultusque divini communionem cum eadem habere & profiteri debeant: neque Vorstius, quando scripsit suas de causis deserendi Papatus, non poenitendas Disputationes. Sed ita illos loqui, quos poeniteat Reformationis, & qui dummodo nobis ægre faciant, lubenter causam prostituunt & tradunt Pontificiis, oportet. Pergunt: Nec majori cum specie dici potest, singulis Magistratibus licere in sua ditione religionem quam probant summa vi tueri, & cæteras dissentientes eliminare. Si enim id licet in Hollandia Calvinistis, cur non quoque in Suecia, Dania, Saxonia Lutheranis, in Gallia, Italia, Hispania Pontificiis, imo in Turcia Mahometanis? in China & Japonia Ethnicis? Parum erat, religionem nostram componere cum Papistis, aliisque in Christianismo, ni etiam in parem ordinem redigeretur cum Muhammedana, & Ethnica. Nemo dicit, tuendam a Magistratu religionem quam probat, sed solam veram. Neque de vi summa, de coactione qua alii ad religionem adigantur, loquimur; sed de verae religionis (quam profanum est comparare cum Gentilium & Turcarum superstitionibus & infidelitate) jure, & comprobatione, quam veram certo sciri haberiqueposse jam dictum, & quo solo fundamento illud niti debet quod vel Magistratus, vel alii pro ejus defensione aut propagatione agunt. Quin tu censes veram religionem defendi à Magistratu Christiano non posse, neque aliquid ei agendum esse, pro religione Christi, etiam qua Magistratus est, quin idem liceat Gentili pro falsa non licere illi superstitiones aliaque mala religioni inimica arcere, & ut commode atque optime potest eliminare, nisi idem liceat Muhammedanis aut Gentilibus adversus Christum, & eius doctrinam? vel denique quod Reformatus Magistratus Papismum, quantum jure & commode potest, non debeat removere, quin idem aeque contra Reformationem concedendum sit ejus Adversariis? loquimur hic, quid liceat de jure, non quid in foro politico usu veniat. Ex quibus liquet, quam periculosa & pernitiosa sint Adversariorum de ista sua tolerantiae Pandora, quam tam late depraedicant, & immane adeo extendunt, ipsis quoque dum Reformati audire etiam volunt, & toti Christianae religioni, fidei nostrae, & veritati (per veritatem autem intelligo, non modo eam, quae ad salutem aeternam obtinendam necessaria est, sed omnem omnino veritatem, imprimis eam, quae ad divinam gloriam, salutem nostram, aliorumque aedificationem promovendam est necessaria, loquor cum Episcopio, respondente ad quaestionem ... ut alii quis propter Remonstrantium articulos, quos ad salutem esse necessarios non putat, perfectionis periculo se exponere temere, nunquam deserendam esse veritatem) denique & Christo domino adversantia thematā. Et vehementer tamen sibi placent in isthoc suo consilio, quasi unum sit ad conjungendos hominum animos, & minuendas inter Christianos lites ac dissidia remedium, vel mutuae, ut Episcopii verbum retineam, quod hac de re habet, in Examine Thesium Capelli: quum revera Christianae religionis opprobrium & pernitiem tendat, hoc si quod aliud, dum & vere religionis illam faciat incertitudinem, & parem ejus, cum quavis falsa, insuper & Ethnica ac Muhammedana conditionem. Quo magis deplorare saeco istorum hominum statum
units.tr: So now we hear the Reformed say: is it unjust for us to condemn Popery? Or is it equally lawful for the Papists to condemn us, and our doctrine as we condemn theirs? Arminius did not teach this in his Disputation, in which he undertook to maintain: that the Reformed Churches did not secede from the Roman Church, and that they act rightly in that they ought to have and profess communion with it in faith and the worship of God. Nor did Vorstius, when he wrote his On the causes of forsaking the Papacy, write disputations that he would need to repent of. But it is fitting that those speak thus who regret the Reformation, and who, provided only that they vex us, gladly betray the cause and hand it over to the Papists. They go on: Nor can it be said with greater plausibility that each magistrate may in his own territory defend with all his might the religion he approves, and drive out the others who dissent. For if this is allowed to the Calvinists in Holland, why not also to the Lutherans in Sweden, Denmark and Saxony, to the Papists in France, Italy and Spain, or even to the Mahometans in Turkey, and to the heathens in China and Japan? It was not enough to put our religion on a level with the Papists and others within Christianity, unless it were also reduced to the same rank as the Mahometan and the heathen. No one says that the magistrate should defend the religion he approves, but only the true one. Nor are we speaking of supreme force, or of compulsion by which others are driven into religion; we speak of the right of the true religion (which it is profane to compare with the superstitions and unbelief of the Gentiles and Turks), and of the approval which, as already said, can be known with certainty to be the true one, and on which alone whatever the magistrate, or others in its defence or propagation, do ought to rest. Or do you think that the true religion cannot be defended by a Christian magistrate, and that nothing is to be done by him for the religion of Christ, even though he is the magistrate; and that the same is not permitted to a heathen, who may not restrain superstitions and other evils hostile to religion, for the false religion, and remove them as conveniently and as well as he can, unless the same is permitted to the Mahometans or the heathens against Christ and his doctrine? Or finally, that a Reformed magistrate ought not to remove Popery as far as he lawfully and conveniently can, unless the same is equally to be conceded to its adversaries against the Reformation? We are speaking here of what is lawful by right, not of what happens in the practice of political affairs. From these things it is clear how dangerous and pernicious are the Pandora's boxes of our adversaries on this matter of toleration, which they proclaim so widely and extend so monstrously, to the detriment of the whole Christian religion, our faith and the truth (by truth I mean not only that which is necessary for obtaining eternal salvation, but all truth whatsoever, above all that which is necessary for promoting the divine glory, our salvation and the edification of others; I speak with Episcopius, answering the question ... that one should not rashly expose himself to the danger of perfection on account of the articles of the Remonstrants, which he does not think necessary to salvation, and that truth is never to be abandoned), and finally to the themes opposed to Christ our Lord. And yet they take great pleasure in this their plan, as if it were a single remedy for joining men's minds and lessening the quarrels and dissensions among Christians, or, to keep Episcopius's word which he uses about this in his Examen of Cappellus's Theses, mutual (remedy); whereas in truth it aims at the disgrace and ruin of the Christian religion, and this more than anything else, since it makes religion itself uncertain and puts it on a par with any false religion, and even with heathen and Mahometan belief. All the more must we deplore the state of these men, who are not instructed in the Christian religion by other teachers, and then the teachers themselves.

units.la: [Remark: the final line and the catchword are partly illegible in the scan; the transcription of the ellipsed and italic passages is approximate.] qui non aliis Doctoribus de religione Christiana instituuntur, tum & Doctores ipsos. Aliud est, disputare de tolerantia quinque istorum articulorum, ex quibus primum enatae lites, tum schisma; aliud, de vaga & universali tolerantia, pro qua nunc disputant, ad omnes Christianismi sectas, quantumcunque errantes ac adversantes, ipsosque etiam idololatras, in unum coetum cogendos; ne de infidelibus quod modo dictum, repetam. Initio disputatum de illa valde fuit, restrictaque semper ad contentionem quinquarticulanam. Sic V Vtenbogardus, in historia vitae suae, sic Grotius Apolog. cap. iv. & v. Nunc de hac etiam, prout quotidie dilapsi Adversarii fuerunt in alias aliasque opiniones & errores: nullibi certo unquam persistente extra Ecclesiam errandi vagandique spiritu. Pacem quoque passim cum omnibus missens, inquit de haereticis suis, lib. Praescriptionum, Tertullianus.
units.tr: It is one thing to dispute about the toleration of those five articles, from which the first quarrels arose, and then the schism; it is another to dispute about a vague and universal toleration, for which they now argue, which would gather into one assembly all the sects of Christianity, however erroneous and hostile, and even the idolaters themselves; not to repeat what has just been said about unbelievers. At first there was much debate about the former, and it was always restricted to the contention over the five articles. So Uytenbogaert, in the history of his life, and Grotius in his Apology, chapters 4 and 5. But now the adversaries, as they have daily slipped into one opinion and error after another, also argue about this wider matter: nowhere, outside the Church, has the spirit of erring and wandering ever settled into a fixed course. Tertullian too, in his book of Prescriptions against heretics, says that he sends peace everywhere to all.

units.la: Longe alia facies Remonstrantium hodie, ac initio turbarum fuit, & omnino alia ratione disputatur iisdem de rebus nunc; praeterquam de plutibus aliis, ac tunc. Exempli causa, quis nescit illorum thesim semper fuisse, electionem a Deo factam esse ex praevisa fide? postea in gratiam Socini; vel ex ista haeresi fluctuantes circa praescientiam in Deo futurorum contingentium, missum fecerunt quod de electione aeterna hactenus docuerant, & coeperunt dicere, eam non ab aeterno, sed in tempore contingere ubi quis actu credit. Quae est ipsa Socini sententia. Apologia Remonstrantium c. XVIII. pag. 189. Si ipsum Scripturae spectes, ἐπλόγην sive ἐλόγην significat actualem sequestrationem quorundam sive hominum sive populorum ex communi turba ratiorum ad certam aliquem finem, id est, ad participandum peculiare aliquod privilegium, quo caeteri carerent. Pag. 190. At ex iis, quae jam a nobis praemissa sunt, patet falsum esse quod electio facta sit ab aeterno: Unus tantum in Scriptura locus est, qui id affirmare videtur, unde communis error iste natus est, locus vid. ad Ephes. 1. 4. ubi Deus elegisse Ephesios dicitur ante jacta mundi fundamenta: sed eligendi verbum ibi hic pro decreto eligendi accipi posse quis dubitat? Nec mirum, nec novum id videri debet, cum Spiritui S. in Scripturis familiare sit, affirmare datum nobis esse ante tempora saecularia, quod, ut nobis daretur, ante tempora saecularia decretum est. Ita verbi gratia salus nobis data dicitur ante tempora saecularia, 2 Tim. 1. 9. Quae si scire velis, unde petierit Apolog. Auctor, Socinum explica in Prælect. cap. XIII. pag. 63. ubi haec leges: Neque huic sententiae nostrae repugnant verba illa Pauli Ephes. 1. 4. Sicut elegit nos in ipso ante mundi constitutionem, &c. Namque eo loco eligendi verbum non proprie usurpatum fuit, nec electionem ipsam sive eligendi decretum, quae loquendi forma sanctis literis per quam familiaris est, praesertim vero apud ipsum Paulum, qui affirmare non dubitat, Deum suos jam glorificasse, Rom. 8. 30. & datam nobis fuisse gratiam in Christo ante tempora saecularia, 2 Tim. 1. 9. & alia ejusmodi non pauca. Iterum Remonstrantes Apolog. pag. 191. Concludunt ergo falsum esse (quamquam hactenus id plerique tenuerunt) electionem in Scripturis uspiam ab aeterno factam dici, aut eam (ut est cum pro decreto sumitur) in Scripturis propensi ad rationem Dei internam sive immanentem, quae in Deo ab aeterno fuerit: & contra verissimum esse, quod electio in Scripturis proponatur ut actio Dei externa sive transiens, & quae in tempore capta est, contra quam hactenus fere creditum est. Similiter negant, reprobationem ab aeterno factam. cap. XX. pag. 220. Quum Arminiana sententia de electione ex praevisa fide niteretur aeterna Dei praescientia, ut Arminius in Declaratione sententiae suae loquitur: Hoc decretum praescientiae Dei innititur, quod ab aeterno fuit, quo ante jacta ejusmodi administrationem mediorum ad conversionem & fidem idoneorum, ex praeveniente ipsius gratia credituri erant & subsequente gratia perseveraturi: quive vero etiam non erant credituri experseveraturi. Haec autem in aliam formam re- sinfinxisse Episcopium haud mirum, postquam ex Socini Theologia circa praescientiam Dei nutare cœpit, uti in Socinianismo Confutato à nobis ostensum, lib. II. cap. VII. & VIII. Ita quoque disputatum fuit initio de mortis Christi universalitate, an pro omnibus mortuus sit? Jam vero videas illos nusquam satisfactionis Christi, ubi de ejus morte & salvatione sermo, mentionem facere; & hæc tamen mortis istius consideratio quidem præcipua, in cujus expositione & vindicatione adversus Socinianos, tum res, & Ecclesiæ usus postulant apertiorem plenioremque fieri illius explicationem: imo in Apologia, cap. VIII, dicunt quidem ob plures Christum causas Servatorem nostrum esse, & præconio, exemplo, & martyrio suo etiam salutem nostram procurasse, ne μὴ interim de satisfactione; ut neque in Catechesi, ubi solum ajunt, Christum propter hominum peccata mactatum, & verbum satisfactionis, & modum hæc de re loquendi in Ecclesia usitatum studiose declinant, contra ad illorum qui Socinianorum est se accommodant, quare quæstionem illam quæ nobis iisdem de morte Christi est, ita proponendam censeo, ut satisfactionem etiam examinemus, tum ad hujus eliciendam confessionem, tum quod ex ejus debita attentione facilius decidituř, an Christus morte suâ satisfecerit pro omnium & singulorum hominum peccatis. Post Arminium, Remonstrantes aut ipsa Socinianorum dogmata, uti in multis, arripuerunt; aut plerosque Theologiæ articulos inflexerunt, & si non in thesi ipsâ, vel eam tradendo integram Socinianam, vel ejus elevando certitudinem aut necessitatem, in illorum gratiam; in ejus explicatione, & defensione, Socinianis, quantum possunt, accessere, & ad eorum mentem phrasim, stylum, omnia accommodarunt. Ut omnino, quemadmodum cum Lutheranis, ubi distinguimus hodiernos & horum quæstiones disputationesque, à doctrinâ qualis primum Lutheri fuit, simili discrimine utendum. sit apud Remonstrantes in Arminianos meros, id est, eos qui Arminio in hærentes manent intra famosos illos quinque de Prædestinatione & annexos articulos; & Remonstranto-Socinianos, quales formavit post Arminium Episcopius. Et prudenter inter utrosque discernendum est. Homines istos alienat ab Ecclesiâ multum factio politica, quod putantes, se aut suos læsos vel politicè vel Ecclesiastice, in muneris aut loci, quem forte tenebant, amissione, ulciscendum hoc opinentur pertinaci ab Ecclesiâ divortio. Perverso sane consilio, in Ecclesiam, & animæ suæ propriam pacem & consolationem vindicare velle, quod homines aliqui forte adversus te commisere, (si hoc ita sit, & non debuerit haud aliter fieri) quod uti factι est, ita nostro non eget patrocinio, minus vindictâ. Verùm illa ubi in oblivionem venerint, aut meliori sententiâ animoque ipsi superaverint, discreto rejectoque palam & sincere à se suâque professione omni Socinianismo, spes est in meliorem mentem, & unionem nobiscum adducendos.
units.tr: The Remonstrants today look very different from how they did at the beginning of the troubles, and the same matters are now argued in an entirely different way, apart from many other points that have changed since then. For example, who does not know that their thesis has always been that God's election was made on the basis of foreseen faith? Later, for the sake of Socinus, or wavering over God's foreknowledge of future contingents under the influence of that heresy, they set aside what they had taught about eternal election up to that point and began to say that election does not take place from eternity but in time, when someone actually believes. This is Socinus' own opinion. Apology of the Remonstrants, ch. 18, p. 189: "If you look at the word of Scripture, ἐπλόγην [eplogēn] or ἐλόγην [elogēn] signifies the actual separation of certain persons or peoples from the common crowd of human beings for a certain end, that is, to share some special privilege which the others lack." P. 190: "But from what we have already set out, it is plain that it is false that election was made from eternity. There is only one passage in Scripture which seems to affirm this, and from it this common error arose: Ephesians 1:4, where God is said to have chosen the Ephesians before the foundations of the world were laid. But who doubts that the word 'chose' can there be taken for the decree to choose? Nor should this seem strange or new, since it is familiar to the Holy Spirit in the Scriptures to affirm that something has been given to us before the ages, which was decreed before the ages so that it might be given to us. Thus, for example, salvation is said to have been given to us before the ages, 2 Tim. 1:9." If you want to know where the author of the Apology got this, look at Socinus in the Prelections, ch. 13, p. 63, where you will read: "Nor do those words of Paul in Ephesians 1:4, 'as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world', etc., contradict this view of ours. For in that place the word 'choose' was not used in its proper sense, nor is election itself or the decree of election meant; this way of speaking is very common in the sacred letters, especially in Paul himself, who does not hesitate to affirm that God has already glorified his own, Rom. 8:30, and that grace was given to us in Christ before the ages, 2 Tim. 1:9, and many other things of this kind." Again the Remonstrants, Apology p. 191: "They conclude therefore that it is false (although most have hitherto held it) that election is said anywhere in Scripture to have been made from eternity, or that it is (as when it is taken for a decree) directed in Scripture to God's internal or immanent reason, which was in God from eternity; and on the contrary that it is most true that election is set forth in Scripture as an external or transient action of God, which was undertaken in time, contrary to what has commonly been believed hitherto." Likewise they deny that reprobation was made from eternity. Ch. XX, p. 220. Since the Arminian doctrine of election from foreseen faith rested on God's eternal foreknowledge, as Arminius puts it in the Declaration of his opinion: "This decree rests on the foreknowledge of God, which was from eternity, by which God foresaw those who, before such an administration of the means suitable for conversion and faith was set in motion, would believe through prevenient grace and would persevere through subsequent grace; and also those who would not believe and would not persevere." It is no surprise that Episcopius recast these things into another form, after he began to waver about God's foreknowledge under the influence of the theology of Socinus, as we showed in our Socinianism Confuted, book II, ch. VII and VIII. So too at the beginning the question was debated about the universality of Christ's death, whether he died for all. Now, however, you will find that they nowhere mention Christ's satisfaction when they speak of his death and our salvation; yet the consideration of that death is the chief one, and both the matter itself and the use of the Church demand that its explanation and defence against the Socinians be made clearer and fuller. Indeed, in the Apology, ch. 8, they do say that Christ is our Saviour for many reasons, and that by his proclamation, example and martyrdom he has secured our salvation, but they say nothing about satisfaction. Likewise in the Catechism they only say that Christ was slain for the sins of men, and they carefully avoid the word satisfaction and the manner of speaking about this matter customary in the Church; on the contrary they accommodate themselves to those of the Socinians. Therefore I think the question that concerns us about Christ's death should be put in such a way that we also examine satisfaction, both to elicit its confession and because from due attention to it the matter will more easily be settled, namely whether Christ by his death satisfied for the sins of all and of each man. After Arminius, the Remonstrants either seized upon the very doctrines of the Socinians, as in many matters, or bent most articles of theology. If they did not do so in the thesis itself, either by setting forth the whole Socinian thesis or by lowering its certainty or necessity, then in its explanation and defence they went over to the Socinians as far as they could, to win their favour, and they adapted their phrasing, style and everything else to the Socinian mind. So altogether, as with the Lutherans, where we distinguish the present-day ones and their questions and disputes from the doctrine as it first was in Luther, a similar distinction must be made among the Remonstrants: between the Arminians proper, that is, those who remain attached to Arminius and within the famous five articles on predestination and their attachments, and the Remonstrant-Socinians, such as Episcopius formed after Arminius. And one must discern prudently between the two. A political faction alienates these men greatly from the Church, since, thinking that they or their people have been wronged, either politically or ecclesiastically, by the loss of an office or position they perhaps held, they suppose this must be avenged by a stubborn separation from the Church. Certainly it is a perverse plan to wish to claim for the Church, and for one's own soul's peace and consolation, what some men may perhaps have done against you (if this is so, and it should not have happened otherwise). What has been done needs no defence from us, still less revenge. But when those injuries have passed into oblivion, or they have overcome them with a better judgement and spirit, and have openly and sincerely rejected all Socinianism from themselves and from their profession, there is hope they may be brought to a better mind and to union with us.

units.la: Vulgus ipsorum si interrogeš, præter repositam alto animo, quam prætendunt, injuriam sibi suisque factam, horrenda aliqua in doctrinam nostram, præsertim de prædestinatione, proferunt opprobria, de Deo auctore peccati &c. quæ vana terriculamenta & calumniæ sunt, quibus doctrinam & Ecclesias nostras contra fas & verum improbè onerant, qui hoc unum sibi agendum existimant, ut simplices homines à communione nostrâ absterreant, & seducant. Diluenda illa convicia passim sunt, & animi hominum de illis melius instruendi. Nemo ex nostris illa docet, quæ isti nobis vulgo objiciunt, & ut aliquis illa scripsisset (quod tamen ita non est), quis in nostris concionibus talia unquam proponi vel doceri audivit? Jam non ex alicujus opinione forte vel scripto judicari de doctrinâ Ecclesiæ debet, sed ex concionibus, ex Confessione: ubi nostra Confessio abominanda talia habet, ac ipsi nobis exprobrant? vel ubi, aut quis unquam pro membro Ecclesiae adoptatus fuit, sub istorum fide & professione? Quorsum ergo fallissimis istiusmodi & prodigiosis consequentiis denigrare & blasphemare doctrinam pergunt, & docent alios? Haec demenda animis hominum praejudicia sunt, & de veritate ac sanctitate doctrinae nostrae sincere & constanter instruendi.
units.tr: If you ask the common people among them, apart from the injury, which they nurse in their hearts and claim was done to them and their own, they produce some horrible reproaches against our doctrine, especially on predestination: that God is the author of sin, and so on. These are empty bugbears and calumnies, with which they wrongly and dishonestly burden our doctrine and our Churches; they think it their sole business to frighten simple people away from our fellowship and to lead them astray. Those slanders must be refuted everywhere, and men's minds must be better instructed about them. None of ours teaches what they commonly throw at us, and even if someone had written such things (which is not so), who ever heard such things proposed or taught in our sermons? Moreover, the doctrine of the Church ought not to be judged from the opinion or perhaps the writing of some individual, but from our sermons and from our Confession. Where does our Confession contain such abominable things, as they charge us with? Or where, and who was ever admitted as a member of the Church under their faith and profession? To what end, then, do they persist in blackening and blaspheming our doctrine with such utterly false and monstrous consequences, and teach others to do the same? These prejudices must be removed from men's minds, and they must be sincerely and steadily instructed about the truth and holiness of our doctrine.

units.la: Ad cognoscendas res Remonstrantica, quod ad Arminiana, faciunt scripta Arminii, Collatio Hagiensis, & Synodus Dordracena; quod ad Socíniana, Apologia Remonstrantium; Catechesis; Scripta Episcopii, & quae cum autorem (significante Curcellaeo) habent, Responsio ad Specimen Professorum Leidensium, Vedelius Rhapsodus, Verus Remonstrans, Theologus. Adversus illa, ex tantâ Scriptorum, quae est, copiâ, lege Gomari theses, Amefium, ad Collationem Hagiensem, & in Anti-Synodalibus: adversus haec, & tum Catechismum ipsorum, habes Voetium, Heidanum; tum Apologiam, Disputationes Antapologeticas Triglandii. Immensa scimus librorum est turba, sed quae Studiosis praesertim seligenda sint, annotamus. Satis superque hic disputatum videri merito potest, nempe quod ad Arminiana, forte & nimium, si respicimus quam promiscue à quibusvis, saepe non satis rerum capacibus, & nimis multis scriptionibus, & coram quibusvis, quoque fere loco & tempore, vulgaris etiam quam pro sublimitate quaestionum, clamatum & tumultuatum, de altissimis fidei & doctrinae mysteriis, sit. Ad Socíniana quod pertinet, de his in genere, tum quantum Remonstrantes tangunt, plus necessariae operae utilisque adhuc superest. Ad observandam vero illam inter dogmata Remonstrantica distinctionem & discrimen est, quod ego Controversias hoc ordine dispono, ut primo loco proponam quinque (tertius & quartus aliquando commodè in unum concontrahuntur ) famosos articulos de Praedestinatione Dei, &c. tum alia (non dico omnia, quasi nullum à me praetermissum sit, de cujus sensu ob sententiae ambiguitatem, an hic collocandum esset, haesi): annotatâ etiam differentiâ, quâ de illis hodie aliter disputant, atque olim.
units.tr: For the Remonstrant matters, as far as the Arminian ones go, the writings of Arminius, the Hague Conference, and the Synod of Dort are useful. As far as the Socinian ones go, the Apology of the Remonstrants, their Catechism, the writings of Episcopius and those which have the author (as Curcellaeus indicates), the Response to the Specimen of the Leiden Professors, Vedelius the Rhapsodist, the True Remonstrant, and Theologus. Against those, from the great abundance of writings that exists, read Gomarus's theses, Amesius on the Hague Conference and in the Anti-Synodalia. Against these, and against their Catechism, you have Voetius and Heidanus; then the Apology and the Antapologetic Disputations of Triglandius. We know the crowd of books is immense, but we note those which students in particular should select. Enough and more than enough may rightly seem to have been disputed here concerning the Arminian matters, perhaps even too much, if we consider how promiscuously, often before people not competent enough for such things, and in too many writings, and in front of anyone at almost every place and time, there has been such common clamouring and tumult about the highest mysteries of faith and doctrine, out of keeping with the sublimity of the questions. As for the Socinians, concerning them in general, and as far as the Remonstrants touch on them, more necessary and useful work still remains. As for observing the distinction and difference among the Remonstrant doctrines, I arrange the controversies in this order: first I will set out the five famous articles on the predestination of God, etc. (the third and fourth are sometimes conveniently combined into one), and then the others. I do not say all of them, as if none had been passed over by me; about one of them I hesitated, because of the ambiguity of its statement, whether it should be placed here. I will also note the difference by which they now dispute about these matters differently than formerly.

units.la: Quisquis fuerit libellh, contra me, vel Summae Controvers. lib. VIII. editi Auctor A. F. P. dignus neutiquam visus fuit, vel tale scriptum, quod à longe gravioribus, quibus distinebar in Iudaismo confutando curis me abstraheret: quin, ad medium fere lectum, inter occupationes istas, abjiciendum, partesque ei dandas in secundâ Summae editione, censebam: eodem modo, quo cum Auctore libelli Ad legem & testimonium antehac me egisse memineram. MeminERAM & ejus, quod Augustinus dixit, in initio libri sec. de Civit. Dei, & tamen quis disceptandi finis erit & loquendi modus, si respondendum esse respondentibus semper existimemus: nam qui vel non possunt intelligere quod dicitur, vel tam dure sunt adversitate mentis, ut etiamsi intellexerint, non obediant, respondent, ut scriptum est, & loquuntur iniquitatem, atque infatigabiliter vani sunt. Quorum dicta contraria si toties velimus refellere, quoties obnixâ fronte statuerunt non curare quid dicant, dum quocunque modo nostris disputationibus contradicant, quam sit erumnosum & infructuosum videre. Interim rogatus ab eximio quo Studioso, ut vel ipse perlegerem libellum, aut ejus examen sibi permitterem, ob nescio quam familiaritatem, quâ cum Remonstrantici Seminarii Sociis fruitur, cum, quem jam alius Studiosus, ac discipulus noster in Academiâ Ultrajectinâ, sub praesidio Cl. Viri D. Matth. Netheni, exossatum dederat, relegi tandem totum, & in quinque distinxi Capita, quae quam nullius negotii sint, & nihil praeter antiquam continent cantilenam, quaeque in Adversariis scriptiunculis observare Studiosos oportebat, ostendere ipsis haud gravate volui.
units.tr: Whoever the author of the little book against me was, or of the edition of the Summa controversiarum, book VIII, signed A. F. P., he seemed by no means worthy, nor was his writing such as to draw me away from the much weightier cares with which I was occupied in refuting Judaism. Indeed, about halfway through reading it, in the midst of those occupations, I judged that it should be cast aside, and that a portion should be given to it in the second edition of the Summa, in the same way as I remembered having dealt earlier with the author of the book Ad legem & testimonium. I remembered also what Augustine said at the beginning of the second book of De Civitate Dei: And yet what end will there be to disputation, and what manner of speech, if we think that whoever answers must always be answered? For those who either cannot understand what is said, or are so hard in mind that, even if they understand, they do not obey, answer, as it is written, and speak iniquity, and are tirelessly vain. If we wanted to refute their contrary statements as often as they, with brazen face, have resolved not to care what they say, so long as they contradict our disputations in any way, how wearisome and unfruitful it is to see. Meanwhile, asked by a distinguished student to read the booklet myself, or to let him examine it, on account of some familiarity he enjoys with the fellows of the Remonstrant seminary, and since another student, our pupil at the Utrecht Academy, under the presidency of the distinguished Matthias Nethenus, had already dissected it, I at last reread the whole and divided it into five chapters. I was not reluctant to show them how trivial these are, containing nothing but the old song, and what students ought to observe in such little adversarial writings.

units.la: Atque primum quod concernit historiam doctrinæ, si-ve nostræ, sive Remonstrantium, gloriatur Auctor, multos ante Augustinum Patres, in antiquâ Ecclesiâ; in Reformatâ, ante Arminium nonnullos, ex Remonstrantium sc. sensu loquutos. Sed quorum nec loca profert, nec verba; & quæ nomina pridem in libellis vulgaribus adducta à suis, à Nostris discussa haud ignorabat; & diluta hoc uno responso, quod de doctrinâ aliquâ non ita sollicitè atque accuratè loquantur homines, eâ nondum in controversiam adducta, vexatâque ab Adversariis, quam postea: ut de doctrinâ & controversiâ Pelagii, non tam audiendi sint, qui ante, quam qui post Augustini tempora; & de Arminio, qui hujus themata nosse potuerunt, atque opiniones. Quem in finem ipsa Augustini verba faciunt, super his ipsis quæstionibus, lib. de Prædest. Sanct. cap. xiv. Quid igitur opus est, ut eorum scrutemur opuscula, qui priusquam ista hæresis oriretur, non habuerunt necessitatem in hac difficili ad solvendum quæstione versari, quod procul dubio facerent, si respondere talibus cogerentur. Unde factum est, ut de gratia Dei quid sentirent, breviter quibusdam Scriptorum suorum locis & transeuntes attingerent; immorarentur vero in eis, quæ adversus alios inimicos Ecclesiæ disputabant. Enarrat. in Psalm. liv. Numquid enim perfectè de Trinitate tractatum est, antequam oblatrarent Ariani? numquid perfectè de pœnitentiâ tractatum est, antequam obsisterent Novatiani? Sic non perfectè de baptismate tractatum est, antequam contradicerent foris positi rebaptizatores: nec de ipsâ Christi unitate enucleatè dicta erant, quæ dicta sunt, nisi postea quam separatio illa urgere cepit fratres infirmos, ut jam illi qui noverant hæc tractare atque dissolvere, ne perirent infirmi sollicitati quæstionibus impiorum, sermonibus & disputationibus suis obscura legis in publicum deducerent. Hoc est, quod & alibi dixit, de Civit. Dei lib. xv i.cap. 11. ab adversario motam quæstionem discendi existere occasionem, atque adversus eos omnia & considerari diligentium; & intelligi clarius, & instantius praedicari solerre. de eo etiam exponens Apostolicum istud, oportet haereses esse. Caeterum ab Augustini aevo, Ecclesiam Catholicam illum, ejusque doctrinam pro suis agnovisse, tam certum, ac nostram cum illa convenire. Quod non Pontificii ignorant, vel diffitentur; in nuperis contentionibus Iansenianis, atque anterioribus Dominicanorum. Quumque non Nostri solum, sed & Pontificii Doctores pro falso habeant quod de Praedestinatorum haeresi, per calumniam doctrinae Ecclesiae, Augustini, nostraeque afficatur, quanta ea mentis male affectae aerugo est in Adversario, quod Praedestinatianorum, Praedestinatorum dicere debuerat, haeresin a Gottschalco renovatam, etiamnum afferere haud erubescat. Super quo instruendus rectius venit ex Vsserio, Vincentio, Iansenio, Auvraeo, Doctore Sorbonico, qui, nullam unquam fuisse Praedestinatorum haeresim, ostendit contra Sirmundi Iesuitae librum Hygini sc. de Praedestinatorum haeresi, &c. in quo palmarios quam plurimos errores & falsitates adnotavit quoque msc. in suo Codice Blondellus.
units.tr: And first, as regards the history of doctrine, whether of ours or of the Remonstrants, the author boasts that many Fathers before Augustine in the ancient Church, and some in the Reformed Church before Arminius, spoke in the sense of the Remonstrants. But he produces neither their passages nor their words, and I was not unaware that these names had long since been brought forward in popular little books by his own side and discussed by ours, and they were answered by this one reply: that men do not speak so carefully and accurately about a doctrine that has not yet been brought into controversy and harassed by the adversaries, as they do afterwards. Thus, concerning the doctrine and controversy of Pelagius, those who came before Augustin's time are not to be heard so much as those who came after; and concerning Arminius, those who could know his themes and opinions. To this end, Augustine's own words, on these very questions, in De Praedestinatione Sanctorum, chapter 14, serve: Why then is there need to examine the little works of those who, before this heresy arose, had no necessity of engaging in this difficult question for its solution, which they would undoubtedly have done if they had been compelled to answer such things? Hence it happened that what they thought about the grace of God they touched on briefly in some passages of their writings, in passing; but they lingered on those things which they argued against other enemies of the Church. In Enarrationes in Psalmos, Ps. 54: Surely the Trinity was not fully treated before the Arians barked? Surely penance was not fully treated before the Novatians resisted? So too baptism was not fully treated before the rebaptizers outside contradicted; nor was the very unity of Christ explained clearly, until that separation began to press upon weak brothers, so that those who knew how to treat and resolve these matters brought the obscure things of the law into the open by their discourses and disputations, lest the weak, troubled by the questions of the impious, should perish. This is what he also said elsewhere, in De Civitate Dei, book XVI, chapter 11: a question raised by an adversary becomes an occasion for learning, and everything is considered more diligently against them, and is understood more clearly and preached more urgently. He also explains that Apostolic saying, there must be heresies, in this sense. Moreover, that the Catholic Church from Augustine's age acknowledged him and his doctrine as its own, and that our doctrine agrees with his, is so certain that the Papists do not ignore or deny it, in the recent Jansenist controversies as well as in the earlier ones of the Dominicans. And since not only our men but also the Popish doctors hold it false that the heresy of the Predestinarians is charged by calumny against the doctrine of the Church, of Augustine and of ours, what a rust of an ill-disposed mind is in the adversary, that he should not blush to assert that the heresy of the Predestinarians, which he ought to have called the heresy of the Predestinatians, was renewed by Gottschalk. On this matter one should be better informed from Ussher, Vincent, Jansenius, Auvray the Doctor of the Sorbonne, who showed against the book of the Jesuit Sirmond, on the heresy of the Predestinarians by Hincmar, etc., that there never was any heresy of the Predestinarians at all, and who noted very many prominent errors and falsehoods in it. Blondel also noted these in writing in his own copy.

units.la: Secundo ad doctrinam quod spectat, vel doctrinalia, Negandum Adversario, Nos, in probanda aliis Scripturae, aut doctrinae veritate objectiva, in testimonio Spiritus S. proram ac puppim constituere: ut hinc Libertini contra nos inclamare possint, quod habet pag. 33. vel, quod pag. 43. Pontificii circulum objicere. Nequit dici, inter Christianos opinionibus inter se dissentientes nondum ullo judicio esse decisum, a quorum parte stet veritas, quamvis in judicio illo, (quod non de caelo pronunciatum, uti pag. 40, sed Spiritus S. in Scriptura loquentis esse dicimus: & Scripturam normam vel indicem & regulam, Spiritum S. judicem passim appellamus,) omnes non acquiescant, & contendere desinunt, uti temere colligit, pag. 35. 45. atque hominum nullus sit infallibilis. pag. 36. 37. Non omnes propterea aut Scepticos facimus, aut Papas. pag. 37. Sed hanc ipsorum argumentationem improbamus, contra veræ religionis defensionem, quam solam Magistratui tribuimus, hoc pacto agentium: Si id licet in Hollandiâ Calvinistis, cur non quoque in Suecia, Daniâ, Saxoniâ Lutheranis, in Galliâ, Italiâ, Hispaniâ Pontifi-cii-ssimo in Turciâ Mahometanis, in Chinâ & Japoniâ Ethnicis? quomodo argutatus Curcellæus fuerat. Hoc dicimus indignum esse Christianis, religionem nostram, ejusque defensionem componere cum Muhammedanâ, vel Ethnicâ: quasi par utriusque & pro se, & contra aliam, jus sit & officium: indignum Reformatum nomen amplexis, in eandem hactenus conditionem referre nostram religionem cum superstitione & idololatriâ Papisticâ. impugnare illud æque regulas & fundamenta politiæ Christianæ, ac Ecclesiæ atque inducere religionum ἀδιαφορίαν & libertinismum. Ad objectionem, quod nemo in propriâ causâ possit esse judex, negandum, similiter causam religionis propriam dici aut posse, aut debere. Sed ipsi argumento eo usi fueramus, à contrariis in re quâcumque nostrâ vulgari aut terrenâ judiciis non pendere veritatem ejus, aut possessionis nostræ. Verum quis non videt, aliud esse in argumentatione, comparationem sumere à re propriâ etiam ad rem religionis; aliud simile utriusque velle facere judicium. Argumentum illud est à minori ad majus; non à pari, contra pag. 47. De mutuâ tolerantiâ quam identidem cantillant Adversarii, jam toties discussum explosumque, & ostensum inanes voces esse, ab ipsorum factis ubique toto cœlo discrepantes, ut verbum addere, supervacaneum merito videri possit. Sat ultro citroque verborum hic insumtum: ad rem deveniatur, & factis ostendant serio se id velle, quod videri volunt. Dixerat D. Curcellæus, Christianos, utpote judicio suo in præcipuis & fundamentalibus religionis dogmatibus consentientes, in unum Ecclesiæ corpus coire debere, ut fratres in Christo: modo caeteros diversa sentientes ad sua non cogerent. Hoc enim est, inquit, tyrannis in Ecclesia non ferenda: cujus qui rei sunt, fundamentum evertere & fraternitatis vinculum abrumpere censendi sunt. Quod etiam de idololatris dictum volo. Postrema haec de idololatris Pontificiis ego dicta accepi relate ad ista non solum, quae de tyrannide, sed & quae de unione Christianorum inter se, attulerat, modo tyrannidem Pontificii omitterent. Quod ex iis meis verbis palam est, quae libellator omittit: dices quidem non te velle resorbere Papismum, & illorum aliorumve adeo probare idololatriam; sed siquidem ipsi ferre vos dissentientes in animum inducant, concordiae locum fore. Ego vero quin facile jam hoc tempore & loco vobis, illa etiam sub conditione, accessuri sint Pontificii, haud dubito. Magnam vero calumniae mihi dicam scribit, quod contra Curcellaei mentem, illa sic explicarim, & Pontificiis etiam ex ipsorum mente, attribuerim. Verum sciat. 1. me verba illa, quod etiam de idololatris dictum volo; non negasse ad posterora ista referri debere, de tyrannide quae dixerat, sed exclusive ad alia, & non quoque ad priora, hoc videre me non potuisse. 11. Obstabat vis & filum argumenti ipsius, quo tum Christianos dixerat in praecipuis & fundamentalibus convenire; tum in reliquis se tolerare invicem debere; atque interim in unum omnes coire Ecclesiae corpus; & tanquam fratres prosequi mutuo semet oportere. Quae, quare non etiam Pontificiis, quippe Christianis, attribuenda sint, nondum fateor me perspicere: modo vid. tyrannidem seponant, atque tolerantiam vestram amplectantur. Non enim aliquos Christianos, sed Christianos in genere consentire dictum; & ut fratres in unum corpus concedere debere. Ergo, nostro judicio, controversia Papistica de idololatria, non est ex praecipuis & fundamentalibus, quae coitionem impediat; vel restringendum illud, de Christianorum in fundamentalibus & praecipuis consensu. 111.
units.tr: Secondly, as for doctrine or doctrinal matters, the Adversary must be denied the claim that we, in proving to others the objective truth of Scripture or of doctrine, make the testimony of the Holy Spirit our prow and stern. From this the Libertines can cry out against us, as he says on p. 33, or, as he says on p. 43, the Papists can object that we argue in a circle. It cannot be said that among Christians who differ in opinion the question has not yet been decided by any judgment as to which side has the truth. Yet, although in that judgment (which we say is not pronounced from heaven, as he says on p. 40, but is the Holy Spirit's own judgment speaking in Scripture, and we often call Scripture the rule and index and the Holy Spirit the judge), not all acquiesce and cease to contend, as he rashly infers on pp. 35, 45, and no human being is infallible (pp. 36, 37), we do not on that account make everyone either sceptics or popes (p. 37). Rather, we disapprove of their argument, which proceeds against the defence of the true religion, the only defence we assign to the magistrate, in this manner: If this is allowed to the Calvinists in Holland, why not also to the Lutherans in Sweden, Denmark and Saxony, to the most Papal Papists in France, Italy and Spain, to the Mahometans in Turkey, and to the heathen in China and Japan? This is how Curcellaeus argued. We say it is unworthy of Christians to set our religion and its defence on a level with the Muhammadan or the heathen religion, as if both had an equal right and duty both in defending themselves and in attacking the other. It is unworthy of those who have embraced the name of Reformed to place our religion in the same position as Papist superstition and idolatry. Such a view would equally overthrow the rules and foundations of Christian polity and of the Church, and would introduce indifference [ἀδιαφορία] of religions and libertinism. To the objection that no one can be judge in his own cause, we deny that the cause of religion can, or should, be called one's own. But the argument we had used was that its truth does not depend on the judgments of adversaries in any of our ordinary or earthly matters, or on our possession of it. Yet who does not see that it is one thing to take a comparison in argument even from one's own affairs to the affairs of religion, and another thing to want to make a judgment that the two are alike? That argument goes from the less to the greater, not from equal to equal, contrary to p. 47. As for the mutual toleration which the Adversaries repeat over and over, it has already been discussed and exploded so many times, and shown to be empty words, utterly at odds with their own deeds, that it could rightly seem superfluous to add a word. Enough words have been spent here on both sides; let us come to the matter, and let them show by their deeds that they seriously wish what they want to appear to wish. Curcellaeus had said that Christians, agreeing in their judgment on the chief and fundamental doctrines of religion, ought to come together into one body of the Church as brothers in Christ, provided they did not force those who think otherwise to their own views. For this, he says, is tyranny that is not to be tolerated in the Church; those who are guilty of it are judged to overthrow the foundation and to break the bond of brotherhood. I want this also said of idolaters. I have taken these last words about idolatrous Papists as referring not only to what he had said about tyranny, but also to what he had brought forward about the union of Christians with one another, provided only that the Papists gave up tyranny. It is plain from my own words, which the libeller leaves out: You will indeed say that you do not wish to swallow up Papism, and that you do not so readily approve the idolatry of them and others; but if they bring themselves to tolerate your dissent, there will be room for concord. I for my part do not doubt that the Papists, even on that condition, would readily come to you here and now. He writes that I am heaping calumny on him, because I have explained those words against Curcellaeus's intention and attributed them to the Papists even according to their own mind. But let him know: first, I could not see that the words I want this also said of idolaters do not require that the latter clauses refer back to the tyranny he had mentioned, but exclusively to the other things, and not also to the earlier ones. Second, the force and thread of the argument itself stood in the way, in which he had said that Christians agree on the chief and fundamental points, and that in other matters they must tolerate one another, and meanwhile that all should come together into one body of the Church and should pursue one another as brothers. I admit I still do not see why these things should not be attributed to Papists as well, since they are Christians, provided they set aside tyranny and embrace your toleration. For it was said not that some Christians but Christians in general agree, and that they ought to come together as brothers into one body. Therefore, in our judgment, the Papist controversy about idolatry is not among the chief and fundamental matters that would prevent coming together; or else that statement about the agreement of Christians in fundamentals and chief matters must be restricted. Third, [...] and all doctri-

units.la: Noveram ex Remonstrantium Apologia, articulos fundamentales agnosci ab ipsis istos, modò, qui adeo in confesso, atque indubii juris sunt, ut de iis neque controverti possit: quare, de Pontificiorum idololatriâ quum quidem maxime controvertatur, hic articulus ipsis fundamentalis esse nequit, qui conjunctionem fraternam impediat: vel articuli religionis & salutis fundamentales aliter constituendi veniunt. IV. Et hic noster Auctor, pag. 38. Atque in his mutuam tolerantiam dissentientibus sancte & inviolate colendam asserimus: cujus generis fere sunt omnes controversiæ, quæ hoc tempore inter Christianos agitantur. & pag. 51. universalem propugnat inter Christianos tolerantiam. Quomodo ergo ab eâ Pontificios, consideratos etiam ut idololatras, modò tyrannidi omni Papali valedicant, excludere possunt? Denique, ut quantopere absimus vel à calumniâ, in quâ nobis irrogandâ impotenter illâ occasione paratragœdiat, vel ab animo cuipiam aliquid præter mentem attribuendi, gratulamur hanc ipsis sententiam, & mentem melius explicatam, si vere dicere queant, & testari, se cum Pontificiis idololatris nullam velle nec posse ecclesiasticam aut fraternam colere communionem, quamvis ita late & generatim loquantur, cum Christiani in præcipuis & fundamentalibus Religionis dogmatibus inter se consentiant, cum, qui superest in aliis levioris momenti dissensum, impedire non debere, quo minus in unum Ecclesiæ corpus coëant, & se ut fratres mutuâ in Christo charitate prosequantur. Si modo, qui ista magni æstimant, cæteros diversum sentientes ad ea suscipienda non cogant. Porro, negandum ei, neminem nostrum prædestinationis, fidei, aut salutis suæ posse esse certum, contra pag. 44. 46. Negandum, veræ religionis defensionem, nisi per atrocem calumniam, persecutionem dici debere: vel non eam aut defendendam vi etiam & armis, vel falsam removendam, eliminandam esse, sic ego, addit is, opprimendam, pag. 48. neque Illud est, in conscientias irruere, vel in Dei jura involare, aut ad nostram religionem suscipiendam cogere homines. pag. 50. Siquidem placeret, aut vacaret mihi multare hominem eadem, quâ mecum egit, ratione, & ubi mea invertit, calumniam clamare, haud pauca hic se offerrent. Dixeram, Episcopium nutare circa praescientiam Dei, quod & probavi suo loco in Socinianismo Confutato: ille refert me dixisse negatam Episcopo Dei praescientiam, pag. 53. Certe qui hoc de Dei praescientia inquit, nisi rationibus omnibus obstarent una divinarum praedictionum irrefragabilis auctoritas, pars negans paene praeponderatura videatur. Addo etiam magnis multisque circa divinam providentiam difficultatibus occurri posse, si actionum humanarum, quas Deus a libera atque aequilibri voluntate suspensas esse voluit, praescientia Deo non tribuatur, mihi quidem nutare circa illam rem videtur haud uno modo. Ego ex Apol. attuleram, quod dicit, falsum esse quod electio facta sit ab aeterno, atque id communem errorem appellat. quod item contra Socinianos plenius discussi. ille de voce electionis, accepta pro decreto eligendi, duntaxat respondet. pag. 53. Sed de re est quaestio, & errore illo, quem dixerat Episcopius, communi; non de solâ voce, vel loci Ephes. 1.4 expositione. Trita & vel pueris refutata est argumentatio, respectu Dei nulla sunt contingentia, ergo contingentium nulla Deo potest attribui praescientia. pag. 54. Quae nobis, nulla nixa consequentia opponere, & talibus libellum illinire Auctor non debuisset, sed illa prius aggredi, quae super hoc ipso copiose à nobis dicta responsaque sunt alibi. Quinam illi sint, inter Theologos, qui dicunt, Deum omnia quidem futura praescire posse si velit, sed non velle omnia praescire, quae possit, quos notat pag. 54. ego quidem ignoro. Desideravi, atque etiamnum desidero, pleniorem ab Adversariis fieri mentionem atque expressionem satisfactionis Christi, nec modo dicant, Christum praeconio, exemplo & martyrio suo etiam salutem nostram procurasse, sed hic, ubi ne μὴ quidem de satisfactione, & locus id tamen postulat, eam, id est, rem & naturam ejus exponere, non post multa tandem, eâ uti voce, quam nec Socinians usurpare reformidant; nam & satisfactionem sibi non negari Eques Polonus, in nupero adversus Ordinum Decretum Scripto contendit. Ruarus se agnoscere dicit, Christum tamquam caput electorum omnium, obedientia sua in vita, & multo magis in morte. Deo praestita, sufficiens λύτρον dedisse pro peccatis nostris, adeoque aequipollens supplicio, quod nos peccatis nostris eramus meriti, non quidem ex se, &c. sed ex clementi Dei acceptatione. Cum autem, inquit, meritum stricte dictum satisfactione excludo; non tamen negó ejus meritum in laxiori significatione. Hoc vero negat, proprie & vere poenam pro peccatis nostris à Christo persolutam. Ut non mirum videri Remonstrantibus debeat, haec ipsorum non satis videri verba, quibus dicunt quod per Christum justitiae Dei, sive amori, quo justitiam amat, & odio habet peccatum, abunde satisfactum fuerit, & imposterum cum genere humano propitius, per eundem Filium suum, agere decreverit. Quae, uti vides, nec Socinianus refugiet affirmare: ut non de voce, sed de re satisfactionis simus solliciti, neque id satis sit, quod Deo satisfactum dicunt, nisi Christum vere & proprie nostri loco poenas peccatorum nostrorum in se suscepisse, ac vera propriaque satisfactione exsolvisse eas, asserant, atque ita aperte distincteque Socinianismum rejiciant. Quem quomodo improbatum in Apologia, dicant, vel hinc dijudicari potest, quod pag. 61. Nostr Socinianos dicit, in Confessione, & Apologia, adversus Cichovium Iesuitam anno 1603 tantum passioni D. Iesu tribuere, ut nemo vel paulo aequior, aliquid merito desiderare queat. Nihil ergo ipsi pro sua aequitate desiderant in Socinianis. Nos vero, & omnes, doctri-
units.tr: I had learned from the Remonstrants' Apology that they acknowledge as fundamental those articles which are so admitted and so certainly of right that they cannot even be disputed. Therefore, since the idolatry of the Papists is in fact the very thing most disputed, this article cannot be fundamental for them in a way that would hinder brotherly union; or else the fundamental articles of religion and salvation must be defined in some other way. Fourth. And this our Author, on p. 38: And in these matters we assert that mutual toleration is to be holily and inviolably observed among those who differ; the kind of controversies which are now debated among Christians are almost all of this sort. And on p. 51: he defends a universal toleration among Christians. How, then, can they exclude the Papists from this toleration, even when they are regarded as idolaters, provided they bid farewell to all Papal tyranny?
