Finally, so that you may see how far we are from the calumny with which he, on this occasion, theatrically and intemperately charges us, or from attributing to anyone something beyond his meaning, we welcome this opinion of theirs, and a better explained meaning, if they can truly say and testify that they wish and are able to have no ecclesiastical or brotherly communion with idolatrous Papists, although they speak so broadly and generally that Christians agree among themselves in the chief and fundamental doctrines of religion, and that the remaining dissent in other matters of lesser weight ought not to hinder them from coming together into one body of the Church and pursuing one another with brotherly charity in Christ, provided that those who value these things highly do not force others who think differently to accept them. Further, it must be denied that any of us can be certain of his predestination, faith, or salvation, contrary to pp. 44, 46. It must be denied that the defence of the true religion ought to be called persecution, unless by atrocious calumny; or that it is not to be defended even by force and arms, or that error is to be removed and eliminated, which, as he says, is to be suppressed (p. 48). Nor is it to rush into consciences, or to usurp the rights of God, or to compel men to accept our religion (p. 50). If it pleased me, or if I had leisure, to repay the man in the same way he dealt with me, and to cry out calumny where he has turned mine, not a few things would present themselves here. I had said that Episcopius wavered about the foreknowledge of God, which I also proved in its place in my Socinianism Refuted. He reports that I said the foreknowledge of God was denied by Episcopius (p. 53). Certainly the man who says this about God's foreknowledge, unless the indisputable authority of the divine predictions stood against all reasons, the denying side would seem almost to outweigh; I add also that many great difficulties about divine providence can arise if the foreknowledge of human actions, which God has willed to be suspended from a free and balanced will, is not attributed to God, seems to me to waver on that matter in more than one way. From the Apology I had cited his statement that it is false that election was made from eternity, and he calls this a common error; I have discussed this more fully against the Socinians as well. He only answers about the word election, taken to mean a decree of choosing (p. 53). But the question is about the matter, and about that error which Episcopius called common, not merely about the word or about the interpretation of the passage Ephesians 1:4. The argument, long worn out and refuted even by children, is that with respect to God there are no contingencies, therefore no foreknowledge can be attributed to God of contingent things (p. 54). He ought not to have smeared his little book with such arguments, which rest on no sound consequence against us, but should have first tackled those things which we have said and answered at length elsewhere on this very point. Which theologians they are who say that God can foreknow all future things if he wishes, but does not wish to foreknow all that he could (whom he marks on p. 54), I indeed do not know. I have wished, and still wish, for a fuller mention and statement by the Adversaries of the satisfaction of Christ; and they should not only say that Christ by his proclamation, example and martyrdom also procured our salvation, but here, where there is not even a single word [μή] about satisfaction, and where the passage nevertheless calls for it, they should explain it, that is, the thing and its nature, not after much delay use that word which not even the Socinians shrink from using. For the Polish knight, in his recent writing against the Decree of the Estates, also contends that satisfaction is not denied to him. Ruarus says he acknowledges that Christ, as head of all the elect, gave by his obedience in life, and much more in death offered to God, a sufficient ransom [λύτρον] for our sins, and so an equivalent of the punishment which we had deserved for our sins, not indeed from himself, etc., but from the merciful acceptance of God. "But when I exclude merit strictly so called from satisfaction," he says, "I do not deny its merit in a looser sense." Yet he denies that the penalty for our sins was properly and truly paid by Christ. So it should not seem strange to the Remonstrants that these words of theirs do not seem sufficient, in which they say that through Christ full satisfaction has been made to the justice of God, or to the love with which he loves justice and hates sin, and that he has decided hereafter to deal kindly with the human race through the same Son of his. As you see, not even a Socinian will shrink from affirming these things. So we are concerned not with the word but with the thing of satisfaction, and it is not enough that they say satisfaction was made to God, unless they assert that Christ truly and properly took upon himself the punishments of our sins in our place, and discharged them by a true and proper satisfaction, and so clearly and distinctly reject Socinianism. That they have not condemned Socinianism in their Apology can be judged from this alone: on p. 61 he says that the Socinians, in the Confession and Apology against the Jesuit Cichovius in 1603, attribute so much to the passion of Jesus that no one, even a little fairer, could desire anything more. So for their own fairness they desire nothing more in the Socinians. But we, and all doctri-

units.la: Ο Etrinam de veritate satisfactionis. Quibus dum se accommodant Remonstrantes, & hic ipse Scriptor, quo animo adeo tumultuatus est in nos, vel quod Socinianismo illos diximus plus æquo indulgentiores, & faventiores; vel quod hac in causa pleniorem ab ipsis petivimus huius rei, contra Socinianos, in publicis Scriptis, Confessione, Catechesi, Apologia, explicationem? Interim tamen & hic si sincere sententiam & doctrinam suam pro veritate fidei istius testati fuerint, & quod de Apologia, suisque dicit, vere rejecerint aperteque Socinianam sententiam, erit quod palam nobis ipsisque iterum gratulemur. Denique quod in initio Auctor haud semel pollicitus erat se ostensurum, ex doctrina nostra sequi Deum peccati auctorem esse; id temere, neque per consequentiam, sed calumniam luce clariorem, probare conatur ineptissime ex maledicentissimis Lutheranorum; ex Actis Synodalibus Remonstrantium; nostra Catechesi, qu. lx. denique Synodo Dordracena cap. i. art. vi. quae talia sunt, ut nemo non facile ad illa responderit, & ad nauseam usque explosas norit blasphemias, responso meo ulteriori indignas, nisi inaniter chartam & tempus, repetendis rebus, commaculare turpiter cum Adversario statuam. Quod si quis, aut D. Curcellaeus operam quaerat, & negotium, age in manus sumat, ne plures dicam, unum Twissum, atque Arminium salvat iis, quibus obriguit hactenus, vinculis: ego me promtum paratumque offero, qui cum eo manus conseram, vel super rancida ista, atque a Bellarmino mutuata, calumnia, de Deo auctore peccati; vel de toto praedestinationis negotio: faxo sentiant, in praedestinationis doguate, quod hic blaterat, victos nos non esse.
units.tr: Concerning the doctrine of the truth of satisfaction. Whatever their agreement with this doctrine, and whatever the Remonstrants' position, what spirit moved this writer to rage so fiercely against us? Was it because we said they were rather too indulgent and favourable towards Socinianism? Or was it because in this matter we asked them for a fuller explanation of this doctrine against the Socinians in our public writings: the Confession, the Catechism and the Apology? Still, if they have sincerely professed their own opinion and doctrine on this article of faith, and if they have truly rejected, as the author says in the Apology and in their own writings, the Socinian opinion, openly and clearly, then we shall have cause to rejoice publicly with them and with ourselves once more. Finally, the author promised more than once at the start that he would show that our doctrine implies that God is the author of sin. He tries to prove this rashly, not "by consequence" but by a "calumny clearer than the light." He does so very clumsily, drawing on the most abusive writings of the Lutherans, the Synodal Acts of the Remonstrants, our Catechism (question 60), and finally the Synod of Dort, chapter 1, article 6. These are of such a kind that anyone can readily answer them, and everyone knows the blasphemies that have been driven out until they are sickening. They are not worth a further reply from me, unless I were foolishly to waste paper and time, and shamefully soil myself by going over the same things again with my opponent. But if anyone, or Mr Curcellaeus, is looking for the matter and wants to take it up, let him (to say no more) take up one Twisse, or Arminius, and free himself from those chains by which he has hitherto been bound. I offer myself, ready and prepared, to cross swords with him, either over this rancid calumny about God as author of sin, borrowed from Bellarmine, or over the whole business of predestination. I will see to it that they find we are not beaten on the doctrine of predestination, whatever this man bawls about it.

units.la: Tertium, quæ de causa schismatis & turbarum Remonstranticarum, quam nobis falso impingit, & solitis historiolis querelisque, ut libellum impleret scilicet, extendit, locum reperient, ubi Cl. Triglandii Historiam Adversarii everterint. Dicimus cum Optato, lib. 1. adversus Parmenianum: clausisti oculos, ne parentes tuos reos agnoscerent: aperuisti eos, ut innocentes & indignos criminis copulares. Omnia pro tempore, nihil pro veritate, quomodo ante dixerat, ut quod illi priores in titulo schismatis fecerant, & vos jam dudum fecisse & nunc facere videamini. Illi ruperunt suis temporibus pacem: vos exterminatis unitatem.
units.tr: Third, as to the cause of the schism and of the Remonstrant disturbances, which he falsely charges on us and extends, to fill out his little book, with his usual little stories and complaints: let them find a place where they can overturn the history of the illustrious Triglandius, the opponent's source. We say with Optatus, in the first book against Parmenianus: You closed your eyes, so that they would not recognise their parents as guilty; you opened them, so that you could join the innocent and the unworthy in crime. Everything for the time, nothing for the truth. He had said earlier that those first men had earned the name of schismatics, and that you now seem to have done, and still do, the same. They broke the peace in their times; you destroy the unity.

units.la: Quartum, quo referendum quod ad amoliendum à suis Socinianismum operose agit, admittemus, ubi essecerit verum esse, quod dicit pag. 14. nullos hic esse Socinianos constat. Quod utinam verum, nosque omnes falsi essemus, & supra modum, supra quam oportet, solliciti! Ita nulli hic Socviniani? & hoc constat? Quaeso unde tot Socviniani libri, & Belgico etiam idiomate? unde tot sermones, disputationes, tot turbae in Sectis, in Ecclesiis, in politiis denique de Socinianismo invehendo, fovendo? unde vestra illa Theologia, ad Socini, supra quam Arminii, opiniones & dogmata, ex quo schisma fecistis, accommodata? Quod nisi ostenderint alii, ostenderim & ego, fidem nolo ullam mereamur. Neque volupe nobis est, haeresim illam vel in aliis deprehendere, vel in vobis. Sed id ipse olim Montacutius, vestris utcunque addictus nimium dogmatibus, palam testatus fuit, in libro Actorum, & Monumentorum cap. 1. pag. 47. ita: multi id haud negaverint, illos, Arminii nempe discipulos, merito ac juste à Calvino, & Beza defecisse, quod ad partes illas rigidiores, quae abditam illam plusque admirandam, quia intellectus minus, doctrinam de praedestinatione ad vitam & mortem concernunt; verum & id omnino dicitur, satisque probabiliter, quod sub eo dissensionis istius pretextu, occulte clam, insensibiliter praejudicatis ac paratis animis non satis attendentibus, nec suspicacibus infundant tales novos, vel redivivos conceptus haereticos, quos licentiosa prophetandi libertas, quam ita appellant, ambitio, oppositio, dissensus, vel curiotur ipsis offerunt. Haec Montacutius. Hoc verò quod dicitur, Socinianos nullos hic esse, aut non id constare, patrocinium eorum arguit ipsis, qui tam benigne de illis loquuntur, cordi esse & curae. Neque clam illud nunc, sed palam satis est, & nemini ignotum esse potest, ne quidem volenti. Rem manifestariam probare nec attinet, nec gratum adeo. Et quantum Socinianis deferat hic ipse Scriptor, in articulo palmario de satisfactione, jam audivimus, ubi nihil in ipsis desiderare, quae passionem D. Iesu concernunt, testatus fuit. Interim & hic, quod supra aliquoties gratulabimur valde, hoc si à suâ parte praestiterint Adversarii sancte & sincere, ne ullos, & apud ipsos, esse hic Socinianos constiterit.
units.tr: Fourth, which belongs to the point where he labours to clear his own side of Socinianism: we will grant it, when they have shown that what he says on page 14 is true, it is established that there are no Socinians here. Would that it were true, and that we were all wrong and anxious beyond measure, beyond what is right! So there are no Socinians here, and this is established? I ask: whence so many Socinian books, even in the Dutch language? Whence so many sermons, disputations, and so many disturbances in the sects, in the churches, and finally in the states, over introducing and fostering Socinianism? Whence that theology of yours, fitted to the opinions and dogmas of Socinus more than of Arminius, for which you made a schism? Unless others can show this, I will show it myself, and I do not want us to earn any belief. Nor is it a pleasure to us to detect this heresy either in others or in you. But Montacutius once bore witness to this openly, though he was too much devoted to your doctrines, in the book of Acts and Monuments, chapter 1, page 47, thus: "Many would not deny that those disciples of Arminius rightly and justly departed from Calvin and Beza, in that they inclined to the stricter party, which concerns that hidden and more admirable doctrine of predestination to life and death, because the mind understands it less. But it is also said altogether, and fairly probably, that under the pretext of this dissension, secretly, unnoticed, with prejudiced and prepared minds that do not pay enough attention and are not suspicious, such men pour in new or revived heretical notions, which the licentious freedom of prophesying (as they call it), ambition, opposition, dissent, or curiosity offers them." So Montacutius. But that there are no Socinians here, or that this is not established, shows the patronage of those who speak so kindly of them and have them at heart. Nor is this now hidden, but is plain enough, and cannot be unknown to anyone, not even to one who wishes it. It is neither necessary nor very welcome to prove a matter so manifest. And how far this same author defers to the Socinians on the cardinal article of satisfaction, we have already heard, where he declared that nothing in them is lacking concerning the passion of Jesus. Still, here too, as we shall rejoice greatly, as we have done several times above, let it be seen that the opponents have done this on their side, sincerely and in good faith, so that it is established that there are no Socinians among them here.

units.la: Quintum libelli caput dandum frequentissimis gravis- simisque calumniis, in doctrinam primò & religionem nostram; tum ejus Professores, ac Doctores; denique & me.
units.tr: The fifth chapter of the booklet deals with its very frequent and very grave calumnies: first against our doctrine and religion, then against its professors and teachers, and finally against me.

units.la: Haec vulgaris ipsorum agendi, cui à multis annis assueverunt, methodus: atque certo consilio singulatim annotanda. Ut & quo animo ad disputationes hasce accedant, & quo fructu tractare eas possint, appareat. Sed vinci in bis, & pro maledictis benedicere, quod ex animo ei facimus, qui atrociter laesit non nos adeo, quam & alios, atque Ecclesiam, ejusque doctrinam, id demum vincere est. Dabo indicem, neque omnium, nam eas annotare tantum instituì, copiâ earum adactus, ubi plurima perlegeram, atque secundo relegere istiusmodi emblematibus exornatum scriptum, ab animo, vel negotiis impetrare haud potui. Quae obiter hic, ibi occurrunt, habe ista. In Doctrinam dicta, pag. 15. horribilia dogmata. monstra errorum. pag. 56. doctrinam nostram esse meré speculativam. pag. 62. Deum authorem peccati constituere. pag. 5. Catechismum non male cum regula lesbia conferri. pag. 10. Synodum Dordracenam ex hominibus partium expertibus non constitisse. Doctores pag. 9. deformatos appellat, pro reformatis: ingeniosâ nimirum mutatione. pag. 29. licet concordiæ studium præ se ferant, animum tamen gerunt à pace alienissimum pag. 26. concionibus debacchari solent, pag. 35. Calvinistæ. pag. 62. conscientias ab ipsis in servitutem redigi. pag. 41. quotquot sunt Calvini sectatores, eadem jure Pontificatum sibi vindicabunt. Quid recenseam, neque hoc adeo gratum vel utile argumentum, non ea καλὰ, vel ἀφίλιμος τῆς ἀνθρώπους. Tit. III. 8. scommata, hæc ejus sc. rhetorica, in Gomarum, pag. 59. Heidanum. pag. 17. & 56. Marefium, pag. 59. Cabeljavium, & du Bois, pag. 23. V Vittewrongelium, pag. 29. Campenses, pag. 22. Denique & in me, pag. 5. convitia, maledicta, calumniæ. Nimirum quia de Arminio dixeram, eum nimium fisum propriis suis speculationibus. Grave scilicet crimen, quod non nisi illis diris exagitandum fuit. Quasi aliter de Arminio omnes judicent, qui cum vel coram, vel ex scriptis noverunt: & non idem etiam publicâ Lectione de eodem dixerit, ante me, eximius in Angliâ Theologus, Iohannes Prideaux, quam periculose versentur in Ecclesiâ subtiliora nonnulla ingenia, quæ meditationem jactant sine lectione, observare est in Arminio. Quod vero de Vorstio dixi, de Episcopio, aliisque istius commaticis viris, latius comprobavi in Apparatu ad Controversi. & Disput. Socin. Quod autem præsens Auctor de Vedelio inquit, Zydlovio, Maccovio, Amyraldo, res prorsus aliter habet, ac scribit. De infantibus quod enim ab illo scriptum, in inferno damnatis; nec alii, nec ego unquam diximus: sed illorum judicium Deo committimus, suspenso nostro: quia de infantibus, ut nec infantibus Scriptura tam copiose loquitur, atque de adultis. De fidelium infantibus in infantiâ morientibus, res clara est, eos ex judicio charitatis habendos pro fœderatis, & salvatis. Zydlovium, in illâ suâ disputatione res imo jusserunt sibi suas habere, qui ei palam se opposuere, Triglandius, Vocius, alii. Nec Maccovii probata sententia communi Theologorum judicio fuit, de objecto fidei falso. Nihil autem à vero magis abest, quam ob illa ulcera ab Amyraldo tacta, hunc Arminianismi accusatum fuisse unquam. Ut nimis rerum imperitus Scriptor hic fuerit, qui se illis immiscere, & calumnias, quam veritatem, sequi maluerit. Quid illas magno numero; in me praesertim cruciatas, persequar? quasi homines pro bestiis habuissem? quum phrasim Apostolicam usurpavi, ubi in disputatione adversus haereticos, cum bestiis luctatos nos dixi. Me nunc inter illos ponit, qui nulla erga ipsos charitate ducuntur, qui persequutionem (à quâ semper longè abfui) in ipsos, in Mennonitas, moliar; alibi tamen cum iis conjungit, qui videri volunt aliquam cum ipsis communionem expetere, quare me jubet ad animum revocare ea, quae nuper in Ecclesiâ Ultrajectinâ, de concordiae rationibus agitata sunt. De quo melius scio judicasse Remonstrantium permultos, quam is facit. Et tamen, hic Scriptor, istâ sua methodo, & scribendi ratione ac reverentiâ, concordiam scilicet promovere se jactat, & mutuae tolerantiae esse imprimis deditum, videlicet quae diris infectationibus & calumniis paratur, quę apprime quadrant libelli frontispicio, ubi pollicetur, eo scilicet de mutuâ inter Christianos opinionibus dissidentes tolerantiâ potissimum disceptari. belle nimirum, & egregie. Nos verò ex animo Deum rogare haud desinimus, ea ut pacis veritatisque consilia omnibus inspiret, quae ad nominis sui gloriam futura sint, & veram, non fucatam, Christianorum inter se concordiam, & tolerantiam. Atque quia Dordracena Synodus ipsis sudes in oculis est, quam continuis impetunt convitiis, non desinam hic apponere, judicium Viri supra omnes judiciosi & magni, & praeter Papicolas, neminí non probati, Pauli nempe Servitae, quod perscripsit ad celeberrimum Danielem Heinsium, post habitam Synodum, missamque sibi Heinsii Homiliam, super eodem argumento. Epistola haec est: Reverendo Domine, furt procul dubio Apostolorum Iohannis & Pauli sententia quam in tua homilia enarrasti; eamque orthodoxam esse soli non credunt, qui caecitate mentis damnati sunt: nam ut Divinae gratia & adoptionis soli electi participes sunt, ita quae sit ejus vis & efficacitas soli agnoscere possunt. Non enim mundus aut caro, vel nycticorax lucem ferre valent, quibus denegata est ea oculorum acies, qua lux perspici potest. Meo judicio nedum fides Divinum beneficium est, verum & recte de ea, ac de illius causis & effectibus existimatio mundanis sapientibus est denegata. Vos felices, quibus caelitus divina mysteria detecta sunt. Christiana ista Synodus Apostolicam sententiam a carnali discrevit, & haec damnata illam pie amplexa est. Et prudenter amplissimi Ordines adversarios vestros, linguam coercere jusserunt, defuncti munere, quod principis est proprium in Ecclesia etc. 4. Kal. Iunii 1620.
units.tr: This is their usual method of proceeding, to which they have been accustomed for many years, and I have deliberately chosen to note the instances one by one, so that it may appear with what spirit they approach these disputations and with what profit they can handle them. But to be conquered in these matters, and to bless when we are cursed, which we do from the heart, is in the end to conquer the man who has grievously wounded not so much us as others, and the Church and its doctrine. I shall give an index, though not of all of them, for I had only set out to note them. I was overwhelmed by their number: after reading through very many, and then reading again a writing so adorned with such emblems, I could not bring myself to continue, whether from inclination or from business. The things that occur here and there, take these. On doctrine, said on p. 15: horrible dogmas, monsters of errors. p. 56: that our doctrine is purely speculative. p. 62: that God is made the author of sin. p. 5: that the Catechism may not badly be compared with the Lesbian rule. p. 10: that the Synod of Dort did not consist of men free from party interest. On the teachers: p. 9, he calls them deformed instead of reformed, by a clever change, of course. p. 29: although they make a show of zeal for concord, they nevertheless bear a mind most alien to peace. p. 26: they are wont to rave in their sermons. p. 35: Calvinists. p. 62: consciences are reduced by them to slavery. p. 41: all who are followers of Calvin will by the same right claim the papacy for themselves. Why should I list more? It is neither a pleasant nor a useful subject, and these are not things that are [καλὰ καὶ ὠφέλιμα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις] (Tit. 3:8). These are his scoffs, his rhetoric: against Gomarus, p. 59; Heidanus, p. 17 and 56; Maresius, p. 59; Cabeljavius and du Bois, p. 23; Vittewrongel, p. 29; the Campenses, p. 22. Finally, against me too, p. 5: insults, abuse, calumnies. Namely, because I had said of Arminius that he trusted too much in his own speculations. A grave crime, forsooth, which could be assailed only with such dire words! As if everyone who has known Arminius, either in person or from his writings, judged otherwise. And as if, before me, the eminent English theologian John Prideaux had not said of the same man in a public lecture: how dangerously some subtle minds behave in the Church, which boast of meditation without reading, may be observed in Arminius. What I said of Vorstius, of Episcopius and of other men of that stamp, I have proved more fully in the Apparatus to the Controversies and the Disputations against the Socinians. As for what the present author says about Vedelius, Zydlovius, Maccovius and Amyraldus, the matter is quite otherwise than he writes. For what was written by him about infants damned in hell, neither others nor I have ever said; rather we commit their judgment to God, suspending our own, because Scripture speaks of infants less copiously than of adults. Concerning the infants of believers who die in infancy, the matter is clear: by a judgment of charity they are to be held as covenanted and saved. As for Zydlovius, in that disputation of his, those who openly opposed him, Triglandius, Vossius and others, indeed told him to keep his opinions to himself. Nor was the opinion of Maccovius, concerning a false object of faith, approved by the common judgment of theologians. Nothing, however, is further from the truth than that Amyraldus, touched by those sores, was ever accused of Arminianism. This author must be so ignorant of affairs that he preferred to mix himself up with those men and to follow calumnies rather than truth. Why should I pursue those many insults, which have been directed especially at me? As if I had treated men as beasts, when I used the apostolic phrase where, in disputation against heretics, I said that we had fought with beasts. He now places me among those who are moved by no charity towards them, who plan persecution (from which I have always been far removed) against them, against the Mennonites. Yet elsewhere he joins me with those who wish to seem to seek some communion with them, and therefore bids me call to mind what was lately debated in the Church of Utrecht concerning the grounds of concord. On this matter I know that many of the Remonstrants judged better than he does. And yet this author, by his method, his manner of writing and his reverence, boasts that he promotes concord and is devoted above all to mutual tolerance, a tolerance prepared, forsooth, with dire invectives and calumnies. These fit very well the frontispiece of the booklet, where it promises that it will discuss chiefly mutual tolerance among Christians who differ in opinions. Beautifully and excellently indeed! But we for our part do not cease to ask God from the heart that he may inspire all men with counsels of peace and truth, which may serve the glory of his name, and a true, not feigned, concord and tolerance among Christians. And since the Synod of Dort is a thorn in their eyes, which they assail with constant insults, I shall not refrain from setting here the judgment of a man above all judicious and great, and approved by nearly everyone except the Papists: Paul the Servite, which he wrote to the very famous Daniel Heinsius after the synod had been held and Heinsius's homily on the same subject had been sent to him. The letter is this: "Reverend Sir, without doubt it is the opinion of the Apostles John and Paul that you set forth in your homily; and only those who are condemned by blindness of mind do not believe it to be orthodox. For as only the elect share in divine grace and adoption, so only they can recognize what its force and efficacy is. For neither the world nor the flesh, nor the owl, can bear the light, to whom that keenness of eye by which light can be perceived has been denied. In my judgment, not only is faith a divine benefit, but right judgment of it, and of its causes and effects, is also denied to worldly wise men. Happy are you, to whom divine mysteries have been revealed from heaven. That Christian Synod has distinguished the apostolic opinion from the carnal, and those who were condemned have piously embraced it. And wisely the most illustrious Orders have commanded your adversaries to restrain their tongues, having discharged the duty which is properly the prince's in the Church, etc. 29 May 1620."

units.la: Iam sequuntur controversiae.
units.tr: Now the controversies follow.

units.la: I. Num causa praedestinationis, quare Deus ab aeterno praedestinavit hominum alios ad salutem, sit propter praevisam eorum fidem: alios autem ad mortem, propter praevisa eorum mala opera? Neg.
units.tr: I. Is the cause of predestination, why God from eternity predestined some men to salvation, that he foresaw their faith; and others to death, that he foresaw their evil works? No.

units.la: Vel:
units.tr: Or:

units.la: Num electio & reprobatio non sint facta ab aeterno, sed in tempore fiant, ad actualem hominum fidem, vel inobedientiam? Neg.
units.tr: Are election and reprobation not made from eternity, but take place in time, in view of men's actual faith or disobedience? No.

units.la: II. Num Christus pro omnibus & singulis hominibus mortuus sit? Neg.
units.tr: II. Did Christ die for all and each of men? No.

units.la: Vel:
units.tr: Or:

units.la: Num Christus morte sua satisfecerit Deo pro omnium & singulorum hominum peccatis? Neg.
units.tr: Did Christ by his death satisfy God for the sins of all and each of men? No.

units.la: III. Num omnibus per Euangelii praedicationem vocatis communis quaepiam a Deo concedatur gratia, qua in ipsorum situm sit potestate, & arbitrio, verbo divino credere & obtemperare? Neg.
units.tr: III. Is some common grace granted by God to all who are called through the preaching of the Gospel, by which it lies within their power and choice to believe the divine word and obey it? No.

units.la: IV. An Spiritus S. singulari operatione in ipsam animam, nimam, conversionem hominis & fidem effectivè producat? Aff.
units.tr: IV. Does the Holy Spirit, by a singular operation, effectively produce the conversion of man and his faith in the very soul? Yes.

units.la: v. Annon Deus fideles ita semper custodiat & regat, ut nunquam à se prorsus deficiant? Aff.
units.tr: V. Does not God so always preserve and guide the faithful that they never fall away from him altogether? Yes.

units.la: vi. Num de simplicitate Dei nihil extet in Scripturis? Neg.
units.tr: VI. Is there nothing in the Scriptures about the simplicity of God? No.

units.la: vii. Annon Scriptura doceat, Deum secundum eli sentiam suam ubique esse? Aff.
units.tr: vii. Does Scripture not teach that God, according to his essence, is present everywhere? Affirmative.

units.la: viii. Annon pro certo ex Scripturis affirmandum sit, Deum habere scientiam futurorum contingentium? Aff.
units.tr: viii. Must it not be affirmed from Scripture with certainty that God has knowledge of future contingent things? Affirmative.

units.la: ix. Num eventus libere futuros Deus norit per scientiam aliquam mediam, ante decretum voluntatis suæ de illis futuris? Neg.
units.tr: ix. Does God know freely future events through some middle knowledge, before his decree of will concerning those future things? Negative.

units.la: x. Num doctrina de Personarum in Deo Trinitate non sit fundamentalis ad salutem, neque usus alicujus practici? Neg.
units.tr: x. Is the doctrine of the persons in the Trinity of God not fundamental to salvation, nor of any practical use? Negative.

units.la: xi. Num de adorando Spiritu Sancto nullum in Scripturâ extet mandatum, exemplum, aut indicium? Neg.
units.tr: xi. Is there in Scripture no command, example, or indication concerning worshipping the Holy Spirit? Negative.

units.la: xii. Num quæstio de justitiâ originali tota inepta & inutilis sit? Neg.
units.tr: xii. Is the question of original righteousness wholly useless and unprofitable? Negative.

units.la: xiii. An providentiæ divinæ vis influat in voluntatem, eam ad actum suum excitando & determinando? Aff.
units.tr: xiii. Does the power of divine providence flow into the will, stirring and determining it to its act? Affirmative.

units.la: Num verò à voluntatis actu ipsa determinetur? Neg.
units.tr: But is it indeed determined by the act of the will itself? Negative.

units.la: xiv. Annon peccatum originale sit proprie dictum peccatum? Aff.
units.tr: xiv. Is original sin not properly called sin? Affirmative.

units.la: xv. Num Christus ob plures alias causas sit Filius Dei, quam ob æternam à Patre generationem? Neg.
units.tr: xv. Is Christ the Son of God for more causes than his eternal generation from the Father? Negative.

units.la: xvi: Num Christus ob alias causas dicatur Salvator, videlicet præconium, exemplum, & martyrium, quam propter nostram à peccatis redemtionem? Neg.
units.tr: xvi. Is Christ called Saviour for other causes, namely proclamation, example, and martyrdom, rather than for our redemption from sins? Negative.

units.la: xvii. Num Christus, tanquam novus à Patre Legislator, legem additione novorum praeceptorum secerit perfectiorem? Neg.
units.tr: xvii. Did Christ, as a new Lawgiver from the Father, make the law more perfect by adding new precepts? Negative.

units.la: xviii. Num fides in Christum salvifica nec praecepta fuerit sub V. T. nec vigerit? Neg.
units.tr: xviii. Was saving faith in Christ neither commanded under the Old Testament nor in force there? Negative.

units.la: xix. Num dicendum sit, Socinum, in capite de justificatione, & de fide, quod ad summam rei, convenire cum Orthodoxis? Neg.
units.tr: xix. Must it be said that Socinus, in the chapter on justification and on faith, agrees with the Orthodox as to the substance of the matter? Negative.

units.la: xx. Num coram Deo justificemur non fide apprehendendo Christi justitiam, quae sola nobis imputetur in remissionem peccatorum, sed fide ut est actus & opus nostrum, includens in se obedientiam operum Evangelicorum, propter quam, quamvis non ex ejus dignitate & merito, justificemur? Neg.
units.tr: xx. Are we justified before God not by faith apprehending the righteousness of Christ, which alone is imputed to us for the remission of sins, but by faith as it is an act and work of ours, including within itself the obedience of evangelical works, on account of which we are justified, though not on account of its worth and merit? Negative.

units.la: xxi. Num credendum sit, omnibus omnino hominibus conferri a Deo communem & generalem gratiam, per quam idonei sint Deo vocanti parere, & cujus beneficio legi naturae obsecundati, Deo grati evadant, & vel salute aeterna per extraordinariam gratiam donentur, vel beneficiis majoribus gradatim a Deo assiciantur, ut ad salutem aeternam pervenire possint? Neg.
units.tr: xxi. Must it be believed that a common and general grace is granted by God to all men without exception, by which they are fit to obey God calling them, and by whose benefit, having obeyed the law of nature, they become pleasing to God, and are given eternal salvation through extraordinary grace, or are gradually favoured by God with greater benefits, so that they can attain eternal salvation? Negative.

units.la: xxii. Num actus intellectus non subjaceant divino mandato? Neg.
units.tr: xxii. Are the acts of the intellect not subject to the divine command? Negative.

units.la: xxiii. Num eo perfectionis hic veniant fideles & regeniti, ut absque omni lucta, praecepta omnia divina praestare aut complere possint? Neg.
units.tr: xxiii. Do the faithful and regenerate reach such a degree of perfection here that they can perform or fulfil all divine precepts without any struggle? Negative.

units.la: xxiv. Num distinctio presbyterorum, in docentes & regentes, sit novitium συνημα? Neg.
units.tr: xxiv. Is the distinction of elders into teachers and rulers a novelty [συνημα]? Negative.

units.la: xxv. Num ordines in Ecclesiis, inter Evangelii ministros, hierarchici, non sint tamquam illiciti improbandi? Neg.
units.tr: xxv. Are the hierarchical orders among the ministers of the Gospel in the churches not to be condemned as unlawful? Negative.

units.la: xxvi. Num vocatio, ad constituendum ministrum Evangelicum, sive ad hoc, ut quisque jure & legitime Evangelium hominibus praedicet, non sit necessaria? Neg.
units.tr: xxvi. Is a call not necessary for appointing a minister of the Gospel, or for anyone to preach the Gospel to men rightly and lawfully? Negative.

units.la: xxvii. Num a quovis fideli aliquando Sacramenta, baptismus, & Coena administrari possint? Neg.
units.tr: xxvii. Can the sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, sometimes be administered by any believer? Negative.

units.la: XXVIII. Num nec ex præcepto Christi, nec ex Apostolica authoritate pædobaptismus urgeri potsit? Neg.
units.tr: XXVIII. Can infant baptism be urged neither by the precept of Christ nor by apostolic authority? Negative.

units.la: XXIX. Num S. Cœna sit tantum in commemorationem mortis Christi, & non quoque in confirmationem & obsignationem gratiæ ac salutis in Christo? Neg.
units.tr: XXIX. Is the Lord's Supper only in commemoration of the death of Christ, and not also for the confirmation and sealing of grace and salvation in Christ? Negative.

units.la: XXX. Num Christiano Magistratui competat jus & potestas architectonica sub Christo suprema in Ecclesiæ regimen, sine cujus authoritate nihil hic agi queat, Ministris Ecclesiæ suam authoritatem non immediate & à Christo, sed subordinatam à Magistratu habentibus? Neg.
units.tr: XXX. Does the Christian magistrate hold, under Christ, the supreme architectonic right and power over the government of the Church, without whose authority nothing can be done here, while the ministers of the Church do not have their authority immediately from Christ, but subordinately from the magistrate? Negative.

units.la: XXXI. Num quæstio de statu animarum à corpore separatarum, contra Socinianos, sit supervacanea? Neg.
units.tr: XXXI. Against the Socinians, is the question about the state of souls separated from the body superfluous? Negative.

units.la: XXXII. Num inutilis sit quæstio, an eadem corpora sint resurrectura? Neg.
units.tr: XXXII. Is the question useless, whether the same bodies will rise again? Negative.

units.la: XXXIII. Num dogmata ad salutem necessaria sint paucissima, & quæ apud Christianos nec controversa, nec controverti possint, sed apud omnes in confesso sint qui Christiani esse velint, aut quibus modo sanum sit sinciput? videlicet hisce tribus comprehensa capitibus, fide divinorum promissorum, obedientia divinorum præceptorum, & debita Scripturis reverentia? Neg.
units.tr: XXXIII. Are the dogmas necessary to salvation very few, and such that they are neither disputed among Christians nor can be disputed, but are admitted by all who wish to be Christians, or whose head is still sound; namely those comprehended under these three heads: faith in the divine promises, obedience to the divine precepts, and due reverence for the Scriptures? Negative.

units.la: XXXIV. Num omnes Christianorum cœtus, sectæque, in illis fundamentalibus pariter consentientes, in unum Ecclesiæ corpus coire oporteat? Neg.
units.tr: XXXIV. Ought all the assemblies and sects of Christians, agreeing alike in those fundamentals, to come together into one body of the Church? Negative.

units.la: XXXV. Num libertas prophetiarum sit, cuilibet permittere ut profiteatur, & doceat talia, ac ex verbo Dei controverti possunt; & ut Deum colat quo modo colendum credit, adeoque quousque illam quisque hic sibi concedi amat? Neg.
units.tr: XXXV. Is there a liberty of prophesying, so that anyone may be permitted to profess and teach such things as can be disputed from the Word of God, and to worship God in whatever manner he believes it should be worshipped, and therefore to grant himself as much freedom here as he likes? Negative.

units.la: Liber Nonus DE LUTHERANIS.
units.tr: Book Nine: On the Lutherans

units.la: De Schismate Lutherano, ejus origine: uti de Luthero, Carolostadio, Zwinglio, eorumque scriptis mutuis. De Augustana Confessione. Controversia ubiquitatis. Libro Concordiae. De Syncretismo. Colloquium Marpurgense. Concordia Wittembergensis. Consensus Sendomiriensis. Judicium de unione iiscum, vel syncretismo. Controversiae, praeter articulum de S. Cana, reliquae. Disputatio.
units.tr: On the Lutheran schism, its origin; likewise concerning Luther, Carlstadt, Zwingli, and their mutual writings. On the Augsburg Confession. The controversy over ubiquity. The Book of Concord. On syncretism. The Colloquy of Marburg. The Concord of Wittenberg. The Consensus of Sandomierz. Judgment on union with them, or syncretism. The controversies, other than the article on the Holy Supper, and the rest. Disputation.

units.la: EST hoc certe triste & pernitiosum Schisma, quod Satan, ut operi Reformationis tanto efficacius obsisteret, ejusque cursum remoraretur, superiori saeculo excitavit, inter Ecclesias Lutheranas, & Nostras: sive partes respiciamus, inter quas obortum, una a Papismo egressas, eique reformandi intentas; sive causam S. Caenae, ob quam excitatum, quum nullum debeat esse Christianae charitatis majus vinculum, quam istud; seu atrocem dissentiendi modum, quo supra omnem modum illi Nostras & Ecclesias & doctrinam inde insectati fuerunt passim atque persequuti. Deplorandum quam maxime illos, qui idem initio fuerunt, vel ejusdem operis Socii, quique post primum animorum divortium uniti aliquoties, semperque uniendi, si causam & originem dissensus considerares, ita & exardescere, & implacabiles fieri, ut discordare ferme pro articulo religionis haberi incipiat. Et quid hoc S. Caenae est, ob quod adeo divelluntur? non profecto, an Caena frequentanda, vel an Sacramentum sit, & de fructu ejus recte faciendo apud anistimum fidelem, quæ ejus summam complectuntur & essentiam; neque de Christi præsentiâ, an præsens ibi Christus, & singularem suæ gratiæ gustum communicantibus præbeat; sed num ejus corpus adsit, num hoc vere & substantialiter edatur, & sanguis ejus bibatur? quod quia nunc defendunt ex corporis & humanæ in Christo naturæ ubiquitate, tota quæstio alium locum vel categoriam occupavit, quam prius, neque tam de Sacramento, quam de statu & conditione corporis Christi quæri videtur. Sed utrumsit, si verum, quod corpus Christi omnipræsens, aut hinc etiam substantialiter in S. Cœnâ adsit, non pendebit hoc ex nostrâ vel opinione, vel fide, sed ex rei veritate; ac proinde si vel erraremus quod illa non ita credimus, (in quo tamen non errare nos probatu facile est), attamen & præsens Christi corpus ubique nihilo secius esset, & à nobis quoque ederetur, quod tantâ contentione defendunt, ab infidelibus quoque & impiis manducari: proinde hæc quantumvis dissensus alicujus causa, Scismatis verò inter Ecclesias esse non debuit; quod quanto-pere piòs omnes à primo ejus ortu hucusque afflig at, nemo unquam satis expresserit. Quoties audita illa pii Melanthonis vox fuit, haud sine grandi animi mœrore atq; ejulatu expressa: non si tantum lacrymarum funderem, quantum hic præterfluens Albis vehit, exhaurire meum dolorem possem, quem fero propter hærentem hanc in Ecclesiis nostris controversiam! Hoc etiam scripsit Vito Theodoro, Ecclesiastæ Noribergensi a. cIↄ Iↄ xlv. ad Albertum Hartenbergium, a. cIↄ Iↄ lı. ad Hencelium, Consulem Augustanum, a. cIↄ Iↄ lv ı. ad alios. Ad Bucerum a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxv, Nulla enim res æque deterret homines ab Evangelio, ac nostra discordia. Dici haud potest, quantum hæc scandalorum ubiq; dederit. Pe scandalis: necesse quidem est venire scandala, sed væ ipsi homini, per quem venit scandalum. Matth. xv 11. 7. De tribus nobis hic differendum venit, de dissidio & scismate Lutheráno, super causâ Sacramentariâ: de sacramento & unione cum iis: tertio, de disputatione, & reliquis ipsorum Controversiis.
units.tr: Certainly this is a sad and pernicious schism, which Satan stirred up in the last century between the Lutheran Churches and ours, so that he might resist the work of the Reformation more effectively and slow its course. We may look at the parties involved, which arose from a single source, both having gone out from Popery and both intent on reforming it. Or we may look at the cause of the Holy Supper, for which the division was raised, although there ought to be no stronger bond of Christian love than that. Or we may look at the savage manner of disagreement, by which they attacked and persecuted our people, our Churches and our doctrine everywhere, beyond all measure. It is most lamentable that those who were at first one and the same, or companions in the same work, and who after the first division of minds were united several times, and always ought to be united, should have become so inflamed and implacable. If one considers the cause and origin of the dispute, the matter has come to be treated almost as an article of religion. And what is this Supper of the Lord, over which they are so torn apart? Surely it is not whether the Supper is to be frequented, or whether it is a sacrament, or how its fruit is rightly to be received by a faithful soul; these things contain its sum and essence. Nor is it about the presence of Christ, whether Christ is present there and gives a singular taste of his grace to those who communicate. Rather, the question is whether his body is there, whether it is truly and substantially eaten, and whether his blood is drunk. Because they now defend this from the ubiquity of Christ's body and of his human nature, the whole question seems to have taken a different place and category than before, and it seems to be asked not so much about the Sacrament as about the state and condition of the body of Christ. But whether it is true that the body of Christ is omnipresent, or whether, on that basis, it is also substantially present in the Holy Supper, will not depend on our opinion or faith, but on the truth of the matter. Therefore, even if we were wrong in not believing it so (though it is easy to prove that we are not wrong in this), nevertheless the present body of Christ would be everywhere all the same, and would also be eaten by us, as they defend so vehemently; it is eaten also by unbelievers and the impious. Hence, however much this disagreement may have been the cause of a dispute, it ought not to have been a schism between Churches. No one has ever adequately expressed how much this schism has afflicted all the godly from its first origin until now. How often was that saying of the pious Melanchthon heard, uttered with great grief and lamentation of mind: "Even if I could pour out as many tears as this Elbe carries past here, I could not drain away my sorrow, which I bear because of this controversy clinging to our Churches!" He wrote this also to Veit Dietrich, minister at Nuremberg, in 1545; to Albert Hartenberg in 1551; to Hencel, consul of Augsburg, in 1551; and to others in 1551. To Bucer in 1535 he wrote: "For nothing so deters men from the Gospel as our discord. It cannot be said how much this has caused scandals everywhere." Concerning offences: "It is necessary that offences come, but woe to that man through whom the offence comes" (Matth. xv 11. 7.). Here we have three things to discuss: first, the schism and division of the Lutherans over the Sacramentarian cause; second, the sacrament and union with them; third, the disputation and their other controversies.

units.la: In Schismatis perstringendâ historiâ, attendenda ejus occasio, tum ruptura, demum variae ejus à multis obfirmationes, & exasperationes, & rupturae productiones, ut minus corrigibilis evaserit. Occasio conjicienda in discordiam Lutheri cum collegâ Carolostadio. Ruptura, in scriptis adversariis non Lutheri tantum & Carolostadii, sed & illius in Zwinglium nominatim, inde Saxonicorum, & Tigurinorum, quibus dein Basileensis accesserunt, aliique. Obfirmationes Schismatis observandae, in contentionibus super Augustanâ Confessione, ab a. MDXXX, & demum in Libro Concordiae, pro canonizando dogmate Ubiquitatis facto, a. MDLXXVII. Circa syncretismum notamus, primo Auctores, qui pro eo sedulam navarunt operam, sive Ecclesiastici, quales inprimis Bucerus, Melanthon, sive politici; inter quos praecipuus Hassiae Langravius Philippus, alii post nominandi. Deinde Consensus quoquo pacto aliquoties initos. Marpurgi primùm anno MDXXIX, tum Witembergae a. MDXXXVI. Denique Sendomiriae, in Poloniâ, anno MDLXX. & alibi. Tertio, judicium de syncretismo caute tractando interponimus. Post quae loco ultimo, de reliquis cum Lutheranis controversiis, illarum origine, & tractandi modo disceptamus.
units.tr: In setting out the history of the schism, we must note its occasion, then its breach, and finally the various hardenings and exasperations by many, and the productions of the breach, by which it became less capable of correction. The occasion is to be found in the disagreement of Luther with his colleague Carlstadt. The breach is found in the writings of adversaries, not only of Luther and Carlstadt, but also of Luther's writings against Zwingli by name; from there came the Saxons and the Zurichers, to whom the Basel people were afterwards added, and others. The hardening of the schism is to be observed in the contentions over the Augsburg Confession from 1530, and finally in the Book of Concord, made in 1577 to canonize the dogma of Ubiquity. Concerning syncretism we note, first, the authors who devoted diligent effort to it, whether ecclesiastical men, such as chiefly Bucer and Melanchthon, or political men, among whom the principal one is Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, and others to be named later. Next, the consensus entered into several times in one way or another: first at Marburg in 1529, then at Wittenberg in 1536, and finally at Sandomierz in Poland in 1570, and elsewhere. Third, we set down a judgment on how syncretism is to be handled with caution. After these things, in the last place, we discuss the other controversies with the Lutherans, their origin, and the manner of treating them.

units.la: In intercessum verò non incongruum videri debet, aliqua de Luthero, de Carolostadio, de Zwinglio praenotasse. Natus est Martinus Lutherus a. MCCCCLXXXIII. d. x. Novembris, Islebiae, quod Comitatus Mansfeldiei oppidum est. Martinus appellatus, eo quod dies, quo baptizabatur infans, isti Sancto dicatus erat. Hoc pro more saeculi. Unde & Urbano Regio suum nomen mire contigit, mulierculis nomen Sancti, cujus die natus erat, oblitis, Sacerdos, quia Urbani diem sciebat haud procul abesse, Urbanum nominavit. Lutherus, emen-sis, lis trivialibus studiis Isenaci, Erphurdiam venit a. cIↄ Iↄ I. ætatis suæ xv ııı. ubi Magister artium renunciatus, Philosophiam docuit, annos natus viginti. Tum & juris aggressus studium fuit. Anno ætatis vigesimo primo, territus, ut volunt, violenta, ex fulmine, commilitonis sui morte, Monasterium ibidem Monachorum Augustinianorum ingressus est: ubi primum incidit in exemplar Bibliorum, nunquam sibi antehac visorum. Interim & sedulus in lectione Augustini, neque minus Scholasticorum, præsertim Gabriëlis, & Cameracensis: Occami scripta & acumen ipsi Thomæ, ac Scoto præferebat. Missam dicere cœpit ibidem ab a. cIↄ Iↄ VII. ætatis xxiv. V Vittembergam verò, ad illustrandam recens ab Electore Friderico erectam Academiam (cujus Ioh. Staupicius primus fuit Theologiæ professor, Ordinis Augustiniani eremitarum Vicarius Generalis per Germaniam, magnus Lutheri patronus; & primus Rector, Mellerstadius) Erphordia vocatus fuit a. cIↄ Iↄ VIII. cum annum ætatis ageret xxv I. Vbi primo Dialecticam & Physicam Aristotelis explicuit: inde, urgente Staupicio, Theologiæ Doctor, sumtus promotionis curante Electore, qui concionantem sæpius audiverat, eoque ejus ingenium demirabatur, factus est a. cIↄ Iↄ xı ı.anno ætatis xxx. Hinc jam prælegere Theologiam, & explicare primùm epistolam Pauli Apostoli ad Romanos, inde Psalmos cœpit, eâ dexteritate, vi, & doctrinæ puritate, in articulo præsertim de justificatione hominis coram Deo, quem tum à Staupicio, tum proprio conscientiæ sensu addidicerat, ut non potuerit quin Iohanni Tecelio, Dominicani Ordinis Monacho, indulgentias venales in Misniâ & Saxoniâ impudenter circumferenti ab a. cIↄ Iↄ xv ı, sic animose opponeret. Unde Reformationis, quod notum, coeptum opus. In quo, magnis multisque cum Adversariis colluctandum ei semper fuit, præter Tecelium, cum Eccio, Prierate, & postea Cajetano. Quin & silen- tium nium promisit aliquoties, modo idem Adversariis suis injungeretur, atque ad Pontificem provocavit, suæ ei lubenter submissurus. Tandem compertus à nimis quam multis, contra ac opinabatur, adeoque à Pontifice & Cardinalibus, illa dogmatum opprobria doceri ac defendi, exuto omni metu, & Romanæ sedis obedientiâ, in opere Reformationis animosè & constanter perrexit: quod factum ab anno clɔ Iɔxx. quando scripsit in litteris ad Spalatinum, inter alia: Ac me quidem facta mihi alea, contemnus est Romanus furor & favor: nolo eis reconciliari nec communicare in perpetuum, damnent extrantque mea. Ego vicissim, nisi ignem habere nequeam, damnabo, publiceque concremabo jus pontificium totum, id est, lernam illam haeresium, & finem habebit humilitatis exhibitæ hactenusque frustrata observantia, quâ nolo amplius inflari hostes Euangelii. Hoc anno Bulla Papæ adversus Lutherum prodiit, quam is, postquam sua scripta Colonienses hoc etiam anno combusserant, una cum jure Pontificio, die x. Decembris hujus ejusdem anni in exstructum rogum palam conjecit, addita hâc exe- cratione: quia te conturbasti Sanctum Domini, conturbet te ignis æternus. Iam anno clɔ Iɔ xv i i i. Heidelbergam, ad capitulum Ordinis, quod ibi habebatur, profectus Lutherus, pro testandâ suâ doctrinæque suæ innocentiâ, disputationem in Monasterio Augustinianorum, quod nunc Collegium Sapientiæ est, habuit de justificatione fidei, cujus theses extant Tom. i. Operum Lutheri Latin. Disputationi illi Bucerus tum temporis interfuit, omniaque, ut poterat, quæ à Luthero dicebantur, annotavit. Reversus inde domum, in prima, quæ cum Pontificiis institura de religione disputatio fuit, Lipsiæ, anno clɔ Iɔ xix. Carolostadius & Lutherus unà fuerunt, addito ipsis Melanthone: ubi cum Eckio primùm Carolostadius, de libero arbitrio, tum Lutherus, de Pontifice Ecclesiæ capite, disputavit. VVormatia reversus anno clɔ Iɔ xxi, ex consilio Electoris Saxoniæ Friderici abductus fuit in solitarium aliquem locum extra hominum notitiam & contubernium, arx fuit V Vartenburg, prope Isenacum (Pathmum appellare solitus), ubi circiter decem menses egit. Quo absente V Vittembergenses, interque eos præcipuus Carolostadius, nihilo segnius pergentes in Ecclesiæ reformatione, privatam missam, & imagines, Confessionem auricularem, discrimina ciborum, invocationem Sanctorum abrogarunt, & celebrare S. Cœnam sub utraque (uti solent loqui) specie, potius parte, instituerunt. Quæ res Lutherum, quod se absente, neque prius consultâ suâ authoritate, facta fuisset, adeo pupugit, ut inconsulto Electore, ex suo eremo V. Vittembergam a. cIↄ Iↄ xxi r. advolarit, ibique illa improbare, & publice etiam pro concione reprehendere inceperit, non tam quod male essent facta, quam quod non à se: veritus hoc pacto nomini & authoritati suæ aliquid derogatum iri.
units.tr: Some account of Luther, of Carlstadt and of Zwingli should be set out here, since it may seem not out of place. Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 at Eisleben, a town in the county of Mansfeld. He was called Martin because the day on which the infant was baptized was dedicated to that saint, as was the custom of the age. Hence it also happened, remarkably, that Urbanus Regius got his name: the women had forgotten the name of the saint on whose day he was born, and the priest, knowing that the day of Urban was not far off, named him Urbanus. Luther, having finished his elementary studies at Eisenach, came to Erfurt in 1501, in the fifteenth year of his age, where he was made Master of Arts and taught philosophy at the age of twenty. Then he also took up the study of law. In his twenty-first year, struck with terror (as they say) by the violent death of a fellow soldier, struck by lightning, he entered the monastery of the Augustinian monks in that same place. There he first came upon a copy of the Bible, which he had never seen before. Meanwhile he was diligent in reading Augustine, and no less the Scholastics, especially Gabriel and Cameracensis; he preferred the writings of Ockham and their acuteness even to Thomas and Scotus. He began to say Mass there from 1507, in his twenty-fourth year. Then, to adorn the Academy at Wittenberg, newly founded by the Elector Frederick (whose first professor of theology was John Staupitz, Vicar General of the Augustinian hermits throughout Germany, and a great patron of Luther; and whose first rector was Mellerstadt), he was summoned to Erfurt in 1508, in his twenty-fifth year. There he first expounded the dialectic and physics of Aristotle. Then, at the urging of Staupitz, and with the costs of his promotion borne by the Elector (who had often heard him preach and marvelled at his talent), he became Doctor of Theology in 1512, in his thirtieth year. From then on he began to lecture on theology, first expounding the Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Romans, and then the Psalms, with such skill, force and purity of doctrine, especially on the article of the justification of man before God, which he had learned both from Staupitz and from the sense of his own conscience, that he could not help opposing so boldly John Tetzel, a Dominican monk who shamelessly carried around indulgences for sale in Meissen and Saxony, from 1517. From this began the work of the Reformation, as is well known. In this work he always had to wrestle with many great adversaries, besides Tetzel, namely Eck, Prierias and later Cajetan. Indeed he promised silence several times, provided the same was enjoined on his adversaries, and he appealed to the Pope, to whom he would gladly submit. Finally, having discovered (contrary to what he had supposed) that those shameful doctrines were taught and defended by very many, and indeed by the Pope and the cardinals, he cast off all fear and obedience to the Roman See, and pressed on boldly and steadfastly in the work of reformation. This happened from 1520, when he wrote in a letter to Spalatin, among other things: "As for me, the die is cast; I despise Roman rage and favour. I do not wish to be reconciled to them nor to communicate with them for ever; let them condemn and burn my writings. For my part, unless I can have no fire, I shall condemn and publicly burn the whole Papal law, that is, that Lernaean hydra of heresies; and there will be an end to the humility I have shown and to the observance, hitherto fruitless, by which I no longer wish to flatter the enemies of the Gospel." In this same year a Bull of the Pope against Luther was issued. After the Cologne men had burned his writings, also this year, he publicly threw that Bull, together with the papal law, into a pyre built for the purpose, on 10 December of the same year, adding this curse: "Because you have troubled the Holy One of the Lord, may the eternal fire trouble you." Already in 1518 Luther had gone to Heidelberg for the chapter of the Order held there, and in order to bear witness to his doctrine and its innocence, he held a disputation in the monastery of the Augustinians, which is now the College of Wisdom, on the justification of faith. The theses of that disputation are found in volume 1 of Luther's Latin works. Bucer was present at that disputation at the time, and he noted down, as far as he could, everything that Luther said. Returning home from there, Carlstadt and Luther were together, with Melanchthon added, at the first disputation on religion held with the Papists, at Leipzig in 1519. There Carlstadt disputed with Eck first, on free will, and then Luther disputed on the headship of the Pope over the Church. Returning to Wittenberg from Worms in 1521, Luther was carried off, by the counsel of the Elector of Saxony Frederick, to a certain solitary place away from human notice and company: this was the castle of Wartburg near Eisenach (which he used to call Patmos), where he spent about ten months. In his absence the Wittenbergers, and among them especially Carlstadt, went on no less vigorously in the reform of the Church. They abolished the private Mass, images, auricular confession, distinctions of foods, and the invocation of the saints, and they instituted the celebration of the Holy Supper under both kinds (as they usually put it), or rather under one part of each. This so stung Luther, because it had been done in his absence and without first consulting his authority, that without the knowledge of the Elector he flew from his hermitage to Wittenberg in 1522, and there he began to disapprove of these things and to rebuke them publicly even from the pulpit. He did this not so much because they had been done badly, as because they had not been done by him, fearing that something would be taken away from his name and authority in this way.

units.la: Andreas Bodenstein Carolostadius, sic dictus ab oppido Franciæ Orientalis, in quo natus, quem ab initialibus nominis & cognominis litteris a b c Melanthon in privatis litteris Alphabetum solebat nominare, primus fuit Theologiæ Doctor in recenti Academiâ V Vittembergensi factus, & Professor Theologiæ: etiamque juris doctor fuit, & Lutherum postea Theologiæ Doctorem creavit: unde & Lutherus ei, ut Præceptori ac majori suo scribit in epistolis. Postquam Lutherus indulgentias oppugnare coepit, ei se mox adjunxit Carolostadius, atque a. cIↄ Iↄ xx, qui fatalis Papatui in illis oris suis, aperte & acriter Papismum oppugnandum desendumque docuit. Unde ejus decem tum temporis Conclusiones quas Christianissimas appellat, quarum tertia erat: Alexander quartus, & omnes post eum Pontifices Romani anathemate se per suas decretales perstrinxerunt, ab a. 1296 usque ad annum 1520 nunc præsentem. IV. Sequitur ergo, quod Leo decimus excommunicare non potest. Quia juxta suas Constitutiones: excommunicatus non potest excommunicare.
units.tr: Andreas Bodenstein Carolostadius, so called after the town in East France where he was born, whom Melanchthon in his private letters used to call "Alphabetum" from the initial letters a, b, c of his name, was the first to be made Doctor of Theology and Professor of Theology in the recently founded Academy of Wittenberg. He was also a doctor of law, and he later created Luther a Doctor of Theology, which is why Luther in his letters addresses him as his teacher and elder. When Luther began to attack indulgences, Carolostadius at once joined him in 1520. As a fatal enemy of the Papacy in those parts, he openly and vigorously taught that Papism must be attacked and defended against. Hence his ten theses of that time, which he calls most Christian. The third of them was: "Alexander IV and all the Roman pontiffs after him have bound themselves with anathema through their decretals, from 1296 down to the present year 1520." IV. It follows, therefore, that Leo X cannot excommunicate, because according to his own constitutions an excommunicated person cannot excommunicate.

units.la: Q q 3
units.tr: Q q 3

units.la: Et quæ sequuntur. Verum reformatione illa in Vittenbergæ, Luthero in Pathmo delitescente, peracta, quam diximus, reversus Lutherus hinc certamen orsus est cum Carolostadio. Quod initium dedit tristis & diuturni dissidii Sacramentarii. Namque aliter hic, aliter ille doctrinam & verba Cœnæ interpretabatur. Carolostadius verba, hoc est enim corpus meum exponebat, quasi per hoc, non panis, sed assidens Christi corpus ab ipso fuisset commonstratum: id est, quasi fracto, distributoque ad comedendum pane Christus sermone & manu ad suum versa corpus, dixisset: hoc est enim corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur. Lutherus aliter, & per hoc, panem denotari volebat. Inde æmulationes & contentiones inter Lutherum atque Carolostadium orta, præsertim quum hic videret, se ab illo aliquoties pro concione publice perstringi. Hinc V Vittembergam defendam sibi Carolostadius judicavit, atque vocatus Orlamundam, quod Thuringiæ oppidum, pastor Ecclesiæ hic constitutus anno clo Iɔxxiv. fuit. Neque ita tamen quievit Lutherus, sed hoc etiam anno Ienam veniens, ad sedandos furentium Anabaptistarum motus & tumultus, concionem habuit, cui & Carolostadius forte intererat. quā primum in Muncerum ejusque deliria invectus, porro ejusdem Alstetensis seditiosi spiritus dixit esse ἐἴφνο μάχτς & baptismi ac Sacramenti altaris destructores: quibus haud obscure Carolostadium designabat. Quod hic sentiens, a concione Lutherum in publico convenit diverso, atque expostulavit multis de injuria sibi palam facta. Ille vero adeo non placandum sibi offensum Carolostadii animum putavit, ut contra vehementius irritarit, protracto aureo nummo illum in scriptionem adversus se publicam cogens, ich beger/das ihr wider mich schreiben solt/ und gibt euch darumb den goldgulden / das ir meine nichts schonen solt / und so dapffer ir mich angreifft / je lieber ir mir fein solt. Hoc initium certaminis Sacramentarii fuit, haec occasio. Atrogantior Lutherus merito in eo visus fuit, quod adeo intemperanter tulit alios praeter se Reformationis ἐγχειρήσεως; quod non minus aegrum ei fecit ergo Huldrichum Zuinglium animum, apud Helvetios reformantem. Tanti mali causa exstitit inter bonos similtra aemulatio. Imprudentiam addidit, quod voluptei fuerit leviter a se atque ob meliorem causam dissentientes fratres pro concione perstringere & impetere: quod animi affectibus obnoxii, & ad turbas proni inefragabile est argumentum. Adde, ubi etiam ad scriptionem minium facile, quia tum alium provocat; tum ipse prosilit, in materia quae extra controversiam concionum, seu scriptionum commodius sopiatur, atque ubi non adversus hostes, sed haereticos, sed cum fratribus res est. Verum sapienter id quidem Deus ita permisit, ac moderatus in Luthero fuit, ut juxta virtutes plane divinas, etiam communis infirmitatis probaret lapsus, ne hominem ignoraremus, neve (quod alteroquin hominis facile committitur, & a quo de hic quidem immunes aliqui fuerunt) idolum ex eo faceremus, quem ad tantum opus Dei adhibebat: tum etiam ut plane hoc Dei opus sciremus, quod in bene reformanda Ecclesia homo aliis ἐργαλεῖον praestitit. Iena Lutherus Ottamundam pergens, ut pastorem agebat Carolostadius, cum nec salutare, nec fratrem appellare sustinuit, utpote aureo nummo sibi (ut dicebat) in adversarium conducto. Facta haec a. cI5 I5xxVI. Postea Carolostadius, jussu Electoris, sed instigante Luthero, quasi Anabaptistarum favet furoribus, Thuringia ejectus, & varia oberrans loca, libellos aliquot scripsit de Coena, quos Basileae edidit. Tandem & Figurum venit, anno cI5 I5 xxx. ubi Zuinglius docebat, qui de Carolostadio judicare solebat, idem ei accidisse quod Tyrioni, cui arma quidem ad pugnandum non deerant, sed animorum peritia. Figuri Carolostadius, quum jam violentam illam suam verborum Coena interpretationem abjecisset, factus fuit Ecclesiae diaconus, quod haud leviter Lutherum commovisse creditum. Post obitum Zuinglii, Basileam concessit, ubi decem annis in Schola & Ecclesia docuit, commorturus ibidem a. CIↄ Iↄ XLI.
units.tr: And so on. But when that reformation at Wittenberg had been carried through, as we have said, while Luther was hiding on Patmos, Luther returned and began a quarrel with Carolostadius. This gave rise to the sad and long-lasting Sacramentarian dispute. For the one interpreted the doctrine and words of the Supper in one way, the other in another. Carolostadius explained the words "hoc est enim corpus meum" as if by them Christ had pointed out the body sitting there, not the bread: that is, as if Christ, with his speech and his hand turned toward the bread, broken and distributed for eating, had said: "This is my body, which is broken for you." Luther wanted it understood otherwise, as signifying the bread. From this arose rivalry and contention between Luther and Carolostadius, especially when the latter saw that he was being openly attacked from the pulpit by Luther more than once. So Carolostadius judged that he must defend himself at Wittenberg, and, being called to Orlamünde, a town in Thuringia, he became minister of the congregation there in 1524. Luther, however, did not rest in this way. In the same year, coming to Jena to quell the riots and tumults of the raging Anabaptists, he preached a sermon, at which Carolostadius happened to be present. In it he first attacked Müntzer and his follies, and then said that the same seditious spirit of Alstedt was the destroyer of baptism and of the Sacrament of the altar, which clearly pointed to Carolostadius. Perceiving this, Carolostadius met Luther publicly after the sermon, and complained at length of the injury done to him openly. Luther, however, thought the offended mind of Carolostadius was so far from being appeased that he rather provoked him more vehemently, offering him a gold coin and urging him to write publicly against him: "I want you to write against me, and I give you a gold gulden for it, so that you spare me nothing, and the more bravely you attack me, the more you will please me." This was the beginning and the occasion of the Sacramentarian conflict. Luther was rightly seen as too arrogant in this, since he bore so intemperately that others besides himself undertook the work of Reformation. This made Huldrych Zwingli, who was reforming among the Swiss, no less sorrowful in mind. The cause of so great an evil among good men was a mutual rivalry. Imprudence was added in that Luther delighted in lightly attacking and assailing from the pulpit brethren who dissented from him, even for a better cause, which is an unfailing sign of a mind prone to passions and inclined to disturbances. Add that he readily provoked to writing when the matter was one that could be more conveniently settled outside the controversies of sermons and writings, and where the business was not with enemies or heretics, but with brethren. Yet God wisely permitted this, and so moderated it in Luther, that, in keeping with his entirely divine virtues, he also showed the lapses of common human weakness, lest we should not know him as a man, and lest (which is otherwise easily committed by man, and from which some were indeed free) we should make an idol of the one whom he used for so great a work of God; and also so that we might clearly know this to be the work of God, namely that in the good reformation of the Church, man served as an instrument for others. When Luther went on to Orlamünde, where Carolostadius acted as minister, he could not bring himself either to greet him or to call him brother, since (as he said) he had been hired against him for a gold coin. This happened in 1526. Afterwards Carolostadius, by order of the Elector but at the instigation of Luther, who was supposedly favouring the frenzies of the Anabaptists, was driven out of Thuringia. Wandering through various places, he wrote several booklets on the Supper, which he published at Basel. At last he came to Zürich in 1530, where Zwingli taught, and who used to judge of Carolostadius that the same thing had happened to him as to the Tyrian, who had arms enough for fighting but lacked skill in handling men's minds. At Zürich, Carolostadius, having by then abandoned that violent interpretation of the words of the Supper, was made deacon of the Church, which is believed to have stirred Luther not a little. After Zwingli's death he withdrew to Basel, where for ten years he taught in the school and the Church, dying there in 1541.

units.la: Huldrichus Zuinglius
units.tr: Huldrych Zwingli

units.la: natus est a. CIↄ CCCC LXXXVII. Kal. Ianuar. Basileae primum litteris operam dedit, ubi & postea easdem in Schola Martiniana docuit. Inde in Philosophia gradum Magisterii adeptus, ad Theologiam se applicuit, in quibus illos fructus fecit, ut non secundum munus vocatus sit, ad pastorale obnoxio, nec audito Lutheri nomine, quando nec annunciare caepit, potissimum in doctrina de justificatione hominis coram Deo, quam a Papismi fermento deputatam didicerat, a praeceptore suo Thoma VVit-tembachio. Glaronae vocatus fuit ad famosissimum tum temporis Virginis Eremitanae templum, ubi collegam habuit Leonem Judae. Lo- se ut Missam celebraret monentibus, aliquando respondit: Si vere Christus est in hostia, indignus sum qui illum intueatur; indignior, qui Basi offeram. Si non est in hostia, vae mihi, si panem pro Deo, pulo adorandum proponam. Glaronae translatus fuit Tigurum anno CIↄ Iↄ XXIX. Kal. Ianuar. quo tempore quam rationem servarit in praedicando Evangelio, ipse postea a. CIↄ Iↄ XXII. exposuit in libro, quem Archetelem inscripsit, qui est Tomo operum: anno abhinc quarto, inquit, (ut rationem praedicationis nostrae Tigurii promulgare habeat) solidum Evangelium secundum Matthaeum praedicavi, quo semper illum nomine nominari quidem audieram, quorum facionis me exemplis, nam antequam ea ad manus vestras venerint, ordinem negotiatio, imo nunc annum fere pollicitus sum, id me fa-
units.tr: was born in the year 1487, on 1 January. At Basel he first devoted himself to literature, and later taught the same subjects in the Martinsschule there. Having obtained the degree of Master in Philosophy, he turned to theology, and made such progress in it that he was called to the pastoral office, though he had not yet heard the name of Luther, and had not yet begun to preach. He taught chiefly the doctrine of man's justification before God, which he had learned from his teacher Thomas Wyttenbach to regard as a leaven of Papism. He was called to Glarus, to the then most famous church of the Hermit Virgin, where his colleague was Leo Jud. When Leo and others urged him to celebrate Mass, he once replied: "If Christ is truly in the host, I am unworthy to look upon him, and still more unworthy to offer him. If he is not in the host, woe to me if I put forward bread to be adored as God." He was transferred from Glarus to Zurich on 1 January 1519. Concerning the method he followed in preaching the Gospel at that time, he himself later explained in 1522, in the book he entitled Archeteles, which is in the volume of his works. "Four years ago," he says, "so that I might set out the method of our preaching at Zurich, I preached the solid Gospel according to Matthew, though I had always heard it called by that name. I have promised to pursue the same method, and now nearly a year..." The sentence continues in the next unit.

units.la: Note: the lower part of the page is faint and partly illegible; the text above is a best reading. facturum. Haec adversus illos dixit, qui eum temere nomine & authoritate Lutheri praegravare conabantur. Et quanto tum temporis in pretio apud ipsos Adversarios habitus fuerit, declarat epistola seu Breve Papae Adriani VI. ad ipsum missum, Papatus ejus anno primo, CIↃ IↃ XXIII. d. XXIII, Januarii, quo & Zuinglium, dilectum filium, & egregiam ejus virtutem, tum quoque affectum erga eum & ipsius commoda honoresque mire deprædicat. Occubuit Zuinglius a. CIↃ IↃ XXXI, die XI. Oct. ætatis anno XLIV, quadriennio Luthero minor. In Carolostadio forte haud immerito majorem desideres prudentiam, & constantiam; in Lutheri moderationem & humilitatem; sed in Zuinglio quid carpas, haud equidem scio, adeo vir prudens & doctus juxta fuit, & in controversia Sacramentaria adversus Lutherum non scripsit prior nominatim, & vulgari lingua, sed Latina, ut eruditis haec potius objicere judicanda, quam ad populum commovendum emittere, secus ac Lutherus; atque ad sententiae & doctrinae suae simplicem expositionem, non Lutheri impugnationem, vel nominis ejus detractionem, videretur. Vide ejus Amicam exegesin, sive expositionem Eucharistici negotii, ad Martinum Lutherum, Oper. Zuinglii, Tom. II. scriptam a. CIↃ IↃ XXVII. ubi in epistola ad Lutherum, inquit: non bellum decrevi, aut ad singulare certamen in harenam descendi, sed fediculum tibi mitto librum: non qui res repetitum, sed compositum vestiat. Vide & expositionis ei nomen praefiximus, quo tibi sententiam nostram ac scripturae fundamentum, quo nitimur, amice exponat, ne ad manus veniatur: quod Pontificii & mordaces quidam, sed mali poetae aliquando anxie optarunt. Ad Lectorem: Dissentiebat a nobis palam Lutherus, ac maledicta in omnia pacis gratia ferentes congerebat, nemo ex nobis mutinabat: ac ne nunc quidem convitiis aget. Quid ergo novi satum erit, ubi nominatim expositionem nostram ad eum damus? quandoquidem ille primus sic a nobis dissentiebat, ut non esset essct contentus scientiam nostram reiicere, nisi nos inter fanatioos quoque & praestigiatores connumerasset: idque libris editis, ut est in epistola ad Rutlingenses, & Carolostadii revocatione. Et nos sine intermissione ipsius argumentis, sed praeterito ejus nomine, respondimus & ad ea, quibus fidebat, perinde atque tunc facturi essemus. Scribebat ergo & antea contra nos nominatim etiam Lutherus, nos contra ipsum, sed tacite ac intacto ejus nomine. Nunc ad eum scribemus nominatim, sed citra contumeliam: si ipse nobis irattus erit, nihil novi fiet: si nos benigne feriemus; nam pote malis jam duratis, quae in nos jaculabitur, iterum novi fiet nihil: prius enim ad eadem tela stetimus incoinciventibus oculis.
units.tr: facturum. He said this against those who tried to disparage him rashly under the name and authority of Luther. How highly he was then regarded by the Adversaries themselves is shown by the letter, or brief, which Pope Adrian VI sent to him in the first year of his pontificate, on 23 January 1523, in which he greatly praises Zwingli, his beloved son, and his outstanding virtue, and also his affection towards the Pope and his advantages and honours. Zwingli died on 11 October 1531, in the forty-fourth year of his age, four years younger than Luther. In Carlstadt you may perhaps rightly miss greater prudence and constancy, and in Luther moderation and humility; but what fault to find with Zwingli I really do not know, so wise and learned a man was he. In the Sacramentarian controversy he did not write against Luther first, nor by name, nor in the vernacular, but in Latin, so that these objections might be judged something to put before the learned rather than to stir up the people, unlike Luther; and he seems to have aimed at a simple exposition of his own opinion and doctrine, not at an attack on Luther or a disparagement of his name. See his Amica exegesis, or exposition of the Eucharistic matter, addressed to Martin Luther, in the Works of Zwingli, vol. II, written in 1527. In the letter to Luther he says: "I have not decided on war, nor have I come down into the arena for single combat, but I send you a little book, not one that repeats the matter but one that sets it out in a composed form. See also that we have prefixed to it the name of an exposition, so that it may explain to you in a friendly way our opinion and the foundation of Scripture on which we rest, lest it come to hand otherwise. This is what the Papists and certain biting but bad poets have sometimes anxiously wished for." To the Reader: "Luther openly dissented from us and heaped curses on all who bore the grace of peace; none of us grumbled, and even now he will not be stopped by reproaches. What, then, will be new if we now give him our exposition by name? Since he first dissented from us in such a way that he was not content to reject our knowledge unless he also counted us among the fanatics and deceivers; and this in published books, as in his letter to the Reutlingers, and in the recall of Carlstadt. And we have answered without interruption his arguments, but without naming him, and we answered those things in which he trusted, just as we would have done then. So Luther too had written against us by name before, and we against him, but tacitly and without touching his name.
