Now we shall write to him by name, but without insult: if he is angry with us, nothing new will happen; if we strike him kindly, nothing new will happen either, since we have already hardened ourselves against the wounds he throws at us, having stood against the same weapons with eyes unblinking."

units.la: Inde Lutherus sermonem a se in Vittembergensi Ecclesia habitum, pro substantialis corporis & sanguinis Christi in Sacramento assertione, contra Swenmeros aut Fanaticos edit; cui reponere Apologiam Zuinglius, a multis ad id rogatus, necesse habuit, sed vide quam sollicite, quamque prudenter, quippe hic primus liber adversus Lutherum ab eo Germanice conscriptus fuit, anno MDXXVII. v. Cal. April. Nec enim hic alios, inquit, tumultus aut turbas quaerimus, sed hoc unum cavere conamur, ne quando vel falsa scriptorum interpretatione vel ignorantia tenebris circumventi decipiamur: praeterea ne quisquam in Christi ecclesia tantum authoritatis sibi vendicare instituat, ne nemini ipsum citra divini verbi quoque testimonium quidvis affirmanti aut huic falsum sensum obtrudenti liceat reprehendere. Deinde: Primum vero diligentissime te admonitum velim, amice Lector, ut excussa omni oscitantia cum judicio legere discas, nec quidquam tò negligentia te adduci patiaris, ut quam primum aliquid vel a Luthero vel Zuinglio dictum scriptumve esse audis, id ipsum statim citra omnem ipsius rei considerationem diligentiorem temere arripere velis, ita ut huic te totum committas: quin potius ad judicii veri regulam singula revocando in am divi-nae veritati verboque Dei aeterno conformia loquantur scribantur considerabis.
units.tr: Then Luther published a sermon he had delivered in the church at Wittenberg, against the Swenckfeldians or fanatics, in support of the substantial presence of the body and blood of Christ in the Sacrament. Zwingli, asked to do so by many, felt obliged to reply to it with an Apology; but see how carefully and how prudently he did so. For this was the first book he wrote against Luther, and he wrote it in German, in the year 1527, on 28 March. "I am not seeking here," he says, "to stir up any other tumults or troubles, but I try to take care of this one thing: that we may not be deceived, surrounded by darkness, through a false interpretation of the writings or through ignorance. Moreover, let no one undertake to claim so much authority in the Church of Christ that he may rebuke whoever is not permitted, without the testimony of God's Word, to assert anything or to force a false sense upon it." Then: "But first I would have you most diligently warned, friendly reader, that you learn to read with judgment, shaking off all sluggishness, and that you do not allow yourself to be led by carelessness into snatching up at once, without any more careful consideration of the matter, whatever you hear as soon as possible was said or written by Luther or Zwingli, so as to commit yourself wholly to it. Rather, you will consider each thing by bringing it back to the rule of true judgment, and whether what is said or written agrees with divine truth and the eternal Word of God."

units.la: Tum in Responsione ad Lutheri librum de Sacramento, eodem anno scriptâ; nostra quidem, inquit, Latine edita, in quibus ad omnia argumenta tua (quae hactenus à nemine adhuc tractata & convicta esse saepe conquestus es) respondimus, peregrina tamen lingua usi, ne quando nos alicujus odii ac invidiae insimulare posses, quasi dedecoris & infamiae tuae siti inflammati nomen tuum universis Germaniae populis invisum & exosum facere cupiamus. De primis Carolostadii hâc in causâ scriptis libellis, unde magnum Zuinglio conflatum ab aliis odium & invidia, vide quam ingenue, & prudenter judicet in primâ ejus de hâc re scriptione, nempe epistolâ de Cœnâ Domini, ad Matthæum Albertum Rutlingensem Ecclesiasten, anno eIↄ Iↄ xx iv. d. xv i. Novemb. Carolostadius, ut neque de isto taceam, qui sive tempestive, sive minus, de improviso hanc rem in vulgus dissipavit, ac libellum quendam trium paginarum de hâc re edidit, sub titulo, De execrabili abusu Eucharistiae; eum legimus, postea quam fratres, praesertim Leo noster, orarent ut legerem, ipsisque prius non esset improbatus: lectus, placuit multis locis, quibusdam displicuit, quod res omnium difficillima non satis humerorum haberet. Quique à sententiâ Carolostadii dissentiebat, ut quem quidem oppugnare falsam, sed nec tamen veram tueri persuasus erat, censebatque tyroni simillimi, cui non quidem animus & arma ad pugnandum deessent, sed armorum peritia, in istâ verò proponendâ quam fuit modestus, quam sanctus! In ipsâ illâ ad Matthæum Rutlingensem epistolâ: Num tametsi ea sententia, quam dicturi sumus, vehementer tibi arridebit, nihil tamen definimus, sed nostra in medium proferimus: ut si Domino placuerit, alii quoque sic sentire doceantur, sed & spiritus, qui nos dimittat, doceat: is enim si voluerit sic intelligi, frustra verba fundemus. Deum ergo Opt. Max. precor, ut vias nostras dirigat: ac sicubi simus Balaam in morem veritati pertinaciter obluctaturi, angelum suum opponat, qui machaerâ suâ minis hunc asinum (insitiam & audaciam dicto nostram, si saltem ex audacia gloriaeque cupiditate quicquam nobis hic agitur) sic ad maceriam adfligat, ut factum pedem, hoc est impurum illotumque carnis sensum auferamus, ne ultra blasphememus nomen domini Dei nostri. Lutherus opinionem de Sacramento suam hauserat vel renovarat ex lectione Cardinalis Aliacensis, in Quartum Sententiarum, ubi is sc. missâ transsubstantiatione, magis inclinare in consubstantiationem, nisi Ecclesiae obstaret decisio, fatetur. De quo Lutherus, in libro de captivitate Babylonica, scripto anno cIↄ Iↄ xx. in hunc modum palam loquutus est: Hic VViglephusta, & sexcentis nominibus haereticus ero. Quid tum? postquam Romanus Episcopus, Episcopus esse desiit, & tyrannus factus est, non formido ejus universa Decreta, cujus non sic esse potestatem, articulos novos fidei condendi, nec Concilii quidem generalis. Dedit mihi quondam, cum Theologiam scholasticam haurirem, occasionem cogitandi D. Cardinalis Cameracensis libro sententiarum quarto, acutissime disputans: multo probabilius esse, & minus superfluorum miraculorum poni, si in altari verum corpus verumque vinum, non autem accidentia esse astruerentur, nisi Ecclesia determinasset contrarium. Postea videns quae esset Ecclesia, quae hoc determinasset, nempe Thomistica, hoc est, Aristotelica, audacior factus sum, et qui interfuerunt et sacrum hereticum, eandem stabiliri consentiam meam, sententia priore, Esse videlicet verum panem verumque vinum, in quibus Christi vera caro vernsque sanguis, non aliter nec minus sit, quam illi sub accidentibus suis ponunt. Hinc ergo accepta Lutheri opinione, disputari super ea coepit a Carolostadio primum, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxii, at scriptis christianis, ab anno cIↄ Iↄ xxiv. non inter istum solum, & Lutherum, sed hunc quoque, & Zuinglium, Oecolampadium, aliosque.
units.tr: Then, in his Reply to Luther's book on the Sacrament, written in the same year, he says: "Ours, indeed, has been published in Latin, in which we have answered all your arguments (which you have often complained no one has yet treated or refuted); but we used a foreign language, lest you might ever accuse us of some hatred or envy, as if, inflamed with thirst for your shame and infamy, we wished to make your name hated and odious to all the peoples of Germany." Concerning the first writings of Carlstadt in this cause, from which great hatred and envy were stirred up against Zwingli by others, see how frankly and prudently he judges in his first writing on this matter, namely the letter on the Lord's Supper, to Matthias Albertus, preacher at Reutlingen, dated 16 November 1524. "Carlstadt, not to pass over him either, who, whether opportunely or not, unexpectedly scattered this matter among the people, and published a little book of three pages on it, under the title On the Execrable Abuse of the Eucharist: this we read, after the brothers, especially our Leo, asked us to read it, and it had not been disapproved by them first. Having read it, many parts pleased, some displeased, because a matter of the greatest difficulty did not have enough shoulders to bear it." And he who dissented from Carlstadt's opinion, since he was persuaded that he was indeed to be opposed as false, but yet not to defend the true view, judged himself most like a beginner, who lacked not spirit and arms for fighting but skill in handling the arms. Yet in setting this forth how modest and how holy he was! In that same letter to Matthias of Reutlingen: "Although the opinion we are about to state will please you greatly, we define nothing, but bring our views forward, so that, if it pleases the Lord, others too may be taught to think so, and the Spirit who lets us go may teach them as well. For if he is willing for it to be understood thus, we shall pour out words in vain." So I pray to God Most Good and Greatest that he may direct our ways; and if we should be about to struggle stubbornly against the truth like Balaam, may he set against us his angel, who with his sword may strike this ass (I call our insolence and audacity so, if indeed anything here is driven by audacity and love of glory) against the wall, so that we may remove the defiled foot, that is, the impure and unwashed sense of the flesh, and no longer blaspheme the name of the Lord our God. Luther had drawn his opinion on the Sacrament from, or renewed it by, reading the Cardinal of Cambrai on the Fourth Book of the Sentences, where he admits that, were it not for the decision of the Church, he would incline from transubstantiation to consubstantiation. On this matter Luther spoke openly in his book On the Babylonian Captivity, written in 1520, in this manner: "Here I shall be a Wycliffite and a heretic in six hundred ways. What then? Since the Roman Bishop has ceased to be a bishop and has become a tyrant, I do not fear all his decrees; his power is not such that he can set up new articles of faith, nor even a general council." Once, when I was drinking in scholastic theology, the most acute disputation of the Lord Cardinal of Cambrai in the fourth book of the Sentences gave me occasion to think it far more probable, and less full of superfluous miracles, to assert that on the altar there is the true body and the true wine, and not accidents, unless the Church had determined otherwise. Afterwards, seeing what Church had determined this, namely the Thomist, that is the Aristotelian, I became bolder, and I was not willing to let my opinion be overturned by a heretical council, since it was determined by the former opinion, namely that there is true bread and true wine, in which the true flesh and true blood of Christ are no differently or less than they posit under their accidents." From this, then, Luther's opinion was taken up, and it began to be disputed about, first by Carlstadt in 1522, and in written Christian works from 1524, not only between him and Luther, but also between him and Zwingli, Oecolampadius, and others.

units.la: Inde natae diversae Confessiones Ecclesiarum Saxonicarum, & Helveticarum, in Comitiis Augustanis anno cIↄ Iↄ xxx. Nam postquam suam, a Luthero, Melanthone, Iusto Iona, & Bugenhagio primum a die xiv. Martii cIↄ Iↄxxx. delineari coeptam, & septemdecim articulis comprehensam, qui Tom. v. Germanico Ienensi Lutheri, & alibi leguntur, & in Annalibus Evangelicis Sculteti, Decad. ii. atque inde à Melanthone, non primum Augustæ compositam, (ut nonnulli scribunt), sed hic exasciatam & in istam formam redactam, iterumque Luthero missam Coburgum, in arce vicinâ, ubi subsistebat, probatamque adeo, ut scriberet se in eâ emendare nihil posse, neque sibi facile futurum suisse, tantâ moderatione ac styli lenitate uti, dan er so sanfft / und leise nicht streiten sollte / uti loquitur, Tom. v. German. Ienens. sol. 22. postquam (dico) illam Confessionem ElectOr Saxoniæ Iohannes, cum Iohanne Friderico, filio; & Georgio Marchione Brandeburgensi; Ernesto, & Francisco fratribus, Ducibus Brunsvicensibus, & Luneburgensibus; Philippo, Hassiæ Lantgravio; V Volfango, Principe Anhaltino, & Legatis civitatum Noribergæ, & Reutlingæ, obtulisse die xxiv. Iunii, lectaque postridie in palatio Cæsaris publice fuisset, aliam quatuor Civitates, Argentoratum, Constantia, Memminga, & Lindavium, auctore Bucero & Capitone, quæ doctrinam de Sacramento apertius, planius, veriusque explicaret, quam illa Saxonica, Imperatori in Comitiis exhibuerunt: inde & Zuinglius, quia variis per Adversarios passim impetebatur calumniis, ob causam doctrinæ, quasi mira horrendaque doceret, singularem sententiæ suæ Consessionem Imperatori misit. Adeo ut triplex in his Comitiis oblata fuerit Confessio, Melanthonis illa Saxonicorum, quæ vulgò Augustana nominatur; & quatuor civitatum; & postremò Zuinglii, Augustanæ Confessionis primos fuisse auctores illos, quos diximus, & quo quantoque tempore primos articulos ruditer consignarint, operæ pretium est audire ex litteris Lutheri ad Justum Ionam, eò magis quò circa horum historiam multos errare comperimus. Ita habet epistola, S. Scri-ptu
units.tr: Hence arose the different Confessions of the Saxon and Helvetic churches at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530. For after their own confession, begun by Luther, Melanchthon, Justus Jonas and Bugenhagen, first drafted from 14 March 1530 and comprised in seventeen articles (which are read in volume 5 of Luther's German Jena edition and elsewhere, and in Scultetus's Annales Evangelici, decade 2), was composed not first at Augsburg by Melanchthon, as some write, but was polished there and reduced to this form, and then sent back to Luther at Coburg, in the nearby fortress where he was staying. It was so approved by him that he wrote that he could change nothing in it, and that it would not have been easy for him to use such moderation and gentleness of style, that he should not argue so gently and quietly, as he puts it (vol. 5 of the German Jena edition, p. 22). After (I say) Elector John of Saxony, together with his son John Frederick; George, Margrave of Brandenburg; Ernest and Francis, brothers, dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg; Philip, Landgrave of Hesse; Wolfgang, Prince of Anhalt; and the envoys of the cities of Nuremberg and Reutlingen, had presented that confession on 24 June, and it had been publicly read the next day in the Emperor's palace, four other cities, Strasbourg, Konstanz, Memmingen and Lindau, under the authorship of Bucer and Capito, presented to the Emperor at the Diet another document, which explained the doctrine of the sacrament more openly, plainly and truly than that Saxon one. Zwingli too, because he was assailed on all sides by the adversaries with various calumnies, as if he taught wonderful and horrible things, sent the Emperor a separate confession of his own opinion. So three confessions were offered at this Diet: Melanchthon's Saxon one, which is commonly called the Augsburg Confession; that of the four cities; and lastly Zwingli's. It is worth hearing from Luther's letters to Justus Jonas who were the first authors of the Augsburg Confession, and how quickly and for how long they roughly drafted its first articles, since we find that many err about this history. The letter reads as follows: The Prince wr

units.la: ptu psit Princeps nobis, id est, tibi, Pomerano, Philippo, & mihi communes literas, ut una simus, & omnibus sepositis aliis rebus, ante Dominicam futuram absolvamus, quæ necessaria sunt ad Comitia 8. Aprilis futura. Carolus enim Cæsar ipse aderit Augustæ, amicè compositurus omnia, ut scribit in suâ bullâ. Quare hodie & cras, licet absente testaciemus nos tres, quantum possumus: tamen & tuum erit, ut Principi voluntati satisfiat, rejectis in socios reliquos laboribus tuis, cras te hicistere nobiscum. Festinata enim sunt omnia. Christus adspiret, ut omnia in gloriam ejus siant. Amen. Hora 12. 14. Martii, 4. 30. Augustæ quum aliquo tempore Saxoniæ Elector, Melanthon, alii morarentur, ante Cæsaris adventum, Elector ad Martinum Lutherum Confessionem à Melanthone revisam retextamque misit, hisce cum litteris, S. Reverende & doctissime nobis dilecte & devote: postquam vos, & alii nostri Theologi Witeberge, nobis clementer mandantibus & petentibus, articulos de religione nostra controversos, scripto brevi delineastis, non volumus vos celare, jam M. Philippum Melanthonem denuò eos hic Augustæ revidisse, & in formam redegisse, quam vobis unà mittimus. Et clementer petimus, ut eosdem articulos accuratius revidere, & expendere non gravemini. Et sive ita, ut scripti sunt, vobis placebunt, sive addendum aliquid aut adimendum esse cogitabitis, scripto sententiam vestram annotare, & per hunc tabellarium sine morâ, bene munitos & obsignatos remittere velitis, ut Cæsare, quem brevi expectamus adveniente, instructi & parati simus. Ita ergo & Luthero, & Melanthoni debetur hæc Confessio, ut præcipuis ejus auctoribus, illi quasi patri, huic matri, quorum ille plus materiæ, hic formæ contulerit, quamque à se aliquoties mutatam variatamque fassus haud semel fuit. In epistolis ad Ioachimum Camerarium, de Actis in Conventu Augustano, part. 1. Consil. Theol. Ego mutabam & refingebam pleraque quotidie. Plura etiam mutatura, si nostri [illegible, ~3 letters] permisissent. Ad ipsum Lutherum:
units.tr: The Prince has written to us, that is, to you, the Pomeranian, Philip and me, asking us to be together and, setting aside all other business, to finish before next Sunday the things needed for the Diet fixed for 8 April. For Emperor Charles himself will be present at Augsburg, to settle everything amicably, as he writes in his bull. So today and tomorrow, although you are absent, we three will bear witness as far as we can; yet it will also be your duty to satisfy the Prince's wish, by passing your labours on to the other colleagues and coming here to us tomorrow. For everything is being hurried. May Christ breathe on us, so that all things are done to his glory. Amen. Hour 12, 14 March, 4.30. At Augsburg, while the Elector of Saxony, Melanthon and the others were staying there before the Emperor's arrival, the Elector sent to Martin Luther the Confession, revised and rewoven by Melanthon, with this letter: Reverend and most learned, our dear and devoted friend: after you and our other theologians at Wittenberg, at our gracious command and request, wrote down briefly the articles of our religion that are in dispute, we do not wish to conceal from you that Master Philip Melanthon has now revised them again here at Augsburg and reduced them to the form which we send you with this letter. And we graciously ask that you not hesitate to review and weigh these same articles more carefully. And whether they please you as they are written, or whether you think something should be added or removed, we ask that you note your opinion in writing and send it back by this messenger without delay, well secured and sealed, so that we may be instructed and prepared for the Emperor, whom we expect to arrive shortly. So this Confession is owed to both Luther and Melanthon, as its chief authors: to the one as father, to the other as mother; the one contributed more of the matter, the other more of the form. Melanthon himself often admitted that it had been changed and varied by him, and not only once. In his letters to Joachim Camerarius, on the proceedings at the Augsburg Diet, part 1, Consilia Theologica: I kept changing and recasting most things every day. I would have changed even more, if our people had allowed it. To Luther himself: Every day we change much in the Apology. He calls the Confession an Apology, as he declares in another letter to the same man: Our Apology is sent to you, though it is more truly a Confession. So it should be no great cause for complaint that something in the Confession was later altered, while Luther was still alive. On this matter John Brenz wrote to Vitus Theodorus in the year 1541 in this manner: I usually compare this later edition of the Apology with the earlier, to see what has been changed, and I find that most things have been altered. I know, however, that Philip does nothing rashly, without judgment. So while I compare and weigh the reasons for the changes, I wonder how much profit I gain from reading it. That change came about from the Wittenberg Concord of the year 1537, when the Confession was revised, corrected and enlarged by Melanthon.

units.la: Ia Apologia quotidie multa mutamus. Apologiam nominat, Confessionem: uti in altera ad eundem declarat epistola: Mittitur tibi Apologia nostra, quamquam verius Confessio est. Ut minus exagitandum fuerit, quod postea etiam aliquid in confessione variatum, ipso adhuc superstite Luthero, fuerit. Qua de re Ioh. Brentius, hunc in modum scripsit ad Vitum Theodorum, anno cIↄ Iↄ xlı. Ego soleo hanc posteriorem editionem Apologiae cum priori conferre, ut videam, quid mutatum sit, & invenio plerasque esse mutatas. Scio autem Philippum citra judicium nil temere mutare. Quare dum confero & expendo causas mutationis, mirum quanto cum fructu a lectione discedam. Mutatio illa contigit a Concordia V Vittembergensi, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxvıı. quando Confessio a Melanthone fuit recognita, emendata, & locupletata.
units.tr: In the Apology we change many things every day. He calls the Confession an Apology, as he declares in another letter to the same man: "Our Apology is sent to you, though it is more truly a Confession." So it should be no great cause for complaint that something in the Confession was later altered, while Luther was still alive. On this matter John Brenz wrote to Vitus Theodorus in the year 1541 in this manner: "I usually compare this later edition of the Apology with the earlier, to see what has been changed, and I find that most things have been altered. I know, however, that Philip does nothing rashly, without judgment." So while I compare and weigh the reasons for the changes, I wonder how much profit I gain from reading it. That change came about from the Wittenberg Concord of the year 1537, when the Confession was revised, corrected and enlarged by Melanthon.

units.la: Decimus articulus, qui de S. Coenâ agit, in prima editione sic legitur. De Coenâ Domini docent, quod corpus & sanguis Christi verè adsint, & distribuantur vescentibus in Coenâ Domini: & improbant secus docentes. In hac autem variata, uti vulgo ad majorem invidiam loquuntur: De Coena Domini docent, quod cum pane & vino vere exhibeantur corpus & sanguis Christi vescentibus in Coenâ Domini. Adeo ut & in ipsa thesi, & adjecto vel omisso anathemate, sit discrepantia. Ibi dicitur Christi corpus adesse & distribui: hic duntaxat exhiberi: ibi secus docentes notantur; hic non.
units.tr: The tenth article, which deals with the Lord's Supper, reads thus in the first edition: "They teach that concerning the Lord's Supper the body and blood of Christ are truly present, and are distributed to those who eat in the Lord's Supper, and they condemn those who teach otherwise." In the altered version, however, which is commonly quoted to heighten the odium, it reads: "They teach that concerning the Lord's Supper the body and blood of Christ are truly exhibited with the bread and wine to those who eat in the Lord's Supper." So there is a difference both in the thesis itself and in the addition or omission of the anathema. There it is said that the body of Christ is present and distributed; here only that it is exhibited. There those who teach otherwise are condemned; here they are not.

units.la: Articulum illum decimum, uti totam Confessionem, certum est ab Auctore ad Pontificiorum sensus nimis fuisse accommodatum, & tantum Adversariis concessum, ut hinc magnam apud suos se invidiam incurrisse multis in litteris ipse Melanthon testatus sit. Ad intimum amicum suum Ioachimum Camerarium: Ego Apologiam parevi scriptam summa verecundia. Neque de his rebus posse mitius dici arbitror. Eodem anno scilicet xxx. ad eundem, Augusta: Non dubitabam, quin Apologia nostra videretur quibusdam futura lenior, quam mereantur improbitas adversarii. fariorum. Ego tamen complexus sum ea, quae sunt in causa praecipua. Iurisdictionem totam, ὡς τὸ ἀξίωμα [?] reddo Episcopis. In alia: Hoc male habet scilicet, quosdam immoderatiores, reddi iurisdictionem, restituì πολιτικὴν Ecclesiasticam. Hoc interpretantur restitutionem dominationis Pontificiae &c. Vtinam, utinam possim non quidem dominationem confirmare, sed administrationem restituere Episcoporum. Video enim, qualem simus habituri Ecclesiam, dissolutā πολιτείαν Ecclesiasticā. Video postea multò intolerabiliorem futuram tyrannidem, quam ante unquam fuit. Adhaec, nihil adhuc concessimus adversariis, praeter ea, quae Lutherus censuit esse reddenda, re bene ac diligenter deliberata ante conventum. Neque ego non additurus eram aliquid quasi auxiliarium, publicae pacis causa. Cujus fortasse aliqui rationem nunc non habent. Ergo ex consensu Lutheri haec egit.
units.tr: It is certain that the author had accommodated this tenth article, like the whole confession, too much to the Papists' views, and had conceded so much to the adversaries that Melanchthon himself testified in many letters that he had thereby incurred great hatred among his own people. To his intimate friend Joachim Camerarius: I drew up the Apology with the greatest restraint. Nor do I think such matters can be put more gently. In the same year, 1530, to the same man from Augsburg: I did not doubt that our Apology would seem to some milder than the wickedness of the adversaries deserves. Yet I have embraced those things which are the main points of the case. I give back the whole jurisdiction to the bishops, as the [dignity] [ὡς τὸ ἀξίωμα]. In another letter: It grieves me, of course, that some of the more intemperate people complain that jurisdiction is being given back, and that I have restored the ecclesiastical polity [πολιτικήν]. They interpret this as the restoration of papal domination, etc. Would that I could, not indeed confirm their domination, but restore the administration of the bishops! For I see what kind of Church we shall have with the ecclesiastical polity [πολιτείαν] dissolved. I see that the tyranny that follows will be far more intolerable than it has ever been. Besides, we have conceded nothing to the adversaries beyond what Luther judged should be given back, after a careful and diligent deliberation before the meeting. Nor was I not going to add something by way of auxiliary, for the sake of public peace. Some of them perhaps take no account of this now. Therefore he acted with Luther's consent.

units.la: ¶Vnde ad Lutherum ipsum postridie Augusti, ejusdem anni, & ex eodem loco: Valde reprehendimur a nostris, quod jurisdictionem Episcopis reddimus. Nam vulgus assuefactum libertati, & semel excusso jugo Episcoporum, aegre patitur sibi rursus imponi illa vetera onera, & maxime oderunt illam dominationem civitates Imperii. De doctrina religionis nihil laborant, tantum de regno & libertate sunt solliciti. In alia, ad eundem: Non credis, quanto in odio sim Noricis, & nescio quibus aliis, propter restitutam Episcopis jurisdictionem. Ita de suo regno, non de Evangelio dimicant socii nostri. Amicus quidam scripsit, me, si quanta voluissem maxima pecunia a Romano Pontifice conductus essem, non potuisse meliorem rationem suscipere restituendae dominationis Pontificiae, quam hanc esse judicent homines, quam instituimus. Ego nullam adhuc articulum, aut deserui aut abjeci, qui ad doctrinam pertineat. Tantum stomachantur de politicis rebus, quae non est nostrum eripere Episcopis. Haec omnia quo minus offenderet Pontificios, nosque ab ipsis, vel pace impertienda redderent alieniores. Eodem anno Melanthon, ad Iohannem Silberbornium; Nos obtinuimus confessio wem fidei, moderatissime scriptam, ut apparet, nos non aborrere à consiliis pacis. Hoc unum petivimus, ne saeviretur in Ecclesias nostras, propter id doctrinae genus, quod ipsi proposuerimus, cum quidem res loquatur ipsa, nos nullum dogma defendere contra Euangelium, aut catholicam Ecclesiam, imo multis locis doctrinae Christianae, qui antea prophanis opinionibus jacuerant oppressi, lumen attulisse, videlicet, de justitia fidei, de poenitentia, de usu Sacramentorum, de auctoritate traditionum humanarum: Quod si hoc ab adversariis impetraremus, ostendebamus, nos prolixè illis concessuros esse omnia, quae ad dignitatem Episcoporum stabiliendam pertinent. Neque enim id egimus unquam, ut politia Ecclesiastica dissolveretur, modò ut Euangelium nos damnarent Pontifices. Ostendimus etiam nos, in ritibus Ecclesiasticis, omnes, qui viderentur ἀλλόφυλοι[?], communiter cum ipsis servaturos esse. Nullum detrectavimus onus, quod sine scelere suscipi posset. Ex tam profusa in Pontificios liberalitate quum scripta Confessio, durissimis temporibus, & à moderatissimi non solum ingenii viro, sed hoc etiam in opere timidissimo, uti ex Lutheri ad ipsum literis ostendi potest, tempore duro non solum, sed quoque exiguo, quid mirum quod & in eâ concinnandâ sæpius nutaverit, & postea ad exactiorem limam revocatam in nonnullis correxerit Melanthon, aut elucidarit: neque hoc inscio, vel improbante unquam Luthero, quo vivo hæc variatio contigit, & sic aliquoties, eo adhuc superstite, recusa. Gratiam nonnullam Papatui in Confessione factam, neque ipsi Papistæ ignorant. Quid? Papa Pius v. in epist. ad Regem Poloniæ Sigismundum Augustum, anno MDLXXI. Augustana autem Confessio, ut solet passim dicere Confusio, etsi similis est caeteris haeresum pravitatibus; tamen ob eam causam periculosior est, quod levius quam caetera à Catholicae fidei professione declinans, speciem quandam religionis retinere videatur; eo perniciosior alia, quò venenum ejus occultius latet, nec eminet foris.
units.tr: Hence to Luther himself, the day after 1 August of the same year, from the same place: We are strongly criticized by our own people for giving back jurisdiction to the bishops. For the common people, accustomed to liberty and once the yoke of the bishops has been shaken off, can hardly bear to have those old burdens imposed on them again, and the free cities of the Empire especially hate that domination. They have no anxiety about the doctrine of religion, only about kingdom and liberty. In another letter, to the same man: You do not believe how much I am hated by the Nurembergers, and I know not who else, on account of the restored jurisdiction of the bishops. Thus our colleagues are fighting about their own kingdom, not about the Gospel. A certain friend wrote that if I had been hired by the Roman Pontiff for the largest sum of money, I could not have taken a better course for restoring papal domination than the one men judge we have adopted. I have not yet abandoned or rejected any article that pertains to doctrine. They only grumble about political matters, which it is not for us to snatch away from the bishops. All these things were done so that they would offend the Papists less and make them less alienated from us, or more ready to grant peace. In the same year Melanchthon wrote to John Silberhorn: We have obtained a confession of faith, written most moderately, as is apparent, showing that we do not shrink from counsels of peace. We asked for this one thing only: that there be no persecution of our churches on account of the kind of doctrine which we have proposed, since the matter itself speaks, that we defend no dogma against the Gospel or the catholic Church; indeed, in many places we have brought light to Christian doctrine which had lain oppressed by profane opinions: namely on the justice of faith, on repentance, on the use of the sacraments, and on the authority of human traditions. If we obtained this from the adversaries, we showed that we would concede to them fully everything that pertains to establishing the dignity of the bishops. For we never aimed to dissolve the ecclesiastical polity, provided that the Pontiffs did not condemn us for the Gospel. We also showed that in ecclesiastical rites we would all, even those who seemed foreign [ἀλλόφυλοι], keep them in common with them. We refused no burden that could be taken up without sin. Since the Confession was written with such lavish generosity towards the Papists, in the most difficult times, and by a man not only of the most moderate disposition but also, in this work, most timid, as can be shown from Luther's letters to him, in a time not only hard but also brief, what wonder is it that Melanchthon wavered often in composing it, and afterwards, when it was called back to a more exact polish, corrected or clarified some points? Nor did Luther ever disapprove of this, or do it without his knowledge, while he was alive, when this variation took place; and so it was printed several times while he was still alive. Some favour shown to the papacy in the Confession is not unknown even to the Papists themselves. What of Pope Pius V in his letter to Sigismund Augustus, King of Poland, in 1571? The Augsburg Confession, which he often calls a Confusion, though it is like the other perverse heresies, is nonetheless more dangerous for this reason, that, departing less than the others from the profession of the Catholic faith, it seems to retain a certain appearance of religion; and it is the more pernicious for this, that its poison lies more hidden and does not stand out to outsiders.

units.la: Primus Eckius, in Colloquio VVormatiensi anno cIↄ Iↄ xlı. controversiam Melanthoni de mutatis Consessionis Exemplaribus movit; sed hic tantum abfuit, ut Melanthon à suis desertus, aut culpatus fuerit, ut Eckio os obturarit, postquam respondisset: Rerum eandem esse sententiam, & si quaedam alicubi in posteriore editione vel magis mitigata vel explicatiora essent. Ne alia addam, quę pro jure & authoritate mutatæ Confessionis, & pro honore Melanthonis, hanc eandem in rem, dici copiosè possunt. Vide Admonitionem Neostadianam, Hospinianum, Histor. Sacramentaria part. II. Pezelium, Part. VIII. Respons. Theolog. pag. 124. & alios. Luculentum certe Recognitæ Confessioni Principes Protestantes testimonium perhibuere litteris anno cIↄ Iↄ lxı. ad Ferdinandum Imp. ex conventu Naumburgico scriptis, in quo de varietate Exemplarium Confessionis disceptatum fuit, & Recognita æque ac prior approbata, quod ea unius ejusdemque sententiæ cum prima illa sit. Quodque in plurimis Colloquiis & disputationibus, quæ cum Adversariis instituta fuerunt, oblata fuit, & in quibusdam articulis eam ob causam copiosius explicata est, ut veritas divina in lucem magis proferretur &c. præsertim cum hanc Recognitam Confessionem sicut a. 40. & 41. typis edita est, hoc ipso tempore constet in Ecclesiis & Scholis nostrarum ditionum potissimum in usu esse, & in manibus omnium versari. De Conventu ìsto Naumburgico etiam Thuanus, lib. xxvııı. Histor. vıı. viri ea conditione assensi sunt, ut præfatio nova adderetur, in qua posterior quoque illa editio Confessionis & apologia tamquam cum priore consentiens approbetur, & loca quaedam in priore illa ad transsubstantiationem alludentia explicentur. Adde & Auctorem Histor. Concil. Tridentini, lib. v. Atque illustre imprimis est Landgravii V. Wilhelmi, hac de re ad Electorem Saxoniæ Augustum, a. lxxvıı. scriptum, occasione libri Concordiæ: Non ignoratis quod antehac bono animo de particula illa (non mutata Augustana Confessio) monuerimus, ac etiamnum vos amanter rogamus, de his rebus ac pe-
units.tr: Eck was the first to raise, at the Colloquy of Worms in 1541, the objection to Melanchthon about the altered copies of the Confession. But Melanchthon was so far from being deserted or blamed by his own people that Eck was silenced once Melanchthon had replied: the meaning of the two is the same, even if some passages in the later edition are somewhere softened or explained more fully. I need not add the other things that can be said at length, in defence of the authority of the altered Confession and of Melanchthon's honour, on this same point. See the Neustadt Admonition, Hospinian, Historia Sacramentaria part II, Pezel, Responsiones theologicae part VIII, p. 124, and others. The Protestant princes certainly gave a clear testimony to the revised Confession in a letter to Emperor Ferdinand written in 1561 from the Naumburg assembly, where the variation of the copies of the Confession was debated. There they approved the revised text as much as the earlier one, saying that it is of one and the same meaning with that first one; and that in most colloquies and disputations held with our opponents it was offered, and in some articles was explained more fully for this reason, so that divine truth might be brought more into the light, etc., especially since this revised Confession, just as it was printed in 1540 and 1541, is known at this very time to be chiefly in use in the churches and schools of our territories and to be in the hands of everyone. Thuanus also, book 28 of his History, book 7, speaks of this Naumburg assembly: the men agreed on this condition, that a new preface be added, in which that later edition of the Confession and the Apology are approved as agreeing with the earlier one, and certain passages in the earlier one that allude to transubstantiation are explained. Add also the author of the History of the Council of Trent, book 5. Especially notable is the letter of Landgrave Wilhelm V on this matter to Augustus, Elector of Saxony, written in 1577 on the occasion of the Book of Concord: You are not unaware that we earlier advised, with good intent, about that particle (the unaltered Augsburg Confession), and we still kindly ask you to think carefully about these matters and the troublesome consequences that flow from them, and to weigh each point diligently.

units.la: ricuscrupulosis inde manantibus consequentiis diligenter cogitare, ac singula studiose perpendere velitis. Etsi namque aequum est, ut Augustanam illam Confessionem, quae Imp. Carolo anno 30. oblata est, nominemus: constat tamen omnibus, quam ob causam deinceps illa Confessio, vivente adhuc Luthero, & tam de ipsius, quam praecipuorum Statuum, Theologorumque consilio, & voluntate, in quibusdam articulis, non sine magno fructu locupletata, ac deinceps in Colloquiis, publico nomine Imperii habitis, proposita & usurpata, imo & a nobis, & a D. Parente nostro, aliisque Electoribus, & Principibus anno 61. Naumburgi appensis sigillis non minus quam prior illa confirmata, & Imp. Ferdinando Francofurti proposita oblataque fuerit. Quae sane omnia unica hac voce (non mutata) improbamus atque rejicimus. Adeo non privata authoritate Melanthonis, ut hodie Lutherani scribunt, sed a Theologis, & Politicis, & Principibus, & Electoribus, a Melanthone non solum, sed a Luthero quoque Confessionis illa recognitio vel variatio approbata fuit. Et mirum, quare post Lutherum ea contentio de variata Confessione incaeperit, cui Lutherus ad octo annos supervixit, & pluries recusam vidit, neque tamen obloquutus unquam fuit, sed calculum suum apposuit semper juxta cum aliis Theologis, Principibusque, & comprobavit. Ipsa prima editio a. cI5 I5 xxx I. jam discrepabat ab exemplari Caesari exhibito, in quo legebatur: Corpus & sanguinem Christi, sub specie panis & vini vere adesse in Cena Domini. nimis profecto ad mentem & sententiam Pontificiorum. Unde in ejus prima Apologia, & Canon Missae, & dictum Theophylacti, de panis mutatione quoque referebantur. Quare his omissis, in prima statim editione positum: Corpus & sanguinem Christi vere adesse, & distribui in Cena Domini. Denique, in editione recognita: Cum panis & vino vere exhiberi corpus & sanguinem Christi recipientibus in Cena Domini. Quid jam est, quod reprehendas, priorem editionem ab altera correctam, mutationemque evenisse, quum passim ut mutata Confessio, ita & editiones fuerint, quarum prima à suo autographo, (ut exemplari in Cancellariâ Casselensi servato ostendi potest) jam tum discrepari. Non quidem dixero, quod tamen Principes viros scribere haud poenituit, vel auctores Confessionis isto tempore adhuc in errore Transubstantiationis haeresis fuisse, vel hunc in Confessione expressum, quod mihi non verosimile de illis Theologis, & tamdiu jam adversus Papatum exercitatis, & à Marpurgico conventu multum doctioribus: sed quidem nimis lata laxaque oratione, & verbis ad Pontificiorum aures ac gratiam directis, sententiam authorum valde timide generatimque declaratam, & quia non aperte & libere magis improbarunt id quod improbandum erat, sua sermonis φλυαρίας nec sibi, neque aliis satisfecisse, sed cothurnum dedisse plus quam uni aptandum pedi, saltem de quo ex verbis non facile constare posset quò spectarent, exiistimo. Hinc ejus ab iisdem suis Authoribus facta mutatio. Sed ulterius ut scias, primam exhibitae Confessionis, tum editae, denique & renovatae lectionem, quas omnes nunc exposui, quem sensum exprimere Confessio voluerit, addam etiam protographum articuli istius decimi, ex septemdecim articulis Lutheri, quos cum Melanthone, Iusto Iona, & Pomerano consignavit, & ex quibus Confessionem postea formavit Melanthon: Quod in Eucharistia seu Sacramento altaris vere praesens sit in pane ac vino verum corpus & sanguis Christi, secundum verba, hoc est corpus meum, hic est sanguis meus: nec tantum sit panis & vinum, ut nunc adversarii quidam contendunt. Flagitant etiam haec verba & confirmant: fidem, & exsuscitant eam in omnibus qui hoc Sacramentum serio petunt, nec contra illud agunt: sicut & baptismus cum petitur, fidem adfert & largitur. Hinc sumtus eformatusque Confessionis articulus ille fuit, aeque frustra ad demulcendos Pontificios, ac ad Nostros perstringendos, quum ex nupero Marpurgensi Colloquio satis sciscirent, quomodo vel minus candide nostra sententia explicaretur, dicendo in S. Coena tantum panem esse vinumque, vel saltem minus distincte, integreque quam ut ita hic fieri oporteret. Certum quoque, non illo primum fine articulos illos vel Confessionem scriptam, ut pro perpetua Ecclesiarum Protestantium norma haberentur, vel symbolo; sed tantum, ut apud Caesarem ac Principes declararent Protestantium doctrinam Christianam, eamque immunem redderent ab illis calumniis & haereticorum, quibus eam Adversarii passim gravabant. Quae causa fuit, quare ad sententiam & loquendi modum Pontificiorum, plus quam decuit, se inclinarit. Neque credendum est, si pro tali scripto habendam Confessionem putassent Auctores, quod tam brevi tempore, & fere ad unius arbitrium, in tanta rerum angustia, neque habitis hac de re prius aliorum & Theologorum, & Politicorum, Principumque suffragiis, levi adeo rudique opera congessissent. Quare non est, quod Lutherani hodie omnes, ex praescripto scilicet libri Concordiae, tantopere clament Augustanam Confessionem invariatam, aut certent pro priori ejus editione, adversus secundam recognitam. An ergo insanierunt omnes Theologi, Principes, & Status, qui recognitam probarunt; & ut a priori non adeo discrepantem, nec ei postponi, nedum opponi, vel quasi minus sanam, aut haereticae alicujus suspectam rejici voluerunt? Sumamus decimum, de S. Coena Domini, articulum: is adeo Pontificiis conveniebat & aptari aeque poterat, Transsubstantiationis dogmate sub illo facile intelligendo, ut in suo de illo judicio Caesar, Principesque annotarent: Decimus articulus in verbis nihil offendit, quando fatentur in Eucharistia post consecrationem legitime factam, corpus & sanguinem Christi substantialiter & vere adesse. An licuit in gratiam Pontificiorum ita cadere articulum istum, qua forma minus illis displiceret, & nefas fuit pro veritate magis explicanda, adde & pro concordiâ cum nostris confirmandâ, saltem non offendendâ, ita exponere, quo sensu intelligendum esse Auctor ipse judicavit? Certè qui adeo pro priori lectione æstuant adversus posteriorem & correctiorem, ostendunt sibi gratius esse, nos, quam Pontificios, damnari. Formula Concordiæ, a. cI͏ↄ I͏ↄ lxxv i i. erecta recognitam Confessionem explodit, & Lutheranos omnes jubet invariatam, ut loquuntur, id est, primam tenere ac sequi. Unde jam tantis buccis & magna scilicet cum ἀδιαφόρῳ[?], Invariatæ socios se jactitant. Atqui inter præcipuas causas negatæ libri Bergensis, seu formulæ Concordiæ à Principibus viris Theologisque subscriptionis fuit, quod correctiorem Consessionis editionem indigne repudiaret, & novo exemplo nomineque solam immutatam præscriberet. Hoc notarunt in articulis Torgensibus, vel in Declaratione controversiarum articulorum, uti primò appellabantur, (ex quibus Formula & Concordia Bergensis post conflata, quando illi ad Principes & Theologos Augustanæ Confessionis per universam Germaniam missi, ad exquirenda aliorum judicia & censuras, antequam in Cœnobio Bergensi confirmarentur, atque referrentur in canonem) Theologi Hassiaci a. cI͏ↄ I͏ↄ lxxv i. d. v. Septembris: uti sic loquuntur: Augustana Confessio, ejusque Apologia in Conventu Naumburgensi Anno 61 à nonnullis Electoribus & Principibus demùm subscripta, & quæ in Imperii Comitiis & Colloquiis oblata & exhibita sunt Consessiones, quibus & Schmalcaldici articuli commemorandi, repetita & Imperatori Ferdinando tradita, ideoque unanimiter approbata sunt. Hoc verò nobis non minus mirum, quam diligenti consideratione dignum videtur, quod vox Immutata Confessioni Augustanæ additur: cum tamen Electores & Principes haud dubiè singulari consilio, & magnis gravibusque de causis, in dicto Conventu Naumburgi, non primam tantum, quæ Imp. Carolo 5. Augusta exhibita fuit, sed etiam alteram, quæ paulò post Anno 40. & 42. copiosius repetita, & ex Scriptura sacra emendata, declarata & locupletata, ac Vuiteberge in lucem edita esset, nullatenus rejecerint, sed ut defensam etiam in VVormatiensi Colloquio adversus Eckium, & sic authenticum scriptum, vivente adhuc Luthero, factum, aeque ac priores Anno 3 c. Imp. Carolo traditas, & Anno 31. Vuiteberge excusas, approbarint: quae omnia verbo Immutata improbantur, ut non modo ob hanc causam Theologi, sed etiam Evangelici Electores & Principes levitatis & inconstantiae argui & accusari possent.
units.tr: Although it is right that we call it the Augsburg Confession, which was presented to Emperor Charles in the year 1530, it is nevertheless known to all why that Confession was afterwards enriched in certain articles, while Luther was still alive, not without great benefit, by the counsel and will of himself and of the chief estates and theologians, and afterwards was put forward and used in colloquies held in the name of the Empire; indeed it was confirmed by us and by our father, and by the other electors and princes, at Naumburg in 1561, with seals appended, no less than the earlier one, and was offered to Emperor Ferdinand at Frankfurt. All these things we certainly reject and condemn by this single word "unaltered". So the revision or variation of the Confession was approved not by the private authority of Melanchthon, as the Lutherans now write, but by theologians, statesmen, princes and electors, and not only by Melanchthon but also by Luther himself. And it is strange why that dispute about the altered Confession began only after Luther, although he survived for eight years after it and saw it reprinted many times, yet never objected, but always added his vote along with the other theologians and princes, and approved it. The very first edition, of 1530, already differed from the copy presented to the Emperor, in which it was read: the body and blood of Christ are truly present under the species of bread and wine in the Lord's Supper, which was indeed too much in line with the mind and opinion of the Papists. Hence in his first Apology, and in the Canon of the Mass and the saying of Theophylact about the change of the bread, these things were also quoted. So these were omitted, and the first edition stated: the body and blood of Christ are truly present and are distributed in the Lord's Supper. Finally, in the revised edition: when bread and wine are truly offered, the body and blood of Christ are received by those who partake in the Lord's Supper. What fault is there, then, in finding the first edition corrected by the second, and the change having taken place, since altered Confessions and editions were everywhere in circulation, of which the first, as can be shown from its autograph (as from the copy kept in the chancery at Kassel), already differed? I do not indeed say, though princes did not hesitate to write it, that the authors of the Confession were at that time still in the error of the heresy of transubstantiation, or that this was expressed in the Confession. That is not likely to me concerning those theologians, who had long been exercised against the Papacy and were much more learned than at the Marburg assembly. But I think they expressed the opinion of the authors, in a rather broad and loose style and in words aimed at the ears and favour of the Papists, and too timidly and in general terms; and because they did not openly and freely reject what needed to be rejected, they satisfied neither themselves nor others with their verbal trifling, but put on a buskin meant for more than one foot, at least one about which, from the words, it could not easily be known where they aimed. Hence the change made by the same authors. But so that you may know the first reading of the Confession as presented, then as published, and finally as renewed, all of which I have now set out, and what meaning the Confession wished to express, I will also add the original of that tenth article, from the seventeen articles of Luther which he signed with Melanchthon, Justus Jonas and Pomeranus, and from which Melanchthon afterwards shaped the Confession: That in the Eucharist, or the Sacrament of the altar, the true body and blood of Christ are truly present in the bread and wine, according to the words, "This is my body, this is my blood"; nor is there merely bread and wine, as some of our opponents now contend. These words also urge and strengthen faith, and stir it up in all who seriously seek this sacrament and do not act against it, just as baptism, when it is sought, brings and bestows faith. From this the article was taken and shaped, and it was no less in vain either to soothe the Papists or to attack our side, since from the recent Marburg colloquy they had learned well enough how our view was explained, though less candidly, by saying that in the Holy Supper there is only bread and wine, or at least less distinctly and completely than it ought to be here. It is also certain that the articles or the written Confession were not first drawn up for this purpose, to be held as a permanent norm of the Protestant churches or as a creed, but only so that they might declare to the Emperor and princes the Christian doctrine of the Protestants, and free it from those calumnies and heretical charges with which our opponents everywhere burdened it. This was the reason why they inclined to the opinion and manner of speaking of the Papists more than was fitting. Nor is it to be believed that, if the authors had thought the Confession should be held as such a writing, they would have put together so light and rough a work in so short a time, and almost at one man's discretion, in such a press of affairs, and without first taking the votes of other theologians, statesmen and princes on this matter. Therefore there is no reason why all Lutherans today, by the prescription of the Book of Concord, cry out so loudly that the Augsburg Confession is unaltered, or contend for its first edition against the second, revised one. Did all the theologians, princes and estates who approved the revised text act like madmen, and wish that it be not much different from the earlier one, not set behind it, let alone opposed to it, or rejected as if less sound or suspected of some heresy? Let us take the tenth article, on the Lord's Supper. It suited the Papists so well, and could equally well be fitted to them, since the dogma of transubstantiation could easily be read into it, that the Emperor and the princes noted in their judgment on it: The tenth article offends nothing in its words, since they confess that in the Eucharist, after the lawful consecration, the body and blood of Christ are substantially and truly present. Was it lawful, to win the favour of the Papists, to frame that article in such a way that it would displease them less, and wrong to explain it more truly and, what is more, to confirm agreement with our own people, or at least not to offend them, by setting it out in the sense which the author himself judged should be understood? Certainly those who are so keen for the earlier reading against the later and more correct one show that they would rather have us condemned than the Papists. The Formula of Concord, erected in 1577, explodes the revised Confession and orders all Lutherans to hold, as they say, the unaltered text, that is, to keep and follow the first. Hence they now boast with such great mouths, and with great indifference[?], of being companions of the Unaltered. Yet among the chief causes of the refusal of subscription to the Book of Bergen, or the Formula of Concord, by eminent princes and theologians, was that it unworthily rejected the more correct edition of the Confession and, by a new example and name, prescribed only the altered one. The Hessian theologians noted this in the Torgau articles, or in the Declaration of the controversial articles, as they were first called (from which the Formula of Concord of Bergen was afterwards put together, when those articles were sent to the princes and theologians of the Augsburg Confession throughout all Germany, to seek the judgments and censures of others, before they were confirmed in the monastery of Bergen and made into a canon), in the words of the Hessian theologians of 5 September 1577: The Augsburg Confession and its Apology, presented at the Naumburg assembly in 1561, were at last signed by some electors and princes, and the Confessions which were offered and exhibited at the Imperial Diets and colloquies, to which the Schmalkald Articles must also be added, were repeated, handed to Emperor Ferdinand, and therefore approved unanimously. But it seems to us no less strange than worthy of careful consideration that the word "unaltered" is added to the Augsburg Confession, since the electors and princes, surely with a special purpose and for great and weighty reasons, at the said Naumburg assembly by no means rejected not only the first one, which was presented to Emperor Charles 5 at Augsburg, but also the second, which a little later, in 1540 and 1542, was repeated more fully, and was corrected, declared and enriched from holy Scripture, and was published at Wittenberg; but, as defended also at the Worms colloquy against Eck, and so an authentic writing made while Luther was still alive, they approved it just as the earlier ones handed to Emperor Charles in 1530 and printed at Wittenberg in 1531. All these things are condemned by the word "unaltered", so that the theologians, and also the Evangelical electors and princes, could be charged and accused not only on this account of levity and inconstancy.

units.la: Quod suorum Theologorum judicium confirmarunt Principes Lantgravii VVilhelmus, & Ludovicus, quando illud ad Saxoniae Electorem, una cum suis mittebant litteris, in quibus: Nam quod solum, & nominatim ad primam immutatam Confessionem Augustanam, quae isto quidem tempore scripta est in summa festinatione & temporis angustia, atque etiam in maximo metu praesentium periculorum, adeoque mollissime, ne offenderetur Caesar, neve Principes Evangelici in summum vitae periculum adducerentur, provocatur, eoque illa quae postea in praecipuis articulis summa cum diligentia & cura locupletata & emendata est, si non rejicitur, saltem suspecta apud alios redditur, id approbare non possumus. Similiter VVilhelmus Langravius, ad Norimbergensem Senatum: ad Iulium Brunsvicensem: iterum ad Augustum Saxoniae Electorem, anno clɔ Iɔ lxxvii. die xx. Decemb. Et a. clɔ Iɔ lxxviii. d. ii. Januar. super eadem re. Iterum a. clɔ Iɔ lxxix. d. xxvi. Octob. quando & propter hanc, & alias causas, ad Legatos trium Electorum, Palatini, Saxonis, & Brandenburgici, ipsum ad subscriptionem Bergensis libri denuo sollicitantes, identidem detrectavit. Neque aliter censuerunt de isthac novitia appellatione Immutatae Confessionis, Ludovicus Elector Palatinus, in litteris ad Saxonem a. clɔ Iɔ lxxvii. d. xvii. Octob. Tum Theologi Magdeburgenses, Bipontini, Anhaltini, aliique Augustanae Confessionis Theologi, qui tamen seu in articulis primum Torgensibus, ipsis ad judjudicandum, seu libro Bergensi, ad subscribendum missis, nominatim hoc de immutata Augustana Confessione graviter reprehenderunt, & pro causa non minima attulere, quo minus iisdem assentirentur. Nostros sciens omitto: quippe satis est, ipsos Augustanae Confessionis Theologos, ac Principes in Formula Bergensis discordiae non tulisse hoc Confessionis mutatae stigma, à paucis recentibusque Theologis suae professioni ac doctrinae iniquè impressum, illosque studuisse in ipso initio hanc à se removere ignominiam & contemtum. Accedit & ratio gravis politica, quo minus Confessionum contrarietas, propter varias editiones, vel ob posteriorem istam Recognitionem, concedi debuerit. Nam dum multi pridem clamarent, & praesertim Iesuitae Dilligenses, Protestantes excidisse pace Religionis, olim ipsis concessa, quia nunc alia docerent ab Augustana Confessione Caesari exhibita, quod inter alia ostendere conabantur ex Augustanae Confessionis variatione, huic plene occurri non potuit, nisi negando, per illam variationem, in Ecclesia, vel doctrina mutationem obtigisse. Confer Johannis Gerhardi Dedicat. ad lib. II Confess. Specialis part. II. Quomodo enim aliter commode responderis? nisi Iesuitis concedere fractam Deo & hominibus fidem, melius videatur: quod quanta cum Principum, aliorumque Augustanae Confessionis Sociorum contumelia & probro conjunctum, quis est qui non videat? Sed quorsum adeo de variata Confessione tumultuantur varii isti homines, qui ne quidem ipsam illam Bergensem formulam, quae mutatam Confessionem tantopere exagitat, immutatam servare aliquamdiu potuere, quin multi de variatione identidem fuerint conquesti? Hoc Helmstadienses Theologi a. cIↄ Ic lxxxiii. in Conventu Quedelburgensi Saxonicis palam objecere, in Concordia Bergensi quaedam post factas subscriptiones mutata fuisse. Idem Hutnio, in Apologetica adversus ipsum epistola, regessit Daniel Hofmannus, a. clo Io xciv. & adversus Pappum, Argentinensem Theologum, turbonem verius, à quo caeptum nostros loco movere, initio facto à venerando sene Iohanne Sturmio, probavit Michael Beutherus, in Declaratione Agendae Ecclesiae Argentinensis. Haec de variata, vel invariata Augustana Confessione paulo latius exponenda fuerunt, ut sciretur quid sibi velit, quod passim tanta cum φαντασία Lutherani vulgo, at temere, jactant de sua invariata Confessione. Quamvis retenta etiam priori lectione, quam omnino fatendum est secundis curis prodiisse emendatiorem, possit verbis dari sensus quoque non incommodus, qui articulo laxe & generaliter concepto aptari, per intellectum & explicationem sacramentalem de Christi praesentia potest; vel, uti inquit Altingius, in Exegesi Augustanae Confess. Corpus & sanguinem Christi vere adesse in Coena bifariam posse intelligi; vel quod adsint spiritualiter oblata verbo promissionis & fide percepta; vel quod adsint corporaliter & substantialiter, inclusa vel abscondita invisibiliter in, cum, sub pane & vino. Quo postremo sensu illud rejicimus.
units.tr: The Landgraves William and Louis, the princes, also confirmed the judgment of their own theologians when they sent it to the Elector of Saxony with their letters, in which they wrote: For as to the fact that the appeal is made solely and by name to the first altered Augsburg Confession, which was indeed written at that time in great haste and under pressure of time, and also in the greatest fear of present dangers, and so very gently, lest Caesar be offended or the evangelical princes be brought into mortal peril; and therefore that later version, which was afterwards enriched and corrected with great diligence and care in the chief articles, if it is not rejected, is at least rendered suspect among others, we cannot approve that. Similarly Landgrave William wrote to the Senate of Nuremberg, to Julius of Brunswick, and again to Augustus, Elector of Saxony, on 20 December 1577, and on 2 January 1578, on the same matter; and again on 26 October 1579, when, both for this reason and others, he repeatedly refused the requests of the envoys of the three electors, Palatine, Saxon and Brandenburg, who were pressing him again to subscribe the Book of Bergen. Louis, Elector Palatine, judged no differently about this new name Altered Confession, in his letter to the Saxon of 17 October 1577. Then the theologians of Magdeburg, Zweibrücken, Anhalt, and other theologians of the Augsburg Confession, who nevertheless, whether in the Torgau articles first sent to them for judgment or in the Book of Bergen sent for subscription, censured this very matter of the altered Augsburg Confession severely, and brought it forward as no small reason why they would not assent to those documents. I knowingly pass over our own men. It is enough that the theologians and princes of the Augsburg Confession, in the Formula of Concord, would not tolerate this stigma of an altered Confession, unjustly stamped on their profession and doctrine by a few recent theologians, and that at the very outset they took pains to remove this disgrace and contempt from themselves. There is also a grave political reason why the contrariety of the Confessions could not be conceded, on account of the various editions or because of that later revision. For while many had long been crying out, especially the Jesuits of Dillingen, that the Protestants had fallen from the peace of religion once granted to them, because they now taught other things than the Augsburg Confession exhibited to Caesar, which they tried to show, among other things, from the variation of the Augsburg Confession, this could not be fully answered except by denying that any change in the Church or in doctrine had come about through that variation. Compare Johann Gerhard, Dedication to Book II of the Confession, Special Part II. For how else could one answer conveniently, unless it seemed better to concede to the Jesuits a faith broken before God and men? How great a disgrace and reproach this would be to the princes and the other allies of the Augsburg Confession, who does not see? But why do these various men make such an uproar about the varied Confession, when they could not even for some time keep unchanged that very Formula of Bergen which so harasses the altered Confession, without many complaining again and again of variation? In 1583, at the Convention of Quedlinburg, the Helmstedt theologians openly objected to the Saxons that certain things in the Concord of Bergen had been changed after the subscriptions were made. Daniel Hofmann gave the same answer to Hutter in 1594, in his letter of apology against him; and Michael Beuther proved it, in the Declaration of the Agenda of the Church of Strasbourg, against Pappus, the Strasbourg theologian (a troublemaker rather than a true theologian), who began to move our men from their place, the start having been made by the venerable old man John Sturm. These things about the varied or unvaried Augsburg Confession had to be set out somewhat more broadly, so that it might be known what the Lutherans mean when they commonly, and rashly, boast with such phantasia [φαντασία] of their unvaried Confession. Although, even with the earlier reading retained, which must certainly be admitted to have come out more correctly in the second revision, words may be given a not inconvenient sense as well, which can be applied to the article, loosely and generally conceived, through a sacramental understanding and explanation of Christ's presence. Or, as Altingius says in his Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession: The body and blood of Christ can be understood to be truly present in the Supper in two ways: either that they are present spiritually, offered by the word of promise and received by faith; or that they are present corporeally and substantially, included or hidden invisibly in, with, and under the bread and wine. It is in this last sense that we reject it.

units.la: Denique hinc factum, quod nostri passim non detrectarint subscribere Augustanae Confessioni, pro sensu Auctorum magis, quam verborum, & in nostram sententiam haud difficulter exponendae. Calvinus, epist. ad Mart. Schallingium, a. clo Io lv ii. Nec vero Augustanam Confessionem repudio, cui pridem volens ac libens subscripsi, sicut eam author ipse interpretatus est. Zanchius, Argentorati quum esset suffectus in locum Caspari Hedionis, rogatus, ut Augustanae subscriberet Confessioni, fecit id quidem, sed hac addita conditione: modo orthodoxe intelligatur. Atque tribus additis capitibus sententiam suam de Coena, cujus causa subscriptio petebatur, explicuit: verum Christi corpus pro nobis traditum, & verum ejus sanguinem, in peccatorum nostrorum remissionem effusum, in Coena vere manducari & bibi. II. Verum id non ore & dentibus corporis, sed vera fide. III. Ideoque à solis fidelibus. In qua explicatione Scholarchae tum temporis acquieverunt. Similiter Petrus Martyr, ex Angliâ redux, & pristino in Argentinensi Scholâ loco restitutus, de Augustanâ Confessione subscribendâ interrogatus, nam tum jam gliscebant ibidem turbae Sacramentariae: Confessionem Augustanam, dixit, & alias quae ab ea non discrepant, si recte atque commode intelligantur, se libenter amplecti, profiteri, ac si opus foerit, velle pro viribus tueri. Sed praeter Confessionem, quando proferebatur Concordia Marpurgensis, cujusque articuli, se illi non subscripsisse, respondit, quod per verbum Dei & conscientiam largiri nequeat, destitutos verâ fide percipiendo sacramenta, corpus Christi sumere. Iudiciosissimus atque religiosissimus vir fuit Petrus Martyr. Hyperius sic subscripsit: Andreas Hyperius in summâ negotii consentit. Passim nostri in Germaniâ Theologi & docent, & exponunt in Scholis Augustanam Confessionem, eique Commentarios scribunt & Exegeses. Moris quoque est, Doctores qui promoventur, eidem jurare: quod nobis exprobrant Remonstrantes, in Apologia cap. x. Neque veriti fuerunt Nostri in variis Imperii Comitiis, sub Augustana Confessione, ejusque Sociis comprehendi, quando de religionis negotio cum Protestantibus actum; quamvis hodie melius in articulis nuperae pacis anno MDCXLVIII. seorsim ab aliis, & proprio nomine veniamus, tresque religiones exserte nominentur, art. VII. De quibus confer nostrum Examen Bullae P. Innocentii X. de Pace Germaniae. pag. 469. &c. Flaccianorum factio fuit, quae ut Melanthoni vivo, etiamque mortuo, ita ejus discipulis studiisque infensissima, quaestionem inter Lutheranos movit, de mutata, vel recognita à Melanthone Confessione: quo hac etiam ratione optimum virum, ejusque meliora sequentes consilia discipulos primum gravibus multorum odiis onerare, inde vexare passim, demum & loco movere possent.
units.tr: Finally, from this it came about that our men did not hesitate often to subscribe the Augsburg Confession, in the sense of its authors rather than its words, which could easily be explained in our opinion. Calvin, in a letter to Martin Schalling, 1552: Nor indeed do I reject the Augsburg Confession, which I long ago subscribed willingly and gladly, as its author himself interpreted it. Zanchius, when at Strasbourg he had been appointed in the place of Caspar Hedio, was asked to subscribe the Augsburg Confession and did so, but with this condition added: provided it is understood orthodoxly. With three chapters added, he explained his opinion on the Supper, for which the subscription was sought: that the true body of Christ given for us, and his true blood poured out for the remission of our sins, are truly eaten and drunk in the Supper. II. Truly, not with the mouth and teeth of the body, but with true faith. III. And therefore only by believers. The scholarchs of that time were content with this explanation. Similarly Peter Martyr, returned from England and restored to his former post in the Strasbourg school, was asked whether he would subscribe the Augsburg Confession, for the sacramentarian disturbances were already growing there. He said: I gladly embrace and profess the Augsburg Confession, and other things that do not differ from it, if they are rightly and fittingly understood, and if need be, I am willing to defend them to the best of my strength. But when the Concord of Marburg and its articles were produced, he replied that he had not subscribed to that, because it could not grant, through the word of God and conscience, that those destitute of true faith take the body of Christ in receiving the sacraments. Peter Martyr was a most judicious and most religious man. Hyperius subscribed thus: Andreas Hyperius agrees in the main point of the business. Our men in Germany everywhere both teach and expound the Augsburg Confession in the schools, and write commentaries and expositions on it. It is also the custom for doctors who are promoted to swear to it, which the Remonstrants throw in our faces in their Apology, chapter 10. Nor were our men afraid, in the various Imperial Diets, to be included under the Augsburg Confession and its allies, when the matter of religion was treated with the Protestants; although today, in the articles of the recent peace of 1648, we are rightly named separately and by our own name, and the three religions are expressly named, art. VII. On these matters compare our Examination of the Bull of Pope Innocent X on the Peace of Germany, p. 469 and following. There was a faction of the Flacians which, as it was most hostile to Melanchthon while he lived and even after he died, and to his disciples and their studies, so it raised the question among the Lutherans about the Confession altered or revised by Melanchthon. By this method too they could burden that excellent man, and his disciples who followed better counsels, first with the grave hatreds of many, then harass them everywhere, and at last drive them from their places.

units.la: Quæ V Vittenbergenses Theologi præ aliis experti fuere: sensisset & ipse non minus Melanthon, nisi fato præventus, mors ipsum insidiis & molitionibus iltis excmisset. Nam quum (quod inter singularia divinæ in opere Reformationis providentiæ colloco) Melanthon moderatiora in dissensione Sacramentaria sequutus consilia, inde & parum, vel nihil à nostris hac in re abesset, cæteri ejus collegæ ac discipuli in Academia V Vittembergensi adeo præferendam Melanthonis, præ Lutheri duritia, modestiam sententiamque censebant, ut post ejus mortem Academia mirum in modum mutata veritati locum daret, & doctrinam de Cœna, ex nostra potius, quam Lutheri sententia, exponere & docere inceperit. Fatentur hoc Academiæ isti evenisse Lutherani omnes. Hinc enim natæ aliorum malefcriatorum adversus V Vittembergenses, & qui tum hisce faciebant, Lipsenses, insectationes, odia, persequutiones, quibus illos loco & professione postea deturbarunt, & in exilium alios, alios in carcerem egerunt. Et ne idem aliquando iterum eveniret, formulam Concordiæ scilicet, excogitarunt, quâ doctrina nostra ad minimas quasi fibras castigatur & damnatur; in quam formulam omnes jurare coëgerunt, ne de cætero illis metus de suis esset, in meliorem forte sententiam mitioremque nobiscum adducendis. Hæc Formula Concordiæ Bergensis appellata, in qua Schisma ipsorum quasi consummatum videri potest. Quam ut eo melius explicemus, de Philippo Melanthone, & Matthæo Flacio Illyrico pauca præmittenda sunt.
units.tr: The Wittenberg theologians experienced these things more than others. Melanchthon too would have felt them no less, had not death, forestalling him, freed him from those plots and machinations. For when Melanchthon followed the more moderate counsels in the Sacramentarian dispute (which I count among the singular providences of God in the work of the Reformation), and so was little or nothing removed from our position in this matter, his other colleagues and disciples in the Wittenberg Academy thought Melanchthon's moderation and opinion so much to be preferred to Luther's harshness that after his death the Academy, wonderfully changed, gave place to truth and began to set out and teach the doctrine of the Supper from our opinion rather than from Luther's. All Lutherans confess that this happened to that Academy. From this arose the attacks, hatreds and persecutions of other malefactors against the Wittenbergers, and against the Leipzigers who then sided with them, by which they afterwards drove them from their posts and profession, sending some into exile and others into prison. And lest the same thing should happen again, they devised that Formula of Concord, by which our doctrine is chastised and condemned down to its smallest fibres. They compelled everyone to swear to it, so that in future they would have no fear of their own men being led over by us to a perhaps better and milder opinion. This is called the Formula of Concord of Bergen, in which their schism can be seen as, so to speak, consummated. To explain it better, a few things must first be said about Philip Melanchthon and Matthias Flacius Illyricus.

units.la: Philippus Melanthon, non sine boni viri elogio nominandus, quem Germania communem merito agnoscit præceptorem, quando natus sit, indicat inscriptio ante paternas ædes, in inferiori Palatinatu, Brettæ oppido, hæc: Dei pietate natus est in hac domo Doctissimus Dn. Philipp. Melanchton, d. xv i. Feb. a. cIↄ cccc xcv i r. Nomen vernaculum fuit Schwarzerd. Heidelbergæ studuit convictor Doctoris Theologi Pallantis, ab anno ætatis suæ duodecimo, id est sæculi cIↄ Iↄ ix. ubi titulum & gradum Baccalaurei adeptus, sextus videlicet inter unum & viginti candidatos. Cum triennio exacto, Magisterium ambiret, atque repulsam ob ætatis defectum à quibusdam ferret, tum etiam ob curam valetudinis, Tubingam concessit. Audivit hic, præter alios in Medicinâ, ac Iure, in Theologiâ Doct. Lempum, de quo non absque justo risu aliquoties retulit, quod explicans dogma Transsubstantiationis, auditoribus suis creta illud depingere in tabulâ solitus esset. Adferebat hoc vulgo Melanthon, quando ei res absona aliqua proponebatur, etiam postea ad retundendum commentum ubiquitatis. De alio quoque Tubingensi Concionatore Monacho narrabat, qui omissâ Euangeliorum doctrinâ, explicabat pro concione Ethica Aristotelis; idque non parvo auditorum studio, qui ista lubentius audiebant, quam vulgares ex putidissimis Legendis fabulas, quæ solæ & semper fere repetebantur. Hæc tenebrosa & tristissima illa tempora, quibus & se haud absimilem tum fuisse deplorare solebat: cohorresco quando cogita, quomodo accesserim ad statuas in Papatu. Tubingæ postquam Magister artium factus, & publice in Academiâ legisset Virgilium, Terentium, Ciceronem, atque etiam aliquandiu præfuisset officinæ Typographicæ, vocatus fuit V Vittembergam, quò ex consilio Capnionis potissimum (qui eum cognatione attingebat, & olim quando in Phorcemiensi Scholâ litteris operam dabat, sorori suæ cohabitantem (Phorcensis, vel Phorcemiensis & Capnio erat) donarat Græcâ Grammaticâ, Lexico Græco, & Bibliorum codice; & ad quem Tubingæ degentem sæpius Capnio divertere, unàque cum eo in Collegio cibum capere solebat, præsertim quando ab indoctis Monachis, Hochstrato, & sui similibus indigne vexaretur, & jam in Germaniâ, jam Romæ hæresis accusaretur, qui solus inter omnes istos quid hæresis ef-set set, credo intelligebat, tantamque litteris & Græcis,& Hebraicis, illo tempore gloriam conciliavit, ut nemo alius, edită à se primum Grammatica Hebræa, & Onomastico) hoc dico Capnione consulente, Melanthon (cujus nomen ex Germanico in Græcum, uti suum ex Reuchlin in Capnionis, Hermolaus Barbarus olim commutarat) Tubingă relictă V Vittembergam concessit a. cIↄ Iↄ xvi ii. ætatis suæ xxii. quo discedente Georgium Simlerum, ejus in Græcis præceptorem dixisse ferunt: deplorandum esse toti civitati ejus abitum; & omnes illos qui Tubingæ viverent, non eo usque progressos esse in studiis, ut quantus hic vir esset, qui discedebat, intelligerent. V Vittembergæ Græcam linguam docuit, magno omnium concursu, fructuque, præsertim Theologorum. Quod Lutherus de eo mox testatus fuit, in literis ad Spalatinum: Auditorium habet refertum auditoribus: imprimis omnes Theologos summos, cum mediis & infimis studiosos facit Græcitatis. Neque hanc solum linguam, sed & Latinam, artesque omnes unà cum litteris, & Philosophiam tam diligenter, tantâque cum laude excoluit, ut hæ omnes illum ceu alterum parentem inde jure meritoque honorare, per Germaniam præsertim, incæperint. Tantoque apparatu præditum, in Theologicis fœlicius versatum quis miretur? ad quæ semper animum ejus studiumque valde accenderat codex ille Biblicus, sibi à cognato suo Capnione olim datus, in cujus lectione adeo fuit assiduus, ut nemo credere posset librum istum, quem sic in sinu semper premebat, sacrum esse, sed profanum aliquem autorem ita ab ipso volvi indesinenter ac tantum non deperiri, vulgo arbitrarentur. Tantum ejus judicio tribuebat Lutherus, ut absque eo nihil magni facile aggrederetur: atque hinc scripsit lib. i. epist. pag. 197. in omni mea professione nihil ducam antiquius Philippi calculo: cujus unius judicium & autoritas mihi stant pro multis millibus sordidorum Ecclesiastum. Neque me pudet, etsi magistrum artium, philosophiæ
units.tr: Philip Melanchthon, who deserves to be named with praise for his goodness, and whom Germany rightly acknowledges as its common teacher, is shown by the inscription before his family home, in the Lower Palatinate at the town of Bretten, to have been born there. The inscription reads: By God's goodness, the most learned Mr. Philip Melanchthon was born in this house on 16 February 1497. His vernacular name was Schwarzerd. At Heidelberg he studied as a boarder with the theologian Pallas, from the age of twelve, that is in 1509, when he took the title and degree of bachelor, sixth out of twenty-one candidates. After three years had passed, he sought the master's degree, but was refused by some on account of his youth, and also because of concern for his health, so he withdrew to Tübingen. There he attended lectures in medicine and law, and in theology those of Doctor Lemp, of whom he often told, not without good cause for laughter, that when explaining the doctrine of transubstantiation he used to paint it on a board with chalk for his hearers. Melanchthon was accustomed to repeat this saying to people when some absurd matter was put before him, and later too he used it to refute the fiction of ubiquity. He also used to tell of another preacher at Tübingen, a monk, who, leaving aside the teaching of the Gospels, expounded Aristotle's Ethics in his sermons. This won no small following among his hearers, who listened to such things more willingly than to the common tales from the most foul legends, which were almost the only things ever repeated. He used to lament those dark and sorrowful times, saying that he himself had then been not very different: I shudder when I think how I came to be before the images in the Papacy. After becoming Master of Arts at Tübingen, and having publicly lectured in the university on Virgil, Terence and Cicero, and having for some time presided over a printing house, he was called to Wittenberg. This happened chiefly on the advice of Capnio (Reuchlin), who was related to him by blood, and who, when Melanchthon was studying at the school of Pforzheim, had given him, living with his sister, a Greek grammar, a Greek lexicon and a copy of the Bible.
