Capnio, while Melanchthon was staying at Tübingen, often used to visit him and eat with him in the college, especially when he was shamefully harassed by the unlearned monks, Hochstraten and men like him, and was accused of heresy now in Germany and now at Rome. Capnio alone among all those men, I believe, understood what heresy was. Melanchthon, with Capnio's advice, left Tübingen for Wittenberg in 1518, at the age of twenty-two. Georg Simler, his teacher in Greek, is reported to have said when he left: It is to be deplored by the whole city that he is going; and all those who live at Tübingen have not progressed so far in their studies as to understand how great a man this is who is leaving. At Wittenberg he taught Greek to a great crowd of hearers, to the great benefit of all, especially of the theologians. Luther soon bore witness to this in a letter to Spalatin: His lecture hall is full of listeners; above all he makes all the leading theologians, and the middling and lowest students too, into Greek scholars. He cultivated not only this language but also Latin, all the arts together with letters, and philosophy, so diligently and with such praise that all of these began, rightly and deservedly, to honour him as a second parent, especially throughout Germany. Who would be surprised that he, endowed with such equipment, was more successful in theology? To this his mind and zeal were always greatly inflamed by that biblical codex which Capnio had once given him as a relative. He was so constant in reading it, and so constantly carried this book, which he always pressed to his bosom, that people generally thought it was not a sacred book but some profane author which he was forever turning over and almost wearing out. Luther attributed so much weight to his judgment that he undertook nothing important without it. Hence he wrote in book 1 of the letters, page 197: In my whole profession I count nothing more valuable than Philip's judgment; his judgment and authority alone outweigh for me many thousands of filthy churchmen. Nor am I ashamed, though I am a Master of Arts, of yielding to his mind, which is distinguished in philosophy and theology and in nearly all the titles of the Church, if it should differ from this little grammarian.

units.la: Melanthon: Philippus Melanchthon. phia & Theologia, & omnibus pene Ecci titulis insignem, si hujus mihi Grammatistae dissenserit ingenium, meo sensu cedere. Quod & sapius feci, & quotidie facio, ob divinum donum, quod Deus in hoc fictile vasculum (Eccio quidem contemptibile) larga benedictione infudit. De titulis quod dicit, hoc est, Melanthon solo Magistri titulo contentus fuit; Doctoris, quem Lutherus habebat, respuit; neque adeo contemsit in aliis, quam quidem neglexit in seipso. Unde de illis, in epistola quadam, loquens de alio: ille adolescens, quisquis est, si non habet certam conditionem, meo judicio rectius faciet, si non properabit ad gradum. Titulus aliquid habet oneris. Vides meum exemplum: nemo me perpellere potuit, ut illum, quamlibet honorificum titulum Doctoris, mihi decerni sinerem. Nec ego gradus illos parvifacia: sed ideo, quia judico esse magna onera & necessaria reipublicae verecunde petendos esse, & conferendos, sentio. Hac ratione Lutherus de eo alibi dixit: quidquid uspiam in artibus & vera philosophia scimus, hoc Philippum praestare titulo quidem humili Magistri insignitum, sed longe omnibus Doctoribus doctiorem. Magna Dei in hoc eluxit sapientia & benignitas, quod singulari adeo providentia, utrumque virum Lutherum & Melanthonem, hunc Tubingae, illum Erphordiae, ad eandem Academiam, inque idem, quod instabat, Reformationis opus, tam extraordinariis donis imbutos, mirum in modum consociaret, ut dum non uni omnia concedere, defectus alterius per alterum corrigi, & mutua studiorum animorumque συμβιβασμός in idem opus incumbere ambos voluerit. Erat in Luthero major animus, & vehementior, in Philippo mitior: ibi plus Theologiae, hic litterarum: Lutherus ad inchoandum valebat, Philippus ad peragendum: pluscul um in illoc Monachi, hic philosophi: in eodem opere fuit utriusque magnus interim & necessarius fructus, atque divina quaedam in eodem attemperatio. Unde & conjunctissimi ambo, quamvis non ejusdem per omnia ingenii genii & indolis, vixere, ac quantum honoris Luthero Melanthon, tantum huic ille amoris vicissim constanterque referebat. Fidelem Luthero in omnibus consiliis & negotiis [illegible, ~1 word] se exhibuit: cum quo una quando esset in primo Colloquio Lipsiaco anno cIↄ Iↄ xix. ac nonnunquam interloqueretur, indignatus Eckius: tace tu Philippe, ac tua studia cura: ne me perturba, iratus dixit: & quando aliquid Luthero in schedula porrigeret, Idem, amove, inquit, ad teistam saccum distinctionum. Per contemtum Eckius Melanthonem, Grammaticum appellare solebat. Postquam cum hic, tum alibi egregia eruditionis Theologicae specimina Melanthon dedisset, toto animo studioque tradendae Theologiae, & reformandae, cum Luthero, Ecclesiae incubuit. Unde in omnibus Ecclesiarum negotiis, quae tum crebra magnaque passim agitabantur, interfuit, sive Consilia de emendandis ecclesiis, sive visitationes earum, sive Comitia, & Colloquia de religionis negotio haberentur. Quod vel una satis testari potest concinnata a se, quamvis ex praelineatis aliis articulis, Augustana Confessio, cujus praecipuum onus ipsi incumbebat: ut minus mirum, si non ita ex sententia fluxerit prima illa ejus scriptio, quin aliquoties fuerit mutanda. Hinc testatum aliquando Melanchtonem in ejus vita refert Melchior Adamus, inter Vitas Theol. German. si nunc mihi ad ornanda esset Confessio illa, accuratius omnino complecterer, quam eo tempore licebat. Et in epistolis ad Flachium, & alios passim: Scripsi Augustanam Confessionem tunc, cum haberem reprehensores multos, adjutorem neminem. Visumque ei initio erat, titulum non facere Confessionis, vel Principum nomine edere, sed potius docentium, seu Theologorum. In controversia Sacramentaria stetit primum a disputatione cum Oecolampadio, super sententia antiquitatis de hac controversia. Imprimis a Conventu Marpurgensi; tum Colloquio Casellano cum Buccero, a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxv. mitius se gessit, & viam concordiæ quum videret nec tantam hic esse quæstionem, nec nos adeo errare, sectatus fuit: denique in nostram tandem etiam plene cessit sententiam, post cultam cum Calvino præcipue integerrimam constantemque familiaritatem. Vide de illis etiam Sculteum, in Curriculo vitæ suæ, pag. 20. ubi refert, quod Peucerum narrantem audierit, socerum suum Melanthonem lecto Dialogo Oecolampadii de Cœna Domini, mutasse de orali manducatione sententiam, & quod postea triumphare solitus fuerit hoc argumento; Patribus doctrina Synusiastarum ignota fuit: Augustinus crassissimus fuit Zuinglianus, ergo &c. Dialogus ille legitur etiam inter epistolas Oecolampadii, & Zuinglii, pag. 130. Docet nos distinguere ipse Melanthon, epist. ad Ioach. Camerarium a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxiv. die x. Ianuar. prout vel Lutheri, vel suam sententiam sequebatur loquens enim de Colloquio Cassellano inter se & Bucerum, ad quod a Philippo Lantgravio evocatus fuerat, inquit: heri denique, hoc est, die nono Ianuarii demum reversus sum ex Cassis, quo me & Bucerum vocarat ὁ μακάριος Philippus Landgravius, ut ego nostrorum, ille suorum sententiam afferret περὶ τῆς διαλλαγῆς in illa pervulgata causa. Meam sententiam noli nunc requirere. Fui enim nuncius alienus, etsi profecto non dissimulabo, quid sentiam, ubi audiero, quid respondeant nostri. Ac de hac tota re coram, aut cum babelo certiores tabellarios, &c. tum de Simonè Grynæo addit: & publica discordia causam nullam præbuit ipse. Etsi autem non facio me judicem, tamen nec nostras plane libero culpâ. Et ad Iohannem Brentium scripsit die xx i. Ianuarii, non aspernandam esse cum Nostris concordiam, quorum sententiæ multi in Galliis & alibi Martyres interficiantur: ea res at verum fateor (inquit) non leviter me cruciat. Certe vehementer hæc res piam & pacificam animam discruciabat. Heu quoties apud amicos, sive iis loqueretur, sive scriscriberet, exclamavit: Si tantum lacrymarum funderem possem, quantum undarum noster Albis pleno vehit alveo, non posset exhaurire meum dolorem ortum ex hac dissensione. Ad Vitum Theodorum, a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxvııı. illud sciaɩ, amplius deteniio nullum diem, nullam noctem abiisse, quin hac de re cogitarim. Ita enim haec cura cum assiduo urebat, haec sollicitudo. Semper ad extremum usque concordiam suasit: quod non nescit quodcunque usquam est Lutheranorum. Pridie quam moreretur, Caspare Peucero, genero suo, dicebat: non morbo moveor, neque ulla est sollicitudo, quae animum meum angat aut perturbet: una cura est, una sollicitudo, ut Ecclesiae sint in Christo Jesu concordes. Hujus Peucceri extat Tractatus Historicus de Phil. Melanthonis sententia, de Controversia Caena Domini; a. cIↄ Iↄ xcvı. editus, qui totum negotium hoc copiose explicans consuli a quovis potest. Ferdinandus Imp. intellecta Melanthonis morte (obiit autem a. cIↄ Iↄ lx. die 19. Aprilis, aetatis suae lxıı. postquam xlıı. annos VVittembergae docuerat) hoc ei modestiae testimonium (cujus ipse ille Ferdinandus variis ex Colloquiis experat documentaj perhibuit: hujus viri consilia semper fuerunt moderata. Adeo hoc nomine apud omnes praedicabatur. Beza, in Epicedio ejus: Et gravis ut huic sis caveas juvenisve senexve. Qui nemini vixit gravis. Quod ab anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxıx. in nostra sententia ilicterit Melanthon, docuit me scripta hoc anno, mense Martio, epistola Argentorato ad Farellum Calvinus, cujus haec, quae de eo agit, pars hic omnino legenda est: Cum Philippo fuit mihi multis de rebus colloquium: de causa concordiae ad eum prius scripseram, ut bonis viris de ipsorum sententia certo possemus testari. Miseram ergo paucos articulos, quibus summam rei breviter perstrinxeram. Iis sine controversia ipse quidem assentitur: sed fatetur esse in illa parte nonnullos, qui crassius aliquid requirant: atque id tanta pertinacia, ne dicam tyrannide, ut diu in periculo fuerit, quod eum videbant a suo sensu nonnihil alienum. Quamquam autem non putat constare solidam consensionem, optat tamen ut hæc concordia, qualiscunque est, foveatur, donec in unitatem suæ veritatis nos Dominus utrinque adduxerit. De ipso nihil dubito, quin penitus nobiscum sentiat. Vivebat adhuc Lutherus, mortuus demum a. xlvi. sed quem exemplo Eliæ excusare prudens vir Melanthon solebat, cujus vocationi nihil quidem fidei authoritatisque decessit, quamvis cultum vitulorum non sustulerit, quum ab idolis aliis gentem illam magno cum zelo repurgasset. Sed propter authoritatem Lutheri, & incommoda multa quæ nimis anxiè metuebat Melanthon, continuit se, ut minus aperte constanterque sententiam, quam tenebat, tueretur, vel exponeret. Unde eum & confirmare & excitare variis litteris Calvinus opus habuit nimis hic pusillanimem, & æque cum suo, ac Ecclesiæ incommodo supra modum moderantem: ne adeo vereretur potius, quam revereretur Lutherum, ut ejus causa minus officio & conscientiæ satisfaceret in exponenda & defendenda sententia, cujus de veritate apud animum satis esset convictus. Quod non ita ad incitandum, quam quidem erigendum ejus animum, si se dictum Calvinus interpretari voluit, epistola ad eum a. cIↄ Iↄ xlv. die xxviii. Junii. Vinam ut me angit, adeoque excruciat mæroris tui συμπαθεια: sic aliquâ ejus parte sublevare te possem. Si ita est, ut dicunt Tigurini, habuerunt justam scribendi causam. Vester autem Pericles quamvis intemperie ad fulminandum rapitur? præsertim cum ejus causa nihilo sit melior. Multum illi debemus omnes, fateor. Nec ego invitus patiar, ut summa authoritate polleat, modo sibi ipsi moderari sciat. Quamquam in Ecclesia semper videndum est, quousque hominibus deferamus. Æquum enim est, ut nemo quispiam plus potest reliquis omnibus: præsertim ubi hoc ipsum non dubitat experiri, quantum possit. In tanta quidem dissipatione, quantam nunc cernimus, difficile est res turbatas componere. Verum si in nobis omnibus esset is animus qui esse debet, aliquod forsan remedium posset inveniri.
units.tr: Melanchthon: Philippus Melanchthon. I am not ashamed, though he is a master of arts, distinguished in philosophy and theology and in almost all the titles of the Church, to yield to my judgment if this schoolmaster of mine disagrees with me. I have often done so, and I do it every day, because of the divine gift which God has poured with a generous blessing into this earthen vessel, which is indeed contemptible to the Church. As for what he says about titles, this means that Melanchthon was content with the title of Master alone. He rejected the title of Doctor, which Luther held, and so he did not despise in others what he neglected in himself. Hence, writing in a certain letter about another man: That young man, whoever he is, if he has no settled position, will in my judgment act more wisely if he does not hurry after a degree. A title carries some burden. You see my example: no one could persuade me to let that most honourable title of Doctor be conferred on me. Nor do I think lightly of those degrees, but because I judge that they are great and necessary burdens for the commonwealth, I feel that they ought to be sought modestly and bestowed with care. In this same spirit Luther said of him elsewhere: Whatever we know anywhere in the arts and in true philosophy, Philip surpasses us, marked with the rather humble title of Master, but far more learned than all the Doctors. Great wisdom and goodness of God shone forth in this, that with such singular providence he joined together in marvellous fashion these two men, Luther and Melanchthon, the one at Tübingen, the other at Erfurt, both endowed with such extraordinary gifts, and brought them to the same Academy and to the same work of Reformation which was then pressing. God willed that neither should be granted everything, that the defects of each should be corrected by the other, and that both should apply themselves to the same work by a mutual agreement [συμβιβασμός] of their studies and minds. Luther had the greater spirit and the more vehement one, Melanchthon the milder. Luther had more theology, Melanchthon more literature. Luther was able to begin, Melanchthon to finish. There was more of the monk in the one, of the philosopher in the other. In the same work there was, meanwhile, great and necessary fruit from each, and a certain divine adjustment in the same work. Hence the two of them, though not alike in every kind of talent and disposition, lived in the closest friendship, and Melanchthon gave back to Luther in turn as much love as he received honour from him. He showed himself a faithful helper to Luther in all his counsels and undertakings. When he was with him at the first Colloquy of Leipzig in 1519, and occasionally spoke up, Eck, angered, said: Be quiet, Philip, and attend to your own studies; do not disturb me. And when he handed Luther a note, Eck said again: Take it away to the sack of distinctions. Eck used to call Melanchthon the Grammarian in contempt. After Melanchthon had given outstanding examples of theological learning here and elsewhere, he devoted himself with all his mind and effort, together with Luther, to teaching theology and reforming the Church. So he took part in all the affairs of the churches that were then being urgently and widely debated, whether counsels on amending the churches, visitations of them, or diets and colloquies on religious matters were being held. One clear witness to this is the Augsburg Confession, which he drew up, although the outline of its articles was prepared by others, and the principal burden of it lay on him. It is therefore less surprising that his first draft did not flow entirely as he wished, and had to be changed more than once. Hence Melchior Adam, in the Lives of the German Theologians, reports Melanchthon's own statement in his life: If I were now to adorn that Confession, I would certainly write it out more carefully than the time then allowed. And in his letters to Flacius and others he writes everywhere: I wrote the Augsburg Confession when I had many critics and no helper at all. At first it seemed good to him not to call it a Confession, nor to publish it in the name of the princes, but rather as the teaching of teachers, that is, of theologians. In the sacramentarian controversy he first took a stand after his dispute with Oecolampadius over the opinion of antiquity on this question, chiefly at the Marburg Conference. Then, at the Cassel Colloquy with Bucer in 1535, he behaved more mildly, and when he saw that the question was not so great here and that we were not so far in error, he pursued the way of concord. Finally he fully came over to our opinion, after cultivating with Calvin a most upright and steadfast friendship. On these matters see also Scultetus, in the Course of his Life, page 20, where he reports that he heard Peucer relate that his father-in-law Melanchthon, after reading Oecolampadius' Dialogue on the Lord's Supper, changed his opinion about the oral eating, and that he afterwards used to triumph with this argument: the Fathers were ignorant of the doctrine of the Synusiasts; Augustine was a very gross Zwinglian; therefore etc. That Dialogue is also read among the letters of Oecolampadius and Zwingli, page 130. Melanchthon himself teaches us to distinguish, in his letter to Joachim Camerarius of 10 January 1534, whether he was following Luther's opinion or his own. Speaking of the Cassel Colloquy between himself and Bucer, to which he had been summoned by Landgrave Philip, he says: Yesterday at last, that is on 9 January, I returned from Cassel, whither the blessed Landgrave Philip had called me and Bucer, so that I might set out the view of our people and he that of his own, concerning [περὶ τῆς διαλλαγῆς] the reconciliation in that well-known cause. Do not ask me now for my own opinion. I am a stranger as messenger, though indeed I will not hide what I think when I have heard what our people reply. And about the whole matter, he adds, in person or with more certain messengers, and about Simon Grynaeus: The public discord itself gave no cause. Yet although I do not make myself judge, I do not entirely free our side from fault. And he wrote to John Brenz on 21 January, that concord with our people should not be spurned, whose opinion many martyrs are being killed for in France and elsewhere: This matter, I confess in truth, torments me not lightly. Certainly this matter tormented that pious and peaceable soul severely. Alas, how often among friends, whether speaking or writing, he cried out: If I could pour out as many tears as our Elbe carries waters in its full channel, I could not exhaust my grief arising from this dissension. To Vitus Theodorus in 1538: Know this, that not a single day or night has passed for more than a while without my thinking about this matter. So constant and so anxious was this care that consumed him. He always urged concord to the very end, which every Lutheran anywhere is well aware of. The day before he died, he said to his son-in-law Caspar Peucer: I am not moved by sickness, nor is there any anxiety that troubles or disturbs my mind. There is one care, one anxiety: that the Churches may be in agreement in Christ Jesus. There is a Historical Treatise by this Peucer, On the Opinion of Philip Melanchthon concerning the Controversy over the Lord's Supper, published in 1596, which anyone may consult, since it explains the whole business at length. When Emperor Ferdinand learned of Melanchthon's death (he died on 19 April 1560, in his sixty-second year, after teaching at Wittenberg for forty-two years), he gave this testimony to his moderation, which he had himself experienced in various colloquies: The counsels of this man were always moderate. So widely was he praised for this quality among all. Beza, in his Funeral Poem for him: And so grave, that you should beware of him whether young or old. He lived grave toward no one. That Melanchthon had from 1539 inclined to our opinion, I learned from a letter which Calvin wrote to Farel from Strasbourg in March of this year; the part of it which deals with him must be read here in full: I had much conversation with Philip on many matters. I had written to him earlier about the cause of concord, so that we could bear certain witness to good men about their opinion. I had sent a few articles, in which I had briefly outlined the sum of the matter. He assents to these without controversy, but he admits that there are some in that party who demand something rather crude, and this with such obstinacy, not to say tyranny, that for a long time he was in danger, since they saw that he was somewhat estranged from their own sense. Although he does not think that a solid agreement exists, he nevertheless wishes that this concord, such as it is, be cherished until the Lord has brought us on both sides into the unity of his truth. I have no doubt about him: he thinks entirely as we do. Luther was still alive, and died only in 1546, but Melanchthon was accustomed to excuse him by the example of Elijah, whose calling certainly lost nothing of faith and authority, although he did not remove the worship of the calves, when he had with great zeal purged that nation of other idols. But because of Luther's authority, and the many inconveniences which Melanchthon feared all too anxiously, he restrained himself, so that he defended or set forth the opinion he held less openly and steadfastly. Hence Calvin needed to encourage and rouse him by various letters, since he was too timid here and, to his own harm and that of the Church, moderated himself beyond measure, so that he feared Luther rather than revered him, and for his sake satisfied duty and conscience less in setting out and defending an opinion of whose truth his mind was sufficiently convinced. Calvin's letter to him of 28 June 1545 was written not so much to provoke as to raise up his spirit, if Calvin wished his words to be understood in that way: Would that I could relieve you in some part of your grief, which so distresses and torments me with its sympathy [συμπαθεια]. If it is as the Zurichers say, they had a just reason for writing. But why is your Pericles carried away into thundering by an intemperance which does not even improve his cause? We all owe him much, I confess. Nor would I be unwilling to see him wield the highest authority, provided he knows how to moderate himself. Yet in the Church we must always see how far we should yield to men. For it is fair that no one should have more power than all the rest, especially when he himself does not hesitate to test how much he can do. In such a great dispersion as we now see, it is difficult to compose troubled affairs. But if in all of us there were that spirit which ought to be there, some remedy might perhaps be found.

units.la: Note: "clo Io xlv." and "clɔ Iɔ lv." read as MDXLV and MDLV, the reversed-C numerals of the printer. Calvinianos, post obitum Lutheri, defecisse. Hinc Philippum duplicem, quin triplicem faciunt. Idem c. xi. Alii distinguunt Philippum publicum, & privatum, partim orthodoxum, partim heterodoxum, uti Calovius, in Critico sacro. Atque Benedictus Morgenstern, epist. ad Schlusselburgium, pag. 107. Germanicarum Ecclesiarum postem Phil. Melanthonem, scribere haud erubescit.
units.tr: Calvinists, after Luther's death. From this they make Philip twofold, or rather threefold. The same author, chapter 11. Others distinguish Philip as public and private, partly orthodox, partly heterodox, as Calovius does in his Critico sacro. And Benedict Morgenstern, in his letter to Schlüsselburg, page 107, does not blush to write that Philip Melanchthon was the plague of the German Churches.

units.la: Non parva tandem inter Lutherum ac Melanthonem ex illâ sententiarum; etiam animorum dissensio, & simultas orta fuit: quin & pro concione se notari aliquando occulte Melanthon sensit, de quo & Sculteus, in Curriculo vitæ suæ, pag. 20. unde (ad quem modum antea diximus Carolostadium abactum, dentaris ejusmodi concionibus) de discessu cogitans, deque adjungendo sibi fidissimo comite Caspar Crucigero, quod nequidquam certe ex re Lutheri fuisset, hic illum ad se accersitum ita composuit placavitque: causa, inquiens, hæc mea est, quam tuebor sine te: tu maneas sano in sententia contraria, si veriorem esse judicas: nec mihi tuo vel patrocinio vel auxilio opus est. In quas leges transactum inter utrumque fuit, servataque mutuo pax & amicitia. Ita palam nunc dissentiebat à Luthero Melanthon, & non ultra ut olim alienæ sententiæ nuncius habebatur, sed dominus suæ. Attamen, utcunque inter ambos ad extremum usque spiritum inviolabilis fuerit concordia, mortuo Lutbero, ejus discipuli aliique in Melanthonem insurgere, impugnare eum, ἀντιλέγειν eo usque coeperunt, ut sic tandem verum esse senserit, quod Calvinus toties præmonuerat, se prolixa suâ moderatione, & timiditate non demulsisse adversarios, sed irritasse, & fecisse adversus se audentiores, quod corrigere, postquam illis tantum indulserat, ac ab exordio resistere, non æque promptum sero nimis pervidit. Unde exilium non sibi jam eligendum, sed metuendum: de quo, ad V. Wolfgangum Musculum, a. clɔ Iɔ xliv. die. xii. Augusti, Nunc domestica bella nova [illegible, ~3 letters] noster Pericles. Totas adversus eos, qui περὶ συμβόλων [?] συμβόλων [?] aliter loquuntur, quam ipse [illegible, ~3 letters] quitur, ac me quoque interdum arripit. Fortassis in hac sen [illegible, ~3 letters] & a brevi mihi exulandum erit. Ego nec defugio aerumn [illegible, ~3 letters] εἰ δὲ συγχαρηναι τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ, nec quidquam tamen [illegible, ~3 letters] moderate faciam. ad Calvinum, a. clɔ Iɔ I i i. Mihi [illegible, ~3 letters] vivam, nova exilia expectanda sunt. Quò si redigeret [illegible, ~3 letters] Calvinum adire, & petere Genevam proposuerat. Qu [illegible, ~3 letters] re si cedendum erit, colloqui tecum decrevi, inquit. [illegible, ~3 letters] Calvinus ad eum: sin vero contigerit, quod times, ei [illegible, ~3 letters] hoc mihi in rebus miseris & luctuosis non leve solatium, [illegible, ~3 letters] dere te prius & amplexi, quam ex hoc mundo migrandu [illegible, ~3 letters] sit. Iterum ille, ad Calvinum, a. clɔ Iɔ I iv. die x i Octob. Non desistero nos colloquuturos esse, antequam [illegible, ~3 letters] hoc mortali carcere mens discedat. Etsi enim propter senectu [illegible, ~3 letters] à meta hujus curriculi non procul absum, tamen quotie [illegible, ~3 letters] nova exilia expecto. Iisdem literis dixerat: Quod vero [illegible, ~3 letters] proximis literis me hortaris, ut reprimam invadentes clam [illegible, ~3 letters] res illorum, qui renovant certamen [illegible, ~3 letters] quosdam præcipue odio mei eam disputationem movere. habeant plausibilem causam ad me opprimendum. Adve [illegible, ~3 letters] sus quæ omnia incommoda, metusque diligenter & [illegible, ~3 letters] hide eum consolatus Calvinus fuit. Egregiè epistolâ clɔ Iɔ Iv. i i i. Non, Martii, Nec vero illa mihi excu [illegible, ~3 letters] tio satisfacit, malevoli quæ te oppressum capiunt, hinc capi [illegible, ~3 letters] re plausibilem materiam. Quid enim factum sunt servi Chri [illegible, ~3 letters] sti, nisi spreta invidia, contemptis ministeriis mundi, pro [illegible, ~3 letters] habito etiam discriminum metu, quæcunque obstacula ingi [illegible, ~3 letters] vit Satan, victrice constantia superent? Certè quantum [illegible, ~3 letters] in te insaniant, nihil tibi durius ab illis impendet, quam [illegible, ~3 letters] migrare istinc cogaris. Quod tibi meo judicio complures [illegible, ~3 letters] causas sponte optandum fecit. Verum ut timendæ sint extr [illegible, ~3 letters] ma quæque, tibi semel statuere necesse est, quid Christo d [illegible, ~3 letters] beas, ne ingenuam veritatis professionem suppriment, ad ea [illegible, ~3 letters] opprimendam quasi tacitum patrocinium improbis hominib [illegible, ~3 letters] accommodes. Ad Albertum Hardenbergium Bremensem Concionatorem Melanthon scripsit a. MD. Ian. die xii. Januar. quo eodem a. obiit, d. xix. Aprilis: Totos jam viginti annos expecto exilia. Ad eundem, si solas expellar, decrevi Palestinam adire, & in illis Hieronymi Lateribris, in invocatione filii Dei, & testimonia perspicua de doctrina scribere, & in morte Deo animam commendare. Alia epistola, Dixerunt Adversarii, se perfecturos esse, ut non sint habituros vestigium, ubi pedem collocare possint in Germania. Etiam hoc cito perficiant, ut Filius Dei ad Judam dicit. Erit mihi vel in caelo vestigium morienti: vel si vivam in hoc corpore apud honestos & doctos viros, vel in Germania, vel alibi. Certe nisi mature (sibi quidem, non item Ecclesiae) cum Deus turbis hisce subduxisset, procul dubio adversarii in eo orsi fuissent tragoediam, quam post in genere ejus Peucero perfecerunt. Unde de eo etiam Thuanus, in fine libri xxvi. Sed qui obviam eam humanitatem in exteris ac diversa sententiibus probavit, longe contrariam fortunam inter suos, & eandem doctrinam profitentes expertus est.
units.tr: Not a small dissension and rivalry, arising from that difference of opinion and also of minds, broke out at last between Luther and Melanthon. Melanthon once sensed that he was being secretly singled out in a sermon, as Sculteus notes in his Curriculum vitae, p. 20. Thinking of leaving, and of attaching to himself as his most loyal companion Caspar Cruciger (which would certainly have done him no good against Luther's position), he was summoned by Luther, who settled and soothed him in these words: This cause is mine, and I will defend it without you. Remain in your contrary opinion, if you judge it the truer. I need neither your patronage nor your help. On these terms an agreement was reached between the two, and peace and friendship were kept on both sides. Melanthon now openly dissented from Luther, and was no longer regarded, as he once had been, as the messenger of another's opinion, but as the master of his own. Yet, although harmony between the two remained unbroken to the last breath, after Luther's death his disciples and others began to rise against Melanthon, to attack him, and to contradict (ἀντιλέγειν [antilegein]) him to such a degree that he at last felt the truth of what Calvin had so often warned: that his long moderation and timidity had not soothed his opponents but provoked them and made them bolder against him. Too late, he saw that he should have resisted from the start rather than indulging them so far. So exile was no longer a thing he could choose but a thing he had to fear. Writing to Wolfgang Musculus, on 12 August 1544, he says: Now new domestic wars [...] our Pericles. Against all those who speak about the creeds [...] otherwise than he himself [...] speaks, he attacks me too at times. Perhaps in this matter [...] and before long I shall have to go into exile. I do not shrink from hardship [...] but if it is right to rejoice in the gospel [εἰ δὲ συγχαρῆναι τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ, ei de sunchairēnai tō euangeliō], I shall nonetheless do nothing [...] immoderately. To Calvin, in 1552: [...] I live, new exiles are to be expected. He had decided to go to Calvin and to ask to be taken to Geneva: if I must give way, I have resolved to talk with you. Calvin replied to him: But if what you fear should come to pass, this will be no slight comfort to me in these wretched and sorrowful circumstances: that I should embrace you before you depart from this world. Again he wrote to Calvin, on 11 October 1554: I shall not cease to say that we shall talk together before the mind departs from this mortal prison. For although on account of my age I am not far from the goal of this course, yet as often as [...] I expect new exiles. In the same letter he had said: As for what you urge me in your last letter, to restrain those who attack [...] their opponents secretly [...] they who renew the contest, and some of them chiefly out of hatred for me, have stirred up that dispute, so that they have a plausible cause for crushing me. Calvin consoled him in all these troubles and fears, and carefully so. In a letter of 3 March 1554 (5 March, by the Roman reckoning) he wrote: Nor does that excuse satisfy me, that the malicious who see you oppressed take from this a plausible matter [for attack]. For what have the servants of Christ done but, scorning envy and despising worldly ministries, overcome with steadfast courage whatever obstacles Satan has put in their way, even when they feared dangers? Certainly, however much they rage against you, nothing harder can threaten you from them than being forced to leave that place. In my judgment, many reasons make that something you should even wish for. But since whatever is to be feared must be faced, you must decide once and for all what you owe to Christ, lest you suppress the open profession of the truth and lend, as it were, a silent protection to wicked men for the suppression of it. Writing to Albert Hardenberg, preacher at Bremen, Melanthon wrote on 12 January 1550 (he died on 19 April of the same year): For now I have been expecting exile for twenty years. To the same man: If I am driven out alone, I have decided to go to Palestine, and there to write, in the Hieronymic letters, on the invocation of the Son of God, and clear testimonies on doctrine, and to commend my soul to God in death. Another letter says: My opponents have said that they will bring it about that they [i.e. we] will not have a trace of a place in Germany where we may set our foot. Even this they will quickly accomplish, as the Son of God said to Judas. I will have a trace in heaven when I die; or if I live in this body, among honest and learned men, either in Germany or elsewhere. Certainly, had God not withdrawn him from these tumults in good time (for himself, though not for the Church), his adversaries would without doubt have begun there the tragedy which they afterwards completed in the person of Peucer. Thuanus also says of him, at the end of book 26: But he who showed such humanity towards those who were foreign and of differing opinions experienced a far different fortune among his own, who professed the same doctrine.

units.la: Luthero, quod adversus Nostros immoderatior extitit, causa magna fuit Amsdorfius: Melanthoni quod illae excitatae turbae; etiam Flacius. Ille Lutherum, quamvis per se acrem satis ad majorem semper incitavit vehementiam, & ab omni cum Argentinensibus & Tigurinis incunda concordia defecit, nisi prius se erasse confiterentur. Natus Nicolaus Amsdorfius, a. MD. ccccc lxxxiii. Luthero aetate aequalis. Magdeburgensium primus concionator fuit: inde, expulsa Iulio Pflug, episcopus Naumburgensis a Luthero, ex consilio & jussu Electoris Saxoniae, ordinatus, sed sexto anno post a Carolo Imp. iterum ejectus, restituto in ejus locum priori Iulio Pflug, Magdeburgum repetiit. Hic Luthero non ita diu ante ejus mortem auctor fuit, ut formulam conciperet, ad quam in ista sententiarum de Coena discrepantia, subscribendam omnes mnes collegas & pastores adigeret, cui prudentior tum Lutherus respondit: Litem hanc suam esse, cui invitum neminem velit implicare. Si quid tale tentaret, plures fortasse adversaturos, quam suffragaturos, & posteriora prioribus futura pejora. Quod utinam monitum simul & vaticinium Formulae Bergensis postea Auctoribus firmius animo insedisset, & fuisset observatum! Hic fuit idem Amsdorfius, qui adversus Georgium Majorem, necessitatem bonorum operum ad salutem negavit, contra crudam, ineptam ac stolidam thesim asserunt, unde qualis vel ingenii vel theologiae vir fuerit, appareret: bona opera ad salutem esse noxia & periculosa. Quasi non posset veritas & puritas doctrinae de gratuita nostri coram Deo justificatione servari, cum bonorum operum necessitate, non ad justificationem, neque ad merendum, sed ut iis à justificatione, tamquam sola via ad salutem regia, per sanctitatem nempe, absque qua nemo Deum visurus est, Hebr. XII. 14 progredientes ad salutis possessionem (non juris adeptionem) perveniamus. Magnas illi homines (qui haec non bene intelligentes, aut conciliantes, de propositione illa: bona opera ad salutem necessaria, impotenter litigarunt,) Melanthoni molestias, & turbas Ecclesiae inanes concitarunt. De quibus vide part. II. Consil. Theol. Melanthonis. Et quum tria in ista propositione essent consideranda, an facienda bona opera? an necessario? an ad salutem? illud neque Amsdorfius negabat, ex cujus praesatione ad Postillam domesticam, haec Melanthon produxit: ich habe allezeit gelehret, das man gute werck thun pflichtig und schuldig ist. Et quia secundum etiam Melanthon astruebat, necessaria esse bona opera, seu obedientiam, ideo sic adversus eum tumultuatum. Tertium vero cedebat lubens, neque asserere audebat ad salutem esse necessaria. Propter has causas, inquit, docemus, necessaria esse bona opera, seu novam obedientiam. Nequaquam tamen assuendum est, bona opera ad salutem & vitam aeternam consequendam necessarie esse. In Responso ad Pastores Saxonicos: tamen hac phrasi non utamur, bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem. Alibi: Plane dico, me non uti hac phrasi: Bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem. Sed has propositiones affirmo veras esse, & proprie, sine sophistica sic dici: Nova obedientia est necessaria, vel, Bona opera sunt necessaria, quia Deo debetur obedientia, juxta dictum, debitores sumus. Sic etiam alibi se declarat. Hac in contentione Flacius se conjunxit adversus Melanthonem, quo magis videlicet praeceptorem suum opprimeret. Unde in propositionibus a. CIↃ IↃ lvı ı. Cosviga ad Melanthonem datis, in propositione tertia: ideoque tollatur corruptela de necessitate operum ad salutem, cum conjunctis. Quin omnino & facienda bona opera, & necessaria, atque ad salutem, non obtinendam vel acquirendam, sed gratis obtentam adeundam & occupandam: libereque haec & intrepide asserenda nobis sunt, nequaquam cum ullo vel gratiae divinae, aut gratuitae justificationis Christique praejudicio, aut Pontificiorum ipsorumque sententiae aliquo ad minimum commodo conjuncta.
units.tr: For Luther, the great cause of his growing harshness towards our people was Amsdorf; for Melanthon, the stirring up of those turmoils was due in part to Flacius. Luther, though already sharp enough by nature, Flacius always spurred on to greater vehemence, and he broke off all harmonious concord with the Strasbourg and Zurich theologians unless they first confessed that they had erred. Nicolaus Amsdorf was born in 1483, Luther's contemporary. He was the first preacher at Magdeburg; later, when Julius Pflug was expelled, he was ordained bishop of Naumburg by Luther, on the advice and by the command of the Elector of Saxony. But six years later he was ejected again by Charles V, and when Julius Pflug was restored to his place, Amsdorf went back to Magdeburg. Shortly before Luther's death, Amsdorf was the originator of a formula, to which he wanted all his colleagues and ministers to subscribe in that dispute over the Lord's Supper. Luther, more prudent at the time, replied that this was a quarrel he did not wish to involve anyone against his will. If they tried anything of the sort, more would perhaps oppose it than support it, and the later outcomes would be worse than the earlier ones. Would that this warning and prophecy had more firmly sunk into the minds of the later authors of the Formula of Bergen, and had been observed! It was the same Amsdorf who, against Georgius Major, denied that good works are necessary to salvation, asserting the crude, foolish and stupid thesis that good works are harmful and dangerous to salvation, by which it appears what kind of man he was, both in intellect and in theology. As if the truth and purity of the doctrine of our free justification before God could not be kept along with the necessity of good works, not as a means to justification or to earning merit, but because by way of them, after justification, as the only royal road to salvation, namely through holiness (without which no one will see God, Heb. 12:14), we come to possess salvation (not to acquire a right to it). Those men, who did not rightly understand or reconcile this proposition, good works are necessary to salvation, quarrelled violently over it, and stirred up vain troubles for Melanthon and disturbances for the Church. On these matters see part II of Melanthon's Consilia Theologica. Since three things in that proposition must be considered (whether good works are to be done, whether they are necessary, and whether they are necessary to salvation), Amsdorf did not deny the first. From the preface of his Postil for home use, Melanthon quoted these words: I have always taught that one is bound and obliged to do good works. And since Melanthon also maintained that good works, or obedience, are necessary, they therefore made an uproar against him. The third point Amsdorf readily conceded, and did not dare to assert that good works are necessary to salvation. For these reasons, he says, we teach that good works, or new obedience, are necessary. Yet we must by no means accustom ourselves to say that good works are necessary for attaining salvation and eternal life. In the Response to the Saxon Pastors: nevertheless we shall not use this phrase, good works are necessary to salvation. Elsewhere: I plainly say that I do not use this phrase, Good works are necessary to salvation. But I affirm these propositions to be true, and to be said properly and without sophistry: New obedience is necessary, or, Good works are necessary, because obedience is owed to God, according to the saying, we are debtors. He explains himself in the same way elsewhere. In this controversy Flacius joined forces against Melanthon, evidently so as the more to crush his own teacher. Hence in the propositions which Cosvig sent to Melanthon in 1551 (the third proposition), the statement reads: and therefore let the corruption about the necessity of works for salvation, together with its supporters, be removed. Indeed, we must assert freely and fearlessly, and in no way in conjunction with any prejudice to divine grace or to free justification and Christ, or with anything at all that would even slightly favour the Papists or their opinion, that good works are to be done, that they are necessary, and that they are necessary to salvation: not to obtain or acquire it, but as the means by which we enter upon and take possession of what is freely obtained.

units.la: Flacius ex praecipuis fuit Melanthonis & V Vittembergensium, in contentione decennali de adiaphoris, adversarius. Vbi si rem ipsam solum spectassent, non improbandum erat, quod remissiori de adiaphoris, quae praetendi vulgo talia solent, non haberi, & revera pons fiunt per quem Papismus reduci queat, sententiae se opponerent, nisi pro inconsiderata sua vehementia, a re ad personam pergentes, studuissent hoc pacto virum optimum Philippum Melanthonem, collegasque & socios saevum in modum opprimere & perdere. Monuerat illum amanter acriterque etiam Calvinus, de illa super adiaphoris contentione, per epistolam: Sed ego te nunc apud teipsum accuso, ne iis qui absentem damnant, cogar subscribere. Haec tua defensionis summa est, modo fessimant doctrinae pueritas, de rebus incertis ipsi esse pernimaciter dimicandum. Atqui si verum est, quod pro certo passim asseritur, tu res medias & indifferentes nimis longè extendis. Cultum Dei mille modis apud Papistas adulteratum non ignoras, Corruptelas, quae minimè tolerabiles erant, sustulimus. Nunc impii, ut de subacto Euangelio triumphum agant, easdem jubent restituere. Si quis recusare non dubitet, hoccine pertinaciae adscribes? Id verò à tua modestia quàm alienum sit, novi. Tu si ad cedendum fuisti mollior, id tibi vitio à multis verti, non est quod mireris. Adde, quod rerum quas tu medias facis, quaedam cum Dei verbo manifestè pugnant. Nimis praecisè fortasse quaedam alii urgent, atque ut in contentionibus fieri solet, odiosè quaedam exagitant, quibus non inest tantum mali. Verùm si quid in rebus divinis intelligo, tam multa Papistis absente concedi non oportuit: partim quia laxasti quae verbo suo Dominus adstrinxit, partim quia proterve Euangelio insultandi materiam dedisti. Unde & cessit postmodum in hac contentione Melanthon lubens. Ad ipsum Flacium, a. MDLVI. Haec postea Consiliarii nominarunt ἀλλόφυλοι[?]. Nam ab ipsis vocabulum initiò nobis propositum est. Sciebam etiam levissimas mutationes ingratas fore populo. Tamen cum doctrina retineretur integra, malui nostros hanc servitutem subire, quam deserere ministerium Euangelii. Et idem consilium Francis me dedisse fateor. Hoc igitur feci. Doctrinam confessionis nunquam mutavi. Ea etiam de ritibus hic mediis nimis pugnavi, quia jam antea in plerisque Ecclesiis harum regionum retenti erant. Postea vos contradicere coepistis. Cessi, nihil pugnavi. Aiax apud Homerum praelians cum Hectore, contentus est, cum cedit Hector; & fatetur, ipsum victorem esse. Pos finem nullum facitis criminandi. Quis hoc hostis facit? ut cedentes & arma abjicientes feriat? vincite, cedo, nihil pugno de ritibus illis, & maximè opto, ut dulcis sit Ecclesiarum concordia. Fateor etiam hac in re à me peccatum esse, & à Deo veniam peto, quod non procul fugi illas insidiosas deliberationes. Sed illa, quae falsa mihi à te & Gallo objiciuntur, refutabo. Eo hac hac de mediis ritibus, quia in epistola tua de his praecipua pars est.
units.tr: Flacius was one of the chief opponents of Melanchthon and the Wittenberg theologians in the ten-year dispute over adiaphora. Had they opposed the matter itself, and not merely the more lenient view that things commonly called adiaphora should not be regarded as such, since they can in fact become a bridge by which Papism might be led back, that would not have been wrong. But in his rash vehemence he passed from the matter to the person, and so set about crushing and destroying that excellent man Philip Melanchthon and his colleagues and associates in a savage manner. Calvin had also warned him lovingly and sharply about that dispute over adiaphora, in a letter: But now I accuse you, in your own mind, lest I be forced to subscribe to those who condemn one who is absent. This is the sum of your defence: that it is with the utmost obstinacy that a fragile schoolboy-like doctrine should fight about uncertain matters. Yet if what is asserted everywhere as certain is true, you stretch indifferent and intermediate things far too widely. You are not unaware that the worship of God was corrupted in a thousand ways among the Papists. We removed the corruptions, which were by no means tolerable. Now the impious, that they may triumph over the conquered Gospel, order the same things to be restored. If anyone hesitates to refuse, will you ascribe this to obstinacy? I know how far that is from your modesty. If you were too soft in yielding, you need not wonder that many have found fault with you for it. Add that some of the things you call intermediate clearly clash with the Word of God. Some men press certain points too narrowly, and, as usually happens in controversies, they harass certain matters hatefully, though these contain no great evil. But if I understand anything of divine matters, so many concessions should not have been made to the Papists in your absence: partly because you relaxed what the Lord has bound by his word, and partly because you gave them occasion to insult the Gospel shamelessly. And so afterwards Melanchthon gladly gave way in this dispute. To Flacius himself, in 1556. Afterwards the councillors called these men foreigners [ἀλλόφυλοι?]. For the name was first proposed to us by them. I knew that even the slightest changes would be unwelcome to the people. Yet, since the doctrine was kept whole, I preferred that our people undergo this servitude rather than abandon the ministry of the Gospel. I confess I gave the same advice to the French. So I did this. I never changed the doctrine of the Confession. I also fought hard here about these intermediate rites, because they were already retained in most churches of these regions. Afterwards you began to contradict me. I yielded; I did not fight at all. Ajax, fighting against Hector in Homer, is content when Hector gives way, and admits that he himself is the victor. You make no end to accusing. What enemy does this? Does he strike those who yield and lay down their arms? Conquer, I yield; I do not contend at all about those rites, and I most of all wish that the concord of the churches may be sweet. I also confess that I sinned in this matter, and I ask God's pardon, because I did not flee far from those insidious deliberations. But I will refute those falsehoods that are objected to me by you and by the Frenchman. I say this about intermediate rites because the chief part of your letter concerns them.

units.la: Fuit ille Matthias Flacius, vel Flachius Flach Germanice, natione Illyricus, (hodie Slavonia dicitur) unde hoc nomine innotuit, natus a. cIↄ Iↄ xx. Cum Venetiis studeret, audiretque celebrem in litteris humanioribus virum I. Baptistam Egnatium, consilium communicavit cum Baldo Lupatino, Franciscanorum provinciali, propinquo suo materno, de ingrediendo Monasterio, quo ad Theologiae eruditionem, cujus vehementer cupidus erat, commodius perveniret, quod tamen ipse Baldus postea dissuasit, & quia hic gustum Reformationis jam perceperat, auctor potius erat, ut in Germaniam secederet, purioris doctrinae Praeceptoribus usurus: quod & fecit. Baldus non diu latere potuit, quin in suspicionem veniret haeresis, ac primum per viginti annos squallido carcere discruciatus, tandem mari mersus supplicium constanter pertulit. Dignus vir, cujus in Martyrologio nomen ne praetereatur. Basileam ergo Flacius, inde VVittembergam venit, ubi Lutherum audivit & Melanthonem, interque studia tantis subinde concutiebatur tentationibus, ut publicae in templo preces pro ipso haberentur. Professor postea constitutus, nonnulla adversus Papistas, & in opere Historiae Ecclesiasticae (Centurias Magdeburgi confecit) haud poenitenda praestitit: sed inquieti, vehementioris & duri quum esset ingenii, tum VVittembergae adversus Melanthonem, tum Antverpiae postmodum, ubi cum Spangerbergio, Hamelmanno & aliis, circa a. cIↄ Iↄ lxv i. ad Colloquium vel Disputationem, cum Nostris habendam (cum nihil Protestantes ab Adversariis timerent, inter se mox digladiari coepernt, inquit hac ipsa de re Thuanus, lib. xl.) vocatus, tantas turbas dedit, ut & hic & ibi amiciae cum libertatis, tum puritatis doctrinae, causa inter primos extiterit. Tacco contentiones suo de peccati originalis substantia dogmagmate aliisque datas, de quibus Eusebius Bohemus, in Epitome Histor. Eccles. pag. 998. &c. Extant Acta Disputationis Vinariensis anni cIↄ Iↄ lvii. inter ipsum, & Victorinum Strigelium, Ienensem Theologum, (quem adversa factio primum Ienae carcere tenuit triennali, inde Lipsiâ abegit: Professor postmodum factus Heidelbergae, ubi & obiit) de quorum tamen editione valde semper conquestus Strigelius fuit, ubi primo loco disputatum fuit: utrum in regeneratione, seu conversione hominis ad Deum tantum mutentur qualitates, sine creatione novae substantiae: an verò cum qualitatibus creetur nova substantia? secundo, de modo agendi, quem Deus in hominis conversione adhibeat? Sed sibi cum homine Barbaro, (adeo crudas incoctasque locutiones proferre solitus erat) rem fuisse, scripsit postea bonus vir Strigelius. Mortuus autem ille est Francofurti ad Moenum a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxv.
units.tr: That Flacius, or Flachius (in German, Flach), was by nation an Illyrian (today called Slavonia), whence he became known by this name, was born in 1520. While he was studying at Venice and listening to the famous humanist scholar Giovanni Battista Egnazio, he discussed with Baldo Lupatino, provincial of the Franciscans, a relative on his mother's side, the idea of entering a monastery, so that he might more conveniently reach the knowledge of theology for which he was eagerly longing. Baldo himself afterwards advised against this; since Flacius had already tasted the Reformation, Baldo rather urged him to withdraw into Germany, to use the teachers of purer doctrine, and he did so. Baldo could not long remain hidden from suspicion of heresy, and, after being tortured for twenty years in a squalid prison, was at last drowned in the sea, bearing his punishment steadfastly. He was a worthy man, whose name should not be passed over in the Martyrology. Flacius therefore went from Basel to Wittenberg, where he heard Luther and Melanchthon. Among his studies he was from time to time shaken by such temptations that public prayers were offered for him in the church. Afterwards he was made a professor, and he did no small service against the Papists and in his work of Church History (he compiled the Magdeburg Centuries). But being restless, of a vehement and harsh disposition, he gave great disturbances, first at Wittenberg against Melanchthon, and then later at Antwerp, where, with Spangenberg, Hamelmann and others, around 1565 he was summoned to a colloquy or disputation with our side (since the Protestants feared nothing from their adversaries, they soon began to fight among themselves, says Thuanus on this very matter, book 40). Among the first, he stood out as the cause of both friendship and liberty and of purity of doctrine, by stirring up so many quarrels here and there. He caused contentions over his dogma on the substance of original sin and other matters, about which Eusebius Bohemus writes in the Epitome Historiae Ecclesiasticae, page 998 and following. The acts of the Disputation of Weimar, of the year 1557, survive, between him and Victorinus Strigelius, theologian of Jena (whom the hostile faction first held in prison at Jena for three years, and then drove out of Leipzig; he was afterwards made professor at Heidelberg, where he also died). Strigelius always complained bitterly about the publication of these acts. The first question disputed was: whether in regeneration, or the conversion of man to God, only qualities are changed without the creation of a new substance, or whether a new substance is created along with the qualities? The second concerned the manner of acting which God employs in the conversion of man. But the good man Strigelius later wrote that he had been dealing with a barbarian (for he was accustomed to put forth such crude and half-cooked expressions). Flacius died at Frankfurt on the Main in 1575.

units.la: Quomodo Melanthon, ita cum sequuti reliqui post ejus obitum V Vittembergenses Theologi, in Controversiâ Sacramentariâ moderationem vehementiae praeferendam censebant, & simpliciter dogma de corporis Christi ubiquitate rejiciebant, librisque ac Propositionibus nonnullis se in totâ doctrinâ magis Philippi, quam Lutheri, sententiam amplecti palam ostendebant. Scripserant inter alia anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxi. Catechismum, in quo ad interrogationem, de Coena Domini, quid sit, respondetur: Est communio corporis & sanguinis Domini nostri Iesu Christi, sicut in verbis Evangelii institua est: in quâ sumtione Filius Dei vere & substantialiter adest, & testatur se applicare credentibus sua beneficia. Ediderant quoque librum Germanicâ linguâ Grundfest / seu Fundamentum firmum VVittebergensium Theologorum, de persona & incarnatione Domini nostri Iesu Christi, contra novos Marcionitas, Samosatenianos, Arianos, Nestorianos, Eutychianos & Monothelitas in Flacianorum grege. Quae valde horum hominum bilem commoverunt. Neque negat Leonhartus Hutterus, V Vittembergensis Professor, illa nostrae esse sententiae, quando in libro adversus Hospinianum, de libro Concordiae cap. 11. de V Vittembergensibus Theologis, ut palam Calvinistis, & de ipsorum Catechismo, ita loquitur: de hoc Catechismo Hospinianus noster satis prolixe disserit, & flosculos ejus elegantiores, Calvinismo manifeste patrocinantes, recitat ac magnifice commendat. Quâ sane in parte posse sibi adversarios non habet. Nam ultro concedimus ipsum scatere erroribus Calvinisticis. Capite quarto inquit: à VVittebergensibus & nonnullis Lipsiensibus, per scripta hactenus ab ipsis edita, Calvinismum in Ecclesias & Scholas introductum fuisse. Cum V Vittembergensibus una stabant Lipsienses; verùm à pluribus passim oppugnabantur, à quibus accusati apud Electorem Augustum, instituto Dresdæ, quod Misniæ oppidum est, variorum Theologorum Conventu, ad a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxi. die x. Octobris, Consensus conscribitur, quo V Vittembergensium sententia & docendi modus probatur, adversus venenatos, uti loquuntur, Flaccianorum dogmata. De negotio Coenae sic se explicuerunt V Vittembergenses: firmiter credimus, praesentiam veri corporis & sanguinis in Coena (quam Lutherus, & horum regionum Doctores contra Papisticam Transsubstantiationem, & localem inclusionem in pane, Sacramentarium item errorem de vacuis, nudis, & inanibus signis, Visionem Sacramentalem vocarunt) ex verbis tantum Institutionis recte probari posse, ut sunt ab Evangelistis magnâ diligentiâ & consensu descripta; & ab Apostolo Paulo fideliter repetita ac declarata. Et hunc in sensum, sed frustra. Sacramentariorum errorem, de inanibus signis, multi, ut haberent scilicet quod improbare possent, rejecerunt: quod & nobis aeque tutum, ac aliis. Articulos autem de naturis Christi, earumque unione, salvis proprietatibus, de Christi adscensione, majestate & gloriâ, adversus corporis ejus ubiquitatem, rectè & plane expositerunt. Haec ergo quum non ex voto succederent Adversarii, supera itaque miscue-runt, quousque alio in Conventu, & Dresdensem consensum annullare, & talem modum formulamque docendi in Ecclesias introducere, quo & de VVittenbergensibus se plene vindicare, & securi esse adversus moderationem in articulo de Coena explicationem, possesent. Quem in finem obtinuere Conventum Torgæ unum, & alterum, & denique tertium in Coenobio Bergensi, prope Magdeburgum, quibus omnia animi sui vota ita tandem perficere, ut excogitata formulâ, quam falsò Concordiæ appellarunt, & corporalem Christi in Coenâ præsentiam, & naturæ ejus humanæ ubiquitatem, in canonem retulerint, atque eliminata moderatiore docendi ratione, & Philippi authoritate, librisque, præsertim Corpore Doctrinæ, damnatisque passim melius sentientibus, infinitis animis laqueum, Ecclesiis suis aliam & diversam formam, nobis ab ipsis dissentientibus aeternam ferè necessitatem hac ratione imposuerunt.
units.tr: Just as Melanchthon did, so the Wittenberg theologians who followed him after his death, in the sacramentarian controversy, judged that moderation should be preferred to vehemence, and they simply rejected the dogma of the ubiquity of Christ's body. In their books and certain propositions they openly showed that in their whole doctrine they embraced the opinion of Philip rather than of Luther. Among other things, in 1571 they had published a Catechism, in which, to the question what the Lord's Supper is, the answer is given: It is the communion of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, as it was instituted in the words of the Gospel; in this receiving the Son of God is truly and substantially present, and testifies that he applies his benefits to believers. They had also published a book in German, the Grundfest, or Firm Foundation of the Wittenberg Theologians, concerning the person and incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, against the new Marcionites, Samosatenes, Arians, Nestorians, Eutychians and Monothelites in the flock of the Flacians. These things greatly stirred the bile of these men. Leonhard Hutter, professor at Wittenberg, does not deny that these were in agreement with our opinion. In his book against Hospinian, on the Book of Concord, chapter 11, speaking of the Wittenberg theologians, and openly as to the Calvinists, he speaks thus about their Catechism: Our Hospinian discourses at considerable length on this Catechism, and recites and magnificently commends its more elegant flowers, which clearly favour Calvinism. In that part, indeed, he can have no adversaries; for we readily concede that it abounds in Calvinistic errors. In chapter 4 he says: that Calvinism was introduced into the churches and schools by the Wittenbergers and some Leipzig men, through the writings they have hitherto published. The Leipzig men stood together with the Wittenbergers, but they were attacked on all sides by many others. Accused by these before the Elector Augustus, a gathering of various theologians was held at Dresden, a town of Meissen, on 10 October 1571, and the Consensus was drawn up, by which the opinion and method of teaching of the Wittenbergers were approved against what they call the poisonous dogmas of the Flacians. The Wittenbergers explained their position on the matter of the Supper thus: We firmly believe that the presence of the true body and blood in the Supper (which Luther, and the teachers of these regions, against the Papistical transubstantiation and local inclusion in the bread, and likewise the sacramentarian error of empty, bare and inane signs, called a sacramental vision) can rightly be proved from the words of institution alone, as they have been described with great diligence and agreement by the Evangelists, and faithfully repeated and declared by the Apostle Paul. They took this sense, but in vain. Many rejected the sacramentarian error about empty signs, so that they might have something to condemn; and this was as safe for us as for others. But they expounded the articles on the natures of Christ and their union, with the properties preserved, and on Christ's ascension, majesty and glory, against the ubiquity of his body, rightly and plainly. Since these things did not turn out as the adversaries wished, they then used every means, until at another gathering, and at Torgau once, and a second time, and finally a third time in the Bergen monastery near Magdeburg, they brought it about that all the desires of their minds were at last fulfilled. They enacted into a canon the so-called formula, which they falsely named the Concord, and the bodily presence of Christ in the Supper and the ubiquity of his human nature. And, having eliminated the more moderate method of teaching and the authority of Philip, and having especially removed the Corpus Doctrinae and the many who thought better, they laid a snare for countless souls, and by this means imposed upon their churches another and different form, and upon us, who dissent from them, an almost eternal necessity.

units.la: Conventus Torgensis primus habitus fuit anno cIↄ Iↄ LXXIV. mense Majo, constituitque quindecim Theologis, inter quos Henricus Salmuth, Paulus Crellius, VVolfgangus Harderus, Daniel Greserus, Nic. Jagenteufel, Petrus Glaserus, & alii, vix noti homines, qui non audiis aliis egregiis præstantissimisque, & de Ecclesiâ optimè meritis viris, considerunt Formulam Concordiæ, ex quâ Bergensis dein data fuit, constantem articulis partim affirmativis, partim negativis, qui tum sententiam de Coenâ eruditorem, quod ad Christi corporis præsentiam continent, decem tribus, ne quid omitti videretur, comprehensum; tum Sacramentariorum (ut loquuntur), nominatim Zuinglii, Oecolampadii, Buceri, Calvini, Bezæ, Martyris, Heidelbergensium &c. errores scilicet acerbissimè damnant, ac rejiciunt, ut fanaticos nempe, furibundos, & quid non? configuratis hunc in finem articulis plus quam viginti. ne videlicet ulla rima in posterum superesset evadendi, quia ubique constricta haereret sententia & expositio quaevis melior, & qui in eam inter ipsos forte propendērent, his tendiculis mox caperentur. Hinc iam in V. Vittembergenses, aliosque Theologos passim, qui Torgensibus articulis, ut veritati, & authoritati doctrinae, Doctorumque hactenus in ipsorum Ecclesiâ celebratorum, & paci quàm maximè infensis, neque debito modo ordinēque compositis nollent subscribere, saevitum acriter. Ac primò V. Vittembergenses Theologi Torgam, ad articulorum subscriptionem evocati, postquam diu multisque restitissent, & varias tum pro Dresdensi Consensu nupero, tum adversus novitios hos articulos afferrent rationes, argumenta, obtestationes, spretis omnibus, captivi abducti fuerunt Torgâ Lipsiam: erant quatuor, Caspar Crucigër, Henricus Mollerus, Christophorus Pezelius, & Fridericus V. Videbramus, qui postmodum Heidelbergam vocatus, ibi obiit. Paulus Crellius primum, inde Georgius Major, ejus socer, Theologi item V. Vittembergenses, turpiter & causam, & Collegas deserebant. Neque in illos solos, quos dixi, ita saevitum, sed in plures, ob eandem causam, & veritatis professionem. Caspar Peucerus jam ante, mense Aprili, in carcerem abductus fuerat, ideo quod auctor haberetur librorum, quos antea diximus, à V. Vittembergensibus editos, & adversarios adeo commovisse. Erat hic gener Melanthonis, Medicinae in Academiâ V. Vittembergensi Professor, fidus semper Socero, & doctrinae ejus religiosus supra reliquos, uti oportuit, sectator. Quare ei, prae aliis, adscripta Academiae V. Vittembergensis in meliorem sententiam, id est, uti vulgo dicebant, Calvinismum mutatio; coque magis, quo in aulâ & Academiâ plurimum pollebat. Capita, ob quae accusatus, quatuor proferebantur. 1. Quod per conspirationes & practicas (ut loquuntur) conatus fuisse {I}nova sacramentaria dogmata in istas terras invehere, {II}quod ipse chartas de his, atque libellos sparsisset, {III}Ad istorum dogmatum defensionem animasset {IV}Theologos. Atque incitasset etiam exteros Theologos, adversus Ecclesiarum Saxonicarum Doctores, In quo nominatim tangebant Bezam, ejusque cum illo familiaritatem. Ad singula Peucerus respondit: sed nihil obtinuit; nisi ut mutato subinde carcere, decem continuos annos in squallore & miseria vitam traheret, non obstantibus quibuscunque pro se intercessionibus, ipsiusque adeo Imperatoris Maximiliani II. qui & usus apud Electorem hac ratione fuerat, dignissima Imperatore; eoque ob quem ab omnibus semper celebratus fuit, animo, Elec\-tore causam incarcerationis dante, quod vellet ministros secum idem sentire in religione: id quidem non perficies, inquit Imperator, neque nostrum est imperare conscientiis, aut ad fidem quempiam vi cogere. Liberatus tandem, mortua Electoris uxore Peucerus, sibi infensissima, ductaque ab illo Principis Anhaldini filia, hujus precibus fuit, cum jam esset aetatis LXII. anno MDLXXXVI; vixitque exinde in aula Anhaltina, usque ad extremum vitae, quod incidit in a. MDLXXVII. die xv. Septemb. Constantiam ejus ipse Elector Augustus praedicavit, quum declarationem postremam ad propositas ei quaestiones legisset, laudabatque egregium animum. Historiam carceris sui ipse conscripsit, quam ediderunt amici, anno post obitum ejus MDLXXXV. Praeter hunc alii fuerunt, quorum idem fatum, de quibus nunc non est dicendi locus.
units.tr: The first Torgau conference was held in May of the year 1574. It appointed fifteen theologians, among them Henricus Salmuth, Paulus Crellius, Wolfgang Harder, Daniel Greser, Nicolaus Jagenteufel, Petrus Glaser and others, men scarcely known, who considered the Formula of Concord, from which the Book of Bergen was afterwards issued, without listening to other eminent and distinguished men who had deserved well of the Church. It consisted of articles partly affirmative and partly negative. As far as they concern the presence of Christ's body, they comprise the teaching on the Supper in ten parts, so that nothing might seem to be left out. They also sharply condemned and rejected the errors of the Sacramentarians (as they call them), namely Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Bucer, Calvin, Beza, Martyr, the Heidelbergers and so on, as fanatics, madmen, and worse, with more than twenty articles drawn up for this purpose. The aim was that no crack should remain in the future through which to escape, since every better opinion and interpretation would be held fast in one fixed form, and any who inclined towards it among themselves would soon be caught in these snares. Hence they raged fiercely against the theologians of Wittenberg and others generally, who refused to subscribe the Torgau articles, since they were hostile to truth, to the authority of the doctrine and of the teachers hitherto celebrated in their own Church, and to peace, and were not composed in a proper manner and order. First, the theologians of Wittenberg were summoned to Torgau to subscribe the articles. After they had resisted for a long time and had put forward various arguments, reasons and entreaties, both for the recent Dresden Consensus and against these novel articles, all their objections were disregarded, and they were led away captive from Torgau to Leipzig. They were four: Caspar Cruciger, Heinrich Moller, Christoph Pezel, and Friedrich Widebram, who was afterwards called to Heidelberg and died there. Paul Crellius first, and then Georg Major, his father-in-law, also theologians of Wittenberg, shamefully deserted both the cause and their colleagues. And it was not only against those I have named that they raged, but against many others, for the same cause and the profession of truth. Caspar Peucer had already been taken to prison in April, because he was thought to be the author of the books which we mentioned earlier, published by the Wittenbergers, and which had so stirred the adversaries. He was the son-in-law of Melanchthon, a professor of medicine in the Academy of Wittenberg, always faithful to his father-in-law and, more than the others, a devoted follower of his teaching, as was fitting. For this reason he was, above others, blamed for the change of the Academy of Wittenberg to a better opinion, that is, as the common people said, to Calvinism; and all the more so because he had great influence at court and in the Academy. Four charges were brought against him: (1) that he had tried, by conspiracies and plots (as they call them), to introduce new Sacramentarian doctrines into these lands; (2) that he had himself scattered papers and pamphlets on these matters; (3) that he had encouraged the theologians to defend these doctrines; and (4) that he had also incited foreign theologians against the teachers of the Saxon Churches. In this charge they especially named Beza and his friendship with him. Peucer answered each point, but gained nothing, except that, his prison being changed from time to time, he spent ten unbroken years in squalor and misery. Neither the intercessions made on his behalf, nor those of the Emperor Maximilian II himself, who had acted in this way with the Elector, a conduct worthy of an emperor, and for which he was always praised by everyone for his spirit, could help him. The Elector gave the cause of the imprisonment as this: that he wished the ministers to think alike with him in religion. The Emperor said: "You will not achieve that; nor is it our business to rule consciences or to force anyone to faith by violence." At last Peucer was freed, after the death of the Elector's wife, who had been most hostile to him, and after he had married the daughter of the Anhalt prince, at her prayers, in the year 1586, when he was already sixty-two years old. From then on he lived at the court of Anhalt until the end of his life, which came on 15 September 1602. The Elector Augustus himself praised his constancy when he read the final declaration in answer to the questions put to him, and he praised his outstanding spirit. He wrote the history of his imprisonment himself, which his friends published in 1585, the year after his death. Besides him there were others with the same fate, of whom there is no place to speak now.

units.la: Alter Torgae Conventus habitus fuit a. MDLXXVI. Neque enim satis erat Flaccianis, primos illos Torgenses articulos tam affirmativos quam negativos concinnasse, nisi & dogma Ubiquitatis, quod in illis neglectum fuerat, throno collocassent, deturbata e contra authoritate & scriptis Melanthonis, ad quae alii idem provocabant; Hutterus cap. XI. in initio Iam mode multò suprà ostendimus Articulos Conventus primi Torgen- sis, licet christianis Calvinismi erroribus essent oppositi, non tamen plane omni imperfectione & impuritate caruisse. Neque enim tum temporis in lucem fuerant protracti errores, quibus Corpus Doctrinae Philippicum scatere postmodum evidentissimè demonstratum fuit. Hujus Conventus praesides fuere sex viri, Iacobus Andreas, Chemnitius, Selneccerus, Chytraeus, Musculus, Cornerus: qui librum Concordiae, ex primis illis Torgensibus articulis, aliisque inde additis construxerunt. Iacobus Andreas, fabri filius, unde cognomentum Schmidlein, interfuit quoque Colloquio VVormatiensi a. MDLVIII. & ad Colloquium Possiacenum missus a Christophoro, Duce VVittembergico, a. MDLXI. post factus fuit Academiae Tubingensis Cancellarius, & a VVittembergico Principe missus ad Colloquium Mompelgartense, cum Theodoro Beza, a. MDLXXXVI: denique colloquium Badenae habuit, cum Ioh. Pistorio Niddano Medico nostrae sententiae addicto, a. MDLXXXIX. post quod, anno sequente, obiit. Vir inquieti tumultuantisque ingenii, arrogantis magis quam docti, & qui haud leve lucrum familiae suae ex novis semper variisque tumultibus, quibus ut plurimum prae erat, attulit. Martinus Chemnitius vir bene doctus, Brunsvicensis Ecclesiae per triginta annos primum coadjutor, quomodo loquuntur, inde Superintendens; quamvis à variis interim expetitus fuerit Principibus, Electoribus, atque à Rege Daniae Friderico, Brunsvigae obiit a. MDLXXXVI. Nicolaus Selneccerus, Theologus Lipsiensis, cui imprimis cum Beza certamen fuit de corporis Christi ubiquitate, super loco Act. 111. 21. [illegible, ~12 letters] obiit Lipsiae a. MDXCII. David Chytraeus, vernacule Rostocke[?] quindecim annos natus, ut multi aetatem mirarentur, Magister artium Tubingae, postea etiam Theol. Doctor in VVittembergensi Academia factus, in Rostochiana docuit Academia, mortuus ibi-
units.tr: The second conference at Torgau was held in the year 1576. For the Flacians it was not enough to have drawn up those first Torgau articles, both affirmative and negative, unless they had also set up on the throne the doctrine of ubiquity, which had been neglected in them, and overthrown, on the other hand, the authority and writings of Melanchthon, to which others too appealed for the same purpose. Hutter, chapter 11, at the beginning: Now indeed we have shown at length that the articles of the first Torgau conference, although opposed to the Christian errors of Calvinism, did not however lack all imperfection and impurity. For at that time the errors had not yet been brought into the light, by which the Philippist corpus of doctrine was afterwards shown most clearly to be full of them. The presidents of this conference were six men: Jacob Andreae, Chemnitz, Selnecker, Chytraeus, Musculus and Cornerus. They built the Book of Concord out of those first Torgau articles and others added from them. Jacob Andreae, a smith's son, from which he got the surname Schmidlein, also took part in the Colloquy of Worms in 1558, and was sent by Christoph, Duke of Württemberg, to the Colloquy of Poissy in 1561. Afterwards he became chancellor of the University of Tübingen, and was sent by the Prince of Württemberg to the Colloquy of Montbéliard with Theodore Beza in 1586. Finally he held a colloquy at Baden with Johann Pistorius of Nidda, a physician who adhered to our opinion, in 1589. After this, he died in the following year. He was a man of restless and tumultuous mind, more arrogant than learned, and who brought no small profit to his family from the constant and varied disturbances over which he mostly presided. Martin Chemnitz, a well-learned man, was for thirty years first assistant, as they say, and then superintendent of the Church of Braunschweig. Although he was often sought after by various princes, electors, and by Frederick, King of Denmark, he died at Braunschweig in 1586. Nicolaus Selnecker, a theologian of Leipzig, had above all a dispute with Beza about the ubiquity of Christ's body, on the passage Acts 1. 21 [illegible]; he died at Leipzig in 1592. David Chytraeus, who, though a boy of fifteen, as many marvelled at his age, became Master of Arts at Tübingen, and later also Doctor of Theology at the University of Wittenberg, taught at the University of Rostock, where he died in 1600, a man well versed in history as well as in theology. He had been asked to draw up the book, or Torgau formula, as it was called, by those six men, for distribution to the others...

units.la: Act. 1. 21 is cited in the Greek; the Greek words are illegible on the scan. dem a. MDC[?] vir, præterquam in Theologiâ, in historiis benè versatus. Librum, seu formulam Torgensem, uti appellabatur, ab illis sexumviris compositam, ad alias per Germaniam Augustanæ Confessionis Ecclesias & Scholas, pro impetrandis omnium super eo judiciis & suffragiis, mitti placuit. Quare ab Electore missus aliis quaquaversum Electoribus, Principibus, Statibus, Academiis, & Scholis, varia, alia pro, alia adversus istum librum judicia & censuras rettulit. Quæ omnia iisdem illis libri, & doctrinæ Vbiquitatis sex conscriptis Patribus, in tertio Conventu Bergensi, in Monasterio, prope Magdeburgum a. MDLXXVII. die xi Maji, tradidit cognoscenda & examinanda, ut ex iis tandem prodiret formula Concordiæ, quæ sic vocatur, & sive à primis conventibus, sive ab hoc ultimo, jam Torgensis, jam Bergensis, appellata fuit. Inde subscripta à multis, ab aliis rejecta, tandem & edita, quamvis multis Augustanæ Confessionis reclamantibus, a. MDLXXX. Subscriptionem detrectarunt una cum Theologis suis & Ecclesiarum ministris, Lantgravii fratres: Princeps Bipontinus: Duces Pomeraniæ: Prussiæ Dux Albertus: Princeps Anhaldinus Joach. Ernestus: Dux Mechelburgensis: Duces Saxoniæ Lauwenbergensis: Comes Hanoviæ Philippus Ludovicus: Comites Nassovii, Iohannes, & Ludovicus V Witgensteinius; urbes Imperii, Magdeburgum, Francofurtum, Spira, V Vormatia: multiqué alii. Rex Daniæ librum Concordiæ regno suo inferri vetuit: eumque dono sibi missum à Sorore suâ, Electoris Saxoniæ conjuge, quamvis auro & holosericoe eximie obductum, in ignem abjecit. Atque adversus eum alii haud aliter animati fuere. Quos multæ movebant rationes, repudiata Augustana Confessio, à Melanthone recognita, quam sub nomine mutatæ odiose exagitabant; proscissa optimi Melanthonis fama, & scripta, approbatum novitium ubiquitatis corporis Christi commentum; da-mnaminatę (quippe damnandi pro improbandi, quâ Confessio usa fuerat, vocem, quamvis ingratiis Principum, adhibuerant) innumerae Ecclesiae, pii Martyres ab illis dissidentes, & quae ejusmodi tum Principes, tum Ecclesiae recusati assensus proferebant argumenta. Omitto Reformatarum Ecclesiarum, & Principum, adversus istum Discordiae librum protestationes: ubi non silenda imprimis Iohannis Casimiri, Comitis Palatini vigilantia, tum Theologorum ipsius scripta a. cI5 I5 Ixxxi. Admonitio Neostadiana, auctore Zacharia Vrsino, pro qua, sub nomine Studiosorum Neostadianorum prodiit Defensio, auctore Marco Beumlero Tigurino, adversus Erfurtensis Apologiae Sophismata, & cavillationes. Illc etiam Iohannes Casimirus causa fuit indicti Francofurtensis Conventus anno cI5 I5 Ixxv1 1. die xxv1. Septembris, nationalis fere omnium Ecclesiarum Reformatarum, ut quid adversus Librum Concordiae, & injustas sui in eo damnationes agendum foret, consulerent. Nam quod Hutterus paulim excipit, formulâ hac non damnatas fuisse exteras Ecclesias, sed tantum ordinem inter suos Theologos constitutum, illud utinam non factum fuisset: quidem non expresse dixerunt, se damnare exteras Ecclesias, verum damnare exteros Doctores, Zuinglium, Oecolampadium, Bezam, & reliquos, horumque doctrinam, & quicunque inter ipsos eam aliquâ ratione sequerentur: quod quid revera aliud fuit, quam exteras damnare Ecclesias? Delegati ad Conventum Francofurtensem venerunt Ecclesiarum Gallicarum, Polonicarum, Hungaricarum, Belgicarum, aliarumque: Bohemicae quoque, & Helveticae invitatae huc à Principe fuerant; sed per graves causas impeditae se voluerunt excusatas.
