Aderant Legati Reginae Angliae, Daniel Rogerius, qui conventum moderabatur, & Robertus Belus; praeter Consiliarios, & Ministros Casimiri Principis. Tria deliberandi fuerunt capita. 1. Quomodo impendens omnium Ecclesiarum exterarum condemnatio, quam Vbiquitarii novi sui Corporis doctrinae subscriptione quaererent; praveniri atque impediri posset? II. An expedia hoc tempore communem ac uniformem fidei Confessionem omnium Ecclesiarum nomine conscribere: Et si expediat, quâ potissimum methodo conscribi debeat? III. Quibus hoc scribendi provincia demandanda sit: & quâ ratione haec Confessio cum praedictis Ecclesiis communicari, & ab iisdem subscribi & comprobari possit? Ad primum caput, decreta fuit, institutaque Coetus nomine Legatio ad Electores & Principes Augustanae Confessionis, pro impediendis atque retundendis condemnationibus Ecclesiarum in Concordiae libro factis. Legationem istam obivit Paulus Knibbius J C. cui ad parandum ubique accessum juvandumque additus Reginae Angliae Legatus, Robertus Belus: nihil autem à Principibus, ad quos missi, praeter verba, retulerunt. Magnificus & perquam celebris iste Ecclesiarum nostrarum Conventus Francofurtensis fuit, cui interfuerunt praestantissimi viri, Vrsinus, Zanchius, Tossanus, Junius, Threcius, Languetus, Dathenus, alii: illudque de communi omnium Ecclesiarum & uniformi Confessione edenda, sic quidem plurimis visum (singulorum judicia videre est in Fragmento notularum Dathenii, ex Bibliotheca Ant. Tysii, exhibito à Cl. Ludovico Gerardo à Renesse, in Notis ad Epist. Apologeticam Belgicarum Ecclesiarum ad Auctores libri Bergensis), & conscriptio ejus demandata Vrsino, ac Zanchio; examen verò Gualthero, & Bezae; scriptaque & missa quoque ad Helvetios, sed postea tamen gravibus de causis opus suspensum intermissumque fuit. Videatur Hospinianus, in eximio opere, de Origine, & progressu libri Concordiae, cui apte titulum fecit: Concordia Discors. eique frustraneo conatu Leonhartus Hutterus, Theologus Vvittebergensis aliud ejusdem argumenti volumen oppositus, tit. Concordia Concors. Etiam Ecclesia Belgica seorsum, uti coepimus dicere, novo isti Libri Bergensis partui se opposuit, scripta ad Auctores illius, sex supra nominatos Theologos, quos & fratrum titulo passim honorant, epistola Apologetica a. cIↄ Iↄ lxix: quae Latine edita, Belgicè, & Germanicè. Ne Papistae dicant, quibus idem liber, & Vbiquitatis monstrosum commentum magno scandalo semper fuit. Inde libri & Disputationes Iesuitarum, aliorumque adversus corporis Christi ubiquitatem, Spertlingi, Busaei, Caspari Francki, Gregorii de Valentia, & Bellarmini Iudicium de libro Concordiae, quod subjunctum legitur ultimo Controversiarum ejus Tomo. Atque hic famosus liber Concordiae, cui titulus, Concordia. Pia & unanimi consensu repetita Confessio fidei & doctrina Electorum, Principum, & Ordinum Imperii, atque eorundem Theologorum, qui Augustanam Confessionem amplectuntur &c. comprehenditque, praeter Praefationem, subscriptam variis Electorum, Principum, Senatuumque nominibus, & tria vulgata Symbola, Apostolicum (ut dicitur), Nicaenum, Athanasianum; Confessionem Augustanam, juxta primam ejus editionem; cum ejusdem Apologia: Articulos Schmalcaldicos, Catechismum Lutheri utrumque, Minorem, & majorem: Epitomen articulorum, de quibus controversiae ortae sunt, inter Theologos Augustanae Confessionis, qui in Repetitione sequenti, secundum verbi Dei praescriptum, pie declarati sunt & conciliati: denique Solidam, planam (sic loquuntur) ac perspicuam Repetitionem, & declarationem quorundam articulorum Augustanae Confessionis, de quibus aliquandiu inter nonnullos Theologos eidem addictos disputatum fuit: continentem earum controversiarum ad normam & analogiam verbi Dei & compendiariam Christianae nostrae doctrinae formulam & rationem, decisionem atque conciliationem. Haec formula illa, & Concordia, vel variarum potius formularum συλλογή & farrago, ad quam Ecclesias & doctrinam, doctoresque suos, multo cum Reformationis opprobrio & detrimento, jam à multis annis xvc̄s. [illegible, ~3 letters]s illi inclementer adegerunt: in quo propterea schismatis Lutherani constituimus vim & complementum. Atque hactenus id egimus, ut rationem dissidii inter nos, atque Lutheranos, quod ad ortum suum & profectum, denique hanc ejus adultam αξιωσις explicaremus: sequitur, juxta ordinem initio praescriptum de syncretismo & unione cum iis, tum prout mista aliquoties, tum quousque inusuda forte adhuc videatur, aliquid ut hoc etiam in loco proferamus.
units.tr: dem in the year 1600 [?], a man well versed in histories, though not in theology. It was agreed to send the book, or formula, which was called the Torgau Book, composed by those six men, to the other Churches and schools of the Augsburg Confession throughout Germany, to obtain everyone's judgments and votes on it. Accordingly, the Elector sent it to the other electors, princes, estates, universities and schools in every direction, and brought back various judgments and censures, some for and some against that book. He handed all of these to the same six authors of the book and of the doctrine of ubiquity, at the third convention of Bergen, in the monastery near Magdeburg, on 11 May 1577, to be read and examined, so that from them there might at last emerge the formula of concord, as it is called; and it was named after Torgau or Bergen, according to the first or the last of these conventions. It was then subscribed by many, rejected by others, and at last published in 1580, though many protested against the Augsburg Confession. The brothers, the landgraves of Hesse, refused to subscribe it, together with their theologians and the ministers of their churches; so did the Prince of Zweibrücken, the Dukes of Pomerania, Duke Albert of Prussia, Prince Joachim Ernest of Anhalt, the Duke of Mecklenburg, the Dukes of Saxe-Lauenburg, Count Philip Louis of Hanau, the Counts of Nassau, John and Louis, and Louis V of Sayn-Wittgenstein; also the free cities of the Empire, Magdeburg, Frankfurt, Speyer and Worms, and many others. The King of Denmark forbade the Book of Concord to be brought into his kingdom, and when his sister, the wife of the Elector of Saxony, sent him a copy as a gift, although it was richly bound in gold and silk, he threw it into the fire. Others were moved against it in no different spirit. Many had their reasons: the Augsburg Confession, revised by Melanchthon, was rejected, and they harshly attacked it under the name of the "altered" Confession; the reputation and writings of the excellent Melanchthon were torn to pieces; the new fiction of the ubiquity of Christ's body was approved; the word "condemn" (used in place of "reject", which the Confession had employed, though against the wishes of the princes) was applied to countless Churches and to pious martyrs who dissented from them; and the princes and Churches who refused their assent put forward arguments of this kind. I pass over the protests of the Reformed Churches and princes against this book of discord, in which the vigilance of John Casimir, Count Palatine, must not be passed over, nor the writings of his theologians in 1581: the Admonitio Neostadiana, by Zacharias Ursinus, for which a Defence was published under the name of the students of Neustadt, by Marcus Beumler of Zurich, against the sophisms and cavils of the Erfurt Apology. John Casimir was also the cause of the Frankfurt convention, called in 1578 on 26 September, made up almost entirely of the Reformed Churches of the nation, to consider what ought to be done against the Book of Concord and its unjust condemnations of them. For as for what Hutter later maintains, that by this formula the foreign Churches were not condemned, but only an order was set up among its own theologians, would that it had not been so. Indeed they did not expressly say that they condemned the foreign Churches, but they condemned the foreign teachers, Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Beza and the rest, and their doctrine, and whoever followed it in any way among them. What was this in truth, other than condemning the foreign Churches? Delegates came to the Frankfurt convention from the Churches of France, Poland, Hungary, the Netherlands and elsewhere; the Bohemian and Helvetic Churches had also been invited there by the prince, but they asked to be excused on account of serious reasons. The legates of the Queen of England were present, Daniel Rogers, who presided over the convention, and Robert Beale; besides the councillors and ministers of Prince Casimir. Three heads were to be considered: (1) how the impending condemnation of all the foreign Churches, which the new ubiquitarians sought to secure by subscription to the doctrine of their new body, could be forestalled and prevented; (2) whether it was now expedient to draw up a common and uniform confession of faith in the name of all the Churches, and, if so, by what method it ought especially to be written; (3) to whom this task of writing should be entrusted, and by what means this confession could be communicated to the said Churches and be subscribed and approved by them. On the first head it was decided, and a delegation was set up in the name of the assembly, to the Electors and princes of the Augsburg Confession, to prevent and blunt the condemnations of the Churches made in the Book of Concord. Paul Knibbe, a jurist, undertook this embassy, and to help him gain access everywhere the legate of the Queen of England, Robert Beale, was added; but they brought back from the princes to whom they were sent nothing but words. That magnificent and very famous Frankfurt convention of our Churches was attended by most distinguished men: Ursinus, Zanzius, Tossanus, Junius, Threcius, Languet, Dathenus, and others. The proposal to publish a common and uniform confession for all the Churches seemed good to most, as one may see from the judgments of individuals in the fragment of Dathenus's notes, taken from the library of Antonius Thysius, published by the distinguished Ludwig Gerard of Renesse in his notes on the Apologetic Letter of the Belgic Churches to the authors of the Bergen book. The drafting of it was entrusted to Ursinus and Zanchius, and the examination to Gualtherus and Beza; it was written and also sent to the Swiss, but afterwards, for grave reasons, the work was suspended and dropped. See Hospinian, in his excellent work on the origin and progress of the Book of Concord, which he aptly titled Concord in Discord; and in vain Leonhard Hutter, theologian of Wittenberg, opposed to it another volume on the same subject, entitled Concord Agreeing. The Belgic Church, as we began to say, also set itself apart and opposed this new birth of the Bergen book, in its Apologetic Letter of 1569 written to the authors of that book, the six theologians named above, whom it everywhere honours with the title of brothers; this was published in Latin, and in Dutch and German. Lest the Papists say so, to whom this same book and the monstrous fiction of ubiquity have always been a great scandal: hence the books and disputations of the Jesuits and others against the ubiquity of Christ's body, of Sperling, Busaeus, Caspar Franck, Gregory of Valencia, and Bellarmine's judgment on the Book of Concord, which is appended at the end of the last volume of his Controversies. And this notorious Book of Concord, whose title is: Concord. A confession of faith and doctrine, repeated with pious and unanimous consent, of the Electors, Princes and Estates of the Empire, and of their theologians who embrace the Augsburg Confession, etc.; it contains, besides a preface signed in the names of various Electors, Princes and senates, and the three commonly circulated creeds, the Apostles' (as it is called), the Nicene, and the Athanasian; the Augsburg Confession, according to its first edition, together with its Apology; the Smalcald Articles; Luther's Catechism, both the Smaller and the Larger; an Epitome of the articles over which controversies arose among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, which in the following repetition were piously explained and reconciled according to the prescription of the Word of God; and finally a solid, plain (as they put it) and clear repetition and declaration of certain articles of the Augsburg Confession, over which for some time there was dispute among some theologians attached to it; containing a decision and reconciliation of those controversies according to the rule and analogy of the Word of God, and a compendious formula and account of our Christian doctrine. This formula, or rather this collection and medley of various formulas, which many years ago, to the great shame and loss of the Reformation, they harshly imposed on the Churches, their teachers and their doctors, is the very strength and completion of the Lutheran schism. So far we have worked to explain the cause of the division between us and the Lutherans, as to its origin and progress, and finally this its mature [ἀξίωσις] claim. It follows, according to the order prescribed at the beginning, to say something in this place also about syncretism and union with them: both how far they are sometimes mixed, and how far they may perhaps still seem unusual.

units.la: De quo quando agimus, antequam de aliis Lutheranorum nobiscum controversiis, vel hoc argumento est, intelligi syncretismum super dissensione de Cœna: non si alias praeterea afferant opiniones aut errores, de quibus ut in negotio Concordiae nunquam actum; ita nec quales sint hic interrogare, solummodo de dissidio Sacramentario componendo, in quo semper laboratum, loqui convenit. Neque dogma Ubiquitatis hic temere immiscendum, quod uti post natum, & pro articulo doctrinae assumtum, interque ipsos Lutheranos semper plurimos habuit obloquutores, nunquam etiam huic consilio ingestum fuit. Dicemus ergo, quid hoc in negotio syncretismi olim factum, quidquid fieri hodie, si non posset, at nostro quidem judicio oporteat. In quo promovendo prae aliis semper laborarunt Theologi Argentinenses, interque eos Bucerus, & Capito: ex Politicis, nullus majori ardore & constantia, quam Landgravius Hassiae, Philippus.
units.tr: When we come to this matter, before the other controversies between us and the Lutherans, it should be understood that syncretism here means agreement on the dissension about the Supper, and not on whatever other opinions or errors they may bring forward. Those other matters were never taken up in the business of the Concord, so it is not for us to ask what they are here. We should speak only of composing the sacramentary dispute, which was always the object of effort. Nor should the dogma of Ubiquity be rashly mixed in here. It came into being later and was adopted as an article of doctrine, and it always had very many opponents even among the Lutherans themselves. It was never pressed on this design. We shall therefore say what was done in the matter of syncretism in the past, and what ought to be done now, in our judgment, if it cannot be done. In promoting this, the Strasbourg theologians always laboured more than others, among them Bucer and Capito. Among the politicians, none showed greater zeal and steadfastness than Philip, Landgrave of Hesse.

units.la: Martinus Bucerus Selestadiensis, natus fuit anno MDXCI. & ex lectis primum Lutheri libris, inde familiaritate cum eo contracta Heidelbergae, denique eadem in Colloquio Wormatiensi renovata confirmataque, puriori Euangelii praedicationi (Ordinis Dominicani Monachus fuit) accessit, atque Argentorati docere coepit a. MDXXXI, ubi cum Collegis diligentem navavit operam in Ecclesiae istius a superstitionibus & corruptelis Papismi reformatione, tum dissidii Eucharistici, quod quantum damni ubique Reformationi adferret satis videbat, inter Lutherum Saxonicosque, & Helveticos aliosque Theologos, compositione. Cuius fini interfuit Colloquio Marpurgensi a. cIↄ Iↄ xxix. & V Vittembergensi a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxvi. quibus concordia inter dissidentes, conscriptis ejus aliquot articulis, sancita fuit.
units.tr: Martin Bucer of Sélestat was born in 1491. Having first read Luther's books, and then entering into friendship with him at Heidelberg, which was renewed and confirmed at the Colloquy of Worms, he turned to the purer preaching of the Gospel (he had been a monk of the Dominican Order). He began to teach at Strasbourg in 1531, where, together with his colleagues, he worked diligently for the reform of that Church from the superstitions and corruptions of Popery. He also worked for the composing of the Eucharistic dispute between Luther and the Saxons on one side and the Helvetic and other theologians on the other. He saw well how much harm this dispute did to the Reformation everywhere. He took part in the Colloquy of Marburg in 1529 and in the Wittenberg one in 1536, where concord was ratified between the disputing parties after some of its articles had been drawn up.

units.la: V Wolfgangus Fabritius Capito, Haganoae natus a. cIↄ cccclxxvii i.trium facultatum, Medicinae primum, tum Theologiae, denique & Iuris doctor factus, concinator primo Archiepiscopi Moguntini Alberti Cardinalis fuit, inde Argentoratum venit a. cIↄ Iↄ xxiii. cum Bucero: ubi Evangelii doctrinam haud segniter promovit, & Buceri in concordiae cum Lutheranis opere assiduus fuit Collega. Uxorem habuit Iohannis Oecolampadii viduam, deinde aliam. Obiit a. cIↄ Iↄ xli.
units.tr: Wolfgang Fabritius Capito was born at Haguenau in 1478. He became doctor of all three faculties: first of medicine, then of theology, and finally of law. At first he was a preacher to the Archbishop of Mainz, Cardinal Albert. From there he came to Strasbourg in 1523 with Bucer. There he promoted the doctrine of the Gospel no less vigorously, and he was Bucer's assiduous colleague in the work of concord with the Lutherans. He had as wife the widow of Johannes Oecolampadius, and afterwards another. He died in 1541.

units.la: Philippus Hassiae Landgravius indefessam ad combinandos utrimque animos collocavit operam, saepiusque hujus & illius partis evocavit ad se Theologos magis moderatos, hinc Bucerum imprimis, inde Melanthonem; autorque extitit primi Conventus Marpurgensis a. cIↄ Iↄ xxix. die 1. Octob. illum in finem habiti: ubi adfuerunt Lutherus, Melanthon, Iustus Ionas, Andreas Osiander, Brentius, Steph. Agricola: ex nostra parte Zuinglius, Oecolampadius, Bucerus, Hedio: & post privatum primo aliquod, tum publica Colloquia, tertio die consensu facta aliquot articulis, & consignatus fuit, uno solo excepto, de modo praesentiae Christi in Coenâ: subscripseruntque omnes, quos dixi. Decimusquartus, sive ultimus articulus de S. Coenâ ita habet: Credimus, & certo statuimus omnes de Cana Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quod utraque parte Coenae secundum institutionem utendum sit. Et quod Missa non sit opus, per quod vivis aut mortuis impetretur gratia: Quod etiam sacramentum altaris sit sacramentum veri Corporis & sanguinis Iesu Christi. Christi: Et quòd spirituali manducatione illius corporis & sanguinis, singulis Christianis praecipuè opus sit. Similiter, quòd usus sacramenti, perinde, ut verbum à Deo omnipotente, sit ordinatus, ut ad veram fidem & delectionem conscientia imbecillles moveantur per Spiritum sanctum. Et quamquam in eo, (An verum corpus & sanguis Christi corporaliter sit in pane & vino) hoc tempore nondum consensimus: Tamen utraque pars, quantum omninò ferre potest cujusque conscientia, caritatem mutuam praestare debet. Utraque etiam pars Deum omnipotentem sedulò invocare debet, ut per Spiritum suum nos in verâ sententiâ confirmare velit. Amen. De hoc Colloquio, Melanthon scripsit ad Camerarium: De congressu Marpurgensi non habeo, quod scribam. De aliis capitibus doctrinae Christianae omnibus convenit. Tantum controversia cana explicari non potuit. Leges capita, quae ibi composita sunt. Tantum triduanum colloquium fuit. Et adversarii leniores visi sunt, quàm fore arbitrabar. Reliqui omnes, praeter Lutherum, fuimus καὶ ἀσφαλῶς. Nam Lantgravius properavit dimittere conventum propter pestilentiam grassantem eo loco. Quo leniores nostri erant, eo durior Lutherus, qui ab initio congressus statim in mensâ, ad quam sedebant, majusculis litteris scripserat: hoc est corpus meum: scilicet ne ab illis abducerëtur. Demum Nostros pro fratribus, utcunque hoc Christianè & laudabiliter ambientes, id est, offerentes, docentesque, fratrum loco mutuo esse oportere, non ita orantes; quamvis, ut de hac re Bucerus scripsit, nos nihil paderet, etiam quemlibet in quo Christi aliquid appareat, precari, ut fratris locum apud se concederet, si ad hoc adprecari satis esset, agnoscere tamen noluit. Nihil autem hic de omnipraesentiâ corporis Christi, ob quam non in articulo de personâ Christi mutuò pleneque consensissent, agitatum. Argumento, quantopere à primâ quaestionum metâ nunc abicrint Adversarii, tum in illâ, tum in aliis contra nos arreptis contentionibus, ubi factâ summariâ articulorum fidei, & si quorum forte controversorum, dinumeratione, nihil extra plenam consensionem tum temporis superfuit, praeter unum illud de modo praesentiae Christi in S. Coena: de quo quae Lutheri sententia, & quomodo intelligenda, vel in quo puncto à nostra diversa, patuit ex voce corporalis, videlicet, an Christi corpus corporaliter esset in Coena.
units.tr: Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, applied tireless effort to bringing the minds of both sides together. He often summoned to himself the more moderate theologians of each party: from our side, Bucer above all; from theirs, Melanchthon. He was the author of the first Colloquy of Marburg, held for this purpose on 1 October 1529. There were present Luther, Melanchthon, Justus Jonas, Andreas Osiander, Brenz and Stephen Agricola; on our side Zwingli, Oecolampadius, Bucer and Hedio. After a private conference at first, and then public colloquies, on the third day agreement was reached on several articles, and these were signed by all those I have named, with one exception: the manner of Christ's presence in the Supper. The fourteenth and last article, on the Lord's Supper, reads thus: We believe and firmly hold, all of us, concerning the Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, that it is to be used by both parts according to the institution. And that the Mass is not a work by which grace is obtained for the living or the dead. Also that the sacrament of the altar is a sacrament of the true body and blood of Jesus Christ. And that a spiritual eating of that body and blood is especially necessary for each Christian. Likewise, that the use of the sacrament, just as the word, was ordained by Almighty God, so that the weak consciences may be moved to true faith and love by the Holy Spirit. And although in this matter (whether the true body and blood of Christ is corporeally in the bread and wine) we have not yet agreed at this time, nevertheless each party ought to show mutual charity, as far as each one's conscience can altogether bear. Each party also ought to invoke Almighty God diligently, that he may by his Spirit be willing to confirm us in the true opinion. Amen. Melanchthon wrote to Camerarius about this Colloquy: I have nothing to write about the Marburg meeting. We agreed on all the other heads of Christian doctrine. Only the controversy about the Supper could not be settled. You will read the heads that were drawn up there. It was only a colloquy of three days. And our opponents appeared milder than I had expected. All of us except Luther were both calm and secure. For the Landgrave hurried to dismiss the conference because of the plague raging in that place. The milder our side was, the harsher Luther was. From the beginning of the meeting he had at once written in large letters on the table at which they sat: This is my body, plainly so that he would not be drawn away from them. At last he asked our men, as brothers, though he sought this in a Christian and commendable way, that is, by offering and teaching, that they should be to him in the place of brothers in return, but not by begging. Yet, as Bucer wrote about this matter, we were unwilling to do anything, even to pray for anyone in whom anything of Christ appears, that he might grant us the place of a brother with him, if it were enough to ask for this. Nor was anything said here about the omnipresence of Christ's body, on account of which they had not fully agreed on the article concerning the person of Christ. This shows how far the opponents have withdrawn, from the first point of the questions, both in that dispute and in the others they have taken up against us. When a summary of the articles of faith, and of any disputed points that might arise, had been counted up, nothing beyond full agreement remained at that time, except that one point about the manner of Christ's presence in the Supper. What Luther's opinion was on this, and how it was to be understood, or at what point it differed from ours, became clear from the word corporeal, namely whether Christ's body is corporeally in the Supper.

units.la: Argentinenses Theologi praecipui auctores fuerunt instituti Conventus, Consensusque in hac causa secundi Wittembergensis, a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxv i. die xx i. Maji. Vbi & in eo, de quo solo in Marpurgensi Conventu dissentiebant, visa fuit inita esse concordia, scriptaque in haec verba communis formula, auctore Melanthone: Audivimus D. Bucerum explicantem suam sententiam de Sacramento corporis & sanguinis Christi, hoc modo: Confitentur juxta verba Irenaei, constare Eucharistiam duabus rebus, terrena & coelesti. Itaque sentiunt & docent, cum pane & vino, vere & substantialiter adesse, exhiberi & sumi, corpus Christi & sanguinem. Et quamquam negant fieri Transsubstantiationem, nec sentiunt fieri localem inclusionem in pane, aut durabilem aliquam conjunctionem extra usum Sacramenti, tamen concedunt Sacramentali unione (Panem esse corpus Christi / Corpus esse cum pane,) Hoc est, sentiunt perrecte pane simul adesse & vere exhiberi corpus Christi. Nam extra usum cum asservatur in pyxide, aut ostenditur in processionibus, ut sit à Papistis, sentiunt non adesse corpus Christi. Deinde hanc institutionem sentiunt valere in Ecclesia, nec pendere ex dignitate Ministri, aut sumentis. Quare sicut Paulus ait, etiam indignos manducare, ita sentiunt porrigi vere corpus & sanguinem Domini, etiam indignis. Et indignos sumere, ubi servantur verba & institutio Christi: Sed tales sumunt ad judicium, ut Paulus ait, quia abutuntur Sacramento, cum sine paenitentia & sine fide accedunt: Ideo enim propositum est, ut testetur illis applicari beneficia Christi, & fieri eos membra ChriChristi, & ablui sanguine Christi, qui agunt pænitentiam & erigunt se fide in Christum. Cum autem pauci convenerimus, & opus sit utrinque hanc rem ad alios concionatores & superiores referre, nondum licet nobis de concordia pacisci, priusquam ad alios retulerimus. Cum autem profiteantur omnes, se juxta confessionem & Apologiam Principum Evangelium profitentium, in omnibus articulis sentire & docere velle, maxime cupimus sarciri & constitui concordiam. Et spes est nobis, si reliqui utrinque ita consenserint, solidam futuram esse concordiam. Subscripserunt d.xx ix. Maji, à nostrâ quidem parte Capito, Bucerus, Frechtus, Ortherus, Gervas. Scholasticus, Joh. Bernhardi, Bonif. Lycosthenes, V. Volf. Musculus, Mart. Germani, Matthæus Aulberus, Joh. Schradinus, Argentinensis, Ulmensis, Eslingensis, Memmingensis, Francofurtensis, Augustanæ, Furfeldensis, Ruthlingensis Ecclesiarum Ministri: ab illâ parte Lutherus, Crucigerus, Bugenhagius, Melanthon, Menius, & Miconius. Hujus Formulæ vel Consensus, in quem coierunt, præcipuus auctor Bucerus fuit, cujus proinde nomen statim in limine occurrit. Probatum quidem variis fuit, quod à Bucero actum: quamvis alii maluissent non illis verbis conceptam formulam, quæ Adversariis plus æquo concedere videtur. Interim de omnibus inter illos conventum religionis articulis, nihilque se in nostris desiderare, sed sibi per omnia satisfactum, Lutherus palam fassus fuit. In Bucero vero multi haud satis probabant immoderatum passim concordandi studium, & hinc indulgentiam nimiam quâ largiebatur ea, quæ tradi Adversariis noluissent: unde eidem accidisse dixerunt, quod illis, qui præ nimia vini aviditate, etiam fæces hauriunt. Non ita ut alii, Capita Concordiæ VVittembergensis placuerunt Basiliensibus, & Helvetiis, qui sententiæ suæ expositionem pleniorem singulari scripto complexam Luthero transmiserunt. In quâ primo enarrant, quam acceptum sibi fuerit, quod Lu-thetherus ipsorum Confessionem, paulo ante scriptam missamque, per Bucerum & Capitonem, in se non improbaverit, sed bene acceperit: saltem Christianae concordiae, quam in Articulo de S. Cena omnes desiderent, promovendae causa, uberiorem declarationem postulaverit: quodque per Concordiae articulos, Confessioni & doctrinae Basiliensi nihil derogaretur, sed eosdem (haec ipsorum verba) fidei & Confessioni nostrae esse consentaneos, & non contrarios: sicque not in Articulorum sensu quantum ad summam, prorsus convenire. Quod quidem, promovendae concordiae causa, nobis pergratum est. Deinde expositā latius doctrinā de ministerio verbi, sacramentis, baptismo, & Coenā, rescripsit tandem illis Lutherus, d. 1. Decemb. a. clo Io xxxv i r. (quum illi ad eum scripsissent a. clo Io xxxv i. mense Novembri) litteris spiritu charitatis & concordiae, ut & invectiva in Stentores Concordiae inimicos, plenissimis. Neque ea mitius, meliusque tanquam, & magis deliberato ac composito animo hac de re ad Nostros scripserit, scio. Vbi haec ejus verba: Erunt enim tam apud vos, quam apud nos aliqui, quibus Concordia haec parum probabitur, sed suspecta erit. Sitamen nos utrinque, quibus illa cordi est, serio sedulóque instabimus: Clementissimus Deus & Pater utique gratiam suam dabit, ut & alii paululum mitescant, & aquae turbidae consident. Rogo itaque peramanter, V. P. hoc agat & curet serio, ut apud vos & vestrates clamosi illi, qui adversus nos & concordiam blaterant, a vociferationibus suis abstineant, ac populum simpliciter doceant. Praeterea hanc Concordiae causam commendet illis, qui ad talia vocati sunt atque idonei: nec eos impediat. Quemadmodum & nos hoc loco tum in scriptis, tum in concionibus tranquillitati studebimus, & ab invectivis in vestros abstinebimus: ne causam ullam Concordiae impediendae praebeamus: quippe quam, Deo teste, toto pectore videre exoptamus. Et laus sit Deo: dixicetum, declamatum hactenus satis plus satis, siquidem aliquid sic professi potuissel. Cum primis vero obnixe rogatos vos volo, ita de me existimetis tanquam de eo, cui res tota summe sit cordi quicque quantum omnino mearum erit virium, nihil eorum sit intermissurus, qua ad Concordiam promovendam pertinere buent. Novit id Deus, quem testem invoco super animam meam. Dissidium enim hoc nec mihi, nec cuiquam profuit: sed plurimum damni dedit: ex quo profecto nihil utilitatis vel commodi speravi potuit, vel etiamnum potest. Deinde ad singulos declaratæ confessionis articulos accedens: In primo inquit, de verbo prædicato, nihil prorsus habeo, quod desiderem. Similiter in articulo 11. de Baptismo nihil differentiæ observo. Tum de S. Cœnâ: Quod ad tertium articulum de Sacramento corporis & sanguinis Christi: non dum quoque docuimus, neque adhuc docemus, Christum è cælo vel à dextra Dei descendere vel ascendere, visibiliter vel invisibiliter. Firmiter tenemus articulum fidei: Ascendit in cælum: sedet ad dextram Dei: unde venturus est judicare, &c. Committimus divinæ omnipotentiæ, quomodo corpus & sanguis ejus in Cœnâ nobis præbeantur, quoties ipsius mandato convenitur, & institutio ejus celebratur. Nem mentionem facimus ullius ascensus vel descensus, qui fieret in Cœnâ: sed simpliciter tenemus verba ejus: Hoc est corpus meum, Hoc est sanguis meus. Verumtamen, si, quod prius dixi, non omnino satis recte mentem mutuo percipimus, hoc in præsens optimum sit, ut invicem amici simus, & optima queque mutuo de nobis invicem polliceamur, donec gluma & fæculenta aqua tandem subsidat. Poterunt hic & in reliquis omnibus D. Capito & Martinus Bucerus optime in medium consulere, modo pectora invicem componamus, ac simultates omnes facessere jubeamus, ut Spiritui sancto locus detur. Atque hoc fundamento iterum fundat concordiam, repetitque: Insuper ut dilectio & amicabilis Concordia inter nos perfecta vigeat, ex parte nostra nihil faciemus reliquum: cum primis ego, quantum ad me, omnem offensam penitus ex animo delebo, vobisque amorem & fidem omnem polliceor. Quantumvis enim nos, qui rem hanc serio agimus, summa queque egerimus, semper tamen auxilio De; Dei & consilio majore indigebimus; quandoquidem Satan summus noster & concordiae hostis, facile suos noverit invenire, per quos summa imis conturbet: ut nihil sit opus, nos diffidentiae vel suspicionibus invicem indulgere. Sed cum primis necessarium, ut corda simul & dextras mutuo porrigamus, ne posteriora fiant deteriora prioribus. Tantum sua tunc bene putavit interesse, ut concordia retineretur. Concludit, De excommunicatione seu clavibus non recordor, aliquando inter nos aliquid fuisse controversum. Forte apud vos rectius habet disciplina quam apud nos: neque in hoc capite, modo in caeteris plene conjuncti simus, volente Domino, laborabit Concordia. Amen. Utinam hic animus idem & constans Luthero semper adfuisset, sed & discipuli hanc potius Praeceptoris sui aemulati fuissent aequitatem ac concordiam, quam intemperiem saepius alias ostensam! Adeo distinguere debemus, quidquid ipsi in Melanthone, in Luthero nos, prout aliquando aurior fuit, vel mitior. Illius intervalla habuit magis crebra; hujus etiam nonnulla, praecipue ubi jam diximus. Responderunt ad illas etiam Lutheri litteras Helvetii, a. cIↄ Iↄ XXXVIII. d. IV. Maji, atque in fine dicunt: Ex his omnibus non possumus aliud perspicere aut sentire, quam inter nos (Deo sit laus) de sensu aut vera substantia hujus articuli unanimem esse consensum, pacemque optimam inter nos sine ulla amplius controversia coaluisse, Deumque ad hanc veram concordiam nos suo auxilio adduxisse, cui nos eam ob rem maximas laudes & gratias agimus in aeternum. Atque ita tum concordia inter Lutherum, ac Tigurinos tandem coaluit: utinam vero firma semper & constans fuisset! Bene Melanthon, in ep. ad Vitum Theodorum: Ego ne longissime recederem a veteribus, posui in usu sacramentalem praesentiam, & dixi datis his rebus, Christum vere adesse, & efficacem esse. Id profecto satis est. Nec addidi inclusionem, aut conjunctionem talem, qua affigeretur τῳ ἀγίῳ τὸ σῶμα, aut ferruminaretur, aut misceretur. Sacramenta pacta sunt, ut rebus sumtis adsit aliud.
units.tr: The chief authors of the Strasbourg conference and the consensus in this matter were the theologians of the second Wittenberg meeting, on 22 May 1535. There, on the one point on which they had disagreed at the Marburg conference, they seemed to have reached agreement, and they set down the following common formula, composed by Melanchthon: We have heard Dr. Bucer explain his opinion concerning the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ, in this way: they confess, following the words of Irenaeus, that the Eucharist consists of two things, earthly and heavenly. Therefore they feel and teach that, together with the bread and wine, the body and blood of Christ are truly and substantially present, offered and received. And although they deny that transubstantiation takes place, and do not think that there is a local enclosure in the bread, or any lasting union outside the use of the sacrament, yet they grant a sacramental union (the bread is the body of Christ / the body is with the bread). That is, they hold that the bread is truly present together with the body of Christ, and that the body is truly offered. For outside the use, when it is kept in a pyx, or displayed in processions, as the Papists do, they hold that the body of Christ is not present. Further, they hold that this institution remains valid in the Church and does not depend on the worthiness of the minister or of the recipient. Therefore, just as Paul says that even the unworthy eat, so they hold that the body and blood of the Lord are truly offered even to the unworthy. And the unworthy receive, where the words and institution of Christ are retained; but such people receive to their judgment, as Paul says, because they abuse the sacrament when they come without repentance and without faith. For it is intended, so that it may witness that the benefits of Christ are applied to them, and that they become members of Christ and are washed in the blood of Christ, for those who repent and raise themselves up by faith in Christ. But since few of us have met, and it is necessary on both sides to refer this matter to other preachers and superiors, we are not yet permitted to make an agreement before we have referred it to others. Yet since all profess that, according to the Confession and Apology of the princes who profess the Gospel, they wish to hold and teach in all the articles, we most earnestly desire that the concord be mended and established. And we hope that, if the others on both sides agree in this way, the concord will be solid. They signed on 29 May: on our side Capito, Bucer, Frecht, Ortherus, Gervasius Scholasticus, Johann Bernhardi, Boniface Lycosthenes, V. Volf, Musculus, Martin Germanus, Matthaeus Aulber, Johann Schradin, the ministers of the churches of Strasbourg, Ulm, Esslingen, Memmingen, Frankfurt, Augsburg, Furfeld and Ruthlingen; on the other side Luther, Crucigerus, Bugenhagen, Melanchthon, Menius and Myconius. The chief author of this formula or consensus, into which they came together, was Bucer, whose name therefore appears at once on the threshold. Indeed, what Bucer did was approved by many, although some would have preferred that the formula had not been worded in those terms, since it seems to concede more than is fair to the adversaries. Meanwhile Luther openly confessed that, concerning all the articles of religion agreed among them, he wanted nothing further in ours, but was completely satisfied. But many did not much approve of Bucer's immoderate eagerness to reach agreement everywhere, and of the excessive indulgence with which he yielded things that they would not have wished handed over to the adversaries; so they said that he had come to the state of those who, from excessive greed for wine, drink even the dregs. It was otherwise with the Confession of Wittenberg concord, which pleased the Basel and Swiss churches, who sent Luther a fuller exposition of their opinion, set out in a separate writing. In it they first describe how welcome it was to them that Luther had not disapproved of their Confession, written and sent shortly before through Bucer and Capito, but had received it kindly; at least he had asked, for the sake of promoting Christian concord, which everyone desires in the article on the Lord's Supper, for a fuller declaration; and that through the articles of concord nothing was taken away from the Basel Confession and doctrine, but that these articles (their own words) were consonant with our faith and Confession, and not contrary to them; and so they agreed entirely in the sum of the articles' meaning. This indeed was most welcome to us, for the sake of promoting concord. Then, after the doctrine concerning the ministry of the Word, the sacraments, baptism and the Supper had been set out more fully, Luther at last wrote back to them on 1 December 1535 (since they had written to him in November 1535), in letters most full of the spirit of charity and concord, as well as with an invective against the trumpeters of discord. I know that he did not write about this to our people more mildly and better, and with a more deliberate and composed mind. His words there are these: For there will be some both among you and among us to whom this concord will hardly be pleasing, but it will be suspect. Yet let us on both sides, who have this at heart, press on earnestly and diligently: the most merciful God and Father will surely give his grace, so that others also may grow a little milder, and the troubled waters may settle. I therefore ask most lovingly, Your Reverence, that you take care and see to it earnestly, that among you and your fellow countrymen those clamorous men who babble against us and against concord may refrain from their outcries, and simply teach the people. Moreover, commend this cause of concord to those who have been called and are fit for such things, and do not hinder them. Just as we too in this place will strive for tranquillity, both in writings and in sermons, and will refrain from invectives against yours, so as not to give any cause for hindering concord, which, God is my witness, we desire with all our heart to see. And let praise be to God: we have said and declaimed enough, more than enough, if we could have professed anything of the kind. Above all, I earnestly want you to think of me as one to whom this whole matter is especially dear, and who, as far as his strength extends, will omit nothing that pertains to promoting concord. God knows this, whom I call as witness upon my soul. For this discord has profited neither me nor anyone else, but has done the greatest harm; from it I could truly have hoped for no advantage or benefit, and I cannot hope for any even now. Then, approaching the individual articles of the declared Confession, he says: In the first, he says, concerning the preached word, I have absolutely nothing that I want. Likewise, in the eleventh article on baptism I see no difference. Then concerning the Lord's Supper: As for the third article on the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ: we have not yet taught, nor do we yet teach, that Christ descends or ascends from heaven, or from the right hand of God, visibly or invisibly. We firmly hold the article of faith: he ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God, from whence he will come to judge, etc. We commit to the divine omnipotence the question of how his body and blood are offered to us in the Supper, whenever we assemble at his command and his institution is celebrated. We make no mention of any ascent or descent that takes place in the Supper; but we simply hold to his words: This is my body, This is my blood. Yet if, as I said before, we do not perceive each other's mind altogether rightly, then for the present it is best that we be friends with one another, and promise each other every good thing, until the sediment and muddy water finally settle. Here, and in all the rest, Dr. Capito and Martin Bucer can very well act as mediators, provided we settle our hearts with one another and bid all enmities depart, so that place may be given to the Holy Spirit. On this foundation he again establishes concord, and repeats: Moreover, so that love and friendly concord may flourish perfectly among us, on our part we will leave nothing undone: above all I, as far as I am concerned, will utterly wipe out every offence from my heart, and I promise you all love and faithfulness. For however much we who handle this matter earnestly have done our utmost, we shall always need the help of God and a greater counsel; since Satan, our chief enemy and the enemy of concord, will easily find those through whom he may throw the highest things into confusion, so that there is no need for us to indulge in distrust or suspicions toward one another. But above all it is necessary that we stretch out to one another both hearts and right hands, lest the latter things become worse than the former. So much did he then think it mattered that concord be kept. He concludes: Concerning excommunication, or the keys, I do not recall that anything was ever disputed between us. Perhaps discipline stands more rightly with you than with us; and in this chapter, provided we are fully united in the rest, by the Lord's will, concord will not suffer. Amen. Would that this same spirit had always remained constant in Luther! Would that his disciples had rather imitated this fairness and concord of their teacher, than the intemperance shown so often on other occasions! So we must distinguish, concerning Melanchthon, and concerning Luther, what in each we attribute to him, as at times he was harsher or milder. He had more frequent intervals of the latter; and some of them in the case of this man too, especially where we have just now spoken. The Swiss also answered Luther's letters, on 4 May 1538, and at the end they say: From all these things we can perceive and feel nothing other than that among us (God be praised) there is unanimous agreement concerning the sense and true substance of this article, and that the best peace has been formed between us without any further controversy, and that God has brought us to this true concord by his help, for which we give the greatest praises and thanks to him for ever. And so at that time concord between Luther and the Zurich churches was at last formed: would that it had always been firm and constant! Melanchthon well, in his letter to Vitus Theodorus: I, so as not to depart very far from the ancients, have set forth the sacramental presence in use, and I have said that, with these things given, Christ is truly present and effective. This is surely enough. Nor have I added any enclosure or such a union, by which the body would be fastened to the holy thing, or welded, or mixed. The sacraments were so arranged that, when the things are taken, something else is present.

units.la: Quod autem de Buceri lenitate, ac indulgentia diximus, ea nec Martyri usquequaque probata: quare nec illius in docendo formulæ dubiæ, obscuræ, & ad aures Adversariorum compositæ magis, quam ad so-liditatem doctrinæ, adsensit. quod tum Argentorati ostendit, quando ibi primum cum Bucero docere incæpit, sed cujus methodum in formulis illiusmodi laxis non sectabatur, tum in Anglia, ubi Martyr Oxonii, Bucerus Cantabrigiæ agebat. atque hic in thesês à Martyre disputatas, inter quas secunda erat: Corpus & sanguis Christi non est carnaliter aut corporaliter in pane & vi-no, nec ut alii dicunt, sub speciebus panis & vini, iltam appositi Censuram, quod optasset thesim sic expressam: Corpus Christi non continetur localiter in pane & vino: nec iis rebus affixum aut adjunctum est, ulla mundi regione. Scilicet ut isto loquendi modo declinaret Lutheranorum sententiam, non refutaret. Hoc cum tempore etiam Calvinus abusque Genevâ monuit, ut magis perspicue de Cœnâ Domini scriberet, ac loqueretur. Et reversò ex Angliâ Petro Martyre Argentoratum, ubi ei proponebatur Concordiæ Vvittembergensis formula, à Bucero cum Luthero inita, subscribere abnuit, quia per conscientiam (dicebat) largiri nequiret destitutos verâ fide, percipiendo sacramenta, corpus Christi sumere. Ex adverso Lutherani Bucerum pro suo habere ausi. Vide Ministros Comitatus Mansfeldici, in Scripto a. cIↄ Iↄ Ixv. adversus Eberum. Quæ res ita sollicitos multorum animos tenuit de Bucero, ut identidem monerent, caveret, ne nimium tribuendo Adversariis, vel veritatem pro mundi captu astutius hinc inde flectendo, inconstantiæ notam sibi inureret; uti ad illum scripsit Georgius, Comes VVurtembergicus anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxv. Similiaque ad eundem aliquoties V Volfgangus Musculus. Vide Annales Sculteti, part. II. p. 343. 387. ubi ad Bucerum Musculus: Urbem Regii factum multis etiam suorum scandalo est. Ejus exemplo tibi etiam multum timeo &c. & p. 398. 413. In historia, sive Curriculo vitae suae narrat, Bullingerum dixisse Dan. Tossano: Mi D: Tossane, tu incides in multos qui de concordia VVittembergica loquuntur: narro igitur tibi, quid à Petro Martyre ego, & Simlerus, & quod Martyr à Bucero in Anglia audierit. Bucerus, ajebat Martyr, dixit, se poenas dare quod causam publicam homo privatus voluisset componere, & tam multa prava dogmata conciliare. Professus est etiam Martyr, se nunquam in illam concordiam conspirasse. Et pag. 39. totum illud Buceri negotium à capite arcessens, scribit, cum à Tigurinis ad Capellas infeliciter pugnatum esset, & Zuinglius cum multis egregiis viris occubuisset, eâque clade, quod paulo ante inter aliquot Helvetiae Civitates, & Argentinam, atque Hassorum Principes coiërat foedus dissolutum esset; Martinum Bucerum Theologum Argentinensem timidiusculum totam can-tam simul periturum putasse, nisi superioris Germaniae Civitates, & imprimis Argentinam suam alicujus novi foederis praesidio munivet. Utroque igitur oculo illum respexisse ad potentissimum Saxoniae Principem, quem ut facilius ad foedus pelliceret, omnibus conatum esse persuadere, Zuinglii & Lutheri sententiam, de Coena Domini, eandem fuisse, sed eos propter λογομαχίαν non potuisse convenire: praestare autem cum Luthero loqui, quàm cum Oecolampadio & Zuinglio, quod ille sublimius, isti humilius de causa ista locuti essent. Quod Bucerus etiam persuaserat Johanni Calvino viro juveni, & Controversiarum Germanicarum ignaro, qua tum temporis ex Gallia Argentinam venerat. Hinc in Germania superiori phrases Bucero-Lutheranae post infelicem praesertim Concordiam VVittembergensem frequenter usurpatas; resque eo devenit, ut demortuis Theologis, quibus Buceriana conciliationis causa nota fuerat, Ulma, Augusta, Memmınga, Lindavia, Argentina denique pro Zuingliana doctrina Lutheranam, & Ubiquitatem tandem ipsam, amplexarentur. ut non immerito scribat Rudolphus Gualterus, Epistolā quādam ad Illustrem Comitem Ludovicum VVitgensteinium seniorem, Bucerum; si hodie viveret, ne ab Argentinā quidem suā agnitum & admissum iri.
units.tr: As for what we said about Bucer's mildness and indulgence, Martyr did not wholly approve of it either. So he did not assent to Bucer's teaching by formulas that were doubtful and obscure, and framed more to suit the ears of opponents than to the solidity of doctrine. He showed this at Strasbourg, when he first began to teach there alongside Bucer, for he did not follow Bucer's habit of lax formulas of this kind. He showed it again in England, where Martyr taught at Oxford and Bucer at Cambridge. Here, in the theses disputed by Martyr, the second of which was: The body and blood of Christ are not in the bread and wine carnally or corporeally, nor, as others say, under the species of bread and wine, he was censured for having preferred the thesis to be expressed thus: The body of Christ is not contained locally in bread and wine, nor is it fixed to or joined with those things in any region of the world. Clearly, by this way of speaking, he was avoiding the Lutheran opinion rather than refuting it. At about the same time Calvin, from far-off Geneva, advised him to write and speak more plainly about the Lord's Supper. When Peter Martyr returned from England to Strasbourg, the formula of the Wittenberg Concord, agreed by Bucer with Luther, was put before him for signature, and he refused to subscribe. He said that in conscience he could not give the body of Christ to those destitute of true faith when they received the sacraments. The Lutherans, on the other hand, dared to claim Bucer as their own. See the ministers of the County of Mansfeld in their writing of 1565 against Eber. This matter troubled the minds of many people about Bucer so much that they repeatedly warned him to take care lest, by yielding too much to his adversaries, or by bending the truth this way and that more craftily to suit the world's taste, he brand himself with the mark of inconstancy. So wrote Georg, Count of Württemberg, to him in 1535. Wolfgang Musculus wrote similar things to him several times. See Scultetus's Annals, part II, pp. 343, 387, where Musculus writes to Bucer: The city's turning royalist has been a scandal to many of your own people. I greatly fear, following its example, for you too, etc. and pp. 398, 413. In his history, or account of his life, Bullinger is reported to have said to Daniel Tossanus: My dear Tossanus, you will fall in with many who talk about the Wittenberg concord. So I will tell you what I, and Simler, heard from Peter Martyr, and what Martyr heard from Bucer in England. Bucer, Martyr said, declared that he was paying the penalty for being a private man who wanted to settle a public cause and reconcile so many wicked doctrines. Martyr also professed that he had never agreed to that concord. And on p. 39, tracing the whole affair of Bucer from its source, he writes that when the Zurich men had fought unsuccessfully at Kappel, and Zwingli had fallen with many outstanding men, and by that disaster the covenant that a little earlier had been made among several Swiss cities, Strasbourg, and the princes of Hesse had been dissolved, the rather timid Strasbourg theologian Martin Bucer thought that the whole cause would perish together unless the cities of upper Germany, and especially his Strasbourg, fortified themselves with the protection of some new covenant. He therefore looked with both eyes to the most powerful prince of Saxony, and tried by every means to win him over to a covenant more easily, persuading him that the views of Zwingli and Luther on the Lord's Supper were the same, but that they could not agree because of a war of words; and that it was better to speak with Luther than with Oecolampadius and Zwingli, because the former had spoken of this matter more loftily and the latter more humbly. Bucer had persuaded this also to John Calvin, a young man ignorant of the German controversies, who had then come to Strasbourg from France. Hence in upper Germany the Bucero-Lutheran phrases were frequently used, especially after the unhappy Wittenberg Concord, and matters came to such a pass that, after the theologians who knew the purpose of Bucer's reconciliation had died, Ulm, Augsburg, Memmingen, Lindau, and finally Strasbourg itself embraced the Lutheran doctrine, and even ubiquity, in place of the Zwinglian. Rudolf Gwalther rightly writes, in a letter to the illustrious Count Ludwig of Wittgenstein the elder, that Bucer, if he were alive today, would not be acknowledged and admitted even in his own Strasbourg.

units.la: Illa quae hactenus de syncretismo Lutheranorum diximus, viventibus dissensionis auctoribus contigerunt, videlicet Consensus Marpurgensis primum, tum VVittembergensis: post illos e medio sublatos, non defuere etiam qui huic operi eximiam navarunt operam; ut divulsae ecclesiae in concordiam vel tolerantiam mutuam coirent. Vnionem dicimus Ecclesiasticam, inter Ecclesias dissidentes, & ab Ecclesiasticis, peculiaribus huc institutis conventibus, conclusam; ubi post duas praecedentes Marpurgensem, & VVittembergensem, tertia secuta, nobisque consideranda venit, post mortem antesignanorum inita, Sendomiriensis in Poloniā, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxx. die xiv. Aprilis: ubi trium Confessionum in Poloniā utrāque, & magno Ducatu Lithuaniae socii; Bohemicae, Augustanae, & Helveticae, adversus Ebionitas, & Anabaptistas, Consensum piè feliciterque hunc in modum stabiliverunt, quod ad articulum de S. Coenā: Deinde vero, quantum ad infelix illud dissidium de Caena Domini attinet: convenimus in sententiā verborum Domini nostri Iesu Christi, ut illa orthodoxè intellecta sint à Patribus, & inprimis Irenaeo: qui duabus rebus scili-cet terrena & caelesti hoc mysterium constare dixit. Neque elementa signaeve nuda & vacua illa esse asserimus, sed simul re ipsā credentibus exhibere & praestare fide quod significant. Denique ut expressius clariusque loquamur, convenimus, ut credamus & confiteamur, substantialem praesentiam Christi non significari duntaxat, sed verè in Caenā eo vescentibus repraesentari, distribui & exhi-beri corpus & sanguinem Domini symbolis adjectis ipsi rei minimè nudis, secundum Sacramentorum naturam. Quae mutui consensi s ratio hactenus omnium optima est, ut junctis, invicemque approbatis Ecclesiarum Confessionibus, vel formula alia omittatur, vel talis constituatur, ac haec, quae ex V Vittembergensi quidem aliqua retinet, sed ubi cardo difficultatis haeret, accuratior illa est, substantialem praesentiam Christi in Coena statuens quidem, non autem corporis, quamvis hoc etiam exhibeatur, sumaturque in symbolis, a credentibus, per fidem: in usu instituto in hac communione vere et substantialiter adesse Christum, et vere exhiberi sumentibus corpus et sanguinem Christi. Quae omnia melius sonant, quam quae in formula V Vittembergensi: vere et substantialiter adesse corpus Christi: Et, porrigi vere corpus et sanguinem Domini, etiam indignis. Atque isto modo in hac placita consensum Sendomiriae, ut missis debinc omnibus odiis, insectationibus, rixis, pro fratribus se mutuo agnoscerent, suasque invicem ecclesias pro orthodoxis: in quo supra Marpurgensem consensum progressi fuerunt: convenimusque, ut quemadmodum illi nos, nostrasque Ecclesias, et confessionem nostram, in hac synodo publicatam, et Fratrum orthodoxas esse testantur: sic etiam nos illarum Ecclesias eadem Christiano amore prosequamur, et orthodoxas faciemur: extremumque Vale dicamus, et altum silentium imponamus omnibus rixis, distractionibus, dissidiis, quibus Evangelii cursus, non sine maxima multorum piorum offensione, impeditus est: et unde adversariis nostris non leve calumniandi, et vere Christianae Religioni nostrae contradicendi occasio fiat subministrata: quin potius pacî et tranquillitati publicae studere, charitatem mutuam exercere, et operas mutuas ad aedificationem Ecclesiae pro fraterna conjunctione nostra praestare debemus. Quinimo pro uno fere Ecclesiarum corpore haberi hinc omnes voluerunt, & ad generales Synodos ex aequo vocari, & convenire: Quamobrem consilia officiare mutua inter nos conferre, et in posterum de conservatione et juramento omnium totius Regni, Lithuaniae, Samogitiae piarum orthodoxarum et reformatarum Ecclesiarum, tanquam de de uno corpore consulere politicis sumus, ac receptimus. Et si quando Synodos generales celebrabunt, nobis quoque significent: & ad nostras etiam generales vocati non gravatim veniant, si opus fuerit. Hęc autem Ecclesiarum unio præstantissima haberi merito debet, ad cujus exemplar se alias componere, omnesque illud sequi æquum sit, & laudabile. Adeoque facilis, ne dicam possibilis, Ecclesiarum nostrarum coitio, quando in probos, modestos, & orthodoxiæ studiosos viros ejus instituendæ eadem consilium Consensum Sendomiriensem eodem anno confirmarunt solemniter in Synodo Posnaniensi: ubi utraque pars, primum Ministri, Patroni, & tota Ecclesia Consessionis Bohemicæ, Poloni, & Germani, utriusque sexus homines, ex templo suo progressi in templum Augustanæ Confessionis, concionem matutinam habuerunt Ministri Fratrum Bohemorum, alter Polonicè, alter Germanicè; à meridie vicissim Augustanæ Consessionis Cœtus processit ad templum fratrum Bohemicorum, & hic Augustanæ Confessionis Ministri, unus iterum Polonis, alter Germanis, concionem habuerunt; atque prælectis utrobique populo consensus, in quem omnes unanimiter concesserunt, sacaque per Ministros ad mutuam concordiam & pacem adhortatione seriâ, maximâ eorum lætitiâ & applausu occentum illud: ecce quam bonum & quam jucundum fratres habitare in unum. Quis obsecro, tantillum modo spiritus Christiani habens, hoc opus non probet, non laudet, & ad animum suum rediens, non exultet pariter in tam sancta concordiâ, quæ ut grata cœlo, ita quod invisa potuerit esse hominibus aliis, quis crederet, nisi hoc Vilnenses Lutherani suo facto, in Synodo a. 1578 probassent, atque improbâ facti hujus commendatione Leonhardus, vel Leominus Hütterus, in scripto suo adversus Panei Irenicum, vere litigioso, & furibundo magis, quam Theologico, cap. XVI confirmaret: sed sibi interim, in illa ... [illegible, ~10 letters] rationali Synodo Sendomiriensi consensum inter Evangelicos initum, & in Synodo Toruniensi quoque confirmatum fuisse a. cIↄ Iↄ xcv. Sic est, postquam in nationali Sendomiriensi Synodo consensus factus, eodem anno die xx Maii, in Synodo provinciali Posnaniensi solemniter illè confirmatus fuit: repetitus in nationali Synodo Cracoviensi, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxiii. d. xxix Septemb. & obsignatus cum exitu Synodi, sacrâ Synaxi ab omnibus trium Ecclesiarum praesentibus Ministris, & delegatis unanimiter celebratâ, juxta ritum Cracoviensis Ecclesiæ. Idemque factum in Synodo Petricoviensi, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxv. die 1. Iunii, & Vlodislaviensi, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxiii. die xxx. Iunii, atque Toruniensi, a. cIↄ Iↄ xcv. die xx Augusti. Denique in nupero Toruniensi Colloquio, a. cIↄ Iↄ cxlv. d. 1. Septemb. Reformati in generali fidei suæ Confessione Sendomiriensem suam, id est, Helveticam, ibidem lingua Polonicâ explicatam conscriptam Confessionem probarunt iterum confirmarunque oblatam antea Sigismundo I. in Comitiis Varsaviensibus a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxii, eique dedicatam postea, quum ederetur a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxiv. & Stephano Regi exhibitam, in Comitiis a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxvii. quæ diligenter considerata, Rex Noster publicum religionis exercitium Cracoviæ concessit. Consensus ille Sendomiriensis a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxv. Torunii primò, lingua LatinoPolonicâ, ex decreto Synodico in lucem datus, feliciter recusus iterum a. cIↄ Iↄ xcii. & a. cIↄ Iↄ xcvi. Heidelbergæ a. cIↄ Iↄ c v. atque pridem utroque idiomate a. cIↄ Iↄ cxxviii. Factâ Sendomiriensi consensione. Proceres Evangelici in Poloniâ, communicato cum Ministris consilio, ad excitandos in similem concordiam Germanorum animos, quibus suo illustri exemplo jam præiverant, litteras, dum Comitia Varsaviensia celebrabantur a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxvii. dederunt d. xxvii. Februarii, ad Electores, & Principes Germaniæ, ad Ludovicum Electorem Palatinum, Saxonem, & Brandenburgensem, ad Ludovicum Electorem Palatinum, Saxonem, & Brandedeburgicum : qui rescripserunt, probari sibi concordiae & unionis studium, illudque se apud suos omni ope promoturos. In epistola ad Electorem Palatinum loquuntur Poloni Proceres, inter alia: Nos certe, qui regno hoc Polonico, & Magno Ducatu Lithuanico, caeterisque provinciis iisdem adnexis continemur, libenter fatemur, uberrimum nos fructum ex ea Concordia, quam collatis & conciliatis tribus fidei confessionibus, Augustana scilicet, fratrum Bohemorum, & Helvetica, beneficio Dei sancte inivimus, summo cum gaudio & animi laetitia percipere, quam ut Deus Opt. Max. nobis perpetuam esse, & eandem caeteris quoque Ecclesiis largiri & tribuere velit, ardentissimis votis eum precamur. Adjunxere suas litteras Theologi, iisdemque unanimiter subscripsere, tum Augustanae Confessionis, tum Reformatarum Ecclesiarum, & Fratrum Bohemicorum Ministri, suo suorumque nomine, servi Iesu Christi, Ministri Evangelici in regno Poloniae &c. In quibus litteris, ad Electorem Palatinum sic loquuntur: Quod si id nobis (in fundamento quidem consentientibus) contingere non possit, ut etiam in singulis religionis nostrae scrupulis idem, eodemque oris tenore loquamur (siquidem Spiritus S. varie & liberè dona sua distribuit, prout & cui vult) monemur nos sacrae literae, ne invicem nos mordeamus. (nam inquit, consumemini) neque tam impotenter nobis in proprio sensu & donis arrideamus, ut servos Domini, sanguine ipsius emtos, condemnemus, sed alii alios invicem honore praevenientes, alii aliorum onera charitate portemus, & pro nobis invicem oremus. Quaeresi quis contentiosus est, nos non habemus eiusmodi morem, neque Ecclesia Dei 1 Corinth. 11. Nos inquam, qui in his Sarmaticis regionibus gregem Christi pascimus, quamvis diversos praeceptores in perdiscendis una eademque caelesti doctrina habuerimus, alii Augustana, alii Bohemica, alii Helvetica confessioni, ritibusque assuefacti & addicti, cum aliquandiu hibinet quisque in suo sensu placentes, invicem contenderimus, & non illeptidam An- tichri. Christo spectaculum praebuimus: tandem anno abhinc octavo, tum authoritate Spiritus S. pacem concordiae & amorem mutuum suadentis, tum etiam malis discordiae permoti, omnibus litibus finem imposuimus, ac contendere jam in more non habemus. Cui concordiae & amori motuo Dominus ita benedicit, ut laetitiam ac fructum inde sequentem verbis satis declarare possimus. Nam non solum illud in nostris conscientiis sentimus: Ecce quam bonum & quam jucundum, fratres habitare in unum: sed etiam manifeste experimur, id Ecclesiae nostrae inter atrocissimos hostes, tam Papistas, quam Arianos versantes, plurimum conducere ad pacem externam, ablationem scandalorum, ad aedificationem Ecclesiae, & ad repressionem ac oppressionem hostium Filii Dei, contra quos conjunctus exercitus Domini, triplici acie, quanto concordius, tanto fortius, & praeclarius contendit. Factum inde, ut ad exemplum Sendomiriensium, in Bohemia ii qui Hussiticam & Bohemicam, atque illi qui Augustanam Confessionem sequebantur, in unum consenserint, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxv. facta communi fidei formulâ, quam & Maximilianus Imp. ratam habuit, viguitque communis consensus inconcussus usque ad a. cIↄ Iↄ c v i. Videre de his licet Hospinianum, Histor. Sacram. part. i i. pag. 342, Historiam Fratrum Bohemorum, Joh. Camerarii Paraeum, in Irenico, cap. xvii. & xviii. & xxii. Historiam Ecclesiarum Sclavonicarum lib. i. pag. 88. 89 64. Consensus illius Sendomiriensis jussi sunt singuli Ecclesiarum per Poloniam &c. Ministri habere exemplar: ita constitutum in Synodo V Vlodislaviensi a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxiii. can. iii, atque in Synodo Torunensi a. cIↄ Iↄ xcv. can. ii. & hic quidem non habere illud tantum, & legere, sed etiam ex praescripto illius & canonum in eo expressorum, tum ipse agere, tum coetum sibi commissum gubernare. Et can. iii. sancitum, ut in Synodis particularibus, & cetibus frequentioribus, quales solent haberi in feriis Paschalibus, aut alio quovis ad id accommodato tempore, ad minimum semel quotannis libellus iste Consensus cum Synodis Generalibus in eo contentis prælegatur, & juxta illum examen fratrum, & membrorum Ecclesiæ Dei instituatur: quique aliquâ in re deliquisse deprehensi fuerint, corrigantur, & in reos fiat executio disciplinæ. Namque deprehendebantur aliqui Consensui isti minus morigeri, quique ei subscribere nolent, de quibus excommunicandis actum d.xxiv Aug. in illâ Synodo. Vtinam vero exemplum istius Consensus permoveat ad similem, Ecclesias quoque alias, præsertim quum non adeo grave vel arduum opus sit, tres Confessiones, Augustanam, Helveticam, Bohemicam in consensum redigere, illæ si in se spectentur; & quas Lutherus ipse aliquando non improbavit. Tum tutissimum hic in Confessionibus concordandis laborare, potius quam Doctoribus. Quid de Helveticâ Confessione, post Concordiam VVittembergensem, sibi missâ judicarit Lutherus, modò vidimus. De Bohemorum fide & sententiâ circa cœnam, jam a.cIↄ Iↄ xxii i. audita eâ ex Legatis fratrum Bohemorum ad se VVittembergam, hoc suum judicium exposuit, in epist. ad Nic. Hausmannum, Tom. ii. epist. De Pighardis (sic quidem etiam, sed per invidiam vulgo appellabantur) jam non male [?]sentro, audita eorum, præsentibus ipsis, fide circa sacramentum Eucharistiæ. Atque ad eundem alibi, explicans simul mentem Bohemorum, & discrimen à sententiâ suâ: Pighardi sic de sacramento sentiunt, quod Christus sub pane non sit corporaliter, quomodo aliqui dicunt, se vidisse ibi sanguinem, & puerulum &c. sed spiritualiter, seu sacramentaliter, hoc est, qui panem accipit visibiliter, vere accipit naturaliter ejus sanguinem, qui à dextris Patris sedet, sed invisibiliter. Vltra hoc non possunt eos damnare. Deinde quod non adorant, admodum referunt, quod non sit ibi visibiliter, ut visiones habeant, sed invisibiliter, hoc est, ad dexteram Patris. In eundem sensum Confessionem illorum à se editam, præfatione suâ laudavit anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxiii. Vt valde mirum sit detestan-
units.tr: What we have so far said about the syncretism of the Lutherans happened while the authors of the dispute were still alive: first the Marburg Consensus, then the Wittenberg one. After those men were removed from the scene, there were also those who devoted real effort to this work, so that the divided churches might come together in concord or at least in mutual toleration. By "ecclesiastical union" we mean a union between churches that disagreed, concluded by churchmen at special meetings convened for this purpose. After the two earlier ones, the Marburg and the Wittenberg, a third followed, which we must now consider. It was made after the death of the leaders, at Sendomir in Poland, on 14 April 1570. There the Polish and Greater Lithuanian sides, allied with the three Confessions, the Bohemian, the Augsburg and the Helvetic, stood together against the Ebionites and the Anabaptists. They established this consensus, piously and happily, in the following manner, as regards the article on the Lord's Supper: Then, as far as concerns that unhappy dispute about the Lord's Supper, we agree in the sense of the words of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they are understood orthodoxly by the Fathers, and especially by Irenaeus, who said that this mystery consists of two things, the earthly and the heavenly. We do not assert that the elements or signs are bare and empty, but that they at the same time exhibit and give to believers, in very deed and by faith, what they signify. Finally, to speak more expressly and clearly, we agree that we should believe and confess that the substantial presence of Christ is not merely signified, but that the body and blood of the Lord are truly present in the Supper to those who eat, and are distributed and exhibited, the signs being added, not to the thing itself bare, but according to the nature of the sacraments. This manner of mutual consent is by far the best so far, so that, with the Confessions of the Churches joined and mutually approved, either another formula is omitted or one is drawn up like this one. It keeps some things from the Wittenberg formula, but where the crux of the difficulty lies it is more accurate: it affirms the substantial presence of Christ in the Supper, though not of the body as such, although the body too is exhibited and taken in the signs by believers, through faith: that in the use instituted in this communion Christ is truly and substantially present, and the body and blood of Christ are truly exhibited to those who receive them. All these things sound better than those in the Wittenberg formula: the body of Christ is truly and substantially present, and the body and blood of the Lord are truly offered, even to the unworthy. In this way, at Sendomir, by these decisions, they agreed that, all hatreds, attacks and quarrels having been laid aside, they should acknowledge one another as brothers and regard each other's churches as orthodox. In this they went beyond the Marburg consensus: and we agree that, just as they attest that we, our churches and our Confession, published at this synod, are orthodox and of the brethren, so we too shall embrace their churches with the same Christian love and shall count them orthodox. And we shall bid a final farewell, and impose deep silence on all quarrels, divisions and dissensions, by which the course of the Gospel has been hindered, not without the greatest offence to many godly people, and which have given our adversaries no slight occasion to slander and to contradict our Christian religion. Rather we ought to labour for peace and public tranquillity, to exercise mutual charity, and to render mutual services for the building up of the Church, for our brotherly union. Indeed, they wished all to be regarded from then on almost as one body of the Churches, and to be called and to meet equally at general synods: Wherefore we have resolved to consult together, to confer mutual counsels, and in future to take thought, as to political matters, for the preservation and oath of all the pious, orthodox and reformed Churches of the whole kingdom, of Lithuania and Samogitia, as if they were one body. And if they hold general synods, they shall also inform us, and if we are summoned to our general synods, they shall come without reluctance, if need be. This union of the Churches ought rightly to be held as most excellent, and it is fair and praiseworthy that others should model themselves on it and follow it. So easy, not to say possible, is the union of our Churches, when men who are upright, modest and zealous for orthodoxy were chosen to bring it about. The same Sendomir consensus was solemnly confirmed in the same year at the Synod of Posen, where each party, first the ministers, patrons and the whole Church of the Bohemian Confession, Poles and Germans, men of both sexes, leaving their own temple, went into the temple of the Augsburg Confession. There the ministers of the Bohemian Brethren preached a morning sermon, one in Polish and the other in German. In the afternoon, in turn, the assembly of the Augsburg Confession went to the temple of the Bohemian Brethren, and there the ministers of the Augsburg Confession, one again for the Poles and the other for the Germans, preached a sermon. When the consensus had been read to the people on each side, and all unanimously agreed to it, and serious exhortations to mutual concord and peace had been spoken by the ministers, the chorus was sung, to their great joy and applause: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. Who, I beg you, having even a little Christian spirit, would not approve this work, not praise it, and, returning to his own mind, not rejoice equally in so holy a concord? Who would believe that something so pleasing to heaven could be hated by other men, unless the Lutherans of Vilna had approved this by their own deed at the synod of 1578, and unless Leonhard, or Leonhardus Hütter, had confirmed in his writing against Pareus's Irenicum, which is more litigious and furious than theological, chapter 16, that the dishonest commendation of this deed... But meanwhile, to himself... [illegible] ...the consensus made among the Evangelicals at the Sendomir synod, and that it was also confirmed at the synod of Thorn in 1595. So it is: after the consensus was reached at the national synod of Sendomir, it was solemnly confirmed in the same year, on 20 May, at the provincial synod of Posen. It was repeated at the national synod of Cracow in 1573, on 29 September, and was sealed at the close of the synod, with the sacred Synaxis celebrated unanimously by all the ministers and delegates of the three Churches present, according to the rite of the Church of Cracow. The same was done at the synod of Pietrkow in 1575, on 1 June, at Włodisław in 1583, on 30 June, and at Thorn in 1595, on 20 August. Finally, at the recent colloquy of Thorn, in 1645, on 1 September, the Reformed, in their general confession of faith, again approved and confirmed their own Sendomir confession, that is the Helvetic, there set out in the Polish language, and they confirmed it, the Confession once offered to Sigismund I at the Diet of Warsaw in 1572, later dedicated to him when it was published in 1574, and presented to King Stephen at the Diet of 1577. After this had been carefully considered, our King granted the public exercise of religion at Cracow. That Sendomir consensus, first published at Thorn in 1585 in Latin and Polish by synodal decree, was happily reprinted again in 1592, and in 1596 at Heidelberg in 1605, and long before in both languages in 1628, after the Sendomir agreement had been made. The Evangelical nobles in Poland, having taken counsel with the ministers, sent letters to the Electors and Princes of Germany, to the Electors Palatine, of Saxony and of Brandenburg, on 27 February, while the Diet of Warsaw was being held in 1577, to stir up the minds of the Germans to a similar concord, to which they had already led the way by their own illustrious example. The Electors replied that they approved the zeal for concord and union, and that they would promote it among their own people by every means. In the letter to the Elector Palatine the Polish nobles speak, among other things: We, who are held in this Polish kingdom, and in the Great Duchy of Lithuania, and the other provinces joined to them, freely confess that we receive with the greatest joy and gladness of mind the very abundant fruit of that concord which we have, by God's grace, sacredly entered upon, through the bringing together and reconciling of the three Confessions of faith, the Augsburg, that is, that of the Bohemian Brethren, and the Helvetic. We pray with most ardent wishes that God, most good and great, may wish this to be perpetual for us, and grant and bestow the same on the other Churches also. The theologians added their letters and unanimously subscribed them, both the ministers of the Augsburg Confession and of the Reformed Churches and of the Bohemian Brethren, in their own name and in that of their people, as servants of Jesus Christ, ministers of the Gospel in the kingdom of Poland, etc. In these letters they speak to the Elector Palatine thus: But if this cannot happen to us, that we should speak with the same voice on each scruple of our religion (since, agreeing in the foundation, the Holy Spirit distributes his gifts variously and freely, as and to whom he wills), the sacred letters warn us not to bite one another (for, it says, you will be consumed), nor to be so intemperately pleased with our own opinion and gifts that we condemn the servants of the Lord, bought with his blood, but that, each anticipating the other in honour, some bear the burdens of others in charity and pray for one another. If anyone asks whether we are contentious, we do not have such a custom, nor does the Church of God (1 Cor. 11). We, I say, who feed the flock of Christ in these Sarmatian regions, though we have had different teachers in learning the one and the same heavenly doctrine, some accustomed and attached to the Augsburg Confession, some to the Bohemian, some to the Helvetic, and rites, when for some time each of us pleased himself in his own opinion, we contended with one another and offered an unseemly spectacle to Christ and the Antichrist. At last, eight years ago, moved both by the authority of the Holy Spirit, who urges peace of concord and mutual love, and by the evils of discord, we put an end to all disputes, and we no longer have the habit of contending. The Lord so blesses this concord and mutual love that we can declare in words enough the joy and fruit that follow from it. For we not only feel in our consciences: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity, but we also manifestly experience that this contributes greatly to our Church among the most savage enemies, who live among both the Papists and the Arians, to external peace, to the removal of scandals, to the building up of the Church, and to the repression and overthrow of the enemies of the Son of God, against whom the united army of the Lord, in threefold battle line, the more harmoniously it fights, the more strongly and splendidly it fights. As a result, following the example of the Sendomirians, in Bohemia those who followed the Hussite and Bohemian faith and those who followed the Augsburg Confession came together in agreement in 1575, a common formula of faith having been made, which Emperor Maximilian also ratified, and the common consensus flourished unshaken until 1616. On these matters one may consult Hospinian, Historia Sacramentaria, part 2, p. 342; the History of the Bohemian Brethren; Johann Camerarius's Paraeus in the Irenicum, chapters 17, 18 and 22; and the History of the Slavonic Churches, book 1, pp. 88, 89, 64. It was ordered that the ministers of the individual Churches throughout Poland, etc., should have a copy of that Sendomir consensus. This was enacted at the Synod of Włodisław in 1583, canon 3, and at the Synod of Thorn in 1595, canon 2. And here it was not enough merely to have it and read it, but, according to its prescription and the canons expressed in it, each was himself to act and to govern the assembly committed to him.
