And canon 3 sanctioned that at particular synods and more frequent gatherings, such as are usually held at the Paschal feasts or at any other suitable time, this little book of consensus, with the general synods contained in it, should be read at least once a year, and that according to it an examination of the brothers and members of the Church of God should be carried out; and those found to have erred in any matter should be corrected, and discipline should be executed against the guilty. For some were found less compliant with that consensus, and some were unwilling to subscribe to it, and concerning their excommunication an act was passed on 24 August at that synod. Would that the example of this consensus might move the other Churches also to bring the three Confessions, the Augsburg, the Helvetic and the Bohemian, into agreement, which is not so very grave or difficult a task, if they are considered in themselves; and which Luther himself once did not disapprove. Then it would be most sound to labour in reconciling the Confessions here rather than the teachers. What Luther judged about the Helvetic Confession sent to him after the Wittenberg Concord, we have just seen. Concerning the faith and opinion of the Bohemians about the Supper, already heard from the envoys of the Bohemian Brethren who came to him at Wittenberg in 1523, he set forth his judgment in a letter to Nicolaus Hausmann, vol. 2, letter On the Pighards (so they were called, though commonly and by way of abuse): I do not disapprove the Pighards, having heard their faith concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist, with themselves present. And in another letter to the same man, explaining at once the mind of the Bohemians and their difference from his own opinion: The Pighards think about the sacrament thus: that Christ is not under the bread bodily, as some say, who claim they have seen there blood and a little child, etc., but spiritually, or sacramentally, that is, whoever visibly receives the bread truly receives naturally the blood of him who sits at the right hand of the Father, but invisibly. Beyond this they cannot condemn them. Then, that they do not adore, they quite refer to the fact that he is not there visibly, so that they might have visions, but invisibly, that is, at the right hand of the Father. In the same sense he praised their Confession, which he had published, in his preface in the year 1533. So it is very strange to detest and to denounce that those who, as they boast, are disciples of Luther, reject the Sendomir Consensus, with so much fairness of the cause and also with the authority of Luther himself, lest Scripture...

units.la: { } Scan shows the text in a mixed roman and italic setting; the italic passages are marked above. testandumque, existere Lutheri ut se iactant discipulos, qui Consensum Sendomiriensem repudiant, tanta tum causæ æquitate, tum Lutheri quoque authoritate, ne Scripturam dicamus, subnixum. Benedictus Morgenstern, in epist. ad Schlusselburgium, impii consensus Sacramentariorum in Polonia, cui subscripserunt Pseudo-Lutherani Calviniste & Fratres Bohemici &c. Exagitavi in meo scripto impium hunc syncretismum, non pro dignitate, (quis enim hoc posset) sed pro viribus in hac senectâ. Sed non aliter hic usuvenit quam ut veritas, ita & charitas odium pariat. Manet nihilominus laudabile Patrum Sendomiriensium institutum, & exemplum istud suum, ad quod alios quaquaversum merito exhortabantur, imitandum.
units.tr: ...and to be detested, that those who boast of being disciples of Luther reject the Consensus of Sendomir, a position supported as much by the fairness of the cause as by the authority of Luther himself, not to mention Scripture. Benedictus Morgenstern, in his letter to Schlusselburg: I have assailed, in my writing, the impious consensus of the Sacramentarians in Poland, to which the Pseudo-Lutherans, the Calvinists and the Bohemian Brethren, etc., subscribed. I have assailed this impious syncretism, not in a manner worthy of it (for who could do that?) but as far as my strength allows in this old age. But here it happens, not otherwise than that hatred gives birth to truth, and charity likewise. Nevertheless the praiseworthy practice of the Fathers of Sendomir remains, and their example, which others were rightly urged to imitate on every side.

units.la: Neque defuerunt viri egregii semper, ut & hos, post tam aliquoties Synodicè unionem, nominemus, qui singulari pietatis & concordiæ zelo Lutheranos ad unionem duxerunt incitandos, qua Politici, qua Ecclesiastici. Inter illos, præter jam memoratos, Christianus I. Elector Saxoniæ: Christophorus, Dux VVurtembergicus, qui Cardinali Lotharingio interroganti, quænam Confessio & religio Germanorum esset, & an ea cum Ministris Gallicis consentiret respondit: se nullum discrimen scire inter Gallicorum ministrorum & Augustanæ Confessionis doctrinam, excepto unico articulo de Cœnâ Domini, qui tamen ita se habeat, ut consensus in eo etiam primo quoque tempore sperari posset, quum certamen magis in verbis, quam in reipsâ consistat. Quæ legi in Protocollo Colloquii inter Ducem, & Cardinalem habiti ad tabernas Alsaticas, a. MDLXI. missio ab ipso Duce ad Electorem Fridericum III. Palatinum, in Archivo Electoralis Cancellariæ manu propriâ Electoris a. aliquot in locis annotato, testis est Hospinianus, Hist. Sacram. part. II. pag. 310. Rex Navarrenus a. MDLXI. Prorex Galliæ, pro Carolo IX. adhuc puero, Daniæ Regis legato Georgio Glucho, roganti ut non CalCalvini & Helvetiorum, sed Lutheri doctrinam per Galliam doceri curaret, lepidè admodum respondit: „Lutherum & Calvinum in quadraginta articulis communiter à Papâ dissentire, inter se in triginta novem „convenire, unum restare controversum: quo non „obstante deberent utrinque junctis animis in Papam „insurgere, & hunc opprimere, deinde etiam de compo-„nendo controverso illo uno articulo seriò dispicere. Referunt Beza & Gallasius, in Commentde statu Relig. in Gallia part. 1. pag. 80. Et Thuanus, Histor. lib. XXVII. In libro Memoriarum Plessæi, legitur Instructio à Rege Navarreno Henrico data Domino de Segur, Legato in Belgium, & Daniam, cui inter alia in mandatis fuerit ut hoc negotium apud Principes Protestantes urgeret, quo in aliquâ Synodo dissidium Sacramentarium componeretur, de quo inter partes conveniebat quod ad „rem, solum de modo rei litigare, quod non satis decorum, de modo ultra modum contendere. Pontificios „nobis longè prudentiores esse, qui quantumvis discrepantes super hâc re ante disputationes Lutheri habuerint inter se sententias decem vel duodecim, tamen „concordiam servarent. Atque hoc multorum Principum studium semper fuit, ut sublato infelici schismate, Ecclesiæ magis conjungerentur. Quod etiam spectarunt literæ Electoris Palatini a. MDCVII. ad Comitem Palatinum Neoburgicum, ad Regem Angliæ, atque ad Illustriss. Ordines.
units.tr: Nor have there ever been lacking distinguished men, and we should name them here too, who, since unions have so often been attempted by synods, were moved by a singular zeal for piety and concord to urge the Lutherans toward union, both the statesmen and the churchmen. Among them, besides those already mentioned, were Christian I, Elector of Saxony, and Christoph, Duke of Württemberg, who, when Cardinal of Lorraine asked him what the confession and religion of the Germans was, and whether it agreed with the French ministers, replied: that he knew of no difference between the teaching of the French ministers and that of the Augsburg Confession, except for the single article on the Lord's Supper; yet that even on this point agreement could be hoped for at any time, since the dispute lies more in words than in the thing itself. That these things were read in the record of the colloquy held between the Duke and the Cardinal at the Alsatian taverns in 1561, and sent by the Duke himself to Elector Frederick III of the Palatinate, is attested by Hospinian, Hist. Sacram. part. II, p. 310, who saw the document in the archive of the Electoral Chancery, annotated in several places in the Elector's own hand. In 1561 the King of Navarre, Viceroy of France on behalf of Charles IX, who was still a boy, answered very wittily the Danish royal envoy Georg Gluch, who asked that the doctrine of Luther rather than that of Calvin and the Swiss be taught in France: "Luther and Calvin agree with each other on thirty-nine articles and differ from the Pope on forty; there remains one point of controversy. Even so, they should join forces to rise up against the Pope and crush him, and afterwards seriously consider settling that one disputed article." Beza and Gallasius report this in Commentary on the State of Religion in France, part 1, p. 80. Thuanus also reports it in Histor., book XXVII. In the book of the Memoirs of Plessis one reads the instruction given by King Henry of Navarre to Lord de Ségur, his envoy to the Low Countries and Denmark, among whose commissions was that he should press this business with the Protestant princes, so that the Sacramentarian dispute might be settled in some synod. The parties agreed that on the matter itself they were disputing only about its manner, and that it was not decent to quarrel about the manner beyond measure. The Papists, he said, were far more prudent than we are: however much they differed among themselves on this matter before Luther's disputations, holding ten or twelve opinions, they still kept concord. And it has always been the aim of many princes that, with this unhappy schism removed, the churches should be joined together more closely. This was also the aim of the letters of the Elector Palatine in 1607 to the Count Palatine of Neuburg, to the King of England, and to the most illustrious Estates.

units.la: Atque uti proprium hoc officium Theologorum, ita à nostrâ quidem parte nescimus unquam ullum fuisse, qui non existimarit, inter Lutherum & Zuinglium, vel Ecclesias Lutheranas & Reformatas, ob dissensionem sacramentalem haud opor tuisse dirimi, aut negari fraternitatem. Inter Lutheranos (quemadmodum supra in ipso Luthero distinguenda diximus intervalla mitiora, ab acrioribus, ut quum scribit ad Iacobum, Præpositum Bremensem: beatus qui non abiit in consilio Sacramen-
units.tr: And just as this is the proper duty of theologians, so on our side we know of no one who has not thought that, because of the sacramental disagreement, Luther and Zwingli, or the Lutheran and Reformed Churches, ought not to have been divided, or their brotherhood denied. Among the Lutherans (as we said above, in Luther himself we must distinguish the milder moods from the harsher ones, as when he writes to Jacob, provost of Bremen: blessed is the man who has not gone into the counsel of the Sacramen-

units.la: tariotarorum, nec stetit in via Zuinglianorum, nec sedit in ca- thedra Tigurinorum. Habes quid sentiam. Quo quid immitius dici potest? taliaque apud ipsum plura: sed quoque alibi meliora habet. In quibus distinguendis vide quam clementer & moderatè se gesserit, quem cane pejus & angue oderunt Lutherani, Calvinus, epistola ad Bullingerum, scripta a. cIↄ Iↄ xliv. die xxv. Novemb. Sæpe dicere solitus sum, etiamsi me diabolum vocaret, me tamen hoc illi honoris habituram, ut insignem Dei servum agnoscam: qui tamen ut pollet eximiis virtuti- bus, ita magnis vitiis laboret) sic dico, inter Lutheranos fatemur quidem esse pacis studiosos, præter illos qui in formulas Vonsensus jam olim jurarunt, atque probos viros, quibus dolet hæc divulsio, & nihil adeo in votis est quam Concordiam, ad Majorum exemplum, resarcire; sed pleramque ipsorum partem litigandi intemperies adeo usque tenet, ut non solum Nos haud ferant, sed neque illos è suis, qui erga Nos modestiores se gerunt; qui nihil prius habent quam dominare, & damnare. De Melanthone jam diximus. Et hic in epistolâ ad V Volffgangum Musculum, anno cIↄ Iↄ xliv. die v. Octob. Meminisfi versum Aristophanis de ollis inter se collisis, [illegible, ~20 letters] sic civiles discordiæ sæpe utrique parti existio sunt: quod & metui antea sæpe, & nunc metuo eventurum nostris ecclesiis, moto rursus θορύβῳ περὶ δείνα. O rem miseram, & omnium lachrymis deplorandam, quod illud ὅσων σύμβολον belli cogitur esse, materia seu occasio! in eandem sententiam scripsit ad eundem, die x. Novembris ejusdem anni. Ad Christophorum Carlevitzium. Consiliarium Saxonicum & Cæsareum, scripsit anno cIↄ Iↄ xlvi, quando exilia sibi prævidebat & metuebat: Quidquid ergo decreverit Princeps, etiamsi quod non probabo, tamen nihil seditiose faciam, sed vel tacebo, vel feram, quidquid accidat. Tutè etiam antea servitutem pæne deformem, cum sæpè Lutherus magis sua natura, inquā Philosophia erat non exigua, quam vel personae suae, vel utilitati communi serviret. Et scio eo- rum ut ab aetatibus ut tempestatum incommoda, ita aliquā in gubernatione vitia modestia arte ferenda et dissimulanda es- se. Quae à Collegis suis crudelia passus gener ejus Peucerus, supra attigimus. Simili modo cum Victorino Strigelio, Urbano Picrio, aliisque actum, quos melioris sententiae modestiaeque homines in duram carcerem compegerunt, ac miserè vexarunt. Non absque lachry- mis legat quis duram Anglo-Belgarum exulum apud Lutheranos Hafniae, Vismariae, Lubeci, & Hamburgia. CIↄ Iↄ Iııı. & Iıv. conditionem, quomodo excep- ti fuerint media acerbaque hieme cum suis mulieribus, gravidis, puerperis, infantibus, aegrotis, senibus, & suspiam hospitium, vel hyemandi saltem spatium nancisci aliquod potuerint, idque propter unum doctrinae istud discrimen in causā sacramenti, super quo variis in locis impetratā à Ministris Lutheranis (aliquando & denegatā) disputatione, ita suam causaeque innocentiam probarunt, ut commiserationem commeritos eo acerbius exagitarint humanitatis ac religionis juxta inimici illi Ministri. Dequibus vide Narrationem Iohannis Vttenhovii, qui illis interfuit, de institutā et dissipatā Belgarum, aliorumque peregrinorum in Anglia, Ecclesiā; quam etiam Historiae suae Sacramentariae inseruit Hospinianus; & Belgicis Annalibus, Emm. Meteranus, lib.
units.tr: tarians, nor stood in the way of the Zwinglians, nor sat in the chair of the Zurichers. You have my view. What could be said more harshly? And he has many such things elsewhere; but he also has better things elsewhere. In distinguishing these, see how gently and moderately he behaved, whom the Lutherans hate worse than a dog or a snake. Calvin, in a letter to Bullinger written on 25 November 1544: I have often said that even if he called me a devil, I would still grant him this honour, that I recognise him as an eminent servant of God; yet as he excels in remarkable virtues, so he labours under great vices.) So I say this: among the Lutherans we admit that there are some who love peace, apart from those who long ago swore to the formulas of concord, and good men who grieve over this division, and who desire nothing so much as to mend the concord, after the example of their forebears. But most of them are so gripped by a intemperance of quarrelling that they not only cannot bear us, but cannot bear even those among their own who behave more moderately toward us, who seek above all else to dominate and to condemn. We have already spoken of Melanchthon. And he, in a letter to Wolfgang Musculus, 5 October 1544: I remember the verse of Aristophanes about the pots knocking together, [illegible, about 20 letters] so civil discords often become the occasion of destruction for both parties; this I feared before, and now I fear it will happen to our churches, once the uproar about such-and-such has been stirred up again [θορύβῳ περὶ δείνα]. O wretched matter, to be lamented with the tears of all, that that sign of ... [ὅσων σύμβολον] is forced to become the material or occasion of war! He wrote to the same man in the same vein on 10 November of that year. To Christoph Karlowitz, Saxon and Imperial councillor, he wrote in 1546, when he foresaw and feared exile: Whatever the Prince decides, even if I do not approve, I will do nothing seditious, but will either be silent or endure whatever happens. Safely too, earlier, I was writing about the almost deformed servitude, since Luther often served not so much his own person or the common good as his nature, that is, his considerable philosophy. And I know that, as the troubles of the ages and the storms of the times are to be borne, so in governing some faults must be borne with moderation and concealed. His son-in-law Peucer, who suffered cruel treatment from his colleagues, we have touched on above. In a similar way Victorinus Strigel, Urban Pierius, and others were treated, men of better opinion and moderation, whom they shut into a harsh prison and miserably harassed. One should read without tears the hard condition of the Anglo-Belgian exiles among the Lutherans at Copenhagen, Wismar, Lübeck and Hamburg in 1553 and 1554: how they were received, in the middle of a bitter winter, with their wives, pregnant women, women in childbed, infants, the sick and the old, and how they could hardly find any lodging, or even a space in which to spend the winter. This happened because of the single point of doctrine on the sacrament, on which they had gained a hearing and debate from the Lutheran ministers in various places (though sometimes it was refused), and in which they proved their cause and innocence so well that, though they deserved pity, their hostile ministers persecuted them all the more bitterly, against all humanity and religion. On these matters see the Narrative of John Utenhove, who was present, on the established and dispersed church of the Belgians and other foreigners in England; Hospinian included it in his Sacramentarian History; and Emmanuel Meteren in the Belgic Annals, book 1. Here belongs what Melanchthon wrote in his Consilia, part II, for the year 1556, in reply to the Westphalians: whether the English and the French are to be tolerated as enemies? He affirms altogether that they must be treated so, and that they too may be granted the use of the sacred ministry. Not to mention how Guilielmus...

units.la: 1. Huc, quod in Consiliis Melanthonis part. 11. ad a. CIↄ Iↄ Ivı. respondit VVestalien-sibus: An Angli et Galli hostes sint tolerandi? quod omnino affirmat agendum, & concedendum eis quoque ministerii sacri usum esse. Ne dicam, quomodo vel cum Guiljelmo Klebitio Heidelbergae Heshusius, insanum in morem a. CIↄ Iↄ lxx. cum Danaeo, Geneva in Hollandiam, ad capessendam Theol. Professionem a. CIↄ Ic lxxxı. proficiscenti, inhumaniter in itinere Argentinenses, omne hospitium ei, & familiae suae intercludendo; cum Saxoniae moniae Cancellario, Doctore Creill. cIↄ Iↄ c v. quem capite multarunt: hodieque cum Nostrae religionis hominibus Dantisci, templum scholamque contra jus & fas eripientes, agant: certe non digni saltem ea Nostrorum humanitate ac benevolentia, fraternaque charitate, quam ubique experiuntur. In Narratione exulum Belgarum Iohannis Vtenhovii, quam diximus, pag. 89. refertur, in Actis ipsorum apud Daniae Regem, quod inter caetera testati fuere, neminem unquam a sua communione, controversiae Sacramentariae nomine, sive in Anglia, sive alibi exclusum fuisse. Et Martinus Micronius, in disputatione Lubeci, a. cIↄ Iↄ l v, d. xxv i. Februarii: Leve esset a professis Christi hostibus talia, aut etiam graviora propter Christum sustinere: sed a vobis, quos pro nostris Fratribus & communis Evangelii Christi professoribus hactenus duximus, ista ipsa experiri, longe nobis est molestissimum. Et hoc tamen eferatorum hominum animos retinere non potuit, quia pios Confessores toto regno, urente hyeme, ocyus expellerent. Atque nisi constaret peccari benignitate, quamvis in immeritos non ita facile, ac rigore aliquo licet non injusto, aliter quoque cum illis agendum censeremus, qui nimia nostra bonitate supra modum abutuntur. Certe haec ostendunt, omnino distinguendos Lutheranos, neque de illis aeque sentiendum, vel promiscue benevolentiam nostram iis offerendam aut prostituendam; sed moderandam prudentia nostram erga illos beneficentiam esse. Sunt quidem inter illos, sed rariores, ut ex omnibus historiis liquet, & suppressi varieque multati a primipilis suis, inferiores aliis numero ac potestate, qui erga nos & Ecclesias nostras melius affecti, moderationem suadent. Cum istis quidem volo nobis negotium esse, non ita cum illis: quamvis & hic parum fructus sperari possit, quandiu non appareat quo pacto qui meliores apud suos queant aut superiores evadere, aut saltem reliquorum clamores & venitaniam faniam coërcere; ne officiant. Interim & probos illos modestosque Theologos non deseri vel negligi, sed juvari firmarique oportet. Talis fuit Petrus Palladius, Superintendens Hassniensis, qui ut est in historiâ Iohannis Vtenhovii jam memorata, exules nostros benignissimè excipiebat, & pro fratribus à se habitis voluisset quidem datum suo loco hospitium, nisi à Rege aliter mandatum fuisset: audita eorum coram frequenti coetu declaratione fidei, aperto ore testatus fuit: Confessionem ipsorum ab omnibus sectis alienam, in praecipuis Christianae religionis capitibus consentire. Exiguum duntaxat dissidium esse circa Coenam Dominicam, non quidem in praecipuâ ejus parte & mysterio, sed duntaxat quaestione de modo praesentiae corporis Christi in Coenâ. Quod saepe dissidium tanti non est (dicebat) ut propterea fraternitatis vinculum rumpi à nobis debeat: praesertim cum in praecipuis articulis Christianae fidei consensus sit. Quapropter nos decet, homines istos in hac fidei ipsorum Confessione pro fratribus complecti, ac pro nostrâ facultate juvare. Ego sane eos pro Christianis & fratribus agnosco, easque apud vos omnes constet, me ita de illis sentire, et publicè eis datâ dextrâ id testatum facio: quod cum amanter admodum fecisset, amicè discessum. Contigit hoc anno MDLXXIII[?]. Similis notae melioris quoque Christophorus Donawerus, Minister Ratisbonensis, qui anno MDLX. Senatui Ecclesiastico exhibuit Moderationis motivem, seu Rationes Moderationis, ob quas nequiret damnare Calvinistas, quae in lucem edita anno MDXXXIII, digne ut non à Germanis solum, sed Latinè etiam ab omnibus legantur. Atque huiusmodi scripta ab alterâ parte edita semper magnifacienda & concelebranda sunt, eo magis quo rariora.
units.tr: 1. Here also belongs what Melanchthon, in part 2 of his Consilia, answered the Westphalians in 1556: Are the English and the French to be tolerated as enemies? He affirms without qualification that they should be tolerated, and that they too may be allowed the use of the sacred ministry. I need not mention how Heshusius at Heidelberg, in 1570, behaved in a barbarous manner toward Wilhelm Klebitz as he set out with Danaeus from Geneva for Holland to take up a professorship of theology in 1581. On the journey the people of Strasbourg inhumanly barred every lodging to him and his household. Nor need I mention how the Chancellor of Saxony, Dr Creil, was beheaded in 1601. Even today, at Danzig, men of our religion are seizing a church and a school against right and law. Such people certainly do not deserve the humanity, kindness and brotherly charity which our own people show them everywhere. In the Narrative of the Belgian exiles by John Utenhove, which I have mentioned, p. 89, it is recorded that in their account before the King of Denmark they testified, among other things, that no one had ever been excluded from their communion on account of the sacramentarian controversy, whether in England or elsewhere. And Martin Micron, in the disputation at Lübeck, on 25 February 1555, said: It would be a light thing to endure such treatment, or even worse, for Christ's sake from those who profess themselves Christ's enemies. But to experience these very things from you, whom until now we have regarded as our brothers and fellow professors of the common Gospel of Christ, is far more grievous to us. Yet this could not restrain the minds of these savage men, for in the midst of winter they drove the godly confessors out of the whole kingdom with all speed. Unless it were established that we sin by kindness, although not easily toward the undeserving, we would judge that they should be dealt with in some other way, with a severity that is not unjust, since they abuse our great goodness beyond measure. Certainly these things show that the Lutherans must be carefully distinguished; we must not feel the same about all of them, nor offer or cheapen our goodwill to them indiscriminately. Our kindness toward them must be tempered by prudence. There are indeed among them, though fewer, as all the histories make clear, men who have been suppressed and variously punished by their leaders, who are inferior to others in number and power, and who are better disposed toward us and our churches and urge moderation. It is with these men that I wish to have dealings, not with the others. Yet even here little fruit can be hoped for, as long as it does not appear how those who are better among their own people might become superior, or at least restrain the clamours of the rest and their frenzied rage, lest these hinder them. Meanwhile it is right that those upright and moderate theologians should not be abandoned or neglected, but helped and strengthened. Such a man was Peter Palladius, superintendent at Hesse, who, as is recorded in the history of John Utenhove already mentioned, received our exiles most kindly, and would have gladly given them lodging in his own place for the brothers he took them to be, had the King not ordered otherwise. Having heard their declaration of faith before a large assembly, he openly testified: Their confession, free from all sects, agrees in the principal heads of the Christian religion. There is only a small disagreement concerning the Lord's Supper, not indeed in its main part and mystery, but only in the question of the manner of the presence of Christ's body in the Supper. This disagreement, which is often a small matter (he said), is not so great that the bond of brotherhood ought therefore to be broken by us, especially since there is agreement on the chief articles of the Christian faith. Wherefore it befits us to embrace these men in this their confession of faith as brothers, and to help them according to our ability. I for my part acknowledge them as Christians and brothers, and I bear witness to this before you all, that you may know how I feel about them, by giving them my right hand in public. When he had done this with great warmth, they parted in friendship. This happened in the year 1573[?]. Christoph Donauer, minister at Regensburg, a man of similar note and better standing, also gave the Ecclesiastical Senate, in 1560, his Motives of Moderation, that is, the reasons for moderation for which he could not condemn the Calvinists. It was published in 1533 and is worthy of being read not only by Germans but in Latin by everyone. Writings of this kind, published by the other side, must always be held in high esteem and celebrated, all the more because they are so rare.

units.la: Nec omittendus Christophorus Pelargus, Theol. Francofurt. ad Oderam, & Superintendens Marchiae: quem acerbè Calvinismi exagitavit Frid. Balduinus V Vittembergensis Theologus: & apostatam in litteris ad eum suis anno MDLXIV. criminantur Cramerras; & Schlusselburgius. Denique merito praedicandum celeberrimi viri Georgi Calixti, Theologi Helmstadiensis; Iudicium, de Controversiis Theologicis, quae inter Lutheranos & Reformatos agitantur. Et de mutua partium Fraternitate atque tolerantia, propter consensum in fundamentis. Una cum Ejusdem Desiderio & Studio Concordiae Ecclesiasticae: Lugduni Batav. impressa, anno praecedente cI(ɔ) Iɔ l. Iudicium versum, prudens, sanctum: cui, quod ad rei summam, totus, lubensque accedo. Nam quamvis aliam ab eo tum in doctrina de Praedestinatione, tum de Coena sententiam amplectar, de cujus alterutrius veritate nec disputat, neque contendendi ibi locus est, existimo tamen, probat ab eo utraque sententia, momentumque proponitur, bene tolerari utramque sic invicem posse, ac debere, quomodo ubi Concordia inter partes vel habetur, vel consulitur, expedire visum fuerit. In tribus Calixtus dissensum nostrum constituit, in articulo de Praedestinatione, de natura Christi, & S. Coena, atque ibi Ubiquitatem corporis Christi aeque ac nos rejicit, hic vero, & illic ira nos a sua sententia discrepare ait, ut normalo animo, sed ibi defendendae luculentius divinae gratiae, hic oppugnandae tanto acrius Missae Papisticae causa videantur sibi in eam, quam tuemur, ire sententiam: quare non de illa re contendendum esse, in qua absque salutis periculo aut errore aut ignorantia possit contingere, & qua non obstante inter Nos ea Ecclesiarum debeat esse & animorum conjunctio, ut fraterno Nos amore mutuo & constanter complectamur. In quo ei accedimus, de illa nostra differentia, & moderate ita judicanti. Quod si cum talibus, ac illc, hac in re semper agendum, facilis foret conciliatio ac consensus.
units.tr: Nor should Christoph Pelargus be omitted, theologian of Frankfurt on the Oder and superintendent of the Mark. Friedrich Balduin, theologian of Wittenberg, attacked him bitterly for Calvinism, and Cramer and Schlüsselburg accuse him of apostasy in their letter to him in 1564. Finally, the work of the most celebrated Georg Calixtus, theologian of Helmstedt, deserves high praise: Judgement on the Theological Controversies which are debated between the Lutherans and the Reformed, and on the mutual fraternity and tolerance of the parties, on account of agreement in the fundamentals. It was printed at Leiden in 1650, together with his Desire and Zeal for Ecclesiastical Concord. It is a wise and holy judgement, and as far as the substance of the matter goes, I subscribe to it entirely and gladly. For although I embrace a different opinion from his, both on the doctrine of predestination and on the Supper, and it is not for me to dispute here the truth of either, nor is there room for controversy in this place, I nonetheless think that he proves, and that it is set forth as a principle, that each of these opinions can and ought to be well tolerated by the other, just as it seems fitting when concord between the parties either exists or is sought. Calixtus identifies our dissent in three points: the article on predestination, the nature of Christ, and the Lord's Supper. There he rejects the ubiquity of Christ's body just as we do, but here and there he says we differ from his opinion, and that we seem to ourselves to go in the direction we defend, in a sincere spirit, though in the former case to defend divine grace more clearly, and in the latter to oppose the Papist Mass more vigorously. Therefore we must not contend over that matter, in which one may err or be ignorant without peril to salvation, and despite which there ought to be among us such union of churches and minds that we embrace one another in constant and brotherly love. In this I agree with him about that difference between us, and with his moderate judgement. If we always dealt with such men, and with him, in this way, conciliation and agreement would be easy.

units.la: Sed alii, & plures, ferme infinitas faciunt inter nos controversias, qualis Henricus Eckhardus, in Fasciculo Controversiarum, an calumniarum? easque, quae sunt, extendere malunt & augere, quam contrahere: qui si- mimum nimium ad disputandum judicandumque adferunt vehementer exulceratum, neque aliquid norunt quam laedere. Atque hi plus nocent, quam alii prosint. Apud Nos nemo, quod sciam, est, qui non censeat, negotium Sacramentarium, ex quo natum schisma fotumque, non eo trahi oportere, ut Ecclesias divellat. Quare pro pace aut retinenda, aut revocanda assidui Nostrorum fuerunt & labores, & scripta. Sic ipse ille Calvinus, cujus nomen tanto odio exagitant, judicavit. Quem in finem legatur vel solus ejus libellus, de optima inter nos concordia ratione, si extra contentionem quaeratur veritas. Ex quo si haec perpenderimus, facile de ejus mente constare poterit: Ne qua vel dubitatio vel suspicio concordiam moretur & impediat, primo loco definiendum est de quibus rebus conveniat inter nos. Nam quae inimitio certaminum maxime exasperarunt utrinque animos, nunc sunt extra controversiam. Odiosissimum erat ab una parte jactari, alligari Spiritus gratiam externis elementis: ab altera modo nudas & inanes figuras & theatricis pompis similes relinqui. Haec contentio nunc sublata est. Deinde: Quisquis autem sano rectoque judicio praeditus, simul compositum affectum & sedatum afferet, fatebitur solum de modo edendi esse certamen. Pergit: "Hoc constituto", licebit admittere loquendi formas, in quibus nonnulli ob ambiguitatem sunt perplexi. Sub pane vel vino panis nobis dari Christi corpus: quia non substantialis unio corruptibilis cibi cum Christi carne, sed sacramentalis notatur conjunctio. Hoc autem controversiae caret apud omnes pios, inseparabile esse vinculum signi & rei significatae in promissione ipsa, quia Deus nihil fallaciter ostentat, sed figuras quod vere & re ipsa praestat. Demum subjungit: "Haec ubi transfacta fuerint, emergit adhuc dubitatio de voce substantiae: cujus sedandae haec videtur esse expedita ratio, ut crassa imaginatio tollatur de manducatione carnis, a: si corporalibus cibis esset similis, qui ore suscepti in ventrem defluunt. Nam ubi haec absurditas remota fuerit, nec est cur negemus substantialiter nos pasci pasci Christi carne, quia verè coalescimus cum ipso in unum corpus per fidem, & ita unum cum ipso efficimur. Quàm, & quam facilis, vel Calvino judice, & quam propinquus, in illis etiam verbis formulisque de quibus maximè contenditur, consensus sit, apparet. Quare etiam se haud mediocriter laetatum adjutumque consensu, licet nondum pleno solidoque, aliquali saltem Marpurgi ante initio, scribit Idem, statim in principio Secundae Defensionis de Sacramentis, adversus VVestphalum. His consimilia Beza aliquoties propositus, in Colloquio Mompelgartensi, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxv i. Unde & Nostri Lutheranos passim fratres in Christo appellarunt: & colendam invicem fraternitatem suo exemplo monuerunt, quamvis non eâ, quâ oportuit, humanitate & amore semper exceptî: ut in Colloquio Marpurgensi, Mulbrunensi, Mompelgartensi, aliisque patuit. Hic cum Beza in Colloquii exitu dixisset: dolemus nos non consentire. Capimus tamen vobiscum fraternitatem colere: & ad dextram fraternitatis porrigendam paratum se ostendisset; Iacobus Andreas excipere, se non fraternitatis, sed quidem humanitatis dexteram ei porrecturum; abrupit Beza, dicens: Quia dexteram fraternitatis nobis porrigere recusatis, & nos pro fratribus agnoscere nolumus, amicitiae dexteram etiam nolo. Et in Colloquio Mulbrunensi, de Vbiquitate corporis Christi, inter Theologos Palatinos, & VVittembergicos a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxv. Nostri illos passim Fratres nominarunt: illi vero, pro more, fraternitatem repudiarunt. Hoc quoque ipsum, quae nonnullorum est vecordia, exprobrare impotenter solent, quod ad pacem ita promti & alacres sumus. Et Langravio Hassiae Mauritio a. cIↄ Iↄ c v. fraternitatis dexteram negabat Balthasar Mentzerus: ut in Actis multuum Marpurgicorum istius anni est. In quibus nescio majoremne nostrorum liberalitatem admirer, an reliquorum inhumanitatem. Denique Sculteus à Theologis Tubingensibus, postquam & coram & per lit[illegible, ~6 letters] iam egerat de concilianda pace, a. cIↄ Iↄ c xvi. Hoc responsum tandem retulit, se in amicitiam politicam nos semper recepisse, recepturosque deinceps in Theolo-gicam, hoc est, fraternitatem Christianam nunquam.
units.tr: But others, and many, make almost endless controversies among us, such as Henricus Eckhard, in his Fasciculus Controversiarum, an calumniarum? He prefers to extend and increase the controversies, which exist, rather than reduce them. Such men bring to disputation and judgement a feeling far too bitter, and they know nothing but how to wound. These men do more harm than others do good. Among us, so far as I know, there is no one who does not think that the sacramentarian dispute, from which the schism arose and was nourished, ought not to be pursued so as to tear churches apart. Therefore our people have laboured and written constantly for the retaining or the restoring of peace. Calvin himself, whose name they pursue with such hatred, judged so. To see this, read at least his little book, On the best method of concord among us, if the truth is sought outside contention. If we weigh this carefully, it will be easy to know his mind: So that no doubt or suspicion may delay and hinder concord, it must first be determined on what matters we agree. For the things which most exasperated the minds of both sides in the heat of strife are now outside the controversy. It was most hateful for one side to proclaim that the grace of the Spirit is bound to external elements, and for the other to leave only bare and empty figures, like theatrical show. This contention has now been removed. Next: Whoever, endowed with sound and right judgement, brings to the matter a calm and composed feeling, will confess that the struggle is only over the manner of eating. He goes on: "This being settled," it will be permitted to admit forms of speech in which some are perplexed by ambiguity. Under the bread or wine, the body of Christ is given to us as bread, because what is marked is not a substantial union of corruptible food with Christ's flesh, but a sacramental conjunction. This is not disputed among all the godly, that the bond between the sign and the thing signified is inseparable in the promise itself, because God does not display figures falsely, but truly performs in deed what he shows. Finally he adds: "When these things have been done, doubt still arises concerning the word substance. The ready way to settle this seems to be to remove the gross imagination of eating the flesh, as if it were like corporeal food which, taken into the mouth, slides down into the belly. For when this absurdity has been removed, there is no reason why we should deny that we are substantially fed on Christ's flesh, because we truly grow together with him into one body through faith, and so are made one with him. How easy and how near, even by Calvin's judgement, the agreement is, even in those very words and formulas about which the dispute is fiercest, is plain. Hence he writes that he rejoiced not a little and was helped by the agreement, though not yet full and solid, at least in part, at the beginning at Marburg, in the very opening of his Second Defence of the Sacraments against Westphal. Beza, on many occasions, proposed things similar to this, at the Colloquy of Montbéliard in 1586. Hence our people also repeatedly called the Lutherans brothers in Christ, and by their own example urged that fraternity be cultivated between us, though they were not always met with the humanity and love that were due, as appeared at the colloquies of Marburg, Mömpelgard (Mulbronn) and others. When Beza, at the end of the colloquy, had said: We grieve that we do not agree. Yet we are willing to cultivate brotherhood with you, and had shown himself ready to extend the right hand of fraternity, Jacob Andreae replied that he would offer him the right hand not of fraternity but of humanity; Beza broke off, saying: Since you refuse to extend to us the right hand of fraternity, and do not wish to acknowledge us as brothers, I also refuse the right hand of friendship. And at the Colloquy of Mulbronn, on the ubiquity of Christ's body, between the Palatine and Wittenberg theologians, in 1575, our people everywhere called the others brothers; but they, as usual, rejected fraternity. This too, as the madness of some people does, they habitually reproach us for with intemperate abuse, because we are so ready and eager for peace. Balthasar Mentzer also refused the right hand of fraternity to Landgrave Maurice of Hesse in 1605, as is recorded in the acts of the Marburg colloquy of that year. In these I do not know whether I should admire more the generosity of our people or the inhumanity of the others. Finally, Sculteus, after he had both in person and through letters already pleaded for the making of peace with the theologians of Tübingen, in 1616, at last brought back this answer: They have always received us into political friendship, and will receive us in future into theological friendship, that is, into Christian fraternity, never.

units.la: Concordiae nostrae nihil adeo objici posse videtur, quam famosus liber Concordiae a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxvii : à sex Doctoribus Lutheranis cusus, indeque omnibus obtrusus. Eo tamen etiam non obstante Nostri, videntes librum illum, hoc quidem animo sineque proposito ut Vbiquitatis commentum in canonem referret, sed tamen eo loquendi modo prudenter usos ejus Architectos ut non adeo aperte exprimerent, tum inter ipsos plurimos semper id nobiscum repudiare, perrexerunt in sua erga Lutheranos benevolentia, & fratres compellarunt, etiam in illa Epistola passim, quam Belgice Ecclesiæ a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxix. ad Sexum-viros Bergenses misserunt, apologeticam & expostulatoriam, inscriptam Honorandis in Christo fratribus &c. Sic & praefatio nomine Ecclesiarum Gallicarum & Belgicarum premissa Syntagmati Confessionum a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxi. quæ etiam huic operi inseruit simul Confessionem Augustanam, Saxonicam, & Wittembergensem. Cujus rationem dat Praefatio: & qui longè discrepare putabantur (ut hactenus de nobis & fratribus Augustanæ confessionis propter privata nimium multorum scripta non prorsus immeritò inter judicatum est) si modò intra confessionum fines stetur, & al sit quidem omnis calumnia, & sophistice, adsit vero & sincera & candida interpretatio, quam proximè in omnibus convenire existimandi sint. Atque hac causa fuit cur Augustanam confessionem, unà etiam cum Saxonicâ & Wittembergensi inserere in hac Harmoniâ voluerimus, ut facilius cognosci possit, & nos cum illis in propriis quibusque fidei capitibus consentire, & quam paucissima superesse inter nos controversia. Nam quod ad illam de Cœnâ Domini controversiam attinet, in re, & de re ipsa nulla pugna est, in adjunctis & circumstantiis quibusdam rei variamus. Similiter Admonitio Neosta-
units.tr: No objection against our Concord seems to be stronger than the notorious Book of Concord of 1577, drawn up by six Lutheran doctors and then forced on everyone. Even so, our people, seeing that this book (though not with the intention of making the ubiquity fiction a article of the canon) was framed in such a way by its architects that they did not express it too openly, and seeing that very many Lutherans themselves had always repudiated it with us, persisted in their goodwill toward the Lutherans and addressed them as brothers. They did so also in that Dutch apologetic and expostulatory letter, headed "To the honourable brothers in Christ, etc.," which the Church of the Netherlands sent in 1579 to the Sexumviri of Bergen. So too the preface, written in the name of the French and Dutch Churches and placed before the Syntagma of Confessions of 1581, which also included in that work the Augsburg, Saxon and Wittenberg Confessions. The preface gives the reason: "and those who were thought to differ widely (as up to now about us and the brethren of the Augsburg Confession, not without good cause, has been judged on account of the too many private writings of many men), if only they stand within the bounds of the confessions, and if all calumny and sophistry is absent, and a sincere and candid interpretation is present, ought to be thought to agree with us almost in everything. And this was the reason why we wished to insert the Augsburg Confession, together with the Saxon and Wittenberg, into this Harmony, so that it might more easily be known that we agree with them in each of the proper heads of faith, and that very few controversies remain between us. For as far as that controversy about the Lord's Supper is concerned, there is no fight over the thing itself, and we differ only in certain circumstances and accessories of the matter." Similarly the Admonitio Neostadiensis [the Admonition of Neustadt]... [the passage continues in the next unit].

units.la: diuina, cap. xi. & xii. ubi de vera Christiane Concordia in Ecclesiis constituenda ratione. Ubiquitatis dogma non agnoverunt olim, neque adhuc agnoscunt Theologi Helmstadienses. Quod apparuit in Conventu primum Quedelburgensi a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxi. ubi Tilemannus Heshusius, Daniel Hofmannus, aliique Ducis Brunsvicensis, & Helmstadiensium Concionatores aperte acriterque illi obloquuti fuerunt: neque intellexerunt eam doceri in libro Concordiae, cujus haec super re verba, in articulo de Persona Christi: Quod autem Christus omnipotentia sua divina, corpore suo, quod collocavit ad dexteram majestatis & potentiae Dei, praesens esse possit, ubicunque vult, praesertim in Sacra sua Coena, quo se in verbo suo alligavit, id facile omnipotentia ejus efficere potest, sine abolitione verae suae humanae naturae. Quae verba non docent actualem corporis Christi omnipraesentiam, neque ubicunque hoc esse, sed ubicunque velit esse. Quamvis primi argumenti ariete illa quidem sic concuti statim possint, ut vel ad hoc, vel ad alia absurda confugere necesse habeant. Dico enim, vel corpus Christi ubicunque vult, & in Coena praesens erit, per temporaneum & transitorium descensum, vel per continuam existentiam. Non illud, quod Lutherus in literis ad Helvetios exserte negavit. Atque hoc si esset, jam vel in pluribus terrae locis Christi corpus continuo existeret, vel omnibus. Utrum sumatur, absonum fuerit, & contrarium fidei, ac humanae in Christo naturae. Deinde adversus Tubingenses Theologos super eadem re disputarunt Helmstadienses, edito a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxv, scripto Apologetico Germanice, adversus calumniam, qua accusabantur als selbst sie von der approbierten formula Concordiae abgefallen seyn, darumb das sie die ungegründte Ubiquitatem carnis Christi nicht billichen. Subscribunt quidem formulae Concordiae; non tamen dogmati Ubiquitatis. Idem & hodie Helmstadienses sunt. Calixtus, in Iudicio suo, pag. 5. infaustum centamen de ubiquitate appellat, motum primò à Iacobo Fabro Stapulensi, atque à Luthero quidem aliquando in fervore contentionis adversus Zwinglium arreptum, sed postea omissum, tandem à Iohanne Brentio, & Iacobo Andreâ tantis viribus resuscitatum, ut scribat, hunc posteriorem, nulli operæ pepercisse, donec ubiquitatem aliis persuasisset, aliis obtrusisset. Neque tamen omnibus Augustanam confessionem amplexis, sive ut vocant Lutheranis persuadere eam potuit, non Danis, non Holsatis, non Norimbergensibus, non Helmstadiensibus, non aliis pluribus. Stat itaque ab ubiquitate hodie saltem aliqua pars eorum, qui Lutherani dicuntur; contra eam verò, quicquid reliquorum est Christianorum, toto Orbe, tum Orientalium, tum Græcorum, tum Pontificiorum, tum Calvinianorum. Neque præter rem censeri potest quod scribit Vir magni Iudicii M. Aneton. de Dominis lib. sua VII. C. XI. n. 5. Ubiquitatem corporis Christi adhuc magis, quam est transfusio substantiæ, absurdam, magisque impossibilem omnis boni Theologi semper respuet: adfirmare eam non est boni Philosophi, neque boni Theologi. Et quis non merito cohorreat ad tam monstrosam corporis Christi ubiquitatem; de quâ Brentius ad Heshusium dixit, in Quedelburgensi Colloquio: Idem corpus Christi etiam Romæ et Athenis fuisse invisibiliter eo tempore, quo Christus in cruce pependit. Hoc cœlum Brentianum, quod se non expectare, neque in eo suum πολίτευμα esse Petrus Martyr, in supremis constitutus, Bullingero respondit. Denique eadem Ubiquitate alter ille ejus patronus Iacobus Andreas ad Langravium Hassiæ VVilhelmum a. cIↄ Iↄ IXXIX. quum eum ad Libri Concordiæ subscriptionem importunius sollicitaret: Christus in adscensione suâ ne pilo quidem à terrâ recessit. Atque ipse quoque Lutherus antea dixerat: Corpus Christi esse in quovis etiam pane taberna pistoria: et in fune sive laqueo, quo Iudas se suspenderit. Quæ verba magno conatu defensum it Leon. Hutterus, lib. Concordia Concors. cap. 1. Verba Pauli, ut implerentur
units.tr: ...diuina, chapters 11 and 12, where the method of establishing true Christian concord in the Churches is set out. The theologians of Helmstedt neither acknowledged the dogma of ubiquity in the past, nor do they acknowledge it now. This appeared first at the colloquy at Quedlinburg in 1581, where Tilemann Heshusius, Daniel Hofmann and others, preachers of the Duke of Brunswick and of Helmstedt, openly and sharply opposed it; nor did they understand that it was taught in the Book of Concord, whose words on this matter, in the article on the Person of Christ, are these: "That Christ, by his divine omnipotence, can be present with his body, which he placed at the right hand of the majesty and power of God, wherever he wills, especially in his Holy Supper, to which he has bound himself in his word, his omnipotence can easily bring about, without the abolition of his true human nature." These words do not teach the actual omnipresence of Christ's body, nor that it is everywhere, but that it is wherever he wills to be. Yet the battering-ram of this first argument can at once be so shaken that they must take refuge in this or other absurdities. For I say: either the body of Christ is wherever it wills and will be present in the Supper through a temporary and transitory descent, or through continuous existence. Not the former, which Luther expressly denied in his letters to the Swiss. And if it were the latter, then Christ's body would already exist continuously either in many places on earth or in all. Whichever is assumed, it would be absurd and contrary to faith and to the human nature of Christ. Then the Helmstedt theologians disputed on the same matter against the Tübingen theologians, publishing in 1585 a German apologetic writing against the calumny by which they were accused of having fallen away from the approved formula of Concord, because they did not approve of the groundless ubiquity of Christ's flesh. They indeed subscribe to the Formula of Concord, but not to the dogma of ubiquity. The Helmstedt men are the same today. Calixtus, in his Judgment, p. 5, calls the ubiquity "an unlucky dispute," set in motion first by James Lefèvre of Étaples, and taken up by Luther in the heat of his contest with Zwingli, but afterwards dropped, and at last revived with such force by John Brenz and Jacob Andreae that, as he writes, the latter "spared no effort until he had persuaded some of ubiquity and imposed it on others." Yet he could not persuade all who embraced the Augsburg Confession, or as they call them, the Lutherans: not the Danes, not the Holsteiners, not the Nurembergers, not the Helmstedt men, nor many others. So today at least some part of those who are called Lutherans stands for ubiquity; but against it stands whatever remains of Christians throughout the whole world, Eastern, Greek, Papist and Calvinist alike. Nor can it be deemed beside the point what Michael Antonius de Dominis writes, a man of great judgment, in book 7, ch. 11, n. 5 of his work: "The ubiquity of Christ's body, being even more absurd and more impossible than transubstantiation, every good theologian will always reject; to affirm it belongs neither to a good philosopher nor to a good theologian." And who would not rightly shudder at so monstrous a ubiquity of Christ's body? Brenz said of it to Heshusius at the Quedlinburg colloquy: "The same body of Christ was also invisibly at Rome and at Athens at the time when Christ hung on the cross." This is the Brenzian heaven, which Peter Martyr, on his deathbed, said he did not expect, and that in it was not his citizenship, in his reply to Bullinger. Finally, the other patron of the same ubiquity, James Andreae, pressing the Landgrave of Hesse, William, in 1579 more insistently to subscribe the Book of Concord, wrote: "Christ at his ascension did not withdraw even a hair's breadth from the earth." Luther himself had said before: "The body of Christ is in every bread, even in a bakery; and in the rope or noose with which Judas hanged himself." Leonhard Hutter defended these words with great effort in his Concordia Concors, ch. 1. Luther explained the words of Paul, "that all things might be filled," as a sack is filled and stretched with grain;

units.la: IXX tur omnia, sic explicuit Lutherus; quemadmodum saccus frumento impletur ac distenditur: Zuinglius, in Exegesi Eucharist. negot. pag. 345. itemum Apol. ad Lutheri Sermon. contra Swermeros, pag. 392. Tom. II. Lubecenses, in disput. cum Mart. Micronio a. cI5 I5 I v. dicebant, Christum ita ubique existere, ut sit in omni gramine terrae. Verum quia Vbiquitas illa non ab omnibus Lutheranis, uti audivimus, defendiatur, Nostri quoque, eâ missâ, inhaerentes controversiae Sacramentariae, hanc fraterne componendam semper existimarunt. Quo faciunt plurima Nostrorum communia scripta, & privata, vel à singularibus, vel communi aliquorum, seu Ecclesiarum, aut Academiarum nomine edita. Theologorum Heidelbergensium lib: Christliche Ermahnung, &c. Barth. Bythneri, nomine Ecclesiarum Polonicarum Exhortatio. Antonii Corvani, diaconi Bellerive, Ministri Antverpiensis, a. cI5 I5 lxvii. epistola ad Socios Augustanae Confessionis, in eâdem urbe: quam refert Borrius, in Annalibus Belgicis, lib. III. Hermanni Pacifici, revera Christophori Herdesiani, Vrbis Norimbergensis syndici, Simplex ac dilucida expositio, quâ ratione controversia de Coenâ Domini orta, facile cognosci & componi possit, anno cI5 I5 lxxvIII. Erasmi Sabini Hohsneri Lutheranorum & Calvinistarum, id est, Ecclesiarum evangelicarum consensus in doctrinâ de Coenâ, & personâ Christi, Germanicè, a. cI5 I5 cvii. Davidis Parei Irenicum, a. cI5 I5 cxv. qui ad hoc scribendum motus quodam libro Germanico, Motiven und Ursachen / Rationes propter quas Principes Lutherani cum Calvinistis in negotio Religionis contra Papistas simul stare nec possint, nec debeant, uti colligere est ex libri capite xxix. quas Motivas omnes ex professo refutat. Et quamvis acerbe ejus Irenicum Hutterus exagitarit, non tamen par pari retulit Pareus, sed modestiâ & charitate alterius malam vicit intemperiem, ostendens quod semel dixerat, atque in brevibus adversus HutHutte[?]um Notis statim initio repetit, nolle se, ut Irenicum suum[?] fieret polemicum. A. clɔ Ⅰɔ xxxi. à iii. Martii ad xxiii. Lipsiæ, in Conventu Electorum & Principum Protestantium Germaniæ, colloquuti inter se diebus aliquot fuerunt, suo tantum nomine, & sine cujusquam, de quo in exordio & fine Colloquii utrimque solemniter protestati, præjudicio, tres à Nostrâ, & totidem ab aliâ parte Theologi. Hinc Matthias Hoë, Polycarpus Lyserus, Henricus Hoffner: à nostrâ parte, Iohannes Bergius, Iohannes Crocius, Theophilus Neoburgus. Egerunt de omnibus Augustanæ Confessionis articulis ordine, quibus Nostri subscripturos se offerebant; atque ad decimum articulum de Cœnâ, quæstionem de modo communicationis suspensam reliquerunt, quomodo olim in Colloquio Marpurgensi. In reliquis etiam parum discrepabant. Præmittebatur hoc ceu tentamen majoris & generalis Concordiæ instituendæ; ad quam tempora, & Conventus iste videbantur invitare. Sequuta variorum hinc inde, qua Theologorum, qua Politicorum studia & consilia in eandem rem, procurante hæc cum primis & promovente Ioh. Du[?]ræo Scoto-Britanno. Qui conquisitis judiciis Theologorum Anglorum, interque eos Davenantii, Mortoni, Halli, à. clɔ Ⅰɔ cxxiv: quæ simul edita, promovendis negotium Archiepiscopis Cantuariensibus, Abbotto primum, deinde Laudo; habitis etiam Theologorum Gallorum, Transylvanorum, Belgarum judiciis, Scotorum quoque; (quorum judicium inseruit Instructionibus Historiæ Theologicæ lib. xxvi. cap. vii.) Ioh. Forbesius, tum temporis in Abredonensi Academiâ Theol. Professor, apud Germanos, & Suecos indefessam posuit operam, ad negotium syncretismi, in Colloquio Lipsiaco inchoati, promovendum, perficiendumque: ad quod quum Nostri se promptos, politici & Principes inter Lutheranos non alienos ostenderent, horum Theologi (neque tamen id de omnibus dictum) primò remoram & obstacula suggerrent, inde totum negotium abrumpere & dissipare annisi sunt, promulgato à V. Vitembergensi Theologo Hulsemanno feralι libro, Calvinismi irreconciliabilis: quo eluserunt suorum Nostrorumque vota & labores pro faciendâ Ecclesiarum unione, non omnino absque fructu jam aliquo usquequam producta. Quibus, a. cIↄ Iↄ c xlı. mense Januario Epistolicam Dissertationem, quâ eos schismatis continuati inter Protestantes merito reos agit, Durœus opposuit. Idem Hulsemannus est, qui in Colloquio nupero Torunensi, a, Iↄ Iↄ c xlv. postquam sess. v. hæc Manifestatio à Reformatis facta fuisset: Quod in hoc Colloquio, alii Catholici Romani, alii Augustani, alii vero Reformati dicantur, id nihil parti quidquam præjudicare, neque ita accipi debet, quod Augustani & Reformati non essent membra Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, vel quasi Augustani non essent Reformati, vel Reformati non essent Augustanæ Confessionis Socii, sed hæ partium appellationes discriminis ergo in hoc Colloquio adhibentur: turbas omnibus movit, & sess. vi re. solemniter reprotestatus est contra prædictam D D. Reformatorum Manifestationem, postquam intellexit eam in Acta relatam esse: se non permissere communionem Augustanæ Confessionis socio rum D D. Reformatis, quoad communionem dogmatum. Atque ita semper homines illi vel tentatis vel initiis Consensionis viis se impotenter opposuere, & intermissæ, vel ruptæ Concordiæ primi ubique extiterunt auctores.
units.tr: ...Zwingli, in his Exegesis of the Eucharistic controversy, p. 345, likewise Apology for Luther's sermon against the Swabian fanatics, p. 392, vol. II. The Lübeck men, in a disputation with Martin Micron in 1555, said that Christ exists everywhere in such a way that he is in every blade of grass on the earth. But since that ubiquity is not, as we have heard, defended by all Lutherans, our people too, setting it aside and keeping to the sacramentarian controversy, have always thought that it should be settled in a brotherly way. To this many common and private writings of our side point, whether published by individuals or in the name of some group, or of Churches or Academies: the Heidelberg theologians' book, Christian Exhortation, etc.; Bartholomew Bythner's Exhortation in the name of the Polish Churches; the letter of Antonius Corvanus, deacon of Bellerive and minister at Antwerp, to the associates of the Augsburg Confession in the same city, in 1567, which Borrius cites in his Belgian Annals, book III; the Simple and Clear Exposition of Hermann Pacificus (really Christoph Herdesian, syndic of the city of Nuremberg), by which the controversy about the Lord's Supper that arose can easily be understood and settled, in 1578; Erasmus Sabinus Hohsner's Consensus of the Lutherans and Calvinists, that is, of the evangelical Churches, on the doctrine of the Supper and the person of Christ, in German, in 1607; David Pareus's Irenicum, in 1615, who, moved to write it by a German book, Motives and Causes (Rationes propter quas Principes Lutherani cum Calvinistis in negotio Religionis contra Papistas simul stare nec possint, nec debeant), as may be gathered from chapter 29 of that book, and who refutes all those Motives expressly. And although Hutter harshly attacked his Irenicum, Pareus did not repay him in kind, but overcame the other's bad temper with moderation and charity, showing what he had once said, and in the short Notes against Hutter repeats at once at the beginning that he did not wish his Irenicum to become polemical. From 3 to 23 March 1631 at Leipzig, at a meeting of the Electors and Protestant Princes of Germany, the theologians of each side, three from ours and as many from the other, spoke together for some days, in their own name only and without prejudice to anyone, as both sides solemnly protested at the beginning and end of the colloquy. From the other side were Matthias Hoë, Polycarp Leyser, Henry Höffner; from ours, John Berg, John Croc, Theophilus Neuburg. They went through all the articles of the Augsburg Confession in order, to which our side offered to subscribe; and at the tenth article, on the Supper, they left the question about the mode of communication undecided, as once at the Colloquy of Marburg. In the other matters too they differed little. This was put forward as a trial of a greater and general concord to be undertaken; to which times and that meeting seemed to invite. There followed on this side and that various studies and counsels, both of theologians and of politicians, on the same business, chiefly undertaken and promoted by John Dury, a Scot-Briton, who, having gathered the judgments of English theologians, among them Davenant, Morton and Hall, published in 1634, these being published together to promote the business by the Archbishops of Canterbury, first Abbot, then Laud; and having also obtained the judgments of French, Transylvanian and Dutch theologians, and of the Scots too (whose judgment he included in his Instructions of Theological History, book 26, ch. 7), John Forbes, at that time professor of theology in the Academy of Aberdeen, spent tireless effort among Germans and Swedes to advance and complete the business of syncretism begun at the Leipzig colloquy. When our people showed themselves ready for it, and the politicians and princes among the Lutherans were not unfavourable, their theologians (though this is not said of all) first suggested hindrances and obstacles, and then strove to break off and scatter the whole business, by publishing the deadly book of an irreconcilable Calvinism by the Wittenberg theologian Hülsemann, by which they mocked the wishes and labours of their own people and ours for achieving union of the Churches, which had already produced some fruit here and there. Against these things, in January 1641, Dury opposed an epistolary dissertation charging them with rightly being guilty of continuing the schism among Protestants. It is the same Hülsemann who, at the recent colloquy of Thorn in 1645, after the fifth session, when this Manifestation had been made by the Reformed (that in this colloquy some are called Roman Catholics, others Augsburgers, and others Reformed; this prejudices nothing for either party, nor should it be understood as meaning that the Augsburgers and Reformed were not members of the Catholic Church, or that the Augsburgers were not Reformed, or the Reformed were not associates of the Augsburg Confession, but these designations of the parties are used in this colloquy for the sake of distinction), stirred up a disturbance among all, and in the sixth session solemnly protested again against the aforesaid Manifestation of the Reformed gentlemen, once he understood that it had been recorded in the Acts: that he did not permit communion with the Reformed gentlemen, associates of the Augsburg Confession, as far as communion in doctrines goes. And so those men, always opposing the attempted ways and beginnings of consensus, have everywhere been the first authors of broken or interrupted concord.

units.la: De syncretismo potius Lipsiæ inito scribit Michael V. Valtherus, in Centuria Miscellan. Theol. cap. xxx. Consensum Marpurgensem primus violavit Lutherus, a. cIↄ Iↄxxxı r. edita ad Marchionem Brandeburgensem epistolâ, quâ in Zuinglianos, ut Sacramentarios, hæreticos, & fanaticos invehitur: similiter anno sequente, ad Francofurtenses. Hic quoque V. Vitembergensem Concordiam fregit, a. cIↄ Iↄ xxx ix. pristinâ acerbitate usus adversus Zuinglium, & Tigurinos, in libro de Concordia. Melancholanthonem improbe vexarunt, ac tantum non in exilium egerint sui V Vittembergenses. Adversus Paulum Eberum, qui in libro, Pia & in verbo Dei fundata assertio de Cœnâ Domini, abhorrere se dicit ab illâ quorundam vehementiâ, qui ita præsentiam corporis Christi in cœnâ defendunt, ut prorsus ab Ecclesiâ & fidei universæ consortio excludant omnes, qui non eodem modo, sicut ipsi consueverunt, de præsentiâ corporis Christi in Cœnâ sentire, & loqui didicerunt: clamarunt mox a. MDLXV. Ministrii Comitatus Mansfeldensis, & acerbe eum insectari fuerunt. Contra Sendomiriensem Consensum vociferati, starim sunt Vilnenses Lutherani: adversus nuperos tractatus & negotia, V Vittrembergenses: atque, ut de Colloquio Lipsiensi loquitur Joh. Micraelius, in Syntagm. Histor. pag. 487. nihil aliud postea effectum est, quam ut D. Hoë & D. Bergius scriptis se invicem lacesserent: Et quanquam alias visum est, illa religionis capita, in quibus utriusque partis Theologi consentiunt, abunde sufficere, tum ad salutem hominis Christiani, tum ad solidiorem pacem in Ecclesiis Dei stabiliendam, non tamen sine causa alii verentur, nisi Deus ipse animos dissidentium, & quidem in fundamentalibus fidei articulis, in viâ veritatis confirmet, ne frustra sit omnis conatus, quem præter Lipsiacos Joh. Duræus hactenus magno studio adhibuit, ut tapita illa controversiarum & reliqua obstacula inter nostrates & Calvinianos tollantur, quæ obstare videntur, quò minus in unum Ecclesiæ corpus coalescamus. Id est, nulla nobis cum illis concordia speranda, nisi illorum accipiamus opiniones salvis sententiis nihil expectandum. Ira semper impedire ac rumpere Concordiam sategerunt inquieti & rixosi homines: quod adeo non dissitentur, ut gloriae ducant. Certe non Christianorum, vel Dei filiorum, aut Theologorum gloriâ. Sed adeo quidem à viis pacis, id est, optimis quibusque absunt, & horrent. Hinc Eckhardus, ante Fasciculum suarum Controversiarum, ubi tum praefigurat Calvinistas, tum fanaticos & versipelles im- postea postares appellat, in prima Præfatione ad Georgium Saxoniæ Ducem, de nobis inquit: Quinto denique angun-tur dissidere se à nobis non in fundamento Religionis, sed in rebus levioribus, quæ parum habeant momenti: nec de quæstionibus numero multis, sed paucissimis controversiam esse, de quibus citra fidei naufragium & pacis atque fraternitatis jacturam dissensio esse queat. Deinde: Ex articulis enim cardinalibus & fundamentalibus, ne unum quidem Theologia Calvinistica inviolatum nobis relinquit. Et in altera Præfatione, ad Saxoniæ Electorem, Christianum 1. eâdem vesania, & vertigine correptus: cum tam inter summum cælum & imam terram tanta non sit distantia, quanta inter Augustanam Confessionem & Calvinistarum ἑτεροδοξίας, nec magis inter Calvinistas & Augustana Confessionis Theologos, quàm inter Christum & Belial, fraternitas, iniri aut conjunctio fieri queat. Postea etiam: In articulis profectò non paucis neque levibus discrepantia summa est: nec magis, quàm inter lucem & tenebras conciliatio tentari potest. Quid agas istis hominibus, vel quam hic mediteris consensionem? Integrum, & satis spissum librum scripsit Nicolaus Hunnius, de fundamentali dissensu doctrinæ Evangelicæ Lutheranæ, & Calviniana seu Reformata. Confer Philippi Nicolai præfat. ad libros suos de Omnipræsentiâ Christi. Feurbornii Dedicat: ad tractatum, de Peccato in Spiritum S. V Vittembergenses adversus Palatinorum Ermahnung/p.27. Hutterum & Sigwartum, contra Ironicum Parei. Hunc præsertim lib.1.c.1. & lib.11.c.1,11, modestior tamen disputat Huttero. Friderico Balduino V Vittembergensi Theologo haud satis fuit disputationes conscribere, easque satis prolixas, de Eucharistia Calvinianorum; de Baptismo Calvinianorum; nisi etiam de Christo Calvinianorum, quasi videlicet alium nos Christum habeamus, disputasset. V Veberi, contra quem disputat Ioh. Lampadius, in Prodromo Concordiæ Evangelicæ, hoc erat argumentum; inter quos Christus est divisus, illi non possunt esse ejusdem doctrinae fratres. Atqui inter Lutheranos & Calvinianos Christus est divisus. Ergo. Michael V. Valtherus, in Centuria Miscellaneorum Theologicorum, xxxviii. pag. 370. Quaesitum fuit à Pastore quodam in Belgio: Num Calviniani verum habeant Coenae Sacramentum? Respondi, minime gentium. Conradus Schlusselburgius, in epistola ad Pelargum, cujus supra meminimus, eum non modo apostatam vocat, sed Calvinianos blasphemos, Sacramentarios, Scripturae Sacrae falsarios, & haereticos manifestos, ipsius Cacodaemonis ministros, errores blasphemos. lueri[?], de nullo fere Christiano articulo doctrinae recte sentire & docere, Berengarium Calvinistarum in Gallia patronum, quamvis errorem revocarit, tamen cum sua aeterna damnatione expectatum veritatem morte animi hunc, & Oecolampadium extinctum, quorum exemplo etiam Pelargus, siquidem in apostasia pervicax manserit, secundum Dei justum judicium aeternum periturus, quare ut eum Deus in apostasia sua perseverantem evertat et confundat, precatur. Se vero Calvinianos perfecto odio tanquam haereticos, secundum Dei mandatum prosequi, scribit. Quis non immani aliquo daemone possessum hominem, talia efflagitantem, putet? Hoccine Christianum, vel Evangelicum est, deiectum aliquem à Lutheranis ad nos, tantis odiis prosequi atque aeterno devovere exitio? sic Lutheranum, certe non est Theologicum, nisi odii istius, quod proverbio locum dedit, Theologici. Quid dicam blasphemum librum Zachaei Fabri, Germanicè scriptum, Beweis das die Calvinische Lehr ärger sey als die Papistische / Calvinistarum multorum religionem multà detestarem esse Papisticâ: ubi in genere de Calvinistis non modo hoc satagit probare, sed & pejores illos esse ipsis, qui Christum crucifixerunt pag. 60. Ethnicis, pag. 89. 118. Turcis pag. 124. quin etiam Diabolo, scribit pag. 126. quod pag. 128. multis supra ducenta ac trecenta argumentis se probaturum mentitur, nempe Calvinistarum dodoctrinam pejorem & damnabiliorem esse ipso Diabolo; quare multis anathematismis execrandam pag. 80. neque in imperio tolerandam, pag. 115. Johannes Affelmannus, Professl. Rostochiensis, scripsit Disputationem, Trias Syllogismorum Anti-Calvinisticorum, ubi hunc primum facit syllogismum, Deus Calvinistarum, est 1. Auctor et causa peccatorum. 2. Vere peccans. 3. Et magis quidem quam homo. 4. Est hypocrita, & dolosus, pessimus. 5. Est iniquissimus & impiissimus. 6. Est Diabolus, immo ۷. Diabolo deterior: Et ejusdem disp. syllogismo tertio: Doctrina Calvinianorum tanta est prophanitas & abominatio, ut fidem Christianam simpliciter salvam e medio, & quemlibet in sua religione salvari posse credant, nec certum est cuiusque religionis non agere sortè, sed religionem ludere, ut testatur. At Doctrina Calvinianorum tanta est prophanitas, impietas & abominatio. Ergo. Ad quae quis non totus contremiscat? Et haec probat, sequiturque Abrahamus Calovius, in Epist. Dedic. ad Criticum sacrum, in Confess. Augustanam: ubi totis viribus se opponit concordiae Ecclesiasticae, ejusque promotoribus Crocio & Duaeo, variisque argumentis apud Succiae Regimen & Proceres sustendere conatur, inter Lutheranos & Reformatos dissensiones esse de fide, non leves, sed praecipuas & fundamentales, in decem articulis nos discrepare ab Augustana Confessione, & in controversiis plusquam triginta gravissimis de doctrina dissidere: quare & consilium unionis pacificae inter Ecclesias & Confessiones hinc inde, verbo Dei è diametro adversari, Samaritanismum sapere, à pietate esse alienum, carnale, subdolum, scandalosum & periculosissimum. Nunc, & cum talibus hominibus pacem expete, vel iis laboriose offer, quam praefracte nolunt, detestantur, oppugnant. Quid similis notae libros recensebo, solis titulis horrendos: Calvinianorum Nestorianismus. Calvinus Judaizans. Calvino Papismus. Dum non vero Deus der Calvinisten. Et si qui similis deteris & plu-
units.tr: Michael Walther writes about the syncretism rather, which was entered into at Leipzig, in his Centuria Miscellaneorum Theologicorum, chapter 30. Luther was the first to violate the Marburg agreement, in 1529, in a letter to the Margrave of Brandenburg in which he attacks the Zwinglians as sacramentarian, heretical and fanatical; he did the same the following year in a letter to the people of Frankfurt. Here too the Wittenbergers broke the Wittenberg Concord, in 1536, using their old harshness against Zwingli and the Zurichers in his book On Concord. The Wittenbergers treated Melanchthon shamefully and all but drove him into exile. Against Paul Eber, who in his book A devout assertion of the Lord's Supper, founded on the Word of God, said that he shrank from that vehemence of some who so defend the presence of Christ's body in the Supper that they utterly exclude from the Church and from the fellowship of the whole faith all who have not learned to think and speak about the presence of Christ's body in the Supper in the same way that they themselves are accustomed to, the ministers of the County of Mansfeld cried out at once, in 1565, and attacked him bitterly. The Lutherans of Vilnius raised an outcry against the Sandomierz Consensus at once, and the Wittenbergers against recent treaties and negotiations. And, as Johann Micraelius says of the Colloquy of Leipzig, in his Syntagma Historicum, page 487: nothing else came of it afterwards than that Dr. Hoë and Dr. Bergius provoked each other with writings. And although at other times it has been thought that those articles of religion on which the theologians of both parties agree are amply sufficient both for the salvation of a Christian and for establishing a firmer peace in the Churches of God, yet others fear, not without reason, that unless God himself confirms the minds of the dissenters, and indeed on the fundamental articles of faith, in the way of truth, all effort is in vain, the effort which, apart from the Leipzig men, John Durr has hitherto applied with great zeal, so that those knotty controversies and the other obstacles between our people and the Calvinists, which seem to stand in the way of our coalescing into one body of the Church, may be removed. That is to say, no concord with them is to be hoped for unless we accept their opinions, the statements of the Augsburg Confession being given up. So restless and quarrelsome men have always striven to hinder and break concord; and they do not deny this so far as to count it a glory. Certainly it is not the glory of Christians, or of the sons of God, or of theologians. But they are so far from the ways of peace, that is, from all the best things, and they shrink from them. Hence Eckhardt, before his Fasciculus of Controversies, where he first censures the Calvinists and then calls the fanatics and the slippery impostors by their names, says in the first preface, addressed to George, Duke of Saxony, concerning us: Lastly, they are at pains to say that they differ from us not on the foundation of religion but in lesser matters of little weight; nor is the controversy over many questions but over very few, on which dissent can exist without shipwreck of the faith and loss of peace and brotherhood. Then: For from the cardinal and fundamental articles he leaves us not even one point of Calvinist theology unviolated. And in the other preface, to the Elector of Saxony, he, seized by the same madness and vertigo, says: since between the highest heaven and the lowest earth there is not so great a distance as between the Augsburg Confession and the heterodoxies of the Calvinists, and no more can brotherhood be entered into or union effected between the Calvinists and the theologians of the Augsburg Confession than between Christ and Belial. Later also: In articles certainly not few or slight the discrepancy is great, and no more than a reconciliation between light and darkness can be attempted. What can one do with such men, or what agreement do you contemplate here? Nicolaus Hunnius wrote a whole and rather thick book on the fundamental disagreement between the Evangelical doctrine of the Lutherans and the Calvinist or Reformed. Compare the preface of Philip Nicolai to his books on the Omnipresence of Christ; the dedication by Feuerborn to his treatise on the sin against the Holy Spirit; the Wittenbergers against the Ermahnung of the Palatines, page 27; Hutter and Sigwart, against the Ironicum of Pareus, especially book 1, chapter 1, and book 11, chapters 1 and 11, though he disputes more modestly than Hutter. Friedrich Balduin, a Wittenberg theologian, was not content to write disputations, and quite long ones, on the Eucharist of the Calvinists and on the Baptism of the Calvinists; he must also dispute about the Christ of the Calvinists, as though we had some other Christ. Weber, against whom John Lampadius disputes in his Prodromus of Evangelical Concord, had this argument: those among whom Christ is divided cannot be brothers in the same doctrine. But among Lutherans and Calvinists Christ is divided. Therefore. Michael Walther, in his Centuria Miscellaneorum Theologicorum, number 38, page 370: a certain pastor in Belgium was asked whether the Calvinists have the true sacrament of the Supper. I answered, by no means. Conrad Schlüsselburg, in his letter to Pelargus, whom we mentioned above, calls him not only an apostate but calls the Calvinists blasphemers, sacramentarians, falsifiers of Holy Scripture, manifest heretics, ministers of the Cacodaemon himself, and propagators of blasphemous errors. Luer(?) writes that they think and teach almost no Christian article of doctrine rightly; he calls Berengar the patron of the Calvinists in France, who, although he revoked his error, nevertheless with his eternal damnation awaits the truth extinguished by the death of his soul, and Oecolampadius likewise; and by their example Pelargus too, if indeed he remains obstinate in apostasy, is destined to perish eternally according to God's just judgment. Therefore he prays that God may overthrow and confound him while he persists in his apostasy. He writes that he himself pursues the Calvinists with perfect hatred as heretics, according to God's command. Who would not think that such a man, who demands such things, is possessed by some monstrous demon? Is it Christian, or evangelical, to pursue with such hatreds, and to doom to eternal destruction, someone cast out from the Lutherans to us? Such a Lutheran is certainly not a theologian, except in that hatred which has given a proverb its place: theological hatred. What shall I say of the blasphemous book of Zacharias Faber, written in German, Proof that the Calvinist doctrine is worse than the Papist, in which, in general, about the Calvinists he not only labours to prove this but also that they are worse than those who crucified Christ, page 60; worse than the heathens, pages 89 and 118; worse than the Turks, page 124; and even worse than the Devil himself, he writes on page 126; and on page 128 he falsely claims that he will prove this by more than two or three hundred arguments, namely that the doctrine of the Calvinists is worse and more damnable than the Devil himself; therefore it is to be execrated with many anathemas on page 80, and not to be tolerated in the Empire, page 115. Johannes Affelmann, professor at Rostock, wrote a disputation, Three Syllogisms against the Calvinists, in which he makes this first syllogism: the God of the Calvinists is (1) the author and cause of sins; (2) truly sinning; (3) and more so than a man; (4) he is a hypocrite and deceiver, most wicked; (5) he is most unjust and most impious; (6) he is the Devil, nay (7) worse than the Devil. And in the third syllogism of the same disputation: the doctrine of the Calvinists is so profane and abominable that they believe the Christian faith is simply removed from the midst, and that anyone can be saved in his own religion, nor is it certain that each religion is not perhaps a matter of chance, but a religion played with, as he testifies. But the doctrine of the Calvinists is so profane, impious and abominable. Therefore. At these things who would not tremble all over?
