And Abraham Calovius approves these things and follows them, in his dedicatory epistle to the Critica sacra, on the Augsburg Confession, where with all his might he sets himself against Church concord and its promoters, Crocius and Duraeus, and by various arguments tries to persuade the government and nobles of Sweden that the disagreements between the Lutherans and the Reformed about faith are not slight but chief and fundamental; that we differ from the Augsburg Confession in ten articles and disagree in more than thirty very grave controversies of doctrine; and that therefore a plan for a peaceful union between the Churches and Confessions on either side is directly opposed to the Word of God, savours of Samaritanism, is alien to piety, and is carnal, deceitful, scandalous and most dangerous. Now you seek peace with such men, or offer it to them with effort, which they stubbornly refuse, detest and assail. Why should I list books of similar note, horrible by their titles alone: The Nestorianism of the Calvinists, Calvin Judaizing, Papism for Calvin, The God of the Calvinists is not the true God, and others of a similar and worse kind, and many more things. Melanchthon long ago saw these things and groaned over them, in his letter to Vitus Theodorus, in 1543: Do you think I hear our people with no great pain, when they sometimes speak much more mildly of the Rhenish Churches than of the Turks? You too sometimes...

units.la: ras res. Haec iam olim Melanthon vidit, & ingemuit, In epistola ad Vitum Theodorum, a. clɔ Iɔ xliii. Ita me magno sine dolore nostros audire putas, qui interdum multo mitius de Ecclesiis Rhenanis loquuntur, quam de Turcis? Te quoque interdum doleo, horridius loqui. nedum ut nos deteriores habeant Pontificii. Lucas Osiander in Conclusione Enchiridii Controversiarum cum Calvinianis, pag. 294. Romanus equidem Antichristus Ecclesiae faciem misere deformavit: non autem meliorem se gerit spiritus Calvinisticus, & in quibusdam etiam Papam superat. Similiter Matthias Hoe, in epist. ad Comitem Ioachimum Andreae Schlick, scripta a. clɔ Iɔcxix die xxiii Augusti, postea edita: Nos orientalem Antichristum appellat, atque componit cum occidentali, ut non multo meliorem. Hoc iam ipsis Pontificiis observatum, nos prae ipsis Lutheranis exosos esse. Famianus Strada Decad. i. Belli Belgici, lib. v. ad annum clɔ Iɔ Ixvii. Lutherani enim odio Calvinianorum, a quibus longe arctius quam a Catholicis dissidebant, non ea tamen sua sangebantur. Loquitur de Lutheranis Antverpiae cladem nostrorum sub Domino Tholoso, haud procul ab urbe, non solum placide spectantibus, sed & adversum Nostros se cum Pontificiis Hispanisque conjungentibus. Neque certe usquequaque sidos illos Nostri sensere. Quod supra lib. iv. pag. 271, de Cardinalis Lotharingi rationario adduximus ex Zanchio, hujus quoque loci est, ut debite perpendatur. Quid, annon ad eam usque rabiem nonnullos illorum abreptos novimus, ut Martyres nostros, quorum tum temporis magnus ubique numerus erat, palam dicere auderent, Diaboli esse Martyres? Melanthon, a. clɔ Iɔ Ivııı, epist. ad Ioachimum Camerarium: Optas Princeps communes multarum gentium colloquium. Mihi videtur recte hoc scribi, ne videamur fremitus lictoris Balsini probare, ubi vocentur quidam martyres Anglicos esse martyres diaboli. Nolim hac continuare afficere Spiritum sanctum, in Latimero, qui annum octo. {Sexagesimum} egressus fuit, & in aliis sanctis viris, quos sup. Iodoch. VVestphalus illud scripsit, in libro contra Ioh. à Lasco: quem Senatui Francofurtanae urbis, ubi Lascus erat, & potestatem erigendae exulum peregrinorum, praesertim Belgarum Ecclesiae, cui & Dathenus praefuit, acceperat, inscripsit: eos, qui pro asserenda veritate, & gloria Dei suum sanguinem effuderunt in Anglia, Belgio, Gallia, & alibi, esse Martyres Diaboli. Scilicet tantum religio potuit suadere malorum. Sunt qui cum talibus fortis pacem expetunt, aut fraternam communionem, qui Spiritui sancto tam manifeste obloquuntur, & Martyres, quos Deus accipit, Ecclesia honorat, ipsique persequutores venerati fuere, Diabolo assignant. Pessimum hominum genus, non dicam Christianorum, qui otio luxuque dissolventes, nunc in contentiones fastumque proni, eos qui salutari cruce & persequutionibus gravissimis exercentur, quosque nocte quovis crudelissima veritatis ac conscientiae puritatem redimunt, contemnunt, convitiantur, damnant. Quod nos docet, in agitandis syncretismi consiliis caute prudenterque versari, & imprimis videre, quibuscum illa tractentur. Sed omnino stratagema Diaboli timorandum, quod inter Lutheranos adversum Nos odii, atque hominum crimina nationibus subest, ut sciamus ex qua causa haec emanent. Est autem hoc, quod sentientes doctrinae nostrae & veritatis vim adversus truda sua dogmata putant, nisi suos homines validis vociferationibus, calumniis & diris a nobis abstrahant, facile doctrinam nostram admissuros esse, unde, ne hoc eveniat, ista methodo agendum sibi censent, sed quam nolint a Pontificiis mutuatam, eoque vel solo nomine debere omnibus esse exosum.
units.tr: Melanchthon saw this long ago and lamented it, in his letter to Vitus Theodorus, 1543: "Do you think I hear our people without great pain, when they sometimes speak much more gently of the Rhenish churches than of the Turks? I too grieve that you sometimes speak more harshly, not to mention that the Papists treat us worse." Lucas Osiander, in the conclusion of his Enchiridion of Controversies with the Calvinists, p. 294: "The Roman Antichrist has wretchedly disfigured the face of the Church; yet the Calvinist spirit does not bear itself any better, and in some respects even surpasses the Pope." Likewise Matthias Hoe, in his letter to Count Joachim Andreas Schlick, written on 23 August 1619 and published later: "He calls us the eastern Antichrist and sets us alongside the western one, as though we were not much better." This has already been observed by the Papists themselves, that we are more hated than the Lutherans are. Famianus Strada, Decade I of the Belgian War, book v, under the year 1567: the Lutherans, out of hatred for the Calvinists, from whom they dissented far more sharply than from the Catholics, were nevertheless not moved to pity by their own sufferings. He speaks of the Lutherans at Antwerp, who watched the defeat of our people under Lord Tholosus, not far from the city, not only calmly, but also joined the Papists and Spaniards against ours. Our people certainly did not find those men trustworthy in every respect. What I cited above from Zanchius, book iv, p. 271, concerning the accountant of the Cardinal of Lorraine, also belongs here and should be weighed carefully. Do we not know that some of them were carried away to such a madness that they dared openly to say that our martyrs, who at that time were numerous everywhere, were martyrs of the Devil? Melanchthon, in 1548, in his letter to Joachim Camerarius: "You wish, Prince, for a common conference of many nations. It seems to me right to write this, lest we seem to approve the roaring of the lictor Balsinus, where some are called the martyrs of the Devil, the English being such martyrs." I would not wish to continue to offend the Holy Spirit by speaking thus of Latimer, who went beyond the age of eighty, and of the other holy men whom Joachim Westphal wrote about above, in his book against John à Lasco. He dedicated it to the Senate of the city of Frankfurt, where Lasco was, and which had granted him authority to set up the church of the foreign exiles, especially the Belgian church, over which Dathenus also presided. In it he stated that those who shed their blood for the defence of the truth and the glory of God in England, Belgium, France and elsewhere are martyrs of the Devil. Clearly religion can persuade people to such evils. There are those who seek peace, or fraternal communion, with such men, who so openly contradict the Holy Spirit, and who assign to the Devil the martyrs whom God receives and the Church honours, while their persecutors have been revered. They are the worst kind of people, I shall not say of Christians, who, dissolute in idleness and luxury, now inclined to quarrels and arrogance, despise, revile and condemn those who are exercised by the saving cross and most severe persecutions, and who, by the most cruel death, redeem the purity of the truth and of conscience. This teaches us to act with caution and prudence in promoting plans for syncretism, and above all to see with whom such matters are being negotiated. But we must certainly beware of the Devil's stratagem, which lies beneath the hatred and the slanders that the Lutherans direct against us, so that we may understand from what cause these come. The reason is this: they feel that the force of our doctrine and of the truth is directed against their dogmas, and they think that unless they draw their own people away from us by loud outcries, calumnies and curses, they will easily admit our doctrine. Therefore, lest this happen, they judge that they must proceed by this method, although it is one they would not want borrowed from the Papists, and for that reason alone ought to be hateful to everyone.

units.la: Ego vero in negotio syncretismi suspectio pedeversandum existimo, & quaedam hic ante omnia praenotanda, & distincte consideranda esse, tum videndum, quid agi, quo modo, quibusque conditionibus oporteat. Atque ut à postremo exordiar, præmitto. I. De Syncretismo hic cogitari, id est, partium adversarium & amicitiæ reconciliatione, ac reductione in mutuam conjunctionem, & communionem aliqualem, non in plenam unionem, vel in unius sententiæ, aut corporis Ecclesiastici consensum: tantùm de duarum, distinctarum, & diversarum Ecclesiarum consociatione, manentE utrimque suâ doctrinæ & rituum quorundam nonnullâ discrepantiâ, sed quæ nec salutis, nec religionis, nec communionis fraternæ inter utramque Ecclesiam, cætera orthodoxam, fundamentum videatur tollere. Atque hac ratione intelligendum quidquid de unione, consensu, aut concordiâ inundâ dicitur, scilicet non de totali & omni, qualis est concedentium in unam sententiam, & ejusdem corporis communionem, quæ hic vix speranda, sed partiali, & quæ secundum quid, qualis duorum in idem fœdus, pacta, leges, conciliationis est concursus & συγκατάθεσις. Plus etiam, quam de tolerantiâ hic agitur, quâ missis convitiis, infectationibus, damnationibus, addendum & persequutionibus, se ferant invicem: nam hoc retrogredi esset, si id nunc demum in consiliorum partem veniret, ut nos hoc pacto tolerarent, qui nunquam aliter à nobis toleratos se dicere possunt. Verùm ultra ista dudum progressum, initaque mutua concordia & fraternitas; huic superstruendum, non retrocedendum, sed promovendum opus illud est & confirmandum, si quid ultra curandum sit. In illiusmodi tolerantiam concedendum facile dicent omnes, ii etiam qui eam minus servant, & abstinendum à calumniis & contentionibus clamabunt quoque rixosissimi, & maledicentissimi hominum. Sed quemadmodum in disputationibus, improbatur si ad priora relabamur themata, progrediendum, & ubi stetit promovendum ultra negotium est: ita in dissidio Ecclesiarum videndum, quousque res productæ tandem fuerint (ad quod nos juvat historia, absque quâ nihil hic agitur); & hic aut in quo haeserit videndum, sin minus ictus consensus, aut si non confirmatus, conservatus, promotus receptusque, in eo laborandum, ut quod bene coeptum perficiatur. Postremum & summum, ad quod Concordia nostra producta fuit, censeo fuisse Consensum Sendomiriensem, tam quoad ipsam Consensionem, quam ejus modum & leges, restat modo hoc ut servatum fuisset, promotumque. Ego in hoc annitendum arbitror, ut illud repetatur, perficiatur, & omnibus persuadeatur, si quid in hoc opere agendum putemus. Tum multas in consultando difficultates tollit exemplum, si ei superaedifices, potius quam ut novas operi leges & regulas mediteris. Distinguenda etiam bene, materia, persona, locus, tempus syncretismi. Ne super quavis materia, vel articulo; neve cum quocunque homine incatur: tum etiam multum facit ratio loci, ubi; denique & quando instituendus. Materiam syncretismi nolo extendi ad quaevis, & quaecunque altera pars de novo possit iterum atque iterum in controversiam vocare: quid si damnatas haereses, aliosve errores paulatim adoptet, ac sequatur? vel pruriat indices novas contentiones, malitque serere eas & fovere, quam cavere aut evellere? Materia dissensus jam non alia facienda est, quam quae ab initio fuit, inter Lutherum, ac Nostros; & de qua in Colloquiis, & formando consensu olim laboratum; vel quae ex mutuis Confessionibus peti monstrarique potest. De hac videndum ut conveniatur, vel in certas leges tolerantia ac fraternitas constituatur, aut potius quae aliquoties ante facta, ut novo parcamus laboriae certaminibus, retineatur. Adeo parum, vel nihil operis est in re, totum fere in affectibus & hominum animis temperandis ac movendis in mutuam convenientiam. Ideo in praecipuo, saltem primo controversiae capite, foedere, in reliquis facilius pergetur, quum illud turbarum initium fuerit, & deinceps semper per ceu-foralis tæda à rixosis arrepta sit ad accendendos omnium animos præten sum vulgo à rixosis, ne paci videretur locus esse. III. Magis adhuc personas distinguo, in moderatos, pios, pacificos, prudentes & contentiosos alios, turbulentos. Neque enim promiscue omnibus pacem offero, vel cum quibuscunque eam aut agito, aut cupio. Sunt qui pacem pervicaciter repudiant, jurati ejus hostes, clamatores contra eam & ejus studiosos validi, nihil prius habentes quam Nos, & doctrinam, & Ecclesiam, adde Martyres sanctissimos damnare, quibuscunque calumniis & convitiis onerare, pro hæreticis, & quodcunque illis pejus dici potest, traducere, id est, quorum unicum studium est contendere, dominari, damnare: cum his uti pacem inire & de pace loqui, frustaneum arbitror. Verum quibus alia sedet mens, & spiritus pacis ac concordiæ molliora & meliora suggerit consilia, quamvis inter suos numero adeo exiguo, ut ferme digitis computari queant (quales habeo Melanthonem, Paulum Eberum, Melanthonis repertorium suo tempore dictum, Palladium, Pelagum, Donawerum, Calixtum &c.) cum istis (dico) tam facile nobis conveniet, ut cum aliis nunquam. Unde simul apparet, quam difficile sit syncretismi opus, quam inconstans, tamque, cum aliquibus eorum, longe paucissimis, & à dominante turbâ oppressis, vel initum, vel repetendum, quousque non aut à meliori parte major, aut Principum & Magistratus authoritate, qui præ Ecclesiasticis suis sapiant, aut denique à populo germanæ probitati dedito (nisi hi & illi à Ministris subjugentur & rapiantur) reliquorum intemperies debito modo coërceatur, & emendetur. Namque moderatiores illos alii pro scismaticis nunc habent. Ut videlicet scisma eos potius novum molituros à sanioribus illis, quam syncretismum nobiscum permissuros, sciamus. Calovius, in Synopsi Controversiarum, non satis habet in fronte Calixtinos, post Calvinianos, constituere
units.tr: For my part, in the matter of syncretism I think we must proceed without suspicion, and certain points must first be noted and carefully considered, and then we must see what ought to be done, in what manner, and under what conditions. And to begin at the end, I first set out this: (1) by Syncretism I mean here the reconciliation of the opposing parties in friendship, and their restoration to mutual union and a certain communion, not a full unity, nor agreement in one opinion or in one ecclesiastical body; only the association of two distinct and different Churches, each retaining some discrepancy in doctrine and certain rites, but one that does not seem to undermine the foundation of salvation, of religion, or of fraternal communion between the two Churches, which are otherwise orthodox. In this sense, whatever is said about union, agreement, or concord in this matter must be understood: not total and complete agreement, such as that of those who assent to one opinion and belong to one body, which can hardly be hoped for here, but partial agreement, which holds in some respects, such as the coming together of two parties in the same covenant, pacts, and laws of reconciliation, that is, their assent [συγκατάθεσις]. Moreover, what is at issue here is more than tolerance, by which the parties, setting aside insults, harassments, condemnations, and persecutions, bear with one another. For that would be a step backward, if it were now at last to come into the plans that they should tolerate us in this way, when they cannot say they have ever tolerated us otherwise. But since we have long since advanced beyond these things, and a mutual concord and fraternity has been entered upon, this work must be built upon, not reversed, but advanced and confirmed, if anything further is to be done. All will readily agree to such tolerance, even those who keep it least, and the most quarrelsome and abusive of men will also loudly cry out that abstaining from calumnies and contentions is necessary. But just as in disputations it is disapproved if we fall back to earlier topics, and one must go forward and advance the matter beyond where it stands, so in the division of the Churches we must see how far matters have been carried (and history helps us in this, without which nothing can be done here), and where they have stuck; and if the agreement struck has not been confirmed, preserved, advanced and received, we must labour that what has been well begun be brought to completion. The last and highest point to which our Concord was brought, I think, was the Consensus of Sendomir, both as to the agreement itself and its manner and laws; it only remains that this be preserved and advanced. In this I think we must strive, that it be taken up again, completed, and persuaded to all, if we think anything should be done in this work. Then, too, the example removes many difficulties in deliberation, if you build upon it rather than devise new rules and regulations for the work. We must also distinguish carefully the matter, person, place, and time of syncretism: not to enter upon any matter or article whatever, nor to treat with any person whatever. The place where it is undertaken also matters greatly, and finally when it is to be undertaken. (2) I do not want the matter of syncretism extended to any matter at all, such that the other party could again and again raise controversy over any point: what if they gradually adopt and follow condemned heresies or other errors? Or what if they itch to sow and foster new disputes rather than guard against or root them out? The matter of dissent must not be other than what it was from the beginning, between Luther and ours, and about which labour was spent in the Colloquies and in forming agreement before; or what can be sought and shown from the mutual Confessions. On this matter we must see that agreement is reached, or that tolerance and fraternity are established on fixed laws, or rather that what was done on several occasions before is kept, so that we may spare ourselves new and laborious contests. So little, or almost nothing, of the work lies in the matter itself; almost all of it lies in calming and moving the feelings and minds of men toward mutual harmony. Therefore, in the chief point, at least the first point of the controversy, we shall proceed more easily in the rest, since that was the beginning of the disturbances, and afterwards the firebrand has always been seized by the quarrelsome to inflame the minds of all, under the pretext commonly put forward by the quarrelsome, so that there would seem to be no room for peace. (3) I distinguish persons even further, into the moderate, the pious, the peaceable, and the prudent, and others who are contentious and turbulent. For I do not offer peace to everyone indiscriminately, nor do I seek or desire it with whomever. There are those who obstinately reject peace, sworn enemies of it, loud and strong opponents of it and of those who pursue it, having nothing more at heart than to condemn us, our doctrine, and our Church, and to add our most holy martyrs, to burden them with whatever calumnies and insults they can, and to slander them as heretics and with whatever worse names can be applied; that is, those whose only aim is to contend, to domineer, and to condemn. To make peace with these men, and to speak of peace with them, I consider a futile thing. But with those whose mind is otherwise, and whose spirit suggests gentler and better counsels of peace and concord, although their number among their own people is so small that they can almost be counted on the fingers (such as I have in Melanchthon, Paul Eber, the Melanchthonis repertorium as it was called in its time, Pallas, Pelagus, Donawerus, Calixtus, etc.), with these men (I say) agreement will come as easily for us as with no others. From this it also becomes clear how difficult the work of syncretism is, how unstable, and how, with some of them, very few indeed, and oppressed by the dominant crowd, it has been either begun or must be resumed, until the disorders of the rest are restrained and corrected in due manner, either by the better part of them, or by the authority of the princes and magistrates, who are wiser than their own churchmen, or finally by the people, devoted to genuine honesty (unless these too are subdued and snatched away by the ministers). For some of the more moderate men are now regarded by others as schismatics, so that we may know that they would sooner set in motion a new schism against the wiser ones than allow syncretism with us. Calovius, in his Synopsis of Controversies, is not content to place the Calixtines in the forefront, after the Calvinists.

units.la: Dicere, semper Synopsin dicit Controversiarum potio-nem, quae Ecclesiae Christi cum haereticis & schismaticis modernis; Socinianis, Anabaptistis, Vvergelianis, Rhomi-fratribus, Pontificiis, Calvinianis, Calixtinis, aliisque intercedunt [?]: verum & praefationem prolixam adversus Calixtum instituit, quâ ei exprobat schisma, haeresin, apostasiam, Samaritanismum, atheismum, & quid non? ut animum à suis aeque, ac nostris, & expetita toties Ecclesiarum unione abhorrentem, cognoscamus. IV. Quare neque aut omnibus sine discrimine, aut aliis quam qui se intrametam doctrinae Lutheri, & Augustanae Confessionis; tum juxta regulas charitatis habituros ostendunt, neque prodige offerendam fraternitatem, praesertim post toties elusam nostram benevolentiam, & obstinatos inde obstinatius Adversariorum animos, neque nimis ambiendam, nedum exterquendam, existimo. Pacis negotia ab utraque parte expetenda, & pari passu prosequenda sunt; si integram, velut & solidam, non coactam, non fucatam, aut damnosam. Nimia indulgentia saepe nimium peccatur, & non probanda bonitas quae cum detrimento sui in indignos erogat, quibus contra auctores ipsos foede abutuntur. Nempe hoc etiam est, sanctum canibus dare, & margaritas coram porcis projicere: quod contra Christi praeceptum, Matth. VII. 6. Videndum est enim primum ne obsit benignitas, inquit in Officiis, Cicero. Nostri, vereor, ne erga Lutheranos passim fuerint aequo benigniores, atque indulgentiores. Quid effecit tandem suo tanto Concordiae ambitu Bucerus, quam ut illis convitiandi, nostris amittendi plurimas Ecclesias & Scholas, suamque ipsius Argentinam, fecerit ansam? Neque nostris probata per omnia illius lenitas fuit, & quibus immoderatius studebat, Compositiones. Scultetus ad A. cIↄ Iↄ xxx. pag. 292. Et sane negari non potest, Capitonem & Bucerum, qui jam tum nisi concordiam cum Lutheo meditabantur, usque adeo ambibignis de Cœnâ Domini phrasibus in Confessione illâ loquitur de Confessione quatuor Civitatum in Comitiis Augustanis oblatâ, ipsos fuisse: ut & in Helveticam, & in Saxonicam trahi ille sententia possent: magno Ecclesiarum illarum, Argentinensis imprimis, malo. Quousque se adeo adversos & paci adversos gerunt Lutherani, nescio quo fructu pax iis identidem offeratur. Satis est Deo probari & hominibus, per nos non stare quo minus Ecclesiae socientur, & ita nos statuere, quod illorum huc deceat æque promptos esse animos atque nostros: de caetero si discordias malint, Deo committenda causa, cui nihilominus placebit pacis nostrum studium, quamvis irritum, & quod iteratis obtestationibus, & priores illis fraternitatem obtulimus, vel saltem commendavimus, ad ejus exemplum, qui prior dilexit nos. 1 Joann. iv. 19. Digna censeo V Volfgangi Musculi verba in epistolâ ad Bucerum, quæ ex autographo exhibet Scultetus, ad a. cIↄ Iↄxxxiiii, postquam Lutherus emisisset epistolam ad Senatum Francofurtensem, in quâ Zuinglianos archidiabolos appellarat, & è suggestu repellendos, atque ditione ejiciendos dixerat, ut & hic legantur: Hoccine scilicet silentio fovenda erat multis jam bonis desiderata illa concordia, quam tu annos aliquot tanto labore tam fideliter parturis? Annon tandem experimur, quàm sitarduum convenire cum eo, qui nostram concordiam augue pejus odit, quique universo cupit orbi testatum, sibi cum nemine minus quàm nobis, cum pessimis videlicet haereticis, esse concordia? Quid quaeso cum hoc homine facies quem quo magis ames & colas, eo majoribus videas furiis agitari? Ego mi Bucere, nihil puto nobis aliud agendum, quam, ut cum summa patientia praestolemur aequam divini judicii lancem, quae procul dubio palam faciet propediem, utra pars Christianae modestia propius accesserit. v. Quod dixi, habendam quoque loci, & temporis rationem, id prudentiae est accurate dispicere, quid loca ferant, & tempora. Nam subinde excitaveris crabrones intempestivâ, quamvis dulcicompellatione, & magnum malum tum tibi creaveris, tum aliis: absque quo non negligenda mollia fandi tempora. Aliis locis, atque alio tempore duriores sunt Adversarii, jam, vel tum; iterum ad pacis consilia nunc aut postea magis vel minus propensi. Captanda haec saepe magis, quam quaerenda: Quod denuo, quam difficile hoc negotium sit, ubi promiscue & universaliter proponitur cum omnibus agitandum, evincit. VI. Neque adeo probo, ut multa Nostri scribant Irenica, vel huc facientes tractatus. Non quod syncretismum improbem, aut promotum nolim, neutiquam sane: sed tum quia hoc nimis quam notum adversariis, certumque omnibus, pacem nos suadere, adeo ut hinc opprobrii in nos causam vulgò sumant; tum quod scriptionum hujusmodi satis extet, sive rationes adferas ad movendos animos; sive modum praescribas quo possit aut debeat inmiri syncretismus, extra Colloquium, vel post tot jam habita hujus argumenti eaque varis, ut vana fere omnis videatur hic poni opera. Sin simpliciter commendandam pacem, & pacifica consilia existimes, habemus Irenicum Franc. Junii, Oper. Tom. I. inscriptum Mauritio, Hassiae Landgravio, in Psal. cxxi. de modo pacis, & Psalm. cxxxi. de illius fructu. Ne Andreae V. Villeti Meditationes dicam, in eundem Psalm. cxxi. vel Erasmi in Psalm. lxxxi. de amabili Ecclesiae concordia: Sin Irenicum in specie cum Lutheranis, extat Partei illud, continens fere omnia ad hanc rem spectantia, seu Theologica, seu historica: ne & alios nominem. Praeterquam quod in ejusmodi scriptis ex nimio concordiae studio saepius contingat Auctores plura quam aequum sit Adversariis largiri, & cum dispendio veritatis charitati incumbere, vel cogitare magis de aliis Ecclesiis, quam suis, & captando aliorum gratiam, domesticam floccifacere, aut amittere. Quum Argentinenses Theologi Erasmi libellum de amabili Ecclesiae concordia, in Germanicam Linguam transfudissent, exemplaraque ejus per Germaniam sparsa essent, aegerrime tulit V. Volfgangus Musculus, qui propterea ad Bucerum, in haec verba scripsit: Displicet omnino institutum hoc vestrum. Et, anxie timeo ne nimia concordia meditatione prolabamini, ut veritati agnitae, praedicatae, publicatae, inculcatae non admodum probe sitis consulturi: id quod Dominus avertat. Tum: Ex corde loquor, quia scio cui loquar. Maledicta sit ea concordia, quae non nisi veritatis et regni Christi praejudicio damnoque sanari potest. Sancte beatus Oecolampadius in disputatione Bergensi admonuit, videndum, ut magis simus in Electorum Christi Ecclesia, quam ille tandem agnituros est, quam in ea, ubi salva conscientia consistere non poterit. Denique in haec desinit verba: vellem tandem huiusmodi libellis finem fieri.
units.tr: Calovius always says, in his Synopsis of Controversies, that the dispute which exists between the Church of Christ and modern heretics and schismatics (Socinians, Anabaptists, Weigelians, Rosicrucian brethren, Papists, Calvinists, Calixtines and others) is one that cannot be settled. He also composes a lengthy preface against Calixtus, in which he charges him with schism, heresy, apostasy, Samaritanism, atheism, and what not, so that we may learn that his mind, like ours, abhors the union of the Churches that has so often been sought. IV. Therefore they show that they will neither deal with all people without distinction, nor with any except those who take their stand on the doctrine of Luther and the Augsburg Confession, at least not according to the rules of charity. Nor do I think that fraternity should be offered lavishly, especially after our goodwill has so often been mocked and the minds of our opponents have been made more obstinate by it, nor that it should be courted too eagerly, much less wrung from them. The business of peace must be sought by both sides and pursued step by step, if it is whole and solid, not forced, not disguised, and not harmful. We often sin by excessive indulgence, and that goodness is not to be approved which, to its own loss, bestows itself on the unworthy, who then shamefully abuse their benefactors. This is indeed to give what is holy to dogs and to cast pearls before swine, which is against Christ's command (Matt. 7:6). For first of all we must take care that kindness does no harm, says Cicero in his De Officiis. I fear that our own people have too often been more generous and indulgent than fitting towards the Lutherans. What did Bucer finally achieve by his great zeal for concord, except to give the Lutherans an occasion to revile him, and to cost us many churches and schools, and his own Strasbourg? Nor was his gentleness, or the compromises towards which he eagerly leaned too much, approved by our side in every respect. Scultetus, at the year 1530, p. 292: And indeed it cannot be denied that Capito and Bucer, who even then were planning concord with Luther, were so ambiguous in the phrases about the Lord's Supper in that Confession (he speaks of the Confession of the four cities presented at the Diet of Augsburg) that that opinion could be drawn both towards the Helvetic and towards the Saxon, to the great harm of those Churches, especially the Strasbourg Church. As long as the Lutherans behave so hostilely and so opposed to peace, I do not know what fruit it is to keep offering them peace. It is enough to be approved by God and by men, that the uniting of the Churches is not held back on our part, and that we show our readiness; the rest is for them: if they prefer discord, let the cause be committed to God, who will nonetheless be pleased with our zeal for peace, however fruitless, and with the fact that, by repeated entreaties, we have offered or at least commended fraternity to them, after the example of him who first loved us (1 John 4:19). I think the words of Wolfgang Musculus are worthy of note, in a letter to Bucer, which Scultetus gives from the autograph, at the year 1534, after Luther had published a letter to the Senate of Frankfurt, in which he had called the Zwinglians archdevils and said they should be expelled from the pulpit and driven out of the territory. They are quoted here as well: Was that concord, which for many good men has long been desired, and which you have so faithfully laboured over for some years, to be cherished by silence? Do we not at last find how hard it is to agree with one who hates our concord more than anyone, and who wishes it to be known to the whole world that he has concord with no one less than with us, that is, with the worst heretics? What, I ask, will you do with this man? The more you love and cultivate him, the more you see him driven by the greatest furies. I, my Bucer, think we should do nothing else than wait with the greatest patience for the fair balance of divine judgment, which will undoubtedly soon make plain which side has come nearer to Christian moderation. V. What I said, that the place and the time must also be taken into account, is a matter of prudence, to examine carefully what places and times allow. For at times you will have stirred up hornets with an ill-timed address, however sweet, and created a great evil both for yourself and for others; so gentle words must not be neglected at the right times. In other places, and at other times, the opponents are harder, now or then, and at one time or another more or less inclined to counsels of peace. These opportunities are often to be seized rather than sought; and this shows again how difficult this business is, when it is proposed indiscriminately and universally, to be debated with everyone. VI. Nor do I greatly approve that many of our people write irenical works, or treatises tending that way. Not that I disapprove of syncretism, or would not wish it promoted, by no means; but because it is only too well known to our adversaries, and certain to everyone, that we urge peace, so that they commonly take from this a cause for reproach against us; and because there is already enough of this kind of writing, whether you bring forward reasons for moving minds, or prescribe a way in which syncretism can or should be brought about outside a colloquy, or after so many discussions of this subject already held and in various ways, so that almost all such effort seems to be in vain. But if you think that peace and peaceful counsels should simply be commended, we have the irenical work of Francis Junius, in his Works, vol. I, addressed to Maurice, Landgrave of Hesse, on Psalm 121, about the way of peace, and on Psalm 131, about its fruit. I say nothing of the Meditations of Andreas Villetus on the same Psalm 121, or of Erasmus on Psalm 81, about the lovable concord of the Church. If an irenical work specifically with the Lutherans exists, it is that of the Party, containing almost everything relevant to this matter, whether theological or historical; I will not name others too. Besides, in such writings it happens rather often, through excessive zeal for concord, that authors concede more to their adversaries than is fair, and devote themselves to charity at the cost of truth, or think more about other Churches than their own, and in seeking the favour of others, despise or lose what is their own. When the Strasbourg theologians had translated Erasmus's little book on the lovable concord of the Church into German, and copies were scattered through Germany, Wolfgang Musculus took it very badly, and wrote to Bucer on this account in these words: I altogether dislike this undertaking of yours. And I anxiously fear that in your too eager pursuit of concord you will slip, so that you will not sufficiently well consult the truth once recognised, preached, published and inculcated; which the Lord forbid. Then: I speak from the heart, because I know to whom I speak. Cursed be that concord which can be healed only at the prejudice and loss of the truth and the kingdom of Christ. Blessed Oecolampadius, in the Bern disputation, warned: we must take care to be more in the Church of Christ's elect, which he will at last recognise, than in that one where, with a good conscience, he cannot remain. Finally, he ends with these words: I would wish that an end be put to books of this kind.

units.la: Atque ad Bucerum Idem antea, quando illius instinctu Argentinenses aliaeque civitates Suevicae subscripsissent Confessioni Augustanae, quod haud absque praejudicio propriae suae rv Civitatum Confessionis factum videbatur: Bucere, inquit, tu scribis ad nos, recessum esse a vestris urbibus in Confessionem Saxonicam, eo quod vera habeat, nihilque aliud videatur pretendere, quam quod Christus in sacramento Eucharistia, vel corpus et sanguis Christi in Caena Domini distribuantur communicantibus, et quod qui secus docent, improbentur. Nobis vero de his verbis non tam anxie curandum scio, quam de illorum interpretatione, quae scilicet Lutherani illa ponant. Atque hanc puto rationem fuisse, quod hanc Saxonicae Confessioni in Comitiis apud nostros habitis subscribere noluerint. Me mirum in modum movet, quomodo hodie vera sint Saxonicae Confessionis verba, cum tum vera non fuerint, quando, si vera sunt, magno Ecclesiarum emolumento admitti poterant. Et quae sequuntur. Satis Irenicorum a nostra parte, quibus tantum abest obaudiant Adversarii, ut acerbissime illa infectentur et respuant. Quod si pax ipsis cordi, nam ad eam faciendam concurrere et illi quoque, si non aeque debent, prodeant tandem semel ipsi suis Irenicis, eaque videamus, vel saltem nostra aequius, si non amantius, ferant. Neque dissimulanda scripta Pelargi, Donaveri, Calixti, addo & Henrici Nicolai: sed utinam iis omnes ipsorum starent, neque illa minori insectatione & odio exciperent, quam nostra! VII. Et quod si nondum velint Lutherani τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης (cum quibus Apostolus conjungit τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς, Rom. XIV. 19. adeo nequeunt, ista divelli) quaeso omittant saltem convitia, uti multorum apud ipsos immanis hactenus adversum nos mos est. Quorsum innoxios & pacificos dicteriis verberare, & assiduis calumniis? quorsum nomina Calvinianorum, Sacramentariorum, Swenckerorum, Fanaticorum, & nescio quid non, in libris, & concionibus contra nos acerbe ejicere? adeone Christiana res non Christiane, ac ne quidem humaniter, tractari debet? Ioh. Pappus, in Epitome Histor. Eccles. in Catalogo haereticorum ponit pag. 956. Sacramentarios, eorumque ibidem scilicet varia illa cognomina, seu convitia Doctor explicat. VIII. Quia autem tam in cavendis maledictis, quam in amplectenda pace officio suo desunt Theologi Lutherani, consultum, ut Magistratus eorum & Principes, quorum hic longe melior mens est suis Ministris, eos in ordinem redigant, & severe iubeant a convitiando abstinere. Neque video aliquid boni expectari posse, priusquam istud saltem habeatur. Fecit hoc olim Fridericus III. Elector Palatinus; Fridericus V. Wilhelmus, administrator Saxoniae a. MDLXXXIII. Elector Brandeburgicus pridem, a. MDLXXIV. Sic & alii Ordines Evangelici, vel eorundem Delegati in Conventu Francofurtico a. MDLXXXIV. post Colloquium Lipsiacum, quod interea temporis omnis ab utraque parte tam in docendo, quam scribendo Christiana moderatio et lenitas suspenda sit, ne sit. Illa animorum conjunctio et conformitas impediatur, sed potius, quantum fieri potest, promoveatur. IX. Neque a maledictis solum, sed & malefactis contra nos abstinere illos oportet, id est, a persequendo, ejiciendo, privando nostros honoribus, facultatibus, locis, vitâ, sepulturâ deniq;, etiam ne violenter auferant templa nobis, scholas, & locum regiminis in Magistratu, quod uti olim Argentorati, atque alibi, ita hodie Dantisci, neglectâ etiam Regis auctoritate, intercessione, minis, agunt. De hoc existimo prius nos debere esse sollicitos, recuperandis videlicet nostris, quam prædicando syncretismo cum illis, qui se tales erga nos gerunt, & in vanum laborare. Quemadmodum Lutherus solebat dicere, ad propositas rationes conciliationis cum Pontificiis, prius ut redderent nobis Martyres nostros ; deinde de concordiâ agerent : sic ante omnia reddant Lutherani nobis ablata, & tum de pace loquamur ac conjunctione mutuâ.
units.tr: Likewise, Musculus wrote earlier to Bucer, when at his instigation the Strasbourg and other Swabian cities had subscribed to the Augsburg Confession, which seemed to be done not without prejudice to the confession of their own four cities: Bucer, he says, you write to us that there has been a withdrawal from your cities to the Saxon Confession, because it holds true things, and seems to claim nothing else than that Christ is distributed in the sacrament of the Eucharist, or the body and blood of Christ in the Lord's Supper, to those who communicate, and that those who teach otherwise are condemned. For my part, I know that we ought not to worry so anxiously about these words as about the way the Lutherans interpret them. And I think this was the reason why our people were unwilling to subscribe to the Saxon Confession at the diets held among us. It strikes me in a remarkable way how the words of the Saxon Confession can be true today, when they were not true then, since, if they are true, they could have been admitted to the great advantage of the Churches. And so on. We on our side have enough irenical works, which our adversaries are so far from obeying that they attack and reject them most bitterly. But if peace is dear to them, for making it both we and they must come together; and let them at last, once and for all, step forward with their own irenical works, and let us see them, or at least let them bear ours more fairly, if not more lovingly. Nor must the writings of Pelargus, Donauer, Calixtus, and I may add Henry Nicolai, be passed over; but would that all of them stood by their own, and did not receive ours with less attack and hatred than they do! VII. And if the Lutherans do not yet wish the things of peace (with which the Apostle joins the things of edification, Rom. 14:19, which cannot be so separated) [τὰ τῆς εἰρήνης] [τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς], I beg them at least to leave off reproaches, as is the huge custom among many of them until now against us. Why do they beat the harmless and peaceable with taunts and constant slanders? Why do they, in books and sermons, bitterly hurl against us the names of Calvinists, Sacramentarians, Swenckfeldians, Fanatics, and I know not what else? Ought a Christian matter to be handled in an unchristian way, not even humanely? John Pappus, in his Epitome of Ecclesiastical History, in the catalogue of heretics, p. 956, lists the Sacramentarians, and the author there explains those various nicknames, or reproaches. VIII. But since the Lutheran theologians fail in their duty, both in avoiding slanders and in embracing peace, it is advisable that their magistrates and princes, whose mind is far better than that of their ministers, bring them into line and sternly order them to abstain from reviling. I see no good can be expected before this at least is done. Frederick III, Elector Palatine, did this long ago; Frederick William, administrator of Saxony, in 1583; the Elector of Brandenburg earlier, in 1574. So too other Evangelical orders, or their delegates, at the Frankfurt Assembly in 1584, after the Colloquy of Leipzig, that in the meantime, on both sides, all Christian moderation and gentleness, both in teaching and in writing, be suspended, lest that union and conformity of minds be hindered, but rather, as far as possible, be promoted. IX. They must abstain from wrongs against us not only in words but also in deeds, that is, from persecuting, expelling, depriving our people of honours, property, places, life, and finally burial, and also from violently taking away from us churches, schools, and places of rule in the magistracy; which they do now at Danzig, disregarding even the authority, intercession and threats of the King, just as once at Strasbourg and elsewhere. About this I think we must first be concerned, that is, with recovering what is ours, rather than by preaching syncretism with those who behave in this way towards us, and labouring in vain. Just as Luther used to say, in reply to the proposed grounds of reconciliation with the Papists, that they should first give back our martyrs and then talk about concord, so before all things let the Lutherans give back what they have taken from us, and then let us speak of peace and mutual union.

units.la: Illis præmissis, si quid ulterius agendum, quod ad syncretismum cum iis, qualem diximus, spectat, hoc non per disputationes fieri debere arbitror: satis quippe de omni inter nos articulo, ac nimium satis disputatum videri jure potest, ut nemo dari queat, qui non ex prostantibus utrimque scriptis veritatem discere, si debite æquoque animo attendat, possit. Probaturque mihi sententia Sculteti, in Curric. vitæ, pag. 45. quam in Senatu Ecclesiastico Heidelbergensi se proposuisse ait, a. cIↄ Iↄ c v ı ı ı .quando deliberabatur, quonam modo continuis tristissimisque Euangelicorum certaminibus occurri posset; è re Ecclesiæ fore, si Re„formati deinceps ab omnibus Apologiis, antilogiis, & „quocunquei nomine vocentur, eristicis scriptis ab„stinerent. Nihil enim dici scribique posse, quod non „pridem dictum scriptumque sit. Extare Ecclesiarum „nostrarum Confessiones, & Confessionum Declara„tiones, quæ hominem veritatis indagandæ cupidum, „abunde satis instruere possint. Neque Colloquiis iterum vel Synodos suadeo, ut alii, in quibus hæc de re discepretur, aut agatur, nisi tam facile sit talem constituere Synodum, istorumque virorum, quales hic requirantur, ac optare & delineare. Vel enim particularem velis, vel universalem, id est, ex omnibus utrimque Ecclesiis, aut Ecclesiarum consensu ac delegatione constantem, vel aliquibus ꝥhæc (meo judicio) rebus quotidie in pejus vergentibus, & divortio se indies magis dilatante, non contrahente, frustra exspectatur, præsertim quum ei, à Nostris aliquando in medium propositæ, Lutherani tantopere & palam reluctentur. Vel ponatur talis Synodus, & quod omnium difficillimum, viri in ea aptissimi, probi, docti, prudentes, moderati: putasne melius conventuros, quam jam antea aliquando convenire visi sunt? ego contrà vereor omnia secus, pejoraque: & plures productum iri quæstiones ac dissensiones, & obstinata magis judicia, & eo minus συγκαταβάσεως, quo adversus priores Consensus semper Adversariorum plurimi & loquuti vehementer fuerunt, & moliti quæcunque. Colloquia ejusmodi, & Synodi, ut quidem earum præclarissimus fructus merito exspectari debet, ita raro bene ceciderunt, nescio an unquam ex utriusque voto, quod tamen deberet, si optatus finis sequeretur, qui hic non disputatio aut victoria, sed consensus mutuus. Sin particularem aliquorum, & non communi omnium nomine. Synodum constituas, præterquam quod eadem fere redeunt difficultates, hoc insuper est, quod ei accedere reliqui vel ex solâ pervicaciâ recusabunt, prout hominum atque adversariorum imprimis, probata tot inante Colloquiis indoles jam fuit. Ego quod meum, sed tenue judicium, uti disputationum, ita & Colloquiorum, fere satis arbitror esse, nisi tale haberi posset, in quo, rebus antea bene præparatis, non ad disputationem vel majorem contentionem, sed ultimam, certam, solennemque compositionem, evitatis, quas supra dixi, difficultatibus & periculis, convenire tur. In quem finem, præter multa à Nostris hanc in rem propositia, præsertim à Paræo, ut consideretur Delineatio pii & fructuosi in Theologicis Colloquii, ab Henrico Nicolai subjuncta suo Irenico, non refragor. Alioqui, quemadmodum de disputationibus, ita & de Colloquiis dico, metuendum ne posteriora prioribus meliora sint, & feliciora. Quemadmodum olim Melanthon scripsit de Ifenacensi Colloquio Lutheri, cum Bucero, ad Vitum Theodorum, ego certis de causis malo eam rem extrahi. Nam si congressus iterum accendet discordiam & certamen, ut certe metuo, quid attinet properare hoc quidem tempore, voluntatibus adeo exulceratis? Et tamen si gravis & vera deliberatio, de hoc ipso articulo, & de aliis quibusdam speranda esset, maxime expeterem conventum. Interim (ne videar obstare rei, & syncretismo bene feriendo, quem ambabus ulnis amplector, & qualis exempli gratia Sendomiriensis ille, omni vi deprædico, & utilem ac necessarium Ecclesiis existimo: sed de modo consultamus) proximum, ut particulares seu Doctores, seu Ecclesiae Consensibus antea saepius feliciterque, quod ad rei summam, factis innitentes, non exspectatis aliis vel Colloquiis vel Synodis, cum Lutheranis aut Ecclesiis, aut Doctoribus, vel aliis quibuscunque pergant tractare, & sicubi visum coire etiam, prout rerum & Ecclesiarum hominumque utilitas singulis in locis videbitur postulare? Habentur, notique & obvii vulgo sunt tum dissensus, tum consensus articuli; jam & ex hominibus alii aliis longius vel minus errant, & etiam conveniunt; denique aliud requirit vel permittit status hujus illiusque Ecclesiae: pro horum omnium debita consideratione prudenter agendum, & ex charitate circumspecta. In dissidio Sacramentario, nam hoc caput rei est, conveniri inter partes posse ac debere omnino statuo. Hoc & exemplo vel authoritate Lutheri, & Consensuum aliquoties factorum, praeterquam tot rationibus & argumentis, ac in hanc rem a Nostris, Christianae charitatis, ad praeceptum Magistri, semper studiosissimis, & a Lutheranis aliquibus quandoque adducta, comprobari facile potest: vel inspectis solum levi opera partis utriusque Confessionibus, ex quibus, de doctrinâ Ecclesiarum, non vero ex sententiis vel dictis Doctorum, judicium fieri debet. Lege hunc in finem, Præfationem Syntagmatis Confessionum, in quo juxta cum aliis Augustana Consessio, cum Saxonicâ & VVittembergensi inserta, nomine Ecclesiarum nostrarum præfixam. Et Lutherus Confessionem Helveticam, uti supra vidimus, approbavit. Denique & detestatum eumquoque sub finem vitæ tristes illas contentiones, scimus ex Iohanne Alesio Theologo in Academiâ Lipsiensi, qui de Luthero protulit, in Responsione suâ ad articulos Lovaniensium Ruardi Tapperi, illum profecturum in patriam, ubi & obiit, loquentem Melanthoni de dissensione sacramentariâ, dixisse: mi Philippe, fateor in negotio sacramenti minimum esse actum. Cumque instaret Philippus, ut leni aliquo scripto hoc emendaretur, respondit: Ego quoque de hâc re sollicite cogitavi, sed sic redderem totam doctrinam suspectam. Itaque hoc bono Deo committam. Agite vos etiam aliquid post mortem meam. Hæc multorum testimoniis vide confirmata, in Admonitione Neostadiensi cap. VI. à pag. 235. Atque pro concordiâ promovendâ scripserat jam a. MDXXXV. ad Argentinenses Pastores: Quare vicissim vobis, oro, persuadeatis, tam cupide me amplecti eam concordiam, quam capide velim mihi Dominum Iesum Christum propitium semper fore. Et non dubitate, quantum in me fuerit, nihil poterit à me exigi aut imperari, quod pro hâc causâ non sim libenter & hilariter facturus & passurus. Similiter anno sequente, post Concordiam V Wittembergensem, ad eosdem scripsit; atque postmodum ad Helvetios. Haberi ergo ex Utriusque partis Confessionibus Vnionem posse existimo, & Ecclesiarum quandam consensionem: non autem probo, ut multo artificio communis aliqua cudatur formula, generalis & flexiloqua, uti antea aliquando factum, in quam dissensiones utrimque reducantur, & sub eâ lateant; quæ agendi ratio neque sincera satis, neque que solida, & nec ex partium usu magis, quam veritatis. Melanthon, epist. ad Ioh. Hencelium, Consulem Augustanum: Non potest tolli dissidium generalibus verbis. Ad Brentium, a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxv: maxime velim concordiam fieri sine ulla sophistica. Potius constitutis utrimque consensus, dissensusque ingenuè articulis, atque super momento ejus habita deliberatione, Unio firmissime stabiliatur, ut quaeque pars alteram ferat; quod Lutherus Consilium Melanthoni ad Colloquium Cassellense cum Bucero profecto a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxiv. dederat: Forte ipsi conscientia minimè mala altero intellectu constricti sunt. Ideoque libenter illos feremus, si innocentes & puri sunt, Christus illos facile liberabit. Interim & ego profecto bona conscientia altero intellectu constrictus sum, nisi id forte mihi accidat, ut memetipsum non agnoscam. Itidem igitur me quoque tolerent, sicut in meam sententiam descendere nequeunt. Vel omisso quaestionis articulo, coque relicto suspenso, maneatur in confessis utrimque, & docendis explicandisque iis, in quibus usus Coenae salutaris situs, quaeque ad salutem & aedificationem haberi satis sit. Quemadmodum Suevi, in Syngrammate suo, Oecolampadio respondebant: Optime Oecolampadi, planè nobis persuasum est, te facile pro agnatâ tibi modestiâ, imò pro Christiano candore, passurum, ut tantisper de pane & vino coena dominica à tuâ opinione dissentiamur, dum Dominus tibi & nobis τὰ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν dederit. Ad quae in Iudicio suo adducta, Calixtus subjungit: Si eâ mente vel hodie essemus, tranquillitati Ecclesiae, & concordiae Christianorum consuleretur. Vel maneatur in loquutionibus, à Scripturâ probatis, juxta eundem: Satius autem fuerit in disputationibus, praesertim contra dissentientes, ne offendantur illi aut turbentur, simpliciter loqui & locutionibus uti, quibus utitur Scriptura, nempe hoc quod accipimus & manducamus, quum benedictus panis sumitur & comeditur, est corpus Christi: Item panis est communicatio corporis Christi. Atque eximia huc in finem est regula ab Henrico
units.tr: With those points granted, if anything further is to be done toward a syncretism with such people as I have described, I do not think it should be done by way of disputations. Indeed, it can rightly be said that every article between us has already been disputed enough, and more than enough, so that no one could fail to learn the truth from the writings of both sides, if he attended to them fairly and with an open mind. I approve the opinion of Scultetus in his Curriculum vitae, page 45, which he says he put forward in the Ecclesiastical Senate at Heidelberg in 1608, when they were deliberating how to meet the constant and most grievous quarrels of the evangelicals. He said it would be for the good of the Church if the Reformed henceforth abstained from all apologies, antilogies, and controversial writings, whatever name they bear. For nothing can be said or written that has not been said and written before. The Confessions of our Churches, and the declarations of those Confessions, exist, and these can amply instruct any man who desires to search out the truth. Nor do I advise, as others do, colloquies or synods in which these matters are argued or treated, unless it is as easy to arrange such a synod, and to choose and describe such men as are required here, as it is to wish for them. For whether you wish for a particular synod or a universal one, that is, one made up of all Churches on both sides, or one resting on the consent and delegation of the Churches, it is waited for in vain, in my judgment, while things are growing worse every day and the divorce is widening day by day rather than closing, especially since, whenever our men have at some time put this proposal forward, the Lutherans have resisted it so strongly and openly. Or suppose such a synod were convened, and (what is most difficult of all) its members were the most fit, upright, learned, prudent, and moderate men: do you think they would meet more happily than they have sometimes been seen to meet before? I, on the contrary, fear everything will turn out otherwise and worse, that more questions and dissensions will be raised, judgments will become more obstinate, and there will be even less [συγκαταβάσεως] condescension, since against the earlier consensus formulas very many of the adversaries have spoken vehemently and have striven by every means. Colloquies of this kind, and synods, though the finest fruit of them ought rightly to be expected, have seldom ended well, and I do not know whether they ever ended according to the wish of both sides. Yet they ought to, if the desired end were to follow, which here is not disputation or victory but mutual consent. But if you were to constitute a synod of some men only, and not in the name of all in common, then, besides the fact that almost the same difficulties would return, this would be the further problem, that the rest would refuse to join it out of sheer obstinacy alone, as the disposition of men and especially of adversaries, already shown by so many colloquies before, has been. As for me, my own judgment, though slight, is that disputations and colloquies are for the most part sufficient, unless one could be held in which, with matters first well prepared, the parties might meet not for a further dispute or greater contention but for a final, certain, and solemn settlement, the difficulties and dangers I have mentioned having been avoided. To this end I do not object to the many proposals made in this matter by our men, especially by Pareus, that there be considered the Delineatio pii & fructuosi in Theologicis Colloquii, appended by Henry Nicolai to his Irenicum. Otherwise, as I say of disputations, so also of colloquies, there is reason to fear that the later ones will be worse than the earlier, and less happy. As Melanchthon once wrote to Vitus Theodorus about Luther's colloquy at Isenach with Bucer: For certain reasons I would rather that the business be drawn out. For if the meeting again kindles discord and strife, as I certainly fear, what is the point of hurrying at this time, with wills so embittered? And yet, if a serious and true deliberation on this very article and on certain others were to be hoped for, I would most eagerly desire a meeting. Meanwhile (lest I seem to stand in the way of the cause, and of a good syncretism, which I embrace with both arms, and which, for example, that Sandomierz agreement I praise with all my power and consider useful and necessary for the Churches; rather, we are deliberating about the manner) I propose that individuals, whether teachers or Churches, as has often and happily been done before with regard to the substance of the matter, relying on facts, and without waiting for other colloquies or synods, should go on treating with the Lutherans, whether with Churches or with teachers or with anyone else, and should come together wherever it seems fit, as the usefulness of things, Churches, and men in each place may seem to require. The disagreements and agreements on the articles are present, and are well known and commonly met with; some men already err more or less far from one another, and some also agree; finally, the state of this or that Church requires or permits something different. Things must be done prudently and with cautious charity, with due consideration of all these matters. In the sacramentarian dispute, for this is the head of the matter, I hold that the parties can and must surely be brought together. This can easily be proved both by the example and authority of Luther, and by the consensus formulas made several times, besides many other reasons and arguments, and by the Christian charity of our men, ever most zealous in obedience to the Master's precept, and by some Lutherans brought forward at times. Or it may be proved by merely glancing with little effort at the Confessions of both parties, from which judgment about the doctrine of the Churches, and not from the opinions or sayings of the teachers, should be made. For this purpose read the Preface to the Syntagma Confessionum, in which, along with others, the Augsburg Confession, inserted together with the Saxon and Wittenberg ones, is prefixed in the name of our Churches. Luther also approved the Helvetic Confession, as we saw above. Finally, we know from John Aless, a theologian in the University of Leipzig, who in his Response to the articles of the Louvain men, Ruard Tapper, reported of Luther that, when he was about to set out for his homeland, where he also died, speaking to Melanchthon about the sacramentarian dispute, he said: My Philip, I confess that in the matter of the sacrament there is very little to do. And when Philip urged that this be corrected by some mild writing, he replied: I too have thought anxiously about this matter, but in that way I would make the whole doctrine suspect. Therefore I will commit this to good God. You men do something about it even after my death. These things are confirmed by the testimony of many, see the Admonitio Neostadiensis, chapter VI, from page 235. And already in 1535, to promote concord, he had written to the Strasbourg ministers: Therefore, I beg you, be persuaded in turn that I embrace that concord as eagerly as I would wish that the Lord Jesus Christ may always be gracious to me. And do not doubt that, so far as lies in me, nothing will be demanded or commanded of me that I shall not gladly and cheerfully do and suffer for this cause. Likewise, in the following year, after the Wittenberg Concord, he wrote to the same men, and afterwards to the Swiss. I therefore think that union can be had from the Confessions of both parties, and a certain agreement of the Churches; but I do not approve that some common formula be hammered out with great craft, general and ambiguous, as has sometimes been done before, into which the disagreements on both sides are brought back and hidden under it. This method of dealing is neither sincere enough nor solid, and it serves the advantage of the parties more than of the truth. Melanchthon, in a letter to John Hencel, consul of Augsburg: Disagreement cannot be removed by general words. To Brenz, in 1535: I would most wish that concord be made without any sophistry. Rather, once the points of consensus and dissensus have been frankly set out on both sides, and a deliberation held on their weight, let the Union be most firmly established, so that each party bears with the other. Luther had given this counsel to Melanchthon for the Cassel colloquy with Bucer, in 1534: Perhaps they are bound by a different understanding, their consciences being in no way evil. Therefore we will gladly bear with them, if they are innocent and pure; Christ will easily set them free. Meanwhile I too, with a good conscience, am bound by a different understanding, unless perhaps it happens to me that I do not recognize myself. Likewise, therefore, let them also tolerate me, just as they cannot come down to my opinion. Or else, with the article of the question set aside and left in suspense, let them abide by what is agreed on both sides, and by teaching and explaining those points in which the use of the saving Supper is set forth, and which are enough to be held for salvation and edification. As the Swabians answered Oecolampadius in their Syngramma: Most excellent Oecolampadius, we are fully persuaded that you, from the modesty native to you, and indeed from Christian candour, will easily allow that we dissent from your opinion for the time being, about the bread and wine of the Lord's Supper, until the Lord gives both you and us [τὰ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν] to think the same thing. To which Calixtus, in his Judicium, adds, after citing these words: If we were today in that mind, the tranquillity of the Church and the concord of Christians would be served. Or let them abide by expressions approved by Scripture, according to the same writer: It would, however, be better in disputations, especially against dissenters, so as not to offend or disturb them, to speak simply and to use the expressions that Scripture uses, namely, that what we receive and eat, when the blessed bread is taken and eaten, is the body of Christ; likewise, the bread is the communication of the body of Christ. And an excellent rule for this purpose is that of Henry Nicolai, a theologian of Danzig, in his Irenicum, written in 1545. The differences among the Religions that have arisen from the manner of setting forth will be shown to be easily removed, if the manners of setting forth are examined, and in place of the empty and ambiguous, the ambiguities and vague expressions are replaced by a clear and determinate sense, and in particular by ones that... (the passage breaks off) by Henry

units.la: Nicolai Gedanensi Theologo, in Irenico suo, scripto anno MDXLV. Quae differentiae Religionum ex modo proponendi ortae sunt, eae facile tolli patebunt, si modi proponendi inspiciantur, et pro tricis ac ambiguis apertis et ambiguitatibus vacui determinatique sensus substituantur, illisque maxime ad modos loquendi in Scriptura usurpatos revocentur, illi bene in sensu Spiritus Sancti natura ac genuino inquirantur, constituantur, in iis ut certissimis et tutissimis quiescatur, ac reliqui in tricas aut contentiones et exagerationes deducentes relegentur. Sic panem in Coena esse ipsum Corpus Christi sub accidentibus panis externis, quantitate, figura, colore, sapore, essentialiter transubstantiatum, et sub ac cum illo pane uno indivisoque comedendi actu ipsam Corporis Christi substantiam ore manducandam esse, modi proponendi humani sunt. Pro illis modus Scripturae adhibeatur, Panis, quem frangimus, vel hujus panis in Coena fractio, distributio, et sumptio, est Corporis Christi communicatio, 1 Cor. 10. Sensus ejus a Spiritu Sancto intentus studiose inquiratur, et in eo, ut certo ac immota, fixatur, et via ad consensum producendum paratior erit. Quicquid de humanis proponendi modis fuerit, sive illi ad rem fuerint, sive a re recesserint.
units.tr: Nicolaus of Danzig, a theologian, in his Irenicum written in 1545, shows that the differences between the religions that arise from the way doctrines are put forward can easily be removed. If the ways of putting them forward are examined, and the vague and ambiguous phrases are replaced by clear and determinate meanings, and these are traced back chiefly to the modes of speaking used in Scripture, and the meanings are sought out and fixed in the sense of the Holy Spirit and its genuine intent, then people may rest in them as most certain and safe, and the rest, which lead to quibbles, contentions and exaggerations, may be set aside. Thus, that the bread in the Supper is the very body of Christ, essentially transubstantiated beneath the outward accidents of the bread (quantity, shape, colour and taste), and that with and under that one and undivided bread the very substance of Christ's body is to be eaten by the mouth in the act of eating: these are human ways of putting things. In place of them let the manner of Scripture be used: "The bread which we break, or the breaking, distribution and taking of this bread in the Supper, is a communion of the body of Christ" (1 Cor. 10). Let its sense, as intended by the Holy Spirit, be studiously sought out and fixed as certain and unchanging, and the way to producing agreement will be easier. Whatever may be the case with human ways of putting things, whether they have been relevant to the matter or have departed from it.

units.la: Quod in exemplo transubstantiationis proponit, de consubstantiatione, vel sententia Lutherana capiatur, uti aeque facile potest, et confecta res est. Cujus ejusdem Auctoris volo banc in rem egregia quoque notari quae habet ejusdem Irenici sive de Differentiis religionum conciliandis Comment. §. 5. 10. 13. 12. Ubi quaerit: An non Scriptura alio modo et verbis de re aliqua loquatur, ut in ejus verbis sisti debeat, et verba hominum tanquam trica, noxia, et a salutari Verborum forma abducentia, rejici debeant, vel suspendi? § 14. An non fundamentum rei et substantia Christianae fidei in simplicitate teneri possit, etiamsi tandem de specialibus istis determinationibus simplex Christianus non aliquid sciat, et explicatas aut propositas satis capere non valeat. Sic panem Coenae communicationem Corporis Christi in usu esse, fundamentum Coenae est. An transsubstantiatione, consubstantiatione, vel substantiali panis & Corporis conjunctione, signi ad signatum relatione, analogica repraesentatione, Symbolica figuratione, expressione, aliave ratione sit, ad varias & Scholasticas determinationes pertinet, & a simplicibus Christianis intelligi non potest, sed ad Scholarum disceptata relinquendum & referendum est. Et omnino firmiter constituendum est, quid, quantum, & quale, ad ipsam fidei Christianae substantiam ac fundamentalem necessitatem pertineat, & in eo, ut consensus fidelium procuretur, imprimis laborandum. Suasit illud olim etiam Melanthon Electori Palatino Friderico.
units.tr: What he proposes in the example of transubstantiation can equally easily be taken as referring to consubstantiation, or to the Lutheran view, and the matter is settled. I wish to point out in this same author's work some excellent remarks on this subject, found in his Irenicum, or On Reconciling the Differences of Religion, commentary §§ 5, 10, 13 and 12. There he asks: "Does not Scripture speak of some matter in another way and in other words, so that one must stand by its words, and the words of men, as captious, harmful, and drawing us away from the wholesome form of the words, must be rejected or suspended?" (§ 14) "Can the foundation of the thing, and the substance of the Christian faith, not be held in its simplicity, even if the simple Christian knows nothing of those special determinations in the end, and cannot grasp them when they are explained or proposed?" Thus, that the bread of the Supper is in use a communion of the body of Christ, this is the foundation of the Supper. Whether it is by transubstantiation, by consubstantiation, or by a substantial conjunction of the bread and the body, by the relation of sign to thing signified, by analogical representation, by symbolic figuration, by expression, or by some other manner, this belongs to various scholastic determinations, which simple Christians cannot understand, and must be left to and referred to the disputations of the schools. And it must be firmly settled what, how much and of what kind is necessary to the very substance of the Christian faith and its fundamental necessity, and in this we must labour above all that the consent of the faithful be secured. Melanchthon once advised this same thing to the Elector Palatine, Frederick.

units.la: III. Secundo, remotis contentiosis, prodest reliquos de una forma verborum convenire. Et in hac controversia optimum esset, retinere verba Pauli: Panis, quem frangimus, κοινωνία ἐστὶ τοῦ σώματος. Et copiose de fracta Coena dicendum est, ut invitentur homines ad amorem hujus pignoris, & crebrum usum. Et vocabulum, κοινωνία, declarandum est. Non dicit, mutari naturam panis, ut Papistae dicunt. Non dicit, ut Bremenses, panem esse substantiale corpus Christi. Non dicit, ut Heshusius, panem esse verum corpus Christi: sed esse κοινωνίαν, id est, hoc, quo fit consociatio cum corpore Christi: quae fit in usu, & quidem non sine cogitatione.
units.tr: III. "Secondly, with contentious matters set aside, it is useful for the rest to agree on one form of words. And in this controversy it would be best to retain the words of Paul: 'The bread which we break is a communion [κοινωνία] of the body.' And the breaking of the Supper should be spoken of at length, so that people may be invited to love this pledge and to frequent use. And the word 'communion' [κοινωνία] should be explained." He does not say that the nature of the bread is changed, as the Papists say. He does not say, as the Bremen men do, that the bread is the substantial body of Christ. He does not say, as Heshusius does, that the bread is the true body of Christ; but that it is a communion [κοινωνία], that is, that by which fellowship with the body of Christ is effected, which takes place in use, and indeed not without thought.

units.la: Nullo vero modo probare potium ut ad formulam aliquam Consensus mutui quasi conglutinandam tradatur Adversariis. Christi corpus in Coena vere & substantialiter praesens dici, in quibus aliqui plus nimium quandoque luxuriarunt, vel indulserunt. Cum Martyre & sentio, & loquor, qui quam accuratus hac in parte fuerit in Colloquio Possiaceno, alibi dixi. Cujus etiam vide epistolam, inter epistolas Zanchii, pag. 404. ad Ioh. Sturmium, Argentinensis Scholae Rectorem, ubi inter alia se declarat: Cum postea rogor: An in Ecclesia Coenam sine corpore & sanguine Christi haberi existimem? Resp. Si de ea praesentia loquamur, quam corporalem, realem, atque substantialem vocant: corpus & sanguinem Christi abesse fateor: neque si adessent, plus utilitatis, satis, commodi, aut emolumenti nobis afferrent: quam inde hauriamus, dum in cœlis manent procul à nobis disjuncta. Eadem tamen dico adesse fidelibus in Cœnâ, præsentiâ fidei, cujus vis & facultas est, ut ea efficiat reddatque præsentia spiritualiter, quæ locorum spacio longè admodum sunt abjuncta. Deinde caro & sanguis Christi nobis præsentia sunt spiritu, gratiâ, & meritis, & aliis admirabilibus fructibus, qui divinitus per ea in nos derivantur, quemadmodum Sol dicitur nobis adesse præsens per lucem, radios, & bonos influxus, quos inde percipimus. Neque enim aut substantiam corporis Christi præsentem, aut oraliter manducari, aut ab indignis sumi, dicendum sed plane, & ingenue id quod res, corpus ejus substantialiter in coelo præsens, hic ejus ut morte fracti fieri ἀνάμνησιν, & per fidem, quæ πνευματικῶς καὶ βλεπομένως, spiritualiter, præsentissime, ac vividissime pasci illius fruitione solos pios. Præsentem Christum in Cœnâ uti omnes fatemur, ita dixisse hic suffecerit. Tum aliud est, vere & substantialiter adesse Christum in Cœnâ; quod utique verum, & sic nonnullos loquutos video: aliud, ejus corpus præsens esse. Vel etiam, verè & substantialiter Christi corpus accipi in cœnâ, & distribui, sacramentaliter videlicet: aliud, ibi per se, vel seipso vere & substantialiter præsens esse. Optime quod ad hanc rem dictum fuit ab antiquis, in Nostro hoc Belgio, V Valdensibus, in suâ Confessione, vel Catechismo (quod egregium antiquitatis nostræ monumentum suæ Historiæ Belgicæ inseruit, cui & eo nomine omnes multum debemus, Cl. Boxhornius, pag. 36.) interrogantes, nam ipsa ponam, ob venerationem suam, verba: Vra VVat ontfangt gy in den broede? Outsangt gy niet het lijff en bloet Iesu Christi? Antw. Dén ik woor maer ick en geloef alsoe niet als maenig doelende menschê doet. Want inden nachtmael en ontfangen ick noch vlesch, noch bloet lichamelicken, maer broet en wijn; welcke broet gebroecken ende wijn
units.tr: But by no means can it be right to hand down to the adversaries some formula, as though to glue together a mutual consent, that the body of Christ is said to be truly and substantially present in the Supper, a point in which some have at times indulged or run to excess. I both feel and speak with Martyr, and I have said elsewhere how exact he was in this respect at the Colloquy of Poissy. See also his letter, among the letters of Zanchius, p. 404, to John Sturm, rector of the school at Strasbourg, where among other things he declares himself: When I am later asked whether I think the Supper is held in the Church without the body and blood of Christ, I answer: if we speak of that presence which they call corporal, real and substantial, I confess that the body and blood of Christ are absent; nor, if they were present, would they bring us any more usefulness, benefit or advantage than we now draw from them, while they remain in heaven, separated far from us. Yet I say that the same are present to the faithful in the Supper, by the presence of faith, whose force and power is to make them present spiritually, though they are at a great distance from us in space. Then the flesh and blood of Christ are present to us by the Spirit, by grace and by merits, and by other admirable fruits which are derived to us from them by divine power, just as the sun is said to be present to us through its light, its rays and the good influences which we receive from it. For it must not be said that either the substance of the body of Christ is present, or that it is eaten orally, or taken by the unworthy; but plainly and ingenuously, what the thing is: his body is substantially present in heaven, and here it is made a remembrance of his breaking in death, and the godly alone are fed by its enjoyment, through faith, which is spiritual and seen [πνευματικῶς καὶ βλεπομένως], most present and most vividly. That Christ is present in the Supper we all acknowledge, and it is enough to have said so here. Then it is one thing to say that Christ is truly and substantially present in the Supper, which is certainly true, and I see that some have spoken in this way; it is another to say that his body is present. Or again, that the body of Christ is truly and substantially received and distributed in the Supper, sacramentally of course: it is another to say that he himself, by himself, is truly and substantially present there. What the ancients said well on this matter in our Netherlands was said by the Waldenses in their Confession or Catechism (an excellent monument of our antiquity, which the distinguished Boxhorn inserted in his Dutch History, p. 36, to which we all owe much on that account). I will set down their words, for the sake of their venerability, asking: "What do you receive in the bread? Do you not receive the body and blood of Jesus Christ?" Answer: "Yes, I say so, but I do not believe as many people do. For in the Supper I receive neither flesh nor blood bodily, but bread and wine; which bread being broken and wine drunk, as the Lord has ordained it, we are at the same time, through the Holy Spirit and faith and the lifting up of our hearts to heaven, made partakers of the body and blood of Christ, which was broken and poured out for us." And with the bread and wine I also receive those benefits which came through the breaking of his body and the pouring out of his blood on the cross for my sins.

units.la: <bl>wijn gedroncken zijnde / gelijck alst den Heere gesordineert heeft / soe wozden wy te gelijcke door den H. Geest/ ende't geloeve/ ende onser herten opheffinge ten hemel / deelachtich des lichaems ende bloet Christi / welke gebroecken ende uytgestort is geweest voor ons.</bl> En metten broede ende wijne ontfange ick oick die weldaden / die gecomen zijn door het breecken zijner lichaem ende uytstorten sijns bloets aen den Cruyce voor mijne sonden.
units.tr: Such is the frankness and sincere explanation of mind. Not to play with ambiguities and generalities: that is not pleasing, and not even to those in whose favour you seem to have acted so. Hence Luther never fully approved of Bucer's zeal, until at last he burst out with these words: "He is a seed-picker, he is nothing..."

units.la: Talis placet ingenuitas, & sincera mentis explicatio. Ludere amphibologiis, & in generalibus, randem nec illis placet, in quorum etiam gratiam sic egisse visus es. Vnde nec Luthero usquequaque probabatur Buceri studium, ut eruperit postremo in haec verba: Spermologus est, nil nisi conciliationes quaerens & tractans, sed apud me conciliationes ipsius nihil amplius habebunt loci &c. quando nempe Bucerus in Articulis Reformationis Coloniensis a. MDXL[?] v. omisisset mentionem corporalis Christi in Coena praesentiae. Calixtus, in suo Iudicio, de Buceriana conciliandi ratione: Ponebat autem fundamentum conciliationis in ambiguis formulis, quas una pars de manducatione figurata, sive spirituali, & praesentia tali, sine quali manducationem istam spiritualem per fidem non peragi statuebant: Altera vero de propria & orali manducatione & vera praesentia corporis (nempe corporis in praedicamento substantiae) acciperet: Vt ita si ad verba obiter ostenderetur, specieterms convenirent, aut saltem convenire crederentur, sive mera verba spectantibus & de sensu non sollicitis, convenire apparerent, etiamsi reapse & sententiis non convenirent. Qualis conciliandi ratio a Luthero & plerisque aliis prudentibus utriusque partis merito rejecta fuit & improbata. Et pag. 141. Rectius autem fuerit utramque partem simpliciter & ingenue, quod sentit, prositeri, quam alteram alteri ambiguis loquendi formulis imponere. Qualem concionandi rationem inierunt olim Philippus & Bucerus, nempe ut scriberentur formulae, quarum verba bis utraque pars amplecteretur, sed singulae suo sensu acciperent & interpretarentur. Quem conatum, quamvis expeditum eoque ingenii concordiae desiderio & studio professum, nulla successus felicitas excepit. Malumus, ut diximus, utramque partem animi sensa sincere & citra fucum exponere.
