Et etiamsi discrepent, nihilominus odia & inimicitias & conviciandi & damnandi libidinem ponere, & mutuam Christianam charitatem, ut Christianos decet, fovere & exercere, donec re inter eruditos erudite & placide disputata & agitata, Deus pleniorem & perfectiorem consensum largiatur. Ad quae quid dici possit, equidem non video. Quae quanto meliora sanioraque eo sunt, quod Theologi Darmstadini, coram Ernesto Landgravio apostatā, quorum cum Calixto negotium fuit, haud semel, praecedenti anno dixerunt: Reformatos in doctrinā fundamentales errores habere, & aeternam salutem destruentes: magno cum Principis, aliorumque scandalo. Certe ille iis scripsit d. vi. Decemb. MDCLV. se miratum fuisse quod non Lutherani aeque Reformatos ad communionem admitterent, ac bi illos, uti fit praesertim in Galliā, quum utriusque tam necessaria sit concordia. Haec ejus verba: Reformati quidem in controversiis cum Lutheranis nullos his fundamentales errores impingunt, ita ut absque opinionis abjuratione quam de S. Eucharistia habent (prout ex Charentonicā Synodo id liquet) eos ad communionem admittant. Unde nobis quoque persuasum erat, pro a Lutheranorum confessioni addictos, idem facturos, studio praesertim concordiae tantopere utriusque necessaria. Eant nunc, qui nihilominus discordias inter nos volunt, sciantque non ordine haberi Pontificios Lutheranos, ac Reformatos, idque etiam illis mirum esse, quod nos adeo dissentimus. Quare ut tandem quoque contrahamus fusius dicta, quosdam ponemus articulos, quibus tuto hactenus convenire possimus, & duritiem aliorum aversari, magis conscientiae & paci litare, quotquot optimi. 1. Vt de sententiae alicujus veritate, ex Scripturā ita de Ecclesiae alicujus sententia, ex confessionibus judicandum: non ex privati alicujus, vel Doctoris dictis, aut scriptis. II. Omnes Confessiones Ecclesiarum, quae Syntagmati Confessionum, publico Ecclesiarum nomine confecto, insertae, ubi & Augustana, & Helvetica, una cum aliis, pro Orthodoxis habendae. III. Ac proinde inter illas omnes Ecclesias, earum Ministros, & membra fraternitas oportet intercedat, & communio. IV. Cui rei, cuicunque istarum Confessionum & Ecclesiarum socio, pro conscientia & officio, quidquid alii secus, incumbendum, & quae privatim, quae publice annitendum, ut pro isto, quo eum Deus collocavit loco & gradu, pacem & communionem foveat ac conservet, & quaevis damna ac praejudicia avertat & caveat, pro fraternae charitatis regula. V. Servata tamen cuique sententiae suae Confessionis, & Ecclesiae diversitate illa, quae de doctrinae momento concordes (quae de doctrinae veritate, & momento distinctio probe semper observanda), de veritate alterutrius sententiae fas sit conferre & disputare, aliosque ad suam sententiam perducere, sed amicabili ubique & fraterno modo, in Scholis plus, in Ecclesia pro concione parcius, at parcissime libris. Haec, quamvis non coalito palam & ubique vulnere, a singulis praestari possunt, & non expectata communi aut universali Ecclesiarum utrarumque combinatione, a singulis erga singulos, seu hominum vulgo; seu Doctoribus, & Ecclesiis particularibus erga alios, nixi argumentis exemplisque supra positis, observari. Atque haec dicta sunto de nostro cum Lutheranis syncretismo, in quo ubi omnia a nostra quidem parte egerimus, at prudenter quoque, quae ad pacem pertinent, totum Deo committendum negotium est, cui quando non placet ad Judam convertere Israelem, sed hic amat in devia abire, ferendum est, & acquiescendum in eo quod bonis semper consiliis, exemplisque praeiverimus. Vult saepe Deus ob arcanas confilii sui rationes, & suorum exercitationem, seorsim habitare duas illas tribus, neque convenire ut antea, & eorundem sacrorum ut quidem oportet, habeti antiquam & constantem communionem. Vbi quando pro reducendis fratribus, in medium consuluerimus, atque haud segniter, ὡς μὴ μεταλύοντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ, licebit securi esse, & bonae conscientiae testimonio tutis, postremo & concludere praestantissimis Zuinglii verbis, quibus is suam ad M. Lutherum Exegesin Eucharistiae, (namque hic si uspiam necesse est bene cognitam habere negotii hujus historiam Ecclesiasticam totam, & ad eam passim recurrere, absque qua parum egeris, nosque ideo crebriores in eâ adducenda hic fuimus): Satis sit oro dissensum, satis tumultuatum, satis seditum. Orire gratissime Lucifer, pretium justitiae sol emica. Cum enim contenditur, negligitur sanctimonia, quam unice à nobis requiris. Vides ut à contentione nunquam redeamus meliores: est enim carnis opus, à quo nemo regredi citra maculam potest. Contra qui ab ea sunt alieni, nunquam non fuerunt optimi. Ab ego igitur nos abstinte, ut nervos omnes quos alioqui ad certandum intendimus, ad virtutis opus accingamus. Hoc & Apostoli monitum est II Tim. II. 22. Sectare justitiam, fidem, charitatem, pacem, cum iis qui invocant Dominum ex puro corde.
units.tr: Such candour and an honest statement of one's mind are welcome. Playing with ambiguities and generalities does not finally please even those in whose favour you seem to have acted. So Luther did not at all approve of Bucer's zeal for reconciliation, and at last broke out in these words: He is a seed-collector, seeking and handling nothing but reconciliations, but his reconciliations will have no further place with me, and so on. This was when Bucer, in the Articles of the Cologne Reformation of 1543 (?), had left out any mention of the bodily presence of Christ in the Supper. Calixtus, in his Judgment, on Bucer's method of reconciling: He laid the foundation of reconciliation in ambiguous formulas, which one party would take of a figurative or spiritual eating and of such a presence without which they held that this spiritual eating could not be accomplished through faith; the other party would take them of a proper and oral eating and of a true presence of the body (namely of the body in the category of substance). So that, if the words were briefly examined, the terms would agree, or at least would seem to agree, or would appear to agree to those who look only at the words and are not concerned about the sense, even though in reality and in their meanings they did not agree. Luther and most other prudent men on both sides rightly rejected and disapproved of this method of reconciling. And on p. 141: It would be better for each party simply and frankly to profess what it thinks, than for one to impose on the other ambiguous forms of speech. The method of preaching once adopted by Philip and Bucer, namely that formulas should be written whose words both parties might embrace, but each would take and interpret in its own sense, was an effort which, although undertaken openly and with a zeal for the desire of concord, no success ever crowned. We prefer, as we have said, that each party set forth the feelings of its mind sincerely and without disguise. And even if they disagree, nevertheless they should lay aside hatreds, enmities, the lust for reviling and condemning, and should cherish and practise mutual Christian love, as becomes Christians, until, the matter having been learnedly and calmly disputed and discussed among the learned, God grants a fuller and more perfect agreement. What can be said against these words, I indeed do not see. How much better and saner they are is shown by the fact that the Darmstadt theologians, who had the dispute with Calixtus, before the apostate Landgrave Ernest, said more than once in the preceding year that the Reformed hold fundamental errors in doctrine which destroy eternal salvation, to the great scandal of the Prince and others. Certainly he wrote to them on 6 December 1655 that he had been amazed that the Lutherans did not admit the Reformed to communion on the same terms as they admitted themselves, as is done especially in France, since the concord of both is so necessary. These are his words: The Reformed, indeed, in their controversies with the Lutherans, charge them with no fundamental errors, so that they admit them to communion without abjuring the opinion they hold concerning the Holy Eucharist (as is clear from the Synod of Charenton). Hence we too were persuaded that those attached to the Confession of the Lutherans would do the same, especially out of zeal for concord, which is so necessary to both. Let those now go who nevertheless want discords between us, and let them know that the Papists are not held in the same order as the Lutherans and the Reformed, and that it would also be surprising to them that we differ so much. Therefore, so that at last we may also draw together what has been said at greater length, we shall lay down some articles on which we can hitherto safely agree, and turn away from the harshness of others, and serve conscience and peace more, as many as are good. 1. As the truth of any opinion is to be judged from Scripture, so the opinion of any Church is to be judged from its confessions, not from the sayings or writings of any private person or teacher. II. All the Confessions of the Churches which are inserted in the Syntagma of Confessions, compiled in the public name of the Churches, where both the Augsburg and the Helvetic, together with the others, are to be held as Orthodox. III. And therefore fraternity and communion ought to exist among all those Churches, their ministers and members. IV. For this matter, every adherent of any of these Confessions and Churches, whatever others may think otherwise, must in conscience and duty strive, both privately and publicly, to foster and preserve peace and communion in the place and rank in which God has set him, and to avert and guard against every loss and prejudice, according to the rule of fraternal charity. V. Yet each person's diversity of opinion within his own Confession and Church being kept, those things on which they agree concerning the importance of doctrine (the distinction between the truth of doctrine and its importance must always be carefully observed) may be compared, and it is lawful to dispute about the truth of the other's opinion and to lead others to one's own opinion, but always in a friendly and brotherly manner: more in the schools, more sparingly in the Church in sermons, and most sparingly in books. These things, though not with an open and universal healing of the wound, can be performed by individuals, and observed, without any expected joint or universal combination of both Churches, by individuals towards individuals, whether among the common people or among teachers and particular Churches towards others, relying on the arguments and examples set out above. And let these things be said of our syncretism with the Lutherans; in which, although we have done all things on our part, and prudently also what pertains to peace, the whole matter must be committed to God. When it does not please Him to turn Israel to Judah, but He loves rather to go astray in byways, it must be borne and acquiesced in, and we shall have gone before them always with good counsels and examples. God often wills, for the hidden reasons of His counsel and for the trial of His people, that those two tribes dwell apart and no longer come together as before, and that they hold the ancient and constant communion of the same sacred rites, as indeed they ought. When we have taken counsel for bringing back the brethren, and that not sluggishly, [ὡς μὴ μεταλύοντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ], we may be safe and secure in the testimony of a good conscience, and finally conclude with the most excellent words of Zwingli, with which he addressed his Exegesis of the Eucharist to Master Luther (for here, if anywhere, it is necessary to have a well-known ecclesiastical history of this whole matter, and to refer to it constantly, without which you will accomplish little; and for that reason we have here often adduced it): I pray, let there be enough disagreement, enough tumult, enough sedition. Rise most welcome Lucifer, sun that shows the price of justice. For when we contend, holiness, which alone you require of us, is neglected. See how we never return from contention better: for it is a work of the flesh, from which no one can withdraw without stain. On the other hand, those who are free from it have never failed to be the best. Let us therefore abstain from it, so that we may apply all the strength which we otherwise direct to striving to the work of virtue. This the Apostle also admonished: 2 Tim. 2:22. Pursue righteousness, faith, love, peace, with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.

units.la: Sequuntur reliquae cum Lutheranis, post sacramentariam de S. Coenâ, controversiae: ubi primum consideranda ea de personâ Christi, ex priori illa nata. Nam quum velint Lutherani, in S. Coenâ adesse non modo Christum, de quo nulla disputatio, sed Christi substantiale corpus, de ejus praesentiâ ita coeptum disputari, ut prior illa huic cedere visa fuerit, & quasi translata belli sede totum ferme praelium in hoc versari, quod est de reali corporis Christi praesentiâ. Quo enim modo hic corpus Christi? quum corpus omne ex sui naturâ certo aliam loco adsit, & Christi corpus adscendeŕit desiit in coelos. Vel enim per descensum, atque in loca frequentatæ duntaxat, Cœnæ, vel in omnia, ubique; aut si non per descensum, tum ex prævia ili omni loco existentia contingat illa omnipræsentia, oportet. Sed quomodo jam adscendit, atque in cœlis sedere dicitur? Hic Lutherus, videns se in arctum cogi, eligendum alterutrum vidit, aut multipræsentiam Christi, multis in locis, vid. S. Cœnæ; aut omnipræsentiam corporis in omnibus locis sine discrimine statuendam. atque adhuc varie nonnunquam de utroque loqui Lutheranos videas. Iam in fervore contentionis, pressus ab Adversario, ad opinionem ubiquitatis confugit. Lutherus, aliquando omisit, solis institutionis Cœnæ verbis adhærens, atque ex iis sequi præsentiam corporis Christi arbitratus, modum quo fieret, in medio reliquit: quo pacto se expediunt inter Lutheranos quotquot ubiquitatem non admittunt, vel rejiciunt. Et quemadmodum sententiam suam de consubstantiatione corporis Christi in Cœnâ, missâ transsubstantiatione. Lutherus à Cardinale Alliacensi sumsit; ita Vbiquitatis commentum debetur Iacobo Fabro Stapulensi; ejusque apud Lutheranos in canonem relatio auctoribus formulæ Bergensis.
units.tr: There follow the remaining controversies with the Lutherans, after the sacramentarian dispute about the Holy Supper. Here we must first consider the question concerning the person of Christ, which arose from the former one. For since the Lutherans want Christ to be present in the Holy Supper not only (which is no matter of dispute) but also as His substantial body, the question of His presence has begun to be debated in such a way that the former question seemed to give way to this one, and, as if the seat of war had been moved, almost the whole battle has come to turn on this: the real presence of the body of Christ. For how is the body of Christ here? Since every body by its nature must be in a certain place, and the body of Christ ascended and ceased to be on earth, going up into heaven. For either it must be by a descent, and only into the places where the Supper is frequently celebrated, or else into all places, everywhere; or, if not by descent, then that omnipresence must come about from a prior existence in every place. But how then did it ascend, and is it said to sit in heaven? Here Luther, seeing himself driven into a corner, saw that one of two things had to be chosen: either a multi-presence of Christ in many places, namely at the Supper, or an omnipresence of the body to be posited in all places without distinction. And you may see the Lutherans still speaking now and then in varied ways about each. Then, in the heat of contention, pressed by the adversary, he took refuge in the opinion of ubiquity. Luther at one time left the question aside, clinging to the words of the institution of the Supper alone, and thinking that the presence of the body of Christ followed from them, he left the manner in which it happens in the middle: this is how all those among the Lutherans who do not admit or reject ubiquity get themselves out of the difficulty. And just as Luther took his opinion of the consubstantiation of the body of Christ in the Supper from Cardinal d'Ailly, under the name of transubstantiation, so the fiction of ubiquity is owed to Jacques Lefèvre of Étaples, and its entry among the Lutherans into the canon is owed to the authors of the Formula of Bergen.

units.la: Iterum, arreptâ corporis Christi omnipræsentiâ, quam jactare facilius, quam exponere & declarare, alia difficultas surrexit omnium maxima, quâ ratione hanc haberet humana natura, cum sit proprietas divinæ? Vbi tum proprietates in Deo divellere ab ejus natura, tum inter se, res merito visa horrenda, & quæ suo præjudicio satis argueret, theses illas, in quarum subsidium hoc advocaretur, pudendas, falsas, & improbandas esse. Sed quemadmodum ii, quibus semel deposità frons, nihil ultra reformidant peccare; ita qui errori suo pertinaciam addunt, subruere omnia malunt, quam illum deponere, nihilque iis tam durum sonat vel absurdum, quod priori commento statuminando non assumant. Ergo admiserunt Lutherani, proprietates divinae naturae in Christo communicatas esse humanae, neque tamen omnes, sed aliquas, praesertim ubiquitatem, in cujus gratiam illud excogitatum fuerat, sed & praeter eam, omnisciemtiam quoque, & omnipotentiam, atque adorabilitatem. Quod quomodo naturas in Christo duas, earumque proprietates salvas relinquat, & à damnato utrinque Eutychianismo distet, quomodoque factum, an vi unionis duarum naturarum, an exaltationis & glorificationis in natura humana, ipsi necdum explicare potuerunt. Vide Frider. VVendelini nuperas Exercitationes Theologicas, adversus Joh. Gerhardi exercit. xlvii. Hanc quaestionem ego secundo loco pono, ideo quod ex priori orta, cujus habenda in his disputationibus potior ratio, quam absque illo, ordinis locorum communium, ubi haec illam praecederet. Atque in hac quaestione non Nos solum, sed & Pontificios adversarios habent, quamvis inter se conveniant, corpus Christi in Coena praesens esse: sed id Pontificii non ex aliqua corporis Christi ubiquitate, nedum proprietatum divinarum cum humana natura communicatione, sed simplici corporis multipraesentia per voluntatem Dei, derivandum censent. Vbique appareret, in coeno Papali mansisse Lutheranos; atque ex eo longius purgatiusque se proripuisse Reformatos.
units.tr: Again, having seized on the omnipresence of Christ's body, which is easier to boast of than to explain and define, another difficulty arose, the greatest of all: how could human nature have this property, when it belongs to the divine nature? Here they tore the properties apart from God's nature and from one another. Men judged this a dreadful thing, and it was enough to show by its very offensiveness that those theses, in whose support this was brought forward, were shameful, false and to be rejected. But as those who have once put aside shame fear nothing further in sinning, so those who add obstinacy to their error would rather overturn everything than give it up, and nothing sounds so harsh or absurd to them that they will not take it up to prop up their earlier invention. So the Lutherans admitted that the properties of the divine nature were communicated to the human nature in Christ, but not all of them, only some: above all omnipresence, for whose sake that doctrine had been devised, but also, besides it, omniscience, omnipotence and adorability. How they can keep the two natures and their properties intact in Christ, and how they differ from the Eutychianism condemned on both sides, and how this comes about, whether by the force of the union of the two natures or by the exaltation and glorification in the human nature, they have not yet been able to explain. See Friedrich Wendelin's recent Theological Exercises, against the forty-seventh exercise of Johann Gerhard. I place this question second, because it arises from the former, and in these disputations it deserves a higher place than it would have in the order of the commonplaces, where it would come before that one. On this question we have as adversaries not only ourselves but also the Papists, although they agree with us that the body of Christ is present in the Supper. But the Papists do not derive this from any ubiquity of Christ's body, much less from a communication of the divine properties to the human nature, but from a simple multipresence of the body by the will of God. It is everywhere plain that the Lutherans remained in the Papal mire, and that the Reformed have dragged themselves further and more cleanly out of it.

units.la: Vivente Luthero nunquam quaestio mota super dogmate Praedestinationis, neque in disputationibus, vel Colloquiis aliquid de illo dictum aut scriptum, adeo nullâ hâc in parte cum Luthero fuit dissensio, sed eandem quam is sententiam, sequuti Nostri fuerunt, quod etiamnum ex ejus scriptis ostendi potest, initisque Consensibus. Et tamen hodie ejus discipuli tantas serè super hoc articulo, ac aliis, turbas cient. Quod argumento est, quàm à Praeceptoris sui sententiâ dissentientes ... cesserint, & materias quęstionum per hodiernos Doctores variare immensum, atque mutari praeter pristinum ipsarum statum. Controversia de Praedestinatione producta, & disputari coepta primum Argentorati, inter Marbachium, & Zanchium, a. clɔ lɔ lxɪ. & lxɪɪ. inde palam in Colloquio Mompelgartensi a. clɔlɔlxxxvɪ, à Iacobo Andreâ, contra Bezam: atque inde pro articulo dissensus haud minimo habita fuit. Cujus instituti Colloquii causas magis politicas, quam Ecclesiasticas, ex Dan. Tossano, narrat eximius rerum Reformatarum historicus, Scultetus, in Curriculo, sive Historia vitae suae, pag. 28. nempe quod se praesente Tossanus Perzelio in causas illius Colloquii inquirenti retulerit, politicas fuisse, non Theologicas, tam à parte Gallorum Mompelgarti exulantium, quam Friderici Principis, Comitis Mompelgartensis. Gallos enim exules ideo Bezam vocasse, quod sperarent, si placide cum Iacobo de controversiis, inter Gallos & Virtembergicos, capitibus conferret, se deinceps Principe usuros benigniore, & forte etiam Ducem Virtembergicum futurum nostrum. Principem Fridericum autem primis aetatis annis à Iacobo in Vbiquitaria doctrina informatum, postea P. Beutrichii suasu Bernam & Genevam profectum, ibi Bezae lectionum & concionum auditorem fuisse, & aliquando libere dixisse: ich habe viel zu Genff und Schreiß gesehen / daron mir nichts gesagt worden / aber wenig davon D. Iacobus gesagt hat / hoc est; Geneva & in Helvetia vidi multa, de quibus nihil, pauca eorum, de quibus saepe audivi ex D. Iacobo. Eundemque ab eo tempore humaniorem erga Gallos fuisse, atque ideo exules suscepisse. Cum autem ei suggestum fuisset, Ducem Virtembergicum prole mascula carere, & Austriacos vix latuos illum successorem, si Hugonotarum partibus faveret, esse illum jam suspectum, & quod Genevae suisset, & quod Gallos exules foveret, his adductum cau-sct, & quod Gallos exules foveret, his adductum causis consensisse in colloquium Bezæ cum Iacobo, non tam ut veritati consuleret, quam ut se de Calvinismo purgaret. Prædestinationem autem defendunt Lutherani, ex fide prævisâ, & generalem in Deo omnes homines salvandi voluntatem, inde & redemtionem, atque gratiam universalem: quarum opinionum jam semina jacta in Libro Concordiæ, c. xi. de æternâ Prædestinatione, & electione Dei. Quamvis in doctrinâ de libero arbitrio ab antiquâ & Catholicâ Ecclesiæ sententiâ, quam norunt & nostram esse, nolint videri dissentire. Neque etiam dissensit Lutherus, uti ostendit ejus liber de servo arbitrio, contra Erasmum, quem non retractatum ab Auctore fuisse Nostri in Disput. cum hodiernis Lutheranis ostendunt, interque alios Marcus Fridericus Vvendelinus, in præfatione Exercitationum Theologicarum, adversus Iohannem Gerhardi: quod, nisi declinarent à semitâ antiquâ hodierni, probare quid attineret? Et nullum librorum suorum majoris semper Lutherus fecit, voluitque pro genuino haberi, ac istum, & Catechismum majorem: quemadmodum ad Capitonem scripsit a. clɔ Iɔ xxxvii. Neque duriores apud Nostrum quemquam loquutionum modi occurrunt, quam apud Lutherum deprehendes: qui adversus easdem calumnias necesse habuit respondere pro doctrinâ, qualibus nostra eadem à Lutheranis infamari solet, ut de Deo auctore peccati, de distinctione duplicis Dei voluntatis occultæ & revelatæ: quod ex ejus ad Antverpienses scriptâ epistolâ, Tom. ii. epist. pag. 281: persici potest. Nulla quidem hac in parte discrepantia observata fuit inter Lutherum ac Nostros, in Consensu Marpurgensi a. clɔ Iɔ xxix. ubi tamen articulus sextus de hoc doctrinæ articulo verba facit. In Confessione Augustanâ, art. xviii. orthodoxe loquuntur. Melanthon in Loc. Comm. & apud Pezelium, Argum. & Resp. part. ii. Chemnitius, in Loc. Comm. Iac. Heerbrandus, passim omnes damnant hic Pelagianos, atque etjam Synergistas, & Pontificios nobiscum egregie refellunt, Chemnitius, in Exam. Conc. Tridentini, Ioh. Gerhardi, Loc. Comm. de lib. arbitrio, pag. 398. & Confess. Catholic. Tom. IV. pag. 536. neque distinctam hoc in articulo, quod alioqui gnaviter solent, praeter illa quae ad locum de Praedestinatione faciunt, annotant cum Calvinistis (quomodo loquuntur) controversiam, non Chemnitius, Luc. Osiander, Mentzerus, Ioh. Gerhardi, neque ipse adeo maledicentissimus Henr. Eckhardi. Et tamen non usquequaque videntur cum Luthero suo, ac communi nostrā doctrinā consentire aliqui, concedentes, in homine potestatem non resistendi verbo Dei, natura esse posse. Cujus quamvis aeque ac aliorum, ubi minori specie quaestiones multiplicant, possent facere ex ipsorum methodo distinctam quoque controversiam, omittere tamen eos studiose arbitror, quia nimis palam à Lutheri, & Catholicā Ecclesiae doctrinā, suaque Confessione dissentire, & ad Pelagianismum deflectere deprehenderentur. Et illud, non resistere, à nobis oriri, inde sequi Spiritus operationem, & efficientiam fidei, videtur statuere Osiander, in Enchiridio Controv. cap. VIII. qu. 11. Quando igitur obedienter, & debitā diligentiā audimus verbum, neque Spiritui sancto resistimus, tum non nos, sed Spiritus sanctus, opus suum in nobis inchoat, & fidem excitat. Et sic, non ex nobis, sed ex Spiritu sancto provenit fides: quam non nos, sed Spiritus ille in nobis excitat. Quum autem in omnibus hominibus à naturae perversitate, & peccandi voluptate sit sacrorum repugnantia & contemptus (Ægid. Hunnius, in tractatu de libero arbitrio, pag. 80. Æquales etiam sunt respectu naturalis illius contemtus, quo animalis homo naturā fastidire solet verbum Dei, stultitia siquidem est illi, nec potest cognoscere, quod spiritualiter dijudicatur. Fastidium naturale, & naturaliter ingenitum appellat, pag. 86. 89.) quomodo (dico) quum hoc nobis ingenitum sit naturae viribus superari fastidium, contemtus, & resistentia potest? cum & ad deponendam naturae pravitatem nobiscum nascentem, nullae nobis supersint vires? uti bene loquitur Joh. Gerhardi Loc. Commun. Tom. II. sol. 444. Ægid. Hommius tractatu jam dicto, pag. 40. inquit: Deus per spiritum suum, hominem ex nolente ac repugnante volentem, consentientem, & obedientem efficit. Neque dissimulanda distinctio, quam dat pag. 46. de duplici velle, eique opposito duplici nolle, quorum prius sit pædagogicum, circa externam ministerii obedientiam; alterum internum, descriptum obedientia fidei & assensione cordis: & illud quidem in nostrarum virium potestate situm vult, non autem hoc. Pagina vero 60. etiam interna hominum non renatorum arbitrio adjungit, qualia, affectum non contradicendi, propositum non blasphemandi, non calumniandi. Quibus conferri potest ejusdem Disp. xxxi. & xxxii. in Volumine Thesium ipsius. Si vero accipiamus, quod in Tractatus illius initio statim dicit: quod in divinis & spiritualibus rebus nullum sit arbitrium humanae voluntatis, sed res de sola titulo; est id in nostris Ecclesiis extra dubitationem positum, quodque pag. 10. in his, inquam, ne modiculum quidem illud de quo Erasmus disputat, superesset homini suis viribus relictio; sed sunt haec unius ac solius Spiritus sancti virtuti & operationi in solidum adscribenda: tum nullus hic controversiae articulus. Atque in illis etiam discrepantia inter Lutheranorum, & Remonstrantium sententia sita; unde diversa utrorumque ad nostram Ecclesiam ratio. Sed ex isto fundamento, si res extra assectus introspiciatur, nulla deberet inter Lutheranos, ac nos esse super dogmate Praedestinationis dissensio. Nam posito contra Pelagianos, Pontificios, & Synergistas themate, non per nostras aut vires, aut concursum esse quod convertimur, sed ex sola & mera spiritus divini gratia atque operatione, sequitur, converti nullos nisi per gratiam illam posse, & sola hac data homines converti. verti. Iam non omnes convertuntur, sed aliqui: hic ergo gratia illa contingit. Numquid non aliis quoque eandem conversionis gratiam dare Deus posset, modo vellet? omnino: non dat autem: quare nec vult dare. Hoc vero quod in tempore facit, & quomodo facit, sic facere decrevit ab æterno: nota enim ei opera sua à sæculo: quare prædestinavit Deus dare illis suam conversionis gratiam, non item aliis, ac proinde etiam salutem, nam hæc solius conversionis adjunctum consequens est. Patet igitur, non omnium æque salutem Deum generali aliquâ voluntate velle vel prædestinatione: neque redemtionem esse universalem; nec gratiam; uti neque salutem: quæ omnia pari sunt latitudinis & extensionis: sed uti his, & non aliis gratiam salutaris conversionis & exhibet Deus, & vult, ita iisdem & Christum redemtorem voluisse docendum quoque est solis, atque salutem. Adeo totum negotium vertitur in dogmate de gratia & libero arbitrio, quo bene asserto, in reliquis vera nequit esse controversia, & nisi Lutheranus sibi, neque concatenatæ huic veritati obloqui potest. De quo videri potest Iohannis Lampadii Bremensis Prodromus concordiæ evangelicæ, ubi de prædestinatione, libero arbitrio, annexisque agitur capitibus, & ex ipsis Lutheranis ostenditur, utriusque partis super illis consensus, quodque novatores nullam exinde fovendi schismatis causam habeant. Distinguitque Auctor, quod non frustra observemus, inter Lutheranos, Euangelicos, & Vbiquitistas Pseudo-Lutheranos. pag. 3. eoque hoc fine suscipiam, ut palam faciam non differre hac in parte Reformatos ab Evangelicis Lutheranis, sed tantum ab Vbiquitistis Pseudo-Lutheranis, quorum Cadmeam fraternitatem obtinere non anxie laborant. Etenim distinguendum inter Lutheranos semper diximus.
units.tr: While Luther was alive, the question of the doctrine of Predestination was never raised, and nothing about it was said or written in disputations or colloquies. There was so little disagreement with Luther on this point that our people followed his opinion, as can still be shown from his writings and from the early consensus statements. Yet today his disciples stir up nearly as much controversy over this article as over the others. This shows how far they have departed from their teacher's opinion, and how greatly the questions have been altered by present-day teachers and moved away from their original state. The controversy about predestination began and was first argued at Strasbourg between Marbach and Zanchius in 1561 and 1562. It then came openly to light at the Colloquy of Mömpelgard in 1586, where Jacob Andreae opposed Beza, and from then on it was regarded as a point of no small disagreement. The historian of the Reformed churches, Scultetus, in his Curriculum, or history of his life, page 28, gives the causes of that colloquy as more political than ecclesiastical. He reports from Daniel Tossanus, who told Pezelius when he inquired into the causes of the colloquy in Scultetus's presence, that they were political and not theological, both on the side of the French exiles living at Mömpelgard and on that of Prince Frederick, Count of Mömpelgard. The French exiles had summoned Beza, they say, because they hoped that if he discussed the controversies between the French and the Württembergers calmly with Jacob, he would thereafter find a kinder prince, and perhaps our Jacob would even become Duke of Württemberg. Prince Frederick, however, had been instructed in the Ubiquitarian doctrine by Jacob in his early years. Later, on the advice of P. Beutrich, he went to Bern and Geneva, where he heard Beza's lectures and sermons. He once said freely, in German: "I saw much at Geneva and Schaffhausen, of which nothing was said to me, but little of what Dr. Jacob has told me," that is, Geneva and Helvetia I saw many things, of which nothing, and few of those things about which I often heard from Dr. Jacob. From that time on he was more humane toward the French, and so he received the exiles. When it was suggested to him that the Duke of Württemberg had no male heir, and that the Austrians would hardly be a gentle successor to him if he favoured the Huguenots's cause, and that he was already under suspicion both because he had been at Geneva and because he fostered the French exiles, he was moved by these reasons to agree to the colloquy between Beza and Jacob. He did so not so much to serve the truth as to clear himself of Calvinism. Lutherans, however, defend predestination on the basis of foreseen faith, and a general will in God that all men be saved, and from this redemption and universal grace. The seeds of these opinions were already sown in the Book of Concord, chapter 11, on the eternal predestination and election of God. Yet on the doctrine of free will they wish not to appear to dissent from the ancient and Catholic opinion of the Church, which they know to be ours too. Nor did Luther dissent, as his book On the Bondage of the Will, against Erasmus, shows. Our people in disputation with the present-day Lutherans show that the author never retracted it, and among others Marcus Friedrich Wendelinus does so in the preface to his Theological Exercises, against Johann Gerhard. Unless the present-day Lutherans have strayed from the ancient path, what would be the point of proving this? Luther always considered none of his books more genuine, and wished none to be held as more so, than this one and his Larger Catechism, as he wrote to Capito in 1537. Nor will you find harsher forms of expression in any of our writers than you will in Luther, who had to answer for the doctrine against the same calumnies with which our teaching is usually defamed by the Lutherans, such as that God is the author of sin, and the distinction between the twofold, hidden and revealed, will of God. This can be verified from his letter written to the people of Antwerp, vol. 2 of the letters, page 281. Indeed no disagreement on this point was observed between Luther and our people in the Marburg Consensus of 1529, although the sixth article there does treat of this doctrinal article. In the Augsburg Confession, article 18, they speak orthodoxly. Melanthon, in the Loci communes and in Pezelius's Arguments and Answers, part 2, Chemnitz in the Loci communes, and Jacob Heerbrand throughout, all condemn the Pelagians here, and also the Synergists, and they refute the Papists splendidly alongside us. Chemnitz does so in his examination of the Council of Trent, and Johann Gerhard in his Loci communes on free will, page 398, and in his Catholic Confession, vol. 4, page 536. None of them, however, though they usually work hard at such things, notes a separate controversy on this article with the Calvinists, as they put it, apart from those points that bear on the place of predestination. Not Chemnitz, not Luke Osiander, not Mentzer, not Johann Gerhard, nor even the most abusive Henry Eckhard. Yet some do not seem altogether to agree with their Luther or with our common doctrine, granting that in man there can be, by nature, the power of not resisting the word of God. Although they could, as with other matters where they multiply questions over lesser points, make out of their own method a separate controversy here too, I think they study to leave it alone, because they would be seen to dissent too plainly from the doctrine of Luther and of the Catholic Church and from their own Confession, and to lean towards Pelagianism. And Osiander seems to hold that this "not resisting" comes from us, and that from it follows the operation of the Spirit and the efficacy of faith, in his Enchiridion of Controversies, chapter 8, question 11: When therefore we hear the word obediently and with due diligence, and do not resist the Holy Spirit, then it is not we but the Holy Spirit who begins his work in us and stirs up faith. And so faith comes not from us but from the Holy Spirit, who stirs it up in us, not we. Yet since in all men there is, from the perversity of nature and the pleasure of sinning, a repugnance and contempt for sacred things (Egidius Hunnius, in his treatise on free will, page 80: They are equal too, with respect to that natural contempt with which the natural man is accustomed to despise the word of God; for it is foolishness to him, nor can he know it, because it is spiritually discerned; he calls it natural disgust, and innately implanted by nature, pages 86 and 89), how, I ask, since this disgust, contempt, and resistance are innate to us, can they be overcome by the powers of nature? When we have no powers left to put off the depravity of nature born with us? So well says Johann Gerhard, Loci communes, vol. 2, page 444. Egidius Hommius, in the treatise already cited, page 40, says: God through his Spirit makes man willing, consenting, and obedient, out of unwilling and resisting. Nor should we pass over the distinction which he gives on page 46, of a twofold willing and its opposite, a twofold unwilling. The first is pedagogical, concerning outward obedience to the ministry; the other is internal, described as obedience of faith and assent of the heart. He wants the first to lie within the power of our faculties, but not the second. On page 60 he even adds to the inward things of unregenerate men's free will such things as the disposition not to contradict, the purpose not to blaspheme or slander. These may be compared with his disputations 31 and 32 in the volume of his Theses. But if we accept what he says at the very beginning of that treatise, that in divine and spiritual things there is no power of the human will, but the matter rests solely on the title; this is placed beyond doubt in our Churches, and what he says on page 10, that in these things, I say, not even that tiny bit about which Erasmus disputes would be left to man by his own powers, but these must be ascribed wholly and solely to the virtue and operation of the Holy Spirit, then there is no controversial article here at all. Indeed the disagreement between the opinion of the Lutherans and that of the Remonstrants lies in these very matters, which is why each side stands in a different relation to our Church. But on this foundation, if the matter is examined apart from feelings, there ought to be no disagreement between the Lutherans and us about the doctrine of predestination. For once it is established against the Pelagians, the Papists, and the Synergists, that what turns us is not done by our own powers or our cooperation, but by the sheer grace and operation of the divine Spirit alone, it follows that none are converted except through that grace, and that men are converted only when this grace is given. Now not all are converted, but some are. Therefore that grace comes to these. Could not God also give the same grace of conversion to others, if he wished? Certainly he could. But he does not give it; therefore he does not will to give it. What he does in time, and how he does it, he decreed to do thus from eternity, for he knows his works from the beginning. Therefore God predestined to give his grace of conversion to these, but not to others, and consequently also salvation, for salvation is the necessary consequence of conversion alone. It is plain, then, that God does not will, by any general will or predestination, the salvation of all men equally; nor is redemption universal, nor is grace, nor is salvation; all these have the same breadth and extent. But just as God bestows and wills the grace of saving conversion on these and not on others, so it must be taught that Christ the Redeemer willed to redeem those same ones only, and to save them. Thus the whole business turns on the doctrine of grace and free will, and once this is rightly asserted, no true controversy can remain on the other points. A Lutheran cannot oppose this interlinked truth unless he opposes himself. On this one may consult Johannes Lampadius of Bremen, Prodromus of the Evangelical Concord, where predestination, free will, and the chapters connected with them are treated, and where it is shown from the Lutherans themselves that both parties agree on them, and that the innovators have no reason from this to foster a schism. The author rightly distinguishes, which we should not neglect, between the Lutherans, the Evangelicals, and the Pseudo-Lutheran Ubiquitists. Page 3: And I undertake this with the purpose of making plain that the Reformed do not differ on this point from the Evangelical Lutherans, but only from the Pseudo-Lutheran Ubiquitists, whose Cadmean brotherhood they do not anxiously labour to keep. Indeed we have always said that a distinction must be made among the Lutherans.

units.la: Super perseverantia Sanctorum nullam unquam litem Nostris movit aut Lutherus, aut Melanthon, aut quis alius veteranorum istius familiae Theologorum. Unde forte aliter verba Confessionis Augustanae art. XII. quo damnatur in fine error aliquis Anabaptistarum, qui dicerent, justificatos Spiritum S. non posse amittere, accipienda esse quam hodierni volunt, conjicere licet: eo magis, quo nec illa sententia Anabaptistarum est, sed contraria, justificatos quidem amittere Spiritum Sanctum. vel ponendum hoc inter illa, de quibus conqueri Melanthon solitus, quod in tanta angustia Confessionem illam adornasset, ut si postmodum conscribenda fuisset, accuratiore studio illam limasset. Adde Nostrorum in hunc articulum exegeses, Altingii, Crocii, aliorum. Super eo disputationem, post vexationes & turbas a Marbachio datas in Schola Argentinensi, iniit Jacobus Andreas, in Colloquio Mompelgartensi, cum Beza, Ægidius Hunnius, in Volumine Thesium, Disput. xxx. hâc de re disputat, ut quaestione Theologica; aliter ac de quaestionibus fidei.
units.tr: Lutherus, Melanthon, and the other veteran theologians of that party never raised any quarrel with our side over the perseverance of the Saints. So one may suspect that the words of the Augsburg Confession, Article XII, where some error of the Anabaptists is condemned at the end, that is, the claim that justified persons cannot lose the Holy Spirit, should be understood differently from the way the moderns want. This is all the more likely because that was not the Anabaptist view at all, which was the opposite, namely that justified persons can indeed lose the Holy Spirit. Or this passage should be placed among those things about which Melanthon was accustomed to complain, that he had drafted that Confession under such pressure of time that, had it been written up afterwards, he would have polished it with more careful study. Add the expositions of our opponents on this article, by Alting, Crocius, and others. Jacob Andreae, after the troubles and disturbances stirred up by Marbach in the school at Strasbourg, took up the matter in the Colloquy of Mömpelgard with Beza. Ægidius Hunnius, in his volume of Theses, Disputation 30, discusses it as a theological question, not in the way one treats questions of faith.

units.la: Et ab illo Mompelgartensi Colloquio, vel Jacobo Andreâ, reliquarum de baptismo, & caeremoniis ritibusque nonnullis quaestionum disputationes coeptae: de quibus non ut contenderent, sed componerent magis erant antea omnes solliciti: tanguntque aut administrationem Sacramentorum, baptismi, & Coenae; aut templa, & cultum publicum: talia, ut disciplinae quidem Ecclesiasticae, non tamen religionis diversitatem indicent; atque ab Adversariis magis ex praxi defendantur pleraque, quam necessitate. Unde in Synodo Posnaniensi a. cIↄ Iↄ lxx. die xx. Maji, quâ consensus Sendomiriensis ante mensem factus confirmabatur art. xviii. benè statuerunt Augustanae Confessionis, & Bohemicae Fratres: Caeremonias & ritus Papisticos sensim auferendos, & omnino rejiciendos esse censemus, ut Exorcismum, imagines idololatricas, Sanctorum reliquias, ipsum superstitiosum candelarum, Consecrationem herbarum, vexilla, cruces aureas & argenteas, ac his similia: ne per illa verbum Dei profanetur, & ne Antichristo patrocinari videamur. Atque in historia Concordiae V Vittembergensis, quam Argentinensibus suis tradidit Bucerus, de Pomerano refert, quum super illis caeremoniis cum eo conferret, ita sibi responsum, quod non multum illa moraretur, quin solere se S. Coenam saepius sine candelis, vestimentorum pompis, & elevationis ritu, fortassis aliquanto etiam simplicius quam apud nos fiat, in suis Ecclesiis celebrare. Haec ita Bucerus, in tractatu dicto, inter Scripta ejus Anglicana, pag. 658.
units.tr: From that Colloquy of Mömpelgard, or from Jacob Andreae, the disputations began on the rest of the questions concerning baptism and certain ceremonies and rites. Before this, everyone had been anxious to settle these matters, not to fight over them. They touch either the administration of the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper, or the churches and public worship. They are of such a kind that they point to differences in church discipline, not to a difference in religion. Moreover, our adversaries defend most of them more from practice than from necessity. Hence at the Synod of Posen, on the 20th day of May 1570, by which the Sandomierz agreement made a month before was confirmed in Article 18, the Brethren of the Augsburg Confession and the Bohemian Brethren wisely decided: We judge that the Papistic ceremonies and rites should gradually be removed and wholly rejected, such as exorcism, idolatrous images, relics of saints, the superstitious use of candles, the consecration of herbs, banners, golden and silver crosses, and things like these, lest the Word of God be profaned by them and we seem to favour the Antichrist. And in the history of the Fifth Wittenberg Concord, which Bucer gave to his people at Strasbourg, Bucer reports about Pomeranus that when he discussed those ceremonies with him, he received this answer: that he did not much care about them, since he was accustomed to celebrate the Holy Supper in his own churches more often without candles, without the pomp of vestments, and without the rite of elevation, and perhaps even somewhat more simply than is done among us. So Bucer, in the treatise titled among his English writings, page 658.

units.la: Quod ad nostras cum Lutheranis spectat disputationes: quemadmodum Adversarii in fingendis & faciendis controversiis strenui sunt, ita in disputando molesti, prolixi, obtusi, passim quoque acerbi & maledicci. Non video adeo necessum esse multos libros scribere, quum eorum satis magna sit copia: minus probo personales impugnationes, tam familiare illis vitium, ut vix ii etiam, qui prae aliis moderati, & erga nos propensi videntur, eo abstinere queant, quin passim Calvinianos nominent, & quodcunque istius generis convicium. Matthias Hoe, V Vittembergensis Theologus, neutiquam inter optimos numerandus, in libello de Disputationibus Theologicis, dum docet scilicet, quomodo instituendae sint, passim ut Sacramentarios nos acerbissime exagitat. Lepidum nempe boni disputatoris exemplum. Acturus tu aliquando cum illis, diutior sis in exponendo controversiae statu; ut Adversarii se expediant: tum ad disputationem accede, & in forma, syllogistice, uti ad Andream Iacobi in Colloquio Mompelgartensi clamabat aliquoties D. Beza, sic syllogismum: id est, disputare oportet perspicue, & amice, uti inter illos, quorum unitae aliquando partes & Ecclesiae fuerunt, & si forte iterum, vel alicubi uniendae. Ideoque & hoc probe observandum, ut sententiam suam quam hodie tenent Adversarii, non solum conentur nobis probare veram, sed illam quoque esse Lutheri, & Confessionis Augustanae: contra nobis id agendum, ut in omnibus ostendamus consensum doctrinae nostrae cum Luthero, & Augustanâ Confessione, vel quomodo se mutuo tolerarint olim dissidentes. Quod egregie & diligenter ostendit in libro Belgico Henricus Alutarius: Speculum dissidentium Lutheranorum. Adeo qui in hisce controversiis aliquid cum fructu praestiturus sit, oportet aeque bonum esse, saltem quod ad res Reformationis primas, historicum, ac Theologum, & tam scire quid actum dictumque olim, quam quod jam agendum vel disputandum sit. Libros consulere oportet, Confessionem Augustanam, Concordiam Bergensem: & Controversiarum tractatores, missis prolixioribus, habes Lucae Osiandri F. Enchiridion; Mentzeri Exegesin Augustanae Confessionis, cui responderunt Altingius, & Crocius; Henrici Eckhardi Fasciculum Controversiarum, hoc solo nomine commendandum, quod quaecunque adversum Nos comminisci iniquiores possunt, una cum suis argumentis, comprehendat, ut ridiculum sit, quod in libri titulo ait, illum continere quaestiones fere omnes, quae inter Augustanae Consessionis Theologos & Calvinianos disceptantur. Imo vel leviter librum inspicienti apparebit non meliorem ei quadrare titulum, quam farraginem calumniarum: & Auctorem perpetuo hoc agere. I. Ut Calvinianis, quomodo loquitur, impingat falso, quae nunquam statuunt. II. Unius Doctoris sententiam imponat toti Ecclesiae, atque omnium faciat communem. III. Quodque pessimum, Doctoris etiam à nostris Ecclesiis reprobati, puta Vorstii. IV. Et non distinguat opinionem alicujus, vel sententiam problematicam, à doctrinâ Ecclesiasticâ. V. Ex Logomachiis faciat quaestiones, & controversias. VI. Exceptiones & instantias ponat, pro quaestionibus principalibus. VII. Atque ut numerum librumque augeret in quo solo sudavit, casdem easdem aliquoties repetit controversias. Quae omnia librum perlustranti, mox liquebunt: quem proinde eo loco habendum censeo, quo dixi. Legendum etiam, ex multis Colloquiis, Mompelgartense, in quo prima multarum rerum, egregiaque habetur disputatio. Tum Admonitio Neostadiana, quem librum ut in Belgicum Nostri converterent, censuit merito Synodus Mediobur-gensis a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxxi. addendique Scriptores polemici Controversiarum Lutheranarum. Commendo Altingium, Alutarium, qui Belgice adversus illos scripsit, uti quoque Acronius, Grevinchovius; & quibus nota lingua Germanica, consulenda istorum Theologorum, hisce in rebus versatissimorum, scripta, interque Heidelbergensium Trewherzige Ermahnung &c. Christophori Pezelii, Historica narratio de Coena, quae etiam Belgice legitur.
units.tr: As for our disputes with the Lutherans: just as our opponents are vigorous in inventing and making up controversies, so in disputing they are tiresome, long-winded, dull, and everywhere also bitter and abusive. I see no need to write many books, since there is already a large enough supply of them. I approve less of personal attacks, a vice so familiar to them that hardly even those who seem more moderate than the rest and well disposed towards us can refrain from it, but everywhere call us Calvinists and utter every insult of that kind. Matthias Hoe, a Wittenberg theologian, by no means to be counted among the best, in his little book on Theological Disputations, while teaching how they ought to be conducted, savagely harasses us everywhere as Sacramentarians. A charming example, indeed, of how a good disputant behaves! When you are at some point going to deal with them, be rather long in setting out the state of the controversy, so that our opponents can extricate themselves. Then come to the disputation and do it in form, syllogistically, as Beza often shouted at Jacob Andreae in the Colloquy of Mömpelgard: sic syllogismum. That is, one must dispute clearly and in a friendly way, as among those whose parts and churches were once united, and perhaps may be united again somewhere. Therefore this too must be carefully observed: our opponents should not only try to prove to us that the opinion they hold today is true, but also that it is the view of Luther and of the Augsburg Confession. On our side we must take care to show in every point the agreement of our doctrine with Luther and the Augsburg Confession, or how they once tolerated each other while in disagreement. Henricus Alutarius has shown this admirably and diligently in his Dutch book Speculum dissidentium Lutheranorum. Hence whoever is going to accomplish anything useful in these controversies must be equally well versed, at least as far as the first matters of the Reformation are concerned, both as a historian and as a theologian, and must know what was once done and said as well as what must now be done or disputed. One should consult the books Augsburg Confession and Concord of Bergen. Among the writers of controversy, leaving aside the lengthier ones, you have Luca Osiander the Younger's Enchiridion; Mentzer's Exegesis of the Augsburg Confession, to which Alting and Crocius replied; and Henricus Eckhard's Fasciculus Controversiarum, which deserves commendation for this alone, that it gathers together whatever the most unfair of men can invent against us, along with their arguments. It is ridiculous that the author says on the title page that it contains nearly all the questions debated between the theologians of the Augsburg Confession and the Calvinists. Indeed, even a light glance at the book will show that a better title would be a farrago of calumnies, and that the author is constantly doing the following: I. He falsely charges the Calvinists, as he puts it, with things they never held. II. He imposes the opinion of one teacher on the whole Church and makes it common to all. III. And worst of all, he does this with teachers rejected by our churches, such as Vorstius. IV. He does not distinguish the opinion of some individual, or a merely problematic view, from the doctrine of the Church. V. He makes questions and controversies out of verbal disputes. VI. He sets up objections and instances in place of the principal questions. VII. And in order to increase the number and bulk of the book, in which alone he has laboured, he repeats the same controversies several times. All of this will soon be clear to anyone who goes through the book, and so I think it should be placed where I have said. The Mömpelgard Colloquy should also be read, among the many colloquies, since it contains the first and an excellent discussion of many matters. Then the Neustadt Admonition, which the Synod of Middelburg rightly decided our people should translate into Dutch, in the year 1581. The polemical writers on the Lutheran controversies should also be added. I commend Alting, and Alutarius, who wrote against them in Dutch, as also Acronius and Grevinchoven. For those who know German, the writings of these theologians, who were most experienced in these matters, should be consulted, among them the Heidelberg Trewherzige Ermahnung etc., and Christoph Pezel's Historical Narrative on the Supper, which is also read in Dutch.

units.la: Varia Lutherani inter se a primis temporibus habuerunt schismata, de quibus ex parte diximus: omnium catalogum exhibent Micraelius, in Syntagmate historico, lib. III. & Iohannes Pappus, in Epitome historiae Ecclesiasticae. Qualia Antinomorum, authore Ioh. Agricola Islebio, ad anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxvIII. Interimistarum, ex libro Interim: authoribus Iulio Pflug, Michaële Sidonio; & Iohanne illo Agricolâ confecto a. cIↄ Iↄ xlvIII: qui controversias religionis inter Protestantes & Pontificios moderabatur, & cui inhaereri usque ad determinationem generalis Concilii volebat quidem Caesar, sed ei neutra pars assensit. Inter Lutheranos alii aliis librum illum magis probabant, vel improbabant. Et quia varia in illo tum circa doctrinam, tum ritus animadvertebantur; de operibus ad salutem necessariis; de hominis ad sui conversionem cooperatione & synergia; de ritibus & caeremoniis; nata hinc tria fere apud Lutheranos schismata. Primum Majoristarum dictum, motum ab Amsdorfio, docente, opera bona dicenda esse non necessaria ad salutem, potius perniciosa. Alterum Synergistarum, partes ducente Victorino Strigelio, seque ex Philippi Melanthonis lib. Corp. Doctrinæ potissimum tutante. Tertium Adiaphoristarum, ritus Papisticos, de quibus litigabatur, dicentium indifferentes esse. Litesque & contentiones adeo exundarunt, ut quamvis satagente illas componere Saxoniæ Electore Augusto, in Colloquio Altemburgico a. cIↄ Iↄ lxiii. inter Theologos Misnicos, & Thuringicos, quorum illi pro Interimisticis erant, hi contra ii, & producta in va-rium disputatione de uno justificationis articulo per quinque integros menses, re infecta tandem discessum sit. Adversus consilia & conatus interimisticos egregie quidem se gessit Andreas Osiander, atque potius loco cedere & Norimbergam relinquere voluit, quam illis se adjungere, sed idem in Academiam Regiomontanam Borussiæ admissus ad professionem Theologicam, alia movere cœpit, non minus mala, schismaticque occasionem dedit, docens ad a. cIↄ Iↄ lı. justificari nos justitia Christi, ut Dei, quæ eadem sit Patris, Filii, & Spiritus Sancti essentialis. Cui dum se oppositus Hebræus, in eádem prius Academia linguæ Professor, Franc. Stankarus, Italus Mantuanus, inde Francofurtum ad Oderam commigratus, ex adversa parte alium errorem edit, de Christo secundum solam humanam naturam mediatore. Quorum illud Osiandrismus dictus, hoc Stancarismus. Qualis vir Osiander fuerit, quamque nil ab indole sua alienum commiserit, turbans suis vanis perversisque dogmatis (nam etiam alia præter hoc, quod diximus, tenebat, uti Christum, quamvis non peccasset, nihilominus tamen incarnandum fuisse, at non crucifigendum, quia nimirum ad ejus imaginem hominem creatum exponebat) Ecclesiam, Calvinus ad Melanthonem significavit, epist. a. cIↄ Iↄ lı ı. Quod se Osiander mihi subduxit, imo non sine violento impetu se præcipuit, non mirum, nec tantopere dolendum. Tu enim expertus pridem es, ex eo esse ferarum genere, quæ nunquam cicuratur: & ego semper inter nostra dedecora eum numeravi. Quo certè die mihi primùm visus est, profanum hominis ingenium, & foedos mores sum detestatus. Quoties suave, ac generosum vinum laudare vellet, has in ore habebat voces, Ego sum qui sum: Item, hic est Filius Dei vivi: quae manifesta Dei ludibria prodirent. Quo magis saepe miratus sum vestrā omnium indulgentiā talem belluam foveri. Praecipuè verò, quum locum in praefatione quādam tuā legerem (ubi post VVormaciensē insaniā specimen plusquam literaliter, abs te Laudatur) obstupui. Sed facessat ille, quem alienissimum à nobis esse expedit. Istiusque deliria Calvinus idem graviter refellit, Iustitut, lib. III. cap. XI. Vide de eodem Melanthonem, in Consiliis part. II. pag. 155. 208. 253. 306. Pezelium, part. V. Resp. Theolog. pag. 117. Conradum Schlusselburgium, in Catalogo haereticorum lib. VI. ubi; quae Nic. Gallus, Ioh. VVigandus, aliique, adversus eundem attulerunt, habes. Fuit Osiander vir alicujus ingenii, animique, sed audacis, ambitiosi, turbidi, vitae non satis ordinatae & sobriae. Vivendi ejus morem descripsit, Enarrat. Evangel. part. IV. Melanthon: Osiander ita sibi abrupit vitam. Solebat „incumbere studiis circa horam nonam noctis, & continuabat ea ad primam vel secundam usque. Saepe eum „convenī, cùm essemus Augustae in conventu. Mane „surgebat, quando erat cibus appositus ad mensam: „descendebat de scalis, & gestabat caligas repositas in „brachiis. Solebam dicere ad eum: Domine Andrea, Ihr „bettet die Suppen schier verschlaffen: respondebat: Ich „weiß die Zeit wolzutreffen: & hilariter prandebat ac bi„bebat: ut Melancholici sunt voraces. Postea ibat de„ambulatum unam vel alteram horam: tertia vel quar„ta hora legebat vel scribebat aliquid: postea coenabat: „& circa horam noctis nonam iterùm ad studia redibat. „Factus est tandem hydropicus: id tribuo illi consuetu„dini. Quando venit in Pruffiam, voluit etiam certare „cum aulicis bibendo: sicut poterat largiter bibere: e,,rat enim robustus vir. Atque quia sibi metuebat à lepra, collo auream catenam, ne illa inficeretur, gestasse scribunt: Opinionem suam de justificatione per justitiam Dei essentialem, à multo tempore præferat[?]. In Colloquio Marpurgensi a. clo Io xxix. cui nomine Norimbergensium interfuit, habita à Luthero concione de nostra coram Deo justitia, eundem quem Lutherus paulo ante, textum sumsit, & explicuit adeo duris novisque loquendi rationibus, tantaque grandiloquentia de justitia nostra disseruit, ut hinc monstri aliquid alere cum omnes animadverterent, & Lutherus, se fastuosum spiritum improbare, palam testaretur. Adfuit etiam Comitiis Augustanis, quando iis offerretur Confessio a.clo Io xxx. Norimbergâ in Borussiam accitus fuit, ab Alberto Marchione Brandeburgico, & summo Borussiæ Magistro: ubi docebant in recenti Academiâ Regiomontanâ Frid. Staphylus, factus postea apostata, Georgius Venetus, Stancarus. Sententiam sic proponebat Osiander: nos solâ essentiali Dei justitiâ justos esse, essentiali ejus vitâ vivere, & victuros esse, essentiali ipsius gloriâ glorificari, essentiali illius charitate ad diligendum Deum & proximum propter ipsum inflammari, & gravissimè errare omnes, qui putent aliâ re, quam solo suo & vivo Deo Patre, Filio, & Spiritu sancto nos posse justificari, vivificari, glorificari: & glacie frigidiora docere, qui doceant, nos tantum propter remissionem peccatorum reputari justos, & non etiam propter justitiam Christi, essentialem & divinam, per fidem in nobis habitantis. Præcipuè se ei opposuit, in Ministerio verbi Collega Ioach. Morlinus, quem ipse ut exceperit, hæc ejus epistola ad Morlinum probat: Infixisti mihi hodie in concione tuâ non modò acerbum, verùm etiam scelerum vulnus. Nemo enim aliter intellexit: accedunt litera tua, nescio an indoctiores, an furiosiores. Verum ut intelligas quàm me terruerit, audi. Ego mihi vehementer gratulor, quod te inimicum habeam apertum potius, quàm amicum incertum.
units.tr: The Lutherans themselves have had various schisms among one another since the earliest times, some of which I have already discussed in part. Micraelius, in his Syntagma historicum, lib. III., and Johannes Pappus, in his Epitome historiae ecclesiasticae, give a complete catalogue of them. Among these were the Antinomians, under Johann Agricola of Eisleben, from about 1538; the Interimists, named after the Interim, whose authors were Julius Pflug and Michael Sidonius, and after that Johann Agricola, who drew it up in 1548. This Interim was meant to settle the controversies of religion between Protestants and Papists. The Emperor wished it to be kept in force until a general council decided the matter, but neither party agreed to this. Among the Lutherans, some approved of that book more and others less. Because various points in it were criticised, both of doctrine and of rites, several schisms arose among the Lutherans. These concerned good works necessary to salvation, the cooperation and synergy of man in his own conversion, and ceremonies and rites. The first, called the Majoristic, was started by Amsdorf, who taught that good works are not necessary to salvation but rather harmful. The second, the Synergistic, was led by Victorinus Strigel, who relied chiefly on Philip Melanchthon's Corpus doctrinae. The third, the Adiaphoristic, consisted of those who said that the Papist rites, over which there was dispute, were indifferent. The quarrels and contentions grew so great that, although Augustus, Elector of Saxony, worked hard to settle them, the Colloquy of Altenburg in 1563 between the theologians of Meissen and those of Thuringia (the former favouring the Interimists, the latter opposing them) ended without result, after a discussion of the single article of justification had lasted five whole months. Andreas Osiander certainly acted admirably against the Interimist plans and efforts, and he preferred to give way and leave Nuremberg rather than join them. Yet when he was admitted to a professorship of theology at the Academy of Königsberg in Prussia, he began to stir up other matters, no less harmful and schismatic. He taught that we are justified by the justice of Christ as God, which is essentially the same in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Against him stood the Hebrew scholar Francis Stancarus, an Italian from Mantua, who had earlier been professor of languages in the same Academy and then moved to Frankfurt on the Oder. From the opposite side he put forward another error, that Christ is mediator only according to his human nature. The first of these was called Osiandrism, the second Stancarism. What sort of man Osiander was, and how little he kept from his own character, disturbing the Church with his empty and perverse doctrines (for besides this point he also held that Christ, though he had not sinned, would nonetheless have been incarnate, but would not have been crucified, since he thought man had been created in the image of that incarnate Christ), Calvin pointed out in a letter to Melanchthon in 1551: That Osiander has slipped away from me, or rather has broken away with violent force, is no surprise, nor should it grieve us so much. You have long known that he belongs to that kind of wild beast which is never tamed, and I have always counted him among our disgraces. On the very day I first saw him I detested the profane character and foul manners of the man. Whenever he wished to praise a sweet and noble wine, he had these words on his lips: "I am who I am", and also "This is the Son of the living God". These were plain mockeries of God. The more often I have wondered that all of you indulge such a beast. Above all, when I read a passage in one of your prefaces (where, after the madness of Worms, you praise him in a way that is more than literal), I was astonished. But let him depart, the man it is best for us to have nothing to do with. Calvin also refuted his delusions severely in the Institutes, lib. III., cap. XI. On the same man see Melanchthon, in Consiliis, part. II., pp. 155, 208, 253, 306; Pezel, part. V. of the Responsa theologica, p. 117; and Conrad Schlüsselburg in the Catalogue of Heretics, lib. VI., where you will find what Nicolaus Gallus, Johann Wigand and others brought against him. Osiander was a man of some talent and spirit, but bold, ambitious, restless, and of a life not sufficiently orderly or sober. Melanchthon describes his manner of living in the Enarrationes evangelicae, part. IV.: "Osiander so broke off his life for himself. He used to apply himself to his studies from about nine o'clock at night, and continued them until one or two. Often I met him when we were at the diet in Augsburg. In the morning he got up when the food was set on the table; he came down the stairs carrying his boots tucked under his arms. I used to say to him, 'Lord Andreas, you will nearly sleep through the soup'. He would answer, 'I know how to time it well', and he would eat and drink merrily, as melancholy men are greedy. Afterwards he walked for an hour or so; in the third or fourth hour he read or wrote something; then he had supper, and about nine at night he returned to his studies. At last he became dropsical, and I put that down to his habits. When he came to Prussia he even wanted to compete with the courtiers in drinking, and he could drink heavily, for he was a robust man. And since he feared leprosy, they write that he wore a gold chain round his neck, lest it be infected." For a long time he had held his opinion about justification by the essential justice of God. At the Colloquy of Marburg in 1529, which he attended on behalf of the Nurembergers, Luther preached a sermon on our justice before God. Osiander took the same text that Luther had just used and expounded it in such harsh and novel modes of speech, and discoursed on our justice with such high-flown rhetoric, that everyone noticed he was hatching some monstrosity, and Luther openly declared that he disapproved of his proud spirit. He was also present at the Diet of Augsburg, when the Confession was presented in 1530. He was summoned from Nuremberg to Prussia by Albert, Margrave of Brandenburg and Grand Master of Prussia. There, in the newly founded Academy of Königsberg, Friedrich Staphylus (who later became an apostate), George Venetus and Stancarus taught. Osiander put forward his view in this way: "We are made just by the essential justice of God alone, we live by his essential life, we shall live, we are glorified by his essential glory, and we are inflamed by his essential love to love God and our neighbour for his sake. Those who think that we can be justified, quickened or glorified by anything other than God himself, his only and living Father, Son and Holy Spirit, err most gravely; and those who teach that we are reckoned just only for the remission of sins, and not also for the essential and divine justice of Christ dwelling in us through faith, teach more coldly than ice." Above all, his colleague in the ministry of the Word, Joachim Mörlin, opposed him, and Osiander's letter to Mörlin shows how deeply he was stung: Today in your sermon you struck me with a wound that is not only bitter but also criminal. For no one understood it otherwise. Your letter arrives as well; I do not know whether it is written with less learning or with more madness. But so that you may understand how much it has frightened me, listen. I greatly congratulate myself that you are an open enemy rather than an uncertain friend.

units.la: Agerem aliter tecum, sed literæ tuæ adimunt mihi spem amicitiæ, concordiæ, & tuæ respiscentiæ. Itaque respondebo tibi, non ut tu vis, neque quomodo tu vis, sed quando, & ut mihi commodum videbitur: & ostendam tibi, Deo adjuvante, coram totius Europæ Ecclesiâ, aliud esse doctum, aliud Doctorem VVittembergensem qui oblitus Filii Dei juravit se non discessurum à confessione Augustanâ, cum omnis homo sit mendax, nec excipiatur Philippus. Hac memoriâ mente repetito 19. April. 1551. In medio certamine, præter omnem exspectationem, interemptus est paroxysmo epileptico, Regiomonti. a. cIↃ IↄIII. die XVII. Octob. Post vero obitum pro eo pugnam continuarunt Funccius, (qui non parvam ei in Commentariorum Chronologicorum fine attexit laudationem, quippe gener ejus erat) Sciurus, & alii, usque ad a. cIↃ Iↄ lxv I. quo sopita lis fuit, Funccio, præcipuo Osiandrismi propugnatore, ob turbas in Borussiâ datas, quod Ducem suasisset, ut inde se cum filio unico, propter insidias scilicet Consiliariorum suorum, proriperet, una cum duobus aliis Consiliariis politicis capite mulctato, Regiomonti, in foro publico anno cIↃ Iↄ lxv I. die XXVIII. Octobris. Franciscus Stankarus] etiam in Academiâ Cracoviensi Hebraæ linguæ Professor fuit, atque in carcerem conjectus ob dogmata Euangelica, sed liberatus industriâ famuli sui Georgii Nigri, concisâ in longas fascias linteo, quibus dimittebatur. Ejus opinio magnas in Ecclesiis Polonicis, sub primis earum initiis, turbas dedit, consultique super ea Melanthon, Calvinus, Martyr, Zanchius, Beza, alii, qui eam solide confutarunt, & Tigurini Theologi, in epist. ad Ecclesias Polonicas, subjecta historicæ narrationi Iohannis Vtenhovii, de peregrinatione exulum Anglorum. Variis Polonicarum Ecclesiarum Synodis agitatum ejus damnatumque dogma, a. cIↃ Iↄ Iv. & cIↃIↄ Iix. usque dum a. cIↃ Iↄ lxxiv. eo Stobnicię mortuo, illud simul vivere desiit. Referunt, ante obitum resipuisse, vel saltem, propter pacem Ecclesiae, litem omisisse, ac deposuisse. Auctor Histor. Eccles. Sclavon. lib. 1. pag. 83. 125. & lib. 11. pag. 228. Filium habuit Franciscum Stancarum, ministerio functum in Ecclesia Oxensi, ab a. MDXCIX. usque ad a. MDCXXI. quo obiit, de quo Idem historicus agit, lib. 111. pag. 414. De Matthaeo Flacio Illyrico supra diximus: hic praeter impetum & violentiam adversus bonum virum Phil. Melanthonem. atque furores Amsdorfii quos detestabatur, bona opera non necessaria ad salutem, sed perniciosa dicentis, alterius schismatis Flacianorum auctor exitit a. MDLXI. in Consessu Vinariensi disputans cum Victorino Strigelio, super negotio peccati originalis, quod hic extenuabat, ille autem plus aequo extendebat, & asserebat esse substantiam: quod multi in eo exagitarunt, praesertim Lipsienses, & V Vittembergenses Theologi, quorum Censuram in librum ejus Clavis scripturae exhibet in sua Epitome historica Pappus. Atque liber Concordiae Bergensis eandem opinionem improbavit: quae cum Cyriaco Spangenberger, qui post Flacium, illa acerrime tutatus fuit, tandem etiam intercidit. Aliud Schisma excitavit Formula Concordiae, inquit Micraelius, in Catalogo Scismatum Lutheranorum pag. 529. quum ei alii subscribere parati essent, alii vero recusarent. Inter illos inepte Helmstadienses, & quidem quasi alterius Scismatis auctores recenset. Samuel Huberus, in Acad. V Vittembergensi Professor Theologus ad a. MDCLXIII. docuit praedestinationem universalem: cui errori se multi tum inter Lutheranos, tum Nostros, oppositerunt. Alia Lutheranorum vel schismata, vel quaestiones vexatas, quomodo appellat in Disput a. MDCXX. d. xxi. Ianuar. Balthasar Meisnerus, nihil attinet pluribus persequi. Controversias autem, quae cum Lutheranis sunt, ad haec revocari capita.
units.tr: I would deal with you otherwise, but your letter takes away my hope of friendship, of harmony, and of your repentance. So I shall answer you not as you wish, nor in the way you wish, but when and as it seems fit to me; and by God's help I shall show you, before the whole Church of Europe, that it is one thing to be learned and another to be the Doctor of Wittenberg, who, forgetting the Son of God, swore that he would not depart from the Augsburg Confession, though every man is a liar and Philip is not excepted. Written from memory and repeated in thought, 19 April 1551. In the midst of the contest, beyond all expectation, he was carried off by an epileptic fit at Königsberg on 17 October 1552. After his death, however, the battle for him was continued by Funck (who added no small praise of him at the end of his Chronological Commentaries, since he was his son-in-law), by Sciurus and others, until 1567, when the quarrel was put to rest. Funck, the chief champion of Osiandrism, was beheaded in the public square at Königsberg on 28 October 1566, together with two other political councillors, because he had persuaded the Duke, on account of the plots of his own councillors, to flee with his only son, and because of the disturbances that had arisen in Prussia. Francis Stancarus was also professor of Hebrew in the Academy of Kraków. He was thrown into prison for his evangelical doctrines, but was freed through the diligence of his servant George Niger, who cut a linen cloth into long strips by which he let himself down. His opinion caused great disturbances in the Polish churches in their early beginnings. Melanchthon, Calvin, Martyr, Zanchius, Beza and others were consulted about it, and they solidly refuted it, as did the Zurich theologians in their letter to the Polish churches, which was appended to John Utenhove's historical account of the exile of the English. This dogma was debated and condemned in various synods of the Polish churches in 1554 and 1569, until in 1574, when Stancarus died at Stobnica, it ceased to live. They report that before his death he repented, or at least, for the peace of the Church, dropped the quarrel and laid down his opinion. See the author of the Historia ecclesiastica Sclavonica, lib. I., pp. 83, 125, and lib. II., p. 228. He had a son, Francis Stancarus, who held the ministry in the Church of Ostrów from 1599 until 1621, when he died; the same historian treats of him in lib. III., p. 414. We have already spoken of Matthias Flacius Illyricus. Besides his violence and fury against the good man Philip Melanchthon, and his support for Amsdorf's view (which Melanchthon abhorred), that good works are not necessary to salvation but harmful, he became the author of another schism, that of the Flacians, when in 1561 at the Synod of Weimar he disputed with Victorinus Strigel about original sin. Strigel played it down, while Flacius extended it beyond measure and maintained that it was a substance. Many criticised this in him, especially the theologians of Leipzig and Wittenberg, whose censure of his book Clavis Scripturae Pappus gives in his historical Epitome. The Book of Concord of Bergen also rejected the same opinion. Cyriacus Spangenberg, who after Flacius defended it most fiercely, eventually perished along with it. "Another schism," says Micraelius in his catalogue of Lutheran schisms, p. 529, "was stirred up by the Formula of Concord, when some were ready to subscribe to it and others refused." Among those who refused he foolishly lists the Helmstedt theologians, as if they were the authors of yet another schism. Samuel Huber, professor of theology at the Academy of Wittenberg, taught universal predestination up to 1613; many, both Lutherans and our own people, opposed this error. It is not worth pursuing at length the other Lutheran schisms, or the vexed questions, as Balthasar Meisner calls them in his disputation of 21 January 1620. The controversies that we have with the Lutherans, however, may be traced back to these heads.

units.la: 1. Num Christi corpus & sanguis vere & substantialiter aliter in S. Coena praesens sit, ita ut oraliter ibi, atque ab infidelibus etiam, sumatur? Neg.
units.tr: 1. Whether the body and blood of Christ are truly and substantially present in the Holy Supper otherwise, so that they are taken orally there, even by unbelievers? No.

units.la: ii. Num humana Christi natura sit ubique praesens, idque ex communicatis sibi realiter divinae naturae proprietatibus, nempe omnipraesentia, omniscientia, omnipotentia, & adorabilitate? Neg.
units.tr: ii. Whether the human nature of Christ is present everywhere, and this from the divine nature's properties really communicated to it, namely omnipresence, omniscience, omnipotence and adorability? No.

units.la: iii. Num generali voluntate Deus velit omnium hominum salutem: atque inde Christus pro omnibus hominibus mortuus sit vel satisfecerit; atque hinc universalis omnibus ad conversionem offeratur gratia: adeoque Deus ex praevisa fide, vel infidelitate homines praedestinarit? Neg.
units.tr: iii. Whether God by a general will wills the salvation of all men, and so Christ died for all men or made satisfaction for them, and hence universal grace is offered to all for conversion, and so God predestined men on the basis of foreseen faith or unbelief? No.

units.la: iv. Num vere fideles & sanctificati quidem etiam plene deficiant a fide, & a Dei gratia in totum excidant? Neg.
units.tr: iv. Whether true believers and sanctified persons may indeed fail completely in faith and fall away wholly from the grace of God? No.

units.la: v. Num baptismus regenerationem & fidem conserat tamquam ordinarium medium huic fini, & ad salutem necessarium sit, supra necessitatem mandati: adeoque in casu necessitatis, etiam privatis & mulieribus baptizare liceat? Neg.
units.tr: v. Whether baptism confers regeneration and faith as the ordinary means to this end, and is necessary to salvation beyond the necessity of the command; and so whether, in a case of necessity, it is lawful for even private persons and women to baptize? No.

units.la: vi. Num in baptismo recte adhibeatur exorcismus? Neg.
units.tr: vi. Whether exorcism is rightly used in baptism? No.

units.la: vii. Num privata Confessio & absolutio in Ecclesiis sit retinenda? Neg.
units.tr: vii. Whether private confession and absolution are to be retained in the Churches? No.

units.la: viii. Num ad celebrationem S.
