Coenae devotionem cereos accendere: Ministrum alba veste indui: altaria, & aureos calices adhibere: non frangere panem cibarium; sed placentulis uti orbicularibus: atque communicantibus non in manus symbola tradere, sed in os ingerere: & aegroto S. Coenam separatim ac privatim administrare, convenit? Neg.
units.tr: viii. Whether it is fitting, for the celebration of the Holy Supper, to light candles out of devotion, to have the minister dressed in a white vestment, to use altars and golden chalices, not to break ordinary bread but to use round wafers, to hand the elements to communicants not into their hands but to put them into their mouths, and to administer the Holy Supper separately and privately to the sick? No.

units.la: ix. Num ad mentionem nominis Iesu genicu-landum, vel detegendum sit caput? Neg.
units.tr: ix. Whether one should kneel at the mention of the name of Jesus, or uncover the head? No.

units.la: x. Num in templis habendae imagines, & in sacris coetibus, cantiones Latinae, contentus harmonici, vel organa Musica? Neg.
units.tr: x. Whether images should be kept in churches, and in sacred assemblies Latin songs, harmonious concerts, or musical organs? No.

units.la: Liber Decimus DE BROWNISTIS, &c.
units.tr: Book Ten: On the Brownists, etc.

units.la: Brownistarum, sive Separatistarum origo, secta, nomen. Articuli illorum non impugnant Ecclesiarum nostrarum doctrinam, sed regimen, & disciplinam, praesertim priscae Anglicanae. Quare alias moverunt olim controversias; alias hodie. Quaedam carpunt, quae Nos etiam non probamus. Cetera quae habent, talia non sunt quin scismatis ea redarguant, & temerariae ab Ecclesia Reformata separationis. Breviter rationes, quas praetendunt, examinantur: & simul retunduntur aliis. Quaestiones reliquae, de Potestate ecclesiastica; Presbyteris; Presbyterio, Classibus, & Synodis. De Independentismo. De Ecclesiae particularis amplitudine. De templis olim idololatricis, similiter de reditibus, & stipendio Ministrorum verbii, confirmatione matrimonii ecclesiastica; formulis precum. Appendix, de Antinomis.
units.tr: The origin, sect and name of the Brownists, or Separatists. Their articles do not attack the doctrine of our Churches, but their government and discipline, especially that of the early English Church. For this reason they have raised some controversies in the past and others today. They find fault with certain things which we also do not approve. The rest of what they hold is of such a kind that it refutes their schism and rash separation from the Reformed Church. Briefly, the reasons they put forward are examined, and at the same time refuted by other arguments. The remaining questions concern ecclesiastical power; elders; the presbytery, classes and synods; Independency; the extent of a particular church; the temples once used for idolatry; likewise the revenues and stipends of ministers of the Word; the ecclesiastical confirmation of marriage; and forms of prayer. Appendix: on the Antinomians.

units.la: Tempore Reginae Elizabethae in Angliâ pullulavit Secta quae Brownistarum dicta, inchoata à Roberto quodam Browne, qui primus segreges ab Ecclesiâ Anglicanâ, ob discrimen regiminis disciplinaeque, egit coetus: at postea errorum convictus & temerarii scismatis, publicam in primario Londini templo fecit palinodiam; neque ita adhuc tranquillus animo, sed variis agitatus conscientiae inquietantis morsibus, postremum desperatione, vitam sibi infelici suspendio ademit. Quare non multum in hoc chorago sequaces ejus jus gloriæ quod ponerent, unquam habuere: agnoscunt autem illum talem, & separati Cœtus seniorem fuisse, recantasse etiam, vitamque laqueo sibi finivisse.
units.tr: In the reign of Queen Elizabeth a sect arose in England called the Brownists, begun by one Robert Browne, who was the first to form separate congregations apart from the English Church, on account of a difference over government and discipline. But afterwards, convicted of his errors and of rash schism, he made a public recantation in the chief church of London. Yet he was not at peace in his mind, but was tormented by the gnawing of a troubled conscience, and at last, in despair, took his own unhappy life by hanging. For this reason his followers have never had much cause to boast of this man as a champion. Still, they acknowledge that he was the senior of the separated congregations, and that he also recanted and ended his life with a noose.

units.la: Sequutus Robertus Browne, à quo Brouwnistarum nomen, primum Ludimagister in Southwarke, dein Verbi minister Islingtoni, prope Londinum, qui partibus Separatistarum se adjungens, una cum suo grege a. MDLXXX. ex Anglia transfretavit Medioburgum Zelandorum, ubi oborta inter ipsos gravi dissensione, pars pleraque ad Anabaptistas deflexit: ipse Browni Angliam repetiit, recantatoque errore, ab Episcopis beneficium impetravit, in quo, & reliquâ vitâ, tum sævitiæ erga uxorem, quam se verberare ajebat, non ut uxorem, sed ut pessimam vetulam, tum injustitiæ erga Capellanum suum, quam ob causam & carcere conclusus diu, denique variorum scandalorum reus actus fuit.
units.tr: Robert Browne, from whom the name Brownists comes, followed him. He was first a schoolmaster in Southwark, then a minister of the Word at Islington, near London. Joining the Separatists, he crossed over from England with his flock to Middelburg in Zeeland in 1580. There a serious dissension arose among them, and most of the party turned aside to the Anabaptists. Browne himself returned to England, recanted his error, and obtained a benefice from the bishops, which he held for the rest of his life. Yet during that time he was guilty both of cruelty towards his wife, whom he said he beat not as a wife but as a wicked old woman, and of injustice towards his chaplain. For this reason he was long imprisoned and finally was convicted of various scandals.

units.la: Quæ agnoscentes sui, id est, separationis sectatores, inde ægre adeo ferunt ab ipso denominari, ut quem in Ægyptum regressum, & à Deo desertum, quia cum ipse prior deseruerat, scribunt. Ioh. Robinsonus, lib. Anglico (nam quia Anglicè prostant, neque noti aliter libri sunt, suis ipsos titulis designare necessum habemus) justification of Separation, against Rich. Bernard, pag. 50.
units.tr: Those of his own followers who acknowledge these facts, that is, the adherents of separation, are so annoyed at being named after him that they write of him as one who, having gone back to Egypt, was deserted by God, because he had first deserted them. John Robinson, in an English book (for since they are published in English, and these books are not known in any other way, we must identify them by their titles), Justification of Separation, against Rich. Bernard, p. 50.

units.la: Henricus Barrow, à quo nomen Barrowistarum (scias distincta esse Brownistarum, & Barrowistarum nomina) vehementissimus & virulentissimus fuit Ecclesiarum nostrarum detractor & adversarius, qui coetui suo alienissimos & adversissimos contra nos infudit spiritus: quod, qui eximie adversus illos scripsit, Richardus Bernardus, planum fecit, cum in libro The Separatists schisme p.22. & 70. tum alio, The errours of Barrow confuted. Tandem hic, post sexennalem incarcerationem, una cum socio Johanne Greenwood, sub Elizabethâ, regno ejus a. xxxvi. Christi a. MDXCIII. in suspendium actus fuit: by the evill advise of the cruell Prelates about hermilo consilio crudelium Praelatorum juxta eam, scribit Robertus Baylie, Glascovensis, lib. à Dissuasive from the errors of the time pag. 14. Unde duos illos Barrow & Greenwodum pro Martyribus Secta ipsorum reputat, & veneratur. Illorum exemplo territi quotquot in Anglia supererant istius familiae, aufugiebant; venerunt-que Amsteldamum, ductore Francisco Johnsono: à quo tempore ibi consederunt. Cum Johnsono, Amsteldamni, ejusdem secta erat Henrico Ainsworth; qui Consessionem ediderunt a. cIↄ Iↄ c ii. Sed Johnsono, viro admodum contentioso, neque cum Fratre primum Georgio, tum nec cum Parente bene convenie bat, quem utrumque etiam excommunicavit. Deinde inter Johnsonum, atque Ainsworthum oborta lite, in duas partes scissa secta fuit, quae se mutuo excommunicabant: & Johnsonus, cum suis, Emdam concessit, ubi cum ejus morte Congregatio soluta fuit & evanuit.
units.tr: Henry Barrow, from whom the name Barrowists comes (you should know that the names Brownists and Barrowists are distinct), was the most vehement and virulent detractor and adversary of our Churches, and he poured into his congregation spirits most hostile and opposed to us. Richard Bernard, who wrote notably against them, made this clear both in his book The Separatists' Schism, pp. 22 and 70, and in another, The Errors of Barrow Confuted. At last, after six years of imprisonment, he was hanged together with his companion John Greenwood, under Elizabeth, in the thirty-sixth year of her reign, in 1593 of Christ; by the evill advise of the cruell Prelates, that is, by the evil counsel of the cruel prelates, as Robert Baillie of Glasgow writes in his book A Dissuasive from the Errors of the Time, p. 14. Hence their sect regards and honours those two, Barrow and Greenwood, as martyrs. Terrified by their example, all who were left of this family in England fled away, and they came to Amsterdam under the leadership of Francis Johnson, and from that time settled there. With Johnson at Amsterdam was Henry Ainsworth, of the same sect; they published a Confession in 1602. But Johnson, a man very contentious, did not get on well either with his brother George, or with his father, both of whom he excommunicated. Then, a quarrel arising between Johnson and Ainsworth, the sect was split into two parts, which excommunicated each other. Johnson, with his people, withdrew to Emden, where, on his death, the congregation was dissolved and vanished.

units.la: Ainsworthus in Hiberniam trajecit, nonnullosque ibi reliquit discipulos, brevi reversus Amsteldamum. Post cujus mortem Coetus Amsteldamensium Brownistarum parum abfuit quin in fumum abiisset, diuque carens Rectoribus, tandem post multas contentiones accepit Johannem Canne, qui, turbata Sectis Anglia, & non admissis modo, sed plurimum quoque ibi pollentibus Brownistis, fastidita exili pauperequo turba sua Amsteldamensi, in Angliam transvolavit, locumque invasit alium, Coetu Amsteldamensi relicto, suo cum interitu luctante.
units.tr: Ainsworth crossed over to Ireland and left some disciples there, and soon returned to Amsterdam. After his death the congregation of the Amsterdam Brownists came close to going up in smoke, and for a long time lacked leaders. At last, after many contentions, it received John Canne, who, when England was thrown into confusion by the sects, and the Brownists were not only tolerated but were very powerful there, grew weary of his poor and lowly Amsterdam flock, and flew back to England. He seized another place, abandoning the Amsterdam congregation, which struggled on to its own ruin.

units.la: Vti Browne, cum suis, Mediobur gum; Johnsonus Amsteldamum; ita Johannes Smith Leidam ex Anglia appulit, fundavitque Congregatiunculam Separatistarum, sive Brownistarum: sed cum antiquioribus ejusdem sectae non diu concors, quos idololatriae accusabat, quod tum in concione ad volumen Bibliorum, tum inter cantandum, Psalterium respicerent, etiam Antichristianismi in regimine Ecclesiae, quod Pastoribus adjungerent alios Doctores, & Rectores, quæ humani commenti dicebat; tandem ad Anabaptistas defecit: & quemadmodum antea non cum Brownistis, ita nec tunc cum Anabaptistis, quibuscunque etiam immixtus, faciebat, cui non tot variæ Anabaptistarum sectæ satis adhuc erant, nisi & novæ formam suo exemplo præbuisset, rebaptizatus non solum, sed & seipsum baptizans, unde Rebaptista dici meruit.
units.tr: As Browne with his followers came to Middelburg, and Johnson to Amsterdam, so John Smith came from England to Leiden and founded a little congregation of Separatists, or Brownists. But he did not agree for long with the older members of the same sect, whom he accused of idolatry, because in preaching they looked to the volume of the Bible, and while singing they looked to the Psalter; and of antichristianism in church government, because they joined other teachers and rulers to the ministers, which he called a human invention. At last he defected to the Anabaptists. And just as before he had not agreed with the Brownists, so then he did not agree with the Anabaptists, into whose company he had mixed himself; they did not yet have enough sects of various kinds unless he too had provided a new form by his example. He was not only rebaptized, but also baptized himself, whence he deserved to be called a Rebaptist.

units.la: Optimus inter illos fuit, de quo postremùm dicendus, Iohannes Robinsonus, quoque Leidensium Separatistarum Minister, vir supra reliquos probus, atque eruditus, qui initio quidem adventus sui ex Anglia in Hollandiam, varios pro separatione ab Ecclesiâ Anglicanâ & nostrâ, illiusque justificatione scripsit tractatus, sed postea crebris Amesii & Parkeri litteris & collationibus admonitus, melius sapere didicit, & de reducendo suo ad Ecclesiam Cœtu, à quâ se secreverat, serio deliberare incæpit, concedens suis saltem communicare Ecclesiæ nostræ verbo, & precibus, quà publicis, quà privatis: super quo scripsit librum, of Communion private, and public. Atque non spem solùm fecerat, de plenâ restaurandâ communione, in Sacramentis etiam, ac disciplina, nisi immaturâ morte fuisset præventus; sed, post obitum ejus, obortâ in Cœtu contentione & scissione, super communione cum Ecclesiâ Anglicanâ in auditione verbi, D. Robinsoni vidua, liberi, reliquique propinqui & amici in communionem Ecclesiæ nostræ recepti fuerunt. Vir ille gratus nostris, dum vixit, fuit, & Theologis Leidensibus familiaris ac honoratus. Apologiam edidit suo, & Ecclesiæ suæ nomine a. cIↄ Iↄ c xix. quæ legitur Latinè, & Anglicè, recusa pridem a. cIↄ Iↄ c xliv. digna quæ à Theologis omnibus serió expendatur. Multa quippe continet & observat haud adeo contemnenda. Scripsit præterea Robinsonus varia contra Arminianos: frequens quippe & acer erat Episcopii in Academiâ adversarius & Opponens. Contrà Anabaptistas item: & Observationes divinas, ac morales, Anglice: Denique Independentismi, de quo postea plura, is ipse auctor extitit.
units.tr: The best of them was the one of whom I am to speak last: John Robinson, minister of the Separatists at Leiden, a man more upright and learned than the rest. At first, after his arrival in Holland from England, he wrote various treatises in favour of separation from the English Church and from ours, and in justification of it. But afterwards, admonished by frequent letters and discussions with Ames and Parker, he learned to think better, and he began to deliberate seriously about bringing his congregation back into the Church from which it had separated. He agreed that his people should at least share in our Church's Word and prayers, both public and private. On this he wrote a book, Of Communion, Private and Public. He had not only raised hopes of full restoration of communion, including in the sacraments and discipline, but would have brought it about had he not been overtaken by an untimely death. After his death, however, a contention and split arose in the congregation over communion with the English Church in hearing the Word. The widow, children, and other relatives and friends of Robinson were received into communion with our Church. That man was welcome to our people while he lived, and he was familiar and honoured among the Leiden theologians. He published an Apology in his own name and that of his Church in 1619. It is read in Latin and in English, and was reprinted in 1644. It deserves to be carefully weighed by all theologians, for it contains and observes much that is not to be despised. Robinson also wrote various works against the Arminians; he was indeed a frequent and sharp opponent of Episcopius in the Academy. He also wrote against the Anabaptists, and Divine and Moral Observations, in English. Finally, he was the very author of Independency, about which more later.

units.la: Anglicana Ecclesia ab initio Reformationis, in regimine & disciplina, hierarchico episcoporum ordine, & ceremoniis prae aliis gravata, plurimis passim scandalum dedit, & conquerendi contendiq; materiam. Qui retenta ibidem multi existimant, ex primorum in Anglia reformatorum cum Protestantibus Germaniae magis, quam Galliae, ubi illa non ita probata, ac illic, convenientia & commercio: accedente forma regiminis politici Monarchica, cui Episcopalis in Ecclesia familiari admodum nexu se accommodat. Restiterunt illis in Anglia vulgo, quibus alia, vel Genevensis, aut post eam Scoticanae Ecclesiae probata simplicitas. Sed hoc discrimine, quod optimi illa ordinis Episcopalis, & caeremoniarum reprehendenda quidem censerent ac reformanda, sed non propterea deserendam Ecclesiae, ubi obtinebant, ut in Anglicana, communionem; sufficere, si hac retenta, illis se non conformarent, unde dicti passim NonConformistae, ad distinctionem illorum, qui ista regiminis & disciplinae probabant etiam, observabantque. Alii pauciores hanc dissensionem tanti faciebant, ut propterea deserendam Ecclesiae, quae illis laborabat, communionem censerent, iique erant qui dicebantur Separatistae, seu Brownistae. Hinc magna ubique requirebatur cautela & prudentia incedendi recta inter Episcopales ab una, atque Brownistas ab altera parte, ne vel illis accederetur in probandis scandalis, vel in nimium illis improbandis aut fugienda detestandaque ideo omni Ecclesiae Anglicanae communione, Schismaticis. Quo enim nomine appellare eos oporteat, incertum. Brownistae appellari, vel ob teterrimum Roberti Browni facinus, omnino respuunt. Unde Iohannes Robinsonus, in Apologiae suae titulo inquit: aeque contumeliose ac communiter dictorum Brownistarum, sive Barrowistarum. Nec hoc, nec illo nomine compellari amant. Confessionem primam quam ediderunt a. cIↄ Iↄ xcv i. extatque Anglicè, Latinè, & Belgicè, cujusque Apologiam scripserunt ad Doctores Oxonienses a.cIↄIↄxcv i i i. se Anglos in Belgio exulantes vocant: Confessio fidei Anglorum quorundam in Belgio exulantium. Nisi quod majori forte cum ipsorum venia dixeris Separatistas, vel separatos, aut separantes se, בדין, unde vocatos Pharisæos nonnulli (an bene, jam non dico) opinantur. Certè integros scribunt libros cum hoc titulo: Justification of Separation: & Ecclesias suas, ecclesias separationis nun cupant. Iohannes Smit, the churches of separation. Ergo illos, nam aliqua nota discernendi, Separatistas nominemus. Solo Robinsono excepto, eoque circa extrema vitæ suæ, omnes magnâ vehementiâ contenderunt, cum Ecclesiis nostris, Anglicis præsertim, non tenendam communionem esse. Quod si vel de Anglicanis verum fuisset, Episcopali ordine, & cæremoniarum onere gravidis, non de hodiernis tant e.1, non de Nostris Belgicis, illorum vacuis, dici unquam potuit. Et cur tamen ab his, nisi & istis quoque, adhuc dum se segregant? Nos ab Anglis continuo Ministros accipimus, vicissimque iis damus, & in ejusdem Ecclesiæ communionem homines utrimque recipimus: cur ab utrisque se separant, & diversos etiamnum coetus agunt, diversam communionem? Olim scripsit inter illos Franciscus Iohnsonus peculiarem hoc titulo, sed anglicè, librum: illicitum esse ullam cum hodierno Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ ministerio vel audire vel habere communionem. Interdicens suis etiam communione verbi, & precum in Ecclesiis Anglicanis; ut cultu superstitioso & vano, quomodo de modo precandi per formulas dixit, in libro contra Giffordum, cui titulum fecit ludicrum, more worke for Priests, Ioh. Greenwood, Christi fidus, uti additur, Martyr. Sed quid hæc ad illos, qui se formulis non alligant; aut ad præsens Anglicanæ Ecclesiæ Ministerium, amoto diu ordine hierarchico? aut quid ad nostras Ecclesias, à quibus tamen seorsim etiam hodie sacra sua illi instituunt? Mitior semper Robinsonus, quin in Apol. cap. ult. quandam se fecisse ab Ecclesiâ Anglicanâ secessionem scribit: quam ipsam etiam jam, siquidem supervixisset, correxisset forte totam.
units.tr: The English Church, from the beginning of the Reformation, was burdened in government and discipline by the hierarchical order of bishops, and by ceremonies more than other churches, and so it everywhere gave scandal to many and provided matter for complaint and contention. Many think that the retention of these things there came from the closer agreement and intercourse of the first English reformers with the Protestants of Germany than with those of France, where such things were not so approved as there. To this was added the monarchical form of civil government, to which episcopal government in the Church accommodates itself with a very close bond. Among the common people of England, those who resisted were drawn to the simplicity approved in the Genevan Church, or afterwards in the Scottish Church. But they differed in this: the best of them judged the episcopal order and ceremonies to be blameworthy and in need of reform, but did not think that the communion of the Church where they prevailed, as the English Church was, should on that account be abandoned. It was enough, they held, that while retaining it they did not conform to these things; hence they were everywhere called Nonconformists, to distinguish them from those who also approved and observed these forms of government and discipline. Others, fewer in number, made so much of this disagreement that they thought the communion of the Church which was troubling them should be abandoned on that account. These were the ones called Separatists, or Brownists. Hence everywhere great caution and prudence were required to walk a straight course between the Episcopalians on one side and the Brownists on the other, lest one either yielded to the Brownists in approving their scandals, or, by condemning the Episcopalians too much, were driven to flee and abhor all communion with the English Church as schismatics. What name it is proper to call them by is uncertain. They utterly reject being called Brownists, on account of the most detestable deed of Robert Browne. Hence John Robinson, in the title of his Apology, says: of the Brownists, or Barrowists, as they are commonly and contemptuously called. They love to be addressed by neither this name nor that. Their first Confession, which they published in 1595, exists in English, Latin, and Dutch; and in their Apology, written to the Oxford teachers in 1598, they call themselves Englishmen in exile in Belgium: The Confession of Faith of certain Englishmen exiled in Belgium. Unless perhaps, with their pardon, you call them Separatists, or the separated, or those separating themselves, [בדין], whence some (whether rightly I do not now say) suppose they were called Pharisees. Certainly they write whole books with this title, Justification of Separation, and they wish their churches to be called churches of separation. John Smith, the churches of separation. So let us call them Separatists, for the sake of some mark of distinction. Except Robinson, and that only near the end of his life, all of them contended with great vehemence that communion was not to be kept with our Churches, especially the English ones. Even if this had been true of the English churches, burdened as they were with episcopal order and the weight of ceremonies, it could never have been said of the present ones, nor of our Belgic churches, which are free of those things. And yet why do they still separate from these and from those as well? We continually receive ministers from the English, and in turn give ministers to them, and we receive people on both sides into communion of the same Church. Why do they separate from both, and keep separate assemblies and a different communion? Formerly Francis Johnson wrote a special book on this, in English, with this title: It is unlawful to hear or to have any communion with the present ministry of the English Church. He forbade his people communion in the Word and prayers in the English Churches, as superstitious and vain worship, as he spoke of praying by set forms, in a book against Gifford, to which he gave a playful title, More Work for Priests. John Greenwood, faithful to Christ, as it is added, martyr. But what does this matter to those who do not bind themselves to forms; or to the present ministry of the English Church, the hierarchical order having long been removed; or to our Churches, from which nevertheless they still today set up their own sacred assemblies apart? Robinson was always milder; indeed, in the last chapter of his Apology he writes that he had made a certain secession from the English Church, which, had he survived, he perhaps would have corrected entirely.

units.la: Nam quod ad doctrinam, exserte fatetur, nihil se in Confessionibus nostris carpere; & reliqui non Confessionis doctrinam in disputationibus adoriuntur, sed Ecclesiarum nostrarum regimen, & disciplinam. Illis se quidem subscripturum testatus Robinsonus fuit, & convenire sibi haud gravate cum nostris, quibus & communionem libens impertiretur: profitemur coram Deo & hominibus, adeo nobis convenire cum Ecclesiis reformatis Belgicis in re religionis, ut omnibus & singulis eandem Ecclesiarum fidei articulis, prout habentur in Hermonia Confessionum fidei, paratissimi subscribere. Deinde, quo jure quàve injuriâ, nos (quibus multo magis in re fidei & religionis convenit cum Ecclesiis Belgicis reformatis, quam plurimis ex eis Ecclesiis, quarum Confessiones tanquam Christianæ conjunctionis symbola, omnibus inspiciendæ proponuntur) ab hoc charitatis vinculo, aut conjunctionis consortio excludi possimus? Ac postea: de Ecclesiis reformatis quid aliud dicam? eas pro veris & genuinis Christi Ecclesiis habemus, cum eisdem in sacris Dei communionem profitemur, & quantum in nobis est, colimus, communes publicas ab illarum pastoribus habitas ex nostris, qui morantur linguam Belgicam frequentant, sacram canam earum mens. Iris, si quae forte nostro casui interfuit nobis cognita, participamus: malis illarum serò ingemiscimus; eisque à Deo sanctam, firmamque pacem ex animo precamur. Hæc in præfatione suæ Apologiæ. Unde & Fratres nos appellat, Apol. c. v 1. Adeo bene isti viro cum Nostris conveniebat, & quam largiri se nostris lubenter communionem scribit, eam ut accepisset tandem etiam cum suis à Nostris, & in nostris Ecclesiis haud levis spes erat.
units.tr: For doctrine, Robinson openly admits that he finds nothing to criticise in our Confessions. The others who dispute with us attack not our doctrine but the government and discipline of our Churches. Robinson himself declared that he would subscribe to them and that he had no serious difficulty in agreeing with us, and he was glad to offer us communion: we profess before God and men that we agree so fully with the Dutch Reformed Churches in matters of religion that we are most ready to subscribe to each and every one of the articles of faith of those Churches, as they are set out in the Harmony of the Confessions of Faith. Then: by what right, or with what injustice, can we (who agree far more in faith and religion with the Dutch Reformed Churches than with most of those Churches whose Confessions are offered to everyone to examine as the creeds of Christian fellowship) be excluded from this bond of charity or this fellowship of union? And later: what else can I say about the Reformed Churches? We hold them to be true and genuine Churches of Christ. We profess communion with them in the holy things of God, and as far as in us lies we cultivate it. We attend the public sermons given by their ministers, and those of us who live among them and frequent the Dutch language take part in their Lord's Supper. If any of their affairs has come to our knowledge, we share in it. We groan over their misfortunes, and from our hearts we pray to God for their holy and firm peace. These are his words in the preface to his Apology, and from them he calls us brethren (Apol. ch. 5, sec. 1). Robinson so clearly agreed with our people, and he writes that he gladly offers us communion, that there was no small hope that, once he had received it, he would one day bring his own people to communion with ours and into our Churches.

units.la: Quamvis in nonnullis à Nostris, discrepare se, constare etiam voluerit: nec placere omnia, quæ in Nostris Ecclesiis geruntur, si non publico instituto (quo non videntur obtinere) consensu tamen fere unanimi, & consuetudine uniformi.
units.tr: Yet he also wished it to be recognised that he differed from us in some matters: nor do all the things that are done in our Churches please me, if not by public institution (which they do not seem to have), yet by an almost unanimous consent and uniform custom.

units.la: Hinc quæstiones Brownisticæ prudenter distinguendæ. Aliæ enim sunt de rebus, quas iiscum non proba-mus; aut de quibus nolimus contendere; nedum scindere Ecclesiæ communionem: quas moverunt aut adversus Ecclesiam Anglicanam: aut etiam Nostram. Quæ ad-versus Anglicanam, ut hinc initium turbarum scismatisque fuit, concernebant aut ordinem Ecclesiasticorum hierarchicum; aut Liturgiam & modum cultus sacri. Ibi, quod Episcopos habebant Angli, & Archiepiscopos, Suffraganeos, Diaconos, Archidiaconos, & reliquam Cleri hierarchico-Papalis turbam. Præterea improbabant quoque quod personæ Ecclesiastica politica tractarent munera & negotia. Iam in cultu divino primum Ceremonias respuebant; tum librum usitatum Communium precum, variis Papatus lemmatis ac superstitionibus refertum. Sed hæc omnia jam sublata, iisque purgata Anglicana Ecclesia est, quibus alii non minus obstiterunt semper ac illi: quique propterea si ab Anglicanâ Ecclesiâ, quare ab Anglo-Belgicâ, & nostris aliisque Ecclesiis, secesserunt? Deinde, quæ in aliis, præter Anglicanam, Ecclesiis Reformatis reprehendunt, talia sunt, ac jam dixi. De libris apocryphis in Ecclesiâ non legendis, quod proferunt, agnoscimus. Neque id apud nos obtinet. De Confessionis nostræ articulo sexto inquit Robinsonus, se toti Confessioni lubenter velle subscribere, modo unius partis sule (ejusdemque non maximi momenti) in Artic. 6. de scriptura, candida & sibi constans adhibeatur interpretatio. Scopus Articuli est (ut ex margine constat) distinguere inter libros Canonicos, & Apocryphos, quos vocant: de quibus tamen Apocryphis creditur, & affirmatur, quod legi in Ecclesiâ possint. Hoc si intelligatur de privatâ eorum per Ecclesiæ
units.tr: Hence the Brownist questions must be carefully distinguished. Some concern things which we do not approve, or about which we are unwilling to contend, much less to break the communion of the Church. These they have raised either against the English Church, or even against ours. Those raised against the English Church, which was the origin of the troubles and the schism, concerned either the hierarchical order of the clergy or the liturgy and manner of divine worship. On the first point, the English had bishops, archbishops, suffragans, deacons, archdeacons, and the rest of the hierarchical and papal crowd of clergy. Moreover, they disapproved of the fact that ecclesiastical persons handled civil offices and business. In divine worship, they first rejected the ceremonies, and then the customary book of Common Prayer, which was filled with various remnants of Popery and superstitions. But all these things have now been removed, and the English Church has been purged of them, and others have opposed them no less than they did. Why, then, have they separated from the English Church, and so from the Anglo-Belgic Church and from ours and other Churches? Furthermore, the things they criticise in the Reformed Churches other than the English are of the kind I have already mentioned. We acknowledge what they put forward about the apocryphal books not being read in the Church. Nor does this prevail among us. Robinson says that concerning the sixth article of our Confession he would gladly subscribe to the whole Confession, provided that an honest and consistent interpretation is applied to one small part (and that of no great importance) of Article 6, on Scripture. The aim of the article is (as the margin shows) to distinguish between the canonical books and those called Apocryphal, of which it is however believed and affirmed that they may be read in the Church. If this is understood of their private reading by the members of the Church,

units.la: nemmembra lectione, libenter annuimus: sin vero de publica, pastorali, & Ecclesiastica, aliter sentimus, neque sufficere mus ullos alios libros apud nos ad tantum dignitatis culmen in Ecclesia vchi, quàm qui à Sanctis Dei hominibus aliis à Spiritu Sancto exarati sunt. Nam quod dicitur, Apocrypha legi etiam in Ecclesia posse, non autem debere, hoc non alium sensum habet, quam quem ipse ponit. Quod vero soliti fuerint in volumine Biblico apocryphi libri, inter Veteris, ac Novi Testamenti libros compingi, loco iis æque convenienti, quàm Turcæ alicui leproso & captivo inter duos præstantissimos Europæ Principes, inquit Robinsonus, correctum jam, cum nova versione Belgica, adeoque in ultimum locum, etiam post Psalterium, Catechesin, Confessionem & Liturgiam rejecti illi libri sunt. Nisi quod illud de Apocryphis in Ecclesia non legendis, aut ad precum formulas quis trahat, ut apocryphas quoque, quemadmodum Ioh. Greenwood, in suo hujus argumenti libro, adversus Giffordum, pag. 29. sive contra Catechismi explicationem, ut Ainsworth, apud Pagetum, Arrow against the Brownists pag. 46. quod tum aliud, & diversum erit. Nam neque Catechismum libris Scripturæ æquamus, sed ex iis tradimus tractamusque eum & non aliter; atque formulas precum nostras, non divinas habemus aut canonicas, sed perinde ac conciones quas facimus, quasque etiam pro rerum usu variamus. Quæ quâ cautela apud Nos observentur, vide ex Amesio, Cas. Consc. lib. IV. cap. XXVI. quaest. I. §. II. & Cap. XVII. quaest. IV. & V. quippe cui Brownistica gravamina vel dogmata erant perspectissima, ad quæ habitá ratione perplura apud eum dicta occurrunt, tum in libro Medulla, tum Casuum; quæ nisi hinc, bene quis intelligat vel explicet. Unde edidit idem quoque accuratum libellum Puritanismi Anglicani auctore Bradshaw.
units.tr: we gladly agree. But if it is understood of public, pastoral and ecclesiastical reading, we think otherwise, and we do not consider that any other books, apart from those written by the holy men of God moved by the Holy Spirit, are fit to be carried to so high a pinnacle of dignity in the Church. For the statement that the Apocrypha may be read in the Church, though not ought to be, has no other sense than the one Robinson himself gives it. As for the custom, which was once common in Bibles, of placing the apocryphal books among the books of the Old and New Testaments, in a place equally suited to them as a leper and captive Turk between two most excellent princes of Europe, as Robinson puts it, those books have now been corrected, together with the new Dutch version, and thrown to the last place, even after the Psalter, the Catechism, the Confession and the Liturgy. Unless someone were to apply what is said about the Apocrypha not being read in the Church to the formulas of prayer, as John Greenwood does in his book on this subject against Gifford (p. 29), or against the explanation of the Catechism, as Ainsworth does (in Paget, Arrow against the Brownists, p. 46). That would be a different and separate matter. For we do not equate the Catechism with the books of Scripture; we teach and handle it from them and in no other way. And we do not regard our forms of prayer as divine or canonical, but in the same way as the sermons we preach, which we also vary according to the needs of the occasion. For the caution with which these things are observed among us, see Amesius, Cases of Conscience, book 4, ch. 26, question 1, sec. 2, and ch. 17, questions 4 and 5. Ames knew the Brownist grievances and doctrines most thoroughly, and many passages dealing with them occur in his works, both in the Medulla and in the Cases; unless one reads these, one can hardly understand or explain them properly. For this reason the same man also published a careful little book, The Puritanism of the English, by Bradshaw.

units.la: Deinde quod de nominibus diorum idololatriis in melius commutandis Brownistæ disputant, facilè omnes approbamus: & quis non malit, ut feriam potius diceremus, quemadmodum in antiquâ Ecclesiâ, vel diem primum, secundum, tertium, quàm Solis, Lunæ, Martis &c. modò usus accederet. Quem penes arbitrium est, & jus & norma loquendi. Ex quo etiam video ipsos Brownistas, præter doctrinæ suæ propositum, subinde sic loqui. Nam quum Henricus Barrow tribus ante mortem, vel (uti dicunt) Martyrium diebus scripserit ex carcere, ad Comitissam aliquam, non Aprilis, sed quarti mensis usurpato nomine: illi, qui Apologiam adversus Oxonienses composuerunt, scribunt illam epistolam datam fuisse mensis Aprilis quarto vel quinto die. Tantus est ille trium litterarum, quod dici solet, tyrannus mos. In Martyrologio Anabaptistico, ad à. cIↄ Iↄ I I I I. lego epistolam cujusdam Iusti Kint, ubi inter alia sic loquitur: scies, quod ego die, quem in Babele Sancti Thomæ vo-cant &c. Ut antiquiora consulamus. In Concilio Narbonensi can. xv. dicunt, diem quintam feriam, qui & dicitur Iovis: Ad nos pervenit, quosdam de populis Catholicæ fidei, execrabili ritu diem quintam feriam, qui & dicitur Iovis, excolere, & operationem non facere. Audi Augustinum, de hoc egregie disserentem, in Psalm. xciii. quæ haud pigebit describere: Quare ergo talem habet titulum, in quarta sabbati? Una sabbati, dies dominicus est: secunda sabbati, secunda feria, quem seculares diem Lunæ vocant: Tertia sabbati, tertia feria, quem diem illi Martis vocant. Quarta ergo sabbatorum quarta feria, qui Mercurii dies dicitur à Paganis & à multis Christianis: sed nolumus ut dicant; atque utinam corrigantur, ut non dicant. Sic enim habent linguam suam, quâ utantur. Non enim & in omnibus gentibus ista dicuntur. Multæ gentes aliæ atque aliæ aliter vocant. Melius ergo de ere Christiano ritus loquendi ecclesiasticus procedit. Tamen si quem forte consuetudo traxerit, ut illud exeat ex ore quod improbat corde, intelligat illos omnes de quorum omnibus appellata sunt sydera, homines fuisse: nec ex eo esse corpissel-ista sydera in caelo, ex quo illi esse coeperunt. Eusebius Emyssenus, homil. xi. de Pascha: mortifera idolatriae consuetudo in tantum homines occaecaverat, ut Solis, Lunae, Martis atque Mercurii, Iovis, Veneris, Saturni, & diversis elementorum, ac daemonum appellationibus dies vocitarent, & luci tenebrarum nomen imponerent. Quin à Paganismo haec veniant, forte ab Ægyptiis, nemini obscurum: nomina vero mensium nostrorum Numam habere auctorem, Plutarchus testis est. Philastrius Brixiensis, in Catalogo Haereticorum, & hanc ponit cap. xi. quae dicit nomina dierum, Solis, Lunae, Martis, Mercurii, Iovis, Veneris, Saturni, à Deo haec ita posita ab origine mundi, non hominum vana praesumptione nuncupata, cum à prima origine usque ad graecos Reges, & Hermen fallacissimum illum, qui haec nomina vanissima, & frivola mentiendo ausus est nuncupare, si quaerere volueris invenies multum fluxisse temporis, & sic paganos, id est, graecos haec nomina posuisse: cum haec nomina etiam secundum septem stellas dixerint hominum generationem consistere, nisi ille ipse delirans hoc definit: Dierum enim numerus primus, secundus, tertius, quartus, quintus, sextus, septimus, à Deo est appellatus, non in hac vanitate nuncupationis turpissima initio enunciatus, aut traditus. Imo supra Ægyptios licet adscendere, & denominationem dierum planetariam arcessere ab antiquis Sabaeis, seu Chaldaeis, quod ex auctore Arabico Said Vaheb docet Hottingerus, in Historia Orientali, lib. 1. cap. VIII. pag. 177. ubi Auctoris illius locum adducit, de Sabaeis sic loquentem: diem primum sacrum faciunt Soli: secundum Lunae: tertium Martis: diem quartum Mercurio: diem quintum Iovi: diem sextum (congregationis) Veneri, cujus nomen est Belsba; diem septimum Saturno. Istae vetustatis est haec dierum nomenclatura, indeque tantam vim in usu apud Graecos, Romanos, & quasvis passim Gentes accepit, ex antiquissima Gentilium astrologia, non demum ex civili aliquo, seu publico instituto: de quo vide Seldenum. num, lib. III. de Iure Natur. Hebraor. cap. xx. &c. Sylvestro Papæ vulgò adscribunt, quod dierum nominationem Ethnicam Solis, Lunæ &c. mutarit in aliam feriarum primæ, secundæ &c. quoque id fecerit rogatu Constantini Imperatoris: verum haud ita est. Nam etiam ante Sylvestri tempora, ut post, simplex illa vel dierum, vel feriarum, aut sabbathorum nominatio in Ecclesiâ obtinuit. Tertullianus, lib. de Ieiunio, contra Psychicos, quos appellat: proinde nec stationes, quæ & ipsæ suos quidem dies habeant, quartæ feriæ, & sextæ. quas eodem libro appellat quoque quartam & sextam sabbathi. Τετράδα, πέμπτην, quartam, quintam, sextam legimus apud Iustinum, & alios, quæ vertunt vulgò feriam, sive respectu habito ad primam anni Ecclesiastici, à Pascha incipientis hebdomadam, quâ sep-tem dies habebantur feriati, ut Scaliger existimat: sive simplici dici intellectu, feriâ, id est, die. Sed quoque apud Iustinum, Clementem, & alios occurrunt nomina dierum planetaria, nimirum ut vulgata. Ille in Apologiâ describens morem concionum: die solis, inquit, omnes convenimus. Clemens, Stromat. lib. VII. novis ipse ieiunii quidem ænigmata horum dierum, τῆς τετράδος, ἡ τῆς πεμπτάδος λόγοι ἐπαφμίζωνται, ἡ μὲν Ἥλιος, ἡ δὲ Ἀφροδίτης. quarti inquam, & sexti. Dicitur autem ille quidem Mercurii, hic vero Veneris. Ut aliam constet fuisse nominationem sacram, & Ecclesiasticam; aliam vulgarem, & profanam. Veteres, ad exemplum Iudæorum, dicebant diem hunc, vel illum sabbathi. Iudæorum Doctores aliqui vel istis Legis verbis memento diei sabbati significatum volunt, ut hinc potius dies, quam à veteri & communi Gentilium usu à Planetis denominarentur. Sic Rabbi Isaac & Abarbanel apud Sel-denum, de Iure Hebr. lib. III. cap. XIX. [?]אלא תספר, non numerabis more, quo numerare solent alii; sed numerabis per nomen sabbati. Quin adeo ab illis abhorrent Iudæi, ut nec in Astronomicis suis libris, aut Calendariis ferant signaturas planetarum vulgares ⊙ ☾ ♂ aut ♈ ♉ ♄ ♃ Schickhardus, in Proœmio Tarich, seu de Regibus Persiæ, pag. 34. Tertullianus parasceven nominat, lib. iv. contra Marcionem. Hieronymus, in Epitaphio Paulæ: dormivit sancta & beata Paula, septimo Kalendarum Februarium, tertia sabbathi, post solis occubitum. Et Augustinus, epist. cxv ii i, ad Ianuarium, sabbatum, & dominicum, & quintam sabbati appellat. Plenissimè Hieronymus, ad Hedibiam, quæst. iv. Vna sabbati dies dominica intelligenda est: quia omnis hebdomadis in Sabbatum, & in primam, & secundam, & tertiam, & quartam, & quintam, & sextam sabbati dividitur: quam ethnici idolorum & elementorum nominibus appellant. Quam loco illius dierum mensiumque nomenclaturæ Ethnicæ approbare nemo non potest. Imperatores Valentiniani, Theodosius, & Arcadius, in Cod. de Feriis, lib. vi. In eadem observatione numeramus & dies solis, quos Dominicos rite dicere majores Constantinum, opinor, respiciunt, qui τὴν κυριακὴν, κυριακὴν, ἡλίου ἡμέραν appellat. ἐν τῇ φωτὸς εἶναι τῇ ἡλίου ἐπιτιμῶν συμβαίνειν. Eusebius, lib. iv. de vita Constantini, cap. xviii. xix. Et Sozomenus, lib. i. cap. viii. Neque video, quare non possint nomina illa dierum vel mensium planetaria, ethnica, & idololatrica mutari, facile etiam, ut in usu Ecclesiastico, ita & civili, ut dicatur & dies, & mensis, primus, secundus, tertius, & sic porro; vel sumta ex anni tempestatibus denominatione: quemadmodum Carolus M. Germanos instituit, de quo Krantzius, Saxon. lib. ii. cap. viii. Mensibus ad propriam linguam nomina impososuit, qui ante id tempus apud Germanos partim Latinis, partim barbaris nominibus enunciabantur. Et Ianuarium quidem appellavit Wintermaen, Februarium, Hornungh: Martium, Lentzmaen: Aprilem, Osstermaen: Majum, Winnemaen: Iunium, Brachmaen: Iulium, Heumaen: Augustum, Ernemaen: Septembrem, Herbstmaen: Octobrem, Harvestmaen: Nouembrem, Wyntmaen. rembrem, Ioremaen / Decembrem, Hellichmaen. Quod quidam etiam in nominibus dierum refigendis tentari, observarique posset? Polydorus Virgilius, de Invent. lib. VI. cap. v. Profectò pudendum est, simulque dolendum, quod non antehàc data sint istis diebus Christiana no-mina, ne dii Gentium inter nos, tam memorabile monumentum haberent. Similiter censet Zanchius, de Operibus Creat. part. II. lib. VI. f. VI. Quomodo Arabes, Turcæ, ac Persæ dies si os aliis quàm Planetarum nominibus designant, primum, secundum, tertium, & sic porro appellantes. Turcæ primum, quem nos solis diem, mercatus alterum, postmercatus diem, tertium Salli, inde quartum, quintum, Giuma, seu festum diem, & congregationis, nam hunc (quem nos vulgò Venerem dicimus) illi sacrum habent; sextum denique vocant postgiuma, sive post-festum. Et Græci hodierni primum diem dicunt Dominicum, inde Δευτέρα, Τρίτη &c. sextam Παρασκευή seu Μεγάλη, tum Σάββατον sive Σαββάτων. Crusius, in Annot. ad Turco-Græciam, pag. 53. Quid obstat, quod non etiam Christiani, omissa idololatricâ appellatione, dies suos nominent inoffensis, si non sacratis vocabulis, prout visum fuerit expedire? Agnosco interim magnam usus vim esse, eoque solo præxim excusari potius, quam probari posse, ut illa usurpemus, quæ nobis ut dicamus conversatio extorquet, quemadmodum hâc in re loquitur Tertullianus. lib. de idololatria. Thomas Campanella, lib. de Monarchiâ Hispaniæ cap. x. Monarcham suum instruit, ut curet ita ordinari menses, ac dies, ut singulis mensibus singula nomina Apostolorum, & septem hebdomadæ diebus septem sacramentorum nomina (loquitur pro sensu Ecclesiæ suæ) attribuantur. Nam revera, inquit, incolæ novi mundi, quando vident in conversationibus Christianis menses & dies Gentilium in usu esse, in admirationem rapiuntur. Non dico quod recta futura esset mutatio talis, ac Campanella proproponit, imo perversam ajo: sed quod is, quod alii, nominibus Gentilibus offensi, non nunc solum, sed & olim, uti in transcursu ostendi, ita mutationem laudandam censemus omnes, nihilque hic Brownistis vel Separatistis adversum Nos superesse quaestionis, quidem adversus inveteratum pravumque osum uti cum aliis.
units.tr: Next, as to the Brownists' dispute about changing the names of the days, which are named after idols, we all readily agree. Who would not prefer that we say, as they did in the ancient Church, "the first day," "the second," "the third," rather than "of the Sun," "of the Moon," "of Mars," and so on, if only custom allowed it? The right and the rule of speaking rest with the one who holds the power over the language. From this I also see that the Brownists themselves, apart from the purpose of their doctrine, sometimes speak in this way. For when Henry Barrow wrote from prison three days before his death, or what they call his martyrdom, to a certain countess, he dated the letter not in April but with the name of the fourth month. Those who composed the Apology against the Oxford men write that the letter was dated the fourth or fifth day of April. Such is the tyranny, as it is commonly called, of the three-letter custom. In the Anabaptist Martyrology, in the year 1534, I read a letter of a certain Just Kint, where among other things he says: you will know that I [wrote] on the day which they call in Babel of St. Thomas, and so on. To consult older sources: in the Council of Narbonne, canon 15, they say: It has come to us that certain people of the Catholic faith, by an execrable custom, observe the fifth day of the week, which is also called Jove's day, and do no work. Hear Augustine, who discusses this admirably in Psalm 93, a passage I will not be sorry to copy out: Why then does it have this title, "on the fourth of the Sabbath"? The first of the Sabbath is the Lord's day; the second of the Sabbath is the second day, which the secular people call the day of the Moon; the third of the Sabbath is the third day, which they call the day of Mars. So the fourth of the Sabbaths is the fourth day, which is called the day of Mercury by the pagans and by many Christians. But we do not wish them to say it; and would that they were corrected so that they would not say it. For they have their own language, which they use. Indeed, these names are not used among all peoples; many other nations call them by different names. It is better, therefore, that the Christian manner of speaking should proceed in the ecclesiastical way. Yet if custom has perhaps drawn someone so that what he disapproves in his heart comes out of his mouth, let him understand that all those from whom the stars were named were men, and that the stars in heaven did not begin to exist from the time those men began to exist. Eusebius of Emesa, homily 11 on the Passover: The deadly custom of idolatry had so blinded men that they called the days by the names of the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and by the various names of the elements and demons, and gave to the light the name of darkness. That these customs come from paganism, perhaps from the Egyptians, is obvious to everyone. But that Numa was the author of the names of our months is attested by Plutarch. Philastrius of Brescia, in his Catalogue of Heretics, chapter 11, also states this: The names of the days, of the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, were not given by the presumption of men but were established by God from the origin of the world. If you wish to inquire, you will find that much time passed from the first origin until the Greek kings and that most deceitful Hermes, who dared to name them with these most vain and frivolous lies; and so the pagans, that is, the Greeks, established these names, since they said that the generation of men depends on the seven stars, unless that raving man himself defined this. For the number of the days, first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, was named by God, and was not announced or handed down at first in this most shameful vanity of naming. Indeed, one may go back even beyond the Egyptians and draw the planetary naming of the days from the ancient Sabaeans or Chaldeans, as Hottinger teaches from the Arabic author Said Vaheb, in his Oriental History, book 1, chapter 8, page 177, where he cites that author's passage speaking of the Sabaeans: They make the first day sacred to the Sun, the second to the Moon, the third to Mars, the fourth to Mercury, the fifth to Jupiter, the sixth (of assembly) to Venus, whose name is Belsba; the seventh to Saturn. This naming of the days is of great antiquity, and from the most ancient astrology of the Gentiles it gained such force in use among the Greeks, Romans, and all nations everywhere, not from any civil or public institution. On this see Selden, De iure naturali et gentium iuxta disciplinam Ebraeorum, book 3, chapter 20, etc. They commonly ascribe to Pope Sylvester the change of the pagan naming of the days, Sun, Moon, and so on, into the other naming, first, second, etc., of the ferias, and say he did this at the request of the Emperor Constantine. But that is not so. For even before the time of Sylvester, and afterwards, that plain naming of the days, or ferias, or sabbaths, prevailed in the Church. Tertullian, in his book On Fasting, against the Psychics, as he calls them: Therefore neither the stations, which have their own days, the fourth and sixth days of the week, which in the same book he also calls the fourth and sixth of the Sabbath. We read [Τετράδα], [πέμπτην], the fourth, fifth, sixth, in Justin and others, which are commonly translated as "feria," either with reference to the first week of the ecclesiastical year, which begins from Easter, in which seven days were kept as festivals, as Scaliger thinks, or in the simple sense of the word, "feria," that is, day. But also in Justin, Clement, and others occur the planetary names of the days, namely as in common use. Justin, describing the custom of sermons in his Apology, says: We all assemble on Sunday. Clement, Stromata book 7: He himself mentions the riddles of the fast of these days, the things of the fourth day [Τῆς τετράδος] and of the fifth [ἡ τῆς πεμπτάδος λόγοι] are called, the one the Sun [ἡ μὲν Ἥλιος], the other Venus [ἡ δὲ Ἀφροδίτης]. I mean the fourth and sixth. The one is called Mercury's day, the other Venus's. Thus it is clear that there was one sacred and ecclesiastical naming, and another common and profane one. The ancients, following the example of the Jews, called this or that day of the Sabbath. Some Jewish teachers, citing those words of the Law, remember the day of the Sabbath, want them to mean that days should be named from the Sabbath rather than from the Planets, after the old and common usage of the Gentiles. So Rabbi Isaac and Abarbanel, cited by Selden, On Hebrew Law, book 3, chapter 19: [לא תספר], you shall not count in the manner in which others are accustomed to count, but you shall count by the name of the Sabbath. Indeed the Jews so shrink from those planetary names that they do not even bear the common signs of the planets, ☉ ☾ ♂ or ♈ ♉ ♄ ♃, in their astronomical books or calendars; see Schickhard, in the preface to his Tarich, or on the Kings of Persia, page 34. Tertullian calls it parasceve, book 4 against Marcion. Jerome, in the Epitaph of Paula: The holy and blessed Paula fell asleep on the seventh day before the Kalends of February, the third of the Sabbath, after sunset. And Augustine, letter 115 to Januarius, calls it the Sabbath, the Lord's day, and the fifth of the Sabbath. Jerome very fully, to Hedibia, question 4: The one day of the Sabbath is to be understood as the Lord's day, because every week is divided into the Sabbath, and the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth of the Sabbath; which the pagans call by the names of idols and elements. Nobody can fail to approve this naming in place of that pagan naming of the days and months. The emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, in the Code, On Ferias, book 6: In the same observance we also count the days of the Sun, which the elders properly call Sundays; they seem to refer to Constantine, who calls it [τὴν κυριακὴν], [κυριακὴν], [ἡλίου ἡμέραν], the Lord's day, the Sun's day [...]. Eusebius, book 4 of the Life of Constantine, chapters 18 and 19; and Sozomen, book 1, chapter 8. Nor do I see why those planetary, pagan, idolatrous names of the days or months could not be changed, easily in civil as in ecclesiastical use, so that the days and months are called first, second, third, and so on, or taken from the seasons of the year: as Charlemagne did for the Germans, of whom Krantz, Saxonia, book 2, chapter 8: He gave names to the months in their own language, which before that time had been called among the Germans partly by Latin and partly by barbarous names. He called January Wintermaen, February Hornungh, March Lentzmaen, April Osstermaen, May Winnemaen, June Brachmaen, July Heumaen, August Ernemaen, September Herbstmaen, October Harvestmaen, November Wyntmaen, December Hellichmaen. Could something of this kind also be attempted, and observed, in the names of the days? Polydore Vergil, On Discoveries, book 6, chapter 5: It is truly shameful and also grievous that Christian names were not given to those days long ago, so that the gods of the Gentiles would not have so memorable a monument among us. Zanchi thinks similarly, On the Works of Creation, part 2, book 6. How the Arabs, Turks, and Persians designate the days by other names than those of the planets, calling them first, second, third, and so on. The Turks call the first, which we call the day of the Sun, the second the day of the market, the third the day after the market, then the fourth, the fifth, Giuma, that is the festival and assembly day (for this one, which we commonly call Venus, they hold sacred); finally they call the sixth the day after Giuma, that is, after the festival. And the modern Greeks call the first day the Lord's day, then [Δευτέρα], [Τρίτη], and so on, the sixth [Παρασκευή] or [Μεγάλη], then [Σάββατον] or [Σαββάτων]. Crusius, in his notes on Turco-Graecia, page 53. What prevents Christians, too, from omitting the idolatrous names and naming their days without offence, if not with sacred words, as it seems expedient? Meanwhile I acknowledge that custom has great force, and that by this alone the practice may be excused rather than approved, so that we use those things which our conversation forces us to say, as Tertullian says in this matter in his book On Idolatry. Thomas Campanella, in his On the Monarchy of Spain, chapter 10, instructs his monarch to see that the months and days are so ordered that each month is given the name of an Apostle and the seven days of the week the names of the seven sacraments (he speaks in the sense of his own Church). For indeed, he says, the inhabitants of the new world, when they see in Christian conversations that the months and days of the Gentiles are in use, are struck with amazement. I do not say that such a change as Campanella proposes would be right; I call it perverse. But since he, like others, is offended by Gentile names, as I have shown in passing, we all judge that the change should be praised, and that nothing remains here of any question for the Brownists or Separatists against us, except perhaps the obstinate and perverse use of the old custom along with others.

units.la: Similiter de divi Dominica sanctificatione frustra est, quod inter articulos dissensus id proponunt, uti fit in Apol. contra Doct. Oxonienses, thes. xi. quum quod hic peccatur a Nostris, uti ab aliis, non probemus, non doceamus, sed contra clamemus sanctificandum diem esse, & hanc Ecclesiae doctrinaeque nostrae manifestam esse sententiam, omnibus satis conspicuam, Robinsono etiam Apol. c. vii.
units.tr: In the same way, it is pointless of them to put forward as a point of disagreement the sanctification of the Lord's Day, as they do in the Apology against the Oxford doctors, thesis 11. Our people, like others, do not approve or teach a violation of that day. On the contrary, we loudly insist that the day must be kept holy, and this is the plain opinion of our Church and of our doctrine, clear enough to everyone, and Robinson too acknowledges it in Apol. ch. 7.

units.la: Neque quod de festorum, seu dierum aliquorum apud nos observatione, ut Paschatis, Pentecostes, Nativitatis, Ecclesiis nostris objici debet, quasi aut dierum sanctitatem venerarentur aliquam, aut etiam simplex istorum observantia probaretur omnium sententiis, aut praxi: praesertim in Ecclesiis Belgicis, ubi ex judicio Synodi Dordracenae anno MDLXXIV. art. III. abrogata illa fuerunt, decretumque Dominico solo contentos esse nos oportere. Ubi iterum usitata praxis Nostros in aliam consuetudinem impulit, testatos interim, optandum esse, ut libertas sex diebus operandi, & sanctificandi solius Dominicae in Ecclesia servata fuisset. Synodus Dordrac. a. MDLXXV. art. LXXV. Idem contra festa usitata constitutum Genevae anno MDLI. de quo Beza, in vita Calvini; Alterum decretum, ut in proximum diem referretur Natalium D. celebratio, nec alii alii festi dies essent, praeter septimum quemque quem Dominicum vocamus. Et Calvinus, epist. ad Hallerum, a. MDLI. inter alia testatur, se ignorante illam mutationem factam, sed quam non adeo aegre ferat: ego tamen neque suasor neque impulsor fui; sic tamen accidisse non molestè fero. namque initio omnia festa eliminata fuisse, scribit: Priusquam urbem unquam ingrederer, nulla prorsus erant feriae praeter diem Dominicum. Idem epist. ad Mompelgardenses a. cIↄ Iↄ xl iii. In festis non recipiendis cupertm vos esse constantiores. Ad Mensonem Poppium a. cIↄIↄ ix. Optandum quidem est ut praeter diem Dominicum pauci retineantur dies festi: nam ut tollantur e medio superstitionum reliquiae, semper ad hoc vitium plus aquo propensi erunt homines. Neque Ecclesia Scotica a primordio Reformationis festa retinuit, quae πυρεισάχθω anno cIↄ Iↄ cxviii. à Synodo Perthensi. Ut neque propter causam festorum, Ecclesias Reformatas culpare aut repudiare debuerint Brovvnistae, quae ipsa multae quoque Ecclesiae cum Reformatione abolev-erunt, aliae nescio quâ consuetudinis necessitate retinuerunt, aut abolita primum denuò admis-ruht.
units.tr: Nor should our churches be charged with the observance of festivals, or certain days, among us, such as Easter, Pentecost and Christmas, as if we revered the holiness of these days, or as if the simple observance of them were approved by everyone's opinion or practice. This is especially so in the Belgic churches, where, by the judgment of the Synod of Dordrecht in 1574, art. III, those days were abolished and it was decreed that we should be content with the Lord's Day alone. Here again, the custom in use drove our people toward another practice, though they testified meanwhile that it was to be wished that the liberty of working six days and keeping only the Lord's Day holy had been preserved in the Church (Synod of Dordrecht, 1575, art. LXXV). Geneva likewise decreed against the usual festivals in 1551, of which Beza speaks in the life of Calvin: "The second decree was that the celebration of Christmas should be moved to the following day, and that there should be no other feast days apart from every seventh day, which we call the Lord's Day." And Calvin, in his letter to Haller in 1551, testifies among other things that he did not know this change had been made, but that he does not take it too badly. "I was neither its advocate nor its promoter, yet I do not greatly regret that it has happened this way. For he writes that at the beginning all festivals had been removed: 'Before I ever entered the city there were absolutely no holidays except the Lord's Day.'" The same Calvin, in his letter to the people of Montbéliard in 1543, says: "In not receiving festivals you ought to be the more constant." To Mention Poppius in 1549 he writes: "It is indeed to be wished that apart from the Lord's Day few festival days be retained; for in order that the remnants of superstition be removed from the midst, men will always be more than enough inclined to this vice." Nor did the Scottish Church retain festivals from the beginning of the Reformation, which were restored (?) by the Synod of Perth in 1618. So the Brownists ought not to blame or reject the Reformed churches on account of the matter of festivals, since many churches themselves abolished them at the Reformation, while others retained them through some necessity of custom, or, having abolished them at first, admitted them again.

units.la: Minus est, quod de gradibus Academicis, ut Papalibus, & de studio profanorum & Ethnicorum Scriptorum in Scholis, objiciunt Adversarii, Apol. contra Oxonienses thes. lxx. de quibus quis contendendum admodum putet, sedum in Ecclesiâ, & ubi agitur, de separatione ab Ecclesiâ instituenda, vel sequenda? Scimus, quae de legendis Gentilium libris olim scripsit Basilius; & quod in Concilio Carthaginensi iv. can. xvi. cautum: Episcopus Gentilium libros non legat: quodque ex Hieronymo in epist. ad Ephes. adducitur à Gratiano quoque 1. dist. xxxvii. Legant episcopi & presbyteri, qui filios suos (adeo maritati tum erant) secularibus erudiunt literis, & faciunt illos comœdias legere, & mimorum turpia scripta cantare, de Ecclesiasticis sumtibus forsitan eruditos. Novimus quae hac in parte pueris & scholis observanda praecipiuntur, etiam de reformatione Gentilismi ex scholis Christianorum, à Ludovico Vive, aliisque pridem monita, majori jure & ratione ac Socrates apud Platonem è suâ Republicâ eliminatas voluit obscoenas & falsas fabulas. Sed quis nostrum illis refragatur? quis improbat, quis prohibet? imo ubi non tum Magistratuum, tum Ecclesiarum in hoc incumbit studium, ut cum litteris vero imbuatur Christianismo & pietate juventus nostra? Iadeo nihil hic quod nobiscum contendanti superest. Illudque de gradibus Academicis levius est, quam ut in censum veniat: quos ipsos nemo nostrum ut rem religionis, sed mere scholarem habet, multique aut negligunt, aut contemnunt. Melanthon, de illis ita scripsit, quae & supra ex eodem attuli, ille adolescens quisquis est, si non habet certam conditionem, meo judicio rectius faciet, si non properabit ad gradum. Titulus aliquid habet oneris. Vides meum exemplum: nemo me perpellere potuit ut illum quamlibet honorificum titulum Doctoris mihi decerni sinerem. Nec ego gradus illos parvifacio: sed ideo quia judico esse magna onera & necessaria rep. verecunde petendos esse, & conferendos, sentio. Zuinglius, in Responsa ad Ioh. Bugenhag. Pomerani epistolam, Oper. Tom. II. pag. 257. Rides etiam me magnum Theologum, qui tam abest ut Theologi nomen unquam ambiverim, ut nonnunquam cum fastidio legam hoc titulos, Doctor aut Professor Theologiae, in illorum libris, qui fortasse Theologi sunt. Ita est, sub illis titulis saepe magna fovetur ambitio. Quin compellationem reverendi, vel reverentiae refugit Zuinglius, Tom. I. ad Valentinum Comparem, pag. 229. qui Din wirde ei dixerat: est vero, quod in te merito reprehendam, quod nimirum nimis ambitioso titulo me aggravas, dum me non meo nomine, sed dignitatis titulo alloqueris. Verum amoto ambitionis vitio, in usurpandis illis titulis, & superstitionis Papalis in conferendis, nihil hic video, ob quod contendi debeat: titulis consideratis, quemadmodum Capito loquebatur lib. IV. epist. Oecolampadii, discriminis loco, in Scholis, ut studiosi ab ignavis discernantur, & exercitati tyronibus praferantur, ac stimulum habeant gloriae honestissimae. Admittimus, sed Scholae magis habita consideratio... deratione, pro docendi promovendique usitata methodo, quam nostri: quo pacto Bucerus, in Cantabrigiensi Angliae Academia admisit, non petiit, se in ordinem & nomen Doctorum adscisci, nullo addito, quod quidem distincte postularat, publico ritu, vel usitata initiandi caeremonia; ubi oratione a se ad promotionem recitata, de usu illorum titulorum disseruit, quae extat inter Scripta ejus Anglicana, sol. 184. adde &c. 871. Eadem fuit ratio Waldensium & Fratrum in Bohemia, improbantium gradus docendi & promovendi in Universitatibus, authoritate Papali observatos, etiam gesticulatoriam insignium collationem, de quibus Clar. Vir Joachimus Camerarius, in Historica Narrat. de Ecclesiis Fratrum in Bohemia & Moravia, pag. 103. Quod si qui etiam locuti sunt contentius de illis ineptiis actionum & verborum nugis, quae conferendo insignia usurparentur, quis non ignoverit paulo prudentior, gravitatis indignationi? Quin etiam, si idem nunc quoque ab aliquo (quocunque sane) fiat, fortasse non immerito fieri, existimandum sit. Vix enim in tanta luce intelligentiae & liberalis institutionis, optimarumque disciplinarum copia, effugere potest obsoleta jocularium observationum usurpatio urbanorum dicta & severiorum stomachum. Eraque ea quoque emendari melius, ut ubique peccata arta corrigerentur, & invecta absurditates removerentur: quibus adhuc locum relinqui apud eos, a quibus veluti jugum excussum est Papalis dominatus, & rejecta impietatis & perversitatis alia onera, quam potest habere comprobationem vel omnino excusationem? Id vero quod Brownistae objiciunt, quod retinemus Scholares titulos, paris est commatis cum eo quod ab altera parte nobis impingunt Lutherani, quod illos cupiamus abolitos. Etenim super eo quaestionem quoque movit Henr. Eckhardus, in Fasciculo Controversiarum Calvinianarum, cap. ult. Adeo quod omnibus undiquaque satisfaciat, vix frustra speres. Denique & Luthero idem objiciunt Pontifi tificii, Gretserus in Lutbero Academico, cap. 111. quod omnes gradus Academicos sustulerit. Quod autem Carolostadio passim istam sententiam objiciant Lutherani, vereor an verum sit, quum solius Lutheri nitatur testimonio, quem iniquiorem erga illum fuisse, & multa non bene de eo interpretatum, novimus, utcunque suo Magistro & promotore: nam Carolostadius Theol. Doctor in recenti Academia Vittembergensi, Lutherum Doctorem creavit a. cIↄIↄxII. Refert in vita Carolostadii Melchior Adamus, ex Iohannis Sturmii Anti-Pappo IV. pag. 20. quod Carolostadius Simoni Grynaeo controversiam moverit, circa annum trigesimum octavum, postulans ab eo, ut si Theologiam publice docere vellet, Theologum se Doctorem creari pateretur. Ad quam controversiam componendam missi fuerint Basileam à Senatu Argentinensi, Capito, Bucerus, & ipse Sturmius. Forte Carolostadius ante discessum suum V Vittembergâ a. cIↄIↄxxII. quo tempore promovebat Doctores V Vestermannum, & Gotschalcum Crapium, & dixisse ferunt, se nullum postea promoturum; movit nonnulla, de titulorum istorum aliquo abusu, quae adversus titulos in se postea expositia de ipso fuerint. Quae omnia haud tanti, ut propterea contentio in Scholis, nedum in Ecclesiis, minime secessio, instituatur. De quibus usurpandis videmus motam à primis Reformationis initiis disputationem. Tomo primo Declamat. Melanthonis à Doctore Iona habita oratio extat, de gradibus in Theologia. Tomo tertio, Iohannis Bugenhagii, super eadem materia. Pezelius, part. VII. Argum. & Respons. Melanth. pag. 265. singulatim agit, de gradibus honorum in Academiis. Confer & Iohannem Gerhardi, Loc. Commun. Tom. VI. de Minist. Ecclesiast. sect. XI. Bradshaw, Englisch Puritanisme pag. 19. Alium librum, à Guide unto Sion, pag. 21.
units.tr: Less weighty is what the adversaries object concerning academic degrees, as though they were papal, and concerning the study of profane and Gentile writers in the schools (Apol. contra Oxonienses, thesis 70). Who would think these matters worth contending over, especially in a church where the question is whether separation from the Church is to be undertaken or followed? We know what Basil once wrote about reading Gentile books; and what the Council of Carthage IV, canon 16, provided: "A bishop shall not read Gentile books." Also what Gratian, dist. 37, cites from Jerome's letter to the Ephesians: "Let bishops and elders, who bring up their sons (for they were then married) in secular letters and make them read comedies and sing the shameful writings of mimes, be educated at ecclesiastical expense, perhaps." We know what has been prescribed in this regard for children and schools, and what Ludovicus Vives and others have long advised concerning the purging of paganism from Christian schools, with greater right and reason than when Socrates in Plato's Republic wished obscene and false fables removed. But which of us opposes these things? Who disapproves of them, who forbids them? Indeed, where is the zeal of magistrates and churches not directed to this, that our youth be imbued with true Christianity and piety along with letters? Therefore there is nothing here for us to dispute with them. And the matter of academic degrees is too trivial to come into account; none of us regards them as a matter of religion but as purely scholastic, and many either neglect or despise them. Melanchthon wrote of them thus, which I have also quoted above from the same author: "That young man, whoever he is, if he has no fixed position, will in my judgment act more rightly if he does not hasten to a degree. A title carries some burden. You see my example: no one has been able to persuade me to allow that most honourable title of Doctor to be conferred on me. Nor do I think lightly of those degrees, but because I judge them to be great and necessary burdens, I feel they are to be sought modestly and conferred with care." Zwingli, in his reply to the letter of Johannes Bugenhagen of Pomerania, Opera vol. II, p. 257: "You even laugh at me as a great theologian, who am so far from ever having sought the name of theologian that I sometimes read with disgust those titles, 'Doctor' or 'Professor of Theology,' in the books of men who perhaps are theologians." Indeed, under such titles great ambition is often nourished. Zwingli, vol. I, to Valentinus Compar, p. 229, even shrank from the title of "reverend" or "reverence," since the man had addressed him as "Din wirde": "Truly, there is something I rightly reprove in you, namely that you burden me with too ambitious a title, since you address me not by my own name but by the title of dignity." But, setting aside the vice of ambition in using those titles and the papal superstition in conferring them, I see nothing here on account of which contention ought to be made, provided the titles are considered as Capito spoke in book IV of Oecolampadius' letters, as a mark of distinction in the schools, "so that the diligent may be distinguished from the idle, and the practised placed before beginners, and so that they may have a spur to most honourable glory." We admit that the consideration of the school is greater than ours in regard to the customary method of teaching and advancing; in this manner Bucer, in the Cambridge Academy of England, admitted, did not seek to be enrolled in the order and name of Doctors without any addition, which he had indeed plainly demanded, by public rite or the usual ceremony of initiation; and in an oration he delivered there at his promotion, he discussed the use of those titles, which is extant among his English writings, p. 184; add also pp. 871 ff. The reasoning was the same for the Waldensians and the Brethren in Bohemia, who disapproved of the degrees of teaching and promotion observed in universities by papal authority, including the ceremonial conferral of insignia; concerning these the distinguished man Joachim Camerarius, in his historical narrative of the Churches of the Brethren in Bohemia and Moravia, p. 103, writes: "But if some have also spoken rather contentiously about those absurdities of actions and words, the trifles that were used in conferring insignia, who would not, if somewhat more prudent, pardon them from indignation at their gravity? Indeed, even if the same thing is done now by someone, whoever he may be, it should perhaps be thought not unjustly done. For hardly, in such great light of understanding, liberal education and abundance of the best disciplines, can the old-fashioned use of jocular observances escape the disgust of serious and urbane minds. And these things too would be better corrected, so that everywhere close sins be amended and introduced absurdities be removed. Yet such room is still left for them among those from whom the yoke of papal domination has been shaken off, and other burdens of impiety and perversity have been cast aside, what approval or even excuse can they have?" But the objection the Brownists make, that we retain scholastic titles, is of the same kind as the objection the Lutherans on the other side bring against us, that we wish them abolished. Indeed Henricus Eckhardus raised this question too in the Fasciculus Controversiarum Calvinianarum, last chapter; one could hardly hope to satisfy everyone on every side. Finally the Papists object the same to Luther, as Gretser does in Lutherus Academicus, ch. 3, that he abolished all academic degrees. But as to the Lutherans' frequent charge that Carlstadt held this view, I doubt whether it is true, since it rests on the testimony of Luther alone, who we know was more hostile to him and interpreted many things about him unfavourably, however much he was his teacher and promoter. For Carlstadt, Doctor of Theology in the recent Academy of Wittenberg, created Luther Doctor in 1512. Melchior Adam reports in the life of Carlstadt, from Johannes Sturmius' Anti-Pappus IV, p. 20, that Carlstadt raised a dispute with Simon Grynaeus around the year 1538, demanding that if he wished to teach theology publicly, he should allow himself to be created Doctor of Theology. To settle this dispute, Capito, Bucer and Sturmius himself were sent to Basel by the Senate of Strasbourg. Perhaps Carlstadt, before his departure from Wittenberg in 1522, when he was promoting the Doctors Westermann and Gotschalk Crapius, is said to have stated that he would promote no one afterwards; he raised some objections concerning an abuse of those titles, and afterwards things were said about him, as against the titles he himself had set forth. All these things are not of such weight that a contention should be started over them in the schools, much less in the Churches, let alone secession. We see that the discussion of their use was raised from the first beginnings of the Reformation. In the first volume of Melanchthon's declamations there is an oration by Doctor Jonas, On the Degrees in Theology. In the third volume, one by Johannes Bugenhagen on the same subject. Pezelius, part VII, Arguments and Replies of Melanchthon, p. 265, treats singly On the Degrees of Honour in Academies. Compare also Johann Gerhard, Loci Communes, vol. VI, On the Ecclesiastical Ministry, sect. XI; Bradshaw, English Puritanisme, p. 19; and another book, A Guide unto Sion, p. 21.

units.la: Verum his missis, accedamus ad veras inter Nos atque que Adversarios Separatistas quaestiones, quorum spectanda nobis est tum veritas, tum momentum, ut constet, an quid tam grave tantique ponderis inter Nos & illos dissidium sit, quod patrocinari illorum scismati queat. Nam utcunque vera essent multa ex parte quae adversus Nos objiciunt; tanta insuper ut sint, ut omnino scindi & dissolvi Ecclesiae unio debeat, probare opus: quod[?] prae illo longe est difficilius. Sed apices omnes (nam de apiculis fere contendunt) recte intuenti liquebit, quam longe & hic & ibi erient a veritate atque, ac Ecclesiâ.
units.tr: But setting these aside, let us come to the real questions between us and our Separatist adversaries. Both their truth and their importance must be weighed, so that we can see whether there is any disagreement between us and them so serious and weighty that it could justify their schism. However true many of the things they object against us may be, it is still necessary to prove that they are so grave that the unity of the Church must be wholly torn apart and dissolved. That is far more difficult than the first task. But anyone who looks at all the points carefully (for they dispute almost over trifles) will see how far both they and we stray from the truth and from the Church.

units.la: Primum enim, quod quidem maximi videtur momenti, est de orthodoxiâ & veritate Ecclesiae Anglicanae, qualis fuit, dum secessionem ab eâ instituerunt: adjunt, non fuisse veram, ac propterea deserendam Ecclesiam. Sed bene distinguenda verum; & perfectum, seu ut Ecclesia aliqua sit imperfecta, vel non vera: quem admodum vere fidelis, pius, adde doctus, diligens, namque in omnibus hoc discrimen obtinet, est, qui non tamen perfectus in illis, sed & multas magnasque imperfectiones admixtas habet. Quare ut detur, variis naevis infectam fuisse Anglicanam Ecclesiam, hoc tamen argumento nondum effecerunt, vel nullatenus pro vera habendam fuisse Ecclesiam, vel deserendam. Audiamus etiam, breviterque, quae pro se adferunt. Dicunt, in primâ Ecclesiae collectione, sub Elizabethâ Reginâ, homines non rite instructos, conversosque fuisse, neque praeeunte solemni confessione & foedere cum Deo, admissos, sed vi fere & authoritate Regiâ ac politicâ, quasi ad sonum tympani, promiscue quosvis, Papistas etiam, improbos, atheos in Ecclesiam actos congregatosque, unde Anglicana illa conflata sit, quae proinde nequeat vera esse. Respondeo, χῇ συγχώρησον, detur verum esse quod de primâ Ecclesiae Anglicanae collectione dicunt, nullo tamen modo sequitur, vel omnes tali tempestate improbos, & non mul-tos
units.tr: First, and this seems to be of the greatest importance, they question the orthodoxy and truth of the English Church as it was when they began to separate from it. They say it was not true, and that for this reason the Church should be abandoned.
