But the true and the perfect must be carefully distinguished, that is, a church may be imperfect without being not true, just as a man may be truly faithful, pious, and, I add, learned and diligent, and yet not perfect in these things, but have many great imperfections mixed in with them. So even if it is granted that the English Church was tainted with various blemishes, they have not yet shown by this argument either that it should be regarded as not true at all, or that it should be abandoned. Let us also briefly hear what they bring forward in their own defence. They say that in the first gathering of the Church under Queen Elizabeth, men were admitted who had not been properly instructed or converted, and who were received without a solemn confession and covenant with God, but almost by force and by royal and political authority, as if at the sound of a drum. Thus any and every sort of person, even Papists, wicked men and atheists, were driven and gathered into the Church, and from this the English Church was put together, which therefore cannot be true. I reply: [χῇ συγχώρησον] grant that what they say about the first gathering of the English Church is true; yet it in no way follows that all men of that time were wicked, or that not many...

units.la: { } Bbb 3 — signature at foot of page. tificii, Gretserus in Luthero Academico, cap. 11. quod omnes gradus Academicos sustulerit. Quod autem Carolostadio passim istam sententiam objiciant Lutherani, vereor an verum sit, quum solius Lutheri nitatur testimonio, quem iniquiorem erga illum fuisse, & multa non bene de eo interpretatum, novimus, utcunque suo Magistro & promotore: nam Carolostadius Theol. Doctor in recenti Academia V Vittembergensi, Lutherum Doctorem creavit a. cIↄ Iↄ xii. Refert in vita Carolostadii Melchior Adamus, ex Iohannis Sturmii Anti-Pappo iv. pag. 20. quod Carolostadius Simonii Grynaeo controversiam moverit, circa annum trigesimum octavum, postulans ab eo, ut si Theologiam publice docere vellet, Theologum se Doctorem creari pateretur. Ad quam controversiam componendam missi fuerint Basileam a Senatu Argentinensi, Capito, Bucerus, & ipse Sturmius. Forte Carolostadius ante discessum suum V Vittembergâ a. cIↄ Iↄ xxii. quo tempore promovebat Doctores V Veltermannum, & Gotschalcum Crapium, & dixisse ferunt, se nullum posthac promoturum; movit nonnulla, de titulorum istorum aliquo abusu, quae adversus titulos in se postea expositae de ipso fuerint. Quae omnia haud tanti, ut propterea contentio in Scholis, nedum in Ecclesiis, minime secessio, instituatur. De quibus usurpandis videmus motam à primis Reformationis initiis disputationem. Tomo primo Declamat. Melanthonis à Doctore Iona habita oratio extat, de gradibus in Theologiâ. Tomo tertio, Iohannis Bugenhagii, super eadem materia. Pezelius, part. vii. Argum. & Respons. Melanth. pag. 265. singulatim agit, de gradibus honorum in Academiis. Confer & Iohannem Gerhardi, Loc. Commun. Tom. vi. de Minist. Ecclesiast. sect. xi. Bradshaw, Englisch Puritanisme pag. 19. Alium librum, à Guide unto Sion, pag. 21.
units.tr: ...of the Papists. Gretser, in his Luther Academicus, ch. 11, says that Luther abolished all academic degrees. As for the charge that the Lutherans commonly bring against Karlstadt with this opinion, I doubt whether it is true, since it rests on the testimony of Luther alone; we know that Luther was less fair to him, and interpreted many of his actions wrongly, although Karlstadt was Luther's own teacher and promoter. For Karlstadt, doctor of theology in the recent academy of Wittenberg, created Luther a doctor in 1512. Melchior Adam, in his life of Karlstadt, cites Johann Sturm's Anti-Pappus, part 4, p. 20, that Karlstadt began a dispute with Simon Grynaeus around the year 1538, demanding that, if Grynaeus wished to teach theology publicly, he should allow himself to be created a doctor of theology by Karlstadt. To settle this dispute, the Senate of Strasbourg sent Capito, Bucer and Sturm himself to Basel. Perhaps before Karlstadt left Wittenberg in 1522, when he was creating the doctors Veltermann and Gotschalk Crapius, he said that he would promote no one after that; he raised some complaints about an abuse of these titles, and afterwards these same complaints were turned against him, and about him. None of these matters is so important that a quarrel should be stirred up in the schools, let alone in the churches, and still less a secession. We see that the dispute over the use of these titles was raised from the first beginnings of the Reformation. In the first volume of Melanchthon's Declamations there is an oration on the degrees in theology delivered by Doctor Jonas. In the third volume there is one by Johannes Bugenhagen on the same subject. Pezel, part 7, Argum. & Respons. Melanth., p. 265, deals with the degrees of honour in the academies one by one. Compare also Johann Gerhard, Loc. Commun., vol. 6, de Minist. Ecclesiast., sect. 11. Bradshaw, English Puritanisme, p. 19. Another book, A Guide unto Sion, p. 21.

Nam utcunque vera essent multa ex parte quae adversus Nos objiciunt; tanta insuper ut sint, ut omnino scindi & dissolvi Ecclesiae unio debeat, probare opus: quod prae illo longe est difficilius. Sed apices omnes (nam de apiculis fere contendunt) recte intuenti liquebit, quam longe & hic & ibi erient a veritate aeque, ac Ecclesia.

However true many of the things they object against us may be, it is still necessary to prove that they are so grave that the unity of the Church must be wholly torn apart and dissolved. That is far more difficult than the first task. But anyone who looks at all the points carefully (for they dispute almost over trifles) will see how far both they and we stray from the truth and from the Church alike.

Sed bene distinguenda verum; & perfectum, seu ut Ecclesia aliqua sit imperfecta, vel non vera: quemadmodum vere fidelis, pius, adde doctus, diligens, namque in omnibus hoc discrimen obtinet, est, qui non tamen perfectus in illis, sed & multas magnasque imperfectiones admixtas habet. Quare ut detur, variis naevis infectam fuisse Anglicanam Ecclesiam, hoc tamen argumento nondum effecerunt, vel nullatenus pro vera habendam fuisse Ecclesiam, vel deserendam.

They say it was not true, and that for this reason the Church should be abandoned. But the true and the perfect must be carefully distinguished, that is, a church may be imperfect without being not true, just as a man may be truly faithful, pious, and, I add, learned and diligent, and yet not perfect in these things, but have many great imperfections mixed in with them. So even if it is granted that the English Church was tainted with various blemishes, they have not yet shown by this argument either that it should be regarded as not true at all, or that it should be abandoned.

units.la: Audiamus etiam, breviterque, quae pro se adferunt. Dicunt, in prima Ecclesiae collectione, sub Elizabetha Regina, homines non rite instructos, conversosque fuisse, neque praecunte solemni confessione & foedere cum Deo, admissos, sed vi fere & authoritate Regia ac politica, quasi ad sonum tympani, promiscue quosvis, Papistas etiam, improbos, atheos in Ecclesiam actos congregatosque, unde Anglicana illa conflata sit, quae proinde nequeat vera esse. Respondeo, <bl>χ</bl> συγχώρησιν, detur verum esse quod de prima Ecclesiae Anglicanae collectione dicunt, nullo tamen modo sequitur, vel omnes tali tempestate improbos, & non multos tos etiam inter illos pios fuisse (neque enim puto, illos hoc negaturos, non de Martyribus, qui sub Henrico, & Maria plures in isthoc regno), vel omnes improbos mansisse, semperque omnes tales, etiam dum Adversarii cum illa Ecclesia communicare noluerunt, perdurasse. Annon, uti in politia, sic quoque in Ecclesia, vitium facile committitur in prima constitutione, vel reformatione, quod deinde succesu temporis corrigitur & emendatur? Vel quemadmodum vitium postmodum accedens non officit toti semper Ecclesiae, ita nec quod sub initio forte accidit. Sed & vitia iliusmodi facti sunt, non doctrinae, non illa si quae intercurrerunt, probavit Ecclesia, neque docuit: quare non magis ea, quam alia, quam perpetua, & communia isti Ecclesiae cum aliis, nec ipsam eximo Separatisticam, peccata Anglicanae objici possunt. At neque rem ita se habere, ut illi jactant, cum Ecclesiae Anglicanae primordiis, certum est. Habuit Ecclesia illa jam sub Eduardo juvene, ne superiora dicam tempora, Doctores, & Ministros, indigenas, exterosque, qui illis, & sequentibus Mariae, usque ad Elizabetham, temporibus, docendo, instruendo, convertendo homines strenuissime laborarunt; quorumque operam ita benedixit Deus, ut florentem sub ipsis persecutionibus, magnam Ecclesiam, multosque sanctissimos Martyres, ante Elizabetham dederit, irrefragabilia verae & orthodoxae Ecclesiae argumenta. Quod si vel in solis Martyrum Anglorum instemus exemplis, intoleranda merito videbuntur illorum, hominum praejudicia illam Ecclesiam condemnantium, & non habentium pro vera. Sumamus ipsam Elizabetham, tantum non Martyrem quoque, & quotquot cum istorum temporum felicitate dati seu reddití Ecclesiae fuerunt; quis tam improbus, qui vel illam, vel alios, aut non bene conversos, aut non vere fideles asserere ausit? Sed vi & mandato Edictorum Regiorum multi in Ecclesiam coacti fuerunt. Num omnes ita? num plerique? nulli alià viâ, & vi verbi? ut nuspiam fuerit vera Ecclesia, verum ministerium, fideles veri? imo nemo vi adactus fuit, ut religionem amplecteretur. Quod si authoritate regiâ in subsidium veniente Ecclesiæ, conata fuerit Regina juvare tum reformationem, tum ejus incrementum, hocne vitio verti potest vel debet? annon Regiam & politicam potestatem ancillari Christo ejusque regno promovendo, & se hâc ratione sacrare Deo, oportet? Vide, quæ sacrorum Principum sequuta hâc in re exempla Regina fuerit, II. Chron. xv. 13. & xxxIII. 16. & xxxIV. 32. 33. Vel peccarint etiam immodico zelo politici, luere hocne Ecclesia tenetur, & toti ei exprobrandum? Num semper & ubique ita egit, & nuspiam, nunquam aliter Elizabetha regina? num & alii Principes? num omnes per totam Angliam? ut à totâ Anglicanâ Ecclesiâ, & perpetuò se segregare debuerint soli Browniståe? vel quid hoc ad Anglicanas, & Belgicas, aliasve Ecclesias transmarinas, ante tempora Elizabethæ etiam collectas, vel ad nostras ab exulibus sub Marianâ persecutione Anglo-Belgis fundatas, ut ab omnibus se semper segreges facere illi voluerint? Sed omissa fuit publici & nationalis fœderis cum Deo, post conversionem & reformationem à Papatu, solemnitas, qualis in Veteri populo, ad ejusmodi negotia, fieri solita. Neque hoc omnino verum. Aliter factum in Coventriensi, Northamtonensi, aliisque diœcesibus, ubi confœderationis istiusmodi habitam rationem scribunt. Verùm probandum prius esset, explicite & exserte debere ab omnibus Ecclesiis vel membris præstari tale fœdus, antequam pro veris haberi possent, & non sufficere ad hoc, fœdus implicitum, substantiale, virtuale, tacitum quandoque, & per varios actus officiaque communionis Ecclesiasticæ erga Deum & homines comprobatum. Cæterùqui solemnitatem ejusmodi publici fœderis non rejicimus, gravi nempe eam invitante occasione, ad exemplum Joluæ, Asæ, Ioasi, Iosiæ, Nehemiæ, de quibus in sacris: quale Respublica & Ecclesia Genevensis, a. clɔ Iɔ xxxvi i. præeunte in sacramentum publico Senatus Scribâ; Regnum & Ecclesia Scotica a, clɔ Iɔ lxxx. præeunte Iacobo Rege, cum suâ familiâ, & nuper Angli, Scoti, Hibernique famoso fœdere inierunt a. clɔ Iɔ c xxxv iii. Sed ut non habeatur vera Ecclesia, ad quam explicata, publica, ac generalis ejusmodi fœderis Confessio non præcesserit, haud admittendum. Præsertim quum ante sacramentorum administrationem à singulis fœdus cum Deo, & quidquid eo comprehendi vel exigi poterit, iniri renovarique, ex Ecclesiæ Reformatæ disciplinâ, soleat. Vide de illis Rob. Parkerum, lib. iii. Polit. Eccles. cap. xvi. Gisbertum Voetium, de Eccles. Institutâ & visib. Disp. iv. v. Guilj. Apollonium, Confideratt. Controverf. Anglic. cap. ii. Denique, nisi hæc objectio neglecti solemnis fœderis Separatistis sit modo prætextus & mera ἀσφαλεια, quum neque post nuper dictum fœdus nationale ab omnibus Anglis, neglecto diuturniori scismate, reversi ad Ecclesiam ocyus fuerint; cur ab illo etiam tempore se separatos gesserunt ab Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ, vel aliarum Reformatarum communione? Sed hoc est ingenium, hæc indoles Schismaticorum, ludere prætextibus. Vti Donatistæ olim, Cæciliani Carthaginensis Episcopi ordinationem calumniabantur, quasi à Traditoribus sacrorum Scripturæ Codicum factam, proinde illegitimam, & hinc falsam Ecclesiam, cui ejusmodi Episcopi darentur, quamvis sæpe convicti haud vera esse in Cæcilianum & Catholicos jactatâ crimina, pertinaci tamen dissensione in schismate perseveraandum, in suâ solum parte Ecclesiam hætere, censuerunt. Adeo quidquid illis dici olim potuit, in nostros quoque homines quadrare comperiemus.
units.tr: Let us hear also, briefly, what they bring forward in their own defence. They say that in the first gathering of the Church under Queen Elizabeth, men were not properly instructed or converted, nor admitted after a solemn confession and covenant with God. Instead, by force and almost by royal and political authority, as if at the beat of a drum, people of every kind, even Papists, wicked men and atheists, were driven and gathered into the Church, and from this the English Church was put together, and so it cannot be true. I reply: granted [συγχώρησιν] that what they say about the first gathering of the English Church is true, it nonetheless does not follow that all were wicked at that time, for many of them, and certainly some godly men, were among them (I do not think they would deny this, especially regarding the martyrs, who were numerous in this kingdom under Henry and Mary). Nor does it follow that all remained wicked, or that all such people persisted in that state, even while our adversaries refused to communicate with that Church. Is it not the case that, in the state as in the Church, a fault is easily committed in the first establishment or reformation, and that this is afterwards corrected and amended as time goes on? Just as a fault that arises later does not harm the whole Church always, so neither does what perhaps happened at the beginning. Moreover, faults of this kind were committed by men; the Church did not approve them, nor did it teach them, nor did it accept any that crept in. Therefore the faults that have been objected to the English Church are no more peculiar to it than to other churches, and they are not peculiar even to the Separatist church itself, since they are perpetual and common to all. But that things are not as those men boast, so far as the beginnings of the English Church are concerned, is certain. Already under the young Edward, not to mention earlier times, that Church had teachers and ministers, native and foreign, who worked most vigorously in teaching, instructing and converting people through the reign of Edward, through Mary's time, and up to Elizabeth. God so blessed their labour that before Elizabeth's time he gave a flourishing Church even under persecutions, and many most holy martyrs, which are irrefutable proofs of a true and orthodox Church. And if we insist on the examples of the English martyrs alone, the prejudices of those men who condemn that Church and do not hold it to be true will rightly appear intolerable. Let us take Elizabeth herself, who was almost a martyr too, and all who were given or restored to the Church with the good fortune of those times: who is so wicked as to dare to assert that she, or others, were either badly converted or not truly faithful? But many were forced into the Church by the force and command of royal edicts. Were all so forced? Were most? Were none brought in by any other way, and by the power of the Word alone, so that nowhere was there a true Church, a true ministry, or true believers? Indeed, no one was forced to embrace the religion. But if the Queen, coming to the aid of the Church by royal authority, tried to help both the reformation and its growth, can this or should this be blamed? Ought not royal and political power to serve Christ and to promote his kingdom, and in this way to dedicate itself to God? See what examples of holy princes the Queen followed in this matter: II Chron. xv. 13, xxxiii. 16 and xxxiv. 32, 33. And if they also sinned through an excessive political zeal, is the Church bound to bear the blame for this, and is it all to be reproached? Did Queen Elizabeth always and everywhere act in this way, and never otherwise, nowhere? And did the other princes? Did all throughout the whole of England? So that the Brownists alone should have been obliged to separate themselves permanently from the whole English Church? Or what does this have to do with the English and Belgic churches, or other churches overseas, which were gathered even before Elizabeth's time, or with our churches founded by exiles from England and the Low Countries under the Marian persecution, that those men should wish to make themselves separate from all of them always? But, it is said, the solemnity of a public and national covenant with God was omitted after the conversion and reformation from Papacy, such as was customary among the old people for matters of this kind. Nor is this altogether true. It was done otherwise in Coventry, Northampton and other dioceses, where, as they write, an account was taken of such a covenant. But it would first have to be proved that such a covenant must be made explicitly and expressly by all churches or members before they could be held to be true, and that it is not enough for this purpose that a covenant implied, substantial, virtual, sometimes tacit, and confirmed through the various acts and duties of ecclesiastical communion towards God and men. Otherwise, we do not reject the solemnity of such a public covenant, namely when a serious occasion invites it, after the example of Joshua, Asa, Joash, Josiah and Nehemiah, of whom we read in the sacred books. Such a covenant was entered into by the Republic and Church of Geneva in 1536, with the public Senate's scribe leading the oath; by the Kingdom and Church of Scotland in 1580, with King James leading, together with his family; and recently the English, Scots and Irish entered into the famous covenant in 1638. But it must not be admitted that a church is not a true church unless an explicit, public and general confession of such a covenant has come before it. Especially since, according to the discipline of the Reformed Church, it is customary for individuals to enter into and renew the covenant with God, and whatever can be included in it or required by it, before the administration of the sacraments. On these matters see Robert Parker, Politia Ecclesiastica, book iii, ch. xvi; Gisbert Voetius, De Ecclesia instituta et visibili, disp. iv and v; William Apollonius, Considerationes controversiarum Anglicarum, ch. ii. Finally, unless this objection about the neglected solemn covenant is merely a pretext for the Separatists and an empty [ἀσφάλεια] safeguard, since after the recent national covenant mentioned above, not all the English returned quickly to the Church, neglecting the longer schism, why have they behaved as separated from the communion of the English Church, or of the other Reformed churches, from that time on? But this is the nature and character of schismatics, to play with pretexts. Just as the Donatists once slandered the ordination of Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, as if it had been performed by traitors who had handed over the sacred Scripture codices, and therefore illegitimate, and hence the Church to which such bishops were given was false; and although they were often convicted that the crimes they had thrown at Caecilian and the Catholics were not true, they nonetheless decided that they should persevere in schism with stubborn dissent and that the Church existed only in their own part. So we will find that whatever could once be said against them can also be fitted to our people.

units.la: Huc pertinent quæ eâdem temeritate disputant nostri stri Adversarii super toleratis in Ecclesia peccatoribus, vel de illa propter eosdem deferenda, aut de non communicando cum alienis peccatis, quod non putant evadi, quando cum ista Ecclesia communionem colimus, quae improbos tolerat, vel eos non statim a se ejicit, atque excommunicat. Respondemus, neutiquam quidem nos negare, quin non alii quam veri pii & fideles Ecclesiam debeant ingredi, atque constituere; quod etiam nullos alios Ecclesia pro suis agnoscere debeat, ac recipere, vel in suam admittere communionem; sed ea quemadmodum de occultis non judicat, sed in externa professione acquiescit, non quasi nil ultra a suis exigat, sed quod judicio suo de hominibus non ulterius penetret, ita quod piis se immisceant passim alii, neque ecclesiae pervicaciter exprobrandum, neque ideo necesse cum pravis aliorum operibus communicare, vel communionem ecclesiasticam stoccipendere aut abrumpere. Robinsonus id agnoscit, cap. ult. Apologia, quando dicit, non adeo inepti nos sumus, vel insani potius, ut in eadem Ecclesia sanctitatem (quoad alios) aliam, quam externam & visibilem desideremus. Aliud est quales intus, vel quales extus, quales coram Deo, aut coram hominibus deprehendamur: & quis status Ecclesiae, hominumque in ea esse debeat, i vel sit, aut esse, per communem conditionis imbecillitatem, hic possit. Occurrit in Ecclesiae area non triticum solum, sed palea, lignum & stipula, probi permixti improbis: ob quos, quamvis ii offendamur, non ideo exire Ecclesia, nisi & mundo quoque, possumus. Non tamen haec ita proponimus, quasi aut non necesse dicamus sanctos esse omnes in Ecclesia debere, aut malos studio vel lubenti animo ac licentiose tolerandos esse, vel quasi satis esset habere modo externam fidei professionem, & non internae etiam virtutes requirantur, vel non istae exigendae quoque & respiciendae Rectoribus Ecclesiarum in admittendis ad S. communionem hominibus sint, quasi ad verum & legitimum Ecclesiæ visibilis membrum constituendum sufficeret, ut quis ore Christum confiteatur, licet Satanam operibus referat, verba sunt Robinsoni; vel quasi vellemus, sanctitatem quandam plane sceniam Dei Ecclesiæ obtrudere: sed ne, quando de singulorum, in Ecclesiam admittendorum verâ fide & conversione per certa signa convicti non sumus, ideo ab Ecclesia faciendam separationem putemus: de quo hic proprie quæri, non de qualitate membrorum Ecclesiæ, bene censuit Rob. Baylie. Posito, Ecclesiam suo officio, & valde multos irrepere improbos hypocritas, committi scandala, tolerari etiam indignos, ac ideo statim secessionem facies, rumpeisque omnem cum Ecclesiâ communionem? non committendum arbitror, dum modo non docentur probanturque scandala, nec ipsa illa desidiosa tolerantia, vel disciplinæ neglectus laudatur, sed carpitur palam, catenus in doctrinâ & in observantiâ, Christi apud illam Ecclesiam commorantis habèri adhuc indicia existimo. Quantumcunque corrupta in pluribus quæ disciplinam, quæ mores, quæ doctrinam quoque ipsam concernebant, esset Ecclesia Corinthiaca, non tamen ab eâ secessionem commendabat Apostolus, quin improbavit etiam quod inter illos essent qui schismata facerent. Vti bene Augustinus inquit, epist. xlviii. ad Vincentium: Non enim propter malos boni deserendi, sed propter bonos mali tolerandi sunt, sicut toleraverunt Prophetæ, contra quos tanta dicebant, nec communionem sacramentorum illius populi relinquebant. Vide Parkerum, Polit. Eccles. lib. i. cap. xiii. xiv. & lib. iii. cap. xvi. qui tertius liber, nescio an bonâ fide, certe male integer omissus est in editione nuperâ a. clɔ Iɔ xxxviii. quæ modo duos ejus libros continet, quum tres sint: quare monitos hic omnes volo, ut sequantur editionem a. clɔ Iɔ c xvi. ubi tres libri, & tertius quidem major duobus prioribus extat. tractans de Ecclesiâ. Non ergo statim deserendam Ecclesiæ communio-
units.tr: To this pertains what our adversaries dispute with the same rashness concerning the tolerated sinners in the Church, or concerning the need to abandon the Church on their account, or concerning not communicating with the sins of others, which they think cannot be avoided when we keep communion with a Church that tolerates the wicked, or does not immediately cast them out from itself and excommunicate them. We reply that we by no means deny that only true and godly people ought to enter and constitute a church, and that the church ought to acknowledge and receive as its own, or admit into its communion, none but such; but just as it does not judge hidden things, and rests in an outward profession, not as if it demanded nothing further from its members, but because its judgment of men does not penetrate further, so it is not to be reproached by the pious for the fact that others mix in among them everywhere, nor is it therefore necessary to share in the wicked works of others, or to break off or abandon ecclesiastical communion. Robinson acknowledges this in the last chapter of his Apology, when he says: We are not so foolish, or rather insane, as to desire in the same church any holiness (as regards others) other than external and visible. It is one thing how people are found to be inwardly, or outwardly, before God or before men, and what state the Church and the men in it ought to be in, or can be in, because of the common weakness of the condition. In the threshing floor of the Church there appears not only wheat but chaff, wood and stubble, the good mixed with the wicked; because of these, although we are offended, we cannot therefore leave the Church, unless we also leave the world. Nor do we put this forward as if we did not say that all in the Church ought to be holy, or as if the wicked should be tolerated deliberately or carelessly and without restraint, or as if it were enough to have merely an outward profession of faith, and inward virtues were not required too, or as if these were not to be demanded and taken into account by the rulers of the churches in admitting people to the holy communion, as if it were sufficient for a man to be a true and lawful member of the visible Church that he confesses Christ with his mouth, though he denies Satan with his works (these are Robinson's words); or as if we wanted to impose some completely imaginary holiness on God's Church. But we do not think that a separation should be made from the Church because we are not convinced by certain signs of the true faith and conversion of individuals who are to be admitted to the Church; and Robert Baillie rightly judged that this is not the proper question here, which concerns not the quality of the members of the Church. Suppose the Church fails in its duty, and very many wicked hypocrites creep in, scandals are committed, and even the unworthy are tolerated; should one therefore at once secede and break off all communion with the Church? I do not think this should be done, provided that scandals are not taught or approved, nor that very slothful toleration or neglect of discipline is praised, but is openly found fault with; so far as doctrine and observance go, I think there are still signs in that Church that Christ dwells there. However corrupt the Church of Corinth was in many matters, concerning discipline, morals and even doctrine itself, the Apostle did not commend secession from it, but even disapproved that among them there were those who made schisms. As Augustine rightly says, letter 48 to Vincentius: For the good are not to be forsaken because of the wicked, but the wicked are to be tolerated because of the good, just as the prophets tolerated those against whom they said such great things, and did not abandon the communion of the sacraments of that people. See Parker, Politia Ecclesiastica, book i, ch. xiii and xiv, and book iii, ch. xvi; that third book, I know not whether in good faith, but certainly carelessly, was left out of the recent edition of 1638, which contains only two of its books, though there are three; therefore I wish all to be warned here to follow the edition of 1616, where there are three books, and the third, which deals with the Church, is larger than the two preceding it. Therefore we do not judge that communion with the Church should at once be abandoned because of some person in the Church who sins publicly and stubbornly and is not excommunicated, nor that the whole Church is so contaminated that no one can share in any sacred office with it, especially since there is no despairing wickedness on the part of the Church, as Robinson rightly warns. The Donatists…

units.la: manio munionem, vel propter aliquem in Ecclesiâ publice ac pertinaciter peccantem, quique non excommunicetur, ita contaminari totam Ecclesiam, ut nemo cum eâ in ullo sacro officio communicare queat, arbitramur: praesertim non accedente Ecclesiae malitiâ desperatâ, uti Robinsonus bene monet. Donatistarum olim vox erat, quod in communione sacramenti mali contaminarent bonos: quae nunc iisdem verbis docent Brovvnistae. Jam vero nec probant, talem Ecclesiae Anglicanae statum fuisse, uti subsumere debent, quo tempore secessionem ab eâ fecerunt, illamque continuarunt: nedum tales fuisse omnes Reformatos: ut, ad summum, si nimium ipsis infesta visa fuisset Anglicana, ad aliam puriorem, nec facto scismate, transire potuissent, nisi temerarium judicium constituissent sequi, prae aedificatione animarum suarum, aut Ecclesiae: quod plane est Donatisticum, & Anabaptisticum. Unde eundem ipsorum errorem refutatum videre licet in Enchiridio Controvers. Anabapt. Osiandri, cap. vi. qu. i. & iii. Et contra Brovvnistas quidem, apud Robertum Abbotum, lib. a Triall of our Church Forsakers pag. 99. 101. &c. Richardum Bernardum, Separatists Schisme, pag. 103. alioque in defensionem illius libri scripto, Plaine Evidences, contra Joh. Smit, & Ainsvvortum, pag. 164. 204. 231. Rutherfurtum, lib. Anglico, pro presbyterio Scotizano; cap. ix. & x. Bayllie, The errours of time, ch. 11. Qui & alium adversus Anabaptistas librum scripsit, apto titulo: Anabaptismus fons Independentismi, Brownismi, Antinomismi, & Familismi, Anglice. Apollonium, Consideratio Controv. cap. i. Spanhemium, epist. ad Buchananum, Quest. i. Denique adversus illos omnes, seu Donatistas, seu Anabaptistas, seu Brovvnistas & recte Augustana Confessio, art. viii. Cum autem in hac vita admixti sint Ecclesiae multi mali & hypocritae, qui tamen societatem habent externorum signorum cum Ecclesiâ, licet uti Sacramentis, quae per malos administrantur ministrantur juxta vocem Christi, Sedent Scribæ & Pharisæi in Cathedra Moisi, &c. Et Sacramenta & verbum Dei propter ordinationem & mandatum Christi sunt efficacia, etiamsi per malos exhibeantur. Damnant Donatistas & similes, qui negabant licere populo uti ministerio malorum in Ecclesia, & sentiebant ministerium malorum inutile & inefficax esse.
units.tr: ...of the communion, whether because of some person in the Church who sins publicly and obstinately and is not excommunicated, we judge that the whole Church is so contaminated that no one can communicate with it in any sacred office. This holds especially when there is no desperate malice in the Church itself, as Robinson rightly observes. It was once the cry of the Donatists that the good are contaminated by communion in the sacrament with the wicked, and the Brownists now teach the same thing in the same words. Moreover, they do not prove that the state of the Anglican Church was such as they must assume it to have been at the time when they seceded from it and continued apart from it, much less that all the Reformed churches were such. At most, if the Anglican Church had seemed too hostile to them, they could have passed over to another, purer church without making a schism, unless they had rashly decided to follow their own judgment, out of concern for the edification of their souls or of the Church. This is plainly Donatist and Anabaptist. Hence one may see their same error refuted in Osiander's Enchiridion of the Anabaptist Controversy, chap. vi, question i and iii. Against the Brownists, see also Robert Abbot, A Triall of our Church Forsakers, pp. 99, 101, etc.; Richard Bernard, Separatists Schisme, p. 103; and in defence of that book, the writing Plaine Evidences against John Smith and Ainsworth, pp. 164, 204, 231; Rutherford, in the English book pro presbyterio Scotizano, chaps. ix and x; Baillie, The Errours of Time, ch. 11. Baillie also wrote another book against the Anabaptists with the apt title Anabaptismus fons Independentismi, Brownismi, Antinomismi, & Familismi, Anglice. See Apollonius, Consideratio Controversiarum, chap. i; Spanheim, Epistle to Buchanan, Question i. Finally, against all of them, whether Donatists, Anabaptists or Brownists, the Augsburg Confession, art. viii, rightly says: "Although in this life many wicked people and hypocrites are mixed with the Church, who nevertheless share in the external signs with the Church, the sacraments administered by the wicked are to be used, according to the voice of Christ: 'The scribes and Pharisees sit in the chair of Moses,' etc. And the sacraments and the Word of God are effective, by reason of the ordinance and command of Christ, even when they are administered by the wicked." It condemns the Donatists and those like them, who denied that the people might use the ministry of the wicked in the Church and held that the ministry of the wicked was useless and ineffective.

units.la: Alteram causam schismatis ab Ecclesia Anglicana prætendunt Separatistæ, præter illam ex primâ ejus collectione, à statu Ecclesiæ deformato per Papalis Antichristianismi reliquias, ordinem Episcopalem, & hierarchicum; Liturgiam, & librum precum; Ceremonias &c. Hoc argumentum ubique late deducunt. In Præfat. ad Confess. a. cIↄ Iↄ xcvi. & Confess. art, xxixx. xxx. xxxi. xxxii. In Apologiâ Ainsworti; Robinsoni, cap. ult. Ainswort, contra Pagetum, & alibi sæpius. Sed jam ante huic responsum. Illa, utcunque probanda non sint, haud tamen necessarium facere & justum à totâ Anglicanâ; & si vel hoc, non ab aliis omnibus Reformatis Ecclesiis, quæ illis caruerunt, schisma: non ab hodiernâ Anglicanâ, quæ illis expurgata, à quâ tamen Schisma, in nostris saltem regionibus, continuant.
units.tr: The Separatists allege a second cause of their schism from the Anglican Church, besides the one from its first formation: the state of the Church deformed by the remnants of Papal Antichristianism, the episcopal and hierarchical order, the liturgy and book of prayers, the ceremonies, and so on. They develop this argument at length everywhere: in the preface to their Confession of 1596, in the Confession, articles xxix, xxx, xxxi, xxxii; in Ainsworth's Apology; in Robinson's Apology, last chapter; in Ainsworth against Paget, and often elsewhere. But this has already been answered. Those things, however they may be disapproved, do not make it necessary or just to separate from the whole Anglican Church. And even if they did, they would not justify a schism from all the other Reformed Churches, which lacked those things. Nor do they justify a schism from the present Anglican Church, which has been purged of them, and yet from which they continue to separate, at least in our regions.

units.la: Objiciunt loca plura, quibus malum omne jubemur cavere, & secernere nos à peccatoribus, exire è Babylone, &c. 1. Thess. v. 22. 1 Cor. vi. 9. 17. 18. Ierem. li. 6. Mich. ii. 10. Apoc. xviii. 4. 11. Cor. vi. 17. Act. xl. 40. Verum est, quod ab omni peccato abstinere debeamus, sed hoc non dicit, ab omni peccatore nos longum abire, vel ab Ecclesiâ aliquando peccante, aut peccatoribus in Ecclesia degentibus, debere, alioqui & mundo exeundum foret. 1 Cor. v. 10. Neque quicunque statim errores viriaque in Ecclesiam admissa, eam deserendam clamant. Sed primo quidem constare debet, vitia non solum ibi esse, sed & doceri, ac probari; errores que doctrinæ foveri capitales seu fundamendamentum fidei & religionis convellentes; tum universaliter, id est à totâ universim Ecclesiâ, non ab uno forte alioveCoetu; & accedere indeclinabilem persequutionem in optimos quosque, quibus haud liceat tutis tali loco esse, aut Deo in puritate conscientiæ servire. Quæ omnia in Ecclesiam Anglicanam, & Reformatas alias dicere Separatistæ nostri non sustinebunt. Unde quam male agant, diffamando Matrem suam Ecclesiam, apparet.
units.tr: They object to many passages by which we are commanded to beware of all evil, to separate ourselves from sinners, to go out of Babylon, and so on: 1 Thess. 5:22; 1 Cor. 6:9, 17, 18; Jer. 51:6; Mic. 2:10; Rev. 18:4; 2 Cor. 6:17; Acts 40:40. It is true that we ought to abstain from all sin, but this does not say that we must keep far away from every sinner, or must at some time leave a Church that sins, or the sinners who live in the Church; otherwise we would have to go out of the world. See 1 Cor. 5:10. Nor do those who immediately cry out to forsake the Church do so because of errors or vices admitted into it. But first it must be established that the vices are not only present there but also taught and approved; that the errors which foster the chief doctrines, or which overturn the foundation of faith and religion, are universal, that is, found in the whole Church and not perhaps in one or another gathering; and that there is an unavoidable persecution of all the best people, so that they cannot be safe in such a place or serve God in purity of conscience. Our Separatists will not be able to assert that these things hold of the Anglican Church and the other Reformed churches. Hence it is evident how wrongly they act in defaming their own mother, the Church.

units.la: Quinimo variis argumentis ostendi potest, & pro vera habendam Ecclesiam Anglicanam, à quâ secesserunt; & temerarium illo unfuisse schisma. Illud, quia quæ Ecclesia doctrinam fidei servat integram, estque, quomodo ecclesiam describit Apostolus, columna & firmamentum veritatis, 1 Tim. iii. 15. ædificata supra fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, Ephes. ii. 20. pro falsâ haberi nequit. Robinsonus, Apolog. cap. ult. Quanto magis Anglicana, in quâ, profligatis plurimis maximisque erroribus Pontificiis, veritas Evangelica (quoad summa capita) tanto studio, zeloque à plurimis piis & doctis viris annunciatur. Deinde, in quâ Ecclesiâ iste fructus doctrinæ cernitur, ut progignat quotidie veros fideles, sanctos, quin & Confessores, Martyres innumeros, quis falsam ausit dicere, & non honoret magis tum doctrinæ, & efficaciæ ejus, tum fideliun, Martyriumque ratione, prout decet? Quoniam ibi sint doctores ... Ephes. iv. 11. 12. ac de eâ Ecclesiâ dicere liceat: adscendamus ad montem Domini, ad domum Dei Jacobi, ut nos doceat de viis suis, atque ambulemus in ejus semitis. Esa. ii. 2. 3. Robinsonus: de personis eorum Dominus proprius judicabit, cui stant, aut cadunt. Fuere ex isto ordine qui temporibus nostris Marianis, veritatis Evangelicæ Confessionem vitæ suæ prætulerunt: Spero & ex illorum successoribus superesse, quisi eadem instaret tempestas (quod Deus avertat) & eidem veritati agnitæ idem testimonium ...
units.tr: Indeed, it can be shown by various arguments that the Anglican Church, from which they seceded, is to be regarded as a true church, and that their schism was rash. First, because a church that keeps the doctrine of faith whole, and is, as the Apostle describes the church, "the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Tim. 3:15), built "upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles" (Eph. 2:20), cannot be held to be false. Robinson, Apology, last chapter: "How much more the Anglican Church, in which, with most of the great Papal errors put to flight, the Evangelical truth (as to its chief heads) is proclaimed with such zeal and care by very many pious and learned men." Next, in what Church is this fruit of doctrine seen, that it daily begets true believers, saints, indeed confessors and countless martyrs? Who would dare to call such a church false, and not honour both the doctrine and its efficacy, and the faithful and their martyrdom, as is fitting? Since there are teachers there (Eph. 4:11, 12), one may say of that Church: "Let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways, and we may walk in his paths" (Isa. 2:2, 3). Robinson: "Their Lord will judge the persons of them, to whom they stand or fall. There were from that order, in the time of our Marian persecution, those who preferred the confession of Evangelical truth to their lives. I hope that some of their successors also survive, should the same storm threaten (which God forbid), and bear the same testimony to the truth acknowledged..."

units.la: stimotestimonium, eodem precio, perhiberent. Tertio, nemo in se descendens, & qui procul sit ab iniquo judicandi affectu, inficiari poterit, se in Ecclesiâ Anglicana certa deprehendere unionis hominum cum Christo & inter se, quod vere fidelium & piorum est, documenta. Robinsonus iterum: fidem salvificam, & veram pietatem multorum cordibus in Ecclesia Anglicana, per Evangelii praedicationem & ingenerari & foveri absit ut vel negemus, vel non eo nomine ingentes gratias Deo optimo maximo, & nostrorum ipsorum, & aliorum respectu debitas fateamur. Adde quod ab omnibus Reformatis Ecclesiis, quarum hic judicium audiendum est, ubi agitur de agnoscendâ, vel repudianda sorore Ecclesiâ, Anglicanâ semper pro vera agnita fuerit: & nunquam propter aliqua schismata personarum, vel regiminis, à communione reliquarum segregata. Bene Augustinus dixit, epist. xlviii. Neque propter paleam relinquimus aream Domini, neque propter pisces malos rumpimus retia Domini. Denique in Ecclesiâ Anglicanâ semper plurimi superfuerunt, qui ordini hierarchico & caeremoniis constanter sunt obloquuti, ut nihil necesse, propter illa, eam totam deserere, & communionem ejus condemnare, in quibus corrigendis intra ipsam Ecclesiam semper sedulo, majorique longe cum fructu, quam à Separatistis ἐκκλησίας, laboratum fuit. Quomodo jam suum probabunt schisma, namque revera fuit, quum nec illa quae secessioni suae praetendunt, sufficientem vel necessariam causam segregandi ab Ecclesia praebeant, neque quamvis in Ecclesia Anglicana scandala fuerint ea, omnibus aliis Reformatis, Scoticis, Gallicis, Belgicis objici potuere, cum quibus saltem retinere communionem, & non ab omnibus seorsim ire maximo cum scandalo, debuissent. Detur, aliquid fuisse quo minus in Ecclesia Anglicâ bene morari potuerint, vel illud de ordine episcopali, & rituum ac caeremoniarum Papalium tale tantumque fuisse, ut reprobanda Ecclesia, quae illa tenet, net, fuerit, quid aliæ Reformatæ Ecclesiæ meruerunt, quod non iis accesserint? vel an illa tanta, quæ contra nostrarum Ecclesiarum in Belgio statum ac regimen habuerunt, in primo suorum appulsu, ut neque nostræ potuerint veræ esse, nec fuerint adeundæ? De Brownistis prima agitata apud nos consilia in Synodo Alcmar. anno MDXCIX. inde Amstel. a. MDCI. ubi pro Schismaticis declarati, eò quod se frustra ab Anglicanâ non solum, sed & aliis Ecclesiis segregassent, prætendentes videlicet I. statum Amsteldamensis Ecclesiæ valde esse confusum. quia nunquam posset simul uno in loco convenire tota Ecclesia, β. neque satis bene sanctificaretur dies Dominicus. γ. nec unquam possent certi esse de præsentiâ membrorum. δ. denique nec possent publici actus sive excommunicationis, sive alii exerceri. I I. quia scilicet Nostri ad baptismum admitterent, quorum parentes non essent membra Ecclesiæ, neque dignam satis curam gererent baptizatorum. III. propter formulas precandi, quibus uterentur. IV. quia non observarent præceptum Christi, Matth. XVIII.15.16.17. V. quod divinum cultum exercerent in templis Antichristianis. VI. quia non eo modo sustentarentur Ecclesiarum ministri, ac Christus & Apostoli ordinarint I.Cor.IX. I[?]II. propter mutationem presbyteriorum apud Nos annuam, qui juxta ipsos debeant esse perpetui. VIII. quia matrimonium confirmarent Nostri in Ecclesiâ, ac si esset actus Ecclesiasticus. IX. quia novo censuræ uterentur modo, suspensione videlicet, quam Christus non instituerit. Matth. XVIII.19. X. quod dies aliquos festos servarent, ut nativitatis Christi, resurrectionis, adscensionis &c. Has decem rationes dabant, quare non ab Anglicanâ solum, sed & nostrâ Ecclesiâ divorterent, (quas ex Fr. Johnsoni Articulis, ag. the French & Dutch Church, reponit in Apol.1 suâ adversus Brownistas, Anglicè, Josephus Hallus) omnes profecto frivolas, quarum aliquæ non
units.tr: testimonium, eodem precio, perhiberent. Thirdly, no one who examines himself, and who is far from an unjust disposition of judgment, will be able to deny that in the Anglican Church he perceives clear evidence of the union of men with Christ and with one another, which is a mark of true believers and the pious. Robinson again: "Far be it from us either to deny that saving faith and true piety are engendered and fostered in the hearts of many in the Anglican Church through the preaching of the Gospel, or not to acknowledge on this account immense thanks to God, the best and greatest, due both on our own behalf and on behalf of others." Add that by all the Reformed churches, whose judgment must be heard when the question is whether to acknowledge or reject a sister church, the Anglican Church has always been recognised as true, and never cut off from the communion of the rest on account of any schisms of persons or of government. Augustine rightly said (Epistle 48): "We do not abandon the threshing floor of the Lord on account of the chaff, nor do we break the nets of the Lord on account of the bad fish." Finally, in the Anglican Church there have always been very many who constantly objected to the hierarchical order and the ceremonies, yet there was no need, on account of these, to desert the whole Church and condemn its communion; rather, these things were always diligently and with far greater fruit laboured over within the Church itself, than by the Separatists' churches [ἐκκλησίας]. How will they now prove their schism? For it truly was one, since the things they put forward as the cause of their secession provide no sufficient or necessary reason for separating from the Church; nor could the scandals that existed in the Anglican Church be objected to all the other Reformed churches, Scottish, French, and Belgic, with which at least they ought to have kept communion, and not gone apart from all of them, with the greatest scandal. Grant that there was something that prevented them from living well in the Anglican Church: was the matter of the episcopal order and of the Papal rites and ceremonies so great and so grave that the Church holding them must be rejected? What, then, did the other Reformed churches deserve, that they should be joined to it? Or were those things so great that they must be regarded as not true churches, and not to be approached, since they had a state and government contrary to that of our churches in the Netherlands, at the first moment of their coming? The first deliberations about the Brownists among us were held at the Synod of Alkmaar in 1599, and then at Amsterdam in 1601, where they were declared schismatics, because they had separated in vain not only from the Anglican but also from other churches, alleging, namely: (1) that the state of the Amsterdam church was very confused, because the whole church could never meet together in one place; (2) that the Lord's Day was not sanctified well enough; (3) that they could never be certain of the presence of the members; (4) and finally that public acts, whether excommunication or other acts, could not be carried out. (5) Because our people admitted to baptism those whose parents were not members of the Church, and did not take sufficient care of the baptised. (6) On account of the forms of prayer they used. (7) Because they did not observe the precept of Christ, Matt. 18:15, 16, 17. (8) Because they performed divine worship in Antichristian temples. (9) Because the ministers of the churches were not supported in the way that Christ and the Apostles ordained (1 Cor. 9). (10) On account of the yearly change of the elders among us, who, in their view, ought to be perpetual. (11) Because our people confirmed marriage in the Church as if it were an ecclesiastical act. (12) Because they used a new mode of censure, namely suspension, which Christ had not instituted (Matt. 18:19). (13) Because they kept certain festival days, such as the birth, resurrection and ascension of Christ, etc. These were the ten reasons (for in the original there are thirteen) they gave for divorcing themselves not only from the Anglican but also from our Church; they are answered from the Articles of Francis Johnson against the French and Dutch Church, and in the Apology of Joseph Hall against the Brownists, written in English. All of them are certainly frivolous; some were not truly alleged, some are not to be approved, or are of no value or weight, at least not sufficient to establish and foster a schism. A cause for leaving the Church must surely be great and pressing, as much by its own right as by extreme necessity; which...

units.la: 1 Apol. Anglicana. non satis vere allate, aliquae non probandae, vel nullius pretii ponderisque, saltem non ad instituendum & fovendum scisma. Magna certe & praegnans tam jure suo, quam extrema necessitate debet esse causa faciendae ab Ecclesia secessionis: quae non apud nostros homines occurrit. Deus nobis imperavit congregationem, sibi servavit separationem, inquit Augustinus. Vbi ergo Deus separationem nec mandat, nec probat: vae homini, qui quae Deus juncta voluit, divellit. Prodeant ipsorum Adversariorum de Ecclesiis nostris judicia ac testimonia, luculenta nonnunquam & honorifica, de Anglicana etiam, quando in ea fatentur veram vigere doctrinam & religionem; de Reformatis aliis, quas pro veris videntur habere, praesertim Belgica nostra, quam saepe non parum depraedicant: quod ergo post haec secessioni ipsorum ab illis omnibus proferri patrocinium poterit, vel argumentum? De Ecclesia quidem Anglicana sic ipse inter illos loquitur Henricus Barrovv, a quo nomen & sectam trahunt, in epistola ad Nobilem Comitissam, paulo ante suum supplicium scripta, quae Brovvnistarum Apologiae inseritur, contra Doctores Oxonienses: ad tertiam accusationem respondi, me libenter amplecti & imitandere communem fidem in hisce regionibus receptam & agnitam, ut omnino sanctam ac puram. Atque in alia ejus epistola, quae ibidem quoque adfertur: annon nos depraedicavimus fidem Martyrum Anglicorum, beatosque illos aestimavimus, utcunque falsa officia, & multam corruptionem in cultu divino exercerent? Iob. Robinsonus, in Apolog. cap. xii. Neque a nostrum quopiam in confessione fidei sua requiritur, ut vel unica vocula, Ecclesiae Anglicanae aut renunciet, aut refragetur. Deinde: Convenit nobis (quatenus Ecclesiis reformatis Belgicis, & aliis) cum Ecclesia Anglicana in Articulis fidei & religionis Christianae capitibus, hujus Ecclesiae nomine conscriptis, prout habentur in Harmonia Confessionum fidei. Si per Ecclesiam intelligas Catholicam Ecclesiam, per universum terrarum orbem sparsum & disseminatam, libenter agnoscimus, ejusdem partem eximiam, eamque visibilem & conspicuam, in Anglia reperiri: quarum etiam communionem in omnibus religionis actibus licitis in se, & rite ordinatis (nostro judicio) sancte profitemur, & colimus. Ibidem: Quod non ita tamen intelligi velim, ac si vel personas Episcoporum, vel authoritatem, qua potiuntur civilem in rebus vel civilibus, vel etiam Ecclesiasticis, omnino aversemur. De personis earum Dominus proprius judicabit, cui stant, aut cadunt. Fuere ex isto ordine qui temporibus nostris Marianis, veritatis Evangelicae Confessionem vitae sua praetulerunt: Spero & ex illorum successoribus super, esse, qui si eadem instaret tempestas (quod Deus avertat) & eidem veritati agnita idem testimonium, eodem precio, perhiberent. Vide, ut honorifice loquatur de ipsa Ecclesia Anglicana, quam alias cum Babylone conferunt, falsam dicunt Ecclesiam, falsumque eius, quem exercet, & superstitiosum cultum. De Reformatis Ecclesiis aliis & in genere, non minus etiam reverenter. Praefat. ad Confess. An. cIↄ Iↄ xcvi. pag. 18. exemplaris Belgici, vel Anglici pag. 7. approbant Ecclesiarum Reformatarum doctrinam, inque eandem sibi convenire cum Confessionibus Belgica, Scotica, Germanica, Gallica, Helvetica, aliarumque orthodoxarum Ecclesiarum, Syntagmate Confessionum contentis, palam attestantur. Joh. Robinsonus, Apol. praefat. pag. 7. De Ecclesiis reformatis quid aliud dicam? Eas pro veris, & genuinis Christi Ecclesiis habemus: cum eisdem in sacris Dei communionem profitemur, & quantum in nobis est, colimus: conciones publicas ab illarum pastoribus habitas ex nostris, qui norunt linguam Belgicam, frequentant. Sacram caenam earum membris, si qua forte nostro coetui intersint nobis cognita, participamus: malis illarum serio ingemiscimus; eisque a Deo sanctam, firmamque pacem ex animo precamur. Ainswortus, contra Pagetum, agnoscimus Reformatas Ecclesias (visis earum Confesfionibus) esse veras Ecclesias, & fratres nostros in Domino. apud Pagetum, Arrow against the Brownistes pag. 43.
units.tr: 1 Apol. Anglicana. The reasons they give are not stated truly enough, some are not to be approved, and some have no weight or value at all, at least not for founding and fostering a schism. The cause that justifies leaving the Church, both by its own right and by extreme necessity, must surely be great and weighty, and no such cause is found among our people. "God commanded us to gather together; He reserved separation to Himself," says Augustine. Where God neither commands nor approves separation, woe to the man who divides what God wished to be joined. Let the judgments and testimonies of our opponents about our churches be brought forward. They are sometimes clear and even honourable: about the English Church, when they admit that true doctrine and religion flourish in it, and about the other Reformed churches, which they regard as true, especially our Belgian church, which they often praise not a little. What defence or argument, then, can be offered for their secession from all of these? Henry Barrow himself, from whom they take their name and sect, speaks thus about the English Church in a letter to a noble countess, written shortly before his execution, which is included in the Brownists' Apology against the Oxford doctors: "To the third accusation I answered that I gladly embrace and imitate the common faith received and acknowledged in these regions, as wholly holy and pure." And in another letter of his, also cited there: "Did we not praise the faith of the English martyrs and count those men blessed, however false their offices were and however much corruption they practised in divine worship?" John Robinson, in his Apology, chapter 12: "None of ours is required in his confession of faith to renounce, or to contradict, even one little word of the Church of England." Then: "We agree (as far as the Reformed Churches of Belgium and others do) with the English Church in the articles of faith and the heads of Christian religion, drawn up in the name of this Church, as they are found in the Harmony of the Confessions of Faith." If by Church you understand the Catholic Church, scattered and spread through the whole world, we gladly acknowledge that an outstanding part of it, and one both visible and conspicuous, is to be found in England; and we solemnly profess and cultivate its communion in all religious acts that are lawful in themselves and rightly ordained (in our judgment). The same author: "I would not wish this to be understood as if we wholly turned away either from the persons of the bishops or from the authority which they hold, civil in civil matters or ecclesiastical too. The Lord alone, to whom they stand or fall, will judge their persons. Among that order there were, in our Marian times, men who preferred the confession of the Gospel truth to their lives. I hope that among their successors too there are some who, if the same storm should threaten (which God forbid), would bear the same witness to the same truth, at the same price." See how honourably he speaks of the English Church itself, which at other times they compare with Babylon, calling it a false Church and its false and superstitious worship. About the other Reformed Churches, and in general, he is no less respectful. In the preface to the Confession of 1596 (page 18 of the Belgian copy, or page 7 of the English) they approve the doctrine of the Reformed Churches, and they openly attest that it agrees with the Confessions of the Belgian, Scottish, German, French, Helvetic and other orthodox Churches contained in the Syntagma of Confessions. John Robinson, Apology, preface, page 7: "What else shall I say of the Reformed Churches? We hold them to be true and genuine Churches of Christ. We profess communion with them in the holy things of God, and, as far as lies in us, we cultivate it. We attend the public sermons given by their ministers, those of us who know the Belgian tongue. We take part in the Lord's Supper with their members, if any of them happen to be present at our assembly and are known to us. We grieve sincerely over their misfortunes, and we pray to God from our hearts for a holy and firm peace for them." Ainsworth, against Paget: "We acknowledge the Reformed Churches (having seen their Confessions) to be true Churches and our brothers in the Lord," quoted by Paget, Arrow against the Brownists, page 43.

units.la: Iam vero de Belgicis nostris, & qui inter illos optimus, Ioh. Robinsonus, Apol. praef. Profitemur coram Deo & hominibus, adeo nobis convenire cum Ecclesiis reformatis Belgicis in re religionis, ut omnibus, & singulis earundem Ecclesiarum fidei Articulis, prout habentur in Harmonia Confessionum fidei, paratissimus subscribere: Et, Ut redeam quo volum. Quum (ut ex praefatione patet) Ecclesiarum Belgicarum propositum sit, in Confessione sua confirmanda, rationem reddere spei, quae in illis est, & apertè sententiam suam aperire in re fidei; ut & in Harmonia confessionum edenda, conjunctionis illius, quae illis arctissima est cum sanctis Dei, & verè Catholica Ecclesia, cumque singulis ejus sanctis, & sanis membris, omnes homines conjungere, quo jure, quàve injuriâ, nos (quibus multo magis in re fidei, & religionis convenit cum Ecclesiis Belgicis reformatis, quàm plurimis ex eis Ecclesiis, quarum confessiones tanquam Christianae conjunctionis symbola, omnibus inspiciendae proponuntur) ab hoc charitatis vinculo, aut conjunctionis consortio excludi possumus? Hinc nos perpetuò Fratres appellat. De dissensionibus inter nos atque illos idem Robinsonus, Apol. praef. satis tenuiter loquitur, & suos solum paulo aliter sentientes, atque ab orbitâ nostra paulum deflectentes dicit; & de nobis ibidem, licet idem quod nos ferè sentiant in omnibus, atque, an fratres de quibus immerito sinistram opinionem concipiunt. De scismate, & separatione suâ, quam imprudenter fecerunt, Robinsonus secessionem quandam illos fecisse ait, cap. xir. atque in fine, quod non sit illis animus ad scismata propensus. Quid ergo est, quod ab illis Ecclesiis, quas adeo probant, & commendant, secessionem fecerunt temerariam & scandalosam? pro quâ quando coguntur loqui, videas homines in maximas redigi angustias, illudentesque ad ejus apologiam provocari, pro quâ nihil rationum, plura verò in contratratium suppetunt. Super quo Separationis articulo legé, praeter alios, qui contra Brownistas, hoc ex professo tractant, Rich. Bernard The Separatists Schisme: ejusque defensionem alio libro, Plaine Evidences, contra Ainsvvortum, & Ioh. Smith. Roberti Abboti Triall of our Church forsakers. Iohn Ball, adversus duos tractatus Ioh. Canni, unum quem inscripsit, de necessitate separationis ab Ecclesiâ Anglicanâ, alterum, quem opposuit Robinsono, & probare annisus fuit, non licere audire Anglicanae Ecclesiae Ministros. Ioh. Halli Apol. contra Brovvnistas, Anglicè.
units.tr: But as for our Belgians, and the best of them, John Robinson, Apology, preface: "We profess before God and men that we agree so closely with the Belgian Reformed Churches in the matter of religion that we are most ready to subscribe to all and each of the articles of faith of those same Churches, as they are found in the Harmony of the Confessions of Faith." And, to return to where I was heading: since (as the preface makes clear) it is the purpose of the Belgian Churches, in confirming their Confession, to give a reason for the hope that is in them, and openly to declare their opinion in matters of faith, and also, in publishing the Harmony of the Confessions, to join all men to that union which they have most closely with the saints of God and the truly Catholic Church, and with each of its holy and sound members, by what right or what wrong could we (who agree with the Belgian Reformed Churches in matters of faith and religion much more than with very many of those Churches whose confessions are set before everyone to be examined as symbols of Christian union) be excluded from this bond of charity or fellowship? Hence they call us brothers forever. Concerning the disagreements between us and them, the same Robinson, in the preface to his Apology, speaks rather meagrely, and says that his own people think only "a little differently and deviate a little from our course"; and about us he says, in the same place, that although they think almost the same as we do in everything, we are brothers about whom they wrongly form an unfavourable opinion. Concerning the schism and their separation, which they made rashly, Robinson says that they made "a certain secession," chapter 12, and at the end, that they have no inclination towards schisms. What then is the reason why they made a rash and scandalous secession from those Churches which they so approve and commend? When they are compelled to speak about it, you may see these men driven into the greatest difficulties, and, mocking, they are called to defend it. For this there are no reasons at all, but many arguments on the other side. On this article of separation read, besides others who treat it professedly against the Brownists, Richard Bernard, The Separatist's Schism, and his defence of it in another book, Plaine Evidences, against Ainsworth and John Smith; Robert Abbot, Triall of our Church forsakers; John Ball, against two treatises of John Canne, one entitled On the necessity of separation from the English Church, and the other which he opposed to Robinson, and he laboured to prove that it is not lawful to hear the ministers of the English Church. John Hall's Apology against the Brownists, in English.

units.la: Id quod hactenus de scismate Brovvnistarum ab Ecclesiâ tum Anglicanâ, tum nostrâ diximus, manifestum fit ex singulis, quas movent, controversiis, inspectâ probè illarum natura. Quippe omnes concernunt Ecclesiae regimen, disciplinam, & constitutionem externam. Primò quaerunt, de potestate Ecclesiasticâ regiminis, ubi resideat? Dicimus nos, penes Rectores, seu presbyteros Ecclesiae, quâ docentes, quâ regentes: illi, penes totam Ecclesiam, etiam plebem. Ecclesia consideratur, vel ut unum corpus in se, absque discrimine eorum qui in illo corpore; vel cum hoc discrimine, quod est inter Rectores, & plebem. Etiam potestas Ecclesiae in se consideratur praecisè; vel distinctè potestas regiminis. Illius subjectum ponendum est corpus Ecclesiae, in genere; huius, quia jam fit distinctio, non plebs, sed Rectores soli. Observatâ divisione Ecclesiae in presbyteros, & plebem, potestas Ecclesiastici regiminis non penes utrosque, non penes plebem est, nec a plebe derivatur in Presbyteros, quamvis cum plebis consensu electio presbyterorum a presbyteris fiat in Ecclesiâ constitutâ, sed electio a quocunque procedat, non confert electo proprie loquendo potestatem ecclesiastici regiminis, nisi per designationem tantum personae aptae, cui immediate Christus potestatem illam confert, nemo alius. Quemadmodum in electione confert, nemo alius. Regis, Senatus populusque designant, eligunt personam ἀξίου, in quam non ab illis revolvitur potestas regia, utique quam ipsi non habent, sed à solo Deo; unde & Dei gratiâ regnare dicuntur. Vel, uti in generatione hominis, parentes corpus suppeditant, & subjectum ostendunt quasi cui Deus vi communis suæ providentiæ animam indat, quæ non ab utroque patente vel ex fœtu corporeo exsuscitatur, sed solum Deum auctorem habet: itaque hic, Ecclesia designat personam regimini suo aptam sibi visam: non autem à plebe, ab infra adscendendo, aut à presbyteris eligentibus devolvitur potestas regiminis in electum, vel ordinatum, sed à Deo, à Christo sola dependet, oritur, conseretur. Circa hanc quidem rem versatur potestas totius Ecclesiæ: nempe est potestas aliqua, quæ non proprie est regiminis, tota autem ecclesia subjectum est totius suæ potestatis: sed potestatem illam distribuendo, secernenda etiam in Ecclesiæ ejus diversa subjecta sunt, ut potestatem regiminis habeant presbyteri, potestatem consentiendi, approbandi, vel improbandi in multis, plebs. Nam & plebis in præcipuis Ecclesiasticæ potestatis actibus seu officiis suæ non contemnendæ partes sunt, in electione pastorum, seniorum, Diaconorum, excommunicatione &c. unde illud in veteri Ecclesia vulgare, cum consensu plebis. Quâ de re videnda elegans dissertatio Davidis Blondelli, de jure plebis in Regimine Ecclesiastico. Ius igitur seu potestas & exercitium regendi Ecclesiam, non penes plebem est, uti Brovniståe existimant; sed penes Rectores Ecclesiæ solos. Potestas Ecclesiæ præcise considerata, non cum additione hujus aut illius rei, vel regiminis, vel assensu apud totam est Ecclesiam. Quemadmodum potestas animæ est in tota anima, sed potestas videntis animæ vel visionis (per visionem corpus regitur) in solis oculis, uti ratiocinationis in capite. Ita potestas Ecclesiæ est in Ecclesiâ; sed regentis, in iis qui Ecclesiæ oculi oculi dicuntur & vigiles, id est. Rectoribus. Iste Brovvnistarum hoc in loco error est, quod plebi etiam as‑signant jus, potestatem, exercitium, & partes regiminis Ecclesiastici. Idemque aliquando in Ecclesiis Gallicis sub a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxı. molitus fuit Joh. Morelljus Minister Parisiensis, à Bezâ, & Sadeele solidè refutatus. Vide Bezam epist. lxviıı. & Comment. Relig. in Gall. part. iv. pag. 19. Atque de quæstione illâ Brovvnistarum, Baylium, The Errours of time, ch. ix. Ioh. Collings, Vindicie Ministerii Evangelii, Anglicè. Iohn. Ferriby, The Lawfull Preacher. Voetium, Disp. iii. & iv. de potestate & polit. Eccles. Apollonium, Considerat. Controv. Anglic. cap. iii. & iv. Spanhemium, epist. Class. ii. qu. ii.
units.tr: What we have said so far about the schism of the Brownists, both from the English Church and from ours, becomes clear from each of the controversies they raise, if their nature is properly examined. For all of them concern the government, the discipline and the external constitution of the Church. First they ask: "Where does ecclesiastical power of government reside?" We say: with the rectors, or elders, of the Church, both as teachers and as governors; they say: with the whole Church, even the common people. The Church is considered either as one body in itself, without distinction among those who are in that body, or with this distinction which exists between the rectors and the people. Also, the power of the Church is considered in itself, precisely; or the power of government is considered distinctly. The subject of the former must be the body of the Church in general; of the latter, since a distinction has now been made, not the people but the rectors alone. With the division of the Church into elders and people observed, the power of ecclesiastical government is neither with both, nor with the people, nor is it derived from the people to the elders. Although the election of elders by the elders, with the consent of the people, takes place in an established Church, nevertheless whoever makes the election does not, properly speaking, confer the power of ecclesiastical government on the one elected, except by designating a suitable person, to whom Christ himself immediately confers that power, and no one else does. Just as in the election of a king, the senate and the people designate and choose a worthy person [ἄξιον], to whom the royal power is not transferred from them (since they do not have it), but from God alone; for which reason kings are said to reign by the grace of God. Or, as in the generation of man, the parents supply the body and show the subject, as it were, into which God by the power of his common providence infuses a soul, which is not produced by either parent or from the bodily offspring, but has God alone as its author: so here the Church designates a person it sees as suitable for its government; but the power of government does not descend to the chosen or ordained person from the people, from below ascending, or from the electing elders; it depends on, arises from and is joined to God and Christ alone. The power of the whole Church is concerned with this matter, namely that it is a certain power which is not strictly that of government, but the whole Church is the subject of its whole power. Yet, by distributing that power, its different subjects are also to be distinguished within the Church: the elders have the power of government, and the people have the power of consenting, approving or disapproving in many matters. For the people also have no small share in the chief acts or duties of ecclesiastical power, in the election of pastors, elders and deacons, in excommunication and so on; whence that common saying in the ancient Church, "with the consent of the people." On this matter see the elegant dissertation of David Blondel, On the right of the people in ecclesiastical government. Therefore the right, or power, and the exercise of governing the Church do not reside with the people, as the Brownists think, but with the rectors of the Church alone. The power of the Church, considered precisely, without the addition of this or that thing, whether of government or of assent, is in the whole Church. As the power of the soul is in the whole soul, but the power of seeing belongs to the eyes alone (the body is directed by vision), and the power of reasoning to the head; so the power of the Church is in the Church, but the power of ruling is in those who are called the eyes and watchmen of the Church, that is, the rectors. This error of the Brownists in this place is that they also assign to the people a right, power, exercise and share in ecclesiastical government. The same thing was once attempted in the French Churches, in the year 1571, by John Morel, minister at Paris, and it was solidly refuted by Beza and Sadeel. See Beza, letter 68, and Commentary on the Religion in France, part 4, page 19. And on that Brownist question, see Bayle, The Errours of time, chapter 9; John Collings, Vindiciae Ministerii Evangelii, in English; John Ferriby, The Lawfull Preacher; Voetius, Disputations 3 and 4, On ecclesiastical power and polity; Apollonius, Considerations on the English controversy, chapters 3 and 4; Spanheim, Classical letter 2, question 2.

units.la: Sequitur disputatio de Presbyterio Ecclesiastico. Vbi hoc quidem nobiscum agnoscunt, presbyteria juris divini esse. Robinson, Apol. pag. 21. Sed tum in presbyteris nostris, tum presbyterium carpunt. 1. quod illi non sunt omnes διδάσκαλοι. Quippe censent, omnes in ordinem Rectorum Ecclesiæ cooptatos illis donis instructos esse oportere, ut possint non domatim solum, & in privato aliquo conclavi, vel consistorio, sed publice etiam in Ecclesiâ docere, pro publici sui muneris ratione. Vtcunque etiam observent discrimen inter presbyteros docentes, & regentes. Illud tamen ut valeant etiam Rectores, quacunque in necessitate, vel usu, absente pastore vel mortuo, aliove casu, decere arbitrantur. ii. Volunt, omnes Presbyteros debere esse perpetuos, non annuos, vel temporarios. Iam vero ut tales sint, vel perpetui, quemadmodum etiam in nostris Ecclesiis alicubi: & ut quam optimis donis instructi seniores, adeo ut quoque docere possint, nemo invidebit; sed ut soli tales, neque alii esse debeant, & in Ecclesiâ doceant quoque publice, uti necdum probatum, ita discrimen, quod tamen agnoscere videntur nobiscum, inter Presbyteros docentes ac regentes ali-quam quantum obscuat. Bucanus, Instit. Theol. loc. xl ii. Quod vero, loquitur de Senioribus Ecclesiae, illis spatium non perpetuum, sed vel annuum, vel longius praescribatur, idcirco fit, 1. Quod plerique munus istud ultro, ut nunc sunt tempora, recusant. 2. Quod expediat interdum eos mutari. 3. Quod Ecclesiae intersit, ad Ecclesiasticam tyrannidem vitandam: ut aliqui etiam ex plebe norint, quid in Consistoriis & Ecclesiastica jurisdictione geratur, & quae recte leges de iis rebus positae observentur. De quibus Ambrosius in 1. ad Timoth. 5. 1. Et Synagoga, & postea Ecclesia seniores ex populo habuit, sine quorum consilio nihil agebatur in Ecclesia. Quod qua diligentia obsoleverit, nescio, nisi forte Doctorum desidia, aut magis superbia, dum soli volunt aliquid videri. Auctor Altaris Damasceni, cap. xi i. pag. 927. Sed haec infelicitas horum temporum, quod non ubique sunt perpetui, licet in plerisque apud nos Ecclesiis sint, & ubi perpetui sunt, bona & opes Ecclesiae non in publicum aerarium Ecclesiae colligantur, sed ab Aulicis, magistratibus, aliisque ordinis inferioris diripiantur. Posse Seniores, praesertim temporarios, de jure suo remittere in tanta aerarii publici angustia, & honorarium suum condonare quis dubitat? Atque antea de Seniorum, seu perpetuorum, seu temporariorum stipendio dixerat, in explicatione loci Apostolici, 1. Tim. v. 17. Etsi igitur non accipiunt in Reformatis Ecclesiis stipendia seniores, non sequitur tamen non esse illos seniores in Ecclesia Apostolica institutos. Si quaeritis an debeatur eis subsidium sustentationis: Respondeo, honorarium debetur, & praemium quoddam propter opus ipsorum, nam operarius est dignus mercede sua, plenum etiam & integrum sustentationis subsidium, si vel quis dono gubernationis praeditus pre aliis ad istud munus provectus fuerit, quia necessariam ejus administrationem Ecclesia judicat, & non habeat, unde se & familiam sustentare posset, vel si quis ad inopiam postea redactus fuerit. De perpetuis potissimum loquor, non de temporariis, quibus honorarium durante administratione debetur, non tamen subsidium integrum sustentationis, si ad egestatem redacti fuerint, debetur ex justitia, hoc est propter opus ipsorum, sed cum non futuri in opere, ex charitate. Perpetuis debetur honorarium ex justitia & propter opus ipsorum, in casu necessitatis, id est inopia vel egestatis etiam integrum & plenum sustentationis subsidium debetur ex justitia propter opus ipsorum.
units.tr: Next comes the disputation on the ecclesiastical presbytery. Here they grant us that presbyteries are of divine right. (Robinson, Apology, p. 21.) But they find fault both with our elders and with the presbytery. (1) Not all of them are teachers [διδάσκαλοι]. They hold that all those co-opted into the order of the Church's rulers ought to be endowed with the gifts needed to teach not only at home and in some private room or consistory, but also publicly in the church, according to the nature of their public office. Although they observe a distinction between teaching and ruling elders, they nevertheless think that ruling elders may act in any case of necessity or practice, when the minister is absent or dead, or in some other such case. (2) They want all elders to be perpetual, not annual or temporary. Now, that some elders should be perpetual, as in some of our churches, and that elders endowed with the best gifts, so that they may also teach, should be recognised by no one as an objection; but that only such men should be elders, and that no others should be, and that they alone should also teach publicly in the church, has not been proved. Thus the distinction, which they seem to accept with us, between teaching and ruling elders is considerably blurred. (Bucanus, Institutes of Theology, loc. 42.) As for the fact that the term of office for the elders of the Church is not perpetual but is fixed as annual or for a longer period, this happens (1) because most men, as the times now are, refuse the office willingly; (2) because it is sometimes useful for them to be changed; and (3) because it is in the Church's interest, to avoid ecclesiastical tyranny, that some even of the laity should know what is done in the consistories and in ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and that the laws rightly laid down about such matters are observed. Ambrose speaks of these things on 1 Timothy 5:1: "Both the synagogue and afterwards the Church had elders from the people, without whose counsel nothing was done in the Church." How this diligence has fallen into disuse I do not know, unless perhaps through the idleness of the teachers, or rather their pride, since they alone want to seem to be doing something. (Author of the Altar of Damascus, ch. 42, p. 927.) But this unhappiness of our times, that elders are not everywhere perpetual, although in most of our churches they are, and where they are perpetual the goods and resources of the Church are not gathered into the public treasury of the Church but are plundered by courtiers, magistrates and others of lower rank, is a further matter. Who doubts that elders, especially temporary ones, can in such straitened public finances give up their right and remit their honorarium? And earlier I had spoken of the stipend of elders, whether perpetual or temporary, in explaining the apostolic passage, 1 Timothy 5:17. So although the elders in the Reformed churches do not receive stipends, it does not follow that they were not instituted as elders in the apostolic Church. If you ask whether they are owed a subsidy for support, I answer: an honorarium is owed, and a certain reward on account of their work, for "the labourer is worthy of his hire"; and a full and complete subsidy for support is owed if someone endowed with the gift of governing has been promoted above others to that office, because the Church judges his administration necessary, and he has no means by which he could support himself and his family, or if someone has afterwards been reduced to poverty. I speak chiefly of perpetual elders, not temporary ones, to whom an honorarium is owed during the period of their administration; however, a full subsidy for support, if they have been reduced to want, is not owed in justice, that is, on account of their work, but out of charity, since they will not be working in the office. To perpetual elders an honorarium is owed in justice and on account of their work; in a case of necessity, that is, of penury or want, a full and complete subsidy for support is also owed in justice on account of their work.

units.la: III. Presbyteria, id est, Senatum & negotia presbyterii non in conclavi aliquo vel secretario Ecclesiae haberi, sed in facie Ecclesiae, eaque tota inspectante, volunt Brownistae. Quod jam etiam discrimen presbyterorum ac plebis tollere videtur, & magnam non potest non inducere & fovere confusionem, atque varias absurditates. Hoc autem sequitur, ex priori illo fundamento, de potestate Ecclesiastica penes plebem residua.
units.tr: III. The Brownists want the presbytery, that is, the senate and the business of the presbytery, to be conducted not in some private room or secretary's office of the Church, but in the sight of the Church, with the whole congregation looking on. This also seems to remove the distinction between elders and the people, and cannot fail to bring in and foster great confusion and various absurdities.
