This follows, however, from that earlier foundation, that ecclesiastical power remains with the people.

units.la: Gravior, quique majores & diuturniores turbas Ecclesiae, Anglicanae praesertim, dedit, est quem vulgo appellamus, Independentismus, a Brownistis ortus, inde ab aliis, qui de caetero Brownistis non associati, arreptus defensuique magna vi ingeniorum, fuit, deinde contentionum seditionumque in Nova Anglia primum, & Belgio, ubi ejus auctores exulabant, hodie potissimum in ipsa Anglicana Ecclesia, & Republica. Primus ejus parens habetur Iohannes Robinsonus, de quo aliquoties diximus, qui & rem, & vocem posuit Apolog. cap. 5. cetus particularis (recte institutus & ordinatus) tota integra, & perfecta Ecclesia ex suis partibus constans immediate & independenter, quoad alias Ecclesias) sub solo Christo. & ante haec Apologia Brownistarum contra Doctores Oxonienses th. IX. Classes, earumque regimen posuit inter regulas regiminis Papistici: ne Ecclesia regatur ex regulis Papisticis, foris, Classibus. Bene observandum, non modo statuendi & explicandi Independentismi diversos esse Brownistas, & inter illos qui a Brownistis in aliis, in hoc quoque a Nobis, quos Presbyteriales vulgo vocant, dissentiunt: quamvis in quam plurimis quotidie magis magisque illis accedant: de quo vide Baylie cap. VI. The errours of time. Sed nos, reliquis particularibus missis, solum Independentismum exponemus, in quo conveniunt. Ubi primo loco sciendum, nolle eos, quos vulgo tales, distinctionis ergo vocant, Independentes dici, uti neque cum Brownistis censeri, quorum scopulos, separationis nempe ab Ecclesia, se diligentissime vitare semper voluisse, restantur initio in Apologia quam ediderunt, vel Apologetica narratione, uti titulus habet, Ministrorum quorundam, antea exulum, nunc vero membrorum Synodi Theologorum, Anglice: subscripta a Thoma Goodwin, Nye, Simpson, Burroughs, Bridge, praecipuis controversiae auctoribus, & patronis. Interim dum se Independentes nominari conquerantur, mirum ipso detestandum omni modo est, quod nos in Apologia audent appellare Calvinianos: quod nomen quanta ignominia nobis ab heterodoxis tribui soleat, illos latere non potest. Ne de nomine Presbyterialium dicam, eo minus distinctivum, quo ipsi quoque presbyteria habent & probant, tantummodo se impugnare ajunt combinatum classico-Presbyteriale regimen. Credo, quod appellari malint Congregationales, quemadmodum pro potestate particularium Congregationum totum est quod distinguunt, & Ecclesias suas vocant Congregationales, uti Ioh. Cottonus libri sui titulum fecit: The way of Congregationall Churches cleared. Pauci numero initio fuerunt qui ab hisce partibus stabant, sed sedulo semper allaborarunt, ut Primores & Proceres regni occuparent atque ad se allicerent, qua via, quod numero defuit, dignitate & momento Patronorum exaequatum, indeque vis & pondus sectae accessit. Robinsonus scripsit Apologiam suam, in qua fundamentum posuit Independentismi anno clIↄ Iↄcxix. verum Coetus ejus, cui Leidae praeerat, quamque ad suam illam regulam gubernabat, valde exiguus secum fere interiit. Ex eo tamen aliqui mare trajicientes in Americam, quo multi hinc inde Angli ducebant colonias, & novam formabant Angliam, in Neo-Plemmuda Coetum Independentem (uti dicitur) erexerunt, circa annum cIↄ Iↄ c xxx. Cui a. cIↄ Iↄ c xxxv. accedens ex Angliâ, cum innumeris aliis pulsus persequutione Episcoporum, Cottonus, horrore ordinis Episcopalis, qui sibi omnia, reliquæ Ecclesiæ nihil concedebant, ex adverso in aliud extremum prolapsi, omnia Ecclesiæ, & plebi, absque vinculo, in quo aliam timebant iterum tyrannidem, aliarum Ecclesiarum, concedebant. Cottonus iste primum in Angliâ alterius longe sententiæ fuerat, unde & plurimorum errorum hæresiumque reus, maximus ordinis vel ἀπξίας istius quaqua versum promotor extitit; atque ad se ex Angliâ attraxit Thomam Goodwin, aliosque, quos suis opinionibus diligenter imbuit; habuitque secum, quemadmodum Montanus olim Maximillam, Hutchinsonam, de quâ varia & prodigiosa referunt. In Belgio nostro Ecclesia Anglica, Roterodamensis hactenus fuerat sub ordine presbyteriali, cum nostrâ Belgicâ, usque ad adventum Hugonis Petri, qui Cottoni, ut creditur, litteris ex novâ Angliâ instructus, illam formavit ad typum Independentismi, sed quam ipse non diu post deseruit, atque confluxit quoque in Novam Angliam. Sequuti eum in Roterodamensi Coetu Bridges, Simson, & VVard, ex Angliâ: qui primum renuntiantes ordinationi Anglicanæ, ex quâ hactenus ministerio functi fuerant, & in privatorum censum redacti, postea à Coetu in Ministros electi fuerunt, atque ordinati. Bridgo ordinante VVardum, tum VVardo illum. Verùm oborta mox gravis dissensio inter Simsonem, & Bridgum, propter exercitium prophetandi, ad morem Brownistarum, quod hic improbabat & impediebat, alter vero urgebat: unde scissa in duas partes Ecclesia, atque coetum proprium erexit Simson, adversus Bridges. Deinde VVardum Bridgi Collegam fastidire Coetus incipiens, non quievit, usque dum sua privata, nam reclamabat Collega, authoritate ministerio exuisset. Quae res scandalum causata, vicinos ejusdem familiae Arnhemienses movit, ut se interponerent, atque Rotterodamum mittentes ministros duos Goodwinum, ac Nye, cum duobus Senioribus, adscito ad se Bridgo, cum suorum nonnullis, constituerunt illam Synodi formam, quam prolixe in Apologia narrant, commendantque supra alias Synodos omnes, videlicet, quum satis temere deposituisset Ministrum suum Coetus Roterodamensis, vel ejus major factio; tum vi legis inter Christianos communis de cavendo scandalo, tum istius de non communicando cum aliorum peccatis (neutiquam authoritate ulla, vel potestate) tenebatur (inquiunt in Apologetica Narratione) Coetus vel ecclesia se submittere plenario atque aperto examini proximarum Ecclesiarum, isto suo facto graviter offensarum: quin in casu impoenitentiae vel pertinaciae potuissent offensae Ecclesiae adversus eam pronunciare sententiam excommunicationis cum ea, aliisque Ecclesiis idem significare, ut cum illa non communicarent usque ad testaram debitam resipiscentiam, non dicunt, excommunicationem: quod bene notandum, quia haec notat potestatem, quam negant ullam supra particularem Ecclesiam vel congregationem dari aut constitui posse: atque in eo casu controversiae ab illis collocatur: sed non communiodem pronunciare, parium est, eorumque quorum interest communionem servare, aut minus. Quare ita hoc in negotio perrexerunt, & sic agendum censent in simili casu, ubi res aliqua Synodum exposcit, quam admittunt quidem, sed non certam aut statam, quia iterum potestatis hoc, aut obligationis vel servitutis, aut inferioritatis erga superiores videtur: sed occasionatam, & pro causae ratione arbitrariam. Arnhemiensis Coetus scripsit ad Roterodamensem, significans datum scandalum, ex temerario Ministri oppressione & depositione, quare ab iis petit paterentur in nomine Christi, & pro vindicando ejus honore, atque in solatium oppressi Ministri, causæ examen coram reliquis suæ nationis Ecclesiis, vel quibuscunque aliis hoc ipsorum facto offensis, instituì, utque se subjicerent (ita loquuntur, to subject them selves) integræ totius negotii actorumque omnium revisioni atque examini. Quod ubi concessissent promto lubentique animo, & advenissent Arnhemo ii, quos supra diximus, institutusque conventus fuisset, præmissa adhortatione, quæ eo spectabat ut docerent, singularem aliquam & particularem Ecclesiam, quæ sibi datam existimat à Christo judicandi eos qui ejusdem secum corporis ac societatis potestatem, non debere sibi arrogare exemtionem à reddendâ ratione, vel à censura aliorum (an exemtion from giving account, or being censurable by any other) sive Magistratus supra, sive proximarum Ecclesiarum juxta se. Tam longe (dicunt) à mente nostra aberat independens illa libertas, quæ nobis vulgo impingitur, etiam tum quando minima nobis à regno Anglicano dependentia, vel revertendi eò spes videbatur reliqua. Hic autem successus atque exitus Synodi illius fuit, ut, habita aliquot dierum causæ cognitione, auditisque & examinatis variis testibus, quomodo in Curiâ aliquâ ubi vel maxime authoritate res agitur, desiderari posset, Cœtus qui offenderat, palam errorem suum agnoverit, & Ministrum confessum etiam in quo forte ipse peccarat, restituerit in pristinum suum locum, indicatoque solemni jejunio, se coram Deo ac hominibus propter peccatum illud suum humiliarit. Verum quod ad divisos Cœtus Simsonis, & Bridgi, intercessit tandem authoritas publica Magistratus, eosque unire iterum coëgit. Maximas autem per horum hominum opiniones & factiones, turbas sensit, atque etiamnum experitur Anglia, postquam hinc inde eò certatim confluxerunt: ubi scissâ & dilacerata miserè Ecclesiâ & Republicâ, interim omnis generis hæreses, errores, sectæ multiplicantur, & dominantur vaga licentia, cum magno veritatis, pietatis, & ordinis præjudicio, ac ruina. Hoc Anglorum peccatum fuit, quod eliminato Episcopatu, non statim paratum habuerunt ordinem, ad quem Ecclesiæ regerentur, sed fluctuantes, sub tantâ tamque diuturnâ & magnâ flagrantibus dissensionibus siverunt illas jactari huc usque miserum in modum & proculcari. Quod eo magis deplorandum, quo non adeo gravis super Independentismo dissensio primùm visa, quin aut semi & tolerari, aut componi, vel in eandem sententiam regiminis Ecclesiastici perduci posse dissentientes, crederetur. Quid enim hoc est, propter aliquem in regimine Ecclesiastico, eumque non summum articulum, regimen non tantum, sed Ecclesiam ipsam indignè lucre? Non de Episcopatu agitur admittendo, non de Senioribus repellendis, agnoscitur regimen Ecclesiæ habendum, & per presbyteros tum docentes, tum regentes: plerumque exilii nostri tempore habuimus tres Seniores in quâlibet congregatione, quibus etiam eramus subjecti, scribunt in Apologiâ, p. 14. Quid jam illud est obsecro, de quo tantopere contendunt? Non id spectat adeo Ecclesiam instituendam, acquidem conjungendam cum aliis: vel nec hoc proprie, nam Synodos Ecclesiarum admittunt ipsi etiam, celebrantque, sed dependentiam, vel potius combinationem Ecclesiarum in Synodos, & horum authoritatem in illas. Hi duo axes sunt, super quibus volvitur omnis disputatio. Existimant, Ecclesiam vel congregationem particularem totam sui juris esse, & habere in se omnem potestatem Ecclesiasticam, supremam, non alteri Ecclesiæ, aut Ecclesiis, aut Ecclesiarum Deputatis vel Synodis subjectam, æque minus ac Episcopis: ideoque & conveniente Synodo, huic nullam proprie & directe in aliam Ecclesiam potestatem competere, quidem ut consilio, & auxilio ecclesiam juvare possit, vel adversus peccantes etiam procedere censurâ, at non ex potestatis alicujus, seu superioris vi, sed collaterali & pari judicio, & pronunciandæ non excommunicationis, quod sit modo in inferiores (ab Ecclesiâ in membra, in quæ potestatem habet), sed non-communionis, uti in partes. Hinc nolunt istas Synodos, solummodò occasionaras. Quidnam vero hic tanti iterum quæro, quod magnarum contentionum & tumultuum causa esse debeat? quodque non vel tolerari, vel componi, si non corrigi facile possit?
units.tr: The more serious error, and the one that has caused the greater and more lasting disturbances, especially in the English Church, is what we commonly call Independentism. It arose from the Brownists, was taken up and defended with great energy by others who were not associated with the Brownists in other respects, and then produced strife and sedition first in New England and in the Netherlands, where its authors went into exile, and today above all in the English Church and commonwealth itself. Its first parent is held to be John Robinson, of whom we have spoken several times, who put forward both the thing and the word in his Apology, chapter 5: a particular congregation (rightly instituted and ordained), a whole, entire and perfect Church made up of its own members, immediately and independently (as far as other Churches are concerned) under Christ alone. Earlier, the Brownists' Apology against the Oxford Doctors, thesis 9, listed classes and their government among the rules of Papist government: the Church is not to be governed by Papist rules, namely by classes. It must be carefully noted that the Brownists are not the only people who differ in defining and explaining Independentism, and that among those who differ from the Brownists on other points there are also some, whom we commonly call Presbyterians, who agree with them on this: although more and more of them come over to these views every day. On this see Baillie, chapter 6, The errours of time. But, setting aside the other sects, we shall explain only the Independentism in which they agree. Here, first, it must be understood that those whom people commonly call by this name, to distinguish them, do not wish to be called Independents, nor to be counted among the Brownists, whose rocks, namely separation from the Church, they have always most carefully tried to avoid. This they state at the beginning of the Apology they published, or Apologetical Narrative, as its title has it: of certain ministers, formerly exiles, but now members of the Synod of Theologians, in English, signed by Thomas Goodwin, Nye, Simpson, Burroughs, Bridge, the chief authors and champions of the controversy. Meanwhile, although they complain of being called Independents, it is strange and in every way detestable that they dare to call us Calvinists in their Apology. They cannot be unaware of how great a disgrace this name is usually thought to bring us from the heterodox. Not to mention the name Presbyterians, which is the less distinctive since they too have and approve presbyteries, and which they say they only oppose as the combined classical-presbyterial government. I believe they would rather be called Congregationalists, since the whole of what they distinguish is the power of particular congregations, and they call their Churches Congregational, as John Cotton named his book The way of Congregational Churches cleared. At first there were few in number who stood on this side, but they always worked hard to win over and attract the leading men and nobles of the kingdom. By this route what they lacked in numbers was made up by the rank and weight of their patrons, and so the strength and influence of the sect increased. Robinson wrote his Apology, in which he laid the foundation of Independentism, in the year 1619; but his congregation, which he led at Leiden and governed by his rule, was very small and almost died out with him. Yet from it some crossed the sea to America, where many Englishmen were then leading colonies from here and there and forming a New England, and in New Plymouth they set up an Independent congregation (as it is called) around the year 1630. In 1635 Cotton joined it from England, driven out with countless others by the persecution of the bishops. Out of horror at the episcopal order, which allowed everything to itself and nothing to the rest of the Church, he fell into the opposite extreme, and granted to every congregation and to the people everything, without any bond, for fear that otherwise they would again suffer the tyranny of other Churches. Cotton had first been in England of quite a different opinion, and so, being guilty of very many errors and heresies, he became the greatest promoter of this order, or rather of this lack of order, everywhere; and he drew to himself from England Thomas Goodwin and others, whom he carefully imbued with his opinions. He had them with him, as Montanus once had Maximilla and Hutchinson, about whom they report various prodigious things. In our Netherlands the English Church at Rotterdam had until then been under presbyterial order, along with our Dutch Church, until the arrival of Hugh Peter, who, as is believed, had been instructed by letters from Cotton in New England, and formed it into the pattern of Independentism. He himself soon afterwards abandoned it, and he too flowed off to New England. Bridges, Simson and Ward from England followed him into the Rotterdam congregation. First, renouncing the English ordination, by which they had until then exercised the ministry, and being reduced to the rank of private persons, they were afterwards elected and ordained ministers by the congregation: Bridges ordained Ward, and then Ward ordained Bridges. But soon a serious dissension arose between Simson and Bridges over the practice of prophesying, in the manner of the Brownists, which Bridges disapproved and hindered, while the other insisted on it. As a result the Church was split into two parts, and Simson set up a separate congregation against Bridges. Then Ward, who began to find his colleague Bridges distasteful, did not rest until he had stripped him of the ministry by his own private authority, since his colleague protested. This matter caused scandal, and moved the neighbouring Arnhem congregations of the same family to intervene. They sent to Rotterdam two ministers, Goodwin and Nye, with two elders, and, having summoned Bridges with some of his supporters, they established that synodal form which they describe at length in their Apology, and commend above all other synods. Namely, since the Rotterdam congregation, or its larger faction, had rashly deposed its minister, the congregation or Church was bound (they say in the Apologetical Narrative), both by the law common among Christians of avoiding scandal and by that law of not communicating in the sins of others, to submit to a full and open examination by the nearby Churches, which had been gravely offended by this act. Indeed, in case of impenitence or obstinacy, the offended Church could have pronounced against it a sentence of excommunication, and with that and other Churches signified the same thing, namely that they would not communicate with it until it showed due repentance. They do not say excommunication. This must be carefully noted, because that word signifies a power which they deny can be given or established over any particular Church or congregation; in that case they place the controversy on this point. But to pronounce non-communion is a matter for equals, and for those whose interest it is to maintain communion, or less. Therefore they have proceeded thus in this business, and think that the same must be done in a similar case, when some matter calls for a synod. They do admit a synod, but not a fixed or standing one, because that would seem to be a power, or an obligation, or servitude, or inferiority towards superiors; rather one called for the occasion, and arbitrary according to the reason of the matter. The Arnhem congregation wrote to the Rotterdam one, pointing out the scandal given by the rash oppression and deposition of the minister. Therefore they asked them to permit, in the name of Christ and to vindicate his honour, and in consolation for the oppressed minister, that an examination of the case be instituted before the remaining Churches of their nation, or before any others offended by their act, and that they should subject themselves (that is how they put it) to a revision and examination of the whole business and of all the acts. When they had agreed to this with ready and willing minds, and those whom we mentioned above had arrived at Arnhem, and a meeting had been convened, a preliminary exhortation was given, aimed at teaching that a single and particular Church, which thinks it has been given by Christ the power of judging those who belong to the same body and society, ought not to claim for itself an exemption from giving account, or from being censured by any other, whether by a magistrate above it or by the neighbouring Churches near it. They say that this independent liberty, which is commonly imputed to us, was far from their mind, even when the slightest dependence on the English kingdom remained to us, or some hope of returning there seemed to remain. The outcome and result of that synod was this: after the case had been heard for some days, and various witnesses had been heard and examined, in the way that might be wanted in any court where matters are handled with the greatest authority, the congregation which had given offence openly acknowledged its error, restored the minister, who had been confessedly wronged, and even in the matter in which perhaps he himself had sinned, to his former place; and, having appointed a solemn fast, it humbled itself before God and men for that sin. But as for the divided congregations of Simson and Bridges, public authority of the magistrate at last intervened and forced them to unite again. Yet England has felt, and still feels, very great disturbances from the opinions and factions of these men, since they have hurried there from every side in rivalry. There, while the Church and commonwealth have been miserably torn and rent apart, all kinds of heresies, errors and sects are multiplying in the meantime and reigning under a wandering licence, with great harm and ruin to truth, piety and order. This was the sin of the English: that, once episcopacy had been removed, they did not at once have a ready order to which the Churches could be restored; instead, wavering, they allowed them, amid such great, long-lasting and fiery dissensions, to be tossed about and trampled down in a miserable manner, even to this day. This is all the more to be lamented, since at first the dissension over Independentism did not seem so grave that the dissenters could not be tolerated, or settled, or brought into agreement with the ecclesiastical government. For what is this, to ruin not merely the government but the Church itself, shamefully, on account of some point in ecclesiastical government, and not even the chief point? The question is not about admitting episcopacy, nor about rejecting elders; they acknowledge that the Church's government must be held, and exercised by presbyters, both teaching and ruling. For the most part during our exile we had three elders in each congregation, to whom we were also subject, they write in the Apology, p. 14. What, I ask you, is that thing over which they contend so vigorously? It does not concern so much the founding of a Church, or even its joining with others; nor properly even this, for they too admit and hold synods of the Churches, but it concerns the dependence, or rather the combination of Churches into synods, and the authority of these over them. These are the two hinges on which the whole disputation turns. They think that a Church or particular congregation is wholly its own master, and has within itself all ecclesiastical power, supreme, and not subject to another Church, or to Churches, or to deputies of Churches, or to synods, any more than to bishops. Therefore, even when a synod is convened, no power properly and directly over another Church belongs to it, except that it may help the Church with counsel and assistance, or even proceed against sinners with censure; but this is not by the force of any power or superior, but by a collateral and equal judgment, and it pronounces not excommunication, which is exercised over inferiors (from the Church upon the members over which it has power), but non-communion, as among equals. Hence they do not want these synods to be permanent, but only occasional. But what I ask again: what is there in this so great that it should be the cause of great contentions and tumults? What is there that could not be tolerated, or settled, if it could not easily be corrected?

units.la: Ecclesiam particularem habere omnem potestatem Ecclesiasticam in se, neque eam accipere à Synodo, vel ab aliis superioribus, certum est. Pone (verbi causa) ut modo una particularis sit ecclesia, vel in mundo, vel in aliquâ mundi parte, vel ut non sint Ecclesiæ quæ sociari in unum possint; aut quod aliqua cum iis sociari nequeat: non hæc eo minus ecclesia est, vel mutila ideo aliquâ sui parte, nedum essentiali. Iam sociari in unum Ecclesias, & convenire in Synodos, haud improbant Adversarii, tantum non dependere à Synodis. Et si bene introspiciamus, dependentia à Synodis non congruè dicitur. Quippe haud existimandum, vel ab aliis superioribus aut Ecclesiis, aut Synodis habere precariam potestatem particularem quamquę Ecclesiam, vel se potestate suâ exuere, quando in Synodum coit, illamque ei tradere. Neutiquam. Synodorum vel usus vel potestas nihil officere potest aut debet Ecclesiarum particularium libertati & potestati, estque non privativa, sed cumulativa potestas, ecclesiaque particularis quælibet manet subjectum proprium & adæquatum plenæ potestatis ecclesiasticæ. Neque Synodi in alias sub eâ comprehensas ecclesias potestatem usurpant imperantem, quæ Dominorum, & superiorum est in inferiores sibi subditos; sed ex communi & libero Ecclesiarum consensu in Synodum, hæc potestatem habet delegatam, & auxiliarem vel ministrantem. Eccle-
units.tr: It is certain that a particular church has all ecclesiastical power in itself and does not receive it from a synod or from any other superior body. Suppose (for example) that there is at present only one particular church, either in the world or in some part of it, or that there are no churches that could be joined together, or that none can be joined with it. That church is no less a church for this, nor is it maimed in any part, let alone an essential one. Now our opponents do not object to churches uniting and meeting in synods, only to their depending on those synods. If we look closely, however, the word "dependence" on synods is not properly used. It should certainly not be thought that a particular church holds its power by grant from other superiors, whether churches or synods, or that it strips itself of its power when it meets in a synod and hands it over. By no means. The practice and authority of synods can neither harm nor ought to harm the liberty and power of particular churches. The power is not exclusive but cumulative, and each particular church remains the proper and adequate subject of full ecclesiastical power. Nor do synods claim a commanding power over the churches comprised under them, such as masters and superiors have over inferiors subject to them. Rather, by the common and free consent of the churches, the synod holds a delegated power, auxiliary or ministerial.

units.la: clcecclesiis voluntaria consensione, ob necessitatem ordinis & aedificationis, Synodis se subjicientibus. Vti quando in Rebus-publicis, vel alibi, ex communi aequalium consilio Collegium erigitur, ad quod communes causae devolvuntur tractandae & definiendae, quod in illas nullam habet potestatem, nisi earum arbitrio & mutuo consensu. Quod in circulis vel dioecesibus Ecclesiarum, quare hae isti, illae alteri Synodo se adjungant & submittant, apparet. Non est ergo proprie haec Ecclesiarum ad Synodum relatio, dependentia dicenda, neque commodo mihi vocabulo Independentismi vel denotata controversia, vel hominum secta videtur: nam bene dici potest, Ecclesiam particularem esse independentem ab alia, vel a Synodis, aut hominibus; pendere autem a solo Christo: submissio potius appellanda fuerat, ut quae venit ex communi consensu Ecclesiarum se illi ordini, ad aedificationem & bene esse Ecclesiae, subjicientium. A qua nomenclatura ipsos non admodum alienos futuros, & molliori verbo rem non malam facilius persuasum ipsis iri confidimus, quum in Apologia dicentes audiverimus, suis se Senioribus subjectionem praestare, & Synodi Roterodamensis sententiae subjectionem a Roterodamensi coetu postulatam, teneri Ecclesiam se submittere aliorum judicio & censurae &c. quae facilius mihi videntur concilianda cum sententia nostra, quam cum nomine dependentiae (quo offenduntur) vel potestatis usurpatae a Synodo in Ecclesias.
units.tr: ...by the voluntary consent of the churches, submitting themselves to synods for the necessity of order and for edification. This is as when, in commonwealths or elsewhere, by the common counsel of equals, a college is set up to which common matters are referred for discussion and decision, and which has no power over those matters except at the discretion and by the mutual consent of the parties. That this is so in the circles or dioceses of churches, where these churches join one synod and those another, is plain. Therefore this relation of churches to a synod is not properly called dependence, nor does the word "Independency" seem to me a suitable term to denote either the controversy or the sect of men. For it can well be said that a particular church is independent of another church, or of synods, or of men, yet depends on Christ alone. It would rather have been called submission, since it arises from the common consent of the churches, which submit themselves to that order for the edification and well-being of the church. We trust they will not be greatly averse to this terminology, and that they will more readily be persuaded that the thing is not bad when it is put in a milder word. For we have heard them say in their Apology that they render submission to their own Elders, and that the Rotterdam congregation was asked to submit to the judgment of the Synod of Rotterdam, and that the church is bound to submit itself to the judgment and censure of others, and so on. These seem to me more easily reconciled with our view than with the name of dependence (which offends them), or with a power usurped by a synod over the churches.

units.la: Verum quid est quod adeo offendere eos possit, si Synodorum potestate ita explicata, & limitata, aliquam iis tribuamus? Censuram stringere in contumacem, pronunciare non-communionem, quid vel ab excommunicatione adeo distat, vel ab usurpata potestate? Illa non-communio passive considerata, quid differt ab excommunicatione? qui extra Sanctorum communionem ponitur, annon idem est quod excommunicatus? vel ecclesia sic damnata non-communione, annon potepotestatem aliquam sentit adversus se exercitam? Adjunt, illa esse remedia efficacia, powerfull & effectuall meanes: quomodo absque omni potestate? Sed improbare se dicunt, Synodorum authoritativam potestatem ecclesiasticam. Certè magis videntur mihi verba horrere, quam rem. Vbi Ecclesia se submittit judicio, censuræ, sententiæ non-communionis, annon se subjicit potestati? Vel coëuntes in Synodum Ministri ac Seniores, annon servant potestatem suam ecclesiasticam, quam semper habent ex ordinatione & functione ministerii, jamque eò magis quò ab Ecclesiis suis ad Synodum deputantur? vel an amittunt potestatem suam, eamque ante Synodum deponunt? quo quid absurdius dici potest? Si ergo potestatem suam ecclesiasticam retinent ii qui Synodum constituunt, quomodo eam quasi vel vacuam vel vanam sine viribus imaginamur? Et non in alias Ecclesias Synodus pronunciat, quam suas, id est, quæ ibi per Legatos suos conveniunt, communesque causas ei subjiciunt, omnino per voluntariam & mutuam submissionem, neque in alienam segetem falcem suam immittit Synodus, sed combinata Ecclesiarum potestas in earundem ecclesiarum bonum invigilat una, & communiter prospicit. Siquidem nolint dici potestatem & authoritatem, ex quâ Synodus sua agat; quid illud tanti refert, ut non res retineri, & conjunctio ecclesiarum animorumque possit? dummodo idem, vel fere idem curetur, quo id cunque nomine fiat, potestatis, an consilii, an utriusque, vix litigandum videtur. Quod gloriantur in Apologiâ, se suâ methodo & viâ æquè, si non melius, negotia in Synodis suis tractare ac absolvere quam nos in nostris; faciant, unaque incumbant in tranquillitatem & ædificationem Ecclesiarum mutuam. Iam de statis Synodis quod regerunt, existimo eos, si permittantur aliquandiu suâ incedere regulâ, potestatem Synodorum propediem magis agnituros, & propter crebra magnaque que variarum Ecclesiarum negotias ipsa duce experientiâ, ad statas Synodos recursuros, atque antiquam & Catholicam Ecclesiæ Christianæ praxim de Synodis, earum potestate, & statis vicibus, haud difficulter probaturos. Præsertim metus amittendarum Synodorum, quando non habentur statæ; firmataque, docere illos deberet, quam adversus Ecclesiæ commodas hic tumultuentur. Quidquid sit, non oportuit ob levidense negotium tantas concitare turbas: nec tanti referret forsitan illis hac in parte indultum nonnihil fuisse, toleratamque infirmitatem, donec ipsos usus & experientia refellisset potius, quam contentio. Quare admodum a. clɔ Ioc xlv. die xiii. Septembris conclusum in Parlamento, ut Deputati utriusque domus, una cum Delegatis Ecclesiæ Scoticanæ, & Synodi Londinensis, dispicerent de compositione & unione Controversiæ in Synodo agitatæ, super Ecclesiastico regimine: vel sin minus hoc obtineri posset, inquirerent in modum, quo tenere conscientiæ, quæ se in omnibus nequeunt subjicere eidem regulæ stabiliendæ, possent tolerari juxta Dei verbum, ad publicam tranquillitatem, & Synodi progressus non diutius illis contentionibus inhibendos. Ad quod variis institutis collationibus, die iv. Decemb. a. clɔ Ioc xlv. Dissentientes fratres (sic passim appellati) consensum suum testati in Confessione fidei cum Ecclesiis Reformatis, quas pro veris amplectuntur, & variarum sententiarum desperantes compositionem petebant tolerari: quod alii non contendendum rati, variis scriptis diu certarunt coram Deputatis Parlamenti & Synodi, nullo tandem eventu. Iterumque a. clɔ Ioc xlviii. Dissentientes Fratres, coram Parlamento disputarunt super tribus Propositionibus Synodi: quarum prima concernebat regimen Presbyteriale; altera, subordinationem congregationum; tertia, potestatem particularis Cœtus in ordinando. De illo Synodi propositio erat, quod
units.tr: But why should it offend them so much if we attribute to synods some power, explained and limited in this way? To impose censure on the contumacious, to pronounce non-communion: how does this differ from excommunication, or from the power usurped? Considered passively, how does that non-communion differ from excommunication? Is not one who is placed outside the communion of the saints the same as an excommunicated person? Or does a church condemned by non-communion not feel some power exercised against itself? They add that these are efficacious remedies, "powerfull & effectuall meanes": how can that be without any power? But they say they disapprove of the synods' authoritative ecclesiastical power. Surely they seem to me to shrink from the words more than from the thing. When a church submits to the judgment, the censure, the sentence of non-communion, does it not submit to a power? Or do the ministers and elders who meet in synod not keep their ecclesiastical power, which they always have from ordination and the office of ministry, and all the more so since they are sent to the synod by their churches? Or do they lose their power and lay it down before the synod? What could be more absurd than that? If, therefore, those who constitute the synod retain their ecclesiastical power, how can we imagine it as if empty or void and without strength? Nor does the synod pronounce on any churches other than its own, that is, those which meet there through their delegates and submit common matters to it, entirely by voluntary and mutual submission. Nor does the synod put its sickle into another's harvest; rather, the combined power of the churches watches over the good of those same churches together and provides for it in common. If they will not have it called power and authority by which their synod acts, what does it matter so much, provided the thing itself is kept and the union of churches and minds can be maintained? So long as the same, or nearly the same, is secured, whatever name it is done under, power, or counsel, or both, it hardly seems worth quarrelling over. As for their boast in the Apology that they conduct and finish business in their synods by their own method and way equally well, if not better, than we do in ours, let them do so, and let them labour together for the tranquillity and mutual edification of the churches. As for what they object concerning fixed synods, I think that if they are allowed for some time to proceed by their own rule, they will in due course come to recognise the power of synods more, and, led by experience itself in the frequent and great affairs of various churches, will return to fixed synods. They will not find it difficult to prove the ancient and catholic practice of the Christian Church concerning synods, their power, and their fixed meetings. Especially the fear of losing synods when they are not held as fixed should teach them, once they are firmly established, how much they stir up tumults against the advantage of the Church. Whatever the case, it was not right to stir up such great disturbances over so slight a matter. Nor would it perhaps have mattered much to have granted them some indulgence in this respect and tolerated their weakness, until experience and practice had refuted them, rather than contention. Hence it was resolved in Parliament, on 13 September 1645, that deputies of both houses, together with delegates of the Scottish Church and of the London Synod, should consider how the controversy debated in the synod over ecclesiastical government might be composed and united; or, if this could not be obtained, should inquire into a way in which consciences that cannot submit in all things to the rule to be established might be tolerated, according to the Word of God, for the public tranquillity, and so that the progress of the Synod would not be hindered any longer by those contentions. To this end, after various conferences held on 4 December 1645, the dissenting brethren (so they were called everywhere) testified their agreement with the Reformed Churches, which they embrace as true, in the Confession of Faith, and, despairing of a composition of the differing opinions, they asked to be tolerated. The others, thinking this should not be contested, disputed for a long time in various writings before the deputies of Parliament and of the Synod, but with no result in the end. And again in 1648, the dissenting brethren disputed before Parliament on three propositions of the Synod. The first of these concerned Presbyterian government; the second, the subordination of congregations; the third, the power of a particular assembly in ordaining. Concerning the first, the proposition of the Synod was that "Scripture declares that several particular congregations may be under one Presbyterian government. Of this, synodical assemblies are of various kinds: Provincial, National, and Ecumenical. Then, it is lawful, and agrees with the Word of God, that there be a subordination of Congregational, Classical, Provincial, and National assemblies to the government of the Church..."

units.la: „Scriptura declarat, plures particulares congregatio„nes posse esse sub uno regimine Presbyteriali. De isto„Congregationes Synodicae variorum generum sunt, „Provinciales, Nationales, & Oecumenicae. Dein, „licet, ac cum verbo Dei congruit, ut sit subordina„tio Conventuum, Congregationalis, Classici, Pro„vincialis, & Nationalis, ad regimen Ecclesiae. Deni„que haec erat propositio tertia: omnino requiritur, ne „singularis Congregatio, quae apte associari potest, si„bi arroget omnem & solam potestatem ordinationis. Has propositiones rationibus variis à Synodo confirmatas, Dissentientes fratres aliis impugnabant, atque ad priores respondebant. Quod semel iterumque aliis instantiis & responsionibus tum ab hac, tum ab illa parte reciprocatum, quę distinctis scriptis comprehensa, om-nia jussu Parlamenti edita fuerunt, atq; ad annum alterumq; protracta: unde factum, ut quo plus disputatum, eo longius discessum, & quo contentionis plus, eo mali divisionisque plus datum fuerit. Facit horum, meique mentionem, sed honorificam satis, quo nomine & gratias publice dico. V.C. Ludovicus Molineus, Historiarum Professor Oxoniensis, in Parenesi, c. xxii. ubi primum de me testatus, quod nemo hactenus presbyterianorum aequior fuit in fratres, nec, quod alii, ut facit Amyraldus, veritis fratres in hominum monstra aut contumelias proscindit, sed tanto candore, tantaque animi lenitate conatur reducere in viam suam, ut vix est ut non ametur etiam ab illis quos non pervicerit & persuaserit. tum meai examinans, aliquot ponit Conclusiones, in quibus nec probamus omnia, neque etiam improbamus. Nam quod primum inquit, fratres quidem negare Ecclesiam particularem ad consociationem ejusdem disciplinae cum aliis obstringi, praecepto divino, attamen nec eam repudiare cum sororibus Ecclesiis, in eadem fide conspirantibus: bene est, modo conjunctio habeatur & colatur, si non ex jure divino, omnibusque universaliter & diserte praescripto, at Ecclesiastico, & pro bono, pace atque soʼꝛꝗ̄ Ecclesiarum mutuâ. Præcertim quum addat, Ecclesiam particularem teneri reddendis rationibus viarum suarum Synodo, aut alteri particulari Ecclesiæ. Deinde agnoscit conventus Synodorum esse de jure divino: sed negat, Synodum quamcunque aut Ecclesiam particularem habere in alias seu Ecclesias, seu Synodos judiciariam authoritatem & potestatem: non omnem, aut qualemcunque, fateor, non à se & suâ sponte, & jure quodam superioritatis proprio in Ecclesias quasi inferiores, & potestatem suam ab aliis seu Ecclesiis seu coetibus mendicantes, sed liberâ duntaxat consociatione, & non sni adeo, quam negotiorum quorundam, difficilium aut ad plures spectantium, submissione mutuâ, obtinere Synodos potestatem, quâ pollent, arbitramur, non privativam Ecclesiarum, sed cumulativam. Nedum ut Ecclesia alia in aliam potestatem ullam ex se habeat, aut imperium. Quod vel primus apud nos dicit ordinis Ecclesiastici articulus; Nulla Ecclesia in aliam, nullus Verbi Minister, Senior, Diaconus nullus in alterum dominium exercebit, verùm unusquisque ab omni dominandi cavebit sibi suspicione & illicito. Synodus Nationalis Emdana, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxı. art. ı. Quod repetitum confirmatumque Synodo Dordracenâ a. cIↄ Iↄ cxix. Ordinis Ecclesiastici canone lxxxıv. Verùm quod Vir. Cl. postmodum addit, uti aliis, id est, civilibus hominum ordinibus, foris, atque societatibus; ita Ecclesiis quoque, Consistoriis, Classibus, & Synodis authoritatem suam esse totam & potestatem regendi à Magistratu civili, id non admittimus, existimantes, Ecclesiam per se corpus esse aut societatem, distinctam à civili, & alterius plane generis, ut non sit imperium in imperio; sed cui auctor fundatorque Christus, de requisitis ad essentiam & integritatem, sive ad esse ejus & bene esse, abunde prospexerit, sive sub Magistratu aliquando inimico, aut nullo actu, sive favente. De quo non est ut impraesens disputemus; uti nec de foris Ecclesiasticis, quot, aut quibus, certe non citra necessitatem multiplicandis. Scripta super Controversiis Dissentientium fratrum, quos vulgo Independentes vocant, extant varia, quaeque ad manus nostras venere praecipua quidem, Syons prerogative Royal, ostendens quod quaelibet particularis Congregatio est independens; is an independant body, not standing under any other ecclesiasticall authoritie out of it selfe. Independentium, qui sic appellantur, Apologia, cum Antapologia Thomae Edwardi, qua illam refutavit. Rationes per Dissentientes fratres oblatae adversus Propositiones concernentes Regimen Presbyteriale, cum Responsionibus Synodi ad illas, Anglice: ubi disputatur de rebus in controversia. Papers for accommodation anno MDCXLIV. in quibus de componendis, aut uniendis, vel tolerandis dissensionibus & dissentientibus hinc inde actum. A survey of the summe of Church discipline, duobus libris, quorum primum scripsit Tho. Hooker; alterum Joh. Cotton, pro ordine Ecclesiarum Congregationalium in Nova Anglia. Adversus illos Rob. Baylie, lib. a Dissuasive from the Errours of the time, ch. III. IV. V. VI. X. Jus divinum Regiminis Ecclesiastici, pro Regimine presbyteriali, per Ministros Londinenses, Anglice. A vindication of the Presbyteriall government, per Ministros Synodi Provincialis Londinensis a. MDCXLIX. Sam. Rutherfurd, lib. The due right of presbyteries: aliique ejusdem tractatus. Joh. Paget, A defence of Church government, adversus Ainsworthum, Davenportium, & Cannum, de potestate presbyterii, Classium, & Synodorum. Samuel Bolton, The Arraignement of Errour, a pag. 268. &c. imprimis a pag. 349. ubi de compositione controversiarum egregie disserit. Cui fini facit etiam Iohn Brinsley, The Arraignement of the present Schisme of new separation in Old England: Ex Nostris, Vocius, Disp. de Classibus, & Synodis. De Ecclesia clesiâ visibili, & institutâ. Apollonius (adversus quem inter Anglos scripsit Nortonus) Consider. Controv. cap. VI. Spanhemius, epist. Class. III.
units.tr: The Scripture declares that several particular congregations may be under one presbyterial government. Of such government there are synodical assemblies of various kinds: provincial, national, and ecumenical. Next, it is lawful, and agrees with the Word of God, that there be a subordination of the assemblies (congregational, classical, provincial, and national) to the government of the Church. Finally, this was the third proposition: it is wholly required that a single congregation, which can suitably be associated with others, should not claim for itself all and sole power of ordination. The dissenting brethren attacked these propositions, which the Synod had confirmed with various arguments, and answered the earlier ones. This was repeated again and again, with further demands and replies from one side and the other. These, set down in separate writings, were all published by order of Parliament and drawn out over a year or more. Hence it came about that the more they disputed, the further they departed from one another, and the more contention there was, the more harm and division it produced. He makes mention of these matters, and of me, but in terms honourable enough, for which I publicly give thanks. The learned Ludovicus Molineus, professor of history at Oxford, in his Parenesis, ch. 22, where he first bears witness concerning me: no one among the Presbyterians has hitherto been fairer toward the brethren, nor does he tear them to pieces with monstrous charges or insults, as others do, as Amyraldus does, but with such candour and such gentleness of mind he tries to lead them back to their own path, that it is hardly possible he should not be loved even by those whom he has not overcome and persuaded. Then, examining my views, he lays down some conclusions, in which we neither approve everything nor disapprove everything. For as to what he says first: that the brethren indeed deny that a particular church is bound by divine precept to join with other churches in the same discipline, yet neither do they reject fellowship with sister churches agreeing in the same faith. This is good, provided that the union is maintained and cultivated, if not by divine right, and prescribed to all universally and expressly, yet by ecclesiastical right and for the good, peace, and mutual [edification] of the churches. This is especially so since he adds that a particular church is bound to render an account of its ways to the Synod, or to another particular church. Next, he acknowledges that assemblies of synods are of divine right. But he denies that any synod, or any particular church, has judicial authority and power over other churches or synods. I grant that it has no power of any kind, nor of any sort whatever, not of itself and of its own accord, nor by some proper right of superiority over churches that are, as it were, inferior, begging its power from other churches or assemblies. We judge rather that synods possess the power they have by free association only, and by mutual submission in certain difficult matters or matters concerning many; a power not private but cumulative to the churches. Far from any church having any power or rule of its own over another. The first article of our ecclesiastical order states this: No church over another, no minister of the Word, elder, or deacon shall exercise lordship over another; rather, each shall guard himself against all suspicion and unlawful desire to dominate. National Synod of Emden, 1571, art. 1. This was repeated and confirmed by the Synod of Dort, 1619, canon 84 of the Ecclesiastical Order. But when the most learned man afterwards adds that, just as other civil orders, offices, and societies of men have their whole authority and power to govern from the civil magistrate, so also churches, consistories, classes, and synods have theirs, we do not admit this. We judge that the Church is in itself a body or society, distinct from the civil and of a plainly different kind, so that it is not an empire within an empire. Christ, its author and founder, has abundantly provided for what is required for its essence and integrity, or for its being and well-being, whether under a magistrate sometimes hostile, or with no action at all, or favourable. We need not dispute about this at present, nor about the ecclesiastical offices, how many or which, certainly not to be multiplied without necessity. Various writings on the controversies of the dissenting brethren, whom commonly they call Independents, exist, and those principal ones which have come into our hands are: Syons prerogative Royal, showing that every particular congregation is independent, is an independant body, not standing under any other ecclesiasticall authoritie out of it selfe. The Apologia of the so-called Independents, with the Antapologia of Thomas Edwards, by which he refuted it. The Rationes offered by the dissenting brethren against the propositions concerning presbyterial government, with the Responses of the Synod to them, in English, where the matters in controversy are discussed. Papers for accommodation, 1644, in which the composing, uniting, or tolerating of dissensions and dissenters on both sides is treated. A survey of the summe of Church discipline, in two books, the first written by Thomas Hooker, the second by John Cotton, for the order of the Congregational churches in New England. Against them Robert Baillie, in A Dissuasive from the Errours of the time, chs. III, IV, V, VI, X. Jus divinum Regiminis Ecclesiastici, for presbyterial government, by the ministers of London, in English. A vindication of the Presbyteriall government, by the ministers of the Provincial Synod of London, 1649. Samuel Rutherford, The due right of presbyteries, and other treatises of the same kind. John Paget, A defence of Church government, against Ainsworth, Davenport, and Cann, on the power of presbytery, of classes, and of synods. Samuel Bolton, The Arraignement of Errour, from p. 268 onward, especially p. 349, where he discusses excellently the composing of controversies. To the same end also John Brinsley, The Arraignement of the present Schisme of new separation in Old England. Among our own: Voetius, Disp. on classes and synods, and on the visible and instituted Church. Apollonius (against whom Norton wrote among the English), Consider. Controv. ch. VI. Spanheim, Epist. Class. III.

units.la: Regredicendo ad thesGes Brownistarum, quamvis eadem ut plurimum sequantur Dissidentes fratres, seu Congregationales, aut quocunque nomine appellare eos placeat, an Independentium, quod aliqui inter ipsos non admodum refugiunt? offert, inter primas se ea, quâ de amplitudine Ecclesiæ particularis quæritur: an non alia ejus mensura capienda sit, quàm à loco, ut Ecclesia particularis sit, quæ commodè uno in loco tota convenire, atque ab uno pastore doceri queat; vel, quæ suo ambitu non plura complectatur membra, quam quæ in unum locum simul coire possint? ita ut totidem in unâ aliquâ urbe censendæ sint ecclesiæ particulares, quot ejusmodi congregationes: vel non potius, ab unitate Synedrii particularis Ecclesia æstimanda sit, quamvis variis locis convenire cogatur, nec uno ob multitudinem suam possit, ita ut habeat pro copia membrorum pastores, locaque apta & copiosa, regatur autem simul ab uno Synedrio, quod ex pluribus Pastoribus constet, unà cum Senioribus? Brownistæ, atque Independentes prius illud volunt. Apologia Brownistarum, thes. VIII. Robinsonus, c. I. Confer Amesium, Medull. Theolog. c. I. lib. I. cap. XXXIX. §. 18. 19. Parkerum, lib. III. Polit. Eccles. cap. XVII. p. 189. Dissentientes Fratres, adversus III Propositionem, de regimine Presbyteriali: quâ Synodus dixerat, plures particulares Congregationes posse esse sub uno regimine presbyteriali, idque ostenderat exemplo Ecclesiæ Ierosolymitanæ, atque Ephesinæ, ubi proculdubio plures fuerint Cœtus, at sub uno presbyterio censita una particularis Ecclesia. Certe modo caveatur, ut pro numero fidelium Ecclesia habeat sufficientes Pastores, & ædes sacris Conventibus aptas, nihil video quare non etiam sub uno Presbyterio illæ congregationes regantur, ha beantur quæ
units.tr: Returning to the theses of the Brownists: although the dissenting brethren, or Congregationalists (or whatever name it pleases them to be called, or Independents, which some among them do not much refuse), mostly follow the same principles, the first question that arises concerns the extent of a particular church. Should it not be measured differently than by place? That is, is a particular church one that can conveniently assemble entire in one place and be taught by one minister, or one that in its compass does not include more members than can gather together in one place at once? On this view, as many particular churches should be counted in a single city as there are such congregations. Or rather, should a particular church be judged by the unity of a particular synod, even though it is compelled to meet in various places and cannot, because of its size, meet in one? Thus it would have ministers in proportion to its numbers, and suitable and spacious places, but would be governed at the same time by one synod, consisting of several ministers together with the elders? The Brownists and the Independents prefer the former. Apologia Brownistarum, thes. VIII. Robinson, ch. I. Compare Amesius, Medull. Theolog. bk. I, ch. XXXIX, §§ 18, 19. Parker, bk. III, Polit. Eccles. ch. XVII, p. 189. The dissenting brethren, against the third proposition concerning presbyterial government, in which the Synod had said that several particular congregations may be under one presbyterial government, and had shown this by the example of the churches of Jerusalem and Ephesus, where there were undoubtedly several assemblies, yet one particular church was counted under one presbytery. Certainly, provided care is taken that the church has enough ministers for the number of the faithful, and buildings suitable for sacred gatherings, I see no reason why those congregations should not also be governed under one presbytery, and be held as one particular church, rather than as many churches as there are assemblies that can be served by one minister perhaps. This makes for a greater union, harmony, and edification of the church and of the ministry. See Voetius, disp. 11, on the institution of the Church; Apollonius, Controv.

units.la: quæ que pro unâ particulari Ecclesiâ, quam ut totidem constituantur Ecclesiæ, ac Cœtus, quot ab uno forte Pastore administrari possunt. Illud ad majorem facit Ecclesiæ, & ministerii unionem, concordiam, atque ædificationem. Vide Voetium, disp. 11. de Eccles. Institut. Apollonium, Controv. Anglic. c. 111. Spanhemium epist. p. 23.
units.tr: which are to be regarded as one particular Church, rather than as as many churches or congregations as one minister might perhaps serve. This makes for greater union, harmony and edification of the Church and ministry. See Voetius, disp. 11, de Eccles. Institut.; Apollonius, Controv. Anglic. c. 111; Spanheim, epist. p. 23.

units.la: Atque etiam super loco sacrorum Conventuum cum Brownistis superest controversia, de templis Papisticis, aut ad gentilem idololatriam olim usurpatis, an ad cultum sacrum inibi peragendum adhiberi queant? Negant Brownistæ, & destrui loca illa jubent, reditusque in usus tantum profanos impendi, ac civiles. Brownistarum Confess. thes. xxxix. & Apolog. contra Oxon. thes. xii. Robinsonus, cap. ix. Neque id de templis solum, sed & campanis, aliisque utensilibus & apparatu omni idololatrico, ac superstitioso intelligunt. Ex adverso quum juxta Apostolum, idolum nihil sit, 1 Cor. VIII. 4. illum istorum usum idololatricum nil curantes, proindeque locum æstimantes communem, naturalem & civilem, quemadmodum Robinsonus etiam distinguit; nihil impedit, quare non ut alium quemvis, ita & illa loca ad cultum peragendum aptemus. Neque enim vel distinctum de diruendis præceptum nobis datum; neque idololatria characterem iis imprimit indelebilem, quin purgari, & sic in quosvis usus impendi possint. Quemadmodum cum fanis Gentilium Veteres Christianos egisse, & Theodosium Alexandrinum scimus Bacchi templum in Christianum commutasse, & statuas in templi utensilia ususque pauperum convertisse. In Angliâ statuit Gregorius episcopus Romanus, scribens Mellito Abbati, ut est apud Bedam, Histor. Eccles. lib. 1. cap. xxx. quod fana idolorum destrui in eadem gente minime debeant; sed ipsa quæ in eis sunt idola destruantur, aqua benedicta fiat, in eisdem fanis aspergatur, aliaria construantur, reliquiæ componantur. Quia si fana eadem bene constructa sunt, necesse est ut à cultu daemonum in obsequia veri Dei debeant commutari, ut dum gens ipsa eadem fana sua non videt destrui, de corde errorem deponat, & Deum verum cognoscens ac adorans, ad loca quae consuevit familiarius concurrat. Caeterum de controversia ista Brownistica, vide Pagetum, adversus Ainsworthum, Arrow against the Brownists pag. 19. & 130. Eandem contra Anabaptistas tractat Osiander, in Enchiridio cap. VI. Coroll. 11. Conatusque fuit Jacobus Andreas in Colloquio Mompelgartensi hac etiam super re controversiam movere, pag. 380. An in iis templis vera Evangelii praedicatio, & Sacramentorum usus celebrari possit, in quibus Pontifícii summam Idololatriam exercuerunt: an vero penitus evertenda, demolienda, & nova extruenda sint? Iterum, pag. 390. Quaeritur autem: An propter Idololatriam, quae passim in Templis Papisticis exercetur, ipsa Templa & altaria Imaginibus, sacris historiis minimè Idololatricis exornata, & dispensationi corporis & sanguinis Christi in Eucharistia destinata, diruenda? Sed frustra. Nam uti Beza bene respondit: De Templorum demolitione in illis tumultibus bellicis facta, nemo nostrum omnia probavit, quae cavere & avertere non potuimus. Iterumque pag. 394. Aliud est eversio templorum, quam minimè probamus, quàm manifestorum Idolorum sublatio, quibus vel nunc abusi fuerint homines, vel probabile est non posse non abuti. Et: Rectè docetur templorum eversio minimè esse necessaria, nec temere probanda. Idem Browniståe statuunt de reditibus Ecclesiasticis. Quin aboleri bona omnia Papalia, quae alias modò escam & alleétamentum Papalium servari videntur: & impendi volunt in usus politicos, neque ex illis sustentari Ministros debere, uti neque ex decimis (quas Judaicas appellant), sed ex voluntariâ collectâ Ecclesiae. Apolog. contra Oxon. thes. VII.
units.tr: There is also a controversy with the Brownists about the place of the sacred assemblies: whether Papist temples, or buildings once used for pagan idolatry, may be used for performing sacred worship there. The Brownists deny it, and order those places to be destroyed, and their revenues to be spent only on profane and civil uses. Brownist Confession, thes. 39; Apology against the Oxford men, thes. 12; Robinson, ch. 9. They understand this not only of temples but also of bells and of all utensils and equipment that is idolatrous and superstitious. On the other hand, since according to the Apostle an idol is nothing (1 Cor. 8:4), we, not caring about their idolatrous use and therefore judging the place to be common, natural and civil (as Robinson also distinguishes), see nothing to prevent us from fitting those places for worship just as any others. For no command to destroy them has been given to us, nor does idolatry stamp on them an indelible character, so that they cannot be cleansed and devoted to any use. Thus we know that the early Christians dealt with the temples of the Gentiles, and that Theodosius of Alexandria turned a temple of Bacchus into a Christian church, and converted statues into church furnishings and into relief for the poor. In England Gregory, bishop of Rome, writing to the abbot Mellitus, laid down (as it is in Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 30) that the temples of idols ought by no means to be destroyed in that nation; but the idols that are in them should be destroyed, holy water be made and sprinkled in the same temples, altars be built, and relics placed. For if those temples are well built, it is necessary that they be changed from the worship of demons to the service of the true God, so that, while the people do not see their own temples destroyed, they may lay aside error from their heart, and, knowing and adoring the true God, may come more familiarly to the places to which they are used to resort. For the rest, on this Brownist controversy, see Paget against Ainsworth, Arrow against the Brownists, pp. 19 and 130. Osiander treats the same question against the Anabaptists in his Enchiridion, chap. 6, corollary 11. James Andreae also tried to raise this controversy at the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. 380: Whether the true preaching of the Gospel and the use of the sacraments can be celebrated in those temples in which the Papists have practised the greatest idolatry, or whether they must be wholly overthrown, demolished, and new ones built? Again, p. 390: But it is asked: whether, on account of the idolatry which is practised everywhere in Papist temples, the temples themselves and the altars, adorned with images and sacred histories by no means idolatrous, and destined for the distribution of the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist, should be destroyed? But in vain. For as Beza well replied: Concerning the demolition of temples carried out in those wartime tumults, none of us approved of everything, which we could not guard against or avert. And again, p. 394: The overthrow of temples, which we by no means approve, is one thing; the removal of manifest idols, which men have now abused or which it is probable they cannot but abuse, is another. And: It is rightly taught that the overthrow of temples is by no means necessary, nor to be rashly approved. The Brownists hold the same view about ecclesiastical revenues. Indeed they want all Papal goods, which otherwise seem to be preserved only as bait and enticement for Papalists, to be abolished and spent on civil uses; they hold that ministers should not be supported from these, nor from tithes (which they call Jewish), but from the voluntary contributions of the Church. Apology against the Oxford men, thes. 7.

units.la: Carpunt itidem in Ecclesiis nostris ac ministerio, quod in Ecclesia à Ministris matrimonium confirmatur, quasi esset res Ecclesiastica, & sacra, cum sit politica & communis. Quin matrimonium tale in se sit, haud ignoramus: verùm ut confirmatio & benedictio ejus sanctè quoque peragatur in Ecclesiâ, quid adeo impedit, præsertim quando non ut necessarium habetur ad essentiam vel matrimonii spectans, vel ministerii; sed ex usu antiquo, & majoris vel sanctioris cautelæ ergo & benedictionis? Sic apud Veteres observatum. Tertullianus, lib. II. ad Vxorem: Unde sufficiam ad enarrandam felicitatem ejus matrimonii, quod Ecclesia conciliat, & confirmat oblatio, & obsignatum Angeli renunciant, pater pro rato habet? Ambrosius, epist. Ixx. Nam cum ipsum conjugium velamine sacerdotali & benedictione sanctificari oporteat, quomodo potest conjugium dici, ubi non est fidei concordia? Possidonius, in vitâ Augustini cap. xxvii. memorat, cum ab Ambrosio hoc tenuisse inter alia, ne uxorem cuiquam unquam posceret, causam dabat, ne conjugati forte jurgarent, & cum maledicerent, per quem conjuncti essent. Sed plane ad hoc sibi jam illi consentientibus petitum interesse debere affirmabat sacerdotem, ut vel eorum jam pacta & placita firmarentur, vel benedicerentur. Mos antiquissimus est, ut benedictio Conjugii, à sacerdote, uti loquuntur Veteres, fiat in Ecclesiâ. Sic in decretis Paparum, Euaristi, & Hormisdæ, adde Soteris apud Platinam, legitur. In Concilio Carthaginensi iv. cap. xiii. Sponsus & sponsa cum benedicendi sunt à Sacerdote, à parentibus vel paranymphis offerantur in Ecclesiâ Sacerdoti: qui cum acceperint benedictionem, eadem nocte pro reverentiâ benedictionis in virginitate permaneant. Vide ii. Decret. Gratiani cap. xxx. qu. v. Atque ita servatum ab antiquo in Ecclesiâ, ut conjugium confirmarent Ministri, eique solemniter benedicerent: tum ad obvianda clandestina matrimonia. Hinc inter canones Iohannis Metropolitæ, in Rerum Moscoviticarum Commentario tario refert Sigismundus Baro Herbersteinii: Matrimonium non nisi publice in Ecclesiis contrahatur. In Papali Ecclesia in excessum abeunt, docentque, debere in Ecclesia confirmari matrimonium, scilicet quia pro sacramento habetur: at male. Ex altera parte Browniste peccant, dicentes, non posse vel non debere in Ecclesia consecrari omnino. Iterum male. Nos medium tenemus, & in Ecclesia à Ministro posse convenienter confirmari matrimonium, non tamen ex ulla necessitate debere, docemus: namque à politico Magistratu confirmatum matrimonium probamus aeque. Lutherani ulterius, etiam privatim domi confirmata matrimonia haud improbantsuti ex epistola Jac. Reneccii ad Schlüsselburgium, quae inter hujus epistolas ultima est, videre licet. Lubet adscribere verba Doctissimi Auctoris Altaris Damasceni, Didoclavii, ut titulus habet, revera Davidis Calderwodi, pag. 866. Coetum etiam frequentiorem probamus, non tamen coetum publicum totius Ecclesiae particularis necessario adesse debere existimamus, & apud nos sapius solent celebrare matrimonia extra sacra & publicum conventum totius Ecclesiae. Nam non est actio ista mere Ecclesiastica, quae desideret praesentiam totius coetus particularis illius Ecclesiae cujus personae contrahentes sunt membra, sicut administratio sacramentorum. Est contractus civilis, sed divinus etiam, quia intervenit Dei auctoritas, id est, institutum, quo statuit vinculum hujus contractus non temere dissolvendum aut violandum, non tamen sequitur non nisi Ecclesiae interventu celebrandum, nisi velimus quaecunque Deus instituit, etiam si non ad usum sacrum, in Ecclesia celebranda. Non excludimus praesentiam totius Ecclesiae, imo nec infidelium, aut quorumvis qui adesse cupiunt, sicut in portis civitatum omnibus accessum patuisse non dubium est, sed necessariam esse ejus praesentiam negaremus. Sufficere existimo si frequentior fuit coetus in loco publico, modo non relinquatur cujusvis arbitrio huius numerum definire. Tempus, locum, coetum, legibus definiri oportet propter in-comcommoda & pericula quæ ex clandestinis matrimoniis emer-gere possunt. Ministri benedictionem tamen non sperninus. Non est de essentia contractus præsentia & benedictio ministri. Sic & apud Nos diversimodè, aut præsente Ecclesia fit, aut dimissâ, Matrimonii consecratio. Conferfis Amefium, Caf. Confc. lib. v. cap. xxxv i. Bucani Institut. Theol. loc. xi i. pag. i N. Bellarminus, de Matrimonio, lib. i. cap. xxxi i. specialem inde cupit facere controversiam,quod Nostrorum quidam videntur causas matrimoniales ad politicum forum rejicere, & non ad Ecclesiasticum. Verùm æquè frustra ac ab aliâ parte Brovvnistæ nobis intentant aliam litem ac disputationem. Apolog. contra Oxonienses thef. vi. & Robinsonus, cap. v i. Quo loco ubi de hoc, uti & de aliis in præcedentibus articulis, egisset, bene subjungit: Atque hæc sunt in quibus ab Ecclesiis Belgicis dissentimus, quæ ut nec tantilla sunt, quæ negligi debeant ab iis quibus nihil è Domini Christi sacro sive ore, sive spiritu prodiens minimum censetur, ita nec tanta, ut fraterna charitatis & communionis vinculum abrumpant. Denique itarem hanc jam determinavit Directorium Cultus publici in Angliâ, c. de confirmatione matrimonii: Quamvis matrimonium non est sacramentum, neque Ecclesiæ Dei proprium, sed commune generi humano, & cujus Reip. quovis in statu interest; tamen quia qui conjugium ineunt, in Domine hoc faciunt, atque in tali statu ad ingressum præcipue opus habent instructione directionis, atque admonitione ex Dei verbo, atque divinâ in nobis benedictione, consultum judicamus, ut matrimonium confirmetur à legitimo Verbi ministro, qui illos simul moneat, atque apprecetur benedictionem.
units.tr: They also find fault in our churches and ministry that in the Church the marriage is confirmed by the ministers, as though it were an ecclesiastical and sacred matter, when it is civil and common. Indeed we are not unaware that marriage is such in itself; but why should it hinder that its confirmation and blessing also be solemnly performed in the Church, especially when it is not held to be necessary to the essence of marriage or of the ministry, but is done by ancient custom, for the sake of greater or holier caution and blessing? This was observed among the ancients. Tertullian, To His Wife, book 2: How shall I be able to tell of the happiness of that marriage which the Church joins together and the oblation confirms, which the angels report and the Father holds as ratified? Ambrose, epistle 70: For since marriage itself ought to be sanctified by the priestly veil and blessing, how can it be called a marriage where there is no agreement of faith? Possidius, in the Life of Augustine, chap. 27, records that Ambrose taught this among other things, and gave as his reason for not asking anyone for a wife that the married might perhaps quarrel, and curse the one through whom they were joined. But he plainly affirmed that the priest ought to be present at such a request, since they were now agreed, so that their pacts and agreements might be either confirmed or blessed. It is the most ancient custom that the blessing of marriage be given by the priest in the Church, as the ancients put it. So it is read in the decrees of the popes Evaristus and Hormisdas (add Sixtus, according to Platina). In the Fourth Council of Carthage, chap. 13: When the bridegroom and bride are to be blessed by the priest, they shall be presented in the Church to the priest by their parents or bridesmen; and when they have received the blessing, they shall remain in virginity that same night out of reverence for the blessing. See Gratian's Decretum, part 2, cause 30, question 5. And so it has been kept from antiquity in the Church, that the ministers should confirm marriage and solemnly bless it, also to prevent clandestine marriages. Hence, among the canons of John the Metropolitan, Sigismund Baron of Herberstein reports in his commentary on Muscovite affairs: Marriage should be contracted only publicly in churches. The Papal Church goes to excess, teaching that marriage ought to be confirmed in the Church, namely because it is held to be a sacrament; but wrongly. On the other side the Brownists err, saying that marriage may not, or ought not, to be consecrated in the Church at all. Again wrongly. We keep the middle course, and teach that marriage may suitably be confirmed in the Church by the minister, yet need not be so from any necessity; for we equally approve marriage confirmed by the civil magistrate. The Lutherans go further and do not disapprove even of marriages confirmed privately at home, as may be seen from the letter of Jacob Rennecker to Schlüsselburg, which is the last of his letters. It is pleasing to quote the words of the most learned author of the Altare Damascenum, Didoclavius, as the title has it (really David Calderwood), p. 866: We approve a more frequent assembly too, yet we do not think that a public assembly of the whole particular Church must necessarily be present; and among us marriages are often celebrated outside the sacred and public gathering of the whole Church. For that action is not purely ecclesiastical, requiring the presence of the whole particular assembly of the Church of which the contracting persons are members, as the administration of the sacraments does. It is a civil contract, but also divine, because the authority of God intervenes, that is, the institution by which he has decreed that the bond of this contract is not to be lightly dissolved or violated; yet it does not follow that it must be celebrated only with the intervention of the Church, unless we wish everything God instituted, even if not for sacred use, to be celebrated in church. We do not exclude the presence of the whole Church, nor even of unbelievers or of anyone else who wishes to be present, just as it is beyond doubt that access to all was open at the gates of the cities; but we would deny that its presence is necessary. I think it is enough if the assembly was more frequent in a public place, provided it is not left to anyone's discretion to define its number. Time, place and assembly ought to be defined by laws, because of the inconveniences and dangers that can arise from clandestine marriages. We nevertheless do not despise the minister's blessing. The presence and blessing of the minister are not of the essence of the contract. So also among us the consecration of marriage takes place in different ways, either with the Church present or dismissed. Compare Amesius, Cas. Consc., book 5, chap. 36; Bucanus, Institutes of Theology, loc. 12, p. 1N; Bellarmine, On Marriage, book 1, chap. 32. He wishes to make a special controversy out of the fact that some of ours seem to refer matrimonial causes to the civil forum rather than the ecclesiastical; but the Brownists bring against us another dispute and quarrel from the other side, just as fruitlessly. Apology against the Oxford men, thes. 6; and Robinson, ch. 6. In the place where he treated this, as well as the other points in the preceding articles, he rightly adds: These are the points on which we dissent from the Belgic Churches; and they are neither so trivial that they should be neglected by those to whom nothing proceeding from the sacred mouth or Spirit of the Lord Christ seems the least thing, nor so great that they break the bond of fraternal charity and communion. Finally, the Directory of Public Worship in England has already settled this point, in the chapter on the confirmation of marriage: Although marriage is not a sacrament, nor peculiar to the Church of God, but common to mankind and in which the commonwealth in any state has an interest; yet because those who enter into marriage do so in the Lord, and in such a state especially need instruction in direction and admonition from the Word of God, and the divine blessing upon them, we judge it fitting that marriage be confirmed by a lawful minister of the Word, who may at the same time admonish them and pray for the blessing.

units.la: Præterea disputant Brovvnistæ super formulis, an adhibere aliquas in precibus liceat, adeoque an orationem Dominicam ipsam, de quâ idem intelligunt, an non? Haud licere contendunt, sive alias quasvis formulas sumamus, sive orationem Dominicam. Imo existimant Antichristianum esse, & superstitiosum: datamque à Christo orationem Dominicam, non ut precandi essem formula, quâ utamur, sed ut pro exemplari solum inserviret, doceretque quomodo & quâ methodo precationes nostras componere & instituere debeamus. Causataque hæc illorum opinio ex libro Communium precum, in Ecclesiâ Anglicanâ olim usitato, cui subscribere anno cIↄ Iↄ lxxı. recusarunt. Verum uti in aliis articulis, ita in hoc peccant, non quod licere putant arbitrariâ ratione & absque formulis precari, quod utique agnoscimus; sed quod existiment, aliter non licere. Nos nequaquam formularum necessitatem urgemus, neque doctrinâ, neque praxi: tantum de jure quæritur, num liceat absque peccato illis quoque uti. Interim ut spiritum precum exeramus & exerceamus, atque adsuescamus pro rerum & temporum ratione liberas ex animo preces formare ac fundere, omnino consultum: sed quod si non liceat formulas, præcipue in gratiam rudium atque imperitiorum, tum etiam consensus testandi causâ, adhibere, necdum videre possumus. Quâ ratione Calvinus scripsit ad Prorectorem Angliæ a. cIↄ Iↄ xlvı. Quod ad formulam precum & rituum Ecclesiasticorum, valde probo, ut certa illa extet, à quâ posteribus discedere in functione sua non liceat, tam ut consulatur quorundam simplicitati et imperitiæ, quam ut certius ita constet omnium inter se Ecclesiarum consensus. Postremò etiam ut obviam eatur desultoriæ quorundam levitati qui novationes quasdam affectant, uti eò pertinere catechismum ipsum ante ostendi. Sic igitur statuum esse catechismum oportet, sacramentorum administrationem, publicam item precum formulam. Sed non hoc eò pertinet ut ipsius politici ordinis in Ecclesiâ occasione, vigor illé nativus prædicationis Evangelii ullo modo consenescat &c. &c. Neque improbasse Calvinum liberam precationum, pro rerum statu, ex animo potius, quam libro, formandarum rationem, vel suo exemplo docuit, quando post Praelectiones suas, passim alias & novas precationes facit, utiex ejus in Iezechielem, & Prophetas minores Commentario apparet. Scilicet hoc est, quod Tertullianus dixit, in Apolog. sine monitore, quia de pectore oramus. Nec debere nos formulas sequi, neque non licere iis uti, sed posse citra vitium adhibere, & cum fructu etiam servare aliquando, asserimus. Harmonia Synodorum Belgicarum, digesta per S. R. edita a Festo Hommio, cap. xi. §. 11. ita habet. Minister preces vel dictante Spiritu, vel certa sibi propositâ formulâ concipiet. Consule Amesium, Cas. Consc. lib. iv. cap. xvii. Balduinum, Cas. Consc. lib. ii. cap. viii. caf. xiii. Professores Leidenses, Synopsi Pur. Theol. Disp. xxxvi. thes. xxxiii. xxxiv. Richard Bernard, The Errours of Barrow confuted, pag. 191. Rheterfurd, pro Presbyterio Scoticano, Anglicè, pag. 326. Rob. Abbot, a Triall of our Churchforsakers pag. 20). 214. Apollonium, cap. vii. Calderwood, in eximio opere Altaris Damasceni, cap. x. pag. 613. adversus Liturgiam Anglicanam disputans, quæ propositio precum libro libertatem precandi tollebat, astringebatque ad præscriptas formas: habemus quidem nos, inquit, in Ecclesiâ nostrâ Scoticâ Agendas, & ordinem in sacris celebrandis servandum, sed nemo alligatur precibus aut exhortationibus liturgiae nostrae, proponuntur tantùm ut paradigmata, quibus precum aut exhortationum materia & forma quoad substantialia indicantur, non ut eisdem verbis adstringantur ministri. Totos ego tredecim annos, quibus functus sum ministerio, sive in sacramentis, sive in aliis sacris celebrandis, exhortationibus aut precibus quae extant in Agenda nostra, nunquam usus sum. Sic etiam alii complures; & omnibus etiam liberum est idem facere. Et postea: Nec tamen adeo rigidus sum, ut rudioribus primùm oraturis hac admi-nicumicula, semper praescriptas verborum formulas omnino denegem, si simul doceantur sic memoriae infigere, ut possint affectui accommodare, & sic affectus verba praecedere possent; & ipsi ad perfectiora tendere, nec in rudimentis ista forma herere. Socrates in historia testatus fuit, lib. v. cap. xxi. In omnibus ubique regionibus non potest reperire duas Ecclesias, quae orando plane consentiant. Adeo non certae, eadem vel communes precum ubique observatae formulae, sed agnita hac in re Ecclesiarum libertas semper fuit. Confessio Helvetica posterior, cap. xxiiii. Neque oportet preces publicas, quoad formam & tempus, in omnibus Ecclesiis esse pares. Libertate enim sua utantur Ecclesiae quaelibet. Iam etiam in Ecclesia Anglicana Directorium cultus publici, authoritate Parlamenti constitutum a. cIↄ Iↄ cxlv. nullas precum formulas continet, solum modum, methodum, & orandi regulas.
