Et orationem Dominicam non esse solum exemplar faciendarum precationum, verum formulam quoque, precationis pro prece dicendam, praeterquam verba Christi, in ejus commendationem prolata, sic igitur orate, Matth. vi. 9. & quando oratis, dicite, Luc. xi. 2. ipsa forma, qua proposita, arguit: nam formulam orationis principium ejus, & finis, totusque contextus significant. Accedit usus, & praxis Ecclesiae Christianae, ea oratione semper usae. Tertullianus, de orat. Deus solus docere potuit, ut se vellet orari. Ab ipso igitur ordinata religio orationis, & de spiritu ipsius jam tunc cum ex ore divino ferretur, animata sua privilegio ascendit in coelum, commendans Patri, quae Filius dixit. Antea, in hac oratione breviarium totius Evangelii comprehendi, dixerat. Cyprianus, de orat. Dominic. Quae enim potest magis spiritualis esse oratio, quam quae a Christo nobis data est, a quo nobis & Spiritus sanctus missus est? quae vera magis apud Patrem precatio, quam quae a Filio, qui est veritas, de ejus ore prolata est? & quae sequuntur. Augustinus, epist. lix. explicans differentiam, quae est 1 Tim. 11. 1. inter precationes, orationes &c. precationes vult esse, quas facimus in celebratione sacramentorum, antequam illud, quod est Domini mensa, incipiat benedici. Deinde, orationes dici, cum benedicitur & sanctificatur, & ad distribuendum comminuitur: quam totam petitionem fere omnis Ecclesia, inquit, Dominica oratione concludit. Observa, Augustinum dicere, cum benedicitur, & sanctificatur sacramentum, orationem Dominicam conjunctim cum illa petitione dici, uti quoque Gregorius, lib. vii. epist. lxiv. orationem vero Dominicam idcirco mox post precem dicimus, quia mos Apostolorum fuit, ut ad ipsam solummodo orationem, oblationis hostiam consecrarent. Vide, ad hanc orationem simpliciter fieri consecrationem, non vero post & super jam consecratum panem demum orationem dici, quomodo illa Gregorii verba trahit & explicat Baronius, Annal. Tom. viii, Anno DXC ix. num. xx. Augustinus, Serm. lxxxiii. de diversis: post orationem Dominicam quam accepistis & reddidistis, dicitur pax vobiscum. Idem, serm. ccxv. de Tempore: Symbolum vel orationem Dominicam & ipsi tenete, & filiis vestris ostendite. Nam nescio qua fronte se Christianum dicat, qui paucos versus in symbolo vel oratione dominica orare dissimulat. Chrysostomus, orat. in Eutropium: aut quomodo hoc casu soluto, sacramenta contrectabitis, & precationem illam dicetis, qua rogare jubemur, dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut & nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris: si a debitore vestro pænam exigatis? Atque huc spectat argumentum illud, quo Orthodoxi pugnabant adversus Pelagianos, eorumque præsumtam perfectionem ex oratione Dominica, quæ jubet dicere: remitte nobis debita nostra. Ter in die orationem Dominicam recitare jubet Auctor Constit. lib. vii. cap. xxv. Et in Concilio Toletano iv. can. ix. carpuntur, qui non quotidie, sed Dominica solum die, orationem illam proferebant: Nonnulli sacerdotes in Hispania reperiuntur tur qui dominicam orationem, quam Salvator noster docet & praecepit, non quotidie, sed tantum die dominica dicunt. Attamen, quia quotidiana oratio est, quotidie quoque ut detur, dici oportet. Lutherus Tom. v. in Catechismo majori, ad Orationis Dominicae explicationem, inde argumentum precandi petit, quod quomodo orare debemus, formulam praescripsit Dominus: Praeter hac unam hoc ipso ad orandum non mediocriter pelliciendi & pertrahendi essemus, quod Deus juxta praeceptum & promissionem etiam antevortit nos, ipse verba ac modum orandi nobis praescribens, ac velut pramanfum in os inferens, quomodo & quid nos orare oporteat. Non tamen haec ita capienda, quasi vel nullam aliam liceret Deo facere orationem, praeter Dominicam; vel illa sola dicenda semper & repetenda ad quosvis casus esset, quod Pontificiorum vitium est, suum Pater noster ad quaevis gementium; vel quasi sola Deo grata esset illa precatio, aut nulla constaret, cui ea non subjungeretur. Vide Amesium, Cas. Consc. lib. iv. cap. xvii. cujus sententiam discussit in Theologia Casuum Consc. Germanice, Andreas Keslerus cap. xi. Sed agnito in Dominica oratione precationum faciendarum exemplari optimo, vel idea, potest & ipsa rite pro prece adhiberi; quod & Robinsonus concedit: non dubito, quin rite & pie asserpari possit in precando Deum, haec ipsa verborum formula: modo absit opinio partim necessaria, qua se astringi putant superstitiosi homines voculis, & syllabis: partim perfectionis, quae plurimi existimant, se tum demum perfecte precatos fuisse, quando hanc formulam conceptis verbis recitarent. Apolog. cap. iii. Neque ego hoc jeci fundamentum repudiatae vobiscum communionis, inquit Ainsworthus, loquens de usu orationis Dominicae: apud Pagetum pag. 63. &c. Augustinus, epist. cxxi. ad Probam: Et si per omnia precationum sanctarum verba discurras: quantum existimo nihil invenies quod non in ipsa dominica contineas & concludas oratio. Unde liberum est.
units.tr: Moreover, the Brownists dispute about set forms: whether it is lawful to use any in prayer, and so whether the Lord's Prayer itself, which they understand in this sense, is lawful. They contend that it is not lawful, whether we use some other set form or the Lord's Prayer. They even think such use is antichristian and superstitious, and that Christ gave the Lord's Prayer not as a form of words for us to use in praying, but only to serve as a model, teaching us how and by what method we ought to compose and arrange our prayers. This opinion of theirs arose from the Book of Common Prayer, once in use in the English Church, which they refused to subscribe in the year 1571. But as they err in other articles, so they err in this one: not because they think it lawful to pray in an arbitrary manner and without forms (which we certainly grant), but because they hold that it is not lawful to pray in any other way. We by no means press the necessity of forms, either in doctrine or in practice. The only question is about right: whether it is lawful, without sin, to use them as well. Meanwhile, it is entirely advisable that we should exercise and practise the spirit of prayer, and accustom ourselves to form and pour out free prayers from the heart, according to the circumstances of things and times. But that it is not lawful to use forms, especially for the sake of the unlearned and inexperienced, and also to bear witness to agreement, we cannot yet see. For this reason Calvin wrote to the Protector of England in the year 1546: As for a form of prayers and of ecclesiastical rites, I greatly approve that there should be a certain established form, from which it is not lawful for those who come after to depart in their office, both so that the simplicity and inexperience of some may be consulted, and so that the agreement of all the Churches among themselves may be more certainly established. Lastly, too, so that a stop may be put to the fickle levity of certain men who aim at novelties, as I showed before that the catechism itself serves this end. Thus it is fitting that there be a catechism set by public authority, the administration of the sacraments, and likewise a public form of prayer. But this is not so that the native vigour of the preaching of the Gospel should in any way grow old through the occasion of the political order itself in the Church, etc., etc. Nor did Calvin, either by his teaching or by his own example, disapprove of the method of forming free prayers from the heart, rather than from a book, according to the state of things; for after his lectures he everywhere makes other and new prayers, as appears from his commentary on Ezekiel and the Minor Prophets. Clearly this is what Tertullian said in the Apology: without a prompter, because we pray from the heart. We assert that we ought not to be bound to forms, nor is it unlawful to use them, but that they may be used without fault and sometimes kept with profit. The Harmony of the Belgic Synods, drawn up by S. R. and published by Festus Hommius, chapter 11, §11, says: The minister shall frame his prayers either by the dictation of the Spirit, or with a certain form set before him. Consult Amesius, Cases of Conscience, book 4, chapter 17; Baldwin, Cases of Conscience, book 2, chapter 8, case 13; the Leiden professors, Synopsis of Pure Theology, disputation 36, theses 33 and 34; Richard Bernard, The Errours of Barrow confuted, p. 191; Rutherford, for the Scottish Presbytery, in English, p. 326; Robert Abbot, A Triall of our Church-forsakers, pp. 20, 214; Apollonius, chapter 7; Calderwood, in his excellent work The Altar of Damascus, chapter 10, p. 613, disputing against the English Liturgy, which proposed prayers in a book and so took away the liberty of praying, and bound men to prescribed forms. He says: We indeed have in our Scottish Church Agendas, and an order to be observed in celebrating the sacred rites, but no one is bound to the prayers or exhortations of our liturgy. They are set forth only as patterns, by which the matter and form of prayers or exhortations are indicated as to their essentials, not so that ministers are bound to the same words. For all the thirteen years in which I have served in the ministry, whether in the sacraments or in other sacred rites, I have never used the exhortations or prayers that are found in our Agenda. So also many others; and it is free for everyone to do the same. And afterwards: Nor am I so rigid as to deny altogether to beginners, who are to pray, these little props of prescribed forms of words, provided they are at the same time taught to fix them in the memory so that they may suit their feeling, and so that feeling may go before the words, and that they may themselves press on to more perfect things, and not cling to that form in the rudiments. Socrates testified in his history, book 5, chapter 21: In all regions everywhere one cannot find two Churches which agree entirely in prayer. So there never were fixed, identical, or common forms of prayer observed everywhere; the liberty of the Churches in this matter has always been recognised. The Second Helvetic Confession, chapter 24: Public prayers need not be alike in all Churches as to form and time. For any Churches may use their liberty. Further, in the English Church the Directory of Public Worship, established by authority of Parliament in the year 1645, contains no set forms of prayer, only the manner, method, and rules of praying. And that the Lord's Prayer is not only a model for making prayers, but also a form of words to be said as a prayer, is shown by the form itself, in which it is set forth, besides the words of Christ, uttered in recommendation of it: Thus therefore pray, Matt. 6:9, and when you pray, say, Luke 11:2. For its beginning, its end, and the whole context signify a formula of prayer. Add to this the custom and practice of the Christian Church, which has always used that prayer. Tertullian, on prayer: God alone could teach us how he wished to be prayed to. So the religion of prayer was ordained by him, and its spirit, already when it was delivered from the divine mouth, ascended into heaven by its own privilege, commending to the Father what the Son had said. Earlier, he had said that in this prayer the summary of the whole Gospel is comprehended. Cyprian, on the Lord's Prayer: For what prayer can be more spiritual than that which was given us by Christ, by whom the Holy Spirit too was sent to us? What prayer is truer before the Father than that which was spoken by the Son, who is the truth, from his own mouth? and what follows. Augustine, in letter 59, explaining the difference which is in 1 Tim. 2:1 between prayers, orations, etc., holds that prayers are those which we make in the celebration of the sacraments, before the thing which is the table of the Lord begins to be blessed. Then they are called orations, when it is blessed and sanctified, and broken for distribution: and, he says, almost the whole Church concludes all this petition with the Lord's Prayer. Observe that Augustine says that when the sacrament is blessed and sanctified, the Lord's Prayer is said together with that petition; so also Gregory, book 7, letter 64. We say the Lord's Prayer immediately after the prayer, because it was the custom of the Apostles to consecrate the sacrificial victim of the oblation only by that prayer itself. Notice that consecration takes place simply at this prayer, and not that the prayer is only said afterwards and over the bread already consecrated, as Baronius twists and explains those words of Gregory, Annals, vol. 8, year 590, n. 20. Augustine, sermon 83, on various subjects: After the Lord's Prayer, which you have received and returned, the peace is said: "Peace be with you." The same, sermon 215, on the time: Hold the creed or the Lord's Prayer yourselves, and show it to your children. For I do not know with what face a man can call himself a Christian who pretends not to pray a few verses of the creed or the Lord's Prayer. Chrysostom, in his oration against Eutropius: Or how, in this condition, will you handle the sacraments, and say that prayer by which we are commanded to ask: "Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors", if you exact punishment from your debtor? To this point also belongs the argument by which the Orthodox fought against the Pelagians and their presumed perfection, drawn from the Lord's Prayer, which bids us say: "Forgive us our debts." The author of the Constitutions, book 7, chapter 25, bids us recite the Lord's Prayer three times a day. And at the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 9, those are rebuked who recited that prayer not daily but on the Lord's Day only: Some priests are found in Spain who say the Lord's Prayer, which our Saviour teaches and commands, not daily, but only on the Lord's Day. Yet, since it is a daily prayer, it ought to be said daily as well. Luther, vol. 5, in the Larger Catechism, in his explanation of the Lord's Prayer, takes from it an argument for praying: since we ought to pray, the Lord prescribed a form; and besides this, we would be not a little enticed and drawn on to pray by the fact that God, according to his command and promise, goes before us, prescribing to us the words and manner of praying, and, as it were, putting a morsel into our mouth, how and what we ought to pray. Yet these things are not to be taken as if it were not allowed to make any other prayer to God besides the Lord's Prayer; or as if that alone were always to be said and repeated for every occasion (which is the fault of the Papists, who have their own "Our Father" for every groaning person); or as if that prayer alone were pleasing to God, or as if no prayer was valid to which it was not added. See Amesius, Cases of Conscience, book 4, chapter 17, whose opinion Andreas Kessler discussed, in German, in his Theology of Cases of Conscience, chapter 11. But, once the Lord's Prayer is acknowledged as the best model, or idea, for making prayers, that very form may also be properly used as a prayer; and Robinson grants this: "I do not doubt that this very form of words may be properly and piously used in praying to God, provided only that there is not the partly necessary opinion, by which superstitious men think themselves bound to little words and syllables, and partly the opinion of perfection, which very many think they have then only prayed perfectly when they recited this formula word for word." Apology, chapter 3. "Nor have I laid this foundation for the rejection of communion with you," says Ainsworth, speaking of the use of the Lord's Prayer, in Paget, p. 63, etc. Augustine, letter 121 to Proba: "And if you run through all the holy words of prayers, you will find, as I think, nothing which you do not contain and enclose in the Lord's Prayer itself. Hence it is free."

units.la: Vide Amesium, Cas. Consc. lib. iv. cap. xvii. est aliis atque aliis verbis, eadem tamen in orando dicere, sed non esse debet liberum alia dicere.
units.tr: See Amesius, Cases of Conscience, book iv, chapter xvii: one may say the same things in prayer in other and different words, but it ought not to be free to say other things.

units.la: Absurdum vero quod ad haec de formulis etiam trabunt usum Catechismorum, quos propter eandem causam explodunt; & Symbolum, quod Apostolicum vulgo dicitur, saltem catholicum est: nempe quia formulæ quædam sint, quas in cultu, vel in religionis officiis observamus. Quæ omnia eliminanda censent, ut apocrypha, tenendumque solum & unicum Dei verbum. Propter eandem causam illorum aliqui abstinent à Psalterio, in formam metricam redacto. Alibi factum, ut abolito cantandi in Ecclesiâ ritu ac consuetudine, unus singulari videlicet ad hoc dono instructus cantaret, quod ei suggessisset Spiritus, audientibus reliquis. Alibi, sive apud Brownistas, sive Independentes, in totum cantionis Ecclesiasticæ praxis omittitur, quasi ceremoniale aliquid, aut pædagogicum, vel Papale sonans, ac referens.
units.tr: It is absurd that they also draw from these matters about forms the use of the Catechisms, which they reject for the same reason, and the Creed commonly called the Apostles', which at least is catholic. Their reason is that these are fixed formulas which we use in worship or in the duties of religion. They judge that all of these should be removed as apocryphal, and that only the Word of God should be held as the one and sole standard. For the same reason some of them abstain from the Psalter, which has been put into metrical form. Elsewhere it has happened that, with the custom and practice of singing in church abolished, one person, gifted for this purpose alone, sang whatever the Spirit had suggested to him while the others listened. Elsewhere, whether among the Brownists or the Independents, the practice of singing in church is omitted altogether, as if it were something ceremonial or childish, or smacked of and recalled the Papacy.

units.la: Et quis recenseat omnia, quæ illi homines, aut illorum aliqui pro singularitate & pervicaciâ suâ contra communem & antiquum Ecclesiæ morem aut observant, aut omittunt, de agapis, de osculo charitatis &c. de quibus Thomas Edwardi, in Antapologiâ contra Independentes; & peculiari libro rit. Gangræna, & ex eo potissimum, Baylie, Honorius Reggius, & libellus Belgicus Tumultuum Anglicorum.
units.tr: And who could list everything that these men, or some of them, either observe or omit against the common and ancient custom of the Church, out of their singularity and obstinacy: concerning the agapae, the kiss of charity, and so on. On these see Thomas Edwards, in his Antapologia against the Independents, and his special book, the Gangraena, and above all from it Baillie, Honorius Reggius, and the Dutch pamphlet Tumults of the English.

units.la: Postremo disputant Brownistæ super baptismo impertiendo infanti, cuius neuter parens sit membrum, & in communione Ecclesiæ: id quod neutiquam faciendum existimant. Apolog. ad Oxoniens. thes. x. Robinsonus, Apol. cap. 11. Lib. A Guide unto Sion. pag. 41. Nos sacramentum uti minime profanandum novimus, neque nisi con fœderatis Christi applicandum, ita ut infantes ex Christianis parentibus natos & oblatos Ecclesiæ, arceamus propter parentum proximorum negligentiam, & quia hi non sint membra Ecclesiæ, in comcommunione S. Coenæ, impetrare à nobis non possumus, neque probare, ut quis sibi arroget judicium Dei, de fœderis sui gratiâ aut amplitudine definiendi, aut ab eo alios amovendi & secludendi, atque existimamus, in dubiis promiores nos debere esse ad judicandum de aliis clementius, quam severius. Ita Calvinus, in epist. ad Ioh. Knoxum, a. MDLIX. epist. pag. 322. ubicunque non intercidit, vel exstincta fuit Christianæ professio, fraudantur jure suo infantes, si à communi symbolo arcentur. lege, si placet, integram epistolam Anicæ ad Farellum, a. MDLIIII. de baptizando infante parentum Papisticorum, sed quem avia offerebat: quem Dominus gratiam suam in multas ætates extendat, eam astringere non est nostrum. Et certe locum hic habet vulgaris regula: favores esse ampliandos. Adde Bezam, epist. x. Zanchium, in iv. Præcept. sol. 743. Confer, quæ hac super re disputat Ioh. Forbesius, Instruct. Historicæ Theolog. lib. x. cap. x. sub finem. Maccovius, Theol. Polemica cap. xxi. qu. iii. Si illi tantum baptizandi qui sunt in fœdere: Ergo liberi excommunicatorum non sunt baptizandi. Verum primùm, Ergo. Resp. Non tantum ratio habenda parentum, sed & avorum & proavorum. Similiter Amesius, de Pædobaptismo, pag. 219. Robertus Puppius. de Pædobaptismo, pag. 64. Rhetersford, pro presbyterio Scoticano, cap. xii. Abbotus, of Churchforsakers, pag. 55. Appollonius, cap. v. qu. iv.
units.tr: Finally, the Brownists dispute about administering baptism to an infant neither of whose parents is a member in communion with the Church, which they think should in no way be done. Apology to the Oxford theses, thesis x. Robinson, Apology, chapter 11; book A Guide unto Sion, p. 41: "We know that the sacrament must by no means be profaned, nor applied except to the confederates of Christ. So we cannot bring ourselves to keep away from the Church infants born of Christian parents and offered to the Church, on account of the negligence of their nearest parents, and because these are not members of the Church, from communion in the Lord's Supper. Nor can we prove that anyone should arrogate to himself the judgment of God, to define the grace and extent of His covenant, or to remove and shut out others from it. We think that in doubtful cases we ought to be more inclined to judge others mercifully than severely." So Calvin, in his letter to John Knox, 1559, p. 322: Wherever the Christian profession has not perished or been extinguished, infants are defrauded of their right if they are kept from the common symbol. Read, if you like, the whole letter of Anna to Farel, 1554, concerning the baptism of the infant of Papist parents which the grandmother offered: May the Lord extend His grace over many generations; it is not ours to restrict it. And certainly the common rule applies here: favours are to be enlarged. Add Beza, letter x; Zanchius, on the fourth Commandment, p. 743. Compare what John Forbes disputes on this matter in his Instructions of Historical Theology, book x, chapter x, near the end. Maccovius, Polemical Theology, chapter xxi, question iii: If only those who are in the covenant are to be baptized, then the children of the excommunicated are not to be baptized. But first, the inference does not follow. Answer: not only the parents, but also the grandparents and great-grandparents must be taken into account. Similarly Amesius, On Infant Baptism, p. 219; Robert Puppius, On Infant Baptism, p. 64; Rutherford, for the Scottish presbytery, chapter xii; Abbot, Of Church-forsakers, p. 55; Apollonius, chapter v, question iv.

units.la: Turbatâ supra modum Angliâ, inter varias hæreses, errores, atque deliria, quæ eam exagitant & discerpunt, quum haud minimam partem faciat etiam Antinomismus, de hoc impræsentiarum nonnihil addere instituti ratio poscere videtur. Ac primùm Antinomorum, sive qui legi morali, ejusque in religione usui variis modis obloquuti semper fuere, tres in Ecclesiâ constituimus periodos. Primam tempore Patrum, in primitivâ Ecclesiâ; alteram, tempore Reformationis, tertiam hodie, præcipuè in Angliâ. Prima fuit tempore PaPatrum, Augustini, & aliorum. Quippe in libro de Haeresibus cap. 1 iv. in describenda haeresi Aetianorum, discipulique ejus Eunomii, ( qui tempore Epiphanii, id est, circa a. cccxt. adhuc superfuit. uti hic scribit lib. 111. contra Haeres. tom. 1. in fine) ferunt etiam inquit; usque adeo fuisse bonis moribus inimicum, ut asseverarent, quod nihil cuiquam obesset quorumlibet peccatorum perpetratio, ac perseverantia peccatorum, si hujus, quae ab illo docebatur, fidei particeps esset. In quod abusos fuisse loco Joannis xvii. 3. Haec est vita aeterna, ut te cognoscant &c. scribit in Annotationibus suis ad illum Augustini locum, Lamb. Danaeus: qui ibidem addit, hoc antiquum dogma fuisse Severianorum. Alios Adversarios legis & Prophetarum nominavit Augustinus, nempe qui scripta eorum everterent. Tomo sexto operum illius duo libri extant, contra Adversarium legis & Prophetarum: cujus inscriptionis rationem dans in ipso primi libri vestibulo, sic scribit: Librum quem misistis fratres dilectissimi, nescio cujus haeretici, inventum sicut scripsistis, in platea maritima, cum venalis codex ipse ferretur, & concurrentibus turbis periculosa curiositate & delectatione legeretur, ut quanto possem compendio responderem, prius quaesivi cujusnam esset Auctoris. Non enim soli Manichaei legem prophetasque condemnant, sed & Marcionistae, & alii nonnulli, quorum secta non ita innotuerant populis Christianis. Iste autem totus adversarius, libri illius anonymi auctor, perpetuo adversus fidem & veritatem Scripturarum Propheticarum disputat. Unde Augustin. lib. 11. Iam nunc ea discutienda sunt, quae iste de novi Testamenti libris suffragari sibi arbitratur adversus propheticas literas, tanquam ex apostoli Christi sua sententia condemnaverint. Quod ergo prophanas & aniles fabulas, & genealogias infinitas appellasse Apostolum existimat divina eloquia legis & prophetarum &c. Adversus quae egregium & sedulum vindicem se Augustinus praebuit. Legem Dei Manichaei, & Marcionitae rejiciebant: & hoc quoque Severiani. Similiter de Eunomianis, Eunomianis, Iohannitis. Verum non id hic spectamus, quod Scripturae legis se quidam opponunt, illam falsam asserendo, quod improbissimum: sed quod Scripturae totius veritatem divinitatemque agnoscentes, de usu legis, quem sub Novo jam Testamento habeat, contendunt.
units.tr: With England thrown beyond measure into turmoil, amid the various heresies, errors and delusions that harass and tear it apart, and since Antinomianism forms by no means the smallest part, the plan of this work seems to require that something be added about it at present. First, then, concerning the Antinomians, or those who have always in various ways objected to the moral law and its use in religion, we distinguish three periods in the Church: the first in the time of the Fathers, in the primitive Church; the second in the time of the Reformation; the third today, especially in England. The first belongs to the time of the Fathers, of Augustine and others. For in his book On Heresies, chapter liv, describing the heresy of the Aetians and of their disciple Eunomius (who was still alive in the time of Epiphanius, that is, about the year 360, as he writes in book iii of Against Heresies, vol. i, near the end), Epiphanius says: "They also say that it is so hostile to good morals that they assert that the commission of any sins whatever, and perseverance in sins, does no harm to anyone, provided he shares in the faith taught by them." Lambert Danaeus, in his notes on Augustine's passage, writes that this was abused on John 17:3, This is eternal life, that they may know thee; and he adds in the same place that this ancient dogma belonged to the Severians. Augustine named others "Adversaries of the Law and the Prophets", that is, those who overturned their writings. Two books of his, Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, survive in the sixth volume of his works. Giving the reason for this title at the very beginning of the first book, he writes: "The book which you sent, dearest brothers, by some heretic whose name I do not know, I found as you wrote, in the maritime street, where the book itself was being sold, and was being read by crowds gathering with a dangerous curiosity and delight. So that I might answer as briefly as I could, I first asked who its author was." For not only the Manichaeans condemn the law and the prophets, but also the Marcionites and some others whose sects were not so well known to Christian peoples. That whole adversary, however, the author of that anonymous book, disputes continually against the faith and truth of the prophetic Scriptures. Hence Augustine, in book ii: "Now must be examined those things which he thinks support him from the books of the New Testament against the prophetic writings, as if the Apostle of Christ had condemned them by his own judgment. Because he thinks the Apostle called the divine oracles of the law and the prophets 'profane and old-wives' fables' and 'endless genealogies'..." Against these things Augustine showed himself an outstanding and diligent defender. The Manichaeans and Marcionites rejected the law of God, and so did the Severians. Likewise with the Eunomians and the Johannites. We are not here concerned, however, with the fact that some men set themselves against the Scriptures of the law, asserting it to be false, which is most wicked; but with those who acknowledge the truth and divinity of all Scripture and yet dispute about the use that the law has under the New Testament.

units.la: Lex autem, vel libros legis notat, illam Scripturae partem, quae Mosi tribuitur; vel in genere tabulam praeceptorum Mosaicorum: quae varia, uti notum, & vel morales sunt, vel caeremoniales, vel judiciales: aut denique solam primam illam praeceptorum partem moralem: quo sensu in praesenti disquisitione legis vocem accipimus.
units.tr: The term "law", however, denotes either that part of Scripture which is ascribed to Moses, or in general the tablet of the Mosaic precepts, which, as is well known, are various: moral, ceremonial, or judicial; or finally only that first part of the precepts, the moral part. It is in this sense that we take the word "law" in the present inquiry.

units.la: Altera periodus Antinomorum fuit tempore Reformationis, quando Iohannes Agricola Islebius, in Schola Islebiâ Theologiae Lector, ad a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxv iii. docere coepit, legem sub Evangelio praedicandam non esse, nec imo Decalogum, neque ejus concione perparandos, concutiendos aut emolliendos hominum animos, videlicet sub gratiâ nunc, non sub paedagogiâ & terrore legis constitutis: solummodo annunciandum Evangelium esse, credendumque vel si meretrix, si scortator, adulter sis &c. te in viâ salutis esse, modo Christum teneas: quidem cavenda peccata, & justitiae operandum, verum non ex concione vel praecepto legis, sed ex libertate spiritus Christi, & Evangelii id faciendum, & peccatis non obstantibus applicandam sibi Christum, ejusque promissiones esse. Apud Lutherum, Tom. i. Oper Latin. extant Antinomi cujusdam (opinor Agricolae) positiones, 1. Poenitentia docenda est non ex Decalogo, aut ullâ lege Mosis, sed ex violatione filii per Evangelium. 6. Ex concionibus Pauli & Barnabae satis manifestum est, non esse opus Lege ad ullam partem justificationis. 13. Quare pro conservandâ puritate doctrinae, resistendum est iis, qui docent, Evangelium non praedicandum, nisi animis prius quassatis & con-
units.tr: The second period of the Antinomians was in the time of the Reformation, when John Agricola of Eisleben, theology lecturer in the school at Eisleben, about the year 1538, began to teach that the law is not to be preached under the Gospel, nor even the Decalogue, and that men's minds are not to be prepared, shaken or softened by sermons, since they are now established under grace and not under the schoolmaster and the terror of the law. Only the Gospel is to be proclaimed, and it is to be believed that, even if you are a harlot, a fornicator, or an adulterer, you are on the way of salvation, provided you hold to Christ. Sins are indeed to be avoided, and righteousness practised, but not from the sermon or command of the law; it is to be done from the freedom of the Spirit of Christ and of the Gospel, and, sins notwithstanding, Christ and His promises are to be applied to oneself. In Luther's Latin Works, vol. i, are the propositions of a certain Antinomian (I think Agricola's): 1. Repentance is to be taught not from the Decalogue, or from any law of Moses, but from the violation of the Son through the Gospel. 6. From the sermons of Paul and Barnabas it is clear enough that there is no need of the Law for any part of justification. 13. Therefore, to preserve the purity of doctrine, we must resist those who teach that the Gospel is not to be preached unless hearts have first been shaken and con-

units.la: contritis tritis per legem. 14. Qui enim affingunt verbis Christi im-proprium sermonem, & dicunt primum Legem, deinde Evangelium docendum esse, hi sunt verborum Christi contortores, non enim consistunt in simplicitate verborum Christi. Postea tanquam impuros articulos rejicit 1. In Visitatione Saxonica, Quia Christus mandat praedicandum esse poenitentiam & remissionem peccatorum in suo nomine, Ergo docendus est Decalogus. 3. In Galat. dicit Lutherus, Legis proprium officium esse, ut eo facilius agnoscat Christum. Tales loci multi sunt in eodem commentario, quos ut erroneos improbamus, ut puritas doctrina conservari possit.
units.tr: contrite, crushed and worn down by the law. 14. For those who attach an improper meaning to the words of Christ, and say that the Law must be taught first and the Gospel afterwards, are twisters of the words of Christ, for they do not keep to the simplicity of Christ's words. Then he rejects as unclean these articles: 1. In the Saxon Visitation: because Christ commands that repentance and the remission of sins be preached in his name, therefore the Decalogue must be taught. 3. In the Galatians commentary Luther says that the proper office of the Law is to lead a man more easily to recognise Christ. There are many such passages in the same commentary, which we reject as erroneous, so that the purity of doctrine may be preserved.

units.la: Adducuntur postea & alii articuli Antinomici, de quibus addubito, an omnes bene Auctoribus suis attribuantur, vel eorum mentem exprimant, ut primus Lex non est digna, ut vocetur verbum Dei. tum ultimi, quibus reprehenditur dictum Petri 11.Pet.1.Certam facientes vocationem vestram per bona opera. Denique 12. Als baldt du gedenckst / So und so solt es in der Christenheit zugehen/es solten seine / erbare / züchtige / heilige / teusche Leute sein/ So hastu des Euang: ist schon gefeilet cap. 6. Luc. Quae neque cum praecedentibus positionibus, neque cum modestia & probitate Theologi, vel Christiani hominis convenire videntur. Caeteras theses illis communiter adscribi videmus: 1. Bistu ein Hure / Bube / Ehebrecher / oder sonst ein Sunder / Gleubstu / so bistu im wege der seligkeit. 3. Wenn du mitten in der sünden steckest und bist aufs höchste / Gleubstu / so bistu mitten in der seligheit. 4. Decalogus gehöret auff das Nathans / nicht auff den Predigstuel. 5. Alle die mit Mose umbgehen / müssen zum Teufel fahren / An gelgen mit Mose. 6. Wir sollen nicht die Menschen bereiten zum Euangelio durch die predigt des Gesetzes / Gott mus es thun / das werck ist seyn. Lutherus illis positionibus & articulis oppositi disputationes quinq; , eodem anno: sextam a.cIↄIↄxl. quibus Antinomorum delìria egregie perstrinxit & confutavit.
units.tr: Afterwards other Antinomian articles are cited, and I doubt whether all of them are rightly attributed to their authors, or express their meaning. Such are the first, The Law is not worthy to be called the word of God, and the last ones, in which the saying of Peter, 2 Pet. 1, Make your calling sure by good works, is found fault with. Finally, number 12: As soon as you think: thus and so it should go in Christendom, it should have its people be honourable, decent, holy, German folk, then you have already polished the Gospel. Luke 6. These do not seem to agree either with the preceding positions or with the modesty and uprightness of a theologian or a Christian man. We see the following theses are commonly ascribed to them: 1. If you are a whore, rascal, adulterer, or otherwise a sinner, believe it, and you are on the way to salvation. 3. If you are stuck in the midst of sin and at the very height of it, believe it, and you are in the midst of blessedness. 4. The Decalogue belongs on Nathan's lips, not in the pulpit. 5. All who deal with Moses must go to the devil; hang them on the gallows with Moses. 6. We should not prepare people for the Gospel by preaching the law; God must do it, that is his work. Luther wrote five disputations against these positions and articles in the same year, and a sixth in 1540, in which he admirably exposed and refuted the raving of the Antinomians.

units.la: Subindicabimus breviter fontes errorum, quibus ostensis facile sit illos redarguere 1. Aliud est legis divinae Scriptura & verbum; aliud lex moralis (de qua impræsentiarum) ipsa. Vtcunque non esset hodie ejus usus sub N. Test. qui fuit olim; haud tamen negari potest, similiter ac de lege cæremoniali, & judiciali, eam tamen vocandam esse verbum Dei. II. Pœnitentia, etiam peccatum, cujus illa est, in suâ latitudine poni debet & transgressionum legalium, & Euangelicarum: quis enim negare posset, utrumque peccatum, & poenitendum esse? III. Vti sub V.T. non adversus legis solùm doctrinam, sed & Euangelii (utraque enim viguit, quod Antinomi non difficebuntur, qui dicunt, legem tantum arguere peccata, & valere ad damnationem. Thesi 16. quare & per doctrinam Euangelii salvatos Patres); ita sub Novo jam, & contra Euangelium peccatur, & legem. IV. Distinguenda sunt, doctrina legis, & doctrina justificationis. V. Iterum, doctrina justificationis, & justificatio ipsa. VI. Aliud, quod ad justificationem requiritur formaliter, aliud quod antecedenter, quod consequenter. Ad justificationem, videlicet ejus materiam, nihil facit præter justitiam Christi: cui non obstat vel quod justificationis passivæ in animo debitam acceptionem antecedit humiliatio, & quamvis non tempore, at ordine naturæ eam sequitur observantia & bona opera. VII. Lex proprie debitum urget, ostenditque peccatum: Euangelium gratiam, & remissionem peccatorum. Iuvat huc adscribere Thesès aliquot Lutheri, rem optime declarantes, ex primâ ejus contra Antinomos Disputatione. 30. Quare prior docendus est Adam (id est, peccatum & mors) qui forma est futuri Christi, postea docendi. 31. Peccatum vero & mors, non per verbum gratiæ & solacii, sed per Legem necesse est ostendi. 32. Experientia est, quod Adam primùm arguitur Legis transgressor, post per Semen Mulieris promissum erigitur &c. 33. Et David primùm Lege per Natan occiditur, dicentem, Tu es ille &c. Post Euangelio servatur dicente, Non moriens &c. 34. Paulus Lege prostratus audit, Quid me persequeris? Post Euangelio vivificatur, Surge &c. 35. Et ipse Mar. 1. Pœnitemini & credite Euangelio, appropinquavit enim regnum Dei. 36. Iterum oportuit in nomine ejus prædicare pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum. 37. Sic & Spiritus primo arguit mundum de peccato, ut fidem doceat in Christum, id est, remissionem peccatorum. 38. Paulus Epistola ad Romanos hanc Methodum servat, ut prius doceat omnes esse peccatores, justificandos per Christum. VIII. Lex & Euangelium aliquando opponuntur, videlicet si illa conetur hominem justificare, id est, si homo per illam justificari quærat; subordinate consideratur lex ad Euangelium, si illa modo declaret, per se neminem justificari posse: atque hoc modo inter utrumque tam bene, ac priori modo neutiquam, convenit. IX. Non prædicanda est Lex sola, absque Euangelio, vel sola ante Euangelium, sed cum Euangelio. X. Ad utriusque prædicationem relinquitur Spiritui libera operatio, quo ordine velit apud hominum animos seu legem urgere, seu Euangelium, quosque convenienter huic, aut illi in homine actus producere primum, aut deinceps. XI. Spiritus divini gratia & operatio non datur per legis prædicationem, vel non hæc ejus ad nos vehiculum est; sed Euangelium. Gal. III. 2. quamvis semel datus, tum legis prædicationem, tum alia plura reddat apud nos efficacia & fructuosa. XII. Euangelium strictè & præcisè sumtum non habet præcepta, solas promissiones: præcepta vero quæ etiam docere videtur & urgere, proprie & in se consideræ sunt præcepta à lege, sed determinantur in Euangelio ad singularem ejus materiam: id est, pœnitentia, fides, resipiscentia, obedientia præcipiuntur in lege, sed in Christum credere, converti ad eum, huic obedire docenti obedientiam legi præstandam esse, Euangelium aperit: sed nil hic novorum à lege præceptorum est (neque enim Christus ut novus à Mose habendus est legislator, vel qui perfectiorem legem tulerit, aut alia superaddiderit legi, quæ perfecta in genere præceptorum & morum satis est) tantummodo præceptorum legalium ad hanc materiam & objectum applicatio: & hac ratione peccata dicuntur Euangelica, quatenus tum non transgrediuntur solum legem, sed incurrunt etiam in benignam & salutarem illorum applicationem in Euangelio, id est, adversus Euangelium quoque. Ergo præcepta proprie non habet Euangelium formaliter, & quasi alia à lege: tantummodo ejus præcepta dicuntur determinative, vel applicative. Duo declinandi sunt circa præcepta in Euangelio commemorata scopuli: tum ne illa Euangelio, quasi sua, aliaque & nova à lege, attribuamus; quod esset Euangelium in legem commutare, & Christum in novum legislatorem. Tum ne illa à doctrinâ Euangelii nimium removeamus, quasi non hujus loci quoque esset, præcepta prædicare: utrumque satis pernitiosum. XIII. Euang. non facit nova præcepta; sed confirmat moralia vetera, eaque corroborat novis argumentis, ut de diligendo Deo, proximo &c. XIV. Quare nisi sub Novo quoque Test. lex obtinebat, nulla erunt hodie præcepta, quibus teneamur, vel quæ docere & urgere oporteat: aut hæc si quæ sint, ea legis oportet esse. Quod Antinomos eo magis stringit argumentum, quo ut extollere videantur Euangelium, legem tollunt. Haud tamen credibile, quod volent Euangelium commutare in legem; aut illi sua facere præcepta, vel alteram ex eo legem, aut priori majorem. XV. Distinguenda probe semper justificatio, & sanctificatio: etiam justitia, quâ justificamur, & sanctitas ad quam sanctificamur: hic legis usus est, ut normam & regulam præstet, juxta quam sanctitas dirigenda; ibi, ut doceat, non suâ vi justificari nunc hominem posse; utque eum dejiciat ab opinione & præsumtione justificationis legalis. Lutherus bene, in Disput. II. Antinomica thes. 9. Et nihil decendum, cogitandum in re justificationis, nisi solum verbum gratiae in Christo exhibita. 10. Ex his autem non sequitur, Legem esse abolendam, & è concionibus Ecclesiæ tollendam. 11. Quin eo magis est necesse eam deseri & urgeri, quod non est necessarium, sed impossibile ad justificationem. 12. Ut homo superbus & de viribus suis præsumens erudiatur, sese per Legem non posse justificari. 13. Nam peccatum & mores eo maxime monstranda sunt, non quod necessaria sint ad vitam innocentem. 14. Sed ut homo agnoscat suam injustitiam & perditionem, & ita humilietur. 15. Si peccatum ignoretur, præsumitur falsa innocentia, sicut in Gentibus, & post in Pelagianis cernitur. 16. Si mors ignoretur, præsumitur hanc vitam esse vitam & nullam in futuro aliam. 17. Cum verò non nisi Lex utrumque doceat, satis claret, Legem esse maxime necessariam & utilem. XVI. Aliud est, necessitatem bonorum operum ponere ad justificationem; aliud ad salutem. XVII. Tum ad salutem promerendam, vel adipiscendam & possidendam. Non ad illud opera faciunt, sed ad hoc. XVIII. Neutiquam ponenda operum præsentia necessaria in actu justificationis; neque dicendum, hoc sequi ex doctrina de necessitate bonorum, quod adversus Joachim Morlinum bene tenuit Paul. Crellius, in Propositionibus V Vitemb. a. MDLXX. Aliud est bona opera considerare ad justificationem, ad fidem, ad salutem; nullum illic locum habent; isthic ad juncta sunt consequentia, & hic antecedentia XIX. Unde aliud est, asserere fidem non esse absque operibus: & tamen justificare absque operibus, XX. Ordine naturæ fides est ante bona opera: tempore, cum bonis operibus. XXI. Quemadmodum Pontificii in eo errant, quod justificationem & sanctificationem confundunt, ita in hoc Antinomi, quod legis usum in hac, & illa non melius distinguunt, & quia non justificat vel etiam non sanctificat lex, quod in dirigenda sanctitate nullum usum præbere eam asserunt. XXII. Namque, non tantum inter justificationem distinguendum, & sanctificationem; verum etiam inter sancti[?]
units.tr: We shall briefly point out the sources of the errors, and once they are shown it will be easy to refute them. 1. The Scripture and word of the divine law is one thing; the moral law itself (which is what we are concerned with at present) is another. Although its use under the New Testament is not today what it was once, it cannot be denied that, as with the ceremonial and judicial law, it must nevertheless be called the word of God. II. Repentance, and the sin of which it is the repentance, must be understood in its full breadth, to include both transgressions of the law and transgressions of the Gospel: for who could deny that both are sins and both must be repented of? III. Under the Old Testament sin was committed not only against the doctrine of the law but also against that of the Gospel (for both flourished then, as the Antinomians will not deny, though they say that the law only convicts of sins and serves for condemnation; see thesis 16; that is why the Fathers were also saved through the doctrine of the Gospel). So under the New Testament too, sin is committed both against the Gospel and against the law. IV. The doctrine of the law and the doctrine of justification must be distinguished. V. Again, the doctrine of justification and justification itself must be distinguished. VI. What is required for justification formally is one thing; what is required antecedently and what consequently is another. Nothing contributes to justification, that is, to its matter, except the righteousness of Christ; and this is not hindered by the fact that humiliation precedes in the mind the due reception of passive justification, nor by the fact that obedience and good works follow it in the order of nature, though not in time. VII. The Law properly presses the debt and shows sin; the Gospel shows grace and the remission of sins. It is helpful to add here some theses of Luther, which set out the matter very clearly, from his first Disputation against the Antinomians. 30. Therefore Adam, that is, sin and death, who is the form of the Christ to come, must be taught first, and afterwards what is to be taught. 31. Sin and death, however, must be shown not through the word of grace and comfort, but through the Law. 32. Experience shows that Adam is first convicted as a transgressor of the Law, and afterwards raised up through the Seed of the Woman promised to him, etc. 33. And David is first struck down by the Law through Nathan, who says, "You are the man," etc. Afterwards he is saved by the Gospel, which says, "You shall not die," etc. 34. Paul, prostrated by the Law, hears, "Why do you persecute me?" Afterwards he is made alive by the Gospel, "Arise," etc. 35. And he himself, Mark 1: "Repent and believe the Gospel, for the kingdom of God is at hand." 36. Again, it was necessary to preach repentance and the remission of sins in his name. 37. So also the Spirit first convicts the world of sin, so that he may teach faith in Christ, that is, the remission of sins. 38. The Epistle to the Romans keeps this method, teaching first that all are sinners, who must be justified through Christ. VIII. Law and Gospel are sometimes opposed, namely when the law tries to justify a man, that is, when a man seeks to be justified by it; the law is considered subordinately to the Gospel when it only shows that no one can be justified by it: and in this way the two agree well with one another, but not at all in the former way. IX. The Law alone must not be preached, without the Gospel, or alone before the Gospel, but with the Gospel. X. In the preaching of each, the Spirit is left free to act in whatever order he wishes, whether to press the law or the Gospel on men's minds, and to produce in a person first one act or the other, or afterwards, in accordance with this. XI. The grace and operation of the divine Spirit are not given through the preaching of the law, nor is the law his vehicle to us; it is the Gospel. Gal. 3:2. Although once given, he then makes both the preaching of the law and many other things effective and fruitful among us. XII. The Gospel, taken strictly and precisely, has no precepts, only promises. The precepts which it also seems to teach and press are, properly and in themselves considered, precepts of the law, but they are determined in the Gospel to its particular matter: that is, repentance, faith, conversion and obedience are commanded in the law; but the Gospel reveals that one must believe in Christ, turn to him, and obey him who teaches that obedience is to be rendered to the law. Yet there is nothing new here from the law (for Christ is not to be regarded as a new lawgiver different from Moses, nor as one who gave a more perfect law or added other things to the law, which in its kind of precepts and morals is already perfect enough); there is merely an application of the legal precepts to this matter and object. And for this reason sins are called evangelical, in that they transgress not only the law but also incur the kindly and saving application of it in the Gospel, that is, they are committed against the Gospel too. Therefore the Gospel does not have precepts formally and as something other and separate from the law; its precepts are only said to be determinative, or applicative. Two rocks must be avoided concerning the precepts recorded in the Gospel: first, that we should not attribute them to the Gospel as its own, and as other and new relative to the law, which would be to change the Gospel into the law and make Christ a new lawgiver; second, that we should not remove them too far from the doctrine of the Gospel, as if it were not also the place to preach precepts. Both are quite pernicious. XIII. The Gospel does not make new precepts, but confirms the old moral precepts and strengthens them with new arguments, such as concerning the love of God, of neighbour, and so on. XIV. Therefore, unless the law also held under the New Testament, there would today be no precepts by which we are bound, or which ought to be taught and pressed; or if there are any, they must belong to the law. This argument presses the Antinomians all the more, since in seeming to exalt the Gospel they abolish the law. Yet it is not credible that they wish to change the Gospel into law, or to make the precepts their own, or to make another law out of it, or one greater than the former. XV. Justification and sanctification must always be carefully distinguished, and also the righteousness by which we are justified and the holiness to which we are sanctified. Here the use of the law is to provide the norm and rule by which holiness is to be directed; there, it is to teach that man cannot now be justified by his own strength, and to cast him down from the opinion and presumption of legal justification. Luther rightly says, in the second Antinomian Disputation, thesis 9: Nor is anything to be yielded to or thought of in the matter of justification except only the word of grace exhibited in Christ. 10. From this, however, it does not follow that the Law is to be abolished and removed from the sermons of the Church. 11. Rather, it is all the more necessary that it be retained and pressed, because it is not necessary but impossible for justification. 12. So that the proud man, presuming on his own powers, may be taught that he cannot be justified by the Law. 13. For sin and the moral precepts must be shown especially not because they are necessary for an innocent life, 14. but so that man may recognise his own injustice and perdition, and thus be humbled. 15. If sin is unknown, a false innocence is presumed, as among the Gentiles, and afterwards among the Pelagians. 16. If death is unknown, it is presumed that this life is the only life and there is no other in the future. 17. Since only the Law teaches both, it is clear enough that the Law is most necessary and useful. XVI. It is one thing to posit the necessity of good works for justification, another for salvation. XVII. Works do not contribute to the former, but to the latter: to earning, attaining and possessing salvation. XVIII. The presence of works must by no means be posited as necessary in the act of justification; nor is it to be said that this follows from the doctrine of the necessity of good works, which Paul Crell rightly maintained against Joachim Morlin in the Wittenberg Propositions V of 1570. It is one thing to consider good works in relation to justification, to faith, and to salvation: in the first they have no place at all; in the second they are consequents joined to it, and in the third they are antecedents. XIX. Hence it is one thing to assert that faith is not without works, and yet to justify without works. XX. In the order of nature faith comes before good works; in time, it comes together with them. XXI. Just as the Papists err in confusing justification and sanctification, so the Antinomians err in not distinguishing the use of the law in the one and the other better, and because they say that the law neither justifies nor even sanctifies, and that it offers no use in directing holiness.

units.la: sancti[?] Eee 4 sanctificationem, & sanctitatem. Lex non sanctificat nos, sed quidem sanctitatem nostram regulat. xxiii. Aliud est principium sanctitatis, vel obedientiae; aliud ipsius regula: illud Spiritus Christi, hoc lex est. xxiv. Aliud est, sub lege esse; vel secundum eam vivere. xxv. Lex ex veteri foedere tantum hominibus praescribitur: ex Novo, cordibus etiam inscribitur. Hebr. viii. 10. xxvi. Aliud est, legem servare legaliter; aliud Evangelice. xxvii. Alia ratione lex docetur apud Pontificios; alia ratione apud Reformatos. Ibi neutro loco bene, neque in negotio justificationis, neque sanctificationis. Haud vero, quia illi graviter hac in re errant, sequitur, aut legis nullum usum rectum esse, aut eam non doceri apud nos. xxviii. Igitur male Antinomi dixerunt, legem non docendam aut praedicandam sub Euangelio, inter Christianos esse, vel quasi non absque praejudicio gratuitae justificationis habere ejus usus legitimus possit, eam totam ex omni religionis ambitu eliminare.
units.tr: Sanctification and holiness. The law does not sanctify us, but it does regulate our holiness. (23) The source of holiness or obedience is one thing, and its rule is another: the former is the Spirit of Christ, the latter is the law. (24) To be under the law is one thing; to live according to it is another. (25) The law is prescribed to men only under the Old Covenant; under the New it is also written on their hearts. Heb. 8:10. (26) To keep the law legally is one thing; to keep it evangelically is another. (27) The law is taught among the Papists on one footing and among the Reformed on another. Neither is right, either in the matter of justification or in the matter of sanctification. Yet because the Papists err gravely in this, it does not follow that there is no right use of the law, or that it is not taught among us. (28) Therefore the Antinomians were wrong to say that the law is not to be taught or preached under the Gospel, that it has no place among Christians, or that its lawful use cannot be had without prejudice to free justification, and that it should be removed altogether from every sphere of religion.

units.la: Adversus quam hypothesim haec perpendere argumenta licet. 1. quod lex in se bona, divina, & perfecta est, nullam habens imperfectionem, qualem lex caeremonialis: quare ergo abolcatur, imperfectionem legis restatur Scriptura. Psal. xix. & cxix. eamque omnimodam defendimus tum adversus Pontificios, tum Socinianos: & quod lex non abrogetur, nisi propter imperfectionem suam, docet Apostolus, Heb. vii. 18. 19. & viii. 7. quod in morali non habet locum. Quae autem abrogantur: vel quod adoptionis ei adscribitur, Rom. viii. 3. non legis est, sed, quomodo ibidem exponitur, nostri, non valentium per nostram impotentiam eam implere, quare nec per eam justificari. ii. Christus & Apostoli in N. T. legem docuerunt, & confirmarunt. Matth. v. 17. &c. & xix. 17. 18. & xxviii. 20. Act. ii. 37. 38. & xx. 21. & xxvi. 17. 18. 20. Rom. iii. 31. & vi. 6. 18. 19. & vii. 22. & viii. 1. 12. & xiii. 8. 9. Cor. vi. 11. Heb. vi. 1. & xii. 14. Iac. ii. 10. ii. Gal. v. 14. adde Malach. iv. 4. ergo sub N. T illa non praetereunda vel negligenda est. iii. Nihil continet lex quod adversetur ullis N. T. vel religionis Christianae articulis: imo tota multum illis inservit: ergo tenenda. iv. necessaria est regula bonorum operum, quae nulla est praeter eam; vel ergo non necessario facienda bona opera, docendaque, aut non juxta certum Dei praescriptum, vel pro eo non admitti lex Dei debet. Deinde, ut virtus, ita nec peccatum ullum haberi poterit, legem si tollamus. Rom. iii. 20. quae omnia, nullam videlicet boni maliq; regulam esse, Christianae religioni eo magis adversantur, quo omnem religionem radicitus evertunt. v. Quorsum lex moralis abrogabitur, ejusque doctrina, quum naturalis maneat, quae cum illa est eadem? imo quam non potest haec deleri unquam, ita nec illa debet, hujus typus & certissima tabula. vi. Summarium legis est amor, sive erga Deum, sive homines. Ille autem quia in N. T. quam maxime vigere, etiam doceri debet, nulla ejus perfectior tabula, quam lex. Rom. xiii. 8. Gal. v. 14. Iac. ii. 10. ii. [?]. Sub N. T. & hujus praedicatione quia semper degunt etiam homines improbi, & pii multam partem adhuc peccato obnoxii sunt, propterea saltem, nec ipsis forte reluctaturis Adversariis, doctrina legis requiri videtur. Lutherus, Disp. iii. th. 35. Vt nulla unquam sit audita vel futura frons impudentior, quam illorum, qui Legem tollendam esse docent. 36. Scilicet miseros homines posse docere & facere, quod ipse Dominus et fecit & docuit. Unde in Praefat. Comment. ad Galat. de horum hominum secta dixit: quae ego minime omnium praevidissem aut sperassem. Quod vero pro opinione Antinomorum adferri argumentum vel quae ratio possit, non scio, quae non ex praemissis facile solvi ac explicari queat. Auctor illorum dogmatum Agricola, Lutheri conterraneus fuit, & Theologiam docuit in Schola Islebia. Comitiisque Augusta-pis nis unà cum Melanthone interfuit, a. cIↄ Iↄ xxx. atque subscripsit Augustanæ confessioni, à quâ primum in deliria Antinomica; inde ad partes Pontificias defecit: auctorque unà cum Iulio Pflugg, & Michaële Sidonio fuit libri Interim: unde eximiis donis locupletati, à Carolo, & Ferdinando fratre, hic episcopatu Merseburgensi, iste Naumburgensi, ille dono quo præsulatio alio, dignitate locum dederunt, chrisma ab ipsis & oleum Pontificium defensa fuisse, quò discederent unctiones. Obiit Agricola Berolini, ubi Electori Brandeburgico à Sacris erat Pontificiis, a. cIↄ Iↄ lxvi. Ab Antinomicis opinionibus Lutherus cum abduxisse videbatur, quando ad publicam illarum recantationem eum egit in Academia Vvittembergensi; quievitque quoad usque Lutherus in vivis fuit: verum hoc mortuo, ad pristinas sordes rediit, & ulteriores.
units.tr: Against this hypothesis the following arguments may be weighed. (1) The law is in itself good, divine and perfect, having no imperfection of the kind found in the ceremonial law. If the law is abrogated, the imperfection of the law must be shown from Scripture: Ps. 19 and 119. We defend its perfection on every count, both against the Papists and against the Socinians. That the law is not abrogated except because of its imperfection, the Apostle teaches, Heb. 7:18–19 and 8:7; this does not apply to the moral law. As for what is abrogated, if something is ascribed to it as weakness, Rom. 8:3, that is not the fault of the law but, as is explained in that same place, of ours, who were unable by our own weakness to fulfil it and so could not be justified by it. (2) Christ and the Apostles in the New Testament taught and confirmed the law: Matt. 5:17ff., 19:17–18, 28:20; Acts 2:37–38, 20:21, 26:17–18, 20; Rom. 3:31, 6:6, 18–19, 7:22, 8:1, 12, 13:8–9; 1 Cor. 6:11; Heb. 6:1, 12:14; James 2:10; Gal. 5:14; add Mal. 4:4. Therefore under the New Testament it is not to be passed over or neglected. (3) The law contains nothing that conflicts with any article of the New Testament or of the Christian religion; indeed, the whole of it serves them greatly. Therefore it is to be retained. (4) A rule of good works is necessary, and there is no such rule apart from the law. Either good works are not necessarily to be done and taught, or they are not to be done according to a certain prescription of God, or else the law of God must be admitted for this purpose. Further, if we take away the law, there can be no knowledge of sin, just as there can be no virtue; Rom. 3:20. All of these things, namely that there would be no rule of good and evil, are the more opposed to the Christian religion because they utterly overthrow all religion. (5) Why should the moral law be abrogated, and its teaching, when it remains natural and is the same as that law? Indeed, just as this cannot ever be destroyed, so neither should that law be; it is the type and most certain tablet of it. (6) The summary of the law is love, both toward God and toward men. Since this love is especially to flourish under the New Testament and must also be taught, there is no more perfect tablet of it than the law: Rom. 13:8; Gal. 5:14; James 2:10. Since men who are wicked still live under the New Testament and under its preaching, and the godly are for the most part still liable to sin, the teaching of the law seems to be required at least for these reasons, and perhaps even the Adversaries, who would not resist it, would agree. Luther, Disp. 3, thes. 35: "So that there has never been heard, nor will there ever be, a more shameless face than that of those who teach that the Law is to be abolished." 36: "Namely, that wretched men are able to teach and do what the Lord himself both did and taught." Hence in the Preface to his Commentary on Galatians he said of the sect of these men: "which I by no means foresaw or hoped for." But what argument or reasoning could be adduced in favour of the Antinomian opinion I do not know, which cannot easily be solved and explained from what has been said. The author of these doctrines was Agricola, a fellow countryman of Luther, who taught theology in the school at Eisleben. He was present at the Diet of Augsburg along with Melanchthon in 1530, and subscribed to the Augsburg Confession, from which he first defected into Antinomian follies, and then went over to the Papist side. He was also, along with Julius Pflug and Michael Sidonius, an author of the Interim; for this he was enriched with splendid gifts by Charles and his brother Ferdinand: the one gave him the bishopric of Merseburg, the other that of Naumburg, and the former gave him a place of dignity in the office of chaplain. It was said that he defended the Pontiffs' chrism and oil, lest the anointings depart from them. Agricola died at Berlin, where he was chaplain to the Elector of Brandenburg with Papist leanings, in 1566. Luther seemed to have drawn him away from the Antinomian opinions when he obliged him to recant them publicly at the University of Wittenberg; and he remained quiet as long as Luther was alive, but after Luther's death he returned to his former filth, and went further.

units.la: Ejusdem ferè commatis fuit Nicolaus Amsdorfius, qui Lutherum comitatus primo ad Colloquium Vormaticense a. cIↄ Iↄ xxi, Magdeburgensium primus concionator fuit; postea, amoto Iulio Pflugg, Naumburgensis Episcopus, quem tamen locum, sextum post annum, cedere iterum Pflugio, à Carolo Cæsare iussus fuit, & Magdeburgum remeare, ad a. cIↄ Iↄ li. Hic adversus Georgium Majorem (qui Magdeburgensis Scholæ Rector, post Casparum Crucigerum, Vvittembergam evocatum, secundus fuit, posteaque etiam Professor Theol. Vvittembergæ) defendentem, bona opera ad salutem esse necessaria, impotentius se opponens, insanam thesim astruxit: bona opera ad salutem esse noxia & pernitiosa. Iam ante Lutherus quoque, Disput. iv. contra Antinomos thes. 8. dixerat: Summa, lex non est utilis nec necessaria ad iustificationem, neque ad ulla bona opera, multo minus ad salutem. Bene quidem non ad merendam salutem, omninò verò ad meritam per Christum nobis adeundam, & occupandam. Quemadmodum respondit Melanthoni, ad quæst. Verum hæc propositio sit vera: justitia operum necessaria est ad salutem? Non, quod operentur, seu impetrent salutem, sed quod fidei impetrantii præsentes seu coram sint: ego necessario adero ad salutem meam. Consil. Theol. Melanth. part. 1. pag. 243. Conati quidem fuerunt Adversarii Majoris Amsdorfius, & Matthias Flacius Illyricus heterodoxam illi, in articulo de justificatione sententiam affricare; sed ex facta ab eo declaratione patuit, meram fuisse τὴν ἀμελείαν et ἀσθενείας, quæ Adversarios primum adversus ipsum, tum quoque adversus rectam & probam docendi rationem egit, dicentes infantientium in morem, bona opera ad salutem esse pernitiosa. Etiam bonum virum Philippum Melanthonem illi, quos diximus, turbones hac contentione vexarunt: unde hic quidem, bona opera esse necessaria, quatenus vid. creatura rationalis Deo semper debet obedientiam, non vero ad salutem esse necessaria, dicere sustinuit. Quæ in parte 11. Conf. Theologicorum Melanthonis videri possunt. Major quoque diserte testatus fuit, se in gratiam illorum, quos forte offenderat sua propositio, lubenter eâ abstenturum. Flacius, in articulis reconciliatoriis cum Melanthone, ann. cIↄ Iↄ lv i 1.art. i i i. Ideoque tollatur corruptela de necessitate operum ad salutem, cum conjunctis. Tantum Clamatores possunt, ubi incidunt in viros honestos & probos, id est, se longe meliores. Tandem autem Liber Concordiæ, ann. cIↄ Iↄ lxxv i i. finem lis contentionibus imposuit, & de tertio legis usu, docuit: quum lex Dei propter tres causas data sit, Primo, ut externa quædam disciplina conservetur, & feri atque intractabiles homines, quasi repagulis quibusdam coërceantur. Secundo, ut per legem homines ad agnitionem suorum peccatorum adducantur. Tertio, ut homines jam renati, quibus tamen omnibus multum adhuc carnis adhaeret, eam ipsam ob causam certam aliquam regulam habeant, ad quam totam suam vitam formare possint & debeant, &c. pernitiosum & falsum dogma esse illorum, qui dicebant legem impiis & infidelibus tantum, & non agentibus poenitentiam, non vero renatis & piis proponendam atque inculcandam, neque eius observantiam apud hos urgendam esse. Primum illum legis usum appellant paedagogicum; alterum spiritualem; tertium renatorum proprium. Quos usu bene dispositos esse, non dico. Dicerem consulendum Conradum Schlusselburgium, Tom. VII. Cat. Haereticorum, quo toto tomo de Majoristis agit, nisi prolixe nimis ineptientem Scriptorem vereret commendare, qui passim impia & blasphema Majori, pro more suae disputationis impingit.
units.tr: Nicolaus Amsdorf was of much the same stamp. He accompanied Luther to the Colloquy of Worms in 1521, and was the first preacher at Magdeburg. Later, when Julius Pflug was removed, he was made bishop of Naumburg, though after six years he was ordered by Emperor Charles to give up that place again to Pflug and return to Magdeburg, in 1551. Here he opposed Georg Major, who had been rector of the school at Magdeburg and, after Caspar Cruciger, the second to be called to Wittenberg, and afterwards also professor of theology at Wittenberg, when Major defended that good works are necessary to salvation. Amsdorf, opposing him too violently, set forth the insane thesis: "good works are harmful and pernicious to salvation." Earlier, Luther too, in Disp. 4 against the Antinomians, thes. 8, had said: "In short, the law is neither useful nor necessary for justification, nor for any good works, much less for salvation." Rightly indeed, not for earning salvation, but certainly for receiving and laying hold of the salvation that is merited for us through Christ. So he answered Melanchthon, in the question: "Whether this proposition is true: the righteousness of works is necessary for salvation?" "No, not because they work out or obtain salvation, but because they are present to faith as it obtains; I shall necessarily be present for my salvation." Melanchthon's Theological Consultations, part 1, p. 243. The Adversaries of Major, Amsdorf and Matthias Flacius Illyricus, indeed tried to fasten on him a heterodox opinion in the article of justification; but from the declaration made by him it became clear that it was a mere carelessness and weakness of expression, which first drove the Adversaries against him, and then also against the sound and proven method of teaching, as they said, in the manner of babblers, that good works are pernicious to salvation. These troubles also vexed the good man Philip Melanchthon, by the same contention which we have mentioned; hence he maintained that good works are necessary insofar as a rational creature always owes obedience to God, but not that they are necessary to salvation. These things may be seen in part 2 of Melanchthon's Theological Consultations. Major too openly testified that, to please those whom his proposition had perhaps offended, he would willingly abstain from it. Flacius, in the Reconciliatory Articles with Melanchthon, in 1551, art. 3: "Let therefore the corruption concerning the necessity of works for salvation, together with its adjuncts, be removed." Only the clamourers can do this when they fall upon honest and upright men, that is, men far better than themselves. Finally, the Book of Concord, in 1577, put an end to these quarrels, and taught concerning the third use of the law: since the law of God was given for three causes. First, that a certain external discipline may be preserved, and that wild and unmanageable men may be restrained as with certain bars. Second, that through the law men may be brought to the knowledge of their sins. Third, that men already reborn, to whom nevertheless much of the flesh still clings, may for that very reason have a certain fixed rule by which they can and ought to form their whole life. It declared that the teaching of those who said that the law is to be proposed and impressed only on the impious and unbelieving, who do not repent, and not on the reborn and the godly, nor is its observance to be urged on these, is a pernicious and false dogma. They call the first use of the law pedagogical, the second spiritual, the third the proper use of the reborn. I do not say that these men are well disposed in their use of it. I would recommend Conrad Schlusselburg, Tom. 7 of the Catalogue of Heretics, in which he treats the Majorists throughout that whole volume, were I not afraid of commending a writer who is too tediously silly, and who everywhere, in the manner of his disputation, heaps impious and blasphemous charges upon Major.

units.la: Tertia periodus Antinomorum hodie est in Anglia: quorum antesignani praecipui habentur Iohannes Eaton, Tobias Crispus, Iohannes Saltmarsh. Huic se opposuit Thomas Gattakerus: & adversus Antinomos in genere scripsit & ex professo Samuel Rutherfurd; quos & alio libro refutavit, Christ dying: Antonius Burges; Ioh. Bisco, alii. Antinomorum themata, vel dogmatum ipsorum capita carptim referunt Honorius Reggius, sive Clariss. vir & Collega Georgius Hornius, in Comment. de Statu Ecclesiarum in Anglia; & libellus Belgicus, de Turbis Anglicanis. Verum mallem, ut ipsi potius qui ita dicuntur Antinomi, per aliquot distinctas & perspicuas theses explicuissent mentem suam, oppositam communi & usitatae hactenus in Ecclesia doctrinae, de usu legis. Namque video, dum ex integris ipsorum dissertationibus, libellis & concionibus theses conficiuntur per Scriptores Adversarios magis, quam per Auctores ipsos, nonnunquam haud satis feliciter illorum sensus capi & exprimi, & tum hinc, tum inde multa quidem dici, at saepe vix intelligi, vel non peti τὸ κεφάλαιον. Pervolvi Tobiae Crispi, Doct. Theologi, & magni illorum patroni, tres libros pro ista causa scriptos, quorum titulum fecit, Christ alone exalted. Quippe hoc spectare videntur illi homines, non malo animo, ut magis Christi solius gloria appareat, dejicere praeter Christum omnia, & opera hominum, dispositiones, & conditiones, fiduciam & reclinationem in operibus qualemcunque, & quae legi aliis tribuuntur, ea soli Christo vindicare. Antinomos, Libertinos praesertim, appellari se aegre patiuntur, potius dici amant Assertores libera gratiae: sic Saltmarsh adversus Gattakerum loquitur. Unde illorum assidui clamores, librorumque tituli, free grace, libera gratia, Certe in hoc argumento explicando non omnino frustra sunt, modo quaepiam, quae cum hoc bene queunt consistere, prudentius distinxissent, conciliassent, aut etiam admisissent. Atque ubi limites illis sui probe assignantur, aliorumque articulorum bene salvatur veritas, multa illius argumenti egregia apud ipsos occurrere & in quibus a communi sententia plus methodi saepe, quam doctrinae ratione discrepant, certum mihi videtur. Tres praecipui (meo judicio) articuli, in quibus exponendis a nobis abeunt: Christi redemptio ejus ad nos applicatio; vitae obedientia, an aut quomodo juxta legem instituenda.
units.tr: The third period of the Antinomians today is in England. Their chief leaders are considered to be John Eaton, Tobias Crisp and John Saltmarsh. Against them stood Thomas Gattaker, and Samuel Rutherford wrote against the Antinomians in general and expressly; he also refuted them in another book, Christ dying. Anthony Burgess, John Bisco and others did the same. Honorius Reggius, or the distinguished man and colleague Georg Horn, in his commentary On the State of the Churches in England, and a Belgic pamphlet, On the English Troubles, briefly set out the themes or main heads of the Antinomians' doctrines. But I would have preferred that those who are called Antinomians had themselves explained their views in several distinct and clear theses, opposed to the common doctrine on the use of the law hitherto received in the Church. For I see that when theses are drawn up from their complete dissertations, books and sermons, they are framed more by the adversary writers than by the authors themselves. Sometimes their meaning is not grasped or expressed very well; much is said here and there, but often it is hardly understood, or the chief point (τὸ κεφάλαιον) is not sought. I have read through three books by Tobias Crisp, Doctor of Theology and the great patron of this party, written for this cause and entitled Christ alone exalted. These men seem to aim at this, not with bad intent: that the glory of Christ alone may appear more clearly, by casting down everything apart from Christ, namely the works, dispositions and conditions of men, trust and reliance on any works whatever, and by claiming for Christ alone whatever others attribute to the law. They are reluctant to suffer being called Antinomians, or Libertines especially; they prefer to be called Assertors of free grace. So Saltmarsh speaks against Gattaker. Hence their constant cries and book titles, free grace, libera gratia. Certainly in explaining this argument they are not altogether wrong, provided they had more prudently distinguished, reconciled or even admitted some things that can well stand with it. Where the limits are properly assigned to them and the truth of the other articles is well preserved, it seems certain to me that many excellent things on this subject occur among them, and that in them they often differ from the common opinion more in method than in the substance of doctrine. There are three chief articles (in my judgement) in which they depart from us in their exposition: Christ's redemption and its application to us; and the obedience of life, whether and how it is to be established according to the law.

units.la: Redemptionem docent aliquam universalem. Male. Atqui id faciunt, ut certos homines reddant de Christo suo salvatore, non ex conditione aliqua, quam apud se hi prae illis deprehendant, fidei videlicet, (quippe vel nomen conditionum in toto salutis negotio horrent; liberam gratiam, id est, ex ipsorum mente, ab omni conditione immunem perpetuo inculcantes) sed ex omnium aequa portione in Christi satisfactione universali. Ut nihil homines ad sui securitatem agere necesse sit, quam ad se derivare & applicare λόγον ac redemptionem in Christo factam, ad modum actionis vel donii universaliter exhibiti & distributi. Quare dicendum vobis (inquit Tob.Crispus, vol. 1. Serm. VII. pag. 163.) non esse meliorem viam cognoscendi vestram in Christo pertionem, quam ex generali oblatione, concludere absolute, quod vester sit, atque ita, absque ulla alia re, accipere ipsum, ut oblatum vobis in verbo: atque hæc ejus acceptio sub generali exhibitione, est summa securitas, quod Christus sit vester. Ejusdem volum. pag. 296. ex 1. Ioan. 11. 2. & 11. Cor. v. 15. colligit universalitatem redemptionis omnium particularium personarum in mundo, quam vis non omnes fiant reconciliationis istius participes. Verum hæc de universali redemtione Christi non conveniunt cum veritate: uti adversus Remonstrantes, aliosque abunde probatum, quæ hic repetere nihil necesse. Deinde nil opus erat, ut hunc errorem suæ thesi adoptarent, quam absque eo etiam possent explicare. Nempe ex, posita particulari redemtione, qui eam sibi applicaret (de modo, quo hoc jubeant fieri, nihil dico), hinc statueret sibi partem in Christo esse, sola ejus rei promissione, non conditione ulla sua fretus. Denique eo convenientius loquerentur, quo applicationem redemptionis ad animam fieri docerent ex solo Dei dono & actione singulari, non ex hominis viribus aut ἐνεργείᾳ aliqua. Quinimo particularem hominum electionem statuentes particularem quoque redemtionem (sunt enim paris ubique latitudinis & extensionis) docere debebant, non universalem.
units.tr: They teach some universal redemption. This is wrong. Yet they do so in order to make certain people certain about Christ their Saviour, not on the basis of some condition which they perceive in themselves over others, namely faith (for they shudder even at the word condition in the whole business of salvation, constantly urging free grace, that is, in their view, grace wholly free of every condition). Rather, they base it on the equal portion of all in Christ's universal satisfaction. Thus men need do nothing for their own security except to derive and apply to themselves the word and the redemption made in Christ, as an act or gift offered and distributed universally. "Hence you must conclude," says Tobias Crisp (vol. 1, Sermon VII, p. 163), "that there is no better way of knowing your election in Christ than from the general offer: to conclude absolutely that he is yours, and so, without any other thing, to receive him as offered to you in the word. This reception under the general offer is the highest security that Christ is yours." In the same volume, p. 296, from 1 John 2:2 and 2 Cor. 5:15 he infers the universality of redemption for all particular persons in the world, although not all become sharers in that reconciliation. But these things about universal redemption do not agree with the truth, as has been abundantly proved against the Remonstrants and others, and there is no need to repeat it here. Moreover, there was no need for them to adopt this error into their thesis, since they could explain it even without it. For, supposing particular redemption, whoever applied it to himself (I say nothing of the manner in which they bid this be done) would conclude that a share in Christ is his, relying on that promise alone and not on any condition of his own. Finally, they would speak more fittingly if they taught that the application of redemption to the soul comes from God's gift and singular action alone, not from man's powers or from any energy of his own.
