Indeed, those who posit a particular election ought also to teach a particular redemption (for the two are of equal breadth and extent everywhere), not a universal one.

units.la: Mirum vero merito videatur, quod in redemtione nostrum peragenda, Christum dicunt non tulisse solum nostrorum peccatorum poenas & reatum, sed peccata ipsa ei impositia fuisse. Pro quo Auctor ille, Vol. 11. Serm. in Isa. 1111. 6. tum ex isto loco, tum aliis argumentis, prolixe per tres integros Sermones, 11. 111. & 1v. disputat. Pag. 74. Deus non solum inflixit Christo demeritum peccati, tum propterea vulnerando, verum etiam iniquitatem ipsam ei imposuit, intelligo iniquitatem ipsorum. Quibus postremis verbis videtur vel obloqui priori sententiæ de universalitate redemtionis (quam tamen etiam alii scribunt ab ipsis tradi); vel illa intelinteslexerit de generalitate electorum; vel duplicem fingat redemtionem, generalem, & particularem, quod omnino absurdum. Sed illud de impositis Christo peccatis nostris, non solis eorum poenis, praeterquam quod impossibile, quia peccatum est actio transiens, quae postquam abiit non reproducitur, nec realiter imponitur vadi, non etiam necessarium, quia sufficit, ut reatus imputetur, pro quo solvendo & expiando luit. Neque unquam aliter intelligitur, quando quis solvere & satisfacere, vel ἀντάλλαγμα dare pro alio, dicitur. Scias autem illos docere, portata a Christo ipsa etiam peccata nostra fuisse, ut eo melius tollerent ab homine dolorem de peccatis, quem impugnant, quatenus Christum illa tulisse, proque iis doluisse, asserunt. Samuel Richardsonus, qui pro Tobiâ Crispo defensionem scripsit, adversus Stephanum Gerce, lib. Divinae Consolationis, pag. 260. verba 11. Cor. v. 21. fecit ipsum peccatum, de peccato ipso, & non de solo reatu exponit, quasi iniquum sit, hunc imponere alicui, absque illo: ipse tamen part. III. libri, pag. 1. 2. explicans Apoc. 1. 5. Lavit nos a peccatis nostris, non de peccato, vel ejus macula, sed de reatu, & maledictione accipit. Doctrinam inde formans hanc: quod Christus Iesus morte suâ crucis, suos plene liberavit, à peccato, hoc est, inquit, à poenâ peccati aeternâ, ita plene ac si ipsi nunquam peccassent.
units.tr: It may well seem strange that, in accomplishing our redemption, they say Christ bore not only the punishments and guilt of our sins, but that the sins themselves were laid upon him. On this point that author (vol. 2, sermons on Isaiah 53:6) argues at length through three whole sermons, the second, third and fourth, both from that passage and from other arguments. At p. 74 he writes: "God not only inflicted on Christ the desert of sin, wounding him for that reason, but also laid on him iniquity itself, I mean their iniquity." By these last words he seems either to contradict his earlier opinion on the universality of redemption (which others nonetheless write is put forward by them too), or he understood it of the generality of the elect, or he invents a double redemption, general and particular, which is wholly absurd. But that our sins themselves, and not merely their punishments, were laid on Christ is both impossible, since sin is a transient act which, once gone, is not reproduced nor really laid upon another, and unnecessary, since it suffices that guilt be imputed, for which he paid and made expiation. Nor is it ever understood otherwise when someone is said to pay, satisfy, or give a ransom for another. Know, however, that they teach that our sins themselves were borne by Christ, so that they might the better remove from men the sorrow for sins which they oppose, insofar as they assert that Christ bore them and grieved for them. Samuel Richardson, who wrote a defence of Tobias Crisp against Stephen Gerce, in his book Divine Consolation (p. 260), explains the words of 2 Cor. 5:21, "he made him to be sin," of sin itself and not of guilt alone, as if it were unjust to impose guilt on someone without the sin. Yet he himself, in part III of the same book (pp. 1–2), explaining Rev. 1:5, "washed us from our sins," takes it not of sin or its stain but of guilt and curse. From this he forms the doctrine: "that Christ Jesus by his death on the cross fully freed his own from sin, that is, he says, from the eternal punishment of sin, as fully as if they had never sinned."

units.la: Quaestio ab iis mota est super justificatione nostrâ, quando facta, aut fiat. Docent, justificationem electorum factam in morte & satisfactione Christi, non fieri actu quando quis credit, sed tum quidem illam apud animum credentis manifestari. Super quo multum contendit Richardsonus: sed quod levi negotio componi potest, distinguendo justificationem activam & passivam: illa est actio Dei justificantis; haec istius terminatio & applicatio ad conscientiam fidelium. Illa facta est cum Christi satisfactione; haec fit tum quando quis actu credit. Haec revera illius est manifestatio; sed quia justificare in suâ plenitudine connotat terminationem ad justificatum vel justificandum, ita non est ea sola manifestatio, neque negandum quia ista manifestatio etiam justificatio dicenda sit. Et hoc sensu justificatio passim in Scriptura accipitur, & in epistolis Paulinis, ubi fidei adscribitur. Quia hic de tempore vel momento justificationis agitur, licet ea sic interpungere: justificatio destinata est ab omni aeternitate, in decreto Praedestinationis; promissa, mox post lapsum; facta in Christi morte, & resurrectione (conjungenda etenim haec sunt Rom. VIII. 34.) ibi à Christo merita, hic à Deo declarata, & ratihabita; applicatur, intimatur; manifestatur apud animum, ad fidem; consummabitur denique gloriosum in modum, tempore ultimi, atque universalis judicii.
units.tr: They have raised a question about our justification: when it was made, or when it is made. They teach that the justification of the elect was accomplished in the death and satisfaction of Christ, and that it is not effected when a person believes, but is then indeed manifested to the mind of the believer. Richardson contends much on this point, but it can be settled with little trouble by distinguishing active and passive justification. The former is the action of God justifying; the latter is its terminus and application to the conscience of the faithful. The former was accomplished with Christ's satisfaction; the latter happens when someone actually believes. The latter is indeed its manifestation; but since to justify in its fullness connotes a terminus toward the justified or the one to be justified, that manifestation is not the only one, and it must not be denied that this manifestation may also be called justification. In this sense justification is taken everywhere in Scripture, and in the Pauline epistles, where it is ascribed to faith. Since the question here concerns the time or moment of justification, it is permissible to punctuate it thus: justification was destined from all eternity in the decree of predestination; promised immediately after the fall; made in Christ's death and resurrection (for these are to be joined, Rom. 8:34), there merited by Christ, here declared and ratified by God; applied, intimated, and manifested to the mind, to faith; and finally it will be consummated in a glorious manner at the time of the last, universal judgement.

units.la: Nihil autem difficilius, quam illorum, de quibus agimus, & Antinomi vulgo audiunt in Angliâ, mentem bene explicare circa applicationem redemptionis, & Christi. Vulgo praeparationes & dispositiones traduntur in homine esse aliquas ante conversionem & fidem, ab omnibus fere Theologis Anglis: dolor & paenitentia de peccato, ex lege potissimum excitata, quae praecedat fidem & unionem nostram cum Christo: fidem esse conditionem Novi foederis: haec omnia vero illi tollunt & impugnant. Ajunt, gratiam omnimode liberam esse, nulli conditioni adstrictam, & applicationem ejus fieri ad hominem nulla qualitate bona praeditum, quâ gratiam aut Christum demereatur, vel fidentius accipiat. Christum, tempore quo Deus se & Filium suum vult revelare in nobis, accedere ad homines nulla vel qualitate meliori aut conditione praeparatos, sed improbos usquequaque & pessimos, quibus, ex electione videlicet quotquot sunt, & spiritum & fidem & omnia communicat. Ajunt, non dolendum, non angendum animo propter peccata esse; neque haec debere antecedere tanquam dispositiones ad recipiendum dum Christum. Et sic quoque fidem non esse conditionem Novi foederis, neque per eam, ceu instrumentum nos Christi fieri participes & justificari: sed per illam tantum animo manifestari reconciliationem & justificationem olim in Christi morte factam. Non attendi hic nostrum accipere, solummodo Dei dare. Quem in finem Vol. I. Serm. VII. pag. 150. hoc utitur simili: ut quum quis pauperem miserumque omni ex parte hominem videt, nec vestitum, nec clamantem, cui & manus & loquela desint vel ad accipiendam vel ad implorandam opem, te nihilominus miserebit ejus, eique poteris benefacere: ita Deus sua propria bonitate motus, nobis exhibet & adaptat Christum, ceu vestem, suis ipse manibus quasi, nobis nec manibus ad accipiendum, vel voce ad orandum praeditis, neque ulla re a nostra parte antecedente, quae Deum aut demereatur, aut hominem ad illa accipienda melius disponat. Distinctionem adhibet duplicis receptionis Christi, passive, & active: illa quasi absque manibus, haec fit cum illis. Illa est quando reluctanti homini Deus Christum suum immittit, ut Medicus aegro quantumvis abnuenti, adhibita potentiori vi, qua ei os adaperiat, potionem infundit, quam novit salutarem esse: quod adducit Jerem. XXXI. 18..19. Ad quam primam receptionem sequitur, quod mox homo incipit agnoscere Christum, aestimare, amplecti, amare, & perpetuo in eo vivere, juxtaque ductum & spiritum ejus se totum componere, quae est receptio Christi activa, ubi pro amico, & fratre, & Salvatore agnitus, quam poterit arctissime recipitur. Deinde distinguit, Christum dari nobis, vel manifestari datum: dari, ante ullam in nobis qualificationem vel conditionem, qui omnem probam qualitatem secum fert, atque in homine primus, solusque operatur: manifestatur (inquit) post fidem. Non est sine fide ejus manifestatio; quidem datio. Haec, nulla re, neque infidelitate praepeditur, quam
units.tr: Nothing, however, is more difficult than to explain properly the view of those we are discussing, whom in England people commonly call Antinomians, on the application of redemption and of Christ. Almost all English theologians teach that in a man there are certain preparations and dispositions before conversion and faith: sorrow and repentance for sin, aroused chiefly by the law, which go before faith and our union with Christ; and that faith is the condition of the New Covenant. These men, however, reject and attack all of this. They say that grace is wholly free, bound to no condition, and that it is applied to a man who has no good quality by which he might deserve grace or Christ, or receive them more confidently. They say that at the time when God wills to reveal himself and his Son in us, Christ comes to men who are prepared by no better quality or condition, but who are altogether wicked and worst of all, and that he imparts to them, namely to all whom he has chosen, both the Spirit and faith and everything else. They say that we need not grieve or be troubled in mind on account of sins, and that these things ought not to go before as dispositions for receiving Christ. Likewise they say that faith is not the condition of the New Covenant, nor are we made partakers of Christ and justified through it as an instrument; rather, through faith only the reconciliation and justification accomplished long ago in the death of Christ are made manifest to the mind. Here, they say, our receiving is not considered; only God's giving is. To this end the author, Vol. I, Sermon VII, p. 150, uses this comparison: when someone sees a poor and wretched man, in every way destitute, neither clothed nor crying out, whose hands and speech are lacking both to receive help and to beg for it, nevertheless you will pity him and will be able to do him good. So God, moved by his own goodness, offers and fits Christ to us as a garment, as it were with his own hands, while we have neither hands to receive nor voice to pray, and no thing on our part going before which might deserve God or better dispose the man to receive these gifts. He makes a distinction between a passive and an active reception of Christ: the first is as it were without hands, the second is done with them. The first is when God sends his Christ into a man who resists, as a physician, with a stronger force, pours a potion, which he knows to be healthful, into a patient who refuses it, opening his mouth; he cites Jeremiah 31:18–19. Following this first reception, the man soon begins to acknowledge Christ, to esteem, embrace, and love him, and to live in him continually, and to shape his whole self according to his guidance and Spirit; this is the active reception of Christ, in which he is recognized as friend, brother, and Saviour and is received as closely as possible. Then he distinguishes between Christ being given to us and Christ being made manifest as given. He is given before any qualification or condition in us, since he brings every good quality with him and alone, first among men, works in them; he is made manifest (he says) after faith. His manifestation is not without faith, but his giving is. The latter is hindered by nothing, not even by unbelief, which it removes; the former, while unbelief lasts, cannot be had except after faith.

units.la: FFf quam tollit: illa, durante infidelitate, neque nisi post fidem, haberi non potest. Deus in datione Christi ad animam (distincta a manifestatione) facit copiam Christi in animâ, quam Christus occupat ante ullam omnimodam qualificationem in eâ existentem: traditurque hic Christus, in novum foedus. Quare intrat, & justificat hominem ante ullam in eo productam qualificationem. Exprimo mentem illorum, cum quibus agimus, quorum etiam verba, quantum licet, retineo. Quod Christus ante omnem qualitatem, & ad eam primo in hominibus efficiendam traditur, exponunt ex Iesa. lx 1. 1. 2. 3. ubi Christus missus dicitur ad religandos confractos corde, & aperiendos oculos caecorum &c. Cumque ad illud posset objici, ergo contritionem cordis antecedere Christi adventum in corda. Respondent, distinguendo fractionem cordis, ab ejus sensu; quemadmodum in bonis, alicujus turbatae res sunt & fractae quasi; deinde collatis omnibus rationibus & libris id ipse videt sentitque. Ajunt, illam cordium fractionem esse in omnibus ante Christum, id est, inopes esse ac miseros; cujus sensum non accipiunt nisi à Christo, & per eum demum sibi secum unitum. Iezech. xxxvi. 26. Christus frangit illorum corda gratiosè, tum etiam religat. Contritio cordis, & quae hinc oriuntur, ex Christo jam praesente, ejusque spiritu fluunt. Zach. xii. 10. non ad eum accipiendum quasi gratae & acceptabiles qualitates, vel conditiones antecedunt. Sic & fides ipsa, non ante accessum Christi in animâ existit, sed post eum, & ex eo. Vade Christus auctor fidei dicitur. Heb. xii. 2. & dona accepisse pro rebellibus. Psalm. lxviii. 18: Ephes. iv. 8. & caput esse Ecclesiae, atque initium, & in omnibus primum. Col. i. 18. qui primus datur nobis in rebus salutis, ante quascunque alias, quarum nihil in nobis locum habere potest, antequam cum animâ actualiter unitus sit. Neque aliunde inchoare „ hic oportet, non ab inhærente nostrâ justitiâ, vel qualificationibus, precibus, lachrymis, humiliatione, dolore, reformatione, aut universali obedientiâ, sed missis omnibus, à solo Christo. Quemadmodum vacuâ antliâ frustra laboremus aquam educere, sed eam primò infundimus aliunde, & sic aquam extrahimus: ita Christum primò immitti in animas, antequam inde aliquid salutare produci queat. Neque primò Christus fidem animæ inserit, ad quam tum demum quasi ab eâ attractus, accedat; sed ipse prior accedit una cum dono fidei, quam animæ præsens intromittit. Vol. III, Serm. XI. Iterum Vol. I. Serm. XIV. pag. 317. non imaginari debes, inquit Crispus, nostram motionem vel nostrum venire ad Christum esse primum mobile, quod Christum moveat ad nos venire, sed vice versa Christi ad nos adventus prior causa est accessus ad eum nostri, acti agimus. Ephes. II. 1. Neque cogitandum, nos aptos esse, vel debere esse, ut ad Christum venire possimus vel liceat: neque enim Christus aptitudinem ullam nostram respicit, absque quâ nos non admittat in sui communionem, sed aptos facit ad eam communionem, ad quam nos destinat. Serm. XI. pag. 288. liberum donum est absque conditione, neque conditionem urget in antecessum, sed sua donat Deus in Christo citra respectum conditionis ullius: neque fides nostra, vel obedientia conditio donorum Dei sunt, Serm. VII. pag. 125. nulla ab hominis parte requiritur conditio in fœdere novo, totum negotium soli Deo incumbit, neque ulla pars ab homine, pro participatione beneficiorum ejus, adimplenda prius. Heb. VIII. 10. Iezech. XXXVI. 25. alioqui (inquit) Christus non esset purum merumque donum; quod ut sit, nihil ab homine exspectare vel accipere, ratione Christi hominibus impartiendi, Deus vult. Consequuntur omnia fœdus novum, ut ejus fructus & effecta, non vero antecedunt. Deinde etiam distinguit, aliud esse facere aliquid respectu fœderis, tamquam ejus conditionem, quod frustra habet; vel respectu officii, Deo tam libere nobiscum contrahentis, debiti. Adde & Serm. VII. seq. Exquibus intelligendum, quod dicit Serm. III. pag. 49. Christus est libera via ebrioso, lenoni, scorto, iniquo ejus, æque ac homini pessimo. Verum ne sinistre capiatis, haud est Christus illis libera via sic in eo ambulandi, & in peccatis illis continuandi, nam neminem, ad quem accedit, in ejusmodi relinquit sordibus, verum accedendi ad eum potestas æque est vilissimis in mundo peccatoribus, ac cuipiam hominum. Qui Christum qualiscunque accipit, ei Christus ad Patrem via est, etiam dum improbus est, & nondum emendatus, atque partem suam in Christo potest reputare æque ac quando est justus. Deus nihil spectat in homine, vel ab eo requirit, ut eum participem Christi faciat. Dicere, Christum esse donum, sed sub conditione, videtur sibi contradictio.
units.tr: Those with whom we are dealing hold that in the giving of Christ to the soul (distinct from his manifestation) God supplies Christ to the soul, and Christ takes possession of it before any qualification whatever exists in it; and Christ is thus delivered into the new covenant. Therefore he enters and justifies the man before any qualification has been produced in him. I set out the mind of those with whom we are dealing, and I keep their own words as far as I can. That Christ is given before any quality and in order first to bring one into being in men, they explain from Isaiah 61:1–3, where Christ is said to be sent to bind up the broken in heart, and to open the eyes of the blind, and so on. And since it could be objected to this, then the breaking of heart goes before Christ's coming into hearts, they answer by distinguishing the breaking of the heart from its sense, just as in goods of some men their affairs are, as it were, disturbed and broken; and then, after weighing all the arguments and books, he himself sees and feels this. They say that this breaking of hearts is in all men before Christ, that is, they are poor and wretched; but they do not receive its sense except from Christ, and at last through him, united to themselves. Ezekiel 36:26: Christ graciously breaks their hearts and then also binds them up. Contrition of heart, and what arises from it, flows from Christ already present and from his Spirit. Zechariah 12:10: no acceptable or pleasing qualities or conditions go before in order to receive him. So also faith itself does not exist in the soul before the coming of Christ, but after him and from him. Christ is called the author of faith, Hebrews 12:2, who received gifts for rebels, Psalm 68:18; Ephesians 4:8, and is the head of the Church and the beginning, and first in all things, Colossians 1:18. He is given to us first in the matters of salvation, before any others, none of which can have any place in us before he is actually united with the soul. Nor, they say, must we begin from anywhere else here: not from our inherent righteousness or qualifications, prayers, tears, humiliation, sorrow, reformation, or universal obedience, but with all these set aside, from Christ alone. Just as we labour in vain to draw water from an empty pump, but first pour it in from elsewhere, and so draw out the water, so Christ must first be sent into souls before anything saving can be produced from them. Nor does Christ first implant faith in the soul, to which he then comes as if drawn by it; rather he comes first, together with the gift of faith, which he introduces into the soul present to him. Vol. III, Sermon XI. Again, Vol. I, Sermon XIV, p. 317: you must not imagine, says Crispus, that our movement or our coming to Christ is the first mover which causes Christ to come to us; but on the contrary, Christ's coming to us is the prior cause of our approach to him, we who are acted upon acting. Ephesians 2:1. Nor should we think that we are, or ought to be, fit or allowed to come to Christ; for Christ does not regard any fitness of ours, without which he would not admit us to his fellowship, but he makes us fit for that fellowship to which he appoints us. Sermon XI, p. 288: it is a free gift without condition; it does not press a condition beforehand, but God gives his gifts in Christ without regard to any condition whatever; neither our faith nor our obedience are conditions of God's gifts. Sermon VII, p. 125: no condition is required on man's part in the New Covenant; the whole business rests on God alone, and no part is to be fulfilled by man beforehand for participation in his benefits. Hebrews 8:10; Ezekiel 36:25. Otherwise (he says) Christ would not be a pure and mere gift; for it to be such, God wills that, in respect of imparting Christ to men, nothing be expected or received from man. All the things that follow are the fruits and effects of the New Covenant, not things that go before it. Then he also distinguishes between doing something with respect to the covenant as its condition, which is in vain, and doing something with respect to the duty owed to God, who contracts with us so freely. Add also Sermon VII and what follows. From these things must be understood what he says in Sermon III, p. 49: Christ is a free way for the drunkard, the pimp, the harlot, and his wicked man, as well as for the very worst man. But lest you take this wrongly, Christ is not a free way for them to walk on in this manner and continue in those sins, for he does not leave in such filth anyone to whom he comes; rather the power of coming to him belongs equally to the most vile sinners in the world and to any man whatever. He who receives Christ, whatever he is, Christ is the way to the Father for him, even while he is wicked and not yet amended, and he can count his share in Christ just as much as when he is righteous. God looks for nothing in man, and requires nothing from him, in order to make him a partaker of Christ. To say that Christ is a gift, but under a condition, seems to them a contradiction.

units.la: Explicanda ad illorum mentem duo imprimis sunt, ratio fœderis gratuiti; tum fidei, quam hæc ad illud habeat. In quo utroque, à modo docendi communi haud parum discedunt. Primo fœdus agnoscunt duplex, operum; & alterum gratiæ in Christo: hoc iterum duplex, vel sacerdotale sub V. Testamento; vel prout à Christo jam administratur sub Novo. Neque unius fœderis diversam œconomiam, sed diversa dicunt fœdera. In quo nec cum veritate satis, neque secum conveniunt. Nam enumerantes differentias utriusque, quas in tribus ponunt I. in eo, quod Christi fœdus illo melius sit, ratione remissionis peccatorum: α. ibi non omnis generis peccatorum, uti hic. β. & conditiones ejus impertiendæ ibi post varias sacrorum & sacrificiorum conditiones. γ. & gradatim ac successive per sacrificia, non ita semel ὡς τὸ [?] concedebatur, ut hic II. discrimen constituunt ratione pacis conscientiæ. „tiæ. 111. libertatis à poenâ, ac irâ Dei: quorum substantiam quidem fatentur sub illo foedere fuisse, sed graduum magnum discrimen inter hoc illudque. Quorsum itaque duplex foedus, & non unius potius dicunt duplicem administrationem? namque hac ratione satis bene explicari, quod duo foedera Apostolus nominat Heb. viii. & ix. potest. Vol 11. Serm. 11. & xi. Atque hinc existimo, Richardsonum, part. 1. Divin. Consolat. pag. 328. negare, quod Circumcisio in se fuerit signum foederis gratiae. Adversus quod disputat Vasavor Powel, l. Christi & Moses excellency, pag. 43. Crispus Vol. 1. Serm. vi. Foedus novum omni à nostrâ parte conditione liberum dicit; contra ac fatetur caetera omnia Dei foedera esse, quæ nituntur stipulatione conditionum ab utraque parte praestandarum. hic secus, ubi à nullâ nostrâ conditione ait pendere, foedus ut firmum sit, vel irritum. Quia nempe hoc foedus est merum liberae gratiae donum: quod alias, inquit, non foret, si conditionem stipularetur Deus aut exigeret. Quidquid à foederatoirequiritur, hoc omne Deus ipse efficit, eique confert, atque id vi foederis, inquit Tom. 111. Serm. 11.
units.tr: Two things must first be explained in their sense: the nature of the gracious covenant, and then the relation which faith bears to it. On both points they depart not a little from the common manner of teaching. First, they acknowledge a twofold covenant: that of works, and the other of grace in Christ. This second is again twofold: either priestly under the Old Testament, or as it is now administered by Christ under the New. They say these are not different arrangements of one covenant but different covenants, and in this they agree neither with the truth nor with themselves. For in listing the differences between the two, which they place in three points, the first is that Christ's covenant is better than the older one in respect of the remission of sins: (α) there, not every kind of sin was forgiven, as here; (β) its conditions were bestowed there only after various conditions of sacred rites and sacrifices; (γ) it was granted gradually and successively through sacrifices, not once for all, as here. Their second point is the difference in respect of peace of conscience, and the third is the difference in respect of liberty from punishment and from the wrath of God. They admit that the substance of these things was present under that covenant too, but they assert a great difference of degree between this and that. Why, then, do they speak of a twofold covenant, rather than of one covenant with a twofold administration? In this way, what the Apostle calls two covenants in Heb. 8 and 9 could be explained quite well. Hence I think Richardson, part. 1 of his Divine Consolation, p. 328, denies that circumcision in itself was a sign of the covenant of grace. Against this disputes Vavasor Powell, in his Excellency of Christ and Moses, p. 43. Crisp, Vol. 1, Serm. 6, says the New Covenant is free from any condition on our part, whereas he admits that all other covenants of God rest on a stipulation of conditions to be performed by both parties. Here, he says, it is otherwise: the covenant does not depend on any condition of ours for being firm or void. This covenant, he says, is purely a gift of free grace, which otherwise it would not be if God stipulated or demanded a condition. Whatever is required of the one who enters the covenant, God himself performs all of it and confers it on him, and he does so by virtue of the covenant, as he says in Tom. 3, Serm. 2.

units.la: Quod ad fidem, negant eam foederis, aut justificationis nostrae conditionem esse: justificationem inquiunt contingere homini, dum impius est; qui postquam „justificatus est, incipiat credere: non fides dicenda „nos justificare, nisi per fidem intelligamus Christum; „qui solus justificat, & justificat hominem antequam „credit, adeo non per fidem. Fides manifestat justificationem, „quam ipso Christus homini impartit, ea„que animae declaratur per fidem in illum. Fides non „est conditio, absque qua nec Christum, neque beneficium ejus recipiamus; sed manifestatio ejus quod „jam omnino factum, receptumque. Quod trahit locum „Apostoli Heb. xi. 1. Non credimus (inquit) ut „justificemur, sed credimus postquam & quia justifica„ti: non justificamur, non sumus in foedere, non de eo participamus per ullam conditionem à nobis præstitam; sed in fœdere sumus, & Christus nos in fœdus suum assumit, absque ullâ in nobis conditione. Christus noster est, antequam habemus ullam qualificationem gratiosam. Crispus, Tom. III. Serm. II. pag. 84. ponit distinctionem inter hæc duo, ut Christus primum noster sit, quod est ante ullam in nobis conditionem, aut qualitatem; & quod noster est, ac manet, sequitur nostrum passim gerit, quod Spiritus Dei in nobis efficaciter ostendit per usum præceptorum ac institutorum divinorum. Vol. III. Serm. VII. Fides dicitur justificare declarativè, non aliter, quatenus justitiam Christi manifestam facit fidelibus. Fides, ut justitiam Christi respicit, non defert eam ad animam, sed declarat solummodo ejus præsentiam in animâ, quæ fuit etiam ante fidem. Homo quippe justificatus & reconciliatus Deo est, antequam credat. Ideoque fides non est instrumentum unionis nostræ cum Christo, sed fructus ex unione ejus ad nos sequens, qui nobis unitus est antequam credimus. Quare vis fidei non intelligenda est instrumentalis ad justificationem, sed ad ejus jam factæ, sed occultæ declarationem. Richardsonus Tom. III. pag. 67. etc. Fidei vox in Scriptura est πολύζηλος: quando dicimur justificari per fidem, fides significat Christum. Gal. III. 16. 19. 23. I. Joann. IV. 9. neque credendo justificamur, sed antequam credimus, per Christum justificati sumus, quando Christus in cruce pro nobis mortuus fuit; quæ justificatio per Spiritum S. cordibus nostris manifestatur, atque fide recipitur: ubi & nonnulla pro sententiâ suâ profert argumenta, sed quam facile solvi possunt. Eundemque vide pag. 125. ejusdem libri. Atque hæc de fide ipsorum, & justificatione.
units.tr: As for faith, they deny that it is a condition of the covenant or of our justification. They say justification befalls a man while he is still ungodly; after he has been justified, he begins to believe. Faith, they say, must not be called what justifies us, unless by faith we mean Christ, who alone justifies, and justifies the man before he believes, so far is it from being through faith. Faith makes manifest the justification which Christ himself imparts to a man, and this is declared to the soul through faith in him. Faith is not a condition without which we cannot receive Christ or his benefit, but the manifestation of what has already been wholly accomplished and received. They draw this from the Apostle's words in Heb. 11:1. "We do not believe," they say, "in order that we may be justified, but we believe after and because we are justified. We are not justified, we are not in the covenant, we do not partake of it through any condition performed by us; but we are in the covenant, and Christ takes us into his covenant with no condition in us. Christ is ours before we have any gracious qualification." Crisp, Tom. 3, Serm. 2, p. 84, draws a distinction between these two: that Christ is first ours, which is before any condition or quality in us; and that he is ours and remains ours; and then follows what we do, which the Spirit of God effectively shows in us through the practice of his precepts and divine ordinances. Vol. 3, Serm. 7: faith is said to justify declaratively, and in no other way, insofar as it makes the righteousness of Christ manifest to believers. Faith, as it regards the righteousness of Christ, does not carry it to the soul, but only declares its presence in the soul, which was there even before faith. For a man is justified and reconciled to God before he believes. Therefore faith is not the instrument of our union with Christ, but the fruit that follows from his union with us, since he is united to us before we believe. Hence the power of faith is not to be understood as instrumental for justification, but for the declaration of a justification already accomplished, though hidden. Richardson, Tom. 3, p. 67 and following. The word "faith" in Scripture is very many-sided: when we are said to be justified by faith, faith signifies Christ (Gal. 3:16, 19, 23; 1 John 4:9). We are not justified by believing, but we were justified through Christ before we believed, when Christ died for us on the cross. This justification is made manifest to our hearts by the Holy Spirit and received by faith. Here too he brings some arguments for his opinion, which can easily be answered. See the same author, p. 125 of the same book. And so much for their view of faith and justification.

units.la: Antea ostendimus, quomodo dicant, Peccata nostra stra omnia, & non solùm eorum poenas, à Christo portata fuisse, atque expiata: unde porrò docent, fidelem de peccatis suis dolere angíque non debet, cum respectu ad eorum demeritum, quum hoc omne à Christo sublatum sit: quare quum cogitamus, ipsa illa à nobis in Christum translata fuisse, ac proinde nos illis vacuos, nil reliquum quod doleamus. Tum (dicunt) remissionis sensum non habere nos jam, uti olim Israelitae, sub foedere sacerdotali, per interstitia & intervalla, interventu sacrificiorum, sed continuum & non interruptum, prout haec natura est foederis novi ab illo diversi. Crisp. Vol. III. Serm. III, IV, V. quod peccatum tantum in Christum translatum sit. Vol. II. Serm. XIII. non
units.tr: Earlier we showed how they say that all our sins, and not only their punishments, were borne and expiated by Christ. From this they further teach that the believer ought not to grieve or be anxious about his sins, with respect to their demerit, since all of this has been taken away by Christ. Therefore, when we consider that those very sins were transferred to Christ, and that we are accordingly empty of them, there is nothing left for us to grieve over. Then (they say) we do not have a sense of remission as the Israelites once did under the priestly covenant, by intervals and gaps, through the intervention of sacrifices, but a continuous and uninterrupted sense, as is the nature of the new covenant, which differs from that one. Crisp, Vol. 3, Serm. 3, 4, 5, that sin was transferred only to Christ. Vol. 2, Serm. 13:

units.la: „debemus dolere de peccatis, poenitere, humiliare, „jejunare, quasi per haec à peccatis effemus purgandi, vel per opera aliqua nostra curandi, aut ex operibus & officiis nostris remedium peccatis vel turbatae „conscientiae quaeramus. Omnes cultus divini partes „obeundae solùm tanquam Dei instituta, in quibus „promisit sese nobis manifestaturum, atque ad eum „glorificandum. Epist. Dedic. ad Vol. III. Vol. I. Serm. alt. pag. 330. Fidelis in quodcunque grave peccatum in„ciderit, adulterium, homicidium &c. mox tamen iter-„um respicere in Christum debet, neque expectare „primum ut humiliatus sit, doleat &c. antequam sibi „praesentem applicet consolationem in Christo, sed an-„te illa sibi aeque potest applicare promissionem remis„sionis, ac post illa, quae praestare quidem oportet, & „habere sensum peccati, & confiteri delicta, sed non ut „per ea gratiam acquirat, sed post adeptam, applicatamque gratiam, & ex hujus sensu. Serm. I. p. 311. „fideles propter peccata sua timere non est necesse, ne„que oportet, quia scilicet sublata & expiata sunt per „Christum. Timent quidem (inquit, cum hac distinctio„ne) peccatum committere, non autem de commissis, quasi aliquid detrimenti ipsis afferre possint. Quo addu-cis locum cum Rom. vii. 15. 19. 24. 25. ubi Apostolum loqui quidem de se ut regenito & fideli existimat, non autem ex propria, ut tum erat, persona, sed alicujus turbati, & præ gravitate inhærentis sibi corruptionis valde angustiati animi. Vti commissa peccata, ita neque afflictionem secundum ipsos, ullæ metum fidelibus injicere debent, quia nil damni inde oboriri potest, è contra nil nisi bonum, prout afflictiones omnes fidelibus in ipsorum immittuntur bonum. Vol. I. Serm. IX. p. 209. Serm. XI. pag. 264.
units.tr: "We ought not to grieve over sins, to repent, to humble ourselves, or to fast, as though by these we were to be purged of sins, or to be cured of them through some works of ours, or as though we sought a remedy for sins or for a troubled conscience from our works and duties. All parts of divine worship are to be performed only as God's institutions, in which he has promised to manifest himself to us and to be glorified. Dedicatory epistle to Vol. 3; Vol. 1, second sermon, p. 330. If a believer falls into any grave sin, adultery, murder, and so on, he ought nevertheless at once to look again to Christ, and not wait first until he is humbled, grieves, and so on, before he applies to himself the present consolation in Christ. Rather, he can apply to himself the promise of remission just as well before those things as after them. Indeed, he ought to do those things, and to have a sense of sin, and to confess his offences, but not so that he may thereby acquire grace; rather, after grace has been obtained and applied, and from the sense of it. Serm. 1, p. 311. Believers need not, and ought not, to fear on account of their sins, because they have been taken away and expiated by Christ. They do indeed fear (he says, with this distinction) to commit sin, but not to be troubled about sins committed, as though these could do them any harm. You bring forward the passage Rom. 7:15, 19, 24, 25, where he thinks the Apostle speaks of himself as a regenerate and faithful man, not out of his own person as he then was, but in the person of someone troubled, whose mind is greatly distressed by the heaviness of the corruption that dwells in him. Just as committed sins, so, according to them, neither should affliction cause fear to believers, because no harm can arise from it; on the contrary, only good, since all afflictions sent to believers turn to their good. Vol. 1, Serm. 9, p. 209; Serm. 11, p. 264.

units.la: His ita expositis de Adversariorum mente, primùm super Christi redemptione, quæque eo spectant; tum illius applicatione; pergendum ad illorum sententiam de credentiâ & observantiâ operum, & an hic legis ullus usus, tum quo fine opera bona facienda sint. Primò non putandum illos, quos vulgò vocant Antinomos, & de quibus nos agimus, bonorum operum hostes esse, vel non illa docere, qualia nonnunquam iis objiciuntur, atque nimis leviter de illis quandoque creduntur: sed de ratione & fine, quomodo bona opera facienda, disceptant. Quod alii legi tribuunt in docendo & exhortando (nam de usu legis in condemnando transgressores, in confesso est, cum per Euangelium, apud fideles, sublatum: nulla enim jam condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu), hi Christo vindicant, ejusque spiritui, quem liberâ & ingenuâ motione hominem agere dicunt, ad serviendum Christo, & Deo, solo ejus & benè vivendi amore allectum: nedum ut aliquos hic ex lege terrores necessum sit adhibere, vel ejus pædagogiâ ducere homines aut constringere. Vtuntur ad hoc vulgò Psal. cx. 3. erit tibi populus voluntarius. Vol. I. Serm. II. p. 31. Serm. IX. p. 191. Richardsonus, part. I. II. p. 17. 38. ita mentem explicat, ut omnino è re sit ejus verba hic describere: Lex est sancta, justa, & bona. Rom. 3. 31. Justitia legis manet, & quilibet tenetur vitam suam componere juxta eam; non recipimus legem, ut datam per Moysen. sent, sed ut datam per Christum; in eandem suis obedientiæ legem dat, licet non iisdem conditionibus, quamvis nil agere possimus ad salutem, bene tamen aliquid agere debemus ad ejus gloriam. Joh. 1 5. 8. Insistamus consulere diligenter bonis operibus, Tit. 3. 8. Vt quis dicat, non teneri nos observare decem præcepta, quæ appellatur lex moralis, decem verba, abominandum; quippe si non obliger observare ea, jam non peccat quando contra ago, neque mirum si tales abominandi sint in ipsorum cordibus & vita. Concedo, liberos nos ab ejus maledictione & pœna, verum non à rebus ea contentis. Lex concernit nostram conversationem, quamvis non salutem. Sitis vos sancti in omni modo conversatione: hinc commendantur sancti, vos qui diligitis Deum, odistis malum, & horretis societatem illorum, qui contemnunt præcepta Dei. Ita si omnes loquantur, haud adeo erit (facta commodâ interpretatione legis per Christum datæ) quod reprehendatur.
units.tr: Having thus set out the views of our opponents about Christ's redemption and what pertains to it, and then about its application, we must go on to their teaching on faith and the observance of works, whether the law has any use here, and for what end good works are to be done. First, we should not think that those whom people commonly call Antinomians, and with whom we are dealing, are enemies of good works, or that they do not teach them. Such charges are sometimes brought against them, and they are sometimes too lightly believed. Their dispute is about the manner and purpose in which good works are to be done. Some of them assign the law's role to teaching and exhorting. (That the law no longer condemns transgressors among believers, since through the Gospel it has been taken away, is admitted: for there is now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.) They ascribe this instead to Christ and to his Spirit, which, they say, moves a man freely and ingenuously to serve Christ and God, drawn only by love of him and of living well. There is no need to employ any terrors from the law here, or to lead or constrain men by its schoolmastering. For this they commonly use Psalm 110:3, your people shall be willing. Vol. I. Serm. II. p. 31. Serm. IX. p. 191. Richardson, part. I. II. p. 17. 38, explains the sense in such a way that it is worth quoting his words here in full: The law is holy, just, and good. Rom. 3:31. The righteousness of the law remains, and everyone is bound to order his life according to it. We do not receive the law as given through Moses, but as given through Christ. He gives the law of his obedience to us, though not on the same conditions. Although we can do nothing for our salvation, we ought nevertheless to do something well for his glory. John 1 5:8. Let us take care to be diligent in good works. Titus 3:8. That someone should say we are not bound to keep the ten commandments, which are called the moral law, the ten words, is an abomination. For if we are not obliged to keep them, then we do not sin when I act against them, and it is no wonder if such men are abominable in their hearts and lives. I grant that we are free from its curse and punishment, but not from the things it contains. The law concerns our conduct, though not our salvation. Be holy in all your conduct. Hence the saints are commended: you who love God, hate evil, and shrink from the company of those who despise God's precepts. If everyone spoke like this, there would be little to find fault with, provided the law given through Christ is interpreted suitably.

units.la: Nusquam magis solliciti sunt, nec hoc absque ratione, quam in distinguendis bonorum operum finibus, usibusque, ut intra metas suas maneant, & ne homo illis ullatenus fidat. Ex negotio justificationis, consolationis, & salvationis, jubent bona opera esse omnino; illaque vel ut nimium laudentur, & suo nomine deprædicentur; aut in relatione ad Christum effertantur, culpant. Vol. 1. Serm. 1. pag. 19. neque admittunt, dici viam ad regnum, utcunque non causa regnandi. Concedunt, esse officium in viâ peragendum, aut concomitantia ad cœlum, & comitari homines eo venturos, non verò viam ipsam, quæ solus Christus. Vol. 1. Serm. 1 v. Richardsonus, part. 111. pag. 58. Condemnamus, nos aliquid agere ad nostram salutem. Fines, ob quos præstanda sint bona opera, assignant. 1. ad testandam nostram erga Deum gratitudinem. 11. in ipsius atque ædificationem proximi. 111. ut in usu & exercitio illorum Deum, juxta promissionem, quod per illa hominibus occursurus sit, ac se manifestaturus, appre-hentendamus, eoque fruamur, non vero quasi per illa, v. g. per jejunia, precationes, & poenitentiam Deum mo-veamus erga nos, aut placemus, sed quod erga nos bene affectus Deus se propria voluntate in ipsius nostris officiis, aut exercitiis nobis videndum praebeat & ge-standum. Vol. I. Serm. VIII. pag. 193. & Serm. IX. pag. 217. Non patiuntur homines in consolationibus, vel acquirenda certitudine ac fiducia salutis, ad opera sua, ad qualificationes, officia, & fructus sanctifi-cationis remitti, vel in examine sui, ad signa, ad notas deflectere, quam viam litigiosam & dubiam vocant, atque quantum fiduciae operum proximioram, tantum Christo ejusque gratiae adversam. Vol. II. Serm. XV. inherentes qualificationes sunt dubia signa est: quod per vulgaria signa discurrendo, universalis obe-dientiae, sinceritatis, & amoris fraterni, ostensum it. Deo tantum agnoscit salutem hominis certo indicantia, Spiritum Christi, attestando illam animis, juxta verbum Dei; & fidem, eam recipiendo. Serm. XVI: XVII. & Vol. II. pag. 93. Serm. I. & II. Dei foedus cum suo populo fundamentum est ipsorum securitatis. Richardso-nus, Divin. Consolat. pag. 243. Ne tua consolatio dependeat ex tua personali sanctificatione, quia hinc non po-test certa fieri & constans consolatio. Consolationem quaerere a nostra sanctificatione, causa multarum turbarum in pluribus infirmis existit. Sanctificationi nihil cum justifi-catione, nec cum salute, ut aliqua causa earum: Sanctifica-tio etiam admittit gradus, verum justificatio nec regulas habet, nec gradus, magisque gloriosa est quam sanctificatio. Justificatio nostra oportet ut nos consoletur. Justificatio non dependet ex nostra apprehensione aut receptione, sed con-sistit in eo quod Dominus Iesus pro nobis fecit. Justificatio per Christum perfecta est; sed fide apprehenditur. Hebr. XI.
units.tr: Nowhere are they more anxious, and not without reason, than in distinguishing the ends and uses of good works, so that they remain within their limits and a man does not in any way trust in them. As regards the business of justification, consolation, and salvation, they command that good works be set aside altogether, and they blame those who praise them excessively and proclaim them by their own name, or who extol them in relation to Christ. Vol. I. Serm. I. p. 19. Nor do they allow it to be said that works are the way to the kingdom, however much they are not the cause of reigning. They concede that good works are a duty to be performed on the way, or accompaniments to heaven, and that men who are going there are accompanied by them; but the way itself, they say, is Christ alone. Vol. I. Serm. I. v. Richardson, part III, p. 58. We condemn the notion that we do anything for our own salvation. They assign the ends for which good works are to be performed as follows. (1) To testify our gratitude to God. (2) For the edification of our neighbour. (3) So that in the use and exercise of them we may apprehend God, as promised, who will meet and reveal himself to men through them, and so enjoy him. Not, however, as though by them, for example by fasting, prayers, and penance, we might move God towards us or appease him; rather, God, well disposed towards us, presents himself to be seen and embraced by us in our duties and exercises, by his own will. Vol. I. Serm. VIII. p. 193. & Serm. IX. p. 217. They do not allow men, in seeking consolation or the assurance and confidence of salvation, to be referred to their works, their qualifications, their duties, and the fruits of sanctification, or to turn aside into self-examination, to signs and marks, which they call a contentious and doubtful way. The more confidence is placed in one's own works, the more it is opposed to Christ and his grace. Vol. II. Serm. XV. inherent qualifications are doubtful signs, which, by running through the common signs of universal obedience, sincerity, and brotherly love, has been shown. Only God knows the signs that certainly indicate a man's salvation: the Spirit of Christ, bearing witness to it in our minds according to the word of God, and faith, receiving it. Serm. XVI, XVII. & Vol. II. p. 93. Serm. I. & II. God's covenant with his people is the foundation of their security. Richardson, Divine Consolation, p. 243. Do not let your consolation depend on your personal sanctification, for from this a certain and constant consolation cannot be made. To seek consolation from our sanctification is the cause of many troubles in most weak people. Sanctification has nothing to do with justification, nor with salvation, as a cause of them. Sanctification also admits of degrees, but justification has neither rules nor degrees, and is more glorious than sanctification. Our justification ought to comfort us. Justification does not depend on our apprehension or reception, but consists in what the Lord Jesus has done for us. Justification through Christ is perfect, but it is apprehended by faith. Heb. 11.

units.la: 1. Spiritus & fides manifestant nobis justificationem nostram, quotquot crediunt sunt justificati. Act. 13. 39. Possibile est habere πληροφορίαν fidei. Hebr. 10. 22. Fides facit in-fefragabilem evidentiam, & quando fides occulta dubiaque est, neque tum justificatio apprehenditur, nisi fide occulta ac dubia, neque sanctificatio est evidens sed dubia. atque ita nec potest nobis manifestare nostram justificationem. Ex sanctificationis effectis est quod homo in quaestionem trahit suam justificationem, quare nullam sanctificationis effectum potest animae monstrare suam justificationem: atque anima quae justificationem suam apprehendit in Christo, non solum novit eam, sed vivit ea, javibusque ejus fruitur fructibus, pace, gaudio, robora, absque ulla in seipso sanctificatione. Quandoquidem Christus factus est sanctificatio fidelium, 1 Cor. 1. 30. quare non ea viveret anima, diceretque, Sanctificationem habeo in Christo, quae perfecta est; nec saepe fallit justitia, verum ejus semper manet. Psalm. 111.3. Quare omnem meam consolationem accersam a Christo, neque per illam justificationem. Et quemadmodum non debemus inferre justificationem nostram ex aliquo effectu justificationis, ita nec illa apprehensio justificationis est a Deo, quae hominem abstrahit a mediis & regulis sanctificationis, namque decet est hominum non ambulare sancte, juxta verbum Dei. Tit. 2. 14. Haec prolixiora quidem, sed digna visa, quia non obvia, quae ex Anglico versa, hic, ubi de illorum, quos impraesens ad partes vocamus, sententia, legerentur, commodissime illam explicantia. Atque hoc hactenus, ad ipsorum exprimendam & explanandam mentem, ex propriis ipsorum scriptis, satis sit. Adjungamus quoque judicium de illis nostrum, qua pote brevitate, & exiguam.
units.tr: 1. The Spirit and faith make our justification manifest to us; all who believe are justified. Acts 13:39. It is possible to have full assurance [πληροφορία] of faith. Heb. 10:22. Faith produces an unshakeable evidence, and when faith is hidden and doubtful, justification is not then apprehended, except by hidden and doubtful faith, and sanctification is not evident but doubtful; and so it cannot make our justification manifest to us. It is from the effects of sanctification that a man calls his justification into question; therefore no effect of sanctification can show the soul its justification. But the soul that apprehends its justification in Christ not only knows it but lives by it, and enjoys its fruits, peace, joy, and strength, without any sanctification in itself. Since Christ has been made the sanctification of believers (1 Cor. 1:30), the soul does not live by that and say, "I have sanctification in Christ, which is perfect"; nor does righteousness often fail, but it always remains. Psalm 111:3. Therefore I will draw all my consolation from Christ, and not from that justification. And just as we ought not to infer our justification from some effect of justification, so that apprehension of justification which draws a man away from the means and rules of sanctification is not from God, for it is not fitting for men not to walk holily according to the word of God (Titus 2:14). These things are rather lengthy, but they seemed worth including, because they are not commonplace, and because they were translated from the English here, where we are dealing with the opinion of those whom we are now calling to account, and they explain it most conveniently. Let this suffice so far for setting out and explaining their view from their own writings. Let us also add our judgement of them, briefly and in a small compass.

units.la: 1. Permultum discrepant a communi docendi methodo. Passim nos docemus, in transitu hominis peccatoris ad statum gratiae, primum locum habere dolorem ac poenitentiam de peccato, inde fidem, justificationem, hinc unionem cum Christo, & sic foedus inter Deum ac hominem: non quod temporis inter illa, sed naturae differentia, actuumque diversorum observetur. Illi plane contrario modo & via philosophantur, & ubi nos incipimus, finiunt, atque in quo finimus, ab eo ordiuntur. Haec magna in methodo mutatio, haud exiguam conceptuum (quamvis in re dissensus haud adeo multus sit) infert varietatem. Primo foedus iniri inter Deum, & hominem peccatorem, & uniri inde cum homine Christum, justificatum esse, hinc credere, tum dolere aliquando de peccatis ut adversus Deum adeo gratiose justificantem commissis, id est, cum Evangelii, non legis intuitu, dicunt. Quae in quibus deficiant, ex sequentibus patebit. II. Concedimus interim nonnulla ab illis bene explicari, ad gratiae in Christo abundantiam significandam, & consolationem ac fiduciam salutis omnem in eo fundandam, & bene doceri, quomodo, misso operum nostrorum & dignitatis qualicumque respectu ac fiducia, oportear in solum Christum recumbere, extra nos. Nominatim a. quando negant ullas in homine, ante Christi gratiam, existere, aut dari posse praeparationes vel dispositiones bonas aut salutares, ad recipiendum Christum, ejusque gratiam: docentes, omne bonum ab illa gratia primum effici in nobis, nihil a nobis vel ex nobis produci posse. Tenenda hic distinctio; aliud ut sit, dispositiones ponere ab homine ortas & viribus suis praestitas, ante & ad gratiam Christi; aliud, ponere dispositiones ab illa Christi gratia effectas, ad gratiae varios actus exerendos, quae non existunt ante vel citra gratiam, sed ex ea, & viam sternunt ad illius gratiae opera edenda alia post alia. b. Quare & bene hoc docent, quomodo initium omnis boni non sit ducendum ex nobis, sed ex Deo & Christo; non nos Deum excitare, vel in eum ferri primos, & quasi a nobis inciperet quodcunque nobis boni contingit, primo respiciendum hominem; sed primas in toto religionis negotio partes Christo & Deo per omnia tribuendas esse. g. Proinde nec debere homines ullis suis fidere dispositionibus, qualitatibus, aut operibus, quasi hinc Deo acceptiores & digniores essent; & non ex solo Christo, Deo grati. III. Neque rejicimus aliquas illorum distinctiones; ut receptione Christi, & gratiae Christi primùm passivæ, tum activæ. Inter justificationem, prout facta in Christo; & prout manifestatur apud animum: quamvis in hujus rei explicatione non per omnia conveniamus. Inter dari Christum nobis, & manifestari. Et Christum nostrum fieri, ac nostrum esse. IV. Ex adverso à non benè observatis nonnullis distinctionibus, illorum errores præcipuè orti. Quales, præter jam datas, sunt. 1. quod aliud sit, conditionem bonam esse in nobis, vel à nobis: utcunque hoc non sit, illud tamen esse. 2. Conditio fœderis pangendi alia est; vel quod jam pactum accipiendi. Hic potest esse conditio, quamvis ibi non sit. 3. Conditio potest esse in accipiendo, quæ non est in dando. 4. Imò donum eo majus, si & rem, & cum ea ipsam quoque conditionem, ad rem accipiendam necessariam quis donet. Uti Deus dat nobis Christum & fidem quoque, quâ eum recipimus. 5. Conditionis præsentia aliud, aliud ejus dignitas. Illa est, quamvis hæc nulla sit. 6. Distinguimus formam regenerationis & novæ vitæ; tum actus ejus varios; neque enim omnes statim simul exseruntur. Quemadmodum in homine vivente, momento quidem infunditur anima, sed quæ varios tunc & jam prodit actus, ut primùm magis vegetativos, inde sensitivos, tum rationales, non viceversa, vel non omnes uno impetu, sed singulos ordine, quorum hi ad illos viam disponunt, qui suo tempore succedunt, quamvis omnes ex unâ & indita semel animæ rationalis formâ. 7. Hâc ratione distinctè consideramus Christi gratiam in homine primùm descendentem; atque inde ejus operationes. Operatur illa quidquid in homine veri & salutaris boni, & formam bonæ ac salutaris vitæ imprimit quidem unâ actione semel, sed hoc non obstat quo minus ad statum & conditionem hominis à peccato ad Deum perducen-di, di ; primo excitet in homine actum pœnitentiæ de peccatis præteritis ; tum fidei, pro eorum habenda sententiaque in Christo remissione ; inde virtutes reliquas. Quemadmodum Crispus loquitur, Vol. I. Serm. VI. pag. 136. substantiam fœderis applicari quidem fidelibus quam primum justificantur ; sed varios ejus fructus demum suo tempore in illis compleri : ita nos hic de gratia, ejusque operationibus in homine loquimur. n. Fœdus gratiæ consideratur vel apud Deum, vel apud hominem : ibi, ut Deus ex illo fœdere homini bene facit, quamvis fœdus vel ignoranti adhuc, vel etiam contemnenti : hic, prout homo à Deo jam ad ipsum conversus, fœdus illud quoque init, eique confœderatur. ꝏ. Nulla conditio nostra ante fœdus, quidem in eo. ˢ. Atque hic jam integra cum Christo nostra unio observatur : ut inde distinguamus Christi primum ad nos accessum, & ejus nobiscum unionem, quæ demum integra concipitur, ubi est reciproca. ɔ. Christus accedit ad nos, & prior, & cum domi ; nos accedimus inde ad Christum, cum nostris officiis : quæ adeo non obstant ejus liberæ donationi, ut ipsa Christi in nobis dona sint. ꝯ. Est unio Christi oblata, & inita : illius fides consequens & fructus est, hujus concomitans. ꝺ. Aptitudo in nobis ad Christum nulla est ; sed quidem ex Christo, ad officia. ɔ. Nulla nostra aptitudo ante Christum, quidem aliqua cum Christo, dum accipitur. Ut non promiscue Christus ebrioso, lenoni, homicidæ &c. prostituendus sit, qualis proponitur fideli. ꝺ. Non pugnant, ut fides declarat nobis justificationem nostram, & quoque justificet, instrumentaliter nempe. ꝺ. Nam non ipse actus credendi justificat ; ut hinc temere argutentur Adversarii, eumque justitiæ Christi opponant : sed Christus fide apprehensus. p. Non pugnant, libere ex spiritu Christi Deo obedire ; & secundum ejus legem. ꝥ. Bona opera in negotio fidei oportet respicere ut ministros, & pedisequos, non ut præcursores. ꝯ. Nulla vero in re illa fiunt sunt opponenda, vel comparanda Christo. Sub Christo, & salvo hujus honore, non verendum est ne nimium praedicentur. g. Aliud est, confirmare salutis certitudinem ex bonis operibus; aliud eam in illis fundare, id quod nullâ ratione probandum. n. Denique aliud, ex signis operum probare virtutum, potius quam status nostri veritatem.
units.tr: 1. They differ considerably from the common method of teaching. We everywhere teach that in the passage of a sinful man to the state of grace, sorrow and repentance for sin come first, then faith and justification, then union with Christ, and so the covenant between God and man. We do not mean that these follow one another in time, but that they differ in order of nature and in kind of act. They reason in the opposite manner and by the opposite route. Where we begin, they end, and where we end, they begin. This great change of method brings no small variety of concepts, although the disagreement in substance is not so great. First they say that a covenant is entered into between God and sinful man, that Christ is united with man from that point, that man is thereby justified, that from this he believes, and that he then at some time grieves over the sins committed against God, who justifies so graciously. They mean that this happens with a view to the Gospel, not to the law. Where these views fail will appear from what follows. II. We nevertheless grant that some things are explained well by them, to signify the abundance of grace in Christ, and that all confidence and assurance of salvation is to be founded in him; and that it is taught well how, setting aside any regard for our works and any dignity or trust in them, we ought to rest in Christ alone, outside ourselves. Namely, (a) when they deny that any good or saving preparations or dispositions for receiving Christ and his grace exist in man before Christ's grace, or can be given, teaching that every good is first effected in us by that grace, and that nothing can be produced by us or from us. The distinction must be kept here. It is one thing to posit dispositions that arise from man and are accomplished by his own powers, before and toward the grace of Christ. It is another to posit dispositions effected by that grace of Christ, for the exercise of its various acts. These do not exist before or apart from grace, but come from it, and pave the way for the works of that grace to be produced one after another. (b) Therefore they also teach well how the beginning of all good is not to be derived from us but from God and Christ. It is not we who stir up God, or who first move toward him, nor should man be looked at first, as if whatever good befalls us began from us. Rather, the first parts in the whole business of religion must be given to Christ and God in all things. (c) Accordingly, men ought not to trust in any of their dispositions, qualities or works, as if by these they were more acceptable and worthy to God, and it is not from Christ alone that they are pleasing to God. III. Nor do we reject some of their distinctions: such as between the reception of Christ and of the grace of Christ, first passive and then active; between justification as accomplished in Christ and justification as made manifest to the mind, although we do not agree in every respect in explaining this matter; between Christ being given to us and Christ being made manifest; and between Christ becoming ours and Christ being ours. IV. On the other hand, their errors have arisen chiefly from certain distinctions that were not well observed. Such are, besides those already given: 1. that it is one thing for a good condition to be in us, and another for it to come from us; however that may be, the condition is still there. 2. The condition of making a covenant is one thing, and that of accepting a covenant already made is another. Here there can be a condition though there is none there. 3. There can be a condition in accepting which is not present in giving. 4. Indeed the gift is greater if someone gives both the thing and, along with it, the very condition necessary for receiving the thing, as God gives us Christ and also the faith by which we receive him. 5. The presence of a condition is one thing, its worth is another. The former may be there while the latter is none. 6. We distinguish the form of regeneration and of new life from its various acts, for not all of them are put forth at once. As in a living man the soul is infused in a moment, yet it then produces various acts, first the more vegetative, then the sensitive, then the rational, and not the reverse; nor are all put forth with one impulse, but singly and in order, each preparing the way for those that succeed in their time, although all come from one rational soul once infused. 7. In this way we distinctly consider Christ's grace first descending into man, and from it its operations. That grace works whatever is true and saving good in man, and imprints the form of a good and saving life by one action, once. But this does not prevent it from first stirring up in man, to bring his state and condition from sin to God, an act of repentance for past sins; then of faith, for holding and judging these sins forgiven in Christ; then the remaining virtues. As Crispus says (Vol. I, Sermon VI, p. 136), the substance of the covenant is indeed applied to believers as soon as they are justified, but its various fruits are completed in them only in their time. So we speak here of grace and its operations in man. (d) The covenant of grace is considered either with God or with man. With God, he does good to man from that covenant, although the man may still be ignorant of it or even despise it. With man, as he is now turned to God by God, he too enters into that covenant and is joined to it in it. (e) No condition of ours exists before the covenant, though one exists within it. (f) And here the full union with Christ is observed, so that we distinguish Christ's first approach to us from his union with us, which is finally conceived as complete when it is mutual. (g) Christ approaches us, and he is first, and comes with his gift; we then approach Christ with our duties, which do not hinder his free giving and are indeed themselves gifts of Christ in us. (h) The union with Christ is offered and entered into; faith is its consequence and fruit, and its accompaniment. (i) There is no aptitude in us for Christ, but there is one from Christ, for duties. (j) There is no aptitude of ours before Christ, though some exists with Christ while he is received. So Christ is not to be offered indiscriminately to a drunkard, a pimp, a murderer and so on, as he is offered to the believer. (k) They do not conflict: faith declares to us our justification, and also justifies, instrumentally of course. (l) For the act of believing does not itself justify; the Adversaries rashly argue this and oppose it to the righteousness of Christ. Rather, Christ is justifying, apprehended by faith. (m) They do not conflict: to obey God freely, from the Spirit of Christ, and according to his law. (n) Good works in the business of faith must be regarded as ministers and attendants, not as forerunners. (o) Yet in that matter no works are to be set against or compared with Christ. Under Christ, and with his honour preserved, there is no need to fear that they are praised too much. (p) It is one thing to confirm the certainty of salvation from good works, and another to found it on them, which cannot be proved by any reasoning. (q) Finally, it is one thing to prove from the signs of works the truth of our virtues, rather than the truth of our status.

units.la: v. Pro hominibus in tentationibus & desertionibus spiritus constitutis, qui nimium ad se, sua opera semper, imperfectiones, & dvaσθνείας recurrunt, non contemnenda aliquando sunt quae urgent Adversarii contra istum hominum in se recursum, & reclinationem, & pro instruendis, erigendis, consolandis, laetandisque animis (adhibitis, quos diximus, limitibus & cautelis) conferri hic ab illis nonnihil, haud difficendum. Certe uti magnae sapientiae est tales bene curare, ita in tractandis illis magna adhibenda prudentia: & uti homines ita afflicti peccant in tacita operum fiducia, cumque eâ symbolizatione, ita non sunt in se retrudendi, & signis vel notis, aut officiis multum vexandi, verum abigendi potius extra se, & in Christo constituendi. Ad quod suis conceptibus non poenitendam forte praestant illi homines operam.
units.tr: v. For people placed in temptations and desertions of spirit, who too often return to themselves, to their own works, their imperfections and their weaknesses, what the Adversaries urge against this human turning back and leaning on oneself is sometimes not to be scorned. It is not difficult for them to contribute something here toward instructing, raising up, comforting and gladdening minds, provided the limits and cautions we have mentioned are observed. Surely, as it takes great wisdom to care well for such people, so great prudence must be used in dealing with them. And since men so afflicted sin through a tacit trust in works, and with it a kind of compact, they are not to be pressed back into themselves nor harassed much with signs, marks or duties, but rather driven out of themselves and established in Christ. In this their own concepts perhaps they render no unwelcome service.

units.la: Denique ut jam & Brownistarum, & aliorum attexamus controversias, en earum syllabum. Cum Brownistis ergo quaeritur:
units.tr: Finally, so that we may now also set out the controversies with the Brownists and others, here is their list. The questions put to the Brownists are these:

units.la: 1. Num Ecclesia Anglicana, & praeter eam Reformatae omnes aliae, adeo fuerint corruptae, ut ab iis secedendi causas satis justas & graves habuerint Angli Brownistae, sive Separatistae; vel, an ab ejus Ecclesiae communione separare nos oporteat, ubi de singulorum in eâ membrorum conversione & probitate non sumus certi, atque convicti? Neg.
units.tr: 1. Were the English Church, and all the other Reformed churches besides it, so corrupted that the English Brownists, or Separatists, had sufficiently just and serious reasons for seceding from them; or ought we to separate from the communion of that Church when we are not certain and convinced of the conversion and integrity of its individual members? No.

units.la: 11. Num potestas gubernandi Ecclesiam sit penes eam totam, & singula ejus membra? adeoque negotia omnia Ecclesiastica, non in ullo Conclavi, sed publice & in facie totius Ecclesiæ, atque ab eâ tractari debeant? Neg.
units.tr: II. Does the power of governing the Church belong to the whole Church and to each of its members, so that all ecclesiastical business ought to be handled not in any private room, but openly and in the sight of the whole Church, and by it? No.

units.la: III. Num Ecclesiæ Seniores omnes debeant esse perpetui, & ex officio quoque διδάσκαλοι? Neg.
units.tr: III. Must all the elders of the Church be perpetual, and also teachers by virtue of their office? No.

units.la: IV. Num particularis quælibet Ecclesia debeat esse non amplior, quam quæ uno ambitu & loco ad sacra celebranda, sub uno Pastore, convenire queat? Neg.
units.tr: IV. Ought any particular congregation to be no larger than can gather in one place and compass to celebrate the sacred rites under one minister? No.

units.la: V. Num regimen singularum Ecclesiarum debeat esse independens, & abstractum à communione cum Ecclesiis aliis, ac combinatione mutuâ in Congregationes Classicas aut Synodicas, easque statas & ordinarias? Neg.
units.tr: V. Ought the government of each individual church to be independent, and cut off from communion with other churches and from mutual combination into classical or synodal assemblies, and those fixed and regular? No.

units.la: VI. Num idololatrica olim Papistarum templa, campanæ &c. non queant ad usus sacros repurgari & adhiberi: neque Ministri verbi ex reditibus, aut decimis, sed ex sola populi collectâ sustentandi sint? Neg.
units.tr: VI. Can the former idolatrous temples of the Papists, their bells and so on, not be purged and used for sacred purposes, and must the ministers of the Word not be supported from revenues or tithes, but only from the money collected from the people? No.

units.la: VII. Num non liceat Ministro in Ecclesiâ conjugium confirmare & benedicere? Neg.
units.tr: VII. Is it not lawful for a minister in the Church to confirm and bless a marriage? No.

units.la: VIII. Num nullas liceat habere precandi formulas, neque adeo ipsam orationem Dominicam pro precatione usurpare? Neg.
units.tr: VIII. Is it not lawful to have any set forms of prayer, nor indeed to use the Lord's Prayer itself as a prayer? No.

units.la: IX. Num infantes non sint baptizandi quorum parentes proximi non sunt membra Ecclesiæ in communione S. Cœnæ, quamvis in Ecclesiâ nati? Neg.
units.tr: IX. Are infants not to be baptized whose parents nearest to them are not members of the Church in communion at the Lord's Supper, although they were born in the Church? No.

units.la: Cum Antinomis hæc quæruntur:
units.tr: These questions are put to the Antinomians:

units.la: I. Num Christus patiendo pro peccatis nostris, ipsa peccata sibi habuerit imputata, & non solum eorum stratum tulerit ac pœnas? Neg.
units.tr: I. Did Christ, in suffering for our sins, have the sins themselves imputed to him, and not merely bear their burden and punishments? No.

units.la: II. Num Christus pro omnibus & singulis hominibus redemptionem dederit universalem? Neg.
units.tr: II. Did Christ give a universal redemption for all and each of mankind? No.

units.la: III. Num ante omnem bonam qualitatem in animâ à Dei gratiâ productam Christus cum eâ unitus sit dicendus & homo cum Deo fœderatus à suâ etiam parte, sibique etiam peccatori improbissimo æque possit applicare omnes promissiones gratiæ, ac fideli? Neg. iv. Num credat homo demum postquam est justificatus, & fides justificationem sequatur? Neg.
units.tr: III. Before any good quality produced in the soul by the grace of God, is Christ to be said to be united with it, and man to be covenanted with God on his own side too, so that he can apply all the promises of grace to the most wicked sinner just as to the believer? No. iv. Does a man believe only after he has been justified, and does faith follow justification? No.

units.la: v. Annon dolere & pœnitere de commissis peccatis, ex intuitu etiam transgressæ legis, & pœnæ demeritæ, indeque humiliari animo oporteat, ut quis se promissionibus Christi soletur, earumque faciat securum? Aff.
units.tr: v. Ought one not to grieve and repent of the sins committed, also from regard to the transgressed law and the deserved punishment, and so humble oneself in mind, that one may comfort oneself with the promises of Christ and make oneself secure in them? Yes.

units.la: vi. Annon fidelibus & regenitis quoque lex moralis prædicanda sit? Aff.
units.tr: vi. Ought the moral law not also to be preached to believers and the regenerate? Yes.

units.la: Liber Undecimus De GRÆCIS, & ORIENTALIBUS.
units.tr: Book Eleven: On the Greeks and the Orientals.

units.la: GRÆCA Ecclesiæ olim præstantissimæ & celeberrimæ. Historia dissensionum, & controversiarum inter Græcos, ac Latinos. Origo illarum, & progressus. Ecclesiarum Scisma, vel secessio. Unio aliquoties tentata. De Concilio Nicæno, & canone ejus vi. super primatu episcopi Romani. Unde prima & gravissima quæstio Græcorum cum Latinis. De Concilio Constantinopolitano, ejusque can. iii, & symbolo. De Ephesino, contra Nestorium. Hinc de Nestorianismo, & quæstione quæ Græcas Ecclesias vehementer concussit, altera. De Chalcedonensi Concilio, & Eutychianismo. De Constantinopol. ii. contra Theodor. Mopsvestenum &c. De Monothelitis, & Conc. Constantinopolitano iii. vel trinisexto. De Concilio Constantinopolitano quinisexto habito in Trullo, variisque eo contentis controversiarum capitibus: de monogamia Clericorum; Canon xxxvi. de paritate Constantinopolitani episcopi cum Romano, de jejunio sabbathi, de esu sanguinis
units.tr: The Greek Church, once the most excellent and most celebrated. History of the disputes and controversies between Greeks and Latins: their origin and progress. The schism or secession of the Churches. Union attempted several times. On the Council of Nicaea and its sixth canon concerning the primacy of the bishop of Rome, whence the first and most serious question between Greeks and Latins arises. On the Council of Constantinople and its third canon, and its creed. On the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius. Hence on Nestorianism, and the second question, which violently shook the Greek Churches. On the Council of Chalcedon and Eutychianism. On the second Council of Constantinople against Theodore of Mopsuestia, etc. On the Monothelites and the third Council of Constantinople, or the Quinisext. On the Quinisext Council of Constantinople held in Trullo, and the various heads of controversy contained in it: on the monogamy of clergy; canon 36, on the equality of the bishop of Constantinople with the Roman; on fasting on the Sabbath; on eating blood and what is strangled.

units.la: ac Juffocati. De Concilio Constantinopolitano VII. adversus cultum imaginum. De septem Graecorum Synodis. De processione Spiritus S. à Patre, Filioque. Leviores aliquot Graecorum cum Romanis quaestiones. De pane S. Coenae azymo. Secessio Ecclesiarum Graecarum, à Latinâ. Tentata aliquoties unio. de Concilio Florentino. Judicium de Graecorum controversiis. De Patriarchâ Constantinopolitano. De Russis, & Moscovitis. De Alexandrino Patriarchâ, & Cophtis. De Abyssinis. De Antiocheno Patriarchâ. De Jerosolymitano. Syri, & Melchitae. Maronitae. Chaldaei. Nestoriani. Armeni. Georgiani. Graecorum Liturgiae, & invocatio Sanctorum. Quinam illorum se cum Romana conjungunt Ecclesiâ, qui minus. De Patriarcharum Constantinopolitanorum, praesertim Jeremiae, & Cyrilli studio ergâ Protestantes. Quid agendum hic sit: quomodo disputandum.
units.tr: On the seventh Council of Constantinople against the veneration of images. On the seven Synods of the Greeks. On the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son (Filioque). Some lesser questions of the Greeks with the Romans. On unleavened bread in the Lord's Supper. The secession of the Greek Churches from the Latin. Union attempted several times; on the Council of Florence. Judgment on the controversies of the Greeks. On the Patriarch of Constantinople. On the Russians and the Muscovites. On the Patriarch of Alexandria and the Copts. On the Abyssinians. On the Patriarch of Antioch. On the Patriarch of Jerusalem. The Syrians and Melchites. The Maronites. The Chaldeans. The Nestorians. The Armenians. The Georgians. The liturgies of the Greeks and the invocation of the saints. Which of them join themselves to the Roman Church, and which less so. On the Patriarchs of Constantinople, especially Jeremiah and Cyril, and their zeal toward the Protestants. What must be done here: how it is to be disputed.

units.la: VAriae temporum, locorumque Ecclesiae observari possunt periodi, & nationum respectu, apud quas ea diversis temporum momentis diversata fuit, tres quidem celebriores notari gentes debent, Hebraei, Græci, Europæi. Apud Hebræos prima fuit Ecclesia; ab hiis ad Græcos; à Græcis ad Europæos, apud quos nunc, desertis illis, & neglectis pœne istis, fere tota commorari videtur. Hactenus, post illa quae de Infidelibus, tribus primis libris, diximus, occupati fuimus in explicandis Ecclesiae Europeae rebus, & variis sectis: sequitur, ut quid Ecclesiae apud Graecos superfit, videamus. In initio praedicationis Apostolicae, communis nationum divisio, & in scriptis Apostolicis usitatissima fuit, Iudaeorum, & Graecorum. Hinc Paulinum istud: Iudaeo primùm, & Graeco: Judaeis & Graecis. Rom. 1.16. & 11. 9. 10. 1.Cor. 1.24. & x. 32. adde Act. xiv. 1. & xviii. 4. & xx. 21. Praeter hoc, Barbari aliquando adjunguntur. Rom. i. 14. Graecis & Barbaris, Col. iii. 11. non refert, in Christo videlicet, Graecus & Iudaeus, circumcisio & praeputium: Barbarus, Scytha: servus, liber. Ubi Iudaeus, Graecus, & Barbarus; inter Barbaros, Scytha. Barbarorum generale nomen, quo & Iudaei, & Graeci, denique & Romani, alias a se nationes denotatunt. Illi quemque extraneum appellant βάρβαρον, quod sua non utatur lingua. Nam modum vel vitium loquendi vox illa sua origine significat. Hinc Apostolus dixit i. Cor. xiv. 11. ἐὰν μὴ εἰδῶ τὴν δύναμιν τῆς φωνῆς, ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος, καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐν ἐμοὶ βάρβαρος. Eademque ratione Graeci alios a se omnes, Romanos quoque; & hi vicissim illos, caeterosque, barbaros dixerunt. Hodieque in Graecia qui aliis correctius loquuntur, reliquos item barbaros vocant. Testis Simeon Cabasilas, in litteris ad Crusium, a. clɔ Iɔ lxxviii. ὡς οἱ τὴν Ἑλλάδα οἰκοῦντες, κατὰ τὰ πολλὰ φθεγγόμενοι, βαρβάρως τοῖς ... ἀποκαλοῦσι, τύττας βαλλοπέ[?]μενοι, ὥσπερ πάνυ τῆς πάλαι ... ἡ Ἀρμενίου.
