Trium hodie sunt ordinum Graece loquentes: quidam corruptissimo utuntur sermone, vix priscis intelligendo, quales sunt Atheniensis. Alii μεγαλοβάρβαροι Graecobarbarum sermonem habent. Denique sunt qui aliis rectius loquuntur, sed hi rariores, quales qui Constantinopolim, Thessalonicam, Peloponesum incolunt. Hunc sermonem in scriptis Cyrilli, nuper Constantinopolitani episcopi; istum, in versione Novi Testamenti a Maximo Calliopolita, in Graecum vulgarem factâ, observare est. Quaeque alibi in scriptis eorum Ecclesiastis cis Graeco-Barbara occurrunt, erudito Glossario explicuit Ioh. Meursius. Inter Barbaros, Scythas nominat Apostolus: an quod ad eos, vel eorum, quocunque loco consisterent, aliquos pervenisset jam Euangelium? an verbi vel exempli gratia illos dixit, inter Barbaros remotissimos, ut ita melius doceret, neminem a Christo, cujuscunque status nationisque, seclusum, qui non per fidem pari in eo jure & beneficiis frueretur? Schytarum alioquin ad ultimam Septentrionem sitorum conversionem ad Christum celebrant, quando de latitudine Ecclesiæ, & acceptæ salutaris prædicationis, loquuntur Patres, Tertullianus, Chrysostomus, Hieronymus. Ille in libro adversus Iudæos: jam Getulorum varietates, & Maurorum multi fines, Hispaniarum omnes termini, & Galliarum diversæ nationes, & Britannorum inaccessa Romanis loca, Christo vero subdita, & Sarmatarum, & Dacorum, & Germanorum, & Schytharum &c. Sic & Christum, & Euangelium illis prædicatum, & creditum Chrysostomus meminit: ubique gentium in regione Romanorum, Persarum, Schytharum, Maurorum, Indorum, & alias orbem nostrum. Hieronymus, Tom. I. epist. ad Lætam: depositis pharetras Armenius, Hunni discunt psalterium, Schythiæ frigora fervent calore fidei. Et Tom. II. epist. illâ celebri ad Euagrium, ubi de paritate Episcoporum agit, & horum à Presbyteris nuperâ distinctione: quid enim facit exceptâ ordinatione Episcopus, quod presbyter non faciat? Nec altera Romanæ urbis Ecclesia, altera totius orbis existimanda est. Et Gallia, & Britannia, & Africa, & Persis, & Oriens, & India, & omnes Barbaræ nationes, unum Christum adorant: unam observant regulam veritatis. Si auctoritas quæritur, orbis major est urbe. Missis tum Barbaris, tum Iudæis, vel quomodo apud hos, aut ab his ad illos Ecclesia discesserit, Græcos impræsentiarum spectabimus, non illos, prout inito prædicationis Euangelii erant Ecclesiæ primæ illustrissimæque, à quibus aliæ fundatæ, & quorum linguæ, post Hebræam, sacra, & usitata Scriptoribus divinis uniformiter fuit, etiam quum ad Romanos, ad Hebræos scriberent, quos in suis epistolis non Hebraeâ, vel Romanâ linguâ. Sed unâ Græcâ alloquuti fuerunt; neque dubito quin & propter eandem causam Matthæi Euan-ge. gelium, & N. Testamenti scripta omnia Græce consignata ab Auctoribus suis fuerint: verùm hodiernos Græcos, & quales apud eos nunc sint Ecclesiæ, videbimus. Illos nominamus, quia in Oriente, vel Orientalibus Ecclesiis præcipui sunt, quamvis præter illos, dicemus quoque de Cophthis, Abyssinis, Armenis: uti de illis qui aut quatuor in Oriente Patriarchatibus subsunt, aut ab illis seorsim vivunt.
units.tr: The periods of the Church may be observed in various times and places, and with respect to the nations among whom it lived at different moments of time. Three especially celebrated nations must be noted: the Hebrews, the Greeks, and the Europeans. The first Church was among the Hebrews; from them it passed to the Greeks, and from the Greeks to the Europeans, among whom, those others now having been deserted and almost neglected, it seems to dwell almost entirely. Hitherto, after what we said about the unbelievers in the first three books, we have been occupied in explaining the affairs of the European Church and its various sects; it follows that we should see what remains of the Church among the Greeks. At the beginning of the apostolic preaching the common division of the nations, and the most usual one in the apostolic writings, was that of Jews and Greeks: hence Paul's phrase "to the Jew first, and also to the Greek" (Rom. 1:16), "Jews and Greeks" (Rom. 1:9–10; 1 Cor. 1:24; 10:32; add Acts 14:1; 18:4; 20:21). Besides this, "barbarians" is sometimes added: "to Greeks and to barbarians" (Rom. 1:14); "where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free" (Col. 3:11). Here Jew, Greek and barbarian are named, and among the barbarians, the Scythian. "Barbarian" was a general name by which Jews, Greeks, and finally Romans also designated the nations other than themselves. Each of them called any foreigner barbarian [βάρβαρον], because he did not use their language, for that word by its origin signifies a manner or defect of speech. Hence the Apostle said: "If I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to him that speaketh, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian to me" (1 Cor. 14:11) [ἐὰν μὴ εἰδῶ τὴν δύναμιν τῆς φωνῆς, ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος, καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐν ἐμοὶ βάρβαρος]. By the same reasoning the Greeks called all others barbarians, the Romans as well, and these in turn called the former and the rest barbarians. Even today in Greece, those who speak more correctly call the rest barbarians too. Witness Simeon Cabasilas, in his letters to Crusius, in the year 1578: as those who inhabit Greece, speaking for the most part, call those who speak otherwise "barbarians" [ὡς οἱ τὴν Ἑλλάδα οἰκοῦντες, κατὰ τὰ πολλὰ φθεγγόμενοι, βαρβάρως τοῖς ἀποκαλοῦσι], as is very much the case with the old... of Armenia. Today there are three orders of those who speak Greek: some use a very corrupt speech, hardly intelligible to the ancients, such as the Athenians; others have a Greek-barbarian speech [μεγαλοβάρβαροι]; finally there are those who speak more correctly than the others, but these are rarer, such as those who live in Constantinople, Thessalonica and the Peloponnese. This speech may be observed in the writings of Cyril, recently bishop of Constantinople; that other in the version of the New Testament made into the vernacular Greek by Maximus of Callipolis. Whatever Greek-barbarian expressions occur elsewhere in the writings of their ecclesiastics, John Meursius has explained in a learned glossary. Among the barbarians the Apostle names the Scythians. Was it because the gospel had already reached them, or wherever they lived? Or did he name them, by way of example, as the most remote among the barbarians, so as to teach better that no one, of whatever condition or nation, is excluded from Christ, who through faith does not enjoy the same right and benefits in him? Indeed, the Fathers celebrate the conversion of the Scythians, who lived at the farthest north, to Christ, when they speak of the breadth of the Church and of the salutary preaching it received: Tertullian, Chrysostom, Jerome. Tertullian, in his book against the Jews: "Already the varieties of the Getulians and the many borders of the Moors, all the boundaries of the Spains, and the diverse nations of the Gauls, and the places of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans, yet subject to Christ, and of the Sarmatians, the Dacians, the Germans and the Scythians, etc." So also Chrysostom mentions Christ and the gospel preached and believed among them: "everywhere among the nations, in the regions of the Romans, Persians, Scythians, Moors, Indians, and the other parts of our world." Jerome, vol. 1, letter to Laeta: "The Armenians lay aside their quivers, the Huns learn the psalter, and the cold of Scythia glows with the warmth of faith." And vol. 2, in that famous letter to Evagrius, where he treats of the equality of bishops and the recent distinction between them and presbyters: "For what does a bishop do, except in ordination, that a presbyter does not do? Nor should the Church of the city of Rome be thought one, and the Church of the whole world another. Both Gaul and Britain and Africa, and Persia, and the East, and India, and all the barbarian nations, worship the one Christ and observe the one rule of truth. If authority is sought, the world is greater than the city." Setting aside the barbarians and the Jews, or how the Church departed among them, or from them to others, we shall now look at the Greeks, not at those first and most illustrious churches of the beginning of the preaching of the gospel, from which others were founded, and whose language, after Hebrew, was uniformly the sacred and customary one for the divine writers, even when they wrote to the Romans and to the Hebrews, whom in their epistles they addressed not in Hebrew or Latin but in Greek alone. Nor do I doubt that for the same reason the Gospel of Matthew and all the writings of the New Testament were written by their authors in Greek. But we shall see the present-day Greeks, and what churches now exist among them. We name them because they are the chief among the Eastern or Oriental Churches, although besides them we shall also speak of the Copts, the Abyssinians and the Armenians, as well as of those who are subject to the four Eastern patriarchates or live separately from them.

units.la: Nam quum quatuor vulgo ex antiquâ distributione habeantur Græcarum Ecclesiarum Patriarchæ, Constantinopolitanus, Alexandrinus, Antiochenus, & Ierosolymitanus, (adnumeratâ Romanâ, quinque Ecclesias universales seu catholicas nominat Nilus, lib. 1. Differ. Eccles.) hi omnes ferè Orientis Ecclesias inter se diviserunt, suisque subdiderunt juribus. Constantinopolitani latissima semper fuit dioecesis, ad quam pertinuerunt Ecclesiæ per Græciam, Mysiam, & Bulgariam, Thraciam, V Valachiam, Moldaviam, Russiam, Moscoviam, insulas Ægæi maris, & Asiam minorem. Ad Alexandrinum, Cophthi & Æthiopes. Ad Antiochenum Syri spectant. Ad Ierosolymitanum alii. Sedes Constantinopolitani est nova Roma, seu Constantinopolis; Alexandrini, hodie Alcairum; Antiocheni, Damascus; Ierosolymitani, ipsa urbs Ierusalem. Undecim Religionis sectas in Oriente numerant alii, Græcos, Syros & Melchitas, Georgianos, Moscovitas seu Russos, Nestorianos, Indos seu S. Thomæ (vulgò dictos) Christianos, Iacobitas, Cophthos, Armenos, Abassinos, Maronitas. Quorum tres præcipui, atque ex quibus reliqui plus vel minus participant, Græci, Nestoriani, & Iacobitæ.
units.tr: For although four Greek Patriarchs of the Churches are commonly held, from the ancient distribution, the Constantinopolitan, the Alexandrian, the Antiochene and the Jerusalemite (adding the Roman, Nilus calls five universal or catholic Churches, Book 1 of the Differences of the Churches), all of these have divided almost all the Eastern Churches among themselves and subjected them to their jurisdictions. The diocese of Constantinople was always the widest, and to it belonged the Churches throughout Greece, Mysia and Bulgaria, Thrace, Wallachia, Moldavia, Russia, Muscovy, the islands of the Aegean Sea, and Asia Minor. To Alexandria belong the Copts and the Ethiopians. To Antioch belong the Syrians. To Jerusalem belong others. The seat of Constantinople is New Rome, or Constantinople; that of Alexandria is today Cairo; that of Antioch, Damascus; that of Jerusalem, the city of Jerusalem itself. Others count eleven religious sects in the East: Greeks, Syrians and Melchites, Georgians, Muscovites or Russians, Nestorians, the so-called Indian or St. Thomas Christians, Jacobites, Copts, Armenians, Abyssinians, and Maronites. Of these three are the chief, and the rest share more or less in them: the Greeks, the Nestorians, and the Jacobites.

units.la: Ac primo quidem oportet inquirere in causas & themata dissensionum inter Græcos ac Latinos, & juxta historiam quando quæque & quâ occasione enata sint, quæ magnas contentiones, inde & divulsionem Ecclesiarum fecerunt, primo res regiminis & disciplinæ Ecclesiarum, tum quoque fidei. Prima disputatio fuit super auctoritate, vel majoritate Episcoporum Orientis, vel Occidentis, nempe Constantinopolitani cum Romano, hoc modo orta. Erecta à Constantino Imp. Constantinopoli, & huc translata Imperii sede, Constantinopolis Romam aemulata, hujus paritatem ubique affectavit, & pro urbis conditione, similiter quoque ejus Episcopus: ut mox simultas & discordia nata sit inter utriusque Romae, Veteris & Novae episcopos, Romanum & Constantinopolitanum, quorum ille parem, hic superiorem ferre recusabat: atque hoc initium contentionum inter utrasque Ecclesias, Occidentis & Orientis, Romanam & Graecas fuit, super primatu, vel suprematu episcopi Romani. Atque emulari primum auctoritatem Romani episcopi, Orientales coeperunt, illamque suis finibus coërcere: quod factum in primo Concilio Nicaeno; adeo à primis initiis haec exorta. Tum paria cum Romano Orientales Constantinopolitano suo attribuere, in Concilio Constantinopolitano: quod confirmarunt iterum in Chalcedonensi. Inde in aliis Synodis alia orta, & in Constantinopolitani quini-sextâ Trullanâ varia imprimis adversus Romanos controversiarum capita, resque tandem eo pervenit, ut scissa in partes Ecclesiâ Orientali & Occidentali, apertum schisma seu secessio facta fuerit: post quae sepius quidem laboratum pro resarciendâ unione, sed frustra, uti in sequentibus ostendemus.
units.tr: First, one must indeed inquire into the causes and subjects of the disputes between the Greeks and the Latins. Following history, one must ask when and on what occasion each arose, since they produced great contentions and then the division of the Churches. These were first matters of church government and discipline, and then matters of faith. The first dispute concerned the authority, or the greater standing, of the bishops of the East or of the West, namely Constantinople against Rome, and it arose in this way. Constantine the Emperor founded Constantinople and transferred the seat of the Empire there. Constantinople, rivalling Rome, sought equality with her in every respect, and its bishop likewise, in keeping with the city's rank. Soon rivalry and discord arose between the bishops of the two Romes, Old and New, the Roman and the Constantinopolitan. The one refused to yield equality, the other refused to yield precedence. This was the beginning of the contentions between the two Churches, Western and Eastern, the Roman and the Greek, over the primacy or supremacy of the Roman bishop. The Eastern bishops began to challenge the authority of the Roman bishop and to confine it within its own limits, which was done at the first Council of Nicaea, so that this dispute arose from the very beginnings. Then the Eastern bishops attributed equal standing to their Constantinopolitan bishop with the Roman one, at the Council of Constantinople, and they confirmed this again at Chalcedon. From there other disputes arose in other synods, and especially at the Quinisext (Trullan) Council of Constantinople, which contained various chapters of controversy against the Romans. At last matters reached such a point that the Church was split into Eastern and Western parts and an open schism or secession occurred. After this there were frequent efforts to repair the union, but in vain, as we shall show in what follows.

units.la: Quae quo melius constent, ab ovo rem exponere necesse erit, initio facto à Concilio Nicaeno, annotatis ubique iis, quae vel Graecorum cum Ecclesiâ Romanâ disceptationes, vel ipsorum inter se motas haereses erroresque, quales Nestorianorum, Eutychianorum &c. quibus permulti ab eo tempore inter ipsos hodieque infecti, concernunt. Synodi habentur duum generum, generales, & particulares, illae etiam Oecumenicae dicuntur, non quod ex toto orbe collectae, sed propter orbem ImpeImperii Romani, οἰκουμενικ dici soliti, & quod ex Oriente Occidenteque Legati iis convenerint, sive quod de rebus & causis generalis fidei decreverint; non autem quod forte à Romano episcopo confirmatæ. Istæ locales συνοδοι τοπικαι dicuntur, & μεγαλαι: illæ οἰκουμενικαι, vel generales. Unde in Synodo Bracarensi I. c. 1. Ioh. xii. Relecti ex Codice coram Concilio tam generalium Synodorum canones, quam localium. Particulares nonnullæ etiam ante Nicænam generalem habitæ fuerunt, sed in ordine & volumine Conciliorum vulgo post Nicænam ponuntur, dignitatis, non temporis, habitâ ratione, quâ Nicæna præcellit. Tales Carthaginenses, sub Cypriano; Antiochena, contra Paulum Samosatenum; Ancyrana; & Neo-cæsariensis; quas confirmat Synodus Constantinopolitana in Trullo, can. 11. & Chalcedonensis, can. 1. jubet observari canones à Patribus constitutos κατὰ ἑκάστην συνοδον.
units.tr: So that these things may be better established, it will be necessary to set out the matter from the beginning, starting from the Council of Nicaea. I shall note everywhere those things which concern either the disputes of the Greeks with the Church of Rome, or the heresies and errors stirred up among themselves, such as those of the Nestorians, the Eutychians, and others, by which very many have been infected from that time down to the present day. Synods are of two kinds, general and particular. The general ones are also called oecumenical, not because they were gathered from the whole world, but on account of the world of the Roman Empire, which were usually called oecumenical [οἰκουμενικαί]. They are also called so because legates from East and West met there, or because they decreed concerning the matters and causes of the general faith, and not because they were perhaps confirmed by the Roman bishop. The local ones are called local synods [συνοδοι τοπικαι] and great [μεγαλαι]; the general ones are oecumenical [οἰκουμενικαι], or general. Hence in the first Synod of Braga, c. 1, John xii: The canons of general synods, as well as of local ones, were read from the codex before the council. Some particular synods were also held before the general Nicene one, but in the order and volumes of the councils they are commonly placed after the Nicene, the order being according to dignity and not time, since Nicaea is pre-eminent. Such are the Carthaginian under Cyprian; the Antiochene against Paul of Samosata; the Ancyran; and the Neocaesarean. The Synod of Constantinople in Trullo confirms them at canon 11, and the Council of Chalcedon, canon 1, orders that the canons established by the Fathers according to each synod [κατὰ ἑκάστην συνοδον] be observed.

units.la: Nicænum Concilium habitum fuit, seculo quarto: at quo ejus anno, haud ita certum; consulatu Paulini, & Iuliani, xiii. Kal. Iulii, ut habent Veteres inscriptiones. Sed quis ille imperii Constantini annus, magis autem Christi, & annon sub aliis Consulibus celebratum, ambigitur: adeo in incerto sunt, præcipuè temporis chronologiam si respicimus, quæ olim acta leguntur. Bene quidem id cautum à Constantino, quod in limine Codicis Theodosiani statim occurrit, si quæ post hæc edicta, sive Constitutiones, sine die & Consule fuerint deprehensa, auctoritate carent: unde non parum luminis hisce obscuritatibus infertur: sed utinam moris tum etiam fuisset, quod multo demum tempore post incœpit, ut Christi annus actis saltem Ecclesiasticis adsignatus fuisset; nam per annos Imperatorum, & Consules omnia numerabantur; ut ita securius pedem in tempore Actorum designando figeremus. Iam & de annis Imperatoris, & de eo ad Christianam chronologiam reducendo valde laboramus. Disputat de tempore & anno habiti Nicaeni Concilii Baronius in Annalibus; & hoc exemplum adfert Iohannes Lydius, vir doctissimus, in praefat. ad Prateolum de Conciliis, à se auctum, quo probet quam incerta temporum in antiquitatibus Ecclesiasticis sit ratio, quia ipsius Nicaeni Concilii tempus quidam ad annum Christi referunt cccxx, quidam, ut Eusebius in Chronico, ad A. cccxxiv. quidam ad cccxxx. Alii ad cccxxiii. ad cccxxxvii. alii. Communior tamen, eaque verior videtur sententia, quae constituit Concilii tempus in annum Christi cccxx. anno imperii Constantini xx. Indictum concilium fuit in urbe Bithyniae Nicaeâ. Fue-runt enim & aliae Niceae, in Galliâ, in Thraciâ. De duabus praecipue illic actum controversiis; de Pascha te, & de doctrinâ Arii; accessit & tertium, quod inter particularia, & ecclesiasticum erat, concernebatque ecclesiam Alexandrinam, ubi graves turbas Episcopo Alexandrino moverat aliquis Meletius, qui & causam dedit decisioni in Synodo factae, super juribus Archiepiscoporum: unde hic, tum Romani in Occidente, tum in Oriente Alexandrini, Antiocheni, & Ierosolymitani episcoporum tanguntur episcopalia, imprasens nobis consideranda, quia & hinc primatum suum Romanus, Graecis semper controversum, constabilire conatus fuit.
units.tr: The Council of Nicaea was held in the fourth century. But the year of it is not very certain: it was in the consulship of Paulinus and Julian, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, as the ancient inscriptions have it. Yet which year of Constantine's reign it was, and still more which year of Christ, is in doubt, and whether it was celebrated under other consuls. They are so uncertain, especially if we look at the chronology of time, in the acts that are read from long ago. Constantine certainly took good precaution in this, as appears at once at the head of the Theodosian Code: if any edicts or constitutions issued after this are found without a day and consul, they lack authority. Thus not a little light is brought to these obscurities. But would that the custom had also existed at that time, which began only much later, that the year of Christ had been assigned at least in the ecclesiastical acts. For everything was numbered by the years of the emperors and consuls, so that we might fix our foot more securely in designating the time of the acts. Even now we labour greatly over the years of the emperor and over reducing them to Christian chronology. Baronius disputes the time and year of the Council of Nicaea in his Annals. John Lydius, a most learned man, adduces this example in his preface to Pratéolus on the Councils, which he enlarged, to prove how uncertain the reckoning of times is in ecclesiastical antiquities. For some refer the time of the Nicene Council itself to the year of Christ 320, some, as Eusebius in his Chronicle, to 324, some to 330, others to 323, to 337, and others. The more common opinion, and it seems the truer one, places the time of the Council in the year of Christ 320, the twentieth year of Constantine's reign. The council was convened in Nicaea, a city of Bithynia. For there were also other Nicaeas, in Gaul and in Thrace. Two controversies were especially treated there: the Easter question, and the doctrine of Arius. A third was added, which was among the particular and ecclesiastical matters, and which concerned the Church of Alexandria, where a certain Meletius had stirred up grave troubles for the Alexandrian bishop. He also gave occasion for the decision made in the Synod concerning the rights of archbishops. Hence the episcopal matters touching the Roman bishop in the West, and the Alexandrian, Antiochene, and Jerusalem bishops in the East, are now to be considered by us, because from this too the Roman bishop tried to establish his primacy, which was always disputed by the Greeks.

units.la: Athanasius, lib. de Synod. duplicem Synodi hujus causam ponit, Syri etenim, Cilices, Mesopotamiani in causa festi claudicabant, atque una cum Iudaeis Pascha celebrant: & jam tum Ariana haeresis, quae contra Ecclesiam insurrexerat, suos propugnatores habebat, qui ipsum defenderent, & qui piis insidias facerent, Eusebianos scilicet. Quod de Paschate celebrando ait, differentiam illam concernit, quâ alii decima quartâ die primi mensis aut aequinoctio verno praecise Pascha observabant, quod idem tempus & Iudaei tenent: alii vero non decimo quarto die, sed sequenti dominico, quo sic magis à Iudaeis viderentur distare, festum illud agebant. Disparitas illa ritus diu in Ecclesiâ fuerat, Asianis decimam quartam tenentibus, Occidentalibus contrà, usque dum in Concilio Nicæno paritas observandi eodem die Paschatis introducta fuit. De quâ disputatione omnino idem dico, quod Nicephorus, histor. lib. xii. cap. xxxii. mihi non recte fecisse videntur, qui olim de festo hoc die tantopere dissidentes contenderunt. Egregiusque hanc in rem apud Socratem locus est, Histor. Eccles. lib. v. cap. xxi. Hoc loco, meâ quidem sententia, opportunum tempus se offert, pauca de Paschate differendi. Neque veteres certè, neque recentes, hi qui Iudaeorum consuetudinem imitari contendunt, satis justam causam, si quid ego judico, habuerunt, cur tantopere de hoc festo digladiarentur: neque praeterea illud cum animis considerarunt, quando religio Iudaica erat in Christianam commutata, accuratas illas Mosaicae legis observationes, & rerum futurarum figuras penitus evanuisse. Cujus rei argumentum certissimum inde capi potest, quòd nulla lex à Christo condita, Christianis fecit potestatem ritus Iudaicos observandi, imò vero contrà Apostolus illud plane vetuit, dum non modò circumcisionem abrogabat: verum etiam hortabatur, ut de festis nulla fieret dissensio. Deinde: Qui quarto decimo die mensis Paschae celebrant, eum morem observandi à Ioanne Apostolo ipsis traditum dicunt: qui autem Romam & alias partes Occidentis incolunt, Petrum & Paulum Apostolos, consuetudinem, quam illi tenent, ipsis reliquisse affirmant. Verùm nemo istorum omnium, testimonium de hu rebus scriptis proferre potest. Et quòd ex consuetudine potius in singulis locis, quam ex ullâ aliâ causâ coepta sit festi Paschatis celebratio, hinc facio conjecturam, &c. Et c. praecedente, canonem refert, in Novatianorum Angarensi Synodo constitutum, quem ἀδιάφορον vocabant, docebantque, dissensionem de festo Paschatis non satis justam causam esse, cur Ecclesiæ pax dirimeretur. Cujus occasione in dissertationem illam de Paschate, & varietate rituum Ecclesiasticorum digreditur c. xxi. Neque hanc
units.tr: Athanasius, in his book On the Synods, gives a twofold cause of this synod. The Syrians, Cilicians, and Mesopotamians were wavering in the matter of the feast, and celebrated Passover together with the Jews. And already at that time the Arian heresy, which had risen up against the Church, had its supporters, who defended it and who laid snares for the pious, namely the Eusebians. What he says about celebrating Easter concerns the difference by which some observed Passover precisely on the fourteenth day of the first month or at the vernal equinox, which the Jews also keep at the same time, while others did not celebrate that feast on the fourteenth day but on the following Sunday, so that they might seem to differ more from the Jews. This difference of rite had existed in the Church for a long time, the Asians keeping the fourteenth day and the Westerners the contrary, until uniformity of observing Easter on the same day was introduced at the Council of Nicaea. On this dispute I say altogether the same thing as Nicephorus, History, book 12, chapter 32: They seem to me not to have acted rightly who once contended so fiercely over this feast day. Socrates has an excellent passage on this matter in his Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 21: Here, in my opinion, a fitting time presents itself to say a few things about the differing of Easter. Neither the ancients nor the moderns, who strive to imitate the custom of the Jews, certainly had a sufficiently just cause, if I judge rightly, for fighting so fiercely over this feast. Moreover, they did not consider with their minds that when the Jewish religion was changed into the Christian, those exact observances of the Mosaic law and the figures of future things had wholly vanished. A most certain proof of this can be drawn from the fact that no law established by Christ gave Christians the power of observing Jewish rites. On the contrary, the Apostle plainly forbade this, when he not only abrogated circumcision but also exhorted that there be no dispute about feasts. Further: those who celebrate Passover on the fourteenth day of the month say that this custom was handed down to them by the Apostle John; but those who live in Rome and the other parts of the West affirm that the Apostles Peter and Paul left them the custom which they keep. But none of them can produce written testimony of these things. And that the celebration of the feast of Passover began from custom in individual places rather than from any other cause, I make this conjecture, etc. And in the preceding chapter he cites the canon established in the Synod of the Novatians at Ancyra, which they called indifferent [ἀδιάφορον]. They taught that a dispute over the feast of Passover was not a sufficiently just cause for the peace of the Church to be broken. On that occasion he digresses in chapter 21 into that discussion about Easter and the variety of ecclesiastical rites. Socrates rightly gives Baronius a good thrashing for this, Annals, vol. 4, at the year 390, and also Binius, Councils, vol. 1, p. 538. But of this elsewhere. Also, the cause of Arius was then debated, and his opinion was condemned, which held that the Son of God…

units.la: { } hanc ob causam bene vapulat Baronio Socrates, Annal. Tom. iv. ad a. cccxc i. tum etiam Binio, Concil. Tom. i. pag. 538. Sed de hoc alias. Atque Arii causa tum quoque agitata, damnata ejus sententia, qui Filium Dei docebat non esse Deum aeternum, sed ὡσὲ ὅτι ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν, ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ἐγένετο ut haec & similia illum, ejusque socios dicere solitum, in epistola sua scribit Alexander presbyter Alexandrinus. Aderant in Synodo recenti atque octodecim episcopi; inter quos qui cum Ario faciebant, princeps erat Eusebius Nicomediensis, vir callidus, & vafer: contra eos potissimi Alexander ille, quem dixi, & Athanasius, Alexandrinae Ecclesiae tum temporis adhuc diaconus. Denique Meletium quod attinet, ejusque causam, erat hic Episcopus Lycopolis, in Thebaide Ægypti, & quia tempore persecutionis sub Diocletiano, idolis sacrificarat, à Petro Alexandrino episcopo de gradu motus fuerat: quod aegre ferens, praeter multas in Petrum, ejusque successores Achillam & Alexandrum injurias, & calumnias, sententiae quoque ipsius inobediens & cedere nolens, schisma instituit, alios Diaconos, episcopos & presbyteros, invito Alexandrino (cui suberat ipse in Ægypto Episcopus) creans, & ordinans, quorum indiculum, seu breviarium à Meletio traditum Alexandro episcopo, refert Athanasius, Apol. ii. Quae tandem causa ad Concilium Nicaenum devoluta, Patres quidem mitius agere cum Meletio, illisque à se ordinatis presbyteris, ut in epistola Synodica ad Ecclesiam Alexandrinam legere est; sed tamen Synodale decretum occasione Meletianorum, turbarumque contra Archiepiscopum motarum, pro inviolata Episcopi Alex. in suas Ecclesias potestate edere ipsos perpulit. can. vi. Τὰ ἀρχαῖα ἔθη κρατείτω, ἀντίχθονα ... Antiqui mores obtineant, ut qui sunt in Ægypto, Libya & Pentapoli, Alexandrinus episcopus horum omnium habeat potestatem. ἐπειδὴ ἡ τοῦ ὁ τῶ Ῥώμῃ ἐπισκόπῳ τοῦτο σύνηθες ἐστιν, quoniam illa est Ro-mano etiam episcopo consuetudo. Similiter autem & in Antiochiâ, & in aliis provinciis privilegia servantur Ecclesiis τὰ πρεσβεῖα σῴζεσθαι τῆς ἐκκλησίας. Illud autem omnino manifestum est, quod si quis praeter sententiam Metropolitani factus sit episcopus, hunc magna Synodus statuit non oportere esse episcopum. Hoc contra Meletianos, eosque a Meletio ordinatos, inscio Metropolitano Alexandrino, Episcopos; uti illa, pro jure metropolico Alexandrini sarto tectoque in posterum conservando. Et sequens canon VII. de Ierosolymitano agens: ἐπειδὴ συνήθεια κατέχει [?] ἀρχαία παράδοσις ... ἐπίσκοπον τιμᾶσθαι [?]. Quoniam consuetudo obtinuit, & antiqua traditio, ut Æliæ episcopus honoretur, habeat ordinem honoris, Metropoli propriâ dignitate servatâ. Recenseri vides episcopos, Romanum, Alexandrinum, Antiochenum, Ierosolymitanum, eosque appellari metropolitanos. Quae ut intelligamus, sciendum, primis Apostolorum temporibus eundem fuisse presbyterum & episcopum; postea autem humanâ & Ecclesiasticâ constitutione discrimen introductum, ut episcopus supra presbyteros constitueretur, primùm quidem non nisi ordinis causâ, ratione habitâ ætatis, vel prioris aut posterioris in ministerio ordinationis: at deinde quoque additâ majori potestate & præfecturâ episcopis in presbyteros, præcipue ut hi ab illis ordinarentur: de quibus viri doctissimi jam abundanter docuerunt, Salmasius, Blondellus, alii. Sed quæ causâ episcopos supra presbyteros evexit, eadem supra Episcopos unum quoque primum constituit; nempe, uti in civitate supra presbyteros episcopus, ita supra plurium civitatum in unâ provinciâ episcopos Metropolitanus vel Archiepiscopus, ratione habitâ civitatum, carumque dignitatis, in formandis episcopis, & archiepiscopis in provinciæ metropoli. Nimium ad normam civilis regiminis constituta ecclesiarum regendarum ratio: quia mos est causarum civilium, idem in negotiis EcEcclesiasticis obtinendum est. Cod. Theodos. lib. xvi. Et sic urbium splendor eousque valuit in Ecclesiasticis quoque disponendis, ut sedes episcoporum confirmaretur, vel tolleretur, pro urbium fortunis. Quod maxime manifestum in episcopatu Constantinopolitano, quando ea urbs per Constantinum evecta, simul eius episcopus, ob urbis dignitatem, plures circum se ecclesias suae potestati mox subjecit, ac depressit. Sic & in aliis. Unde in Concilio Tauritanensi, paulo post obitum Ambrosii celebrato, super contentione inter episcopos Arelatensem, & Viennensem, uter illorum primatum obineret, definitum can. 1. ut qui ex eis comprobaverit suam civitatem esse metropolim, is totius provinciae honorem primatus obtineat. Ut stupendus error vel contumacia sit Baronii, in canonem Concilii Constantinopolitani quintum negantis, juxta rationem civitatum, ordines illos Ecclesiasticos compositos fuisse. Uti supra variarum civitatum episcopos Archiepiscopus, vel primus episcopus, qui ratione urbis, quam incoleret ecclesia major, dicebatur Metropolitanus, obi metropolim provinciae; ita quando sub Constantino variae in unam dioecesim reductae fuerunt provinciae, supra Metropolitanos quoque paulo post constituti fuerunt Primates superiores, Exarchi dioecesium, ut Metropolitani exarchi provinciarum, qui peculiari nomine appellabantur Patriarchae, vel Patriarchae episcopi. Hi necdum noti concilio Nicaeno, Metropolitani quidem: sed haud ita multo post fundamenta istius quoque ordinis jacta, per mutatam provinciarum in dioeceses formam civilem, atque nomen & res Patriarcharum in Concilio Chalcedonensi palam audita saeculo sequenti. Hi ergo gradus, sed praeter verbum & institutionem Apostolorum, per viam secularis fastus, supra presbyteros in Ecclesiam post se invicem surrepsere, 1. Episcoporum. 11. Metropolitanorum. 111. Patriarcharum: omnia paulatim, ex consuetudine primum, verum quam deinceps
units.tr: For this reason Socrates is rightly given a sound thrashing by Baronius, Annals, vol. iv, under the year 390, and likewise by Binius, Councils, vol. i, p. 538. But more on this elsewhere. The cause of Arius was also debated at that time, and his opinion was condemned: he taught that the Son of God was not eternal God, but there was when he was not, and he came from things that were not [ὡσὲ ὅτι ἦν ὅτε οὐκ ἦν, ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων ἐγένετο]. Alexander, presbyter of Alexandria, writes in his letter that Arius and his companions used to say such things and similar ones. At the recent synod there were also eighteen bishops. Among those who sided with Arius the leader was Eusebius of Nicomedia, a shrewd and crafty man. Against them stood chiefly that Alexander I have mentioned, and Athanasius, who was then still only a deacon of the Church of Alexandria. As for Meletius and his cause: he was bishop of Lycopolis in the Thebaid of Egypt, and because in the time of the persecution under Diocletian he had sacrificed to idols, he was removed from his rank by Peter, bishop of Alexandria. Taking this badly, and apart from many injuries and calumnies against Peter and his successors Achillas and Alexander, and refusing to obey or yield to their sentence, he set up a schism. Without the consent of the Alexandrian bishop, under whose authority he himself stood in Egypt, he created and ordained other deacons, bishops and presbyters. Athanasius, in his second Apology, gives the list or summary of these men which Meletius handed to Alexander the bishop. This cause was at last referred to the Council of Nicaea. The Fathers indeed dealt more gently with Meletius, and with the presbyters he had ordained, as can be read in the synodal letter to the Church of Alexandria. Yet the synodal decree, prompted by the Meletians and the disturbances raised against the archbishop, compelled them to issue a ruling for the inviolable power of the Alexandrian bishop over his churches (canon 6): Let the ancient customs prevail [Τὰ ἀρχαῖα ἔθη κρατείτω], that the bishop of Alexandria have authority over all who are in Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis, since this is the custom also for the bishop of Rome [ἐπειδὴ ἡ τοῦ ὁ τῶ Ῥώμῃ ἐπισκόπῳ τοῦτο σύνηθες ἐστιν], for that is the custom also for the Roman bishop. Likewise also in Antioch, and in the other provinces the privileges of the churches are preserved [τὰ πρεσβεῖα σῴζεσθαι τῆς ἐκκλησίας]. Moreover, this is altogether plain: if anyone is made bishop without the approval of the metropolitan, the great synod decrees that he ought not to be bishop. This was aimed against the Meletians, and the bishops ordained by Meletius without the knowledge of the Alexandrian metropolitan; the canon likewise sought to keep the metropolitan rights of Alexandria safe and secure for the future. The following canon 7, dealing with Jerusalem, says: Since custom has prevailed and ancient tradition [ἐπειδὴ συνήθεια κατέχει ... ἀρχαία παράδοσις ... ἐπίσκοπον τιμᾶσθαι], that the bishop of Aelia be honoured, let him have the order of honour, the dignity of the metropolis being preserved. You see that the bishops of Rome, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem are listed, and are called metropolitans. To understand this, we must know that in the earliest times of the apostles presbyter and bishop were the same; but later, by human and ecclesiastical arrangement, a distinction was introduced, so that a bishop was set over the presbyters. At first this was only for the sake of order, with regard to age or to the earlier or later date of ordination in the ministry. Later, greater power and oversight were also given to bishops over presbyters, especially so that the presbyters should be ordained by them. The most learned men have already written about this at length: Salmasius, Blondel and others. But the same cause that raised bishops above presbyters also set one primate above the bishops. Just as in a city the bishop is above the presbyters, so over the bishops of several cities in one province stands the metropolitan or archbishop, with regard to the cities and their dignity, in appointing bishops and archbishops in the metropolis of the province. The arrangement for governing the churches was set up too much on the model of civil government: because it is the custom in civil cases, the same should be observed in ecclesiastical affairs (Cod. Theodos. lib. xvi). And so the splendour of cities held such weight even in arranging ecclesiastical matters that the sees of bishops were confirmed or abolished according to the fortunes of cities. This is most evident in the see of Constantinople, when that city was raised up by Constantine: at once its bishop, on account of the city's dignity, brought many churches round about under his power and lowered their status. So also in other cases. Hence at the Council of Tauris, held shortly after the death of Ambrose, when the bishops of Arles and Vienne contended over which of them should hold the primacy, it was decided (canon 1): that whichever of them proves that his city is the metropolis, let him hold the honour of primacy over the whole province. How amazing is the error, or the obstinacy, of Baronius, who denies that those ecclesiastical orders were arranged according to the rank of cities, as stated in the fifth canon of the Council of Constantinople. Just as the archbishop, or first bishop, over the bishops of several cities, who was called metropolitan because the greater church was in the city where he lived, was the metropolis of the province, so when under Constantine several provinces were brought together into one diocese, primates were set up a little later above the metropolitans as well: the exarchs of dioceses, as the metropolitans were exarchs of provinces, who were called by the special name of patriarchs, or patriarch-bishops. These were not yet known at the Council of Nicaea, which knew only metropolitans. But not long after, the foundations of this order too were laid, through the change of provinces into civil dioceses, and the name and reality of patriarchs were openly heard of at the Council of Chalcedon in the following century. These grades, then, were slipped into the Church one after another above the presbyters, through the path of worldly pride, and without the word or institution of the apostles: 1. bishops; 2. metropolitans; 3. patriarchs. All of them gradually grew up, first from custom, but afterwards the canons confirmed them.

units.la: Cod. Theodos. lib. xvi. ceps canones confirmarunt. In Metropolitanis id manifestissimum, de quibus in Conc. Nicæno: origo enim eorundem petitur non aliunde, quam ex antiquâ consuetudine, sive de Alexandrino loquantur, sive de Romano, sive de Ierosolymitano, ubi vis est ἀρχαία ἐξουσία, συνηθὲς, παράδοσις δικαία, neutiquam ex sacris, vel divinâ institutione horum derivatur aut jus aut praxis. Alexandrino Episcopo defertur potestas, vel corroboratur potius, in Ecclesias Ægypti, ubi turbas dederat Meletius, & in Ecclesias Libyæ, ac Pentapolis: idque ex duplici ratione, primùm, quia ita jam antiqui mores obtinuerant. Omnium prima fuit Ecclesia Alexandrina, quæ speciem distincti episcopatus supra presbyteros habuit; uti è contrario Africana omnium ultima. Testatur id de Alexandrinâ Ecclesiâ Hieronymus, in epist. ad Euagrium, cos à Marco Euangelista, usque ad Heraclam & Dionysium presbyteros, semper unum ex se electum in excelsioris gradu collocasse, quem episcopum nominabant. Atque hic uti Episcopi, ita primò omnium Patriarchæ nomen auditum. Sed & altera ratio confirmati in dioecesi suâ juris illæsi Alexandrino episcopo, erat exemplum Episcopi Romani, quod apud eum quoque consuetudo illa esset, ut haberet potestatem ecclesiarum sibi subjectarum. Ergo id volunt, quemadmodum Romanus in suâ, sic Alexandrinus, sic Antiochenus in suis provinciis supremi ut sint, & quæ jura Metropolitano Romano constant, eadem ut in suas Ecclesias servarent Alexandrinus, & Antiochenus. Vides id hoc canone agi, ut quieta & salva maneant Metropolitanis sua ἀρχαία ἐξουσία, æque Alexandrino, æque Antiocheno, ac Romano. Par ordo istorum constituitur in suos inferiores; nulla vero potestas alicui in parem; Metropolitano in Metropolitanum. Frustra est Baronius, reliquique cum eo Papæ assentatores, dum aliter hunc Nicænum canonem legunt, & longè adhuc aliter interpretantur. In exordio præfigunt ea verba:
units.tr: Cod. Theodos. lib. xvi. The matter is most evident with the metropolitans, of whom the Council of Nicaea speaks. For their origin is sought from nothing other than ancient custom, whether one speaks of the Alexandrian, the Roman or the Jerusalem metropolitan, where there is talk of ancient authority, custom, just tradition [ἀρχαία ἐξουσία, συνηθὲς, παράδοσις δικαία]. Neither their right nor their practice is derived from sacred or divine institution. Power was given, or rather confirmed, to the Alexandrian bishop over the churches of Egypt, where Meletius had caused disturbances, and over the churches of Libya and Pentapolis. This was for a double reason. First, because the ancient customs had already prevailed in this way. The Church of Alexandria was the first of all to have the appearance of a bishop set distinctly above the presbyters, just as, on the contrary, the African Church was the last of all. Jerome bears witness to this of the Alexandrian Church in his letter to Evagrius: from Mark the evangelist down to Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters always chose one from among themselves and placed him in a higher rank, which they called bishop. And here, just as the title of bishop, so also the name of patriarch was first heard, above all others. The second reason for confirming the Alexandrian bishop in his undisturbed right within his diocese was the example of the Roman bishop, for he too had that custom, that he should have power over the churches subject to him. So they want it that, just as the Roman is supreme in his own provinces, so the Alexandrian and the Antiochene should be supreme in theirs, and that the Alexandrian and the Antiochene should keep for their churches whatever rights are established for the Roman metropolitan. You see that this canon is intended so that the ancient authority of the metropolitans, of Alexandria, Antioch and Rome alike, should remain quiet and safe. A like order is set among their subordinates; but no power is given to one over an equal, that is, a metropolitan over a metropolitan. Baronius is wrong, and the other flatterers of the Pope with him, when they read this Nicene canon otherwise, and interpret it far differently. At the beginning they put these words in front:

units.la: Quod Romana Ecclesia semper habuit primatum. Ad quod tum sequatur: Tenuit autem & Ægyptus, ut Episcopus Alexandriæ omnium habeat potestatem &c. quomodo illa citavit in Conc. Chalcedonensi Legatus Ecclesiæ Romanæ, episcopus Paschasinus; vel uti vertit Dionysius Exiguus: Ecclesia Romana semper habuit primatum, mos autem antiquus perduret &c. Atque ad finem canonis conjungunt septimum illum de episcopo Æliæ, cum sexto, ex quo unum faciunt. At parum esset, si vel illa inscriptio aut titulus de primatu Romano praefixus esset canoni Nicæno, quamvis titulum nolit esse Cardinalis, sed ipsius sexti canonis verba, argumento sane futili, & nullo, quod absque eo exordio sensus reddatur plane obscurus, ac mutilus, quod falsum. Sed nec illud alicujus momenti, si vel primatus Ecclesiæ Romanæ adscriberetur: cum & idem reliquis sit metropolitanis: primatus enim intelligitur respectu subjectorum episcoporum & Ecclesiarum, non respectu Metropolitani unius ad alterum. Et si vel omnino primatus intelligeretur in ordine ipsorum Metropolitanorum inter se, & quidem Romani ut primi ad secundum Alexandrinum, & tertium Antiochenum; non de eo admodum contendunt Græci. Nilus, lib. 1. de causis dissens. Eccles. neque vero illud in causa est, quod Latini affirmant, nos nobis Primatum arrogare velle, & in secundis post Romanorum principatum nolle consistere: sanèque idcirco pacem detrectare. Neque enim unquam cum Romanâ Ecclesiâ de Primatu contendimus; neque de secundo loco nunc agitur. Sed nullo pacto hinc educitur, quod ex primatu Ecclesiæ Romanæ fluat omne jus quod habet Episcopus Alexandrinus in suâ, uti ex illâ de Primatu Romano ante canonem Nicænum præfatione colligit Baronius. Nilus loco jam citato: porro Primatus, quem Episcopus Romanus obtinet in alios universales Episcopos, non est æqualis ei quem obtinet unius gentis in subditos. Illic enim Primatus ordinis tantum est, & in verbis mi-[?]
units.tr: That the Roman Church has always held the primacy. To this there follows: But Egypt also has held that the Bishop of Alexandria should have authority over all, etc., as the Legate of the Roman Church, Bishop Paschasinus, quoted it at the Council of Chalcedon, or as Dionysius Exiguus renders it: The Roman Church has always held the primacy, but the ancient custom shall endure, etc. At the end of the canon they also join the seventh canon, concerning the bishop of Aelia, to the sixth, and make one canon of the two. But it would matter little if either that inscription or title about the Roman primacy were prefixed to the Nicene canon, even though the Cardinal does not wish it to be a title but the very words of the sixth canon. That is a plainly futile argument, and it proves nothing, since without that preface the sense would be entirely obscure and maimed, which is false. Nor would it be of any great moment if the primacy of the Roman Church were ascribed to it, since the same primacy belongs to the other metropolitans too. A primacy is understood with respect to the subject bishops and churches, not with respect to one metropolitan over another. And even if a primacy were understood among the metropolitans themselves, namely that the Roman, as first, stands over the Alexandrian as second and the Antiochene as third, the Greeks do not contend very much about that. Nilus, book 1 of On the Causes of the Dissension of the Churches: Nor is it the case, as the Latins affirm, that we wish to arrogate the primacy to ourselves and are unwilling to stand in second place after the Roman principate, and that for this reason we refuse peace. For we have never contended with the Roman Church about the primacy, nor is the question now about the second place. But by no means does it follow from this that all the right which the Bishop of Alexandria has in his own province flows from the primacy of the Roman Church, as Baronius gathers from that preface on the Roman primacy placed before the Nicene canon. Nilus, in the place already cited: Moreover, the primacy which the Roman bishop holds over the other universal bishops is not equal to that which he holds over the subjects of one nation. For that primacy is only one of order, and rests in words rather than in things, since equality is looked for in most matters. The primacy which from the Nicene Synod is acknowledged in the Roman bishop is acknowledged in the Alexandrian as well, and likewise in the other greater churches, as Paschasinus recited these things from the Nicene canon at the Council of Chalcedon. Similarly also&

units.la: mi-[?] magis quam in rebus positus, cum in plurimis æqualitas spectetur. Primatus qui à Nicænâ Synodo in Romano, idem agnoscitur in Alexandrino, idem in reliquis Ecclesiis majoribus: uti hæc ex canone Nicæno recitavit in Concilio Chalcedonensi Paschasinus: similiter autem & qui in Antiochiâ constitutus est, & in cæteris provinciis primatus habeant Ecclesiæ civitatum ampliorum. Latini Nicænorum canonum interpretes haud aliter legunt, & disputunt, ac nos, Dionysius Exiguus, Isidorus Mercator, similiter in Iure canonico Gratianus, 1. dist. lxv. c. Mos antiquus & Ruffinus in historiâ lib. 1. cap. vi. ut apud Alexandriam, & in urbe Româ vetusta consuetudo servetur, ut vel ille Ægypti, vel hic suburbicariarum Ecclesiarum sollicitudinem gerat. Suburbicarias ecclesias intelligit sub urbe, ejusque sollicitudine, & provinciâ metropolitanâ constitutas: quâ de re, si lubet, consule Illustrem Salmasium, peculiari tractatu, adversus Iac. Sirmondum, Eucharisticon pro Adventoriâ, de Regionibus, & Ecclesiis Suburbicariis, absque auctoris nomine. & in libro de Primatu Papæ, cap. vii. Non ausim dicere, quod Balsamon ad can. vi. Nicænum, quatuor Patriarchas hic constitui, Romanum, Alexandrinum, Antiochenum, & Ierosolymitanum: quamvis & in Arabicâ canonum lxxx. Nicænorum compilatione, edita primò per Alfonsum Pisanum, tum per Franciscum Turrianum, utrumque Iesuitam, sæpius Patriarcharum fiat mentio; & can. viii. qui respondet Græco sexto, episcopus Ægypti, id est, Patriarcha, similiter Episcopus Antiochiæ eodem canone Patriarcha dicatur, & pluribus locis. Neque solum synonymice episcopus Metropolitanus dicitur Patriarcha, ut quoque ante distinctum Metropolitanorum atque Patriarcharum gradum, Patriarchæ aliquando dictus, sed distinctio etiam inter Patriarcham, ut episcopis & Archiepiscopis superior constituitur, ac potestas Patriarcharum indicatur, Archiepiscopos atque episcopos ordinandi. Can. xxxiii. de episcopo Seleucię appellando Catholico, possit iis adi- mare archiepiscopos, sicut faciunt Patriarchę, & non sit in- juria Patriarchę Antiocheno, siquidem ipse consensit post- quam hoc ab eo Synodus petivit, ne de sublatâ potestate ist â i- rrogaretur. Eidemque, quia tenet locum Patriarchę in Oriente, assignatur sedes in Concilio, post episcopum Ierosolymitanum sexta. Tum can. xxxiv. & can. xli. statuitur, ut omnes Archiepiscopi semel per annum apud Patriarcham suum conveniant. Adde can. xlv. de querelis Archiepiscopi unius contra Patriarcham. & can. xlvi. de querelis unius Archiepiscopi adversus alium, non facile à Patriarchâ accipiendis. Sed quod maximè Arabicorum canonum fidem elevat, [praeterquam quod] toties Patriarcharum meminerint, qui titulus in scriptis Ecclesiasticis, & conciliis, & literis episcoporum ignotus adhuc erat, est, quod omnino apparet illum horum canonum vel Auctoris illorum scopum fuisse, ut Patriarchas in Oriente agnoscat quidem. sed Romanum episcopum omnibus praeferat, eique potestatem in illos attribuat. Can. xxxix. Archiepiscopum inter Episcopos constituit ut fratrem; sed Patriarcham loco Patris: sicque praest Patriarchę iis omnibus, qui sub potestate ejus sunt, sicut ille, qui tenet sedem Romę, caput est & Princeps omnium Patriarcharum. Quamdoquidem ipse est primus, sicut Petrus, cui data est potestas in omnes principes Christianos & omnes populos eorum, ut qui sit vicarius Christi Domini nostri, super cunctos populos & cunctam Ecclesiam Christianam. Et quicunque contradixerit, à Synodo excommunicatur. Quod profecto muquam dixisset Synodus, non accepisset Constantinus, non tolerassent reliqui in Oriente Patriarchae, ut omnes Romano subjecti fuissent, & quidem ex auctoritate quasi & institutione Christi. Imo hoc rectà adversatur canoni Nicaeno sexto genuino, ubi episcopi, Alexandrinus & Antiochenus Romano aequiparantur: & quaecunque ordinis vel primatus istius sunt, non ex divina, non ex Christi institutione arcessuntur, sed ex sola consuetudine, & aemulatione aliorum. Quorsum ergo spectet Papistarum operosa de canonibus Synodi Nicenae maximam partem deperditis disputatio, & pro horum Arabicorum commendatione, liquet: videlicet ut alios nobis cudant, & sub auctoritate tam celebris & maxime venerandae Synodi commendent canones, vel pro transubstantiatione, si placet; vel praecipue quidem pro usurpata Episcopi Romani potestate: illosque accipiamus, si non veros, at commentitios: qua de fraude haud semel convicti Romani egregieque retusa fuit aliquoties eorum improbitas & audacia, dum ex actis Nicaenis suam illam potestatem confirmare satagerent. Quod experti fuere tum in Chalcedonensi concilio, tum in Carthaginensi sexto, sub Aurelio, Carthaginensi episcopo, a. CCCCXIX. Quando apud Africanos nonnulli in rebus controversis & contentiosis provocarent ultra mare ad episcopum Romanum, Africani non ferendum hoc rati, quaestionem super eo moverunt, agitataque res in Concilio Carthaginensi fuit: ubi Faustinus Ecclesiae Rom. Legatus, ad confirmandum hoc jus Episcopo Romano, provocavit ad Acta Concilii Nicaeni, quibus illud Romano episcopo assignaretur: ad quod attoniti Patres, consensere quidem se non refragari, siquidem ita in Concilio Nicaeno conclusum, lubentesque se ejus auctoritati acquieturos; sed Alippius episcopus Tagastensis, Legatus provinciae Numidiae, dixit: hoc tantum me movet, quoniam cum inspiceremus graeca exemplaria hujus Synodi Nicaenae, ista ibi, nescio qua ratione, minime invenimus. prudenter & cordate, neque vel Nicaeni Concilii, vel Romani episcopi auctoritati quid detractum videri voluit: solum verti in quaestione, an illud quod Romani jactabant, illustrissimae Synodi Actis comprobaretur. Non solum ex hujus sententia rem decidi cupiebant, sed permittebant frui Romanum privilegio isto, sto, quousque ex genuinis Nicaeni Concilii Actis constaret, quid hac de re esset. Quare mox petita ab Oriente vera Nicaeni Concilii exemplaria fuerunt, scriptumque ad Constantinopolitanum episcopum, apud quem Concilii exemplar authenticum haberi dicebatur, etiam ad Alexandrinum, & Antiochenum, ut sua si quae haberent, transmitterent Nicaenae Synodi exemplaria, e quibus haec quaestio decidi posset; etiam ad episc. Rom. Bonifacium, Zosimi successorem scribunt, ut ipse litteras ad Ecclesias Orientales adderet, eadem petentes exemplaria. Quo pacto cum non solum non agnoscebant aut supremum quaestionum arbitrum, aut infallibili praeditum judicio, vel summa & non controversa pollere authoritate, sed quoque tum sibi, tum Orientalibus episcopis subjectum significabant, & ab illis, suaque Synodo sententiam expectare debere, quod non magis ejus auctoritatem concernebat, quam fidem, quae utraque satis manifeste in dubium vocabatur. In litteris ad eum suis scribunt Carthaginenses Patres perquam humaniter, vel eorum nomine quicunque a litteris fuit: nullo modo nos talia, qualia commemorare jam volumus, intelligunt provocationes transmarinas, de quibus disputabatur, vel tolerare cogeremur, vel intolerabilia pateremur, sed credimus adjuvante misericordia Domini Dei nostri, quod tua sanctitate Romanae Ecclesiae praesidente, non sumus jam istum typhum passuri, & servabimur ergo ea, quae nobis etiam non differentibus custodiri debeant cum fraterna charitate, quae secundum sapientiam & justitiam quam tibi donavit Altissimus, etiam ipse perspicis esse servanda, si forte aliter habent canones Nicaeni concilii. Quamvis enim plurimos codices legerimus, sed nusquam in Nicaeno concilio Latinis in codicibus legimus, quemadmodum in praedicto commonitorio mihi directa sunt, ea tamen quia hic in nullo graeco codice potuimus invenire, ex orientalibus Ecclesiis ubi perhibentur eadem decreta posse etiam authentica reperiri, magis nobis desideramus afferri &c. Non agnosciunt omnia jura & veritatem in scrinio pectoris Romani haerere, vel cum Supremum omnium controversiarum judicem, dum ab ipso provocant ad alios noscendae veritatis causa, idque in quaestione quae ipsum, ejusque authoritatem tam signanter petebat: quin cum jubent quoque ad eosdem Magistros abire, qui verius ipsum omnesque de causae hujus certitudine essent instructuri. Utique si in hoc substitisset Africanorum Patrum generositas & Nicaena exemplaria vel non missa ex Oriente suissent ad rem hanc decidendam; vel non alia ab exemplaribus Papae, vel non coacti fuissent omnes fraudem Romani episcopi detegere & propalare? Sed missis a Cyrillo Alexandrino, & Attico Constantinopolitano Nicaenae Synodi exemplaribus, impostura deprehensa, & convicti falsitatis Romani fuerunt, neque alii Synodi quam xx. canones vulgo noti prodierunt, quibus non modo nulla ad Romanum episcopum provocatio continetur, ejusque ne gru quidem occurrit, in quibus tale aliquid non potuimus reperire, scribunt postea Caelestino Papae Africani; sed omnes quaestiones Nicaeni Patres committunt Metropolitanis. Unde Africani monere jam Romanum, ne Clericos suos ultra mittere, quamvis ab aliquibus forte ultra mare ad negotia quaecunque dirimenda vocatos. Quia scilicet Nicaeni (sic loquuntur) prudentissime justissimeque viderunt quaecunque negotia in suis locis ubi orta sunt finienda, nec unicuique providentiae gratiam sancti spiritus defuturam, quae aequitas a Christi sacerdotibus & prudenter videatur, & constantissime teneatur. Pergunt, neque enim refugimus illa describere, quae illi tanto cum zelo & animositate Episcopo Romano, ejusque usurpationi postquam post exploratam Graecorum exemplaria in iis canonES a Zosimo citatos non reperissent: (sic ipse loquitur ad hoc Concilium Severinus Binius) repositurunt: Nam ut aliqui tanquam a tuae sanctitatis latere mittantur, nulla inveniuntur Patrum Synodo constitutum, quia illud quod pridem per eundem coepiscepum nostrum Faustinum, tanquam ex parte Nicaeni Concilii exinde transmisistis, in Conciliis veteribus quae accipiuntur Nicaenis à sancto Cyrillo coepiscopo nostro Alexandrinae Ecclesiae, & à venerabili Attico Constantinopolitano Antistite, ex Authentico missis &c. tale aliquid non potuimus reperire. Executores etiam Clericos vestros quibuscunque petentibus nolite mittere, nolite concedere, ne famosum typhum scculi in Ecclesiam Christi, quae lucem simplicitatis & humilitatis, diem Domini videre cupientibus praefert, videantur inducere. Eat nunc, habeatque Roma pudorem. Falsi convicti Papae Legati, Episcopi, pro causa sui Papae, in adducendo canone & auctoritate magnae Synodi Nicaenae. Quid illis amplius credas, qui palam deprehensi falsi testes, & actorum publicorum, ecclesiasticorum, in gratiam pudendae ambitionis suae, ac Romanae tyrannidis, corruptores? Manifestaria res est, in oculis Africanae & Orientalis Ecclesiae fraus patuit, & exposita coram orbe fuit vani Episcopi intoleranda ambitio. Hic jam habes Orientales cum Africanis una contra Papae Romani suprematum pugnantes, atque triumphum de superato ejus typho & profligato palam reportantes. Ille, quem sub nomine Nicaenae Synodi citarat Faustinus Legatus canon, est inter Iulii primi, ex ejus epistolâ de Conc. Nicaeno canones, quos pro Nicenis impudenterque falsoque venditant Romani. Quae cum Romani episcopi Leonis Legatis disputatio super canonibus Nicaenis fuerit in Concilio Chalcedonensi, suo loco videbimus. Canone Nicaeno vi. de Metropolitanis actum diximus, agnitosque fuisse pro talibus Romanum, Alexandrinum, Antiochenum, denique & Ierosolymitanum. Atque ad exemplum Romani episcopi stabilitum par jus in suis provinciis Alexandrino, tum & Antiocheno. Can. vii. de Ierosolymitano quidem agitur, honorque antiquus, quem jam olim habebat, ei confirmatur; sed tamen ut propria dignitas non auferatur Metropolitano, qui erat episcopiscopus Cæsareensis, cui suberat Ierosolymitanus, & a quo ordinabatur, ut in civilibus metropolis Syriæ Palestinæ erat quoque Cæsarea. Verùm honor is datus Ierosolymitano, ut honorarius esset Metropolitanus, atque honoraretur quasi talis τῆ ἀχωλαθίας τ' πρώτης, atque inter Antistites sederet, & cum iis subscriberet, sed nequidquam immutata propria Metropolitani dignitate reali, τῆ μιλοποτόλεως συζομίνυ τῶ οἰκείῳ ἀξιώματι ⊙ s quam omnem tamen postea gnaviter arripuit, sibique arrogavit Ierosolymitanus, subjecto sibi suo Metropolitano, & Palæstinis Ecclesiis. Canon Arabicus, qui canoni VII. Nicæno respondet, quamvis in Arabico sit decimus, ita habet: quia est consuetudo honorandi Episcopum Heliæ nomine Patriarchæ, cum est dignus honore, propter sanctitatem loci, & propter probitatem ejus: præsit illi provinciæ, & locis ei vicinis, reddatque Archiepiscopo ejus loci debitum honorem; & vocetur ille exarchus, id est, major quam Archiepiscopus. ex versione Turriani: quæ paulo aliter leguntur ex editione Alph. Pisani; sed in eundem sensum. Can. xxxv I. de Patriarchâ Æthiopum loquuntur, sub potestate ejus sit, qui tenet sedem Alexandriæ. Sit tamen apud eos loco Patriarchæ, & appelletur Catholicus, non tamen jus habeat constituendi Archiepiscopos, ut habet Patriarcha, siquidem non habet talem potestatem. Vidimus in Synodo Nicæna quo loco fuerint episcopi, Romanus, Alexandrinus, Antiochenus, Ierosolymitanus. At de Constantinopolitano nihil: quod haud mirum, quum nonnullis demum annis post habitum Concilium, quidam septem dicunt, alii quinque, alii decem, quidam eodem anno, sed post peractum Concilium, Constantinopolis à Constantino dedicata sit, quæ olim Byzantium erat. Inde tum novam urbem efferre studuit Constantinus, & alteram Romam facere, quæ in omnibus ex æquo, si liceret, Veteri Romæ responderet, uti loquitur ipse Baronius, ad Ann. cccxxx. Hactenus episcopus Byzantinus Heracleensi subserat Metropolitano, ab eoque ordinabatur; nam & Byzan- tium olim Perinthionum, sive Heracleensi jurisdictio- ni subjectum, ex quo à Romanis sub Severo occupatum, & ferè diruptum fuit. Glycas, Annal. part. iv. Diuque postea obtinuit, quamvis Heracleënsis Constantinopolitano subjectus esset, ut tamen hic ab illo ordinaretur. Zonaras, Annal. Tom. iii. in vita Constantini, Leonis Filii, Polyeuctus Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus ὑπὸ τῶν Κωνσταντίας κεχειροτόνηται, à Cæsa- rensi ordinabatur; sed quia Heracleensis Imperatorem offendérat, suo jure privabatur, ὁ δὲ Ἡρακλείας ἀποστ- ραφεὶς τὴν τοῦ βασιλέως, ὀφειλόμενος τῆς ἀποστολῆς αὐτὸς. Erat tempore Nicæni Concilii Byzantinus episcopus Metrophanes, Probi prædecessoris Episcopi Frater. Psellus, de septem Synodis, primam in Nicæâ habitam dicit.
units.tr: mi-[?] magis quam in rebus positus, cum in plurimis æqualitas spectetur. The primacy recognised at the Nicene Synod in the Roman bishop is acknowledged also in the Alexandrian, and likewise in the other greater Churches. Paschasinus recited this from the Nicene canon at the Council of Chalcedon: similarly, those who are established in Antioch and in the other provinces shall have the primacy of the Churches of the greater cities. The Latin interpreters of the Nicene canons, Dionysius Exiguus and Isidore Mercator, read and argue no differently from us, and so does Gratian in canon law, dist. 65, c. Mos antiquus, and Rufinus in his history, book 1, chapter 6: so that the ancient custom is kept at Alexandria and in the old city of Rome, that the one should care for Egypt and the other for the suburbicarian Churches. By the suburbicarian Churches he means those established around the city, under its care and within its metropolitan province. On this matter, if you wish, consult the illustrious Salmasius, in his separate treatise against Jacques Sirmond, Eucharisticon pro Adventoria, de Regionibus, et Ecclesiis Suburbicariis, published without the author's name, and in his book de Primatu Papæ, chapter 7. I would not dare to say, with Balsamon on Nicene canon 6, that four patriarchs were appointed here: Rome, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem. Yet in the Arabic compilation of the eighty Nicene canons, first published by Alfonso Pisano and then by Francesco Turriano, both Jesuits, mention of the patriarchs recurs frequently; and canon 8, which corresponds to the sixth Greek canon, says the bishop of Egypt, that is, the patriarch, and in the same way the bishop of Antioch is called patriarch by the same canon, and in many places. Nor is the metropolitan bishop called patriarch only as a synonym, as was sometimes done even before the distinct grades of metropolitans and patriarchs were drawn; the distinction is also made that the patriarch is set above bishops and archbishops, and the power of patriarchs is indicated as that of ordaining archbishops and bishops. Canon 33, on the bishop of Seleucia being called Catholicus: he may take away from them the archbishops, as the patriarchs do, and there is no injury to the patriarch of Antioch, since he himself agreed after the synod asked this of him, lest he be questioned about the power taken away. To the same man, because he holds the place of patriarch in the East, a seat in the Council is assigned, sixth after the bishop of Jerusalem. Then canons 34 and 41 lay down that all archbishops shall meet once a year with their patriarch. Add canon 45, on complaints of one archbishop against a patriarch, and canon 46, on complaints of one archbishop against another, which are not to be readily received by the patriarch. But what most of all weakens the credit of these Arabic canons is this: although they so often mention patriarchs, a title still unknown in ecclesiastical writings, councils and the letters of bishops, it clearly appears that the aim of these canons, or of their author, was to acknowledge patriarchs in the East, but to place the Roman bishop above them all and to give him power over them. Canon 39 makes the archbishop a brother among bishops, but the patriarch takes the place of a father: thus the patriarch presides over all those who are under his power, just as he who holds the see of Rome is the head and prince of all the patriarchs. Since he is first, like Peter, to whom power has been given over all Christian princes and all their peoples, as the vicar of Christ our Lord over all peoples and the whole Christian Church. And whoever contradicts him is excommunicated by the Synod. The Synod would certainly never have said this; Constantine would not have accepted it; the other patriarchs in the East would not have tolerated that all should be subject to Rome, and that by a kind of authority and institution of Christ. Indeed this directly contradicts the genuine sixth Nicene canon, where the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch are made equal to the bishop of Rome; and whatever belongs to this order or primacy is derived not from divine or Christ's institution, but from custom alone and the rivalry of others. What then the Papists aim at in their laboured dispute about the canons of the Nicene Synod, most of which are lost, and in their commendation of these Arabic canons, is plain: namely, that they may forge others for us and, under the authority of so famous and most venerable a Synod, recommend the canons either for transubstantiation, if they like, or especially for the usurped power of the Roman bishop; and that we should accept them, if not as genuine, at least as fabricated. By this fraud the Romanists have more than once been convicted, and their impudence and audacity were several times thoroughly repulsed, when they strove to confirm that power from the acts of Nicaea. They experienced this both at the Council of Chalcedon and at the Sixth Council of Carthage, under Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, in 419. When some Africans in controversial and contentious matters appealed overseas to the Roman bishop, the Africans, thinking this not to be borne, raised the question, and the matter was debated in the Council of Carthage. There Faustinus, legate of the Roman Church, to confirm this right for the Roman bishop, appealed to the acts of the Nicene Council, in which that right was supposedly assigned to the Roman bishop. At this the astonished fathers agreed that they would not oppose it, since it had been so concluded at the Nicene Council, and they would gladly abide by its authority; but Alippius, bishop of Tagaste, legate of the province of Numidia, said: this alone moves me, that when we examined the Greek copies of this Nicene Synod, we found nowhere in them, I know not why, those things. He spoke prudently and wisely, and wished that nothing be taken away from either the authority of the Nicene Council or of the Roman bishop; he only raised the question whether what the Romans boasted of was confirmed by the acts of that most illustrious Synod. They wished the matter settled not merely by his opinion, but they also allowed the Roman to enjoy that privilege until it was established from the genuine acts of the Nicene Council what the truth of the matter was. Therefore genuine copies of the Nicene Council were soon sought from the East, and they wrote to the bishop of Constantinople, where it was said that an authentic copy of the Council was kept, and also to the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, asking them to send, if they had any, copies of the Nicene Synod, from which this question might be decided. They also wrote to Bishop Boniface of Rome, successor of Zosimus, asking him to add his letters to the Eastern Churches, seeking the same copies. By this course, since they not only did not acknowledge either a supreme arbiter of questions or one endowed with an infallible judgment, nor believed that he possessed the highest and undisputed authority, but also indicated that he was subject both to themselves and to the Eastern bishops, and that he ought to await the opinion of them and of their Synod, the matter concerned not so much his authority as his faith, and both were called into doubt quite openly. In their letter to him the Carthaginian fathers write, very courteously, or in the name of whoever was in charge of the letters: by no means could we tolerate, or else we would suffer intolerable things, such things as we now wish to mention, they understand the overseas appeals under debate, but we believe, with the help of the mercy of our Lord God, that under your holiness presiding over the Roman Church we shall not now suffer that arrogance; and so we shall be preserved in those things which, even without delay, ought to be observed with brotherly charity, which, according to the wisdom and justice that the Most High has given you, you yourself clearly see ought to be kept, if perhaps the canons of the Nicene Council say otherwise. For although we have read very many codices, yet nowhere in the Nicene Council have we read in Latin codices what has been sent to me in the aforesaid letter; since we could not find them in any Greek codex, we rather desire that they be brought to us from the Eastern Churches, where the same decrees are said to be found even in authentic form, etc. They do not acknowledge that all rights and truth lie in the treasury of the Roman breast, since they appeal from him, the supreme judge of all controversies, to others for the sake of knowing the truth, and this in a question that so pointedly concerned him and his authority. Indeed they even bid them go to those same teachers who would more truly instruct him and all others about the certainty of this cause. Surely, if the nobility of the African fathers had rested in this, and no Nicene copies had been sent from the East to settle the matter, or had they not differed from the copies of the Pope, would they not have been forced to uncover and expose the fraud of the Roman bishop? But when copies of the Nicene Synod were sent by Cyril of Alexandria and Atticus of Constantinople, the imposture was detected, and the Romans were convicted of falsehood; and no other synod came out than the twenty canons commonly known, which contain no appeal at all to the Roman bishop, nor is any trace of his name found in them: in which we could find nothing of the kind, the Africans later wrote to Pope Celestine; but the Nicene fathers commit all questions to the metropolitans. Hence the Africans now warn Rome not to send its clergy any more, even if perhaps some have been called overseas to settle any business whatever. Because, namely, the Nicene fathers (so they speak) most prudently and most justly saw that whatever business arises should be settled in the places where it arose, nor will the grace of the Holy Spirit be lacking to each provision, which fairness should be seen and most firmly held by the priests of Christ. They go on, for we do not shrink from describing those things which they, with such zeal and animosity, set against the Roman bishop and his usurpation, after they had found, on examining the Greek copies, that the canons cited by Zosimus were not in them (so Severinus Binius speaks of this Council): For although some are sent as if from your holiness's side, no such thing is found decreed in the synods of the fathers, because what was previously sent to us by your means, through our fellow bishop Faustinus, as if from the Nicene Council, in the ancient councils which are received as Nicene, from our fellow bishop Cyril of the Alexandrian Church and from the venerable Atticus, the Constantinopolitan prelate, sent from the authentic copies, etc., we could find nothing of the kind. Do not send, do not grant, your clerks as executors to whoever asks, lest they seem to bring the arrogance of the world into the Church of Christ, which prefers the light of simplicity and humility to those who wish to see the day of the Lord. Let Rome go now and have shame. Papal legates, bishops, convicted of falsehood, in pleading for their Pope, in citing a canon and the authority of the great Nicene Synod. Why should you believe them any more, who were openly detected as false witnesses and as corrupters of public and ecclesiastical acts, for the sake of their shameful ambition and of Roman tyranny? The matter is manifest: the fraud lay open in the eyes of the African and Eastern Church, and the intolerable ambition of the vain bishop was exposed before the world. Here you already have the Easterns and Africans together fighting against the supremacy of the Roman Pope and openly winning a triumph over the defeated and overthrown arrogance of his. That canon which the legate Faustinus had cited under the name of the Nicene Synod is among the canons of Julius I, from his letter about the Nicene Council, which the Romans shamelessly and falsely hawk as Nicene. What dispute there was about the Nicene canons at the Council of Chalcedon, between the legates of the Roman bishop Leo, we shall see in its place. We have said that the sixth Nicene canon dealt with metropolitans, and that Rome, Alexandria, Antioch and finally Jerusalem were acknowledged as such. And on the model of the Roman bishop, an equal right was established for the Alexandrian in his provinces, and so too for the Antiochene. Canon 7 deals with Jerusalem, and its ancient honour, which it had long held, is confirmed to it; but yet so that the proper dignity is not taken from the metropolitan, who was the bishop of Caesarea, to whom the Jerusalem bishop was subject, and by whom he was ordained, since Caesarea was also the metropolis of Syria Palaestina in civil matters. But the honour given to Jerusalem was that it should be honorary as a metropolis, and be honoured as such, [τῇ ἀκολουθίᾳ τῆς πρώτης] in the order of first precedence, and sit among the bishops and subscribe with them; but it was to be without any change in the real dignity of the metropolitan [τῇ μητροπόλεως συζῶντι τῷ οἰκείῳ ἀξιώματι], which nevertheless the Jerusalem bishop afterwards eagerly seized and claimed for himself, subjecting to himself his own metropolitan and the Palestinian Churches. The Arabic canon, which corresponds to Nicene canon 7, although in the Arabic it is the tenth, reads thus: because it is the custom to honour the bishop of Elia with the name of patriarch, when he is worthy of honour, on account of the holiness of the place and of his probity: let him preside over the province and the places near it, and render to the archbishop of that place the due honour; and let him be called exarch, that is, greater than an archbishop. This is from the translation of Turriano; it reads a little differently in the edition of Alphonso Pisano, but to the same sense. Canon 31 speaks of the patriarch of the Ethiopians: let him be under the power of him who holds the see of Alexandria. Yet let him be among them in place of a patriarch, and be called Catholicus; but let him not have the right of appointing archbishops, as the patriarch has, since he does not have such power. We have seen at the Nicene Synod in what place the bishops of Rome, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem sat. But nothing is said of Constantinople; which is no wonder, since some years after the Council was held, some say seven, others five, others ten, and some say in the same year but after the Council was finished, Constantinople was dedicated by Constantine, which was formerly Byzantium. Then Constantine set about raising a new city, and to make another Rome, which in all things would correspond equally, if it were allowed, to the Old Rome, as Baronius himself says, at the year 330. Until then the bishop of Byzantium was subordinate to the metropolitan of Heraclea, and was ordained by him; for Byzantium was formerly Perinthus, and was subject to the jurisdiction of Heraclea, until it was occupied by the Romans under Severus and almost destroyed. Glycas, Annals, part 4. And for a long time afterwards it held this position, although Heraclea was subject to Constantinople, so that nevertheless it was ordained by Constantinople. Zonaras, Annals, vol. 3, in the life of Constantine, son of Leo: Polyeuctus, patriarch of Constantinople, [ὑπὸ τῶν Κωνσταντίας κεχειροτόνηται] was ordained by the bishop of Caesarea; but because he had offended the Emperor at Heraclea, he was deprived of his right, [ὁ δὲ Ἡρακλείας ἀποστραφεὶς τὴν τοῦ βασιλέως, ὀφειλόμενος τῆς ἀποστολῆς αὐτὸς]. At the time of the Nicene Council the bishop of Byzantium was Metrophanes, brother of Probus, the bishop before him. Psellus, on the seven synods, says that the first was held at Nicaea.

units.la: Est in Sacerdotii dignitate præcellens Constantinopoli Ter pio & animo & sermone Metrophanes.
