units.tr: Among the bishops of Constantinople, Metrophanes is outstanding in dignity, both in his piety of mind and in his eloquence.

units.la: Verùm ipse Metrophanes, ob ætatem, non interfuit Synodo; sed ejus nomine presbyter ejus Alexander, cum Diacono, Paulo, qui duo deinceps succedere in sedem episcopalem. Idem ille Alexander est, ad quem extat Alexandri, episc. Alexandrini de Ario, epistola; & quamvis non legatur ejus nomen inter eos, qui Concilio subscripserunt, ut quoque aliorum ibi desideratur nomina, qui egregiam operam Synodo navarunt, inter illos tamen occurrit, cum Diacono Paulo, qui decreta Synodi ad suas singuli Ecclesias perscripserunt, & hic ad Ecclesias Cycladum Insularum, uti auctor est Gelasius, vel Dalmatius, cujus ille scripta sequutus fuit, & edidit, Cyzicenus, de Actis Conc. Nicæni. Quantumvis autem hoc in Concilio non contenderint inter se Romana Græcaque Ecclesia, ut quidem in aliis postmodum, attamen quia ex hoc, vel hujus canone, quem hactenus spectavimus, sexto multa controversia deinceps agitata fuit inter utramque Ecclesiam, super primario dissensionis mutuæ articulo, de Primatu Papae, & inter Generales Synodos, quam Legati Orientalis & Occidentalis Ecclesiae constituerunt, primum obtineat locum, de eo dicendum antequomnia fuit.
units.tr: Yet Metrophanes himself did not take part in the Synod, on account of his age; instead, in his name, his presbyter Alexander attended, together with the deacon Paul, who afterwards succeeded in turn to the episcopal see. This is the same Alexander to whom there survives a letter of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, concerning Arius. And although his name is not read among those who subscribed to the Council, just as the names of others who rendered outstanding service to the Synod are missing there, nevertheless he does appear among them, together with the deacon Paul, who each drew up the decrees of the Synod for their own churches; and this Paul did so for the churches of the Cyclades islands, as Gelasius or Dalmatius reports (Cyzicenus, who followed his writings and published them, in his work on the Acts of the Council of Nicaea). Although the Roman and Greek Churches did not contend with one another at this Council, as they later did at others, nevertheless, because much controversy was afterwards stirred up between the two Churches over the sixth canon, which we have so far considered, or over its wording, concerning the primacy of the Pope, which is the first point of their mutual disagreement, and because of the General Councils which the legates of the Eastern and Western Churches convened, it must be discussed before all else.

units.la: Verùm quod in Nicaeno attigerunt solùm sub ratione juris Metropolitici, & in parem ordinem redegerunt Metropolitanos omnes, Romanum, Alexandrinum, Antiochenum, id clarius decisum in sequenti Concilio Constantinopolitano I. ubi hujus sedis archiepiscopo concessus honor primatus post Romanum, ob aequalem in hoc & illo dignitatis causam, urbis videlicet praecellentiam. Unde inter utrumque episcopum, mox & Ecclesias prima perpetuaque contentionis extitit occasio, super Papae Romani primatu, quem hic semper supra omnes, Constantinopolitanus secundum juxta illum, cupiit. Habitum Constantinopolitanum concilium fuit sub Theodosio Seniore, à quo & convocatum, confirmatumque pro more fuit: unde ei scribunt in epistolâ Synodicâ Patres, dum canones mittunt; rogamus igitur tuam clementiam, ut per litteras quoque tuae pietatis ratum habeatur concilii decretum: ut sicuti litteris, quibus nos convocasti, Ecclesiam honore prosecutus es, ita etiam finem eorum, quae decreta sunt, obsignes. Constantinopolim convenerunt Synodi causa Patres centum & quinquaginta, Anno Christi cccLxxxI. duplici potissimum de causâ, fidei iterum, & disciplinae, quam Macedonius, & Maximus, hic disciplinam, ille fidem, uterque episcopus Constantinopolitanus, turbarant. Socrates, histor. Eccles. lib. v. cap. VIII. Imperator nullâ morâ interposita, Concilium Episcoporum, ipsius fidem amplectentium, convocat, quo tum fides Concilii Nicaeni corroboraretur, tum Constantinopoli designaretur Episcopus. Fides Nicaena scilicet, contra haereum, quae Spiritus S. Deitatem negabat, cujus Macedonius auctor erat; deinde quia contra Gregorium Nazianzenum Constantinopolitanae Ecclesiae designatum Episcopum, Aegyptii Episcopi, Maximum Philosophum olim Cynicum, postea ad haeresim Apollinaris prolapsum tumultuarie intruserat, thronus (uti loquuntur) Gregorio vindicandus erat; qui sponte tamen paulo post invidiae suorum cessit, in ejus locum communibus suffragiis constituto episcopo Nectario. Hoc quo melius intelligatur, series Constantinopolitanorum episcoporum obiter exhibenda, à Metrophane, sub quo habitum Concilium Nicaenum modo diximus, ad hujus Synodi tempora. Post Metrophanem, episcopus successit ejus presbyter, qui Concilio Nicaeno interfuerat, Alexander, vixitque episcopus annis viginti tribus. Post Alexandrum, Paulus, qui de sede ejectus per Constantium, x. annis praefuit. Hinc Eusebius, ex favore & fide scilicet Constantii Imp. Arianus, annis xi. Tum ejusdem furoris vir, atque deinde apertus Spiritus S. ejusque Deitatis oppugnator, Macedonius, ejusdem Ecclesiae antea presbyter, annis xi. unde Macedoniani haeretici dicti pneumatomachi. Tum Eudoxius, etiam Arianus, qui primum Germanicae, hinc Antiochiae, tum Constantinopoli episcopus, annis viii. sub Juliano & rursumque Joviano praefuit. Demophilus inde, quoque Arianus, annis xi. mensibus v. Successit Eusigrius, Orthodoxus; sed in exilium actus à Valente Imp. postquam Ecclesiam illam rexisset annis quatuor. Denique Gregorius Nazianzenus, is, cujus causa, nimirum ut vel in sede confirmaretur, vel eo ejecto, haberetur ejus loco Maximus Cynicus, ab Aegyptiis intrusus, Synodus Constantinopolitana habita: ubi de eo haud segniter disceptatum fuit. Ac tandem, quum videret Gregorius, mortuo Meletio episcopo Antiocheno, qui acerrime pro Gregorio, una cum Gregorii fratre Nysseno steterat, furere contra eum nihilo secius Aegyptios, sola invidia motos, sponte se abdicavit, habuitque eum in finem celebrem in Synodo ad centum & quinquaginta episcopos orationem, quâ dimissionem suam petiit, & obtinuit: substituitque in ejus locum communibus [?] omnium suffragiis, adeoque concordibus, ut locus, quo hoc contingebat, concordia hinc nominata fuerit, Nectarius, vir orthodoxus & pius, senatorii tum ordinis. Elegantissima certe fuit Nazianzeni ad Patres Synodales valedictoria oratio, quâ & precatur eos: diuturnis laboribus nos levate, ac recreate. Moveas vos hæc canicies, sit apud vos honori nostra peregrinatio. Alium subrogate, qui pro vobis vexetur, qui pueris sit manibus, qui voce sit non inerudita, qui omnibus in rebus vobis obsequi, curasque ecclesiasticas simul perferre possit: quandoquidem tales præsertim hoc tempus flagitat. At mihi cernitis quomodo corpus etiam hoc se habeat, nimirum & tempore, & morbo, & labore confectum. Quid vobis timido & ignavo sene opus est, atque in dies singulos, ut ita loquar, non corpore tantum, sed etiam caris moriente? qui vix hæc quoque ad vos loquor. Ne Magistri voci fidem denegetis: neque enim unquam denegastis. Lassus sum, dum mihi toties multitudo criminis vertitur. Lassus sum, dum & cum sermone & cum invidia, & cum hostibus, & cum nostris pugno. Ad crimina sibi intentata deveniens, inter alia, ad hoc de non observata episcopali pompa & φαυλισμόν [?], egregiè respondet: quin hæc quoque fortasse nobis exprobraverint (jam enim exprobrarunt) quod nec mensa lauta & opipara, nec magnifica venerandaque veste utimur, nec splendide in publicum prodimus, nec ad eos, à quibus convenimur, gravitatem adhibemus. Nesciebam scilicet nobis cum Consulibus, & Præfectis, clarissimisque belli ducibus, qui tot opibus copiisque circumfluunt, ut, quo sua projiciant, non habeant, certamen esse &c. Et de alio sibi subrogando, hæc monet, omni observatione, & designando describendoque optimo pastore dignissima: quem igitur tibi substituemus? dicet aliquis. Providebit sibi Dominus pastorem ad præfecturam, quemadmodum ovem providit ad holocaustum. Hoc unum requiro, ut ex eorum numero sit, qui aliis invidie sunt, non miserationi; qui non in omnibus rebus cunctis obsequuntur, sed qui in quibusdam quoquoque ob recti studium, in hominum offensionem incurrunt, alterum enim in præsens jucundissimum est: alterum in posterum utilissimum. Ac vos quidem orationes discessui meo congruentes parate: ego autem his verbis extremum vos salutabo: Vale Anastasia, nomen à pietate habens &c. Templum intelligit in urbe Constantinopoli augustum, sic dictum, quia in eo Nicænæ fidei doctrina publice revixisset quasi, postquam per varios Constantinopolitanæ ecclesiæ prædecessores episcopos Macedonium, Eudoxium, Demophilum, Arianos, diutius fuisset suppressa & labefactata. Et contra Maximum quidem factus à Patribus Concilii canon 1v. de Maximo Cynico, & ejus inordinatâ constitutione, quæ Constantinopoli facta est, placuit. Maximum neque episcopum fuisse, aut esse, nec qui ab eo ordinati sunt in quocunque gradu cleri, earumbus, quæ ab illo facta sunt, infirmatis. Sic ejectus sede, quam occuparat, Maximus fuit, & ipse, aliique per eum constituti in clero, synodaliter depositi: unde etiam in catalogo Episcoporum Constantinop. non recensetur. Contraque Ægyptios, qui ipsum, ex odio & livore in bonum Gregorium, intruserant, editus fuit canon secundus, iterum de limitibus diœcesium Episcopalium, juxta statuta Synodi Nicænæ: Qui sunt supra ὑπὲρ διοικήσεις, vel ultra, ut vertit Gentianus Hervetus, diœcesim Episcopi, ad ecclesias extra fines terminos sitas ne accedant, neque confundant ecclesias. Sed secundum canones, Alexandriæ quidem Episcopus, qui sunt in Ægypto tantum administret. Orientis autem Episcopi Orientem solum gubernent: servatis privilegiis, quæ Antiochenæ Ecclesiæ Nicænis canonibus tributa sunt. Et Asiæ diœceseos episcopi, Asianam diœcesim tantum gubernent. Nec non & Pontica diœceseos ea tantum quæ ad Ponticam diœcesim pertinent, & Thraciæ, quæ sunt in Thraciâ gubernent. Non vocati autem Episcopi super diœcesim, non accedant propter ordinationem, vel alias dispensationes faciendas. Servato autem suprascripto de diœcesibus canone, manifestum est, quod ea, quae ad unumquemque provinciam pertinent, synodus provinciae administret. Ita condemnati Ægyptii, qui ultra suam dioecesim, in Constantinopolitanâ Ecclesia episcopum constituerant, confirmatique canones Nicæni de salvis Archiepiscoporum, seu Metropolitanorum, per provincias suas juribus: utque, si qua difficultas vel quæstio sub oriretur, Synodus provincialis illam componeret, & decideret, cautum. Episcopo Alexandrino, Antiocheno, Asianis, & Ponticæ, & Thraciæ, singulis suæ assignatæ ἐπαρχίας, & dioeceses, μαλεπαρχίας explicat Socrates. Et episcopos Patriarchas appellabat jam tum in oratione suâ Gregorius Nazianzenus: quid non passi sumus, inquit, ἀ ὑπερβύλιοι, ἐ πισκόπων, διοικήτορων ἡ μαλιμέχων ἐπῶν, ἐφορῶν δημοσίας, annon publicas presbyterorum, Episcoporum, aut ut proprie loquar, Patriarcharum cædes? Atque historiae Metrophanem appellant Patriarcham novae Romae. Et Zonaras, in Annal Tom. II. ita indigitat Metropolitanos. Verum discrimen & distinctionem horum aperte exponit Imp. Iustinianus, Novell. vi. sanctissimi Patriarchae uniuscujusque dioecesis & Deo amabiles Metropolitae, & reliqui reverendissimi episcopi atque Clerici. Deinceps: sanctissimi siquidem Patriarchae uniuscujusque dioecesis haec proponant in ecclesiis sub se constitutis; & manifesta faciant Deo amabilibus Metropolitis, quae a nobis constituta sunt. Illi quoque rursus etiam ipsi proponant ea in Metropolitana sanctissimâ ecclesiâ, & constitutis sub se episcopis haec manifesta faciant. Illorum vero singuli in propria ecclesia haec proponant. Similiter in Novella vi. i. & xl. ii. atque alibi. Supra presbyteros erant Episcopi; supra Episcopos Metropolitani; supra Metropolitanos, Patriarchae, qui & Archiepiscopi Patriarchae dicuntur, & œcumenici, Novell. xl. & xli. & lxx. ix. Mennæ ἀρχιεπίσκοπος ἡ οἰκουμενικὸς μαλεπαρχῶν; atqui ita sepius. Haud satis fuit Patribus Constantinopolitanis Maximum episcopum exauctorasse, & jura Episcoporum stoporum in suis provinciis, juxta canones Nicaenos, iterum constituisse, adversus alienae dioecesis invasores ἐπηρείας: sed & pro honore sedis Constantinopolitanae fecerunt canonem III, Τὸν μὲν τῆς Κωνσταντινουπόλεως ἐπίσκοπον ἔχειν τὰ πρεσβεῖα μετὰ τὸν τῆς Ῥώμης ἐπίσκοπον, διὰ τὸ εἶναι αὐτὴν νέαν Ῥώμην. Quae constitutio vehementer oculos semper confixit episcopi Romani, quod videret hic, auctoritate Synodali, Constantinopolitanum nuper demum emersum sibi aequiparari. Constantinopolitanae civitatis episcopus habet privilegia honoris post Romanum episcopum, eo quod sit ipsa nova Roma. Bene attendenda ratio est, ob quam Patres hanc dignitatem Constantinopolitano attribuunt, videlicet splendor urbis; ut quia nova Roma Veteri par habebatur, ejus quoque episcopus Romano non cederet, aemulam enim hanc Romae constituerunt Imperatores, inque omnibus partem, Eo quod sit ipsa nova Roma. Indicant simul quod fundamentum sit honoris, cujusque primi in Episcopo Romano, prima nempe urbs: & haec quia jam secunda, alterum ab eo locum obtinere debebat. Cod. de sacrof. Eccles. l. vi. Ecclesiae urbis Constantinopolitanae, quae Romae veteris praerogativa laetatur. C. de piivil. urbis Constantinop. Urbs Constantinopolitana non solum juris Italici, sed etiam ipsius Romae veteris praerogativa laetatur. Menna episcopo Constantinop. scribit Imp. Justinianus in Novella lxi i. τῇ ἀγιωτάτῃ ἀρχιεπισκόπῳ τῆς βασιλίδος πάντης πόλεως, ἡ οἰκουμενικὴ προσηγορία. Dicitur passim Constantinopolis, nova Roma, & πάντων τῆς πόλεως βασιλίς. Et Novell. cxxx i. Διοπίζομεν τῇ τῆς ἐκκλησιαστικῆς ἐξουσίας ὅρος, τὴν ἀγιότητα τῆς πρεσβυτέρας Ῥώμης πάντων πρῶτον εἶναι πάντων τῆς ἰσχύος, τὴν δὲ μακαριωτάτην ἀρχιεπισκοπὴν Κωνσταντινουπόλεως τῆς νέας Ῥώμης δευτέραν ἰσχύειν, μετὰ τὴν ἀγιότητα τῆς πρεσβυτέρας Ῥώμης, τὴν ἄλλην ἀποκρίσασθαι. Romanus Papa primus est omnium sacerdotum, ex Veteribus canonum Ecclesiae cleclesiasticorum constitutionibus, quia est episcopus senioris Romae: Constantinopolitanus, secundum post eum jubetur tenere locum, caeterisque omnibus praeponitur, quia & ipse novae Romae episcopus est. Cedunt ei jam locum Alexandrinus, Antiochenus, Hierosolymitanus, & reliqui: primusque in hoc Concilio subscripsit ideo Nectarius Constantinopolitanus, tum Timotheus Alexandrinus, Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus, Meletius Antiochenus. In Concilio Nicaeno, post Hosium, ex Orientalibus subscripsit primus, Provinciae Aegypti Metropolitanus Alexandrinae Ecclesiae Alexander. Canonem Constantinopolitanum ita vertit Dionysius Exiguus: Verumtamen Constantinopolitanus episcopus habeat honoris primatum post Romanum episcopum. Significanter dixit, honoris primatum, πρεσβεία τῆς τιμῆς, eumque Constantinopolitano deberi post Romanum: primatum ergo habet & Constantinopolitanus, habent & omnes, quibus Canones attribuunt πρεσβεῖα τῆς τιμῆς id est, & Alexandrinus, & Antiochenus, & omnes denique Archiepiscopi. Dicitur que primatus, non in ordine ad Coëpiscopos, sic enim non posset primatus post Romanum attribui Constantinopolitano: verum in ordine ad subiectos sibi in sua provincia episcopos: & primus locus Romani episcopi in ordine ad Constantinopolitanum, qui ei secundus est, ordinem notat, non vero potestatem, quae ambobus par est, ob parilem urbis, vel Veteris, vel Novae rationem, & dignitatem. Scribit Theodorus Balsamon in hunc canonem, esse, qui praepositionem μετὰ post non intelligant de submissione honoris, sed de ratione temporis, quod primatus Constantinopolitano contigerit posterius Romano. Unde apparet, quam acriter suis adversus Romanum honoribus intendant Constantinopolitani, & cum eo Graeci alii, quamque diligenter super hujus canonis sententia, & primatu duarum istarum sedium, inter Graecos Latinosque controvertatur. units.tr: But what they touched on at Nicaea only under the heading of metropolitan right, and placed all the metropolitans in one rank, Rome, Alexandria and Antioch, was decided more clearly at the following Council of Constantinople I, where the archbishop of this see was granted the honour of primacy after Rome, because of the equal ground of dignity in this city and that one, namely the pre-eminence of the city. From this arose the first and lasting occasion of contention between the two bishops, and between the Churches, over the primacy of the Roman Pope, which the Constantinopolitan wanted to be above all others, and the second after him. The Council of Constantinople was held under Theodosius the Elder, by whom it was also convened and confirmed, as was customary. So the Fathers write to him in the synodal letter, when they send the canons: "We therefore ask your clemency that the decree of the council be ratified by the letters of your piety too, so that, just as you honoured the Church with the letters by which you summoned us, so you may also set your seal to the end of those things which have been decreed." About 150 bishops gathered at Constantinople in the year of Christ 381, chiefly for two reasons: first for the faith, and then for discipline, which Macedonius and Maximus, the one troubling the faith, the other discipline, both bishops of Constantinople, had disturbed. Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 8: "The emperor, without delay, summons a council of bishops who embrace his faith, by which the faith of the Council of Nicaea might be strengthened and a bishop might be appointed for Constantinople." The faith of Nicaea was of course maintained against the heretics who denied the Deity of the Holy Spirit, of whom Macedonius was the author. Then, since Maximus the Philosopher, formerly a Cynic and later fallen into the heresy of Apollinaris, had been tumultuously thrust in by the Egyptian bishops against Gregory Nazianzen, who had been designated bishop of the Church of Constantinople, the throne, as they say, had to be vindicated for Gregory. Yet he soon yielded of his own accord to the envy of his own people, and by common vote Nectarius was appointed bishop in his place. To understand this better, the succession of the Constantinopolitan bishops should be set out briefly, from Metrophanes, under whom the Council of Nicaea was held, as we have just said, down to the times of this Synod. After Metrophanes, his presbyter Alexander succeeded him as bishop; he had been present at the Council of Nicaea and lived as bishop for twenty-three years. After Alexander came Paul, who was removed from his see by Constantius and presided for ten years. Then Eusebius, an Arian by the favour and faith of the Emperor Constantius, for eleven years. Then Macedonius, a man of the same madness, and then an open opponent of the Holy Spirit and of his Deity, formerly a presbyter of the same Church, for eleven years; hence the Macedonian heretics were called Pneumatomachi. Then Eudoxius, also an Arian, who was first bishop of Germanicia, then of Antioch, and then of Constantinople; he presided for eight years, under Julian and again under Jovian. Then Demophilus, likewise an Arian, for eleven years and five months. Eusignius succeeded him, an Orthodox man, but he was driven into exile by the Emperor Valens after he had ruled that Church for four years. Last came Gregory Nazianzen, whose cause, namely that he should either be confirmed in the see or, if he were removed, that Maximus the Cynic, thrust in by the Egyptians, should take his place, led to the holding of the Synod of Constantinople, where the matter was debated not without vigour. And at last, when Gregory saw that, after the death of Meletius, bishop of Antioch, who had stood most fiercely for Gregory along with Gregory's brother Gregory of Nyssa, the Egyptians, moved by envy alone, were raging against him no less than before, he resigned of his own accord. To that end he delivered before the synod of about 150 bishops a famous speech in which he asked for his dismissal, and obtained it. By the common vote of all, and so unanimously that the place where this happened was afterwards named Concord, he put in his place Nectarius, a man orthodox and pious, then of senatorial rank. Certainly Nazianzen's farewell speech to the synodal Fathers was most elegant, in which he also begs them: "Relieve and refresh us from our long labours. Let this grey hair move you; let our sojourn among you be held in honour. Appoint another who will be harassed on your behalf, who has hands unburdened by children, who has a voice not unlearned, who can obey you in all things and at the same time bear the cares of the Church, since this time especially calls for such men. But you see how this body of mine is, worn out by time, by sickness and by toil. What need have you of a timid and idle old man, who is dying day by day, so to speak, not only in body but also in the dear ones? I scarcely speak even these things to you. Do not refuse credit to the voice of your teacher, for you never have refused it. I am weary, while the mass of accusations is constantly turned against me. I am weary, while I struggle with words, with envy, with enemies, and with my own people." Coming to the charges brought against him, among other things, to the one concerning the neglect of episcopal pomp and his "contempt" (phaulismos), he answers admirably: "Perhaps they will also reproach us with this (indeed they have already reproached us), that we do not use a lavish and sumptuous table, nor magnificent and venerable robes, nor do we go out in public in splendour, nor do we assume gravity towards those by whom we are visited. I did not know that we were in competition with consuls and prefects and the most famous generals of war, who overflow with such wealth and resources that they have nowhere to throw their goods," and so on. About the man to be substituted for himself he gives this advice, describing and depicting the best shepherd, worthy of every observance: "Whom then shall we put in your place? someone will say. The Lord will provide a shepherd for the office, just as he provided a sheep for the burnt offering. I ask only this, that he be one of those who are an object of envy to others, not of pity; who do not obey in all things, but who in some matters incur offence among men through their zeal for what is right. For the one is pleasant for the present; the other is most useful for the future. And you, prepare speeches fitting my departure; but I will bid you farewell in these words for the last time: Farewell, Anastasia, which has its name from piety, etc." By Anastasia he means the august church in the city of Constantinople, so called because in it the doctrine of the Nicene faith had, as it were, publicly revived, after it had been long suppressed and weakened under the earlier bishops of the Constantinopolitan Church, Macedonius, Eudoxius, Demophilus, who were Arians. And against Maximus, canon 4 was made by the Fathers of the council, concerning Maximus the Cynic and his disorderly appointment, which was made at Constantinople: it was resolved that Maximus was not and could not be a bishop, and that those ordained by him in any grade of the clergy, and whatever was done by him, were invalid. So Maximus was removed from the see he had seized, and he himself and the others appointed by him to the clergy were deposed by synodal decision; hence he is not even listed in the catalogue of the bishops of Constantinople. Against the Egyptians, who out of hatred and jealousy had thrust him in to the harm of Gregory, the second canon was issued, again concerning the limits of episcopal dioceses, according to the decrees of the Synod of Nicaea: "Bishops are not to go beyond their dioceses [hyper dioikēseis], or beyond, as Gentian Hervet translates it, to churches situated outside their bounds, nor are they to confuse churches. But according to the canons, the bishop of Alexandria shall administer only those in Egypt; the bishops of the East shall govern only the East, the privileges granted to the Church of Antioch by the Nicene canons being preserved; and the bishops of the diocese of Asia shall govern only the Asian diocese; likewise the Pontic diocese only those things that pertain to the Pontic diocese, and those in Thrace only those in Thrace. Bishops are not to go to another diocese uninvited, for ordinations or other business. And with the canon concerning dioceses preserved as above, it is clear that the provincial synod shall manage the matters that belong to each province." So the Egyptians, who had appointed a bishop in the Church of Constantinople beyond their own diocese, were condemned, and the Nicene canons were confirmed, that the rights of the archbishops or metropolitans within their provinces be safe, and that, if any difficulty or question should arise, the provincial synod should settle and decide it. Socrates explains that the bishops of Alexandria, Antioch, Asia, Pontus and Thrace were each assigned their own eparchy and diocese, which he calls [malepárchia]. Already in his speech Gregory Nazianzen called the bishops patriarchs: "What have we not suffered," he says, "from [hyperbolioi], bishops, diocesan governors or [malimecha], the public slaughter of presbyters, bishops, or, to speak properly, of patriarchs?" And the histories call Metrophanes the patriarch of New Rome. And Zonaras, in his Annals, volume 2, so designates the metropolitans. But the difference and distinction between these is clearly set out by the Emperor Justinian, Novel 6: "the most holy patriarchs of each diocese and the metropolitans beloved of God, and the remaining most reverend bishops and clergy." And further: "for the most holy patriarchs of each diocese are to set forth these things in the churches under them, and make them known to the metropolitans beloved of God, which we have established. These in turn are to set them forth in the most holy metropolitan church, and make them known to the bishops under them. Each of these is to set them forth in his own church." Similarly in Novels 6, 1 and 40, 2, and elsewhere. Above the presbyters were the bishops; above the bishops, the metropolitans; above the metropolitans, the patriarchs, who are also called archbishops-patriarchs and ecumenical, Novels 40, 41 and 70, 9; Menas, "archbishop and ecumenical [of the] metropolitans" (Mēnas archiepiskopos ē oikoumenikos [metropolitōn]); and so often elsewhere. It was not enough for the Constantinopolitan Fathers to have deposed the bishop Maximus and to have re-established, in accordance with the Nicene canons, the rights of the bishops in their own provinces against the violent invaders of another's diocese. They also, for the honour of the see of Constantinople, made canon 3: "The bishop of Constantinople shall have the primacy of honour after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome" [Ton men tēs Konstantinoupoleōs episkopon echein ta presbeia meta ton tēs Rhōmēs episkopon, dia to einai autēn neran Rhōmēn]. This decree has always fixed the eyes of the Roman bishop sharply, because he saw that the Constantinopolitan, recently risen up, was by synodal authority made his equal. "The bishop of the city of Constantinople has the privileges of honour after the Roman bishop, because it is itself New Rome." We must weigh carefully the reason for which the Fathers gave this dignity to the Constantinopolitan, namely the splendour of the city: since New Rome was regarded as equal to Old Rome, its bishop too should yield nothing to the Roman. For the emperors set up this rival to Rome, and in all things... "Because it is itself New Rome." They indicate at the same time that the basis of honour, which belongs first to the Roman bishop, is the first city, and that this city, already second, ought to hold the place next after it. Code, On the Holy Churches, book 6: "the churches of the city of Constantinople, which rejoices in the prerogative of Old Rome." Code, On the Privileges of the City of Constantinople: "The city of Constantinople rejoices not only in the Italian law, but also in the very prerogative of Old Rome." The Emperor Justinian writes to Menas, bishop of Constantinople, in Novel 131... [ tē hagiōtatē archiepiskopō tēs basilidos pantēs poleōs, hē oikoumenikē prosēgoria] ... Constantinople is everywhere called New Rome, and "queen of all cities" (pantōn tēs poleōs basilis). And in Novel 131 (Latin 131): "We define the limit of ecclesiastical authority: that the holiness of elder Rome is first of all, and the most blessed archbishopric of Constantinople, New Rome, shall hold second place after the holiness of elder Rome, the others being put after." The Roman Pope is first of all priests, according to the ancient canons and constitutions of the ecclesiastical churches, because he is bishop of Old Rome; the Constantinopolitan is ordered to hold the second place after him, and is placed before all the others, because he too is bishop of New Rome. Already the Alexandrian, the Antiochene, the Jerusalemite and the rest yield place to him; and at this council Nectarius of Constantinople subscribed first, then Timothy of Alexandria, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Meletius of Antioch. At the Council of Nicaea, after Hosius, the first of the Easterners to subscribe was Alexander, metropolitan of the province of Egypt and of the Church of Alexandria. Dionysius Exiguus translates the Constantinopolitan canon thus: "Nevertheless, the bishop of Constantinople shall have the primacy of honour after the bishop of Rome." He said significantly "primacy of honour" (presbeia tēs timēs), and that it is owed to the Constantinopolitan after the Roman. So the Constantinopolitan also has a primacy, and so have all to whom the canons attribute the presbeia tēs timēs, that is, the Alexandrian, the Antiochene, and in short all archbishops. And this primacy is said not in relation to fellow bishops, for in that sense a primacy after the Roman could not be attributed to the Constantinopolitan; it is said in relation to the bishops subject to them in their own province. And the first place of the Roman bishop, in relation to the Constantinopolitan, who is second to him, denotes order, not power, which is equal for both, because of the equal rank and dignity of the city, whether Old or New. Theodore Balsamon, commenting on this canon, writes that there are those who do not understand the preposition "after" (meta) as referring to a submission of honour, but to the order of time, namely that the primacy came to the Constantinopolitan later than to the Roman. From this it appears how fiercely the Constantinopolitans, and the other Greeks with them, strive against the honours of Rome, and how diligently the Greeks and Latins dispute over the meaning of this canon and the primacy of these two sees. Hence arose the first and perpetual dispute between the two sides, since this canon attributed to the Constantinopolitan bishop a dignity equal to the Roman, and so balanced both Romes as on one scale. And here the Constantinopolitan [see] is given not only [hyperbas] ... after Rome, but also in the Council of Chalcedon...

units.la: & & perpetua inter utrosq; viguit disputatio ; Constantinopolitano hoc canone suo episcopo parem attribuente dignitatem cum Romano, atque in eandem quasi lanteram appendente utramq; Romam. Atq; hic Constantinop. non tantum ὑπερβᾶσ τ̀ πμ̃ς, post Romanum; sed & in Chalcedonensi Concilio ὶσω ὑπερβᾶσ accepit: quum tam aegre parem Romanus ferret, ac alter superiorem. Multum quidem clamitant Romani adversus hunc Concilii canonem, surreptitium dicentes, falsum, à Romanâ ecclesiâ nunquam receptum, sed damnatum, & quid non? verum quantumcunque tumultuentur, à Constantinop. Patribus in Concilio Generali factus canon est. Hoc Socrates, hoc Sozomenus testantur, qui canonem recitant; neque Baronius infitiatur it: & in Concilio Chalcedonensi clamaverunt Constantinopolitanae ecclesiae Clerici: ea, quae sanctorum Patrum centum quinquaginta sunt, teneant privilegia Constantinopolis, ne depereant. Novella Iustiniani cxxx i. in honore isto sedis Constantinopolitanae agnoscendo ait se sequi canonum ecclesiasticorum definitiones. Sed dicunt, canon ille post Nectarii electionem sancitus, ab iis, qui remanserant Constantinopoli Episcopi Orientales; verba sunt Baronii, Annal. Tom. iv. ad A. ccclxxx i. num. xxxv i. sed unde id constat? quae huius assertionis, vel conjecturae ratio? quidve ad rem facit, sive post Nectarii electionem canon conditus sit, sive antea? quum postea demum Concilio, & hisce ejus canonibus, cum reliquis subscripsit primus Nectarius. Et electio Nectarii praesente ac consentiente totâ Synodo facta, uti scribunt ad Damasum Papam Patres Constantinop. Reverendissimum, Deoque dilectissimum Nectarium in Concilio Generali, communi omnium consensu, praesente Theodosio Imperatore religiosissimo, totius denique cleri, totiusque civitatis suffragiis Episcopum constituimus. Et in Catalogo Episcoporum Byzantii, apud Marquardum Freherum, Iuris Graeco-Romani Tom. I. lib. IV, dicitur Nectarius, qui ante electionem erat ἀξιωματικὸς[?] Magistratum gerens, à Patribus cl. simul & baptizatus, & ordinatus. Photius ait, illum nuper baptizatum, quando ad episcopatum promoveretur. Post istam electionem demum factus sit hic canon, quid tum porro? at discesserant jam plerique ex Synodo. Hoc autem proba: neque enim credemus, antequam valere jussa ratione, cogamur simpliciter admittere placita Romanorum, non vero ea examinare. Imo & ob hanc causam maxime manere debuerunt omnes, quia propter illa, quae statum ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae concernebant, vocati cum primis erant. Itane abiissent, re non confecta? hoc tulisset scilicet Imperator, hoc ipse recens creatus Nectarius. Abiecerint etiam ante absolutam Synodum, vel saltem ante firmatum hunc canonem, non tamen dissenserunt, nec unquam Graeci hanc ob rem, vel canonem, dissensum suum aut indignationem testati unquam fuerunt, quin contra eum semper utroque (quod ajunt) pollice comprobarunt. Ipseque Papa Damasus, acceptis Synodi canonibus, eos probavit. Testis Photius, in lib. de septem Synodis. Neque Papistae aliter agnoscunt hanc Synodum oecumenicam, seu generalem, nisi ex Papae approbatione. Nobis vero tanti non est, Papae confirmatio accesserit, vel non: parumque referre putamus, an dicatur haec Synodus generalis, quum, quod alioqui Generales Synodos facit, hic defuerit, nempe ex Occidentali Ecclesia legati: neque nisi cum vulgo, & ob celebritatem Synodi, vel quod Occidentalis quoque Ecclesia consensum suum in hanc Synodum postea declaravit, praecipue ob generalem fidei adversus haeresim definitionem, inter Generales dictas collocamus. Sed Damasus, & Romana Ecclesia non recepit Synodum, nisi in rebus fidei contra Macedonium, aliosque haereticos; haud in iis, quae de regimine Ecclesiarum constituta sunt. Ergo nec etiam in confirmatis ab hac Synodo canonibus Nicaenis de terminis diœcesium? Vel si hoc, quare non etiam ubi de juribus & ratione sedis Constantinopolitanæ agitur? Novimus quidem sequentibus temporibus Romanos obloquutos frustra fuisse huic Constantinop. canoni; sed de Damaso id non probabunt, ullam ab eo hic factam exceptionem. Convocarat quidem Orientales in Synodum Romæ habendam; sed multis de causis, & propter itineris longinquitatem ac difficultatem, atque ob metum hæreticorum Ecclesiis orientalibus infestantium, se excusabant in epistola Synodica ad Damasum Constantinopolitani Patres. Nihil autem turpius commentito à Papistis Concilio Romano IV. sub Damaso habito, ejusque canone, quo se ecclesia Romana supra cæteras omnes effert, atque Constantinopolitanum inter Orientis Episcopos ne nominat quidem. Damasus subdoratus, affectatam ab Orientalibus Constantinopolitanæ Ecclesiæ patriarchalem sedem ac dignitatem, ipsi nihil hac de re in suâ ad Concilium Synodicâ meminerit, canonem in Collectione Crescioniana, & Vaticano aliisve codicibus, post anathematismos supra descriptos extantem, edidisse videtur, inquit Severinus Binius, in Notis ad hoc Concilium. Istud videtur sane est salsissimum; neque certe si verum putarent Romani, adeo dubitanter de eo loquerentur. Damasus sic disposuisset de episcopatibus Orientalium? & directe adeo contra Concilium Constantinopolitanum? quod tamen approbavit? cur nihil istius meminit in Synodica ad Concilium epistola? Sed bene est, quod subdoratus Damasus fuit affectatam ab Orientalibus Constantinopolitanæ Ecclesiæ Patriarchalem dignitatem, id est, sententiam canonis Constantinopolitani: ergo non falsus, non subreptitius canon, cujus gestum mox acceperit Papa Damasus. Accipe commentitium illum Damasi canonem: post has omnes Prophetic-as, & Evangelicas, & Apostolicas, quas superius deprompsimus, Scripturas, quibus Ecclesia Catholica per gra- tiam[?] iam Dei fundata est; etiam existimandum putavimus, quod quamvis per orbem Catholicæ diffusa Ecclesiæ quasi unus thalamus Christi sit, sancta tamen Romana Ecclesia non nullis Synodicis constitutionibus cæteris Ecclesiis prælata est; sed & Evangelicâ voce Domini salvatoris nostri Primatum obtinuit: Tu es Petrus &c. Est ergo prima Petri Apostoli sedes Romana Ecclesia, non habens maculam, neque rugam, neque aliud huiusmodi. Secunda autem sedes apud Alexandriam &c. Tertia autem sedes est apud Antiochiam &c. Mendacissima definitio, quæ dicit nonnullis Synodicis constitutionibus Romanæ Ecclesiæ primatum supra reliquas ecclesias decretum fuisse. Ne ulla quidem Synodus, nedum nonnullæ, quæ hunc primatum memorent, produci possunt. Num Nicæna? atqui ista Romano Alexandrinum atque Antiochenum, in suâ dioecesi quemque pares fecit, neque ultra dioeceses vel provincias suas exire, non [illegible, ~6 letters] ut explicant Constantinopolitani Patres ad mentem Nicænorum, permittit. An aliæ particulares & nonnullæ Synodi? in ne unâ quidem sive Orientalium, sive Occidentalium, de hoc Rom. Ecclesiæ primatu vel levissima fit mentio. Quam ergo impudens est figmentum hujus constitutionis, quasi a Damaso formatæ, ubi Romana Ecclesia primatum dicitur habere nonnullis Synodicis constitutionibus, quem tum adhuc nec habebat, neque ei Synodi ullæ attribuerant? Postea Canon ille Constantinopolitanus usu quodam, & tacito Romanæ sedis consensu confirmatus, & ab Innocentio III. renovatus fuit in Lateranensi Concilio, inquit Binius. Denique & symbolum fidei in hoc Concilio, idem cum Nicæno, nisi quod id quod in Nicæno breviter & simpliciter dictum fuerat: Et in Spiritum sanctum, magis pro præsenti necessitate, adversus hæresim Macedonii, explicarint: credimus in Spiritum Sanctum, Dominum & vivificantem, ex patre procedentem, & cum Patre, & Filio adorandum, & conglorificandum, [illegible, ~4 letters].
units.tr: Between the two sides there has been a constant and lasting dispute. By this canon of theirs the Constantinopolitan bishop is given a dignity equal to that of the Roman, and both Romes are hung in the same balance pan. Here Constantinople received not only ὑπερβᾶσ τ̀ πμ̃ς [the prerogative of honour after Rome], but also, at the Council of Chalcedon, ὶσω ὑπερβᾶσ [equal honour]. The Romans bore it with great bitterness that the other should be made their equal, and not their inferior. The Romans indeed cry out loudly against this canon of the Council, calling it surreptitious, false, never received by the Roman Church, but condemned, and what not. Yet however much they make an uproar, the canon was enacted by the Constantinopolitan Fathers in a General Council. Socrates and Sozomen bear witness to this, reciting the canon, and Baronius does not deny it. And at the Council of Chalcedon the clergy of the Constantinopolitan church cried out: let the privileges of Constantinople, which are those of the holy Fathers of the hundred and fifty, be kept, lest they perish. Justinian's 131st Novel, in acknowledging this honour of the see of Constantinople, says that he follows the decrees of the ecclesiastical canons. But they say that this canon was sanctioned after the election of Nectarius, by the Eastern bishops who had stayed behind at Constantinople; these are Baronius's words, Annals, vol. 4, at the year 381, no. 36. But how is that established? What is the ground or conjecture for this assertion? And what does it matter whether the canon was framed after the election of Nectarius or before it, since Nectarius himself was the first to subscribe to the Council and its canons, along with the rest? Moreover, Nectarius's election was made with the whole Synod present and consenting, as the Constantinopolitan Fathers write to Pope Damasus: we have appointed the most reverend Nectarius, beloved of God, as bishop in the General Council, by the common consent of all, with the most pious Emperor Theodosius present, and by the votes of the whole clergy and the whole city. And in the catalogue of the bishops of Byzantium, in Marquard Freher's Jus Graeco-Romanum, vol. 1, book 4, Nectarius is described as one who before his election was ἀξιωματικὸς[?] holding the office of magistrate, and was both baptized and ordained by the Fathers together. Photius says that he had been baptized only recently, when he was promoted to the episcopate. Suppose the canon was enacted only after that election; what then? But by then many had already left the Synod. Test this, however: we will not believe, before we have weighed the reasons, that we must simply accept the Romans' opinions without examining them. Indeed, for this very reason all of them ought most of all to have remained, because they had been summoned chiefly on account of matters which concerned the state of the Constantinopolitan church. Would they have left with the business unfinished? The Emperor would certainly not have allowed it, nor Nectarius, newly created as he was. Even if they left before the Synod was concluded, or at least before this canon was ratified, they did not dissent; nor did the Greeks ever bear witness to any dissent or indignation over this matter or the canon, but on the contrary always approved it with both thumbs up, as they say. And Pope Damasus himself, having received the canons of the Synod, approved them. Photius bears witness to this in his book On the Seven Synods. Nor do the Papists otherwise acknowledge this Synod as oecumenical, or general, except by the Pope's approval. For our part, it is of no great concern to us whether the Pope's confirmation came or not, and we think it matters little whether this Synod is called general, since the thing that otherwise makes Synods general, namely legates from the Western Church, was lacking here. We count it among the General Councils not merely because of common usage and the fame of the Synod, but also because the Western Church afterwards declared its consent to this Synod, chiefly on account of its general definition of the faith against heresy. But Damasus and the Roman Church did not receive the Synod, except in matters of faith against Macedonius and other heretics; not in those things which were decreed concerning the government of the churches. Therefore they did not receive even the canons of this Synod confirmed from Nicaea concerning the boundaries of dioceses? Or if they did receive this, why not also where the rights and standing of the see of Constantinople are treated? We know indeed that in later times the Romans protested in vain against this Constantinopolitan canon; but they will not prove that Damasus made any objection to it here. Indeed he had summoned the Eastern bishops to a Synod to be held at Rome; but the Constantinopolitan Fathers, in their synodal letter to Damasus, excused themselves for many reasons, including the length and difficulty of the journey and the fear of the heretics who were harassing the Eastern churches. Nothing is more shameful than the invention by the Papists of a Roman Council of the fourth year under Damasus, and of its canon, by which the Roman Church exalts itself above all others, and does not even name the Constantinopolitan among the bishops of the East. Damasus, having caught a whiff that the Orientals were aiming at a patriarchal see and dignity for the Church of Constantinople, seems to have published a canon, found in the Cresconian collection and in the Vatican and other codices after the anathemas described above, without making any mention of this matter in his synodal letter to the Council, says Severinus Binius in his notes on this Council. It seems is surely most silly; nor would the Romans speak so doubtfully about it if they thought it true. Would Damasus have so arranged the bishoprics of the Orientals, and directly against the Council of Constantinople, which he nevertheless approved? Why does he make no mention of this in the synodal letter to the Council? But it is well that Damasus caught a whiff that the Orientals were aiming at a patriarchal dignity for the Church of Constantinople, that is, at the sense of the Constantinopolitan canon. So the canon was not false or surreptitious, since Pope Damasus received its acts soon after. Take that invented canon of Damasus: after all these Prophetic, Evangelical and Apostolic Scriptures, which we have drawn out above, by which the Catholic Church has been founded through the grace [?] of God, we have also thought it right to hold that, although the Church spread throughout the world as one bridal chamber of Christ, the holy Roman Church has been placed before the other churches by some synodal constitutions; and it has also obtained the primacy by the evangelical voice of our Lord and Saviour: You are Peter, etc. Therefore the Roman Church is the first see of the Apostle Peter, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the kind. The second see is at Alexandria, etc. The third see is at Antioch, etc. A most lying definition, which says that the primacy of the Roman Church over the other churches was decreed by some synodal constitutions. No Synod at all, let alone several, which mention this primacy can be produced. Is it the Nicene? But that Synod made the Alexandrian and Antiochene bishops equal to the Roman within their own dioceses, and does not permit anyone to go beyond his own dioceses or provinces, as the Constantinopolitan Fathers explain in keeping with the mind of the Nicene Fathers. Or some other particular and several Synods? Yet in not one, whether of the East or of the West, is there even the slightest mention of this primacy of the Roman Church. How impudent, then, is the fiction of this constitution, as if it had been formed by Damasus, where the Roman Church is said to hold the primacy by several synodal constitutions, which it did not yet hold at that time, nor did any Synods attribute it to it? Afterwards that Constantinopolitan canon, confirmed by a certain usage and by the tacit consent of the Roman see, was renewed by Innocent III in the Lateran Council, says Binius. Finally, the creed of faith in this Council is the same as the Nicene, except that what was said briefly and simply at Nicaea, and in the Holy Spirit, they expanded, more because of the present need against the heresy of Macedonius: we believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, and with the Father and the Son to be adored and glorified together, [illegible, ~4 letters].

units.la: πνεύματος ἐκπορευόμενον, qui locutus est per Prophetas. Additum & hoc: Et unam catholicam & Apostolicam Ecclesiam confitemur, unum baptisma in remissionem peccatorum, expectamus resurrectionem mortuorum, & vitam futuri seculi. Amen. Illud de Spiritus Sancti processione, postea gravem inter Latinos ac Graecos contentionem movit, postquam Latini symbolo huic, inconsultis Graecis, addidissent, Spiritum S. procedere à Filio, quomodo apud Latinos symbolum legitur, auctoritate Leonis Pontificis, ab Episcopis Hispanis, contra Priscillianistas primum, uti dicitur, symbolo adjectum. De quo in sequentibus plura. Iohannes Zonaras, Annal. Tom. III. ubi de Concilio Nicaeno loquutus fuisset, ἡ δὲ θεολογία, Theologi vero de Spiritu Sancto post in secundo concilio contra Macedonium congregato, ea quaestione agitata, adjecta est, inquit. Θεολογίαν Patres appellant, doctrinam de Deo, vel S. Trinitate in se consideratam; at in opere redemtionis, & doctrinam de Christo, ejusque incarnatione, οἰκονομίαν. Ita Chrysostomus dixit de tribus Evangelistis, quod instar fulguris sonuerint τὴν οἰκονομίαν; Iohannes vero tonuerit τὴν θεολογίαν. Et Eusebius, historiam suam exordiens, se de Christi Servatoris sublimissima oeconomia, & Theologia, οἰκονομίας τε καὶ θεολογίας initium sermonis facere, ait.
units.tr: proceeding [ἐκπορευόμενον] from the Spirit, who spoke through the Prophets [τὸ λαλῆσαν διὰ τῶν προφητῶν]. This was added as well: "We confess one holy catholic and Apostolic Church, we acknowledge one baptism for the remission of sins, we look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come. Amen." That clause on the procession of the Holy Spirit later caused a serious dispute between the Latins and the Greeks, after the Latins, without consulting the Greeks, had added to this creed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, as the creed is read among the Latins. By the authority of Pope Leo, this phrase is said to have been first added to the creed by the Spanish bishops against the Priscillianists. More on this below. John Zonaras, Annals, Vol. III, after speaking of the Council of Nicaea, says: "But the theology [ἡ δὲ θεολογία] concerning the Holy Spirit was added later, at the second council gathered against Macedonius, when that question had been debated." The Fathers call θεολογία the doctrine of God, or of the Holy Trinity considered in itself; but the doctrine of the work of redemption, and of Christ and his incarnation, they call οἰκονομία. So Chrysostom said that the three Evangelists thundered like lightning τὴν οἰκονομίαν [the economy], while John thundered τὴν θεολογίαν [the theology]. And Eusebius, beginning his history, says that he makes the start of his discourse with the most sublime οἰκονομίας τε καὶ θεολογίας [economy and theology] of Christ our Saviour.

units.la: A. ccccxxx I. jussu Theodosii, & Valentiniani Impp. habitum Concilium Ephesinum generale, adversus Nestorium, Ecclesiae Constantinopolitanae episcopum, ex presbytero Antiocheno factum, anno cccccxxviii. qui quia in concione ad populum aliquando dixerat: se eum qui spatiis menstruis adolevisset, Deum non appellare; neque Mariam Θεοτόκον, commoti adversus eum alii, praecipuè Alexandrinus episcopus Cyrillus, & cum hoc Memnon Ephesinus, effecerunt ut in Synodo Romanâ, per Coelestinum episcopum, tum in Alexandrinâ, per Cyrillum, demique & in generali Ephesinâ Nestorius haereseos notatus, & depositus, atque in exilium actus fuerit, suffecto in ejus locum Maximiano: Contendebant ejus tempore, an Maria dicenda esset θεοτόκος, an ἀνθρωποτόκος? Nestorius hanc litem ut vel evitaret, vel dirimeret, dicendam ajebat χριστοτόκος. Deum autem ex ipsa natum, dicere reformidabat. Non negabat Christum Deum, non duas in eo naturas, non harum in Christo unionem: faciliusque ex Synodi Actis deprehendes quae bene, quam quae male dixerit, aut quae non bene explicari forte potuerint. Tom. II. Act. CVIII. ex scriptis Nestorii adducuntur aliqua, ob quae notatus heterodoxiae fuerit. Interque ea occurrit primum, ex ejus Dogmatico, quaternione septimo decimo (nam non per folia veterum libri notabantur, ut hodie, sed per quaterniones, qui signabantur, non illorum paginae) Unde in Actis Concilii Constantinopolitani VI. Act. III. Codicem, praeferentem Sermonem Mennae episcopi Constant. ad Vigilium P. quintae Synodo Constantinopoli exhibitum, a Monothelitis falsatum fuisse deprehenderunt: nam cum aperientes ac discernentes, invenerunt tres quaternniones in principio libri additos, non habentes subnotationem numeri, qui secundum consuetudinem affigitur in quaternionibus, sed in quarto quaternione habente primum numerum, & in sequenti quaternione secundum, & tertium, atque quartum subsequenter.) Sic & Nestorius: Cum divina Scriptura de Christi ortu, ex Maria Virgine, aut de ejusdem morte aliquid dictura est, nusquam Dei, sed semper Christi, aut filii, aut Domini nomen usurpare deprehenditur. Quandoquidem tria haec duarum naturarum notionem complectuntur. Et modo quidem hanc, modo verò illam, nonnunquam autem utramque simul insinuat; exempli causa: Cum sacra scriptura Christi ex sacra Virgine generationem nobis enarrat, non dicit: Misit Deus Verbum suum Deum, sed ait: Misit Deus filium suum: illud enim nomen accipit, quod utriusque naturae symbolum est. Quia enim Filius simul Deus, & homo est, idem dicit Misit Deus filium suum factum ex muliere: hoc autem cum addis, nec in nomen, quod utramque naturam denotat, & premitur, mentis oculos conjicis; natumque ex Maria Virgine, Filii quidem nomine appellas: (siquidem Christum ex Virgine Filium Dei genuit) attamen quia Filius Dei duplicis naturae existit, non Dei Filium, sed humanam tantum naturam peperisse cogites, quae propter Filium adjunctam, filii quoque appellatione afficitur. Quod initio ait, Scripturam nusquam, ubi de Christi morte verba facit. Dei nomen usurpare, in eo falsus fuit, quia Act. xx. 28. dicitur Deus Ecclesiam suo sanguine acquisivisse. & 1. Cor. 11. 8. Dominus gloriae crucifixus. At in ceteris agnoscere cum videmus, duas in Christo Iesu naturas, & quod simul Deus & homo sit, quemadmodum quoque in sequentibus, utramque in Christo naturam, dualitatem naturarum, passim dicit. Id videtur totum declinare voluisse, ne diceretur Filius Dei, vel Deus a Matre genitus. Unde statim in sequenti excerpto: Deum ex Christipara Virgine processisse, id per divinas Scripturas edoctus sum: quod autem Deus ipse ipsa natus sit, id nusquam scriptum comperi. Iterum: Sacra proinde Scriptura Deum ex Christipara Virgine genitum esse nusquam affirmat, sed Iesum Christum, sed Filium, sed Dominum. Quem in finem adducens, quod Angelus dixit Iosepho: surge & accipe puerum & matrem ejus; non dictum, non: surge & accipe Deum, & matrem ejus; sed surge & accipe puerum & matrem ejus, Ex eodem ejus libro, vel quaternione: Sed neque impedio, si quis Verbum in carne exitisse, vel cum carne conjunctum fuisse, dicere voluerit. Aliud enim est nasci, aliud cum nato conjungi. Dicit itaque, quod in ea natum est, de Spiritu Sancto est, hoc est, Spiritus Sanctus, quod in ea est, condidit. Quia ergo Patres divinarum Scripturarum peritissimi animadvertebant, si Deum Verbum, quod incarnatum dicunt, pervidetur, hoc est, genitum dicerent, necessario confessuros Deum Verbum filium esse Spiritus Sancti, & per consequens sequens, duos habere Patres: Si vero γενητὸν, hoc est, factum assererent, hinc rursum inferri posse, Deum Verbum Spiritus sancti creaturam esse: quare generationis voce rejecta, posuerunt: Qui descendit propter nos, & propter nostram salutem, & incarnatus est. At quid est, inquis, hoc: Et incarnatus est? Quidvis potius, quam ex divinitate in carnem versus est. In carne Verbum, & cum carne unitum, atque incarnatum, ait; non in carne factum, vel generatum, vel per carnem natum. Pergit; Sanè Deus Verbum ante incarnationem & Filius erat, & Deus erat, & Patri conjunctus erat. At vero in novissimis temporibus servilem quoque formam assumpsit. Caeterum cùm ante Filius esset, & Filius appellaretur; post carnem tamen assumptam seorsim per se Filii nomine appellari non debet, ne duos Filios videamur inducere. Sic quoque potest quàm homo illi semel unitus est, qui ab initio Filius est, & nunc homini indissociabili vinculo conjunctus est, quod quidem ad filiationis dignitatem attinet, divisionem nequaquam recipit; secundum dignitatem dico filiationis, non secundum naturas. Unde quòd Deus Verbum perpetuam cum Christo unionem retineat, & Christus quoque appellatur. Si volueris non ponendos in Christo duos Filios, quamvis duas naturas, benè hoc. Deinde: Inconfusam igitur naturarum conjunctionem retineamus, & Deum in homine confiteamur: Hominem divino quodam nexu praepotenti Deo conjunctum, una cum Deo adoremus. Si tantum intenderit Nestorius, deitatem Christi, vel divinam ejus naturam, aut ipsum Deum non posse dici in, vel ex Maria genitum, aut factum, tamque non illâ ratione θεοτόκον, ut generatio vel partus ad θεὸν, aut divinam naturam terminarit, quasi haec generata fuerit, bene explicari ejus dicta potuerunt: quadia haec ejus. Non per se, & secundum se Deus est, quod in utero formatum est: Non per se, & secundum se Deus est, quod Spiritus sancti opera effectum est: Non per se, & secundum se Deus est, quod in monumento conditum est: Alias enim Anthropolatræ & necrolatræ, hoc est, hominum mortuorumque cultores essemus. At vero quia Deus in homine assumpto existit, assumptus assumenti conjunctus, propter assumentem Deus appellatur. Sic est, Deus non fuit formaliter in utero factus vel genitus; sed humanam naturam in utero factam assumsit. Nisi humanam non naturam, sed personam intelligat assumtam: unde hominem hic passim dixerit. Deumque verbum ei duntaxat peculiari modo adhæsisse, vel inhabitasse, ut loquitur; & non personaliter unitum cum humana natura fuisse, quæ valde obscure ejus verbis innuuntur, si innuuntur: nam res facti est, non an bene reprobata damnataque hæresis sit, quæ illa in Christo negat, docetque quod in Nestorio rejecerunt Patres; sed, an revera ita Nestorius docuerit. Miror, non clariora ex ejus Scriptis producta adversus ipsum documenta fuisse, ut ad illa statim absque ulteriori discussione clamatum anathema fuerit, pronunciataque in hanc formam sententia, die xxi Junii, quum propriidie Synodum demum inchoassent: Igitur Dominus noster Iesus Christus, quem suis ille blasphemis vocibus impetivit, per sacram hanc Synodum eundem Nestorium, omni prorsus Episcopali dignitate privatum, & ab universo nihilominus Sacerdotum consortio & cæteris alienum esse decernit. Quod ducenti & ultra episcopi approbarunt: & postridie ipsi Nestorio hoc modo significatum: Sacra Synodus juxta Religiosissimorum Christianissimorumque Imperatorum assertorum præscriptum, in Ephesiorum Metropoli per gratiam Dei congregata, Nestorio novo Iudæ. Agnosce te, propter impias convictiones tuas, obstinatamque adversus sacros Canones contumaciam, consumacemque obstinationem vigesimo secundo mensis Junii jam decurrentis, juxta Ecclesiasticorum sanctionum decreta, a sacra Synodo ex auctoritate, atque ab omni Ecclesiastica dignitatis gradu amotum esse. Ex Cyrilli Alexandrini [?]consensus in hac Synodo permagna fuit authoritas, & favor, quemque religiose admodum reliqui sequebantur) Anathematismis xii. contra Nestorium, quibus præcipue Patrum sententia innixa fuit & fundata; opposita quæ Nestorio adscripta fuit dilucidius apparet. Ex primo: Si quis non confitetur, Emmanuelem verum Deum esse; adeoque sanctam Virginem, quæ incarnatum Dei Patris Verbum secundum carnem genuit, Deiparam esse, anathema sit. Tertio: Si quis post naturarum unionem, subsistentias in uno Christo dividit (unicuique nimirum suam propriam assignans) naturaque ea tantum copula connectit, quæ est secundum dignitatem, vel authoritatem, non ea autem coitione, quæ sit secundum physicam unitionem, anathema sit. Quinto: Si quis dicere audet, Christum hominem tantum Deiferum, non verum quoque Deum, unicumque ac naturalem Dei Filium esse; quatenus nimirum Dei Verbum caro factum, perinde ac nos ex nobis carni & sanguini communicavit, anathema sit. Ex quibus colligas, Nestorium duas in Christo personas, Christum hominem Deiferum, eaque ratione Mariam non esse Θεοτόκον[?], existimasse. Cyrillianis, alios xii Anathematismos oppositos Nestorius, quibus non suam exponit aut vindicat sententiam, sed eam, quam Cyrilli & adversariorum esse putabat, oppugnat, de Filii Dei in Maria generatione, aut mutatione, & naturæ utriusque in eo confusione, hinc & divinæ aut deitatis in ipso passione &c. Anathem. iii. Si quis non secundum conjunctionem unum dixerit Christum, qui est etiam Emmanuel secundum naturam, ex utraque etiam substantia; tam Dei Verbi, quam etiam ab eo hominis suscepti, in unā Filii connexione, quam etiam nunc inconfuse servamus, minime confitetur, anathema sit. Anathem. vi. Si quis hominem, qui in Virgine creatus est, hunc esse Unigenitum dixerit, qui ex utero Patris ante Luciferum natus est, & non magis propter unitionem eum, qui est naturaliter Unigenitus, Patris ingeniti appellatione confitetur eum participem factum; Iesum quoque alterum, quempiam præter Emmanuelem dicat, anathema sit. Et vii. Si quis servi formam pro seipso, hoc est, secundum propriæ naturæ rationem, arbitrandam esse dixerit, & non omnium Dominam, & mptiùs per societatem, quàm beatam, & ex se naturali Domini Vnigeniti naturæ conjuncta est, veneratur, anathema sit. Istud imprimis spectasse Nestorium apparet, ut confitendo duas in Christo unitas naturas, divinam ab omni mutatione, & confusione immunem servaret, & distincta utriusque idiomata, si non personaliter etiam divisa, eâque ratione non genitum Filium aut De-um à Mariâ, quare neque hanc Θεοτόκον. Vnde in lit-teris ad Cyrillum, ante habitam Synodum, ita illum affatur, super sententiâ Patrum Nicænorum: Penitus, si ita videtur, illorum dicta introspice, & plane mente sensa comperies, Divinum illum Patrum chorum nusquam decisse, homousiam Divinitatem patibilem esse; aut, quæ Patri coæva est, recens natam esse; aut, quæ templum solutum excitavit, excitatam esse. Qualia vel sentire Cyrillum, vel saltem ex eius sequi sententiâ, persuasum habebat; quamvis temerè. Addit: Quò idem nimirum Christus patibilis simul & impatibilis citra fidei discrimen concipi queat. Illud quidem secundum humanam naturam; hoc verò secundum Divinam. Et pergens: In eo autem non injuria te laudo, quòd distinctionem naturarum, secundum Divinitatis & humanitatis rationem, harumque in una droxaxat persona conjunctionem prædicas; quodque Deum Verbum altero illo, qui videlicet ex muliere est, ortu minimè indiguisse affirmas, & quod Divinitatem tandem pati non potuisse, diserte pronuncias. distinctas naturas ait, & in una quoque persona: quæ si ita revera se habent cum sententia eius, & non fuco ac dolo malo pronunciata, dicere quidem licebit, doctrinam à Synodo damnatam falsam, hæreticamque; sed, an ea ipsa Nestorii fuerit, dubium esse. Putabat Nestorius, Cyrillianos dicentes Mariam Θεοτόκον, statuere divinam Christi naturam à Mariâ, vel in eâ genitam, quare mutationi, & passioni quoque subjectam. Vnde ita in iisdem literis se declarat: claratr Vbicunque igitur Divinæ Scripturæ Dominicæ dispensationis mentionem faciunt, cum incarnationem, tum ipsam quoque mortem & passionem non Divinæ; sed humanæ Christi naturæ semper tribuunt. Quâpropter si rem diligentius consideremus, sacra Virgo non Deipara; sed Christipara appellanda erit. Audi quomodo Evangelistæ istuc proclament: Liber (inquiunt) generationis Iesu Christi, Filii David, Filii Abraham: Atqui perspicuum est, Deum Verbum non extitisse Davidis filium. Accipe, si placet aliud hic testimonium: Iacob (ait) genuit Ioseph virum Mariæ, de quâ natus est Iesus, qui vocatur Christus. Perpende rursum aliam Evangelii vocem, veritatem hanc diserte confirmantem: Christi (inquit) generatio sic erat, cum esset desponsata mater ejus Maria Ioseph, inventa est habens in utero de Spiritu sancto. Quis autem ita desipiat, ut Unigeniti Divinitatem Spiritus sancti creaturam esse credat? Adde his illud quoque: Erat mater Iesu ibi; rursum: Cum Maria matre Iesu; & illud: Quod in ea natum est, de Spiritu sancto est; & illud: Accipe puerum & matrem ejus, & fuge in Ægyptum; & illud: De Filio suo, qui factus est ei ex semine David secundum carnem; & illud rursum de ejusdem passione: Deus Filium suum mittens in similitudinem carnis peccati, & de peccato condemnavit peccatum; & illud iterum: Christus mortuus est pro peccatis nostris; & rursum: Christo carne passo. Denique: (hoc est,) non mea Divinitas, sed (corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur.) Sunt alia innumera sententiæ, quæ. Divinitatem neque nuper natam, neque corporeæ passionis capacem esse, mortalium generi testatum faciunt, sed ipsam carnem, quæ Divinæ conjuncta est natura. Subjungit: Rectum proinde Evangelicaque traditioni consentaneum est, ut Christi corpus Divinitatis templum esse confiteamur; illudque nexu usque adeo sublimi, Divinoque & admirabili ipsi conjunctum esse statuamus, uti Divina natura ea sibi vendicet, quæ corporis aliqua sunt propria. Verum propter eam, sive communicationis sive appropriationis notionem, nem, nativitatem, passionem, mortem caeterasque rerum proprietates Divino Verbo adscribere, id demens, ut puto, mentis est paganorum more vere errantis, aut certe ipsam Apollinarii, & Arii aliorumque haereticorum male [?]alio etiam graviori laborantis. Nam qui appropriatum vocabulum ita detorquent, illos Deum Verbum laetantes participem, & succedanei incrementi capacem, & ob formidinem passionis tempore declaratum, Angelicis praesidio indigum extitisse, fateri oportet. Cum alii proprietates divinae naturae transfunderent in humanam: Nestorius verebatur, ne per Cyrillum, proprietates humanae imputarentur divinae naturae. De hoc similiter scripserat ad Coelestinum, Romanum Episcopum: Malus enim etiam nobis labor hic celebratur, dum elaboramus eruere sordidissimam impietatem pessimae opinionis Apollinarii, & Arii de Ecclesia Dei: nescio enim quemadmodum quidam de Ecclesiasticis quandam contemperationis imaginem ex Deitate & humanitate Unigeniti accipientes aegritudine praedictorum haereticorum, dum & corporis passiones audent superfundere Deitati Unigeniti, & immutabilitatem Deitatis ad naturam corporis transisse confingunt: & utramque naturam, quae per conjunctionem summam & inconfusam in una persona Unigeniti adoratur, contemperationis mutabilitate confundunt. Caeci, qui nec superiorum illorum Patrum expositionem meminerunt, aperte ad eos reclamantes: Credimus in unum Dominum Iesum Christum Filium Dei incarnatum ex Spiritu Sancto & Maria Virgine. Hoc enim vox in nomine quod significat utramque naturam, id est, Christus est Deitatis patris Homousios, humanitas vero posterioribus temporibus nata est ex sancta Virgine, quae propter conjunctionem Deitatis ab Angelis & hominibus simul colitur. Existimabat Nestorius, se zelare adversus Apollinaris haeresim, cui valde affine judicabat, quod aliqui docebant de contemperatione deitatis & humanitatis in Christo: forte etiam aliqui justo longius progressi fuerant, quemadmodum scimus Eutychem, Constantinopolitanae Ecclesiae diaconum, qui adversus haeresim Nestorii se egregie gesserat in Concilio Ephesino, postmodum in eandem confusionis naturarum in Christo vertiginem prolapsum, causam sui damnandi dedisse in sequenti generali Synodo Chalcedonensi. Et jam tum adeo gliscebat illa haeresis, ut Cyrillus ipse ad Iohannem Antiochenum scribere necesse habuerit: Tum vero sanctitas illorum ora comprimere dignetur, qui commixtionem, vel confusionem, vel commistionem Verbi Dei carne factam esse dicunt. Eis namque verisimile non defuturos, qui ista quoque de me invulgent, taliaque me sensisse, vel docuisse spargant. Hoc autem maxime impugnabat Nestorius, quod forte quis aut vellet, aut videretur confundere in Christo naturas, & passiones corporis Deitati attribueret, aut Dei immutabilitatem ullo pacto infringeret. Caeterum & duas in Christo naturas, & homoousion profitebatur, & illarum summam inconfusamque conjunctionem, adde quoque, quod in eo maxime notandum, in una persona. Unde verba illa quae pro concione dixit, quaeque omnium deinceps turbarum scaturigo habita fuerunt: Mariam Deiparam nemo vocato, homo enim fuit, ab homine autem Deus nasci non potest, in bonum sensum, quamvis & malum quoque, capi potuerunt. Non potest ab homine Deus nasci formaliter, sed materialiter is qui Deus, quidem. Admodum miror, non extare ipsius Nestorii alia, in quibus sententiam declaraverit eam, quae in ipso a Synodo damnata fuit, & non in ipsa Synodo, praeter Cyrilli anathematismos, habitas fuisse disputationes, ex quibus certius & liquidius de ejus doctrina constare potuerit: nam quae hic lecta fuerunt, Nestorii litterae, & Excerpta ex ejus libris, vel sor ne magis juvare Nestorianos, quam damnare videamur. Verum hoc nihil praejudicat doctrinae in Synodo stabilitae, ejusque in repudianda contraria, vel in Nestorio vere, vel saltem sub ejus nomine (nam istud fafactum concernit, non fidem) auctoritati, cui multum ponderis dedit Alexandrini, & Romani episcoporum, pro illa confirmanda, nomen & consensus. Magni nominis in Ecclesia fuit Nestorius, & fervidi contra haereticos zeli, unde dum de extero in sedem Constantinopolitanam sufficiendo, post obitum Sisinnii, & non ex clero Constantinopolitano, qualis Sisinnius, ante eum Atticus, & Atticus fuerant, agi retur, hic, uti antea Chrysostomus, Antiochia, propter eximiam suam famam, & dotes accersitus fuit, & in throno (ut loquebantur) collocatus.
units.tr: In the year 430, by the order of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, the general Council of Ephesus was held against Nestorius, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, who had been made from an Antiochene presbyter in the year 428. He had once said in a sermon to the people that he would not call God one who had grown up through the months of pregnancy, nor call Mary Theotokos [θεοτόκον]. Others were roused against him, above all Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and with him Memnon of Ephesus. They brought it about that Nestorius was marked as a heretic and deposed, first by the Roman synod under bishop Celestine, then by the Alexandrian synod under Cyril, and finally by the general Synod of Ephesus, and was driven into exile, Maximian being appointed in his place. In his time they were disputing whether Mary should be called theotokos [θεοτόκος] or anthropotokos [ἀνθρωποτόκος]. Nestorius, to avoid or settle this quarrel, said she should be called christotokos [χριστοτόκος]. He shrank from saying that God had been born of her. He did not deny that Christ was God, nor that there were two natures, nor their union in Christ. You will more easily see from the Acts of the Synod which of his words were sound and which were bad, or which could perhaps not be well explained. In Tom. II, Act. CVIII, some passages from the writings of Nestorius are quoted, for which he was branded as heterodox. Among them the first to appear is from his Dogmatic, quire seventeen. (For in those days books were not marked by the leaves, as today, but by quires, which were numbered, and not by their pages.) Hence in the Acts of the Sixth Council of Constantinople, Act. III, they found that a codex containing the sermon of Mennas, bishop of Constantinople, to Pope Vigilius, which had been produced at the Fifth Synod at Constantinople, had been falsified by the Monothelites. When they opened and examined it, they found three quires added at the beginning of the book, which did not have the number mark that is customarily attached to quires, but the fourth quire had the first number, the following quire the second and third, and the fourth in sequence. So too Nestorius: When divine Scripture is about to say anything of Christ's birth from the Virgin Mary, or of his death, it is found never to use the name of God, but always the name of Christ, or of Son, or of Lord. For these three names embrace the notion of the two natures. Now it signifies one nature, now the other, and sometimes both at once. For example, when Holy Scripture tells us of the generation of Christ from the holy Virgin, it does not say: "God sent his Word, God," but says: "God sent his Son." For it takes that name which is the symbol of both natures. For since the Son is at once God and man, the same text says: God sent his Son made of a woman. But when you add this, you turn the eyes of the mind to the name that denotes and embraces both natures; and when you call him, born of the Virgin Mary, by the name of Son (for indeed she bore Christ, the Son of God), yet because the Son of God exists in a twofold nature, you think that she bore not the Son of God but only the human nature, which, being joined to the Son, is also given the name of son. In saying at the beginning that Scripture nowhere uses the name of God when it speaks of Christ's death, he was wrong, because Acts 20:28 says that God acquired the Church with his own blood, and 1 Cor. 2:8 speaks of the Lord of glory crucified. But when we see him acknowledging in other places two natures in Jesus Christ, and that he is at once God and man, as he also does in what follows, he speaks throughout of both natures in Christ, the duality of natures. He seems to have wanted to avoid all this, lest it be said that the Son of God, or God, was begotten of a mother. Hence immediately in the following excerpt: I have been taught through the divine Scriptures that God proceeded from the Virgin who bore Christ; but I have found nowhere written that God himself was born of her. Again: Holy Scripture therefore nowhere affirms that God was begotten of the Virgin who bore Christ, but that Jesus Christ, or the Son, or the Lord, was. To this end he cites what the angel said to Joseph: "Arise and take the child and his mother," not "Arise and take God and his mother," but "Arise and take the child and his mother." From the same book, or quire: Nor do I hinder anyone who wishes to say that the Word was in the flesh, or was joined to the flesh. For it is one thing to be born, another to be joined to the one born. Thus what was born in her is of the Holy Spirit, that is, the Holy Spirit formed what is in her. Therefore, since the Fathers, most skilled in the divine Scriptures, noticed that if they said that the Word of God, whom they call incarnate, was begotten, that is, born, they would necessarily have to confess that the Word of God was the Son of the Holy Spirit, and consequently (following) that he had two fathers; but if they asserted that he was gennēton [γενητὸν], that is, made, it could be inferred again that the Word of God was a creature of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, rejecting the word "begotten," they wrote: "who came down for us and for our salvation, and was incarnate." But what, you ask, is this: "and was incarnate"? Anything rather than that he was turned from divinity into flesh. He says that the Word was in the flesh, and was united with the flesh and made flesh, not that he was made or begotten in the flesh or born through the flesh. He goes on: Certainly God the Word was both Son and God before the incarnation, and was joined to the Father. But in these last times he also took on the form of a servant. Yet although he was Son before, and was called Son, after assuming the flesh he ought not to be called Son apart by himself, lest we seem to introduce two Sons. So too the man who was once united to him, who is Son from the beginning and is now joined to the man by an indissoluble bond, as far as the dignity of sonship goes, admits no division. I mean the dignity of sonship, not the natures. Hence, since God the Word keeps a perpetual union with Christ, Christ is also called by his name. If you want us not to posit two Sons in Christ, though two natures, then this is well. Then: Let us therefore keep the unconfused conjunction of the natures, and confess God in the man, and let us adore together with God the man joined to God by a certain divine bond of mighty power. If Nestorius only meant that the deity of Christ, or his divine nature, or God himself, could not be said to be born or made in or from Mary, and that she was not called Theotokos in the sense that the birth or bearing was directed to God or the divine nature, as if that were begotten, then his words could be well explained, since these are his words: That which was formed in the womb is not God in himself and of himself; that which was made by the work of the Holy Spirit is not God in himself and of himself; that which was laid in the tomb is not God in himself and of himself. Otherwise we would be worshippers of men and of the dead, that is, of dead men. But because God exists in the assumed man, the assumed is joined to the assumer, and is called God on account of the assumer. So it is: God was not formally made or begotten in the womb, but assumed a human nature made in the womb. Unless he means that the man, not the nature, was assumed; hence he often says "man" here. And that the divine Word had clung to him, or dwelt in him, in a peculiar manner, as he puts it, and was not united in person with the human nature, which is very obscurely hinted at in his words, if it is hinted at at all. For the question is one of fact, not whether the heresy which denies those things in Christ and teaches what the Fathers rejected in Nestorius was rightly rejected and condemned, but whether Nestorius really taught it in this way. I am surprised that clearer proofs were not produced from his writings against him, so that anathema was pronounced at once, without further discussion, and sentence was passed in this form on 21 June, when the Synod had only just begun the day before: Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he assailed with his blasphemous words, through this holy Synod decrees that this same Nestorius, stripped of all episcopal dignity, is also to be separated from the whole fellowship of priests and from all others. More than two hundred bishops approved this, and the next day it was announced to Nestorius himself in this way: The holy Synod, gathered in the metropolis of the Ephesians by the grace of God, in accordance with the prescription of the most religious and most Christian emperors, to Nestorius the new Judas: Know that, on account of your impious convictions, your stubborn disobedience against the holy canons, and your obstinacy, you have been removed by the holy Synod, on the authority of the decrees of ecclesiastical sanctions, from every grade of ecclesiastical dignity, on the twenty-second day of the current month of June. Cyril of Alexandria's consensus had very great authority and favour in this Synod, and the rest followed it devoutly. The twelve anathemas against Nestorius, on which the opinion of the Fathers chiefly rested and was founded, make clearer what was opposed to Nestorius. From the first: If anyone does not confess that Emmanuel is true God, and therefore that the holy Virgin, who bore according to the flesh the Word of God the Father made flesh, is the Mother of God, let him be anathema. Third: If anyone, after the union of the natures, divides the subsistences in the one Christ, assigning to each its own, and joins them only by a connection which is according to dignity or authority, and not by that coming together which is according to physical union, let him be anathema. Fifth: If anyone dares to say that Christ is only a man bearing God, not also true God, and the one natural Son of God, in that the Word of God, made flesh, shared in flesh and blood just as we do, let him be anathema. From these you may gather that Nestorius held that there were two persons in Christ, that Christ was a man bearing God, and that for this reason Mary was not Theotokos [Θεοτόκον]. The Cyrillian side. Nestorius opposed twelve other anathemas, in which he does not set out or defend his own opinion, but attacks what he thought was the opinion of Cyril and his adherents, concerning the generation or change of the Son of God in Mary, and the confusion of both natures in him, and hence the suffering of the divine or deity in him, etc. Anathema iii: If anyone does not confess that Christ, who is also Emmanuel according to the nature, is one according to the conjunction, from both substances, both of the divine Word and of the man assumed by him, in the one connection of the Son, which we also now keep unconfused, let him be anathema.
