Anathema vi: If anyone says that the man who was created in the Virgin is the Only-begotten, who was born from the womb of the Father before the morning star, and does not rather confess that he who is naturally the Only-begotten was made a sharer, by reason of the union, in the title of the unbegotten Father, and says that Jesus is another beside Emmanuel, let him be anathema. And vii: If anyone says that the form of a servant is to be regarded as his own, that is, according to the reason of his own nature, and does not worship it as the Lady of all, and as joined by a companionship rather than by a blessed union to the natural nature of the Only-begotten Lord, let him be anathema. It appears that Nestorius was chiefly concerned, in confessing two natures united in Christ, to keep the divine nature free from all change and confusion, and to keep the distinct properties of each, if not also divided in person, and for this reason not to say that the Son or God was begotten of Mary, and so not to call her Theotokos. Hence in his letter to Cyril, before the Synod was held, he addresses him thus about the opinion of the Nicene Fathers: Look carefully, if you will, into their words, and you will plainly find with a clear mind that that divine band of Fathers never decided that the consubstantial Deity is passible, or that the one coeval with the Father was recently born, or that the one who raised the temple when it was destroyed was raised. He was persuaded that Cyril either held such things or at least followed from his opinion, though rashly. He adds: So that the same Christ may be conceived as passible and impassible at once, without danger to the faith: the former according to the human nature, the latter according to the divine. And going on: In this I rightly praise you, that you affirm the distinction of the natures according to the reason of divinity and humanity, and their conjunction in the one person; and that you plainly declare that the Word of God did not at all need that other birth, which is of the woman, and that the Deity could not at last suffer. He says the natures are distinct, and also in the one person. If these really are his opinions, and were not put forward with deceit and evil intent, it may indeed be said that the doctrine condemned by the Synod was false and heretical; but whether it was Nestorius's own doctrine is doubtful. Nestorius thought that the Cyrillians, in calling Mary Theotokos, held that the divine nature of Christ was from Mary, or was begotten in her, and therefore subject also to change and suffering. Hence in the same letter he declares: Wherever, then, the divine Scriptures make mention of the Lord's dispensation, they always attribute both the incarnation and the death and passion itself not to the divine but to the human nature of Christ. Therefore, if we consider the matter more carefully, the holy Virgin should be called not Deipara but Christipara. Hear how the Evangelists proclaim this: "The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham." Yet it is plain that God the Word was not a son of David. Take, if you please, another testimony here: "Jacob (he says) begat Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." Consider again another voice of the Gospel, clearly confirming this truth: "The generation of Christ was thus: when his mother Mary had been betrothed to Joseph, she was found to have in her womb of the Holy Spirit." But who is so foolish as to believe that the divinity of the Only-begotten is a creature of the Holy Spirit? Add to these also: "Mary the mother of Jesus was there"; again: "with Mary the mother of Jesus"; and: "What was born in her is of the Holy Spirit"; and: "Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt"; and: "Concerning his Son, who was made of the seed of David according to the flesh"; and again concerning the same passion: "God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh"; and again: "Christ died for our sins"; and again: "Christ suffering in the flesh." Finally: (that is,) "not my divinity, but (my body, which is broken for you)." There are countless other sayings which show to the human race that the divinity was neither newly born nor capable of bodily suffering, but the flesh itself, which is joined to the divine nature. He adds: It is right, therefore, and consonant with the gospel tradition, that we confess the body of Christ to be the temple of the divinity, and that we hold it to be joined to him by a bond so lofty, divine and wonderful, that the divine nature claims for itself those things which are properties of the body. But on account of that notion of communication or appropriation, to ascribe to the Divine Word the nativity, the passion, the death and the other properties of things is, as I think, the act of a madman, of a mind wandering in the manner of the pagans, or certainly of one suffering from the error of Apollinaris and Arius and other heretics, and even worse. For those who thus twist the term "appropriated" must confess that those who say that the Word of God shared in joy and was capable of gradual growth, and who was shown at the time of fear to be in need of the help of angels, were in existence. Since others transferred the properties of the divine nature to the human, Nestorius feared lest, through Cyril, the human properties would be imputed to the divine nature. He had written similarly about this to Celestine, bishop of Rome: For this is also a troublesome labour for us, while we toil to uproot the most filthy impiety of the wicked opinion of Apollinaris and Arius concerning the Church of God. For I do not know how some of the churchmen, taking from the Deity and humanity of the Only-begotten an image of a certain blending, by the sickness of the aforesaid heretics dare to pour the sufferings of the body upon the Deity of the Only-begotten, and feign that the immutability of the Deity has passed into the nature of the body, and so confound both natures, which are worshipped in the one person of the Only-begotten through the highest and unconfused union, by the mutability of a blending. Blind men, who neither remember the exposition of those earlier Fathers, cry out clearly against them: We believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary. For this word "in the name" signifies both natures, that is, Christ is consubstantial with the Deity of the Father, and the humanity was born in later times of the holy Virgin, who, on account of the union with the Deity, is worshipped together by angels and men. Nestorius thought that he was zealous against the heresy of Apollinaris, to which he judged that certain teachings about a blending of deity and humanity in Christ were closely akin; perhaps some had gone rather too far, as we know Eutyches, deacon of the Church of Constantinople, did. He had acted nobly against the heresy of Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus, but afterwards, falling into the same whirl of confusion of natures in Christ, he gave cause for his own condemnation at the later general Synod of Chalcedon. And already that heresy was so rampant that Cyril himself was obliged to write to John of Antioch: May the holiness of those who say that the Word of God was made by mixture, or confusion, or commixture with the flesh, be pleased to restrain their mouths. For it is likely that there will not be lacking those who spread these things about me too, and who spread the report that I held or taught such things. But Nestorius especially opposed this: that someone might wish, or seem, to confound the natures in Christ, and attribute the sufferings of the body to the Deity, or in any way break the immutability of God. Otherwise he professed both two natures in Christ and the consubstantial, and their highest and unconfused union, which, add also, is especially to be noted in him, is in one person. Hence those words which he spoke in a sermon, and which were afterwards regarded as the fountain of all the disturbances: Let no one call Mary Deipara; for she was a man, and God cannot be born of a man, could be taken in a good sense, though also in a bad one. God cannot be formally born of a man, but he who is God is materially so. I am very surprised that there are no other writings of Nestorius himself in which he declared the opinion which was condemned in him by the Synod, nor that, apart from the anathemas of Cyril, disputations were not held in the Synod itself, from which the doctrine of Nestorius could have been established more certainly and clearly. For the things read here, the letters of Nestorius and excerpts from his books, seem rather to help the Nestorians than to condemn them. Yet this does not prejudice the doctrine established in the Synod, nor its rejection of the contrary, whether it was truly in Nestorius, or at least under his name (for that concerns a matter of fact, not of faith). The authority of the bishops of Alexandria and Rome, which gave much weight to the confirmation of that doctrine, lent its name and consent to it. Nestorius was a man of great name in the Church, and of fervent zeal against heretics. Hence, when the election of a successor to the see of Constantinople was discussed, after the death of Sisinnius, and not from the clergy of Constantinople, as Sisinnius had been, and before him Atticus and Atticus had been, he was summoned from Antioch, as Chrysostom had been before, on account of his remarkable fame and gifts, and was placed on the throne, as they said.

units.la: In prima sua concione Imperatorem hunc in modum affatus dicitur: da mihi, o Imperator, terram ab haereticis liberam & purum, & ego tibi caelum reddam. Tu mihi haereticos extirpa, & ego tibi Persis delendis adero. Etiam postquam depositus fuit, inque Monasterium S. Euprepii, in quo primum egerat, non longe distans Antiochia, retrusus, variis interim honoribus, muneribusque a Theodosio auctum, scribit Euagrius. Damnato illo, non ideo pacata statim omnia erant.
units.tr: In his first sermon, he is reported to have addressed the emperor in these words: Give me, O Emperor, a land free and pure from heretics, and I will give you heaven. You root out the heretics for me, and I will be at your side in destroying the Persians. Evagrius writes that even after he was deposed and confined to the monastery of St Euprepius, where he had first lived, not far from Antioch, Theodosius kept heaping various honours and gifts upon him. Once he had been condemned, however, not everything was immediately quiet.

units.la: Iohannes Antiochenus episcopus, tum quod cum Nestorio sentiret, tum quod se absente damnatio eius contigerat, ubi Ephesum venit, omnia adversus Cyrillum, & Concilium commovere & incitare; tum suos quos adduxerat Clericos, tum alios, & Imperatores ipsos, coepit. Vsque dum Imperator videns illas inter Cyrillum Alexandrinorum, & Iohannem Antiochenorum episcopum contentiones turbare pacem Ecclesiae, & non parum quoque Imperii, utramque solum Nicomediam, ad ineundam pacem, evocavit: quod Iohannes declinandum, & antevertendum ratus, misso ad Cyrillum, suo, suorumque nomine, Paulo Emileno, pacem cum eo iniit, & tum damnationi Nestorii, tum electioni Maximiniani, in illius locum, consensit. Unde non pauci in Orientali dioecesi, cui Antiochenus praesit, & tunc, & deinceps Nestorianorum partium sectatores extitere. Adversus Nestorium hoc pacto dum disputatum, alii ex adverso, ne duas in Christo personas dicerent, duas in eo naturas negabant, quorum dux fuit in Ecclesia item Constantinopolitana, quique adversus Nestorium valide se gesserat, Eutyches, presbyter monachus, abbas, archimandrita apud Graecos appellatur, Papa dicitur quoque in Actis Concilii Chalcedonensis. Hic ante unionem duas quidem naturas posuit, sed post unionem, non amplius duas in Christo, sed unam, unde & nobis in humana natura consubstantialem negavit. Quemadmodum haec duo doctrinae ejus, & haeresis capita distincte annotat Flavianus episc. Constantinopolitanus, in epist. ad Leonem, epist. Romanum, cui scribit suo Consacerdoti. Indeque in Concilio PseudoEphesino 11. Barsumas, & omnes Aegyptii, quorum caput erat Dioscorus Alexandrinus, clamabant: qui dicit duas naturas, Nestorianus est. contra Orientales episcopi: anathema Nestorio, & Eutychi. Quodque Theodosius junior adductus fuit, ut Concilium Ephesinum, & quae in eo contra Flavianum, & Eusebium gesta, probaret, hoc solo motus fecit, quod persuasum sibi esset, illos Nestorianam haeresim iterum moliri, & quod eandem revocare tragoediam conarentur. Quod quoque Leo putavit, episcopus Romanus, in suis ad Eutychem litteris, inter epistolas ejus VI. Quod utcunque falsum, ex illo tamen occasionem captasse Eutychianos, certum. Sententiam eorum ita expositi in Concilio Chalcedonensi Dioscorus, art. 1. non oportet dicere post adorationem duas naturas, sed unam naturam Dei verbi incarnatam. Ipseque Eutyches, in Constantinopolitana Synodo act. VII. quae in Ephesina lecta, & in Chalcedonensi art. 1. relecta fuere: usque ad hodiernum diem non dixi corpus Domini & Dei nostri consubstantiale nobis. Sanctam autem virginem confiteor nobis esse consubstantialem. Deinde: Confiteor ex duabus naturis fuisse Dominum nostrum ante adunationem, post vero adunatadunationem, unam naturam confiteor. Quomodo ante adunationem, potest constare duabus naturis, & non in adunatione, atque post eam? Inde in Constantinopolitano concilio, cui Flavianus Constantinopolitanus episcopus praefuit, a. cccc xlviii. d. xxiii. Novemb. damnatus fuit Eutyches, in hanc formam: Lachrymantes & lugentes perfectam eius perditionem, decrevimus per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum ab eo blasphematum, execrandum eum esse ab omni officio sacerdotali, & a nostra communione & primatu monasterii. Scientibus hoc omnibus qui postea colloquentur ei & ad eum convenerint, quae res erunt & ipsi paene excommunicationis, sicut non recedentes ab eius collocutione. At in Ephesino postea restitutus, & depositus Flavianus: cui subscripserunt Dioscorus episc. Alexandrinus; Iuvenalis, episcopus Ierosolymitanus; Domnus, episcopus Antiochenus; Stephanus, Ephesi episcopus; Thalassius, episcopus Caesareae Cappadociae, & plurimi alii. Propter quae habitum iterum Chalcedonense Concilium, à Martiano Imp. indictum, primo Niceae Bithyniae, non in Italia, uti petierat Leo Romanus episcopus, (tantum abest, quod Severinus Binius, in notis ad hoc Concilium dicit, ut vel authoritate Leonis indictum à Martiano fuisset, vel rogatus ille, ut locum, tempus, modum celebrandi Concilii praescriberet,) inde etiam paulo post translatum Chalcedonem, ejusdem provinciae civitatem, ad vii. Id. Octob. a. cccc li. Cui interfuere Anatolius: Constantinopolitanus (Flavianus iam obierat); Dioscorus, Alexandrinus; Maximus, Antiochenus; Iuvenalis, Ierosolymitanus; Quintillus, Heracleensis episcopus, aliique numero sexcenti triginta, (de quo numero confer Baronium) damnaruntque Octobris die xiii. Dioscorum, Ecclesiae Alexandrinae Episcopum, eo quod Eutychem, adversus Flavianum, restituisset, & magna crudelitate pro opinione Eutychis aestuans, tum Flavianum, tum alios quosque verversum indigne fuisset perfequutus. Definitio verò Synodi post confirmata decreta Concilii Niceni, Constantinopolitani, & Ephesini, duas in unâ Christi persona naturas asseruit: Christum Iesum filium, Dominum unigenitum, quem in duabus naturis inconfusè & incommutabiliter, indivisè, atque inseparabiliter omnes agnoscimus, nunquam sublata differentia naturarum propter unitionem, sed potius utriusque naturæ proprietate servata, & in unam concurrente personam, non in duas dedu&um divisumve personas, sed unum & eundem filium unigenitum, Deum verbum, Dominum Iesum Christum, confessi. Atque ita in Chalcedonensi Concilio damnatus Eutychianismus: qui varias in Ecclesiis Græcis, non tum solùm temporis, sed deinceps dedit contentiones. Nam & Eutychiani hodie in Orientis Ecclesiis varii sunt: quare in hoc articulo aliam cum Græcis controversiam notare nos oportet. Cæterum in Chalcedonensi repetitus etiam, confirmatusque canon est de privilegiis Ecclesiæ Constantinopolitanæ, novæ Romæ. Quod valde pupugit Romanæ Ecclesiæ præsentes Legatos, qui postridie de eo coram totâ Synodo conquesti, quasi ipsis absentibus constitutus fuisset, & vi ab aliis extortus. Respondit primùm Aëtius, archidiaconus Constantinopolitanus, hoc pro more fieri, ut absolutis illis, quæ ad fidem spectant, alia quædam necessaria Ecclesias concernentia pertractentur. Ad hæc etiam rogatos Romanos fuisse, ut manere vellent, & adessent tractandis, sed ipsos recusasse. Postea &c omnes acclamarunt, non se coactos fuisse ad subscribendum, & singuli de novo idem contestati fuerunt, se sponte & voluntarie subscripsisse. Nihilque morati Patres indignationem & minas Romanensium, perstiterunt in confirmatione canonis Constantinopolitanæ Synodi, de pari dignitate Constantinopolitanæ Ecclesiæ, post Romanam. Et studio videntur exspectasse finem Synodi, ne hæc res rebus fidei gravioribus, &cconconsensui Ecclesiarum in rejiciendo Eutychis ac Dioscori dogmate remoram injiceret. Interim nec oblivisci istius canonis Constantinopolitani debuerunt, dum Act. xv, capite primo constituerant, servandos praecedentium Synodorum canones: Regulas sanctorum Patrum per singula nunc usque concilia constitutas, primum robur obtinere decrevimus, atque canonem illum de praerogativa Constantin. episcopi, adversus falsas & usurpationes Romanas diligenter semper observandum viderunt. Tandem auditis, & Nicaenae, & Constantinopolitanae Synodi canonibus, Patrumque iteratis suffragiis, judices dixerunt: eamdem quidem primatus et honorem praecipuum, secundum canones, antiquae Romae Deo amantissimo Archiepiscopo conservari. Oportere autem sanctissimum archiepiscopum regiae Constantinopolis urbis Romae, eisdem primatibus honoris et ipsum dignum esse. Primatus utrique attributitur; & Romano, qui hic simpliciter archiepiscopus dicitur, & Constantinopolitano, in suis videlicet aeque exercendus, tantum ut secundo loco nominaretur Constantinopolitanus, pari de caetero gaudens potestate & jure, uti nulla in re inferior veteri nova Roma haberi volebat, ex quo urbis intuitu oriebatur dignitas illa, vel contentio saecularis de mutua dignitate. Et utcunque oggrunnirent Legati Romani, se ad Papam relaturos, ut ipse aut de sua sede injuria, aut de canonum eversione possit ferre sententiam: nihil commoti Patres perrexerunt tamen, & Romanorum archiepiscopo Leoni (neque aliter loquuntur) scribunt in Synodali, de gestis suis, epistola, se confirmasse etiam canonem Concilii Constantinopolitani de hujus episcopi honore, cui Legati ejus vehementer fuisset reluctati. Unde scævo semper obtutu illum Rom. Pontif. respexerunt canonem, & improbarunt, neque ideo in Codice canonum Ecclesiae Romanae, ubi tamen Veterum Synodorum, & Chalcedonenses quoque canones, comparet. Liberatus, Diaconus Carthaginensis ginensis, in Breviario causæ Nestorianæ & Eutychianæ. cap. xiii. de hisce concilii Chalcedonensis Actis & licet sedes Apostolica nunc usque contradicat, quod à Synodo firmatum est, Imperatoris patrocinio permanet quodammodo. Adeo hoc à primis inde temporibus magnum inter has illasque Ecclesias extitit contentionis argumentum. Tantæ autem venerationis in Ecclesiis Orientalibus Chalcedonensis illa Synodus, ut anniversariam ejus colant memoriam, ad d. xvi. Iulii. Unde & in Synodo Constantinopolitanâ contra Antimum, a. Io. xviii. quando Chalcedonensis Concilii nomen è sacris tabulis expunctum, & Orthodoxorum Patrum deleta nomina; in eadem sacra Diptycha, exposcente populo, revocata fuerunt, & per Samuelem diaconum celebritas Chalcedonensis Synodi in diem crastinum habenda, hoc pacto proclamata: Notificamus vestra charitati, quod crastinâ die persiciemus memoriam sanctorum Patrum nostrorum Episcoporum in Chalcedonensi metropoli congregatorum, qui una cum sanctis Patribus Constantinopoli & in Epheso congregati confirmaverint Symbolum trecentorum decem & octo Patrum in Nicæa congregatorum. Atque hoc dictum de quatuor concilijs, primarijs, aut generalibus, ita appellari solitis, vel quod delegati ex Ecclesiis Imperii Orientis, Occidentisque ea constituerunt, vel quod in illis de primarijs & generalibus fidei articulis tractatum definitumque fuit. Ineptum & ridiculum est, appellationis illius vim petere ex Pontificis Romani accedente approbatione vel auctoritate; quæ nec necessaria, nec exspectata, neque postulata, aut sequuta in multis fuit. Sed operæ pretium est observare, quo ordine tum Diabolus per suas varias hæreses præcipua fidei fundamenta labefactare conatus sit, tum Deus eadem adversus frustraneos ejus conatus in Synodis maximè illustribus confirmari studio & zelo piissimorum Doctorum voluerit. Quum nihil prius habeat Christiana religio quam fidem in Deum
units.tr: John, bishop of Antioch, because he agreed with Nestorius and because the condemnation had taken place in his absence, came to Ephesus and began to stir up and incite everything against Cyril and the Council. He did this with the clergy he had brought with him, with others, and even with the emperors themselves. Finally the emperor, seeing that these disputes between Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and John, bishop of Antioch, were disturbing the peace of the Church and no small part of the empire, summoned both of them to Nicomedia alone, to make peace. John, thinking it best to avoid this and to get ahead of it, sent Paulus Aemilianus to Cyril in his own name and that of his followers, made peace with him, and consented both to the condemnation of Nestorius and to the election of Maximian in his place. As a result, not a few in the Eastern diocese, over which the Antiochene bishop presides, became followers of the Nestorian party, both then and afterwards. While the dispute against Nestorius was carried on in this way, others on the opposite side, lest they should speak of two persons in Christ, denied that there were two natures in him. The leader of these in the Church of Constantinople, who had acted vigorously against Nestorius, was Eutyches, a presbyter and monk. Among the Greeks he is called abbot and archimandrite, and in the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon he is also called Pope. Before the union, he did indeed posit two natures, but after the union he no longer held two natures in Christ, only one; hence he also denied that Christ was consubstantial with us in his human nature. Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, in his letter to Leo, the Roman bishop, whom he addresses as his fellow priest, carefully notes these two points of Eutyches' teaching and heresy. Hence at the pseudo-Council of Ephesus, in the eleventh session, Barsumas and all the Egyptians, whose head was Dioscorus of Alexandria, shouted: Whoever says two natures is a Nestorian. The Eastern bishops replied: Anathema to Nestorius and to Eutyches. Theodosius the Younger was induced to approve the Council of Ephesus, and the acts done there against Flavian and Eusebius, and he was moved to do so by this alone: he was persuaded that these men were again plotting the Nestorian heresy and trying to bring back the same tragedy. Leo, the Roman bishop, also thought this, in his letters to Eutyches, among his epistles, number 6. Whatever the truth of that, it is certain that the Eutychians seized on this as an occasion. Dioscorus, in the first session of the Council of Chalcedon, set out their opinion in this way: It is not right to say, after the union, two natures, but one incarnate nature of the Word of God. Eutyches himself, in the seventh session of the Synod of Constantinople, which was read in the Council of Ephesus and read again in the first session of Chalcedon, said: Up to the present day I have not said that the body of our Lord and God is consubstantial with us. But I confess that the holy Virgin is consubstantial with us. Then: I confess that our Lord was of two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature. How can before the union be consistent with two natures, and not with the union and what follows it? Then in the Council of Constantinople, presided over by Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, in the year 448, on 23 November, Eutyches was condemned in this form: Weeping and mourning over his complete ruin, we have decided, through our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he has blasphemed, that he is to be cast out from every priestly office, from our communion, and from the primacy of the monastery. Let all who afterwards talk with him or meet him know that they will themselves be in danger of excommunication if they do not withdraw from conversation with him. But afterwards, at Ephesus, Flavian was restored and then deposed. The following signed the deposition: Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria; Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem; Domnus, bishop of Antioch; Stephen, bishop of Ephesus; Thalassius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; and many others. Because of these matters, the Council of Chalcedon was convened again, indicted by the emperor Marcian. It first met at Nicaea in Bithynia, not in Italy as Leo, the Roman bishop, had asked. (Severinus Binius, in his notes on this Council, is so far from saying that it was convened by Marcian on the authority of Leo, or that Leo had asked him to prescribe the place, time, and manner of holding the Council, that the contrary is true.) Soon afterwards it was moved to Chalcedon, a city of the same province, and met on 9 October 451. Those present included Anatolius of Constantinople (Flavian had already died), Dioscorus of Alexandria, Maximus of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Quintillus, bishop of Heraclea, and others, six hundred and thirty in number (on this number compare Baronius). On 13 October they condemned Dioscorus, bishop of the Church of Alexandria, because he had restored Eutyches against Flavian, and because, burning with great cruelty in defence of Eutyches' opinion, he had persecuted Flavian and many others most unworthily. The definition of the Synod, after confirming the decrees of the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, and Ephesus, asserted two natures in one person of Christ. It confessed: Christ Jesus, the Son, the only-begotten Lord, whom we all acknowledge in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation, the difference of natures never being taken away because of the union, but rather the properties of each nature being preserved and concurring into one person; not divided or split into two persons, but one and the same Son, only-begotten, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ. In this way Eutychianism was condemned at Chalcedon, and it caused various disputes in the Greek Churches, not only at that time but afterwards. For Eutychians are even today to be found in various Eastern Churches; therefore we must note here a different controversy with the Greeks. Moreover, at Chalcedon the canon concerning the privileges of the Church of Constantinople, the new Rome, was also repeated and confirmed. This greatly annoyed the Roman legates present, who the next day complained about it before the whole Synod, saying that it had been set up in their absence and forced through by others. First Aëtius, archdeacon of Constantinople, replied that this was the custom: after those matters which concern the faith were settled, certain other matters necessary for the Churches were dealt with. He added that the Romans had been asked to stay and attend to these matters, but that they had refused. Afterwards all the bishops cried out that they had not been forced to sign, and each one again declared that he had signed freely and willingly. Undisturbed by the indignation and threats of the Romans, the Fathers persisted in confirming the canon of the Synod of Constantinople concerning the equal dignity of the Church of Constantinople after the Roman. They seem to have deliberately waited for the end of the Synod, so that this matter, less weighty than the matters of faith, might not hinder the agreement of the Churches in rejecting the doctrine of Eutyches and Dioscorus. Nor should they have forgotten that canon of Constantinople, since in the fifteenth act, in its first chapter, they had decided that the canons of the earlier Synods should be observed: We have decided that the rules established by the holy Fathers in each council up to now should first have force, and we have resolved always to observe carefully that canon concerning the prerogative of the bishop of Constantinople against the false claims and usurpations of Rome. Finally, after the canons of the Synods of Nicaea and Constantinople had been heard, and after the votes of the Fathers had been repeated, the judges declared: The same primacy and pre-eminent honour, according to the canons, shall be preserved to the most beloved of God, the archbishop of Old Rome. And the most holy archbishop of Constantinople, the royal city, shall also be worthy of the same primacy of honour as Rome. Primacy is attributed to both. The Roman bishop, who here is simply called archbishop, and the bishop of Constantinople were to exercise it equally in their own sees, except that Constantinople was named in the second place. In other respects Constantinople was to enjoy equal power and right, since it did not want to be regarded as inferior to old Rome in anything. From the fact that it was a city came that dignity, or the secular rivalry about mutual dignity. Although the Roman legates grumbled that they would report to the Pope, so that he himself might pass sentence either on the injury done to his see or on the overthrow of the canons, the Fathers, unmoved, went on regardless. In their synodal letter about their proceedings, they write to Leo, archbishop of Rome (they speak in no other way), that they had also confirmed the canon of the Council of Constantinople concerning the honour of this bishop, against which his legates had strongly objected. Hence the Roman Pontiff has always looked upon that canon with disfavour and rejected it, and for this reason it does not appear in the Code of canons of the Roman Church, where, however, the canons of the older Synods and also those of Chalcedon are found. Liberatus, deacon of Carthage, in his Breviarium of the Nestorian and Eutychian case, chapter 13, says about these acts of the Council of Chalcedon: Although the Apostolic See has until now contradicted what was confirmed by the Synod, it remains in some way in force through the emperor's protection. So from the earliest times this has been a great subject of contention between these Churches and those. The Council of Chalcedon is so highly revered in the Eastern Churches that they keep its anniversary on 16 July. Hence also, at the Synod of Constantinople against Antimus, in the year 518, when the name of the Council of Chalcedon had been struck from the sacred tablets and the names of the orthodox Fathers had been erased, at the people's demand the same sacred diptychs were restored, and through Samuel the deacon the celebration of the Synod of Chalcedon was proclaimed for the following day in this way: We notify your charity that tomorrow we shall celebrate the memory of our holy Fathers, the bishops gathered in the metropolis of Chalcedon, who, together with the holy Fathers gathered at Constantinople and at Ephesus, confirmed the creed of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers gathered at Nicaea. This is said of the four councils, called primary or general, as they are customarily named, either because delegates from the Churches of the Eastern and Western Empires constituted them, or because matters concerning the primary and general articles of faith were treated and defined in them. It is foolish and ridiculous to seek the force of that title from the approval or authority of the Roman Pontiff, which was neither necessary, nor expected, nor requested, and in many cases did not follow. But it is worth observing in what order the Devil, through his various heresies, tried to shake the chief foundations of the faith, and how God, in the most illustrious Synods, willed that these same foundations be confirmed against his futile attempts, through the zeal and devotion of the most pious teachers. Since the Christian religion has nothing more important than faith in God, and in Christ, and here the Devil has tried to overthrow nothing beyond the doctrine of the Trinity and of the wonderful incarnation of Christ, he first attacked the deity of Christ, and then that of the Holy Spirit. Therefore that truth was affirmed at the first Council of Nicaea against Arius, and this one at Constantinople against…

units.la: Quum ni-hil prius habeat... Deum, & in Christum, & hic nihil supra doctrinam Trinitatis, atque admirandæ Christi incarnationis, convellere ibi studuit Diabolus Christi Deitatem primùm, tum Spiritus sancti: quare illa veritas in primo Nicæno, adversus Arium; hæc in Constantinopolitano, adversus Macedonium confirmata fuit. Deinde assertâ Christi, ut & Spiritus Sancti Deitate verâ, reliquum Diabolo videbatur, ut quum duas in Christo naturas admittere cogeretur, illarum unionem impugnaret: quare hanc adorsus, jam divellere eam, jam ex adverso confundere molitus fuit. Unde Ecclesia iterum sic unionem naturarum explicare debuit, ut non duas personas poneret, quod factum adversus Nestorium, in Ephesinâ; atque ita unam personam, ne tamen duas naturas negaret, adversus Eutychem, in Synodo Chalcedonensi. Quæ quatuor Concilia, neutiquam tamen, quod P. Gregorius fecit, & post eum alii, quatuor Evangeliis æquiparanda, quamvis quidem illorum doctrina ab Evangelicâ non discrepet, fere intra sæculum habita. Primum Nicænum, a. ccc xxv. alterum Constantinopolitanum, a. ccc lxxx i. tertium Ephesinum, a. cccc xxx i. ultimum Chalcedonense, a. cccc i. Atque ex illis, ut ad singula observavimus, petenda fundamenta dissensionum inter Ecclesias Orientales, & Occidentales, vel adversus Romanam, super causa primatus Episcopalis; vel in negotio fidei, quod Orientales ab eâ transversos egit, inque errores multifarios & diuturnos, quique hodie illos occupant, Nestorianismi, & Eutychianismi, quorum permulti apud eos etiamnum sectatores, quod in sequentibus videbitur.
units.tr: Since the Christian religion holds nothing more important than faith in God, and in Christ, the Devil has here tried to overthrow nothing above the doctrine of the Trinity and of Christ's wonderful incarnation. He first attacked the deity of Christ and then that of the Holy Spirit, so that the first truth was confirmed at Nicaea against Arius, and the second at Constantinople against Macedonius. Once the true deity of Christ and of the Holy Spirit had been asserted, the Devil seems to have been left with the task of attacking the union of the two natures in Christ, since he was forced to admit two natures. He therefore went after this union, sometimes trying to tear it apart and sometimes to confound it. Hence the Church had to explain the union of the natures again, so that it neither posited two persons, which was done against Nestorius at Ephesus, nor, while avoiding two persons, denied the two natures, which was done against Eutyches at the Council of Chalcedon. These four councils were, however, by no means regarded as to be placed on a level with the four Gospels, as Pope Gregory did and others after him, although their teaching does not differ from the Gospel. They were held within about a century: the first, Nicaea, in 325; the second, Constantinople, in 381; the third, Ephesus, in 431; and the last, Chalcedon, in 451. From these councils, as we have noted for each one, must be sought the grounds of the disputes between the Eastern and Western Churches, or with the Roman Church, over the primacy of the bishop; and in matters of faith, in which the Easterners have deviated from the Church and fallen into many and long-lasting errors, which still hold them today, namely Nestorianism and Eutychianism. Many of their followers still adhere to these, as will be seen below.

units.la: Sed quia adhuc dum in eruendis controversiis, quas Orientales cum aliis Ecclesiis habent, earumque fundamento & origine indaganda versantur, insequendus per historias, præsertim per Concilia, fluxus temporis est, ut quid, quando enatum; vel agitatum dissidium, tencateneamus. Non enim damnatis licet hæresium Auctoribus, interquieverunt illæ, sed alios & alios porro patronos & defensores in Orientis Ecclesiis nactæ fuerunt. Adversus Synodum Chalcedonensem, pro Eutyche, ejusque opinione, jam manifeste, tum clam & indutis aliis atque aliis formis, multi varia deinceps moliti fuerunt. De quibus vide Breviarium Liberati, à cap. xv. deinceps. Atque ita alii Nestorianarum partium, alii Eutychianarum, potissimam Orientalium Ecclesiarum partem duæ illæ hæreses supra modum semper infestarunt. Monachi Armeniæ Nestorianam sectantur hæresim, sub nominibus & scriptis Diodori Tarsensis, Theodori Mopsvesteni episcopi, & Ibæ: quæ condemnata fuerunt in Concilio Constantinopolitano generali. v. a. Ioliii. super tribus, uti dicebatur, capitulis coacto, nempe super condemnatione Theodori Mopsvesteni, & epistolæ Ibæ Edesseni, atque scriptorum Theodoreti Cyrensis, adversus Cyrillum. Sed Eutychianismus plures sui ramos hic ibi dissudit, sub aliis, & aliis nominibus. Hujus enim opinionis fuerunt Dioscorus Alexandrinus, cum Eutyche in Concilio Chalcedonensi damnatus. Post hunc Petrus Moggus, quartus ab eo Alexandrinus quoque episcopus. Petrus Antiochenus, cognomento Gnapheus, sive Fullo, qui post trisagium, quod cantabatur in Ecclesia, de suo addebat crucifixus propter nos, damnatus in Synodo primum Romana, sub Felice III. a. cccc lxxxiii. tum Constantinopolitana, sub Acacio, sedis ejus episcopo, multisque variorum scriptis, & anathematismis, præsertim Quintiani episcopi duodecim, ad exemplum xii. anathematismorum Cyrilli, contra Nestorium, suppressus. Quin in Synodo Sidoniæ Palestinæ a. Ioxii. ferme octoginta episcopi Eutychianarum partium, Chalcedonensem Synodum anathematis & Flavianum Antiochenum episcopum, præter alios orthodoxos, exilio multare conati fuerunt. Cum quibus quantum isto tempore negotium orthodoxis fecit, atque Hormisdae Papae inter caeteros, ex hujus epistolis liquet.
units.tr: But since, in the course of looking into the controversies which the Eastern Churches have with the others, and in searching out their foundation and origin, we must follow the sequence of time through the histories, especially the councils, let us keep hold of what arose and when, and what dissension was stirred up. For the heresies were not put to rest by the condemnation of their authors; instead they found other and still other patrons and defenders in the Churches of the East. After the Council of Chalcedon, many men, first openly and then secretly and under various other guises, pursued various schemes in favour of Eutyches and his opinion. On these see the Breviary of Liberatus, from chapter 15 onward. Thus these two heresies, one held by the party of Nestorius and the other by the party of Eutyches, always troubled beyond measure the greater part of the Eastern Churches. The monks of Armenia follow the Nestorian heresy under the names and writings of Diodore of Tarsus, Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, and Ibas, which were condemned at the general Council of Constantinople, the fifth, held in 553 on the so-called Three Chapters, that is, on the condemnation of Theodore of Mopsuestia, the letter of Ibas of Edessa, and the writings of Theodoret of Cyrrhus against Cyril. But Eutychianism sent out several branches here and there under different names. Its adherents included Dioscorus of Alexandria, who was condemned with Eutyches at the Council of Chalcedon; after him Peter Mongus, the fourth bishop of Alexandria from him; and Peter of Antioch, surnamed Gnapheus or the Fuller, who, after the trisagion sung in the Church, added of his own accord "crucified for us". He was condemned first at the Roman Synod under Felix III in 483, and then at the Synod of Constantinople under Acacius, bishop of that see, and was suppressed by many writings and anathemas, especially the twelve anathemas of Quintian, bishop, modelled on the twelve anathemas of Cyril against Nestorius. Indeed, at the Synod of Sidon in Palestine in 512, almost eighty bishops of the Eutychian party tried to condemn the Council of Chalcedon with an anathema and to drive Flavian, bishop of Antioch, into exile, along with other orthodox bishops. How much trouble this caused the orthodox at that time, and especially Pope Hormisdas, is clear from his letters.

units.la: Acephali qui dicti (discrepant Scriptores, unde iis impositum nomen sit. Liberatus, in Breviario, cap. ix. ita appellatos ait, quod quem sequerentur suae opinionis authorem non edicerent.) Eutychianarum quoque partium fuerunt. Ejusque factionis erat Severus, a restituto Gnaphaeo, tertius in sede Antiochena episcopus: quique cum sequuti appellati sunt Severiani: cum quibus habita Collatio Constantinopolitana, sub Iustiniano Imp. a. Ib xxxir. quique in Concilio Constantinopolitano, sub Menna, ejus sedis episcopo, a Ib xxxvi. una cum Antimo Constantinopolitanae sedis, ante Mennam, invasore, aliisque ejusdem cohortis, condemnatus fuit. In Syria latissime haeresis Eutychiana vagata fuit, sedulo eam promovente Jacobo quodam Syro, (Baradeum dicit Gabriel Sionita) obscuro admodum nulliusque pretii homine, inde & Zanzalus, propter summam tenuitatem dictus, ejusque sequaces Jacobitae, quorum magnus inde in Syria, atque Oriente numerus extitit, ab a. Ib lxxv. Hi Orthodoxos nominabant Melchitas, eo quod Chalcedonensem Synodum & Imperatoris fidem (Melchi Syris Rex est) sequerentur. Eundemque Armeniorum sectae principem facit Nicephorus, lib. xviii. cap. iii. & iiii. Armenii quippe Iacobitae sunt, seu Eutychiani. Utramque Armeniam, & Syriam passim pervagata illa haeresis fuit. Unde postea in Concilio Hispalensi ii. a. Ib clvii. cap. xii. legitur: Duodecima actione ingressus est ad nos quidam ex haeresi Acephalorum, natione Syrus (ut asserit ipse) Episcopus, duarum in Christo naturarum proprietatem abnegans, & deitatem passibilem asserens.
units.tr: The so-called Acephali (writers disagree about why they were given this name; Liberatus, in his Breviary, chapter 9, says they were so called because they would not name the author of the opinion they followed) were also of the Eutychian party. Severus, the third bishop of Antioch after the restored Gnapheus, belonged to this faction, and his followers were called Severiani. A conference was held with them at Constantinople under the Emperor Justinian in 534, and they were condemned at the Council of Constantinople under Menas, bishop of that see, in 536, together with Anthimus, who had seized the see of Constantinople before Menas, and others of the same band. The Eutychian heresy spread very widely in Syria, promoted diligently by a certain Syrian named Jacobus (Gabriel Sionita calls him Baradaeus), a very obscure man of no worth, from whom Zanzalus, so called for his extreme meanness, and his followers, the Jacobitae, took their name. From 575 their number grew large in Syria and the East. These men called the orthodox Melchites, because they followed the Council of Chalcedon and the faith of the Emperor (Melchi means king in Syriac). Nicephorus makes this same man the leader of the Armenian sect, in book 18, chapters 3 and 4. For the Armenians are indeed Jacobites, that is, Eutychians. That heresy spread everywhere through both Armenia and Syria. Hence it is later read in the Second Council of Seville, in 657, chapter 12: In the twelfth session there came to us a certain man of the heresy of the Acephali, a Syrian by birth (as he himself claims), a bishop, who denied the property of the two natures in Christ and asserted a passible deity.

units.la: Sectae Monothelitarum, dicentium, unam duntaxat in Christo esse voluntatem, & unam operationem Divinitatem auctores praecipui fuerunt, Sergius, & Pyrrhus,
units.tr: The leading authors of the sect of the Monothelites, who said that there is only one will and one operation in Christ, were Sergius and Pyrrhus,

units.la: Constantinopolitani Episcopi, cum quo Pyrrho Disputatio habita à Maximo monacho, coram Gregorio Patricio, a. Iɔ c xlv, quam Baronius ad finem Tom. VIII. Graecam, & ex versione Francisci Turriani Iesuitae latinam primus edidit. In Lateranensi Synodo, sub Martino I. a. Iɔ cxlii. auctores istius sectae hoc modo proponuntur, in libello Stephani, Dorensis episcopi: primum quidem Theodorus Pharanitanae ecclesiae quondam episcopus: postmodum autem Cyrus Alexandrinus antistes, item Sergius Constantinopolitanus, nec non successores eius Pyrrhus & Paulus. Hi namque Apollinaris & Severi dogmata haereticorum renovare ausi sunt, per hoc, quod praedicaverunt unam voluntatem & operationem divinitatis & humanitatis Christi dogmatizare. Condemnati autem sunt in illa Lateranensi Synodo, & Constantinopolitana III. generali VI. unde trinisexta appellatur, sub Constantino Pogonato, a. Iɔ c lxxx. ubi inter Monothelitarum patronos illos, quos diximus, constituitur quoque Papa antiquae Romae, Honorius, Actione I, & VIII. & XIII. & XV. Quod idem Balsamo scribit, patriarcha Antiochenus, in hanc Synodum. Et Synodus quinisexta Trullana can. 1. Monothelitica haeresis surculus quidem est Eutychianismi, sed in hoc tamen ab Eutyche discrepare videri vult, quod duas naturas fatetur, quamvis unam earum subsistentiam, voluntatem, & operationem. Macarius Antiochenus in Synodo Constantinop. VI. Act. VIII. Nec enim carnem dicimus in Divinitatis transfire naturam, neque iterum in naturam carnis ineffabilem Dei verbi derivari naturam, sicut Apollinarius, Eutyches, & Severus impudenter asseruerunt. Nusquam enim propter unitionem differentia naturarum evanuescit. Salvatur autem magis proprietas utriusque naturae in una persona, unaque substantia. Unitum quippe ist carni secundum subsistentiam consitentes verbum, unum illum adoramus, filium unigenitum, Deum verum, Dominum omnium nostrum Iesum Christum, in duabus naturis inconfusè & indivisè cognoscendum, non per partes pa-rentes, ac segregantes hominem & Deum, neque idem quidem operatum fuisse miracula, hunc vero passum fuisse, quae humana sunt, sicut dividentes Theodorus[?] & Nestorius dicunt. quos deinceps etiam condemnant. Deinde: Neque enim quae divina sunt, secundum Deum: neque rursus quae sunt hominis, secundum hominem: sed humanatus Deus verbum, novam quandam Deivirilem operationem, & hanc totam vivificatricem demonstrat. Antea dixerat: Non dico duas voluntates, aut duas operationes in incarnationis dispensatione domini nostri Iesu Christi, sed unam voluntatem & Deivirilem operationem. Et postea, Non dico duas naturales voluntates, aut duas operationes naturales in incarnationis dispensatione Domini nostri Iesu Christi, nec si membratim incidar, & mittar in mare.
units.tr: patriarchs of Constantinople. A disputation was held with Pyrrhus by the monk Maximus, in the presence of the patrician Gregory, in 645; Baronius first published it in Greek at the end of volume 8, and in Latin from the translation of Francis Turrianus the Jesuit. At the Lateran Synod under Martin I, in 649, the authors of this sect were named as follows, in the libel of Stephen, bishop of Dora: first, indeed, Theodore, once bishop of the church of Pharan; afterwards Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria; likewise Sergius of Constantinople, and also his successors Pyrrhus and Paul. For these dared to renew the dogmas of the heretics Apollinaris and Severus, by teaching that there is one will and one operation of the deity and humanity of Christ. They were condemned at that Lateran Synod, and at the Third General Council of Constantinople, the sixth, which is therefore called the Quinisext (Trisexta), under Constantine Pogonatus, in 680, where among the patrons of Monothelitism named above is also the Pope of Old Rome, Honorius, in the first, eighth, thirteenth and fifteenth sessions. Balsamon, the patriarch of Antioch, writes the same about this council. And the Quinisext Synod of Trullo, canon 1, also says so. The Monothelite heresy is indeed an offshoot of Eutychianism, but in this it wishes to seem to differ from Eutyches, that it confesses two natures, though it holds that they have one subsistence, will and operation. Macarius of Antioch, at the Sixth Council of Constantinople, Act 8: For we do not say that the flesh passes over into the nature of the deity, nor again that the nature of the word of God is derived into the ineffable nature of the flesh, as Apollinaris, Eutyches and Severus shamelessly asserted. For the difference of the natures does not vanish on account of the union. Rather, the property of each nature is preserved in one person and one substance. For we confess that the Word, united to the flesh according to subsistence, is the one whom we adore, the only-begotten Son, true God, Lord of us all, Jesus Christ, to be recognized in two natures without confusion and without division, not dividing and separating man and God into parts, nor saying that the same one worked the miracles and that another suffered the human things, as Theodore and Nestorius, who divide, say, and whom they afterwards also condemn. Then: For the divine things are not according to God, nor again are the human things according to man; but God the Word, made man, shows a certain new divine-human operation, and this one entirely life-giving. He had said earlier: I do not say two wills or two operations in the dispensation of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, but one will and a divine-human operation. And afterwards: I do not say two natural wills or two natural operations in the dispensation of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, not even if I were cut limb from limb and thrown into the sea.

units.la: Sequitur Synodus quinisexta Constantinopolitana, habita sub Iustiniano Iuniore Rinotmeto, sive truncati nasi, in Trullo, id est, Imperialis palatii Secretario sic dicto, a. DCXCI[?]. vocatur quinisexta, quia quum nec quinta generalis sub Iustiniano Imp. nec sexta sub Constantino, ad normam aliarum quatuor generalium Synodorum canones condidissent, quod quintae sextaeque proinde defuit, haec supplere visa est, factis CIII canonibus, quare πενθεκτη à Graecis dicta fuit, & quamvis reclamantibus Latinis, pro generali habita. Ubi primum approbatis quatuor generalibus Conciliis Nicaeno, Constantinopolitano, Ephesino, & Chalcedonensi, varia deinceps condita fuere, adversus Ecclesiae Romanae disciplinam & mores: ex quibus alia disputationum inter utrosque argumenta, perpetuaque materia nata fuit. De conjugio clericorum, quod suis Graeci aliquâ ratione indulgent contra ac apud Romanos fit. Vt bigamum, nisi resipiscentem, non tolerant in catalogo sacerdotali vel clericali: neque post ordinationem conjugatum, nisi lectorem, aut cantorem: neque conjugatum, nisi ad inferiores gradus diaconatus, & presbyterii, non episcopatus; at ut nullo modo clerico haud liceat esse conjugato, quod Romanis visum, improbant. Unde expresse quidem Romanos in suis hic canonibus pungunt, atque reprehendunt. Vide Can. III. VI. XII. XIIII. XLVIII. Canone XIII. dicunt:
units.tr: The next council is the Quinisext Synod of Constantinople, held under Justinian II, called Rhinotmetus or "the Slit-Nosed," in the Trullus, that is, in the hall of the imperial palace so named, in the year DCXCI[?]. It is called Quinisext because, since the fifth general council under Justinian and the sixth under Constantine had not drawn up canons on the pattern of the other four general synods, this council seemed to supply what the fifth and sixth had lacked. It issued 103 canons, and for this reason the Greeks called it the Pentekte. Although the Latins protested, it was counted as a general council. After the four general councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus and Chalcedon had been approved, various canons were subsequently enacted against the discipline and customs of the Roman Church. From these arose disputes between the two sides and a constant subject of controversy. (a) On the marriage of clergy: the Greeks allow it in some measure, contrary to the practice among the Romans. They do not tolerate a bigamist in the sacerdotal or clerical list unless he repents. Nor do they tolerate a man who is married after ordination, except a reader or cantor. Nor do they allow a married man to be ordained except to the lower grades of deacon and presbyter, not bishop. They disapprove of the Roman view that a cleric may in no way be married. Accordingly, in these canons they expressly sting and rebuke the Romans. See canons III, VI, XII, XIV and XLVIII. Canon XIII says:

units.la: Quoniam Romana Ecclesia pro canone traditum esse cognovimus, ut diaconi vel presbyteri, qui digni qui ordinentur existimandi sunt, profiteantur se non amplius suis uxoribus conjungendos, nos antiquum canonem Apostolice perfectionis ordinisque servantes, hominum qui sunt in sacris, conjugia deinceps ex hoc temporis momento firma & stabilia esse volumus, nequaquam eorum cum uxoribus conjunctionem dissolventes, vel eos mutua tempore convenienti consuetudine privantes. Quamobrem si quis dignus inventus fuerit, qui hypodiaconus, vel diaconus, vel presbyter ordinetur, is ad talem gradum assumi nequaquam prohibeatur, si cum legitima uxore cohabitet. Sed neque ordinationis tempore ab eo postuletur, ut profiteatur se a legitima cum uxore consuetudine abstenturum: ne ex eo a Deo constitutas & sua praesentia benedictas nuptias injuria afficere cogamur, Evangelica voce exclamante, quae Deus conjunxit, homo non separet: & Apostolo docente, Honorabiles nuptias, & torum immaculatum, & Alligatus es uxori? ne quaere solutionem. Qui canon citatur quoque Gratiano 1. dist. XXXI. Hinc ergo controversia Graecorum cum Latinis, super conjugio clericorum. Verum & aliae in hac Synodo tanguntur inter utrosque controversiae, ut de jejunio Sabbathi, quo Romani etiam jejunare solent; Graeci autem interdicunt, excepto uno Sabbatho ante Paschali, quod appellant magnum. Hinc non solum rem definiunt pro se Graeci in hac Synodo, sed iterum Romanos tangunt atque reprehendunt. Can. IV. Quoniam intelleximus in Romanorum civitate, in sanctis Quadragesima jejunii, in ejus Sabbathis jejunari, praeter Ecclesiasticam traditam consequentiam: sancta Synodo visum est, est, ut in Romanorum quoque Ecclesia inconsulte viue habeat canon qui dicit: Si quis clericus inventus fuerit in sancto Dominico vel Sabbatho jejunans, praeter unum & solum, deponatur: sin autem laicus, segregetur. adde & can. lxxxii. Praeterea disputatur hic de esu sanguinis & suffocati, quem Graeci omnino illicitum censent, Romani contra Can. lxvii. Divina nobis scriptura mandavit, a sanguine & suffocato, & fornicatione abstinere. Eos ergo, qui propter lautum & delicatum ventrem, cujuscunque animalis sanguinem atque aliquá esculentum condiunt ac infirmas, ut par est, incusamus ac punimus. Si quis ergo deinceps animalis sanguinem quovis modo comedere aggrediatur, si fit quidem clericus, deponatur; sin autem laicus, segregetur. Atque hae quaestiones in Synodo motae agitataeque: ubi & illud de primatu Constantinopolitani, contra Romanum, iterum confirmatum can. xxxvi. Remanentes quae a sancti. 140. Patribus qui in hac Dei obser vatrice & regia urbe convenerunt, & sexcentorum triginta qui Chalcedone convenere, constituta sunt, decernentes ut thronus Constantinopolitanus aequalia privilegia cum antiquo Romae throno obtineat, & in Ecclesiasticis ut ille magni fiat, ut qui sit secundus post illum. Post quem magnae Alexandrinorum civitatis numeratur thronus: deinde Antiochiae, & post eum Hierosolymitanae civitatis. Ut haud mirum sit, Romanos adeo stomachari, atque invehi contra istam Synodum, quae quaestiones varias determinat contra Romanos, & authoritate generalis Synodi (quo quali illam Graeci habent) confirmat: ut ab hoc tempore intermissam Graecorum cum Latina ecclesia communionem Graecos scribere, annotet Baronius, Annal. tom. VIII. ad a. 692. Atque hinc jam numerandae aestimandaeque sunt Graecorum controversiae. Prima super primatu episcopi Romani, a Concilio Nicaeno, a. cccxxv. Dein: super oppositio ei pari dignitatis episcopo Constantinopolitano, ab a. ccclxxxi. in Concilio Constantinopolitano. Altera, quae Graecitas vexavit Ecclesias, de errore vel haeresi Nestorii, ab a. cccc xxxi. condemnatâ in Concilio Ephesino. Tertia, de haeresi Eutychis, ab a. cccclı. seu Concilio Chalcedonensi. Quarta, de Monothelitarum haeresi, ab a. Iɔ c lxxx. seu Synodo Constantinopolitana III. Quinta, de Conjugio clericorum, ab a. Iɔ c xc ı ı. in Synodo Trullanâ, quinisextâ. Indeque Sexta, de jejunio abbathi. & Septima, de esu sanguinis.
units.tr: Since we have learned that the Roman Church has received as a canon that deacons or presbyters who are judged worthy to be ordained should promise that they will no longer live with their wives, we, keeping the ancient canon of apostolic perfection and order, wish that the marriages of those who are in holy orders from this moment on shall be firm and stable, in no way dissolving their union with their wives or depriving them of conjugal intercourse at the appropriate time. Therefore, if anyone is found worthy to be ordained subdeacon, deacon or presbyter, he shall by no means be forbidden to be advanced to such a grade on the ground that he lives with his lawful wife. Nor shall he be required at the time of ordination to promise that he will abstain from lawful relations with his wife, lest we be compelled to wrong the marriage which God has established and blessed by his presence, the gospel voice crying out, "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder" (Matt. 19:6), and the Apostle teaching, "Marriage is honourable, and the bed undefiled" (Heb. 13:4), and "Art thou bound unto a wife? Seek not to be loosed" (1 Cor. 7:27). This canon is also cited by Gratian, Dist. XXXI. Hence arises the Greek controversy with the Latins over the marriage of clergy. Yet other controversies between the two sides are touched on in this synod, such as the fast on Saturday, which the Romans also customarily keep, whereas the Greeks forbid it, except for the one Saturday before Easter, which they call the Great Saturday. Here the Greeks not only settle the matter in their own favour in this synod, but again touch on and rebuke the Romans. Canon IV: Since we have understood that in the city of Rome, in the holy fast of Lent, fasting is practised on its Saturdays, contrary to the tradition handed down by the Church, it has seemed good to the holy synod that in the Roman Church too, an uncontested canon should stand which says: If any cleric is found fasting on the holy Lord's Day or on Saturday, except for one alone, he shall be deposed; but if a layman, he shall be excommunicated. Add also canon LXXXII. Furthermore, this synod disputes about the eating of blood and of what is strangled, which the Greeks consider wholly unlawful, while the Romans, contrary to canon LXVII, do not. Canon LXVII: Holy Scripture has commanded us to abstain from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. Therefore we rebuke and punish those who, for the sake of a dainty and delicate belly, season the blood of any animal and some food with it, as is proper. If anyone therefore henceforth attempts to eat the blood of any animal in any way, if he is a cleric he shall be deposed, but if a layman, excommunicated. These questions were raised and debated in the synod. There too the primacy of Constantinople against Rome was again confirmed in canon XXXVI. The remaining decisions of the holy fathers who gathered in this God-protected royal city, and of the six hundred and thirty who met at Chalcedon, decree that the throne of Constantinople shall enjoy privileges equal to those of the ancient throne of Rome, and that in ecclesiastical affairs it shall be exalted like it, being second after it. After it the throne of the great city of Alexandria is counted, then Antioch, and after that the city of Jerusalem. So it is no wonder that the Romans were so angry and inveighed against this synod, which settles various questions against the Romans and confirms them with the authority of a general synod (which the Greeks regard it as being). Baronius, in Annals vol. VIII, at the year 692, notes that from this time the Greeks broke off communion with the Latin Church. From here on, the Greek controversies must be counted and assessed. The first, concerning the primacy of the Roman bishop, arose at the Council of Nicaea in 325. Next, the opposition to the bishop of Constantinople, who was given equal dignity, arose from the year 381 at the Council of Constantinople. The second, which vexed the Greek churches, concerned the error or heresy of Nestorius, condemned from the year 431 at the Council of Ephesus. The third, concerning the heresy of Eutyches, dates from the year 451, that is, the Council of Chalcedon. The fourth, concerning the heresy of the Monothelites, dates from the year 680, that is, the third Council of Constantinople. The fifth, concerning the marriage of clergy, dates from the year 692, at the Trullan or Quinisext Synod. Then the sixth, concerning the fast on Saturday, and the seventh, concerning the eating of blood.

units.la: Sequuta fuit seculo octavo alia de cultu imaginum, in Concilio Constantinop. VII. generali, in Blachernis habito, seu Basilicâ S. Mariæ, ubi a. Iɔ cclɪv. sub Constant. Copronymo, à cccxxxviii. episcopis, per sex menses congregatis, religiosus imaginum cultus damnatus fuit: ejusque Acta inserta Concilio Nicæno II. a. Iɔ cc lxxxvii. sub Constantino, ejusque matre Irene, quod pro cultu imaginum gestum, Act. VI. Unde quæstio inter Græcos Latinosque hæsit super sex prima generali Synodo, illis dicentibus, eam Constantinopolitanam esse, his Nicænam: quarum hæc probavit, quod illa rejecit, videlicet cultum imaginum.
units.tr: In the eighth century there followed another controversy, concerning the veneration of images, at the seventh general Council of Constantinople, held at Blachernae, that is, in the Church of St. Mary, where in the year 754, under Constantine Copronymus, the religious veneration of images was condemned by 338 bishops who met over six months. Its acts were included in the second Council of Nicaea in 787, under Constantine and his mother Irene, which dealt with the veneration of images in its sixth session. From this arose a dispute between Greeks and Latins over which was the sixth general synod: the former said it was the Constantinopolitan, the latter the Nicene. The Latins approved that synod which the Greeks rejected, namely the veneration of images.

units.la: Illi Definit. XIV. dixerunt: Si quis in formâ Dei existentem Deum verbum servi formam in propriâ hypostasi assumentem, & per omnia nobis similem factum sine peccato, conatus fuerit materialibus coloribus figurare, veluti si nudus homo fuisset, & hoc modo ab inseparabili & incommutabili deitate sejungere, veluti quae ternitatem induituram in sanctam & vivificantem Trinitatem, anathema. Definit. XVI. Si quis sanctorum omnium ideas in imaginibus inanimatis & mutis materialibus coloribus depingere studeat, cum nullum omnino usum adferant picturae, anathema: Vana enim est excogitatio, & diabolicae insidiationis inventio. Nonne enim sationis fuerit illorum virtutes & virilia facta, quae nobis per scriptas historias traditae sunt, veluti vivas quasdam imagines in seipso depingere, & ad eadem ista seipsum zelo instimodi excitare, quemadmodum sancti patres nos docuerunt mus? Atque pro confirmatione Synodi, tandem decunt; Si quis hanc nostram sacram universalem septimam Synodum non receperit, sed eam quacunque modo calumniatus fuerit, & cum satisfactione omnia quae in ea desiderantur doctrina à Deo afflata, non amplexus fuerit, anathema sit à Patre, & Filio & Sancto Spiritu, & à septem sanctis universalibus synodis. Ita quidem tum Graeci: & fervide causam adversus imagines egerunt ipsorum Imperatores, de quibus in Collectione Iuris Orientalis, Bonefidius, lib. 1. sub constitutione Theophili: Michael pater ejus edixerunt ne ulli picta imagini, ubicunque ea esset nomen Sanctus imprimeretur, quod id nulli res praeterquam soli Deo congruere putabat. Leo autem, & filius ejus Coprony mus, omni earum adoratione prorsus interdixerunt. Theophilus autem ne pingi quidem eas calendas concessit: abjectis dicens animi esse talium rerum admirationem, ipsamque solam spectandam esse veritatem. Atque ita in Ecclesia tumultuatum super causa imaginum, Concilio Constantinopolitano anno IDCCCXIV. pro septima Constantinopolitana Nicaena II. improbante: è contra iterum alio Constantinopolitano a. IDCCCXLII. cultum imaginum, ejecto Iohanne patriarcha, alioque in ejus locum surrogato Methodio, revocante. Verum deflexerunt postea Graeci, & barbaries hanc etiam superstitionem invexit, quae circa imagines occupatur. Unde & loco septimae Constantinopolitanae Pseudo-Nicaenam arripuerunt, magnaque in veneratione habuerunt passim septem illas Synodos: de quibus Michaelis Psellii, & Photii Constantinopolitani extant libelli, & Photii Nomocanon Tit. I. can. II. ibidemque Balsamo Antiochenus, & Glycas, Annal. Tom. IV. Hinc & Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha recens ordinatus in suis systaticis scribere solet, ut et in Iure Graeco Romano Leunclavii, edito à Marq. Frehero, lib. VI. ἀσπάζομαι τὰς ἁγίας εἰκόνας ...
units.tr: The Greeks said in their Definition XIV: If anyone, attempting to depict with material colours God the Word, who exists in the form of God, who took on the form of a servant in his own hypostasis, and who was made like us in all things without sin, and so separates him from the inseparable and unchangeable deity, as if he were to be clothed in the Holy and Life-giving Trinity, let him be anathema. Definition XVI: If anyone seeks to paint with material colours in lifeless and dumb images the ideas of all the saints, since such pictures are of no use at all, let him be anathema. For it is an empty invention and a devilish contrivance. Would it not rather be fitting to portray in oneself their virtues and manly deeds, which have been handed down to us through written histories, as living images, and so to stir oneself up with a zeal of this kind, just as the holy fathers taught us? And finally, to confirm the synod, they say: If anyone does not receive this our holy universal seventh Synod, but falsely accuses it in any way, and does not embrace with full satisfaction all the teaching inspired by God that is found in it, let him be anathema from the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and from the seven holy universal synods. Thus the Greeks in those days; and their emperors fiercely pleaded the cause against images. Bonefidius, in the Collection of Eastern Law, book 1, under the constitution of Theophilus, writes: His father Michael decreed that no name of Saint should be stamped on any painted image wherever it was, since he thought that such honour fitted none but God alone. Leo, and his son Copronymus, wholly forbade any adoration of them. Theophilus, however, did not even allow them to be painted, saying that the admiration of such things belongs to the mind that has been cast off, and that truth alone is to be looked upon. And so in the Church there was tumult over the matter of images: the Constantinopolitan council of 814 approved the seventh synod of Constantinople, which was the second Nicene, while on the other hand another council at Constantinople in 842, with Patriarch John expelled and Methodius put in his place, revoked the veneration of images. But the Greeks later changed their minds, and barbarism introduced this superstition too, which is concerned with images. Hence, in place of the seventh Council of Constantinople, they seized upon the pseudo-Nicene one, and everywhere they held those seven synods in great reverence. There are treatises on them by Michael Psellus and Photius of Constantinople, and Photius' Nomocanon, title I, canon II, and likewise Balsamon of Antioch and Glycas, Annals vol. IV. Hence also the newly ordained Patriarch of Constantinople is accustomed to write in his synodal letters, as in Leunclavius's Greco-Roman Law, edited by Marquard Freher, book VI: [ἀσπάζομαι τὰς ἁγίας εἰκόνας ...] I embrace the holy icons...

units.la: Greek text at the foot of the page continues below the last line and is illegible in detail. [illegible, ~12 letters] amplecter sanctas VII. Synodos universales, & ab eis statuta recipio & accepto omnia. In Menologio autem, ad d. XVI. Julii, quo memoriam celebrant veterum Synodorum generalium, septima omittitur. Sic enim habet: Memoria Patrum Nicaenorum CCCXVIII. Patrum Secunda Synodi Constantinop. CL. Tertia Ephesina CC. Quarta Chalcedonensis DCXXX, Quinta, CLX. Sexta CLXX.
units.tr: The Greek text at the foot of the page continues below the last line and is illegible in detail. [illegible, about 12 letters] I embrace the holy VII. Universal Synods, and I accept all the things established by them. In the Menologion, however, under 16 July, on which day they celebrate the memory of the ancient general Synods, the seventh is omitted. It reads thus: Memory of the Nicene Fathers CCCXVIII. Of the Fathers of the Second Synod of Constantinople CL. Third, Ephesine CC. Fourth, Chalcedonian DCXXX, Fifth, CLX. Sixth CLXX.

units.la: Circa illa tempora moveri coepit quaestio ista famosa de processione Spiritus Sancti à Patre, Filioque: Graecis exprobrantibus Latinis, quod istud temere symbolo apposuissent: agitataque primùm quaestio fuit inter Gallos, & Graecos, in Synodo Gentiliacensi, a. MCCLXVI. Et haec multarum turbarum controversia, magnis animorum agitata contentionibus, praecipuumque divortii Graecorum à Latinis argumentum semper extitit. Neque adeo res erat, ob quam Graeci Latinos tam vehementer exagitarent, quam quod hi, illis inscriis & non auditis, Symbolo ingerere fuissent ausi lemma istud, Filioque. Unde Petrus Antiochenus, in epistola ad Michaelem Cerularium Constantinop. apud Baronium, Tom. XI. ad a. MLIV. Sed malum est illud & malorum pessimum, additio in symbolo. Si enim nostra Evangelia eadem sunt cum illorum Evangeliis, unde illa plura, qua nos edocti hujusmodi alienam additionem fecerunt? Dein: Illos itaque qui Symbolo aliquid addunt, vel auferunt, anathemate damnamus.
units.tr: About this time there began to be stirred up that famous question concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, the Greeks reproaching the Latins that they had rashly added it to the creed. The question was first debated between the French and the Greeks at the Synod of Gentilly in 1266. This controversy over many disputes, pursued with great heat of spirit, always remained the chief ground of the Greeks' separation from the Latins. Nor was there any matter for which the Greeks harassed the Latins so fiercely as that the latter had dared to insert that phrase, Filioque, into the creed without consulting or asking them. Hence Peter of Antioch, in his letter to Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, quoted by Baronius, vol. XI, under the year 1054: But the addition to the creed is an evil, and the worst of evils. For if our Gospels are the same as theirs, whence do those many additions come, which they have taught us to make to it? Then: We condemn with anathema those who add anything to the creed, or take anything away.

units.la: Alia insuper fuerunt, de quibus Graeci contendebant cum Romanis, super pane in S. Coenâ adhibendo, an fermentato, ut Graeci; an azymo, ut Latini? de quo Michaël Constantinopolitanus, & Leo, archiepiscopus Acridiae Bulgarorum, scribunt in epistola ad Iohannem Tranensem, apud Baronium, Tom. XI. a. MLIII quasi cum Iudaeis hac in parte Romani, & quicunque cum ipsis, facerent, in servandis azymis, ac sabbathis, vel horum per quadragesimam jejunio. Ac de azymis quidem: dem: Vos quidem panem, nos ἄρτον dicimus. Artos autem interpretatur elevatus & sursum portatus, à fermento & sale calorem & elevationem habens: azyma autem nil distant à lapide sine animâ, & luto lateris deorsum confusæ terræ, & sicco luto comparatæ, quas cum azymis Moyses comedere miseris Iudæis semel in anno legem constituit.
units.tr: There were also other matters over which the Greeks contended with the Romans: whether leavened bread, as the Greeks use, or unleavened bread, as the Latins use, should be employed in the Lord's Supper. Michael of Constantinople and Leo, archbishop of Acrida of the Bulgarians, write about this in a letter to John of Trani, quoted by Baronius, vol. XI, under the year 1053, as if the Romans, and all who followed them, in this respect did what the Jews do, in keeping the unleavened bread and the sabbaths, or in fasting through Lent. On the unleavened bread they say: You indeed say "panem", we say "artos". Artos means something raised and carried up, having warmth and elevation from leaven and salt; but unleavened bread is nothing different from a stone without life, or from the mud of a brick, or from earth mixed and dried like mud, which Moses, in his wretched law, commanded the Jews to eat with unleavened bread once a year.

units.la: Alia leviora, super halleluja in quadragesima cantando, vel omittendo; quorum hoc Latini, illud Græci observant: de sacerdotum barbis, quas Latini radunt; alunt Græci: de annulis episcoporum, quos Latini gestant, at reprehendant Græci, nec hi, nec illi merito tanti faciebant. Unde Petrus Antioch. in epist. ad Michaelem Cerularium: Quicunque verè à toto sunt commissi Romanorum errores, percurrimus: & alios quidem illorum execrandos duxi, atque vitandos, alios verò incertos, & alios prætermittendos. Quid enim nostra interest, quòd illorum sacerdotes barbam radant? quid etiam, quòd illis annulos gestent in Symbolum contracti cum sanctâ Dei Ecclesiâ connubii? Nos etenim etiam coronam in capite gestamus.
units.tr: Other lesser matters concerned singing or omitting the alleluia in Lent: the Latins observe the one, the Greeks the other. There was the matter of priests' beards, which the Latins shave and the Greeks grow. There was the matter of the rings of bishops, which the Latins wear and the Greeks find fault with; neither side, however, rightly made so much of these things. Hence Peter of Antioch, in his letter to Michael Cerularius: We have run through all the errors of the Romans that have truly been committed, and some of them I have thought detestable and to be avoided, others doubtful, and others to be passed over. For what does it matter to us that their priests shave their beards? What does it matter that they wear rings, having entered into a bond with the holy Church of God by a symbol? For we too wear a crown on our heads.

units.la: Nec illud de azymo præcipuum dissensus argumentum faciunt. Iohannes Episcopus Citri, in Responso ad Constantinum Cabasilam, Dyrrhacii archiepiscopum: Duo sunt manifesta & magna, quæ inter nos & Latinos faciunt differentiam. Primum & majus, doctrina de Sancto Spiritu. Secundum autem, nec tanti momenti, azymorum oblatio: est inter Responsa Patriarcharum, in Iure Græcorum canonico. Atque illud primum vim suam trahit non tam ex articuli naturâ, quam arrogatâ Papæ Romani potestate, quâ in symbolum dicitur articulum illum ingessisse. Unde uti prima, ita gravissima semper inter Græcos Latinosque viguit contentio super Papæ Romani primatu. Quod demonstrat Nilus, archiepiscopus Thessalonicensis, lib. περὶ ἀζύμων [?] ἐκκλησιαστικῶς, ubi ostendit, μὴ ἄλλο τι τὸ διαφέρον [?] τῶν Λατίνων ἐν ἀζύμοις ἢ ἡμῶν μίγνυσθαι τῷ ζύμῃ [?], ἄλλως
units.tr: Nor do they make that matter about unleavened bread the chief ground of dissent. John, bishop of Citrus, in his Reply to Constantine Cabasilas, archbishop of Dyrrhachium: There are two clear and great things that make the difference between us and the Latins. The first and greater is the doctrine concerning the Holy Spirit. The second, of no such importance, is the offering of unleavened bread. This is among the Replies of the Patriarchs, in the Greek canon law. And the first point draws its force not so much from the nature of the article as from the claimed power of the Roman Pope, by which he is said to have thrust that article into the creed. Hence, as the first, so the gravest contention has always prevailed between Greeks and Latins over the primacy of the Roman Pope. Nilus, archbishop of Thessalonica, shows this in his book On the Unleavened Bread, ecclesiastically [περὶ ἀζύμων ἐκκλησιαστικῶς], where he shows that the difference of the Latins in the matter of unleavened bread is nothing other than that we mix leaven into it [μὴ ἄλλο τι τὸ διαφέρον τῶν Λατίνων ἐν ἀζύμοις ἢ ἡμῶν μίγνυσθαι τῷ ζύμῃ]; otherwise

units.la: ἀλλὰ [?] ἔσεσθαι [?] εἵνεκ[?], non aliam dissidii Ecclesiarum Latinarum, & Græcanicarum causam esse, quam quod Papa ejus quod controversum est, cognitionem ac judicium ad Oecumenicam Synodum deferre detrectet; sed ipse solus controversiæ Magister ac judex sedere velit, reliquos vero discipulorum instar dicto audientes habere. Quod quidem ab Apostolorum & Patrum legibus actionibusque est alienum. Respicit controversiam de processione Spiritus Sancti. Atque ita impagati sumus Græcorum quæstiones & controversias, assignato earundem tempore, & origine: patetque has esse, nempe servato temporis ordine, quo quæque enatæ, præcipuas, de primatu episcopi Romani; de hæresi Nestoriana; Eutychiana; Monothelitica; de conjugio clericorum: jejunio sabbathi; esu sanguinis; cultu imaginum; processione Spiritus Sancti a Filio; & de azymis: postea addita quoque quæstio, de igne purgatorio, a. MCCLXXIV. Super quibus, iisque præsertim quæ Romanam concernunt Ecclesiam, disputatione aliquandiu fota, tandem scisma Ecclesiarum subsequutum fuit. Quod quomodo, & quando contigerit, secundo loco exponendum nobis est.
units.tr: but [ ... ] will be [ ... ]. The quarrel between the Latin and Greek Churches has no other cause, he says, than that the Pope refuses to refer to an Ecumenical Synod the knowledge and judgment of the matter in dispute, but wishes to sit alone as master and judge of the controversy, and to have the rest as obedient disciples. This is indeed alien to the laws and acts of the Apostles and the Fathers. He refers to the controversy about the procession of the Holy Spirit. Thus we have sufficiently examined the Greek questions and controversies, with their time and origin assigned; and it is clear that these are, in the order of time in which each arose, the chief ones: concerning the primacy of the Roman bishop; concerning the Nestorian heresy; the Eutychian; the Monothelite; concerning the marriage of clergy; the fast of the sabbath; the eating of blood; the worship of images; the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son; and the unleavened bread. Afterwards was also added the question of purgatory fire, in 1274. Over these matters, and especially those that concern the Roman Church, a dispute was carried on for some time, until at last a schism of the Churches followed. How and when this happened we must set out in our second place.

units.la: Quando in Oriente Imperium tenuit Michaël III. in Occidente Ludovicus II. episcopo urbis Romæ Nicolao I, Constantinopolitanæ Ecclesiæ præfuit episcopus Ignatius; quo rejecto, sedem, operâ Michaëlis Imp. occupavit Photius a. DCCCLVIII. ipse ille, cujus est celebris Nomocanon, sive canonum & legum collectio uno codice per certos titulos digesta; & Μυριόβιβλος, sive Bibliotheca. Ignatii depositionem, & Photii in ejus locum surrogationem ægerrimo animo tulit Nicolaus Papa: eâque de causâ graviter expostulavit apud Imp.
