Michaëlem, Photium ipsum, & alios, misitque Legatos suos Constantinopolim, Radualdum Portuensem, & Zachariam Anagninum episcopos, qui rem omnem perquirerent, atque ad examen & judicium suum referrent, interim communionem omnem cum Photio sedulò caverent. Quod minus observarunt illi, & Constantinopolim venientes in Synodo ccc XVIII. episcoporum anno Io ccc lxi. consenserunt in Ignatii depositionem iterato tum factam, & cum Photio communicarunt: eòque postea domum reversi excommunicationis sententiam incurrerunt. Hinc in Synodo Romanâ propter causam illam indi-ctâ anno Io ccc lxiii. Pontifex Photium excommunicare, Ignatium vero in pristinam sedem reponere conatus fuit. Unde offensis valde utrinque animis, hinc Michaëlis Imp. & Photii, inde Nicolai P. acrem Pontifici Nicolao mittit epistolam Imperator, exprobrans ei usurpatam auctoritatem in Ecclesiam, vel Praesules Constantinopolitanos, quo nihil dici ingratius Pontifici potuit, magno fastu illam potestatem semper ambienti, quare is in aliâ ad Imperatorem epistolâ monenda minatur istius epistolæ, cæterorumque hâc in causâ contra Ignatium scriptorum Auctoribus, ni alio decreto illa revocaret Imperator, & publice traderet comberenda, ab omni Christianâ compage remotos, Apostolicâ fe-auctoritate, diris anathematis vinculis innodabimus. Quod & repetit: alioquin (ut jam praefati sumus) sic, Deo fa-vente, de caetero vigilabimus, & studiis quibus possumus, insistemus, ut inter examines computentur qui auctoritatem Petri non senserint, immò Dei hanc ordinantis in Petro non intellexerint: ita ut nec ista, quae permitiose compilata sunt defendere, sed nec his similia, ut non dicam scripto tradere, vel in mentem volvere quis ulterius audeat. Denique pergit ad se Romam vocare Ignatium, & Photium, ut coram eorum causa agitari & definiri posset, atque hac viâ illos adigere ad agnoscendam sententiamque suam in ipsos potestatem. Erat & alia causa quae distrahebat Romanorum & Constantinopolitanorum animos in partes, Bulgarorum regio & Ecclesiæ, quas ad se pertinere dicebat Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha, ex jure imperii Orientalis, quod illos comprehendebat; de-inde inde quia Graecis uterentur Sacerdotibus, unde regimen Ecclesiarum, atque ordinatio episcoporum ac sacerdotum ad se spectaret: contra Nicolaus Papa illos suae sedi ac potestati subjectos ajebat, illorumque regimen ad se trahebat, eo quod a sua sede Doctores & doctrinam petiissent. Unde non parva dissensio, & turbae: de quibus conqueritur Nicolaus, in epist. ad Hincmarum Rhemensem, apud Baronium, Tom. X. ad a. DCCCLXVII. Capita vero decem a Graecis sibi objecta Nicolaus haec testabatur, de jejunio sabbathi, processione Spiritus S. a Filio, caelibatu clericorum, de chrismate baptizatorum quod fiat a presbyteris, de aqua pro chrismate usurpanda, de edendo caseo vel ovis in quadragesima, quod agnus tempore Paschatis una cum corpore Christi super altare offerretur, quod Occidentales clerici barbam raderent, & diaconi non suscepto presbyteratu ad episcopatum transirent, denique libellus fidei exigeretur a Legatis sedis Romanae: quorum aliqua vera, alia futilia, nonnulla falso vel a Graecis dicta, vel pro talibus a Romanis accepta fuerunt. Mortuo exin Nicolao, in ejus locum successit Adrianus II. qui praedecessorem suum adeo per omnia sequebatur, ut hinc Nicolaitanus palam diceretur.
units.tr: When Michael III held the empire in the East and Louis II in the West, while Nicholas I was bishop of the city of Rome, the bishop Ignatius presided over the Church of Constantinople. When he was deposed, Photius, by the work of the emperor Michael, took his seat in 858: the same Photius who wrote the famous Nomocanon, that is, a collection of canons and laws arranged under certain titles in a single book, and the Myriobiblos, or Bibliotheca. Pope Nicholas took the deposition of Ignatius and the substitution of Photius in his place very badly, and for this reason he sharply complained to the Emperor Michael and to Photius himself and others. He sent his legates to Constantinople, the bishops Radoald of Porto and Zachary of Anagni, to inquire into the whole matter and refer it to his examination and judgment, and meanwhile to take great care to have no communion with Photius. These men did not keep this instruction fully, and on coming to Constantinople, in a synod of 318 bishops in the year 861, they agreed to the deposition of Ignatius, which had been carried out again at that time, and communicated with Photius; and afterwards, on returning home, they incurred the sentence of excommunication. Hence, in a Roman Synod held in 863 on account of that matter, the Pontiff tried to excommunicate Photius and restore Ignatius to his former see. Hence, with minds greatly offended on both sides, the Emperor Michael and Photius on one side, and Pope Nicholas on the other, the Emperor sent a sharp letter to Pope Nicholas, reproaching him for the authority he had usurped over the Church or the bishops of Constantinople, than which nothing could be said more unwelcome to a Pontiff who always sought that power with great pride. Therefore in another letter to the Emperor he threatens, warning him, that unless the Emperor revokes that decree and hands over that letter, and the other writings composed in this cause against Ignatius by their authors, to be publicly burned, we will bind them with the chains of dreadful anathema, removed from every Christian fellowship by Apostolic authority. He repeats this: otherwise (as we have already said) we will, with God's favour, watch from now on, and will apply ourselves with all the zeal we can, so that those who have not perceived the authority of Peter, nay, have not understood God's appointment of it in Peter, are counted among the unbelievers, so that no one further dares to defend those things that have been wickedly compiled, still less to write down or call to mind anything similar. Finally he goes on to summon Ignatius and Photius to Rome, so that their case could be argued and decided in their presence, and by this means to compel them to acknowledge his judgment and power over them. There was also another cause that divided the minds of the Romans and Constantinopolitans: the region and Churches of the Bulgarians, which the Patriarch of Constantinople claimed belonged to him, by the right of the Eastern Empire, which included them; and then because they used Greek priests, so that the government of the Churches and the ordination of bishops and priests belonged to him. Against this, Pope Nicholas said that they were subject to his see and authority, and he claimed their government for himself, because they had sought teachers and doctrine from his see. Hence arose no small dissension and disturbance, of which Nicholas complains in his letter to Hincmar of Reims, quoted by Baronius, vol. X, under the year 867. Nicholas also declared that the ten chapters the Greeks objected to him were these: the fast of the sabbath; the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son; the celibacy of clergy; the chrism of the baptized, which was made by priests; the water to be used for the chrism; the eating of cheese or eggs in Lent; that a lamb was offered on the altar at Easter together with the body of Christ; that Western clergy shaved their beards; that deacons, without having received the presbyterate, passed over to the episcopate; and finally that a creed was demanded from the legates of the Roman see. Some of these were true, others trifling, and some were either said falsely by the Greeks or accepted by the Romans as if they were true. Nicholas died after this, and was succeeded in his place by Adrian II, who followed his predecessor so closely in everything that he was openly called a Nicholaitan.

units.la: Hic ope Basilii Imp. qui, interfecto sua opera Michaele, successerat, Ignatium restitui pristinum in locum, pulso Photio, curavit in Synodo Constantinopolitana IV, quam Romani octavam universalem indigetant, a. DCCCLXIX. Res autem Ignatii, & Photii, tum Michaelis & Basilii, atque pro Ignatio, describit in hujus vita Nicetas Paphlagonius, qui in Tomo Conciliorum tertio Binii legitur, parte secunda, in Historia Concilii Constantinopolitani VIII. Nullibi vero major varietas in designandis Conciliis quam in hoc octavo, quod vulgo oecumenicum vocant. Siquidem ita appellatur & Constantinopolitanum illud a. DCCCLXI. quo Ignatius fuit depositus, & in locum ejus surrogatus Photius: tum hoc, quod sub Basilio & Adriano II. celebratum, pro Ignatio, contra Photium aliud, in quo Photius sedem recepit, a.Ↄ ccc lxix[?]. Denique ita etiam inscribitur Ferrariense, seu Florentinum, quod fuerit œcumenicum VIII. Græci quidem pro octavâ generali Synodo non habent illam Constantinopolitanam contra Photium, sub Basilio, & Adriano celebratam; sed ex adverso sequentem anni Ⅰↄ ccc lxxix. pro Photio: unde & canonem, sub nomine octavæ Synodi producit in suâ Iuris collectione Gratianus. Sed & in Concilio Ferrariensi (quod pluris est momenti) sess. VI. Marcus Ephesinus palam affirmavit: concilium illud inter generalia commemorandum non esse: sed potius sequens concilium sub Iohanne VIII. de quo ita: Is deinde Ioannes aliud Concilium habuit, quod item appellavit Octavum, quod Acta ipsius Concilii, quod vos Octavum fuisse dicitis, improbavit, Photiumque restituit. In quo plane Concilio inter alia fuerat decretum, ut hæc eadem Symboli additio tolleretur, quod vos non ignorare putamus. Si quidem igitur ipsius concilii Acta reprobas videntur, non est congruum rationi, ut de his aliqua mentio fiat, cum alterum octavum Concilium sequi potius debeeremus. Propterea tempore ex eo in Constantinopolitanâ Ecclesiâ hucusque solet ita celebrari: Quicunque in sanctos Patriarchas Ignatium & Photium scripta vel dicta sunt, anathema sunto. Apparet hinc, Græcos illa quæ in causâ Ignatii & Photii olim gesta utraque sic composuisse, ut nec in hunc, in illum dicta recipi voluerint. Verùm ad illud Garci Ephesini in Concilio Ferrariensi Iulianus Cardinalis respondens, Ephesino apertè succubuit, ajens: Hoc autem metu vos libero, præstantissimi Patres: nam nihil de ipso Concilio, Octavo scilicet recitabitur. Sed quoniam in eo volumine nonnulla Sexti, Septimique Concilii Acta sunt scripta: idcirco ea videre volemus: nam de Octavo Concilio nobis cura non est. Ob quod responsum quàm indignè vapulet Baronio, non est impræsentia-rum tum animus discutere. Ergo Concilium Constantinopoli ultimum in causa Photii anno Iↄ cccLxxix cogit Basilius Imp. cccLxxxv episcoporum, inque eo, mortuo jam Ignatio, restitutio Photii in sedem episcopalem, praesentibus iterum Legatis Pontificiis, confirmatur: Quod etiam approbavit Johannes Papa, tum aliis, tum singularibus ad ipsum Photium litteris; quae inter epistolas ejus CC I. Unde, quod scilicet Johannes Papa imbelli animo hoc commisit contra praedecessoris sui, & Synodi Constantinopolitanae, octavae Latinis dictae, sententiam, à Photio, Eunucho ut ajunt, circumventus, fabulam de Johanne Papissa natam existimat Baronius; quasi quod hoc in negotio foeminam se potius, quam virum ostendisset. Neque hoc solum egit Constantinopolitana sub Photio Synodus, ut ejus restitutionem confirmaret, sed & superiorem dictam abrogavit, & e symbolo particulam illam Filioque, ubi de processione Spiritus Sancti, sustulit, eaque etiam ratione Romanae Ecclesiae se lubens opposuit. Neque quod Nicolaus de Bulgaris moveret, & cujus spe Johannes seipsum jactarat, Photius ulla ratione concedendum putavit, sed Bulgaros, eorumque Ecclesias sedi Constantinopolitanae subesse, non Romanae, tenuit, atque ad Imperatorem negotium rejecit. Quin nec in eo gratificari voluit Romano episcopo Adriano Ignatius, utcunque ab eo valde adjutus, inque sedem episcopalem pristinam magno illius studio restitutus. Quare de eo conquestus ille fuit in epistola ad Basilium Imp. (inter epistolas Adriani quinta) quod ejus favore Ignatius in Bulgarum regione consecrare praesumsisset antistitem. Sub illo Photio Constantinopolitano inchoavit divulsio Ecclesiarum Graecarum à Latinis, inque Synodo Constantinopolitana habita anno Iↄ cccLxxix. perquam gravia adversus Ecclesiam Romanam, ejusque episcopos Nicolaum & Adrianum constituta fuerunt: illaque, omnium illorum quae actitati
units.tr: Here Basil the Emperor, who had succeeded Michael after arranging his murder, saw to it that Ignatius was restored to his former place, with Photius driven out, at the Fourth Synod of Constantinople, which the Romans call the eighth ecumenical council, in 869. The affairs of Ignatius and Photius, of Michael and Basil, and the struggle on Ignatius's behalf, are described in the life of Ignatius by Nicetas Paphlagonius, which is read in the third volume of Binius's Councils, part two, in the history of the Eighth Council of Constantinople. Nowhere is there greater variety in naming the councils than in the case of this eighth one, which is commonly called ecumenical. For the Constantinopolitan council of 861, at which Ignatius was deposed and Photius put in his place, is also called the eighth; so is the council held under Basil and Adrian II in favour of Ignatius and against Photius, and another in which Photius regained his see, in 879. Finally, the Council of Ferrara, or Florence, is also entitled the eighth ecumenical council. The Greeks, indeed, do not count as the eighth general synod that Constantinopolitan council against Photius held under Basil and Adrian, but instead the following one of the year 879, held for Photius; this is why Gratian, in his collection of law, cites a canon under the name of the eighth synod. Moreover, at the Council of Ferrara (which carries more weight), in the sixth session, Mark of Ephesus openly declared that that council is not to be reckoned among the general councils, but rather the later council under John VIII, of which he says: John then held another council, which he likewise called the eighth. The acts of that very council, which you say was the eighth, he rejected, and he restored Photius. In that council, among other things, it had been decreed that this same addition to the Creed should be removed, which we think you are not unaware of. If, then, you seem to reject the acts of that council, it is not reasonable that any mention be made of them, since we ought rather to follow the other eighth council. For this reason, from that time until now, the Church of Constantinople has customarily celebrated in this way: Whatever has been written or said against the holy Patriarchs Ignatius and Photius, let it be anathema. It appears from this that the Greeks, having composed the proceedings in the case of Ignatius and Photius, arranged both so that nothing said for one or against the other should be admitted. But when Julian the Cardinal answered the remark of Mark of Ephesus at the Council of Ferrara, he plainly yielded to Ephesus, saying: I release you from this fear, most excellent Fathers. For nothing will be read out concerning the council itself, namely the eighth. But since certain acts of the Sixth and Seventh Councils are written in that volume, we wish to see them, for we are not concerned about the Eighth Council. I have no wish to examine now how shamefully Baronius is lashed for this reply. So the last Constantinopolitan council in the case of Photius was convened in 879 by Emperor Basil, with 385 bishops present; and at it, with Ignatius now dead, the restoration of Photius to his episcopal see was confirmed, again in the presence of the papal legates. Pope John also approved this, both in other ways and in particular letters to Photius himself, which are numbered CCI among his letters. Hence Baronius thinks the tale of Pope Joan arose from the fact that John, with a weak spirit, entrusted this matter, against the judgment of his predecessor and of the Constantinopolitan synod called the eighth by the Latins, having been circumvented by Photius, a eunuch as they say; as though in this business he had shown himself a woman rather than a man. Nor did the Constantinopolitan synod under Photius only confirm his restoration; it also repealed the earlier decision, and removed from the Creed that clause Filioque, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, and by this means too it willingly set itself against the Roman Church. Nor did Photius think that he ought in any way to concede the matter of the Bulgarians, which Nicholas had pressed and in the hope of which John had boasted; instead he held that the Bulgarians and their churches were subject to the see of Constantinople, not to Rome, and referred the matter back to the Emperor. Nor did Ignatius, though he had been greatly helped by the Roman bishop Adrian and restored to his former episcopal see through his great zeal, wish to oblige him in this. Hence Adrian complained of him in a letter to Emperor Basil (the fifth among Adrian's letters) that Ignatius, through his favour, had presumed to consecrate a bishop in the region of the Bulgarians. Under that Photius of Constantinople the separation of the Greek churches from the Latins began; and in the synod of Constantinople held in 879 very severe decisions were made against the Church of Rome and its bishops Nicholas and Adrian; and the origin of all the evils that were done, the Greeks openly [?].

units.la: [The last line is partly illegible.] runt malorum originem, Græci palam [?]. Et jam se mutuo de hæresi variisque facinoribus accusabant Græci & Romani, atque excommunicabant alii alios. Photio Romani primam schismatis culpam attribuunt. Baronius: primus ergo Photius aperte se ab Ecclesia Romana sejunxit, qui non mediocrem ansam posteris, ut in schismate perseverarent.
units.tr: [The last line is partly illegible.] Thus the Greeks and the Romans were already accusing each other of heresy and various crimes, and each excommunicated the other. The Romans attribute the first guilt of the schism to Photius. Baronius: Photius, therefore, was the first openly to separate himself from the Roman Church, which gave no small occasion to posterity to persevere in the schism.

units.la: Postea a. cIↄ IIII. sub Constantino Monomacho valde recruduit contentio inter Romanum episcopum Leonem (qui vulgo dicitur nonus), & Michaelem Cerularium, Constantinopolitanum, occasione epistolæ Michaëlis & Leonis, archiepiscopo Acridiæ, quæ metropolis Bulgarorum (qui unà stabant), ad Ioh. Trenensem episcopum, super notis controversiis de azymis, jejunio sabbathi, suffocatis &c. Cui respondit Leo, & significat quam illi inclementer Romani excepissent, Latinam ecclesiam palam damnando, & Latinorum apud se templa omnia claudendo, eorumque monasteria auferendo; & quamvis amice, ac fraterne videretur scribere ad Michaëlem, mutuaque de concordia agere, passim quippe Leo illum Fratrem & confratrem salutat, charissime nobis & adhuc dicendo in Christo Frater & Antistes Constantinopolitane: tamen illam addit conditionem, quâ non potuit non graviter offendi Michaël, quem satis pro authoritate Romanus devovit, scribens ad eum (est inter epist. Leonis sexta) Credimus enim propter quod & loquimur atque constanter profitemur: Romana Ecclesia adeo non est sola, sicut tu putas una, ut in toto orbe terrarum quæcunque dissentit superbè ab eâ, non sit jam dicenda vel habenda ecclesia aliqua, sed omnino nulla: quinpotius conciliabulum hæreticorum, aut conventiculum schismaticorum, & synagoga Satanæ. Nam nos cum pertinacibus & in errore permanentibus pacem aliquam habere non possumus. Ergo hæreses & schismata, & diligentibus legem Dei non erit scandalum, sed pax multa. Quicunque gloriatur ChriChristiano nomine, cesset Romanam, sanctam & Apostolicam ecclesiam maledicere & lacessere. Unde qua ratione purgerent & perimerent se mutuo, quamvis sub blanda pacis & fraternitatis allocutione, vel sub tractatione mutuae concordiae, apparet. Legati Leonis Humbertus episcopus Silvae candidae, Fridericus Archidiaconus Cancellarius, ambo Cardinales, & Petrus Episcopus Amalphitanus postquam Constantinopolim venissent, & cum Imperatore, cum Patriarcha, aliisque diu egissent, Patriarcham tandem Michaelem, & Leonem Acridanum episcopum, omnesque illorum complices auctoritate Apostolica damnarunt, Leo Ostiensis, lib. II. cap. lxxxix. Ibique jam volitare hinc inde jacula anathematum, & damnare se mutuo Latini aeque, ac Graeci. Humbertus Cardinalis, Disputationem suam, quam cum illis habuit, & primus edidit Baronius, in Appendice ad Tom. XI. Annalium, talibus spiculis infulcit, ut ejus sufficiat audivisse conclusionem; Pro quibus omnibus, & aliis, quos longum est scripto prosequi, erroribus nisi respuerit, & digne satisfecerit, irrevocabile anathema hic & in futuro erit a Deo, & ab omnibus Catholicis, pro quibus Christus animam suam posuit. Acriori adhuc stylo disputavit Idem, adversus Nicetam Pectoratum, Monachum, quem & exquisitis conspuit in initio dicteris: ve tibi Sarabaita, qui nulla coenobitali est animatus disciplina, voluntate atque voluptate ductus propria contra sanctam Romanam & Apostolicam Ecclesiam, & omnium sanctorum Patrum Concilia horribiliter latrasti, & pultior asino, frontem leonis, & murum adamantinum frangere tentasti, in quo utique conatu non es victor erroris, sed victus errore, nec presbyter, sed inveteratus diurnum malorum, & puer centum annorum maledictus, potius dicendus Epicurus, quam monachus: nec credendus es degere in monasterio Studii, sed in amphitheatro aut lupanari, quo (sicut quondam Patrum dixit) quicunque vult, intrat, & solvit asinum. Quidam vere praenominaris Pectoratus, quoniam tum serpente antiquo super pectus tuum gradieris. Es abo- dantia enim cordis os loquitur. Ejusdemque sufficis plura sequuntur, atque in conclusione sic illum dimittit: Tu vero miserrime Niceta, donec resipiscas, sis anathema ab omni Christi Ecclesia cum omnibus qui tibi acquiescunt in una perversa doctrina. Unde non minum illos ad solemnem Michaelis, aliorumque eorum sententium process excommunicationem, neque nisi hoc primum patrato facinore, unde divortium Graecorum magis exasperatum, discedere voluisse. Quippe a. clɔlv. die xvii. Kalend. Augusti, in templo S. Sophiae charta excommunicationis posita super altare praecipuum, egressi templo Papae Legati, pulverem pedum suorum excutere in limine, proclamantes: videat Deus, & judicet. Atque ita ordinatis in urbe Ecclesiis Latinorum, anathemate cunctis dicto, qui deinceps ex manu Graeci Romanos vituperantis, communicarent, in osculo sanctae pacis abivere, xv. Kal. Augusti. Charta excommunicationis satis erat magna, & conclusio talis: Michael abusivus Patriarcha neophytus & solo habitum monachorum adeptus, nunc etiam criminibus pessimis a multis diffamatus; atque cum eo Leo Acridanus Episcopus dictus, & Sacellarius ipse Michaelis Constantinopolitanus, qui Latinorum sacrificium profanis conculcavit pedibus; & omnes sequaces eorum in praefatis erroribus & praesumptionibus, sint Anathema Maranatha cum Simoniacis, Valesii, Arriani, Donatistae, Nicolaitae, Severiani, Pneumatomachis, Manichaeis, & Nazarenis, & cum omnibus haereticis, immo cum diabolo & angelis ejus, nisi forte resipuerint. Amen, Amen, Amen. Deinde etiam alia promulgata fuit excommunicatio generalis contra omnes Romanae sedis adversarios: Quicunque Fidei sanctae Romanae & Apostolicae Sedis, ejusque sacrificio pertinaciter contradixerit, sit Anathema Maranatha, nec habeatur Christianus Catholicus, sed azymita haereticus. Fiat, Fiat, Fiat. Atque hoc pacto in nervum erupit Graecorum Latinorumque discordia. na contentio, divulsaeque à communione mutuâ ecclesiae, pro innatâ Romanorum indole, quâ nequeunt pari cum aliis jugo incedere, vel cum aliis à disciplinâ suâ alienis juxta vivere, sed omnibus dominari affectant, & imperitare. Neque ideo cessrunt Graeci, sed quemadmodum intolerandam Legatorum Papae arrogantiam notarat Michaël, in epist. ad Petrum Antiochenum, quod ad Imperatorem venissent, gravi quidem & superbo habitu, & gressu, & supercilio, se vero nec trivialî salutatione dignatos, neque sua capita vel modicum inclinasse; ita illos omnino aversari necesse esse, scribit: Cum itaque hoc pacto vivant, & ejusmodi moribus sint educati, & quae aperte sint legibus vetita, & interdicta, & execrata, facere audeant; quomodo inter eos, qui Orthodoxi sunt, collocandi ab iis, qui recte sentiunt, judicabuntur? Numquid equidem id ego crederem? Qui vero ista sentientes recte facere fuerint arbitrati, eandem cum illis sortiantur portionem. Nunquam enim nos ipsos aemulabimur in hac ipsorum concordia & confessione. Nec ita, inquam, mente capti erimus, vel nostro sensu privati, ut hanc sequamur viam. Haec vero hâc de causâ volumus nos percurrere, ut scire valens tua beatitudo, quae ab istis peragantur, non putet eos circa azyma tantum errare, quemadmodum nos etiam hactenus putavimus: sed cum noverit alios praeter hæc ipsorum errores, cum illis eos numeret, cum quibus digni sunt ut connumerentur. Quod vero omnium est gravissimum, & intolerabile, & eorum amentiam satis superque declarat, illud est, Dicunt enim quod non acceperunt haec, tanquam ut ab aliis edocerentur, sed potius ut alios ipsi docerent: fore etiam ut persuadeant nobis sequi eorum dogmata. Et hoc inquiunt cum imperii potestate, & inverecundia majore. Vides, ut par pari referat Constantinopolitanus Latinis, & quod nil minus tolerari potuerint Graeci, quam istorum fastum & impudentem arrogantiam. Petrus etiam Antiochenus, in suâ ad Michaëlem responsione, quamvis non in omnibus cum eo convenit, pro summo adversus Romanos crimine urget, additionem ad symbolum, de quâ pronunciare haud veretur: Ac itaque qui symbolo aliquid addunt vel auferunt, anathematizamus. Haec de scismate, seu ruptura & secessione Ecclesiarum Graecarum à Latinis breviter dicta sunt. Tertio loco agendum de unione aliquoties inter utrosque tentatâ & agitatâ, atque quo loco res istae hodie sint, quoque statu vel animo Graeci erga Occidentales, seu Pontificios, seu Protestantes, inquirendum.
units.tr: Afterwards, in the year 1054, under Constantine Monomachus, the dispute between the Roman bishop Leo, commonly called the ninth, and Michael Cerularius, patriarch of Constantinople, flared up again badly. It arose from a letter of Michael and Leo, archbishop of Acrida, the metropolis of the Bulgarians (who were standing with him), to John, bishop of Trani, about the well-known controversies over unleavened bread, fasting on the Sabbath, things strangled, and so on. Leo replied to this, and showed how harshly the Romans had been treated by the Greeks, who openly condemned the Latin Church, closed all the Latin churches in their domain and seized their monasteries. Although he seemed to write amiably and fraternally to Michael and to discuss mutual concord, Leo greeted him repeatedly as brother and fellow-brother, saying most dear to us, and still in Christ, brother and bishop of Constantinople. Yet he added a condition by which Michael could not help being gravely offended, and the Roman bishop, true to his authority, condemned him sharply in a letter to him (it is the sixth of Leo's letters): For we believe, and therefore speak and constantly profess, that the Roman Church is by no means alone, as you think, to be one. In the whole world, whoever disagrees proudly with her is no longer to be called or regarded as a church at all, but is wholly nothing; rather, a conventicle of heretics, a gathering of schismatics, and a synagogue of Satan. For we cannot have any peace with the obstinate and those who remain in error. Therefore heresies and schisms will be no stumbling block to those who love the law of God, but a source of great peace. Whoever glories in the Christian name should cease to revile and provoke the Roman, holy and Apostolic Church. From this it is plain that they cleansed and destroyed one another by such means, even under the flattering address of peace and brotherhood, or under the pretext of mutual concord. The legates of Leo, Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida, Frederick, archdeacon and chancellor, both cardinals, and Peter, bishop of Amalfi, came to Constantinople and, after long dealings with the emperor, the patriarch and others, at last condemned the patriarch Michael, and Leo, bishop of Acrida, and all their accomplices, by apostolic authority (Leo of Ostia, book 2, chapter 89). Then the darts of anathemas were already flying here and there, and Latins and Greeks alike were condemning one another. Cardinal Humbert, in his disputation with them, which Baronius first published in the appendix to volume 11 of the Annals, drove home his points with such shafts that it suffices to hear his conclusion: Unless they renounce these and all the other errors, which it would take too long to pursue in writing, and make due satisfaction, they will be under an irrevocable anathema here and in the future, from God and from all Catholics, for whom Christ laid down his soul. He argued again in an even harsher style against Niceta Pectoratus, a monk, whom he at the outset assailed with carefully chosen insults: Woe to you, Sarabaite, who have been animated by no monastic discipline, but led by your own will and pleasure, have barked horribly against the holy Roman and Apostolic Church and the councils of all the holy Fathers, and, more stubborn than an ass, have tried to break the lion's brow and the adamantine wall. In that attempt you were not the conqueror of error, but conquered by error; you are not a priest, but an old man full of daily evils, a cursed boy of a hundred years, to be called Epicurus rather than a monk. Nor are you to be believed to live in the monastery of the Studium, but in an amphitheatre or a brothel, where, as one of the Fathers once said, whoever wishes enters and unties the ass. Rightly is your name Pectoratus, since you walk upon your breast like the old serpent. For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. Much more follows in the same vein, and in the conclusion he dismisses him thus: As for you, most wretched Niceta, until you repent, may you be an anathema from the whole Church of Christ, together with all who assent to you in your one perverse doctrine. Hence the Greeks were not willing to depart from the solemn excommunication of Michael and his partisans, nor from the sentence once pronounced, unless this first deed had been done, by which the Greek divorce was made more bitter. Indeed, in the year 1054, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the church of St Sophia, a charter of excommunication was placed upon the principal altar; the Pope's legates went out of the temple, shaking the dust of their feet from the threshold and crying: May God see and judge. Thus, after the Latin churches in the city had been closed, with an anathema pronounced on all who thereafter communicated with the Romans' detractors at the hand of a Greek, they departed with the kiss of holy peace, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August. The charter of excommunication was quite long, and its conclusion ran thus: Michael, the abusive patriarch, a neophyte who has obtained only the habit of a monk, now also defamed by many for the worst crimes; and with him Leo, called bishop of Acrida, and the sacristan of Michael himself at Constantinople, who trampled the Latin sacrifice underfoot with profane feet; and all their followers in the aforesaid errors and presumptions, let them be an anathema, Maranatha, with the Simonians, Valesians, Arians, Donatists, Nicolaitans, Severians, Pneumatomachi, Manichaeans and Nazarenes, and with all heretics, yes, with the devil and his angels, unless perhaps they repent. Amen, amen, amen. Then also a general excommunication was proclaimed against all opponents of the Roman see: Whoever has obstinately opposed the faith of the holy Roman and Apostolic See, and its sacrifice, let him be an anathema, Maranatha, and let him not be held a Christian Catholic, but a heretic who uses unleavened bread. So be it, so be it, so be it. In this way the discord between Greeks and Latins broke out into open strife, and the churches were separated from mutual communion, because of the innate character of the Romans, who cannot walk under a yoke equal with others, or live alongside others who are foreign to their discipline, but aim to dominate and rule over all. Nor did the Greeks give way on that account. Just as Michael had noted the intolerable arrogance of the Pope's legates, in his letter to Peter of Antioch, because when they came before the emperor they had a grave and proud bearing, gait and haughty brow, and did not deign to give even an ordinary greeting, nor bow their heads in the slightest, so he writes that it was altogether necessary to shun them: Since, therefore, they live in this way, and have been brought up with such customs, and dare to do what is plainly forbidden, prohibited and execrated by the laws, how shall they be judged fit to be placed among those who are Orthodox by those who think rightly? Surely I would not believe it myself. Those who, holding these views, think they do right, let them share the same lot with them. For we shall never imitate them in this their concord and confession. Nor, I say, shall we be so out of our minds or deprived of our sense as to follow this path. We wish to run through these matters for this reason, so that your blessedness, who knows what they are doing, may not think that they err only about unleavened bread, as we too have hitherto thought; but, knowing that they have other errors besides these, may count them with those with whom they deserve to be counted. And what is most grievous of all, and intolerable, and declares their madness sufficiently and more than enough, is this: they say that they did not receive these things as though to be taught by others, but rather that they might teach others themselves, and that they will also persuade us to follow their doctrines. And they say this with the power of an empire and with greater shamelessness. You see how the Constantinopolitan pays the Latins back in their own coin, and how the Greeks could bear nothing less than their haughtiness and shameless arrogance. Peter of Antioch too, in his reply to Michael, though he did not agree with him on all points, urges against the Romans as the highest crime an addition to the creed, about which he does not hesitate to pronounce: Therefore we anathematize those who add anything to the creed or take anything away. These matters concerning the schism, or the rupture and secession of the Greek churches from the Latins, have been briefly set out. Third, we must treat of the union attempted and debated several times between the two, and inquire where those matters now stand, and what the condition and attitude of the Greeks is towards Westerners, whether Papists or Protestants.

units.la: Pro conciliandis Graecis cum Latinis primò actum lego in Concilio Barensi, a. MXCVIII [?]. cui Anselmus Cantuariensis interfuit, ubi & magnâ cum laude disputavit adversus illos de processione Spiritus Sancti à Patre: quâ occasione postmodum scripsit epistolam, seu librum, de processione Spiritus Sanctiŏ, itemque ad Vualramum episcopum, de fermentato & azymo. Acta autem Concilii illius Barensis interciderunt. Sed in instruendis & convincendis Graecis, praesertim in controversiâ de processione Spiritus Sancti à Patre, primâ Latinorum cum Graecis fuit opera. Quò spectavit Chrysolani, Mediolanensium episcopi, P. Paschalis II. ad Alexium Comnenum Legati a. MCXVI. habita oratio, quae est apud Baronium, Tom. XIX. quam Chrysolanum adversâ disputatione exceperunt Graecorum plurimi. Etiam pro uniendis cum Latinâ Ecclesiâ Graecis scripsit P. Innocentius III. ad Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum, a. MCXCVIII. quae est epistolarum ejus CCCLIIII. Deinde in aliâ ad eundem epistolâ rationes reddit primatus sui, quare Ecclesia Romana dicatur universalis, quod perpetuum Graecis contra Romanos fuit offendiculum: minaturque Patriarcham Papa, ut Romanae Ecclesiae reverentiam & obedientiam debitam impendat, secus in ipsum, & Graecorum Ecclesias, pro more, processurus. Habebat in urbe Constantinopolitanâ vicarium Sedis suae Innocentius, pro Latinis ibi degentibus: postea Balduino Flandriae Comite facto Imperatore, etiam ex Latinis in Patriarcham assumtus fuit primus Thomas Maurocenus. Dein a. cIↄ ccxxxı P. Gregorius ıx. scripsit prolixam epistolam (quæ est epist: lxv.) ad Patriarcham Constantinopolitanum Germanum: sed iterum, quia primatu Romano offensus iste erat, in illo pertractando argumento, & si posset probando, totam epistolam insumit. Idem saxum volvit cum Michaële Palæologo Imp. Constantinopolitano P. Vrbanus ıv. eumque postea secutus Gregorius x. Qui huc in finem convocavit Concilium Lugdunense, a. cIↄ cc lxxıv. plusquam quingentorum episcoporum, ubi præter varios Principes, & Legatos, interfuerunt quoque ex Oriente tum Imperatoris, tum Patriarcharum, aliorumque Legati, actumque de tribus articulis, subsidio terræ sanctæ, & super unione Græcorum, & super reformatione morum, uti illa prima sessione ipse Gregorius proposuit. Pertracti hic Græci in publicam cum Romana Ecclesia unionem vel ad ejus potius subjectionem, nam primatum ejus omni tempore ab ipsis negatum & retusum, nunc agnoscere coacti fuerunt, sed non adeo ex sensu religionis ac fidei, quam ex metu tum Caroli Siciliæ Regis, tum Balduini Constantinop. Imperatoris Latini, præeunte Græcis suis Imp. Palæologo. Vocatus (ut id obiter dicam) ad hoc Lugdunense celebre concilium erat quoque Thomas Aquinas, ut contra Græcos de processione Spiritus Sancti pro acumine ingenii sui, dignâ tanto vindice quæstione, disputaret; at morte præventus obiit, nonis Martii, in Monasterio Fossæ novæ, prope Terracinam, quando mensis Maji septimâ die Concilium inchoabat. Circa hæc tempora scripsit Nilus, Thessalonicensis Monachus, de causis dissensionum, inter Orientales atque Occidentales Ecclesias, libros duos, „ostendens, non aliam dissidii istius causam esse, quam „quod Papa ejus quod controversum est cognitionem „ac judicium ad Oecumenicam Synodum deferre detrectet: sed ipse solus controversiae magister & iudex sedere velit; reliquos vero discipulorum instar docto audientes habere. Quod quidem ab Apostolorum & Patrum legibus actionibusque alienum. Scripsit etiam librum, de Igne purgatorio Latinorum, quem nobis egregiisque argumentis explodit. Etiam Barlaam Monachus scripsit, contra Papae principatum, libellum. Cujus nequaquam sunt epistolae Barlaami Hieracensis episcopi, qui a. MCCCXIII. vixisse ponitur, edita ab Henrico Canisio Tom. VI. Antiq. Lectionum, atque de Romani episcopi potestate & authoritate, coram Barlaam Monachus, loquuntur, multisque de processione Spiritus Sancti a Filio: cujus etiam Epistolam exhibet eodem Tomo Canisius. Quem recte confundit cum Barlaamo monacho Abrahamus Bzovius, in Continuatione Annalium Baronii, Tom. XIV. ad anno MCCCXXXII. Monachum illum appellando, quum hic episcopus, & alter Monachus fuerit, tum diversissimae sententiae circa primatum Romanum uterque, & ille Graece, hic Latine scripsisse videatur.
units.tr: To bring the Greeks together with the Latins, I read that the first step was taken at the Council of Bari in the year 1098 [?]. Anselm of Canterbury took part in it, and there he argued with great credit against the Greeks on the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father. On that occasion he afterwards wrote a letter, or book, on the procession of the Holy Spirit, and also a work to Bishop Walram on leavened and unleavened bread. The records of that Council of Bari have perished. But in instructing and convincing the Greeks, especially in the controversy over the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father, the chief labour was that of the Latins. To this purpose belongs the speech delivered by Chrysolanus, bishop of Milan, on behalf of Pope Paschal II to Alexius Comnenus, in the year 1116. It is found in Baronius, vol. XIX, and many of the Greeks answered it with a hostile dispute. Pope Innocent III also wrote, in the year 1198, to the Patriarch of Constantinople to bring the Greeks into union with the Latin Church; this is letter 354 of his letters. Then in another letter to the same man he gives the reasons for his primacy, why the Roman Church is called universal, which had always been a stumbling block for the Greeks against the Romans. The Pope threatens the Patriarch that he must render the reverence and due obedience owed to the Roman Church, otherwise he will proceed against him and the churches of the Greeks as is his custom. Innocent kept a vicar of his see in the city of Constantinople for the Latins living there. Later, when Baldwin, Count of Flanders, had become emperor, Thomas Morosini, the first Latin to be appointed Patriarch, was also taken from the Latins. Then in the year 1231 Pope Gregory IX wrote a lengthy letter (it is letter 65) to the Patriarch of Constantinople, Germanus. But because that man was offended by the Roman primacy, he spends the whole letter on that subject, trying, if he could, to prove it. Pope Urban IV rolled the same stone with Michael Palaeologus, the Emperor of Constantinople, and after him Gregory X did the same. To this end Gregory X called the Council of Lyons in the year 1274, with more than five hundred bishops. Besides various princes and legates, there were present legates from the East, both of the Emperor and of the patriarchs and others. Three articles were dealt with: aid for the Holy Land, and concerning the union of the Greeks, and concerning the reform of morals, as Gregory himself proposed at the first session. Here the Greeks were brought to a public union with the Roman Church, or rather to its subjection; for although they had always denied and rejected its primacy, they were now forced to acknowledge it. Yet this was not so much from a sense of religion and faith as from fear of Charles, King of Sicily, and of Baldwin, the Latin Emperor of Constantinople, with the Emperor Palaeologus going before his Greeks. (I may mention in passing that Thomas Aquinas was also invited to this famous Council of Lyons, so that by the keenness of his mind he might dispute against the Greeks on the procession of the Holy Spirit, a question worthy of so great a champion; but he was overtaken by death and died on 7 March in the monastery of Fossanova near Terracina, when the Council was opening on 7 May.) Around these times Nilus, a monk of Thessalonica, wrote two books on the causes of the dissensions between the Eastern and Western Churches, showing that there is no other cause of this division than that the Pope refuses to refer the disputed matter to the cognition and judgment of an ecumenical synod, but wishes to sit alone as master and judge of the controversy, while the rest he wants to have as disciples, listening as taught. This, he says, is foreign to the laws and practices of the Apostles and Fathers. He also wrote a book on the Latins' purgatory, which he refutes with clear and strong arguments. The monk Barlaam also wrote a little book against the primacy of the Pope. Not at all the letters of Barlaam, bishop of Hierapolis, who is said to have lived in 1313, published by Henricus Canisius in vol. VI of the Antiquae Lectiones, speak of the power and authority of the Roman bishop in the presence of the monk Barlaam; they say much about the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. Canisius also gives his letter in the same volume. Abraham Bzovius, in the continuation of Baronius's Annals, vol. XIV, under the year 1332, rightly distinguishes him from the monk Barlaam, calling him a monk, although he was a bishop and the other a monk; and both held very different views on the Roman primacy, and the one seems to have written in Greek, the other in Latin.

units.la: Posteaquam aliquoties hinc a Latinis, inde a Graecis negotium mutuae unionis fuisset propositum, & literis, libris, legatis utrimque utrisque communicatam, Graecis urgentibus in frequenti, generali, liberā Synodo rem peragi debere, in Concilio Basileensi, quod inchoatum quidem, a. MCCCCXXXI. finitum a. MCCCCXLI. in quod Legati Orientalis Imperatoris Iosephi Palaeologi, & Constantinopolitani Patriarchae, Demetrius Palaeologus, Isidorus Abbas, & Iohannes Dissipatis una convenerant, sess. XIX. a. MCCCCXXXIV. VII. Id. Septembris decreverunt, rem in manus suscipiendam, & junctis animis operisque perficiendam esse. Vbi de urbe primo actum, in qua Synodus pro hac re generalis haberetur, Basileensibus Patribus Basileam, & praesens Concilium urgentibus, Graecis autem ConConstantinopolim: propositâ Synodi nomine alia quoque loca fuerunt, sin minus placeret Basilea, nempe Calabria, Ancona, vel locus alius maritimus, Bononia, Mediolanum, aliave civitas Italiae; vel extra Italiam, Buda in Hungariâ, in Austriâ Vienna, ultimo & Sabaudia; Graeci verò Eugenium P. magis, quam Basileense Concilium sequuti, Ferrariam deligunt, quò aliqui etiam ex Basileensi concilio, hoc neglecto, se contulerunt. Inchoatum Ferrariense Concilium fuit a. cIↄ cccc xxxvIII. d. 12. Aprilis, habitae hic sessiones xvi, translatoque inde propter pestem Concilio Florentiam, absolutum post xxv. sessiones, alias Ferrariae, reliquas Florentiae, finiit a. cIↄ cccc xxx ix. pridie Nonas Iulii.
units.tr: After the matter of mutual union had been proposed several times, on the one side by the Latins and on the other by the Greeks, and had been communicated by letters, books and legates on both sides, the Greeks insisted that the business must be carried out in a large, general and free synod. Accordingly, at the Council of Basel, which began in 1431 and ended in 1441, where the legates of the Eastern Emperor John Palaeologus and of the Patriarch of Constantinople, Demetrius Palaeologus, Isidore the abbot and John Dissipatis had met together, in the nineteenth session, on 7 September 1434, they decided that the matter must be taken up and carried through with united minds and effort. There the question was first raised of the city in which a general synod for this purpose should be held. The fathers at Basel urged Basel and the present council, but the Greeks urged Constantinople. Other places were also proposed in the name of the synod, if Basel did not please: namely Calabria, Ancona, or another seaside place, Bologna, Milan, or some other city of Italy; or outside Italy, Buda in Hungary, Vienna in Austria, and last of all Savoy. The Greeks, however, followed Pope Eugenius rather than the Council of Basel, and chose Ferrara, to which some from the Council of Basel also went, neglecting it. The Council of Ferrara began on 12 April 1438. Sixteen sessions were held here; then, because of the plague, the Council was transferred from there to Florence, and it was concluded after twenty-five sessions, some at Ferrara and the rest at Florence, on 6 July 1439.

units.la: Imperator Graecorum Iohannes Palaeologus, & Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus Iosephus ipsi cum multis Orientalium Antistibus advenere, Latinis, uti promissum à Basileensi Concilio fuerat, sumtus curantibus, magno cum honore & pompâ excepti, atque ad urbem Ferrariam, tum Concilium adducti fuerunt. Hinc quatuor elapsis mensibus, quo tempore velitationes aliquot disputationum habitae, prima sessio incœpit die viii. mensis Octobris, ac deinceps rem aggressi, disputarunt perpetuò de processione Spiritus Sancti à Filio, vel potius de additione illius Filioque ad symbolum: Graecis causatis, hinc schisma Ecclesiarum originem accepisse, quod Romani suo arbitrio, non expectato generalis concilii, & quoque Orientalis Ecclesiae judicio, illud symbolo addidissent: praesertim quum Synodo generali tertiâ Ephesinâ, contra Nestorium cautum fuisset, ne cui liceret symbolo quid addere, vel demere. Latini verò dicebant, illud non esse habendum pro additione symboli, solummodo explanatione & declaratione: neque contra veritatem aut doctrinam Ecclesiae illo articulo quidpiam comprehendi. Graeci schismatis causam in Romanos jaciebant. Unde Marcus Ephesinus, cujus potissimae in dicendo partes tes fuerunt, sess. 111. sic exorsus fuit: At quoniam quidem altero bono, id est, a mutua erga sororem suam amicitia Ecclesiam benevolentiâ Romana Ecclesia iam defecerat, daque sibi proprium finxerat, ac sibi perpetuo conservarat, quod neque litteris sacris relictum, neque ab universalibus Concilijs celebratum, neque a maioribus nostris suscepting et tractatum fuerat. Idque propterea solvende nostrae amicitiae causam, simulatque nostrarum initium, dubio procul fuisse constat. Innuit dogma de processione Spiritus Sancti, de quo solo per omnes sessiones disputatum. Eandemque schismatis causam fuisse disseruit Archiepiscopus Nicaenus Bessarion, postea factus Cardinalis, in Oratione, habita in Synodo, pro union. Per longam acremque inter partes disputationem, rem in contentionem abeunte, Graeci sessiones publicas deferebant: atque post xxv. sive ultimam sessionem, quando privatim solum, in aedibus Patriarchae convenicbant, (qui synodo propter imbecillitatem interesse nequivit, ex quâ ibidem obiit) missis ad Eugenium Pontificem (qui praerat) Nuncijs significabant, se nolle amplius cum Latinis differre: quandoquidem disputatio nil aliud praeter contentionem maximam parit, nec non ipsi Latini in respondendo nunquam defecerunt, ita ut infinita fieret disputatio, si cum ipsis vellent contendere. Similiter Imperator, Iuliano Cardinali: Dico equidem, P. amp. nos amplius vobiscum disputare nolle, quandoquidem verbis abundatis, ac ipsa dialectica vobis venit, ut nunquam satiari velitis, verum semper differre, ad extremum autem vehementissime perorare, statimque consurgere, ac sessionem dimittere, ut animos auditorum ad vestram orationem flectatis. Omisso igitur multiloquio, viam quâ Dei benignitate coniungi possimus, excogitemus. Idemque ad Papam, significans suorum indignationem, & quo minus vel Latinis consentire, vel ad hoc per ipsum cogi possent: Nonnulli praesules nostri, Latinorum petitionem credentes congruam rationi non esse, volunt ei acquiescere; difficileque eis videtur, dogma majorsuorum tam subito dimittere, cum semper crediderint, Latinorum fuisse sententiam, Spiritum sanctum duas subsistentiales causas habere, propterea quæ noluerint illud, Ex Filioque suscipientes nobiscum pacem componere. Nobis ergo non esse est, ut patrias leges moresque servemus. Ego vero qui conventui nostro (ut paulo ante dixi) non impero, ipsum tyrannice cogere nolo, ut quicquam præter ejus voluntatem dicat vel agat, ita ut in hoc quod à me, pater beatissime, petis, minime tibi satisfacere valeam. Tandem ad faciendam unionem stimulante hinc Imperatore, propter commodum quod Imperio suo proventurum sperabat, inde Papa sumtus suos & studia identidem exprobrante, Græcorum aliqui cum Romanis coëundum censuerunt, alii minus, & custodiendas potius Patrum suorum sanctiones ac placita, inter quos præcipuus Marcus Ephesius, qui primus à sessionibus publicis abstinuit, unaque cum eo Heraclëensis Antistes, Patriarchæ Alexandrini, uti ille Antiocheni, vicarius, qui proinde sess. xxv. adversus Græcorum alios, unionem flagrantius expetentes in hunc modum verba fecit: Num Occidentales doctores sanctis nostris doctoribus, ac synodorum patribus plures sunt? qui quidem sancti nostri Spiritum sanctum ex patre, non autem ex filio procedere, litteris mandaverunt. Quem sermonem Ephesius excipiens prolixam habuit orationem, in peroratione autem protulit Latinos hæreticos, nedum schismaticos esse, idque Orientalem ecclesiam tolerasse, quod genus ipsorum majus ac fortius esset, propterea que Græcos tot annos ab eis disjunctos esse, quod hæretici sunt. Dicebat igitur, se cum Latinis nequaquam debere conjungi, prius quam additionem illam à symbolo prorsus auferant. Hinc porro in Actis Concilii legitur: Tum Græcorum conventus in duas partes divisus fuit: nam altera pacem cum Latinis vehementer desiderabat, altera vero dissidii authoribus favens, ab eâ mirum in modum abhorrebat. Cui quoque parti Græcorum nobilium & laicorum plurimi vehementer favebant, singulis tamen diebus frequentes abs- que quæ Latinis conveniebant, ut quidem agerent, Latinis responderent, inter se consulerent. Attamen perfunctè denique Græci, quod quamvis Latina Ecclesia docet Spiritum procedere à Patre Filioque, non statuerit idcò duo principia, vel ex duobus principiis, causis & spirationibus Spiritum Sanctum procedere, sed ex uno, ex Patre, per Filium, acquievere: factaque unionis litteræ, quibus testati, ut hæc fidei veritas ab omnibus Christianis credatur & suscipiatur, sicque omnes profiteantur, quia Spiritus sanctus ex Patre & Filio æternaliter est, & essentiam suam, suumque esse subsistens habet ex Patre simul & Filio, & ex utroque æternaliter tanquam ab uno principio & unicâ spiratione procedit, declarantes quòd id quòd sancti doctores & patres dicunt, ex patre per filium procedere Spiritum sanctum, ad hanc intelligentiam tendit. Subscripserunt-que tum Græci, excepto Marco Ephesino, & Latini anno MCCCCXXXIX. pridie Nonas Iulii. Disputatum fuit de illo solum articulo, processionis Spiritus, neque concessum Græcis alias quæstiones ingredi: unde quum Pontifex sedulo insisteret, ut eodem pacto etiam reliquas absolverent controversias, de purgatorio igne, & de summi pontificis primatu, & de azymo & fermentato pane, de divina denique panis transmutatione, respondebant Græci: Nos, pater sanctissime, nullam adhuc respondendi facultatem habemus. Perrexerunt autem suo nomine atque in arena respondere ad gratiam Pontificis, non vero ad sensum & sententiam suarum Ecclesiarum: quod perfunctorie & obiter Pontifex (neque hæc in Synodo acta, sed privatim cum Pontifice) attamen avide arripuit, atque unionis litteris inseruit, contra ac Græci testati erant, ne de alia quæstione præter illam de Spiritus sancti processione, in unionis litteris ulla mentio fieret. Atque antea dixerant: se sine totius Orientalis Ecclesiæ authoritate quæstionem aliam tractare non posse, cum pro illa tantum de Spiritus Sancti processione Synodus convocata fuerit. Ipseque
units.tr: The Emperor of the Greeks, John Palaeologus, and the Patriarch of Constantinople, Joseph, came to Ferrara with many of the Eastern prelates. The Latins, as the Council of Basel had promised, bore the costs. They were received with great honour and splendour and were conducted to the city of Ferrara, where the Council then sat. Four months later, during which some skirmishes of disputation took place, the first session began on the eighth day of October. They then took up the matter in earnest and debated continuously about the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, or rather about the addition of the Filioque to the creed. The Greeks argued that the schism between the Churches had its origin here: the Romans had added it on their own authority, without waiting for a general council and without the judgment of the Eastern Church. This was especially so because the Third General Council of Ephesus, against Nestorius, had laid down that no one might be permitted to add to or take away from the creed. The Latins, however, said that this should not be regarded as an addition to the creed but only as an explanation and declaration, and that nothing contrary to the truth or to the doctrine of the Church was contained in that article. The Greeks laid the blame for the schism on the Romans. Hence Mark of Ephesus, who took the leading part in the speaking, began the third session in this way: But since, indeed, the Roman Church had already fallen away from the other good thing, that is, from the mutual goodwill of friendship towards its sister Church, and had feigned for itself a private right, and had kept it for itself perpetually, which was neither left in the sacred letters, nor celebrated by the universal councils, nor received and handled by our forefathers, and it is certain beyond doubt that this was the reason for dissolving our friendship as soon as it began. He was hinting at the dogma of the procession of the Holy Spirit, the only matter discussed through all the sessions. The Archbishop of Nicaea, Bessarion, who was afterwards made a Cardinal, likewise argued that this was the cause of the schism, in his oration delivered in the Council, in favour of union. After a long and sharp disputation between the parties, when the matter had turned into strife, the Greeks withdrew from the public sessions. After the twenty-fifth, or last, session, when they met only privately in the house of the Patriarch (who could not attend the Council because of his weakness, and of which he died there), they sent messengers to Pope Eugenius, who presided, and declared that they were unwilling to delay any longer with the Latins, since the disputation produces nothing but the greatest contention, and since the Latins never failed in answering, so that the disputation would go on endlessly if they wished to contend with them. The Emperor likewise said to Cardinal Julian: I say indeed, most reverend Father, that we are unwilling to dispute any longer with you, since you have such an abundance of words and such dialectic skill that you never wish to be satisfied but always to delay, and finally to plead most vehemently, and at once to rise and dismiss the session, so that you may turn the minds of the hearers to your oration. Therefore, setting aside much talk, let us devise a way by which, by God's kindness, we may be joined. He said the same to the Pope, indicating the indignation of his people and that they could not be brought, either by the Latins or by him, to agree to this: Some of our prelates, believing that the Latins' request is not reasonable, wish to yield to it; yet it seems difficult to them to let go so suddenly of the greater dogma of our people, since they have always believed that the teaching of the Latins was that the Holy Spirit has two subsistential causes; therefore they were unwilling to make peace with us by accepting the Filioque. For us, then, it is not possible to do otherwise than keep our country's laws and customs. As for me, I do not (as I said a little earlier) command our assembly, and I am unwilling to force it tyrannically to say or do anything beyond its own will; so that in what you, most blessed Father, ask of me, I am by no means able to satisfy you. At last, to bring about the union, the Emperor urged it on account of the advantage which he hoped would result for his empire, while the Pope on the other side repeatedly reproached them for his expenses and efforts. Some of the Greeks thought that they should unite with the Romans, others less so, and that they should rather guard the decrees and opinions of their Fathers. Among these the chief was Mark of Ephesus, who first abstained from the public sessions, and together with him the Bishop of Heraclea, vicar of the Patriarch of Alexandria, as the former was of Antioch. He therefore, in the twenty-fifth session, spoke in this way against the other Greeks, who were more eagerly seeking union: Are the Western teachers more numerous than our holy teachers and the Fathers of the synods? Yet our holy men have committed to writing that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, not from the Son. Ephesus took up this speech and delivered a long oration; in his peroration he brought out that the Latins are heretics, not merely schismatics, and that the Eastern Church had tolerated this, because their kind was greater and stronger, and for that reason the Greeks had been separated from them for so many years, because they are heretics. He therefore said that he ought by no means to be joined with the Latins before they had altogether removed that addition from the creed. Hence in the Acts of the Council we read: Then the assembly of the Greeks was divided into two parts; for one part greatly desired peace with the Latins, while the other, favouring the authors of the dissension, shrank from it in a remarkable manner. Very many of the Greek nobles and laymen also strongly favoured this latter part, yet every day they regularly went away from the meetings with the Latins, where they were to act, answer the Latins, and consult among themselves. At length, however, the Greeks, cursorily, agreed that although the Latin Church teaches that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, it has not thereby decided that the Holy Spirit proceeds from two principles, or from two principles, causes and spirations, but from one, from the Father through the Son. The letters of union were made, in which they attested that this truth of faith is to be believed and accepted by all Christians, and so all profess that the Holy Spirit is eternally from the Father and the Son, and has his essence and his subsisting being from the Father together with the Son, and eternally proceeds from both as from one principle and one spiration, declaring that what the holy doctors and Fathers say, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, tends to this understanding. The Greeks, except Mark of Ephesus, and the Latins then subscribed, in the year 1439, on the day before the Nones of July. The dispute concerned only that one article, the procession of the Spirit, and the Greeks were not allowed to enter into other questions. Hence, when the Pontiff pressed earnestly that they should in the same way settle the remaining controversies, concerning purgatorial fire, concerning the primacy of the supreme pontiff, concerning unleavened and leavened bread, and finally concerning the divine transmutation of the bread, the Greeks replied: Most holy Father, we have as yet no faculty for answering these. They went on, however, to answer in their own name and in the arena, in response to the Pontiff's favour, and not to the sense and opinion of their Churches. The Pontiff seized on this cursorily and in passing (and these things were not done in the Council but privately with the Pontiff), yet eagerly, and inserted it in the letters of union, contrary to what the Greeks had attested, namely that there should be no mention in the letters of union of any question other than that concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. And earlier they had said that they could not treat any other question without the authority of the whole Eastern Church, since the Synod had been convened only for that question about the procession of the Holy Spirit. And the Emperor himself

units.la: quæ que Imperator, velim, ne à Latinis cogamur, ut sacro symbolo nostro quicquam apponamus, vel ceremoniarum aliquid in Ecclesiâ nostrâ mutemus. Atque ante frequentatas Ferrariæ sessiones, quando mota fuisset quæstio de Purgatorio, Græci inter se non convenichant, aliis cum Latinis se conjungentibus, aliis minus: ut jam postquam ita omnia Florentiæ conclusa, & in partes Latinorum ubique transissent Græci, domum reversi ad suos, haud mirandum quod minus grati acceptique fuerint, nec probatum omnibus illorum studium, minime quod de purgatorio igne, & primatu Papæ Romani videbantur segnius concessisse. Itaque nihil minus quam servata unio Florentina fuit. Annalium Glycæ continuatio, pag. 599. Redeuntes autem domum Græci, non amplius iis, quæ in Italiâ pacta conventaque fuisse diximus, stare voluerunt. Quapropter motus Rom. Pontifex, doctos quosdam viros Byzantium misit, ut cum Græcis in colloquium venirent, qui synodum in Italiâ coactam, ejusque decreta non admitterent. Marcus enim archiepiscopus Ephesi, & Scholarium Græcorum doctissimus, ut antea, sic nec tum quidem Latinis adsentiri volebat. Ubi ad colloquium & disputationem ventum esset, nihil efficere Romani potuerunt: sed infectâ re domum reversi sunt.
units.tr: also: I wish that we might not be forced by the Latins to add anything to our holy creed or to change anything of the ceremonies in our Church. Before the sessions at Ferrara were frequented, when the question of Purgatory had been raised, the Greeks did not agree among themselves, some joining themselves with the Latins, others less so. So, after everything had been concluded thus at Florence and the Greeks had passed everywhere to the Latin side, it is no wonder that when they returned home to their own people they were less welcome and less approved, and that their zeal was not pleasing to all, especially because they seemed to have yielded more slackly on the fire of purgatory and on the primacy of the Roman Pope. So the union of Florence was by no means kept. Continuation of the Annals of Glycas, p. 599. Returning home, the Greeks did not wish any longer to abide by what, as we have said, had been agreed and settled in Italy. Therefore the Roman Pontiff, moved by this, sent some learned men to Byzantium to come into conference with the Greeks, who would not admit the synod gathered in Italy and its decrees. For Mark, archbishop of Ephesus, and the most learned of the Greek scholars, as before, so not even then was willing to agree with the Latins. When they came to conference and disputation, the Romans could effect nothing, but returned home with the business undone.

units.la: De eodem, Auctor Turcograeciæ, lib. 1. Qui vero in urbe degebant Clerici, Hieromonachi, sacerdotes, Abbates, confessionibus audiendis præpositi (Pneumatici dicti) ac cæteri, iis molebant liturgias & sacra cum illis, qui venerant, celebrare, aut in precibus mentionem ipsorum facere, sed ab eis recedebant, tanquam qui pietatem (ut ita dicam) abjecissent. Multi sacerdotio etiam renuntiarunt. Denique unitatem divisio, concordiam discordia consecuta est.
units.tr: On the same subject, the author of the Turcograecia, book 1: "Those clergy who lived in the city, the hieromonks, priests, abbots, those set over hearing confessions (called Pneumatics), and the rest, were unwilling to celebrate liturgies and sacred rites with those who had come, or to mention them in their prayers, but withdrew from them as men who had, so to speak, cast off piety." Many also renounced the priesthood. In the end, division followed unity and discord followed concord.

units.la: Idem de Ruthenis refert, in Rerum Moscoviticarum Commentario, Sigismundus Baro: Erat quidam Metropolitanus Russiæ, Isidorum intelligit, quem Papa fecerat, cum Bessarione, Cardinalem, utpote de se egregie in Concilio, ad reducendos
units.tr: Sigismund Baron says the same about the Ruthenians in his Commentary on Muscovite Affairs: "There was a certain Metropolitan of Russia, I mean Isidore, whom the Pope had made a cardinal along with Bessarion, because he had served well at the Council in bringing the Greeks back, or rather leading them astray,

units.la: vel seducendos Graecos, meritos, qui ad nefandam Pa-pa Synodum accesserat, ubi & Ecclesiae erant unitas, reversus in patriam captus, omnibus bonis spoliatur, atque in carceres conjicitur: ex quibus tandem evasit. Hanc gravem a suis retulerunt Graeci, & Rutheni vel Russi, ex Syno-do reversi. Neque hoc mihi adeo mirum videtur, quod non majoris fructus fuerit aut Florentinum Concilium, aut composita ibi unio, quum Graecos convenisse videam actos non sensu religionis adeo, quam spe subsidii a Latinis hoc pacto impetrandi, pro conservatione Imperii, & rerum suarum, atque in eadem crimen turpiter elusos quoque a Papa, quando Imperatori illud petenti respondit simpliciter, sibi Graecorum imperium curae futurum, neque cessaturum Germanos & Hungaros ad arma adversus Turcas incitare. Quod fecit quidem, sed poenitenda oppido arte, ad persidiam & perjurium stimulatis Christianis; quod trisli ad Varnam clade, & superata Constantinopoli IV. Kal. Iul. a. MCCCCLIII. tredecim ferme post Concilium Florentinum annis; alii ponunt annum MCCCCLIII. luere Christiani debuerunt. Biennio ante captam urbem, scripsit Constantinop: Ecclesia ad Bohemos, ut fidei ejusdem socios, petens iisdem uniri: haud secundum illam Florentiae unionem simulatam, a recto verogue consilio abhorrentem, quae directio a veritate appellanda esset: quamobrem illam minime admisimus, imo prorsus ausibile vimus. Facile erat Papae, famelicos Graecos & omnium inopes ad se allectos alere sua quasi manu, variis promissis ac beneficiis demulcere, & in nassam pertrahere, suoque arbitrio subjicere, qui Imperatorem sperato subsidio, episcopos Cardinalitia dignitate, uti fecit in Bessarione Trapezuntio, & Isidoro Sarmatiae antistite, sibi devincire potuit. Atque illa necessitatis causa commovit passim Imperatores Orientis Paparum gratiam atque amicitiam ambire. Quod etiam procemium indicat Constitutionis Michaelis Palaeologi in Corpore juris Constit. penult. Proinde tot difficultatibus circumventus Imperator, ac paene ad desperationem compulsus, legatos ad Papam misit, de ineundâ Veteris & novae Romae ecclesiarum concordiâ, modo Caroli expeditionem everteret. Quis, diligenter observans acta Florentinae Synodi, non videt Graecos, quam acres initio erant, tam leves postmodum & temerarios fuisse ad ineundam pacem, conditionibus multum gravioribus, quam initio admissuri videbantur, quum tantâ contentione disputabant de additione ad symbolum, & postea non hoc tantum, sed majora multo, de primatu Papae, & Purgatorio &c. insimul tradiderunt, citra ullam molestiam, vel certamen, non habitâ super illis, nec singulis, nec omnibus, ullâ solemni aut seriâ disputatione, nedum sessione, vel Synodo. Vt quâvis aliâ re potius motos dicas Graecos in illorum assensum, quam ex conscientiâ veritatis. Actumque de illis non in Concilio, sed post, in privatis congressibus, in quibus privata negotia atque emolumenta liberius feliciusque tractari assolent. Quantum Graeci restiterunt initio tum Latinis, tum eorum sententiae ac dogmati, unioni quoque dum constantes adhuc in suorum dogmatum defensione perstabant, tam aegre & invitis trepidisque animis adacti postea in unionem fuerunt, quam variis cautelis moderari, ne suis nimis officeret, conabantur quidem, at frustra. Illud etiam quod Graecorum Patriarcha nunquam Synodo interfuit, qui solus Patriarcharum Orientalium aderat, cum reliquorum vicariis; & subitanea ejus mors; denique reperta ab eo ultimo scripta schedâ, in quâ agnoscere se dicit episcopi Romani suprematum, & ignem Purgatorium, eo majorem suspicionem generant, quo necdum de his articulis actum, nedum definitum quid fuerat: quae proinde tam desidiose tradidisse Patriarcham, illud inprimis de potestate Papae, quae vera & propria semper schismatis aut divisionis causa fuit, quis arbitretur?
units.tr: for he had gone to that nefarious synod of the Pope, where there was said to be unity of the Church. On returning to his homeland he was seized, stripped of all his goods, and thrown into prison, from which he at last escaped." The Greeks and the Ruthenians or Russians, returning from the synod, brought back a grave report of this. Nor does it seem to me so surprising that the Council of Florence, or the union agreed there, bore no great fruit, since I see that the Greeks came together not so much from a sense of religion as from hope of obtaining support from the Latins in this way, for the preservation of their empire and their property; and in that matter they were shamefully deceived by the Pope too, when he simply answered the Emperor, who asked for it, that the empire of the Greeks would be his concern, and that he would not cease to stir up the Germans and Hungarians to arms against the Turks. This he did indeed, but by a most shameful device, spurring Christians on to treachery and perjury; and for this the Christians had to pay with the sad defeat at Varna and the fall of Constantinople on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the year 1453, roughly thirteen years after the Council of Florence (others place the year at 1453). Two years before the city was taken, the Church of Constantinople wrote to the Bohemians, as companions in the same faith, asking to be united with them. That union at Florence was not the true and genuine one, but a feigned one, far removed from right and true counsel, and it ought to be called a deviation from the truth; for this reason we did not admit it at all, but rather saw it as utterly to be avoided. It was easy for the Pope, who drew the famished Greeks and the destitute of every kind to himself, to feed them with his own hand, to soothe them with various promises and benefits, to draw them into the net and bring them under his will. He could bind to himself the Emperor, with the hoped-for support, and the bishops with cardinalitial dignity, as he did with Bessarion of Trebizond and Isidore, bishop of Sarmatia. And it was out of this necessity that the Emperors of the East moved on all sides to court the favour and friendship of the Popes. The preamble of the constitution of Michael Palaeologus in the Corpus Juris also indicates this: Therefore the Emperor, beset by so many difficulties and almost driven to despair, sent envoys to the Pope concerning the forming of concord between the churches of Old and New Rome, if only he might overturn the expedition of Charles. Who, carefully observing the proceedings of the Florentine Synod, does not see that the Greeks, however fierce they were at first, afterwards became so light and rash in making peace, on terms far more burdensome than they seemed at first willing to accept? For they disputed with such great contention about an addition to the creed, and afterwards handed over not only this but far greater matters, concerning the primacy of the Pope, Purgatory, and so on, all together, without any trouble or struggle, with no solemn or serious disputation about them, either individually or collectively, let alone a session or a synod. So that you might say the Greeks were moved to assent to them by anything rather than by conscience of the truth. And the matter was settled not in the Council but afterwards, in private meetings, in which private affairs and advantages are wont to be handled more freely and more successfully. However stoutly the Greeks at first resisted the Latins, and their opinion and doctrine, and while they still stood firm in defending their own dogmas against union, they were afterwards driven into union so reluctantly, with unwilling and anxious minds, that they tried indeed, but in vain, to moderate it with various safeguards, lest it harm their own position too much. Also, the Patriarch of the Greeks never attended the Synod; he alone of the Eastern Patriarchs was present, with the vicars of the others. His sudden death, and the paper written by him at the end, in which he says he acknowledges the supremacy of the Roman bishop and the fire of Purgatory, give rise to all the more suspicion, since these articles had not yet been discussed, let alone defined. Who would think that the Patriarch handed these down so carelessly, especially the matter of the power of the Pope, which has always been the true and proper cause of schism or division?

units.la: Quidquid etiam his de rebus sit, hoc constat, Graecis ad sedes suas reversis, nec alios, nec ipsos quoque probasse acta Florentina, sed repudiata unionis formula, constanter recusasse colla sua subdere episcopo Romano, vel in ejus doctrinam & statuta descendere. Quare dum hic non potuit coalescere scisma, & unio tam aegre obtenta probari servarique, deinceps negotium longius abiit, patuitque tandem frustra concordiam inter Romanam Ecclesiam, & Graecos Orientales quaeri aut institui. Ut minoris facienda sint quae jam & tum magno cum strepitu jactat, vel fingit aliquorum Orientalium ad se accessum Romana Ecclesia, quorum nonnulla confecta, alia emendicata, vel paucorum hominum sunt, pauca spontanea, vel libera, nedum universalia.
units.tr: Whatever the truth of these matters, this is certain: when the Greeks returned to their own sees, neither others nor they themselves approved the Florentine proceedings, but, rejecting the formula of union, they steadfastly refused to bow their necks to the Roman bishop or to submit to his doctrine and decrees. Hence, since schism could not take hold here, and a union so reluctantly obtained could not be approved or preserved, the business went on for a long time afterwards, and it became plain at last that concord between the Roman Church and the Eastern Greeks was sought and attempted in vain. So less weight should be given to what the Roman Church already then boasted of with great noise, or pretended, namely that some Easterners had come over to it; some of these arrangements were made, others were begged for, and they belong to a few men; few were spontaneous or free, let alone universal.

units.la: Et quam non mirum aliquos semper reperiri, qui speciem beneficiorum impetrandorum, vel metu alienae potentiae, ad Romanam Ecclesiam vel confugisse, vel confugere se simulant, ita minus hoc, quod sincera mente nequeant alii impetrare a se ut cum Ecclesia se conjungant, quae potestatem tyrannicam in quoscunque exercet suo fastuoso Papae primatu: qui articulus primus & perpetuus fuit disjuncti a Latinis Orientis. Ut ipse Bellarminus dicat, in Praefatione, ad lib. de Rom. Pontifice: Primi, qui serio primatum Romani Pontificis oppugnarunt, videntur fuisse Graeci. Eamque fere unicam divortii Graecorum a Latinis causam fuisse nil necesse probare post Nilum Thessalonicensem archiepiscopum, qui hoc ipsum singulari libello demonstravit, de causis dissensionum Ecclesiasticarum. Atque inter Romanos Papistas Abrahamus Bzovius, Annal. Tom. XVI. ad a. CIↃ CCCC XXXVIII in initio, dissidiorum inter Graecos Latinosque causam conjicit in Constantinopolitanam Ecclesiam, quae Romanae sedis semper aemula fuerit potestatem. Nolo equidem Constantinopolitanorum veteri partes, qui & ipsi quoque nimis imprudenter affectarunt Romani episcopi factum, eadem acti vanitate & ambitione. Quod tamen minus ferendum in Romano fuit, quo non in plures, uti ille, sed in omnes, atque, quod ille nunquam in istum tentavit, hic in illum etiam, & reliquos omnes Patriarchas deberi sibi supremam & Christi vicariam potestatem, temere asseruit. Quis hoc aequo animo ferat uno in homine, in episcopo, ut non satis ei videatur suis dominari, nisi etiam exteris, alienis, & omnibus imperitet, & seu Urbis se efferat principatu, seu vana Petri successione, non cogitet, Petri Christique successores, ad eorum exemplum nil prius decere quam animi humilitatem, & dominationis fugam atque odium? Revera doctores humiles duces superbi, uti Gregorius I. Romanus episcopus dicebat de Iohanne Constantinopolitano, quando se universalem episcopum incipiebat scribere, qui titulus aeque Romano, & Constantinopolitano ab illo tempore usurpatus, neque alia ex causa ab illo in isto reprehensus, nisi quod sibi soli arrogatum cuperet, saltem ejus successores, superbi atque pompatici sermonis inventionem, uti de eo ipse ille Gregorius scribit ad Imp. Mauritium. Absit a cordibus Christianorum nomen blasphemiae, in quo omnium fere detestabilis honor adimitur, dum ab uno sibi dementer arrogatur. Nolo ingredi de Primatu Papae controversiam, hoc tantum dico, illis rationibus cum a Graecis confessum, quibus a Protestantibus solet, ut unius sententiae apparet nos esse cum illis, & vix requiri ut aliis contundatur quam quibus a Graecis factum id videmus argumentis. Quod ad Petrum Apostolum spectat, a cujus exemplo & successione primatum suum deducunt Romani, respondet Barlaam monachus, quod Petro, idem reliquis concessum fuisse Apostolis ἰσοτίμως. Et non a Petro derivari illud, quodcunque is habuerit, ad successores Romanos, cum nec Petrum Romae episcopum fuisse, aut quod Clemens ordinarit primatum, unquam quis dixerit: etiam quod hoc primatum, non magis pro Romano possit adferri, quam pro Alexandrino, vel etiam Ierosolymitano, quorum hic sedem istam tenet, ubi Christus (quod magis ei, quam si forte Petrus Romae) mortuus. Praeterea, inquit Balaam, quam absurdum illud est & à ratione abhorrens; ut eorum quidem Apostolorum unusquisque nostrum communem pastorem orbis terrarum, perinde atque Petrum, fuisse: eorum autem neminem, praeter solum Petrum, successorem reliquisse?
