Illo etiam argumento Nilus usus, de Primatu Papae, dicens: Si vero, quia Petrus Romae diem suum obiit, idcirco Romanam sedem magnam essse; profecto Hierosolymorum sedes major digniorque erit, in qua Servator noster Iesus Christus vivificam mortem obiit. Iam vero à Patribus & Regibus dicunt episcopum Romanum primariam dignitatem tenere, non à Christo, vel à Petro: illudque propter dignitatem urbis, ad exemplum ordinis politici, [illegible, ~6 letters] [?] Sed paria jura Patres concesserunt Constantinopolitano, secundo quidem à Romano, ordine, non dignitate vel potestate inferiori, non ut ab illo creretur, quandoquidem nec hic, nec alius quispiam Patriarcharum à Papa ordinabatur. Nilus, si vero, quia primus est in numeratione, idcirco denominatus accipiis, concede hoc ipsum etiam Constantinopolitano, nam & hic praeponitur Alexandrino. Alexandrinus vero eadem ratione sub se habet Antiochenum, hic vero rursum Hierosolymitanae sedi praefert. [Greek, illegible, ~8 words] quod autem Papa primatus coordinatus est, non exceptus, liquet. Ipsumque non esse majoris ordinis quam episcopum, Nilus hinc probat, quia non modo episcopus à Patribus vocatur, sed quoque ab episcopis ipse ordinatur, quod non fieret, si ipse episcopo major esset. Neque enim quispiam alteri impertiri potest, quod ipsemet non habuit. Deinde ex Dionysio ostendit, quomodo eo tempore omnis ecclesiastica hierarchia divisa fuit in diaconos, sacerdotes, & episcopos, ut tunc nulla dignitas major majot vel superior fuerit episcopali. Quod autem Romanam vocant sedem apostolicam, quasi hoc pacto singulare aut superius quid ei attribuatur, ostendit Nilus, appellationem illam aliis quoque catholicis fratribus communem esse, ut ipsorum sedes dicantur sedes apostolicae; catholicam vero Ecclesiam Romanam temere dici, Barlaam probat. Atque contra infallibilitatem Papae, objiciunt exemplum P. Honorii, a sexta Synodo propter haeresim anathemate perculsi, quod apud Nilum aliquoties repetitur; & Papissam Iohannam profert Barlaamus. Atque ita in reliquis. Ut omnino constet, Graecos adferre adversus Papae principatum tam egregia solidaque arma, ac quis alius: prae quibus levia & inania sunt, quae ad aucupandam Papae gratiam mercenarii Graeci Bessarion, aut Gennadius, protulerunt.
units.tr: How unsurprising it is that there are always some who, either from fear of another's power or in hope of gaining benefices, pretend to have fled, or to be fleeing, to the Roman Church. It is far less surprising that others cannot sincerely bring themselves to join the Church, which exercises tyrannical power over whomever it likes through its proud papal primacy. This article was the first and perpetual cause of the Eastern separation from the Latins. Bellarmine himself says, in the preface to his book on the Roman Pontiff: "The first who seriously attacked the primacy of the Roman Pontiff seem to have been the Greeks." That this was almost the sole cause of the Greeks' divorce from the Latins need not be proved, since Nilus, archbishop of Thessalonica, demonstrated exactly this in a separate little book, on the causes of ecclesiastical dissensions. Among the Roman Papists, Abraham Bzovius, in the opening of his Annals, vol. XVI, under the year 1438, traces the cause of the disagreements between Greeks and Latins to the Church of Constantinople, which has always been jealous of the power of the Roman See. I am not inclined to defend the old partisans of Constantinople, who also too rashly aspired to the position of Roman bishop, driven by the same vanity and ambition. Yet this was less intolerable in the case of Rome, since Rome did not claim this power over some, as Constantinople did, but over all; and, what Constantinople never attempted against Rome, Rome rashly asserted against Constantinople and all the other patriarchs, that supreme power as Christ's vicar was owed to itself. Who could bear this with equanimity in one man, in one bishop, so that it seems not enough for him to rule over his own people unless he also lords it over outsiders, aliens and everyone else, whether he exalts himself by the princedom of the City or by the empty succession of Peter, and does not consider that the successors of Peter and of Christ ought, following their example, to think of nothing sooner than humility of spirit and the flight from and hatred of domination? Indeed, "humble teachers, proud leaders", as Gregory I, Roman bishop, said of John of Constantinople when that man began to style himself universal bishop. This title, once usurped by John, was afterwards used equally by the Roman and the Constantinopolitan bishops, and Gregory rebuked it in him for no other reason than that he wished it to be claimed for himself alone, or at least that his successors should not invent "a proud and pompous form of speech", as Gregory himself writes of him to the emperor Maurice. "Let the name of blasphemy be far from the hearts of Christians, a name by which the honour of almost all others is taken away, while it is arrogated to himself by one man in his madness." I do not wish to enter into the controversy over the primacy of the Pope. I say only this: the Greeks have conceded it on the same grounds on which the Protestants usually argue, so that it appears we agree with them in opinion, and it is hardly needed to refute it with other arguments than those by which we see the Greeks have done so. As for the Apostle Peter, from whose example and succession the Romans derive their primacy, the monk Barlaam replies that the same power was granted to the other Apostles on equal terms [ἰσοτίμως]; that whatever Peter had did not pass from him to the Roman successors, since no one has ever said that Peter was bishop of Rome, or that Clement ordained the primacy; and that this primacy can be claimed for the Roman see no more than for Alexandria, or even for Jerusalem, where Christ, rather than Peter, died, if Peter had perhaps died at Rome. Moreover, says Barlaam, "how absurd and contrary to reason it is that each of those Apostles should be considered our common pastor of the whole world, just as Peter was, and yet none of them, except Peter alone, should have left a successor!" Nilus also used this argument, saying in his book on the primacy of the Pope: "If indeed the Roman see is great because Peter ended his days at Rome, then surely the see of Jerusalem will be greater and worthier, where our Saviour Jesus Christ died the death that gives life." Moreover, the Fathers and kings say that the Roman bishop holds the first dignity, not from Christ or from Peter, but because of the dignity of the city, as a pattern of the political order, [illegible, ~6 letters] [?]. But the Fathers granted equal rights to the Constantinopolitan bishop, who was second to the Roman in order, though not inferior in dignity or power, and not so that he should be created by Rome, since neither he nor any other patriarch was ordained by the Pope. Nilus says: "If indeed you accept that he is named first because he is first in the numbering, then grant this to the Constantinopolitan as well, for he too is placed before the Alexandrian. The Alexandrian, by the same reasoning, has the Antiochene under him, and he in turn places the Jerusalem see after himself." [Greek, illegible, ~8 words] "That the Pope, however, was co-ordinated and not excepted, is clear." Nilus also proves from this that he is not of a higher order than a bishop, because he is called bishop not only by the Fathers but is also ordained by bishops himself, "which would not happen if he were greater than a bishop. For no one can impart to another what he himself does not have." Then, from Dionysius, he shows how at that time the whole ecclesiastical hierarchy was divided into deacons, priests and bishops, so that no dignity was then greater or higher than the episcopal. As for their calling the Roman See the apostolic see, as if some singular or higher privilege were attributed to it by this means, Nilus shows that this title is common to other Catholic brethren as well, so that their sees too are called apostolic; and Barlaam proves that calling the Roman Church catholic is rash. Against the infallibility of the Pope, they bring forward the example of Pope Honorius, struck with anathema by the sixth Synod for heresy, which Nilus repeats several times; and Barlaam produces Pope Joan. And so on through the rest. So it is clear that the Greeks brought against the primacy of the Pope arms as excellent and solid as any others; beside them, the light and empty things which the mercenary Greeks Bessarion or Gennadius put forward to win the Pope's favour are trivial.

units.la: Quod deinde Nestorianam, vel Eutychianam, aut hinc enatas haereses concernit, & Orientales infecit Ecclesias, id non adeo consideramus ut quid ipsorum adversus Latinos, quam quod adversus veritatem, & communem Ecclesiarum orthodoxiam suas his Ecclesias deformarunt, quorum apud se, ac apud nos, aliosque habent adversarios quamplurimos. Sed quia non exiguam Orientalium Ecclesiarum partem a longissimo tempore illa infestarunt, hodieque asseclas habent non paucos, catenus attendenda illa nobis sunt atque examinanda, omissa disputatione, quae in Veterum scriptis hodieque extantibus copiose legi potest. Videantur Gelasius episc. Romanus, de duabus naturis in Christo, adversus Nestorium, & Eutychem: Vigilius, contra Eutychem, libris v. extant quoque in Bibliotheca Patrum. Leontius Byzantinus contra Nestorium, & Eutychem, libris iii. Maximi Disputatio, cum Pyrrho Constantinopolitano; aliique.
units.tr: As for the Nestorian or Eutychian heresies, or those born from them, which infected the Eastern Churches, we are not so concerned with what they have done against the Latins as with how, against the truth and the common orthodoxy of the Churches, they have deformed these Churches with their errors; and they have very many opponents among themselves, among us, and among others. But since these heresies have troubled no small part of the Eastern Churches from a very long time, and still have not a few followers today, we must attend to them and examine them so far as is needed, leaving aside a dispute which can be read at length in the writings of the Ancients that still survive today. Let the following be consulted: Gelasius, Roman bishop, On the Two Natures in Christ, against Nestorius and Eutyches; Vigilius, against Eutyches, in five books, which are also extant in the Bibliotheca Patrum; Leontius of Byzantium, against Nestorius and Eutyches, in three books; the Disputation of Maximus with Pyrrhus of Constantinople; and others.

units.la: In quaestione de coniugio, vel caelibatu Clericorum, in praecipuo nobiscum conveniunt, contra Romanos, quod non repugnare contendunt, ut quis simul sit con-jugatus, & Ecclesiastico fungatur munere. At excipiunt, ne sit bigamus; id est, ne ad alteras transferit nuptias, quod non admittunt in Clerico: non quidem damnant, sed non coronant, etiam in laico: castitas omnino reiiciunt. Unde in Unione Ruffonum Polonorum cum Romana Ecclesia, a. MDXCV. expresso articulo stipulati fuerunt: matrimonia sacerdotalis ut integra consistent, exceptis bigamis. Novella cxxiii. cap. xii. Clericos non aliter ordinari permittimus, nisi liberos suscipiant, & rectam fidem, vitamque habeant irreprehensibilem: & neque concubinam aut naturales habuerint aut habeant filios, sed caste viventes, aut uxorem legitimam, & ipsam unam & primam habentes; neque viduam, neque separatam a viro; neque aliter legibus aut sacris canonibus interdictam. Tam pro hoc, quam illo, id est, quod uxorem habere liceat, & tantum unam oporteat, proferunt Scripturae quaedam loca. Confessio Æthiopum, apud Damianum à Goës: Et id, quod Presbyteri apud nos uxores possideant, ex Paulo accepimus, qui mavult clericum & laicum nubere, quam uri. Is quoque inquit, oportere Episcopum virum unius uxoris esse, & irreprehensibilem, sobrium: parique modo vult esse diaconos. Patres Trullani, can. xiii. pro non dissolvendis Sacerdotum conjugiis, adferebant tum Christi illud: quod Deus conjunxit, homo ne separet; tum Pauli, ligatus es uxori, ne quaeras solutionem: Quam fit hodiernorum Graecorum hac super re constans sententia, discces optime ex Ieremiae Patriarchae Constantinop. Responso ad Tubingenses Theologos: Secundo dicitis, melius esse matrimonium contrahere, quam uri: secundum illud unius mulieris virum, & cetera D. Pauli praecepta. Ideo nos quoque illis Sacerdotibus, qui se continere non possunt, antequam Sacerdotes consecrati sunt, conjugii usum permittimus. Deus enim conjugium praecepit. Nec ignoramus, conjugio Sacerdotibus interdicto, turpia ab ipsis commissi. Qui vero castae[?]sem vovit, castitatem servet: tali, post votum factum, marito esse non permittimus. Nemo enim qui manu suâ aratro impositâ, se retrò verlit, idoneus est ad Regnum cœleste. Quod si infirmitate humanâ lapsus fit, castigamus eum, poenitendo, confitendo, caeteras frictiones subeundo, & à malis abstinendo, donec ablutus sit: tunc miserticordia Dei non reprobabit ipsum. In diaconum autem nemo consecratur, nisi conjugatus. Unde plerunque & nuptias celebrare, & in gradum diaconatus simul ordinari solent. Si vero sponsa diaconi male audit, in diaconum ipse, nisi integræ famæ uxorem duxerit, non consecratur. Mortua conjuge, sacerdos à sacris obeundis prorsus suspenditur: si caste tamen vivit, officiis ac aliis rebus divinis, cum cæteris Ecclesiæ ministris, choro tanquam minister interesse potest. Erat quidem antea consuetudo, ut vidui caste viventes, sine reprehensione sacra peragerent. Sed nunc mos invaluit, ut nullus viduorum ad sacra facienda permittatur, nisi monasterium aliquod ingrediatur, juxtaque regulam vivat. Quicunque sacerdos viduus, ad secundas nuptias, quod cuique liberum est, transierit, nihil habet cum clero commune. Hæc de illis Sigismundus Baro. Alexander Guagninus Veronensis, in Descriptione Moscoviæ, cap. 11. Sacerdotes Romanos confundunt, qui cœlibem vitam ducere Iese juramento obstringunt, cum sancta Synodus, quæ fuit in Gangra, scribat in quarto canone: qui spernit sacerdotem secundum legem uxorem habentem, dicens quod non liceat de manibus ejus sacramentum sumere, anathema sit. Id eadem Synodus dicit, ut omnis sacerdos & diaconus propriam uxorem dimittens, sacerdotio privetur. Ita & Scripturam, & canones pro suâ sententiâ adferunt. Denique Latinis applicat illud Pauli 1 Tim. 1v. 2. doctrinis dæmonum prohibentium nubere, Nicetas Pectoratus, in libello contrà Latinos, ad quem respondit Humbertus Cardinalis. Verùm quod ad locum Apostoli pro monogamis, qui & pluribus, praeter Graecos, difficultatem movit, 1 Tim. 111. 2. decet episcopum esse unius uxoris: cum alii ita intelligunt, ut non liceat episcopo plures habere uxores, sive ex usitata polygamia, sive ex temerario repudio assumtas; alii quod numquam liceat episcopo plures habere aut habuisse, quem in sensum Graeci illud capiunt, & ex Latinis plures: quibus hactenus accedunt Pontificii; Bellarminus, lib. 1. de Clericis, cap. xxiii. ex Nostris Salmasius, lib. de Trapezitico foenore, pag. 51. &c. Priorem expositionem vulgo sequuntur Theologi nostri, seu locum illum interpretantur in suis Commentariis, seu vindicent in disputatione cum Pontificiis: ortamque regulam ajunt ex perversa sive Iudaeorum, sive Gentilium consuetudine, ubi uni marito plures, nec intercedente morte, sed vel per polygamiam cumulativam, aut et repudio diversarum, contingebant aliquando uxores, quod in episcopo non tolerandum Apostolus censuit. Dicere, tum temporis bigamiam aut polygamiam cumulativam in usu aut more non fuisse, valde dubito ne satis certum sit: quum Seneca, cujus aetate Paulus vixit, in hunc morem invehatur, lib. 111. de beneficiis, cap. xvi. postquam dixisset, quomodo pudorem ri tolleret peccantium multitudo, & commune maledictum desineret esse probri loco, quod exemplo hoc commonstraturus, nunquid jam illa, inquit, repudia erubescit, postquam illustres quaedam ac nobiles feminae, non consulum numero, sed maritorum annos suos computant, & exeunt matrimonii causa, nubunt parricidii? Tam diu illud timebatur, quamdiu rarum erat. Idemque Juvenalis exprobrat, Satyra vi.
units.tr: In the question of marriage or celibacy of the clergy, they agree with us on the main point, against the Romans, in holding that it is not inconsistent for a man to be married and also to discharge an ecclesiastical office. But they make one exception: he must not be a bigamist, that is, he must not have passed to a second marriage, and this they do not allow in a cleric. They do not condemn such a man outright, but they do not crown him, and this applies to a layman as well. They wholly reject celibacy. Hence, in the Union of the Ruthenian Poles with the Roman Church in 1595, by an expressly stated article they stipulated: that the marriages of priests should remain intact, except for bigamists. Novella 123, chapter 12: We permit clerics to be ordained only if they have children, hold the right faith, and live an irreproachable life, and if they have neither a concubine nor natural children, or, if they have them, they live chastely; or if they have a lawful wife, and that wife is his one and first wife; and not a widow, nor one separated from her husband, nor one otherwise forbidden by the laws or the sacred canons. They adduce certain passages of Scripture both for this view and for the other, namely that it is permissible to have a wife, and that one only ought to be had. The Confession of the Ethiopians, as reported by Damian a Goes: That the priests among us have wives we have received from Paul, who prefers that a cleric and a layman marry rather than burn. He also says that a bishop ought to be the husband of one wife, irreproachable and sober; and he wishes deacons to be likewise. The Trullan Fathers, canon 13, in favour of not dissolving the marriages of priests, then cited the words of Christ, what God has joined together, let not man put asunder, and the words of Paul, you are bound to a wife, do not seek a release. How firm the present opinion of the Greeks is on this matter you may learn very well from the reply of Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople, to the Tübingen theologians: Secondly, you say that it is better to marry than to burn, according to the saying "the husband of one wife," and the other precepts of St. Paul. Therefore we too permit the use of marriage to those priests who cannot contain themselves, before they are consecrated priests. For God commanded marriage. Nor are we unaware that, although marriage is forbidden to priests, they have committed shameful things. But whoever has vowed chastity, let him keep it: we do not permit such a man to be married after the vow has been made. For no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven. But if he has fallen through human weakness, we chastise him by repentance, confession, undergoing the other penances, and abstaining from evil, until he is cleansed; then the mercy of God will not reject him. No one is consecrated deacon unless he is married. Hence they usually celebrate the wedding and are ordained to the rank of deacon at the same time. If, however, the betrothed of a deacon is ill spoken of, the deacon himself is not consecrated, unless he has taken a wife of unblemished reputation. When a wife has died, a priest is wholly suspended from performing sacred duties; yet if he lives chastely, he may take part in the services and other divine offices, with the other ministers of the Church, in the choir, as a minister. Formerly it was indeed the custom that widowers who lived chastely might perform sacred rites without reproach. But now the custom has prevailed that none of the widowers is permitted to perform sacred rites unless he enters some monastery and lives according to its rule. Whatever priest, being a widower, passes to a second marriage, which is free to everyone, has nothing more in common with the clergy. These things are reported by Sigismund Baron (Herberstein). Alexander Guagninus of Verona, in his Description of Muscovy, chapter 11: They confound the Roman priests, who bind themselves by oath to lead a celibate life, since the holy Synod that was held at Gangra writes in its fourth canon: whoever despises a priest who has a wife according to the law, saying that it is not lawful to receive the sacrament from his hands, let him be anathema. The same Synod says that every priest and deacon who puts away his own wife shall be deprived of the priesthood. Thus they bring forward both Scripture and the canons in support of their view. Finally, they apply to the Latins that saying of Paul, 1 Tim. 4. 2, doctrines of demons forbidding to marry, as Nicetas Pectoratus does in his little book against the Latins, to which Cardinal Humbert replied. But as for the passage of the Apostle concerning monogamists, which has caused difficulty for others besides the Greeks, 1 Tim. 3. 2, a bishop must be the husband of one wife: some understand it to mean that a bishop may not have several wives, whether taken in the customary manner of polygamy or by the rash practice of divorce; others that a bishop may never have had or have several. In this sense the Greeks take it, and among the Latins several do. To these up to now the Papists also add themselves: Bellarmine, book 1, On Clerics, chapter 23; and among our own, Salmasius, in his On Banking Interest, p. 51, etc. Our theologians generally follow the former interpretation, whether they explain that passage in their commentaries or defend it in disputation with the Papists. They say that the rule arose from the perverse custom either of the Jews or of the Gentiles, where a single husband sometimes had several wives, not because of death intervening, but through cumulative polygamy or through the divorce of several. The Apostle judged that this could not be tolerated in a bishop. I very much doubt whether it is sufficiently certain that at that time bigamy or cumulative polygamy was not in use or custom, since Seneca, in whose lifetime Paul lived, inveighs against this practice in book 3 On Benefits, chapter 16. After saying how the multitude of sinners removes shame and how the common reproach ceases to be a disgrace, intending to illustrate this with an example, he says: Does not the divorce now blush, since certain illustrious and noble women count their years not by the number of consuls but by the number of their husbands, and leave a marriage for the sake of marriage, and marry for the sake of murder? That practice was feared as long as it was rare. The same Juvenal reproaches it in Satire 6.

units.la: sic sunt octo mariti
units.tr: Thus there are eight husbands

units.la: Quinque per autumnos: titulo res digna sepulchri.
units.tr: Five by autumns: a thing worthy of a tomb for its title.

units.la: Isti hominum mores erant, ea consuetudo: & quod in mulieribus, id in viris quoque, & in his quidem prius, iterabatur, utcunque contra leges inter ipsos latas, rectamque rationem, & placita sapien-tum committeretur. Atque apud Iudaeos ad sua usque tempora servatum memorat Iustinus, coram Tryphone Iudaeo, ut ex Magistrorum suorum scitis liceret cuique quatuor aut quinque uxores habere: & quod siquis formosam conspicatus eam concupisceret, Iacobi & aliorum Patriarcharum exemplo id excusarent probarentque. Quod Iudaeis, & Gentilibus usitatum olim fuisse, scribit in Apostoli locum Theodoretus. Ut non tam alte inclamare opus sit, quasi hoc nuspiam moris fuisset Apostolorum aevo, quod in Episcopo videtur Apostolus improbare, si plurium uxorum, & non morte succedentium, vir fuerit. Quin in Consultis Bulgarorum, ad quae respondit P. Nicolaus I. id adhuc fuit, cap. 11. Si liceat uno tempore habere duas uxores? Atque ad Iudaeorum morem Paulum respexisse Chrysostomus quoque indicat, dum locum exponens, ait: Iudaeis autem licitum erat, ἡ δὲ δύο ἔχειν τὰς γυναῖκας , id est, bigamis esse successive & cumulative. Itaque plerique passim exponunt, Apostolum velle ut episcopus sit unius uxoris vir, non plurium, sive per simplicem polygamiam, sive quod propius accedit, per temerarium unius alteriusve repudium, & amplexus promiscuos. Quod in laicis reprehendit canon dictus Apostolicus XLVII. εἴ τις λαικὸς τὴν ἰδίαν γυναῖκα ἐκβάλλων, ἐπέχει βάλη, ἢ παρ' ἄλλης ἀπολελυμένην, ἀφορίζεσθω. Ex versione Gentiani Herveti: si quis laicus uxorem propriam pellens, alteram vel ab alio dimissam duxerit, communione privetur. Quod multo magis reprehendendum in episcopo. Ut autem dicam quod sentio, existimo per istud μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνδρα Apostolum non velle an unius, an plurium uxorum possit esse episcopus vir, sed simpliciter ut uxoratus sit, non de necessitate quidem, sed quantum ad σωφροσύνην requiri videtur: ut μιᾶς non sit unius, sed aliquis uxoris vir. Quemadmodum εἷς, μία, in scriptis Novi Testamenti aliquoties sumitur. Matth. VIII. 19. εἶς γραμματεύς, προσελθὼν εἶπεν αὐτῷ, Magister, sequar te quocunque ieris. Item Marc. XII. 19. μία γυνή? cap. XXI. 19. μίαν ... vers. 24. interrogabo & ego vos λόγον ... cap. XXVI. 69. & venit ad ipsum μία παιδίσκη. Ioan. VI. 9. ἓν παιδάριον. Luc. V. 12. ἐν μιᾷ τῶν πόλεων. Εἷς & μία pro τις, vel ἑνὸς, ut apud Marcum, XIV. 51. Ergo μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνήρ, alicuius uxoris vir. Vel pone, bigamiam Apostolus taxarit, censeo quod si tamen post primum conjugium episcopus videret se non posse vivere ἀσυμπλήρωτον extra nuptias, canon is (si nempe ita intelligendus) cedere deberet graviori sti, qui in natura fundatus est, in religione matrimonii, de conjugio incundo ad compescendos ignes carnis: haec enim moralis & naturalis lex est, illa modo Ecclesiastica, & ordinis, non naturae, & quae tenet modo ne priori obsit. Neque digamia damnatur, in quocunque etiam homine, quomodo fornicatio. Chrysostomus διπλοπαρακοίτης non carere quidem dicit criminatione, πᾶσάς ἔχει τὸ γέγονος παρθένος: haud tamen peccatum constituit, quum non contra leges sit. Qua ratione Hieronymus dixit, contra Iovinianum, quod est in Iure Canonico Gratiani c. XXX I. q. I. c. Aperiant. Non damno digamos, imo nec trigamos, & si dici potest, octogamos. Alii locum Apostolicum explicarunt de matrimonio post baptismum contracto, ut tantum unum deberet esse in episcopo, quantumvis forte pluribus fuisset implicatus ante baptismum. In quem sensum profertur canon Apostolorum XVI. ὁ ἀδελφὸς γάμος συναλλάξεις μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα, ἢ παλαιὰν γυναῖκα ἔχων, ... ἢ ἀπερίστερος, ἢ ἄλλης ξένης ἀλλ' ἢ ἐγκλήμα. Atqui si de licitis nuptiis intelligatur, quare non semper licitae? vel quomodo post baptismum offendunt, quae ante baptismum licuerunt? si de illicitis, id est de vera ac prohibita polygamia, ea merito arcet ab episcopatu: atque simultanea
units.tr: Such were the manners of those people and such their custom. What was done among women was done among men too, and among men indeed it was done first, however much it was committed against the laws made among themselves, against right reason, and against the decisions of the wise. Theodoret, I think, recalls that the Jews, before the Jews' own time, kept this custom as well. Justin, in his dispute with the Jew Trypho, says that by the decrees of their own teachers it was lawful for each man to have four or five wives, and that they excused and approved any man who saw a beautiful woman and desired her, citing the example of Jacob and the other patriarchs. Theodoret, commenting on the Apostle's passage, writes that this was once common among Jews and Gentiles. We need not cry out so loudly, as though this had never been the custom in the Apostles' age, since the Apostle seems to disapprove of a bishop who has had several wives, and wives who did not succeed by death. Indeed, in the Consultations of the Bulgarians, to which Pope Nicholas I replied, chapter 11, the question was still being asked: whether it is lawful to have two wives at one time? Chrysostom also shows that Paul had in view the Jewish custom, when, expounding the passage, he says: "the Jews were allowed to have two wives" [ἡ δὲ δύο ἔχειν τὰς γυναῖκας], that is, to be bigamists in succession and at the same time. Accordingly, most commentators everywhere explain that the Apostle wants a bishop to be the husband of one wife, not of several, whether through simple polygamy or, what comes closer, through the rash divorce of one wife or another and promiscuous embraces. The canon called Apostolic, number 47, censures this in laymen: "If any layman, casting out his own wife, takes another who has been dismissed by someone else, let him be cut off" [εἴ τις λαικὸς τὴν ἰδίαν γυναῖκα ἐκβάλλων, ἐπέχει βάλη, ἢ παρ' ἄλλης ἀπολελυμένην, ἀφορίζεσθω]. In the translation of Gentian Hervet: "if any layman, putting away his own wife, takes another, or one dismissed by another, let him be deprived of communion." This ought to be censured much more in a bishop. But to say what I think: I hold that by the phrase husband of one wife [μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἀνδρα] the Apostle does not mean whether a bishop may be the husband of one wife or of several, but simply that he should be married. This is not required of necessity, but it seems to be required for sobriety [σωφροσύνην]; so that one [μιᾶς] does not mean only one, but some wife's husband. Just so, εἷς and μία are used in the writings of the New Testament in several places: Matthew 8:19, "a certain scribe [εἶς γραμματεύς] came up and said to him, Master, I will follow you wherever you go"; likewise Mark 12:19, "a wife [μία γυνή]"; chapter 21:19, "one [μίαν]"; verse 24, "I will ask you also one [λόγον] question"; chapter 26:69, "a maid [μία παιδίσκη] came to him"; John 6:9, "a little boy [ἓν παιδάριον]"; Luke 5:12, "in one [ἐν μιᾷ] of the cities." Also εἷς and μία stand for τις or ἑνὸς, as in Mark 14:51. So husband of one wife means husband of a certain wife. Or, suppose the Apostle did censure bigamy. I think that if a bishop, after his first marriage, found that he could not live unfulfilled [ἀσυμπλήρωτον] outside marriage, that canon (if it is indeed to be understood so) ought to give way to the weightier law, which is founded in nature and in the sacred character of marriage, namely the entering of marriage to quench the fires of the flesh. For that is the moral and natural law, whereas the canon is merely ecclesiastical and a rule of order, not of nature, and it holds only so far as it does no harm to the earlier marriage. Nor is second marriage condemned in any man whatever, as fornication is. Chrysostom says that the man who has had two wives [διπλοπαρακοίτης] does not indeed lack reproach, since he has had a previous wife [πᾶσάς ἔχει τὸ γέγονος παρθένος], yet he does not thereby commit sin, since it is not against the laws. For this reason Jerome, against Jovinian, said what is in Gratian's Canon Law, 31 q. 1, c. Aperiant: "I do not condemn digamists, nay, not even trigamists, and, if one may say so, octogamists." Others have explained the Apostle's passage of a marriage contracted after baptism, so that a bishop should have only one wife, however much he may have been entangled with several before baptism. In this sense the Apostolic canon 16 is quoted: "a brother who after baptism marries, or who has an old wife... or who is unmarried, or who takes another stranger, except for a charge..." But if this is understood of lawful marriages, why are they not always lawful? Or how do those things offend after baptism which were allowed before baptism? If it is understood of unlawful marriages, that is of true and forbidden polygamy, then it is rightly kept from the episcopate; and there the simultaneous or cumulative sense seems to be meant, because he is said to be caught up in those entanglements [συμπλοκαῖς], that is, in two marriages at once. Whatever the truth about the Apostle's passage, the Greeks have always been harsher against digamists, and against trigamists or polygamists who marry in succession, with ecclesiastical penalties laid down against them, namely exclusion from holy communion. Perhaps the third canon of the Synod of Neocaesarea is to be understood of this. Basil, in his canonical letter to Amphilochius, canon 4, expressly places a digamist outside communion for a year, sometimes for two years, and a trigamist often for three, four, or even five years. They did not indeed bar such people altogether from the Church, though from holy communion they did; but they admitted them to hearing [ἀκροάσεως], so that they might stand among the hearers for two or three years; then they were allowed to stand among the faithful [ὑποπίπτοντες], yet still for a long time [ἀπὸ χαλᾶς τῆς ἀγαθῆς χρονίας], until, their repentance having been proved, they were admitted to participation in communion in its proper place. A fourth marriage, however, they condemned not only ecclesiastically but also civilly, by a decree published every year in July from the platform, in the definition of Constantine Porphyrogenitus: "no one should dare to contract marriage [πίπτει γάμον μηδένι τολμῆσαι]; but if anyone should want to enter such a marriage, he is to be deprived of every ecclesiastical assembly and kept from entering the holy temple, as long as he remains in that marriage." For this, they say, also seemed good to the holy Fathers who went before us. We, making the sentence more explicit, cast him out as alien to the Christian commonwealth. As for trigamists, they limit the rule so that if he has passed forty years of age and has children from the earlier marriages, he is by no means permitted to go on to a third; but if he has no children, the trigamy is made subject to a penalty of abstention from holy communion for five years. But he who is thirty years old, and has had children from the earlier marriages, is joined to a third wife under the penalty of excommunication until the fourth year; if, however, he has no children, he is indulged to some extent, and is punished by a lighter penalty, though still a penalty. All these rules are harsh beyond fairness, as they often exercised a harsher discipline where none, or a milder one, ought to have been applied. So it should now seem less surprising to anyone that in dispensations concerning bigamy the Greeks dispense less; although it is read, in the confession of the Ethiopians made by Christopher Licanatus, or Zaga Zabo, that the patriarch of the Ethiopians also sometimes dispensed in this matter for the public good. Balsamon, on Apostolic canon 16, also indicates that some bigamists have sometimes been promoted to higher orders against the canons. In blessing marriage the Greeks use the crowning: hence the apolytroseis and stephanoseis in their liturgy, or euchologion, when the priest first places crowns on the bridegroom and then on the bride, with a solemn blessing, and they take the crowns off again on the eighth day; but in the case of bigamists they omit this. The priest indeed blesses their marriages, using the forms and prayers common for this purpose, but he does not crown bigamists; nor is this office performed during the celebration of the sacred rites, as on other occasions; and a bigamist is not admitted to it unless the period of penance has been completed. Yet this observance about the crowns is not universal.

units.la: „Stantinum episcopum est: An qui ad secundas convolat „nuptias, accipere possit bigami precationem a regionis „antistite? Responsio. Exacta quidem disciplina bigamos „coronare non novit: magnae autem ecclesiae consue„tudo haec non observat, sed bigamus etiam sponsalitias coronas imponit: nec ullus unquam per eam „causam incusatus est. Ideoque calumniam non formidabit quisquam, si tales coronaverit, nisi quod annum unum aut alterum a sacrorum mysteriorum „communione arceri debeant: nec eum qui precationem concepit, simul cum iis cibum sumere oportet.
units.tr: "Whether the bishop of Constantinople..." Is it lawful for a man who hastens into a second marriage to receive a blessing for bigamists from the bishop of the region? Answer: Strictly speaking, the discipline does not know of crowning bigamists. But the custom of the great Church does not observe this; the bigamist even receives the bridal crowns, and no one has ever been accused on that account. So no one need fear a charge of calumny if he has crowned such people, except that they ought to be kept from communion in the sacred mysteries for a year or so, and the one who has pronounced the blessing ought not to eat with them at the same time.

units.la: Ergo Graeci, qui à Romanis distant in eo, quod conjugia Ecclesiasticis relinquunt, quae isti tollunt, à nobis vero dissentiunt in hoc de bigamia; & quod ante ordinationem clericalem, non post eam, permittant conjungi; & in reliquis gradibus, excepto episcopatu: quum tamen de episcopo dicat Apostolus, quod debeat unius uxoris vir esse. & Chrysost. Apostolum haereticorum ora obstruere, qui damnabant nuptias, eumque contra ostendere, rem eam culpa carere, quin & adeo esse honoratam, ut cum ipsa etiam possit quispiam ad S. episcopatus solium subvehi, ὡς μετ' αὐτὸν διάδοχος τῆς ἐπὶ τὸ ἅγιον ἀναβάσεως θρόνου. Confer Novell. Iustin. cxxii. c. xxiii. Imp. Leonis Constit. ii. & iii.
units.tr: So the Greeks, who differ from the Romans in that they leave marriage to the clergy (which the Romans forbid), and differ from us on bigamy in this: they allow marriage before clerical ordination, not after it, and in the lower orders, except for the episcopate. Yet the Apostle says of a bishop that he must be the husband of one wife. And Chrysostom says that the Apostle stopped the mouths of the heretics who condemned marriage, and showed on the contrary that it is blameless, and so honoured that by means of it a man may even be raised to the holy episcopal throne, "as the successor after him to the seat of that holy ascent" [ὡς μετ' αὐτὸν διάδοχος τῆς ἐπὶ τὸ ἅγιον ἀναβάσεως θρόνου]. Compare Novel 122 of Justinian, ch. 23, and the Constitutions ii and iii of the Emperor Leo.

units.la: Circa Iejunium sabbathi Graeci observatum volunt Apostolorum (ut dicitur) canonem lxv. sec. alios lxvi, si quis clericus inventus fuerit die dominico jejunare vel sabbato, praeterquam uno solo, deponatur: sin laicus, segregetur. Apud Ignatium, epist. ad Philippenses: quicunque dominicam aut sabbatum jejunaverit, praeter unum sabbatum Paschae, ipse est Christi interfector. Et Clemens, Constitut. lib. vii. c. xxiv. aut quintâ & sextâ feriâ: Quoniam quarta quidem judicium in Dominum pronunciatum est, postquam Judas proditionem pecuniâ promiserat: Sextâ verò mortem in cruce sub Pontio Pilato passus est. Sabbatum tamen, & Dominicum festos dies agitate, quod ille quidem dies recordatio sit fabricationis mundi, hic verò resurrectionis. Unum verò tantummodo sabbatum nobis toto anno observandum est, sabbatum scilicet sepulturae Christi: quo quidem jejunare deceat, non autem celebrare festum. Dum enim auctor mundi sub terra est, superat lucis mortis latitiam effectionis universi; quod ipse effector praestantior sit naturâ, & dignitate rebus à se effectis. Non die dominico jejunari volunt, in quo convenit orientali cum occidentali ecclesiâ, quod propter resurrectionem Christi videatur dici laetitiae: non sabbato, ne cum Iudaeis hoc pacto facere videantur, & teneri religione sabbathi; excepto [?] no sabbato magno, ante Pascha, quo recolas silicet Christum in sepulchro jacuisse, quasi illud sequentes quod dictum: quando ablatus ab eis fuerit sponsus, tunc jejunabunt. Canonem illum adduxerunt Trullani Patres in Synodo quinisexta c. iv. ubi Romanae Ecclesiae morem aperte taxabant, quod sabbatis quoque, per totam quadragesimam jejunarent; quod etiam reliquis extra quadragesimam facerent. Hispani in Concilio Eliberitano, secuti morem Ecclesiae Romanae, jejunium sabbaticum confirmarunt, can. xxvi. Errorem placuit corrigi, ut omni sabbathi die superpositiones celebremus. Sic Garcias Loaisa: alia editio legit, ut jejuniorum superpositiones celebremus. Superpositiones sunt ὑπερθέσεις Graecis, dictaque sic jejunia, quod cibanoa superponuntur. Iudaizare illa ratione Latinos, Graeci dicebant. Unde Michael Cerularius, in epist. ad Iohannem Tranensem episcopum: Sabbata vero quomodo in quadragesima Iudaice observari? Atque Sabbatarias appellabat Nicetas Pectoratus. At vero quantumvis illa antiquissima inter utramque Ecclesiam sit controversia, ex diversa jejunandi apud utrosque a primis inde temporibus consuetudine orta, non tamen tanti haberi debuit, ut ullam concitaret litem, abolendis potius utrimque statis illis, neque superstitione carentibus jejuniis, de quibus nemo praeceptum ullum divinum adferre potuit, ὡς δεῖς ἐνίσχυσε ἐχω ἀδίκως ἐφύλαξε, uti loquitur Socrates, lib. v. cap. xx. In aliis sequendus potius mos ac consuetudo Ecclesiae, ubi quis degit, citra vel necessitatem aut superstitionem, alteriusve Ecclesiae aut moris infestationem: sicuti de hoc jejuniorum negotio diversimode apud Ecclesias quoque occidentales observato responderunt Hieronymus, & Augustinus. Ille, epist. ad Lucinum: De Sabbatho quod quaeris, utrum jejunandum sit, & de eucharistia, an accipienda quotidie, quod Romana ecclesia & Hispanica observare perhibentur, scripsit quidem & Hip-
units.tr: Concerning the fasting on the Sabbath, the Greeks maintain the canon of the Apostles (as it is called), number 65, or according to others 66: if any clergyman is found fasting on the Lord's day or on the Sabbath, except for one day alone, let him be deposed; but if a layman, let him be cut off. In Ignatius, in the letter to the Philippians: whoever fasts on the Lord's day or on the Sabbath, except the one Sabbath of the Passover, is a murderer of Christ. And Clement, Constitutions book 7, ch. 24: or on the fifth and sixth day. For on the fourth day judgment was pronounced against the Lord, when Judas had promised the betrayal for money; but on the sixth he suffered death on the cross under Pontius Pilate. Keep the Sabbath and the Lord's day as festal days, because the one is the memorial of the creation of the world, the other of the resurrection. Only one Sabbath is to be observed by us throughout the year, namely the Sabbath of the burial of Christ, on which it is fitting to fast, but not to keep a feast. For while the author of the world is under the earth, he surpasses the joy of the light by the death of the creation; because the Maker is greater in nature and dignity than the things he has made. They do not want fasting on the Lord's day, on which the Eastern and Western Churches agree, since it seems to be a day of joy because of the resurrection of Christ; nor on the Sabbath, lest they seem to act in this way like the Jews and be bound by the religion of the Sabbath; except on the great Sabbath before Easter, when we recall that Christ lay in the tomb, following that saying: when the bridegroom is taken away from them, then they will fast. The Trullan Fathers in the Synod of Quinisext, canon 64, adduced that canon, where they openly rebuked the custom of the Roman Church, which fasted also on the Sabbaths throughout the whole of Lent, and which fasted on them also outside Lent. The Spaniards at the Council of Elvira, following the custom of the Roman Church, confirmed the Sabbath fast, canon 26: it has seemed good to correct the error, so that we keep the fasts on every Sabbath day. So Garcia de Loaysa; another edition reads, so that we keep the fasts of the Sabbath. The Greeks call such fasts hypertheseis (superpositions), and fasts are so called because food is placed above them. The Greeks said that the Latins Judaized in this way. Hence Michael Cerularius, in his letter to John, bishop of Trani: But how are the Sabbaths observed Jewishly in Lent? And Nicetas Pectoratus called them Sabbatarians. Yet however ancient this controversy between the two Churches may be, arising from the different custom of fasting among both from the earliest times, it ought not to be held of such importance as to stir up any quarrel; rather both sides should abolish those fasts, which are fixed and not free from superstition, and for which no one has been able to bring forward any divine precept, "as he held it without reason, he kept it unjustly" [ὡς δεῖς ἐνίσχυσε ἐχω ἀδίκως ἐφύλαξε], as Socrates says, book 5, ch. 22. In other matters the custom and usage of the Church where one lives should be followed, provided there is no necessity or superstition, and no offence to another Church or custom; just as Jerome and Augustine answered concerning this matter of fasting, which was observed differently among the Western Churches too. Jerome, in his letter to Lucinus: As to the Sabbath, which you ask about, whether it ought to be fasted, and about the Eucharist, whether it ought to be received daily, which the Roman and Spanish Church are said to observe, Hippolytus, a most eloquent man, has indeed written on it

units.la: polyp. polytus vir disertissimus, & carptim diversi scriptores ex variis autoribus edidere. Sed ego illud te breviter admonendum puto, traditiones ecclesiasticas (praesertim quae fidei non officiant) ita observandas sunt ut a majoribus traditae sunt. Nec aliorum consuetudinem aliorum contrario more subvertit. Atque utinam omni tempore jejunare possemus, quod in Actis Apostolorum diebus Pentecostes, & die Dominico apostolum Paulum, & cum eo credentes fecisse legimus. Ille, epist. cxviii. ad Ianuarium: Quod enim neque contra fidem, neque contra bonos mores injungitur, indifferenter est habendum, & pro eorum inter quos vivitur societate servandum est. Credite aliquando ex me audisse, sed tamen etiam nunc commemoro. Mater tua Mediolanum me consecuta, invenit ecclesiam sabbatho non jejunantem: caperas perturbari & fluctuare quid ageret. Tunc ego talis non curabam, sed propter ipsum consului de hac re beatissimae memoriae virum Ambrosium. Respondit, se nihil docere me posse, nisi quod ipse faceret, quia si melius nosset id potius observaret. Cumque ego putassem nulla reddita ratione auctoritate sola sua nos voluisse admonere ne sabbato jejunaremus, subsecutus est, & ait mihi: Cum Romam venio jejuno sabbato, cum hic sumus non jejuno: Sic etiam tu, ad quam forte ecclesiam veneris, ejus morem serva, si cuiquam non vis esse scandalo, nec quemquam tibi. Hoc cum matri renuntiassem, libenter amplexa est. Ego vero de hac sententia etiam atque etiam cogitans, ita suscepi ut habui, tanquam eam caelesti oraculo susceperim.
units.tr: and various writers have published scattered notes from various authors. But I think you should be briefly reminded of this: ecclesiastical traditions (especially those which do not harm the faith) are to be observed just as they were handed down by our elders, and one custom should not overturn another's contrary custom. And would that we could fast at all times, as we read that the Apostle Paul and those who believed with him did on the day of Pentecost and on the Lord's day in the Acts of the Apostles. Augustine, letter 118, to Januarius: For what is enjoined neither against the faith nor against good morals is to be regarded as indifferent, and is to be kept for the sake of fellowship with those among whom one lives. Believe me, I heard this from you at some time, but I still recall it now. When your mother followed me to Milan, she found the church not fasting on the Sabbath; she was troubled and wavered about what to do. Then I, who did not care about such things, consulted about this matter the man of most blessed memory, Ambrose. He replied that he could teach me nothing except what he himself did, because if he knew better he would observe that rather. And when I thought that he wished to warn us, without giving any reason, only by his own authority, not to fast on the Sabbath, he followed on and said to me: When I come to Rome I fast on the Sabbath; when we are here I do not fast. So you too, to whatever church you come, keep its custom, if you do not want to be a scandal to anyone, nor anyone to you. When I reported this to my mother, she gladly embraced it. As for me, thinking on this opinion again and again, I have held it as I have held it, as if I had received it from a heavenly oracle.

units.la: Sensi enim saepe dolens & gemens multas infirmorum perturbationes fieri, per quorundam fratrum contentiosam obstinationem & superstitiosam timiditatem, quae in rebus hujusmodi quae neque scripturae sanctae auctoritate, neque universali Ecclesiae traditione, neque vitae corrigendae utilitate ad certum possunt terminum pervenire, tantum quia subest qualiscunque ratiocinatio cogitationis, aut quia in sua patria sic ipse consuevit, aut quia ibi vidit ubi peregrinationem suam quo remotiorem a suis, eo doctiorem factam putat, tam litigiosas excitant quaestiones, ut nisi quod ipsi faciunt nihil rectum existimant. Optimè. Caeterum in jejuniis, iisque statis frequentes sunt Græci. Observant quadragesimam, jejunium festi S. Apostolorum, & natalis Christi, & obdormitionis S. Deiparæ, & Christi idque non eâdem, sed diversimodâ ciborum abstinentiâ. De quibus Balsamon in Responsis ad Marcum Alexandrinum. De Moscovitis, Sigismundus Baro, in Commentario Rer. Moscovit. Paulus Iovius, in Legatione Moscovit. Universus populus quater in anno, & pluribus super diebus jejunare consuevit, abstinetque ab esu carnium, ovorum, & lactis. In vere primum, more Latino, post dies Cinerum: mox adulta æstate, in honorem divorum Petri & Pauli: & initio autumni dimm, cum assumpta in cœlum Maria virginis memoriam celebramus: postremò sub ipsum hyemem, cum adventus Domini prænunciatur. Per hebdomadam vero, diem Mercurii sine carnibus. Veneris autem sine ovis lacteque inedia sunt, sed Saturni dies mensis omnibus obsonuis opiparè, referta hilaritate exolvitur. Cæteris sicut ac non solemnes, nullas festorum dierum vigilias observant. Additur Alexander Guagninus, in descript. Moscov. cap. 11.
units.tr: For I have often felt, grieving and sighing, that much disturbance of the weak arises from the contentious obstinacy and superstitious timidity of certain brothers, who in matters of this kind, which cannot be brought to a fixed conclusion either by the authority of Holy Scripture, or by universal tradition of the Church, or by the usefulness of amending life, but only because some kind of reasoning of thought underlies them, or because one has been accustomed to it in one's own country, or because one has seen it where one thinks one's pilgrimage, the further it is from one's own people, has made one the more learned, stir up such litigious questions that they think nothing right except what they themselves do. Very good. Moreover, the Greeks are frequent in fasts, and in set fasts. They observe Lent, the fast of the feast of the holy Apostles, the fast of the birth of Christ, and of the Dormition of the holy Mother of God and of Christ, and not with the same but with different abstinence from food. Concerning these, Balsamon in his Responses to Mark of Alexandria. Concerning the Muscovites, Sigismund Baron, in his Commentary on Muscovite affairs, and Paulo Giovio, in the Embassy to Muscovy: The whole people are accustomed to fast four times in the year and on many days besides, and abstain from eating meat, eggs and milk. In spring first, in the Latin manner, after Ash Wednesday; then in the height of summer, in honour of the saints Peter and Paul; and at the beginning of autumn, when we celebrate the memory of the Virgin Mary's assumption into heaven; and lastly just before winter, when the coming of the Lord is announced. Each week they go without meat on Wednesday, and on Friday without eggs and milk; but Saturday is spent in a feast of all kinds of dainties, with great cheerfulness. On other days, which are not solemn, they observe no vigils of feast days. Alexander Guagnini is added, in the Description of Muscovy, ch. 11.

units.la: In abstinentia ab esu sanguinis & suffocati Græci primo loco objiciunt canonem Apostolorum, ex Actis cap. xv. 29., atque hac in re olim convenerunt multi diuque, quamvis non pari omnes aut observantiâ, aut necessitate. Et quia hodieque nonnulli cum Græcis canonem illum intelligunt, de eo, ut de re attentius videndum nobis est, quid statuere oporteat. Act. xv. 28. Ἔδοξε γὰρ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι καὶ ἡμῖν, μηδὲν πλέον ἐπιτίθεσθαι ὑμῖν βάρος πλὴν τῶν ἐπάναγκες τούτων. 29. Ἀπέχεσθαι εἰδωλοθύτων καὶ αἵματος καὶ πνικτοῦ καὶ πορνείας· ἐξ ὧν διατηροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς εὖ πράξετε. Vana quæ circa hunc Synodi Apostolicæ canonem vel disputantur, aut quæri possunt, omittimus: ut, quid εἴδωλοθύτων sit? vide 1. Corinth. VIII. an σῶμα & σῶμα duo constituant capita, an unum? præcipuè quum cap. xi.
units.tr: In abstaining from blood and from what has been strangled, the Greeks first of all object to the canon of the Apostles, Acts 15:29, and on this point many have agreed for a long time, though not all with the same observance or the same necessity. Because some even today understand that canon together with the Greeks, we must look at it more carefully and decide what ought to be held about it. Acts 15:28: "For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things" [Ἔδοξε γὰρ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι καὶ ἡμῖν, μηδὲν πλέον ἐπιτίθεσθαι ὑμῖν βάρος πλὴν τῶν ἐπάναγκες τούτων]. Verse 29: "That you abstain from things offered to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication; keeping yourselves from these things you will do well" [Ἀπέχεσθαι εἰδωλοθύτων καὶ αἵματος καὶ πνικτοῦ καὶ πορνείας· ἐξ ὧν διατηροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς εὖ πράξετε]. We omit the idle questions that are argued or can be raised about this canon of the Apostolic Synod: what εἰδωλοθύτων means, see 1 Cor. 8; whether blood and what is strangled [αἷμα, πνικτόν] make two heads or one, especially since ch. xi.

units.la: xxi. 25. huius libri intercisum inter utrumque habetur, ᾗ τὸ αἷμα, ᾗ πνικτόν: vel╌ um sive intercisum ponatur, sive non, eodem res redit, ut sanguinis eius prohibeatur, sive in suffocato, sive extra illud: etenim propter sanguinem est, quod suffocatum habetur illicitum, illudque generis, hoc speciei communissimae rationem obtinet. Per sanguinem & suffocatum, humanum sanguinem, eiusque effusionem intelligere, quod Patres Tertullianus, Cyprianus, Theophylactus, nimis a proposito abludit. Θηρίων sunt qui explicant non fornicationem simpliciter, sed eius speciem & gradum turpissimum, adulterium atque incestum: exemplo, 1 Cor. v. 1. Ita Seldenus lib. VI. de jure natur. Hebraeor. cap. XII. Alii fornicationem spiritualem, id est, idololatriam, quamque committebant accumbendo in idoleo. Heinsius, πορνείας, ῥυσίαν victimam meretricians, quam meretrices mercede poëtioque meretricio emtam partamque Diis suis offerebant. Nos simpliciter & juxta communem vocis acceptionem, fornicationem explicamus. Denique sunt Codices, qui praeter illa memorata capita in hac Synodo constituta, leguntque additam conclusionem: ᾧ ὅσα μὴ θέλετε ἑαυτοῖς γίνεσθαι, ἑτέροις μὴ ποιεῖτε. Et quae non vultis vobis fieri, aliis nec facite. Quomodo videntur legisse Irenaeus, ac Cyprianus. Habent id quoque versio Aethiopica, Complutensis, Regia, Montani, exemplar Cantabrigiense, & nonnulli MSS. de quibus Beza in Notis, Junius, Lud. de Dieu, Seldenus, loc. cit. Nos illa non multum movent, qui stamus fide plurimorum & vulgatiorum, atque probatissimorum codicum. Ut neque quod alii videntur non legisse praeceptum de suffocato: Vide Baronium, Tom. I. ad A. 51. Verum istis & aliis missis, interdictum illud sanguinis & suffocati, quale est? an juris moralis, vel saltem perpetui? ita ut nunquam liceat comedere de suffocato, aut sanguine? Certe multi semper fuerunt, de Christianis loquor, quor, atque ii etiamnum, qui illicitum esse putant, & contra praeceptum, quod ut juris moralis, ita perpetuae voluntate esse observantiae. Graeci communiter: atque ex Patribus aliis etiam plurimi. Cuius argumento est, quod ad objectionem vel calumniam de Thyestis epulis, sibi a Gentilibus passim objectis, Christiani vulgo ita respondebant, ut dicerent, se ab omni etiam animalis sanguine religiose abstinere, neque illum inter edulia admittere, quanto magis sanguinem humanum: quo in suis epulis vesci Christianos, Ethnici palam calumniabantur. Deinde per botulos cruore distentos, vel intestina animalium sanguine oppleta, farcimina, Christianos probari solitos, Tertullianus scribit: adeo hinc dignoscebantur, quod illa refugerent. Tertulliani verba sunt in Apologetico: Erubescunt error pter Christianis, qui ne animalium quidem sanguinem in epulis esculentis habemus, qui propterea quoque suffocatis et morticino abstinemus, ne quo sanguine contaminemur, vel intra viscera sepulto. Denique inter tentamenta Christianorum botulos etiam cruore distentos admovetis. Porro quale est, ut quos sanguinem pecoris horrere considiis, humano inhiare credatis? nisi forte suaviorem eum expetitis. Similiter Minutius Felix, in Octavio: tantum ab humano sanguine caremus, ut nec edulium pecorum in cibis sanguinem nove gerimus. Unde Biblis martyr, apud Eusebium, lib. v. cap. 1. & Baronium, Tom. II. ad A. 176. respondet tortoribus: Quomodo infantes edere ibi, quibus ne irrationalium quidem pecudum sanguine vesci liceat? Rem ita explicat Origenes, contra Celsum, lib. VIII. Suffocata autem fuerint, sanguine non expresso demortua: quam utique daemonum esse asserunt cibum, ex cujus nitore hi nutriantur. Haec id circo divinus prohibet sermone ne in cibum sumantur, ne forte daemonum cibis contrahantur: perinde ac nobiscum istiusmodi spiritus colantur, si suffocatis vescamur. Inter Canones Apostolorum, LXIII. ita habet: si quis episcopus, vel presbyter, vel diaconus, vel omnino ex sacerdotali catalogo, comederit carnem in sanguine animæ ipsorum, ὁ πνικτὸν, ἢ ἀπὸ θηρίου ... vel quid à feris captum, aut morticinium, deponatur, hoc enim lex prohibuit: si autem sit laicus, segregetur, ἀποξενούσθω. illud, carnes in sanguine animæ suæ, est τὸ πνικτόν. Synodus VI. in Trullo, can. lxviii. Divina nobis Scriptura mandavit, à sanguine & suffocato & fornicatione abstinere. Eos ergo, qui propter lautum & delicatum ventrem, cujuscunque animalis sanguinem atque aliquid esculentum condiunt ac instruunt, & si illo vescuntur, ut par est, incusamus ac punimus: si quis ergo deinceps animalis sanguinem quovis modo comedere aggrediatur, si sit quidem clericus, deponatur: sin autem laicus, segregetur. Propter illos hic canon constitutus, qui se à sanguine abstinere dicebant, interim esculenta, in quibus sanguis deliciarum causa admiscebatur, cupiebant: quare noluerunt Patres, ullo modo sanguine, sive solo, sive eduliis ἐκ τῶν αἱμάτων factis, frui. Præterea & aliæ Synodi suffocati vel sanguinis esu quoque interdicunt. Photii Nomocanon, tit. xi. cap. xiii. De Laicis, qui comedunt idolis immolata, vel carnes in sanguine, vel suffocata, vel à feris capta, vel morticinia, Post. can. lxiv. Syn. Ancyr. canon iii. Gangr. Syn. canon ii. Syn. vi. canon lxviii. Gregorii Thaumaturgi epistola, quæ est de iis qui immolata comederunt. Basilii canon lxxxi, adde Concil. Aurelianense ii. can. xx. Inde & Leonis Imp. Novella constit. lviii, ὁ μυ-σ-θ-ὸς τὸ αἷμα βρῶμα ποιεῖσθαι, certe supra modum severa, scelus vocans, si quis sarciminibus, hodieque ussitatissimis, quin in ptelio & honore aliquo, vescatur; insuper gravi & pecuniaria, & corporali multa illud vindicans: quæ videatur Const. siquidem prolixior est, quam ut illam describamus. Inde Græci, & Moscovitæ, Abyssini, Armeni à suffocato & sanguine communiter abstinent: atque aliter facientes Romani nos, vel hanc ob causam, condemnant. Balsamon, ad can. Apost. lxiii. Quae autem à venatoris avibus vel canibus capiuntur, & suffocantur, quomodo ab aliquibus comedantur, nescio. Nota ergo canonem, propter Latinos, qui suffocata indiscriminatim comedunt. Epistola Michaelis Cerularii, contra Latinos, apud Baronium, Tom. xi. A. 1053. De Moscovitis Sigismundus Baro, in suo rerum Moscoviticarum Commentario, ex Canonibus cujusdam Iohannis Metropolitae, qui Propheta apud illos habitus: Animalia, volucres ab avibus vel feris laceratae, non comedantur: qui vero comederint, aut in azymis dormiverint, vel in septuagesima carne usi fuerint, vel sanguinem voraverint, corrigantur, Aves, animalia suffocata non comedantur. Ieremias Patriarcha Constantinop. in Responso i. ad Tubingenses, circa hoc: nec quod suffocatum est apud nos in cibum adhibetur, in hodiernum usque diem: sed aversamur, Patribus & Apostolis constanter obedientes. De Iudeis res nota. Caput septimum praeceptorum Noachi est, de non comedendo membro animalis vivi. Mikkotzi, Praecepto negativo cxxxiii. Caro animantis per se mortui non comedenda. Deut. 14. Et si animal non fit ipsi ut debet mactatum, ejus ejusque est interdictus. Idem judicium est de vitulo aut agno qui octavum nondum attigit diem. Praecepto seq. Prohibitum est edere de animali rapto. Raptum vocatur, quod bestia silvestris laceravit, aut avis rapax unguibus discerpsit. Sic si animal rapiatur & non moriatur, adhuc prohibitus est esus. Ut si lupus abduxerit capram auribus, & aliquis insequens eripiat pecus ex ore lupi, prohibitus est esus, ideoque canibus projiciendum est. Idem est judicium de bove aut alio pecore quod de tecto cadit, aut quod jaculo vulneratur. Excipiunt tamen sanguinem piscium. Praecepto cxxxvii. Nullus sanguis comedendus. Levit. 17. Excipitur sanguis piscium, qui licitus est. Atque Muhammedani idem cavent. Muhammed in Alcorano saepius, cum carne porcina, simul prohibet esum sanguinis, ac suffocati. Surata II. & V. & VI. Prohibuit vobis morticinia, sanguinem, carnem porcinam, & super quod laudes dicta sunt aliis quàm Deo. Hoc est, idolothyta. Diu fuit, fateor, quòd Christianorum multi, quasi ex legis divinae reverentiâ, suffocato sanguine- que inter edendum abstinuerunt. Hodieque non desunt viri cum primis erud. ti, pii, & maximi, qui idem censent, non licere sanguine vesci, praeceptumque illud Apostolicum constanter ac perpetuò omnes obligare. Beatus Rhenanus, in Tertulliani locum, ex ejus Apologiâ supra adductum: Non diu est, quod Christiani suffocato vescimur & morticinâ carne. Nam Beatus presbyter, & item Rabanus in poenitentiario, sed & quotquot de hâc re supra 400. annos tradiderunt, certum poenitentiae tempus prescribunt, si quis Apostolicam hanc legem fuerit prævaricatus. Exstat in Actis, sed & cadaver animalis tangere piaculum erat. Hodie in illam sententiam disputant, Christianus Becmannus, in Exercit. Theologicis, cap. XXVI. qui & multos se nosse, legem illam religiosè custodientes, testatur: inque eundem finem adducit Sebastianum Castellionem, & Danielem Angelocratorem. Claudius Salmasius, lib. de Trapezitico fenore pag. 438. praeceptum Apostolicum de non comedendo sanguine contendit non propter συγγνώμην Iudaeorum, ne hi à Gentilibus promiscuè sanguine & suffocato vescentibus nimium offenderentur, sed tanquam rem omnino necessariam positum, ut caput legis caeremonialis quod impositum semper, æque ut illud de non scortando, observandum esset. Ex adversa plures censent, legem illam de abstinendo à sanguine & suffocato temporariam fuisse, neque perpetuum obligare. Sic disputant, sic vivunt plerique, nihil ut discriminis, propter conscientiam scilicet, inter cibos observent, sed & sanguine ac suffocato peraeque vescantur. Baronius, Annal. Tom. I. ad A. 51. Quidam Apostolici culmini reverentiâ, illud ipsum institutum aliquandiu retinendum putarunt; quod demum tamen Occidentalis Ecclesia consensu est æquè laudabiliter antiquatum. Tacitâ dissuetudine, & quod nullum amplius à Gentilibus, vel Iudæis scandalum verendum videbatur, lex illa vulgo observari desiit. Neque nunc demum, sed & olim, quando etiam ab aliquibus observabatur, aliì meliori freti libertate, eam omiserunt, & promiscuè sanguine quoque inter esculenta usi fuerunt. Iam tempore Augustini. Quod testantur ea, quæ habet adversus Faustum Manichæum, lib. xxxii. cap. xiii. Et in Actibus apostolorum hoc lege præceptum ab apostolis, ut abstinerent gentes tantùm à fornicatione & ab suffocato & sanguine: id est, nequaquam ederent carnem, cuius sanguis non esset effusus. Quod alii non sic intelligunt, sed à sanguine præceptum esse abstinendum, ne quis homicidio se contaminet. Hoc nunc discutere tempus est, & non necessarium: quia & si hoc tunc apostoli præceperunt, ut ab animalium sanguine abstinerent Christiani, ne præfocatis carnibus vescerentur, elegisse mihi videntur pro tempore rem facilem, & nequaquam observantibus onerosam, in quâ cum Israëlitis etiam gentes, propter angularem illum lapidem, duos parietes in se coeuntes, aliquid communiter observarent: simul & admonerent, in ipsâ arcâ Noë, quando Deus hoc iussit, ecclesiam omnium gentium fuisse præfiguratam: cuius facti prophetia, iam gentibus ad fidem accedentibus, incipiebat impleri. Transacto verò illo tempore, quo illi duo parietes, unus ex circumcisione, alter ex præputio venientes, quamvis in angulari lapide concordarent, tamen suis quibusdam proprietatibus distinctiùs eminebant: & ubi ecclesia gentium talis effecta est, ut in eâ nullus Israëlita carnalis appareat, quis iam hoc Christianus observat, ut surdos vel mutos vel claudos non attingat, nisi quorum sanguis effusus est? aut leporem non edat, si manu à cervice percussus, nullo cruento vulnere occisus est? Et qui forte pauci adhuc tangere ista formidant, à caeteris irridentur. Ita omnium animos in hac re fecit.
units.tr: Xxi. 25. In this book the text is broken between the two parts, "that which is blood" and "that which is strangled." Whether the break is made or not, the matter comes to the same thing: the blood is forbidden, whether it is in the strangled animal or apart from it. The reason the strangled animal is held unlawful is the blood, and the strangled is a kind of the genus, the blood being the most general ground. By "blood" and "strangled" the Fathers Tertullian and Cyprian and Theophylact understood human blood and its shedding, but that reading departs far from the purpose of the text. Some explain "fornication" not simply but as its most shameful species and degree, adultery and incest, citing 1 Cor. 5:1. So Selden, book 6 of De iure naturali Hebraeorum, chapter 12. Others take it as spiritual fornication, that is, idolatry, which they committed by reclining at idol feasts. Heinsius takes porneia together with rhysian (a sacrifice) as the victim of prostitutes, which harlots bought with their wages and the price of their trade and offered to their gods. We explain it simply, according to the common meaning of the word, as fornication. Finally, there are manuscripts which, besides the heads mentioned above laid down in this Synod, read an added conclusion: "Whatever you do not wish to be done to yourselves, do not do to others" [ὃ μὴ θέλετε ἑαυτοῖς γίνεσθαι, ἑτέροις μὴ ποιεῖτε]. "What you do not want done to you, do not do to others." Irenaeus and Cyprian seem to have read it this way. The Ethiopic version, the Complutensian, the Royal, Montanus, the Cambridge copy and some manuscripts also have it, as Beza notes in his Notes, and Junius, Lud. de Dieu and Selden, loc. cit. We are not much moved by these, since we stand by the agreement of the majority, the more widespread and the most approved manuscripts. Nor should the precept about the strangled be troubled by the fact that others seem not to have read it; see Baronius, vol. 1, at the year 51. But setting these and other things aside, what is the nature of that prohibition of blood and of the strangled? Is it of moral law, or at least perpetual, so that it is never lawful to eat what is strangled or blood? Certainly there have always been many, I speak of Christians, and there are still some, who think it unlawful, and that the precept binds with the force of moral law and with a perpetual observance. The Greeks commonly hold this, and many of the other Fathers too. The proof of this is that when the Gentiles repeatedly objected to Christians the calumny about the feasts of Thyestes, Christians generally answered that they abstained religiously from the blood of every animal and did not admit it among their foods, much less human blood, which the heathens openly slandered the Christians as eating at their feasts. Tertullian also writes that Christians were commonly tested by sausages and blood puddings, or animal intestines filled with blood; so far were they known by refusing these things. Tertullian's words in the Apology are: "The Gentiles blush for their error, since we Christians do not even have the blood of animals in our edible feasts, and for that reason we also abstain from strangled and carrion meat, lest we be defiled by any blood, even blood buried in the entrails. Finally, among the tests of Christians you bring forward blood puddings swollen with gore." Again, how likely is it that those who shudder at the blood of cattle would lust after human blood? Unless perhaps you seek it because it tastes sweeter. Similarly Minucius Felix, in the Octavius: "We are so far from human blood that we do not even knowingly take the blood of cattle into our food." Hence Blandina the martyr, in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 1, and Baronius, vol. 2, at the year 176, answers her torturers: "How could they eat infants, to whom it is not lawful even to taste the blood of irrational beasts?" Origen explains the matter against Celsus, book 8: "Animals that are strangled die without their blood being let out; and they say this is the food of demons, by whose vapour these are nourished. Scripture therefore forbids these things as food, lest we be contaminated by the food of demons, just as such spirits would be worshipped among us if we ate strangled things." Among the Canons of the Apostles, number 63, it reads: "If any bishop, or presbyter, or deacon, or in general anyone from the priestly list, eats flesh with the blood of its life [en tō haimati autou], or what is strangled, or what has been taken by beasts, or carrion, let him be deposed, for the law forbids this; but if he is a layman, let him be separated." That phrase, "flesh in the blood of its life," means what is strangled. The Sixth Synod in Trullo, canon 68: "Divine Scripture has commanded us to abstain from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. Therefore those who, for the sake of a dainty and delicate stomach, season and prepare the blood of any animal and some edible thing, and eat it, we rightly censure and punish. If anyone henceforth undertakes to eat the blood of an animal in any way, let him be deposed if he is a cleric, but if a layman, let him be separated." This canon was framed against those who claimed to abstain from blood while in the meantime desiring dishes in which blood was mixed for the sake of pleasure; so the Fathers would not allow the use of blood in any way, whether alone or in foods made ek tōn haimatōn [from the bloods]. Moreover, other Synods also forbid eating what is strangled or blood. Photius's Nomocanon, title 11, chapter 13: "Concerning laymen who eat things sacrificed to idols, or flesh in blood, or what is strangled, or what has been taken by beasts, or carrion." Then canon 64 of the Synod of Ancyra, canon 3; the Synod of Gangra, canon 2; the Synod of the Sixth, canon 68; "The Epistle of Gregory Thaumaturgus, which is concerning those who have eaten sacrifices." Basil's canon 81; add the Council of Orléans II, canon 20. Thence also the Novel of the Emperor Leo, constitution 58, which calls it an abomination to make blood a food: certainly beyond measure severe, calling it a crime if anyone eats blood sausages, still very common today, or any dish of honour made from it; it punishes this besides with a heavy fine, both monetary and corporal. That constitution is, indeed, too long for us to describe. Hence the Greeks, the Muscovites, the Abyssinians and the Armenians commonly abstain from what is strangled and from blood, and the Romans, who do otherwise, condemn us for this reason among others. Balsamon, on the Canon of the Apostles 63: "But how things taken by hunting birds or dogs and strangled are eaten by some, I do not know. Note therefore the canon, because of the Latins, who eat strangled things without distinction." The letter of Michael Cerularius against the Latins, in Baronius, vol. 11, at the year 1053. Concerning the Muscovites, Sigismund Baron, in his commentary on Muscovite affairs, cites the canons of a certain John, Metropolitan, whom they regard as a prophet: "Animals and birds torn by birds or beasts are not to be eaten; those who have eaten them, or slept among unleavened bread, or eaten the seventy-day meat, or swallowed blood, must be corrected. Birds and strangled animals are not to be eaten." Jeremiah, Patriarch of Constantinople, in his first Response to the Tübingen theologians, on this point: "Nor is what is strangled used as food among us, even to this day; but we turn away from it, constantly obeying the Fathers and Apostles." The matter concerning the Jews is well known. The seventh of the precepts of Noah is not to eat a member of a living animal. Mikkotzi, negative precept 133: "The flesh of an animal that has died of itself is not to be eaten." Deut. 14: "And if the animal is not slaughtered as it should be, it is forbidden; the same judgment applies to a calf or lamb that has not yet reached its eighth day." Next precept: "It is forbidden to eat what has been torn by a beast. That is called torn which a wild beast has mangled, or which a rapacious bird has torn with its talons. So if an animal is seized and does not die, eating it is still forbidden. As if a wolf has carried off a goat by the ear, and someone pursuing takes the flock out of the wolf's mouth, eating it is still forbidden, and it must be thrown to the dogs. The same judgment applies to an ox or other cattle that falls from a roof, or that is wounded by a javelin." They do, however, except the blood of fish. Precept 137: "No blood is to be eaten." Lev. 17: "The blood of fish is excepted, which is lawful." And the Muslims observe the same. Muhammad in the Qur'an, often together with the prohibition of pork, forbids the eating of blood and of what is strangled: sura 2, 5 and 6: "He has forbidden you carrion, blood, pork, and that over which words have been said other than God's." That is, things sacrificed to idols. "It was long, I confess, that many Christians, as if out of reverence for the divine law, abstained from strangled meat and from blood when eating. Even today there are not lacking men, very learned, pious and great, who think the same, that it is not lawful to eat blood, and that the Apostolic precept binds all constantly and perpetually." Beatus Rhenanus, on the passage of Tertullian's Apology cited above: "It is not long since Christians ate strangled meat and carrion. For Beatus the presbyter, and likewise Rabanus in his penitential book, and all who have written on this matter for over four hundred years, prescribe a fixed time of repentance for anyone who has transgressed this Apostolic law. It is found in the Acts; even touching the carcass of an animal was an offence." Today Christian Becmann argues for the same view in his Exercitationes theologicae, chapter 26, and he testifies that he knows many who keep that law scrupulously; to the same end he cites Sebastian Castellio and Daniel Angelocrator. Claudius Salmasius, in his book De Trapezitico fenore, page 438, contends that the Apostolic precept about not eating blood was laid down not as an indulgence to the Jews, lest they be too offended by Gentiles who ate blood and strangled meat indiscriminately, but as a thing altogether necessary, a head of the ceremonial law which, like the precept against fornication, was to be observed always. On the other side, many think that the law about abstaining from blood and from what is strangled was temporary and does not bind perpetually. Such men argue and live thus, observing no distinction among foods on grounds of conscience, but eating blood and what is strangled alike. Baronius, Annals, vol. 1, at the year 51: "Some thought that out of reverence for the Apostolic authority that very institution should be kept for a time; but at last the Western Church, by common consent, abolished it, as laudably as it had been established. By tacit disuse, and because no further scandal from Gentiles or Jews seemed to be feared, that law fell into general neglect. Nor only now, but long ago, when some did observe it, others, trusting in a better liberty, omitted it and used blood indiscriminately among their foods." Already in the time of Augustine this is attested by what he writes against Faustus the Manichaean, book 32, chapter 13: "And in the Acts of the Apostles it is read that the Apostles commanded the Gentiles to abstain only from fornication and from what is strangled and from blood; that is, that they should in no way eat flesh whose blood had not been poured out." Others do not understand it this way, but hold that abstinence from blood was commanded so that no one might defile himself by murder. It is now time to examine this, though it is not necessary: for even if the Apostles then commanded Christians to abstain from the blood of animals so that they would not eat strangled flesh, they seem to me to have chosen for the time a thing easy and in no way burdensome to those who observed it, in which the Gentiles together with the Israelites might share a common observance, because of that corner stone joining the two walls; and at the same time they would remind us that in Noah's ark itself, when God commanded it, the Church of all nations was foreshadowed, and the prophecy of this fact was then beginning to be fulfilled as the Gentiles came to the faith. But when that time had passed, the two walls, one from circumcision and the other from uncircumcision, although they agreed in the corner stone, nevertheless stood out more distinctly with certain peculiarities of their own; and when the Church of the Gentiles became such that no carnal Israelite appears in it, who among Christians now observes not to touch the deaf, mute or lame, unless their blood has been shed? Or who does not eat a hare, if it was struck on the neck by a hand and killed without any bloody wound? And those who perhaps still fear to touch such things, the others laugh at. Thus it has affected the minds of all in this matter.

units.la: Ita omnium animos in hac re sensit. sensuit illa sententia veritatis. Non quod intrat in os vestrum, vos coinquinat, sed quod exit, nullam cibi naturam, quam societas admittit humana, sed quae iniquitas commisit, peccata condemnans. Observa, quod & pauci erant, & ab aliis passim irridebantur, quibus sanguine vesci religio videbatur. Euantus, vetus auctor, sed qui post tempora Gregorii vixit (hujus enim adducit librum Pastoralem;) scripsit epistolam, contra eos, qui sanguinem animalium immundum esse judicabant: cujus opinionis dicit extitisse quosdam in partibus Caesar Augustanis, adeo non communis aut constans sententia vel praxis erat abstinendi ab esu sanguinis: atque adversus id quod ex hoc loco Act. xv. objiciebant, respondit, id pro tempore constitutum, propter infirmitatem Judaeorum, vel Christianorum ex Judaeis: Quod si forte objiciunt, ista in canonibus haberi. Nec ego me ista fateor ignorare, sed in antiquis canonibus ista reperiuntur, quando ecclesia ex circumcisione & praeputio ad fidem congregabatur; quando adhuc non solido cibo, sed lacte nutriebatur. Talia quid ad Corinthios Apostolum dixisse noverint, & in Actibus Apostolorum facta invenient. Nunc vero ecclesia Dei solido cibo fide roborata consistit, ut viriliter contra impetus haereticorum pugnet, non in infantium mollitie enervata succumbat. Allegat quoque in suam sententiam Augustinum, contra Faustum Manichaeum; & Hieronymum: ne alia dicam. Epistola illa edita a Canisio est, ex MS. monasterii S. Galli, extatque Lectionum ejus Antiquarum Tom. V. part. II. Passim Auctores se illo Augustini loco expediunt. Nicolaus I. in Responso ad Consulta Bulgarorum, cap. xc.
