Vide & Humbertum Cardinalem, in Disputatione adversus Graecos, apud Baronium, in Appendice Tom. xi. pag. 783. Adeoque nunquam communiter illa opinio & praxis obtinuit de abstinentia a suffocato & sanguine, quin plurimi semper contrarium sectati fuerint. Scholastici in hanc sententiam pronunciant: Thomas I. II. qu. CIII. art. IV. prohibita illa Act. xv. dicit fuisse pro tempore solutum, non in perpetuum, quousque coaluisceret unio Gentilium, & Iudaeorum. Erasmus, in Annotat. ad 1. Cor. vii. de decreto isto similiter: Quod ibi decretum est, adeo ut quantum, ut nunc Iudaizare crederetur, qui abhorrent à gallina suffocata, aut sanguine distentis. Nec ledimus interim Apostolicam majestatem, tantùm existimamus hoc ad tempus fuisse constitutum ob placandos Iudaeorum animos. Quid Commentatores dicant in locum ipsum Act. xv. quilibet viderit: nobis curae non est impraesentiarum illos consulere, vel evolvere. Augustana Confessio huius meminit, art. ult. circa finem: Apostoli iusserunt abstinere à sanguine, quis nunc observat? neque tamen peccant, qui non observant, quia nec ipsi quidem Apostoli voluerunt conscientias tali servitute: sed ad tempus prohibuerunt, propter scandalum. Est enim perpetua voluntas Ecclesiae consideranda in decreto. Duo sunt potissima argumenta, quae abstinentiam à sanguine imperare videntur. Primum, legis Noachicae illud Gen. ix. 4. Alterum ex canone Apostolico Act. xv. 29. petitum. Adferuntur & alia, ex lege Mosaicâ, Levit. iii. 17. & vii. 26. & xvii. 26. Deut. xii. 16. 23. & xv. ult. 1 Sam. xiv. 32. sed quae ex communi regulâ de abrogatione caeremonialium facilè solvuntur. Illud urgere magis videtur, quod ante legem Mosaicam praeceptum hoc tenuit, inde à Noacho: unde nonnulli existimant, juris Noachici caput ab Apostolis hic confirmatum, & in canonem relatum fuisse: quod refellit Seldenus, lib. vii. de jure Natur. Ebraeor. sed ad illud Genes. ix. 4. similiter respondetur, multa caeremonialia ante Mosem obtinuisse. Iam à primâ mundi aetate sacrificia in usu fuerunt, atque observata ratio primitiarum, decimarum &c. quae non idcirco perpetuae legis sunt. Argumentum ex Act. xv. 29. validius est, neque nullam continet difficultatem. Nam & ab Apostolis, sub N. Testamenmento, ubi agitur de lege caeremoniali vel servanda, vel abroganda, ubi de instruenda Ecclesia, imperatur, atque ex reliqua lege retinetur, quin ut εἰπωμένων, & juxta cum scortationis cavendae praecepto observandum. Respondemus autem, nobis haud videri canonem istum de sanguine & suffocato perpetuae legis habendum esse: sed pro tali, qui quid isto tempore, in gratiam Iudaeorum χεισταυιζόντων à Gentilibus Christianis fieri oportuerit, in facili cujusdam actus omissione, edixit. Adeo ut ex capite de esu libertatis Christianae, hoc quoque de esu sanguinis decidi & explicari debeat. Legis caeremonialis est, inter alia, ut à sanguine & suffocato abstineatur. Videtur subesse moralis ratio, & fundamentum analogiae in detestatione omnis crudelitatis & feritatis morum: uti omnia caeremonialia in aliquo aut legis, aut Euangelii fundamento analogiam suam habent: sed unde imperite admodum argumentum fieret, ad ipsius legis observantiam, ad quam nisi mediate per accedentem divinam jussionem concludi nequit: sed quod praecipue Apostolos commoverit ad prohibendum sanguinis & suffocati esum, est rei facilitas, sita in sola omissione, in temperanda libertate circa cibum: in quo argumento ut libertas procacius aliquando jactari contingit, ita saepius ab Apostolis circumscripta: Vide Rom. xiv. 1 Cor. viii. Atque in hoc nostro canone primum caput est de idolothyto, videlicet non comedendo: an nunquam? non hoc vult doctrina Apostolica. 1 Cor. viii. & x. 19. id tamen inter capita necessaria ponitur, & primo quidem loco. Sed quia quod ad cavendam fratris offensionem debet fieri, ex necessaria fit charitate & charitatis mutuae lege, hinc quod offendiculi cavendi causa, ne fratrem temere tristemur, aut conscientiam ejus verberemus, uti Apostolus loquitur, esum idolothythi, simul etiam sanguinis ac suffocati, ut omittamus, inter necessaria Apostolicae disciplinae capita recensetur.
units.tr: He thus moved the minds of everyone in this matter. That saying of the truth prevailed: "What goes into the mouth does not defile you, but what comes out of it does." No natural kind of food that human society admits is condemned, only the wickedness that a person commits, which is what condemns sins. Notice that there were few who held this view, and that others mocked them on every side, since to them abstaining from blood seemed a matter of religion. Euantus, an ancient author who lived after the time of Gregory (for he cites Gregory's Pastoral Rule), wrote a letter against those who judged the blood of animals to be unclean. He says that some such people existed in the regions of Caesar Augusta, so far was abstaining from eating blood from being a common or settled opinion or practice. Against what they objected from Acts 15, he replied that this was ordained for the time, because of the weakness of the Jews, or of Christians who came from the Jews: "But if they perhaps object that these things are held in the canons, I do not confess that I am ignorant of them. Yet these things are found in the ancient canons, when the Church was gathered to the faith out of circumcision and uncircumcision, when it was still nourished not with solid food but with milk. As for what the Apostle said to the Corinthians on such matters, they may know it, and they will find it done in the Acts of the Apostles. But now the Church of God stands strengthened by faith with solid food, so that it may fight bravely against the assaults of heretics and not give way, enervated by the softness of infants." He also cites, in support of his view, Augustine against Faustus the Manichaean, and Jerome, to say nothing of others. That letter has been published by Canisius from a manuscript of the monastery of St Gall, and it is found in his Antiquae Lectiones, vol. 5, part 2. Authors commonly extricate themselves by that passage of Augustine. Nicholas I, in his Responsa ad consulta Bulgarorum, ch. 90. See also Cardinal Humbert, in his disputation against the Greeks, in Baronius, in the appendix to vol. 11, p. 783. And so that opinion and practice of abstaining from what is strangled and from blood never prevailed generally, but very many always held the contrary. The Scholastics pronounce in this sense: Thomas (1-2, q. 103, art. 4) says that the prohibition of Acts 15 was loosed for the time, not for ever, until the union of Gentiles and Jews should grow strong. Erasmus, in his Annotations on 1 Corinthians 7, likewise says of that decree: "What was decreed there was such that anyone who now shrinks from a strangled hen or from blood would seem to be Judaizing. Nor in the meantime do we diminish the apostolic authority; we only judge that this was ordained for the time, to placate the minds of the Jews." What the commentators say on Acts 15 itself, anyone may see; it is not our concern at present to consult or go through them. The Augsburg Confession mentions this in its last article, near the end: "The Apostles ordered abstinence from blood. Who now observes it? Yet those who do not observe it do not sin, since not even the Apostles themselves wished to bind consciences with such servitude, but for a time forbade it on account of scandal. For the perpetual will of the Church is to be considered in the decree." There are two main arguments that seem to enjoin abstinence from blood. The first is that of the Noachic law, Genesis 9:4. The second is taken from the Apostolic canon, Acts 15:29. Other passages are also adduced from the Mosaic law: Leviticus 3:17, 7:26 and 17:26, Deuteronomy 12:16, 23 and 15 at the end, and 1 Samuel 14:32; but these are easily resolved by the common rule about the abrogation of ceremonial laws. What seems to press more is that this precept was held before the Mosaic law, from Noah onwards; whence some think that a chapter of the Noachic law was confirmed here by the Apostles and placed in the canon. Selden refutes this, in his De jure naturali et gentium iuxta disciplinam Ebraeorum, book 7. But to that passage, Genesis 9:4, one answers similarly that many ceremonial things held sway before Moses. From the first age of the world sacrifices were in use, and the practice of firstfruits and tithes was observed, which are not for that reason part of a perpetual law. The argument from Acts 15:29 is stronger, and it is not without difficulty. For the Apostles, under the New Testament, where the question concerns whether the ceremonial law is to be kept or abrogated, and where the Church is being instructed, command it, and retain it from the rest of the law, not as "said" [εἰπωμένων], and to be observed together with the precept to avoid fornication. We reply, however, that this canon about blood and what is strangled does not seem to us to be of perpetual law, but was laid down as a matter of a certain easy omission, for the sake of the Jews who were "Judaizing" [Ἰουδαΐζοντων] at that time, so that Gentile Christians should do what was needful. So this matter of eating blood must be settled and explained from the chapter on the eating of Christian liberty. It is a part of the ceremonial law, among other things, that one abstain from blood and from what is strangled. A moral reason seems to underlie it, and a ground of analogy in the detestation of all cruelty and savagery of manners, just as all ceremonial things have their analogy in some ground of the law or of the Gospel. But it would be very unskilful to make an argument from this for the observance of the law itself, to which one cannot conclude except mediately, through the divine command that comes with it. What chiefly moved the Apostles to forbid eating blood and what is strangled is the ease of the matter, which lies solely in an omission, in moderating liberty about food. In this argument, as liberty sometimes happens to be boasted of rather boldly, so more often the Apostles curbed it. See Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8. And in this canon of ours the first head is about what is offered to idols, namely, not eating it. Is it never to be eaten? The Apostolic doctrine does not mean that (1 Corinthians 8 and 10:19). Yet that is placed among the necessary heads, and indeed in the first place. But because what must be done to avoid offending a brother is done out of necessary charity and the law of mutual love, therefore the eating of what is offered to idols, together with blood and what is strangled, is reckoned among the necessary heads of Apostolic discipline, for the sake of avoiding a stumbling block, so that we do not rashly grieve our brother or wound his conscience, as the Apostle puts it; to say nothing of the rest.

units.la: Sed, cur non potius, si gratificari hac in re Iudaeis Apostoli voluerint, eorumque infirmitati cedere libertatem Christianam, indulserunt vel injunxerunt circumcisionem? quam maxime quidem cupiebant Iudaei, & quae causam συζητησεως[?] & concilio dederat. Nempe, quia immane quantum differt circumcisio, ab esu sanguinis, aut suffocati: & dum indulgendum duntaxat Iudaeis aliqua in re videbatur, non magni alicujus capitis, sed levicula potius rei gratia facienda fuit, praecipue quum negotium principale interim quoque agi commendarique debebat, de lege caeremoniali abroganda, sepeliendaque. Accedit, quod circumcisio in tota hac quaestione, sive a Iudaeis eam urgentibus, sive ab Apostolis ei reclamantibus, semper considerata fuit, ut unum aliquod singulare legis caput, sed talis, quod totius legis caeremonialis observantiam involveret, essetque ejus compendium. Gal. v. 3. Unde quodvis potius aliud legalis caeremoniae praestari vel imponi potuit, quam istud. Praeterquam quod longe aliud sit in omni dispensatione, rem quampiam, & licitam solummodo, omittere, praesertim in quotidiana vivendi consuetudine, circa cibum & esum, ubi & aliorum copia abundat, quam committere, patrare, vel peragere aliquid, quodque in solo, ac praecipuo religionis capite versatur, quale est circumcisio. Quare dum hoc negotium nunc incumbebat Apostolis, docere quomodo legis caeremonialis tempus expirasset, eaque non observanda esset amplius, interim etiam pro prudentia & charitate vellent agere cum Iudaeis, id est Christianis ex Iudaismo venientibus, qui haerebant, atque ad hunc praesertim allidebant vulgo lapidem, consultum arbitrati fuerunt, ne intempestivo forte aliquo zelo Christiani reliqui libertate in contemptum atque offensionem fratrum aliorum abuterentur, non sint totam legem caeremonialem, omne ejus ἀσ-[?], vel maximum aliquod caput observarent, sed abstinendo abstinerent duntaxat pauculis & levioribus, in quibus cedebant solùm de suo jure, de eo quod aliàs licitum erat, ab idololytho, à sanguine, à suffocato comedendis. Quae causa ubi cessat, scandali nempe, cessat autem hodie, quare non quibusvis, & dictis illis rebus frui vescique liceat, ego non video. Quamvis utcunque nunc desinente offensione Iudæorum ad religionem accedentium, nolim etiam eâ procaciter aut jactanter uti libertate, ubi quis Christianus ex infirmitate, non ob legis caeremonialis reverentiam vel auctoritatem (quae verius haeresis esset, quam infirmitas) sed propter canonem Apostolicum opinaretur abstinendum suffocato & sanguine esse. Vide Rom. xiv. 1 Cor. viii. 13. Adeo faciles in re facili oportet nos esse, ubi multum refert, an de nostro, idque nullo incommodo, cedamus, an verò fratris conscientia tristetur, laedatur, corrumpatur. Et quamvis dicantur illa necessariò observanda, ἐπιάναγκες, in decreto Apostolico (minimè placet, ex arbitrio mutare lectionem in ἐπ' ἀνάγκης), non tamen sequitur pari vel æquali necessitate omnia ista capita servanda esse. Scortatio de necessitate perpetua & morali cavenda est: esus autem idolothytorum, & suffocati quidem necessariò aliquando, sed demum, ubi casus ponitur offensionis aut scandali: extra eum non. Placet ergò magis observatio Cloppenburgii, in Scholâ sacrifi. circa finem, ἐπιάναγκες ad verbialiter sumi, & notare aliquam μείων necessarii, quomodo in ἐπιθυμίας, ἐπιδέσμους, ἐπίγαμ, moribundus, fere mortuus, aliquantum densus, subflavus, aliisque ejusmodi. Praeterea ad locum Apostolicum responderi potest, intelligi non sanguinem & suffocatum in genere; sed immolatitium, in Gentilium sacrificiis; ubi non semel una cum carnibus, sanguinem etiam victimarum devorabant. Vide Seldenum loc. cit. pag. 717. Certè alibi fit tantùm mentio idololatriae & fornicationis, Apoc. 11. 14. Maimonides, More Nevochim, part. III. c. XLVI. illam rationem dat prohibiti sanguinis, quod Sabii seu gentiles idololatrae solitи erant cum victimâ ejus sanguinem comedere, in sacramentum communionis cum Daemonibus: observatque, eâdem phrasi Deum uti, quando adversus comedentem sanguinem, atque immolantem Molocho loquitur, & nusquam alias: ponam faciem meam contra virum illum. Levit. XVII. 10. & XX. 3. Quia, inquit Maimonides, illius comestio ad speciem aliquam idololatriae, Daemonum videlicet cultum, ansam & occasionem praebeat. Et Mikkotzi, praecepto negativo CLXXI. Atque juxta eam sententiam respondet Thomas à Iesu, lib. VI. de Converf. Gent. cap. I. non advertunt Graeci, inquit, contra quos ibi disputat, illud Apostolorum decretum contra idolorum cultores latum fuisse, qui immolatum & idolatriticum edebant. Quare tantum illud servandum erit sicut à Catholicis servatur, ubicunque inter gentes quae idola adorant immolatitia sunt. Porro illo Apostolorum decreto tantum immolatitia & non alia prohiberi, docent gravissimi Orientalium Patres, B. Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus in 4. Catechesi, D. Gregor. Nazian. Serm. in sanctam Pascha, Iustin. Martyr q. 43. Origenes, lib. 8. contra Celsum, & alii. Argumenta pro sententiâ nostrâ haec habeo.
units.tr: But why did the Apostles not rather, if they wished to gratify the Jews in this matter and yield Christian liberty to their weakness, grant or enjoin circumcision? The Jews indeed desired this most of all, and it had been the cause of the dispute and the council. Certainly circumcision differs enormously from abstaining from blood or from what is strangled. While some concession seemed to be made to the Jews in a matter of this kind, it was not to be made for the sake of any great chapter of the law but rather for a trifling thing, especially since the principal business meanwhile had also to be pursued and recommended: the abrogation and burial of the ceremonial law. Add to this that in the whole of this question, whether the Jews pressed for circumcision or the Apostles opposed it, circumcision was always considered as one singular chapter of the law, yet such that it embraced the observance of the whole ceremonial law and was its summary (Gal. 5:3). Hence any other part of the ceremonial law could have been granted or imposed rather than that. Moreover, in every dispensation there is a great difference between omitting something that is lawful only, especially in the daily customs of living, concerning food and eating, where there is also an abundance of other things, and committing, performing or carrying out something that lies in the sole and chief article of religion, as circumcision does. Therefore, while the Apostles were now engaged in the task of teaching how the time of the ceremonial law had expired and that it was no longer to be observed, yet meanwhile they wished to act with prudence and charity towards the Jews, that is, the Christians coming from Judaism, who clung to the law and especially stuck fast to this stone, they judged it expedient, lest some ill-timed zeal lead the remaining Christians to abuse their liberty to the contempt and offence of other brothers, that they should not observe the whole ceremonial law, all of it, or its greatest chapter, but by abstaining should abstain only from a few and lighter things, in which they yielded only some of their right, namely from eating what was offered to idols, from blood and from what is strangled, things otherwise lawful. Where this reason ceases, namely the offence, and it ceases today, I do not see why it should not be lawful to enjoy and eat all those things mentioned. Although, now that the offence of the Jews coming to the faith has ceased, I would not wish to use that liberty rashly or boastfully, where a Christian, from weakness and not from reverence or authority of the ceremonial law (which would be more a heresy than a weakness), but because of the apostolic canon, thought that he must abstain from what is strangled and from blood. See Rom. 14; 1 Cor. 8:13. So readily ought we to yield in an easy matter, where it matters much whether we give up what is ours, and that without any inconvenience, or whether the brother's conscience is saddened, hurt or corrupted. And although those things are said to be necessary to be observed [ἐπιάναγκες] in the Apostolic decree (I by no means like changing the reading arbitrarily to ἐπ' ἀνάγκης), it does not follow that all these chapters must be kept with equal or the same necessity. Fornication must be avoided out of perpetual and moral necessity; but eating of things offered to idols, and of what is strangled, is necessary indeed at some times, but only when the case of offence or scandal arises; apart from that case, not. Therefore I prefer the view of Cloppenburg, in his Scholā sacrifi., near the end, that [ἐπιάναγκες] is to be taken adverbially and to denote a certain diminution of necessity, as in [ἐπιθυμίας], [ἐπιδέσμους], [ἐπίγαμ], moribundus, almost dead, somewhat thick, yellowish, and other expressions of this kind. Besides, it can be answered to the apostolic passage that blood and what is strangled are not to be understood in general, but the things offered in sacrifices to the Gentiles, where they not once devoured the blood of the victims together with the flesh. See Selden, loc. cit., p. 717. Certainly elsewhere only idolatry and fornication are mentioned (Rev. 2:14, 20). Maimonides, More Nevochim, part III, ch. 46, gives this reason for the prohibition of blood: that the Sabians or Gentile idolaters were accustomed to eat the blood with the victim, as a sacrament of communion with the demons; and he observes that God uses the same phrase when He speaks against the one eating blood and sacrificing to Molech, and nowhere else: "I will set my face against that man" (Lev. 17:10; 20:3). Because, says Maimonides, eating it would offer some appearance and occasion of idolatry, namely the worship of demons. And Mikkotzi, negative precept 171, and in accordance with that opinion Thomas à Jesu responds, book VI of De Conversione Gentium, ch. 1: the Greeks, against whom he disputes there, do not notice, he says, that the apostolic decree was issued against the worshippers of idols, who ate what was sacrificed and offered to idols. Therefore that alone must be observed, as it is observed by Catholics, wherever among the nations that worship idols there are things sacrificed to idols. Moreover, that the apostolic decree forbade only things sacrificed to idols and no others, the most weighty Fathers of the East teach: St Cyril of Jerusalem in his fourth Catechesis, St Gregory Nazianzen in his sermon on holy Pascha, Justin Martyr, question 43, Origen, book 8 against Celsus, and others. These are the arguments I have for our opinion.

units.la: 1. Quia discrimen esculiorum, proinde abstinentia à sanguine & suffocato, non est juris naturalis, vel moralis; quare nec perpetui usus, vel observantiae, vel ad nos ulla vi legis pertinens. Hoc fundamento nititur, quod disputant Nostri adversum Pontificios, non licere Ecclesiae, novas praeter Dei verbum leges condere, neque aliis Christianis objicere, quàm quas Dei lex comprobat: & quod respondent ad Act. xv. non ibi novum quid Apostolos instituisse aut decrevisse; sed tantum legem mutuae charitatis, & de cavendâ proximi offensione explicasse ad prudentem libertatis, in iis dierum gratiam, attemperationem, quatenus pro tempore expediebat ab idolothyto, sanguine, & suffocato abstinere. Vi de Calvinum, Institut. lib. IV. cap. x. §. 21. 22. Et Nostrorum Disputationes, adversus Bellarminum, lib. IV. de Rom. Pontifice, cap. XVI. Secundò argumentamur, ex statu Novi Test. ubi lex cæremonialis abrogata, discrimen ciborum sublatum, & libertas hâc etiam in parte fidelibus acquisita. Primò ergo hic consideranda est legis cæremonialis abrogatio, cujus est caput illud de discrimine ciborum, de non edendo sanguine. Quò minus illorum sententiam conciliàre possum, qui exserte fatentur legis cæremonialis hoc esse, & quoque adhuc observandum. Quum nihil certius, nihil in Theologiâ notius sit, quàm cæremonias legis omnes cum Christo evânuisse, hodieque illarum observantiam ita esse mortiferam, uti antea fuit laudabilis. Quæ ante Christum debuit observari lex, quamquam ante destructum templum, utcunque in Christo intermortuam, aliquâ tamen ratione licuit ex parte servare, ut nempe cum honore Synagoga sepeliretur, hodie nefas est revocare, vel resuscitare bene sepultam. Col. II. 16. 17. 20. 21. 22. 23. Heb. IX. 10. Ex illo deinde est, quod sub Novo nunc Testamento omnes cibi quod ad usum pariter sunt liciti, nihilque illorum ultra immundum. Matth. XV. 11. Act. X. 15. Rom. XIV. 2. 14. 17. 20. 1 Cor. VIII. 8. & X. 25. 1 Tim. IV. V. 5. Tit. I. 14. Denique pars libertatis Christianæ est, in quam per Christum vindicati sumus, quæque adeo, ne ullo cæremonialis legis onere nos iterùm sinamus implicari, defendenda, nullum discrimen in cibo vel potu constituere aut observare. 1 Cor. VIII. 4. Gal. V. 1. 9. 13. & IV. 9. 10. 11. cum. Rom. XIV. 2. 5. Tertiò, ex hoc ipso loco Act. XV. 28. sic de Apostolorum mente arguo, quod ea non fuerit, omnibus & perpetuò legem sigere de cavendo sanguine: quia exserte testantur se non posse, ideoque nolle ζυγὸν vers. 10. βαρεῖν, videlicet cæremoniarum imponere fidelibus, quale interim fatentur esse & hoc de vitando sanguine: clarum ergo, non sensisse eos hoc, quod ex lege caeremoniali praescribunt hic observan- dum, legis, aut perpetuae obligationis vim sortiri debere, sed potius tempori indulgeri, citra praejudicium nostrae ab illo onere liberationis. Praesertim quum alibi, ubi de caeremoniarum abolitione loquuntur Apostoli, quod non semel fit, integram & universalem cam docent, non excepto ullo legis capite, quod ex eâ servandum ulterius sit, quodque simul arguat non illam sublatam totam. Vti nec cum ullâ limitatione vel exceptione loquuntur hic Petrus & Jacobus, quando ad propositam quaestionem simpliciter suis in orationibus vel suffragiis docent, legem caeremonialem frustra amplius urgeri. Tunc & id rogatum velim alios, an putent, idololbyti esum interdictum semper & ubique esse, etiam extra periculum scandali & offensionis? Sijant, velim ad contrariam Apostoli sententiam 1 Cor. VIII. mihi tum responderi: sin negent illicitum esse, tum quidni idem in suffocato? utraque capita conjunguntur, & ejusdem generis censenda sunt, ut utrumque canon non propter legem, sed propter offensionem caveri jusserit. Leve est, quod objicitur, de fornicatione addito interdicto: quod si à vi perpetuum est: neque tum aliis me hic torqueri sinam, quomodo cum praecepto legis perpetuo, quale est prohibitio fornicationis, jungantur alia (nostro judicio) non propter se prohibita, sed pro tempore tantum cavenda. Quid enim difficultatis continet, quod res diversi generis jun- guntur in unâ sententiâ? id quod saepe contingit; praecipuè ubi aliquo modo conveniunt, ut una vel impetrentur, vel prohibeantur, quantumvis non aequaliter? cogita, quod si pariter ex lege observari debeant omnia ista capita, tam cavendi idolothytha, sanguinem, suffocatum, quam idololatriam: ad quam legem referes priora? illud de prohibitâ fornicatione constat, legis moralis esse, adeoque naturalis: cui jungantur alia legis caeremonialis: quae si necessario observanda, jam fesequetur, legem cæremonialem, saltem quoad illa perpetuò observandam esse: quod quomodo cum analogia fidei conveniat, equidem non video. Idem de illis judicium, qui & suillâ carne ex religione abstinent. Quales olim quoque fuisse nonnullos, si non etiam hodie, colligere est ex Basilii canone xxv i i i. quæ citatur in epitome Canonum Harmenopuli, sect. v. de Laicis, tit. i i. Qui se promisit abstinere velle à suillis carnibus, ridiculus est. Quippe nulla Dei creatura rejicienda est, quæ cum gratiarum actione sumatur. Argumentum pro nostra sententia tertium inde sumo, quod, quando maximè viguit prohibitio sanguinis, & suffocati, sub V. T. licuit proselytis tamen ista comedere, Deut. xiv. 21. Unde apparet, non in se illud, aut suâ natura, tanquam ex vi legis perpetuæ illicitum habitum vel tum fuisse. Accedit, quod Iudæi interdictum de sanguine non accipiunt nisi de sanguine pecorum, ferarum, volucrum, non piscium, locustarum, aliorumve id genus animalium, quæ edere quamvis cum sanguine licitum sibi habuerunt, nempe nisi immunda fuissent. Docet hoc Maimonides, Halach. Schecita cap. i. ubi inquit: Non opus est ut adhibeantur ritus mactationis piscibus & locustis. Certum collectio eorum tantum licitos eos facit. Nam Moses, Num. xxi. 22. nunquid oves & boves mactabantur pro eis, qui sufficiant eis? vel omnes pisces maris colligentur pro eis? collectio seu congregatio, ipsa captura piscium, velut mactatio bovum & pecorum. Alibi item collectio locustarum memoratur, ut in Prophetis Isai. xxxiii. 4. ut quæ sola sufficeret. Unde etiam, tametsi ex se morerentur in aquis, liciti erant pisces, quos etiam vivos comedere (ut ostrea nos solemus) licuit. Adde Mikkotzi, præcepto supra allegato.
units.tr: 1. Because the distinction between foods, and therefore abstinence from blood and from what is strangled, is not part of natural or moral law, it has no permanent force or observance, and does not bind us by any power of law. Our writers rest on this foundation when they argue against the Papists that the Church may not make new laws beyond the Word of God, nor impose on other Christians anything except what God's law approves. They answer that Acts 15 does not show the Apostles instituting or decreeing anything new, but only explaining the law of mutual charity and of avoiding offence to a neighbour, so that, for the time being and as the circumstances required, Christians should abstain from meat offered to idols, from blood, and from what is strangled, out of prudent consideration for the weak in the exercise of liberty. See Calvin, Institutes, bk. IV, ch. x, §§ 21, 22, and our disputations against Bellarmine, bk. IV, On the Roman Pontiff, ch. XVI. Second, we argue from the state of the New Testament, in which the ceremonial law has been abrogated, the distinction of foods removed, and liberty in this matter also won for the faithful. First, then, we must consider the abrogation of the ceremonial law, of which the rule about the distinction of foods, and about not eating blood, is a part. I cannot reconcile myself with those who openly admit that this is part of the ceremonial law and still to be observed. Nothing is more certain or better known in theology than that all the ceremonies of the law vanished with Christ, and that to observe them now is as deadly as it once was praiseworthy. The law which ought to have been observed before Christ, and which, though in Christ it had died out, was in some respect permitted to be kept until the temple was destroyed, so that the synagogue might be buried with honour, is now unlawful to revive, or to raise up again once it has been buried. (Col. 2:16, 17, 20–23; Heb. 9:10.) From this it follows that under the New Testament all foods are equally lawful for use, and none is any longer unclean (Matt. 15:11; Acts 10:15; Rom. 14:2, 14, 17, 20; 1 Cor. 8:8; 10:25; 1 Tim. 4:4, 5; Tit. 1:14). Finally, it is part of the liberty of the Christian, into which we have been claimed through Christ, and which must be defended so that we do not again allow ourselves to be burdened with any yoke of the ceremonial law, to set up or observe no distinction in food or drink (1 Cor. 8:4; Gal. 5:1, 9, 13; 4:9–11; compare Rom. 14:2, 5). Third, from this very passage, Acts 15:28, I argue about the mind of the Apostles thus: they did not intend to impose on all men, and for ever, a law about abstaining from blood, because they expressly testify that they neither could nor would lay on the faithful "a yoke [ζυγὸν] (Acts 15:10) or a burden [βαρεῖν]", that is, the burden of ceremonies, which they admit this prohibition about avoiding blood also to be. It is clear, therefore, that they did not mean that what they prescribe here from the ceremonial law should have the force of a law or of perpetual obligation, but rather that they yielded to the times, without prejudice to our liberation from that burden. This is especially so since, where the Apostles speak elsewhere about the abolition of the ceremonies, which they do more than once, they teach that abolition as complete and universal, with no exception of any chapter of the law that is to be kept further, which in itself shows that the law was not abolished in part. Nor do Peter and James speak with any limitation or exception here, when, in their speeches or votes on the question proposed, they simply teach that the ceremonial law is no longer to be urged in vain. I would also like others to be asked whether they think that eating meat offered to idols is forbidden always and everywhere, even outside the danger of scandal and offence. If they say it is, I would like them to answer me with the contrary opinion of the Apostle in 1 Cor. 8. But if they deny that it is unlawful, why not the same for what is strangled? The two heads are joined together, and are to be judged of the same kind, so that the canon ordered both to be avoided not on account of the law but on account of offence. What is objected about fornication, with a prohibition added, is a light matter; for if that prohibition is perpetual in force, I will not let myself here be tormented by how other things, which in my judgment were not forbidden in themselves but were to be avoided only for the time, are joined to a precept of perpetual law, such as the prohibition of fornication. For what difficulty is there in things of different kinds being joined in one sentence? This happens often, especially where they agree in some way, so that they are either enjoined or forbidden together, however unequally. Consider: if all these heads, the avoiding of meat offered to idols, of blood, and of what is strangled, as well as of idolatry, ought to be observed equally by law, to which law will you refer the former ones? It is certain that the prohibition of fornication belongs to the moral and therefore natural law, and that other things belonging to the ceremonial law are joined to it. If these must necessarily be observed, it will follow that the ceremonial law, at least in those points, must be observed for ever; and how this agrees with the analogy of faith, I certainly do not see. The same judgment applies to those who abstain from pork out of religious scruple. There were once some of this kind, if not still today, as may be gathered from canon 28 of Basil, which is cited in the epitome of the Canons of Harmenopulus, sect. v, on laymen, tit. ii: "He who has promised that he will abstain from pork is ridiculous. For no creature of God is to be rejected, which is taken with thanksgiving." I draw a third argument for our view from this: when the prohibition of blood and of what is strangled was most in force under the Old Testament, it was still permitted to proselytes to eat these things (Deut. 14:21). Hence it appears that these things were not unlawful in themselves, or by the force of a perpetual law, even then. Besides, the Jews do not understand the prohibition about blood except of the blood of cattle, wild beasts, and birds, not of fish, locusts, or other animals of that kind, which they held it lawful to eat even with blood, namely unless they were unclean. Maimonides teaches this in Halakhot Shechitah, ch. i, where he says: "There is no need for the rite of slaughter to be applied to fish and locusts. Gathering them alone makes them lawful. For Moses, in Num. 11:22, asks: Are sheep and oxen to be slaughtered for them, to suffice for them? Or are all the fish of the sea to be gathered together for them? The gathering, the very catching of fish, is like the slaughter of oxen and cattle. Elsewhere too the gathering of locusts is mentioned, as in Isaiah 33:4, since that alone would suffice." Hence also fish, even though they die of themselves in the water, were lawful, and it was permitted to eat them alive, as we are accustomed to do with oysters. Add Mikkotzi, on the precept cited above.

units.la: Circa cultum imaginum pristina quidem Ecclesiæ Græcæ fuit sententia, neque faciendas, neque colendas esse; ut ex Actis Synodi Constantinopolitanæ sub Constantino Copronymo a. Io ccl iv. variisque Impp. editis videre dere est, de quibus in Iuris Orientalis lib. 1. legitur sub Constitutionibus Theophili: Michaël pater ejus edixerat ne ullï pictæ imagini, ubicunque ea essent, nomen Sanctæ imprimeretur, quòd id nulli rei præterquam soli Deo congruere putabat. Leo autem, & filius ejus Constantinus omni earum adoratione prorsus interdixerant. Theophilus autem ne pingi quidem eas coloribus concessit: abjecti animi esse talium rerum admirationem, ipsamque solam spectandam esse veritatem. Inde autem à pristinâ pietate ac zelo adeo desciverunt, ut detestari hoc duntaxat videantur, si quis fusas aut statuas veneretur, circa pictas alias, earumve cultum negligentiores: quamvis neque illud etiam satis observent, præsertim in figurâ crucis habendâ, venerandaque, & præsertim in S. Nicolai effigie Moscovitæ: hi in singulis ædibus & habitationibus habent imagines sanctorum, pictas, aut fusas, ico honorificentiore, & cum alius alium accedit, ingressus habitaculum, continuo caput aperit, ac ubi imago sit, circumspicit: quâ visâ, ter se crucis signo munit, caputque inclinans inquit: Domine miserere. Dein salutat hospitem: uti refert Sigismundus Baro. Vide etiam in Christiani V Voldimari Principis Daniæ, Responso cap. VIII. ad scriptum Iosephi Moscovitarum Patriarchæ a. cIↄ Iↄ cIV. Solas picturas venerantur Abyssini, non statuas. Armeni autem imagines non adorant: quin adoratores earum palam condemnant. Refert Edwin Sandis, Anglus, in Relat. de Statu Relig. cap. XLI. adeo diversas esse effigies Christi, & Mariæ (quas unicè venerantur) apud Græcos, ab illis quas Latini colunt, ut nullâ ratione sibi sint similes. Quodque magis mirum aut ridiculum, imaginem Mariæ in Laureto conspici facie Æthiopissæ. Neque aliter oportuit prostitui rei hujus turpitudinem ac superstitionem. Atque uti in hoc de imaginibus, ita etiam de cultu & veneratione Sanctorum (hæc enim sibi mutuò affinia) à Scripturæ & veterum suorum Patrum doctrinâ immane quantum Græci desciverunt. verunt, illos communi more invocando, præsertim Mariam. Cujus locuple testimonium in ipsorum Euchologio, sive Ritvali; & Horologio, sive officio singularum horarum. Ieremias Patriarcha, Respons. I. cap. xxi, & Resp. II. cap. v. & Resp. III. cap. iv. Addunt & alios pro sanctis. Chaldæi Nestorium invocant, & Theodorum Mopsvestenum. Iacobitæ, Cophthi, & Æthiopes Severum. Dioscorum, & Iacobum. Armeni Thaddæum Apostolum: à quo ajunt suos primum conversos, S. Georgium Georgiani. S. Nicolaum, & Angelum Michaelem Russi. Omnes male.
units.tr: Concerning the worship of images, the earlier view of the Greek Church was indeed that they are neither to be made nor worshipped. This may be seen from the Acts of the Synod of Constantinople under Constantine Copronymus in the year 754, and from edicts of various emperors, of which we read in the Oriental Law, bk. 1, under the Constitutions of Theophilus: "Michael, his father, had ordered that the name of a Saint should not be placed on any painted image wherever it might be, because he thought this suited no thing except God alone. Leo, however, and his son Constantine had utterly forbidden all adoration of them. Theophilus did not even allow them to be painted in colours: the admiration of such things is a mark of a base mind, and only the truth itself is to be looked upon." But from their earlier piety and zeal they have so far departed that they seem to detest this only if someone venerates cast or carved images, and are more careless about other painted ones and their cult; though they do not even keep this strictly, especially in the matter of having and venerating the figure of the cross, and especially in the Muscovite images of St. Nicholas. These have in every house and dwelling images of the saints, painted or cast, and honour them more reverently; and when one comes to another, on entering the dwelling he at once uncovers his head and looks round for the image, and having seen it, he signs himself three times with the sign of the cross, and bowing his head says: "Lord, have mercy." Then he greets the host, as Sigismund Baron reports. See also the Christian V of Voldemar, Prince of Denmark, Response, ch. VIII, to the writing of Joseph, Patriarch of the Muscovites, of the year 1604. The Abyssinians venerate only pictures, not statues. The Armenians, however, do not adore images; indeed they openly condemn those who worship them. Edwin Sandys, an Englishman, reports in his Relation of the State of Religion, ch. XLI, that the images of Christ and Mary (which alone they venerate) among the Greeks are so different from those the Latins worship that they are in no way like each other. And what is more wonderful or ridiculous, an image of Mary at Loreto is seen with the face of an Ethiopian woman. Nor could the shame and superstition of this matter have been more openly displayed. And just as in this matter of images, so too in the cult and veneration of the saints (for these are closely related) the Greeks have departed to an immense degree from the teaching of Scripture and of their own ancient Fathers, invoking them in the common manner, especially Mary. Their Euchologion, or Ritual, and their Horologion, or office of the individual hours, give ample testimony to this. Jeremiah the Patriarch (Response I, ch. xxi; Response II, ch. v; Response III, ch. iv) adds other examples of invoking saints. The Chaldeans invoke Nestorius and Theodore of Mopsuestia; the Jacobites, Copts, and Ethiopians invoke Severus, Dioscorus, and James. The Armenians invoke the Apostle Thaddeus, by whom they say their people were first converted; the Georgians invoke St. George; the Russians, St. Nicholas and the Archangel Michael. All of them wrongly.

units.la: Quæstio de processione Spiritus Sancti à Patre, Fili- oque, gravis quidem præ cæteris visa est, quia primarium fi- dei de Deo articulum tangere videtur.
units.tr: The question about the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son seemed, among the others, a grave one, since it appears to touch the primary article of faith concerning God.

units.la: sed bene introspecta non hoc adeo impetebant Græci, ac quod symbolo particula illa addita fuisset, Latinorum arbitrio, non exspectata Synodi generalis sententia, neque audito Orientalis Ecclesiæ hac super re judicio: quare potissimum hujus contentionis posteriora ex alio fluxit capite, quod est de auctoritate Ecclesiæ Romanæ, ejusque primatu. Deinde in re ipsa præjudiciis aberratum fuit, putantibus Græcis Latinos statuere, quod ex duplici causa vel principio pendeat Spiritus Sancti processio, & non ex uno oriatur: quum non aliter docerent Latini quam à Patre Filioque procedere ex uno spirandi principio, à Patre per Filium. Denique nec hæc res sola vel tanta, vel tam aperte decisa in S. Dei verbo, ut propterea, siquidem in reliquis conveniretur, vel anathema mutuò dicendum, vel discerpendæ Ecclesiæ essent. Quomodo hàc in disputatione convenerint Græci, Latinique in Concilio Florentino, cui mox Græci reclamarunt, supra diximus. Facilius concedunt, Spiritum S. procedere à Patre, per Filium, quam à Patre, Filioque. Cæterùm in professione fidei, quam faciunt sub tempus ordinationis Græcorum episcopi, & archiepiscopi, dicunt inter alia, de Spiritu S. solummodo τὸ ἐκ τοῦ ΠαἉλλὰ ἐπιπροσθῶσι ... nil de Filio. Neque ait Ieremias Patriarcha Constantinop. in Responso ad Tubingenses. Qui dum non procedere eum à Filio contendit, distinguit, uti Graecorum alii, inter processionem personalem in Deo, & missionem externam ac temporariam Spiritus S. vel donorum ipsius in homines. Contendit quidem hoc à Filio fieri quoque: non autem inde recte illud prius inferri existimat. Ita nullo modo sequuntur Graeci suorum in Concilio Florentino factam cum Latinis unionem: juxta quam Gennadius Patriarcha, qui illi interfuit, scripsit defensionem ejus ad suos Graecos, qui nihilo dimoti à sententia, suos in Florentino Concilio ad faciendam unionem moribus emptos fuisse, palam affirmarunt: quod proinde in Scripti sui initio amovere à se Gennadius molitur. Atque hic utcunque Latinorum sententiae fuerit, tamen in Confessione fidei facta coram Mahomete II. non diu post captam urbem, a. MCCCCLIII, de Spiritu S. satis habuit dixisse: Ἁλλὰ ... ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς ... ἐκ τοῦ Υἱοῦ. Quidquid sit, non videtur, prout à Graecis haec quaestio agitatur, aut itaque fundamentalis esse, aut ita necessaria explicatu, ut ecclesias, si caetera conveniant, scindere debeat. Verum, uti aliquoties jam diximus, non articulus ille vel quaestio adeo fuit, quae tantopere Graecos offenderit, quam ejus ad symbolum additio, incons ulta inauditaque Orientali ecclesiae, quae hactenus idem cum Occidentali symbolum tenuerat, imo ab Oriental symbolum acceperat Occidentalis, id est, non ferebat hoc argumentum praetensae à Romana auctoritatis potestatisque in alias Ecclesias Graecas. Quando vero, verba sunt Thomae à Iesu Carmelitani Monachi, lib. VI. de Convers. Gentium, cap. III. Fuerit à Latinis facta illa additio Filioque, licet id clare non constet, verisimile creditur fuisse facta circa annum sexcentesimum. Nam in Concilio Toletano octavo celebrato circa annum sexcentesimum mum quinquagesimum tertium, recitatur symbolum cum hac additione: & cum ante hoc tempus, non inveniatur cum illa, ut constat ex Concilio Toletano tertio, anno quingentesimo octuagesimo nono celebrato, signum evidens est, illo medio tempore, fuisse à Romano Pontifice additionem factam, ut creditur in Concilio ingenti Latinorum Patrum propter dissensiones quasdam exortas inter Galliam, & Hispaniam: quamvis non constet quale fuerit illud Concilium, ut notavit D. Thom. 1. p. q. 36. art. 2. unde quamvis certò non possit explorari, neque locus neque tempus huius additionis, certum tamen est, vel in aliquo Concilio generali, vel authoritate alicujus summi Pontificis additum esse. Auctoritate Romani Pontificis Leonis symbolo superadditum scribit Severinus Binius, in Notis ad Conc. Constantinop. 1. Deque re, seu articulo illo arduo processionis Spiritus Sancti disputant subtiliter, pro more Scholastici, ad Thomam, 1. qu. xxxvi. Gabriel Vasquez, Disp. cxlv. Iohannes de Rada, Controversf. inter Thomam & Scotum, Controv. xv. & xvi. Theod. Smising, de Deo Trino, Disp. iv. qu. 1. & 11. alii.
units.tr: But on closer inspection the Greeks did not so much attack this point itself, as the fact that the particle had been added to the creed at the discretion of the Latins, without waiting for the judgment of a general council and without hearing the opinion of the Eastern Church on the matter. So the later stages of this dispute flowed mainly from another source, namely the authority of the Roman Church and its primacy. Further, the matter itself was misunderstood through prejudice, the Greeks supposing that the Latins held that the procession of the Holy Spirit depends on a double cause or principle and does not arise from one alone, since the Latins taught nothing other than that he proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one principle of spiration, from the Father through the Son. Finally, this question was not so important, nor so clearly settled in the holy Word of God, that, if they agreed on the rest, they should have to pronounce anathema on each other or tear the Church apart. How the Greeks and Latins came to terms on this disputed point at the Council of Florence, which the Greeks soon repudiated, we have said above. They more readily concede that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son than from the Father and the Son. Moreover, in the profession of faith which Greek bishops and archbishops make at the time of their ordination, they say among other things, concerning the Holy Spirit only [τὸ ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς ἐκπορευόμενον], "proceeding from the Father", and say nothing about the Son. Nor does Jeremias, Patriarch of Constantinople, say so in his Answer to the Tübingen theologians. While he contends that the Spirit does not proceed from the Son, he distinguishes, as some other Greeks do, between the personal procession in God and the external and temporal mission of the Holy Spirit, or of his gifts, to human beings. He does indeed contend that this mission also comes from the Son, but he does not think that the former may rightly be inferred from it. Thus the Greeks in no way follow the union made at Florence with the Latins by their own people: Gennadius, Patriarch, who was present there, wrote a defence of it to his fellow Greeks, who, not at all moved from their view, openly declared that their representatives at the Council of Florence had been bought with money to bring about the union; which is why Gennadius, at the beginning of his writing, labours to clear himself of this charge. And however the Latin view may be, in the confession of faith made before Mahomet II, not long after the capture of the city, in 1453, he was content to say about the Holy Spirit only: [ἀλλὰ ... ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς ... ἐκ τοῦ Υἱοῦ] "but ... from the Father ... from the Son". Whatever the case, as the Greeks conduct this question, it does not seem either to be fundamental, or so necessary to explain that it ought to split the churches if they agree on the rest. Yet, as we have said several times already, it was not that article or question which so offended the Greeks, but its addition to the creed, made without consultation and without the knowledge of the Eastern Church, which until then had held the same creed as the Western Church, and indeed the Western Church had received the creed from the Eastern. That is, they did not tolerate this claimed authority and power of the Roman Church over the other Greek churches. When, however, this addition of the word Filioque was made by the Latins, the words are those of Thomas à Jesu, a Carmelite monk, in book VI of De Conversione Gentium, chapter III: although it is not clearly established, it is believed to have been made about the year 600. For in the Eighth Council of Toledo, held around the year 653, the creed is recited with this addition; and since before this time it is not found with it, as is clear from the Third Council of Toledo, held in the year 589, there is clear evidence that in that intervening time the addition was made by the Roman Pontiff, as is believed, or in some great council of Latin Fathers, on account of certain disputes that had arisen between Gaul and Spain; although it is not certain what that council was, as Thomas (Aquinas) noted in 1 p. q. 36 art. 2. So, although the place and time of this addition cannot be determined with certainty, it is certain that it was added either in some general council or by the authority of some supreme Pontiff. Severinus Binius, in his Notes on the First Council of Constantinople, writes that it was added to the creed on the authority of the Roman Pontiff Leo. And concerning this matter, or that difficult article of the procession of the Holy Spirit, the Scholastics, following the usual method, dispute subtly with reference to Thomas, 1 qu. xxxvi: Gabriel Vasquez, Disp. cxlv; Juan de Rada, Controversies between Thomas and Scotus, Controv. xv and xvi; Theodor Smising, On the Triune God, Disp. iv, qu. 1 and 2; and others.

units.la: Super azymo, sive an S. Coena celebranda sit in fermentato, ut Graeci; an infermentato, ut Latini, eo minor superest contentio, quo hi concedunt, & in hoc, & illo aequè sacramentum perfici: non ergo hic adeo impugnant Graecos Latini, ac suum de azymo tueri conantur morem. Nos cum Graecis facimus, utrumque fermentato, videlicet quia communis panis est; quali utendum res ipsa ostendit. Non verò in hoc Graecis accedimus, quod ad probationem suae thesis assumunt, vel azymum non esse panem, non ἄρτον, scilicet quia non ἄζυμον tollitur fermento in altum; vel quod Christus in primâ Coenâ fermentato fuerit usus. Nam quod aiunt, Christum dicam Paschatis anticipasse, & alio à Iudaeis die luna decimaquarta suum Pascha, tum S. Coenam celebrasse, non ita statuimus, sed eodem quo ex lege comedendum Pascha, tum Iudaeis id Christum quoque obseruasse: quamuis non eiusdem diei sed tem-pore, sed pridie comederit, certum tamen quod quia in azymis Pascha celebrabatur, quocunque demum die hoc Christus peregerit, non alio pane, quam infermentato obseruasse. Res leuior videtur, quam ut de ea magnopere contendatur, vel ut per sex integra secula ea habita fuerit scismatis materia: nam incepit quaestio 2. cap. liii. uti Leo ix. scribit in epist. ad Michaelem Constantinop. episcopum, de quo supra vidimus. Neque adeo in Latinis reprehenderemus, quod azymo utantur in Coena, si pane solido, sed quod eius spumam et minutias farinaceas leuissimas, panis nomine uti eignas adhibent, magis improbamus. Vti olim circa cl.lx. de eo scripsit Berenoldus, Constantiensis presbyter, quem in Liturgicis adducit Cassander, cap. xxv. ii. qui illa per contemptum minutiae numeri arenarum et latarum appellat, imaginarium et umbratilem leuitatem illis tribuit, et indignas esse panis vocabulo pro sua censura, ac propter eas officium atque religionem ecclesiastica officia multum per omnem modum confundi asserit. Deinde et hoc Graeci melius quam Latini, quod in Coena communionem celebrant, sub utraque Sacramenti parte: adeo ut Ruteni quoque, quando se cum Romana conjungerent Ecclesia a. cl.lo lx.xcv. stipulati inter alia fuerint: Sacramenta sanctissimi corporis et sanguinis Domini nostri Iesu Christi ut nobis ita, quemadmodum hucusque ab fuerunt, sub utraque specie panis et vini, temporibus perpetuis integre inviolabiliterque conseruentur. Ieremias Patriarcha, cap. xxi. - Dicitis itaque primum, in S. Coena percipiendam esse utramque speciem: et recte dicitis. Sic enim et nos facimus, quando venerandum percipimus mysterium, quod quidem dignissimum.
units.tr: Concerning the unleavened bread, that is, whether the Holy Supper is to be celebrated in leavened bread, as the Greeks hold, or in unleavened bread, as the Latins hold, the dispute is the smaller, since the Latins concede that the sacrament is equally performed with either. The Latins therefore do not fight the Greeks so hard here as they strive to defend their own custom regarding unleavened bread. We agree with the Greeks that both should be leavened, namely because it is ordinary bread, which is what the thing itself shows should be used. We do not, however, agree with the Greeks in the arguments they adduce for their thesis: that unleavened bread is not bread [ἄρτον], namely because the unleavened [ἄζυμον] is not raised up by leaven; or that Christ used leavened bread at the first Supper. For as to their claim that Christ anticipated the Passover by a day, and celebrated his Passover on the fourteenth day of the moon at a different time from the Jews and then the Holy Supper, we do not hold this. We hold rather that Christ observed the Passover on the same day on which the law required it to be eaten, as the Jews did. Though he ate it not on the same day but a day earlier, it is certain that, since the Passover was celebrated with unleavened bread, whatever day Christ kept it he kept it with no bread but unleavened. The matter seems too trivial to be contended over so vigorously, or to have been the material of schism for six whole centuries. For the question arose (ii, chap. liii), as Leo IX writes in his letter to Michael, bishop of Constantinople, whom we saw above. Nor would we blame the Latins for using unleavened bread in the Supper, if it were solid bread; but we disapprove much more that they use, under the name of bread, the froth and the very light, floury crumbs of it. Berenoldus, presbyter of Constance, wrote about this long ago, around the year 1060; Cassander cites him in his Liturgica, chap. xxv. In contempt he calls these crumbs "a number of grains of sand" and "flakes," ascribes to them an imaginary and shadowy lightness, and, by his own judgment, says they are unworthy of the name of bread; and he asserts that on account of them the office and the religion of ecclesiastical offices are greatly confounded in every way. Further, the Greeks do better than the Latins in this too, that in the Supper they celebrate communion under both parts of the sacrament. So much so that the Ruthenians, when they joined themselves to the Roman Church in the year 1595, stipulated among other things: The sacraments of the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ shall be preserved whole and inviolable for perpetual times, as they have been hitherto, under both kinds of bread and wine. Jeremias the Patriarch, chap. xxi: You say first that in the Holy Supper both kinds are to be received, and you are right. For so we also do, when we receive the venerable mystery, which is most worthy.

units.la: Similiter a Romana Ecclesia dissident Graeci super Purgatorio igne, quem nullum esse singulari libro demonstravit Nilus, idque ex Patrum suorum perpetua, uti ait, sententia, qui nunquam talem ignem docue-runt. runt. Quamvis nec per omnia Graeci orthodoxè se gerant, ignem quidem purgandis animabus destruunt, interim tamen locum caliginosum alium, tristem, ac calamitosum constituunt, in quo animæ post hanc vitam purgentur, antequam ad Deum accedant. Ignem autem esse, & corporeum improbant, eò quòd animam à tali igne pati non posse videatur. Quare nullum nisi æternum ignem inferni norunt: deque eo explicant locum Apostoli, hàc in materià vulgò adferri solitum, 1 Cor. 3.1. 15. servabitur, quasi per ignem: in Concilio Florentino. Nilus exponit, de die judicii. Atque illic quidem ita se declararunt Graeci; nam ipsi purgatorium, non ignem, sed obscurum quendam locum, ac laborum plenum esse censemus, in quo quidem existentes animæ lumine divino privantur, donec coadjuvante ecclesiâ, ut suprà dictum est, expientur, ac liberentur. Intercessiones pro mortuis probant Graeci, & faciunt. Jeremias Patriarcha, in Resp. ad Tubingenses cap. xv. Et liberatæ, vel sanctæ animæ, juxta illos, ante judicii diem, non fruuntur divina in cœlo visione ac fruitione, nisi post diem judicii, sed alio quodam loco eo usque continentur, quem paradysum appellant: similiter de animabus impiorum dicunt, servari eas in loco quodam alio ab inferno, in quem post judicii diem sint conjiciendæ. Quâ de re disputat Gennadius Constantinopolitan. pro defens. Concil. Florent. cap. iv. Thomas à Jesu, de Conver. Gent. lib. vi. cap. vi. Sigismundus Baro, in Comment. Rer. Moscovit. Purgatorium nullum credunt: sed dicunt, unicuique vitâ defuncto, secundum meritum suum esse locum: piis quidem laetidum, cum angelis placidis: impiis autem obscurum, & caecâ caligine obductum, cum angelis terribilibus destinatum esse, in quo extremum expectant judicium. Ex loco & angelis placidis cognoscunt animæ gratiam Dei semper petunt extremum judicium: alii contra. Neque animam à corpore separatam, poenis obnoxiam esse putant. Nam cum anima in corpore se contaminaverit, cum corpore esse expiandem. Quod autem pro defunctis funebre sacrum faciunt, eo dicunt eo posse tolerabiliorem animabus eorum ac [?] locum, in quo facilius expectare futurum judicium queant. Idemque de illis refert Alexander Guagninus. Maniacha, in quae Graeci hodie post longam oppressionem, et sequutam immanissimam barbariem prolapsi sunt errorum capita, ea hactenus prosequuntur quae antiqua et communiter nota a multis seculis dissensionum argumenta fuere. Nunc vero iis subjugatis a crudelissimis tyrannis, neque parum religionis, ac libertatis apud ipsos videtur reliquum. Stupenda sane rerum sacrarum et Christianae religionis illic dominatur ignorantia, non in plebe solum et laicis, quos vocant, sed et sacerdotibus, ac clero. Retinent tamen aliquod ordinis hierarchici, numerantque Patriarchas, Metropolitas, episcopos, hieromonachos, Presbyteros sive Papas, Monachos, Diaconos, Hypodiaconos, & Anagnostas: Monachi suos Archimandritas, seu Abbates: suntque omnes ordinis Basilii, fundatoris Monachatus in Oriente, uti Benedictus in occidente: calogeri dicti καλόγεροι, quod nomen a bona senectute primo datum senioribus aetatis provectioris monachis, q. d. boni senes; inde omnibus Hic ordinis. Quod ad religionem, vulgo servant preces, lassas & liturgiam, sermone ac precibus, superstitiosas non omnino vacuis, peraeque fere barbaram: virque ultra quid sciunt, de vulgo loquor, quam horulas suas, & diebus sacris homilias, aegre ipsis intellectas: tanta apud illos hodie & litterarum & religionis raditas, societate aliorumque meliorumque Christianorum destitutos, atque tyrannide Turcarum oppressos nimis dejectosque. Unde & in reliquis fidei articulis aut probum sensum, aut confessionem ab illis temere exspectes. Commentum habent luminis in Christi sepulchro miraculose quotannis die sabbati sancti accensi, quod mirum dictu quantopere homines simplices in fide ergo Christum retinent, absque quo verentur eos ad Mahometismum hammedissimum defecturos. Quod fallum miraculum, ab aliquo sacerdote templum ingresso, qui orando scilicet impetrarit luminis istius accensionem, quodque tantum per horae spatium durat, & sustentatur in matceriae [?] in lampade ardentis, patratum: uti videre est in Commentario Adae, Archimandritae Chaldaeorum Babylonensium, de conciliatione fidei Orientalium, cum Romana, cap. VI. apud Bzovium, Annal. Tom. XIV. ad a. clɔ ccc xxx.
units.tr: The Greeks likewise differ from the Roman Church over the fire of Purgatory, which Nilus has shown in a single book to be nonexistent, relying, as he says, on the constant opinion of their Fathers, who never taught any such fire. Yet the Greeks do not behave entirely orthodoxly even here. They deny that the fire purges souls, but they posit another dark, sad and calamitous place in which souls are cleansed after this life, before they come to God. They deny that this fire is corporeal, because it seems that a soul cannot suffer from such a fire. Hence they know only the eternal fire of hell, and they explain the passage of the Apostle commonly cited on this subject, 1 Cor. 3. 15. "he shall be saved, yet so as by fire", as referring to the day of judgment; this is the view of Nilus, and the Council of Florence also reports it. In that place the Greeks declared themselves as follows: "For we hold that purgatory is not a fire but a dark and toilsome place, in which souls, existing there, are deprived of the divine light until, with the help of the Church, as was said above, they are cleansed and freed." The Greeks approve and practise intercessions for the dead. Jeremiah the Patriarch, in his reply to the Tübingen theologians, chapter 15. According to them, souls that have been freed, or are holy, do not enjoy the divine vision and fruition in heaven before the day of judgment; they are kept until then in some other place, which they call paradise. Similarly, they say of the souls of the impious that they are kept in a certain place other than hell, into which they are to be cast after the day of judgment. Gennadius of Constantinople discusses this matter in his defence of the Council of Florence, chapter 4. Thomas à Jesu, On the Conversion of the Gentiles, book 6, chapter 6. Sigismund Baron, in his Commentary on Muscovite affairs: "They believe in no purgatory, but say that after death each person has a place according to his merit: for the pious a place of joy, with gentle angels; for the impious a place dark and covered in blind mist, assigned to terrible angels, where they await the final judgment. From the place and the gentle angels the souls know the grace of God and always seek the final judgment; the others do not. Nor do they think that a soul separated from the body is liable to punishments; for when the soul has defiled itself in the body, it must be cleansed along with the body. As for the funeral rites they perform for the dead, they say that by these the souls are made more tolerable, and their place more bearable, so that they can more easily await the coming judgment." Alexander Guagninus reports the same things about them. Concerning the errors into which the Greeks have fallen today, after long oppression and a most savage barbarism, they still maintain those matters which for many centuries have been the old and commonly known grounds of dissension. But now that they have been subjected to the most cruel tyrants, little of religion or liberty seems to remain among them. Truly, a stupendous ignorance of sacred things and of the Christian religion reigns there, not only among the common people and the so-called laity, but also among the priests and the clergy. Still, they retain some hierarchical order, and they count patriarchs, metropolitans, bishops, hieromonks, presbyters or papas, monks, deacons, subdeacons and readers. Their monks have archimandrites, or abbots. All belong to the order of Basil, founder of monasticism in the East, as Benedict is in the West; they are called kalogeroi [καλόγεροι], a name first given from good old age to the elder monks, as if to say "good old men," and thence applied to all of this order. As to religion, the common people keep the prayers, the litanies and the liturgy, in a language and with prayers that are not entirely free of superstition and are almost equally barbarous. And they know little beyond their little hours and, on holy days, sermons which they hardly understand. Such is the decline of learning and religion among them today, cut off from the fellowship of other and better Christians, and oppressed and sorely cast down by the tyranny of the Turks. Hence you can rashly expect from them either a sound sense or a confession in the remaining articles of the faith. They have a fiction about the light in Christ's sepulchre, which is miraculously lit every year on Holy Saturday. It is remarkable how strongly simple people cling to Christ for the sake of this faith, fearing that without it they would fall away to the most accursed Mahometanism. This false miracle, as is shown in the commentary of Adam, archimandrite of the Chaldeans of Babylon, On the Reconciliation of the Faith of the Orientals with the Roman, chapter 6, was performed by some priest who entered the church and, by praying, obtained the kindling of this light, which lasts only for the space of an hour and is kept burning in a lamp by some material. It is found in Bzovius, Annals, volume 14, at the year 1330.

units.la: Miserrimus à capta urbe, Graecorum, Ecclesiarumque Christianarum in Oriente status fuit, quando Turcis corpora & animas fere Christianorum, bonaque & religionem pariter in praedam cessisse cognovimus. Quaeque adhuc habent miseri homines, si quae habent, quaeque omnium pretiosissima merito computamus, vita & religio, vestigalia. Capiebatur urbs à Mahomete II. a. clɔ cccc liii. al. liiii. d. xxix. Maji, tanta cum irruentium & obsessorum strage, ut nec qui foris erant, ingredi, neque qui intus, egredi possent.
units.tr: The condition of the Greeks and of the Christian churches in the East has been most wretched since the capture of the city, when we learned that the bodies and souls of the Christians, their goods and their religion alike, passed as plunder to the Turks. And the things that these poor people still have, if they have any, and which we rightly count most precious of all, namely life and religion, are merely taxes. The city was taken by Mahomet II in the year 1453, on the 29th day of May, with such a slaughter of the attackers and the besieged that those outside could not enter nor those inside get out.

units.la: Nullus, post Michaelem Florentiae mortuum, iis fuerat Patriarcha, quumque quaereret Mahometes, quis apud eos tunc Patriarcha esset, miraretur que nullum esse, copiam fecit eligendi quem vellent: quare coacta Synodo constituerunt Patriarcham Georgium Scholarium, olim Iudicis munere functum, quique Concilio Florentino interfuerat, & pro unione steterat, unde & librum conscripsit, in Defensionem quinque Capitum Synodicae unionis, à Fabio Benevolentio Latinè editum a. clɔ Iɔ lxxxi. Ex Georgio factum ei, pro Graecorum more, qui eorum quos in Patriarchas eligunt nomen commutant in aliud ab eadem littera incipiens, nomen Gennadii: sicut postea Manuelis nomen in Maximi, qui octavus ab eo fuit Patriarcha. Gennadius de fide & religione interrogatus à MachometE Confessionem illam edidit, quae lib. II: Turco Graecie, & post Orationem Davidis Chytraei, de Statu Ecclesiarum Orientis, extat: quā audita Turcarum Imperator edictum pro Christianis edidit, ne quis illos quocunque modo laederet vel convitiaretur. Sequutus Gennadium fuit Isidorus hieromonachus. Post hunc Iosephus. Tum Marcus Xylocarabes, sub quo primo τοκισμὸν pescesium introductum fuit, quod est tributum mille aureorum Sultano deinceps pendi solitum pro creando novo Patriarcha: ubi antea solerent Imperatores ipsi munera dare novo Patriarchae. Affinxerunt nonnulli Marco isti, quod Pescesium primus promisisset, sed per calumniam, ut eum loco movere concitata contra ipsum hac invidia, aliumque Simeonem hieromonachum Trapezuntium ejus loco constituere possent, oblato Sultano quoque pescesio, dicentes: quia Patriarcha Majestatis tuae summa ducatorum mille φλωρίων χιλιὰς promisit, ecce damus id & nos, ut Patriarcham faciamus nostrum Monachum: quia communis populus, & unā Clericorum chorus non ferunt Patriarcham Marcum. Quae lubenter arripiens Sultanus legem inde fecit, ut unusquisque Patriarcha istum censum suae ordinationis perferret in fiscum regium. Unde factum postmodo, ut pro arbitrio Sultani, ejusque ἀλλαγῆς, aut populi tumultibus & studiis, jam hunc tum illum cupientis Patriarcham, nihil levius usitatiusque fuerit quam Patriarchas amovere & revocare, prostituentibus se suaque turpiter Sultano Christianis, ejusque adversus se tyrannidem impudenter hoc pacto, cum religionis & facultatum suarum summo dispendio, confirmantibus. Facto ita Patriarcha Symeone Trapezuntio, contendentibusque inter se continuo pro Patriarchali sede Marco, & Symeone, quibus hinc inde alii in populo ac clero adhaerebant, Sukani noverca Maria lites astute diremtura, favens Dionysio cuidam Philippopolitano Metropolitae, tum ut huic, & Sultano gratificaretur, accepto pescesio duorum millium ducatorum, impetravit, ut rejectis Marco atque Symeone, Dionysius in illorum locum surrogaretur: quâ ratione confirmatus pescepefcefiusus, auctusque duplo census fuit. Dionysius ille non ferens continuas suorum molestias & calumnias, dicentium ipsum a Turcis circumcisum esse, deserto Patriarchatu, in Monasterium aufugit: unde restitutus iterum in locum pristinum fuit Symeon Trapezuntius, redditumque denuo pescesium, quod Symeonis illius culpa primo introductum in Ecclesiam fuerat. Quod quum nunc offerrent mille ducatorum, Quaestor regius accipere noluit, respondens, se in rationibus fisci reperire duo millia pro pescesio a Dionysio exhibita, quare tantundem nunc quoque praestare illos debere, nec prius se acquieturum. Quare dandum fuit pescesium bis mille aureorum: quod merito ab eo extortum, qui primus pescesii auctor exiterat, cujusque deinde bona omnia, & vasa ecclesiastica fisco regio, post mortem suam, cesserunt. Neque tamen hoc pacto quiescere ei licuit, sed quam artem prior excogitarat adversus Marcum, eadem usus alius iterum adversus ipsum fuit Raphael, Hieromonachus Servius, qui charatzium introduxit, id est, annuum tributum duorum millium aureorum, pendendum regio aerario, pro patriarchio. Qua ratione detrusus iterum Symeon, inque ejus locum constitutus fuit Raphael. Post hunc Maximus, primum vocatus Manuel, qui in Patriarchatus sui exordio ad Sultanum adductus, obtulit pro pescesio Io. aureos; deinde & singulis annis bis mille aureorum, pro charatzio. Omniaque illa contigerunt, sub imperio Machometis II. qui urbem occupavit: post quem successit ejus filius Bajazetus, a. MCCCCLXXXII. Postque Maximum Patriarcha in ordine illo decimus, videlicet a superata urbe, Nipho, Metropolita Thessalonicensis: hoc ejecto revocatus prior ille Dionysius; post hunc Maximus: hoc quoque retruso, superior iterum Nipho revocatur: quem excepit Ioachimus, sub quo charatzium crevit ad trium millium ducatorum. Sequutus Pachomius, sub quo charatzium auctum quingentis ducatis. Eo ejecto restitutus superior Ioachim. Et hoc mortuo, prior iterum Pachomius, additis quinquaginta ducatis supra tria millia & quingenta; tum Theoleptus. Post eum Hieremias. Hinc Ioannicius, sub quo charatzium auctum centum ducatis. Sequutus Dionysius, sub quo Pescesium, quod initio aureorum quingentorum fuit, ad tria millia perductum. Successor autem Ioasaphus magno studio atque efficit, ut ad bis mille reductum sit. Post Ioasaphum Metrophanes, & hunc Hieremias, Larissae antea Metropolita successit, cum quo Tubingensibus epistolaris illa concertatio fuit, quae satis nota, & suo etiam loco a nobis memorabitur. Ita nunc Ecclesiae Graecae miseram trahunt servitutem, & quidquid ultra sunt vel possunt, in praedam cedit Turcis. Cujus ipsi Graeci magna causa, nisi unica, dum nimis impotenti fastu inanem dignitatem ambientes, eam conquisita pecuniae summa a Bassa obtinent, qui novos emtores vel liberaliores avidissime admittit, quo una opera aerarium suum ditet, atque Christianos omni sua vi, auctoritate & opibus exsugat. Sin minus Christiani ex contentione & ambitione suos Patriarchas exagitent commutentque ipsi, artem nunc edoctus ipse Christianorum, priores deponit, ut ex novis semper alia tributa corroget censumque. Primo impertiens Patriarchae, postquam a Metropolitanis & archiepiscopis electus est, (retinent adhuc σχῆμα icтud) χειροτονίαν, vel ut hodie Graeci loquuntur, μητρόπολις diploma Imperiale, quo potestas sacrorum datur, & authoritas in omnes infra se Christianos, ac Christianorum ecclesias. Pro pescesio accipit Turca duo ducatorum millia; praeterea pro charatzio χαράτζιον, annui census loco, die S. Georgii, quatuor mille & centum ducatos. Constantinopolitani Patriarchae olim amplissima fuit dioecesis, cujus hodie vix umbram retinet. Quandiu Romanos vel Graecos habuit Imperatores (sic quippe Graeci Constantinopolitanos suos Romanos quoque: unde Romanorum orum aut Romanorum Imperatores illos passim appellatos legas, propter νέω Ῥώμης: Veteris Romae Ἀυτὸς, aut φραγγῖς Latinos, Francos dicunt) floruit, imo luxuriavit Patriarcharum potestas, habuitque sub se, ex Veteri distributione, Ponticam, Asiam, Thraciam, in quarum Ecclesias hodieque sibi quid arrogat, praeterea antiquum titulum oecumenici. Ex prisco adeo more, ab Heracleensi Antistite confirmari solet, quod à primis inde temporibus obtinuit, quum Byzantium ante creatam Constantinopolim Heraclea fuerit subje-ctum. Et Heracleensis Antistes, post Constantinopolitanum, in subscriptionibus adhuc secundum tenet locum. Ex Ecclesiarum subjectarum collectâ vivit hodie Patriarcha, reditibusque illarum annuis. Subsunt ei septuaginta quatuor Metropolitani, qui sub se alios iterum habent episcopos, ut Thessalonicensis decem, Athenien-sis pauciores, alii plures &c.
units.tr: No one had been Patriarch among them after Michael died at Florence. When Mahomet asked who their Patriarch was at that time, and was astonished to learn there was none, he gave them leave to elect whomever they wished. A synod was therefore convened, and they appointed as Patriarch Georgius Scholarius, formerly a judge, who had attended the Council of Florence and had stood for union. He also wrote the book in defence of the five chapters of the synodal union, which Fabius Benevolentius published in Latin in 1581. Georgius was given the name Gennadii, as was the Greek custom: those they elect as Patriarchs change their name to another beginning with the same letter. Later Manuel was given the name Maximus in the same way, and he was the eighth Patriarch after him. When Mahomet questioned Gennadius about faith and religion, Gennadius published that Confessionem, which is found in the second book of Turco Graecia, and after the oration of David Chytraeus, de Statu Ecclesiarum Orientis. When the Turkish Emperor heard this confession, he issued an edict for the Christians, forbidding anyone to harm or revile them in any way. Gennadius was followed by Isidorus, a hieromonk, and after him by Iosephus. Then came Marcus Xylocarabes, under whom the τοκισμὸν of the pescesium was first introduced. This was a tribute of a thousand gold pieces, which was afterwards regularly paid to the Sultan for the creation of a new Patriarch. Before this, the Emperors themselves used to give gifts to a new Patriarch. Some men then charged this Marcus with having first promised the pescesium, but falsely, so that they could stir up envy against him, remove him from his post, and install in his place another, Simeon, a hieromonk of Trebizond. They offered the Sultan the pescesium too, saying: "Because the Patriarch Marcus promised your Majesty a sum of a thousand ducats, φλωρίων χιλιάς, behold, we also give it, so that we may make our own monk Patriarch, because the common people and the whole choir of clergy cannot bear Patriarch Marcus." The Sultan eagerly seized this offer and made it a law that every Patriarch should pay this sum for his ordination into the royal treasury. As a result, it later happened that, at the Sultan's discretion and at his ἀλλαγῆς, or through the tumults and partisanship of the people, whichever Patriarch they desired at the time, nothing was easier or more common than to remove Patriarchs and recall them. The Christians shamefully prostituted themselves and their possessions to the Sultan, and by this means, to their own great loss in religion and property, they confirmed his tyranny against themselves. When Simeon of Trebizond had been installed in this way, and Marcus and Simeon kept contending with each other for the Patriarchal see, each supported by different factions among the people and clergy, the Sultan's stepmother Maria, intending to settle the quarrel cleverly and favouring a certain Dionysius, Metropolitan of Philippopolis, obtained for two thousand ducats from the pescesium, with the aim of pleasing both him and the Sultan. Marcus and Simeon were rejected, and Dionysius was substituted in their place. By this arrangement the pescesium was confirmed and doubled. That Dionysius, unable to bear the constant troubles and slanders of his own people, who said he had been circumcised by the Turks, abandoned the Patriarchate and fled to a monastery. Simeon of Trebizond was then restored to his former place, and the pescesium was again demanded, though it was through Simeon's fault that it had first been introduced into the Church. When they now offered a thousand ducats, the royal Quaestor refused to accept them, replying that in the accounts of the treasury he found two thousand paid for the pescesium by Dionysius, and therefore they must now pay the same amount, and he would not give way until they did. So they had to give two thousand gold pieces for the pescesium. This was rightly extorted from the man who had been the first author of the pescesium, and after his death all his goods and church vessels passed to the royal treasury. Nevertheless, he was not allowed to rest in this way. The same trick that the earlier man had devised against Marcus was used by another, Raphael, a Serbian hieromonk, against Simeon himself. He introduced the charatzium, that is, an annual tribute of two thousand gold pieces, to be paid to the royal treasury for the Patriarchate. By this method Simeon was again thrust out, and Raphael was installed in his place. After him came Maximus, first called Manuel, who, when he was brought before the Sultan at the beginning of his Patriarchate, offered ten gold pieces for the pescesium, and then two thousand gold pieces every year for the charatzium. All these things happened under Mahomet II, who captured the city, and after him his son Bajazet succeeded, in 1482. After Maximus, the Patriarch in that order who was tenth from the taking of the city was Nipho, Metropolitan of Thessalonica. When he was ejected, that former Dionysius was recalled. After him came Maximus again, and when he too was thrust out, the earlier Nipho was recalled. He was succeeded by Ioachimus, under whom the charatzium grew to three thousand ducats. Then came Pachomius, under whom the charatzium was increased by five hundred ducats. When he was ousted, the former Ioachim was restored, and when he died, Pachomius again took office, with fifty ducats added to the three thousand five hundred. Then came Theoleptus, and after him Hieremias. Next was Ioannicius, under whom the charatzium was increased by a hundred ducats. Then came Dionysius, under whom the pescesium, which at the start had been five hundred gold pieces, was raised to three thousand. His successor, Ioasaphus, with great effort brought it down again to two thousand. After Ioasaphus came Metrophanes, and then Hieremias, previously Metropolitan of Larissa, with whom there was that exchange of letters with the Tübingen scholars, which is well known and which I will mention in its proper place. Thus the Greek Church now drags out a wretched servitude, and whatever it still is or has, falls as plunder to the Turks.
