The Greeks themselves are the great cause of this, if not the sole cause: while they court an empty dignity with excessive and powerless pride, they obtain it by paying a large sum of money to the Pasha, who most eagerly admits new buyers, or more generous ones, so that he may enrich his own treasury at the same time and drain the Christians with all his power, authority and resources. If the Christians do not do so, through their strife and ambition they harass and change their own Patriarchs, and the Turk, now schooled in this practice, deposes the earlier ones so that he may always extract new taxes and revenues from the new ones. First, the Patriarch, after he has been elected by the Metropolitans and archbishops, (they still retain this rank) must pay for his χειροτονίαν, or, as the Greeks say today, μητρόπολις, an imperial diploma by which the power of sacred things is given, and authority over all Christians and Christian churches beneath him. For the pescesium the Turk takes two thousand ducats, and besides this, for the charatzium, which takes the place of an annual rent, on St George's day, four thousand one hundred ducats. The diocese of the Patriarch of Constantinople was once very extensive, though today it barely keeps a shadow of it. As long as it had Roman or Greek Emperors (for the Greeks call their Constantinopolitans Romans too, so that you may read of them everywhere called Romans or Roman Emperors, on account of νέα Ῥώμη, New Rome, as opposed to Old Rome, αὐτός; and they call the Latins φράγγοι, Franks), the power of the Patriarchs flourished, indeed it grew luxuriant. By the ancient division it had under it Pontus, Asia and Thrace, over whose churches it still claims something for itself today, as well as the old title of ecumenical. By ancient custom it is usually confirmed by the Bishop of Heraclea, as it has been from the earliest times, since Byzantium was subject to Heraclea before Constantinople was founded. The Bishop of Heraclea still holds the second place in the signatures after the Bishop of Constantinople. The Patriarch today lives on the revenues of the churches subject to him, collected each year. Seventy-four Metropolitans are under him, and they in turn have other bishops under them, for example ten at Thessalonica, fewer at Athens, others more, and so on.

units.la: Suberant ei quoque olim Moscovitae, seu Russi vel Rutheni, (nam Russiae maxima pars, alba vulgo dicta Imperatori Moscorum: caeteri Russiae nigrae, vel rubrae Regi Poloniae subjecti sunt, horumque nonnulli cum Romana se conjunxerunt Ecclesiâ a. MDXCV.) at nunc proprium habent Patriarcham, quem Princeps eligit, confirmant sui suffraganei: quod inchoatum precedenti seculo à duce Basilio M. qui, quem pro more Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha miserat Metropolitam, eò quod sua valde carperet vitia & peccata, in carcerem conjecit, neque eo, quamvis ipsius Turcarum Imperatoris fatigatus precibus, liberavit. Unde deinceps ipsi suum constituere Patriarcham Moscorum Duces: quem sui episcopi tum ordinant. Mittit attamen in signum pristini moris ac subjectionis Moscorum Imperator Constantinopolitano Patriarchae quotannis, sed quasi in eleemosynam, quingentos aureos. Duo ei subsunt Metropolitae, Novogardiensis, & Roftoviensis: his, alii episcopi. A Graecis, & studio praesertim Constantinopolitani e-piscopisco̅pi certum est, Russos primam Christianæ religionis institutionem accepisse, quamvis ægre hoc fateantur, & potius ab Andrea Apostolo se conversos ad fidem factent: indeque est, quod ad Constantinopolitanum Patriarcham ipsorum Ecclesiæ semper spectarint, eique fuerint subjectæ, qui (uti Romanus in Occidente) per plurimarum gentium ad Christum, operâ suorum conversionem, jurisdictionem suam haud segniter quoque promovit. A quo, ejusque obedientiâ desciverunt Russi, potius quàm ab ipsorum religione. Nam Græcā sequuntur, nisi quod peculiaria nonnulla habeant. Præsertim venerantur S. Nicolaum Barensem, cen tutelarem suum. Pueros septem annorum admittunt ad communionem Eucharisticam: quia eâ ætate dicunt quod peccare incipiant contra Deum. Diaconum vel sacerdotem non habent nisi conjugatum, videlicet ante, non post suam ordinationem. Possevinus ait, eos negare, simplicem fornicationem peccatum esse; ut quoque usuram. Vti politicè, sic & Ecclesiasticè distinguuntur Russi. Hi qui Poloniæ Regi subjecti, vel eorum aliqui a. MDXCV. die XXIII. Decemb. unionem inierunt cum Ecclesiâ Romanâ, ejusque Papâ Clemente VIII, de quo Baronius, ad calcem Tom. VII. Possevinus in Apparatu, voce Rutheni. Thomas à Iesu, l. VI. Cardinalis Ossatus, l. II. epist. XXXVII. Et ante omnia Historia Eccles. Sclavon. lib. IV. Atque antequam ad unionem accederent, primò expressè stipulati fuerunt illorum nomine Adamus V Vlachinensis, & Cyrillus Luceorensis V Vladicæ, suis varia à Romanâ Ecclesiâ concedi, inter quæ & hæc erant: Sacramentum Sanctissimi Corporis & sanguinis Domini Nostri Iesu Christi nobis ita, quemadmodum hucusque usi sumus, sub utraque specie panis & vini, temporibus perpetuis integrè inviolabiliterque conservetur. Sacramentum Baptismi & forma ipsius ut nobis integrè, prout in hanc usque diem datur, sine omni additamento constat. De Purgatorio nullam litem movemovemus, sed volumus doceri ab Ecclesia sancta Romana. Calendarium novum, si secundum morem antiquum fieri possit, suscipiemus. Ad processionem pro festo Corporis Christi faciendam ne adigamur: hoc est ne simili ratione processionis cum Sacramento faciendae nobis necessitas imponatur, quandoquidem apud nos alius est modus & usus Sacramentorum. Tum & ante festum Paschae, ad consecrationem ignis, ut etiam pulsationem asperibus compactis loco campanae, & alias ceremonias quibus hucusque caruimus, ne compellamur: quin potius secundum ritum & consuetudinem Ecclesiae nostrae integre conserventur. Matrimonia sacerdotalia ut integra constent, exceptis bigamis. Propter literas confirmationis Romanum ut Episcopi ritus Graeci non mittant. Haec illis indulgere Papa coactus fuit. Caeteri Russi, qui Duci Moscorum subjecti, horrent quam maximè Romanam communionem, & nisi ferente necessitate iiscum comedere, vel celebrare minimè sustinent. Vide hanc in rem epistolam Iohannis Metropolitae Russi ad archiepiscopum, ut ipsi dicunt, Romanum; ejusque canones, apud Sigismundum Baronem. Cujus & haec pag. 12. verba sunt: nulli homini infensior Moscus, quam summo Pontifici, quem non nisi Doctoris titulo dignatur. Caeterum de Russorum religione plurimi scripserunt, qui videri possunt & singulari volumine extat Theologia Moscovitica, variorum Auctorum, Spirae edita a. cIↄ Iↄ lxxx ii. Tum a. cIↄ Iↄ c Francofurti, Rerum Moscoviticarum Auctores varii: ubi, Commentarii Sigismundi Baronis Herbersteinii; Paulus Iovius, de legatione Basilii M. Principis Moscoviae; Iohannes Faber, de Religione Moscovitarum: Alex. Guagnini Descriptio Moscovia. Praeterea ejusdem argumenti, Possevinus de rebus Moscoviticis. Oderbornius, de Russorum Religione, ad Davidem Chytraeum.
units.tr: The Muscovites, or Russians and Ruthenians, were formerly also subject to him. Most of Russia, commonly called White Russia, is under the Emperor of the Muscovites, while the rest of Russia, Black or Red, is subject to the King of Poland, and some of these in 1595 joined the Roman Church. Now, however, they have their own Patriarch, whom the Prince elects and his suffragans confirm. This began in the previous century under Duke Basil the Great, who threw into prison the Metropolitan whom the Patriarch of Constantinople had sent him, as was customary, because he sharply censured his vices and sins. Basil did not release him even when the Turkish Emperor himself wearied him with requests. From then on the Dukes of Muscovy set up their own Patriarch, whom their bishops ordain. As a sign of their former custom and subjection, however, the Emperor of the Muscovites still sends the Patriarch of Constantinople five hundred gold pieces every year, though it is given as an alms. Two Metropolitans are subject to him, those of Novgorod and Rostov, and other bishops are subject to them. It is certain, from the Greeks and especially from the zeal of the Patriarch of Constantinople, that the Russians received the first instruction in the Christian religion from the Greeks, although they reluctantly admit this and prefer to claim that they were converted by the Apostle Andrew. For this reason their Church has always looked to the Patriarch of Constantinople and been subject to him, who, like the Roman in the West, did not slowly extend his jurisdiction through the conversion of very many peoples to Christ by the work of his own men. The Russians abandoned him and his obedience, but not their religion. For they follow the Greek rite, except that they have certain peculiarities. In particular they venerate Saint Nicholas of Bari as their patron. They admit boys of seven years old to Eucharistic communion, because they say that at that age they begin to sin against God. They have no deacon or priest who is not married, and that marriage must come before, not after, his ordination. Possevinus says that they deny that simple fornication is a sin, and likewise usury. The Russians are divided in both civil and ecclesiastical matters. Those who are subject to the King of Poland, or some of them, entered into union with the Roman Church and its Pope Clement VIII on 23 December 1595. On this see Baronius, at the end of volume VII; Possevinus in the Apparatus, under the word Ruthenians; Thomas à Jesu, book VI; Cardinal Ossat, book II, letter XXXVII; and above all the Historia Ecclesiae Sclavonicae, book IV. Before they came to the union, Adam, Bishop of Vladimir, and Cyril, Bishop of Luck, expressly stipulated on their behalf that various concessions be made to them by the Roman Church, among which were these: The sacrament of the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ shall be preserved for us entire and inviolable, in the same way as we have used it until now, under both kinds of bread and wine, for all time. The sacrament of baptism and its form shall stand for us wholly, as it has been given until this day, without any addition. We shall raise no dispute about purgatory, but we wish to be taught by the holy Roman Church. We shall accept the new calendar, if it can be done according to the old custom. We are not to be compelled to the procession for the feast of Corpus Christi, that is, that no necessity be imposed on us for a similar procession with the sacrament, since among us the manner and custom of the sacraments is different. Likewise we are not to be compelled to the consecration of fire before Easter, nor to the striking of boards in place of the bell, nor to other ceremonies which we have lacked until now; rather they shall be kept whole according to the rite and custom of our Church. Priests' marriages shall stand whole, except for bigamists. The Romans shall not send letters of confirmation to bishops of the Greek rite. The Pope was compelled to grant these things to them. The other Russians, who are subject to the Duke of Muscovy, shrink with the greatest horror from communion with Rome, and unless necessity compels it they cannot bring themselves to eat with Romanists or to celebrate with them. On this matter see the letter of John, Metropolitan of Russia, to the archbishop, as they call him, of Rome, and its canons, in Sigismund Baron. Of him, on page 12, these words also appear: No man is more hostile to the Muscovites than the supreme Pontiff, whom they deign to honour only with the title of Doctor. Otherwise, many have written about the religion of the Russians, and they can be consulted. There is a separate volume, Theologia Moscovitica, by various authors, published at Speyer in 1582. Then in 1600 at Frankfurt, Rerum Moscoviticarum Auctores varii, where there are the Commentarii of Sigismund Baron von Herberstein; Paulus Jovius, de legatione Basilii M. Principis Moscoviae; Johannes Faber, de Religione Moscovitarum; and Alexander Guagnini, Descriptio Moscoviae. Besides these, on the same subject, Possevinus, de rebus Moscoviticis, and Oderborn, de Russorum Religione, addressed to David Chytraeus.

units.la: Alexandrino episcopo (cujus hodie sedes est Alcairi) olim ex Synodo Nicaena attributa Ægyptus, Libya, & Pentapolis: tres enim primò Ægypti fuere provinciae, postea sex factae, demum aliae additae, ut decem in universum fuerint. Cum tot enim metropolitanis jubetur ad Chalcedonensem Synodum venire Dioscorus, Actione Synodi primâ: Igitur & tam Sanctus sanctis secum decem metropolitanis episcopis, qui sub tuis degunt diœcesi, & aliis similiter decem sanctis episcopis, Kalendis Augusti, Ephesum metropolim Asiæ venire festinare. Alexandrini primum suum episcopum Marcum dictum Evangelistam, qui Hananiam post se ordinarit, & duodecim presbyteros, ex iisque unum semper eligendum in protopresbyterum, sive episcopum, alio semper in ejus locum cooptando presbytero. Quò respicit Hieronymus in celebri illo loco, epist. ad Evagrium: & Alexandriæ à Marco Evangelistâ usque ad Heraclam & Dionysium episcopos, presbyteri semper unum ex se electum, in excelsiori gradu collocatum episcopum nominare. Ubi & illud non minus egregium, compescendæque episcoporum arrogantiæ, dictum: ubicumque fueris episcopus sive Romæ, sive Eugubii, sive Constantinopoli, sive Rhegii, sive Alexandriæ, sive Tanis, ejusdem meriti, ejusdem est sacerdotii. Morem eligendi episcopum vel presbyterum durasse ad tempora usque Concilii Nicæni, quando ejus loco Alexander qui Concilio interfuit, instituit ut Patriarcham (sic loquitur) non presbyteri ex suo collegio, sed episcopi quemcunque virum aliàs idoneum crearent, scribit Eutychius Patriarcha Alexandrinus, in Ecclesiâ suâ Originibus, quem Seldenus edidit, cum eruditissimis annotationibus. Additque, à Marco ad Demetrium, qui nonus in ordine Patriarcharum fuit, nullum in provinciis Ægypti fuisse episcopum, sed eum primum tres; & post hunc, Heraclam viginti constituisse episcopos: à cujus tempore quoque Patriarcha dictus est Papa, seu avus: uti episcopus, abba. Atque ita etiamnum scribunt, [illegible, ~12 letters] μεγάλης πόλεως Ἀλεξανδρείας. Quia autem ex Alexandrinâ Ecclesiâ Dioscorus, ista Ecclesia præ aliis semper infecta ejus hæresi fuit, quæcum Eutychianâ convenit, quamvis
units.tr: Formerly, by the Synod of Nicaea, Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis were assigned to the Bishop of Alexandria (whose see is today at Cairo). For at first Egypt consisted of three provinces, afterwards it was made six, and finally others were added, so that there were ten in all. For in the first session of the Council of Chalcedon Dioscorus is ordered to come with as many metropolitans: "Therefore let the holy one come to Ephesus, the metropolis of Asia, in haste on the first of August, together with ten metropolitan bishops who dwell in your diocese and likewise ten other holy bishops." The Alexandrians had as their first bishop Mark, called the Evangelist, who ordained Hananiah after himself, and twelve presbyters, from whom one was always chosen to be protopresbyter, or bishop, another presbyter always being co-opted into his place. Jerome alludes to this in that famous passage in his letter to Evagrius: "And at Alexandria, from Mark the Evangelist down to the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, the presbyters always named one of their own, placed in a higher rank, as bishop." Here also is that no less notable saying, which serves to check the arrogance of bishops: "Wherever you are a bishop, whether at Rome, at Eugubium, at Constantinople, at Rhegium, at Alexandria or at Tanis, you have the same merit and the same priesthood." That the custom of electing a bishop or presbyter lasted down to the time of the Council of Nicaea, when Alexander, who attended the Council, instituted that instead of this the presbyters of their own college should not create a Patriarch (so he speaks) but any suitable man chosen from among the bishops, is written by Eutychius, Patriarch of Alexandria, in his Origines of his Church, which Selden published with the most learned annotations. He adds that from Mark to Demetrius, who was ninth in order of the Patriarchs, there was no bishop in the provinces of Egypt, but then first three, and after him Heraclas appointed twenty bishops. From his time too the Patriarch was called Pope, or grandfather, just as a bishop was called abba. And so they still write, [illegible] of the great city of Alexandria [μεγάλης πόλεως Ἀλεξανδρείας]. But since Dioscorus came from the Church of Alexandria, that Church above the others was always tainted with his heresy, which agrees with the Eutychian one, although

units.la: Greek line at the foot of the paragraph: not fully legible on the scan; the Greek words are reproduced as far as they can be read. ris diversam contendant Dioscori ab Eutyche fuisse sententiam, justeque hunc damnatum, at illum injustissime. Confundere illum in Christo duas naturas; sed hunc duas in Christo naturas unitas docere, unamquE factam naturam personatam ex naturis non personatis, sine mixtione tamen aut confusione. Dioscorum sui pro Sancto habent, ac venerantur, minimeque patiuntur illum damnatum dici in Chalcedonensi Concilio. Appellantur Copti, secundum aliquos quasi Ægyptii, Qbti vel Ægyptii: alii dictos censent a circumcisione, quâ illa gens antiquitus usa perhibetur, sed quam hodie omittunt: alii a primo Ægyptiorum rege Chibe dicto: melius ab urbe Ægypti celeberrimâ olim, & Thebaidos metropoli, Copto. Unde & Copti dicendi, vel Coptitae, non Cophthi, quomodo illos Mahammedani appellant, per contemtum, quasi dicas incisos: unde & nomen hoc veniri, & scriptionem esse Cophthi, sive ab usurpatâ olim circumcisione, sive exprobratâ, nonnullis visum. Habent suum Patriarcham nationis Coptorum dictum. Et Alexandriae aliquando duo simul Patriarchae, Orthodoxorum unus, Coptorum alter, seu Iacobitarum: nam Copti Iacobitae sunt, & in liturgiâ suâ celebrant Severum, Dioscorum & Iacobum, Syrum illum, Iacobitica secta auctorem. Quamvis Iacobitae qui per Syriam, Mesopotamiam & Babyloniam innumeri proprium habeant Patriarcham, in civitate Mesopotamiae Caramit, qui se numcupat patriarcham Antiochenum, secta quoque suae ecclesias habeant frequentissimas atque episcopos, Ierusalemi, Damasci, Aleppi, aliisque ibidem locis. De Copti Thom. à Iesu refert, quod à Pontifice Romano se segregarint jam inde à tempore Chalcedonensis Concilii; quodque eum errare posse in iis quae sunt fidei, opinantur. Quod baptismum ratum non habent, ne quidem in summa necessitate, si ab alio quam sacerdote conseratur. Quod in S. Coena, seu missâ, uti loquuntur. communicant omnes sub utraque specie. Iohannis non administratur oleum, &c. Et quantum in Orientali Ecclesia variae sectae, Coptorum, Abyssinorum, Armenorum, &c. in multis cum Protestantium doctrina ac Ecclesia conveniant, non in omnibus, à multis pridem annotatum fuit. Inter Anglos, à Richardo Field in libris de Ecclesia. Edwardo Bicrewodo, in diversarum linguarum et religionum. Ephraemo Pagit, in Christianographia. Neque est quod in illorum cognoscendis sententiis doctrinaque Pontificios Scriptores, Alphonsum Castrensem dico, Praeconem, aliosque borum sectatores coecos, inter quos & Bzovius, turò consulas vel sequaris, nisi in iis quae contra ipsos, solitos omnia ex placito Papatus sui aestimare, & pro hujus genio ac indole haereses interpretari, non ex veritate.
units.tr: some contend that the opinion of Dioscorus was different from that of Eutyches, and that the one was rightly condemned while the other was most unjustly condemned. Eutyches confounded the two natures in Christ; but Dioscorus taught that the two natures in Christ were united, and that from non-personal natures one personal nature was made, yet without mixture or confusion. The Copts regard Dioscorus as a saint, venerate him, and by no means allow him to be called condemned at the Council of Chalcedon. They are called Copts, according to some as if they were Egyptians, Qbti or Egyptians; others think they are named from circumcision, which that people is said to have practised in antiquity but which they now omit; others from Chibe, the first king of Egypt; the better view is that they are named from Coptos, once a very famous city of Egypt and the metropolis of the Thebaid. Hence they should be called Copts, or Coptites, not Cophthi, as the Mohammedans call them, by way of contempt, as if you were to say "the cut ones." Hence some have thought that this name is derived from the circumcision once practised, or from the reproach of it, and that the spelling should be Cophthi. They have their own Patriarch, called the Patriarch of the nation of the Copts. At one time there were even two Patriarchs of Alexandria at once, one of the Orthodox and another of the Copts, or Jacobites; for the Copts are Jacobites, and in their liturgy they celebrate Severus, Dioscorus and Jacob, that Syrian who was the author of the Jacobite sect. Although the Jacobites, who are countless through Syria, Mesopotamia and Babylonia, have their own Patriarch in the Mesopotamian city of Caramit, who styles himself Patriarch of Antioch, the sect also has very numerous churches and bishops at Jerusalem, Damascus, Aleppo and other places there. Thomas à Jesu reports of the Copts that they have separated from the Roman Pontiff since the time of the Council of Chalcedon, and that they think he can err in matters of faith. They do not regard baptism as valid, not even in extreme necessity, if it is administered by anyone other than a priest. In the holy Supper, or Mass, as they call it, all communicate under both kinds. The oil of John is not administered, etc. That in the Eastern Church various sects, of the Copts, Abyssinians, Armenians and others, agree in many things, though not in all, with the doctrine and Church of the Protestants, has long been noted by many. Among the English this was noted by Richard Field in his books on the Church, by Edward Brerewood in on the diversity of languages and religions, and by Ephraim Pagitt in Christianographia. Nor is there any reason for you to consult or follow the Popish writers, I mean Alphonsus Castrensis, Praco, and others, their blind followers, among whom is also Baronius, in learning the opinions and doctrine of these people, except where they judge everything against them according to the decree of their own papacy, and interpret heresies in accordance with its spirit and character rather than with the truth.

units.la: Patriarchas suum proprium habent (Abuna vocant, seu Patrem nostrum, etiam Pinys v. P. ep. [?] Catholicum appellat) Abyssini, qui Aethiopiam incolunt amplissima natio, sub Imperatore, cui temere nomen presbyteri Iohannis, vel Petro-Iohannis imponitur, quum hoc nomen & Imperium Prestegani longe alteri-us, quam Abyssinorum Imperatoris, nam in Asia imperavit, diu desiit, sed Lusitani Abyssinorum Imperatorem, putantes eum esse decantatum illum Presbyterum Iohannem, magis fama & nomine notum, quam certe rei veritate, dum apud illum nonnulla viderunt, quae de Presbytero Iohanne passim jactabantur, cum primo sic nominarunt, atque inde manavit, ut Abyssinorum Imperator ab Europeis habitus pro Presbytero Iohanne fuerit, sed ex errore, quem utriusque Imperii distantia, aetas, & Abyssinorum propria confessio redarguunt.
units.tr: The Abyssinians, who inhabit Ethiopia, a very large nation, have their own patriarch. They call him Abuna, that is, our Father, and Pinys also calls him Catholicus. They live under an emperor who is rashly given the name Presbyter John, or Petro-John. That name and the empire of Prestegan, which was quite different from the Abyssinian emperor's (for it lay in Asia), had long since ceased to exist. But the Portuguese, thinking that the emperor of the Abyssinians was that famous Presbyter John, known more by fame and name than by the truth of the matter, saw in him several things that were commonly claimed about Presbyter John. They first named him thus, and from this it came about that Europeans regarded the emperor of the Abyssinians as Presbyter John. This was an error, however, which the distance between the two empires, their different ages, and the Abyssinians' own confession refute.

units.la: Presbyter Iohannes male vulgo dicitur, quum sit Prestegan, vox Persica, significans Legatum: vel quod aliis placet mancipiorum regum, [illegible, ~8 letters] Presbyter [?] Abyssinorum ille Imperator episcopatus, & beneficia ecclesiastica, non patriarcha, confert; & mortuo Patriarchâ, omnes ejus proventus, bonaque ad se rapit. Olim subjecti fuere Patriarchæ Alexandrino, hodieque nonnullam ab eo dependentiam agnoscunt. Nam & ex ejus dioecesi Alexandrinum aliquem Patriarcham eligunt Abyssini Monachi, qui Ierusalemi ad S. Sepulchrum, uti dicunt, commorantur, Monachorum ordinis S. Antonii, quem Alexandrinus confirmat: propterque illo in liturgiâ precantur, ante suum Patriarcham. Et ab illo chrisma confectum singulo septennio ad Æthiopes mitti, dicit Tecla Maria, Abyssinus presbyter, apud Thomam à Iesu, lib. VI 1. cap. XIII. Unde & eadem cum Alexandrinis sapiunt, id est, sunt utrique Iacobitæ, dicentes, in Christo post unionem esse unam naturam, unam voluntatem, unam operationem, sine tamen mixtione & confusione: uti idem Tecla aperte professus Romæ fuit. Quapropter neque Concilium Chalcedonense accipiunt: & Papam Leonem qui ejus patronus & magna pars fuit, condemnant: & Dioscorum, Iacobum, ac Severum pro sanctis habent & venerantur. Eâdem insuper æra utuntur Copti & Æthiopes, quam appellant æram Martyrum, ab anno XIX. Diocletiani, Christi CCCII. quo gravis adeo in Christianos & Ægyptios, Æthiopes, aliosque viguit persecutio, ut Coptorum centum quadraginta quatuor millia trucidata, septingenta in exilium acta dicantur: quam æram martyrum Copti; annum gratiæ Æthiopes vocant. Rogatusque Tecla, an in aliquibus discrepent Copti, & Abyssini, respondit, nullam esse differentiam inter eos, & in omnibus rebus concordare. Sunt enim sub ejusdem Patriarchæ obedientiâ. Idemque demonstrat in Prodromo Coptico cap. II. Athanasius Kircherus. Quæ illorum religio, qui mores, apud varios expositum reperias, præsertim apud Damianum à Goes, equitem Lusitanum, qui Confessionem fidei Æthiopum edidit, factam à Legato Imp. Æthiopum Davidis ad Iohannem III. Portugalliæ regem, Christophoro Licanato, patriâ. suâ lingua dicto Zaga Zabo, anno cIↄ Iↄ xxxiv. Apud Thom. à Iesu. Nicol. Codignum, de rebus Abyssin. Francisc. Alvarezium, in Hist. Æthiopum. Matth. Dresserum, Lipsiensem, de Ecclesiâ Æthiopicâ. Bernh. Varenium, libello de diversis Gentium religionibus, post descript. regni Iaponiæ, aliosque. Ipsi notarunt Pontificii, in quam multis Abyssini à se discrepant. Licet reverentiam aliquam Romano Pontifici exhibeant, nam firmiter sententiam de primatu Romanæ Ecclesiæ, inquit Thom. à Iesu. Idemque de sacramento confirmationis Ⅰ_que extremæ unctionis non invenio apud Æthiopes scriptores expressam aliquam mentionem. Credunt, animas infantium decedentium ante baptismum, eo solum salvari qui orti sunt à parentibus fidelibus. Praeterea traditiones sanctorum non admittunt, solumque verbo Dei scripto fidem habere, ut Alvarezius cap. 78. Nullas pro defunctis oblationes habent, nec sacra faciunt pro vivis, forte, vel quia existimant illis non prodesse, aut quia Purgatorium cum Græcis non agnoscunt. Ministrantque Eucharistiam etiam laicis sub utraque specie. Hæc de illis Thomas à Iesu, monachus Carmelitanus. Adde Confessionem Zagæ Zabo, qui inter alia: Et sacramentum Eucharistiæ non servant apud nos in templis, ut sit hic apud Europeos. Nec in ministerio sacramentum Eucharistiæ ostenditur, ut hic video fieri. Monachis non licet vicatim mendicare, nec à plebe aliquid eleemosynarum extorquere. Et nullam pro remissione animarum facimus Missam. Præterea constitutum est à sanctis Apostolis in Synodorum libris, Clericis uxores licere ducere. De animarum propagatione, omnes sine ulla hæsitatione in hac sententia versamur, omnium hominum animas ab Adam profluxisse, et ut caro nostra est ex femina carnis Adæ: ita quoque anima nostra, quasi lucerna in anima Adæ accensa, originem suam et naturam ex Adam trahit. Ex quo apparet, nos omnes semen esse Adæ ex carne et anima, etc. Communiter statuunt animarum traducem. Atque circumcisionem olim quidem etiam admiserunt, non ita hodie, sed & tum ex politica & nationis antiqua consuetudine, uti praeter Hebraeos plurimae gentes, Ægyptii aliique, non ex religione, vel sacramento illam observare solíti fuerunt, quamvis ad imitationem procul dubio Hebraeorum. Pontificios adeo quidem execrantur, ut Ioh. Maffæus referat histor. Indic. l. ult. sub finem, quod quando suasu Regis, Abyssinorum Patriarcha disputaturus esset cum Iesuita Rhoterigio, id non solum abnuerit, dicens, nullum sibi cum haereticis commercium sermonis esse, sed Regi etiam graviter interminatus fuerit, si legere scripta illorum pergeret. Atque haec de Ecclesiis Copto-Æthiopicis; sive Abyssinis.
units.tr: Presbyter John is wrongly called this in common usage, since the word is Prestegan, a Persian word meaning legate; or, as others prefer, of the king's servants [illegible, about eight letters] Presbyter [?] the Abyssinian emperor, who confers episcopal and ecclesiastical benefices himself, not the patriarch; and when the patriarch dies, the emperor seizes all his revenues and goods for himself. Formerly they were subject to the patriarch of Alexandria, and even today they acknowledge some dependence on him. For the Abyssinian monks, who dwell at Jerusalem by the Holy Sepulchre, as they say, and who belong to the order of St Anthony, choose an Alexandrian as their patriarch, and he is confirmed by the patriarch of Alexandria. For this reason they pray in their liturgy before their own patriarch. Tecla Maria, an Abyssinian priest, says, in Thomas à Jesu, book VI, chapter XIII, that the chrism is made by him and sent to the Ethiopians every seven years. Hence they also agree with the Alexandrians, that is, both are Jacobites, saying that in Christ after the union there is one nature, one will, one operation, yet without mixture or confusion; as Tecla himself openly professed at Rome. For this reason they do not accept the Council of Chalcedon, they condemn Pope Leo, who was its champion and chief supporter, and they regard Dioscorus, James and Severus as saints and venerate them. Moreover, the Copts and Ethiopians use the same era, which they call the era of the Martyrs, reckoned from the nineteenth year of Diocletian, that is, 302 of Christ, when a severe persecution raged against Christians, Egyptians, Ethiopians and others, so that it is said that 144,000 Copts were slaughtered and 700 sent into exile. The Copts call this the era of the Martyrs, the Ethiopians call it the year of grace. When Tecla was asked whether the Copts and Abyssinians differed in any respects, he replied that there was no difference between them and that they agreed in all things, for they are under the obedience of the same patriarch. Athanasius Kircher shows the same in his Coptic Prodromus, chapter II. Their religion and customs may be found set out by various writers, especially by Damian à Goes, a Portuguese knight, who published the confession of faith of the Ethiopians, made by the legate of the Ethiopian emperor David to John III, king of Portugal, Christophorus Licanatus, called Zaga Zabo in his own language, in 1534; also in Thomas à Jesu, Nicolas Godignus, on the affairs of Abyssinia, Francisco Alvarez, in his History of the Ethiopians, Matthias Dresser of Leipzig, on the Ethiopian Church, Bernhard Varenius in his little book on the various religions of the nations, after his description of the kingdom of Japan, and others. The Papists themselves have noted in how many points the Abyssinians differ from them. Although they show some reverence to the Roman Pontiff, for they firmly hold an opinion about the primacy of the Roman Church, says Thomas à Jesu. Likewise I find no clear mention of the sacrament of confirmation or of extreme unction among the Ethiopian writers. They believe that the souls of infants who die before baptism are saved only if they were born of faithful parents. Moreover, they do not admit the traditions of the saints, and hold the faith only by the written word of God, as Alvarez says in chapter 78. They make no offerings for the dead, nor do they celebrate sacred rites for the living, perhaps either because they think these do not benefit them, or because they do not acknowledge purgatory with the Greeks. They also administer the Eucharist to laymen under both kinds. These things about them are told by Thomas à Jesu, a Carmelite monk. Add the confession of Zaga Zabo, who says among other things: And we do not keep the sacrament of the Eucharist in our churches, as is done here among the Europeans. Nor is the sacrament of the Eucharist displayed in the ministry, as I see done here. Monks may not beg from village to village, nor extort any alms from the common people. We do not celebrate any Mass for the remission of souls. Moreover, it has been laid down by the holy Apostles in the books of the Synods that clergy may take wives. Concerning the propagation of souls, we all hold without any hesitation this opinion, that the souls of all men have flowed from Adam, and just as our flesh is from the woman's flesh of Adam, so also our soul, like a lamp kindled in the soul of Adam, draws its origin and nature from Adam. From this it appears that we all are the seed of Adam, in flesh and soul, etc. They commonly hold the traducianist view of the soul. They once also admitted circumcision, though not so today; but this too they observed from civil custom and ancient national usage, as many nations besides the Hebrews, such as the Egyptians and others, were accustomed to observe it, not from religion or as a sacrament, though doubtless in imitation of the Hebrews. They so detest the Papists that John Maffei, in his Histories of the Indies, last book, near the end, reports that when, at the king's urging, the patriarch of the Abyssinians was about to debate with the Jesuit Rodriguez, he not only refused, saying that he had no dealings in discourse with heretics, but also sternly threatened the king if he should go on reading their writings. So much concerning the Coptic-Ethiopian churches, or the Abyssinians.

units.la: Orientis numeratae olim 7. dioeceses, Oriens, Ægyptus, Asiana, Pontica, Thracia, Macedonia, & Dacia. Macedoniae & Daciae provinciae communi Illyrici nomine comprehenduntur, uti ab uno olim Illyrici praesecto regebantur: dein ab uno utriusque primate metropolitâ Thessalonicensi: denique ad Bulgarorum reductae dioeceses, quorum metropolita sui juris diu fuit, nulli alii subjectus. Reliquas dioeceses caeteri Patriarchae inter se, non eodem semper modo, distribuerunt. Alexandrino, authoritate Synodi Nicaenae, cessit Ægyptus, Libya, & Pentapolis. Antiocheno Orient, speciatim sic dictus. Unde Orientis patriarcha vulgo a Veteribus appellatus. Orientis autem dioeceses fuerunt latissimae, Syria prima, & secunda, Palaestina, Phoenice, Cilicia, Mesopotamia, Arabia &c. Ex quibus Hierosolymitano assignatae tres Palaestinae, quibus illé posset ἐπισκοπεῖν. Quod definitum in Concilio Chalcedonensi a. cccc li. ubi obortâ quaestione inter Maximum Antiochenum, & Iuvenalem Hierosolymitanum episcopum, super limitibus dioecesium, statutum, ut Antiochenus haberet duas sub se Phoenicias, & Arabiam; Hierosolymitanus, tres Palaestinas. Concilio dein Constantinopolitano, sub Iustiniano Imp. a. Ⅰ​ⅠⅠ. superibus Capitulis Nestorianismi, Hierosolymitana epispiscopalis in Patriarchalem erecta fuit, propter reverentiam (dicebant) sanctæ resurrectionis; ideoque dum in confinio Alexandrini Ierosolymitanus habitaret & Antiocheni, utrique huic subtracti aliqui, & Ierosolymitano concessi episcopatus, quibus ad formam aliorum quoque præsideret Patriarcha. Constantinopolitano Chalcedonense Concilium attribuit Asianam, Ponticam, & Thraciam.
units.tr: The East was formerly counted as having seven dioceses: Oriens, Egypt, Asiana, Pontica, Thracia, Macedonia and Dacia. The provinces of Macedonia and Dacia were included under the common name of Illyricum, since they were once governed by a single prefect of Illyricum, and afterwards by one metropolitan of both, the bishop of Thessalonica. Finally the dioceses were restored to the Bulgarians, whose metropolitan was for a long time independent and subject to no other. The other patriarchs divided the remaining dioceses among themselves, not always in the same way. By the authority of the Council of Nicaea, Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis passed to the patriarch of Alexandria. To the patriarch of Antioch fell the Orient, specifically so called, whence the patriarch of the Orient was commonly named by the ancients. The dioceses of the Orient were very extensive: Syria, the first and second, Palestine, Phoenicia, Cilicia, Mesopotamia, Arabia and so on. Of these, three Palestines were assigned to Jerusalem, over which it could exercise oversight. This was determined at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, when, a dispute having arisen between Maximus of Antioch and Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, over the boundaries of the dioceses, it was decided that Antioch should have the two Phoenicias and Arabia under it, and Jerusalem the three Palestines. Later, at the Council of Constantinople under the emperor Justinian in 553, when the Nestorian Three Chapters were condemned, the episcopal see of Jerusalem was raised to a patriarchate, out of reverence, as they said, for the holy resurrection. Therefore, since Jerusalem lay on the border between Alexandria and Antioch, some bishoprics were withdrawn from each of these and granted to Jerusalem, so that its patriarch might preside over them in the same way as the others. The Council of Chalcedon assigned Asiana, Pontica and Thrace to Constantinople.

units.la: Atque hactenus de Orientalium sectis egimus, juxta illorum sedes patriarchales, quibus aut subjecti fuerunt, aut ad quas olim spectarunt, proximeve referri possunt: uti ad Constantinopolitanum, qui urbis ratione primatum mox obtinuit, de Moscovitis & Russis: ad Alexandrinum, de Coptis, & Abyssinis: nunc sequitur ut ad Antiocheni dicecesim videamus de Syris seu Melchitis, qui per illam frequentes degunt, cujus archiepiscopi sedes hodie est, non Antiochia, sed Damascus. Syri dicti a regione, quam incolunt: Melchitæ, a religione, quod eam tum ipsi, tum ipsorum episcopi sequuti sunt, quæ Regis seu Imperatoris erat. Id est, quum post Chalcedonensem Synodum, in quâ Eutyches ac Dioscorus fuere condemnati, alii Synodum sequerentur, alii secus, Imp. Leo sequentesque Synodum amplectentes urgentesque, causam aliis dedere, orthodoxos per calumniam Melchitas appellandi, quia nempe religionem tenebant Imperatoris. Cæterum orthodoxi sunt, Eutychianismum aversati, secus ac alii; & per Orientem frequentissimi. Communia Græcorum sequuntur dogmata, de processione Spiritus S. à solo Patre, jejunio sabbathi, conjugio & bigamia sacerdotum; prætera ad versus Latinos Eucharistiam celebrant sub utraque parte; negant Purgatorium ignem, aliaque, quæ in Latinâ Ecclesiâ dudum carpsit & castigavit Orientalis. Primatum Romanum eo constantius rejiciunt, quo Petrum ajunt Antiochiæ sedisse, antequam ad Romanos proficisceretur, unde se Romano submittere episcopo omnino renuunt. Hinc de illis Gabriel Sionita, lib. de Vrbibus Oriental. cap. iv. testatur, quod odium intestinum in summum Pontificem, atque in omnes ei in spiritualibus subjectos gerunt, quodque eidem primum pertinaciter abnegant. Contrà ac Maronitæ, montis Libani incolæ, qui ab aliquo tempore se Romanis subjecere, ab a. cIↄ cIxxxvi. quod refert VVilhelmus Tyrius, de bello sacro lib. xxii. cap. viii. A quo tempore iterum relapsi ad priorem Græcorum religionem & dogmata, sed reversi denuò sunt, sub Gregorio xiii. & Clemente viii. Unde autem sic dicti sint, incertum valde est. An à Marone hæretico Monothelitâ, cui errori olim una cum aliis fuerint deditissimi, ut VVilhelmus Tyrius, rerum istarum peritus, colligit: cum per annos pene quingentos cujusdam Maronis hæresiarchæ errorem fuisse secuti. Deinde: Maronis autem error, & sequacium ejus est, & fuit (sicut ex sexta Synodo legitur, quæ contra eos lata esse dignoscitur, & in quâ damnationis sententiam pertulerunt) quod in Domino nostro Iesu Christo una tantum sit, & fuerit ab initio, & voluntas, & operatio. Similiter Bernardus Lutzemburgensis; & Praeeolus, in Elencho hæres. voce Maronitæ. Quod alii ægerrimè ferunt, illorum inde derivari nomenclaturam, malunt que à Sancto quodam Marone, abbate deducere, cujus mentio occurrit in Concilio Constantinopolitano, sub Menna, in subscriptione libelli Monachorum Apameæ, Act. v. quæ in aliis editionibus est actio i. ubi primus Alexander presbyter & archimandrita monasterii beati Maronis, à quo Maronitas nominatos, ut à Studio Constantinopolitano monasterio, Studitas, colligit Baronius, Tom. vii. ad a. ixxviii. Alii à terrâ Maronlâ dictos autumant, apud Gabrielem Sionitam, de Vrbib. Arabiæ, cap. vi. Baronium, Tom. xii. ad a. cIↄ clxxxii. Quidquid de ipsorum nomine sit, undecunque acceperint, exiguo præ aliis numero, in Cypro, AlepAleppi, Damasci, praesertim vero in Libano vexantur, atque à Turcis vehementer opprimuntur & exsugiuntur. Patriarcha ipsorum, qui se Petrum semper, vel Iacobitarum Patriarcha Ignatium, appellat, octo vel novem sub se habet suffraganeos. Et hi sedem agnoscunt Romanum Pontificem, & sedem Apostolicam, unde ex omnibus Orientis populis se integram restituerunt, inquit Possevinus, in Apparatu, tit. Maronitae: unde & Romae seminarium Maronitarum, pro juvandis illis, excitum.
units.tr: So far we have treated of the Eastern sects, according to their patriarchal sees to which they were either subject or formerly belonged, or to which they can most closely be referred: thus, to the see of Constantinople, which soon gained primacy on account of its city, belong the Muscovites and Russians; to that of Alexandria, the Copts and Abyssinians. Now it follows that we should look, in the diocese of Antioch, at the Syrians or Melchites, who live there in large numbers, and whose archbishop's see is today not Antioch but Damascus. They were called Syrians from the region they inhabit, and Melchites from their religion, because both they and their bishops followed the religion of the king or emperor. That is, when after the Council of Chalcedon, at which Eutyches and Dioscorus were condemned, some followed the Council and others did not, the emperor Leo and those who followed him, embracing and pressing the Council, gave others occasion to call the orthodox Melchites by way of slander, because they held the religion of the emperor. Yet they are orthodox, having rejected Eutychianism, unlike others, and they are very numerous throughout the East. They follow the common doctrines of the Greeks: on the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father alone, on fasting on the Sabbath, on the marriage and bigamy of priests. Besides, against the Latins they celebrate the Eucharist under both kinds; they deny purgatorial fire, and other things which the Eastern Church long ago attacked and rebuked in the Latin Church. They reject Roman primacy all the more firmly because they say Peter sat at Antioch before he went to Rome, and so they utterly refuse to submit themselves to the Roman bishop. Hence Gabriel Sionita, in his book on the cities of the East, chapter IV, testifies that they bear an inner hatred toward the supreme Pontiff and toward all who are subject to him in spiritual matters, and that they stubbornly deny him first place. In contrast to them are the Maronites, inhabitants of Mount Lebanon, who for some time past submitted themselves to the Romans, from 1186, as William of Tyre reports, On the Holy War, book xxii, chapter viii. From that time they relapsed again into the earlier religion and doctrines of the Greeks, but returned again under Gregory XIII and Clement VIII. It is very uncertain, however, how they came to be so called. Whether it was from Maro, a Monothelite heretic, to whose error they were once most devoted together with others, as William of Tyre, well versed in these matters, infers: since for nearly five hundred years they had followed the error of a certain heresiarch Maro. Then: But the error of Maro and his followers is, and was (as is read from the sixth Synod, which is known to have been passed against them, and in which they underwent the sentence of condemnation), that in our Lord Jesus Christ there is, and was from the beginning, only one will and one operation. Bernard of Luxembourg and Prateolus, in his Catalogue of Heresies, under the word Maronites, agree. Others, who take it very ill that their name is derived from this, prefer to derive it from a certain St Maro, an abbot, whose mention occurs in the Council of Constantinople under Menas, in the subscription of the petition of the monks of Apamea, Act v, which in other editions is act i, where the first is Alexander the presbyter and archimandrite of the monastery of the blessed Maro, from whom the Maronites are named, just as the Studites are named from the Studium monastery at Constantinople, as Baronius infers, vol. vii, under the year 878. Others think they were named from the land of Maronia, as Gabriel Sionita states in his book on the cities of Arabia, chapter vi, and Baronius, vol. xii, under the year 1182. Whatever the origin of their name, and wherever they received it, they are few in number compared with others, and are harassed in Cyprus, Aleppo and Damascus, but especially on Lebanon, and are severely oppressed and drained by the Turks. Their patriarch, who always calls himself Peter, or the patriarch of the Jacobites, Ignatius, has eight or nine suffragans under him. These acknowledge the Roman Pontiff and the Apostolic See, by which, says Possevinus in the Apparatus, under the title Maronites, they restored themselves entire from all the peoples of the East; and for this reason a seminary of Maronites was set up at Rome to help them.

units.la: Quintum post quatuor Patriarchas olim locum in Synodis, earumque subscriptionibus tenebat episcopus Seleuciensis, cujus authoritatem hodie arrogat Patriarcha Muzal, in Mesopotamia, qui Chaldaeorum seu Nestorianorum summus est episcopus, cognomine antiquo catholicus, sequeque scribit quintum Patriarchan. Elias Patriarcha Babylonis, in epist. ad P. Paulum v. circa 1 cx. Ego Elias etc. cui per gratiam, & praeter sua merita, credita est sedes quinta Babylonis. Cujus modo nomen ac rudera superstunt, sedes ac dignitas Seleuciensi (nam in Babylonis antiquae locum Seleucia concessit) contigit, cum quâ Seleucia quidam idem faciunt hodierno Muzal, quae amplissima Mesopotamiae urbs est, Tygri adjacens, sed non, verum è regione veteris Ninivae sita est, quae ad orientalem Tigris partem in Assyriâ, hæc ad ejus occidentalem in Mesopotamiâ. In epistolâ a. circa 1 1 1. ad P. Iulium iii. scribunt, se convenisse ex omnibus civitatibus & pagis, circa civitatem Mozal, hoc est Athur in vicinia Ninives. Patriarchalis sedes, quae olim Seleuciae, nunc in Muzal est, ejusve proximo monasterio: quodque olim illi Patriarchae datum, hodiernus sibi quoque arrogat. Quid autem id sit, videri ex Synodo Nicaenâ potest, can. xxiii. Sit praeterea honorandus, qui tenet sedem Seleuciae, quae et in provinciâ Orientali, qui debet etiam appellari nomine Catholici, sitque obediendum est, & possit is ordinare Archi. chiepiscopos, sicut faciunt Patriarchæ, & non fiet injuria Patriarchæ Antiocheno, siquidem ipse consensit, postquam hoc ab eo Synodus petivit, ne de sublatâ potestate istâ irascerentur. Quod quidem factum est, ut illius provinciæ fideles pace & quiete frueretur, simul etiam, ut is, qui tenet sedem Seleuciæ, nomine catholici honoraretur. Et cap. xxxiv. Si convenerint Episcopi ad habendum Concilium in Græciâ, & fuerit præsens præl atus Seleuciæ, quæ est provincia Babylonie, in aditu Zabur, quæ hodie vocantur civitatula: oportet honorare eum multum, & magnificare atque extollere supra omnes episcopos Græciæ. Siquidem ipse tenet locum Patriarchæ in Oriente, & sedes ejus in Concilio debet esse sexta post episcopum Hierosolymitanum. Et quicunque hanc constitutionem violaverit, synodus eum excommunicat. ex Actis Concilii Nicæni Arabici, Alphonsi Pisani, lib. II. De hoc ergo Patriarchâ, post Antiochenum, & Ierosolymitanum, jam suo loco egimus. Est vero is Nestorianorum, qui regionis istius ratione appellantur vulgo, caput, atque latissimas occupant regiones, non Mesopotamiam solum & Assyriam, sed in Tartariam, & Indiam usque suæ sectæ professores diffundunt. Chaldæorum Nestorianorum nonnulli, sub P. Iulio III. se Romanæ Ecclesiæ subjecerunt, ab eaque acceperunt Patriarchas; quorum primum confirmavit Sulakam, ordinis S. Pachomii monachum a. 1551. Cui successit Abdiesu, obtentoque à Papâ Pio IV. pallio, ad Concilium Tridentinum perrexit, ubi habuit orationem, contra quam protestatus Orator Lusitaniæ fuit, Regem suum, apud Antistites Orientales sibi parentes neminem Patriarcham superiorem scire: quæ protestatio multorum excitabat animos ad varia absurda in oratione Patriarchæ exequenda, quæ alii haud segniter supprimebant, & occultabant. Histor. Conc. Trident. lib. vi. Sed hi Romanenses Chaldæi nequaquam comparandi cum reliquis numero, à quibus sunt repulsi sugarique: Nestorianis Chaldæis, ipsorumque Patriarchâ, nomen, sedem potestatemque pristinam reinetė. Denique a. cIɔ Iɔ ex. Patriarcha Babylonis Elias, per Adam Archidiaconum, ad P. Paulum V. se contulit, cuque se submisit: quo apud suos consensu autem eventu, incertum. Historiam habes insertam Annalibus Baronii, Tom. XIV, & apud Petrum Strozam, qui cum Adamo Legato Eliae, saepius Romae contulit, & hinc disputationem suam conscripsit, De dogmatibus Chaldaeorum. Nestoriani Chaldaei, potentissimi ac numerosissimi sequuntur dogmata Graecorum, & Nestorianorum, de quibus quia dictum a nobis in praecedentibus, hic multa addere supervacuum. Et quidquid fit de Nestorio, & cujus ille sententiae doctrinaeque super eo quod in Ephesino Concilio ei attributum fuerit, Nestoriani hodie tenent damnatam in Nestorio haeresin, necnon solum Nestorium tuentur ac praedicant. Haec enim excerpta articulorum controversorum inter se & Latinos exhibuit Patriarchae suo Eliae Ada archimandritae: Dominus Papa, cum omnibus Patribus magnae Ecclesiae Romae vocant Virginem sanctam Mariam, Dei Genitricem, Nos vero Orientales eam Genitricem Christi vocamus. Illi duas naturas Christi confitentur, duas virtutes, & duas voluntates. Nos autem fatemur unam virtutem & unam voluntatem. Illi etiam unam personam fatentur in Christo. Nos quidem fatemur duas personas. Et dicunt, quod Spir. ex Patre & Filio procedit. Nos vero fatemur, quod ex Patre Spiritus procedit.
units.tr: Fifth after the four patriarchs, in the synods and in the order of their signatures, came the bishop of Seleucia, whose authority the present Patriarch of Mosul in Mesopotamia now claims. He is the chief bishop of the Chaldeans, or Nestorians, and is called catholicus by an old title, and he writes himself the fifth patriarch. Elias, Patriarch of Babylon, in a letter to Pope Paul V about 1 cx., writes: "I, Elias, etc., to whom, by grace and beyond my own merits, the fifth see of Babylon has been entrusted." Only the name and ruins of that see now survive. The see and dignity passed to Seleucia, since Seleucia took the place of ancient Babylon, and some people identify the present Mosul with Seleucia. Mosul is a very large city of Mesopotamia, lying beside the Tigris, but not opposite old Nineveh: Nineveh lies on the eastern side of the Tigris in Assyria, while Mosul lies on its western side in Mesopotamia. In a letter of about 111 to Pope Julius III they write that they had gathered from all the towns and villages around the city of Mosul, that is, Athur, near Nineveh. The patriarchal see, which was once at Seleucia, is now at Mosul or in a monastery nearby, and the present patriarch claims for himself what was once granted to that earlier patriarch. What this grant was can be seen from the Council of Nicaea, canon 23: "The one who holds the see of Seleucia, which is in the Eastern province, is to be honoured, and he is also to be called by the name of catholicus. He is to be obeyed, and he may ordain archbishops, as the patriarchs do, and no injury shall be done to the Patriarch of Antioch, since he himself agreed when the synod asked him, lest he be angry that this power was taken away. This was done so that the faithful of that province might enjoy peace and quiet, and so that the one who holds the see of Seleucia might be honoured with the name of catholicus." And canon 34: "If the bishops meet to hold a council in Greece, and the prelate of Seleucia, which is the province of Babylon, at the entrance of Zabur (which today is called a little town) is present, he must be greatly honoured, and exalted above all the bishops of Greece. For he holds the place of patriarch in the East, and his seat in the council must be sixth, after the bishop of Jerusalem. Whoever violates this constitution, the synod excommunicates." This is from the Acts of the Arabic Council of Nicaea, in Alphonsus of Pisa, book 2. We have already dealt with this patriarch, after Antioch and Jerusalem, in its proper place. He is the head of the Nestorians, who are commonly named after this region, and they occupy very wide lands. They spread their sect not only through Mesopotamia and Assyria but also into Tartary and India. Some of the Chaldean Nestorians submitted themselves to the Roman Church under Pope Julius III and received patriarchs from it. The first of these, Sulaka, a monk of the order of St Pachomius, was confirmed in 1551. He was succeeded by Abdiesu, who received the pallium from Pope Pius IV and went to the Council of Trent, where he delivered an oration. Against this the envoy of Portugal protested, saying that his king knew of no patriarch superior to himself among the eastern prelates who were subject to him. This protest stirred the minds of many to carry out various absurdities in the patriarch's oration, which others did not hesitate to suppress and conceal. (History of the Council of Trent, book 6.) But these Roman Chaldeans cannot be compared in number with the rest, from whom they have been driven and drained. The name, see and former power of the patriarch belong to the Nestorian Chaldeans. Finally, in 1551 (sic) the Patriarch of Babylon, Elias, through Adam the archdeacon, submitted himself to Pope Paul V and placed himself under him; whether this had the consent of his people, or what its outcome was, is uncertain. You have the history inserted in the Annals of Baronius, vol. XIV, and in Peter Strozza, who often conferred at Rome with Adam, Elias's legate, and from this wrote his disputation, On the Doctrines of the Chaldeans. The Nestorian Chaldeans, who are very powerful and very numerous, follow the doctrines of the Greeks and of the Nestorians, which I have discussed above, so there is no need to add much here. Whatever may be the truth about Nestorius, and whatever his opinion and teaching may have been on the matter attributed to him at the Council of Ephesus, the Nestorians today hold the heresy condemned in Nestorius, and they only defend and proclaim Nestorius himself. Indeed, Ada, archimandrite, gave to his patriarch Elias this extract of the points in controversy between themselves and the Latins: "The Lord Pope, with all the Fathers of the great Church of Rome, call the holy Virgin Mary the Mother of God, but we Easterners call her the Mother of Christ. They confess two natures of Christ, two powers and two wills. But we confess one power and one will. They also confess one person in Christ; we indeed confess two persons. And they say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, but we say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father."

units.la: Armenii scio olim pertinuerunt ad Patriarchatum Constantinopolitanum, quia erant provinciae Ponticae, sed a longo tempore ab eo defeciverunt, & loca vicina incolentes iis, in quibus modo versamur, de illis iam dicemus. Binos habent Patriarchas, quos quoque Catholicos vocant, nemini subjectos: alterum Armeniae majoris, dictae ab occupatione Turcarum, Turcomania; alterum minoris, cis Euphratem: utramque enim fluvius iste dissecat & disterminat. Illius antiqua sedes fuit Sebastia, Armeniae majoris metropolis, & hodierna in monasterio Ecmeazin, apud civitatem Persiae Ervan: hujus olim sedes Melitene, Armeniae minoris metropolis, hodie in civitate Sis, Ciliciae prope Tarsum: nam per hanc etiam, dictam nunc Caramaniam, se diffundit Patriarchae illius jurisdictio. Armeni, praeterquam hic, in variis per Asiam locis, Europae etiam, in Tartaria, Russia, Lithuania, ubi propria habent templa, dispersi sunt, praesertim in locis mercatus, nam ad mercaturam prae aliis valent, unde & apud Turcas passim acceptiores: addunt alii & hanc rationem, quare Turcae magis faveant Armenis, quam ullis aliis Christianorum, quia scilicet Armenus quidam Sacerdos Muhammedi aliquando praedixit & vaticinatus fuit illam suam, quam deinde obtinuit, potestatem. Theologia & dogmata ipsorum valde incerta sunt, compertumque absona & dira nonnulla, praeter veritatem, iis impacta fuisse. A qualibus ipse eos Genebrardus purgat, Chronolog. lib. IV. pag. 927. an bona & propria motus causa, non dico: hoc interim de Graecis Scriptoribus addit, se eos suspectos habere, quotiescunque de Syris, Maronitis, Aethiopibus, Persis, Indis, Georgianis, Aegyptiis scribunt, eosque vel Jacobitas, vel Nestorianos asserunt: quum qui apud illos peregrinantur, saepius orthodoxos deprehendant ac catholicos. Constans autem scriptorum consensus est, esse Jacobitas, & post quartum concilium Chalcedonense, opera Echanii cujusdam Armeni, qui & Mandacumes appellabatur, sententiam Eutychis, Dioscori & Monophysitarum sequutos: uti scribit Euthymius monachus Zigabenus, ubi adversus illos disputat, Panoplia part. II. tit. xx. Vtebanturque hoc simili, quod quemadmodum gutta aliqua mellis vel aceti in mare demersa non amplius servat suam naturam, neque cernitur ultra, aut subsistit, ita corpus Christi in divinitatis pelago demersum quasi absumtumque non amplius suam ipsius naturam servare ac proprietates, atque inde non duas in Christo esse naturas, sed unam, eandemque divinitatis. Quidquid hac de re sit, pro pessimis hominibus habitos Armenios scimus, suone merito, an aliorum invidia, incertum. Hinc Niconis scriptum, de pessimâ Armenorum religione, in Bibliothecâ Patrum; & apud Balsamonem, in Can. epist. pag. 1097. Baron. Tom. X. cujus stare judicio nolim, praesertim in iis, quae Armenis in articulo de Trinitate objicit. Rogatus Iohannes Cypri episcopus, à Constantino Cabasilâ, Dyrrachii archiepiscopo, de tolerandis Armenis, & permittendo iis aedificare templa, respondet, quod inter Responsa Patriarcharum, Tom. III. Iuris Graeco Latini, nec abs re est, ut hic legatur: Ab initio quidem indultum est, ut in Christianorum regionibus & civitatibus diverse linguae & religionis homines habitarent, ut puta Iudaei, Armeni, Ismaelitae, Agareni, & alii ejusmodi, non promiscue tamen, sed seorsim. Unde etiam harum tribuum cuique intra civitatem, vel extra, loci determinantur: ut bis circumscribantur, nec ulterius eorum habitationes extendantur. Illud autem veteribus principibus excogitatum est, tribus, ut opinor, & causis. Una quidem, ut habitationis angustiis & defectu, sensum capiant, se propter haeresin rejiciendos judicari. Alia autem, ut propter frequentem cum Christianis consuetudinem paulatim ad mutationem convertantur: si non omnes, aliqui saltem, quos salus dilexerit. Tertia etiam, ut industria ipsorum fructus referant, qui iis ad vitam opus habent. Armeni ergo, si quo loco circumscripti sunt, templa aedificant, & faciunt quae ad haeresin ipsorum pertinent, extra calumniam manent. Idem enim Iudaeis licet & Ismaelitis, qui Christianas civitates incolunt. Quod si defuerint sibi habitationis egrediuntur terminos, non ipsi tantum prohibentur, sed & aedificia eorum, qualiacunque fuerint, diruuntur. Indulgentiam enim talium & licentiam jamdudum concesserunt. Unde quo loco Armeni habitant, dudum fuerunt, pari fere cum Iudaeis & Agarenis, liquet. Tantumque Graecis cum Armenis odium esse scribit Varenius, ut illi cibum sumere cum iis, aut eodem ex poculo bibere recusent. Interim hi ipsi Armeni pluria habent veteris ἀποδόσεως monumenta. Iuxtaque ea, quæ ipsi de illis Pontificii referunt, aliique imagines nec crucem adorant: sed adorantes feriunt anathemate. Negant, verum Christi corpus realiter in sacramento Eucharistiæ sub panis; & sanguinem, sub vini speciebus contineri. Præterea etiam sacramentis virtutem conferendi gratiam, negant. Rursus sic vinum in calice apponunt, ut nullam penitus misceant aquam, eam afferentes minimè miscendam esse. Negant, in nuptiis contrahendis aliquod esse sacramentum, asseverantes, illam maris & fœminæ indissolubilem conjunctionem non esse sacramentum, neque per illam, aliquam gratiam conferri conjunctis. Dicunt etiam, esse aliqua peccata ita prorsus irremissibilia, ut à nullo sacerdote remitti possint.
units.tr: I know that the Armenians once belonged to the Patriarchate of Constantinople, because they were in the provinces of Pontus, but for a long time they have broken away from it. Living in the places near those in which we now are, we shall now speak of them. They have two patriarchs, whom they also call catholici, and who are subject to no one: one of Greater Armenia, which is called Turcomania from the Turkish occupation, and one of Lesser Armenia, on this side of the Euphrates, for that river divides and separates the two. The ancient see of the former was Sebastia, the metropolis of Greater Armenia, and today it is in the monastery of Echmiadzin, near the Persian city of Erivan. The see of the latter was formerly Melitene, the metropolis of Lesser Armenia, and today it is in the city of Sis, in Cilicia, near Tarsus. For his jurisdiction of the patriarch of that see also extends through Caramania, as it is now called. Armenians are scattered not only here but in various places across Asia, and also in Europe, in Tartary, Russia and Lithuania, where they have their own churches. They are especially found in trading centres, for they excel in commerce above others, and so they are more acceptable to the Turks everywhere. Some add this further reason why the Turks favour the Armenians more than any other Christians: an Armenian priest once predicted to Muhammad and foretold that power which he afterwards obtained. Their theology and doctrines are very uncertain, and it is known that some absurd and dreadful things, apart from the truth, have been attached to them. Genebrard clears them of these charges, (Chronology, book 4, p. 927), though I do not say whether he does so from good and proper motives. Meanwhile he adds, concerning Greek writers, that he holds them under suspicion whenever they write about the Syrians, Maronites, Ethiopians, Persians, Indians, Georgians and Egyptians, and declare them to be Jacobites or Nestorians, since those who travel among them often find them orthodox and catholic. There is, however, a constant consensus of writers that they are Jacobites, and that after the Fourth Council of Chalcedon, through the work of a certain Armenian named Echanius, who was also called Mandacumes, they followed the opinion of Eutyches, Dioscorus and the Monophysites. So Euthymius Zigabenus, a monk, writes when he disputes against them (Panoplia, part 2, title 20). They used this comparison: just as a drop of honey or vinegar sunk in the sea no longer keeps its nature, nor can it be seen or endure any more, so the body of Christ, sunk and as it were consumed in the sea of the godhead, no longer keeps its own nature and properties; hence there are not two natures in Christ, but one and the same divine nature. Whatever the truth of this matter, we know that the Armenians have been regarded as very wicked people, but whether this is deserved or comes from the envy of others is uncertain. Hence the writing of Nicon, On the Most Wicked Religion of the Armenians, in the Library of the Fathers, and in Balsamon, on the canonical letters, p. 1097; Baronius, vol. X. I would not wish to abide by their judgment, especially in what Nicon objects to the Armenians on the article of the Trinity. John, bishop of Cyprus, when asked by Constantine Cabasilas, archbishop of Dyrrachium, whether the Armenians should be tolerated and allowed to build churches, replies in the Responses of the Patriarchs, vol. III of the Greco-Latin Law, and it is not out of place to read it here: "At the beginning it was indeed granted that people of different languages and religions should live in Christian lands and cities, such as Jews, Armenians, Ishmaelites, Agarenes and others of that kind, but not mixed together; rather, each apart. So the places of each of these tribes are fixed, within or outside the city, so that they are confined within these limits and their dwellings are not extended further. Now the ancient princes devised this, I think, for three reasons. One is that, through the narrowness and lack of room, they may come to feel that they are judged to be rejected because of their heresy. Another is that, through frequent association with Christians, they may gradually turn to a change, if not all, at least some whom salvation has loved. A third is that they may bring to bear the industry from which they draw the means they need for life. So if the Armenians are confined to some place, they build churches and do what pertains to their heresy, and they remain free from calumny. For it is equally permitted to Jews and Ishmaelites who inhabit Christian cities. But if they lack room for dwelling and go beyond their boundaries, not only are they themselves forbidden, but their buildings, of whatever kind, are torn down. For a long time they have granted such indulgence and licence. Hence it is clear that in the place where the Armenians live, they were long ago, almost on a par with the Jews and Agarenes." Varenius writes that there is such hatred between the Greeks and the Armenians that they refuse to take food with them or drink from the same cup. Meanwhile these same Armenians keep many monuments of the ancient apodosis [ἀποδόσεως]. And, according to what the Papists themselves report of them, they do not adore images or the cross; rather, they strike with an anathema those who adore them. They deny that the true body of Christ is really contained in the sacrament of the Eucharist under the appearance of bread, and the blood under the species of wine. Moreover, they deny that the sacraments confer grace. Again, they place wine in the chalice without mixing any water at all, asserting that water must by no means be mixed in. They deny that there is any sacrament in contracting marriage, asserting that the indissoluble union of man and woman is not a sacrament, nor is any grace conferred on the couple through it. They also say that there are some sins so utterly unforgivable that no priest can forgive them.

units.la: Asserunt præterea, nullum esse purgatorium locum, in quo animæ ab hac luce migrantes purgentur à sordibus, quas in corpore contraxerant, antequam in æterna tabernacula recipiantur. Item, beatos essentiam Dei non videre, sed claritatem quandam illius essentiæ; in quâ visione afferunt supremam constare beatitudinem. Diem natalis Domini nesciunt, nullaque festa, nec Vigilias custodiunt, nec quatuor tempora. Præterea in sabbatho, & in Dominicâ carnes comedunt. Rebaptizant eos, qui semel baptismum susceperunt in ecclesiâ Romanâ, dicentes, in eâ non esse verum baptisma, propterea quod apud Latinos non esse veram catholicam ecclesiam credant, sed solum penès ipsos. Proprium habent Primatem, quem Catholicum appellant, & cui velut summo Pontifici per omnia optemperant. Romanum siquidem antistitem contemnunt, cumque dicunt non esse cæteris superiorem. Hæc ex Nicone, Prateolo, Thomâ à Iesu, Armeniorum adversariis. Chytræus quoque in Orat. de Statu Eccles. pag. 22. 23. in sacris non alia quàm ipsis vernaculâ & vulgò notâ linguâ utuntur. Quem morem, Ruthenos, ac Moscovitas, & Moldavos, aliasque gentes, Byzantino Patriarchæ subjectas, & alias in Oriente & Africâ ecclesias Christianas, hodie etiam servare scimus. Habentque Biblia suâ Armenorum linguâ, quæ versio facta dicitur à Chrysostomo, apud ipsos exulante. In Liturgiâ suâ omnibus integrum sacramentum distribuunt: nec ulla, sine distributione sacramenti, Missa celebratur: neque sacerdotes mariti ab administratione sacrorum arcentur. Unde facilè credo, à scriptoribus Pontificiis nonnulla temerè Armenis afficta fuisse. Quomodo quæso convenit, Armenos imagines religiosas earumque cultum vehementer execrari; & simul effigiare imagines Patris, Filii, & S.S.: illis attribuere, quod peccatum originale negant; & quod dicerent quoque omnes homines ante passionem Christi fuisse damnatos ob primorum parentum peccatum atque transgressionem? Quod faterentur Deum esse mendacem? talia ac iis admodum ineptè adscribit Prateolus. Operæ pretium foret, ut quis nos certius de ipsorum religione & fide doceret, quos suspicor magis reformatos esse, quam quidem communis ferat opinio. Eugenius P. perquam studiosè conatus fuit illos in unionem secum attrahere, quâ formâ Græcorum alios, catatque in Florentinâ Synodo formula unionis Armenorum, sed parem illa apud hos successum habuit, quam apud Græcos altera: quod testatur Thomas à Iesu, lib. VII. cap. XIX. At postea in Concilio Florentino, tempore Eugenii IV. celebrata est Armenorum unio cum Ecclesiâ Catholicâ, quamvis nunc apud Armenos ipsos, sicut nec apud Græcos, unionis in illo celeberrimo Concilio, præsente Imperatore Palæologo facta, nullum fere exstat vestigium.
units.tr: They further assert that there is no purgatory, in which souls leaving this life are cleansed of the stains they contracted in the body before they are received into the eternal tabernacles. Likewise, they say that the blessed do not see the essence of God but a certain brightness of that essence, and they hold that the supreme blessedness consists in this vision. They do not know the day of the Lord's birth, and they keep no feasts, nor vigils, nor the Ember days. Moreover, they eat meat on the Sabbath and on the Lord's day. They rebaptize those who have already received baptism in the Roman Church, saying that there is no true baptism in it, because they believe the Latins do not have the true catholic Church, which exists only among themselves. They have their own Primate, whom they call Catholic, and to whom, as to a supreme Pontiff, they conform in everything. They despise the Roman bishop and say that he is not superior to the others. These things are reported by Nicon, Prateolus and Thomas à Jesu, adversaries of the Armenians. Chytraeus also, in his oration on the state of the Church, pp. 22-23, says that in sacred matters they use no language but their own vernacular, commonly known tongue. We know that the Ruthenians, Muscovites, Moldavians and other peoples subject to the Byzantine Patriarch, and other Christian churches in the East and in Africa, still observe this custom today. They have the Bible in their own Armenian language, a version said to have been made by Chrysostom while he was in exile among them. In their liturgy they distribute the whole sacrament to all; no Mass is celebrated without the distribution of the sacrament; nor are married priests barred from administering the sacred rites. Hence I readily believe that some things were rashly attributed to the Armenians by Papist writers. How, I ask, does it agree that the Armenians vehemently abhor religious images and their worship, and yet depict images of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit? How does it agree that they deny original sin, and that they would say all men before Christ's passion were condemned because of the sin and transgression of the first parents? Would they confess that God is a liar? Prateolus ascribes such things and others to them quite absurdly. It would be worth while if someone instructed us more certainly about their religion and faith, which I suspect are more reformed than common opinion holds. Pope Eugenius very eagerly tried to draw them into union with himself, just as he did with some of the Greeks, and a formula of union with the Armenians was drawn up at the Synod of Florence; but it had as little success among them as the other one had among the Greeks. Thomas à Jesu testifies to this, book VII, chapter XIX: But afterwards, at the Council of Florence, celebrated in the time of Eugenius IV, the union of the Armenians with the Catholic Church was effected; yet now among the Armenians themselves, as also among the Greeks, scarcely any trace remains of the union made at that most famous council in the presence of the Emperor Palaeologus.

units.la: Supra Armenos ad Septentrionem, inter Pontum Euxinum, & mare Caspium, degunt qui vulgò dicuntur Georgiani, ïque, sicut illi, olim Constantinopolitasano peruenerunt Patriarchæ, sed jam proprium habent, in monte Sinâ, in claustro S. Catharinæ. Tantum autem inter utrosque odium esse dicitur, ut hi jubeant: Si quis vestrum habeat spinam in pede sixam transiens ante Armenorum Ecclesiam, debet spinam sustinere, nec se ad pedem suum evellendi causâ inclinare, ne per hoc videatur ante Armenorum Ecclesiam, ab omnibus Christianis, pilipendendam, inclinare. Referente Thomâ à Iesu, lib. VII. cap. XVIII. Georgianos à S. Georgio distos communiter scribunt, quia eum supra modum venerentur, quasi primum apud ipsos Euangelii prædicatorem, cujus ideoque signum in vexillis circumferant adversus alios præliaturi. Est certè gens bellicissima, & Schytharum more, quorum contermini, vivens. Nomen hoc non à S. Georgio ipsorum regio, sed jam à tempore Melæ, ac plinii habuit. Neque Georgianos & Iberos eosdem censeo, quamvis non longe dissitos. Mela: super Schytæ Schytarumque desertæ, inquit, ac super Caspium sinum, Comani, Massagetæ, Cadufii, Hircani, Hiberi. Super Amazonas & Hyperboreos, Cimmerii, Scythæ, Eniochæ, Georgi, Mosci &c. Diversos facit Hiberos, & Georgos. Hi sunt, quos nunc Gorgianos appellamus. Regio ipsorum vulgò Gorgestan, vel Georgia. Videsis Antoninum, histor. part. III. tit. XIX. cap. VIII. §. IX. X. Cujus princeps Teimurazes, totaque natio impudenter delusa fuit haud ita pridem anno cIɔ Iɔ cxiv. à Iesuitis, qui Reginæ Cetabæ, matris, apud Persas ob religionem Christianam interfectæ, caput se mittere Regi persuaserant, quod magno aliquamdiu honore omnes prosequuti, usque dum Cetabæ ancilla & fraudem Iesuitarum, & corpus Dominæ produxit, quod Rex à Persis magnâ dein pecuniâ redemit. Historiam descripsit Gregorius Hieromonachus, Trapezuntinus, eamque alii ad illum annum commemorant. Conversos autem Iberos primum exemplo & operâ captivæ alicujus mulieris Christianæ, quæ pietate suâ & religiosâ admodum vitâ, tum miraculis tantum stuporem incusserat Reginæ aliisque ejus loci, ut religionem Christianam edoceri hinc ardentissime expetierint, passim scribunt Historici Rufinus, lib. 11. cap. x. Sozomenus, Socrates, alii. Georgios illos vel Georgestanos hodie cum Græcis convenire in religione atque liturgia, asserunt.
units.tr: Beyond the Armenians, to the north, between the Euxine Sea and the Caspian Sea, live those commonly called Georgians, who, like the Armenians, once came under the Patriarch of Constantinople, but now have their own at the monastery of St Catherine on Mount Sinai. There is said to be such hatred between the two that the Georgians order: If any of you has a thorn stuck in his foot while passing before the church of the Armenians, he must endure the thorn and not bend down to pull it out of his foot, lest by this he seem to bow before the church of the Armenians, which is to be despised by all Christians. This is reported by Thomas à Jesu, book VII, chapter XVIII. Writers commonly say that the Georgians are so called from St George, because they venerate him beyond measure, as the first preacher of the Gospel among them; and therefore they carry his sign on their banners when they go out to fight against others. They are certainly a most warlike people, living in the manner of the Scythians, whose neighbours they are. Their land had this name not from St George but already from the time of Mela and Pliny. Nor do I think the Georgians and the Iberians are the same, although they are not far apart. Mela: beyond the Scythians and the deserted Scythian lands, he says, and beyond the Caspian gulf, dwell the Comani, Massagetae, Cadusii, Hyrcani, Iberi. Beyond the Amazons and Hyperboreans, the Cimmerii, Scythians, Eniochi, Georgi, Mosci, etc. He makes the Iberians and the Georgians different peoples. These are the ones we now call Georgians. Their region is commonly called Gorgestan, or Georgia. See Antoninus, history, part III, title XIX, chapter VIII, §§ IX-X. Their prince Teimurazes and the whole nation were shamelessly deceived not long ago, in the year 1614, by the Jesuits, who had persuaded the King to send them the head of the Queen Mother Ketevan, who had been put to death among the Persians for the Christian religion. The king honoured it with great reverence for some time, until a maidservant of Ketevan revealed the Jesuits' fraud and the body of the Lady, which the King afterwards ransomed from the Persians for a large sum of money. Gregory the Hieromonk of Trebizond described this history, and others mention it for that year. Historians such as Rufinus, book II, chapter X, Sozomen, Socrates and others write that the Iberians were first converted through the example and efforts of a certain captive Christian woman, whose piety and very religious life, together with miracles, struck such awe into the Queen and others of that place that they eagerly desired to be taught the Christian religion. They assert that these Georgians, or Georgestanians, today agree with the Greeks in religion and liturgy.

units.la: Varia autem Græcorum & Orientalium est Liturgia, ordoque agendorum Ecclesiasticorum, postquam nimis in formulas & formalitates λειτουργικὰ dediti, tot tandem librorum sacrorum nacti sunt genera, ut numerare molestum sit. Præter Liturgias Iacobi, Clementis, Petri, Matthæi, quæ Æthiopum, Marci, de quibus alias diximus, earumque ostendimus vanitatem & vitia, tenent præsertim Liturgiam Chrysostomi, ac Basilii: sed quas omnes temere illis auctoribus adscribi, viri docti copiose ostendunt. Rivetus, in Critico sacro. Rob. Cocus, in Censura scriptorum veterum. Hospinianus, in histor. Sacramentaria. Mornæus, de Missa lib. 1. cap. 11. Molinæus, de Missa lib. iv. Casaubonus, Exercit. xiv. in Baronium, num. 8. Ioh. Gerhardi, Confess. lib. 1. part. 11. cap. viii. Et nos de illis agimus, ubi de Theologia Patrum. Vulgatam præterea habent liturgiam, præsertim in quadragesima, τὰ προηγιασμένα, ante sanctificatorum, id est sanctificatorum panum, vel panis partium in die dominico, quas per hebdomadam singulis diebus capiunt, ante jam sanctificaras. Cæteraque ipsorum officia videre licet, in Euchologio, quod variis additis diversorum exemplarium lectionibus, & notis, edidit nuper Iacobus Goar, Parisinus, Missus antehac Apostolicus (quemadmodum scribunt) in Orientem. Præterea habent libros, horologium officiorum ad singulas dei horas: Diurnale dicerent Latini: uti & Typicum totius anni: Paracleticum, Psalterium, Triodium, Pentecostarium, Anthologium, aliaque, de quibus Leo Allatius, singulari libro, vel dissertatione una, nâ, & altera de libris Ecclesiasticis Græcorum. Omnibus illis subservit Menologium, quod est Calendarium sacrum, à mense Septembri, unde Græci annum inchoant, incipiens, totius anni festa digerens ac solemnitates.
