Quale ex versione Cardinalis Sirleti, Canisius in Lectionibus antiquis, & Bibliotheca Patrum aliud ex versione Genebrardi exhibet: nam pluria, eaque valde diversa passim occurrunt. Arcudium indicarem, qui multa de hodiernis Græcorum Ecclesiis scripsit, deque Consensu Græca Ecclesia cum Romana, sed hactenus mihi quæsitus quidem, at non visus: interim Leonem Allatium, & Iacobum Goar video in plurimis cum non leviter carpere & castigare. Ille in fine Dissertationis I. de Arcudii Anthologio novo loquutus, hanc subdit censuram: Sane si intra Sanctorum Patrum terminos se continuisset Arcudius, neque plus sapere, quam ipse divinus spiritus voluisset, opus neque inutile, neque incommodum Orientalibus etiam Græcis fuisset. Verumtamen cum vetera immutat, integra obtruncat, perfecta immiscet, & de suo addit incompta atque insulsa, neque cum Græcis ipsis communia, stomachum sapientibus movit, & opus aliud laudabile dehonestavit. Ille, in suis ad Menologium Notis, haud semel Arcudium quoque perstringit: quorum judicium usque dum lectio Auctoris illius mihi contingat, sepono. Scripsit & Allatius, de Ecclesia Occidentalis & Orientalis perpetuâ consensione libros tres, ad votum suum & Papatus magis, quam ad veritatem, ut ab Ecclesiâ suâ amoliatur crimen, quo laborat, defectionis nempe à Græcis: digNum opus altiori discussione & censurâ. Neque jam dicere de variis Græcorum in peragendis sacris ritibus est animus, qui & pro sectis diversi sunt, & apud Auctores indicatos videri possunt: adde Iob. Bapt. Casalium, de sacris Christianorum ritibus, cap. XCI, & Christophorum Angelum, Græcum, de Statu & ritibus Græca Ecclesiæ, Latine versum à Georgio Phelario, Dantiscano. Duo præcipue in Græcorum Liturgigicis reprehendimus, formalitates omnium & singulorum officiorum nimias; ad quas hoc pacto homines supra modum adstringuntur; & multifaria; quae in illis intercurrit superstitio, ac sanctorum, aliarumque rerum improbanda veneratio. Quippe turpiter hodie se prostituunt in sanctorum cultu Orientales. Quae eo magis nunc excrevere, quod oppressi saeva Turcarum tyrannide, & restincto inde valde studiorum omnium ac religionis apud eos ardore, in paucis ejusmodi preculis, earumque fere sola recitatione segniter vulgo amant acquiescere & immori. Tanta apud illos hodie regnat barbaries, & rerum optimarum neglectus ac torpor. In quo propius accedunt ad Pontificios, & Ecclesiae Papalis morem, quam nostrum: eoque ab iis facilius alicíendi, & secum conjungendi: quod pauci tamen etiam ex tanta Orientalium copia hactenus fecerunt. Russi aliquot, & Maronitae. Reliqui Papam tanquam pejus & angue oderunt. Quin Papam Graeci quotannis, feriâ quintâ ante Pascha, palam excommunicare solent. Quodque in Concilio Lateranensi, a. cl◊ cc xv. annotatum, adeo detestati Latinos fuerunt Graeci, ut in altari, quo Latinus forte celebrasset, non prius sacra perageret Sacerdos Graecus, antequam altare ab illo inquinamento aqua fuisset bene expurgatum. Quocum convenit, quod Balsamon, Patriarcha Antiochenus respondit, ad Interrogata Marci Alexandrini: an Latinis captivis, accedentibus ad Graecorum ecclesias, communio concedenda esset, nec ne? Qui non est mecum, contra me est (inquit divinum Evangelium) & qui non colligit mecum, dispergit. Quoniam igitur ante annos multos, occidentalis ecclesia (Roma inquam) celebris conventus divisus est ab aliorum quatuor sanctorum patriarcharum spirituali communione, & ad mores institutaque diversa a catholica ecclesia, & ab orthodoxis aliena: quam ab consensu neque Papa in divinis sacrificationibus communi patriarcharum nominum relatione dignus habetur: non debet Latinos
units.tr: The liturgy of the Greeks and Orientals is varied, and the order of their ecclesiastical services, since they have given themselves too much to formulas and formalities (λειτουργικά [liturgika]), has come to have so many kinds of sacred books that it is tiresome to count them. Besides the liturgies of James, Clement, Peter and Matthew, which belong to the Ethiopians, and that of Mark, about which we have spoken elsewhere and shown its vanity and faults, they especially hold the liturgies of Chrysostom and Basil; but learned men have amply shown that all of these were rashly ascribed to those authors: Rivetus, in his Critici sacri; Rob. Cocus, in his Censura scriptorum veterum; Hospinian, in his Historia sacramentaria; Mornaeus, de Missa, book I, chapter 11; Molinaeus, de Missa, book IV; Casaubon, Exercitatio XIV against Baronius, num. 8; John Gerhard, Confessio, book I, part II, chapter viii. We too deal with these matters where we treat of the Theology of the Fathers. Moreover they have a common liturgy, especially in Lent, called the presanctified [τὰ προηγιασμένα], that is, the presanctified bread or parts of bread consecrated on the Lord's day, which they take each day of the week from those already consecrated. The rest of their offices may be seen in the Euchologion, which Jacob Goar of Paris, formerly sent (as they write) as an apostolic envoy to the East, recently published with various additions, different readings of copies, and notes. They also have books: the Horologion of offices for each of the canonical hours, which the Latins would call the Diurnale; likewise the Typicon for the whole year; the Paracletike, Psalter, Triodion, Pentecostarion, Anthologion, and others, about which Leo Allatius wrote in one separate book or in one or two dissertations, on the ecclesiastical books of the Greeks. All these are served by the Menologion, which is a sacred calendar, beginning from September, from which the Greeks start their year, setting out the feasts and solemnities of the whole year. Canisius, in his Antiquae lectiones, and the Bibliotheca Patrum, present one version from Cardinal Sirleto, and another from Genebrardus, for many different and quite diverse versions occur everywhere. I would point out Arcudius, who wrote much about the present Greek Churches, and about the Agreement of the Greek Church with the Roman; but I have so far sought him in vain and not seen him. Meanwhile I see that Leo Allatius and Jacob Goar criticize and castigate him in many places, not lightly. Allatius, speaking at the end of his first dissertation on Arcudius' New Anthologion, adds this censure: Certainly, if Arcudius had kept within the limits of the holy Fathers, and had not been wiser than the divine Spirit himself, the work would have been neither useless nor inconvenient even for the Eastern Greeks. But since he changes what is old, mutilates what is whole, mixes in what is perfect, and adds of his own things that are unpolished and insipid, which are not held in common with the Greeks themselves, he has stirred the disgust of the wise and dishonoured another laudable work. Allatius, in his Notes on the Menologion, more than once also attacks Arcudius; I set aside their judgement until I may read that author. Allatius also wrote three books, On the Perpetual Agreement of the Western and Eastern Church, more according to his wish and the interest of the Papacy than according to the truth, so that the charge under which his Church labours, namely defection from the Greeks, may be removed; a work worthy of deeper examination and censure. Nor is it my intention now to speak of the various rites of the Greeks in performing their sacred offices, who are also divided by sects, and who may be seen in the authors indicated. Add Giovanni Battista Casali, de sacris Christianorum ritibus, chapter XCI, and Christopher Angelus, a Greek, de statu et ritibus Graecae Ecclesiae, translated into Latin by Georg Phelarius of Danzig. We chiefly reproach two things in the Greek liturgies: the excessive formalities of all and each of the offices, by which people are bound beyond measure; and the many superstitions that intrude into them, and the condemnable veneration of saints and of other things. For the Orientals today shamefully prostitute themselves in the cult of the saints, and this has grown the more now that, oppressed by the savage tyranny of the Turks, and with the zeal for all good studies and religion thereby almost extinguished among them, they are content, in a few such prayers and almost only in their recitation, to remain sluggish and to linger. Such barbarism rules among them today, and such neglect and torpor of the best things. In this they come closer to the Papists and the custom of the Papal Church than to ours, and so they can more easily be enticed by them and joined to them; yet even from so great a multitude of Orientals, few have so far done so: a few Russians and the Maronites. The rest hate the Pope as worse than a snake. Indeed the Greeks customarily excommunicate the Pope publicly every year on the Friday before Easter. And what was noted at the Lateran Council in 1215 shows how greatly the Greeks detested the Latins: a Greek priest would not perform the sacred rites at an altar on which a Latin had perhaps celebrated, until the altar had been thoroughly cleansed with water from that pollution. With this agrees what Balsamon, Patriarch of Antioch, answered to the questions of Mark of Alexandria: whether communion should be granted to Latin captives who come to the churches of the Greeks, or not? He who is not with me is against me, says the divine Gospel, and he who does not gather with me scatters. Therefore, since many years ago the Western Church, that famous assembly (Rome, I mean), has been separated from the spiritual communion of the other four holy patriarchs, and has adopted customs and institutions diverse from the catholic Church and alien to the orthodox, and since the Pope, in agreement with them, is not thought worthy in divine sacrifices of having his name mentioned in common by the patriarchs, the Latins ought not to...

units.la: Rom. rum genus manu sacerdotali per divina & immaculata mysteria sanctificari, nisi deponat prius, se à Latinis institutis & consuetudinibus abstenturum, & secundum canones in- structus fuerit, & orthodoxis adaequatus. Nobiscum in pluribus conveniunt, & convenire possunt Græci: qui- dem apud nos obstacula illa non sunt, quæ ipsis Romani objiciunt: nos enim etiam Papatum Romanum oppugnamus, ignem purgatorium, aliaque quæ ipsi non ferunt; iterum communionem sub utráque Cœnæ parte, conjugium Ecclesiasticorum, usum Linguæ vulgaris in sacris, & plura tenemus, in quibus ipsorum nobiscum tum doctrina, tum praxis concordant. Inque plurimis articulis principalibus consensum inter Nos- tros & Orientales Ecclesias esse, à pluribus demonstratum. Varii hodie in istis Ecclesiis defectus, erroresque vigent, sed ex iis multi non sunt universales omnium; neque antiqui adeo, & quos non pertinaciter essent retenturi, si ab externâ tyrannide libertas, & ab aliis rectior pleniorque institutio obtingeret. Iam verò hinc destituti, oppressi inde, minus mirum quod omnia refrigeant apud ipsos & dilabantur. Pontificii haud segniter huic negotio incumbunt, ut eos ad se pelliciant, eorumque ad se accessu Ecclesiæ suæ amplitudinem distendant, commendentque. Neque etiam fraudibus in hoc parcunt, dum vera desunt, ut Orientalium ad se Legationes miras magnasque fingant & mentiantur: præsertim ut nobis scilicet hæreticis illa objiciant, quasi aliunde tantundem illis accederet, ac nos illis auferimus & nocemus. Vnde magnâ pompâ introductus in Concilium Tridentinum Chaldæorum Legatus Abdiesus: in cujus narratione Patres varia notassent absurda, nisi totum negotium protinus suppressum, consilio atque astutiâ Lusitanorum Præsulum, fuisset. Et ut fallere alios illo excogitato artificio Romani solent, conducto forte qui se mentiatur regionum longissimè sitarum legatum accedere, præstiturum obedientiam sedi Romanæ, ubi falsus facile deprehenditur Legatus, falsum quod aliorum nomine veniat, aut integrarum nationum, fidem subjectionemque Romanae ecclesiae amplectentium, ita nec mirum, nec novum, decipi aliquando & ipsos ab ejusmodi circumcellionibus, qui tali accupio illorum vanam ambitionem ludere, & magna mercede sua ipsis mendacia venditare sciunt. Quod factum inter alia tempore Clementis VIII. quando magnifica Ecclesiae Alexandrinae ad Romanum Pontificem venire misa legatio, a Gabriele Patriarcha scilicet, ut Ægypti & Æthiopes primatum ac fidem Romanae Ecclesiae agnoscerent: magnaq; pompa a Legatis facta fidei confessionis quae immensum quantum deprædicat Caesar Baronius in Appendice Tomi VI. nobisque superbe insultans magno effert encomio: at deprehensa postea (quod Anastasia tum nescivit: sed unde cum pudore post discere potuit, quam vana plerumque ejus contra illos, quos haereticos & Novatores criminatur, sit gloriatio, praesertim ex consensu vel concordia Orientalium secum) omnia falsa esse & confiteta a mendaci quodam Bartone. Sic Thomas a Iesu Carmelita Monachus, lib. VII. de convers. Gent. cap. VI. pag. 364. (qui make Legationem a Patriarcha Marco adornatam ait, quum a Gabriele Patriarcha institua fuerit, at qui se, quemadmodum Alexandrini omnes, S. Marci Evangelistae scribebat successorem): summum Ecclesiae caput universumque Pastorem agnoscebant, ut late in fine 6. Tomi Cardinalis Baron. scribit: re tamen postea diligentius examinata cujusdam Bartonis impostoris fuisse mendacium ac figmentum apparuit. Hoc lemma fastuosae Cardinalis gloriationi adjiciendum fuerat. Idem Thuanus indicat, Histor. lib. CXIV. ad a. CIↃ IↃ XCV.
units.tr: Rom. that their people should be sanctified by priestly hands through the divine and immaculate mysteries, unless they first renounce the Latin institutions and customs, and are instructed according to the canons and brought into agreement with the orthodox. The Greeks agree and can agree with us in many matters. Those obstacles which the Romans raise against them do not exist among us, for we also oppose the Roman papacy, purgatory fire, and other things which they do not tolerate. We also hold to communion under both kinds of the Lord's Supper, to the marriage of ecclesiastics, to the use of the vernacular in worship, and to many other things in which their doctrine and practice agree with ours. It has been shown by many writers that there is agreement between our churches and the Eastern churches on most of the principal articles. Today many defects and errors flourish in those churches, but many of them are not universal among all, nor so ancient that they would hold on to them stubbornly if liberty from external tyranny and a more correct and fuller instruction came to them from elsewhere. Now that they are deprived of help here and oppressed there, it is less surprising that everything among them grows cold and falls apart. The Papists apply themselves without sloth to this business, so as to entice them to themselves and to puff up and commend the greatness of their church through their coming over to it. Nor do they spare deceits in this, when true reports are lacking; they invent and lie about grand and splendid embassies from the Easterners to themselves, chiefly so that they can throw these things in our faces, as though they gained as much from elsewhere as we take from them and harm them. Hence the Chaldean envoy Abdiesus was introduced with great pomp into the Council of Trent; in his account the Fathers would have noted various absurdities, had not the whole business been quickly suppressed by the counsel and cunning of the Portuguese prelates. And just as the Romans are accustomed to deceive others by this contrived trick, by hiring someone to pretend that he is an envoy from very distant regions, who will render obedience to the Roman see, and the envoy is easily found out to be false, so it is neither surprising nor new that they themselves are sometimes deceived by such vagabond hangers-on, who know how to play upon their vain ambition and sell lies to them for a great price. This happened, among other times, in the time of Clement VIII, when a splendid embassy was sent to the Roman Pontiff from the church of Alexandria, namely from the patriarch Gabriel, so that Egypt and Ethiopia would acknowledge the primacy and faith of the Roman Church. With great pomp the envoys made a profession of faith, which Caesar Baronius immensely extols in the Appendix to Volume VI, and he proudly insults us and praises it with great eulogy. But it was afterwards discovered (which Anastasius did not know at the time, but he could later learn with shame how empty is so often his boasting against those whom he accuses of being heretics and innovators, especially given the agreement and concord of the Easterners with them) that everything was false and had been fabricated by a certain liar, Barton. So Thomas a Jesu, the Carmelite monk, book VII, On the Conversion of the Gentiles, chapter VI, page 364, (who says that the embassy was arranged by the patriarch Marcus, although it was set up by the patriarch Gabriel, who, like all the Alexandrians, wrote that he was the successor of St Mark the Evangelist) says: they acknowledged the supreme head of the Church and the universal Shepherd, as Cardinal Baronius writes at length at the end of the sixth volume; yet when the matter was afterwards examined more carefully, it appeared to be the lie and fabrication of a certain impostor, Barton. This label ought to have been attached to the boastful Cardinal's glorying. Thuanus also points this out, Histor., book CXIV, at the year 1595.

units.la: Ad nos autem quod spectat, existimo omnino majorem curam impendendam esse Orientalibus, eorumque Ecclesiis, plusque opis nostrae & auxilii, quam hactenus solet. Oportet magis constare nobis & nota exploranque esse istarum ecclesiarum negotia, statum ac res: tam quoque juvare illos; & qua civilem, qua ecclesiasticam & spiritualem iis offerre operam. Nimium certe ab aliis Ecclesiis & longius distinctis avulsos nos gerimus atque alienos: & vix aliquid certi scimus de praesenti illarum statu. Quod contra communionem Sanctorum videtur, ubi nempe major haberi potest ac debet; & praeter disciplinam Ecclesiarum. Quanto esset melius, quam nobis, quamque illis utilius & suavius, communionem habere magis intimam frequentemque, & commercium inter nos existere artius & solidum ad mutuam in fide & charitate aedificationem, atque consolationem! Tale inter Ecclesias Orientis & Occidentis vinculum fuit Apostolorum aevo, diuque in Ecclesia mansit per multa saecula; nihilque ad Ecclesiam aliquam destruendam efficacius esse, quam si a reliquo corpore nimis temere aut deseratur, aut recedat sponte, vel quoquo pacto divellatur, observatum plurimis exemplis fuit. Hoc Diabolus negotium sumit, ut dirimat animos, & Ecclesias scindat: contra divini spiritus opus est & argumentum, tenere συνδέσμου unionis & communionis sacrae inviolabile. Aut quid tantae difficultatis esset, vel quotannis, vel qua alia occasione, si non per Legatos, Apocrisiarios olim dictos, Ecclesiarum aut Synodorum mutuos; per litteras, quales encyclicae olim fuerunt, vel communicatorias, & formatas, ea quae pacis & aedificationis curare ac promovere ad invicem? de quo Optatus Milevitanus dixit, lib. II. Ecclesias per totum orbem commercio formatarum in una communionis societate potuisse concordare. Sed de hoc alias dicendi uberior erit locus. Certum est, quod cum Europaeis propius conjungi orientales amant: deinde, quod cum nullis in Europa Ecclesiis in consensum melius reduci possunt, ac cum nostris, modo in nonnullis rectius instruantur. Ostendunt hoc ipsorum cum Nostris crebrae tractationes. Constantinop. Eccles. epistola ad
units.tr: As for us, I think that far greater care must be devoted to the Easterners and their churches, and more help and assistance must be given than has been customary until now. We ought to know more of these churches' affairs, condition and circumstances, and to explore them more thoroughly; and we should help them both in civil matters and in ecclesiastical and spiritual ones. Certainly we act as if we were cut off and estranged from other churches, and distant from them, and we scarcely know anything certain about their present state. This seems contrary to the communion of the saints, where indeed a greater communion can and should be had, and beyond the discipline of the churches. How much better it would be, and how much more useful and pleasant both for us and for them, to have a closer and more frequent communion, and a firmer and more solid intercourse between us, for mutual edification and comfort in faith and charity! Such a bond existed between the churches of East and West in the age of the Apostles, and it remained in the Church for many centuries; and it has been observed by many examples that nothing is more effective for destroying a church than when it is either too rashly deserted by the rest of the body, or withdraws of its own accord, or is torn away in any way. This is the work the Devil undertakes, to divide minds and split churches; but it is the work and mark of the divine Spirit to hold fast the bond [συνδέσμου] of union and sacred communion inviolable. Or what great difficulty would there be, either yearly or on some other occasion, in caring for and promoting peace and edification among one another, if not through envoys, formerly called apocrisiarii, of the churches or synods, then through letters, such as the encyclical letters once were, or letters of communion, and formal ones? Concerning this Optatus of Milevis said, in book II, that churches throughout the whole world could agree in one fellowship of communion by the exchange of formal letters. But there will be a fuller opportunity to speak of this elsewhere. It is certain that the Eastern peoples love to be joined more closely to the Europeans; and further, that they can be brought into agreement with no churches in Europe better than with ours, provided that they are instructed more correctly in some matters. Their frequent dealings with ours show this.

units.la: Bohæmos scripta, biennio ante captam urbem, die xviii. Ianuar. anno MCCCCL. ex bibliotheca Pragensi Carolina primò edita in lucem, inde variis in scriptis exhibita ac memorata, ad unionem secum inennndam Bohæmos, qui Romanorum innovationibus resistebant, id est, fratres Hussitas jam tum exhortabantur: certiores facti sumus, ut nullis attentatis innovationibus ad-versus Ecclesiam Christi per nonnullos factis, sed in fundamento fidei substructi estis, quae nobis tradita est à nostro Domino, suisque discipulis; quare decrevit illico hanc sacrosanctam Ecclesiam ad vos scribere, & ad unionem pariter secum adhortari, haud secundum illam Florentiae unionem simulatam, à recto utque consilio abalienatam, quae direpta à veritate appellanda esset. Quamobrem illam minimè admittimus, imò prorsus annihilavimus: at secundum immobilem & immutabile decretum, in quo solo verè ac tutò manere possumus. Nec ambigis Christi Ecclesia ex his, quae de vobis laeta ac accepit, ut dictum est, quod, cum equidem periculosis Romae innovationibus obstare censuistis, concordes huic per omnia eritis, mediante adeò sacra scriptura vero judice: ex dubium ante de vobis famam habebamus, vos quasi haud Romanis innovationibus resistere solere. Itaque dilectissimi fratres atque filii, si sic est, ut audimus & speramus, mature pariter nobiscum unionem. Fratres autem Bohæmos valde sollicitè ac diligenter per multas terræ regiones, in Occidente non solùm, sed & in Oriente, apud Græcos quoque investigasse coetus fidelium secum Papam reclamantium, scimus ex illorum historiâ edità à Camerario; & Historia Ecclesiastica Sclavonicorum. Forte nimiâ sollicitudine illos quæsiverunt, quoad hunc finem, ut ab illis ordinatos reciperent ministros. Nec defuere Græci tempore Reformationis quoque rebus nostris, quin & suis, atque V Wittembergam Patriarcha Constantinopolitanus Iosephus misit Ecclesiæ suæ diaconum Demetrium, qui in res Reformatorum, & doctrinam Ecclesiasque inquireret, deinde referret ad suos. Hic ubi per semestre V Vittembergæ commoratus fuisset, ad suos reversus a. MDLXIX, Græcum Consessionis Augustanæ exemplar, à Melanthone conscriptum, sub nomine Pauli Dolscii, ad Patriarcham suum retulit; de quo in quâdam ad Bordingum epistolâ Melanthon: mitto tibi interpretationem Græcam confessionis, sine meo consilio editam. Probo tamen phrasin, ac misi Constantinopolin per virum doctum, qui ibi Diaconi officio fungitur, & tota æstate noster hospes fuit, ac narravit, multas adhuc ecclesias in Asia & in Thracia & vicinis regionibus esse; sed paulatim propter servitutis ærumnas diminui frequentiam. Epistola illa Melanthonis edita Basileæ a. MDLXVI. cum Poëmatibus &c. Græcis Mart. Crusii.
units.tr: A letter of the Church of Constantinople written to the Bohemians, two years before the capture of the city, on the 18th of January 1450, first published from the Carolina library at Prague, and afterwards exhibited and mentioned in various writings, urged the Bohemians, who resisted the innovations of the Romans, that is, the Hussite brethren, already at that time, to form a union with them: We have been informed that you are not moved by any attempted innovations against the Church of Christ made by some, but are founded on the foundation of faith which was handed down to us by our Lord and his disciples. Therefore this holy Church has resolved to write to you at once, and likewise to urge you to union with her; not according to that pretended union of Florence, which has been estranged from right and sound counsel and which ought to be called torn away from the truth. Therefore we do not admit it at all, indeed we have utterly annulled it; but we hold to the unmoving and unchangeable decree, in which alone we can truly and safely remain. Nor do you doubt that the Church of Christ, from what has been reported to her about you with joy, as has been said, that since you have judged that the dangerous innovations of Rome should be opposed, you will be in agreement with her in everything, indeed through holy Scripture as the true judge. Before this we had a doubtful report about you, that you were not accustomed to resist the innovations of Rome. Therefore, most beloved brothers and sons, if it is so, as we hear and hope, be quick to join union with us. We know from the history of Camerarius, and from the Ecclesiastical History of the Slavonians, that the Bohemian brethren very anxiously and diligently sought out, in many regions of the earth, not only in the West but also in the East, among the Greeks too, assemblies of the faithful who protested against the Pope with them. Perhaps they sought these with excessive anxiety, for this purpose, so that they might receive ministers ordained by them. Nor were the Greeks lacking in the time of the Reformation, both to our affairs and to their own; and Joseph, patriarch of Constantinople, sent to Wittenberg his deacon Demetrius, who was to inquire into the affairs of the Reformers, their doctrine and churches, and then report back to his own people. When he had stayed at Wittenberg for six months, he returned to his own people in 1569, and brought back to his patriarch a Greek copy of the Augsburg Confession, written by Melanchthon under the name of Paul Dolscius. Concerning this, Melanchthon wrote in a letter to Bording: I send you a Greek translation of the Confession, published without my counsel. Yet I approve the phrasing, and I sent it to Constantinople through a learned man who holds the office of deacon there, and who was our guest the whole summer; and he reported that there are still many churches in Asia and in Thrace and the neighbouring regions, but that their number is gradually diminishing because of the hardships of slavery. That letter of Melanchthon was published at Basel in 1566, with the Greek poems etc. of Martin Crusius.

units.la: Sequutus fuit in Patriarchatum Ieremias, vir juxta doctus ac humanus, quocum Tubingensibus (ὑποδιακόνοις[?] Stephano Gerlachio, & Martino Crusio) ab a. MDLXXV. ad a. MDLXXXI. commercium litterarum, & epistolaris concertatio fuit super nonnullis fidei articulis, Confessione Augustanâ comprehensis, quam Græcam Tubingenses miserant Patriarchæ. Omniaque Græcè & Latinè ab illis edita V Vittembergæ, anno MDLXXXIV. vindicata à criminationibus Stanislai Socolovii, qui Patriarchæ Responsum ad missam ei Augustanam Confessionem, quasi Censuram contra Lutheranos, ediderat biennio ante, acerbissimis annotationibus instructam. De quo videri etiam potest Thuanus, Histor. lib. lxxiii. ad a. MDLXXXI. Et quamvis de gravissimis inter se disputarint, Patriarcha tamen semper unionem atque concordiam urgere haud destitit, gratulatusque in secundo Responso fuit, statim ab initio, quod doctrina Ecclesiarum in adeo multis inter se concordet. Atque Iohannes Zygomalas, in litteris ad Crusium, anno MDLXXVI. die xv. Maji: perspicuum tibi & omnibus futurum est, quod in continuis & causam fidei præcipuè continentibus articulis consentiamus. Quæ autem videntur consensum inter vos & nos impedire, talia sunt, si velit quis, ut facile ea corrigere possit, &c. Gaudium enim in cœlo & super terram erit, si cubs in unitatem utraque ecclesia, & idem sentientes & simul vivemus, in omni concordia & pace secundum Deum, & in sincera caritatis vinculo. Ægre etiam inter alia ferebat Zaga zabo Abyssinorum in Lusitaniam Legatus, ad Iohannem III. Portugalliæ Regem, a. cIↄ Iↄ xxxiv. exponens Æthiopum suorum fidem, quod ob discrepantiam nonnullam in fide ac moribus infensos adeo se præberent Orientalibus alienigenis Europæi: Quamobrem indignum est, peregrinos Christianos tam acriter & hostiliter reprehendi, ut ego de hac re, & de aliis, quæ minime ad veram fidem spectabant, reprehensus fuit: Sed multo consultius erit, huiusmodi Christianos homines, sive Græcos, sive Armenios, sive Æthiopes, sive ex quavis septem Christianarum Ecclesiarum, in charitate & Christi amplexibus sustinere, eos sine contumeliis permittere inter alios fratres Christianos vivere & versari, quoniam omnes sicut baptismi sumus, & de vera fide unanimiter sentimus. Nec est causa, cur tam acriter de ceremoniis disceptetur, nisi ut unusquisque suas observet, sine odio & infestatione aliorum, nec commercii Ecclesiæ ob id excludendus est, si peregrè in alienis provinciis domesticos ritus observet &c. Ac ne quis malesanus nos sugillet, quod illa quæ Lutheranis oblata, nobis applicamus, sciat, præter alia quæ ad hoc dici possunt, ad Generalem Synodum Torunensem in Polonia, a. cIↄ Iↄ xcv. in quâ syncretismus Reformatorum cum Lutheranis ante quindecim annos Sendomiriæ initus confirmabatur, legationem ab Ecclesiâ Græca venisse, pro feriendâ secum pace ac concordiâ: uti hâc de re in actis Synodi illius perscriptum: Præterea multæ insignes legationes hinc inde ad eandem Synodum missæ, cum literis & commendatione fraterni amoris, nec non promtitudinis animi in recipiendis & amplectendis iis omnibus, quæ in hâc Generali Synodo ex Verbo Dei, juxta priorum Synodorum Decreta concordibus suffragiis sancita esset[?]. sent. Inter quas altera erat ab Illustr. Domino Constantino Duce ab Ostrog. Palatino Cijoviensi, Græcæ Religioni addicto, officia amicitiæ Ecclesiis Evangelicis offerente, & cum iis nomine suo ac suorum conjunctionem in verâ Religione expetente, satis honorificè missa, & per Legatum præsentem Dominum Casparum Lusz[?]kowium expedita. Hoc seculo a.MDCXVI. ad Cantuariensem in Anglia Archiepiscopum Georgium Abbotum scripsit Cyrillus, Patriarcha Alexandrinus, & alumnum misit Græcum, presbyterum, ut in religione plenius institueretur, in Academia Oxoniensi. In litteris suis, quas ita subscripsit, Cyrillus Dei gratiâ Papa, & Patriarcha magnæ urbis Alexandriæ, & Index œcumenicus, gratulatur suis Ecclesiis pacem contingere à Turcâ, Christiani nominis inimico infensissimo, verùm à Papistis dicti haud exiguum ipsis metum esse, à canibus & operariis subdolis, hypocritis dicto, quibus solenne est, aliud clausum habere in pectore, aliud promptum in lingua; qui Deum ipsum projecta audacia impetere haud erubescunt, dummodo Romani pontificis tyrannidi quoque modo velificentur: hi emissarii terrorem mirum in modum nobis incutiunt, nostraque imponunt simplicitati, cui mancipanda variis admovent machinas, maxime freti eruditionis fuco, & spinosarum disputationum aculeis, cum nos inter eâ eruditorum penuriâ laboremus, qui cum sciolis istis æquo marte congrediantur. Etenim propter peccata nostra desperabiles facti sumus præ omnibus gentibus, & cum imperii quoque liberales amisimus. Quo major incumbit cura & sollicitudo, providere ut quovis modo, sive per nostrum ad ipsos, sive ipsorum ad nos accessum, cum in aliis doctrinis, tum præcipuè in religione uberius instruantur, & illud à nobis referant suorum erga nos olim beneficiorum fructum (quippe ab illis nos studia, & religionem acceperimus), ut nostra juventur doctrinâ & doctoribus. Ulterius post Patriarchiam Jeremiam, cum Nostris convenit Meletius, Alexandrinus primùm, tum Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha, qui quando impostores aliqui Graeci a. cIↄ Iↄ xcv. sub nomine Patriarchae Alexandrini Gabrielis, Confessionem Romae, ad placitum Papae, ediderint, quo tempore Meletius, non Gabriel aliquis Patriarcham tenuit, audito ille negotio valde infremuit tale quid de Alexandrinis, se inscio, spargi, qui ab illiusmodi Confessione, vel subjectione Papae Romano facienda erat alienissimus. Quae attingit Thuanus, lib. cxiv. & plenius ex literis Junioris Douzae, ad Janum Douzam patrem, constant. Quamque in nostras Ecclesias, non Pontificias, propensus fuerit Meletius, vir in linguis, Hebraeā, Syrā, Arabicā, & Theologicā cognitione doctissimus, ostendit tum in litteris ad Hypatium Pociey, Ruthenae primatem, a. cIↄ Iↄ xcix. tum Sigismundum III. Poloniae Regem, scriptis a. cIↄ Iↄ c. quando adhuc erat Patriarcha Alexandriae, super negotio unionis cum Romanā Ecclesiā initae, à Russo-Graecis aliquibus regno Poloniae subditis, invitis quamvis & reclamantibus aliis: Perspiceret Majestas Tua, Nos, cum Majoribus nostris, non ignorare (quem precaris et agnoscamus) Romanum Pontificem, (id quod sese autumat) Pontificem sIlicet Romanum, veluti & Constantinopolitanum Pontificem, Pontificem Constantinopolitanum, cæterosque Apostolicarum Sedium Pontifices, caterarumque certarumque sedium Apostolicarum Pontifices. Qui non unus omnium, sed inter omnes & ipsum, &c. Unum Universale Caput, quod sit D. N. Iesus Christus est, alius esse non potest, nisi biceps aliquod sit corpus, aut potius monstrum corporis. Perspiceres, Rex Serenissime, (ut interim de Concilio illo Florentino, veluti de re silentio digna, taceam) non Nos, è Patriâ, tum Orientalium tum Occidentalium dogmatibus, traditionibusque, quae per septem Universalia Concilia Nobis consignarunt, atque obsignarunt, egressos. Illos egressos, qui novitatibus in dies delectantur. Quibus iisdem litteris Cyrillum commendat Regi, de quo statim dicturi sumus, exarchum tum temporis Alexandrinum: A Tua vero Clementiā, hoc quidem tempore peti. petimus, ut Reverendum Patrem Cyrillum Lucari, Exarchum hujus Apostolicæ Sedis, & Filium nostrum favore Regio dignetur, hominem & probitate & eruditione Regio favore dignissimum. Sub hoc Meletio conventus fuit habitus Vilnæ Polonorum anno MDXCIX. die xv. Maji, inter Euangelicos, id est, juxta Consensum Sendomiriensem, Augustanos, Bohæmos, Reformatos unà, & Græcos vel Russos non unitos (duum quippe generum Russi sunt, alii unionem cum Romanis sequuntur; horrent eam alii: de quibus Auctor Histor. Eccles. Slavon. lib. iv.) & primo politica confœderatio pro mutuâ adversus quascunque, præsertim Romanensium, oppressiones, facta, tum ad ecclesiasticam quoque progressum, scriptumque eâ super re ad Constantinopolitanum Patriarcham, & Meletium, à Nostris, hanc in formam: Nobis cum primis in votis est, ut cum iis quoque coalescamus, qui à Nobis remotiores, Pontifici Romano jam dudum nuntio remisso, pariori doctrinæ favent; & licet locis disjunctis, pietatis professione & religione ad nos propius accedunt. Qualem quidem semper putavimus esse Ecclesiam Orientalem in Græciâ, & inter ejusdem nobiscum linguæ homines in Moscoviâ, in Russiâ & Lituaniâ, cui non sine insigni laude R. P. V. tempestate nostrâ præesse scimus. Quamobrem etiam hoc summopere expetimus, ut datâ occasione, cum R. P. V. de Religionis negotio agamus, & ratio-nem, quâ cætus Nostri Orthodoxi Vestris Ecclesiis, per sanctam in Jesu Christo consensionem uniri, & arctiore quodam charitatis vinculo in posterum conglutinari possent, colla-tis sententiis ineamus. Unde etiam cum ad Nos crebris nun-tiis rumor is delatus esset, quosdam harum Regionum Antistites Vestrates, qui antea solíti sunt in omnibus suffragiis R. P. V. accedere, eique obedire, observantiæ jugo excusso, Pontifici Romano, itinere ad ipsum sat longinquo suscepto, obedientiam, fidelitatem, & subjectionem omnem, idque nomine omnium Ecclesiarum Græcarum Religionem in Polonia Regno profitentium, (sed falso, utpote insciis plerif-que.
units.tr: Jeremiah succeeded to the Patriarchate, a man learned and courteous in equal measure. With him the Tübingen scholars (to the subdeacons [ὑποδιακόνοις?], Stephen Gerlach and Martin Crusius) carried on a correspondence from 1575 to 1581, and an exchange of letters on several articles of faith contained in the Augsburg Confession, which the Tübingen men had sent to the Patriarch in Greek. All of it was published in Greek and Latin at Wittenberg in 1584, and defended against the charges of Stanislaus Socolovius, who two years earlier had published, with very bitter annotations, the Patriarch's reply to the Augsburg Confession sent to him, which he presented as a censure of the Lutherans. On this matter Thuanus may also be consulted, Histor. book 73, under the year 1581. Although they disputed sharply on the gravest points, the Patriarch nevertheless never ceased to press for union and concord, and in his second reply he rejoiced, right at the outset, that the teaching of the Churches agreed so closely. John Zygomalas, in a letter to Crusius dated 15 May 1576, wrote: It will be plain to you and to all that we agree in the continuous articles which chiefly contain the cause of faith. Those matters which seem to hinder agreement between you and us are such that anyone who wishes can easily correct them, etc. For there will be joy in heaven and upon earth if both Churches come into unity, think the same, and live together in all concord and peace according to God, and in the sincere bond of love. The envoy of the Abyssinians, Zagazabo, also took it hard, among other things, when he addressed John III, King of Portugal, in 1534 and set out the faith of his Ethiopians: because of some difference in faith and morals, Europeans showed themselves so hostile to Eastern foreigners. It is therefore unworthy that Christian strangers be rebuked so bitterly and hostilely, as I was rebuked over this matter and over others which did not touch the true faith at all. Much more advisable will it be to bear with such Christians, whether Greeks, Armenians, Ethiopians, or from any of the seven Christian Churches, in charity and in the embrace of Christ, to allow them to live and move among other Christian brothers without insult, since we are all baptised and think unanimously about the true faith. Nor is there any reason why ceremonies should be disputed so bitterly, except that each may keep his own without hatred and harassment of others. Nor should anyone be shut out of fellowship of the Church on that account if, abroad in foreign provinces, he keeps the rites of his homeland, etc. And lest some madman sneer at us that we apply to ourselves what was offered to the Lutherans, let him know that, besides other things that can be said to this, a legation came from the Greek Church to the General Synod of Thorn in Poland in 1595, the synod in which the syncretism of the Reformed with the Lutherans, entered into at Sandomierz fifteen years before, was confirmed, seeking peace and concord with them. This is recorded in the acts of that synod. Besides, many distinguished legations were sent from various quarters to the same synod, with letters and commendation of brotherly love, and also of readiness to receive and embrace all those things which, from the Word of God and in accordance with the decrees of earlier synods, were to be sanctioned in this General Synod by common vote. Among these there was another, sent quite honourably by the Illustrious Lord Constantine, Duke of Ostrog, Palatine of Kiev, who was devoted to the Greek religion, offering the offices of friendship to the Evangelical Churches, and in his own name and that of his people seeking union with them in the true religion. It was carried out through the present envoy, Lord Caspar Luszkowski. In this century, in 1616, Cyril, Patriarch of Alexandria, wrote to George Abbot, Archbishop of Canterbury in England, and sent a Greek presbyter as a pupil, that he might be more fully instructed in religion at the University of Oxford. In his letter, which he subscribed thus, Cyril, by the grace of God Pope and Patriarch of the great city of Alexandria, and Ecumenical Judge, he rejoices that peace has come to his Churches from the Turk, the most bitter enemy of the Christian name; but that the Papists, so called, cause them no small fear. They are dogs and deceitful workers, hypocrites, whose habit it is to have one thing shut up in the breast and another ready on the tongue; who are not ashamed to assail God himself with shameless boldness, provided they somehow fawn on the tyranny of the Roman pontiff. These emissaries strike us with a wonderful terror and impose upon our simplicity, to which they apply various machines to enslave us, relying chiefly on the veneer of learning and on the prickly stings of contentious disputes, since we labour under such a scarcity of learned men that we cannot contend on equal terms with those smatterers. For on account of our sins we have become despised beyond all nations, and we have also lost our liberal rule. All the greater, therefore, is the care and concern that presses upon us to provide, in whatever way, whether by our going to them or their coming to us, that they be more fully instructed, both in other doctrines and especially in religion, and that they may bring back to us the fruit of past benefits from us to them (for indeed from them we received our learning and our religion), so that our teaching and our teachers may be helped. Afterwards, following the Patriarch Jeremiah, Meletius, first Patriarch of Alexandria and then of Constantinople, came together with ours. When certain impostors among the Greeks, in 1595, under the name of the Alexandrian Patriarch Gabriel, published at Rome a Confession at the pleasure of the Pope, at a time when Meletius, not some Gabriel, held the Patriarchate, he, having heard of the matter, fumed greatly that anything of the kind was being spread about the Alexandrians without his knowledge, since he was utterly opposed to such a Confession or to submission to the Roman Pope. Thuanus touches on these things in book 114, and they are set out more fully in the letters of the younger Douza to his father Janus Douza. How inclined Meletius was toward our Churches, and not toward the Papist ones, he showed, a man most learned in languages, Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, and in theological knowledge, both in his letter to Hypatius Pociej, Primate of Ruthenia, in 1599, and in his letter to Sigismund III, King of Poland, written in 1600 while he was still Patriarch of Alexandria, concerning the union entered into with the Roman Church by some Russo-Greeks subject to the kingdom of Poland, though others protested and objected: Let Your Majesty understand that we, together with our forefathers, are not ignorant (whom you ask, and whom we acknowledge) that the Roman Pontiff, as he himself claims, is indeed the Roman Pontiff, just as the Constantinopolitan Pontiff is the Constantinopolitan Pontiff, and the other Pontiffs of the Apostolic Sees and of the other certain Apostolic Sees. These are not one over all, but among all and with him himself, etc. There is one universal Head, who is our Lord Jesus Christ; there cannot be another, unless the body were two-headed, or rather a monstrous body. Your Majesty would see, most Serene King (to keep silent for the moment about that Council of Florence, as a matter unworthy of mention), that we have not departed from our homeland, from the doctrines and traditions of both the Eastern and the Western Church, which through the seven Ecumenical Councils have been delivered to us and sealed for us. They departed, those who delight daily in novelties. In the same letter he commends to the King Cyril, then Exarch of Alexandria, of whom we are about to speak at once: From Your Clemency, however, we ask at this time that Your Majesty deign to show royal favour to the Reverend Father Cyril Lucaris, Exarch of this Apostolic See and our son, a man most worthy of royal favour both for his uprightness and his learning. Under this Meletius a conference was held at Vilnius in Poland on 15 May 1599, among the Evangelicals, that is, according to the Consensus of Sandomierz, the Augustana, the Bohemians, and the Reformed together, and the Greeks or non-united Russians (for there are two kinds of Russians: some follow union with the Romans, others shun it; on these see the author of the Histor. Eccles. Slavon. book 4). First a political confederation was made for mutual defence against all oppressions, especially those of the Romanists, and then also for progress in ecclesiastical matters. Our men wrote on this subject to the Constantinopolitan Patriarch and to Meletius in this form: Our chief wish is that we also may unite with those who, though more remote from us, having long since sent back the Roman Pontiff, favour a purer teaching, and though separated in place, draw nearer to us in profession of piety and religion. Such indeed we have always thought the Eastern Church to be, in Greece, and among those of our own language in Muscovy, Russia, and Lithuania, over which we know Your Reverence presides, not without distinguished praise in our time. Therefore we also very earnestly desire that, when an occasion is given, we may discuss matters of religion with Your Reverence, and enter upon a comparison of opinions by which the assemblies of our Orthodox could be united with your Churches through holy agreement in Jesus Christ, and be bound together in a closer bond of charity in future. Hence also, since a rumour had been reported to us by frequent messages that some of your bishops of these regions, who had formerly been accustomed to agree with Your Reverence in all votes and to obey him, had shaken off the yoke of reverence, and, having undertaken a journey to the Roman Pontiff a long way off, had promised obedience, fidelity, and every subjection to him, in the name of all the Greek Churches professing the religion in the kingdom of Poland (but falsely, since most people were ignorant and many contradicted and were unwilling), we have indeed grieved that they, as we ought, have fallen away from the former doctrine to the worst errors and the battles of Antichrist, and have bound themselves to him.

units.la: Text continues on the next page. que, multis contradicentibus & invitis) promisisse, se-que ei addixisse, doluimus sanè, pro eo, ac debuimus, ipsos à priori doctrinâ, ad pessimos errores, & pugnas Antichristi defecisse. Quia verò, tum professio nostra Christiana, tum pericula undique imminentia Nobis suadent, ut cum Vestris Ecclesiis Graecis, quarum non exiguum numerum Ore Lituanica & Ruthenica continent, pacem foveamus & concordiam colamus: de eo imprimis R. P. V. cum Reverendissimo Patriarcha Alexandria compellandum, & ab eo consilium pianumque operam petendam existimavimus: ut si quâ ratione fieri possit, sublatis iis quae ab Evangelica veritate abhorrere videantur, Deo uno & Trino, sub uno Capite Christo, in fidei unitate & sacrâ fraternâ charitate serviamus. Rescripsit Patriarcha per Cyrillum suum: qui quia minus gratum responsum Regi, & Pontificiis intellexerat, id nec reddidit nec publicavit: uti ipse testatus est in epistolâ, relictâ apud Archiepiscopum Leopoliensem, quam in Concionibus suis Miscellaneis refert Iesuita Scarga. Atque ita hoc opus discedentibus nostris Vilnae die v. Iunii, intermissum.
units.tr: Text continues on the next page. We were indeed grieved, as we ought to have been, that they had fallen away from the former doctrine into the worst errors and the battles of Antichrist. But since both our Christian profession and the dangers threatening us on every side urge us to cherish peace and concord with your Greek churches, of which a not inconsiderable number use the Lithuanian and Ruthenian tongues, we judged that this matter should be laid before the most reverend Patriarch of Alexandria, and his counsel and effort sought, so that, if it could in any way be done, with whatever is clearly repugnant to the Gospel truth removed, we might serve the one triune God, under the one Head Christ, in unity of faith and holy brotherly love. The Patriarch replied through his Cyril, but since Cyril understood that the reply was less welcome to the King and the Papists, he neither delivered nor published it, as he himself attested in a letter left with the Archbishop of Lviv, which the Jesuit Scarga cites in his Miscellaneous Sermons. And so this work was interrupted when our men left Vilnius on the fifth day of June.

units.la: Cyrillus autem Lucaris, qui primum Rector Scholae Ruthenorum Ostrogensis, inque ea Linguae Graecae Professor, postea exarchus & Archimandrita, tandem Patriarcha Constantinopol., consensum cum nostris Ecclesiis, earumque doctrina plenissimè perfecit, edita eleganti Confessione, primum Latinè a. MDCXXXI. tum Graecè quoque, suo & Ecclesiae Orientalis nomine, cum variis in fine Responsionibus, a. MDCXXXI. Quae condemnata quidem à successoribus ejus Cyrillo Berrhoensi, & Parthenio; ab illo a. MDCXXXVIII. ab hoc, a. MDCXLI. at non alium fere in finem, quam ut hinc certius constaret, illam Cyrilli Confessionem esse, de quâ nonnulli antea malitiosè, imprudenter alii dubitabant, sedulo id fovent ibus hinc Pontificiis, inde Remonstrantibus, ideo quod Cyrillus in nostram incidisset sententiam de Dei Praedestinatione, in quem finem Grotius edi curavit famosas & latrocinales contra Cyrillum, tum Berrhoënsis, tum Parthenii Synodos: qui ipsi Pseudo-Patriarchæ scelerum quoque pœnas, sedibus suis ejecti, postea dederunt: quemadmodum antea Anastasius Pattelarius Cretensis, Cyrilli beneficio factus Metropolita Thessalonicensis, pulso in exilium Cyrillo, sedem vix mensem tenuit, revocato in suum locum Cyrillo, & in eandem insulam Tenedum relegato Pattelario. Atque ita variis primum fractus injuriis, exiliis, & persequutionibus Cyrillus noster, tandem a. cIɔIɔcxxxvııı.infatigabili inimicorum suorum malitiâ, à Iesuitis excitati, ultimum sustinuit verae religionis martyrium, à Turcico Bassâ nefariè strangulatus. Quod ideo facinus omnino partem facere debuit in Appendice mysteriorum Patrum Iesuitarum.
units.tr: Cyril Lucaris, who was first rector of the Ruthenian school at Ostrog and professor of Greek there, and afterwards exarch, archimandrite, and at last Patriarch of Constantinople, fully established agreement with our churches and with their doctrine, by publishing an elegant Confession, first in Latin in 1631, and then also in Greek, in his own name and in the name of the Eastern Church, with various responses at the end, in 1631. These were indeed condemned by his successors Cyril of Berrhoea and Parthenius, the former in 1638 and the latter in 1641; but they did so for almost no other purpose than to make it more certain that this was Cyril's Confession. Some had previously doubted it maliciously or rashly, and the Papists on one side and the Remonstrants on the other eagerly fostered this doubt, because Cyril had come round to our opinion on God's predestination. To this end Grotius had the notorious and robber-like synods against Cyril published, both that of Berrhoea and that of Parthenius. Those men later paid the penalty for their crimes to the pseudo-Patriarch himself, having been ejected from their sees. Just as earlier Anastasius Pattelarius of Crete, made Metropolitan of Thessalonica through Cyril's kindness, held his see scarcely a month after Cyril had been driven into exile, and Cyril was restored to his place while Pattelarius was relegated to the same island of Tenedos. And so our Cyril, first broken by various injuries, exiles and persecutions, and at last by the tireless malice of his enemies, stirred up by the Jesuits, suffered the final martyrdom of the true religion, being wickedly strangled by the Turkish Pasha. This crime ought surely to form a part of the Appendix of the Jesuit Fathers' Mysteries.

units.la: In Tenedo insulâ quum exul degeret, mortem continuò operiens, nec de fide ejus & constantiâ ulli dubitarent, scripsit ad amicum epistolam, quam exhibet Rivetus in libro adversus Silvestrum Petrasanctam cap. xı. Per ciò ho voluto scriver à V.R. è protestarvi che mi siate testimonio se jo morè que jo mora Catholico Orthodoxo nella fede del N.S. Iesù Christo, nella dottrina Evangelica conforme la confessione Belgica, la confessione mia, & le altre d'ello chiese Evangeliche che sono tutti conformi: abhorrisco li errori delli Papisti & le superstitioni delli Greci, provo & abbraccio la dottrina del Dottor meritissimo Giovanni Calvino, & di tutti quelli che sentono con lui. In questo voglio che mi siate testimonio, per che con sincera conscienza così tengo, così professo è confesso, come anco la mia confessione mostra: & recommando à voi questo deposito, caso che morissi, di farne partecipi tutti li fratelli Christiani orthodoxi, è mi recomando alle preghiere di V.R. alli 15. 23. Marzo. Cyrillo Patriarcha di Constantinopoli. Ipsissima sunt Cyrilli nostri verba. Cujus cum Calvino in religionis articulis consensus unicum fuit, quod tantum ei Papistarum, & aliorum conflavit odium: & ob quod Parthenius palam professus fuit se (optimi senis & martyris) Cyrilli doctrinam ferire anathemate, perquam diro & horrendo, in illum non modo, sed & Confessionis ejus Lectores: sunto æterno anathemati obnoxii, & segregati à Patre, Filio, & Spiritu Sancto sine secundum naturam solo Deo; & in hoc futuroque sæculo maledicti, & expertes veniæ, & insolubiles post mortem, & æternæ damnationis participes. Quam vero levis, ingratus, crudelis, improbus homo iste Parthenius fuerit, ostendit in vindicando Cyrillo à contumeliis Remonstrantium Abrah. Heidanus, in Præfat. ad Cassam Dei. Adde Ioh. Henrici Hottingeri Dissert. VIII. Analect. Historico-Theologicorum. Alter sequutus illos Parthenius fuit, qui Cyrilli partes & famam adversus hostes tutatus fuit. Certe optima, atque examussim convenit cum nostra Confessio Cyrilli, pro quâ multum ei, multum Græcis Patriarchæ suum sequentibus, debemus. Unde etiam operis nostri cum Græcis peragendi major apparet, cum necessitate, facilitas. Duo autem præsertim hac in causa accuranda: primum, ut illos in religionis articulis uberius instruamus, deinde nobiscum artius coniungamus. Non hoc absque illo curatum volo: verum ἀληθὲς ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ. Quemadmodum in Colloquio Vilnensi a. cIↄ Iↄ xc ix, nostri dicebant, consessum cum Græcis pari ratione stabiliendum esse, ac cum hominibus Augustanæ Confessionis; quos, etsi in quibusdam discedant à nobis, toleramus tamen & pro fratribus agnoscimus. Illud autem si obtineri contingeret, quantam (bone Deus!) illis Ecclesiis salutem, nostris solamen, & contra hostes omnes robur ac gloriam, cœlo denique ipsi gaudium conciliaret? Quare ut huc tandem consilia ac studia nostra dirigantur, præsens à me instituta de Græcis atque Orientalibus Ecclesiis dissertatio fuit. Nihil enim mihi antiquius, quam compositis apud nos Ecclesiæ rebus, ad exteros & remotos hinc cogitationes operamque que convertere, & pro illis convertendis, juvandis, & nobis propius conciliandis, missis levioribus, istique negotio noxiis saepe contentionibus, laborare. Quod nostri esse officii, & non in nostris solis haerere aut rebus aut disputationibus, semper existimavi. Atque hoc pacto constabit etiam, quam non sit tanta Pontificiae Ecclesiae amplitudo, vel nostrae tenuitas, ac Adversarii putant, Orientalibus Ecclesiis se cum nostris, contra Papales, associantibus.
units.tr: While he was living in exile on the island of Tenedos, expecting death at any moment, and no one doubted his faith and constancy, he wrote a letter to a friend. Rivetus gives it in his book against Silvestro Petrasancta, chapter 11. Therefore I have wanted to write to you, Reverend Sir, and to declare that you may bear witness for me that if I die, I die a Catholic and orthodox Christian in the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the Evangelical doctrine according to the Belgic Confession, my own confession, and the other confessions of the Evangelical churches, which all agree. I abhor the errors of the Papists and the superstitions of the Greeks. I approve and embrace the doctrine of the most worthy teacher John Calvin and of all who think with him. On this point I want you to be my witness, for with a sincere conscience I hold, profess and confess this, as my confession also shows. I commend to you this deposit: if I should die, please make all the orthodox Christian brethren partakers of it. And I commend myself to your prayers. 15/23 March. Cyril, Patriarch of Constantinople. These are the very words of our Cyril. His agreement with Calvin on the articles of religion was the only thing that stirred up the hatred of the Papists and others against him. Because of it, Parthenius openly professed that he would strike the teaching of that excellent old man and martyr with a most dire and dreadful anathema, not only against him but also against the readers of his Confession: Let them be liable to the eternal anathema, and cut off from the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and from God alone according to nature; and let them be cursed in this age and the age to come, without pardon, unable to be loosed after death, and sharers in eternal damnation. How light, ungrateful, cruel and wicked this man Parthenius was, Abraham Heidanus shows in defending Cyril against the insults of the Remonstrants, in his Preface to Casses Dei. Add Johann Heinrich Hottinger, Dissertation VIII, in the Analecta Historico-Theologica. Another Parthenius followed these, who defended Cyril's cause and reputation against his enemies. Certainly the Confession of Cyril is very good and agrees exactly with ours, and for it we owe much to him and to the Greeks who follow their patriarch. Hence the greater ease, along with the need, of carrying on our work with the Greeks also appears. Two things, however, must be attended to in this matter, especially: first, that we instruct them more fully in the articles of religion, and second, that we join them more closely with us. I do not want this done without that, but truth in love [ἀληθὲς ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ]. Just as our men said at the Colloquy of Vilnius in 1599, a fellowship with the Greeks should be established on the same footing as with those of the Augsburg Confession, whom, although they differ from us on some points, we tolerate and acknowledge as brethren. But if that could be obtained, what salvation (good God!) it would bring to those churches, what comfort to ours, what strength and glory against all enemies, and finally what joy to heaven itself! Therefore, that our counsels and efforts may at last be directed to this end, the present dissertation on the Greek and Oriental churches was undertaken by me. For nothing is more important to me than, once the affairs of the Church among us are settled, to turn thoughts and labour to those who are outside and far off, and to work for their conversion and help, and for drawing them closer to us, setting aside lesser matters and contentions that often harm this undertaking. I have always thought this to be our duty, and not to cling only to our own affairs and disputes. In this way it will also be clear how far from true is what our adversaries think: that the Papal Church is so great, or ours so small, when the Eastern churches join with ours against the Papists.

units.la: Quare probo, ut Seminaria apud nos (ne Roma in hoc diutius se extollat) habeantur pro Orientalibus juvandis, in quibus aut nostri homines eo mittendi, aut ab illis huc ad studia ablegati, probe erudiantur, & sic nobis curae esse Ecclesiae Catholicae statum ac communionem, omnibus probemus. Romae & seminaria illorum habent, & inter Cardinales Protectorem Ecclesiarum Orientalium.
units.tr: Therefore I approve that seminaries be maintained among us for the help of the Eastern churches (so that Rome may not boast of this any longer), in which either our own men are to be sent there, or men sent away from them here to study, are to be thoroughly trained; and thus we shall show everyone that we care for the state and communion of the Catholic Church. Rome also has seminaries for them, and among the Cardinals one who is Protector of the Eastern Churches.

units.la: Quod vel solum exemplum ad aemulationem excitare oportebat, & studium nostrum provocare erga illos, quos Romanis infensos, ipsi haud ignorant. Romanis universisque Latinis, insito quodam odio infensissimi sunt, inquit de illis Socolovius, in Praefat. ad P.Gregorium XIII. ante suam Censuram Orientalem, de qua supra loquuti fuimus. Hoc & ipsis Judaeis observatum: Benjamini Tudelensi, in Itinerario, ubi de Constantinopoli: & hic Graecorum Papa est; quia religioni Papae Romani non consentiunt. Huc ergo, uti diximus, flectendi oculi & cura nostra, quo a nobis erudiri & juvari queant, atque ad Ecclesiae communionem postliminio reduci. Huc quilibet quodcunque, pro loco quem tenet, & donis sibi a Deo concessis, potest, conferat oportet: & nos ut ad hoc officium omnes cohortaremur, in praesenti negotio diuscule fuimus versati. Desideramus autem, ut in compendium contraham, ferme ista. I. ut certior uberiorque contingat notitia praesentis status Ecclesiarum Orientalium & Graecarum, sive per literas, sive per exploratores eo missos. II. majorem apud nos curam & studium pro illis juvandis: apud Ecclesias nostras, politias, & Academias. Quae in finem seminaria, quae diximus, fructu haud carerent. III. Institutionem pleniorem uberioremque illis à nobis impartiendam. IV. Tum de propius illis nobiscum ineundis prudens ac sanctum consilium. V. Continuamque cum illis Correspondentiam, seu communionem, aut per epistolas, aut legatos Ecclesiasticos. Nullo autem modo praetereundum nobis studium DD. Ordinum Belgii in hanc rem haud ita pridem demonstratum, quando suis sumptibus N. Testamentum, & Catechismum nostrum curarunt hic à Graecis in vulgarem ipsorum linguam conversi, postquam consensum suum cum doctrinâ & Ecclesiis nostris declarassent, ab a. cIↄ Iↄ c xlv. deinceps. In erudiendis illis disputationi locus erit, eique non rixosae, non asperae, sed quae collationem magis, quam contentionem referat, atque ad compositionem tendat, & conjunctionem. Quomodo Nostri se exposuerunt in Colloquio Vilnen-si: Quod si aliquam evolverint Confessionem, & disputare voluerint, de aliquo articulo, fiat sine; sed quam minissime ac mollissime, in spiritu lenitatis, velitatione quadam amicâ, magis ad intelligendum eorum argumenta, (quae diligenter consignanda, etiam minutissima,) quam ad confun-dendum eos, ut omnes Christo lucrifacere queamus. Dixe-rant initio: Quandoquidem nos Evangelii Graecorum Re-ligionem censemus esse veriorem & propiorem doctrinae Apostolicae, in plerisque articulis, quam Romanam; eosque ita pro Fratribus Christianis reputamus, ut cum eis conversari, in concordiâ & charitate vivere, in iis quae sunt ad communonstrandum viam salutis, juxtâ & in temporibus praesto adesse, injurias communi consilio & auxilio propulsare, & plane cum eis, tanquam cum Fratribus dilectis mirì & foedus pangere juxta Canonem S. Scripturae S. possimus. Querendum est eis. I. Virum & illi ejusdem sint in nos affectus, talemque εὐσχημοσύνην esse bonam, gloria Dei. incremento Ecclesiae ejus, communi societatio, ac pacis adversus hostes inservire intelligant? Et, Virum eam, aeque ac Nos, exceptent atque capiant? Ita dissimili ratione cum his agendum, ac cum aliis. In disputatione permultum stant authoritati Patrum Graecorum, in quorum proinde lectione bene versatum decet esse, qui illos sit aggressurus. Super ardua & contentiosa quaestione de processione Spiritus S. bene hoc etiam Vilnenses proposuerunt: In Articulo, de fide in Spiritum S. possumus acquiescere in eo, quod majores eorum confessi sunt: Spiritum S. procedere a Patre per Filium, & tam a Patre quam a Filio missi & dari; S. S. id palam asserente. Cumque aut de religionis articulis disputandum, aut de ritibus, de his pro re nata agendum, neque eorum a nostris moribus discrepantium catalogum dare multum opus, sufficerit, pro ratione instituti, subnectere praecipuas super doctrina aliorum controversias, quae sunt: I. Num in Christo sint duae personae? Neg. II. An duae in Christo distinctae semper naturae, voluntates, atque operationes? Aff. III. Annon quibuscunque personis Ecclesiasticis concessum sit matrimonium, & quandocunque, sive ante, sive post ordinationem contrahere liceat, seu semel, seu aliquoties? Aff. IV. Num illicitum sit, edere sanguinem aut suffocatum? Neg. V. Num liceat imagines seu picturas, seu fusas vel statuas religiose colere? Neg. VI. Spiritus S. in Deo an procedat a Patre, & Filio? Aff. VII. Num Sancti coelestes ullo modo a nobis invocandi? Neg.
units.tr: This example alone ought to stir us to emulation and provoke our zeal toward those whom, as they themselves well know, are hostile to the Romans. They are most hostile to the Romans and to all Latins, with a certain innate hatred, says Socolovius of them, in the preface to Pope Gregory XIII, before his Eastern Censure, which we discussed above. The Jews too have noted this. Benjamin of Tudela, in his Itinerary, on Constantinople: and here is the Pope of the Greeks, because they do not agree with the religion of the Roman Pope. Therefore, as we have said, our eyes and our care must be turned in this direction, so that they may be taught and helped by us and restored by right of return to communion with the Church. Anyone should contribute whatever he can, according to the place he holds and the gifts God has granted him. In the present matter we have dwelt at some length in order to urge all to this task. To sum up, we desire mainly the following. (1) That a more certain and fuller knowledge of the present state of the Eastern and Greek Churches be obtained, either by letters or by agents sent there. (2) That we show greater care and zeal among our own churches, polities and academies for helping them; to this end the seminaries we have mentioned would not be without benefit. (3) That we impart fuller and richer instruction to them. (4) That there be a prudent and holy plan for entering into closer relations with them. (5) That we keep up a continual correspondence or communion with them, either by letters or by ecclesiastical envoys. Nor must we pass over in silence the zeal recently shown in this matter by the Lords States of Belgium, who, at their own expense, had the New Testament and our Catechism translated here by the Greeks into their vernacular tongue, after they had declared their agreement with our doctrine and Churches, from the year 1645 onward. In instructing them there will be room for disputation, but a disputation that is not quarrelsome or harsh, but one that resembles a conference rather than a contest, and tends toward reconciliation and union. Our men conducted themselves thus at the Colloquy of Vilna: if they unfolded some Confession and wished to dispute about some article, let it be done, but as gently and softly as possible, in a spirit of meekness, with a kind of friendly skirmish, aiming more at understanding their arguments (which must be carefully recorded, even the smallest points) than at confounding them, so that we may all gain Christ. At the outset they had said: since we judge the religion of the Greek Evangelicals to be truer and closer to apostolic doctrine than the Roman religion on most articles, and since we regard them as Christian brethren, so that we may associate with them, live in concord and charity, in those things which lead to showing the way of salvation, and likewise be present to them in times of need, repel injuries by common counsel and help, and plainly make a covenant with them as with beloved brothers, in accordance with the canon of Holy Scripture. They must be asked: (1) whether they also feel the same toward us, and understand that such decency [εὐσχημοσύνην] is good and serves the glory of God, the growth of his Church, common fellowship, and peace against enemies; and whether they receive and embrace it as we do. Thus the matter must be handled differently with these people than with others. In the disputation, much weight rests on the authority of the Greek Fathers, so whoever is about to attack them ought to be well versed in reading them. On the difficult and contentious question of the procession of the Holy Spirit, the men of Vilna also proposed well: on the article concerning faith in the Holy Spirit, we can acquiesce in what their elders confessed, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, and is sent and given both by the Father and by the Son, the Holy Spirit openly asserting this. And since we must either dispute about articles of religion, or deal with rites as occasion arises, it will be enough, given the purpose of this work, not to give a long catalogue of their customs that differ from ours, but to append the main controversies over their doctrine, which are these: (I) Are there two persons in Christ? No. (II) Are there always two distinct natures, wills and operations in Christ? Yes. (III) Is marriage permitted to all ecclesiastical persons, and may they marry whenever they like, either before or after ordination, once or several times? Yes. (IV) Is it unlawful to eat blood or what has been strangled? No. (V) May images or pictures, or cast or carved statues, be venerated religiously? No. (VI) Does the Holy Spirit in God proceed from the Father and the Son? Yes. (VII) Are the heavenly saints in any way to be invoked by us? No.

units.la: ADDENDA
units.tr: ADDENDA

units.la: Ad pag. 266. Parisiis instituta primum disputatio erat in aedibus Ducis Montpensierii, propterea quod ejus filia nupta erat Duci Bullionaeo, & religionis reformatae: non vero habita disputatio, quia Pontifici Nostris, ut preces dicerent, vel in aedibus, vel se praeferte, omni vi obstabant, dicente Rusaeo, doctore [?]sacrificio, quod si Ministris precari placeret, ipse immunitatum iret, quae si les Ministres vouloyent [?]pour [?]iroit pisser, durant la priere: tandem resumta disputatio fuit, in aedibus Nivernianis, die IX. Iulii: cum disputandum esset de Missa, aliis rebus, vid. controversia de authoritate Ecclesiae, de Dei omnipotentia, sermone primum, dein scripto ad XIV. Augusti, quo tempore aegrotante Vigoreo, & absente de Sacramentis. Nostris etiam discedendi potestas a Nivernensi Duce facta fuit, die XXVI. Augusti. Acta impressa extant Argentorati, anno MDLXVII.
units.tr: To p. 266. The first disputation at Paris was held in the house of the Duke of Montpensier, because his daughter was married to the Duke of Bouillon, who belonged to the Reformed religion. The disputation did not take place, however, because our men were prevented by every means from saying their prayers, whether in the house or in the open, Rusaeus the doctor [?]sacrifice saying that if the Ministers wished to pray, he would go and piss during the prayer, if the Ministers wanted to. At last the disputation was resumed in the house of the Duke of Nevers on 9 July. They were to dispute about the Mass and other matters, namely the controversy concerning the authority of the Church and God's omnipotence, first by speech and then in writing, up to 14 August, when Vigor fell ill and was absent, and the matter of the sacraments was taken up. Our men were also given permission to leave by the Duke of Nevers on 26 August. The printed acts are extant at Strasbourg, in the year 1567.

units.la: Pag. 303. A. MDLXXXIX. Colloquium Badense, inter Iacobum Andreae, cum Iacobo Heerbrando, & partis Pontificiae Ioh. Pistorium Niddanum, & Theod. Bulaeum, Iesuitam. Disputarunt de Ecclesia, & Indice Controversiarum. Acta utrinque edita fuerunt, Tubingae, a. MDXC. & Coloniae.
units.tr: P. 303. In 1589 the Colloquy of Baden, between Jacob Andreae with Jacob Heerbrand on one side, and on the Papist side Johann Pistorius of Nidda and Theodore Bulaeus, a Jesuit. They disputed about the Church and the Index of Controversies. The acts were published on both sides, at Tübingen in 1590, and at Cologne.

units.la: Pag. 304. MDXCVIII. Disputatio Thonoesi habita, in Ducatu Sabaudiae, prope Genevam, die XIV. Martii, inter Hermannum Lignardum, Professorem Genevensem, & Capucini ordinis Monachum: de Romana ecclesia.
units.tr: P. 304. In 1598 a disputation was held at Thonon, in the Duchy of Savoy, near Geneva, on 14 March, between Hermann Lignardus, Professor at Geneva, and a monk of the Capuchin order, concerning the Roman Church.

units.la: A. MDCIX. DXI. Aprilis, Parisiis, inter Molinaeum, & Gontierum, qui cum probare vellet, episcopos in N.T. facultatem accepisse instituendi sacerdotes, nominans cap. 11. & v. ex 1. ad Timotheum, neque ipsum, quem intendebat, locum assignare valens, ab ipso tandem Molinaeo adjutus fuit, qui locum Adversario ario suggerebat, haberi cum nempe, non capitibus ab ipso dictis, sed cap. IV. 22. manus ne quispiam cito im-ponere.
units.tr: In 1609, on 11 April, at Paris, between Molinaeus and Gontier. Gontier, wishing to prove that bishops in the New Testament had received the power of ordaining priests, cited chapter 11 and a verse from 1 Timothy, but was unable to point to the passage he intended. He was at last helped by Molinaeus himself, who suggested to his opponent a passage, namely not the chapter cited by him, but chapter 4, verse 22: lay hands on no one hastily.

units.la: Eodem anno, die XIV. Septemb. Fontenaci, inter Petrum Valladum, & Capucinae sectae Angelum Raconis, de libris Machabaeorum apocryphis.
units.tr: In the same year, on 14 September, at Fontenay, between Peter Vallade and Angelus Raconis of the Capuchin sect, concerning the apocryphal books of the Maccabees.

units.la: A. MDCXI. In Xantonibus, aede nobili Rometana, inter Guiljelmum Rivetum, & P. Vergerium, de notis Ecclesiae.
units.tr: In 1611, at Saintes, in the noble house of Rometa, between William Rivet and P. Vergerius, concerning the marks of the Church.

units.la: A. MDCXIII. die xx. Junii. Durlaci, inter Georgium Fridericum, Marchionem Badensem, & Franciscum Lotharingiae ducem, qui secum adduxerat P. Gontierum, disputatum fuisset de variis Augustanae Confessionis articulis, nova methodo Jesuitica, at ex Scriptura & Bibliis, aequivalentibus verbis, & iisdem in terminis controversiarum decisio ostenderetur: quod quum ineptum merito videbatur, & contra omnes disputandi leges, in fumum abiit totum negotium.
units.tr: In 1613, on 20 June, at Durlach, between George Frederick, Margrave of Baden, and Francis, Duke of Lorraine, who had brought with him P. Gontier, a disputation was to be held on various articles of the Augsburg Confession, by a new Jesuit method, in which the decision of the controversies was to be shown from Scripture and the Bibles, with equivalent words and the very same terms. Since this seemed rightly absurd and contrary to all the laws of disputation, the whole business went up in smoke.

units.la: A. MDCXV. die XXIV. & XXV. Aprilis, Burdegalae, inter Johannem Cameronem, & Parent, notario Sam. Bochtarto, de Romanae Ecclesiae fallibilitate.
units.tr: In 1615, on 24 and 25 April, at Bordeaux, between John Cameron and Parent, a notary, and Samuel Bochart, concerning the fallibility of the Roman Church.

units.la: A. MDCXVIII. die XXVI. Novembris, inter Joh. Maximilianum Anglaeum, Ministrum Rothomagensem, & Fr. Verronum, de Missa.
units.tr: In 1618, on 26 November, between John Maximilian Anglaeus, minister at Rouen, and Fr. Verron, concerning the Mass.

units.la: Eodem anno, die XIX. Decembris Vezesi, prope Tolleburgum, inter Guilj. Rivetum, cum D. de Londe, atque Tessierum Jesuitam, & Despruels, de potestate Petri Papali.
units.tr: In the same year, on 19 December, at Vezet, near Tolleburg, between William Rivet with D. de Londe, and Tessier the Jesuit and Després, concerning the power of the Pope as Peter's successor.

units.la: A. MDCXIX. die XXIX. Aprilis, & V. VII. X Junii, in Castello Montis, in Gallia, inter Cuvillum Ecclesiae Reformatae ministrum, & Nicolaum Chichon, ex ordine Minimorum, de Judice controversiarum.
units.tr: In 1619, on 29 April, and on 5, 7 and 10 June, in the castle of Mont, in France, between Cuvillus, minister of the Reformed Church, and Nicholas Chichon of the order of Minims, concerning the judge of controversies.

units.la: A. MDCXXVIII. d. XXII. Septembris Cadomi, inter Sam. Bochartum, & Fr. Verronum, de falsificationibus Bibliorum Genevensium; deinde, de Eucharistia.
units.tr: In 1628, on 22 September, at Caen, between Samuel Bochart and Fr. Verron, concerning the falsifications of the Geneva Bibles; then concerning the Eucharist.

units.la: A. MDCXXXI[?] Iⅆ. XIX. Augusti, Lim-burgi, inter Godefridum Hottonum, cum Ioh. Iacobo du Bois, notario Henrico Blanchetefte, & partis Pontificis Matthiam Hauzeur, & Iohannem Pery: de invocatione Sanctorum.
units.tr: In 1631[?], on 19 August, at Limburg, between Godfrey Hotton, with John James du Bois, a notary Henry Blanchetefte, and on the Papist side Matthias Hauzeur and John Pery, concerning the invocation of the saints.

units.tr: FINIS
