units.la: Judicium Facultatis Theologicæ IN ACADEMIA LEYD, de Sectâ Fratrum Roseæ Crucis. AD Nobilissimum, Amplissimum, Curiæ Præsidem, & Senatum Curiæ.
units.tr: Judgment of the Theological Faculty at the University of Leiden on the Sect of the Brothers of the Rosy Cross. To the most noble, most distinguished President and Senate of the Court.

units.la: Quum Nobilissimus, Amplissimus & Clarissimus Curiæ Provincialis Hollandiæ & VVest-Frisiæ Senatus, pro suâ, quâ erga Dei & Domini nostri Jesu Christi Ecclesiam, ejusque integritatem fertur, pietate & studio, per Clarissimum Virum & Consiliarium Dom. de VVitte atque ejus Consessus Secretarium, à Facultate nostrâ Theologicâ, de Fraternitate Roseæ Crucis (ut vocant) ac potissimùm de ejus Religione, sententiam nostram; deinde modum rationemque, quâ gliscenti, & sese in Belgium quoque nostrum effundenti, obviam iri possit, exquireret; Facultas nostra, toto pectore & animo hanc sanctam curam & solicitudinem Curiæ amplectens, sui esse officii, Clarissimi Amplissimique Consessus postulationi, quoad ejus fieri potuit, satisfacere.
units.tr: Since the most noble, most distinguished and most illustrious Provincial Senate of the Court of Holland and West Friesland, out of its piety and zeal for the Church of God and our Lord Jesus Christ and for her integrity, has asked through the most illustrious Councillor, Lord de Witte, and the Secretary of that assembly, for our Theological Faculty's opinion on the Fraternity of the Rosy Cross (as they call it), and especially on its religion, and then for the method and manner by which one might meet this growing movement, which is spreading also into our Belgium: our Faculty, embracing this holy care and concern of the Court with its whole heart and mind, considers it its duty to satisfy the request of this most illustrious assembly as far as it can.

units.la: Ad primum itaque propositi Membrum quod attinet; libris à Clarissimo Senatore prædicto sibi exhibitis, lectis, excussis, dijudicatisque; ac inprimis eo, qui Famæ & Confessionis Roseæ-crucis nomen inscriptum habet, quem omnes pro publico ac genuino Fratrum illorum scripto agnoscunt, reliquis eorum fautorum popotius, quàm Mystarum seu Mystagogorum existentibus; eadem Facultas, quantum quidem ex eo illorum mentem, quam usquenùm obscuris & generalibus terminis involvere & celare satagunt, indagare & perscrutari potuit, hæc ex illis capita enotavit; quæ, si opus fuerit, eadem Facultas parata est uberius declarare. Cu-jusmodi sunt:
units.tr: Accordingly, as to the first part of the proposal: after the books shown to us by the aforementioned Senator had been read, examined and weighed, and above all the one bearing the title Fama and Confessio Fraternitatis Rosae Crucis, which everyone acknowledges as the genuine public writing of those Brothers, while the rest of their supporters are rather the followers than the initiates or mystagogues, this Faculty has noted down the following heads from them, as far as it could search out and examine their mind, which they have so far labored to wrap and conceal in obscure and general terms. If necessary, the same Faculty is ready to explain them more fully. These are of the following kind:

units.la: 1. Biblia sacra commendant quidem; sed eorum sententiam à suis pendere, & ad suos viam sternere volunt; eosque, qui ad ea vitam instituunt, sui similliimos & maximè propinquos faciunt. p.40. & 41. Unde paret aliquam perfectionem supra sacram Scripturam in Sect suâ constituere.
units.tr: 1. They do indeed commend the holy Bible, but they want their own opinion to depend on their writings and to pave the way for their own; and they make those who order their lives by these writings very like themselves and closest to them. pp. 40 and 41. Whence it appears that they set up in their Sect some perfection above Holy Scripture.

units.la: 2. Librum Patris sui Rosencrucii, prænotatum T. (putamus esse Theologiam) sibi posthàc à sacris Bibliis supremum suum thesaurum fore, ac jure meritoque non facilè censuræ ac reprehensioni mundi subjiciendum esse, scribere non verentur. p. 20. Quo etiam sacris Bibliis eum adjungunt, & authoritate comparant.
units.tr: 2. They do not hesitate to write that the book of their father Rosencreutz, marked T. (we suppose it is Theologia), will henceforth be their supreme treasure next to the holy Bibles, and that it ought rightly and deservedly not to be easily subjected to the censure and criticism of the world. p. 20. By this they also join it to the holy Bibles and give it equal authority.

units.la: 3. Eum Librum talem esse pronunciant, ut ex eo solo, omnia simul quæ in omnibus qui antehàc fuerunt adhuc sunt, & dehinc succedent aut edentur, reperitur, aut posthàc reperientur, legere, intelligere & retinere possis. p. 32. 33. Quin cogitationes, inquisitiones & observationes Patris sui evehunt super omnia quæ inde à principio mundi ab humano intellectu, sive Divinâ revelatione & patefactione, sive Spirituum & Angelorum ministerio, sive ingenii subtilitate, aut longi & diuturnâ observatione, exercitio & experientiâ, inventa, excogitata, producta, emendata, & usquenam prolata & propagata sunt; imò tam eximias & grandes fuisse ajunt, ut si omnes cujuscunque sapientiæ libri perirent, eam ex hoc solo posteri certiùs & facilius reparare possent. p. 31. 32. Quibus illum sacris Bibliis quoad perfectionem longè præferunt.
units.tr: 3. They declare that the book is of such a kind that from it alone one can read, understand and retain everything that has existed in all people up to now, and that will follow and be published afterwards, or will be found hereafter. pp. 32 and 33. Moreover, they exalt the thoughts, inquiries and observations of their father above all things that from the beginning of the world have been discovered, thought out, produced, corrected, and brought forth and spread anywhere by human understanding, whether by divine revelation and disclosure, by the ministry of spirits and angels, by subtlety of wit, or by long and continual observation, practice and experience. Indeed, they say they were so remarkable and great that, even if all the books of every kind of wisdom perished, posterity could recover that wisdom more surely and easily from this book alone. pp. 31 and 32. By these claims they put it far above the holy Bibles as to perfection.

units.la: 4. Divinam hanc revelationem non tantùm in Patre suo, quem ajunt Divinis revelationibus ad coelestia & humana mysteria admissu, ut est in Sepulchrali Eulogio, p. 20; sed & in sociis ejus & fratribus consequentibus jactitant. p. 10. Spiritusque Divini impulsum, p. 44. ac passim praesidenter propheticum Spiritum jactitant, ut p. 40. Et dum ajunt, ut Mathematici Eclipses Lunae, ita seu obtenebrationem, obscurationem Ecclesiae, (praenunciare), prophetas agunt. p. 37. & alibi.
units.tr: 4. They boast of this divine revelation not only in their father, whom they say was admitted to divine revelations of heavenly and human mysteries, as is stated in the Sepulchral Eulogy, p. 20; but also in their companions and their following brothers. p. 10. They also boast of the impulse of the divine Spirit, p. 44, and everywhere claim the prophetic Spirit in a leading way, as on p. 40. And while they say, like mathematicians predicting eclipses of the moon, that they foretell the darkening and obscuring of the Church, they play the prophets. p. 37, and elsewhere.

units.la: 5. Angelorum insuper bonorum alloquio & patefactione se frui, p. 42. In Diabolos vero se plenam potestatem habere & exercere gloriantur. p. 19. & 25. Ita ut illorum ministerio, horum vero servitio, ut quos vi cogant, utantur: Quae omnia enthusiasmum & fanaticum quid extra Dei Verbum exhibent.
units.tr: 5. They further claim to enjoy the speech and disclosure of good angels, p. 42. But they boast that they have full power over devils and exercise it, pp. 19 and 25. So they use the ministry of the one and the service of the others as spirits they force by power. All these things present enthusiasm and a kind of fanaticism outside the Word of God.

units.la: 6. Adeoque & Magiam, ut scientiae & potentiae suae effectricem, profitentur; quam occultam Philosophiam vocant. p. 12. eamque Patrem eorum ab Arabibus una cum Lib. M. (id est Magias) praenotato, & a se versO, & inde a Fezensibus in ea mire exercitatis accepisse, p. 4. 5. 8. 11. Quam non tantum naturalem, sed & curiosam & improbam esse, constat ex supernaturalibus actibus, qui pag. 4. de illis referuntur; puta, quod Rosencrucium ad se ex Germ. in Damascum accedentem, non ut hospitem, sed ut notum suo nomine salutarint, & Coenobii aliaque arcana panderint. p. 4. quae publico testimonio, & Dei, & Apostolica authoritate damnantur in Simone & Elyma mago, Act. 8. in puellis illis Pythonicis, quae Paulo testimonium dabant, c. 16. 16. in iis qui curiosas artes exercuerant, qui insolitos libros suos maximi precii exusserunt, c. 19. 18. quin quod Fezensiu Magiam non omnino puram ipsorum Pater confessus sit, p. 6. deniqSex iis quae de Diaboli servitute & usu ante annotata sunt, quodque p. 33. dicitur, Quam hoc mirandum foret si ita canere possis, ut loco animantium & ferarum Spiritus ad te allicere, & loco infernalis Plutonis potentes Principatus mundi commovere? In quibus bus magna incantatio & Diab. impostura sese profert.
units.tr: 6. They also profess magic, as the producer of their knowledge and power, which they call occult philosophy. p. 12. They say their father received it from the Arabs, together with the book M. (that is, Magia) mentioned above and translated by himself, and from the Fezians who were wonderfully practiced in it. pp. 4, 5, 8, 11. That this magic is not only natural but also curious and wicked is clear from the supernatural acts that are reported of them on p. 4: for example, that when Rosencreutz came to them from Germany into Damascus, they greeted him not as a stranger but as one known by his own name, and revealed the convent and other secrets. p. 4. These things are condemned by public testimony, by God, and by apostolic authority: in Simon and Elymas the magician, Acts 8; in those Pythonic girls who bore witness to Paul, ch. 16:16; in those who had practiced curious arts and burned their unusual books of great value, ch. 19:18. Moreover, the fact that their father himself confessed that the magic of the Fezians was not wholly pure, p. 6; and finally, from what has been noted above about the servitude and use of the devil, and from what is said on p. 33: "How remarkable it would be if you could sing so as to draw spirits to you in place of animals and wild beasts, and to stir up the powerful principalities of the world in place of infernal Pluto!" In these words a great incantation and diabolical imposture shows itself.

units.la: 7. Magiae & Caballam adjungunt, quam ipse Ro‐senerucius à praeceptoribus Mahometanis Arabibus & Africanis hauserit, ac fatetur contaminatam fuisse do‐rum Religione: sed utramque & Magiam & Caballam pulchrè in suum usum, & ad majus fundamentum sa‐cr fidei accommodasse ajunt. p. 5. & 6. quae & ipsa vanita‐tis habet plurimū; & ex quo de genere doctrinae ac disci‐plinae, curiosi scilicet & superstitiosi ex Mahometanis deducto, judicare licet.
units.tr: 7. They join to magic the Cabbala, which Rosencreutz himself is said to have drawn from his Mahometan teachers, Arabs and Africans, and admits that their religion was tainted; but they claim that they have adapted both magic and Cabbala beautifully to their own use and to a greater foundation of the holy faith. pp. 5 and 6. This too contains a great deal of vanity; and from it one may judge what kind of doctrine and discipline it is, curious and superstitious, derived from the Mahometans.

units.la: 8. Istis Principiis Sectae hujus Pater, Fratres & Socii universalem rerum omnium scientiam sibi, & quidem tantam quantam Deus homini scire permisit, p. 8. arrogant. p. 3. Ac plura & majora à Deo edoctos, quàm humana mens possit capere, asserunt. p. 18. imò talem, qualem Sapientia ipsa de se in libro Sap. pronunciat; quamquam Adam in Paradyso habuit & neglexit; atque Enoch, Abraham, Moses, Salomon singulari Dei gratiâ acceperunt. In praefat. ad Fraternitatis Famam & p. 24. 31. Eamque certò & finaliter Deum per ipsos mundo ante ejus interitum, qui brevi instat, decrevisse communicare & tribuere, praedicunt & praedicant, ibid. & p. 37. Quae sanè praesumptuosa, & supra consuetum modum humanae naturae & infirmitatis sunt.
units.tr: 8. On these principles the father of this sect, its Brothers and companions claim for themselves universal knowledge of all things, as much as God has permitted man to know. p. 8. They claim that they have been taught by God more and greater things than the human mind can grasp. p. 18. Indeed, they claim such knowledge as Wisdom itself declares of itself in the book of Wisdom, although Adam had it in Paradise and neglected it, and Enoch, Abraham, Moses and Solomon received it by a singular grace of God. In the preface to the Fama of the Fraternity, and pp. 24 and 31. They proclaim and preach that God has decreed to communicate and grant this knowledge through them to the world before its end, which is near at hand, ibid. and p. 37. These claims are truly presumptuous and beyond the usual measure of human nature and weakness.

units.la: 9. Ac proinde perfectionem & reformationem rerum omnium Divinarum & humanarum sese instituere jactitant. p. 23. Inprimis verò Theologiae. Et ut id totum quale sit intelligatur, in Fornice sepulchrali quatuor aetates & revelationes inter se conferunt, quatuor figuris in uno circulo conclusis designatas, quarum in ambitu haec inscripta fuerint. 1. Nullo modo inane. 2. Iugum Legis. 3. Libertas Euangelica. 4. Immaculata Dei gloria. p. 18; quorum postremum ad suam doctrinam ejusque explicationem referunt. Atque ita perfectionem ad se suumque seculum transferunt, quam futuro seculo deputavit Deus.
units.tr: 9. Accordingly, they boast that they set up the perfection and reformation of all things, divine and human. p. 23. Above all of theology. And so that the whole of this may be understood, in the sepulchral vault they compare four ages and revelations with one another, designated by four figures enclosed in one circle, around whose rim the following was inscribed: 1. Nothing vain in any way. 2. The yoke of the Law. 3. Evangelical liberty. 4. The spotless glory of God. p. 18. The last of these they refer to their own doctrine and its explanation. And so they transfer to themselves and to their own age the perfection that God has assigned to the age to come.

units.la: 10. Ad Theologiam & Religionem quod attinet, quamvis Christianos se profitentur, Machometem & ejus assecla; (quos tamen Pater ipsorum praeceptores habuit. pag. 20) Papam, haereticosque omnes, detestentur. pag. 27. atque Evangelicis & Reformatis sese in speciem aggregent. p. 23. attamen quidam eorum in lib. cui Echo nomen, nomina Lutheri & Calvini refugit, ut singularia. Ita ut peculiarem Religionem ab iis videantur meditari; ac dum Theoph. Paracelsi Theologiam commendant in praefat. fanaticam se meditari indicent.
units.tr: 10. As for theology and religion, although they profess themselves Christians, they detest Muhammad and his followers (whom nevertheless their Father had as teachers, p. 20), the Pope, and all heretics (p. 27). They present themselves in appearance as joining the Evangelicals and the Reformed (p. 23). Yet some of them, in the book called Echo, avoid the names of Luther and Calvin as if they were peculiar, so that they seem to be devising a religion of their own. And while they commend the theology of Theophrastus Paracelsus in the preface, they show that they are meditating a fanatical one.

units.la: 11. Sacrosanctam Trinitatem verbis saltem agnoscunt, Christum Sapientiam & Verbum Dei se pure & sincere confiteri dicunt, adeo ut pater ipsorum pro Symbolo habuerit; Christus mihi omnia. p. 18. Sed qualem nobis Christum fingant satis indicant; dum ajunt, se talem Philosophiam agnoscere, quae cum Iesu penitus & plane omnibus partibus conveniat; ita ut quemadmodum ipse ipsissima Imago Patris, ita illa ipsius sit. p. 24. Quod est pro Christo nescio quod mentis figmentum supponere.
units.tr: 11. At least in words they acknowledge the Holy Trinity. They say they confess Christ as the Wisdom and Word of God purely and sincerely, so much so that their father took as his motto: "Christ is all things to me" (p. 18). But what sort of Christ they imagine for us they sufficiently indicate when they say that they recognise such a philosophy as agrees with Jesus completely and in every part, so that just as he is the very image of the Father, so that philosophy is his own (p. 24). This amounts to putting in place of Christ some figment of the mind, I know not what.

units.la: 12. Perfectionem Ecclesiae, ejusque a tyrannide Papae reformationem, Patrem & Fratres, (quamvis Ecclesia ipsorum aevo nondum repurgata) agnovisse & ad eam anhelasse, atque postremis hisce seculis ex parte institutam approbare, testantur. p. 12. 13. 23. sed ejus plenam & totalem reformationem ad se suaque tempora referunt. p. 23. 40. 43. insigni sc. praesumtione & ausu.
units.tr: 12. They testify that they have recognised the perfection of the Church and its reformation from the tyranny of the Pope (though their own Church was not yet purged in their age), that they have longed for it, and that they approve it as partly brought about in these last ages (pp. 12, 13, 23). But they refer its full and total reformation to themselves and their own times (pp. 23, 40, 43), with remarkable presumption and audacity.

units.la: 13. Eandem reformationem & perfectionem in reliquis Facultatibus, totaque Philosophia, promittunt. p. 7. 24. 29. quod si non manifestam impietatem, plurimam tamen habet vanitatem.
units.tr: 13. They promise the same reformation and perfection in the remaining faculties and in all of philosophy (pp. 7, 24, 29). If this is not manifest impiety, it nonetheless has a great deal of vanity.

units.la: 14. Ac primum in Mathesi, cujus & scientiam & reformationem omni ex parte sibi arrogant, multum Astrologiae judiciariae tribuere videntur. p. 36. 39. 40. quae sane scientia ut est vanissima, ita a pietate non parum abest.
units.tr: 14. First, in mathematics, whose science and reform they claim for themselves in every respect, they seem to attribute much to judicial astrology (pp. 36, 39, 40). This science, indeed, is as utterly vain as it is far from piety.

units.la: 1 5. In Physicis pària pollicentur. Et de Chymiâ & Alchymiâ, (cujus abusum, ut videri volunt, execrantur) hæc pronunciant, Artem conficiendi aurum & argenti quam deprimere, sed eam ipsam pœrgama & rem levem ac ludicram esse; cujusmodi multa millia, eaque melius habeant. p. 25. Atque ejusmodi societatem in Europâ instituere, quæ auri, argenti & preciosorum Lapidum habeat plus satis; adeò ut & Regibus, si ita usus ferret, communicare possit. p. 8. Loquuntur de abundantiâ auro, quàm Rex Hispaniæ ex utrâque Indiâ reportat. p. 14. Summo capiti Romani Imperii præter preces & Mysteria sua, offerunt ingentes auri thesauros. p. 29. Iactitant se totum mundum posse ditare; ac promittunt magna bona ac divitias illis, qui se ipsis adjungunt. p. 45. Adeò ut à paupertate futuri immunes. Vnde & inter promissiones illas amplissimas hæc est; Nonne beatum foret, ut quis sibi à fame & paupertate non metuat? p. 32. Item, Quàm jucundum esset, ut ita canere possis, ut loco suppli-um meum margaritas & pretiosos Lapides ad te attrahas? p. 33. Quæ omnia impostnram & ludificationem habent: ne quid deterius dicamus.
units.tr: 15. In physics they promise equal things. About chemistry and alchemy (whose abuse they profess to execrate) they pronounce as follows: the art of making gold and silver is not to be despised, but it is itself mere rubbish and a light and playful thing; they have many thousands of such things, and better ones. (p. 25). And they set up in Europe a society of this kind, which has more than enough gold, silver and precious stones, so that it could share them even with kings, if custom should require it. (p. 8). They speak of the abundance of gold which the King of Spain brings back from both Indies (p. 14). They offer to the supreme head of the Roman Empire, besides prayers and their mysteries, huge treasures of gold (p. 29). They boast that they can enrich the whole world, and they promise great goods and riches to those who join themselves to them (p. 45), so that those men will be free from future poverty. Hence among those most ample promises is this: Would it not be a blessing if someone need not fear hunger and poverty for himself? (p. 32). Likewise: How pleasant would it be if you could sing in such a way that, instead of a supplication, you could draw pearls and precious stones to yourself? (p. 33). All of these things have imposture and mockery in them, not to say worse.

units.la: 1 6. Medicinæ quoque maximam scientiam & reformationem sibi vendicant; quam ex Lege Patris sui Fratres & facere, & gratis facere, tenētur. p. 12. Paracelsum passim laudant. p. 8. 19. Panaceam, seu Medicinam profitentur, quæ omnibus simul morbis medetur. 45. Imò inter ampla illa promissa, pag. 32. inquiunt; Bonum foret, ut quis non habeat quòd sibi à senio & morbo metuat; & in præfat. Famæ. Perfectissima hæc medicina ad omnem morbum, &c. ab hominibus amovendi. Vnde de Societatis authore commemorant, quòd annos 106. natus, naturæ, non morbi necessitate, quem nunquam in corpore senserit, Divini Spir. evocatione, animam suam Deo reddiderit, illiusque corpus 120. annis pulchrum, præclarum, illæsum & planè inabsumptum permanserit. p. 20, 21, quódquç reliquorum patrum
units.tr: 16. They also claim for themselves the greatest science and reform of medicine, which their brothers are bound by their Father's law both to practise and to practise free of charge (p. 12). They praise Paracelsus everywhere (pp. 8, 19). They profess a panacea, or medicine, which cures all diseases at once (p. 45). Indeed, among those ample promises (p. 32) they say: "It would be good if no one had anything to fear for himself from old age and disease"; and in the preface to Fama: "This most perfect medicine removes every disease from men," and so on. Hence they record of the founder of the Society that at the age of 106, by the necessity of nature and not of disease (which he never felt in his body), at the summons of the Divine Spirit, he rendered his soul back to God, and that his body remained beautiful, splendid, unharmed and quite incorruptible for 120 years (pp. 20, 21). And likewise of their other fathers:

units.la: feo suorum corpora à morbo & doloribus vacua fuerint; quamvis momentum resolutionis animę ipsorum à corpore transilire nequiverint. Quæ omnia contra Dei humano generi ex peccato impositam, ut mortis, ita morborum necessitatem, sunt; & adeo insolentia, inusitata; & quiddam naturâ homineque superius habent.
units.tr: their bodies were free from disease and pains, although they could not avoid the moment when their soul departed from the body. All these things are contrary to the necessity of death and of disease, which God imposed on the human race because of sin. They are so unusual and unaccustomed, and they have something above nature and above man.

units.la: 17. In Ethicâ seu Morum Philosophiâ, similia de ejus perfectione & reformatione ingerunt. p. 7. Atque sigillatim de Politiâ dicunt quidem, se in nullius propositi & ausus contra politiam suscepti suspicionem venire posse. p. 29. agnoscere se in Politiâ Rom. Imperium, & quartam Monarchiam, pro suo & Christianorum capite. p. 23. & 24. Attamen asserunt universum mundum renovandum & reformandum, tum in Iurisprudentiâ tum Politiâ, adeò ut novus se proferat & appareat. p. 30. & 24. Quamvis, inquiunt, satis novimus quales mutationes propinquæ sint, quas etiam aliis theodidactis ex animo & libenter communicare volumus; attamen id quod in manibus habemus, nostra subsignatio & sigillum esto. Imò difertius, p. 31. Vbi proposito exemplo Arabum in civitate Damear degentium, qui longè aliam politiam habent atque cæteri Arabes, hæc subjiciunt; Ad horum exemplar etiam Regimen in Europâ (qualiter illius descriptionem habemus à quodam Patrum nostrorum conscriptam) instituetur, postea quam illud fiet & peragetur quod antecedere necesse erit, & nostra buccina sonoro clangore & ingenti clamore personabit; hoc est, quando id quod à paucis in præsentiâ indicatur, & ut futurum in signis & imaginibus arcanè proponitur, totum terrarum orbem implebit, & liberè ac publicè proclamabitur, &c. p. 35. Vnde sanè illos non modò mutationè in Imperio prædicere, sed & secundum suam imaginationem moliri evidens est. Imo dicunt se ita tectos Divinâ nube, ut nullius publicæ cognitioni, animadversioni, proscriptioni, violentiæ subjectos. &i sint.p. 24. 34. 37. ut plenius à nobis põst dictum; quae manifestam seditionem prae se ferunt.
units.tr: 17. In ethics, or moral philosophy, they press similar claims about its perfection and reform (p. 7). And concerning politics in particular, they say indeed that they can fall under no suspicion of any purpose or undertaking against the state (p. 29). They acknowledge in politics the Roman Empire, and the fourth monarchy, as the head both of themselves and of Christians (pp. 23, 24). Yet they assert that the whole world must be renewed and reformed, both in jurisprudence and in politics, so that a new order comes forth and appears (pp. 30, 24). "Although," they say, "we know well what changes are at hand, which we also wish to share from our hearts and willingly with other God-taught men, yet let what we have in hand be our signature and seal." More plainly still (p. 31), having proposed the example of the Arabs who live in the city of Damear, who have a quite different polity from other Arabs, they add: "On the model of these, government will also be established in Europe (of which we have a description written by one of our Fathers), after that has been done and accomplished which must go before; and our trumpet will sound with a resounding blast and a great clamour. That is, when what is indicated by a few for the present, and secretly set forth as future in signs and images, fills the whole orb of the earth, and is proclaimed freely and publicly," and so on (p. 35). Hence it is clear that they not only predict a change in the empire but also plan it according to their own imagination. Indeed they say that they are so covered by a divine cloud that, even if they should be, they are subject to no public knowledge, observation, proscription or violence (pp. 24, 34, 37). As we shall say more fully later, these claims bear the marks of open sedition.

units.la: 18. Praeter hanc Philosophiae & Facultatum omnium scientiam, Linguarum quoque similiter omnium, praesertim earum gentium inter quas degunt, notitiam & usum sibi vendicant. Fatentur quidem, se in aliis Linguis non perinde esse eloquentes: neque id mirum esse, ut qui sciant, eas nullatenus cum primi parentis nostri Adami aut Enochi Linguâ convenire; utpote quae Babylonicâ confusione tota sit abscondita. p. 40. Interea tamen & aliarum Linguarum, quamvis non diserte, generaliter tamen cognitionem se habere indicant: quip. 26. ajunt, cujuscunque judicium, quâcunque Linguâ fiat, ad se perventurum esse. Quin in illo programmate, quod Fraternitatis illius socii Parisiis affixerunt, declarant, se & omnes Scientias sine libris docere; & loqui Linguis in populis inter quos habitant, usitatis. Quod & ipsum supra humanam sortem est, ac semel tantum Apostolis in universum orbem emittendis ad Evang. omnibus gentibus praedicandum, divinitus tributum est.
units.tr: 18. Besides this knowledge of philosophy and of all the faculties, they also claim for themselves a similar knowledge and use of all languages, especially those of the peoples among whom they live. They admit indeed that they are not equally eloquent in other languages. Nor is this surprising, since they know that these languages in no way agree with the language of our first parent Adam or of Enoch, being wholly hidden under the Babylonian confusion (p. 40). Meanwhile, however, they indicate that they have a general, though not express, knowledge of other languages as well, for they say (p. 26) that anyone's judgment, in whatever language it is made, will come to them. Indeed, in that programme which the companions of that Brotherhood posted at Paris, they declare that they teach all sciences without books, and speak in the languages customary among the peoples with whom they dwell. This too is beyond the human lot, and was granted divinely only once, to the Apostles sent out into the whole world to preach the Gospel to all nations.

units.la: 19. Neque in his, nempe generalium rerum atque Linguarum omnium notitiâ ipsorum scientia continetur ac terminatur; sed insuper se profert ad singularum rerum, cogitationum, actionum & eventuum, scilicet praeteritorum, praesentium, & futurorum cognitionem. Ut diserte declaratur in amplissimis illis promissis, p. 32. Nonne, inquiunt, res preciosa foret, si omnis horae interire possent, quasi jam inde à principio mundi usque in praesens tempus vixisses, & ad finem usque mundi victurus esses? Nonne id foret magnificum & eximium, ut in aliquâ mundi parte ita habitare possis, ut neque populi qui altera flumina Gangem degunt res suas te celare, neque qui in Persiâ vivunt consilia sua abs te abscondere possint? Excluditur tantum infelicitas & mors cujusque, ut est p. 14. Sed id, ajunt, in laudem Dei hoc ipso publicè profitemur, quicquid sanè arcani ex Libro M. (id est Magiae) reperimus, quamvis in-gina [?] ginem & picturam totius mundi ante oculos habere possimus, samen nostra miseriae & infelicitas & hora mortis nobis ignota est: quod magnus ille Deus sibi reservavit, ut nos parationes perpetuo habeamus. Quae sane omnia modulum humanae scientiae cum excedant, facile cognoscere est, quis huius cognitionis sit modus & ratio; nempe eadem illa, quā Arabes illi Rosencrucium hospitem ad se adventantem, ut ante commemoravimus, non ut hospitē, sed ut notum salutarunt, & coenobii arcana enarrarunt. p. 4. scilicet Magiam; ut aperto ipsorum judicio hic testatissimum est.
units.tr: 19. Nor is their science contained and bounded in this, namely the knowledge of general things and of all languages. It further extends to the knowledge of individual things, thoughts, actions and events, that is, of past, present and future. This is plainly declared in those most ample promises (p. 32): "Would it not, they say, be a precious thing if you could live through every hour, as if you had lived from the beginning of the world up to the present time, and were to live until the world's end? Would it not be magnificent and excellent if you could dwell in some part of the world in such a way that neither the peoples who dwell beyond the Ganges could hide their affairs from you, nor those who live in Persia could conceal their plans from you?" Only misfortune and each man's death are excluded, as is said on p. 14. "But this," they say, "we publicly profess to the praise of God: whatever secret things we find in the Book M. (that is, of Magic), we can have before our eyes the image [?] and picture of the whole world; yet our misery and unhappiness and the hour of our death are unknown to us. That great God has reserved this to himself, so that we may always be prepared." Since all these things indeed exceed the measure of human knowledge, it is easy to recognise what the manner and method of this knowledge is: namely the same by which those Arabs greeted Rosencreutz, a guest coming to them, as we mentioned before, not as a stranger but as one known to them, and related to him the secrets of the monastery (p. 4). That is, Magic; as their own judgment makes most plain here.

units.la: 20. Denique non tantum rerum omnium & generalium, seu universalium, & particulariu seu singularium scientiam, sed & potentiam ac virtutem sibi singularem & naturā superiorem attribuunt, puta, se ut omnia cognoscunt, ita à nemine videri aut cognosci, nedum laedi posse, sed exeantos ab externa vi & potentia. Sic p. 34. Deus nos fas, ut inquirant, luce obtexit, ut nobis suis servis nulla vis inferri possit. Unde etiam à nemine, etiamsi haberet oculos aquilinos, videri & cognosci queunt; & de suis illis pronunciant, quod invisa, intactaque manebunt. p. 24. 26. & 27.
units.tr: 20. Finally, they attribute to themselves not only knowledge of all things, general and universal as well as particular and singular, but also a power and virtue peculiar to themselves and superior to nature. That is, just as they know all things, so they cannot be seen or known by anyone, much less harmed, and they are exempt from external force and power. So on p. 34 God has covered us with light so that those who would pry cannot find us, and no force can be brought against us, his servants. For this reason, they claim, no one can see or know them, not even someone with eagle eyes; and they declare that they will remain unseen and untouched. See p. 24, 26 and 27.

units.la: His omnibus consideratis, riteque expensis, colligimus & concludimus banc Sectam (si non potius commentum est capitis cujusdam male feriati Fraternitatem hujusmodi commentiti) à Patre Christiano Rosencrucio institutam, à Fratribus vero propagatam & confirmatam, & quę hoc jam agit ut maxime se proferat, esse in Religione quidē erroneam, neq; abesse ab haeresi, quinimò, Fanaticam, superstitiosam, Magicamque: In Philosophiā autem praesumptuosam, malē comparati cerebri phantasiam, & animi chimaeram vanam inutilemq;, atque impostuŗ plenam; in Republ. deniq; seditiosam, adeoque ei in Belgio nostro contrā Ecclesiam & Rempublicam glisceni maturē occurrendum esse. Atque id quidem respondendum duximus ad primum consultationis
units.tr: Having considered all these things and weighed them properly, we gather and conclude that this sect (unless it is rather the invention of some half-crazed head who made up such a brotherhood), founded by Father Christian Rosencreutz, spread and confirmed by the Brothers, and now working hard to make itself as widely known as possible, is erroneous in religion, and is not free from heresy; indeed it is fanatical, superstitious and magical. In philosophy it is presumptuous, a fantasy of a badly constituted brain, an empty and useless chimera of the mind, and full of deceit; and in the commonwealth it is seditious. Therefore it must be met early in our Belgium, before it grows strong against the Church and the State. This is what we thought fit to answer to the first point of the consultation of the most noble and most distinguished Senate...

units.la: Nobilissimi & Amplissimi Senatus caput.
units.tr: The Chapter of the Most Noble and Most Honourable Senate.

units.la: Alterum vero quod attinet, de modo quo haec Secta occurri possit, censemus, Prudentiae vestrae esse, de illo dispicere, quomodo huic modum ponat. Hoc tantum Dignitati vestrę subjicimus, quum tota fere haec Secta vanitatis sit plena, & à delirio vix abesse videatur, vanis & insanis Magistris id remedium videri adhibendum, quod ipsorum morbus deposcit. Verùm, si qui sunt qui vanam & insanam hanc suam opinionem & imaginationem ad malitiam traducant, aliorumque simplicitate abutentes Ecclesiae integritatem violare atque Rëipublicę juxtà tranquillitatem turbare satagant, ei verius paulò coërceri posse, ne quid Ecclesia aut Reipubl. detrimenti accipiat. Dat. Lugd. Batav. x. Maij Anno 1625.
units.tr: As for the second matter, namely the manner in which this sect may be met, we are of the opinion that it belongs to your Prudence to consider how a remedy may be set upon it. We only submit this to your Dignity: since nearly the whole of this sect is full of vanity and hardly seems free from madness, it seems that the remedy which their disease demands should be applied to these vain and insane teachers. But if there are some who turn this vain and insane opinion and imagination of theirs to malice, and, abusing the simplicity of others, strive to violate the integrity of the Church and to disturb the tranquillity of the Commonwealth, then it may be more truly held in check somewhat, lest the Church or the Commonwealth suffer any harm. Given at Leiden, 10 May, in the year 1625.

units.la: Ita censemus nos Sacrę Theologiæ Doctores & Profess. Academ. Lugdunensis.
units.tr: Thus we, the Doctors of Sacred Theology and Professors of the Academy of Leiden, have judged.
